## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY—ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL—OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COLLATION WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY THE DISCOVERY OF ALL WORKS WHICH, AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES, HAVE APPEARED; PROVIDED WITH INDIVIDUAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER SET BELOW; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, PROVIDED THEY POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any theme; THE OTHER, OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon individual Scriptural texts, and in what places in their works.**

**A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clerical Library, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. # In the Year of the Lord 1125  
Cosmas of Prague  
## The Chronicle of the Bohemians by Cosmas

(Edited by Dr Rudolf Köpke, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, vol. IX, p. 1.)

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomena: The Age, Birth, and Deeds of Cosmas of Prague

[Col. 0009A] Cosmas of Prague—whom scholars who have rendered excellent service in investigating the deeds of the Bohemians have justly adorned with the splendid titles of father of Bohemian history and Herodotus—also holds, among writers on German affairs, a place by no means to be denied him, whether one considers the material of events which he enclosed in his book or the method and plan he pursued in writing history. Nor without reason do we too seem able to claim him as our own, since, though descended from the Bohemian people, he was joined to the German Empire by a community alike of divine and human concerns. For although his Slavonic blood boiled with hatred rather than affection toward the Germans, whom he regarded as enemies and oppressors of his country [Note: [Col. 0009B] II, 8, 14.], nevertheless he did not dare either to reject the supreme authority of the German emperor, which even the Bohemians were bound to observe, or to call into question the ecclesiastical discipline of the Archbishop of Mainz. Nor could he compose a history of the Bohemians while taking no account whatever of German affairs; for he could scarcely fill even one or two pages without encountering events both performed and recorded by Germans, and without having to commit German names to writing. Let this, then, be the glory of the Bohemians: that so useful a writer of events was given them from among their own people. But let them leave to us this second Cosmas, who, as he himself testifies, was imbued with German learning and letters and cultivated for the apprehension of higher meanings [Col. 0010A].

Yet there is another distinction which ought by no means to be taken from the Bohemians. A German indeed was the first to bring Cosmas’s chronicle before the public; but it was exceedingly learned Bohemian men who devoted the greatest labor and diligence to reading and explaining it. Examining it again and again with renewed care, they penetrated so deeply into the inner recesses of that book that they led the way for the Germans and left us almost nothing that could be newly brought forward. First was Dobner [Note: [Col. 0009B] In *Ad Hajecii Annales Bohemorum* I, 172 ff.], to whom Bohemian history owes so much, who by his learning elucidated [Col. 0010B] the life and book of Cosmas. After Dobner came Dobrovský [Note: [Col. 0009B] In the preface to *Scriptores Rerum Bohemicarum* I, p. VII ff.]—a man of the highest merit in Czech history, who, had fate not stood in the way, would have been able to fulfill his promise to the *Monumenta Germaniae* [Note: [Col. 0009B] *Archiv* IV, 35.] of a new edition of Cosmas. After Dobrovský came Palacký, who in his book laid the new foundations of Bohemian history [Note: [Col. 0009B] *Würdigung der alten Böhmischen Geschichtschreiber*, p. 1. Of less importance are the earlier discussions of Cosmas by Oudin, *Commentar. de scriptor. eccles.* II, 766; Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis* I, 331; Menken in the preface to vol. I of *Scriptores Rerum Germanicarum*; Ceillier XXI, 576; Hamberger, *Zuverlässige Nachrichten* IV, 104; Pubitschka, *Geschichte von Böhmen* IV, 225; Meinert, in the essay “Die Böhmischen Geschichtschreiber des ersten Zeitraums,” *Wiener Jahrbücher* XV, advertisement supplement, p. 27.]. After so many and such great men, supremely deserving in the field of Bohemian affairs, scarcely any sounder plan can be followed in our own undertaking than to proceed along the path which we see fortified by such authority, and especially to note those points which seemed to us to be otherwise than they had judged [Col. 0011A].

The testimonies left to us concerning the life of Cosmas are indeed not so few; but, as happens almost everywhere in the case of writers who sought glory not through deeds but through writing, they must be sought from the author’s own book. For exceedingly few things are found to have been added later by others, more by chance than by design. Yet he inserted testimonies about himself into his book with a freer hand than is usual with other writers. His life must therefore be constructed from his own words.

Cosmas, born about the year 1045 [Note: [Col. 0011C] The testimony which Cosmas himself gave concerning himself at III, 59, where he says that in 1125 he was an octogenarian, has been followed by Pelzel, Dobrovský, Palacký, and almost all the rest. Although I do not embrace that view with every doubt removed, I am led to it by the following arguments. For it seems impossible to reconcile it with the other testimony which he gave at II, 34, under the year 1074: it is scarcely clear how the man whom Cosmas meets there could have addressed the author, a young man in his twenty-ninth year, with the greeting “good boy.” Nor did the author portray himself there as anything other than a boy, as is sufficiently apparent from the words, “while we were still placed in the schools”; these must not be interpreted, as Palacký seemed to think, to mean that Cosmas served as master in that school. Can one believe that he who was a boy in 1074 had been born in 1045? I think I see one way of resolving this difficulty, already noticed by Dobner in *Ad Hajecium* I, 174: the word *octogenarius* at III, 59 need not be pressed so strictly. Perhaps it should be explained thus: we should suppose—though I freely admit that I cannot establish this by other examples—that the author meant to indicate that he had passed his seventieth year of life and had already entered his eighth decade. Yet, unless I am mistaken, this period can be bounded more narrowly. Adelung, in his *Manual Glossary*, proved from an example taken from a diploma that *boni pueri* (“good boys”) were called *scholares* (“schoolboys” or “students”). Therefore he was undoubtedly to be called a *puer* who was not yet of an age to obtain holy orders; from this it appears that in 1074 Cosmas had not yet reached his twenty-fifth year. If all this is accepted, the year of his birth must neither be placed later than 1054 nor moved earlier than 1050.], of not altogether obscure station [Note: [Col. 0011D] At III, 51 he noted the death of Berthold, the client of his son Henry; he certainly would not have done so had that client been some lowly household servant. It is also clear from elsewhere that the squires of soldiers were called *clientes*; if Cosmas’s son was to be counted among soldiers, neither does his father seem likely to have been born in so lowly a station.], derived his origin, I believe, from a family brought from Poland [Col. 0011B]. For his great-grandfather [Note: [Col. 0012C] Pelzel and Dobrovský wished the passage II, 5, where we read, “Among whom, alas, my great-grandfather was taken captive, a fellow in the clergy, a priest in office,” to refer not to a natural great-grandfather but merely to an elder among the clergy to whose number Cosmas himself belonged; they did not establish this view by examples. Undoubtedly, however, the author speaks not of a grandfather but of his great-grandfather; he uses the same word in much the same manner at II, 13, where Duke Břetislav calls St Wenceslas and Boleslaus, his ancestors, *atavi* (“great-grandfathers”). Compare also II, 26, and what Pubitschka observed concerning this imprecise usage, *Chronologische Geschichte von Böhmen* III, 157, 341. Thus nothing appears to prevent us from believing that Cosmas’s great-grandfather preserved for his descendants the memory of that captivity [Col. 0012D].], a priest who was still alive only a few years before Cosmas came into the light of day, was brought captive to Prague in 1039 by the Bohemians, returning as victors to their homeland with the relics of St Adalbert, together with a company of Polish nobles. Cosmas was committed to the schools of Prague for education, so that he might soon be enrolled among the clergy; and in 1074 we still find him remaining in the school for boys.

After he had emerged from the rudiments of letters, Cosmas went to Liège, which at that time flourished above the other thriving schools of Lotharingia under the direction of Master Franco; there he diligently applied himself to grammar and dialectic. The intellectual resources which he acquired [Col. 0012A] are attested by the brilliant classical authors with whom he filled his book, and by his very manner of writing. How deeply there he absorbed his love of learning, and how faithfully he retained it to the end of old age, is shown by the fitting and full eulogy with which, near the conclusion of his book, he attempted to erect a monument to Master Franco [Note: [Col. 0012D] III, 59.]. When this course of studies had been completed [Note: [Col. 0012D] At what time this occurred is not clear. I would conjecture between 1075 and 1084, years which he passed over in his chronicle in profound silence. It is also greatly to be regretted that the year of Master Franco’s death is wholly unknown. Sigebert writes that he was already flourishing in 1047.], we see him active in public affairs. There can scarcely be doubt that he was admitted to the duke’s court; for he was involved in public business of such a kind as would seem capable of being entrusted only to a man approved by the duke. When a synod met at Mainz in 1086, he attended those solemn ceremonies at which Emperor Henry made Duke Vratislaus king of Bohemia. He saw the emperor himself affixing his signature [Col. 0012B] by hand to the diploma which assigned Moravia to the diocese of Prague and confirmed the boundaries of that ancient bishopric [Note: [Col. 0012D] II, 37: “which I saw Caesar himself noting with his own hands.”]. For he seems to have been received into the closer friendship of Gebhard of Prague as that bishop’s companion on this journey; indeed, he depicted for us the bishop’s austere and holy life with such authority as to declare that he had seen all these things himself [Note: [Col. 0012D] II, 47: “I wish to speak of these things which we ourselves have seen.”]. In 1091 he saw a certain miracle of Saints Wenceslas and Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0012D] II, 46: “which we ourselves saw.”], and shortly afterward he set out for Italy. For in 1092, in the company of Cosmas, bishop of Prague [Note: [Col. 0012D] The view formerly held by some—for example Pontanus, *Bohemia pia*, p. 3—that Cosmas the bishop and Cosmas the dean were one and the same person, was already refuted by Balbín, *Epitome rerum Bohemicarum*, p. 211.], and Andrew of Olomouc, who were journeying to Italy to receive investiture, he came to Mantua and heard at Verona that King Vratislaus had died [Note: [Col. 0012D] II, 49, 50: “rumor beats upon our ears.”]. Likewise, when in 1094 those same bishops [Col. 0013A] were sent to Mainz to be initiated into holy orders by the Archbishop of Mainz, Cosmas accompanied them, as he himself indicated in recording their return home [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 3: “we spent the night in the middle of a field.”]. Then, in 1099, he again became the companion of Herman, the new bishop of Prague, in obtaining holy orders; for both Herman and Cosmas were advanced by Seraphin, Archbishop of Esztergom, to the same rank of priesthood in the bishop’s own see [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 9: “and promoted me …”]. In 1100 he was present at Prague for the consecration of the church of St Peter the Apostle, and for that remarkable examination by which Bishop Herman ordered the authenticity of the relics of St Ludmila to be tested [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 11: “as we ourselves saw.”]. In 1108 he was present as a witness of the most cruel slaughter by which the family of the Vršovci was destroyed [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 24: “for we saw them miserably dragged into the marketplace.”]. From these passages it is sufficiently clear that he was undoubtedly among [Col. 0013B] those clerics of the chapter of St Vitus at Prague who possessed the highest authority in administering the affairs of the Church. By 1100 he was already enrolled in their number. For when Otto, Duke of Moravia, tried to take from them the marketplace in the village of Sekyrkostel, which the parents of the canons of Prague had given them, Cosmas was sent as envoy to Duke Vladislav in order to repair the loss by his effort and prudence; and he brought the undertaking to the happiest outcome [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 33: “I was sent on behalf of the brethren.”]. Finally, that he attained the dignity of dean sometime between 1119 and 1122 will appear from what we shall say below concerning the time at which he composed his book. Cosmas therefore saw those times in which both the Church and the Roman Empire were shaken as if by most violent storms, [Col. 0013C] and he was in vigorous manhood when the bitterest controversy concerning the marriages of priests arose. All the more astonishing, then, is it that amid those tempests he kept a wife at home almost untouched by them, and that in 1117, after her death, he raised in his book a memorial to her in certain verses as to a most faithful spouse and the unwavering companion of all his fortunes, to use his own words [Note: [Col. 0013D] III, 43.]. In 1123 he mentioned his son Henry [Note: [Col. 0013D] This is Henry Zdik, who afterward, from 1126 to 1150, performed the office of Bishop of Olomouc with the greatest distinction among his countrymen and wielded great influence in public administration among the dukes of Bohemia. That his name was very famous in those times appears from the numerous testimonies supplied by the continuators of Cosmas. The origin of Henry proposed by Palacký, I, 440, is shown beyond doubt by the bishop’s charter of donation made for the souls of his parents, in Boczek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae* I, p. 264. Although it contains no names, it gives the dates of death of Cosmas and Božetěcha, precisely agreeing with those in Cosmas III, 43, 62. The ducal origin of Henry invented by Augustin and repeated by others has already been sufficiently shown by others to be without foundation. See Augustin, *Series episcoporum Olomucensium*, ed. Richter, Olomouc, 1831, p. 22.]. Finally, in 1125, when Duke Soběslav was raised to the throne, Cosmas died on 21 October, as another person noted at the end of his book, having lived a life not devoid of honors to nearly his eightieth year [Note: [Col. 0014D] III, 62. The Bohemian necrology in Dobner, *Monumenta historica Bohemica* III, 15, agrees, where one reads: “12 Kalends of November: Cosmas, dean of the Church of Prague.”].

From the things that Cosmas had heard among his countrymen and foreign peoples, seen, or finally performed himself as a participant in events, he composed, as it were, a summary of his life in his Chronicle of Bohemia [Col. 0014A]. Having undertaken to write only in old age, he left it to posterity as the ripe fruit of a vigorous old age. He indicated quite exactly the time when he took up the pen to write, defining it in his letter to Gervasius as follows: “This chronicle was composed while Henry IV reigned as Roman emperor, while Pope Calixtus governed God’s holy Church, and in the time jointly of Vladislav, duke of the Bohemians, and Herman, bishop of the Church of Prague.” Calixtus II obtained the papal see in 1119, and Bishop Herman died in 1122, as Cosmas himself recorded [Note: [Col. 0014D] III, 49.]; this interval is confirmed by the mention of Emperor Henry and [Col. 0014B] the duke of Bohemia. This accords well with the fact that in one passage of the first book he touched upon events performed in 1110 [Note: [Col. 0014D] I, 35; III, 32.].

He did not compose the three books of which the chronicle consists in one continuous course, nor certainly did he publish them all at one and the same time. For he dedicated the individual books, as gifts, to different persons. He sent the first book to Master Gervasius, whom he honors with the title *archigeronta* (“chief elder”), with a dedicatory letter, in order that it might undergo his judgment; in explicit terms he declares that he depends wholly upon that judgment, and that at Gervasius’s command he would either gird himself for writing the rest or stop at the end of the first book. He wrote it at a time when he had not yet attained the honor of the deanery, for he calls himself by the modest title of servant of the servants of St Wenceslas. He dedicated the second book to the man at whose exhortation he had begun to write it [Col. 0014C]; he also presented the first book, which he had “formerly” sent to Gervasius, to that same Clement, Abbot of Břevnov [Note: [Col. 0014D] II, prologue.]. But he composed the second book not very long after the first and, I think, before the death of Bishop Herman in 1122. He composed the final part of the third book, which he furnished only with a preface and not with a dedicatory letter, after Herman’s death [Note: [Col. 0014D] III, 49.], and carried it down to 1125. At the death of Duke Vladislav he intended to lay down his pen, as is proved by the verse:

> Let the book end where our duke’s end is.  
> [Note: [Col. 0014D] III, 58.]

But afterward he added several other matters which seemed worthy of remembrance. From this it is apparent that Cosmas did not add the words quoted above concerning the time at which the chronicle was composed [Col. 0015A] to his letter to Gervasius after the whole work had been completed [Note: [Col. 0015D] As Pelzel and Dobrovský, p. XIV, thought.]; they were undoubtedly written at the same time as the first book. Finally, he sent all three books to Severus, provost of Mělník, together with a dedicatory letter which he afterward placed at the beginning of the whole work. Yet his mind was so timid that he asked Severus above all else: “Whether these senile trifles please you alone or displease you, I beg that no third eye may see them.” He therefore seems to have shared the book with him in private friendship rather than to have issued it publicly. He wrote this letter, like that preceding the second book, when he had already reached the deanery of St Vitus. This must therefore have occurred between 1119 and 1122. Thus he wrote down the events themselves as they occurred, and seems to have continued doing so until the very end [Col. 0015B] of his life, until the pen fell from him in death.

The kinds of resources he employed in writing are diverse: some are written, others unwritten. The latter too are of different kinds: things either seen by the author himself, heard from eyewitnesses, or finally drawn from common report and the accounts of old men. The written resources are public charters, letters, and books. From the nature of the matter itself it is clear that the former kind of sources was more often used toward the end of the book, the latter near its beginning. Nothing need be added to the passages already mentioned above in which Cosmas explicitly indicated what he himself had seen. As to events performed at Prague in the last fifty years, he was either himself an eyewitness or could very readily obtain such authorities [Col. 0015C] as knew the true causes and circumstances of affairs. Thus, with a few exceptions here and there, from the year 1074 to the end of the chronicle he wrote everywhere as a contemporary, and very often as an eyewitness. Nor did he conceal in silence what he had drawn from the narratives of other witnesses; near the end of the first book he wrote: “Now, with the aid of God and St Adalbert, my mind is inclined to relate those things which we ourselves saw, or which we truthfully heard from persons recounting what they had seen.” The former words appear to concern the latter part of the second book; and what had occurred from 1039 onward, where the second book begins, he could undoubtedly investigate from men who had themselves seen the events. He expressly praises eyewitness narratives under the year 1109, concerning the death of Duke Svatopluk [Col. 0016A] [Note: [Col. 0015D] II, 27: “as we afterward heard from those reporting it.”]; concerning the defeat of the Bohemians in 1124 [Note: [Col. 0015D] III, 56: “a priest alone escaped and reported it.”]; and in that little story “On the Lustful Priest” [Note: [Col. 0015D] III, 62: “for he himself secretly told me.”].

Another kind of historical authority must be joined to these testimonies, and the author used it very frequently. These are monuments or remains of diverse kinds which, down to Cosmas’s time, either were truly preserved or were believed to have been preserved by people with a kind of religious superstition. Such monuments include Crocco’s fortress [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 3: “from whose name it is recognized that the fortress, now overgrown with trees, is situated in the forest …”]; the burial mound of his daughter Kazi [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 4: “the mound is visible to this day”]; the boots of Prince Přemysl [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 7: “they are preserved at Vyšehrad … to this day”]; the burial mound of the very brave man Tyr, who commanded the army of Duke Neklan [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 12: “and even today it is called … Tyr’s tomb”]; the alder tree on which Děring hanged himself [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 13: “that alder … because it stood beside the road, was called,” etc.]; the Roman-style work by which Duke Boleslaus fortified the castle of Bunzlau [Note: [Col. 0015D] “with Roman work, as is visible today,” I, 19.]; the vestments given to St Adalbert by Emperor Otto [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 38: “they are honorably kept to this day in the Church of Prague”]; the mill-chain [Col. 0016B] which Duke Břetislav was said to have broken with a single blow of his sword [Note: [Col. 0015D] I, 40: “which is visible to this day”]; the honors granted to Dovora and her descendants, and retained down to Cosmas’s time [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 34: “from then until now their descendants possess them through the generations”]; the chalice by the consecration of which the soul of Emperor Henry II was saved [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 37: “which is kept to this day … at Bamberg”]; and, finally, the monastery of St Wenceslas situated on the Elbe [Note: [Col. 0016D] II, 7: “in which, as is visible even today …”].

To these writing resources are added tales and common report, transmitted orally from ancient times among people. Cosmas cites it now as “the fabulous relation of old men” [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, prologue.], now as “the report of the truly faithful” [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 13.], now by saying “it is commonly said” [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 14.], and now as something he heard “as report has it” [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 10; III, 43.]. From these sources, then—perhaps in part from popular songs [Note: [Col. 0016D] This is the view of Palacký and Šafařík in *Die ältesten Denkmale der Böhmischen Sprache*, pp. 84, 179.]—he drew what he recorded in the earlier part of the first book [Note: [Col. 0016D] I, 1–15.]: the origins of the Bohemians; the first inhabitants; the daughters of Crocco; Prince Přemysl and Libuše; the founding of the city of Prague; the war [Col. 0016C] between the maidens and young men of the Bohemians; Vladislav and Neklan; and Děring, the false schoolmaster.

With this material of events drawn from popular rumor Cosmas joined, as the order of events seemed to require, what he had obtained from other books. These were not numerous, as one might expect in a learned man. Yet since, in describing Bohemian affairs, he had no one in whose footsteps he could follow, only very few matters needed to be sought from books. His resources were: the chronicle of Regino and its continuator [Note: [Col. 0016D] Although Palacký thought otherwise, *Würdigung*, p. 22, passages I, 1 and III, 14 were undoubtedly taken from Regino, and I, 19–20 from the continuator.], from which he copied one passage exactly word for word; Gumpold’s *Life of St Wenceslas*, which he cited rather than copied [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 15, 17; III, 55.]; [Col. 0017A] the earlier *Life of St Adalbert* [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 26, 29, 30.]; the *Life of St Ulrich*, which he merely named [Note: [Col. 0017D] III, 42.]; and certain necrologies [Note: [Col. 0017D] Meinert conjectured that these belonged to the monasteries of St Vitus, St George, Břevnov, and Mělník.].

Finally, to books must be added public charters and letters, which he partly cited and from which he drew a few things, and which he partly inserted into his text entire. These are: the Privilege of the Moravian Church and the Epitome of Moravia, resources which we now regret to have been lost, and of which he made only mention [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 15.]; the forged bull ascribed to Pope John XIII, concerning the foundation of the bishopric of Prague and likewise the foundation of the monastery of St George, by which document the author himself was deceived [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 22, 34.]; and the genuine decree of Emperor Henry IV concerning the restoration of the diocese of the bishopric of Prague [Note: [Col. 0017D] II, 37.]. The letters are those of Duke Boleslaus I to Emperor Otto I concerning [Col. 0017B] the appointment of Dětmar as bishop of Prague [Note: [Col. 0017D] I, 23.], and of Duke Boleslaus of the Poles to Duke Vladislav of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0017D] III, 41.]. Whether I may add the letter of Countess Matilda to Duke Welf is very doubtful [Note: [Col. 0017D] II, 32.], because it is in part composed in those homoeoteleutic verses, ending with similar sounds, which Cosmas uses very frequently. Nor does any different conclusion seem warranted concerning the speeches which he very frequently makes kings and dukes deliver.

Now a second question arises: how Cosmas arranged such abundant and copious material for writing, and how, amid so great a multitude of events, he exercised critical judgment with historical fidelity. Nor will you here find wanting the sound judgment by which he makes it very clear that he can distinguish truth from falsehood, nor was he unaware [Col. 0017C] how far copper differs from lupins. He arranged all his material quite suitably in three books. The first he carried down to Duke Břetislav I, the founder of the glory of the ducal house and of the Bohemians—that is, to the year 1039; the second down to Břetislav II, in the year 1092. Thus the first book contained those periods in writing of which he followed popular report or the books of others; the second, what he had heard from eyewitnesses or had himself seen in youth; the third, what he had learned as a man and old man, whether in his homeland or among foreign peoples.

He knew well that the most ancient times of the Bohemians lacked every written authority. He writes freely to Gervasius [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, prologue]:

> “I began to arrange the years of the Lord’s Incarnation from the times of Bořivoj [Col. 0017D], the first Catholic duke, because at the beginning of this book I neither wished to invent nor was able to find a chronicle, so that I might know when, or in what times, those things which you will presently read in what follows were done.”

[Col. 0018A] And elsewhere, concerning the same period, he adds [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 9]:

> “Because there was no one at that time to entrust the deeds of those men to memory by the pen.”

Accordingly, he takes good care not to assign definite years to events occurring before, and shortly after, the baptism of Duke Bořivoj, nor to describe their date more precisely—something he declares impossible. “Between these years,” he writes [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 15], “which we have noted below, occurred those things which we have touched upon above; for we could not know in what years or at what times they were done.” In describing them he turns to the fabulous narrative of old men, intending to commit it to writing “not from an ambition for human praise, but lest the things reported be altogether handed over to oblivion—according to our power and knowledge, and insofar as it has been permitted us to know” [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, prologue]; and he solemnly declares that in all these matters he has invented nothing [Col. 0018B].

Following this principle of narration, he also exercised such carefulness in his book that he would present nothing as certain which he had not sufficiently established, or which seemed capable of being undermined by some doubt. He expressed this in explicit terms in quite a few places. At one time, “he preferred to be silent rather than state an unverified matter” [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 1]; at another he confesses that he himself is uncertain how things stood [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 12, 19, 36]; and whatever he could not investigate thoroughly, he openly says that he does not know [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 15, 18; II, 12, 40; III, 24, 58]. Yet even from matters which he knew well, he did not wish to pour forth a great mass of events as though from a sack, but with restrained judgment he pruned excessive abundance. Lest he repeat what had already been said, he prefers “to pass it over rather than cause weariness to readers, because we read that it has already been written by others” [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 15, 27, 30]; and sometimes [Col. 0018C], “where more things worthy of report might be said,” he thinks they ought to be veiled in silence [Note: [Col. 0018D] II, 26]. Conversely, “he judges that those things must not be passed over which he sees to have been omitted by others” [Note: [Col. 0018D] I, 29].

This prudent and modest plan of writing, which he chiefly followed in the first two books, he somewhat altered in the third book—or, more accurately, pressed too far. For in committing the events of his own time to writing, he shows himself excessively cautious and, scarcely as one would expect, timid. It seemed exceedingly difficult to him to report upon his contemporaries, and especially upon the more recent dukes of Bohemia, in such a way as to avoid the two rocks of flattery and harshness. These anxieties burden the third book, as he expounded at greater length in its very prologue:

> “For concerning modern [Col. 0018D] men or times, it is more useful that we remain altogether silent than, by speaking the truth, incur some loss, because truth always begets hatred. But if, departing from truth, we write otherwise than matters [Col. 0019A] actually stand, since the causes are known to almost everyone, nonetheless we incur the stigma of flattery and falsehood. If we set forth their deeds fully with the pen, because some things were not done in accordance with God, we shall undoubtedly not escape the offense of certain persons who are still alive; for the fault and the judgment are alike, whether one has kept back the truth or admitted falsehood.”

From all this he drew for himself a rule of writing which, although it makes the writer of events safer, is not equally salutary for matters that must be handed down to posterity.

> “Therefore it seems to us far safer to recount a dream, to which no one bears witness, than to write the deeds of present men; for which reason let us leave their deeds to be more fully explained by posterity.”

Elsewhere [Col. 0019B], overcome by the same fear, he breaks off the thread of narrative. He does not dare add more concerning the destruction of the Vršovci family, lest he seem to have written a tragedy [Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 24]. He does not wish to speak freely of the virtues and glory of Duke Vladislav, “while he remains in this life, lest he incur either the charge of flattery, or, by writing too little concerning his praises, the offense of detraction” [Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 28]. He left untouched the virtues of Hermann, bishop of Prague, although he could have offered several matters worthy of report, “on account of the men of the present time, who, themselves doing no good, refuse to believe upon hearing of the good deeds of others” [Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 49]. And he does not consider it lawful to investigate why Duke Bořivoj was twice elevated to the throne and twice rejected [Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 54]. Indeed, he was brought so far that, although in the first book he had written that he did not wish to invent, he made an almost contrary pronouncement concerning that same [Col. 0019C] Bořivoj in this verse:

> Now, my Muse, check your little lip with your finger.  
> If you are wisely taught, take care not to speak the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 46.]

These very weighty words, drawn from Cosmas’s own disposition, seem to require this interpretation: that he wished neither to invent falsehoods nor openly to declare the true causes of events, which he knew well. That in the third book he really departed from the most salutary policy which he had formerly adopted is also apparent from this: scarcely anyone will deny that the character and nature of the whole chronicle are changed in the latter part of that book.

If you examine somewhat more carefully the method by which he composed his work, it will become evident of itself that he wished to write Annals of the Bohemians, proceeding simply year by year [Col. 0019D]. But matters turned out somewhat differently in the first two books. Here and there he did indeed insert certain disconnected notices, which, by the nature of annals, are held together by no bond; but where he could or wished to pour forth the abundance of events with a full hand, [Col. 0020A] he himself, as though swept along by a fuller stream of narrative, observed those narrow bounds of years less precisely and set forth events in an agreeable narrative with freedom of spirit. In the third book, however, where fear prevented him from disclosing everything he knew, he followed the series of years more exactly, more often set down with the same pen matters having no connection with one another, and more than once adopted a meager and dry style of writing. This is plainly apparent near the end of the third book, which he concluded with an almost childish little story about a lustful priest, altogether unworthy of such a book [Note: [Col. 0019D] III, 62].

But another matter remains which cannot be passed over in silence. For Cosmas, whom we have seen to be so circumspect a writer, did not always and everywhere adequately avoid more serious errors in writing the events themselves [Col. 0020B]. In this respect he must certainly be forgiven, since never to stumble anywhere amid so great an abundance of events almost exceeds human nature. He often fell into the very error he most strove to avoid: in describing dates more accurately, he slipped more than once. This is not at all surprising in the most ancient times, where he lacked a tested guide; but it happened even where a clearer light had already shone.

Falsely, for example, he assigned the baptism of Duke Bořivoj to the year 894, and the death of Duke St Wenceslas, who died in 935, to the year 929 [Note: [Col. 0019D] I, 14, 17]. The bishopric of Prague was founded not in 967, but not before 973 [Note: [Col. 0019D] I, 22]. Thietmar, the first bishop of Prague, died not in 969, as Cosmas wishes, but only in 982 [Note: [Col. 0019D] I, 24]. He confused the dates of St Adalbert’s journeys to Rome [Note: [Col. 0019D] I, 28, 29]; [Col. 0020C] falsely assigned the death of Emperor Otto II to 984, and that of St Adalbert to 996 [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 31]. He says that Jaromír was expelled from the kingdom by his brother Oldřich in 1002, whereas we know that this took place only in 1012 [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 36]. He writes that Judith was abducted by Břetislav in 1021, though this cannot have occurred before 1029 [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 40]. He did not describe accurately enough the time when Emperor Henry III waged war against the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0020D] II, 12]. He falsely assigns to 1074 the battle fought at Mailberg in 1082 by Duke Vratislav and Leopold, margrave of Austria [Note: [Col. 0020D] II, 35]. If you seek further examples, you may add them without any difficulty.

He confused persons no less than dates. He makes St Adalbert, the friend of Otto III, the friend [Col. 0020D] of Otto II [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 28]; he confuses Duke Bolesław of Poland with his father Mieszko [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 34]; he falsely ascribes to Oldřich the brother the capture of Prague by Jaromír in 1002 [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 36]; he makes Henry II the son of Otto III [Note: [Col. 0020D] I, 37]; he falsely calls Judith the daughter of Margrave Otto, [Col. 0021A] whose sister she was [Note: [Col. 0021C] I, 40]. Likewise, he errs in establishing the genealogy of Jaromír and Oldřich, whom he made sons of Bolesław II and grandsons of Bolesław III [Note: [Col. 0021C] I, 32]; he silently omits the Pole Vladivoj from the succession of Bohemian dukes [Note: [Col. 0021C] I, 34], and frequently stumbles in narrating these periods. He described less accurately the wars of Duke Břetislav I with the Poles and Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0021C] I, 40], and reported falsehoods concerning Duke Casimir of Poland [Note: [Col. 0021C] II, 2; all these errors were formerly enumerated by Palacký in his book *Würdigung*, p. 25].

What, however, is especially surprising in a man so modest and restrained is that in describing more recent times he undoubtedly erred in one or two places because he allowed himself to be carried away by anger or partisanship, although he seemed to have guarded himself so well. In narrating the dispute concerning the bishoprics of Prague and Olomouc, he strongly favors Gebhard, bishop of Prague, a rash [Col. 0021B] and indeed cruel man; and, as Dobner and Palacký have already observed, he seems to exercise a harsher judgment upon Vratislav, a strong and energetic duke, because the latter had raised up rivals to the bishops of Prague in the bishops of Olomouc [Note: [Col. 0021D] II, 21]. His sharper attacks upon the Germans may more readily be pardoned in a man full of love for his homeland. In narrating miracles he shows himself modest and sound-minded, and the things which he committed to writing, arising from the character of those times, exceed neither belief nor sound judgment, with perhaps one or two exceptions [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 37; II, 4, 34, 47; III, 11, 57].

That Cosmas came to writing equipped with no small resources of learning is sufficiently proved by the lights of ancient writers, which he held so well in mind that they flowed spontaneously from his pen. Above all he read Latin poets: Terence [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 13; III, prologue]; Virgil [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 1, 4, 10, 11, 40; II, 8, 12, 14, 33, 35, 39, 45; III, 3, 13, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 27, 29, 31, 49, 58, 59]; Horace [Note: [Col. 0021D] *Odes* I, 1, 4, 9, 35; II, 10, 18, 35; *Satires* I, preface, 34; II, 1; *Epistles* I, prologue, 9, 25; II, 14, 33; III, 29]; Lucan [Note: [Col. 0021D] II, 3, 10, 12, 14, 35, 39, 45; III, 12, 29]; Juvenal [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 9, 19, 38]; Statius [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 40]; and Prudentius [Note: [Col. 0021D] III, 19]. Among prose writers I could detect only Sallust [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 9, 11; II, 35, 39] and Boethius [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 3; II, 23]. He used authors of Christian antiquity more rarely; nevertheless, he cited Jerome [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 42] and Augustine [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 4] in one or two places, nor did he cite passages of Holy Scripture very often.

His language is neither pure nor correct [Col. 0022A], and it contains much which, though pardonable for those times when not everything was reduced to grammatical rules, must nevertheless be corrected even by a less severe critic. At other times he narrated events well and clearly and painted persons not infrequently in such vivid colors that you might think yourself reading an epic poem; therefore you might judge him not unworthy of the title “Herodotus of the Bohemians.” The stream of narrative itself often swept him away so that he composed not only speeches of dukes and kings, but narrative itself, in hexameters, dactylic verses, rhythmic language, and homoeoteleuton—rhyme or like-sounding endings—which, as we know, writers of the twelfth century used very frequently. Concerning such verses he wrote to Clement, abbot of Břevnov:

> “But as for finding in certain places what are, as it were, metrical [Col. 0022B] verses, know that I did this knowingly in ignorance, while I made verses.”

[Note: [Col. 0021D] II, preface.]

But since almost half the entire work is composed in that homoeoteleutic style, we should seem to exceed the limits set for us if we marked it in our text whenever it occurred; it was sufficient to do so in only a few places.

There are writers of later times who took Cosmas as their guide in narrating events and plundered his book more or less. Whether I should include among them those responsible for the popular poems of the Queen’s Court Manuscript, or rather say that both the authors of those poems and Cosmas followed old tales circulating among the people, I hesitate to decide and gladly leave the judgment to those more expert. [Col. 0022C] This one thing I hold firmly: Cosmas did not follow the recension of the poems which we possess [Note: [Col. 0021D] I, 4, 10, 12, 13, 36. Šafařík and Palacký, *Die ältesten Denkmäler der Böhmischen Sprache* [The Oldest Monuments of the Bohemian Language], p. 179].

Palacký has noted in his book the names of the rest who genuinely copied Cosmas. They are the Saxon annalist, from whom I consider it superfluous to cite examples; Hildegard of Hradisko, who wrote in 1127 and 1147 [Note: [Col. 0022C] See what Boczek published in *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae* I, p. 114 ff.]; the Prague Annals [Note: [Col. 0022C] I cannot persuade myself that the Prague Annals should be counted among Cosmas’s sources; on the contrary, I believe that they flowed from Cosmas himself. For the author himself expressly declares that he could nowhere find a chronicle setting forth in what times the most ancient events of the Bohemians occurred. He therefore produced the false chronological notices not from tenth-century annals, in which they would scarcely have been tolerable, but from his own invention. Yet the same chronological errors found in the author—writing a century and a half after the beginnings of Bohemia—will certainly trouble no one in either Cosmas or the Annals; and the very words agree here and there so closely that the Annals seem to be a very copious abridgment [Col. 0023C] of the matters narrated by Cosmas.

> To dispose of this here as well: that the Sázava continuation was copied from the author of the Prague Annals is proved by passages under 990 concerning the town of Němci; 1053 concerning St Procopius; 1130 concerning Meinhard, bishop of Prague; 1132 concerning Přibyslava; 1134 concerning John, the eleventh bishop of Prague—for from this point the Prague bishops are designated by number, as in the Sázava continuation, whereas this had not previously been done either in Cosmas or in the Annals; 1139 concerning Sylvester, abbot of Sázava; and 1143 concerning the marriages of clerics. In the years 1160–1193 the writer of the Annals [Col. 0023D] seems to have had Gerlach, abbot of Milevsko, before his eyes, and also to have sought some other matters elsewhere. This appears both from the double account of the death of Emperor Frederick I and from the mention in 1182 of Duke Henry, whom we know to have acquired the duchy only in 1193. Since the author calls the same man “lord bishop,” suppressing his name, the conjecture arises all the more easily that the Annals were composed before Henry’s death—which is not recorded in them—namely, between 1193 and 1197, since the following years, 1216–1220, were added by another, though contemporary, hand, as the distinguished Pertz observed. We have judged it necessary to add all this here because the Prague Annals are of the highest importance, as will become evident a little below, in examining Cosmas’s second continuation.]

the monk of Opatovice [Note: [Col. 0022D] From the year 894 onward; compare also the years 1028 and 1068, and others. Palacký proved, p. 68, that he followed a manuscript containing the Sázava interpolation, by the example of 1091, which he took from the interpolated text.]; [Col. 0023A] Marignola [Note: [Col. 0023D] He copied Cosmas almost everywhere in the most ancient tales. Compare also the passages concerning St Adalbert, the abduction of Judith, and the war of Henry III against the Bohemians, in Dobner, *Monumenta historica Bohemica* II, 140, 157, [Col. 0024C] 166, 169.]; Neplach of Opatovice [Note: [Col. 0024C] Compare the years 894, 984, 994, etc.; ibid., IV.]; Pulkava [Note: [Col. 0024C] Compare the most ancient tales, the years 967, 1002, 1021, etc.; ibid., vol. III.]; Dalimil and Hájek [Note: [Col. 0024C] See Palacký’s *Würdigung*, p. 115. Hájek himself cites Cosmas as an author.].

To these I would add another: the author of the Life of St Adalbert composed in verse, which Dobner published from Cosmas’s Prague manuscript [Note: [Col. 0024C] *Monumenta historica Bohemica* II, 1]. Dobner himself, and after him Dobrovský and Palacký, considered it attributable to Cosmas himself. Yet whoever the author of that Life may be, he copied Cosmas’s chronicle; I can scarcely persuade myself that Cosmas himself was its author. Dobner declared that Cosmas’s name was neither prefixed to that little book nor could any indication be found in the Life itself pointing to Cosmas, apart from certain passages taken from the chronicle and adapted into verse. Certainly another could easily have done this, since its rhythmic language itself seemed to invite conversion into regular and complete verses [Col. 0023B].

The words by which Cosmas seemed to have indicated to Dobner that he had also composed a Life of St Adalbert—that he did not wish to say twice what had been said [Note: [Col. 0024C] I, 30]—can plainly be referred without difficulty to the earlier Lives of St Adalbert. Nor is the similarity of literary style which Dobner thought he had detected in those books of sufficient weight for me to believe that Cosmas composed both the chronicle and the Life. Nor, it seems, can another judgment be made concerning the continuation of the Life of St Wenceslas, found in the same manuscript, which Pelzel and Dobrovský held to be attributable to Cosmas. Yet, if one may offer such an opinion without examining the manuscript itself, it appears to be nothing but a fragment of Cosmas’s chronicle attached to that Life. So much for this.

[Col. 0023C] When the pen, as it were, fell from the hands of the dying Cosmas, who had directed his mind to the deeds of the Bohemians up to his final day, there arose another writer of events. Although not endowed with the same happy gift for writing history, he took up the part left by Cosmas with no less concern for posterity and for the usefulness of history [Col. 0024A]. This is the “canon of Vyšehrad,” sufficiently designated by the broad title of Cosmas’s first continuator, who composed Annals of Bohemia from 1125 to 1142 and included in his book the times and deeds of Duke Soběslav I, who ruled the Bohemians for fifteen years down to 1140, not without glory.

Since this author seemed especially to have had before his eyes the aim of exalting Soběslav with the highest praises, Palacký, relying on one passage of the little work [Note: [Col. 0024C] Under 1140: “For he [Soběslav] knew, from the report of his household chaplains, that Blessed Gregory had said,” etc. And shortly afterward: “They summon the chaplain Vincent, than whom no other was more faithful to him” [Col. 0024D]], proposed the conjecture that the writer of the Annals was that same Vincent, the duke’s chaplain, whom we hear the author affirming with all his heart to have been most faithful to him. Though the opinion is very attractive [Col. 0024B], it must nevertheless be left undecided. The author himself appears to have wished to conceal his name; for it is found nowhere, neither in his book nor in other writers.

He was a Bohemian by nationality, as is confirmed both by the greatest zeal with which he favors the Bohemians against the Germans [Note: [Col. 0024D] For example, in 1126, in narrating the war of Emperor Lothair and Duke Soběslav] and no less by explicit words [Note: [Col. 0024D] In 1126 and 1136 recur the words “neither our fathers nor our grandfathers nor our great-grandfathers”; in 1126 the Germans are “our enemies,” and the author speaks of “us” and “our people”; in 1137 they are the Bohemians]. Against Pessina [Note: [Col. 0024D] In a marginal gloss entered in the metropolitan manuscript itself; see Pelzel and Dobrovský I, preface, p. XXXIII], Dobrovský [Note: [Col. 0024D] Loc. cit.], and Meinert [Note: [Col. 0024D] *Wiener Jahrbücher*, XV, *Anzeigeblatt*, p. 31], who attempted to prove that he was a Prague canon, Palacký demonstrated from the book itself that he was a canon of Vyšehrad [Note: [Col. 0024D] *Würdigung*, p. 37]. For the author speaks at greater length about the foundation of the monastery of Vyšehrad, and only someone who saw daily with his own eyes the sacred ornaments with which Soběslav had adorned that church could describe them so accurately [Note: [Col. 0024D] Under 1129. Meinert, loc. cit., persuaded himself on arguments I do not know that the passage in which some words of the false charter concerning the Church of Vyšehrad recur—see Cosmas under 1070—is interpolated].

Finally, there is the zeal with which he preferred the [Col. 0024C] canons of Vyšehrad to those of Prague. For he attacked some of the latter very bitterly—an invective which one could scarcely suppose had been directed by him against brothers and colleagues [Note: [Col. 0024D] Under 1131 and 1133. In 1130 he sets himself and his own people—he says “us”—against the canons of Prague; and in 1131 he testifies that the bishop of Münster celebrated Mass in the church of Vyšehrad]. Therefore there can be no doubt [Col. 0025A] that by the words “supporter of this Church,” which he used under 1137, he meant Vyšehrad.

Only a few things need be said concerning the sources from which he drew, for almost everywhere he selected his material from the broadest and clearest stream of the events themselves. His narrative presents the highest appearance of truthfulness, and the writer of the Annals himself explicitly indicates his authority. So far as I know, he erred almost nowhere in narrating events; following the course of chronological order with the greatest accuracy, he proceeds with a modest and restrained step. Though he does not attract the minds of readers by native charm as Cosmas does, he is by no means to be deprived of the praise due to his diligence and usefulness.

In more than one place he clearly teaches that he was an eyewitness of the events themselves: thus, in describing heavenly portents [Col. 0025B] under 1131, we read the phrases “as I saw” and “while we were looking on.” Nor did he fail to support his history by reports of eyewitnesses. He undoubtedly heard accounts from participants in the battle of Chlumec in 1126 [Note: [Col. 0025D] “But I do not wish you to be unaware . . . . . of what I heard.”]; and he reports accurately what others saw concerning celestial apparitions [Note: [Col. 0025D] Under 1128 and 1139]. He “has ascertained” how great Soběslav’s favor was with Emperor Lothair and what disagreement existed between Duke Vratislav of Brno and Henry, bishop of Olomouc [Note: [Col. 0025D] Under 1135 and 1136]. From “the report of truthful men” [Note: [Col. 0025D] Under 1137] he derived other matters; and he openly confesses ignorance of what had not been established for him, or marks it, as it were, with the stamp of suspicion by the words “if report is to be believed” and “as is said” [Note: [Col. 0025D] Under 1133].

And, unless I am mistaken, what adds the greatest weight of authority to the book [Col. 0025C] is that he composed his Annals while events themselves were unfolding, and did not permit what he had heard or seen to be obscured by oblivion in any way. The most accurate descriptions of natural phenomena and the author’s own words are witnesses. To supplement what he had written under 1130 concerning two stars seen in heaven, he added under 1131:

> “Afterward I could by no means explain anything about them in my narrative, because they moved in different directions. But meanwhile, when I am entirely free from other business, I shall explain how I saw them.”

This passage shows that a fairly long interval elapsed between the writing of those words and these. He does not dare commit to paper the counsels of the nobles taken shortly before Soběslav’s death in 1140, “lest he incur hatred.” Prayers composed for the salvation of that duke’s soul reveal the grief of his very recent death. To these must be added [Col. 0026A] what is read under 1141 concerning the journey of Henry, bishop of Olomouc, against the Prussians, and concerning his return.

He used a fairly pure and simple style; he set forth certain matters, such as the conspiracy against Soběslav, clearly. Nor does he lack literary resources: acquaintance with ancient literature is not wanting, for the years 1134 and 1136 show that he had read Horace and Virgil.

Not very long after the canon of Vyšehrad, about fifty years after Cosmas, a certain monk of Sázava [Note: [Col. 0025D] Palacký rightly and undoubtedly refuted Meinert’s opinion, loc. cit., p. 32, that this Sázava continuation was composed not by one author but by several; *Würdigung*, p. 46. Both the manner of writing and the very words reveal the same author, since he frequently refers back to things said above or ahead to things to be said below: under 1133 to what he said under 1097; and under 1123 and 1161 to the year 1134] turned his mind to writing annals. Neither his name was handed down to posterity nor can the time when he composed his book be more precisely fixed. This alone is proved by his own words: he belonged to that monastery of the order of St Benedict [Col. 0026B] which drew its name from the river Sázava, flowing by it and emptying into the Vltava [Note: [Col. 0025D] He described with the greatest accuracy the relics of saints kept among the monks of Sázava and the holy places, under [Col. 0026D] 1095; under 1155 we read “our brothers,” and under 1156 “in this monastery,” “among us”].

This monastery, easily among the most celebrated of Bohemian monasteries, deserves mention especially because St Procopius, whom it found in 1038 as its founder and originator [Note: [Col. 0026D] We cannot depart from this year, transmitted by the Sázava monk himself, in fixing the time when that monastery was founded], established that sacred rites should be celebrated according to the Slavonic rite and order. These were preserved until the end of the eleventh century, not without the gravest danger to the monks, according to the chronicler’s own testimony. The same Procopius was the first man of the Bohemian people whom the Roman pontiffs received into the company of saints [Note: [Col. 0026D] This occurred in 1204; see below, the second continuation of Cosmas and the Life of St Procopius in *Acta Sanctorum*, July 2, p. 138. Though dedicated to Severus, bishop of Prague, it appears to have been composed after the Sázava monk. Palacký, *Würdigung*, pp. 51, 297].

The monk of Sázava carried his chronicle down to 1162, but he did not lay down his pen in that very year; rather, he seems to have composed his book about 1170, unless I am mistaken [Col. 0026C]. For he testifies that Soběslav II was delivered into chains in 1161 “to be worn down for a long time.” But that man was not called from prison to the throne until 1173, as we know. Whether those words were written before or after that year cannot be extracted from them.

Without doubt the monk had spent many years at Sázava before 1173, in the time of Abbot Sylvester, who ruled the monastery from 1134 to 1161 with the highest praise from all. The author lavished such full-handed praise upon him that you may readily persuade yourself that the illustrious abbot could have been so celebrated only by one admitted to his familiarity [Note: [Col. 0026D] Under 1134]. Moreover, the author himself teaches that what is read under 1097 was not written before 1134 [Note: [Col. 0026D] He accurately defined the years during which Diethard, who died in 1134, held the office of abbot of Sázava]; and it is sufficiently evident that he was contemporary with events occurring in [Col. 0027A] 1126 and 1132. For in the former place, concerning the peace between Soběslav and Otto which did not last long, he used these words: “A contrary outcome received our joys”; and in the latter he writes that he saw Groznata’s widow, who had died in that year.

It is therefore permissible to conjecture that, like Cosmas, he left us a book as the fruit of old age, and committed events to the memory of posterity almost half a century after they had occurred. Accordingly, it is not at all surprising that here and there, though very rarely, he fell into error [Note: [Col. 0027D] Under 1126 and 1157].

If you ask, he seems to have adopted a twofold plan in composing his chronicle: first, to add certain supplements to Cosmas’s chronicle and include matters which he saw had been omitted by him; second, to carry the history of the Bohemians down to his own time [Col. 0027B]. This twofold plan did not succeed equally well. For the former portion, consisting of interpolations, is of the slightest importance, since we owe absolutely nothing to the author himself down to the year 1038. The interpolations not concerning the monastery of Sázava he drew from the Hersfeld Annals, which Waitz demonstrated to be a source of the Quedlinburg Annals [Note: [Col. 0027D] I cannot persuade myself either, with Palacký, that the Hildesheim Annals are the source of the Sázava interpolations, or, with Waitz, that the Quedlinburg Annals are; *Archiv*, VI, p. 690. For in the Sázava text certain things occur which are absent from the former—for example, under 989, 996, and 998—and others absent from the latter. For matters missing in our copy of the Quedlinburg Annals under 963, 973, and 975 agree here and there word for word in the Sázava text with the Hildesheim Annals. Yet certain variant readings, though of slight importance, prevent us from referring everything to Quedlinburg: readings agreeing with Hildesheim occur in passages which recur word for word in Quedlinburg. Thus, under 958, the same material occurs in the Hildesheim, Quedlinburg, and Sázava Annals; but in the variant reading *illis autem* (“but to those”), the Sázava Annals agree [Col. 0028D] with Hildesheim, while *autem* is absent from Quedlinburg. Under 960, in the words *paganico ritu* (“by pagan rite”), Quedlinburg has *paganismo* (“by paganism”); under 986, the Sázava text has *venit* (“came”) against Quedlinburg’s reading *perrexit* (“proceeded”). Yet since scarcely anyone would suppose that the monk copied both the Hildesheim and Quedlinburg Annals, only this conclusion seems to remain: that he drew from the source of both.].

No other books, so far as I can see, were called in by the author for assistance, with the possible exception of a Sázava necrology [Note: [Col. 0028D] I seem to have detected its traces under the years 1045, 1053, 1126, 1127, 1130, 1132–1134, 1139, 1140, 1142, 1147, 1150, and 1155]. Under 1038 he had before him the charter of Duke Břetislav I’s foundation of the monastery of Sázava, and under 1132 the charter of the donation of Přibyslava, a noblewoman.

In the latter part, in which the monk attempted by his own effort to write the history of his country, one hears in more than one place a sensible [Col. 0027C] and learned man speaking, whom one can scarcely deny to be a continuator worthy of Cosmas. What he committed to writing concerning the origin of the monastery he owed both to popular report and to the narratives of old monks, whom the author seems to cite in 1038 by the phrases “as is said” and “by the truthful report of the faithful.” The holy places of the monastery of Sázava also supplied the monk with ample material for writing, which he pointed out, as it were, with his finger in such expressions as: “As is seen today,” “as appears on the present day” [Note: [Col. 0028D] Under 1038; compare also 1070, 1095, 1097, and 1146].

Almost everything we read from 1126 onward he derived from his own resources, and I do not hesitate to say that his reliability is established in these matters. One can only regret that he did not hand down the rest to posterity in the same manner in which [Col. 0028A] he described the origin of the monastery of Sázava in 1038, Lothair’s war with Duke Soběslav in 1126, Emperor Frederick I’s Italian expedition in 1158, and the life and character of Abbot Sylvester in 1134; instead, almost everywhere he pursued excessive brevity of narration.

In the ecclesiastical schism, lest I pass this over, which had arisen in those times, he supports, as the Bohemians were accustomed to do, the side of Frederick I and Victor IV against Alexander III [Note: [Col. 0028D] Under 1159]. He was adequately furnished with learning: among Latin poets Juvenal occurs [Note: [Col. 0028D] Under 1038], and among the Fathers of the Church, Gregory the Great and the “wondrous Father” [Note: [Col. 0028D] Under 1097 and 1162]. His manner of writing is plain and clear, unless one chooses to criticize this—which indeed is far from praise—that he pursued rarer and somehow [Col. 0028B] obsolete words.

This great and extensive collection of Bohemian events from the years 1140–1283, which the editors have called Cosmas’s second continuation and which we subsume under the common title “Continuation of the Prague Canons,” gives rise to far greater difficulty. For, even after this little book has been examined with the greatest care, many exceedingly difficult knots remain attached to it, and very serious questions arise concerning the individual parts of the annals: concerning the method and procedure by which this mass of materials was put together, the authors by whom it was written, and what should be attributed to each. Our hope of removing these difficulties is the slighter because this continuation rests upon only one Prague metropolitan manuscript—and that not an autograph, [Col. 0028C] but rather a copy from the middle of the fourteenth century. After the first continuation, with a blank space of one line left, as Dobrovský testifies [Note: [Col. 0028D] I, p. XXXIV.], this more extensive second continuation follows without any title.

For a long time, all those who have devoted themselves to Bohemian history have been much troubled by the origin of this little book. Balbín, who both saw and read this manuscript, persuaded himself that the author of the continuation from the year 1126 to 1200 was the same suspect Jaroslav, a monk of Strahov, whom Hájek, in the list of authors prefixed to his book, declares that he had among his sources. What follows down to 1283 he called Jaroslav’s appendix. He indicated this opinion both in the margin of the manuscript itself [Note: [Col. 0029D] “Here Jaroslav of Strahov seems to begin his chronicle.”], and repeatedly adopted it in his *Epitome of Bohemian Affairs* (*Epitome rerum Bohemicarum*) [Note: [Col. 0029D] pp. 221 ff.].

Pessina of Czechorod adopted nearly the same opinion, though in the manuscript itself, at the year 1154, he noted that the remainder had been written by an anonymous canon of the Church of Prague [Note: [Col. 0029D] Pelzel and Dobrovský I, p. XXXVII. See further Pessina’s *Moravian Mars* (*Mars Maravicus*), Prague, 1677, fol., pp. 293 ff., and his *Seven-horned Phosphorus* (*Phosphorus septicornis*), Prague, 1673, quarto, pp. 37, 558.]. But Pelzel and Dobrovský sufficiently proved that the things Hájek alleged on the authority of the fabulous Jaroslav are nowhere found in this continuation, and that Balbín’s conjecture can be supported by no arguments whatsoever. Their own view was that a Prague canon contemporary with the events wrote the history of his own time from 1249 to 1283, while deriving what preceded from older sources [Note: [Col. 0029D] I, p. XXXVIII. Pelzel himself, however, had earlier assigned the name Jaroslav to the continuator, in the essay entitled “Whether the Imperial Crown Was Offered to King Ottokar” (*Ob dem König Ottokar die Kaiserkrone angetragen worden*), in Born’s *Proceedings of a Private Society in Bohemia* (*Abhandlungen einer Privatgesellschaft in Böhmen*), Prague, II, 74.]. Meinert restricted this view by maintaining that only what is read from about the year 1260 onward [Col. 0029B] should be credited to a contemporary author [Note: [Col. 0029D] *Vienna Yearbooks* (*Wiener Jahrbücher*) XV, Anzeiger, p. 36.].

Finally, the first to perceive the truth with penetrating intelligence was Palacký [Note: [Col. 0029D] *Assessment* (*Würdigung*), p. 94; he certainly confirmed this in the essay “The Mongol Invasion of 1241” (*Der Mongoleneinfall von 1241*), in *Transactions of the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences* (*Abhandlungen der Königlich Böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften*), series V, vol. II, p. 387.]. On the basis of the very different manner of writing and character of the narratives, he judged that the years 1250–1283 had been written by two Prague canons and had perhaps been fused into a single book by some compiler in the fourteenth century [Note: [Col. 0029D] *Assessment* (*Würdigung*), p. 94; he certainly confirmed this in the essay “The Mongol Invasion of 1241” (*Der Mongoleneinfall von 1241*), in *Transactions of the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences* (*Abhandlungen der Königlich Böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften*), series V, vol. II, p. 387.].

Since, therefore, in such great obscurity no illumination is to be sought from the manuscript, this one course must be followed: we must examine the book itself, to see whether indications of its origin may perhaps be drawn from its language, the colouring of its narrative, and the individual opinions that disclose the author’s character. Yet everyone sees how uncertain all such considerations are in a medieval writer, in whom a fixed and consistent manner of writing is found only rather seldom. [Col. 0029C] Accordingly, I am very far from believing that the opinion which I shall set forth below is free from every doubt, or incapable of being refuted.

For anyone who merely glances over the whole collection of annals, one fact presents itself spontaneously: whoever its author may have been, he by no means composed on his own initiative everything read from the year 1140 onward. Indeed, it is clear that the earlier part, which he borrowed from others, must be wholly removed from the present question. For all that he wrote concerning the years 1140–1193 he derived from sources still accessible today, taking the most distinguished writers of earlier Bohemian history as his guides.

With very few changes, or reduced [Col. 0030A] to a compendium, he took from Abbot Gerlach of Mühlhausen the years 1140, 1171, 1176, and 1182 [Note: [Col. 0030D] Dobner, *Historical Monuments of Bohemia* (*Monumenta historica Bohemiae*) I, p. 79 ff.], as Pelzel and Dobrovský observed; from the book on Frederick I’s Italian expedition by Vincent, chaplain of Daniel, bishop of Prague, the years 1154, 1159, and 1162 [Note: [Col. 0030D] Ibid. I, p. 29 ff.]; and from the more obscure Prague annals he adapted for his own use the years 1160, 1164, 1168, 1172–1178, 1182–1186, and 1189–1193. Finally, one passage under the year 1159 seems to be owed to Cosmas’s first continuator.

A larger gap is also apparent. For the author proceeds from the year 1140 to 1154, leaving blank the remaining years not mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0030D] The conjecture proposed by Pelzel and Dobrovský I, p. XXXVII, is attractive: that at an earlier time manuscripts existed in which the gap of 1142–1154 had been filled from Vincent’s chronicle. For, according to their testimony, Lupáč’s and Veleslavín’s calendars state, on Cosmas’s authority, that Count Hroznata, returning from Jerusalem, died on 16 October 1152. Yet in none of the continuations that they grouped under Cosmas’s own name is anything of the kind read, though it does in fact occur in Vincent. It follows that our manuscript did not correspond to the older copies that existed, but that its text had been somewhat altered—a fact which, unless I am mistaken, seems capable of lending somewhat greater support to the opinion I shall propose.].

All these things prove that he lived toward the close of the thirteenth century, since Gerlach is known to have composed his chronicle after 1214 [Col. 0030B] [Note: [Col. 0030D] Palacký, *Assessment* (*Würdigung*), p. 81.]. Yet upon closer examination there remain nevertheless a few things, indeed very few, not found in those authors. In copying Vincent, he was undoubtedly able to use a manuscript of better quality than the one published by Dobner, and thus not a few variant readings arose. But he added to Vincent materials from other sources: namely, the years 1155, 1157, and 1159.

Of far greater importance are the things he inserted among the Prague annals: the passages concerning Duke Soběslav in 1176, the years 1187 and 1188, and the somewhat fuller narrative in 1192 concerning Dukes Wenceslas, Přemysl, and Henry. All of these things, however, breathe the style found in the Prague annals and adhere so closely to their text that I arrive at the firm conviction [Col. 0030C] that both portions of the history were written by one and the same author; thus the complete Prague annals are to be restored from Cosmas’s continuator.

He seems, indeed, to have had before his eyes that copy of the annals which ended in 1193, for he followed them as far as that point. But what is read in the Prague annals for the years 1216–1220 is sought in vain in this author. If what I have proposed is true, there existed a fuller recension of the Prague annals than that presented in the Cassinese manuscript; and several fragments have here been preserved which are all the less to be despised because the surviving resources for Bohemian history at the end of the twelfth century are not numerous. Following, therefore, in the footsteps of these guides, [Col. 0031A] the compiler descended as far as the year 1193, where he was deprived of them—as the end of the Prague annals and the reckless confusion of the events that follow prove beyond all certainty.

But what resources did the continuator have in this part of his narrative? This is the question most difficult to explain. Anyone who surveys the very extensive material of events from 1196 to 1283 will readily conclude that it could not have been written by a single author. First, one is struck by the recurrence of the same events two or three times, now expressed in different words, now assigned to different years [Note: [Col. 0031C] There are two notices of the death of Bishop Henry, under 1196 and 1198: there he is called Henry, here Bracislav. The death of Bishop Frederick is recorded under 1178 and 1199; Prague is said in the same words to have been besieged by Conrad, duke of Moravia, under 1183 and 1203; likewise, in the same words, the Bohemians are said to have engaged in war with the Moravians in 1184 and 1204. Under 1190 and 1210 we read [Col. 0031D] that Conrad died in Apulia. Here too the compiler betrays himself, because the individual years differ from one another by twenty in their numerals. Duke Přemysl is said twice to have become king, under 1197 and 1199; the exile of the chamberlain Cyrin is recorded under 1211 and 1212. Under 1248 it is written very briefly that King Wenceslas was driven from the throne; under 1249 it is narrated at great length that, in the rebellion stirred up by his son Otakar, he was not at all driven from the throne but emerged victorious. Otakar’s victory over the Hungarians is first mentioned only in passing under 1260, and then expounded in a most copious narrative. The years 1182, 1199, 1249, 1256, 1264, 1266, 1271, 1278, and 1281 occur twice; the years 1258 and 1282 occur three times.].

Moreover, everything read from the year 1279 onward is so shamefully disordered that one seems to be proceeding along an almost inexplicable path. These accounts differ from one another to such an extent [Col. 0031B] that only a very few can be attributed to scribal carelessness—though that must certainly not be denied. For who could believe that an author, unless he were a reckless and unreflective compiler, could narrate the same events in such radically different ways almost in one breath?

But another argument may be added, and it is by no means of slight importance. In everything we read from about 1212 to the end, the clearest traces of an eyewitness are not likely to escape anyone. What we have, for example, concerning the excommunication imposed upon the people of Prague by Bishop Andrew in 1216 and 1217 is furnished with a description of the time so precise that no one but a contemporary can be judged to have written it in this way. The words read under 1261, “We received Cunigunda, the queen,” [Col. 0031C] clearly betray one who was present at the events themselves; and the dreadful famine of 1283 could have been depicted in this fashion only by someone who had seen its abominable and horrifying deeds with his own eyes.

But plainly no one could have transmitted as an eyewitness to posterity the memory of events occurring across seventy years. This itself proves with certainty that the second part of the continuation is composed of diverse pieces; and different authorial temperaments are clearly displayed by the different [Col. 0032A] styles. For the character of the material related in 1196–1248 differs greatly from that narrated in 1249–1283. Those fifty-two years are comprised in annals that are sometimes extremely brief, whereas the thirty-five later years demand almost the whole little book in a very copious narrative.

Let us examine the individual parts of the annals a little more closely. From 1212 to 1249, to begin with this section, the annals bear the appearance of unimpeachable authority, both in dates [Note: [Col. 0031D] Years 1216, 1217, 1227, 1228, 1230, 1236, 1240, 1248, 1249.] and in their accurate descriptions of sacred places in Prague [Note: [Col. 0031D] Years 1226–1228, 1232, 1234, 1244, 1245.]. That they were composed by a Prague canon is evident from the entries for 1235 and 1241, where we read that Vít, a canon, subsequently became dean of the Prague chapter [Col. 0032B]—a fact that could only have been committed to writing after Vít had gained for himself a distinguished reputation in administering the deanery. I would therefore suppose that these annals were not written by the author to whom we owe the following material, but were merely adapted to his own use and combined with his own writings.

In the subsequent material, from 1250 onward, where the abundance of narrative flows much more richly, no one will easily fail to observe that, down to about 1278, the author recorded with the utmost diligence the quantity and quality of the weather each year, when hail fell, and what the harvests were like. He scarcely omitted a single year in which he did not report these natural matters with the greatest precision and in almost the same words everywhere [Note: [Col. 0031D] Under 1251 we read: “The grain crop turned out badly, especially the winter crop.” Under 1252: “The winter crops turned out moderately in most regions; the summer crops almost entirely failed, millet excepted.” Under 1254: “The autumn grain crop and tree-fruits turned out badly; wine failed altogether.” Under 1266: “Grain, tree-fruits, and wine turned out badly in Bohemia because of damage caused by hail and drought.” Under 1270: “Almost all grain, both winter and spring, perished throughout nearly the whole of Bohemia; [Col. 0032D] the fruits of trees turned out moderately.” Under 1251: “Heavy snow fell in most parts of Bohemia, such as our age does not remember.” Under 1252: “Snow fell in most places.” Under 1254: “Our age does not remember the extent of this failure of wine.” Under 1258: “In this year frost damaged tree-fruits and vineyards.” Under 1260: “In this year too the crops, vineyards, and tree-fruits were damaged—some by drought, some by hail—in most regions.” Under 1262: “Crops of diverse kinds, both winter and summer, almost entirely perished in most parts of Bohemia, both from hail and from drought.” Under 1251: “A great force of winds arose … under whose violent blast many buildings fell.” Under 1256: “A great force of winds.” Under 1264: “A great force of winds arose; at their onset many buildings and many granaries collapsed.” Under 1250: “Very many buildings and granaries were destroyed by a whirlwind.” Under 1257: “There occurred a very great inundation of waters, which brought grave and extensive damage throughout the whole diocese of Prague.” Under 1264: “There occurred [Col. 0033D] a great inundation of waters throughout all Bohemia, by whose unusual flooding very much damage was done to buildings.” Many other examples could be added, for instance under 1250, 1252, 1259, and 1260.].
