In the examples set forth in the note [Col. 0032C], I think no one will fail to discern the most evident traces of one and the same manner of writing, by which it seems possible to prove with reasonable certainty that the same author continues down to 1278. Nor do you find him consistent only in describing weather and crops: he also devoted more attention than befits a historian to other matters of less importance in the writing of history. [Col. 0033A] For he writes copiously about the consecration of clerics, churches, and altars [Note: [Col. 0033D] Years 1251, 1258, 1259, 1274.], churches built in his own time [Note: [Col. 0033D] 1252, 1253, 1257, 1269, 1276, 1278.], and translations of relics [Note: [Col. 0033D] 1251, 1253.]. He did not, indeed, turn his attention away from public affairs, but he dwells principally upon the journeys of papal legates into Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0033D] 1252–1254, 1256, 1267.]; he touched the rest only lightly.

For he nowhere set himself the task—one that we shall see undertaken in certain other parts of the annals—of presenting before the eyes the particular deeds and characters of individuals. His style is rather crude, confused, and lowly. He takes no care to connect individual matters somewhat more closely, but pours everything out, as it were, from a sack without order. If you ask down to what year this annalist guided us through such a great mass of events, I think I have found [Col. 0033B] his last traces in the enumeration of Prague buildings under 1278, from the words: “In the same year, winter,” etc. For in the very extensive narrative that follows, those regular notices concerning weather and crops finally fall almost wholly silent. Moreover, the descriptions of the weather in 1280 and the famine in 1282 do not agree at all with the former ones.

From all that I have proposed, I readily convince myself that it is clearer than daylight that the author was contemporary with the events. Who, I ask, after a considerable lapse of time would have cared to transmit such prodigies to posterity so accurately? The author was a canon of the Prague chapter, who himself testified in explicit words that he had appeared in public [Note: [Col. 0033D] Under 1260: “We received Otakar as he returned from that expedition.” Under 1261.]. Many other things are read that could have been written only by a contemporary Prague canon [Col. 0033C] [Note: [Col. 0033D] Under 1253: “What the bishops did with the king remains unknown.” Under 1256: “Conrad, archbishop [Col. 0033C] of Cologne, … came—as we believe—to negotiate,” etc. [Col. 0034D] Under 1261, concerning Queen Margaret’s repudiation, he says: “God knows for what reasons.” He knows well what penalties Bartholomew the canon paid in 1251, and how much money the Prague chapter gave to Bernard, the papal legate, in 1254 and 1256. He accurately recorded the chapels and altars built or demolished each year in the Prague Church, and likewise when loss was inflicted upon the chapter’s estates in 1265.].

Accordingly, he recorded most accurately and truthfully those matters that concern the city of Prague; and therefore we seem justified in calling his book the first part of the Prague annals. No one should wonder that he sometimes erred in establishing chronology; nor is it everywhere clear whether the errors should be assigned to him or to the copyist [Note: [Col. 0034D] The copyist or compiler seems to have erred in the years 1240, 1249, and 1272. Other erroneous year-numbers occur in 1239, 1245, and 1274, all one less than the proper number—a mistake that occurred frequently.].

Within the limits just established, however, there are quite a few other passages whose character is so foreign to this one that surely no one would wish to attribute both them and those weather annals to a single author. First we have the extensive history of King Wenceslas I, which in the years 1248 and 1249 demonstrates a contemporary author, one who knew the events well and knew how to write of them well. [Col. 0033D] A brilliant narrative of events follows the dry and extremely brief annals; and what is read from the words “Therefore [Col. 0034A] King Wenceslas—dragged away in chains” can be connected in no way either with what precedes or with what follows.

The annals had been carried down to 1249, and now we are thrown back as far as Wenceslas’s first year, that is, 1228. The subsequent times are designated not by years from Christ’s birth but by the fifteenth, sixteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first years of Wenceslas’s reign—a method of reckoning which you seek in vain elsewhere in the entire book. Moreover, certain matters already mentioned under 1226 and 1231 recur in this narrative. This is therefore a distinct history of Wenceslas I, written by some unknown contemporary author, which can readily be separated from the remaining parts of the continuation. That its author was likewise attached to the Prague chapter seems proved by what is read concerning the privilege granted by the king to the canons. [Col. 0034B] The double use of the word “then,” employed by the author, prevents us from conjecturing that this was written in the very year 1249; but it was undoubtedly committed to writing before the king’s death in September 1253.

Several other parts of the annals raise greater doubts. Under 1260, for example, there is a lucid and very exact description of the victory won by Otakar II over the Hungarians. Here, as if in vivid colours, are depicted matters that the first Prague canon had noted a little above in certain meagre words. This author, whose little book we have tried to separate from the aggregate of the remaining annals under the title *Otakarian Annals*, seems especially to have aimed at celebrating “such a great and mighty victory as worthily to be ascribed to God alone and to His saints with fitting [Col. 0034C] acts of thanksgiving and praise,” and Otakar the king through whom the victory was won.

He also pursued a loftier manner of writing. Preserving the reverence due to royal dignity, he almost everywhere calls Otakar “lord of the kingdom of Bohemia,” and carefully observes this courtly, so to speak, style in mentioning others as well. The dukes of Carinthia and Silesia are “illustrious” to him; the counts are “men distinguished in rank”; others are “renowned warriors.” Nor did he less frequently embellish his narrative with rhetorical ornaments, whether his own or drawn from elsewhere; and he so often indulged his temperament that he interrupts the course of his speech with exclamations and interjections. All this is wholly remote from the character [Col. 0034D] we found in the first author.

Nearly the same style, I think, is found under 1264, [Col. 0035A] where the peace made between the kings of Bohemia and Hungary is related no less gloriously, and such praises of King Otakar occur as: “Who could fail to marvel at so magnificent a king, who was called from his mother’s womb a golden king?” I would not without reason venture to assign to the same author those parts of the continuation in which he far exceeds the limits of a barren and narrow historical compendium: the account, under 1254 and 1255, of Otakar’s expedition against the Prussians—something sufficiently confirmed also by the double mention of this war—the lavishly bestowed praises of Dean Vít in 1271, the narrative under 1272 of the German imperial crown offered to Otakar [Note: [Col. 0035C] Again he is exalted with the highest praises: he is “the most serene king”; the electors ask that he might deign to assume the insignia of imperial dignity; he rewards the envoys with magnificent gifts of gold, silver, etc.], the account under 1278 of the character of John, bishop of Prague, and, in the same place, the panegyric and, so to speak, dirge for Otakar, [Col. 0035B] in which his dreadful death after a magnificent life is bitterly lamented [Note: [Col. 0035C] “In the same year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, there was a measure …” [Col. 0035D] That these were written by one and the same author can be proved from the author’s own words. Of Dean Vít in 1271 he writes: “But lest, by pursuing in fuller detail the deeds of each virtue divinely bestowed upon him, I seem to incur the reproach of flattery, I prefer, laying aside my pen, to leave [them] to posterity,” etc. Of Otakar in 1278: “Putting aside my pen, lest by pursuing the truth I seem to incur the reproach of flattery, I leave his deeds … to posterity.” Under 1276: “What was done there … I preferred to pass over, lest, by recounting each matter as it occurred, I perhaps incur someone’s hatred.” In 1271, of Vít: “For he enlightened the minds of men as a shining lamp”; in 1278, of Bishop John: “A shining lamp … enlightened the hearts of men.” Under 1271 he speaks of Vít’s imitation of truth and justice; in 1278 John is “a follower of justice, an imitator of truth.” Vít also distributed denarii to the poor; in 1278 Otakar is said to be “giving each man a solidus denarius.” Of Vít in 1271: “Every Church will recount his alms”; under 1278: “The human mind cannot even recount how generous he was.”].

Yet I think I have found no small similarity of style and almost the same authorial temperament also in those parts where, in certain respects, we hear him criticizing Otakar under 1276 and 1278 [Note: [Col. 0036C] Under 1272: “He is said to have used such words”; under 1276: “He is reported to have given such an answer”; under 1278: “His fates continually lead him unwilling, drag him willing”; under 1260: “The fates lead the unwilling, drag the willing.” Under 1278: “Terror and dread fell upon the army”; under 1260: “Fear and trembling fell upon the impious.”]. Here he depicts even King Rudolf for us as “a prudent and discerning man,” and is far from pursuing his country’s enemy with hatred; rather, he sets a wise and self-consistent man in contrast to Otakar, a most daring and splendid man.

This author too was a Prague canon [Note: [Col. 0036D] Under 1260: “Jarosius … reported orally before the bishop, provost, dean, and canons of Prague in the Prague chapter.”]. For only one who had, for a long time, seen the eminent man discharge the office of dean as his colleague could have described Dean Vít’s character and life so accurately. In other matters too, [Col. 0035C] he had access to clearer sources. Concerning the Hungarian defeat in 1260, he had before his eyes Otakar’s letter sent to the pope; and he either himself sought testimony from the captive Hungarians or received it from others [Note: [Col. 0036D] Under 1260: “These same unbelievers and the rest … as they themselves later reported.”].

Indeed, he has King Otakar himself as a witness [Note: [Col. 0036D] “For as the oft-mentioned prince of Bohemia and the other princes, barons, and knights jointly reported.” I would not infer from the words “between us and the river called Morava” that the author himself was present at the battle; it is undoubtedly a more vivid form of expression.], and he heard John the knight, “a man in every respect worthy of belief,” and many others concerning the miracles performed on the same day. He saw Otakar often, as he testifies in his words about him under 1278: “These things we have seen and bear witness to.” [Col. 0036A] The king’s most terrible defeat and his country’s irremediable miseries moved his inmost heart with the greatest force.

In narrating events he is modest and cautious, taking good care not recklessly to overstep the bounds of truth. He indicates this in such expressions as: “unless I am mistaken; whether by design or by error, I do not know” [Note: [Col. 0036D] Under 1260.]; “it remains difficult to recount” [Note: [Col. 0036D] Under 1277.]; and, concerning Otakar’s death, he says that he can say “nothing certain,” “because different people say different things” [Note: [Col. 0036D] Under 1278.]. Although, as is most worthy of a historian, he carefully avoids incurring the reproach of hatred or flattery [Note: [Col. 0036D] Years 1271, 1276, 1278.], nevertheless in one or two places he allowed himself to be carried away by devotion to Otakar: he says that the German imperial crown was offered to the king “repeatedly,” and he dared to assert that, apart from his final defeat, Otakar had never been conquered by enemies [Col. 0036B] [Note: [Col. 0036D] Years 1272, 1278.]. He sometimes erred in chronology; nor can everything he says about the peace concluded between the kings in 1276 be measured by the standard of truth.

A third author, I think, wrote the years 1278–1281. It is true that expressions are found here and there which occur in earlier parts as well; nevertheless, the manner of writing is different and the author’s intended aim is different. The first author tried to include in his annals everything that came to his knowledge; the second directed his attention to public affairs and especially Otakar’s fortune; the third, though his narrative has its merits, turned away from the public events that supplied the richest material, and seems principally to have rested content with transmitting as accurately as possible to posterity the election of Tobias, bishop of Prague.

[Col. 0036C] He also has a peculiar habit found nowhere among the others: he cannot mention the Prague canons without adorning them with some honorific title [Note: [Col. 0036D] In 1278 they are “men certainly honourable and prudent”; in 1279, “men prudent and of outstanding discernment,” and their [Col. 0037D] assembly is “honourable.” The archbishop of Mainz is “most reverend,” the bishop of Olomouc “honourable,” and Tobias is bishop “by the favour of divine clemency.”], and embellishes his style with such words as “humbly,” “devoutly,” “kindly,” and “graciously.” The author, himself a canon, recorded not only what the Prague canons did or thought, but even what they ate or drank. He set down the events with his pen at almost the same time as they occurred, as appears from words under 1279 [Note: [Col. 0037D] See also the prayers offered for Tobias, the new bishop, in 1279, undoubtedly written shortly after the election, and the narrative concerning Spakmann and his companions in 1281.], concerning Bruno, bishop of Olomouc: “for this was always his custom, and is,” although Bruno died shortly after 18 February 1281 [Note: [Col. 0037D] Richter, *List of the Bishops of Olomouc* (*Series episcoporum Olomucensium*), p. 67.]. We have called this continuation the second part of the Prague annals.

There remains, finally, one author, likewise a Prague canon, succeeding the one who had descended to 1281. He again goes back as far as 1279, in order, as it were, to supplement the latter’s annals with a narrative of the calamities and public miseries by which Bohemia was at that time almost overwhelmed. This is the third part of the Prague annals. He depicted for us in the most forceful and pungent words such an image of the most unhappy land that one could scarcely look upon it without genuine emotion of heart. [Col. 0037B] Nor should one wonder that the same author allowed himself to be carried away by a very great, almost deadly hatred of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0037D] Under 1279: “It is the custom of the Germans, with excessive zeal, [Col. 0038D] to rage against the Bohemians.” Under 1281: “As bats hide themselves at dawn when daylight breaks, so the Germans vanished away like smoke.”], of which in the earlier writers one finds only the slightest trace, or almost none at all.

The author seems to have been among the envoys of the Prague chapter sent to the bishop of Brandenburg to request that its possessions not be wholly plundered. “Whoever heard this,” he says, “his ears tingled.” He saw his country’s most grievous calamities with his own eyes. “And,” he says, “we heard and saw more and more various torments in these times than we read in books” [Note: [Col. 0038D] Under 1279, where these words also occur: “All these things in these times poured out upon the Bohemians,” etc.—“May He now turn our mourning into joy, that while living we may praise Him at all times.”].

Thus his manner of writing is extremely vehement and violent, and burns, as it were, with that hatred of his country’s enemies. In this too the author struck out upon his own path: he tried to explain his opinions more fully [Col. 0037C] and adorn them with a certain learning. A witness is that long series of examples drawn from Holy Scripture and other testimonies taken, as one seeks in vain among the preceding writers, from the laws of the Roman emperors. His learning and literary cultivation are further demonstrated by ornaments from Horace, Ovid, and other Roman poets—though I freely confess that I have been unable to discover to whom he owes them—and by passages drawn from books of Gregory the Great and Ekkehard of Aura [Note: [Col. 0038D] Years 1279, 1282, 1283.].

Finally, there remain a few fragments of Bohemian history which seem in part to have been written by a Prague canon—perhaps by one of those whom we have considered above. These passages are: under 1258, “was consecrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September”; and under 1266, [Col. 0037D] “passing through again—carry off the rye.” In part, they seem to owe their origin to some monk of Strahov: under 1256, “Lord Conrad—Mount Sion”; and under 1258, “the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November—completed.” The man who gave the annals their final revision [Col. 0038A] abridged these notices in some unknown manner and inserted them in suitable places.

The annals finally end by repeating the opening chapters of Cosmas, followed by a catalogue of the princes of Bohemia from Přemysl down to King Wenceslaus II. I can scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—persuade myself that these additions were made by the author whom we placed fourth, since they are connected with what precedes by loose, or almost no, ties, and their very wording seems to reveal the hand of a compiler. That the author of this, so to speak, epilogue had before him the complete continuation as we possess it is apparent from his statement that he intends to present a catalogue of princes, “with this reservation, however, that whenever in these writings the reader encounters a knot of uncertainty, he should, in order to dispel error, refer back [Col. 0038B] to what is written above; for there he will find it more fully recorded.” The catalogue of princes itself further confirms this, since it embraces the whole history of Bohemia described by Cosmas and his continuators. Finally, in its concluding words the compiler attempted to arrange somewhat more clearly the entire mass of the annals.

For, of the three divisions of history which he made, the first, carried down to the death of King Vratislaus I in 1092, comprises the first two books of Cosmas; the second, down to King Vladislaus II in 1140, comprises Cosmas’s third book and the first continuation; while the third, extending to King Wenceslaus II in 1283, corresponds most exactly to the very extensive second continuation. Why such an ending was imposed upon the book is indicated by these words: “Because the minds of many people are disturbed by anxiety concerning the investigation [Col. 0038C] of the sequence and descent of the progeny of the dukes and kings of the kingdom of Bohemia, in what manner,” etc. Yet surely people’s minds were troubled for a weightier reason: that Wenceslaus, still a boy, was the last member of the most ancient stock of the Přemyslids; and his son Wenceslaus III, born in 1289 [Note: [Col. 0038D] See the genealogical table in Palacký, II, 2.], doubtless relieved men’s anxieties a little concerning that most illustrious royal house, soon to perish. Thus, if I see rightly, both the catalogue and the whole body of annals which we possess were compiled between the years 1283 and 1289.

Add, finally, that the portions of the earlier annals were shamefully scattered and a kind of new ordering of events established, so that materials corresponding to one another from the individual annals were at last written out in what seems a continuous stroke of the pen. Whoever reflects upon this will not doubt that all these things could have been so wretchedly fused together only by a compiler [Col. 0038D]. Without doubt this is likewise the compiler best suited to have filled the great gap which we find in the years 1142–1196 with scraps gathered from Vincentius, Gerlach, and the Prague annals [Col. 0039A]. This was done for no other purpose than to connect the first continuation with the second by some bond of association; and this certainly succeeded very badly. The same author, finally, is suggested by those words inserted after the year 1260 without any connection to the rest of the text, as though they were a gloss, concerning the adversities that were to break in after that year; anyone can see that these words were interpolated only at a later time. What he confused into a single heap of events, we have endeavoured to arrange and disentangle, restoring to each author what is due to him.

Nor, to dispatch this point also briefly, were writers of later times lacking who resorted to these continuations of Cosmas as an exceptionally abundant source for Bohemian history and drew from them draughts [Col. 0039B] of the fullest kind. I had formerly readily persuaded myself that perhaps from these writers the annals might be restored in the complete form in which they had been composed by their authors; but it is now sufficiently clear that this hope cannot be brought to fulfilment. For all the historical writers known to me both read and adapted to their own purposes the compilation of annals which we possess. These are Francis, canon of Prague [Note: [Col. 0039D] At the years 1265 and 1278; see Pelzel and Dobrowsky, II.], who copied only the second continuation; Neplach, abbot of Opatovice, who followed the lead of all the continuators [Note: [Col. 0039D] The Vyšehrad canon at the years 1129, 1130; the Sázava monk at 1139, 1140, 1161, 1162; the Prague canons at the years 1199–1271. To these it is useful to add the words by which he described his source at the year 1265: “And down to this year the things that happened are written in the chronicle; but the matters that follow I collected from certain quires.”” Compare with them Meinert, monk of Opatovice, *Weiner Jahrbücher*, XLVIII, *Anzeigeblatt*.]; Marignola, who had the Vyšehrad continuation and the Prague continuations before his eyes [Note: [Col. 0039D] At the years 1126, 1127, 1130, 1138, 1142, and at 1141, 1283.]; and no less Pulkava, both before and after the year 1250 [Note: [Col. 0039D] See, for example, in Pulkava the years 1201, 1204, 1214, 1216, 1224.]. In the earlier portion, however, certain other materials are also found in him which appear so closely connected with those [Col. 0039C] drawn from the continuation of Cosmas that one might conjecture that the genuine form of the annals is to be discovered there—if anything certain could be determined concerning Pulkava himself before the chronicle circulated under his name has been more carefully tested by the standards of criticism.

Let us now see what manuscripts there are upon which we can build this edition of Cosmas as upon a new and firm foundation. We have indeed had a far richer harvest of manuscripts than had come into the hands of earlier editors. Freher and Menken had two manuscripts; Pelzel and Dobrowsky six; Palacký listed eight; we know thirteen, of which we ourselves collated three—the oldest, those of Leipzig, Bautzen, and Dresden [Col. 0040A]; four others were either collated or inspected on behalf of our edition by others; and, finally, Pelzel’s and Dobrowsky’s edition supplied variant readings of the rest, or at least Palacký gave notice of them. With these resources, even if a wholly new text of Cosmas could not be established, it nevertheless comes much closer to the authentic form of the chronicle in which its author himself gave the book to the public.

We did not obtain the autograph, certainly, but we acquired two exceedingly weighty manuscripts which, by a singular accident, seemed to have entirely escaped the notice of learned men. We cannot therefore set before the reader how Cosmas’s book gradually, as it were, grew; but with the aid of the manuscripts we have advanced far enough to say that two recensions of the chronicle were made. The two editions do not differ greatly in the facts themselves [Col. 0040B]; yet, if one considers the manner of writing, one can scarcely deny that the second is somewhat more polished. For not infrequently, without doubt, the author himself substituted for an earlier expression another which seemed to correspond better to the sense.

We have established two classes of manuscripts. One, A, presents the earlier recension of the text; the other, B, the later.

The class A consists of only one manuscript, and that a very ancient one: the Leipzig manuscript, written on parchment in octavo at the end of the twelfth century [Note: [Col. 0039D] *Archiv*, VIII, 282.]. It was graciously sent to us for collation by the distinguished Gersdorf, librarian of Leipzig. Palaeographical evidence persuades us that the codex, entitled *Book of Blessed Mary the Virgin at Huysburg*, was written not very long after Cosmas’s death; and the catalogue of Roman pontiffs added at [Col. 0040C] folio 136 extends to Adrian IV, that is, to 1154. The author’s own death is entered under the year 1125, as in the other manuscripts. The manuscript is carefully written in a full, rounded hand; its ruling is in brownish ink; and not infrequently a contemporary hand corrected mistakes or supplied in the margin words which had escaped the copyist.

That this manuscript served as the exemplar of none of the others is shown by certain lacunae [Note: [Col. 0039D] Not infrequently one or two words are missing, [Col. 0040D] and no less often six or seven; for example, I, 6, the words: “They were now approaching the village to which they were going.” In the same place, the verse: “And they display garments and spread them beneath the horse.” I, 13, the words: “And, as if forewarned by a divine oracle, I protected you and your descendants from the coming calamity”; I, 29, the words: “And he traces his origin from the lords of this land.”], which are not found in the others, and by variant readings occurring in the Leipzig manuscript alone [Note: [Col. 0040D] I, preface: A has *inbuto* (“imbued”), the others *delibuto* (“anointed”); I, 2: A, *dolores* (“pains”), the others *labores* (“labours”); I, 4: A, *rehabere* (“to regain”), the others *recuperare* (“to recover”); ibid.: A, *thoris* (“beds”), the others *stratis* (“couches”); I, 7: A, *deditos* (“given over”), the others *commissos* (“entrusted”); I, 18: A, *reperire* (“to find”), the others *percipere* (“to perceive”); I, 26: A, *pastoralem curam* (“pastoral care”), the others *virgam* (“staff”); I, 33: A, *misericordiam* (“mercy”), the others *gratiam* (“grace”); I, 38: A, *pectora* (“breasts/hearts”), the others *corpora* (“bodies”); ibid.: A, *est* (“is”), the others *constituetur* (“will be established”); II, 15: A, *negotia* (“affairs”), the others *judicia* (“judgements”); III, 51: A, *mansit* (“remained”), the others *conversatus est* (“dwelt/lived”).]. Nor is the following the least argument: in this same manuscript the arrangement of words differs so often and so greatly from all the others that one recognizes in this manuscript alone a distinct recension of the text [Col. 0041A]. We have given a specimen of the manuscript and a rather crude drawing of Cosmas on its final folio.

Only the authority which we have marked A* agrees with this manuscript: namely, the Saxon annalist, who, shortly after 1137, copied Cosmas almost word for word, though not accurately enough to be used in restoring the text. Yet most certain traces are found that he had before him the text of recension A [Note: [Col. 0041C] For example, in the Saxon annalist is found the reading occurring only in manuscript A: I, 26, *curam* (“care”); I, 29, in both are absent the words *et hujus—ducis* (“and of this—duke”); ibid., they read *recedunt* (“they withdraw”), the others *redeunt* (“they return”); ibid., they lack *maximo* (“greatest”); II, 16, they have *negotia* (“affairs”); II, 49, they agree in the reading *in post suo tempore* (“afterwards in his time”); III, 26, they have *coadunato iterum* (“having again assembled”); III, 51, *mansit* (“remained”).]. We have therefore recorded the Saxon annalist’s reading only in a few places, so that it may be plain how the two witnesses are connected.

With the siglum B we designate all the remaining manuscripts, which agree among themselves in departing from manuscript A. Foremost among them is:

[Col. 0041B] **1) The Bautzen manuscript**, Gersdorf Library, MS 7, parchment, thirteenth century, taller than it is broad, written on seventy-three folios, the last of which are severely damaged by decay. Most regrettably, the manuscript is not complete: the first folio, on which the dedicatory letter was written, has been cut out; after the seventh, one and a half folios of another are missing. Everything is absent that is found from II, 46, from the words “therefore now certain of mercy,” etc., to the words “whose anger he had kindled,” etc., III, 15. A seventeenth-century hand has noted: “Much is lacking here.” Again, two leaves are missing in the eighth quire; two others, grimy on the outer side, show traces of a bookbinder’s hand. They seem already to have adhered to the covering of another book, and the remaining leaves of the same quire [Col. 0041C] have been shamefully dispersed. All this seems to prove our opinion that the codex, already torn apart in the seventeenth century, was subsequently gathered together, perhaps haphazardly, in order that the damage might be repaired.

It is written in not very large but fairly handsome minuscule letters; the ink is brownish; scribal abbreviations are not very frequent. The letter *i* is always without an overstroke, while *í* is written. Final *e* occurs very frequently in words: *luce, apprime, curte*; similarly, *e* stands in place of *ae*: *cesus, penitencia*; and *c* and *cc* stand for *t* and *ct*: *porcio, eleccio*. The accent *â* is not lacking. Here and there the chapters are marked, though not numbered, by the word *item*, likewise written in red; no consistent rule in the division of chapters can be sought. On the first folio appears a certain illustration, undoubtedly painted at the same time as the codex, in which Lech and Čech seem to be depicted quite neatly.

The scribe often erred [Note: [Col. 0041D] For example, I, 10, he wrote *convincie* for *conditione*; I, 12, *mirabiles* for *miserabiles*; I, 21, *sociuntur* for *sortiuntur*; I, 34, *concilio* for *condicto*; I, 39, *correcta* for *correpta*; ibid., *morte* for *more*; I, 42, *concius* for *tercius*; II, preface, *optari* for *optasti*; besides other instances.]. His carelessness is further proved by the fact that glosses which he found here and there in his exemplar he incorporated into the text in such a way that he wrote the earlier reading and the gloss in one continuous stroke of the pen. There also occur Bohemian glosses written above the text in a slightly later hand; we have supplied them in their proper places. Yet these very glosses persuade us that this manuscript is of superior quality.

For we do not hesitate to embrace the opinion that, after recension A had been completed, the glosses not found there were added by the author himself [Col. 0042B]. They are such in character that no one can doubt that they were appended by the author himself as he polished his book again and again; for they do not serve interpretation at all, but show the author hesitating whether he should write one way or another in a better style. These glosses passed into nearly all the other manuscripts; they are not found in the single manuscript A [Note: [Col. 0041D] I, 11: A alone reads *magnus terror ingruerit* (“a great terror shall break in”); B1 has *magnus post te vel fragor vel terror ingruerit* (“after you a great crash or terror shall break in”), with which the others either agree or present only *fragor* (“crash”). I, 12: A has *vincendi conditio* (“the condition of conquering”); B1 and the others add *vel ratio* (“or method”). In the same place, A reads *mansoleum in saecula nominativum* (“a mausoleum famous for ages”); B1, with some others, gives *vel memoriale* (“or memorial”). I, 13: A, *sub glacie nitida* (“beneath shining ice”); 1, *sub glacie nova vel nitida* (“beneath new or shining ice”); ibid., A, *tradidit eam* (“he handed it over”); 1, *vel civitatem eam* (“or the city itself”); ibid., A, *in domini sui vitam* (“against the life of his lord”); 1 adds *vitam vel necesse* (“life or necessity”), in place of which meaningless reading all the remaining manuscripts have *vel necem* (“or death”). I, 30: A, *rapidis lupis* (“swift wolves”); 1, *rabidis vel cruentis lupis* (“raging or bloody wolves”), and all the others repeat *cruentis* (“bloody”). I, 37: A, *ad venationem saepe faciens* (“often engaging in hunting”); 1, wrongly, *venatum ire vellet ad venationem saepe faciens* (“he wished to go hunting, often engaging in hunting”); ibid., A, *urgentes* (“pressing on”); 1, *urgentes impingentes* (“pressing and striking”). I, 37: A, *in coelestem patriam vel habitationem* (“into the heavenly fatherland or dwelling-place”); 1 omits *patriam vel* (“fatherland or”). I, 40: A, *cupidinis* (“of desire”); 1, *Veneris* (“of Venus”), but a contemporary hand writes above it *telo laesa cupidinis* (“of desire wounded by an arrow”). I, 41: A, *ecclesiae injuriam* (“injury to the church”); 1, *damnum vel injuriam* (“damage or injury”). II, 3: A, *intrant* (“they enter”); 1, *adeunt intrant* (“they approach [and] enter”); ibid., A, *ecclesiae limina* (“the thresholds of the church”); 1, *limina adita* (“thresholds approached”). II, 39: A, *eventu prospero* (“with a prosperous outcome”); 1, *propicio vel prospero* (“favourable or prosperous”).].

What, then, could be clearer than that these two families of manuscripts must be established? Since, therefore, all this seemed to leave us unable to doubt that the scribe of B1 followed a manuscript in which the author’s second revisions had been preserved, we have made the text of B1 our principal foundation. The other manuscripts provide support, above all A, which we have followed, almost contemporary as it is with Cosmas, in the spelling of both Germanic and Bohemian names [Col. 0042C]; in the remaining manuscripts these are written according to the usage of later Bohemians. The origin of the remaining manuscripts is not to be sought in B1; for quite a few readings occur in B1 alone [Note: [Col. 0042D] For example, B1 has: I, preface, *placere cupio* (“I desire to please”), the others *glisco* (“I strive”); I, 14, 1, *pariter* (“equally”), the others *partim* (“partly”); I, 30, 1, *deprecor* (“I entreat”), the others *deprecamur* (“we entreat”); I, 37, 1, *fulgurea* (“lightning-like”), the others *sulfurea* (“sulphurous”); I, 42, 1, *decet* (“it is fitting”), the others *par est* (“it is proper”); I, 38, 1, *fundant* (“they pour forth”), the others *sudant* (“they sweat”); I, 37, *candelabra aurea* (“golden lamps”), the others *argentea* (“silver”); I, 42, 1, *ferentibus* (“bearing”), the others *referentibus* (“reporting”).]. But very close to manuscript 1 comes another, which we have marked with the number:

**2) The Prague metropolitan manuscript**, fourteenth century. Pelzel and Dobrowsky gave a most abundant description of it in their preface [Note: [Col. 0042D] P. XV.], which may here be repeated:

> “A parchment manuscript written between the years 1320 and 1313 [Col. 0043A] in rather large characters, preserved in the library of the chapter of the metropolitan church of Prague. On the second folio, which has the number I written in red on its lower margin, among other decorations of the initial letter in various colours and gold, two coats of arms may be seen: one of the Prague chapter; the other of the barons of Dražice, displaying a green branch. From this family came John III (d. 1278) and John IV (d. 1343), bishops of Prague. That the manuscript was copied for John IV, bishop of Prague—who was also responsible for Francis the canon’s writing of the second part of the Prague chronicle—is certain from the notice of the death of William Lepus in 1320, entered at the end of the second continuation.
>
> “There are, moreover, significant indications in the metropolitan manuscript that it was bound together from two volumes. For the writing in which Francis’s chronicle—called by its author the second part of the Prague chronicle—is written in this manuscript differs from that in which the first part, namely Cosmas with the Prague continuators, is copied. The parchment leaves are also ruled differently, so that every column of the first part contains thirty-eight lines, but that of the second forty-four. The quires, or gatherings of parchment, of which sixteen are counted in the first part, are again numbered from the beginning, or from number 1, in the second. Finally, these two volumes were gathered into one, which now consists of one hundred and ninety-nine folios marked in red. ——— Cosmas’s chronicle is read from folio 48 to folio 105. Then his continuators follow, in the same hand and ink, to folio 148. On both pages of this folio a hand later than the first, though still ancient, had written in other ink and different letters a series of Prague bishops down to Arnošt, the first archbishop. After this there appears the trace of a leaf cut out at a later time, which was the eighth leaf of the sixteenth gathering, or quire, as printers call it. The numbers written in red on the lower margin, by which the individual leaves are marked, therefore seem to have been added later; for, without counting the excised leaf, they proceed in continuous sequence to the end.
>
> “The folio marked no. 149 [Col. 0043D], which is the first leaf of the first quire of the second part, was left blank. From folio 150 to folio 185, Francis’s chronicle, or the second part of the Prague chronicle, is copied in different characters and ink. Folios 185 and 186 contain certain more recent seventeenth-century [Col. 0044A] memorial notes concerning the archbishops of Prague; the remainder to the end of the manuscript is blank.”

At the beginning of the codex are read the Passions of St Adalbert and St Wenceslaus. That this manuscript comes very close to 1 is apparent from quite a few places where it agrees with that manuscript alone, both in correct and in erroneous readings [Note: [Col. 0043D] I, 1: 1 and 2 wrongly read *historiaca* for *historica*; I, 5: both wrongly read *Herecynthiam* for *Berecynthiam*; ibid., both *thalitarium* for *thalarium*; I, 13: both wrongly *abscidens* (“cutting off”) for *abscondens* (“hiding”). Only in MSS 1 and 2 is the gloss *telo laesa cupidinis* (“desire wounded by an arrow”) read; II, 4: both have *partam* for *paratam*; II, 39: both *arripiunt* for *corripiunt*.].

Yet this manuscript bears another particular mark of its own. There are certain extremely brief notes of no importance whatever which Pelzel and Dobrowsky, having no better manuscripts, attributed to Cosmas. But now no one can doubt that, since they are not found in the two oldest manuscripts, they were inserted by some interpolator, apparently of the fourteenth century. We have therefore entered them among the variant readings. They occur at the years [Col. 0044B] 1008, 1011, 1014, 1015, 1026, 1032, 1041, 1053, 1061, 1081, and 1084, copied from annals of some unknown kind. In rejecting these little notes Palacký’s judgement [Note: [Col. 0043D] *Würdigung*, p. 16.] did not fail him at all. But we do not think that all the brief notices which interrupt, as we see, the most abundant stream of narrative ought to be cut out, if only because they are found in very ancient manuscripts, whose authority cannot be surpassed in such a matter. This could the less be done because, as we have already attempted to prove above, the author himself adopted the manner of annals in composing his book; therefore, where he had nothing else to relate, he inserted the briefest notices. By means of the aforementioned little notes we have obtained a most reliable indication that two other manuscripts are most closely connected with it.

[Col. 0044C] **2a) The Roudnice manuscript**, fifteenth century, on paper, in the Lobkowicz Library, was brought to light by Palacký in 1826. The text of the first continuator is also read in it. The same distinguished scholar gave a description and certain variant readings in his book [Note: [Col. 0043D] *Würdigung*, pp. 13–15.], which we have incorporated in their proper places into our text. Palacký had already observed that this manuscript repeats nearly everywhere the text of manuscript 2. Yet although all the little notes mentioned above are repeated, and the same readings occur in both manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0044D] II, preface: both read *arvis* (“fields”) for *armis* (“arms”); II, 5: both wrongly *Foromatas* for *Soromatas*; II, 10: these alone read *fluvium quae est circa Belinam* (“the river which is around Bělina”) for *quae est circa fluvium Belinam* (“which is around the river Bělina”); III, 42: these alone have the corrupt *sco* for *nomine* (“name”); III, 60: both *incertum* (“uncertain”) for *inceptum* (“undertaken”).], it is nevertheless proved that it did not derive from 2 by the words *respondit—praesulem* (“he answered—the bishop”), which occur under the year 1140 in this manuscript alone and not in manuscript 2.

**2b) The Břevnov manuscript**, preserved in the library of the monastery of Břevnov, was described as follows by [Col. 0044D] Pelzel and Dobrowsky [Note: [Col. 0044D] P. XXIII.]:

> “It is written on paper, in folio, in the sixteenth century. Although this manuscript is later, it is nevertheless to be held in the highest esteem because it contains a great many good readings. Nor do we doubt that it was copied from a most ancient manuscript of the best quality, since we have certainly recognized this from the old spelling of names and other [Col. 0045A] indications. It was also collated with a certain older manuscript by some careful person who formerly used this codex. Besides the complete three books of Cosmas’s chronicle, this codex also contains Cosmas’s first Prague continuator, from the beginning to the words: ‘But on the following day the Moravians with the fugitive Bohemians’; and on the lower margin the words: ‘upon Vladislaus and his brother,’ which display the beginning of the next folio, missing together with all the rest. This continuation of Cosmas was copied by another hand, namely that which had added variant readings in Cosmas’s books. It bears the prefixed title: ‘Supplementary Matters to Cosmas, composed, as appears, by a certain monk.’”

The extremely brief notes of manuscript 2 recur at the years [Col. 0045B] 1015, 1026, 1032, 1041, 1052, 1082, and 1084. Thus it does not agree completely with 2 in these matters; other readings of the manuscript also prove that it was not copied from 2 [Note: [Col. 0045D] I, 1: 2b reads *terrae* (“of the earth”), 2 and the others *orbis* (“of the world”); I, 3: *paupertatis amabilitatem* (“the loveliness of poverty”), 2 and the others *paupertatem emabilem* (“lovable poverty”); I, 5: *cibis* (“foods”) for *herbis* (“plants”); I, 6: *praescius* (“foreknowing”) for *inscius* (“unaware”); II, 4: *paratam* (“prepared”), 2 *partam* (“obtained”); II, 8 adds *Franciae* (“of France”), absent from the others; II, 40, *et resiliens* (“and springing back”), lacking in 2.].

**3) The Stockholm manuscript**, parchment, thirteenth century, a gigantic codex—one cubit and a half in height—most splendidly written. It was described by Dobrowsky [Note: [Col. 0045D] *Litterarische Nachrichten von einer Reise nach Schweden und Russland im J. 1792*, p. 35; Palacký, *Würdigung*, p. 7.], who also provided several variant readings. It is the basis of Freher’s edition of 1607; and it may be permitted to repeat here his words from the dedicatory epistle to Peter Wok of Rosenberg:

> “I rejoice that I have also brought back this fruit of the Bohemian and Polish journey undertaken five years ago at my prince’s command: while staying in the royal city of Prague, good fortune placed in my hands that memorable monument of native antiquity [Col. 0045C], and placed it there complete—of which previously I had included a portion among my Bohemian writings to general praise—would that it had been equally free from errors and blemishes! Although I had to rely on a single copy, and one transcribed from old parchment manuscripts by no very fortunate hand, I nevertheless took pains through careful rereading that, after the stains had been removed as far as was possible at that time, it might offend the eyes of the fair-minded reader as little as possible. I shall also do more hereafter if any person devoted to the public good, as I hope, will assist me with other copies.”

The manuscript was afterwards carried off by the Swedes and is today kept at Stockholm. Since we were unable to inspect the manuscript itself, we retained among the variant readings, under siglum 3, the readings given by Freher; not, however, in every place, because very often [Col. 0045D] an erroneous reading originated from mistakes of the copyist or printer. It is not easy to pronounce a judgement upon the genuine readings of this manuscript; this is not very regrettable, since it is sufficiently certain that it is not older than the manuscripts employed by us, A and 1 [Col. 0046A]. The foundation charter of Vyšehrad is not read in this manuscript, as Dobrowsky testifies. The story of the five martyr brothers in Poland is also absent [Note: [Col. 0046D] I, 38.], as is that licentious story concerning the priest [Note: [Col. 0046D] III, 62.]. Yet the manuscript must be assigned to family B, as is shown by the glosses found in most places [Note: [Col. 0046D] I, 11, 12, 13.]. In quite a few places, however, it agrees with the next two manuscripts, which we have called 4 and 4a.

**3b) Vienna manuscript 7391**, paper, sixteenth century, is a copy of manuscript 3, made in 1574. It was inspected at Vienna by the distinguished Pertz; where the text appeared to require it, the distinguished Chmel, director of the Imperial Library, most generously communicated its readings to us.

**4) Dresden manuscript I, 43**, a folio parchment manuscript preserved in the Royal Library [Col. 0046B] at Dresden [Note: [Col. 0046D] *Archiv*, VI, 225.], was most generously sent to us for examination by the distinguished Falkenstein. Before Menken, who gave variant readings [Note: [Col. 0046D] *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, III.], and Dobrowsky, who believed it to have been written in the thirteenth century, it had already been seen by Lupacius, Georg Fabricius, and Albinus [Note: [Col. 0046D] Pelzel and Dobrowsky, preface, p. XXVIII; Albinus, *Neue Meissnische Chronik*, Wittenberg, 1580, p. 737.]. But this manuscript was written in the twelfth century.

The text is written most splendidly in two columns; the lines are ruled in ink; the minuscule letters are very beautifully written; the initials are painted in colours. Cosmas’s text occupies seven quires and six folios. Abbreviations are neither frequent nor unusual. The use of *e* for *ae* is very common; *e* is rarer; plain *i* without an overstroke occurs; a syllable divided at the end of a line is marked with a sign resembling 1. Cosmas’s text is bound together with Solinus’s book and that of Theophilus on colours, written in the same manner and almost in the same hand. Here a contemporary hand notes in uncial letters that the book belongs to the monastery of Altzella; from this one may conjecture that Cosmas’s chronicle was written in the same place. On the wooden cover of the book are read the words *Gesta* and certain other faded words which I think I have read as *Corb.* and the name *Cosmas Pragensis*, written in a fifteenth-century hand, at which time that wooden cover also seems to have been made.

But the manuscript is of the greatest importance because of the interpolations and the continuation by the anonymous monk who lived in the Benedictine monastery of Sázava in the time of Abbot Silvester, in the middle of the twelfth century. This continuation, down to the year 1162, is copied as though it were the fourth book of the Chronicle of the Bohemians, but in such a way that here it begins already [Col. 0046D] from Cosmas’s own words found at III, 59. The interpolations are neither few nor unimportant. The later ones, from the year 1038 onward, when the foundation of Sázava monastery is narrated at length, [Col. 0047A] concern the monastery itself. The interpolations are read at the years 958, 960, 962, 973, 975, 985, 986–990, 995, 998, 1038, 1045, 1053, 1070, 1088, 1089, 1095, 1097, 1116, 1122, 1123, and 1125. We have removed all of these from our text and shall give them in their proper place together with the continuation. The extremely brief notes of manuscript 2 are not found in these interpolations, sufficiently proving that it has no connection with them.

That it was copied from another interpolated manuscript is apparent even from this: whenever the word *dux*, *rex*, or *episcopus* occurs, the scribe inserted in the text the proper name which he undoubtedly found written above it in his exemplar. He omitted nothing except one verse at I, 6 and the two verses for the year 1117 in which Cosmas laments his wife; in their place he added two verses concerning Herman [Col. 0047B], bishop of Prague. The chapters of the text are divided by red letters but not numbered; we have retained these in our edition. They largely agree with the likewise unnumbered chapters given by Pelzel and Dobrowsky, whom we have followed where the manuscript fails us. Once the interpolations have been cut away, the text is fairly pure and corrected, and it sometimes supplies excellent readings [Note: [Col. 0047D] I, 30: it adds *possideam* (“may I possess”), where manuscript 1 alone reads *habeam* (“may I have”), while the word is lacking in all the others; with A and 1 it supplies the lacuna in II, 1, *moribus—placabiles* (“in manners—peaceable”); correctly, with A, it reads II, 16, *ire properat* (“he hastens to go”).]. For example, II, 5: manuscript 4, and 4a alone with it, has the words *attavus meus* (“my great-great-grandfather”), wrongly absent from all the remaining manuscripts, which restore the true sense of the words. This single example sufficiently shows that it was copied from none of the manuscripts we have reviewed. It seems especially closely connected with the Stockholm manuscript [Note: [Col. 0047D] I, 41: both read *furnas* for *furvas*; I, 42: *ventris* (“of the belly”), the others *noctis* (“of the night”), *corporis* (“of the body”), etc.; II, 39: only 3 and 4 read *prospero* (“prosperous”) without a gloss; II, 42: in both the word *damnum* (“loss, injury”) is absent; II, 47: they add *regis* (“of the king”).]. From this manuscript was copied:

**4a) Vienna manuscript 1544–508**, parchment, thirteenth century. Formerly kept at Prague in the Clementinum college of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, after the suppression of that institution it was presented by Peter Wokaun of Wokaun in 1780 to the Imperial Library at Vienna, as Pelzel and Dobrowsky report [Note: [Col. 0047D] P. XXIX.]. They supplied variant readings and described the manuscript as follows:

> “It is written on parchment in quarto, in clear characters, in the thirteenth century, so far as may be judged from various indications. We ourselves handled this exemplar while it was at Prague. It contains all those additions which, in the description of the Dresden manuscript, we said must be attributed to the monk of Sázava. It is regrettable that several folios are absent from this [Col. 0047D] most excellent manuscript. For all that is found from the year 923 to the year 994 is missing, as are the words: ‘… I flee honours, I despise the pomps of the world,’ etc. Its peculiar feature is that it superfluously repeats the proper names of dukes and other persons. For in most places where Cosmas employs a pronoun or the appellative title of the duke under discussion, it customarily adds the duke’s proper name.”

Most recently the distinguished Pertz inspected the manuscript at Vienna; besides Cosmas’s text, it contains the Life of St Elizabeth and certain letters. In almost all readings it agrees so thoroughly with manuscript 4 that I am now convinced of what Pelzel and Dobrowsky hesitated to say: that it derived from that manuscript. For, following a new collation of the Dresden manuscript, the examples by which they believed they could support the contrary [Col. 0048B] view must almost be rejected; those examples arose from Menken’s less accurate collation. We consider it superfluous to offer examples for our opinion, since they will occur of themselves to every reader.

**C)** To these complete manuscripts of Cosmas are added certain others, largely mutilated and therefore not available for consultation everywhere, but by no means to be rejected for that reason, since some are very ancient.

**5) The Brno manuscript**, paper, folio, fifteenth century, now preserved in the Franciscan museum. Meinert discovered it at Třebová in Moravia in 1819 [Note: [Col. 0047D] He described it and supplied variant readings in Hormayr, *Archiv für Geographie, Historie*, 1819, p. 65; Palacký repeated this in *Würdigung*, p. 11.]. It is more complete than the other manuscripts of this kind. The person who wrote this manuscript reduced Cosmas’s chronicle to an abridgement; he entirely cut out the charters inserted in the text, or gave fragments of them, and wholly suppressed other things which we have given in their proper place [Note: [Col. 0047D] For example, I, 3, the words *ad stabula—habuere* (“to the stables—they possessed”); [Col. 0048D] I, 5, *vosipsos—tollat* (“yourselves—may remove”); I, 38, the story of the five martyrs in Poland is omitted.]. Certain glosses have been written above the text in a later hand [Note: [Col. 0048D] I, 12, 13.].

**6) The Karlov manuscript**, paper, fifteenth century, must be included among these. It was collated by Bonaventure Piter, provost of the monastery of Rajhrad in Moravia, who, among the materials for a collection of writers on Bohemian affairs, had collated the five oldest manuscripts of Cosmas. A note proves that this manuscript was given in 1465 to the canons of the Augustinian monastery at Karlov [Note: [Col. 0048D] Dobner on Hájek, I, 176; Pelzel and Dobrowsky, preface, p. XXXII.]. But, buried in oblivion, the manuscript awaits its discoverer in the hiding-place of some unknown monastery or library. Nor need we greatly regret the loss of this manuscript, for it was mutilated. Palacký reports [Col. 0048D] [Note: [Col. 0048D] *Würdigung*, p. 15. The knight von Schwabenau testifies, in a dissertation on Conrad II, duke of Znojmo, in the *Monatschrift des Böhmischen Museums*, year I, October, p. 49, that he saw Piter’s apparatus and that variant readings of the Karlov manuscript had been entered there. That the manuscript was partly mutilated and partly interpolated is sufficiently evident from the remaining reports. Whether the Vyšehrad charter, which he testifies that he found there, occurred only in Piter’s apparatus or actually in the manuscript itself cannot be said.] that, besides certain other lacunae, everything [Col. 0049A] found after the year 1091 was missing; that is, the copyist omitted almost half of the book.

7) Codex Argentinensis, a parchment codex in folio, twelfth century. [Note: [Col. 0049D] *Archiv* I, 392; VIII, 464.] The distinguished Engelhard collated it with the first edition of Freher as early as 1825 for our use. [Note: [Col. 0049D] *Archiv* V, 700–701.]

[Col. 0050A] It consists of only fourteen leaves. It was carefully written in brownish ink; the ruled lines were likewise drawn in ink, while the headings were written in red. Abbreviations are not especially frequent. On the first leaf the following verses are read:

Henry the Twelfth, Duke of the Bavarian people,

Filled with noble descent from a fleeting life,  
[Note: [Col. 0049D] That is, with a lineage (*schema*), here equivalent to descent (*stemma*).]

That noble man, begotten by a famous duke as father,

Born noble on his mother’s side, from the blood of kings.  
[Note: [Col. 0049D] Henry the Proud, Duke of Bavaria, and Gertrude, daughter of the Emperor Lothair.]

After them he shines forth in outstanding nobility.

For this, his country rejoices, happy in his virtue.

This happy man was once blessed with a distinguished wife.

She was a king’s daughter, she whom bitter death removed.  
[Note: [Col. 0049D] Matilda, daughter of Henry II, king of England, died in 1189. [Col. 0050D]]

The duke has thereupon left the fatherland twice four heirs,

Clothed in the garb of outstanding virtue.  
[Note: [Col. 0050D] Meibom, *Rerum Germanicarum* III, 166.]

The inhabitant of Bavaria rejoices in the honor of his lords,

Whom he sees flourishing splendidly in marvellous beauty.

The father himself too rejoices, knowing that his offspring will be happy;

May the mother also rejoice, passing her life in peace.

As a rose, added to diverse flowers, appears more beautiful,

So the father, bound to excellent boys, shines brightly.

And that he might know the life of the ancients through the writings of their predecessors,

And through their customs might understand their wretched condition.

[Col. 0049B] The distinguished Engelhard seems rightly to have conjectured that these verses were written for Henry the Lion. If this is so, the codex was written shortly after 1189. Its exceedingly scanty harvest of variant readings proves that the first edition of Freher was not prepared so negligently. The copyist grievously mutilated Cosmas’s chronicle, preserving scarcely a tenth part of the whole work: Book I, prologue–15 and 21–23; Book II, 37 and 38; everything else is lacking. In addition there is the spurious bull of Pope Alexander II concerning the foundation of the church of Vyšehrad, which no one who reads it with even slight attention can regard as genuine; we have included it among the variant readings. [Note: [Col. 0050D] II, 26.] Where manuscript 7 can be compared with the other codices, its text is not wholly to be rejected; the glosses at I, 13 prove that it must be assigned to family B. Finally, it is the latest manuscript of this kind which we possess.

7a) The Munich paper codex, fifteenth century, whose description we owe to the distinguished Föhringer. This manuscript too is very mutilated and contains the false bull of Alexander II. Yet it preserves certain other fragments of the chronicle that are absent from the Strasbourg codex. The Munich manuscript contains Book I, prologue–19, except for the years 895–929; I, 21–26 and 29–31, down to the words “the seventh day before the Kalends of May.” Then follows the Vyšehrad bull; everything else is lacking. Thus, I think, no one will doubt the common origin of these codices. And, unless I am mistaken, the purpose of the person who inserted the false bull of Alexander II into Cosmas’s mutilated chronicle is sufficiently clear. In this single forged document the mutilated text is distorted; and some Vyšehrad forger seems to have inserted it not very long after Cosmas, intending thereby to claim Cosmas as a witness to the antiquity of the Vyšehrad church. He seemed to have sufficiently achieved his purpose if he miserably clothed and, as it were, adorned his offspring with certain scraps rashly torn from the chronicle.

The manuscripts which we have now reviewed, together with the considerable number that had come to the notice of Pelzel and Dobrowski but could not be found by them, prove that Cosmas’s chronicle was read with the utmost diligence by later generations. Emperor Charles IV ordered three copies to be made, as Neplach testifies under the year 1125 in these words: [Note: [Col. 0050D] Dobner, *Monumenta historica Bohemiae*, vol. IV. I do not know what sort of codex Simler had before him in his *Epitome bibliothecae Conradi Gesneri*, Zurich, 1555.]

> “At the same time Cosmas, dean of the Church of Prague, passed to the world above. He wrote chronicles concerning Bohemia, which Plych, dean of Prague, copied three times on parchment at the insistence of the most illustrious king of the Bohemians, Charles, when they had been rotted by moths and age.”

Pelzel and Dobrowski conjectured that these manuscripts had been given as gifts to foreign princes and therefore were not lying hidden in Bohemia. Furthermore, the catalogue of Bohuslaus of Hassenstein shows that a codex existed in his library, which, as we read, was consumed by fire in 1570.

There are five editions of Cosmas’s chronicle, the first two of which were published by Marquard Freher:

1) In *Scriptores rerum Bohemicarum*, Hanover, [Col. 0050D] 1602, pp. 1–14. As is now sufficiently clear, this was issued according to the Strasbourg codex; it should be called a copy of the manuscript rather than a true edition of the chronicle.

2) He published the second edition in 1607, at Hanover, from the Wechel press, pp. 1–172, from the codex now at Stockholm, then at Prague, as Dobrowski sufficiently proved. But he supplemented the earlier edition from the Stockholm codex rather than establishing a new text on the basis of its complete authority, for he retained the false bull of Alexander II from the Strasbourg codex. As we saw above, Freher himself remarked that the copyist had transcribed the codex with no very fortunate hand. Thus proper names are shamefully corrupted, and six hundred times, for example, *tamen* (“nevertheless”) is read where the codices have *enim* (“for”). Freher also indulged his own conjectures here and there, as he himself sufficiently clearly indicated in the preface to his edition.

3) The third edition is nothing but a repetition of the second, although the title page bears the year 1620.

4) In 1728 Menken repeated Freher’s text of the chronicle in the first volume of his collection of writers on Saxon affairs, pp. 1967–2132. Later, in the third volume, he supplied the variant readings and interpolations of the monk of Sázava from the Dresden codex. He further adorned his edition with the annotations of Christian Theophilus Schwarz, professor at Altdorf. From these annotations, diligently gathered from other chronicles, we have repeated a few and copied other matters that seemed useful for explaining events, since the annotations themselves exceeded both the character and the limits of our work.

[Col. 0051C] 5) The fifth edition, and the best—one which even today is by no means undeserving of its reputation—was published at Prague in 1783 by Pelzel and Dobrowski in the first volume of *Scriptores rerum Bohemicarum*, pp. 1–282. They built it upon a critical foundation and a sufficiently extensive apparatus of codices. It rests chiefly on the Prague codex, [Col. 0052A] to which the editors added the Břevnov codex and Freher’s texts; they also sought out with the utmost care everything that seemed to concern Cosmas. With what benefit we have incorporated into our edition the collection of variant readings which they supplied will be evident to anyone who inspects it even casually. From their edition we took the readings of those codices which, after Pertz had proved by his examination of the metropolitan codex that it was exceedingly accurate, seemed unlikely to yield any benefit if consulted again.

The first person, so far as I know, who made larger fragments of the continuation from the metropolitan codex public was Pessina of Czechorod. In composing his books he was permitted to bring this manuscript, together with others, to light from the archives of the Prague chapter. If one gathers in a single place the passages which he had printed in the *Phosphorus Septicornis* [Note: [Col. 0051C] For example, p. 536, year 1140; p. 182, year 1249; p. 536, year 1271; pp. 1281–1283.] and in the *Mars Moravicus* [Note: [Col. 0051C] P. 346, year 1249; p. 361, year 1254; p. 368, [Col. 0052C] years 1261–1265; p. 370, year 1271; p. 381, year 1278.], one already has a respectable portion of all the continuations; but these passages were not published very accurately. This happened much more markedly in the first complete edition that we possess, issued under the title *Continuation of the Bohemian Chronicle formerly composed by Cosmas, now brought forth from a Prague manuscript*, edited by Joachim Krakovský of Kolowrat, under the presidency of Baptist Piker. Vienna, 1752. Quarto. Pelzel and Dobrowski sufficiently demonstrated how negligently this edition had been prepared, compiling a catalogue of its foulest errors. [Note: [Col. 0052C] I, p. XXXIX.] We have followed the accurate edition of those men, adding the various readings which Palacký supplied from other codices. Even so, the question raised by the earlier editors must be repeated: it is not possible in every passage to elicit the author’s true meaning, nor to correct all the faults of the copyists; these perhaps will be healed by some other codex still concealed in the libraries.

I wrote at Berlin in May 1847.

RUDOLPHUS KOEPKE.

[Col. 0055]

[CHRONICLE OF THE BOHEMIANS.]

THE PROLOGUE TO SEVERUS, PROVOST OF MĚLNÍK, BEGINS.  
[Note: [Col. 0055D] Mělník.]  
[Note: [Col. 0055] Thus A and 1. “Of Mělník” is absent in 2, 4, and 4a. “To the provost of Mělník” in 2a. “Prologue of Cosmas, dean of Prague, to the chronicle of the Bohemians, addressed to Severus the provost” in 3. “The preface to the chronicle of the Bohemians begins” in 5. “The prologue to the chronicle of the Bohemians begins” in 7. “Prologue of the book of the Bohemians” in 7a.]

[Col. 0055A] To Lord Severus, provost of the church of Mělník—endowed alike with literary learning [Note: [Col. 0055] *Scientia*, “learning,” is omitted in 5 and 7.] and spiritual understanding—Cosmas, dean of the church of Prague in name alone, wishes the prize in the heavenly kingdom after the course of this life. How deeply, in devotion and affection of mind, I submit myself to your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0055] “Fatherhood” in A and 1; “brotherhood” in the others.] I cannot express, calling God to witness. For love is not great if human reason can comprehend it. True love can possess nothing of its own, nothing private or hidden, which it cannot disclose to the one whom it loves with sincere affection. Had this not been present in me [Note: [Col. 0055] *Affuissent*, “had been present,” in 4 and 4a.], I should never have presumed to offer these senile trifles of mine to a man of such [Col. 0056A] authority. For I sought and sought what pleasant, what idle thing I might offer you; but I found nothing so ridiculous as my little work. If we laugh pleasantly when we see someone stumble with his foot against a stone, how many stumblings of mine, how many synaloephas against the rules of grammar, will you see in this work! If you wish to laugh at each of them, you can exercise the characteristic faculty of man beyond measure. [Note: [Col. 0055] Here 2 and 2a add either “that you may be able to read” or “farewell”; 2b adds “or.”] Whether these senile trifles please or displease you alone [Note: [Col. 0055] “Or whether they please you alone” in 7.], I beg that no third eye may see them. [Note: [Col. 0055] “Eye” is absent in 4 and 4a; “farewell” is added in 4 and 4a.]

ALSO, A PREFACE TO MASTER GERVASIUS FOR THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS.  
[Note: [Col. 0055] “For the work that follows” is absent in 4.]

[Col. 0055B] To Gervasius, chief elder, fully steeped in every study of the liberal arts and imbued with the wisdom of every kind of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0055] “Entirely” in 4 and 4a; *inbuto*, “imbued,” in A.], Cosmas—who is said to be unworthy even to be called such, yet is servant of the servants of God and of Saint Wenceslas [Note: [Col. 0055] *Wencezlao* in 2b, 4, and 4a.]—sends the offering of due prayer and the pledge of mutual affection.

When you receive [Note: [Col. 0055] “Receive” in A.] this little sheet [Note: [Col. 0055] *Cedulam* in 2; *schedulam* in 2b.], know [Note: [Col. 0055] “Know” in 2b, 3, and 4a.] that I have sent you the chronicle of the Bohemians, which I have resolved to submit for examination to your singular prudence. I have polished it with no elegance of grammatical art, but have arranged it simply and scarcely in Latin, so that by your discerning judgment it may either be wholly rejected, lest anyone read it, or, if it is judged worthy of reading, may first be polished exactly by the file of your examination—or rather, which I ask more earnestly, may through you be elucidated anew in more Latinate language. [Note: [Col. 0055] *Latialius* in A; *enudetur*, “be laid bare,” in A.]

For I judged this alone to be the reward of my labor: that either you, to whom wisdom has been granted by God, or others more eminent in wisdom or learning, might use this work of mine as material, just as Virgil had the destruction of Troy [Note: [Col. 0055] *Eacidia* in A.] and Statius the Aeacid, so that they might make their learning known to posterity and magnify for themselves a memorial name through the ages.

Therefore I have taken the beginning of this narrative from the first inhabitants of the land of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0055] *Boemiorum* in A at this point.] and, prompted not by ambition for human praise but lest what has been related should altogether be consigned to oblivion, I set forth, to the best of my ability and knowledge, for the love of all good men, the very few things which I learned from the fabulous reports of old men. I always desire to please the good and the learned [Note: [Col. 0055] “For” is added in all manuscripts except A and 1; “I strive” in all except A and 1.]; but I do not fear to displease the ignorant and ill-bred.

For I know that some jealous critics will appear and die of derisive laughter when they see the form [Note: [Col. 0055] *Schema* in 2b; plural *scemata* in 4 and 4a.] of this undertaking. They are learned only in disparaging others, while of themselves they know how to produce nothing good. Of such men [Col. 0056C] the prophet sings: “They are wise to do evil, but to do good they do not know” (Jeremiah 4:22). These men inspect only those things with lynx-eyed gaze [Note: [Col. 0056D] Horace, *Satires* I.2.90.] and engrave upon their hearts, as though upon diamond, whatever has been said improperly or wherever my drowsing mind has stumbled. What wonder? “Sometimes even good Homer nods.” [Note: [Col. 0057B] Horace, *Epistle to the Pisones* 359.]

Therefore I am neither frightened by their envious disparagements nor flattered by their ironic praises. Let those who wish read; let those who do not wish reject it. But you, dearest brother [Note: [Col. 0057] “Dearest” in 2b.], if you love me as your friend, if you are moved by my prayers, gird the loins of your mind and take into your hand a razor [Note: [Col. 0057] *Rosarium*, “rosary,” in 7.], a file, and a pen, so that you may scrape away what is superfluous and add what is absent; change what is improperly said into proper expression [Note: [Col. 0057] “Change” in A.], so that my ignorance [Note: [Col. 0057] “Ignorance” in all except A and 1; “borne up” in 4 and 4a.] may be upheld by your wit.

For I am not ashamed to be corrected by a friend—I who earnestly request to be amended with the deepest affection even by friends [Note: [Col. 0057] “Friend” in 4 and 4a; “enemies” in Freher.] The first book contains, then, the deeds of the Bohemians, arranged as far as I have been able to know them, down to the time of the first Břetislav [Note: [Col. 0057] Thus A and 1; *Brzieezislavi* in 2; *Bracizlavi* in 2b and 7a; *Bracizlai* in 4 and 4a; *Bratizlavi* in 7.], son of Duke Oldřich [Note: [Col. 0057] *Odaldrici* in A; *Udaldrici* in 2b and 7; *Oalrici* in 3; *Odalrici*, with *u* written above the *O*, in 4 and 4a; *Udalrici* in 7a.].

[Col. 0058A] I began to arrange the years of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0057] After *incarnationis*, 2b has three asterisks.] from the time of Bořivoj [Note: [Col. 0057] *Borivoy* in 2b; *Boriwoi* in 4; *Boriwoy* in 4a; *Borivoii* in 7; *Borivoi* in 7a.], the first Catholic duke, because at the beginning of this book I neither wished to invent nor was able to find a chronicle from which I might know when, or in what times, the events which you will presently read in what follows were done. Farewell; and at your command I shall either gird myself to unfold the rest, or stop my step there and set a limit to my foolish undertaking.

Live and farewell; do not reject my desires, but fulfill them.

This chronicle was composed while Henry IV was reigning as Roman emperor [Note: [Col. 0057] “Emperor of the Romans” in 2b, 3, 4a, and 7.] and Pope Calixtus was governing God’s holy church [Note: [Col. 0057] “Pope Calixtus” is omitted in 4 and 4a; “the second” is added in 5.], in the time [Note: [Col. 0057] “Times” in 2b, 3, 4a, and 7.] of Vladislav, duke of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0057] *Wladislai* in 2.], and likewise of Herman, bishop of the church of Prague, as is made known in what follows to all who wish to know in what years of Christ or indictions these things were done.

THE FIRST LITTLE BOOK OF THE CHRONICLE OF THE BOHEMIANS, COMPOSED BY COSMAS, DEAN OF THE CHURCH OF PRAGUE, BEGINS.  
[Note: [Col. 0057] “The little book into the chronicle of the Bohemians” in 1. “The first book of the Chronicle of the Bohemians begins” in 3. “The first little book of Cosmas, dean of the church of Prague, into the Chronicle of the Bohemians begins” in 4. “The Chronicle of the Bohemians, composed by Cosmas, begins” in 7.]

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057B] 1. After the outpouring of the Flood, after the confusion of the men wickedly minded who built the tower, the human race—which then consisted of about seventy-two men—was divided by divine vengeance, for such unlawful and rash attempts [Note: [Col. 0057] *Ausibus*, “attempts,” in 4 and 4a.], into as many different kinds of languages as there were heads of men. As we have learned from historical report [Note: [Col. 0057] *Historica* in A; *hystoriaca* in 1; *historiaca* in 2 and 2b, with the *a* before *c* deleted.], each of them, wandering and an exile, dispersed far and wide, roamed through different expanses of lands; and, though diminishing in body from day to day, multiplied manifoldly into generations and generations.

Thus the human race, with God’s will ordering all things, was so spread throughout the world that after many ages it at last reached even these regions of Germany. For all that region [Note: [Col. 0057] *Illa* is omitted in 4 and 4a.] situated beneath the northern pole, from the Tanais [Note: [Col. 0057] *Thanaytenos* in 1; *Tanaytenus* in 2b.] as far as the west [Note: [Col. 0057] *Occiduam* in 1, 4, and 4a.], although its individual places are called by their own names, is nevertheless called Germany by a general designation [Note: [Col. 0057] *Vocatur*, “is called,” in A.]. [Note: [Col. 0057B] These are words of Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards* I.1, taken by the author from Regino’s *Chronicle* under the year 889.]

We have mentioned these things in order that we may better pursue the purpose of our undertaking. Yet first, before we come to the beginning of the narrative, we shall attempt briefly to explain the situation of this Bohemian land [Note: [Col. 0057] “Bohemian” rather than “Bohemia” in 7.] and the origin of its name.

2. In the division of the world [Note: [Col. 0057] “Of the earth” instead of “of the world” in 2b.], according to geometers, Asia under its own name occupies one half of the world, while Europe and Africa occupy the other half. [Note: [Col. 0057] *Africa* in 1.] Germany lies in Europe. In its northern parts there is a place spread out very broadly [Note: [Col. 0057] *Difusus*, “spread out,” in 1.], encircled on every side by mountains in a ring [Note: [Col. 0057] *Cinctusque*, “and encircled,” in 2b.], which extend in so marvellous a fashion around the whole land [Note: [Col. 0059] “Of the whole world,” deleted, then “of the land,” in 1.] that to the eye they appear as one continuous mountain surrounding and fortifying all that country. [Note: [Col. 0059] *Mirum*, “marvellous,” is absent in 4a; *circuiat*, “circles around,” in A.]

The surface of that land was at that time occupied by vast wildernesses of forest, without human inhabitant [Note: [Col. 0059] “Without habitation” in 2b.]; yet they resounded greatly with swarms of bees and the varied songs of birds.

The beasts of the woods were countless as the sand of the sea [Note: [Col. 0059] *Arena*, “sand,” in 1.], or as the stars in heaven [Note: [Col. 0059] *Hethere* in A; *heterrae*, corrected to *heterae*, in 1.]; unfrightened by anyone, they roamed through the trackless land, and the earth scarcely sufficed for the herds of beasts. The herds of cattle could scarcely equal in number the locusts leaping across the fields in summer. The waters there were exceedingly clear and wholesome for human use; likewise the fish were pleasant and healthful to eat.

A remarkable thing—and from it you may perceive how high in the air this region hangs—is that no foreign water flows into it; rather, however many streams, small and great, rise from its various mountains, all, received by the greater water called the Elbe, flow northward to the sea. [Note: [Col. 0059D] He derives the Eger not from the source known to us but from the origin of the Teplá, which flows into the Eger a little below the thermal springs of Karlovy Vary. See Dobner’s commentary on Hájek, *Annales* II, 129.]

And because this region then lay untouched by the plough [Note: [Col. 0059] *Pendeat*, “hangs,” is additionally written in 5.], and no man had yet entered it to cultivate it, it seemed preferable to say nothing of its fertility or barrenness rather than make a statement about an untried matter [Note: [Col. 0059] *Ineptam*, “unfitting,” in 4 and 4a.].

Whoever that man was—it is uncertain how many souls were with him—after entering these wildernesses and seeking places suitable for human dwellings, surveyed with keen sight the mountains, valleys, wild places, and pleasant dales; and, as I think, near Mount Říp [Note: [Col. 0059] *Rip* in 1; *Rzip* in 2; *Rip*, corrected to *Rzip*, in 2b. [Col. 0059D] Mount Saint George, situated between the mouths of the Eger and Moldau rivers.], between two rivers, namely the Ohře [Note: [Col. 0059] *Ocram* in 7. [Col. 0059D] This is the Teplá river and the part of the Eger which receives it; Ogra is so named in Slavonic because of its warm waters. The remaining part of the Eger is Cosmas’s Chub. Compare below II, 37, and Dobner II, 130.] and the Vltava [Note: [Col. 0059] Thus A and 1; *Wultauam* in 3; *Wiltavam* in 5; *Wltavam* in the others. [Col. 0060D] The Moldau.], he first set down his seats, first founded homes and dwellings, and rejoiced to set upon the ground the household gods which he had carried with him on his shoulders. [Note: [Col. 0059D] Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.598.]

Then the elder, whom the others accompanied as though their lord, addressed his followers thus:
