“O companions, who have more than once endured grievous labors [Note: [Col. 0059] *Dolores*, “pains,” in A.] with me through the pathless forests [Note: [Col. 0060D] Horace, *Odes* I.7.31.], halt your steps [Note: [Col. 0060D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.465.]; offer your household gods a welcome libation, by whose aid [Note: [Col. 0059] *Ope*, “aid,” in 2b and 4.] you have at last reached this country, marvellously predestined for you long ago by fate [Note: [Col. 0059] *Fatum*, “fate,” corrected to *fato*, “by fate,” in A.]. This is that land, that land [Note: [Col. 0059] The second phrase was added by a second hand in A; it is omitted once in 2b.] which I remember often promising you: a land subject to no one, full of wild beasts and birds, moist with the nectar of honey and milk, and, as you yourselves see, delightful in climate for habitation. Waters abound on every side and are beyond measure full of fish. Here nothing will be lacking to you, because no one will harm you [Note: [Col. 0059] The phrase from “because” to “harm you” is omitted in 4a.]. But since such a region, so beautiful and so great, is in your hands, consider what name is fitting for the land.”

Immediately, as though instructed by a divine oracle, they said: “From where shall we find a better or more fitting name than this: since you, father, are called Boemus, let the land too be called Bohemia?” [Note: [Col. 0059] The reading *et dicatur* is corrected to *dicatur et* in A.]

Then the elder, moved by the omen of his companions, began in joy to kiss the earth, glad that it was to be called by his own name; and, rising and stretching both palms toward the stars [Note: [Col. 0060D] Virgil, *Aeneid* V.253, 256.], he began to speak thus:

“Greetings, land of destiny, sought by us with a thousand vows, once bereft of man in the time of the Flood; now preserve us unharmed, as though memorials of humankind, and multiply our offspring from generation to generation.”

3. [Note: [Col. 0059] Chapter numbers are absent from the manuscripts; in their place manuscript 1 sometimes writes “Likewise.” In arranging the chapters we have followed manuscript 4, in which the individual chapters are continually marked not by numbers but by colored capital letters.]

If anyone should attempt to tell at length what manners, what uprightness, what great simplicity [Note: [Col. 0059] *Simplicitudinis*, corrected to *simplicitatis*, in A.], what admirable goodness men then possessed; how faithful they were among themselves and merciful to one another [Note: [Col. 0059] *Inter* in 1.]; what moderation, sobriety, and self-restraint they displayed—men who imitate things quite contrary to all this in these modern times—he would become exceedingly tiresome [Note: [Col. 0059] *Fastigium*, “height,” corrected to *fastidium*, “weariness,” in A.]. Therefore we pass these matters over and wish to say a few true things concerning the character of that first age.

That age was exceedingly happy,  
[Note: [Col. 0060D] From “That age was exceedingly happy” through “acorns” are verses of Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, metrum 5, with a few changes.]

Content with modest expense, and not puffed up with swollen pride.

They did not know the gifts of Ceres and Bacchus, for they did not yet exist.

They broke their late fasts with acorns or the flesh of wild beasts.

Uncorrupted streams gave healthful draughts.

As the sunlight or the moisture of water,

so fields and forests, and even marriages themselves, were common to them.

For, after the manner of cattle, every night they entered new marriages [Note: [Col. 0061] Manuscript 1 has “new, or they entered marriages”; 4 and 4a have “they approve, they enter”; 7 has “they brought forth.”] and, when dawn arose, they broke the union of the three Graces and the secret [Note: [Col. 0061] Thus A; *ferrea*, “iron,” in 1 and the other manuscripts.] bonds of love. Wherever night had overtaken each person [Note: [Col. 0061] *Occupaverat*, “had overtaken,” in 4; *occupavit*, “overtook,” in 1.], there, stretched out upon the grass beneath the shade of a leafy tree, he gathered sweet sleep. They knew neither the use nor the clothing of wool or linen; in winter they used the skins of wild beasts or sheep as garments. [Note: [Col. 0061D] The expressions are taken from Regino under the year 887.]

No one knew how to say “mine,” but, after the pattern of monastic life, whatever they had, they called “ours” with mouth, heart, and deed. Their cattle-folds had no barriers [Note: [Col. 0061] The passage from “Their cattle-folds” through “possessed” is absent in 5.], nor did they close their doors to the poor, because there was neither thief nor robber nor any needy person [Note: [Col. 0061] *Nec* occurs three times in A.]; no crime among them was more serious than theft and robbery. They saw no weapons of any people, but possessed only arrows, and these for striking wild beasts.

Why say more? Alas! Prosperity turns into its opposite, and what was common into private property. They avoid and flee secure poverty, once lovable [Note: [Col. 0061] “The loveliness of poverty” in 2b.], as though it were a filthy wheel, because the love of possessing, fiercer than the fires of Etna, burns in everyone. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Boethius, the same passage.]

When these and such evils arose, day by day one bore more and more patiently the injury inflicted upon him by another—an injury which no one had previously known how to inflict—and he had neither judge nor ruler before whom to lament his complaint. After this, whoever was considered more eminent in his tribe or lineage, in person, character, and wealth, men flocked to him of their own accord, without exaction and without seal [Note: [Col. 0061] *Sigillo* in A.]; and, preserving their liberty, they debated doubtful cases and injuries done to them [Note: [Col. 0061] *Confluebat* and *disputabat*, singular, in A.].

Among them there arose a man by birth named Krok [Note: [Col. 0061] *Croh* in 3; *Crecko* in 4 and 4a.], from whose name a castle, now overgrown with trees, is known to stand in the forest adjoining the village of Stříbrná [Note: [Col. 0061] *Ztibene* in 1 and 7; *Ztbecne* in 4 and 4a; *Stibene* in 5; *Ztibene* in 7a.]. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Křakov, not far from the town of Rakovník.]

This man was in his generation perfect to the last degree, endowed with abundance of worldly goods [Note: [Col. 0061] This phrase is absent in 7.] and discerning in the deliberation of judgments. To him, from their own tribes and from the peoples of the entire province, all flocked like bees to their hives to settle disputes [Note: [Col. 0061] *Convolant*, “flock,” in 4a.]. This great and notable man had no male offspring; nevertheless, he begot three daughters, to whom nature gave riches of wisdom no less than she is accustomed to give men.

4. The eldest of these was called Kazi. She yielded neither to Medea of Colchis in herbs and incantation [Note: [Col. 0061] “Grass” in 4.] nor to the Paeonian master [Note: [Col. 0061] *Paeonio*, “Paeonian,” appears as *ponio* in 4.] in the art of healing, because she often made the Fates cease from their work of ending life,

And made the Fates themselves obey her commands by her incantation. [Note: [Col. 0061] *Facta*, “deeds,” in 1; *carmina*, “incantations,” in 3.]

Hence, when the inhabitants of this land have lost something and despair of being able to recover it [Note: [Col. 0061] *Habere*, “to have,” in A.], they use this proverb concerning her: “Not even Kazi herself can recover that.” [Note: [Col. 0061] *Rehabere*, “recover,” in A.]

Here is the place where she was carried off to the tyrant, Ceres’ daughter [the transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain]; her mound may still be seen today, raised very high by the inhabitants of the land in memory of their mistress, above the bank of the river Mže [Note: [Col. 0061] *Mzie* in 2; *Msae* in 2b; *Alsae* in 7. [Col. 0061D] The Mže, which empties into the Moldau at Zbraslav; see Dobner on Hájek II, 116.], beside the road which goes toward the district of Bechyně [Note: [Col. 0061] *Behin* in 1, 4, and 4a.], over the mountain called Ossek [Note: [Col. 0061] “The mountains called” in A; *Ossiek* in 2. [Col. 0061D] Wosek and Brdy. See Kropf’s essay, “The Oldest Division of the Land of Bohemia,” [Col. 0062D] in *Jahrbücher des Böhmischen Museums* II, 442.]

Worthy of praise, but second in age, was Tetka [Note: [Col. 0061] *Tethka* in 1, 2b, 3, and 7; *Tetaka* in 4 and 4a; *Thetka* in 5; *Thechka* in 7a.],
A woman ignorant even of the sea, yet sharp-nosed, built from her own name the fortress of Tethin, naturally most secure in position, on the summit of a precipitous cliff beside the river Msa.

[Note: [Col. 0061] *maris* corrected to *naris* in A.]

[Note: [Col. 0061] *Thethin* 1; *Thetin* 2b, 4, 4a; *Tethin* 7; *Thechin* 7a.]

[Note: [Col. 0062D] Dobner testifies that he saw remains of Tethin’s walls not far from the town of Beraun: II, 117.]

She established and taught that foolish and senseless people should worship and venerate Oreads,

[Note: [Col. 0061] *Oriadas* 4, 4a.]

Dryads,

[Note: [Col. 0061] omitted in 1.]

Hamadryads,

[Note: [Col. 0061] “Dryads, Hamadryads” omitted in 4, 4a.]

and every superstitious sect,

[Note: [Col. 0062D] That is, manner of life.]

together with sacrilegious rites.

[Note: [Col. 0061] *ritus* corrected from *usus* in 1.]

Thus even now many peasants, like pagans, worship springs or fires; one venerates groves

[Note: [Col. 0061] *locus* 1.]

and trees, or

[Note: [Col. 0061] *seu* 7.]

stones; another makes offerings to mountains or

[Note: [Col. 0061] *et* A.]

hills; another begs and prays to the deaf and dumb idols which he himself has made, that they may govern his house

[Note: [Col. 0061] *suam* omitted in 2.]

and himself.

The third, younger in age

[Col. 0062C]

[Note: [Col. 0061] omitted in 4.]

but greater in wisdom, was called Lubossa.

[Note: [Col. 0061] Thus A, 7, and henceforth; *Libussie* 2; *Libussa* 5.]

She also built a city, then exceedingly powerful, beside the forest stretching toward the village of Stebecna,

[Note: [Col. 0061] *Ztibecinam* 1, 2b, 5; *Ztibecznam* 2; *Zubecnam* 3; *Ztbecnam* 4, 4a; *Zitbecinam* 7; *Zeibecinam* 7a.]

and called it Lubossin from her own name.

[Note: [Col. 0061] omitted in A.]

[Note: [Col. 0061] *Lubosin* 1; *Libossin* 2; *Lubossam* 7, 7a; *Lubossin* otherwise.]

[Note: [Col. 0062D] Palacký conjectured that this city was Libossin in the domain of Smecna, in his book *Würdigung*, etc., p. 23.]

Among women she was uniquely a woman prudent in counsel, vigorous in speech, chaste in body, upright in character; in settling the people’s lawsuits, second to none; gracious to all, yet more lovable still; the ornament and glory of the female sex, prudently directing affairs proper to men. But because no one is blessed in every respect

[Col. 0063A]

[Note: [Col. 0063] A adds *et*.]

[Note: [Col. 0063D] Horace, *Odes* II.16.27.]

this woman of such and so great renown—alas for the dreadful human condition!—was a diviner.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *fitonissa* 2; *phytonissa* 2b; *phitonissa* 4a.]

And because she foretold many future events to the people, and foretold them truly, the entire nation, forming a common plan,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *inigens*, with *g* deleted, A.]

after her father’s death appointed her as their judge.

[Note: [Col. 0063] “And because … as their judge” omitted in 4, 4a.]

At that time a considerable dispute arose between two citizens, more eminent in wealth and birth and seemingly leaders of the people, concerning the boundary of an adjoining field.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *continui determinio* A.]

They burst out into such mutual quarrelling that each flew at the other’s thick beard with his nails; shamefully reviling one another and gesturing beneath their noses with bared fingers, they came raging into the court. With great uproar they approached their mistress and humbly asked her to settle the doubtful case between them according to the rule of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *diremit* corrected to *dirimat* in A.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *supliciter* 1.]

Meanwhile she, as is the wanton softness of women when she has no man to fear,

[Col. 0063B]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *lit* A.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *timeat* A.]

was reclining very luxuriously, propped upon her elbow, as though she had borne a boy, high upon embroidered bedding.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *thoris* A.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *acubabat* 1.]

And as she proceeded along the path of justice,

[Note: [Col. 0063] Thus corrected by another hand in 4, for *indecens*; *indecens* 4a.]

having no regard for persons,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *aspiciens* 2.]

and brought the cause of the entire controversy between them to a state of equity, then the man whose cause did not win

[Note: [Col. 0063] second hand in A.]

the victory in court, angered beyond measure, shook his head three

[Note: [Col. 0063] *ter* 4, 4a.]

and four times, struck the ground three times with his staff,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *baculis* 2.]

and, spattering his beard with a mouthful of saliva,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *conspuens* A; *aspergens* 4, 4a.]

cried out:

[Note: [Col. 0063] *exclamat* 2, 3, 4, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0063D] In the popular poem *The Judgment of Libuše* (cf. the book published by the most distinguished gentlemen Šafařík and Palacký, *The Oldest Monuments of the Bohemian Language*, Prague, 1840), concerning whose authenticity a great controversy has arisen among leading scholars, the following is read there, p. 47:

> And all his limbs trembled in rage,  
> He swings his arm and bellows like an aurochs.

[Col. 0064D]

[lacuna]

> Woe to men when a woman rules!]

“O insult intolerable to men! A leaky woman deceitfully turns over manly judgments in her mind. We know certainly that a woman, whether standing

[Note: [Col. 0063] *stat* 4, 4a.]

or sitting upon a throne,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *resideat*, corrected by another hand in 4; *licet* added in 4, 4a.]

has little sense;

[Note: [Col. 0063] *sapiat* 4, 4a, 7.]

how much less when she reclines upon bedding? Indeed, then

[Col. 0063C]

she is better suited to receive a husband than to dictate laws to soldiers. For it is certain that all women have long hair but short understanding. It is better to die than for men to endure such things. Nature has left us alone exposed to the reproach of nations and peoples: we lack a ruler and masculine discipline, and womanly laws oppress us.”

To this the mistress,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *domna* 1; “Lubossa” added in 4, 4a.]

concealing the insult inflicted upon her and hiding her grief of heart with womanly modesty, smiled and said: “It is as you say. I am a woman; I live as a woman. But

[Col. 0064A]

for that reason I seem to you to have little understanding, because I do not judge you with an iron rod.”

[Note: [Col. 0064D] In the popular poem, p. 48:

> Choose a man from among your equals,  
> That he may rule you with iron.]

“And

[Note: [Col. 0063] *sed* 4.]

because you live without fear,

[Note: [Col. 0063] “without pain and fear” 4, 4a.]

you rightly despise me. For where there is fear, there also is

[Note: [Col. 0063] second hand in A.]

honour.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *est* added in 3, 4a.]

But now it is very necessary that you have a ruler stronger than a woman.”

[Note: [Col. 0063] omitted in 1, 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *ferociorem* 1, 4, 7.]

“Thus once the doves despised the whitish

[Note: [Col. 0064D] Should one read *albidulum*, ‘somewhat whitish’?]

kite,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *milvium* 7.]

whom they had chosen

[Note: [Col. 0063] *que* 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *elegerunt* 3.]

as their king, as you despise me; and they set over themselves as leader a hawk much stronger,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *ferociorem* 1, 4, 7.]

who, inventing charges against both guilty and innocent, began to kill them. From that time until today the hawk feeds upon doves. Go home now, so that tomorrow you may choose as your lord the man whom I shall take as my husband.”

Meanwhile she summoned her aforementioned sisters, whom like furies no less fierce possessed, and by their magical art and her own she deceived the people in every way. Lubossa herself

[Col. 0064B]

was, as we have said, a diviner like the Cumaean Sibyl; the second, a sorceress like Colchian Medea;

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Cholhis* A; *Chcohis* 1.]

the third, a witch like Aeaean Circe.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *AE AE AE* 2, 2a, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] Thus A, 1.]

What plan those three Eumenides formed that night, or what secret act they performed, though it was unknown, nevertheless became clearer than daylight to all in the morning, when their sister Lubossa named both the place where the future duke lay hidden and who he was. For who would believe that they would appoint a duke for themselves from the plough? Or who would know where the man who was to become ruler of the people was ploughing? What does prophetic frenzy not know? Or what is there that magical art cannot accomplish?

[Note: [Col. 0063] *sufficit* 2.]

The Sibyl was able to foretell to the Roman people the sequence of fates almost to the Day of Judgment; she also, if it be lawful to believe it, prophesied concerning Christ, as a certain doctor in a sermon introduces verses of Virgil

[Col. 0064C]

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Virgili* 1; *Vigilii* 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0064D] Compare Augustine, *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, *Works* III.2, p. 629, and Virgil, *Eclogue* IV, addressed to Pollio.]

composed in the person of the Sibyl concerning the coming of the Lord. Medea was able, by herbs

[Note: [Col. 0063] *cibis*, “foods,” 2b.]

and incantation, often to draw Hyperion

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Yporionem* A.]

and Berecyntia

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Herecinthiam* 1, 2.]

down from heaven; she could draw rain, lightning, and

[Note: [Col. 0063] *et* omitted in A.]

thunder from the clouds;

[Note: [Col. 0063] *ducere* 4, 4a.]

she could make King Aeacus young from old.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Egacum* 1, 2, 4, 7.]

By Circe’s song,

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Cirnis* 4a.]

the companions of Ulysses

[Note: [Col. 0063] *Ulixes* 1, 2.]

were changed

[Note: [Col. 0064D] Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII.69–70.]

into various forms of wild beasts, and King Picus into the bird now called a woodpecker.

[Note: [Col. 0063] *qui* 4, 4a.]

What wonder? How great were the deeds accomplished by Egyptian magicians through their arts,

[Col. 0065A]

who by their incantations performed almost as many marvels as Moses, servant of God, is reported to have displayed by the power of God.

[Note: [Col. 0065] *hab.* corrected to *exh.* in A.]

So far concerning these matters.

### 5.

On the following day, as had been ordered, without delay they summon an assembly and gather the people. All meet together in one place. The woman,

[Note: [Col. 0065] “Lubossa” added in 4.]

seated on a lofty throne, addresses the countrymen:

[Note: [Col. 0065] “saying” added in 4, 4a.]

“O people most wretched, who do not know how to live free, and whom no good man loses except with his life: though not unwilling, you flee that liberty and voluntarily submit your necks to unfamiliar slavery. Alas, too late and in vain you will repent, as the frogs repented

[Note: [Col. 0065] “as the frogs repented” absent in 7.]

when the water-snake (*hydrus*),

[Note: [Col. 0065] *ydrus* corrected to *ydra* in A.]

whom they had made their king,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *quam* A, corrected by a second hand.]

began to kill them. Or, if you do not know what the laws of a duke are,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *sint* A.]

I shall try to tell them to you in a few words. First,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *Inprime* corrected to *Inprimo* in 1.]

it is easy to set up a duke, but

[Col. 0065B]

difficult to depose one who has been set up. For he who is now in your power, depending on whether you appoint him duke or not, once appointed, you and all that is yours will be in his power. Before his presence your knees will tremble with fever,

[Note: [Col. 0065] 1 reads *febricita habet*; 3, 7 read *febricitata labentur*, “will totter in fever.”]

and your tongue, speechless, will cling to your dry palate. At his voice, from excessive terror, you will scarcely answer: ‘Yes, lord, yes, lord,’”

[Note: [Col. 0065] A reads *i. d. semet legit*, perhaps an internal scribal reading.]

“while he, by his nod alone and without any prior judgment on your part, will condemn this man, behead that man, order one to be cast into prison and another hanged on the gallows. He will make you yourselves,

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in A; “you yourselves … will take” absent in 5.]

and whichever among you he pleases, some slaves, some peasants, some tributaries, some tax-collectors, some torturers, some

[Note: [Col. 0065] *alios* omitted in 4, 4a.]

heralds, some cooks or bakers

[Note: [Col. 0065] *piscatores*, “fishermen,” 4, 4a.]

or millers. He will also appoint for himself tribunes, centurions, stewards, cultivators of vineyards,

[Col. 0065C]

and fields, harvesters of crops, makers of weapons, and cobblers of various skins and leathers. He will place your sons and daughters in his service. From your oxen and horses, mares and flocks, he will take every best thing

[Col. 0066A]

to his palace.

[Note: [Col. 0065] *placitum*, “pleasure,” in A and 1; remaining witnesses read *palatium*.]

All your better possessions,

[Note: [Col. 0065] “all the livestock” 4, 4a.]

in villages, fields, farmlands, meadows, and vineyards, he will take away and turn to his own uses. Why do I delay with many words? Or why do I say this as though to frighten you,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *vos uterream* 1.]

as though I wished to terrify you? If you persist in your undertaking

[Note: [Col. 0065] *in cepto* 4, 4a.]

and do not break your pledge, I shall now disclose to you both the duke’s name and the place where he is.”

At this the common rabble rejoices with a confused

[Note: [Col. 0065] *exaltante* 4, 4a.]

shout. All with one voice demand that a duke be given them. To them she says: “Look—look beyond those

[Note: [Col. 0065] *vos* A.]

mountains”—and she pointed to the mountains—“there is

[Note: [Col. 0065] *ubi* 2.]

a not very large river called Belina,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *Belena* 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0065D] The Bilin in the district of Litoměřice, which flows into the Elbe near Aussig.]

on whose bank there is known to be

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in 4, 4a.]

a village called Stadici.

[Note: [Col. 0065] *Ztadiczi* 1, 3, 7; *Ztadici* 2, 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Staditz.]

In its territory

[Note: [Col. 0065] *teriorio* A; *teritorio* 1.]

there is a single clearing, twenty-two

[Note: [Col. 0065] Twelve in 1, 2, 7.]

paces in length and breadth,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *in* omitted in 2b; “and in breadth” absent in 4, 4a.]

which, wonderfully enough, though situated in the midst of so many fields,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *tantos*, “so great,” 2.]

belongs to no field.

[Col. 0066B]

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Even in our own day the people call this field Königsfeld. Compare Palacký, *History of Bohemia* I, 87.]

There your duke ploughs with two piebald oxen. One ox is girded with whiteness and has a white head;

[Note: [Col. 0065] *et* added in A.]

the other is white from forehead to back,

[Note: [Col. 0065] *tegrum* 1.]

and has white hind feet. Now, if it please you, take my slippers

[Note: [Col. 0065] Thus A; *thalitarium* 1.]

and cloak, and garments fit for a duke,

[Note: [Col. 0066D] That is, clothing.]

go and report the commands of the people and

[Note: [Col. 0065] *ac* A, 2b.]

my own to the man; bring him to yourselves as duke and to me as husband. The man’s name is

[Note: [Col. 0065] *est* omitted in A.]

Premizl,

[Note: [Col. 0065] Thus A; *Primizl* in all witnesses except 2; *Prziemysl* and thereafter.]

who will devise many laws over your necks and heads—for this name in Latin means ‘one who thinks beforehand’ or ‘one who devises above and beyond.’

[Note: [Col. 0066D] Compare Dobner on Hájek II, 158.]

His later offspring

[Note: [Col. 0065] *postea* 2b.]

shall reign throughout this

[Note: [Col. 0065] *haec* 1.]

whole land forever

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in A.]

and beyond.”

### 6.

Meanwhile messengers are appointed to carry the commands of the mistress and people to the man. When the mistress saw them,

[Col. 0066C]

as though uncertain of the route, hesitate, she said: “Why do you hesitate? Go safely; follow my horse. He himself will lead you

[Note: [Col. 0065] *adducet* A; *deducet* 4, 4a.]

by the straight way and bring you back, because that path has more than once been trodden by him.

“Empty rumour flies, and likewise false opinion, that the mistress herself

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in 4a.]

was accustomed always to travel there at dead of night by phantom riding, and return before cockcrow: let the Jew Apella believe that.”

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0066D] Horace, *Satires* I.5.100.]

“What then?”

[Note: [Col. 0065] *tamen* A; *dum* 7.]

The messengers proceed, wisely unlearned; they go knowingly ignorant, following the horse’s tracks. They had already crossed the mountains and were now approaching the village to which they were going,

[Note: [Col. 0065] “already, already … to which they were going” absent in A.]

[Col. 0066C]

when

[Note: [Col. 0065] *tunc* 4, 4a; *dum* 7.]

a boy ran to meet them. Questioning him, they said:

[Note: [Col. 0065] omitted in 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0065] “to him” added in 4, 4a.]

“Ho, well-born boy, is this village named Stadici,

[Note: [Col. 0065] Thus A; *Ztadici* in the other witnesses; *Ztadiczi* 7a.]

or, if it is, is there in it a man named Premizl?” “It is the village you seek,” he said,

[Col. 0067A]

“and look: Premizl is nearby in the field, urging on his oxen so that he may finish more quickly the work he is doing.”

[Note: [Col. 0067] *opus* omitted in 2.]

Approaching him, the messengers say:

> “Fortunate man, duke born to us from the gods!”

And, as is the custom of rustics, it did not suffice

[Note: [Col. 0067] plural *sufficiunt* 1.]

to say it once; but with puffed cheeks they repeat:

> “Hail, duke; hail,
>
> [Note: [Col. 0067] “duke” repeated in 4, 4a.]
>
> most worthy of great praise!
>
> Unyoke the oxen, change your clothes, mount the horse!”

And

[Note: [Col. 0067] “And … horse” written in the margin of manuscript A; absent in 4, 4a; “and all except A sneezing” is a corrupt/uncertain variant.]

they show him the garments and saddle the horse. “Our mistress Lubossa and the whole people

[Note: [Col. 0067] *immensa*, “immense,” 2.]

command you to come quickly and receive the fated kingdom for yourself and your descendants. All that is ours, and we ourselves, are in your hand. We choose you as duke, judge, ruler, protector—choose you alone as our lord.”

At these words the prudent man,

[Note: [Col. 0067] “Premizl” added in 4, 4a.]

as though ignorant of the future,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *praescius*, “foreknowing,” with *inscius* deleted, 2b.]

[Col. 0067B]

stood still. He planted in the ground the goad he held in his hand and, unyoking the oxen, said: “Go back to the place from which you came!” Immediately, quicker than speech, they vanished from sight and were never seen again. But the hazel stick

[Note: [Col. 0067] *autem* omitted in A.]

which he planted in the ground put forth three tall shoots; and, more wonderful still, it produced leaves and nuts. The men,

[Note: [Col. 0067] omitted in A.]

seeing such things happen thus,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *ibi* A.]

stood stupefied. In return for their welcome, he invites them hospitably to breakfast, shakes from a bag woven of cork

[Note: [Col. 0067] *subure* 4.]

mouldy

[Note: [Col. 0067] Thus A, 1, 2b, 3; *nucidum* in the margin, *muscidum* in an ancient hand, 2; *muscidum* 4, 4a; *mucidum* or *muscidum* 7.]

bread and part of a cheese, and places the bag itself upon the turf as a table, together with a coarse cloth and the other things.

[Note: [Col. 0067] *7'c* A.]

Meanwhile, while they eat breakfast

[Note: [Col. 0067] “while they eat breakfast” omitted in 4, 4a.]

and drink water from a jar, two shoots, or two little branches,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *seu* 2b; “or two little branches” absent in 5.]

wither and fall, but the third grows much taller and broader.

[Note: [Col. 0067] *altius* A.]

[Col. 0067C]

Thus the guests’ amazement, mixed with fear, increased.

[Note: [Col. 0067] *ammir-* consistently in A, 4.]

And he said: “Why are you astonished? Know that many lords shall be born from our lineage,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *propagine*, “shoot,” A.]

but one shall always rule. Yet if your mistress were not in such haste in this matter,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *re* omitted in 4a.]

but waited for the course of fate for a little while,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *si* 7; “after me … are absent” 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0067] *per* omitted in 4, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0067] *dum* added in 1.]

so that she did not send for me so quickly:

[Note: [Col. 0067] *numeret* 1.]

as many sons fit to rule as nature might bring forth, so many lords your land would have.”

### 7.

After this, dressed in princely clothing and shod with royal footwear, the ploughman mounts the spirited horse. Yet not forgetful of his condition, he takes with him his boots sewn all over with cork. He caused them to be preserved for the future, and they are preserved at Wissegrad

[Note: [Col. 0067] *WISSEGRAR* A; *Wisegrad* 1, 4, 7.]

in the duke’s chamber to this day and forever.

[Col. 0067D]

Now it happened, as they travelled by the shortcuts

[Note: [Col. 0067] *compita*, “crossroads,” in the margin of 2.]

of the roads, that the messengers still did not dare speak familiarly to their new

[Col. 0068A]

lord,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *familiaris* 7.]

but, like doves when some strange bird approaches them, at first fear her and soon, in flight itself, grow accustomed to her

[Note: [Col. 0067] *asuefaciunt* 1.]

and

[Note: [Col. 0067] *et e: tamquam* A, 1; *p. f.* added in A’s margin.]

make her as it were their own and love her; so they, riding and conversing, shortened the journey with talk, and by joking

[Note: [Col. 0067] *jocundo* A.]

and coarse remarks beguiled the fatigue. One of them, bolder and more ready of tongue, said: “Lord, tell us, for we cannot sufficiently wonder why you caused us to preserve these cork-sewn boots, fit for nothing except

[Note: [Col. 0067] *nisi* omitted in 2.]

being thrown away.”

[Note: [Col. 0067] *propiciantur* 1.]

He replied: “I caused them to be made and shall cause them to be preserved forever for this purpose: that our descendants may know from what stock they arose,

[Note: [Col. 0067] *st.* A.]

and may always live in fear and suspicion, and may not

[Note: [Col. 0067] corrected from *ne* 1; *ita* 2, 4; *neu* 7.]

unjustly oppress through pride the people entrusted

[Note: [Col. 0067] *deditos*, “given over,” A.]

to them by God, because all of us have been made equal by nature.

[Col. 0068B]

“Now permit me in turn to ask you

[Note: [Col. 0067] “you in turn” absent in 2; “ask you one another” 4, 4a.]

whether it is more praiseworthy to rise from poverty to dignity, or to be reduced from dignity to poverty. Without doubt you will answer

[Note: [Col. 0067] *respondetis* 4, 4a.]

me that it is better to rise to glory than to be reduced to want. Yet there are some born of noble kinship who are afterwards reduced to shameful poverty and made wretched. When they proclaim to others that their parents were glorious and powerful, they do not fail to know that they thereby bring greater shame and disgrace upon themselves, since through their own idleness they have lost what their forebears possessed through industry. For Fortune always plays this game with her wheel: now she raises some to the heights, now she plunges others into

[Note: [Col. 0067] *ad* A, 2b.]

the depths. Thus it comes about that earthly dignity, which once tended

[Col. 0068C]

to glory, when lost turns to disgrace. But poverty overcome by virtue does not hide itself beneath a wolf’s skin; rather, it raises its conqueror to the stars, though once it had dragged him down to the lower world.”

[Note: [Col. 0067] *infima*, “depths,” 2; *inferna*, “hell,” 5.]

### 8.

After they had completed their journey

[Note: [Col. 0067] *cum* 2b.]

and were now very near the city, the mistress hastened to meet them, surrounded by her attendants. Joining right hands, they entered the house with great rejoicing, reclined upon couches, refreshed their bodies with Ceres and Bacchus, and devoted the remaining hours of the night to Venus

[Note: [Col. 0067] *veri* A.]

and Hymen.

[Note: [Col. 0067] *imineo* 1.]

This man, who truly ought to be called a man by merit of his excellence, curbed this savage nation with laws, subdued an untamed people under his authority, and subjected them to the servitude under which they are now oppressed. He alone, together with Lubossa alone, dictated all

[Col. 0068D]

the laws by which this land is governed and ruled.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] The same little tale is also found in the oldest collections of Bohemian laws.]

[Col. 0069A]

### 9.

During these beginnings of the laws, one day the aforesaid mistress, stirred by the Python-spirit, with her husband Premizl and the other elders of the people

[Note: [Col. 0069] *populis* 1.]

standing by, prophesied as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0069] *vocitata* 4, 4a.]

> “I behold a city whose fame shall touch the stars.
>
> There is a place in the forest, a village that is
>
> thirty stadia distant from this place,
>
> which the waters of the Wlitava bound.”

[Note: [Col. 0069] Thus A; *Wiltava* 4a and elsewhere.]

“This place is strongly defended on the northern side by a deep valley and the little stream Brusnica;

[Note: [Col. 0069] *aquilonari* 4, 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *munitur* 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *valde* 2, 2b.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] Thus A; *Bruzinca* 2; *Bruznice* 4, 4a; *Bruznica* otherwise.]

but on the southern side a very broad, rocky mountain, called Petrin from its rocks,

[Note: [Col. 0069] *Paetrin* 1; *Petrin* 2b, 4, 4a, 5; *Petrun* 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Today Saint Lawrence’s Mountain; Dobner on Hájek II, 119.]

rises over the site. The mountain of the place curves in the shape of a dolphin or sea-pig, extending to

[Note: [Col. 0069] *ad* A.]

the aforesaid river. When you arrive there,

[Note: [Col. 0069] *dum* 4, 4a.]

you will find a man in the middle

[Note: [Col. 0069] *medii* 1.]

of the forest making a threshold for a house. And because even great lords bow themselves at a low threshold,

[Col. 0069B]

you shall call the city which you will build Prague, from the event itself.”

[Note: [Col. 0069] *regi* corrected to *rei* in A, 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0069D] For “threshold” in Bohemian is *prag*. Compare Palacký I, 88. See also Pelzel’s essay, “On the Origin and Name of the City of Prague,” *Newer Treatises of the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences* II, 112.]

“In this city, at some future time, two golden olive trees shall rise; with their summits they shall pierce even the seventh

[Note: [Col. 0069] *sempiternum*, “eternal,” A.]

heaven, and throughout the whole world shall shine brightly in signs and miracles. All the tribes of the land of Bohemia and the remaining nations shall honour and worship them with sacrifices and gifts. One of these shall be called

[Note: [Col. 0069] *vocabitur* omitted in 4; a fifteenth-century hand in 1 adds ‘Wiceslaw and Woytiech’; 3 inserts *Wechlava* in Latin; 3a *Weceslava*; D corrects to *Weczlava*.]

‘Greater Glory,’ the other

[Note: [Col. 0069] 3 inserts *Tressivoya* in Latin; D corrects *Tiessiwoya*.]

‘Consolation of the Army.’”

[Note: [Col. 0069D] This refers to Saints Wenceslaus and Adalbert; compare Dobner on Hájek III, 413; IV, 206, concerning these etymologies.]

She would have said more, had not the pestilent, prophesying spirit fled from God’s creature.

[Note: [Col. 0069] *fuisset* 2, 2a, 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *sed* 7.]

Immediately they go to the old forest and, after finding the given sign in

[Note: [Col. 0069] omitted in A.]

the specified place, build Prague, the mistress of all Bohemia.

[Note: [Col. 0069] *aedificavit* 3, 7.]

And because at that time the maidens of this land, reaching maturity without a yoke, like Amazons aspiring to military arms,

[Col. 0069C]

and making themselves leaders, served as soldiers just like recruits,

[Note: [Col. 0069] *thyornes* A.]

pursued hunting manfully through the forests, and were not taken by men but themselves took men as husbands whenever and whomsoever they wished; and because, like the Scythian nation of the Plauci

[Note: [Col. 0069] Thus A, 1, 2, 4, 7; *Planci* elsewhere.]

or

[Note: [Col. 0069] *seu*, written above *sive*, 2b.]

Picenatici, men and women had no distinction in dress—therefore womanly

[Col. 0070A]

boldness grew to such a degree

[Note: [Col. 0069] *femina*, with *rum* added, 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *exercuit* 2; an early marginal hand corrects to *excrevit*.]

that they built for themselves, on a cliff not far from the aforesaid city, a stronghold naturally secure in position, to which the name Divin was given from the word for ‘maiden.’

[Note: [Col. 0069] *opidum* A.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *Devin* 1, 7; *Dewin* 2b, 4, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Thus *Devin* in Bohemian is the same as what among us is Magdeburg, that is, “City of Maidens” (*Parthenopolis*). The Annals of Fulda, under 864, read: “Rastislaus besieged a certain city which in the language of that people is called Dewin, that is, ‘maiden.’”]

When the young men saw this, indignantly aroused against them by excessive zeal, they assembled in far greater numbers and built a city amid thickets on another cliff, no farther away than the sound of one trumpet.

[Note: [Col. 0069] *bucinae* A, 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *altâ* corrected to *alta* in 1.]

Modern people call it Wissegrad; then it derived its name, Hrasten, from

[Note: [Col. 0069] *ab* omitted in 7.]

the thickets.

[Note: [Col. 0069] *Huasten* corrected to *Hrasten* in A, 5; *Hurasten* 1, 2, 2b, 7; *Nurasten* 3; *Wrasten* 4, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] From Bohemian *Chrast*. Dobrovský.]

And because the maidens often became more ingenious in deceiving the young men,

[Note: [Col. 0069] *virgines* corrected to *juvenes* in 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *f. s. a. i.* added in A’s margin.]

while the young men often proved stronger than the maidens,

[Note: [Col. 0069] *ferociores* 7.]

war and peace by turns were conducted between them. And when they enjoy a peace arranged between them, both sides resolved to provide a common feast of food

[Note: [Col. 0069] singular *componeret* 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *et cibis* 4a.]

and drink, and to celebrate together for three days a solemn festival without arms in an appointed place.

[Col. 0070B]

What more need be said? The young men entered into feasting with the girls no differently than ravenous wolves seeking food

[Note: [Col. 0069] *edilia* 2; *u* added by an ancient hand.]

in order that they might enter sheepfolds.

[Note: [Col. 0069] *ut* erased in 2.]

They spent the first day merrily in feasting and excessive drinking.

> “And while they wished to quench their thirst, another thirst increased;
>
> The young men scarcely postpone their delight until nightfall:

[Note: [Col. 0069] *hilarem* omitted in 4, 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] *noctu* A, 1, 2; *noctu* overwritten with *noctis* 2b; *noctis* 4a.]

[Note: [Col. 0069] “until nightfall” omitted in A.]

> Night had come, and the moon shone in a clear sky.”

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Horace, *Epodes* XV.1.]

Then one man, blowing a trumpet, gave them this signal, saying:

> “You have played enough, eaten enough, and drunk enough;

[Note: [Col. 0069] *satisque* 7.]

“If it were right for a leader to add courage to his soldiers by words, I would detain you with many circumlocutions of speech. But because the enemy stands before your eyes and little time remains for exhortation,

> Let it be permitted me to kindle you even with a few words.

All have the same devotion to fight in war, but not the same prospect of victory. They fight for the glory of a few; we fight for our country, for the freedom of the people and ourselves, and for our ultimate safety. They fight to seize what belongs to others; we, to defend our sweet pledges and dear marriages. Take courage and be men. For you have appeased with vows the gods whom you formerly had offended, by the offerings by which they wished to be appeased. Therefore do not fear their terror, because those whose courage is harmed by fear in battle are involved in the greatest danger; but boldness is held in place of a wall, and the gods themselves assist the bold. Believe me: beyond those camps lies your safety and glory. But if you turn your backs to the enemy, you will nevertheless not escape death. Yet would that it were death! Something worse than death will be done: they will violate your wives before your eyes, slaughter infants with the sword in their mothers’ bosoms, and give the mothers puppies to suckle. For the conquered have one virtue only: to refuse the victors nothing.”

And after he had carried out his stepmother’s orders, escaping in swift flight before the rest, he hurried home, and behold, his wife was being mourned as dead. When her husband saw her and uncovered her face—a tale resembling fiction—it appeared that the corpse had a wound in its womanly breast and both ears cut off. Then the man, recalling what had been done in the battle, brought out from his purse the bloody ears with their earrings and recognized her as being in the likeness of the person whom he had killed in battle as an adversary.

Among the spoil they found the young lord’s son hiding with a certain old woman. When the duke saw him, though a pagan, he nevertheless, like a good Catholic, was moved to mercy by the child’s tender age and beauty and spared him. He built a new town on level ground, named Dragus, on the bank of the river Ogre near the village of Postolopirth—where the monastery of Saint Mary is now seen—and entrusted both town and boy to the tutor to whom the boy’s father had formerly committed him. This was a man named Duringo, of Sribian stock, surpassing ordinary human wickedness, worse than the worst man and more cruel than every beast.

Without delay he brought these fatal gifts, hoping to obtain countless rewards for such a deed. He found the duke in the Prague palace, sitting in council with all the nobles. Thinking it best to lay his crime before them all, he entered, greeted the duke, and, after receiving his greeting, stood waiting. When permission to speak was given him, he said:

[Note: Col. 0079. Corrected in another hand, 1.]

“Behold—I, behold—I alone have achieved with my axe that you may all sleep secure on both ears. For often one tiny spark, which the keeper of a house has carelessly left beneath a thin ash, kindles great fires and envelops and burns not only the house but its very masters. Foreseeing and guarding against this spark, which would harm you in the future, I extinguished it and protected you and your descendants from the coming disaster, as though forewarned by a divine oracle. You, however, who are the heads of the land, devise a name for this deed. If it is a merit, make all men know how much I have deserved; but if you say it is a crime, you owe me all the more because you yourselves do not commit crimes. Or should you have spared the child because his father wished to kill your children and set puppies to suck your wives? Certainly neither the flesh of a mad dog nor the broth of a wolf is sweet. Behold, the avenger of his father’s blood lies defeated without your blood, though he would someday harm you as well. Go then instead: take the kingdom swiftly, which you will possess more happily for ever without fear.”

[Note: Col. 0079. en en 1.]

[Note: Col. 0079. Once only, 4a.]

[Note: Col. 0079C. Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* II.3.101.]

Then at once he produced the tender head upon a dish, in which nothing of the living man had yet been destroyed, except only that it had been deprived of speech. The duke was horrified; the hearts of the nobles trembled; a confused murmur shuddered in horror. Then the duke turned his head away from the impious gift and uttered these words:

> “Take from our sight your gifts, criminal one;  
> Your crimes exceed measure and pardon, and find no punishment adequate to them.  
> For this outrage no fitting judgment can be devised, nor any equal penalty.  
> Do you think that I could not have done what you did, had I wished?  
> It was lawful for me to kill an enemy, but not for you to kill your lord.  
> This sin which you have committed is a sin greater than can be called a sin.  
> Certainly, whoever kills you or judges that you are to be killed  
> Incurs not one sin only but a double sin:  
> Both the sin that you are killed,  
> And the sin that you killed your lord;

But in truth, having come to himself, when he recognized that he had unjustly taken up arms against his lord, Emperor Arnolph, his spiritual co-father, as though forgetful of his benefaction—Arnolph, who had subjected to him not only Bohemia but also other regions, from there as far as the river Ogram, and thence toward Hungary as far as the river Gron—he was led by repentance. Through the darkness of midnight, with no one aware, he mounted a horse, crossed his camp, and fled to a place situated on the side of Mount Zober. There, long before, three hermits had built, with his assistance and help, a church amid a great forest inaccessible to men.

Cf. Dobner on Hájek III, 544.]. When he had happily entered upon the way of all flesh, Spitigneum succeeded to his father’s principality [Note: [Col. 0081] *Zpitigneu* in 2b, 7; *Zpitignen* in 3.]; after his death Wratizlav [Note: [Col. 0081] *Wratislav* in 2; *Wratislau* in 3; *Wratizlaus* in 4, 4a.] obtained the duchy [Note: [Col. 0082C] The periods of these princes are shrouded in scarcely penetrable darkness. Dobner III, 502. He assigned Spitigneum’s death to 922 and Wratizlav’s to 925, but this rests more on conjecture than on firm evidence.]. He took as wife a woman named Dragomira, from the exceedingly hard Lutician people, herself harder than stones to bring to faith, from the province named Stodor [Note: [Col. 0081] *Stotor* in 7.] [Note: [Col. 0082C] This is called Hevellun. Thietmar IV, 20. Compare also Adam of Bremen II, 18.].

She bore two sons [Note: [Col. 0081] Omitted in 1.], Wencezlaus [Note: [Col. 0081] *Wenceslaum* in 2.], pleasing to God and humankind, and Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0081] *Boleslaum* in 2.], detestable for his brother’s murder. But how Duke Borivoj [Note: [Col. 0081] “duke” omitted in 2b, 3, 4, 4a.], with God’s grace always going before and everywhere following, received the sacrament of baptism; or how, through his successors, the holy religion of the Catholic faith advanced [Note: [Col. 0081] “advanced” in 2.] day by day in these regions; or which duke, believing, first built what churches, or how many, for the praise of God—we have preferred [Col. 0082A] [Note: [Col. 0081] *malumus* in 3.] to pass these matters over rather than burden readers with tedium, since we have already read them written by others: some things in the privilege of the Moravian church, some in the epilogue [Note: [Col. 0081] *ephilogo* in 1.] of that land and of Bohemia, and some in the Life or Passion of our most holy patron and martyr [Note: [Col. 0081] “of Christ” added by 4, 4a.] Wencezlaus [Note: [Col. 0081] *Wencezlavi* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0082C] This is the Life of St Wencezlaus written by Gumpold, bishop of Mantua, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* IV, 213.]; for even foods taken too often become hateful.

The numbers of the ensuing years are absent in 7a.].

On the fourth day before the Kalends of October [28 September], Saint Wencezlaus, duke of the Bohemians, martyred by the treachery of his brother Bolezlav [Col. 0083B] [Note: [Col. 0083C] Bunzlau.] [Note: [Col. 0083] 3 reads “into the city,” omitting “Boleslav.”], entered happily into the everlasting hall of heaven [Note: [Col. 0083] “into the hall” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0083C] Cf. Gumpold’s *Life of Wencezlaus*, chapters 17–19. Cosmas went very far astray in establishing the chronology: St Wenceslaus was killed in 935. Compare *Jahrbücher des deutschen Reichs unter den Sächsischen Kaisern* I, 2, p. 7.].

Now how Bolezlaus, scarcely worthy to be called the holy man’s full brother, deceitfully invited his brother to a feast, though he was in fact plotting to kill him in order to retain the governance of the kingdom; and how he concealed before men, though not before God, the guilt of fratricide—I think this has been sufficiently related in the triumph of the Passion of that holy man [Note: [Col. 0083C] That is, in the book in which his death is celebrated.]. After the reward of his life, another Cain, Bolezlaus—alas!—obtained the ill-gotten duchy.

But amid those feasts—execrable for brotherly slaughter, as we have recounted above—a remarkable child was born to Duke Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0083] *Bolezlavi* in 1.] by an excellent wife. From the event he was given the name [Col. 0083C] Ztrahquaz [Note: [Col. 0083] Thus in A, 1; *Ztrahkwas* in 2; *Strahquaz* in the others.], a name meaning “terrible feast.” For what feast can be more terrible than one at which fratricide is committed? Therefore Duke Bolezlaus, conscious of his crime [Note: [Col. 0083] “conscious of the crime committed” in 1.], fearing the penalties of Tartarus, and continually pondering with anxious mind how God might in some way be appeased for this crime, made a vow to the Lord, saying: “If this my son,” he said [Note: [Col. 0083] “Strahquaz” added by 4.], “survives, I vow him to God with all my heart: that he shall be a cleric and serve Christ all the days of his life, for my sin and for the people of this land” [Note: [Col. 0083] “for” is omitted in A.].

18. After this, the father, mindful of his vow, when the boy had become teachable and very dear to his parents, could not bear for him to learn away from his sight [Note: [Col. 0083] “for him to depart” in 3.], and sent him to Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0083] *Ratisbonam* in 2, here and henceforth.], entrusting him beneath the regular wings of the abbot of Saint Emmeram the martyr [Note: [Col. 0083C] Michael, bishop of Regensburg and abbot of St Emmeram, who exercised this office from 944 onward. Compare the Lesser Annals of St Emmeram, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* I, 94.]. There he was instructed in ecclesiastical and monastic ordinances [Note: [Col. 0083] “and” added by the collator in 2b.]; there he was clothed in the monastic habit; there he was brought up to manhood. The further course of his life will be sufficiently revealed in what follows.

As for the deeds of Duke Bolezlaus, I could learn [Note: [Col. 0083] “find” in A.] nothing else worthy of report except one matter, which I judged worth setting before you. For the servant of God Wencezlaus had built a church in the metropolitan city of Prague in honour of Saint Vitus the martyr, but, prevented by death, had left it unconsecrated. Duke Bolezlaus humbly sent envoys with great gifts and still greater promises and assurances to Michael, the bishop then presiding over the church of Regensburg, and with difficulty obtained his agreement to consecrate it [Col. 0084B] [Note: [Col. 0084C] Gumpold reports that the church was consecrated in St Wencezlaus’s lifetime by Tuto, chapter 15. Tuto died no later than 932, in which year his successor Isengrimus attended the synod of Dingolfing; see Mansi XVIII, 361. Compare moreover Dobner’s discussion of this matter in his notes on Hájek III, 624.].

The bishop certainly would not have consented, unless, for the commemoration of the soul and salvation [Note: [Col. 0083] “of the blessed” is added by 4.] of his friend Wencezlaus, now slain, he had resolved that it should be done; for, while he had flourished in the flesh, the man of God Wencezlaus had honoured him with deep affection as his spiritual father [Note: [Col. 0083] *spiritalem* in 1, 4.] and most gracious bishop. Bishop Michael likewise had adopted him as a most beloved son, often instructing him in the fear and love of God [Note: [Col. 0083] “fear and love” in A.], and often sending him gifts [Note: [Col. 0083] “through” is added by A, 2.] of which the new church of Christ stood in especial need at that time.

As soon as the duke had gained his desire, all the people, nobles, and clergy devoutly rushed to meet the arriving bishop and received him with great honour and joy into the buildings of the metropolitan city of Prague [Note: [Col. 0083] “in” is omitted in 2.]. In short: on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September], the church of Saint Vitus the martyr was dedicated [Note: [Col. 0083] Thus in A; absent in the other witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0083] “of Saint Vitus the martyr” is absent in 3.], and the joyful bishop returned [Note: [Col. 0083] Corrected by another hand in 1; “was returning” in 3.] to his own place.

19. [REG.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 930, Otto, son of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0083] *Henrici* in A.], married Edith [Note: [Col. 0083] Corrected in A; *Edgid* in the remaining witnesses; absent in 5.], daughter of the king of the English.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 931, Emperor Henry made the king of the Obotrites and the king of the Danes Christians [Note: [Col. 0083] What is read under this and the preceding year is absent in 4.].

[Col. 0085A] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 932 [Note: [Col. 0085] *DCCCCXXXI* in 4.], on the fourth [Note: [Col. 0085] “within the Nones” in 3.] day before the Nones of March [4 March], the body of Saint Wencezlaus the martyr was transferred from the town of Bolezlav [Note: [Col. 0085] *Bolezlau* in 1, and henceforth.] to the city of Prague because of his envious brother’s hatred [Note: [Col. 0085C] Gumpold’s *Life of St Wencezlaus*, chapter 23. This must have taken place in 938 if his bones were in fact transferred to Prague three years after his martyrdom.]. For his brother Bolezlaus, doing worse and worse day by day [Note: [Col. 0085] “earlier” in A.], pierced by no repentance for his crime, could not bear in his pride [Note: [Col. 0085] “for” in 4.] that God displayed countless miracles at the tomb [Note: [Col. 0085] “mound” in 3.] of the holy martyr Wencezlaus [Note: [Col. 0085] “his” in A, 4.] through his merits. He secretly ordered trustworthy retainers to transfer him to Prague and bury him in the ground by night in the church of Saint Vitus, so that, if God should show any wonders to his saints for their glory, they might be ascribed to the merits not of his brother, but of Saint Vitus the martyr.

I have judged neither his other evil deeds worthy of narration nor reliably established them. Yet we wish to tell your charity of one sufficiently bold [Col. 0085B] and memorable act which he performed formerly in his youth. This Duke Bolezlaus—for if he should be called a duke, who was impious and a tyrant, more savage than Herod, more brutal than Nero, surpassing Decius in the enormity of his crimes and Diocletian in cruelty, whence he assumed for himself the byname “the Cruel” [Note: [Col. 0085] “name” in 2; “surname” in 2b.] Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0085] “so that he might be called” is corrupt or incomplete in A.]—was so harsh that he governed nothing by counsel, nothing by reason, but did everything according to his own will and the impulse of his mind.

It therefore happened that he conceived the plan of founding for himself a town constructed in Roman fashion [Note: [Col. 0085C] That is, a town fortified with stone walls; cf. Thietmar I, 10.]. At once he summoned together all the leading men of the people, without exception [Note: [Col. 0085] “the leading men of the people” in A.], led them into a grove [Note: [Col. 0085] “place” in the other witnesses.] beside the river Elbe [Note: [Col. 0085] *Albe* in 1, added by another hand; *Albim* in 2b.] [Note: [Col. 0086C] The Albis, that is, the Elbe.], marked out the site, and disclosed to them the secret of his heart [Note: [Col. 0085] Plural “secrets” in 4.]. “Here,” he said, [Col. 0085C] “I will and command you to build me, in Roman fashion, an exceedingly high wall around the circuit of the town” [Note: [Col. 0085] “for me” is omitted in 4.].

They replied: “We who are the leaders [Note: [Col. 0086C] That is, the head, the chief men.] of the people and bear the insignia of rank renounce you, for we neither know nor wish to do what you command; nor did our fathers previously do such a thing [Note: [Col. 0085] Corrected in 1.]. Behold, we stand before your eyes [Note: [Col. 0085] “sight” in 3.], and we submit our necks rather to your sword than to the unbearable yoke of servitude. Do what you will, for we shall not obey your commands [Note: [Col. 0085] “obey” in 2, 2b.].”

Then Duke Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0085] “Bolezlaus” added by 4.] flew into a dreadful rage. Leaping up, he stood upon a rotten trunk which happened then to lie in the grove [Note: [Col. 0085] “mud” in 2; “grove” in 2b; *to* is placed over *co*.], drew his sword, and said: “O cowards and sons of cowardly fathers! If you are not half-men [Note: [Col. 0085] “not” is omitted by A, 1, 2b, 4.] or less worthy than the very pear tree [Note: [Col. 0085] *pili*, corrected to *piri* in 2b; the wording is materially uncertain.], prove your words by deeds; and test whether it is easier to submit your necks to the sword or to the yoke of servitude [Note: [Col. 0085] Corrected in A.]”

It was a sight worth seeing and astonishing for the bold insolence of the duke. For even if he had possessed a thousand armed right hands in one body [Note: [Col. 0085] “and” added by 4.], he could not have terrified so great a company of men more [Note: [Col. 0085] Another hand in 1 supplied *i. t.*, the transmitted abbreviation at *in tantum* (“to such an extent”); the source gives no fuller expansion.]. When the duke [Note: [Col. 0085] “Bolezlaus” added by 4.] saw them paler than boxwood from fear, he seized by the locks of his head [Note: [Col. 0085] Thus corrected in 1; *cinninos* in A; *circinos* in the other witnesses.] one man who was foremost among the elders and, striking him with all his strength, cut off his head as though it were the head of a tender poppy [Note: [Col. 0085] “he cuts off” in 1.]. Then he said:

> Thus I will; thus I shall do: let my will stand in place of reason.  
> [Note: [Col. 0086C] Juvenal, *Satires* VI, 223.]

The others, seeing this, led by belated repentance, fell at the duke’s knees [Note: [Col. 0085] “of Bolezlaus” added by 4.], begging forgiveness with tears. “Now, lord,” they said, “spare our offences. We shall now obey all your commands; we shall willingly do whatever you wish [Note: [Col. 0085] A omits *jam ultro* (“now willingly”).] Do not be cruel to us any longer.” And at once, in accordance with the duke’s will, they built a city with a thick and high wall [Note: [Col. 0085] “high” is supplied above the line in A.], in Roman fashion, as it may still be seen today; and it is called Bolezlav [Note: [Col. 0085] Accusative *Boleslaum* in 3.] after the name of its founder [Note: [Col. 0085] What follows is absent in codex 7a as far as the year 967.].

20. [CONTINUATION OF REGINO.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 933, the eastern Hungarians, devastating East Francia, Alemannia, and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0085] *Calliam* in 2.], returned through Italy.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 934, King Henry [Note: [Col. 0085] Thus in A at this point; *Heinricus* in 3, and so thereafter.] struck down the Hungarians in a great slaughter and captured many of them [Note: [Col. 0085] “most of them” in 3.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 935, King Henry was struck with paralysis. [Col. 0086C] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 936, King Henry died; his son, Emperor Otto, succeeded him in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0085] “in the kingdom” added by 4.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 937, Arnulf, duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0085] “duke of the Bavarians” in 2b; “king of Bavaria” in 3.], died. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 938, the Hungarians were again devastated by the Saxons in a great slaughter, and the sons of Duke Arnulf rebelled [Note: [Col. 0085] “fought” in 2.] against King Otto. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 939, King Louis married Gerberga, widow of Giselbert [Note: [Col. 0085] *Gisalbum* in 3; *Giselberti* in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0085] “In the same year a comet appeared” added by 4.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 940, [CONTINUATION OF REGINO] the duchy of Lotharingia was entrusted to Henry, the king’s brother, and in the same year he was expelled from it. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 941 [Note: [Col. 0085] “The year of the Lord’s Incarnation 941” is absent in 1.], Henry, brother of King Otto [Col. 0087A] [Note: [Col. 0087] “Otto’s” added above the text in 2b.], conspired with certain Saxons against the king but was unable to do any harm. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 942, a star like a comet was seen for fourteen nights, and an immense mortality of cattle [Note: [Col. 0087] *bovum* in 1.] followed. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 943, Duke Otto died; Conrad, son of Werner [Note: [Col. 0087] *Werinari* in A; *Verneri* in 3.], succeeded him in the duchy [Note: [Col. 0087] “in the duchy” in 2b, 3.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 944, the Hungarians were slaughtered by the Carantanians [Note: [Col. 0087] “Carinthians” in 3.] in a great massacre. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 945, Berthold [Note: [Col. 0087] *Berdoldus* in 1; *Bertoldus* in 2.] duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0087] “of Bavaria” in 3.] died, and Henry, the king’s brother, succeeded him. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 946, King Louis was expelled from his kingdom by his own people [Note: [Col. 0087] “by his own people” is absent in A; *assuis suo* in 1, 4.]. [Col. 0087B] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 947, Lady Queen Edith [Note: [Col. 0087] *Edid*, with *domina* omitted, in 3; *domna Hedgyd* in 4.] died. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 948, a synod was held at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0087] *Ingelenheim* in 3; *Inglinheim* in 4.] by thirty-four bishops [Note: [Col. 0087] “by 34” in 2a, 2b, 4; the number is absent in A; *XXXIV* in 2a, 2b, 4, but in the margin of 2b: “others: 30.” In 2, after “Ingelheim,” everything is omitted, with a trace of erasure remaining.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 949, a daughter, Mathilda [Note: [Col. 0087] *Mechtildis* in 3.], was born to Liudolf, the king’s son. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 950, Bolezlaus, duke of the Bohemians, rebelled against the king [Note: [Col. 0087] “rebels” in A; “rebelled” in 3.]; the king attacked him with a strong hand and subjected him wholly to his authority [Note: [Col. 0087] “subjugated” in 3.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 951, King Otto went into Italy.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 952 [Note: [Col. 0087] The two oldest codices, A and 1, contain only the numbers of the years 952–966; the remainder lack them altogether. In codex 2 the words that follow under 967, “from a bramble, a grape … his father’s namesake,” are wrongly distributed across 952–957; misled by this strange error, Dobrowski admitted them into his text. In 4, the year 951 is repeated.]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 953. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 954. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 955. [Col. 0087C] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 956. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 957. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 958. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 959. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 960. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 961. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 963. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 964. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 965. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 966.

21. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967 [Note: [Col. 0087] *DCCCCLXII*. In 4 the years of the Lord’s Incarnation 968, 969, 970, and 971 follow, and the death of Bolezlaus is recorded under 972. What is narrated under 967 is also found in 7 and 7a.], on the Ides of July [15 July], the duke surnamed [Col. 0088A] “the Cruel,” Bolezlaus, lost both the duchy, badly purchased with his brother’s blood, and his life. His son and namesake succeeded to the principality, very unlike his father in good character and spiritual manner of life [Note: [Col. 0087] *spiritali* in 7.].

O wondrous mercy of God! O how incomprehensible are his judgments! Behold, from a bramble comes a noble grape, from thorns a rose, from thistles a fig [Note: [Col. 0087] Corrected in A.]: that is, from a fratricide there emerges a worshipper of Christ; from a wolf, a lamb; from a tyrant [Note: [Col. 0087] *tirranno* in 1.], a modest man. From the impious Bolezlaus is born a pious second Duke Bolezlaus, second to none in excellence. Nor is he stained by sharing the name of his wicked father, in whom true [Note: [Col. 0087] Corrected in A.] love of Christ and pure charity [Note: [Col. 0087] *dileccio* in 1.] burned fervently. For just as many receive [Note: [Col. 0087] *sociuntur* in 1.] the names of saints but do not attain holiness [Note: [Col. 0087] *sanctitate* in 7.], so holiness and wickedness are not known in a person from a name, but each is recognized by merit [Note: [Col. 0087] Singular *dinoscitur* in A; “in a name” in 4.].

22. This second Prince Bolezlaus was a most Christian man, Catholic in faith, father of orphans [Note: [Col. 0087] “and” added by A.], defender of widows, comforter of those who mourn, kindly receiver of clerics and pilgrims, and outstanding founder of God’s churches. For, as we read in the privilege of the church of Saint George [Note: [Col. 0087] *Georii*; *Georgii* in 1.], he faithfully established twenty churches for the Christian religion and sufficiently endowed them with all the resources pertaining to ecclesiastical use.

He had a full sister named Mlada, a virgin devoted to God, learned in sacred letters [Note: [Col. 0087] Omitted in 5.], dedicated to the Christian religion, endowed with humility [Note: [Col. 0087] *Humilitati* in 2; the text from *humilitate* through “generous” is omitted in 5.], gentle in speech, generous patroness of the poor and orphans, and adorned with every moral virtue. When she came to Rome on a matter of prayer [Note: [Col. 0087] “to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul” added by 4.], she was kindly received by the Apostolic Lord [Note: [Col. 0087C] John XIII.]. After remaining there for some time, she was sufficiently trained in monastic discipline. Finally, Pope John, by counsel of his cardinals [Note: [Col. 0087] *ex c. card.* in A.]—or rather, wishing to aid the new church with his gracious [Note: [Col. 0087] *benigniss.* in 3.] support—consecrated her abbess [Note: [Col. 0087] Corrected in 1.], changed her name to Maria [Note: [Col. 0087] *Maria* in 3.], and gave her the Rule of Saint Benedict and the abbatial staff.

Thereafter the new abbess, bringing [Note: [Col. 0087] *alatura* in 1.] a new and holy monastic [Note: [Col. 0087] *monahicam* in 1.] rule to the land of Bohemia, received apostolic permission and blessing and rode with her greatly rejoicing company to her sweet homeland. [Col. 0089A] They reached the royal city of Prague, and Duke Bolezlaus honourably received his long-desired and most beloved sister. Joining hands, they entered the royal residence. There, while seated together and long enjoying mutually exchanged conversation, she told her brother of many things that she had seen or heard at Rome, worthy of report and admiration [Note: [Col. 0089] “worthy of report and admiration” is absent in 4.]; moreover, she presented him with a letter sent to her on the Apostolic Lord’s behalf [Note: [Col. 0089] “handed over” in 2b; above, “presented.”], whose form was as follows:

> John [Note: [Col. 0089] “bishop” added by 7; the letter is mutilated in 5.], servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0089] “servant of the servants of God” in A.], sends apostolic blessing to Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0089] “duke” added by 4.], foster-child of the Catholic faith.
>
> It is right to lend kindly ears to just petitions, because God is justice; those who love God [Note: [Col. 0089] “him” in 7; in 2b the collator noted: “another has *eum*.”] shall be justified, and all things work together for good to those who love God’s justice [Note: [Col. 0089] “God’s justice” in A.]. Our daughter, your kinswoman [Note: [Col. 0089D] With Dobner IV, 173, *filia* should have been supplied, so that the bull might appear to have been sent not to Bolezlaus II but to his father Bolezlaus; unless Dobner, like Cosmas, was deceived even by this forged letter. Assemani, *Origines ecclesiasticae Studii*, III, part II, p. 169, was the first to question the genuineness of this letter; since he did not provide his arguments, Pubitschka, *Geschichte von Böhmen* III, 7, seems to me to have sufficiently proved the matter. Palacký, *Würdigung*, p. 26, accepted their view: Cosmas appeared, by the words “whose form was as follows,” to indicate that he was giving the text not from a copy but only from memory.], named Mlada, also Maria, brought to our heart, among other petitions not to be rejected, your dear prayers: namely, that with our assent it might be permitted in your principality to establish a bishopric for the praise and glory of God [Note: [Col. 0089] “and” is added by 7.]. Receiving this request with joyful mind, we rendered thanks [Note: [Col. 0089] *grates* in 1, 4, 7.] to God, who always and everywhere enlarges and magnifies his Church among all nations.
>
> Therefore, by apostolic authority and the power of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—whose vicars we are, though unworthy [Note: [Col. 0089] *vicarii sumus* in A.]—we grant, approve [Note: [Col. 0089] “approve” is omitted in 2.], and canonically establish that at the church of Saints Vitus and Wenceslaus, martyrs [Note: [Col. 0089] A, 1: “Saint Vitus and Wenceslaus”; 2: “let there be Saint V. W.”; 2b, 3, 7: “Saints Vitus and Wenceslaus, martyrs”; 4: “Saints Vitus, Wenceslaus, and Adalbert.”], there shall be an episcopal seat; but at the church of Saint George the martyr, under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the obedience of our daughter Maria, abbess, a congregation of nuns shall be established [Note: [Col. 0089] *monialium* in A.].
>
> Yet not according to the rites or sect of the Bulgarian people, or of the Rus’ [Note: [Col. 0089D] Pubitschka takes these words as proof against the forger, since in Pope John XIII’s time the Bulgarians belonged to the Catholic Church and the Rus’ did not yet profess the Christian faith.], or of the Slavonic language [Note: [Col. 0089] *Slavonicae* in 2b.], but rather, following apostolic institutions and decrees, choose, as you see fit, for this work one more suitable cleric from the whole Church, educated in Latin from his earliest letters, who may be able with the ploughshare of the word to break up the fallow ground of gentile hearts, sow the wheat of good works, and bring to Christ sheaves of the fruits of your faith. Farewell.

And immediately, as had been commanded, by the counsel of the duke and the abbess, the church of Saint Vitus [Note: [Col. 0089] “the church of Saint Vitus” in A.] was appointed for the future bishop [Note: [Col. 0090D] Not in 967 at all, but not before 973, through the help and counsel of St Wolfgang, who gained the see of Regensburg in 972, was the episcopal chair of Prague established. A witness is Henry IV in the diploma copied by Cosmas himself at II, 37, which states that the bishopric of Prague was confirmed by Otto I and Pope Benedict—namely Benedict VI, who reigned in 972–974. Dobner discussed this extensively and acutely in IV, 213. See further Pubitschka III, 18; Othlo, *Life of St Wolfgang*, chapter 29, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* IV; and the Annals of St Emmeram, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* I.]; the church of Saint George the martyr [Note: [Col. 0090D] Established by Duke Vratislav I in Prague Castle.] was for the time being granted to the abbess Maria, the duke’s sister.

23. Accordingly, there was a certain man from Saxony, of remarkable eloquence and learning, named Dethmar [Note: [Col. 0089] *Dietmarus* in 2; *Diehtmarus* in 7.], a priest by rank and monk by profession. Some time before, he had come to Prague on a matter of prayer. When he came to the notice of the second Duke Bolezlaus, he quickly acquired great favour and friendship with him [Col. 0090B]. Because he knew the Slavonic language perfectly [Note: [Col. 0089] *l. perf.* in A; *perferre* in 1.], the duke summoned him through his envoys, called together the clergy, the chief men of the land, and the people, and by his entreaties and exhortations secured their unanimous election of him as bishop [Note: [Col. 0089] *affectu* in A; *consensu* in 2b.].

On the following day, as the duke wished, Dethmar was elected bishop by the favourable acclamation of all, and sent to the most Christian Emperor Otto [Note: [Col. 0090D] According to Othlo, at the cited passage, in the time of Otto II—that is, Otto the Great’s son—the first bishop of Prague was elected. Palacký I, 229, thought this occurred at Easter 973, which Otto I celebrated at Quedlinburg; cf. the *Annals of Quedlinburg*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* III.], son of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0089] A later hand in 7 added in the margin: “of the first king.”], on behalf of the duke and all the clergy and people, with this letter [Note: [Col. 0089] Corrected in 1.]:

> O most glorious emperor and greatest champion of the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0089] Supplied above the line by another hand in A.], mercifully receive our prayers, those of all the clergy and people. We humbly entreat that this man, Dethmar [Note: [Col. 0089] *Diethmarum* in 1 and elsewhere]—proved in every respect [Note: [Col. 0089] “approved” in 3.]—whom we choose as our shepherd [Note: [Col. 0089] “whom we have chosen” in 2b.] may, by your most holy approval [Note: [Col. 0089] Omitted in 1.] and command, be ordained bishop.

Then the emperor, as a lover of the divine law, taking counsel with dukes and princes, but especially bishops, and providing for the welfare and newness of the Christian people, commanded the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0091C] Ruotbert.], who then presided over the court, to ordain him [Note: [Col. 0091] Omitted in A.] bishop. Then the bishop, crowned with the mitre, joyfully returned, new to a new diocese of all Bohemia; and, on arriving at the metropolitan city of Prague, he was enthroned beside the altar of Saint Vitus by everyone [Note: [Col. 0091] “by the people” in 7.], while all the clergy sang:

> We praise thee, O God.

But the duke [Note: [Col. 0091] “Bolezlaus” added by 4.] and nobles answered:

> Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy; and may all the saints help us, Lord, have mercy; and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0091] Codex 1, the oldest, reads: *Xpc keinando kiriel unddi gallihcenalle helfuent unse kiriel*—“Christ, have mercy, Lord; and may all the saints help us, Lord.” Codices 2, 2a, and 3 have *Christe keinado et cetera*; 2 omits *Christe keinado*, but 2b supplies *Christe keynado* in the margin; 4 has *Christe kreynab et cetera*; 7, *C. keynado et cetera*; and 7a, *Christo keynado.*]

The simpler and unlearned people cried, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) [Note: [Col. 0091] *krilesu* in A; *krlessu* in 1, 2b, 4; *kyrie eleyson* in 3; *krlesu* in 7, 7a.]; and thus, according to their custom, they spent the entire day joyfully [Note: [Col. 0091] In codex 7 the foundation of the church of Vyšehrad in 1070 follows; all the rest is absent as far as II, 37.].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 968, Count Vok died [Note: [Col. 0091] *Wok comes* in A and 2b, also in the margin; *Wolkomes* in 3; *comes Wok* in 4.].

[Col. 0091B] 24. Thereafter Bishop Dethmar consecrated churches built by the faithful in many places for the praise of God; and, baptizing the gentile people, he made very many of them faithful to Christ. Not many days later, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 969 [Note: [Col. 0091C] Again he is mistaken: Bishop Dethmar lived until 982, as appears from the *Life of St Adalbert*, chapter 8, cited above; Dobner proved this with several arguments in his notes on Hájek IV, 284. Already under the year 982 the Saxon annalist, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores* VI, criticized this error in our author.], on the fourth day before the Nones of January [2 January] [Note: [Col. 0091C] The Bohemian Necrology agrees concerning the day; in Dobner, *Monumenta Bohemica* II, 9.], freed from the bonds of the flesh, he returned to Christ a hundredfold the talent entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0091] *ceutuplum* in A.].

---

## Supplementary apparatus restored from the supplied source

The 181 inline note blocks above preserve the already translated apparatus. Sequence comparison found 50 omitted source notes and one incompletely represented note; they are restored in the following 48 grouped entries. They are restored here in canonical order, with the source forms, witness scope, and English meaning. Proper-name variants are identified as spellings of the same person or place; unexplained scribal abbreviations are preserved without invented expansions.

1. **§15, epilogue (0081):** in A another hand added *-dem* (“same”) to form *ejusdem* (“of the same”).
2. **§17, *haud* (0083):** *haud* (“not”) was corrected by another hand in A; the note supplies no rejected form.
3. **§17, *quam* (0083):** *quam* (“than/as”) was corrected by another hand in A; the note supplies no rejected form.
4. **§17, plot against Wencezlaus (0083):** codex 1 reads subjunctive *machinaretur* (“he might be plotting”) beside narrative *machinabatur* (“he was plotting”).
5. **§17, rule (0083):** 2b reads singular *gubernaculum* (“helm/government”) for plural *gubernacula* (“reins of government”).
6. **§17, birth of Ztrahquaz (0083):** codex 3 omits *quae* (“which”), and 4 lacks *ut* (“as”), in the clause introducing the feasts during which he was born.
7. **§17, terrible feast (0083):** another hand in A wrote the unexplained abbreviation *i. q.* above the line at *quam in quo* (“than one in which”).
8. **§18 opening (0083):** codex 1 has *Pot*, a defective spelling of *Post* (“after”).
9. **§18, education (0083):** codex 4 omits the entire clause *ibi ecclesiasticis … imbutus* (“there he was instructed in ecclesiastical … [ordinances]”).
10. **§18, church of St Vitus (0083):** the lemma at *Wencezlaus ecclesiam* (“Wencezlaus [built] the church”) was supplied above the line by another hand in 1.
11. **§18, Duke Bolezlaus (0083):** codex 4 adds *Boemorum* (“of the Bohemians”) after “duke.”
12. **§18, bishop’s assent (0083):** 2b reads present *impetrat* (“he obtains”) for perfect *impetravit* (“he obtained”).
13. **§18, *quod utique* (0083):** A omits *quod utique* (“which indeed”).
14. **§18, *haud annuisset* (0083):** *haud* (“not”) was corrected by another hand in A and 1; the note gives no discarded form.
15. **§18, Wencezlaus’s devotion (0083):** codex 2 reads *cum* (“when/with”) for *quia* (“because”).
16. **§18, Michael’s affection (0083):** A omits *nam et* (“for also”).
17. **§18, instruction (0083):** codex 4 omits the span *tum … Dei* (“then/often … of God”), covering Michael’s instruction in the fear and love of God.
18. **§19 heading (0083):** A has the malformed abbreviation *incarnan.* for *incarnationis* (“of the Incarnation”).
