19. **§19, Bolezlaus’s pride (0085):** codex 1 reads *intulit* (“brought upon”) for *tulit* (“bore/endured”).
20. **§19, byname (0085):** A has the abbreviation *dr* at *ut diceretur* (“so that he might be called”); its exact expansion is not supplied.
21. **§19, defiance (0085):** codex 1 reads *consistimus* (“we stand together”) for *assistimus* (“we stand before [you]”).
22. **§19, insult (0085):** codex 3 reads *cultores* (“cultivators/worshippers”) for *viliores* (“more worthless”).
23. **§19, sword or yoke (0085):** codex 1 reads *levi* (“light,” ablative/dative) for comparative *levius* (“lighter”).
24. **§19, terror (0085):** another hand in 1 supplied *i. t.*, evidently the transmitted abbreviation at *in tantum* (“to such an extent”); no fuller reading is given.
25. **§19, submission (0085):** A omits *jam ultro* (“now willingly”) in the promise to obey.
26. **§20, year 934 (0085):** A has the abbreviated word order *Ung. H. r.* (“the Hungarians—Henry—the king”) where the text reads “King Henry [struck] the Hungarians.”
27. **§20, year 938 (0085):** A omits *et* (“and”) before “the sons of Duke Arnulf.”
28. **§20, year 943 (0087):** codex 5 omits the whole span *filius … successit* (“[Conrad], son [of Werner], succeeded”).
29. **§20, year 946 (0087):** A has abbreviated *exp. r.*, representing “was expelled from the kingdom”; the source does not expand the abbreviation further.
30. **§21, Bolezlaus’s byname (0087):** 2b reads *cognomen* (“surname”) for *agnomen* (“byname”).
31. **§21, divine mercy (0087):** A has abbreviated *cl. D.* (“the mercy of God”) at *Dei clementia* (“God’s mercy”).
32. **§22 opening (0087):** the opening wording *erat autem iste* (“this man, moreover, was”) was corrected in A; no rejected form is recorded.
33. **§22, privilege (0087):** 2b reads *uti* (“as”) for *ut* (“as”).
34. **§22, papal aid (0087):** *subvenire* (“to aid”) was added in the margin of A.
35. **§22, Roman report (0089):** 2b reads *seu* (“or”) for *sive* (“or”), a synonymous form.
36. **§22, report to her brother (0089):** *fratri suo refert* (“she reports to her brother”) was corrected by another hand in 1; no rejected form is supplied.
37. **§22, papal petition (0089):** A has a corrected reading at *haud* (“not”); 1 reads corrupt *aud*, and 7 reads *non* (“not”).
38. **§22, *ut nostro assensu* (0089):** codex 1 originally read *in* (“in”), corrected by another hand to *ut* (“so that”).
39. **§22, assent (0089):** codex 1 has misspelled *asensu* for *assensu* (“assent”).
40. **§22, papal vicars (0089):** A abbreviates *vicarii sumus* (“we are vicars”) as *v. s.*.
41. **§22, canonically establish (0089):** A and 2b read *quod* (“that/which”) for *quo ad* (“so that at”) before the church designation.
42. **§22, Bulgarians and Rus’ (0089):** 2b reads *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”).
43. **§22, Rus’ (0089):** codex 3 spells the name *Russiae* and 4 *Rusciae*, for the text’s *Ruziae*; all mean “of Rus’.”
44. **§22, apostolic decrees (0089):** codex 4 reads plural *sequentes* (“following,” plural) for singular *sequens* (“following,” singular).
45. **§22, church for the bishop (0089):** the word *ecclesia* (“church”) was added in the margin of A.
46. **§23, Dethmar’s arrival (0089):** codex 3 reads imperfect subjunctive *veniret* (“he might be coming”) for pluperfect *venerat* (“he had come”).
47. **§23, next day (0089):** another hand in 1 wrote *r* above the line at *postera* (“the following”); the source gives no expansion.
48. **§23, acclamation and ordination (0089–0091):** 2b corrects *favorali* to *favorabili* (“favourable”); codex 5 omits *O gloriosissime … exoramus* (“O most glorious … we entreat”); A omits *per omnia … nobis* (“in every respect … for us”); and 4 adds *venerandus Diethmarus* (“the venerable Dethmar”) after his ordination.

25. Meanwhile, returning from the military camps to philosophy, where [Note: [Col. 0091C] At Magdeburg under Master Otric. See John Canaparius, *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 3, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 582.] he had served for ten or more [Note: [Col. 0091] *militaverat* 3, *militavit* 4.] years [Note: [Col. 0092C] How many years he studied is uncertain. Ibid., ch. 5.], bringing back with him no small quantity of books, there appeared a distinguished hero named Wogtech [Note: [Col. 0091] Thus A. *Woytiech* 2; *Woytech* in others.], still in the rank of subdeacon. Like a tender lamb among the sheep mourning over the death [Note: [Col. 0091] *de* A, A*.] of their shepherd, he diligently performed the funeral rites; persevering in prayers by day and night alike, he commended to God the soul of the universal father by abundant alms [Col. 0091C] and holy prayers. Seeing him devoted to so good a work and hoping that he would be more devoted in the future, Duke Boleslaus and his nobles [Note: [Col. 0091] *obtimantes* 1.], inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, seize the exceedingly unwilling young man [Note: [Col. 0091] *woytech* added by 4.], bring him into their midst, and say:

“Whether you wish it or not, you shall be our bishop, and bishop of Prague [Note: [Col. 0091] Omitted in A; *urbis* (‘of the city’) added by 4.], even against your will [Col. 0092A]. Your nobility, your character, and your deeds agree most fittingly with the honour of the episcopate.

> You are known to us from head to sole [Note: [Col. 0092C] Cf. Horace, *Epistles* II.2.4.].  
> You know well how to show us the way by which one goes to the heavenly homeland.  
> We must be as willing to follow your commands as we are able.  
> All the clergy acclaim you as worthy, and all the people as fit for the episcopate.”

This election took place not far from the city of Prague, in the town of Levý Hradec, on 11 Kalends of March, in the same year in which Bishop Dethmar died [Note: [Col. 0091] “at the time and in the year,” omitting “bishop,” 3; *anno* omitted in 4.].

26. At that time [Note: [Col. 0091] *vero* (“indeed”) added by 4.] [Note: [Col. 0092C] “At that time”—“occupied the cathedra” is taken from the *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 8, with a few additions by the author.] the most eminent Emperor Otto II, a lover of peace and cultivator of justice, returned from the war against the Saracens and came [Note: [Col. 0091] *abiit* (“went away”) 1.] to the city of Verona. More glorious than his most glorious father, Otto I, he was a victor most victorious in every battle [Note: [Col. 0091] Omitted in A; corrected by another hand in 1.] [Col. 0092B].

To him the Slavonic company of Bohemia went with its bishop-elect, bearing an embassy on behalf of the duke and a petition from all the clergy and people, asking that by an imperial nod he confirm their common election [Note: [Col. 0091] *Sclavonica* (“Slavonic”) 1; *munifica* (“generous”) 2. *quo* (“that”) A, 1, 3; *qui* 2; *confirmaret* 2 and the rest.]. Therefore the most serene emperor, yielding to their worthy [Note: [Col. 0091] Omitted in A.] petition, on 3 Nones of June [Note: [Col. 0091] Omitted in 5.] gave him a ring [Note: [Col. 0091] *an. dat ei* A.] and a pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 0091] *curam* (“care”) A, A*.]. Willigis, archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0091] *Willegisus* 2b; *archiepiscopus* 4.], whose suffragan he was and who happened to be present there [Note: [Col. 0091] The words “who … archbishop” were added in the margin of A by another hand; *tunc* (“then”) added by 4.], consecrated him as bishop at the emperor’s command, under the name Adalbert.

For Adalbert, archbishop of the church of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0091] *Magburgensis* 1, 3.], had formerly confirmed him with chrism and had called him by this, his own, name [Note: [Col. 0091] *vocitaverat* A, A*.]. Consecrated [Note: [Col. 0091] “Saint Adalbert was,” added by 4.] on 3 Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0091] Thus 4 alone; all the others read 3 Ides of June.] [Note: [Col. 0092C] Correctly: St Adalbert was consecrated on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, that is, 3 Kalends of July; cf. *Life of Adalbert*, ch. 8.], he rides with his followers [Note: [Col. 0091] *sequentibus* 3.] to his sweet homeland; and, when he reached the holy [Note: [Col. 0091] *sanctam* added by 4.] city of Prague, barefoot and humble in heart, while the clergy and all the populace sang for joy [Note: [Col. 0091] *kyrieleyson* added by 4.], he took possession of the episcopal cathedra.

By the counsel of this most illustrious shepherd Adalbert and through the intervention of his aforesaid and beloved sister, Abbess Maria [Note: [Col. 0091] *Mariae ab.* A.], Duke Boleslaus, with free generosity, granted to each [Note: [Col. 0093] *utrisque* A.] whatever the bishop of Prague possesses or holds to this day in his bishopric, and whatever the abbess desired [Col. 0093A] to be granted and done for the benefit of her monastery; and he confirmed this by the sacred authority of the canons [Note: [Col. 0093] Everything down to the year 994 is lacking in 7a.].

27. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 970. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 971. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 972 Saint Ulrich departed from the world [Note: [Col. 0093] These words are absent in A, 2a, 5.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] He died on 4 July 973. Cf. Gerhard, *Life of St Udalric*, ch. 27, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, p. 414.]. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 973. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 974. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 975. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 976. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 977 [Note: [Col. 0093] What follows is assigned to the preceding year in Freher.] Dubrauca died. Because she was exceedingly wanton, when, already a woman of advanced age, she married the Polish duke [Note: [Col. 0093D] Mieszko; compare what Thietmar IV.35–36 records concerning that Dubrauca, daughter of Boleslaus I, duke of the Bohemians, and Röpell, *Geschichte von Polen* I, 622.], she laid aside the head-veil and put upon herself a maiden’s crown [Col. 0093B]; and this was great folly in a woman. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 978. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 979. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 980.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 981 Slavník [Note: [Col. 0093] *Zlaunik* 1, 2b; *Slawnik* 2; *Zlaunik dux* 4.] died, the father of Saint Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0093] “15 Kalends of April,” added by 4.]. Although many things worthy of remembrance shine forth concerning his character and life [Note: [Col. 0093] *memoria* 2b.], nevertheless, if we were to report even a few of them [Note: [Col. 0093] *refferamus* 1.], we should interrupt the work we have begun.

For he was a man most cheerful in countenance toward everyone, most serene in mind in counsel [Note: [Col. 0093] *vitae* (“of life”) 3.], most gracious in conversation [Note: [Col. 0093] The preceding words are absent in 5.], rich in both worldly and spiritual wealth. In his house [Note: [Col. 0093] “In his house”—“defence” is absent in 5.] honourableness shone, together with sincere affection, upright judgment, and a multitude of nobles [Note: [Col. 0093] Corrected by another hand in 1.]. His deeds included knowledge of the laws, the feeding of the poor, the consolation of the sorrowful [Col. 0093C], the reception of pilgrims, and the defence of widows and orphans [Note: [Col. 0093] “and orphans” absent in 4.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] Compare the *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. …].

The capital of this most distinguished duke was Libice [Note: [Col. 0093D] Libicz in the Bidschow district; cf. Schaller XVI, 21.], situated where the River Cidlina [Note: [Col. 0093] *Cidlina* 1, 3; *Cidlinia* 2; *Cydlina* 4.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] The Czidlina, a river which flows into the Elbe near Libicz. Ibid.] loses its name by entering the river Labe, a watercourse of freer flow [Note: [Col. 0093] *atque* (“and”) 1.]. The boundaries of his principality were as follows [Note: [Col. 0093] *os*, corrected by another hand to *hos*, 1.].

On the western side, toward Bohemia, were the brook Surina [Note: [Col. 0093] *Sirina*, corrected in 1; *Surma* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] The Bílá, which flows into the Elbe near Aussig. Ibid., V, 14.] and the castle situated upon Mount Oseca [Note: [Col. 0093] *Ossieka* 2.] beside the River Mže [Note: [Col. 0093] *Mzie* 2.]. Likewise, on the southern side toward the eastern Germans, the following towns formed his boundary: Chýnov [Note: [Col. 0093] *Chinov* 1, 2b, 4; *Hinou* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0093D] Cheynow.], Doudleby [Note: [Col. 0093D] Daudleb.], and Netolice [Note: [Col. 0093] *Netholici* 1; *Notoliczi* 2; *Notholici* 2b, originally, but corrected to *Netholici*, with the final *i* deleted and *e* written above it; *Netholici* 3.] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Netolitz.], as far as the middle of the forest.

Likewise, toward sunrise and the kingdom of Moravia, there was the castle beneath the forest called Litomyšl [Note: [Col. 0093] *Lutomisl* 1, 4; *Liutomysl* 2; *Lutomizl* 2b; *Lutomis*, with the name omitted, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Leutomischl.], as far as the brook Svitava [Note: [Col. 0093] *Zuitava* 1, 2b; *Zuitawa* 2; *Suttava* 3; *Zwitana* 4.], which lies in the middle of the forest. Likewise, on the northern side toward Poland, there was the castle of Kłodzko [Note: [Col. 0093] *Kladzcho* 1, 2b; *Kladsko* 2; *Kladsco* 3; *Glecz* added by a recent hand in 5.] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Glatz.], situated beside the river called Nysa [Note: [Col. 0093] *Nisam*, corrected by another hand to *Nizam*, 1; *Mzam* 2; *Nizzam* 3; *Nizan* 4.] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Neisse.]. This Duke Slavník lived happily as long as he lived [Col. 0094B].

28. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 982. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 983.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 984 Emperor Otto II died at Rome [Note: [Col. 0094D] It is certain that he died in the preceding year.]. Bishop Adalbert of Prague was so intimate with and dear to this emperor [Note: [Col. 0093] “the second” added by 4.] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Rather, with Otto III; cf. *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 22.] because of his services that, at the Lord’s Easter [Note: [Col. 0093] Omitted in 3.], celebrated by the king at Aachen in the palace before all the bishops, he raised him to this high office: namely, that he should place the crown upon him and celebrate the greater Mass, an act which it was lawful for an archbishop alone to perform [Note: [Col. 0094D] One must by no means think of Otto III’s coronation, but of the placing of the crown, as was customary on feast days; this is sufficiently apparent from the author’s own words. When it occurred is not clear. The records prove that Otto celebrated Easter at Aachen in 995; see Böhmer, *Regesta*, no. 746. The author of his *Life* appears to suggest, chs. 19–20, that St Adalbert was in Germany at approximately the same time.].

After the feast, when he had already received [Note: [Col. 0093] *accepisset* 3.] leave from the emperor to return home, the emperor called [Note: [Col. 0093] *clam vocat* (“calls secretly”) 4.] him aside into his private chamber. Having confessed his sins, he commended himself [Col. 0094C] to the bishop’s pious remembrance in prayer. Moreover, he gave him the vestments in which he had celebrated [Note: [Col. 0093] *celebravit* 4; *celebraret* 3, with correction in 2b.] Mass at Easter: an alb, dalmatic, chasuble, cope [Col. 0095A], and towel (*faciterium*) [Note: [Col. 0095] *facitersium*, corrected in 2; *facitergium* 3.], so that he might possess them in remembrance of him. To this day these are honourably kept in the church of Prague and are called the vestments of Saint Adalbert.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 985 [Note: [Col. 0095] The number was added in the margin of A by another hand.]. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 986. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 987 Střezislava [Note: [Col. 0095] *Zrezizlava* 1, 2b, 4; *Strziezislawa* 2; *Zrezizlana* 3; *Ztrelizizlava* 5.] [Note: [Col. 0095C] Of a most noble distinguished Slavonic family; cf. Bruno, *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 1.] died, the venerable and God-pleasing matron, mother of Saint Adalbert, worthy to be called and to be the mother of offspring so great and so holy [Note: [Col. 0095] Corrected in 1.]. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 988. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 989. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 990 [Note: [Col. 0095C] Already at Christmas 988 St Adalbert seems to have been staying in Rome; cf. Wilmans, *Otto III*, p. 92.] Saint Adalbert became a monk at Saint Alexius in Rome, the abbot not knowing who he was. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 991. [Col. 0095B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 992. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 993. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 994.

29. Nor do I think that what I see has been passed over by others should be skipped [Note: [Col. 0095] Here manuscript 7a begins again.]. For Bishop Adalbert, seeing that the flock entrusted to him was always heading for ruin and that he could not turn it back to the right path, feared that he too would perish with the perishing [Note: [Col. 0095] *perheunte* 1.] people. He did not dare to remain with them any longer, nor did he permit his labour of preaching to be expended further in vain [Note: [Col. 0095] Corrected in 1.].

But when he was just about to set out for Rome [Note: [Col. 0095] Second *jamque* omitted in 1, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0095C] This was St Adalbert’s first journey to Rome; accordingly, it cannot with Cosmas be assigned to the year 994.], by chance, at that very time Strachkvas [Note: [Col. 0095] *Ztrahquaz* 1, 4.], of whom we have spoken above, had come from Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0095] *Radispona* 1.] with his abbot’s permission, after many years, to see his sweet homeland, his relatives, and his brother [Col. 0095C], duke of Bohemia. The man of God, Bishop Adalbert, sought a private interview with him and complained at length of the people’s unfaithfulness and wickedness, of incestuous unions and of the unlawful dissolutions [Note: [Col. 0095] *dissidia* 2b, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0096C] *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 12.] of unstable marriage, of the clergy’s disobedience and negligence, and of the arrogance and intolerable power of the counts.

Finally, he disclosed to him his heart’s whole intention [Note: [Col. 0095] *aperit* (“discloses”) A, A*.]: that he wished to go to Rome to consult the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0096C] John XVI, who held office in the years 985–996.] and never to return to the apostate [Note: [Col. 0095] *apostaticam* 3.] people. Among these remarks he added this:

“It is well,” he said, “that you are known as the duke’s brother and derive your origin from the lords [Note: [Col. 0095] *et*, corrected to *ex*, 1; *dominis*, corrected from *domini*, 1. The words ‘and … derive’ are absent in A, A*.] of this land [Col. 0096A]. This people prefers you [Note: [Col. 0095] *magis vult* 4.] to rule and obeys you more willingly than me. By the counsel and help of your brother [Note: [Col. 0095] *tui* omitted in A, A*.] you will be able to restrain the proud, rebuke the negligent, correct the disobedient, and reproach the unfaithful. Your rank and learning, and the holiness of your conduct, accord greatly [Note: [Col. 0095] *multum* omitted in 2.] with episcopal government. In order that this may come about, I grant it to you by God’s will and my own authority; and, that it may be permitted for you to be bishop here during my lifetime, I shall intercede with every prayer before the Apostolic See” [Note: [Col. 0095] *intendam* 3.].

And he placed in Strachkvas’s lap the episcopal staff which he perhaps held in his hand. But the latter, as though mad, threw it to the ground and added these words:

“I do not wish to have [Note: [Col. 0095] Omitted in all manuscripts; written above the line by another hand in 1.] any rank in the world [Note: [Col. 0095] *possideam* 4.]; I flee honours [Col. 0096B] [Note: [Col. 0095] From the words *honores fugio* the chronicle continues in manuscript 4a.], I despise worldly pomp. I judge myself unworthy of the episcopal dignity, and I am unable to bear so great a burden of pastoral care. I am a monk; I am dead: I cannot bury the dead.”

To this the bishop [Note: [Col. 0095] “Adalbert,” added by 4, 4a.] replied: “Know, brother [Note: [Col. 0095] “Strachkvas,” added by 4, 4a.], know that what you now fail to do for good, you will do later, but to your own very great [Note: [Col. 0095] Omitted in A, A*.] harm.”

After this the bishop [Note: [Col. 0095] “Adalbert,” added by 4.] set out for Rome as he had intended and left behind the people disobedient to his commands [Note: [Col. 0095] *reliquit* 2.]. And because at that time the duke was not his own master but subject to the counts [Note: [Col. 0095] *ducum* A; *ducis* A*.], the counts, turned to hatred of God, the most wicked sons of wicked fathers, committed a very wicked [Note: [Col. 0095] *scelus* 4, 4a.] and unjust deed.

For on a certain feast day [Note: [Col. 0095] *die festivo* A, A*; *festivitate* 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0096C] The feast of St Wenceslaus; cf. Bruno, *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 21. But this occurred after his second journey to Rome, in 996.] they secretly burst into the town of Libice, where the brothers of Saint Adalbert and all the town’s soldiers, like innocent sheep, were attending the solemn rites of the Mass and celebrating the feast [Col. 0096C]. But they, like savage wolves, broke through the city walls, killed every male and female without exception, beheaded four [Note: [Col. 0095] *universis* 3.] brothers of Saint Adalbert with all their offspring before the very altar, burned the town [Note: [Col. 0095] “Libice,” added by 4, 4a.], drenched its streets with blood, and, laden with bloody spoils and cruel plunder [Note: [Col. 0095] Corrected by another hand in 1.], merrily returned [Note: [Col. 0095] Thus A, 1; *recedunt* (“depart”) A, A*.] to their own homes.

Five brothers of Saint Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0095] “the bishop,” added by 4, 4a.] were killed in the town of Libice in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 995. Their names [Note: [Col. 0095] “their names” omitted in 2. A line in different ink is drawn after the words “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 995.”] [Col. 0097A] are these: Soběbor, Spytimír [Note: [Col. 0097] Formerly *Spitimur* 2; *Sptimir* 4, 4a.], Dobroslav [Note: [Col. 0097] *Bobrazlau* 1, 2b; formerly *Bobraslau* in 2, then the second *b* altered to *h*, *ra* deleted, and *II* written above, thus corrected to *Bobuslau*; *Bohrazlau* according to the collator of 2b; *Drobozlau* 3; *Pobrazlau* 4, 4a.], Porej [Note: [Col. 0097] *Poreii* 3.], and Čáslav [Note: [Col. 0097] *Cazlav* 1 and the rest; *Czaslau* 2; *Chazlaw* 5.].

30. When these things had thus [Note: [Col. 0097] *itaque* 2a.] occurred, Duke Boleslaus, after taking counsel with the clergy, addressed the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0097] Omitted in A.] in these words:

“Either bring back to us our shepherd Adalbert, which we prefer, or ordain another for us in his place, which we ask unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0097] *possimus*, corrected by another hand to *poscimus*, 1.]. For Christ’s sheepfolds, still new to the faith among this people, unless the watchful protection of a shepherd attends them, become rich and ready food for bloody [Note: [Col. 0097] *rapidis vel rabidis cruentis* 1.] wolves [Note: [Col. 0097] *recte* 2b, 4, 4a; *fient* 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0097] *edilia* 2, corrected by another hand to *edulia*.].”

Then the metropolitan of Mainz, anxious lest a people newly [Note: [Col. 0097] *a* added by 2.] won for Christ should relapse and perish in its ancient sacrilegious rites, sent envoys to the Apostolic See and asked that it either send back a husband to the widowed church of Prague [Note: [Col. 0097C] *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 18.] or permit another to be ordained in his place [Note: [Col. 0097] *suo ordinare* 4, 4a.].

And because the servant of God Adalbert, freed from the custody of the Lord’s flock by the Apostolic See’s command, dwelt in the monastery of Saint Alexius [Note: [Col. 0097] “the confessor,” added by 4, 4a.] with the senators of heaven beneath the pleasant court of earthly Elysium [Note: [Col. 0097] *conversabantur*, corrected to *conversabatur*, 1.],

> The lord pope and his own pious abbot together [Note: [Col. 0097C] Leo, abbot of the monastery of St Alexius.],  
> comfort the sorrowful man with such friendly words:  
>
> “O sweetest son and most beloved brother [Note: [Col. 0097] “Adalbert,” added by 4a.],  
> we beseech you by the love of God [Note: [Col. 0097] *deprecor* (“I beseech”) 1.]  
> and implore you by love of your neighbour,  
> graciously return to your diocese [Note: [Col. 0097] The letter *c* added above the line by another hand in 1.]  
> and diligently resume the governance of your sheep.  
>
> If they listen to you, thanks be to God; if they do not listen, flee them as they flee you [Note: [Col. 0097] Omitted in 4, 4a.],  
> lest you perish with those who perish; and may you have leave to preach among foreign nations.”

Greatly cheered by this ruling, Bishop Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0097] “Adalbert,” added by 4, 4a.]—because he had been granted [Note: [Col. 0097] *est* 1.] permission to teach foreign peoples—did not leave the sweet fellowship of the brethren without great sorrow [Note: [Col. 0097] *liquit* 2b.]. With Bishop Nothar [Note: [Col. 0097] *Votharino*, corrected in 2b; *Notario* 4a.], a man of the highest discernment [Note: [Col. 0097C] Bishop of Liège; cf. *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 21. But this occurred on the second journey to Rome, in 996; the author confuses the two journeys.], he went [Note: [Col. 0097] Omitted in 4, 4a.] to the archbishop of Mainz [Col. 0098B] and asked him in his palace to learn through his messengers whether his flock would be willing to receive him [Note: [Col. 0097] The words “flock … his” were inserted in the margin of A by another hand; corrected by another hand in 1.].

> What answer his flock gave him in this matter,  
> why it did not receive him,  
> to what peoples he then went,  
> how great his temperance was throughout all the days of his episcopate,  
> and how brightly he shone in uprightness of character—  
> one may learn who has read his *Life* or [Note: [Col. 0097] *sive* 2.] *Passion*.  
>
> For I do not wish to repeat what has already been said twice [Note: [Col. 0097] *biis* 1.].

Then Strachkvas [Note: [Col. 0097] *Strahquas* 2, and so thereafter.], the duke’s brother, whom we have mentioned above, seeing that the bishop had seemingly been rejected by his own people lawfully and canonically [Note: [Col. 0097] *regaliter* (“royally”) 2a.], burned with swollen pride for the episcopate. And since it is easy to compel one who is willing, the wicked people immediately raised this ignoramus and impostor to the episcopal cathedra [Note: [Col. 0097] *locat* (“places”) 3.].

For thus, thus God often permits, by his providence [Col. 0098B], the power of evil men to prevail, just as in this irregular [Note: [Col. 0097] The syllable *in-* added above the line by another hand in A; *regulari* 4, 4a.] farcical [Note: [Col. 0097] *ludrica* A; *ludicitus* 3.] election the offspring of Ceres [Note: [Col. 0097] *genere*, corrected to *generi*, A.] prevailed [Note: [Col. 0097] *praevalere*, corrected by another hand to *praevaluere*, A; *praevalere* 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0098C] That is, of the devil.]. For this Strachkvas was orderly in dress, swollen in mind, dissolute in deeds, wandering in eyes, empty in speech, a hypocrite in character, the director of every error, and in every evil deed an arch-leader of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0097] *archigeron* 4.] [Col. 0098C].

> I am ashamed to recount more concerning Strachkvas, the false bishop.

A few things suffice in place of many [Note: [Col. 0099] *sufficiant* 2b, 3, 4.]. He had come to the archbishop of the see of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0099] Added above the line by another hand in A; *episcopum* 3.] [Col. 0099A]. There, after all that had to be done had been carried out in due order, as is customary, after the episcopal examination, while the choir sang the litany [Note: [Col. 0099] *laetamini*, corrected to *laetaniam*, 2b; *laetamina* 3.] [Col. 0100A], the mitred archbishop prostrated himself before the altar upon the carpets, and after him, between two suffragans,

> Strachkvas, who was to be ordained, lay prostrate in the middle [Note: [Col. 0099] Omitted in A.],  
> when—alas for the dreadful condition!—he was seized by a cruel demon;  
> and what the servant [Note: [Col. 0099] *serus*, corrected by another hand to *servus*, 1.] of God [Note: [Col. 0099] “Adalbert,” added by 4, 4a.] had once foretold to him secretly  
> became openly manifest before the clergy and all the people.

Let it suffice to have inserted these matters so far [Note: [Col. 0099] *sufficiant* 3; “Let it suffice … so far” absent in 5; “so far … 996” absent in 7a.] [Note: [Col. 0099C] Pubitschka attempted to prove, III, 224, that this is a mere fable.].

31. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 996 [Note: [Col. 0099C] St Adalbert died in 997; cf. Palacký, *Würdigung*, p. 28.], after the distinguished standard-bearer of Christ, Bishop Adalbert, had caught Pannonia and Poland alike in the nets of faith, at last, while sowing God’s word in Prussia [Note: [Col. 0099] *Brussia* 2, 3.], he happily ended this present life for Christ by martyrdom on 9 Kalends of May, a Friday [Note: [Col. 0099] The remainder of this book is entirely lacking in 7a. The foundation of the church of Vyšehrad in 1070 follows.]. In that year Easter fell on 7 Kalends [Note: [Col. 0099] 6 Kalends 3.] of May [Note: [Col. 0099C] *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 30. Easter in the year 996 was celebrated on 12 April.].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 997, the often-mentioned Duke Boleslaus, seeing that the church of Prague was bereft of its shepherd, sent his envoys to Emperor Otto III, asking [Note: [Col. 0099] Omitted in 3.] him to give the Bohemian church a spouse worthy by merit, lest [Note: [Col. 0099] “that … does not return” 2.] the flock newly dedicated to Christ return to its former rites of vanity and wicked deeds. Indeed, he declared that at that time no cleric worthy of the episcopate was to be found in all Bohemia.

Immediately Emperor Otto Augustus, as he was most prudent in divine and human affairs, assented to their petition and began to consider more carefully which of his own clerics he should send for this difficult task. By chance there was at the royal court [Note: [Col. 0099C] Theodagus was not at the emperor’s court but at that of Duke Boleslaus II. A monk of New Corvey, skilled in medicine, he had restored the duke to health; cf. Thietmar VII.41, who nevertheless confirms that Theodagus received from Otto the government of the see of Prague.] a chaplain named Theodagus [Note: [Col. 0099] *Thegdagus* 1, 3 and thereafter; corrected to *Thedgadus* 2b.], honourable in deeds and adorned in character, thoroughly educated in the liberal studies, Saxon by birth, and perfectly versed in the Slavonic language [Note: [Col. 0099] *proferre* (“to speak”) 1, 3; *Slavica* 4, 4a.]. Since chance had presented him, the whole senate of the royal court and the emperor himself, greatly pleased, chose and commended him as bishop of the church of Prague; and they ordered the archbishop of Mainz by message to consecrate him swiftly as bishop.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 998, on the Nones of July, Theodagus was consecrated. He was honourably received by the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0099] “and people” omitted in 2b.] of the church of Prague [Col. 0100A], and with great rejoicing enthroned at the corner of the altar of Saint Vitus. The duke rejoices greatly because a good shepherd smiles upon his flock, and the happy flock plays about its new [Note: [Col. 0099] *suo* (“its own”) 2b.] shepherd.

32. This most excellent prince, Boleslaus [Col. 0100B], ruled the duchy for thirty-two years after his father’s death. He was a most ardent champion of justice, the Catholic [Note: [Col. 0099] *chatolice* 1.] faith, and the Christian religion; under him [Note: [Col. 0099] *christianae* repeated in 1.] no one obtained either ecclesiastical or secular rank through money [Note: [Col. 0099] *pro pecunia* 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]. He was also [Note: [Col. 0099] *et* 2b, 3, 4, 4a.], as events prove, a victor most victorious in battle, yet a most merciful pardoner of the conquered and an outstanding lover of peace. He had immense wealth, implements of war, and a sweet delight in arms. For he loved the hardness of iron more than the glitter of gold. In his eyes no useful man was displeasing, and no useless man ever pleasing. He was gentle to his own people and terrible to his enemies.

This most glorious duke [Note: [Col. 0099] “Boleslaus,” added by 4, 4a.] had Hemma as his wife, who was nobler than others in birth [Note: [Col. 0100C] Dobner IV, 432 conjectures that she was a daughter of King Conrad of Burgundy.] [Col. 0100C], but, more worthy of praise, far superior in nobility of character [Note: [Col. 0099] Corrected by another hand in 1.]. By her he had two sons of excellent disposition [Note: [Col. 0100C] Rather four: besides the named Wenceslaus and Boleslaus, Jaromír and Ulrich—whom Cosmas wrongly thinks were sons of Boleslaus III—were sons of Boleslaus II, according to Thietmar V.15.], namely Wenceslaus and Boleslaus. But Wenceslaus exchanged this frail life for eternity from his earliest age [Note: [Col. 0099] *hanc* omitted in 2, 2b, 3.]. After his father’s departure, Boleslaus took up the reins of princely rule, as will be explained below [Note: [Col. 0099] *declaratur* A.].

33. When the days of the aforesaid Duke Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 0099] *appropinquaret* 3; “duke” omitted in 2, 2b, 3.] drew near, in which he was now to exchange life for eternal death [Note: [Col. 0099] *com. m. v. aet.* A.], he summoned his namesake and surviving son [Note: [Col. 0099] *natu* 4, 4a.]. With his wife Hemma [Note: [Col. 0099] *Hemina* 2.] [Note: [Col. 0100C] The very obscure origin of this Emma greatly vexed investigators of Bohemian history. See Pubitschka III, 153; Palacký I.] and a great company of nobles present [Col. 0101A] [Note: [Col. 0101] *turoa* 2.], his words already broken by sobbing [Note: [Col. 0101] *interrupente* A.], he addressed his beloved son as best he could in these words:

“If it were permitted for a mother to bestow upon the infant of her womb gifts of wisdom just as she gives breasts of milk [Note: [Col. 0101] *suae utit infantis* 1.], then not nature, but created man, would rule over creation. Yet God has bestowed certain gifts upon human beings, as upon Noah, Isaac, Tobit, and Mattathias; but only in this way: that those whom they blessed, God blessed; and those whom they appointed beforehand to a life of good conduct, God also granted perseverance [Note: [Col. 0101] *benedixerit* 2; corrected to *benedixerunt* in 3. *praeordinaverit* 3.].

“So also today, my son, unless the mercy of the Holy Spirit is present, the boastfulness of my words profits little. ‘I have made you duke,’ says God [Note: [Col. 0101] Added by another hand in 1, 2.]; ‘do not be exalted, but be as one of them’ [Note: [Col. 0101] *eis* 4, 4a.]. That is [Note: [Col. 0101] *i.* A.], if you feel yourself loftier than others, nevertheless know yourself to be mortal [Note: [Col. 0101] *tamen* added by another hand in A; omitted in 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0101] *esse* omitted in 4a.]; do not [Note: [Col. 0101] *ne* 2, 2b, 3.] look to the glory of rank by which you are raised in the world, but attend to the work which you will carry with you to the underworld [Col. 0101B].

“Write these precepts of God in your heart, and do not neglect these commands of your father. Visit the thresholds of churches often; worship God; honour his priests. Do not be wise in your own eyes, but consult many men, if they are wise in the same matter [Note: [Col. 0101] “but … matter” absent in A.].

> Strive to please many, but consider what sort they are.  
> Discuss everything with friends, but first discuss your friends themselves.  
> Judge justly, but not without mercy.  
> Do not despise the widow and stranger standing at your door [Note: [Col. 0101] Corrected by another hand in 1.].  
>
> Love the denarius, but love its form sparingly.

“For the commonwealth, though it has been greatly enlarged [Note: [Col. 0101] Omitted in 4, 4a.], will swiftly be reduced to nothing by a false form of coinage [Note: [Col. 0101] A recent hand has written *autem* (‘however’) above the line in red.].

“There is something, my son, which Charles [Col. 0101C], a king most wise and mighty in hand [Note: [Col. 0101] Omitted in 4, 4a.], not to be compared [Note: [Col. 0101] Thus corrected in A; *equipperandus* 1.] with us very humble men [Note: [Col. 0101] Over the words ‘not … humble’ are written in 2 these Bohemian glosses: *gesto mi nizizi hide nemnozem si geczin wronelati* [reading and meaning materially uncertain].], did when he intended to raise his son Pippin to the throne after him. He bound him with a terrible oath [Note: [Col. 0101] *cum terribili eum* 2, 2b; *eum terribili cum* 3.] that no deceitful [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *chytra*, ‘cunning, deceitful’.] and corrupt assessment [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *czena*, ‘assessment, valuation’.] of weight [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *promiena*, ‘alteration, change’.] or coinage should occur in his kingdom.

“Certainly no disaster [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *wahy zahuba*, ‘destruction of weight’], no plague [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *mor*, ‘pestilence’.], no mortality, nor even if enemies should lay waste the whole land with plunder [Note: [Col. 0101] *et* added in 2b, 3; Bohemian gloss: *lupezem*, ‘with plunder’.] and fire [Note: [Col. 0101] *devastantes* 3.], would harm God’s people more than the frequent alteration and fraudulent debasement of coinage [Note: [Col. 0101] In 2 the reading is difficult, so that one might read *invitatio* rather than *immutatio*; but the margin has *mutatio*.].

“What plague, or what infernal Fury, plunders, destroys, and diminishes Christians more cruelly than fraud in the lord’s coinage [Col. 0102A]? And yet, when justice grows old and wickedness gains strength, there will arise not dukes but thieves, not rulers of God’s people but wicked exactors, men most avaricious and without mercy, fearing not God who sees all things [Note: [Col. 0101] *metuentes* 3.]. By changing the coinage three or four times a year [Note: [Col. 0101] Omitted in 5.] they will go [Note: [Col. 0101] *ruunt* 3; *eunt* 4, 4a.] into the devil’s snare [Note: [Col. 0101] Bohemian gloss: *kosidla*, ‘snares’; *diablowa*, ‘of the devil’.], to the ruin of God’s people. By such wicked devices and by defiance of the laws, they will narrow the borders of this kingdom which I enlarged, by God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0101] *misericordiam* (‘mercy’) A.] and the people’s abundance, as far as the mountains beyond Kraków [Note: [Col. 0101] *Crakov* 1, and so thereafter; *Krakou* 3.] called Triti [Note: [Col. 0101] *Triti* A; *Trytri* 1; *Tryu* 2; *Tryti* 2b, but corrected by the corrector to *Trnin*; *Triti* 3; *Tritri* 4, 4a.].

> For the wealth of the people is the king’s praise and glory,
Poverty that serves is burdensome not to itself but to its master. [Note: [Col. 0101] *premit* “presses,” written above the line by a later hand in 1; “which burdens him whom it serves” 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0101C] Lucan, *Pharsalia* III.152.] [Col. 0102B] He would have said more, but his final hour closed the prince’s lips [Note: [Col. 0101] *diriguerat* 3.]; and, sooner than speech could tell, he fell asleep in the Lord, and great mourning arose over him. The day of his death was 7 February, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 999.

### 34.

In the same year Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 0101] “archbishop” added by 4a.], also called Radim [Note: [Col. 0101] Radun 3.], brother of Saint Adalbert, was ordained bishop [Note: [Col. 0101] “bishop” absent from 4, 4a.] to the see of the church of Gniezno [Note: [Col. 0101] Genezdensis 1.] [Note: [Col. 0101C] Already in the table for the year 999 mention is made of Archbishop Gaudentius; cf. Wilmans, *Otto III*, p. 113.].

This most glorious Duke Boleslaus II—truly, even today, not sufficiently mourned [Note: [Col. 0101] corrected in A.], [Note: [Col. 0101] *satis* (“sufficiently”) absent from A, 1, 2, 2a, 4, 4a, 5; both *haud* (“not”) and *satis* absent from 2b.], whose memory is a blessing—extended and enlarged by the sword the boundaries of his duchy, as apostolic authority attests in the privilege concerning the same bishopric of Prague. [Note: [Col. 0101] “by enlarging he extended” 2b.] [Note: [Col. 0101C] I doubt whether Cosmas rightly inferred, from the description of the diocese of Prague in the papal privilege, that Boleslaus had enlarged the frontiers of the kingdom by the sword.]

After his death his son, Boleslaus III [Col. 0102C] [Note: [Col. 0102C] Surnamed Rufus, according to Thietmar V.7.], as related above [Note: [Col. 0101] “we related” 4, 4a.], succeeded to the duchy; but he neither retained the boundaries acquired by his father with the same success in affairs nor under his father’s auspices. For Duke Mieszko of Poland [Note: [Col. 0101] Mesko 1, and so thereafter.] [Note: [Col. 0102C] Rather, this was Boleslaus surnamed Chrobry, son of Mieszko.], than whom no man was more deceitful, soon seized the city of Cracow by treachery, putting to the sword all the Bohemians whom he found there. [Note: [Col. 0102C] Krakan.]

Now Duke Boleslaus had by a noble wife two brothers [Note: [Col. 0101] absent from A.], [Note: [Col. 0101] Bolezlao 1.], [Note: [Col. 0101] “two [sisters],” omitting “brothers,” 3.], born to the glory of a fruitful mother [Note: [Col. 0101] “second” 2, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0102C] See above: this is false.], namely Udalric [Note: [Col. 0101] Oodaldricus 1; Udalricus 2b; Oalrilcus 3, and so thereafter; Odelricus 4; Oudalricus 4a; Dedalricus 5.] and Jaromir. Jaromir, while still a youth, was reared in his father’s court; but Udalric [Col. 0103A] [Note: [Col. 0103] Odaldricus 1.] had from childhood been entrusted to the court of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0103] Henrici A.], that he might learn its manners [Note: [Col. 0103] thus corrected in 1; *morem*, “custom,” A and the rest.] and its [Note: [Col. 0103] absent from A.] cunning, and the German language. [Note: [Col. 0103D] They had fled to Germany because Boleslaus had ordered Jaromir to be castrated and Udalric to be suffocated in a bath; cf. Thietmar V.15. From the order of events itself it is clear that Henry was at that time by no means emperor, but duke of Bavaria.]

After this, when no long time had passed [Note: [Col. 0103D] That is, in 1003. Cosmas overlooks the fact that Boleslaus was expelled from Bohemia in 1002 and restored in 1003 by Boleslaus of Poland, while in the intervening period the Pole Wladiboi and Jaromir held the kingdom for a few months. On all these matters see Thietmar, cited passage.], the two aforesaid rulers, Mieszko and Boleslaus, meet for a conference at an appointed place [Note: [Col. 0103] “council” 1.]. Having pledged their faith and confirmed peace between themselves by oath, Duke Mieszko invites Boleslaus to deign to come to his [Note: [Col. 0103] “to his … come” A.] banquet. But he, being—as he was—a dovelike man without gall [Note: [Col. 0103D] In Thietmar V.7 he is the author of boundless impiety, and deservedly so; compare what Thietmar himself relates in V.18.], said on the advice of his household followers that he wished to do all things.

But what pest is more harmful than enemies within one’s household? Since he could not oppose their deceitful counsels—indeed, now yielding to his destiny—alas for the duke’s foreboding mind! He summons to himself the nobler men and those whom he was about to leave in the kingdom, who seemed to him the more faithful, [Col. 0103B] and addresses them in these words:

“If perchance anything should happen to me in Poland—God forbid!—other than, and contrary to, faith and expectation, I entrust this my son Jaromir to your fidelity [Note: [Col. 0103] erased in 1.], and leave him to you as duke in my place.”

Having thus arranged the affairs of the kingdom, he goes to be deprived of sight, and enters the city of Cracow, under the sinister omen [Note: [Col. 0103] *homine*, “man,” 1.] of the treacherous Duke Mieszko, for [Note: [Col. 0103] absent from 4, 4a.] the banquet. For immediately during the meal peace, pledged faith, and the law of hospitality are broken: Duke Boleslaus is captured and deprived of his eyes [Note: [Col. 0103D] He did not die until 1037, as the Prague Annals attest.], and his followers—some are slaughtered, [Note: [Col. 0103] “the others are slaughtered” absent from 4, 4a.] others butchered, others handed over to prison.

Meanwhile the household followers and domestic enemies of Duke Boleslaus—the hateful people, the evil generation, the Vršovci [Note: [Col. 0103] Wirsovici 1; Wirssevici 2b; Versovici 3; Wrssovici 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0104D] This is a patronymic: the sons or descendants of Wrs; cf. Palacký, *Geschichte Böhmens*, I, 163, 363.]—were perpetrating an abominable evil, unheard of in former ages. [Note: [Col. 0103] “are perpetrating” 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0104D] At what time this happened is not sufficiently clear. Dobner V, 57 assigns the crime to the year 1012.] The first among them, and as it were the head of all iniquity, was Kochan [Note: [Col. 0103] *c* written above the line by another hand in A; Kohan 1, 2b, 4, 4a; Cohan 3.], [Col. 0103C] a most wicked man and the worst of all evil men.

He and his kinsmen, wicked men [Note: [Col. 0103] “wicked men” absent from A, 1.], came with the duke and his son Jaromir to a hunting-place called Weliz [Note: [Col. 0103] Veliz 2; Weliz 2b, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0104D] In later times there stood at this place a provostship dedicated to St John the Baptist, situated not far from Rakonicz and destroyed in the Hussite war. Cf. Pubitschka III, 205.]. When report brought them news of what had happened to the duke in Poland, they said:

“Who is this little man [Note: [Col. 0103] *h* written above the line by another hand in 1.], [Col. 0104A] more worthless than seaweed [Note: [Col. 0104D] Horace, *Satires* II.2.8.], who ought [Note: [Col. 0103] “ought” A, 2, 4.] to be greater than we and be called lord? Is no better man to be found among us, one more worthy to rule?”

Ah, evil mind, evil spirit! What they ponder sober, they do openly when drunk. For when their iniquity grew hot [Note: [Col. 0103] written above the line in A.] and took on horns through wine, they seize their lord and cruelly bind him; naked and lying face upward, they fasten his arms and feet to the ground with wooden [Note: [Col. 0103] “wooden” absent from 2b, 4, 4a.] nails. Then, playing a military game, they dance a dance [Note: [Col. 0103] absent from 4, 4a.], leaping on horseback over the body of their lord. [Note: [Col. 0103] “omit” 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0103] *eri* corrected to *heri*, “lord,” by another hand in 1.]

Seeing this, one of the converts [Note: [Col. 0103] “his own” added by 3.] named Dovora [Note: [Col. 0103] Hovora 2a, and so thereafter; Dowora 4.], ran swiftly to Prague:

> He reported to the duke’s friends what had been done [Note: [Col. 0103] “to the duke” 2.], [Note: [Col. 0103] *nunctat* A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]  
> and in that same hour [Note: [Col. 0103] *ora* corrected to *hora*, “hour,” in 1.] led them without delay to the shameful prize.

When the workers of iniquity [Col. 0104B] saw them [Note: [Col. 0103] “what” 4.] suddenly rushing upon them armed, they scattered like bats through the hiding places of the woods. [Note: [Col. 0103] “darknesses” A.] But when the others found the duke grievously torn by flies and half-dead—for, as a swarm of bees, so a host of flies was mounting upon his naked body—they released him, placed him in a vehicle, and carried him into the city of Vyšehrad. [Note: [Col. 0103] Wisegrad 1; Wissograd 2.]

But to Dovora, the servant worthy of all praise and the duke’s friend, such favor was rendered for his service. [Note: [Col. 0103] absent from 2.] For it was proclaimed everywhere in the marketplaces by a herald’s voice [Note: [Col. 0103] falsely repeated in 1: “for his service.”], [Note: [Col. 0103] *praeconia*, “proclamations,” A, 3, 4, 4a.] that Dovora himself and his descendants after him should be forever and beyond counted among the nobles and freeborn. [Note: [Col. 0103] “the duke’s friends” added by corrected 2b.] Moreover, they grant him the hunting dignity belonging to the estate of Stebecna [Note: [Col. 0103] Stebecznam 2; Sthecnam 3; Stbecnam 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0104D] Zbecna in the district of Žatec.], which from that time until now his descendants have possessed generation after generation.

[Col. 0104C]

### 35.

While these things were happening in Bohemia, Duke Mieszko came with a strong Polish force, invaded the city of Prague, and held it for two periods of years, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1000 and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1001. [Note: [Col. 0104D] The duke of Poland held Prague in the years 1003 and 1004; see the Quedlinburg Annals and Thietmar VI.9.] But the city of Vyšehrad [Note: [Col. 0103] Wissehrad 4, 4a.] remained faithful [Note: [Col. 0103] “faithfully” 3.] to its duke, undaunted and unconquered.

In those same [Col. 0105A] [Note: [Col. 0105] *isdem* 1.] days the same Duke Mieszko [Note: [Col. 0105] *i* with *isdem* written above it by another hand in A.] sends envoys to the emperor, giving and promising him boundless money, [Note: [Col. 0105] “and promising” absent from A.] so that he might send the son of Duke Boleslaus, named Udalric [Note: [Col. 0105] Oaldricum 1.], who was in his service, bound in chains [Note: [Col. 0105] “the son of Duke Boleslaus … might be sent chained” 4, 4a.] into custody. [Note: [Col. 0105D] Thietmar V.19 tells the story otherwise: Henry did not side with the Poles, but helped the exiled Bohemian princes.]

O unconquerable hunger for gold! Where is the most powerful law of the Roman Empire? Behold: the possessor of gold, weighed down by the weight of the duke’s gold, obeys the duke’s commands; and the emperor, corrupted by gold, becomes torturer and jailer.

Nor is it surprising that he obeyed the duke [Note: [Col. 0105] corrected to “the duke’s persuasions” in 2b, with *e* written above the line by another hand.], since in our own times [Note: [Col. 0105D] In the year 1110; cf. below III.32.] Wacek [Note: [Col. 0105] Wacec 1; Wack 2, 2a; Wak 2b; Vecek 3.], born beneath a peasant’s millstone, dragged King Henry III [Note: [Col. 0105D] He was Henry V.]—O shameful [Note: [Col. 0105] “for shameful” 2; “O worthy” 4, 4a.] deed [Note: [Col. 0105] “crime” 4, 4a.]!—into Bohemia by a golden chain as though he were a Molossian hound. What the servant of servants commands, the lord of lords obeys; and the king sends Duke Bořivoj [Note: [Col. 0105] corrected to Udalric in 2b; absent from 5.], [Col. 0105B] tenacious of what is just [Note: [Col. 0105D] Horace, *Odes* III.3.1.], a truthful man, shackled to the knees, into custody as if he were an unjust [Note: [Col. 0105] “enemy” written above the line by another hand; *iniquum*, “unjust,” A.] and lying man. But these matters will be set out more fully in their proper place.

### 36.

It happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002 [Note: [Col. 0105] “done” 2b, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0105D] In the year 1004.], when Christ was already looking upon the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0105] two *s*’s written above the line by another hand in 1.] and Saint Wenceslas was aiding his own. Whether he escaped secretly by flight or was released by order of the emperor is uncertain to us. Duke Udalric [Note: [Col. 0105D] According to Thietmar V.9, it was Jaromir who captured Prague.] returned to [Note: [Col. 0105] “to” A, 2, 2b, 3.] his homeland and entered a most strongly fortified [Note: [Col. 0105] “unconquered” 3.] castle called Drevic [Note: [Col. 0105] Drevis 3; Drewic 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0105D] It lay between Rokov and Kornhaus; Palacký I, 259.]. From there he sends a soldier faithful to himself [Note: [Col. 0105] “sends a soldier” A.] and instructs him, entering the city of Prague by night, to terrify the unsuspecting enemy with the blast [Note: [Col. 0105] *clangorem*, accusative, 2.] of a trumpet.

The faithful retainer quickly does as commanded. At night he climbs an elevated place in the middle of the city called [Note: [Col. 0105] “which is called” absent from 2.] [Col. 0105C] Zizi [Note: [Col. 0105] Zizi, with dots above each z, 2; Sizi 2a; Zizi 2b. A corrector adds in the margin: “it is now called Strahow.” Zicis 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0105D] It is now called Strahovia. Pulkawa.], sounds the trumpet, and repeatedly cries aloud:

> “The Poles flee [Note: [Col. 0105] *fugiunt* written once only in 4, 4a.], the Poles flee [Note: [Col. 0105] Poloni 2b, 3.] shamefully in confusion! Rush in, armed Bohemians, rush in fiercely!”

[Note: [Col. 0105D] In the popular poem *Udalrich und Jarmir*, p. 155:
>
> “A shepherd goes forth as early morning dawns;  
> he calls up, that they may open the gate for him.  
> The watch hears the shepherd’s loud call  
> and opens for him the gate upon the Moldau stream. [Col. 0106D]  
> The shepherd steps upon the bridge and blows loudly—”
>
> According to Thietmar, the signal for revolt was given by the bells of Vyšehrad.]

At this cry fear and terror came upon them, through the wondrous permission of God and the intercession of Saint Wenceslas. All scatter: one, forgetting himself and [Note: [Col. 0105] “and” absent from 4, 4a.] his weapons, naked mounts a naked horse and flees; [Note: [Col. 0105] “onto” added in A.] another, just as he had slept, hastens in flight even [Note: [Col. 0105] “and” 2b, 3.] without breeches. [Note: [Col. 0105] *braccis* corrected in 2b, 3.] Some of those fleeing plunge from the bridge, because the bridge had been broken in order to entrap the enemy. Others flee along the precipitous route—called popularly “by the tail of the city”—and, crowded into the narrow postern through the constriction of its exit, countless men are crushed there. [Note: [Col. 0105] “through” absent from 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0106D] In the popular poem, cited passage:
>
> “Terror seizes all the Polish warriors:  
> Ha! the Poles seize their weapons;  
> Ha! the counts strike mighty blows!  
> And the Poles gallop here and there,  
> run through ditches toward the gate in a crush,  
> run, run before the valiant blows.”]

Duke Mieszko himself scarcely escaped with a few men. And so it happened, as usually happens when men flee from fear [Note: [Col. 0105] *prae t, f*, A.]—they are frightened even by the stirring of a breeze, and fear itself increases their fear—that, though no one [Note: [Col. 0105] “so that these,” with *ut* erased in A; “so that these” 1; “thus men” 2; “thus these” in the rest.] [Col. 0106B] was pursuing [Note: [Col. 0105] “following” 2, 2b, 3.] them, rocks and walls seemed to cry out behind them and pursue the fugitives.

On the following day Duke Udalric [Note: [Col. 0105] *dux*, “duke,” 1, A.] [Note: [Col. 0105] Odaldicus 1.] enters the city of Prague. At the deceitful instigation of those same household enemies of whom we have spoken above [Note: [Col. 0105] “these” 2b, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0106D] The Vršovci family; cf. I.34.], on the third day he deprives his brother Jaromir of sight. [Note: [Col. 0106D] Jaromir ruled Bohemia for eight years; he was not expelled by his brother until 1012 and was deprived of sight in 1034. Thietmar VI.45 and the Hildesheim Annals.]

No offspring was born to him from lawful marriage because of his wife’s barrenness. But by a certain woman named Božena [Note: [Col. 0105] Boziena 2.], who was Křesina’s [Note: [Col. 0105] Kresine 1, 2; Krezmae 3; Krizine 4, 4a.], he had a son of outstanding beauty, whom he caused to be called Břetislav. [Note: [Col. 0105] Brzieczislaum 2; Bratizlau 2b; Brecislaum 3; Brazizlau 4a; Bratislaw 5.] [Note: [Col. 0106D] Since Cosmas seems to make this occur after Udalric had gained the duchy, Udalric’s union with Božena must, with Dobner, undoubtedly be assigned to a time after 1012.]

For one day, as he was returning from the hunt [Note: [Col. 0105] absent from 4a.] through a rustic village, he saw this woman of whom we have spoken washing clothes at a well. Looking at her from head to foot, he drank into his breast no small fires of love. [Col. 0106C] For her figure was remarkable [Note: [Col. 0105] *abitudo*, corrected to *albitudo*, “whiteness,” 1; *habitudo*, “figure,” in the rest.]: whiter than snow, softer than a swan, brighter than ancient ivory, [Col. 0107A] more beautiful than sapphire.

The duke at once sent for her and made her his own. Yet he did not dissolve his former marriage, because at that time, as each person pleased, it was permitted to have two or three wives [Note: [Col. 0107] written in the margin by another hand in A.]; nor was it held wicked for a man to take another’s wife by force, or for a wife to marry another’s husband. What is now reckoned a matter of modesty was then a great disgrace [Note: [Col. 0107] thus 1, 2b, 3; *decorari*, “to be adorned,” corrected to *decori*, “disgrace,” A; *decori* 2, 4, 4a, though in the latter manuscripts *de* has been erased.], if a man lived content with one wife or a wife with one husband. For they lived [Note: [Col. 0107] *videbant*, “they saw,” A, corrected by another hand to *vivebant*, “they lived.”] like [Note: [Col. 0107] added in the margin by another hand in A.] brute animals, holding their marriages in common.

### 37.

In the same year:

> Otto III departed from this world,  
> that he may live [Note: [Col. 0107] absent from 4, 4a.] in heaven, where every faithful person lives.

He was succeeded by his son [Note: [Col. 0107] “his son” absent from 2.], Emperor Henry. [Note: [Col. 0107C] How far Cosmas here departs from the truth is clear to everyone. I do not know from where he drew the following little tale. Shortly before Cosmas, Leo of Ostia, II.47, told it not of St George but of St Lawrence; after him Adalbert told it in the *Life of St Henry*, ch. 33. Both expressed nearly the same matter in very different words, so that no bond of dependence can be supposed among these three authors. Yet we read the same little narrative in exactly the words found in Cosmas in Crusius, *Annales Suevici* II, 186, who testifies: “These things are in that great volume, in which the ecclesiastical and monastic community wished not only to be grateful to its benefactor for his very great generosity, but also to invite other magnates and wealthy men to similar and equal beneficence.” But he does not state in what monastery this little book was written. Since Cosmas’s rhythmic discourse is found in the same fragment, it is beyond doubt that it was drawn not from an original work but from Cosmas’s own Chronicle.]

Among the other great deeds that he performed in his life for Christ’s name, [Note: [Col. 0107] “all” 2.] he built [Col. 0107B] a monastery [Note: [Col. 0107] “castle” 1, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] on a certain mountain, bought at no small expense from the owner of the place, named Pabo. From him it took the name Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0107] “the name it took” A; Babenberk 1; Pabenbergk 3; Babenberg 4.], that is, “Pabo’s mountain.” There too he established [Note: [Col. 0107] “built” 1.] a bishopric, which he enlarged so greatly in resources and episcopal dignities that throughout eastern Francia it is regarded not as the last but as the second bishopric after the first. [Note: [Col. 0107] “bishopric” 2.]

There he also built [Note: [Col. 0107] “he also built … monastery” absent from 5.] a church of marvelous size [Col. 0108A] in honor [Note: [Col. 0107] “into honor” 2b, 3.] of Saint Mary the Virgin and Saint George, Christ’s martyr. He likewise enriched it so greatly with church endowments, ornaments of gold and silver, and other royal [Note: [Col. 0107] thus 1; “royally” in the rest.] furnishings that it seems to me better to keep silence about these things than to say less than the reality contains.

> Yet of the many deeds accomplished I shall relate one useful example. [Note: [Col. 0107] absent from A.]

Not far from the aforesaid city there was a certain anchorite [Note: [Col. 0107] *anachorita* 1.], an archimandrite of holy virtues. To him the emperor would often come secretly with only one attendant, pretending that he wished to go hunting, or contriving some other pretext, [Note: [Col. 0107] *at*, “but,” A.] [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 adds “for hunting”; A, 2, 2b, “often making a journey for hunting”; erroneously “for an arrival” 2; “a hunting journey” 3; “wished to go hunting” 4, 4a.] and commend himself to the anchorite’s prayers.

When the emperor [Note: [Col. 0107] “Henry” added by 4.] learned that he wished to go to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0107] Hierosolimam 1, 4a; Ierozolymam 2, 4.] to pray, [Note: [Col. 0107] “that” 2b.] he entrusted to him a golden chalice for the body and blood of the Lord. Because of its size, it had two handles on either side, which we commonly call “ears,” so that it could easily be lifted by someone. [Col. 0108B] The emperor commands and asks him to immerse it [Note: [Col. 0107] *intingat* 2b, 3.] three times [Note: [Col. 0107] “threefold” 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] in the Jordan, where [Note: [Col. 0107] “Jesus” added by 4.] Christ was baptized by John; and he gives him enough money for the journey.

Why say more? The man of God goes to Jerusalem and fulfills the command, dipping the chalice three times in the water of the Jordan. [Note: [Col. 0107] “into the water” 4, 4a.]

> Returning afterward through Constantinople, he passed [Note: [Col. 0107] “was passing” A, 4.] through Bulgaria.
>
> There was a certain [Note: [Col. 0107] “there was a certain” A.] hermit there, living a holy life, [Note: [Col. 0107] “leading a holy life” A; “living a holy life” 3.]
>
> to whom this pilgrim from Jerusalem came.
>
> After many sweet and holy conversations,
>
> he humbly begged him to pray to God [Note: [Col. 0107] “the Lord” A.] for the well-being of Emperor Henry.

[Col. 0107C] The hermit replied: “There is no need to pray for his well-being, for he has been taken from this valley of tears and has already entered the rest of the blessed.”

The other insists and begs him to say how he knows this. And the hermit says: “Last night, when I was neither fully awake nor altogether asleep, a lofty vision carried me up to a great plain, very level, exceedingly broad, and delightful. There [Col. 0108C] I saw most hideous evil spirits, from whose mouths and nostrils a sulphurous [Note: [Col. 0107] “lightning-like” 1.] flame issued. They were dragging Emperor Henry by [Note: [Col. 0107] “and” 1.] the beard against his will, as though to judgment. [Note: [Col. 0107] “and … judgment” absent from A.] [Note: [Col. 0107] “were holding” 3.] Others, joyfully pressing [Note: [Col. 0107] “urging” A, 4, 4a; “pressing, urging” 1.] his neck with iron forks, shouted: [Note: [Col. 0107] “saying” added by corrector 2b, 4, 4a.] ‘He is ours, he is ours.’

“Saint Mary and Saint George followed them from afar [Note: [Col. 0107] omitted in 2.], as if sorrowful and wishing to rescue [Col. 0109A] him, disputing with them, until a balance was hung in the middle of the field. Its capacity was broader than two miles. [Note: [Col. 0109] “thousand [paces]” 1.]

“On the left side the evil party put immense and countless weights upon it: these were evil deeds. [Note: [Col. 0109] “which are” absent from 4, 4a.] But on the other side I saw Saint George place a great monastery with the entire cloister; I saw golden crosses heavy with precious stones; I saw so many large service-books rich with gems and gold; I saw golden [Note: [Col. 0109] thus 1; “silver” A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] candlesticks, censers, and innumerable cloths, [Note: [Col. 0109] corrected in 1.] and whatever good the king had done in life. Yet the evil side still outweighed the other, and cried, ‘He is ours, he is ours.’” [Note: [Col. 0109] the second “he is ours” absent from 1.]

“Then Saint Mary received the great golden chalice from Saint George’s hand, shook her head three times, and said, ‘Certainly [Note: [Col. 0109] written above the line in 1.] he is not yours, but ours.’” [Note: [Col. 0109] omitted in 4, 4a.] “Then, in great indignation, [Col. 0109B] she threw the chalice against the wall of the church, and [Note: [Col. 0109] “when” 3.] one [Note: [Col. 0109] “part” added by 2.] handle of the chalice broke. At its ringing [Note: [Col. 0109] “trembling” 3.] the fiery host immediately vanished. [Note: [Col. 0109] written above the line in 1 by another hand.] Saint Mary took the emperor by the right hand, and Saint George by the left, [Note: [Col. 0109] “Henry” added in 4, 4a.] and led [Note: [Col. 0109] “led” A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] him away with them, as I believe, to a heavenly [Note: [Col. 0109] “homeland, or he has” A.] dwelling.”

The pilgrim from Jerusalem pondered in his heart what had been said, went down to his baggage, and found the chalice’s handle broken, as the hermit had foretold. To this day it is kept as evidence of a great miracle in the monastery of Saint George at Bamberg. [Note: [Col. 0109] “martyr” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0109] “in the church of St George” A.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003, the Vršovci were slain. [Note: [Col. 0109] Wrisevici 1; the rest as above.] [Note: [Col. 0109C] Without doubt this was the very cruel massacre perpetrated by order of Boleslaus III, which Thietmar related in V.18.]

### 38.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1004 [Note: [Col. 0109] “Saint” added in 4, 4a.], Benedict was martyred with his companions. [Note: [Col. 0109] “the five brothers were martyred” 3.]

In the time [Col. 0109C] [Note: [Col. 0109] Everything following, down to and including “and John,” is absent from 5.] of Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0109] Heinridi 1.], who ruled the Roman Empire after Otto [Col. 0110A] III, there were in the regions of Poland five monks and hermits, true [Note: [Col. 0109] “men” A, 2, 2b, 3.] Israelites: Benedict, Matthew, John, Isaac, Christinus [Note: [Col. 0109] Crispinus 3.], and a sixth, Barnabas. No deceit was found in their mouth, nor wicked work in their hands.

Though I might write much concerning the lives of these fathers, I have preferred to write little, because food is always sweeter when served more sparingly. [Note: [Col. 0110C] Peter Damian also dealt with these holy men in the *Life of St Romuald*, above, *SS.* vol. IV, p. 852.] Their manner of life was praiseworthy, acceptable to God, admirable to men, and worthy of imitation by those who wished to follow it. [Note: [Col. 0109] inserted in the margin of A.] [Note: [Col. 0109] What follows, down to “But they suffered,” is absent from 3. After “worthy of imitation by those who wish to follow it,” 3 adds: “Thus far these things.”] For we admire the merits of the saints [Note: [Col. 0109] “their” A.] in order that, by imitating them, we ourselves may become admirable. [Note: [Col. 0109] *amiramur* 4a.]

We may not unfittingly compare these five men [Note: [Col. 0109] Codex A gives this passage thus: “These five men [may be compared] with the five prudent virgins abounding in the oil of mercy, and them” (*eos* deleted) “not” (written above by another hand) “unfittingly compare either with the five porches” (*onibus* deleted and *tibus* written above) “of the sheep-pool, because,” etc.] to the five porches of the Sheep Pool, or to the five prudent virgins [Col. 0110B] abounding in the oil of mercy, [Note: [Col. 0109] Codex A gives this passage thus: “These five men [may be compared] with the five prudent virgins abounding in the oil of mercy, and them” (*eos* deleted) “not” (written above by another hand) “unfittingly compare either with the five porches” (*onibus* deleted and *tibus* written above) “of the sheep-pool, because,” etc.] because, poor themselves, they supplied poor people of Christ, whom they sheltered in their dwellings [Note: [Col. 0109] “them” added in 4, 4a.], with the expenditures of mercy according to their means.

Their power of abstinence was such that one ate twice and another once in the week, but none ate daily. [Note: [Col. 0109] *dictim* 1.] Their food was vegetables cultivated by their own hands; bread they had rarely, fish never. They were permitted to take legumes or millet [Note: [Col. 0109] “fish” 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0109] “but” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0109] absent from 2.] [Note: [Col. 0109] absent from A.] only at Easter [Note: [Col. 0109] “or Pentecost” added in 4, 4a.]. They drank unspoiled water, and that in measured sips. Flesh as food was abominable to them [Note: [Col. 0109] *habom.* 1.], and the sight of a woman detestable.

Their clothing was shaggy and rough [Note: [Col. 0109] “and” added in A.], woven from horses’ tails and manes. [Note: [Col. 0109] *dequinis* 1.] In their bed a stone supported the head and a mat served as bedding, a mat, exceedingly old and single.

> They had no rest at all: all night they stood lamenting  
> both their own sin and guilt, and that of the little common folk.
>
> [Col. 0109C] Now their bruised breasts resound with repeated beatings;
>
> now [Note: [Col. 0109] *tunc*, “then,” corrected to *nunc*, “now,” 1.] their bodies sweat [Note: [Col. 0109] “pour forth” 1.] [Note: [Col. 0109] “breasts” A.] and grow weary with countless genuflections;
>
> now, with hands outstretched and eyes raised,
>
> each urgently prays in panting supplication that he may live in heaven.

They never spoke to one another, except to a guest who had arrived, [Col. 0109C] and to him only briefly. Truly they were doers of the law, not hearers; truly they crucified themselves with the vices and desires of the world, bore Christ’s cross in mind and body, and offered to God an acceptable sacrifice, not [Col. 0110C] from another’s [Note: [Col. 0109] written above the line by another hand in A.] beast but from their own body. [Note: [Col. 0109] “were offering” A.] For every day they took turns receiving blows.

Such was their custom: on every [Col. 0111A] day [Note: [Col. 0111] “each” 1, 2, 2b, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0111] “day” A.],

> after Prime, the back was softened down to the loins. [Note: [Col. 0111] *mollirier* 2, in the text. Another hand has drawn a line through this word and written in the margin *detegunt*, “they uncover”; *mollire* 4, 4a.]
>
> Then brother, falling face down before brother, [Note: [Col. 0111] “brother to brother,” omitting “before,” 2.] said:
>
> “If you spare me when you strike, you sin; do not spare me.”
>
> And the other, standing with the scourge, answered:
>
> “As you wish, so be it”; and he prays to Christ and scourges his brother, saying:
>
> “May merciful Christ absolve your sins through these deeds [Note: [Col. 0111] “completed deeds” 2b; “aforesaid deeds” 4, 4a.],
>
> and then, falling again, he in turn offers his back.”
>
> Nor did one brother feel pain when he struck the other, [Note: [Col. 0111] “when” A.]
>
> but he sang, “Have mercy upon me, O God,” or “Bless me.”
>
> For each lightly bears what he willingly endures.

God, looking down from on high upon their patience [Col. 0111A]

> and innocence of life, and perseverance in faith and work,
>
> when he wished to render the reward of the labors of his saints, [Note: [Col. 0111] “of these men themselves” in place of “of his saints” 4, 4a.]
>
> and to lead them by a wondrous way
>
> [Col. 0111] to their exultant homeland, [Note: [Col. 0111] “bring them through” 2b.]

Duke Mieszko, hearing of their good reputation and holy way of life, [Col. 0111A]

> came with a few men to commend himself to the holy men.
>
> And when he learned of their poverty, he gave them an abundant supply of wealth, [Note: [Col. 0111] “with” A.] [Note: [Col. 0111C] According to Romuald, gold was given them so that, traveling to Rome, they might obtain a royal crown for him from the supreme pontiff.]
>
> namely, a purse filled with a hundred marks.

Receiving from them brotherhood and a share in their prayers, [Col. 0111B] he went joyfully back to his court, [Note: [Col. 0111] “court, palace” 1, but “palace” deleted.] earnestly [Note: [Col. 0111] “many [times]” 2b.] begging and commending himself to them, that they should remember him.

But they did not know [Note: [Col. 0111] “not knowing” A.] what to do [Note: [Col. 0111] “they should do” A.] with the money, because they had never possessed anything [Col. 0112B] like it. They stood astonished; and since for half a year they had spoken nothing to one another, one of them opened his mouth and said:

> [Col. 0111] The weight of silver and gold is a snare of death, [Note: [Col. 0111] “the snare is” A, 2.]
>
> and for those whose biting purse is ever [Col. 0111B] abundant, [Note: [Col. 0111] “always” 4, 4a.]
>
> the pleasant places of Elysium will not easily lie open;
>
> but punishment full of infernal horror [Note: [Col. 0111] “of horror” 4, 4a.]
>
> will torment [Note: [Col. 0111] “was tormenting” 2.] them on Etna. [Note: [Col. 0111] Hetna 1.]
>
> Doubtless this is the temptation of the enemy of the human race,
>
> that he may make us enemies of Christ.
>
> For whoever is a friend of the world will be made [Note: [Col. 0111] “is” A; “is made” 4, 4a.] an enemy of God. [Note: [Col. 0111] in place of an erased word, 1.]
>
> For those who do not keep God’s commands oppose God.
>
> For God said: “No one can [Note: [Col. 0111] “You cannot” A.] serve two masters,”
>
> and, as if explaining himself, added: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” [Note: [Col. 0112C] Matthew 6:24.]
>
> We who until now have been free from frugality shall become servants of Mammon.
>
> [Col. 0111] Will not a man carrying gold tremble at the stirring of a breeze?
>
> Will not an empty-handed traveler sing before a robber? [Note: [Col. 0111] “before a robber, traveler” A.] [Note: [Col. 0112C] Juvenal, *Satires* X.22.]

Source preparation: Canonical local restored source checked directly; no foreign-text recoveries occurred in this chunk.

Did robbers not very often come to us [Note: [Col. 0111] “come,” 4, 4a], and, finding no reason why they should kill us [Note: [Col. 0111] *and* is absent in 2b], depart—at one time after inflicting blows on us, at another after receiving blessings from us? Certainly the report is now flying through the world that we love the world and the things that are in the world. This money itself, which never knows how to be silent, cries out against us; and now, any moment, the wicked hand of robbers will be at the door, because very many know what lords do—indeed, that the nourishment of death, the sustenance of evil, and the ruin of the soul should rather be thrown out more quickly and returned to him whose silver this is. [Note: [Col. 0111] “also,” 2; “deaths,” A.]

And they send one of the brethren, named Barnabas, who had always handled external affairs, to report these matters [Note: [Col. 0111] *these matters* is absent in 4, 4a] on behalf of the brethren to the duke: “Although we are sinners and unworthy [Note: [Col. 0111] “most unworthy,” A; “are,” 4], nevertheless we keep continual remembrance of you in our prayers. We have never possessed silver, nor do we wish to possess it. For our Lord Jesus Christ demands from us not silver but the twofold talent of good work. If a monk has an obol, the obol is of no use to him. Behold, take what is yours, the silver; it is not lawful for us to possess unlawful things.” [Note: [Col. 0113] “it is lawful,” A.]

When he had departed for the duke’s court, at once in the first watch of the night an enemy band arrived; bursting suddenly through the doors of the house [Note: [Col. 0113] *walvas*, 1], they found them singing and chanting psalms to the Lord. Holding swords to their throats, they said:

> If you wish to live in good peace,  
> Give us now the silver that you possess, and spare yourselves.  
> For we know truly that you possess the king’s revenue.

But they swore before God, firmly denied the revenue, and said: “The money which you seek is now in the duke’s chamber, because it was not necessary for us. And if you do not believe us, behold our house: search as much as you please, only do not harm us.” [Note: [Col. 0113] “anything,” A.]

But they, harder than rocks, said: “Words are of no use. Either restore to us the duke’s money, or you shall undergo the dreadful sentence of death.” [Note: [Col. 0113] *or* is written above the line by another hand in 1.] They immediately bound them cruelly and afflicted them throughout the whole night with diverse punishments. At last they killed all of them together by the edge of the sword. Thus the fury of the wicked bore them away to the kingdoms of the heavens. These five brethren—Benedict, Matthew, Isaac, Christian, and John—suffered in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1004, on the third Ides of November. [Note: [Col. 0113] These five proper names are absent in 3; “second Ides,” 2, 2b; “Ides of November,” A.]

### 39. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1005

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1006 [Note: [Col. 0113] What follows is joined to the preceding year in 4, 4a.], Lady Hemma, a jewel of the female sex, having been seized by fever [Note: [Col. 0113] “corrected,” 1], was released from the bonds of the flesh. Her epitaph, published in these little verses, I either saw or remember having seen:

> She who was like a jewel, behold, Hemma lies here as worthless ash.  
> Say, I pray: “Lord, grant forgiveness to this soul.”

[Note: [Col. 0113] “in,” 1; “me” written above the line by another hand in 1 and omitted in 2; “published” omitted in 3.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1007. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1008.* [Note: * Stephen, king of the Hungarians, flourished, 2, 2a.] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1009. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1010. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1011.** [Note: ** Dedication of the church of Bamberg, 2, 2a.] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1012. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1013. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1014.*** In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1015. + In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1016. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1017. [Note: [Col. 0113] 4.]

In June [Note: [Col. 0113] Thus 1, 2; “the fourth Ides of June” is absent in 4, 4a], Teadagus, the fourth bishop of the church of Prague [Note: [Col. 0113] “holy” is added in 4, 4a], died. [Note: [Col. 0113C] Thietmar VII.41 and the Bohemian Necrology agree.] This Teadagus [Note: [Col. 0113] *this* is absent in 4] was a worthy successor of the holy bishop Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0113] written in the margin of 1 by another hand]: virginal in body, golden in conduct, purple in deeds; following the footsteps of his predecessor, pursuing the crimes of the people entrusted to him, and, if not in body, yet suffering martyrdom in mind. He did not die after the manner of men [Note: [Col. 0113] “death,” 1], but, following the Lord, “sleeps and rests in peace together” [Note: [Col. 0113] “slept,” 4, 4a]. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1018 [Note: [Col. 0113] “1019,” 1; “Amen” instead of *to whom* in 2b; “in the same year,” 4, 4a] he was succeeded by Bishop Heccardus. [Note: [Col. 0113] Eccardus, 1, 4a; corrected by a later hand to Erhardus; Ekkardus, 2; Eckardus, 4. He had previously been abbot of Nienburg and was consecrated on 6 October: Thietmar VII.48.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1019. [Note: [Col. 0113] This line is wanting in 1.] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1020.

### 40
