Meanwhile Bracizlaus, the duke’s son, passing from boyhood into youth, went from strength to strength. Before others he possessed success in action [Note: [Col. 0113] “help,” 3], stature of body, beauty of form, greatness of strength [Note: [Col. 0113] “virtues,” 1] and wisdom, fortitude in adversity, and measured gentleness in prosperity.

At the same time there was in the German lands a very powerful count, Otto surnamed the White [Note: [Col. 0113] “Albertus,” 3], sprung by blood from a royal ancestral stock. He had an only daughter, Judith [Note: [Col. 0113] “born,” A, 2, 4, 4a; [Col. 0114C] she was daughter of Henry and sister of Otto, margrave of Schweinfurt. See the genealogical table supplied by Schwarz in note 108 to Cosmas; see also Pubitschka III, 265.], whose beauty surpassed beneath Phoebus all maidens. Her good father and excellent mother had entrusted her, to learn the psalter, to the monastery called Zuinprod [Note: [Col. 0113] Zuinprid, 1; Zumbrod, 3; Zuinbrod, 4, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0114C] That is, Schweinfurt, where Eila, Judith’s grandmother, is shown by *Annalista Saxo* under 1015 to have founded a convent of nuns.], a place exceedingly well fortified by position and walls.

But what towers [Note: [Col. 0113] *quae* (“what”) is absent in 3], however lofty, or what walls, however strong [Note: [Col. 0113] “strongest,” 4], can resist love and exclude a lover [Note: [Col. 0113] “drive out,” 2, 2b]?

> Love conquers all [Note: [Col. 0114C] Virgil, *Eclogues* X.69]: king and duke yield to love.

Therefore Bracizlaus, most handsome of youths and fiercest of heroes, having heard many accounts of the extraordinary beauty, moral excellence, and noble lineage of the aforesaid maiden, could no longer contain himself. He began to ponder within himself whether to attempt to carry her off by force [Note: [Col. 0113] “take,” A] or to prepare a marriage with a dowry. But he preferred to act manfully rather than bow his neck in supplication. For he considered the inborn pride of the Germans, and how they have always held Slavs and their language in contempt with swollen arrogance.

But the more difficult love’s access always becomes, the more strongly Venus’s son kindles fire in the lover. [Note: [Col. 0115] The words from “fire” to “youth” are wanting in 2; supplied in a recent hand in the margin.] The young man’s mind, wounded by Venus’s fire [Note: [Col. 0115] “by desire,” A; over “by Venus’s fire,” a contemporary hand writes “wounded by the dart of desire”; similarly in 2 and 5; 4 reads “by the dart of fire,” though *dart* has been deleted in 4a], wavers as Etna boils with fires. And he melodiously utters this apostrophe to himself [Note: [Col. 0115] *ahuc*, 1; *apostrapham*, 3, 4a]:

> Either I shall enjoy an outstanding marriage,  
> Or I shall be plunged for ever into mockery.  
> It cannot be that Judith shall not be mine—  
> Born of noble stock, a maiden fair to behold,  
> Much to be loved, brighter than the sun’s light,  
> Dearer to me than life. May praise of God endure for ever while she lives.

[Note: [Col. 0115] “might be,” 3; “in place of,” 3.]

At once [Note: [Col. 0115] The words *quos inter* (“among whom”) are absent in 1] he orders that horses be prepared—tested horses, most fit for labour—for those among his men whom he knew to be readier of hand and more faithful to him. He pretended that he would swiftly go to the emperor and return still more swiftly. His men obey their lord’s commands, but do not know what he intends. They wonder among themselves why they are travelling so quickly; and, as if undertaking a journey of seven days, they enter, in the manner of guests [Note: [Col. 0115] *hospitii* (“of lodging”), 3], the court of the aforesaid monastery.

The duke’s son had forbidden all his men to make known to anyone who or whence he was [Note: [Col. 0115] A and 2 read *quis et unde*, “who and whence”], but to treat him as one of themselves. Let the Ithacan yield the credit of having cleverly discovered the son of Thetis (*Thetides*) [Note: [Col. 0115] *Tethidis*, 2b; *Cheridis*, 3; *Thechidis*, 4; *Tchechidis*, 4a; cf. Statius, *Achilleid* II.44.]; nor let the Trojan shepherd boast of having carried off the Tyndarid from Amyclae—Helen, that is [Note: [Col. 0115] “i.e. Helen,” written above the line in A by another hand]—for this youth Bracizlaus goes before both [Note: [Col. 0115] *praeit*, “goes before,” 3, 4, 4a] in courage and in the savage enormity of his deed.

For after they had been granted permission to lodge there for the night, Bracizlaus, like a wolf prowling round sheepfolds and seeking the side on which he may break in to snatch a sleek lamb, surveyed the cloister with keen sight [Note: [Col. 0115] “effort,” 4, 4a] and high spirit. He wished to break in by force, but did not dare, because he did not have with him so great a number of soldiers. By chance there came a feast-day; and behold, Judith the maiden, the object of a thousand desires, came out of the cloister with girls of her own age, as tender girls were accustomed to ring the bells for Vespers in the middle of the church.

When the most daring ravisher saw her, forgetful of himself for joy, he rushed from hiding like a wolf, seized the lamb, and fled conscious of his deed, with tail tucked down, seeking a more distant hiding place. Thus he too fled with the maiden seized. When he came to the gate, he found it bound fast with a miller’s chain and a very thick rope, and the way out blocked. He immediately drew his sword and cut it through as sharply as if it were a straw. The cut of that most powerful stroke is still seen today in testimony.

But his other companions knew nothing of this and remained in their tents. They were seized by the enemies rushing in; some had their eyes torn out and noses cut off, others had hands and feet mutilated. The duke, with a few men and the abducted maiden, scarcely escaped through the darkness of night.

The maiden Judith was abducted in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021. [Note: [Col. 0115C] Cosmas incorrectly assigns this year. What follows proves that Judith was carried off after Moravia had been conquered by the Bohemians. Moravia was undoubtedly recovered in 1029, the year in which Emperor Conrad II moved arms against the Poles; this was demonstrated by Dobner V, 156, and after him Roepell I, 166. For the son of Bracizlaus and Judith, born in 1031, see below.]

And so that the Germans might not be given a just opportunity to accuse the Bohemians—as though in immediate retaliation for the injury done—Bracizlaus, with his new bride, after greeting his father Duke Oudalricus, set out directly for Moravia. [Note: [Col. 0115C] A charter in Boczek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae* I, 111, lacking chronological notes, was written at the time “when our lord Duke B. came to Olomouc with his beautiful wife before the numerous assembly of the nobles of his land.”]

For earlier his father had committed to his power that entire land, after driving all the Poles [Note: [Col. 0115] *Poloniis*; “Polonis,” 1, 3] from its cities [Note: [Col. 0115] absent in 4, 4a]. [Note: [Col. 0116C] Not only over the Poles, but also over the Hungarians, who had taken Moravia from them, Bracizlaus won victory, as that prince himself testifies in a charter in which he calls himself duke of Moravia: Boczek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae* I, 112. It lacks chronological notes and was drawn up at Olomouc. Another charter, dated 1031, proves that Bracizlaus lived there in 1031 with his wife and little son Spitigneu: Boczek I, 114.] He had ordered many of those captured to be sold, in successive hundreds bound in chains, into Hungary and beyond; for in truth, after the death of the second Boleslaus, the Poles had seized by force not only the city of Prague but all Moravia.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1022 there was a persecution of Christians in Poland. [Note: [Col. 0115] “persecution of Christians,” A; nothing concerning this year in 4, 4a. [Col. 0116C] Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1023, on the sixth Ides of August, Occardus [Note: [Col. 0115] *Oggardus*, 2; *Okkardus*, 2b; *Ekardus*, 3; *Eccardus*, 4; *Heccardus*, 4a], the fourth bishop [Note: [Col. 0115] “holy” is added in 4, 4a] of the church of Prague, passed from this light to live eternal life [Note: [Col. 0115] “passed,” 4, 4a; “perpetual life,” V and A; “to eternal life,” 3]. [Note: [Col. 0116C] This took place in 1034, after the death of Mieszko II; cf. the *Annals of Hildesheim*.]

This bishop [Note: [Col. 0115] absent in 4] was resolute against the powerful, kind and modest toward the humble and gentle [Note: [Col. 0115] *and* is omitted in 4, 4a], a most eloquent preacher, a generous giver of alms, and a faithful steward of the Lord’s household in the measure of wheat.

He decreed that for the tithe every person—powerful, rich, or poor—who had ploughland from his own fief [Note: [Col. 0117] a correction or addition written above the line in A] or allod [Note: [Col. 0117] *allidio*, 4a] should pay the bishop two modii, each of five palms and two fingers: one of wheat and the other of oats. Formerly, as had been decreed under the first bishop Dethmarus [Note: [Col. 0117] *Diethmarus*, 1], they gave two harvest stacks for the tithe; by a stack we mean one containing fifty sheaves [Note: [Col. 0117] 3 reads “or for fifty,” apparently because its exemplar had *L*, which the scribe read as *vel*]. After his death Izo [Note: [Col. 0117] *Izzo*, 1, 2, 2b, 3] obtained the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0117] “bishopric,” A, 2, 3], and was ordained in that same year [Note: [Col. 0117] addition by another hand in A], on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, by the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0117] “by the archbishop of Mainz” is absent in 4, 4a]. [Note: [Col. 0117C] The *Annals of Quedlinburg* confirm this.]

### 41

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1024, on the fourth Ides of July, King Heinrich died. [Note: [Col. 0117] “fourth Ides”; “king” is absent in 5; 4 and 4a add “of the Germans,” with the remaining words somewhat transposed.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1025, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, King Boleslaus died. [Note: [Col. 0117] In 2b, *king* has been deleted and *duke* written above it; in 4a, *king* has been erased by a later hand. [Col. 0117C] Cf. Roepell, *Geschichte Polens* I, 162.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1026.* [Note: * King Conrad is consecrated at Rome, 2, 2a, 2b.] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1027. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1028. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1029.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1030, Duke Bracizlaus [Note: [Col. 0117] *Bolezlaus*, 1] slaughtered the Hungarians in great numbers and devastated their land as far as the city of Strigonia. [Note: [Col. 0117C] Gran, where the Gran flows into the Danube. This seems to be the war mentioned above, note 17.]

In the same year, on the third day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0117] Thus 1; “Kalends” corrected to “Ides” in A], Izo [Note: [Col. 0117C] The Bohemian Necrology agrees], the fifth bishop of the church of Prague,

> Passed from this world and enjoys the joyous prize. [Note: [Col. 0117] “passed,” 4, 4a; “enjoys,” A.]

He was noble by birth, but nobler in deed, first doing what he commanded to be done. For no man knew his own home better than he knew the prison and the dwellings of the sick. Nor was he unaware how many human heads were restored to life,

> Or how many souls death sent down to the dusky shades. [Note: [Col. 0117] “furies,” A; “furnaces,” 3, 4, 4a.]

Moreover, he customarily fed forty poor people every day; after providing them abundantly with food and drink, he himself blessed it and himself distributed it cheerfully. His bodily beauty also was remarkable: his head was whiter in hair than a swan. Hence he acquired the surname by which he was called Izo, the white and gracious bishop.

After him Bishop Severus succeeded, sixth in order. In the time of his youth he shone with wondrous beauty of agility. For, surpassing all who were at the duke’s court in his services, he rendered to his lord diligent and, above all, faithful service [Note: [Col. 0117] *and* for *because*, 4, 4a]. He was foremost in clerical duties [Note: [Col. 0117] *officiis*, with *iis* written above the line by another hand in 1], but no less devoted to lay pursuits; he was always the duke’s inseparable companion in hunts. He was first at the killing of the wild boar, and, cutting off its tail [Note: [Col. 0117] absent in A], cleaned and prepared it as he knew the duke wished, then gave it ready to his approaching lord to eat. Hence Duke Oudalricus is often reported to have said to him:

> O Severus, truly I tell you:  
> For this very sweet dish, you are worthy of a bishopric.

By these and similar pursuits he possessed the duke’s favour and pleased everyone.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1031 [Note: [Col. 0117] 1032, 4a], on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Severus was ordained bishop by the archbishop of Mainz. In the same year Spitigneu [Note: [Col. 0117] *Zpitigneu*, 1, 2b; *Zpitigneus*, 4; *Spitigneus*, 4a, and likewise thereafter], son of Duke Bracizlaus, was born.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1032.** [Note: ** Beginning of the church of Sázava, 2, 2a; in 2b this is attached to the following year: “The beginning was made, etc.”] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1033. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1034. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1035. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1036. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1037, Duke Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 0117] *Bolezaus*, 1] died, whom Mieszko [Note: [Col. 0117] *Mesko*, 2, 4a] had deprived of sight [Note: [Col. 0117] “deprived,” 4, 4a].

### 42

In the same year, on the fifth Ides of November [Note: [Col. 0118C] On his shameful death, see the *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1034], Duke Oudalricus,

> Leaving earthly things, seeks the heavenly kingdoms. [Note: [Col. 0118C] The *Annals of Hildesheim* show that Cosmas was not well informed about Udalricus’s final fate.]

Then Jaromir, whom we mentioned above, blind, to whom Duke Oudalricus had assigned residence in the little settlement of Liza [Note: [Col. 0117] *destinarat*, 4, 4a; *daretur* is written above a deleted word by another hand in A; *Licza*, 1; *Lisza*, 2 and 4; *Lizza*, 3; 4 and 4a read *in viculo* (“in a hamlet”), while the remaining witnesses read *in vinculo* (“in bonds”). [Col. 0118C] Lysa is a castle.], on hearing that his brother had departed from this world, rose at dawn and ordered himself to be carried in a vehicle to the city of Prague. When he arrived, he found that his brother had already been borne to the church of Saint George [Note: [Col. 0117] “martyr” is added in 4, 4a]. Standing beside the bier at his brother’s funeral, he moved and shook the hearts of all those standing around with this lament:

> Alas for me! What can I say except, again and again, “Alas for me”?  
> Alas for me, brother! Alas, bitter death’s dreadful condition!  
> Behold, you lie dead; neither you nor I now rejoice  
> In the fleeting summit of this earthly kingdom.  
> The day before yesterday a noble duke, today a motionless trunk;  
> Tomorrow food for worms, afterwards thin ash,  
> And you will be an empty little tale.  
> You deprived me of sight; you did not love your brother as a brother.  
> You would now wish that you had not done what you did to me.  
> Now I know that, if you could, you would wish to restore my sight,  
> Since your deeds, whether well or ill done, are naked and exposed.  
> But now, brother, I forgive you from my whole heart,  
> That almighty God in his mercy may spare you,  
> And that hereafter your spirit may rest in peace.

After the funeral rites had duly been completed, he took his cousin Bracizlaus and led him to the princely seat. As they always do at the election of a duke, they scattered ten thousand coins, or more, among the people through the railings of the upper hall, so that they might not crush the duke on the throne, but rather snatch at the scattered coins. Then, when the duke had been placed on the throne and silence made, Jaromir took his cousin’s right hand and said to the people: “Behold your duke!” And they cried out three times: “Krilessu” [Note: [Col. 0119] *Kryelesu*, 1; *Krlesu*, 2b; *Kirlessu*, 3; *Krlessu*, 4, 4a], which is *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.” [Note: [Col. 0119] This explanation is absent in A.]

Again Jaromir said to the people: “Let those of the family of Muncia come forward! Let those of the family of Tepea come forward!” [Note: [Col. 0119] In Palacký’s opinion, *Munici* should be written; they are descendants of Mun and Tepta.] And he called by name those whom he knew to be more powerful in arms, better in loyalty, stronger in soldiery, and more eminent in wealth. When he perceived them present, he said:

“Since my deeds do not permit me to be your duke, we appoint and commend to you this man as duke [Note: [Col. 0119] “judge,” 3], so that you may obey him, as is fitting for a duke, and render to your prince the loyalty that is due [Note: [Col. 0119] Thus 1, with a contemporary hand in an erasure; the other witnesses read “as is proper”]. And you, my son, I advise—and repeatedly will advise [Note: [Col. 0119] *atque*, “and,” is added in A]—that you honour these men as fathers, love them as brothers, and have them as counsellors in all affairs. Entrust to them the government of cities and people; for through them the kingdom of Bohemia stands, has stood, and shall stand for ever [Note: [Col. 0119] “for ever” is absent in A].

“But avoid the Vršovci, the wicked sons of wicked fathers [Note: [Col. 0119] absent in 2], domestic enemies of our lineage, familiar foes, as you would a filthy wheel; shun their company, for they were never loyal to us. Behold, they first bound me, innocent as I was and their own prince, and subjected me to various humiliations. Then, by the treacheries natural to them and their fraudulent counsels, they contrived that my brother should deprive me of these eyes. My son, keep always in mind the prophecies of Saint Adalbert, who on account of their cruel acts affirmed with his holy mouth that destruction should come upon them three times, and excommunicated them in the church. [Note: [Col. 0119B] Cf. Bruno, *Life of Saint Adalbert*, ch. 21.] By God’s will these things have already occurred twice; anxious fates still await the third destruction to come upon them [Note: [Col. 0119] “destructions” is absent in all the other witnesses; 1 reads “fates” for “things].”

Hearing this, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him like lions. Not many days later Kohan, of whom we spoke above, sent his executioner [Note: [Col. 0119] *lictore*, corrected from *litore* in 1]. While Jaromir, blind, was relieving himself in the privy at the hour of night [Note: [Col. 0119] *noctis*, corrected from *notis* by another hand in A], the assassin pierced him in the rear with a very sharp dagger, even to the innermost parts of the heart [Note: [Col. 0119] A and 1 read “to the innermost parts of the body”; 2 omits the phrase; 2b reads “of the body”; 3, 4, and 4a read “of the belly”]. Thus the righteous man, as a martyr of God, Duke Jaromir died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038, on the day before the Nones of November [Note: [Col. 0119] “or,” and “the day before,” written above the line by the same hand in A; absent in 1], that is, 4 November. [Note: [Col. 0120B] Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.]

Thus far the first book contains the deeds of ancient times.

But because, as blessed Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0120B] Jerome, *Works*, ed. Vallarsi II, 521], things seen are narrated differently from things heard, and things heard differently from things invented; and because we report better what we know better, now, with the help of God and Saint Adalbert, I am moved to tell those things which we ourselves have seen, or which we have truthfully heard from persons recounting them who saw them. [Note: [Col. 0119] In A *heard* is written above *commanded* by a later hand; in 2 another hand has placed *a* over *i*; *and* is absent in A; 1 reads “for”; 3 reads “because”; 1 reads *ferentibus* for *referentibus*.]

**Here ends the first book of the Chronicles of the Bohemians.**

## Here begins the prologue to Clement, Abbot of the Church of Břevnov

[Note: [Col. 0121] *Breunensis*, 1; 4 and 4a read: “Prologue to Clement, Abbot of Břevnov.”]

To Father Clement of the spiritual monastery of Břevnov [Note: [Col. 0121] *Breunovensis*, 4], whose name truly corresponds to his character, ever devoted to contemplation [Note: [Col. 0121] “theoretical,” A], Cosmas, unworthy to be called dean, wishes fellowship in the angelic senate [Note: [Col. 0121] “angelic,” 3; “of fellowship,” 4, 4a].

While I was considering much within myself what I should especially send in the bond of charity to a man of such great holiness—for whom weights of gold and silver are worthless, and only spiritual things pleasing—I judged it best to comply solely with your wish [Note: [Col. 0121] “the best course,” 4, 4a]. For through your cleric, named Deocarus, who secretly and confidentially made it known to me, I understood that you wished gladly to see my trifles which I had once written for Master Gervasius [Note: [Col. 0121] “master” is added in 4, 4a].

Strengthened by this opportunity—indeed compelled by the persuasion of a dear friend—I presume to disclose to your fatherhood not only what you desired, but also, as it were, the second little book of the same narrative, arranged, as far as I have been able to learn, from the time of Bracizlaus, son of Duke Oudalricus, down to his namesake son, King Wratizlaus. [Note: [Col. 0121] “to be desired,” 1.]

Although, venerable father, you never cease to drink deeply of the divine Scriptures and continually draw from the profound springs of philosophy, do not disdain to moisten your sacred lips with this very thin draught.

> For it often happens that after strong wines and sleep-inducing cups [Note: [Col. 0121] “soporific,” 4, 4a],  
> A natural thirst comes upon a person [Note: [Col. 0121] “comes,” 2, 2b, 3];  
> And a draught of pure water [Note: [Col. 0121] “pure,” 4, 4a] becomes sweeter than sweet drinks.
>
> It often happens that the soldier of Mars, sweating under arms [Note: [Col. 0121] “in the fields,” 2, 2a, 4, 4a; a later hand writes “in arms” over *mis* in 1],  
> Rejoices to mingle in maidenly dances [Note: [Col. 0121] “rejoices,” 4; “mingling,” 1];  
> Or delights to play with a boy’s hoop in the circus [Note: [Col. 0121] “in the circus” is absent in A; “therefore,” 4, 4a; “of a little boy,” 4a; “hoop,” 3].

So you, most holy father, put aside now your great and syllogistic volumes, and read these my little works, childish in sense and rustic in style. There you may find some things worthy of mockery and derision [Note: [Col. 0121] “ridicule,” 2b]; commit these to memory precisely so that you may someday correct them to the utmost with the wisdom bestowed upon you by God [Note: [Col. 0121] a correction in A, with the ending of the word supplied by another hand].

And when in certain places you find what seem to be metrical verses, know that I made verses knowingly as one ignorant of the art. Farewell.

## Here begins the second book

[Note: [Col. 0121] 4 reads: “Here begins Book II of the Chronicle of the Bohemians.”]

### 1

Thus Duke Bracizlaus, now strengthened on his father’s throne, treading in the footsteps of his fathers through deeds pleasing both to God and to men, and surpassing them by the unbroken citadel of his virtues [Note: [Col. 0121] 3 reads *arte* (“by skill”) for *arce* (“citadel”)], was like the sun, which in its strength conceals and dims the starry light [Note: [Col. 0121] absent in A] and the excessive splendour of the moon. So Bracizlaus, a new Achilles, a new son of Thetis (*Thetides*), by new triumphs diminishes and obscures the brave deeds and most victorious laurels of his ancestors. [Note: [Col. 0121] *Tithides*, 2; *Tydides*, 2b; *Tychides*, 4, 4a; “new Tithides” is omitted in 3.]

For God bestowed upon him such grace that the virtues which he grants separately and individually to individual men he bestowed upon this man generally and without failing.

> He attained such an accumulation of virtues  
> That in warlike affairs he surpassed Gideon in valour,  
> Excelled Samson in bodily strength,  
> And, by a special prerogative of wisdom, went before Solomon.
>
> Hence in every battle he emerged victorious like Joshua;  
> He was richer in gold and silver than the kings of Arabia;  
> He overflowed everywhere with inexhaustible wealth,  
> And did not fail in the giving of gifts.
>
> He may be compared to water, whose stream never fails.

His wife Judith, most noble in lineage and most fruitful in offspring, bore five sons, distinguished and towering in body like the mountains of Haematia [Note: [Col. 0123] *Hemat iae*, 1; *Hemacie*, 4], singular in wisdom, unequalled in virtue, pleasing in manners, merciful to offenders [Note: [Col. 0123] the phrase from “pleasing in manners” to “merciful to offenders” is absent in 2, 2b, and 3], and praiseworthy in every honourable virtue.

The firstborn was named Spitignev; the second in age, Wratizlav; the third in lineage, Conradus [Note: [Col. 0123] *Chonradus*, 1, 2b, 4, 4a]; the fourth by birth, Jaromir [Note: [Col. 0123] *Iaromir*, 4a]; and the fifth and last, Otto the most handsome. Their lives and glory will be sufficiently explained in their proper places, as abundance of words permits. Their father greatly marvelled to see them still of childish years [Note: [Col. 0123] “years” is omitted in 3], yet vigorous in manly studies [Note: [Col. 0123] “studying,” A]:

> Beholding the noble glory and noble pair of brothers [Note: [Col. 0123B] Horace, *Satires* II.3.243].

No less did her joys trouble the mother, happy at the great advancement [Note: [Col. 0123] “progress,” 2b] of her sons and the condition of their magnificent glory.

## Restored textual apparatus

The following source-order readings complete the apparatus omitted from the repair candidate. Forms are retained with their witnesses; “absent” means that the named words are omitted by that witness.

### Judith and Bracizlaus

- **[Col. 0113]** *interea* (“meanwhile”), 4 and 4a; *capere* (“to seize”), A; the words from *ignem* (“fire”) through *juvenis* (“young man”) are absent in 2 and supplied by a later marginal hand.
- **[Col. 0115]** *fluctuatque* (“and he/she wavers”), 2b and 3. A has *cupidinis* (“of desire”); in 1, *telo lesa cupidinis* (“wounded by the dart of desire”) is written above *igne* by a contemporary Venetian hand; 2 and 5 likewise have *telo igne*; 4 has *telo igne*, and 4a reads the same with *telo* struck through.
- **[Col. 0115]** 1 reads *ahuc* for text *hanc* (“this”); 3 and 4a read *apostrapham* for text *apostropham* (“apostrophe/address”). MS 1 omits the second *aut ego* (“or I”) in *Aut ego conjugio fungar egregio, aut ego ludibrio mergar perpetuo* (“Either I shall enjoy an outstanding marriage, or I shall be plunged forever into mockery”). MS 3 reads *potuit* (“was able”) for text *poterit* (“will be able”), and *vice* (“in place/turn”) for text *vita* (“life”).
- **[Col. 0115]** *Tethidis*, 2b; *Cheridis*, 3; *Thechidis*, 4; *Tchechidis*, 4a. The source cites Statius, *Achilleid* II.44. In 1, *jacet* (“lies”) was corrected by a later hand from *jactet*; A has *i. Helenam* (“that is, Helen”) supralinearly.
- **[Col. 0115]** *praeit* (“goes before”), 3, 4, 4a; *sicut* (“just as”), 2; 2b and 4 read *sic* (“thus”) with *et* omitted; *nisu* (“by effort”), 4 and 4a; 2 omits *tantam copiam militum* (“so great a company of soldiers”); *exiit* (“went out”), 4 and 4a; at *sicut puellae solebant* (“as young girls used to do”), 1 has a correction. 4 and 4a omit *sui prae gaudio factus immemor* (“made forgetful of himself through joy”); 2 has *causam* (“cause”), with an erased *s*, for *caudam* (“tail”).
- **[Col. 0115]** Both readings attached to the chained gate are absent in 3. The source’s dating note says Cosmas has given the year incorrectly: the subsequent narrative shows Judith was seized after Moravia was conquered by the Bohemians; Moravia was recovered in 1029, when Conrad II made war on the Poles; it cites Dobner V.156, Roepell I.166, and the birth of Bracizlaus and Judith’s son in 1031.
- **[Col. 0115]** *Et ne justa* (“and lest just [things]”), A; *ilico heros* (“at once, the hero”) is absent in 4; *cum nova* (“with new [things/news]”) is absent in 4 and 4a; *ante* (“before”), 2b, for printed *antea* (“previously”). The words *de civitatibus* (“from/of the cities”) are absent in 4 and 4a; 1 and 3 read *Polonis* (“Poles”).

### Obituaries, tithe, and Boleslaus

- **[Col. 0115–0116C]** Name forms: *Oggardus*, 2; *Okkardus*, 2b; *Ekardus*, 3; *Eccardus*, 4; *Heccardus*, 4a. 4 and 4a add *sanctae* (“holy”); they read *transiit* (“passed away”); A has *perpetua* (“everlasting”), while 3 has *perpetem vitam* (“unending life”). The editorial note dates the event to 1034 after Mieszko II’s death and cites the *Annals of Hildesheim*.
- **[Col. 0115]** 4 and 4a add *Heccardus*; in the same notice they read *mansuetus* (“gentle”), with *et* omitted. 2, 2b, and 3 omit *et* (“and”).
- **[Col. 0117]** *sive* (“or”) is omitted in 4 and 4a. At *pheodo* (“fief”), A has a reading written supralinearly by another hand; 4a reads *allidio* (“allod”). 1 reads *Diethmaro* for *Dethmaro*. A and 4 omit *enim* (“for”) in *dicimus enim acervum* (“for we call a heap…”). 3 reads *vel* (“or”) for *quinquaginta* (“fifty”); the editor thinks its exemplar had *L*, which the scribe read as *vel*. Name forms include *Izzo* (1, 2, 2b, 3) and *episcopatum* (“bishopric,” A, 2, 3); at *ab eodem anno* (“in that same year”), A has a supralinear correction, while 4 and 4a omit *ab arch. Mog.* (“by the archbishop of Mainz”).
- **[Col. 0117]** Witness 5 lacks the entire notice from *IV. Id.* through *rex* (“king”); 4 and 4a add *Theutonicorum* (“of the Germans”), with some transposition. Witness 5 likewise lacks the notice from *XV. Kal. I.* through *rex*; in 2b, *rex* was struck out and *dux* (“duke”) written above it, while in 4a *rex* was erased later.

### Jaromir

- **[Col. 0117–0118C]** A reads *monasterium* (“monastery”); another hand inserts *ecclesiam* (“church”) in the margin. 2 and 2b lack *in eccl.* (“in church”), but a correction adds *ad monasterium* (“to the monastery”). 4 and 4a add *martyris* (“of the martyr”); 3 has *convertit* (“turned”). Lysa is identified by the source as a castle.
- **[Col. 0119]** In the lament: *Heri* (“yesterday”), 3; *fruituri* (“about to enjoy”), 4 and 4a; *concius* (“stirred up”), 1; 4 and 4a insert *et jam es* (“and now you are”) after *favilla* (“ash”); they read *sint* (“may be”) and 2b omits *nuda et* (“naked and”); 2b reads *utque* (“and as”).
- **[Col. 0119]** For the funeral/acclamation: A’s *hexpl.* is corrected to *expl.* (“completed”); A, 4, and 4a read *funebriis* (“funeral rites”), while 1 corrects *funebris* to *funeriis* (“funerals”); 2b has *obsequiis* (“obsequies”) and *accepit* (“received”); 4a has *superiores* (“higher/earlier”); 2b has *in* (“in”); 2 omits the passage from *ut* through *non*; 2b and 3 read *isti* (“those”); 4 and 4b read *subclamabant* (“were crying out”).
- **[Col. 0119]** Name variants: *Muncina*, 4 and 4a; *Tepea*, 2b. The editor says Palacký I.168 suggests *Munici* and identifies descendants of Mun and Tepta. In A, *ducem* (“leader,” accusative) is corrected by another hand to *dux* (“leader,” nominative); 3 has *judicem* (“judge”). For *ut decet suo principi* (“as befits his prince”), 1 has the printed form written by a contemporary hand over an erasure, while the remaining witnesses read *par est* (“it is fitting”). A adds *atque* (“and”) to *iterum atque iterumque* (“again and again”).
- **[Col. 0119]** At *His urbes et populum ad regendum committas* (“Entrust cities and people to their governance”), 1 has a correction at *urbes* (“cities”). A omits *in sempiternum* (“for ever”). At *iniquorum patrum nequam filii* (“the wicked sons of unjust fathers”), 2 omits *nequam* (“wicked”). 1 reads *generi* (“son-in-law/kind”) for printed *generis* (“of [our] stock”). The source cites Bruno’s *Life of St Adalbert*, ch. 21. In 2b, *ex* (“from/out of”) is corrected for *in* in *excommunicavit eos in ecclesia* (“he excommunicated them in the church”).
- **[Col. 0119]** The full repeated clause is *tercio ut fiant super eos excidia* — “for a third time, that destructions may come upon them”: it appears in 1 alone and is absent from all other witnesses. 1 reads *facta* (“deeds/things done”) for *fata* (“fates”). The prophecy therefore keeps plural *excidia* (“destructions”), as the source does.
- **[Col. 0119]** 2 reads *discalceabantur* (“were being unshod”); an old hand deleted *ei* and wrote *dissecabantur* (“were being cut apart”) in the margin. In 1, *litore* (“shore”) is corrected from *lictore* (“lictors’ attendant”); A’s *notis* is corrected by another hand from *noctis* (“night”); A and 1 have *noctis*, A has *cordis* (“heart”) written above it by another hand, 2 omits it, 2b reads *corporis* (“body”), and 3, 4, 4a read *ventris* (“belly”).
- **[Col. 0119]** At both distinct occurrences, A has *vel et pridie* (“or also the day before”) written supralinearly by the same hand over *pridie* (“the day before”); witness 1 omits it. The source’s death description is *velut martyr Dei*: “like a martyr of God,” not an unqualified identification as one.

### Prologue and Book II

- **[Col. 0121]** 1 reads *Breunensis*; 4 and 4a title the piece *prohemium ad Clementem Breunensem abbatem* (“prologue to Clement, abbot of Břevnov”). *Spirituali* (“spiritual”), 2b, 3, 4, 4a; 4 has *Breunovensis*; A has *theorice* (“theoretically”); 3 has *angelica* (“angelic”); 4 and 4a have *consortii* (“of fellowship”) and omit *optimum* (“best”) in *optimum fore duxi* (“I judged it best”).
- **[Col. 0121]** 2 has *tyrum*; 4 and 4a add *magistro* (“to the master”); 1 has *optari* (“to be desired”) and *debuit* (“ought”); 4 and 4a have *sopifera* (“sleep-inducing”); 2, 2b, 3 have *incidit* (“fell into”); 1 has *sicque* (“and thus”); 4 and 4a have *purae* (“pure”). In 1, *mortis* (“of death”) is corrected to *fortis* (“strong”).
- **[Col. 0121]** A has *mis* written supralinearly by another hand; 2, 2a, 4, 4a have *arvis* (“fields”); 4 has *ita* (“thus”), while the rest have *gaudet* (“rejoices”); 1 has *commiscens* (“mingling”); A lacks *in c.*; 4 and 4a have *idcirco* (“therefore”); 4a has *pueruli* (“little boy”); 3 has *trocho* (“hoop”); 2b has *irrisione* (“mockery”); A has *nem* written above the line by another hand.
- **[Col. 0121]** 4 has *I. l. s. in chronica Boemorum* (“Book I, line/section, in the Chronicle of the Bohemians”); 3 has *vestigium* (“footprint/trace”) and *arte* (“by skill”) for *arce* (“citadel”); A omits *in* in *sicut sol in virtute sua* (“as the sun in its power”); 4 and 4a have *syderum* (“of the stars”); 3 has *ebethat*, reading *hebetat* (“dulls/blunts”).

# Cosmas of Prague, *Chronicle of the Bohemians*, Book II, §§2–8

*Translation status: complete after independent canonical-source adjudication. Initial translation by GPT-5.6 Terra; saved repair by GPT-5.6 Luna; repair review by GPT-5.6 Terra; full apparatus translation and final source adjudication by GPT-5.6 Sol.*

## 2

At that time [Note: “But then” is added in manuscript 4], when Kazimir [Note: “Cazimir,” MSS. 4 and 4a], the most illustrious duke of the Poles, had been taken from this life [Note: Cosmas badly confuses Polish affairs. Kazimir died after Bracizlaus, in 1058, and did not leave infant sons; rather, he himself was left an infant by his father Mieszko II. Cf. Martinus Gallus I, 48, ed. Bandtke], and his sons Boleslaus and Wladizlaus [Note: Besides these two, Kazimir had other sons, Mieszko and Otto. Cf. Martinus Gallus I, 19] were still infants at the breast [Note: “At the breast” is absent in manuscript 1], the wretched Poles, fleeing through various places, had only one hope of safety in their miserable flight [Note: “There was no hope” in MSS. 4 and 4a].

When Duke Bracizlaus observed this, in the fourth year of his dukedom [Note: That is, according to Cosmas’s reckoning, A.D. 1041; cf. above I, 42. But he is mistaken here, as is clear from the more accurate dates concerning the translation of St Adalbert, II, 5], judging it best not to let pass the opportunity offered for attacking his enemies, indeed for avenging the injuries once inflicted upon the Bohemians by Duke Mieszko [Note: “Bracizlaus” is erased in manuscript 1], he resolved, as soon as possible, after taking counsel with his men, to invade them. Immediately he issued a terrible decree, sending throughout the whole province of Bohemia, as a sign of his command, a collar twisted from cork [Note: “From corkwood” in MSS. 2, 2b, 4, and 4a; manuscript 1 corrects the reading], so that whoever came out to the camp too slowly after the signal had been given might know without doubt that he would be hanged on the gallows by such a collar [Note: “The second ‘himself’ is absent in MSS. 4 and 4a].

When they had been assembled in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, every last man, he entered Poland, bereft of its prince, and invaded it as an enemy. Like a huge storm he raged, wreaked havoc, and laid everything low; thus he devastated villages with slaughter, plunder, and fire, and burst into the strongholds [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “into the fortifications” instead of “in the strongholds”]. Entering Cracow, their metropolis, he overturned it from its summit and seized its spoils [Note: In manuscript A, another hand has written the letter *t* above the erasure in manuscript 1]. Moreover, he uncovered the ancient treasures hidden in the treasury by former dukes, namely an exceedingly vast quantity of gold and silver. Likewise, he set the other cities afire and destroyed them to the ground.

When they had reached the fortress of Gedec [Note: Its location is not sufficiently clear. Some have conjectured that it was Giecz, which Długosz writes was once a ducal fortress situated between Gniezno and Poznań. Cf. Roepell I, 177] [Note: The reading is corrected in manuscript A from “Gnezden”; manuscript 1 has “Gradec,” MSS. 2 and 2a “Gdec,” manuscript 2b “Gdee,” and MSS. 4 and 4a “Goec”], the castellan and the villagers who had taken refuge there [Note: The final syllable is written above the line by another hand in manuscript 2], unable to withstand the duke’s attack, came out to meet him carrying a golden rod, which was the sign of surrender. They humbly begged him to transfer them peacefully into Bohemia with their cattle and all their other possessions [Note: Manuscript A corrects “other” to “remaining” in MSS. 4 and 4a]. The duke granted their request. After bringing them into Bohemia [Note: “To Bohemia” is “to” in manuscript 2b], he gave them a considerable portion of a forest called Crinin [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Cirum,” though “Ciruin” may also be read; MSS. 2a and 4 have “Cirnin,” and manuscript 2b “Ciruin”] [Note: Which forest this was is not clear. See the differing opinions in Pubitschka III, 301]. He appointed one of them as their governor [Note: “One of them” is “he appointed one” in manuscript A] and judge [Note: “Perfectum” is corrected to “praefectum” in manuscript 1], and decreed that both they and their descendants should live forever under the law which they had possessed in Poland. Derived from the name of their city, they are called Gedcani [Note: “Gedeane” in MSS. 2b and 3] even to the present day [Note: Palacký observes that two villages may still exist in the Rakovník district, Hedecvko and Hecvdany. Palacký I, 280].

## 3

Not far from the aforementioned city they came to the metropolis of Gnezden [Note: “Gnesen”], strong by the nature of its site and its outer defenses, yet easily captured by enemies, because few citizens inhabited it. There, at that time [Note: Absent in manuscript A], in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, rested the most precious treasure: the body of the most blessed martyr Adalbert [Note: “The body” is absent in manuscript 2].

The Bohemians quickly took the city without battle [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “without death,” rather than “without Mars”] and entered with great joy the sanctuary [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “they approached and entered”; another hand has written “they approached” above “entered” in manuscript 2] of the holy church. Setting aside all other booty [Note: Corrected by another hand in manuscript 1], they asked that the precious mass of the sacred body, which had suffered for Christ, alone be granted them.

When their bishop Severus saw their rashness and perceived their disposition ready for every right and wrong [Note: “Every right and wrong” is “every right and wrong deed” in manuscript 4; the phrase echoes Lucan, *Pharsalia* V, 313; VI, 147], he tried by the following address to recall them from their unlawful attempts [Note: Manuscript A corrects “causis” to “ausis”]:

“My brothers and sons of God’s Church, it is not as easy as you think for any mortal to presume so rashly to touch this sacred portion of the body, full of divine powers. For I greatly fear that we may be struck with loss of memory, blindness, or some weakness of our limbs if we presumptuously undertake this deed. Therefore, first fast for three days, do penance for your sins, renounce all the abominations which he himself has abominated in you [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “and do penance from all abominations”], and promise from your whole heart that you will not commit them again [Note: This is absent in manuscript 2]. For I hope in the mercy of God and of our patron Saint Adalbert that we shall not be deprived of hope for our petition if we persevere in the bond of faith [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “federation” rather than “faith”] and in constant prayer.”

But his words seemed to them like ravings. Immediately, stopping up their ears [Note: Manuscript A reads “continuantes”; manuscript 2 “continniantes”], they rushed forward to seize the sacred body. Since it had been deposited behind the altar beside the wall [Note: In manuscript 1 the letters *ar* are written above the line by another hand] and could not otherwise be removed unless the altar were first destroyed [Note: “First” is added in MSS. 4 and 4a], their wicked hands [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “thus”] with beastly minds set about profane work. But divine vengeance was not lacking. In the very act of their rashness they stood stupefied in their senses [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “stupefied” in the plural], and for nearly three hours they had neither speech, sensation, nor sight, until, by God’s grace, they recovered their former faculties.

Then, though late, moved to penitence, they carried out the bishop’s commands. And the more plainly they had been chastised by divine will, the more devoutly they persisted, untiring in prayer, fasting for three days and asking forgiveness.

## 4

On the third night, after the morning synaxis, Saint Adalbert appeared in a vision to Bishop Severus while he rested [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “Saint Adalbert, appearing in a vision”]:

“Tell the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Bracizlaus”] and his companions this: the Father from heaven will grant what you seek, if you do not repeat the evils which you renounced at the font of baptism [Note: Manuscript A reads “in baptism,” and manuscript A* likewise].”

When the bishop made this known to the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Severus”] and his companions in the morning, they at once rejoiced, entered Saint Mary’s church, and prostrated themselves on the ground before the tomb of Saint Adalbert [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “the martyr”]. After long common prayer, the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a specify “Bracizlaus”] rose and, standing in the pulpit [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “ambo”], broke the silence with these words [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “saying”]:

“Do you wish to amend your transgressions and repent of wicked deeds?”

They cried out with tears [Note: The repeated “they cried out” in manuscript 1 is erased] saying [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “saying”]: “We are prepared to amend whatever our fathers or we sinners have transgressed against God’s holy Adalbert [Note: Added in MSS. 4 and 4a], and to cease from every wicked work [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “with all our mind”].”

Then the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Bracizlaus”], stretching out his hand over the sacred tomb, began thus to the assembled people [Note: “Crowd” is corrected to “people” in manuscript 1; MSS. 4 and 4a read “troop”]:

“Stretch out together, brothers [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “dearest”], your right hands to the Lord [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “God”] and heed my words, which I wish you to confirm by the sacrament of your faith. Therefore let this be my foremost and first decree [Note: Manuscript A and MSS. 2, 2b, 3, 4, and 4a read ‘greatest’ rather than ‘nearest’]: that your marriages, which until now you have treated as brothels and as common to you like brute animals [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a insert ‘are’], shall henceforth, according to the ordinances of the canons, be lawful, private, and indissoluble—provided only that one man live content with one wife and one wife with one husband.

“But if wife rejects husband, or husband wife, and quarrelling between them has boiled over into separation [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read ‘has grown hot’], whoever of them [Note: Manuscript A reads ‘of these’] refuses to return to the former lawfully celebrated union, I do not wish, according to the custom of our land, that the violator of this matter [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read ‘transgressor’] be reduced to slavery; rather, whatever his rank, he shall be deported by forced service into Hungary under our irrevocable decree. Nor may he ransom himself with money or return to this land, lest the contagion of one little sheep spread through Christ’s whole fold.”

Bishop Severus said: “Whoever acts otherwise, let him be anathema.”

The same punishment shall be imposed on virgins, widows, and adulteresses who are known to have lost their good name, corrupted their chastity, and conceived through fornication. Since they have freedom to marry, why do they commit adultery and procure abortions for their conceptions [Note: Manuscript A reads “abortions”; manuscript 3 has another form], which is the worst crime of crimes?

Then the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Bracizlaus”] added:

“If, however, a woman complains that she is not loved in equal measure, but is cruelly afflicted and abused by her husband [Note: ‘By her husband’ is absent in manuscript 3], let the judgment of God be given between them, and whoever is found guilty shall suffer the penalty of guilt.

“Likewise, concerning those notorious for homicides: let the archpriest enter their names before the count of that city, and let the count summon them. If they are rebellious [Note: Written above the line in manuscript A], let him put them in prison until either they perform fitting penance or, if they deny the charge, they are tested by red-hot iron or consecrated water to determine whether they are guilty.

“But fratricides, parricides, murderers of priests, and those implicated in crimes of this capital kind, let the archpriest deliver to the count or duke, who shall expel them from the realm with their hands and bellies bound in iron [Note: Manuscript A reads “or ... or”; manuscript 2b “or,” and manuscript 3 another equivalent], so that like Cain [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “dogs”] they may wander as fugitives over the earth [Note: Manuscript 1 originally read “they wandered,” later corrected].”

Bishop Severus said: “Let this determination of the duke be just and confirmed by anathema. For this purpose, you dukes have the sword hanging at your thigh: that you may often wash your hands in the sinner’s blood [Note: ‘Often’ is omitted in manuscript 2].”

Again the duke said:

“The tavern [Note: Manuscript A reads “the tavern” in a different form], which is the root of all evils, from which proceed thefts, homicides [Note: Manuscript 4a reads a corrupt form], adulteries [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add ‘fornications and drunkenness’], and other evils, and both he who prepares drink and he who buys what has been prepared [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read ‘what has been prepared’ in a different form—‘what has been poured’]—”

Bishop Severus said: “Let him be anathema.”

And the duke again: “Whoever is caught, being a tavern-keeper and a violator of this decree, shall be hung upon a pole in the middle of the marketplace, flogged until the crier is weary, and shaved. Yet his property shall not be confiscated [Note: Manuscript 2b reads ‘confiscated’]; only the drink shall be poured onto the ground [Note: Manuscript A reads ‘rather’], lest anyone be polluted by that accursed draught. Drinkers, if caught [Note: Manuscript 1 has a corrected corrupt reading], shall not leave prison until each has paid 300 coins into the duke’s treasury.”

Bishop Severus said: “What the duke judges, our authority confirms.”

The duke continued [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Bracizlaus”]:

“Further, we altogether forbid markets to be held on Sundays. They are especially held in these regions so that people may devote the other days to their work. If anyone is found publicly engaged on Sundays or feast days [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read ‘both on Sundays and feast days’] in any servile work, on days proclaimed as holidays for the church [Note: Manuscript A reads ‘on Sundays and feast days’], let the archpriest take away the work itself and whatever is found engaged in the work, including the beast of burden [Note: Absent in manuscripts A and A*], and let him pay 300 coins into the duke’s treasury [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read ‘to the duke’].

“Likewise, those who bury their dead in fields or woods: the perpetrators of this presumption shall pay an ox to the archdeacon [Note: MSS. 4a reads ‘the archdeacon’] and 300 coins into the duke’s treasury [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read ‘to the duke’]. But let them bury the dead anew in the cemetery of the faithful [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 omit ‘coins’].

“These are the things God hates; weary of these, Saint Adalbert abandoned us, his sheep, and preferred to go and teach foreign nations. That we shall not do these things again, we confirm together by the sacrament of our faith and yours.”

Thus spoke the duke. Then the bishop [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Severus”], having invoked the name of the Holy Trinity and taken up a hammer, while the other clergy [Note: Omitted in MSS. 4 and 4a] chanted seven psalms [Note: Manuscript 4a reads six] and other prayers appropriate to this holy work [Note: Absent in manuscript 3], began gently to dismantle the top of the tomb, destroying it down to the depths of the sacred treasure.

When they opened the sarcophagus, all who were present in the church were filled with such a fragrance of the sweetest odor [Note: Manuscript 1 and MSS. 4 read a corrupt form; a gloss in manuscript 1 gives “fragrance”] that for three days, as though filled with rich dishes [Note: Manuscript A reads “excellent dishes,” and MSS. 4 and 4a “best dishes”], they forgot to take food. Indeed, very many sick persons were healed at that same hour [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “on that day,” while the other manuscripts read “at that hour”].

Then the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Bracizlaus”] and the bishop [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Severus”], with a few counts, looked upon the saint of God [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Adalbert”]. When they saw him so radiant in face and bearing, and his body entirely whole, as if he had celebrated the sacred solemnities of Mass that very day, the clergy sang *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God”—and the laity sang *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy” [Note: Manuscript A has “krilès”; manuscript 4 “kyrt”]. Their voices resounded to the heavens [Note: Manuscript 1 reads a corrupt form].

When these things had been done, the duke, his face flooded with tears of joy, prayed [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “saying”]:

“O martyr of Christ, blessed Adalbert [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “Adabert”], who hast always and everywhere had mercy upon us [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “have mercy”], now look upon us with thy customary compassion; be gracious to us sinners, and do not disdain to be brought by us—though sinners—to thy seat of the holy Church of Prague [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “holy”].”

A marvellous and most astonishing thing: he whose tomb they had been unable to touch three days earlier, the duke and bishop immediately lifted from the sarcophagus without hindrance. Covering the body with silk, they placed it upon the upper altar, so that the people might discharge the vows which they had made to God and His saint. On that same day 200 marks were allotted to the altar in the fortress [Note: The words “altar in the fortress” are absent in manuscript A].

> O almighty God, who turnest the world through the ages,  
> who ever reignest, who alone rulest all things:  
> nothing is done, nor has been done, nor shall be done in the world, good Christ, without thy will.

What mortal could ever have believed that he would permit his body, already crowned in the heavenly kingdom, to be carried back to apostate nations—nations whose crimes he had despised and whose company he had fled while still alive? Yet, if we consider the greater and ancient miracles of God—how the people of Israel crossed the sea on dry foot; how waters flowed from the dry rock [Note: Manuscript 2b reads “may have flowed”]; or how the Maker of the world appeared in the world, born of the Virgin Mary—we ought not to marvel, but rather to humble ourselves before God, who did and can do whatever He wills, and ascribe everything to His grace.

By the inspiration of that grace, it entered the duke’s heart likewise to translate the body of the archbishop of the same city, named Gaudentius [Note: A note discusses the claim that these bones were given by the Poles, through pious fraud, as the relics of St Adalbert and transferred by the Bohemians. Długosz and others tried to prove this. On the Polish side, Martinus Gallus I, 19, maintains Cosmas’s account. Cf. Balbinus, *Epitome rerum Bohemicarum* III, 4; Dobner on Hájek V, 235; Meinert, *Wiener Jahrbücher* XLVIII, Anzeiger, p. 48], who perhaps rested in the same church [Note: Manuscript A reads “almost”].

As we have related above [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “thus”; the others “as”], he was not only the carnal but also the spiritual brother [Note: Manuscript 1 has the spelling “spiritali”] of Saint Adalbert, and his inseparable companion in every labor and hardship. Although he did not suffer martyrdom bodily with him [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “he endured”], he endured it through the compassion of his mind. For it could not be that a sword did not pierce his soul when he saw his own brother cut into pieces by the swords of the pagans, while he himself greatly desired to be slain with him [Note: Manuscript A originally read “had desired,” later corrected].

It further seemed good to the duke [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “the most noble”] and bishop to transfer with the greatest care, together with the holy body, the relics of the Five Brothers, holy martyrs [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a insert “of the holy martyrs”], whose life and passion we have sufficiently related above [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “with God’s help we shall relate”] [Note: Cf. I, 38], and who rested in the same city, though in another church [Note: Manuscript A has “not” written above the line], together with him.

What more need be said?

## 5

They arrived in Bohemia with all the sacred burden in prosperity and joy. On the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “vigils”] they pitched camp near the metropolitan city of Prague, beside the stream Rokitnica [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Kocitnica,” manuscript 2b “Rokitniczam”] [Note: Rokytnice]. At dawn the clergy and the whole populace came out in procession to meet them, and the plain could scarcely contain its long line.

What was this procession like? The duke himself and the bishop, supporting the sweet burden upon their shoulders, bore the martyr of Christ, Adalbert. Behind them abbots carried the relics of the Five Brothers [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “holy”]. Then the archpriests rejoiced in bearing the burden of Archbishop Gaudentius. They were followed by twelve chosen priests [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read twenty], who could scarcely support the weight of a golden crucifix [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “body”]; for Duke Mieszko had weighed himself against gold three times [Note: “Three times” is absent in manuscript 1]. In fifth place they carried three plates heavy with gold, which had been placed around the altar where the holy body had rested [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “had been placed”].

The largest plate was five cubits long and ten palms broad, richly adorned with precious stones and crystal objects [Note: The meaning of *sachis* is uncertain, perhaps “things” or “objects”]. Upon its border was inscribed this verse:

> This work had weighed three hundred pounds of gold.

Finally they drew immense bells and all the treasures of Poland in more than a hundred wagons. An innumerable band of noble men followed, bound with iron manacles [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “with bound hands”] and with their necks crushed by iron collars [Note: Perhaps “iron rings”; another note explains the term as “strong circles”]. Among them—alas!—taken captive to his misfortune, was brought my great-great-grandfather [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “my ancestor”; the words are absent from MSS. A, 1, 2, 2a, 2b, and 3]:

> A partner among the clergy, a priest by office.

O day worthy of honor among the Bohemians and of commemoration through the ages,  
to be celebrated with sacred mysteries, proclaimed with worthy praises,  
reverenced with the most devout praises,  
abounding in joy for the rich, desired by the weak,  
delightful to the poor, adorned by the giving of alms,  
and cultivated by every good endeavor—a day on which feast-days shine, heaped upon feast-days.

O Prague, most happy metropolis,  
formerly exalted by the holy duke Wenceslaus [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Wenceslaus”], now adorned by the blessed bishop Adalbert [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Adalbert”],  
thou receivest doubled joys bestowed upon thee by the Lord God;  
and through these two olives of mercy thou fliest in renown beyond the Sarmatians and the Sarigas [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “thus”; manuscript A “Solamatas”; MSS. 2 and 2a “Foramatas”; manuscript 2b “Sarmatas”; manuscript 3 “Sauromatas”; MSS. 4 and 4a “Soramatas”] [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “Iazyges”].

This translation of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Adalbert, took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1039 [Note: The Prague Annals agree]. Manuscript 2b dates it “the ninth day before the Kalends of September”; MSS. 4 and 4a, “the eighth.” MSS. 4 and 4a add: “In the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.”

## 6

But although these successes had been granted by God [Note: Manuscript A reads “by the Lord”], a wicked informer was not lacking [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “did not desist”]. He reported these deeds to the Apostolic See [Note: This phrase is absent in manuscript 3] and proclaimed that the duke of Bohemia and the bishop had violated the divine sanctions and the traditions of the holy Fathers; and that, if the lord pope did not punish this [Note: Benedict, pope from A.D. 1033 to 1048], he would diminish throughout the world the authority of the rights of the Apostolic See.

Immediately a sacred assembly was held; the canons were recited and the Holy Scriptures examined. The duke and bishop, though absent, were accused of presumption. Some decreed that the duke should be deprived of all rank and exiled for three years; others judged that the bishop should be suspended from every pontifical office and dwell in a monastery of monks for the rest of his life; others cried that both should be struck with the sword of anathema.

## 7

Meanwhile, the envoys of the duke and bishop of the Bohemians came to Rome on behalf of the whole people and of the two men themselves, bringing petitions more polished by gifts than by eloquent words [Note: Manuscript A reads “by eloquence of words”; manuscript 3 has the same sense]. When opportunity to speak was given them, they set forth the cause of their embassy before the Apostolic lord and the sacred council in this address [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “before his presence”; MSS. 2, 4, and 4a use a different form]:

“O most holy governor of the Catholic faith and Apostolic See, and O fathers enrolled in the book of life [Note: Absent in manuscript A], to whom God has granted the power both to judge and to show mercy: have mercy upon those who confess that they have sinned; spare those who repent and ask forgiveness.

“We confess that we acted unlawfully and contrary to the decrees of the canons, because from such remote regions and within so brief a space of time we could not obtain a messenger for your holy undertaking [Note: Omitted in MSS. 4 and 4a]. Yet whatever it is that we have done, know, O fathers—know [Note: Manuscript 1 reads thus; the other manuscripts omit the repetition]—ye enrolled, that we did it not from rashness, but for the great benefit of the Christian religion and with good intention. Or, if good intention ever falls into fault, O most holy fathers, we are prepared, according to your judgment, to amend our offense.”

To this the Apostolic lord replied briefly: “If one repents, the error does no harm.”

The envoys, removed from the council [Note: Manuscript A reads “thus”; manuscript 1 “to the council”; manuscript 2 “to the business”; the remaining manuscripts “from the council”], obtained lodging, to render account in judgment on the following day.

That night, however, the duke’s and bishop’s envoys went about bribing the cleverness of the cardinals with money; with gold they undermined justice, bought mercy at a price, and softened the judicial sentence with gifts [Note: Manuscript 1 corrects “they buy” to “they soften”].

On the next day, when the envoys were again presented before the sacred council in the Capitol [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “chapter-house”], the Apostolic lord opened his holy mouth, full of weighty words and authority:

“As a harsher vengeance ought to be exercised against those obstinate in the guilt of impiety [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a read “in impieties”], so we readily grant assent to those who acknowledge their guilt and desire penitence [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “assent” in a corrupt form], and we apply the antidote of mercy to wounds inflicted by the enemy [Note: Manuscript 2b reads “by enemies”; manuscript 1 has an interlinear correction].

“For it is a great sin to seize what belongs to others; but it is greater and utterly abominable not only to despoil Christians but also to take them captive and sell captives like brute animals [Note: MSS. 2b and 3 read “those taken captive”]. That you committed this in Poland has been reported to us by truthful messengers.

“The canons testify, the decrees of the Fathers forbid [Note: Manuscript 2b reads “affirm”], and the divine utterances command that those who presume such a deed [Note: MSS. 2b and 3 read “of this kind”] be struck with the sword of anathema: no one may transfer a holy body from place to place without our permission.

“But because you did this either through ignorance or by favor of a good intention, we command [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “under holy obedience”] that for this rash presumption your duke and bishop build, in a suitable place, a monastery sufficiently endowed for all ecclesiastical uses and honors. Let them establish, according to custom, approved persons and the offices of the serving clergy, so that diligent service may be rendered there to God forever, both for the living faithful and for the dead; thus perhaps even in this way the transgression of your guilt may be wiped away in the sight of God.”

The envoys departed greatly rejoicing [Note: Omitted in manuscript 2] and reported the Apostolic lord’s commands to the duke. The duke, obeying them as divine commands, built a most beautiful monastery in honor of Saint Wenceslaus the martyr in the city of Boleslau [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Boleslaw,” manuscript 3 “Boleslaus,” and manuscript 4a “Bolezlaus”], beside the River Labe [Note: Alt-Bunzlau on the Elbe], where that saint had once gloriously completed his martyrdom [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Wenceslaus”]. There, as may still be seen today, a numerous company of brothers serves God, and there are a provostship and a very devout basilica [Note: This matter was not adjudicated until A.D. 1046].

## 8

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1040, Rumor—than which no worse evil flourishes in the world—growing fat on lies and, mingling many things with few and false things with true, increasing as it flies [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 174–175], carried to the ears of the second Emperor Henry [Note: Cosmas counts the emperors named Henry] the report that the Bohemians had carried off from Poland a hundredfold more gold and silver than was true.

Then the emperor [Note: MSS. 4 and 4a add “Henry”] began to seek pretexts against them, in whatever way he might seize from them the gold that had been reported to him. Sending commissioners, he threatened war unless they sent him, within the appointed term, every last obol [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “obovlum”] of the silver they had plundered in Poland.

To this the Slavs replied:

“Always, while the terms of our law were preserved, we have been—and today are—under the rule of King Charles and his successors. Our nation has never been rebellious, and in every war it has remained and will always remain faithful to you, if only you are willing to do us justice [Note: Manuscript A reads “only to us”; manuscript 2b “only”].

“For Pippin, son of the great King Charles, established this law for us: each year we are to pay the successors of the emperors 120 selected oxen and 500 marks. By a mark of our coinage we mean 200 coins [Note: Dobner, in his notes on Hájek II, 433, maintains that one coin of that period had the value, in his own day, of four and a half coins bearing the cross, that is, Kreuzers; the Bohemian tribute therefore amounted to 7,500 florins in the currency of his day].

“This is attested by the age of our people from generation to generation [Note: Manuscript A reads “the age of our generations”; MSS. 2b, 3, 4, and 4a read “from generation to generation”]. Every year we pay this without resistance [Note: Manuscript A reads “reflagration”; manuscript 1 has the same corrupt form], and we wish to pay it to you and your successors. But if you wish to burden us with any yoke of law beyond the customary one [Note: Manuscript 4 reads “of the king”], we are readier to die than to bear an unfamiliar burden.”

The emperor replied [Note: Manuscript 2b reads “replying, said”]:

“It is the custom of kings always to add something new to the earlier law. For no body of law was established at a single time; rather, through successive rulers the sequence of laws has grown. Those who rule laws are not ruled by laws, because, as people commonly say, the law has a wax nose [Note: The words from ‘because’ through ‘nose’ are absent in manuscript A], while the king has a long and iron hand, so that he may bend it wherever he pleases.

“King Pippin [Note: Manuscript 2b adds “of France”] did what he wished; but unless you do what I wish, I shall show you how many painted shields I possess and what I can accomplish in war.”

---

## Complete textual and historical apparatus

The following register translates all 240 apparatus notes in source order. Latin readings are retained in italics because spelling, inflection, and word order often cannot be represented distinctly in English. “Text” identifies the reading printed in the narrative; “adds” and “omits” preserve the source note’s direction.

1. **Col. 0123, opening:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] vero addit 4.` Translation and direction: MS 4 adds *vero* (“but/indeed”) after *Ea* (“that”).
2. **Col. 0123B, Kazimir:** Source note: `[Col. 0123B] Male confundit Cosmas res Polonorum; Kazimir obiit post Bracizlaum a. 1058, neque reliquit filios pueros, sed ipse relictus est puer a patre Misecone II; cfr. Martinus Gallus I, 48, ed. Bandikte.` Translation and direction: Cosmas badly confuses Polish affairs: Kazimir died after Bracizlaus, in 1058, and did not leave sons who were children; rather, his father Mieszko II left Kazimir himself as a child. Cf. Martinus Gallus I.48, ed. Bandtke.
3. **Col. 0123, Kazimir:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] Cazimir 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a spell the name *Cazimir*.
4. **Col. 0123B, Kazimir’s sons:** Source note: `[Col. 0123B] Praeter hos duos alios habebat filios Kazimir Miseconem et Ottonem. Cfr. Martin. Gall. I, 19.` Translation and direction: Besides Boleslaus and Wladizlaus, Kazimir had the sons Mieszko and Otto. Cf. Martinus Gallus I.19.
5. **Col. 0123, infancy:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] deest 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 omits *ad ubera lactis* (“at the breasts for milk,” hence “still nursing”).
6. **Col. 0123, Polish hope:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] nulla 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *nulla* (“no [hope]”) for text *una* (“one [hope]”).
7. **Col. 0123, Bracizlaus notices:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] igitur advertens 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *igitur advertens* (“therefore noticing”) for text *Quod animadvertens* (“noticing this”).
8. **Col. 0123B, fourth year:** Source note: `[Col. 0123B] i. e. ex ipsius Cosmae computatione a. 1041; cfr. supra I, 42; sed hoc loco errat, ut ex accuratioribus notis de translatione S. Adalberti II, 5, patet.` Translation and direction: According to Cosmas’s own computation this was 1041; cf. I.42. He errs here, as the more accurate dates for the translation of St Adalbert in II.5 show.
9. **Col. 0123, Mieszko:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] Bracizlaus erasum 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 erased *Bracizlaus* after *dux Mesco*; the erased word would have misidentified Duke Mieszko as Bracizlaus.
10. **Col. 0123, speed:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] quanto cicius A.` Translation and direction: A reads *quanto cicius* for text *quantocius*; both mean “as quickly as possible,” with the former written as two words.
11. **Col. 0123, decree:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] dux Bracizlaus addunt 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *dux Bracizlaus* (“Duke Bracizlaus”) as the subject of *dictat* (“issues”).
12. **Col. 0123, all Bohemia:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] deest A.` Translation and direction: A omits *per* (“throughout”) before *provinciam*.
13. **Col. 0123, province:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] provinciae A.` Translation and direction: A reads genitive *provinciae* (“of the province”) for accusative *provinciam* (“province”).
14. **Col. 0123, cork:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] subure 2, 2b, 4, 4a, corr. 1.` Translation and direction: MSS 2, 2b, 4, and 4a read *subure* for text *subere* (“cork”); MS 1 has a correction.
15. **Col. 0123, the laggard himself:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] se deest 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a omit *se* (“himself”) from *tali torque se ... suspendendum* (“that he himself would be hanged by such a collar”).
16. **Col. 0123, fortifications:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] vi pro in 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *vi* (“by force”) for text *in* (“into/in”) in the sentence about storming strongholds.
17. **Col. 0123, spoils:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] ti superscr. al. man. A. in rasura 1.` Translation and direction: In A another hand wrote *ti* above the line; in MS 1 it stands in an erasure, completing the form at *obtinuit* (“obtained/seized”).
18. **Col. 0124B, Gedec:** Source note: `[Col. 0124B] Quod ubi situm fuerit non satis liquet; conjecerunt nonnulli esse Giecz, quam ducalem quondam arcem inter Gnesnam et Posnaniam sitam esse scribit Dlugosz. Cfr. Roepell I, 177.` Translation and direction: Its location is uncertain. Some conjecture Giecz, which Długosz says was once a ducal fortress between Gniezno and Poznań. Cf. Roepell I, 177.
19. **Col. 0123, Gedec:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] ita corr. A. pro Gnezden. Gradec 1. Gdec 2, 2a. Gdee 2b. Goec 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: A corrects the text’s *Gedec* from *Gnezden*; MS 1 reads *Gradec*, MSS 2 and 2a *Gdec*, MS 2b *Gdee*, and MSS 4 and 4a *Goec*—variant spellings of the fortress.
20. **Col. 0123, villagers:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] ni al. man. superscr. 2.` Translation and direction: In MS 2 another hand added *ni* above the line to the word *villani* (“villagers”).
21. **Col. 0123, other possessions:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] corr. A. caeterum 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: A has a correction at the text’s *caeteris* (“other”); MSS 4 and 4a read *caeterum* (“the rest/remaining property”).
22. **Col. 0123, brought them:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] duxit A.` Translation and direction: A reads *duxit* (“led/brought”) for text *perduxit* (“led all the way/brought”).
23. **Col. 0123, Bohemia:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] ad 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2b reads *ad Boemiam* (“to Bohemia”) for text *in Boemiam* (“into Bohemia”).
24. **Col. 0123, Crinin:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] Cirum 2. quamvis et legi possit Ciruin; Cirnin 2a, 4. Ciruin 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2 reads *Cirum*, though it may also be read *Ciruin*; MSS 2a and 4 read *Cirnin*, and MS 2b *Ciruin*—spellings of the forest name printed as *Crinin*.
25. **Col. 0124B, the forest:** Source note: `[Col. 0124B] Quae fuerit illa silva, non patet. Diversorum sententias vide apud Pubitschkam III, 301.` Translation and direction: Which forest this was is unclear; see the differing opinions in Pubitschka III, 301.
26. **Col. 0123, appointed for them:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] U. eis A.` Translation and direction: At *constituens eis unum* (“appointing one for them”), A has the abbreviation *U. eis*; the note supplies no expanded alternative.
27. **Col. 0123, governor:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] perfectum corr. praef. 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 corrects *perfectum* (“perfect/completed”) to abbreviated *praef.* = *praefectum* (“prefect/governor”).
28. **Col. 0123, Gedcani:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] Gedeane 2b, 3.` Translation and direction: MSS 2b and 3 read *Gedeane* for text *Gedcane*, variant forms of the inhabitants’ name.
29. **Col. 0124B, descendants:** Source note: `[Col. 0124B] Vel hodie duas exstare villas in circulo Raconicensi Hedecvko et Hecvdany observat Palacky I, 280.` Translation and direction: Palacký I, 280 observes that two villages, Hedecvko and Hecvdany, may still exist in the Rakovník district.
30. **Col. 0123, distance:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] non A.` Translation and direction: A reads *non longe* (“not far”) for text *Nec longe* (“nor far”).
31. **Col. 0124B, Gnezden:** Source note: `[Col. 0124B] Gnesen.` Translation and direction: The note supplies the place-name form *Gnesen*.
32. **Col. 0123, easily captured:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] facile 4, 4a,` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read nominative *facile* for text accusative *facilem* (“easy [to capture]”).
33. **Col. 0123, few citizens:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] ratis al. manu superscr. paucis 1.` Translation and direction: In MS 1 another hand wrote *ratis* above *paucis* (“few”); the resulting reading is corrupt or uncertain.
34. **Col. 0123, at that time:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] deest A.` Translation and direction: A omits *tunc temporis* (“at that time”).
35. **Col. 0123, precious treasure:** Source note: `[Col. 0123] preciosissime 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 reads adverbial *preciosissime* (“most preciously”) for text adjectival *preciosissimus* (“most precious”).
36. **Col. 0125, body:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] deest 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 omits *martiris* (“of the martyr”) before *corpus* (“body”).
37. **Col. 0125, without battle:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] morte 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 reads *sine morte* (“without death”) for text *sine Marte* (“without Mars,” hence “without battle”).
38. **Col. 0125, enter:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] adeunt intrant 1. supra intrant manus alia scripsit adeunt 2.` Translation and direction: MS 1 reads *adeunt intrant* (“they approach, they enter”); in MS 2 another hand wrote *adeunt* (“they approach”) above *intrant* (“they enter”).
39. **Col. 0125, sanctuary:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] limina adita 1. adita alia manu suprascript. limina 2. adyta 2b. limina 4.` Translation and direction: For text *sanctae ecclesiae adita* (“the approaches/sanctuary of the holy church”), MS 1 reads *limina adita* (“the thresholds approached”), MS 2 has *adita* with *limina* added above by another hand, MS 2b *adyta* (“inner sanctuary”), and MS 4 *limina* (“thresholds”).
40. **Col. 0125, booty:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] corr. al. manu 1.` Translation and direction: In MS 1 another hand corrected the reading at *omni praeda* (“all booty”); no rejected form is supplied.
41. **Col. 0125, disposition:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] et rasum 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 erased *et* (“and”) after *temeritatem* (“rashness”).
42. **Col. 0125, right and wrong:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] fasque 4.` Translation and direction: MS 4 reads *fasque* (“and right”) for text *fas* (“right”) before *nefasque* (“and wrong”).
43. **Col. 0125C, right and wrong:** Source note: `[Col. 0125C] Lucan., Pharsal. V, 313; VI, 147.` Translation and direction: Compare Lucan, *Pharsalia* V.313 and VI.147.
44. **Col. 0125, attempts:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] corr. A. pro causis.` Translation and direction: A corrects *causis* (“causes/cases”) to text *ausis* (“attempts/daring deeds”).
45. **Col. 0125, presume:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] praesumamus 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 reads present subjunctive *praesumamus* (“we may presume”) for text perfect subjunctive *praesumpserimus* (“we may have presumed/undertaken”).
46. **Col. 0125, address:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] karissimi addunt 4, 4a` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *karissimi* (“dearest”) after *Quapropter* (“therefore”).
47. **Col. 0125, penance:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] et poenitentiam agite ab omnibus 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *et poenitentiam agite ab omnibus* (“and do penance from all”) before the text’s *ab omnibus abhominationibus* (“from all abominations”).
48. **Col. 0125, renunciation:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] deest 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 omits *et* (“and”) before *ab omnibus abhominationibus ... abrenunciate* (“renounce all abominations”).
49. **Col. 0125, bond:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] federi 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *federi* (“covenant/federation”) for text *fidei* (“faith”) in *fidei ... vinculo* (“bond of faith”).
50. **Col. 0125, prayer:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] deest 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 omits *in* (“in”) before *oratione continua* (“constant prayer”).
51. **Col. 0125, stopping their ears:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] continuentes A continnientes 2.` Translation and direction: A reads *continuentes* and MS 2 *continnientes* for text *continentes*; these are variant or corrupt spellings of “holding/stopping.”
