52. **Col. 0125, behind the altar:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] litterae ar al. manu superscr. 1` Translation and direction: In MS 1 another hand wrote the letters *ar* above the line at the phrase *post altare* (“behind the altar”).
53. **Col. 0125, first:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] prius add 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *prius* (“first”) before the altar’s destruction.
54. **Col. 0125, altar destroyed:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] destrueret 2b, 3.` Translation and direction: MSS 2b and 3 read active *destrueret* (“he/it might destroy”) for text passive *destrueretur* (“it might be destroyed”).
55. **Col. 0125, hands:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] ita 1, 2.` Translation and direction: MSS 1 and 2 read *ita* (“thus”) at the transition to *manus inproba* (“wicked hands”); the construction differs from the text.
56. **Col. 0125, wicked:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] ita corr. A. pro inpio.` Translation and direction: A corrects *inpio* (“impious,” singular form) to text *inproba* (“wicked,” agreeing with *manus*, “hands”).
57. **Col. 0125, stupefied:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] obstupefacti 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read nominative plural *obstupefacti* (“stupefied”) for text ablative plural *sensibus obstupefactis* (“with their senses stupefied”).
58. **Col. 0125, apparition:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] sanctus Adalbertus in visione apparens 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a reorder the text as *sanctus Adalbertus in visione apparens* (“Saint Adalbert, appearing in a vision”).
59. **Col. 0125, tell the duke:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] Bracizlao add 4, 4.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *Bracizlao* (“to Bracizlaus”) after *duci* (“to the duke”; the source prints “4, 4.”).
60. **Col. 0125, baptismal font:** Source note: `[Col. 0125] fronte eraso r A.` Translation and direction: A erased *r* in *fronte* (“forehead”) to produce text *fonte* (“font”).

150. **Cols. 0129B–0130B, Gaudentius’s bones:** Source note: `[Col. 0129B] Hujus ossa loco reliquiarum S. Adalberti a Polonis pia fraude data et a Bohemis translata esse probare conatus est Dlugosz et post eum alii; sed e parte Cosmae Polonus stat auctor Martinus Gallus I, 19. Cfr. Balbini Epitome rer. Bohem. III, 4. Dobner ad Haiec. V. 235. Meinert Wiener Jahrbucher [Col. 0130B] XLVIII. Anz., p. 48.` Translation and direction: Długosz and later writers tried to prove that the Poles, by a pious fraud, gave these bones as St Adalbert’s relics and that the Bohemians transferred them. On Cosmas’s side stands the Polish author Martinus Gallus I.19. Cf. Balbinus, *Epitome rerum Bohemicarum* III.4; Dobner on Hájek V, 235; Meinert, *Wiener Jahrbücher* XLVIII, *Anzeiger*, p. 48.

199. **Col. 0131, presence:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] conspectum 2, 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 2, 4, and 4a read accusative *conspectum* for text ablative *conspectu* in *in conspectu apostolici* (“in the presence of the Apostolic lord”).
200. **Col. 0131, pursued their case:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] persecuti 3.` Translation and direction: MS 3 reads *persecuti* (“pursued”) for text *prosecuti* (“set forth/pursued”).

202. **Col. 0131, remote regions:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] terra 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 reads *terra* (“land”) for text *tam* (“so”) in *de tam longinquis partibus* (“from such remote regions”).
203. **Col. 0131, your holy business:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] omittunt 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a omit *vestrum* (“your”) from *ad tam sanctum negotium vestrum* (“for your so holy business”).
204. **Col. 0131, know:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] ita 1. deest in rell.` Translation and direction: MS 1 repeats *sciatis* (“know”) as printed—“know, O fathers, know”; the remaining manuscripts omit the repetition.
205. **Col. 0131, removed from council:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] ita A. ad concilio 1. negotio 2. concilio rell.` Translation and direction: A has text *summoti a concilio* (“removed from the council”); MS 1 reads *ad concilio* (ungrammatical, apparently “to the council”), MS 2 *negotio* (“business”), and the remaining manuscripts *concilio* (“council”).
206. **Col. 0131, going about:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] circuientes A.` Translation and direction: A reads *circuientes* for text *circueuntes* (“going around”), a spelling/form variant.
207. **Col. 0131, soften the sentence:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] emunt corr. 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 corrects *emunt* (“they buy”) to text *leniunt* (“they soften”) in “with gifts they soften the judicial sentence.”
208. **Col. 0131, Capitol:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] capitulo 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *capitulo* (“in the chapter-house/chapter”) for text *capitolio* (“in the Capitol”).
209. **Col. 0131, guilt of impiety:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] impietatibus pro culpa 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a read *impietatibus* (“impieties”) in place of *culpa* (“guilt”), producing “obstinate in impieties.”
210. **Col. 0131, exact vengeance:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] exercenda 2b, 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 2b, 4, and 4a read *exercenda* (“to be exercised”) for text *exerenda* (“to be exacted/inflicted”).
211. **Col. 0131, assent:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] asensum 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 spells *asensum* for text *assensum* (“assent”).
212. **Col. 0131, enemy:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] hostibus 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2b reads plural *hostibus* (“by enemies”) for singular *hoste* (“by the enemy”).
213. **Col. 0131, apply:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] h. al. manu superscr. 1. ut saepius.` Translation and direction: In MS 1 another hand repeatedly supplied *h.* above the line at *adhibemus* (“we apply”); the abbreviation is not expanded.
214. **Col. 0131, captives:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] captivatos 2b, 3.` Translation and direction: MSS 2b and 3 read *captivatos* (“those taken captive”) for text *captivos* (“captives”) in “sell captives like brute animals.”
215. **Col. 0131, decrees:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] perhibent 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2b reads *perhibent* (“affirm/testify”) for text *prohibent* (“forbid”): “the decrees of the Fathers affirm” rather than “forbid.”
216. **Col. 0131, such a deed:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] hujusmodi 2b, 3.` Translation and direction: MSS 2b and 3 read *hujusmodi* for text *hujuscemodi*; both mean “of this kind/such.”
217. **Col. 0131, command:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] per sanctam obedientiam addunt 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *per sanctam obedientiam* (“under/by holy obedience”) after *praecipimus* (“we command”).
218. **Col. 0131, rash presumption:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] temera 3.` Translation and direction: MS 3 reads feminine *temera* for text genitive *temeri* (“rash”) in *tam temeri praesumptione* (“so rash a presumption”); its construction is irregular.
219. **Col. 0131, suitable place:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] compenti corr. al. man. competenti A.` Translation and direction: In A another hand corrects *compenti* to *competenti* (“suitable”).
220. **Col. 0131, rejoicing:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] deest 2.` Translation and direction: MS 2 omits *valde* (“greatly”) from *legati valde exhylarati* (“the envoys, greatly rejoicing”).
221. **Col. 0131, Boleslau:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] Boleslaw 2. Boleslai 3. Bolezlai 4a.` Translation and direction: MS 2 reads *Boleslaw*, MS 3 *Boleslai*, and MS 4a *Bolezlai* for text *Boleslau*, forms of the city’s name.
222. **Col. 0131C, Boleslau and Labe:** Source note: `[Col. 0131C] Al-Bunzlau ad Albim.` Translation and direction: The editor identifies the place as Alt-Bunzlau on the Elbe.
223. **Col. 0131, saint:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] Wencezlas addunt 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *Wencezlas* (“Wenceslaus”) after *idem sanctus* (“that same saint”).
224. **Col. 0131C, judgment:** Source note: `[Col. 0131C] Haec res anno demum 1046 diiudicata est.` Translation and direction: This matter was not adjudicated until the year 1046.
225. **Col. 0132C, Rumor:** Source note: `[Col. 0132C] Virg. Aen. IV, 174, 175.` Translation and direction: Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.174–175.
226. **Col. 0132C, second Henry:** Source note: `[Col. 0132C] Heinricos imperatores numerat Cosmas.` Translation and direction: Cosmas counts the emperors named Henry; this explains his numbering “the second Emperor Henry.”
227. **Col. 0131, emperor:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] Henricus addunt 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: MSS 4 and 4a add *Henricus* (“Henry”) after *imperator* (“emperor”).
228. **Col. 0131, however:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] quomodo 2, 2b, 3, 4.` Translation and direction: MSS 2, 2b, 3, and 4 read *quomodo* (“how”) for text *quoquomodo* (“in whatever way/however”).
229. **Col. 0131, reported gold:** Source note: `[Col. 0131] ut addit A.` Translation and direction: A adds *ut* (“that/so that”) before *ab eis quod sibi dictum fuerat eriperet aurum* (“he might seize from them the gold that had been reported to him”), altering the clause’s linkage.
230. **Col. 0133, obol:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] obovlum 1.` Translation and direction: MS 1 reads *obovlum* for text *obulum* (“obol”), a spelling variant.
231. **Col. 0133, justice:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] t. n. A. tantummodo 2b.` Translation and direction: At *si justiciam nobis tantum facere velis* (“if only you are willing to do us justice”), A abbreviates *t. n.* and MS 2b reads *tantummodo* (“only”) for text *tantum* (“only”).
232. **Col. 0133C, Pippin/Charles:** Source note: `[Col. 0133C] Carolus erat, Caroli Magni filius, qui a. 805 expeditionem in Boemos fecit teste Einhardo in Annalibus.` Translation and direction: It was Charles, son of Charlemagne, who made an expedition against the Bohemians in 805, as Einhard attests in the *Annals*; the narrative’s attribution to Pippin is erroneous.
233. **Col. 0133C, value of tribute:** Source note: `[Col. 0133C] Dobner ad Haiec. II, 433, docet nummum unum illorum temporum idem valuisse quod nostris diebus quatuor et dimidium nummos cruce signatos (Kreuzer), Bohemicum igitur censum fuisse 7500 florenos nostrae monetae.` Translation and direction: Dobner on Hájek II, 433 teaches that one coin of that period was worth four and a half cross-marked coins (*Kreuzer*) in his own day; the Bohemian tribute therefore amounted to 7,500 florins in the currency of his day.
234. **Col. 0133, generation to generation:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] nostrarum etas etatum A. aetate 2b, 3, 4, 4a.` Translation and direction: A reads *nostrarum etas etatum* (“the age of our generations”) for text *nostratum aetas in aetatem* (“the age of our people from age to age”); MSS 2b, 3, 4, and 4a read *aetate* (“in/by an age”).
235. **Col. 0133, without resistance:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] reflagratione A. 1.` Translation and direction: A and MS 1 read *reflagratione* (“blazing back,” nonsensical here) for text *refragatione* (“opposition/resistance”).
236. **Col. 0133, customary law:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] regis 4.` Translation and direction: MS 4 reads *regis* (“of the king”) for text *legis* (“of the law”) in “beyond the customary yoke of law.”
237. **Col. 0133, emperor replied:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] respondens dixit 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2b reads *respondens dixit* (“answering, he said”) for text *respondit* (“replied”).
238. **Col. 0133, wax nose:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] quia ut---lex nasum desunt A.` Translation and direction: A omits the entire span *quia lex, ut aiunt vulgo, cereum habet nasum* (“because, as people commonly say, the law has a wax nose”).
239. **Col. 0133, Pippin:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] Franciae addit 2b.` Translation and direction: MS 2b adds *Franciae* (“of France”) after “King Pippin.”
240. **Col. 0133, how many shields:** Source note: `[Col. 0133] quod corr. quot A. 1. quot super quod 2b.` Translation and direction: A and MS 1 correct *quod* (“that/what”) to *quot* (“how many”); in MS 2b *quot* is written above *quod*. The resulting text is *quot pictos habeam clipeos* (“how many painted shields I possess”).

9. And immediately, sending letters throughout the whole realm, he gathered a very strong army.  
[Note: [Col. 0133C] The author passed over in silence Henry III’s first Bohemian expedition, in 1039, in which Bretislaus gave his eldest son as a hostage. Cf. Hermann of Reichenau, s.a. 1039.]

By the other route, which leads through Zribia,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *ad* 2b; Zrbia 3.]

and has an exit from the forest into that land by way of the castle of Hlumec,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Hlymec 1; Hlymee 2; Hlumer 3.]  
[Note: [Col. 0133C] Dobner V, 256 conjectures that the name survives in modern Kuml and that ruins of the castle remain on Mount Geyersberg. See also Kropf’s discussion in *Monatschrift der Gesellschaft des vaterländischen Museums in Böhmen*, I, December, p. 37.]

he ordered the Saxons to enter Bohemia. Their leader at that time was Occard,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *princeps* 4, 4a; Okkardus 2; Okardus 3 and throughout.]  
[Note: [Col. 0134C] Margrave of Meissen.]

and all Saxony obeyed him in every respect as though he were a king. For he was a man of great judgment, endowed with singular skill in arranging the affairs of the realm,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *ordinandi* 4, 4a.]

and devoted to military matters from childhood; yet he never achieved successful results in war.

The emperor himself pitched camp on both banks of the River Rezne.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Rezene 1.]  
[Note: [Col. 0134C] The Regen.]

Then, on the following day, passing the castle of Kanb,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Thus corrected in A; Kamb 1, 2, 2b; Kamba 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0134C] Kamb in Bavaria.]

as he was advancing his eagles toward the forest which separates Bavaria from Bohemia,  
[Note: [Col. 0134C] Dobner discusses at greater length, in the cited place, the site of this Bohemian victory. He believes that the battle was fought on the borders of Bavaria and the Pilsen district, not far from the town of Taus.]

when he learned that the Bohemians were blocking the paths through the forest,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *quod* inserted by 2; *silvas* 4, 4a.]

he was enraged, remained silent for a little, and, shaking his head, conceived three angers worthy of a Caesar,  
[Note: [Col. 0134C] Cf. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.50; I.166, 181.]  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *caesari* 4, 4a; in A a corrector altered these words thus: *cepit irasci*, erasing the syllables *con* and *sare*, and expunging *dignas*.]

and broke into these words:

Though they build walls higher than the forests,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Corrected by another hand in 1.]

though they raise lofty towers up to the clouds, just as a net is vainly cast before the eyes of winged creatures, so the Bohemians’ defences avail nothing against the Teutons.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] A reads: “the Bohemians fight.”]

Or if they rise above the clouds, or shut themselves  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *includent* A.]

among the stars,

these things will help that ruined and miserable people not at all.

So he spoke and ordered all to burst into the forest. He himself,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] A adds *super*, “above.”]

preceding them, climbed a high mountain situated in the middle of the forest,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] 4, 4a insert “great and.”]

and, seated upon a tripod, said to the nobles of the whole realm who stood by:

In this valley a cowardly band of Bohemians lies hidden,

like a field-mouse in its sheltering caves.

But his opinion deceived the emperor, for their fortification lay beyond the next mountain. Then the emperor, calling each man by name—first the margraves, then sending ahead all the more distinguished armed men—ordered the infantry to go into battle, promising them victory in these words:

“There is no need for you to undergo a toilsome contest. Only go down: surely they themselves will flee in fear,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *fugiunt*, “they flee,” 4, 4a.]

for they cannot bear your attack. Go, my falcons, go; seize the frightened doves. And, like fierce lions in the manner of wolves, who, when they break into sheepfolds,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] *omnium*, “of all,” 4, 4a.]

take no account of their number and obtain food only when the whole flock has been slaughtered.”

[Col. 0135A] 10. At once, in obedience to the king’s command, the mail-clad ranks rush forward; the nobles contend for the first place in battle.

The bright battle-lines gleam like shining ice,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *prospicuae* A.]

and when the sun flashed upon their arms, the foliage of the woods and the summits of the mountains shone back from them. But when they descended into the valley, they found no one, because the forest was dense on both sides and the terrain impassable. And, as often happens in every engagement, those following drive the men before them into battle even against their will; so the nobles, already weary, were again forced by those following  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Corrected in 1 as *conpelluntur*; the rest read *coguntur*, “are forced.”]

to cross the next mountain.

But now, in the dry heat and thirst, their tongue clings to the palate; their strength fails, their right arms grow weak, they draw sickly breaths from their breasts, and nevertheless cannot halt their step.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *aestu* omitted in 3; *sicca* 2b; *queunt* supplied above the line by another hand in A, absent from 1, 2, 2b, 3; 4, 4a read *valent*, “are able.”]

Some cast their mail coats upon their shields; others stand leaning against trees, vainly gasping for empty air; others lie like logs—stout men unaccustomed to marching and fighting on foot. And when they had reached the fortification, a cry arose from every side,  
[Note: [Col. 0135C] Vergil, *Aeneid* XII.756.]

and vapour, like a cloud, rose over the forest from their exhausted bodies.

When the Bohemians saw this, they hesitated for a short time; then, once they understood that their strength had failed, they boldly sprang out from the fortification.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *prosiliunt*, with *-unt* supplied above the line by another hand in 1.]

Bellona, Fortune’s unconquered sister, gave them boldness.

O Fortune! You are never permanently good;  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *sors fortuna* 4, 4a.]

and with your unstable wheel you plunge the great into the depths.

The faces of fortunate men, once worthy of reverence,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] A reads *opera*, with a *t* supplied above the line by another hand, producing *operta*, “covered.”]

the iron-shod hoof of prancing horses defiles;  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *ferrea*, “iron,” 4, 4a.]

and a nag  
[Note: [Col. 0135C] A horse.]

bursts with its foot the bellies accustomed to luxury, and the loins girded with twice crimson-dyed belts,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *his* A; *cocco* with letters uncertainly supplied above the line in A; *tinctus* 2; *praecinctis* 4, 4a; *rancinus* 2b.]

and scatters their intestines and entrails like a bandage or the bindings of a leg.

I am ashamed to tell more of the sudden death of such great nobility, or of things unworthy to be brought forth in writing.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] 1 originally read *detente*, corrected by another hand to *detantae*.]

For so great was the slaughter there of noble men  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Omitted by 2b, 3.]

as neither on the fields of Emathia,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *Amathiae* 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0135C] Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.1.]

nor in the time of Sulla, nor in any plague of mortals, nor ever by an enemy sword, is said to have destroyed at one time so much Teutonic nobility.

Meanwhile the emperor, sitting on the brow of the mountain, was deceived by the prophecy of his own mind. For while he did not suppose that his men were being conquered by the enemy, when he saw the victors arrive, bloodstained, he leapt onto the back of his swift-footed horse,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *semipedis* A, 1, 2, 3.]

clung to its mane, and

the emperor set spurs to the flanks of his four-footed beast.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] A later hand supplied *t* in red ink above *admove*.]

Had he not had it ready, the Roman emperor would that very hour have gone down without delay into Orcus.  
[Note: [Col. 0135C] On Henry’s defeat on 22 August 1040, cf. Hermann of Reichenau and the Greater St Gall Annals.]

11. While these events were taking place there, the Saxons, with Duke Okard, of whom I have spoken above, entered Bohemia and ravaged hostilely a small region about the River Belina.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Okarado 1; “the river” omitted in 4a; 2 and 2a read “the river which is about Belina”; 2b, “the river which is around Belina.”]

Meanwhile, when their duke received the unwelcome report that the Slavs had defeated the emperor, he halted at the bridge of Gnevin  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Gneum 3; Ghnevin 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0136C] Gnenin, Brüx, on the Bílina in the Saaz district; cf. Pubitschka III, 319.]

beside the River Belina,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Bilinam 4a.]

deeply uncertain whether to test fortune in battle or return home with such disgrace. Nevertheless, he preferred first to test the duke’s disposition and, addressing him through envoys with friendly words, persuaded him thus:

“You who now rejoice that you have conquered by fighting—if you had conquered by supplication, you would have been a far better victor.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *pugnare* 1; *multo* supplied above the line by another hand in A; *victor* omitted in 4, 4a.]

Therefore do not vainly exalt yourself above yourself, because it is hard for you to kick against the goad. For he who lately entered your land with few men, as though sparing and pitying you—unless in the meantime you gain his favour—will soon come upon you with so great a multitude of armies that not even your springs will suffice for them, and your little country will scarcely contain them. Then the latter things will be worse than the former. Therefore I advise and counsel you again: do not lose everything that you seem to possess.

Send to the emperor through friends faithful to you no small sum of queenly money,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *regina* 3.]  
[Note: [Col. 0136C] Horace, *Epistles* I.6.37.]

which surpasses everything, appeases the angry, and reconciles enemies, so that it may itself intercede for you and secure his favour for you.”  
[Note: [Col. 0135] In 1 *fideles* was repeated but expunged; 4, 4a omit *tibi*, “for you.”]

At this Duke Bracizlaus, stirred by anger, rejected the wholesome warnings and, resting his hand upon the hilt, spoke thus:

“Tell your Occard:  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *viro*, “man,” 1; Okardus 2 and thereafter; Ockardus 4, 4a.]

I have counsel enough, and do not suppose that you have gained anything by advising me. Let Saxons harder than rocks listen to you, and any foolish men who think you possess some wisdom. But unless within three days you leave this province of mine without any violence, I shall cut off your head with this sword and put your mouth at your backside.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] *satis consilii* A; *ne* 2; *ne me* 4, 4a; *se* for *te* in 4; *inconsultu* 4, 4a.]

What is done at the emperor’s court is no concern of mine.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Supplied above the line by another hand in A.]

As long as a sword hangs at Bracizlaus’s thigh, milk shall not flow from the emperor’s side, but blood like milk.”

When these words had been reported to the duke,  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *dum* 2, 3; *duci* absent in A; 4, 4a add “to Occard.”]

although he took them very grievously, he nevertheless withdrew unwillingly like a wolf which, when it loses its prey, lowers its tail before the pursuing hounds and returns to the forest. So Duke Occard went back to Saxony in great disgrace.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] The clause “when it loses its prey …” is absent in 4.]

Duke Bracizlaus was likewise informed about Count Pricos,  
[Note: [Col. 0137] Prikos 1; Prycos 2, 2b; Picos 3.]

who was in command in the city of Belina,  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *fuit* 4, 4a; Belin 1, 2, 4; Bolin 3.]

that, bribed by Saxon money, he had not stood guard opposite the fortification, but had placed garrisons where woods were passable to the enemy.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *posuissent* 1.]  
[Note: [Col. 0137D] In 1043 Eppo was prefect of Bílina; see Boczek I, 116.]

For the duke had put him in command of the entire cohort from Moravia and of three legions sent as assistance from Hungary.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *tote* 4, 4a; *fuerunt* 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0137D] From Peter, king of the Hungarians and ally of Bracizlaus. Since the Hildesheim Annals assign these events to 1041, there can be no doubt that Count Pricos’s betrayal and the date 1041 in the text must be referred back to II.11.]

The enraged duke immediately had his eyes gouged out, his hands and feet cut off, and ordered him thrown into the abyss of the river,  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *praecipitare* 3; *abissum* 1; “Duke Bracizlaus” added in 4a; 4, 4a omit *statim*.]

in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1041.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] 4a adds: “The year of the Lord’s incarnation 1041 pertains to this event.”]

*Emperor Henry fights Duke Brzieczislaus and is shamefully put to flight.* 2, 2a, 2b.

12. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1042.  
[Note: [Col. 0137D] These events occurred in 1041; cf. Hermann of Reichenau and the St Gall Annals.]

The emperor Henry, ever a magnificent conqueror, wishing to avenge the destruction of his illustrious men, entered the land of the Bohemians by three routes, ravaged nearly all of it in hostile fashion, and set fire to many towns which they had abandoned because they could not defend them. When he came to the city of Prague, he planted his eagles opposite it at Sibenica, on a hillock.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] Sibenice 1; Sybenice 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0137D] The hill later called Mount Žižka.]

There I have discovered nothing worthy of narration, except that Bishop Severus

fled secretly by night from the city to the emperor’s camp, fearing, as I suppose, that, as one rebellious against his lord, he might be deprived of the honour of his episcopal see.

When Duke Bracizlaus saw this,

He knew not what to do; grief troubled his mind on every side.

Now he regretted having once fought against the emperor;  
[Note: [Col. 0137] The words “now he regretted … emperor” are omitted in 4, 4a.]

now he regretted having rejected Duke Occard’s warnings;  
[Note: [Col. 0137] The words from *sprevisse* to *eum* were placed in A’s margin by another hand.]

now he preferred to fight with prayers and to overcome by prayers him whom formerly he had overcome in battle.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *maluit* 2, 2b, 3; 4, 4a read “to overcome”; 2, 2b, 3 add *nam*, “for.”]

And with these words he attempted to turn aside the emperor’s dreadful anger:

You wage wars, Caesar, that will have no triumphs.  
[Note: [Col. 0137D] Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.12.]

Our land is your treasury; we are yours, and desire to be yours.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *nostra* and “and desire to be yours” absent in A.]

For one who rages against his own subjects

is known to be more cruel than a cruel enemy. If you look to the strength of your army, we are not even a moment’s concern to you. Why do you display your power as though against a leaf carried away by the wind? For the wind fails where nothing opposes it. Whatever you wish to be, you are already victor.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *vitrici* 2b, 3; perhaps an erroneous reading.]

Now bind your victorious temples with laurel.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *tempora* 2, 2b, 4; *tempora* 3; *tympora* absent in 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0138D] Vergil, *Aeneid* V.539.]

Furthermore, he promised him fifteen hundred marks of denarii, which was the tribute for the three years already passed.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *jam* omitted in 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0138D] The Saxon annalist testifies that in autumn, at the feast of St Michael, Henry made peace with the Bohemians at Prague in 1042.]

Soon, just as a great fire blazes with flames when someone pours an excessive quantity of water over it—the water gradually checks its force, and the fire fails before the prevailing waves—

so queenly money extinguished the emperor’s anger.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *fundat* 2b, 3; *sexus* corrected to *secus* in A.]

For he who had formerly entered this land harshly, after receiving the money returned gently, peace having been established.

13. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1043 there was so great a famine in Bohemia that a third of the people perished from hunger.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1044.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1045, Gunther the monk died, on 9 October.  
[Note: [Col. 0138D] On Gunther, hermit in the Bohemian forest, see Hermann of Reichenau, 1045; the *Life of St Gotthard, Bishop of Hildesheim*, in Leibniz I, 487; and Bracizlaus’s charter of 1045, Boczek I, 120; the *Life of St Gunther*, *Acta Sanctorum*, October IV, 1068.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1046, a monastery in the city of Boleslav was dedicated on 19 May by Severus, sixth bishop of the church of Prague.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] 3 reads “29 December”; 4, 4a read “by Lord Severus of holy Prague.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0138D] See above II.7, and Bracizlaus’s charter, Boczek I, 125.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1047.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1048.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1049.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1050.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1051.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1052, Bozena, wife of Duke Oudalric, mother of Bracizlaus, died.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] *Bona*, with *ze* supplied above the line by another hand in A; Boziena 2.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Odalrici 2; Udalrici 2b; this belongs under 1050 in A.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1053, Saint Procopius, abbot, died. 2, 2a, 2b.  
[Note: [Col. 0139D] Of Sázava.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1054,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Written in A’s upper margin by another hand, but incorrectly, as 1053.]

the city of Wratizlav [Breslau] and other cities were restored by Duke Bracizlaus to the Poles, on condition that they should pay him and his successors every year five hundred marks of silver and thirty of gold.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Wratislaw 2; Wratislai 3; Wratislau 2b, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139D] Breslau.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139] 2b, 4, 4a add “Bohemian.”]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1055,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] A has “1053,” supplied above the line by another hand.]

Duke Bracizlaus,

renowned at the summit of virtues,

the jewel of the Bohemians, the bright light of his fathers,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *Sclavorum*, “of the Slavs,” 4, 4a.]

after, with God’s help, subduing all Poland to himself and gaining victory twice, had now proposed to invade Pannonia for the third time.  
[Note: [Col. 0139D] Palacký I, 291 doubts whether Bratislaus really intended to undertake a war against the Hungarians in winter.]

While he awaited his advancing army, he was struck by a severe illness in the city of Hrudim.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Chrudim 2; Hrudin 3.]

When he felt it growing ever more severe and the strength of his body ebbing away, he summoned those leading men of the land who happened to be present. With them standing by, he spoke these words:

“Since my fates summon me and dark death now flies before my eyes, I wish to designate and entrust to your loyalty the man who ought to govern the commonwealth after me.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *qui*, “who,” erased and supplied above the line in A.]

You know that our princely line, partly through barrenness and partly through deaths at an untimely age, had been reduced to me alone.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *principalis* absent in A; *in* absent in 2, 3, 4, 4a; *usque* corrected by another hand in A; *imum*, “lowest,” 2.]

But now, as you yourselves see, God has given me five sons. It does not seem useful to me to divide the kingdom of Bohemia among them, because every kingdom divided against itself shall be desolated.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] A has *in se ipso*, with *i. s. ipso* added in the margin by another hand.]

And because, from the origin of the world, from the beginning of the Roman empire, and down to these times, brotherly affection has been rare, established examples testify to us.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *quod* 2b; *oriente* 1; *fratrum* omitted in A, 1, 2, 2a, 4a; read in 3, 4, and placed in the margin of 2b.]

For Cain and Abel, Romulus and Remus, and my great-grandfathers Bolezlaus and Saint Wencezlaus—if you consider what two brothers did, what will five brothers do?  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Chain 1; *fuerint* for *fecerint* in 3; *quinterni*, “five each,” 3.]

Therefore, the more outstanding and powerful I see them to be, the more my foreboding mind predicts worse things. Alas for the mind of parents, always anxious enough about the uncertain future of their children!  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *ego* in the remaining witnesses; *Heu mens* supplied above the line by another hand in 1.]

It must therefore be foreseen that after my death no discord may arise among them concerning the acquisition of the reins of government.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *providendum* A; *facta* corrected to *fata* in A.]

For this reason I ask you by the Lord, and bind your loyalty by oath, that among my sons or grandsons the elder by birth shall always hold supreme right and the princely throne, and that all his brothers, or those born from the lordly tribe, shall be under his dominion.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *Deum* 2b, 3; *minor*, “younger,” 3; 4 adds *et omnes*.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139D] Cosmas below, III.13, calls this law “the justice of the Bohemians.”]

Believe me: unless one monarch governs this duchy, great harm will come to you nobles at the throat and to the people.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] 1 alone reads *monachos*, “monks,” supplied above the line by another hand; 2b reads *nec monarchos*, “nor monarchs”; 3, *si monarcha*, “if a monarch”; *deveniret* was erased in 1.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139D] A charter written in 1054, mentioning his son Wratislaus as duke of Moravia, shows that Bratislaus did not establish this arrangement only at his death; Boczek I, 130.]

He had spoken; and, leaving his bodily limbs in the hands of those standing by, his breath sought heaven on 10 January.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] 4a omits this date.]  
[Note: [Col. 0140D] The Bohemian Necrology agrees.]

Immediately a great lamentation was raised over him.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *est hoc loco* supplied above the line in A.]

But as to how great Duke Bracizlaus’s frugality was,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *fragilitatis* corrected to *frugilitatis* in A.]

or how great his discernment in divine laws and human judgments,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *regibus*, “kings,” 1.]

or how generous a giver of alms and how pious a protector he was of churches and widows, the eloquence of Tully would have failed before it had explained his individual merits.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *dator* repeated in 1; *explicuissent*, “they had explained,” A.]

14. After his death, all the Bohemian people, great and small alike, by common counsel and unanimous will chose his firstborn son, named Spitignev, as their duke, singing the sweet chant *Kyrie eleison*.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] Zpitignev 1, 2b; Spitigneu 2; Zpingnen 3; Zpitigneum 4; Spitigneum 4a, and so thereafter.]  
[Note: [Col. 0139] 4, 4a read “judge,” omitting “as duke.”]

For he was a very handsome man, with hair blacker than dark pitch, a long beard, a cheerful face, cheeks whiter than snow and faintly flushed in the middle.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *barbara* corrected to *barba* in A; *lata*, “broad,” 4.]

Why say more?

He was a good man and handsome from head to the lowest ankles.  
[Note: [Col. 0140D] Horace, *Epistles* II.2.4.]

On the first day on which he was enthroned,  
[Note: [Col. 0139] 4, 4a insert *autem*, “however.”]

he performed a great and remarkable deed, memorable through all ages: for every person of Teutonic race found in Bohemia—rich, poor, or traveller—he ordered all together to be expelled from the land of Bohemia within three days.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] *seu* 4.]  
[Note: [Col. 0140D] Yet he did not expel all Teutons from Bohemia; rather, as the monk of Sázava reports, he deprived Abbot Vitus of Sázava, who was of Slavic origin, of his office and installed a Teutonic abbot in the monastery.]

He did not even allow his own mother to remain—the daughter of Otto, named Judith, whom we mentioned above.  
[Note: [Col. 0140D] I.40.]

Likewise he expelled the abbess of Saint George, daughter of Bruno,  
[Note: [Col. 0140D] From a charter of Ottokar I, Dobner V, 329 seems to infer that her name was Adelaide.]

because she had earlier offended him with bitter words.

For when his father Bracizlaus was rebuilding the walls round the whole city of Prague, and this aforementioned hero held the province of Satec, granted to him by his father,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *haec* 1; Satc 2; Satcz 2; Sate 2b; Sathec 4, 4a; *h* supplied above the line by another hand in 1.]

he happened to go out with his men to construct the wall near Saint George’s cloister. Since the wall could in no way be properly placed unless the abbess’s oven that happened to stand there were destroyed, a rope was thrown around its middle. Then, while the others hesitated to do this, the lord’s son approached and, making as though it were a joke, with a great burst of laughter ordered it immediately thrown into the stream Bruzinca, saying: “Today the lady abbess shall not taste hot cakes.”  
[Note: [Col. 0141] A corrected *qui*; 4, 4a omit it; *chachinno* 1, 4a; Brusnicam 1; Bruznicam 2b, 4, 4a; Brucitucam 3.]

Recognizing this, the abbess angrily came out of the cloister and, taking his words very ill, attacked and confounded him with these ironic sayings:

Noble, distinguished man, brave and famed in arms,

what great towers and cities he has now conquered!

And from an oven he carries off a famous triumph;

now let him bind his victorious temples with laurel and gold.

Let the clergy ring out many kinds of songs with bells;  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *campanas* corrected to *campanis* in A; *campanas* 4, 4a; *personat*, “rings out,” 3.]

for the duke has thrown down an oven and performed a wondrous deed.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *dejicit*, “throws down,” 4a.]

Ah, it shames one to utter what does not shame him to do.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Ach 4; *ea fari* 4, 4a.]

The man stiffened in body, and his voice stuck in his throat;  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] Vergil, *Aeneid* III.48.]

and, indignant, he restrained his anger with a groan.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *indignamque* 3.]  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX.166.]

Because the duke had kept these sayings of the abbess stored deep in his mind,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *quum* 2b, 3.]  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] Vergil, *Aeneid* I.26.]

after he was enthroned, before he had entered Saint George’s church, he expelled the abbess,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *reservaret* 1; *pq* 1; *intrat* A; *intraret* 4, 4a; 1 adds *ad*; the reading *expellit* was supplied in A by another, contemporary hand and is absent in the remaining witnesses.]

sending her this message:

“Now it is more fitting that the clergy should resound with songs and ring bells when the abbess is cast out of this land,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] 4, 4a omit *et*; A reads *ejicitur de terra*.]

than when her oven is thrown down. Behold: the brave man, famous in arms, wins a celebrated triumph and binds his temples with laurel today not by conquering towers or cities, but by expelling you, abbess, mistress of that oven.”  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *abbatissa* 3; the *m* of *abbatissem* supplied above the line in A; the *n* of *fornacis* supplied above the line in 1; *ejici ipio* 1; corrected in 1.]

And as had been ordered, the abbess was set upon a two-wheeled cart, carried away swiftly, and expelled from the borders of that land quicker than speech.

15. After these things had been done,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] A corrects to *ita*; 1 reads *itaque*, “therefore.”]

the new duke went to arrange the new kingdom of Moravia. His father had formerly divided it among his sons, giving one half to Wratizlaus, and the other to Chonrad and Otto.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Wratizlavo 1; Conrado A, 2; Chunrado 2b, 4a; Cunrado 4; Otoni 1.]  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] Wratislaus had his seat at Olomouc, Conrad at Znojmo, and Otto at Brno; cf. Boczek I, 129.]

But Jaromir, still devoted to study, moved among the wings of schoolboys.

Duke Spitignev sent letters beforehand to the leading men of that land,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Supplied above the line by another hand in A.]

naming in them three hundred men, whom he knew to be the best and noblest from all the towns,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *vidit*, “saw,” 2; “and noblest” omitted in 4, 4a.]

and commanding them, upon the safety of his own head, to meet him at the city of Hrudim.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Grudim 1; *occurrant* in the remaining witnesses.]

They did the man’s commands and came to meet the duke beyond the gatehouse, in the fields of Grutov.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *etiam* 4, 4a; Grutou 2, 2b; Chruton 3; Grothou 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] The fields of Grutau, situated beyond the town of Chrudim; the Moravians travelled farther than the duke had ordered.]

The duke immediately ordered them arrested, angry because they had not met him at the appointed place, and sent them in chains to be held under guard, distributing them among individual towns of Bohemia. Their horses and weapons he distributed among his own men, and he continued on his way into Moravia.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] 4, 4a add “Spitignev.”]

When his brother Wratizlaus heard of this, he greatly feared him and withdrew into the regions of Pannonia, leaving his wife in the city of Olomouc.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *suus* A; *Poloniae*, “Poland,” 4, 4a; Olomucz 2, 4, 4a.]  
[Note: [Col. 0142D] On 20 April 1055 Wratizlaus still resided at Olomouc, as his charter proves; Boczek I, 132.]  
[Note: [Col. 0142D] Olomouc.]

King Andrew received him graciously and treated him honourably as long as he remained with him.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Corrected in A.]

Therefore Duke Spitignev, after arranging everything in Moravia as he pleased,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *palatium*, “palace,” 4, 4a.]

took his brothers to remain with him at court. He put Conrad in charge of the huntsmen and made Otto master over the bakers and cooks.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Conratum 1; Cunradum 4, 4a; 4, 4a read “made [him] master of the bakers and cooks.”]

He seized his sister-in-law and sent her to a very strongly fortified castle named Lescen,  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *castellum* A; name omitted in 3; Lesczen 2.]  
[Note: [Col. 0142D] Lesten.]

entrusting her to the custody of a count named Mstis.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] Name omitted in 4a; Mztis 1, 2, 4.]

That man guarded her not as befitted such a lady; every night he fastened her foot to his own with a shackle.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *cum pede* absent in 2.]

When her husband heard this, he took it grievously; what recompense he later rendered the count for so rash a deed will appear in what follows.  
[Note: [Col. 0142D] II.19.]

16. But after one month had elapsed, through the intervention of Bishop Severus and the counts, he released his sister-in-law and, giving her an escort, caused her to return to her husband.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] *messem*, corrected by another hand above the line to *mensem*, 1; *et* supplied in A by another, contemporary hand and absent elsewhere; “caused her” absent in 4, 4a.]

Because she was near childbirth, as she hurried on her way, she injured her womb and within three days breathed out her spirit, the most beautiful of women, because she could not deliver the immature burden of her womb.  
[Note: [Col. 0141] In 1 another hand corrected *te* to *ire*; 2, 2b read “while you hurry”; 3, “while [she] hurries”; *spiritus* 2; corrected in 1; *poterat*, “was able,” 3.]

When King Andrew saw his guest grieving to such a degree at her death,  
[Note: [Col. 0143] 2 adds *audiens*, “on hearing”; *Andreas* absent in 2.]

he comforted the sorrowful young man with these friendly words:  
[Note: [Col. 0143D] Vergil, *Aeneid* V.770.]

“O my dear guest, may God grant that you be safe. Henceforth cast your care upon the Lord and hope in him, and he himself will bring it about that this grief may more quickly turn to joy.  
[Note: [Col. 0143] *Deum* 2b, 3; *tuus*, “your,” 3.]

For it often happens that from where a man expects less advantage, he receives greater profit.  
[Note: [Col. 0143] *profectus* 3; corrected in 1.]

But concerning the death of your wife, be a brave man, and do not exceed due measure in grieving, as though something new had happened to you alone, when it is known to be certain to all men,
Source preparation: Canonical local restored source checked directly; the recovered Greek form is retained and translated in the apparatus.

Every human body returns to its own garden. Having spoken thus, he led his sorrowful guest to the table, where they were refreshed with rich dishes and made cheerful by mellow wine. By chance this king had an only daughter, named Adleyta [A, A*: Adlegta], already of marriageable age, very beautiful, and an object of excessive envy to many suitors. [She was the sister of Andrew I, king of the Hungarians, daughter of Ladislaus; cf. Pubitschka III, 361.] When the guest saw her, he fell miserably in love with her; the good king did not refuse, and after a few days joined her to him in marriage.

[Apparatus: “to return” appears as “to give back” in A; “he had led” in witness 3; “palace” in A; “is lacking” in A; Adleyta appears as Adlegta in A and A*; the initial *h* is superscript in another hand in witness 1; “marital bed” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; “only a few days later” is absent in witness 1, abbreviated by several witnesses, and occurs after “several days” in witness 3.]

When Duke Spitignev heard this, prudently foreseeing lest perhaps his brother, together with the Hungarians, should invade the whole of Moravia, he sent messengers, recalled him from Hungary, and restored to him the towns which his father had formerly given him in Moravia. [A charter in Boczek I, 135 proves that Wratizlaus was staying at Olomouc in 1059.] For Duke Spitignev was a prudent man in affairs of danger, knowing how to bend and relax his bow at the fitting time. Among his other virtues, we set forth here the following practice as especially worthy of remembrance for posterity and indeed as an example to be imitated.

[Apparatus: “the whole land” appears in M, c, U, and A; “kingdom” in A; “he restored” appears as “he gave back” in witness 1 and “he gives back to him” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “before” appears as “previously” in witness 2b and 3; “prudent” is absent in witness 3 and appears as “most prudent” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “at an opportune time” appears as “at an inopportune time” in witness 4 and “in an opportune time” in witness 4a; “we shall set forth” appears in witnesses 2, 2b, and 3.]

For it was his custom always, during Lent, to dwell in the cloister either of monks or of canons; he devoted himself to almsgiving, attended to the divine offices, and persevered in vigils and prayers, yet in such a way that before the morning chant he would recite the entire psalmody, either with outstretched hands or with genuflections. After Compline, moreover, following the example of monks, he kept silence until the time of Prime. And as long as he was fasting, he arranged ecclesiastical business; after dinner, however, he handled secular judicial matters. The episcopal fur garment and clerical tunic which he put on at the beginning of the fast and wore throughout all Lent, he gave on Maundy Thursday to his chaplain-chamberlain, judging rightly and piously that he who had shared the labor during the season of penitence ought not to be left without a share on the day of the great feast.

[Apparatus: “during the Lenten season” appears with a correction in witness 1; “vigils and prayers” appears as “vigils and fasts” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “he observes” appears instead of “he observed” in the main reading, while witness 3 has the past tense; “the ecclesiastical matters” appears as “he explains” in A and “he was arranging” in witness 3; “secular judgments” appears as “secular affairs” in A; “the episcopal fur garment” is absent in A; “putting it on over his clothing” appears as “dressed” in witness 3; “the day of the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” is added by witnesses 4 and 4a; “shared the labor” is absent in witness 2.]

### 17

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1056.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1057.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1058. On the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August; the Bohemian Necrology confirms the date], Judith, wife of Bracizlaus and duchess of the Bohemians, died. Since her son Spitignev had driven her from his realm, and she could not otherwise avenge upon her son the injury done to herself, she had married Peter, king of the Hungarians, to the disgrace of him and of all the Bohemians. [Peter had been deprived of his kingdom and blinded in 1046, but his former wife was then alive; see Hermann of Reichenau, 1046. Pubitschka III, 330 questions that marriage.]

Later her son Duke Wratizlaus brought her thence and buried her at Prague beside her husband Bracizlaus, honorably, in the church of the holy martyrs Vitus, Wenceslaus, and Adalbert.

[Apparatus: “afterward” appears as “after” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “and buried her” is omitted in witnesses 4 and 4a; “Vitus, Wenceslaus, and Adalbert” appears abbreviated as “V., W., A.” in witness 1; “honorably” is rendered “thus” in A and is absent from the remaining witnesses.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1060, when Duke Spitignev had come to Prague for the feast of Saint Wenceslaus, he saw that the church of Saint Vitus was not sufficiently large and could not contain the people gathering for the holy festival. Saint Wenceslaus himself had built it round, in the likeness of the Roman church, and in it rested the body of that same Saint Wenceslaus. He likewise saw another small church, adjoining and situated, as it were, in a part of the same church; in its middle, in an exceedingly cramped place, stood the mausoleum of Saint Adalbert. He judged it best to destroy both and to build one large church for both patrons. At once he marked out the site of the church in a broad circuit, laid the foundations, and the work grew hot; the wall rose. [Virgil, *Georgics* IV.169.] But foolish death soon interrupted his fortunate undertaking in the following year.

[Apparatus: “he had constructed it” appears as “he built it” in witness 1; “holy” is added by witness 4; “of that same” is absent in A; “another little church” appears as “another church” in witnesses 2b, 3, 4, and 4a; “in a portion” is the printed reading, while other witnesses have “in a narrow place” or related forms; “mausoleum” appears with variant spellings in witnesses 2b, 4, and 4a; “blessed” appears instead of “Saint” in witness 3; “destroyed” appears as “built” in witness 1; “the work grows hot” appears with a correction in witness 1 and as “he hastens” in witnesses 4 and 4a.]

At the time of that same year when the legions were marching to war—perhaps, if I am not mistaken, to bring with a German army, on King Henry’s advice, aid to Andrew, king of the Hungarians, against Béla, as Lambert recorded in 1061 concerning an unnamed Bohemian duke whose arrival the Germans had not expected—when the duke, with the military standards already raised, was making what seemed to be a one-day journey, he met a widow. Weeping, wailing, kissing his feet, and running after him, she cried:

“Lord, avenge me upon my adversary.”

And he said, “I shall do so when I return from the expedition.”

But she said, “What if you do not return? To whom do you leave me to be avenged? Or why do you neglect the reward which you are to receive from God?”

Immediately, at the petition of one widow, he broke off the expedition and gave her justice against her adversary. What do you, modern princes, say to this—you who do not heed the cries of so many widows and so many orphans, but despise them in the swelling arrogance of pride? By such bowels of mercy as we have described above, Duke Spitignev acquired for himself this byname: all called him “father of clerics” and “defender of widows.”

[Apparatus: “Spitignev” is added by witnesses 4 and 4a; “a certain widow” is added by those witnesses; “one day” has a correction by another hand in witness 1; the widow’s running after him is marked by a correction in A; “when I return from the expedition” has a superscript addition in witness 1; “what if,” “she said,” is absent in witness 2; “to whom you leave me to be avenged” is expanded by witnesses 4 and 4a, while witness 2b has “whom you send me back to”; “the expedition” is absent in witness 2; “he immediately interrupts the expedition” is the printed reading; “fasts” appears instead of “prayers” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “he arranges” appears as “he arranged” in witness 3; “judgments” appears as “affairs” in A.]

But because we often see, by God’s hidden judgment, evil men left behind and good men removed from the midst, this man of such integrity was taken from this light on the fifth day before the Kalends of February [28 January; the Bohemian Necrology agrees], in the sixth year of his dukedom, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1061.

[Apparatus: “removed” is misspelled in witness 1; “of such integrity” has a correction in witness 1; the phrase “was” is absent in witnesses 2b and 3; “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation” is absent from the remaining witnesses; “LXI” is absent in witness 1.]

Spitignev, duke of the Bohemians, died. [Witnesses 2 and 2a.]

### 18

After his death his brother Wratizlaus, with the favor of all the Bohemians, was raised to the throne. He immediately divided the realm of Moravia equally among his brothers: he gave Otto the eastern region—namely, the Olomouc region—which he himself had formerly held, better suited for hunting and richer in fish; and he gave Conrad the western region—namely, the Brno region—which lies toward the Germans, and Conrad himself knew the German language. That region is flatter and more open country, and more fertile in grain.

[Apparatus: “his brother” appears as “his own brother” in witness 2b; “immediately” appears as “at once” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “the region which he himself had previously held” is the reading; “which” appears as “who” in witness 2; “hunting” appears as “the taking of game” in witness 3; “the western region” is absent in A; the phrase “which is” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; “the western region” is identified editorially as the Brno region; “the eastern region” is identified as the Olomouc region.]

Meanwhile, when the sun was remaining in the first part of Pisces, the well-disposed youth Jaromir, hearing of the death of his brother Spitignev, whom he had honored with fear and love no less than a father, laid aside his childish fear and returned from his studies, hoping that he would have some portion of the inheritance in his paternal realm. When his brother Duke Wratizlaus perceived that he was more eager for secular than for sacred service, he reproved his obstinacy in these words:

“Do not, brother, do not by apostasy cut yourself off from the head of which you have become a member, and be cast into hell. Long ago divine grace, by its providence, chose you for the rank of priesthood; therefore our father committed you to the exercise of letters, so that you might be considered a suitable successor to Bishop Severus—provided only that, with God’s favor, you survive.”

[Apparatus: “returns” appears instead of “returned” in A; “some part” appears as “a portion” in A; “more eager” is corrected in witness 1 and appears as “to be eager” in A and witnesses 3, 4, and 4a; “apostasy” has a spelling variant in witness 1; “be cut off” appears with a spelling variant in witness 3; “by his providence” appears as “for his providence” in witness 2b; “chose” appears as “chooses” in witness 2; “instruction” appears instead of “ordinance” in witness 3.]

Then, when March began, on the first day of the week, when holy orders were conferred, he had him tonsured, though unwilling, compelled, and resisting strongly. In the duke’s own presence he was ordained as far as the office of deacon; he publicly read the Gospel and, according to custom, served the bishop while he celebrated Mass.

After this, the new deacon—or rather Julian the Apostate, as he should be called—having not rightly cast off the shield of sacred warfare [Horace, *Odes* II.7.10], and having neglected the grace which he had received by the laying on of hands, put on the military belt and fled with his followers to the duke of Poland, Boleslaus II. He remained with him until the death of Bishop Severus.

[Apparatus: “they celebrated” appears instead of “they were conferred” in witness 2b; “he received” appears in witnesses 4 and 4a; “the new deacon, indeed the old one” is omitted in those witnesses and altered in A; A reads *parma*, “buckler,” while the remaining witnesses read *per arma*, “through arms”;  “grace” appears as “the grace” in A and witnesses 2b, 3, 4, and 4a; “neglected” appears as “neglected” in witnesses 2b, 3, and 4a; “Bishop Severus” is absent in A and in witnesses 4 and 4a.]

### 19

At that time Mztis, count of the town of Belina, son of Boris, was a man of great boldness, greater eloquence, and no less prudence. Although he did not forget that he had a mistrustful duke, because he had at one time held in custody the duke’s wife, entrusted to him by his lord [II.15], nevertheless he boldly entered the duke’s palace and addressed him with this humble petition:

“By your brother’s favor, I have built a church in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle. Deign, I beg you, to come to the solemnity of its dedication, and at the same time gladden the town by your arrival; do not despise my suppliant prayers.”

Although the duke did not forget the injury formerly done him regarding his wife, nevertheless, because of his new position, he concealed in his heart the anger which he felt and said: “I shall come; I shall gladden my town; and I shall do what the matter and justice require.”

The count did not understand the prince’s words. Giving the duke many thanks, he departed gladly and prepared what was necessary for great banquets. The duke and Bishop Severus came; the church, which stood in the suburb, was immediately dedicated; and the duke went up into the town for dinner. The bishop and the count, however, reclined at their own court, which stood before the church, with tables laid and food set out.

While they were dining, a messenger came and said in the count’s ear: “The prefecture of the town has been taken from you and given to Koyata, son of Wssebor, who at that time was first in the duke’s palace.”

To this the count replied: “The duke is lord; let him do what pleases him with his town. But what my church possesses today, the duke has no power to take away.”

Unless that night he had escaped by the counsel of Bishop Severus and with assistance, he would undoubtedly have lost his eyes and the foot which he had formerly shackled together with the duke’s wife’s foot.

[Apparatus: Belina appears as Relina in witness 2; “he had held” appears as “he held” in witness 2b and “he had held” in A, 4, and 4a; “the injury” is absent in witnesses 2b and 3; “his wife” is added in A; “in his heart” is expanded by A and witnesses 4 and 4a; “his anger” is added in A; “I shall gladden my town” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; “the count Mztis” is added in those witnesses; “thanks” appears as “gratitude” in witness 2b; “to dine” appears instead of “for dinner” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “Bishop Severus” is added by those witnesses; “which is situated” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; Koyata’s name has numerous spelling variants; Wssebor appears as Wseboris, Vseboris, and related forms; “what” appears as “whatever” in witnesses 2b and 3; “without doubt” is absent in witness 1; the final clause is variously punctuated and transmitted.]

### 20

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1062, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January], Duchess Adleyth died, mother of Judith and Ludmila, and likewise of the younger Bracizlaus and Wratizlaus, who was slain in the first flower of youth on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].

After almost a year had elapsed following the death of Duchess Adleyth, in the year 1063, Duke Wratizlaus took a wife named Zuatava [Swatislawa], daughter of Casimir, duke of the Poles, and sister of Boleslaus and Uladizlaus. By her he had four sons, men of good character: Boleslaus, Borivoy, Wladizlaus, and Sobezlaus.

[Cosmas omitted to mention Judith, a daughter born of the same marriage. She married Count Wipert of Groitzsch, afterwards margrave of Meissen and Lusatia. When this Judith and her husband Wipert founded the celebrated abbey of Pegau, anniversaries of Judith’s parents and brothers were also celebrated there. Thus we read in the Pegau Calendar: “On the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February: King Fratislaus, father of the foundress, one thousand talents.” And: “On the Kalends of September: Queen Zwatislawa, mother of our foundress.” SCHWARZ. Cf. below, II.40.]

Of these persons, in their proper places, as God grants, there will be sufficiently ample treatment.

[Apparatus: “Adleyth” appears as Adlegth and Adleyta in other witnesses; “the younger Bracizlaus” is absent in A; “was slain” appears as “fell” in witness 3; “and” before Wladizlaus is added in witnesses 4 and 4a; Sobezlaus has the variants Zobzlavum, Sobieslaum, Zobezlaum, Sobeslaum, and Zobislaum.]

### 21

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1063.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1064.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1065.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1066.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1067.

On the Ides of December [13 December], Severus, the sixth bishop of the church of Prague, departed from this world and enjoys a pleasant reward. [The monk of Gradice, the lists of Prague bishops, and the Bohemian Necrology agree as to the day and year.]

[Apparatus: “he departed” appears in A, witness 3, and witness 4, while the remaining witnesses have “he departed” in the perfect tense; “from this world” appears as “from this age” in witnesses 4 and 4a.]

He experienced both kinds of fortune, prosperity and adversity, in full measure. For at one time he was seized by Duke Bracizlaus, chained, and committed to prison—perhaps because, after abandoning the duke, he had gone over to the emperor [II.12]—and endured martyrdom both secretly and openly. During almost the whole period of his episcopate, without opposition or contradiction, he governed Bohemia and Moravia as though they were one undivided bishopric. And he would have continued to do so, had he not, after the death of Spitignev, overcome by Duke Wratizlaus’s excessive importunity, consented to the promotion of John as bishop in Moravia—that is, at Olomouc.

[Palacký I, 301 seems not without reason to conjecture that the plan of establishing the Olomouc bishopric was undertaken at Olomouc toward the end of 1052. For in Boczek I, 138 there survives a charter of an exchange containing these words: “In the presence of my illustrious brothers Wratizlaus and Conrad, of the venerable Bishop Severus, and of several counts from Bohemia and Moravia. Done at Olomouc in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1062, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December].” In the year 1065, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], Boczek I, 139 first mentions John, the first bishop of Olomouc.]

Yet first, in the presence of many witnesses, a carefully considered arrangement of fief and allod, or exchange, was made: the bishop of Prague was to choose, in return for that bishopric, twelve of the foremost villages in all Bohemia; moreover, he was to receive annually one hundred marks of silver from the duke’s treasury. The estate in Moravia at Sekircostel, with its appurtenances, he was to possess as before and thereafter; likewise the village of Sliunica with its market, and the castle there situated in the midst of the water called Zuratka, named Podivin after its founder Podiva, a Jew but later a Catholic.

[Apparatus: “bishopric” appears as “episcopate” in witness 2 and 2b; “Sekircostel with its appurtenances” is absent in A; its name has several spelling variants; “likewise” appears in A and witness 1, while witness 2 reads “Sliunica”; Zuratka has several transmitted forms; Podivin appears with variants including Poduin, Podiun, and Podium.]

[Dobner observes that Podivín still survives today as a place in Moravia, not far from Lundenburg, called by some Kostel. Either Cosmas is mistaken, or, led astray by zeal for the Prague Church, he departed from the truth, as Palacký thought. For Hildegard’s manuscript Chronicle of Gradice, in Boczek I, 139, shows that the estate of Sekir-Kostel and the castle of Podivín were in fact transferred by the Prague bishop to the bishop of Olomouc. Finally, in 1068, Duke Otto of Moravia restored—these are the words of another charter, Boczek I, 140—to the elected bishop of Prague, in compensation for the one hundred marks annually to be paid from the treasury which had been withheld from him by the duke, the castle of Podivín in Moravia with the market of the adjacent town of Sekure, as it had passed into the right of the men of Prague, in the time of blessed Adalbert, from the union of parishes.]

It is reported, however, that before Severus’s time there was in Moravia a certain bishop, as I think, named Wracen.

[The memory of two bishops of Olomouc before Severus’s time has been preserved. John, an archbishop who was sent into the land of the Moravians, is mentioned in a letter of Theotmar, archbishop of Salzburg, to Pope John IX, written about the year 900. Another, Silvester, appears around the year 940 in the codex called the *Granum* (“Grain”) of the Catalogue of Moravian Prelates. In 974 a certain Moravian bishop, whose name we regret has not been preserved, attended the synod held by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz; cf. Guden, *Codex diplomaticus* I, 352. Dobner IV, 245 conjectured that this bishop was Wracen. See Richter, *Series episcoporum Olomucensium*, p. 5 ff.]

How great a conflict Severus’s successor Jaromir had with the aforesaid Bishop John concerning this diocese will be declared in its proper place.

### 22

Then Conrad and Otto, hearing that the bishop of Prague had departed to Christ, sent for and recalled their brother Jaromir from Poland. They unbelted him from his military girdle, and he again took on clerical dress and tonsure. Meanwhile Duke Wratizlaus, making provision for himself in the future and fearing that, once his brother had become bishop, he might conspire against him with the brothers just mentioned, began silently to deliberate with himself how he might in some way deprive him of the bishopric.

At that time there was in the duke’s court a certain chaplain Lanczo, born of noble Saxon stock, a man of distinguished appearance and highly learned, raised to the provostship of the church of Litoměřice. His manners and life were not at variance with episcopal honor. Because he had always remained faithful to the duke, the duke strove by every means that he should become bishop of Prague.

Meanwhile Conrad and Otto came from Moravia, bringing their brother Jaromir with them, and earnestly petitioned the duke for him: that he should remember brotherhood, remember their father’s ordinance, remember the oaths by which their father had bound the loyalty of the counts, namely that after the death of Bishop Severus they should choose Jaromir as bishop. But he, being a clever and deceitful man in feigning and concealing the grounds of actions—like the little fox that flees nowhere except where it has tossed its tail—kept one thing hidden in his breast and expressed another to his brothers with his mouth.

“It is not for one man to manage this affair, which calls for the common deliberation of all. But since now, meanwhile, the greater part of the people and military nobles has gone forward to the camp, nowhere, I think, will this matter be discussed better than at the guarded passes of this land. There will be all the elders of this people, the nobles and counts, and the best among the clergy; and the episcopal election rests in their judgment.”

The duke did this so that there, among his own soldiers, surrounded by arms and secured by garrisons, he might oppose the will of his brothers and raise to the bishopric Lanczo, whom he wanted. But the duke’s sinister intention was frustrated, because all power is from God, and no one can be bishop unless it has been predestined or permitted by God.

[Apparatus: “he received” appears as “he had received” in witnesses 4 and 4a; “in the future for himself” has a variant in A; “conspire” appears in the plural in witness 3; Lanczo appears as Janczo in witness 2; the editorial note explains that he was apparently a man distinguished in bodily dignity and beauty; the church’s name appears as Lucomiricensis and Lutomiricensis; “he works” appears instead of “he strove” in A; “bringing” appears as “offering” in A and several witnesses; “earnestly” has a corrected form in A; “on his behalf” is absent in A; “instruction” appears as “ordinance” in witness 3; “he should choose” contains a superscript correction in witness 1; the fox comparison has variants: “flees only there” in witness 2b and “pretends” in witness 1; “he promised” appears instead of “he promises” in the remaining witnesses; “part” has variants in witnesses 1 and 2; “the guarded passes” is explained editorially as mountain narrows or defiles; “oppose” appears as “resist” in witness 2b; Lanczo’s name has a superscript correction in witness 1.]

### 23

Why say more? They had come to the guarded gate through which one goes into Poland, at the place called Dobenina—according to Palacký’s conjecture, today’s Döberle, not far from Trautenau, on the road to Silesia. The duke summoned the people and nobles to an assembly. His brothers stood at his right and left; the clerics and counts sat in a wide circle; and behind them all the soldiers stood. He called Lanczo and, placing him in the middle, praised and commended him to the people, saying to him in a loud voice:

“Your outstanding loyalty, proven to me daily, requires this of me and compels me to do today what I am about to do, so that through this posterity may learn how faithfully they ought to serve their lords. Behold, receive the ring and staff; be the bridegroom of the church of Prague and shepherd of the holy sheep.”

There was murmuring among the people, and no voice of congratulation sounded, as it always does at the time of an episcopal election. Then Koyata, son of Wsebor, count palatine, bearing this very impatiently—for he was truthful in speech and straightforward in word—stood at the right hand of Otto, the duke’s brother, and sharply struck his side, saying:

“Why do you stand there? Are you an ὄνος λύρας—‘an ass at the lyre’? Why do you not aid your brother? Do you not see that your brother, the duke’s son, is rejected, while a proselyte and stranger, who came into this land without breeches, is raised to the throne? And if the duke violates his father’s oath, far be it from us that the spirits of our ancestors should render account to God or suffer punishment for this oath.

“For we know—and strive, so far as we can, for this—that your father Bracizlaus bound us and our fathers by an oath of faith that, after Bishop Severus’s death, your brother Jaromir should be bishop. Or, if your brother displeases you, why is our not inconsiderable native clergy, as well endowed with learning as this German, held in contempt? Oh, if only you had as many bishoprics as you see chaplains born in this land who are worthy of the episcopate! Do you think that an alien will love us more, or desire better things for this land, than a native? For human nature is such that each man, whatever his country, loves his own people more than a foreign one; indeed, if he could, he would divert foreign rivers into his native land.

“Therefore we would rather—rather!—put a dog’s tail or an ass’s dung than Lanczo upon the holy chair. Your brother Spitignev, of blessed memory, had some sense: in one day he expelled all Germans from this land. The Roman emperor Henry is still alive—and long may he live! Yet you make yourself him when, usurping his authority, you give the episcopal staff and ring to a hungry dog. Certainly neither you nor your bishop will bear this unpunished, if Koyata son of Wsebor lives.”

[The Greek words are to be read and derived from Boethius I.4, as Dobrowski first recognized. He had previously thought that he discerned Czech words in the corrupt reading. Cf. his essay in *Monatsschrift der Gesellschaft des vaterländischen Museums in Böhmen* I, 48, K; see also Diogenian, cent. VII.33, and Leutsch’s note in *Paroemiographi Graeci*, p. 291. GROTEFEND.]

[Apparatus: Dobenina appears with the variants Bobenina, Dobevina, and Debonina; “the nobles and the people” is the order in witness 3; “his brothers” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; “at the right” has several forms; “standing” appears as “being seated” or “sitting” in other witnesses; Lanczo’s praise has a correction from “comments” to “commends” in witness 1; “will be” appears instead of “requires” in A before correction; “faithful” is corrected in witness 1 and appears as “servants” in witness 4a; Koyata’s name appears with several spellings; Wsebor appears as Vsebor and Swebor; “an ass at the lyre” is transmitted in severely corrupt forms in the witnesses, including *ananocayapac*, *ananoc aypac*, and related readings; “an alien” appears as “a proselyte” or “proselytizing” in other witnesses; “without breeches” has a correction from “without thighs” in another hand; “if” is absent in A and appears as “and as if” in witness 4a; “the spirits” appears as “empty spirits,” while an old marginal hand identifies the reading as *manes*, that is, ancestral spirits; “for this oath” has a correction in witness 1; the phrase “we know” is followed by a large capital N in witnesses 1 and 2, perhaps representing *nomen*; “the episcopate” appears as “the bishopric” in witness 2; “a dog’s tail or an ass’s dung” has variant word orders, including “a dog’s dung or an ass’s tail”; “to place” appears as “to be placed” in A and witnesses 4 and 4a; “and the ring” is absent in witnesses 4 and 4a; “with impunity” has a corrected reading in witness 1; the final clause is absent in witness 2.]

### 24

Then Zmil son of Bozeni, prefect in the town of Satec, together with Koyata, took Conrad, Otto, and Jaromir by the right hands and said:

“Let us go and see whether the cunning and feigned justice of one man prevails, or the justice and remarkable fairness of the three brothers excels—the brothers whom equal age, one will, and the same authority unite, and whom a greater multitude of soldiers supports.”

No small commotion of the people arose through the camps. Each cried, “To arms! To arms!” That reckless episcopal election was hateful to all. Therefore the greater part of the army went over to those three lords, and they pitched camp at and below the town of Opocen [Opocno].

Since another part of the soldiers had already gone ahead into the forest, the duke, seeing himself as though deserted and not sufficiently secure from his brothers’ attack, fled as quickly as he could, fearing that they might seize Prague or the fortress-city of Wissegrad first.

Yet from the road he sent a messenger to his brothers, saying:

“It was not on account of the boastful tongue of Koyata son of Wsebor, or of Zmil son of Bozen—whose mouth contains honey and whose heart contains gall—that I had done what was done through their wicked and deceitful counsels—those men, if I live! But I shall restrain myself. Rather, now more mindful of my father’s ordinance, of his oaths, and of what justice and brotherly love demand, I shall act.” Only follow me to the city of Prague.”

When they arrived, they pitched camp in the meadows near the village of Gostivar [Hostiwar in the district of Kaurzim] and sent to the duke to ask whether he was willing to confirm his words by deeds. He received them peacefully, chose his brother Jaromir as bishop, and, after oaths had been given and received between them, sent Conrad and Otto back to Moravia in peace.

But Zmil and Koyata, although they had spoken what was true and just among the princes, would have been punished by the duke, without any hearing, as enemies of the commonwealth, unless they had slipped away by night and concealed themselves in flight.

This election took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1068, when the sun entered the twenty-fifth degree of Gemini. [Dobner V, 394 establishes this as 15 June, the feast of Saint Vitus.]
