## Restored textual apparatus

These source-order entries restore the readings required for the places where the repair candidate had dropped, displaced, or altered apparatus. Latin forms are retained with their witnesses and English glosses.

### Opening and Lent

- **[Col. 0143]** A reads *reddere* (“to give back”); 3, *duxerat* (“had led”); at *ferculis reficiuntur* (“they are refreshed by dishes”), 1 has a correction; A, *regia* (“royal”); A omits *unica* (“only”). A reads *nata* (“born”) for *gnata* (“born daughter”); A and A* have *Adlegta*. The editor identifies her as sister of King Andrew I of Hungary and daughter of Ladislaus, citing Pubitschka III.361.
- **[Col. 0143]** In 1, *h* is written supralinearly in *thoro* (“marriage-bed”) by another hand; 4 and 4a omit *thoro maritali* (“for the marriage-bed”); *tempestiva* (“ripe/ready”) remains. The phrase *atque … copulavit* (“and … joined [her in marriage]”) is absent in 1; A and 2 omit *paucos* (“a few”); 3 reads *post dies aliquot* (“after several days”). M, c, U, and A read *totam terram* (“the whole land”); 1 reads *redidit* (“gave back”), and 4/4a *reddit ei* (“gives it back to him”); 2b and 3 read *antea* (“previously”).
- **[Col. 0143]** The Lent readings are: 3 omits *dux* (“duke”) in *Erat enim dux Spitignev*; 4/4a *prudentissimus* (“most prudent”); 4 *importuno* (“troublesome”), 4a *in portuno* (“in harbour”); 2, 2b, 3 *proferemus* (“we shall bring forward”); 1 *tempt.* (abbreviation for *tempore*, “time”); 4/4a *jejuniis* (“fasts”); 3 *servabat* (“was keeping”), against main *servat* (“keeps”); A *spacium* (“space/time”); A *exponit* (“sets out”), 3 *disponebat* (“was arranging”); 3 *tractabat* (“was treating/discussing”); A *negotia* (“business”); A omits *pelliciam* (“fur garment”); 3 *indutus* (“clothed”); 2 omits *laboris* (“of labour”); and 4/4a add *resurrectionis Jesu Christi domini nostri* (“of the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord”).

### Spitignev, Jaromir, and Mztis

- **[Col. 0143–0144D]** A has *ulcirisci* (“to avenge”), corrected; 4/4a *post* (“after”); 4/4a omit *et est* (“and is”); A and 1 *V. W.*; A alone has *filius* (“son”), absent from the rest; 1 *construcxerat* (“had built”); 4 adds *sanctae* (“holy”); A omits *ecclesiam* (“church”); 2b, 3, 4, 4a *ecclesiam* (“church”); A has *in arto* (“in narrow straits”) written by another hand above the line; 2b, 4, 4a *mauseolum* (“mausoleum”); 3 *beati* (“blessed”); 1 *construeret* (“might build”); A omits *destrueret* (“might destroy”); 1 corrects that verb, while 4/4a *accelerat* (“hastens”). The source quotes Vergil, *Georgics* IV.169 and identifies the intended 1061 Hungarian campaign: Andrew I sought German help against Béla at Henry’s advice, as Lambert records.
- **[Col. 0143]** At Spitignev’s death, 4/4a add *Spitigneus*; A and 1 have *V. W.*; A alone has *filius* (“son”); 4/4a omit *et est* (“and is”) in the dated-incarnation formula. The Bohemian Necrology confirms the date.
- **[Col. 0145]** In the Mztis episode, A, 2b, 3, 4, 4a have *gratiam* (“favour”); 2b, 3, 4a *neglectam* (“neglected”); 4/4a omit *quam sibi impenderat* (“which he had bestowed on him”); A omits *quod* (“that”); 2 *Relinae*; 2b *habuit* (“had”); A *tenuit* (“held”), whereas 4/4a have *tenuerat* (“had held”); 2b and 3 omit *tamen* (“nevertheless”); 4/4a *advenire* (“to arrive”); 1 has *et* (“and”) supralinearly; A adds *sua* (“his/her own”), while A/4/4a add *suo* (“his own”); A *suam* (“his/her own”); 4/4a omit *Mztis*; and 4/4a add *Mztis* at the following name-position.
- **[Col. 0145]** The invitation/escape readings are: 2b *gratias* (“thanks”); 4/4a add *Severus*; 4/4a omit *ad convivium* (“to the banquet”); 4/4a *prandendum* (“a meal to be eaten”), 2b *prandium* (“meal”); A, 2b, 3 *in aurem* (“into [the] ear”); A has *Kovate* corrected to *Koyate*, 1 *Coyate*, 4 *Koiethe*, 4a *Koietae*; 1/4/4a *Wseboris*, 2b/3 *Vseboris*; 2b/3 *quid* (“what”); 4 adds *Severi*; 4 omits *et auxilio* (“and help”); 1 omits *procul dubio* (“without doubt”); 1 has *pr. d. amisisset*, abbreviating *procul dubio amisisset* (“would undoubtedly have lost [it]”); the others have the printed reading; A *nomine* (“by name”); 1 *Adlegth*, 3 *Adleyta*; A omits *est* (“is”); and 3 *cecidit* (“fell”).

### Sections 21–23 and names

- **[Col. 0147]** 2 reads *episcopatum* (“bishopric”); A/2 have *refraglatione*, with 1 corrected from *reflagracione*, for printed *refragatio* (“opposition”); 3 *Spingnei*, 4/4a *Spitignei*, for *Zpitigneu*. 1 omits *Olomucensis* (“of Olomouc”); 4 has *ut* struck out and 4a adds it; 2/2b *episcopatu* (“bishopric”).
- **[Col. 0147–0148C]** The property formula is *pheodo et alliodo sive concambio*: “as fief and freehold, or by exchange.” A lacks the passage from *ad Sekirkostel* through *similiter*; 1 *castel*, 2 *Sekirkostel*, 3 *Sekir costel*, 4/4a *Sekyrcostel*. A/1/2b retain the printed place-name; 2 has *Slivincam* (its damaged dotting permits another reading), 3 *Slinnicam*. A/1/4 *Zuartka*, corrected in A to *Zuratka*; 2b *Zwarka* with c added above r; 3 *Zuracka*. 2 permits *Poduin* or *Podiun*, and 3 *Podium*. The source’s historical notes identify Podivín and discuss the disputed transfer.
- **[Col. 0149]** Name and place forms include *Wracen* (1, 2b, 3, 4, 4a), *Wraczen* (2); *Lucomiricensis* (3), *Lutomiricensis* (4, 4a); *Bobenina* (A), *Dobevina* (2b), *Debonina* (4, 4a). The editor conjectures modern Döberle near Trutnov. 3 reads *proceres et populum* (“nobles and people”); 4/4a omit *in unum congregatis* (“gathered together”); A/1 *addextris* (“at the right”), 4/4a *astantibus* (“standing by”); 2 *consedentibus* (“sitting together”), 4/4a *residentibus* (“sitting”).

### The Greek proverb and final speech

- **[Col. 0149]** A has *Ananocayapac*, 1 *ananoc aypac*, 2b *A nanoc aypac*, 5 *ananocaypac*, 4/4a *Ana. noc aipac*, for the restored Greek **ὄνος λύρας**, the corruptly transmitted form of the “ass and lyre” proverb (a lyre unsuited to a donkey). The editor attributes the correct identification and Boethius I.4 source to Dobrowski and cites Diogenianus VII.33 and Leutsch’s note.
- **[Col. 0149]** 2b/3/4 read *Cur* (“why”) for *Quare* (“wherefore”); 2b *quod* (“because/that”) for *quia* (“because”); A *proselita*, 2a and A (first hand), 2b *proselytans* (“proselytising”); 1 has *al.* written above *femoribus* (“thighs”); A omits *si* (“if”), 4a *ac quasi* (“and as if”); 4/4a omit *utique* (“certainly”) and *nostris* (“our”); 2b *vobis* (“to you”).
- **[Col. 0149]** 2 has *inanes* (“empty”); an old marginal hand writes *i. aie manes*, explained as *animae manes* (“spirits of the dead”); 3 has *manus* (“hand”), a distinct reading. 1 corrects *hac* (“this [ablative]”) to *hoc* (“this [neuter]”); 1 and 2 use a large *N* for *enim* (“for”), which elsewhere signifies *nomen* (“name”).
- **[Col. 0151]** 3 *quod* (“because/that”); A omits *frater vester* (“your brother”); 2 *episcopatu*; A’s *nat.* is so written and 1 repeats it; 1 corrects *natus* (“born”); A omits *est* (“is”); 2b inserts *rati*. A has the abbreviated *a. asininam m.*; 4/4a expand it as *caninam merdam aut asininam caudam* (“dog dung or an ass’s tail”). A/4/4a *locari* (“to be placed”); 2 *tu metipsum*, 4a *tu met te ipsum* (“you yourself”); 4/4a omit *et anulum* (“and a ring”); 1 corrects *impute* to *impune* (“with impunity”).
- **[Col. 0151]** For the Koyata/Zmil speech, A corrects *impute* to *impune* (“with impunity”); 4a omits *quia vivet* (“because he will live”); 2 omits *Certe … vivet* (“Certainly … he will live”); name forms are *fil. B. Zmil* (A), *Boren* (1), *Bozen* (4). A corrects *Koyata*; A/4 *Conrandum et* (“Conrad and”); A *Jaromirum*; 4 omits *dux* (“duke”); 2 *Opoczen*, 2b *Opecen* (Opocno); 4/4a add *Wratizlaus*. A has *destutum* with *tu* supplied above by another hand; A adds *et*, which 4 omits; 1 *Wisegrad*; 1 *filium*; A has *me* written supralinearly; A corrects *me* to *ne*, while 4/4a have *reperiam* (“I shall find”).
- **[Col. 0151]** The textual history of *reprimam me* is preserved exactly: it is written in A’s margin by another hand and in 1 over an erasure; in A *reprimam* is supplied supralinearly over erased *puniam* (“I shall punish”). This supports “But I shall restrain myself,” and does not turn the unfinished threat into a punishment. Name forms: *Goztivar* (1, 4), *Goslivar* (2b, 3), *Gostiwar* (4a); the editor identifies Hostivař in the Kouřim district. 1 has *aducem*, corrected by another hand to *ad d.*; 4/4a *elegit* (“chose”); 1 *Kmyl*, 2 *Smil*; A omits *est* (“is”); 1 has *et* supplied supralinearly; 4/4a *publice* (“publicly”); A *Acta* (“done”); A *quartam* (“fourth”); A corrects *gemorum* to *geminorum* (“twins”), while 1 corrects *genitorum* to *gemin.* The editor identifies the date as 15 June, St Vitus’s feast.

Source preparation: Canonical local restored source checked directly; no foreign-text recoveries occurred in this chunk.

25. Without delay, Duke Wratizlaus sends Counts Severus, Alexius, and Marquard the German, together with his brother Jaromir, now elected, to the emperor Henry the Second. [Note: [Col. 0151C] Everyone agrees that Henry was neither emperor nor “the Second.”]

They arrived on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist and approached Caesar in the city of Mainz, where he was conducting imperial business with bishops and princes. They presented their elected candidate and asked, on behalf of the duke and the whole people, that he deign by his authority to confirm their election. [Col. 0152C] The emperor assented to their request and, on the third day—that is, 6 Kalends of July, Monday—gave him the ring and pastoral staff. On the following Sunday, 6 Nones of July, [Note: [Col. 0152C] Neither 6 Kalends of July fell on a Monday nor 6 Nones of July on a Sunday. This was observed by the investigators of Bohemian affairs, Assemani, Pubitschka, and Dobner. Following Assemani’s Monday and Sunday, they wished in both places to restore 2 Kalends of July and 2 Nones of July.] Jaromir, his name changed to Gebeard, was ordained bishop by the bishop of Mainz.

On that same day, while crossing the Rhine, one of his knights, Willalmus, sat after dinner on the bank with his feet lowered into the riverbed. [Note: [Col. 0151] “River” is inserted in manuscript 4a.] The new bishop secretly approached from behind and, unaware that deep water lay concealed there, pushed him into the waters of the Rhine, saying, “I baptize you anew, Willalmus.” After being submerged for a long time, he finally emerged, turning his head and grasping at the waves, and said, “If this is how you baptize, bishop, you are quite mad.” [Note: [Col. 0153] “Bishop” is absent from manuscript 3.] Had this man not known how to swim well, Gebeard the bishop would in a single day both have taken up and lost the episcopate. [Note: The witnesses vary in this passage: *Willehalmus* (1, 2b, 3), *Willelmus* (2), and *Wilchelmus* (4, 4a); *transfretantes* (“crossing over”) is corrected from *transferantes*; *sedet* (“sits”) appears in one witness instead of *sederet* (“was sitting”); and *dimissis* (“released”) occurs in some witnesses instead of *demissis* (“lowered”).]

26. When he had arrived at Prague, on the day when, according to custom, he took possession of the episcopal chair, he gave the provostship of that church to his chaplain Mark. He was nobly born, according to human lineage, from the ancestry of great-great-grandfathers, tracing his origin to the German people, and excelling in wisdom beyond all whom the land of Bohemia then possessed. [Note: [Col. 0153] One witness has *Boemia* instead of *Boemica*.]

For in all the liberal arts he was a very good scholar, [Col. 0153B] one who could be called—and indeed was—the teacher of many masters; in Holy Scripture a marvellous interpreter; and in Catholic faith and ecclesiastical law a magnificent doctor. [Note: [Col. 0153] The words “and in ecclesiastical law” are absent from manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

Whatever religious observance, whatever regular institution, whatever honour there is in this church, he instructed and ordered by his prudence. [Note: [Col. 0153] One witness reads “wisdom” instead of “prudence.”] For before this they were irregular and canons in name only: uncultivated, unlearned, and serving in the choir in lay dress, living like headless men or brutish centaurs. [Note: [Col. 0153] One witness adds “uncultivated”; others read “as bulls” instead of “like centaurs.”]

The prudent Mark instructed them by his words and examples, and, choosing the better men from among many, like flowers gathered from a meadow, with divine assistance cooperating, he established twenty-five brethren, giving them the religious habit and, according to the rule, an equal measure of food and drink.

But since the brethren’s prebend was often interrupted, either through the negligence of the ministers [Col. 0153C] or on account of some matter involving their superiors, [Note: [Col. 0153] The words “or on account of their superiors” are added in another hand in the margin.] and the brethren often afflicted him on that account with their complaints, wishing to satisfy them in every respect, he assigned to himself a fourth part of their tithe and divided three parts among the brethren. Thus each brother received annually thirty measures of wheat and as many of oats, and in addition four denarii weekly for meat, without interruption. [Note: [Col. 0153] “Was given” is added by one witness.] [Note: [Col. 0153D] Dobner observes that four denarii were approximately equal to twenty crusader-coins.]

Many things worthy of report might be said concerning his deeds pleasing to God, but it is better to be silent about them than to seem, out of many things, to have spoken only a few. [Note: [Col. 0153] One witness has “many things worthy of report could be said,” omitting “to be spoken.”] This provost of blessed memory, Mark, after thirty years during which he governed the provostship of this church, was now to receive in the heavenly kingdom the blessed return on the talent entrusted to him, on 18 Kalends of December. [Note: [Col. 0153D] That is, 1098.]

He passes from these shadows to the pleasant places of everlasting light. [Note: [Col. 0153] Another hand adds: “to the light of the pleasant and eternal paradise.”] *

\* [Note: [Col. 0153] The account of the foundation of the Wissehrad church that follows is found in only two manuscripts, 7 and 7a.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1070, [Note: [Col. 0153D] Whether the Wissehrad church was actually founded, or began to be founded, in 1070 is even more doubtful, since all later writers—on whom no suspicion of the kind attaching to Cosmas’s interpolator rests—unanimously state that the church was founded only in 1088. The names of the bishops mentioned in Wratizlaus’s own foundation charter, printed in Boczek I, 183, although the charter wholly lacks chronological indicators, prove that it was written in that same year. See Dobner on Hajek V, 540. Dobner also correctly observed that the ensuing bull of Alexander II is forged, and that it is sufficiently clear from what Gregory VII wrote to Wratizlaus concerning the Wissehrad church in 1074 that Alexander could not have granted such a privilege: “Concerning the relics and privilege about which you asked us: since your messenger, after the church had been completed and finished, sought counsel from us about its consecration, we shall graciously take care to satisfy your wish.”]

Duke Wratislaus, beloved by God and men in character and likewise a distinguished soldier in warfare, admonished by divine inspiration, devoutly resolved, with God’s help, to build a monastery in the chief city of Bohemia, called Wissegrad, which is as it were the mother and mistress of all the cities of that land.

Deliberating with no ordinary earnestness upon plans for carrying out this purpose, [Col. 0154B] he judged it fitting to commend to the pontiff of the holy Roman Church, for governance and diligent protection against every adversity, the monastery which, through God’s cooperating grace, he had devoutly promised to complete, together with the canons of the same church.

Accordingly Peter, provost of the church of Saint George, was sent to Rome and faithfully laid before the apostolic lord the devout message of his duke. [Note: [Col. 0154D] For the true reason for Peter’s embassy, see what Cosmas narrates below at II.29. Compare also Cosmas’s first continuation under the year 1129.]

When he heard this, the venerable Pope Alexander II gave thanks to God for so happy a desire in the aforesaid prince and immediately called a synod, at which there were seventy-two bishops. After he had recited to them all the words of the aforesaid duke, all, with one heart and voice glorifying God, who does not cease to enlarge his holy Church throughout the whole world, answered, “Amen.” The lord pope therefore sent Provost Peter back to his lord with a privilege in these words:

> “Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops of the city of Rome and to his successor popes, and also to the Catholic bishops and all those subject to the holy Roman Church: prosperity in both lives and apostolic blessing from the Most High God together with all the saints. [Note: [Col. 0154D] Everyone can see how far this opening departs from genuine bulls of the Roman pontiffs.]
>
> “Those things which the Lord God has deigned by his clemency to grant for the increase of the apostolic see, we wish to have disseminated under this charter for the knowledge of peoples of every language. First, we plainly proclaim the mercy of God poured out upon us.
>
> “Wratizlaus, duke of the Bohemians, a Christian man, a most upright lover of the faith, a magnificent victor in warfare, as has shone forth most clearly throughout all lands, daily visiting the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul through honourable envoys, and passing by neither us nor the rest who are most devoted in God’s service without benefaction, has made himself known through the devotion of his pious mind: ‘Long ago I made a vow to God which I have as yet in no way fulfilled. I wish, with the protection of our Saviour by which I am everywhere defended, and with the help of your piety, to build a church in his honour.’
>
> “When such words had been heard, we, together with the seventy-two holy Fathers, approved them altogether by common counsel, so that the pontifical dignity might be increased. [Note: [Col. 0155C] The words from “the Fathers” through “approved” are copied from Cosmas’s first continuator under the year 1129.]
>
> “Therefore, to accomplish these things, we sent John, bishop of Tusculum, to lay the foundation. In his presence the aforesaid duke himself was seen to carry on his own shoulders twelve baskets loaded with earth. [Note: [Col. 0155C] The words from “baskets” through “was seen” appear to have been taken from the same source.] [Note: [Col. 0155C] Dobner rightly observed the ridiculous contradiction: in the same diploma permission is granted to build a church in the future, while mention is also made of the foundation of a church already built.]
>
> “The place in which it has been erected is called Wissegrada, which literally means ‘higher than the cities.’ We have decreed that this most holy church be called and venerated as the head of the whole province; we have found it suitably enriched with estates, dependants, gold, silver, and other ornaments.
>
> “Its bishops, under their authority, have set apart from their tithes three hundred men for that church: the bishop of Prague two hundred, and the bishop of Olomouc one hundred, with the consent of his brothers Conrad and Otto. [Note: [Col. 0155C] The words from “the bishop” through “appointed” are copied, with some alterations, from Wratizlaus’s foundation charter granted to the Wissehrad church; compare Boczek I, 183.]
>
> “He has likewise firmly commended this sanctuary to the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all who shall sit in his see. He has ordained that twelve marks from the same church be offered every year, under Christ’s witness, at the feet of whatever pope shall be universal pope.
>
> “By virtue of this provision, so that it might appear higher than all churches in that region, we command that the provost, priest, deacon, and subdeacon of that church proceed with mitre and sandals, in the same manner and with whatever ceremonial the seven cardinals strive to minister at the altar of Saint Peter. We permit that the praises which we customarily proclaim on appointed days under the diadem be solemnly offered to Christ with the utmost care only in this church, when the duke is present.
>
> “[Col. 0155C] If the bishop of that place, moved by the envy of the devil, should presume to refuse chrism for baptism or the consecration of clerics, let that church seek and receive these, by judgment of our decree, from [Col. 0156A] any bishop whatsoever. Let it freely proclaim before the Roman synod every injury, no one hindering it.
>
> “We have placed this writing, sealed with our seal, upon the venerable body of the blessed apostle Peter, especially for this reason: that whoever, an enemy of God and despiser of his commands, may wish to see this may know himself condemned forever by Almighty God and that he will have nothing in common with the companies of the saints, but will burn eternally with the devil in the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.
>
> “Given into the hands of Peter, provost of Saint George, in the Lateran palace, under King Henry, son of the most glorious Emperor Henry, on 7 Ides of May.”

[Note: [Col. 0155C] A later hand has written the number 7 beneath the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0155] Here manuscript 7a ends. In manuscript 7, everything from this point through the year 1086 is lacking.]

But behold: while we treat of our own payments, we have wandered far from the work begun, through the losses of the roads. [Note: [Col. 0155] Manuscript A reads “from our payments.”] Now let us return to the matters we promised above [Note: [Col. 0155] One witness reads “previously mentioned” instead of “promised.”] and see what cause made so great a conflict blaze forth [Col. 0156B] between two angelic men. O avarice and ambition of the world, execrable plague and enemy of the human race, which by your arts even pursue the priests of God!

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1069. [Note: [Col. 0155] The supplied note reads *ita A. 1. in rell.*, “thus in A and 1; in the remaining witnesses …”; the latter reading is not specified.]

27. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1070, on 6 Ides of June, Bishop Gebeard consecrated his church [Note: [Col. 0155] “His church” is absent from manuscript 3.] at the new court called Zricinaves. [Note: [Col. 0155] The name appears variously as *Serczinauez*, *Sercinaw*, *Sremavez*, and *Scircinawez* in the manuscripts.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1071. [Note: [Col. 0155C–D] Under this year he omitted to note the grave dissension that then arose between the dukes of Poland and Bohemia; see Lambert under this year, Schwarz.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1072.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1073. After Bishop Gebeard saw that his labour had come to nothing, because he could not bend his brother Wratizlaus by prayers, gifts, or friends to receive back his compensation—that is, the things given to Gebeard to offset the loss sustained by the church of Prague when the bishopric of Olomouc was established—and to remove Bishop John and reunite the two bishoprics, [Note: [Col. 0155D] A letter of Alexander II to Duke Wratizlaus survives, urging him to make peace with his brother and testifying that he had already written often concerning the suppression of that dispute; Boczek I, 141. The testimony of Hildegard of Gradice is no less conclusive; Boczek printed its fragment at I, 142, where the date 1071 is preserved, so that the beginning of this contention must be referred to 1071. There is also the letter of Archbishop Sigefrid of Mainz, which Dobner and Boczek printed from the codex of Udalric, I, 145. From this letter it is evident that Pope Alexander II excommunicated Gebhard. It is useful to append these words of Sigefrid:

> “Finally, an unfavourable report concerning our brother and suffragan, the bishop of Prague, was made to that most holy father Alexander; and, without my knowledge, he was accused before him by enemies. A singular and hitherto unheard-of edict proceeded from him: that he should suspend our brother and fellow bishop, who had not previously been canonically heard among his brethren, nor canonically summoned before him, nor charged with the fault of disobedience; and should not only suspend him from his office but wholly strip and expel him from the property and revenues of his church, so that, by dispatching messengers, he publicly caused it to be announced among clergy and people that, regarding him as excommunicated, they should neither seek nor receive from him anything belonging to a bishop. … But now our brother and fellow bishop is a wanderer and fugitive from his see,” etc.

It appears from Gregory’s letters written in 1074 that Wratizlaus took from his brother the provostship and the castle of Saint Wenceslas.]

he turned himself, like Prometheus, to the form of another trick: “Since,” he said, “for four years or more I have been unable by supplication to obtain what I want, I shall do what I can; and, God being witness, either I shall reunite both bishoprics or I shall lack them both.” [Note: [Col. 0157] One witness has “episcopate” instead of “bishoprics.”]

Without delay he makes arrangements to go to his court at Zekir Kostel in Moravia. [Note: [Col. 0157] The place appears as *Zekircastel*, *Zekir Kostel*, “the place called Sekir Costel,” and *Sekircoztel* in the witnesses.] Turning aside from his route, already about to inflict harm openly and as though intending to visit his brother Otto, [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Otto” is supplied by the editor.] he went to Bishop John in the city of Olomouc. [Note: [Col. 0157] The city appears as *Olomuce* and *Olomuz* in the witnesses.]

John received him hospitably. “Oh,” he said, “if I had known of your arrival, I would have prepared for you an episcopal meal.” But Gebeard, a lioness driven by hunger, who had long been flashing savage glances at him, replied: “There is one time for taking food; now another business is at hand. But come,” he said, “we must enter a secluded place and begin a private conversation.” [Col. 0157B] [Note: [Col. 0157] The words “a secluded place” are absent from manuscript A.]

Then the bishop, ignorant of what was to come, led him into his bedchamber. You would have seen no differently than if a gentle lamb were leading a rabid wolf into its stall, freely offering itself for slaughter.

When Jaromir saw before the bed a half-eaten cheese, a piece of savory, an onion upon a small dish, and a toasted morsel of bread—perhaps what had remained to the bishop after yesterday’s little meal—he became exceedingly indignant, as if a great crime worthy of the cross had been discovered, and said: “Why do you live sparingly? Or for whom are you sparing, wretch and beggar? By Hercules, it does not become a bishop to live sparingly. What then?”

Forgetting his sacred order, forgetting brotherhood, unmindful of humanity, just as a leopard snatches a little hare or a lion a lamb, so that furious guest seized his little bishop-brother by the hair with both hands, lifted him high, and threw him to the floor as one throws a bundle. [Note: [Col. 0157] “John” is supplied in manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

Immediately, those who had been prepared for this crime acted: one sat on his neck, another on his feet, and a third, flogging the bishop, said with a smile: “Learn to suffer, boy of a hundred years, invader of other men’s sheep.” [Note: [Col. 0157] Manuscript A has *aligenarum*, with the letter *g* erased, for *alienarum* (“of other men’s”).]

As the humble monk was beaten, he sang, as was his custom in the cloister, “Have mercy upon me, O God.” [Note: [Col. 0157C] Gregory VII says in a letter to Wratizlaus dated 16 April 1074 that Gebeard offered this excuse at Rome: that he himself had not struck Bishop John of Moravia, nor ordered that the servants of that bishop have their hair cut off or their beards shaved. See Boczek I, 152.]

To the malicious man who beheld such things there was great laughter and applause; he laughed at no one except one whom he saw ill-treated. And just as a valiant soldier, when he boldly breaks by night into an enemy camp and attacks the sleeping enemy, swiftly flees lest he be captured by them, so Bishop Jaromir, having dishonoured his brother John [Note: [Col. 0158C] That is, John.] and sweetened by the gall of his wickedness, left the city of Olomouc [Note: [Col. 0157] “Olomouc” is supplied by manuscripts 4 and 4a.] and went to his court, where he had long ago arranged to go. [Note: [Col. 0157] Some witnesses read “to his own places.”]

28. This was the first cause, tinder, and beginning of the whole discord which afterward arose between the two pillars of the Church on the occasion of this accusation. [Note: [Col. 0157] One witness has “these were”; manuscript A omits “and.”] For Bishop John, having suffered so great an injury, immediately sends his messenger to Duke Wratizlaus, urgently appealing to him in this complaint:

> “If you look with equanimity upon the inhuman insult inflicted on me by your brother Gebeard, make trial, so that all may know that this is not my injury but yours. For what have I done wrong, or what have I deserved—I who have done nothing except what pleased you? Behold, though unworthy, I was nevertheless called bishop through your favour; beaten with whips like a public crier, even to disgust, I would rather never have attained the pontifical height. Certainly, either restore me, though late, to my abbot, or bear this insult with me in equal spirit and share it; and send either me or my messenger to the apostolic see.”

When he heard this, Duke Wratizlaus was greatly inflamed with zeal and could not restrain his tears amid so grave a crisis. At once a legion of soldiers was sent for Bishop John, so that he might be present at the duke’s conference without danger to his life. For the duke feared that his brother Jaromir might remove him by treachery. [Note: [Col. 0157] “Wratizlaus” is supplied by manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

In the chapel of Bishop John there was a cleric named Hagno, a German, a member of philosophy’s household, [Note: [Col. 0158C] Apparently the head of a school.] and a pupil of Ciceronian eloquence. The duke called him aside, bound him by many promises, and entrusted to him, in writings and words alike, many matters concerning his brother Gebeard, many concerning the injury inflicted on Bishop John, and many concerning the state of the Church, so that he might report them to the apostolic lord. [Note: [Col. 0157] The words from “many matters” through “Gebeard” are absent from manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

While travelling, he passed through Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0157] The name appears as *Radispona* in one witness and is corrected to *Ratisbona*.] and, under an unlucky omen, lodged with a certain citizen named Kompold, [Note: [Col. 0159A] One witness reads “Jaromir” instead of “Gebeard.”] who was a knight of Bishop Gebeard and received from him an annual benefice of thirty marks of silver. [Note: [Col. 0159] “From him” is absent from one witness.]

After supper, over the cups, he shrewdly investigated—as a host commonly does of a guest—who he was, whence he came, and what was the reason for his journey. When he learned that Hagno was conducting an embassy against Bishop Gebeard, he could not endure that an accusation be carried against his lord. On the following day he sent robbers after him to hinder the purpose of his journey by some injury. They seized him on the road, stripped him of his money, cut off his nose, and threatened him with death at sword-point unless he returned. [Note: [Col. 0159] One witness reads *differri* (“be delayed”) for *deferri* (“be carried”); another reads *deliberationem* for *delationem* (“accusation”).]

Fearing, however disgraceful it was, to lose his life, he returned to his bishop John in Moravia. [Note: [Col. 0159] “John” is supplied by manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

[Col. 0159B] 29. Immediately the duke’s indignation grew greater from so great a cause, and another embassy to Rome was resolved upon, but with more cautious counsel and the aid of a safer route. [Note: [Col. 0159] “Wratizlaus’s” is supplied by manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

There was in the duke’s chapel a priest named Peter, son of Podiwa, who held the provostship of Saint George and surpassed the others in knowledge of letters. He knew both languages equally, German and Latin. The duke sent him to Rome, together with a count named Preda, son of Bys, and with a large sum of money, informing them in a concise written statement of the first and last injuries inflicted on himself and Bishop John by his brother, so that they might bring them to the ears of the apostolic lord. [Note: [Col. 0159] The names vary: *Preda* and *Podiva*; *Bys* and *Buz*.]

To enable them to make the journey more safely, he entrusted them to a count palatine of the Roman emperor named Rapota, earnestly begging him that his envoys might go to Rome and return under his escort. [Note: [Col. 0159] The name also appears as *Rapotha*.] For this count possessed such power that all the way to Rome he had his own villages or estates and loyal soldiers in fortresses at successive places. He also received from the aforesaid duke one hundred and fifty marks of silver yearly as a benefice.

When the envoys reached Rome under his escort, they presented to the apostolic lord letters greased with two hundred marks. When these had been read aloud by a notary before all, the Roman pontiff asked them whether they would substantiate in words what the letters said. The envoys replied that it would be very improper for their letters to say one thing and their mouths utter another.

Then he who sat second after the pope, taking counsel with all present in the assembly, judged that such a scandal must be extirpated from the Church by apostolic command.

Immediately Rudolf, apocrisiary and counsellor of Pope Gregory, was sent to Bohemia, [Note: [Col. 0159C] Rather, Rudolf was sent by Alexander II in 1072; for Gregory’s envoys, already mentioned in a letter dated 8 July 1073, were Bernard and Gregory. Boczek I, 143.] with instructions that, if the matter stood as it had been reported to the supreme pontiff, he should correct errors in the pope’s stead, rebuke the disobedient, reprove the unfaithful, strike the negligent with anathema, and, if anything exceeded the limits of correction, defer it and compel the parties to appear for the fuller hearing of the apostolic see. [Note: [Col. 0159] The witnesses vary between “if there are matters” and “if there are matters that exceed the limits of correction”; one reads “reprove” in the present tense instead of “reprove” in the subjunctive.]

30. When the apostolic envoy arrived, he found Duke Wratizlaus in Prague. Offering him apostolic blessing and the adoptive sonship of the universal father, [Note: [Col. 0159C] Alexander II sent Wratizlaus a mitre. See Gregory’s letter, Boczek I, 144.] he exercised such authority and power as though the supreme pontiff himself were present. [Col. 0160B]

Finally, he commanded the duke to summon to a holy synod all the princes of the land, as well as abbots and provosts of churches, and also John, bishop of Moravia. [Note: [Col. 0159] “Of God” is added by manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

Bishop Gebeard, summoned once and twice by name, refused to come, and at last is said to have given this answer:

> “According to the rulings of the canons, with pontifical dignity and justice preserved, I do not come at your pleasure unless my master, the metropolitan of Mainz, is present, together with a gathering of the other fellow bishops.” [Note: [Col. 0159] A later hand has supplied the letter “I” in the margin.]

For he knew that there he would fall into a snare, penalties, and scandal. [Note: [Col. 0159] “There” is absent from one witness.] But when the Roman envoy saw that he had been despised and dishonoured, moved by anger he suspended him from every sacerdotal office and deprived him of episcopal dignity.

[Col. 0160C] When they heard this, not only the canons but also all the clerics in the chapels tore their *oraria* [priestly vestments] and laid themselves bare, as altars are on Good Friday. [Note: [Col. 0160C] *Oraria* means priestly vestments.] The brow of Mother Church is furrowed by no small wrinkle, because priestly offices are silent; and unless their pastor’s former honour and rank are restored, the whole clergy prefers to lose its own ranks forever.

But when the cardinal saw that a greater tumult was arising among the people, compelled by necessity, he restored to the bishop only the sacerdotal office. Unless the two bishops should in that same year render an account to the Roman pontiff of the matters at issue, he bound both of them under ban. [Note: [Col. 0160C–0161C] These events must be referred to the year 1074. In a letter written on 31 January 1074, Gregory orders Gebeard to come to the apostolic thresholds on Palm Sunday; Boczek I, 149.]

[Col. 0161A] Without delay the aforesaid bishops set out for Rome and presented to the apostolic lord a copy of their letters. When these had been read, their case was neither admitted nor rejected nor examined; they were ordered to go to their lodgings until they should be summoned to a general synod on an appointed day.

160. **[Col. 0159]** Another hand in manuscript 1 writes the letter *I* above the line at *metropolita* (“metropolitan”); the apparatus records the added letter without assigning it a further word or interpretation.
161. **[Col. 0160C]** For how Archbishop Sigefrid of Mainz involved himself in these affairs, see above; see also Gregory VII’s letter severely rebuking him, Boczek I, 150.
162. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 2 omits *ibi*, “there,” from “he knew that there he would fall into a snare.”
163. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscripts 4 and 4a read *retributionem*, “punishment/recompense,” singular, for *retributiones*, plural.
164. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 1 corrects *audiens*, “hearing,” to *audientes*, “hearing [this],” agreeing with the canons and clerics.
165. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 4a omits *oraria* (“priestly vestments”) from the clerics’ act of tearing their vestments.
166. **[Col. 0160C]** *Oraria* means priestly vestments.
167. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 2 reads *dimidiaverunt*, “they halved,” for *denudaverunt*, “they stripped/bared [the altars],” as on Good Friday.
168. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscripts 4 and 4a add *sanctae*, “holy,” to Mother Church.
169. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 2 reads *fons*, “spring/fountain,” for *frons*, “brow,” in the image of the Church’s furrowed brow.
170. **[Col. 0159]** A, 4, and 4a read *quod*, “because/that,” for *quia*, “because,” before “the priestly offices are silent.”
171. **[Col. 0159]** A omits *pristinus*, “former,” from the pastor’s former honour and rank.
172. **[Col. 0159]** A, 2, 2b, and 3 read *reddit*, “restores,” for *reddidit*, “restored”; 4 and 4a add *Gebeardo*, “to Gebeard,” to the restoration of the sacerdotal office.
173. **[Col. 0159]** Manuscript 4 reads *reddant*, “they should render,” for *reddat*, “he should render,” in the requirement imposed on both bishops.
174. **[Col. 0159]** The note reads *constrinxit A. corr. alia manu confringit 1*: A has *constrinxit*, “bound”; *confringit*, “breaks,” is recorded in manuscript 1 with a correction by another hand. The earlier corrected form is not specified. The main text has *constringit*, “binds,” under ban.
175. **[Col. 0160C–0161C]** These events should be assigned to 1074: in a letter dated 31 January 1074 Gregory orders Gebeard to visit the apostolic thresholds on Palm Sunday; Boczek I, 149.
176. **[Col. 0161]** A abbreviates *praedicti episcopi*, “the aforesaid bishops,” as *praed. ep.*
177. **[Col. 0161]** Manuscript 1 has *ospicia*, a spelling of *hospicia*, “lodgings.”
178. **[Col. 0161]** Manuscript 1 has a correction at *revocarentur*, “they should be summoned back,” to the general synod.

31. In those same days, Matilda [Apparatus, col. 0161: *Mahtildis* in manuscripts 1, 2, 4], a most powerful lady, had come to Rome. After the death of her father Boniface, she assumed the government of the whole of Lombardy and Burgundy alike, possessing the power to elect, enthrone, or remove more than 120 bishops. [Editorial note, col. 0161: Everyone can see that this was exaggerated by popular rumour.] At the bidding of this lady, as though she were their own sovereign [Apparatus, col. 0161: “another hand superscribed it”; *omnis* is absent in manuscript 1], the entire senatorial order obeyed, and Pope Gregory himself arranged divine and human affairs through her, because she was a most wise counsellor and, in every adversity or necessity of the Roman Church, its greatest supporter. [Col. 0161B]

Bishop Gebehard, descended through his mother’s blood from her lineage [Apparatus, col. 0161: *analogia* in manuscript A instead of *genealogia*; “through his mother’s blood” is omitted in manuscripts 4 and 4a], established a bond of affinity with her. [Col. 0161C. Editorial note: What precisely that bond of affinity was is not sufficiently clear. Schwarz pursued one line of proof, Pfeffel another in his essay in *Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie* I, p. 185, and Dobner another. Palacký followed Pfeffel, who believed that he had discovered that Matilda’s grandmother Matilda and the unnamed mother of Judith, wife of Duke Břetislav, were daughters of Hermann II, Duke of Swabia.]

When, as he himself related, the aforesaid lady recognized that he was her blood-relative, she began greatly to honour him, commend him to the apostolic lord, and, as far as she could, treat him honourably as though he were her brother. Certainly Bishop Gebehard would have lost his good name and honour together with his rank, had she not been present at Rome. Through her intervention, and after she had wearied the apostolic lord with many petitions, peace was made between the aforesaid bishops on this condition: that they should live quietly in peace and remain content with their own bishoprics; but otherwise, after ten years, they should return to the Apostolic See to receive judgment concerning this same case. [Apparatus, col. 0161: *supra* (“above”) in manuscript 4a; *ipso* corrected from *ipse* in A; *domino* for *domno* in A; *si ... affuisset* was added in another hand in the margin of A, while manuscripts 4 and 4a read *fuisset*.]

[Editorial note, col. 0161D: Cosmas has confused two journeys to Rome by those bishops into one. Gebehard had already attempted in 1074 to defend himself before the pope against that accusation; compare note 35 above. In another letter of Gregory, dated the sixth day before the Nones of March, indiction 13 (1075), the following is read:

“For when this case—that of Gebehard and John—was brought, in the second year of our pontificate, before our hearing and that of the whole council assembled there, while many brethren sat with us in the basilica of St Saviour and the aforesaid bishops too had been summoned and placed before us, it appeared, after long and extensive inquiry and examination, to be so entangled in ambiguity and complications that it could not be brought to a clear investigation of truth and justice by the judicial means then employed. Yet, lest their dispute, without the intervention of peace, should for a longer time give rise either to fraternal hatreds or to dangerous enterprises on one side or the other, we resolved, with the counsel of our brethren, that the case should be settled equitably in this manner: everything concerning which there was contention between them should be divided equally, and one should meanwhile hold one part and the other the other part without any disturbance, until they might search most diligently for clearer evidence, whether in writing or through suitable witnesses. And, lest an endless opportunity for renewing the lawsuit perhaps be afforded to either party, we also fixed a term of ten years for doing this, so that whoever trusts that he can establish his right by definite proofs may, within the aforesaid term, have leave and authority to lay claim to and obtain the right of his church,” etc. Boczek I, 158. In the Prague Annals Gebehard’s restoration is assigned to the year 1074.]

Thus, through Pope Gregory, with Matilda acting in the matter, Bishop Gebehard was restored to his former rank and honour in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1074, when the sun entered the fifteenth degree of Virgo. [Apparatus, col. 0161: manuscripts 2 and 2b read “LXXIII,” although traces of erasure by a later hand appear, apparently attempting to change III into IV.]

Moreover, through Matilda’s intervention in this affair, the lord pope gave letters to the Bohemian envoys [Apparatus, col. 0161: *tradidit* (“gave”) in manuscripts 2b and 3], in which he commanded and enjoined Duke Wratizlaus [*Wratizlaus* is added in manuscripts 4 and 4a] to receive his brother Jaromir honourably, obey him in all things as his father and shepherd, and live with him in peace under God’s blessing.

32. But since mention has been made of Matilda [Apparatus, col. 0161: *Machtylda* in manuscript 4], I shall briefly recount one deed which that woman performed manfully, lest I weary the reader. Thus, when the aforesaid maiden, always victorious amid many wars [the words “always victorious ... lived unmarried” are absent in manuscript 4; *victrix* is absent in 4a], was living a celibate life after the death of her father Boniface, Marquis of Tuscany [col. 0162D: Cosmas omits the fact that she married Gozelo, Duke of Lorraine], and alone ruled the exceedingly extensive kingdom of Lombardy, it seemed good to the princes of the land, the counts, and the bishops to persuade her to take a husband, lest royal eminence, together with its offspring, fail without an heir.

Acceding to their counsels, she sent a letter to a Duke of Swabia named Welf [the name is absent in manuscript 4a], containing much in few words:

> “I am sending you these letters not from feminine frivolity or rashness, but for the advantage of my whole kingdom. When you have received them, receive me and the whole kingdom of Lombardy. I shall give you so many cities, so many castles, so many illustrious palaces, gold and silver without measure; above all these things, you shall have a renowned name, if you make yourself dear to me. [Apparatus: *clarum* (“renowned/bright”) in manuscript 2; *casum* corrected to *carum* (“dear”) in manuscript 1.]
>
> “Yet do not charge me with the reproach of boldness because I now address you first. For it is lawful for both the male and female sex to seek a legitimate marriage. Nor does it matter whether a man or a woman first touches the line of love, provided only that an indissoluble marriage results. But this cannot happen except by the consent of both parties. Farewell.”

[Editorial note, col. 0162D: Bernold, who asserts that the younger Welf entered into marriage with Matilda only in 1089 and divorced her in 1095, testifies that he had never touched her. Compare the Monk of Weingarten, p. 789; Stenzel, *Fränkische Kaiser* I, p. 553. Cosmas therefore strayed far from the truth here, deceived by popular rumour.]

What Duke Welf replied to this, on what grounds he consented, how many thousands of armed men Lady Matilda sent ahead to receive the duke at the borders of Lombardy, how honourably she herself received him, or with what magnificence she held the banquet—if anyone wished to know, daylight would fail before he had read all these things. Let King Ahasuerus yield with his displays, he who gave his soldiers a magnificent feast for 120 days [Apparatus, col. 0163: “superscribed” in manuscript 1]; let the Queen of Sheba cease to marvel at Solomon’s table and royal food. For all that was there in its entirety—here a hundredth part was greater than the whole. [Apparatus, col. 0163: *maxima* (“greatest”) is added in manuscript 2.]

Why say more? Night came; they entered the bedchamber; the pair took their places upon the high bed: Duke Welf without Venus, with the maiden Matilda. There, among other things, and after such things as occur between such persons, Duke Welf said:

> “Lady, what did you intend? Why did you summon me—to make sport of me and make me an object of mockery among peoples and a shaking of the head? [Col. 0164D: Shaking the head is a sign of derision and mockery.]
>
> “You bring greater shame upon yourself if you wish to shame me. Surely, either by your command or through your maidservants, some sorcery lies hidden either in your garments or in the bedding. Believe me: if I had been of a cold nature, I should never have come at your bidding.”

When the duke had made these reproaches to the lady on the first and second nights, on the third day she led the man alone into the bedchamber, placed tripods in the middle, set a tabletop upon them, and displayed herself naked as from her mother’s womb, saying:

> “Behold: whatever is hidden, all is open to you, and there is nowhere for any sorcery to lie concealed.”

But he stood with lowered ears, like an ass of evil mind [col. 0164D: Horace, *Epistles* I.9.20], or like a butcher who, sharpening a long knife, stands in the slaughterhouse over a fat flayed cow, desiring to disembowel it. After the woman had sat for a long time upon the table and, like a goose making herself a nest, had vainly moved her tail this way and that, at last the naked woman rose in anger, seized the half-man by the forelock with her left hand, spat into her right palm, gave him a great slap, and thrust him outside, saying:

> “Go far from here, monster; do not defile our kingdom.”

> “You are more worthless than a grub (*galba*), more worthless than cast-off seaweed.” [Col. 0163D: Vergil, *Eclogues* VII.42. The zoological reference of *galba* is uncertain.]

> “If you are seen by me tomorrow, you shall die an evil death.”

[Apparatus: *I* was corrected in A; manuscript 1 omits the gloss “that is, go”; *glaba* in manuscript 1. *Sinciput* (“forelock”) appears as *anticiput* in the main text; *exspuens* (“spitting”) is absent in manuscript 3; *ei* (“to him”) appears in A instead of *sibi*.]

Thus humiliated, Duke Welf fled and brought everlasting disgrace upon all his followers. This is enough to have said briefly—though I wish I had not said it! [This closing sentence is absent in manuscripts 4 and 4a.]

33. Now after Bishop Gebehard returned from the city of Rome, all the nobles who were his clients, rejoicing greatly at his return, came to meet him at the very edge of the forest. Having welcomed them joyfully, he related what had been done at Rome and how he had relied on the assistance of Lady Matilda. Then, jesting with one of them, whom he loved above the rest, named Belec [*Belecz* in manuscripts 1 and 4], he said: “See what a beard I have brought back,” and, stroking it with his hand: “Surely,” he said, “it is worthy of Caesar.”

But the other replied: “Everything that you praise, lord, is pleasing; but I should praise it more if you brought back a changed mind along with your beard:

> “If only you had changed it, thereafter you would have been at peace.”

34. Nor do I wish to pass over what, in that same year, happened to us while we were still at school to hear and see. One day, while I stood in the crypt of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, meditating upon little psalms, a certain man came carrying a candle and a silver thread by which, according to the command of a vision, he had measured the limbs of his body [Apparatus: *est* (“is”) in manuscript 2; *fuerat* (“had been”) in 2b]. Approaching me, he said:

> “Hey, good boy, tell me: where lies Saint Radim, brother of Saint Adalbert?”

I said to him:

> “He whom you call a saint has not yet been canonized by apostolic authority [*canonizatus* in manuscript 4a]; we still celebrate his Mass as for the dead.”

And he said:

> “I know nothing of such things, but I know this one thing: when I had been confined for three years in an underground prison in the city of Kraków [*Krakow* in manuscript 2], in which there was one small window above through which bread and water were rarely handed to me, while my life was passing in that distress, one day a man stood before me. His garments were white as snow and his face shone like the sun. That much I remember; immediately I fell into ecstasy, and, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, I felt myself standing outside the city. And he who had appeared to me in prison, standing beside me, said:

> “‘Go to Prague; fear no one. Enter the church of Saint Vitus; in the crypt of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian offer your gift at my tomb. I am Radim, brother of Saint Adalbert.’

“He said this to me and immediately vanished from my sight. Behold, these hairs and the emaciation of my face testify that what is related to you is true. Moreover, the guardians of the church often see visions in that same crypt when they visit the candle that is lit there at night.”

35. Nor do I think it should be omitted that Duke Wratizlaus and his brothers Chounrad and Otto fought a battle against the eastern margrave Lupold [*Leupoldum* in manuscript 2; *Ludolphum* in 3], son of Lucz. [Editorial note, col. 0165D: In fact, he was the son of Margrave Ernest, who was killed in the battle fought on the river Unstrut in 1078. Cosmas himself shows below that this battle took place only in 1082; compare the Annals of Hildesheim and the Chronicle of Klosterneuburg. On the year 1082, compare also Dobner on Hájek V, p. 495.]

But first one must see whence arose so great an enmity between Lupold and Chonrad, joint ruler of Moravia; previously they had always been friends with one another. [Editorial note, col. 0166D: The true cause escaped Cosmas: Margrave Leopold had expelled the supporters of Henry IV, and Wratizlaus, on the king’s advice, took arms against him, as the author of the *Life of Altmann, Bishop of Passau*, testifies.]

Since the boundaries of the two provinces were divided neither by forest, mountains, nor any obstacle, but were scarcely marked by a little stream named Dia [*Dya* in manuscripts 2 and 4; *Dyia* in 3], flowing through level country [the phrase is absent in manuscript 1], wicked men continually committed robberies by night on both sides in turn, plundering cattle and ravaging villages, and made booty for themselves from both peoples. And just as a small spark often kindles a great fire, so these lords of whom we have spoken, because they would not extinguish the harmful tinder [manuscript A has a later correction; variants include *novicium* and *nocuum*], came through these insignificant matters to their own great destruction.

For although Chounrad frequently sent to the margrave concerning the suppression of this disorder [*pro huiusmodi* (“concerning such matters”) in manuscripts 4 and 4a; *werra* appears in 4 and 4a instead of *seditio*], the latter looked down with swollen pride upon his words. Therefore Chounrad humbly approached his brother Wratizlaus, Duke of the Bohemians, asking him for assistance against the arrogance of the Germans. Though not distrusting his own forces, Wratizlaus hired, for payment, one troop of selected soldiers from the Bishop of Regensburg [col. 0166D: Otto] to aid him.

The duke did not conceal his arrival from the margrave. Rather, sending one of his magnates and speaking, as it were, by antiphrasis, he instructed him to prepare a great feast for him; he promised that he himself would soon come to play a game of Mars. At this the margrave became glad, and ordered everyone, from swineherd to oxherd [*publicum* in manuscripts 4 and 4a instead of *bubulcum*], to be armed for battle with every sort of iron implement, from awl to goad. [The phrase “armed ... to awl” is absent in manuscript A.]

Duke Wratizlaus had arrived with the Bohemians and also with the Germans who belonged to the Bishop of Regensburg [*Radisperonensis* in manuscript 1]; while Otto and Conrad joined them with all the soldiers in the whole of Moravia. When the margrave saw them coming from afar across the open plain, he arranged his men in the form of a wooden wedge and strengthened their courage with an address of this kind:

> “O soldiers, whose strength I have tested sufficiently in many battles of fortune, do not fear those fugitive shadows. I greatly regret that an open field lies before them for flight. For I know that they dare not join battle with you. Do you not see how weakness of strength condemns those whom fear has forced into a single mass? No appearance of arms is visible there. They are sheep, I think, and food for wolves. Why do you stand, ravening wolves and fierce lion-cubs? Rush upon the flocks of sheep and tear apart bodies which stand bloodless, destined to fall before seeing battle, and soon to feed our kites and vultures. O Hell, what great victims we shall give you today! Open your workshops to receive the souls of the Bohemians. For I know that they are men hateful to God and His saints, without mercy, entering this land in order to plunder not merely our possessions but our wives and their offspring also—may God avert it far from us. Yet if it should befall any one of you to die, this is one death happier than every other death: sweet it is to die for one’s country.” [Horace, *Odes* III.2.13.]

He would have said more, but the attack of the Bohemians cut short his speech. For when Duke Wratizlaus saw that the enemy would not yield their position, he ordered the Germans to break into the right wing, while he stationed his brothers Chounrad and Otto to fight in the left wing [the reading *ala* (“wing”) appears as *alia* in manuscripts 1, 2, 4, and 5]. He himself, where the enemy line was thickest [compare Sallust, *Catiline* 60], at the very front of Mars [Lucan, *Pharsalia* VII.220], ordered his army to descend upon the enemy and fight the opponents in hand-to-hand combat.

They at once leapt from their horses [*desilientes* in manuscript 4a], raised a cry of exhortation [*exhortandi* in manuscripts 4 and 4a], and, as fire raging when cast into dry stubble consumes everything in a moment [Vergil, *Georgics* III.99], so they crushed the enemy’s strength with the sword, threw them to the ground, and of so great a multitude scarcely one survivor escaped with the margrave himself.

Thus the flocks of sheep suckled the lion-cubs; and, having lost few of their own men, the Bohemians carried away a famous triumph from the eastern march. In this slaughter there were killed Ztan [*Zdan* in manuscript 2; *Zthan* in 4 and 4a] with his brother Radim [*Radvim* in manuscript 1], Gridon [*Grydon* in manuscripts 1 and 2b; *Grdon* in 3], son of Zanek [*Zanec* in 1; *Zauek* in 2b; *Janek* in 3], and Dobrogost, son of Hines [*Hynes* in manuscripts 1 and 2; *Hones* in 3], together with others, though not very many, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, on the fourth day before the Ides of May. [Editorial note, col. 0167D: On 12 May 1082 at Mouriberch, that is, Mailberg; *Life of St Altmann*.]

*King Henry besieged Rome for two years.* [Manuscripts 2, 2a, and 2b.]

36. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084.

**King Henry became emperor.** [Manuscripts 2, 2a, and 2b.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Judith [manuscripts 2b and 4a add *ductrix*, “ruler/lady”], wife of Wladizlaus, Duke of the Poles [*Polonorum* in manuscript 2], died. She was the daughter of Wratizlaus, Duke of the Bohemians. [Editorial note, col. 0167D: She was the daughter of Adelaide; see above, II.20.]

Because she was barren, she continually offered herself as a living sacrifice to God with tears; devoting herself to almsgiving, she helped widows and orphans, distributing gold and silver most generously among monasteries [*dispensans* (“distributing”) in A; *dispertiens* in manuscripts 2b, 3, 4, and 4a]. She commended herself to the prayers of priests, so that through the intercessions of the saints she might obtain by divine grace the offspring which nature had denied her.

Moreover, she sent her chaplain, named Peter, to bring her vows to the tomb of Saint Giles [manuscript 4a adds “the confessor”], and other small gifts to the abbot and his brethren, so that through their intercession God might hear her petition. [Editorial note, col. 0167D: Martin Gallus, p. 78, and Kadłubek, p. 17, report this matter in almost the same fashion.]

As soon as he had fulfilled his lady’s commands and was about to return home, the abbot is said to have addressed him in almost prophetic words:

> “Go with God’s blessing, and tell your lady: ‘Hope in God and do not waver at all in faith, for you shall conceive and bear a son.’ For there is no one who has not obtained what he faithfully asked of Saint Giles. But I fear lest perhaps we offend God when we weary Him with prayers contrary to fate, although through the merits of this our patron, Saint Giles, He sometimes grants to petitioners what nature forbids.”

When he had reported these things to his lady, she conceived in due time; and after she had borne a son, she died on the third day, at the first cockcrow, on the aforesaid date. Her son was afterwards named Boleslav at baptism after his paternal uncle. [Apparatus: In A another hand corrected *patrui* (“of the paternal uncle”) to *patris* (“of the father”); manuscript 1 also reads *patris*; manuscript 3 omits the word. Manuscripts 4 and 4a add that the son received in baptism the name of his father, Boleslav.]

37. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1086, by the command and under the direction of Henry III, august emperor of the Romans [this is omitted in manuscript 2; the following material through II.38 is also found in manuscript 7], a great synod was held in the city of Mainz. [Manuscript A: *Maguntina*; manuscript 4: *Maguntia*; manuscript 7: *Magoncia*. Editorial note, col. 0167D: Dobner, in his notes to Hájek V, p. 515, proved that this synod must not be confused with another held at Mainz in 1085 by bishops supporting Henry.]

Four archbishops and twelve bishops, whose names we shall give later, sat together with the abbots of monasteries and the other faithful, and confirmed in writing many decrees concerning the condition of the holy Church.

At this assembly, with all the great men of his kingdom—dukes, margraves, magnates, and bishops—assenting and applauding, the same emperor set Wratizlaus, Duke of the Bohemians, over both Bohemia and Poland. [Editorial note, col. 0167D: It is not sufficiently clear how Henry could at that time have placed Wratizlaus over Poland, since at approximately the same time Wladizlaus, Duke of Poland, married Judith, the emperor’s sister. See Roepell, *Geschichte von Polen* I, p. 208.] Placing the royal circlet upon his head with his own hand, he ordered Egilbert, Archbishop of Trier [*Trierensis* is absent in A; *Treveriensis* appears in manuscript 1 with the *i* deleted], to anoint him king in his metropolitan seat at Prague and place the diadem upon his head. [Editorial note, col. 0168D: The Monk of Pegau relates that Wratizlaus bought royal dignity from Henry for 4,000 marks of silver and was crowned at Würzburg by the bishops of Mainz, Constance, and Würzburg.]

At the same council, Bishop Gebehard of Prague [*Jaromir* in manuscript 3; other manuscripts read *Gebehardus*] laid before it the written record of his old complaint concerning John, the Bishop of Moravia mentioned above. Although John had already departed this world in that same year [editorial note: according to the ancient catalogue of the bishops of Olomouc in Richter’s series, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of December], the aforesaid bishop, taking great precautions for the future and acting through friends, importuned the emperor’s ears so that another bishop might not again be substituted in the same place. Before all present he repeated the privilege formerly confirmed for his predecessor, Saint Adalbert the bishop, by both Pope Benedict and the first Emperor Otto.

Moved by this just complaint, at the prayers of Duke Wratizlaus, brother of Bishop Gebehard himself, and by the counsel of Wezelo, Archbishop of Mainz [*Wezzelonis* in manuscript 4], and other good men who favoured justice, the emperor added a new privilege, nearly of the same tenor as the old, and confirmed it with the imperial seal, as will appear in what follows. We do not judge it superfluous to insert the form of this privilege into our work [manuscript 1 reads *opere* (“work”) instead of *operi*], for it contains this text, or one of this sort:

# PL 166.0016 — apparatus notes 1–80

1. [Col. 0161] MSS 1, 2, and 4 read *Mahtildis*, the spelling “Matilda.”
2. [Col. 0161] MS 2b reads *suscipit*, “receives/takes up,” at the corresponding verb.
3. [Col. 0161] MS 4a reads *supra*, “above/before.”
4. [Col. 0161C] “Everyone sees that this popular rumour has been exaggerated.”
5. [Col. 0161] The reading was written above the line by another hand in A.
6. [Col. 0161] MS 1 omits *omnis*, “every/all,” in *ad nutum omnis* (“at the will of every [one]”).
7. [Col. 0161] A and 1 read *analogia*, “analogy.”
8. [Col. 0161] MSS 4 and 4a omit *materno sanguine*, “by maternal blood/descent.”
9. [Col. 0161] MS 1 omits *praesul Gebeardus descendens*, “Bishop Gebehard, descending [from].”
10. [Cols. 0161C–D] “What precisely that bond of kinship was is not sufficiently clear. Schwarz pursued one way of proving it, Pfeffel another in his essay in the *Proceedings of the Bavarian Academy* I, 185, and Dobner another. Palacký followed Pfeffel, who thought he had discovered that Matilda’s grandmother Matilda and the unnamed mother of Judith, wife of Duke Bracizlaus, were daughters of Hermann II, duke of Swabia.”
11. [Col. 0161] A has *ipso*, “himself/the very [one],” corrected.
12. [Col. 0161] A reads *Domino*, “to/by the Lord.”
13. [Col. 0161] A omits the following connective *et*, “and,” after the sentence about honourably receiving him as a brother.
14. [Col. 0161] In A another hand wrote the span *si … affuisset*, “if … had been present,” in the margin; 4 and 4a read *fuisset*, “had been.”
15. [Col. 0161] MS 1 reads *fidem*, “faith/pledge.”
16. [Col. 0161] MS 1 reads *accepuri*, a corrupt spelling for “to receive/having received.”
17. [Cols. 0161D–0162D] “Cosmas has conflated two Roman journeys of those bishops into one. Gebhard had already attempted in 1074 to defend himself before the pope from that accusation. In another letter of Gregory, dated 6 March, indiction 13 (1075), the pope says that the cause of Gebhard and John had been brought before him and the assembled council in St Saviour’s basilica in his second pontifical year; after long inquiry it remained so entangled that truth and justice could not be reached by the procedures then used. To prevent their dispute from prolonging fraternal hatreds and dangerous partisan efforts, the brothers decided an equal division: each should hold one half without disturbance, pending diligent inquiry by documents or suitable witnesses. A ten-year limit was fixed, so that whoever trusted he could establish his right could claim and obtain his church’s right within that period.
