# Cosmas of Prague, *Chronicle of the Bohemians*, Book II, §§37–42

*Translation status: complete after independent canonical-source adjudication. Initial translation by GPT-5.6 Terra; saved repair by GPT-5.6 Luna; repair review by GPT-5.6 Terra; complete apparatus translation and final adjudication by GPT-5.6 Sol.*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry the Third, by the favour of divine clemency August Emperor of the Romans.

We know that it accords with royal rank and imperial dignity that, assisting everywhere the interests of the churches of God, we should repel whatever losses or injuries may need to be repelled from them. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God and of our realm, both future and present, how our faithful servant Gebhard, bishop of Prague, repeatedly complained to his brethren and fellow bishops, to our other princes, and finally to us, that the bishopric of Prague—which from the beginning had been established as one and whole throughout the entire duchy of Bohemia and Moravia, and had thus been confirmed both by Pope Benedict and by the first Emperor Otto—had later been divided and diminished, with a new bishop intruded within its boundaries by the sole power of those ruling, with the consent of his predecessors.

When at Mainz, before the legates of the Apostolic See, in our presence and that of many leading men of our realm, he had brought forward the same complaint, that original diocese, with the whole circuit of its boundaries, was adjudged to the see of Prague by the archbishops Wezlo of Mainz, Sigewin of Cologne, Egilbert of Trier, and Liemar of Bremen; by the bishops also Theodoric of Verdun, Conrad of Utrecht, Ulrich of Eichstätt, and Otto of Regensburg; and, with the assent of the laymen, by Wratislaus, duke of the Bohemians, his brother Conrad, Duke Frederick, Duke Lutold, Count Palatine Rapoto, and all who had assembled there.

Its boundaries toward the west are as follows: Tugost [the mountain range called Fichtelgebirge], which extends to the middle of the river Chub [the Eger]; Zelza; Zedlica [the Elbogen district]; Liusena; Dasena [the Tetschen district]; Lutomerici [Leitmeritz]; and Lemuzi, as far as the middle of the forest by which Bohemia is bounded.

The manuscripts give the following variants: Tugost, Tugast, Iugast, Tugozc, and Cugast; *quae* (“which,” feminine) instead of *qui* (“which,” masculine); Zelza is absent in some witnesses; Zedlica also appears as Zedlea and Zedlicane, and is omitted in others. The editor remarks that Zelza and Zedlica may be variant readings of a single name. Liusena is also read as Luisena, Lucsane, and Luczko; learned men thought it might be the place called Luczane or Luczko, frequently mentioned by Cosmas—that is, the royal city of Saaz—but the identification is left undecided. Dasena is also read Dacane, Decane, and Daciane; the editor identifies it tentatively with the Tetschen district, while Dobner wondered whether the name preferred by the duke was the ancient Daxan, situated between Saaz and Leitmeritz. Lemuzi is also read Lemuci; its identity is uncertain, and the editor doubts whether Dobner rightly found the district of Zittau here.

Toward the north its boundaries are: Psovane; Ghrvvati; and another Chrowati [Chrowatia]; Slasane [Silesia as far as Mount Zobten]; Trebowane; Bobrane [the region along the river Bober]; Dedosane [between the Oder and the Bober]; as far as the middle of the forest where the boundaries of the Milciani [in Upper Lusatia] meet.

The witnesses read Psovane or Psovuane; Ghrvvati also appears as Chrowati, Chowati, and Crouati; the second Chrowati is absent from one witness and appears as Hrouati in another. Slasane is also read Zlasane. Trebowane appears as Trebouane and Trewobane. Dobner thought it referred to the territory of Görlitz; he believed the name Trebowane concealed Drenow, mentioned in Cosmas under the year 1131, though the editor doubts that this can stand. Kropf identified it with Triebel in Lower Lusatia. Bobrane is also read Boborane and Poborane. Dedosane appears as Dedosese, Dedossene, and Dedosesi; the editor identifies the district as lying between the Oder and the Bober and compares Thietmar IV.28.

Thence, toward the east, it has these rivers as boundaries: namely Bug [Bug] and Ztir [Styr, which flows into the Bipetz], together with the city of Cracow and the province called Vag, with all the districts belonging to the aforesaid city, which is Cracow. Thence, with the borders of the Hungarians added, it extends as far as the mountains called Tritri [the Carpathian mountains, the Tatra].

The witnesses give Bug also as Buo, and Ztir also as Ztiz and Zur. Cracova appears as Krakova, Krakovia, Krakoua, Cracoua, and Chracoua; the city is also called Krakow. Ungarorum is also transmitted as Ungariorum. Tritri is read Tatri in one witness; the name occurs frequently in Długosz and refers to the Carpathian, or Tatra, mountains.

Then, on the side looking south, with the region of Moravia added as far as the river called Wag, and the middle of the forest called Moure [Matra], and of that same mountain, the same diocese extends where Bavaria is bounded.

Moure is transmitted in various forms: Md’re, which may be read Mudre; More; Mderre; and Mure. The note identifies it as the Matra. One witness reads *ejus* (“of that same”) rather than *ejusdem*.

[In manuscript 5 the following occurs here: “But whoever wishes to know better how this diocese was enlarged and confirmed should seek it in the privilege of that same church.” The remainder is lacking.]

Accordingly, through our mediation and with the common concurrence of the princes, it was done that Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia, and his brother Conrad should wholly acknowledge again and restore to the aforesaid bishop of Prague, their brother, the diocese claimed in due judicial order.

Therefore, reasonably moved by the petition of that bishop, we confirm and establish by the decree of our imperial authority the restoration of the bishopric of Prague for him and his successors, decreeing inviolably that henceforth no person of whatsoever condition, nor any association of men, shall presume to alienate from the church of Prague anything of its right within the aforementioned boundaries.

So that the authority of this restoration and confirmation may remain firm and unshaken for all ages, we have ordered this charter to be drawn up and, as appears below, to be marked with the impression of our sign, which we have laboured to ratify with our own hand.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of May [29 April], in the year 1086 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the ninth indiction, in the thirty-second year indeed of Lord Henry’s reign and the third of his empire.

The sign of Lord Henry the Third, August Emperor of the Romans.

[In place of the monogram is an empty circle drawn in yellow. The lines of the monogram itself are drawn alternately in black, yellow, and red. A.]

[Col. 0172A] I myself saw the emperor mark this with his own hands in the privilege of the bishopric of Prague.

### 38

Likewise in the same year, at the command of Emperor Henry and through the intervention of Wezlo, archbishop of Mainz, Pope Clement, through the legates of the Apostolic See who had attended that council, confirmed by his privilege the bishopric of Prague according to the boundaries stated above. This was requested and represented by Bishop Gebhard through his chaplain named Albin, whom he had sent from Mainz to Rome with the legates of the Apostolic See concerning this same matter.

In the same year, on the fifth day before the Ides of June [9 June; one witness reads July], Otto, duke of Moravia, brother of Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia, died. The Bohemian necrology confirms this date.

Meanwhile Egilbert, archbishop of Trier, obeying the emperor’s commands, came to the metropolitan city of Prague and, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June], amid the solemn rites of Mass, anointed Wratislaus—clothed in royal robes—as king. He placed the diadem upon the head both of Wratislaus himself and of his wife Svatava, clad in a royal mantle, while the clergy and all the magnates cried out three times:

> “To Wratislaus, king both of Bohemia and of Poland, glorious and peaceable, crowned by God: life, health, and victory!”

The manuscripts vary in the name Svatava, which also appears as Suatava, Zuathava, and Zuatawa. One witness ends after “victory”; another reads “praise” instead of “health and victory.”

He is called king “of Poland” because a portion of Poland beyond the Oder, namely Silesia, was under Wratislaus’s power. In Wratislaus’s charter concerning the foundation of the church of Vyšehrad, dated 1088 and printed in Boczek I, 183, occur these words: “The confirmation also of Lord Egilbert, archbishop of Trier, from whom I likewise received the anointing of royal consecration.”

Three days afterwards, the archbishop, enriched according to royal magnificence with an immense weight of gold and silver and endowed with other gifts and presents, returned joyfully and with great honour to his own country.

### 39

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1087, King Wratislaus, having collected an army, entered Zribia [the March of Meissen], which Emperor Henry had formerly granted him to possess in perpetuity. While he was rebuilding near the city of Meissen a certain castle called Gvozdek [Guoz-Burzward in the district of Nisan], he sent two detachments of chosen soldiers, under his son Břetislav, to avenge an injury formerly inflicted upon him, while the others continued their work.

The note explains that Zribia was the March of Meissen, which Henry had taken from Margrave Eckbert in 1076, as Lambert records, and had entrusted to Wratislaus because of his proven loyalty. Gvozdek is identified as Guoz, Burzward’s stronghold in the district of Nisan. See also Pelzel’s essay, “On the Rule of the Bohemians in Meissen,” in the *Abhandlungen der Böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften* (1787), p. 39. The manuscripts read Zribiam or Zrbiam; Gvozdek also appears as Guozdec and Gnozdec; Meissen is transmitted as Missen, Misen, Misnam, and Missn.

For some time before, as he was returning from the emperor’s court, it happened by chance that he spent the night in a very large village called Kileb. There, when a disturbance arose at night between his men and the townspeople, two brothers were killed by the villagers: Nacarat and Bznata, sons of Count Taz, foremost among the nobles, mighty pillars of this country, illustrious in the light of their virtues.

Nacarat is also read Nakarat and Nacharat; Bznata appears as Wznata; Taz as Iaz, Thaz, and other forms. The witnesses vary between *lumine* (“in the light”) and *nomine* (“in the name”).

Those who had been sent hastened by day and night according to the king’s command. On the third day, at first light, they attacked the aforesaid village with great force, plundered all their possessions, stripped them and their wives even to the strap of their shoes, utterly overthrew the buildings by burning them with fire, and, driving off horses and livestock together, made their way back unhurt.

When noon had come and they were crossing a river, the lord’s son, finding pleasant places along the river, ordered the shield-bearers to go on ahead with the plunder, while he invited the men stronger in battle to take a meal there with him. Since the heat was great, the duke’s son, burning with excessive warmth, refreshed himself for a short time after the meal by swimming in the water. Then Count Alexius sent him this message:

> “You are not swimming here in your Vltava or your Ohře. Stop delaying; carry off the treasures of brave men.”

The manuscripts vary in the forms of Vltava and Ohře; one omits *in* before Ohře. The words “Stop delaying” are from Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.281.

The young man replied: “It is natural for old men always to tremble at a breath of wind, and, though their destinies are already impending, to fear them more than young men do.”

When this was reported to Alexius, he said:

> “May God grant it; but may there now be such a favourable and inescapable opportunity of fortune that young men may see whether old men or they themselves fear fate more.”

While the aforesaid count was saying this, behold: more than twenty horsemen sent by the Saxons appeared, in order to provoke them with a *cimbellum* [a little bell or taunting signal; the reading is uncertain], just as a weasel, wishing to strangle its enemy the asp, entices it from its hole by the shadow of its tail.

The manuscripts read *cimbello*, *cimpello*, *cum bello* (“with battle”), *cum dolo* (“with deceit”), and *cymbello*. The printed reading *cimbello* is retained.

When our men saw them—rash men, more bold than discerning—they rushed to their doom in pursuit of the enemy, although Alexius vehemently opposed, forbade, and recalled them.

For at once the iron legion of the Saxons leapt forth from ambush, and not one of our men who had pursued the enemy escaped. But when those remaining in the camp saw a cloud of dust rising to heaven as though in a whirlwind, although sudden and unexpected reverses commonly disturb even the bravest warriors in battle, they nevertheless seized their arms as quickly as possible, received the enemy manfully, and a battle was joined with utmost force. The crash of arms and the shouting of men rose to the clouds; spears were broken in the first encounter; the matter was decided by swords, until, God bringing aid, the Saxons were turned to flight. Our men won the victory, but one too bloody.

The phrases “the crash of arms” and “rose to the clouds” echo Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.569, and Virgil, *Aeneid* II.313. One witness reads *turbare* (“to disturb”) instead of *turbare soleant*; another has *quanto citius* (“as quickly as possible”) rather than *quam cicius*. One manuscript first read *corripiunt* (“seize”) and later corrected it to *arripiunt* (“snatch up”). The reading concerning God’s aid is transmitted with the phrase *ferente* (“bringing”) supplied by correction; another marginal reading gives *Boemis* (“to the Bohemians”).

Since the soldiers of the second rank had already gone on with the plunder, only nobles perished in this battle: Count Alexius; his son-in-law Ratibor; Branis with his brother Zlava; and very many others. Count Preda, having lost a foot, barely escaped death. The duke’s son was wounded beneath his right thumb; and unless the hilt of the sword which he held in his hand had checked the blow, he would have lost the whole hand. This slaughter took place on the sixth day before the Nones of July [2 July].

Branis is also read Bravis and Bratus. One witness omits “his son-in-law” after Ratibor.

### 40

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1088.

> In these same times occurred the deeds here related.  
> There was a certain knight named Beneda,  
> A great-souled young man, of such outstanding bodily form  
> As handsome Hector or Turnus in arms.  
> Born of Jurata, whose first ancestor was Taz.

The year-number is joined to this chapter in some witnesses. The note indicates that a large initial *H* is written in the manuscript.

For some reason, King Wratislaus too had then been angered with him. Fleeing into Poland, Beneda became a knight of Lady Judith, wife of Duke Wladislaus. When two years had passed, he returned from Poland and approached Wigbert, the king’s son-in-law, asking that through Wigbert’s support he might return to his lord’s former favour.

Judith had died in 1085; see above II.35. The note compares II.20 and refers to the *Life of Wipert*, chapter 2, in Hofmann’s *Scriptores rerum Lusaticarum*, for the circumstances that brought Margrave Wipert to Bohemia. The manuscripts read Jurata also as Iurzata; Taz as Iaz and Thaz. One witness omits *rogans* (“asking”).

But Wigbert was a man of very sound judgment and did not wish to offend his father-in-law in anything. He advised Beneda to remain meanwhile more safely with the bishop of Meissen, named Benno, and likewise to procure him as an intercessor.

Benno was restored to his see in 1088. The manuscripts vary between *tutius* (“more safely”) and *tutus* (“safe”), and one reverses the order of *sibi similiter* (“likewise for himself”).

Meanwhile it happened that King Wratislaus again entered Zribia with his army, in order to transfer the aforesaid castle Gvozdek to another, stronger site. Learning that Beneda was in the city of Meissen, the king sent for him to come under a pledge of good faith.

When the king saw him arrive, he began to consider how he might ensnare him by deceit. After many words, spoken indiscriminately, and certain things plausibly feigned, the king deceitfully took him by the right hand and led him apart beyond the camp, as though to speak secrets there.

Then, seeing the golden hilt and pommel of the sword with which the knight was girded, he asked him in the course of their conversation how much his sword was worth.

Beneda replied: “If you put a millstone upon a helmet, with this sword I shall cut both together, head and body down to the thigh, in one stroke.”

The king marvelled deceitfully, praised the sword, and asked him to show it to him. Suspecting no evil, Beneda gave the king the sword drawn from its sheath. The king seized it, brandished it in his hand, and said:

> “What do you say now, son of a woman who attacks a man unprovoked?”

Then he said to the chamberlain standing with him—the only person there besides him—a man worse than the worst, Vít Seliboríc:

> “Seize him! Seize the exalted man and bind him on all fours!”

The manuscripts vary in the name Vít Seliboríc, including Vseborio. One group omits the passage beginning “the king seized it” through “brandished it,” though a later hand supplied it in the margin.

But because boldness is never safe in dealings with bold men, the bold knight at once seized by its hilt the sword from the chamberlain’s thigh, cut his loins through the middle, and left him kicking upon the ground half alive.

Nor did the fierce knight flee, though he could have escaped; rather, like Hercules leaping and recoiling about the Lernaean hydra:

> Three times he slightly wounds the vile king with his sword;  
> Yet he himself receives no blow from the duke’s right hand,

until, at the outcry, men rushed from the camp.

But Cucata was the first of all to fly to the scene, and, as though receiving a wild boar charging upon him, he received the knight on a broad hunting-spear. Then King Wratislaus, as though he could take vengeance upon a dead man, ordered him bound by the feet to a horse’s tail and dragged this way and that through thorns.

### 41

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1089.

[“The establishment of the church of Vyšehrad,” manuscripts 2a and 2b.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1090, that ancient *chelidrus*—the serpent-like monster and enemy of humankind—who never slumbers but always disturbs the peaceful,

> Could no longer endure that the brothers should live at peace—  
> Namely King Wratislaus and Bishop Gebhard.

Vain glory and ambition tormented the latter; arrogance and the swollen pride of haughtiness agitated the former. Yet neither would yield to the other, nor could either overcome the other. The one did not wish to have his brother as an equal; the other did not wish to be regarded as less than his brother. The one wished to rule over; the other did not wish to be subject. The one wished, as if king, to dominate and surpass; the other refused to obey his commands, but professed his service to the emperor alone, from whom he had received the bishopric.

The manuscripts vary between *episcopium* (“bishopric”) and *episcopatum* (“bishopric”). The passage beginning “the one did not wish” appears to have been written by another hand in one witness.

They sometimes differed with such manly spirit that the king often had no bishop to place the crown upon him on feast-days. Driven both by this necessity and by ambition, the king, not by lawful process but solely by his own dominion, again installed his chaplain named Wezlo as bishop in the territory of Moravia.

A note observes that this schism had already occurred in 1088, as is proved by the privilege of the church of Vyšehrad, confirmed by Jaromir, bishop of Prague, and Vecelo, bishop of Olomouc. It suggests that the act arose because King Wratislaus had abandoned the party of Pope Clement and gone over to Urban II.

By this act he plainly made himself notorious: he had not only disregarded what he himself had approved before the emperor and his bishops—that the two bishoprics should be one—but had also violated the privilege of Pope Clement, by which he had confirmed the boundaries of that bishopric.

Bishop Gebhard intended to complain before the Apostolic See of this injustice inflicted upon the Church. He was about to go to Rome, but, after taking counsel with his household, first visited his old friend Wladislaus, king of Pannonia. Revealing to him the injury done to his church, he requested aid for the journey to Rome.

The manuscripts vary between *damnum* (“loss”) and *injuriam* (“injury”), and some preserve both.

> Alas, unaware that his own imminent fate was already close at hand.

For on the first day on which he visited the king he fell into grievous bodily illness. Since he was near the city of Esztergom, the king sent him there by ship, entrusting his care to the bishop of that city.

> Alas, what sufferings he endured through six days!  
> Tears impede me, and I cannot utter them in words.  
> On the seventh day, as evening was already falling,  
> When the July sun touches the sixth day before the Kalends [26 June],  
> The jewel of priests, the light of all Bohemians,  
> Gebhard, the pious bishop, renowned for learning,  
> Departed from this world, that he might live in Christ.

The Bohemian necrology agrees with this account; the catalogue of the bishops of Olomouc gives the tenth day before the Kalends of July. Palacký assigned Gebhard’s death to 1089. The manuscripts vary between *advesperascente* (“as evening was falling”) and *advesperante* (“as evening approached”). One witness reads “words” rather than “sayings” in the second line.

> Of whose character and life my mind desires to say much,  
> But feeling fails within my breast.  
> Yet I gladly speak these few things which I myself have seen.

### 42

During Lent this was his custom. Always wearing haircloth beneath and episcopal clothing above, by day he presented himself to human eyes; but at night, clothed in a sack, he secretly entered the church and, prostrate on the pavement, persevered in prayer until the ground on which he lay was wet from a copious rain of tears.

Then he rose to make an *agape*—that is, to provide alms for the poor. Before he began to recite the psalms, he abundantly relieved, by good works, the need of all wretches whom he found before the church; when the Psalter was completed, he did the same.

After matins he distributed among the poor forty quarter-loaves of bread and as many herrings, or portions of some other food.

When daylight was approaching for the fourth time, he washed the feet of twelve pilgrims, according to the number of the apostles:

> To these he distributes twice six coins of denarii.

Having placed them until the hour of dinner in a private room or hut, he himself set before them necessities in abundance and blessed their food and drink with his own right hand. Then he went to the public table and fed forty needy persons with himself.

One manuscript reads *missam* (“Mass”) rather than *mensam* (“table”).

Likewise, at his see in Prague he established that forty poor persons should be fed every day and clothed twice each year, from the strap of the shoe to the fastening of the cap. The note explains that *mastiga* means the clasp or buckle of the cap.

He also bound certain visiting guests and poor clerics by very generous gifts, on condition that, remaining with him throughout Lent, they should read through psalters both for the living and for the dead.

At each and every solemn celebration of Mass held daily in the chapel, he caused three sums of denarii to be given.

On every Sunday he offered twelve silver coins upon the pyx of holy relics; on feasts of the apostles and other greater solemnities, two hundred.

If, wise reader, you wish to know how generous he was, he never wore an episcopal fur garment for an entire year, but gave one winter garment to his chaplains at Easter and another, a summer garment, on the feast of Saint Wenceslaus. Know that he was equally generous in his other gifts.

After his death, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1091, on the fourth day before the Nones of March [4 March], Cosmas was chosen bishop by King Wratislaus and by all the clergy and people of the Bohemians, while Henry the Third, the August Emperor, was reigning but was then occupied with imperial affairs in Lombardy.

## Complete textual, geographical, and historical apparatus

The following register translates all 255 canonical apparatus notes in source order. Exact source forms are retained because spelling, grammar, and word order often cannot be distinguished in English alone.

1. **Source note:** `[Col. 0167] et individuae desunt A.` **Translation and direction:** A omits *et individuae*, “and indivisible,” from the Trinitarian invocation.
2. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] al. man superscr. A.` **Translation and direction:** Another hand added a reading above the line in A at *novimus*, “we know”; the letters are not supplied.
3. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] dignitatibus 2.` **Translation and direction:** MS 2 reads *dignitatibus*, “dignities,” for *utilitatibus*, “needs/benefits.”
4. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] dampnabiles injurias 4, 4a` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a read *dampnabiles injurias*, “condemnable injuries,” for *dampna vel injurias*, “losses or injuries.”
5. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] quiapropter 1.` **Translation and direction:** MS 1 spells *quiapropter* for *Quapropter*, “therefore.”
6. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] deest 4.` **Translation and direction:** MS 4 omits *universis*, “to all.”
7. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] cum fratribus 4. 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a read *cum fratribus*, “with brothers,” for *confratribus*, “fellow bishops/brothers.”
8. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] per totum desunt 7.` **Translation and direction:** MS 7 omits *per totum*, “throughout the whole.”
9. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] ducatuum 7.` **Translation and direction:** MS 7 reads plural *ducatuum*, “duchies,” for singular *ducatum*, “duchy.”
10. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Sigevino 2. Sicevino 2b.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2 and 2b spell the name *Sigevino* and *Sicevino* for text *Sigewino*.
11. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Lyemaro 4. 4a` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a spell *Lyemaro* for *Liemaro*.
12. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Tietrico 1. Liederico 3, Theoderico 4. Thyederico 4a.` **Translation and direction:** The witnesses spell Bishop Tiedric’s name *Tietrico* (1), *Liederico* (3), *Theoderico* (4), and *Thyederico* (4a).
13. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Cunrado 4, Cuuonrado 7.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 7 spell Chounrad *Cunrado* and *Cuuonrado*.
14. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Ovdaldrico 1. Ovdalrico 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 1 and 4a spell Oudalric *Ovdaldrico* and *Ovdalrico*.
15. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Cistetensi A. Heysthetensi 4. 4a` **Translation and direction:** A reads *Cistetensi* and MSS 4 and 4a *Heysthetensi* for *Eistetensi*, “of Eichstätt.”
16. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Ch. ducis, 1.` **Translation and direction:** MS 1 abbreviates “Chounrad, duke” as *Ch. ducis*.
17. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] al. man. in margine 1. adscriptum.` **Translation and direction:** In MS 1 another hand added a reading in the margin at *Friderici*, “Frederick”; the text is not supplied.
18. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Lutholdi 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a spell Duke Lutold’s name *Lutholdi*.
19. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Rapothonis 1, 2b, 4, 4a, 7. Rapotae 3.` **Translation and direction:** Rapoto’s name appears as *Rapothonis* in 1, 2b, 4, 4a, and 7, and *Rapotae* in 3.
20. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] De geographica hac descriptione Pragensis episcopatus vid. Dobner ad Hajec. IV, 217---229; Palacky I, 227.` **Translation and direction:** For this geographical description of the Prague bishopric, see Dobner on Hájek IV, 217–229, and Palacký I, 227.
21. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Tugast 1, 2, 2b, Iugast 3, Tugozc 4, 4a, Cugast 7.` **Translation and direction:** Tugost is spelled *Tugast* in 1, 2, 2b; *Iugast* in 3; *Tugozc* in 4, 4a; and *Cugast* in 7.
22. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Est saltus, qui vocatur Fichtelgebirge.` **Translation and direction:** Tugost is the forest called the Fichtelgebirge.
23. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] quae 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 4a, 7.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 4a, and 7 read feminine *quae*, “which,” for masculine *qui*.
24. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Eger.` **Translation and direction:** The river Chub is the Eger.
25. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] deest A. 3, Zeyza 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** A and 3 omit *Zelza*; MSS 4 and 4a read *Zeyza*.
26. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Dobner in hoc nomine fines episcopatus Citicensis sibi deprehendisse videbatur. Kropf in commentatione supra laudata regionem Pilsenensem.` **Translation and direction:** Dobner thought the name marked the boundary of the diocese of Zeitz; Kropf instead identified the Plzeň region.
27. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Zedlea 3, Zedlicane 4, 4a. Omissum 2a 7. Videnturque haec duo nomina Zelza et Zedlica unius vocis lectiones variantes esse DOBR.` **Translation and direction:** MS 3 reads *Zedlea*; 4 and 4a *Zedlicane*; 2a and 7 omit the name. Dobrovský thought Zelza and Zedlica were variant readings of one name.
28. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Elbogensis circulus.` **Translation and direction:** Zedlica is the Elbogen district.
29. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] In 2, legi potest Liusena et Luisena. Luisena 2b. Liusena 3, 7. Lucsane omisso et 4, 4a` **Translation and direction:** In 2 the name may be read *Liusena* or *Luisena*; 2b reads *Luisena*; 3 and 7 *Liusena*; 4 and 4a *Lucsane* and omit *et*, “and.”
30. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Idem esse videbatur viris doctis, quod Luczane vel Luczko, cujus saepius mentionem fecit Cosmas, i. e. Satecensis regia, quod ego in medio relinquo.` **Translation and direction:** Scholars thought this the same as Luczane or Luczko, often mentioned by Cosmas, namely the Žatec region; the editor leaves the question open.
31. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] ita A. 1, 2, 2b, 3, 7. add. 1. Dacane, Decane 2, In 2b corrector in margine adnotavit: aliter Dacane. Daciane 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** A, 1, 2, 2b, 3, and 7 read *Dasena*; MS 1 adds a reading; 2 has *Dacane, Decane*; a corrector in 2b notes “otherwise Dacane”; 4 and 4a read *Daciane*.
32. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Tetschenensis circulus; Dobner dubitavit num praeferat dux, quod veteribus erat Daxan, medio inter Satecium et Lutomericium situm.` **Translation and direction:** This is the Děčín district. Dobner doubted whether to prefer a form connected with ancient Daxan, between Žatec and Litoměřice.
33. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Liutomerici 2, 3, 7. Luthomirici 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2, 3, and 7 read *Liutomerici*; 4 and 4a *Luthomirici* for *Lutomerici*.
34. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Leitmeritz.` **Translation and direction:** Lutomerici is Leitmeritz/Litoměřice.
35. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Lemuci 4.` **Translation and direction:** MS 4 reads *Lemuci* for *Lemuzi*.
36. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169C] Quid sit, incertum est; Dobner num jure Zittaviensem regionem hic repererit dubito` **Translation and direction:** The identification is uncertain; the editor doubts Dobner’s identification with the Zittau region.
37. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] aquilonem 3, 4, 4a, 7` **Translation and direction:** MSS 3, 4, 4a, and 7 read *aquilonem*, “the north,” for adjectival *aquilonalem*, “northern.”
38. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Psovuane 2.` **Translation and direction:** MS 2 spells *Psovuane* for *Psovane*.
39. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Num eadem regio de qua supra I, 15?` **Translation and direction:** The editor asks whether this is the same region mentioned above at I.15.
40. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Chrowati 1, 2b. Chowati 3, Crouati 4. Chowati 7.` **Translation and direction:** Ghrvvati is spelled *Chrowati* in 1 and 2b, *Chowati* in 3 and 7, and *Crouati* in 4.
41. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] deest A. 1, Chrowati 2, 4, 4a. Hrouati 3.` **Translation and direction:** A and 1 omit *et altera Chrowati*, “and the other Croatia”; 2, 4, 4a read *Chrowati*, and 3 *Hrouati*.
42. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Chrowatia.` **Translation and direction:** The place is Croatia/Chrowatia.
43. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Zlasane 1, 2, 4.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 1, 2, and 4 spell *Zlasane* for *Slasane*.
44. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Silesia ad montem Zobten.` **Translation and direction:** Slasane is Silesia near Mount Zobten.
45. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Trebouane 2, 3, 4, 4a. Trewobane 7.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2, 3, 4, and 4a read *Trebouane*; MS 7 *Trewobane* for *Trebowane*.
46. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Dobnero videbatur territorium Goerlicense. In nomine Trebouane latere opinabatur Drenow de quo contin. Cosmae ad 1131; quod num stare possit dubito. Kropfio est Triebel in Lusatia inferiori.` **Translation and direction:** Dobner identified the Görlitz territory and thought *Trebouane* concealed Drenow, mentioned under 1131, though the editor doubts it; Kropf identified Triebel in Lower Lusatia.
47. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Boborane 1. Boborane 2, 2b, 4, 4a, 7. Poborane 3.` **Translation and direction:** Bobrane is spelled *Boborane* in 1, 2, 2b, 4, 4a, 7 and *Poborane* in 3.
48. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Regio ad fluvium Bober.` **Translation and direction:** Bobrane is the region on the Bober River.
49. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Dedosese 1, 2, 2b Dedossene 3, Dedosesi 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** Dedosane is spelled *Dedosese* in 1, 2, 2b; *Dedossene* in 3; *Dedosesi* in 4, 4a.
50. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Inter Oderam et Boberam; cfr. Thietmar IV, 28.` **Translation and direction:** Dedosane lies between the Oder and Bober; compare Thietmar IV.28.
51. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Milcanorum 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a read *Milcanorum* for *Milcianorum*, “of the Milciani.”
52. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] In Lusatia superiori; cfr. Thietmar. I, 9.` **Translation and direction:** The Milciani were in Upper Lusatia; compare Thietmar I.9.
53. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Buo 7.` **Translation and direction:** MS 7 reads *Buo* for the river *Bug*.
54. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Bug.` **Translation and direction:** The river is the Bug.
55. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] feliciter 1.` **Translation and direction:** MS 1 reads *feliciter*, “happily,” for *scilicet*, “namely.”
56. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Ztiz 2b. Zur 4a` **Translation and direction:** MS 2b reads *Ztiz* and 4a *Zur* for *Ztir*.
57. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Styr qui in fluvium Bipetz exundat.` **Translation and direction:** This is the Styr, which flows into the Bipetz.
58. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Krakova 1. Krakovia 2. Krakoua 2b. 7, Cracoua 3. Chracoua 4a.` **Translation and direction:** Cracow is spelled *Krakova* in 1, *Krakovia* in 2, *Krakoua* in 2b and 7, *Cracoua* in 3, and *Chracoua* in 4a.
59. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] ita A. Wag rell.` **Translation and direction:** A reads *Vag*; all remaining witnesses read *Wag*, the region’s name.
60. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Krakow 2, 2b, 3.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2, 2b, and 3 spell Cracow *Krakow*.
61. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Ungariorum 4, 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 4 and 4a read *Ungariorum* for *Ungarorum*, “of the Hungarians.”
62. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] Tatri 2a` **Translation and direction:** MS 2a reads *Tatri* for *Tritri*.
63. **Source note:** `[Col. 0170C] Apud Dlugossum saepius occurrens; montes Karpathici, Tatra.` **Translation and direction:** Długosz frequently mentions these mountains: the Carpathians, or Tatra.
64. **Source note:** `[Col. 0169] dilata 4a.` **Translation and direction:** MS 4a reads *dilata*, “spread out,” for *dilatata*, “extended.”
65. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171] Md're signo contractionis apposito super d. 2, ita ut Md're legi possit Mudre. More 2a. Mderre 2b. Mure 4, 4a. More 7.` **Translation and direction:** MS 2 writes abbreviated *Md're*, with a contraction sign above *d*, possibly *Mudre*; 2a and 7 read *More*, 2b *Mderre*, 4 and 4a *Mure*.
66. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171D] Matra.` **Translation and direction:** The mountain is the Mátra.
67. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171] ejus A. More` **Translation and direction:** A reads *ejus*, “of it,” for *ejusdem*, “of the same,” before “mountain”; the note also prints *More*.
68. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171] limitatur 2, 4. Hoc loco sequuntur in 5. Qualiter autem hec parochia dilatata fuerit et confirmata, qui vult melius scire, querat in privilegio ejusdem ecclesie. Reliqua desunt.` **Translation and direction:** MSS 2 and 4 read *limitatur*, “is bounded,” for *liminatur*, same sense. MS 5 then adds: “But whoever wishes to know better how this diocese was enlarged and confirmed should seek it in the privilege of that church”; the remainder is absent from 5.
69. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171] per erasum factum A, per factum 1, pactum 3, factum 4, 4a, 7.` **Translation and direction:** In A *per* was erased before *factum*; MS 1 reads *per factum*, “through the deed,” MS 3 *pactum*, “agreement,” and 4, 4a, 7 *factum*, “it was done.”
70. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171D] Difficultas, quae inde nascitur quod Wratislaus paulo ante regis nomine salutatus hoc in diplomate dux nominatur, Dobnero V, 517 ita solvi posse videbatur, ut diceret hoc factum esse ob Clementis papae reverentiam, qui nondum regalem Wratislai titulum agnoerat. Idem testatur diplomati fundationis Wissehradensis duplicem sigillum appensum esse, in quorum altero Wratislaus sex, in altero dux appelletur.` **Translation and direction:** Dobner V, 517 explained the difficulty that the charter calls Wratislaus “duke” soon after he was acclaimed king as deference to Pope Clement, who had not recognized his royal title. Dobner also says the Vyšehrad foundation charter bore two seals, calling him king on one and duke on the other.

107. **Source note:** `[Col. 0171D] Ita nominatur quia pars Poloniae Oderanae i. e. Silesiae in potestate erat Wratislai. In Wratislai [Col. 0172D] praecepto de fundatione ecclesiae Wissehradensis a 1088 apud Boczek 1, 183 haec leguntur verba: (Confirmatio) domini etiam Egilberti Trevirensis archiepiscopi a quo simul et unctionem regalis consecrationis accepi.` **Translation and direction:** He is called Polish because Wratislaus controlled the Oder part of Poland, Silesia. Wratislaus’s 1088 Vyšehrad foundation charter in Boczek I, 183 records confirmation by Egilbert of Trier, from whom he received royal anointing.

### 43.

In the same year, on 17 April, the fourth weekday in the second week of Easter, the monastery of the holy martyrs Vitus, Wenceslaus, and Adalbert in the city of Prague was burned.

> [Note: “[In the same year—Prague” is written in the lower margin of A.]  
> [Note: These chronological indications were observed by Palacký I, 321 not to agree with one another; he therefore thought that the number XV before *Kalends of May* should be deleted, that the fire of St Vitus should be assigned to the preceding year, and likewise what follows concerning Wratislaus’s Moravian war. In the Prague annals the fire of St Vitus is recorded under the year 1091.]  
> [Note: “monastery” at this point in A.]

In the same year King Wratislaus was greatly angered against his brother Conrad, because, mindful of their mutual affection, Conrad supported the party of the sons of his brother Otto—namely Svatopluk and Ottík.

> [Note: 4 and 4a insert “15 Kalends of May.”]  
> [Note: Omitted in A.]  
> [Note: “party”: *pati* 1.]  
> [Note: *Zuatoplik* A; *Zvatoplivc* 1; *Zuatoplik* 2.]  
> [Note: Omitted in 4.]  
> [Note: *Otic* 2; *Otik* 2b; *Ortik* 3.]  
> [Note: A third son, Bretislaus, must be added to these, as is clear from a certain donation made by their mother Euphemia to the monasteries of Hradisko and Rajhrad for the soul of Otto on the day of the burial of her dearest husband. The chronological particulars are absent. Boczek I, 176.]

After they had been expelled from their paternal inheritance, the king had entrusted to his son Boleslaus the city of Olomouc and other towns; not long afterwards, in that same city, Boleslaus was overtaken by untimely death on 11 August.

> [Note: The monk Hildegard of Hradisko, in Boczek I, 185, testifies that Boleslaus, the king’s son, had already died in 1089. For the monks’ consolatory letters addressed to Wratislaus, see ibid., pp. 184–185.]

And because those three brothers—Jaromír, Otto, and Conrad—were, so long as they lived, so united in mind that the king could not divide them by any devices—just as, it is said, a lion feared three young bulls standing with their horns joined together—he had never dared to attack his brothers. But when, after his brothers’ deaths, he saw Conrad alone, deprived on every side of fraternal support, he entered Moravia with an army, intending likewise to drive him from the province which had fallen to Conrad by paternal inheritance, by lot and by the cord of inheritance, and by rightful grant.

> [Note: “These”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “namely” omitted in 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “and” omitted by A, 3, and 4.]  
> [Note: A reads “the king could divide them.”]  
> [Note: A reads “his brothers.”]  
> [Note: *aut* A; *ac* supplied above the line in another hand.]  
> [Note: Corrected in 1.]

They came to the city named Brno.

> [Note: *Brinen* 1; *Bruno* 2; *Brynen* 2b; *Bruen* 3; *Brneu* 4; *Brnen* in an erasure in 4a.]  
> [Note: Brünn.]

There, while the king was arranging the siege in a circuit, with the magnates of the land standing round him, and assigning the places where each count should pitch his tents, Zderad the steward—a deceitful man as he was—gave the king a sidelong signal with his eyes and marked out young Bretislaus, who was standing among the nobles before his father, with the charcoal mark of disgrace. “For,” he said, “your son, lord king, gladly plays in the river and swims in summer. If it please your Majesty, let him place his tents with his men by the river on this side of the city.”

> [Note: “standing around”: 3.]  
> [Note: “chief men”: 3.]  
> [Note: *Zderad* 1, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “with a black mark”: *elogio* A, 2, 2b, 3; *elogio vel carbone* 1; *elogio carbone* 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “since”: *quandoquidem* 4a.]  
> [Note: The Svitava.]  

He said this because formerly, in Saxony, when the young man in question was swimming in a river at midday, enemies rushed upon him from the opposite side and attacked them, as we have related above.

> [Note: “because”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: Corrected in another ink in 1.]  
> [Note: II.39.]

This saying sank too deeply into the young man’s heart; he grieved no less than if a poisoned arrow had wounded his heart. He went sorrowfully to camp and took no food until the stars of night. But beneath the dark night, having summoned a troop of his own men, he disclosed the wounds of his heart and deliberated how he might take vengeance upon the wicked steward.

> [Note: “young man”: *juvens* 1.]  
> [Note: “to”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: Omitted in A.]  
> [Note: “of night” omitted in 4a.]  
> [Note: “in someone”: 4, 4a.]

That same night he secretly sent to his uncle Conrad, explaining the insult done to him and by whom it had been inflicted, and seeking his advice as to what ought to be done. Conrad replied: “If you recognize who you are, do not fear to extinguish the fire that burns me no less than you; it is not honourable to disregard it.”

> [Note: “and … had been inflicted” are absent from A.]  
> [Note: 4a reads “extinguish.”]

For Conrad was not unaware that the king did all this at Zderad’s counsel. When the messenger had reported his uncle’s words to Bretislaus, all approved and assented, praising the duke’s judgement as though it had been given them by God, since they themselves had repeatedly advised this before.

> [Note: *itentidem* 2, 2b.]

Why say more? Throughout that whole night the deed was arranged which was accomplished in the morning.

### 41.

For at daybreak Bretislaus sent to the aforesaid steward, directing him to enter with him into a private consultation wherever he pleased. Suspecting no evil, the latter took Count Držimír; the two of them alone set out. When the young man saw them from afar, he sprang forward from his own men to meet them by the distance of a stone’s throw. For he had given his soldiers the sign that, when he threw his glove into the man’s bosom, they should do what they had promised to do.

> [Note: “to the aforesaid”: A corrects an omission; omitted in 1.]  
> [Note: “consultation”: 3.]  
> [Note: *Drysimir* 1; *Drsimir* 3; *Disimir* 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “only those two”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: Supplied above the line in A.]  
> [Note: A reads *prosilit*, “sprang.”]  
> [Note: A reads *ictus*, “stroke.”]  
> [Note: From “he sprang forward from his own men,” 4 and 4a read somewhat differently: “He withdrew from his soldiers, so that they might recognize the sign which he had promised to make.”]

After reproaching him briefly for the things by which he had often offended him, Bretislaus said: “The allegiance which I promised, behold, I renounce it to you.” Then, turning his horse, he threw his glove in the man’s face.

> [Note: “There”: A reads *Un*, in an erasure and another ink.]  
> [Note: “him”: A.]  
> [Note: *cyrotecam* 1, 4; *cyrothecam* 2, 4a.]

Just as an enraged lion raises its mane, lowers its tail, strikes its own brow with the knot at the tail’s end, and pricks its hindquarters with the sting beneath its tail, and is borne against everything that stands in its way, so immediately from the battle-line sprang the fiery armed youths Nozislav and his brother Držikraj, sons of Lubomír, and a third, Borša, son of Olen. They raised the vainly fleeing Zderad high in the air upon three spears, threw him to earth like a bundle, trampled him beneath their horses’ hooves, and again and again wounded him and pinned his body to the ground with missiles.

> [Note: “As soon as he had spurred himself with the lash of his savage tail / and raised his mane, the lion …” Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.208.]  
> [Note: “fighting”: *pugnens* 1.]  
> [Note: “breasts”: A; “his” added in 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: *Nozizlaw* 2, 4a; *Nozislaus* 3.]  
> [Note: *Drysimir* 1; *Dyrzkray* 2; *Drsikrai* 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “but”: 4.]  
> [Note: “fleeing”: 3.]  
> [Note: Omitted in 4, 4a.]

By such a death treacherous Fortune cast down her friend Zderad from the summit of her wheel, on 11 July.

Count Držimír, pale-faced, flew to the camp and reported to the king what had happened. The king alone mourned and wept; everyone praised the young man, though they did not dare praise him openly. Bretislaus, however, moved his camp separately a little more than one hill away; the greater part of the army, and the stronger in war, followed him.

> [Note: *Dyrzimir* 2; *Drismir* 2b; *Drsimir* 3; *Disimir* 4; *Drzimir* 4a.]  
> [Note: “report”: 1, with *n* cancelled.]  
> [Note: “to the king” omitted in A.]  
> [Note: 4, 4a add “Bretislaus.”]  
> [Note: 4, 4a add “and glorified.”]  
> [Note: A has *vis* supplied above the line.]  
> [Note: 1 reads “they praise.”]  
> [Note: 1 reads “will move.”]  
> [Note: “more fierce”: 2b.]  
> [Note: “in war” omitted in 3.]

### 45.

Meanwhile Conrad’s wife, named Wirpirk, one of the number of prudent women, came to the king’s camp without her husband’s knowledge.

> [Note: *Wirbirk* 3.]  
> [Note: Her name was Hilburg, as is clear from a charter of Duke Conrad: Boczek I, 188.]

When she was announced to the king, he summoned the nobles into an assembly; and, bidden to come, she stood before the king, her face profusely drenched with tears. At last, as sobs interrupted her speech, she forced her way into utterance and spoke thus:

> [Note: 4, 4a: “and ordered her to come. And she stood.”]  
> [Note: “poured forth”: 3.]  
> [Note: “face”: A, 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.64–65.]  
> [Note: 4, 4a add “saying.”]

> I am no longer worthy, gracious king, to be called your daughter-in-law;  
> Yet as a suppliant I have not rashly come to your knees.

> [Note: A originally had *aut*, corrected in another ink to *haud*, “not.”]  
> [Note: “gracious” omitted in 4.]  
> [Note: “nor”: 2b.]

And she fell upon her face and did homage to the king. Ordered to rise, she stood and said:

“My lord king, you will find in these regions no cause for war; from here you will bring back no victory from battle. You wage a war more than civil. But if you decree that we and our possessions shall be booty for your soldiers, you turn your own weapons against yourself when you despoil your brother—whose protector you ought to be—by bloody plunder.

> [Note: “none”: 4.]  
> [Note: “here”: 1.]  
> [Note: Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.1.]  
> [Note: “we and” omitted in 1.]  
> [Note: “ought”: *debebas* 3.]

“He who attacks his own goes against God. For whatever spoils you seek to possess here, far within your own borders, I shall show you richer ones situated in the midst of your kingdom. Nowhere will you be better enriched or made more splendid than in the suburb of Prague and the settlement of Vyšehrad. There are Jews most full of gold and silver; there are merchants of every nation, exceedingly rich; there are moneyers exceedingly wealthy; there is a market in which abundant booty overflows for your soldiers.

> [Note: “better” omitted in 1.]  
> [Note: *dicaberis*, corrected to *ditaberis*, “you will be enriched,” 1.]  
> [Note: “nor more splendid”: 4; omitted in 4a.]  
> [Note: *Uisegr.* 1; *Wissogradensi* 2.]  
> [Note: Corrected in A by another hand.]  
> [Note: “there” omitted in 4a.]

“Or, if you delight to see how Troy burned, nowhere will you see Vulcan rage more fiercely than when you see those two aforesaid cities burning. Yet you will say: ‘They are mine.’ And whose do you suppose are those things which you are devastating as an enemy? Are not we and ours yours? But if you sharpen only your thunderbolts against your brother’s throat, far be it that you should be accounted another Cain.

> [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* II.581.]  
> [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* V.662.]  
> [Note: “when” omitted in 3.]  
> [Note: *Cain* 1.]

“Saving your favour, Greece lies open to your brother, Dalmatia lies open; he would rather travel abroad than charge you with fratricide. Rather receive what he sends you, now not as a brother but as your servant.” And she drew from her bosom pincers and a bundle of twigs. “And if brother has sinned against brother,” she said, “correct him; but entrust the land, which is yours, to whom you prefer.”

> [Note: “your”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “as it were your” omitted in 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: *forpices* A.]  
> [Note: *exiquid* corrected above the line in 1.]  
> [Note: “she says” omitted in 4a.]  
> [Note: 1 adds “your.”]

She had spoken, and so touched the king’s heart and moved the hearts of the princes that no one could restrain himself from tears. The king ordered her to sit at his side. But before she sat down, she said: “Since I have found favour in your eyes, I ask yet one petition: I beg you, do not put me to shame. A little punishment is enough for a father for the great sin of his son.”

> [Note: A has *hos*, with *se* supplied above the line.]  
> [Note: 4 adds “Wiw.”]

Then the king said: “I know where you are going. But go on, rather, and bring my brother and my son to me all the more quickly, in a holy kiss and a bond of peace.” And he kissed her. For the king had greatly feared that his brother and son might conspire against him.

> [Note: 4, 4a omit “and my son”; 4 reads “and my son.”]  
> [Note: “to me” omitted in 1, 3.]  
> [Note: Omitted in 4.]  
> [Note: *ulde* 1.]

When, under Lady Wirpirk’s escort, they came to the king, he gave them the kiss of peace and said to his son: “My son, if you have done well, none will fare better than you; but if ill, your sin will lie at the door.”

> [Note: *convenissent*, corrected in another hand to *cum venissent*, 1.]  
> [Note: “under … Wirpirk” absent from A; *Wirpyrk* 1; *Wirbik* 3.]  
> [Note: The latter half of the saying is absent in 4, 4a.]

### 46.

After this Bretislaus, understanding that his father had made peace not from his heart but from necessity, withdrew with all those who had crossed over to his battle-line into the region of the city of Hradec. There he remained, vainly awaiting an uncertain turn of fortune.

> [Note: “city” omitted in 2.]  
> [Note: Königgrätz.]

For of all who had followed him, none dared revisit his own home, because they greatly feared the king whom they had offended, lest he seize them and either cast them into chains or condemn them to capital punishment. But when the king saw that he could not take vengeance upon his son or his followers as he wished, he summoned his brother Conrad, assembled the elder men of the land, and strengthened by the oath of all the counts the agreement that, after his death, his brother Conrad should possess the throne and duchy of Bohemia.

> [Note: “visit”: A.]  
> [Note: “and”: 2; omitted in 3.]  
> [Note: *sequatibus* A.]  
> [Note: A: “the elders of the land.”]  
> [Note: “common”: 2b; “pledge” 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: “that”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: A has *ob, suum*.]

Then the king, strengthened by his brother’s counsel and aid, began openly to devise how he might take vengeance upon his son. Nor did this escape his son Bretislaus. Without delay more than three thousand valiant men assembled to him; hastening forward, they pitched camp around the brook Rokytnice, ready on the following day to join battle against the king.

> [Note: “of his brother” omitted in A.]  
> [Note: A reads *hec*.]  
> [Note: “this” omitted in A.]  
> [Note: 4 reads “the king’s son.”]  
> [Note: *Rokytniczam* 2; *Rokitincam* 3.]  
> [Note: Not far from Prague.]

For he had sent a messenger beforehand to his father, saying: “Behold, behold, I stand far off, whom you were going to seek. What you are going to do hereafter, do today.” Nor should it pass in silence that, in the dead of that same night, divine revelation deigned to work. For if we reveal human acts according to the measure of our knowledge, it is unworthy that we should keep silent about the mighty works of God which we ourselves have seen.

> [Note: “which” written in A’s margin.]  
> [Note: Omitted in 4a.]  
> [Note: “council”: 1.]

### 47.

Accordingly, on the aforesaid night, while the matters mentioned above were taking place among the princes, our patrons, namely St Wenceslaus and St Adalbert, visited those placed in prison and, in their overwhelming affliction, released them by their most holy gracious intervention. First they tore away the outer doorposts together with the door; immediately they broke the prison’s own small iron door with its bars; and they also shattered from outside and cast away the block in which the feet of the condemned were cruelly confined.

> [Note: “little door”: A.]  
> [Note: “trample”: 4a.]

At once a merciful voice sounded in the ears of the condemned, saying: “Until now our aid has failed you and this our country, because you proved unworthy of the grace of God, from the time when these princes waged this more-than-civil war between Bohemia and Moravia. But since grace, mercy, and regard belong to the saints and elect of God, and we are directed wherever that grace has looked, certainly our presence can nowhere come in aid where it has not first been present in mercy.”

“Therefore, now certain of God’s mercy, arise; hasten to the church of God; and announce to all that we, specifically St Wenceslaus and St Adalbert, have absolved you and brought peace.” Immediately, as though awakened from a heavy sleep and released from their chains while the guards were still sleeping, they went out free and fulfilled what had been commanded.

> [Note: 4, 4a add “and.”]  
> [Note: A reads thus; omitted in the remaining witnesses.]

Previously they had disagreed to such an extent that, each suspicious of the other, the one fearing lest he be deprived of the throne, the other lest he be seized by his father, they greatly feared one another.

> [Note: “because”: 2.]  
> [Note: “they were in discord”: 3, 4a; corrected in 4.]  
> [Note: “both”: 3.]

The young man was accompanied by men of his own age and by the greater part of the nobles, more ready of hand and stronger in war. The other was favoured and reverently honoured with great devotion by Bishop Cosmas, the provosts of the churches, all the magnates of the land, men more advanced in age and more useful in counsel, together with the whole militia of the people. And indeed, at that time, the worst crime since Prague’s foundation would have been committed, had not the holy gracious intervention of most blessed Wenceslaus and the great mercy of almighty God brought peace according to the desire of all the princes and people.

### 48.

Seeing this, the counts who had remained in the camp sent to Bretislaus, saying: “If you trust your father and return to your former favour with him, we do not trust him at all, for we know well enough his cunning craftiness. We fear his friendships more than his enmities. For just as a bear suffers not the slightest blow unavenged, so he will never cease from vengeance until he has left unavenged not one iota of all things by which we have offended him.

> [Note: Omitted in 2.]  
> [Note: “enough”: 2, 2b, 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: A first had *nimium*, corrected above the line to *minimum*, “the least.”]

“Therefore either allow us, for your sake, to depart to any region of the earth, or seek higher palaces with us wherever in the world they may be. For we are prepared to serve no lord more readily than you, our lord.”

> [Note: Omitted in 2.]  
> [Note: “more” omitted in A.]

But Bretislaus saw that, just as a soldier without arms is deprived of his proper function, so a duke without soldiers does not even possess the name of duke. He preferred to seek foreign bread with them rather than, alone and without a soldier, to enjoy domestic peace with his father.

Without delay, after gathering all their livestock and servants, more than two thousand soldiers set out with Duke Bretislaus for the Pannonian king. ### 49.

In the same year, through the arrangement of King Wratislaus, Cosmas, elected to the church of Prague, and Andrew, likewise elected to the see of Olomouc, came to Mantua under the escort of the Count Palatine Rapota. They were presented to Emperor Henry III Augustus at the beginning of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, on the Kalends of January.

> [Note: 3, 4, 4a insert “was.”]

After a long silence, the handsome Caesar opened his fair lips, saying:

> [Note: “the day before”: 4.]  
> [Note: “assembled”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: A reads *aberit lab.*; 3, “opened his lips”; 4, “opened.”]

“These brothers have been sent to us by our faithful friend Wratislaus, king of Bohemia, so that according to canonical and apostolic institution we may confirm their election by our authority. Yet we do not wish to make a determination without your consent.”

> [Note: The reading is corrupt in 2 and 4a.]

Then the bishop of Münster, Erpo, who had come from Jerusalem at that time, rose and, leaning on the table on which episcopal staffs, rings, and relics of saints had been placed, said: “It is very dangerous for what has been confirmed by the decree of many to be destroyed by a few. For many bishops were present, many princes of the Roman empire, and envoys of the Apostolic See were present, when you confirmed by your privilege that the two bishoprics, Prague and Moravia alike, should remain, as they had been from the beginning, one and undivided.”

The emperor replied: “Allow me now to do what my friend has asked of me; but concerning these matters I shall decide later, at the proper time, in their proper place.” Immediately he betrothed them with rings to their respective churches, giving them pastoral staffs. When this had been done, both bishops were ordered to return to Verona and wait there until Count Palatine Rapota, once the royal business had been completed, should again conduct them with him to their homeland.

### 50.

Meanwhile an ominous rumour struck our ears: King Wratislaus had passed to Christ on 14 January, and his brother Conrad had succeeded to the rulership.

> [Note: “XVIII,” 2.]  
> [Note: The Bohemian Necrology and the Pegau Calendar agree.]  
> [Note: The monk of Pegau and the Hildesheim Annals testify that he fell from a horse while hunting.]

Conrad immediately sent a courier to the emperor and, promising him money, asked that the election of the bishops mentioned above be annulled. But the emperor, taking more thought for justice than consenting to the money of iniquity, said: “What I have done, I have done; nor can I alter my deed.” The envoy named Woclin went away sad because he had not obtained what he had requested on the duke’s behalf.

> [Note: *cessari*, corrected in another hand to *cassari*, “be annulled,” A.]

The duke, whose disposition had now changed, received them kindly and celebrated Easter with them at Vyšehrad, on 28 March.

During that Easter week, around the Kalends of April, a great snow fell, and a cold mixed with ice became so severe as rarely occurs even in the middle of winter.

> [Note: A: “occurred in mid-…”; *contingit* 2b.]

We have not much to write about the deeds of this Duke Conrad, because in the same year in which he assumed the duchy, after seven months and seventeen days, he lost it together with his life on 6 September. He was succeeded by the younger Bretislaus—that is, the second Bretislaus.

Bishop Cosmas himself, with the clergy and a splendid procession, received him at the city gate before the church of St Mary, led him to the throne, and, according to the rite of that land, the younger Duke Bretislaus was enthroned by all the counts and nobles on 14 September.

### 51.

In the same year an eclipse of the sun occurred on 20 September, on the sixth weekday after noon.

On the Kalends of October of that year, a certain false bishop named Routpert came into this land. He declared that he had governed the church of Cavaillon in the province of Vasconia for many years. Since our brother Osel, also called “the Ass,” recognized him and testified that he had formerly acted as bishop when travelling with him from Hungary to Jerusalem, Duke Bretislaus and Cosmas the elect received him gladly and allowed him to perform the divine office, or canonical hours, as a bishop.

> [Note: 4, 4a: “on the Kalends of October of the same year”; 2b, 3: “on the third Kalends of October.” In the latter, *tertiis* was deleted and *in* written above.]  
> [Note: *Rd’pertus*, with a contraction-mark placed over the d, 2; *Rupertus* 2b; *Rutpertus* 3, 4, 4a, and thereafter.]

> [Note: “him” supplied above the line in A.]

Why say more? He consecrated many churches, ordained many clerics in March, and on Maundy Thursday exorcised the most holy chrism. At Easter a cleric came to him, plainly conscious of his own error, and something or other became known to him secretly. A remarkable thing: neither the duke nor the elect could obtain that he should remain even for a short time; rather, during that very Easter week he hurriedly took the road towards Saxony.

> [Note: As is clear from what precedes, this happened in 1093.]  
> [Note: *sacrosacrum* 2b.]

Later, when it became known that he had been a false bishop, they sent one of the Latins, named Constantius, into Vasconia. Through him Bishop Desiderius of the church of Cavaillon reported in writing that that church had never had a bishop named Routpert. They also sent to Pope Clement, seeking his authoritative advice concerning what ought to be done amid so great a crisis.

> [Note: “they send”: 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: *Constantinum* 4, 4a.]  
> [Note: Thus A; “named” is absent from the remaining witnesses.]

In reply he ordered the churches to be consecrated again in full; those baptized with the false bishop’s chrism were not to be rebaptized, but only confirmed; likewise, those ordained by him were not to be reordained, but only to stand among the ordinands for ordination and receive the blessing by the laying on of hands alone.

> [Note: “to rebaptize”: 3.]  
> [Note: “order”: 4, 4a.]

Thus the wounds inflicted upon Mother Church by the enemy were healed by the antidote of justice, while Pope Clement III governed the state of the Catholic faith, and Jesus Christ our Lord reigned with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.
