> [Note: This entire verse is absent from 3.]

**Here ends the Second Book of the Chronicle of the Bohemians.**

> [Note: “Here ends … work” written in red in A and 4.]

**Here begins the Apology of the Same Dean, Entitled Above, for the Third Book of the Work, Again.**

> [Note: “above” omitted in 2b.]  
> [Note: “entitled”: 4a.]  
> [Note: *ittendidem* A; “of this” 2b; “of the same” 4a.]  
> [Note: “Apology of the same dean for the third book of the chronicles”: 4; “Apology to the reader”: 3.]

> Now, with God’s promised favouring mercy, I have accomplished  
> Whatever I think I promised you, reader.

> [Note: 2b: “whatever I think I promised you, pious reader,” with *pious* written above and *good* above it, for “I think I promised you, reader.”]

Now, recalling a few things out of many concerning past events or times gone by [Note: Column 0187: *transactis* (“completed”) in witnesses 4 and 4a], I have brought the history of my narrative down to the time of Duke Bretislaus the Younger [Note: Column 0187: *ipia*, corrected in another hand to *tempora* (“times”), witness A]. Why, then, I have thought it worthwhile now to cease from the work in hand is not without reason [Note: Column 0187: *opere* (“work”) in A; *abs re* (“without reason”) in 2b and 4a]. For concerning modern people or times, it is more useful for us to keep wholly silent than, by speaking the truth—for truth always breeds hatred [Note: Column 0187: two or three words were written above this in A but erased; Column 0187C: Terence, *Andria* I.1.41]—to incur some loss [Note: Column 0187: A reads *ignoramus* (“we do not know”), expunged in the margin and replaced by *incurramus* (“we incur”); *stipendium* (“pay”) in A, 2, 2a, and 3, but in 2 corrected by an older hand to *dispendium* (“loss”)].

But if, departing from the truth, we write otherwise than matters stand [Note: Column 0187: *habent* (“stand”) in 2 and 4], since the facts are known to almost everyone, we nonetheless incur the charge of flattery and falsehood [Column 0187C]. Indeed, the people of this age, stripped of virtues, delight in being clothed with praises [Note: Column 0187: *ditari* (“enriched”) in 4 and 4a]; their greatest folly [Note: Column 0187: omitted in 4 and 4a] is to wish to be adorned with favours [Note: Column 0187: *dicorari*, a variant spelling in 3 and 4a], while doing by no means those things worthy of favour [Note: Column 0187: corrected in A].

Yet it was not so among the ancients, who, although they were most worthy of praise, nevertheless fled the praises which modern people seek [Column 0188B]; and what was shameful to them is held honourable by these men. If we were to set forth their deeds fully in writing, because some things were not done with God, we should doubtless fail to escape the offence of certain persons who are still alive—new-made men [Note: Column 0187: *neophytici* (“neophytic”) in 3] and *itaci* [Note: Column 0187: *ytaci* in 4; *vertaci* in 4a; Column 0188C: Cosmas himself explains what an *itacus* is]—who, at the duke’s word, have nothing readier on their lips than “Yes, lord”; another, “It is so, lord”; a third, “Do so, lord.” But it was not thus of old.

For the duke especially honoured the man who, by the reasoning of justice, set a shield against wrongdoing in opposition to it, and who restrained evil counsellors and those departing from the path of equity by a single word of truth. Such men now are either none or few; and if they exist, while they are silent, they are as though they did not exist. For the fault and the judgment are alike: either to have kept silent about truth [Column 0188C] or to have conceded falsehood.

Therefore it seems to us far safer to tell a dream, to which no one bears witness, than to write the deeds of people now living. Wherefore we leave their deeds to be explained more fully by posterity [Note: Column 0187: omitted in 4]; yet, lest anyone accuse us of having passed them over untouched, we shall take care to note a few matters summarily.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SAME WORK

[Note: Column 0187: written in red in A; 2 reads “of the work above”; 2b, “of the chronicle”; 3, “Here begins the third book”; 4 and 4a, “Here begins the third book of the chronicles.”]

### 1

Therefore the new duke, Bretislaus the Younger—mature in age, but more mature in understanding [Note: Column 0187: *maturis* (“mature,” plural) in 2]—after he had worthily celebrated, according to the custom of this land and with due observances, the feast-day of his patron Saint Wenceslas in the city of Prague (28 September) [Note: Column 0187: *suum* (“his own”) is added in 2], and had provided a magnificent banquet for all the magnates and counts for three days, there, in view of his accession [Note: Column 0187: *nativitate* (“birth”) in 3], decreeing certain measures as far as he could for the advantage of the Church and establishing others for the convenience of this land—just as from the very beginning of his life he had placed all his hope in God’s protection alone [Column 0189A], so now, at the outset of his rule, inflamed with an exceeding zeal for the Christian religion, he drove from the midst of his realm all magicians [Note: Column 0189: *et* (“and”) is added in 3 and 4a], diviners, and sorcerers [Note: Column 0189: corrected in A]. Likewise he uprooted and burned with fire the groves or trees which the common and ignoble populace worshipped in many places.

He also abolished superstitious observances which the peasants, still half pagan, kept on the Tuesday or Wednesday of Pentecost: they offered libations over springs, slaughtered victims, and sacrificed to demons. He likewise abolished burials made in woods and fields, and the displays [Note: Column 0189: *cenas* (“banquets”) in 4 and 4a; Column 0189D: that is, apparatus or pageants; compare what is read in Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 15] which, in accordance with pagan custom, they held at crossroads and three-way crossings [Note: Column 0189: *quas* (“which”) is omitted in 3], as though for the repose of souls [Column 0189D: that is, rest]—likewise the profane games which they performed over their dead, summoning empty shades [Note: Column 0189: *inanescentes manes* in 3; in 4 and 4a, *inanes cientes manes* and the following words are omitted] and, putting masks upon their faces, practising Bacchic revelry.

These abominations and other sacrilegious inventions the good duke extirpated [Note: Column 0189: *exterminat* (“extirpates”) in 2b], lest they should any longer occur among the people of God. And because he always worshipped God alone and truly with a pure heart, and possessed zeal for Him, he pleased all lovers of God.

For he was a distinguished prince, a duke welcome in camps, a soldier unconquerable in arms [Note: Column 0189: *spectabilis* (“distinguished”) in A, expunged and replaced above by another hand with *acceptabilis* (“welcome”)]. Whenever he invaded Poland, he always returned with great triumph. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, the first of his dukedom, he devastated it by such frequent incursions that, on this side of the river Oder, from the fortress of Recen to the city of Głogów [Note: Column 0189: *Glogau*], no human being lived, except in the town of Niemcza [Column 0189D: Nimptsch] alone.

Nor did he desist from ravaging it until Wladislaus, prince of Poland, with great supplication, paid in full, down to the last penny, the tribute for the preceding and present years. The total of this tribute was 1,000 marks of silver and 60 of gold [Note: Column 0189: one witness reads “forty” instead of “sixty”; Column 0189D: compare above II.13. Martin the Gaul reported the same matter differently, p. 82; compare Palacký I, 340, and Roepell I, 217].

The duke also handed over to his son Boleslaus the cities belonging to the province called Kladsko [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Kladsko*, *Kladzko*, *Kladzco], and committed him by formal act of delivery and pledge of faith to Duke Bretislaus, so that, obeying his maternal uncle, he might peacefully possess the province entrusted to him by his father [Note: Column 0189: “by his father” in witness 2]. Duke Wladislaus himself swore an oath that he would annually pay him, at a fixed time, for the peace granted, the tribute formerly established under Duke Bretislaus: 500 marks of silver and 30 of gold.

### 2

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, while Emperor Henry III was still beyond the mountains in Lombardy [Note: Column 0189: “being there” in A; “six” is expunged] attending to imperial affairs [Note: Column 0189: one witness reads “nuptial affairs”], a general synod was summoned by all the bishops and princes of the Roman Empire at Mainz [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Magontia*], for mid-Lent.

To it Duke Bretislaus sent the elected bishops Cosmas and Andrew, entrusting and formally delivering them to the Count Palatine Rapota, often mentioned already [Note: Column 0189: added in the margin of A by another hand], and asking him to present them to the Archbishop of Mainz for ordination [Note: Column 0189: “bishop” in 3 and 4a]. Rapota intervened for them and testified before the archbishop and the universal synod that their election had formerly been confirmed by the emperor in the city of Mantua [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Mantoua*]. With all the suffragans approving, Cosmas and Andrew were ordained bishops on 12 March, the fourth Ides of March, by the Archbishop of Mainz, named Ruthard [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Routhardus*].

### 3

In the same year there was a mortality among human beings [Note: Column 0189: “in Bohemia” is added in 4 and 4a], especially great in the German regions [Column 0190D: compare Bernold’s chronicle for the year 1094, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores V].

For when the aforesaid bishops were returning from Mainz [Note: Column 0189: A reads *Magutia*] and passed through a certain village called Amberk [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Ainbeck*, *Hamberk*, and *Bamberk], they could not enter the parish church [Note: Column 0189: omitted in 4 and 4a], though it was quite spacious and stood outside the village, in order to hear Mass, because its entire pavement was filled with corpses to the very last spot [Note: Column 0189: A reads “was,” expunged]. Similarly, in the city of Kaker there was no house in which there were not three or four human corpses. Passing it by, we spent the night in the open country not far from the city.

In the same year, in September, Duke Bretislaus married a Bavarian noblewoman named Lukarth [Note: Column 0189: variants include *Lukardam*], sister of Count Albert [Note: Column 0189: omitted in 3 and 4; Column 0190D: her origin is sufficiently obscure; see Pubitschka IV, 72].

Likewise, in the same year and at the command of the same duke, Bishop Cosmas consecrated, on 27 September, the altar of Saint Vitus the Martyr [Note: Column 0189: “in the city of Prague” is added in 4 and 4a], because the monastery had not yet been brought to completion.

### 4

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, for many nights a reddish northern light appeared in the sky [Note: Column 0189: *aquilonaris* (“northern”) in 4].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, on 14 April, at the command of the most glorious duke of the Bohemians, Bretislaus [Note: Column 0189: 3 reads “Kalends of May”; 4 and 4a omit the date], the monastery of the holy martyrs Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert was consecrated by the venerable Bishop Cosmas.

In the same year there was such a movement [Note: Column 0189: “of Christians” is added in 4 and 4a]—indeed, such a divine compunction—among the people to set out for Jerusalem that very few settlers remained in the German regions [Column 0191A], and especially in eastern Franconia, in cities and villages [Note: Column 0191: one witness reads “remained permanently”].

Since, because of the size of the host, they could not all proceed together by one road, some of them, passing through this our land, by God’s permission fell upon the Jews and baptized them against their will; those who resisted they slaughtered. Seeing these things done contrary to the decrees of the canons, Bishop Cosmas, moved by zeal for justice, tried in vain to prevent their baptizing them unwillingly, because he had no one to assist him.

For Duke Bretislaus at that time, with his whole army in Poland on the bank of the river called Nysa [Note: Column 0191: *Nizzam* in 3], after destroying their fortress called Brido [Note: Column 0191: variants include *Brydo*, *Byrdo*, and *Bryd*; Column 0191C: Wartha, on the borders of the county of Glatz and Silesia], was also building, farther down the same river, a very strong fortress upon a high rock, from which it took the name Kamenec [Note: Column 0191: variants include *Kamenez*, *Kamene*, and *Camener*; Column 0191C: on the river Nysa, not far from the county of Glatz, the fortress of Kamenz, later a Cistercian monastery; Schwarz].

That the Jews, however, not many days later cast off from themselves the yoke of Christ, despised the grace of baptism and the salvation of the Catholic faith, and again bowed their necks beneath the yoke of Mosaic law [Note: Column 0191: *sed* (“but”) is omitted in A, 2b, 3, 4, and 4a], could be ascribed to the negligence of the bishops and prelates of the Church.

When the aforesaid fortress of Kamenec had been founded, before Duke Bretislaus departed thence, he took aside Mutina, son of Bosa [Note: Column 0191: *Boza* in 2b], his kinsman and secretary [Note: Column 0191: *consecrarium* (“associate”) in 4 and 4a], reproached him greatly for the many things by which he had often offended him [Note: Column 0191: *quia* (“because”) in 2b], and said:

> “If I did not fear to offend God [Note: Column 0191: A reads “if I did not fear”], I would certainly tear out your eyes [Note: Column 0191: A places *oculos* (“eyes”) after *profecto*; another reading has “your eyes”], as you deserve; but I do not wish to do so, because it is a great crime to mar what God’s finger has wrought in a human being.”

Allowing him only two knights to remain with him, he removed him from his sight and presence, sent him into Bohemia, and ordered all his property confiscated.

Without delay, as he was returning, the duke sent men to seize Bosey [Note: Column 0191: variants include *Boziey*, *Bosen*], son of Cac, Mutina’s kinsman; for he had always hated that clan, the Vršovci [Note: Column 0191: variants include *Vrsseuicz*, *Wryssouic*, *Versouiae*, and *Wirssowic*], because he knew it to be very proud and deceitful.

When they had seized him at once, as commanded, he was put aboard ship with his wife and two sons and banished to Zribia [Note: Column 0191: variants include *Zbriam*, *Zirbiam*, and *Zrbiam*]. From there he proceeded into Poland and found there his brother Mutina; the duke of Poland received them quite kindly.

### 5

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, Duke Bretislaus summoned Udalric, son of Conrad [Column 0192C: Duke of Brno], ordered him seized, and sent him to the fortress of Kladsko to be held in custody.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, it was reported [Note: Column 0191: “related” in 4 and 4a] to Duke Bretislaus that certain Jews, having escaped in flight, were secretly removing some of their wealth, partly to Poland and partly to Pannonia.

Greatly angered, the duke sent his chamberlain with several knights to strip them from head to heel [Note: Column 0191: “to the soles of their feet” in 4 and 4a]. On arriving, he summoned the elder Jews to him [Note: Column 0191: “those arriving he summons” in 4] and began thus to address them:

> O race sprung from the *manzerim* [Note: Column 0191: *manzeribus* (“sons of a harlot”), with variants *manseribus* and *mansoribus*; Column 0192C: that is, “sons of a harlot”],  
> Ishmaelites,  
> The duke commands you to tell him why you flee,  
> And why you diminish without cause the treasures you have acquired [Note: Column 0191: *partas* (“acquired”) in 4 and 4a; corrected by the corrector of 2b].  
> Meanwhile, whatever is mine is wholly mine.  
> You carried away neither goods nor riches from Jerusalem.  
> For one denarius, thirty were proscribed under  
> Caesar Vespasian; thus you were scattered throughout the world.  
> You came lean; lean go wherever you wish [Note: Column 0191: “lean also” in 3].  
> God is my witness that you were baptized.  
> These deeds were performed not by me, but at the lord’s command [Note: Column 0191: the word order is reversed in 2].  
> But since you have again fallen back into Judaism,  
> Let Bishop Cosmas see what he ought to do about it.

He had spoken this on the duke’s behalf, and immediately they burst in, overthrew the houses, took the treasures and whatever household goods they found of greatest value. They left them nothing except grain of wheat for food [Note: Column 0191: *nihil nisi* (“nothing except”) is omitted in 3; *quod solum* (“which alone”) is omitted in 2b].

O how much money was taken from those wretched Jews that day [Note: Column 0191: added in the margin of A]! Not even from burning Troy was so much wealth gathered upon the Euboean shore.

### 6

In the same year, on 10 December [Column 0192C: confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology], Bishop Cosmas departed to Christ.

This prelate was humble, simple, patient, and very merciful; he bore calmly injuries inflicted by any person; he was a kindly forgiver of those acknowledging their faults, no deaf hearer of widows, no slow helper of orphans [Note: Column 0191: *adjutor* (“helper”) is corrected in A in another ink; “no slow helper of orphans” is omitted in 3; in 4 and 4a it is inserted after “diligent visitor,” and 4a reads *auditor* (“hearer”) for *adjutor*], a diligent visitor of the sick, mindful of the lowest estate, and prompt in performing funeral rites.

### 7

After his death, Duke Bretislaus, having care for souls and considering the authority granted him by God to choose a spouse for the Church, began anxiously and sleeplessly [Note: Column 0191: omitted in 2] to examine in his silent mind the character of his clergy [Note: Column 0191: “and” is added in 3] and to investigate each person’s life and conduct, considering whom above all he should advance to the highest degree of the priesthood.

Though he himself knew what was in each cleric among his own people [Note: Column 0193: the words “among his own people” were added in the margin of A by another hand], he nevertheless recalled Solomon’s saying:

> “My son, do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent”  
> (Ecclesiasticus 32:24).

[Note: Column 0193: MS 3 omits *fili*, “my son”; MSS 4 and 4a add *et post factum non peniteberis*, “and after doing it you will not repent.”]

He summoned Wigbert, his kinsman by marriage through his sister [literally *generum*, “son-in-law”; here the relationship is through his sister], a wise man very learned and discerning in such affairs [Note: Column 0193: *et* (“and”) is omitted in 2b], and said to him:

> “In the time of my father King Wratizlaus [Note: Column 0193: omitted in 2b], you were always first among his friends at court. You have observed the character and life of the Bohemians; you know all, not only laymen but also clerics [Note: Column 0193: omitted in A], inside and out. By your counsel I now wish to choose a bishop.”

To this the nobleman answered in words well suited to his own character:

> “Formerly, while your father the king flourished, my counsel prevailed. Now there live men of such character [Note: Column 0193: “the character of men” in 3] as think themselves something when they are nothing, and to whom no counsel pleases except that which they themselves devise [Note: Column 0193: corrected in A].
>
> “But you know better that, in so holy an undertaking, those who consult for the advantage of Holy Church ought to be free from anger and hatred, from pity and friendship [Note: Column 0193: the latter phrase is omitted in A]; for where these hinder the mind, human judgment is deceived [Column 0193C: Sallust, *Catiline* 47].
>
> “Yet neither friendship with anyone binds me, nor pity overthrows me, nor hatred agitates me, nor anger inflames me, so as to prevent me from telling you, dear lord, what the order of justice requires.
>
> “There is your father’s, and now your own, chaplain, whom you know better than I, named Herman. He has always been steadfast in the king’s service [Note: Column 0193: added in the margin of A], faithful in what was entrusted to him, a trustworthy executor in conducting embassies; chaste, sober, humble, and modest; neither drunken [Note: Column 0193: *violentus* (“violent”) corrected in A to *vinolentus* (“drunken”); 2b also reads “violent”], nor ambitious, nor proud; and, what is the foremost virtue in a cleric, thoroughly learned.
>
> “So far as human judgment can discern, he appears a good man and perfect to the fingernail [Note: Column 0193: corrected in A], provided only that his being a foreigner is no impediment [Note: Column 0193: *solum* (“only”) in A, 2b, 3, and 4].”

Then the duke, marvelling at the unanimity of his own will and Wigbert’s, said [Note: Column 0193: “Bretislaus” is added in 4a]:

> “Your heart thinks no differently from mine [Note: Column 0193: *aut* (“or”) corrected in A to *haud* (“not”)]. And because he is a foreigner, he will benefit the Church more: no family connexion will drain him, no concern for children will burden him, no crowd of kinsmen will despoil him [Note: Column 0193: corrected in A; 2b reads “despoil”]. Whatever comes to him from any source, his bride and mother, the Church, shall have it all.”

“Therefore I shall make this man bishop of Prague.”

Without delay, the chief men of the land and the provosts of the Church having been summoned to the duke’s assembly in the city of Boleslav [Column 0194A; Note: Column 0193: “palace” in 4 and 4a], with all the clergy approving [Note: Column 0193: “and all the people approving” in 2b] and the people favouring, Herman, a deacon by promotion and raised to the provostship of Boleslav, was, unwillingly, appointed to the still higher honour of the episcopate [Note: Column 0193: *rogatur* (“is asked”) in 3].

This election was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, on the day before the Kalends of March, 28 February [Note: Column 0193: witnesses 2, 3, 4, and 4a read “the second”; the date is therefore 28 February].

### 8

Because in the same year Emperor Henry III celebrated Easter at Regensburg (10 April) [Note: Column 0193: the emperor’s name is omitted in 2b; Column 0193C: compare Henry IV’s diploma issued at Regensburg in Böhmer, 1959], Duke Bretislaus was ordered to come there with his elect. After celebrating Easter in the city of Vyšehrad, he came to Regensburg on the third day after the octave of Easter (19 April) [Note: Column 0193: “in” is added in 4 and 4a].

Since before the feast he had sent gifts in friendship both to the emperor and to his magnates [Note: Column 0193: corrected in A], all his friends who were at court came out to meet him for nearly three miles [Note: Column 0193: omitted in 4 and 4a], and conducted him into the city with great honour.

At his first request [Note: Column 0193: “first request” is corrupted to *immam* in 2b] the emperor confirmed the Bohemians’ election, giving Herman a ring and episcopal staff. He also obtained by his prayers from the emperor that he should give a banner to his brother Borivoy and entrust him to all the Bohemians who had come with him, so that after his death they might raise his brother Borivoy to the throne [Column 0194C: this was done contrary to the law of succession to the kingdom established by Bretislaus I; compare above II.13].

### 9

In the same year Duke Bretislaus came with an army into Moravia, rebuilt the fortress of Podivin [Note: Column 0193: variants include *Podwin* and *Podiwin*], and restored it, as it had formerly been, to the authority of Bishop Herman [Note: Column 0193: “him” in A and 2; omitted in 4]. There, in the village of Zlaunica [Note: Column 0193: variants include *Zliunica*, *Zluinica*, *Slivnica*, and *Slaunica*], he celebrated Pentecost (29 May).

Then, meeting Coloman, king of Pannonia [Note: Column 0193: variants include *Chlomannus* and *Colomannus*], in the field called Luczko [Note: Column 0193: *Luczo* in 4], they spoke much with one another, negotiating an agreement satisfactory to both parties [Note: Column 0193: “to him” in 2b; “agreement” is omitted in A]. After exchanging immense gifts, they renewed the old treaties of friendship and peace [Note: Column 0193: “and peace” is omitted in 4 and 4a] and confirmed them with oaths.

There Duke Bretislaus entrusted his elect, Deacon Herman [Note: Column 0193: A reads “Bishop Herman”; the other witnesses read “Deacon”], to Archbishop Seraphim [Note: Column 0193: *Seraphyn* in 4] for ordination. When Herman came to the archbishop’s seat in the city of Esztergom at the time when holy orders were conferred, on 11 June, the third Ides of June, he ordained him priest, and likewise advanced me, though unworthy, to the same rank.

After holding the council, the duke returned and pitched camp near the city of Brno [Note: Column 0193: variants include *Brinen* and *Bruen]. For he was greatly angered against Udalric and Lutold [Note: Column 0195: *Luitold* in 2b and 3], sons of his uncle Conrad.

Fleeing from him, they shut themselves up in fortified towns [Note: Column 0195: “in” is omitted in 3] and sent over the other cities to him, fearing that he would ravage the country as an enemy.

Meanwhile, Duke Bretislaus stationed garrisons in the cities that had been surrendered to him, entrusted them to his brother Borivoy, and returned to Bohemia. But Suatopluk and Otto, sons of Otto [Column 0195D: Duke of Olomouc], together with their mother Eufemia [Column 0195D: she was the daughter of Béla I, king of Hungary], were very obedient and faithful to the duke [Note: Column 0195: variants of *Suatopluk* and *Otto* are recorded in the witnesses].

Likewise in the same year, at the Nativity of the Lord (25 December), Duke Bretislaus invited Boleslaus, his relative through his sister, to a banquet arranged in the city of Žatec. At that very feast, with the consent of all the counts of Bohemia, Boleslaus was made sword-bearer to his maternal uncle.

After the feast the duke sent him back to his own lands, gave him a gift [Note: Column 0195: “gifts” in 2b, 3, 4, and 4a], and ordained that, as payment for the service attached to the dignity of sword-bearer [Note: Column 0195: an additional syllable is written above the word in A], he should receive from the tribute which his father Wladislaus always paid annually 100 marks of silver and 10 talents of gold [Note: Column 0195: *habebat* (“he had”) corrected in A to *habeat* (“he should have”)].

### 10

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, Duke Bretislaus learned for certain from certain reports that the emperor intended to celebrate Easter at Mainz (2 April). Thinking it best to send there his elect Herman [Note: Column 0195: *suum el* is written in A], both to bring his gifts to the emperor and to receive from his master the blessing for which he waited, he entrusted him to Wigbert, who was likewise to attend the imperial court, and asked him to favour all Herman’s business at the proper time [Note: Column 0195: omitted in 4 and 4a].

But because Archbishop Ruthard, accused of the simoniacal heresy, had left Mainz and was then staying in Saxony [Note: Column 0195: “in those days” in A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, and 4a], Herman was ordained bishop on 8 April, in the octave of Easter, the sixth Ides of April [Note: Column 0195: A reads “the seventh”], by Cardinal Rupert, envoy of Pope Clement, who happened to be present there, at the emperor’s command and with the approval of all the suffragans of the Church of Mainz [Note: Column 0195: “lord” is inserted in 4 and 4a; A reads *Maguncie*].

### 11

In the same year [Column 0195D: the following makes clear that in 1100 Ludmila had not yet been received without dispute among the number of the saints], we disclose to your charity an admirable miracle, memorable for ages, which divine grace deigned to reveal through the merits of the most holy mother Ludmila [Note: Column 0195: *sanctissima* (“most holy,” feminine) in 3; *mris* is an abbreviation in 1], as we ourselves saw it.

Lady Abbess Windelmuth [Column 0195D: abbess of the monastery of Saint George], a devoted servant of God, rebuilt to completion the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, which stood on the territory of the monastery over which she presided and had fallen into ruin from its foundation through age.

When the abbess had obtained the bishop’s agreement to consecrate it [Note: Column 0195: *praesul* (“bishop”) is omitted in 4], and he was, as customary, placing relics of saints in a pyx, the lady offered the bishop, among other things, a cloth one palm broad, which she had received from Saint Ludmila’s veil, asking him likewise to put it among the holy relics in the pyx.

Then the bishop, as though indignant, said: “Lady, be silent about her sanctity! Let the old grandmother rest in peace” [Note: Column 0195: one witness reads “old grandfather”; another “the lady”; 4 omits the phrase].

The abbess replied: “Do not, lord, do not say such things [Note: Column 0195: these words are omitted in A]. For God daily works many mighty deeds through her merits.”

Immediately, at the bishop’s command, a large frying-pan full of glowing coals was brought [Note: Column 0195: “offered” in 2b]. Invoking the name of the Holy Trinity, the bishop threw the cloth upon the flame-belching coals. A marvellous thing: smoke and a small flame flashed around the cloth, but did it no harm.

And this too greatly increased the miracle: because of the excessive heat, the cloth could not be taken from the flames for a long time; yet when at last it was removed, it appeared so whole and strong as though it had been woven that very day.

Overcome by so manifest a miracle, the bishop and all of us shed tears of joy [Note: Column 0195: “we were moved to tears” in 2; “we shed tears” in 4] and gave thanks to Christ. The church was dedicated in honour of Saint Peter the Apostle on 3 October, the fifth Nones of October [Note: Column 0195: “the sixth” in 3].

### 12

Likewise in the same year, on 18 October, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [Column 0196C], Borivoy, brother of Duke Bretislaus, gave a most magnificent banquet in the city of Znojmo [Note: Column 0195: *Znoyem* in 3; Column 0195D: *Znavm*] and married a wife named Helbirk [Note: Column 0195: variants include *Helbyrk*, *Helluck*, and *Kerberk*; Column 0196D: compare the Chronicle of Klosterneuburg in Pez], sister of Leopold, the eastern margrave [Column 0196D: Leopold is Saint Leopold; Helbirk is the daughter of Leopold the Fair].

Because in those same days Lutold, son of Conrad [Note: Column 0195: variants include *Luitoldus* and *Lutholdus], had been admitted to the fortress of Rakouz by the permission of Gotfrid [Note: Column 0195: *Godfrid* in 3; Column 0196D: apparently the brother of Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, and son of Count Arnold, who held the fortress of Lambach on the Traun; compare the Life of Adalbero in Pez II.7], he inflicted many injuries upon Borivoy, devastating his villages every night and taking refuge in the aforesaid fortress [Column 0196D: Retz in Austria].

Therefore Duke Bretislaus, greatly angered, again gathered an army and marched into Moravia, intending to avenge his brother’s injury. But first he sent to Gotfrid, beseeching him by the bonds of their ancient friendship [Note: Column 0197: “faith” in A] either to send Lutold to him without delay in chains [Note: Column 0197: corrected in A] or to drive him from his fortress that very hour.

When Lutold became aware of this, he deceitfully shut the castlemen out and himself forcibly seized the fortress with his knights. Then Gotfrid [Note: Column 0197: *Gothfrid* in 4], with the envoys who had been sent to him, met the duke near the town of Wranov, and before all men cried out that Lutold was a traitor and an enemy of the commonwealth. The fortress, which had been entrusted to him in friendly faith [Note: Column 0197: the phrase is corrected in A], he now asked the duke to help him besiege as an enemy [Note: Column 0197: “in” is added in 2].

The duke did not refuse his request, but moved his army around the city. For six weeks battle was fiercely joined night and day, until hunger—which conquers strong cities [Column 0197C: compare Lucan, *Pharsalia* IV.410]—prevailed in the fortress.

Conquered by this [Note: Column 0197: “conquered” is added in 4; “victory” in 4a] and broken by war, Lutold secretly escaped by night and scarcely fled away alone, leaving his knights there [Note: Column 0197: “having lost” in 3; “all” is corrected in A]. When morning came, they surrendered themselves and the fortress into the duke’s hand.

Meanwhile, while this battle was being fought, Paulic [Note: Column 0197: variants include *Paulik*], son of Marquard [Note: Column 0197: *Markward* in 2], tutor of Wladislaus, died by an arrow. Likewise Dobes [Note: Column 0197: *Doles* in 3], son of Lstimir [Note: Column 0197: variants include *Lyztimir*, *Istimir*, and *Lztimir*], was killed while keeping his turn of the night watch.

Having lost these two men and restored the city to Gotfrid, the victorious duke returned with his men to Bohemia.

### 13

Now, as the Nativity of Christ drew near and the duke was staying for hunting in the village of Stibecna [Note: Column 0197: variants include *Stbeczna*, *Stebna*, *Sebecna*, and *Sbencna], he is said one day, while dining, to have spoken to a certain hunter [Note: Column 0197: omitted in 4 and 4a] who was sitting not far from him at the fourth table:

> “Ho, Cucata! Do you think I do not know who among you is seeking to kill me?”

And he, being a man vehement in speech, cried out [Note: Column 0197: “proclaimed” in 4 and 4a]:

> “May God avert this far from us, and may your eye not behold it—that he himself may more swiftly be killed who plots such things!”

To this the duke said: “Ah, good man [Note: Column 0197: “Ah, ah” in 4], it is granted to no one to avoid unavoidable fate.”

On the following day (21 December), because it was the vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle, he heard Mass in the morning and went hunting. As he was returning at night, attendants carrying lanterns and torches [Note: Column 0197: *facibus* (“torches”) corrected in A from *fascibus* (“bundles”); “and weapons” is added in 4 and 4a] met him before the village.

Immediately Lorck [Note: Column 0197: variants include *Lork* and *Lark*], an impious robber sent by the devil, sprang from his hiding place, girded with a sword, and with all the force he could struck the duke [Note: Column 0197: “Bretislaus” is added in 4 and 4a] in the very entrails with a hunting-spear [Note: Column 0197: corrected in A].

The duke fell in the middle of the grove [Note: Column 0197: *luto* (“mud”) in A, 2, 2b, and 4], just as though bright Lucifer had fallen from high heaven:

> If bright Lucifer had fallen from high heaven.

At once the grieving company of his men flew to him; drawing out the spear [Note: Column 0197: *asta* (“shaft”) in A], they lifted up the half-dead duke.

But that servant of Satan, hastening in flight through the dark night, fell with his horse into a cistern,

> which a rushing torrent, descending in rain, had made.

It is uncertain whether by his own hand, or because the sword slipped from its sheath, he was cut across the middle of the belly, so that all his entrails flowed out [Note: Column 0197: one witness reads “into” rather than “through”].

Tumult arose throughout the village: some leapt upon horses, others ran here and there with weapons [Note: Column 0197: A reads “here and there”; 4 reads “here and there also”], seeking the contriver of so great an evil.

Soon one man found him half alive; and although his wound was quite sufficient for death [Note: Column 0197: *habuerit* (“had”) in 2b], he nevertheless cut off his head with a sword, saying:

> You shall not go guiltless to the dark shades of hell— [Note: Column 0197: *furias* (“Furies”) in A; *furnas* in 4 and 4a].

[The supplied source ends here, with the verse incomplete.]

## Restored textual apparatus

- **[Col. 0187, ch. 1]** Before *triviis* (“crossroads”), 4a omits *in* (“in”); 2b has *ad* (“at/to”) for *ob* (“because of”); 4 reads *ut est* (“as it is”). These readings belong to the pagan rites and games passage.
- **[Col. 0189, ch. 4]** At Zribia, A corrects *revelatus* (“unveiled/revealed”) to *revectus* (“carried back”). For *a capite usque ad calcem* (“from head to heel”), the whole phrase is a marginal addition in A by another hand.
- **[Cols. 0191 and 0193, ch. 7]** MS 2 omits *et* (“and”) between *sollicitus* and *pervigil* (“anxious” and “watchful”); MS 3 adds *et* (“and”) after *clericorum* (“of the clerics”). In A another hand supplies *ad* (“to”) above the line before *summum sacerdotii gradum* (“the highest degree of priesthood”); A omits *summum* (“highest”). Another hand writes *inter suos* (“among his own people”) in A’s margin, and *esset* (“was/might be”) above the line at *clerico* (“cleric”). MS 2b reads *quoque* (“each”) for *quoquam* (“any”). MS 3 omits *fili* (“my son”); MSS 4/4a add *et post factum non peniteberis* (“and after doing it you will not repent”). MS 2b omits *et* (“and”) at *cui et ait* (“and he said to him”), and *regis* (“King”) before Wratizlaus. A omits *omnes* (“all”) after *clericos* (“clerics”). At *Ad haec* (“to these things”), A has *quem* (“whom”). MS 3 has *hominum mores* (“the characters of men”) for *homines morum* (“men of [such] characters”). A has *quod* (“what/that which”) in its margin and a correction at *placet* (“pleases”). A omits *sanctae* (“holy”) from *sanctae ecclesiae utilitati* (“the advantage of Holy Church”), not that whole phrase; it omits *a misericordia et amicitia* (“from pity and friendship”) and *humana* (“human”) from *humana fallitur opinio* (“human judgment is deceived”). *In servicio* (“in service”) is in A’s margin. MS 2b reads *nec* (“nor”) for *non* (“not”); A corrects *violentus* (“violent”) to *vinolentus* (“drunken”), while 2b has abbreviated *viol.* A records a correction at *unguem* (“fingernail”), without identifying the earlier form. A/2b/3/4 have *solum* for *solummodo*, both “only.” MS 4a adds *Bracizlaus*. A corrects *aut* (“or”) to *haud* (“not”). The reading *despoliabit* (“will despoil”) is corrected in A and appears in 2b; the others have *despoliet* (“may despoil”). MSS 4/4a have *palatium* (“palace”) for *placitum* (“assembly/pleasure”); 2b has *cunctoque populo* (“and all the people”). MS 3 has *rogatur* (“is asked”) for *subrogatur* (“is appointed in another’s place”). The dating note gives *II* in 3/4/4a, “the second day [before the Kalends],” corresponding to *pridie* (“the day before”).
- **[Col. 0193, ch. 8]** 2b reads *praemisit* (“sent ahead”) for printed *praemiserat* (“had sent ahead”); at *satrapis* (“to the magnates”), A has a correction. 4/4a omit *fere* (“about”) from *tria fere miliaria* (“about three miles”); 2b *ad civitatem* (“to the city”) for *in civitatem* (“into the city”); *cum* (“with”), in *cum magna honorificentia* (“with great honour”), is written above the line by another hand in A; 2b *immam* for *primam* (“first”); 2b *hic* (“this [man]”) for *hoc* (“this [thing]”); A omits *precibus* (“by prayers”); at printed *ejus* (“his”), the note records a correction in A and *suum* (“his own”), without making the direction explicit; 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a read *sublevarent* (“might raise/relieve”) for *sublimarent* (“might exalt”); 2b *ad solium* (“to the throne”) for *in solium* (“onto the throne”).
- **[Col. 0193–0195, ch. 9]** 3 reads *ibidem* (“there”) for *idem* (“the same”); Podivín is *Podwin* (2), *Podiwin* (2b, 4a); A/2 *eum* (“him”) and 4 omits *id* (“it”); Zlaunica forms are *Zliunica* (2,2b), *Zluinica* (3), *Slivnica* (4), *Slaunica* (4a); Cholomanno forms are *Chlomanno* (2d), *Colomanno* (3), *Colmanno* (4), and Luczko is *Luczo* (4). 2b adds *sibi* (“to themselves”), A omits *placitantes* (“negotiating”), 4 *utrumque* (“either”) for *utrarumque* (“of both”), 2/2b/3 omit *immensis* (“immense”), and 4/4a omit *et pacis* (“and peace”). A has *episcopum* (“bishop”), other witnesses *diaconum* (“deacon”); 4 *Seraphyn*; Brno forms are *Brinen* (2b), *Bruen* (3); 2b/3 *Luitoldo*; 3 omits *in*; Suatopluk is *Zwatoplik* (2), *Zuatoplyk* (2b), *Zuatopluk* (all remaining witnesses); Otto is the printed A form, *Ottek* (3), *Ottik* (all remaining witnesses). The editorial note identifies Eufemia as daughter of Béla I of Hungary.
- **[Cols. 0195–0196, ch. 11]** A omits *aviam* (“grandmother”) and *Ad haec* (“to these things”); A’s marginal reading is *abbatissa h. l.* (“the abbess at this point”), and A has *noli dom.* (“do not, lord”) for the printed division. 2b *offertur* (“is offered”) for *affertur* (“is brought”); 2 *lacrymis fundimur* (“we are flooded with tears”), 4 *fudimus* (“we shed”), for printed *lacrimas fundimus* (“we shed tears”); 3 *VI* for the date. In 4, *praesul* (“bishop”) is omitted from the consecration clause.

[Col. 0198B] And remember to report my deeds to Ceres’ son-in-law.  
*[Note: [Col. 0197] “ceris” in A; another hand has written “Cereris” above it.]*  
*[Note: [Col. 0197C] Virgil, *Aeneid* II.549.]*

But the duke [Bracizlaus added by MSS 4, 4a], although plunged into such pain and grief, during that night and the following day did not relax his spirit or his lips from the praise of God: now offering tearful repentance, now confessing his sins both to Bishop Herman and to the other priests of God. The tribute brought from Poland at that time, and whatever he found in his treasury [variant: “found in his treasury” in A], he caused to be distributed among the monasteries through the hands of the bishop [variant: “to give” in MSS 3, 4a].

When he had arranged everything that needed to be arranged for his soul, he said: “Give my little son my staff and my spear; the rest is not mine to give him, for God has placed it in his own power.”

And so, on the following night, after cockcrow, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, like a good athlete of God, he divided the two substances of man at their respective origins; and beyond doubt we believe that he has either already received, or will receive, the heavenly fellowship [the first *jam* is absent in MS 3; the second in MSS A, 4, 4a].

One of the clergy, following his bier as far as the grave, repeatedly uttered this lament:

> “May the soul of Bracizlaus live—Sabaoth, Adonai—free from death; Bracislaus [is] strong.”

*[Note: [Col. 0197] The manuscripts read *yskiroî*; MSS 3 reads *yskyros*, and MSS 4, 4a read *yscbyros*.]*  
*[Note: [Col. 0197C] Greek ἴσχυρος, “strong.”]*

A remarkable thing occurred: by his lament he so stirred the clergy and the people alike to weeping that, while you wept, you wished to weep still more.

He was buried amid the greatest lamentation of his people in the common burial-ground outside the church of St Wenceslas, before the gate on the left, as he himself had directed. There his sister Ludmila, a devout handmaid of God, built an arched chapel above the vaults in honour of St Thomas the Apostle, and ordained that Mass for the dead should be celebrated there every day.  
*[Note: [Col. 0197] “A devout handmaid of God” is written in A as “a handmaid, devout to God.”]*

And because a report immediately spread among the people that Duke Bracizlaus had been killed by the counsel of Bosey and Mutina, whom the duke had previously expelled from his realm, some are accustomed to ask whether the person who gives the counsel is guiltier than the person who agrees to carry it out. But in truth both are guilty; nevertheless, guiltier is the one who devises the homicide, because he also accuses himself concerning another [the Latin *de alium* is corrupt or uncertain]. Therefore you killed Bracizlaus—you who gave counsel that he should be killed.

The bishop and the counts immediately sent a messenger in haste to Borivoy in Moravia, so that he might hasten to receive the duchy of all Bohemia formerly granted to him by the emperor. He came quickly and, on the very day of Christ’s Nativity, 25 December, was enthroned with the unanimous support of all.

Then Cillenia completely erased her traces, scarcely impressed in Bohemia, when, hating earthly lands, she sought the heavenly ones. For it was the law of the Bohemians that the eldest among their princes should always possess the princely throne.

### 14.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1101 [MS A falsely reads 1102], Uodalricus and Lutoldus, sons of Conrad, expelled the garrisons from Moravia that Borivoy had left there for its protection when he departed, and recovered their cities. Likewise Bosey and Mutina returned from Poland; Duke Borivoy granted them his favour, not from the heart but because of the necessity of the time [this clause is omitted by MSS 4, 4a], and they recovered the cities they had formerly held: Satec to Bosey and Lutomerice to Mutina [variants: *Liutomierziczie* in MS 2; *Lutomiricae* in MSS 3, 4a].

### 15.

[Col. 0199C] In the same year Uodalricus went to the emperor in the city of Regensburg and, through friends, importuned him with prayers and wearied him with immense promises, asking that he restore to him the duchy of Bohemia, unjustly snatched away by his younger brother Borivoy.  
*[Note: [Col. 0199C] Everyone can see that these men were not brothers. On this usage see Pubitschka IV, 101.]*

Having received money from him, the emperor gave him the insignia and banner of the duchy; but he left the attainment of election as duke to the discretion of the Bohemians.

Uodalricus then sent an extremely eloquent man as envoy, named Neusse, son of Dobremil. He accused his brother Borivoy, rebuked the counts, threatened them, declared himself older in age, and demanded, according to the custom of the country, the honour of the principal seat, wrongfully taken from him by his younger brother [here “younger” means the younger son of his paternal uncle].

Although he had a just cause, he grasped vainly at the tail while losing the horns [the manuscripts preserve corrupt readings here; the sense is proverbial]. Thus Udalricus tried too late to drive his brother Borivoy, already confirmed upon the throne, from the realm.

When Udalricus learned through the report of his envoy that neither his brother would yield the throne nor the counts accept his counsel, he obtained only this by his entreaties: permission from the emperor to invade by force the province due to him [the words “by force” are omitted by MSS 4, 4a].

He was soon joined in fellowship by men vigorous in war: Count Sigardus of the town of Sala; his brother, Udalricus, bishop of Freising; and his son-in-law through his sister, named Frederick.  
*[Note: [Col. 0199C–0200C] Schwarz observed that no Udalricus is found among the bishops of Freising of that period. A record in Meichelbeck, *Historia Frisingensis* I.2, no. 1282, proves that Henry held that office from 1098 to 1137; he was the brother of Count Frederick of Pilstein.]*

He had inflamed their minds with eagerness for war by promising them mountains of gold and declaring that all the elder men of Bohemia were his supporters. Moreover, wherever he could, he enlisted no small number of Germans as auxiliaries. In their foolishness they imagined that heaps of gold and silver would lie scattered and exposed in the streets of Bohemia.

When all these had been gathered together, Uodalricus and his brother Lutoldus entered Bohemia in the month of August, but under an unlucky star. For Borivoy, having assembled an army, met them and pitched camp above two hills near the town of Malin [variant: *Malyn* in MS 1], ready to give battle to them on the following day.  
*[Note: [Col. 0200C] The city of Kuttenberg now stands there.]*

The Germans pitched their camp not far away on the other side of the stream Vysplisa [variants: *Wyzplisa*, *Wyzpliza*, *Wzalsa*, *Wzlipsa*, *Wzlypsa*], so that each army could see the other.

When they perceived that the Bohemians were unanimous in their steadfastness with Duke Borivoy, they said to Udalricus: “Where are those elder men of Bohemia whom you said were your supporters? You have lied to your own destruction; you deceived us and led us into great danger.”

They wished to return, but could not, because along the same road behind them Suatopluk was coming with his brother Otto, bringing two squadrons to Duke Borivoy’s assistance. What were they to do? Hemmed in by great distress on every side, they hastened by night into a shameful flight along the narrow road and exceedingly confined path through the forest toward Gabr [variant: *ADGABR* in MS 1].  
*[Note: [Col. 0200C] Habern, by which one goes into Moravia.]*

There the bishop of Freising lost his chapel-equipment—the sacred vessels and ornaments used by priests for worship, as well as the casket in which the relics of the saints are kept. There, because of the difficult road, the whole army threw away its baggage and ordinary belongings [variants include *omnem* and *omnis*].

When morning came, the Bohemians arrived and plundered the spoils left without an enemy.

At that time Borivoy and Suatopluk were harmonious and united with one another. But to explain how discord arose between them, I shall briefly return to its earlier beginnings.

### 16.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1102, Wladizlaus, duke of Poland, had two sons: one born of a concubine, named Sbignev [variants: *Izbigneu*, *Zbingnen*, *Zpitigneu*]; the other born of Judith, daughter of King Wratizlaus, named Bolezlaus. He divided his kingdom between them equally.  
*[Note: [Col. 0201D] His father gave Masovia to Sbignev; to Bolezlaus he gave the principal seats of the kingdom at Cracow, Sandomierz, and Wroclaw, as Martinus Gallus reports, II.8. On the brothers’ dissension see the same work, II.24.]*

But since, according to the Lord’s saying, “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” (Luke 11:17), and house shall fall upon house; and since, as the common saying goes, two cats caught in one sack cannot remain together, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1103, immediately after his father’s death, Sbignev took up arms against his brother. By promising money, he secured Duke Borivoy as an ally.

Borivoy immediately sent for Zuatopluk in Moravia, and they met and pitched camp together near the town of Recen.  
*[Note: [Col. 0201D] Rützen, in the region of Troppau.]*

On hearing this, Bolezlaus sent his tutor Skribimir [variant spellings: *Zribimir*, *Zkrybimir*, *Zkribimir*, *Zkarbimir*, *Zkrbimir*], and begged Duke Borivoy to remember their kinship. Through Judith, his sister, he said, Borivoy was more closely related to him; moreover, he offered him on the spot ten purses filled with one thousand marks.

*[Note: [Col. 0202D] Martinus Gallus calls him the palatine Skarbimirus.]*

O money, queen of every evil, companion of fraud, enemy and foe of fidelity! You suppress justice and overthrow righteous judgments. Grabissa and Protiven [variants: *Protyven*, *Protiwen*], Borivoy’s corrupt counsellors, compelled the duke himself to repudiate the fidelity he had promised to Sbignev.

He immediately accepted the money and returned home [MS A reads “to his homeland”]. And because he had given not even a single obol to Zuatopluk, the latter, deeply indignant and inflamed with anger, is said to have departed saying: “I shall extinguish my fire by ruin.”  
*[Note: Sallust, *Catiline* 31.]*

### 17.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1104, John [the Third] was elected bishop of Moravia.

In the same year Suatopluk sent into Bohemia trackers of wickedness, informers against justice, sowers of discord, and inventors of every evil art—men who

> Could arm brothers, once united, for battle.

*[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.335.]*

These men went through almost all the cities of Bohemia: they corrupted some with money, bound others with gifts, and others with promises. Everyone whom they knew to be eager for revolution, deprived of office, changeable, or unstable in mind they enlisted by their cunning into the party of Duke Suatopluk [MS 1 reads *afficiunt* for *asciscunt*].

Once this had been done, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1105, when the sun was in the tenth degree of Libra, Zuatopluk entered Bohemia with his company [MSS 4, 4a read “army”]. Companies of traitors came to meet him, while some expected that he would be received through the open gates of Prague within the walls.

But earlier that same day Duke Borivoy, arriving very early, occupied the city first, stationed strong garrisons there, entrusted it to Bishop Herman, and withdrew with his men to Vyšehrad.

*[Note: [Col. 0201] A seventeenth-century hand notes in the margin of MS 1 that some material is missing here: apparently two folios are lacking, containing what followed up to chapter 21, through the words “corrupted and greedy.”]*

And behold, Zuatopluk appeared in the plain with six legions, handsomely and orderly equipped. Since no one came out from the city to meet him, he paused for a little while, uncertain and doubtful. Then, after crossing the river Vltava below the village called Bubni [variants: *Bubin*, *Burni*], they approached the city. But they found the gates shut and soldiers resisting strongly from the walls.

There they were disgracefully confounded by a maidservant standing upon the walls. Returning by the same route, they pitched their tents between the two cities, at the place where trading takes place on Saturdays.  
*[Note: [Col. 0202D] On the right bank of the Moldau, in that part of Prague where the Jewish graves are now located; Palacký I, 353.]*

They supposed that their conspirators from both cities would gather to them that night. When this did not happen at all, Suatopluk summoned an assembly in the morning and began as follows:

“Although this is not now a time for me to use a lengthy address, nevertheless I shall say a few words for the matter at hand, lest anyone think that I fear an occasion of death. For the timid and cowardly, to whom miserable life seems sweet, death is most fitting; but for a brave man, to undergo death in battle is sweeter than liquid nectar.  
*[Note: MS A originally had, but then expunged, the words: “captus oculis et mentula est privatus” (“deprived of his eyes and penis”).]*

“For I long ago resolved either to obtain bread and higher honour, or, fighting, to succumb to an honourable death. But the one death you must now avoid is that any one of you should be captured, bound by the hands behind his back, made a spectacle for the enemy, and, like an ox led to sacrifice, fall slain to be cut to pieces.

“For the defeated there is one victory and a memory worthy of praise: that the enemy may not obtain a bloodless victory.”

Having spoken, he immediately turned back toward Moravia with his company. Then Wacek [variant: *Waczek*, *Vecek*] said to the count:

“O miserable condition of fortune, by which I am now compelled to sit upon the ground like an owl, though I seemed, like an agile eagle, to have risen almost to the clouds.”

Vacko replied: “My lord, do not let this adversity break you; happier prosperity will follow it more swiftly, for the brightness of the sun shines more brilliantly after a watery cloud [the manuscripts variously read “after water,” “after a watery,” or “after water and”]. Such indeed is the alternation of all things in the world.”

Duke Borivoy pursued them with his men. Although he had seven times as many soldiers, he did not dare to engage them in battle, because he feared the treachery of his own men, lest they abandon his camp and transfer themselves to the enemy’s service. He followed them from afar as far as the entrance to the forest.  
*[Note: [Col. 0203D] That this occurred already in 1104 is proved by the Hildesheim Annals and the Saxon Annals.]*

### 18.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1106, while the devil, inventor of discord, was sowing dissensions throughout the whole world, certain German nobles became his fellow-workers. They seduced the emperor’s son, namely King Henry IV, and persuaded him to take up arms against his father.

The father, fleeing before his son, fortified himself with a few troops in the city of Regensburg and sent for Duke Borivoy, asking him to come to his aid with his army.

Without delay the Bohemians arrived and pitched camp not far from Regensburg beside the river Regen. On the other side of the same river was the camp of the emperor’s son.

Then those who had seemed to be the emperor’s supporters began to desert him. First Margrave Lupold of the East fled by night and returned home with his men. Depoldus [variants: *Dupoldus*, *Diepoldus*] and Berengerus [variants: *Rerengerus*, *Regnerus*], margraves, transferred themselves to the camp of King Henry the Younger.  
*[Note: [Col. 0203D] Depoldus was count of Vohburg and margrave of Nordgau; he had already gone over to Henry the Younger. See the Hildesheim Annals, 1104. Berengerus was of Sulzbach. Ekkehard’s *Chronicle* for 1106 agrees concerning these men.]*

When the Bohemians saw that they were abandoned on every side, they too hastened as quickly as they could into flight by night.

On seeing this, the emperor left Regensburg and, crossing through the southern region by the road leading to Netoliz [variants: *Netolicz*, *Necholic*, *Netholic*], entered Bohemia. Duke Borivoy received him honourably and, as the emperor himself had arranged, gave him an escort through his land toward Saxony worthy of an emperor, conducting him as far as his son-in-law Wicbertus [variant: *Wigbertus*].  
*[Note: [Col. 0204D] As far as the Wissechore Mountains, that is, the metalliferous mountains of Saxony. See the monk of Opatovice under 1105 in Palacký, *Würdigung*, p. 55.]*

From there, passing through Saxony and crossing the Rhine, he proceeded to Liège, where not many days later he lost both his life and his empire, on the seventh day before the Ides of August.  
*[Variant: MSS 4, 4a read “the sixth day.”]*

### 19.

In the same year Suatopluk summoned those who had followed him from Bohemia and asked their counsel about what should now be done in the enterprise already begun.

Then Budivoy, son of Hren [variants: *Chren*], older than the rest in age and more eloquent in speech, a man even-tempered in adversity and prosperity, trained from youth in such affairs and full of cunning, addressed them as follows:

“The outcome of battle is variable: now these men, now those, prevail in war. But we, brothers, have not yet fought unto blood; we have not yet made a bridge of our heads by which one goes up to the throne [MSS 4, 4a read “a road by which one goes”], which we shall certainly make if fortune compels us to do so.

“But since one reaches the lofty heights of honour not always by arms but more often by deceit, let us now lay aside our arms and employ guile. By such arts Troy was captured from the Argives in the tenth year, and Prudentius says in the *Psychomachia*:

> It makes no difference whether victory’s palm comes by arms or by guile.

*[Note: Prudentius, *Psychomachia* v. 550.]*

Without delay, another, so to speak, shape-shifting Sinon was sent into Bohemia, equipped with many kinds of deceit: the nephew of Gapata [variants: *Gapati*, *Sapacae*, *Gapathe*]. Prepared for either fortune, he did not fear the chance of death; his name aptly sounded manly, because he acted manfully.

For just as Sinon of old drew the armed Argives, concealed in the horse, into the walls of Troy by his lies, so through this man’s deceitful contrivances conquered Bohemia lay open to Duke Suatopluk.

When he reached Duke Borivoy, he fell at his knees, wet the duke’s feet with feigned tears, and, finally ordered to rise, spoke as follows:

> “Wretched me! I have scarcely hidden myself by flight and scarcely escaped the wicked hands of the impious Suatopluk. If he had captured me, beyond doubt he would have torn out these eyes. Since I cannot otherwise avenge myself upon him, O almighty God, let it be lawful for me to reveal his secrets; let it be lawful for me to betray all those who are his intimates in this land.”

*[Note: [Col. 0204D] The allusion is to Virgil, *Aeneid* II.61.]*

Thus, mixing truth with falsehood, he charged Suatopluk with many crimes and, so that he might be believed more readily, confirmed his statements with oaths.

By such arts and snares the good and simple Duke Borivoy was deceived and, excessively credulous of lies, rashly cut off the sturdy branches upon which he himself rested and upon which his honour depended, and fell from the high summit.

For he often wished to seize his faithful friends Bosey and Mutina and punish them as enemies of the commonwealth. But because he had as his counsellors Grabissa and Protiven [variant: *Protucen*], men full of cracks—that is, unreliable and leaky—his intention did not remain hidden from the said counts.

They immediately transferred themselves to his brother Wladizlaus and added spurs to one already raging and furious, so that he might rage still more fiercely against his brother Borivoy. Wladizlaus had already renounced his loyalty, brotherhood, and friendship toward Borivoy, and had openly sent Pulon, brother of Vilalmi [variants: *Wilhelmi*, *Willehalmi*, *Willalmi*; *Polon* in one witness], to Suatopluk in Moravia.

When Wladizlaus and the other counts received him—alas, senseless men, almost enemies of themselves and foes of their country—they brought the raging wolf into the sheepfold, to their own destruction: a wolf who would tear apart not only the sheep but also the shepherds themselves.

Therefore Borivoy, gentle as a lamb, was deprived of the kingdom, and Suatopluk, fiercer than a tiger and more savage than a lion, was enthroned in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1107, on the day before the Ides of May.  
*[Note: [Col. 0205D] The Prague Annals agree; see also the charter in Boczek I, 191.]*

### 20.

The neighbouring peoples marvelled at this novelty, never before seen in Bohemia, and by omens predicted worse things in the future for the Bohemians of foolish mind.

On one side the sons of Pannonia, the Cassandri, rejoiced; on the other, Poland’s worthless *trapi* congratulated themselves with uncircumcised lips.  
*[Note: [Col. 0205D] A *trapus* is a rag; thus here the word means people of the lowest sort.]*

For while these princes troubled themselves, those others enjoyed peace.

Many of the counts whom Borivoy himself had raised from newcomers into counts accompanied him and set out with him for Poland. Sobezlaus [variants: *Sobieslaus*, *Zobezlaus*, *Zobeslaus*], third in age after Borivoy, already a young man of good character, saw what was happening and followed his brother into Poland.

At the same time King Henry IV happened to be in Saxony.  
*[Note: [Col. 0206D] Henry was staying at Goslar in July; see Böhmer no. 1981.]*

Borivoy hastened to him, lamented the injury inflicted upon him, and promised to give immense weights of gold and silver if he would restore to him the duchy of Bohemia, unjustly taken away.  
*[Note: [Col. 0206D] See the Hildesheim Annals, 1107.]*

The king immediately sent one of his high officers and gave Suatopluk this brief command:

“By the crown upon my head I command and order you to come to me without delay; or, if you delay in coming, I myself shall quickly visit you and your Prague in justice and judgment.”

Suatopluk immediately gathered an army. At the very entrance of the forest near the town of Hlumec [variant: *Hlimecz*, *Hlymec*], he summoned the nobles and high officers and presented his brother Otto to them, saying:

“I alone shall go, and at the peril of my head shall test the king’s doubtful friends. You wait here for uncertain happenings in uncertain circumstances. Henceforth may almighty God go before and follow after our deeds.”

Taking a few men with him, he rashly went forward, rushing into an open snare. O foolish wisdom of the man—or rather, the bold audacity of the duke! He went, not unaware of what the king, corrupted by gold and greedy as hell, would do to him.  
*[Note: [Col. 0205] In MS 1 the bookbinder has scattered the following folios out of order.]*

When Suatopluk arrived, the king ordered him, without any hearing, to be thrust into custody. Summoning those who had come with him, he entrusted Duke Borivoy to them, so that they might take him back to Prague and restore him once more to the principal throne.

Returning with him, they pitched camp on the third day near the castle of Donin.  
*[Note: [Col. 0206D] Dohna.]*

When Otto heard this, he said to his men:

“What are we waiting for here? What we feared has already happened, and what we dreaded has come to pass. Let us go and see the new duke—whether the king’s right hand protects him from our spear.”  
*[Note: [Col. 0206D] That is, from the spear.]*

He organized six legions from chosen soldiers, crossed the mountains by night, and at dawn attacked Borivoy’s camp. But Borivoy, already aware of the danger, had slipped away in flight and concealed himself, because a deserter from Otto’s camp had secretly informed him of the matter.

### 21.

Bishop Herman, a prudent and just man, placed amid the shifting fortunes of the two dukes as though between Scylla and Charybdis, withdrew to his friend Otto, bishop of the church of Bamberg [variants: *Babenbergensis*, *Bamberiensis*], lest he seem to have followed either of their uncertain parties.

Borivoy, although he had not obtained what he had sought, nevertheless paid the king the money he had promised. But since all men, according to circumstances, are great or small, behold: a duke of great name, cast into custody, obeys the commands of any very insignificant person and is torn by the insults of those less worthy.

> Ah, how many cares he turns over in his breast, whenever he tries through the foremost men of the palace to bend the king’s anger!

*[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* V.702.]*

But since a king’s door is knocked upon in vain with an empty hand, whereas a greased hand breaks diamonds, he promised the king ten thousand marks of silver. Ah, what will a man not give when a sword hangs over his neck? Who, placed in extremity, would not willingly give for himself whatever he possessed? Indeed, if the king demanded a hundred thousand talents from him, would he not be no less foolish if he did not promise even mountains of gold for his life?

For this reason the king received from him an oath of fidelity, released him, and sent with him one of his retainers to receive the specified payment. When this man came to Prague, he immediately despoiled the sacred shrines, gathered women’s ornaments, and swept together whatever glittered of gold and silver in Bohemia. He scarcely collected seven thousand marks; for the remainder, he gave his brother Otto to the king as hostage.

Likewise Bishop Herman, on arriving, supplied the duke from the endowment of the holy church with seventy marks of refined gold. Also, five cloths belonging to the same church, with their borders, were pledged among the Jews at Regensburg for five hundred marks of silver.

Certainly there was no abbot, no provost, no cleric, no layman, no Jew, no merchant, no money-changer, and no cithara-player who did not unwillingly contribute something to the duke from his storehouse [MS 1 reads “to the king”; MSS 4, 4a omit the final phrase].

After a few days Otto escaped by flight and returned from the royal court to his brother, which greatly displeased the king.

### 22.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1108, as often happens when male and female lie together in one bed as two,

> A third person is immediately begotten,

so the noble wife of Duke Zuatopluk—

*[Note: From the Saxon annalist some have convinced themselves that Zuatopluk’s wife was named Ita. But without doubt the annalist was misled by the little word *ita*, “thus,” which we read here in Cosmas and which he mistakenly thought indicated a name.]*

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete: “the noble wife of Duke Zuatopluk …”]

## Complete source-order textual apparatus

2. **0197C** Vergil, *Aeneid* II.549.
3. **0197** *Bracizlaus* is added by 4 and 4a.
4. **0197** *nunc … confitendo* (“now … by confessing”) is a marginal addition by another hand in A.
5. **0197** A reads *invenit in sua* (“found in his own [place]”).
6. **0197** 3 and 4a read *dare* (“to give”).
7. **0197** 3 reads *sic* (“thus”).
8. **0197** A reads *Dei bonus* (“God’s good [servant]”).
9. **0197** 3 omits the first *jam* (“already”) in *aut jam accepisse* (“either already to have received”).
10. **0197** A, 4, and 4a omit the second *jam* in *aut jam accepturum* (“or already about to receive”).
11. **0197** 3 reads *planctu* (“by lamentation”).
12. **0197** 3 has *yskyros*; 4 and 4a *yscbyros*, for the lament’s Greek *ischyros* (“strong”).
13. **0197C** Greek *ἴσχυρος*: “strong.”
14. **0197** 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a read *ciebat* (“was stirring”).
15. **0197** A *podiandro*; 3 *polyandrio* (“many-men/tomb”).
16. **0197** A abbreviates *famula Dei devota* (“a devoted handmaid of God”).
17. **0199** 4 reads *Bracizlaum*.
18. **0199** 2 reads *Bozsey*, and so thereafter.
19. **0199** *dux* (“duke”) is erased in A and absent in 3.
20. **0199** 2 has *sanctior* (“holier”) in the text, corrected in an old margin to *sontior* (“more guilty”).
21. **0199** 4 and 4a read *legatos* (“envoys”).
22. **0199** A, 2b, 3, 4, 4a read *olim sibi a caesare* (“formerly to him by the emperor”).
23. **0199** 2b, 3, 4, 4a read *Cyllenia*.
24. **0199** A reads *dolet* (“grieves”).
25. **0199** A has a reading deleted and supplied above by another hand.
26. **0199** A reads *liquerat* (“had left”).
27. **0199** 2 reads *Christi* (“of Christ”).
28. **0199** A has *Mill. CII* (“1102”), falsely.
29. **0199** A reads *in* (“in”).
30. **0199** 4 and 4a omit *gratiam suam* (“his favour”) after Borivoy’s reluctant concession.
31. **0199** 2 *Liutomierziczie*; 3 and 4a *Lutomiricae*.
32. **0199** 4 and 4a read *adiit* (“approached”).
33. **0199** 2 reads *salutat* (“greets”).
34. **0199** 2 omits *injuste* (“unjustly”) in the request for restoration.
35. **0199** A corrects *praeereptum* to *praereptum*; 2, 2a, 2b, 4a retain *praeereptum* (“snatched away”).
36. **0199C** The editor says these men plainly were not brothers; see Pubitschka IV.101 on this manner of speaking.
37. **0199** A corrects marginal *sibi tradat* (“may hand over to him”) from *tradit* (“hands over”).
38. **0199** 4 and 4a have *disertum valde* (“very eloquent”), omitting *legatum* (“envoy”).
39. **0199** 4 and 4a read *Neussa*.
40. **0199** 4 and 4a omit *filium* (“son”) in “Neusse by name, son of Dobremil.”

She bore and hung the tender newborn at her breast [Note: [Col. 0207] “named Wacezlaus” added by 4, 4a.]. For him King Henry sent after five months, lifted him from the sacred font of baptism, and called him Henry after his own name. Sending him back to his father [Col. 0208A] [Note: [Col. 0207] “his own” added by 4, 4a.], he remitted to his godfather Suatopluk the entire debt, namely 3,000 talents, and ordered him to be ready to join him on an expedition against the savagery of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0207D] Álmos, expelled by his brother King Coloman, had sought help from Henry V; cf. Ekkehard of Aura.]. At the request of certain Germans, he had resolved to go there and avenge the slaughter of the Jerusalemites, whom that people, because of its cruelty [Note: [Col. 0207] *credulitatem*, “credulity,” corrected to *crudelitatem*, “cruelty,” in A.], had in part killed by the sword and in part reduced to their own slavery [Note: [Col. 0207] “their own” added by 4.].

And now, in September, while Duke Suatopluk was staying with the king in Pannonia near the city of Possen [Note: [Col. 0208D] Pressburg; see Henry V’s diploma, issued there on 29 September 1108, Boelimer 1991. Ekkehard calls it the fortress of Bresburg; Otto of Freising, VII.13, Posonium.], Borivoy entered Bohemia with the Poles as an enemy. Wacko [Note: [Col. 0207] Waczkone 2; Veckone 3; and so thereafter.] and Mutina, together with their garrisons, were put to flight from the fortress which had been strongly established toward the Polish frontier; for, when Duke Suatopluk departed, he had entrusted all his care to these two and had set them over all men as protectors of Bohemia [Col. 0208B]. When Wacko saw that his companion Mutina was neither fighting fiercely nor resisting the enemy manfully at the fortress, he concluded from this circumstance that Borivoy was entering Bohemia by Mutina’s counsel. He immediately sent one of his knights secretly to report all this to Duke Suatopluk. Likewise he equipped another knight with deceit and sent him into Duke Borivoy’s camp. Prepared for either outcome,

> To practise deceits alike, or to yield to death.  
> [Note: [Col. 0208D] Virgil, *Aeneid* II.62.]

Coming to the aforesaid Duke Borivoy, he pretended that he had fled [Note: [Col. 0207] *aufugisse*, “fled away,” 4.] from Duke Suatopluk’s camp; he announced that Suatopluk had now [Note: [Col. 0207] “him now,” A.] returned from Hungary, and affirmed under oath that on the following day he would fight them [Note: [Col. 0207] “into the fortress,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0207] *confirmans*, “affirming,” 4; “through” omitted.]. Terrified by these lies [Note: [Col. 0207] omitted by 4.], they returned that same night to Poland.

When he heard this [Col. 0208C], King Henry is said to have told his godfather Suatopluk: “Unless I avenge your wrongs upon the Poles, may I always be thought more worthless than cast-off seaweed” [Note: [Col. 0207] omitted by 2, 2b.] [Note: [Col. 0208D] Virgil, *Eclogues* VII.42.].

Meanwhile Suatopluk, ablaze with anger, while absent ground his teeth against absent Mutina, flashed with his eyes, and sighed deeply. He could scarcely await the day on which to pour out his wrath upon him. He thought it too little merely to punish Mutina; already, with dreadful promises [Note: [Col. 0207] *praemissis*, “previously made,” 4a.] and an oath, he bound himself to extinguish that whole lineage with the sword as one extinguishes a lamp. And because he had certain of them before his eyes in his own service [Note: [Col. 0207] A: another hand in the margin, *se*; 2, *se*; 2b, *se*, with *sibi* written above and perhaps *suo* added in the margin; 3, *sibi*; 4, 4a, *suo*.], he grieved in his heart, but presented a cheerful face [Note: [Col. 0207] *ylarem* 1; *hilari* 2b.] to everyone.

As he approached afterwards, at the very edge of the forest near the town of Lutomisl [Note: [Col. 0207] Liutomysl 2; Luconis 3; Lutomizl 4, 4a.], Wacek [Col. 0209A] and Mutina met him. On that day Mutina was informed three times by his friends that, unless he fled, he would beyond doubt lose either his life or his eyes. But because his fate was now pressing upon him, his friends’ words seemed to him like ravings [Note: [Col. 0209] *liramenta* 3.]. “He is not,” he said, “a brave man who fears the fate of death.”

### 23

But when they entered the fortress of Wratizlau [Note: [Col. 0209] Vratizlu 1; Wratislai 3.] [Note: [Col. 0209D] Wratislaw, not far from the town of Hohenmaut.], on the following day, early in the morning, he summoned all the magnates to an assembly. When they had gathered together, just as a lion released from its cage stands roaring in the theatre and, its mane erect, awaits food, so Suatopluk entered the hall and sat in the middle on the block of the stove, more inflamed with rage than the stove which is kindled by flame [Note: [Col. 0209] *quae*, “which [feminine],” 3.]. Looking around at them all, and fixing Mutina with fierce eyes, he opened his mouth in indignation as follows [Col. 0209B] [Note: [Col. 0209D] Cf. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII.190.]:

“O race detested and offspring hateful to the gods! O worthless sons of Vrisovici [Note: [Col. 0209] Wrisowici 1; Wrissevici 2b; Wersovici 3; Wrssowic 4, 4a.], hereditary enemies of our family! Shall it ever pass from my memory what you made of my great-grandfather Jaromir on Mount Veliz [Note: [Col. 0209] Weliz 1, 2.]—sport indeed for you, but everlasting mockery for us [Note: [Col. 0209] *quidem*, “indeed,” 2.]? [Note: [Col. 0209D] (705), I.34.] Shall I forget that you and your brother Bosey, by wicked treachery [Note: [Col. 0209] *malicia*, “wickedness,” 1.], killed my brother Bracizlaus [Note: [Col. 0209] omitted by 3.] [Note: [Col. 0209] supplied above the line by another hand in A, in place of Bolezlaus.], that outstanding star among rulers in the whole world? [Note: [Col. 0210D] III.13.] And what had my brother Borivoy deserved, who ruled under your power and obeyed you in every respect as though he were your own purchased slave? Yet, because of the pride innate in you, you could not endure the duke’s moderation; and you harassed me with all your accustomed cunning, until I yielded to your wicked counsels and grievously sinned against my brother Borivoy [Col. 0209C], because [Note: [Col. 0209] *quod*, “because,” 2b.] I deprived him of his throne. This is the one thing that pains me and will pain me for ever.

“Listen still once more, O my magnates, to what this son of iniquity and head of all impiety, this Mutina, has done—Mutina whom I lately, when I was going with you [Note: [Col. 0209] *veni*, “came,” 3.] on campaign, left behind me as second governor and commander of the rest of this land. That worthy man, pretending to go hunting [Note: [Col. 0209] *se* omitted by 3; *ire* omitted by A, 2, 2b, 4.], did not fear to go by night into Poland, to the town of Zvini [Note: [Col. 0209] Swidnicz 2; Zwini 2b, 4; Swini, with *noctu ire* repeated before *Swini*, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0210D] Schweidnitz.], in order to devise with his uncle Nemoy how he might drive me from the throne.”

A confused murmur arose [Note: [Col. 0209] *confissum*, “confessed,” A.], and by their assent they made the duke’s angered mind burn ever more fiercely [Col. 0210A]. Then the duke [Note: [Col. 0209] “Suatopluk” added by 4, 4a.], giving a sidelong signal to Iictor, who stood by and knew of his undertaking [Note: [Col. 0209] *ex obliquo*, “sideways,” omitted by 2b.], went outside [Note: [Col. 0209] *exit*, “goes out,” 2, 3, 4.]. Iictor immediately rushed upon Mutina, who feared nothing of the kind.

O wondrous patience of the count! At two blows he sat unmoving; at the third, when he tried to rise [Note: [Col. 0209] *fugere*, “flee,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0209] repeated and deleted in A.], he was struck in the head. At the same hour and in the same hall, Unezlav [Note: [Col. 0209] Unislaw 2; Uinzlau 2b; Unislau 3; Unizlau 4; Unizlaw 4a.], Domasa [Note: [Col. 0209] Domassa 2, 4; Damassa 3.], and Mutina’s two sons were seized. But Neusa [Note: [Col. 0209] Neussa 1, 4; Neusse 3.], who was of another people but very close to Mutina, saw what was happening and fled. He would have escaped [Note: [Col. 0209] *et* corrected by another hand to *ut* in A; *ut* inserted by 2, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0209] *aufugerat*, “had fled,” 2b, 3, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0209] *jamque*, “and now,” A.] [Note: [Col. 0209] *fugerat*, “had fled,” A.] through the thickets outside the town, had not his red tunic made him conspicuous. He was immediately captured and deprived of his eyes and penis [Note: [Col. 0209] passage from “who” to “deprived” omitted in A.].
