And as often happens when a bloodthirsty wolf bursts into a sheepfold: it rages, slaughters, and does not quell its fury or cease from killing [Note: [Col. 0209] omitted by 4, 4a.] until [Col. 0210B] [Note: [Col. 0209] *quomodo*, “how,” 4.] it has killed all the sheep—so Suatopluk, no longer mindful of the killing of one man, flared into rage and ordered that all that people, without distinction of age and without delay, should be beheaded. Standing amid the company of counts, he said: “Whoever does not shrink from carrying out my commands shall receive a great mass of gold. But whoever kills Bosey and his son shall receive a hundredfold and possess their inheritance.”

No more swiftly do the winds fly forth when their king Aeolus [Note: [Col. 0209] *eolus* 1.] pierces with his spear the sides of the mountain [Note: [Col. 0210D] Virgil, *Aeneid* I.81.] beneath which they are held imprisoned [Note: [Col. 0209] omitted by 3.], than the magnates Vacula [Note: [Col. 0209] Vacl’a, which should be read Vacula, 2; Wacula, the rest.], Hermannus, Kirassa [Note: [Col. 0209] Kyrassa 1, 2; Kraissa 4, 4a.], and very many others leapt upon their horses [Note: [Col. 0209] *eos*, “them,” 2.] and sped with winged [Note: [Col. 0209] *perpeti*, “enduring,” 3, 4, 4a.] course to the doom of Bosey and his son. The rest ran over the country and searched, to remove that whole race from the midst [Note: [Col. 0209] omitted in A.].

### 24

[Col. 0210C] Meanwhile, Bosey in the village of Lubic—alas, ignorant of his doom—sat down to dine with his son and wife [Note: [Col. 0209] *prandendum*, “to dine,” 4.]. A boy came and said: “Look, lord, many men are running hastily and in disorder across the field.” But he said: “They are returning from the campaign; let them come to us with God’s blessing” [Note: [Col. 0209] “let them come … blessing” omitted by 2b.]. As he spoke, behold, the savage [Note: [Col. 0209] *trunculentus*, 2, 4a.] Kyrasa [Note: [Col. 0209] Kirassa 1, 4.] opened the doors and, flashing his drawn sword, cried [Note: [Col. 0209] “saying” added by 4, 4a.]: “Come out, criminal! Come out, you who have wickedly gathered allies, for you killed my kinsman Thomas without cause in the season of Lent.”

His son Boruth [Note: [Col. 0209] Boruch 3.] rose and said: “What are you doing, brothers? If we have been ordered to be taken, we can be taken without weapons and disturbance.” But, unsuspecting, he received the sword [Col. 0211A] up to the hilt [Note: [Col. 0211] omitted by 2b.] through the middle [Note: [Col. 0211] *medium*, “middle [neuter],” 4.] of his belly. Without delay, the father too received the sword in his throat, still wet with his son’s blood [Note: [Col. 0211] *madantem*, 2; *madente nati sanguine*, “wet with the son’s blood,” 4a.].

But those attackers, like conquerors of cities [Note: [Col. 0211] *in*, “in,” added by 1.] [Note: [Col. 0211] *impugnatores*, “attackers,” 2.], plundered immense treasures; and, as Cato says:

> What is gained over a long time slips away in a brief moment.

For of such great riches not even one garment remained with which their bodies might be covered [Note: [Col. 0211] *ita*, “thus,” 1; *jamque*, “and now,” the rest.]. But Bosey [Note: [Col. 0211] Bosei 1.] and his son Boruth [Note: [Col. 0211] “his son,” A.] were thrown naked into a ditch like beasts of burden, without coffin or funeral rites, on 27 October [6 Kalends of November; Note: [Col. 0211D] Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.].

I was unable to learn how many heads of that people were given over to death, because they were killed neither in one day nor in one place. Some were led into the marketplace and slaughtered like brute animals; others were beheaded on Mount Petrin [Col. 0211B] [Note: [Col. 0211] Petrzin 2.] [Note: [Col. 0211D] Mount St Lawrence near Prague.]; many were massacred in houses or in streets [Note: [Col. 0211] omitted in A.]. What should I say of the death of Mutina’s sons, whose death appeared more cruel than every death [Note: [Col. 0211] *omnium*, “of all,” 2b.]? They were boys of good disposition, handsome in face, lovable to behold [Note: [Col. 0211] *justi*, “just,” 2.], such as neither a skilful craftsman can fashion in white ivory nor a painter portray on a wall. We saw them dragged pitiably into the marketplace, often crying [Note: [Col. 0211] “and weeping” added by 4, 4a.], “Mother mine! Mother mine!” while the bloody executioner [Note: [Col. 0211] *artifex*, “craftsman,” A, 1.] killed both, like piglets, under the armpit with a knife [Note: [Col. 0211] *cutello*, A.].

> All fled away, beating their breasts, lest they should see [Note: [Col. 0211] *videant*, “may see,” A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] the executioner committing so cruel a deed.

The rest who survived of that race concealed themselves in flight: some in Poland, others, fleeing, in Pannonia. Although their destruction and dispersal [Col. 0211C] [Note: [Col. 0211] *dissidio*, “division,” 2b.] provide ample [Note: [Col. 0211] *apostolicam*, “apostolic,” 1.] material for writing, lest we seem to have unfolded a tragedy with a goatish song [Note: [Col. 0211] *yrcino*, “goatish,” 1.], let us return from our slight digression to the chronicle [Note: [Col. 0211D] Compare what Dodechinus, under 1108, and the monk of Pegau report of this race’s most cruel slaughter. Dodechinus testifies that three thousand men were killed; the Pegau monk maintains that it was done at Henry V’s counsel.].

### 25

It happened, after King Henry had returned from the city of Possen when the siege had been lifted, that King Coloman of Hungary [Note: [Col. 0211] Colomannus 1, 2b; Cholomannus 3; Colmannus 4.] shortly afterwards, wishing to avenge on Duke Suatopluk the injuries inflicted upon him, entered Moravia and began to lay it waste as an enemy. For while King Henry, intent upon warfare, was besieging the city of Possen on every side [Note: [Col. 0211] *obsidionem*, “siege [accusative],” 4.], the aforesaid duke with his Bohemians had left nothing unburned on this side of the River Vag [Note: [Col. 0211] Wag 2.], from Trencinopolis [Note: [Col. 0211] Atrentinopolim 2; a Trentinoplim 2b; Atrenemopolim 3; a Trencinopolim 4.] [Note: [Col. 0212D] Trenczin.] as far as the point where the aforesaid river flows [Note: [Col. 0211] *influit*, “flows,” 2, 3, 4, 4a.] into the Danube [Col. 0212A].

The same duke had often seized scouts or spies sent by the Pannonian king [Note: [Col. 0211] *faculatores*, 2.] and deprived them of nose and sight. Likewise, one day he learned in advance that more than a thousand men, selected [Note: [Col. 0211] omitted by 2.] [Note: [Col. 0211] *electos*, “selected [accusative],” 2.] soldiers sent by the aforesaid king for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0211] *ad haec*, “for these things,” 2.] were hiding among marshes [Note: [Col. 0211] *palludes*, 1.]: they were to seize by ambush either foraging shield-bearers [Note: [Col. 0211] thus corrected in A; *seurarios* 1, 4a; *scrutarios* 2, 2b, 3, 4.] or unsuspecting Germans by night. Suatopluk suddenly fell upon them and ordered all, to the last man, caught like fish in a cast net, to be killed or hung on the rack [Note: [Col. 0211] “he ordered some killed, others hung on the rack,” 3.]; but to a few he granted life after receiving a large payment.

Because of such acts and others of the same kind, by which Duke Suatopluk had afflicted the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0211] *afflicxerat*, 1.], when he heard that King Coloman had invaded Moravia, he immediately assembled [Col. 0212B] [Note: [Col. 0211] present tense, *coadunat*, 2b, 3.] both the army of Bohemia and that of Moravia. As he hastened through a dark forest at night, burning to surprise the enemy secretly and join battle with him on the following day, among so many thousands of soldiers [Note: [Col. 0211] *milium*, 1.] hurrying with him, a remarkable thing happened: a broken branch projecting badly into the pupil [Note: [Col. 0211] *puplla*, 1.] of the duke’s eye became lodged so firmly that, when the shoot was scarcely drawn out together with the eye, they lifted the duke up half-dead. The army returned sorrowfully home on the day before the Ides of November [12 November].

### 26

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1109, on 23 January [10 Kalends of February], because a great frost had set in and all waters were completely frozen, Duke Suatopluk, his wound healed after the eye had been removed, immediately assembled an army again [Col. 0212C] [Note: [Col. 0211] “assembled again,” A, A*.]. For three days and three nights he hurried without stopping, entered Hungary, and, before any of its inhabitants knew, unexpectedly arrived with his army at the city of Nitra [Note: [Col. 0212D] Neitra.]. He would have burst into it [Note: [Col. 0211] *irruisset*, “would have rushed in,” 3.], had not the guards who were always posted there shut the gate. After laying waste and setting fire to its suburb, they encountered companies of many persons fleeing in carts and on horses toward the aforesaid city. They gathered them all together like sheaves in a field [Note: [Col. 0211] *agris*, “fields,” 4.], burned their villages, devastated the entire region [Note: [Col. 0211] *reg. illa*, A.], and returned joyfully to their own homes, laden with a very great abundance of beasts of burden and other things [Note: [Col. 0211] *capia* corrected by another hand to *copia*, “abundance,” 1.].

### 27

In the same year the most excellent King Henry [Note: [Col. 0211] “king most excellent,” A.] [Note: [Col. 0213] “Henry” omitted by 3; “king” omitted by 4a.], remembering his anger and indignation against the duke of Poland named Bolezlaus, and remembering the promise which he had made to his godfather Suatopluk [Note: [Col. 0213] Zuatoplyk 1.] near the city of Possen [Note: [Col. 0213] Bossen 3.], as we related above, set out through Saxony. He took with him Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0213] Bavarios 1, 2b, 3.] as well as Alemanni [Note: [Col. 0213] *Alamnnos*, with *a* written above by another hand in A; Almannos 2; Alemannos 2b.] and East Franks, and those who live about the Rhine, from Cologne of Agrippina to the western boundaries of his empire. Nor were the Saxons, harder than rocks, absent, with their long spears [Note: [Col. 0213] *austis* corrected to *hastis*, “spears,” 1.].

When the Bohemians had also joined them, he entered Poland in September [Note: [Col. 0213D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1109. Yet Henry had already crossed the Oder on St Bartholomew the Apostle’s Day, 24 August, according to Martin the Pole.] [Note: [Col. 0213D] See Martin the Pole, *Chronicle* III.82, and the excursus on Henry V’s expedition into Poland, no. 10, in Roepell I, 669.]. Having established a siege around its first town, Glogov [Note: [Col. 0213] Glogow 2; Glogou 4.], he ravaged the land [Col. 0214A] [Note: [Col. 0213] omitted by 2, 4a.] on both sides of the River Oder, from that town to the castle of Recen [Note: [Col. 0214D] Ritschen.], and then returned to camp with great booty.

There, when he had decided that on the following day he would dismiss Duke Suatopluk and his army, they spent the whole day until nightfall on royal business [Note: [Col. 0213] *duxerunt*, 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]. Meanwhile, a certain knight, bolder than the boldest [Note: [Col. 0213] *audacissimus*, “very bold,” 1.], came into the camp. As we later heard from those reporting it, he had been sent by John, son of Csta [Note: [Col. 0213] Cysta 1, 2, 2b.], of the race of Wrissovici [Note: [Col. 0213] Wrissovic 1; Vrssevicz 2; Werssevic 2b; Warsovici 3; Wrssowic 4.] [Note: [Col. 0214D] The *Chronicle of Pegau* states that he was sent by Count Wipert of Groitzsch.]. Ready either [Note: [Col. 0213] *utroque*, “either [ablative],” 4, 4a.]

> To win a fame acquired by great daring,  
> [Note: [Col. 0213] “To win” omitted in A.]  
>
> Or to lose this life together with the duke’s death,  
> [Note: [Col. 0213] “Suatopluk” inserted by 4, 4a.]

he stood beneath a spreading beech [Note: [Col. 0214D] Virgil, *Eclogues* I.1.] beside the road leading to the royal court, watching for the duke’s return as he came back from the king’s court.

> When, at the first twilight of night, he saw him  
>
> Surrounded by a great company of attending knights  
> [Note: [Col. 0213] “Suatopluk” inserted by 4, 4a.],  
>
> He leapt on his horse and for a short while mingled himself with the middle of the column;  
>
> And, with the full exertion of his strength, hurling his javelin between the duke’s shoulders  
> [Note: [Col. 0213] *ingente*, “huge,” 3, 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0213] *vibrans*, “hurling,” thus corrected in A; *et*, “and,” 3, 4; *librans*, “poising,” the rest.],  
>
> He pierced his inmost breast with deadly steel.  
> [Col. 0213] [Note: [Col. 0214D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.347.]

He breathed out his spirit more swiftly than he could touch the ground—namely, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October (21 September).

> His company, not without grief, lifts his body, now bereft of life  
> [Note: [Col. 0213] *exanimem*, 2; *exanimum*, 2b; *exanime*, with *et* omitted, 3, 4, 4a.],  
>
> And weeps, and weeping carries it back to its camp;  
>
> Throughout the camp there is much tumult during the night.

[Col. 0213B] For men wandered hither and thither [Note: [Col. 0213] *balantes*, 4.], fled, and then returned, until Purcardus [Note: [Col. 0213] Purchardus 1.], sent by the king, scarcely calmed the people’s uncertain movements. But when morning came, the king [Note: [Col. 0213] “Henry” added by 4.] came to mourn over his godfather [Note: [Col. 0213] “Suatopluk” inserted by 4, 4a.]. In the presence of all the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0213] *immensis*, “immense,” 3.], he granted that they might choose as duke whichever one they wished from among their princes’ sons [Note: [Col. 0213] singular *voluisset*, 1.].

Then Wacko, sorrowful as he was, begged with tears welling up [Note: [Col. 0213] *t* by another hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 0213] *exortis*, “arisen,” A; *abortis*, “miscarried,” 2.] that he appoint Otto, brother of the slain prince, as their duke [Note: [Col. 0213] *decertat* corrected by another hand to *decernat*, “appoint,” 1.]. The king at once approved him, and the foolish people shouted *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) three times through the camp. Without delay, and with few aware of it, a son of Bugsa [Note: [Col. 0213] Bosa 1; Busa 2, 2b, 4, 4a; “son of Bussae,” 3.] named Detrih [Note: [Col. 0213] Detrisek 1, 2b, 4, 4a; Dietrzisek 2; Detrissik 3.] ran swiftly [Note: [Col. 0213] *clanculo*, “secretly,” written above by another hand in 1.] and, at first light on the fourth day, brought Otto to Prague. Wacko [Note: [Col. 0213] Uacek 1.] and all those who were from Moravia were eager to raise him to the height of the princely seat [Col. 0213C].

[Note: [Col. 0213] Two or three leaves are missing from manuscript 1; taken together with the leaves mentioned above, everything is lacking down to III.32, “his brother Wladizlaus.”]

Because they attempted to accomplish this without the consent of the Bohemians and the bishop, their rashness was thwarted [Col. 0214B], and the oaths formerly given were recited in the midst of the council. For when they enthroned Duke Suatopluk [Note: [Col. 0213] omitted in A.], all the Bohemians had confirmed by oaths that after his death Wladizlaus, if he survived, should be raised to the throne.

### 28

Amid these great disturbances of the people, Bishop Hermannus and Count Fabianus, governor in the city of Wissegrad—who excelled the rest in wisdom as well as rank—prevailed by their counsel and exerted every effort to ensure both that the oaths should remain inviolate [Note: [Col. 0213] *essent*, “might be,” 3.] and that Wladizlaus, with everyone’s consent, should possess the rights of the principate lawfully conferred. He was raised to the throne when the sun was in the ninth degree of Libra, 2 October.

It seems to me that we should for the present keep silence concerning his virtues [Col. 0214C] and glory, while he lives [Col. 0215A], lest we incur the charge either of flattery or, by writing too little of his praises [Note: [Col. 0215] *ejus*, “his,” 3, 4a.], of disparagement. Thus someone advises, saying: “Praise a duke’s virtue, but only after the prize of this life.”

But when Borivoy heard that his younger brother Wladizlaus had obtained the throne of the realm after Suatopluk’s death, he immediately came down from Poland and went into Zribiam to Wigbert, his brother-in-law through his sister. Trusting in his counsel and assistance, and also relying on the promised support of certain traitors among our own people, early on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, 24 December, he entered Prague without resistance [Note: [Col. 0215] *urbem*, “city,” omitted by 2b.]—alas, for the ruin and the emptying of many purses.

### 29

[Col. 0215B] At this unexpected turn of events, the townspeople, greatly disturbed, trembled uncertain what course they ought to follow amid the sudden shifts of fortune [Note: [Col. 0215] *trepidabant*, “were trembling,” 4, 4a.]. Many of them [Note: [Col. 0215] present in A, omitted by the rest.], whose lot was more fortunate,

> Leaving their possessions in the city with their dear children,  
>
> They flee, unable to know which camp to follow.

Many, desirous of political change, rejoiced and exulted, and insulted those who fled [Note: [Col. 0215] *fugentibusque*, A.], because, with Duke Borivoy’s permission, they plundered their goods. Bishop Hermannus, caught in his palace as though surrounded by enemies, was kept shut in by his own peaceful retainers; for they knew that he would gladly flee if he could.

Amid these divided fears of the people, Fabianus, governor of the city of Wissegrad [Note: [Col. 0215] *praef. W.*, A.], uncertain where to turn [Note: [Col. 0215] *vertat*, “may turn,” the rest; thus corrected in A.],

> Preferred to be elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0215] *audire*, “hear,” corrected to *habire*, “be elsewhere,” in A; *audire* in the rest.] rather than to see abominations close at hand;  
>
> And, leaving the city entrusted to him behind,  
>
> Having greatly lamented the commonwealth, whose care was his alone,  
>
> He stood and spoke these sad words:
>
> “Woe to you, Bohemia, which, though not so very large,  
>
> Are held in common and subject to many masters.  
>
> Of the lordly stock and male sex  
>
> There are now twice ten petty lords, unless I am mistaken.  
>
> Hence the learned poet Lucan is said to have declared:  
> [Note: [Col. 0215D] *Pharsalia* III.152: “The poverty which serves is burdensome not to itself but to its master.”]
>
> Power increased too greatly is burdensome not to itself but to the people;  
>
> For whatever madness the leaders commit, the people suffer.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0215D] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14.]

Having spoken, and, as was said above, having left the city of Wissegrad behind [Note: [Col. 0215] omitted by 4.],

> [Col. 0215D] he stayed in villages in its neighbourhood,  
>
> [Col. 0216A] suspended in fortune’s uncertainty.
>
> Meanwhile Rumour, swifter than winds and lightning,  
> [Note: [Col. 0215D] Virgil, *Aeneid* V.319.]  
>
> Fills every city with diverse reports,  
> [Note: [Col. 0215D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.549.]  
>
> And there is great tumult among the people throughout the land.

For many, lacking worthy pursuits and delighting in the novelty of events, roamed hither and thither through the villages [Note: [Col. 0215] *balantes*, 4.], laid them waste, and awaited fortune’s uncertain changes. But others, whose minds were loftier and faith purer, made for the princely seat, the city of Prague. What were they to do? Not unaware, they rushed into an open pit, and willingly or unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0215] *fide puriores*, “purer in faith,” added by A, omitted by the rest.] [Note: [Col. 0215] *volantes nolantesque*, “flying and unwilling,” A.] entered Duke Borivoy’s perilous throw of the dice [Note: [Col. 0216D] Lucan, *Pharsalia* V.7.].

He received them kindly, bound them by oaths and many promises, entrusted them to Count Gabrissa [Note: [Col. 0215] Grabissi 4, 4a.], and that same day transferred himself with others to the safer walls [Col. 0216B] of the city of Wissegrad. From there, at the first hour on the morning of the feast day itself, 25 December, he returned to Prague. He was received with a great procession of clergy, heard Mass there, and again returned to the aforesaid city.

### 30

That same night Otto, Suatopluk’s brother, and Count Wacek came from the fortress of Gradec [Note: [Col. 0215] Gradeck 3.] with three divisions of knights and pitched camp near the stream of Rokitnica [Note: [Col. 0215] Rokytniczam 2; Bruznicam 3.]. At daybreak they came to the town of Wissegrad and blocked every road around it with guards [Note: [Col. 0215] *oppitulaverunt*, with *tu* erased in A; “and they … blocked” omitted by 4, 4a.], so that no one could leave or enter [Note: [Col. 0215] “no one could either leave or enter,” 3; “no one could leave, nor could anyone enter,” 4, 4a.] to bring assistance to Borivoy.

For Duke Wladizlaus had earlier arranged to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0216C] in the aforesaid city of Gradec. But because in the meantime he was obliged, at King Henry’s summons [Note: [Col. 0215] *natione*, “nation,” 2.], to attend the royal synod at Regensburg in the octave of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0215] “of the Nativity” inserted by 2b.], 1 January [Note: [Col. 0216D] Ekkehard testifies that Henry held a conference with the princes at Regensburg on the Epiphany of the Lord.], he had instructed Count Wacek to provide, as diligently as possible, a banquet for Otto, whom he had invited to the feast.

But he himself, hastening because of the king’s command, remained with the other counts in the city of Plizen [Note: [Col. 0215] Plzen 2; Pilzen 3; Plrzen 4, 4a.] for two feast days. On the third day, when he learned what was taking place in Prague, he delayed and set aside the king’s commands; and on the feast of St John the Apostle and Evangelist, 27 December, he flew with those who had been with him at court [Note: [Col. 0215] *eis*, “those,” 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0215] *urbe*, “city,” 2b.] to the walls of the aforesaid city, but found the gates closed,

> And saw men armed and ready to fight him.

[Col. 0216D] Addressing those who stood aloft upon the battlements, he began thus: “I come to you peacefully. Recognize [Col. 0217A] me, and open your gates to your lord” [Note: [Col. 0217] *vestros*, “your [plural],” 4a.]. When no one answered these words of the duke, he grew greatly angry [Note: [Col. 0217] “Borivoy” inserted by 4, 4a.] and made many threats against them. He then turned [Note: [Col. 0217] *vertit*, “turned,” 2b.] his course across the stream Bruznica [Note: [Col. 0217] Bruzincam 2.], and, when he ascended the brow of a hill, he saw from afar [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted by 3.] a long line of armed men in the field. Wacezlau [Note: [Col. 0217] Waczlaw 2; Waceslaus 3.], son of Wigbert, was coming among them to assist Borivoy [Note: [Col. 0217D] In Wipert’s *Life* and the Calendar of Pegau only two sons of Wipert occur, Wipert and Henry, as Schwarz observes; he conjectures that the Bohemians’ Waceslaus was the Meisseners’ younger Wipert.].

Sending one of his satraps [Note: [Col. 0217] “of the satraps” omitted in A.], he investigated whether they came as enemies or in peace. But when, through a messenger [Note: [Col. 0217] *nuncium*, “messenger,” A.], each side recognized the other, the aforesaid young man was alarmed. He turned back no differently than if he had trodden upon a hard viper lurking in brambles [Note: [Col. 0217] *retrorsit*, A, 1, 2.], gathered his men into one troop [Note: [Col. 0217] *maniplum*, 2.], and said: “No avenue of flight lies open to us, nor is it hidden from us that we must, against our will, enter upon the hazard of battle [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted in A.]. Only do this: do not let them carry off this battle [Col. 0217B] [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted by 2.] unpunished.”

He spoke, and they unfurled [Note: [Col. 0217] *expendunt*, 3.] their standard, and loudly invoked Holy Mary [Note: [Col. 0217] *nimis*, “excessively,” inserted by 3.] [Note: [Col. 0217] “and St Wenceslaus” added by 4, 4a.] for aid. But the duke [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted in A.], because in his native integrity [Note: [Col. 0217] *ignatam* corrected by another hand to *innatam*, “innate,” in A.] he had always hated civil wars, held both their cry and themselves cheap, and wished to pass them by [Note: [Col. 0217] *nolebat*, “did not wish,” 3.].

### 31

Then Detrisek, son of Busa [Note: [Col. 0217] Bussae 3.], fuel of evil and instigator [Note: [Col. 0217] *inventor*, “inventor,” 3.] of crime, said: “If your own injury, inflicted on you by men less worthy than yourself, neither bites nor moves you, at least pardon us, so that you may learn whether we are living flesh or dead” [Note: [Col. 0217] *utram*, “which [feminine],” 3.].

To this Duke Wladizlaus replied: “If this is attributed not to mercy but to cowardice, this very hour you shall see [Note: [Col. 0217] plural *videbitis*, “you shall see,” A.]

> How often this my sword shall here be wielded.”

And sooner than said [Note: [Col. 0217] “Duke Wladizlaus” inserted by 4, 4a.], he seized his shield [Note: [Col. 0217] *gladio*, “sword,” in the text of 2, with *clypeo*, “shield,” in the margin.], sprang far ahead of the line, and was first to thunder into the hostile battle-line. Like a bristling boar surrounded by a pack of dogs, so [Col. 0217C] the duke, encircled by enemies, trampled some and struck down others,

> Until, wholly drenched in human blood,

he came victorious to his camp, now stationed at the foot of the city of Wissegrad, having lost only one count, Wacena [Note: [Col. 0217] Waczena 2; Wecena 3.]. Great shouting for joy arose in the camp because they had received their duke safe from battle.

But Wigbert’s son, like a snake [Note: [Col. 0217] *agnus*, “lamb,” A, 3.] which a shepherd has broken in the middle with his footstep [Note: [Col. 0217] “which a shepherd” omitted by 2.] [Note: [Col. 0218D] That is, by the imprint of a human foot, *pede*.]—the snake, lifting its head after losing its tail, scarcely crawls—so the aforesaid youth, having lost some men and had others grievously wounded [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted by 2b.],

> Deeply sorrowing in his heart, entered the lofty walls  
> [Note: [Col. 0217] *subiit*, “entered,” 4.] [Note: [Col. 0218D] Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.745.]

of Prague. [Col. 0218A] A thing like a portent: all who were wounded died.

Why should we wonder if, for one crime of the sons of Pelops [Note: [Col. 0217] *Pelei* written above *Pelonis* in 2b; Pelopis 4.], the sun hid its eyes and darkened its rays over the city of Argos, when such worse crimes have been committed between these neighbouring cities? For civil war is conducted more cruelly, where son challenges father in war and father challenges son to single combat, one man summons [Note: [Col. 0217] *scit*, “knows,” with *s* erased in A; *citat*, “summons,” 4a.] his own brother to a duel, another binds and strips his brother taken as an enemy, another cuts down his kinsman, another slaughters his friend as though an enemy. Everywhere a foul deed is done [Note: [Col. 0217] omitted by 2, 2b, 3.] and an abominable crime committed.

O Jesus, good Lord! What things do you suffer in humankind? How patiently do you wait, until you have fewer people whom you must punish according to their deserts? [Note: [Col. 0217] *habebas*, “you had,” corrected to *habeas*, “you may have,” in A.] [Note: [Col. 0217] *debebas*, “you ought,” corrected to *debeas*, “you may have to,” in A.]

[Col. 0218B] **32.** Meanwhile Duke Wladizlaus had long since sent Counts Hermann and Zezeman [Note: [Col. 0217] Thus superscribed by another hand in A, with *proposuerat* erased.] [Note: [Col. 0217] *Sazemam* in 2b, 3, 4a.] to King Henry, who happened to be celebrating the approaching feast of the Lord’s Nativity (25 December) in the city of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0217] *Celebrarat* (“had celebrated”) in 2, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.]. Promising him 500 marks of silver [Note: [Col. 0217] X in A.] [Note: [Col. 0218D] Compare above I, 35], he humbly begged him to deign, either personally or through his envoys, to restore to him the duchy [Note: [Col. 0217] 4 and 4a add “or the kingdom”] which had been taken from him by his brother Borivoy at Wicbert’s instigation. Although the king was then very angry with Wicbert [Note: [Col. 0217] Superscribed by another hand in A], he was nevertheless more inflamed by love of the promised payment; immediately raising an army, at the beginning of the year 1110 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he entered Bohemia on the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0217] “The third before the Kalends” in 3; 4 and 4a add “King Henry.”].

Sending ahead the two margraves Depold [Note: [Col. 0217] Diepold in 2, 4, 4a; Diepuld in 2b; Dipold in 3.] and Bernger [Note: [Col. 0217] Pernger, corrected to Bernger, in A; Bereng and Beringer in 2 and 4, 4a.], he ordered that, after peace had been arranged, Borivoy and his brother Wladizlaus, together with Bishop Hermann, Wicbert’s son [Note: [Col. 0217] Wigbert in 1], and the other leading men of Bohemia, should meet him at the bishop’s court in the village of Rokican [Note: [Col. 0217] Rokyczan in 2; Rokizan in 3.]. When they had arrived there according to the king’s command, Borivoy and Wicbert’s son were seized without any hearing [Note: [Col. 0217] “They were seized” in 4 and 4a]; but the bishop’s cause was found to be just, the king’s hand having been anointed with gold [Note: [Col. 0217] *Manus* (“hand”) in A.].

After this, by order of Duke Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0217] Wladizlu in 1; Wladislaw in 2; Wladislao in 3], all Borivoy’s supporters were either deprived of sight and property, or merely stripped of their substantial possessions [Note: [Col. 0217] *Antum* in A]; the rest who were able to escape this calamity fled to Zoblezlaus, the king’s son, in Poland. Among them John, son of Csta, of the clan of the Wrissovici, of whom we have spoken above [III, 27] [Note: [Col. 0218D] III, 27], was captured and, by order of Vacek [Note: [Col. 0217] *Wack* superscribed by another hand in 1], deprived of sight [Col. 0219A] and of his nose.

Privitan [Note: [Col. 0219] Priwitan in 2; Priwithan in 4; Priuithan in 4a] likewise, having been seized in the same revolt, and appearing to be the chief man in the city of Prague, had a huge mangy dog, drunk with yesterday’s broth, tied upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 0219] *Allito* in 1. The words “huge … drunk” are absent from 1, but supplied in a recent hand in the margin]. He was dragged three times by his beard around the market-place, while the dog barked and defiled its bearer [Note: [Col. 0219] *Demer dare* corrected to *demerdante* in A; *immundante* (“defiling”) in 4 and 4a, written there by another hand, which erased the old word apparently out of modesty]. A herald cried aloud: “Such honour is borne by one who repudiates the pledged faith promised to Duke Wladizlaus.” And, while the whole market looked on, his beard was cut off over a board, and he was banished toward Poland into exile.

**33.** Yet even then there were not lacking faithless men and sowers of discord, who sowed such thorns of dissension [Note: [Col. 0219] *Spinas* (“thorns”) is superscribed in A; 3 reads “sowed dissensions,” omitting “thorns.”] between the harmonious brothers [Note: [Col. 0219D] They were cousins.]—namely Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0219] “Wladizlaus” in A] and Otto—that they feared mutual plots against one another. Therefore Otto, invited by his brother [Note: [Col. 0219] 4 and 4a insert “by Wladizlaus”], was afraid to come to the feast of Easter (10 April). But after Easter, on the Kalends [Note: [Col. 0219] The third before the Kalends in 2b and 3] of May, at the third summons, Otto came to his brother Wladizlaus in the appointed village called Tinec [Note: [Col. 0219] Tinecz in 2; “Teynecz on the Hills” added in the margin of 2b for explanation; Tynec in 4 and 4a] above the little hills [Note: [Col. 0219D] Teynec on the Elbe]. There they conferred all day about various matters and, after oaths had been given and received between them, appeared to be reconciled.

But because this same Otto had forbidden us to hold a market in the village of Sekir Kostel [Note: [Col. 0219] Costel in 1], which his father and mother had granted in perpetuity to God and Saint Wenceslaus, to be held by us, servants of God and Saint Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0219] *Familiaribus* (“members of the household”) in 1], for the remedy of their souls, I was sent on behalf of the brethren and complained before the duke and his counts against Otto [Note: [Col. 0219] *Ottonem* in A]: that [Note: [Col. 0219] *Quia* (“because”) in 4a] he was extinguishing the lamp of his parents, which he ought to have kept burning [Col. 0219C]. He replied: “I do not extinguish the lamp of my parents; but I do not wish that what I know was given especially to you should be under the authority of the bishop. And now I restore the aforesaid market not to the bishop, nor to any person, but to God and Saint Wenceslaus, for you, servants of God and Saint Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0219] *Familiaribus* in 1].” Thus, after the market had been restored to us in the presence of the duke [Note: [Col. 0219] 4 and 4a insert “Wladizlaus”] and his counts, Otto returned to Moravia on the following day [Note: [Col. 0219] *Restituo* (“I restore”) in 1; “the market restored to us” in A; “to you” in 1].

**34.** Likewise, in the same year, on the third Ides of July, a general synod was summoned for all the princes of the land of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0219] “Bohemia” in A] at the court of Sacz [Note: [Col. 0219] Saczka in 1, 2b, 4, 4a; Saczska in 2; Sacska in 3], which is situated amid meadows. Otto too was summoned there and came incautiously with few men, relying greatly on the oaths recently given and received between them [Note: [Col. 0219] “And received” is absent in A]. On the third day, [Col. 0220A] when all business had already been settled [Note: [Col. 0219] Omitted in 2], Otto rose in the morning and ordered the officials in the camp to be ready with what they needed for the return journey [Note: [Col. 0219] *Praecepit* (“ordered”) in 2b]. He himself went up to the court [Note: [Col. 0219] “Court” in 4 and 4a], to receive leave from his brother.

Why linger over many words? Why do I not sooner tell what was done without delay [Note: [Col. 0219] These words are absent in 2b]? Immediately Otto was seized like a most ferocious lion [Note: [Col. 0219] “A very brave” in A] by Duke Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0219] “The lord” inserted in 4 and 4a], as though by a most gentle lamb. When his counsellors urged him to deprive Otto of his sight, he said [Note: [Col. 0219] Absent in A]: “By no means shall I imitate Duke Boleslaus of Poland, who deceitfully summoned his brother Sbigneu [Note: [Col. 0219] Izbigneu in 1 and 2; Zpigneum in 4a] under sworn pledges of faith and on the third day deprived him of his eyes. I do not wish to enter into perpetual discord with my brother; rather, I wish to punish him, so that, chastened, he may come to his senses and understand, and so that his descendants may learn that the land of [Col. 0220B] Moravia and its rulers are always subject to the authority of the prince of the Bohemians, as our grandfather of pious memory, Bracizlaus, ordained—he who first subjected it to his dominion” [Note: [Col. 0220D] Compare Martin of Gallus, *Chronicle*, and Roepel I, 260].

But what is too strong for a strong man? Behold, the strong man Otto danced amid armed hands, and, committed to chains, went with cheerful face and joyful countenance, as though invited to a feast [Note: [Col. 0219] 3 has “and from”; 4 and 4a add “rejoicing”], until he was thrust into custody in the city of Vissegrad [Note: [Col. 0219] *Custodia* (“custody”) in A]. There he is reported to have said to the soldiers who watched over him by turns:

> Friends of a lying tongue are like a bee:  
> From its mouth flows honey, but its hindmost tail stings [Note: [Col. 0219] “Its” in 4].  
> Believe that I have been deceived by such a fraud; [Col. 0220C]  
> Yet one must endure the accidents of changing fortune.  
>
> My brother does not do this to me [Note: [Col. 0219] Absent in 4], but an unjust man does:  
> Thus Wacek willed it; thus it is done, Prostey being judge [Note: [Col. 0219] Roscthey in 1 and 4; Rosciey in 3; Wsethey in 4a].  
> Those men—if I live, I shall deal with them; but for the present I shall restrain myself.

Not long afterward, when the very strong castle of Krivoplat [Note: [Col. 0219] Krziwoklat in 2; Krivoklat in 2b and 4a] [Note: [Col. 0220D] Bürglitz], in the forest beside the river Msa [Note: [Col. 0219] Mzam in 2], had been refortified, Otto was handed over there to armed guards, to be kept for nearly three years.

**35.** In the same year, while Duke Wladizlaus and all the people of Bohemia joyfully and gladly celebrated the birthday feast of their patron [Note: [Col. 0219] Absent in A; “his” in 1; “saint” in 2, 2b, 3; “most holy” in 4 and 4a] Wenceslaus (28 September), a messenger came to the duke and reported:

“While you feast here in tranquillity and safety, but your brother Sobezlaus [Note: [Col. 0219] Sobieslaus in 2; Zobeslaus in 2b and 3; Zobezlaus in 4] and Boleslaus, duke of the Poles, are devastating this land [Col. 0221A] and plundering the people like heaps of worthless harvest, I scarcely escaped alone [Note: [Col. 0221] *Efugi* (“I escaped”) in 2b] to bring you this news. Hasten on the march; shut your storehouses now [Note: [Col. 0221] *Accelerat* (“he hastens”) in 4]; leave your banquets. Mars summons you to battle; tomorrow the enemy’s armed thousands [Note: [Col. 0221] “Armed” is absent in 2 and 2b; “thousands” is absent in A] will be here.”

They immediately rose from the feast, quickly assembled an army, and met them on this side of the river Cydlina [Note: [Col. 0221] Cidlina in 1 and 2], near the village called Lucica [Note: [Col. 0221] Luczica in 2] [Note: [Col. 0221D] In the district of Chlumec]. But on the other side of the same river the Polish phalanxes advanced without pillage or burning [Note: [Col. 0221] *Incendentes* (“burning”) in A], until, reaching the town of Oldris [Note: [Col. 0221] Olokis in 4 and 4a], they came to the waters of the river Elbe. From there they sent word deceitfully [Note: [Col. 0221] Absent in 4] to Duke Wladizlaus:

> We bear no hostile weapons [Note: [Col. 0221] “Arms” in 4a],  
> nor have we come to fight, but to reconcile you with your brother [Note: [Col. 0221] “Your brother” in A; “your brother” in 2].  
> But if you are unwilling to comply with our counsel,  
> tomorrow we shall cross the river, and all else thereafter. Amen.

To this Duke Wladizlaus briefly replied:

> This year, I think, there will be no peace without much blood [Note: [Col. 0221] Absent in 3],  
> because no one comes armed for a treaty of peace [Note: [Col. 0221] Superscribed in A].  
> You will cross the river; afterward there will be no “Amen.”  
> You will cross the river, but you shall not return unpunished [Note: [Col. 0221] “Depart” in A; “return” superscribed over “depart” in 1].  
> I shall do what you say; do what else you wish.

Then, too ready to trust the enemy’s deceitful words, he and his men forded the river that night before sunrise and came to the opposite bank of the same river [Note: [Col. 0221] *Rupis* (“rock”) in 2]. When the Poles saw that their tricks had succeeded [Note: [Col. 0221] 4 and 4a insert *non* (“not”); *perfecisse* (“had been accomplished”) in 2b], they launched an attack upon the land. Ravaging it with fires and plunder, laden with immense booty [Note: [Col. 0221] “All” in 3], they pitched camp near the bridges of Criucy [Note: [Col. 0221] Crinici in 1 and 3; Cryuczi in 2; Criuci in 2b; Kruici in 4 and 4a]. Our men, however, exhausted from that night and unable so quickly to ford back across [Note: [Col. 0221] *Transvadare* in 1 and 2b; *transvadere* in 3], stood bewildered.

**36.** When Duke Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0221] Omitted in 3] understood that he had been deceived by treachery, and perceived the cowardly spirits of some of his men in fighting, anger, indignation, and conscious courage blazed up in the duke [Note: [Col. 0221] *Ducis* (“of the duke”) in 4 and 4a]. Like a powerful trumpet [Note: [Col. 0221] Added in the margin by another hand in A] which rouses soldiers to war, so his speech awakened the sluggish minds of his followers:

“O Bohemians,” he said, “once renowned by land and sea, outstanding in courage, eminent in triumphs! Now your tributaries, whom you have always made to fear, insult you while you are still alive [Col. 0221C] and devastate your land. Do you have *tilienses* [Note: [Col. 0221] *Tylienses* in 4] hanging at your thigh—mere rattling swords lacking an edge [Note: [Col. 0221D] *Tillacei* or *tiliaginei*, that is, merely noisy, lacking an edge]?্বাস Or do the Poles alone possess iron swords? Why do you still live [Note: [Col. 0221] *Nobis* (“for us”) in A, 2, 3, 4, 4a]? O everlasting disgrace to us and to our descendants! Behold, your Ceres is smouldering [Note: [Col. 0221] “Our” in 4 and 4a]; your household gods smoke up to the clouds; Vulcan rages over the whole surface of the land—and still your hearts, colder than ice, do not burn? Or, if your heart melts away, why does not at least your stomach, already languishing with hunger’s zeal [Note: [Col. 0221] *Languescet* (“will languish”) in 1 and 2], blaze with zeal for justice? Does not the lamentation and howling of women move you,

> which with hoarse cries reaches the lofty stars? [Col. 0222B]

Who does not feel with bitter heart the sobs of infants at the breast [Note: [Col. 0221] *Lactaniium* in 4 and 4a], the groans of a pregnant woman [Note: [Col. 0221] “Pregnant women” in 3], or of a wife carried off by pagans? Who can restrain tears when he sees his children, bleating like lambs [Note: [Col. 0221] *Angellos* in 1; *angelos* in 2], killed or torn from their mother’s breast [Note: [Col. 0221] “Mothers” in 1]? Yet this grief would be less grievous if such pain had not been inflicted by those less worthy than ourselves [Note: [Col. 0221] *Minis* in 4a]. Certainly, if I had only three shields, I would not today leave the double hazard of war untried.”

Immediately the duke [Note: [Col. 0221] Omitted in A; “Duke Wladizlaus” added in 4 and 4a] and the whole army, as each stood upon the bank, sought no longer for fords but leapt in disorder and swam across the water [Note: [Col. 0221] “And” added in 2b], eager to die for their country. Grief and the injury inflicted made them men. They hastened by whatever means they could, even at the cost of their lives, to shatter the enemy’s joyful triumph.

But on the following day the often-mentioned duke of Poland, crossing the stream Trutina [Col. 0222C] [Note: [Col. 0222D] Trautenau], because it is not everywhere passable, ordered his men with the booty and all the weak to go ahead. He himself, at a place suitable for battle [Note: [Col. 0221] “Open” in 4 and 4a], stood with his unencumbered horsemen, ready to fight in defence of his men [Note: [Col. 0221] “To fight” in A].

Seeing this, Detrich [Note: [Col. 0221] Detrisek in 1 and 4], son of Busa [Note: [Col. 0221] Bosa in 1; Bussae in 3; Buza in 4 and 4a], whom we have often mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0221] “More often” in 3; omitted in 4a], withdrew with the soldiers attached to his side to one place and said to them: “My brothers and fellow-soldiers, whoever has in his bodily flesh any little piece that is cowardly or afraid to die [Note: [Col. 0221] Thus in 3; superscribed by another hand in A; absent in 1, 2, 2b, 4, 4a] must either cut it off first, or [Col. 0223A] now depart from our battle-line [Note: [Col. 0223] *Abscedat* (“depart”) in 3]. For he who does not know how beautiful it is to die in arms [Note: [Col. 0223] *Est* (“is”) in A] is more worthless than seaweed.”

When he saw their spirits eager for battle—for there were about a hundred soldiers—he rushed unexpectedly upon the enemy from an exposed flank with a great charge, like a wolf that seeks secretly to burst from its hiding-place into a flock [Note: [Col. 0223] “Into” added in 4]. After about a thousand opponents had been struck down, this soldier is said, like a raging tigress, to have cut with his sharp sword through the thickest wedges of the enemy, and those opposing him on the right and left, as though they were ears of tender grain [Note: [Col. 0223] Omitted in 2], until overwhelmed by the immense force of missiles [Note: [Col. 0223] “Excessive” in 3] he fell upon a vast heap of slain.

But the Bohemians who fought in the opposing front of Mars, alas, fell into an unfamiliar flight and turned their backs. Sobezlaus [Note: [Col. 0223] Zobezlav in 1 and thereafter], with the Poles, won an ill-starred victory, because it was more than a civil war. This slaughter took place on the eighth Ides of October [Note: [Col. 0223] Omitted in 4a], and in it fell the brothers Nosizlav [Note: [Col. 0223] Nozizlav in 1 and 4; Nozislaw in 2; Nozzislau in 2b; Nozislau in 3] and Drisicray [Note: [Col. 0223] Drisykray in 1; Driskray in 2b; Driskray, with *et* omitted, in 3; Drsicray in 4 and 4a], sons of Lubomir [Note: [Col. 0223] Liubomir in 2; Labomir in 3], and very many others [Note: [Col. 0223] “Brothers” absent in A].

**37.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, Queen Svatava [Note: [Col. 0223] Zuatava in 1; Swatava in 2] labouring among her children, with Bishop Hermann acting as intermediary, and Count Palatine Wacek supporting the matter, though against his own safety [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus in A, 1, and 4; “doing” in the others], Duke Wladizlaus recalled his brother Sobieslaw [Note: [Col. 0223] Sobeslaus in 3; Sobezlaus in 4 and 4a] from Poland and gave him the city of Satec with the whole province belonging to it.

**38.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1112, in accordance with the ordinance of the ancient kings [Note: [Col. 0223] *Tum* superscribed by another hand in A.] and at the command of King Henry IV, Duke Wladizlaus sent his nephew, Bracizlaus’s son and namesake, with an armed force of 300 shields [Col. 0223C] to Rome [Note: [Col. 0223] “Region” in 2] [Note: [Col. 0223D] It is established that this had already happened in 1110; compare Stenzel, *Fränkische Kaiser* I, 630].

But since the king had gone far ahead, the aforesaid youth with his men, crossing the Bavarian Alps, found the king in Verona and celebrated Pentecost there with him (21 May) [Note: [Col. 0223D] It was in 1111, as the Hildesheim Annals and three charters of Henry V prove, issued at Verona on 19–22 May 1111. Compare Boehmer 1999–2001].

In August the king entered Rome with an immense multitude of different peoples and languages [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus in A; the other witnesses differ.], to receive the imperial insignia according to the custom of kings [Note: [Col. 0224D] Henry was crowned emperor on 13 April]. Because this same king had formerly risen against his father, Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0223] *Paschalus*, corrected by another hand in 1; absent in 3], judging him infamous, would not fulfil his will. The king immediately ordered him seized and, applying a sword to his throat [Note: [Col. 0223] *Ensis*, corrected by another hand in 1], began to threaten him with death. Fearing death, he consented to the king’s will; and on the third day, reconciled with one another, amid the favourable acclamations of all the Roman people [Col. 0224A] and clergy, he was proclaimed and installed as Augustus and emperor [Note: [Col. 0223] “And” added in 1 and 4] [Note: [Col. 0224D] This had already happened in February 1111. See the *Roman Annals*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS V, 471].

On the following day the new emperor sent the apostolic see such great gifts [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus in 1; “gifts” in the others] that, in proportion to their magnitude, they might have been believed sufficient for human greed. When these things had been accomplished, the emperor returned to Bavaria, and our countrymen returned safely to their homeland.

**39.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113 [Note: [Col. 0223] *A* added in 4a], certain men who more willingly spread vain and uncertain reports told Sobezlaus that his brother, Duke Wladizlaus, wished to seize him, Wacek the count having suggested and advised this against him. He replied: “Either I shall die, or he who plans such things shall die before I am captured.” And, so that he might think the report the more likely to be true [Note: [Col. 0223] *Crederet* (“believed”) in A; *crederetur* (“was believed”) in 4 and 4a.], at that very hour a messenger came calling him to his brother’s court [Note: [Col. 0224B] *Hora* (“hour”) in 1].

Taking about three hundred soldiers, he approached [Note: [Col. 0223] *Adiit* (“approached”) in A.] his brother’s court [Note: [Col. 0223] *Curiam* (“court”) in 4 and 4a.] with a few men, but made the rest stand armed no farther away than the distance of one stadium. There, after greeting his brother and taking a meal, the duke went ahead, ordering his brother to follow him to the city of Wissegrad. They were not far from the city, but about ten stadia away [Note: [Col. 0223] *Distabat* (“it was distant”) in A, 4, 4a].

Then Sobezlaus sent to ask Count Wacek that they might walk together along the road and converse [Note: [Col. 0223] “With him” in A]. After they had spoken a little on the way [Note: [Col. 0223] “On the way” absent in 4 and 4a], Wacek, the unsuspecting and innocent count, was struck from both sides and behind:

> His breast was pierced by three death-bearing wounds, [Col. 0224C]  
> on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of Quintilis.

Sobezlaus immediately returned to his own men and took the road intending to pass through Zribia into Poland, for he greatly feared his brother’s presence. When he had crossed the forest, Erkembertus [Note: [Col. 0223] Erkembertus in 4], commander of Donin castle, a man full of the deceptive stratagems of treacherous Sribia [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus corrected in 1; *pellacis* in A, 2, 4], met him. Pretending friendship, he promised him much [Note: [Col. 0223] “Having promised” in 4 and 4a]: that through the emperor’s favour he would obtain all the redress due to him if he came into the emperor’s presence. By tricks he humbly invited him to enter the fortress with a few companions for a meal [Note: [Col. 0223] “To eat” in A and 2]; for at that time the said castle was under the emperor’s authority.

Soon, during the meal, armed men were brought in; he shut the door upon his guest [Note: [Col. 0223] *Clausum* (“closed”) in 2 and 4a], and after a few days sent him bound toward Saxony to a very strong castle, whose name is [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0225] The name is absent in A, 3, and 4; blank space remains in 1, 2, 2a, 2b, and 4a], entrusting him to his cleric named Woudalric [Note: [Col. 0225] Odaldridus in 1] to guard. When the military companions [Note: [Col. 0225] *Nulicre* in 2] saw that their lord had been captured by fraud, some fled into Poland and others returned to Bohemia.

After one month, however, through Christ’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0225] Omitted in 4 and 4a], Sobeslaus was released by that same cleric in the following way. He was lowered in a basket by a rope tied to a column between the railings of an upper building [Note: [Col. 0225] *Ligatam* (“tied,” feminine) in 3; *ligato* (“tied,” masculine/neuter) in 4a], down the wall; and the aforesaid cleric likewise descended by the same rope [Note: [Col. 0225] *Eundem* (“the same,” masculine) in 3 and 4a], together with a knight named Counrad, son of Rivin [Note: [Col. 0225] Ritan in 2; blank space in 2a; Kram in 2b], who was also privy to the deed and had brought horses beneath the wall that same night. And just as a bird released from its cage flees and returns to the forest, so they sped away in swift flight [Note: [Col. 0225] *Celeri* (“swift”) superscribed over an erasure of *clerici* in A] toward Poland.

In the same year, in December, Duke Wladizlaus released his brother Otto from chains and restored to him the province comprising one half of all Moravia with its cities, which Otto had formerly held after the death of his brother Zuatopluk.

**40.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, in May, by command of Lord Otto, Prostey [Note: [Col. 0225] Rosctey in 1; Rosetey in 2b; Rosethey in 4 and 4a] and his son-in-law, who was called “gentle Wacek” [Note: [Col. 0225] *Cognominatur* (“is called”) in 1], of whom we have spoken above [III, 34] [Note: [Col. 0225D] III, 34], were both deprived of sight [Note: [Col. 0225] “Of their eyes” in 4 and 4a].

In the same year Sobezlaus, taking some Poles with him, came to the castle of Kladsco [Note: [Col. 0225] Kladzko in 1] and sought through many entreaties and promises to induce the citizens to open the city gates to him. When they did not consent but resisted manfully, the aforesaid young man [Note: [Col. 0225] “Sobezlaus” added in 4 and 4a], inflamed with anger, set fire to the palace situated near the wall. A contrary wind then arose, and the battlements at the top of the tower, which happened to stand in the outer defensive work near the walls, caught fire [Note: [Col. 0225] *Stabat* (“stood”) in 2, 2b, 4, 4a]. The townspeople, greatly distressed [Note: [Col. 0225] Omitted in A] and now despairing of safety, asked that a peaceful pledge be given merely for their lives and individual safety. Peace having been granted to them, they barely escaped the peril of death [Note: [Col. 0225] The words “for their lives … peril” are absent in 2b]; the whole city was burned and utterly destroyed [Note: [Col. 0225] “Was utterly destroyed” in A].

**41.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, in January, Boleslaus, duke of the Poles [Note: [Col. 0225] Belezlaus in 1], sent his uncle Wladizlaus a supplicatory letter, written in these words:

“If my prayers have power with you and obtain for your full brother Sobezlaus a place of forgiveness, I believe that the bond of our peace and friendship will be firm and lasting. For if I were entreating you on behalf of enemies [Note: [Col. 0225] “You on behalf of enemies” in A], you certainly ought to comply; how much more may I now intercede that you should be reconciled, you whom one mother bore in her womb under one heart? Indeed, when Saint Peter asked whether he should forgive a brother sinning seven times in a day [Note: [Col. 0225] *Sciscitante* (“while asking”) in A and 3], the Lord said: ‘Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven’ (Matthew 18:22) [Note: [Col. 0225] “But up to” is absent in A.]. Therefore this example teaches us to forgive our brothers as many times as they can sin against us [Note: [Col. 0225] “Can” in 2b and 3; “can sin” superscribed by another hand in A].”

Moved by these examples and prayers, or rather by the compassion toward his brother innate in him [Note: [Col. 0225] Thus in 1 and 4; absent in the others], Duke Wladizlaus in March again restored him to his former favour [Note: [Col. 0225] Absent in A; thus in 1, and “in” in the others] and gave him the city of Gradec and the whole adjoining province with four castles [Note: [Col. 0225] *Circumjacentem* (“surrounding”) in 4].

In July of the same year Duke Wladizlaus and his brothers Otto and Sobezlaus met Boleslaus, duke of the Poles, beside the waters of the river Nizam [Note: [Col. 0225] Nizzam in 3], at an appointed conference [Note: [Col. 0225] *In condictum* in A; “to the appointed place” in 4 and 4a]. Having given and received oaths among themselves, they confirmed treaties of peace. The next day, after huge gifts had been exchanged between them, they returned cheerfully to their own homes.

Meanwhile Wdalric [Note: [Col. 0225] Odalric in 1], son of Duke Cuonrad [Note: [Col. 0225] Conrad in A], having been removed from the midst of men by inevitable fate [Note: [Col. 0225D] On the Nones of January, as the Pegau calendar proves], and his younger brother Lutold having likewise been taken from this light long before, while their sons were still young in years [Note: [Col. 0225] “Their sons” in 2b], Duke Wladizlaus gave his full brother Sobezlaus the whole province with its cities—namely the territories of Brno and Znojmo [Note: [Col. 0226D] The Brno and Znojmo territories]—which their father Cuonrad had once held [Note: [Col. 0225] “The whole province” in A].

**42.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1116, the Hungarian nation, great in strength, rich in resources, exceedingly powerful in military arms [Note: [Col. 0225] *Praeponens* (“putting before”), corrected by another hand to *praepotens* (“exceedingly powerful”) in 1], and capable of fighting with any king on earth, after the death of its king Coloman [Note: [Col. 0226D] He died in 1114], sent its princes to Duke Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0225] *Intrant* (“they enter”) in 3], asking him to renew and strengthen the ancient peace and friendship with the new king named Stephen [Note: [Col. 0225] Thus in A, 1, and 4a; “that is, holy” in 2 and 2a; “namely” in 3; “and” added in A] [Note: [Col. 0226D] Stephen II]. The duke assented to their wish and promised that he would do what pertained to peace [Note: [Col. 0227] “Replied” in 2 and 4a].

They came to the brook Olzava [Note: [Col. 0227] Olzawa in 1 and 2; Olzava in 3; Olzana in 4 and 4a], which divides the kingdoms of Pannonia and Moravia. The innumerable Hungarian people had already covered the entire surface of the land in the field of Lucsco [Note: [Col. 0227] Luzko in 1, 2, 4, and 2b] [Note: [Col. 0227D] As Palacký conjectures, near Hluk, between Hungarian Brod and Ostrava], like locusts, or like the sand of the sea or drops of rain [Note: [Col. 0227] “As” in 1; absent in 3]. The duke, however, pitched camp on the other side of the aforesaid stream [Note: [Col. 0227] *Annis*, corrected by another hand to *amnis* (“stream”) in 1].

But, as Scripture says, “Woe to the land whose king is a child” (Ecclesiastes 10:16) [Note: [Col. 0227] Corrected in 1], their princes, wandering through their innate pride, returned answers to the duke’s peaceful words that provoked quarrelling rather than conveyed the kiss of peace [Note: [Col. 0227] “Returned answers to peaceful words” in A]. Therefore the duke deferred going to the conference that day. Taking this ill and suspecting that matters were otherwise, they ordered three armed legions, called *hospites*, to go outside their camp [Col. 0227B] and stand on the opposite side of the stream for their defence [Note: [Col. 0227] Corrected in 1].

Duke Wladizlaus [Note: [Col. 0227] Added in 4 and 4a], thinking that they were about to break forth to battle [Note: [Col. 0227] *Aestimans eos* (“thinking them”) in A], ordered his men to take up their arms [Note: [Col. 0227] *Rapere* (“snatch”) in 4]; and, sooner than it could be spoken, they leapt across the boundary stream against them. A sudden, unexpected, unanticipated, dreadful, and bloody battle was joined [Note: [Col. 0227] *Inprospera* (“unsuccessful”) in A; “unexpected and unlooked-for” in 4 and 4a].

In it the son of Sdan [Note: [Col. 0227] Stan in 1 and 2; Scan in 3; Szthan in 4 and 4a], whom we mentioned above, named Iurik [Note: [Col. 0227] Iurzik in 2; Turick in 3], commander of the city of Satec and a most valiant soldier, fell fighting fiercely with other nobles of that city on the third Ides of May [Note: [Col. 0227] June in 3]. But while the others turned their backs, the duke himself [Note: [Col. 0227] “Wladizlaus” inserted in 4 and 4a] was forced into flight [Note: [Col. 0227] *Compunctus* (“pierced”) in 1].

Otto and Sobezlaus, however, having four strong phalanxes [Note: [Col. 0227] *Phalanges* in 2b and 3] and receiving as many valiant Bohemian cohorts [Note: [Col. 0227] Superscribed by another hand in A; *choortes* in 1], went around a hill which happened to separate them [Note: [Col. 0227] *Circumierunt* in 3] and suddenly charged with great force upon the Hungarian camp. There the king and his nobles with the bishops, knowing nothing of the battle that had taken place [Note: [Col. 0227] *Depuna*, corrected to *de pugna* (“of the battle”) in 1], sat drinking and feasting splendidly. In short, unless Archbishop Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0227D] Of Gran] had fled more quickly with the king [Note: [Col. 0227] Omitted in A], he himself would not have escaped the danger of death.

Certainly, so many noble and common Hungarians perished there [Note: [Col. 0227] “Pannonians” in A; “Pannonians” in the other copies, with “or Hungarians” superscribed in 1] as are not reported to have perished even in the time of Saint Udalric beside the river Lech [Note: [Col. 0227D] *Life of Saint Udalric*, ch. 12, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, SS IV, 400]. The legions of *hospites* mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0227] Omitted in A; *hospitae* in 3], which had prevailed in battle even against our duke, returned from the slaughter. When they saw their own men routed, others lying in heaps, and the enemy exulting in the camp [Note: [Col. 0227] The words “exulting … camp” are absent in 2b], they took to disgraceful flight.

When they saw from afar the king’s camp [Note: [Col. 0227] “The bridge Belin” superscribed by another hand in A; Belun corrected to Belin in 1; Bebin in 3; Belin in 4 and 4a]—for the camp had already been set beyond the bridge Belim [Note: [Col. 0227] “Of the king” added in A] in the fields [Note: [Col. 0227] “Of the king” added in A]—thinking that hostile battle-lines were still pursuing them, many more fled in terror and were drowned in the river Wag. Our men, victorious, pitched their tents in their camp that night and plundered the Hungarian soldiers’ treasures, namely a lavish abundance of gold and silver vessels [the printed *ambicisaom*, perhaps *ambiciosam*, is uncertain],

> and the common people distributed the remaining goods for their own use.

**43.** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1117, on the third Nones of January [Note: [Col. 0227D] Dodechin agrees concerning the earthquake; but it was Wednesday, unless one supposes that Cosmas, following Bohemian usage, regarded the first hour of sunset as the first hour of the day; compare below, ch. 49, and Pubitschka IV, 187], when it was Thursday, at about evening, there was a great earthquake, but a far greater one in the regions of Lombardy. For, as we learned from a report, many buildings there fell, many castles were destroyed, many monasteries or shrines collapsed [Note: [Col. 0227] Corrected in 1], and crushed many people.

In the same year:

> The steadfast companion of all my affairs [Note: [Col. 0227] These two verses are absent in 5],  
> on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, Bozetecha died [Note: [Col. 0227] Bozetcha in 1; Bosetehcd in 3].

# Cosmas of Prague, *Chronicle of the Bohemians*, Book III, §§43–57

*Complete after canonical-source adjudication. Initial translation by GPT-5.6 Terra; repair by GPT-5.6 Luna; review by GPT-5.6 Terra; full apparatus and final adjudication by GPT-5.6 Sol.*

Likewise, in the same year—[Note: absent in 4, 4a; “by the will of the Almighty” inserted in 4, 4a.]—with our lord Jesus Christ always reigning, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, and by whose merciful inspiration—[Note: “who” in 2.]—Duke Vladislav remembered his brother Bořivoj, [Note: He was held in chains at Hammerstein Castle until 1116.] whose humility the Lord—[Note: “God” in 3.]—looking down from the throne of heaven—[Note: “ete” in 1.]—had pitied in his affliction and misery. For the man toward whom God shows mercy cannot fail to show mercy himself—[Note: “whose” in 4, 4a; “God has shown mercy … God” absent in 3.] Therefore the aforesaid duke, already prompted by a divine nod and doing everything on Bishop Herman’s advice—[Note: “with counsel,” A.]—sent for and recalled his brother Bořivoj from exile in December; and, satisfying him and submitting himself—[Note: “himself” in 4.]—to his authority, he again placed him on the princely throne. O marvelous kindness of a duke, but still more admirable equanimity: he is delighted neither by secular rank nor saddened when the height of honor is laid aside!

> Power, when assumed, pleased the duke; power, when relinquished, pleased him.

Who, I ask, has ever heard of deeds such as these?—[Note: absent in A.] Would that Coloman—[Note: *Cholomannus* 1; *Kolmannus* 4; *Colmannus* in the rest.]—king of Pannonia, if he were alive, might hear of them! Fearing that his brother Álmos would reign after him, he deprived both him and his son of their penis and their sight. [Note: Compare the *Life of St. Otto, Bishop of Bamberg* III.42.] But Bořivoj, not forgetful of the benefit he had received—[Note: absent in A.]—gave his brother half of his duchy, which lies—[Note: “is,” added by another hand in 1.]—beyond the River Elbe—[Note: “and,” added above the line in 1.]—and stretches northward. Although younger, he obeyed his brother Vladislav—[Note: inserted in 4, 4a.]—in all things, always anticipating him in honor—[Note: “in honor,” added in 4, 4a.]—and did nothing without his counsel—[Note: absent in 3.]

### 44. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118

In September there was so great a flooding of waters—[Note: “in Bohemia,” inserted in 4, 4a.]—as I do not think has occurred anywhere in the world since the Flood. For our River Vltava, suddenly bursting violently from its bed—ah! [Note: “ach ach” in 4.]—how many villages, how many houses in this suburb—[Note: *domos*, “houses,” in 3, 4.]—cottages, and churches it swept away in its force! At other times, although this rarely happens, the overflowing water—[Note: From the margin of an older manuscript in 2: *i.*, “invading”; through a scribe’s error, *mundans* for *i.*; 2b also reads *inundans*, “flooding,” in the margin.] scarcely touched the bridge’s decking; but this flood rose more than ten ells above the bridge.

### 45. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119

On the third day before the Kalends of August [30 July], a Wednesday, when the day had already declined—[Note: “renowned,” A.]—a violent wind—[Note: absent in 4.]—indeed Satan himself in a whirlwind—suddenly rushing from the south upon the duke’s palace in the city of Vyšehrad, utterly overthrew an ancient and exceedingly strong wall. And what is still more remarkable: although both the front and rear portions remained whole and unshaken, half the palace was torn out down to the ground. More quickly than you could break a straw, the force of the wind shattered the lower and upper beams together—[Note: *ita* in A; absent in the rest.]—with the building itself into fragments and scattered them—[Note: *discerpsit*, “tore apart,” in 4, 4a.] This storm was so powerful that, wherever it struck, it threw down by its force the forests and planted trees—[Note: “plants,” 2b.]—and everything else that stood in its way in this land.

### 46. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1120

> Now, my Muse, restrain your lip with your finger.  
> If you are wise in your learning, beware lest you speak truth—[Note: “falsehood” in the margin, by another hand, 2.]  
> If you would be wise with me, say only briefly:  
> “Bořivoj has again been driven from the summit of rule.”  
> These things happened on the fourth day after the Ides of August. [Note: “fourth,” 3.]

### 47. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121

The crops were greatly diminished—[Note: “excessively,” 3.]—because of the excessive drought that lasted for three—[Note: absent in A.]—consecutive—[Note: “contiguous,” 1.]—months, namely March, April, and May.

In the same year—[Note: From this point through the word *Zuratka*, everything is absent in 4, 4a.]—Duke Vladislav rebuilt—[Note: “rebuilds,” 2b.]—the town of Donín—[Note: *Douin*, 3.]—and likewise the fortress of Podivín—[Note: *Podwin*, 2; *Podiwin*, 2b; *Podiuin*, 3.]—which is situated—[Note: absent in A.]—in Moravia—[Note: *Moravie*, A.]—below the river Žuratka—[Note: *Zuracka*, 3.]

### 48. In the same year

Certain Germans—[Note: *Theutoni*, 2.]—within the borders of Bohemia, in the forest reached by way of the village of Bělá, built—[Note: singular *aedificavit*, 2, 2b, 3.]—a castle on a precipitous—[Note: “interrupted,” 3.]—rock. Hearing this, Duke Vladislav—[Note: corrected in A.]—took three companies of chosen knights and, suddenly attacking by surprise, captured the castle. [Note: The entire sentence from “Hearing this” through “castle” is absent in 4.] At the first approach, arrows shot from the wall wounded, though not fatally, two of the duke’s knights: Oudálric, son of Wacemil—[Note: *Odaldicus*, 2; *Waczemil*, 2; *Wacemi*, 2b; *Vecenul*, with the following words omitted, 3.]—and Olen, son of Borsa. Unless Count Albert—[Note: *Adalbertus*, 4, 4a.]—had arrived and, by many entreaties and his native shrewdness, secured the release of those Germans who were captured in the castle, the duke would undoubtedly already have ordered all of them hanged in that same forest. [Note: “the duke” absent in 2; “Vladislav” inserted in 4, 4a.]

The winter of that same year—[Note: “in the same year,” 4, 4a.]—was exceedingly windy—[Note: *ventuosa*, 2, 4, 4a.] and warm, and there was a great flood of waters.

### 49. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1122

On the ninth day before the Kalends of April [24 March]—[Note: absent in A, 1, 2, 2b, 3.]—there was an eclipse of the moon at midnight, when it was the Jewish Passover. [Note: *phase*, 1, 2, 4; *pasche*, 2b.]

In the same year:

> The holy man Herman, bright with the light of learning,  
> Met his fate fifteen days before the Kalends of October [17 September],  
> As Sunday was already dawning—[Note: *illucente*, corrected by another hand; *illucescente*, A.]—  
> On the feast of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr.

[Note: Confirmed by the *Bohemian Necrology*.]

During his lifetime he had most devoutly observed that saint’s feast, because he was descended from the town of Trajectum and from the same Lotharingian lineage—[Note: Thus A, 1; corrected by a later hand in A; *Lotharingia*, 4; *de Lothrimia*, 4a.] Holding the pontifical see for the ninth time, he ruled this church for twenty-two years, six months, and seventeen days. [Note: “VII,” 3.] He was distinguished, formidable to strangers, gracious to his household, incomparable in excellence of character: a lamp shining and burning in the world, set not under a bushel but upon a lampstand. By the word of teaching and by example he illuminated the hearts of unbelievers—[Note: “not,” absent in 3.] Although many other worthy deeds of his shine forth as deserving of narration, we leave them untouched because of the men of the present time, who themselves do no good and refuse to believe the good deeds of others when they hear of them.

Yet it should not seem absurd if we recount in reverse order—[Note: *prae-* added above the line by another hand in 1.]—what we ought earlier to have narrated. For when the aforesaid bishop—[Note: “Hermannus,” 4.]—felt his illness worsening and saw a few attendants standing around his bed—[Note: “his,” inserted in 4, 4a; *assistere*, “attending,” A.]—he groaned and said: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine; woe is me!” [Note: Thus A; “woe is me” absent in the rest.] And he fell silent.

They stood amazed—[Note: “utterly amazed,” 3.]—and silently looked into one another’s faces. Shortly afterward the bishop again opened his mouth and said:

“I ought once, when I was healthy, to have spoken these things while standing in the pulpit, which I am now compelled to confess in the agony of my spirit. For I confess that I, a sinner—[Note: “and unworthy,” inserted in 4, 4a.]—did not rebuke fellow sinners for their sin; and I not only honored but even loved those who petitioned while acting wickedly and committing offenses, although I ought to have rebuked them and, if they would not obey, excommunicated them. For after the younger Břetislav—[Note: “Duke,” inserted in 4; compare above, III.13.]—than whom there neither was nor will be a better duke—died, wickedness flourished in this land, pride sprouted, deceit, guile, and injustice put forth shoots. And I constantly grieved with sorrow that I had not been permitted to die together with the good duke.

“Woe is me! [Note: Repeated in 4, 4a.] For I kept silent; [Note: “that,” 2b.] I did not call back the apostate people, nor did I fight for Christ with the sword of anathema. Instead, through the touch of a hand with an unholy people, I allowed myself and the Christian people to be defiled, as it is written: ‘Whoever touches an unclean thing shall be unclean’ (Leviticus 22:4); [Note: *immundam*, 2; *immundum*, 2b, 3, 4, 4a.] and, ‘Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it’ (Ecclesiasticus 13:1); [Note: *inquinatur*, “is defiled,” 3.] or, ‘What agreement has Christ with Belial?’ (2 Corinthians 6:15).

“By ‘apostate people’ I mean the Jews, who through our negligence relapsed into Judaism after baptism. Therefore I greatly fear that Christ may charge this against me and cast me down into the lower hell. For in the dead of night I heard a voice saying to me: ‘You did not go up into opposition, nor build up a wall for the house of Israel, so as to stand in battle on the day of the Lord; [Note: “on the day” absent in A; “house,” 2.] and you allowed the Lord’s flock, redeemed not with gold or silver but with Christ’s precious—[Note: absent in 3.]—blood, to be polluted by one diseased little sheep and banished from the heavenly kingdom.’

“Alas for wretched me! What sort of man I should wish to be, how different from what I once was! Now I myself displease myself, because I see that I have done too little good.”

He had spoken, and immediately, as we related above:

> His spirit, fleeing into the empty air, vanished. [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.278.]

After him Megnard—[Note: Thus A, 4; *Meynardus*, 1, 2, and the rest.]—became the tenth bishop in succession.

### 50. In the same year

In March Count Bznata—[Note: *Wznata*, 2, 4, 4a.]—returned from Jerusalem—[Note: *Hieros.*, 1.]—and Galicia together, and on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November [16 October] of that same year he died. Likewise, in the same year—[Note: From “In the same year” through this point, all is absent in 4, 4a.]—honey and the vintage abounded in full measure, and the crops had grown sufficiently; but the grain did not abound in the ears. [Note: Corrected by another hand from *astris*, “stars,” in A.] This year was followed by a warm winter, and consequently in the following summer we lacked stored ice.

### 51. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123

In March Count Dlugomil—[Note: *Dlygomil*, 1, 2b; *Dlubomil*, 2.] and Gumpreht—[Note: *Gumperht*, 1; *Gumpreth*, 3.]—and Gilbert—[Note: *Gisilbertus*, 4, 4a.]—and Henry, also called Sdik—[Note: *Zdik*, 2; *Sdik*, 3, 4, 4a.]—together with others, set out for Jerusalem—[Note: *per Hierosolymam*, A.] Some of them returned in November—[Note: September, 2; in 2 a very recent hand deleted *Sept.* and wrote *Nov.* above it.]—and some died there. For Count Dlugomil—[Note: *Dlygomil*, 1, 2; *Dligomil*, 2b.]—already while returning—[Note: absent in 4, 4a; absent in A.]—died on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July]. Likewise Berthold—[Note: *Bertoldus*, 1, 2, 4.]—retainer of my son Henry, died on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August]. [Note: “died,” 3.]

I am hindered by tears and cannot utter it in writing:

> What madness, or what discord, drove brothers of one mind,  
> Like twin boars—[Note: Thus A; “bulls” written above, or “boars,” 1; “bulls” in the rest.]—into dreadful rage?

For Duke Vladislav, stirred by immense anger, took up arms against his brother Soběslav in March, expelled him with all his followers from Moravia, and restored his inheritance to Conrad, son of Luitpold—[Note: the Province of Znojmo.] He gave Otto, brother of Duke Svatopluk, the fourth part of that kingdom which had belonged to the tetrarch Oudálric—[Note: the Province of Brno.]—brother of the aforesaid Luitpold.

Soběslav fled from the presence of his brother and went to the emperor in the city of Mainz—[Note: thus 1; “in the city of Mainz,” 4; absent in the rest.]—but his affairs made little progress, for without money a man’s entreaties are vain before all kings, and the justice of laws falls silent. Then, like a wolf that, gaping, attacks a flock and, seeking prey in vain when it grasps nothing, lowers its tail and returns to the forest—[Note: A has “returns to the forest, lowering its tail when it grasps nothing.”]—so Soběslav, his cause unsuccessful before the emperor, went to Wipert—[Note: *tetendit*, “went,” 4, 4a.]—and stayed with him for seven months. [Note: A reads “remained”; the sentence is absent in A.]

Then in November he crossed—[Note: “crosses,” 2, 2b, 3.]—into Poland. Duke Bolesław honorably received him into his own household; but King Stephen of Pannonia gladly received his wife, the daughter of Duke Álmos—[Note: Her name was Adelaide. King Stephen was the son of Coloman, brother of Duke Álmos.]—recognizing her as his kinswoman.

Likewise, during Lent, almost throughout the whole world—[Note: “city,” 1.]—aerial powers, like very many stars, although they did not fall, were nevertheless seen to have fallen—[Note: “to have fallen back,” 3.]—to the earth. The Lord says something similar in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

### 52. In the same year

There was the greatest abundance in crops sown both in autumn and in spring, except that hail did harm in many places. Honey was plentiful in the open country, but very scarce in wooded places. The winter was exceedingly harsh—[Note: absent in 4, 4a.]—and snowy.

As that same year was drawing to its close—[Note: “pressing,” 2, 3; “being vigorous,” 2b.]—the final branch of Margrave Dedi’s line was uprooted by fate. [Note: Deda, 3. He belonged to the Buzici family; compare Thietmar VI.34. The last was the younger Henry, Margrave of Meissen; compare the *Life of Wipert*, chapter 11.] Emperor Henry IV, considering the margraviate of the aforesaid Dedi vacant of an heir, had granted it to Wipert’s power. But in Saxony there was a man named Conrad—[Note: Count of Wettin.]—born of the same lineage as Dedi, to whose hands that margraviate rightfully belonged. Therefore Duke Lutera—[Note: *Ludera* corrected to *Lutera* in A.]—and the other Saxons, greatly angered against the emperor, undertook war against Wipert.

### 53. In those same days

Duke Vladislav and Otto, as the emperor had commanded them, assembled an army from both Bohemia and Moravia, crossed the forest, and pitched camp beyond—[Note: “around,” 2.]—the town of Guozdec—[Note: *Guozdecz*, 2.]—opposite the aforesaid duke. The Archbishop of Mainz and Count Wipert stood on this side of the River Mulde—[Note: *Mlidava*; *Multaua*, 3; *Mildeua*, 4, 4a; the marginal form is *Mulde*.] with a heavy—[Note: absent in 3.]—armed multitude; while the Saxons, encamped between them, kept the opposing forces apart and did not allow their adversaries to come together—[Note: “saw” in 4, 4a; “nor … their own,” in the margin of 1.]

Then the Duke of Bohemia and Otto sent word to the Saxons, saying:

“We have not taken up arms against you through pride; rather, by the emperor’s command we have come to aid the Archbishop of Mainz—[Note: “chief bishop,” in the rest; the marginal note identifies him as Albert.]—and Count Wipert.
