But since those who ought to be present and to initiate the first battle are absent, merely—[Note: absent in 1.]—yield us the ground, so that we may have grounds for returning—[Note: “reporting back,” 3.]—namely, that you yielded and we stood—[Note: “and we stood,” absent in 1.]—and waited for them—[Note: “you,” 4, 4a.]—in the appointed place.”

To this Duke Lutera—[Note: corrected in A; *Ludera*, 2, 4.]—replied:

“I am astonished that you, prudent men, do not plainly perceive the stratagems by which you have been induced to take up arms in vain against us innocent men—[Note: *deprehendere*, “perceive,”; *reprehendere*, “reproach,” 1.] Do you think that the counsels of Albert, the archbishop of Mainz, lack any trickery?—[Note: *nulla*, “none,” in 4, 4a.] Have you not yet sufficiently experienced his Attic cleverness? Thus, thus Wipert is known to you: another Ulysses—[Note: *Ultres*, 2; *Ulysses*, 2b.]—who has been instructed in the tricks of that same bishop.

“Why do they themselves not come to greet us, who would gladly return their greeting? It is safer to wait at a distance than to join battle hand to hand, and to procure one’s own advantage by another’s disadvantage. Certainly any bleary-eyed man can see clearly—[Note: Horace, *Satires* I.3.25.]—what they are plotting by their guile. For they know and understand well that, if you conquer the Saxons—which you cannot achieve without great loss to yourselves—[Note: “not,” absent in A.]—or if we are able to prevail powerfully against you—[Note: *nos*, “us,” in A and the other witnesses; *vobis*, “you,” in the corrected reading.]—they will more easily invade Bohemia once it has been bereft of its defenders—[Note: *inquirere*, “investigate,” in 2.] This is what the emperor desires; this is what the Archbishop of Mainz devises—[Note: *consiliator*, “counselor,” 1.]—and thus your son-in-law Wipert always makes friends with the Bohemians.

“For your own brother Soběslav, whom Wipert recently, at your wish—[Note: “his,” 2, 2b, 3.]—deceitfully drove into Poland—unless he quickly returns to that same Wipert, let no one believe me any longer.

“We, however, want you to know that we are more ready to meet you in battle than to yield you the place.”

When they heard these deceptively composed words, the over-credulous Bohemians ravaged the district around the city of Meissen and returned home, when the sun was in the fifteenth degree of Sagittarius [24 November]. [Note: “fortress,” 1.]

### 54. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124

On the second day before the Ides of February [12 February], Herman, brother of William, and Lutobor, son of Martin—[Note: *Liutober*, 2, 2a, 4, 4a.]—set out for Jerusalem.

In the same year—[Note: From “the second day before the Ides” through this point, all is absent in 4, 4a.]—

> Duke Bořivoj, on the twice-two Nones  
> Of the month of Pluto [February], [Note: IV Nones of February, according to the Pegau Calendar and the Bohemian Necrology. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.13: “He dedicated the second month to the god Februus, who is believed to have power over purifications; for it was necessary that the city be purified in that month in which he ordained that rites be paid to the gods of the dead.” Compare Ovid, *Fasti* II.33 ff.; Plutarch, *Numa* 20; John Lydus, *On Months*, p. 68. According to the ancient Etruscans, Februus was a god of the underworld, or Pluto’s father, or Pluto himself. Grottefend.]  
> An exile in Hungary, his bodily frame dissolved,  
> Passed to Christ, whom he worshiped with a pure mind,  
> And with whom he now rejoices in the spacious court of heaven.  
>
> After all the labors of this life and world,  
> Which he endured while living in exile for fifteen years,  
> And the twice three years which he suffered shut in prison,  
> Twice raised to the throne, why twice rejected—  
> It is not lawful for me to investigate or utter such things.  
> God, who creates all things and governs what he has created, knows.  
> Let whoever reads this say: “May Duke Bořivoj now live there—”  
> [Note: Thus 1; “rest,” written above the line by the same hand, as A and the rest read.]  
> Where there is a portion and rest for holy souls. [Note: “Peace” written above *portion* in 2b; this verse is absent in A.]

He was buried in the metropolitan city of Prague, in that leap year then ending, on the day before the Ides of March [14 March], at the principal church of the holy martyrs Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert—[Note: “and Adalbert,” absent in 3, 4a.]—in the crypt of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor—[Note: “bishop and confessor,” absent in A.]

### 55. Likewise, in the Lent of that same year

On the ninth—[Note: “eighth,” A, 2, 4.]—day before the Kalends of April [24 March], Bishop Megnard—[Note: *Meinardus*, 1; *Meynhardus*, 2; *Meginhardus*, 2b.]—happened to find Podivín’s bones in the sacristy and buried them in the chapel beneath the tower, between the altar of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor—[Note: “and confessor,” absent in A.]—and the tomb of Bishop Gebhard. This man was the servant and inseparable companion in the labor and hardship of Saint Wenceslas the martyr; anyone wishing to know may learn enough about his deeds in the life of that saint. [Note: Absent in A, 3, 4a.]

For in his time Severus, the sixth bishop of this see, enlarging—[Note: “building,” written above the line by a later hand in 1.]—the chapel around the sacred tomb of the aforesaid patron, dug up the bones of the aforesaid servant, because otherwise the wall could not be founded; placing them in a sarcophagus, he had set them in the chamber where ecclesiastical gifts were kept.

Likewise, on the eighth day before the Ides of April [6 April], on Easter Day, Emperor Henry IV sent letters to all the princes and bishops of his realm, ordering them, all excuses set aside, to gather for his court on 4 Nones of May [4 May] in the city of Bamberg—[Note: *Bamberch*; *Bamberk* in the margin of A; *Babenberch*, 4.] [Note: Compare Ekkehard’s *Chronicle*.]

### 56. Meanwhile, Soběslav

Soběslav, brother of our duke, left Poland and set out with all his followers—[Note: “all his followers,” A.]—for Duke Lothair of Saxony, hoping to obtain both the counsel and aid of so great a man. He was honorably received as a guest and obtained the desired consolation of his hope. For when the aforesaid duke learned that the ruler of Bohemia—[Note: “Vladislav,” added in A; absent in the rest.]—was attending the royal court—[Note: *Wladizlai*, added in A; absent in the rest.]—he sent an envoy with his guest to the emperor, saying:

“It accords with royal power and imperial dignity mercifully to aid those who suffer injury, and royally to oppose those who inflict it with the severity of justice. You will furnish to us and all nations proof of such grace and of princely authority if, doing justice to this innocent man, Soběslav, who suffers wrong, you reconcile him to his brother.”

The emperor, greatly angered, looked upon his entire assembly and said:

“The margrave has spoken enough on behalf of imperial authority; he himself wrongs us and demands vengeance for wrong. For if, as he admits, it becomes me to avenge the injuries of others, why should I not first avenge my own? Or what greater injury can there be than that, though summoned, he did not come to our councils? Therefore let anyone whom zeal for justice and this injury stings now pledge faith upon the holy Gospels, that he will take up arms and follow me into Saxony after the feast of Saint James the Apostle [25 July].”

All the princes assented and approved, and swore to wage war against the Saxons according to the emperor’s edict.

In these same days—[Note: 22 May; this agrees with the *Life of Wipert*, chapter 12, and the Pegau Calendar.]—Wipert, son-in-law of King Vratislav, died; we have sufficiently mentioned him above. [Note: “I have mentioned,” 3.] But Soběslav, seeing that fortune and the king’s resources—[Note: *censum*, corrected by another hand in A; *census*, 2b; *censura*, 3.]—favored his elder brother more, turned aside to Wipert’s son, Henry—[Note: Wipert’s elder son had died before his father.]—in order to console his kinsman through his sister over the death of his father—[Note: *fratris*, “brother,” corrected by another hand in the margin of A to *patris*, “father.”] From there he sent Count Stephen to the ruler of Poland; for through him he arranged all his plans.

As Stephen crossed the forest lying between Saxony and Poland, he fell into the armed hands of robbers. Standing at a distance, they said to him and his companions:

“We spare you and have pity on you, and grant you your lives. Go your way in peace, but leave us your horses and all that you carry; for a few of you cannot resist or escape many.”

Stephen, unafraid, said: “Give us a little time to take counsel.” [Note: Absent in 3.] When they granted it, the count said:

“O brothers and companions, do not fear now the chance of death, the final lot of fortune. Who will break bread for us if we shamefully turn to flight? Or, after a life shamefully prolonged, who will provide us with life’s necessities? And we do not know whether these barbarians will grant us even this. Alas, too late and in vain we shall regret not having died like men, when, after diverse torments, they make us a proverb and a byword among all peoples—one of us with his nose cut off, another deprived of his eyes.”

And they unanimously said: “Let us die, let us die; but let us see that we do not die unavenged.”

When the pagans saw them arming themselves more for battle than for flight—[Note: *aptarier*, 1, corrected in 2; *aptari*, 4.]—they suddenly rushed upon them. A monstrous battle took place between five *ancilia* and fifty shields of strong men. A priest among them, to whom they had commended their souls, fled with bow and quiver. One robber, seeing the unarmed man—[Note: “seeing the man,” A.]—pursued him as he fled. But the priest, unable to escape, shot an arrow backward and struck the horse in the middle of its forehead; the horse and its rider fell backward. Thus the priest alone escaped and reported in the city of Głogów—[Note: *Gloglou*, 4.]—what had happened.

The prefect of that city, named Nozizlav—[Note: *Voyzlav*, 1; *Voyzlau*, 2b, 3; *Woyzlaus*, 4, 4a.]—hastened there with many armed men—[Note: absent in A.]—and found Stephen half alive in the middle of the River Bóbr—[Note: *Boler*, 3; *Borb*, 4, 4a; *Bober*.]—clinging to bushes. For when the barbarians saw that many of their own men had been killed and others wounded, they were greatly angered and hurled him into that river—[Note: “himself,” A.] The aforesaid prefect took him up—[Note: *suspiciens*, “looking up,” corrected by another hand to *suscipiens*, “taking up,” 1.]—and brought him and his companions, still half alive, to his castle. There Stephen died on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], a Sunday. [Note: “third,” 2b, 3.]

At this time Soběslav was staying with Wipert’s son, because after his father’s death that youth—[Note: That is, “young man,” as Schwarz observes; he had already participated in the battle of Welfesholz in 1115. Compare the *Life of Wipert*, chapter 11.]—was fiercely pressed on every side by enemies.

In July of the same year Duke Vladislav gave his firstborn daughter, named Svatava—[Note: Called Luitgard by the Germans.]—in marriage to Frederick, a man very famous among the Bavarian nobles—[Note: Count of Bogen.]—with a great display of feminine adornment and an excessive provision of wealth.

### 57. In the same year

The power of Christ, the power and wisdom of God—[Note: “of God,” absent in 3.]—governing all things by its own sustaining will, deigned in its mercy to rescue this little land from the snare of Satan and of his son Jacob Apella—[Note: That is, a Jew, from Horace: “Let the Jew Apella believe it.”] Whatever his pitch-black right hand touched, it defiled; and the breath of his mouth, fetid like that of a basilisk, killed those upon whom it blew—[Note: *afflaverat*, “had blown,” with *necat*, “kills,” omitted in 3.] Very many truthful persons also testify that Satan was often seen in human form clinging to his side and rendering him services.

Thus Satan raised him by his arts to such audacity—indeed madness—that, exceeding his proper station, this most wicked man performed after the duke the office of *vicedominus*—[Note: *vice Deum*, “in place of God,” in 3; *vicedomni*, 4, 4a.]—and this was a great chaos for the Christian people. This same man—[Note: “Jacob,” inserted in 4, 4a.]—became an apostate after baptism. At night he destroyed the altar that had been built and consecrated in their synagogue, and, taking the sacred relics, did not fear to throw them into his privy.

Duke Vladislav, full of God and zealous with Christ’s zeal—[Note: *zelatus*, “zealous,” 4, 4a.]—seized this sacrilegious and evil-working Jew—[Note: “Jew,” inserted in 4, 4a.]—on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August [22 July] and ordered him held under strict guard. Ah, how much of the mammon of iniquity was taken from the house of that deceiver and carried into the duke’s treasury—[Note: “Vladislav’s,” added in 4, 4a.]! Moreover, his fellow Jews in crime agreed to pay the duke three thousand pounds of silver and one hundred pounds of gold, lest the aforesaid bastard be punished with death. [Note: This is absent in 4, 4a.]

But the duke—[Note: “receiving this,” in 4, 4a.]—prompted by God’s grace, redeemed Christian slaves from all the Jews and decreed that no Christian should thereafter serve them—[Note: “the Jews,” 4, 4a.]—amen, amen, I say. Whatever sins he had ever committed, he wiped away all of them by this praiseworthy act and acquired for himself an eternal name:

> O pious handmaid of Christ, Mary Magdalene,  
> Her people ever faithfully offer vows to you,  
> Since on your feast they were delivered from a hostile enemy.

Likewise, in the same year, on the third day before the Ides of August [11 August], at the eleventh hour of daylight, there was an eclipse of the sun. A very great pestilence among cattle, sheep, and swine followed—[Note: “and swine,” absent in 4, 4a.]—many bees died, and there was an extreme scarcity of honey. Autumn and spring crops alike failed, except millet and peas. [Note: “The crops and peas” are absent in A.]

## Canonical apparatus, notes 91–180

91. `[Col. 0231] a verbis Eodem anno usque ad hunc locum omnia desunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit everything from *Eodem anno* (“In the same year”) through this point.
92. `[Col. 0231] ita corr. al. man. pro astris A.` In A another hand corrects *astris* (“stars”) to *aristis* (“ears of grain”).
93. `[Col. 0231] Dlygomil. 1, 2b, Dlubomil. 2.` Dlugomil is spelled *Dlygomil* in 1 and 2b and *Dlubomil* in 2.
94. `[Col. 0231] Gumperht 1, Gumpreth 3.` Gumpreht is spelled *Gumperht* in 1 and *Gumpreth* in 3.
95. `[Col. 0231] Gisilbertus 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *Gisilbertus* for Gilbertus.
96. `[Col. 0231] Zdik 2, Sdik 3, 4, 4a.` Sdic is spelled *Zdik* in 2 and *Sdik* in 3, 4, 4a.
97. `[Col. 0231] atque A.` A reads *atque* (“and”) for *et* (“and”).
98. `[Col. 0231] per Hier. A.` A abbreviates/reorders the journey as *per Hier.*, “through/to Jerusalem.”
99. `[Col. 0231] Septembri 2, in quo recentissima manus deleto Sept. supra scripsit Nov.` MS 2 first read *Septembri* (“in September”); a very recent hand deleted *Sept.* and wrote *Nov.* (“November”) above it.
100. `[Col. 0231] Dlygomil 1, 2, Dligomil 2b.` Dlugomil is *Dlygomil* in 1 and 2 and *Dligomil* in 2b.
101. `[Col. 0231] deest 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit *jam* (“already”).
102. `[Col. 0231] deest A.` A omits *in* (“while/in”) before *revertendo* (“returning”).
103. `[Col. 0231] Bertoldus 1, 2, 4.` MSS 1, 2, and 4 spell Berthold *Bertoldus*.
104. `[Col. 0231] obiit 3.` MS 3 reads *obiit* (“died”) for *moritur* (“dies”).
105. `[Col. 0231] ita A, tauros superscr. vel apros 1, tauros rell.` A has *apros* (“boars”) as printed; MS 1 writes *tauros* (“bulls”) above it with “or boars”; the remaining witnesses read *tauros*.
106. `[Col. 0231] deest 3, 4a.` MSS 3 and 4a omit the clause introducing Vladislav’s anger and arms against Soběslav.
107. `[Col. 0231D] Provinciam Znaymensem.` The inheritance is the province of Znojmo.
108. `[Col. 0232D] Provinciam Brunnensem.` The fourth part is the province of Brno.
109. `[Col. 0231] ita 1, in urbe Maguntina 4, deest rell.` MS 1 reads *in Maguntia urbe* (“in the city of Mainz”) as printed; MS 4 *in urbe Maguntina*; the remaining witnesses omit the phrase.
110. `[Col. 0231] deest A.` A omits *sed parum sua profecit legatione* (“but he accomplished little by his embassy”).
111. `[Col. 0231] deest 4.` MS 4 omits *inhians* (“gaping/ravenous”) in the wolf simile.
112. `[Col. 0231] comprehendit 2, 4a, prendit 3, 4.` MSS 2 and 4a read *comprehendit* (“seizes”) and 3 and 4 *prendit* (“takes”) for *prehendit* (“catches”).
113. `[Col. 0231] repetit silvam subm. caud. cum nil preh. A.` A reorders the words: “he returns to the forest, lowering his tail, when he catches nothing.”
114. `[Col. 0231] tetendit 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read perfect *tetendit* (“went”) for present *tendit* (“goes”).
115. `[Col. 0231] mansit A, A*, hoc loco.` A and A* add *mansit* (“he remained”) at this point, after Wipert.
116. `[Col. 0231] deest A.` A omits *per septem menses conversatus est* (“he stayed for seven months”).
117. `[Col. 0231] transit 2, 2b, 3.` MSS 2, 2b, and 3 read present *transit* (“crosses”) for perfect *transiit* (“crossed”).
118. `[Col. 0232D] Nomen ei erat Adelheidae. Stephanus rex erat filius Colomanni, fratris Almi ducis.` Her name was Adelaide. King Stephen was the son of Coloman, brother of Duke Almus.
119. `[Col. 0231] natam corr. A.` A corrects *natam* (“daughter”) to *gnatam* (“daughter/offspring”).
120. `[Col. 0231] urbem 1.` MS 1 reads *urbem* (“city”) for *orbem* (“world”).
121. `[Col. 0231] recidisse 3.` MS 3 reads *recidisse* (“to have fallen back”) for *cecidisse* (“to have fallen”).
122. `[Col. 0233] deest 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit *Hiemps aspera fuit nimis* (“The winter was exceedingly harsh”).
123. `[Col. 0233] urgente 2, 3, vigente 2b.` MSS 2 and 3 read *urgente* (“pressing”) and 2b *vigente* (“flourishing”) for *vergente* (“drawing to a close”).
124. `[Col. 0233] an. verg. A,` A abbreviates/reorders *anno vergente* (“as the year drew to a close”) as *an. verg.*
125. `[Col. 0233] Deda 3.` MS 3 reads *Deda* for the name Dedius.
126. `[Col. 0233C] De tribu Buzici cfr. Thietmar. VI, 34.` On the Buzici family, compare Thietmar VI.34.
127. `[Col. 0233C] Ultimus erat Heinricus junior marchio Misuensis. Cfr. Vita Wiperti, c. 11.` The last of the line was Henry the Younger, margrave of Meissen; compare *Life of Wipert* 11.
128. `[Col. 0233] tum al. man. 1.` In MS 1 another hand adds *tum* above the line, completing *marchionatum* (“margraviate”).
129. `[Col. 0233] quid in Sax. 1.` MS 1 abbreviates *quidam in Saxonia* (“a certain man in Saxony”) as *quid in Sax.*
130. `[Col. 0233C] Comes Wettinensis.` Conrad was count of Wettin.
131. `[Col. 0233] Ludera corr. Lutera A.` A corrects *Ludera* to *Lutera*, Duke Lothair’s name.
132. `[Col. 0233] circa 2.` MS 2 reads *circa* (“around”) for *ultra* (“beyond”).
133. `[Col. 0233] Guozdecz 2.` MS 2 spells Guozdec *Guozdecz*.
134. `[Col. 0233] circa 3, 4.` MSS 3 and 4 read *circa* (“around”) for *citra* (“on this side of”).
135. `[Col. 0233] Multaua 3, Mildeua 4, 4a.` MS 3 reads *Multaua* and MSS 4, 4a *Mildeua* for river *Mlidava*.
136. `[Col. 0233C] Mulde.` The river is the Mulde.
137. `[Col. 0233] deest 3.` MS 3 omits *gravi* (“heavy”) before “armed multitude.”
138. `[Col. 0233] videbant 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *videbant* (“saw”) for *sinebant* (“allowed”).
139. `[Col. 0233] nec---suos in margine 1.` In MS 1 the span *nec ... suos* (“nor ... their own/adversaries”) is in the margin.
140. `[Col. 0233] ita 1, archipraesuli rell.` MS 1 reads *archiepiscopo* (“archbishop”) as printed; the remaining witnesses read *archipraesuli* (“chief bishop”).
141. `[Col. 0234C] Alberto.` The archbishop is Albert.
142. `[Col. 0233] deest 1.` MS 1 omits *vos* (“you”) before *tantummodo cedite* (“merely yield”).
143. `[Col. 0233] referendi 3.` MS 3 reads *referendi* (“reporting back”) for *revertendi* (“returning”).
144. `[Col. 0233] et nos stetisse desunt 1.` MS 1 omits *et nos stetisse* (“and that we stood”).
145. `[Col. 0233] vos 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *vos* (“you”) for *eos* (“them”) in “waited for them.”
146. `[Col. 0233] corr. A, Ludera 2, 4.` A corrects the name *Lutera*; MSS 2 and 4 read *Ludera*.
147. `[Col. 0233] reprehendere 1.` MS 1 reads *reprehendere* (“reproach”) for *deprehendere* (“perceive/detect”).
148. `[Col. 0233] nulla 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *nulla* (“no”) for *ulla* (“any”) trickery.
149. `[Col. 0233] si sic 3.` MS 3 reads *si sic* (“if thus”) for repeated *Sic* (“Thus, thus”).
150. `[Col. 0233] Ultres 2, Ulysses 2b.` MS 2 reads corrupt *Ultres* and 2b *Ulysses* for *Ulixes* (“Ulysses”).
151. `[Col. 0233] nos corr. hos A, nos 1, rell.` A corrects *nos* (“us”) to *hos* (“these men”); MS 1 and the remaining witnesses read *nos*.
152. `[Col. 0233] incommodum corr. al. m. 1.` In MS 1 another hand corrects accusative *incommodum* (“disadvantage”) to ablative *incommodo* (“by another’s disadvantage”).
153. `[Col. 0233] parare 2b.` MS 2b reads *parare* (“prepare”) for *comparare* (“procure”).
154. `[Col. 0233] ita A, corr. al. man. quis 1, rell.` A has *quivis* (“anyone”) as printed; another hand corrects it, and MS 1 and the remaining witnesses read *quis* (“who/anyone”).
155. `[Col. 0233] lippus est 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read singular *lippus est* (“is bleary-eyed”) for plural/ablative *lippis* (“to bleary eyes”).
156. `[Col. 0233] prospicere 3.` MS 3 reads *prospicere* (“look forward/see”) for *perspicere* (“perceive clearly”).
157. `[Col. 0234C] Hor., serm. I, 3, 25.` Compare Horace, *Satires* I.3.25.
158. `[Col. 0233] quod 2b.` MS 2b reads *quod* (“that/which”) for interrogative *quid* (“what”).
159. `[Col. 0233] deest A.` A omits *non* (“not”) in “which you cannot [achieve].”
160. `[Col. 0233] non A. h. l.` A reads *non* (“not”) at this locus in the loss clause; the note’s *h. l.* means “in this place.”
161. `[Col. 0233] Sacxones 1.` MS 1 spells Saxons *Sacxones*.
162. `[Col. 0233] ita corr. 1, nos A. et rell.` MS 1 has corrected *vobis* (“against/over you”) as printed; A and the remaining witnesses read *nos* (“us”).
163. `[Col. 0233] poter 1.` MS 1 reads incomplete *poter* for *potenter* (“powerfully”).
164. `[Col. 0233] corr. A.` A has a correction at *Boemiam* (“Bohemia”); no rejected form is supplied.
165. `[Col. 0233] inquirere 2.` MS 2 reads *inquirere* (“investigate”) for *invadere* (“invade”).
166. `[Col. 0233] consiliator 1.` MS 1 reads *consiliator* (“counselor”) for verb *consiliatur* (“devises/takes counsel”).
167. `[Col. 0233] tuus 4.` MS 4 reads *tuus* (“your”) for *suus* (“his”) before Soběslav.
168. `[Col. 0233] ad A.` A reads *ad* (“according to/toward”) for *ob* (“because of/at”) before “your wish.”
169. `[Col. 0233] suam 2, 2b, 3.` MSS 2, 2b, and 3 read *suam* (“his own”) for *tuam* (“your”) wish.
170. `[Col. 0233] arce 1.` MS 1 reads *arce* (“fortress”) for *parte* (“degree/part”) in the Sagittarius date.
171. `[Col. 0233] Liutober 2, 2a, 4, 4a.` MSS 2, 2a, 4, 4a spell Lutobor *Liutober*.
172. `[Col. 0233] a verbis II. Idus usque ad hunc locum omnia desunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit everything from *II. Idus* (“the second day before the Ides”) through this point.
173. `[Col. 0233] Boemomorum inserunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a insert corrupt *Boemomorum* (“of the Bohemians”) after *Dux* (“Duke”).
174. `[Col. 0234C] 4. Non. Febr. testibus Kalendario Pegaviensi et Necrologio Bohemico. K.---Macrob. Saturn. I, 13: Secundum (mensem) dicavit Februo deo, [Col. 0235C] qui lustrationum potens creditur; lustrari autem eo mense civitatem necesse erat, quo statuit, ut justa diis Manibus solverentur. Cf. Ovid., Fast. II, 33, sq.; Plut. Numa 20, Joanne Lydo auctore (de mens. p. 68.) Februus apud veteres Etruscos deus inferiorum erat, aut pater Plutonis, aut idem qui Pluto. GROTTEFEND.` The Pegau Calendar and Bohemian Necrology attest *IV Nonas Februarii*, “the fourth Nones of February.” Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.13 says the second month was dedicated to Februus, god of purifications, because the city had to be purified when rites were paid to the dead. Compare Ovid, *Fasti* II.33ff.; Plutarch, *Numa* 20; John Lydus, *On Months*, p. 68. Among ancient Etruscans Februus was god of the underworld, Pluto’s father, or Pluto himself; Grottefend.
175. `[Col. 0233] compaga corr. al. man. compage 1.` In MS 1 another hand corrects *compaga* to ablative *compage* (“frame/bond”).
176. `[Col. 0233] saluta corr. al. man. soluto 1.` In MS 1 another hand corrects *saluta* to *soluto* (“dissolved/released”), differing from printed feminine *soluta*.
177. `[Col. 0233] omnis 4a.` MS 4a reads singular *omnis* (“every”) for plural *omnes* (“all”) labors.
178. `[Col. 0233] quo 1.` MS 1 reads singular *quo* (“which”) for plural *quos* (“which [labors]”).
179. `[Col. 0233] ita 1, 4. 4a. supersc. eadem. m. 1. in textu sex annos; ita quoque A. et rell.` MSS 1, 4, 4a have *bis ternos* (“twice three”) as printed; in 1 the same hand also writes it above the text’s *sex annos* (“six years”), the reading of A and the remaining witnesses.
180. `[Col. 0233] turbis 2b. his 3.` MS 2b reads *turbis* (“by disturbances”) and 3 *his* (“by these”) for *cur bis* (“why twice”).

## Canonical apparatus, notes 181–271

181. `[Col. 0233] reprobatur 3.` MS 3 reads present passive *reprobatur* (“is rejected”) for perfect participle *reprobatus* (“having been rejected”).
182. `[Col. 0233] ita A. scrutari superscr. vel rimari 1. eadem manu scrutari rell.` A reads *rimari* (“investigate”) as printed; in 1 the same hand writes *scrutari* (“examine”) above it with “or rimari”; the remaining witnesses read *scrutari*.
183. `[Col. 0233] ita 1. superscr. ead. man. loco requiescat, quod A. et rell.` MS 1 reads *ibi vivat* (“may he live there”) as printed, with *loco requiescat* (“may he rest in the place”) above it by the same hand; A and the rest read the latter.
184. `[Col. 0233] super vocem pars adscriptum pax 2b.` In 2b *pax* (“peace”) is written above *pars* (“portion”).
185. `[Col. 0233] deest hic versus A.` A omits the entire verse *Est ubi sanctarum pars et requies animarum* (“Where there is a portion and rest for holy souls”).
186. `[Col. 0233] habenti 2.` MS 2 reads *habenti* (“having”) for *labenti* (“ending/passing”) of the year.
187. `[Col. 0233] sextali A.` A reads *sextali* (“sixth”) for *bissextili* (“leap [year]”).
188. `[Col. 0235] deest 3, 4a.` MSS 3 and 4a omit *atque Adalberti* (“and Adalbert”).
189. `[Col. 0235] episcopi et confessoris desunt A.` A omits *episcopi et confessoris* (“bishop and confessor”) after St Martin.
190. `[Col. 0235] VIII. A. 2, 4.` A, 2, and 4 read *VIII* (“eighth”) for *9* before the Kalends of April.
191. `[Col. 0235] deest 3.` MS 3 omits *praesul* (“bishop”).
192. `[Col. 0235] Meinardus 1. Meynhardus 2. Meginhardus 2b.` Megnard is spelled *Meinardus* in 1, *Meynhardus* in 2, and *Meginhardus* in 2b.
193. `[Col. 0235] Podiuen 1. 2b, 4, 4a. Pediuen 3.` Podiwin is spelled *Podiuen* in 1, 2b, 4, 4a and *Pediuen* in 3.
194. `[Col. 0235] et confessoris desunt A.` A omits *et confessoris* (“and confessor”) after St Nicholas.
195. `[Col. 0235] deest A. 3, 4a.` A, 3, and 4a omit *in vita ipsius sancti* (“in the life of that saint”).
196. `[Col. 0235] autem A.` A reads *autem* (“however”) for *enim* (“for”).
197. `[Col. 0235] recentiori man. superscr. fabricans 1.` In MS 1 a later hand writes *fabricans* (“building”) above *dilatans* (“enlarging”).
198. `[Col. 0235] in margine A. Bamberk 1. Babenberch 4.` A has *Bamberch* in the margin; MS 1 reads *Bamberk* and 4 *Babenberch*.
199. `[Col. 0236C] Cfr. Ekkehardi Chronicon.` Compare Ekkehard’s *Chronicle*.
200. `[Col. 0235] omn. suis A.` A reverses/abbreviates *cum suis omnibus* (“with all his followers”) as *omn. suis*.
201. `[Col. 0235] ita 1. Luderam A.` MS 1 reads *Luteram* as printed; A reads *Luderam*, Lothair’s name.
202. `[Col. 0235] et op. erasa 1.` MS 1 erased *et op.*, the beginning of *et optato* (“and desired”).
203. `[Col. 0235] deest A.` A omits *principem Boemiae* (“the ruler of Bohemia”).
204. `[Col. 0235] Wladizlai addit A. deest in rell.` A alone adds *Wladizlai* (“Vladislav”) after “ruler”; the name is absent from the rest.
205. `[Col. 0235] corr. 1.` MS 1 has a correction at *obviare* (“oppose”); no rejected form is supplied.
206. `[Col. 0235] omnibus 4.` MS 4 reads *omnibus* (“all”) for *cunctis* (“all”).
207. `[Col. 0235] dabis 2b.` MS 2b reads singular *dabis* (“you will give”) for plural *dabitis* (“you will give”).
208. `[Col. 0235] suum coet. A.` A reverses/abbreviates *coetum suum* (“his assembly”) as *suum coet.*
209. `[Col. 0235] dicens corr. dixit A. 1. dicens 2.` A and 1 correct *dicens* (“saying”) to *dixit* (“said”); MS 2 retains *dicens*.
210. `[Col. 0235] deest 2b.` MS 2b omits *iste* (“that man/he”) before “margrave.”
211. `[Col. 0235] uti 2, 2b, 4.` MSS 2, 2b, and 4 read *uti* (“as/to use”) for *ut* (“that”).
212. `[Col. 0235] quaecunque 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read neuter plural *quaecunque* (“whatever things”) for masculine singular *quemcunque* (“whoever”).
213. `[Col. 0236C] XI Kal. Jun. Consentiunt Vita Wiperti, c. 12, et Kalendarium Pegaviense.` The date is the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, 22 May; *Life of Wipert* 12 and the Pegau Calendar agree.
214. `[Col. 0235] memini 3.` MS 3 reads singular *memini* (“I have mentioned”) for plural *meminimus* (“we have mentioned”).
215. `[Col. 0235] corr. al. manu A.` Another hand corrects A at *regis* (“of the king”); the rejected form is not supplied.
216. `[Col. 0235] census 2b. censura 3.` MS 2b reads *census* (“resources/revenue”) and 3 *censura* (“judgment”) for *censum* (“resources”).
217. `[Col. 0236C] Heinricum. Wipertus filius major natu ante patrem obierat.` The son was Henry; Wipert’s elder son had died before his father.
218. `[Col. 0235] eum superscr. al. man. 1.` In MS 1 another hand writes *eum* (“him”) above *quo consolaretur*, making the object of “console” explicit.
219. `[Col. 0235] fratris corr. alia manu in margine patris A.` In A another hand corrects *fratris* (“brother’s”) in the margin to *patris* (“father’s”): Henry is consoled over his father’s death.
220. `[Col. 0235] deest A.` A omits *et* (“and”) before “from there he sent.”
221. `[Col. 0235] princ. Pol. A.` A abbreviates/reorders *Poloniae principem* (“ruler of Poland”) as *princ. Pol.*
222. `[Col. 0235] deest 3.` MS 3 omits Stephen’s request *Parvum ... date nobis spacium* (“Give us a little time”).
223. `[Col. 0235] deest A.` A omits *ultimae jam* (“now the final”) before “lot of fortune and death.”
224. `[Col. 0235] deest 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit *suum* (“his/our”) before “bread.”
225. `[Col. 0235] inversis 1. sed corr. 3.` MS 1 reads *inversis* (“turned back”) for *versis* (“turned”); MS 3 has a correction.
226. `[Col. 0235] en 1.` MS 1 reads *en* (“behold”) for *Et* (“And”).
227. `[Col. 0235] babati 1.` MS 1 has corrupt *babati* for *barbari* (“barbarians”).
228. `[Col. 0235] nobis hanc A.` A reverses *hanc ... nobis* (“this ... to us”) as *nobis hanc*.
229. `[Col. 0235] poenitebit 1.` MS 1 supplies/reads *poenitebit* (“it will cause regret”); the note gives no contrasting form.
230. `[Col. 0235] vos 2.` MS 2 reads *vos* (“you”) for *nos* (“us”) in “make us a proverb.”
231. `[Col. 0235] aptarier 1. corr. aptarier 2. aptari 4.` MS 1 reads archaic passive *aptarier* (“to be armed/prepared”); MS 2 corrects to that form; MS 4 reads *aptari* with the same meaning.
232. `[Col. 0235] corr. A` A has a correction at *irruunt* (“they rush”); no rejected form is supplied.
233. `[Col. 0237] inter add. 3.` MS 3 adds *inter* (“between”) before the opposed forces.
234. `[Col. 0237] virum vid. A.` A reverses/abbreviates *videns virum* (“seeing the man”) as *virum vid.*
235. `[Col. 0237] deest 4.` MS 4 omits *At ille* (“But he,” the priest).
236. `[Col. 0237] Gloglou 4.` MS 4 spells Głogów *Gloglou*.
237. `[Col. 0237] Voyzlav 1. Voyzlau 2b, 3. Woyzlaus 4, 4a.` Nozizlav is *Voyzlav* in 1, *Voyzlau* in 2b and 3, and *Woyzlaus* in 4 and 4a.
238. `[Col. 0237] al. manu superscr. A.` In A another hand writes a reading above *cum* (“with”); its letters are not supplied.
239. `[Col. 0237] deest A.` A omits *multis* (“many”) before “armed men.”
240. `[Col. 0237] Boler 3. Borb 4, 4a.` The Bóbr is spelled *Boler* in 3 and *Borb* in 4 and 4a.
241. `[Col. 0237C] Bober.` The river is the Bober/Bóbr.
242. `[Col. 0237] ipsum A.` A reads *ipsum* (“him himself”) for *eum* (“him”).
243. `[Col. 0237] suspiciens corr. al. m. suscip. 1.` In MS 1 another hand corrects *suspiciens* (“looking up”) to *suscipiens* (“taking up”).
244. `[Col. 0237] ubi 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *ubi* (“where”) for *ibique* (“and there”).
245. `[Col. 0237] tertio 2b. III. 3.` MS 2b spells out *tertio* (“third”) and MS 3 uses *III* for the third day before the Kalends of June.
246. `[Col. 0237C] I. e. juvenis, ut observat Schwarz; interfuit enim jam anno 1115 praelio Wolfesholzensi efr. Vita Wiperti, c. 11.` *Puer* means “young man,” as Schwarz observes; he had already fought at Welfesholz in 1115. Compare *Life of Wipert* 11.
247. `[Col. 0237] undique ab in. A.` A reverses/abbreviates *ab inimicis undique* (“by enemies on every side”) as *undique ab in.*
248. `[Col. 0238C] Germanis Luitgarda.` The Germans called Svatava Luitgard.
249. `[Col. 0237] Bavaricos 1. in turba varios 2.` MS 1 reads *Bavaricos* (“Bavarians”) for *Bavaros*; MS 2 reads *in turba varios* (“various men in the crowd”).
250. `[Col. 0238C] Comiti Bogensi.` Frederick was count of Bogen.
251. `[Col. 0237] ita 1. X A.` MS 1 reads the chapter number as printed; A reads *X* (“ten”).
252. `[Col. 0237] deest 3.` MS 3 omits the second *Dei* (“of God”) in “the power of God and wisdom of God.”
253. `[Col. 0237] sub 4.` MS 4 reads *sub* (“under”) for *suo* (“his own”) before “sustaining will.”
254. `[Col. 0237] satanaeae 1.` MS 1 has corrupt *satanaeae* for *Satanae* (“of Satan”).
255. `[Col. 0237] ocroicnica vel tale quid superscr. al. man. 1.` In MS 1 another hand writes *ocroicnica*, or something similar, above Jacob Apella’s name; the reading is unexplained.
256. `[Col. 0238C] I. e. Judaei, ex Horatiano: Credat Judaeus Apella.` This means a Jew, from Horace: “Let the Jew Apella believe it.”
257. `[Col. 0237] quemcunque 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read masculine *quemcunque* (“whomever”) for neuter plural *quaecunque* (“whatever things”).
258. `[Col. 0237] afflaverat omisso necat 3.` MS 3 reads *afflaverat* (“had breathed upon”) and omits *necat* (“kills”).
259. `[Col. 0237] est 2.` MS 2 reads indicative *est* (“is/was”) for subjunctive *sit* (“may have been”) after “was seen.”
260. `[Col. 0237] vice Deum 3. vicedomni 4, 4a.` MS 3 reads *vice Deum* (“in place of God”) and MSS 4, 4a *vicedomni* for *vicedomini*, the deputy lord’s office.
261. `[Col. 0237] Jacobus inserunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a insert *Jacobus* (“Jacob”) after “this same man.”
262. `[Col. 0237] Judaeum inserunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a insert *Judaeum* (“Jew”) after “such a man.”
263. `[Col. 0237] zelatus 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *zelatus* (“having been zealous”) for *zelans* (“being zealous”).
264. `[Col. 0237] an repetunt 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a repeat the exclamation as *an* for *Ah*.
265. `[Col. 0237] Wladizlai add. 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a add *Wladizlai* (“Vladislav’s”) after “duke’s treasury.”
266. `[Col. 0237] deest 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a omit the whole ransom statement: three thousand pounds of silver and one hundred of gold paid to avert his execution.
267. `[Col. 0237] quod accipiens 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a add *quod accipiens* (“receiving this”) before the duke’s redemptive act.
268. `[Col. 0237] Judaeis 4, 4a.` MSS 4 and 4a read *Judaeis* (“the Jews”) for pronoun *eis* (“them”).
269. `[Col. 0237] o pia Chr. A.` A reads abbreviated *O pia Christi* (“O pious [female] servant of Christ”) for the invocation’s fuller form.

In the same year Duke Vladislaus, a distinguished and venerable man, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord (25 December) and Epiphany (6 January) in the village of Stebečná. Then, because he had fallen ill, he moved to the city of Vyšehrad and remained there until his death. In that winter, as spring began, exceedingly violent winds prevailed throughout the entire lunar month of March.

[Note: “Duke” in manuscript 3; omitted by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Since” in 2b; “because” in 3.]

[Note: “He ordered himself to be transferred” in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Until” added by 2b, 4, and 4a.]

[Note: “March” in manuscript 1. In codex A the following verses, absent from the remaining manuscripts, follow:]

> In the year one thousand, sixty less ten,  
> The English felt the comet’s fiery hair.  
>
> In the year one thousand, one hundred less one,  
> The Franks capture Jerusalem by mighty valour.

### 58. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1125

Soběslav, hearing that his brother Vladislaus was gravely ill, having adopted the sound counsel of his friends—or rather, as the divine will had already so ordained—returned from Saxony with all his company. On the fourth day before the Nones of February, he arrived by night near the city of Prague, in the forest surrounding the monastery of Břevnov. What he himself had decided should be done in this matter remains concealed; for a hero of such character would not have entered this land so rashly unless certain of the nobles had existed upon whose advice, as I suppose, he acted.

[Note: “Vladislaus” added by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “The city” absent from A.]

[Note: Brzewnow 2; Breunen 2b; Breunou 3; Breunev 4 and 4a.]

For that same night, turning back, he secretly ranged through the land, now through forests, now through villages, hither and thither, inflicting violence upon no one, but continually seeking his brother’s favour.

[Note: “Now” is absent from A.]

[Note: “Always” is absent from A.]

[Note: “Seeking” is absent from A.]

All the Bohemians of the first and second rank loved him and favoured his cause; only the duchess and a few with her supported Otto. Since he had married her sister Sophia, she strove by every means to ensure that Otto, after her husband, should possess the ducal throne.

[Note: “Others” in manuscript 2.]

[Note: “Ranks” in manuscript 1.]

[Note: A later hand in the margin of A has *patri*, “father,” in place of *parti*, “party.”]

[Note: The duchess was Richsa, daughter of Count Henry of Beringen. See Pubitschka IV, 157.]

[Note: “Sophia.”]

[Note: “Had married” in A.]

Meanwhile the duke’s increasingly severe illness greatly exhausted his body. In the midst of this, the magnates of the land, troubled like fish in muddy water and wavering uncertainly in their minds, were dismayed. Queen Svatava, the duke’s mother, forewarned and instructed by Soběslav’s friends, came to visit her son and spoke to him thus:

[Note: “Troubled” in A.]

[Note: “Wavered” in 3.]

[Note: Zuatava 1; Zwatava 4.]

[Note: “Soběslav by friends” in A.]

“Since I am your mother and a queen, I come as a suppliant and in fear to your knees; with the knees with which I received you when you were little, I now fall before you on trembling knees for your brother. For I ask not what may rightly be denied, but what is pleasing to God and acceptable to men. For it pleases God, as He himself said: ‘Honour thy father and thy mother,’ that you should graciously receive my aged prayers, and I beg you not to put to shame this wrinkled face flooded with tears.

[Note: *Ex* in 1.]

[Note: *Abortam* in 2; *obrutam* in 2b.]

[Note: “With” in A.]

[Note: “Soběslav” inserted by 4 and 4a.]

“Let it be permitted to me, an old mother, to obtain from my son what all the people of Bohemia, lying prostrate, ask and petition for. Let it be permitted to me, worn out with age, to see you at peace, whom I see, born from my womb in equal condition and, by the grace of God, well brought up. May it happen to me, an old woman soon to die, that I do not die before God grants relief to this incomparable grief of mine. Rightly indeed do I grieve, because the savage Erinys reigns in this land and arms you brothers—once united—in battle.

[Note: “If not” in 3.]

[Note: Corrected in A.]

[Note: Corrected in A.]

[Note: “I deserve” in 1; “I die” in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.335.]

“For who does not know that a shirt is nearer to the body than a tunic? Nature, which by birth has made one nearer, causes him to be more closely attached to his own people and more zealous in every concern. But that man—yes, that man—whom you make your brother, and to whom you now entrust and commit the care and guardianship of your offspring and dear wife, believe me, your mother: he will be the first to become for them a snare, a pit, and a stumbling-block. But this man whom you keep distant from yourself and count almost as a stranger, though he is your full brother, will be far more merciful to your people than the son of your paternal uncle, to whom after you, you assign the throne of your paternal duchy.”

[Note: Omitted in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Among you” in 4 and 4a.]

She had spoken,

> And wept, and distressed her son with her weeping.

[Note: “Naumque” in 1.]

[Note: “His” in 3.]

When she saw him weeping with her, she added: “My son, I do not lament your fate, which cannot be avoided by humankind; rather, I bewail your brother’s life, more pitiable than death. As a fugitive, wanderer, and exile, he would now rather die happily than live unhappily.”

[Note: “Deeds” in 1.]

[Note: “Could” above the line, corrected by another hand to “would,” in 1; “may prefer” in 3.]

And her son Vladislaus, his face bathed in tears, said: “I will do it, my mother; I will do what you urge. I was not born from adamant or from the accursed Charybdis, so as not to remember my brother born of the same womb.”

[Note: “Vladislaus” inserted by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Nor” in 3 and 4.]

[Note: Thus A; the other manuscripts have “from Charybdis”; *ex* is absent in 3 and 4a.]

[Note: “My” added by 4 and 4a.]

Meanwhile Otto, bishop of the church of Bamberg, a soldier of Christ of illustrious character, returned after conquering and destroying the idols of the Pomeranians, and visited the duke, whose strength was now failing through illness. After the duke had entrusted himself and his soul to him through holy confession, the bishop promised that pardon could neither be given nor obtained before he had promised true and firm peace and favour to his brother.

[Note: “The bishop returned” in A.]

[Note: Bamberiensis 1; Babenbergensis 4.]

[Note: “Illustrious” in 3 and 4a.]

[Note: “Vladislaus” inserted by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Otto” added by 4.]

[Note: Absent from A, 2b, 3, 4, and 4a.]

Then the aforesaid bishop, entrusting the care of his soul and the task of bringing peace to Bishop Meinhard, richly laden with gifts in accordance with princely generosity, continued on his way. For he was hastening to reach his see before the Lord’s Supper.

[Note: Corrected in 1 from *perficiente* to *perficiendae*.]

[Note: Meginardus in 1.]

[Note: “The Lord’s Supper” in A.]

[Note: He returned on the most holy Saturday of Easter, as Ekkehard relates under 1125.]

Soběslav was immediately summoned; and that which had formerly been plotted in secret was now openly discussed among the people.

When Otto, prince of Moravia, who always clung to the duke’s side, perceived that these things were taking place, he returned sadly to Moravia, fearing that perhaps he might be captured. Vladislaus was reconciled with his brother Soběslav on Wednesday of Holy Week (25 March). Then, after the octave of Easter, on the second day before the Ides of April, a Sunday which that year was the Sunday *Misericordia Domini*, the pious and merciful Duke Vladislaus passed to Christ, not without great lamentation from his followers. The mercy which he had always shown to the poor for Christ’s name, he doubtless then received from the merciful Lord himself.

[Note: “At the duke’s side” in A.]

[Note: “Perhaps” in 2; “possibly” in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “His brother Soběslav” added by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: Absent from A.]

[Note: Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.]

He was buried in the church of Saint Mary the Virgin, which he himself built and sufficiently enriched for Christ and his mother with every ecclesiastical privilege; there he established a highly honourable abbey of monks. The place is named Kladruby.

[Note: “There” in 3.]

[Note: Kladruby 2; Kladaruby 3.]

[Note: Kladrau.]

> What a duke this was while spirit ruled his limbs,  
> From his deeds already written you may learn  
> What praise he deserves, and with what honour he should be revered.  
> Let the book end where our duke’s life ends.

[Note: “Fifth” in 3.]

[Note: In 2a the following words occur: “Here begins the prologue to the fourth book.” In 4: “The book ends. Here begins the illustrious [work] of the Chronicle of the Bohemians”; in 4a these words were added in the margin, but by a later hand.]

### 59.

Since at the beginning of the first book I remember having said that this chronicle was composed in the time of Duke Vladislaus and Bishop Herman, and since they have now by fate crossed from this valley of tears to places perhaps delightful, while the subject matter of deeds still abounds, I consider whether there I should fix my anchor on the shore, or instead

> Now, while the east winds rage, spread my sails upon the deep.

[Note: “First” absent from 3.]

[Note: “Was composed” in A.]

[Note: “Valley” in A.]

[Note: “Of tears” in A.]

[Note: “For himself” in 2.]

[Note: “Reader” in 2a.]

[Note: “Cares” in 4.]

Consult, fair Muse, my instructress, now on my behalf. For you, who never grow old, do not cease to trouble me, an old man, toward youthful studies. You do not fail to know that in any old man, as in me, the understanding is childish and the spirit weak. Oh, if God, now that I am eighty years old, would restore to me the years gone by, in which long ago at Liège, under Master Franco, in the green meadows of grammar and dialectic, you played enough with me!

[Note: “Courses” corrected by another hand to “studies” in 1.]

[Note: “Or” corrected to “not” in A.]

[Note: “Man” in 3.]

[Note: “Each one” in 2b.]

[Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.560.]

[Note: “Indeed” in 2.]

[Note: “Of the Franks” in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Green” in A; *virectis* in 1 and 4.]

O most lovable and sweet one to young men, always chaste yet never old: why do you seek me out in old age? Why do you stimulate my dull mind? Now aged years bend my back; now wrinkled skin disfigures my face; now my breast pants like a tired war-horse; now my hoarse voice hisses like a goose; and diseased old age weakens my senses. Certainly soft bread and toasted morsels please me more than your sophistries, which once, while reclining softly under your armpit, we sweetly sucked from your tender breast.

[Note: “All” in 2.]

[Note: “Wrinkled [things]” in 3.]

[Note: “Please” in 2b.]

O horn-butting sophistry, eagerly to be sought by syllogistic men but sufficiently experienced by us already, leave old men and seek young men like yourself: sharp in intellect and ingenious in the arts of learning. They have lately fed on delectable banquets at the great table of Lady Philosophy and exhausted all the treasures of France; they return as new philosophers! The renowned virtue of Duke Soběslav awaits such orators, who may splendidly gild his wondrous deeds with a golden pen. To them I, too, an old man, humbly commit whatever foolishness I utter, to be polished to perfection.

[Note: *deonae* in 4.]

[Note: *philosophye* in 1.]

[Note: “May be able,” corrected by another hand to *queunt*, in 1.]

[Note: Thus corrected by another hand in 1; *eliminandum* in 3.]

With the permission of these men and of all who read this, let it be permitted to me to derive something from the many deeds of the aforesaid duke which have been recorded. And you who criticize me as an old man—being yourself wise—bring the treasure of your learning into the light, and use this rough text as your material.

[Note: In 2a follow the words: “Here begins the fourth book concerning the elevation of Soběslav as duke of the Bohemians.”]

### 60.

Under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, almighty God, three and one, as we have related above, when Duke Vladislaus was taken from this light, his brother Soběslav—though younger in age, yet more mature in mature wisdom, generous of hand, welcome to the citizens, pleasing to the people of both sexes and every age—was raised, with all the Bohemians together favouring him, by hereditary right to the ancestral throne of the principate on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: “Though” absent from 2.]

[Note: “Mature” absent from 2.]

[Note: “To the throne of the principate” in A.]

> O Thou who governest the world by everlasting reason,  
> Who would have hoped, or who could have believed,  
> That peace would be made in this year without great bloodshed?

[Note: Omitted in 4a.]

[Note: “That” in 4 and 4a.]

Especially since Lord Otto, induced by the counsel of certain men, had bound himself by such an oath that he would not depart from the city of Vyšehrad until either, defeated, he suffered capital punishment, or, victorious, he gained possession of the summit of the princely seat. But our Lord Jesus Christ, who scatters and rejects the counsels of princes, through the merit of the most holy martyr Wenceslaus, mercifully arranged matters as your charity knows well enough from what I have related above.

[Note: Thus corrected in 1; *instinctus* in A, 2, 2b, 3, 4, and 4a.]

[Note: “Oath” in 2b.]

[Note: “Martyr Wenceslaus” in A.]

Therefore let the good duke now cease to be angry and indignant alike at his brother and at Otto. Let him believe that all things are governed by God’s reason and that nothing can be done without Him. But since, as Solomon testifies, “anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:10), far be it from the most reverend duke to stain his eminent virtues by anger and indignation, or to defile his worthy acts by impatience.

[Note: “Not” in 4.]

[Note: “God’s reason” in A; “God” omitted in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Most reverend” in 3.]

[Note: “Patience” in 3.]

Indeed, if anyone should undertake to set out his deeds individually for the sake of his praise, daylight and the page would fail before the work begun could be completed. Nevertheless, we disclose to your charity one principal memorial of him, in which he ought in fact to be preferred in action to almost all others: that a duke of such power never

> Defiled his lips with honeyed drink, the robber of the mind.

[Note: “If anyone” added by another hand in the margin of A.]

[Note: *Lau.* in 1.]

[Note: “For the sake of his praise” omitted in 2b.]

[Note: “Individually” in 3.]

[Note: “Uncertain” in A and 2; “begun” in 2a.]

[Note: *Polluit* in A; *proluit* in 2.]

[Note: A drink mixed with honey.]

Certainly it is no small virtue for a powerful man to restrain his mouth and to reject not the dregs but the allurements of his natural drink.

### 61.

In the same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, when it was Wednesday in the holy week of Pentecost, great snow fell in certain wooded places; in the following days severe cold arose, and it greatly injured crops of every kind, especially those sown in autumn, as well as vineyards and trees. Thus in many places shrubs dried up from the roots, and lesser streams were frozen stiff with frost.

[Note: “Sixteenth” in 4; “sixth” in the remaining manuscripts; “thirteenth” in 4a.]

[Note: It fell on 17 May.]

[Note: “Likewise” in 2b.]

[Note: Absent from 3, 4, and 4a.]

[Note: “Thus” written above the line in A.]

[Note: The words “and lesser streams were frozen stiff with frost” are absent from 2; *g.* is written above the line by another hand in 1.]

On the Saturday of that week, the third day before the Kalends of June, Emperor Henry IV died. With him, his imperial line came to an end, partly through the barrenness of the female sex, partly because from his earliest age every royal male line had been brought by a destructive fate to its conclusion.

[Note: “Tenth” in 4a.]

[Note: He died on 23 May; compare Ekkehard and the Saxon annalist under 1125. That day fell on the Saturday of Pentecost week. The error does not appear to be Cosmas’s, but a corruption in all our manuscripts.]

[Note: “His own” in 3; *et* omitted in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: The words from “female” to “from his earliest age” are absent in 1.]

[Note: *Li* written above the line by another hand in A.]

### 62.

Meanwhile, by God’s grace, when the renowned Duke Soběslav had established peace throughout his whole realm, let us pause from heroic chronicles and relate how a certain priest extinguished the inciting flames of his heart by the burning of raw greens. He himself told me this confidentially and begged me in Christ, as a friend, not to reveal his name to anyone. I believe him, as I believe myself, because his praiseworthy life gives credence to his words.

[Note: “While” absent from 3.]

[Note: “Codices” in 4 and 4a. These manuscripts omit everything from “Meanwhile” to this point and insert: “Although this matter lies outside the order of our narrative, yet because we believe it suitable for the edification of the faithful,” etc.]

[Note: “Had extinguished” in 1; “extinguished” in 2.]

He said that after the Lord had taken his wife from him, he had vowed to God in a devout mind that he would know no woman thereafter. But because it is very difficult to uproot from the mind something to which one is accustomed, I do not know how many years later so great a temptation of the flesh assailed him that, almost forgetting the vow he had made to God, overcome by lust, he nearly fell into the devil’s snare.

[Note: *Aigebat*, with the *g* erased, in A.]

[Note: “Priesthood” in 2b; *presbiteruram* corrected in A.]

[Note: *Asueta* in A.]

[Note: Absent from 2.]

[Note: “That” in 1 and 2.]

What was he to do? He had once read in the *Dialogues* how Saint Benedict checked the burning of hostile flesh by the fiery stimulus of nettles. Suddenly, visited by heavenly grace and returning to himself, seeking a suitable place for a like deed and finding no secluded place, he secretly gathered a handful of nettles, furtively entered his chamber, shut the little door upon himself, and threw off every garment from his body, down to a single thread.

[Note: “Stimulus” in 4 and 4a.]

Ah! If anyone had then seen that sane priest raging like a madman, even if he had buried a beloved parent on that same day, willing or unwilling he would surely have laughed. Certainly no cruel schoolmaster rages against a pupil, nor an angry lord against a slave, as fiercely as the priest, inflamed against himself and made senseless by anger, scourged his genitals and buttocks with nettles.

[Note: “Your” corrected to “then” in 1.]

[Note: “Although” in 4a.]

[Note: “Returned” in 2.]

Then he turned back to his heart, and raging much more cruelly about his breast, he said: “You, yes you, most wicked heart, always torment me; I will now torment you in this manner. For from you come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, and lusts.”

[Note: *Exin* in 2b.]

[Note: “Most wicked heart” in 2b.]

[Note: The words “most wicked heart, always torment me” are absent in 5, with a blank space left.]

[Note: “If” corrected by another hand to “thus” in 1.]

[Note: “Pride” added by 4 and 4a.]

Thus, gratifying his fury, the furious priest, afflicted with such pains, lay as if dying for three days. Yet, not considering that he had done enough for the remedies of his soul, he gathered a bundle of nettles and hung it in his chamber so that he might always have them before his eyes. Whenever he saw them, whether hanging, cut down, or flourishing by the roadside, his heart trembled, and his evil mind, mindful of evil, wholly vanished.

[Note: Absent from 5.]

[Note: “Weakened” in 2b; “drawn” in 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Me” corrected to “himself” in 1.]

[Note: Corrected in 1.]

[Note: Corrected by another hand in A.]

[Note: Absent from 2b.]

But let us turn this priest’s imitable severity toward the preservation of virtues, and let us do in the mind what he did in the body. For the words of the Lord are true words, when He says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). For behold: while the priest burned outwardly in punishment, by God’s grace he extinguished that which burned unlawfully within; he conquered sin because he changed the fire.

[Note: “Let us turn toward virtues” in A.]

[Note: “In” added by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: Omitted by 4 and 4a.]

[Note: “Sinfully” in 2b.]

[Note: “Will burn,” corrected to “burned,” in 1.]

[Note: Codex 3 ends with these words: “Thus far the work of Cosmas, dean of Prague.”]

Let all the faithful in Christ know that the composer of this chronicle, namely the most reverend Cosmas, dean of the church of Prague, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November in the same year in which Duke Soběslav is known to have been enthroned. Amen. Farewell, brethren.

[Note: “Namely” absent from 2b.]

[Note: In manuscript 2, a later hand added 1125. In 4 and 4a: “In this same year Cosmas, the most reverend dean of the church of Prague, composer of this chronicle, departed this life on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.”]

[Note: “Thus” in 1; “Amen” in A.]

[Col. 0245]

## Continuation of Cosmas by the Canon of Vyšehrad

### In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126

Soběslav came into Moravia and, having taken the province from Otto, restored Vratislaus, son of Dědálec, to his paternal seat. Otto, duke of Moravia, met Lothair at Regensburg. Soběslav devastated Moravia, Otto’s portion.

[Note: “In the year of the Lord” in 2b, and so thereafter.]

[Note: That is, Udalricus; compare Cosmas III.41.]

[Note: “Native land” in 2a.]

[Note: Luderius in 2 and 2b.]

[Note: See below, Continuation of Sázava, under 1126.]

[Note: “Was devastating” in 2b.]

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, at daybreak, a sign of lightning was seen. Some thought that it had appeared before Christmas, others on the vigil of the Nativity; but it was plainly seen on the night of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. That winter there was such a quantity of snow as no man said he had ever seen; many people died in it. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March there was a flood of water; ice damaged many things.

[Note: “Lightning was seen” in 2b.]

Lothair, king of the Saxons, led astray by Otto, duke of Moravia, puffed up with great pride, greed for money, malice, and iniquity, came with his army against the Bohemians near the stronghold named Chlumec. There Duke Soběslav, with God’s help and his company, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, struck down five hundred of their magnates, not counting the shield-bearers, among whom the aforesaid Duke Otto fell. In so great a battle only three Slavs perished; but he spared the king of the Saxons with the others and dismissed him in peace. Thus Lord Soběslav and the Bohemians returned unhurt with great honour and glory.

[Note: “Lothair” in 2b.]

[Note: “Of Saxony” in 2b.]

[Note: Sixteenth in 2b.]

[Note: *Scuriferis* in 2.]

There was indescribable joy among clergy and laity throughout the whole household of Saint Wenceslaus, because neither our fathers nor grandfathers nor great-grandfathers had possessed such honour as almighty God, by His grace, granted to us: by His right hand and just judgment He defeated them. Amen.

[Note: “Wonderful” in 2b.]

[Note: “Because” in 2; “Saint Wenceslaus [rather] than” in 2a; “that” in 2b.]

But I do not wish, fathers and mothers, that you should be ignorant of what I heard.

[Note: “But I do not wish” is absent from 2 and 2a.]

I announce to you the truth of the aid of almighty God, which was seen by almost both armies: an eagle flying that day, before battle was joined between Saxons and Bohemians, cried out over the Saxons, foreknowing by God’s will their corpses; and a bell was heard ringing. Again, while almost a hundred Bohemian magnates, provosts, and chaplains stood around and guarded Saint Wenceslaus’s lance, one chaplain, a worthy man of noble birth named Vitus, who, according to custom, was holding the lance of the aforesaid saint, clothed in a mail-shirt and helmet like Achilles, cried weeping for joy to his companions:

[Note: “From those standing around” in 2b.]

[Note: “Guards” in 2 and 2a.]

[Note: “Of the Bohemians” in 2b.]

“O comrades and brothers, stand firm! For I see Saint Wenceslaus seated upon a white horse and clothed in a white garment above the summit of the holy lance, fighting for us. You also, behold!”

[Note: “Previously named” in 2b.]

[Note: “Cried” in 2b.]

[Note: “Summits” in 2b.]

They, astonished, looked this way and that and saw nothing—for the miracle had not been given by God to all, but only to the worthy. In grief and tears, groaning to God with all their heart, stretching eyes and hands toward heaven, they cried “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy”—until almighty God, in His mercy and through His holy messenger Wenceslaus, our protector, defeated our enemies. Amen.

[Note: “And” added by 2b.]

[Note: “Into” in 2a and 2b.]

[Note: *Kyr.* in 2.]

[Note: “Amen” absent from 2b.]

While Duke Soběslav did all these things, he sent his chaplain to the village called Vrbčany, where the matter was known. He found on the wall of the church the banner of Saint Adalbert the bishop; it was hung upon the lance of Saint Wenceslaus the martyr at the time of battle against the Saxons, where God defeated them. Amen.

[Note: Wrbczane 2; “to the village of Wrbczany” in 2b.]

[Note: “The Lord” in 2b.]

[Note: “Amen” absent from 2b.]

In the same year, on the fifth day before the Nones of October, Zdik was canonically elected bishop to the see of Olomouc and was ordained by his archbishop of Mainz, Adalbert; at his ordination, his barbarian name being removed, he was called Henry.

[Note: Zdiko in 2b, and so thereafter.]

[Note: “The bishopric of Olomouc” in 2 and 2a.]

[Note: “Adalbert.”]

[Note: Absent from 2b.]

In the same year Duke Soběslav and King Stephen II of the Hungarians met for conference and exchanged gifts. On his return Soběslav seized Břetislav, bound him in chains, and brought him to the castle called Dohna.

[Note: “Břetislav” in 2b.]

[Note: Son of Duke Břetislav II, who was killed in 1100.]

[Note: “To” in 2b.]

[Note: “Called” in 2b.]

[Note: Dohna.]

In the same year many people died of famine throughout the world. Then, after three months had passed, Břetislav was confined in the fortress of Jaroměř. At the same time the Bohemians rebuilt certain fortifications, which in Slavonic are called Přimda, Zhořelec, and Tachov. During the same period a chapel on Mount Říp was named. The most serene Duke Soběslav rebuilt it when it had been destroyed, and Zdik, venerable bishop of the holy church of Olomouc, with the utmost reverence consecrated it after restoring its former endowment-right.

[Note: Jaromierz in the district of Königgrätz.]

[Note: “Year” in 2b.]

[Note: “Slavonic” in 2b.]

[Note: Przimda 2; Przinda 2b.]

[Note: Frauenberg in the district of Čáslav.]

[Note: Yzcorzelik in 2b.]

[Note: Görlitz.]

[Note: Dachau.]

[Note: “The chapel … named” in 2b.]

[Note: Absent from 2b.]

[Note: “Of the former” in 2 and 2a; “former right,” with *dotis* omitted, in 2b.]

### In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127

On the seventh day before the Kalends of March, the head of Saint Adalbert, martyr and bishop, was discovered in the city of Gniezno, in the very place where the same martyr had been crowned by martyrdom and buried.

[Note: “Body” in 2b.]

[Note: Guizno in 2b.]

[Note: The words from “the seventh day before the Kalends” to “buried” are struck through by a light pen-stroke in 2.]

Soběslav, duke of the Bohemians, was then reconciled to Lothair, king of the Germans, and, moved by his favour and affection, besieged the castle of Nuremberg with a great force, ravaged and burned Bavaria almost as far as the Danube. After ten weeks had elapsed, when the undertaking had been completed, he returned home with great pomp and triumph. But the Bavarians and Swabians, inflamed by fury and indignation, established Duke Conrad of Franconia, of the Staufen family, as their king; and thus, alas, they brought about in the realm a final error worse than the first.

[Note: On the feast of Pentecost, 22 May, at Merseburg; compare Jaffé, *Geschichte des Deutschen Reichs unter Lothar*, p. 58.]

[Note: Nuremberk in 2b.]

[Note: Absent from 2b.]

[Note: Absent from 2.]

[Note: On 18 August 1127 Lothair was staying at Bamberg: Böhmer 2100.]

[Note: Duke of Franconia, of the Staufen house.]

### In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1128

On Easter Day (22 April), King Lothair lifted from the baptismal font the son of Duke Soběslav, and they became intimate friends. After confirmation, Wigbert’s son promised this child, at the end of his own life, his entire fief, the Saxon magnates being present there.

[Note: Henry.]

[Note: Of Groitzsch.]

In the same year Soběslav undertook an expedition to assist his compatriot King Lothair, who was besieging Speyer, against King Conrad; on the following day he returned home with thanksgiving. Not long thereafter, Conrad, son of Liutold, was captured by Soběslav and confined in the cloister of the church of Vyšehrad. The summer was dry.

[Note: “Interval” added by 2b.]

[Note: Compare Cosmas III.41.]

[Note: “In the castle of Vyšehrad” in 2b.]

In the same year many Bohemian princes were captured, chained, and held in custody by Duke Soběslav. Břetislav was taken to the castle of Děčín, and Conrad to Henry, son of Wigbert.

[Note: “Magnates” in 2a and 2b.]

[Note: Daczin 2; Dieczin 2b.]

[Note: Tetschen.]

In the same year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, called *Prosince* in Slavonic, there was a red eclipse of the moon. I shall report what certain persons saw: the remaining portion tossed itself this way and that until it disappeared; many stars surrounded it, one of which flew around the moon, while another shot toward the north. Ten days later, at night, red signs appeared in the sky from the north.

[Note: “And in Slavonic Prosince” omitted in 2b.]

[Note: “From which” in 2 and 2a.]

[Note: “Toward the north” in 2a.]

### In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1129

Vratislaus, son of Dědálec, was captured by Soběslav and afterwards sent into exile. The castle of Kladsko was restored and fortified by Soběslav.

[Note: “Thereafter” in 2b.]

In the same year Duke Soběslav renewed the monastery of Vyšehrad, which his father, King Vratislaus of blessed memory, had built for the sake of his own soul, his wife’s soul, and his offspring, with the approval and authority of the most glorious Pope Alexander and seventy-two fathers. The aforesaid pontiff of the holy Roman Church, to confirm the dignity of that holy foundation, deigned, through John bishop of Tusculum and Peter provost of Saint George the Martyr, to grant in perpetuity to the ministers of the aforesaid church—namely priest, deacon, subdeacon, and provost—the use of sandals and mitres as a mark of apostolic authority.

[Note: “Duke” in 2b.]

[Note: The reading should apparently be *dignitatem*, “dignity.” Concerning this foundation, compare Cosmas under 1070.]

[Note: “And” added by 2b.]

[Note: “And also the provost” omitted in 2b.]

Thus disposed and ordained, the aforesaid king subjected this monastery, which he had founded in this fashion, to the holy Roman Church. Carrying twelve baskets full of stones upon his own shoulders in honour of the Saviour, he acted as Emperor Constantine founded the Roman Church. For that reason he made it free. Soběslav, as we have said, renewed it and enlarged it after its renewal, for he had its walls painted; he hung in it a golden crown weighing twelve marks of gold, and eighty marks of silver; he added bronze and iron without number; adorned its pavement with polished stones; added surrounding porticoes; installed ceilings along two sides; covered the entire summit and roofs with tiles; ordered the cloister and all the offices to be roofed; and moreover increased the number of canons of the same church and augmented their stipends, estates, and other goods.

[Note: “Which” in 2b; “who” in 2 and 2a.]

In the same year Lord Meinhard, bishop of the church of Prague, restored the tomb of Saint Adalbert the bishop with gold, silver, and crystal.

[Note: “Restored” in 2a and 2b.]

In the same year Wenceslaus, duke of Olomouc, son of Svatopluk, was sent into Hungary by Duke Soběslav to aid King Stephen against the Greeks. He returned in peace, but after living four months consumed by quartan fevers, he died on the day before the Kalends of March.

[Note: “Indeed” added by 2.]

[Note: Zuatoplik in 2a and 2b.]

[Note: “Duke” in 2b.]

[Note: The Anonymous of Hradisko has the eighth day before the Kalends of March; Richter, *series episcoporum Olomucensium*, p. 23.]

### In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130

On the very day of the Nativity (25 December), as dawn arose, Lucifer rose—a thing never seen or heard before. Lord Meinhard, bishop of the church of Prague, set out for Jerusalem for the sake of prayer.

In the same year Duke Soběslav, setting out for Regensburg for a conference with King Lothair, by God’s grace escaped drowning in a certain stream called the Regen [Note: Col. 0249: omitted in 2; 2a reads it; 2b reads it]. Remaining in that city for a week, he destroyed twenty fortifications, and so returned to his own land safe and joyful. While Lord Duke Soběslav was doing these things, and was both before and still then entirely unharmed in all respects, he arrived at the castle of Kladsko [Col. 0249B; Note: Col. 0249: Kladsk, 2] with a large retinue. Having fortified it more diligently and strongly than before, he intended to proceed into Moravia.

But, as God’s mercy revealed—for he himself says, “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be known” (Matt. 10:26), and so forth—the plots and betrayals long before contrived against him then came to light on that very journey, and thus temporarily prevented the intended expedition into Moravia. Therefore, on the following Sunday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, while still on the journey, he learned that two retainers were lying in wait for his life. He summoned his companions, Zdeslav [Note: Col. 0249: Sdeslaus, 2], son of Blahoň [Note: Col. 0249: Blago, 2], and another named Diviš, asking their pledge that they would not oppose his will in a certain confidential matter. They gave the duke their pledge willingly.

Pointing out the traitors before their eyes, he said: “These are the betrayers of my life [Col. 0249C; Note: Col. 0249: omitted in 2 and 2a], its ambushers and murderers. As you promised me a little earlier [Note: Col. 0249: *paulo ante* is absent in 2a], lead them unpunished until they are brought before us, so that we may learn more fully and clearly the truth of every betrayal, whether suspected or manifest.” One of them was apprehended with a spear and a poisoned dagger almost two cubits long; the other escaped by flight.

Then Lord Soběslav, by God’s wisdom [Note: Col. 0249: “grace,” 2b], like Solomon forewarned, summoned certain of his huntsmen, yet concealing the matter, and said: “A garment [Note: Col. 0250D: a kind of garment] has been stolen from one of my squires. Send out tracking dogs to follow the thief’s footprints.” They did not disregard their lord’s command, but swiftly pursued him and captured him in a certain village. They brought him bound before the duke; he had a sword smeared with poison.

Before the leading men of Bohemia [Col. 0249D], the duke questioned the wicked robbers, saying: “For what reason, and on whose advice, did you wish to perpetrate a crime so great and so wicked? And whose soldiers are you?” The sons of iniquity could not conceal so atrocious a deed. Thus one declared himself a soldier of Miroslav, son of Count John, and the other a soldier of his younger brother, Střezimír [Note: Col. 0249: thus 2a; Col. 0250A].

These words began their cursed statement: “O good and merciful prince, if you seek the reason and the sequence of events, this is the truth, with every cloud of falsehood removed: Miroslav sent us wretches to destroy your illustrious life.” Miroslav, who was on that same expedition, was placed in very harsh chains. Střezimír, however, having planned the matter with his brother, pretended that his mother was gravely ill and requested leave from the duke to return home from the expedition. He too was captured in a certain village, and both brothers were taken to Vyšehrad.

After these events, Lord Soběslav proceeded to the metropolitan city of Prague for prayer, barefoot and in changed clothing, like the king of the Ninevites. All received him as he entered with great triumph and honour [Note: Col. 0249: “all the churches rejoice,” 2], rejoicing as was fitting over his deliverance, singing the angelic hymn, and ringing bells. When he had prayed there, he departed for Vyšehrad, where he was received by the canons of his father—that is, King Vratislav—with indescribable joy.

On the next day, as bees commonly flock to their leader and mother, so the Bohemian nobles, having learned that their prince had escaped such great dangers, assembled in the upper city of Vyšehrad. Finding him there [Note: Col. 0249: “meeting him,” 2b], they rejoiced at his safety as a mother rejoices over an only son.

On the following day Duke Soběslav gathered nobles and commoners in the palace of Vyšehrad, including the Prague canons; we too were there. The multitude of men at that council was nearly three thousand [Col. 0250C]. The monarch of the Bohemians himself, standing in the midst of us all, raised his voice and spoke through tears, like a son entreating his father for all his disobedience:

“O Bohemian magnates and shield of the Bohemian land! I neither praise nor extol myself, but speak the truth: when I was an exile, I was everywhere fortunate by God’s grace and possessed sufficiently those things necessary to me. Now, however, I say weeping: while my brother Duke Vladislav was still living, I obtained neither this duchy nor this honour by shield or by any other force, but by God’s mercy, by the election of my brother still living, and by that of all of you. For this reason and by this justice, I judge that I have possessed it justly and reasonably.

“Yet some of the more distinguished men of this province [Note: Col. 0249: “province,” 2a], stirred by Satan’s prompting [Note: Col. 0249: “warned,” 2 and 2b], wished—alas!—to kill me [Col. 0250D], just as their forefathers once killed my brother Duke Břetislav, most prudent of men, and likewise killed Svatopluk without cause. I, however, who have laboured for the good of my country and equally for your honour, they wished to destroy, I know not for what reason; but, with God’s grace assisting me, they could not accomplish it.

“Do you not see [Col. 0251A] how great was the hardness and impiety of their hearts? Those upon whom I bestowed the richer gifts of my favour, whom I honoured with a dearer affection than others, and whom I caused fittingly to sit at my side—their malicious will contrived my destruction. Yet lest I seem to condemn them out of ambition or envy, let your dignity be pleased to hear the testimony of their own mouths.”

After this the aforesaid sons of Satan were presented to the prince and those seated at table with him. The men who had been commanded by their superiors to seek the duke’s life could not conceal their wicked deed. They accused Miroslav, son of John, in all these matters, saying that everything they had wished to do had been commanded them by him [Note: Col. 0251: omitted in 2 and 2a], for they had been his servants.

Miroslav was ordered to stand before the duke [Col. 0251B], and one of the leading men was instructed to ask him whether he had dared devise such a crime from his own malice or at another’s suggestion, and who had been the author of the conspiracy. He replied:

“Most merciful prince, I can by no means conceal my great sin, which I planned through the greatest misfortune; but I wish to disclose it in your presence and that of those seated here. At one time a soldier of Břetislav named Bolesa visited me three times in order to urge this sin upon me, but I refused to agree to his advice. At last Bosík [Note: Col. 0251: Božík, 2 and 2b], our [Note: Col. 0251: ‘your,’ 2b] chaplain, came to me and began to exhort me in this manner:

“‘Was not your father in this province [Col. 0251C] nobler and wiser than any other? Yet among the nobles of this land you are regarded as of no account; moreover, you suffer your own brother to endure many evils for nothing, long held in chains. It is therefore better that, after this most arrogant duke has been killed, we enthrone such a man as will undoubtedly allow us to have whatever we please. If you do not believe me, I shall lead you to one whom you can believe without hesitation.’

“When this speech had ended, I, to my sin, accepted his counsel. Thus he led me to Bishop Meinhard, who was staying in a certain village called in Slavonic [Note: Col. 0251: omitted in 2b] Zircinaves [Note: Col. 0251: Zerzinawes, 2b]. He did this as though wishing to commend me to the bishop for service; there the whole beginning of this conspiracy was made.”

Then, questioned by the duke about the aforesaid conspiracy [Col. 0251D], he gravely accused the bishop in every respect, saying:

“Bishop Meinhard, to keep us steadfast in this undertaking, placed two fingers upon the relics of the saints and addressed me in words of this kind: ‘If you destroy the duke’s life, you shall without doubt possess with honour whichever you choose among these five—namely Žatec, Litoměřice, the chamber, the table [Col. 0252A], and the office of marshal [*agazonia*; Note: Col. 0251: *agosonia*, 2; *gosina*, 2a; Col. 0251D: the office of marshal]—I promising it and Duke Břetislav granting it.’”

After he had accused himself and others with his own mouth, he was led out from the council with his associates. On the following day he, his brother Střezimír, and a certain physician were deprived of all their limbs in the marketplace.

The two aforementioned sons of Satan underwent an unheard-of punishment: bound tightly upon a wheel, their eyes torn out, their hands and tongues cut off, and their legs broken, they were placed upon the posts prepared for their death [Note: Col. 0251: “death,” 2], and ended their miserable lives.

Křivosud, Miroslav’s uncle, and two others, one called Váčemil [Note: Col. 0251: Vicemil, 2b] and the other Henry—men accused by the aforesaid Miroslav before the duke and the said assembly [Col. 0252B]—were sent for judgment at Prague and underwent the ordeal by iron. Thus condemned by almighty God, they were found truly guilty; it was therefore decreed that they should undergo capital punishment. Finally, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, they were led to the marketplace and beheaded with an axe.

Chaplain Bosík also [Note: Col. 0251: “also,” inserted in 2b] was among the crowd of people, as though at a spectacle.
