I do not know whether he came to erase the crime imputed to him, or whether, as the devil had been the contriver of this affair and its guide in every respect, he brought him to watch the death of his companions, unwilling that his champion should wander any longer from the fellowship of his associates. For he who had previously been a fugitive and exile, conscious of his guilt, now by God’s grace appeared openly before all. One of the leading men, seeing him [Col. 0252C], seized him and brought him to the duke. When questioned about the matter, he differed in no respect from his companions’ account; thus he was bound with an iron chain and immediately [Note: Col. 0251: “at once,” 2b] assigned to custody under the royal steward. On the following week, the second day before the Kalends of July [Note: Col. 0251: “June,” 2], Břetislav was blinded.

In the same year, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, a certain monster resembling a serpent was seen in a single moment—that is, about sunset—to fly throughout all Bohemia and many other places. Afterwards another sign, exceedingly bright, was seen by some people in the morning. Vratislav, son of Dětřich, was brought back from exile.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1131, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April [Note: Col. 0251D: according to other witnesses, the pope had already come to Liège on 22 March; Jaffé, p. 97], that is, on the Sunday on which *Laetare* is sung, King Lothair assembled with a great company of clergy and laity in the city called Liège [Col. 0252D]. At this assembly they chose the fugitive Pope Innocent [Note: Col. 0252D: the Second], namely the man whom Peter, son of Leo [Note: Col. 0252D: Anacletus II], had driven from the pontifical see with the clergy and people of the Roman Church.

For this reason they sent the bishop of the church of Münster [Note: Col. 0252D: Ekbert; Note: Col. 0251: omitted in 2a], to announce [Col. 0253A; Note: Col. 0253: “because of,” 2a; “to announce”] to Pope Peter and all the Romans that the king of the Germans would come to them with an army after five months. Fearing the false king Conrad, he departed from the straight road and came into Bohemia. In the metropolitan city of Vyšehrad he celebrated, with great honour and with the canons of that church, the Mass of the Finding of the Holy Cross (3 May). At length, suitably rewarded by Duke Soběslav, he passed through the territory of Margrave Racud [Note: Col. 0253: Racd’sis, 2; Vacilsis, 2a; Raedep, 2b] and, travelling through many provinces, returned home. But the matter came to nothing and perished like dust carried away by the wind.

Meanwhile, as time passed, Duke Soběslav built a castle at the foot of a certain village called Tachov, on the borders of Mže, and named it after the neighbouring village [Col. 0253B]. He also built another in the district of Milevsko beside the river Nisa and called it Yzhorelik; formerly it had been called Drenov [Note: Col. 0253: Orenow, 2a; Drzewniow, 2b].

At this point Lord Bishop Meinhard returned sound and unharmed to the seat of his bishopric. To clear himself of the crime laid to his charge, he submitted himself to every judgment before Duke Soběslav and all [Note: Col. 0253: omitted in 2a] the nobles of Bohemia. Therefore two canons of the Prague church were sent, one on behalf of the lord bishop—namely an unlearned man called Herold, who, though this was improper, had been vicar and chaplain of the bishop of Bamberg and archpriest [Note: Col. 0253: “archpriest,” 2a] of Plzeň. Miroslav, son of John, had said that this man had been present in the chapel at Zircinew, where the oath was made between Bishop Meinhard, Bosík, and Miroslav. The other was Tutha [Col. 0253C], on behalf of the duke. These two were sent to the archbishop of Mainz and the bishop of Bamberg [Note: Col. 0253D: St Otto], so that Meinhard would accept with equanimity whatever judgment they might impose upon him [Note: Col. 0253: “might be imposed,” 2b].

Concerning the two stars, O Bohemians [Note: Col. 0253: omitted in 2 and 2b], mentioned by you eleven years ago [Note: Col. 0253: “years,” 2; Col. 0253D: “months” seems to be required, for these things undoubtedly refer to the year 1130], I could afterwards explain nothing about them in my account, because they moved in different ways. But now, while wholly at leisure from other affairs, I shall explain, as far as the grace of the Holy Spirit has furnished my understanding, both what I saw and how it occurred.

The star which rose at dawn, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, at the approach of spring—which you Bohemians called Lucifer—set, when the winter sunset of the sun approached, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [Note: Col. 0253: “occasion,” 2 and 2a].

In the same year another, brighter star appeared at sunrise on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0253D]. Gradually descending lower, it was no longer visible on the second day before the Ides of January. Which of these, then, should be called Lucifer [Note: Col. 0253: “was called,” 2 and 2b], I do not think any human beings know; but God, creator of all things, knows—the God through whom many signs and portents have occurred before our eyes [Col. 0254A], some of which I have noted above [Note: Col. 0253: “noted,” 2a]. There was an eclipse of the moon, but a small part remained until it became wholly full again [Note: Col. 0253: “refilled,” 2b].

Let us return to what precedes. On the fourth day before the Kalends of October, the bishop of Bamberg [Note: Col. 0253D: for Otto’s letter to Meinhard on this matter, see Boczek I, 202] and the bishop of Olomouc [Note: Col. 0254D: Henry], together with seven Bohemian abbots, while Duke Soběslav, people, and clergy stood by, cleared Meinhard, bishop of the holy Prague church, of every charge previously brought against him, by laying aside their stoles. They professed that Bishop Meinhard had devised nothing hostile against Duke Soběslav, but had laboured solely to procure Břetislav’s release from chains [Note: Col. 0253: “uncle,” 2a].

Bishop Meinhard then went to Rheims for the council [Note: Col. 0253: “of the council,” 2 and 2a; Col. 0254D: held at Rheims]. At that synod the aforementioned fugitive Pope Innocent [Note: Col. 0253: thus 2a; “ppter” in 2; “pope” omitted in 2b] was present with fifty bishops besides abbots [Col. 0254B]. There they excommunicated Pope Peter, then presiding over the Roman Church, and King Conrad, “extinguishing lights” [Note: Col. 0253: omitted in 2].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1132, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, varied red signs [Note: Col. 0253: “various,” 2b] appeared in the sky toward the north. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, while Lord Meinhard was staying in a certain village called Chuchel [Note: Col. 0254D: Kuchel in the district of Beroun], an unheard-of and most terrible portent occurred at twilight one day.

For, when he was already weighed down with sleep and was mounting his bed, and his servants stood before him, a horrible noise, as though coming from a cave, suddenly sounded in their ears and seemed to threaten the house where he was. Terrified by the noise [Col. 0254C], they fled, leaving their lord alone [Note: Col. 0253: “having been left,” 2]. Not knowing what to do, he leapt from bed and, as though in ecstasy, stood beside the wall of the fireplace. And behold: a stone of marvellous size came down from the mountain, crushed two walls together with the bishop’s bed, and came to rest there. Thus the lord bishop escaped unharmed. Amen.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, there was an eclipse of the moon, and it was entirely blood-red [Note: Col. 0253: omitted in 2 and 2a]. Duke Soběslav set out for Bamberg for the council of King Lothair [Note: Col. 0254D: according to the Saxon annalist, the king was there on the feast of the Purification of Mary, 2 February].

When the whole council had assembled in the royal palace, and King Lothair and Duke Soběslav were sitting privately in a small chamber beside the palace, behold—whether through the age of the building or some evil person, I do not know—the floor of the royal [Note: Col. 0253: “king’s,” 2 and 2a] palace collapsed, with all those who were inside [Col. 0254D]. In that collapse many Germans were wounded; others, gravely injured, scarcely escaped death. All the Bohemians, however, remained unharmed.

Not long afterwards King Lothair assembled for a council in the castle of Plzeň [Note: Col. 0253: Plizn, 2b] with many Germans [Col. 0255A]. Again [Note: Col. 0255: “and again,” 2b] the palace in which they had assembled collapsed with all in it, but by God’s grace all escaped safely.

At the same time a council was held by the king at Goslar. When the palace collapsed with everyone in it, by God’s grace it injured no one. In the following week after the Lord’s resurrection (10 April) [Note: Col. 0255: “of the Lord also,” 2b], terrible thunder and unheard-of lightning appeared. The tower of St Wenceslas was set on fire; but, by God’s protecting grace and the aid of the prayers of the holy martyrs Wenceslas and Adalbert, only the tower was burned, while the church remained safe from fire.

Blessed Gotthard, confessor and bishop, shone through the outstanding miracles worked by his merits in the city of Hildesheim [Note: Col. 0255: Wildensi, 2 and 2b; Col. 0255D: the translation of St Gotthard occurred in this year; cf. *Annals of Hildesheim*, 1132]. When news of this event spread among many peoples of the faithful [Col. 0255B], many came to the fortress of Hildesheim [Note: Col. 0255: Hildessense, 2b], both to see his miracles and, above all, that through his merits and prayers they might be released from every bond of sin and deserve to be counted among the children of God.

At the same time the most powerful city of Regensburg was almost entirely burned, except for forty houses which scarcely escaped. Fire also did great harm in many places that year.

Duke Soběslav sent three hundred soldiers to aid King Lothair as he proceeded to Rome, placing over them Jaromír, son of Duke Bořivoj [Note: Col. 0255D: duke of Olomouc]. Having left their own land, they came to a place called Omberk [Note: Col. 0255D: Augsburg; this disaster occurred on 28 August], and there fought the Germans in the market of that place. With God’s help they defeated them.

Duke Vratislav, son of Dětřich, ruler of the part of Moravia called Brněnsko [Col. 0255C], married a wife from Rus’, surpassing Helen, queen of the Greeks, in beauty. She also [Note: Col. 0255: this seems to be the correct reading in P; “because,” edition] shone with such extraordinary fairness of complexion that the ruddy brilliance of gold seemed to stain the whiteness of her body with certain red marks.

In the same year the duke of the Poles set out for Hungary with an innumerable army, wishing, after driving out the blind king called Béla [Note: Col. 0256D: Béla II, son of Álmos], to enthrone against the Hungarians’ will the son of Coloman [Note: Col. 0255D: Borich, son of Anastasia, who was descended from the family of the princes of Rus’, had been married to Coloman, and, on suspicion of infidelity, had been repudiated by the king. Coloman died in 1114; cf. Katona, *Historia critica regum Hungariae*, vol. III].

For the mother of that young man, repudiated by her husband King Coloman while pregnant, returned to her father [Note: Col. 0256D: Vladimir Monomakh, prince of Rus’], and there bore the child. The duke of the Poles wished to set him over the Hungarians as king, but divine providence frustrated his plan. The blind king met him with his army [Note: Col. 0256D: at the river Sajó], and Bolesław [Col. 0255D; Note: Col. 0256D: the Third] and his men, terrified, waited for night and then fled [Col. 0256A]. The Hungarians pursued them and, with God’s help, killed many in the flight.

Meanwhile Duke Soběslav [Note: Col. 0256D: who had married Adelaide, sister of King Béla], fortified by God’s mercy and the prayers of St Wenceslas [Note: Col. 0255: thus 2a and 2b; “unwilling,” 2; “fortified” in the margin], entered Poland with his army on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November. He utterly consumed with fire all that part of the region called Silesia [Note: Col. 0255: Slansko, 2a and 2b]. He took away many captives, countless riches, and not a few herds of untamed mares [Note: Col. 0255: “brought,” 2], and so, with God’s grace favouring him, returned to his homeland amid great triumph and rejoicing.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1133, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, the moon suffered an eclipse, but a quarter of it was darkened; thus it set as sunrise approached. A very great mortality among men followed this eclipse. On the seventeenth [Note: Col. 0255: eighteenth, 2b] day before the Kalends of February, the vigorous Duke Soběslav invaded Poland for the second time [Col. 0256B], ravaged it with a splendid victory, carried off many captives, burned nearly three hundred villages, and at last returned home victoriously through God’s granting.

At the same time an apostolic legate arrived and accused Bishop Meinhard of many detestable crimes. He ordered the accused man to come before an apostolic hearing and clear himself of the charge brought against him. For certain perverse brothers of his monastery had conspired against him, seeking shamefully to drive him from his see after stripping him of his dignity. God’s grace did not permit their execrable and unjust scheme to take effect.

Duke Soběslav, proceeding to Hungary to his brother-in-law, the king of the Hungarians, pitched camp on this side of a district called Vag. Having remained there a long time [Col. 0256C], he finally completed [Note: Col. 0255: “having set out,” 2] his business and returned home.

On the fourth day before the Nones of August a solar eclipse appeared in a marvellous fashion. The sun gradually failed and was so reduced that a crescent-like rim passed toward the south; afterwards it turned eastward, then westward, and finally returned to its former condition. In many places too in the German lands, if report is to be believed, blood seemed to fall like rain [Note: Col. 0255: “to rain,” 2b] that very day. It is further reported that, in a certain place in the German lands, a piece [Note: Col. 0255: “open,” 2 and 2b] of flesh descended at that same hour together with the bloody rain. It was so large that scarcely twelve men could have lifted it.

After this Bishop Meinhard, nurtured in holy piety [Col. 0256D; 0257A], went to Mainz to defend himself before his archbishop. Many bishops had assembled there, and in their hearing he duly cleared himself of the charge brought against him [Note: Col. 0257: “he excused and cleared himself,” 2b]. He mercifully forgave his accusers every crime by which they had dared rise against him [Note: Col. 0257: “every” omitted in 2].

In the same year (4 June), King Lothair, having received the imperial insignia, was consecrated by Pope Innocent in the monastery of St John the Baptist in the Lateran. He did not dare proceed to the church of St Peter the Apostle, fearing Peter, son of Leo, who was then presiding over the holy Roman Church.

In the same year the unruly young man Vladislav, namesake of his distinguished father [Note: Col. 0257D: Vladislav I, Soběslav’s brother], fled into the Bavarian regions with many illustrious men of the Bohemian land.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1134, unfortunate Poland, under the protection of the imprudent [Note: Col. 0257: “fearless,” 2a] Duke Bolesław, already repeatedly ravaged in war by Bohemians and Moravians, was again entered and despoiled by the aforesaid armies of both Bohemians and Moravians. It was wholly devastated with fire and sword as far as the river called the Oder. Yet of the Bohemians there were few besides men from Hradec, Chrudim, Boleslav, Čáslav, and Kladsko.

The illustrious Prince Soběslav, conspicuous alike for strength of spirit and bodily power and deserving of frequent praise, met Emperor Lothair for a conference in the city called Plzeň [Note: Col. 0257D: whether this is Pilsen in Bohemia, as some have wished, is doubtful; for at nearly the same time Lothair was staying among the Saxons; see Jaffé, p. 153]. The reason for this was as follows [Col. 0257C].

The blind king of the Pannonians [Note: Col. 0257: “the king,” inserted in 2 and 2a] had sent Peter, bishop of the city of Alba [Note: Col. 0258D: Stuhlweissenburg], to the emperor with great gifts, to lay before the emperor and his princes the injuries inflicted upon him by the Polish duke. But because, as commonly happens in such affairs, the embassy of an inferior party accomplishes little or nothing with a superior unless a mediator intervenes, the aforesaid bishop came to Duke Soběslav in Bohemia, so that his embassy might succeed through Soběslav’s mediation and intercession.

For this reason Duke Soběslav went to the emperor. When he arrived, the emperor received him graciously and honourably, and he obtained every request kindly: namely, that the imperial will concerning the king of Hungary and the duke of Poland should proceed according to Duke Soběslav’s will [Col. 0257D; Note: Col. 0257: “dignity,” 2b].

The gifts offered to the emperor by the Hungarians were these: two white horses, suitably caparisoned [Note: Col. 0257: omitted in 2a], whose saddles contained twenty-six marks of gold, together with many other things [Col. 0258A]. Therefore the aforesaid Peter, bishop of Alba, having obtained the embassy he desired and having also been given many valuable gifts by the emperor and his consort [Note: Col. 0257: *conthorali*, 2a and 2b; Col. 0258D: Richenza], returned home rejoicing.

Meanwhile, the Bohemians, unable to remain at peace, entered Poland on the fourth day before the Kalends of March; by chance it was Monday of Quinquagesima [Note: Col. 0257: “Quadragesima,” 2b]. The Poles, judging that no enemy would now come as the beginning of Lent drew near, had left their camps and various fortifications and were staying in their villages. Therefore, while they wished in security [Note: Col. 0257: “secure,” 2b] to enjoy the calm times of peace, enemies suddenly [Note: Col. 0257: omitted in 2a] and unexpectedly came upon them and carried them off like sheep from sheepfolds, with no protector.

Although the Bohemians entered the enemy land without Duke Soběslav [Col. 0258B], they nevertheless brought back such plunder that it surpassed all the booty which all the dukes of Bohemia had taken in Poland. O miserable land subjected to a foolish ruler! For whatever madness kings commit, the Greeks are punished [Note: Col. 0258D: Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14].

The often-mentioned king of the Pannonians [Note: Col. 0257: “of Pannonia,” 2a], Béla, blinded by fraternal cruelty [Note: Col. 0258D: that is, by Coloman, who was the cousin-german of Álmos, Béla’s father], asked his son-in-law, Duke Soběslav, to lift his infant from the font of holy regeneration. No one ought to wonder at this, since such spiritual kinship is arranged between brother-in-law and son-in-law, between sister and brother. For our descendants will yet see ages proceeding more marvellously—indeed, more miserably—when, as is already clear in many events, a child’s begetter becomes his own child’s godfather.

Now indeed holy faith, though it has sought the stars after abandoning worldly aids, nevertheless looks down somewhat from above upon earthly things [Col. 0258C]. But afterwards, when the more calamitous pest of faithlessness [Note: Col. 0257: “faithless,” 2] has grown stronger, it will seek loftier hiding-places and will not even wish to turn its gaze toward us [Note: Col. 0257: “toward wrath,” 2 and 2a].

King Béla therefore asked his son-in-law concerning the infant. Duke Soběslav did not refuse his request, but sent the venerable Bishop Meinhard of the Prague [Note: Col. 0257: “Prague,” 2a] church and very many other leading men with the child into Hungary. When they arrived, King Béla received Bishop Meinhard with no less honour than when, first adorned with pontifical mitre, he had come to the chief seat of his bishopric.

After the infant had been baptized on Pentecost (3 June), the aforesaid bishop was rewarded by the king with many precious gifts and returned home [Col. 0258D; Note: Col. 0257: “returns,” 2 and 2b]. But, as God, the gracious rewarder of faithful servants, was approaching the day on which he had determined to lead Meinhard, a faithful and worthy steward of His household, from the hardships of this life into everlasting joy [Col. 0259A], Meinhard was seized by illness on that very return journey [Note: Col. 0259: “confined,” 2b]. As his illness worsened and he could not travel farther, he took to his bed in a village belonging to his bishopric called Sekyr.

Meanwhile Duke Soběslav asked his brother-in-law, the king of Hungary, to give the sister of his wife [Note: Col. 0259D: that is, of Coloman; she was Maria, born in Serbia], namely Queen Helena [Note: Col. 0259D], in marriage to Prince Conrad of Znojmo, so that the alliance made between them might endure more firmly, strengthened by such ties.

When she had been betrothed and he heard that the bishop was held by illness, he first grieved, overflowing as he was with compassionate feeling; then he hurried to return as quickly as possible, that he might find alive the man whom he loved with deepest affection [Col. 0259B]. Returning from Hungary, the aforesaid prince came to his bishop and gave fitting consolations of kindness to the man suffering from illness [Note: Col. 0259: “in,” inserted in 2; “now,” inserted in 2b].

The bishop, sensing the approaching dissolution of his body, gave his duke all the gifts he had received from the Hungarian king. Having accepted them and visited his pastor, the duke returned home. After his departure, the venerable bishop Meinhard, ever to be remembered with pious love, rendered to his highest Creditor the profit of the talent entrusted to him, multiplied by a double yield. He passed from the perilous disturbances of human life to the blessed dwellings of the saints, there to rejoice in everlasting reward.

When his venerable body had been brought to the metropolitan city of his bishopric, Henry, bishop of Olomouc, who was performing the office due at his funeral [Col. 0259C], tearfully entreated Duke Soběslav and all there present, clergy and laity alike, that if, prompted rather by malignant impulse than by any truth of right, they had held any disagreement with the unhappy foreigner during his life, they should at least show forbearance toward his pitiable funeral.

When the funeral rites were completed, he buried him fittingly in the church of the holy martyrs Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert. Whoever wishes to know the course of his life and the many adversities which he endured in his bishopric through the plotting of the adversary of humankind and destroyer of every good, the devil, should turn back to what has been written above.

Meanwhile, after Bishop Megnard, as has already been said, had been removed from this world by the law of death, very many persons arose—secretly, however—of whom some, through the intervention of friends and kinsmen, while others through wealth, which corrupts even holy men, importuned Duke Soběslav and Emperor Lothair, thinking by their permission, but without the divine will of Saint Adalbert the martyr, to obtain his see. The supreme Judge, the truest inspector of all things, frustrated the wicked and God-hated desires of all these men by destroying their unjust hidden wishes [Note: “[indeed” is added by MS 2a.]; his providence is not deceived in its ordering, and what he has firmly predestined is in no respect frustrated. He turned Duke Soběslav far away from their scheme and, by the power of his divinity, compelled him to seek a suitable shepherd for his faithful.

Therefore the aforesaid prince, filled with the spirit of discernment [Note: “thus I emend; P. has *refert*, as do the editions”], lest he remain any longer without his own bishop, held a council in his metropolitan city of Prague on 3 Kalends of October [29 September]. All the magnates of Bohemia, clerical as well as lay, were present; for perhaps they had gathered there because of the feast of our blessed patron, the martyr Wenceslas. When, therefore, a rumour contrary to divine reason [Note: MS 2b has “diverse”] ran through the council, so that one group shouted that this man, another that man, was worthy of the episcopate, and none among them found a suitable candidate, John—chosen by God before the ages—was at last called forward.

At that time he governed the provostship of the holy church of Vyšehrad, surpassing all in person, pleasing all by his affability, and acceptable to God and men in his other habits of life. He therefore deserved to be chosen to the summit of the episcopate and appointed shepherd and ruler of those subject to him.

The winter was unsettled: at one time there was frost, at another the earth thawed as in the season of spring, so that the River Elbe was bound by ice twice and thawed twice. The River Vltava, which by its channel divides our metropolitan cities, Prague and Vyšehrad, froze four times, and its ice dissolved four times; moreover, there was a scarcity of snow. This unseasonable weather, beginning in November, omitted no month throughout the entire course of the following year without raging violently either at the beginning or at the end of every month. At last, in the second year, on 5 Kalends of November [28 October], during the evening hours, a most savage storm of winds arose throughout the whole world. Raging until night, it destroyed, in the first dusk of night, churches both of stone and of wood, as well as buildings, fences, and piles in barns, so that not even one sheaf remained upon another; it uprooted trees utterly throughout the forests.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, John, bishop-elect of the holy church of Prague, set out for the emperor, [Note: “Who was at Quedlinburg at the beginning of February [Col. 0260D]. Jaffé, p. 277.”] so that his election might be strengthened by imperial assent and approval. When he arrived, he was honoured with so high a distinction that the emperor caused him to be received with a procession, and then himself went out to meet him. After he had handed him the episcopal insignia, namely staff and ring [Note: “This was contrary to the agreements of Calixtus in the year 1122.”], he sent him to the Archbishop of Mainz, that he might ordain him a bishop worthy of God [Note: “The words ‘a worthy bishop’ are absent in MS 2a.”].

Thus Bishop John, ordained by his archbishop on 13 Kalends of March [17 February], returned with great gladness and joy. But before he came to the metropolitan city of his bishopric, he consecrated [Note: MSS 2a and 2b have “dedicated”] the church of one of the leading men, which happened to lie on his route. While he was performing the mystical offices of dedication according to custom, on the Nones [Note: MS 2a has “on the ninth”] of March [7 March] a sign appeared in the sun. There were four [Note: MS 2b has “smaller”] circles, joined together by certain configurations: one in the middle, larger than the others; a second to the east; a third to the west; and a fourth to the north. Beneath them many signs, like false suns, appeared around the true sun, and they remained thus for almost three hours. Traces of the sign were visible until the eleventh hour of the day. When Bishop John had dedicated the aforesaid church and came to the seat of his episcopate, he was received with great rejoicing by clergy and people.

In the same year Prague, the metropolis of Bohemia, began to be rebuilt in the manner of Latin [Note: “That is, Italian.”] cities. While Duke Soběslav and Bolesław [Note: MS 2b adds “of Poland”] remained in the discord into which, through the machinations of the enemy of humankind, they had begun to fall against one another, and none of their peers could suitably restore peace between them by mediation, Emperor Lothair, compelled, indeed, by divine inspiration, caused both to come at an appointed time to his court [Note: “At Merseburg, where a council was held beginning on 15 August; compare Jaffé, p. 164.”].

As each hurried with his duchy at full speed to carry out the imperial commands, the emperor frequently urged his sworn kinsman Soběslav, the most faithful supporter of the realm, through envoys, to arrive before Bolesław. As we learned, he did this chiefly for this reason: he wished to determine at his own discretion with what, or with what kind of, honour he should receive Duke Bolesław. When Duke Bolesław arrived and the emperor and his princes were taking counsel about the matter, Duke Soběslav rose and said, in the hearing of all present: “No honour is fitting for Duke Bolesław before God except that he become the emperor’s lictor.” [Note: MS 2b has “Botestaus” for Soběslav and “Sobieslao” for Bolesław; MS 2 has “was made.”] [Note: “Bolesław performed homage to the emperor and, bearing his sword, went before him in the procession, according to the testimony of the Annals and the Saxon Chronicle.”]

When he had said this, all the German princes answered unanimously that no one was so faithful and intimate a friend of the emperor as Duke Soběslav; and although he had previously been regarded before the emperor as unfaithful and an enemy, in this present affair he had plainly proved himself the emperor’s most friendly and faithful supporter. Bolesław therefore came; and when they had taken their seats in council, Duke Soběslav sat at the emperor’s right hand, and [Note: MSS 2 and 2b have “but”] the other princes sat on the other side. A seat, however, was placed before his presence for Bolesław, as for a lictor. At length, after many matters had been debated there with much deliberation [Note: MS 2 has “councils”], peace remained incomplete, but a truce was established, and each returned home.

At the same time envoys of the Greek emperor [Note: “John I Comnenus.”] came to the emperor, bringing many great gifts, for the following reason. A certain duke named Roger [Note: “Roger II, son of Roger I, the first king of Sicily.”], living beyond Sicily, was ravaging Greek territory; and the Greek emperor requested that the emperor restrain him.

In Thuringia, in a certain level field, a stone of wondrous size, like a large house, descended through the air. Its sound was heard for the space of the preceding three days by people living near that place. After it fell downward, half of it sank into the depths of the earth, and for three days it lay hot like steel drawn from the fire.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, the feast of Saint Benedict the Confessor (21 March) fell to be celebrated on Great Saturday, that is, on the vigil of the Lord’s Resurrection, which rarely happens. I shall relate a detestable and rarely heard occurrence, as I have learned it.

At one time Henry, Bishop of Olomouc, was about to build a church in the village called Blansko [Note: “Blankenstein in the Leitmeritz district.”]—for this village had long before been under the authority of his predecessors. But Vratislav, one of the dukes of Moravia [Note: “Duke of Brno, son of Duke Ulrich, who died in 1115; compare Cosmas III, 41.”], when he learned of the good purpose of the good bishop, began eagerly to consider how he might destroy this undertaking. He did this chiefly because he had learned that a great quantity of goods was stored in the bishop’s storehouse in that village; if he could seize them in any way, he was most greedily intent upon doing so.

It therefore happened that the aforesaid bishop, together with Duke Conrad and Duke Vratislav, met in a certain monastery called Rajhrad, intending to hold various councils [Note: MSS 2a and 2b have “conduct matters”]. When their business had been transacted, Duke Vratislav forbade Bishop Henry to build a church in the aforesaid village, asserting that it belonged more to himself than to the bishop. At last, after many councils had been held there, peace remained incomplete, but a truce was established, and each returned home.

As Emperor Lothair was about to go to Rome, he sought help from Duke Soběslav. Soběslav consented to the imperial request and, having assembled an army, placed at its head Vladislav, who had recently been recalled from exile. When he distributed a gift to the soldiers, he gave Vladislav nine hundred marks of denarii; having received them, Vladislav secretly took flight with his companions.

In the same year, on 17 Kalends of August [16 July], the star called Lucifer appeared at the winter rising-point of the sun. Maintaining its course above, it finally reached the place where the sun is accustomed to rise on 8 Kalends of July [24 June], namely the very day on which the days begin to shorten and the nights to increase. When it had remained there for some time, a new star appeared after it, one seen neither by us nor by our fathers, indeed not even by our grandfathers. Within a short space of time it passed the former star; and not long afterward the former returned by the same route to its place and there set, while this one proceeded in a straight course toward the west.

I record this especially for modern readers and posterity, so that those who are less diligent [Note: MS 2a has “more cautious”] may know that a new star appeared; but if they observe this fact with sleepless care, let them know how to proclaim God wonderful in his works and glorious, and let them pray that he may deign so to order all that he visibly works that, praising his omnipotence in all things, they may deserve to receive the gifts of salvation promised by him. For these are the works of him of whom that eminent author says:

> You number the stars, whose names you alone know;  
> You know their signs, powers, courses, places, and times.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1137 [the text reads “1037”], I am pleased, setting aside for a little while the matters mentioned above, to insert a new and wonderful work of divine mercy and power, which I learned from truthful report. In the district of Čáslav [Note: “thus MS 2a”] there is a village called Beztuina [Note: “thus MS 2a”] [Note: “Today Bestwin in the Čáslav district.”]. In it a certain woman had lived from her virginity for many years with her husband, preserving toward him faithfulness and affection as was fitting. But after a long time, when she was already declining into old age [Note: perhaps “old age” should be corrected], she was seized by so grave an illness that she could by no means walk upright or stand, but was carried out and brought back on a litter by others. In short, she was held by this illness for several years.

It happened that, during the celebrations of the Lord’s Nativity, when according to the custom of our people all were occupied with common feasting, this woman, deprived of the ability to act, lay alone at home. Her neighbouring women came to her and asked that they might carry her over, so that, even if she could not sit, she might at least recline somehow [Note: MS 2b has “certainly”] among their company. She did not refuse their request but promised to do so. Carried among the feasters, she lay there until much murmuring and noise, as commonly happens among guests, began to arise. Calling one of her attendants, she asked to be carried home, and this was done.

That day was the feast of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr (26 December), and a Saturday. As she sat alone at home and no one else was with her, she suddenly heard a sweet sound, like the sound of a bell. Somewhat indignant, she said: “Alas, how much my brother has devoted himself to feasting, since he performs the divine office at such an unsuitable time!” For her own brother was parish priest of the church built there.

As she said this, behold, the door of the house in which she sat opened, and the sound which she had heard resounded as though a bell hung in her house. Terrified, she looked toward the door and saw two noble men standing there, clad in episcopal countenance and dress. One of them touched her with the staff he held and said: “Rise; give glory to God. I am John the Evangelist, whose festival faithful people throughout the world are to celebrate tomorrow. This is my brother Saint Gotthard. Know that you have been healed through our prayer.” Raising her up, they led her out and, as divine power willed, brought her to the village called Zlapi, where a certain noble and powerful man named Mladota had built a church in honour of Blessed Gotthard, bishop and confessor.

When they had arrived there, they set her down before the church. She stood with such firm step as though she had never been touched by illness. Taking her by the hand, they brought her inside; and behold, men of radiant countenance, clothed in white garments, were singing praises to God. But how great an odour and how great a splendour she said that she perceived there cannot be uttered by human speech.

While this occurred, her husband came back from the gathering of the neighbours. Not finding his wife, he thought that she had been led away by some temptation of the Evil One; and, summoning the neighbours, they sought her everywhere around the village, through marshes and thickets. Failing to find her, they gathered and sat weeping at home.

Meanwhile, after making her prayer, she was about to offer the earrings she had received upon the altar, when Saint John the Evangelist forbade her, saying: “Tomorrow, when the people assemble for Mass in the place [Note: MS 2b adds “your”], then [Note: absent in MS 2a] offer these earrings upon the altar in your church, and tell of the mighty works of God which the grace of God has wrought in you through us; and do not remain any longer with your husband.”

When these things had been done, the same saints brought her back, set her before the gate of her house, and immediately disappeared. Rejoicing, she entered her home and found them weeping. Telling them of God’s power, she showed what and how great things God had wrought in her. But they, with roles reversed [Note: MS 2b has “voice”], wept not so much for her return as for joy at her healing. When the following day dawned and the whole neighbourhood flocked together to hear the mysteries of the Mass, the aforesaid woman, as the saints had commanded her, placed her earrings upon the altar before all those standing there and recounted in order everything that had been divinely done in her. Hearing these things and seeing her well, they rendered immeasurable thanks to God and the saints.

The venerable Bishop Henry [Note: MS 2b adds “also called Zdík”] resolved to go to the Lord’s tomb. Having received leave from Duke Soběslav, he celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity (25 December) at Prague with his brother, Bishop John. When it was over, both went to Moravia and there celebrated the feast of the Epiphany (6 January) at Olomouc, the seat of the bishopric. John returned home, but Henry set out on his journey. Many from both regions went with him, among them Bolecay [Note: “This seems to be the correct reading; MS 1 has *Boleslai*, MS 2b *Boleslaus*”], our acquaintance and a most faithful supporter of this church.

But because they were detained for a long time at Constantinople—for perhaps the emperor was conducting wars in distant regions—they could not reach Jerusalem before the Saturday before Easter (11 April). After they arrived, the bishop remained there to await another Easter feast. His travelling companions, however, having worshipped at the Lord’s tomb, returned. They suffered many dangers at sea because of storms, and many of them died while wandering on the sea. Among these the aforesaid Bolecay [Note: MS 2b has “Boleslaus”] died and was buried on a certain deserted island; the rest escaped with great difficulty.

In the same year, during Lent (28 February), Duke Soběslav met his brother-in-law, the king of Hungary. After many and varied matters had been discussed, he celebrated holy Easter at the castle of Olomouc; for he could not reach his metropolis of Vyšehrad before Easter.

The noble duchess Adelaide [Note: MS 2b has “Adelheid”], eagerly desiring to attend the feast of Blessed Stephen, king and confessor (2 September), went to Pannonia. But she was detained there longer by her brother, until she buried her father Álmos. For Álmos, blinded by his brother Coloman, ended his life in exile in Greek territory. His unburied body thus remained for ten years, until his son King Béla, himself deprived of sight by the same aforesaid tyrant, carried it into his own kingdom. After her father had been buried [Note: “In MS 2 ‘brother’ was first written, but corrected to ‘father’ by the same ancient hand.”], Duchess Adelaide, since she could not return home for the feast of Saint Wenceslas the martyr (29 September), celebrated his feast in the aforesaid castle of Olomouc.

Prince Soběslav and Duke Bolesław met in the castle of Kladsko, on the Bohemian frontier, on the feast of Pentecost (30 May), and there entered into a treaty of peace. When this was concluded, they returned home. After the feast, Vladislav, son of Bolesław [Note: MSS 2a and 2b have “of Vladislav”], lifted from the font the infant son of Duke Soběslav in the castle of Němci and gave him the name Wenceslas [Note: “The words ‘in the castle … gave him’ are absent in MS 2, but read by MS 2b.”].

But while we describe in sequence the affairs of mortal things, it remains for us to add something briefly about heavenly matters. Since in the preceding year we spoke of two stars, we shall now speak also of three. A third star, equal in brightness to the two previously mentioned, appeared on 3 Ides of September [11 September]. It rose before the dusk of day in the place where the sun travels in the sign of Leo. The second, called Lucifer, rose on 5 Kalends of January [28 December], likewise before the dusk of day. The third, which had been seen in the preceding year, did not appear with these.

Emperor Lothair, joined to our prince Soběslav by spiritual kinship, was removed from the midst by the law of death in the castle of Rodburk [Note: “He died at the village of Breitenwang; compare Mascov, *Commentary on Lothair*, p. 340. Other names are given by others; compare Jaffé, p. 223.”] and passed to the world above [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “from those above”]. He was buried in a castle called Brunswick.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, on 4 Kalends of March [26 February], a sign in the form of a serpent was seen after sunset flying throughout all Bohemia toward the west. Suddenly vanishing, it left behind signs like red marks. Within the Easter season, on 5 Ides of May [11 May], red signs appeared in the northern sky in the form of columns. Divided into two parts, they seemed to contend, at one moment rushing together, at another retreating.

After King Conrad had been elected, all the princes and all the leading men and retainers of his kingdom decreed that on the holy solemnity of Pentecost, which fell on 11 Kalends of June [22 May; Note: MS 2b has “July”], they should hold a court and council in the city of Bamberg; that all belonging to his kingdom should gather there at the appointed time [Note: “For the princes, including Soběslav, who assembled there in support of Conrad’s cause, see the charter which Conrad ordered to be written there, in Herrgott, *Genealogia gentis Habsburgicae*, II, 158.”]; that his election should likewise be confirmed by all; and that the royal insignia should be received before all the princes from the Duke of Regensburg [Note: “That is, Henry the Proud, Duke of Bavaria and Saxony, Lothair’s son-in-law.”].

When all had assembled together as decreed, the Duke of Regensburg neither wished himself to be present at the gathering nor returned the royal insignia. After the council had been held and many matters transacted, as each was returning home, our Duke Soběslav came to the king, who was still remaining in the same place, during the feast just mentioned. Received by the king with great honour, he remained there for several days. By the king’s favour he also obtained that his son Vladislav should succeed him in the government of the duchy. Although a boy, Vladislav received the banner from the king in his father’s presence; to confirm this, all the Bohemian nobles swore oaths upon the relics of the saints before the king.

When these things had been done, Duke Soběslav, filled with joy according to his desire, returned home with his men. When the solemnity of the Apostles Peter and Paul (29 June) approached for celebration by the faithful, Duke Soběslav ordered the knights of the first and second rank to assemble before him at once at Sačka. When this had been done, the duke himself partly begged and partly commanded them to confirm by oath in his presence the loyalty which they were willing to keep for his son after his death; and this was done.

In the same year, as the feast of our blessed patron Wenceslas (29 September) approached, Duke Soběslav joined his daughter Mary in lawful marriage to the son [Note: “He died on 28 October 1139; compare Roeppel, I, 297.”] of Leopold [Note: “Leopold.”], margrave of the East, and endowed her with five hundred marks of silver. These nuptials took place in Moravia, in the district of Olomouc.

On the day before the Ides of October [14 October], at the first dusk of night, red signs appeared in the north. On the second night, namely the Ides themselves, the same happened at the same hour. On the third night, 17 Kalends of November [16 October], around dawn, they appeared in the same way. Duke Bolesław died [Note: “the Fourth.”].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, Duke Soběslav redeemed several castles from Wigbert’s wife for seven hundred marks of silver. He furthermore gave her the third penny in the castle of Donín. Having confirmed [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “confirming”] the soldiers who guarded [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “should guard”] the castles, Duke Soběslav was returning one day with his army. When he was at the entrance to his land, in the midst of a forest, a most violent wind blew, uprooting not only buildings and every sort of obstacle, but [Note: MS 2 adds “and”] also the great trees of the forests. Meanwhile [Note: MS 2 omits “in”], the Bohemians, placed in great danger, were so terrified that one of the castellans, approaching the duke, said: “Behold, my lord duke, before God and his saints, with your own favour as witness, I promise that, if the omnipotence of God deigns to deliver me from this danger with my life, you shall know that I shall as soon as possible take up the habit of monastic profession.”

But under God’s protection only seven men in the whole army perished through falling trees; the rest returned safely. On the seventh [Note: “Perhaps the sixth should be read.”] Nones of March [1 March], red signs were seen in an unusual place from the beginning of the night to its end. In this year the solemnities of the holy martyrs Adalbert and George were celebrated by the faithful on 9 Kalends of May [23 April] [Note: “They fall on 23 April.”]. That same day shone with the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection.

At the same time Duke Soběslav met his brother-in-law, Béla, king of Pannonia, for this King Béla was giving his daughter [Note: “Sophia.”] to the son [Note: “Henry, who died before his father.”] of Conrad, king of the Germans. These nuptials were celebrated on the feast of Pentecost (11 June).

On the fourteenth Kalends of August [19 July], a darkness of the air occurred: smoke of an unusual stench exhaled like a mist, nor did it cease smoking by day or by night, the darkness continuing thus for a week. On 9 Kalends of the same month [24 July], a denser blackness than usual darkened the air about noon with a most putrid stench, as though an odour issuing from hell had blown over people’s senses of smell. There were also some who said that they had seen something like a fissure in the sun.

When the Saxons resisted King Conrad and refused to give assent and favour to his election, he resolved to subdue to his kingdom men tested in wars [Note: “This expedition was decreed in the council of princes held at Strasbourg on 28 May; compare Jaffé, *Conrad III*, p. 23. The expedition itself began on 25 July, according to the Chronicle of St Pantaleon.”]. As he gathered reinforcements for his army through many retainers, he requested among the others our Duke Soběslav to take part with his men in the aforesaid war, for he placed very great hope of victory in the strength of Soběslav’s fighters.

When king and Duke Soběslav entered Saxony by different routes [Note: “Not without the mediation of Albero, Archbishop of Trier.”], the Saxons, unable to bear the force of the newcomers, fled to their camps. They did not dare to appear before the king until, through the mediation of Duke Soběslav, they submitted themselves to the king’s authority and obtained his peace in every respect. Thus, with the king’s honour preserved, a victory was accomplished without arms. Returning thence, they ravaged a certain place and carried off great plunder.

At that time John, Bishop of Prague, worn down by a long illness, passed to the world above on 6 Ides of August [8 August; Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “from the world above”]. He had been afflicted by illness from March until 6 Ides of August, as we have said. He was buried in the chapel of Saint Gotthard, bishop and confessor, which he himself had ordered built to the north by piercing the wall of the church of Saint Wenceslas.

Sylvester, abbot of Sázava, succeeded him under an ill omen. His election was made on 3 Kalends of October [29 September]; but because he was not consecrated before the duke, by whose will he had been chosen, ended his life, his election lasted only a short time, as will become clear in what follows.

After this Duke Soběslav went to his estate called Chvojno [Note: MS 2 has “Chwoyno”; Note: “By Palacký’s conjecture, I. 413: Königgrätz.”], and while staying there began to rebuild the castle called Hostin Hradec [Note: MSS have “Goscin,” “Hosczin Hradek”; Note: “Arnau.”]. For he intended, if God willed, to create discord between himself and the dukes of Poland and perhaps in some degree to subjugate them to his dominion; for this reason he was fortifying the castles on their side. But divine providence had determined otherwise: before he had brought the aforesaid castle to completion, on the Sunday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord (17 December), he was struck by a deadly illness and laid low in bed.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, as the illness grew ever more severe, he was taken from Chvojno [Note: MS 2b has “Chwoyna”] and carried to the castle mentioned above. Meanwhile, I judged it more prudent to pass over in silence the many rumours and counsels which the Bohemian nobles entertained, lest perhaps, by narrating individual events as they occurred, I incur someone’s hatred. For all the chief men of Bohemia had gathered in the city [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “city,” ablative] of Vyšehrad. Deliberating day and night, one group strove to elect and enthrone this man, another that man. Yet the whole assembly looked only to Nacerat [Note: “thus MS 4; Naczerath in MSS 2, 2a, and 2b”], so that all might unanimously submit to whichever candidate he favoured.

While these things were taking place, those about Duke Soběslav, together with his lady wife, seeing in him no sign of returning health, anointed him with oil. Then, as bodily weakness increased more and more, he received the viaticum and departed this world on 16 Kalends of March [14 February].

Alas! It is hard to relate with what anxiety and disturbance Bohemia was then shaken. It grieved deservedly at the loss of so great a defender and father. He was bound by such love for his country that, caring for all, he was most ready to die for the liberty and honour of his subjects. For this reason he avoided in every way [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “in all ways”] the wantonness of the flesh, which is accustomed to weaken many men [Note: MS 2b has “weaken”; MS 2 has “relate”].

Soběslav, a vigorous duke [Note: MS 2b has “a holy man and duke”], eminent above all in person, gracious in speech, energetic in warfare, prudent in counsel, and generous in almsgiving—for, as his fellow-chaplains reported to him, he knew that Blessed Gregory had said: “Why then are you slow to give, when what you extend to one lying on the earth, you give to one sitting in heaven?”—also took anxious and diligent care of the poor. For he was not a deaf hearer of the Gospel command: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Although he was occupied with great care not only for his own principality, but also devoted attention to Moravia and Serbia [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “Scribia”], and, as I have sufficiently shown above, often gave his counsel to the king of the Pannonians in many matters, he nevertheless frequently reflected within himself lest his soul, entangled in occupations of this kind, should perish through lack of foresight [Note: MS 2 has “improvident”]. Therefore, as though instructed by the words of a certain wise man saying:

> Gifts that a man gives when dying are not gifts,

he undertook a saving plan with his consort, Lady Adelaide [Note: MS 2b has *conthorali*, “wife”]. They hastened before the day of their death to placate the supreme Judge and inspector of consciences, particularly considering that after their death no one would be so faithful or intimate to them as to distribute their goods to the poor and to servants of God as they themselves had done while alive.

In short, they [Note: MS 2b has the singular “summoned”] summoned the chaplain Vincent, than whom no one was more faithful to them. They revealed to him in order the entire plan of their holy intention and at the same time ordered and begged him, on their behalf, to ask the canons of the holy churches of Vyšehrad and Prague, as well as the fellow-soldiers of Saint Benedict and the nuns, together with all the clergy dwelling within the city, to perform the offices for the dead according to custom: namely, on the first, second, third, and seventh [Note: MS 2b has “sixth”] days; and thereafter to make commemorations for them until the anniversary. Some were to say Masses for the salvation of the living, others for sins, others for the faithful departed.

It was therefore decided to appoint the first day on the feast of All Saints (1 November). To show how affectionately and devoutly the praiseworthy Duke Soběslav performed this almsgiving, when the anniversary came he himself held a meal in the cloister of Vyšehrad with the canons of that monastery and all the devout clergy assembled from the suburb [Note: absent in MSS 2 and 2a], and there, amid rich display, showed a rich [Note: MS 2 has “to the rich”] intention.

The same noble Duke Soběslav, among the other great deeds of his life, subjected to Emperor Lothair and King Conrad the Saxons and Bavarians, as well as others at times hostile to the Roman Empire. Surrounded by these and many other honours of this kind [Note: MSS 2 and 2a have “of this world”], the aforesaid duke was overtaken by death on 16 Kalends of March [14 February]. May God, the rewarder of all good things, for whose love the aforesaid duke performed this good work, now deign to cherish his soul according to the generous will of the cheerful giver. Amen. [Note: MS 2b has “May you deign, Lord.”]

Vladislav [Note: “the Second.”] succeeded him. Abbot Sylvester lost the bishopric. Vladislav, with his followers, met at Bamberg his brother-in-law King Conrad [Note: “Vladislav’s wife was Gertrude, daughter of Leopold IV, Margrave of Austria; through her mother Agnes, she was sister of King Conrad III [Col. 0270D].”] [Note: “Apparently in April; compare Jaffé, *Conrad III*, p. 47.”], and, having received the banner from the king, returned home.

In the same year Otto proceeded to the ordination of the bishopric. Having received it, he returned home with great honour and joy on 5 Kalends of June [28 May], from the metropolitan city of Mainz, ordained by Archbishop Albert.

In the same year Duchess Adelaide, honourable and illustrious in character, after no long course of this life, was touched by the sorrows of her heart. Having lived seven months after the death of her husband, she departed this world on 17 Kalends of October [15 September].

The River Sázava, which flows beside the monastery of the same name, Sázava, suffered a rupture on 15 Kalends of December, for more than twenty stadia in length from above to below; and the mill of that monastery, which from ancient times had never lacked water, then stood dry. [Note: [Col. 0269] “disruption,” 2b.] The abbot and brethren of that monastery, with their servants, came to the bank; observing the marvel, and in order to make it more widely known, they gathered large fish and crabs from the dry riverbed, contrary to the usual custom. From the first hour until the sixth, moreover, the aforesaid river was, by divine dispensation, held in this altered condition. [Note: [Col. 0271] “alteration,” 2, 2b.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation (25 December) 1141, Duke Vladislav celebrated the feast of the Nativity of the Lord at the village called Siwohost, [Note: [Col. 0271] Czijhosst’ in the margin of 2b.] where, on the very feast-day, when night had covered the whole world, the boy Vladislav [Note: [Col. 0271D] son of the deceased Duke Soběslav I.] fled to his maternal uncle named Béla, who was then reigning in Hungary. That winter was variable. Béla, king of the Hungarians, died, and our exiles grieved with bowed heads.

In this year, during Lent, many men throughout the whole region of Bohemia were hanged on the gallows, especially on Mount Šibenica. [Note: [Col. 0271D] Today Mount Žižka.] Of these, several escaped and took flight. On 17 Kalends of May, the flooding of the River Vltava, which flows between the cities of Vyšehrad and Prague, became excessive and greatly damaged neighboring property. On 9 Kalends of May a new Lucifer arose, but it differed in its changes from the earlier Lucifer which I mentioned before: that one arose on 17 Kalends of August; this one was seen on 9 Kalends of May, and thus pursues varied courses.

Here Bishop Zdík of the church of Olomouc, receiving the cross from the holy altar of Saint Peter, weeping for joy and singing this antiphon, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross” (Mark II, 31), etc., mounted his horse with his men against the pagans called Prussians, in order to instill in them faith in the Holy Trinity and baptize them. [Note: [Col. 0271D] See concerning this matter the letters given by Pope Innocent II to Bishop Henry in the year 1141; Boczek I, 212.] Yet it is better to be silent concerning his journey: [Note: [Col. 0271] “who then,” 2.] he labored in vain, [Note: [Col. 0271] “than,” 2.] and one may rejoice at his return.

[Col. 0271C]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, while Conrad, not yet Roman emperor, was reigning, and Vladislav, prince of the Bohemians, who had succeeded his uncle, the illustrious Soběslav, was enthroned, a mad sedition arose among the Bohemians. Agitated by the spur of treachery, it divided them into two parties; the better and nobler party went over to Conrad, duke of Moravia, [Note: [Col. 0271D] The other Moravian dukes favored him: Otto of Olomouc, Vratislav of Brno, and others. Compare Vincent of Prague, under this year.] while the lesser and younger party remained with Vladislav.

These things having taken place, peace was suddenly cast aside and a hasty war declared. They assembled in an appointed place, deliberated under arms concerning the expulsion of Vladislav and the election of Conrad, and established no firm basis for concord and peace. On the following day, however, the Moravians with the Bohemian exiles unexpectedly rose against Vladislav and his brothers Theobald [Note: [Col. 0271] Everything that follows is absent in 2b.] and Henry [Note: [Col. 0272D] Likewise a brother of Vladislav II.], and compelled them, together with their whole army, to flee. While they resisted as best they could, the chief leaders in the war—Nacerat, Smil, Ben, [Note: [Col. 0271] Beneda, 2; Ben., 2a.] and very many others on both sides—fell. [Note: [Col. 0272D] This occurred in the battle at Mount Vysoká, in the Čáslav district, between Suchdol and Malešov, on 25 April. See Vincent of Prague I. I., and Palacký I, 419.]

Then the Bohemians, seeing that the Moravians were gaining strength and that they themselves lacked God’s help, all fled to save themselves. Entering Prague, the metropolitan city, with Theobald they strengthened the fortifications, and promptly sent Vladislav to the king of the Germans to obtain assistance. Conrad therefore, inflamed by desire for the duchy, pursued the fugitives and besieged Prague. He stationed armed men on every side, prepared siege-engines, crossbows, and archers, and at last set fire to monasteries, cloisters, and buildings.

Alas for sorrow! An abominable crime, unheard-of distress, unwonted grief, anxiety, fear, and trembling seized the suburban inhabitants and their neighbors. The nuns beloved by God and men, from the monastery of Saint George the martyr and Saint Ludmila the martyr, seeing all their sanctuaries and dwellings burned, terrified and half-dead amid groaning and heavy sighing, scarcely able to lift eyes and hands to heaven, cried: “Lord, have mercy upon us and look upon us.” Suddenly finding an exit from the city, they fled and withdrew to one place beneath Mount Petřín. In the church of Saint John the Baptist they remained, as exiles, sorrowful and tearful, until they should see the restoration of their own place.

After a few days had elapsed—days not counted because of grief and affliction—the coming of King Conrad of the Germans, together with those accompanying him, Duke Vladislav, and Bishop Zdík, a man of venerable and holy memory, thundered forth with a strong force. On hearing of this, the tetrarch Conrad secretly fled with his followers into his own land and thereafter appeared. King Conrad therefore came and restored the duke in firm peace; [Note: [Col. 0272D] He entered Prague on the feast of Pentecost, that is, 7 June, according to Vincent.] having received the promised money, he departed for his own country.

Then all who had been in sorrow rejoiced as though awakened from a heavy sleep. They began to rebuild what had been violated and to renew what had been wholly destroyed. Thus the lady nuns, daughters of holiness and of the Catholic faith, living in the aforesaid place, said day and night in tearful voices, according to the desire of righteous Simeon: “When shall we leave here? When shall we dwell in the cloister? When shall we pray to God with full joy?” Soon heard by the Lord, they learned from the report of the guards of the walls, fishermen, and poor men laboring at night that flames had been seen issuing from their church [Note: [Col. 0271] “their,” 2, 2b.] and stretching to heaven.

Admonished by the Holy Spirit through this report, they visited the cloister, surveyed the church, inspected the altars, and above all sought with tears the relics of Saint Ludmila, their patroness. They summoned Wernher, a stonecutter and mason, and urged him to search among the stones and firebrands. Behold: by God’s will Wernher found the sarcophagus intact and untouched by fire. He returned joyfully to the ladies and, asking a reward in his joy, announced the glad news.

O holy God! O wondrous one in your saints! O blessed one in your works! With what exultation you deigned to fill your handmaids; with what solace of visitation to inundate them; with what great joy of your manifestation to gladden them! Giving thanks to God, they fell to the ground, drenched the place with tears, and, forgetting their sorrow, ran to raise the shrine. But, as though stupefied, they restrained their presumption. Calling the priest Pudo, with whose counsel and help they attempted to carry it outside, they went to the city gate and found it blocked, barred, and, as it were, set against their exit. Though shaken with great exertion and assailed with excessive labor, they were in no way able to open it. Stricken by this miracle, they returned to the place from which they had come and, sending a messenger to Bishop Otto, begged him to come and decide what should be done. He replied that he did not dare act unless he first sent to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0273] The words “he replied … bishop” occur as one passage in 2a.]

Again they implored Bishop Zdík of Moravia to fulfill their desire. [Note: [Col. 0274] “fulfill,” 2.] He promised that he would do so if he obtained their bishop’s permission. Therefore the cloister-dwellers, not abandoning their purpose, with the counsel of Lord Henry, dean of Prague, Peter the archdeacon, and the others of the convent, raised the sarcophagus, opened it, and joyfully placed it again in the spot prepared beside the altar.

Nor should this be passed over: the wondrous theft of Wernher, a tale to be proclaimed through the ages. Having secretly taken away a portion of the body of blessed Ludmila, Christ’s athlete, he returned to his homeland. He hired two men to build a church to God; having begun the work, they died. In the next year two others died, and in the third he himself died. Seeing these things, his son, at the command of neighbors and relatives, entered Bohemia, related what had happened to his kinsman Gervasius, the chancellor, and, admonished through him, restored the stolen things to the church, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0273]

## Continuation of Cosmas by the Monk of Sázava

### On the Chronicle of Saint Jerome and the Computation of Years

[Col. 0273B]

Blessed Jerome, in the chronicle which he compiled with his own hands, records as follows: From Adam to the Flood, 2,242 years; from the Flood to Abraham, 942 years; from Abraham to the Nativity of the Lord, 2,015 years. Their sum is found to be five thousand one hundred and ninety-nine years. Years from the Incarnation of the Lord:

932. [Quedlinburg Annals.] In the same year King Henry subdued the Abodrites.

958. The sign of the cross appeared on men’s garments; it brought death to those who held it in derision, but inflicted no harm upon those who reverently and devoutly venerated it.

960. In this year envoys of the people of Rus’ came to King Otto and begged him to send one of his bishops to show them the way of truth. They professed that they wished to abandon pagan observance and receive the name and religion of Christianity. He consented to their petition and sent Bishop Adalbert, sound in the Catholic faith. They lied in every respect, as the later outcome proved; for that aforesaid bishop did not escape the deadly peril of their ambushes.

962. [Quedlinburg Annals?] Tuto, bishop of the church of Regensburg, died.

963. A great synodal council was held at Rome in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle. There Emperor Otto Augustus presided with a great multitude of bishops, abbots, monks, provosts, and clerics. Pope Benedict was deposed from the Apostolic See, entrusted to Bishop Adaldag, and taken into Saxony, where he ended his life. In that same year, pestilence attacked the army of Emperor Otto.

972. Saint Ulrich, bishop of the church of Augsburg, departed from this world on 4 Nones of July. His body was buried by Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg.

973. Otto, the first pious emperor of the Germans—alas, alas for sorrow!—died on the Nones of May; his son Otto succeeded him.

975. A winter exceedingly harsh and inappropriately long. On the Ides of May, newly fallen snow covered the earth.

In the same year Archbishop Rudbert died, and Willigis succeeded him.

985. [Quedlinburg Annals.] The Saxons invaded Slavonia, and Duke Mieszko came with a great army to reinforce them. They devastated the whole Slavonic land with fires and slaughter.

986. King Otto, still a very young boy, came into Slavonia with a great Saxon army, and they devastated it with many fires and killings.

987. In the same year the Saxons again invaded Slavonia, and finally the Slavs themselves were subjected to the king’s rule. The fortresses beside the River Elbe were restored anew. A mighty wind cast down many buildings.

[Col. 0275A]

988. In this year the immense heat of summer consumed almost all crops, and soon a great mortality among men followed.

989. [COSMAS.] In the same year comets appeared, followed by a great pestilence among men and beasts of burden, especially oxen.

990. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 12 Kalends of November, at the fifth hour of the day. In the same year Saint Adalbert, bishop of the holy church of Prague, at Rome, at Saints Alexius the Confessor and Boniface, became a monk without the abbot’s knowing who he was. Likewise in the same year Niemcza was lost. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Nimtsch in Silesia. Compare the Prague Annals and Wilmans, Otto III, Excursus VIII, p. 219.]

995. And they were buried in the church of Saint Boniface the martyr on 6 Ides of October. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Namely, the five brothers of Saint Adalbert; this is a gloss on Cosmas I, 29.]

[Quedlinburg Annals.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 996, Saint Adalbert, the second bishop of the Bohemians from the city of Prague, was crowned with glorious martyrdom by the Prussians on 9 Kalends of May. Theodagus succeeded him.

998. In the same year, during July, there was a terrible earthquake throughout all Saxony, and two stones set ablaze by thunder fell: one in the city of Magdeburg itself, the other beyond the River Elbe.

999. In the same year Pope Bruno died; in the Roman manner he was called Gregory.

1000. Before Emperor Otto visited his homeland, he went in humble devotion to Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr, newly crowned for Christ in Poland; he earnestly sought his intercession. There he was received with the utmost exertion by Boleslav, duke of the Slavs, and was dutifully honored with gifts of every kind of wealth. Thereupon Emperor Otto returned to his homeland and celebrated the day of the Lord’s resurrection festively at Quedlinburg with the services of due veneration. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Quidiligensi, 4a.]

1001. Duke Mieszko of Poland gained possession of the city of Prague.

### On the Beginning of the Monastery of Sázava

Here it seems fitting not to pass over how the monastery of Sázava took its beginning through the grace of divine dispensation; under which princes, and in what way, from a humble origin, it grew—with God as its author—to the greatness seen today. Thus, in this work as in the other works of his mercy, may the magnificence of divine goodness be praised by all the faithful.

In the time of the aforesaid Duke Ulrich, a man magnificent in divine worship, there was a hermit named Procopius, a Bohemian by birth, from the village of Chotun. [Note: [Col. 0275D] In the Kouřim district. Palacký demonstrated, Würdigung, p. 51, that the Life of Saint Procopius written in Bohemian verse—which Dobner conjectured to have flowed from very ancient sources, at Hájek IV, 246—was derived from the Chronicle of Sázava.] He was thoroughly instructed in Slavonic letters, formerly devised and established canonically by the most holy Bishop Cyril. In the world he had been an eminent priest, of honorable life and celebrating the sacred mysteries chastely; afterwards, armed with the mitre of monastic profession, [Note: [Col. 0276D] That is, “fortified.”] he dwelt alone with the one God, unwavering in the pledge of faith.

Burning with all the ardor of his spirit for love of Jesus Christ, he despised the wretched vanity of this world. Renouncing house and wife, fields, kinsmen and friends—indeed, denying himself to himself—he bade farewell to the deceitful world and its miserable pomps. Fleeing its tumultuous whirlwind, he sought the hidden places of solitude. On the brow of a certain deserted cave, [Note: [Col. 0276D] Not far from Kouřim, by the River Sázava, which flows into the Moldau.] said to have been inhabited by a thousand demons, he took his seat, clad in heavenly armor. There he constructed the defensive works of virtues by which he could protect himself, [Note: [Col. 0276D] That is, “fortifications.”] and, dashing against the Rock which is Christ the arrows of spiritual wickedness and suggestion, the dogs of vices and their assault, through prayers, vigils, and fasts, he began to fight manfully.

As he thus labored tirelessly for God for a long time in the solitude dear to him, free from the shipwreck of worldly tumult and hidden from all, the merciful dispensation of the Godhead would not allow a city set upon a hill to remain concealed, nor a lamp hidden beneath a bushel, but willed that it should shine openly, to the praise and glory of his name, as an example to many faithful persons.

For, by the prompting of heavenly grace, when the same duke at one time came hunting to the place he had especially chosen for the chase, while he was pursuing the hunt, he followed one stag from the multitude as it fled to the more secret part of the wood. He came to the summit of the aforesaid cave and found Procopius in a poor hut, a man in monastic dress cultivating the life of a hermit. The prince, then, with the measured manner proper to princely dignity, cheerfulness of mind, and sweet affability of speech, first inquired in order concerning every aspect of this new matter: who he was, from what regions he had come, and for what reason a man of such character had wished to inhabit solitudes so rough.

To these questions Procopius responded briefly and humbly, setting forth the whole truth in order as it stood. Finally he added that, for love of God and hope of heavenly reward, he had wholly renounced the world and wished, if it pleased God, to remain in that desert until the end.

The wise prince marveled in the Lord at so arduous a purpose in the man and, observing his countenance graced by holy religion, stretched both hands toward heaven and blessed God amid tears. Then he earnestly commended himself to Procopius’s prayers, adopted him as his spiritual father, gave support with a generous hand, and returned joyfully to the station of his soldiers.

Thereafter the fame of his virtues, spreading in manifold report, increased so greatly far and wide along every road that people of that province came in crowds at the report of him, brought gifts, and devoutly entrusted themselves to his prayers. He was full of the ardor of charity, piously endowed with hospitality, fittingly adorned with holy wisdom, pure in chastity, provident in the mercy of humility, distinguished by temperance, and full of an abundance of zeal for faith. By the word of holy preaching, as a timely shower poured down in its fitting season, he watered the hearts of his hearers; with the plowshare of his teaching he most profitably renewed their minds.

He received the poor with such abundance of divinely implanted compassion, and ministered to them with such ready and joyful solicitude of service, as if Christ himself were visibly present, that the beggars and *pifaudi* [Note: [Col. 0277D] Apparently the same as the French *pifre*, that is, “gluttonous, hungry.”] of all his territory were fed through his labor. A multitude of believers hurried to him, desiring in their hearts to renounce the gains of the world and remain with him until the end. He received and cherished them kindly, as a hen her chicks under her wings.

When a short interval of time had passed, blessed Father Procopius, having collected whatever resources he could, laid a foundation in the name of the Lord and built a basilica in honor of the most holy Mother of God Mary and Saint John the Baptist. He gathered certain brethren religious in life and conduct, and, since they agreed spiritually in unanimous charity, established monastic observances and divine mysteries for them according to the model of the life-giving Father Benedict, himself becoming the least among the least.

No one’s eloquence is sufficient worthily to describe how prudent and effective were the diligence, industry, and concern of his mind, or how abundant was his pious charity toward the brethren. The aforesaid duke and the chief men of the court [Note: [Col. 0277D] That is, “the company of nobles.”] were accustomed to call him father and to commend themselves to him. They also fittingly desired to love him with filial reverence. Therefore the same duke, magnanimously taking counsel with the discerning intelligence and prudent judgment of his magnates, determined that he should be advanced to the investiture of the abbacy. He suitably supplied certain necessities for monastic use and promised others, which he afterward fittingly fulfilled.

But Procopius, fearing to prefer himself to others, wholly refused, through the highest profit of meekness and humility. He declared that he was an unlearned and unworthy man, unable to bestow the service of obedience upon those not subject to him, calling God—the sole knower of all secrets—as witness of his inward examination.

Meanwhile Duke Ulrich, of pious memory, was removed from this light, and his son Břetislav obtained the sovereignty of the realm, a man in every respect loving the worship of divine religion. He resolved to bring to complete fulfillment, with every diligent exercise of wisdom, the work which his father had left unfinished. Hearing the holy reputation of the blessed man, he rejoiced with his magnates in an exultation beyond belief. Joyfully commending himself to Procopius’s prayers, he took him aside and urged him to accept the mitre of the abbacy. Then, a second time, in the presence of all courtly dignitaries, he addressed him with persuasive words: whether willing or unwilling, he ought to undertake the governance of pastoral care.

But the man of God, persisting in his accustomed firmness and declaring himself altogether unworthy, could by no means be bent to the duke’s consent. Yet who can oppose divine ordinance? Overcome by every insistence of prayers, every exhortation of affection, and the affability of the magnates, he was forcibly ordained abbot.

After this celebrated promotion, Duke Břetislav first confirmed by princely authority the gift which his father had made to the same father before he accepted the abbacy: namely, the river flowing below Amilobuz [Note: [Col. 0277D] According to Schaller X, 128, this is the River Sázava.] as far as the cave popularly called Zákolnica, together with the meadows and surrounding wood. [Note: [Col. 0278D] Which is lacking.] Then, when subsequent heirs [Note: [Col. 0277] “heresies” wrongly in 4.] attempted to seize this gift and claim it as their own right, unwilling to annul his father’s enactments, he intervened, settled the dispute, and restored to Father Procopius all use of water and woodland within the aforesaid boundaries. He redeemed the adjoining fields [Note: [Col. 0277] “but” is absent in 4.] and meadows on both sides for the price of six hundred denarii, under the testimony and confirmation of his son Vratislav and his princes, and conveyed them to Abbot Procopius by written instruments and lawful witnesses.
