Finally, from his own generosity, he granted in perpetual possession to the same abbot and his successors, for the salvation of his soul, the land lying around it as far as the wood of Strnounic, together with the village of Zcramnik, one pond, and timber works for fishing purchased for one hundred denarii.

Thus, having become abbot under so fortunate a course of events, he did not exalt himself above himself. Rather, founded on firmer solidity of virtues and established in the steadfast excellence of humility and charity, he was so cheerful and restrained in kindly affection that he was held by those subject to him more in love than in fear. Publicly and individually he never ceased to give them salutary admonitions and many teachings embellished with examples of the ancients. [Note: [Col. 0278D] That is, “adorned”; this appears to be the proper reading instead of *piamenta*, given by the manuscript.]

In his time abundance of every kind of thing was not lacking. Yet he sustained himself by the work of his hands, relieved the need of the poor, bore the care of all who were in sorrow, and, like a wise physician, restored them as sick persons with a fatherly antidote and consolation. While he led such a blessed and illustrious life, he shone in the temple of God like the sun by signs of virtue until the end of his life. Indeed, through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he was illustrious in the mystery of prophecy, foreknowing future things.

Two days before the end of his earthly dissolution, he knew beforehand through the revelation of divine grace. Summoning his nephew Vitus, a man of good character, together with Emmeram, Vitus’s son of pious disposition, he set forth future events to them in order, as later the outcome proved, and said sobbing in this noble manner:

> “My dearest little sons, whom I have reared as a hen her chicks, consider that the time of my departure is at hand. Most certainly, on the third day, if the Lord permits, I shall depart from this tabernacle of flesh, commending you to God. But I make known to your prudence that after my departure you will be violently shaken by the changeful waves of slanders; you will be afflicted by the pestilential shipwreck of persecutions; and for six years you will become exiles in a foreign land. This place will be handed over by the strong hand of the duke to the power [Note: [Col. 0279D] That is, “authority.”] of foreigners.
>
> “But you, my dearest little sons, do not therefore suffer shipwreck in faith. Strengthen your brethren; praise God with a spirit ever ready; [Note: [Col. 0279D] That is, with a mind always ready for the praises of God.] bless him in prosperity; pray to him in adversity; give thanks in joyful circumstances; seek him in sorrowful events. By the magnificence of his mercy you will at length be consoled. For when the six years of your exile have passed, he will have mercy, restore for you a state of peace, render deserved retribution to your slanderers, and bring you back to the harbor of consolation.
>
> “For when the present pious Prince Břetislav has died, [Col. 0279C] Spytihněv will succeed, and he will persecute you. When he has died, Vratislav, a God-fearing and kindly man, [Note: [Col. 0279D] “fearing God.”] will receive the government of the Bohemian principality. He will bring you back from exile, and our Lord Jesus Christ will give you peace and security in this place all the days of your life. Amen.”

Now, as the following day was ending, after the evening synaxis and Compline had been canonically completed, he was sitting on his little bed when he was seized by a severe illness. Though placed at the point of death and drawing his last breath, he nevertheless did not cease, with arm outstretched, manfully to strike at the ancient enemy with the sword of prayer. He ordered the brethren to be present. When they had turned to an affliction of sorrow and inconsolable weeping, he strengthened them with the consolation of paternal instruction; and, admonishing them concerning his body and the shipwreck of this world, he departed to the Lord: from servitude to kingship, from labor to rest, from death to everlasting life, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and is glorified as one God in perfect Trinity for infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Blessed Abbot Procopius happily completed the course of his life in the Lord in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1053, on 8 Kalends of April of that year. In the presence of Severus, bishop of Prague, he was honorably committed to burial in the church of the holy Mother of God Mary, which he himself had built.

After the departure of the most blessed Father Procopius, the associated community by its own choice elected from its congregation his nephew Vitus. He was elected without deceit and ordained without venality: a man fitted for human and divine affairs, an enemy of this world, nobly mannered, wakefully wise, reverend in appearance, gracious in speech, and gentle in placability.

While he was living effectively in the abbacy, Duke Břetislav bade his final farewell to the world, and Spytihněv took up in his place the reins of sovereignty. At this time the sequence of Saint Father Procopius’s prophecy was fulfilled. For, prompted by the zeal of the Devil, many jealous men conspired in the court of the duke with feigned, poisonous slanders, began to set snares of caviling against Abbot Vitus and his brethren, and, clouding the prince’s ears with favorably contrived lies, publicly charged them with manifold reproaches. They said, namely, that by means of Slavonic letters they were manifestly ensnared by the sect of heresy and hypocrisy and wholly perverse. Therefore, they steadfastly declared, it was altogether proper that these men be expelled and an abbot and brethren of Latin authority be installed in their place.

O envy, an inextricable zeal of malice! O detestable envy, all manner of malice gathered together, an unquenchable fire! Yet truly, as a garment is consumed by moths, so he who fosters envy makes him whom he envies more illustrious.

Thus Abbot Vitus, taking with him his brethren, whom unity of charity had joined in concord, departed as an exile into the land of the Huns.

[Col. 0280C]

Now we have considered it worthwhile to commit to the charitable memory of the faithful, in a brief account and a truthful report, one among the many miracles of the blessed man which the magnificence of our Lord deigned to reveal through his merits after his death.

When the aforesaid duke caused Abbot Vitus, his nephew Emmeram, and the brethren whom unity of charity had joined in concord to depart into exile in the land of the Huns, he followed the counsel and decision of his own supporters and installed as abbot in that place a man of German stock, [Note: [Col. 0280D] For Spytihněv’s disposition toward Germans, see Cosmas II, 14.] full of turbulent indignation.

On the first night after his arrival, as he was proceeding as usual to the morning synaxis and approached the church doors, the holy man Procopius appeared, leaning inside the entrance of the oratory, and said to him: “Whence comes your authority to dwell here? What do you seek?”

But he replied: “The sovereign majesty of the duke and the unshaken eminence of his primacy have entrusted this monastery to the governance of my power until the end of my life.”

The holy father said to him: “Depart most swiftly, without the shame of disgrace; and if you do not do so, divine vengeance will come upon you.” Having said this, he vanished.

But the other, believing it to be a delusion of Satan, regarded it as of no value whatsoever. When on the second and third nights he made light of the warning, on the fourth night the holy man appeared to him as he was going to the morning service and said:

> “Why did you refuse to obey my friendly warnings? I obtained this place from the Lord for my spiritual sons, not for you, who entered by usurpation. And if this authority has hitherto been granted to you by your lord the duke, from me it shall henceforth be forbidden.”

Saying this, he began violently to strike him with the strongest blows of the pastoral staff (*cambutta*) [Note: [Col. 0281D] A pastoral rod.] which he carried in his hand. Immediately, as though struck by Bellona’s frenzy, [Note: [Col. 0281D] Juvenal, *Satires* IV, 123.] the man left the place without delay, hurried with winged speed to the duke of the land, and disclosed to him the entire event. Astonished, the duke began to waver in vehement amazement; caught in the snare of uncertainty, he remained so until the end of his life.

After Duke Spytihněv had died, the Godhead entrusted to his faithful servant Vratislav the government of the duchy under a memorable title. Since Vratislav singularly loved the divine worship of the church, he also loved that place with all the affection of his heart. Sending envoys to the king of the Huns, [Note: [Col. 0281D] Solomon, as Dobner IV, 382 thought; he considers the monks to have been recalled in 1064.] he brought Abbot Vitus and his brethren back honorably from exile and fittingly restored them to their place.

Through the merits and prayers of their blessed patron Procopius, the propitious consolation of almighty God attended them. It renewed that place, abounding and overflowing in the increase of every good thing, to its former—indeed, to a greater—honor. [Note: [Col. 0282D] That is, “initiated, restored.”]

The happy Abbot Vitus, a man of great ability and counsel, as the end of his life approached, with the brethren’s consent entrusted the right of abbatial governance of his monastery (*arcisterium*) [Note: [Col. 0282D] That is, *asceterium*, “monastery.”] to his kinsman Emmeram, a man conspicuous for holiness, in the assembly of the duke [Note: [Col. 0282D] Thus Vitus died before the year 1086, when Vratislav obtained the kingship.] and his magnates. He himself afterward, when a brief span of days had passed, closed his final day, to live with the Lord forever. His body was buried beside the doors on the left side, at the entrance of the church of the holy Mother of God Mary.

After his departure, the kindly Abbot Emmeram—an individual of dove-like simplicity—shone in the merits of holy life and the jewels of virtues. Admitting no serpentine prudence into his mind, while he lived he maintained an unshaken steadfastness in the Catholic faith and firmly established many wavering hearts in the faith of Christ. In every respect he was a man of evident blessedness and generosity toward all.

He called money nothing other than evil. Holding it wholly as nothing, he would not touch it even with his hand; indeed, he judged that it ought to be trampled beneath the feet, following the footsteps of the holy apostles, who avoided touching with their sacred right hands the prices of things sold, but left us examples that treasure ought to be trampled like mud beneath our feet.

Thus, when the blessed abbot was praised among men as a father of outstanding perfection in holy conduct under the order of monastic soldiery, and flourished exceedingly in the affection of righteous love—because, according to Truth, neither a city set upon a hill nor a lamp under a bushel can remain hidden (Matt. V, 14)—the dispensation of the Godhead sent the chastisements of infirmities into every member of his body. This was lest the flattery of those praising him instill exaltation in him, lest his mind incur self-exaltation through human commendations, before, safe from the perilous navigation of this great and broad sea, he reached the harbor of blessedness.

Accordingly, for a long time, as our Lord willed, afflicted everywhere by many sufferings of calamity, he was removed from human affairs: to be mourned by his many successors because he had departed, but to be accompanied with every joy because he had reached the heavenly kingdoms. The united body of brethren buried him on the right side of the entrance of the door of the aforesaid church.

At this time King Wratislaus, worthy of commemoration for his piety, who gladly enriched the church of the monastery already mentioned, governed the summit of the Bohemian monarchy [Note: [Col. 0281] “battle-line” in 4a.]. By his pious will and the election of the brethren, Bozethecus obtained the dignity of abbot in the place of Father Emmerammus, a man exceedingly accessible to all and generous toward everyone. He was skilled at painting most beautifully; he knew very well how to model or carve in wood and stone and turn bone. A man of great eloquence and ready memory, but eager for popular acclaim, presumptuous, hot-tempered, and somewhat given to vices. For he commendably adorned that place with every ornament, as appears to this day; he established the church by enlarging it most beautifully in [Col. 0282C] length, breadth, and height—indeed, he adorned it with hangings, bells, crosses, and every monastic furnishing, and renewed the whole monastery in every respect with buildings and all equipment.

His zeal watched over every necessity useful to monastic life. Hence a great tinderbox of dissensions arose among the monastery’s brethren against him, with the Devil’s envy inciting and serving it; and a lamentable rage began to bubble up, namely through the wretched brethren Demetrius, Cananus, and Golisson, priests—men then incompetent and injurious—and their other accomplices and supporters, who raged like Bacchants, behaving savagely against him in shameful deed and speech. But the aforesaid king, a most Christian man, loved him uniquely; through whose favour [Col. 0282D] the same abbot had been raised so high that he appeared to surpass almost all the Bohemian abbots in dignity.

For this reason the same abbot, acting presumptuously, usurped his bishop’s office at a certain high feast. For he placed a crown upon the head of the above-named king, though his bishop Cosmas [Note: [Col. 0281] Thus 4 and 4a read it.] [Col. 0283A] [Note: [Col. 0283D] He was elected bishop in the year 1091. Compare Cosmas II.12.] ought to have done so. Bishop Cosmas was therefore angry with him in unquenchable fury, and, because he had inflicted injuries upon him through false accusations, tried to depose him. Yet, unable to resist the continual prayers of the royal magnates, he scarcely forgave his debtor, Abbot Bozethecus, the debt of wrath—not, however, from his whole heart—on this condition, as the same bishop finally answered him:

> “But because you, abbot, know well how to carve and turn, by the command of our holy obedience, to wipe away your fault—which you presumptuously committed through your contumacy—we command you to have made an image of the Crucified One as large as your own height and breadth, and to carry it, with the cross, upon your back as far as Rome, and place it in the metropolitan church of Saint Peter the Apostle.”

The abbot did not delay to accomplish this willingly and with contrition of heart [Col. 0283B], and made satisfaction to the episcopal majesty.

After some time, it is beyond all proper telling how greatly the monastery’s brethren mentioned above conspired against him with the poison of jealousy, like deadly serpents; for each of them sought accusations against him, but suitable testimony was not found. For these same brethren, limbs of Satan, thought that, if the already named abbot could be expelled by any means, one of their accomplices in these errors would, they hoped, assume the rights of the abbacy. King Wratislaus had meanwhile passed to the Lord; his successor at that time, Bracizlaus, held the eminence of the Bohemian dukedom. When the above-mentioned brethren, personally and through friends, continually assailed his ears with many fabricated and innumerable reproaches composed against their abbot Bozethecus [Col. 0283C], the same duke uprooted the named abbot from the aforesaid place and expelled the brethren. There the words of Truth were fulfilled: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26:31).

Accordingly, once the abbot had been expelled, those of his brethren who had been the authors of treachery against him thereafter wandered everywhere as roaming vagrants through uncertain places, until at last some, pierced in heart, were scarcely received back in their own place; unfit for that place, they ended their lives there, and the books in their language were wholly erased and scattered, and will never again be read in that place.

1045. Gunther, monk and hermit, died on the seventh Ides of October, and was buried in the monastery of Saints Adalbert and Benedict before the altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

[Col. 0283D] 1053. Procopius, first abbot of the monastery of Sázava, bringing the course of his life to a happy end, departed this world’s arena on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, to receive the prize of eternal blessedness.

1070. In the fourth indiction, sixth epact, and second concurrent, on the third day before the Kalends of July, Bishop Gebehard consecrated the church at Sázava in honour of the Holy Cross. Its altar contains relics of the Holy Cross, of the garment of [Col. 0284A] Saint Mary, of Saint Peter the Apostle, of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and of Saint George the Martyr.

1088. Thus [Note: [Col. 0284D] Compare Cosmas II.40.] the righteous man, Beneda the soldier, as though a martyr of God, died on the fifth Ides of July and was buried in the city of Meissen before the gate of the monastery of Saint [Note: [Col. 0283] “Saint” is absent in 4a.] John the Apostle and Evangelist.

1089. Lord Megnhard, abbot of Saint Adalbert’s monastery at Břevnov, died; the monastery had been built by him. Adalbert succeeded him.

1091. And during the winter there was neither snow nor rain.

1095. In the same year, on the second Ides of October, the oratory at Sázava was consecrated by Cosmas, the venerable eighth bishop of the holy church of Prague. Bozetech, abbot of the same place, whom we mentioned above, built it during his administration, beginning on the right [Col. 0284B] from the altar of Saint Martin and on the left from the altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, extending to the end of the crypt. In the middle of the oratory, where the altar stands, are contained relics of Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Andrew, Saint Bartholomew, Saint Thomas, Saint James, Saint Philip, Saint Luke the Evangelist, Saint Barnabas, and all the apostles.

On the following day, namely the Ides of October, three altars were consecrated: one above the crypt, containing relics of the Lord’s shroud, his crown of thorns, his tomb, the Holy Cross, Saint Mary, Saint John the Baptist, and Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist; another altar beneath the crypt, containing relics of Saints Cosmas and his brethren; likewise, in the chapel on the left side of the church, an altar [Col. 0284C] containing relics of the Holy Cross, Saint Lawrence the martyr, Saint Blaise the bishop and martyr, Saint Maurice the martyr, and Saint Pancras the martyr.

Then, on the third day, namely the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, two altars were consecrated. One was on the right and contained relics of Saint Martin; Saints John and Paul; Saint Tiburtius the martyr; Saint Gleb and his companion; Saints Benedict, John, Isaac, Matthew, Christian, Nicholas, Jerome, Ulrich, Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 0283] “Fortunatus” in 4.], Odolphus, and Lazarus. The other altar was on the left and contained relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr; Saints Andrew and Thomas the Apostles; Saint Clement, pope and martyr; Saint George the martyr; and Saint Pantaleon the martyr.

[Col. 0284D] 1097. Duke Bracizlaus, with the approval of all the magnates of the land and the election of Bishop Cosmas, joyfully conferred the title of the abbacy of Sázava, on the third Nones of January, upon Diethard [Note: [Col. 0283] “Dethard” in 4a.], provost of Břevnov [Note: [Col. 0283] “of Břevnov” in 4.]—a man sufficiently trained in Latin letters, then regarded as outstanding in monastic religion. He was an excellent man: handsome in appearance, ingenious in intellect, serious in disposition, agreeable in conduct, exceedingly polished in speech, sparing in speech [Col. 0285A], hostile to vices, and so tranquil that he changed his expression neither from joy nor from sorrow. He was ordained abbot by Cosmas, bishop of Prague, on the eighth Ides of March.

When he first arrived at the place whose abbot he had been named, he found the monastic furnishings utterly reduced to nothing, to such an extent that he and the brethren could not have been sustained for even one month on the provisions found there, had not the above-named duke supplied help from his own treasury. But divine mercy did not fail that place while this abbot lived: through him it increased assistance for the place and made it abound and overflow with every good thing. The abbot himself wrote, by immense labour night and day, the books which he did not find in the place entrusted to him, apart from the Slavonic books; some he bought, some he hired scribes to write, and in every way acquired them. He renewed the oratory with tiles and other ornaments.

He confirmed in perpetuity, strengthening by the commands and inviolable decrees of the dukes of the land, the endowments acquired under the authority of his predecessors; and he increased them himself: namely dwellings, possessions, slaves, chartered dependants, offered persons [Note: [Col. 0285D] Those who had offered or subjected themselves and all that they possessed to the monastery.], male and female servants, lands and vineyards, forests with mountains and plains, waters and watercourses and fisheries. He also undertook manual labour beyond his strength, especially applying himself to planting and to the cultivation of vineyards; and he kept entirely watchful over all the monastery’s affairs, always turning in his mind the saying of the admirable father: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.” Throughout his life he regarded as displeasing that brother [Col. 0285C] who made himself incapable of the work enjoined upon him and dull through laziness, saying that refusal to submit to obedience was like the crime of divination.

As long as he lived, embracing and consoling all the brethren in good will and living piously among them as a father among sons, he summoned them toward the heavenly kingdom, as an eagle hovering invites its young to fly. In him, indeed, the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High was fulfilled while he lived. At last, when he had already reached mature age, God sent the chastisement of illness into his limbs, as he himself had requested; for “whom the Lord loves he chastens.” Thus he was wearied in his entrails by grievous suffering night and day, until he entered upon the way of all flesh on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January. He governed the same place for thirty-seven years, nine months, [Col. 0285D] and eleven days [Note: [Col. 0285] 4 and 4a continue: “In the same year the duke, etc.”].

1116. In the same year, while Hermann flourishes in the bishopric of Prague, Silvester is raised to the priesthood. [Note: [Col. 0285] The monk of Sázava wished to erase the memory of Cosmas’s wife, and in place of the verses which Cosmas composed about her in III.43, inserted these.]

1122. In the same year, on the third Nones of January, the distinguished father and honourable worshipper of Christ, Koyatha, underwent the law of mortal condition.

[Col. 0286A] 1123. In the same year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Silvester, prompted by divine mercy and kindled with ardour for cenobitic life, renounced the ruinous wiles of the world. In the monastery of Sázava, under the rule of Abbot Diethard of good memory [Note: [Col. 0285] “Dethard” in 4a.], he changed his secular habit and wholly devoted himself to divine pursuits; that is, after the embraces of bleary-eyed Leah, he delighted in Rachel’s beauty, and after Martha’s labour desired to attain Mary’s consolation. How great his diligence was in enlarging divine and ecclesiastical matters will be told in its place.

1125. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, at the feast of Saint Benedict the abbot, Silvester made his profession and, having become a monk, by God’s agency advanced so far in the exercise of divine religion that he was deservedly esteemed by all as both [Col. 0286B] honourable and lovable. Hence it subsequently happened that he was raised, like a second father, to the honour of the deanery within the community.

1126. Therefore, when the glorious Duke Sobezlaus [Note: [Col. 0285D] He is Ulrich to Otto of Freising and others.] was raised to the throne of paternal glory amid the rejoicing of all the princes of Bohemia, great joy arose among all, because heavenly grace, as could be seen, attended the beginnings of the good duke, and because in that year—something difficult to believe—no bloodshed took place between the duke himself and Otto [Note: [Col. 0285D] This is mistaken: at the end of 1125 Sobezlaus had devastated Moravia in a military expedition [Col. 0286D].]. But alas! As the madness of the ancient enemy pressed on, sowing discord and civil wars everywhere, an adverse outcome overtook our joys.

For in the following year the aforesaid Duke Otto, exceedingly distressed because the desire of his hope had been frustrated, judged it the best course—though providing too little cautiously for his future—to hasten with his men to King Lothar and all the princes of Saxony. Received with fitting honour [Note: [Col. 0286D] At Regensburg, where Lothar was staying on 27 November 1125; Böhmer, Reg. 2095. Otto had already met the king in the preceding year.], he seized the opportunity of place and time and set forth before all the cause of his journey: namely, that Duke Sobezlaus had entered Bohemia by stealthy steps and violently seized the princely throne, due to him by hereditary right and designated and confirmed by oath by all the Bohemian magnates. Finally he added these words briefly:

> “Let not the mercy of your graciousness [Note: [Col. 0285] “indignation” in 4.], most excellent emperor, refuse to provide for this matter. The grace of divine dispensation has raised your imperial excellence above all the princes of the whole realm to the dignity of empire [Col. 0286D], so that from your benignity mercy and justice may be shown to all who seek them in whatever hardships concern them. We indeed know that we ought in all matters to be subject to the commands of your majesty, and therefore that justice should nonetheless not be denied us by your graciousness.”

By a gracious reply the king calmed [Col. 0287A] the duke’s mind and is said to have spoken before all the princes of Saxony in these terms:

> “The dukedom of Bohemia, as we have learned from our predecessors, has from the beginning stood within the power of the Roman emperor; nor has it ever been lawful for the election or elevation of any duke in that land to take place unless the imperial majesty, by the authority of its power, initiated, completed, and confirmed it. Therefore, whoever has attempted to presume against this settlement is plainly a contemner of our majesty, and has inflicted no small insult not only upon you but also upon us and the whole realm—an insult which is by no means to be borne calmly.”

What more need be said? The king, all the princes, and all the foremost men of Saxony gave and confirmed their pledge to Duke Otto that no one other than he [Col. 0287B] would rule in Bohemia. Meanwhile the cunning—or rather exceedingly imprudent—duke strove to approach each of the Saxon magnates individually, promising boundless gifts and, as the saying goes, mountains of gold, so that he might have all their minds most ready to bring him aid.

It was therefore reported to Duke Sobezlaus that King Lothar was threatening the Bohemians, preparing war, and devising the devastation of the realm unless they quickly agreed, after Sobezlaus had been expelled, to install Otto as their duke. But Duke Sobezlaus, wholly unmoved by these rumours, replied briefly in a measured voice:

> “I hope in God’s mercy and in the merits of the holy martyrs of Christ, Wenceslas and Adalbert, that our land will not be delivered into the hands of foreigners.”

Then the most prudent [Col. 0287C] duke, casting all his thought upon the Lord, visited all the monasteries, imploring divine assistance to support him amid adverse events. When he learned that King Lothar was approaching the Bohemian borders with a strong Saxon force, he hurried to meet him at the castle called Chlumec [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Chlumec” in 4a.]. On the following day, as Duke Sobezlaus sat with his men at dinner, men came saying:

> “Excellent duke, you are attending to the delights of food and acting too carelessly, for behold: unless you meet them swiftly, the swords of the enemy will rule over our necks.”

At once a cry arose in the camp that everyone should be ready. Meanwhile Duke Sobezlaus sent ahead envoys—Nazcerat, Mirozlaus, Zmilon, and others of his magnates—bearing these words to the king:

> “Sobezlaus says this: Your discernment, good emperor, ought to know that the election of the Duke of Bohemia, as we have received it from our predecessors, has never stood in the emperor’s discretion, but always in that of the princes of Bohemia [Col. 0288A]; in your power lies only the confirmation of the Bohemian election. Without cause you endeavour to bind us beneath the yoke of a new law. Know that we shall by no means consent to this; rather, we piously choose to die for justice than to yield to unjust decrees. And indeed, unless you desist from this undertaking, the judgment of almighty God is near, to display between us a prodigy memorable to ages to come.”

These words appeared to the king and his whole army like ravings. Duke Otto assured the king of complete security, because all the leading Bohemians had made him a firm pledge of their loyalty; and he said there was no need for arms, but that those who wished could enter the land with falcons and hawks [Note: [Col. 0287D] He seems to imitate Cosmas in I.12 and II.9.] without any hindrance. Therefore, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [Col. 0288B], bands of Saxons, dangerously confident, advanced between two mountains [Note: [Col. 0287D] The Annals of Hildesheim, under 1126, read: “The forests which divide Bohemia from Saxony.”]. Because very heavy snow had made the road difficult, many, having put aside their arms, proceeded on foot.

But when they had entered the narrow pass between the two mountains, where, as though shut in from heaven, every possibility of escape was taken away, Duke Sobezlaus divided his men into three battle-lines, rushed upon them with sudden attack, and put to the sword every man who stood on the opposing side. There Duke Otto, minister of this evil, fell [Note: [Col. 0287D] In a certain charter written in 1126, in Boczek I, 200, these words occur: “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, Otto, duke of Moravia, called by his father’s name, was slain in [Col. 0288D] battle.” On the date compare Jaffé, *Geschichte des deutschen Reichs unter Lothar*, p. 50.]; there many Saxon magnates were struck down [Note: [Col. 0288D] They are enumerated by the Saxon annalist.], and scarcely anyone could escape, except perhaps those who had remained at a distance to guard the baggage or beside the king’s flank.

Once that day’s most wretched slaughter had been accomplished, the king sent messengers [Note: [Col. 0288D] Henry of Groitzsch, Sobezlaus’s nephew, according to Otto of Freising.] for Duke Sobezlaus, ordering and [Col. 0288C] asking him to come. Fearing no misfortune, he went to the king with a few of his magnates. Standing [Note: [Col. 0288D] Prostrate at Lothar’s feet, according to the same Otto.] before him, he first addressed him in these words:

> “No insolence of our rashness, excellent king, drove us to injure you; no proud presumption moved us to shed the blood of your nobles. Certainly we devised no harm or disgrace for your majesty. Rather, as we repeatedly made known to you before through our envoys, we refused to submit our necks to the yoke of a new law which not even our fathers were able to bear. And behold: divine judgment has furnished a plain indication of the justice of us both and has removed every occasion of an unjust quarrel between the two parties. Let, therefore, every cause of discord now cease; let the unity of concord return. We too are prepared, at the appropriate place and time, to render with our possessions and our person every duty of justice which our predecessors rendered to royal majesty.”

To this the king replied: “Unless Duke Otto had compelled us by the supreme force of his prayers to oppose your purpose, no compelling reason whatsoever could have bent our mind to this, so that any prince might have been permitted even to raise a finger against you. Therefore, with God’s assent and favour, enjoy the honour and throne of your father’s dukedom; preserve unbroken for us and the whole realm the bond of mutual love and friendship.” Saying this, he handed [Note: [Col. 0289] “delivered” in 4a.] him the standard, emblem of the dukedom, by his hand. Thus, after mutual kisses had been exchanged, Sobezlaus returned to his dear capital with the greatest glory and honour and amid the immense rejoicing of his followers; for sixteen years he possessed the throne he had desired.

In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, John [Note: [Col. 0289D] The third; according to the Bohemian Necrology, he died on the ninth day before the Kalends of March.], sixth bishop of the holy church of Olomouc, released from the bonds of flesh, returned to Christ the talent entrusted to him [Col. 0289B] increased a hundredfold. After him Bishop Sdico [Note: [Col. 0289] “Zdico” in 4a.] succeeded as seventh in order, and in the same year was ordained on the sixth Nones of October.

In the same year Queen Zvatava, mother of Duke Sobezlaus, died on the Kalends of September.

1127. Lord Clemens, abbot of the monastery of Saints Adalbert and Benedict at Břevnov, died; Uodalricus succeeded him.

In the same year Mileysi, a handmaid devoted to God and second to none in piety, earnestly attentive in heart to conduct pleasing to God, in order that through divine grace forgiveness might be granted her for her transgressions, visited at Rome the thresholds of the holy apostles. In the same year, having returned, she departed the course of this life in a happy consummation on the fourth Ides of July.

[Col. 0289C] 1128.

1129.

1130. Meginhart [Note: [Col. 0289] “Meginbert” in 4.], bishop of the Bohemians, went to Jerusalem. Likewise, in this year, on the Kalends of March, Wacezlaus, duke of Moravia [Note: [Col. 0289D] The Bohemian Necrology agrees.], father of all Christendom and lover of clerics, died. In the same year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, an immense sign appeared and dreadful thunder was heard. In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, Duke Sobezlaus of the Bohemians publicly beheaded certain plotters against his life in the marketplace at Prague; he deprived others of feet, hands, tongues, and sight. Bracizlaus, son of Duke Bracizlaus, was deprived of his eyes.

1131. The relics of Saint Godehard [Note: [Col. 0289] “Gothard” in 4a.], bishop and confessor, a man of remarkable holiness, were elevated. In the same year Silvester, prior of the monastery of Sázava, went to [Col. 0289D] Rome.

1132. Pribizlawa [Note: [Col. 0289] “Pbrzlava” in 4a.], wife of Groznata, ended her life. We judge it greatly fitting to commit briefly to the service of the pen, for the memory of the faithful, something concerning her pious way of life. While she lived in the flesh, we are confident that she pleased God; and we saw in her conduct a mirror of every kind [Col. 0290A] of virtue for people who love God. Throughout her life she made it her familiar practice to love God’s worship deeply, to prefer nothing to his love, to show herself from the depths of compassion a mother to Christ’s poor, and, with complete sincerity and [Note: [Col. 0289] “and” in 4.] devotion of mind, as circumstances required, to offer honour and aid to persons dedicated to God’s service. She was good indeed when lawfully joined to her husband; better thereafter when she remained in widowhood; best when, after the mournful burial of her beloved and only son Severus, she shone forth.

Burning with desire to see the Lord’s tomb, she went to Jerusalem with Lord Bishop Megnhard and others, and returned safely to her own country. But when the time of her departure from this life drew near and she perceived that bodily strength was failing her, [Col. 0290B] she summoned all the senior and most honoured members of her kin. With all her relatives consenting to this, she offered and confirmed under lawful witnesses to the hospital of God and Saint John the Baptist at Sázava the village of Goztivar with its adjoining forest, fields, meadows, and every property that she possessed there, together with all her household, and also the village of Bosakonic. And so, after a few intervening days, she left the affliction of this world on the fifth Nones of May, in that same monastery awaiting the day of the general resurrection and to enjoy blessed rest.

1133. Abbot Diethard [Note: [Col. 0289] “Dethard” in 4.], whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0289D] Under the year 1097; this shows that the author here erred in writing the year-number [Col. 0290D]. Diethard died in 1134.], in a good old age commended his blessed soul to the Lord on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January. In the same year the Bohemians devastated Poland. In the same year there was an eclipse of the sun [Col. 0290C] at midday.

1134. Bogudar died on the Kalends of February. After the death of the pious Father Diethard, Silvester, prior of the monastery of Sázava, was elected abbot of the same monastery on the ninth day before the Kalends of May by the unanimous counsel and concordant vote of the brethren. He was a man lovable to all for the honourableness of his conduct, very gracious in conversation, exceptional in abstinence, a friend of humility, and a close disciple of true charity. He bound himself to the whole congregation of brethren by such a bond of intimacy and affection that he was regarded by all as belonging more to love than to fear. When the cycle of that year had passed, again on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, having received the abbatial crozier at the metropolitan see [Note: [Col. 0289] “to the metropolitan see” in 4.] from the hand of Duke Sobezlaus, he was ordained by the venerable Bishop John.

Thus raised by God to so fitting an honour, the good shepherd returned to the sheepfold entrusted to his governance [Col. 0290D] amid the rejoicing of all his people. Here an occasion presents itself to fulfill what we promised above [Note: [Col. 0290D] Under the year 1123.]: namely, how ardently he burned with love in the pursuit of holy religion, and how diligent his care was in improving and enlarging the monastery’s affairs. So far as he could and knew how, he was accustomed frequently to instill the entire monastic [Col. 0291A] discipline into the hearts of his brethren. He taught that it was a most grave crime to possess superfluous private goods unlawfully, saying that a monk who had food and clothing ought to be content with these. He also presented to all in himself a special example of humility and patience, always reflecting upon the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.”

During his administration he built a chapel to the holy Mother of God; he decorated the monastery of Saint John the Baptist with beautiful painting; he inserted walls with apses in the middle of the oratory, between the altars of Saint Stephen and Saint Martin; he adorned the church floor with polished stones brought from Mount Petrin; and he built most beautifully the dormitory, refectory, cellar, kitchen, and the cloister court [Col. 0291B] around its circuit with little columns and little apses. In the village called Mnichovici [Note: [Col. 0291D] Měchnov in the district of Kouřim.] he built a basilica in honour of Saint Michael and all the heavenly powers. What more need be said? All his intention, study, and solicitude, so long as he lived, persisted especially in this: to make himself useful in every respect to the house of God.

In the same year Lord Megnhard, tenth bishop of the holy church of Prague, died on the fifth Nones of July [Note: [Col. 0291D] Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.], a true lover of monks and clerics and a pious comforter of the poor and pilgrims. John succeeded him.

1135. On the third day before the Kalends of March, Lord John was ordained eleventh bishop of Prague. In the same year [Col. 0291C], Pope Innocent confirmed the Order of Saint Augustine for the church at Prémontré, in the city of Pisa, on the fifth Nones of May.

1136.

1137. Abbot Silvester, together with Lord Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0291] “Henricus” in 4a.], bishop of Olomouc, and others, under the prompting of divine inspiration, travelled to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, entrusting meanwhile the administration of his monastery to Lord Bero, dean of that place. In the same year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, he returned under favourable south winds. On this journey the soldier Ruzin, devoted to God, died on the third Ides of October. In the same year, on the second Nones of December [Note: [Col. 0291D] It is uncertain whether he died on the third or fourth day of December. See Jaffé, p. 224.], Lothar, emperor of the Romans, pious comforter of the poor and pilgrims, departed this world; Cuonradus [Note: [Col. 0291] “Chunradus” in 4a.] succeeded him. [Col. 0291D] Duke Lupoldus [Note: [Col. 0291] “Leopoldus” in 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0291D] Of Olomouc, son of Boriwoy II.] was expelled from Moravia.

1138.

[Col. 0292A] 1139. Lord Heinricus, most reverend bishop of Olomouc, set out for Rome for the sake of prayer. In the same year Lord John, eleventh bishop of the holy church of Prague, a true lover of clerics and monks and pious comforter of poor people and pilgrims, departed this world on the sixth Ides of August [Note: [Col. 0291D] Confirmed by the Bohemian Necrology.]. In the same year Silvester, abbot of the church of Sázava, a truly Israelite man, succeeded to the bishopric. But in the following year, prompted by God, from whom all good things proceed, he adopted sound counsel, often reconsidering with himself that he was insufficient for so great a burden of episcopal government, and the apostolic saying, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4), and so forth. He willingly relinquished the same bishopric [Col. 0292B] and recovered his abbacy.

1140. Duke Sobezlaus of Bohemia, stripped of his limbs, entered the way of all flesh on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. In the same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, Wladizlaus, son of Duke Wladizlaus, succeeded him in the principate. At the same time, since Lord Abbot Silvester declined the Bohemian bishopric, Otto, canon and provost of the church of Prague, was elected bishop, and was ordained in the same year on the seventh day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0291D] This seems to require correction from “July” on the evidence of the first continuation of Cosmas under 1140; see above, p. 146.]. In the same year, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, Duchess Adleyth died [Note: [Col. 0291D] The Necrology gives the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.].

1141. Spitigneus, son of Duke Boriwoy [Note: [Col. 0291D] The second, who died in 1124.], Mirozlaus, and Mukar went to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer in the month of January. In the same year there was a flooding of waters in Bohemia.

1142. Count Nacerat [Note: [Col. 0291] “Nazerat” in 4.] and other Bohemian magnates [Col. 0292C] conspired against Duke Wladizlaus; joining with the Moravians, they entered Bohemia as a great hostile force. Then, after battle was joined and the Bohemians gave way, they besieged Prague and devastated by fire the monasteries of Saints Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert, and of Saint George. At last, when Cuonradus, king of the Romans, arrived [Note: [Col. 0292D] On Pentecost, as Vincent of Prague confirms.], they withdrew from the siege of the city and returned to Moravia. Through the intervention of Cardinal Wido [Note: [Col. 0292D] “Guido, cardinal-deacon—whom we send from our side to those regions to correct abuses,” writes Pope Innocent II on 21 August 1142; Boczek I, 215.] and the bishops Otto and Heinricus, and of the abbots, they came into a treaty of peace by rendering fitting satisfaction.

In the same year the synagogue of the Jews and many buildings were burned [Note: [Col. 0291] We follow the punctuation of 4a; 4 attaches the words “in the suburb of Prague” to the preceding sentence.]. In the suburb of Prague a serpent was seen flying. In the same year, on the third Ides of July, Kerberk [Note: [Col. 0291] “Kerbek” in 4a.] [Note: [Col. 0292D] The Necrology, in which the reading is the fourth Ides of July, has Gertrude; compare Cosmas III.12.], wife of Boriwoy, died.

1143. Duke Wladislaus of the Bohemians devastated Moravia by fire [Col. 0292D] [Note: [Col. 0292D] Compare Vincent under this year.]. In the same year the papal legate separated priests from their wives [Note: [Col. 0292D] See Guido’s letters on this matter, Boczek I, 223.]. In the same [Col. 0293A] year, the discovery of the head of Saint Adalbert, bishop and martyr, in the city of Prague in the church of Saint Vitus the martyr, and the discovery of Saint Wenceslas’s hair-shirt, took place. In the same year the venerable dedication of the monastery of Saints Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert was performed on the second day before the Kalends of October by three bishops: Otto of Prague, Heinricus of Olomouc, and the bishop of Bamberg. In the same year the devout Pope Innocent passed to the Lord.

1144. Guido, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, provoked by the baseless denunciations of certain persons, suspended Abbot Silvester from office; but in the following year, through Lord Heinricus, bishop of Olomouc, upon his return, he restored him.

1145.

[Col. 0293B] 1146. The chapel of Saint Mary at Sázava, built by Lord Abbot Silvester, was dedicated by the venerable Bishop Otto.

1147. Bernard, venerable abbot of Clairvaux, beloved by God and men, hearing of the invasion and persecution which the pagan Sanguin [Note: [Col. 0293D] Zenghi, prince of Mosul.] inflicted upon the frontier of Jerusalem, exhorted King Louis [Note: [Col. 0293] “Ludwicus” in 4a.] of France and all the peoples of the Franks, just as Mattathias exhorted his sons [Note: [Col. 0293D] The example is drawn from letters of Pope Eugenius III, issued concerning aid for the Holy Land; Boczek I, 241. For Saint Bernard’s letter to Duke Wladislaus, see ibid., 255.], to go to Jerusalem in God’s expedition with armed hand, to lay down their lives for their brethren, and, with God’s help, to free the Christian people from the sword of the pagans. At his admonition the peoples of France, England, Lotharingia, Saxony, Bohemia, Swabia, and Bavaria, together with the fierce Franks, prepared for the Lord’s expedition. There was a mobilization of Christians against the pagans.

At the same time the renowned Bishop Sdico of Moravia went among the Prussians [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Pomeranians, according to Vincent.] with Heinricus, dean of the church of Prague, to preach, and returned in the same year. In the same year, on the second Ides of June, Izcizlaus [Note: [Col. 0293] “Czcislaus” in 4a.], fifth abbot of the church of Postoloprty, died. Bero, dean of the monastery of Sázava, succeeded him and was ordained in the same year on the seventh Ides of December.

1148. On the sixth Ides of July, Otto, the twelfth bishop of the holy church of Prague, died [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Necrology and Vincent agree.], and Daniel, provost of the same church, succeeded him.

1149. Daniel was consecrated bishop by the archbishop of Mainz.

[Col. 0293D] 1150. The distinguished Sdico, seventh bishop of the church of Olomouc, was withdrawn from this world, to live the life everlasting [Note: [Col. 0294D] On 25 June, as confirmed by the Necrology and the catalogue of the bishops of Olomouc in Richter, p. 24.]. He was succeeded by John [Note: [Col. 0294D] the fourth.], a canon from Mount Strahov [Note: [Col. 0293] Zragor, manuscript 4a.]. In the same year Gertrude, duchess of Bohemia, died [Note: [Col. 0294D] Wife of Vladislav II and daughter of Leopold IV, duke of Austria.].

1152.

[Col. 0294A] 1153. Pope Eugenius died [Note: [Col. 0294D] the Third.], a man eminent in life; Anastasius succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0294D] the Fourth.].

1154. As daylight was already failing and nightfall began to draw on, the moon suffered an eclipse. Afterwards a very great mortality spread among humankind.

1155. Our brethren Arsenius, Sizna, and Radosta departed this life.

1156. Bero, abbot of Postoloprty, on the fifth Ides of May—alas!—ended his days in untimely death. In the second watch of his life, inspired by the Lord’s grace, he had offered himself in this monastery as a whole burnt offering to God upon the altar of Christ’s cross. He was a man full of the power of charity, simple and chaste in conduct, and a singular friend of voluntary poverty. For the merit of his holy religious life, he was first elevated among us to the honour of the deanery and then, through Lord Otto the bishop, to the summit of the abbacy in the monastery of Postoloprty. [Col. 0294B] He governed that church for eight years, four months, and thirty-five days.

1157. On the fifth Ides of January, Duke Spytihněv—indeed, the flower and glory of dukes—alas, received the end of this present life through a death far too premature. He was magnificently endowed beyond others with the gift of divine mercy and, to say it with the consent of all, wholly fashioned from every grace of virtue; whoever recalls him worthily cannot be without grief and tears. For the golden shield of God’s Church fell: father of clerics, mother of orphans, most intimate comforter of the needy, most zealous investigator of all uprightness and goodness. Virtue was his love and vice his horror; [Col. 0294C] in judgment mercy and truth always won for him the citadel of victory. None was readier than he to show compassion; none slower to be angered with, or to exact vengeance upon, the guilty.

God also chastised him for a long time in this world with the rod of His gracious correction, but reserved for him the staff of consolation, by which to receive the rewards of the life to come. Having endured long and difficult exiles among foreign peoples, he was at last restored to his homeland by both the command and the petition of Frederick, Roman emperor, to Duke Vladislav. Yet after a short interval, compelled by fate, he departed from this world, blessed for the compensation of temporal loss by the consolation of eternal happiness.

In the same year, on the thirteenth Kalends of February, Frederick, abbot [Col. 0294D] of Postoloprty, a man of the highest discernment in divine and human affairs, of devout sincerity toward God and people, and inward affability toward all, had set out with Lord Daniel the bishop on a journey to the land of the Hungarians. For that prelate and Henry, brother of Duke Vladislav, together with other leading men of the Bohemian [Col. 0295A] land, were escorting the daughter [Note: [Col. 0295D] Elizabeth.] of the Hungarian king [Note: [Col. 0295D] Géza II.] to be betrothed to Frederick, son of the same duke. On his return, when he arrived at one of his villages to rest, after an illness of three days he breathed out his final spirit.

Also in that year, on the eleventh Kalends of March, John, bishop of the church of Olomouc, who had been taken from the monastery of St Augustine at Strahov, ended his present life. He stood indeed in the very flower of youth, but was mature in nobility of character. In defence of justice and of the condition and honour of God’s holy Church, he always remained, insofar as lay in him, an unyielding combatant: stern toward the disobedient, but gentle, ready, and gracious toward those who loved God. From the time when he received the episcopal mitre, [Col. 0295B] he always guarded humility above all in heart, bearing, and speech; so much so that he often even refused veneration from persons humbler than himself, saying that he ought not demand honour from human beings, since he too had been formed from the same clay.

### On the excellence of King Vladislav and his brother Duke Theobald

In the same year Emperor Frederick, having joined to himself Duke Vladislav and his brother Theobald, entered Poland with a powerful army [Note: [Col. 0295D] On 22 August Frederick crossed the Oder, according to Rahewin, who, like Vincent of Prague, treated this expedition more fully.]. He subjected its princes, Bolesław [Note: [Col. 0295D] the Fourth.] and Mieszko [Note: [Col. 0295D] the Third; they were sons of Bolesław III.], to his authority; received an immense sum of gold and silver; and, taking their sons as hostages [Note: [Col. 0295D] Rather, his brother Casimir and other nobles, as Rahewin confirms.] for the future confirmation and stability of peace, returned having obtained the victory he desired.

For the conclusion of this peace the illustrious energy of Duke Vladislav was especially active. He showed himself so favourably disposed toward the imperial will that he wished, by himself and his own men alone, either to compel the aforesaid princes to submit or, should the need require it, to be the first to begin battle with them. The emperor, however [Note: [Col. 0295D] In October he was staying at Besançon; cf. Böhmer, Regesta, no. 2376.], having obtained the honour he sought, returned to his own seat.

Then, with the year 1158 from the Incarnation already begun, he deliberated with the princes of the realm how he ought to reward the Bohemian duke for his service [Note: [Col. 0295D] At Regensburg, on 16 January, Frederick I issued the charter granting the golden circlet to Vladislav and all his successors; see Boczek I, 267.]. While many of them declared that, in accordance with imperial munificence, he seemed worthy to be rewarded with the finest gifts of gold and silver, the emperor, [Col. 0295D] employing [Col. 0296A] a more generous counsel, addressed the duke, whom he had summoned to him, in these noble words:

> “The constancy of your valour has greatly pleased us. For the sincerity of your fidelity toward us has become manifest to the whole realm: how faithfully, devoutly, and deeply you love, according to God, the unimpaired welfare of us—indeed, of the entire kingdom—when in our necessities and in the affairs of the commonwealth of the whole realm you have never hesitated to expose your own life and those of your men to danger. Therefore, considering and cherishing this outstanding virtue in you, and desiring that henceforth you be regarded as faithful and unchanging toward our imperial serenity, we have decreed to honour you, according to our liberality, with whatever honour you may choose. Yet because we know that your land abounds in gold, silver, and every abundance of precious things, [Col. 0296B] and that nothing of this kind is rare for you, receive, by God’s grace and our goodwill, the crown of a kingdom which we confer upon you, together with the dignity of royal power and honour in your own realm.”

As he said this, he ordered a golden crown to be brought forth, wonderfully adorned with gems and precious stones, which the emperor himself was said to use at the highest festivals [Note: [Col. 0296D] This is erroneous. By Frederick’s ordinance Vladislav was permitted, on the same feast days on which the emperor wore a crown, to be publicly adorned with a circlet by the bishops of Prague and Olomouc. The emperor claims the crown or diadem for himself, and the circlet for Vladislav. Dobner attempted to prove in a special dissertation that this circlet was a true crown, in *Born, Abhandlungen einer Privatgesellschaft in Böhmen*, V, 1.]. Thus elevated by such divinely granted honour, the glorious Duke Vladislav returned to his own country amid the great rejoicing and gladness of his people.

Then, in May of the same year [Note: [Col. 0296D] On 14 June 1158 Frederick was still staying at Augsburg; Böhmer, no. 2402.], the king and his brother Duke Theobald set out with Caesar Frederick for Italy against the Milanese. The latter were then deeply hostile to the emperor because of a certain uprising made against the people of Lodi and those of the city of Nola [Note: [Col. 0296D] Nola is a city of Campania; the author seems to have had the city of Como in mind.]. For the emperor had resolved not to withdraw with his army until he had repaid his enemies, with fire and sword, the vengeance they deserved [Note: [Col. 0296D] Milan was besieged from 6 August 1158 onward, according to Rahewin.].

There the glorious and truly glorifiable Vladislav, with his chief men, like Judas Maccabaeus of old—now crushing the foreheads of his adversaries, now pursuing them from behind, now pressing them fiercely from right and left—fought so many battles gloriously and victoriously that it would take long to recount them. Yet since the outcome of victory in military contests is commonly uncertain, and various chances play differing and difficult turns in such matters, it could not be otherwise than that he too should lose some of his leading men there.

Therefore the citizens of Milan, [Col. 0296D] considering his exceptional valour and energy [Col. 0297A] and recognizing that he was most acceptable to Caesar, sent envoys and petitions to him, begging that he serve as mediator between themselves and Caesar in offering suitable satisfaction and arranging peace [Note: [Col. 0297D] Peace was established on 3 September; see Vincent of Prague’s ample account.]. With his prudent counsel and diligent assistance, the citizens of the aforesaid city obtained peace.

1159. Bishop Daniel set out for Milan to Caesar Frederick [Note: [Col. 0297D] He had come to Italy with the king in the preceding year.], by whom he was received graciously and honourably. The emperor kept him for two years, occupied in his service and in the affairs of himself and the realm.

Meanwhile, when Anastasius, pontiff of the Apostolic See, had died at Rome, a serious disturbance arose, and two men of opposing parties were elected to preside over the Apostolic See: Alexander [Note: [Col. 0297D] the Third.] and Victor [Note: [Col. 0298D] the Fourth.]. To settle this dispute Bishop Daniel was sent to Rome, so that [Col. 0297B] both persons might appear before the council of Caesar and the whole realm, and that, in accordance with public and canonical ordinance, the one more suitable should obtain primacy over the Apostolic See.

At that council [Note: [Col. 0297] In manuscript 4, in the margin beside the passage “At that—received,” a contemporary hand wrote, one letter beneath another, the word *mentiris*, “you lie.”] [Note: [Col. 0298D] held at Pavia early in the year 1160.], before all the princes of the realm and 150 bishops, Victor won the victory of justice and, by the unanimous vote and acclamation of all, received the supreme office of the Apostolic See. These matters having been duly concluded, Bishop Daniel, raised to great honour by Caesar and the pope and also exercising the distinction of an apostolic legation, proceeded to the king of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 0298D] Géza II.], and thence, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1160, returned to his own episcopal seat at Prague, prospering in all things by God’s help.

1161. On the fourth Ides of February, Sylvester, abbot of Sázava, [Col. 0297C] in the twenty-eighth year of his rule, passed from the darkness of this bodily region to the homeland of everlasting dwelling, to receive, for the labour of the present life, the prize of blessed recompense. He was fittingly distinguished by the discipline and grace of every virtue, and so devoted to the exercises of practice and the love of contemplation that one could clearly have perceived a man still placed in the flesh, yet already established wholly in heavenly things by the ardour of his spirit.

He was a particular friend of frugality, abhorring richer foods and cups of wine as certain sources of disease, while delighting in simple food and the pure water of the river. He detested the banquets of the powerful and of all worldly persons; for this reason he was less loved by many, because in such matters he made himself the companion of no one. Much might indeed be said about the praiseworthy quality of his life, as an example of devout living and a pattern of uprightness; but since I remember having already spoken of this in part above, and especially since clear testimonies remain concerning the greatness of his works in that monastery [Col. 0297D] and the extent [Col. 0298A] of his labours for the honour of divine worship, let these things suffice here. This alone, with all due respect to everyone, I shall say:

> That place scarcely found for itself such a father  
> In morals and in life as Abbot Sylvester was.

After his death Božata, prior of the same place, succeeded to the abbacy in that same year through the election of King Vladislav and Bishop Daniel. Within a short time—after completing the span of one year—he voluntarily laid aside responsibility for his rule. For he had already completed thirty years in monastic life and had made himself so remote from the turmoil of secular affairs that he would not permit himself to know even slightly what was being done in [Col. 0298B] the world. Thus he was wholly inexperienced in arranging the monastery’s outward concerns or examining judgments in disputes among laypeople. Moreover, he was burdened with so many and such grave ailments that scarcely ever, even when the greatest necessity required it for the church’s benefit, could he go beyond the walls of the monastery. Overcome by these and similar difficulties, after the cycle of a year he laid down the burden of government he had undertaken.

In the same year the young Duke Soběslav [Note: [Col. 0298D] Son of Soběslav I.] made a night attack upon the city of Olomouc with sixty armed knights; nearly all whom he found there he caused to be dishonoured with diverse insults. This soon

> Flying Rumour struck the ears of King Vladislav,

[Col. 0298C] who, having assembled an army, surrounded the said city. But seeing that the city’s entrance would be inaccessible to himself and his men because of the strong guard of soldiers, he judged it wiser to test the youthful prince’s mind by cunning rather than by war. Through intermediaries he invited the duke to peace—indeed, he pledged and assured him that he would accept whatever condition of peace he wished.

The prince, therefore, like the simplest lamb, suspecting nothing adverse, went into the king’s hands. Peace and the condition of peace were confirmed by the oath of a sworn pledge. There John, bishop of Moravia, and here every leading man of Bohemia swore, as the king prescribed, to confirm peace and fidelity. But where was fidelity? The oaths were violated, the agreement of peace was rendered void; the prince, of exceptional worth, was seized and chained, and shut up for a long time [Note: [Col. 0298D] Until the year 1173.] to be worn down under most stringent [Col. 0298D] guard in the very strong castle of Přimda [Note: [Col. 0298D] Frauenberg in the Pilsen district.].

1162. By the assent of divine mercy, and through the active intervention of King Vladislav and also Lord Bishop Daniel, Regnard received the helm of government in the monastery of Sázava. He had first governed the monastery of Sedlec [Col. 0299A] [Note: [Col. 0299D] Selau in the Čáslav district.] very honourably and magnificently enlarged its possessions of various kinds by his own labour.

But in the first year of Lord Bishop Daniel’s ordination, certain wicked men rose against this venerable abbot. Whatever criminal allegations they could invent against him, they did not hesitate to drive into the bishop’s ears by frequent and importunate denunciation. And because, as blessed Gregory says, “a mind occupied with many matters is easily deceived by flatterers,” the bishop believed the matter to be as it had been fabricated. Thus the venerable Regnard, scarcely—without canonical hearing, without being convicted by lawful accusers or witnesses, and without having confessed the crime alleged against him—was deprived of the honour of the abbacy and expelled from the monastery with the entire congregation dear to him.

[Col. 0299B] It is indeed remarkable of so great a man, namely the lord bishop, that he could pronounce so cruel and precipitous a sentence upon both shepherd and flock, and that he judged that no one at all should be spared on the accusation of one person—unless perhaps, as some then conjectured and as the subsequent outcome of events proved, he did this on that pretext in order to entrust the same place to certain regular canons of the Augustinian order brought in from foreign lands.

The aforesaid Lord Reginhard, in the fourteenth year after he had been deposed from his office, [Col. 0300A] was made abbot of the monastery of Sázava, when the Lord mercifully regarded his tribulations and patience. A native of Metz, he was a most discerning guide of monastic life, endowed with the grace of affection and affability, most steadfast in the strength of humility and gentleness, and in every elegance of conduct comparable in all respects with the best.

He always gave the most vigilant care to standing in defence of his people. Neither royal majesty nor the power of princes could ever instil fear or shame in him when truth had to be asserted. Neither did prosperity ever soften his spirit into empty joy, nor adversity cast it down into destructive sadness: in every event he was a man whose countenance always showed the same cheerfulness. He strove to preside over the whole congregation more through love than terror. He had subjected himself so completely to humility that, though he was worthier and more exalted than all in the congregation, in all his actions he presented himself as subject.

No one was readier, swifter, or more effective than he at every humble task. He had skill in painting or carving any images in wood, bone, or metal of various kinds. Nor was he ignorant of craftsmanship, or of every composition customarily made from glass [Note: [Col. 0299] Here the text ends in both manuscripts 4 and 4a; what follows is the supplement of the monk of Sázava. In manuscript 4 there follows a very brief Life of St Ludmila, published by Menken, at the end of which are read the words: “Here ends the book of this man in the Chronicle of the Bohemians.”].

[Col. 0299]

## CONTINUATIONS OF COSMAS BY THE CANONS OF PRAGUE

[Col. 0299C] **[GERLACH.]** In those days, when King Conrad ruled in the kingdom of the Romans and Duke Soběslav held power in Bohemia, Zdík—also called Henry—the revered bishop of Olomouc, had taken up our habit, which he had seen at Jerusalem over the tomb of life, amid, as they relate, a great shower of tears. Having there renounced both the eating of flesh and the other enticements of life, he brought back to the said duke and to the Bohemians, as it were, both a new man and a new order.

When that duke died shortly afterward, his successor, the illustrious Vladislav, together with his most noble wife Gertrude, sister of the aforesaid King Conrad, were kindled by the example and exhortation of the said bishop. They established a new church for a new order, raising a most beautiful structure on Mount Strahov and changing its name to [Col. 0299D] Mount Zion, in the year of the Lord 1140. The same bishop cooperated most effectively with them, especially in spiritual matters, gathering religious brethren from wherever he could, [Col. 0300C] and first placing at their head a certain Blasius.

But after he learned clearly concerning the institution of the church of Prémontré—that from it came the origin of the order and the teaching of regular life—he immediately held consultation with the founders themselves. By unanimous decision they sent envoys and requested a convent from the house of Steinfeld. At that time our order, though not yet widely extended, nevertheless burned with great zeal, both at Prémontré and in all the churches of our order, especially in the church of Steinfeld, which had no equal in religious life and has none now.

Drawn by its most sweet fragrance, princes of lands everywhere rejoiced to found new churches and summon persons of the order for the illumination of their provinces. Among these were the founders now under discussion. They first presented their petition to the chapter, then to the church of Steinfeld, and obtained in full effect what they devoutly requested. For the matter was entrusted to the provost of Steinfeld, that he should advance their undertaking and grant their desire.

The provost, a man full of God, did not delay in what he had been commanded, but, taking brethren with him and Lord Godescalc—who was afterwards made abbot at Sedlec—set out for Bohemia. He came to Prague, was devoutly received, pledged himself to accept the place, and at last, returning home, left there at his side the aforementioned Godescalc with brethren, who meanwhile were to prepare wooden dwellings for the convent. Once these were ready, after the cycle of another year the same provost returned, bringing with him a convent of clerics and the abbot whom they had elected, named Gezo. Gezo would gladly have kept Lord Godescalc with him; but his provost ordered him to return to [Col. 0301B] Steinfeld to await what had been divinely ordained for him.

Nor do I think it unsuitable to relate briefly how this same Gezo, the first abbot of Strahov, first came to conversion at Steinfeld. In this, indeed, those will confess the Lord’s mercies who understand that He calls His predestined in wondrous ways. While Gezo was keeper of the canons and of the greater church at Cologne, a wealthy and refined man, one night he dreamed that his fellow canons were seated, as it were, in a circle, with himself in their midst. Then there stood before them a man terrible in appearance. With the rod he carried in his hand, he struck first one on the head, then another, then a third; and so he scourged them all, on both his right and his left. Finally, when he intended to strike Gezo too, Gezo avoided the blow and so awoke.

The death of these men followed the vision: all were shortly removed from this light, in precisely the order in which they had been struck in the vision. Seeing this and fearing death, he fled like a unicorn and took refuge in Steinfeld, at the harbour of the monastery. There he lived justly and according to the rule until the day when he was raised to the abbacy.

Gezo was indeed a man of complete integrity and diligence, a prudent administrator in spiritual as well as temporal matters, and a great champion of discipline. The church of Strahov still flourishes and is governed by his institution. Thus his memory is blessed: after death he does not die, [Col. 0301D] and his ever-living works proclaim that he still lives.

**[VINCENT.]** In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, King Conrad entered upon the way of all flesh. In his place Frederick, his cousin, duke of Swabia and a knight vigorous in arms, was elected king and began to govern the affairs of the whole world.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1155, Duke Vladislav was received into the greatest favour by King Frederick. The sons of Soběslav, exiles, faithfully attached themselves to Lord King Frederick and were honourably treated by him and his princes.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1156, King Frederick gathered a very great multitude of princes and other knights. With Duke Henry of Saxony, Frederick son of King Conrad, and other princes joined to him, [Col. 0302A] he set out for Rome with a strong force of soldiers, that Pope Adrian might consecrate him emperor according to due right.

When, leaving the Alps, they reached the impregnable castle of Gervarda before the city of Verona, the Veronese prohibited him and his men from passing, claiming this as their right. They said that he had not been consecrated emperor and that, on this account, by their law he ought to pay them money if he wished to go that way to Rome; once they had received him as consecrated emperor, they would then pay him the honour due to an emperor—but not before.

On hearing this King Frederick restrained his anger and, concealing it, offered fine words and promised the money they demanded. Thus, as though security had been given in the matter, he passed Verona with his armies unharmed. When the royal armies had been posted beyond [Col. 0302B] the city, he ordered the Veronese to come for the money owed. Trusting his words, they sent thirteen of their noblest men, accompanied by many nobles, to the king for the promised payment.

The king received them with a cheerful countenance and, after offering them the finest assurances concerning the money promised, ordered them seized. When one of them said that he was the king’s relative in a closer degree and proved this by testimony, the king ordered him for that reason to be hanged higher, as being nobler—leaving this example to posterity and instilling fear in others, that they might not presume to act thus against their lords.

**[VINCENT.]** Meanwhile the Pavians and Cremonese, as to their most dear lord, came to meet him with a large and select force of knights and proceeded along the royal road in his service. At last the king entered the Rome he had desired and, at the appointed time, was consecrated emperor by Lord Pope Adrian.

When the consecration had been completed and they were taking food by right in the royal encampments, set in a most beautiful plain before the royal city of Rome, the Romans, dreaming of their ancient pride and indignant that the lord emperor’s consecration had taken place as though against their will, armed themselves powerfully against him. What more need be said? Armed battle-lines advanced toward the Tiber. When the emperor heard this, he armed his forces in response and ordered no attack to be made upon them until they came out onto the plain.

The Lateran forces came out into the open field against the emperor’s army. The foremost battle-lines joined; battle began. Yet [Col. 0302D] while Emperor Frederick, with the son of King Conrad and other princes, was striking them manfully in front, Henry, duke of Saxony, a warrior of war, fiercely attacked them from behind at the bridge over the Tiber. When they had nearly reached the iron gate standing in the middle of the bridge, the Lateran men saw this and, choosing the lesser of two evils, shut the iron gate against both their enemies and their own side. They were thus miserably overthrown: some died by the sword, some by drowning; the rest were captured, four hundred in number, and presented to the lord emperor.

The emperor entrusted them to Peter, prefect of the city of Rome, who had faithfully adhered to him. They had destroyed both his palaces in Rome and his other fortifications. [Col. 0303A] The prefect of the city punished some for so bold a deed by hanging, and received a great deal of money from others to rebuild his ruined palaces. Thus the emperor won the victory he desired on the level plain.

After this victory the emperor made a treaty and agreement with Lord Pope Adrian: neither the Romans, who had made themselves enemies of the empire, nor the king of Sicily, who did not obey the empire, should be received into favour without the counsel and will of the lord pope; and conversely, the lord pope should not receive them without the counsel and will of the lord emperor. He then returned happily to Lombardy.

Not forgetting the injury done by the Milanese, he besieged the city of Tortona, which, after Spoleto not far from Rome had already been destroyed, had sworn alliance with Milan against the emperor. Surrounding it with a strong force of knights, with the Pavians, Cremonese, and other Lombard cities lending assistance, he destroyed it utterly after many had been killed on both sides, granting the defeated only their lives.

This other royal and very strong city, neighboring Tortona, seeing what had happened—having joined the Milanese in their oaths—fled to the lord emperor. According to his will it destroyed all its towers and fortifications, and appeased him by its service.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1157, Emperor Frederick summoned a general court of his princes at Würzburg for the feast of Pentecost. There he joined to himself in marriage Lady Beatrice, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, who in appearance and beauty seemed in some measure to surpass human form, as though she were offspring of divinity. Duke Vladislav attended these wedding festivities among the other princes with Lord Daniel, bishop of Prague; as befitted so great an emperor, the wedding was celebrated splendidly.

There the lord emperor revealed to his princes the intolerable arrogance of the Milanese. On hearing it, they advised that, as enemies of the empire, they should be corrected with fitting punishment.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, Emperor Frederick, taking pity on Duke Vladislav of Poland, then in exile, and on his own sister, who had been joined to the duke in marriage, prepared an army to restore him to his duchy in Poland. Entering it with very numerous forces, he cruelly devastated it. Since the princes of Poland could not resist such strength, through the mediation of Duke Vladislav of Bohemia [Col. 0303D] they came into his favour—on the condition that, carrying naked swords above their necks, they should be presented to the imperial majesty. They were received into the favour of the lord emperor, after hostages had been given in satisfaction and oaths received that they should send three hundred armed knights to assist the lord emperor against Milan.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, the lord emperor summoned a solemn court of his princes to Magdeburg at Christmas. After the royal insignia had been displayed and the ceremony happily completed, he urged and entreated them, mindful of their royal blood, to provide him aid in crushing Milanese arrogance. His princes faithfully promised this by unanimous decision.

[Col. 0304A] Duke Vladislav of Bohemia, too, seeing so many and such great princes already under arms against Milan, promised that he himself, with his troops, would come to the emperor’s aid. Lord Daniel, bishop of Prague, likewise did not refuse to undertake this labour against Milan with his duke. For so great a service the emperor adorned Duke Vladislav of Bohemia with the royal diadem, making a king from a duke.

Frederick’s imperial court ended; arms were prepared against Milan; from every side the siege of Milan resounded. At the appointed time armies moved from different parts of the world to besiege Milan. Emperor Frederick, with his dukes, margraves, and other princes, advanced against Milan.
