King Vladislav of Bohemia crossed the Alps first. Passing safely through Verona, [Col. 0304B] he stationed his royal forces before the city of Brescia. The Brescian people, not daring to come out against them or commit themselves to so great an army, merely guarded their walls. The whole Brescian territory was devastated by the Bohemians.

Soon afterward the imperial forces arrived. All the armies rejoiced exuberantly at the emperor’s arrival. The emperor’s royal encampment was established above the River Olio. They came to the very swift River Adda, where they found the bridges broken and a vast multitude of people from the Milanese territory preventing them from crossing the water. On the bank beside the ruined bridge the imperial tents were pitched, filling the plains in every direction. Nearly a mile below these encampments stood the tents of Lord Vladislav, [Col. 0304C] king of Bohemia, Lord Daniel, bishop of Prague, and the other Bohemian princes; after so many labours, sweet food was taken.

Meanwhile Odolen, son of Zris, a vigorous knight, tried with two knights to find a ford. Finding none, he committed himself to the midst of the current, followed by only one companion. We saw them whirled about in the middle of the waves so that now they seemed to be above their horses, now their horses above them. At last, with God’s help, they crossed the river safely. Their third companion, either because his horse or his courage was weak, returned to the bank.

When this was reported to the king of Bohemia—that two knights had found a ford—the planks were thrown down and the drum, the signal for battle, was struck. The knights armed themselves, and Vladislav himself, king of Bohemia, a vigorous and illustrious knight, leading them, drove their warhorses into the very midst of the rushing waves. Preserved by divine mercy, they overcame currents so violent and so precipitous, though many knights there were lost by drowning.

Thus the king of Bohemia, having passed the currents with his strong armed force, fell upon his enemies, surrounding them on every side with armed troops. Very many were struck down, bound, and captured. Cries rose to heaven from both sides: the Bohemians’ joyful cries at victory and the Milanese’s mournful cries at their unforeseen disaster.

At first the emperor’s army thought that the Milanese had come to their assistance; but when they saw the Bohemians manfully striking their adversaries, rejoicing in so great a victory [Col. 0305A] and raising happy cries to heaven, they marvelled how and by what skill they had overcome such rushing currents.

**[VINCENT.]** Having thus overcome them, the Bohemians took castles, villages, and plunder, and committed as much as they could to fire. Meanwhile the king moved over to the emperor’s bridge, anxious to repair it. Beams useful for the bridge were brought together from both sides, both from the emperor’s men and the king’s. Night interrupted so great a labour.

At earliest dawn a messenger arrived: the Milanese had come with their forces to defend the ford.

No delay was made: the soldiery armed, the battle was fought fiercely, and the Milanese, defeated, took to flight; nor is this surprising, for in such a situation death must be avoided either by the sword or by one’s feet. The Bohemians, having killed very many of them, captured eighty of the more noble [Col. 0305B] members of the Milanese soldiery and delivered them into the royal power; the king of Bohemia in turn delivered them to the imperial majesty, to the latter’s honour. The lord emperor, with his armies, happily crossed the river Adda by the repaired bridges. He besieged Trenez, a most strongly fortified castle of the Milanese, and captured it in a short time. From there they came to a very noble city called Lodi, which the Milanese had utterly destroyed. In the midst of the ruined city the imperial tents were pitched; and the emperor, considering its destruction, laboured all the more for the destruction of Milan.

While these things were taking place, the Milanese came, under the emperor’s safe-conduct, to the court of the lord emperor, offering him fitting satisfaction for their offences. When the princes heard this, they advised [Col. 0305C] that the lord emperor receive them again into his favour. But Anselm, archbishop of the church of Ravenna, rose and replied against this:

> “You do not know,” he said, “the cunning of the Milanese. They offer you words indeed sweet and humble, but they keep a crafty fox within their breasts. Let the measure with which they measured for others be measured back to them. They destroyed the churches of God and the emperor’s free cities; let Milan, theirs, be destroyed. They showed mercy to none; nor should they obtain it.”

When the lord emperor and his princes heard this, he accepted his counsel; and, by casting down his glove, according to the custom of the ancient emperors, [Col. 0305D] he publicly placed them under his ban, thereby declaring them manifest enemies of the empire. At this the joyful young men clamoured for arms. The armed soldiery marched toward Milan; it was proclaimed that all the troops should be ready under arms at the signal of the lord emperor. Day rose, bringing death to many and victory to many.

On the very level plains before Milan, most suitable for armies, the imperial forces armed themselves. In the first line of battle was Louis, the emperor’s brother, Count Palatine of the Rhine, in the first flower of his youth. By the dignity of his ancient predecessors [Note: [Col. 0305] “successors,” Dobr.] of Swabia, he advanced into the plain with an armed [Col. 0306A] force of Swabians, reinforced by the troops of Pavia and Cremona, who had been the makers of this expedition.

Frederick, son of King Conrad, Duke of Rothenburg [Note: [Col. 0305] “Rotennburg,” Vincent], still in his youth, held the second position with his strong force. To increase this army Hugh, marquis of Montferrat, joined it with the strong troops of Verona, Brescia, and Mantua. Vladislaus, king of Bohemia, held the third position with his army, which he had assembled into one body from all his soldiery, a very great and strong host. In the fourth position Henry, duke of Austria, was stationed with his very large army. In the fifth was Otto, Count Palatine of Regensburg, together with his brothers Frederick and Otto and a great force of Bavarians. In the sixth place was the emperor himself, [Col. 0306B] Frederick, with an army whose length and breadth were exceedingly difficult to comprehend. In the seventh position advanced Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, with the army of the German and Lombard princes, gathered in great strength.

[Continuation of Cosmas, 1136.] After these came a multitude of princes whom no one could number—whose standards, powers, movements, positions, and times thou, O God, knowest.

[Vincent.] Thus so many and such great armies, terrible in the brightness of iron, advanced toward the Milanese gate—called the Roman Gate—and, with no one obstructing them, came to the long-desired city. The Milanese, not daring to commit themselves to battle in the open fields against such numerous and powerful armies, strengthened their ditches and fortifications which they had made around the walls, and guarded them [Col. 0306C] with an armed force.

But the lord emperor, seeing that they did not dare to come out beyond their fortifications, ordered his tents to be pitched before the aforesaid gate, called the Roman Gate, greater both in name and in fact. He also ordered the tents of other princes to be pitched around the other Milanese gates; and what he ordered was quickly done: the tents of different princes were pitched before the different gates.

The Milanese considered from what direction they might attack them. They decided to direct their effort against the army in the first line, that of Louis, the emperor’s brother, who had stationed his forces at the Gate of Saint Dionysius; and about the evening hour they advanced to battle with an armed hand as vigorously as they could. The aforesaid prince [Col. 0306D] met them, like a valiant soldier, with his strong force. Battle took place on both sides; the bravest soldiers were struck down; now these men prevailed, now those.

When Vladislaus, king of Bohemia, heard this, he ordered the drum, the signal of war, to be beaten. There was no delay: the soldiery armed, and marched to the aid of those fighting. Louis, the emperor’s brother, pressed more vigorously to drive the Milanese back from himself.

Meanwhile Vladislaus, king of Bohemia, splendid in his arms, attacked with his soldiery the first Milanese line and pierced with his lance through the middle their commander and standard-bearer, Dacius, who [Col. 0307A] fell there, pierced through. The remaining soldiers, both Bohemian and German, rushed upon the enemy wherever they could. Shield-boss struck shield-boss, foot was crushed against foot, and the mightiest blows of valiant men resounded. On both sides the bravest soldiers were struck down. The battle lasted from the evening hour until twilight. The defeated Milanese, with very many killed and captured, withdrew within the walls.

By such a ring of soldiers the Milanese were surrounded on every side. The lord emperor did not cease every day to march around Milan with his armies, so that none might be able to leave it. Every day different assaults were made upon them; they were sorely pressed by many killings and captures—terror within and the sword without ravaged them.

[Prague Annals.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1160.

[Col. 0307B] In this year Bishop Daniel returned from Milan.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1161.

[Vincent.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, Theobald went with the king’s son to aid the emperor, and Soběslav was captured. [Note: [Col. 0307D] See the monk of Sázava for evidence that this occurred in 1161.]

In the year of the Lord 1163.

1164. [Prague Annals.] King Vladislaus entered the land of the Huns, drove the Greek king out of it, and pacified the magnates of the Hungarians.

1165.

1166.

1167.

1168. [Prague Annals.] Duke Theobald and Bishop Daniel died in Italy; Frederick succeeded him as the fourteenth bishop. [Note: [Col. 0307D] In 1167, according to Gerlach.]

[Col. 0307C] 1169.

1170.

[Gerlach.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1171, Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, was martyred.

1172. [Prague Annals.] King Vladislaus entered Poland with the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Rather, in 1157; compare the continuation of Sázava.]

1173.

1174. Soběslav was released from his chains [Note: [Col. 0307D] He was released in 1173.] and made duke.

1175. Duke Oldřich, brother of Soběslav, went to Milan.

1176. Duke Soběslav devastated Austria by fire. Excessive drought reduced the crops. Soběslav fought [Col. 0307D] against Frederick in Bohemia. [Gerlach.] In the same year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, King Vladislaus, founder of Strahov, died. [Note: [Col. 0307D] He died in 1174.]

[Col. 0308A] 1177. [Prague Annals.] Duke Oldřich was captured by his brother Soběslav. Soběslav himself was driven from the throne by the Bohemians. [Note: [Col. 0307D] According to Gerlach, in 1177.] Frederick, son of King Vladislaus, was enthroned. Soběslav died in exile. [Note: [Col. 0307D] According to the same witness, in 1180.]

1178. Bishop Frederick died [Note: [Col. 0307D] According to the same witness, in 1179.], and Valentine succeeded him as the fifteenth bishop.

1179.

1180.

1181.

[Gerlach.] In the year of the Lord 1182, the church of Strahov was dedicated for the second time, namely on the seventh [Note: [Col. 0307] “sixth,” Gerlach.] day before the Kalends of May, by the venerable Lord Adalbert, archbishop of Salzburg. This was for the following reason: the high altar had been moved [Note: [Col. 0307] Gerlach reads “new” for “moved.”], and the choir had been raised. Present were nearly all the canons of the Prague church [Col. 0308B] and many abbots, among whom one, and the foremost—though in his own judgment the humblest—was Abbot Gottschalk, who adorned so great a solemnity with his discourse. Among other things that he said, he also said this:

> “I am present, dearest brethren, at your second dedication, having also been present at the first; and I seem to myself to see the condition of this house very different from what it then was. For then it was poor in possessions and rich in merits; now, the condition having been reversed, it has increased in possessions and declined in discipline.”

And, rebuking what deserved rebuke in this manner and urging them toward honourable conduct, he offered them counsels of salvation.

1182. [Prague Annals.] Bishop Valentine died. Henry succeeded as the sixteenth bishop; later, while bishop, he obtained the duchy.

[Col. 0308C] 1183. Conrad, duke of Moravia, besieged Prague. [Note: [Col. 0307D] This occurred in 1182.]

1184. The Bohemians began war with the Moravians. [Note: [Col. 0308D] Gerlach narrates this at length under 1185.]

1185. Duke Wenceslaus was compelled to besiege Prague, but departed disappointed in his hope. [Note: [Col. 0308D] In 1184.]

1186. There was an eclipse of the sun. A mortality of men occurred.

1187. Duke Frederick, with all the chief men of his land, and likewise Lord Bishop Henry [Note: [Col. 0308D] Bishop Henry, son of Henry, was, like Duke Frederick, a grandson of Vladislaus I, duke of Bohemia.], with the abbots and all the clergy, were summoned to the emperor’s court, and a great synod was held. [Note: [Col. 0308D] At Regensburg during Lent, according to Gerlach.] In the same year Theobald was ordered by his brother [Note: [Col. 0308D] His paternal cousin; Theobald was the son of Theobald I and grandson of Vladislaus I.] Frederick to be captured; but forewarned by certain [Col. 0308D] supporters, he escaped by flight.

1188. Jerusalem was besieged by the pagans and surrendered to Saladin.

[Col. 0309A] 1189. Duke Frederick died. Conrad, the worthy duke of Moravia, succeeded. Theobald recovered his provinces. The Roman emperor also, intending to fight the pagans with an innumerable multitude of Christians, took the route across the sea; there he ended his life in a shipwreck and rests buried at Antioch. Many noble chief men of the Bohemian land who had followed him, together with Duke Theobald, were likewise overtaken by unexpected death.

1190. Duke Conrad set out with the emperor’s son for Apulia, where, having won for himself a most renowned triumph, alas, he was overtaken by untimely death. His bones were brought and buried at Prague, [Col. 0309B] while those who mourned and grieved from the heart over him wept:

> “Ah, ah, Conrad, duke often to be remembered!  
> May you live in Christ, translated from this world!”

1191. Duke Wenceslaus sat upon his father’s throne [Note: [Col. 0309D] He was the son of Soběslav I.], which he possessed scarcely for three months.

1192. Duke Wenceslaus was driven from the throne. Duke Přemysl was established. The city of Prague was surrounded by siege, but was not taken. At last, after three months, with [Col. 0310A] Duke Wenceslaus himself permitting it, it was announced through the emperor’s envoy that it was handed over into the hands of the lord bishop. But while Duke Wenceslaus was travelling on the borders of Serbia, he was captured through the ambushes of the treacherous [Note: [Col. 0309] “vrsipellis,” manuscript 2.] margrave [Note: [Col. 0309D] Otto of Meissen.] of that province and shut in most secure custody, Spytihněv alone escaping. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Duke of Brno.] In the same year Duke Přemysl [Note: [Col. 0309D] Son of King Vladislaus II.] ravaged the province of certain Germans [Note: [Col. 0309D] Bavarians.] and thereby stirred the emperor [Note: [Col. 0309D] Henry VI.] to anger. The lord bishop also set out for the shrine of Saint James the Apostle for the sake of prayer; the emperor detained him because of money promised to him, and thus hindered he returned to Bohemia.

1193. At the beginning of March Lord Bishop Henry [Note: [Col. 0309] In an old but not contemporary hand, “Břetislav” is written above.] returned to the emperor’s court, and at the beginning of [Col. 0310B] August he returned to Bohemia with great glory and honour, accompanied by the young Duke Spytihněv and bearing the standards of the duchy entrusted to him by the emperor, yet without relinquishing the name and dignity of his bishopric.

1194.

1195.

# I. History of King Wenceslaus I

[Col. 0309]

[Col. 0309C] Therefore King Wenceslaus, in the first and several subsequent years of his reign, greatly loved the secular and regular clergy and willingly honoured the churches of God and their ministers. As time went on, however, after his father had already entered upon the way of all flesh, he had the city of Prague enclosed with walls and ordered other market towns—called *civitates* in our vernacular—to be fortified with wood or stone, compelling religious and secular clerics to construct the fortifications or ditches of those towns.

During his reign, for many years good peace prevailed. Robbers, thieves, persecutors of churches, and very many other evildoers ceased to inflict injuries or troubles; or, if they inflicted them, they were caught and suffered the sentence of death. In his time too the sport of tournaments was introduced [Col. 0309D] into Bohemia, in 1245, the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0309] “fifth,” manuscript 2.]—or sixteenth—year of King Wenceslaus’s reign. The same king, devoted to the desire of his flesh, began to love a solitary life and to inhabit alone, with a few companions, castles or houses built for this purpose; nevertheless, good peace and quiet still prevailed throughout all his kingdom.

In the time of his reign several houses of religious were built [Col. 0310C] in the city of Prague: namely, those of the Friars Preachers at Saint Clement’s; the Friars Minor at Saint James’s; the Poor Ladies at Saint Francis’s; the Templars at Saint Lawrence’s; and the Hospitallers, or Crusaders of the Star, at Saint Peter’s in the German quarter. Several houses of the same orders were also built in the kingdom of Bohemia with the aforesaid king’s approval.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1249 [Note: [Col. 0309D] The narrative itself shows that what follows occurred in 1248.], the twentieth year of King Wenceslaus’s reign, on the second day before the Kalends of August, the nobles and elders of the land of Bohemia accepted the said king’s son, named Přemysl, as their duke or king; and in the cloister of the Prague [Col. 0310D] church they swore him fealty, with his father wholly unaware. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Concerning these times, Otakar, in a charter written in 1256 and cited by Palacký II, 131, reports this: “In the time of our affliction and misery, when that is, the dire and cruel persecution of our parents wished, in disregard of pity and without fault on our part, to drive us beyond the boundaries of our land,” etc.] When the father heard this, he took it ill, but with discretion natural to him he concealed his feelings.

But in the twenty-first year of King Wenceslaus’s reign, the aforesaid king entered Bohemia with a large army of Bohemians, Austrians, and Hungarians, and on the Ides of February established himself with his army in his castle at Vyšehrad. On the eighth day he departed from there and safely forded the river Vltava [Col. 0311A] below the village of Bubeneč with his entire army. Coming to the monastery on Mount Sion [Note: [Col. 0311D] That is, Strahov.], he remained there for several days, while his army stayed around and beyond the hill and at the monastery of Břevnov. Departing thence on the sixth day, he came to the city of Žatec and subjected it to his rule without battle; he devastated, plundered, and burned many other towns. Toward the end of that year and the beginning of the next, though it was winter, many burnings took place in the kingdom of Bohemia.

Accordingly, after peace had been arranged, concord confirmed by oaths, and documents concerning it drawn up, the king made his way toward Litoměřice. He ordered all the prelates and canons of the churches in the diocese of Prague to meet him within eight days and not fail to assist him according to [Col. 0311B] their means. The bishop of Meissen had been appointed executor in this matter by Pope Innocent IV, [Note: [Col. 0311D] The letter of Innocent IV to Conrad, bishop of Meissen, dated 22 April 1249, is printed in Boczek III, 106. It reads: “But the same Otakar, led astray and seduced by the wicked persuasions of certain barons of the kingdom of Bohemia, together with them cruelly persecutes the aforesaid king and attacks him with hostile persecution, to the detriment of the person and estate of that kingdom; and he is shamefully entering into a treaty of friendship and alliance with Conrad, son of the late Emperor Frederick, duke of Bavaria, and other persecutors of the Church. In all these matters the hand of the bishop of Prague and of certain other ecclesiastical persons [Col. 0312D] of the same kingdom is said to be involved.” To this should be joined the following letter concerning the absolution of the king from the oath which he had sworn to his son concerning the cession of the kingdom.] and it was decreed that, if the prelates of the churches of Bohemia and the canons did not take care to meet and assist the king according to their means, they should be struck with excommunication and eventually deprived of their benefices. In the same matter a letter of the new king of the Germans [Note: [Col. 0312D] William.] containing a similar penalty was presented and publicly read in the Prague church to the canons and other clerics.

But the king’s son, believing that this peace was genuine rather than feigned, came with his men to live at Prague, placing a most secure guard over town and city; afterwards he went on to the other [Col. 0311C] towns and castles which had fallen to his lot.

Meanwhile the king, delaying at Litoměřice, gathered a large army within several weeks. Many prelates of churches and some canons came to him there, offering him their persons, varied gifts of goods, and faithful service. While the king was holding his court in the same city with his faithful men, an edict was issued and proclaimed throughout all the neighbouring markets, under promise of royal favour and threat of the penalty of capital sentence, that all oppression by injuries, the plundering of towns, and robberies must cease, and that all alike, nobles and poor, should enjoy tranquil peace.

After the court had been held and very secret counsel taken, the king set out with his army, proceeding [Col. 0311D] toward Saczska. In this march he spent several [Col. 0312A] nights, during which many hardships were inflicted upon the poor, many towns were stripped of all goods, and various unheard-of crimes were committed. At last he reached Saczska and rested in his fortress, saying that he would proceed toward Moravia and then toward Hungary; but the outcome proved otherwise.

For, as the feast of the Assumption of the glorious Virgin approached, on 15 August, while the king’s son was staying in Prague Castle, the king sent his knights on the Nones of August and took the city [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Old Town, now called Altstadt.], as is believed, certain citizens having handed it over to him. That same day after noon he entered it with his followers. Bishop Nicholas, together with the Friars Minor, solemnly came out to meet him, received him honourably with a procession and a great multitude of both sexes, while bells sounded in all the churches of the city, [Col. 0312B] and led him to the church of Saint Francis amid great rejoicing of the people.

But the king’s son, who was then staying in the castle, learned that his father’s agreement had been wholly violated and saw that the city had been taken against his will. Having entrusted Prague Castle to his faithful followers for its defence, he withdrew to safer places. Certain of his more faithful adherents, to whom the defence of the episcopal court [Note: [Col. 0312D] That part of the city today called the Lesser Town.] had been entrusted, saw that their forces could not suffice for its protection. Taking away by night all the goods in it, they set it on fire that same night, and, laden with diverse property, fled to the castle. On the following day, 6 August, the king sent knights and captured without resistance the tower standing at the foot [Col. 0312C] of the bridge and the episcopal court still smoking; he stationed in them a garrison of stout men.

Thereupon, after taking counsel with his followers and now violating for a second time the agreement which he had in good faith promised to his son and the nobles of the land, he arranged an army to storm the Prague stronghold [Note: [Col. 0312D] The castle.], stationing fighting men to east, west, and north to attack the aforesaid stronghold [Note: [Col. 0311] “had attacked,” manuscript 2.] and permit no one to enter or leave it. He also brought wicked men from Jihlava [Note: [Col. 0312D] These were miners working in the mines of Jihlava, skilled in constructing siege-machines.] and set up many engines against the stronghold; he likewise ordered the ladies to leave the monastery [Note: [Col. 0312D] Of Saint George.]. But certain nobles with their ministeriales, who had been left for the defence of the aforesaid stronghold, resisted in every way and valiantly defended its walls with bows and crossbows.

When the Assumption [Col. 0313A] of the glorious Virgin arrived, the king imposed a truce on his soldiers and the defenders of the castle, so that on so solemn a day none of his own men or the adversaries should suffer any annoyance or hurt. Yet he granted no inhabitant of the castle permission to come into the city. There was an extreme shortage of water among the men besieged in the castle and such a lack of fodder for horses and livestock that, if the siege of the castle were prolonged for more days, men, horses, and livestock alike would be compelled to die from excessive want of water and fodder.

When the solemnity of the Blessed Virgin had passed, the king celebrated his feast safely and peacefully on the following day, 16 August, and caused a magnificent banquet to be prepared for his [Note: [Col. 0313] Manuscript 2 reads thus, with the contraction mark for *-er* erroneously placed above the *u*, as though *servis*, “servants,” were to be read.] princes, clerics, and laymen. For on that day, clothed in all royal ornaments, he came to the church of Saint Francis and received the royal crown placed upon his head by the hands of the bishops—those of Prague and Olomouc. Thus, clothed in a royal mantle and carrying orb and sceptre in his hands, he entered the church to hear the solemn rites of Mass; and he heard most devoutly the Mass celebrated by the bishop of Olomouc, who procured many candles for his office through the king’s favour or patronage.

When these rites were completed, they came to the banquet, which had been prepared with royal magnificence. The aforesaid bishops and prelates of other churches attended it. The nobles of Bohemia, adorned with diverse displays of splendour according to the offices of their benefices, served at it fittingly. [Col. 0313C] The king also sent for his son and the barons adhering to him, that they should come with all speed into his presence and confer with him concerning the restoration of peace and a better condition of the land.

At last the son came to his father, submitted himself to his father in every respect, and pleaded for all the nobles who had offended him. In response to the humility of his entreaties, the king received his son and the nobles into the fullness of his favour and that same day gave all of them kisses of peace with tears. Meanwhile the son, at the urging of his men—or rather, as I should say, through necessity—surrendered Prague Castle and the other castles into his father’s hands. Wholly submitting [Col. 0314A] to his father, he commended himself with all his followers to his father’s favour, saying that he would most willingly be content with whatever his father’s generosity wished him to be content with.

After much deliberation on this matter, the king granted his son the margraviate of Moravia with all its appurtenances, retaining for himself only half the coinage of Jihlava; and thus he allowed him freely to depart. Afterwards the king, having formed salutary counsel with his faithful men, entered Prague Castle on foot on the Friday around twilight, which then fell on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September. First, however, he expelled all those who had been guards of that castle. At the castle gate he was received by the prelates and clergy of the church in procession, and was honourably led to the church with hymns and praises, [Col. 0314B] while the great bells of the principal church rang and the people and nobles of the land then present resounded, “Hospodin promiluy ny”—“Lord, have mercy upon us.”

While the king was then staying within the castle, a charter granting every liberty which they had sought was conceded to the lord bishop and canons of the principal church; it was written, confirmed by royal seals, and given in duplicate into the bishop’s hands. The king remained in the castle for three days; when he had arranged matters according to the pleasure of his will, on the fourth day—which then fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of September—he left the castle early in the morning and set out for his castles, in which he had formerly been accustomed to reside.

After four weeks had passed, while the king was staying in a castle called Týřov [Note: [Col. 0313C] Situated in the district of Pilsen, fifteen miles from Prague; Pubitschka IV, 2, p. 238.], his son came to him with certain [Col. 0314C] nobles to seek a fuller favour for himself and his faithful men, which the king had promised through several envoys to the son and nobles if he would come into his presence in the aforesaid castle. Then the king, having found an opportunity which he had long conceived in his mind, detained his son and certain nobles in that castle. Wholly forgetful of his promise, he sent his son to be guarded in a very strong fortress [Note: [Col. 0313C] Frauenberg.]. He sent the nobles of the land back to Prague Castle, commanding most strictly that they be thrown into separate prisons, two by two, in chains.

# II. First Part of the Prague Annals

[Col. 0313C]

1196. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, Bishop Henry died [Note: [Col. 0313] The same hand has written “Břetislav” above here.], [Note: [Col. 0313C] He died in 1197, according to Gerlach and a bull of confirmation issued by Pope Celestine III to the monastery of Teplá on 7 August 1197. There one reads: “Henry, bishop of Prague, of blessed memory, while he administered the care of the duchy of Bohemia.” The Vienna editor of the continuation mentions this bull, p. 62. The Doksany calendar gives 14 June as Henry’s final day; Balbín, *Epitome historiae Bohemicae*, p. 247.] who had been duke of Bohemia.

[Col. 0314C] 1197. Duke Spytihněv defeated Duke Přemysl. In the same year he was blinded. This Přemysl was crowned by Emperor Philip.

[Col. 0315A] 1199. King [Note: [Col. 0315] In the margin of manuscript 2, in a somewhat later hand: “duke.”] Přemysl was elevated to kingship [Note: [Col. 0315C] At Mainz, at the same time when King Philip was crowned; see Gerlach’s final words.]; having dismissed his wife [Note: [Col. 0315C] Adela, daughter of Otto, margrave of Meissen. Concerning this divorce Pope Innocent III wrote to the archbishop of Magdeburg on 1 October 1199; Boczek II, 353.], he married Constance, sister of the king of Hungary. [Note: [Col. 0315C] Andrew.]

[Col. 0316A] 1198. Duke and Bishop Břetislav departed from this world. [Note: [Col. 0315C] The Vienna editor, p. 61, produced evidence from charters concerning this double name of Henry.]

1199. Frederick, the fourteenth bishop, died. Daniel II was chosen bishop. Vladislaus [Note: [Col. 0315] “Wadislaus,” manuscript 2.] yielded the duchy to his brother Přemysl, who thereupon took up the duchy. [Note: [Col. 0315C] Rather, these events occurred in 1197.]

[Col. 0315A] 1200.

1201. There was an earthquake everywhere.

1202.

1203. Conrad, duke of Moravia, besieged Prague. [Note: [Col. 0315] The words “Conrad ... besieged” have been struck through with a light stroke of the pen in manuscript 2.] King Přemysl, rebelling against King Philip, did homage to Emperor Otto. [Note: [Col. 0315C] See Innocent III’s letters dated 11 December 1203, Boczek III, 19, and Otto IV’s letter to the Roman pontiff, ibid.; in the same year, 1204, the pope confirmed the royal title of the Bohemians. See Palacký II, 67.]

1204. Saint Procopius was canonized. In the same year the Bohemians began war with the Moravians.

1205. King Přemysl returned to Philip’s favour and gave hostages for 7,000 marks.

1206. Duke Leszek [Note: [Col. 0315C] That is, Leszek, duke of Cracow and Sandomierz.] and his brother Conrad [Note: [Col. 0315C] Duke of Masovia.] killed Roman, king of the Prussians. [Note: [Col. 0315C] This is erroneous: “of the Ruthenians” must be read. Roman was duke of Vladimir and Halych; those brothers routed him in 1205 near Zawichost, not far from Sandomierz. Roepell discusses this more fully, I, 407.] Philip captured the bishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0316C] Bruno, concerning whom Arnold of Lübeck, VII, 5.] and drove out Otto.

1207. The sun suffered an eclipse. In the same year Kunigunde, daughter of King Philip, was given in marriage to Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0316C] Who had been born in 1205.], son of King Přemysl.

1208. Emperor Philip was killed by Otto, Count Palatine.

1209. Otto was made emperor at Rome.

1210. Duke Conrad died in Apulia. Otto was excommunicated.

[Col. 0316B] 1211. King Přemysl rebelled against the emperor, and Černín was expelled from Bohemia.

[Col. 0315B] 1212. The relics of the Apostles Thomas, James, and Thaddaeus, and of Saint Maurice, were brought from Germany to Prague. Černín, [Note: [Col. 0316C] Černín appears to have supported the party of Vladislaus, Otakar’s elder son, whom Otto IV had made king of Bohemia at Nuremberg in 1212; Palacký II, 73.] chamberlain of the king of Bohemia, was driven from the province by the king and all the chief men. Frederick, king of Sicily, came into Germany.

1213. The queen of Hungary was killed. [Note: [Col. 0316C] Gertrude, by Benedict, ban of Croatia.]

1214. Daniel II, bishop of the church of Prague, died; Andrew succeeded him.

1215. Andrew was ordained bishop of Prague at Rome on the feast of Saint Cecilia, 22 November. A council was held at Rome.

1216. The brethren of Saint Adalbert were brought to Prague. In the same year, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, Bishop Andrew placed Bohemia under interdict, excluding it from divine offices and burial [Note: [Col. 0316C] Because liberty of the Church had been denied and lay investiture practised.], then withdrew to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0316C] He entered it in March 1217; compare the Prague Annals.]

1217. On the fourth day before the Kalends of June, the archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0316C] Siegfried.] relaxed the interdict on Bohemia. [Note: [Col. 0316C] Compare letters of Honorius III written on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August 1214, Boczek II, 93, and subsequent letters issued in 1218 and 1219.] In the same year a multitude of Christians set out overseas.

1218. Bishop Lawrence of Wrocław, together with Duke Theobald [Note: [Col. 0316C] The third; see Voigt, *Geschichte von Preussen*, I, 445.] of Bohemia, departed for Prussia.

1219. The winter was warm and rainy. In the same year Bishop Andrew of Prague for a second time placed Bohemia under interdict.

[Col. 0317] 1220. The Poles were killed by the Prussians, slain by the rage of the sword of the Ruthenians, and miserably perished, massacred by gold-miners.

1221. Cardinal Gregory [Note: [Col. 0317] Gregory of Crescentio, ordained deacon of Saint Theodore, who was sent as legate to the northern lands. See letters of Honorius III issued in 1220 and 1221; Boczek II, 119.], honourably received by King Přemysl and all the clergy, opened the churches and relaxed the interdict. Pope Honorius [Note: [Col. 0317] The Third.] confirmed the Order of Preachers.

1222. Duke Vladislaus of Moravia, brother of King Přemysl, died. [Note: [Col. 0317] In an ordinance issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of September 1222, the king remembers his brother Vladislaus of pious memory; Boczek II, 142.] In the same year a star of unusual brightness appeared in the western sky.

1223.

1224. Bishop Andrew of Prague died in exile while at Rome. In the same year Peregrinus was elected bishop of Prague.

1225. Cardinal Conrad [Note: [Col. 0317] Bishop of Porto and cardinal of Saint Rufina, who stayed at Prague in May; ibid., II, 165.] entered Bohemia. Vladislaus, margrave of Moravia [Note: [Col. 0317] Son of King Otakar, successor of the Vladislaus mentioned above.], brother of King Wenceslaus, died.

1226. The Preachers received a house in the city of Prague.

1227. On the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 0317] “Twenty-third” had been written, but was corrected by a contemporary hand to “fourteenth.”] day before the Kalends of January, Bishop John [Note: [Col. 0317] The Second.] was consecrated. [Note: [Col. 0317] Peregrinus, whom Bishop Andrew had excommunicated, had resigned his office by order of Honorius III in 1225.] On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, the altar of Saint Catherine the Virgin was consecrated.

1228. King Wenceslaus was consecrated with his wife Queen Kunigunde in the Prague church by the venerable Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, on the Sunday on which is sung *Esto mihi* (“Be unto me”). On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, the chapel of Saint Thomas was consecrated. [Note: [Col. 0317] Concerning the coronation, Kings Otakar and Wenceslaus ordered a charter to be written in 1228; see Boczek II, 186.]

1229. The apostolic legate called Simon sought a tenth of all revenues from the Church. The same Simon suspended all conventual churches from divine office.

1230. Duke Přemysl died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

1231.

1232. The Friars Minor received a house at Prague. Saint Elizabeth was canonized.

1233. Agnes, daughter of King Přemysl, assumed the habit of the Poor Ladies.

1234. The cloister of the church of Prague was repaired in stone and vaulted.

1235. Vitus was made a canon of the church of Prague on 2 Kalends of January [31 December].

1236. John, the twenty-first bishop of Prague, died on 16 Kalends of September [17 August]; Bernard succeeded him.

1237.

1238.

1239. Bernard, bishop of Prague, died [Note: [Col. 0318] in the year 1240. Cf. Palacký, *Italienische Reise*, p. 28.], and Nicholas succeeded him.

1240. Great fear of the Tartars fell upon the Bohemians. In the same year Bishop Nicholas returned after being consecrated at Rome, and was received in his see on 5 Kalends of August [28 July; Note: [Col. 0318] this occurred in 1241.]. Queen Constance died on the Ides of December [13 December; Note: [Col. 0318] A numeral seems to have dropped out; for Constance’s testament was written on the Nones of December [5 December] 1240, and on the seventh day before the Ides of December Wenceslas the king says that his mother had entered upon the way of all flesh. Cf. Boczek II, 380, 381.].

1241. The pagans called Tartars destroyed many Christian kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0318] On the devastation wrought by the Tartars, cf. the letters of King Wenceslas and Pope Gregory IX in Boczek III, 8–29, and Palacký’s essay, “Ueber den Mongoleneinfall von 1241,” in *Abhandlungen der königl. Böhm. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften*, V, 2, p. 371.]; and Vitus, the dean, was elected in the church of Prague on 10 Kalends of October [22 September]. They shot Coloman, brother of the king of Hungary, devastated all Hungary, and killed Duke Henry [Note: [Col. 0318] of Wrocław.] of Poland, with his army, in battle in Poland itself [Note: [Col. 0318] not far from Legnica, on the fields of Wahlstatt.]. On 3 Nones of October [5 October] an eclipse of the sun occurred after noon, so that people thought it was twilight.

1242. Frederick, duke of Austria, ravaged Moravia; but he departed from it in confusion and with great loss, when Wenceslas, king of Bohemia, entered Moravia in order to test the fortune of war [Note: [Col. 0318] Cf. the *Chronicon Garstense* for this year, in Rauch, *SS. rerum Austriae*, I, 32.].

[Col. 0319] 1243. The Sultan of Babylon, with a very great multitude of pagans called Corozini, entered the Holy Land and wholly destroyed the holy city of Jerusalem and the Temple together with the holy sepulchre of the Lord; indiscriminately he killed men, women, and children. The long walk of the cloister towards the north was painted.

1244. He consecrated the church of St James of the Friars Minor. In the same year the Prague cloister was painted.

1245. The altar of St Wenceslas was reconsecrated, and the altar of the holy Evangelists was consecrated on 2 Nones of October [6 October]. Pope Innocent held a council at Lyons, in which, by a definitive sentence, he deposed Emperor Frederick, excluding him from the communion of the faithful because of heresy proved against him. In his place Henry, landgrave of Thuringia, was elected king of Germany [Note: [Col. 0319] This occurred at Hochheim on 22 May 1246. Cf. Böhmer, *Regesta imperii*, 1246–1313, p. 1.]. At the same council Conrad was deposed, having been intruded into the bishopric of Olomouc by secular power [Note: [Col. 0319] Conrad, canon of Hildesheim and brother of Emperor Frederick, against whom they had set up Master William; on him see the letters of Gregory IX, dated Ides of April 1241, in Boczek III, 1, and of Innocent IV, 1243, ibid., p. 29.]; Lord Bruno was substituted for him [Note: [Col. 0319] formerly provost of Lübeck, descended from the house of the counts of Holstein; he was elected when William had voluntarily resigned his office. Letter of Innocent IV, dated 20 September 1245, *loc. cit.* and following.].

1246. Frederick, duke of Austria, was killed by the Hungarians in battle [Note: [Col. 0319] in the battle fought on the Leitha on 15 June 1246.]; and the daughter [Note: [Col. 0319] Gertrude; cf. Pernoldus under 1246.] of his elder brother, the late Henry, duke of Austria, married Wladislaus, son of the king of Bohemia. By this marriage Wladislaus possessed the duchy of Austria. When Duke Mieszko of Poland also died at that time without children [Note: [Col. 0320] He was duke of Opole.], the leading men of that duchy accepted the said Wladislaus as their duke, wholly subjecting themselves and their possessions to his jurisdiction.

1247. Wladislaus, son of King Wenceslas, died; he had succeeded Frederick in the duchy of Austria.

1248. King Wenceslas was driven from his throne. Queen Cunigunde died on the Ides of September [13 September]. The *studium* at Prague perished [Note: [Col. 0320] Balbín, Pubitschka, and Palacký sought in vain to determine the meaning of these words.]. Many houses in the city of Prague and very many villages throughout the kingdom of Bohemia were burned. The custodians withdrew from the church of Prague. The king of France crossed the sea with his army on the Friday before Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0320] Louis IX left Paris in June, when Pentecost was celebrated; on 25 August 1248 he put out to sea.]. The Bohemians and Moravians, defeated at Ponte [Note: [Col. 0320] That is, at the castle of Brüx; those who had raised a revolt against King Wenceslas were put to flight there. Cf. Pulkava for this year.], fled.

1249. On 11 Kalends of April [22 March], Bishop Nicholas suspended the churches established in his diocese from the ringing of bells and from every solemn church ornament; only the ringing of two very small bells and Lenten ornament for the feast and office were permitted, even should a feast of however great a rank occur [Note: [Col. 0320] For at first the bishop favoured the party of the king’s enemies.]. In the same year the church at Vyšehrad was burned.

1250. On 6 Nones of July [2 July], after noon, a great hailstorm fell. It inflicted much damage upon autumn and spring crops, vineyards, fruit-trees, and other things; it made great slaughter among cattle, birds of diverse kinds, and even killed many wild animals. In most places in the kingdom of Bohemia, and especially around Prague, many people and beasts of burden were drowned, and very many buildings and granaries were demolished by the tempest. This hail remained unmelted for seven days; it was of marvellous size and triangular, and some of it was mixed with moss. An excessive flood caused by rain followed it.

In the same year King Wenceslas levied a tax throughout his entire kingdom, taking it from every ploughland.

In the same year, on 16 Kalends of January [17 December], at the third hour, while the knight Pertold was crossing the bridge and had come to the tower at its end, two ravens dislodged a stone from the summit of the prison-tower. It fell upon Pertold’s head; struck by it, he fell from his horse and immediately expired. In the same year, on 16 Kalends of December [16 November], Vitus, dean of Prague, having received King Wenceslas’s command, came to him at Tyrov Castle; on the following day, by the king’s command, he girded with the sword Ursus, the king’s reeve at Veliš, in the church of St John the Baptist, before certain nobles of Bohemia. In the same year Cztibor, the judge, was beheaded by the sword on 4 Kalends of January [29 December] on Mount Petřín, and his son Jaros was broken on the wheel outside the walls of the city [Note: [Col. 0320] On these matters see Palacký II, 436.].

1251. On 18 Kalends of February [15 January], relics sent by the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0320] Innocent IV.] to Agnes, sister of King Wenceslas, and brought by other Friars Minor, were received with the gathering of nearly the entire people and with the procession of all the clergy of the city outside its walls towards Vyšehrad; they were carried into the church of St Francis.

In the same year Wenceslas, king of Bohemia, set out on an expedition towards Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0320] This occurred because the dukes of Bavaria were endeavouring to recover Austria.] with a great army of Bohemians and Moravians. As they passed through Bohemia they committed many evils—plunder, burnings, and innumerable other injuries—while unhappy people wept in many villages. Meanwhile, as the king returned with his men [Col. 0321] to his camp, his son entered Bavaria with the whole army and ravaged, burned, and afflicted a great part of it with various evils. At last, when a truce had been arranged at the plea of the duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0321] Otto.] until the Kalends of May [1 May], he returned home. The returning Bohemians brought much livestock from Bavaria with them, especially the men of Plzeň. At the Purification of St Mary [2 February], while the bishop was preaching, a great force of winds arose and the air grew dark, so that men’s faces could scarcely be distinguished. Afterwards great snow fell in most parts of Bohemia, such as our age does not remember. On 5 Ides of March [11 March], Bishop Nicholas conferred orders at Týn [Note: [Col. 0321] Týnec Horsšovský in the district of Plzeň.], in the church of St Christopher, and there ordained the bishop-elect of Passau [Note: [Col. 0321] Berthold.] deacon.

In the same year Gallus was made sacristan. On the Kalends of April [1 April], Bishop Nicholas conferred orders in the church of St Francis, where he ordained the archbishop-elect of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0321] Philip, son of Bernard, duke of Carinthia, and nephew of King Wenceslas.] deacon and the bishop-elect of Passau priest. On 5 Ides of April [9 April; Note: [Col. 0321] This is the correct reading, not “Ides of April,” as the manuscript has it, since Palm Sunday fell on 9 April.], Palm Sunday, Berthold, bishop-elect of Passau, was promoted to the episcopate in the church of Prague, five bishops being present and blessing him, together with the sixth, the archbishop-elect of Salzburg. On that day an indulgence of seven years and 280 days was granted: each bishop and the elect granted one year and forty days. On 8 Ides of August [6 August], at first twilight, there arose a great force of winds, lightning, and thunder. Likewise, on 49 Kalends of September [15 July], similar and terrible phenomena arose. Again, on 15 Kalends of the same month [18 August], at midnight, similar phenomena arose; by their violent force many buildings fell, granaries were utterly overthrown, many people were struck by lightning, crops were beaten by hail, fruit was knocked from the trees, and vineyards were damaged throughout the entire diocese of Prague. Grain yielded badly, especially winter grain. In the same year the pope demanded one thousand marks of silver from the clergy of Bohemia. Likewise in the same year, near the feast of St Wenceslas [29 September], money in gold to the value of one thousand marks of silver, reckoned by the Polish weight [Note: [Col. 0321] On the Polish weight, which was of lower value than the Bohemian, see Pubitschka IV, 2, p. 247.], was collected from all the clergy of the kingdom of Bohemia, taken to Poland, and assigned to Lord Thomas, bishop of Wrocław.

Also in the same year, foals were born which, to those who saw them, displayed signs as though they were three years old. There was also excessive drought, so that people could not sow in August, September, or the middle of October. In this year likewise grain, wine, and tree-fruits yielded badly. A certain priest from Bernartice, named Martin, was seized and miserably shut up, stripped, in the public prison at the foot of the bridge; on 13 Kalends of December [19 November] he was released from prison. On the day before the Kalends of December [30 November], the abbot of Milevsk [Note: [Col. 0321] Mühlhausen.], the provost, prior, subprior, ecclesiastic, parish priest of Červen, the estate-masters of that monastery, and all their churches were excommunicated and publicly denounced in the church of Prague, and their churches placed under interdict because of Martin’s complaint.

In the same year, on 11 Kalends of December [21 November], Austria submitted to Wenceslas, king of the Bohemians. His son Přemysl was sent to take possession of it; he entered the city of Vienna and other cities, towns, and castles [Note: [Col. 0321] Otakar himself, in a charter written on 29 April 1253, thus testifies: “After the death of the noble princes of Austria and Styria, since those principalities were so grievously distressed by excessively insolent disorder that justice and equity had already gone into exile beyond those provinces [Col. 0322], we, moved by the clemency of innate piety to meet so great a danger, and prudently invited by the nobles, counts, and barons of those duchies, etc.” Cf. Hormayr, *Archiv*, 1828, no. 61. Yet already on 16 November Otakar calls himself duke of Austria; Boczek III, 144.].

In the same year Bartholomew, canon of Prague, was deprived of his prebend by the chapter of Prague, Bishop Nicholas consenting and confirming the chapter’s sentence. Bartholomew himself had pronounced and recorded this sentence against himself in the preceding year because of various offences and his continual absence from choir. The winter was mild, neither too harsh nor too gentle.

1252. Přemysl, son of King Wenceslas, celebrated his wedding at Hainburg [Note: [Col. 0322] Haimburg.] on 3 Ides of February [11 February; Note: [Col. 0322] According to Pernoldus, the marriage was celebrated on 8 April 1252.], marrying Lady Margaret, widow [Note: [Col. 0322] of King Henry VII, son of Emperor Frederick II; she was the sister by birth of Frederick, the last duke of Austria, forty-five years old when she married the young Otakar. On Margaret see Lambacher, *Oesterreichisches Interregnum*, pp. v, 45.] and daughter of the long-dead Leopold, duke of Austria.

In the same year, in Lent, which fell on 13 Kalends of March [17 February], Brother Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of St Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0322] He was already staying at Prague late in 1251, as his letters in Boczek III, 154 prove.], received procurations, in the name of his legation, from the clergy of Bohemia, both religious and secular, although he was stationed in Germany.

In the same year, during spring and before the beginning of summer, the choir of the church of Prague was raised, the chapel of St Michael was enlarged, and the palace was built on its western side. In the same year, on 14 Kalends of June [19 May], [Col. 0323] the feast of Pentecost fell; then, on the vigil of Pentecost and on the holy day itself, severe cold set in and snow fell in most places. Through its severity many horses, sheep, and cattle died. In the same year the chapel of St Michael in the church of Prague was dedicated on 12 Kalends of June [21 May] by the venerable father, Lord Nicholas, bishop of Prague. There was a great shortage of fodder or straw. Almost the whole spring was dry, though its end was rather wet; there was a severe famine at the end of spring and the beginning of summer.

At the same time a multitude of Cumans [Note: [Col. 0323] The Cumans, a Turkish people, are called *Polowci* by the Slavs and *Falones* and *Valvae* by the Germans, as in Otto of Freising VI, 10, and Arnold of Lübeck VI, 5. Because of their extreme cruelty they inspired the greatest terror among western peoples. Cf. Zeuss, *Die Deutschen und die Nachbarstämme*, p. 743. They were sent out from Hungary by King Béla IV, who was assisting his son-in-law Henry, duke of Bavaria, against Otakar in occupying Austria, while himself claiming the province of Styria.] broke out from the borders of Hungary and killed many thousands of Christians in Moravia, sparing absolutely neither sex nor age. Many clerics perished among them.

On the Ides of June [13 June], blood flowed from the foot of the crucifix in the church of St George at Prague, while Pomien, judge of the king of the Bohemians, was worshipping and wiping the blood from the foot of the crucifix with his hand.

In the same year winter crops yielded moderately in most regions, while summer crops almost entirely failed, except millet.

In the same year, on 12 Kalends of June [21 May], the hospital at the foot of the bridge, on the bank of the Vltava, was founded by the Knights of the Cross with the Red Star in honour of the Holy Spirit. This year the winter was harsh, and the ice was two ells thick. In the same year the towers of Prague Castle and those at the foot of the bridge were fortified.

1253. Near the feast of the Annunciation [25 March], several bishops gathered before the king of Bohemia at the old castle. Among them were the archbishop-elect of Salzburg, the bishop of Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0324] Henry.], of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0324] Albert.], of Meissen, of Passau, of Olomouc, and other bishops. King Wenceslas received them all kindly and entertained them honourably for several days at great expense. Why they came, or what they did with the king, remains unknown.

The legate of the Apostolic See, Brother Hugh, also, through Brother Gerhard of the Order of Preachers, demanded for the second time and received fifty marks from the clergy of the diocese of Prague. On the fourth day before the Ides of June [10 June], the Paschal candle in the church of Prague fell about midnight and was shattered into many pieces; its top remained hanging in the portico.

In the same year the city of Prague was walled on the north and west; the episcopal court situated at the foot of the bridge was alienated from Nicholas, bishop of Prague, and fortified with a ditch and defensive works. The church of St Mary of the Cross-bearers was likewise fortified with a ditch, wall, and defensive works. Great fear of the Cumans and other foreigners also came upon the Bohemians. Foreseeing their attack, King Wenceslas collected provisions in grain, wine, honey, hams, salt, and cheeses from all religious persons of the diocese of Prague, from his reeves, and from certain towns, assigning to each a fixed quantity to be rendered by number and measure. He stored these things in the church of St George in Prague Castle; the religious women of that church were compelled to leave their cloister and dwell in the city. This occurred on 16 Kalends of July [16 June]. The Cumans, breaking out from Hungary—or other brigands with them—on 7 Kalends of July [25 June] killed many thousands of Christians in Moravia around Olomouc, and countless persons were drowned while fleeing before them. At the same time the king of Hungary arrived with an innumerable multitude of his own men and of other nations, inflicted great damage upon Moravia, killed some by the sword, took others captive and sent them into exile, spared neither sex nor age, and devastated almost all Moravia by plunder and fire [Note: [Col. 0324] On this devastation see the letters of Otakar and Bishop Bruno of 1255 in Boczek III, 197, 200.]. They devastated and burned most of the fortified places which they could take; they seized and carried away church bells and relics from broken altars; having reduced churches to ashes, they profaned the sacraments of the Church, and crucified many people in contempt of the Crucified One. Meanwhile the legate of the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0324] And his penitentiary Walascus.] arrived before the king of Hungary, restrained him, and compelled him to return home.

In the same year King Wenceslas died [Note: [Col. 0324] At Pocápl Castle.] on 10 Kalends of October [22 September], in the twenty-fourth year and eighth month of his reign. His only son Přemysl, returning from Austria, was honourably received in the seat of his kingdom by the prelates of the churches and the clergy on 16 Kalends of November [17 October].

In the same year the sanctuary of the greater church was painted, through the agency of Bishop Nicholas, on 3 Kalends of April [30 March]. In the same year relics of St Stanislaus the martyr were brought from Cracow on 11 Kalends of November [22 October] and received in the church of Prague with a solemn procession.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1254, on 8 Kalends of February [25 January], the nobleman Borso was arrested and imprisoned in chains at Prague [Note: [Col. 0324] According to Pubitschka’s conjecture, IV, 2, p. 268, this was Borso of Opek, otherwise of Riesenburg, who during the civil war had stoutly defended Brüx Castle against Otakar and his friends. Cf. Pulkava under 1248.]. In the same year, on 6 Ides of July [10 July], Přemysl, son of King Wenceslas, restored to the church of Prague the chapel [Col. 0325] of St Bartholomew, which his father, while still living, had granted to that church in return for certain possessions taken away.

Likewise in the same year, on 12 Kalends of July [20 June], Bernard of Naples, elect and legate of the Apostolic See, came to Prague [Note: [Col. 0325B] For the letters given to him by the pope concerning the establishment of peace between the kings of Bohemia and Hungary, see Boczek III, 183.] and was received in the church of Prague with a solemn procession. He stayed with his entire household on Mount Sion until 12 Kalends of September [21 August]. During this period he exacted and received from the clergy of the diocese of Prague two hundred marks of pure silver for his procurations; of this sum the Prague chapter paid eighteen marks. It paid three marks to another messenger of Cardinal Peter Capucci. The aforesaid Legate Bernard held stations in many churches and granted generous indulgences. In some churches, when he celebrated, he gave an indulgence of one year and forty days; in other churches, on each day until the octave, one year and forty days and a fourth part of venial sins.

In the same year the Prague canons Herman, provost of Litoměřice, died on 5 Nones of March [3 March]; John on 3 Nones of July [5 July]; and George on 12 Kalends of September [21 August]. In this year, too, autumn grain and tree-fruits yielded badly, and wine failed entirely. Our age does not remember an earlier failure of such magnitude. In this year also, on the Kalends of May [1 May], peace was restored between the king of Hungary and the prince of Bohemia, son of King Wenceslas [Note: [Col. 0325B] At Buda, on the Friday before Palm Sunday 1254, peace was made by the kings’ envoys; its terms were recorded in a document, see Boczek III, 181. Styria, over which war had chiefly broken out, was divided between the Bohemians and Hungarians. Cf. also John of Victring I, 4.]. The aforesaid prince, however, returning from Austria brought with him a certain chest, which the clerics of his court called Noah’s Ark, and in which offerings of various gifts were stored. In the same year Master Dionysius died on 4 Nones of October [4 October] at Friuli.

In the year of the Lord 1255. The prince of Bohemia and the margrave of Brandenburg entered Prussia, ravaged it by plunder, fire, and robbery, and killed very many people by manifold deaths, sparing neither sex nor age. Nearly all the spring of this year was cold, windy, and wet.

As time passed, Queen Margaret, wife of Přemysl, son of King Wenceslas, left Austria and entered Bohemia. On 5 Ides of July [11 July] she was received before the walls of Prague by all the clergy and people of that city, with processions, great rejoicing, and diverse musical instruments. On the following day she was received at the gate of Prague Castle by the bishop and canons of Prague with a solemn procession. Present at this procession were Martin, abbot of Břevnov, and John, abbot of Mount Sion, with his entire convent, dressed in solemn copes. In the same year new organs were made in the church of Prague, costing twenty-six marks of silver, but they were completed in Lent of the following year. On 3 Kalends of January [30 December], the sun underwent an eclipse.

[Col. 0325A] [Note: [Col. 0325] In Migne, the textual sections “In the year of the Lord 1256, in the first watch … all the bells were rung” and “In the year of the Lord 1256, Lord Conrad … Mount Sion” are printed in parallel.]

In the year of the Lord 1256. In the first watch of the night, on 5 Kalends of February [28 January], a great light arose in various parts of Bohemia; lightning flashed and thunder was heard. The winter was harsher than usual, though intermittent. A great force of winds arose, but severe cold set in on 7 Kalends of November [26 October] of the preceding year.

In the same year, on 3 Ides of May [13 May], Peter of Ponte Curvo [Note: [Col. 0326B] On him see the letters of Urban IV dated 3 May 1262, Boczek III, 336, and others written in the following year, ibid., 360. This Peter was archdeacon of Gradec.], messenger of the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0326B] Alexander IV.], came to Prague and exacted a procuration from the clergy of the whole diocese of Prague [Note: [Col. 0326B] “Diocese” must be supplied.]; the Prague chapter paid three and a half marks of this sum. On 5 Ides of June [9 June], the same messenger placed the city of Prague under interdict, with the consent of the bishop of Prague and the other prelates, because a certain monk of Porta Apostolorum had been detained, robbed, and shamefully [Col. 0325B] dishonoured by citizens at Prague. He added to his commands that the divine office should be performed in a low voice, with those under interdict and excommunicated persons excluded; he also commanded that, at the evening hour each day, all the bells should be rung three times—

[Col. 0326A] In the year of the Lord 1256, Lord Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, received confraternity in the church of Mount Sion, namely on the feast-day of Blessed Mary Magdalene [22 July], together with other noblemen: Lord Provost Henry of Sefflica, Philip count of Falkenstein, Henry count of Wirrenburg, Werner count of Bolant, the noble Dietrich of Milendunk, Godfrey, the archbishop’s notary, and other nobles. In that same year, on the feast of St Lawrence [10 August], the aforesaid Archbishop Conrad granted this indulgence to the aforementioned monastery of Strahov: on the day of the church’s dedication, on every solemnity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on the feast-days of St Augustine the bishop and Blessed Mary Magdalene, and within the octaves of those solemnities, one year and forty days; and this was done with the permission [Col. 0326B] of Lord Nicholas, bishop of Prague, and the indulgence shall endure for ever. In the same year one entire body of the eleven thousand holy virgins was brought from Cologne and placed in the church of Mount Sion [Note: [Col. 0325] “Lord Conrad … Sion” is not found at this point in manuscript 2, but before the beginning of Cosmas’s first continuator.].

[Col. 0327]—in every church, with the extinguishing of candles, against all those detaining or despoiling clerics. This interdict endured until 9 Kalends of July [23 June]; it was relaxed on the same day because of the oath and promised satisfaction of the citizens of Prague.

In the same year, on 16 Kalends of August [17 July], Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, came to Prague and lodged for several days on Mount Sion. He was honourably received by the prince of the land and provided for at his expense, and, as we believe, came to discuss the Empire with the prince of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0327B] For King William had been killed by the Frisians on 28 January 1256. Cf. Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 36. John of Victring I, 5, relates that Otakar, elected by the princes, replied: “He was content with the glory divinely given him.” See also Pelzel’s dissertation on this matter in Born, *Abhandlungen einer Privatgesellschaft in Böhmen*, II, 74.]. At length, having been richly rewarded by that prince with many and varied gifts, he returned home on 4 Ides of August [10 August]. Yet this archbishop did not wish to be received in the church of Prague with a solemn procession, but came humbly in secular dress to pay reverence to the holy martyrs.

In the same year there was abundance of grain in most areas, but a lack of wine and apples. In Lent of the same year Pope Alexander confirmed a certain new religious order called that of the Blessed Martyrs [Note: [Col. 0327B] This is the Order of the Brethren of the Cross, the Blessed Martyrs of Penance, to whom Pope Alexander III had given a rule of life in 1179.]; its brethren appeared at Prague before the feast of St Wenceslas [29 September].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1257. Přemysl, lord of the kingdom of the Bohemians and son of King Wenceslas, in the third [Note: [Col. 0327B] Fourth.] year of his dukedom, at the beginning of spring expelled the Bohemians from the suburb and settled foreigners there.

In the same year, Lord Eberhard, on the Kalends of April [1 April], bought a certain property in the village called Bělok and granted it to the altar of the Blessed Virgin; he assigned to the same altar another property previously bought in the village of Draškovo. In the same year, in the middle of spring, Lord Nicholas, bishop of Prague, renewed the ceiling, commonly called the “heaven,” after the old one had been demolished.

In the same year, with the beginning of the Kalends of August [1 August], there was an exceedingly great flood, which inflicted grave and extensive damage throughout the diocese of Prague upon gardens, sown fields, and buildings situated near riverbanks; it also drowned many people.

In the same year the prince of Bohemia, taking with him certain Bohemians, Moravians, and Austrians, set out towards Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0328B] This was done to assist his cousin Philip, archbishop of Salzburg—against Duke Henry of Bavaria—after they had elected Ulrich, bishop of Seckau, in Philip’s place.]. There he ravaged, plundered, and burned many villages and churches; but at last he returned home with great disgrace and loss of his nobles, knights, and possessions. Some of his men were killed, some drowned [Note: [Col. 0328B] As they were crossing the Inn, the bridge broke; Hermann of Altaich describes this disaster of Otakar’s precisely in Böhmer, *Fontes*, II. Otakar suffered this defeat at Mühldorf on 25 August.], and some, having lost everything and their horses, returned home on foot in great poverty. The winter was very harsh that year.

[Col. 0327A] [Note: [Col. 0327] In Migne, the textual sections “In the year of grace 1258, Bishop Nicholas … 18 Kalends of September” and “In the year of the Lord 1258, 14 Kalends of November … 17 Kalends of September” are printed in parallel.]

In the year of grace 1258. Bishop Nicholas died on 16 Kalends of February [17 January]. In the same year, on the Kalends of February [1 February], John [Note: [Col. 0328B] The third.] was elected bishop of Prague; in the same year he was confirmed in the church of Prague by Lord Bruno of Olomouc, acting by the authority of Mainz, on 6 Ides of March [10 March]. This year the winter, the beginning of spring, and mid-spring were very severe and cold; the ice on the Vltava was excessively thick and endured until Easter, which then fell on 9 Kalends of April [24 March]. John was consecrated bishop at Vienna in Austria on 4 Ides of May [12 May], since Pentecost then fell on Sunday. He was received in his see at Prague on 7 Kalends of June [26 May], and installed in his cathedra with great rejoicing of clergy and people; on that same day he celebrated his first Mass of the glorious Virgin. This [Col. 0327B] year frost damaged tree-fruits and vineyards, and there was a mortality among sheep. There was an eclipse of the moon on 14 Kalends of June [19 May], and the feast of the Holy Trinity was then celebrated on Sunday. The same John reconsecrated the altar of St Andrew the Apostle and St Stephen the Protomartyr on 2 Kalends of July [30 June]; afterwards he built and consecrated another altar in honour of St Nicholas the Confessor and Blessed Ludmila the Martyr on 18 Kalends of September [15 August].

[Col. 0328A] In the year of the Lord 1258, on 14 Kalends of November [19 October], in the first watch of the night, called the *intempesta*, the church of the cloister of Mount Sion, also called Strahov, caught fire from a candle which a certain brother accustomed to sleep there had carelessly placed by his bed at night. By the Lord’s permission—whose providence had foreseen that it would be adorned in a fairer form—it was devastated by the violence of fire, together with all the buildings continuously adjoining it round the circuit of the cloister. The venerable Lord John, then abbot of that place, by his prudent industry—though effective in other respects, yet conspicuous as more effective in this—unexpectedly restored within five years these ruins, which because of their magnitude had seemed scarcely capable of repair even in a long course of years, to their former state, indeed to one far more beautiful. Finally, besides the other things which he restored more excellently, he completed, on 15 Kalends of October [17 September] in the fifth year after the fire, the church, rebuilt almost from its foundations and vaulted, adding at its side a new chapel of Blessed Ursula; this was a sufficiently splendid work.

In the year of the Lord 1258, the altar of St Andrew the Apostle, St Stephen the Protomartyr, and the holy martyrs [Col. 0330A] Gervasius and Protasius was consecrated on 2 Kalends of July [30 June]. In the same year the altar of St Nicholas the Confessor and Ludmila was consecrated on 17 Kalends of September [16 August].

[Col. 0329A] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1259, the altar of the holy martyrs Stanislaus and Oswald was consecrated on 2 Nones of June [4 June]. Wine of remarkable value was produced throughout all Bohemia. Eberhard, founder of the *bonifantes*, died on the Nones of August [5 August].

[Col. 0329A] [Note: [Col. 0329] In Migne, the textual sections “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation … yielded abundantly” and “1260. In this year also … 11 Kalends of September” are printed in parallel.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1260, on 4 Nones of March [4 March], Přemysl, prince of the land, having assembled a great multitude, set out on an expedition against Hungary. Bohemia was greatly harmed by plundering and robbery as his armies passed through. In this year also crops, vineyards, and tree-fruits were damaged in most regions, some by drought and some by hail. But in other regions [Col. 0329B] wine was produced abundantly.

[Col. 0330A] 1260. In this year also, the prince of the land, having gathered many armies of diverse nations, marched against the Hungarians, who had previously violated the peace made. There he gained a triumph and struck down many thousands of Hungarians and other Saracens, divine and manifest aid assisting him. On his return from that expedition we received him with [Col. 0330B] a solemn procession on 11 Kalends of September [22 August].

[Col. 0329B] In the same year Judith, abbess of St George’s, was consecrated in the church of Prague by John III, twenty-fourth bishop of Prague, on 18 Kalends of September [15 August]. In the same year Lord Tobias, provost of the church of Prague, from his own resources established and endowed one perpetual vicarage in the choir of Prague.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1261, in the month of April, agreement and peace were made between the kings of Hungary and the prince of Bohemia, secured by a monetary penalty, namely 11,000 marks of silver. [Note: [Col. 0329C] The king of Hungary ceded Styria and the castle of Ptuj; furthermore, it was stipulated that Béla, son of Béla IV, should marry Cunegund, daughter of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, and niece of Otakar. This took place in 1264. See the Brandenburg Chronicle in Pulkava. For the remaining chronicles see Lambacher, *Interregnum*, p. 70, and the ordinances of the bishops of Passau, Olomouc, and Prague, written 31 March and 7 April 1261, Boczek III, 307. These prove that, in establishing this peace, the envoys were Louis, commander of the Teutonic Order, Jaros, burgrave of Prague, and Wokko, marshal of the kingdom of Bohemia.]

Queen Margaret left Bohemia for Austria on 15 Kalends of November [18 October], for reasons known to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0329C] Urban IV, in letters addressed to Otakar in 1262, writes as follows: “For it was set forth before us on your behalf that formerly the noblewoman Margaret, once queen of the Romans, having taken a solemn vow of chastity at the provincial chapter of the Friars Preachers assembled at Trier, and having promised obedience in the hands of H., then provincial prior in Germany of the same Friars Preachers, and that she would observe the order of sisters living according to the institutions of the Friars Preachers, likewise assumed the religious habit. Then, transferring herself to the monastery of the sisters of St Mark at Würzburg, who lived according to the aforesaid institutions, and whose care and government that prior himself exercised, she remained for a year and more in that monastery under the same habit.” Boczek III, 332. Compare also Pubitschka IV, 2, 312; Palacký II, 187.]

In the same year, on 8 Kalends of November [25 October], the prince of the kingdom of the Bohemians took as wife Cunegund, [Note: [Col. 0329C] She was a granddaughter of King Béla IV through his daughter Anna, whom Rostislav Mstislavich, prince of Halych, had married. See the genealogical table supplied by Palacký in his essay “Über Formelbücher,” in *Abhandlungen der Königl. Böhmischen Gesellschaft*, V, 2, p. 232.] daughter of Rostislav, duke of the Bulgarians, at a castle in Hungary popularly called in Hungarian Possen, [Note: [Col. 0330C] Pressburg.] and we received her, when she came to Prague, with a solemn procession in Prague church on 10 Kalends of January [23 December].

On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the prince of the Bohemians called Přemysl was consecrated king, [Note: [Col. 0330C] From this time onward Otakar styled himself king of the Bohemians in his charters, whereas previously he had called himself lord of the kingdom of Bohemia.] together with this Cunegund, in Prague church by the venerable father Werner, archbishop of Mainz by name, [Note: [Col. 0330C] From Guden’s *Codex diplomaticus*, Boczek III, 323 publishes a document which Godfrey of Eppstein, Frederick of Bichelingen, Henry of Willenowe, Diether of Katzenelnbogen, Günther of Schwarzburg, and Werner of Bolanden caused to be drawn up. In it they testify: “That we, together with the venerable father and our kinsman, Lord Werner, archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, were present in Prague church in the year of the Lord 1262, on the Sunday of the Nativity of the Lord, where that lord archbishop anointed and crowned as king Lord Otakar, heir of the kingdom of Bohemia, and his wife Cunegund as queen. The same king, who was also duke of Austria and Styria and margrave of Moravia, had taken us at Erfurt into his own expense and escort on our journey to Prague, where he provided for us for eighteen days, and on our return as far as Erfurt—for us, for the aforesaid lord archbishop, and for his whole household, with their persons and goods. He also supplied us all with abundant provisions. Moreover, he gave the lord archbishop 100 marks of gold for his due, and likewise 64 marks to the chapter of Mainz for the due of the court, to buy something for the church’s adornment. In addition, he honoured us handsomely and suitably, as befitted him, with geldings and gifts.” To this should be joined two other charters given to Otakar by the archbishop of Mainz; see the same place.] in the presence of six bishops: John of Prague; the bishop of Moravia; the bishop of Passau [Note: [Col. 0330D] Otto.]; and two from Prussia [Note: [Col. 0330D] Apparently the bishops of Warmia and Sambia.]; also in the presence of the margrave of Brandenburg with his wife, sons, and daughters; likewise in the presence of the dukes of Poland and many other nobles, counts, burgraves, župans, and other foreigners, and an innumerable multitude of Bohemians. For all those aforesaid he held a most magnificent feast [Col. 0331] for two days in the field called Letná, lying between the villages named Owenez, [Note: [Col. 0331A] Výšerov–Bubeneč in the Rakovník district.] Holisovicz, [Note: [Col. 0331A] Holešovice.] and Buben, in buildings solemnly prepared for this purpose.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1262, crops of various seed, winter as well as summer crops, almost wholly perished throughout most parts of Bohemia—partly from hail, partly from drought, partly from the army passing into Hungary—except millet alone; thus neither people had sufficient provisions nor horses and cattle sufficient fodder. Yet in very few parts of the same land grain grew in abundant quantity; there was also only a scant yield of wine and tree-fruits. In this same year there were many fires in towns and villages in Moravia, Bohemia, and Austria.

In the year of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ 1263, there was a very great dearth of grain, hay, and fodder in Bohemia and Moravia, so that a royal measure of rye was sold for 120 Prague denarii, sometimes more and sometimes less; wheat for much more, and peas for 150.
