Then there was also the greatest famine among the people, so that many peasants and craftsmen of various kinds, having sold their livestock and other goods and being unable to support themselves, were compelled to beg alms door to door. Many also, leaving their homes in the countryside, went begging with their wives and children. Much livestock and many draft animals likewise died because of the extreme shortage of fodder and the severity of the winter, which this year had become harsher than usual.

In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1264, a great force of winds arose on 5 Kalends of February [28 January]. Driven by them, many buildings and many granaries collapsed in the city of Prague and throughout the kingdom of Bohemia. Many trees in woods and groves were uprooted; the glass windows of Prague church were also shattered.

Likewise, in the same year, on 11 Kalends of March [19 February], the structure of the tower of Prague church, popularly called the bell-tower, collapsed; and many other church buildings fell down.

In this year the chapel of All Saints, built in the year of grace 1263, was consecrated on 3 Nones of February [3 February] by the venerable John III, bishop of Prague, under King Přemysl, son of King Wenceslas.

In the same year, in December, a great inundation of waters occurred throughout all Bohemia. This unusual flooding caused very great damage to buildings, provisions of various kinds, and many other things.

In the year of grace 1265 King Přemysl celebrated a most magnificent feast for the baptism of his first-born daughter, [Note: [Col. 0331A] Cunegund.] whom three bishops of Prague, Olomouc, and Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0331A] Should one read “Brandenburg”? See below, under Otakar, 1164.] lifted from the font. This was on the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary [2 February], all the nobles of Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria having been invited to the celebration. On that day the same king, crowned with the royal crown, came to the procession and heard Mass at the altar of St Mary in Prague church; and for two days he held a banquet with the aforesaid bishops and nobles of the aforesaid lands in the royal hall in Prague castle.

In the same year a great dispute arose between the king of Bohemia and the duke of Bavaria. [Note: [Col. 0331A] It concerned the archbishopric of Salzburg, which was given to Wladislaus, provost of Vyšehrad, son of Henry II, [Col. 0332A] duke of Silesia, and Anna, niece of Otakar I. Compare the Salzburg Chronicle for this year.] Compelled by this necessity, the king sent nobles to guard the borders of Bohemia; passing through, they inflicted much damage on the villages of the bishop of Prague and on those of other churches and canons. Moravians also crossed over to defend the borders of Bohemia and inflicted very great damage, both on church villages in Bohemia and beyond the borders in Bavaria.

[Col. 0331A] [Note: [Col. 0331] In Migne, the text sections “Anno vero 1266 . . . siliginis perierunt” and “Anno dominicae . . . siccitatis laesionem” are printed in parallel.]

In the year 1266, moreover, Bohemians and Moravians again passed through around the Purification of St Mary [2 February] and during Lent, and again inflicted very great damage on the villages of the bishop and of other churches of diverse religious orders. The winter and spring were wet at first, and many rye crops perished.

[Col. 0332A] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1266, on 7 Ides of August [7 August], Otakar by name, who was also Přemysl, king of the Bohemians, marched into Bavaria with a great multitude of Bohemians, Moravians, Austrians, Carinthians, and Poles. Some of these preceded the king, some accompanied him, and some followed after him. On this journey they did very great damage in the kingdom of Bohemia, grievously oppressing the poor and the villages of churches with plundering, robbery, and arson. [Note: [Col. 0332A] He captured the castles of Cham, Regenstauf, and Nittau; compare Hermann of Altaich for this year in Böhmer, *Fontes*, II. See also Duke Henry’s letter in Palacký’s essay “Über Formelbücher,” p. 277.] Entering Bavaria, they inflicted far heavier damage, cruelly devastating by plunder, robbery, and fire the part lying as far as Regensburg, and burning very many men and women. In this same year grain, [Col. 0334A] tree-fruit, and wine turned out poorly in Bohemia because of damage from hail and drought.

[Col. 0333] In the year of the Lord 1267, on 6 Ides of April [8 April], the legate of the Apostolic See, namely Brother Guy of the Cistercian Order, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Holy Apostles, [Note: [Col. 0333B] In a document issued 15 June 1267, Boczek III, 395, he calls himself cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina.] came to Prague and remained there until 5 Kalends of May [27 April]. [Note: [Col. 0333B] This should be read in place of “5 Kalends of April,” which the manuscript has; see Pubitschka IV, 2, p. 353.] He received from the clergy of Bohemia 150 marks of silver for expenses. Thence, coming into Austria, he stayed in Vienna and held a council there on 6 Ides of May [10 May]. John, bishop of Prague, attended that council with several canons. [Note: [Col. 0333B] And the other bishops: Peter of Passau, Bruno of Brixen, Conrad of Freising, and Leo of Regensburg; compare Mansi XXIII, 1169.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1268, King Otakar ordered pits to be made in every village, with a goose or piglet placed over the pits to catch wolves. In the same year he ordered weights and measures to be renewed and marked with his own sign, which had not previously been done. [Note: [Col. 0333B] Pubitschka IV, 2, p. 362.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1269, a daughter was born to King Otakar [Note: [Col. 0333B] Agnes. Compare Cunegund’s letters in Palacký’s essay “Über Formelbücher,” p. 293.] on the Nones of September [5 September]. A pulpit and altar were erected in Prague church, which Bishop John dedicated on St Martin’s Day in honour of St Matthias the Apostle and the holy confessors Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and very many other saints.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1270, almost all winter and spring grain perished throughout nearly the whole of Bohemia; tree-fruit was of moderate yield, and wine was abundant. The tower of Prague church, which had fallen many years earlier, was repaired through the care of the venerable Lord John, bishop. There was much unseasonable weather in this year, and much flooding rain in autumn. King Otakar built many houses and castles in various places of his kingdom this year. In the same year a stone tower was erected in the middle of the cloister of Prague church to hold a light in it, Gregory, knight of the king and queen, managing its expenses.

In the year of the Lord 1272, on 6 Kalends of December [26 November], Rudolf was elected emperor. [Note: [Col. 0333B] The author is mistaken both in the year and the day: Rudolf was elected at Frankfurt on 29 September 1273; for the witnesses see Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 51. This happened despite the opposition of Otakar’s envoys. On the matter the king himself wrote thus to Pope Gregory X: “The princes of Germany, who possess the power of electing the emperor, unanimously directed their votes toward a certain less suitable count, our solemn envoys—whom we had sent as our procurators to Frankfurt, where the election was to be held—opposing and protesting; and they invested the same man, to the detriment of the Empire and to our prejudice, [Col. 0334B] with the majesty of the sacred diadem.” Compare Dölliner, *Codex epistolaris Otakari regis*, p. 17, and Kurz, *Österreich unter Otakar*, p. 27. Otakar’s envoy was Berthold, bishop of Bamberg; compare Rudolf’s charter of 1275, printed in Lambacher, *Urkundenbuch*, p. 76.] In the same year Prague bridge broke in the middle of the river Vltava on 4 Ides of March [12 March].

In the year of the Lord 1273, on 15 Kalends of September [18 August], a great cleansing-out of waters took place in the river Vltava, so that the wooden chapel situated before the bridge at Pesek [Note: [Col. 0333] A somewhat later hand corrected this to Piesek.] was wholly swept away with its foundations. Of another stone church situated below the bridge on the island, its middle part was struck down; and all the mills around the city of Prague were shattered and swept away by the water. It drowned very many people and overturned buildings. In the fields, grain and hay from the meadows were carried away by the flood; it ruined vegetable gardens, and flowed through the city of Prague, extending its channels as far as the church of St Giles and the church of St Nicholas, flowing through the entire Jewish quarter as far as the church of St Francis.

In the year of the Lord 1274, the nobleman Borso withdrew from the king, having lost the king’s favour without fault of his own, because his rivals reported hostile things about him to the king. [Note: [Col. 0334B] On 5 November 1275, Borso, lord of Rýzmburk, caused a charter of donation to be drawn up in his castle of Rýzmburk; see it in Boczek IV, 166. Letters printed by Bodmann, 12, 30, 44, show that Otakar’s traitor secretly favoured Rudolf’s party. The first of these reads: “Although, therefore, for the present you may briefly suffer some passing adversity, bear all things patiently.”]

In the year of the Lord 1275, on the Kalends of May [1 May], Pope Gregory X held a council at Lyons. [Note: [Col. 0334B] This council was assembled in 1274 and began on the Nones of May [7 May].] Two years earlier, this Gregory had summoned the bishops of all lands where the Christian faith flourishes and the Lord’s name is invoked, so that they should assemble to celebrate a council at the aforesaid time. The council lasted within seven weeks. [Note: [Col. 0334B] It ended on 16 Kalends of August [17 July]; it therefore lasted almost ten weeks.] John, bishop of Prague, attended it with certain canons. Returning to his see at Prague, he ordered throughout his diocese, in accordance with the apostolic command, that hollow collection-boxes be placed in all churches, to gather offerings of the faithful in aid of the Holy Land.

[Col. 0335A] At the same council Pope Gregory confirmed Rudolf’s election, [Note: [Col. 0335B] In these very few words he reports matters of the utmost importance to the king of Bohemia. On 26 September 1274 Pope Gregory wrote to Otakar that he had confirmed Rudolf’s election. Compare Boczek IV, 135, 136, 141, and the preceding letters of Otakar and his envoy Bruno, bishop of Olomouc.] and assigned to Rudolf, the elect, for his benefit the tithes that had been collected throughout Germany in aid of the Holy Land.

In the year of the Lord 1276, John, bishop of Prague, roofed the cathedral church of St Vitus with stone tiles of beautiful and durable workmanship. He also made two large windows of delicate and costly workmanship and glazed them; in them was depicted material from the Old and New Testaments. He likewise erected there two pulpits of elegant and magnificent workmanship, one at the altar of Blessed Dionysius and the other at the altar of Blessed Mary Magdalene; the work could scarcely be completed during the entire following year.

In the same year the Vítkovci [Note: [Col. 0335B] This was the very noble kindred of the Vítkovci, from which descended Záviš of Rosenberg, the king’s enemy. What is related here is confirmed by Henry of Heimburg, an author of the late thirteenth century, whose as-yet unpublished Chronicle we shall publish in its proper place.] withdrew from the king with a huge armed force and inflicted many evils upon the poor and monastic communities throughout the kingdom of Bohemia, at a time when the king had an excessive need of their aid. For it often happens that, while princes disagree among themselves, their enemies gain victory. Also in this year a very great multitude of wolves was seen before the gates of Prague castle, howling loudly on both sides; by this omen they foretold an adverse event for the Bohemian people.

1278. In the same year Henry, canon of Prague and notary of the royal court, was detained on 18 Kalends of October [14 September] by order of Queen Cunegund, and was despoiled in his house of many possessions and of money. Because of this detention Bishop John imposed an interdict in Prague church on 11 Kalends of October [21 September]; this interdict had occurred around and after the feast of Blessed Wenceslas [28 September]. The same Henry was released from custody on 3 Kalends of October [29 September], and divine offices were restored in Prague church. In the same year winter and autumn were warm, foggy, wet, and marked by great violence of winds; passage over the ice was impossible. In this same year two ditches were made before Prague castle, one lined with stones and the other, larger one without stones, forty cubits wide and thirty deep; the length of each extended from the stream Bruska to Obora. The old ditch too, nearer the castle wall, was renewed and on one side raised with a masonry wall; its other side was not renewed. It was forty cubits wide and fifty high. On the other side of the castle, called by the Lesser Gate, a ditch was dug from the Bruska stream and carried across Mount Opis to the court of the lord bishop beyond the river Vltava.

## III. THE OTAKAR ANNALS

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335A] 1254. On 19 Kalends of January [14 December], Přemysl, son of King Wenceslas, set out for Prussia, girded with the sign of the cross, to fight the Prussians. He was followed by a great throng of nobles from Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria, and other soldiers of lower rank. [Note: [Col. 0335B] Peter of Dusburg writes in *Chronicle of Prussia* III, 70 that the army of crusaders exceeded sixty thousand men, and he enumerates the other German princes who undertook this expedition to conquer the land of Sambia. Alexander IV commanded Bartholomew of the Order of Friars Minor to preach the word of the cross against the Lithuanians in Poland, Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria; Boczek III, 192. See also Voigt, *Geschichte von Prussen*, III, 76.]

Coming to Wrocław, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [25 December], and was honourably received by the dukes of Poland [Note: [Col. 0336B] Henry III and Conrad II, dukes of Wrocław and Legnica. They were sons of Anna, daughter of Otakar I.] and by the nobles and bishop of Wrocław, [Note: [Col. 0336B] Thomas.] and for several days was most honourably provided for with his entire army. While he was staying at Wrocław, the margrave of Brandenburg [Note: [Col. 0336B] Otto III, who had married Beatrice, daughter of Wenceslas I, in 1244. Compare the Brandenburg Chronicle in Pulkava.] came to him with his army, and the two set out together for Prussia, leading with them a great multitude.

1255. Meanwhile the powerful and leading men of the land of Prussia, struck with divine fear, as we believe, and having heard the prince of Bohemia’s name, came to the same prince with every humility, surrendering themselves with all that was theirs to his lordship and to the Christian faith. The most pious prince graciously received them, invited them to the grace of baptism, himself lifted one of the more powerful men among them from the sacred font, and gave him his own name, calling him Otakar. The margrave of Brandenburg lifted another from the font and named him after himself. Then many nobles lifted others from the womb of Mother Church, named them after themselves, and gave them their own garments, though precious. Then, coming to a certain hill which they called the Royal Mount, they built a fortification for the greater strengthening of the Christian faith. [Note: [Col. 0336B] Königsberg, capital of the Prussian kingdom.] Then, after very many Prussian peoples had been baptized by the lord bishop of Olomouc and other bishops, the prince of the land of Bohemia and the margrave of Brandenburg, having strengthened the neophytes in the faith of Christ Jesus [Col. 0337A] and received hostages from them, entrusted land and people to the crusaders of the Teutonic Order and returned home with every prosperity and joy.

The prince of Bohemia therefore arrived at Opava [Note: [Col. 0337D] Troppau.] on 8 Ides of February [6 February], then hurried to Austria, where he spent all Lent. Afterwards, in the octave of Easter [21 March], he came to Bohemia, and on 6 Ides of April [8 April] was honourably received with great rejoicing of the clergy and people of the city of Prague, with processions, and in the cathedral church by the bishop and the canons of that church. As the prince was leaving Prague castle, a great force of winds arose in a whirlwind. It threw from the bridge before the castle a knight following the prince; his horse died in the fall, but he himself [Col. 0337B] escaped unhurt. At the same hour a wooden bell-tower with bells within the walls of St Mary fell down, driven by the great force of the wind, and many other collapses occurred in the city and throughout the villages.

At the beginning of the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1260, a conflict more bitter than the former one was again stirred up between closely related princes of exalted blood: namely, on the one side, Přemysl, lord and heir of the kingdom of Bohemia, duke of Austria and Styria, and margrave of Moravia; and on the other, Béla and his son Stephen, kings of Hungary. The occasion—or rather the cause—had been given some years before by the Hungarian kings themselves.

For the elder Hungarian king Béla, contrary to the form of agreement formerly entered into with his nephew, [Note: [Col. 0337D] Through Constance, wife of Otakar I; see above.] the said lord of the kingdom of Bohemia, and confirmed on both sides by oaths personally sworn and by public instruments subsequently drawn up, appeared, in the very year in which that agreement was concluded, to occupy the borders of Moravia, Austria, and that part of Styria which, by the preceding agreement, had fallen to the share of his aforesaid nephew. [Note: [Col. 0337D] Already in 1257 Otakar ordered a fortification or town to be prepared and built on the Hungarian frontier for the necessity and preservation of the land, as he testifies in a charter printed in Boczek III, 246. This was the town of Hradiště, situated on an island belonging to the monastery of Velehrad.]

Moreover his son, King Stephen, proving an even more abundant emulator of his ancestors’ tyranny and slaughter against Christ’s innocent flock, led an army of unbelievers—that is, savage Cuman men—against the illustrious duke of Carinthia, Ulrich, and his brother Philip, once elected archbishop of Salzburg, [Note: [Col. 0337D] Later patriarch of Aquileia.] cousins of the said king of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0338D] They were sons of Bernard, duke of Carinthia, who had married Jutta, daughter of Otakar I. Compare John of Viktring I, 5.] and included in the aforesaid peace. In a grievous and indiscriminate slaughter of monks, clerics, and ordinary laypeople [Col. 0338A] with their little children; in the abduction and violation of nuns and matrons; in the removal of such women and of young men to be converted to another rite; and in the burning of monasteries, other churches, and a great part of Carinthia, he wickedly perpetrated exceedingly dreadful outrages. [Note: [Col. 0337] MS 2 has *perpetratam*.] [Note: [Col. 0338D] This occurred in 1259.]

For these offences against his oath, and others which I omit for brevity’s sake, since no satisfaction followed, the said lord of the kingdom of Bohemia, at the urging of the Styrian nobles and towns, and on the advice of the illustrious Count Otto of Hardegg, certain Austrians, and very few Moravians, received the Styrians into his protection. [Note: [Col. 0338D] According to Pernold, this was done at Vienna in 1259; he writes that the Styrian rebellion was instigated by Otakar.] Although almost all Styria was then in King Stephen’s power, and the Hungarians held the garrisons of every castle and town there, yet within a short time the said lord, with Count Hardegg and certain Austrians and Styrians, drove King Stephen and the Hungarians very forcefully from Styria, beyond human expectation, taking the towns and castles there. The castle of Ptuj, however, in which the wife of King Stephen—Cuman by nation [Note: [Col. 0338D] Elizabeth.], though initiated into the sacraments of the faith—was then personally residing, remained for a time in King Stephen’s power together with the town and a few other castles.

Whence, [Note: [Col. 0338D] Some words have fallen out. Should one read *patratorum*, “of deeds perpetrated”?] from acts committed through Moravia and Austria to the injury of the aforesaid lord of the kingdom of Bohemia—indeed, to Christ’s offence—and from the envy of hatred and jealousy thereby conceived, and from the deceitful wound of grief swelling with the spirit of indignation, [Col. 0338C] there burst forth openly into public view, as though a scar had ruptured. Thus, at the beginning of the year of the Lord 1260, hostilities were again publicly declared between the aforesaid princes, so that in the Lenten season of that same year [21 February] they brought strong armies against each other. But because both armies lacked necessities, especially for the horses, the princes named were compelled to extend truces—hoped to be preliminaries to peace—until the approaching feast of St John the Baptist [24 June]. Yet, alas, the contrary occurred. For, [the reading *in fallar* is uncertain], what happened before and afterwards were the beginnings of the sorrows that were done.

Therefore, as the appointed term of the truce approached, Stephen, the younger king of Hungary, prepared, with the stronger and chosen Hungarian and Cuman warriors, to ambush the army coming from Bohemia and Poland in scattered detachments, intending to fall upon the unwary, whoever first encountered him. Having determined secretly to attack and strike the camps pitched in the meadows near Pohorliz [Note: [Col. 0339D] Porlitz.] by the venerable Lord Bruno, bishop of Olomouc, and the illustrious dukes Henry of Silesia and Wladislaus of Opole, he travelled through the whole rainy and cloudy night to accomplish this. But, his guide erring, he arrived unintentionally at dawn near Walkenstein and Stozecz [Note: [Col. 0339D] Staats.], where, nearby, was a place in the meadows by the stronghold called Lawa [Note: [Col. 0339D] Laa.]. There, as agreed, the whole army of the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia was to assemble around the feast of St John the Baptist.

To this place the brothers Otto and Conrad, counts of Hardegg and Plain—men noble by birth, illustrious in valour, and eminent in rank—were the first to arrive with all their men. They were advised to withdraw into the town of Laa until the army arrived, lest they perhaps be caught unprotected by Cuman and Hungarian ambushes. Yet, as men strong in spirit and strength—indeed, excessively bold—they refused to do this. Instead, though few in number, they pitched their tents in the field and remained there day and night.

Then, on Saturday, the third day after the feast of St John the Baptist [26 June], the army of the lord of the kingdom [Col. 0339C] of Bohemia began to appear, converging from different directions at the agreed place in the meadows near Laa. Those who arrived, burdened by their armour and exhausted by their labours—the men from Bohemia and Moravia with their lord prince; others from Saxony with [Note: [Col. 0339] This is the correct reading; the manuscript has *et*, “and.”] the margrave of Brandenburg; and some with the venerable lord bishop of Olomouc and the illustrious dukes of Silesia and Opole already mentioned—pitched their camps there. Suddenly a report rang through the camp that the Cumans were very near, plundering and slaughtering the neighbouring region and setting it ablaze.

Accordingly, a general commotion arose in the camp. All, astonishingly eager in spirit and equipped with arms, went out to fight in ordered ranks. When they had thus gone into the field, whether deliberately or by mistake I do not know—God knows—it was suddenly reported that only a few of the unbelieving enemy had done these things and that they had now fled. Thereupon, by the deceptive consent of all, which produced the worst sense of security, each returned to camp. The aforesaid counts of Plain, however, and the valiant knight Cadold, surnamed Orphan, with a few others, remained in the field as if for the army’s guard. [Note: [Col. 0340D] On these men see Hermann of Altaich for this year.]

Although they had often experienced the cunning of Cumans and other enemies in battle, nevertheless—as the maxim says, [Col. 0340A] “The fates lead the unwilling and drag the willing”—they rashly gave themselves over to pursuing at a distance enemies feigning flight. Some of our great and noble men followed them here and there without order; caught from behind by the same enemies lying in ambush, they were afterwards killed. [Note: [Col. 0339] This is the correct reading; MS 2 has *conclusis—interemptis*.] Some were then ensnared alike in the snares of death, others in those of captivity.

When this news, uncertain and conflicting though it was, reached the camp—some reporting that the aforesaid counts, Cadold, and the others with them were engaged with the enemy and sought help; others, by contrast, reporting that they had rather been overtaken by the enemy, as later events proved to be truer—the princes rose at once from table. Soldiers and retainers hurried breathlessly to arms; armoured, shielded, and helmeted, and some on barded horses, they rushed against the enemy in great haste.

When they found the illustrious warriors just named—Cadold, the counts, and some others—lying lifeless on the ground on the road at the place of battle, with most of them completely stripped, some of their brave men, struck by fear at the sight, froze like stone, and very many turned their backs upon the enemy. Nevertheless, the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia with a few men, and the lord bishop of Olomouc ahead of all, together with the margrave of Brandenburg and his men, pursued the fleeing enemy.

When the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia and the bishop of Olomouc, first of all, had drawn near, while the margrave of Brandenburg still followed from [Col. 0340C] a distance, the others were seen to halt and draw up their battle-lines opposite them. But when the same margrave came nearer, a great darkening of the air occurred; and amid the agitation and sound of thunder, and the noise of heavy rain with flashing lightning, the impious men turned to flight, though no one pursued them, because the horses of the Christian army had become exceedingly exhausted.

Since the river Morava [Note: [Col. 0340D] The March.] had then greatly overflowed, as though the floodgates of heaven had been opened and a deluge poured down from above, very many of the enemy are reliably said to have perished drowned in it. Nevertheless, because of the grievous fate of Cadold, the counts, and the others, the Christian army was cast down almost to despair. O what grief! O what lamentations among the Minorite brothers at Laa, [Col. 0340D] when the corpses of almost all those who had fallen were brought to them from every side amid the wailing and mourning of all!

What the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia, weakened by grief as commander of so great an army, would do henceforth was uncertain. Many urged a return; but, avoiding the stain on their valour and being, like the children of this world, wiser than the children of light, especially the princes and chief barons each worked through others to make that course both urged and thought advisable. [Col. 0341A] From this there arose dissension which, through the occasion of salutary unity and victory, would finally bring forth salvation.

For when it was charged against the said dukes Henry of Silesia [Note: [Col. 0341] H. Zelzie 2.] and of Opole that they were the first to intend to return home from the site of the camp, and would thus shamefully give the army cause for dissolution, they, as vigorous and prudent men, denied the allegation concerning themselves and attributed the origin or root of such counsel to the Margrave of Brandenburg. Thereupon, all controversy having ceased, the entire army, by common counsel and unanimous decision, marched to the place where the king of Hungary was reported to have pitched his camp.

Accordingly, when Lord Philip, formerly elected archbishop of Salzburg, and his brother Ulrich, illustrious duke of Carinthia and Styria, had joined them there, on the Sunday [Col. 0341B] within the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul (4 July), after Masses had been heard at dawn, the great army of the faithful appeared before the enemy, fully armed as was necessary by common agreement and by the command of the prince who was its head and of the other princes; advancing in ordered battle-lines and covering both mountains and plains. The often-mentioned lord of the kingdom of Bohemia, with his men beneath the banner of the most glorious martyr Wenceslas, surveyed the enemy camp from a slope of a mountain, on the highest [Note: [Col. 0341] *supremo* 2.] elevation of the plain. [Note: [Col. 0341D] *spectantem* 2.] The same unbelievers and the others who were with them, as they themselves afterwards reported, would immediately then have turned to flight, had they not placed confidence in the river called the Morava, which made a chasm between us and them; [Col. 0341C] nor is this surprising, for fear and trembling fell upon the ungodly when they saw Manaym—that is, “the camps of God”—coming against them.

Indeed, the devotion and pious purposes and vows then conceived by the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia and certain princes—by which they bound themselves to the Lord, promising to change their own lives and the condition of their lands for the better in regard to coinage and other matters—and perhaps also the conversion, born of fear, of very many barons and other knights who had fled to confession and to the sign of the holy cross; moreover, the solemn prayers poured out to God for them by a great part of Christendom as far as Cologne the Great and beyond—divine aid and the course and outcome of the angelic [Col. 0342A] war [lacuna: material is missing in the source].

Let the reader read the following letter, sent on behalf of the lord of the kingdom of Bohemia to the most holy father in Christ and lord Alexander, by the grace of God the fourth pope of that name, which is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Here something is missing. A more careful account of the battle must be sought in the following letter of King Otakar to Pope Alexander, from which what is lacking here may be supplied. On other writers by whom that most splendid victory is related, see Palacký II, 182.]

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Because excessive glory is ascribed to the Bohemians in this letter, doubts concerning its historical trustworthiness were raised by Pray, *Annales Hungariae* I, 309, and Katona, *Historia critica Hungariae* VI, 312.]

> “To the most holy father in Christ and lord Alexander, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church, Otakar, by the same grace lord of the kingdom of Bohemia, duke of Austria and Styria, and margrave of Moravia, and so forth.
>
> Since the rescue of his sheep from wolves delights a pious shepherd, and the prosperity of children together with their safety gladdens a kindly father, we have, with God as author, waged a grave war against Béla and his son Stephen, illustrious kings of Hungary; against Daniel, king of Rusʹ [Note: [Col. 0341D] This is Daniel Romanowicz, prince of Halych, who, with the permission of Innocent IV, had acquired royal dignity. Röpell, *Geschichte Polens* V, 1, 522.], and his sons [Note: [Col. 0341D] One of these, Leo, had married Constance, daughter of Béla IV; another, Roman, Gertrude, [Col. 0342D] widow of Wladislaus, the elder brother of King Otakar II; cf. above, 1246.], and the other Ruthenians and Tatars who had come to his aid; [Col. 0342B] against Boleslaus of Cracow [Note: [Col. 0342D] He too was a son-in-law of Béla IV, whose daughter Cunigunda had married Boleslaus.], and the young Leszek, dukes of Łęczyca [Note: [Col. 0342D] Duke of Łęczyca.]; and against an innumerable multitude [Note: [Col. 0342D] The Anonymous of Leobium relates that Béla’s army consisted of 140,000 horsemen, while Otakar numbered 100,000 horsemen, among whom were 7,000 men in full armour.] of inhuman Cumans, Hungarians, and diverse Slavs; likewise Szeklers [Note: [Col. 0342D] These are the inhabitants of Aluta, called Seklers.], Vlachs, Besermins [Note: [Col. 0342D] A Turkish people; by others called Bessi or Bisseni, and also Pechenegs. Zeuss, p. 742.], Ishmaelites, schismatics—namely Greeks, Bulgarians, and Ruthenians—and Bosnian heretics. And we judged that the course of the victory given us from heaven, and of the peace restored after victory between ourselves on the one side and the said kings on the other, should not without reason be truthfully made known in this letter to your fatherhood.
>
> For when we came with our armies to the river called the Morava, about two miles from the castle and town of Hainburg, where it marks the frontier of Hungary and Austria, [Col. 0342C] we found the said kings and their armies encamped there on the opposite bank. Thus the aforementioned river alone divided our camp [Note: [Col. 0342D] Palacký observes that Otakar’s camp was situated between the villages of Wagram and Gross-Enzersdorf.] from that of our adversaries.
>
> Since the position of the place was such that we could not gain the desired access to the enemy without irreparable loss among our own men, and since peace between us and the same kings had repeatedly been attempted in many ways on both sides, but the kings changed their intentions from day to day and hour to hour, so that [Col. 0342D] no room for peace remained—the Lord of Vengeances doubtless hardening their hearts after the manner of Pharaoh [Col. 0343A]—we finally offered the opposing side a choice between one of two alternatives: either they should yield that side to us, so that we might cross to it for the purpose of making war, or we should grant the same to the opposing side.
>
> Of these alternatives the opposing party chose the latter: that we should withdraw and, by our withdrawal, give them a place to cross. So that this might appear possible with every obstacle removed, the said kings, their bans and counts, through suitable envoys, granted us truces established and secured by their oaths for the whole feast-day of blessed Margaret (12 July) immediately preceding, and for half of the day of the feast itself (13 July). But these men, accustomed to violate their agreements and oaths, crossed by fords [Col. 0343B] which they had discovered and prepared long before, during the night, to our side with all their army. And while we said, ‘Peace and security!’ they suddenly appeared against us, unprepared as we were, in the field with an innumerable multitude. [Note: [Col. 0343D] The battle was joined at the place of Kressenbrunn.]
>
> And because scarcely a tenth part of our army remained with us under the expectation of the truce for the protection of our person—for many of our men had crossed the Danube and entered the town of Hainburg, while others had gone down with the wagons to the stations and camp-sites—our enemies, full of treachery, surrounded us in a semicircle in ordered battle-lines, and would perhaps have swallowed us alive had the Lord not helped us.
>
> Therefore, placed at so unavoidable a crisis of necessity, reflecting that power is heavenly and that victory is given, not through the multitude of an army, but from heaven by the gift of the great God, placing all our hope in the help of the Most High, we first exhorted our helpers and fellow-soldiers and, with confidence given us from heaven, boldly charged into the many wedges of the enemy. God terrified, struck down, and put them to flight through our hands and those of our men—indeed, of His own soldiers—so that, as the fugitives rushed onward and crushed one another, the said river Morava, in accordance with the etymology foretelling its name, was reddened with the abundant blood of the slain, like the Red Sea for the Egyptians, and thus became for those submerged and perishing in it a way of death. [Note: [Col. 0343D] According to the *Chronicon Augustanum*, fourteen thousand enemies perished.]
>
> For so great a multitude of sinners fleeing from the face of God perished in that river that some of our men entered the enemy camp over the bodies of men and horses as though [Col. 0343D] over bridges made for that purpose, and seized wagons, tents, provisions, and every kind of precious spoil.
>
> Although, therefore, after the triumph divinely granted to us, we might, as was commonly apparent, have subjected the kingdom of Hungary to our dominion and [Col. 0344A] reduced it to perpetual servitude, nevertheless, considering that it is better to have a good neighbour in concord than to overcome and exterminate a rebel, and also that the emperor Constantine said, ‘Friendships often become sweeter when, after causes of enmity, they have been restored to concord,’ we preferred to renew treaties of peace with the princes and close kinsmen of our high blood—the said kings of Hungary, the lady queen [Note: [Col. 0343D] Maria, daughter of Theodore, emperor of Nicaea.], and the young King Béla [Note: [Col. 0343D] Son of Béla IV.]—according to the terms offered us by the great count Roland and Pozsony, rather than, by devastating and weakening the great kingdom of Hungary, open an entrance to the Tatars against it and against the lands of our own dominion.
>
> Therefore, sending to your apostolic authority the terms of the aforesaid settlement, sealed with the seals of the said kings, queen, and Duke Béla, we humbly ask that they be confirmed by the Apostolic See and, as is fitting, strengthened forever by apostolic protection.”

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Otakar’s letter ends here. What follows is the wording of the canon of Prague, which Hájek first falsely joined to the preceding material as though it were part of the letter, thereby leading Balbín, Pubitschka, and Boczek, who followed them, into the same error. Cf. Dobrovský, “Erläuternde Bemerkungen über die Geschichte Ottokars,” *Monatsschrift des Böhmischen Museums*, II, January, p. 41.]

Accordingly, such a great victory should worthily be ascribed to God alone and to His saints, with fitting thanksgivings and praises; this is also confirmed by certain revelations. For many report that certain men appointed in the rear to guard the army, when battle was imminent, said that they had seen a bird shaped in outline like an eagle, but whiter than snow in colour, with a golden head and neck, inseparably following the banner of blessed Wenceslas, formerly duke and always [Col. 0344C] patron of the Bohemians, the renowned martyr. As it was seen in different places accompanying them as they advanced toward the battle, it grew until it covered the entire Christian army with its body and feathers.

On the same day, the noble, devout, and in every respect trustworthy knight John, son of Swojslav, while ill in his own house, saw in ecstasy, about the third hour, that he was as if stationed in the field of battle with his army. Seeing it small and disordered, he at the same time saw the glorious patrons of Bohemia proceeding to a bright field in this order. First he saw Saint Wenceslas advancing, clad in mail, wearing his helmet upon his head, carrying his sword in a sheath adorned with gold and gems [Col. 0344D] beneath his left arm, and bearing his own banner in his right hand. Immediately after him followed Saint Adalbert, like a great and powerful man, suitably arrayed in pontifical vestments. After these he saw blessed Procopius, like an abbot with his pastoral staff, following close behind the holy bishop; [Col. 0345A] last of all he saw five martyr brothers following, as though dressed in their own tunics.

Then the same knight heard Saint Wenceslas say in a clear voice to those companions of his glory: “Our army is weak; let us hasten at once into God’s presence.” Having said this, he extended his banner against the enemy, who were immediately seen universally to turn in flight.

External revelations also agreed with inward consolation. For, as the often-mentioned prince of Bohemia and the other princes, barons, and knights jointly reported, although a little earlier they had been almost dead and deprived of all strength, yet at the very hour of conflict almost all and each of them received within themselves an assurance, with an unprecedented joy of spirit and body, that victory would be gained; they were ready [Col. 0345B] not merely to charge, but even boldly to break through iron walls.

Jaros, burgrave of Prague, a trustworthy man, likewise declared orally before the bishop of Prague, the provost, dean, and canons assembled in the chapter of Prague, that his army, in whose midst the banner of Saint Wenceslas the martyr was borne, sustained no wound or loss among men or horses; wherever it turned, the enemy fled, turning their backs before it. Moreover, the iron of the lance-staff upon which the said martyr’s banner hung was seen by many to shine like a most brilliant ray of the sun.

The envoys of the king of Hungary, sent by him to the prince of Bohemia, reported before that prince and his barons that, at the hour when the armies [Col. 0345C] joined battle, as the Bohemians lifted a mighty cry to heaven and sang the hymn composed by Saint Adalbert which the people sing in procession every Sunday and on other feast-days, the enemy horses took flight against their riders’ will.

A certain investigator of the Scriptures, especially curious in those writings to explore the mysteries of numbers in their prophetic sense, says:

> “After the year 1260, the times and seasons henceforth appear suspect to me.”

—We judge that this gloss of an interpolator ought to be removed from the text.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1264, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of the glorious patron Saint Wenceslas, [Col. 0345D] the same King Přemysl, hastening to the chief church and most devoutly commending himself to the prayers of clergy and laity alike, met his dearly beloved son-in-law Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, and his sister at Čáslav. They had brought with them their daughter, whom the lord king, lest any spark of discord should remain between himself and the king of Hungary, his uncle, betrothed in marriage to the king’s son Béla before Pozsony, in return for the truces previously concluded and for perpetual peace between their lands, in the presence of three bishops—those of Prague, Olomouc, [Col. 0346A] and Brandenburg. [Note: [Col. 0345D] The marriage was celebrated in the fields called Vizze, where the Fischa flows into the Danube, not far from Vienna, as the writers on Austrian affairs establish. Palacký II, 192.]

Nor should it be omitted how the expenses of the banquets were provided for dukes and margraves of various lands, as well as for the inhabitants of the country, throughout their territories—Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria—until the conclusion of the festival. What more need be said? The king of Hungary came, wearing golden necklaces [Note: [Col. 0346D] These are chains made of gold; see Adelung’s glossary under this word.] hanging down beside his temples, accompanied by few men, to see his son’s bride at the tents of the king of Bohemia; and he arranged her dowry for the wedding.

After he departed, his son Béla, handsome in form above the sons of many, having heard the solemnities of Mass, placed a golden crown upon the head of the girl given to him in marriage. One of his nobles then drew his sword and, brandishing it over the bride’s head, removed the crown, according to the custom of his [Col. 0346B] people. He then took her by ship homeward, not without the greatest lamentation of the parents.

On the same day the king of Bohemia, in a new tent prepared in the manner of a church and covered on every side with various cloths, made four margraves and a fifth man, the duke of Poland, knights, besides other counts and nobles who were splendidly honoured. With them he held military games of various kinds and seated the elder king of Hungary at table in tents lavishly prepared for that purpose, together with diverse princes, serving them graciously and abundantly, on the third day before the Nones of October.

Who could fail to marvel at so magnificent a prince, called from his mother’s womb the Golden King [Note: [Col. 0346D] He was called the Iron King by the Tatars, according to the Erfurt Chronicle of Saint Peter, in Mencken III, 291.], who, by means of gold, silver, and wisdom given him from above, wonderfully and skilfully constructed for his armies, now for a second time, a bridge over the Danube upon great ships, [Col. 0346C] for their crossing and return? When the celebration was ended, King Otakar returned to Prague healthy and unharmed with all his men.

In the year of the Lord 1271, Vitus, dean of Prague, died on the Kalends of May. By preaching the word of life and teaching the faithful of Christ, he disseminated saving knowledge, exchanging earthly things for heavenly in hope of more abundant fruit in return for his merits and labours. For he illumined the minds of men like a shining lamp; every Sunday and feast-day the nobles of the land, burghers, and also craftsmen and labourers flocked to the church of Prague on account of his preaching, so that they might preserve in the little treasury of their memory [Col. 0346D] the word of salvation to the praise and honour of God and for their own advancement.

The Lord had bestowed upon him no small grace of eloquence in setting forth His word, had filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding; and he himself sent forth the sayings of his wisdom like rain, by which he watered the dry hearts of men. This man devoted his whole self and all that was his to the work of the Church for the name of Jesus Christ. With great labour and vigils he compiled the lectionary called the Matutinal. Previously, each book used by [Col. 0347A] the Church during the cycle of the year was provided separately in individual volumes for Matins, according to the division and determination of the seasons: Isaiah in Advent, the Epistles of Paul after the octave of Epiphany, the homilies or Genesis during Lent, Jeremiah in the Passion season, and so on with each book. This shifting produced inconvenience and error among those less trained in the office.

He also caused many musical books belonging to the office of divine worship to be written at his own expense, taking care that nothing be omitted and adding the Epistles and Gospels sung on solemn feast-days. The old service-books were plain, and some were already worn out through age, useless and producing no benefit; through them error and confusion [Col. 0347B] frequently arose in the divine office. The books written at the price and expense of Dean Vitus are missals, graduals, musical antiphonaries, psalters, hymnals, collectaries, baptismal books, breviaries, and many other books of sermons, through which he enlightened the church of Prague in divine worship. Many other conventual and parish churches were likewise corrected and enlightened in the divine office through copies of the Prague books; and we do not doubt that this was meritorious for Lord Vitus the dean, author of this work, and beneficial to his soul.

He also enlarged the church of Prague by constructing altars. At his own expense he erected a vaulted pulpit and placed an altar of the holy Evangelists on the left side of the choir of Saint Mary. [Col. 0347C] He erected another pulpit where the vicars customarily sing “Lord, have mercy” on Maundy Thursday, at Matins on Good Friday, and on the vigil of Easter; and he built an altar of Saint Matthias, assigning suitable provision to the minister appointed for the altar.

Through him the work of the cloister on the long northern side was also completed, with carved columns, vaulting, and the painting of the entire cloister. He enlarged the chapel of Saint Michael, where the ministers vest to celebrate Mass, with vaulted chambers below and above, and placed an altar of Saint Michael there. He also caused it to be painted and endowed it with suitable provision, assigning land in the village of Hornetice and other land in Prziboj, which he bought with his own money. He likewise established a perpetual vicar [Col. 0347D] for the deanery of Prague, assigning land in the village of Bicos from which that vicar might be suitably maintained.

The same lord dean also induced Czeczon, judge of the whole kingdom of Bohemia, to build the church of All Saints, situated at the exit from the cloister toward the royal court. That church was built, the same dean procuring and employing masons and other workmen until the aforesaid work was completed. Two priests were established in it to perform the office. Provision was also made for them through farmland, movable and immovable endowment, and rent-paying persons in two villages, namely [Col. 0348A] Dyrhkov and Visin.

This man Vitus, with pious affection and lavish generosity, was ardent in giving alms. For his possessions were established in the Lord, and the whole church of the saints will recount his alms. Every day he gathered to his table three poor scholars, sometimes four, and ordered that they be served abundantly. He also distributed money to poor lay men and women in the secluded and darker corners of the church while visiting altars in veneration of relics, mindful of the Gospel saying: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3).

He did not seek human praise, in accordance with that philosophical saying:

> “The wise man places the fruit of virtue in conscience; the less perfect man in glory. For the wise man, content with the reward of conscience, does not seek glory.”

He helped not only scholars serving the church of Prague, but also, according to his means and with heartfelt concern, provided for those studying in the general school, as was evident in very many cases. He embraced relatives, kinsmen, and every connection with special affection, suitably relieving their defects and needs, not forgetful of the maxim:

> “When wealth remains to you at the end of old age,  
> Be generous; while you live, do not be sparing toward friends.”

This man, who earned the remembrance of others, [Note: [Col. 0347D] Cf. Vergil, *Aeneid* VI, 664.] had indeed reached mature age and was approaching old age, and the saying of Wisdom suited him: “Venerable old age is not that which has endured long, nor is it measured by the number of years; for its grey hair is understanding, and a spotless life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4:9). [Col. 0348C]

This man performed many pious offices in the house of the Lord, bearing the burden and heat of the day for His praise, and he is not inappropriately compared with the prophet Samuel, who, after he was weaned, was offered in the house of the Lord with three measures of flour and an amphora of wine, to serve the Lord all the days of his life. Likewise, from his youth he offered himself—without compulsion, since God is angered by forced services, but by the free movement of his own will—to the temple of the Lord, namely the church of Prague, serving with untiring mind, manly and steadfast courage, and continual presence, for the service, praise, and glory of Jesus Christ and of the blessed martyrs [Col. 0348D] Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert, throughout all the days of his life; and he fulfilled this service to the end.

Thus it was said of Samuel: “All from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (Judges 20:1). The grace of virtues that shone in this man spread his name, by reason of the exercise of his works for the praise of God’s house, throughout the entire diocese of Prague, all its borders, and every boundary of the whole kingdom of Bohemia. For he shone in the temple of God like a lamp set not under a bushel but upon a lampstand.

He also rose from his bed at midnight before [Col. 0349A] the time for Matins, visiting all the altars in veneration of relics with genuflections and prayers. Sometimes he read through a third part of the Psalter, which we call a “fifty,” if time of such length presented itself before the ringing for Matins. Then he awakened the bell-ringers to ring for Matins, and during the ringing of the bells, leaving the church, went about knocking at the chambers of the clergy and summoning them to the office of Matins. Afterwards he entered the church and came to the choir; if he saw the priest assigned for the week, he gave him the signal to begin Matins, but if the weekly priest was absent, he did not disdain personally to perform his duties. For he delighted, in the divine office, personally to make good every deficiency in the Church neglected by its ministers.

This man never heard the secular legal cases of his dependants, but entrusted them to others to hear. He never exacted, nor accepted when offered, the fines imposed on those condemned by judges to pay a penalty. Instead, in fatherly kindness, he corrected them as sons and sometimes rebuked them more sharply, with sterner words, lest they commit like offences. For he observed the Gospel saying, “Do not judge, that you may not be judged” (Matthew 7:1), and so forth. By every means he avoided involving himself in secular affairs.

In the village commonly called Veliká Ves, where Eberhard, canon of Prague of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 0349D] Cf. above, 1257 and 1259.] had acquired certain goods for the salvation of his soul and assigned them to the church of Prague for feeding [Col. 0349C] and clothing twelve scholars, called *bonifantes* or “good boys,” who were continuously bound to serve in the said church in singing, reading, and psalmody, the same Dean Vitus built up a church in honour of Saint Lawrence, and at his own expense erected there a tower as an ornament to the work. He also obtained from Bishop John an indulgence of forty days, to be granted to the faithful of Christ who came on the dedication anniversary of the church and on other principal feast-days.

At his own expense he built another church in the village of Kojětice in honour of Saint Vitus, with stone walls and roof, and raised a tower. In the village of Sluhy [Note: [Col. 0349D] Sluch, in the district of Kouřim.] he learned by common report that the church was utterly ruined and deserted, so that not even doors remained in it; swine, wolves, [Col. 0349D] and dogs had free and frequent access to it. Lord Vitus, dean of Prague, rebuilt it from its foundations with a structure of most noble workmanship at his own cost, and erected in it a most beautiful tower in veneration of Saint Adalbert the martyr.

He also built an altar in the church of Strahov [Col. 0350A] beneath the tower, in honour of Saint Matthias the Apostle. The same dean improved a half-prebend in the village of Strachkov [Note: [Col. 0349] It was written *Strahow*, but corrected in an old hand to *Strachkow*.] by buying with his own money the manor and inheritance of a knight named [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 0349] A blank space in the manuscript.], through whom many evils had been inflicted upon that half-prebend.

Much could be said about his virtues which deserves to be related: concerning his chastity, continence, observance of fasts, sobriety, fidelity and piety, compassion for neighbours, observance of the divine commandments, and imitation of truth and justice. But lest, by more fully pursuing the deeds of each virtue divinely bestowed upon him, I should seem to incur the reproach of flattery, I have put aside my pen and preferred to leave the matter to posterity, because there are some whose memories preserve his deeds [Col. 0350B] much better.

For every gift of virtue had flowed together in him through the bounty of Almighty God, and he did not glory in this. The world was dead to him, and he to the world. For the world is said to be dead to the person whom it does not bind by its enticements; and a person is said to be dead to the world who desires nothing of the world. He did not hanker after idle talk, spectacles, or actors.

His epitaph:

> Grant, O God, that Vitus may ascend the heavenly heavens,  
> And under a holy name know the star-bearing heaven,  
> And forever enjoy an age without the laws of death. Amen.

This epitaph too was written on the stone placed over his tomb:

> He took the name Vitus from life, truly living,  
> Whose life was adorned with the morals of faith.

[Col. 0350C] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1272 [Note: [Col. 0349D] It should be read thus, and not 1271 as the manuscript has it, an error followed by writers of Bohemian history, as Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 52, observed. Richard had died on 2 April of the same year; see ibid., [Col. 0350D] p. 51.], the archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0350D] Engelbert, whom Pessina III, 7, in the passage he cited from this Chronicle, called Conrad.] and many other nobles with him were sent to King Otakar, asking him on behalf of the electors, who possessed the authority and right to elect to the imperial dignity, to deign to assume the insignia of the imperial dignity.

King Otakar, most serene, received them kindly and graciously and treated them most honourably over the course of several days. Calling together the more eminent Bohemian knights and those more mature in age and distinguished in wisdom, he carefully asked what should be done in such a matter. When the magnates and chief men had assembled in one place by royal command and deliberated, one of them, pre-eminent in rank, who at that time was chamberlain of the kingdom and [Col. 0350D] more eloquent, named Andrew [Note: [Col. 0350D] Francis I, 3, calls him “of Rýžany”; Pelzel and Dobrovský, *Scriptores rerum Bohemicarum* II.], is said to have spoken as follows:

> “O most invincible and excellent king, what mortal on earth can be compared with your power? God reigns in heaven; you rule on earth by His permission, and you exercise lordship over dukes and princes of lands, nor is there anyone who resists your [Col. 0351A] will. The peoples of diverse nations to which you are invited are unknown to you, and the outcome of events is uncertain. Sit upon the throne of your fathers. Your kingdom and power are spread more famously through the regions of the world, and your name has sounded even to the sea [Note: [Col. 0351C] The Adriatic; after the death of Duke Ulrich of Carinthia in 1269, Otakar had occupied Carinthia, Istria, and part of Friuli. See the Anonymous of Leobium. The Veronese, Feltrines, and Trevisans also submitted themselves to Otakar’s protection. Cf. Aeneas Silvius, *History of Bohemia*, ch. 27.]; now all princes of lands obey your nod. Even the emperor himself, should need arise, will obey your commands with shield and buckler in aid of your necessity.”

King Otakar, having heard these words and considering that his power was being exalted and magnified, accepted this counsel; yet declining to rise to the burdens of so great a dignity, he rewarded the envoys with magnificent gifts of gold, silver, precious gems, rings, war-horses, palfreys, and diverse and various precious objects. Having clothed them and their whole court, [Col. 0351B] he sent them back to the electors with fuller expressions of thanks.

Envoys also came several times [Note: [Col. 0351C] This seems capable of being called into doubt.] bearing the same proposal. The king received them kindly but in no way agreed to their requests; rather, after honouring them with gifts, he sent them back to the electors, returning thanks for their summons to so great a dignity.

### 276.

In the fifth year of his election, Rudolf sent envoys to Ottokar, king of Bohemia, demanding the restoration to himself of the lands, namely Styria, Austria, Carinthia, the Port of Naonis, Fioletum, and Friuli, asserting that they belonged to the Empire and were subject to his lordship.

> [Note: Col. 0351C] It was so; the first proceedings in these matters took place at Nuremberg, at the court held there by Rudolf on 19 November 1274. Ottokar was not present, although the matter concerned fiefs which he had occupied during the interregnum. Compare *Monumenta Germaniae, Leges*, II, 399, and Rudolf’s Letter 60 in Bodmann.

> [Note: Col. 0351C] Portenau Castle, Pordenone, situated in the province of Friuli, was a fief of the Church of Aquileia. In Boczek IV, 41, we find a charter of Ottokar dated 12 January 1270, in which he styles himself king of Bohemia, duke of Austria and Styria, and margrave of Moravia [Col. 0351D]. This is followed by another, written 16 February 1270, in which he adds the titles duke of Carinthia and lord of Carniola, the March, and Eger; and, on 28 August 1270, lord of the Port of Naonis. On these provinces see Ottokar’s peace with Stephen, king of Hungary, made in 1271, Boczek IV, 45.

But King Ottokar, a man of great spirit, endowed with singular skill in arranging the affairs of his realm and devoted to warfare from childhood, to whom Bellona, Fortune’s unconquered sister, gave boldness [Col. 0351C], together with success in war—confident in his power and always desirous of fighting and making war—is said to have given the envoys of Rudolf, elected emperor, the following answer:

> “The lands which Rudolf demands have never been in his possession, nor ever shall be. Some were given me as a dowry by reason of my marriage to Margaret, daughter of Leopold, duke of Austria; others I acquired with victorious hand and sword and reduced beneath my lordship. Therefore let him rule in the lands of his Empire; but over the lands which he demands from me he shall never rule.”

> [Note: Col. 0351D] In two letters written to the pope on 9 May 1275, Ottokar confirms that he is willing to submit himself to the pontiff’s arbitration, and asks that both he and Rudolf be enjoined not to attack one another while he prepares himself, in fulfilment of a vow, to bring aid to the Holy Land. In the other letter the following is said of Rudolf: “At the court held at Nuremberg he strove, and still strives, by his judgments to attempt certain measures tending to the detriment of our honour and the no small injury of our lands [Col. 0352C]; and, by his enactments, wholly contrary to every right, he devises manifold evil against us contrary to justice, as a public enemy and manifest adversary.” Compare Boczek IV, 142.

King Rudolf therefore saw and considered that he could achieve nothing by words. After the first and second admonitions, inflamed with angry wrath, he resolved to overcome King Ottokar by arms and prepared himself for war as swiftly as he could.

> [Note: Col. 352C] The second summons directed Ottokar to Würzburg, where a court was held on 23 January 1275; the third summoned him to Augsburg on 15 May of the same year. Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 68. Finally, in 1276 Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg, was sent to Ottokar in order to recall him, as one affected by the imperial ban, to peace for the last time. See Anonymous of Leoben, under 1274, and Böhmer I. I.

> [Note: Col. 0352C] You may say this is true if you read such things in Rudolf’s Letter 8 in Bodmann: “The public enemy of ourselves and of the same Empire, the most abominable betrayer of father and fatherland, whom all Austria has openly vomited forth as inveterate in the malice of perfidy.”

> [Note: Col. 0352C] This was begun on 24 June 1276; Böhmer, [Col. 0352D] p. 77.

When the king of the Bohemians learned that Rudolf was attempting to enter [Col. 0352B] his borders, he sent armies to meet him near Teplá and resist him, lest he enter his territories; but the king himself remained occupied with hunting, games, and other pleasures of courtiers.

> [Note: Col. 0352D] The plan of war first adopted by Rudolf was described by Frederick, bishop of Salzburg, in Letter 15 in Bodmann: “First harass the king of Bohemia in the regions about Bohemia, so that he may be compelled to withdraw from Austria.” But after making peace with the duke of Bavaria he changed his plan: he attacked not Bohemia, as Ottokar himself supposed, but Austria.

King Rudolf, knowing that King Ottokar had resolved to send armed Bohemian forces against him, lest he enter the land of the Bohemians, turned his steps elsewhere. He advanced along the other side of the Danube—[Note: Col. 0352D] which he had crossed at Regensburg—toward Austria, seizing castles, towns, cities, and villages, subjecting all to his authority. Passing through Passau as far as Linz, he encamped there with his forces.

> [Note: Col. 0352D] Linz, where he was in camp on 10 October; Lambacher II, 110.

When King Ottokar heard this, he ordered his forces, which were near Teplá, to come as quickly as possible to Droznovice [Col. 0352C].

> [Note: Col. 0352D] The same place as the Drosendorf mentioned a little below, on the Thaya, on the left bank of the Danube in Lower Austria.

Passing from Teplá through the provinces of Plzeň, Bechyně, and Prachatice, and [Col. 0353A] through woods and forests, they endured many evils, wandering where there was no road and not upon a road. Yet, through their innate wickedness, they did not cease from plundering the poor, sparing absolutely neither sex nor age—a fact most keenly experienced by the men of those southern provinces.

> [Note: Col. 0353C] On this devastation compare the *Chronicle of Klosterneuburg* in Rauch I.

At length, arriving at the appointed place, Drozndorf, they occupied the territory of the adjoining provinces for a length and breadth of four miles. There they pitched their tents and made camp, King Ottokar now dwelling among them, while King Rudolf was on the other side of the Danube with his forces near Korneuburg.

When the aforesaid princes had remained with their armies for seven weeks in the places mentioned above, on either side of the Danube, and saw men weakened [Col. 0353B] and failing from excessive distress, lack of provisions, and the great shortage of fodder for the horses, they sent envoys to and fro. With a truce established and security given under oath, they chose an island called Kamberk as a place to negotiate a friendly settlement and restoration of peace, Concord, the nurse of harmony, acting as mediator.

> [Note: Col. 0353C] It should be observed that Rudolf at this time advanced from Linz as far as Vienna. He began to besiege Vienna on 18 October and kept it under siege for five weeks. See the *Chronicle of Austria* in Rauch II.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] On this famine see the *Salzburg Chronicle*.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] Peace was made in the camp before Vienna, as Frederick of Salzburg proves in a letter to the pope, Pubitschka IV, 2, 420. Ottokar, in Letter 30 in Dolliner, says that the agreement was concluded beside the Danube.

Then, on the appointed day, both princes entered the aforesaid island with a few persons specially summoned for this purpose. After a lengthy discussion, they concluded the following alliance in a marriage contract: Wenceslas, son of the king of Bohemia, should take as his wife the daughter of Rudolf, the elected king; and conversely Rudolf’s son should take as his wife Ottokar’s daughter.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] Guta.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] Hartmann.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] Kunigunde.

This agreement was confirmed by the oath of each prince, in the presence of many bishops and numerous other noble ecclesiastical and secular persons. Instruments concerning the same agreement were also drawn up and authenticated by the seals of many princes as testimony.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] Werner, archbishop of Mainz; Frederick of Salzburg; Berthold of Bamberg; Leo of Regensburg; Peter of Passau; Conrad of Freising; Bruno of Brixen; Dietrich of Gurk; and John of Chiemsee. They are listed in the royal charter issued on 26 November 1276, *Monumenta Germaniae, Leges*, II, 408.

> [Note: Col. 0353D] The terms of peace were written in a charter in the camp before Vienna on 21 November 1276, through the mediation of Berthold, bishop of Würzburg; Bruno, bishop of Olomouc; Louis, count palatine of the Rhine; and Otto, [Col. 0354C] margrave of Brandenburg. This charter contains the following: “Lord O., king of Bohemia, simply and expressly relinquishes every right which he had, or seemed to have, in the lands and persons of whatever condition, namely Austria, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, the March, Eger, and the Port of Naonis.” *Monumenta Germaniae, Leges*, II, 408.

King Ottokar, seeing himself joined to Rudolf, [Col. 0354A] the elected king, by such a confederation and friendship, at Rudolf’s urging and request, and induced also by the counsel of some of his own men, offered him five banners as a sign of submission, hoping that these same banners, together with the lands which he had resigned, would immediately be restored to him.

But Rudolf, a prudent and discerning man, after consultation with his magnates, followed more mature advice and restored two banners to King Ottokar, with the lands of Bohemia and Moravia. He held him in hope of the restoration of the other lands also, alleging that he was burdened by necessities, need, and lack of resources.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] All these matters are arranged in one and the same charter of peace; therefore this author’s narrative seems scarcely deserving of belief.

These things having been completed, while the bond of peace endured most firmly between them and the roots of friendship remained unshaken, they returned joyfully to their own homes. These events took place in the year of the Lord 1276, from 12 Kalends of September to [Col. 0354B] the Kalends of December.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] The letters by which Rudolf invested Ottokar with Bohemia and Moravia were issued at Vienna on 25 November 1276; Boczek IV, 183.

Some matters that were done there at Kamberk I have preferred to pass over in silence, lest, by relating each thing as it happened, I incur the hatred of certain persons.

In the year of the Lord 1277, on 6 Ides of September, King Ottokar, forgetful of his promise, placed his daughter—whom he had betrothed to N., son of Rudolf, the elected king of the Romans—in the monastery of Saint Francis, submitting her to the rule and religious order called the Order of Poor Ladies.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] Born in 1265; compare above.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] Kunigunde did this voluntarily, if one follows Francis in Pelzel and Dobrowski II, 29.

Ten other virgins entered with her, to live under the same rule, desiring to lead a celibate life and to serve almighty God to the best of their power and as the rule of that community commanded. This girl’s entrance into, and adoption of, monastic life was regarded not only by the wise but [Col. 0354C] also by simple country laypeople as the beginning of all evil and of the ruin of the kingdom of Bohemia.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] This can scarcely be believed, since peace between Rudolf and Ottokar was again confirmed on 6 May and 12 September 1277, with certain conditions altered. Compare Böhmer, pp. 84, 88. Lambacher I, 208, and Palacký II, 267, have already proved that the cause of war here falsely alleged by our author was not the true cause.

By whose prompting or counsel King Ottokar was enticed to do this, or consented to its being done, is difficult to relate, since the matter concerns exalted persons.

> [Note: Col. 0354D] He appears to mean Queen Kunigunde, whom the monk of Fürstenfeld and, after him, many others declared to have been the author of the war.

Nor was the ancient enemy absent from the others. Supplying fuel for his deceit [Col. 0355A] and scattering seeds of discord, he never ceases to entangle humankind. He so inflamed King Ottokar’s mind with a zeal for war that, forgetting all his promises to the elected king of the Romans, he could scarcely wait for the day on which he might pour out his wrath upon him. He sends him letters more calculated to provoke quarrelling than to offer the kiss of peace.

> [Note: Col. 0355D] These he wrote at Poděbrady on 31 October 1277 concerning the Vítkovci, whom Rudolf had determined should be included in his peace with Ottokar. Compare Dolliner, p. 79.

In the same year a windmill was erected in the garden at Strahov.

In the year of the Lord 1278, on 5 Kalends of July, King Ottokar set out on an expedition against Rudolf, the elected king, toward Moravia. He stayed at Brno, awaiting the dukes of Poland and their soldiery, as well as the nobles of Bohemia and Moravia, by whose [Col. 0355B] assistance he hoped to gain victory and again subject to his dominion the lands taken from him.

> [Note: Col. 0355D] See Ottokar’s letters to the dukes of Poland in Dolliner, p. 93, in which he invites them to bring him aid. Their names, however, have been suppressed. Compare Dolliner’s observations there concerning Ottokar’s allies.

He did not reflect that the outcome of wars is uncertain; for the issue of battle is variable, and now these men, now those prevail in war. Whomever his fates oppress, they immediately lead against his will and drag though he is willing.

Having assembled their forces, they advanced to the Láva, and remained there so long as they could obtain fodder for their horses and provisions by plundering the poor.

> [Note: Col. 0355D] About the feast of Saint James, that is, 25 July, Ottokar entered Austria, according to Henry of Heimburg.

Then, arriving, they came to the fortress called Drozndorf. There they encamped, surrounded the said fortress, and set up engines and various other instruments for its assault. Seeing what was being done, Messover, a valiant knight who commanded that fortress, [Col. 0355C] and recognizing that he could not resist, surrendered the town, himself, and all that he possessed to the king’s authority.

> [Note: Col. 0355D] Stephen of Mizow in Henry of Heimburg.

When these things became known to Rudolf, the elected king—who had long since assembled a great multitude of Hungarians, Cumans, Swabians, Saxons, Austrians, Styrians, men of Cologne, Rhenish men, and other diverse peoples—he crossed the Danube and came to meet Ottokar.

> [Note: Col. 0355D] Böhmer, p. 95, has proved that not nearly as many imperial princes came to Rudolf’s assistance as the author seems to have imagined, and as Lambacher inferred from a certain charter. The author of the *Salzburg Chronicle* teaches that, apart from the bishops of Salzburg and Basel and the count of Zollern, [Col. 0356D] there were very few.

> [Note: Col. 0356D] This was done at Hainburg on the fourteenth day of August, according to the same chronicle.

King Ottokar was already near the place popularly called “Usadwora Lova Lovistie,” a wooded hill near the River Morava [COSMAS].

Meanwhile Rudolf, the elected king, prudent and wise in [Col. 0356A] a crisis, knowing when to bend and relax his bow, learned through his scouts that the king and his forces had no expectation of the enemy’s arrival, and were dispersed here and there—as is the custom of the Bohemians—in order to seize booty, while the king remained with a few men. Suddenly he rushed upon them, unprepared and unarmed; enclosing them in the form of a semicircle with innumerable forces arranged in battle lines, he shattered their tents and their army.

Fear and terror fell upon the soldiery of King Ottokar at the greatness of the arm of the elected king of the Romans. Terrified and utterly astounded, unable to resist their power, they fled. Thus it commonly happens that when men flee from [Col. 0356B] fear, they are frightened even by a movement of the breeze, and fear itself increases their fear. The strong, armed cavalry of Rudolf’s army pursued the fugitives; they killed some and wounded others.

Many of the more noble men of Bohemia, Moravia, and Poland were captured, surrounded on every side and shut in like swine in a sty. The more eminent, wealthier, and better men were selected and carried off to towns and fortresses. Imprisoned in dungeons, iron manacles, and fetters, they were tortured with most grievous torments and diverse punishments, so that they might give no small quantity of silver and gold to their captors.

But the prisoners, seeing themselves increasingly afflicted from every side by distress, tribulation, and torture, and unable by any remedy or assistance to escape the hands of their persecutors—whose demands for money remained unmet—sold their ancestral goods and ransomed themselves, desiring to preserve their lives. What would a man not give when the sword hangs over his neck? Who, placed in distress, would not gladly give for himself whatever he possessed?

Some of the fugitives, hoping to escape the enemy’s pursuit by the protection of flight, threw themselves into the River Morava, since the conflict of battle was fought beside that river, and were soon drowned.

> [Note: Col. 0356D] John of Vicenza II, 4, describes this battle with sufficient accuracy. The place where it was fought has been described differently by different writers: the town of March, the field of Gänserndorf, Stillfried, the field of Jedenspeigen near the March, and the field of Marchfeld are named now by one historian, now by another. Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 95, has carefully collected their testimonies. The battle was fought on 26 August 1278. As Rudolf himself wrote to the pope, on the day after Saint Bartholomew he pitched camp not far from Ottokar’s army; on the morning of the following Friday they came to arms—on a Friday, as Henry of Heimburg states.

> [Note: Col. 0356D] This Rudolf confirms in his letter to the pope.

Of King Ottokar’s death, however, we can say nothing certain, because different persons say different things. And so, while many wavered, it was commonly proclaimed that he [Col. 0357A] had hidden among the armies and did not appear again.

> [Note: Col. 0357D] In the monk of Fürstenfeld, printed by Böhmer, *Fontes rerum Germanicarum* I, 8, we read that Ottokar’s body was placed in an elevated spot so that those present and future might have no doubtful opinion about him and might not say that he had been carried away. Rudolf, in Letter 92 to the pope in Bodmann, left the following testimony concerning his enemy for posterity: “With gigantic bearing and spirit he defended himself with remarkable valour until some of our knights threw him down, mortally wounded, together with his charger; then at last that magnificent king lost his life along with the victory.” See also the Life of Wilbirgis in Pez II, 263.

An innumerable quantity of booty was taken by King Rudolf’s party from the wagons of the opposing side: gold, silver, vessels, silver dishes, baldachins, and other valuables and various goods; the ornaments of the royal chapel; weapons; the chargers of nobles; and other horses of greater and lesser value. Human calculation cannot estimate the loss and destruction of goods.

> [Note: Col. 0357D] That is, *baldekinus*: a most precious covering woven from gold threads and silk.

Great fear and confusion arose throughout all Bohemia and Moravia, such as had not existed since the kingdom of Bohemia began. For many plunderings and innumerable despoilings of churches were committed in the monasteries of monks, crusaders, nuns, in the houses of the Friars Minor, and in communities of other religious orders.
