> [Note: Col. 0357D] Dobrowski’s conjecture: “legions,” 2.

The Germans, having expelled, driven out, and thrust the monks of the Island Monastery [Col. 0357B] out by the neck, remained in the cloister for six weeks. They consumed all the provisions prepared for the monks, who there diligently performed the divine office and unceasingly offered their prayers to God for their benefactors, for the salvation of the living, and for the dead.

> [Note: Col. 0357D] Ostrov Monastery.

They plundered twenty-four villages belonging to that monastery of movable and immovable property, so that neither a hair nor a grain could be found. What shall I say of the other houses of religious? At Corona, where a new monastic house was being built, not even signs can be found of where the monastery had stood.

> [Note: Col. 0357D] Golden Crown.

What shall we say of the Grey Friars at Osek, of the Benedictines at Břevnov, of the ladies at Teplice and at Světec?

> [Note: Col. 0357D] Schwatz, in the Litoměřice district.

All were afflicted with like torments and similar sufferings, in grief and [Col. 0357C] bitterness. I do not dare speak of the more remote monasteries from the city of Prague, which suffered similar things, because they suffered many worse things. Of these, Vilémov was especially injured, because King Rudolf with all his power twice remained near it, and the margrave of Brandenburg and the dukes of Poland assembled there.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] The Benedictine monastery of Vilémov in the Čáslav district.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] This doubtless occurred in September or October 1278, when he had entered Moravia and Bohemia.

There were also innumerable burnings throughout Bohemia, in villages and towns; plundering of the poor of cattle, beasts of burden, other animals, and poultry of every kind; of garments, grain, and fodder for four-footed beasts.

The kingdom of Bohemia was broken up [Col. 0357D] and divided according to the pleasure and will [Col. 0358A] of Rudolf, the elected king of the Romans. The margrave of Brandenburg obtained Prague Castle with the greater part of Bohemia; the duke of Poland obtained the province of Kłodzko; and the queen received a portion together with her son Wenceslas.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] Henry IV, duke of Wrocław.

And the Gospel saying was fulfilled: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” (Matthew 12:25). Even worse omens of vain imagination were foretold for the Bohemians in the future. Moravia also is said to have been divided into several parts.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] For purposes of civil administration, Moravia was divided by King Rudolf between the bishops of Olomouc and Basel. This is established by the contemporary annalist of Zábrdovice, from whose book Boczek published fragments in his study, *Mähren unter König Rudolf I.*, *Abhandlungen der königlichen böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften*, New Series IV, 25.

Alas! With what distress and agitation Bohemia and Moravia were shaken neither I nor the more eloquent multitude of men can explain.

In the same year, on 12 Kalends of November, John, the twenty-fourth bishop of Prague, died. Exercising the office of the pontifical see, he governed the church of Prague for twenty-two years.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] The twenty-first year was not completed; see above under 1258.

He was of distinguished appearance, formidable to strangers, affable to his household, an imitator of truth, an untiring pursuer of justice, prudent in judgment, illustrious and incomparable in every quality of upright conduct; a pious comforter of mourners and a kindly receiver and visitor of guests and pilgrims. Most eloquent in both the Bohemian and Latin tongues, he was a lamp shining and burning in the world—not under a bushel, but set upon a candlestick—illuminating human hearts by the word of truth, deeds, and examples.

Although many further deeds of his and other illustrious actions are worthy of record, we leave them untouched, because some persons, themselves doing nothing good, never cease to envy the good works of others. His greatest pleasure was to seek and embrace the companionship of learned men, by whose eloquence he delighted [Col. 0358C] his mind and drank the colours of their thoughts more sweetly than liquid nectar.

For another light shone forth, like the noonday sun, surpassing in splendour, through his magnificent power, all kings, dukes, and princes: namely, Ottokar, most serene king of the Bohemians. From the very beginning of his life, placing all his hope in the protection of God alone, this Ottokar ruled the dominion of his kingdom with manly courage. He was a prince of distinguished appearance, an unconquerable king, a welcome leader in camp. Whenever he moved an army to war against any king or duke, he always returned joyfully to his own lands with great triumph.

> [Note: Col. 0358D] That this did not always happen, see above under 1257.

He was also, in the rule of his principality, inflamed with an exceeding zeal of piety [Col. 0358D] [Col. 0359A]: a merciful forgiver of those acknowledging their faults, no deaf hearer of widows, no tardy helper of orphans.

During Lent, at night, content with a single servant, he secretly entered a church and lay prostrate upon the floor, persevering in prayer until the ground on which he lay was wet with a copious rain of tears. Rising from there, he called before sunrise the official entrusted with care of the poor, in order to make the *agape*, and asked whether he had all things ready for feeding the poor.

For it was his custom throughout every Lent to feed five hundred poor persons and, on Good Friday, to clothe the same persons. At the Lord’s Supper he also washed the feet of poor persons, according to the number of the twelve apostles, giving each one a solidus of denarii.

[Col. 0359B] During Lent he also came personally to the church of Prague and approached the priests, persuading them by his requests to sing Masses for the salvation of the living, others for the souls of the faithful departed, and likewise votive Masses of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Spirit, Our Lady, the patrons, Saint Nicholas, and very many others, provided only that so many priests could be found. To the hand of every priest celebrating Mass he offered two gold coins or twelve silver denarii. We have seen these things and bear witness.

How generous this prince was, the human mind can neither comprehend [Col. 0360A] nor describe. I cannot express the innumerable gifts which he gave to foreign dukes and princes in gold, silver, horses, rings, and garments. The number of soldiers, princes, and crossbowmen in his daily retinue could not be counted.

Nobles of the land, weep in the bitterness of your hearts for your king, who clothed you in scarlet amid delights, supplied golden ornaments for your apparel, and girded you with coverings of the most precious decorations, from whose borders, dyed with purple, shining threads also hung down—the pomp of the world smiling upon you, while worldly pride swelled.

The furnishings of the royal chapel were made only from the most precious baldachins, purple, and fine linen, woven into chasubles, dalmatics, copes, and other vestments. Certain chalices were of gold and silver; and the other vessels appointed for [Col. 0360B] divine service, even down to the basins, were all made of gold. The dishes of his table also, fashioned from pure gold and finely wrought silver, were brought forward for every course, however countless the courses of his table.

What more need be said? From sunrise to sunset there was at that time no king to be found who shone with such generosity, power, and uprightness of character. How lavish and prodigal he was in gifts bestowed, I leave his deeds to posterity to explain better and more truly; I set my pen aside lest, in pursuing truth, I seem to incur the charge of flattery. For the immensity of his largesses was measureless.

> [Note: Col. 0359D] A very recent hand has here unnecessarily added *sine* (“without”), 2.

> [Note: Col. 0359D] Palacký II, 297, collected and examined the testimonies of both his supporters and his adversaries.

## IV. SECOND PART OF THE PRAGUE ANNALS

[Col. 0359]

[Col. 0359C] In the year of the Lord 1278, after Bishop John had entered upon the way of all flesh, Tobias, provost of Prague, a man of noble lineage and canonical age, was elected bishop of the see of Prague, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, by divine favour, with the willing and unanimous consent of the canons, though he himself strongly refused, on 17 Kalends of September.

> [Note: Col. 0359D] This seems to be a scribal error, for the narrative itself makes it sufficiently clear that [Col. 0360D] Tobias was elected in November, as Pessina observed in the *Phosphorus*.

While he was still holding the office of provost, he received not only the clergy of the church or city of Prague, but indeed persons arriving from whatever part of the world, with cheerful generosity as though in Christ’s gracious stead; and with charitable affection he supplied them with the necessities of life.

The canons of the church of Prague, wishing with all their strength to bring his election to completion, drew up a decree according to the form of election already observed, fortified by the seals [Col. 0359D] of all the canons. Through solemn envoys—Master Gregory, dean of Prague; Alexius, provost of Olomouc; and Theodoric, canon of Prague, men indeed honourable and prudent—they presented it to the metropolitan, the archbishop of the see of Mainz [Col. 0360C], humbly and devoutly requesting with many urgent prayers that he would mercifully deign, in his customary kindness, to confirm the election held by the Prague chapter.

They excused the absence of the elect both because of the dangers of the roads—since at that time there was the greatest upheaval and disturbance throughout the whole kingdom of Bohemia, after the king’s death, in the midst of plundering and oppression—and because of the distance of the places. They also made before the most reverend archbishop two further necessary petitions in this matter, humbly beseeching him to entrust his authority to the honourable Bruno, bishop of Olomouc, so that he might promote their elect to the rank of priest and, with two neighbouring fellow bishops joined to him, consecrate him to the dignity of the episcopal [Col. 0360D] rank.

> [Note: Col. 0360D] Werner.

The metropolitan, therefore, being a prudent and discerning man, carefully examined the decree in a regular and canonical manner with his canons and other men learned in canon law. Finding in it no ground for censure, mercifully sympathizing [Col. 0361A] with the needs of his subjects, and knowing already the grievous condition of the Bohemian land, he recognized that the Prague elect could not conveniently come into his presence because of the perils of the roads. Assenting to their just requests, and considering also that any confirmation which he might make of an absent elect would be invalid, he entrusted his authority to the bishop of Olomouc in accordance with the form of their petitions, so that, after all the articles and circumstances of the articles pertaining to the nature of the affair had been required and examined, he should grant to the elect as bishop of Prague the gifts or benefits of confirmation, promotion to the priestly rank, and consecration.

Thus the envoys of the Prague chapter obtained from the archbishop of Mainz the fulfilment [Col. 0361B] of their petitions. Having abundantly expressed their thanks according to the purpose of their desire, and received his blessing, they joyfully returned to Bohemia. On reaching the city of Prague, they were received with joy by the elect and the honourable body of canons and clergy on 11 Kalends of January.

In the year of the Lord 1279, on the Nones of January, Tobias, bishop-elect of Prague, having first sent envoys with letters of commission to the venerable bishop of Olomouc concerning confirmation of his election on behalf of the archbishop of Mainz, set out for Moravia with the honourable men Master Gregory, dean of Prague, Alexius, provost of Olomouc, and Theodoric, canons of Prague, who accompanied him, together with other chaplains of lesser and greater rank, and a large retinue of secular noblemen. [Col. 0361C] They found the bishop of Olomouc in the episcopal city called Ostrava [Note: [Col. 0361D] Ostrau.], situated beyond the province of Opava, on the borders of Poland and Moravia.

When the bishop of Olomouc learned of their arrival, he received them honourably and treated them graciously and kindly [Note: [Col. 0361D] See the very full praises of Bruno, which Richter published from the Olomouc Carthusian manuscript, p. 84.]. For it was always his custom, and still is, to rejoice at the arrival of guests. For he follows the authority which says: “It is a special consolation for noble men to receive with hospitality and to treat kindly those arriving from whatever region of the earth; and if anyone, moved by zeal for piety, receives strangers, then, inflamed by the love of charity, he burns yet more warmly toward his neighbours.”

Their business having thus been disclosed and the letters of commission presented, he [Note: [Col. 0361D] Tobias.] humbly requested that the bishop proceed in accordance with the form entrusted to him in the commission [Col. 0361D] concerning the matters promised. The bishop of Olomouc, giving ready heed to their just and honourable petitions, knowing how to sympathize with those wearied by labour and to bring consolation to the sorrowful, promised to carry out as swiftly as possible the mandate laid upon him.

At that time he had joined with him as colleague the bishop of Basel [Note: [Col. 0361D] Henry, whom Rudolf had appointed over Moravia together with Bruno.] for the performance of the royal embassies of Rudolf, king-elect of the Romans. Having accordingly taken that same bishop of Basel to execute the commission, he proceeded, according to the form entrusted to him, to an examination; and, making a diligent and careful inquiry into the circumstances, omitting nothing relevant to the execution of this affair, he brought it to completion.

When all these matters had thus been duly performed, the name of Jesus Christ having been invoked, and the privilege of confirmation having been drawn up and issued, by the authority of his metropolitan he confirmed, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, the election of Tobias as bishop of Prague, regularly and canonically celebrated by the chapter of Prague.

In the same year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0362D] An error; the following proves that this occurred before 18 February.], Tobias the elect set out, [Col. 0362B] taking from the honourable body of the church of Prague prudent men of outstanding discernment and greater learning [Note: [Col. 0361] *peritiores*, “more learned,” 2.]: namely, Master Gregory, dean of Prague; Thomas the provost; Gotfrid the provost; Werner, Ulric, Alexius, Theodoric, Peter, Sdeslaus, and Benes, canons of Prague; and other chaplains of the episcopal court. All were fully clothed in the most precious variegated undergarments and marten furs; likewise he clothed completely the nobles, knights, and squires of his court, high, middle, and low alike, with garments for each, namely with an arrow bent round the ears and marked with the insignia of their forebears. He went into Moravia, to the city of Brno, to the venerable Bruno, bishop of Olomouc. [Col. 0362C]

There he was promoted to the priestly rank by the most honourable and highly praiseworthy bishop of Seckau, on the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0362D] Pubitschka IV, 2, p. 471 observed that XII Kal. Mart. should be read, since the Sunday *Reminiscere* fell on 19 February.]. On the following day he was consecrated bishop of the see of Prague by the venerable bishops Bruno of Olomouc, of Seckau, and of Basel, on the Sunday (19 February) on which *Reminiscere* is sung, in the house of the Preachers and the church of Saint Mary the Virgin. On that day an indulgence of one year and forty days was granted.

On that same day he gave all who came, both those invited and those who came of their own accord, a solemn meal, and celebrated a most magnificent banquet, so that this day may rightly be called his birthday in every yearly cycle. Having therefore received through consecration the character of pontifical dignity, and having completed [Col. 0362D] the magnificent banquet of his birthday, while all remained healthy and unharmed, he returned joyfully to his own people with great rejoicing. The whole congregation of Prague [Note: [Col. 0361] Thus it should be read: “by the whole congregation of Prague,” 2.] and others, clergy both regular and secular, and civic clergy, received him with immense [Col. 0363A] joy—as sad children longing for the arrival of their father—on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the church of Mount Sion, with banners and processions: the clergy singing, “Behold the priest”; the laity, “*Hospodin pomiluy ny*” [“Lord, have mercy upon us”].

This occurred while, alas, the kingdom of Bohemia was still in a bad condition. For that reason the burgraves who controlled the city of Prague did not dare admit Lord Tobias, bishop of Prague, when he wished to enter, although a great multitude accompanied him. May the almighty Creator and Governor of the whole world, who has decreed that you should ascend to pontifical honour [Note: [Col. 0363] A later hand inserted this here, not 2.] by your merits, deign to grant you, for the profit gained from the sheep entrusted to you, the crown of glory.

In the same year, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, when the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary then fell, Lord Tobias, bishop of Prague, [Col. 0363B] wishing to celebrate the first Mass after his episcopal consecration in the cathedral church of Saint Vitus, was denied entrance to Prague Castle by the burgraves, who seemed to govern the commonwealth of the Bohemian land in the manner of men too simple and slow of understanding [Note: [Col. 0363] *videbantur*, “seemed,” 2.], though, to speak more truly, they were striving to destroy it.

He celebrated the solemn Mass of the Annunciation of the glorious Virgin in the church of Mount Sion, not without a considerable furrowing of his brow; yet he was moved by a just and pious reason to perform there the offices of the Blessed Virgin, since that church had been consecrated in honour of Blessed Mary, and the height, breadth, and length of the church, as well as the beauty of its work like that of Solomon’s temple, together with the great multitude of people coming there, prompted him to do so.

How great a concourse was assembled for the celebration of that first Mass—clerics, nobles, barons, knights, citizens, laymen, country people, married women, beguines, widows, children, youths, and virgins—may be understood from this: if that same multitude had been armed and united by the will of all into one body, the city of Prague, while their pledged resolve endured, would have remained unconquerable and unshaken through many periods of time [Note: [Col. 0364] *permanerent*, “would remain,” 2.]. On that day of the Blessed Virgin, the canons of Prague and all clerics were served in the house of the lord bishop with an abundance of fish, wine, and mead.

In the year of the Lord 1280 [Note: [Col. 0363D] It should be read “the year 1280”; see below. The manuscript falsely gives the number 1282.], autumn ended warmly, but winter was harsh and snowy. Its severity lasted until the Annunciation of Blessed Mary (25 [Col. 0363D] March); and after the melting of the snow there was, within twenty days, a great [Col. 0364A] flooding of waters, such that mills could not, because of the excessive abundance of water, be restored to their places and properly set up during the days mentioned.

In the same year there was a great dearth of all things: grain, meat, fish, cheese, and eggs; scarcely two hens’ eggs could be bought for a penny, although many still remembered that, not many years previously, fifty eggs had been bought for a penny in the city of Prague.

In the same year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, a truce was made between Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, and the nobles of the land [Note: [Col. 0363D] This peace was at last established when Rudolf made his second expedition into Bohemia in 1280; he eventually compelled Margrave Otto to cease hostilities, as Henry of Heimburg proves. Compare the Chronicle of Osterhof, in Rauch I, 516, and the Austrian Chronicle, ibid., II, 276. Rudolf himself was still in camp on 18 November 1280, in the district of Čáslav. Böhmer, *Regesta*, p. 104. These also prove that the events recorded here occurred not in 1282 but in 1280, as Palacký observed, II, 329.]. Yet many hoped rather that peace had been made, because from that time wrongdoers ceased inflicting injuries, plundering, violating churches, carrying off cattle and [Col. 0364B] draught animals, detaining and torturing people, and compelling them to wear sacks, mats, and litters.

Nothing was sown that year for winter crops except in districts remote from Prague; and where it was sown, it was nevertheless only in small quantity. Therefore grievous famine tormented the poor, and many needy persons, overcome by hunger, died.

In the same year, on the Nones of January, all the bells in Prague began to ring at the highest pitch [Note: [Col. 0363D] The narrative itself sufficiently shows that this could not have occurred in that year, but in the following year, 1281; and it is also apparent from the fact that above Tobias, bishop of Prague, is said to have been forbidden to enter the church in February 1279. Here we see that this exclusion lasted two years.]. For two years they had not rung, for many reasons, since neither the guards nor the bell-ringers of the Prague church were admitted into the castle to perform their office in the church. Indeed, more than this: even the vicars and the canons of Prague themselves, wishing to render to God the office due to Him, were not granted entrance to the castle, except for a few: [Col. 0364C] namely Andrew alone, sacrist and canon of Prague; Chwalec, the cantor; George, sub-sacrist, priest, minister of the altar of Saint Mary, and vicar; and Master Gregory, although he was dean of the same church, was nevertheless frequently denied entrance to the city.

In the year of the Lord 1281 [Note: [Col. 0364D] The matters following from this point to the end are, chronologically considered, disordered and partly scattered through scribal carelessness. Yet the material here down to the words “abundant supply” must in fact be assigned to 1281. I am chiefly persuaded by the fact that the third year of Bishop Tobias is reckoned (cf. 1278), and that the author shortly above relates that the bishop and canons had been prevented from entering the church of Prague until 5 January 1281.], on the eighth day before the Ides of March, Tobias, by God’s grace bishop of Prague, held ordinations in the church of Prague, the first since the ordination of his episcopate. The multitude of candidates for consecration was great; the ordination, begun in the morning, could scarcely be completed in the whole day. Thus communion of the Eucharist for those then ordained priests was postponed until the following day. On the same day Master Gregory, dean of Prague, was ordained priest.

And [Col. 0364D] although at this time many worldly cares and the surging waves of various disturbances were increasing against the same lord bishop—alienations of episcopal possessions, innumerable plunderings of the goods of the bishopric and of his poor—so that some scarcely thought he could supply sustenance for himself and his court even from provisions, nevertheless, on the day after the promotion of the clergy, on the Sunday on which *Reminiscere* is sung, the anniversary of his consecration, sparing neither the labours he had endured in ordaining the clergy nor the expense, he placed, according to the custom of his predecessors, an episcopal candle in the church of Prague, containing 220 pounds of wax, in honour and praise of the blessed martyrs Vitus, Wenceslas, and Adalbert, in the third year of his pontificate.

He also personally celebrated [Col. 0365B] the offices of the Mass on that day, and most generously provided a meal for the canons of Prague and all other arrivals, with an abundance of fish of different kinds and a plentiful supply of wine and mead.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of July of the preceding year [Note: [Col. 0365D] That is, 1280, which the Austrian Chronicle in Rauch II reports to have abounded in floods and storms.], that is, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, rain fell after noon in the greatest quantity and caused much severe damage. It utterly overthrew the masonry buildings in Prague Castle around the church of Saint George; it tore out the castle wall facing north from its foundations and hurled it with force into the stream Bruska.

Likewise, in the Prague church, all the vaults of the cloister in the long northern passage were broken; and half of the whole cloister and the refectory [Note: [Col. 0365] *refectorio*, “refectory,” 2.], together with the castle wall, [Col. 0365C] were shifted from their place, and all threatened collapse. In woods beside running streams, countless trees were uprooted by the force of the rain. Moreover, countless hills and caves collapsed from the abundance and violence of the rainwater. How many buildings—vineyard walls, houses inside and outside the walls of Prague city, beyond counting—it carried away and swept into the rivers!

It erased and dug up public roads and other ways in its course, like ditches around fortified castles—some places six cubits deep and twelve wide, and each place more or less accordingly. In the fields before the city walls, at the place called *na Skitine*, such [Col. 0366A] a gathering of water occurred that boats could have been steered there by sailors as on the Tiber or the Danube. This water, flowing down to the church of Saint Peter in the German quarter, caused much damage: it overthrew the walls of their court, and flowing into the church, cast down a great quantity of grain which the parishioners had stored for fear of the war then being waged between Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, and the barons of the kingdom of Bohemia and the citizens of Prague.

From there the rain-swollen stream carried away twelve houses and swept them into the river Vltava; and the very many evils arising from the course of that rain could not be explained in a long sequence of words.

Nor should the violence of the winds be omitted. In the same year, on the third day before the Nones of December, that is, on the feast day of Blessed Barbara, they arose and by their force and swift violence [Col. 0366B] threw down exceedingly heavy and strong structures from towers. On the tower called the Greater Gate of Prague Castle, the first building fell to the ground; the second building opposite the house and court of the lord bishop, formerly called the Episcopal Tower, built at the front of the castle with very strong and skilful workmanship, also fell. A third structure, upon the tower near the foot of the bridge, a noble and exceedingly strong work, was driven down by the force of the winds and collapsed to the ground.

We cannot specify the other smaller buildings constructed on the towers of the fortifications or battlements; but according to what we have learned from reliable report, twenty-four tower buildings within Prague Castle and the city walls fell through the force of the winds. There is no need to count how many houses fell by the force of the wind in Prague and outside it. In the countryside, barns were demolished by the winds, as were fruit trees and forest trees—events of a kind which are not said to have occurred from ancient days.

What good or ill Spakmannus, Syberk, and Sazema, with their companies, did at their stations beneath Mount Petřín during that unsettled time need not be set forth in writing, since it is believed to be sufficiently recorded among those who endured the troubles of diverse sufferings and the loss of their property. The windmill at Strahov utterly collapsed through the force of the wind and was rebuilt in the same year.

## V. THIRD PART OF THE ANNALS OF PRAGUE

[Col. 0365D] In the year of the Lord 1279 [Note: [Col. 0365] 1282, 2.] [Note: [Col. 0365D] That this narrative must be connected with the year 1279, since Margrave Otto had already come into Bohemia in 1278, is attested by the anonymous author of Zábrdovice in Bruk’s *Mähren unter Kaiser Rudolf I*, and by the Salzburg and Austrian Chronicles. If one follows Pulkava, Otto undertook the guardianship of the kingdom by Otakar’s own disposition.], Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, guardian of Duke Wenceslas, son of the most serene [Col. 0366D] King Otakar of Bohemia, and of the whole kingdom [Note: [Col. 0366D] In his charters Otto called himself the guardian and captain-general of the illustrious Lord Wenceslas in the kingdom of Bohemia. See Palacký’s commentary, *Ueber Formelbücher*, p. 315.], on the seventh day before the Ides of January sent certain Prague canons, [Col. 0367A] his chaplains, to search for certain charters of King Otakar.

He also, pricked by the spur of greed and avarice, sent knights and many Germans under deceit and fraud, forgetful of eternal salvation, secretly commanding them to seek out and discover where the money of Prosinco, King Otakar’s *vulerius* [Note: [Col. 0367] This appears to be the same as *bladerius*, *wladarius*, that is, a seller of grain or a steward.] and *gratiarius* [an official designation of uncertain meaning], and of many others, had been deposited. For the land of Bohemia was still then in a bad state, disturbed by plundering, robbery, and fires; and many laymen and clerics had therefore carried together their possessions and deposited them in the treasury of Prague: gold and silver, cups, rings, necklaces, and all manner of precious clothing. For no better, firmer, or safer refuge could be found than the sanctuary of the Prague church for keeping deposited goods [Col. 0367B] [Note: [Col. 0367D] *dispositarum*, “of goods placed there,” 2.].

Entering, therefore, the sanctuary of Jesus Christ and the blessed martyrs, they trampled the priestly ornaments underfoot, defiled and overturned the relics of the saints, and, laying impious hands upon them, searched for treasures of money, thinking permissible what, because of the sanctity of the place, was not permitted them. They seized chests; weighing the heavier boxes, they broke them open with axe and hatchet.

Seeing the commission of so grave a crime and the inhuman profanation of the holy things in the sanctuary by the sons of God, the canons of Prague and the other ministers of the church, touched by overwhelming grief, said with kneelings and groans: “Lord Jesus Christ, thy holy things have been trampled and defiled; thy priests lie in mourning and humiliation; and behold, the nations have gathered together to destroy us” [Col. 0367C] (1 Maccabees 3:51).

But they, harder than stones—as is the most savage nature of the Germans—kindled by the heat of anger and readily rushing headlong into evil, dishonoured the ministers of the church. Setting aside fear of God, they abused them with insults, contumelious words, and blows, thrusting fists beneath their beards; they struck others, dragged them away roughly, and expelled them. Having violently taken the sacristy keys from the sacrist, they shut and bolted the doors, set guards, and departed.

Then, entering the chapel of Saint Wenceslas, they rushed to his tomb, examining and feeling it everywhere above and below, seeking money where it can scarcely or never be found when it has not been placed there. One of those Germans, a servant of the devil, had at his instigation [Col. 0367D] secretly stolen a silver censer in the chapel of Saint Wenceslas; but, by the favour of divine grace and the aid of the blessed martyrs, struck by extreme fear, he returned it safe and sound to the ministers of the church.

Then, like tracking hounds, entering the crypt of Saints Cosmas and Damian, they ran about from corner to corner; and, finding nothing, they counted the chests deposited there, tested the heavier ones by lifting them, and carefully marked them, lest they be exchanged and lighter ones put in their place. They deliberated [Col. 0368A] concerning the keys—whether the keys should be taken and presented to the margrave or left with the sacrist.

Finally, having taken the keys by force from the sacrist, they set guards in the crypt and chapel, within and outside the church on every side, commanding them to guard carefully and diligently, as they loved to preserve the eyes in their heads; then they withdrew. Thus for two days and a night neither books, candles, nor any equipment necessary for the worship of the divine office could be obtained from them.

On the next day, not departing from their original purpose, in accordance with the command imposed upon them, they opened the doors, entered the sanctuary of the blessed martyrs, seized an immeasurable quantity of money, and immediately presented it to their lord. Nor did they regard the perpetration of such a deed as horrible, because by doing similar things they had already made a practice of it in many monasteries and other churches. Unless they are restrained from such utterly criminal presumptions by the power of Jesus Christ, they cannot be held back by human shame or correction.

Although elsewhere it is said: “In the propagation of offences, licence cannot be abolished unless censure follows among them for the correction of discipline.” And we remember that it has been promulgated in the laws of the emperors: “We determine that crimes not committed only once shall not receive pardon, nor shall the humanity of imperial liberality be extended to those who have reckoned impunity for an earlier offence as an encouragement to habit rather than to amendment.”

O money, queen of every evil, friend of fraud and deceit, enemy and foe of faith and soul: you suppress justice and overturn just judgments; you are consuming fire, the seditious tinder; you recall humankind from the worship of God and cause it to wander, placing it in the place of error and perdition of the soul! At your instigation, inflamed by the spur of greed and avarice, the Brandenburgers seized what belonged to others, knowing it was not theirs. They gave no heed to the fact that in the Old Testament not robbery only, but even avaricious retention is punished, as Blessed Gregory explains in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke: “With what punishment must one be punished who steals another’s goods, if he is struck with the damnation of hell because he does not give away his own?”

For secular laws and imperial constitutions have likewise provided that it is lawful for no one forcibly to seize another’s property. Even one who, led by some error, thinks a thing his own and, ignorant of the law, seizes it with the intention that an owner may take his own property by force from possessors, is subject to an established penalty, so that robbers may not exercise their avarice with impunity—indeed, to prevent even such thoughts. This is to be understood of a thing lent, hired, pledged, or deposited.

We know also that a canon of *latae sententiae* has been promulgated against all violators of churches, by which they are stained with the mark of infamy and excluded from lawful acts, unless, after first rendering appropriate satisfaction, they are absolved by the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0369A] In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, Paul Beruth forcibly occupied the fortress of Lord Tobias, bishop of Prague, at Roudnice, and the town, and subjected it to his own lordship. He also occupied the court of the lord bishop in the city of Prague, where a great supply of grain, wine, hams, and cheeses had been stored, and appropriated it to his own control.

That same margrave of Brandenburg, touched by no repentance for the perpetration of so grave a crime, his mind still savage and not receding from his conceived evil purpose, did not fear, in the storm of night, while all things lay silent and given to sleep, to disturb the most serene queen of Bohemia with her only and tender son Wenceslas. He ordered his knights and servants to carry her and the boy, unwilling and resisting, scantily clothed, to [Col. 0369B] a carriage and take them to Bezděz Castle [Note: [Col. 0369D] Besig, in the district of Boleslav. See Peter, abbot, *Chronicle of Aula Regia*, ch. 9, in Dobner, vol. V.] through precipitous ways and the hiding places of darkness, although even in broad daylight such a journey, because of the excessive speed of travel, was scarcely possible for people so delicate without immense terror and alarm.

What disturbance with grief of heart, what weeping and groaning then arose from the lady queen, her son, the entire court and household of the queen, and especially the ladies, I do not believe is recorded as having had its equal even in the slaughter of the Innocents and the children of Rachel.

Having brought the lady queen with her dearest son, they placed her, as the margrave commanded, in the very strong fortress of Bezděz, in a confined place under the guard of the most savage foreign Germans, altogether denying all Bohemians [Col. 0369C] entrance to them, except scarcely three persons, who supplied them with food and other necessities required for the sustenance of human life. From that hour the court and household of the lady queen, which had grown very numerous in noble squires, young ladies, and servants and officials of other knights, was diminished and dispersed.

Seeing the lady queen and her son distressed by overwhelming anxiety of grief and intense affliction of sorrow, the barons and elders of Bohemia wished to provide them some remedy. At a general assembly held on behalf of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, at which oaths of loyalty were demanded from all nobles, these nobles among the other negotiations obtained from the margrave, by their petitions, that he should bring the lady queen and her son back from Bezděz Castle and place them in Prague, where the seat of the king of Bohemia and of the whole kingdom is undoubtedly situated, and where the young duke had been born and brought up. For children take greater comfort in dwelling in the place of their birth.

The lord margrave assented to the nobles’ petitions and indeed promised generously, but [Col. 0370A] did not fulfil his promise at all. When the lady queen learned of the margrave’s fraud and deceit and the breach of his promises—that none of them had been put into effect; that he had not consented to the nobles’ petitions; and that, imprisoned in such a confined place, she could not escape the severe troubles and hardships which she suffered each day by any remedy—she silently considered in her heart how she might escape such most bitter afflictions [Note: [Col. 0369D] See Cunigunde’s letters written to Rudolf concerning Margrave Otto, Bodmann, p. 96.].

For she feared, from so sinister a beginning, that a worse fortune would follow; for authority says: “From such a sinister beginning a greater calamity in the future is feared more than a fortunate outcome is hoped for”; and again: “Things begun with an evil beginning scarcely come to a good end.”

The lady queen therefore began at intervals to ask permission [Col. 0370B] from Burgrave Hermann, who was in charge of that castle at Bezděz, to visit the town of Vristad, where a church in honour of Saint George the martyr stood, for the purpose of prayer. For on that day the feast of Saint George occurred. The same Burgrave Hermann, assenting to the lady queen’s request, gave her free permission to go wherever she pleased, but on condition that she leave the children in the castle and, once her business was done, return to the children. And this was done in the manner stated: she came and returned.

Again, after several days, she requested permission to visit the Grey Monks at Hradišt; obtaining it, she went, and on that day ate in the same town, the monastery providing her food. A third time, receiving permission, she came to the city of Mělník, which [Col. 0370C] was specially hers; she stayed there three days at the expense of the townspeople, and returned to Bezděz.

She further sought permission to come to Prague to her sister [Note: [Col. 0369D] Daughter of Otakar.] Agnes. Having obtained it, she came; and after arranging her affairs there, she pretended that she wished to go into Moravia for the funeral rites of her husband, King Otakar. Having set out, although she was expected to go to Moravia, she turned her steps toward Opava [Note: [Col. 0370D] To Nicholas, duke of Troppau, illegitimate son of King Otakar. See Pulkava, under this year.], and thus cleverly and wisely escaped the hardships and vexations she suffered at German hands. For lies sometimes are useful: to be deceived in matters not pertaining to faith is either no sin or a slight one.

After a few days, Otto the margrave appointed the bishop of Brandenburg [Note: [Col. 0370D] Eberhard. See Peter of Aula Regia, chs. 9–11.] over the whole kingdom, giving him [Col. 0370D] all authority and power as to a true protector, that he might govern, protect, and defend it and punish wrongdoers. Then, saying that he was hindered by most pressing necessities, he departed for Saxony.

The bishop of Brandenburg, therefore, set to the care of others, was bound by the office and authority entrusted to him, together with the others appointed with him for this purpose, to punish by the penalties established in secular law those transgressors who committed robberies, plundering, and harassment of all oppressed persons, inflicting due punishments upon the guilty. Yet he passed by with deaf ear and blind eye and consented to the deeds of evildoers, who through the works of their hands and their most criminal acts are without any doubt assigned to hell. He gave no heed to the decrees of the holy Fathers, who say: “He is convicted of consenting who, when able, neglects to oppose the wicked.” Nor is one free from the stain of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

At that time all monasteries of monks—Cistercians, Grey Monks, Black Monks, Cross-bearers, nuns, canons, and other clerics—throughout the kingdom of Bohemia were despoiled. The possessions also of poor country people were not once but repeatedly, indeed innumerably, consumed by fire to ashes: horses, cattle, and all things that [Col. 0371B] could be found. No day passed without plunder.

Meanwhile, Lord Gregory, dean of Prague, came with such other canons as he could obtain to the presence of the bishop of Brandenburg, humbly asking that the goods of the Prague provostship should not be plundered. For at that time nearly the entire property of the provostship of Prague had been despoiled: in the city of Prague—in the custody of the provostship, more than three hundred royal measures of grain of different kinds had been taken away—and in the villages, not merely horses, cattle of diverse kinds, and grain, but in most places all had been reduced to ashes. Some buildings had been carried off, and among all poultry not a hair nor feather could be found.

But the bishop of Brandenburg did not grant the just and so humble prayers of Master [Col. 0371C] Gregory, dean of Prague, and of the other canons, nor did he pity the church’s loss and damage. Burning with excessive fury—as it is the custom of Germans to rage with extreme zeal against Bohemians—he uttered so terrible a statement that the ears of whoever heard it rang.

The statement was this: “Not only shall the property of Provost Gotfrid be plundered, but also that of the other canons, especially those who follow Lady Queen Cunigunde and serve as her chaplains. We add also that we shall pursue the goods of the bishop, not only in property but also in his person, wherever we can.”

Would that their arrow were turned back upon themselves! For:

> No law is more just  
> [Col. 0371D] than that the contriver of death be slain by his own art.  
> [Note: [Col. 0371D] Ovid, *Ars amatoria* I, 655.]

But alas: affliction is still added to the afflicted. For from that time such indignation of the Lord arose against the Bohemians, especially the country people, that, as has been said:

“Whenever kings run mad, the Achaeans pay the penalty” [Note: [Col. 0371D] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14.]. God punished them through the peoples of various nations, just as he once punished and afflicted the people of Israel when it sinned. They wandered through mountains, caves, and hollows of the earth, concealing their goods and their bodies in forests and wooded places of desolation, until winter came and snow fell. Then they could find no places suitable for dwelling, where they might shelter themselves along with their possessions and livestock, [Col. 0372A] for, pursued by enemies, they were tracked down like wild beasts by hounds following footprints impressed in the snow, and captured. Once captured, they were stripped of their goods and clothes and subjected to grievous tortures so that they might ransom themselves with money. Those stripped of clothing and goods, who lacked money, went about in sacks, bedding-cloths, and mats, covering their shameful nakedness [Note: [Col. 0372D] This refers to what is read above under the year 1280.], tormented by the stings of diverse punishments. At Mělník many were stretched upon wheels, hurled from a hill into the River Elbe, and drowned; others were butchered, others killed by the sword, others reduced to bondage in chains, others burned by fire. Some, too, afflicted by severe hunger and bitter cold, expired under innumerable other and various sufferings.

We heard and saw more and more varied tortures in these times [Col. 0372B] than we read of in books. And although in the times of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian the greatest persecution of Christians is said to have occurred, this one seems, when its cause is considered, to have been greater. There, people of differing worship—pagans and Saracens—were against Christians; here, both sides were baptized. There, the faithlessness of pagans and heretics was flourishing; here, the Christian faith endured in the firmness of its strength. There, the purpose was that Christians should depart from the faith and rite of the Christian religion; here, no mention was made of such things, and, with not even a trace of guilt apparent in other matters, they were oppressed like sheep by wolves. And that prophetic utterance came upon them: “The king of Assyria shall lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to Egypt’s shame” (Isa. 20:4), etc.

Many clergy also, [Col. 0372C] both secular and religious, and laypeople who had gathered in lodgings in fortified towns, together with the other inhabitants, were stripped of their goods, worn down by disturbances, afflicted by tribulations, harassed by various persecutions, dried up by heavy sorrows and unutterable groans, lacerated by reproaches, plunged into the depths of misery by the various pains of tempests, and terrified by harsh threats. Some, outside the walls of towns, breathed forth their souls to heaven after being fatally wounded with cruel wounds. And that prophetic saying was fulfilled: “Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and inside terror” (Deut. 32:25).

As for the fact that in Prague Castle, in the royal palace, very many people from whom money was hoped for were tortured to death by punishments of various kinds, [Col. 0372D] I preferred to pass it over in silence rather than recount in writing the shameful deeds perpetrated there, lest so solemn a place, worthy of every praise, be polluted by the filth of most unclean defilements and the foul utterance of words.

In many places in books we find that an entire household or province ought to be punished for the sin of one person; indeed, this is evident from very many examples. Because of Ahab’s sin, his descendants lost the throne of the kingdom. Because of David’s sin, the sword of the Lord raged against the people; yet the glory of a king lies in a populous nation, while the diminishing of the people is the ruler’s ruin. Therefore he who took pride in the multitude of his people was justly punished through its diminution, as is read in the histories [Col. 0373A] of the kings, where David, struck with grief, lamented, saying: “It is I who have sinned; I have acted wickedly. But what have these sheep done?” (2 Sam. 24:17).

Because of the sin of the Sodomites, their little children, who through the privilege of age did not know their fathers’ crimes, were consumed by heavenly fire. Because of the sin of the Amalekites, not only their little children but also their brute animals were commanded by the Lord to be destroyed. Because of the sin of Dathan and Abiram, authors of schism against Moses, not only they themselves, but all their possessions, together with them and their children, went down to hell. Because of the sin of the citizens, the treasures of Jericho were placed under the ban; hence Achan, who stole a golden bar and certain other precious objects, is said to have taken from what was under the ban. Because of the sin of the Egyptians, their possessions were delivered to hail, and their beasts [Col. 0373B] and firstborn were consumed by death. Because of the sin of the Israelites, the ark of the Lord was delivered to the Philistines. Because of Achan’s sin, the Israelite people was defeated by the hand of its enemies. Because of the sin of Eli’s sons, the people fell into the hands of the Philistines. Because of Ham’s sin, his son Canaan was cursed. Because of Gehazi, who sold Naaman the gift of healing, he was made leprous by Elisha’s vindication and lost that same gift of health.

In the Book of Kings one reads also of other kings to whom, by divine will, it was permitted to afflict, take captive, and conquer by war the people of Israel and other nations. Yet those who ascribed the victories they had won to their own power rather than to divine power were punished by God. Nebuchadnezzar, who had gained Egypt and Ethiopia, when in pride he said, [Col. 0373C] “Is not this Babylon, which I have built as the throne of my kingdom?” (Dan. 4:27), etc., was immediately deprived by God of his rational mind and clothed with brutish bestiality, so that, fleeing from people, he lived among beasts. Against the pride of Sennacherib, who gloried in the victory he had gained, ascribing it to his own power rather than to divine power, the Lord said: “Shall the saw boast against him who saws with it? Shall the axe exalt itself against him who hews with it?” (Isa. 10:15).

Concerning Antiochus and other kings who fell because of their sins, it is likewise read that God punished the Amorites, Canaanites, and other nations through the children of Israel, giving their lands for possession to the Israelites as they came forth from Egyptian bondage. One reads [Col. 0373D] also in the Book of Judges concerning Jabin, king of the Canaanites, and the Midianites, that because of the people’s idolatry God raised them up to afflict Israel and occupy its land. But when the people of God, long afflicted under their hands, acknowledged their sin and appeased the Lord through repentance, Barak, accompanied by Deborah, prophetess and wife of Lapidoth, by God’s command crushed Jabin, king of the Canaanites, [Col. 0374A] and Sisera, commander of his army; Gideon delivered Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of the Midianites, and Oreb and Zeeb, their leaders, to death.

All these things set forth above befell the Bohemians in those times; but whether by God’s judgment this came because of the sin of the king, the princes, persons of middling rank, or the lowliest, is unknown. Yet we know that he fed us with the bread of tears and gave us drink in tears by measure; nevertheless, we rejoiced for the days in which he humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evils. May he have mercy on Zion, for the time to pity her has come—indeed, the time has come. May he now turn our mourning into joy, so that, living, we may praise him at every time. Divine vengeance rebukes a ruler together with his sinning people, and the character of the retribution shows the magnitude of the offense.

[Col. 0374B] In the year of the Lord 1281 [Note: [Col. 0373] An ancient hand noted the year 1282 in the margin.], Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, guardian of Wenceslas, duke of the Bohemians, held a conference between the Nativity of the Lord (25 December) [Note: [Col. 0373] 1280.] and the Circumcision (1 January) with Tobias, bishop of Prague, and the nobles of the land, knights, barons, and also citizens of fortified towns. At this conference, with the consent of all, the margrave appointed Tobias, bishop of Prague, chief governor of the entire land, to whom all who were oppressed by violence, despoilment, or any injuries whatsoever might have recourse. He also associated with the lord bishop Theobald [Note: [Col. 0374D] *Theobad’* in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0373D] Of Riesenburg. Palacký II, 333.], judge of the whole kingdom, and other officials, to correct secular offenses and crimes, restrain criminals and all evildoers by sentences of worldly law, and, if the crime [Col. 0374C] deserved it, assign them even to capital punishment.

For in those times so great a multitude of Germans of various foreign nations—nobles, persons of middling rank, and the lowest—had poured into the land of Bohemia that many judged their number to exceed the multitude of flies. But the lord bishop, as a prudent and discerning man, wishing accordingly to assist the safety of the commonwealth, and considering it an extreme evil that so great a multitude of alien nations had crept into the land of the Bohemians, through whom it was being laid waste in goods and persons, first conceived in his mind a reduction of their numbers. He persuaded the nobles of the land to support petitions to be presented to Otto the margrave [Note: [Col. 0374D] There is an error; it seems one should read: “petitions of this kind to be presented.”], and, to the extent of their power, to watch over the project of inducing the lord margrave so that they might be utterly [Col. 0374D] uprooted from Bohemia.

All the nobles of the land also promised to obey the just commands of the lord margrave and to render him in all things the reverence due to him as their true lord. Therefore the lord margrave, having heard and seen the innumerable evils committed by the Germans of foreign nations [Col. 0375A] and considering also the obedience and submission which the nobles had promised to render, accepted their petitions, promising to bring the matter to effect as soon as possible. Thus, making little delay—or, rather, none—he ordered messengers to be sent through the towns and market places, to proclaim and announce by the voice of a herald that all foreign Germans who had entered Bohemia for the purpose of seizing plunder must depart freely, without any hindrance, within three days, setting aside every delay. He added the penalty that, should any of them not depart within three days, they should be punished by the grave sentence by which robbers, thieves, brigands, and nocturnal housebreakers are punished.

When the Germans heard this, allowing themselves no interval of delay, they set out in haste as though wounded by a poisoned dart; and, as bats hide themselves at dawn when daylight shines, so the Germans vanished as smoke vanishes. From that time, the inhabitants of the land, knowing of the Germans’ departure, were restored in more cheerful spirit. Those who had been dwelling in forests and woods returned to their own homes; and from that hour each person set hand to work: the ploughman began to labor at the plough, the smith in his forge, the carpenter at building, the woman with distaff and spindle, and every craftsman began to toil at his own work, holding fuller confidence in the concord of the princes and the growth of peace.

At the same conference, moreover, an agreement was made between the lord margrave and the nobles of the land in the following form: on the feast of the apostles Philip and James (1 May) of the same [Col. 0375C] year, the nobles of Bohemia were to give the margrave of Brandenburg, from a general levy upon the entire land, 15,000 marks of Prague-weight silver. The lord margrave, after bringing Duke Wenceslas [Note: [Col. 0375D] Whom, according to Peter of Zittau, he had ordered taken into Saxony, that is, the land of Brandenburg.] back to Prague Castle, to the seat of his father King Ottokar, was to entrust him for safekeeping to Tobias, lord bishop of Prague, and to other nobles of the land, with certain Brandenburgers and certain trustworthy citizens of Prague attached, so that they might care for him under diligent custody according to the arrangement which the lord margrave and the nobles of the land should decree.

When the stated term arrived, namely the feast of the apostles Philip and James, the lord margrave sent his messengers and letters to excuse [Col. 0375D] his absence, saying that he was occupied by very pressing affairs and could therefore not be present at the appointed term. Nor did he promise to present Duke Wenceslas to their sight, but requested that another date be assigned to him—the Nativity of St John the Baptist (24 June)—on which, without any hesitation or pretense, he promised to present Duke Wenceslas to the nobles’ view according to the form set down above. When the assembly of Bohemian nobles heard this, although they were greatly troubled at the frustration of their hope and the impulses of their minds differed in many wishes, [Col. 0376A] nevertheless, lest a greater evil follow, they acquiesced in the appointed date, content with the proverb: “The lips of princes ought not to be polluted by the invention of a lie.”

In the year of the Lord 1282, a most severe famine of all things fit for human consumption destroyed the people of many lands [Note: [Col. 0376D] On this most savage famine see also the monk of Fürstenfeld in Böhmer I.]. But, passing over foreign matters, I shall proceed to the pressures and straits of the Bohemians’ calamities, for evils without number surrounded Bohemia on every side. Through oppressions, despoiling, nocturnal breakings-in, arson, and the consuming of every sort of possession, enemies brought famine into their midst; pursuing their lives, they seized their life upon the earth and reduced their glory to [Col. 0376B] dust.

Therefore the heart of the Bohemians was troubled within them, and the fear of death fell upon them, because God exalted the right hand of those who crushed down the king of Bohemia; he made his enemies rejoice, turned back the sword of his assistance, did not aid him in battle, destroyed him, dashed the seat of his throne to the ground, shortened the days of his time, drenched him in confusion, brought him down to hell, and numbered him among the dead. Since not only kings themselves but also peoples are punished for the sins of kings, as the prophet testifies, who, seeing the angel striking the people, said: “It is I who have sinned; I have acted wickedly. But what have these sheep done?” (2 Sam. 24:17); and in Pharaoh, who not only was himself drowned in the Red Sea while pursuing the Israelite people, [Col. 0376C] but not one of them survived; and similar things happened to many other kings.

It remains, therefore, to speak of the poorer Bohemians, who had formerly abounded in goods and great wealth. Having lost all these through raids and plundering, they went from door to door begging with the destitute, and fell from hunger into death. Thus the poor, compelled by extreme hunger, went about the lanes, streets, and citizens’ houses of Prague, asking alms. Since the multitude of poor people had now grown excessive, the wealthier people were unable to suffice for them in distributing alms. So they turned away at evening and suffered hunger like dogs; pressed by starvation, they murmured. And that saying of David was fulfilled: “They shall wander about for food; if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur” [Col. 0376D] (Ps. 53:16).

Countless craftsmen and workers in various trades also begged—some of whom had possessed property worth one hundred marks of silver. Stripped of all this, some, their household resources exhausted, sold their wives’ bracelets, earrings, necklaces, and every ornament belonging to female dress, wishing, by driving hunger away, to preserve the safety of their lives. Yet many of these, after consuming all that they had, ended [Col. 0377A] their lives in a wretched death, begging with the destitute from door to door.

All poor persons had indeed been allowed to enter citizens’ houses to request alms. But when rustic beggars, whose number was beyond counting, entered Prague, because of their excessive multitude they began to steal pots from beside the fire with food being prepared for the citizens to eat, and they carried off other household goods, whatever they could seize, to their own harm and the hatred of all. Consequently, from that time entrance into houses was denied to all poor people; nor were they received for lodging within or outside the city, because many evils came upon the citizens through their shameful conduct. Some poor persons, received for the night outside the city walls, rose at night, killed their host [Col. 0377B] and destroyed his household, took the better goods, and departed. Such things, and others like them, happened in very many places.

One female beggar received a poor woman for the night in her hut at Obora. She had no property except five little pieces of bread in a bag; the covering of her body was not worth two eggs. Yet the mistress of the house, impelled by the devil and by the extreme starvation of hunger, committed the crime of homicide by slaughtering her as she slept at night with an axe, as one slaughters a pig. This mistress of the house also had a twelve-year-old son, who, through the fomenting assistance of the malignant enemy, had been an accomplice in this crime. But divine providence does not permit crimes of this kind to pass unpunished. [Col. 0377C] It was the day of Preparation (27 March) on which this horrible crime was committed, a day on which Christ’s faithful customarily make devotional circuits through the churches. By chance some women, as they passed, saw a corpse tied with a rope and being dragged into a sarcophagus near the church of St John, where human bodies were then buried.

But since the son of that vile and utterly wicked mother could not drag the body, the aforesaid women, wishing in Christ’s name to take part in the office of burial, approached the corpse and endeavored, with such help as they could give, to bring the undertaking to completion. One of them, more discerning in mind, looked at the bloody body and wondered greatly, reflecting [Col. 0377D] that bodies of people who have died a natural death are wholly free from an effusion of blood. While the women considered separately, in a longer consultation, what ought to be done in this matter, the perpetrator of the crime—the mother of the boy dragging the body by the rope—escaped death by taking flight. But the boy was detained by the women and handed over to the city judge. The judge, having learned the truth from the boy’s confession, sentenced him under secular law to be hanged.

A certain woman, displaying beautiful fruit from trees to a well-dressed boy of four years—as fathers generally love and clothe their children more carefully at that age—deceitfully lured him by flattering and pleasant words into her house. [Col. 0378A] Having shut the doors, she killed him; after stripping him, she buried his body. Without a moment’s delay she ran with the clothes of the murdered boy to the market to sell them, hoping to gain profit from her wickedness, although fraud and deceit scarcely, if ever, can provide protection to anyone.

A butcher saw the woman carrying the clothes over her shoulder, as garments offered for sale are customarily carried according to the practice of cloth-workers. He approached her and began to ask how much the clothes cost. He was the neighbor of the man whose son had been murdered; recognizing the clothes, he led her to his butcher’s stall, saying that he wished to buy them and pay at once. She followed him. Once they had come to the aforesaid place, the butcher took the clothes [Col. 0378B] and carefully began to inspect them, to see whether they were the clothes of his neighbor’s son, as he suspected. When he had fully recognized them, he asked her where she had obtained the clothes. She replied: “A certain lady gave them to me to sell.” But he said: “The clothes were stolen,” and, retaining them, hung them in his stall above a pole. He kept her in lengthy conversation, during which the matter could be reported to the person concerned. While the woman was already more heatedly demanding the return of the clothes, servants soon appeared seeking the boy. Recognizing the clothes, they detained the woman and presented her to the father along with the murdered boy’s clothes. The father, having learned the truth, brought her before the judge; the judge consigned her to the gallows.

[Col. 0378C] A certain woman, her husband and all her household buried, with only one daughter surviving, lived a miserable life with her daughter. They sought sustenance by alms and were now as if half alive, for many poor people, begging from door to door the whole day, could obtain—not a mouthful or morsel, but not even a crumb or fragment of bread—with which to revive their wretched lives. Oh, if only the husks of swine were at hand!

One day, after fruitless efforts to obtain alms, the exhausted and hungry mother entered her home around nightfall. Afterwards her daughter came and knocked at the door, wishing to enter the dwelling as she had done each day. Her mother forbade her entry, saying: “Why have you come? Are you not already as good as dead? You bear a wrinkled [Col. 0378D] and pale face; you will die in the hut, and there will be no one to carry you to burial.” And she did not admit her. It then happened that the mother herself died that same night; and the daughter, coming on the following day, cast her mother into a pit and survived for a long time.

In those times, because of the extreme severity of hunger, a father knew no means of offering consolation to his son, nor conversely did a son to his father; a mother did not recognize her daughter, nor a daughter her mother; a brother was unknown to his brother. For awareness of their natural kinship was taken away from them because of lack of possessions, and that prophetic saying was fulfilled: “I have become a stranger to my brothers and an alien to the sons of my mother” (Ps. 68:4). Thus raging want took away their ability to recognize their relatives. [Col. 0379A] Often the opposite happened, as the author says:

> Beauty, popular favor, youthful ardor, and wealth  
> have taken from you the knowledge of what a human being is;

and again:

> There are four things by which a person without measure exalts himself:  
> luxury of wealth, noble offspring, learning, and beauty.

[COSMAS I.3.] Among the ancients all things were common to all, and no one called what he possessed his own. But now, when the root of desire and avarice had sprouted and the starvation of hunger pressed them, a brother, seeing his brother crushed by extreme poverty and at the point of death for want of food, was not ashamed—not merely to refuse nourishment, but even to deny him a mouthful of bread—although they were one flesh [Col. 0379B] and the same blood, as branches propagated from the same stock. He paid no heed to John’s words: “If anyone has the goods of this world and sees his brother suffering need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17); and again: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15). To such people it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for you from the beginning of the world. I was a stranger and you did not receive me; I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:41).

In ancient times the life-giving breath supplied healthful breezes to the whole world; their abundance, mingling with the intemperance of scorched air, tempered the seeds, imparted health to human bodies, [Col. 0379C] and made every kind and species according to its nature fruitful. Therefore the first ages were not undeservedly called golden. For human beings were rough and simple, and among them was simplicity ignorant of evil and still inexperienced in cunning; this gave the first ages their name of gold. But afterwards nature, degenerating through baser metals, stained its final ages with iron through the negligence of its improvidence. Thus in our times, threatening a dreadful pestilence to human intercourse, it brought panting fires and the poisons of numbing cold, and compelled them to range abroad in afflicting the world; for the more human use advanced toward the cultivation of things and arts, the more easily rivalry crept into minds. At first beginning well, it secretly passes into envy, nature being its teacher; and from this there now arises [Col. 0379D] whatever the human race experiences in the ages that follow.

Since poor people were denied entry into the houses of Prague and were not received for lodging because of the thefts committed by them, they lay at night in lanes and streets like swine wallowing in dung thrown into the streets from horse stables, because of their nakedness and the severity of the cold. It was winter, with a bitterly cold and unceasing wind. Thus in summer they died only through hunger; but in winter the evil was doubled, for death entered the world not through a window but through the door, knowing no mercy for humankind. [Col. 0380A] It had strong companions—hunger, nakedness, and the severity of the cold—whose power swiftly penetrated every region of all Bohemia, killed the greater part of mortals, and left no one to bury them.

Oh, where were the religious men in those times? Those who otherwise feign extraordinary devotion—why did they not administer the ecclesiastical sacraments, at least to a few people, in such dangers and afflictions, indeed to those at the hour of death, or, to speak more plainly, already in death itself? Priests are appointed to this by the office of their order and by the ordinances of the holy fathers. Who is culpable for these negligences, when so many thousands of people died without ecclesiastical sacraments, is a matter to be debated; but it will be determined when the Son of Man comes in his majesty.

[Col. 0380B] Therefore all the councillors and leading men of the city assembled. After lengthy deliberation over what should be done to cleanse away such a disgrace, they finally decreed by common counsel and consent to hire laborers to dig very large graves, in which many human bodies might be placed. They were three *lastra* deep and ten cubits wide on every side; each grave held a thousand bodies, more or less. There were eight of these horrifying graves because of their size: one at St Peter’s in the German quarter, into which 2,000 bodies were cast; two trenches near the church of St Lazarus among the lepers; two graves near the church of St John at the Pool; two graves at Psarz; [Col. 0380C] and one near the church of St John at Obora. All these graves were filled with human bodies within six months.

When spring days came and the earth had thawed, with winter winds receding, corpses were buried on sandy islands and in fields before the city walls. Several men were appointed to the work of burial, yet, sweating at their labors throughout the day, they could scarcely carry to the graves all the bodies that had died that day before sunset. But because the old city on the other side of the bridge was more populous, bodies were drawn in carts for burial. If so many thousands are recorded to have died in one city within a short time, how many thousands of people throughout the whole kingdom of Bohemia were reckoned to have fallen in comparison with that one city, [Col. 0380D] when Prague alone is demonstrably not even a thirtieth part of the whole kingdom of Bohemia? Thus it is unquestionably reported that the greater part of the population perished throughout the kingdom.

Many people at the point of death also said: “Oh, if only we had not been born, and no one’s eye had seen us! Oh, that we had been carried from our mother’s womb to the grave, so that at least the hands of relatives might attend to the office of burial; for

> Sweeter lie the bones buried by the hands of their own people.

For it was better for us to die well than to live badly, since authority also says:

> The losses of grief are not well weighed by the happy;  
> one who lives dies more than a wretch can exist.”

Some most miserable and unhappy people, crushed by [Col. 0381A] extreme want and unable to sustain their bodily nature with customary food, devoured the carcasses of beasts of burden, livestock, every kind of animal, and dead dogs. Indeed—even though this is horrible and abominable to hear, we cannot pass it over in silence because it has been heard by many—some, barking like dogs, killed and devoured human beings in this shipwreck of misery to sustain their bodies. Others, with the fear of God cast away and human shame abandoned, were not afraid to eat in Lent persons hanged on the gallows, secretly taking them down at night.

Moreover, in the same year, in a village called Horaz belonging to the church of Saczsen, a daughter, having laid aside all piety and forgotten maternal love, cut her [Col. 0381B] mother into pieces, cooked her, and ate her.

Because in this time many evils befell the Bohemians, and because they were goaded by the stings of diverse punishments, as appeared in the foregoing—brought about by Saxon enterprise, or rather, lest we seem to depart from the path of truth by disguising it, principally by Saxon malice and deceit—we shall set forth openly the origin of their fraudulent and deceitful acts, by describing their beginnings in connection with their deeds, so that their acts of fraud and guile may appear more clearly. [EKKEHARD.]

For concerning the origin of the Saxon people there are various opinions. Some think that they derived their origin from the Danes and Northmen; others—to whom the Greeks too are said to agree—that they were remnants of the Macedonian army which followed Alexander the Great and, after his death, was scattered throughout the whole world. [Col. 0381C] We also find in the writings of a certain historian that, according to ancient tradition, they departed from the Angles, inhabitants of Britain, and, sailing across the ocean, came by deliberate search and necessity for settlements to the shores of Germany [Note: [Col. 0381D] “but by force,” 2.], at a place called Hathuloga, at the time when Theodoric, king of the Franks, fighting against Irminfrid, duke of the Thuringians, cruelly devastated their land with sword and fire.

When they first landed, the inhabitants of that land, who are called Thuringians, deeply resenting their arrival, took up arms against them. But the Saxons, resisting fiercely, held the harbor. At length, after they had fought among themselves for a long time and many had fallen on both sides, both parties agreed to negotiate peace. A treaty was made on the condition that the Saxons should have freedom to sell and buy, but should refrain from the fields, from killing men, and from plundering. This treaty remained inviolate for many days.

But when the Saxons’ money had now failed and they had nothing with which to buy or sell, they judged the peace useless to themselves. At that time it happened that a certain young man came out from the ships laden with much gold, wearing a golden torque and likewise golden armlets. A Thuringian met him and said: “What is the meaning of such an immense quantity of gold about your starving neck?” “I am seeking a buyer,” he replied. “I wear this gold for no other purpose; for, being pressed by hunger, what delight do I take in gold?” When the other asked the quality and quantity of the price, he said: “The price makes no difference to me; whatever you give, I accept gratefully.” Smiling, the Thuringian said: “What if I fill your lap with this dust?” Now there was in that place a very large heap of earth. Without hesitation the Saxon opened his lap and received the earth, immediately handing over the gold to the Thuringian; and each went happily to his own people.

The Thuringians exalted their fellow Thuringian with praises to heaven because he had deceived the Saxon by a noble trick; they declared him the luckiest of all mortals, since he had acquired so great an amount of gold for a trifling price. Meanwhile the Saxon, deprived of gold but laden with much earth, [Col. 0382B] approached the ships. His companions met him and wondered what he was doing. Some of his friends began to mock him, others to reproach him; all alike believed him mad. But, requesting silence, he said: “Follow me, excellent Saxons, and you will prove my madness useful to you.” Though doubtful, they nevertheless followed him. Taking the earth, he scattered it as carefully as he could over the neighboring fields and occupied places for camps.

When the Thuringians saw the Saxons occupying camp-sites, the matter seemed intolerable to them; sending envoys, they complained that the treaty had been violated and the agreement broken by the Saxons. The Saxons replied that they had hitherto observed the treaty inviolably, but that they wished peacefully to retain the land bought with their own gold, or else to defend it by arms. [Col. 0382C] Hearing this, the inhabitants of Thuringia cursed the Saxon gold, and acknowledged that the man whom shortly before they had proclaimed fortunate was the author of their own and their country’s ruin. Thus, inflamed by blind warfare, without order or counsel they rushed upon the camp. But the Saxons, prepared, received and overthrew their enemies; and, their enterprise succeeding, they occupied by right of war the neighboring districts round about.

After they had fought on both sides for a long time, and the Thuringians saw themselves overcome by the Saxons, they sought through intermediaries to make peace with them and allowed them to settle in the land which they had acquired. We have inserted this account so that the prudent reader may recognize what great perfidy, deceit, and fraud they employed.

Ignorant of God, the Creator of heaven and earth, of the sea and of those dwelling therein, they worshipped those who by nature were not gods, [Col. 0382D] and especially Mercury, to whom on appointed days they sacrificed even human victims. They thought it unlawful, in view of the greatness and dignity of divinity, either to confine their gods within temples or to assimilate them to any human form.
