Consecrating groves and woods and calling them by the names of gods, they contemplated that mystery through reverence alone.

They observed omens and lots with the greatest care. Their custom of casting lots was simple. They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree into small twigs, distinguished them by certain marks, and scattered them at random and by chance over a white garment. [Col. 0383A] Then, if the consultation was public, the priest of the people, or, if private, the head of the household himself, after praying to the gods and looking up to heaven, took up three twigs, one at a time; and, according to the mark impressed beforehand and raised up, if permission was granted, confirmation of the issue was still required. [Note: [Col. 0383] “he knew,” 2. Written in haste; several words are lacking.] To inquire into birds’ cries and flights was characteristic of that people; they also tested the omens and movements of horses, observing neighing here and snorting there. No omen was credited more highly [Note: [Col. 0383] Corrected by the same hand from “lesser.”], not only among the common people but also among the nobles.

There was another form of observing omens by which they used to determine the outcome of grave wars: they captured by whatever means a prisoner of the people with whom war was to be fought, pitted him against a chosen man of their own people, both in their native arms, and made the victory of one or the other the basis of their forecast. [Col. 0383B] They showed veneration to leafy trees and springs. They also worshipped in the open air a trunk of wood of no small size, erected upright; in their native language they called it *Irminsul*, which in Latin is called “the universal column,” as though sustaining all things.

How, moreover, on certain days, when the moon was either beginning or full, they believed that the most auspicious beginning for undertakings should be made; and how they observed countless other kinds of vain superstition by which they were ensnared—these things we have committed to writing so that the prudent reader may recognize from how great darkness of errors those were freed by God’s grace who had been devoted to the worship of demons and opposed to true religion, regarding it as neither unlawful nor dishonorable to transgress divine and human law alike.

Whenever they were defeated by some king, they surrendered themselves to him as suppliants, promised to perform what was commanded, gave without delay the hostages demanded, and received the envoys sent. Sometimes they were so subdued and softened that they even promised entirely to abandon the worship of demons and submit themselves to the Christian religion; but as they were at times ready to do these things, so they were always hasty to overturn them.

In the year of the Lord 1283, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January—that is, on the feast of Saint Stephen—there occurred something that rarely happens. A rainbow of marvelous beauty appeared, encircling the whole city of Prague: one end extended beyond the city walls toward the south, the other over the river Vltava, on the other side of the city [Col. 0383D] toward the northern quarter. From this certain Jews and some Christian women foretold, by the omen of fate, a future event of good fortune for the whole kingdom of Bohemia. They maintained that, just as the rainbow set against storm-rains restrains the violence of tempests, so, with the Lord God, governor of the whole world, granting it, it would preserve the inhabitants of the kingdom of Bohemia from pressures and diverse afflictions.

Likewise, from another sign—namely, a star seen on the Nones of April, shining with a most brilliant radiance above [Col. 0384A] the horn of the moon—learned and literate men foretold the arrival of their prince and heir of the kingdom of Bohemia, Wenceslaus, who was staying with Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, his guardian. When he arrived, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, the barons and other knights met him many miles away. The clergy of the entire city, coming out with the people, received him in processions, honorably singing before the gates of the castle: “You have come, O desired one,” together with other hymns and songs; and the people also sang: “Hospodin pomiluy ny” [“Lord, have mercy upon us”]. Tobias the bishop was present at this procession with the canons of his church, together with the other monastic communities: those of Břevnov and Strahov, the Preachers, the Friars Minor, and the rectors of all churches, [Col. 0384B] secular men and women, and all the other artisans of every craft.

The same margrave of Brandenburg, when his office of guardianship had ended, ought, according to legal rule, to have rendered an account of his administration of that office, as the imperial laws teach in the *Institutes*, in the title *On the Atilian Guardian*, where it is said (Justinian, *Institutes* 1.20.7): “When guardians administer the affairs of male or female wards, after the term of guardianship has elapsed, they render accounts in a judicial proceeding.” The same margrave, having previously received 15,000 marks of silver from the general levy, was still inflamed by the spur of greed; casting aside human shame, he exacted from the duke of the Bohemians 20,000 marks of silver for release from his guardianship. He gave no heed to what is found promulgated in the same laws: [Col. 0384C] that not only guardians or curators are liable to wards, adults, and other persons for their administration, but that the wards themselves also have a subsidiary action against those who receive securities, which may afford them a final remedy.

For this same sum of money, moreover, the margrave held as pledges the very strong fortifications of Děčín, Ústí [Note: [Col. 0383D] Aussig.], Most, Ronov [Note: [Col. 0384D] Ronov in the Čáslav district.], and the castle of Bezděz, together with their towns, until the aforesaid sum of money should be paid in full.

That same year the whole spring was dry. In the same year, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, frost damaged the vines and the fruits of the trees so extraordinarily that they bore absolutely no fruit. It also damaged throughout Bohemia the winter and summer grain crops—wheat, rye, barley, peas, and other [Col. 0384D] seeds—so that in very many places they were cut down because of their barrenness, since they appeared to provide little or no nourishment for human use.

In the same year the church of Saint Nicholas in the Prague suburb was consecrated by the venerable father and lord Tobias, by God’s grace bishop of Prague, on the second day before the Ides of January. At this consecration a certain cripple was made upright through the merits and prayers of Saint Nicholas. In the same year, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, drops of blood flowed [Col. 0385A] from the foot of the crucifix placed near the tomb of Saint Ludmila in the church of Saint George. Trustworthy men bear witness concerning these occurrences, which happened a second time as well, saying that they saw such things.

Nor do I think it should be omitted, since it is worthy of commemoration, that Lord Tobias, by God’s grace bishop of Prague, although by the office of his government he was bound to foster all the churches of his diocese, nevertheless cherished the church of Prague—whose spouse and lord he was—with special affection. He provided it with precious ornaments and ecclesiastical books for the honor and praise of divine worship, and also of the blessed martyrs Vitus, Wenceslaus, and Adalbert. The donation of these things was as follows:

A chasuble, dalmatic, and tunicle [Note: [Col. 0385D] A vestment of subdeacons.] of white samite [Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, *exametum*, German *Sammt* (“velvet”).] with broad borders [Note: [Col. 0385D] Fringes.]; [Col. 0385B] likewise he gave another black vestment-set woven with gold; likewise an altar-cloth of white *baldachin*, lined with red *cendatus* [Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, a silk cloth was sewn underneath.]; likewise another altar-cloth bearing a lion and an eagle in embroidered work [Note: [Col. 0386D] The work was painted with a needle.]; likewise three altar cloths with broad ornamental bands; likewise a striped samite cloth, which is placed beneath relics on Good Friday; and a fourth long altar cloth, likewise placed beneath relics.

He also gave a large missal containing all epistles and gospels, both for weekdays and festivals, written with musical notation, together with graduals and sequences; likewise a large nocturnal book, with rubrics and chant marked in musical notation throughout the entire antiphonary. He also gave a breviary in large lettering according to the Prague use, the ancient rite and custom of the church being preserved. [Col. 0385C] Such a provider, indeed, is said to be “shod on both feet,” who is judged to have provided fittingly not only for himself but also for his church. For he guarded against the reproach of that authority which says: “Whoever, upon receiving an office of rule, begins to enjoy it in a worldly fashion readily forgets whatever he had thought in a religious fashion.”

Because [Note: [Col. 0386D] Epilogue of the interpolator.] many people’s minds are troubled by the desire to investigate the succession and descent of the line of dukes and kings of the kingdom of Bohemia—how many there were from the first duke Přemysl down to these times, who succeeded whom in the duchy, and where the dignity of royal majesty also first arose—I shall endeavor to explain it as concisely as I can, omitting prolixity of words, which is accustomed to displease the wise [Col. 0385D] and even to produce weariness in some. This qualification, however, is retained: wherever in these writings the reader encounters a knot of uncertainty, let him return above to the written accounts in order to dispel the error; for there he will find the matter recorded more fully.

[COSMAS I, 2.] In the division of the world according to the geometers, Asia, under its own name, occupies half of the world, while Africa and Europe occupy the other half. Germany is situated in Europe; in its northern regions [Col. 0386A] Bohemia is found to lie. A man named Bohemus is said to have entered it with a few souls, and from him the whole land was called Bohemia. This man Bohemus established his first settlements around Mount Říp, between two rivers, namely the Ohře and the Vltava.

[I, 3.] Later, as time passed, a certain man named Crocco arose, native among them; to him all flocked, both from their own tribes and from the whole people, for the settlement of judgments. This man, lacking male offspring, nevertheless begot three prophetess daughters, the first of whom was called Kazi, the second Teta, and the third Libuše. [I, 4.] This Libuše, though younger in age, shone forth as far greater in wisdom. The whole people, taking common counsel, appointed her judge over themselves after her father’s death.

In those same times, however, no small discord arose among the people. Bringing complaints to their lady and demanding that she quickly pronounce final judgments, she is reported to have answered: “For settling judgments, knowledge of the cases is necessary; for without knowledge, the righteous would often be condemned.” And she could not immediately satisfy their petitions. Then the people despised their lady and her judgments, saying that any woman was better fitted for male embraces than to dictate laws to warriors. Seeing the great insult inflicted on her by the people, Libuše concealed and veiled the injury in feminine modesty and said [I, 5.]: “If I am not worthy to preside over you, go and choose a lord for yourselves; and he whom you choose shall be your duke and my husband.”

[I, 6.] Immediately, giving them royal garments and naming the village called Stadice, which is situated near the river Bílina, she sent them forth. She also gave them her horse, to which the road leading to that village was known, saying to them [I, 5.]: “You will find near the named village a man called Přemysl, ploughing a field with varied oxen; bring him, and he shall be your duke and my husband.” [I, 6.] Going forth, they fulfilled everything according to their lady’s command. [I, 7.] This man—who truly deserves to be called a man by reason of his virtue, who devised and dictated all the laws by which this land is used and governed—was the first duke of Bohemia.

I. Duke Přemysl. II. Nezamysl. III. Mnata. [Col. 0386D] IV. Vojen. V. Unislav. VI. Křesomysl. VII. Neklan. VIII. Hostivít. IX. Bořivoj, the first Christian, was baptized by Methodius, bishop of Moravia, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 894 [Note: [Col. 0386D] Cosmas I.10.]. X. Spytihněv. XI. Vratislav. [Col. 0387A] XII. Saint Wenceslaus, martyred through his brother’s treachery on the fourth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0387B] Cosmas I.17.]. XIII. Boleslaus the Fierce, fratricide. XIV. Boleslaus the Pious, founder of the bishopric of Prague [Note: [Col. 0387B] Compare Cosmas I.21.]. XV. Boleslaus the Mild. XVI. Vladivoj. XVII. Jaromír [Note: [Col. 0388B] These dukes are absent in Cosmas.]. XVIII. Oldřich. XIX. Břetislav. XX. Spytihněv, founder of the church of Prague. XXI. Vratislav, duke and first king of Bohemia. XXII. Duke Conrad. XXIII. Duke Břetislav. XXIV. Duke Bořivoj. [Col. 0387B] XXV. Duke Svatopluk. XXVI. Duke Vladislav. XXVII. Duke Soběslav. XXVIII. Duke Vladislav and second king of Bohemia, founder of the church of Strahov. XXIX. Duke Frederick. [Col. 0388A] XXX. Duke Soběslav. XXXI. Duke Conrad. XXXII. Henry, duke and bishop. XXXIII. Duke Vladislav. XXXIV. Duke Přemysl, the third king of Bohemia, who was also called Ottokar. XXXV. King Wenceslaus. XXXVI. King Přemysl. XXXVII. King Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0387] The following was inserted into the text from the margin of an older codex: “In the year of the Lord 1320, William Hare (*Lepus*) died, most faithful to the kings of Bohemia and guardian of the Bohemian people.”].

And because we have briefly set down here the number and order of the dukes and kings, we thought it fitting to describe the number of years and the intervals of time among them. From the first Christian duke, Bořivoj, to Vratislav, first king of Bohemia, twelve dukes are read to have succeeded one another; [Col. 0388B] within this period forty *lustra* [five-year periods] are reckoned. From Vratislav, the first king, to Vladislav, the second king, there were six dukes, within whose times I have calculated [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 0387] The final words are lacking.]

The chronicle ends; he who has died is buried.

## ABOUT THE YEAR 1125: ALBERT OF AIX

[Col. 0387]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I.)

[Col. 0387] Albert, or Alberic, of Aix in Gaul, custodian of the church, wrote—on the testimony of those who were present [Note: [Col. 0387] See Book I, chapters 1, 24, 25; Book II, chapter 33; Book III, chapters 2, 65; Book IV, chapters 53, 55; Book VI, chapters 24, 50; and Book VIII, chapter 21.]—an accurate history of the Jerusalem expedition, or *On the Passage of Godfrey of Bouillon and Other Princes*, down to the second year of Baldwin II; that is, from the year 1095 to 1121, in twelve books. First published without its author’s name together with the chronology of Henry Meibom by Reiner Reineccius, at Helmstedt in 1584, quarto, under the title *Chronicle of Jerusalem concerning the Holy War*. It was afterward restored to its author in Jacques Bongars’s *Deeds of God through the Franks*, vol. I, pp. 184–318, Hanover, 1611, folio. David Hoeschel first disclosed the author’s name in the preface to Anna Comnena’s *Alexiad*, written in 1610.

[Col. 0389]

# HERE BEGINS THE HISTORY OF THE JERUSALEM EXPEDITION, EDITED BY ALBERIC, CANON AND CUSTODIAN OF THE CHURCH OF AIX, ON THE PASSAGE OF GODFREY OF BOUILLON AND OTHER PRINCES

(Bongars, *Gesta Dei per Francos*, I, 184.)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER I.—Prologue to the following work

[Col. 0389A]

Here begins the first book of the expedition to the city of Jerusalem, in which are narrated the renowned deeds of the most illustrious duke Godfrey. Through his labor and zeal the holy city was liberated from the unbelievers and restored to the children of the holy Church.

For a long time and often until these days, on account of events unheard-of and greatly marvelous, I was frequently inflamed with the desire for that same expedition and to offer prayer there, while I burned with longing. But because, owing to various impediments, my intention was granted no fulfillment, I decided, in rash boldness, at least to commit some things to memory from what might become known by report and disclosure from those who had been present, so that I might labor not in idleness but, as it were, on the road—if not in body, then with my whole mind and soul as a companion.

Therefore I have presumed, with our slender powers and in a childish and unguarded style, [Col. 0389B] to write concerning the labor and miseries, the confirmed faith, and the worthy concord in Christ’s love of strong princes and other men: how they left homeland, kindred, wives, sons and daughters, cities, castles, fields, kingdoms, and every sweetness of this world; how, exchanging certainties for uncertainties, they sought exile in the name of Jesus; how, with a strong hand and mighty army, they made their way to Jerusalem and, triumphing in bold assault, slew legions of Turks and Saracens thousands upon thousands of times; how they opened the entrance and access to the sacred sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ; and how they wholly remitted the dues and tributes of pilgrims wishing to enter there. [Col. 0389C]

### CHAPTER II.—How Peter the Hermit was the first instigator of the expedition to Jerusalem

A certain priest, Peter by name, formerly a hermit and born in the city of Amiens, which lies in the western part of the kingdom of the Franks, first exhorted men with every means at his command to steadfastness in this journey. He became a preacher in the Berry region of the aforesaid kingdom, in every exhortation and sermon. By his continual exhortation and summons bishops, abbots, clerics, and [Col. 0390A] monks, then the noblest laymen, princes of diverse kingdoms, and the whole populace—both chaste and unchaste, adulterers, murderers, thieves, perjurers, robbers, indeed every kind of person professing Christianity, and even women—were led by penitence joyfully to flock to this journey. By what occasion and intention this same hermit preached this journey and became its first leader the present page will declare.

### CHAPTER III.—How he approached the patriarch

This priest, some years before the beginning of this journey, set out for Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. There, in the oratory of the Lord’s Sepulchre—alas!—he learned with sorrowful heart of certain unlawful and nefarious things seen there, and his spirit groaned; he appealed to the Lord himself, the judge, concerning these wrongs. At length, stirred by the impious deeds, he sought the patriarch of the holy church of Jerusalem and asked why he permitted the pagans and impious to defile the holy places, to carry away the offerings of the faithful, likewise to use churches as brothels, to strike Christians with blows, and to despoil holy pilgrims of their possessions by unjust payment and oppress them with many hardships. [Col. 0390B]

### CHAPTER IV.—What the patriarch replied to Peter, and how he summoned Christian aid

The patriarch, the venerable priest of the Lord’s Sepulchre, hearing this, made a devout and faithful reply: “Most faithful of Christians, why do you press and trouble our fatherhood about these matters, when our strength or power is reckoned no greater than a tiny ant against the arrogance of so many? For our lives are redeemed either by continual tributes or are assigned to deadly punishments. And we expect greater dangers to be at hand day by day, unless Christian assistance should arrive, which we invite through your embassy.”

Peter replied to him as follows: “Reverend Father, we have sufficiently learned, and now understand and see, how feeble is the force of Christians dwelling here with you, and under how many oppressions of the pagans they lie. For this reason, by the Lord’s favor and for your liberation and the cleansing of the holy places, God accompanying me and my life being preserved, on my return I shall first seek the apostolic lord, then all the foremost Christian kings, dukes, counts, and holders of princely power, making known to all the misery of your servitude and the endurance of your distresses. Now all these messages appear alike ready to be carried out among themselves.” [Col. 0391A]

### CHAPTER V.—How the majesty of the Lord Jesus appeared to Peter in a dream and addressed him

Meanwhile, when darkness had fallen all around from heaven, Peter returned to the holy sepulchre to pray. There, wearied by vigils and prayers, he was overcome by sleep. In a vision the majesty of the Lord Jesus appeared to him and deigned thus to address a mortal and frail man:

“Peter, most beloved son among Christians, arise. You shall visit our patriarch and receive from him letters of our embassy bearing the seal of the holy cross; then hasten as quickly as possible on your journey to the land of your kindred. You shall disclose the wrongs and injuries inflicted upon our people and the holy place, and you shall stir up the hearts of the faithful to cleanse the holy places of Jerusalem and restore the observances of the saints. For through various dangers and trials the gates of paradise shall now be opened to those who are called and chosen.” [Col. 0391B]

### CHAPTER VI.—How Peter came to Rome, reported the apostolic embassy, and concerning the earthquake

At this marvelous revelation, worthy of the Lord, when the vision had departed, Peter awoke from sleep. At the first dawn of day he went out from the temple threshold, sought the patriarch, set forth to him in order the Lord’s vision, and requested letters of the divine embassy with the sign of the holy cross. The patriarch did not refuse to give them, but granted them with thanksgiving. Having received leave, Peter returned to his native regions in obedience to the embassy.

After a voyage across the sea undertaken with no small anxiety, he was carried back to the city of Bari. Once restored to land, he proceeded without delay to Rome. There, having found the apostolic lord, he reported the embassy which he had heard and received from God and the patriarch, concerning the uncleanness of the pagans and the injuries done to saints and pilgrims. The apostolic lord received these things with willing and attentive mind and promised in every respect to obey the commands of the holy prayers. [Col. 0391C]

For this reason, anxious in mind, he came to the city of Vercelli; after crossing the Alps, he decreed that an assembly of all western France and a council should be held at Le Puy, the city of Saint Mary. He then proceeded to Clermont in Auvergne. There, having heard the divine embassy and the apostolic exhortation, the bishops of all France, dukes and counts, and great princes of every order and rank assented to an expedition at their own expense to the Lord’s sepulchre itself. In that most extensive realm, indeed, a holy confederation and sworn compact for this journey arose among the mightiest men, with hands joined. At their affirmation a great earthquake occurred, foretelling nothing other than the movement of armies from diverse kingdoms upon the journey, [Col. 0392A] from the kingdom of France and the land of Lorraine, and likewise of Germans, Englishmen, and the Danish region.

### CHAPTER VII.—Concerning a certain Walter going to Jerusalem: what he did and suffered

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the fourth indiction, under Henry, fourth king and third Roman emperor Augustus, in the forty-third year of his reign and the thirteenth of his empire, and under Urban II, also called Odardus, apostolic lord, on the eighth day of March, Walter, surnamed Senzavehor, a distinguished knight, with a great company of Frankish foot-soldiers but having only eight knights, entered the kingdom of Hungary at the beginning of the Jerusalem journey, through the exhortation of the aforesaid Peter the Hermit. [Col. 0392B]

There, when his valor and the purpose and cause of his undertaken journey had become known, he was kindly received by Lord Coloman, the most Christian king of the Hungarians. Peaceful passage through the entire territory of his kingdom, together with permission to purchase supplies, was granted him. Thus he advanced without injury or hostile attack as far as Belgrade, a city of the Bulgarians, passing through Malevilla, where the bounds of the Hungarian kingdom end. There he peacefully crossed the river Morava by boat.

But at the same place, Malevilla, sixteen members of his company remained behind to purchase arms, without Walter’s knowledge, for he had long since crossed the river. Certain Hungarians of perverse mind, seeing from afar that Walter and his army were absent, laid hands upon those sixteen men. They stripped them of arms, clothes, gold, and silver, and so allowed them to depart naked and empty-handed. Grieving, bereft of possessions and arms, they hastened on to the aforesaid Belgrade, where Walter, with all his force, had pitched tents for lodging outside the walls, and they recounted to him every misfortune that had befallen them. But Walter received the news calmly, since a return for vengeance was wearisome.

In that same night in which his naked and destitute companions were received, Walter requested from the prince of the Bulgarians and the city magistrate provisions necessary for life. But, thinking them spies and deceivers of the land, they prohibited all goods from being sold to them. Therefore Walter and his whole company, deeply angered, began to seize and drive off by force the cattle, oxen, and sheep of the Bulgarians, which wandered everywhere through [Col. 0392D] the fields, sent out to graze upon grass. A grave conflict accordingly began to grow between the pilgrims and the Bulgarians, who were reclaiming their herds, and to become a battle.

At length, as the Bulgarians’ strength prevailed, certain men separated from the pilgrim army by the multitude of the opposing force—up to one hundred and forty thousand—fled into a certain chapel. But the Bulgarians, their own force increasing and Walter failing and fleeing with his whole company, besieged the chapel, burned sixty of those shut inside, and severely wounded many of the rest, who barely escaped the enemies and the chapel in defense of their lives.

After this disaster and destruction of his men, [Col. 0393A] Walter fled, leaving his companions scattered about. After making his way through the forests of the Bulgarians for eight days, he withdrew to a very wealthy city called Niš, in the middle of the Bulgarian kingdom. There he found the duke and prince of the land, reported the injury and loss inflicted upon him, and graciously obtained justice from him in every matter. The prince also bestowed arms and money upon him in reconciliation, and gave him peaceful escort and permission to buy supplies through the Bulgarian cities of Sternitz, Philippopolis, and Adrianople, until he came down with all his company to the imperial city Constantinople, capital of the entire kingdom of the Greeks.

When he had arrived, he begged the emperor himself with every earnestness of most humble petition [Col. 0393B] that he might be allowed to remain peacefully in the emperor’s kingdom, with permission to buy life’s necessities, until Peter the Hermit—by whose exhortation and prompting they had begun this journey—should arrive as his companion; and that, when their thousands had thus been joined, they might cross the arm of the Sea of Saint George by ship and so be better able to resist the Turks and all the battle-lines of the pagans. This was done, and the lord emperor, named Alexius, kindly answered and granted every request.

### CHAPTER VIII.—How Peter, setting out for Jerusalem with a numerous army, avenged his companions in Hungary
After this, and after no long interval of time, the aforesaid Peter and his numerous army—innumerable as the sand of the sea [Col. 0393C], because men from different realms had assembled to join him, namely Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, and Lotharingians—continued together on the road to Jerusalem. Entering the kingdom of Hungary on their journey, they pitched their tents before the gate of Cyperon, with all the army which he had led forth.

Once these had been set in place, he immediately sent messengers to the ruler of Hungary, asking that entrance and passage through the midst of his kingdom be opened to him and his companions. This was granted him, on the condition that no plundering should take place in the king’s land, but that he should proceed peaceably, and that everything needed by the army should be obtained for payment, without quarrelling or dispute.

Peter therefore, hearing of the king’s goodwill toward himself and his companions, rejoiced [Col. 0393D]. He crossed the kingdom of Hungary peacefully, giving and receiving everything necessary for use according to number, justice, and measure; and thus, without disturbance, he proceeded with all his host as far as Malevilla.

But when he drew near the borders of the aforesaid place, a report reached his ears and those of his followers: that the count of that region, named Guz, one of the chief men of the king of Hungary, corrupted by greed, had gathered an armed force of soldiers and formed a most wicked plan with the aforesaid duke, named Nichita, prince of the Bulgarians and governor of the city of Belegrave. The plan was that Nichita too, having assembled the strength of his retainers, should defeat and kill the vanguard of Peter’s host, while Guz should cut down the rear by pursuit with his soldiers; so that they might seize and divide among themselves all the spoils of so great an army—horses [Col. 0394A], gold, silver, and clothing.

Hearing this, Peter would not at all believe that the Hungarians and Bulgarians, being Christians, could commit so great a crime. But when they came to Malevilla, his companions saw hanging upon the battlements and walls the arms and spoils of sixteen companions of Walter, whom the Hungarians had shortly before dared treacherously to strip after they had fallen behind.

Peter, having learned of this injury to his brethren and seen their arms and spoils, urged his companions to vengeance. They sounded the trumpeters’ signals loudly, rushed with raised standards against the walls, and assailed them with a hail of arrows. They shot these with such unceasing and incredible density at those standing upon the walls that the Hungarians, unable to withstand the force of the attacking Franks, withdrew from the wall, if perhaps they might remain within the city beyond their enemies’ reach.

Then a certain Godfrey, surnamed Burel, born in the city of Étampes, master and standard-bearer of two hundred foot-soldiers, himself also on foot and a man of great strength, seeing the adversaries fleeing away from the walls, leapt over the wall by a ladder which he happened to find there. Reinold of the castle of Breis, a distinguished knight, his head covered with a helmet and clad in a hauberk, likewise climbed the walls after Godfrey, until all alike, horsemen and foot-soldiers, strove to enter.

The Hungarians, seeing the extremity of their danger and the imminent peril to their lives, massed some seven thousand for defence. They went out through another gate facing eastward and took their stand upon the summit of a lofty rock, past which [Col. 0394C] the Danube flows, on the side where the stronghold was impregnable. Most of them, unable to escape swiftly through the gate because of its narrow entrance, fell before the very gateway by the sword’s edge. Others, who hoped to save themselves on the mountaintop, were slaughtered by the pursuing pilgrims; others, thrown down from the summit of the mountain, were swallowed in the waves of the Danube itself. Yet more escaped by boat.

About four thousand Hungarians fell there; only one hundred pilgrims, apart from the wounded, were killed in that place. Having won this victory, Peter remained with all his men in that castle of Malevilla for five days, because of the abundance of provisions which he found there: grain, flocks of sheep [Col. 0394D], herds of cattle, abundant drink, and an infinite number of horses.

## CHAPTER IX.—How he crossed the river Maroa with difficulty.

When news of this victory and bloody slaughter of the Hungarians became known, and when the bodies of the Hungarians cut down by the sword were seen—many of them destroyed by cruel wounds and borne by the Danube in its turbulent waters to Belegrave, where, turning back its channel, it continues its course, a mile distant from Malevilla—the aforesaid duke Nichita summoned his men. Having taken counsel of all, shaken with fear, he refused to await Peter any longer at Belegrave. Rather, hoping to defend himself against the strength of the Franks, Romans, and Germans, he resolved to move to Niczh, because that city was protected by the strength of its walls. He carried with him all the treasures of Belegrave [Col. 0395A].

He sent its citizens fleeing with their herds through woods, mountains, and deserted places, until, having summoned assistance from the emperor of Constantinople, he might resist Peter’s companions and take vengeance for the Hungarians, on account of the friendship and alliance which he had made with Guz, count and prince of Malevilla.

Six days later, a messenger from the settlement of the Frankish newcomers was swiftly sent to Peter, to convey this certain message of threats. He said:

> “The king of Hungary, having gathered the army of his whole kingdom, is about to come down against you to avenge his people. It is not certain that even one of you will escape his arms; for grief over the slain and the lamentations have stirred the king and all their relatives and friends. Therefore, cross the river Maroa [Col. 0395B] as quickly as possible, and hasten your journey from here.”

Peter, understanding the king’s anger and his most formidable gathering, left Malevilla with all his companions, taking with him all the spoils, flocks, and captured horses, and determined to cross the Maroa. But upon the entire shore he found only a few vessels, one hundred and fifty in all, by which so great a multitude might swiftly cross and escape, because of fear of the king, who was approaching in great force.

Accordingly, very many whose supply of boats failed strove to cross upon rafts of joined timbers and woven wattles. But many were killed by the Pincenarii, who inhabited Bulgaria: while floating upon those joined timbers and wattles without a helmsman, and sometimes separated from their company, they were struck by arrows and perished.

Peter, seeing the destruction and drowning of his people, commanded the Bavarians, Alemanni, and other Germans, in accordance with their pledge of obedience, to come to the assistance of their Frankish brethren. They immediately boarded seven rafts, sank seven small boats of the Pincenarii with their occupants, and captured only seven alive. Brought into Peter’s presence, these seven were slaughtered at his command.

After this vengeance for his people had been exacted, and the river Maroa crossed, Peter entered the immense and most extensive forests of the Bulgarians with wagons of provisions, all his equipment, and the spoils of Belegrave. Having spent seven days in that vast woodland, he and his men came to the strongly walled city of Niczh. There, after crossing a certain river [Col. 0395D] by a stone bridge before the city, they occupied with pitched tents a meadow delightful for its greenness and breadth, and the riverbank.

## CHAPTER X.—How hostages were given to the duke of the Bulgarians; and how, after their reception, a serious conflict arose with the Bulgarians.

The pilgrim host having thus been lodged, Peter’s prudence and the counsel of the leading men produced an embassy to Duke Nichita, prince of the Bulgarians, who was then present in that city, to obtain permission to buy food. He graciously agreed, but on condition that hostages be given him, lest some injury or violence, as at Belegrave, be committed by so great a multitude.

Walter, son of Walram of the castle of Bretoil, which is near Belvatium, and Godfrey [Col. 0396A] Burel of Étampes, were appointed and given to the duke as hostages. When they had been sent and received by the duke, an abundance of every kind of thing was granted them for purchase from all sides. To those who had nothing with which to buy, the city bestowed abundant alms.

That night therefore passed in complete tranquillity, and the hostages were faithfully returned to Peter by the prince. Then one hundred Alemanni, because of a most trivial dispute with a certain Bulgarian in an evening transaction of buying and selling, having fallen a little behind Peter’s host, set fire to seven mills which stood beneath the aforesaid bridge in the river and reduced them to ashes. They also set some houses outside the city ablaze with a similar fire, in vengeance for their anger.

The citizens, seeing the buildings of their people blazing [Col. 0396B] with fire, came together unanimously before their duke Nichita. They declared that Peter and all his followers were false Christians, mere robbers and not peaceful men: men who had killed the Pincenarii of the duke of Belegrave and so many Hungarians at Malevilla, and who had now dared commit this arson, making no return whatever for benefits received.

## CHAPTER XI.—How the duke pursued the army and seized much plunder.

The duke, hearing this injury and the complaint of his people, commanded all to hasten to arms with all the cavalry which he had assembled there after learning of the attack on Malevilla. Without delay, they were to pursue the pilgrims and repay upon their heads all the evils [Col. 0396C] inflicted upon him.

At this command of the duke, Bulgarians, Comans, many Hungarians, and Pincenarii—who had come by agreement for payment to defend the city—seized horn and bone bows and put on their hauberks. With standards fastened to their lances, they pursued Peter and his army, who were proceeding unsuspectingly. They did not spare the slow and rearmost members of the host, cutting them down and piercing them. They seized the wagons and carts that followed at a slow pace, carrying away matrons, maidens, and tender children; these, as exiles and captives in the land of Bulgaria, were found down to the present day with all their possessions and herds.

Immediately amid this sudden disorder and slaughter of the pilgrims, a certain Lambert escaped by the speed of his horse and reached Peter [Col. 0396D]. Peter did not know of the matter, and Lambert related to him all that had happened, and how these beginnings of evils and sorrows had arisen from the Alemanni because of the fire which they had made.

Peter, a mile away, knew nothing of all this. Greatly troubled by the messenger’s words, he summoned the wisest and most prudent men of the army and spoke to them as follows:

## CHAPTER XII.—How, when Peter returned with the army to meet the duke for peace, a great number of young men were struck down.

> “A grievous and harsh misfortune, arising from the fury of foolish Germans, hangs over us. Very many of our men, together with the Alemanni, have fallen beneath the bow and sword of Duke Nichita and his retainers in vengeance [Col. 0397A] for the fire, of which I knew absolutely nothing. All our wagons too, together with our wealth and herds, have been seized. I see nothing more useful in this matter than that we return to meet the duke and make peace with him, because our men have acted unjustly toward him, although his citizens peacefully supplied us with all necessities.”

At Peter’s declaration and decision, the army retraced its journey to the city of Niczh itself and pitched their tents again in the aforesaid meadow, so that Peter might excuse himself and the whole host that had gone before. Thus, once the duke had been appeased, they hoped to recover their captives and wagons.

While Peter with the more prudent men was diligently engaged in this purpose and plan, and was framing his apology in cautious words, one thousand young men of the foolish sort, of excessive rashness and [Col. 0397B] stubborn neck—a wild and unbridled people—went without cause or reason across the aforesaid stone bridge toward the walls and gate of the city in a violent assault. A further thousand youths of the same rashness, running across the fords and the bridge itself, joined them in support with tremendous shouting and fury. They refused to heed Peter, their leader, who forbade these actions and wished peace to be made, or any of the prudent men.

In this most serious dissension of the conflicting hosts, the whole army remained with Peter, who was restraining this uprising, except for those two thousand; and none of the rest came to their aid. The Bulgarians, seeing this division among the people and that these two thousand could easily be overcome, burst forth from two gates with arrows, lances, and severe blows. Thus they overwhelmed them all with great force and put them to flight.

Twenty of them fell from the bridge and were submerged and suffocated in the waters. Three hundred others fled along the side of the bridge toward unknown fords; some of these perished by arms, others in the waters. At last, those who had been recalled from this madness and remained with Peter in the meadow on the other side of the river saw their people being destroyed by so cruel a martyrdom and could no longer restrain themselves from giving aid. Clad in hauberks and helmets, whether Peter wished it or not, they rushed to the bridge itself.

There a cruel battle began on both sides, with arrows, swords, and lances. But the Bulgarians had seized the ford and bridge first; therefore they could not cross, but were vigorously driven back in flight. Peter, seeing this crushing [Col. 0397D] and flight of his people, sent an embassy to the aforesaid duke through a certain Bulgarian who had resolved to undertake the holy journey to Jerusalem, asking him to deign to hold a brief conference with him and that they might make peace in the Lord’s name on both sides. This was done.

## CHAPTER XIII.—How the army was for the most part scattered, and was again gathered to thirty thousand.

When this peace had been announced among Peter’s people and the turmoil calmed, until everything might return to concord, the rebellious and incorrigible common foot-soldiers repaired and loaded their wagons and carts and pressed onward on the road. Peter, Folcker, and Reinold forbade them to proceed until they could see whether the conference would result in agreement; but they could by no means turn the foolish and rebellious men from their undertaking.

The citizens, seeing that Peter [Col. 0398A] and the leaders of the army impeded those setting out and obstructed the wagons and carts, supposed that they were preparing to flee with the common people. Therefore, leaping out from the city gate with the duke’s soldiers, they pursued them in strong force. For two miles, those who had been delayed from the army suffered severe slaughter and capture.

The wagon upon which was Peter’s chest, full of countless gold and silver, was captured and retained. It was brought back to Niczh with the captives and placed in the duke’s treasury. The remaining spoils were divided among the soldiers. Men without number were slain; boys were carried off with their mothers; and married and unmarried women alike—whose number is unknown.

Peter and all his company who could escape fled hastily like sheep from wolves, scattered through a dark and vast forest: some over precipitous mountains, some through [Col. 0398B] deserted places. At length Peter, Reinold of Breis, Walter son of Walram of Bretoil, Godfrey Burel, and Folcker of Orléans—all these men with only five hundred others—happened to gather after this flight on the summit of a certain mountain. For no more than these appeared to remain out of forty thousand.

Peter then, considering how grievously diminished his people and army were, anxiously pondered various courses. With deep sighing he grieved for the scattered hosts and for the many thousands of his men who had fallen, while only one Bulgarian had perished. He wondered whether anyone at all from the forty thousand fugitives and scattered persons was still alive.

Therefore, at his direction and on seeing this, those fugitives who stood with him upon the mountain summit sounded standards and horns, so that the pilgrims, wherever they were scattered through mountains, forests, and deserted places, might hear the signal of Peter and his companions, return and assemble together, and resume the journey which they had begun. Before the first day had declined, seven thousand had assembled at the sound of the signal.

Thus gathered and returned from dispersion, they again took up the road and came to a certain city empty of property and inhabitants. Pitching camp there, they awaited their fugitive and scattered companions. Yet they could not find or obtain any food in those deserted places, suffering extreme want, for they had lost more than two thousand wagons and carts carrying wheat, barley, and meat for eating, and found no one to see or to offer them anything.

These adversities befell them in the month of July [Col. 0398D], when grain and crops in that region, now ripe for harvest, were already turning yellow. The people being distressed by hunger, the men of most prudent counsel thought it best to roast with fire the ripe crops found in the fields of the deserted and empty city, and to shake out the roasted grain, by which the hungry people might be sustained. By this provision the people lived with difficulty for three days, until the fugitives and scattered persons had reassembled to thirty thousand, apart from the ten thousand who had perished.

## CHAPTER XIV.—How the emperor sent envoys to Peter, that he might come to Constantinople.

Meanwhile, the duke’s messengers had gone before to the lord emperor at Constantinople. They reported to him all the evil [Col. 0399A] concerning these actions and misfortunes: namely, how the army had killed Hungarians at Malevilla; how, coming to the city of Niczh, it had repaid the citizens’ good deeds with evil; but also how it had not committed this crime unpunished.

Hearing these things, the emperor sent envoys to Peter. They found Peter, having left the empty and deserted city, on his way with all his company to the city of Sternitz. In accordance with the emperor’s edict, they delivered this message:

> “Peter, serious complaints concerning you and your people have been brought to the lord emperor, because your army has committed plunder and sedition in his realm. Therefore, by his command, you are forbidden to remain more than three days in any city of his kingdom, until you enter the city of Constantinople. We further command all the cities through which [Col. 0399B] you will pass, by imperial order, to sell peaceably all things to you and your people, and, because you are a Christian and your companions are Christians, not to hinder your journey further. And whatever your retainers have done in pride and fury against Duke Nichita, he wholly pardons you; for he knows that you have paid a severe penalty for this injury.”

On hearing this peaceful embassy from the lord emperor, Peter rejoiced greatly and wept for joy. He gave thanks to God, who, after an exceedingly severe correction—and not an undeserved one—had granted grace to him and his people in the sight of so magnificent and renowned an emperor.

## CHAPTER XV.—How Peter received the emperor’s second embassy, ordering him to hasten his journey to Constantinople.

[Col. 0399C] Obeying the emperor’s commands, Peter departed from the city of Sternitz and went with all his people to the city of Phinopolis. There, when all his misfortune and disaster had been recounted in the hearing of all the Greek citizens, he received many gifts of Byzantine coins, silver, horses, and mules, for Jesus’ name and the fear of God, because all had been moved with compassion for him.

Then, after the third dawn, cheerful and glad, and supplied abundantly with necessary things, he departed for Adrianople. Having remained there only two days in lodging outside the city walls, he left on the third dawn. For a second embassy of the emperor urged him to hasten his journey to Constantinople, because the emperor burned with the desire to see Peter himself, on account of the report he had heard concerning him.

When Constantinople was reached [Col. 0399D], Peter’s army was ordered to lodge at a distance from the city, and full permission to buy provisions was granted them.

## CHAPTER XVI.—How Peter and the army were graciously received by the emperor, and thereafter crossed the sea.

Peter, small in stature but great in speech and heart, was brought by the emperor’s envoys into the emperor’s presence with Folcker alone, so that he might see whether he was as rumour represented him. Peter, entering confidently, greeted the emperor in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. He set out in detail how, out of love and grace for Christ, he had left his homeland to visit His holy sepulchre; and he recalled the adversities which he had already suffered in so short a time.

He announced that very powerful men, most noble counts and dukes, would shortly follow him, who, for the sake of seeing the Lord’s sepulchre, had likewise resolved in most ardent desire to set out upon the road to Jerusalem [Col. 0400A].

The emperor, having seen Peter and learned from his own words the purpose of his heart, asked what he wanted or desired from him. Peter prayed that he might receive him mercifully and provide the means for himself and his companions to sustain life, declaring how many and how innumerable goods he had lost through his followers’ imprudence and rebellion.

Hearing Peter’s humility, the emperor was moved to compassion. He ordered two hundred gold byzantii to be given him, and he distributed to his army one modius of the coin called *tartaron*. Thereafter Peter returned from the conference and palace of the emperor, having been graciously commended by him.

He rested only five days in the fields and estate near Constantinople [Col. 0400B], where Walter Senzavehor also pitched his tents. From that day onward Walter became his companion, their forces, arms, and every necessity being joined together.

Then, when five days had been completed, they struck their tents and crossed by ship, with the emperor’s aid, the arm of the sea of Saint George. Entering the borders of Cappadocia, they passed through mountainous country to Nicomedia, where they spent the night. Afterwards they encamped at the harbour called Civitot. Merchants constantly brought there ships laden with provisions—wine, wheat, oil, barley, and an abundance of cheeses—selling all things to the pilgrims fairly and by measure.

While they rejoiced in this abundance of necessities and tended their weary bodies, messengers of the most Christian [Col. 0400C] emperor arrived. They forbade Peter and his army to proceed toward the mountains of the city of Nicaea because of Turkish ambushes and attacks, until a larger number of the Christians expected to come should join them. Peter, hearing this, accepted the emperor’s embassy and counsel, as did all the Christian people. They remained there for two months, feasting in peace and joy, sleeping secure from every hostile attack.

## CHAPTER XVII.—How the young men made plunder in the territory of the city of Nicaea, and captured a certain castle of Solyman.

After two months, made wanton and unbridled by idleness and an immeasurable abundance of food, they would not heed Peter’s voice. Against his will, they entered through the mountains into the land of the city of Nicaea and the realm of Solyman, duke of the Turks. They plundered cattle, oxen, sheep, goats, and the flocks of Greeks serving the Turks, and brought them back to their companions.

Peter, seeing this, took it sadly, knowing that they would not go unpunished. Therefore he repeatedly warned them not further to engage in this plundering, in accordance with the emperor’s counsel; but he spoke in vain to a foolish and rebellious people.

Because these enterprises had succeeded and they still feared no resistance to their plundering, the bold and boastful young men resolved to take a force from the army and seize and carry off, before the walls of Nicaea and in the Turks’ sight, plunder from the meadows and pastures. Accordingly, some seven thousand foot-soldiers [Col. 0401A], together with only three hundred armoured horsemen, marched forth amid the raising of their standards and great uproar. They drove seven hundred oxen, besides other livestock, from the meadows of the city of Nicaea. Returning to Peter’s tents, they made a full and rich feast; indeed, they sold much of the herd to Greeks and sailors subject to the emperor.

But when the Germans saw that the Romans and Franks had succeeded well, and that they had so often returned with booty without hindrance, they too were inflamed by the greed of plunder. They assembled three thousand foot-soldiers and only two hundred horsemen. With standards of scarlet and purple, they entered the path through the same mountains and came to a certain castle of Solyman, the magnificent man, duke and prince of the Turks, where the mountains [Col. 0401B] and forest end, three miles distant from Nicaea.

They attacked the aforesaid castle with all the strength of their arms and with martial clamour, until they put its defeated inhabitants to the sword, sparing only Greek Christians. All the others found in that stronghold were either killed or driven out. Having taken the stronghold and expelled its inhabitants, they rejoiced in the abundance of food found there. Delighted by this victory, they counselled one another to remain in that fortress, easily gain control of Solyman’s lands and principality through their strength, gather plunder and food from every side, and safely weaken Solyman until the promised army of the great princes should draw near.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—How Duke Solyman, after gathering the Turks, took the aforesaid castle, led some away captive, and killed the rest.

[Col. 0401C]

Solyman, duke and prince of the Turkish army, hearing of the Christians’ arrival and of the plunder and robberies, gathered fifteen thousand of his men from all Romania and the kingdom of Corrozan: men most skilled in war with horn and bone bows, and most swift archers. When these had assembled, two days after the Germans’ victory, he returned from a distant land with a most powerful host to the city of Nicaea. There his anger and grief were further increased by the news concerning the Germans, the seizure of the stronghold which he had lost, and the slaughter and expulsion of his men.

Then, at sunrise on the third day, Solyman camped with all his company [Col. 0401D] and advanced from Nicaea to the stronghold seized by the Germans. His standard-bearers, attacking forcefully in the strength of their archers, cruelly struck and exhausted the Germans who resisted fiercely on the walls with arrows, until they could no longer stand in defence. Driven back from the walls and battlements by the excessive hail of arrows, they sought within the fortress shelter from the missiles, exposed and distressed.

When the Turks saw that they had forced the Germans back from the walls and battlements, they prepared to climb over them. But the Germans inside the stronghold, solicitous and zealous for life, opposed lances to those seeking to enter; others resisted them face-to-face with swords and double-headed axes, until they no longer dared to climb up [Col. 0402A].

Therefore, unable to frighten the Germans by the assault and excessive hail of arrows, the Turks brought every sort of timber to the very gate of the fortress. Setting fire beneath it, they burned it, along with many buildings in the citadel. As flame and heat grew stronger, some were burned alive; others, hoping for safety, leapt down from the walls. But the Turks outside slaughtered those who came out and fled with the sword. They led away captive about two hundred others, handsome youths in face and body; all the rest were destroyed by sword and arrow.

## CHAPTER XIX.—How the army waited eight days for Peter, and how the Turks beheaded certain men of the army.

After Solyman had returned with his men and German captives, having exacted this severe vengeance [Col. 0402B], news of the Germans’ most cruel slaughter reached Peter’s camp. Therefore the spirits and hearts of all were violently shaken with grief at the death of their brethren.

Moved by this misfortune to their people, they repeatedly debated among themselves whether they should immediately rise to avenge them or wait for Peter. For some days before, Peter had gone to Constantinople to petition the emperor on his army’s behalf, that he might ease for them the purchase of necessities.

While they were taking counsel, Walter Senzavehor wholly opposed going to avenge the brethren until the outcome of the affair was clearly known and Peter himself was present, by whose counsel they would undertake everything. The people were calmed by Walter’s counsel for eight days [Col. 0402C], awaiting Peter’s arrival. Yet Peter had still been unable to obtain leave from the emperor to return.

On the eighth day, one hundred Turks, military men renowned in the art of war, rose from the city of Nicaea and ranged through the region and towns situated in the mountains, wishing to learn about the plunder and robberies carried off by the Franks. On that very day they are said to have beheaded many pilgrims wandering here and there in various places, sometimes ten, sometimes fifteen, or more.

When this report was again spread through Peter’s camp—that the Turks were present and had beheaded their scattered men—they refused altogether to believe that the Turks had come down so far from Nicaea. Nevertheless, some advised pursuing them [Col. 0402D], if they might still be found within those borders.

## CHAPTER XX.—How, when the army had armed itself to avenge its companions, Solyman met it with a great force to fight.

Meanwhile, once the truth was known, a tumult arose among the people. The foot-soldiers unanimously came to Reinold of Breis, Walter Senzavehor, Walter of Bretoil, and Folcker of Orléans, who were the leaders of Peter’s army, urging them to rise against the Turks’ audacity in vengeance for their brethren.

But they wholly refused to go until they had Peter present and his counsel. Godfrey Burel, however, master of the foot-soldiers, hearing their replies, declared that such distinguished soldiers who were timid could be of no use in war. With harsh speech he repeatedly reproached [Col. 0403A] these men, who were preventing the other companions from pursuing the Turks in vengeance for their brethren.

By contrast, the leaders of the host, unable any longer to endure the insults and reproaches of him and his followers, deeply stirred by anger and indignation, promised to go against the Turks’ strength and ambushes, even if it should happen that they died in battle.

Without delay, when the first dawn of the fourth day broke, all horsemen and foot-soldiers throughout the camp were ordered to arm, to sound the trumpeters’ signals, and to assemble for battle. Only the unarmed and infirm, with innumerable women, were left in the camp.

Armed and altogether assembled, twenty-five thousand foot-soldiers and five hundred armoured horsemen set out upon the road to the city of Nicaea, in order to challenge Duke Solyman and the other Turks to battle [Col. 0403B] in vengeance for their brethren. Divided and arrayed in six battle-lines, each assigned to its standards, they advanced on right and left.

They had scarcely gone three miles from the harbour and station of Civitot. Peter was absent and knew nothing of everything. Through the aforesaid forest and mountains they advanced glorifying, shouting, and sounding loudly amid violent clamour and tumult. And behold: Solyman, with all his company, had entered the same forest from the opposite side, coming down from the city of Nicaea, intending suddenly to fall upon the Franks in their camp and destroy and wipe them all out by the sword while they were unaware and unprepared.

Hearing the Christians’ approach and vehement noise, he wondered greatly what this tumult might mean, for all that the Christians had resolved was concealed from him. As soon as he understood that the pilgrims were present, he spoke to his men:

> “Behold, the Franks whom we are seeking are here. Let it be certain to you that they come to fight against us. But let us withdraw as swiftly as possible from the forest and mountains into the open plain of the fields, where we may freely join battle with them and they may find no refuge.”

This was done at Solyman’s command; in great silence they emerged from the woods and mountains.

## CHAPTER XXI.—How the Turks fought fiercely with the Christians.

The Franks, unaware of Solyman’s approach, came out from the woods and mountains with shouting and loud cries. Then for the first time they saw Solyman’s battle-lines [Col. 0403D] in the middle of the plain, waiting for them for battle. Seeing them, they began to encourage one another in the Lord’s name, and sent forward two battle-lines containing five hundred horsemen.

Solyman, seeing the two battle-lines sent forward, immediately gave his horse rein, and his men did the same. With unheard-of and intolerable shouting they rendered the Catholic soldiers stunned and astonished. Then, with a hail of arrows, they charged through the middle of the battle-lines. The latter, severely battered and scattered, were separated from the multitude following them.

Hearing this clash of arms and the cruel pursuit of the shouting Turks, the rear of the army, which had not yet emerged from the forest, gathered together in the narrow path by which they had come, to resist and hold the narrow pass [Col. 0404A] and the mountainous ground. But the aforesaid battle-lines, through which the Turks had charged after separating them from their company, having no return to the forest and mountains, took the road toward Nicaea.

Immediately turning back from it, they flew strongly, shouting, through the midst of the Turks. Horsemen and foot-soldiers encouraged one another, and in a moment killed two hundred Turkish soldiers. But the Turks, seeing that the strength of the horsemen had prevailed in the struggle against their own men, wounded their horses with volleys of arrows, and thus made Christ’s bravest champions into foot-soldiers.

## CHAPTER XXII.—How the Turks slew an innumerable multitude of Christians.

Where Walter Sans-Avoir fell, pierced through corselet and vitals by seven arrows [Col. 0404B], Rainald of Breis and Fulcher of Chartres, men of greatest renown in their own land, likewise fell, consumed by martyrdom at the hands of the enemy—though not without great slaughter among the Turks. But Walter of Breteuil, son of Walram, and Godfrey Burel, commander of the infantry, escaped by flight among thorn-bushes and thickets; they returned by the narrow path along which the entire force, withdrawn from battle and gathered together, was being held. When their flight and the destruction of the others became known, all turned to flight, hastening by the same road by which they had come toward Civitot, offering little resistance to their enemies.

The Turks, rejoicing in the successful outcome of their victory, cut down the wretched company of pilgrims, pursuing them with slaughter for three miles as far as Peter’s tents [Col. 0404C]. Entering the tents, they put to the sword all whom they found sick and weak: clerics, monks, elderly women, nursing infants, and persons of every age. They carried off only tender girls and nuns whose faces and appearance pleased their eyes, as well as beardless youths and handsome young men; and they transported to Nicaea money, clothing, mules, horses, and every more valuable possession, together with the tents themselves.

Above the seashore, near the aforesaid Civitot, stood an old and deserted fortification. Three thousand fleeing pilgrims entered this ruined stronghold in hope of defense. But, finding no gates or barriers, distressed and bereft of aid, they rolled shields to the entrance in place of a gate, together with a huge mass of stones [Col. 0404D]. With lances alone, wooden bows, and stones thrown as missiles, they defended themselves bravely against their enemies, compelled by the necessity of preserving life.

But the Turks, seeing that they made little progress in slaughtering those shut within, surrounded the roofless stronghold on every side, shooting arrows high into the air so that, falling back from the sky upon the heads and bodies of those enclosed, they might kill the poor wretches and compel the survivors, at the sight, to surrender. Very many are reported to have been wounded and killed there in this way; yet, fearing a punishment more cruel from the impious enemy, they were not compelled to come out either by arms or by force.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—How the three thousand Christians who had escaped, besieged by the Turks, were delivered by the emperor’s aid.

The sun had already passed the middle of the day when these three thousand, having entered the stronghold, were besieged by the Turks [Col. 0405A]. Yet, defending themselves bravely from the necessity of preserving life, they could not be dislodged from this fortification by any device, even under the cover of that night, until a certain faithful and Catholic Greek messenger crossed the sea by boat at night, found Peter in the imperial city, and reported to him all their dangers, together with the downfall and destruction of the rest.

Peter, recognizing the peril of his followers and the misfortune of those destroyed, mourned and grieved, and humbly begged the emperor to aid, in the name of Jesus Christ, the few wretched pilgrims—the remnants of so many thousands—and not to allow them, abandoned and distressed, to be destroyed by such executioners. When the emperor heard from Peter of the disaster and siege of his people, he was moved to pity. Summoning Turcopoles from every quarter [Col. 0405B], together with all the peoples of his realm, he ordered them with all haste to cross the arm of the sea and aid the fugitive and besieged Christians, and to drive away the Turks from the siege after defeating them.

But when the Turks learned of the emperor’s command, they withdrew from the stronghold at midnight with their Christian captives and abundant spoils. Thus the enclosed and besieged pilgrim soldiers were delivered from the impious.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How a certain Gottschalk gathered a great company for the same expedition.

Not long after Peter’s crossing, a certain priest named Gottschalk, a German by nation and an inhabitant of the Rhine region, inflamed by Peter’s exhortation with love and longing for the same journey to Jerusalem, stirred by his preaching the hearts of very many people of diverse nations to press forward together upon the road [Col. 0405C]. From various regions of Lorraine, eastern Francia, Bavaria, and Alamannia, he gathered more than fifteen thousand persons, both soldiers and common footmen. Having collected an immense sum of money along with other necessary things, they are said to have continued their journey peacefully as far as the kingdom of Hungary.

Arriving by the favor of King Coloman at the gate and fortress of Meseburg, they were honorably admitted. They were also granted permission to buy the necessities of life; and peace was proclaimed on both sides at the king’s command, lest any disturbance arise from so large an army. But while they delayed there for several days and began to wander about, the Bavarians and Swabians—a spirited people—and other fools exceeded measure in drinking. They violated the proclaimed peace, gradually taking wine, barley, and other necessities from the Hungarians; at last they seized sheep and cattle from the fields and slaughtered them, and killed those who resisted or attempted to recover their goods. They perpetrated many other outrages, which we cannot all recount: acts characteristic of a people coarse in rustic fashion, undisciplined, and ungovernable [Col. 0405D].

As those present relate, they impaled a certain young Hungarian through his private parts with a stake in the marketplace over a most trifling quarrel. Complaint of this deed and of the other injuries was carried to the ears of the king and his princes.

## CHAPTER XXV.—How the entire army of Gottschalk, behaving insolently in Hungary, was destroyed.

[Col. 0406A]

Disturbed by this disgrace, and with all his household thrown into commotion, the king ordered his retainers to arm themselves, and, by signal, ordered all Hungary to rise in vengeance for this crime and the other insults, sparing none of the pilgrims because they had committed a shameful deed.

As soon as Gottschalk’s army understood this cruel command of the king, directed to their annihilation, they sounded their signals throughout all their companies and assembled on the plain of Belgrade beside the chapel of St. Martin. Without delay, the royal force of the whole kingdom of Hungary appeared under arms to scatter the assembled people. But they found the Germans strongly resisting, as men in distress and anxious for their lives, with swords, lances, and arrows [Col. 0406B]. Therefore the Hungarians themselves dared not attack them readily.

Seeing, then, that the matter concerned the pilgrims’ very lives, and that they could not engage the Franks without incalculable loss, they spoke deceptively to them in these words:

> “A complaint has reached our lord king concerning the injuries which you have inflicted upon his realm. Yet he judges that not all of you are guilty of this crime, since many sensible men are known to be among you, and the violation of the peace has troubled you no less than it has the king himself and his people. Therefore, if you wish to make satisfaction to the lord king and appease the princes of the land, it is proper and necessary that you surrender all your arms into the hand of the lord king; and, following our counsel, show yourselves peaceable. Enter the king’s power with all the money you possess, mitigate his anger, and thus find favor in his eyes. But if you act otherwise, not even one of you will be able to live before him and his men, because you have committed excessive insult and injury within his kingdom.”

Gottschalk and the other sensible men, hearing this, believed these words to be spoken in good faith. Since the Hungarians professed Christianity, they advised the whole assembly, in accordance with this speech, to surrender their arms in order to make satisfaction to the king, so that all might return to peace and concord. All accepted this counsel. They gave into the hands of the king’s officials their mail shirts, helmets, every weapon, and all their money—the provision, that is, for their lives in Jerusalem—and, humbled and trembling [Col. 0406C–D], submitted their necks to the king, confident that they would obtain from him every mercy and kindness.

But the king’s servants and soldiers carried all the arms into a chamber of the royal palace, while the money and the other more valuable possessions accumulated by so large an army they assigned to the royal treasury. Thus, after the weapons of all had been stored in the chamber, they proved false to every promise that the king would show mercy to the people. Rather, rushing upon them in cruel slaughter, they cut down the unarmed and naked and inflicted a most savage massacre upon them. So great was it that, as those who were present and barely escaped affirm as true, the whole plain of Belgrade was covered with dead and slain bodies and blood; few were freed from this martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—How an abundant people from diverse kingdoms assembled for the same expedition.

[Col. 0407A]

In the same year, at the beginning of summer, when Peter and Gottschalk had gone ahead with their gathered armies, thereafter an abundant and innumerable multitude of Christians from diverse kingdoms and lands—namely, from the kingdom of France, England, Flanders, and Lorraine—burning with the fire of divine love and having taken up the sign of the cross, continually flocked together in companies from every side. They came with all their household goods, property, and equipment of arms needed by those setting out for Jerusalem.

But although thus collected in companies from diverse kingdoms and cities, they had by no means turned away from illicit and fornicate intercourse. Their feasting was immoderate; there was continual indulgence with women and girls who had set out under the same frivolous intention [Col. 0407B]; and under the pretext of this journey they gloried in every kind of recklessness.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—On the slaughter of the Jews at Cologne.

For this reason—whether, I do not know, by the judgment of the Lord or through some error of mind—they rose in a spirit of cruelty against the Jewish people scattered through the various cities. They inflicted a most cruel slaughter upon them, especially in the kingdom of Lorraine, asserting that this was the beginning of their expedition and service against the enemies of the Christian faith.

This slaughter of the Jews was first perpetrated by citizens in the city of Cologne. Suddenly attacking their small number, they cut down many with grievous wounds, demolished their houses and synagogues, and divided a great quantity of money among themselves. Seeing this cruelty, about two hundred fled by boat in the silence of the night to Neuss [Col. 0407C]. When the pilgrims and those signed with the cross discovered them, they left not even one alive, but subjected them to a like slaughter and stripped them of all their possessions.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On a similar slaughter perpetrated at Mainz.

Without delay, pursuing the road as they had vowed, they arrived at Mainz in a vast multitude. There Count Emicho, a man most noble and most powerful in that region, was awaiting the arrival of the pilgrims with an immense German force, as they streamed there by the royal road from various places.

The Jews of that city, learning of the slaughter of their fellow Jews and realizing that they could not escape the hands of so great a multitude, fled in hope of salvation to Bishop Rothard. They entrusted boundless treasures to his protection and good faith [Col. 0407D], placing great confidence in his protection because he was bishop of that city. This chief priest of the city carefully stored away the extraordinary sum he had received from them, and placed the Jews in the most spacious upper chamber of his house, out of sight of Count Emicho and his followers, so that they might remain there safe and sound in a most secure and strong dwelling.

But Emicho and the rest of the band, having taken counsel, attacked the Jews in the upper chamber at sunrise with arrows and lances. Breaking bolts and doors, they overcame and killed as many as seven hundred, who resisted in vain against the strength and assault of so many thousands. They slaughtered the women likewise and struck tender children of every age and sex with the sword. But the Jews, seeing their Christian enemies rise against themselves and their little ones, sparing no age [Col. 0408A], likewise turned upon themselves, their fellow Jews, their children, women, mothers, and sisters, and killed them in mutual slaughter. Mothers—horrible to relate—cut the throats of their nursing children with the sword; others pierced them, choosing rather to perish by their own hands than to be destroyed by the weapons of the uncircumcised.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—How the army, denied passage, fought with the Hungarians.

After this most cruel slaughter of the Jews had been carried out, with few escaping and few baptized more from fear of death than love of Christian profession, Count Emicho, Clarebold of Vandeuil, Thomas, and all that intolerable company of men and women continued their road to Jerusalem [Col. 0408B]. They headed toward the kingdom of Hungary, where passage by the royal road was customarily not denied to pilgrims.

But when they came to the king’s fortress of Meseburg, which the rivers Danube and Lintax secure by marshes, they found the bridge and gate of the fortress closed by order of the king of Hungary. Great fear had seized all the Hungarians because of the slaughter inflicted upon their fellow Christians; the bodies of the slain still stank, while so great an army followed. There were two hundred thousand horsemen and foot soldiers, though the number of cavalry was scarcely reckoned at three thousand.

With the gate closed and passage through the kingdom denied to all, they pitched camp across the plain. They sent messengers to the king and sought peace, but they were not heard concerning their peace or their promise [Col. 0408C]. Thereupon Emicho, Thomas, and Clarebold—men distinguished in military action—took counsel with the more cautious among them: they would ravage the king’s lands lying on this side, and would not depart until a bridge had been laid across the marsh and the river Lintax. By it, approaching the wall of the fortress by some contrivance, they would pierce it, so that passage might thus be opened by their strength.

For many days from the middle of June they sat before the fortress and constructed a bridge. They frequently assaulted those shut in, while the defenders of the fortress resisted bravely, shooting missiles from both sides and causing much slaughter on either side. At times the latter sallied from the citadel in the strength of their mailed men and fiercely pressed the Franks on this side of the river and bridge. At times the Franks prevailed and drove the Hungarians, worn down by battle and wounds, back into the fortress [Col. 0408D].

One day, about the ninth hour, Thomas, Clarebold, and William, with three hundred soldiers trained in horsemanship and clad in mail and helmets, descended to lie in ambush at the place where the Hungarians often crossed by boat in order to defend their land. They hoped that an opportunity might arise to fight and begin battle with them, or to plunder their herds if found. While they descended in this expectation, seven hundred of the king’s soldiers came on horseback and in arms to reconnoiter the Christian army. Seeing that they could by no means escape, they suddenly attacked the Frankish companies. Joining battle, they were defeated, wounded, and grievously battered [Col. 0409A]; they fled by routes known to them and returned sadly and painfully by boat to their own land.

In this engagement William attacked and beheaded the commander of the Hungarian army and the king’s close kinsman, a distinguished man with shining white hair. Because of this victory all the legions spent that whole night awake in rejoicing, and they held many Hungarians captive.
