## CHAPTER XXX.—How, when the army was suddenly thrown into disorder, an innumerable multitude perished.

After these many clashes and daily slaughters over a long period, the army, overcome with weariness and weakened by want of food, appointed a day on which some, in the strength of their mailed men, crossed the bridge they had constructed, while others, spread through the marshes, fiercely attacked the fortress of Meseburg [Col. 0409B]. Bringing up siege-engines, they pierced the walls in two places and pressed the Hungarians hard, so that, if they persisted on the next day, nearly everything would be open to them.

But King Coloman and all his retinue mounted their horses early, ready to flee toward the kingdom of Rus’ if they should see so great a Frankish force, having overcome the fortress, enter the land. They had repaired bridges ruined by long age, by which they could cross the marshes and rivers into the land of Rus’ if necessity compelled them.

Yet when nearly everything had succeeded favorably for the Christians and they had penetrated the walls through a great breach, by some chance or misfortune unknown to me such great fear seized the whole army that all turned together to flight. Like sheep scattered and terrified by attacking wolves [Col. 0409C], seeking escape here and there, they forgot their companions. Seeing such strong warriors suddenly fail and hasten their flight, the Hungarians sprang from the gates with the king in great force. Without delay they pursued the fugitives, slaughtering very many, taking many captive, and often spending most of the night in pursuit.

The slaughter of the common foot-people of both sexes was so great that the waters of the Danube and Lintax were changed into bloody waves. Very many, indeed a number beyond comparison, hoping to save themselves by water, rushed with blind daring into the waves of the Danube for fear of the impending slaughter and were drowned by the violent waters. Wonderful to tell: so great was the drowning of the fugitives that for some time the waters of so broad a river could not be seen because of the bodies of so many thousands [Col. 0410A].

Emicho, Thomas, Clarebold, William, and a few others whose horses still had strength for running escaped unharmed, as did some who concealed themselves in marsh grass and thickets or were able to flee in the dark of night. Emicho and some of his men took flight back by the road on which they had come; Thomas, Clarebold, and many of their men escaped in flight toward Carinthia and Italy.

Thus the hand of the Lord is believed to have been against the pilgrims, who had sinned too greatly in his sight through uncleanness and fornicate intercourse, and who had slaughtered the exiled Jews—although opposed to Christ—in grievous massacre more through greed for money than for the justice of the Lord [Col. 0410B]. For the Lord is a just judge and commands no one unwilling or compelled to come beneath the yoke of the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On the superstition concerning a goose and a she-goat.

There was also another detestable crime among this gathering of foolish common people of frenzied frivolity—an act hateful to the Lord and, beyond doubt, incredible to all believers. They asserted that a certain goose was inspired by the divine Spirit, and that a she-goat was no less filled with that same Spirit. They made these animals their guides for this second journey to Jerusalem, venerated them excessively, and, in bestial fashion, attended to them with their whole heart.

Far be it from faithful hearts to suppose that the Lord Jesus wished the tomb of his most holy body to be visited by brute and senseless animals [Col. 0410C], or that these should become guides of Christian souls, whom he deigned to redeem by the price of his blood after recalling them from the filth of idols. When about to ascend to heaven, he appointed as guides and rulers of his people most holy bishops and abbots worthy of God—not brute, senseless animals.

But why should it be surprising if, in modern times, such abominations and so foul crimes were found among some companies of so many thousands, which the Lord repaid upon their own heads? For in the times of Moses, Joshua, and the other servants of the Lord, iniquity was found in the midst of the righteous, and was corrected and purged by the rod of his majesty, who is the Lord of avengings.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0409]

## CHAPTER I.—With whom and at what time Duke Godfrey undertook the second departure.

[Col. 0409D]

Accordingly, after the departure of Peter the Hermit; after the killing of the distinguished knight Walter Sans-Avoir and the most grievous disaster of his army; then, after a short interval, after the cruel slaughter of the priest Gottschalk and his army; after the misfortune of Count Emicho of Alemannia and of the other valiant men and leaders from the land of France—namely Drogo of Nahella [Col. 0410D], Clarebold of Vandeuil—and after the cruel destruction of their army in the kingdom of Hungary at the gate of Meseburg: Godfrey, Duke of Lorraine, a most noble man, together with his full brother Baldwin; Werner of Greis, the duke’s kinsman; Baldwin of Burg; Count Rainard of Toul and his brother Peter; Dudo of Cons; Henry of Ascha and his brother Godfrey—most valiant knights and most distinguished leaders—set out for Jerusalem by the direct road in the middle of August of that same year.

They took lodging for three weeks of September in the land of Austria, at the city of Tollenburg, where the river Lintax bounds and divides the kingdom of France [Col. 0411A], so that they might hear and learn on what occasion the uprising had arisen by which the army of pilgrims had perished only a few days before, had been turned aside from its purpose of going to Jerusalem with its leaders and commanders, and was now returning toward them in despair.

## CHAPTER II.—The leaders summoned the king of Pannonia through envoys, asking why he had destroyed the people of God.

At length, after much troubling report, while they repeatedly debated what they should first do, and what they should do more cautiously and prudently, in order to investigate the affair and the cruelty which the Hungarians had committed against their Christian brethren [Col. 0411B], all judged this counsel useful: that they should send no one among the most renowned and commanding men to investigate such a monstrous murder and crime, except Godfrey of Ascha. He was known to Coloman, king of that land, since long before this expedition he had been sent to the same king of the Hungarians as envoy of Duke Godfrey.

They sent with him twelve others selected from the duke’s household—namely Balderic of Stavelot and others whose names are unknown—that they might present the embassy of so great leaders in this manner:

> “To CALOMAN, king of the Hungarians, Godfrey, duke of the Lorrainers, and the other leading men of France: greeting and every good thing in Christ. Our lords and leaders wonder, since you profess Christianity, why you have destroyed the army of the living God in so cruel a martyrdom, forbidden them to pass through your land and kingdom, and afflicted them with various charges. Therefore, shaken now by fear and uncertainty, they have resolved to remain at Tollenburg until they learn from the king’s own mouth why so cruel a crime has been committed by Christians, persecutors of Christians.”

## CHAPTER III.—The king’s reply, and how he summoned the duke.

The king replied, with the entire assembly of his men listening:

> “We are not persecutors of Christians. Whatever cruelty we showed or committed in their destruction, we did under compulsion of extreme necessity. For when we had supplied everything to your first army, which Peter the Hermit gathered; when permission to buy had been granted under fair measure and weight; and when we had arranged for them peaceful passage through the land of Hungary, they repaid us evil for good. They not only carried off gold and silver, horses, mules, and livestock from our country, but also destroyed cities and fortresses, killed as many as four thousand of our people, and stripped them of property and clothing.
>
> “After these innumerable injuries, inflicted unjustly upon us by Peter’s company, the following army of Gottschalk—and the army recently crushed, which you have encountered fleeing—besieged Meseburg, a castle and stronghold of our kingdom. In the pride and unrestrained power of their strength, they wished to enter against us [Col. 0411D–0412A], so that they might punish and destroy us; from them, with God’s help, we scarcely defended ourselves.”

Having made this reply, the king ordered the duke’s envoys to be honorably lodged in his palace, in a place called Pannonia. For eight days every necessity was generously supplied to them from the king’s own table. Then, after eight days, the king took counsel with his chief men concerning the duke’s embassy and sent the envoys back, accompanied by envoys from his own household, to convey this answer to the duke and the leaders of the army:

> “King CALOMAN to Duke GODEFREY and all Christians: greeting and unfeigned affection. I have heard that you are a powerful man and a leader in your land, and that you are found faithful by all who know you. Therefore, loving you always solely on account of your good reputation, I now desire to see and know you. Accordingly I have determined that you should come down to us at the castle of Cyperon, without expectation of any danger; and, sitting on the opposite banks of the marsh, we may conduct a full conference concerning everything you ask of us and for which you consider us guilty.”

## CHAPTER IV.—How the duke, entering Pannonia, was honorably received, and what was agreed between him and the chief men of the kingdom.

Upon hearing the king’s message, the duke left the whole assembly behind. By counsel of the leading men, he took only three hundred knights and went to the king at the designated place. With the retinues on each side left behind, the duke brought only Werner of Greis, a most noble man and his kinsman, Rainard of Toul, and Peter. He ascended the bridge which lay over the marsh and, finding the king upon it [Col. 0412C], greeted him very graciously and kissed him with humble devotion.

Thereafter they held various discussions with one another concerning the concord and reconciliation of Christians, until this arrangement of peace and affection proceeded so firmly that the duke, trusting the king’s good faith, took twelve men from the three hundred and, with them, went down with the king into Pannonia and the land of the Hungarians. He appointed his brother Baldwin, leaving the three hundred men behind, to govern and provide for the people at Tollenburg.

When the duke entered Pannonia, the king himself and his chief men received him honorably. All things necessary and fitting for so eminent a man were kindly and abundantly prepared for him from the king’s household and table. Then, over eight days, while the king held a large assembly of his men, who had also gathered to see so celebrated a leader, he sought counsel as to on what pledge and assurance he could admit such a great armed army without danger to his kingdom and the possessions of his people [Col. 0412D].

At last a plan was found and explained to the duke: unless eminent men and leading figures of the army were given as hostages, passage would be granted neither to him nor to his men. Otherwise, under some pretext and in the power of such an innumerable multitude, the king might lose his land and kingdom. Hearing this, the duke yielded to the king’s wish in all things and did not refuse to provide the hostages he asked, but on this condition: that both the present army of pilgrims and any future one should pass through his land without any obstruction and peacefully obtain necessities of life by purchase.

Without delay, the king concluded a treaty with the duke; and all the leaders of his kingdom swore an oath that they would no longer injure pilgrims passing through. Once these matters had thus been confirmed on both sides in true faith, the king, by counsel of his men, demanded that Baldwin, the duke’s brother, become a hostage, together with his wife and household. The duke allowed this to be done without objection. Immediately, after eight days, he sent an embassy and ordered the whole army to hasten to the castle of Cyperon and to place their tents on the far bank of the river and marsh [Col. 0413A].

## CHAPTER V.—Where the army pitched camp by order of the duke.

At this embassy from the duke, the army began to rejoice exceedingly. All rejoiced, having formerly been anxious during the duke’s prolonged absence and believing that he had been betrayed by false faith and killed. But now, as though waking from a deep sleep, they arose and came in accordance with the duke’s command, pitching camp on the bank of the river and marsh [Col. 0413B].

When the tents had been set up, the duke returned from the kingdom of Hungary and was restored to his men. He reported how much care and honor the king had shown him; all that he had agreed with the king and his leaders; and how the king had demanded his brother Baldwin as a hostage with his wife and household until the people should pass in quiet and peace—otherwise, no permission to cross would be granted to them.

Shortly afterward he urged his brother Baldwin to become hostage for the people, as had been decreed. Baldwin began to resist and object vehemently, until the duke, disturbed by his hesitation, resolved that Baldwin should take charge of the army of God while he himself would not hesitate to become hostage for his brethren. At last Baldwin, having cast aside every wavering of mind, agreed to become a hostage and to be carried into exile for the safety of his brethren [Col. 0413C].

## CHAPTER VI.—How, after hostages were given, they passed through Hungary.

Accordingly, once so illustrious a leader had been made hostage and the king had returned with him into Pannonia, the whole army, by the king’s command and permission, was admitted over the bridge beyond the marsh and pitched camp at the river Lintax. When camp had been established and all had been accommodated in lodgings, Duke Godfrey ordered heralds to proclaim through every dwelling and tent, under penalty of death, that no one should touch anything or seize anything by violence in the kingdom of Hungary, nor cause any disturbance, but should obtain everything at a fair price.

Likewise the king ordered proclamation throughout his kingdom that the army should find every abundance of necessary things—bread, wine, grain, barley, beasts of the field, and birds of the air. Under penalty of life, the Hungarians were ordered not to burden or disturb the army with unjust prices, but rather to make all saleable goods readily available to them.

Thus, day after day, in quiet and peace, with fair measure and just purchase, the duke and people passed through the kingdom of Hungary and came to the river Drava. There, after making a structure of piled timber and binding together much wickerwork [Col. 0414A], they crossed the river. The king, with a very strong force of horsemen, constantly advanced on their left, together with Baldwin and the other hostages, until they came to the place called Francavilla.

They remained there for three days, obtaining by purchase the necessities of life and what the army required. Then, with all their people, they went down to Malevilla and spent five nights on the bank of the Sava. There the duke and the other leaders of the army learned that an intolerably strong force of the emperor of Constantinople’s soldiers had arrived to prevent the pilgrims’ passage through the kingdom of Bulgaria. Therefore the duke and all the others took counsel to send part of the army, armed, across the river ahead of the rest to restrain the emperor’s hostile soldiers until the people crossed by water. For no more than three ships were found there; by them a thousand mailed horsemen were sent across to secure the shore [Col. 0414B]. The rest of the multitude crossed the riverbed on rafts of bound timber and wickerwork.

## CHAPTER VII.—Where the king returned the hostages, and how the king of Greece addressed the duke through envoys.

Hardly had the people and their leader crossed the water when behold, the king arrived with all his retinue, bringing the duke’s brother Baldwin, his wife, and all the hostages. There he restored them into the duke’s hand. Then, commending the duke and his brother with great affection through many gifts and the kiss of peace, he returned to his own kingdom.

The duke and his entire army, stationed on the far bank, spent the night lodged in the Bulgarian town of Belgrade [Col. 0414C], which Peter and his army had plundered and burned not long before. In the morning the duke and his army rose and entered the immense and unfamiliar forests of the Bulgarian kingdom. There envoys of the emperor met them, delivering this message:

> “ALEXIUS, emperor of Constantinople and of the Greek realm, to Duke GODEFREY and his followers: undiminished affection. I ask you, most Christian duke, not to permit your people to ravage and plunder my kingdom and lands, into which you have entered; rather, obtain permission to buy, so that your people may find, throughout our dominion, all things sufficient for buying and selling.”

Understanding this embassy of the emperor, the duke promised to obey the emperor’s commands in every respect. Therefore it was proclaimed to all that thereafter no one should take anything by unjust force, except fodder for horses. Passing peacefully at the emperor’s request, they came to Niczh, one of his fortresses [Col. 0414D]. There, by the emperor’s gift, a marvelous abundance of food was offered to the duke—grain, barley, wine, oil, and much game—while the rest were granted permission to buy and sell. They were refreshed there for four days in every plenty and delight.

After this, the duke marched with the whole army to Sternitz, where no less richly were they supplied with gifts from the emperor. Then, after several days, he departed and came down to Philippopolis, a distinguished city. There likewise, by the emperor’s gift, he had every abundance of necessities for eight days [Col. 0415A]. There news was brought to him that the emperor had held Hugh the Great, brother of the king of France, Drogo, and Clarebold in chains and prison.

## CHAPTER VIII.—What message the duke sent in reply to the king, and what he did concerning the detained leaders.

Hearing this, the duke sent an embassy to the emperor, demanding that he restore to liberty those princes of his land whom he held captive; otherwise, he could not preserve faith and friendship with him. Baldwin, count of Hainaut, and Henry of Ascha, having learned of the duke’s embassy sent to the emperor, set out at first light, without the duke’s knowledge, and hastened on the road to Constantinople, so that, by arriving before the envoys, they might obtain greater gifts from the emperor. The duke, on hearing this, took it grievously [Col. 0415B]; yet, concealing his anger, he proceeded to Adrianople. There, having crossed a certain river by swimming the horses, he pitched his tents and spent the night.

The bridge which stretches across the river through the middle of the city was then forbidden by the inhabitants to him and his men. Rising thereafter and hurrying toward Salabria, they pitched their tents in the pleasant places of the meadows. There the duke’s envoys returned from the emperor and reported that he had by no means released the captive princes. Therefore the duke and all the company blazed up in anger, and were unwilling any longer to preserve faith or a treaty of peace with him. Immediately, by the duke’s command, all that land was given over as plunder to the pilgrim and foreign soldiers. Remaining there for eight days, they devastated the entire region.

## CHAPTER IX.—How the Greek emperor, having released the captive princes, provided for his realm, while summoning the duke.

[Col. 0415C]

The emperor, learning that the region was being ravaged, sent to the duke Ralph Peel of Lan and Rotger, son of Dagobert, most eloquent men, from the land and kinship of the Franks, begging that the army should cease from plundering and laying waste his kingdom; and that he would without delay return the captives whom the duke demanded.

The duke, having taken counsel with the other princes, accepted the emperor’s embassy; and, moving his camp and forbidding plunder, he withdrew to the very city of Constantinople with the entire company of pilgrims. Having pitched their tents there, they encamped in a powerful and formidable body, equipped with mail-coats and every kind of martial armour. And behold: Hugh the Great, Drogo, William the Carpenter, and Clarebold, released by the emperor, came to the duke, rejoicing at his arrival and at that of his multitude; falling into the embrace of the duke and the others with many kisses.

Likewise the aforesaid envoys of the emperor met the duke, begging him to enter the emperor’s palace with some of the foremost men of the army, that he might hear the king’s word, while the rest of the multitude remained outside the city walls. The duke scarcely accepted this embassy when certain newcomers from the land of the Franks secretly came to him in the camp. They strongly warned him to beware the emperor’s tricks, poisoned garments, and deceitful words; and not to enter to him because of any flattering promise, but, remaining outside the walls, safely to receive whatever might be offered him [Col. 0416A].

Accordingly, forewarned by the newcomers and instructed concerning Greek deceptions, the duke did not enter to the emperor at all. Therefore the emperor, violently angered against the duke and his whole army, forbade them leave to buy and sell. Baldwin, the duke’s brother, recognizing this indignation of the emperor and seeing the people’s need and the extreme shortage of necessities, persuaded the duke and the magnates of the army that they should again gather plunder through the regions and lands of the Greeks and bring in provisions, until the emperor, compelled by these calamities, should once more grant leave to buy and sell. The emperor therefore, seeing plundering and disaster fall upon the lands of his kingdom, renewed for all the permission to sell and buy.

## CHAPTER X.—After some hostilities on both sides, the duke at last makes peace with the emperor.

[Col. 0416B]

It was the Nativity of the Lord; and therefore, in so solemn a season and in days of peace and joy, it seemed to all good, praiseworthy, and acceptable before God that concord should be renewed on both sides, between the emperor’s household and the duke and all the mighty men of the army. Thus peace having been made, they restrained their hands from every act of plunder and injury. During these four holy days, therefore, they remained before the walls of Constantinople in complete quiet and enjoyment.

## CHAPTER XI.—At the emperor’s request, the duke changes the site of the camp; he sends envoys of goodwill to him, but, when asked, declines to come.

After four days, the emperor’s embassy came forth [Col. 0416C] to the duke, asking him, for the emperor’s sake and at his request, to move his camp and lodge with his army inside the palaces situated upon the shore of the sea-channel, because of the severe cold of snow and winter impending in the rainy season, lest their tents, soaked and worn away, should perish.

At last the duke and the other chief men yielded to the emperor’s will. Having removed their tents, they lodged throughout palaces and turreted houses extending for thirty miles along the seashore, with the whole army of Christians. From that day onward, by the emperor’s command, they found and bought every abundance of food and necessary things.

Shortly afterwards the emperor’s embassy again came to the duke, urging him to enter to the emperor and hear his words. The duke altogether refused this, having been warned by newcomer-citizens of that man’s treachery; but he sent to him distinguished envoys, Count Conon of Montaigu, Baldwin of Bourg, and Godfrey of Ascha, to excuse him and speak in this manner:

> “Godfrey the duke offers faith and service to the emperor. Gladly, and as I desire, I would enter to you and behold the honours and riches of your house; but the many evils which have reached my ears concerning you have frightened me. Yet I do not know whether these things have been invented and circulated through envy or hatred of you.”

Hearing this, the emperor greatly excused himself in all matters, saying that the duke, or anyone from his company, ought never to fear any deceit from him; rather, that he would keep and honour him and his men as a son and friends. The duke’s envoys returned and favourably reported all that they had heard promised generously and faithfully from the emperor’s own mouth [Col. 0417A]. Yet the duke, still not believing his honeyed promises, wholly rejected an interview with him. Thus fifteen days passed amid these messages sent back and forth.

## CHAPTER XII.—The emperor withdraws provisions for sale; the army invades parts of Greece.

The emperor, therefore, recognizing the duke’s firmness and that he could not be induced to come into his presence, was again greatly offended. He withdrew barley and fish from sale, then the provision of bread, so that the duke, forced even thus, might not refuse the emperor’s presence.

But since the emperor did not succeed in softening the duke’s mind, one day, at the emperor’s instigation, five hundred Turcopoles, conveyed by ships across the sea-channel [Col. 0417B], armed with bow and quiver, struck the duke’s soldiers early in the morning with arrows. Some they killed; others they wounded and drove away from the shore, so that they might not buy provisions there as usual.

This cruel report was immediately brought to the duke’s seat. He at once ordered the horns to sound, the whole people to arm, and a return to the front of Constantinople itself, with the tents to be pitched again. At this command of the duke, when the trumpeters’ signal was given, all rushed to arms; and they devastated some of the palaces and towers in which they had lodged by fire, and demolished others, inflicting irreparable damage upon Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The duke’s brother, at risk, leads the duke’s people across; he separates the contending sides.

When the report of such violent fire and destruction had now arisen in the palace [Col. 0417C], the duke was exceedingly alarmed. He feared that, when the flame of the buildings and the tumult of the moving army were perceived, the emperor’s soldiers and archers might suddenly seize by force the bridge by which they had passed from the city of Constantinople to the palace lodgings.

Therefore, without delay, he sent ahead his brother Baldwin with five hundred mailed knights to secure the bridge, lest some force of the emperor, arriving first, should destroy it and thereby deny the pilgrims passage and return across it. Baldwin had scarcely taken his stand in the middle of the bridge when, behold, from right and left, Turcopoles—the emperor’s soldiers—borne about by ships, attacked the crossing men everywhere with arrows and fought fiercely.

Having no means of resisting them from the bridge [Col. 0417D], Baldwin hurried to escape their arrows. Having crossed the bridge, he quickly moved onto dry ground at its other end, taking and guarding the bridge in the direction of the walls of the ruling and mistress-city, until the whole army had crossed. The duke, with his men, kept guard in the rear.

Meanwhile, from the gates toward Saint Argenius, an innumerable host of Turcopoles and soldiers of every kind sprang forth, with arrows and varied armour, to attack Baldwin and the whole company of the Christian people. But Baldwin, unmoved and unconquerable under every assault, held his position until, from morning until evening, the people had been brought across the bridge before the city walls and had lodged after pitching camp. Then, with five hundred mailed knights, he vigorously charged the same Turcopoles who had come out from the gates and were attacking the people.

A fierce battle was joined on both sides; very many fell on either side, and many Frankish horses perished from arrows. But in the end Baldwin prevailed, forcing these emperor’s soldiers, burdened and fleeing, to make for the gates; and he powerfully took possession of the fields and victory [Col. 0418A].

The Turcopoles and the emperor’s soldiers, angered at having been defeated and put to flight in battle, repeatedly came pouring more thickly out of the gates to provoke and attack the army. Until the duke arrived, because it was night, and settled everything in peace, instructing his brother and all the men to return to camp and, in the darkness of night, to withhold their hands and arms from this battle. Likewise the emperor, fearing that this storm of war would fall more heavily and fiercely, and that in the shadowy evening his men would fail and perish, himself ordered peace to be made, rejoicing that the duke had wished to restrain his men from war [Col. 0418B].

## CHAPTER XIV.—The emperor, promising hostages, invites the duke to himself; and what the duke answered the envoys of Bohemond.

At the dawn of the next day, the people rose at the duke’s command and, ranging through the emperor’s land and kingdom, plundered heavily for a course of six days, so that at least in this way the pride of the emperor and his men might seem humbled. When he learned this, the emperor began to grieve and lament that his land and kingdom were being thus devastated.

He immediately took counsel and sent an embassy to the duke, requesting him to stop the plunder and burning, and saying that he would satisfy him in all things, in these words [Col. 0418C]:

> “Let enmities between us and you cease, and let the duke enter to me, receiving from me, without any doubt, assurance and hostages that he shall come and return unharmed, certain of every honour and glory that we can bestow upon him and his men.”

The duke graciously accepted this, provided hostages were given such as he could trust concerning his life and safety; and then, without doubt, he would go down to the emperor and willingly speak with him in person, mouth to mouth.

The emperor’s envoys had scarcely departed after this answer of the duke when, behold, certain other envoys came to the same duke on Bohemond’s behalf and greeted him, saying:

> “Bohemond, the very wealthy prince of Sicily and Calabria, asks you by no means to return to agreement [Col. 0418D] with the emperor, but to withdraw into the Bulgarian cities of Adrianople and Philippopolis and spend the winter there. Be certain that, when March begins, Bohemond himself will come with all his forces to your aid, to defeat this emperor and invade his kingdom.”

Having heard Bohemond’s embassy, the duke deferred making any answer in return until the next day dawned. Then, by counsel of his men, he replied:

> “He had not left his land and kindred for gain or for the destruction of Christians, but had undertaken, in Christ’s name, the journey to Jerusalem; and he wished to complete and fulfil it by the emperor’s counsel, if he could recover and preserve the emperor’s favour and goodwill.”

The envoys of Bohemond, understanding this intention and reply of the duke, were graciously commended by the duke and returned to Apulia [Col. 0419A], reporting everything as they had learned it from his own mouth.

## CHAPTER XV.—Having received the emperor’s son as hostage, the duke enters the court.

The emperor, learning of this new embassy and proposal of Bohemond, pressed the duke and his friends still more concerning an agreement: if the duke wished to be reconciled with him and pass peacefully through his land, and to present himself to him face to face for an interview, he would give his dearest son, named John, as a hostage to the duke; and would furnish him and his men with all necessities and leave to buy.

When the duke understood that these promises of the emperor were decreed and confirmed, he moved his camp away from the city wall. Again crossing the bridge, he withdrew for lodging to the fortified buildings on the sea-channel [Col. 0419B], instructing the whole people to remain peaceful and buy necessities without disturbance.

At dawn the next day, he ordered Count Conon of Montaigu and Baldwin of Bourg, most noble men and most eloquent in every utterance, to appear before him; and confidently sent them to receive the emperor’s son as hostage. This was done. The emperor’s son, now taken as hostage and placed in the power of the duke and his men under faithful guard, the duke without delay was conveyed by ship across the sea-channel to Constantinople.

Taking with him distinguished men—Werner of Greis, Peter of *[name incomplete in the source]*, and the other princes—he boldly entered the emperor’s court and stood before him face to face, that he might hear his word [Col. 0419C] and answer him orally concerning everything he might demand, or put any matter to him. Baldwin, however, did not then enter the emperor’s palace, but remained on the shore with the multitude.

## CHAPTER XVI.—How gloriously the duke was received and entertained by the emperor, and what was agreed between them.

The emperor, seeing so magnificent and honourable a duke and his followers, in the splendour and adornment of costly garments—both purple and gold embroidery, and snow-white ermine work, marten, grey fur, and vair, which the princes of Gaul especially use—was greatly amazed at their honour and elegance. First he graciously received the duke with a kiss; then he did not delay to honour all his chief men and companions with the same kiss of peace.

The emperor, however, sat according to his custom in majesty upon the throne of his kingdom. He rose neither for the duke nor for anyone to offer kisses; rather, the duke bent with knees bowed, and his men also bent to kiss the most glorious and mighty emperor [Col. 0419D].

When all had been kissed in turn, he spoke to the duke in these words:

> “I have heard of you that in your land you are a most powerful knight and prince, and a man of the greatest prudence and perfect faith. Therefore I receive you as an adopted son; and I place in your power all that I possess, so that through you my empire and land may be delivered and preserved from the present and coming multitude.”

Pleased and won over by these peaceful and kindly words of the emperor, the duke rendered himself to him not only as son, as is the custom of that land, but also as vassal, with joined hands, together with all the leading men then present and those who afterwards followed [Col. 0420A].

Without delay, gifts beyond valuation were brought from the emperor’s treasury for the duke and all who had assembled: gold and silver, purple cloth of various kinds, mules and horses, and everything most precious that he possessed. Thus the emperor and duke were bound together by an indissoluble bond of perfect faith and friendship. From the time of the Lord’s Incarnation when this agreement occurred until a few days before Pentecost, each week four men, laden with gold Byzantine coins and with ten modii of tartaron coinage, were sent from the emperor’s household to the duke, by which the soldiers could be supported.

Wonderful to relate! Everything which the duke distributed among the soldiers from the emperor’s gift immediately returned to the king’s treasury in exchange for provisions [Col. 0420B]; and not only these funds, but also whatever the army had collected there from beneath the whole world. Nor is this surprising: throughout the entire kingdom no goods except the emperor’s were sold, whether wine and oil, wheat and barley, or any food. Thus the king’s treasury, continually rich in money, could not be exhausted by any expenditure.

## CHAPTER XVII.—At the emperor’s advice, the people of the Lord move into Cappadocia. The duke repeatedly petitions the emperor concerning necessities.

When peace and agreement between emperor and duke had been confirmed on the condition mentioned above, the duke was brought back to the lodgings in the buildings by the sea-channel and honourably returned the emperor’s son, the hostage, now assured of the faith and friendship received from the emperor [Col. 0420C].

On the following day it was proclaimed by the duke’s command throughout the whole army that peace and honour should henceforth be shown to the emperor and all his men, and that justice should be observed in every measure of buying and selling. Likewise, the emperor prohibited throughout his realm, on pain of death, anyone from harming or defrauding anyone of the army; all things were to be sold to the pilgrims at fair weight and measure, and the price was to be reduced.

After this, when the season of Lent began, the emperor summoned the duke into his presence. He urgently adjured and begged him, by their friendship and plighted faith, to cross the water and pitch his tents in the land of Cappadocia, because the unruly people were destroying the buildings [Col. 0420D]. The duke graciously agreed. Having crossed the water, he and the whole people pitched camp and stayed in the meadows of Cappadocia on the other shore.

From that time onward, goods were gradually sold dearly to the pilgrims; yet the emperor’s gifts to the duke were not diminished at all, for he feared him greatly. But the duke, observing the scarcity in the sale of necessities and receiving the people’s outcry with distress, frequently went by ship to meet the emperor and reproached him over the excessive cost of goods for sale. The emperor, pretending ignorance and that he did not wish this to happen, again reduced the prices of all things for the pilgrims.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Bohemond arrives and is with difficulty persuaded to become the emperor’s man.

While these matters were being conducted between the duke and the emperor [Col. 0421A], and holy Easter had passed three weeks earlier, Bohemond, having ten thousand cavalry and very numerous forces of infantry, came down through Valona, Durazzo, and the other cities of the Bulgarian kingdom, and stood in great strength before the walls of Constantinople.

At the emperor’s request, the duke, taking twenty leading men from his army, met him so as to bring him, under firm assurance, into the emperor’s presence before he laid down his arms or pitched his tents. At last, after they had greeted one another and the duke had spoken long with Bohemond and sought, with many conciliatory words, to persuade him to enter the court to hear the emperor’s word, Bohemond absolutely refused. He said that he greatly feared the emperor, because he was regarded as a crafty and deceitful man.

In the end, overcome by the duke’s good promise and persuasion, he entered the emperor’s palace confidently and was received with the kiss of peace and with every favour and honour [Col. 0421B]. Afterwards, after various discussions and counsels between them, Bohemond became the emperor’s man, agreeing with him under oath and pledged faith that he would retain nothing of the emperor’s kingdom except by his grace and consent.

At once there were brought to Bohemond, as to Godfrey, gifts: marvellous and unheard-of treasures in gold and silver, precious vessels remarkable for workmanship and beauty, and gifts far greater than anyone could estimate.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Bohemond’s nephew secretly departs; the duke and his men are honourably dismissed by the emperor; Count Robert.

While this agreement and treaty between the emperor and Bohemond were being made [Col. 0421C], Tancred, Bohemond’s sister’s son, crossed the sea-channel with his entire company and equipment, both his own and Bohemond’s, without the knowledge of the emperor, duke, or Bohemond, lest he too should become subject to the emperor.

When the emperor heard of this bold action of Tancred, he took it badly, because Tancred had avoided an interview with him. Yet prudently concealing this, he sent Bohemond and the duke, commended with affection, immense honour, and a lavish bestowal of gifts, across the water to the army.

A short while later Robert of Flanders arrived with immense forces. He too, having heard of the agreement of the duke and Bohemond with the emperor, made a treaty and became the emperor’s man. Therefore he also, like them, deserved to receive great gifts from the emperor’s hand [Col. 0421D]. After some days, he was graciously commended by the emperor; and, having crossed the water of the aforesaid sea-channel, he joined his companions and the Christian princes in the region and meadows of Cappadocia, allied with them in arms and forces.

## CHAPTER XX.—The army directs its march toward Nicaea; concerning Count Raymond, Peter the Hermit, and certain other princes.

Not long thereafter, when such distinguished men had assembled in one body, it pleased them by common counsel, now that the fitting time for the expedition had appeared, to continue henceforth the journey, as they had vowed, toward the city of Nicaea. The heathen power of the Turks had unjustly wrested it from the emperor [Col. 0422A] and subjected it to its own rule.

On the same day on which they moved camp, they reached Rufinel. And behold, an embassy from Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, came, reporting that he too had entered the city of Constantinople and made a treaty with the emperor. He asked and earnestly entreated them to await him and the bishop of Le Puy, named Reymer.

But they declared that they would by no means wait for him or remain longer in those parts. They would advance gradually; the count himself could follow by a direct route without excessive haste, once he had prudently and diligently arranged his affairs with the emperor.

At Rufinel itself Peter the Hermit, having waited for the princes, joined them with the few survivors of his worn-down multitude. Raymond’s envoys, having received the duke’s answer, returned to Constantinople [Col. 0422B]. The duke, Bohemond, and Robert of Flanders, honoured with precious gifts from the king and highly commended, continued their journey. Raymond, having become favoured and beloved by the emperor, remained fifteen days in Constantinople, receiving much honour and many gifts from the emperor, and becoming his man under pledged faith and oath.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Concerning the siege of the city of Nicaea.

In these days Robert, count of the Normans, Stephen of Blois, and Eustace, brother of the aforesaid duke, likewise arrived with a great host of cavalry and infantry. They too made a treaty and friendship with the emperor, became his men under an oath of faith, and were honoured by him with very great gifts.

Meanwhile the duke and those with him came to the city of Nicaea [Col. 0422C]. There the duke was the first to establish the siege, pitching camp before the city’s greater gate. When the other princes followed, they had very little rest in the regions of Cappadocia beyond the aforesaid channel of the Sea of Saint George; instead, hastening on their way, they too encamped and took their positions around Nicaea. The city seemed unconquerable through walls, ramparts, and the fortifications of towers.

In this ancient and very strong city, Solymanus, one of the princes of the Turks, a most noble but heathen man, held authority. On hearing of the Christians’ intended arrival, he strengthened the city with every kind of armour and with valiant men. He also brought in abundant provisions gathered from every direction, and secured all the gates everywhere with the strongest bolts.

When the aforesaid princes gathered around Nicaea and its walls on their swiftest horses [Col. 0422D], some took delight in charges and movements of cavalry, admiring the towers, the very strong walls, and their double walls. Yet, though they had surveyed these things, they could not be shaken by any fear. Rather, animated with every sort of courage and military array, they assaulted and attacked the city. Others, attacking on foot, harassed the city’s defenders in war with bows and arrows no less vigorously. But many were worn down by the very heavy blows and missiles of defenders above, because they rashly dared, in blind and sudden onset and commotion, to attempt battle close to the walls.

## CHAPTER XXII.—Further disposition of the siege: which parts of the city were assigned to which princes.

The princes of the army, seeing the people thus perish vainly and uselessly in battle [Col. 0423A], without being able to harm in any way those enclosed in this stronghold, judged that nothing was better than to surround the city on every side with a siege and constrain both the city and the guards upon the walls.

Thus, in the first disposition of the siege, Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, prince and lord of the castle of Bouillon, was stationed with the whole company of Lorrainers. Bohemond, prince of Sicily and Calabria, a Norman by nation, a man of high courage and remarkable intelligence, most capable in every military virtue in war, and exceedingly rich, established his position nearby. Tancred, an illustrious young knight, was assigned to take his position beside the same Bohemond, his uncle, with his companions.

A certain Tatinus, of mutilated nose, a confidant of the emperor of Constantinople and privy to his secrets, was leader of the Christian army because the places of the region were known to him. With an auxiliary force of the emperor’s soldiers, he pressed the city on the side assigned to him [Col. 0423B].

Robert, count of Flanders, inferior to none of them in arms, wealth, or strength; and Count Robert, prince of Normandy, the most fierce son of the king of England, exceedingly rich in arms and military resources, were stationed in order beside the aforesaid men in the siege of the same city.

Werner of the castle of Greis, an irreproachable knight in military skill; Eustace, brother of the aforesaid Duke Godfrey; and their brother Baldwin, a very famous man and unconquered in war, likewise took their places in order.

Baldwin of Montcastle, count and prince of Hainaut, a most illustrious man in every military undertaking; Thomas of the castle of Feria, a Frank and a most resolute knight; together with Baldwin of Bourg, Drogo of Nahella, Gerard of Keresicastle, Anselm of Riburgismont, Count Hugh of Saint-Pol, Engilrad, son of the same Hugh and a distinguished knight, Guy of the castle of Porsessa, a most valiant young knight in arms, Baldwin of the castle of Ghent, and another Baldwin, a man renowned in war, surnamed Count Calderim; together with William of the castle of Foreis, distinguished in every military virtue and power—all these very brave men took their places on the side assigned to them, to watch the city, scarcely conquerable by human strength [Col. 0423C].

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Further concerning the same.

The bishop of Le Puy, named Reymer, filled with every goodness, strengthened the forces around the city with a not inconsiderable body of men and equipment. Stephen, count of Blois, the head and foremost man in counsel throughout the whole army, guarded the city on one side with a great multitude. Hugh, surnamed the Great, brother of the king of France and a most illustrious companion, took his place in his own order to guard the city.

Robert, son of Gerard; Raymond surnamed Pellez; Bonwanker of the castle of Capis; Milo, surnamed Lover, a most valiant knight; Stephen of Albemarle, son of Odo, count of Champagne; Walter of Dromedart and his most beloved son Bernard, delightful in every deed and appearance; Gerard of Gorna; Gothard, son of Godfrey, a most distinguished youth; Ralph, very rich in forces; Lord Alan, surnamed Ferrans; and Conan also, both princes of the Bretons; Reinold of the city of Beauvais; Walo of Calmont; and William of Montpellier—undaunted men—pitched their tents and encamped with the other aforesaid men around the circuit of the city [Col. 0424A].

Castus of the city of Berdeiz; Gebard of the city of Roselon; Gilbert of Treves, one of the princes of Burgundy; Oliver of the castle of Jussy, a bold and warlike knight; Achar of Motinerla, white-haired; Reimbold, count of the city of Oringis, than whom none was more valiant; Louis of Monzons, remarkable in military action, son of Count Diric of Monthiliart; Dudo of Cons, red-haired and most skilled in war; Gozelo and his brother Lambert, most expert in war, with their father Conon of Montaigu, a most illustrious man—set their tents beside those of the aforesaid men.

Peter of Stadeneis, Reinard of the city of Toul, Walter of Verveis, Arnulf of Tyr, John of Namecca, and Herebrand of Bouillon—all these, tireless for every blaze of war, surrounded the city [Col. 0424B].

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Concerning men of the sacred order and the unarmed populace, and the city’s lake.

There is no doubt that with so many leading captains there were present not a few followers and lesser persons: male and female servants, married and unmarried women, men and women of every rank. Bishops, abbots, monks, canons, and priests were set over all these to instruct and strengthen them.

The whole city was enclosed by these forces, except for the place which they had assigned to Count Raymond to guard, but which had been left vacant. So numerous an army allowed no food, nor anything necessary for the body, to be brought in through any gate [Col. 0424C].

But on one side of the city walls there was a lake of extraordinary breadth and length, deep like the sea and suitable for oars and vessels. Through it a way of entrance and departure often lay open for Solymanus’s men bringing in necessities, and for Solymanus himself. Raymond, the aforesaid count from the land of Saint-Gilles, called Provence, had not yet contributed his forces and assistance; for he was lingering at Constantinople with his divisions in alliance with the emperor, greatly bound to him by the magnificent gifts which were increased day by day from the king’s household.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Concerning the prince of the city of Nicaea and his scouts.

[Col. 0424D]

Solymanus, hearing of the assembly of so many warrior-men, left the garrison of Nicaea to seek the assistance of the other Turks and heathens. He laboured for very many days, until he gathered from all Romania five hundred thousand fighting men and armoured horsemen.

When these had been assembled and instructed from every side, the report of the siege of Nicaea and of the Christian army reached his ears, together with the statement that a number above four hundred thousand had encamped there. Stunned by this report, he set out through the mountains with all his gathered forces toward the walls of Nicaea, hoping from a rocky lookout to discern with his own eyes whether so many thousands as he had heard had indeed gathered there, and on what side [Col. 0425A] he might most advantageously attack them.

At last, by counsel of his men, after the fourth day of the siege had passed, this same Solymanus sent two of his men, under a false Christian appearance and in the guise of pilgrims, to spy out the strength and actions of the Christian army. They were to bring this message to the guards of the citadel and defenders of the city of Nicaea:

> “Know that Solymanus, prince and lord of our city, sends us to you, so that you may hold the firmest hope in his aid. Let no fear be instilled into you by those besieging you, for they are exhausted by a long journey and have come here into exile; they are to be reckoned fools. He will deal with them by a similar punishment and martyrdom as he dealt with the companies of Peter a few days ago, and he is ready shortly to aid you with a mighty hand and countless thousands.”

Having received this message from Solymanus, the two men sent ahead took known and indirect paths toward the place where the city was under siege, in hope that they might secretly sail to the city’s defenders and make known what Solymanus had commanded them: namely, that Solymanus, having formed his battle-lines, would shortly attack the pilgrims, and that all the strength of the Turks should burst out from the gates and, joining in force, destroy the people of the Lord [Col. 0425B].

But by the Lord’s will, Christian guards had been posted all around to protect the places and paths, lest any deceit or hostile force should do harm. These two men sent by Solymanus were captured and detained. One was killed in the encounter; the other was brought before the Christian princes.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Further concerning one of those scouts, and how carefully the people of the Lord awaited the coming of the heathens.

[Col. 0425C]

Godfrey, Bohemond, and the others compelled the man who had been seized, by threats of torture, to explain truthfully why he had been sent. Terrified by the threats of so many chosen princes, recognizing that his life stood at the point of death, and trembling in every limb, he pleaded earnestly for his life and safety in a tearful voice, with downcast face and an unceasing flood of tears. He promised to disclose the truth of the matter and what would be useful and salutary for the whole people.

He confessed that he had been sent by Solyman, who, he said, was encamped among the mountain ridges with an innumerable host and was so near [Col. 0425D] that they expected him to arrive for battle on the following day about the third hour. He also said that Solyman’s stratagems and sudden attacks could be forestalled by his report. He begged that he be kept in custody until the stated hour, until the truth of the matter and Solyman’s arrival might be proved; but if he had deceived them in any respect, he asked that his life by no means be spared, but that he should perish with his neck cut off. He also pressed with much humble entreaty to receive baptism by professing Christianity and to share with Christians in Christian law. Yet he sought this more from fear of the death he had incurred than from any love of the Catholic faith.

At last the hearts of the leading men of the army were softened by his pitiable weeping and his excessive promise of Christianity. Taking pity on him, they granted him his life; nevertheless [Col. 0426A] he was sent into the custody he had requested. From then on the whole Christian army was kept alert with sleepless care, day and night, furnished with arms and equipment, until the hour at which, on the captive’s promise, they had learned that Solyman’s innumerable forces would pour forth from the Alps.

Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, Robert of Flanders, and all who were present sent a message throughout that night to Count Raymond, urging him to hasten his march more than usual if he wished to engage the Turks in battle and aid his companions. For they knew that he had lately been released by the emperor, who had commended him with many honors and riches. When he learned of the embassy from such great princes and of Solyman’s so swiftly impending arrival, he made no further delay, but hastened his journey throughout that night. At the first hour of day, when the sun was already filling the world with light, he arrived with the bishop of Le Puy, under standards of diverse colors and adornment, with a cavalry and infantry force in cuirasses and helmets, of mighty strength.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Solyman’s arrival; the exhortation of the bishop of Le Puy; the battle and victory of the Christian people.

Hardly had the count’s tents been pitched when Solyman descended from the mountain heights about the third hour, with all his following overflowing like the sand of the sea, advancing in battle-lines along various paths: all were very brave men, exceedingly skilled in war, heavily armed with cuirasses, helmets, and golden shields, and bearing in their hands many standards of marvelous beauty. In their first battle-line, about ten thousand men, all [Col. 0426C] archers, had hurried ahead into the valley of Nicaea, carrying in their hands horn and bone bows, exceedingly stiff for striking, all mounted upon horses very swift in running and well suited to war.

Thus Solyman and his men, descending, strove to burst violently through the city gate which the aforesaid Count Raymond had besieged in order to guard it. But they were severely driven back and defeated by the count himself and by Baldwin, the duke’s brother, who met them from the opposite side with Baldwin of Calderim and a great force.

Amid the clash of this most cruel war, among men rushing hand to hand, the bishop’s speech comforted the people thus:

> “O people dedicated to God, you have left all things for the love of God—riches, fields, vineyards, and castles. Now everlasting life lies ready for him to whom it may fall to be crowned with martyrdom in this battle. Without doubt, attack these enemies who are opposed to the living God; with God granting it, today you shall receive victory.”

At this exhortation Pagan of Garlande, steward of the king of the Franks, Wido of Porsessa, Tancred, Rotger of Barnaville, Robert of Flanders, and Robert, prince of the Normans, immediately came to the aid of their brethren in Christ, charging through the midst of the battle-lines with lightning blows and the speed of their horses. Duke Godfrey and Bohemond, not delaying their horses, flew with loose reins through the midst of the enemy, piercing some with lances, throwing others from their horses, and often exhorting their companions with manly encouragement to slaughter the enemy.

There was heard there no slight crash of lances, no slight ringing of swords and helmets in this contest [Col. 0427A] of war; no slight destruction of Turks was wrought by these distinguished men and their companions. When, by God’s grace, this victory had been won by the Catholic people, Solyman and his followers returned in flight to the mountains, no longer daring to attack the people of God in this siege with battle.

From that day the faithful of Christ showed every kindness to Solyman’s captive envoy, because they found him true and faithful in his promise; as a private person, he was loved among the households of the highest princes. The Christians cut off the heads of the slain and wounded and carried them to their tents fastened to the straps of their saddles as tokens of victory. They returned joyfully [Col. 0427B] to their companions, some of whom had been left in the tents around the city to prevent the enclosed men from escaping.

When the storm of this first battle around Nicaea had been calmed, they hurled the severed heads of Turks inside the city walls, to terrify the commanders of the citadel and the guards of the walls. Then they collected a thousand Turkish heads, placed them in carts, sacks, and wagons, carried them to the port called Civitot, and sent them by ship to the emperor at Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—The emperor’s generosity toward the princes, and the Turk who was a Christian in name only.

When the emperor saw so many heads of his adversaries and of Solyman’s soldiers—Solyman, by whose unjust violence he had deceitfully lost the city of Nicaea—he rejoiced greatly in this triumph of the faithful and arranged for them to receive a great reward for their military labor. Accordingly, he sent no small sum of money [Col. 0427C], various kinds of purple cloth, and every necessity for rewarding each powerful man, in mule- and horse-drawn vehicles. He also granted countless provisions, and throughout his kingdom the fullest liberty of selling and buying.

At the emperor’s command sailors and merchants competed in traversing the sea in ships full of food—wheat, meat, wine, oil, and barley—until they cast anchor at the port of Civitot. There the companies of the faithful found everything for sale to restore bodies previously weakened by fasting. Enjoying and rejoicing in this abundance of food, they agreed and declared that they would not depart until the city had been overcome, captured, and restored to the emperor’s authority. For by oath they had promised to retain nothing of the emperor’s realm—not forts [Col. 0427D] nor cities—except by his will or gift.

When he learned and investigated this, and saw the Christians’ victory and the Turks’ exceedingly bloody slaughter, that captive whom we mentioned above, despairing of his life and thinking to escape the yoke of Christianity, one day, seeing a most favorable opportunity and negligence in the guard, leaped lightly over the city’s wall. He continually called and begged the Turks who were present upon the walls, then free from warfare, to help him. Without delay, lowering a rope from the walls, they drew him up within the walls amid the hands of the treacherous fugitive—hanging upon it and clinging with his hands—with no small outcry and tumult within and without. Yet none of the Christians [Col. 0428A] dared pursue or seize the fugitive because of the Turks’ missiles raining down from above.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—The leading men who died in the same siege.

While, under the firmest resolve to besiege and destroy the city, seven weeks were passing there around its walls, and while some princes prepared projectiles and stone-throwing engines to reduce the walls and towers, others assembled iron-headed battering rams, devised various engines, and delivered many assaults, Baldwin of Calderim, attacking the walls incessantly and rushing forward with too rash and daring an effort, expired when his neck was broken by the blow of a launched stone.

Baldwin of Ghent, while laboring in the assault on the city and rashly approaching the walls, breathed out his life when his head was pierced by an arrow in the attack. After this, when by the counsel and decree of the princes the army renewed the assault, the count of Forez and another man from the island of Flanders, named Walo—exceedingly ardent in the same assault and fierce in war—were pierced by arrows and died while provoking the enemy. Wido of Porsessa, a distinguished knight, was seized by illness there and died.

The whole people of the Catholics mourned for them, because they were regarded as brave counselors and authors of important undertakings. Bishops and abbots buried such very noble men with every honor and religious rite, distributing no small alms to the poor and beggars for the salvation of their souls.

## CHAPTER XXX.—Likewise concerning others who perished there.

[Col. 0428C] Then one day, while the structures and engines of many princes were being set against the wall of Nicaea, and some labored not in vain while others labored fruitlessly, Henry of Esch and Count Hartmann, one of the greatest men of Germany, built at their own expense a *fox*—a covered siege-engine—of oak beams. Around it they wove protective walls, so that it might withstand the Turks’ heaviest weapon-strokes and every kind of missile, and so that those remaining inside it might safely and unharmed pierce the city by attacking it bravely.

When this engine called the *fox* had at last been completed in every detail by workmanship and fastenings, about twenty armored knights of the aforesaid princes were placed under its protection. But when, with a great mass and effort of men, it was applied near the walls, it did not settle upon level ground [Col. 0428D] or move under a straight thrust and even guidance. Thus its beams, posts, and every fastening were shattered, and in an instant it crushed the men hiding within it.

Hartmann and Henry grieved and mourned deeply over the disaster of their men. They honorably committed the dead to burial, yet they could rejoice not a little that they themselves had not perished with their men in that momentary suffocation.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—The assault upon the walls, and especially upon a certain tower.

On another day thereafter, when the frequent assaults of many were being spent in vain, Count Raymond vigorously attacked a certain tower, shaken by two stone-throwing engines commonly called *mangenae* [mangonels]. [Col. 0429A] Yet not even one stone could be reduced or dislodged from that ancient work, whose mortar was scarcely soluble, by such mighty throwing. Finally, more stone-shattering engines were added; by these the shaken walls at last developed cracks in places, and some stones, under the incessant bombardment, began to crumble and slip with their mortar.

Seeing this, the army of the living God assembled in force, formed a wicker-covered shelter, surmounted the rampart, and attacked the walls with bold advance. They strove to break through and pierce the tower rising above the walls with hooked mattocks. The Turks had filled it within with a mass of stones, so that it might stand more strongly by the density of the stones and, should the outer wall be broken by the Franks, the infinite heap of stones would impede those wishing to enter.

[Col. 0429B] But the people of the living God, their anger increasingly inflamed and moved by the slaughter of their men, worked through the tower with the sharp edge of biting iron, until with such force they made an opening through the tower that the gap in the hollowed wall seemed large enough to admit two men at once. These men might remove and reduce the mass of stones one by one and openly clear a way to the enemy. But not even so could they make progress.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—The people of the Lord surround the aforesaid lake with a naval blockade.

One night, after this struggle and its many efforts of slaughter, while the people around the city were exhausted and at intervals withdrawn to camp, it was discovered that the Turks often went out by ship across the lake from the city [Col. 0429C], secretly bringing in auxiliary men, arms, and every necessity; that merchants gathered there from all quarters; and that every kind of merchandise could be found from the Turks upon that same lake.

Therefore the princes held many consultations about what they should do or undertake, how the lake might be denied to them and exit and entry by ship thereafter refused to those shut inside. They said that otherwise they could not accomplish their assaults or their labor. At last, after much deliberation, this plan was found: unless so broad a lake were guarded by a naval watch, the enemy could not be restrained and the city could not be deprived of provisions.

Accordingly, great and small alike being summoned together, it was decreed by common counsel that innumerable forces of mounted and foot soldiers [Col. 0429D] should be sent to the port of Civitot, so that they might convey to Lake Nicaea the ships obtained from the lord emperor and granted by his gift. The ships were to be drawn from the sea across dry land on wheeled vehicles, skillfully fitted with timber, hemp ropes, and ox-hide straps laid upon the shoulders and necks of men and horses.

This was done. Drawing them for seven miles in the silence of night, they brought at sunrise to the aforesaid place these ships of marvelous weight and size, capable of holding a hundred men, and set them upon the shore and waters. Without delay the leaders of the army rose and came from every side to the lake to see and inspect the ships. They rejoiced that their men had returned safe and unharmed by enemy attack and that the ships had been received without damage.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—The profane defenders severely harass Christ’s followers. Here the duke himself shot through the most warlike Turk with an arrow.

[Col. 0430A]

The ships having thus been received safe and unharmed, the bravest Frankish knights were placed in them to prevent the Turks from leaving and to permit no necessities whatsoever to be brought to them. In one ship were archers from the emperor’s Turcopoles, men accustomed to prevail greatly in naval fighting upon the water.

When the Turks and all the guards of the garrison understood the commotion among the people around the lake and the princes’ unusually early gathering, they ran to the walls facing the river. They were greatly amazed by the newly brought ships, which they would doubtless have thought their own had not their own vessels still appeared on the opposite shore [Col. 0430B], chained with iron and bolts beside the city walls.

Thus, after the lake had been secured by naval blockade and an armored force of soldiers, armed with lances, bows, and arrows, had been left there upon the water, Count Raymond, his knights, and a large force from the army again attacked the aforesaid tower. They multiplied their assaults and stone-throwing, harassed and attacked the Turks without sparing them, and drove an iron-headed battering ram against the walls amid the continual shouting of men.

When the Turks saw the walls repeatedly struck and shaken by the ram and the tower bored through with mattocks, they poured from the walls fat, oil, and pitch mixed with tow and blazing torches. These entirely consumed the battering-ram engine and the wicker screens. Others killed many with arrows and horn bows; others crushed with stones those laboring beside the walls and tower.

[Col. 0430C] In this Turkish defense and resistance, one of their knights, of exceedingly fierce mind and heart, labored unceasingly with bow and missiles. And—what is marvelous to relate—though he despaired of life because of wounds inflicted upon him, he threw his shield far away and openly exposed his breast to the missiles of all. With both hands he hurled rocky stones into the midst of the crowd. Although, as those present truly report, he was burdened with twenty arrows still lodged in his chest, he did not stop his hands from throwing stones and striking the Franks, but inflicted even greater and fiercer injury upon the people.

Duke Godfrey, seeing this most ferocious and cruel man raging, not weakened by the embedding of so many arrows and causing more of the faithful to perish by his shooting, took [Col. 0430D] a Balearic bow and, standing behind the shields of two companions, struck that Turk through the vital parts of the heart. Thus he stopped him, now dead, from further dreadful slaughter.

At last, when the Christian people were exhausted, the sun declined, and so horrible an assault had subsided, the Turks, hard pressed before the opening of the tower, again carried heaps of stones inside during the silence of night, lest easy entrance be found on the following day.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—The killing of a Christian warrior, whom the Turks hang on the wall to mock the faithful.

When the sun returned in the morning, the people of God were encouraged and armed to renew the assault and enlarge the tower’s inner breach. But when they saw and recognized that a fresh deposit of stones had again been placed in the new opening, remembering the danger and anguish they had endured on the preceding day, [Col. 0431A] they began to lose heart, and each urged another to go first.

At last a distinguished knight sprang out from the tents of the aforesaid Count Robert of the Normans. Covered by helmet and cuirass and protected by a shield, he fearlessly crossed the rampart, attacked the walls, hastened to the tower, and tried to remove the heaps of stones from the breach and clear the entrance blocked with stones. But he abandoned his undertaking because of a hail of stones and the continual shower of missiles.

Seeing that he was deprived of all help and could make no progress under the crushing weight of immense stones, the same knight pressed close to the wall, to avoid the Turks’ missiles, which were exhausting the noble man without interruption. Yet even thus no way or possibility of escaping their hands was shown to him.

At last, when his shield had been torn away, he was overwhelmed beside the walls by so many thousands of stones upon his neck and head; his neck broken, he died in his cuirass and helmet in sight of all the faithful, who did not come to his aid. [Col. 0431B] Then, seeing that the man lay motionless and had already died, the Turks cast down from that accursed tower a chain furnished, by crafted design and workmanship, with very sharp and grasping iron claws like hooks. Fastened into the ring of the dead knight’s cuirass, it seized and held him and raised him, dead body and all, within the walls.

Then they took the knight’s body, though dead, and hung it in a noose of rope from the walls, so that by this inhumanity they might further offend the Christians. All were offended and sorrowful, lamenting that their brother had died by so cruel a death and been treated so vilely. After this prolonged mockery, when he had been thrown naked from the walls, they received him honorably and buried him with the other aforesaid faithful who had been killed there, amid distributions of alms and the prayers of priests.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—How a certain Lombard constructed a new kind of engine.

Troubled by this loss of brave men and the Christians’ repeated casualties, which they suffered daily in assaulting the city, and because they could inflict no damage upon the walls by any effort of engines, ballistas, or force of arms [Col. 0431D]—while all their labor and strength were spent in vain—a Lombard by birth, a master and inventor of great arts and works, seeing the Christians’ misery and slaughter, voluntarily presented himself to the aforesaid princes. He encouraged their minds with this consolation and promise:

> “I see that every work of our engines labors in vain; your men are continually diminished by death beside the walls, and the lives of those who remain are still exposed to great dangers. For the Turks shut within confidently and securely resist from the towers and walls, burying the unwary and unprotected under arrows and stones. Indeed, the wall, founded by the ingenuity of the ancients, cannot be cut through by iron or any strength.
>
> “Therefore, since I have perceived all your force thus to be frustrated, I have resolved to approach and urge your lordships [Col. 0432A] that, if you accept my counsel and I receive some reward for my labor from you, then, with God’s help, I will force this tower—which appears strong and insuperable—to fall to the ground without harm or danger to your fellow-soldiers. Through it a way of access will lie open to your enemies, who are opposed to you. Only let the necessities for my art be supplied by common expense and assistance.”

Having heard the man’s promise, they gladly agreed with every goodwill to give him fifteen pounds of Cartanensian currency as the reward for his labor, and to supply without ceasing whatever the work required. They rejoiced and trusted in hope of the promised device.

The master of the art, this agreement having been made, fitted together his contrivances, joined sloping walls, and attached wicker screens by a marvelous construction [Col. 0432B], under whose protection he and those laboring with him might keep their heads safe from the Turks’ missiles hurled from above.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—The destruction of the monstrous tower, and how the lady of the city was captured.

When the protective device had been finished in every detail, Christian men in cuirasses and with shields gathered around the machine. Drawing it with their strength across the ditch, they placed it close beside the walls, despite the resistance and attempts to prevent them of all the Turks above. The master of the art was left safely within it with his other workmen, while the troops of the faithful withdrew without great injury.

The Turks, seeing that this engine might prevail to the city’s harm, threw burning torches with [Col. 0432C] pitch and fat upon the machine and rolled masses of stone from the walls, trying by such means to destroy the device brought against the wall and drive away those enclosed within it. But all they threw or attempted was in vain, because the sloping walls retained neither fire nor stone cast upon them.

The master of the art, hidden confidently in the engine with his companions, did not cease to dig the earth beneath the foundation of the tower with mattocks and very sharp iron. He did so until he had arranged beams, posts, and other enormous timbers in the excavation beneath the foundation, to support the walls after the earth had been removed, lest they suddenly collapse upon those still digging.

When a very great excavation had been made in breadth and length, by the master’s instruction all in the army, small and great alike, brought branches, straw, roof-tiles, dry reeds, tow, and every fuel for fire. They piled these among the posts, beams, and huge timbers, the excavation on every side being filled with this wood. [Col. 0432D] Then the master of the work set fire to it. The blaze was stirred by a mighty draught until the roaring, spreading, irresistible flame grew increasingly powerful and reduced the posts, beams, and all the wood laid beneath to ashes.

When these had thus been reduced to embers and the foundations lacked support from both earth and wood, the structure of the most ancient tower collapsed backward in an instant at midnight, making such a sound that it seemed like the crash of thunder and woke all from sleep. Although the intolerable mass of the fallen tower fell suddenly, it did not break into many pieces through the collision of mortar or stones. Rather, the shaken and damaged walls of the citadel lay broken and gaped with cracks in places, offering an entrance, though a difficult one. [Col. 0433A]

In this collapse and destruction of the tower, Solyman’s most noble wife, greatly terrified and no longer trusting in the city’s protection, was put by her people onto the waters of the lake in the silence of night, in order to escape the Christians by ship. But when her departure was noticed, she was captured by the soldiers guarding the lake, rowing in the newly brought vessels, and was placed in the custody of the princes with her two very young sons.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—The surrender of the city of Nicaea, and a captive nun.

[Col. 0433B] The Turks and defenders of the citadel alike, terrified by the tower’s fall and stunned by the capture of this noblewoman, despairing henceforth of passage across the lake, grievously weakened within by the loss of their men, exhausted by the long siege, and seeing that they could not escape, took counsel together concerning their lives and bodily safety. They begged the Christian army to spare them, promising to deliver the keys of the city into the hands of the emperor of Constantinople, under whose dominion the city had originally been held by hereditary right, until Solyman seized it and subjected it to himself by unjust force.

Tatinus the Snub-nosed, a familiar of the emperor, acting in accordance with the counsel of the leading men of the army, received and returned assurances on both sides and interceded for them before the Christian nobles [Col. 0433C] on this condition: that they should leave the city unharmed and come under the emperor’s surrender, together with Solyman’s most noble wife, who had recently been captured and was held in the custody of the Frankish princes with her two young sons.

Thus, when the assault had been suspended on both sides, while various plans for surrendering the city were under discussion and many Christian captives were restored, a certain nun from the monastery of St Mary at the granaries of the Church of Trier was restored and released with the others into the hands of the Christian army.
