She declared that she had been captured and carried off from Peter’s shattered host; she complained that she had had little respite from the foul and abominable intercourse of a certain Turk and of others.

While she uttered pitiful groans over these wrongs in the hearing of the Christians, [Col. 0433D] she recognized among Christ’s nobles and soldiers Henry of Esch Castle. Calling him by name in a tearful and humble voice, she urged him to help secure redress for her. As soon as he recognized her, he was moved by her misfortune and obtained, with all the effort and mercy he could, from Duke Godfrey that the venerable Bishop Reymer might give her counsel of penance concerning such incest.

At last, after counsel had been received from the clergy, she was granted remission for her unlawful union with the Turk and a mitigated penance, because she had suffered this foul violation by force and unwillingly at the hands of impious and most wicked men. But after a short interval of only one night, through the messenger of that same Turk who had violated her and taken her from the others, she was invited back to unlawful and incestuous marriage by much persuasion and flattering promise.

For that Turk had burned with desire for her incomparable beauty and therefore bore her absence with great distress. He had promised her such rewards that they had so taken root in her mind that she returned to her abominable husband. The same Turk promised that he would soon become a Christian, if only he escaped the emperor’s captivity and chains. At last the poor woman—if she had previously sinned under compulsion—now, deceived by blandishments and vain hope, returned to her impious spouse and adulterous marriage, the entire army unaware of the trick and wantonness by which she had slipped away from them.

Afterwards it became known from informants that she had returned to that same Turk in the exile where he was [Col. 0434B], for no reason other than an inability to endure the deprivation of lust. The storm of war having now been calmed, Christian captives restored from the city, and Turks received and transferred into the emperor’s surrender, the army of the living God spent that day in the camp in great joy and exultation, because all things were still turning out for them according to hope.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—How, by counsel of the princes, the people of God were divided into two parts.

When the following day dawned, after taking what was necessary for use, the whole people set out, traveling safely through the middle of Romania and fearing no impending adversity. After marching together for two days through mountain ridges and narrow mountain passes, they resolved that so great an army should be divided [Col. 0434C], so that the people might occupy camp more freely and spaciously and, thus divided, might be more abundantly supplied with food and fodder for the horses.

They assembled between two mountain peaks, where, after crossing a river by a bridge, Bohemond with all his following companies was wholly separated from Duke Godfrey. Certain great nobles followed him: Count Robert of the Normans and Stephen, prince of Blois. They kept and regulated the road always to the right, so as not to be more than a mile from their brethren.

The duke and his companions, with the bishop of Le Puy and Count Raymond, always went to the right. Thus the division having been made, Bohemond with his whole army descended about the ninth hour into the valley of Dogorganhi, called Ozellis by modern men [Col. 0434D], where his companions had spread out over the grass on all sides for lodging, so that they might place camp in locations suited with streams, meadows, food, and other necessities.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—The most dreadful slaughter of Christians through the ambush of the prince of Nicaea.

Hardly had Bohemond and the other bravest men dismounted when Solyman appeared in violent attack and overwhelming multitude. Since the time he had fled from the city of Nicaea, he had gathered aid and forces from Antioch, Tarsus, Aleppo, and the other cities of Romania, from Turks stationed in scattered places.

There was no delay and no rest from slaughtering and attacking the army and rushing through the camp: some were pierced by arrows, others cut down by the sword, and some captured by that most cruel enemy. A great cry and terror arose everywhere among the people; married and unmarried women alike, together with men and little children, were cut down. Robert of Paris, wishing to aid the wretched, was pierced by a flying arrow and killed.

Stunned by this most grievous slaughter, Bohemond and the other leaders remounted their horses, hastened to their cuirasses and arms, gathered together, and, defending themselves as best they could against the unexpected attack, fought battles with the enemy for a long time. William, a most daring young man and a most handsome knight, brother of Tancred, while resisting vigorously in arms and repeatedly piercing Turks with his lance, fell struck by an arrow in Bohemond’s sight. [Col. 0435B] Tancred, defending himself manfully with the sword, barely escaped alive, but left there with his brother the emblem of beauty which he had carried upon his lance.

The Turks, with their prince Solyman, growing stronger and stronger, violently burst into the camp, shooting and killing infantrymen, pilgrims, girls, women, little children, and old men with arrows and horn bows, sparing no age. Stupefied by this cruelty of most atrocious death, the tender and most noble girls hurried to adorn themselves with clothing and offered themselves to the Turks, hoping that at least the Turks, inflamed and softened by love for their handsome appearance, might learn to pity captive women.

## CHAPTER XL.—The messenger of Christ’s faithful to the duke.

While the flocks of the faithful were thus afflicted and Bohemond’s force was becoming less able to resist, because the Turks had unexpectedly fallen upon him and his men while unarmed, and about four thousand of the Christian army had already fallen into the enemy’s hand, a messenger flew without delay on horseback over the mountain precipices until he reached the duke’s camp, sorrowful and exhausted in spirit.

When Duke Godfrey, having stepped some distance from the entrance of his tent to look upon his companions, saw him from afar hurrying at rapid speed and pale with grief, he asked why he had hastened his journey, that he might report and explain it to him and the other leaders. The messenger brought bitter and grievous news:

> “Our princes, with Bohemond himself, are enduring the harshest toil of war, and the whole following multitude has already undergone the sentence of death; our lord princes too will presently fall unless your hand hastens to their aid. The Turks have burst into our camp and, descending through the valley called Ozellis, or the Terrible Valley, do not cease slaughtering pilgrims in the valley of Degorganhi. They have already killed Robert of Paris by cutting off his head; they have struck down the noble young William, Bohemond’s sister’s son, worthy of lamentation. Therefore the whole company calls you to bring aid: let no delay or postponement hinder or retard you.”

## CHAPTER XLI.—Where the duke and those with him aid the perishing.

Having heard of this misery and the Turks’ audacity, the duke ordered horns to sound throughout all the ranks, all companions to be summoned, arms taken up, standards raised, and aid given to their companions without any delay or rest. As if summoned to a banquet of every delight, they hastened to take up arms, put on cuirasses, gird on swords, put bridles on their horses, saddles on their backs, and take up shields. Some sixty thousand horsemen came forth from the camp with the remaining infantry force.

The brightest day had already dawned and the sun shone with utmost brilliance. Its splendor gleamed upon golden shields and iron garments; standards and banners, shining with jewels and purple, raised and fixed upon lances, flashed. Swift horses were urged by spurs. No one waited for companion or brother; each pressed onward as quickly as he could toward the aid and vengeance of the Christians.

When the Turks suddenly perceived that these men, in so strong a force, armed and clad in iron and with light-bearing standards raised for battle, were rushing with all speed and martial ardor to aid their companions, they took flight. Shaken by fear, they turned from dreadful slaughter, some making their escape through trackless places, others by familiar paths. [Col. 0436B] But Solyman, having escaped in flight with a larger force and denser battle-lines, halted upon the mountain summit and resolved there to meet the pursuing Christians and resist them face to face.

## CHAPTER XLII.—Where the duke and certain other nobles are named, who then acted bravely for God.

Duke Godfrey, who alone, with fifty companions, had ridden ahead at full speed, when the forces of the people following him had quickly assembled, boldly climbed the steep heights of the mountain to strike and join battle with the Turks [Col. 0436C], whom he saw massed and motionless on the mountain summit, prepared to resist. And now, with his own men gathered and joined to him from every side, he charged the stationary enemy, aimed lances at them, and urged his companions in a manly voice to attack them steadfastly.

But the Turks, with their leader Solyman, seeing that Duke Godfrey and his men did not at all lose heart for the present battle, prepared to flee from the mountain top at the speed of their horses, reins loosened. The duke pursued them for six miles; he struck some with the sword’s edge, took several captive with his men, seized no small amount of their booty and spoils, and rescued from the enemy girls, young men, and everything which they hoped to carry off or lead away.

[Col. 0436D] Gerard of Keresi, mounted upon a distinguished horse, during the same pursuit of the enemy saw on the brow of the mountain a Turk who still remained and showed excessive boldness. Protected by his shield, he charged him courageously with his lance. Gerard’s arrow, shot forth and discharged from the shield, pierced the Turk through liver and lung; Gerard carried away the horse of the dying and falling man. Baldwin, count of the Hamaic people, a man generous in great almsgiving, together with Robert of Flanders, struck down the fleeing Turks. He urged his companions, rushing together from every side, to strike and slaughter, and never to appear to slacken in their pursuit or restrain their hands.

Baldwin of Burg, Thomas of the Castle of Feria, Reynold of Beauvais, Walo of Calmont, Gothard son of Godfrey, Gastus of Berdeiz, and also Rudolph [Col. 0437A]—all these laboured together in the struggle of battle, pursuing and cutting through the Turkish ranks with martial prowess. The heavy panting of the horses resounded; smoke from their very breath thickened into a dense cloud amid the lines. The Turks, however, sometimes recovering their strength and trusting in the power of their numbers, resisted bravely amid a hail of thickly flying and falling arrows. But when the storm of this hail had swiftly passed, the companies of the faithful, holding their missiles in their hands, thinned and destroyed their masses, and at last compelled the defeated men to scatter by the byways of the roads and the steep places of the mountains, whose paths they knew.

## Chapter XLIII.—What was agreed among the Lord’s faithful after the victory, and how the sacred order cared for the bodies of the fallen

[Col. 0437B] Therefore the victorious Christians carried off everything that the Turks had brought as provisions for their expedition: grain, no small quantity of wine, buffaloes, oxen and rams, camels, asses, horses and mules; in addition, precious gold and countless silver, and tents of remarkable beauty and workmanship. In the favourable outcome of this victory [Col. 0438A], all unanimously—Bohemond, that is, and the other aforesaid princes, who were the leaders and pillars of the army—returned to concord and counsel. From that day, pooling food and every necessary thing, they decreed that all should be held in common. And this was done.

In this clash of battle and flight of the Turks, some Christian soldiers, wounded by arrows, died; but three thousand Turks are said to have fallen. When this most cruel conflict had ended, the Christian soldiers rested for three days beside a certain river and its reed-bed, restoring bodies utterly exhausted with the abundance of food left behind by the slain Turks. The bishops, priests, and monks who were present committed the bodies of the dead to the earth, commending their faithful souls [Col. 0438B] into the hand of Jesus Christ with prayers and psalms.

Solyman, defeated once more, had scarcely escaped and descended through the mountains of Romania. He had no further hope for the city of Nicaea, for his wife and children; and he made excessive lament for his men, whom he had lost a few days earlier, killed by the Franks in the plain of Nicaea, and now for those whom he had left captured and slain in the valley of Gorgonia.

# Book Three

[Col. 0437]

## Chapter I.—Where Christ’s faithful pitched camp after the victory; and how many died when cruelly afflicted by thirst

[Col. 0437C]

After the enemy attack had withdrawn, at the dawn that preceded the fourth day, the Franks, Lotharingians, Alemanni, Bavarians, Flemings, and the entire German people moved camp with all their necessary belongings and Turkish spoil. They encamped and lodged for the night on the summit of the Black Mountains. When morning came, the Normans, Burgundians, Bretons, Alemanni, Bavarians, Teutons—in short, the whole army—descended from there into a valley called Malabyumas. Because of the difficulty of the terrain and the narrow defiles among the rocks, they shortened their daily march, and this also because of their innumerable multitude [Col. 0437D] and the excessive heat of August.

Then, on a certain Saturday of that same month, a great shortage of water increased among the people. Therefore, severely oppressed by distress, very many persons of both sexes who were present, as they say—about five hundred—breathed their last on that day. Horses, asses, camels, mules, oxen, and many animals likewise perished from the same end: most grievous thirst.

## Chapter II.—Likewise concerning the same matter

We learned there not merely by hearsay, but from the truthful report of those who had themselves shared in this affliction, that in this crisis of thirst miserable men and women endured torments at which the mind recoils, the ear is terrified, and one shudders for one’s own people at such a wretched disaster.

For very many pregnant women [Col. 0438C], their throats dried, their internal organs parched, and all the veins of their bodies exhausted by the immeasurable burning of the sun and scorching heat, gave birth in the middle of the road before everyone’s eyes and left their infants there. Other wretched women rolled about beside their infants on the public road, forgetful of all shame and of their private parts because of the exceedingly grievous suffering of the aforesaid thirst. They were not compelled to give birth by the course of their months or by the hour at hand, but were forced into labour by the sun’s heat, weariness from the roads, accumulated thirst, and long remoteness from water. Their infants were found in the middle of the road, some dead and others half-alive.

Very many men, failing from sweat and heat, with mouths open and throats gaping, drew in the thinnest air in an attempt to relieve their thirst; but it could offer no help. [Col. 0438D] For, as we said above, a large part of them is reported to have perished there that day. Indeed, hawks also—the tame and highly prized birds of magnates and nobles—died in the hands of those carrying them from the same heat and thirst. Likewise, dogs renowned in the art of hunting died in their masters’ hands.

When all were thus afflicted by this pestilence, a desired and eagerly sought river came into view. Hastening toward it, each person strove, in the great crush caused by excessive desire, to get ahead of another. They observed no moderation in drinking, until very many persons and beasts of burden, weakened by excessive drinking, died.

## Chapter III.—They proceed further; the army is divided into two parts; the leading men pursue the hunt

After they had emerged from the narrow rocky passes, it was decreed by common agreement, because of the excessive size of the people, that the army should be divided into parts. Tancred and Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, departed with their men and passed through the midst of the valleys of Ozellis. But Tancred, going ahead with his followers, descended to the neighbouring towns of Reclei and Stancona, in which Christian citizens lived, subject to the Turks, the men of Solyman.

Baldwin and his men proceeded along winding mountain paths, heavily burdened, together with all his company, by a grievous shortage of food; indeed, as fodder failed, the horses could scarcely follow, much less carry men. Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, Robert, and Raymond followed at a distance by the royal road. Turning toward Lesser Antioch, situated beside Reclei, they decided to halt there for lodging at the ninth hour of the day. [Col. 0439B]

When evening came, Duke Godfrey and the other leading men pitched their tents near the mountains in pleasant meadowland. They considered the region suitable and delightful, and exceedingly fertile in game, in which the nobility delight and take exercise. Reclining there, with arms and all equipment laid aside, they found a woodland highly suitable for hunting. Taking bow and quiver and girding on swords, they entered the mountain glades adjoining it, in case something might appear which they could strike and pursue with the keen scent of their hounds.

## Chapter IV.—The duke, fighting a bear, is seriously wounded; but, with another knight’s aid, the beast is killed and he is rescued alive

At last, when each man had dispersed through the shady parts of the wood along his own path, laying ambushes for wild beasts, Duke Godfrey [Col. 0439C] saw a most monstrous bear, of dreadful size, attack a destitute pilgrim gathering brushwood and pursue him around a tree in order to devour him—as, according to the local people’s report, it was accustomed to devour shepherds of the region or persons entering the wood.

But the duke, as he was accustomed and ready in every adversity to come to the aid of his Christian brethren, swiftly drew his sword, spurred his horse vigorously, and flew to the poor man. He hastened to rescue him, in anguish, from the teeth and claws of the butcher; speeding through the thickets with a great cry, he presented himself to the cruel enemy.

The bear, seeing the horse and its rider pressing upon it in rapid course, trusted in its ferocity and the rapacity of its claws. Not sluggishly, it confronted the duke face to face, opened its jaws to cut his throat, raised its whole body to resist—or rather, to attack—and stretched out its sharpest claws to tear him. Carefully withdrawing its head and forelegs from the blow of the sword, it repeatedly deceived him as he sought to strike; indeed, with a terrifying roar it shook all the woodland and mountains, so that all who could hear it wondered.

The duke, seeing the cunning and most wicked beast resist with audacious savagery, was stirred in spirit and became fiercely indignant. Turning the sword-point, he approached the beast in a rash and blind assault in order to pierce its liver. But by an unlucky chance the beast evaded the sword-stroke, suddenly fastened its curved claws in the duke’s tunic, embraced him with its forelegs, cast him from his horse, pressed him to the ground, and hastened to cut his throat with its teeth. [Col. 0440A]

The duke, therefore, in distress, remembered his many distinguished deeds and how he had hitherto been nobly rescued from every danger; now grieved that he should be suffocated by a bloody beast in a vile death, he recovered his strength and immediately rose to his feet. In this sudden fall from the horse and struggle with the frenzied beast, his sword had become entangled around his own legs. Snatching it swiftly at the beast’s throat and gripping the hilt, he cut through the calves and sinews of his own leg with a grievous slash.

Yet although his blood poured forth in an unceasing stream and the duke’s strength ebbed, he did not yield to the wicked beast, but stood with utmost fierceness in defence, until a certain Husechin by name, one of his companions dispersed through the wood, heard the great cry of the poor man delivered from the bear and the violent roar of the butcher [Col. 0440B], and came at speed on horseback to help the duke. Drawing his sword, he attacked the horrible beast and, together with the duke, pierced its liver and ribs.

Thus at last the most savage beast was killed. First through the pain of the wound and then through excessive loss of blood, the duke began to fail in heart, grow pale in face, and throw the whole army into turmoil through the dreadful report. All ran to the place where the champion and man of counsel, the head of the pilgrims, was said to have been wounded. The princes of the army placed him on a litter and carried him to camp amid great mourning, men’s lamentation, and women’s wailing, employing most skilled physicians to heal him. Dividing the beast among themselves, they confessed that they had never before seen one equal to it in size.

## Chapter V.—Tancred, pitching his tents beside the city of Tarsus, negotiates with the citizens for the surrender of the city, now with threats and now with persuasion

[Col. 0440C]

While the duke was thus hindered by a grave wound and the army followed at a slower pace, Tancred, who had gone ahead and was keeping the royal road toward the coast, arrived before Baldwin, the duke’s brother. Having crossed the cliffs through the valley of Buetrenton, he entered through the gate called Juda and descended to the city called Tarsus, commonly named Tursolt. The Turks, chiefs under Solyman, held it in subjection together with its towers.

There an Armenian who had stayed for some time with Tancred and knew him promised that he would persuade the citizens of the city, oppressed beneath the harsh Turkish yoke, to surrender the city secretly into Tancred’s hands without the Turks’ knowledge, should they find an occasion and opportunity. [Col. 0440D] But because the frightened citizens did not accept the Armenian brother’s counsel, owing to the Turks’ presence and guard, Tancred, who had come first, plundered the districts adjoining the aforesaid city. Having gathered limitless supplies of booty for the purposes of a siege, he spread his tents around the walls.

Once the tents had been set up, Tancred brought many threats against the Turks spread along the walls and towers, invoking the arrival of Bohemond and the strength of the army that followed. Unless they came out and opened the city gates, he declared, the relieving army would not depart from this siege until Nicaea itself, together with all its inhabitants, had been taken by assault. But if they yielded to his will and opened the city, they would find not only favour and life in Bohemond’s eyes, but would also receive many rewards and deserve to hold authority in that city and in other strongholds.

## Chapter VI.—The citizens promise surrender; men of God’s army, widely separated from each other, suspect enemies to be present

Softened by these blandishments and promises, sometimes excessively grand, the Turks promised Tancred the city on the condition that no danger or disturbance should thereafter be inflicted upon them by any force following behind until they submitted, with the city’s garrison, to Bohemond’s authority. Tancred did not refuse at all, but undertook to bind an agreement with them on these terms: they should raise Tancred’s banner on the summit of the chief citadel as a sign that [Col. 0441B] Tancred, preceding Bohemond, had claimed this city, and that it should thus remain thereafter untouched by every hostile attack.

But Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey; Count Peter of Staden; Count Reynard of the city of Toul, a man of great resource; and Baldwin of Burg, a distinguished young man, joined in friendship but separated by another route, wandered for three days from the army through deserted and unknown mountain places. Severely afflicted by hunger and shortage of necessities, they eventually came by chance, through the confusion of winding roads, to stand upon the summit of a certain mountain. From it they observed Tancred’s tents set across the plain before besieged Tarsus and were greatly afraid, supposing this display to be Turkish.

Tancred, no less, seeing men from afar on the mountain summit [Col. 0441C], was alarmed. He thought Turks were present, hastening to aid their comrades shut within the city. As the others descended, despairing of life and half-alive from hunger, Tancred, as a most valiant knight, warned his companions that they must defend their lives.

## Chapter VII.—The hostages break the treaty; Tancred and Baldwin unite their forces, renew the siege, and the site of the city

The Turks, however, who had assembled to the number of five hundred upon the towers and walls for observation and defence, likewise supposed Baldwin and his company to be ranks of Turks. Reproaching Tancred, they threatened him in these words:

> “Behold the force hurrying to assist us. We are not in your power, as you thought; rather, you and your men are today to be crushed in our hand and strength. Therefore consider yourself now deceived in the treaty which we made in vain. We have kept you delaying in your camp for no other reason than because we awaited the hope of aid in these ranks which you see, for the destruction of you and yours.”

Tancred, an undaunted young man, held the Turks’ threats in contempt and replied briefly to their insults:

> “If these are accounted your soldiers or leaders, we hold them in contempt in God’s name; we do not fear to approach them. If, with God’s help, they are defeated by us, your pride and boasting will not escape punishment. But if, because of our sin standing against us, we cannot hold our ground, you will nevertheless not escape the hand of Bohemond and his army which follows.”

Having said this, [Col. 0442A] Tancred, with all the force which had gathered around him, splendid in arms, helmets, and coats of mail and mounted on very swift horses, hastened to meet Baldwin. The Turks, meanwhile, sounded terrifying blasts from trumpets and horns from the walls to frighten Tancred. But when both parties recognized the signs of Christianity and saw friends and fellow countrymen, they wept for joy that through God’s grace they had now been delivered from punishments and dangers.

Without delay, having united their forces, they jointly set their tents again before the city walls by common agreement. From cattle and herds which they had collected as booty from the mountains and surrounding country, they slaughtered and prepared food, placing it on the fire. Long hunger compelled them to eat it cooked without salt, since bread was entirely lacking there for all. [Col. 0442B] The city was fortified on every side, well supplied and convenient in inhabitants, streams, and meadows, and situated in fertile plains. Its walls were considered so exceptionally strong that they were believed impossible to overcome by human power unless God gave assent.

## Chapter VIII.—The mutual quarrel of certain princes; and how the people of Tarsus wish Tancred to rule them

When the next day dawned, Baldwin rose with his followers and went toward the city walls. They saw Tancred’s very well-known banner placed upon the upper citadel of a lofty tower, with the Turks’ agreement and treaty. Consequently they were inflamed with excessive indignation and anger, and burst into bitter and seditious words against Tancred and his followers [Col. 0442C], treating Tancred’s and Bohemond’s boasting and leadership with contempt and equating them with mud and dregs.

These and similar bitter words nearly came to arms, had not peaceable and prudent men intervened with the proposal that Armenian citizens themselves, through representatives of both sides, should be asked under whose lordship and authority they preferred the city to be placed, and to which party they inclined by better choice. All immediately answered that they would rather submit to and trust Tancred than the rule of any other prince. They said this not from devotion of heart, but because they always feared an invasion by Bohemond. Nor was this surprising: long before this expedition, Bohemond’s fame had always shone and war had inspired terror in the regions of Greece, Romania, and Syria; whereas the name of Duke Godfrey [Col. 0442D] had only now first begun to gleam.

## Chapter IX.—Concerning the same matter

Having heard this, Baldwin was raised to fiercer anger against Tancred. In Tancred’s presence, through an interpreter, he addressed both citizens and Turks in more grievous words:

> “Do not believe that Bohemond and this Tancred, whom you so venerate and fear, are greater and more powerful masters of the Christian army; nor are they in any respect comparable with my brother Godfrey, duke and prince of the whole military force of Gaul, or with any member of his house. For my brother, Duke Godfrey, is a prince honoured by the entire army through the hereditary right of his noble forebears, of a great kingdom and of Augustus, the first emperor of the Romans. Great and small alike do not cease to obey his voice and counsels in all things, since he has been chosen and appointed by all as head and lord.

> “Know indeed that you and all that is yours, and the city as well, will be destroyed and consumed by that duke with the sword and flames; neither Bohemond nor this Tancred will stand as your champions or defenders. Nor will this Tancred, on whom you rely, escape our hands today, unless you cast down from the summit of the tower the banner which he has raised as an insult to us and for his own glory, and cause the gates to be opened to us. But if you satisfy our will by casting out this banner and surrendering the city, we shall exalt you above all those dwelling within these borders, and you shall always be honoured with worthy gifts and be glorious in the sight of my lord and brother, the duke.” [Col. 0443B]

Enticed by this hope of a fair and pleasing promise, the citizens and Turks, with Tancred entirely unaware, established an agreement and friendship with Baldwin. Without delay, Tancred’s banner was removed from the summit of the tower and contemptuously cast away far from the walls in a marshy place; Baldwin’s banner was raised at the top of the same tower.

## Chapter X.—Concerning the same matter, and how Tancred entered the city of Azara

Tancred, seeing Baldwin’s banner raised and his own removed, bore it patiently, although saddened. Perceiving that this change of banner was causing discord between his own men and Baldwin’s followers, and because his party was inferior in numbers and arms, he did not wish to remain longer in this quarrel. Instead, he went to the nearby city called Azara, fortified and wealthy. Finding its gates shut, he was not permitted to enter.

A certain Welf, a distinguished knight from the kingdom of Burgundy, held this city. Having driven out and crushed the Turks, Welf had taken possession of the city and found there gold and silver, precious cloths, provisions, sheep, oxen, wine, oil, wheat, barley, and every necessity. This Welf had gone ahead with others separated from the army. Tancred, finding the city gates closed and learning that a Christian prince held the city, sent messengers and, under pledge of faith, requested admission for lodging and a share of provisions at a fair sale and purchase. [Col. 0443D] Welf heard the request, ordered the city opened, admitted the man with his companions, and supplied them with all necessities of life.

## Chapter XI.—Baldwin, made ruler of the city, refuses to admit Christians of Tancred’s party

After Tancred’s departure, Baldwin again urged and pressed the Turks, promising that, if they opened the city and admitted him and his followers with hands pledged in faith, he would obtain immense honours and rewards from the duke and be placed in authority over not only that city but other cities as well. The Turks and Armenians, seeing Tancred’s flight and absence but Baldwin’s power prevailing, gave and confirmed mutual assurances, opened the city gates, and admitted Baldwin and his men. Yet they resolved to retain possession of all the fortified towers [Col. 0444A] until Duke Godfrey and the army following him came near. Then, through the duke’s gift and favour, they would arrange with them concerning that city and all other matters, according to Baldwin’s promise, whether they chose to persist in their Christian profession or in the rite of the gentiles.

They granted Baldwin only two chief towers, in which he could remain and rest securely and confidently. The rest of the army’s multitude dispersed through the houses and places of the city. After Baldwin and his men had thus been admitted with their prince and restored by the quiet of lodging, on the following day, as evening approached, three hundred men separated from the pilgrims’ army and following Tancred’s tracks—members of Bohemond’s household and people—stood before the city walls in arms and bearing shields. By Baldwin’s order and the counsel of the leading men, the city and its gate were forbidden to them.

Wearied by a long journey and devoid and exhausted of necessities, they earnestly begged for the city’s hospitality and for necessities to be sold to them. Common people among Baldwin’s company also pleaded for them, because they were brethren and professed Christianity. But Baldwin did not hear their prayers, for this reason: they had gone down to aid Tancred, and because of the agreement which he had confirmed with the Turks and Armenians, no one but his own men was to be received or admitted into the city before Duke Godfrey’s arrival.

## Chapter XII.—The Christians remaining outside the city gate are killed by the gentiles at night

[Col. 0444C] The brethren and fellow pilgrims of Baldwin’s company, seeing that the excluded men could by no means obtain admission, took pity on them because they saw them endangered by hunger. They decided to hand them bread at the gates and lower livestock by ropes for food. When these men had thus been refreshed and, in the silence of night, had fallen into deep sleep through the weariness of their journey, the Turks stationed in the tower-garrisons under the protection of the treaty, wholly desperate and not fully trusting Baldwin and his fellow Christians, secretly took counsel among themselves.

Three hundred of them, taking with them all their treasures and other belongings, left secretly by the fords of a river known to them which flowed through the middle of the city. Baldwin and all his men were asleep [Col. 0444D]. They left only two hundred of their lowly retainers and household in the garrisons, lest any suspicion of their flight arise among the Christians. Having gone out, they suddenly fell upon the Christian men, who had given their weary limbs to sleep in the meadows before the city. They beheaded some, slaughtered others, pierced others with arrows, and left no one—or very few—alive.

## Chapter XIII.—God’s people blame Baldwin for this slaughter and rush to arms; having justified himself, he rises fiercely against the remaining enemies of God

When morning came, the Christians inside the city rose from sleep and went to the walls to discover and see whether their Christian brethren still remained in the meadows. They saw them all cut to pieces by Turkish weapons [Col. 0445A], and the meadows exceedingly soaked and overflowing with their blood. Thus the Turks’ treachery and wickedness were revealed.

Without delay, an uproar arose throughout the city among the Catholic people. Everyone took up arms; to avenge the blood of their brethren treacherously killed, they hastened to break open the towers and destroy the Turks found there, stirring no small tumult with trumpets and a great cry. Startled by such violent noise and the people’s tumultuous rush, Baldwin flew on horseback from the tower-garrison through the middle of the city. He urged the armed companies to cease from battle and return to their lodgings, lest the mutual treaty so recently made should be broken before the slaughter of the Christians had been fully reported to him.

But as the tumult increased more and more [Col. 0445B], the people bore the Christians’ death with indignation and cried that Baldwin was guilty of this killing, as though it had been a murderous plan. Such a great rush and discharge of arrows was made against him that, compelled by the need of refuge and preservation of his life, he had to enter a tower. Immediately coming to himself, laying aside the fierceness of his spirit, he sought to satisfy the people. He excused himself in every respect and declared that he had known nothing of the Turks’ cruelty; he had excluded God’s people for no other reason than that he had sworn to the Turks and Armenians that no one besides his own men should be admitted to the city before the duke’s arrival.

Thus Baldwin was excused and reconciled with his people. He attacked and stormed the Turks remaining in the individual towers, men of the lowly household and retainers; his men also stormed them, and nearly two hundred were beheaded in vengeance for their own people. [Col. 0445C] Many distinguished women of the city accused those Turks, showing the ears and noses which the Turks had cut off from them because they had been unable to find the women compliant with their violation. This disgraceful and dreadful accusation caused the people of Jesus Christ to blaze still more in hatred against the Turks and multiply their slaughter all the more.

## Chapter XIV.—Baldwin’s men make an alliance with Christian pirates and proceed together to Tarsus

After a few days had passed, Baldwin’s men, stationed along the walls, saw from afar a multitude of ships of diverse kinds and construction in the middle of the sea, more than three miles from the city. Their masts, of extraordinary size and height, were covered with purest gold and shone in the sun’s rays. They also saw men coming down from these ships to the sea-shore and dividing among themselves much spoil which they had accumulated over a long time, nearly eight years. [Col. 0445D]

Seeing this, they thought that hostile forces had been summoned by those who had escaped at night after killing the Christians. Therefore they rushed to arms; some on horseback and others on foot ran to the shore itself, boldly asking why they had come and from what nation they had proceeded. The newcomers replied that they were soldiers professing Christianity; they acknowledged that they had come from Flanders, Antwerp, Frisia, and other regions of Gaul, and that they had been pirates for eight years up to that day.

They in turn asked those who had arrived why they had left the regions of the Romans and Germans [Col. 0446A] and come into distant exile among so many barbarous peoples. The latter testified that they had come because of pilgrimage and to worship in Jerusalem. Thus, recognizing each other by language and speech, they pledged hands and made an agreement together to go to Jerusalem.

Among this naval fellowship was a certain Winemar, the head and master of all the companions, from the land of Boulogne and the household of Count Eustace, the distinguished prince of that land. Once their mutual faith had been confirmed on both sides, they left their ships and entered the city of Tarsus with Baldwin, along with their spoil and all their baggage. For several days they enjoyed and feasted there upon every good thing of the land.

Then, after taking counsel together, they selected three hundred men from the naval force for the city’s guard and defence, while two hundred were assigned from Baldwin’s legion. [Col. 0446B] When these arrangements had been ordered and established, Baldwin and his men departed from Tarsus. Joining arms and forces, they marched along the royal road with trumpets, horns, and great power.

## Chapter XV.—Tancred captures the city of Mamistra by force and, at a certain Richard’s prompting, attacks Baldwin’s camp as an enemy

Meanwhile Tancred departed from the city of Azara and from Welf, ruler of that city, and descended upon Mamistra, a city held and fortified by the Turks. He assaulted it with an armoured force while it stoutly resisted and opposed him. In a short time he cast its walls to the ground, broke down its gates and iron bars, and crushed with a cruel slaughter the Turkish arrogance ruling there.

Having expelled the enemy in this manner, Tancred fortified the towers with guards from among his own men. Finding there abundant food, clothing, gold, and silver, he distributed these among his Christian companions and remained there for several days. While he stayed there securely and attended diligently to guarding the city, Baldwin, the duke’s brother, travelling along the royal road with arms and companions, entered the territory of that city. In a spacious orchard planted with trees beside the city, he and his followers and chief men pitched their tents in order.

A certain Richard, prince of the Italian city of Salerno, of Norman stock and a close associate of Tancred, saw this and took it badly. He addressed Tancred in very bitter words:

> “Ah, Tancred! Today you have become the most contemptible of all men. You see Baldwin here, through whose injustice and envy you lost Tarsus. Ah, if you had any courage in you now, you would stir up your men and repay upon his head the injury done to you.”

On hearing this, Tancred raged in spirit. At once he summoned arms and soldiers, sent his archers ahead in great strength to provoke the enemies in their tents and wound the horses roaming through pastures and meadows. He himself, with five hundred armoured horsemen, suddenly rushed upon Baldwin’s camp and followers, in order to take worthy revenge for every injury Baldwin had inflicted upon him.

## Chapter XVI.—Baldwin and Tancred engage in battle, in which Tancred is found inferior

Without delay Baldwin, together with Baldwin of Burg [Col. 0447A], his namesake, Giselbert of Clermont, and all his company, recognized Tancred’s sudden assault and attack. They put on armour, raised their standards, and, after exhorting their companions in manly voice, swiftly presented themselves against Tancred amid the loud shouting of crowds and horns. Both sides engaged in fierce battle and fell under grave wounds.

But Tancred’s force, inferior in numbers and strength, turned its back, unable to bear the weight of battle. It barely escaped the storm of war by fleeing with Tancred into the city’s stronghold across a narrow water-bridge. In the constriction of that bridge, Richard, prince of Salerno and Tancred’s close associate, and Robert of the city of Ansa, most valiant knights, were delayed, captured, and held. Many horsemen and foot-soldiers of Tancred’s company were lost—some slain, others wounded. Giselbert of Clermont alone pursued too far, became surrounded amid the enemy, and was captured and carried away in the narrow passage of the bridge. Baldwin and his men thought him dead and lamented him with great mourning.

## Chapter XVII.—Tancred and Baldwin restore peace between themselves
With the dawn of the following day, both sides grieving over the absence of their noble captive men, and remembering that both had done wrong by violating the devotion owed to the holy road to Jerusalem, made a firm peace upon the counsel of the chief men of their host, restoring captives for captives to one another. Once this peace had been arranged and all the spoils, together with the captives, restored, Baldwin [Col. 0447C], with his seven hundred knights divided into detachments, entered the land of Armenia on the counsel of an Armenian knight named Pancratius, and besieged a stronghold of remarkable construction and strength called Turbaysel. When its Armenian inhabitants, men professing Christianity, saw this, they secretly took counsel with Prince Baldwin himself, expelled the Turks who commanded the citadel, and handed it over to him, preferring to serve under a Christian leader rather than under heathen rule.

Having thus subdued this town together with its fortified citadel and placed his own men there, he likewise besieged and took Ravenel, a fortress impregnable by human strength. The Turks, terrified by the capture of Turbaysel, are reported to have fled and departed from it. He also took many towns with their castles in the surrounding country, terrified by the approach of the army [Col. 0447D] advancing toward Antioch; the Turks, who had long held them in subjection, now shaken by fear, abandoned them by night and fled. Baldwin entrusted the captured Ravenel to the aforesaid Armenian Pancratius, a fickle man of great treachery. He had detained him at Nicaea after his escape from the bonds of the Greek emperor, because he had heard that he was a warlike man of versatile intelligence and that all Armenia, Syria, and Greece were familiar to him. Pancratius, being treacherous and crafty, and very well known to the Turks, judged that through the strength of the fortress of Ravenel entrusted to him he could gain possession of the country. Admitting no one from Baldwin’s company, he installed there his own distinguished young son; yet, while travelling and residing with Baldwin, he concealed that this was being done by fraud.

## Chapter XVIII.—On Baldwin’s successful outcome in capturing fortifications, and on the treachery of a certain Armenian. At last, against his will, this Armenian restores the fortress entrusted to him.

[Col. 0448A]

At length certain Armenian princes, who, having heard of Baldwin’s energy and nobility, had made an alliance with him—one of whom was Fer, governor of Turbaysel, while the other was named Nicusus, whose extensive castles and fortified places lay adjacent to Turbaysel—understood the treachery which Pancratius was plotting with the Turks. Knowing him to be a dangerous and unreliable man, they reported it to Baldwin, maintaining that, if he entrusted the fortress of Ravenel any longer to such a man, so criminal and perjured toward the emperor, he might soon lose the land that he had subdued.

When Baldwin heard this [Col. 0448B] from these trustworthy and faithful men, having himself often experienced that man’s treacheries, he demanded back the fortress entrusted to him. But Pancratius, obstinate in spirit, refused to surrender it into the hands or custody of the Franks. Finally, angered after repeatedly demanding the fortress, Baldwin one day ordered Pancratius, who stood by him and resisted, to be seized, bound in chains, and tortured until compelled to restore the fortress. Yet even then, compelled neither by the suffering of any torture nor by the necessity of saving his life, he still would not surrender it. Baldwin, wearied by his tortures, finally ordered that he be torn limb from limb alive unless he gave satisfaction concerning the surrender of the fortress. Fearing this cruel tearing apart of limbs and sinews, he sent a letter through Fer to his son, ordering him quickly to surrender the fortress to Baldwin for the deliverance of his life and limbs [Col. 0448C]. This was done; Pancratius was released from his bonds and thereafter separated from Baldwin’s fellowship.

Baldwin therefore entrusted the recovered fortress to the guardianship and loyalty of his Franks, and departed from Turbaysel, which is called Bersabee, conquering the country and region on every side and subjecting them to his authority.

## Chapter XIX.—The ruler of the city of Rohas summons Baldwin for aid; Baldwin, summoned, sets out; prevented by the Turks, he returns and hastens anew.

After several days had passed, Baldwin’s fame spread far and wide, and the valor of his wars was proclaimed above all his enemies. The ruler of the city of Rohas, called Edessa, situated in the region of Mesopotamia [Col. 0448D], sent to Baldwin the bishop of that city together with twelve leading men of the city, by whose counsel the entire administration of the region was conducted. They asked him to come down to the city with Frankish knights, defend the country against Turkish attacks, and, together with the ruler, hold in common power and lordship all revenues and tributes.

At length Baldwin accepted their counsel and descended with only five hundred knights, leaving the rest of his force at Turbaysel and Ravenel and in many places which, after the expulsion of the Turks, were now under his authority. But as they had hastened on their way and were preparing to cross the great river Euphrates, the Turks and other hostile forces, brought out at the counsel and instigation of Pancratius, whom he had released from his bonds, gathered together from every direction [Col. 0449A]. Some twenty thousand were present to oppose those wishing to cross. Baldwin, however, perceiving their force and cavalry and being unable at that time to withstand and defeat so many thousands, returned by the way he had come to Turbaysel. Then, after the Turks had dispersed and returned to their own refuges, Baldwin again set out for Rohas with two hundred knights, under the guidance of faithful men, completing his journey without hindrance or hostile attack and crossing the Euphrates with complete success.

## Chapter XX.—How Baldwin was received in the city of Rohas, how nobly he rejected that ruler’s gifts, and the request of the leading men.

When news of the arrival of this most excellent and renowned prince reached the ears of the city’s senators [Col. 0449B], joy and gladness arose among all who heard it. With trumpets and every kind of music, both great and small came out to meet him with every honor and rejoicing suitable to so great a man, and led him into the city. After this man had been so honorably introduced and magnificently established with his companions within the city gates and in lodging, the ruler who had summoned him, with the advice of the twelve senators, to resist the city’s enemies, became indignant at the praises and honors which people and senate had given him. Deep within his heart he began fiercely to envy him. He also forbade him altogether to exercise authority over the city or country, or to share equally with him in any revenues or tributes.

For he said that he would give him a great abundance [Col. 0449C] of gold, silver, purple cloth, mules, horses, and arms, if he would not refuse to be defender and helper to himself, the citizens, and the country, in positions assigned to him, against Turkish plots and assaults. Baldwin wholly rejected the ruler’s gifts, which were to be accepted under so contemptible a compact. He asked only that, under the assurance of his safe-conduct, he might be able to return, unharmed and uninjured, without danger or wicked contrivance, to Duke Godfrey and his brother.

When the twelve senatorial magnates and foremost men of the city, together with the rest of the populace, heard this—that he could not be retained by gold, silver, or any precious gifts—they approached the ruler. By every means and with entreaties they urged him not to permit such a noble man and most powerful defender to depart or estrange him from them, but to make him his partner in the kingdom and city, so that city and country might always be defended by his protection and [Col. 0449D] military aid; nor should he vex the man concerning what had been promised.

## Chapter XXI.—Baldwin is adopted as son by the ruler of Rohas; at his request he attacks the city of Samusart, but returns empty-handed when the undertaking fails.

Seeing the constancy and goodwill of the twelve governors and all the citizens toward Baldwin, the ruler, though unwilling, granted their request and made Baldwin his adopted son, according to the custom of that region and people. He embraced him against his bare breast and once clothed him beneath the garment nearest his own flesh, faith being given and received by both sides.

Thus their fatherhood and sonship being confirmed, one day the ruler admonished Baldwin as a son [Col. 0450A] that, having summoned all his own men-at-arms and paid troops and also taken with him the citizens of Rohas, he should march against the fortress of Samusart, near the Euphrates, and expel Balduc, prince of the Turks, who had unjustly seized and held that citadel belonging to Rohas. For Balduc had inflicted intolerable injury upon the citizens: by threats he had extorted from them as hostages not a few sons of the leading men of the city, because of the annual revenues and tributes in Byzantine coinage which they had agreed to pay him to ransom their vineyards and crops.

Baldwin did not refuse this first request of the ruler and the city’s leading men. Taking two hundred companions and the entire infantry and cavalry of the city, he attacked the castle of Samusart and inflicted great force upon the enemy through the valor of his men. But [Col. 0450B] Balduc and his followers, meeting them amid a hail of arrows and the shrieking of trumpets, repelled them severely. There an innumerable crowd of effeminate Armenian citizens, fighting carelessly and sluggishly, fell; only six brave and worthy knights of Baldwin were slain, pierced by arrows. When their funeral rites had been completed in Christian fashion, great mourning and grief arose throughout the city.

Baldwin, seeing that the citadel-fortress of Samusart was unconquerable and that within it were Turks most valiant and tireless in war, left his men at St. John’s, a position in the fortified district not far from the citadel, equipped with hauberks, helmets, and horses, so that they might always meet the Turks in resistance and harass them with continual warfare. He himself returned to Rohas with only twelve Franks.

## Chapter XXII.—Baldwin, wishing to repress the plot of the conspiring populace against its ruler, achieves nothing.

[Col. 0450C]

A few days later, the whole senate and all the citizens, considering Baldwin’s wisdom and steadfastness against Turkish plots, and recognizing that under his hand the city and its fortifications could be greatly preserved and defended, assembled together. They summoned Constantine of the mountains, a most powerful man, to a common council, in order to kill their ruler and raise Baldwin in his place as ruler and lord.

For that ruler was very hostile to them. He had oppressed them with many exactions and had taken gold and silver from all without measure. If anyone resisted, he stirred up against him the enmity and hatred of the Turks, not only endangering his life [Col. 0450D] but also causing his vineyards and crops to be cut down and his flocks to be plundered. When this plan became known, on a certain day all the small and great men of the city ran to arms. Armed and clad in hauberks, they came to Baldwin, urging him to hasten with them to the destruction of their ruler, declaring that by common counsel they had resolved to make him lord and ruler in his place.

Baldwin utterly refused to undertake such a crime, since he had been established as the ruler’s son and had as yet found in him no ground or evil by which he should become an accomplice and partner in his ruin. He said: “It would be an immeasurable sin before God for me to lay hands without cause upon this man, whom I have accepted as a father and to whom I have also pledged faith. But I pray you, do not allow me to be polluted by his blood and death, nor make my name despised among the princes of the Christian army [Col. 0451A]. I also ask that I be allowed to speak with him face to face in the chamber of the tower, upon which, raised up by your gift, he has been accustomed to dwell until now.”

They immediately granted this. And, ascending the tower, Baldwin spoke to him thus: “All the citizens and governors of this city have conspired to kill you and are hastening in fury and impetuosity, armed in every kind of weapon, toward this tower. I grieve and am distressed by this. Yet I have not neglected to provide some means by which you may be saved, or to forestall them by a gift of your possessions.” Hardly had the ruler heard Baldwin speaking with him when, behold, a multitude of citizens surged around the tower in siege and assault, battering the walls and doors of the tower with an unceasing discharge of mangonels and arrows.

## Chapter XXIII.—How miserably this same ruler was killed.

[Col. 0451B]

Seeing the peril to his life, the ruler revealed to Baldwin his incomparable treasures—purple cloth, gold and silver vessels, and abundant Byzantine coinage—and begged him to accept them, so that he might intervene with the citizens for his life and safety and they might allow him to leave and go from the tower naked and empty-handed. Baldwin heard his pleas and, moved with pity for the desperate man, earnestly exhorted and pressed the leaders of the people to spare their ruler and not kill him, and not refuse to divide among themselves the countless treasures which he had seen.

But neither the senate nor all the citizens listened to Baldwin or to the promise of treasures. With one voice they cried that he should not escape alive or safe in exchange for any compensation or gift of possessions [Col. 0451C], recounting the wrongs and exactions which they had often endured under him and from the Turks at his instigation. Therefore, despairing of his life and seeing that neither his entreaties nor any precious gifts availed him, the ruler sent Baldwin away from the tower. Lowering himself from the chamber through a window by a rope, he came out. They pierced him with a thousand arrows in an instant, killed him, cast him into the middle of the street, cut off his head, fixed it on a spear in mockery, and carried it through every lane of the city.

## Chapter XXIV.—After the ruler’s death, Baldwin, appointed in his place, at first scorns to buy the saleable fortress of Samusart; afterward, on his men’s counsel, he purchases it with very precious goods.

[Col. 0451D]

On the following day they established Baldwin, who strongly resisted and objected, as ruler and prince of the city. They granted him the impregnable tower, together with all the treasures of the slain ruler found within it, and became subject and faithful to him by oath. When Balduc heard of this new elevation of Baldwin, he was struck with great fear that, through a siege conducted by the valor of the Franks, men of war, he might lose the fortress of Samusart. Therefore he sent an embassy to Baldwin, offering the citadel for sale for ten thousand Byzantine coins, and promising that from then onward he would serve him faithfully in return for a paid stipend.

Baldwin paid no attention to his words, because he had unjustly taken this fortress from Christians, to whose city of Rohas it had belonged not long before [Col. 0452A]. Balduc, seeing the fierceness and firmness of Duke Baldwin, said that he would consume the citadel by fire, behead the many hostages of the citizens and governors whom he held, and continually devise plots against Baldwin by night and day. At last, as time generally passed, Baldwin took the counsel of his men and gave Balduc a talent of gold and silver, precious purple fabrics and dye, horses, and mules of considerable value. Thus he redeemed the fortress of Samusart from hostile hand and power.

From that day onward Balduc became subject to Baldwin and was established among the Franks as a member of his household and familiar companion. Baldwin strengthened the recovered fortress with the faithful guard of his own men and restored [Col. 0452B] to their leading men and citizens the hostages found there. After this, because pagans and Christians do not readily agree and are always mutually suspicious, Baldwin demanded Balduc’s wife and sons as hostages to secure the stability of his loyalty. He assented kindly, but from day to day, finding an excuse, delayed surrendering these hostages.

## Chapter XXV.—The fortress of Sororgia is handed over to Baldwin, not without difficulty, and Balduc is marked as deceitful.

Once Duke Baldwin had been thus elevated and his military achievement had become widely known, Balas [Col. 0452B], himself ruler and usurper of the fortress-city of Sororgia, sent an embassy to Duke Baldwin. He asked him to gather an army and descend upon the city, which lay apart from the fortress and mountains and still resisted in rebellion, so that, once citizens and city had been overcome, he might without delay place the fortress in Baldwin’s hands [Col. 0452C]. The citizens resisting him were Saracens and despised paying tribute.

Trusting Balas’s promises and having made a mutual treaty, Baldwin resolved to besiege and capture the city with all his equipment, until the defeated citizens yielded and thereafter became tributaries. But the citizens, learning from Balas’s message of Baldwin’s arrival and anger, summoned Balduc, with paid troops and other Turkish soldiers whom they had attracted with many rewards, hoping under their protection to hold and defend the city walls. Balduc, a knight and one of the Turkish rulers, already corrupted by greed for Byzantine coinage, came with his men to the city, hoping still to rule and dominate it.

When Baldwin learned this [Col. 0452D], he resolved, on an appointed day and with strong hand, to set out for the siege of Sororgia with mangonels and every kind of military equipment by which the city might be breached or taken. But when the citizens and Saracen soldiers heard of the overwhelming preparations, shaken with fear, they sent word asking him to come down peacefully to them, receive the city without opposition, and accept their annual revenues under his lordship. Baldwin yielded to their entreaties and fixed a day on which all these matters should be settled in peace and trustworthy good faith.

Balduc, seeing that the citizens had abandoned defense and, terror-stricken, could not resist so great a prince, left the city with his men and came down to Baldwin at Rohas, pretending loyalty in these words: “Do not believe, or suppose, that I entered the city of Sororgia in order to bring aid to its citizens against you. Rather, I came in order to call them back [Col. 0453A] by whatever counsel I could from their begun rebellion and make them subject and tributary to you.” Baldwin patiently accepted this, allowing Balduc from that day to remain with him under this excuse; nevertheless, he did not at all trust his loyalty.

Without delay the city was handed over to Baldwin, and the citizens became tributaries. Balas placed in his hands and under the custody of his men the fortress which stood preeminent in the mountains. Having received city and fortress, Baldwin left there Folker of Chartres, a military man highly skilled in war, to administer and defend the walls; he himself returned to Rohas in great glory.

## Chapter XXVI.—Tancred destroys fortresses harmful to Christians, and prudently stores the gifts offered him by enemies.

[Col. 0453B]

Tancred, separated from Baldwin and remaining at Mamistra on the coast, reinforced his own strength from the naval army which Baldwin had brought. He besieged and captured the Castle of Maidens, commonly called Batesses; likewise, having taken the Castle of Shepherds, he destroyed it. He also overthrew and crushed the Castle of Young Men, called Bakelers—fortified places in the mountains—held by strong soldiers. He subdued Lesser Alexandria, after destroying its gates and walls. He put the Turks found there to the sword. All castles and fortresses that had hitherto harmed the pilgrims he either captured or burned; of the pagan enemies found in them, he killed some and held others captive [Col. 0453C].

The enemies who, after subduing Christians, had scattered through the mountains and unjustly seized Christian fortresses and places, on hearing of his military prowess either took flight or sent horses, mules, and precious gifts of gold and silver, joining themselves to his friendship so that they might find him peaceable in all they possessed. Tancred rejected none of what was offered; but, cautious and provident, he received and stored everything, mindful of past hardships and expecting still greater future ones.

## Chapter XXVII.—On the city of Maresch, where Baldwin’s wife also died.

Meanwhile, the entire equipment and great strength of the army hastened onward by the direct route through the middle of Romania [Col. 0453D], proceeding across mountain precipices and down the slopes of valleys. Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, Count Raymond, Robert of Flanders, Reymer, bishop of Le Puy, Robert of Normandy, governed it by common counsel and equal leadership. Descending in force upon the city called Maresch, they lodged there overnight, spreading their tents in green places before the city walls. They inflicted no violence upon the Christians dwelling there, but peacefully obtained for purchase from the city the necessities of life.

The Turks, who had learned of the arrival of so many and such great princes, fled from the city’s fortress, which they had oppressed for many years with wrongful force and unjust tributes. In this region of Maresch, Baldwin’s most noble wife, whom he had brought from the kingdom of England, worn down by prolonged bodily illness and entrusted to Duke Godfrey, breathed out her life. She was buried with Catholic rites; her name was Godwera [Col. 0454A]. Udelrard, likewise struck by illness from Wizan, died there and was honorably placed in a tomb: a blameless knight, useful in every counsel and action of war, of Duke Godfrey’s household, and more than all others always privy to his secrets.

## Chapter XXVIII.—On the city of Arthesia, where Christian Armenians, cutting off the heads of the Turks residing among them, kindly receive their brethren.

The aforesaid princes, leaving the mountains and the region of Maresch with all their following companies, learned from certain Syrian Christians who met them [Col. 0454B] that the city of Arthesia was not far away, rich in necessities of life, but possessed by Turks. Learning this, Robert of Flanders, taking with him the most prudent men—Rotger of Roscit and Gozelo, son of Count Cuno of Montaigu—and a thousand mailed men, left the army and descended upon Arthesia. It was a city very strongly fortified with wall, ramparts, and a towered citadel, in which the Turks had reduced the resident Christian Armenians to a servile yoke.

As they approached the city and its walls with standards raised, each most beautiful in its color, and with bronze helmets shining brightly with gold, the renown of their arrival shook the whole region. The Turks on Arthesia’s walls and in its fortress, terrified by this sudden [Col. 0454C] encounter with the Franks, stood ready for defense and resistance, securing the city gates with bars and bolts. But the Armenian citizens, who had been oppressed by these Turks in long servitude and were confined with them in the same fortifications, remembered the wrongs they had long suffered from those Turks: the seizure of wives and daughters, the commission of other wicked deeds, and the exaction of unjust tributes. Now relying on the aid and arrival of Christians, they attacked the Turks, put them to the sword, cut off their heads, and threw them from windows and walls. Opening the city gates to their Christian brethren, they gave them safe entry amid the slaughter of pagans and the casting out of the dead bodies. They kindly welcomed their faithful brethren with every pious reception, familiarly relieved them of arms [Col. 0454D] and baggage, refreshed them with varied food and friendly drinks, and supplied abundant fodder for their horses and mules.

## Chapter XXIX.—The people of God, surrounded by a profane multitude, open a way for themselves by the sword and barely escape; the besieged act with confidence.

From this city station to Antioch ten miles are reckoned. News of the new slaughter of Turks flew swiftly and summoned twenty thousand Turks from Antioch and all its territories as far as the aforesaid city of Arthesia. Of these thousands of Turks, thirty of the cleverest and most agile, mounted on horses running like the wind, advanced deceitfully, leaving the ambush of the entire army behind them [Col. 0455A], so that with horn-and-bone bows they might provoke and draw the Franks out of the fortress.

The Franks, ignorant of the fraud and hidden ambushes, armed on foot and horseback and clothed in hauberks, met them in the open fields in order to engage the enemy. But no success in any encounter could befall them. For the Turks lying in ambush, by a cross-route, occupied the road in great numbers so that the Franks might have neither return nor refuge in the city, but be overwhelmed with sudden destruction.

At the sight of this sudden and unexpected attack, Robert of Flanders, Rotger, and the other leaders of the army, vigorously exhorting their companions and gathering them into one body, drew back their reins and sped across the plain through the dense Turkish ranks. With rigid lances they charged the enemy [Col. 0455B]. The whole company also charged with manly boldness, until they rushed unharmed from the hands of their enemies within the gates and walls. The Turks pursued those who escaped at the gates with a hail of a thousand arrows, trying to enter the gates with them. But they were driven back from the threshold by a force strong though small, and were not allowed to enter the gates with the Franks.

Nevertheless, in the sudden showers of arrows, many squires, horsemen, and foot soldiers on both sides were wounded, as were mules and horses. Seeing that they had achieved nothing, yet still trusting in their own numbers, the Turks established a siege around the aforesaid city. But the faithful who were shut in, because of the abundance of food found in the citadel and its firm, impregnable strength of wall, remained secure and at ease. There, in the fortress of Arthesia, Gozelo, son of Count Cuno [Col. 0455C], overcome by most severe illness, died after a few days and received honorable and Catholic burial from his Christian brethren.

## Chapter XXX.—The pagans besieging Arthesia, informed by scouts of the approaching Christian army, nevertheless do not raise the siege until night.

Meanwhile, at no great distance, the great Christian army hastened on its way. Hidden among them were scouts who, secretly slipping away from the army when opportunity arose, reported to the Turks what they had heard about the arrival and plans of the Catholic host. When these informers heard that news of the siege of their men at Arthesia had reached Prince Godfrey, Bohemond, and the others, and that they had formed a plan to bring relief, they hastened back to the Turkish camp [Col. 0455D]. They announced that Romans, Franks, and Germans were already approaching nearby; that the Turks could neither withstand their strength nor escape their hands unless they quickly abandoned the city and returned to their own refuges.

Yet, warned by these unfavorable reports, they were not at all afraid, trusting excessively in their aforesaid thousands. Instead, throughout the full hours of one day they assaulted the city and labored in repeated attacks. But they spent their effort in vain, since the Franks did not spare in resisting them from the citadel and walls.

## Chapter XXXI.—When the army of God arrives, Arthesia is secured under the protection of the faithful; Baldwin, illustrious in triumph, is honored by a new marriage.

Then, when night had returned and darkness was falling [Col. 0456A], after many consultations among themselves they resolved that, at the first appearance of dawn, they should prepare to withdraw to the bridge of the river Ferna and enter Antioch safely—a city fortified and founded with towers, unconquerable by human strength—lest, if the bridge were seized in advance and they were cut off by the river from the Christian army, they should suffer the peril of defeat and death.

Hardly had the aforesaid Turks entered Antioch when, at the dawn of the following day, the great army of Catholics [Col. 0456B] pitched camp in the territory of Arthesia and spent the night there in joy and gladness. By decree of the leading men, fifteen hundred chosen mailed men were sent to Arthesia to assist the brethren in the fortress, so that, safe and unharmed, strengthened by their common resources and forces and less anxious about hostile attack, they might return by the common road to the army. Once the city of Arthesia had been secured under the protection of Christian faith, they returned to the army without any injury.

Tancred also returned from Lesser Alexandria and the coastal regions, as did all those who had been sent out and dispersed in various places to subdue country, castles, and cities, except Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey. He had gone south into Armenia to conquer the Turks and had subjected Turbaysel, Ravenel, and the other fortresses to his authority. This Baldwin, increasingly growing day by day in wars and triumphs, at the counsel of the twelve governors of the city, married in magnificent and lawful wedding rites a most noble wife of Armenian lineage. She was the daughter of a certain prince, Taphnuz by name, who was Constantine’s brother and possessed fortresses and many strongholds in the mountains; he made Baldwin heir of all of them [Col. 0456C].

He also promised to give him sixty thousand Byzantine coins, from which he could pay his soldiers’ stipulated wages and powerfully hold the country against Turkish attacks. He promised this indeed, but gave him only seven thousand; he delayed the rest from day to day. After Baldwin’s wedding had been celebrated with immeasurable magnificence, it was decreed by the common counsel of the chief men of city and country that this Taphnuz should discuss the condition of the land and the welfare of the city with his son-in-law, because he was a man of advanced age and sounder counsel, and that they should mutually anticipate one another in honor. This was done.

## Chapter XXXII.—The assembled people of Christ are no longer divided; the bishop of Le Puy addresses them paternally, urging vigilance.

[Col. 0456D]

After they had assembled together, from that day onward they were no longer divided, because of the innumerable Turkish forces who, fleeing from the mountains and all Romania, had hastened for defense to Antioch, a city of immeasurable strength of walls and unconquerable. Without delay Reymer, bishop of Le Puy, addressed the people and with such exhortation paternally warned and instructed them all, as the pressing necessity and constant reports concerning the excessively near city of Antioch required:

“O dearest brothers and sons, know, as we have learned, that the very nearby city of Antioch [Col. 0457A] is founded upon the strongest fortification of walls, which cannot be broken by iron or the hurling of stones, built with masonry of unheard-of and indissoluble cement and with masses of great stones. In it, without doubt, all enemies of the Christian name—the Turks, Saracens, and Arabs—fleeing before us from the mountains of Romania and from every direction, have assembled. Therefore we must take the utmost care no longer to divide any of our people or rashly press ahead; but in common and unanimous strength, tomorrow we have most prudently resolved to advance as far as the bridge of Ferna.”

## Chapter XXXIII.—Leaving Romania, following the selected standard-bearers, they arrive at the bridge of the river Farfar, where they are received in battle by the Turks.

[Col. 0457B]

Therefore all the people obeyed the admonition of the venerable priest. On the following sunrise, having recovered their companions from Arthesia, with Tancred and Welf of Boulogne, and with all the Frankish companions from the coastal regions returned, together with camels, asses, and every conveyance of baggage and necessities, they set out as one company, trusting in their arms, toward the bridge of the river Ferna, called Farfar, leaving behind the rugged Alps and valleys of harsh Romania.

On this day Robert, count of the Normans, was selected with his knights to lead the army, as is customary in every military host, so that if any hostile force lay concealed, notice might be brought to the leaders and princes of the Catholic army, that they might hasten as quickly as possible to arms, hauberks, and the formation of battle-lines. Among these thousands, Rotger of Barneville and Everhard of Poisat, knights praiseworthy in every military undertaking, bore the standards and commanded the cavalry until they halted without delay at the aforesaid bridge [Col. 0457C].

This bridge, made by marvelous art and ancient workmanship, was formed in the shape of an arch, beneath which the swift-flowing river Farfar of Damascus, commonly called Ferna, washed its channel. At either end of the bridge stood two projecting towers, impervious to iron and most suitable for resistance; Turks always guarded them. A company of two thousand excellent infantrymen followed and halted at the bridge, but they were not permitted to cross. For about a hundred Turks stationed in the bridge towers [Col. 0457D] for defense vigorously resisted those wishing to cross with bow and hail of arrows; they wounded horses with repeated blows and pierced many riders through the protection of their hauberks with flying arrows.

## Chapter XXXIV.—The fierce conflict of the faithful and Turks over crossing the bridge.

Such a grave contest arose on both sides: the one side wishing to cross, the other opposing the crossing and still prevailing. Seven hundred Turks summoned from Antioch, seeing the steadfastness and defense of their men on the bridge, flew up on very swift horses, greatly emboldened for war, and seized the fords so that no Christian might obtain leave to cross.

The Christian horsemen and foot soldiers [Col. 0458A], seeing the forces of armored Turks spread along the riverbank to resist them, themselves spread out broadly along the opposite bank. On both sides, arrows were bent and discharged with manly effort; a long struggle ensued, and very many men and horses, pierced through on either bank, fell dying and expired. At last the Turks were prevailing greatly, leading and persevering in archery and combat. The army of the faithful, ready in arms and horses, hastened from every side to aid the companions sent ahead. Yet the Turks did not then withdraw from the bank; they preferred to die rather than yield, continually striving to oppose those attempting to cross.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—At the admonition of the Bishop of Le Puy they force the bridge; battle having been joined, Christ’s warriors return victorious; grievous news strikes the prince of Antioch.

[Col. 0458B]

The Bishop of Le Puy, who, having heard of so grave a conflict, had gone on before the main army, saw that the hearts of his men were somewhat failing through fear, because of the wounding of their horses and the piercing of their bodies.
