He repeated his exhortation and thus strengthened the people of the living God for defence:

> “Do not fear the assault of your adversaries. Stand manfully; rise up against these biting dogs. For today God will fight for you.”

At these words and admonitions of so distinguished a pontiff, they formed a tortoise-shell of shields, covered their heads with helmets, clothed their breasts in mail, and boldly forced their way over the bridge, driving the enemy back from it and putting them to flight. Others, seeing that the whole army had come to their aid, entered the fords with great confidence and swam their horses across. [Col. 0458C] Others, having found the fords on foot, hastened to cross the waters in their desire to engage in battle. Enduring the blows of their assailants and the slingers, they attacked the Turks in a blind charge, drove them from their position, and took their stand on the dry bank on the other side of the river.

Wido, seneschal of the king of France, charged the Turks with horse and lance. Reinold of Beauvais, a most fierce young knight, paying no heed to the shafts of arrows, advanced amid the enemy with lance and sword and wrought a most savage slaughter. On both sides the ranks of faithful and unbelievers clashed with violent force; they grew hot with the sweat of battle and inflicted killing and slaughter. Bohemond, Godfrey, Raymond, Robert, and Roger commanded the battle-lines and the exceedingly beautiful standards of various colours, until [Col. 0458D] the Turks, taking flight upon their swiftest horses, returned to Antioch by the mountain descents and routes known to them.

The victorious Christians, returning from their pursuit and great slaughter of the enemy, pursued the foe no farther, since the walls of Antioch appeared far too near and the strength of all the pagans had gathered within it. They spent the night beside the river Fernae. They collected plunder and spoils from every quarter, and released from their bonds many of Peter’s army whom the Turks had scattered throughout the region of Antioch.

When Darsian, prince and head of the city, learned this adverse news and that the fortunes of his own men had turned against them, his countenance fell, his heart was crushed with fear, and he was gripped by great anguish. He pondered what he should do if there should befall him what had befallen Solyman in the loss of Nicaea. [Col. 0459A] Without delay, busily taking frequent counsel, he strove unceasingly to bring in provisions and gather weapons and the forces of his allies; nor did he cease to strengthen the gates and walls with faithful guards.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—The march to Antioch is proclaimed; the bishop addresses the people, and through him those who should lead the army and those who should guard the rear are appointed.

Moreover, at daybreak Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, and all the commanders of the army arose, again put on their arms, mail, and helmets, and ordered all to resume the interrupted march to the city of Antioch, with every necessary provision and every sort of livestock and carts bearing food, of which [Col. 0459B] so great an army had need.

When these had been assembled and made ready for the journey, the provident bishop spoke as follows:

> “Brethren and most beloved sons, hear carefully the words which I address to you, and do not be reluctant to heed them. The city of Antioch is near and close to us: there are four miles between it and us. This remarkable city, a work unheard of by us, was founded by the king of Antioch with enormous stones and towers, whose number is reckoned at three hundred and sixty.
>
> “We know that Sansadonia, son of King Darsian, a most valiant prince, rules within it; and we have learned that four most noble and powerful ammirals, as though they were kings, summoned by Darsian’s command, have assembled there and, in fear of our coming, have prudently placed themselves and their men under strong protection and armed them. [Col. 0459C] Their names are Adorsonius, Copatrix, Rosseleon, and Carcornutus; over all of them Darsian is said to be king, head, and lord.
>
> “These four ammirals hold, by Darsian’s gift and favour, the four richest of the thirty cities which belong to Antioch far and wide throughout the surrounding region and were tributary to King Darsian; each holds one city with a hundred castles. Therefore, warned by Darsian himself, king of Syria and all Armenia, they are said to have come in no small strength to resist us and defend the city, mistress of all these cities and kingdoms.
>
> “It is therefore necessary that we proceed cautiously and in good order. As you know, we joined battle late in the day; we are weary, and our horses’ strength is spent. Let Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, [Col. 0459D] Reinard of Toul, Peter of Staden, Everhard of Poisat, Tancred, Werner of Greis, and Henry of Ascha lead the army at the front in formed battle-lines. Let Robert of Flanders, Count Robert of the Normans, Stephen of Blois, Count Raymond, Tatinus, servant of the emperor of Constantinople, Adam son of Michael, and Robert of Barnavilla, if this counsel is pleasing to you, guard the rearmost battle-lines of cavalry and infantry.”

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—What they did upon arriving at Antioch, and how great the army of God was estimated to be.

When this plan had thus been arranged for all by the bishop and the other prudent men, they advanced in unity along the royal road to the very formidable walls [Col. 0460A] of Antioch. They went forth splendidly arrayed in shields of gold, green, red, and every other colour; with raised standards decorated with gold and with every work of purple dye, beautiful to behold; with horses most fit for war; and with most splendid mail and helmets. They vigorously spread their tents beside the place called Altalon.

There they cut down and uprooted orchards and trees of various kinds with axe and hatchet, taking possession of the ground with their outstretched tents. Once these had been pitched, they eagerly set about preparing food, sounding a thousand and a thousand horns, and busied themselves everywhere with plunder and fodder for the horses. Their roar and clamour was said to be audible for almost a mile.

Nor is this surprising, since the number of so great an army was without doubt reckoned by all at six hundred thousand fighting men, apart from the women and children who followed, whose thousands seemed very numerous. [Col. 0460B] At this arrival of the Christians and the beginning of the siege, the city that day remained so silent that neither sound nor noise was heard from it, and the city was believed to be empty of defenders—although it abounded exceedingly in weapons and pagan forces in all its towers and garrisons.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Description of the manner in which the city was besieged.

Wednesday dawned, when they entered the territory of Antioch and besieged its walls. On that day Tancred was the first to establish his position beside Altalon. Roger of Barnavilla was stationed beside him; Adam son of Michael was placed nearby with his followers, so that no supplies might be brought to the Turks on that side.

At the gate facing the Persian quarter, where the mountain ridges begin to fail, Bohemond occupied a position with a band of strong men; and, having established a secure garrison there, he remained safe. Tatinus, servant of the emperor, somewhat farther from the city, pitched his tent in a field named Combrus, always intent upon flight. Before this same Tatinus Baldwin, count of Hama, established his position with his band. [Col. 0460C]

Next, Count Robert of the Normans and Robert of Flanders were stationed with all their cavalry to besiege the walls. Stephen of Blois likewise took his place in formation beside the aforesaid leaders in order to encircle the city. Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of France, likewise sat down at this siege with his companions.

This city of Antioch, they say, measures fully two miles in length and one and a half in breadth. The aforementioned river Farfar flows past it. It is occupied by walls and towers, whose fortification and masonry extend to the brow of the mountain, where the principal citadel—the mistress of the city and of all its towers—has been founded and rises above them. Around this citadel four unconquerable towers are said to have been placed for the protection of the central fortress standing in their midst; the aforesaid ammirals were designated as the constant guards and defenders of King Darsian over them. [Col. 0460D]

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—Again concerning the same matter.

Still further, at the siege of Antioch—which, as you have heard, is so extensive—the bishop himself took his position at the gate now called Warfaru, an impregnable gate, together with Count Raymond. With them the Provençals, Gascons, and all their followers encamped.

At the farther point, where a bridge made by joining ships was later constructed, Duke Godfrey besieged one gate of the city on the riverbank with all the thousands of Lotharingians, Saxons, Alemanni, and Bavarians, men most savage with the sword. With that duke were Reinard of Toul and Peter of Staden, who, having been separated at Mamistra from Baldwin, the duke’s brother, had returned to the army and the duke; also Cuno of Montacute, Henry of Ascha, and his brother Godfrey—knights ever most dangerous to their enemies—who likewise encamped to prevent the Turks’ entrance and exit. [Col. 0461A] Here the more intense and greater labour fell upon them.

### CHAPTER XL.—Concerning the bridge over the river, for the destruction of which specially devised engines are constructed.

Over this aforementioned river, which, flowing in a very long channel past the walls, stretches onward to the sea, a stone bridge extends from the city itself. It was an ancient work, but had no tower; when the army had completely taken up its positions, this point remained unbesieged. Through this bridge the Turks frequently came out; before the army’s eyes, they made sorties, brought in necessities, and returned. Frequently, when they learned that the people of Jesus Christ had dispersed through the countryside and mountains to seek food or fodder for their horses, they came out by that same bridge and slaughtered them.

Likewise, from the very gate of Warfaru, watched by Bishop Reymerus and Raymond, another threatening bridge, built by the skill of the ancients, extended across a certain marsh, very muddy and exceedingly deep because of the force and flooding of a constantly flowing spring which issued outside the city near its walls. [Col. 0461B] By this bridge the Turks sometimes came out, whether by day or in the darkness of night, when the army had forgotten to guard against ambushes; they shot arrows or struck some men with the sword in their charge, and by a sudden retreat over the same bridge escaped into the city’s protection.

The bishop and all the leaders lamented the menace of this bridge; having taken counsel, they agreed upon its destruction. On an appointed day they went out from the camp with iron hammers, mattocks, and axes. Yet their force in no way prevailed in destroying the bridge, for it was an indestructible work founded upon the cement and ingenuity of the ancients.

The army’s attempt with hammers having thus failed, the leaders resolved to construct an engine out of a pile of timber interwoven with wickerwork. Its iron-forged and joined fastenings they covered with horse-, ox-, and camel-hides, lest the Turks should burn it with fire cast upon it together with pitch and sulphur. [Col. 0461C] When it had been completed, they brought it by the strength of armoured men as far as the middle of the bridge facing the gate of Warfaru, and appointed Count Raymond its guard and commander.

### CHAPTER XLI.—A fierce engagement at the bridge, where the Christians’ engine is reduced to ashes and other instruments are prepared.

[Col. 0462A]

When the Turks saw this structure, they rushed to the walls and fought on the bridge, striking the Franks with arrows and shots from mangonels, so that, after being struck, they might be driven away from the bridge and the engine. Conversely, the Christians resisted with arrows and the Balearic bow, fiercely attacking the enemies upon the walls, until they pierced the liver of the son of a certain ammiral with an arrow.

Angered by his death and by the resistance of the faithful, the Turks burned with greater fury. At last, gathering all their strength together, they suddenly opened the gate, came out boldly, and attacked the engine. They pressed upon and overcame its guards, vigorously throwing fire, pitch-soaked torches, and sulphurous kindling into the engine, [Col. 0462B] reducing it entirely to ashes. Fearing for their lives, its guards, though unwilling, were forced to flee headlong, scarcely defended and escaped.

Since the knights and leaders of the pilgrims saw that they gained nothing by this device, on the following day they set against the bridge three mangonels—called *barbicales* by the Franks—to batter and wear down the gate of Warfaru, its gate-tower, and its walls with repeated shots and the impact of stones, and to break into many pieces the outer walls before the main wall. Yet even so they were unable to breach the gate.

When they accomplished nothing, one day, by common counsel, a thousand armoured men rolled immense and scarcely movable tree-trunks, and stones of remarkable weight and size, across the bridge toward the gate, obstructing the Turks who wished to come out and do harm. [Col. 0462C]

### CHAPTER XLII.—Concerning the Christians’ ship-bridge, intended to avoid the Turks’ ambushes.

Because many losses and attacks were inflicted upon the Christian army from these two bridges, and because the gate and bridge of Warfaru were now occupied and blocked with timber and enormous stones, ambushes were more often made to destroy the faithful from the bridge on the other side of the city, across the river Farfar—the bridge from which, as we have said, the Turks made their sorties and which, owing to the city’s extent, had remained unbesieged.

They therefore resolved to construct a bridge out of ships, secured by ropes, by which they might have free passage to the port of Simeon the Hermit. Previously they had waited on either bank and crossed one by one and slowly in a small boat. [Col. 0462D] This ship-bridge was now constructed for the purpose that, if Turks came out over Farfar’s stone bridge to ambush the Christians, the Franks might swiftly meet them over this wooden bridge, aid their own men bringing provisions from the seaport, and repel the Turks without delay. From the stone bridge of the aforesaid river to the ship-bridge fitted with rope-bound wicker hurdles, the distance is reckoned as half a mile.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—How the Turks secretly attacked Christians sent out for horse fodder.

When the bridge had been completed through the gathering and joining of ships, three hundred Christians, cavalry and infantry alike, crossed the river Farfar one day to seek fodder for their horses and supplies necessary for life. The Turks, observing this and watching from the walls, rapidly gathered their comrades, took arms and quivers, and came out together on horseback over the city’s stone bridge. They unexpectedly fell upon the Christians sent for fodder from behind. They left many bodies lying upon the ground with their heads cut off; the rest, who had an opportunity to flee, they pursued as far as the new bridge. Fortunate were those able to escape such cruel enemies. [Col. 0463A] Others, rushing toward the fords, were overwhelmed and drowned in the waves while fleeing from the Turks; the new bridge was unavailable to them because of the multitude crossing it.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—The faithful, rising to avenge their men, are partly destroyed by swords after mutual slaughter and partly drowned in the river.

[Col. 0463B]

When this grave disaster was reported to the army’s leaders, nearly five thousand armed men, many clad in mail and mounted on horses, flew from their tents to repress the rash enemy. Henry, son of Fredelo of the castle of Ascha, eager to pursue the enemy and renowned as he was in warfare and deeds, swam his horse across the river, though burdened with mail, helmet, and shield; for he had been unable to wait for passage across the ship-bridge because of the long delay.

As he rashly entered the ford with his horse, the waves of the very deep water covered his head. Yet, under God’s protection—for whose sake he exposed his life to danger—he reached the dry bank alive and safe, still seated upon his horse, together with the others who swam across. [Col. 0463C] Persisting vigorously in the pursuit of the Turks, he continually exhorted cavalry and infantry alike to follow fearlessly as far as the bridge itself.

Some Turks were held back and others barely escaped. Their companions, massed at the bridge of Farfar and at the gate, loudly called out for help. They came forth, turned back their horses at the reins amid the rush and clamour of those coming to aid them, and drove the Franks, who had thus far pressed them, into a disastrous flight as far as the very bridge which they had constructed of ships.

In this severe counterattack and flood of Turks, and in the Christians’ swift flight and return to the bridge, many infantrymen perished, pierced by Turkish arrows. Others, seeing immediate death behind them and hoping to be saved by water alone, plunged into the waves of the deep river; no small number were seen to perish and die, submerged and suffocated by the stream. [Col. 0463D] Others, because of the pressure of fugitives, fell from the bridge together with their horses, helmets, and mail; drowned and extinguished in the waves, they were never found again.

### CHAPTER XLV.—The guard of a gate is entrusted to Tancred for an agreed payment.

Since the Turks frequently came forth to injure the people from this bridge and from the gate through which the city was later delivered—a gate situated high in the mountains and offering an exit—the army’s leaders took counsel that Tancred, with a garrison stationed there, should keep guard and suddenly suppress Turks who dared to come out from either gate. For this guard he was to receive by agreement forty marks of silver each month from the army.

One day, while he was keeping guard at the post established in the mountains, beside the Turks’ altars and across the river Farfar, namely at the place where the river flows nearly half a mile from the city, he boldly charged the Turks as they crossed the fords according to their custom. [Col. 0464A] Joining battle with them, he at length prevailed, killed four Turks with the sword, and put the rest to flight across the river, as far as the place where their livestock grazed on grass. Having driven them beyond the river, he took booty from their herds, including one camel, and returned victorious to the new post which he had fortified.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—Concerning a cleric and a noblewoman, who, while playing dice, were treacherously killed.

With these two gates—the one toward the mountains, the other at the stone bridge—under Tancred’s guard, and the Christian army settled and somewhat secure from military affairs, some companions occasionally occupied themselves idly with dice. It happened one day that Adelberon, son of Count Conrad of Luxembourg, a cleric and archdeacon of the Church of Metz, a most noble young man of royal blood and a kinsman of Henry III, Roman emperor, amused and occupied himself in playing dice with a certain noblewoman of great birth and beauty.

They were in an orchard full of fruit-bearing trees and abundant grass, and in the wood beside the camp and the same gate of the city which Duke Godfrey and the contingent of Germans were pressing by siege. [Col. 0464B] While they were, as stated, occupied with leisure and play, the Turks, intent upon ambushing and killing Christians, secretly emerged from the gate. Carefully concealing themselves among the tall overgrown grass and thick trees, they rushed with a sudden cry upon the unknowing and startled archdeacon and the woman playing with him, shooting arrows; they scattered and wounded their companions who had gathered as judges of the game and had now, through fear, forgotten the dice.

They cut off the archdeacon’s head and, returning rapidly through the gate as soon as this had been done, carried it away with them. The noblewoman, however, they seized alive and unharmed by weapons, dragged into the city, and throughout the whole night abused her in the incestuous intercourse of their unrestrained lust, showing her no humanity. [Col. 0464C] At last, after abusing her through the abominable and most wicked violation by many men, they brought her to the walls and killed her by capital sentence. They immediately placed her head, together with the archdeacon’s, in their mangonels and hurled them far from the walls into the midst of the fields.

When the heads of both were found, they were brought and shown to Duke Godfrey. Recognizing the archdeacon’s head, he ordered the grave of his already buried body to be opened and the head restored to its proper place, lest the limbs of so noble a man should remain unburied.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—Concerning a knight struck down through his own carelessness, and the orchard, harmful to the faithful, which is cut down.

[Col. 0465A]

On another day the Turks, rejoicing in the success of their treachery and believing that they could still inflict a like deception upon the Christians, came out of the gate and secretly approached through thick rushes and frail reeds in a marshy place. They attacked certain pilgrims in the aforementioned orchard with their customary ferocity and shouting; but the knights who came to their aid drove them back and forced them to flee.

No one was then struck or wounded by them except Arnolph of the castle of Tyrs, a knight always ardent and prudent in war. On this occasion, however, heedlessly and without shield-cover or iron armour, he had rushed at the pilgrims’ cry into the orchard. There he was pierced by the blind, flying shaft of a Turkish arrow with a mortal wound and died. [Col. 0465B]

The duke and his fellow-campaigners, grievously offended that the Turks made ambushes against Christians from this orchard and that such distinguished men had fallen there through treachery, decided that Christians from the army should gather with tools and axes and utterly root it out, cutting down the grass, rushes, and reeds, so that no deceitful hand could thereafter hide or cause harm there.

When the Turks saw that their deceits at and from this gate were being forestalled by the people of the living God, they again came out through the gate of Farfar. They watched for the destruction of pilgrims crossing by the ship-bridge, carrying bundles of wood or seeking grass and fodder for horses; and whenever from their mountain lookout they saw men wandering here or there for necessities, they immediately pursued and killed them with swords and arrows. [Col. 0465C]

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—Concerning Count Hugh, who, grieving over the slaughter of the faithful, prudently countered the Turks’ treachery.

Since these killings, ambushes, and attacks occurred every day, morning, noon, and evening, and daily laments for the slain were heard in the camp, while Tancred could not so often encounter the enemy because of the varied forms of hostile treachery—and they frequently burst forth from the city over the bridge without his knowledge—Count Hugh of Saint-Pol, from the kingdom of France, was moved to pity by this daily slaughter of the faithful: his own retainers and those of other powerful men, who brought in necessities.

He therefore urged his son Engelrad, a young knight agile in arms, by paternal counsel, to exhort his own retainers likewise, so that, burning with a single resolve, they might desire to free and avenge their poor dependants and Christian brethren from so many Turkish killings and assaults, and frighten away the enemies who pursued them so often. [Col. 0465D]

This done, and volunteers having been found, the aged father himself first called for arms and a horse and mounted. Crossing the ship-bridge under cover of night, he hid with his beloved son and his chosen companions near the mountains in a sheltered valley. At the first light of dawn he left an infantryman in the open plain, where he would be plainly visible to Turkish eyes.

The Turks, not forgetting their cruelty and slaughter of Christians, again came out from the city over the bridge of the river Farfar and took their stand on a mountaintop, as was their custom. From there a view extends from mountain to mountain across the level plain for nearly two miles. [Col. 0466A] Seeing the lone pilgrim wandering and gathering brushwood, they rushed at full speed on horseback to kill him. With a sudden cry they pursued him, frightened, as he fled toward the mountains and thickets, passing close by the ambush of the concealed Christians.

When the pilgrim had hidden himself in the mountains, these four Turks turned back, expecting confidently to retrace their way near the Christians’ ambush. But immediately the count and his men rose from the valley and rushed upon them at speed. They left two crushed upon the ground in an instant, carrying away their horses and weapons; the other two they spared alive, bound, and brought to the army.

Pilgrims of every rank, noble and humble, flocked from all directions to see the captive Turks, giving glory to God for this favourable outcome and heaping praise upon Count Hugh and his son Engelrad, by whose prudence and manly boldness such harmful adversaries had been captured and crushed. [Col. 0466B]

### CHAPTER XLIX.—Where the count’s son, after several perils to his life, strikes down a most savage Turk and returns victorious.

The Turkish leaders and all their force, hearing of the crushing of their men, added anger to grief. They took counsel how they might shortly repay the Christians with more cruel losses in vengeance for their own. Therefore twenty of the bolder and fiercer men, selected from their thousands, were sent on horses swift as the wind to provoke the Christians as far as the ship-bridge.

Making many close passes along the bank beside the bridge and shooting arrows, they tried to stir the whole army behind them, so that the forces of their companions, rapidly pouring out of the city, might overwhelm some with grievous martyrdom, as they were accustomed to do. But Christ’s faithful, sufficiently and repeatedly experienced in their deceits, restrained the people from rash pursuit. [Col. 0466C] Yet, lest the Turks claim that they had been overcome by weariness of war, they sent Engelrad, son of the aforesaid Hugh, with several companions to meet them, so that, like the Turks, wheeling their horses in rapid passes, they might try to deceive the deceitful enemy in reciprocal combat.

Without delay they crossed the bridge and harried their horses to and fro in different mutual charges; one side directed lances to strike, the other shot arrows to pierce. Finally, after extensive rivalry in these charges, the honour and praise of victory, with God’s help, fell to Engelrad. For outrunning a Turk more distinguished and fiercer than the rest, before the eyes of his father and all who had gathered on the opposite bank to observe the outcome, he threw him from his horse and pierced him with his lance. [Col. 0466D] The others, shaken by his fall and disaster and immediately turned to flight, he fiercely pursued with his Christian companions, though not far from the bridge, because ambushes frequently emerged from the city and resisted their pursuers.

When his son and the other companions had safely returned, the heart of the aged father rose into exceeding joy; amid the favour and applause of great and small alike, the glorious young man was exalted together with his helpers and comrades.

### CHAPTER L.—When necessities of food fail, leaders chosen for this purpose carry off innumerable spoils from the surrounding lands.

Amid these continual disturbances and very frequent attacks, after some time had passed, the people of God began to be reduced in supplies and food, because so great an army had exhausted the cities and regions round about. As famine increased daily and the army was dying from want—especially the common people—pitiful groans and grief pressed upon and troubled the most pious bishop and all the commanders of the host, that they might provide counsel in these miseries as to how the people could be sustained. [Col. 0467A]

Since no means was found to relieve the people, it seemed good to all that Bohemond, Tancred, and Robert of Flanders should be sent with a company of cavalry and infantry into the exceedingly wealthy land of the Saracens, still untouched by plunder, to collect spoils and necessities by which hunger might be extinguished and the people relieved of want. Tancred had by then completed his guard-duty and returned from the mountains to the army.

Bohemond, Robert, and Tancred—since it had been decreed at the outset that neither great nor small should oppose whatever the army ordered—took fifteen thousand infantry and two thousand chosen cavalry under arms. Within three days they entered the kingdoms of the pagans and amassed unheard-of quantities of plunder, sheep, and herds of every kind, which they carried off unimpeded for two days. [Col. 0467B] But when evening fell on the third day, weary from the march and with their whole company weighed down by the burden of plunder, they decided to rest in a level plain beside the mountains.

### CHAPTER LI.—Where the pagans strip away the booty.

Meanwhile the report and outcry throughout all the surrounding regions hastened to the ears of the pagan leaders and brought out so many thousands from diverse places and mountain settlements to pursue Bohemond, Robert, their people, and to seize their booty, that it is marvellous to speak or hear of it.

Bohemond, however, knew nothing of this and expected no future adversity. While he slept securely with Robert, at the first dawn of day the aforementioned thousands of enemies appeared. They saw themselves and their men so surrounded that they might have wondered whether a most dense forest had suddenly grown on every side. [Col. 0467C] Astonished by this sight and despairing of life, they immediately summoned the cavalry around them and declared that they must join battle and could not withstand the strength of so many thousands.

They therefore formed a tortoise-shell of shields and a dense front of knights, seeking a route and escape where the enemy’s concentration appeared thinner and weaker. Then, drawing their swords and giving their bridles free rein for the charge, they rushed forward unanimously and broke through the opposing battle-lines. Intent solely upon flight, they hastened to the mountains, leaving behind the deserted infantry together with the whole collection of booty and spoils.

When they had escaped by the steep mountain paths and byways—though many of their followers had been held and destroyed—the pagan ranks enveloped the wretched fleeing infantry. They did not spare them from destruction by sword and arrow; but they captured many, stripped them of their arms, and carried back the plunder and everything taken from them for themselves and their own men. [Col. 0468A]

### CHAPTER LII.—Concerning the booty of Count Robert and, as famine grew, what the lesser people did or suffered.

After this most wretched rout of Bohemond, when he returned to the army and his brethren with humbly tearful countenance, the people mourned greatly—women, young men, children, fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters who had lost beloved friends, sons, and kinsmen.

Robert of Flanders, who had gone down with Bohemond into the land of the Saracens to plunder, had withdrawn separately from him, though unwillingly, when Bohemond and his forces were crushed and put to flight. On the following day, having regrouped two hundred horsemen, he encountered Turks and Saracens who were scattered and proceeding carelessly in the opposite direction. Fighting them boldly, he won a glorious victory and put them to flight. [Col. 0468B] He returned to the camp at Antioch with immense quantities of booty which the fleeing Turks had left behind there, giving great relief to a people despairing amid Bohemond’s calamity.

A short time afterwards, when a few days had passed and Robert’s booty had been consumed, no one dared any longer seek plunder far from the army because of the cruel killing of Bohemond’s companions. A greater and harsher famine began to multiply among the people; an incalculable mortality arose among the common folk; and the army dwindled. Nor is this surprising. A single small loaf, which had formerly been obtainable for one denarius of Luculan coinage, was now sold to the needy for two solidi. An ox was sold for two marks, though a little earlier it could have been bought for ten solidi; a lamb was valued at five solidi.

Thus, when this very severe scarcity oppressed the people of the living God, many scattered throughout the whole region of Antioch in search of food, banding together in groups of two or three hundred for defence against Turkish ambushes and for an equal division of everything that they might find or seize. [Col. 0468C] Hearing and understanding the people’s distress, the misery of famine, Bohemond’s very recent and severe defeat, and the army’s continual dispersal, the Turks came out at nearby hours from the gate on that side of the city which projected into the mountains and was unbesieged, at a great distance from the gate watched by Bohemond. Descending the rocky slopes, they pursued Christ’s faithful scattered on every side and destroyed them in savage slaughter.

### CHAPTER LIII.—The most cruel death of a certain archdeacon and his companions.

One day, as the famine grew more severe and pressed upon many nobles and common people alike, a certain archdeacon of the Church of Toul, named Louis, compelled by the failure of his provisions and overcome by the sword of hunger, withdrew from the army with three hundred other clerics and laymen. Forced by want, they went to places famous for their abundance of food, situated in the mountains of Antioch three miles away, where they thought they could safely plunder and remain. But the Turks, having learned of their departure through informers who continually lived among the peoples under a false pretense of brotherhood, secretly left the city and its aforesaid gate by familiar mountain paths—about sixty armed horsemen—and pursued the Christians to the place toward which they were making their way in hope of obtaining food. Shouting fiercely, they attacked them, piercing them with arrows through head, side, and entrails; like wolves they tore apart the whole company and scattered them in flight.

The archdeacon himself, attempting in vain to flee toward the mountains, was pursued by a Turk on a very swift horse. He was struck through by a rapid arrow; then the Turk drew his sword and, with a terrible wound across both sides of his neck, cut through his shoulders. Thus, while a stream of blood flowed to the ground, he gave up the breath of life. When the leading men of the army learned this most cruel news, their spirits were troubled with grief. They were indignant that so many massacres were being carried out daily by the Turks through the unbesieged gate; and now they grieved still more over the death of so distinguished an archdeacon, while frequent wailings were heard at the loss of each man’s friends.

## CHAPTER LIV.—On the death of the son of the king of the Danes, of a certain noblewoman Florine, and of those killed in the baths.

Amid these many still recent misfortunes, a grievous report struck the ears of the whole holy host: after Nicaea had been defeated and captured, the son of the king of the Danes, named Sveno, a most noble and very handsome man, had been delayed for several days. He had been kindly received and commended by the emperor of Constantinople, and, having heard of the Christians’ victory, was travelling safely through the heart of Romania. He was bringing with him fifteen hundred fighting men to assist in the siege of Antioch.

But Solyman, who, defeated in the mountains, had escaped the Franks, lay encamped in the dense forest of hamlets and reeds between Finiminis and Ferna, cities of Romania. There Sveno was slain in a hail of arrows, and all his company was destroyed in the same martyrdom by wicked executioners. Nor is it surprising that they all perished, overwhelmed by the forces of the Turks. For they had been exposed by the treachery of certain wicked Christians—that is, Greeks—and were unexpectedly surrounded by Solyman’s force assembled from the mountains.

Nevertheless, the king’s son Sveno, resisting with much defense of arms, laid many Turks low with the sword; and his men did the same. But at last, exhausted and stripped of their weapons, unable to withstand the unspeakable multitude of their enemies, they perished together, transfixed by arrows.

There too was a certain noblewoman named Florine, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, joined in marriage to the prince of the Philippians, but now miserably widowed. She was in the same Danish company, hoping, after the triumph of the faithful, to be united with so great and distinguished a husband. But Turkish ferocity cut short this hope. As she fled toward the mountains seated on a mule, six arrows pierced her. Though struck, she did not fall from her mule, continually believing that she would escape death; but at last, overcome in the flight, she was put to death together with the king’s son by capital sentence.

Then Solyman’s Turkish soldiers, rejoicing in their victorious outcome and in the most terrible slaughter of Christians, swiftly rushed to the lake of hot springs which smoked there near Finiminis. Finding beggarly and fever-stricken pilgrims in them, treating their weakened bodies, they transfixed them with arrows and made all the water bloody. Others, hiding their heads beneath the water to escape the blows, they compelled to perish by the cruel end of drowning.

## CHAPTER LV.—A gate deadly to the Christians; Count Raymond somewhat restrains the profane from attacking the faithful.

Troubled by these very frequent Turkish ambushes and continual sorties from the aforesaid gate, and by the most miserable disasters suffered by their own men, the leaders of the army were inflamed with greater anger. Since the said gate could not be besieged because of the difficulty of the mountains and unevenness of the rocks, they decided to obstruct it in this way: they would place a fortification on the back of a projecting rock at the foot of the mountains—a very firm barrier of valley and piled stones. For there was a shortage of timber there.

Accordingly, each of the leading men kept guard there in his allotted turn. From the lookout on the rock and fortification, they watched the Turks’ departures from the gate by the familiar mountain and valley paths; and, pursuing at once those who descended into the plain of the country, they prevented them from slaughtering Christians.

When the aforesaid fortification had at last been built, Count Raymond was keeping watch there in the order of his turn. One day, after stationing an ambush of his soldiers in hiding, nearly two hundred armed and mailed Turkish horsemen rose at the first dawn, left by their usual gate, descended the mountain slopes, and rushed in a sudden attack upon the fortification. They assaulted its guards and attempted to demolish the pile of walls, because it hindered their sorties and ambushes.

While they laboured in vain against the new fortification, Count Raymond’s ambush rose up. Hastening on the swiftest horses to help their companions in the garrison, they pressed hard in pursuit upon the Turks, who now feared their last day and were preparing to retreat uphill to the gate. They retained only one youth born of noble parentage; the rest escaped in flight.

Having captured the youth and put the others to flight, Count Raymond’s soldiers returned to the camp and army in joy and victory. The Turks likewise returned sorrowfully to their own people, and for several days remained quiet, no longer daring from that day onward to pursue Christians wandering about.

## CHAPTER LVI.—For the ransom of a captive youth, his parents, wishing to surrender their tower to the Christians, are expelled; and the youth is killed by the Christians.

On the following day, the Christian leaders learned that this captive was born of noble Turks. Wishing to bring great grief upon the hearts of his people, they presented the youth to his blood-relations in a fortress of towers established by King Darsian for defense, in the hope that, moved by pity to ransom him, they might surrender the fortress over which they presided and secretly admit Christians.

They absolutely refused to surrender the fortress, but offered an immense sum for his ransom and life. The Christians rejected everything except the city and the fortress. Yet because they knew him to be of high lineage, the hearts of his kinsmen began to soften, and private discussions were held between them and the Christians. At length the matter was disclosed to Sensadonia, son of King Darsian: an agreement was being made between the captive youth’s relatives and the Christians for his ransom, by which the city might soon be lost unless precautions were taken.

Therefore King Darsian and his son Sensadonia, perceiving this, took counsel with their leading men and ordered all the captive youth’s relatives, his brothers, and all their dependents expelled from the tower over which they presided, lest through that same tower the city should be handed over to the Christians in return for the ransom of their kinsman.

After they had been expelled and their plans exposed, the Christians had no further hope that the tower would be surrendered, since they had conducted everything too openly. After long torment and various tortures inflicted upon him, they dragged the wretched youth, tortured for almost a month and scarcely still breathing from his sufferings, before all the Turks beneath the walls of the city; they cut off his head and killed him. He was killed especially upon the accusation of Greek Christians, who declared that he had personally put to death more than a thousand Christians.

## CHAPTER LVII.—A decree of the people of God, and the punishment of two persons caught in adultery.

After these events, when the persecution of the Christians had been somewhat checked by the new fortification and by this decapitation, the Christian leaders reflected upon the adversities of their people and of Bohemond’s weakened company. Recalling the pestilence of famine and the devastation of mortality among the people, they asserted that these things were happening because of the multitude of sins.

For this reason, having taken counsel with the bishops and all the clergy present, they decreed that every injustice and impurity should be cut away from the army:

> “No one shall deceive a fellow Christian in weight or measure, in the desire for gold or silver, or in any exchange or business transaction. No one shall dare theft. No one shall be defiled by fornication or adultery. But if anyone transgresses this command, once caught he shall suffer a most severe punishment; and thus the people of God shall be sanctified from iniquity and uncleanness.”

Many who violated this decree were severely punished by the appointed judges. Some were put in chains, some beaten with rods, and others shaved and branded, for the correction and improvement of the whole host.

A man and woman caught there in adultery were stripped before the whole army. Their hands were bound behind their backs, and they were severely scourged with rods by the punishers. They were compelled to go around the whole army, so that, seeing their most savage wounds, the rest might be deterred from such a wicked and abominable crime.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—Duke Godfrey, now restored to health, and Count Raymond are sent separately through the regions to gather supplies of plunder.

Once this justice had been established among the people of God by the judgment of their elders, in order that the Lord’s anger might be appeased, Duke Godfrey had already recovered from the weakness caused by his wound. The army sent him into the land of the Saracens and Turks to recover the booty and spoils which the weakened and fugitive Bohemond had left behind, so that he might bring joy to the hungry and afflicted people out of their misfortune. This was done with God’s favor; but he gathered no great abundance of booty.

For from the time when Bohemond entered their land and carried away plunder, the Saracens and pagans had taken precautions: they hid their herds, all their goods, and their money in the mountains and inaccessible places. Count Raymond and the other leaders were sent out in the same way by decree of the army. But they gathered little booty, because the Saracens were dispersing through the mountains and distant country with their possessions, herds, and flocks.

## CHAPTER LIX.—An embassy of the king of Babylon to the people of God; how Winemar boldly captured Laodicea and foolishly lost it.

After some passage of this long siege, while the people suffered the most grievous pains from the labours of watchfulness, famine, pestilence, and the frequent attacks of the Turks, Ammirabilis, king of Babylon—because serious discord and hatred had long existed between himself and the Turks before this Christian expedition—sent fifteen envoys to the army of the living God. Through a certain abbot, having learned of the Christians’ embassy and purpose, he sent men skilled in languages of various kinds, bearing this message concerning a reciprocal alliance of peace and kingdom:

> “King Ammirabilis of Babylon rejoices at your arrival and that you have so far acted successfully; he sends greetings to the great and humble leaders of the Christians. The Turks, a foreign people hostile to me and to my kingdom, have often invaded our lands, holding the city of Jerusalem, which belongs to our jurisdiction. But now, before your arrival, we have recovered it by our own strength and expelled the Turks. We enter into an alliance and friendship with you. We shall restore to the Christian people the Holy City, the Tower of David, and Mount Sion. We shall discuss the profession of the Christian faith; when it has been examined, if it pleases us, we are prepared to embrace it. But if we remain in the law and rite of paganism, the alliance which we have made with one another shall nevertheless not be broken. We ask and urge you not to withdraw from this city of Antioch until it has been restored into your hands, it having been unjustly taken from the Greek emperor and the Christians.”

Winemar, who had withdrawn from Baldwin and Tancred at Mamistra to the coast, hastened again by ship to Laodicea with all the armament of the naval force. Having surrounded it with a naval blockade and captured it by the valour of his men, he gave or shared none of all that he had acquired with his fellow Christians sitting before Antioch.

While he held captured Laodicea securely, and his fellow-soldiers and confederates were at leisure and enjoying the goods of the land and city, they were deliberately slaughtered and overcome by the Turcopoles and soldiers of the Greek king. The citadel of the city was recovered; Winemar himself was captured and placed in prison, while Duke Godfrey and the other leaders still knew nothing of these events at Antioch.

## CHAPTER LX.—The plan of the besieged Antiochenes is disclosed to the Catholics; the bishop of Le Puy and Duke Godfrey encourage the people of God with consoling words.

Meanwhile the Turks besieged within Antioch did not delay to seek help and alert their friends. From the mountains and neighboring regions they gathered large and abundant Turkish forces, which soon amounted to thirty thousand men assembled together.

The besieged had planned and resolved that, at the first dawn, the outside force should attack the holy people of God; then the men inside the city should rush out to strengthen and increase the assault. They would wear down the Christians with weapons and a hail of arrows, until, slaughtered, they were consumed beneath the sword’s edge.

Information about these utterly wicked plans and criminal conspiracy reached the camp of the Catholic men—Duke Godfrey, the bishop of Le Puy, and the other leaders. Because of scarcity of provisions, prolonged exhaustion, and various disasters, they had no more than a thousand serviceable horses.

Then the bishop gave this counsel:

> “Most Christian men, chosen flower of Gaul, I do not know what course in counsel would now be more useful, except that, placing hope in the name of the Lord Jesus, you should meet them unexpectedly. Although the pagans, assembled everywhere in such thousands as you have heard, are approaching unburdened by any labours, not having left their own land and been exhausted by a long journey, and have already advanced as far as the city of Barich, nevertheless it is not difficult for God to enclose so many thousands in His hand and to destroy them by your few forces.”

To these words of the bishop Duke Godfrey, ever unwearied in the duty of war, replied before the assembled host:

> “We are worshippers of the living God and Lord Jesus Christ, in whose name we serve as soldiers. They are gathered in their own strength; but we are gathered in the name of the living God. Trusting in His grace, let us not hesitate to attack the impious and unbelieving; for whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. Yet just as we love salvation and life, so it is fitting that this word should not become public, lest the enemies, made alert and cautious about our arrival and attack, become too frightened and decline to fight with us.”

## CHAPTER LXI.—Chosen knights attack the enemy camp and are not frightened by the arrival of a great multitude.

At the duke’s urging and exhortation, seven hundred fighting horsemen were chosen. The matter, however, was entirely concealed except from a few leaders of the army; for most men lacked horses because of the various disasters already described, and very few sound horses remained. Thus some rode pack animals, some mules, and some asses, as necessity allowed.

In the silence of the deep night they began their march, crossing the bridge of ships without the knowledge of the Turks who were stationed in Antioch for its defense. Bohemond, Tancred, Robert of Flanders, Robert of Normandy, and Duke Godfrey gathered together at the appointed place. Rotger of Barnaville was summoned and was also present. Constantly involved in ambushes against the Turks and often inflicting slaughter, he had gained such renown among them that he frequently served as intermediary between the Christians and themselves concerning every agreement about prisoners and any other matter. The bishop likewise followed, their companion in every holy exhortation, to strengthen the men of God.

When they had already travelled through the night and were hastening toward the Turkish camp, Bohemond sent ahead with Walter of Drommedart a certain man of Turkish descent. Having recognized the truth, which is Christ, he had received the grace of baptism; recently raised from the sacred font by Prince Bohemond, he had been given Bohemond’s name. They advanced most cautiously until, at the first light of dawn, they observed from the woods and thickets an innumerable people hastening from every side to the help of the Antiochenes.

Having seen the enemy from afar, they prepared to return. With loosened reins they rode back to their seven hundred companions, disclosing matters as they were, but removing all terror by sound encouragement.

## CHAPTER LXII.—Strengthened by the bishop’s speech, the pilgrims openly triumph over the enemy with seven hundred men and dishonour them by cutting off their heads.

The distinguished bishop, having heard Walter’s and Bohemond’s report, warned the companions, who were somewhat wavering with fear and anxiety, not to hesitate to die for the love of Him whose footsteps they had followed under the sign of the holy cross, and for whose sake they had left homeland, kindred, and everything. They were certain that whoever should die there that day with the Lord God Zebaoth would possess heaven.

Strengthened by this blessed exhortation, they unanimously resolved that they would rather die than shamefully turn their backs upon their enemies. Then Count Raymond, joyfully brandishing his lance and covering his breast with his shield, and Duke Godfrey, no less aflame with the desire to engage in battle, together with the other seven hundred warriors, suddenly rushed through the midst of them. Breaking and scattering their large multitude, they received the palm of victory through God’s gift, while the Turks were crushed and put to flight.

Moreover, by God’s aid and mercy, the strings of the Turkish bows had been softened and weakened by rain and were of no use; this greatly impeded them and increased the faithful’s triumph. Made victorious, the Christians saw that they had prevailed and that few of their own men had fallen. Dismounting, they cut off the heads of the slain, tied them to their saddles, and carried them joyfully, together with a thousand good horses and much booty taken from their defeated enemies, to certain companions awaiting the outcome at the camp before Antioch.

The envoys of the king of Babylon were present in that battle. They too carried Turkish heads, cut off and fastened to saddles, to the army. This victory of the Christians by a small force occurred on the day preceding the beginning of the fast.

As the faithful returned in great glory to their people, leaving the Turkish tents in the meadows of Antioch, the Turks under siege, who awaited help from the shattered multitude, stood on their walls and watched the victorious standards of the faithful from afar. Thinking them to be those of their expected people, they suddenly rushed to arms amid a crash of shouting and the blare of horns. Pouring boldly from the gates, they believed they would in a moment destroy the whole holy host from within and without.

But as the Christians came near, and the Turks saw the heads of their countrymen and recognized their spoils and horses, they ceased their shouting and trumpet-blasts. They stopped rejoicing and fled swiftly back into their fortifications. To increase the Turks’ grief, the Christians threw Turkish heads over the battlements and walls; nearly two hundred others they carried on spears and stakes and displayed before all those standing upon the walls.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—While Bohemond and his companions try to make the bridge impassable to the enemy, some are killed and others wounded; the news is sorrowfully brought to Duke Godfrey.

At dawn the following day, the leaders of the faithful, happy over their recent victory, considered how they might place the protection of a certain engine beside the aforementioned city bridge, which stretched across the river Farfar. By setting up the engine, they would cut off entrance to and exit from the city for those passing through, bringing in food, or plotting ambushes against the Christians by means of that bridge.

When the plan had at last been adopted, they sent Bohemond, prince of Sicily; Everard of Poisat; Count Raymond of Provence; and Werner of Greis to the seaport called that of Simeon the Hermit, to buy food with many foot-soldiers. They were also to summon assistance from companions who remained on that seashore because of the ships bringing provisions.

They also sent back in the same company the envoys of the king of Babylon, honouring them with magnificent gifts and returning them safely by ship in good faith.

When informers learned and revealed the plan and departure of such distinguished men, the Turks rejoiced greatly. Taking four thousand chosen soldiers, they left the city by the said bridge and pursued the aforementioned leaders by paths known to themselves. Unknown to the great army, they laid ambushes among brambles and thickets in the mountains, until the leaders who had been sent to the seaport should return.

As the companions returned, both mounted and on foot, four thousand had already gathered at Bohemond’s and the other leaders’ summons. The Turks rushed suddenly from their ambushes against the unsuspecting men laden with food, piercing some through breast and entrails with arrows and slaughtering others with the sword. Since victory was in their hands, they did not cease from slaughtering the faithful until they had killed five hundred through forests and fields, cutting off their heads. The wounded and captives were beyond number.

Bohemond, who guarded the rear with the other distinguished men, learned of this most cruel slaughter. Seeing his men half-dead, hiding among mountain precipices and dark places, and fleeing here and there, he realized that he could not help the fugitives and defeated, but that death was readily at hand for himself. Drawing back his reins, he withdrew with his mounted companions and, abandoning the road, made his way with a few men back toward the coast.

Without delay, a certain man who had barely escaped the weapons by the speed of his horse down the slopes of the hills brought grievous news to Duke Godfrey. The duke, having come from the army across the bridge of ships, stood in the middle of the fields and, on the bishop’s advice, had compelled the Turks and their herds to return to the city. The messenger declared that Bohemond and the other leading men were hemmed in by enemy ambushes and at the point of death, and described the cruelty with which the people returning from the gate had been cut to pieces.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—As the faithful rise to avenge their people, a doubtful battle is fought for a long time by both sides.

Hearing this, the duke sent messengers through all the tents to announce the cruel report and direct the men to be prepared for every danger now confronting them. All the faithful, troubled and terrified, immediately streamed forth from the tents. They put scaled iron garments upon their shoulders, fastened banners to their lances, quickly equipped their horses with bridles and saddles, arranged their battle lines, and prepared to seek by the swift route the approach to the bridge and city, where they expected the enemy to return to the city’s protection.

As they crossed the bridge of ships without delay and found Duke Godfrey in the middle of the fields, his countenance changed with grief over the death of his companions, another messenger arrived. He warned the duke and the other leaders standing with him in the field that they should return to the tents because of Turkish ambushes and attacks. This messenger came from the forces of Bohemond, Raymond, Werner, and the others fleeing through the mountains; they judged the Turkish force and multitude more intolerable than it had been before.

But the duke, undaunted and thirsting to avenge the faithful who had been cut down, utterly rejected withdrawing from the place or abandoning it through any fear. He swore that either that day he would climb the mountain on which the enemy stronghold stood, or he would lose his life there with his men.

While the duke gave this answer and declaration and everyone made ready, Bohemond, Raymond, and Werner themselves arrived safely. At their arrival and survival everyone rejoiced and was strengthened. They advanced toward the aforesaid mountain before the city bridge, and sent ten knights chosen from the multitude ahead to the mountain summit, to see whether another Turkish ambush lay in the valley of the mountain near the highlands.

The ten mounted knights had scarcely taken their stand upon the mountain height when they saw the whole Turkish force: that is, those who had secretly returned through the mountains and familiar paths after the recent slaughter of Christians. They saw twenty horsemen riding forward against them, to drive the ten from the summit. When the ten Christians withdrew because the Turkish ambush was too near, and the twenty held the mountain summit, thirty Christian brethren came to their aid. Charging the twenty boldly, they drove them in flight from the mountain top down to the very Turkish ambush.

As the twenty hurried in flight to their companions, sixty Turkish horsemen—very brave men and highly skilled riders—burst out of the ambush. They quickly drove back the thirty Christian horsemen with bow and arrow and remained there. Seeing their audacity and charge, sixty Christian horsemen likewise went to meet the sixty Turks on the mountain. Meanwhile the whole Christian army approached and suddenly drove them from the mountain, forcing them in swift flight into the valley where the Turkish force and strength had assembled near the mountains.

At this the entire Turkish force rose from its ambush and began to press the sixty Frankish horsemen, who now occupied the mountain paths, with the most violent pursuit. They drove them back across the middle summit of the mountain as far as the valley itself, which the approaching Christian army had occupied.

## CHAPTER LXV.—Here the duke splits a mailed Turk in two with one blow; and after a bloody battle victory attends the faithful.

When the Turks saw that they had advanced too far and that the Christian army remained immovable, unable to be turned from its purpose by any fear and hastening to meet them, they took flight in vain. The Franks nevertheless pressed on in pursuit. Soon mingled together, because they had rushed into close combat, they made a bloody slaughter of the Turks in vengeance for their own men who had been cut down while returning from the port of Simeon.

During this Turkish flight and the Christians’ close pursuit, in which they killed without mercy, a great force of Turks and others had gathered from the walls on every side to the gate, awaiting the return of their people. But, not seeing their fortunes overturned and their plight most wretched, they opened the gate and marched armed into the open fields, intending to strengthen their own men and give them confidence to enter the city.

Mounted and foot soldiers of the faithful and unbelievers were now mingled on both sides. Duke Godfrey, whose hand was most skilled in war, is reported by men who witnessed it with their own eyes to have cut off many heads there, though protected by helmets. As he laboured intensely in the fighting and wrought great slaughter among the enemy, he split in two with a very sharp sword—a remarkable thing to tell—a Turk clothed in mail who was troubling him with a bow. One half of the body, from the breast upward, fell upon the sand; the other, still clasping the horse with its legs, was carried to the middle of the bridge before the city walls, where it fell and remained.

Rejoicing in this successful outcome, Robert of Flanders, Robert count of the Normans, Cano of Montacute, Count Raymond, and all the Frankish nobility present broke through the enemy with the charge of their horses. They pierced many with lance and sword and forced the dying to make for the bridge. There, because of the excessive pressure—which the bridge could not bear, since its breadth did not suffice for so many fugitives—very many fell from the bridge and were engulfed in the waters of the Ferna.

Bohemond, who had escaped by the rocky ridges passable only to wild goats and had returned safely by God’s grace with his companions, toiled fiercely in the same work of bloodshed. He exhorted and comforted his companions; and he slew with the sword enemies falling from the bridge after piercing them with his lance.

The foot-soldiers, delighted by this triumph, attacked with spears those who were falling and packed densely at the edge of the bridge and bank of the stream. They did not restrain their hands from slaughter until the whole river was changed by the blood of the slain.

When these things had thus been successfully accomplished, the Christians had reassembled and were still pursuing the Turks on the bridge and trying to enter the gate with them. But those inside immediately shut the gate, leaving their companions, miserably excluded, in the hands of the attackers. These battles and the Christians’ recent victory occurred on one holy day in March. The Turks killed in battle or drowned in the waters were counted at fifteen hundred.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—Some of those besieged in Antioch secretly defect to the Christians, and the stronghold built beside the bridge is entrusted to Raymond’s guard.

After the most fierce Turkish squadrons had been defeated in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, forced by cruel slaughter and flight into the city gate, and after the Christians had returned to their tents with the great glory of victory, the courage of the pagans began from that day onward to melt away. Their formerly frequent assaults altogether ceased, their ambushes fell quiet, and their strength languished. Fear seized very many of them so deeply that some, separating themselves from the city and their own company, departed by night and, declaring that they wished to become Christians, entrusted themselves to the Christian leaders.

Having been received and joined to the Christian bands, they described the losses their people had suffered and the lamentations made throughout the entire city over their defeat. They further asserted that twelve of King Darsian’s most remarkable and powerful men had fallen in that battle that evening; grief and groaning for their death disturbed all Antioch.

On the fourth day thereafter, Duke Godfrey and all the leaders of the army of God came forth from the tents in great strength. They built the stronghold they had planned upon the summit of the aforesaid mountain before the bridge and city gate, using a mass of stones and mortar of weak clay. They enclosed it with a most secure rampart and appointed Count Raymond to guard it with five hundred men of military courage and skill.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER I.—When the prince of Antioch hears of the Christians’ victory, he asks his faithful men what must be done.

At last, after Duke Godfrey and the people of the faithful had triumphed over the adversaries of the Christian people and thrust them into the river’s whirlpool, and after the stronghold had been established without opposition, a Turkish messenger swiftly flew to the tower and palace of Darsian, ruler of Antioch, situated in the mountains. He reported how great the losses of their people had been, and that unless Darsian provided carefully and diligently, he would soon lose Antioch and his other neighboring territories.

King Darsian, an old man, heard that the stronghold had been established and that his men’s destruction was irreparable. Until then he had been secure in every conflict and changing outcome, as though sleeping upon his throne; now, for the first time, he was distressed with sighing. He summoned his son Sansadonia and all the leading men subject to him to his council.

## CHAPTER II.—The instructions given by Darsian’s messengers, and whom he summons for assistance.

Solyman was present before the same scepter-bearing ruler. He had been expelled from the city of Nicaea and from the territories of Romania. Darsian earnestly requested him to serve as messenger for his embassy, knowing him to be an eloquent man, renowned throughout all pagan kingdoms. He said to him:

> “You, my kinsman, will depart with my twelve envoys and with my son Sansadonia for Corrozan, the land and kingdom of our birth. Compatrix and Odorsonius, two of my most faithful leaders, will be with you in this embassy to make complaint of the wrongs done to us. As you travel, urge Brodeas of the city of Aleppo, our brother and friend, to come to our aid. Likewise call upon Pulait, whose soldiers and arms are abundant, to give us assistance, since he has always been joined to us by alliance. Set forth our adversities and calamities to Soldan, the scepter-bearing ruler of Corrozan, who is head and prince of the Turks; and urge Corbahan, servant of that ruler, to furnish me with familiar aid and forces. Let my scribe and notary therefore be summoned, so that you may carry my seal and letters with you, and men may more confidently believe our need. For many days have passed since my son Buldagis went before you to Corrozan at the beginning of this city’s siege, in order to make known to our brethren and leaders the arrival of the Christian people and urge them all to assist us against it.”

## CHAPTER III.—The presentation of the case before the king of Corrozan.

Having heard the king’s will and command, and having received his letters with their seal, they departed from the city and the king’s palace and set out for the land of Corrozan. They came [Col. 0480A], indeed, with great retinue and expenditure and in great splendour to the great city of Samnarcha, which belonged to the kingdom of Corrozan. There they found the great prince and sceptre-bearing Sultan, supreme over all the kings and princes of the eastern region, together with Prince Corbahan, second only to the king, in great magnificence. Solyman, because he was older and most renowned for ability and eloquence, greeted him. Having greeted the king, before opening the embassy, according to the Turkish custom of those complaining of misfortune and injuries, they threw their caps from their heads onto the ground in the presence of that great and most powerful king and his attendants, tore their beards with savage nails, and drew sighs amid great lamentations. Seeing these Turkish gestures of tearing themselves, King Corrozan replied [Col. 0480B] with great pride:

> “Solyman, our friend and brother, explain what has happened to you and reveal the injuries done to you. Whoever he may be who has presumed to trouble you shall by no means be able to live before our face.”

Rejoicing and trusting in the answer and power of so mighty a king, Solyman recounted in order the bitterness which he grievously held in his heart and the whole matter; what he could not recount orally, he set forth by the testimony of letters:

> “Nicaea,” he said, “which you know to be very famous, and the land which they call Romania, of the kingdom of the Greeks—land which, by your aid and strength, through your gift and favour bestowed upon us, we acquired—a people suddenly arriving, called Christians, from the kingdom of Francia, [Col. 0480C] have taken from us by a strong hand and mighty army. They captured it and delivered it, together with my wife and my two sons, to the emperor of Constantinople. Having crushed and put me to flight by their strength, they pursued me to the city of Antioch, where I hoped to remain. There they have besieged by armed force not only me and mine, but also King Darsian, a most noble man of our race, subject and friend to you, who holds city and lands by your gift. That same prince Darsian, your subject, our elder and kinsman, has therefore sent us to you, that you may deign to help him with the great force at your command; for necessity demands it exceedingly, beyond what we can believe. Our people and army are shattered; our land and country laid waste; our life and [Col. 0480D] all that is ours are now in your hand.” We have no hope other than in you.”

### CHAPTER IV.—How the king received the messengers’ words.

King Corrozan received these words and complaints with laughter and derision, giving them little heed. Before his assembled followers, he declared that he did not believe such calamities could be inflicted upon the Turks by any region of the world, holding in slight account Solyman’s strength, hitherto so renowned, and the boldness of his soldiery.

[Col. 0481A] Solyman, as one who had recently experienced the Christians’ power, did not take the king’s judgment lightly. Since he had been unable to explain everything orally, he opened Darsian’s sealed letters. In them were inscribed the names of the kingdoms and of all the Christian princes defeating the Turks, together with the size of their armies and their forces. But when the king and all the chief men of the pagans who were with him had recognized the letters and learned the circumstances and strength of the Franks, they were dismayed in spirit; lowering their faces to the ground, they no longer vainly marvelled at Solyman’s complaints.

Thereupon, without delay, he sent embassies throughout every land of his kingdom and ordered all his leading men and admirals to assemble on one day, fixed as then seemed most suitable. [Col. 0481B] When the day arrived, they assembled unanimously by the king’s decree and command. The king disclosed to them Solyman’s words and complaints and the wrongs inflicted by the Christians, saying:

> “All of you who have gathered, consider this as it ought to be considered: unless they are restrained, the Christians who have come upon us will do to us what they have done to our other cities and to our friends and brethren.”

### CHAPTER V.—Corbahan’s insult against the people of God before those summoned by the king.

Corbahan, the king’s intimate, first at court and second after the king in the kingdom of Corrozan—a headstrong man full of arrogant ferocity—made light of the Christians’ prowess and burst out in these proud words:

[Col. 0481C]

> “I marvel at the words and complaint of Solyman and of Sansadonia and Buldagis, sons of King Darsian, concerning the Christians’ attack, by whose siege Solyman lost his lands and cities—places which could scarcely have been defended more easily if they had been besieged by so many wretched brute animals. Long ago I laid low a hundred thousand Christians, cutting off their heads, near Civitot, where the mountains end, when summoned to Solyman’s aid against the emperor of the Greeks; I scattered his army and drove him from the siege of Nicaea. After this, my soldiers, sent to Solyman’s aid, crushed the innumerable bands of Peter the Hermit, and the fields of that region will never be cleared of their corpses and bones.”

### CHAPTER VI.—The prince driven from Nicaea describes the strength of the Christian army.

[Col. 0481D]

Solyman, a man of remarkable and great ability, heard his pride and boastful words and answered him calmly:

> “O Corbahan, our brother and friend, why do you so despise us, calling us faint-hearted, and assert that you overcame us by your aid and crushed the emperor of Constantinople and Peter the Hermit’s unheard-of multitudes? The emperor’s army—the soft and effeminate Greek people, rarely tried by the exercises of war—could easily be overcome by the strength of hardy men, and, once overcome, be beheaded. Likewise, I found Peter the Hermit’s bands to be a small and beggarly force, an idle crowd of women, all foot-soldiers wearied by a long journey, with truly no more than five hundred horsemen. [Col. 0482A] It was not very difficult for us to destroy them by a light attack and slaughter.

> “But these men, whose names, prowess, wars, and skill you have learned from the letters, and against whom it is difficult to undertake war—know that they are very brave men, trained in a remarkable multitude of horses, not to be terrified in battle by death or any kind of weapon. Their garments are of iron; their shields are inlaid with gold and gems and painted in varied colours. Their helmets, shining upon their heads with a brightness surpassing the sun’s brilliance, flash. Their ash spears, tipped in their hands with sharpest iron, are like great poles. Their horses are exceedingly well trained for speed and war. Their banners, on their spears, with golden knots and silver fringes, make the surrounding mountains gleam with an immense splendour of light.

[Col. 0482B]

> “Know that their boldness is so great that none of their horsemen, once he has advanced to battle, hesitates to confront twenty thousand of our men, flashing like lions and boars with the deadly blows of weapons. I myself thought their strength insignificant and did not believe that they could stand against me when I had assembled my forces. I hoped to crush their strength as I had shortly before destroyed Peter the Hermit’s army. I also hoped, by the strength of my men, to drive them from Nicaea and to free my wife, sons, soldiers, and princes who were inside its walls. I joined battle with them again; but, my labour spent in vain, I barely escaped their hands through the mountain ridges, leaving behind many of my own slain.

> “[Col. 0482C]

> “They, after wearing down my men and not bearing their own losses equally, returned to Nicaea and renewed the siege more firmly and securely than before, until, holding my defeated people together with my wife and sons in surrender, they handed the city over with its keys to the emperor of Constantinople. Moreover, having conquered and subdued the towns and castles of Romania that were under my rule, they restored them to that emperor and seized very many of our fortresses. Of all the lands, cities, and strongholds which I held, nothing remains to me except the fortress of Foloraca, near the sea and the borders of the kingdom of Russia.

> “Furthermore, these Christian soldiers, whom you believe weak, hold Tursolt, Azaram, and Mamistra, cities of Romania, together with many captured strongholds. [Col. 0482D] They have forced under their power by sword and force the Armenian cities and castles of Dandronuch, Harimnu, and Turbaysel, the mountains of Constantine, prince of Armenia, and of Pancratius, and the land of Duke Corrovassilius. They hold the city of Rohas, most strongly fortified by walls and masonry and especially renowned for its fertility. One prince, Baldewin, head and leader of this Christian people, married the daughter of the prince of that land; and, after the duke’s death, having been raised by the citizens in his place, he made the whole land and country tributary to himself. Thus these Christians have seized all places and kingdoms as far as Malatina.

> “Now, after subduing these places on their right and left, they are besieging Antioch. These peoples are of marvellous endurance and training; they care for no bodily delay or rest, but day by day seek out enemies and opponents; once they find and conquer them, they consign them to destruction.”

### CHAPTER VII.—Corbahan, in great pride, threatens that he will soon test Christian strength.

[Col. 0483A]

Proud Corbahan, after hearing Solyman’s account, opened his mouth still further in boasting and vaunting, saying:

> “If I remain safe and alive, six months shall not pass before I test these Christians, whether they are as strong as you assert. By my god I swear that I shall destroy them in such a manner that all their descendants will lament it.”

### CHAPTER VIII.—King Corrozan consults magicians about the outcome of the war, and the Turkish princes are summoned by name.

[Col. 0483B]

As Corbahan and Solyman disputed with one another, King Corrozan summoned the magicians, diviners, and sacrificers of his gods and inquired about the coming victory. They promised that everything would prosper, that the Christians would triumph, and that the Christians would overcome the king in an easy war.
