Upon hearing this reply of their divinities—a reply in which the king fixed his heart and counsel—Corbahan sent repeated embassies throughout the whole kingdom of Corrozan. By the king’s magnificent command he invited all the chief and noblest men to prepare an expedition with arms, arrows, and wagons of provisions. He ordered craftsmen living throughout every land to make chains and fetters in which the bound and captured pilgrims might be led away to barbarian lands.

Pulait, one of the mightiest Turks, who lived beside the river Euphrates, and Brodoam of the illustrious city of Alapia, himself rich in retainers, were invited by a unanimous embassy of King Corrozan to avenge the Turks and the injuries which Christians had inflicted upon Solyman and King Darsian of Antioch, friends and kinsmen of the Turks. The embassy explained the situation and announced the pressing need. [Col. 0483C] The same report and embassy also reached and warned the prince of the Damascenes, who had himself subdued a great part of Syria and was powerful through the fertility of his soil and the strength of his cavalry. The king’s embassy likewise urged Amasa of the region of Niz, situated beside Corrozan, whose fame for military skill and boldness was exceedingly widespread, because he was always regarded as standard-bearer in the front line in every danger.

[Col. 0483D] This Amasa’s spear and arrow were beyond comparison with the arrows of all the Turks; with the bow he surpassed all in shooting. For every expedition he was equipped with no fewer than a hundred exceedingly swift horses, so that, if one were struck by an arrow or perished through some adverse mishap, others might suffice for the continuous demands of war; thus he was always borne forward, swift and troublesome to his enemies. Boesas, of the same Turkish sect and not unlike him in equipment and arms, was invited. Another Amasa, from the very extensive and rich land of Curzh, abundant in archers, was likewise summoned by royal command. Badas of the stronghold of Amacha and the city of Sororgia, Balduc of Samusart—crafty Turks, but soldiers renowned in arms and war—and Karageth of Karan, a city very strongly fortified by ramparts and walls, were commanded to be present on the same day for the expedition.

[Col. 0484A] These, whether they held authority in Corrozan’s kingdom by royal summons or were dispersed in other kingdoms, were called to this expedition from the beginning of the siege of Antioch and from the day when King Darsian’s second embassy was made through Solyman. In Corrozan they attended to necessary matters, armed soldiers, and burned without interruption with zeal for every preparation for war.

### CHAPTER IX.—Baldewin’s generosity toward the princes, and the tent sent to the duke.

The Christian army and all the princes engaged in the siege and hardship around Antioch were wholly unaware of this expedition. Yet day by day they were pressed not only by a shortage of food but also by a lack of horses and weapons; above all other anxieties, severe want made everyone troubled. [Col. 0484B] While this want grew more and more over a long period, and many despaired because necessary provisions had diminished, Baldewin—who, having been raised as duke of Edessa, or Rohas, had subdued that city—sent great talents of gold and silver through Gerard, one very close to him, to his brother Duke Godefrid, Robert of Flanders, Robert count of the Normans, Reymund, and the other most powerful men, in order to repair the deficiency which he learned that such great and noble princes were enduring. He also sent his brother and the other princes swift and handsome horses, with honourable trappings of saddles and bridles, [Col. 0484C] as well as arms of marvellous honour and beauty.

Then, after a few days, Nicusus, an Armenian prince from the region of Turbaysel, sent Duke Godefrid a tent of marvellous workmanship and beauty, in order to win his favour and friendship. But through an ambush set by Pancratius, the tent was taken from Nicusus’s servants and sent to Boemund as though from his gift. When Duke Godefrid and Robert of Flanders, who were most devoted friends and allied companions, learned from Nicusus’s words that it had been brought for them, they peacefully urged Boemund to restore what he had unjustly received. He wholly resisted their warning and request. The aforesaid princes, therefore angered, again demanded the tent which had been taken, by advice of the greater men. But he declared that he would by no means return it, and by his harsh answer stirred the minds of the aforesaid princes against himself.

[Col. 0484D] Angered, they decided to attack Boemund in the camp with their assembled followers unless he quickly restored what he had unjustly received. At last, by the counsel of the chief men of the army, lest there be discord among the people, Boemund restored the tent to the duke; peace having been arranged, they again became friends with one another. Thereafter, as famine grew worse and provisions failed in the region around Antioch, Baldewin assigned to Duke Godefrid, his brother by the same mother, all the revenues of Turbaysel in grain, wine, barley, and oil, and fifty thousand Byzantines in gold each year.

### CHAPTER X.—The gathering of the nations hastening to the siege of the Christians, and the accusation against Baldewin.

[Col. 0485A]

The fixed day of King Corrozan’s expedition, long proclaimed and prepared, now drew near. And behold, all the nations of his kingdom and the aforementioned princes, scattered through Armenia, Syria, and Romania, gathered at the fortress of Sooch, armed and with abundant equipment. They had two hundred thousand fighting horsemen, apart from the common people and women, beasts of burden and camels, and other animals, which could not be counted by any number.

Corbahan also came, prince and head of the army, surpassing all in wagons of provisions, in troops and soldiers’ arms, in tents, and in lavish equipment. All the assembled princes and peoples honoured him as their lord and listened to him in all things as master and commander. Having gathered his army into one body, he advanced slowly for many days because of the loads of wagons and the burdens of beasts and camels, until he entered the land and city of Rohas, where he stayed and spent several nights.

[Col. 0485B] While he was descending through this country and shortening the journey over several days because of the great pressure of people and beasts, many persons came running from different places and reported much concerning the army and siege of Antioch. Among these reports and others, Baldewin was accused before him because, having crushed and destroyed the Turks, he had subjected not only the city of Rohas but also every surrounding stronghold to his rule.

### CHAPTER XI.—As the pagans prepare to besiege Rohas, Baldewin meets them, fights, and triumphs.

[Col. 0485C]

On hearing this, Corbahan and the leaders of his army consulted together about besieging and capturing Rohas, taking Baldewin and his fellow Christians captive and punishing them, and restoring the city and territory to Turkish control. But Baldewin, whom neither threats nor any terrors could move, learned of Corbahan’s arrival and of his plan against him and the city of Rohas. He summoned and armed all his men and, mounted upon swift horses, met Corbahan’s soldiers who had been sent ahead to besiege Rohas. Attacking them strongly and fighting them with Armenian bow and Frankish lance, [Col. 0485D] he drove them in flight as far as Corbahan’s camp, bringing their spoils—namely camels and beasts of burden with necessary supplies—into the city of Rohas.

Corbahan greatly marvelled that Baldewin had dared this against him while he was present, much less when he was absent. Angered at his audacity, he swore by his god that he would never abandon the siege of Rohas, but would exhort his army and break into it immediately, taking Baldewin captive.

### CHAPTER XII.—For three days Corbahan besieges Rohas in vain; Baldewin pursues him in war as he withdraws.

Corbahan, a dreadful prince and man, had scarcely exhorted his companions when, behold, they all rose and besieged the city of Rohas with the shriek and tumult of trumpets and horns. [Col. 0486A] For three days they brought very great force and assaults against the city walls and gates. But, seeing themselves stoutly resisted by the city’s defenders and guards, and unable to make progress in a moment or short space, because the city was impregnable by its walls and towers, they advised Corbahan to move camp away from the siege for the time being, hasten on the intended road to Antioch, and, after Antioch had been conquered, return to renew the siege of Rohas, until he slaughtered Baldewin and his followers like sheep in a fold.

Accepting this counsel, Corbahan continued his march toward Antioch. Because of the difficulties of the mountains, he divided the unheard-of thousands of his army into separate divisions. Since it would take a long time for so many thousands to cross the great river Euphrates by boat, [Col. 0486B] Baldewin and those with him in the city did not lose heart in distress at so great a multitude. When Corbahan withdrew from before the city, they mounted their horses and pursued the rearmost of his army, in case some division might lag behind and they could attack it. But since they achieved little because of the Turks’ forethought and vigilance, they returned to Rohas, praying the Lord of heaven to have mercy upon Duke Godefrid, Robert, Reymund, Boemund, and all Christians, and to defend and preserve them by His grace from the hand of enemies advancing in such great strength.

Before long, reports of Corbahan’s arrival and that of his soldiers began to spread through the Christian army by Syrian and Armenian informers. [Col. 0486C] Some refused to believe; others, believing, urged the duke to make provision.

### CHAPTER XIII.—Some of the Christian army withdraw from the camp, and capable men go out to scout the approaching pagans.

Amid these varying opinions, Stephen of Blois, for some reason, repeatedly claimed that illness afflicted him severely and that he could no longer remain at the siege. Commending the brethren and departing from them on this pretext of illness, he set out toward the coast, for Lesser Alexandria. When he withdrew, four thousand fighting men of his following went with him.

Duke Godefrid, Boemund, Robert, and Reymund, commanders of the army, more and more alarmed by the report of the approaching pagans, unanimously decided to choose capable men from the army and send them ahead through the mountains and difficult places, from which they might scout more safely, to discover the truth of the matter. [Col. 0486D] Thus Drogo of Nahella, Clarebold of Vinduil, Ivo of the kingdom of the Franks, and Reinard of Toul—very distinguished men—were sent, so that if they heard anything reliable concerning the pagans’ arrival, or perceived it with their own eyes, they should report back to the army without delay. Forewarned, the princes would fear the missiles of their assailants less.

The soldiers and scouts sent out were dispersed: some toward Arthesia, some toward Rossa, and some toward the road of Romania, to discover the truth. They saw an army boiling forth from the mountains and by various roads on every side, like the sand of the sea; they marvelled at its countless thousands and could not count them.

[Col. 0487A]

### CHAPTER XIV.—Having learned of the nations’ equipment, the counsel taken by the princes.

When they had seen those many thousands, Corbahan’s incomparable armament, and the splendour of his resources, they returned to Antioch with all speed, seven days before Corbahan and his battle-lines reached the borders and plains of the Antiochene region. On their return, they secretly reported to the duke and the other princes, as they had learned and seen with their own eyes, Corbahan’s coming, all his equipment, and all the soldiery he had led out, lest the people—terrified because they were exhausted by a long siege and grievous scarcity—should despair, offer less resistance, and prepare to flee when darkness came.

[Col. 0487B] The next day, after the soldiers sent to scout Corbahan’s army had returned, Duke Godefrid, Robert, Reymund, Boemund, Eustachius, Tankrad, and all the chief men assembled together. They discussed what course they should follow and what sounder counsel they should adopt, lest they be suddenly overwhelmed and consumed by the swords and bows of the enemy’s rushing thousands. Duke Godefrid, Robert, and many others urged that they rise in mail, helmets, and shields, with standards raised and battle-lines ordered, meet Corbahan advancing with his thousands, place all their hope in the Lord Jesus, join battle with them, and there end their lives in martyrdom in God’s name. Others advised that part should remain at the siege, lest the Turks burst out from the city to assist Corbahan, while the stronger part, in accordance with the counsel of the duke and Robert of Flanders, should go to meet the enemy no farther than two miles away.

[Col. 0487C]

### CHAPTER XV.—The secret mystery of Boemund’s counsel concerning the betrayal of Antioch.

While each man was offering his opinion in these deliberations, Boemund, a man notably prudent and cunning, took Godefrid, Robert of Flanders, and Reymund apart from the assembly of their companions to a secret place. Speaking thus, he disclosed to them all that he had in his heart:

> “My lords and dearest brothers, I have a secret which I shall now reveal to your trust, and by it, if God grants and helps, all our army and princes can be freed and saved. Seven months have now passed since it was promised to me that the city of Antioch would be delivered into my hand. The agreement between myself and the betrayer has thus been secured by the obligation of his faith so that it cannot be dissolved or altered: at whatever hour I give notice, one of the towers leading into the city, in which that betrayer lives, shall be surrendered into my hand.

> “I have laboured greatly in this affair, seeing that the city could not be overcome by human power. I have agreed to give him much and immeasurable money; and I have promised, under firm pledge of faith, to raise and enrich him among my friends no less than Tankrad, my sister’s son. Boemund, my namesake, a man of Turkish race, has been the agent of this secret agreement and surrender from the beginning of his Christianity. The matter has now reached the point where he will by no means fail in anything that the betrayer promised, and where he will find me prepared to bestow upon him the great reward I promised.

[Col. 0488A]

> “Therefore, because I must give him no small talent, and bear the whole burden of this affair, I disclose one thing privately to you, who are the pillars and commanders of the army: namely, that, if it be your will and that of the others, when the city has been captured it shall be given into my hand. I shall carry this agreement and plan through to completion, and I am prepared without delay to give from my own resources what I promised the betrayer.”

Hearing this, the princes rejoiced greatly and, with complete goodwill, granted the city to Boemund; they likewise made all the other leaders willing to accept this same gift and concession.

[Col. 0488B]

### CHAPTER XVI.—How prudently this plan was debated among the chief men while the others remained ignorant.

Once all the commanders had consented, they pledged one another their hands under the strongest injunction of faith and ordered that this matter should not be made public, but should be hidden in silence and revealed to no one. Some also say that, amid a clash and assault in which men fought on both sides, a young son of this same Turk was captured and came into Boemund’s hands. For the sake of redeeming him, the boy’s father began to associate privately with Boemund. At last, preferring his son’s life to the safety of all the inhabitants, he undertook treachery against King Darsian, entered into an agreement of faith with Boemund for the restoration of his son, and thus admitted Christ’s faithful soldiers into the city.

* The city was granted to Boemund if it should be taken.

Accordingly, as evening was already covering the land, it was decided by his counsel that Godefrid and Robert of Flanders should take seven hundred distinguished soldiers from the army and, while the Turks were dispersed on the walls and were then occupied with domestic concerns, make their way in the shadow of night toward the mountains, as though they were going to ambush some of Corbahan’s army advancing toward the city.

[Col. 0488C] While these seven hundred were already moving in the darkness of night toward the mountains through trackless and scarcely passable places and narrow defiles, under the guidance of Boemund, recently become a Christian, Duke Godefrid firmly charged them all, saying:

> “Brethren and pilgrims devoted to God, we have decided to go to meet the Turks and other hostile men encamped near us, and to fight them, if perhaps some opportunity of victory may be granted us. We forbid, on pain of your lives, any tumult or noise among us.”

But his mind held something other than what he said to the people. For, hastening in the mountains with companions alone aware of the matter, toward that side where the city and Darsian’s citadel stood upon the highest summit, he crossed valleys and precipitous mountain slopes. Far from the city and in secret, he halted with Robert of Flanders in a valley and carefully arranged all that was to be done cautiously and diligently concerning the city’s betrayal.

[Col. 0488D]

### CHAPTER XVII.—How cautiously the interpreter of the faithful and the betrayer of the city came to an agreement.

[Col. 0489A]

When all had been arranged by prudent counsel, they sent ahead to the tower guarded by the betrayer a certain interpreter of languages, a Lombard by birth and one of Boemund’s household, so that on Boemund’s behalf he might remind him of the agreement for admitting the Christians, hear his answer, and report it to the princes. Reaching the walls, he addressed in Greek the betrayer, who on that appointed night was keeping watch at a window of the tower, awaiting the Franks. He asked whether he was alone, so that he could speak with him more safely concerning Boemund’s embassy.

When the betrayer recognized Boemund’s words and most certain signs—namely, by the ring which Boemund had received from him and was now [Col. 0489B] returning as a token—he did not reject the interpreter’s words as unworthy of belief, but carefully asked whether Boemund or his men were present. Hearing that the betrayer was not speaking deceitfully to him, the interpreter declared that Boemund’s soldiers were not far away and ready to do everything that should be undertaken according to his counsel. The betrayer urged them to approach without doubt or fear, to climb the walls safely, and not delay in the least because only a short space of night remained and daylight was drawing near. He urged them especially for this reason: lest the guard of the walls, carrying a torch in hand in the course of his watch and inspecting the city’s ramparts, walls, and towers, should discover those climbing up; then, when the enemy had been awakened, they would be in danger of their lives.

### CHAPTER XVIII.—Godefrid and Robert exhort the men chosen for this enterprise not to dread the first ascent of the walls.

[Col. 0489C]

Having heard the betrayer’s counsel, the interpreter hurried with swift step to the princes left in the mountains, reported everything he had heard, and urgently pressed them to choose whichever men they thought braver, so that they might climb the walls without delay and be admitted into the city. Men were immediately selected for the ascent of the walls; but fear and uncertainty shook their hearts, and each, hesitating at the first entrance and ascent, strongly resisted. Duke Godefrid and Robert, seeing the men so frightened and finding no one willing to go first because they distrusted the Turk’s promise, thinking these devices a trick, raged greatly in spirit. [Col. 0489D] They restored all by this encouragement:

> “Remember in whose name you left your land and kindred, and how you renounced earthly life, fearing no dangers of death for Christ. You must therefore believe that you will happily live with Christ, and, for his grace and love, receive with calm and willing hearts whatever may meet you on this path. Come then, most beloved soldiers of Christ: you do not incur this danger for earthly reward, but await the merit of him who knows how to give his own the rewards of eternal life after present death. For we must die in whatever manner. Already the morning light reveals [Col. 0490A] our plan; if the citizens and Turks perceive us, not even one of us will escape alive. Go, and by climbing offer your lives to God, knowing God’s love to be this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.”

### CHAPTER XIX.—How resolute men were admitted by a leather ladder.

At these words and encouragements of the most high-minded princes, the uncertainty in many minds was wiped away. Taking a ladder made of oxhide, especially suitable for this undertaking, they gradually approached the wall with their interpreter, where the betrayer awaited the arriving men by the ramparts. When some of those sent ahead had arrived—some from the duke’s household, some from Robert’s following, and some from Boemund’s household—the interpreter addressed the Turk waiting for them at the walls, asking him to throw down a rope from the battlements, so that the ladder might be fastened to it and hoisted to the walls, by which soldiers could climb and be admitted.

[Col. 0490B] As he had promised, the Turk raised the ladder by the rope, fastened it firmly around the battlements, and, encouraging the men in a subdued voice, urged them to climb without hesitation. Without delay, bold men, clad in mail and helmets, girded with swords, leaning upon their spears and drawing themselves up by hand, climbed the ladder. Others followed them, in uncertain hope of life, until about twenty-five had been admitted. Once these had entered and remained in profound silence, their brothers waiting beside the walls and awaiting the outcome, but hearing no one, thought that the men admitted had been slaughtered and suddenly strangled by false faith. Therefore they delayed climbing and following.

### CHAPTER XX.—When the ladder broke, some perished; but once it had been repaired, they climbed again confidently.

[Col. 0490C]

The soldiers who had entered, understanding that fear had so seized their Christian companions that they were withdrawing from the ladder and departing, leaned down over the wall and urged their companions in subdued voices to climb, declaring that they would suffer no danger there. Hearing the voices of their brethren still alive, they strove eagerly to climb the ladder and enter the city. But because of the excessive pressure and weight, the ancient and decayed battlements broke apart: stones and mortar came loose and fell, and the ladder, deprived of its fastening, fell completely to the ground with the men still standing upon it.

Spears had been planted and set upright beside the walls; those who fell were impaled upon them. Others were crushed by stones falling from the wall and left half-dead; some died. [Col. 0490D] The people of God were greatly horrified, supposing that all this had occurred through Turkish treachery and that now, doubt dispelled, all those admitted had perished by an unjust death. Yet no sound or crash, although one had been enormous from the falling and impaled men, was heard in the city or on the walls; for the Lord God had raised a fiercely blowing wind that night.

The Turk, keeping the faith which he had pledged to Boemund in surrendering the city, again lowered the rope to raise the ladder. Once more fastening it around stronger battlements in the same place, he summoned back through the interpreter those who were desolate and terrified and faithfully urged them all to repeat the ascent. [Col. 0491A] The men hesitated no longer; strengthened by the interpreter’s words and recognizing the safety of their brethren, they again climbed the ladder and were brought onto the walls, until nearly sixty had mounted and taken their stand above the ramparts.

### Chapter XXI.—Those admitted carry out a slaughter of the guards; other pagans, awakened from sleep, attack the Christians.

Meanwhile, the guard of the walls, making the circuit of the city and, having inspected the ramparts, going to visit and rouse the Turkish watchmen, encountered the men who had been admitted, carrying a torch in his hand. But in an instant his head was cut off by a sword-stroke; and they passed on into the neighbouring tower. Finding everyone there still weighed down by sleep, they struck them down at the sword’s edge; then, rushing in the same onslaught into other towers, they wrought a very great slaughter, until they had killed, without any outcry, the guards of nearly ten towers in that part of the city, sunk in deep sleep. [Col. 0491B]

When these had thus been laid low by the sword, a large force of seven hundred was admitted through a certain postern in the hills near the very place where they had climbed up, its bars suddenly broken. Sounding their horns loudly, they summoned Godfrey, Robert, and the other leaders, so that they might hasten as quickly as possible to help those admitted and enter the city. Hearing the horns and recognizing them as the agreed signal, since they shared every secret of the affair, these men came running in strong force, striving to enter by the gate projecting above in the hills. But Turks rising from the chief citadel of Darsian, which was close to that gate, drove the Franks back with a shower of stones when they heard the tumult, and did not allow the companions of those admitted to reach the gate and open it. [Col. 0491C]

The knights who had entered the city by ladder therefore returned to the aforesaid postern. With exceedingly sharp iron tools prepared by Turkish ingenuity, they broke through its inner passage and widened the opening in the wall; and thus the princes and their companions were admitted in ample numbers, mounted and on foot.

### Chapter XXII.—As the two sides raise an uproar, the princes first announce to the multitude that the city has been handed over.

The Turks, awakened by this sudden shouting, tumult, and shrill blast of trumpets and horns, hastened to arms. They seized bows and arrows, defended the towers, and engaged one another in fierce combat, above and below. In this noisy contention on both sides, [Col. 0491D] the soldiers of Darsian, stationed on the summit of the mountain and in the higher citadel, sounded their horns loudly, so that the Turks in the city and in the tower-garrisons—still snoring in the earliest dawn—might awaken and rise to assist their companions, and so resist the Christians who had been admitted.

The great army which was still encamped outside the walls in another part of the spacious city supposed that those in the hills and citadel were raising their voices, sounding horns, and fighting because of the arrival and entry of Corbahan; they were wholly unaware that the city had been betrayed and captured into the hands of the Franks. Bohemond, Raymond, and Tancred, to whom the entire affair was known and who had remained at the siege, put on their mail-shirts, girded themselves with arms, and rushed with raised standards to attack the city from without. They greatly encouraged those ignorant of what had happened to assault the city, explaining the entire matter to them. [Col. 0492A]

### Chapter XXIII.—The faithful open the city gates; Bohemond’s banner is prominent on the citadel; at first light most warlike combat is waged.

Meanwhile, while the Turks were thus pressed hard by battle within and without, Greek, Syrian, and Armenian citizens, and men professing Christianity, gladly hastened to open the gates and break the bars, through which Bohemond and the entire army were admitted. Bohemond’s banner, crimson in colour, gleamed at the first dawn in that part of the hills where the city had been handed over, above the walls, so that it might be plain to everyone that, by God’s grace and assistance, [Col. 0492B] the city—unconquerable by human power—had been handed over and captured into the hands of Bohemond and all Christ’s faithful.

Thus, when the bars had been torn away and the gates opened everywhere, all, marvelling and rejoicing that this plan had not been known to everyone, quickly took up arms. One urged another on, and all, armed, hastened at a run to enter the city and its gates. One might have gone a mile before the whole multitude of Christians had entered. Immediately, at the mighty crash and noise of so many thousands entering, the dreadful sound of trumpets, the raising of innumerable banners, the immense shouting of armed men, and the neighing of horses, the Turks were stunned; some, still resting in their beds, awoke unexpectedly and unarmed. [Col. 0492C]

Some of them at once gathered in hope of defense, taking up bows and weapons; others, holding out in the towers and strongpoints, struck down with arrows many unsuspecting Christians of the unarmed populace, men and women. Charges and varied conflicts took place and were fought in blind confusion. The Christians, whose strength and numbers were pouring in ever more abundantly, prevailed; throughout the houses, squares, and streets of the city they struck the scattered and wandering Turks down at the sword’s edge. They spared neither age nor sex among the pagan people, until the ground was covered with blood and the corpses of the slain; many lifeless bodies of Christians also lay there, Franks, Greeks, Syrians, and Armenians intermixed. Nor is this surprising: with daylight scarcely recognized, darkness still lay over the earth, [Col. 0492D] and they wholly did not know whom they ought to spare and whom to strike. For many Turks and Saracens, shouting out in fear of death with the voice and sign of Christian profession, deceived the pilgrims and therefore lost their lives in the general slaughter. Ten thousand were killed, their bodies cut down in the lanes and streets of the city and slain by Frankish swords.

### Chapter XXIV.—The pagans flee wherever each can; some, falling from the highest cliffs, are dashed to pieces and killed.

Very many Turks, seeing the exceedingly severe slaughter taking place and that the entire city overflowed with Frankish arms and strength, despaired of life. Fleeing from the towers and garrisons of the city, they made for the hills, by knowledge of the intricate roads entering the refuge of the chief citadel, [Col. 0493A] and escaped the weapons of the pursuing Franks. This citadel and palace, situated in the hills, could be overcome by no art and no force; no one could oppose or harm those remaining within it.

Others, about a thousand, summoned from distant regions to give aid and admitted into the city, were terrified by the shrill sound of trumpets and horns and driven to despair by the immense killing of their own people. Entirely ignorant of the roads and of escape, they too hastened together toward the hills and the upper refuge to avoid the Christian force, but in blind error fell upon a narrow and unknown path. There, the way failing altogether, they had no possibility of turning back on the high ridge; instead, falling downward with horses and mules through precipitous slopes and extremely narrow, impassable rocks, with necks, [Col. 0493B] legs, arms, and every limb broken, all perished in an incalculable and astonishing disaster.

### Chapter XXV.—On the wealth found in the city, and on the day on which the city was captured.

But the people of the living God, returning from the slaughter and pursuit of the pagans fleeing to the refuge and hills, when the sun was already shining higher and the day far advanced, searched the city and looked for food, but found little. They found only oysters of various sorts and colours, pepper also and many spices, clothing, tents of the pagans, gaming counters and dice, and money, though not much. Nor was this surprising, since, during the long siege of nine months, so many thousands of pagans gathered there had consumed everything.

It was Thursday, a most serene day, [Col. 0493C] when, on the third day before the Nones of June [3 June], the city of Antioch was handed over and captured into Christian hands, the Turks having been overthrown and put to flight.

### Chapter XXVI.—On the flight and death of the king of Antioch.

Darsian, king of Antioch, understood that his men were fleeing and that the whole refuge and citadel were now filled with fugitives. Fearing that, once the city had been captured, the Frankish force surrounding the refuge would storm it, he mounted a mule and went out to hide among the trackless mountain paths, until he might learn more fully the outcome and conclusion of the matter, and whether the citadel could be held by his men against the Franks.

As he wandered alone in flight through the mountain paths, some Syrians who professed Christianity and were travelling through the hills for necessary supplies saw and recognized the prince from afar. They wondered greatly [Col. 0493D] why he had gone alone from the citadel’s refuge by way of the remote paths. They said to one another: “Behold our lord and king Darsian, travelling through these deserted mountain places not without reason. Perhaps the city has been taken, his men killed, and he is plainly intent upon flight. Let us see to it that he does not escape our hands, since we have endured so many losses, injuries, and wrongs from him.”

Thus three Syrians discussed in good faith how to kill him, while concealing everything. Bowing their heads, they showed him false reverence and greeted him deceitfully as they approached, until they had taken and drawn his sword. They threw him from his mule, cut off his head, and put it in a sack. They soon brought it to the city of Antioch before the sight of [Col. 0494A] all the Christians and princes. The head was of remarkable size; its ears were very broad and hairy, and its grey hair was joined by a beard flowing from his chin down to his navel.

### Chapter XXVII.—On Rotger, who confronted in battle the pagans advancing before the army, and was overtaken by an unexpected death.

When they learned that Corbahan and his men were now close at hand, and that little food had been found in Antioch, they sent in haste to the port of Simeon the Hermit and borrowed, with money, provisions brought by ship, each according to his means. These they carried into Antioch that evening and the following morning.

After these matters had been completed, with the Turks partly killed and partly fled into the refuge, and the Franks dispersed everywhere through towers, houses, palaces, [Col. 0494B] and walls, on the following day, Friday, three hundred Turkish horsemen of Corbahan’s people, armed with bow, quiver, and arrows and distinguished by oysters, rode ahead of the whole pagan army, to bring sudden destruction upon any faithful men whom they might find unprepared outside the walls.

Of these three hundred, thirty rode in advance. They were men highly skilled in war and very swift on horseback. They gave their horses rein toward the city walls and gates, having left their companions behind them in a certain valley to ambush and attack the faithful, should any pursue the thirty sent ahead as far as the valley, and rush upon the men in hiding. As these thirty approached the wall of the city and fiercely provoked with their bows the faithful of Christ scattered over the ramparts, Rotger of Barnaville, mounted with fifteen most proven companions, clothed in arms and mail, hastened out from the city to meet them, in order to accomplish some notable deed against them.

But without delay the thirty Turkish men sent ahead turned their horses to flight and made for the ambush, drawing Rotger after them as he pressed them in rapid pursuit, as far as the place of ambush. When the men in ambush rose from the valley, Rotger turned back and swiftly retraced the road to the city with his companions. The Turks pursued the fugitive with no less speed until he and his men, approaching the city wall, had almost escaped across the fords of the Farfar. But, by adverse fortune, before the eyes of all standing on the walls, this most noble champion was overtaken by the faster horse of a Turkish soldier. An arrow lodged in his back pierced his liver and lung; falling from his horse, [Col. 0494D] he died.

When so distinguished a man had been killed and was deprived of his companions’ aid, the most cruel Turkish executioners dismounted, cut his head from his neck, and returned to Corbahan and his army, carrying the head fixed upon a spear as a display of their recent and now first victory. Glorying in this success, they greatly encouraged the pagan legions, because they had acted so boldly near the walls and had seen no pilgrim leave the city to help Rotger, killed and beheaded, or dare to do so.

### Chapter XXVIII.—The brothers’ explanation of why they did not aid him as he perished before their eyes.

Let no one think this surprising, nor suppose that the Franks had become faint-hearted through dullness of mind or terror at the approaching multitude, and were therefore slow to aid and avenge their brother, struck down and beheaded before the eyes of all; for no land in the world produces men more daring and readier for war than Gaul. Rather, let him believe beyond doubt that they were delayed by the lack of horses, which they had sometimes lost through disease, prolonged hunger, or at times the deceptive Turkish arrow. [Col. 0495A]

For scarcely one hundred and fifty horses remained to the Franks, and these too were weakened by lack of fodder; whereas the Turks’ horses were fat and untired. Therefore the Turks could escape at speed, and the Franks could by no means overtake them. Only four hundred Turkish horses had been found and captured in Antioch; the Franks had not yet tamed them in their accustomed manner for riding, nor learned to turn them in pursuit of enemies and urge them on with spurs. After the Turks’ departure, the pilgrims, sad and grieving, brought Rotger’s dead body into the city with great lamentation and weeping. They groaned that one of the strongest men of the people had fallen—one ever watchful in ambushes and in the slaughter of pagans, whose notable deeds were greater than our pen can recount.

Indeed, his fame had preceded him among all the Turks, and they gladly used to see and hear him in every matter they transacted with Christians, whether concerning the mutual restoration of captives or when they at times made peace with one another. That most valiant knight was buried in Antioch, in the porch of the basilica of St Peter the Apostle, by the Christian princes, [Col. 0495C] by the lord bishop of Le Puy, and by all the Catholic clergy present. His soul was commended to Christ the Lord through sacrificial prayers and hymns of psalms; for Christ’s love and honour he had become an exile and had not hesitated to die.

### Chapter XXIX.—The siege of the nations around Antioch.

Hardly had the funeral rites of the illustrious knight been completed when, on the very morning of Saturday—the third day after the city had been taken—all the barbarian nations and pagan legions appeared in abundant array. Corbahan had gathered them from every kingdom, land, and place in the eastern region. They pitched tents in the fields and plain and laid siege around the walls and ramparts of the spacious city.

Then, on the third day after he had besieged Christ’s faithful while remaining far from the walls, Corbahan took counsel and moved his camp closer to the city. In the strength of his multitude he established his position in the hills around the chief citadel and in the area where the city had been captured, on the heights of the cliffs, that he might be a support to Sensadonia and Buldage, sons of Darsian, and the others remaining in the refuge; and that he might see the place through which the city had been handed over and the Christians admitted. [Col. 0495D]

Likewise, in the same hills, other men of Corbahan’s people forcibly pitched their tents on the right side of the refuge, along the mountain slopes opposite the place where Duke Godfrey guarded the tower and gate below, by which Bohemond had previously encamped outside the city before its capture, so that the Christians might not be granted any freedom or opportunity to go out in any direction.

### Chapter XXX.—Duke Godfrey, fighting, is put to flight, and many of his companions perish by different deaths.

[Col. 0496A]

Duke Godfrey, seeing that their power and resolution had grown exceedingly strong against him, immediately went out through the gate with a great body of his men against the enemy, to attack and frighten the tents pitched outside the walls and drive the Turks away after defeating them. But behold, the Turks rose to meet the duke in defense of the tents. There, after a long battle on both sides, the struggle became most severe; the duke and his men, exhausted in strength and wearied by fighting, were turned to flight and barely escaped by returning through the gate by which they had gone out. Many others, about two hundred, to whom the narrow gate was denied, were killed, [Col. 0496B] wounded, or captured.

Thus, with the duke routed and driven back, and many of his men crushed at the gate, the Turks burst out from the refuge and its gate. Because they had prevailed against the duke, they came by known paths and a winding valley to the walls, suddenly attacked wandering Christians with shouts, wounded them with arrows in the rush, and without delay returned to the citadel and hills. As they sprang out from the hills and valley morning, noon, and evening to assault the Christians, Bohemond and Raymond, stirred to anger, determined without delay to provide protection for their men by constructing an immense ditch, called a *fossatum*, lying below between the hills and the city, and strengthening it above with a certain wall-like structure. Thus enemies suddenly breaking out from the hills might not strike down with weapons and arrows the pilgrim soldiers wandering incautiously through the open spaces of the city.

But the Turks still holding the refuge in the hills often burst out against this new fortification, made attacks, and sorely harassed and killed its guards and defenders by a hail of arrows and force of arms. Yet the Christian knights Walbricus, Ivo, Rudolph of Fontaines, Everhard of Poisat, Reibold Creton, and Peter son of Gisia, guards and commanders of the new fortification, resisted the Turks no less vigorously with lance and all their arms. They barred them the route of the valley, sometimes suffering, on both sides, grievous slaughter and wounds. [Col. 0496C]

### Chapter XXXI.—Bohemond is fiercely attacked, but prevails through the help of the brethren; and why the pagans pitched camp farther away out of necessity.

[Col. 0496D]

While these most frequent Turkish attacks were made against the new fortification and the Turks were fiercely repelled by the Franks, Corbahan’s soldiers formed an infantry column, entered through the impregnable gate of the refuge, left the hills and remote paths, and—knowing that Bohemond was in the new fortification—assaulted him vigorously. A fierce contest of war arose, and very many were killed. Bohemond and his men would almost have been defeated, had not Christians streamed in from the whole city: Count Robert of Flanders, Duke Godfrey—though defeated in the first assault—Robert, prince of the Normans, and the other illustrious lords contributed their forces and resources, and, by the force of their mailed troops, drove the Turks back from the city and the new fortification. [Col. 0497A]

The Turks, thus driven back with their prince Corbahan, remained for two days in the hills outside the gate and walls, thinking still to harm the Christians. But because they found no grass-fodder on the hills sufficient for their horses, they moved their camp. Crossing the ford of the river Farfar, they encamped a half-mile from the city. On the following day Corbahan, by the counsel of his men, divided his numerous army, amounting to many thousands, around the city to besiege all the gates, so that the enclosed pilgrims had no entrance open to them from either right or left, nor any exit.

### Chapter XXXII.—Where Corbahan distributes men at each gate, and Tancred attacks those assailing the walls.

[Col. 0497B]

With the siege thus established on every side, and after a few days had passed, on a very bright day certain Turkish soldiers rode out of camp and hastened on horseback to the walls of Antioch. With arrow and horn bow they challenged the Franks, hoping to prevail with the same success in which they had earlier gloried at Rotger’s beheading and to gain distinguished fame in Corbahan’s camp. Therefore they laboured more vigorously in assaulting the walls. They dismounted so that, standing at the wall, they might attack more freely and without injury to their horses; now on foot, they could more easily hurl missiles at the pilgrims.

But Tancred, a most fierce knight, never sated with Turkish blood and always eager for their slaughter, learned of their recklessness. With indignation and boldness he clothed limbs accustomed to iron in mail; taking companions highly skilled with horse and lance, he secretly went out from the gate which Bohemond had guarded while the siege was still underway, passing between the walls and the outer defensive wall, commonly called the Barbican. [Col. 0497C] He suddenly raised the war-cry against the Turks intent on battle, assaulted them fiercely, crushed and pierced them while unprepared. Seeing the danger of death, they had no opportunity to return to their horses before six were struck down, beheaded before the walls in vengeance for Rotger’s head, and lost their own heads to the sword. Tancred returned to the city to his brethren in great glory and joy, carrying the Turkish heads with him as proof of victory.

### Chapter XXXIII.—The Christians, despairing of being able to retain the fortification, destroy it by fire.

[Col. 0497D]

On the next day, after Corbahan had positioned his camp and arranged each contingent, and after the exits and entrances of the roads had been blocked on every side around the besieged, the pagans jointly decided that two thousand Turkish soldiers should be selected to storm and destroy the fortification which Duke Godfrey and the other leaders had secured in great victory and strength—as you have heard—when the defeated Turks were drowned in the waters of the river Ferna beneath the very bridge extending from the city across the river. In this fortification Raymond had kept guard until the city was taken by the Christians.

But now, since it was neglected and empty, Count Robert of Flanders, having summoned [Col. 0498A] five hundred fighting men, entered the fortification upon hearing of the pagans’ advance and resolved to defend it, lest Turkish power, suddenly occupying it, should greatly impede the pilgrims wishing to cross the bridge and water. The aforesaid two thousand Turks assigned to destroy the fortification assembled at it in great strength and amid tumult of arms, rushing in and attacking from every side with missiles and bows. At last, on foot, they strove to run across the rampart, amid a huge screaming of crowds and their customary roaring shouts, grievously harassing the defenders from morning until the decline of day.

But Robert and his companions, seeing danger threatening them from the enemy and knowing that they would be destroyed cruelly if defeated and subjected to their power, resisted their enemies bravely for their lives. With lances and crossbows they vigorously attacked the enemy and kept them by force from the rampart. Both sides are said to have suffered severe wounds that day. [Col. 0498B] The Turks, seeing that they gained nothing but were spending all their labour in vain, abandoned those barely defended in the fortification and returned to Corbahan, prince of the multitude. They asked that still more men be added to their force, asserting that on the next day the fortification and its defenders could thus be destroyed.

Robert and those with him, seeing that the Turks had withdrawn, remembered that the enemy would return with greater aid. Therefore, after taking counsel, they left the fortified position under cover of night, since it seemed too weak against the force of so many soldiers. They set the whole fortification on fire, demolished its rampart, [Col. 0498C] and were received by their brethren into the city of Antioch.

### Chapter XXXIV.—On the greatness of the famine among the people of God, and the high prices at which the cheapest things were sold.

On the next day at sunrise, two thousand pagans—added by Corbahan’s order to the two thousand already mentioned—approached the fortification in strong force, with trumpets and horns, hoping to overthrow it by sudden attack and swiftly destroy those enclosed within it, exhausted by the previous day’s defense. But finding the rampart demolished and the fortification burned, they returned to their tents deceived and frustrated.

Thus, with the city besieged on every side, the pagan forces increasing day by day, and every exit blocked, such famine prevailed among the Christians that, [Col. 0498D] when bread failed, they did not shrink merely from eating camels, asses, horses, and mules. They also ate hides which had been found in houses, hardened and decayed for three or six years, after soaking and softening them in hot water; likewise hides freshly stripped from cattle, seasoned with pepper, cumin, or any spice whatever. So severe was the famine that constrained them.

I know that ears shudder on hearing the evils and torments of this unheard-of famine by which God’s enclosed people were oppressed. For one hen’s egg, if one could be found, six denarii of Lucchese currency were paid; for ten beans, one denarius; for the head of one ass, horse, ox, or camel, one Byzantine coin was given; for a foot or an ear, six denarii; for the entrails [Col. 0499A] of any of these animals, five solidi were received in exchange. Finally, the poor and insignificant populace were compelled by the pressure of hunger to devour their leather shoes. Many others filled their wretched bellies with nettle roots and whatever wild herbs they could find, cooked and softened by fire; weakened thus, they dwindled daily by dying.

Duke Godfrey, as those present report, spent fifteen marks of silver on the meat of a most worthless camel; and his steward Baldric is said beyond doubt to have paid the seller three marks for a goat.

### Chapter XXXV.—The Turks, attempting secretly to recover the city, are cast down; after a long struggle they are driven from the wall and perish miserably.

After several days, once Corbahan had strengthened [Col. 0499B] the siege around Antioch, closed every exit and entrance of the city, harassed the people of God with diverse assaults, and forbidden food to be brought in from any side, the Christians—afflicted and wearied by slaughter, prolonged abstinence, and military exertion—began to be less watchful in guarding the city and walls.

Accordingly, a certain tower toward the hills remained unguarded. It was at the place where a defense of brittle mud mixed with bitumen had been made, to check enemies issuing from the besieged gate through the hills and pursuing scattered pilgrims; and where the young man captured by the Provençals had been taken, for whose ransom a certain tower had been demanded but refused by his relatives and friends, and who was therefore put to death under capital sentence.

Certain most daring Turkish soldiers, learning that this aforesaid tower was vacant of inhabitants, secretly placed their ladders and engines against the wall, hoping in the silence of night to bring some pagans in through it and thus recover the city they had lost. Meanwhile, a certain man walking about the city on necessary business lifted his eyes and saw Turks carelessly moving about halfway up the top of that tower. Without delay, making a loud uproar, he alerted the companions staying in the neighbouring tower, declared that the Turks had invaded the city, and so stirred up great alarm among the people. [Col. 0499C]

At this, Henry of Ascha Castle, a knight of great renown in his own land, son of Fridelon and one of Duke Godfrey’s close companions, heard the cry and tumult. Taking shield and sword, he hurried to the top of the tower with two worthy young men, Franko and Sigemar, relatives by blood and inhabitants of the village called Mechela on the river Meuse. They intended to drive the enemies who had entered from the tower, believing that they had been betrayed together with the city by certain brethren corrupted with gold or silver.

But the Turks, realizing that they had been detected and could not free themselves from the pilgrims’ hands by any device, came forward at the tower entrance with their sole hope placed in defense and resisted with savage sword-strokes. They struck Franko, who was fighting with great force, in the brain with a severe and scarcely curable wound. Sigemar, trying to aid his kinsman, they pierced through the belly with a sword up to the hilt; and by an extraordinary and unheard-of effort they held Christ’s faithful back from the entrance. [Col. 0499D]

At length, as the aid of the faithful increased on every side and their strength was reinforced, the Turks, exhausted and spent in spirit by excessive exertion, began to fail in defense and to lower their weapons and arms. Four of them fell by the sword; others, thrown down from the height, died with their necks, legs, and arms broken. [Col. 0500A]

### Chapter XXXVI.—On certain Christians seeking food outside the walls, and on the killing of sailors selling provisions to the besieged.

After this, the pilgrims were compelled by the pressure of famine, as you have heard—and much more besides—and, because of the siege established on every side, found no access for bringing in or obtaining food. Some of the common people, exposing their lives to danger, secretly left the city in great uncertainty and fear under cover of night. Going down to the port of Simeon the Hermit, once a hermit there in the hills, they received food from sailors and merchants for payment, and used to return before dawn through thorns and brushwood in the darkness. [Col. 0500B]

Those who brought grain sold an eighth part of the Laodicean measure for three marks; Flemish cheese for five solidi; and a little wine or oil, or any, however small, means of sustaining life, they exchanged for gold or silver at a heavy and unheard-of price. Some of these men are said to have lingered longer than usual one day; since the night was short, they were exposed by the very swift daylight and were slaughtered and despoiled by the Turks. A few, hiding in thickets and brushwood, scarcely escaped and returned to the city.

Taking occasion from this event, the Turks gathered two thousand men and proceeded to the aforesaid port. By sudden assault they overwhelmed all the sailors found there, pierced them with arrows, burned the ships by setting fire to them, and violently seized and carried away the food and everything brought by ship. [Col. 0500C] Thereafter they frightened sellers and buyers away from the port, so that no further sustenance of food could be found there by the Christians.

When the most cruel report of this reached the ears of the Christians, suffering under the weight of unprecedented famine, the various Turkish attacks now became an added burden to them, and the minds of many wavered in different directions as to how they might escape this siege and the dangers threatening them. Thus, at last, very many men, seeking an exit by whatever effort or opportunity, withdrew themselves from the army by night.

### Chapter XXXVII.—How certain leading men fled secretly from the city in despair of survival.

[Col. 0500D]

As such fear and despair of survival grew more intense, and thoughts rose in many hearts beneath the weight of daily tribulation, certain leading men of the army—William Carpenter and another William, formerly a familiar and household servant of the emperor of Constantinople, who had married the sister of Bohemond, prince of Sicily—were shaken by such great terrors that, in the silence of night, by common counsel, they secretly withdrew from their companions. They went toward the hills and were lowered by ropes from the walls and rampart.

Having been lowered, they travelled without rest through mountain paths because of Turkish ambushes, until they reached Lesser Alexandria. There Stephen of Blois, separated from the siege of Antioch because of illness, was staying to learn the outcome of the affair and the fate of his companions. [Col. 0501A] In that place Stephen learned from these men that the dangers faced by his brethren had increased daily: namely, intolerable famine, Turkish boasting and assaults, and the destruction of men and horses. He despaired of survival, judging himself unsafe even in that place; and, not daring to take the overland route, he prepared his return and flight by ship with the aforesaid leaders.

When the report spread through Antioch that such distinguished nobles had left the city through fear of the attacking Turks, many likewise contemplated flight, the hearts even of strong men failed from fear, and they were no longer as ready as formerly in defense. They defended more sluggishly the new fortification they had established in the middle of the city against the citadel in the hills, being desperate and intent on flight. [Col. 0501B]

### Chapter XXXVIII.—The consoling words of a certain cleric to the people.

A certain most faithful brother, a Lombard by birth and a cleric by life and rank, standing beside the aforesaid new fortification, gave great comfort to the desolate soldiers of Christ—all who were there, clergy and laity, noble and humble alike—and raised the wavering, fear-stricken hearts of all, saying:

> “All you brothers who suffer from famine and pestilence, who, surrounded by crowds of Turks and pagans, expect to undergo temporal death: do not believe that you endure this hardship for nothing. Rather, hear and consider the reward which the Lord Jesus will render to all who are to die on this journey for love and grace of him.
>
> “At the beginning of this journey, a certain priest—a man of good repute and exceptional manner of life—living in the regions of Italy, known to me from my childhood, was one day, as usual, making his way alone across a certain small field to the diocese entrusted to him, intending to celebrate Mass. A pilgrim joined him in friendly companionship and asked him, concerning the urgency of this journey, what he had heard about it, or what he himself first thought of the fact that so many kingdoms, so many princes, and the whole Christian people had flocked with one purpose and desire to the tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the holy city of Jerusalem.” [Col. 0501C–D]

He replied:

> “Different people think differently about this journey. Some say that this desire has been stirred up in all the pilgrims by God and by our Lord Jesus Christ. Others hold that the Frankish leaders and a very great multitude undertake it from fickleness of mind, and that this is why so many obstacles have confronted the pilgrims in the kingdom of Hungary and in other kingdoms; they think, therefore, that their purpose cannot attain its end. Hence my mind still hesitates, though I have long been touched by desire for this journey and am wholly absorbed in that purpose.”

The aforesaid pilgrim immediately said to him:

> “Do not believe that this journey began through fickleness or without cause, but that it was ordained by God, to whom nothing is impossible. And know without doubt that all who are overtaken by death on this journey will be numbered among Christ’s martyrs in the court of heaven, enrolled there and happily crowned—provided that, having become exiles in the name of Jesus, they persevere with pure and whole hearts in the love of God, and keep themselves from avarice, theft, adultery, and fornication.” [Col. 0502A]

The priest, astonished at the pilgrim’s words and promise, asked who he was, from what region he came, and how he had learned with certainty that those who died in this expedition were to be crowned with the blessed in heavenly glory. The pilgrim at once disclosed the full truth of the matter to the inquiring priest as follows:

> “I am Ambrose, bishop of Milan, servant of Christ. And let this be a sign to you and to all Catholic peoples following this road, that I do not deceive you in anything you have heard from my mouth: know that, when three years have elapsed from this day, the Christians who survive, after many labours, will happily gain the holy city of Jerusalem and victory over all barbarian nations.”

Having said this, he vanished without delay and was never seen again thereafter. That distinguished priest declared with the utmost truth that he had seen and heard these things from the holy bishop of God. Now, since that vision and promise were made, two years have been completed; it is certain to all that the third still remains. Thereafter, as Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, had foretold, in the third year the pilgrim soldiers of Christ and their princes gained Jerusalem and cleansed the holy places there, driving out and crushing the Saracens. [Col. 0502B–C]

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—A further exhortation of the leading men, and how the fugitive princes began to sail for Constantinople.

When this vision and promise had been heard from the truthful brother’s report, all who until then had wavered through fear of losing their present life, and had been troubled by the departure of the fugitive princes, were kindled with hope and desire for heavenly life. They became steadfast in spirit and declared that they would no longer withdraw from their brethren and the city for any fear of death, but would live and die with them and endure everything for Christ.

Duke Godfrey likewise, together with Robert of Flanders, wonderfully recalled by their humble consolation almost all the princes, who had been so shaken by terror that they had already conspired to flee, without the common people knowing it; and they restored them to steadfastness for every danger, speaking in this manner:

> “Why do you despair, distrusting God’s help amid all the adversities that have come upon us? Why have you resolved, now that your faith has failed, to abandon your brethren—the humble common people on foot—or to begin flight? Stand firm, and with manly courage endure what opposes you for Christ’s name. Do not abandon your brethren in tribulation, lest you incur the wrath of God, whose grace and mercy will not fail those who trust in him.” [Col. 0502D]

While they spoke these words to the desolate leading men with tears and deep sighs, the spirit of all revived; thereafter they remained steadfast with them in every distress, no longer contemplating flight.

William and likewise William, Stephen, and their fearful, fugitive companions prepared ships, put oars and sails out upon the open sea, and planned to return to Constantinople, leaving their brethren under siege, whom they believed could never be freed from Corbahan’s hands. [Col. 0503A]

## CHAPTER XL.—How the aforesaid men turned back the Greek emperor from helping their brethren.

After they had sailed for some time, lodging on certain islands of the Greek empire or delaying because of the movement of the sea, they learned that the Christian emperor of the Greeks had arrived at the city of Finiminis with a great retinue and abundant equipment, to assist the pilgrims as he had faithfully promised when, after oath and treaty had been struck, they had joined him in friendship.

He had assembled some forty thousand men: Turcopoles, Pincenarii, Cumans, Bulgars skilled with bow and arrow, Danes highly experienced in fighting with the equipment of the double-headed axe, Frankish exiles, a hired army besides, and people of diverse races from desert places, mountain regions, and maritime islands—in short, from every part of his most extensive realm. [Col. 0503B]

The aforesaid princes found him thus strong in armed men and horses, and richly supplied with food, tents, mules, and camels. With him they found also a new army of Franks, about forty thousand strong, gathered through the long winter; and likewise Tatinus of the mutilated nose, who, stunned by fear, had departed from his companions in false faith for the emperor, supposedly to carry an embassy concerning the promised aid. He performed this most unfaithfully, never returning thereafter to Antioch.

The emperor, recognizing the princes when they came to him, was greatly amazed that they had been separated from their companions. He asked about the condition of Christ’s faithful fellow-soldiers, the safety of Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond, and the bishop of Le Puy, and whether their cause stood in prosperity or adversity.

They answered that they were by no means in prosperity or safety, but were so besieged by Corbahan, prince of Khorasan, and the pagan nations that not even a single entrance or exit from that very spacious city lay open to them; nor could they escape their hands except perhaps if some slipped away secretly. They reported how tightly famine pressed them, and how the Turks, in hatred of them, had destroyed merchants and ships. They declared that none of them could survive before so great a multitude, and that they themselves had scarcely saved themselves by their own cunning. They urged the emperor to return and not uselessly harass his army against such vast enemy forces. [Col. 0503C–D]

## CHAPTER XLI.—Certain other princes, contemplating flight, are restrained by the exhortations of good men.

When the emperor heard these dangers to the Christians and learned the strength of the pagans, he held counsel with his chief men; trembling and stupefied, he immediately ordered the whole army to return. Indeed, he ravaged with fire and plunder the land of Romania, formerly unjustly taken from him by Solyman but now restored by the strength of the pilgrims; he overthrew all its cities and garrisons, lest, if Solyman recovered them, they should benefit him in his service.

The great rumour of the emperor’s return and the dispersal of his army flew over Antioch’s walls, struck the pilgrims’ hearts with deep grief, and drove much courage from their minds. Therefore the princes of Christ’s army frequently took counsel whether, by some device, they might leave the city secretly and abandon the humble common people there in danger.

When Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and the bishop of Le Puy learned this, they again began to strengthen them, addressing all in these words:

> “Do not be troubled, nor let your hearts be afraid because this return of the emperor has been reported. God is able to deliver us from our enemies’ hands. Only remain steadfast in the love of Christ, and never commit this treachery against your brethren, by secretly withdrawing from them and taking flight. For without doubt, if you flee through fear of the enemy, Corbahan and all his multitude will pursue you; and you will by no means escape their hands when news of your flight first reaches their ears. Let us therefore stand fast, and in the purpose of our life let us die in the Lord’s name.” [Col. 0504A–B]

At these words all became steadfast, resolving to die and live with their brethren.

## CHAPTER XLII.—Concerning a Christian knight whose horse fell while he was fleeing.

Corbahan and all the legions of the pagans, having heard of the emperor’s withdrawal, increased their attacks still more. Emerging in bodies from their camp, they lay in wait to cut down, according to their custom, anyone who came out of the city.

One day Christians on the city walls saw some Turks, forty horsemen in a single troop, leaving the lodging-place of their tents for this same purpose. Though saddened and terrified by their adverse circumstances, some armed Christians immediately met them across the ford of the Ferna. But the Turks at once drove them back; fleeing across the ford, they stood on another bank, seeing that they could not compete with the speed of their famine-weakened horses. [Col. 0504C]

At last, after a great shower of arrows, as the Turks were withdrawing some distance from the river, a knight of stout heart, still trusting in his horse’s strength and thinking that his companions’ forces followed behind him, pursued them at reckless speed. But since none of his companions dared follow to help him, two most fierce riders wheeled their horses out from the troop toward the pilgrim, with loose reins, and rapidly urged them back in flight along the same way through the cultivated fields toward their companions.

In the charge, when its foot struck an obstacle, his horse fell completely to the ground; thus he was almost at the end of his life. As he lay fallen and wholly abandoned by assistance, when the executioners were already close at hand to strike him, their horses stood motionless, as though they had forgotten their spurs and, as if struck upon the forehead, were compelled to go backward—until the pilgrim knight mounted his horse as it rose to its feet and, by the gift of God and the Lord Jesus Christ, repeated his flight to his companions’ position. [Col. 0504D]

All standing on the bank and upon the walls wept for joy when their brother was received safe and sound; in his deliverance they had plainly experienced the finger of God.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—Concerning the discovery of the Lord’s lance.

[Col. 0505A]

In this affliction of famine of which you have heard, amid fear from the siege and anxiety caused by the ambushes and attacks which the Turks still constantly made from outside, when the people of God were humbled and despairing, a certain cleric from the land of Provence declared that a lance had been revealed to him in a vision—the lance with which our Lord Jesus Christ was pierced in the side.

This cleric reported to the bishop of Le Puy, Lord Reymerus, and to Count Raymond the place where they might find the precious treasure of the lance: namely, in the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He attested his vision with all the truthfulness he could. Believing his words, they came by common resolution to the place which the cleric named. Digging there, they found the lance, as they had learned from the cleric; and, having found it, they brought it forth in that very oratory before all the Christian princes. They spread its fame widely and wrapped it in precious purple cloth. [Col. 0505B]

At its discovery great hope and joy arose among the Christian people, who venerated it with no small celebration and with offerings of countless gold and silver pieces.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—Peter serves as envoy to Corbahan, commander of the siege.

After several days had passed, all the chief men and leaders of the Christian army still wavered and despaired of life amid so many adversities, famine and pestilence; and they feared to join battle with so many nations because their human strength and their horses’ condition had been exhausted. Having taken counsel, they resolved to send an embassy to Corbahan, master and commander of the army and siege. [Col. 0505C]

But they found no one who dared speak to so fierce and proud a man, until Peter, who had been the originator of this journey, firmly offered to go and to deliver magnificent words to the man. Without delay, entrusted with the embassy by Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, and the other princes, the aforesaid Peter—small in stature but great in merit—dared to make his way alone, under God’s protection, to Corbahan’s tent in the midst of the pagans.

Through interpreters he delivered the Christian message to him in this manner:

> “Corbahan, most illustrious and glorious prince in your realm, I am the envoy of Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, and the princes of the entire Christian multitude. Do not disdain to receive the decree and counsel which I bring. The leaders of the Christian army have decreed that, if you will consent to believe in Christ the Lord, who is the true God and Son of God, and renounce the foul rites of the pagans, they are prepared to become your soldiers and, restoring the city of Antioch to your hand, to serve you as their lord and prince.” [Col. 0505D]

He scorned even to hear this, much less to do it. Instead, he instructed Peter the Hermit in his sacrilegious rites and the pagan sect, declaring that he would never depart from it.

## CHAPTER XLV.—Further concerning the same matter, and how haughtily the prince received the embassy’s words.

Peter, hearing Corbahan receive the name and admonition of the Christian faith with mockery, laid before him another message:

> “It has seemed good,” he said, “to the Christian princes, since you refuse to subject to yourself such distinguished men and reject becoming a Christian, that you choose twenty young men from your multitude, and the Christians will do the same. After hostages have been given on both sides and an oath made by each side—you by your god and they by their God—let them fight in single combat in the midst. If victory does not fall to the Christians, they shall return peacefully and without injury to their own land, surrendering Antioch to you. But if your men cannot triumph, you and yours shall peacefully withdraw from the siege, leaving the city and land to us; nor shall you allow so great an army to perish in mutual conflict. But if you disdain this decree of the Christians, be certain that at tomorrow’s dawn all will join battle with you.” [Col. 0506A]

Corbahan, hearing this, answered Peter with great pride:

> “Peter, I want you to know one thing: the Christians are to choose that all beardless youths come over to us, to serve me and my lord, the king of Khorasan; we shall enrich them with great benefits and gifts. Likewise, let girls still untouched come to us and have permission to live. But bearded men and those with any greyness, together with married women, are to be beheaded. Otherwise I shall spare no age, but shall destroy all by the sword’s edge; and those whom I choose I shall carry away in chains and iron fetters.” [Col. 0506B]

Having said this, he showed him an innumerable and unheard-of abundance of chains and fetters of every kind.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—Peter returns; the answer is reported to the leaders, and they deliberate together about what must be done.

[Col. 0506C]

Peter, having received leave from Corbahan to return, entered the city of Antioch, intending to report the boastful words he had heard from Corbahan. And behold, all the princes gathered round Peter with the other Christian soldiers, desiring to hear what Corbahan had answered and to know whether he had brought war or established some treaty for making peace.

Surrounded by crowds of the faithful, Peter declared that Corbahan desired war and had spoken of nothing except in great pride and confidence in his multitude; he began to recount the rest of the threats he had heard. But Duke Godfrey did not allow him to proceed further. Taking him aside, he warned him not to disclose to anyone anything he had heard, lest the people, failing through fear and distress, withdraw from battle.

The period of three weeks and as many days had now passed since the besieged Christian people began to be distressed by want of necessities and failure of bread. Since they could endure these things no longer, great and small alike took counsel together, saying that it was more useful to die in battle than to perish through such cruel famine, while the people daily grew weaker and died. [Col. 0506D]

## CHAPTER XLVII.—War is proclaimed; all prepare as though to die on the morrow, and the divisions are arranged under their commanders.

At this outcry of the lamenting people, battle was proclaimed for the following day. All were commanded to spend the night in prayer and, purified by confession of their sins, to fortify themselves with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; then, at the first light of day, they were to put on their arms.

When morning came, all the Christian soldiers assembled in arms, hauberks, and helmets on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], and formed their battle-lines while still remaining within the city. They appointed Hugh the Great, brother of the king of France, commander of the first division and standard-bearer of both horse and foot. Robert, count of Flanders, and Robert, prince of the Normans, were set over two divisions; thus these two kinsmen were stationed together on one side. [Col. 0507A]

The bishop of Le Puy directed his own division separately toward the mountains, with the lance they had found raised in the middle of its wedge formation and placed in the hands of a certain cleric. Peter of Stadeneis, Reinard of Toul, his brother Werner of Greis, Henry of Ascha, Reinard of Hemersbach, and Walter of Dromedart were appointed to command their formation toward these mountains and the road leading to the port of Saint Simeon, formerly associated with the aforesaid hermit. Count Reinbold of Oringis, Lodewicus of Monzons, and Lambert, son of Cuno of Montaigu, were appointed to command the order of one division.

Duke Godfrey formed his own division from two thousand horsemen and foot soldiers—Teutons, Alemanni, Bavarians, Saxons, and Lotharingians—whose hand and sword were accustomed to be most fierce upon the necks of their enemies. Tancred alone formed his own division from horsemen and foot soldiers. [Col. 0507B]

Hugh of Saint-Pol and his son Engelrad; Thomas of the castle of Fère; Baldwin of Bourcq; Robert, son of Gerard; Raymond of Peleiz; Reynold of Beauvais; Walo of Calmont; Everhard of Poisat; Drogo of Monzei; Rudolf, son of Godfrey; Conan the Breton; and likewise Rudolf the Breton: all these were chosen to command two divisions. Gaston of Berdeiz, Gerard of the city of Roussillon, and William of Montpellier were content with only one division. Bohemond of Sicily was named commander, with horsemen and foot soldiers, of the last division, which was the most densely formed, so that he might protect the other divisions and help those who perhaps needed assistance. [Col. 0507C]

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—Count Raymond is left in the city; the faithful burst out through the gates, and the pagans, alerted by a signal from the chief citadel, meet them.

[Col. 0507D]

When all these things had been arranged and disposed, they left Count Raymond, somewhat ill, to guard the city against the Turks who were in the higher citadel with Sansadonia, son of Darsian, along with a very great force of Christians.

This done, all unanimously resolved to advance against the barbarian legions, in the order in which they had been arranged, each prince with his own division, through the open gate by which the stone bridge stretches across the Ferna. They went forth in a thousand varied and splendid banners, hauberks, and helmets.
