Corbahan likewise and Solyman stationed many divisions on the right and left wings, in front and behind; holding bows of bone and horn for battle, they advanced swiftly from camp to charge against the Christians, intending to begin the combat first with a shower of arrows, while sounding trumpets, horns, and bugles with unbearable clamour. [Col. 0508A]

They had made provision not only because of Peter’s embassy, which had told them that battle would take place on the following day; they were also daily suspicious and anxious lest the Christians suddenly begin battle against them. Therefore they constantly sent messengers to Sansadonia’s citadel, asking him to notify them whenever he perceived the Christians arming or being urged to battle. For from the citadel, situated upon the brow of the mountain, he had a view in every direction of all that occurred in the city; thus they could meet them prepared and in formation, and harm the Franks before they were ready.

Sansadonia refused to send messages, but promised to raise upon the summit of his citadel, fixed to the top of spears, a very broad cloth of blackest and dreadful colour; then he would sound a terrible bugle loudly, thereby making the pagans certain of the Christians’ preparations for war. He therefore raised this dark cloth in the mountains as a signal for commencing war, fastening it above the aforesaid citadel at the very hour when the Christians’ preparations began at earliest dawn and the divisions were being formed, so that, once this signal was seen, the pagans too might prepare to resist, arranging their weapons and formations. [Col. 0508B]

Immediately forewarned by the sign of this cloth and the crash of the loudly sounding, dreadful bugle, they massed and formed ranks, advancing to meet the Christian troops. About two thousand dismounted from their horses to prevent passage over the bridge and across its river.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—Christ’s people, victorious in the first division, are impeded by smoke raised by the pagans.

[Col. 0508C]

The Christian princes, formed and massed at that gate, suspecting and foreseeing that the Turks would oppose their departure with bow and arrow, sent forward from the gate across the bridge and the river Farfar all their foot archers from the common people. With God’s favour, these gained the bridge first and rushed upon the hostile Turks with arrows. Resisting with breasts protected by shields, they drove them from the place until Christian arrows flew as far as the Turks’ station of horses.

The Turks, who had dismounted and run forward on foot to the bridge, saw that they could neither resist nor drive the Christian men from it, but that their horses might be destroyed by a shower of arrows. Turning to flight and hastening as swiftly as possible to their horses, they mounted them and thus, though unwillingly, granted the Christians a free exit. [Col. 0508D]

At this, Anselm of Ribourg-en-Mont, who was stationed in this first division with Hugh the Great, rejoicing in the prosperous outcome and the faithful’s first victory, brandished his lance and plunged into the midst of the Turks. He knocked down some, pierced others, threw still others backwards, and wrought a great slaughter among them.

Hugh the Great, seeing that Anselm had repelled the enemy without any fear of death, rushed forward without delay, inflicting like slaughter on the enemy bands. Robert of Flanders, Robert count of the Normans, Baldwin, prince of Hainaut, and Eustace also struggled boldly and bravely against the hostile formations, killing them with no small carnage. [Col. 0509A]

But Solyman, leader of the Turks, a most savage warrior, and his companion Rossilion, one of the four chief men of Antioch under King Darsian, separated from the rest of the multitude with their formations numbering about fifteen thousand, hurried toward these mountains and the road facing the port of Saint Simeon. Their purpose was that, if the Christians were defeated and perhaps planned flight toward the coast, they might meet them and crush them unawares.

Burning eagerly with this purpose, and hastening along the road more quickly than usual, they unexpectedly fell upon the division of Count Reinard, Peter of Stradeneis, Walter of Dromedart, Henry of Ascha, Reinard of Hemersbach, the most illustrious knight, and Werner of Greis. As an obstacle, they suddenly cast fire from pots onto the ground in front of them, where their route lay toward their Christian companions. [Col. 0509B]

When the fire caught the earth and seized dry grasses and the dry leaves of thorn-bushes, it immediately grew in height and breadth; thus, as a cloud was stirred up by the wind, a dark smoke thickened, overshadowing only the eyes of the faithful and obstructing their sight.

## CHAPTER L.—The pilgrims are scattered in various ways; Bohemond’s division, brought to the point of death, is reported to Duke Godfrey.

The Turks then cunningly followed them behind the smoky cloud. Some, separated by the error of the darkness, they slaughtered; others they pierced with arrows. Only those mounted on horses escaped through the horses’ speed, though not entirely unhurt by arrows. Of the foot soldiers, three hundred were killed and some were kept in chains. [Col. 0509C]

Karieth the Turk of the city of Caran, seeing Solyman’s successful destruction of the division of Reinard, Peter, Werner, and the others, pressed forward more confidently. Together with the prince of Damascus, he came down in a circuit from the mountains beside the city and the river Ferna. Brodoan of the Turkish city of Aleppo likewise approached, to encircle Bohemond’s division, which was last and densely packed with foot soldiers and Franks. Attacking it, they attempted to break into it and scatter it with arrows and the strength of their own men.

Overborne by Turkish power and surrounded by the trickery of cunning men, Bohemond’s company was forced into a pitiable and anguished mass, like sheep about to perish among wolves. They could resist no longer, and the moment was near when they would die, enclosed on every side by troops of unbelievers. [Col. 0509D]

But a messenger, running the length of a road and crying aloud, struck Duke Godfrey—who was fighting fiercely against Buldagi, Amasa, Boesa, and Balduc and triumphing in the name of Jesus, Son of the living God—with a sorrowful plea and warning. He begged him to look and see how desperate the condition of Bohemond and his company had become, declaring that unless he hurried to their aid, all would shortly be destroyed by the Turks.

## CHAPTER LI.—The duke puts the enemies to flight and crushes them, bringing his brethren out from the gate of death.

Duke Godfrey, learning from the swift messenger of the Turkish attack upon Bohemond and his own division, almost surrounded, raised his eyes and saw how Bohemond’s strength and his cohorts were exhausted by the weight of battle and scarcely endured the enemy’s force. Therefore he hurried to confront the adversaries with the Alemanni, Bavarians, Saxons, Lotharingians, Teutons, and Romans in his division, flying forward under varied and splendid purple banners, in order to repel the pagans’ strength and assist those in distress. [Col. 0510A]

Hugh the Great, who at the exit of the first division from the bridge that extends from the city across the Farfar, after driving off and crushing the Turks, held the open field in victory with the Christian foot archers sent ahead, saw that Duke Godfrey’s division and banners were turning back along the road leading to the river Farfar. He himself hurried by the same route, with his legion, to join the duke’s division and increase its strength and arms, knowing that the greater pressure of battle threatened on that side. Both princes moderated the pace of their cavalry according to the ability of the foot soldiers to come near. [Col. 0510B]

When the Turks saw without doubt that they were advancing against them to assist their Christian allies, they began gradually to withdraw from their attack and assault; turning their backs and retracing their way, they fled to their tents, while the duke with the Christian young warriors pursued and slaughtered them fiercely.

## CHAPTER LII.—Further concerning the same matter.

At last, after crossing a certain low and small torrent flowing down from the mountains, where the Christian soldiers had been delayed a little in the valley, the Turks halted on the summit of a mountain, turned their reins toward defence, and tried to frighten off the pursuing Franks with their arrows. The Teutonic pilgrims, however, possessing fearless hearts and invoking Christ’s mercy with loud cries, boldly charged the resisting Turks. Then and thereafter they so drove them into continual flight that none of them dared stand or strike back in that conflict. [Col. 0510C]

Therefore Bohemond, the great prince, and Adam son of Michael, seeing the strength of Godfrey resisting and relieving the people, and seeing that he thundered with his men through the enemy ranks in slaughter, broke off delay with all the division and force which he commanded at the rear. In charge and shouting, they plunged through the middle of the Turkish formations. Such a most savage slaughter was made that the fields were covered with the bodies of the slain, as though the formations had been violently mingled from side to side like hail.

But, with God’s help, battle pressed heavily upon the pagans, and the whole weight of the conflict was turned against them. Corbahan, however, in his pride, had kept larger forces and resources for himself and occupied a position on the Christians’ left; he could by no means hasten to aid his fleeing and crushed companions. For the bishop of Le Puy, with all the force of the Provençals, bravely resisted him face to face and continually opposed to him the Lord’s lance. [Col. 0510D]

From this it is to be inferred that, through the working of God and our Lord Jesus, Corbahan’s strength failed when fear was divinely instilled into him, and the hearts of his men were thrown into tumult; for he remained motionless in obstruction and in the sight of heavenly armour, as though, forgetful of all battle, he and his innumerable following had been held fast. [Col. 0511A]

## CHAPTER LIII.—Corbahan, his forces defeated, places his hope of survival in flight; the bishop of Le Puy pursues him.

Thus, by God’s will, while he stood in stupefaction and ecstasy, someone came to him bearing adverse news and said:

> “Corbahan, most illustrious prince, why do you prolong delay any further against this Christian division? Do you not see how the army which you led out has been defeated and crushed and dispersed in flight? Behold, the Franks are spread through your camp and those of your men, carrying off spoil and gathering all things; and behold, they will come to you without delay.”

Struck by this sad and harsh message, Corbahan raised his eyes, saw his divisions flowing away in flight, and immediately turned his back with all his retinue and fled by the road on which he had come, heading toward the kingdom of Khorasan and the river Euphrates. [Col. 0511B]

The holy bishop pursued him with his whole division, though not far, because of the exhaustion of the horses and the weariness of the foot soldiers. For the horses which the Christians had brought from Gaul had failed because of their many wounds, as those who were present truthfully affirm. Indeed, scarcely two hundred horses fit for battle remained on the day when they engaged in battle with so many pagan nations.

## CHAPTER LIV.—The princes who begged because of want are noted.

Very many distinguished and most noble knights, whose number is unknown, their horses having died and themselves being consumed by scarcity caused by famine, were counted among the foot soldiers and learned to fight on foot, though from boyhood they had always been accustomed to horses and had ordinarily entered battle mounted. Of these distinguished men, anyone who could then obtain a mule, an ass, a cheap beast of burden, or a palfrey used it as a horse. Among them princes, bravest and richest in their own lands, entered battle riding asses—and this is no wonder. [Col. 0511C]

For, when their own means had long failed them, they had begged in poverty; having sold their own weapons because of need, they used Turkish weapons, unfamiliar and ill-suited to battle. Among their number, Hartmann, reputed to have been wealthy and very noble, one of the most powerful men in the land of Germany, is said to have ridden an ass and possessed only a Turk’s shield-boss and sword for battle on that day. Nor is this surprising: exhausted of all resources, after selling his hauberk, helmet, and weapons, he had long begged and had nearly reached the point at which he could not live even by begging. [Col. 0511D]

Henry of Ascha, a noble knight worthy of martial praise, had reached the same condition. But the glorious Duke Godfrey, taking pity on them, assigned Hartmann one loaf of bread with a portion of meat or fish from his own supplies; and he named Henry his table-companion and fellow diner, because he was a knight and his man, who had served him for many years and in the perils of war.

## CHAPTER LV.—Concerning the same matter, and the flight and slaughter of the enemy.

[Cols. 0512A–0514A]

Over these miseries and impoverishments of the noble magnates, only those marvel who have never heard anything like them nor seen the evils that befell such outstanding men in so long an exile. They do not marvel, however, who testify that they saw Duke Godfrey himself and Robert, prince of Flanders, at last lack possessions and horses. For Duke Godfrey was in want: the horse on which he rode on the day of the great battle he received as a gift from Count Raymond, obtained only by much entreaty. For his money had failed through the distress of the aforementioned famine and through the excessive generosity of the alms and goods which he spent on beggars and impoverished soldiers. Robert likewise was in want—the very rich and powerful prince of fertile Flanders—whom those present and eyewitnesses declare often begged within the army; and, as we have learned from the report of many, he acquired by begging the very horse which he mounted on the day of battle. With these horses, acquired through hardship, these most distinguished princes, now unconquered against the battle-lines of the unbelievers on the day of battle, seeing Corbahan and all his company turn their backs, directed their reins swiftly after him, and, striking down and overthrowing those failing in flight and those fleeing, pursued them without pause for a distance of three miles. Tancred also, who commanded the Christian battle-line, as soon as he perceived the enemies’ flight, promptly joined in their slaughter with a body of cavalry; he pursued them as they fled along a road of six miles. Corbahan, seeing the dispersal of his own men and the rout of his army, continued fleeing until, arriving at the great river Euphrates, he escaped with his followers by boat.

### CHAPTER LVI.—On the plundering of the camps and the variety of fetters. [Cols. 0512B–0513A]

While the aforesaid Christian princes were eagerly occupied in slaying and pursuing their enemies, the company of Count Raymond and Bishop Raymer, greedily intent upon booty and the spoils of the Turks, remained in the very place where victory had been granted, pursuing only a little; and they plundered great spoils of gold, Byzantine coins, grain, wine, garments, and tents. Others, who had been intent upon the battle, saw them lay hands upon the spoils and, corrupted by the same greed, likewise set their hands to plunder. They returned to Antioch with abundant and immeasurable spoils, amid praise, joy, and cries of exultation; and those who had formerly been poor and hungry were now filled with every good thing.

In those same camps of the heathen they found innumerable books, in which were written the sacrilegious rites of Saracens and Turks, and the abominable crimes of diviners and soothsayers, together with execrable characters. There were also found in the tents various kinds of chains, fetters, and nooses, made of ropes, iron, and bulls’ and horses’ hides, for binding Christians. All these were brought to Antioch in an immense and countless quantity, together with many goods and tents, including Corbahan’s own tent, built in the manner of a city, with towers and walls of various colours and precious silk. This remarkable tent had streets branching out from it, in which, it is reported, two thousand persons lived spaciously.

Women, tender children, and infants still at the breast—however many were found in the camps—some slaughtered and others trampled beneath horses’ feet, filled the fields with their wretched, mangled corpses, abandoned by the aid of their heathen people who had turned their backs in battle. The other events done in this battle, among both the Christian and heathen peoples, as also the marvellous and unheard-of deeds performed in the siege of Antioch, are reported to have been so many and so varied that I judge they can be retained by no pen and no memory.

# BOOK V [Col. 0513]

## CHAPTER I.—On the restoration of the divine mysteries and the reinstatement of the patriarch. [Cols. 0513A–D]

After this victory had been gained in the plain of Antioch, the great and royal city of Syria, the bishop of Le Puy and the other princes, returning from the rout and slaughter of Corbahan’s army within the walls of the aforesaid city, cleansed the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, which the Turks had profaned by their sacrilegious rites, from every defilement. They rebuilt with all fitting dignity the holy altars which had been overturned; and they restored with the highest reverence the image of our Lord Jesus Christ and the figures of the saints, which the Turks had darkened and covered over with cement, as though blinding living persons. They reinstated Catholic worshippers for the celebration there of the divine mysteries, among all the clergy, both Greek and Latin.

Then, from the purest purple, precious silk, and the remaining ornaments found in Antioch, they ordered mitres, dalmatics, copes, and every adornment for the use of the churches of the living God to be made, so that priests and ministers who were to celebrate the divine offices in the church of St Peter might be vested in them; or when, on Sundays or on a solemn feast, they went in psalms and hymns to the oratory of St Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. This oratory, situated a short distance from the church of St Peter, had remained unharmed and untouched by those same Turks, and had been granted solely to Christians dwelling among the Turks, by the Turks’ gift and permission, after the Turks had subjected the city.

They also fittingly restored to his cathedra and appointed as head of Antioch, with all submission and reverence, the patriarch of the city, a most distinguished and most Christian man. While the Turks were still surrounded by the Christians’ siege, they had often bound him with ropes and hung him alive upon the walls before all eyes, in order to increase the sufferings of the Christian people; and they had frequently worn away his feet by the injury of fetters.

## CHAPTER II.—To which princes Antioch was subject. [Cols. 0513D–0514B]

When these divine matters had thus been attended to and arranged, they established Bohemond as lord and advocate of the city, because he had expended much effort in bringing about the city’s surrender and had borne very great labour in placing guards upon the towers and walls against Turkish plots. Bohemond, having assumed power and lordship over the city, established the residence and guard of his men in the fortress situated in the higher mountainous ground, no Turkish defence there opposing him. For, when they heard of the flight and destruction of their own people, Sansadonius and those who were in the citadel fled likewise through the mountains, leaving the fortress empty and undefended.

But Count Raymond of the region of Provence, ever insatiable in his desire to acquire, seized the tower overlooking the bridge of Fernae toward the port of St Simeon, fortified it with his own retainers, and compelled this portion of the city to be subject to his authority. The other princes—Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, Robert prince of the Normans, and all who had borne no less labour around the city—did not seek to rule the city or to have its revenues or tributes apportioned to themselves, unwilling to violate the faith and oath they had made to the emperor of Constantinople. For they had sworn to him that, if Antioch were taken, since it belonged to his realm, they would preserve it for him and restore it to his majesty, just as they had done with Nicaea and all the castles and cities belonging to his kingdom. From that time onward Bohemond began to envy Count Raymond, though secretly.

## CHAPTER III.—On two princes sent forth, one of whom perished and the other barely escaped. [Cols. 0514C–0515A]

The aforesaid princes, who were concerned to keep faith and their oath, shortly after the victory granted by God sent Baldwin, count of Hama, together with Hugh the Great, brother of the king of France, as envoys to the emperor of the Greeks himself. They were to inquire from him why he had behaved so impiously toward the people of God; and why, in so great a necessity, he had neglected to provide the aid he had promised, when he had not yet been able to find them deceitful or treacherous in any respect.

They were also instructed to tell the emperor that the leaders of the army were released from every promise and oath made to him, because, at the prompting of cowards and fugitives, he had lied concerning all the assistance that he had promised. Thus these two princes, undertaking the embassy of their brother-companions, set out for the emperor by way of the middle of Romania. At the borders of Nicaea they happened to fall into an ambush of Turcopoles, unable to turn aside either to the right or to the left.

The Turcopoles, an impious people, Christian in name but not in deed, born of Turkish fathers and Greek mothers, saw these men placed within their grasp and suddenly rushed upon them. Baldwin, who had gone a little ahead of Hugh, they say, was pierced with arrows; others assert that he was carried off alive as a captive. But to this very day it remains unknown by what end so noble and Christian a prince perished. Hugh the Great, who was following Baldwin’s route at a short distance, seeing that man’s deadly peril, retraced his way at a swift gallop to a certain wood adjoining the mountains, and, protected by its concealment, escaped the hands of the impious.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the plague of mortality that befell the people of God. [Cols. 0515A–C]

After this, as ships frequently arrived from every direction at the port of St Simeon carrying provisions, and as the pilgrims were delivered from the siege of the barbarians through God’s victory, in the midst of a happy abundance of food and every necessary provision, a plague of great mortality arose within Antioch. By it a vast and innumerable multitude of the Christian army, both noble magnates and humble commoners, was consumed.

The venerable bishop of Le Puy was first struck by this deadly disaster, and he ended his life on the Kalends of August [1 August]. Nobles and common people bewailed him with excessive lamentation and buried him in the basilica of St Peter, in the very place where the Lord’s lance had been found. After so venerable a priest had been buried, this most savage plague grew broader and more grievous; and the Christian army began to be so diminished by death that for nearly six months scarcely a day arose on which at least thirty, and often one hundred and fifty, both noble and humble, did not breathe out the spirit of life.

Through the violence of this same calamity Henry of Ascha, a knight noble by birth, died in the castle of Turbaysel and was there buried as a Catholic. Likewise Reinard of Hemersbach, a knight most distinguished in deeds and lineage, lost his life and was buried in the courtyard of the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Moreover, more than one hundred thousand persons—knights and foot-soldiers, noble and humble, monks and clerics, small and great, and even women—perished by death without the sword.

## CHAPTER V.—On Turkish ambushes, and on a certain Folker and his wife. [Cols. 0515C–0516A]

Meanwhile, many who rejoiced in peace and victory and avoided this mortality, while frequently travelling the road to Rohas for necessary provisions in the hope of receiving something from Baldwin’s hand, suffered many ambushes and killings from the Turks dwelling in the fortress of Hasart; and some were often captured and carried away.

One day a certain Folker, an outstanding knight born in the castle of Bouillon, was travelling to Rohas with his wife, a woman of elegant beauty, and with other brethren. He happened to fall into the hands of Turks lying in ambush. After much resistance, he was immediately overcome and beheaded along with the others. Because she was very pleasing to their eyes on account of the beauty of her face, his wife was captured and taken to the fortress of Hasart. The prince and lord of the fortress ordered her to be treated honourably, while he waited to see whether he might obtain something of great value for her ransom.

Not long afterwards, a most illustrious Turkish knight, who had come to the lord of the fortress of Hasart concerning an agreement in solidi, was seized by desire for the beauty of Folker’s wife and inflamed with immoderate love. He urgently begged the lord of the fortress to grant her to him as a gift, in return for the agreed sum of solidi, so that he might be permitted to take her in marriage. And this was done.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the hostilities between Brodoan of Aleppo and the prince of Hasart. [Cols. 0516A–B]

The Turkish knight, delighted by this marriage, laid ambushes and made war upon the enemies of the lord of Hasart far more than was his custom. He often carried off booty from the great city of Aleppo belonging to Brodoan, a certain Turkish prince; and he frequently captured those pursuing him to recover the spoils or cut them down when defeated. For Brodoan of Aleppo and the prince of Hasart bore mutual hatred and bitter enmity toward one another.

After several days had passed, Brodoan, indignant because the aforesaid knight and the body of soldiers from Hasart so often opposed him, gathered from every quarter of the city of Aleppo the Turks subject to his dominion, intending on an appointed day to besiege Hasart with a strong force and storm it. When he learned this, the prince of Hasart anxiously considered how he might summon auxiliary forces capable of confronting Brodoan’s many thousands when they had assembled.

## CHAPTER VII.—The counsel of the Turk, husband of a Christian woman, on gaining the friendship of the Christians. [Cols. 0516B–D]

Amid the various discussions that took place, the Turkish knight who had married the Christian woman, at his wife’s prompting, urged the prince of Hasart as follows:

> “Do you see how Brodoan gathers Turkish troops and strength from every side, intending with many thousands to surround and storm you and your fortress? Now, if you are willing to trust my counsel, do not delay to make Godfrey, duke of the Christian army, your friend by joining hands with him. He holds Antioch in strength, having put Corbahan to flight; and in this pressing need you may be assured that you will gain all the aid and company of the Christians. For you know that this Christian people surpasses every nation in military skill and boldness, and that none compares with them in fidelity and honour. Therefore do not hold this counsel cheap; but without delay secure his friendship for yourself. Thus, once he is your ally, know that all Christians will willingly give you every assistance.”

Knowing this counsel to be sound, and knowing that he could thus resist Brodoan and his innumerable forces, the prince sent to Duke Godfrey at Antioch a messenger who professed Christianity, a Syrian by birth and a man of remarkable prudence, speaking in these words.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The embassy of the prince of Hasart to Duke Godfrey, and how the duke hesitates to make an alliance with the Turks. [Cols. 0516D–0517A]

> “The prince of Hasart sends greeting, and every good that can be wished, to Godfrey, great prince and duke of the Christians. By the counsel of our people we have sent to you, to establish peace and concord between us, to establish faith and friendship, and that our arms may be shared in every need of war. For we have learned how powerful a man and prince you are in resources, that you are able to bring aid to those allied with you, and that no fickleness can loosen you from the bond of your faith. Therefore we have chosen you above all others, we seek you out, we ask your help, and we strike an alliance with this assurance: that you may always be certain of our loyalty. Brodoan of the city of Aleppo has become our enemy; he has assembled Turkish reinforcements from every side and will shortly come against our fortress of Hasart in great force and with a numerous army. I have determined not to meet and resist him by the aid of other Turkish princes, but by your hand, if you will not refuse to trust and assist me.”

When Duke Godfrey heard this embassy, he took counsel with his men and sought assurance for establishing peace, hesitating lest Turkish treachery, after the alliance had been corrupted through some wicked contrivance or pretext, might harm him and his followers through some unjust device.

## CHAPTER IX.—Mahumet, the prince’s son, is given to Duke Godfrey as a hostage; carrier-pigeons of the alliance are sent forth. [Cols. 0517B–D]

When the prince of Hasart learned from his envoy’s report that the duke and his men hesitated concerning this agreement and did not place much confidence in Turkish promises, he sent the duke his beloved son, named Mahumet, as a hostage, so that the peace and alliance to be established between them might henceforth be made more certain. The duke, having received his son as hostage, made a compact of faith and friendship with him, and by a firm oath promised to aid him in every adversity and never fail him.

Once these promises had been made, he appointed a fixed day on which he would lead the Christian army to aid him against Brodoan and, with the help of the Lord his God Jesus Christ, drive the Turkish legions away from the siege of Hasart. While the duke steadfastly made these promises, the envoys from the fortress of Hasart were greatly delighted and rejoiced. Without delay they drew from their bosoms two doves, tame and well-trained birds which they had brought with them; and, fastening with thread to their tails a written sheet bearing the duke’s faithful replies and promises, they released them from their hands to carry the joyful news.

The duke and all who were with him marvelled at this sending forth of birds. But the envoys at once answered why these messages were conveyed by birds:

> “Let not our lord the duke and his faithful men wonder at the doves we have sent forth. We did not send them in childishness or vainly, but for this reason: so that by their swift and unceasing flight they may hasten the message of loyalty which you bear toward him, and assure him of your assistance, whatever chance or obstacle may meet us on the road. There is also another reason why these birds are sent in advance with their little letters: if they should be found in our bosoms by any of our Turkish brethren, we would be condemned to certain death.””

The birds, entrusted with the letters, now flew away and faithfully returned to the throne-room and table of the duke of Hasart. Receiving his domestic birds kindly according to his usual custom, the prince of Hasart untied the inscribed sheets from their tails, read through Duke Godfrey’s secret message, and learned the day of his coming to give aid and with how many thousands the Christian army would come to assist.

## CHAPTER X.—Brodoan besieges Hasart; the Christian army arrives. [Cols. 0517D–0518B]

Having read and understood these things, and certain of Godfrey’s friendship and loyalty, the fortress of Hasart was strongly furnished with very many soldiers, arms, and Turkish forces summoned to aid it from various places. And behold, Brodoan descended into the plains of Hasart with a strong force numbering forty thousand Turkish men; pitching his tents around its walls, he established his camp and attacked the walls and towers day after day with a fierce assault.

He had been encamped barely five days when, behold, Duke Godfrey set out from Antioch in great strength, with banners of wonderful beauty, coats of mail and helmets, and the arrows of horsemen and foot-soldiers, travelling for three days. When one day’s journey had been completed, Baldwin, his brother, setting out from Rohas with three thousand fighting men, met him under banners glittering through the air, having been summoned by the duke’s message.

But Bohemond and Raymond were greatly angered by envy because the prince of Hasart had first sent to Godfrey, made an alliance with him, and given his own son to him as a hostage of mutual fidelity. Therefore they altogether refused to join the duke’s expedition.

## CHAPTER XI.—Bohemond and Raymond join Duke Godfrey; the siege is raised, but certain Christians are slain by ambush. [Cols. 0518B–D]

When the duke had already completed one day’s journey and saw that these princes had remained behind out of envy, and that they could be moved neither by gentle admonitions nor humble entreaty to come, he sent them another embassy, speaking in this manner:

> “It is not fitting for you, who are pillars and leaders of the Christian army, to leave your brothers and fellow Christians deprived of your aid, taking a false pretext against us when we have never yet failed you in any distress or need, but have always been prepared, even for your sakes, to die on this journey. Believe without doubt that if today you remain behind and refuse us aid in this undertaking, we shall be your enemies, and henceforth our foot shall not move in any cause that concerns you.”

Bohemond and Raymond saw that the entire Christian host, at Duke Godfrey’s command, was proceeding on the road to Hasart, and that the duke and their other brother-companions spoke to them in anger. Remembering that they had acted unjustly toward their brethren, they were remorseful. Gathering about four thousand of their own companions, both horsemen and foot-soldiers, they followed Godfrey by the royal road and joined him in the territory of Hasart. The number of assembled princes and their army was thirty thousand fighting men.

Brodoan and those who had gathered with him for the siege of Hasart learned that the Christian columns had entered the neighbouring plains. Seeing from afar the fires of their camps shining in the night and a cloud of smoke ascending, they withdrew their camp from the siege by common counsel and agreement, knowing that they were by no means able to resist so many thousands. About ten thousand of them, travelling around by known paths and mountainous country over a long detour, fell upon the delayed, following pilgrims and the rearmost of the army with arrows from behind. Unknown to the duke and to those who had gone ahead over a distance of two miles, they suddenly attacked and terrified six hundred men and struck them with the sword’s edge.

## CHAPTER XII.—Duke Godfrey is received by the prince of Hasart with great thanksgiving; the alliance is renewed. [Cols. 0519A–B]

When the duke and his men learned this cruel news, they rode swiftly against the Turks who were returning from this slaughter, meeting them by a hurried route in a valley among the mountains of the region of Hasart. There they inflicted no small slaughter upon them with lances and swords. Having crushed them, and with the Turks scattering in flight through the mountains and dense thickets, the duke and the other princes came to the fortress of Hasart.

Its prince met them with three hundred men covered in shining helmets and mail, offering many thanksgivings to the duke for all the victories that had befallen them through his help against the forces of their enemies. At once, after the alliance had been renewed, he joined himself to the duke in inviolable friendship before all who were present, promising to remain steadfast and never to be alienated from the company of the duke or from fellowship and affection for the Christians.

On the counsel of his men, the duke gave his allied friend a helmet wonderfully inlaid with gold and silver, and a very fine coat of mail, which Herebrand of Bouillon, a knight noble and distinguished in military deeds, used always to wear when about to engage in battle. Thus Brodoan was driven from the siege of Hasart; the prince of that fortress was kindly commended by the duke and all the leading men and restored peacefully to his own domain; and the army returned to Antioch. All the princes remained there in great victory and peace.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The duke, compelled by the times as the pestilence increased, withdrew from Antioch. [Col. 0519C]

After this, as the outbreak of the aforementioned pestilence came on more extensively and severely, and many princes together with the common multitude were dying, Duke Godfrey remembered how he had formerly been afflicted at Rome by a very similar disaster during the expedition which he made with Henry, fourth king and third Roman emperor. He remembered how there, in the pestilential month of August, five hundred most valiant knights and many other nobles had died, and how many, terrified, had departed the city with the emperor himself.

Fearing the same evil now, he withdrew from Antioch and retired toward the mountains of Pancratius and Corovassilius. He lived in the towns of Ravenel and Turbaysel, which his brother Baldwin had subdued before the siege of Antioch and, after Baldwin’s migration to Rohas, had left to that brother and the duke.

## CHAPTER XIV.—The duke himself, with a few Christians, destroys hostile strongholds. [Cols. 0519D–0520B]

In those same fortresses certain Armenian brethren, serving God in monastic habit, had suffered many wrongs from the soldiers of Pancratius who lived in a fortress neighbouring the aforesaid places of Ravenel and Turbaysel. Seeing that the duke was a peaceable man and a lover of justice, they approached him, complaining of the injuries inflicted upon them and of the fortress of Pancratius, ever hostile to those same castles and their inhabitants.

The most Christian duke, stirred by the complaints of Christ’s poor and not forgetting the injuries which this same Pancratius had inflicted upon him while the Christians’ siege still lay around the walls of Antioch, took the matter grievously and devised every means of taking vengeance. For Pancratius had despoiled the envoys of Baldwin, the duke’s brother, of great and honourable gifts, both money and other things, while they travelled through his land and country. Yet he had not been afraid to send all these things to Prince Bohemond in order to establish friendship with him.

Moved now by these injuries and the complaints of the poor, the duke chose fifty knights from among his followers. Armed with coats of mail, shields, lances, crossbows, and Armenian lances, he proceeded to the neighbouring fortress in which Pancratius’s harmful robbers lived. Pressing the attack with all his strength, he stormed it in a sudden assault. Once it had been captured, he caused it to be brought down to the ground by flame and fire, after twenty of the soldiers whom he found there had been blinded by his order, in recompense and vengeance for the arrogance and injuries which Pancratius had presumed to inflict upon him and Christ’s poor.

Likewise the fortress and stronghold of Corrovassilius, because of the various wrongs and injuries it had inflicted on Christians, was assaulted and overcome by the strength of the duke’s soldiers, burned, and thrown down to the ground.

## CHAPTER XV.—Baldwin rewards the Christians who gather to him with many gifts, and subdues the Turks. [Cols. 0520B–D]

After Duke Godfrey had returned from Hasart to Antioch, then left the hostage Mahumet in Antioch in the hands and custody of his men and departed for Turbaysel and Ravenel, while Baldwin returned from Hasart with his men to Rohas, very many noble and humble men from the army came to the city of Rohas. Drogo of Nahella, Reinard of Toul, Gastus of Berdeiz, Folker of Chartres, and other leaders and fellow-soldiers came in groups of hundreds and fifties, some on horseback and some on foot, so that they might earn rewards from Baldwin, now made duke and prince in the city and region, for military service, remaining with him for some time.

For they were oppressed by the utmost need and exhausted of necessary resources by the long expedition. They flowed in and increased daily in number and strength, until almost the entire city was besieged by the Franks and occupied by their hospitality. Baldwin bestowed very many gifts day by day in Byzantine gold coins, talents, and silver vessels. He subdued in battle the regions and everything that opposed him; he brought the Turks and all the surrounding peoples under his control, until the nobler and more powerful men of the land made an alliance with him.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Baldwin proscribes and imprisons those conspiring against him. [Cols. 0520D–0521B]

Twelve princes and native inhabitants of the city of Rohas, or Edessa, observed how the Frankish people were pouring out from Antioch and every place, prevailing in every undertaking and skill; how Baldwin preferred their counsels to their own, conducted every matter and business of the land with them, and neglected them and their decrees more than usual. They burned with fierce indignation against Baldwin and his followers. Fearing that they would be wholly driven out by these men, they greatly regretted having appointed Baldwin duke and lord over the city.

Therefore, forming a secret conspiracy and sending an embassy to the Turks, they plotted treachery against Baldwin—how he and his followers might be either killed or expelled from the city. While they were arranging this in frequent and secret meetings, one of them, named Enxhu, who preserved pure loyalty toward Baldwin in his inmost heart and mind, disclosed in order the inventors of the treachery and their accomplices. He therefore declared that it was necessary for Baldwin, his followers, and the entrances to the city to be guarded by night and day against their treason, lest Turkish forces and ambushes find them unsuspecting and unprepared.

Baldwin learned that they were plotting such great treachery, now from a truthful report, now from the change in their troubled expressions. Sending a body of Franks devoted and familiar to him, he ordered all of them seized and committed to prison custody. He ordered all their unheard-of wealth and money brought into his palace, and he spent it unsparingly upon his followers in reward for military service.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Baldwin, exhausted by excessive giving, accepts gifts for the prisoners’ ransom, tortures some, and expels others from the city. [Cols. 0521B–D]

After many days had passed, they repeatedly begged him for their lives and the safety of their limbs, made many excuses, and offered no small gifts through intercessors for their ransom. Yet Baldwin, always guided by the counsel of his men, aimed at greater things, knowing from informers that in neighbouring castles and fortified places they had hidden from the Christian army more ample treasures and whatever they possessed of greater value.

At last, exhausted by excessive giving and by the agreement concerning solidi, and by the magnitude of the gifts which he had bestowed not only upon the leading Franks but also upon the lower ranks, Baldwin allowed gifts to be accepted for the redemption of the prisoners. He refused the gifts of only two men, whom, judged especially blameworthy and guilty of treachery, he ordered to be blinded. He ordered many common accomplices in the crime, condemned after their noses, hands, or feet had been cut off, to be expelled from the city.

No less than twenty thousand, thirty thousand, or sixty thousand Byzantine coins were brought into Duke Baldwin’s treasury from each person ransomed, apart from mules and horses, silver vessels, and very many precious ornaments. From that day onward Duke Baldwin became feared in the city of Rohas, and his name, illustrious for valour, was spread to the very ends of the land.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Baldwin’s father-in-law and on Balas’s deceit at the fortress of Amacha. [Cols. 0521D–0522A]

Baldwin’s father-in-law, named Taphnuz, saw how Baldwin had exacted vengeance from the men guilty of treachery and afflicted them with the loss of possessions and mutilation of limbs. Taking the opportunity, he fled in terror to his strongholds in the mountains and could not thereafter be recalled, fearing that he might suffer capital punishment because of money which he still owed.

Balas also, of the city of Sororgia, frustrated in his hope of recovering the city from Baldwin’s hand or obtaining anything from him because of the influx of Franks, and because his heart was wholly bent upon deceiving them, began secretly to devise how he might by crafty counsel bring Baldwin to destruction. At last, having found a way of wicked fraud by which he might deceive or destroy him, he approached Baldwin one day as though with a sincerity of faith and spoke as follows:

> “I know that you are a man of great power and ability, and that you reward without stint those who willingly place themselves at your military service. Therefore I have secretly resolved that I will entrust not only myself, my sons, and my wife to your hand, but will also surrender to you my fortress of Amacha, by which you may subdue a very large territory, on whatever day you choose as most suitable for receiving it.”

Baldwin, delighted at the prospect of receiving the fortress, readily believed one who spoke so kindly and faithfully to him. He appointed a day on which, according to Balas’s word, the fortress would be surrendered to him without any impediment.

## CHAPTER XIX.—How certain prudent men protect Baldwin against the Turk’s treachery. [Cols. 0522B–C]

As the day drew near, Balas, not forgetful of his deceit, brought one hundred Turks, armed and protected by coats of mail, into the castle of Amacha, and concealed ambushes here and there in the small chambers of the fortress. Thus they were to seize Baldwin and his companions alive as they entered and subject them to his authority.

Unaware of this fraud, Baldwin took two hundred knights, stout for every work of war, and advanced to the fortress of Amacha. He found Balas, as he had promised, ready to surrender the stronghold. Balas earnestly begged him and, with honeyed words, flattered him deceitfully to enter and receive the fortress with a few chosen companions, and then to arrange for whatever faithful men he wished to leave behind in its custody. Baldwin nearly listened and believed him; he was already preparing to select companions to go up and enter with him, and arranging who should remain outside.

But behold, certain prudent Frankish men, maintaining that there was nothing trustworthy in this man’s words and promises, led Baldwin aside and sharply reproached him because he had so suddenly believed the words of this heathen Turk and was willing, without a hostage, confidently to enter his fortress with a small force.

## CHAPTER XX.—How Baldwin discovers the Turk’s treachery in the capture of his men. [Cols. 0522D–0523A]

At last, after much doubt and much deliberation on the matter, and after they had entirely turned Baldwin away from entering the fortress, both parties agreed that Baldwin should wait with his companions in the valley and send ahead twelve companions in whom he trusted to receive the citadel. Taking its keys and bars, they were to bring it forcibly under his authority.

Without delay, twelve men chosen to receive the citadel, clad in armour and coats of mail, entered the fortress and tower of Amacha. As soon as they stood in the midst of the ambushes, one hundred Turks sprang out in a rush from the small chambers, surrounded the men with weapons and arrows, and captured them, able to make little resistance against so many.

Only two of the twelve, wrenching themselves from the enemy’s hands through manly and strenuous resistance, suddenly escaped into a hall with windows overlooking the valley. Drawing their swords, they defended themselves so stoutly against the pursuing enemies that, thrusting their heads out of the windows, they warned Baldwin, standing with his men at the foot of the mountain, to beware of treachery. They declared that ten had been captured through false faith and that they themselves were plainly in danger of death.

### Chapter XXI.—Baldwin is grievously distressed at the capture of his knights.

Baldwin, learning from their anguished cries that the whole affair had turned to disaster and that Balas’s treachery was manifest, was tortured with great grief over the captivity of his men. But what he should do, or what course he should pursue to free them, he could discover by no counsel. For the fortress stood on a lofty crag, impregnable by human ingenuity or strength.

At length Baldwin, grieving over the misfortune of such distinguished men [Col. 0523B], sharply reproached Balas for his wicked deceit, reminded him of his oath, and offered to receive back his captives by giving him a weight of gold and Byzantine coins for their ransom. But Balas rejected every offer and demanded only the city of Sororgia. Baldwin swore by God that he would never surrender the city to him, even if Balas were to mutilate before his eyes, limb by limb, every man whom he had captured. Thus, since Balas would neither heed Baldwin’s entreaties and remonstrances nor value any gifts except Sororgia, Baldwin returned sorrowful to Edessa, lamenting bitterly for his captives. From that day he began to hold the Turks—their counsel, assistance, and intercourse—in vehement hatred.

### Chapter XXII.—Balduc is beheaded; six of Baldwin’s companions are restored.

[Col. 0523C]

Not many days later, Balduc of Samosata, who was to have given his wife and children to Baldwin as hostages but had deceitfully delayed this for many days, entered Baldwin’s palace with flattering words. By Baldwin’s order he was seized by the Franks and beheaded.

Baldwin stationed Folker of Chartres in the city of Sororgia with one hundred worthy knights experienced in war, so that they might continually harass Amacha by assault and endeavour to exact from Balas a fitting return in vengeance for his captive brethren. Accordingly, one day Folker and his men went out to seize booty in the territory of Amacha. Having sent some companions ahead, they drew the Turks from the fortress as far as the place where Folker’s ambush lay. Then battle was joined, and six Turks and soldiers of Balas were captured [Col. 0523D] and carried away.

When these had been captured and taken off, Balas restored six of Baldwin’s companions in exchange for his own men; six he retained in his custody at Jerusalem until that day. Afterwards four escaped through the guards’ negligence and their prolonged weariness. But Balas ordered Gerard, Baldwin’s confidential servant and secretary, together with Piscellus, son of the sister of Ubelhard—a distinguished and very noble knight of Wizam—to be beheaded.

### Chapter XXIII.—A multitude of Germans arriving is consumed by the aforesaid plague.

While Godfrey, because of the widespread destruction caused by so severe a pestilence throughout Antioch, was staying at Ravendel and Turbessel, at the same time fifteen hundred men of the German people, united and chosen from Regensburg, a city on the Danube, and from other cities on the Rhine, were brought by sea to the city of Antioch. They landed at the port of St. Symeon, intending to increase the Christian companies going to Jerusalem with comfort and assistance.

But when this band joined the recently victorious pilgrims in the month of August, it was consumed and devastated by the same plague so completely that not even one of the fifteen hundred seemed anywhere to have survived. [Col. 0524A]

### Chapter XXIV.—Sansadonius ransoms his mother with two sons; Winemar returns; the hostage Mahomet is carefully guarded; ships are repaired.

At the same time, after the Christians’ victory, Sansadonius, son of Darsian, king of Antioch, ransomed his mother [Col. 0524B] together with his two sons for the price of three thousand Byzantine coins from the hand of William, a most noble man, fellow-soldier and compatriot of Count Raymond of Provence. This William had captured them, overcome by sleep, at dawn during the first attack and entry into Antioch.

At the same time Winemar of the land of Boulogne, captured at Laodicea by the Turcopoles of the Greek emperor, was released at Duke Godfrey’s request after long bonds and prolonged imprisonment. Though afflicted by severe punishment, he returned to Antioch.

But the boy Mahomet, son of the prince of Hasart, given to Godfrey as a hostage, remained at Antioch under careful guard: both under that of his own twelve servants and under the vigilant care of Godfrey’s household. Nothing necessary was lacking to him at any hour from the duke’s household. [Col. 0524C]

For many, seeing that the duke and other powerful men had left the places around Antioch because of the impending pestilence—some attributing this mortality to the unhealthiness of the place, others to the pestilential month of August—set out, at the beginning of September, for the port of the aforesaid Symeon in order to remain there. There, after the Turks’ slaughter and Kerbogha’s flight, sailors refitted their ships, bringing the necessities of life and selling everything in sufficient quantity to those in need.

### Chapter XXV.—On a portent shown from heaven, and diverse interpretations of it.

Then, at mid-month, in the silence of a certain night, when all things are ordinarily refreshed by the rest of sleep, a marvellous vision appeared in the summit of heaven to all who were keeping watch. It was as though stars from the whole sky had gathered into one mass and, densely packed together, flashed with fiery brilliance—like embers burning in a furnace and gathered into a globe—within an area as broad as one court containing three acres. [Col. 0524D]

After this prolonged and terrible burning, they became thinner and encircled the heavens in the form of a crown over the space occupied by the fortified city. Remaining thus a long time in an unbroken circle, they finally opened a passage and way by being parted on one side of their circle.

Alarmed by the appearance of this sign, the Christian watchmen roused all those sunk in sleep with tumultuous cries, that they might behold this token of a portent. All marvelled and offered various opinions as to what it foretold. Some maintained that it signified the city of Jerusalem densely filled with bands of heathen Turks [Col. 0525A], and that these would become sparse and scattered through the weakening of their strength and density, so that at last an entrance would seem to be afforded to the Christian sons.

Others said that it signified the Christian army, still gathered in its strength and burning with the fervour of divine devotion, which, afterwards divided throughout the land and the cities unjustly possessed by the nations, would prevail and exercise power in the circuit of Jerusalem and Antioch. Yet others said that it signified the present pestilence and the abundant population of pilgrims, who, gathered together like a dense cloud, would be thinned and diminished. Thus they contended in differing interpretations.

But, by God’s will, as they say, the meaning of the vision was changed for the better. For when Duke Godfrey, summoned from every place together with all the Christian allies, had returned to Antioch in October, after the heat of August had abated, Count Raymond, Robert of Flanders, Robert, prince of the Normans, Bohemond, and the other princes who still remained assembled in Antioch, became united in one purpose. They dispersed through the lands and cities around Antioch, besieged those who resisted and rebelled, and subjected them to their dominion. [Col. 0525B]

### Chapter XXVI.—The deeds of the princes, and Bohemond’s lordship in Antioch.

They first advanced with armed divisions against the city of Albara, exceedingly rich in wealth. Having taken it after no great labour, they struck down with the sword [Col. 0525C] the Turks and Saracens found there. Then, as victory followed victory, Count Raymond, Robert prince of the Normans, Eustace brother of Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, Bohemond—now prince of Antioch—and Duke Godfrey turned aside toward Maarrat, a city of the Turks rich in arms and strength.

But Godfrey, Bohemond, and Robert of Flanders remained there in siege only fifteen days. Then these three returned to Antioch, leaving Count Raymond, Robert prince of the Normans, Eustace, and Tancred around the city of Maarrat with their thousands.

After several days Duke Godfrey, taking forty companions strong in arms and horsemanship, set out toward the city of Edessa [Col. 0525D], which lies seven days’ journey from Antioch. There his brother Baldwin, who held that city with all its dependencies, met him halfway beyond the great river Euphrates in order that they might confer together.

Bohemond, whose heart was gnawed by the deepest envy and indignation against Count Raymond, saw the opportunity provided by Godfrey’s departure and Raymond’s absence. Having alerted and gathered his companions by the trumpet signal, he attacked with great force the tower overlooking the bridge of Ferna. He drove from the fortress and city, by battle and arrows, Count Raymond’s knights who had remained there; and thus he alone obtained dominion over Antioch.

### Chapter XXVII.—How Duke Godfrey detected a Turkish ambush and struck down many in a narrow pass.

[Col. 0526A]

Afterward, Duke Godfrey, having conferred with his brother and taken leave of him, set out quickly for Antioch, where he intended to return to his brethren and the princes with the aforesaid forty companions. He was received peacefully and favourably as a guest at Turbessel, Ravendel, and other places.

Then, hastening along the road into the region called the Bishopric, he halted one day with his companions for a meal beside a certain spring in a grassy meadow. He set down wineskins filled with wine and the other necessities of life which they had carried with them on mules and horses. While he was dining there securely with his companions, boys whom he had sent to scout out Turkish ambushes informed him that one hundred Turks lay hidden in a reedy and marshy place beside a large lake rich in fish, near the mountains, five miles from the city of Antioch, waiting there for the duke’s return. [Col. 0526B]

As soon as their ambush was revealed, the duke postponed the meal and suddenly mounted with those attached to him. Seizing their arms and putting on their hauberks, they hastened toward the enemy. The Turks, no less promptly turning their reins against them, vigorously joined battle with bows and arrows. But victory was granted to the duke and his few men, fighting for their lives.

At last the duke and his men prevailed: they pierced the fleeing Turks with lances, beheaded others, and carried their heads, hanging from their saddles, to the city of Antioch together with their spoils and horses. There the duke found Bohemond, now prince of the whole city, and reported everything to him and to the other princes and brethren—how so many Turks had been conquered and crushed by the hand of so few. [Col. 0526C]

### Chapter XXVIII.—On the Christians’ murmuring and the conference of the princes.

After Duke Godfrey’s return with this victory, some time later the Christian people unanimously complained that they were being kept merely in Antioch and by no means advancing upon the road to Jerusalem, for the desire of which they had left their native lands and endured so many adversities. Great dissension arose among the people, and many withdrew from the forces of Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and Bohemond, having no confidence in their replies and words concerning a long-delayed journey to Jerusalem. [Col. 0526D]

At length the aforesaid princes, recognizing that the people, overcome by weariness, were gradually slipping away, prohibited anyone from preparing a return by sea; they posted guards at every maritime port. They decreed that an assembly and conference concerning the people’s complaint should be held on the fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February].

Accordingly, when they had assembled and held conference within Antioch, it was decreed by all, great and small alike, that on the Kalends of March [1 March] they should meet together at Laodicea, which was under Christian authority. Having gathered strength there from every side and henceforward taking no account of danger to life, they should delay no longer in setting out on the road to Jerusalem.

### Chapter XXIX.—On the dreadful extremity of famine during the siege of Maarrat.

[Col. 0527A]

Meanwhile Count Raymond and all those remaining with his company were wearied by a prolonged siege of five weeks around the city of Maarrat. Long encamped around the city and severely pressed by the Turks, they endured great extremity of hunger. Nor is this surprising: because of the long siege of Antioch, and now of these cities, many surrounding regions had been exhausted of provisions, and a great part of the inhabitants had fled into the mountains with their possessions and herds.

There were ten thousand in the army of Count Raymond and his chief associates. Marvellous to tell and dreadful to hear! Such was the extremity of famine that afflicted these cities that it is shameful to speak of it, much less to do it. For the Christians, in the scarcity you have heard of, did not shrink from eating not merely Turks or Saracens who had been killed, but even dogs seized and cooked over fire. [Col. 0527B] But what wonder? “No sword is sharper than hunger long endured.”

### Chapter XXX.—How Count Raymond destroyed a fortress and captured Maarrat.

Count Raymond, seeing the distress and pain of a people failing from hunger, took a force of knights and went into the mountains. From time to time he brought back innumerable quantities of booty and provisions, by which God’s people were often refreshed. There, throughout the wildernesses and mountains of Lebanon, many Christians seeking food, driven by the aforesaid necessity, were found slain by the Turks.

Finally, ambushes often came out from Damascus, which was the Turks’ principal stronghold; they fell upon men scattered and wandering away from the army and siege, slaughtering some and piercing others with deadly arrows. But Count Raymond, learning of the evils inflicted upon his men encamped around the city through Turkish ambushes, was deeply troubled and considered every means of ending this calamity.

Accordingly he attacked Talaria, a fortress situated in the mountains. Having stormed and destroyed it by the strength of valiant men, together with the Turks found in it, he brought timber from that fortress. From it he constructed a siege-engine for overcoming the aforesaid city of Maarrat, which was very strongly fortified with walls and ramparts. [Col. 0527C]

When the engine had been constructed and the siege-machines arranged, the city was overcome, captured, and overthrown after no long time by Count Raymond and the other princes, Robert, Tancred, and Eustace. Christian knights, shielded and armoured, stood in great force in the middle of the city and struck with the sword the Turks, who resisted fiercely and defended themselves. They pursued others fleeing to the citadel and burned them. They remained there peacefully for three weeks, finding few provisions except an abundance of oil.

Engelrad, son of Count Hugh, a young man of remarkable boldness, died in this city after being overcome by illness. His body was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Andrew. [Col. 0527D]

### Chapter XXXI.—How Raymond, having stormed Turkish and Saracen strongholds, besieged the fortress of Arqa, and of the difficulty of that siege.

[Col. 0528A]

After the aforesaid city of Maarrat had been conquered and destroyed, the army of the aforesaid princes descended to a valley which they called Joy. Having found an abundance of necessities, they refreshed their bodies, worn out and emaciated by hunger, for eight days, after storming two mountain strongholds inhabited by Turks and Saracens.

Then, having stormed and captured the city of Tortosa without much labour, and placed it in Count Raymond’s power and under his guard, they continued their journey and came to the valley called the Valley of Camels. There they gathered much booty and food, and then advanced against a certain fortress called Arqa, impregnable by siege-engines and human strength. [Col. 0528B] Pitching their tents there, they determined to remain for some time until that fortress should be taken by defeating its defenders.

There they constructed siege-engines and mangonels, hurling masses of stones violently against towers and ancient walls, in order to terrify and drive off the knights shut up in the stronghold. But they found the defenders tireless and most unconquerable. From within, they resisted with the like discharge of mangonels and force of stones, inflicting damage upon the Christian host with arrows and stones alike.

They struck Anselm of Riburgis Monte, a most noble and warlike man who was inflicting great force upon the defenders of the fortress, with a stone hurled from that same castle; his brain shattered, he was killed. [Col. 0528C] Grieved and troubled by the death of their most illustrious brother and fellow-soldier and by the resistance of the enclosed Saracens, the princes resolved to excavate the mountains beneath the foundations of the fortress’s walls, so that, once the foundation had collapsed together with the ramparts and walls, the heathens standing on these or in the citadel might perish, overwhelmed beneath the ruins of stones and roofs.

But this labour was spent in vain. For those inside dug in the opposite direction, caught the Christians’ implements by their own devices, and did not allow their work to come to completion.

### Chapter XXXII.—How a dispute arose concerning the Lord’s lance; and how the hostage boy Mahomet died and was honourably sent by Duke Godfrey to his father.

[Col. 0528D]

There, during that same siege, a contention and dispute arose concerning the Lord’s lance: whether or not it was the lance by which the Lord’s side had been opened. For many doubted, and division existed among them. Therefore the author and propagator of that discovery passed through fire and, as they say, emerged unharmed. Count Raymond of Provence himself and Raymond Pilet drew him away from the hands and pressure of his jealous opponents; and from that day they venerated the lance together with all their company.

Afterwards it was reported by some that the same cleric had been so seriously injured by the burning ordeal that he died and was buried shortly thereafter. Consequently the lance began to be held in less reverence by the faithful, who believed that all had been done more by Raymond’s avarice and contrivance [Col. 0529A] than by any truth of divinity.

While these sieges were being conducted around Maarrat, Tortosa, and Arqa, the boy Mahomet, who had been sent as a hostage to Antioch by his father, the prince of Hasart, and entrusted to the faith and guardianship of Duke Godfrey, was seized by illness and died. In accordance with the custom of the heathen, Godfrey sent him back to his father wrapped in costly purple cloth. He excused himself with every sincerity of good faith, declaring that the boy had not died through any negligence on his part; he also protested that he grieved at the boy’s death no less than at that of his own brother Baldwin.

The father received the duke’s excuse kindly and learned the truth from those whom he had sent from his own household as guardians of the boy. He was not in the least moved away from the faith he had promised, but remained steadfast in every compact and peace with the duke and his brother Baldwin.

### Chapter XXXIII.—How Duke Godfrey and Robert of Flanders besieged the city of Gibelet, and how Count Raymond, corrupted by money, recalled these princes from the siege by a deceitful embassy.

[Col. 0529B]

Meanwhile, when the Kalends of March had arrived in due order, Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, Bohemond, and all the princes still remaining at Antioch, as they had decreed, assembled their army at Laodicea—some twenty thousand horsemen and foot soldiers—and pitched camp before the city of Gibelet, situated on the seashore and rich in wealth. They laid siege around it, in order to overcome and bring to an end the Saracens and all heathens stationed there for its defence.

But Bohemond returned from Laodicea [Col. 0529C] and went back with his men to Antioch, ever anxious and suspicious lest he should lose that city, impregnable by human strength, through some treachery or hatred.

Before long, when the destruction of Albara and Maarrat and the slaughter of their Turkish inhabitants had been heard of, as well as the present long siege and capture of Arqa, the Saracen soldiers, having taken counsel with the citizens, offered an immense sum of money to Duke Godfrey and Robert of Flanders. They asked that the city of Gibelet, with its citizens, vineyards, and all crops, might remain untouched in their sight, and that their army should move elsewhere. The aforesaid princes wholly refused this, unless the city with its keys were surrendered to their authority.

Therefore the citizens and magistrates of the city, understanding that those princes could not be bribed by money or precious gifts to remove their camp, secretly sent messengers to Count Raymond at Arqa, renowned among the foremost of the heathen for his deeds and power. They asked him to accept the money which the duke and the others had rejected, and to persuade the Christian princes by entreaty or some device to withdraw from the siege. [Col. 0529D]

The count, insatiable for gold and silver, turned over schemes and devices by which he might remove those most powerful men from the siege of Gibelet, free the citizens and their vineyards and crops in return for the money to be received; for he had no confidence whatever that he could turn them from their undertaking by entreaties. He therefore invented this pretext: that the Turks, of whom there was a great multitude in Damascus, had formed a plan with the Saracens, Arabs, and all nations to wage imminent war against him at Arqa, and had already assembled in great and abundant preparation upon his borders.

Having arranged this fabrication, he sent messengers to the aforesaid princes, who had now been encamped around Gibelet for a week, asking them to hurry swiftly to his aid at Arqa; otherwise, he and the brethren with him could not escape the danger of death at the hands of the heathen, and they themselves might thereafter expect a similar martyrdom. [Col. 0530A]

### Chapter XXXIV.—How the princes struck camp from the siege of Gibelet and hurried to Raymond’s aid.

When Count Raymond’s envoys had been heard, and the danger and fear said to arise from the approaching multitude of heathen considered, the duke and the other chief men unanimously took counsel. Every heart and tongue was directed to this conclusion:

> “When the great Christian army was still whole and undivided together at Antioch, it was scarcely defended against innumerable heathen nations and arms. But now one part has been left at Antioch, one part is divided in this siege of Gibelet, one part is at Arqa, and another has gone to storm the enemy’s fortresses and cities. Thus our forces are reduced and will by no means now be able to stand against so many thousands of heathen, as we have learned from Count Raymond’s report. If, by adverse fortune, the strength of our men at Arqa should be crushed, we must without doubt expect the same fate ourselves. Therefore Gibelet, which we cannot suddenly strike and conquer, must at this time be left untouched; we must bring our camp and army to the aid of our men at Arqa and meet the heathen in battle together with our companions. As God wills in heaven, so let it be.” [Col. 0530B–C]

As all saw and declared this counsel to be good and useful, the camp was removed from the siege of Gibelet. Duke Godfrey and Robert of Flanders, with all the others, set out fully armed and with every preparation for war. In about three days they came to Arqa, to strengthen and assist their Christian companions.

But they learned from Tancred and many others that no forces or threats of heathen were present; rather, that Count Raymond had falsely alleged this gathering of enemies and summoned them to his aid for no other reason than to receive the money which the inhabitants of Gibelet had promised for their own liberation, so that by his stratagem he might turn the Christians away from besieging the walls. [Col. 0530D]

### Chapter XXXV.—The aforesaid princes, deceived by a false embassy, withdraw from Raymond’s company; he recalls them to concord by flattery and gifts.

When the aforesaid princes understood that Count Raymond had deceived them through this trick and false embassy, they took it painfully and gravely. They withdrew from his association and fellowship, pitched their tents two miles apart from him, brought him no assistance whatever in the attack upon Arqa, and held no friendly conversation with him. [Col. 0531A]

For grave hostilities had arisen at Arqa between Count Raymond and Tancred because of the agreement concerning the solidi and Byzantine coins which the count owed Tancred for military service, but did not pay in proportion to the labour and number of knights which Tancred provided and led. From the very day when Duke Godfrey had come there with the other powerful men, Tancred repeatedly reminded the count of his agreement. But the count gave him no answer containing any hope. Tancred remained with the duke, faithfully bound to him in every military subordination, and utterly scorned the count.

Henceforth, avenging the injuries inflicted upon him by the count, he did not spare the count’s companions and friends, but harmed them by ambushes and every possible means. Count Raymond, therefore, seeing that Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and all who were with them bore him grave hatred because he had deceived them by a false embassy, being corrupted by avarice began to soothe the duke’s mind with his flatteries and the craft in which he had been trained and schooled from boyhood. Thus in the end he entirely softened Tancred’s anger.

Then the count sent the duke a horse of great value and handsome form, so that he might more completely placate his mind and, by these gifts, draw him back with himself to the assault on Arqa. For he knew him to be a man of great patience and affection; once he had been placated and reconciled, the others too might return in goodwill to concord. Finally the princes on both sides, except Tancred, became reconciled. With a joint assault and siege they pressed hard upon the fortress of Arqa, and from the day the duke came there they remained encamped for the course of four weeks. [Col. 0531B–C]

### Chapter XXXVI.—How murmuring grew among the people of God because they delayed the road to Jerusalem so long.

At length, when all were wearied by the assault on the fortress and their excavation of the mountain had failed through intolerable labour, incalculable resistance from within, and lack of life’s necessities, murmuring grew among the people of the duke and Robert of Flanders. All declared that they could remain no longer in siege there, and that this fortress, impregnable by force and skill, could scarcely be taken even in the course of a year, even if it might then be conquered by the sword of hunger. [Col. 0531D]

Therefore all, small and great, urgently pressed the duke to remove the camp from the siege and set out for Jerusalem, as they had decreed—the Jerusalem for whose desire and to behold the tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ they had departed from their native lands.

On the contrary, Count Raymond used every means and promise to induce them to remain with him for some further time, until the fortress and the heathens shut up in it should be captured by force or skill. He recounted how Anselm of Riburgis Monte had fallen there and been killed, and how several of his fellow-soldiers had been condemned by those same Saracens, some to death, others to exceedingly cruel wounds.

But, unable to keep them from their desire and purpose by any contrivance of flattery or promise, he declared that he and his own would remain in that place until the hostile fortress was consumed by ruin in vengeance for his men who had been crushed. [Col. 0532A]

### Chapter XXXVII.—The siege of Arqa is raised; the princes pitch their tents far from the city of Tripoli; the people suck sweet canes found on the plains.

While the count persisted in this intention and by many devices sought to prevent his brethren’s departure, one day Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and Tancred also, together with all their followers, set fire to their camp and departed from the siege of Arqa. Many from Raymond’s company joined them: exhausted by prolonged weariness, they had unwillingly remained at Arqa, especially because of their continual desire to go to Jerusalem. For from the beginning they had sat with the count for two and a half months around the fortress of Arqa. [Col. 0532B]

When the count saw that all the people were following the duke, that his force had melted away, and that few remained with him as helpers, he followed the duke’s and the others’ footsteps, willingly or unwillingly. With the others he brought his company into the territory of the city of Tripoli, or Triple, situated on the seashore.

There, at a distance from the city, all spread their tents, lest so great an army injure the inhabitants’ crops and vineyards. For mediators and envoys from that city had repeatedly come down to Arqa to the aforesaid princes, bringing many gifts and promising greater ones if they would spare the city and its possessions and not do to it what they had done to Albara, Maarrat, and the other cities. For this reason the army and all its leaders settled at a distance from the city, until they should see by what arrangement, treaty, or offering of gifts they might be appeased and mutually establish friendship. [Col. 0532C]

There the people sucked in abundance the sweet canes found across the plain of the fields, called *zucra*, delighting in their wholesome juice; and because of their sweetness they could scarcely be satisfied after tasting them. This kind of herb is cultivated annually with great labour by farmers.
