Then, when ripe at harvest-time, the natives crush it in small mortars and store its collected juice in vessels until it coagulates and hardens with the appearance of snow or white salt. Scraping it off, they mix it with bread or dissolve it in water and take it as a food; when tasted with honeycomb, it seems sweet and wholesome. [Col. 0532D]

Some say that it was the kind of honey which Jonathan, son of King Saul, found upon the face of the ground and presumed to taste in disobedience. Thus the people, greatly tormented by dreadful hunger during the sieges of Albara, Maarrat, and Arqa, were refreshed by these sweet-flavoured canes.

### Chapter XXXVIII.—Having made a treaty, the governor of Tripoli provided the people of God with a guide, under whose direction they passed through the most difficult places.

The governor of the glorious and wealthy city of Triple, understanding that the legions of the faithful had encamped at a considerable distance before the city’s walls and gates, sent to the leading men of the army—Duke Godfrey, Count Robert of Flanders [Col. 0533A], Count Raymond, and Robert prince of the Normans—that they might receive gifts from him, so that he might keep his own land safe from them, as well as the land of Gibelet and the fortress of Arqa.

At length, after deliberation, the governor came in great friendship to the duke’s tents. Satisfying the princes with gifts and peaceful words, he provided them with an elderly man as a guide through the mountains beside the seacoast, where the paths were intricate and unknown. From the seashore this man led them by a winding way through narrow mountain defiles along so tight a path that scarcely could one man follow another, or one animal another.

This mountain extends from the highlands in great length as far as the sea. At its summit a tower projected over the road, built across it by means of a gateway. Six men could stand in the tower’s chamber, and by their defence the road could be denied to all who live under heaven. But at that time no one resisted those passing, because of the army’s presence and the escort of the governor of Triple. [Col. 0533B]

Having overcome these very narrow and difficult defiles through the knowledge of their Saracen guide and travelling companion, and returning to the way along the seacoast, they reached the city of Gibelet, on whose behalf the governor of Tripoli had interceded. Leaving it untouched in accordance with their promise, they travelled only one mile farther and spent the night beside a river of sweet water. They remained there also the following day, waiting for the weak common people, worn out by the toil of travelling through pathless and rocky ground.

### Chapter XXXIX.—On the difficulty of the journey and how they made a treaty with the inhabitants of Beirut.

[Col. 0533C]

On the third day thereafter, moving camp and again continuing their road along the seashore, they entered a mountain path of astonishing and unheard-of narrowness. It is said to have been created by a sudden flood and erosion from rain rushing headlong downwards, and to be the route for travellers passing that way.

This mountain is struck by the sea’s waves, so close and continual, that no one can turn in any way either to the right or left, lest he be in danger of falling readily into the depths of the sea. Having completed this difficult passage and also passed, through the mountains, another fortified tower as impregnable as the tower mentioned above—both of which remained wholly without defence because fear instilled by God, not by man, had struck the Saracen guards—they arrived at evening and lodged near the city of Baurim, or Baruth [Beirut]. Their Saracen guide and travelling companion continually went before and led them. [Col. 0533D]

The inhabitants of Baurim, recognizing the Christians’ arrival and that the army was already encamped across the city’s fields, sent acceptable gifts and peaceful words to the aforesaid princes in this form:

> “We pray that you may pass peacefully, without devastating our trees, vines, and crops. And if, with favourable fortune, you fulfil your purpose of taking Jerusalem, we shall serve you with all our possessions.”

Appeased by these entreaties, promises, and gifts of the inhabitants of Baurim, the aforesaid princes rose with the whole Christian army and again continued their journey along the seashore, through the same defiles and harsh rocky places against which the storms of the sea continually beat. [Col. 0534A]

### Chapter XL.—How many perished from serpents in the region of Sidon, and concerning the loss of a certain Walter.

Having left these places, they descended into the plain containing the city called Sagitta, where they remained encamped beside the bank of a certain fresh-water river. There they found very many heaps of stones, among which, while an innumerable host of weak and poor folk rested and lay down in weariness, some, bitten by serpents called *Tarenta*, died from swelling and an unbearable thirst, their limbs distended by an extraordinary inflammation. [Col. 0534B]

There too the Saracens, trusting in their strength and coming out from the city of Sidon, dared to harass the army, killing pilgrims who were seeking provisions and necessities in the district of that city. But, severely repelled by the Christian cavalry, some were slain by weapons, while others, reckoning that their hope of safety lay in the waters, were drowned and perished, suffocated by the waves. The Christians would doubtless have besieged and reduced this city in vengeance for their people; but they turned aside because of their desire to go to Jerusalem.

While many in this region of Sidon were endangered by the aforesaid fiery serpents, and great groaning and lamentation arose over those who were dying, the natives taught them the following remedy: that everyone bitten by serpents should approach one of the nobler and more powerful men [Col. 0534C] of the army, because, if the wound of the sting were touched and enclosed by that man’s right hand, the poison diffused through the limbs would thereafter appear unable to harm him. They were likewise taught another remedy: that a man who had been bitten should without delay have intercourse with a woman, and a woman with a man; and thus either should be freed from every swelling caused by the poison.

The Christian people also learned from the inhabitants to strike stones continually against one another by hand, or to make a sound by repeatedly beating their shields; thus, when the serpents had been terrified by this sound and clamor, their companions could sleep safely. Then, at dawn on the following day, a certain fellow-brother of the Christians, a man and knight born of noble family, Walter by name, of the castle of Verna, taking some companions [Col. 0534D] from his company, set out into the mountains. There he gathered a great abundance of booty, which he entrusted to squires and some of his companions and sent to the army. He himself desired to seek out still greater quantities in every direction, and entered, by a narrow and difficult approach, into a place enclosed by mountains where there were vast herds and Saracen possessions. There, surrounded by them, it remains unknown to this day by what end he perished.

## CHAPTER XLI.—How they passed through the cities of Tyre, Ptolemais, Caiphas, and Caesarea, and thus celebrated Pentecost.

The aforesaid princes and all their company, not knowing why the distinguished knight delayed beyond the appointed time, remained for a third day in the district of the city of Sidon, in case the honorable knight might perhaps [Col. 0535A] return from the mountains, or they might learn something of his arrival. But when he was found neither at the first light nor at the second, they departed from the city’s station.

Thence, having the level plain of the fields before them as far as Tyre, now called Sur, they descended with their guide and pitched camp there across the plain of the fields. For there a spring flows forth, raised by a walled and arched structure in such a way that, by the force and abundance of its waters, it produces at its source so great a stream that the whole army could not exhaust it.

On the following day, leaving Sur, they arrived at the city named Ptolemais, which modern people now call Accaron, because it is the city of God, Accaron. Leaving it on their right upon the seashore, they spent two nights beside a sweet-tasting river which there flows into the sea. [Col. 0535B] There two roads divide: one leads by Damascus and the River Jordan, on the left, to Jerusalem; the other continues on the right beside the shore of the aforesaid sea to Jerusalem.

Since among fifty thousand men scarcely twenty thousand capable in war could be found, they resolved not to pass through Damascus, because of the multitude of Turks inhabiting Damascus and because of the open expanse of plains there, where they seemed liable to enemy attack on every side. Therefore, taking the road along the shore between the sea and the mountains, where they could travel with confidence, protected on their right by the sea and by the inaccessible height of the mountains, they passed the city of Caiphas, named after Caiaphas, once chief priest. [Col. 0535C] On the same day they remained encamped in the territory of Caesarea—the city once called Strato’s Tower, rebuilt later by Herod in honor of Caesar and named Caesarea.

There, at the foot of a mountain, a spring flows and enters the city through the open plain of the fields. Duke Godfrey and Robert of Flanders pitched their tents and lodged there. Count Raymond and Robert, prince of the Normans, pitched camp after them, at some distance away on the same river, separated by a very extensive marsh formed by that river. Having stayed there for four days, they celebrated most devoutly the Saturday of holy Pentecost and the very day of the coming of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLII.—How they found and occupied the city of Ramla, and established a bishop in it.

[Col. 0535D]

Passing the aforesaid cities untouched, they continued their journey on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday through the territory and broad plain of the aforementioned Caesarea of Cornelius, in the land of the Palestinians. On Thursday they brought their camp to the river of the city of Rama, or Rames, and, pitching their tents on the bank of that riverbed, decided to spend the night.

Robert of Flanders and Gaston, a fighting man from Bordeaux, taking five hundred fellow recruits, sent on ahead from the company, advanced to the gates and to scout out the walls. They entered through gates which stood open and unbarred, finding no one in the city. For, having heard of the distress and misfortune of the pagans round about and of the capture of Antioch, [Col. 0536A] all the citizens had fled from the face of the Christians into mountain and desert places, concealing themselves with their children, wives, herds, and treasures.

Thus, finding the city of Rames empty of citizens and arms, they hastily sent a message to the Catholic people encamped on the riverbank, bidding all come to enter and possess the city and refresh their bodies, which great and prolonged labors had afflicted. On hearing this, the pilgrims went without delay to the city and rested there for three days, refreshed by the wine, oil, and abundant grain they found. They also appointed a certain Robert bishop there, leaving Christian inhabitants in it to cultivate the land, administer justice, and render the produce of fields and vineyards.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—While the army advanced toward the mountains, an eclipse of the moon appeared at night.

[Col. 0536B]

Then, when the fourth day dawned, the pilgrims set out together, leaving the city of Rames. They resolved to proceed as far as the place where these mountains begin—the mountains which surround the city of Jerusalem, situated in their midst, on every side. But in that place there was an extreme shortage of water. Therefore, having learned from the report of their Saracen companion and guide that cisterns and watered springs were to be found at the castle of Emmaus three miles away, they sent a large band of armed men, who brought back not only an abundance of water but also plentiful fodder for the horses.

That very night there occurred an eclipse of the moon, which was on the fifteenth day. It failed entirely of its brightness [Col. 0536C] and, changed wholly into a blood-red color until the middle of the night, brought no small fear upon all who saw it—unless they received this consolation from certain persons knowledgeable about the stars. For these said that the portent did not foretell an evil omen for the Christians, but that the moon’s eclipse and its bloody darkness undoubtedly signified the destruction of the Saracens. An eclipse of the sun, however, they declared to be an ominous portent for Christians.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—How the Christian inhabitants of Bethlehem sent envoys to Duke Godfrey, urging him to hasten to their aid; and concerning the joyful reception of their companions.

[Col. 0536D]

After the Christians had encamped in that same place near the mountains of Jerusalem with the whole army, and evening was now approaching, an embassy from the Catholic inhabitants of the city of Bethlehem was made known to Duke Godfrey—especially from those whom the Saracens, suspecting them of treachery upon the Christians’ approach, had expelled from Jerusalem while still threatening them with death. They begged that, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the duke should hasten without any delay to come to their aid. For pagans from every region of the kingdom of Babylon, having heard of the Christians’ arrival, were gathering in Jerusalem for the city’s defense and for their slaughter.

When the duke heard the embassy, its prayers, and the Christians’ peril, that same night he sent ahead about one hundred mailed horsemen chosen from [Col. 0537A] his camp and company to assist the distressed and gathered faithful of Christ in Bethlehem. Obeying the Christian duke’s command, they mounted their horses and, quickly covering six miles through the whole night, arrived at Bethlehem at the first light of day.

When the Christian citizens learned of their arrival, they went out to meet them with hymns, praises, and sprinkling of consecrated water, and joyfully received the Christian horsemen, kissing their eyes and hands and saying to them:

> “Thanks be to God, because in our own times we now see what has always been our desire: namely, that you, our Christian brothers, are here to shake off the yoke of our servitude; to restore the holy places of Jerusalem; and to remove the rites of the pagans and their uncleannesses [Col. 0537B] from the holy place.”

## CHAPTER XLV.—How the army hastened to Jerusalem upon learning of the embassy from Bethlehem; concerning booty carried off from the city’s neighbors; and how they stood before Jerusalem’s walls in praises and hymns.

Hardly had the horsemen sent ahead departed from the camp when, behold, word reached the ears of the leaders and the whole army that an embassy had come to the duke from Bethlehem. For this reason, scarcely had midnight passed when all, small and great alike, struck camp and took the narrow road through constricted paths and tight mountain passes. Every horseman eagerly pressed ahead and hastened the march, lest, as the narrow passages of the paths were flooded by a multitude of foot soldiers, a great obstacle should arise for the cavalry. [Col. 0537C] Great and small alike indeed hastened toward Jerusalem with equal zeal.

The soldiers who had been sent ahead, returning from Bethlehem, joined them on the road at the very time when the heat of the morning sun usually dries the dew upon the grass. Gaston of the city of Bordeaux, withdrawing secretly from the army with thirty men skilled in battle and ambush, prudently knowing that the citizens and soldiers of Jerusalem were still unaware of the approaching pilgrims’ strength, gave his reins free course with his men through the borders of that city and gathered and drove off booty from every side.

But when his bold action became known, the booty was recovered by the citizens and Saracen soldiers, who pursued Gaston and his companions as far as the ascent of a certain rock. From that same rock Tancred was descending from the opposite side, having likewise gone ahead of the army to seek necessities, [Col. 0537D] when Gaston encountered him. Gaston informed him of the Saracens’ sortie from the city and the recovery of his booty, and greatly inflamed Tancred’s spirit to pursue those enemies. Therefore, both, combining their companies’ forces, vigorously urged their horses against the enemy’s rear, putting them to flight as far as the gate of Jerusalem. They retained the booty and brought it to the following Christian army.

When the herds of booty and the returning brethren were seen, all asked whence they had brought away this abundance of spoil. They declared that they had seized and carried it away from the plain of Jerusalem. Hearing Jerusalem named, all flowed into tears of joy [Col. 0538A] because they were so near the holy place of the desired city, for which they had endured so many labors, so many dangers, and so many kinds of death. Immediately, from their longing for the city they had heard named and their love of seeing the holy city, they forgot their labor and weariness and hastened their journey more than usual. No delay whatever was made until about sixty thousand persons of both sexes stood before the walls of Jerusalem, weeping for joy amid shouts of praise and hymns.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—How and by which leaders the city was besieged.

When the most Christian army had assembled in these places under diverse banners and arms, the city gates were closed by the soldiers of the king of Babylon; the Tower of David was fortified with an armed garrison; and all the citizens were spread along the walls to hinder and resist the Catholic people. For the king of Babylon had broken the treaty which his envoys, sent to Antioch, had made with the Christian leaders. He had no cause against them except that Count Raymond had taken the city of Tortosa and besieged the fortress of Arqa for many days.

The Christians, seeing the king’s soldiery, the city’s fortifications, and the resistance of the pagans, encircled the walls with a positioned siege. They stationed Duke Godfrey—powerful in counsel and strength—with the Germans, most fierce in war, on the side of the Tower of David, where the greatest force of defense was concentrated. With him they placed Count Tancred; and they resolved that Raymond, with two bishops from Italy and his company, should take position before the gate [Col. 0538C] of that same tower.

Then Robert of Flanders and the aged Hugh of Saint-Pol chose, with their companions, to take position and besiege the city walls in the sloping part of the plain. Robert, prince of the Normans, and the count of Brittany extended their tents with their companies beside the walls where the oratory of Stephen, the protomartyr, stands. Count Reinbold of the city of Orange, Louis of Monzun, Cuno of Montaigu and his son Lambert, Gaston of Bordeaux, Gerard of Roussillon, Baldwin of Bourg, and Thomas of the castle of Feria took positions all around the city.

Count Raymond, seeing that he might make progress elsewhere, removed his camp from the siege [Col. 0538D] of the gates of the Tower of David, leaving certain companions to guard the gates; and, having pitched his tents upon Mount Sion, he went to besiege the city. When this encircling siege had been established by the leading Franks, and the places had been reconnoitered lest any unoccupied or suitable opening be exposed to ambush, they came to the Mount of Olives. There they also posted a guard of valiant men, lest an attack come unexpectedly from that side and the ambushes of pagans descending through the ridges deceive the unwary Christians.

The Valley of Jehoshaphat, above which the city stood and over which its buildings projected, remained unbesieged because of the difficulty of the terrain and the depth of the valleys. Nevertheless, Christians maintained continual watches and guards there by night and day.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0539]

## CHAPTER I.—On the first day of fighting, different persons are variously afflicted.

[Col. 0539A]

Once the holy city had thus been enclosed on every side, on the fifth day of the siege, by counsel and command of the aforesaid leaders, the Christians donned mail-coats and helmets, formed a tortoise-shell formation of shields, and attacked the walls and ramparts. They fiercely challenged the Saracen men in battle, with javelins, stones, slings, and arrows flying over the walls, fighting within and without for a long part of the day. Many of the faithful were wounded, battered, and crushed by stones; some lost their eyes from the piercing of arrows. Yet none of the leaders was struck that day, by God’s gift.

Grieved at the people’s suffering, the Christians applied themselves more intensely to labor and battle. They fiercely attacked the outer walls, called barbicans, and partly broke them with iron hammers and mattocks. [Col. 0539B] Yet they made little progress on that day.

## CHAPTER II.—The leaders’ deliberation concerning how the city might be taken.

When at last this storm of war had subsided, the duke and the leaders of the army saw that the city was invincible by arms and assault. They withdrew from the attack to camp and took common counsel: unless the city were gained by the contrivances of siege-towers and mangonels, it could never be overcome by any force of arms. This counsel seemed useful to all: siege-towers, mangonels, and rams were to be constructed.

But timber was lacking, of which there is great scarcity in those regions. At this point a certain Christian brother, a Syrian by nation, showed the pilgrims a place where wood suitable for constructing engines [Col. 0539C] could be found: namely, in certain mountains toward Arabia. Once the location of the timber had been revealed, Robert of Flanders, Robert lord of the Normans, and Gerard of Keresi, taking a force of horsemen and foot soldiers, journeyed four miles. Having found the wood, they loaded it on camels’ backs and returned unharmed to their companions’ encampment.

## CHAPTER III.—Concerning the engines brought up to conquer the city.

At the first light of the following day, all the workmen set themselves to the construction of the siege-tower, mangonels, and ram: some with axes, others with augers. Within four weeks the work of the siege-tower, ram, and mangonels was completed in every detail before the Tower of David, in sight of all who remained in that stronghold.

Then young men, old men, boys, girls, and women were instructed [Col. 0539D] to assemble in the valley of Bethlehem, all bringing brushwood on mules and asses or on their own shoulders. From it triple wicker screens were woven, with which the covered siege-tower might disregard the Saracens’ missiles. This was done: abundant twigs and brushwood were brought, and the woven screens were covered with horse-, bull-, and camel-hides [Col. 0540A] so that the siege-tower might not easily be burned by hostile fire.

## CHAPTER IV.—Certain men of the people, while seeking food farther away, meet death.

Meanwhile, during this delay of the long siege and the protracted, laborious construction of the engines, want of necessities compelled certain men to leave the army and seek provisions. But when by chance they entered the neighboring districts of Rames, the aforesaid city, carried off booty, and drove together herds, they were battered by Saracen ambushes. The Saracens had come down from Ascalon, city of the king of Babylon, and retained the booty.

Giselbert of Treves and Achar of Motinerla, brave Christian leaders and noble men, fell there cut to pieces after much fighting. The rest of their companions, put to flight, hurried by the mountain route to Jerusalem. Thereupon Baldwin of Bourg, who had gone out with Thomas of the castle of Feria and a force of horsemen upon the same business of collecting food, met the fugitive and disordered brethren. [Col. 0540B] Learning their affair and misfortune, he comforted them all and urged them to return with him to avenge their injuries. Immediately the pilgrims, encouraged by the consolation of the brave men, returned unanimously and afresh in pursuit of their enemies. After fighting long with them, many on both sides were killed and wounded. Baldwin of Bourg was wounded in the chest by an enemy missile.

## CHAPTER V.—Where one distinguished pagan and two noble Christians are slain.

At length the Christians gained strength and forced the Saracens into flight. They captured one of their most noble knights, a man bald in the forehead, tall of stature, aged, and corpulent. Taking him to Jerusalem, they bound him in fetters in the tent of the aforesaid Baldwin; but he seated himself nobly upon Baldwin’s throne, which was covered with most precious purple.

When the Christian leaders saw that this Saracen was a prudent, noble, and brave man, they often questioned and conversed with him concerning his life and customs, seeking to call him to the Christian faith. But utterly renouncing this profession in every way, he was brought before the Tower of David and beheaded by Baldwin’s squire before everyone, to frighten the guards of the citadel.

The aforesaid leaders, Giselbert and Achar, slain by pagan ambushes, were brought back to the place of siege [Col. 0540D] amid great lamentation. Christian priests rendered them Catholic funeral rites and laid their bones in the tomb of their Christian brethren outside the city.

## CHAPTER VI.—When the city was besieged, and concerning the scarcity of drink.

The holy city—our mother [Col. 0541A] Jerusalem, which illegitimate sons had invaded and denied to her legitimate sons—was besieged on Tuesday in the second week of July, a month deemed unbearable because of heat and the sun’s burning, especially in these eastern regions. There not only do streams fail, but even living springs and small sources are found only at intervals of three miles.

The Christian people suffered grievously in this siege from the most blazing heat of the sun, the unbearable lack of water, and immeasurable dryness. When their companions were sent out in scattered groups to draw water and search for springs, they sometimes returned safely after drawing from a spring; at other times they were endangered by pagan ambushes, their heads cut off. They brought back muddy, turbid water, made so by the struggle of the multitude drawing it, in goatskins containing slippery leech-worms. [Col. 0541B] From this water, as much as each person’s mouth could take in through the narrow opening of the skin—even though it was old and rotten, or drawn from foul marshes or ancient cisterns—was sold for two coins.

Very many among the helpless common people, driven hard by unbearable thirst, when thus permitted to drink, swallowed the slippery water-creatures and worms and so died with their throats or bellies swollen. Only a very small rivulet flows from Mount Sion. Its subterranean conduit runs from Solomon’s palace for the distance of an arrow-shot, to the place where there stands a walled, square structure in the form of a cloister. During the night the rivulet gathers in its middle; from it the citizens drink by day and water their animals.

## CHAPTER VII.—The counsel of a certain enclosed man concerning the undertaking begun.

[Col. 0541C]

The army was refreshed from this exceedingly frequent drawing of water, although the citizens within the siege often hurled missiles at those drawing it from this source and labored to drive the Christians entirely away from it. The leaders, and those who had means, always had an abundance of grapes and wine; but among the needy, whose resources had been exhausted, there was, as you have heard, an extreme lack even of water.

Therefore, as this pestilence of thirst increased and the Catholic people labored long in the siege, the leading men of the people, on the counsel of the bishops and clergy present, decided to consult a certain man of God. He was a solitary dwelling [Col. 0541D] in an ancient tower of great height on the Mount of Olives. They asked what they should do and what they should undertake first, disclosing to him how ardently they desired to enter the city and see the Lord’s sepulchre, and how many dangers they had endured on the journey for this faith and vow.

When the man of God heard their intention and desire, he gave this counsel: that they should first devote themselves to the affliction of fasting and to continuous prayers; and then, with God’s help, make attack more safely upon the walls and the Saracens.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Concerning the appointed procession and what was then done.

Following the man of God’s counsel, the bishops and clergy proclaimed a three-day fast. On Friday all the Christians made a procession around the city and then came to the Mount of Olives, to the place where the Lord Jesus ascended into heaven. Then they proceeded to another place where he taught his disciples to pray, and there stood in all devotion and humility.

There, at that place on the mountain, Peter the Hermit and Arnulf of the castle of Rohes in Flanders, a cleric of great learning and eloquence, addressed the people and extinguished the great discord which had grown up among the pilgrims from various causes. They also reconciled in concordant affection the disagreement long prevailing between Count Raymond and Tancred because of an agreement concerning solidi, which the count had unjustly withheld from him, once both leaders had been moved to compunction by spiritual admonition. When these had been reconciled and restored to concord [Col. 0542B] with many other Christian brethren, the whole Christian procession descended from the place on the aforementioned Mount of Olives and assembled on the nearby Mount Sion, in the church of the holy Mother of God.

There the clerics, clad in white and reverently carrying relics of saints, were joined by many worthy laymen who were struck by the arrows of Saracens watching their passage from the city walls. The city lies near this church of Sion, at the distance of an arrow’s flight. At this place, to stir up the Christians’ anger, the Saracens set up crosses in mockery and insult; they either spat upon them or did not shrink from urinating upon them before all eyes.

## CHAPTER IX.—The engines being brought to the wall, the contrivances of the opposing sides clash.

[Col. 0542C]

After the fast, holy procession, litany, and prayer had ended, and the sky was already covered by darkness, the siege-tower was moved by sections, together with the entire mass of mangonels, in the stillness of night, to the very place of the city where the oratory of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr lies toward the Valley of Jehoshaphat. On Saturday, after the tents around the siege-tower had been moved from their former station, they were set up around it. There the siege-tower and every apparatus of the mangonels and ram were completed in every detail.

But on the leaders’ counsel, engines of three mangonels were set up, so that by their first attack and impact the Christians might drive the Saracen citizens away from the walls and ramparts and, by sudden casting of stones, strike the wall-works. At length, seeing that this attack and bombardment violently shook and damaged the walls, the Saracens fastened to the walls and ramparts sacks stuffed with tow and straw and tightly woven ropes of great thickness from ships, [Col. 0542D] so that they might receive softly the impact and castings of the mangonels and prevent harm to the walls and ramparts.

The duke, seeing this obstruction placed against his engines, immediately shot flaming arrows, drawn from the fire, from a Balearic bow at the ropes and sacks. When they lodged in the dry material, a slight breeze kindled a small flame; gaining strength, it consumed the sacks and ropes, and the impacts again damaged the walls and ramparts.

## CHAPTER X.—The besieged endeavor to destroy the ram that is piercing the walls.

[Col. 0543A]

Meanwhile, to increase the ruin and destruction of the walls, the aforesaid ram, of dreadful weight and construction and covered with wicker screens, was brought up. Driven by force and by the immeasurable mass of men, it immediately shattered and cast down with heavy blows the barbicans—that is, the outer walls set opposite the city’s level ditch—by the men pushing the ram. It opened a way for the siege-tower to the inner and ancient walls and broke through, making an immense and dreadful opening already extending into the city.

When the defenders saw this opening through the city walls and could endure the danger no longer, they kindled sulphurous fire with pitch and wax and set fire to the ram, which stood too near the walls, [Col. 0543B] so that it might no longer batter the walls with its iron head or enlarge the breach. Then the people of God, stirred by a sudden cry, brought water from tents and huts on every side, and at last extinguished the ram’s fire.

## CHAPTER XI.—Those appointed to command the siege-tower on every side are assigned.

Meanwhile, while the ram was being extinguished, the continual castings and impacts of the mangonels damaged the walls and drove the guards and defenders from the ramparts. Without delay, amid these events, the siege-tower was raised with its entire structure. Its walls, platforms, and screens were covered with bull-, horse-, and camel-hides. In it were stationed knights who might assault the city and more easily wear down those resisting them in battle.

Having labored on the work and framework of this siege-tower from Saturday until Thursday, they completed the protracted work in the evening. They appointed Duke Godfrey and his brother Eustace, likewise the two brothers Ludolf and Engelbert, natives of the city of Tournai, [Col. 0543C] to defend the siege-tower and provoke the city to battle. They determined that the duke and his men should remain in the upper platform; Ludolf with his brother and their other followers in the middle platform; and those who were to pull the siege-tower and bring it up to the city in the lower one.

After the barbicans had been destroyed and the ditch filled level, the Christians voluntarily burned the ram with their own fire. Since its removal was so difficult and burdensome, they did not wish a structure of such great strength and size to obstruct the mobile siege-tower.

## CHAPTER XII.—With what pressure the citizens are harassed from outside by the engines.

Then, when Friday morning came, the Saracen soldiers and the city’s citizens, seeing the siege-tower raised and mailed men occupying it, were astonished and terrified. They marvelled that soldiers, so early and ready for battle, appeared in the siege-tower, striking all who moved through the city with arrows and bows, and incessantly assailing with javelins and stones every person seen in the city from the siege-tower projecting above the walls.

Therefore the pagans massed together within the city and did not cease to harm the duke and resist with the flying missiles of arrows; scattered over the ramparts, they wounded the pilgrims. [Col. 0544A] But the pilgrims stoutly resisted in return. In this violent battering from within and without, men and knights in the siege-tower—which surpassed the city and its ramparts by the height of an ash spear—hurled enormous stones to damage the walls and drive the citizens from defending the ramparts, striking all who roamed through the city with arrows and stones.

On the other side of the city above Mount Sion, the soldiers of Count Raymond’s single siege-tower hurled stones and missiles, damaging the walls and those standing upon the ramparts and vainly seeking to harm that siege-tower. It had been raised and brought up to the walls on the very same night and hour as the duke’s tower.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Guards are assigned to the gate through which messengers of Babylon had passage.

[Col. 0544B]

When the siege of the holy city had already become wearisome and the Christians were zealously exerting themselves in every manner and by every work for its capture, and much became known concerning the threats and power of the king of Babylon, word reached the leaders of the army, through the same informers who had revealed to brother Tancred the money and ornaments of the Lord’s Temple before the city’s capture. They learned that continual embassies were sent to the king of Babylon from Jerusalem, by the unbesieged gate at the Mount of Olives and the Valley of Jehoshaphat, reporting everything that was being done; and that the king’s messages and counsels were repeatedly and secretly carried back by the same gate to the city’s defenders, able to create a great obstacle for the Christians.

Therefore, after cautious deliberation, the Christian leaders secretly stationed an ambush [Col. 0544C] in the valley and at the outlet of the same mountain in the silence of night. They fortified the paths of the road before and behind with vigilant guards, lest anyone should come down from Ascalon, Babylon, or any part of this kingdom, or should leave by the unbesieged gate upon an embassy according to the usual practice. Such a person, falling into the ambush, would be suddenly captured and would not escape from the watchers’ hands by any flight, concealed before their very sides.

## CHAPTER XIV.—Concerning two messengers of the king of Babylon who perish by different kinds of death.

After the road guards had thus been arranged and posted at the place of the aforesaid Mount of Olives, two Saracens hastening from Ascalon and carrying the king of Babylon’s messages to the city’s defenders came at the approach of night’s silence and stood amid the guards, hoping to enter the city without any obstacle. But they were suddenly captured and detained by the soldiers and guards of the unbesieged gate. One, pierced by a spear wielded by an uncontrolled young man, immediately gave up his spirit. The other was brought alive and unhurt into the presence of the Christian leaders, so that by threats or a promise of life they might extract from him the purpose for which the messengers had come, [Col. 0544D] and thus the foreseen missiles might do less harm.

Being greatly anxious and concerned for his life, he revealed much concerning the king of Babylon’s counsel and embassy, and how the king had now instructed his faithful soldiers, together with the citizens, through them: not to fail under any terror or wearying oppression, but, consoling one another, to persevere steadfastly in defense. They were to know that after fifteen days he had resolved to come in great force to Jerusalem to aid them, exterminate the Franks, and free his own people.

After this and other reports, he was handed back to the soldiers and placed in the sling of a certain mangonel with his hands and feet bound, so that he might be thrown over the walls after the first and second discharge. But the sling of the mangonel, weighed down by his excessive weight, did not throw the wretch far. Falling immediately beside the walls upon sharp stones, with neck, sinews, and bones broken, he is reported to have died at once.

## CHAPTER XV.—Concerning the engines of the profane against the engines of the faithful.

[Col. 0545B] But the citizens and soldiers of the king of Babylon, seeing that the king’s embassy had thus been scattered, that the Christians were attacking the city more boldly, and that engines on both sides were grievously assailing the city, set about erecting fourteen mangonels of their own. By their force and impact stones were continually hurled against the engines, so that, stunned by their frequent blows, they might be shaken to pieces and destroyed, and those stationed in them might perish together with their collapse. Of these fourteen mangonels, nine were directed against Count Raymond’s engine, together with an innumerable host and force of citizens. By their intolerable and repeated impact the engine was violently shaken and battered, and its joints came apart. Therefore all the fighting men in it, severely battered and stunned by the unexpected [Col. 0545C] destruction, scarcely escaped the danger of death.

Accordingly, because they could not endure so many incessant blows of stones and the protection of the engine had failed, the engine was withdrawn far from the walls; nor was anyone thereafter found who would again mount it and harass the citizens by attacking them. The remaining five, however, were set up against the duke’s engine, so that they might strike and batter it with equal force and discharge. But, under God’s protection, although it was repeatedly struck and shaken so as to threaten collapse, it remained whole and uninjured; protected by wicker screens, it bravely endured the extraordinary impacts of stones, softly receiving them.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Concerning the crucifix which the madness of the faithless could not harm.

On the summit of that same engine stood a cross bearing a most resplendent golden image [Col. 0545D] of the Lord Jesus. The same Saracens continually tried to strike it with the discharge of mangonels, but no power either to hit or to remove it was granted them. While they repeatedly attempted to hurl stones against this cross, a stone flying by chance struck a certain soldier standing at the duke’s side violently on the head; his brain was fractured and his neck broken, and he was killed in an instant.

The duke himself, scarcely preserved from so sudden a blow, persistently shot at the citizens and the mangonels with a balearic bow; and from time to time he repaired and bound again with ropes the screens which had been torn away from the engine by the impact.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Likewise concerning the various engines of the faithless.

The Saracen soldiers, seeing that the blows of the mangonels could not penetrate [Col. 0546A] the wicker screens, sometimes threw fire-spewing pots upon the screens protecting the engine, so that the embers or sparks, clinging to the dry material and stirred up by a light breeze, might grow and consume the engine. But the ingenuity of the Franks forestalled art with art. For the engine and its screens were covered with slippery hides, which did not retain the flames or embers thrown upon them; rather, the fire immediately slid from the hides, fell to the ground, and went out.

At length, hard pressed by the continual blows of these five mangonels, the duke and his men brought the engine close to the walls and ramparts under the protection of the Christian forces, so that it might thus resist the engines more safely. The mangonels, unable to be drawn back into an open space because of the buildings of houses and towers, cast less effectively and could not strike the engine. Now that the engine had been brought close to the walls, and the five mangonels could find no spacious retreat from it, a stone discharged and released in its course flew over the engine, which was too near, or, sometimes failing in its flight, fell beside the walls and crushed the Saracens. [Col. 0546B]

At last the Saracens understood that fearless men stood in the engine, whom they could not injure by the art of mangonels. Therefore they fortified a certain tower near the engine with sacks filled with straw, hay, or chaff, likewise with wicker screens and a dense covering of ships’ ropes, sheltered on every side against the Christians’ mangonels. They placed fighting men in it, to cast masses of stones continually into the engine with slings or little mangonels, and to harass its occupants with the various terrors of weapons. [Col. 0546C] Yet the engine of Duke Godfrey did not yield, nor were its guards driven back by the assault; rather, they grew stronger and fiercer. The Saracen artificers accordingly devised another contrivance by which the engine and those occupying it might be consumed beyond recovery.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Where fire is quenched by vinegar, and the chain of the heathen is pulled away by force.

They brought together a huge and extremely heavy beam of timber, entirely fastened with iron nails and hooks. They packed the nails with tow steeped and greased with pitch, wax, and oil, and with every kind of material for feeding fire. They also fixed a heavy iron chain in the middle of the beam, so that it could not readily be carried off or removed by the curved iron hooks of the pilgrims when the aforesaid timber was thrown over the walls and ramparts to burn the engine. [Col. 0546D]

When this construction of timber had been fitted together and completed, one day all the citizens and soldiers of the king of Babylon assembled within the city and gathered around this work. With ladders, spears, and their equipment, they set the heavy timber alight with a fire which no water could quench and, with great force, swiftly lowered it over the walls, casting it between the walls and the engine. Their purpose was that the posts supporting the whole engine, caught by its most fierce heat, should burn, and that its occupants should suffer its collapse; nor could any water extinguish so vehement a fire until the whole engine, together with the aforesaid beam, had fallen reduced to ashes.

But the Christians learned from native fellow Christians that this fire, inextinguishable by water, could be quenched by vinegar alone. Therefore vinegar, provided beforehand in skins within the engine, was poured out over the fire which had been cast upon them. Thus the great blaze was extinguished and could do the engine no further harm. [Col. 0547A] Finally, a rush of pilgrims was made to extinguish this timber. Seizing the chain, they entered into a struggle with all their strength: some pulling from outside, others holding it from within. But, with God’s favour, the Christians’ strength prevailed; and so the chain was torn from the Saracens and retained by the faithful.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Who first gained possession of the holy city.

While this contest over the chain was taking place within and without, and while the five mangonels, now uselessly hurling their missiles from inside, had failed, the duke, who had taken up his position in the upper chamber of the citadel, hurled with his men every kind of missile and stone into the massed crowd below, and continuously drove those standing on the wall away from the ramparts. Three Christian mangonels, indeed, without rest and with unceasing discharge, flew over the walls and drove the guards back far from the ramparts on either side. [Col. 0547B]

Moreover, the previously named brothers Ludolf and Engelbert, seeing that the Saracens were languishing in inactivity, withholding their hands from defence, and standing far back from both sides of the walls because of the attacks of the mangonels and other engines, immediately—being nearest to the wall—extended timbers from the second chamber in which they were lodged and cast them onto the walls. They were the first to descend into the city, armed with force, after all the guards of the walls had been put to flight. [Col. 0547C] The duke and his brother Eustace, learning that these men had now entered the city, at once descended from the upper citadel; soon they too stood upon the walls and went down to assist them. Seeing this, the whole people, crying out with immeasurable shouting that the princes had already gained the city, hastened to climb and enter by ladders placed everywhere against the wall.

## CHAPTER XX.—Concerning the flight and destruction of the lost.

The citizens and defenders of the city, beholding the captured walls and ramparts, Christian men standing in the midst of the city, and the whole city inundated with Frankish arms, were seized with terror and stupefaction of mind. Suddenly taking flight, a great multitude fled in hope of protection to the palace of King Solomon, which was spacious and extremely strong. The Franks vigorously pursued them with lances and swords, entered the palace gates together with the fleeing men, and continued the immense slaughter of the heathen. [Col. 0547D]

About four hundred horsemen, sent by the king of Babylon and continually patrolling the city to exhort its defence and comfort its citizens, saw the straits and flight of their own people and turned their horses at full speed toward the refuge of the Tower of David. But as the Franks pressed them in fierce pursuit, they scarcely gained the gate; all dismounted before the entrance and left their horses there. [Col. 0548A] The Christians seized these horses and led them away with their bridles and saddles, keeping them.

## CHAPTER XXI.—What happened when the whole people burst in through the gates.

Meanwhile certain pilgrims ran to the city gates, tore away the bars and iron bolts, and admitted the whole multitude to assist. Such was the press and distress of those entering this gate, it is said, that even the horses, weighed down by excessive crushing, attacked many with their teeth, mouths open to bite, against the will of their riders, while pouring with unheard-of sweat. Therefore about sixteen men, trampled, torn apart, and suffocated beneath the feet of horses, mules, and people, gave up the breath of life.

Through the breach in the walls, too, which the iron-headed battering ram had broken open from the front, many thousands of men and women entered. [Col. 0548B] All these gathered together and, with great shouting and noise, rushed to the aforesaid palace and brought aid to the brothers who had gone before, laying the Saracens low throughout the spacious house in a cruel slaughter. So great was the shedding of their blood that streams ran across the pavements of the royal hall itself, and the poured-out blood rose to the ankles. The Saracens, sometimes recovering spirit and strength, rose in vain to defend themselves; nevertheless, they pierced many unwary members of the faithful in mutual slaughter.

## CHAPTER XXII.—Concerning the cistern of the royal palace.

Many Saracens fled into the royal cistern, which lay before the doors of this palace. Excavated to the breadth and size of a lake, it had above it a vaulted roof supported everywhere by marble columns; they entered by steps leading down to draw water. Some of them were drowned in the water; others were killed by pursuing Christians on the very steps where they attempted defence. [Col. 0548C] Through the openings in the vault, which were like the mouths of wells, Christians and Saracens alike, falling in precipitous flight and blind running, were endangered not only by drowning but were also killed through broken throats and necks or ruptured entrails.

During the entire siege of the city, water from this royal cistern was customarily issued in measured portions to citizens and soldiers in need, for watering horses, flocks, and all beasts of burden, and for every necessary use. It is filled by the convergence of all the rainwater dripping from the channels of the roof of the palace itself, from the vault of the Temple of the Lord, and from the roofs of many buildings, abundantly supplying cold and wholesome water throughout the year to all who lived there in the city. [Col. 0548D]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Likewise concerning the general slaughter of the citizens and the plundering of the Temple of the Lord.

After the Christians had emerged victorious from the palace following the immense and bloody slaughter of the Saracens—ten thousand of whom they killed in that place—they struck down with the sword many bands of heathen wandering through the streets of the city, fleeing in terror of death. They stabbed with the sword women who had fled into the towers and upper chambers of the palace. Infants still at the breast, seized by the sole of the foot from their mothers’ bosoms or from their cradles, they dashed against walls or door thresholds, breaking their necks; some they slaughtered with weapons, others they crushed beneath stones. They spared absolutely no age or sex among the heathen. [Col. 0549A]

Whoever first entered a house or palace took peaceful possession of it together with all its furnishings, grain, oil, barley and wine, money, clothing, and whatever property it contained. Thus they became possessors of the entire city. Once Christians had entered the city, while the long slaughter was raging in the palace and city and men eagerly sought Saracen spoils and riches, Tancred, hastening ahead to the Temple at the first entrance into the city, tore away its bars and entered. With the strength and help of his following, he stripped incomparable quantities of gold and silver money from the gilded surrounding walls, columns, and pillars. For two days he laboured at the plundering of this treasure, which the Turks had assembled to adorn the sanctuary. [Col. 0549B]

Two Saracens, who had left the city during the siege, are said to have disclosed this treasure to Tancred, in order to find favour and safety for their lives in his eyes. After the aforesaid interval of days, he opened the Temple gates and faithfully divided the money he carried away with Duke Godfrey, whose knight he was. The whole mass, as they say, could scarcely have been carried by six camels or mules.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Account of the Temple of the Lord.

This Temple, called the Temple of the Lord, must not be understood to be that ancient and marvellous work of King Solomon. For the whole city of Jerusalem was destroyed long before the Lord’s Incarnation, first by King Nebuchadnezzar and then by King Antiochus; Solomon’s Temple was razed from its foundations and stripped of its ornaments and sacred vessels. Again, after the Incarnation, in fulfilment of the prediction of the Lord Jesus, Jerusalem was utterly destroyed together with its inhabitants by the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus, so that, according to the Lord’s saying, not one stone was left upon another. [Col. 0549C]

Rather, many attest that this Temple was later rebuilt by modern Christian worshippers, namely on the place where peaceful Solomon had established the former tabernacle of God out of cedar wood and Parian stone, and the Holy of Holies within it. In the middle of this modern sanctuary rises a naturally formed rocky mound, occupying nearly a third of a jugerum in breadth and standing two cubits high. On one side it has steps leading down into hollow places; on the other side, as those who then examined it report truthfully, it has a little stone door, always sealed. According to the opinion of some, certain things of the Holy of Holies are still kept there.

In the middle of the vault of this modern Temple—which now encloses, around the walls, wondrously fashioned ornamentation above—is said to be fixed a circular chain from which there always hangs a vessel of gleaming gold and workmanship, weighing about two hundred marks. Some maintain that it is a golden urn; others, that the blood of the Lord or manna is hidden in it. Thus diverse opinions lead to different conclusions. [Col. 0550A]

## CHAPTER XXV.—Concerning the sanctuaries of the holy city, and how devoutly the duke visited the Lord’s sepulchre.

This vessel and the projection which, as we have said, rises in the middle of the Temple remained untouched by Tancred, because the Turks themselves, venerating both with every devotion, had preserved them inviolate. They enriched the sanctuary with every honour and ornament and, excluding all other peoples, alone devoted themselves there to the observance of their ceremonies. They likewise revered the aforesaid Temple itself with the highest reverence and protection for performing the rites of their error. They also spared only the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and its Christian worshippers, because of the tribute continually paid them from the offerings of the faithful, together with the church of St Mary of the Latins, which also paid tribute. [Col. 0550B]

But in the remaining sanctuaries of the holy city, Turks and Saracens exercised their tyranny with immense slaughter, entirely expelling Catholic worshippers from them. Accordingly, as has been said, Tancred turned his course toward the Temple of the Lord because of the money disclosed to him through greed. Others swiftly pursued the fugitives toward the refuge of the Tower of David; all the princes coveted Turkish goods and buildings; and the whole multitude made for Solomon’s palace, carrying out a cruel and immense slaughter of the Saracens. Duke Godfrey, however, abstained from all slaughter. Retaining only three of his men—Baldric, Adelbold, and Stabulo—he immediately took off his hauberk, put on a woollen garment, and, barefoot, went out through the walls. [Col. 0550C] He proceeded humbly around the city and entered through the gate facing the Mount of Olives. He presented himself at the Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, persevering in tears, prayers, and divine praises, and giving thanks to God because he had been permitted to see what had always been his supreme desire.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—A certain man’s vision concerning the duke.

For, when the duke’s pious purpose had been fulfilled, the vision of this dream was proved to have been truly fulfilled. Before the beginning of this journey, while the same duke often sighed and his chief desire above all things was to visit the holy city of Jerusalem and see the sepulchre of the Lord Jesus, he frequently disclosed the purpose of his heart to his private attendants. To one of his household, namely Stabulo, a vision was shown in this manner. [Col. 0550D]

He saw a golden ladder of great length stretched from the axis of heaven to the earth. The duke himself, burning with great desire, attempted to climb it with a certain steward of his cup, named Rothard, who carried a lamp in his hand. But when the steward had reached the middle of the ladder, the lamp which he carried in his hand went out, and the middle step of the ladder by which he was ascending to the lofty throne of heaven was severely damaged and worn away. Thus the cup-steward returned to the lower regions and, through fear, could no longer reach and knock at the heavenly gate with the duke.

But Stabulo, whose vision this was, relit the extinguished lamp and confidently climbed the ladder [Col. 0551A] which the unworthy cupbearer had not deserved to ascend. Carrying a lamp that thereafter did not fail, he entered the heavenly court with the duke, where they found a table prepared for them and filled with every sweetness of delights. There the duke reclined with the elect and those worthy of it, and shared in all the sweetness of delight that was present.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Interpretation of the dream.

What is signified by this ladder leading to the heavenly palace, if not the way which the duke embraced with the whole intention of his mind toward the city of Jerusalem, the gate of the heavenly homeland? The ladder was of purest gold because one must come to this way and gate of heaven with a pure heart and perfect humility. In the middle of the ladder, the cup-steward’s lamp goes out; the damaged step gives way; ascent is denied, because he abandoned halfway through the labour, along with many others, the work and burden of the holy journey which he had vowed together with the duke in good and pure intention, as you have heard. [Col. 0551B]

For, through distrust and the approaching hardships, he withdrew from the duke at Antioch; thus becoming an apostate, he returned to the plough of miseries. He did not thereafter enter the heavenly gate by the ladder with the duke, nor was he worthy to share in the table of the saints. Stabulo, however, the duke’s chamberlain, received the lamp from his hand and rekindled it, because he strongly retained the good intention of this journey which he had first undertaken; amid the various wavering impulses of the mind, he rekindled the lamp of good will and held firmly to his blazing vow. Thus, upon an unbreakable step, he climbed the ladder with the duke. Moreover, steadfastly his companion in every tribulation and a faithful servant of God, he reached Jerusalem with him and deserved to enter and pray at the Lord’s Sepulchre, which is the table and the object of the saints’ entire desire for sweetness. [Col. 0551C]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—Concerning the greed of Raymond and Tancred, and the killing of certain heathen.

After the duke had returned in joy and exultation of heart from the sanctuary of the Lord’s Sepulchre, following the victory accomplished there, and had retired to lodging for rest, the whole army had now ceased from slaughtering the heathen. On that night the labour weighed down everyone’s eyes, because Jerusalem, the city of the living God and our mother, had been restored to her children in a great victory on Friday, the solemn day of the Division of the Apostles, which fell on the Ides of July. Count Raymond, corrupted by greed, allowed the Saracen soldiers whom he had besieged in the Tower of David after they had escaped there in flight to depart unharmed upon receipt of a great sum of money. [Col. 0551D] He retained, however, all their weapons, provisions, and spoils along with that fortress.

At the dawn of the following Saturday, about three hundred Saracens, who had escaped the weapons and fled in hope of life to the summit of the roof of Solomon’s lofty house, pleaded earnestly for their lives. Standing at the point of death, they did not dare to come down trusting in any pledge or promise, until they received Tancred’s banner as a sign of protection for life. But it profited the wretches nothing. For many were indignant at this, and the Christians, stirred to fury, left not even one of them alive.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—Where Tancred’s anger is calmed by the counsel of the elders.

[Col. 0552A]

Tancred, a glorious knight, was inflamed with violent anger at this injury done to him; his rage would not have subsided without discord and severe revenge, had not the counsel and judgment of the elder and wiser men soothed his mind with these words:

> “Jerusalem, city of the most high God, as you all know, was recovered with great difficulty and not without loss to our people. Today it has been restored to its own children and freed from the hand of the king of Babylon and the yoke of the Turks. But we must now take care lest, through greed, sloth, or mercy shown to enemies, we lose it by sparing captives and heathen still remaining in the city. For if perhaps the king of Babylon should attack us with a great multitude, [Col. 0552B] we shall immediately be attacked from within and without and so be carried into perpetual exile. Therefore our first and faithful counsel seems to be that all Saracens and heathen who are held captive, whether to be redeemed for money or already redeemed, should without delay fall by the sword, lest some adversity arise against us through their deceit or cunning.”

## CHAPTER XXX.—The extermination of the surviving heathen.

This counsel having been accepted, on the third day after the victory the leading men issued their decree. Behold, all seized weapons and rose up in a pitiful slaughter against the entire remaining multitude of heathen: some they brought forth from bonds and beheaded; others, found in the streets and squares of the city, they slaughtered, though previously they had spared them for money or out of human compassion. [Col. 0552C]

Girls, women, noble matrons, and pregnant women together with little girls they cut down or crushed beneath stones, regarding no age among any of them. Conversely, girls, women, and matrons, distressed by the fear of immediate death and shaken by the horror of an exceedingly cruel killing, embraced their Christian persecutors, who were raging and wreaking slaughter at the throats of both sexes, in order to save their lives. Some threw themselves at their feet, urgently begging them for life and safety with piteous weeping and wailing. Little boys of five or three years, seeing the cruel fate of their mothers and fathers, multiplied their wretched cries and tears together.

But these signs of pity and mercy were made in vain. For the Christians had so wholly given their minds over to killing that no nursing male or female child—much less a living infant of one year—escaped the hand of the striker. [Col. 0552D] Thus the streets of the whole city of Jerusalem are said to have been so strewn and covered with the dead bodies of men and women and the mangled limbs of infants that an innumerable abundance of slain persons was found not only in streets, halls, and palaces but even in places of deserted solitude.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Concerning the former Turkish dominion in the city of Jerusalem.

From the day on which the holy city was besieged, fortified, and defended by the Saracens until this day on which it was captured, conquered, and restored to its own people, no Turk was found in it. Yet shortly before, the Turks had taken it by force, held it for a long time, and exacted heavy tribute [Col. 0553A] from Saracens, from Christ’s pilgrims, and from native believers alike. There were three hundred Turks who had captured the holy city and ruled it for a long time, making many surrounding cities of Syria and the region of Palestine tributary to themselves—cities which the king of Babylon had formerly been accustomed to hold powerfully, together with Jerusalem, as subject and appended to his kingdom.

Now, as you have heard, once the Christian army had assembled for the siege of Antioch after the capture of Nicaea, that same king of Babylon, hearing of the renown, strength, and victory of the Christian princes and of the humiliation of the Turks, besieged Jerusalem, which he had lost, with three hundred Turks and an abundant army. He wore them down through many assaults and the impact of mangonels, although they resisted and fought vigorously, but not without great losses among his own men. [Col. 0553B]

## CHAPTER XXXII.—How the Turks were expelled, and concerning the false promise of the king of Babylon.

Solyman, prince and head of these Turks, was a most fierce knight and always an enemy to the king of Babylon and his kingdom. At last the Turks and their prince, seeing that their small force could not bear the weight of war and the assaults of so many thousands, exchanged pledges and hands concerning their lives and safety. They obtained terms that, upon surrendering the city, they might leave in peace and have the king’s safe-conduct as far as Damascus. There, it is said, the brother of the mighty prince Doniman rules; he has now been expelled from Jerusalem with the aforesaid Turks.

After they had been expelled and had the king’s safe-conduct as far as Damascus, the king entered Jerusalem and approached the Temple of the Lord with the highest reverence and humility according to the rite of the heathen. [Col. 0553C] Then he entered the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre with all the demeanour of heathen devotion, surveying everything peacefully and turning no Christian away from the faith and observance of his rite. Afterward he returned and provided the city with a faithful guard; he fortified the Tower of David with his own retinue and assigned Solomon’s palace and the other royal buildings and defensive works to his own jurisdiction.

Having restored this city to his dominion after the expulsion of the Turks, he rejoiced greatly. Yet, still fearing that the Turks at Damascus might oppose him, he sent envoys to the Christian princes dwelling around the city of Antioch. He reported how he had expelled the Turks from Jerusalem and his kingdom, that he wished to satisfy their wishes in every matter concerning the holy city, and that he would submit to their counsel concerning faith in Christ and the profession of Christianity. But he lied in everything and spoke deceitfully. [Col. 0553D] For he denied pilgrims entry into the city with every defensive resource and military force at his disposal, until now, as you have heard, they were admitted by the aid of the heavenly King, after the Saracens had been killed in cruel slaughter.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—The elevation of the glorious duke in Jerusalem.

Once this lamentable slaughter of the Saracens had been completed, on the following Sunday the faithful and leading Christians held counsel and decreed that the lordship of the city and custody of the Lord’s Sepulchre should be given to Count Raymond. [Col. 0554A] When he refused, and all the other captains had in turn been selected for that office, Duke Godfrey was at last elevated—though unwillingly—to protect the principality of the city.

Having been elevated by the counsel and goodwill of all the Christians, he demanded the royal Tower of David, which Raymond himself had seized after allowing the fleeing Saracens to depart. But Raymond utterly refused to surrender it, until he was compelled to restore it by the duke’s threats and those of the Christians. This duke’s election and elevation must not be thought to have occurred by human will; rather, it was wholly accomplished by God’s ordering and grace. For beyond doubt we have learned from the vision of a certain good and truthful knight that, ten years before this expedition, this man had been chosen and appointed by God as leader, prince, and commander of the Christian army, [Col. 0554B] more blessed than all other leaders in deed, victory, and counsel, and more whole in faith and truth.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—A certain knight’s dream concerning the duke.

One night the aforesaid knight, named Hezelo, from the village of Kinwilre, which is in the Rubuary, was weary from hunting with the duke in a forest called Kettena. He fell into a light sleep and was immediately transported in spirit to Mount Sinai, where Moses, servant of the Lord, after completing a fast of forty days, was granted to see the brightness of God’s glory and to receive the law from God’s hand. He saw the aforesaid duke ascending easily to the summit of this mountain with fear and gentleness; and two men in white garments and priestly dress hastened to meet him, saying:

> “May you be filled with the blessings of the living God and find grace in his sight—the God who bestowed blessing and grace upon his servant and faithful man Moses. May you be established as leader and commander of his Christian people in all faith and truth.” [Col. 0554C]

When this was said, the knight woke from sleep, arose, and the vision was withdrawn.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Explanation of the dream.

What ought to be understood in this vision, if not that in the spirit and gentleness of Moses a spiritual leader of Israel should arise, foreordained by God and established as prince of the people? We therefore know that this vision and blessing were truly and manifestly fulfilled in him. For indeed, although many princes and powerful men, bishops and counts, and sons of kings had undertaken this expedition before and after him and had been leaders of the Christian armies, God did not make their journeys prosper, nor did they obtain the objects of their desire. Rather, many adversities were inflicted upon them and upon all their armies by kings and barbarian peoples, because they were not those through whom salvation was to come to Israel. [Col. 0554D]

But when Duke Godfrey, following all those previously sent, undertook the expedition and became leader and prince of the despairing army, every adversity was changed into prosperity. There was nothing to impede the journey, nor any adversity capable of harm; wrongdoing was found only among the wicked and transgressors. When wrongdoing was found, true divine justice brought retribution after it, by which the host also was sanctified. Thus, after the sons had been chastened now by hunger, now by the sword, they were at last happy and cleansed from defilements; fulfilling their blessed desire with their leader and prince, they deserved to enter the holy city of Jerusalem and worship the Lord’s Sepulchre. Having taken possession of the walls by God’s providence and will, they most gloriously appointed him governor of the city and commander of the people. [Col. 0555A]

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—Likewise, a vision concerning the duke of a cleric of Aachen.

Furthermore, it was revealed to a certain Catholic brother and canon of St Mary at Aachen, named Giselbert, in the seventh month of that same duke’s departure and pilgrimage, that he was foreknown and appointed by God to be the future head and prince of all in Jerusalem. For while the brother was still asleep, he seemed to see the aforesaid duke sitting powerfully in the sun, [Col. 0555B] while countless multitudes of every kind of bird beneath heaven had gathered around him. One part gradually began to lessen as it flew away, but the larger part remained fixed and immovable on his right and left. After this, the sun was obscured for the most part by the rays of its own brightness; within a short interval the duke’s seat was utterly removed, and nearly the whole multitude of birds that had remained flew away.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—Explanation of the vision.

The duke took his seat in the sun when he was elevated to the throne of the kingdom of Jerusalem, which surpasses all the cities of the world in renown and holiness as the sun surpasses all the stars of heaven in brightness. Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who is the true sun of righteousness, illuminated and exalted it by his divinity when he was crucified, suffered, [Col. 0555C] died, and was buried there, rose from the dead on the third day, and appeared alive to those who loved him.

The birds of heaven gathered around the man seated there when people, great and small, noble and ignoble, from all the kingdoms of Christians associated themselves with and became subject to him. The birds flew away when a great multitude of pilgrims returned to the land of their kindred with his consent and permission. But very many birds remained fixed and immovable when many, bound to him by devout affection and delighted by his familiar conversation, resolved to remain with him still longer. After this, within a short interval the sun was darkened and the duke’s seat was taken away, when Jerusalem, bereft after a little while of so magnificent a prince by his death, was greatly diminished in its renown and glory, and weakened in his fall by the loss of many knights and fighting men. [Col. 0555D]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—How a portion of the saving wood was found.

Following the foreshadowing of these dreams, by God’s ordering and the goodwill of the Christian people, Godfrey was elevated as prince and ruler of his fellow brethren upon the throne of the kingdom of Jerusalem. A most faithful Christian, a native of the city and fully instructed in Christ’s law, declared that he had hidden a certain gold-clad cross half an ell in length, with a portion of the Lord’s wood inserted in its middle, otherwise devoid of craftsmanship and bare, in a low and dusty place in an abandoned house. He had hidden it for fear of the Saracens, lest in the turmoil of the siege the cross should be found and stripped of its gold [Col. 0556A] and the Lord’s wood treated unworthily by them.

All the faithful who were present rejoiced at this holy revelation of the Lord’s wood. On Friday, the day of the Lord’s Passion, clergy and people assembled in an honourable procession, in complete abstinence and purity of discipline, at the place where the venerable wood had been hidden. They received it with fear and reverence and resolved to carry it with every devotion and with the singing of hymns to the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and to place it there.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—Concerning the death of the patriarch of Jerusalem.

After these events it pleased the whole assembly of the faithful, and seemed useful and acceptable before God, that, since the entire body of the gentiles and their sacrilegious rites had been expelled from the Holy City [Col. 0556B], and Godfrey, prince of the Christians, had been raised to the throne of Jerusalem to protect the city and its inhabitants, a pastor and patriarch also should be restored, to preside over the flock of the faithful and the holy Church. For the Church had been bereft of its pastor: the patriarch, a most holy man, had been taken from this life on the island of Cyprus during the siege of Jerusalem. This patriarch had left Jerusalem and the Lord’s Sepulchre when he heard of the arrival and settlement of the Christians around the walls of Antioch; he departed for Cyprus because of Turkish threats and Saracen harassment. He was indeed an aged man and a faithful servant of Christ, who from that island sent many charitable gifts to Duke Godfrey and the other princes at the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem: at one time the fruit called pomegranate [Col. 0556C], at another precious citrons of Lebanon, at another fattened peacocks or excellent wine, and whatever else he could obtain according to his means. He hoped that, once the holy Church had been restored under those same princes, he might peacefully and securely serve and preside at the Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God. But after the faithful recovered Jerusalem and renewed its holy Church, this most Christian patriarch departed this life; and thus the Church remained deprived of its pastor.

Therefore, after counsel had been held and repeatedly debated among the Christian princes, as has been said, no one was found worthy in so great honour and divine governance to succeed so great a man. Accordingly, the matter was delayed until someone fit for this pontifical office might be found [Col. 0556D]. Meanwhile they appointed Arnulf of Rohes alone—a cleric of remarkable prudence and eloquence—as chancellor of the holy Church of Jerusalem, administrator of the holy relics, and guardian of the alms of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XL.—Concerning the clerics and the bell-signals established at the Lord’s Sepulchre.

Arnulf having now been promoted to this dignity of the holy and new Church, until a patriarch acceptable to God and the people should be chosen, it pleased the supreme prince of Jerusalem, Duke Godfrey, and all the rest, that twenty brothers in Christ, ministers of the divine office, should be established in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre. They were to sing continually to the living Lord God in praises and hymns [Col. 0557A], devoutly offer the sacrifice of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, and then receive their daily support assigned from the offerings of the faithful.

Thus, when divine worship had fittingly been restored by the Catholic duke and the Christian princes, they ordered bells to be made of bronze and other metals. When the brothers heard their signal, they were immediately to hasten to the church to celebrate the praises of the Psalms and the prayers of the Masses; and the people were likewise to hurry together to hear them. For sounds or signals of this kind had neither been seen nor heard in Jerusalem before those days.

## CHAPTER XLI.—How the duke went out to meet the enemy forces.

Then, after the course of five weeks had passed, Duke Godfrey, having heard reports concerning the gentiles, secured the Tower of David with a faithful guard [Col. 0557B] and, taking with him his companions Robert of Flanders and Tancred, set out for the plain of Ascalon to learn and discover the affairs and plans of the gentiles.
