There, by chance, a messenger met him and reported that Meravis, second to the king of Babylon, and the whole multitude of gentiles, as innumerable as the sand of the sea, had already landed by ship at Ascalon at the king’s command. They had brought infinite supplies of arms, food, and herds, with every abundant preparation for war; and they had resolved to besiege Jerusalem and the Christian exiles.

For the nation of the publicans, the people of very dark complexion from the land of Ethiopia, commonly called Azepart, and all the barbarian nations belonging to the kingdom of Babylon, had determined to assemble there at the city of Ascalon [Col. 0557C]. Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, Tancred, and Eustace, the duke’s brother, having learned the report of the approaching gentile forces and arms, encamped in the mountainous country extending from Jerusalem. Then they sent envoys to Count Raymond at Jerusalem and to Robert, prince of the Normans, commanding that everything be disclosed to them: namely, how great a host of gentiles had occupied Ascalon and had resolved to hold the road as far as Jerusalem. They summoned these princes with all their cavalry and infantry to resist the unbelievers. They also instructed Peter the Hermit and Arnulf—whom they had appointed chancellor and guardian of the Lord’s Sepulchre—to come without delay to Ascalon, bearing the wood of the Lord, to meet the troops of the unbelievers [Col. 0557D]. Yet they decided that a few faithful men should remain for the protection and defence of the city.

## CHAPTER XLII.—The people, forewarned about the gentiles’ booty, abstain.

When these arrangements had been made and the army had spread through the city, those warned by the embassy of the duke and the leading men quickly put aside, repaired, and took up again their horses and arms. Advancing through the mountains amid horns, trumpets, instruments, lyres, and every sound of exultation and joy, they joined Duke Godfrey, who was stationed on the borders of Ascalon; they encamped in the meadows and open country.

Count Raymond alone, still raging with the sting of envy against Duke Godfrey because he had lost the Tower of David, refused when invited to come with the whole body of his followers [Col. 0558A]. At last, compelled anew by the duke and all the princes through threats and admonitions, he rose; and, proceeding through the mountains by the royal road, he joined the duke and the aforesaid princes in the plains with a great force of his men.

Herds, camels, asses, oxen, buffaloes, and every kind of domestic livestock had been deceitfully sent forward and scattered in vast numbers through those plains by the Saracens, so that the Christian people, seized by desire, might plunder and drive them off, turn their thoughts to booty, and thus, hindered by plundering, be more easily overcome by the enemy. But a most noble Saracen, formerly governor of the city of Ramla, who, after Jerusalem had been conquered, had made peace and an alliance with the duke, now came—though a gentile—to assist Duke Godfrey with faithful intention. He exposed the Babylonians’ deceit, saying that the Saracens, Arabs, and all the gentiles had sent the herds ahead for no other reason than to hinder the pilgrims, so that they might devote themselves more to booty than to defence [Col. 0558B].

Forewarned by this gentile prince, the duke and all the commanders of the Christian army took precautions. They established an edict throughout the whole Catholic host that any pilgrim who touched booty before the battle should be punished by having his ears and nose cut off. In accordance with this proclamation and edict, all kept their hands from what was forbidden, taking only what would suffice for food that night.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—The duke explains to the gentile governor why the people go to battle.

[Col. 0558C] On the following day, as the first dawn shone, the whole people of the living God armed themselves for war. In sounds of rejoicing and every sweet melody of gladness, with lyres and instruments, they proceeded as though going to a banquet. Strengthened by the purity of confession, they were fortified and signed with the sign of the holy cross by Arnulf, Peter, and the other priests. Under their anathema, booty and every act of plunder before the contest were again forbidden.

The governor of the city of Ramla, seeing the people rejoicing and singing psalms amid pipes, lyres, instrumental sounds, and cries of exultation, as though invited to a feast of every delight, was exceedingly astonished. He asked the duke about this, saying: “I marvel, and cannot marvel sufficiently, at the source of this people’s great joy and exultant cry, as though they were going to a banquet, when death is present for them today, present martyrdom awaits them all, the issue of war is uncertain, and the great and intolerable force of their opponents has now assembled and pitched its camp not far from here” [Col. 0558D].

To this the duke, full of Christ’s faith and equipped with a spiritual answer, wisely explained to the inquiring man why, in the hope of death that day and of the imminent battle, the Christian people delighted in great joy and sweet melody. For he said:

> “Know that this people whom you see and hear hastening with exultant cries against their enemies, and undertaking battle in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, are certain today of the crown of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0559A]. They know that they will pass into a better life, in which they will first begin to live more happily, if they are deemed worthy to die in this battle for His name and grace. Therefore our hearts are lifted up in joy and jubilation, because, if perhaps we fall into the hands of our enemies, the Lord Jesus, our God, has power to place our souls in the paradise of His glory.
>
> “Therefore we do not fear death before the enemy’s assault, because after temporal death we are certain of His sure recompense. This sign of the holy cross, by which we are defended and sanctified, is without doubt a spiritual shield for us against the missiles of our enemies; trusting in it, we dare to stand more safely against every danger. Indeed, by this wood of the holy cross we were redeemed from the hand of death and hell, and from the power of the wicked angel [Col. 0559B]. And, cleansed in the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, from every defilement of our former error, we have confidence in eternal life.”

## CHAPTER XLIV.—The Christian host, signed with the cross, advances to meet the armed enemy.

Having heard the duke’s answer, the aforesaid gentile was asked, for instruction in everlasting life, that, since he too was about to fight for the cause of the most Christian duke and the Catholic people against his own nation and fellow-countrymen, he should be defended and sanctified by the same sign of the holy cross, so that through faith and hope in that holy cross and in the Crucified One he might be preserved unharmed from the enemies’ weapons and snares. Whether he received baptism immediately or after the battle we do not know, except that some assert [Col. 0559C] that, when he saw the valour and victory of the Christians, he received the grace of baptism.

When the whole Christian assembly, together with the gentile prince, had been sanctified by the sign of this holy cross from Arnulf’s hand, all turned their effort and attention to taking up arms, putting on mail-shirts, arranging battle-lines, and raising standards upon lances. There was no desire for the herds and forbidden flocks. Rather, the flocks and herds sent forward to deceive Christ’s faithful were astonished by the glitter of arms, helmets, and shields; stunned by the violent tumult and shouting of the army, they marvelled. Their ears raised in amazement, they stood motionless for a long time. At length they joined the horsemen and foot soldiers; mingled with the armed formations, they went when the troops went and stood when they stood. Raising a cloud of dust [Col. 0559D], they struck fear into the Saracens, who did not understand the matter and stood at a distance with their numerous multitude.

## CHAPTER XLV.—How their battle-line was arranged.

After the Christians had come down from the mountains and taken their stand in the valley and open plain where the tents of the Saracens, Arabs, Moors, and publicans had been pitched and their battle-lines drawn up, the flocks and all the herds, which no one could number, separated and made their way of their own accord, without keepers or masters, to a nearby place of good pasture. It was as if, forewarned and commanded by divine prompting, they voluntarily yielded place to the Catholic formations, lest they impede them; remaining there in the pasture, they could be found by the Christians after the victory [Col. 0560A].

Without delay, after the animals had been separated and the troops of the unbelievers sighted, the battle-lines of the Franks were prepared for war as they had been arranged: some in the front, some on the right and left, and others to fight in the rear. All the Christian horsemen and foot soldiers gathered in companies around their standards and banners.

Duke Godfrey, supreme lord of Jerusalem after the Lord, with two thousand horsemen and three thousand foot soldiers fully armed with mail-shirts, helmets, shields, lances, and arrows, besieged the gates of Ascalon, so that no force of inhabitants might burst out of the city on that side and unexpectedly attack the Franks from behind. Count Raymond, on the right, drew up his battle-line with a great force of his men toward the spacious and very dense orchards outside the walls, so that when battle came [Col. 0560B] he might strengthen his allies in force and resources and raise hearts weakened by fear from their impending distress. Robert, prince of the Normans, Robert of Flanders, Oliver of Jussy, Gerard of Kersey, and Reynard of Toul commanded closely massed battle-lines on the left against the Moors and every kind of gentile in the plains, ready to join battle. All the Christian horsemen and foot soldiers, formed in a compact mass around their standards and banners, stood there with equal resolve to resist.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—After the second engagements, the enemy side flees.

Thus, as both sides stood face to face, a cruel battle began. For the Azopart, who according to their custom usually commence battle on bended knees, were sent forward and fiercely attacked the Franks at the front of the battle with a hail of arrows [Col. 0560C], sounding trumpets and drums in order to terrify horses and men by such dreadful noise and drive them from the battle and the open plain. These same Azopart—hideous and utterly foul men—also had exceedingly cruel iron whips, with which they pierced mail-shirts and shields by heavy blows, struck horses on the forehead, and made a terrible noise throughout all the ranks of the faithful.

The Arabs, Saracens, and publicans, approaching in their thousands, fought against the Christian lines with lances, arrows, slings, and every sort of weapon, multiplying the engagements and consuming much of the day. Against them, the small Christian force, surrounded in the midst of so many innumerable thousands, fought unceasingly, wearing down and diminishing the enemy’s formations [Col. 0560D]. At last, as the battle grew fiercer and the gentile ranks were broken with God’s help, the entire army of the king of Babylon took flight. Dispersing across the level fields toward the sea, it fled from those who struck and pursued it.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—Concerning the slaughter and spoils of the slain.

Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond, Eustace, Tancred, Cuno of Montaigu, and his son Lambert, seeing that the gentile army and its strength were failing and giving way, rushed into the midst of the enemy with a charge of horses, a violent onset, and the shouting of the foot soldiers. Raging among them with great slaughter, they brought substantial aid to their brothers. The Arabs and the other peoples, seeing that they could no longer endure the battle, scattered and broken, took flight through the fields and narrow paths [Col. 0561A]. But they were slaughtered everywhere by the pursuing and victorious soldiers like wretched cattle.

An innumerable part of them, beaten and retreating, were pressed by the Christian pursuit and, in hope of safety and escape, hurried to the ships and the seashore. There Count Raymond happened to encounter them. Cruelly cutting them down and pursuing them, he forced as many as three thousand, fleeing into the sea, to drown under repeated blows of weapons. When the Saracen companies had thus been terrified by this savage slaughter—some planning flight to the sea, others toward orchards, and many seeking to enter the gate of Ascalon—the victorious Christians spread through the gentiles’ tents. Some seized precious purple cloth, others garments and silver vessels and a large quantity of both more precious metals; others took camels, mules, horses, dromedaries, and powerful asses. Like men hungry and worn down by long abstinence, now forgetful of the whole war, each laid hands upon whatever booty he could [Col. 0561B].

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—The people eager for plunder are struck down; those who restrain their hands prevail.

But the gentiles, whose innumerable multitude still filled the seashore and open country, saw that the people of Gaul were wholly intent on plunder and booty and had ceased pursuit. Leaving their companions everywhere, and reassembling their forces at the signal of trumpets and horns, they bravely attacked the men intent on booty and forgetful of war. They inflicted severe slaughter upon the unsuspecting, and would have made the Christians’ entire victory bloody [Col. 0561C], had not Duke Godfrey, supreme prince of Jerusalem, who was directing the outermost battle-lines toward the mountains, perceived their danger and that greed had blinded them. Without delay he flew to confront the enemy, prohibited the plunder, and sharply urged them all to defend themselves:

> “O rebellious and incorrigible men, who has bewitched you, that your hands should turn to forbidden and unlawful booty before your enemies, with God’s aid, had fallen by the sword? Come, leave the booty and press upon the enemy; do not now yield to those who rise again and seek bitter vengeance upon you.”

He spoke, then broke through the midst of the battle-lines with drawn swords, and dealt a grievous destruction to the enemy at the hands of his followers [Col. 0561D]. He then summoned all whom he had recalled from plunder with him to renew the work of battle. Once more defeated, the gentiles turned their backs and hastened in flight toward the city of Ascalon under the most frequent blows of weapons.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—Further concerning the slaughter of the doomed.

The duke and those with him pursued the fugitives, horsemen and foot soldiers alike, never falling back from the enemies’ rear; pursuing them amid the gravest slaughter, they continued as far as the gate of Ascalon. Fortunate were those received into the gate or able to gain admission. For the press of fleeing and entering Saracens at the very gateways of the city was said to have been so great that two thousand or more, killed or suffocated beneath the feet of people entering, horses, and mules, perished dead in and before the gates [Col. 0562A].

Those last in the flight and slower to flee, seeing distress for their lives on both sides, the difficult entrance to the gates, and, in this terror of weapons, that the gates had been shut and they had been excluded from the city, hastened to climb palm trees, or branches of olive or fig trees, hoping at least to hide or save themselves in the thickness of branches and leaves. But the Christian foot soldiers, very near at hand, immediately pierced with arrows the wretches seen and exposed in the trees; like birds struck by a flying missile, they compelled them, dying, to fall from the branches of the trees to the ground, and made the earth cover many of them.

## CHAPTER L.—When this battle was fought, and concerning the deeds done there.

[Col. 0562B] This battle was joined on Friday, the day before the Ides of August, by twenty thousand Christians against three hundred thousand gentiles: Saracens, Arabs, publicans, and Moors from the land of Ethiopia. Those present in the conflict reported to us that thirty thousand of them fell on the open plain of the fields, besides two thousand suffocated and killed at the city gate, and apart from those who, thinking to escape the dangers of weapons, perished without number, drowned in the waves of the sea’s abyss. No distinguished Christian men fell there, as was learned without doubt from truthful brothers, except a few of the common foot soldiers.

After the gentiles’ flight and overthrow, and the Christians’ victory, Robert, prince of the Normans, captured the long spear wholly covered in silver [Col. 0562C], called the *Standard*, which was borne as the ensign before the army of the king of Babylon. Around it the principal strength had gathered, and to it the defeated and scattered men returned. It was sent to the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and has been displayed there even to the present day in memory of the Christian victory.

Now that this storm of war had been calmed and Meravis—held second to the king in every decree and counsel—had been overcome with all his people, joy in booty was given to the Christians: in tents and herds, camels, buffaloes, asses, sheep, goats, oxen, and every kind of thing. Laden and refreshed by these goods, many travelled throughout the night and returned to Jerusalem with gladness of heart and cries of exultation. Before the most holy Sepulchre they rendered praises and thanks to God [Col. 0562D] for all that had happened to them prosperously and gloriously.

## CHAPTER LI.—Count Raymond, by his counsel, fortifies Ascalon and Asur against the Christians.

Duke Godfrey, having gathered again about two thousand horsemen and foot soldiers, besieged the gates of Ascalon on every side, so that its citizens and soldiers, stupefied and trembling after the new slaughter and recent victory, might surrender the city. They had lost all hope of aid from the king of Babylon, since the assembled strength of his entire kingdom had now been violently crushed and scattered.

But when some part of the night had passed and the people of Ascalon had held much counsel concerning surrendering the city and sparing their lives, Count Raymond, envious of all Duke Godfrey’s glory because of the Tower of David that he had lost, secretly sent this embassy to the Saracen citizens [Col. 0563A]:

> “Be most courageous men, and do not be frightened by Duke Godfrey’s threats into surrendering the city into his hands. For all our princes have resolved to return to the land of their kindred once the war is completed, and you should know that only a small body of fighting men remains with him around the city tonight.”

Encouraged by this embassy and reassurance from the count, the citizens and soldiers turned away from surrendering the city and giving pledges. At sunrise they took their stand on the walls for defence, keeping the duke and his men from the siege of the city with arrows, slings, and every kind of weapon. But the duke, seeing their boldness and resistance, and seeing that no more than seven hundred horsemen of all his forces remained with him, while all the princes had departed at the instigation and persuasion of that same count, proceeding along the seashore, also broke camp from the siege. Following the leading men along the royal road beside the sea, he caught up with them as far as the city of Asur [Col. 0563B].

There Count Raymond had conducted a siege around Asur for one day and night, thinking that, shaken by the new slaughter and recent victory, its citizens would surrender the city into his hands. He also made many threats and terrors against them, sometimes promising that they would obtain life, safety, and every favour from him if they surrendered the city. But when Godfrey’s arrival was known, Raymond—conscious of the treachery he had committed against him from envy—withdrew from the siege of Asur with all his following. He urged the citizens not to fear Godfrey and not to open the city to him under any threat or military attack, strongly assuring them that none of the princes who had gone ahead would return to help him [Col. 0563C].

## CHAPTER LII.—Duke Godfrey and Count Raymond are reconciled.

After exhorting the citizens in this way to hinder the duke, Raymond hurried on and, in the region between Caesarea and the city of Caiphas, beside a certain freshwater stream, joined Robert of Flanders, his namesake Robert, prince of the Normans, and the other leading men. Duke Godfrey, arriving at Asur, besieged the city for one day, in case by some chance or fear instilled in the Asurians it might be handed over to him. But, through Raymond’s persuasion and assurances, finding them—like the people of Ascalon—rebellious and resistant, he turned sadly away from the city. He urged his companions to attack Raymond in the camp and make all the wrongdoing which he had committed against him fall upon Raymond’s own head [Col. 0563D].

They immediately put on their mail-shirts. As they entered the camp with banners raised and prepared in anger to march against the count, while Raymond likewise, armed beforehand, had resolved to meet and resist them, Robert of Flanders and the other distinguished men intervened. They sternly rebuked the men and finally, with much effort, reconciled them on both sides and restored them to concord.

## CHAPTER LIII.—As the princes wish to return home, the duke bids them farewell; the citizens of Asur ally themselves with the duke.

Now that these men had been restored to concord by the favour of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, Robert of Flanders [Col. 0564A], Robert, prince of the Normans, Raymond of Provence likewise, and all the princes revealed to the duke their intention of returning home. In a conversation held with humble and gentle disposition, they found him kindly disposed toward all that they had in mind.

The duke, yielding in every respect to the will of his brothers, resolved to return to Jerusalem, because the power of the city had been entrusted to his protection and defence. Long embracing the necks of his companions and kindly kissing all of them, he earnestly and tearfully commended them with good wishes, begging that they remember him and exhort their Christian brethren not to hesitate to come to the Lord’s Sepulchre, and to bring day-by-day assistance against so many barbarous nations to him and the other companions who remained in exile.

The men and citizens of Asur, hearing that the duke was returning and had been reconciled with Raymond and the others, made a treaty with the duke for the city’s safety and peace, providing him hostages for tribute and for the city [Col. 0564B]. In turn, they received from the duke as a hostage for the security of faith and peace Gerard, a knight devoted to him and born at the castle of Avesnes.

## CHAPTER LIV.—Concerning the other faithful who returned home.

And behold: after so many battles and so many labours, unheard of in all ages, had been brought to completion in victory and a good end, and after the duke and all his companions had mutually commended one another, great and small, leaders and subjects, prepared to return from their long exile to their native land. They bore the palms of victory in their hands, overflowing with tears because of their exceeding affection for the brothers left in exile [Col. 0564C].

Giving them the kiss of love and bidding them farewell, they retraced their route through the same cities and mountain difficulties along the Palestinian sea by which they had come to Jerusalem. All the aforesaid cities—Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, Tripoli, Baurim, and the remaining cities—gave them leave to buy and sell the necessities of life. All peoples and their cities ceased from every attack and ambush against them, fearful and trembling at the overthrow of the king of Babylon and the victory bestowed by the living God upon the faithful.

Thus passing safely and peacefully through these places, carrying few weapons but palms in their hands as a sign of victory, they turned aside into the territory of the city of Jbail, exceedingly rich in crops and vines. There, at a distance from the city walls, because of its convenient streams and pastures, they pitched their tents on the open plain and for two days enjoyed the abundant good things of that land [Col. 0564D].

## CHAPTER LV.—Bohemond besieges Laodicea, a city of Christians.

While they were staying in these places, news was brought to them that Bohemond, insatiable in his greed to amass and acquire, had laid siege to Laodicea, a city and dwelling-place of Catholic Greeks, for a long time. With the assistance and naval assault of the Pisans and Genoese, he had already seized two towers of the city situated on the seashore, which controlled the city by levying tribute from sailors. Some of their Catholic guards he had slaughtered; others he had blinded and thrown down from the fortress itself [Col. 0565A].

Yet the Pisans and Genoese are not greatly to be blamed for these wrongs, for they had learned from Bohemond’s own mouth that matters stood far otherwise than they actually did. At his false urging, therefore, they blockaded the aforesaid towers with two hundred ships; and, with the tall masts of their ships touching the clouds and wicker baskets fixed at their tops, they severely pressed the garrison guards, attacking the towers and their defenders from the overhanging timber with very frequent volleys of stones and arrows.

When Bohemond, that deceitful prince and greedy brother, heard of the arrival of the Pisans and Genoese, he met them six miles from Antioch, near Laodicea, and recounted every evil and great crime concerning the citizens of Laodicea. He declared them to be harmful calumniators of Christians, so that by this device he might more easily incite all minds to hatred of the citizens and to the siege of the city [Col. 0565B]. Thus it came about that those who credulously accepted his word first besieged the towers and compelled their guards to surrender; then, having overcome the towers by their skill or force, they encircled the city. Harassing its citizens with a severe and prolonged assault, they had already firmly placed two bridges across the rampart of the walls, through which access to the walls was more readily open to them. Thus the hard-pressed city would shortly be surrendered to Bohemond. It was near at hand that, with engines of this kind applied, the city would be taken, its citizens punished, and everything unjustly given over to Bohemond.

It was indeed unjust, for during the siege of Antioch that same Laodicea, with the aforesaid towers, had been overcome and captured in a naval siege and assault by Winemar of Boulogne, master of pirates, and certain Christians [Col. 0565C]. Having gathered ships from various lands and realms—namely from Antwerp, Tiel, Frisia, and Flanders—and having joined by sea the Provençals in the land of Saint-Gilles, under Count Raymond’s authority, they sailed round the circuit of the world as far as the city of Laodicea itself. Capturing and storming it, they struck down with the sword the Turks and Saracens found there, its unjust rulers; and, having seized the city and its walls, after the siege of Antioch they entrusted it, together with those towers, to Count Raymond.

Winemar, master and leader of the pirates, was later captured by Turcopoles and soldiers of the Greek emperor and committed to prison; but, through Duke Godfrey’s intervention, he was released from prison and bonds after a very long time [Col. 0565D]. Count Raymond, after the capture of Antioch, when his route to Jerusalem had been settled with the others, restored Laodicea—taken from the Turks and gentiles—to the emperor of Constantinople, and thus kept faith with him inviolate. For, together with Godfrey and the other princes, he had sworn and made a treaty with the emperor that, of all cities, castles, and lands belonging to his realm, they would retain or falsely claim nothing at all.

For this reason, the princes, returning from Jerusalem and encamped in the territory of Jbail, learning that Bohemond had unjustly besieged Laodicea and had wronged the emperor and Count Raymond [Col. 0566A], appointed envoys. They were to urge him amicably and peacefully, by the embassy and request of their Christian brethren returning from Jerusalem in God’s victory, to withdraw from the siege of the city and inflict no further injury upon Christians.

## CHAPTER LVI.—The bishop of Pisa humbly greets the returning pilgrims.

Meanwhile, while envoys were being chosen for this purpose, the bishop of the Pisans, named Dagobert, having learned of the arrival and return from Jerusalem of the Christian pilgrims—whose fame or memory had been known for a very long time down to that day—hastened to visit his brethren, taking with him several eminent men from his following. When he found them in the aforesaid region [Col. 0566B], he could not in any way restrain himself from weeping for joy. Throwing himself upon the necks of all, great and small alike, he began tearfully to kiss them all, saying:

> “Truly and without any doubt I confess that you are sons and friends of the living God. You have renounced not only your possessions, cities, castles, estates, wives, sons, and daughters, but have not spared even your lives, since you did not hesitate to undertake this expedition of God and our Lord Jesus Christ into nations so remote and barbarous. As we have learned, you have endured so many adversities for the grace of our Redeemer.
>
> “Since Christ’s birth it has not been heard that any Christian army, passing through so many kingdoms and dangers, captured Jerusalem by strength and might, expelled its illegitimate sons and inhabitants [Col. 0566C], purified the holy places, and after victory raised up there to guard them the magnificent Christian prince Godfrey—as we have now learned concerning his and your glory and valour. Therefore, rejoicing in the desire to see, greet, and converse with you, we have resolved to come here.”

## CHAPTER LVII.—The mutual conversation of the bishop and the pilgrims.

To this the faithful pilgrims answered the venerable bishop as follows:

“If you rejoice in the prosperity of the Christians and smile upon their safety, why have you unjustly used violence against Christian fellow-citizens, namely those of the city of Laodicea? Why have you seized their towers, slaughtered their guards, and still ravaged their city by siege?”

On hearing this, the bishop [Col. 0566D] excused himself kindly and patiently, declaring that he and his people had sinned in all these matters through ignorance. He said:

“We are free from bloodguilt in this matter. For when we came by ship into these regions, inexperienced and wholly ignorant of warfare, Bohemond met us coming from Antioch. He asserted that the citizens of Laodicea were false Christians; he further persistently reported that they were always hostile to their Christian brethren and had been traitors to the pilgrims among the Turks and Saracens. He begged for our help and strength to avenge this. Believing his words and assertions, and judging these citizens to be most wicked, we gave him our forces and assistance to besiege the city and its inhabitants, thinking that in killing them we were rendering service to God. But now [Col. 0567A] we have learned the truth from your own mouths: namely, that Bohemond persecutes these people out of envy and avarice, not by the grace of God; and that he has miserably deceived us into besieging and punishing Christians. Therefore, returning to our people without delay, we shall reveal the matter and thus restrain them from the city and from every attack upon it.”

## CHAPTER LVIII.—Bohemond, unwilling to raise the siege, is abandoned by all.

Having said this, the envoys of the army of Jerusalem departed with the bishop of Pisa. But finding Bohemond obstinately fixed in his excessive avarice, they courteously explained to him the embassy of his brethren and fellow-princes, urging him to remove his arms and forces from Laodicea, lest they violate the pledged faith given to the emperor of the Greeks and suffer a most serious obstruction to their return within [Col. 0567B] his realm. But Bohemond, having heard the envoys’ words, utterly despised the petition and warning of the faithful, declaring that he would never withdraw from the walls and fortifications of Laodicea until the city and its citizens had been subjected to his authority.

The envoys, reporting all Bohemond’s answers, harsh words, and impatience to the army, informed the leading men. Sharply stirring the anger of all, they moved their minds so that everyone, great and small, was ordered to procure arms and prepare for war. When the bishop learned Bohemond’s purpose and answer, he went down into the camp and fleet of his own people and explained to all in his company the cause and the warning issued by the Christian army. Thus he recalled all the Pisans [Col. 0567C] and Genoese, moved to compunction in the Lord God, from the siege of the city and from aiding Bohemond, lest they presume any longer to raise a hand against the citizens in his support.

Bohemond, therefore, seeing that he had been deprived of assistance and that his forces had been greatly weakened, and that Christ’s faithful and the princes had conspired to remove him by war and force of arms, withdrew far from the siege of the walls with all his force at evening, when darkness covered heaven and earth. Whether from affection or fear, willingly or unwillingly, he obeyed his brethren’s will.

## CHAPTER LIX.—The armed faithful arrive at Laodicea and find that Bohemond has fled.

The following day, when the matter had been reported everywhere, the whole multitude of pilgrims put on arms and mail-coats. Setting out on the march, and after most of the day had passed, they came to Laodicea with crimson banners and a multitude of trumpets. [Col. 0567D] Finding no resistance from opponents, they entered peacefully through the gates of the city, [Col. 0568A] which the citizens themselves had opened to them freely, amid every kind reception.

They were told that Bohemond had withdrawn some distance away and had encamped only half a mile from there. Count Raymond, therefore, with five hundred brethren of his company, entered the city’s stronghold and raised his well-known banner upon the summit of its loftiest tower, placing guards of his own men throughout all the towers of Laodicea. The other brethren and fellow-princes were distributed through all the buildings, inside and outside the houses, for lodging.

The number of Jerusalem pilgrims was about twenty thousand when, returning from Jerusalem, they entered the territory of Laodicea. The sellers supplied them abundantly with everything necessary for life. It was the month of September, the season of autumn, when they reached Laodicea. There, enjoying an exceptional abundance of wheat, grapes, new wine, oil, and barley, they spent fifteen days joyfully, while the city’s inhabitants and the Pisan and Genoese pilgrims showed one another every reciprocal kindness of familiarity and friendliness. [Col. 0568B]

## CHAPTER LX.—Bohemond is reconciled with the people of Laodicea and with certain others.

Meanwhile, recalling their shared Christian name, their common tribulation and suffering, and their former affection, amid these mutual joys of charity, the Christians on both sides appointed intermediaries. They were to rebuke Bohemond for his injustice and appeal to him for reconciliation, so that, moved to compunction, he might not refuse reconciliation with his brethren; and so that the brethren, in turn, might kindly receive him into concord and charity when he had made satisfaction.

Bohemond, hearing these envoys, was moved to compunction over everything and hastened back into unity and affection. For on an appointed day, after a conference had been held in the plains of Laodicea—especially between the two counts, Raymond and Bohemond, and afterwards among the others—peace and friendship were confirmed, and every former hatred was wholly put away. Bohemond then remained with them for three days, in the service of charity inquiring into the victory of Jerusalem; afterwards he returned with his men to Antioch.

Robert of Flanders, Robert likewise prince of the Normans, Gaston of Bordeaux, Cuno of Montaigu, and their other companions decided, after some days, to return by ship to [Col. 0568D] their native land. But Count Raymond, fearing that through Bohemond’s avarice and instability he might lose the cities of Laodicea and Tortosa, which he had subdued with difficult labor, remained with a large body of his followers.

# BOOK VII

[Col. 0567]

## CHAPTER I.—The citizens of Assur, breakers of the treaty, are besieged again by the duke.

[Col. 0567D]

After the citizens of Assur, commonly called Arsid, at the counsel of envious persons, had altogether refused, terrified by the victory which Duke Godfrey had won near Ascalon, to surrender the city and render the revenues which they had agreed [Col. 0568D] to give him each year, they unjustly detained his hostages, given under the treaty of friendship. Rejoicing at the return of their own men [Col. 0569A] who had escaped the duke’s custody by ill-kept faith, they fortified themselves still further against the duke’s presence by strong defenses.

Therefore the king, moved by anger, together with the other nobles and common men who had remained with him—namely William of Montpellier, Werner of Greiz, Geldemar Carpentarius, Wicker the German, and all the Christian knights and foot-soldiers, numbering three thousand—surrounded the city and spread their tents around it. Their tents having been placed on every side, they prepared siege engines and mangonel apparatus, constructing them with the greatest effort over seven weeks.

## CHAPTER II.—A tearful account of the knight Gerhard.

At last, when the engines had been brought up to the wall, they attacked the citizens vigorously. The latter likewise resisted no less energetically for their lives from their towered citadel and walls. [Col. 0569B] But seeing that they labored in vain in defense, they raised aloft a ship’s mast of great height, which lay in the middle of the city, securing it with ropes and chains. Upon it they fastened one of the duke’s hostages, the aforesaid Gerhard, a distinguished knight of the lineage of the Hamaic people, from the garrison of Avennis, in the manner of one crucified, stretching out his hands and feet with ropes. The Christians believed that he had long since been worn away by tortures inflicted by executioners.

But Gerhard himself, raised and fastened upon the summit of the mast, burst forth weeping into this pitiful cry and addressed the duke:

“O most illustrious duke, remember now how, at your command, I was sent here as a hostage and exile among barbarous nations and impious men. Therefore I ask that you be moved by some mercy or human feeling toward me, and do not allow me [Col. 0569C] to perish under so grievous and cruel a martyrdom.”

The duke replied:

“By no means, O Gerhard, bravest of knights, can I pity you and turn so many men away from vengeance upon this city. Even if you were my full brother, like Eustace, you could not be set free on the condition that the city should remain unharmed. For you must die; and it is more expedient that you alone should die than that the decree and oath of our men be violated, and that this city should remain forever hostile to pilgrims. For if you die from this present life, you shall live with Christ in heaven.”

Gerhard, understanding this and seeing that no entreaty of tears availed him, earnestly begged the duke to present his horse and arms to the Holy Sepulchre, so that they might be bestowed there upon those serving God for the remedy of his soul.

Thereupon the duke and the whole multitude of Christians fiercely assaulted the city, forgetting every feeling of pity and mercy toward their brother Gerhard, and attacked the defenders of the city on every side with arrows, slings, and mangonels. And already, among the many arrows carelessly discharged, Gerhard’s body was pierced and wounded by ten arrows. [Col. 0569D]

## CHAPTER III.—When the duke’s engine collapsed, many Christians were burned with it.

The pagans, seeing that this valiant man, all pity having been excluded from the hearts of his own people, was being wounded, reproached the duke and the entire Christian people with great blasphemies, saying:

“Impious and cruel nation, you have not troubled yourselves in the least to spare your brother and fellow-Christian; rather, seeing him and his destruction, you have attacked the city and its citizens [Col. 0570A] all the more fiercely!”

Having said this, they resisted manfully from within with mangonels, crossbows, and arrows, striving to drive back the duke’s soldiers attacking the city from the engine. For they hurled from the walls, in a continual shower, sharp iron stakes wrapped with oil, tow, pitch, and combustible material—wholly inextinguishable by water—through the ox-horns, with which the wicker screens were covered, in order to ward off the fires cast upon it.

At last, however, the flame was gradually kindled and, seizing upon the dry material on every side, burned the entire engine. It collapsed to the ground with its three upper stories. More than fifty fighting men, appointed there by the duke and the other leading men, were caught everywhere in the invasion of flames and fell with the machine in its ruin. Some had their necks and throats broken; others had their legs or arms cut almost away; some had their entrails burst by the unbearable mass of timber. Unable to be rescued by any help, they were reduced to ashes and cinders together with the wood. Among them, Franco of the town of Mechela, which stands on the river Meuse, a fearless knight, was seen by all to be caught by a blazing beam and burned in that same inextinguishable fire. [Col. 0570B]

## CHAPTER IV.—The duke’s exhortation to the knights.

Immediately, without delay, Rothold, a most valiant knight, seeing that the Saracens’ skill and fire had prevailed and that the engine with its occupants had fallen to the ground, leaped swiftly down from the city walls. Before the fire, he had descended from the engine onto those walls together with Peter the Lombard, a distinguished knight. Since no aid was being brought to them, they stood unharmed in the ditch beside the walls. The Saracens, seeing them fallen near the walls, strove to crush the men with iron-tipped stakes and a huge mass of stones. But, protected by God and with their very strong helmets enduring the repeated blows, they returned alive and unhurt to the company of Christians. [Col. 0570C]

The duke, seeing that his boldest knights had thus fallen in grievous destruction and ruin—some slain and burned, others disabled—and that all the work of the engine had been consumed by swift devastation and devouring flame, while many of the Christian company were losing heart and contemplating flight, began in sorrow and grief to call all the despairing back to the assault on the city, the destruction of their enemies, and the strengthening of the siege, [Col. 0570D] saying:

“Ah, wretched and useless men! Why did you leave your land and kindred, except to give your souls unto death for the name of Jesus and for the redemption of the holy Church and the deliverance of your brethren? Behold, this city and all the nations round about are hostile to the city of Jerusalem and lie in wait for our safety; this is one of those cities which you have besieged. Take care that you do not abandon your purpose and, made womanish in so base a fashion, leave this city unconquered. Therefore repent of your most shameful lust, which you have practiced incestuously on this holy journey, and of all your iniquities by which you have offended the grace of God. Thus, cleansed by pardon and confession of your sins, make the Lord of heaven—before whom there is no iniquity—favorable to you; for without him you can do nothing.” [Col. 0571A]

## CHAPTER V.—Penance is imposed upon the people; but, when a similar engine is burned, they are again afflicted.

At this voice and admonition of the duke, all who had been intent on flight and shaken by fear were strengthened by consolation. They established the siege around Assur more firmly and vigorously than before, until another engine, rebuilt once more, could be brought to the walls, through which the city might be taken.

When all was ready, at the first dawn of the following day Arnulf, chancellor of the Lord’s Sepulchre, an illustrious clerk devoted to God, began to rebuke the duke himself and all, great and small, for the treachery and hardness of heart by which they had sinned against their brethren Gerhard and Lambert, fastened to the mast [malo] and left as hostages among the Assyrians. [Col. 0571B] He therefore fatherly exhorted them all to confess and correct this impiety and the shamefulness of all their sins.

Thus, as he exhorted them to compunction of heart and forgiveness of their faults, they shed tears and rose with one purpose to continue the siege of the city. Rebuilding the engine and stone-throwing artillery, they spent a long time around the walls. This second engine was made and assembled to equal the first in size. It was brought across the ditch to the city walls amid the strength of armored men and a multitude of men and women; and very strong and daring men were posted in its upper stories to bring battle against the citizens.

While this engine was being drawn across the ditch [Col. 0571C] so as greatly to surpass the city walls in height, and while the men upon it attacked the fortifications with bow, javelin, and lance and sorely harassed the citizens standing on the walls, the Saracens struck it with a similar discharge of burning stakes, as they had the former engine. The growing flame seized and burned the screens, posts, and beams.

Immediately men and women from the whole army and the tents ran together to extinguish the engine, each carrying water in individual vessels. But this great pouring on of water achieved nothing. For this kind of fire was inextinguishable by water, and its flame was great and unconquerable. Therefore the engine could not be put out until it was wholly consumed. Falling in a great collapse, it crushed very many of the men and women standing nearby with various blows. [Col. 0571D] Some lay dead there; others were disabled by injuries to their limbs; some, half-dead, vomited purple blood from shattered entrails; others, choked by the flames and unable to be rescued by anyone, perished miserably. There was one shared grief among those dying, and no rest.

## CHAPTER VI.—The siege of Assur is raised; Bohemond and Baldwin enter the Holy City.

Since the duke accomplished nothing with these engines, he took counsel with his men. Because the city of Assur, at the onset of that very severe winter, was considered unconquerable because of cold and snow, he returned to Jerusalem in mid-December. Yet he assigned one hundred knights and two hundred foot-soldiers to Rames, or Ramla, to attack and provoke the citizens of Assur continuously [Col. 0572A] in war. The citizens, however, taking precautions lest any sudden assault or ambush should harm them, never went far from the walls. Accordingly, the duke’s knights plundered their crops and vineyards every day.

At length those same Christian knights, seeing that they gained nothing by ambush or assault, likewise returned to Jerusalem and for two months restrained themselves from every attack and harassment. The people of Assur, thus made secure and fearing no further adversity, gradually began carelessly to go out from the city for their occupations and cultivate their vines and fields.

Bohemond, at Antioch, heard of the Christians’ victory and of Duke Godfrey’s glory and exaltation in Jerusalem through the words and report of Robert of Flanders, Robert [Col. 0572B] prince of the Normans, and the other men returning home. Urged by envoys from Baldwin, the duke’s brother, he decided to take the road to Jerusalem in order to visit the place of the Lord’s Sepulchre. Dagobert, bishop of Pisa, who with all his company had remained for a long time—three months—in the region of Laodicea, now joined them upon this journey. Having exchanged gifts, he entered into a friendship with both parties, from day to day, in every word and deed of their feigned religion, and was exceedingly welcome to all.

When the Nativity of the Lord was close at hand, the aforesaid princes entered Jerusalem with great honor and a company of Christians. Duke Godfrey met them gloriously and, from joy and his intense desire to see them, gave them devout kisses.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Pisan bishop’s ambition for the patriarchate.

After some days had passed, the bishop of Pisa, having acquired many supporters among Baldwin’s and Bohemond’s followers, began to become so pleasing and beloved to the duke that he succeeded in being advanced to the dignity of patriarch—rather through a contribution of money than through affection for the new church.

This Dagobert, while he was still bishop of Pisa, had been sent by Urban, supreme pontiff of the Romans, to Spain as a legate for Christian worship and religion. He was honorably received by the king, named Alfonso, and was enriched and honored by all the bishops and archbishops of that kingdom with obedience and affection, and also with precious and magnificent gifts in gold, silver, and purple cloth, bestowed upon him by the king himself and all the leading men. [Col. 0572D]

It also became known to many how that illustrious king had sent, by Dagobert’s hand, a golden ram of marvelous beauty and workmanship as a gift to the apostolic lord out of charity. But Dagobert, burning with avarice, retained it secretly, together with the other money collected from every side. And, as those say to whom the matter became known, after Pope Urban’s death he brought this large talent-mass and golden ram to Jerusalem; bribing Bohemond and Baldwin, he gave the ram and the other gifts to Duke Godfrey. Thus he was elevated to the honor of the patriarchate.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The princes go with the duke to the Jordan.

Dagobert having now been installed as patriarch in the chair of the see of Jerusalem and consecrated by Robert, bishop of the city of Ramla, commonly called Rames, [Col. 0573A] and the Nativity of the Lord having been celebrated by the catholic men and princes in every joy and gladness, Bohemond, Baldwin, and the patriarch himself obtained from the duke that they should arrange their journey so as to meet at the River Jordan on the vigil of the Lord’s Epiphany, where the Lord Jesus had deigned to be baptized by John.

The duke, satisfying their wish and desire, went down with them to that river in full array and with the power of foot-soldiers and knights. There they bathed and rejoiced with joy. Afterwards Baldwin and Bohemond, rejoicing with the duke in all gladness and mutual goodwill, parted from one another there in the region of the Jordan after giving each other a tearful kiss. Godfrey returned to Jerusalem with the patriarch; Bohemond and Baldwin returned respectively to Antioch and Edessa. [Col. 0573B]

## CHAPTER IX.—The citizens of Assur are punished by severe mutilation.

Then, in the middle of February, while the citizens of Assur were confidently engaged from day to day in all their occupations and peacefully went out to cultivate their vineyards and fields, a certain Saracen from among the citizens of Assur, wishing to find favor in the duke’s eyes, revealed everything: how confidently the citizens went out of the city to obtain all that was necessary to them, with no thought of death.

When the duke heard the Saracen, he gave him a kindly hearing in all matters and took care to flatter the man all the more. Accordingly, [Col. 0573C] that traitor appointed a day on which he could kill some of them and capture others while they were laboring in vineyards and fields. At dawn on that day Duke Godfrey placed forty armed knights in ambush near Rames. They fell upon about a thousand Saracens who had gone out, in a sudden charge of horses. Killing them with cruel wounds, they left more than five hundred half alive in the field, with noses cut off and with hands or feet removed. The victors themselves returned to Jerusalem with their captive wives and children.

When this most grievous slaughter became known, the whole city of Assur and all who lived in it were stirred to grief and lamentation. Without delay they sent messengers to the king of Babylon with news of this cruel report and loss. [Col. 0573C]

## CHAPTER X.—Ten Christian knights put thirty pagan horsemen to flight and kill them.

[Col. 0573D]

When Meravis, who ruled second after the king and whose word all citizens and all cities of the kingdom of Babylon obeyed, heard this cruel report, he was greatly disturbed. At once he promised to send one hundred Arab horsemen and two hundred Azoparts to aid the citizens and defend the city. He did not allow so grave an embassy to reach the ears of the lord king of Babylon, the Ammirabilis, lest his heart be too heavily burdened.

Learning of this promised aid from Meravis, the citizens of Assur rejoiced greatly. From that day onward, with the gates open, they and all their herds went securely into the fields, though not far from the city. Then, after eight days had passed, the king of Babylon’s aid and forces came to them: one hundred Arab horsemen and two hundred Azoparts. At their command and encouragement, the citizens ventured to go farther from the city and gate than they had been accustomed to do. [Col. 0574A]

When word of their arrival was heard in Jerusalem, ten Christian knights set out secretly from the duke and halted on the border of Ramla to discover the truth of the matter: whether the Babylonian soldiers had indeed come to help the city of Assur. They immediately sent five squires before the city walls to provoke and draw out the men of whose arrival there was report; the ten knights themselves went down into the plain of Assur.

As the squires rode about before the city walls on horseback according to the plan of the ten knights, thirty armed Arab horsemen suddenly came out of the city and pursued them fiercely, leaving the ambush behind them. The squires fled as swiftly as possible on their horses to the ten Christian knights. Their ten lords immediately came to their aid on horseback and in arms. They put the thirty Arabs to flight and pursued them to the gates and walls of Assur, killing three of them at once. Their heads were cut off by the squires; bringing these with the horses and spoils of the slain, they returned joyfully to Jerusalem. [Col. 0574B]

## CHAPTER XI.—The Babylonians are again cut down near Assur by the duke’s knights.

When this victory and the highly praiseworthy boldness of the ten knights became known, the duke and all his men rejoiced. He accordingly summoned one hundred and forty horsemen and placed them in ambush toward Rames under the leadership of Werner of Greiz and Robert, a worthy knight from Apulia. They were to provoke the Arab soldiers by some stratagem, draw them out from the city of Assur, surround them, and accomplish some notable exploit against them.

These Christian knights of the duke remained in ambush near Rames for two days, until, on the third day, the citizens of Assur, trusting in their own soldiers and ignorant of all danger, began to wander safely through the fields with their flocks. As they wandered without regard for danger, twenty knights immediately came out from the ambush and company of Christians, gathered booty from every side, and carried it off by force; but it was soon recovered by the soldiers of Assur.

At this the whole Christian force rose from the ambush and charged boldly. The Arab and Azopart soldiers, with all their foot-soldiers, did the same, and a severe battle was joined on both sides. At last the Christians prevailed, killing the greater part of them. Retaining the booty, with many horses and soldiers captured there, they returned to Jerusalem in glory and joy. The remaining Saracens, few as they were, barely escaped and returned to Babylon with mournful news; there can be no doubt that they increased the king’s anger and the Babylonians’ fear. Duke Godfrey, finally, rejoiced not a little at the successful outcome of his men. [Col. 0574D]

## CHAPTER XII.—The city of Assur becomes tributary, and Joppa is restored.

Thus at last the city of Assur, worn out, and seeing that it could not resist even with the aid of its king, made peace, offered the duke the keys of its gates and towers, and became tributary to him. The duke granted its tribute, under an agreement of payment in solidi, to Robert, the distinguished knight from Apulia.

After this, wishing still more strongly to press and subdue the city of Ascalon and to overthrow and wage war upon the other cities under the kingdom of Babylon, the duke determined to rebuild and fortify with walls Joppa, commonly called Japhet, which had long been destroyed. There a harbor for ships might be established, and thence there might be a place for resistance against, and injury to, the other cities of the pagans.

Once the city of Japhet had been strengthened and fortified, Christian merchants from every kingdom and island came to its harbor bearing necessities of life. Pilgrims arriving from every direction likewise landed there safely and cared for their bodies with lodging and rest. [Col. 0575B]

## CHAPTER XIII.—The rulers of neighboring cities freely offer themselves as tributaries to the duke.

The Saracens became sorrowful and distressed, because, from the rebuilding and restoration of this city, all the surrounding cities of the pagans were to be subdued, attacked, and devastated, while the Christian forces arriving by sea increased from day to day. In all their deliberation, the pagans thought of nothing better to do than to hasten an embassy from Ascalon, Caesarea, and Ptolemais or Accaron, bearing greetings to the duke on behalf of the ammirals of those cities.

Without delay the embassy was brought before the duke and all his chief men in Jerusalem [Col. 0575C] in this form:

“The ammiral of Ascalon, the ammiral of Caesarea, and likewise the ammiral of Ptolemais send every greeting to Duke Godfrey. We entreat you, most glorious and magnificent duke, that by your favor and permission our citizens may go securely and peacefully about their business. We shall send you ten strong horses and three handsome mules; and every month we shall pay five thousand Byzantines as tribute.”

By this pact peace was greatly established and confirmed; moreover, friendship began to grow day by day, especially between the duke and the ammiral of Ascalon. Gifts flowed increasingly to the duke in wheat, wine, barley, and oil, more than can be spoken or recalled. Caesarea and Accaron likewise, after giving gifts of gold and silver, obtained peace and security. For fear of the most Christian duke had fallen upon all the lands and regions of the pagans. [Col. 0575D]

## CHAPTER XIV.—On the same matter, and how the duke established peace on land.

Thereafter the rulers of Arabia, learning of the duke’s most glorious fame, likewise made peace and friendship with him, on the condition that their merchants might peacefully bring everything necessary for the body to Jerusalem and Joppa and exchange it with Christians for a price, without prohibition. This was done. All things were brought in abundance, both to Joppa and to Jerusalem: herds, cattle, sheep, horses, clothing, and provisions; and they exchanged everything with Christians [Col. 0576A] at a fair price. Thus great joy arose among the people.

But the duke forbade every exchange and departure by sea to all pagans. Guards and ambushes were spread over the sea, lest the pagans bring anything by ship to their cities that might make those cities rich in necessary resources and confident enough to grow proudly rebellious; they might then neglect the treaty which they had made with the duke and, grown strong, resist him. If any came by ship from Alexandria, Damietta, or Africa, they were captured with their goods by the duke’s soldiers and cut to pieces. Likewise, the Saracens kept no peace with Christians at sea. They established peace and treaty with one another only on land.

This peace between the duke and the ammiral of Ascalon grew so great that the inhabitants of that city peacefully entered with merchandise, and Christian men likewise traveled to Ascalon without hindrance. [Col. 0576B]

## CHAPTER XV.—The aforesaid Gerhard is sent back unharmed and honored with benefices.

As this peace increased so greatly and their friendship became more and more closely joined, one day the same governor and ammiral of Ascalon sent back to the most Christian duke of Jerusalem Gerhard of the garrison of Avennis. He had been healed of every wound, honorably dressed in clothing, and mounted on an excellent horse. The duke and all the Christians had thought for many days that he had died in Assur, not knowing that he had been taken down from the mast and sent from Assur to that same ammiral.

When the duke saw Gerhard and received him safe and sound—his beloved knight and excellent young man—he rejoiced exceedingly. At once, in reward for his great labor, he granted him, in the presence of all the faithful who were there, extensive landed benefices valued at one hundred marks, together with the castle called Saint Abraham’s. From that day onward peace on land began to multiply more and more on both sides, until it became wearisome to the warlike knights of Gaul. [Col. 0576C]

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the obstinacy of Grossus Rusticus.

Not long afterwards Tancred met the duke of Jerusalem at the coming feast of the Nativity of the Lord. He came from the fortress of Tiberias, which the duke had rebuilt on a steep mountain with a rampart and impregnable fortification, and which Tancred had received as a gift from the duke to defend. Tancred complained greatly and asked for help because the land and city [Col. 0576D] of Grossus Rusticus, adjoining the kingdom of Egypt, were rebelling against him and disdaining to render their revenues.

When the duke heard and took this ill, he granted Tancred’s request after eight days. With two hundred horsemen and one thousand foot-soldiers, he entered the land and regions of Grossus Rusticus. Having gathered innumerable booty from every side, he ordered some pagan men to be slaughtered and others taken captive, while he reduced everything else everywhere to fire and slaughter.

While the duke stayed in this region for eight days, committing slaughter and arson, Grossus Rusticus, ruler of the region, sent an embassy to seek aid from the Turks, hoping that, supported perhaps by their strength, he might meet and resist the duke. This ruler was called Grossus Rusticus by the Franks because of his excessive fatness and bulk and his contemptible appearance, in which he seemed altogether rustic. [Col. 0577A]

When the ruler of the Turks and king of Damascus heard his embassy, he immediately sent him five hundred Turks as aid. The Christian knights had already departed from Rusticus’s land after their lengthy and severe ravaging. The duke marched always at the front with booty of flocks, clothing, and other things; Tancred, far behind, provided the rear guard with one hundred horsemen.

And behold, shortly afterwards Turkish soldiers were seen hastening toward them. Tancred met them without delay and joined battle with them. On both sides there were hard-fought losses that day: some were killed and others wounded; Tancred barely escaped. When evening came, the duke and all his force encamped in the open country, laying aside their arms for the night. Not knowing how Tancred had engaged in battle with the Turks, he remained wholly uncertain of Tancred’s outcome until, in the middle of that night, Tancred arrived safe with his companions, though some of them had been badly wounded by arrows. [Col. 0577B]

When the duke learned how the Turks had pursued Tancred from Damascus and fought a battle with him, he ordered battle-lines to be formed at the first light of the following day and to meet the Turks who had pursued them. But not one of them was found in that region. For, sensing that the presence of the distinguished duke was very near, they had returned to their own country throughout the night and ceased further pursuit of Tancred.

Afterwards the duke returned to Jerusalem. Tancred likewise returned with his men to Tiberias. With sixty knights, he stayed there and every day attacked Damascus and the Turkish strongholds, carrying off booty from their land and region.

This fortress of Tiberias stands near the place called the Sea of Tiberias; it measures two miles in length and two in breadth. Tancred held it as a benefice after it had been subdued by the most Christian duke and rebuilt with a garrison, because he had found favor in the duke’s eyes, was proven worthy in military service, and seemed unfailing in resistance to the enemies of Christians. [Col. 0577C]

## CHAPTER XVII.—The ruler of Damascus kills Tancred’s envoys; the duke invades his land and compels Grossus Rusticus to make a treaty.

The Turks, seeing Tancred grow stronger day by day, and that Duke Godfrey’s forces were always [Col. 0577D] at his side, resolved for a time to make peace with him on this condition: that, after the term of this peace, when they had taken common counsel, they would either wish to be subject to him or would altogether refuse to enter into an alliance with him. Tancred, having taken counsel with the duke on these matters, agreed to the Turks’ request; and, receiving from them and from Grossus Rusticus many gifts of Byzantine gold, silver, and purple cloth, thereafter did not disturb their land by war.

Then, after several days had passed, Tancred sent six knights, eloquent and highly experienced men, to the prince of the Turks at Damascus, demanding that he surrender the city to him and adopt the Christian faith, if indeed he wished by Tancred’s gift or consent to dwell or live in any part of that region [Col. 0578A]; otherwise, that he could not preserve friendship with him for gold, silver, or other gifts. When he heard this, the prince of Damascus was moved by violent anger and ordered five of the men who had been seized to be beheaded. The sixth, because he embraced the Turkish sect, he commanded to be spared.

When news of the most bloody slaughter of these distinguished envoys reached the duke’s ears, he was greatly distressed together with Tancred and the whole Church. Immediately mustering forces of horsemen and foot soldiers from every side, he descended into the land of Damascus against the killers of his brethren. For fifteen days he devastated the land and its districts, no one resisting him. Seeing therefore that nothing, whether belonging to himself or to the Turks, remained untouched before the Christians [Col. 0578B], Grossus Rusticus, prince of the region, whether willing or unwilling, made an alliance with the duke and Tancred; but he rejected the Turks, by whose aid he was wholly unable to stand before the face of the most Christian duke.

## Chapter XVIII.—Where the glorious duke began to fall ill

After this treaty with the aforesaid prince had been confirmed on terms of tribute, the duke intended to return by way of Ptolemais, Caesarea, and Caiphas. The admiral of Caesarea came to meet him and courteously offered him a meal. But the duke declined food, tasting only a citron, with all gentleness and thanksgiving. Soon afterward he was seized by a grave illness. Turning aside to Joppa, he found the bishop and duke of the Venetians there with an abundant equipment and a multitude of arms. When he learned that they were fellow Christians and not [Col. 0578C] a hostile gathering, he entered secretly, with a few companions, the lodging that had newly been built for him. For he was oppressed as his bodily affliction grew worse.

Four of his close attendants stood by him: some received his feet into their laps; others placed their own breasts beneath his head to support it as he reclined; while others wept excessively and sorrowfully over his suffering, because they feared that in this long exile they would be deprived of so great a prince.

## Chapter XIX.—The duke is honoured by Venetian gifts, and afterward is more severely afflicted by illness

When the Christian pilgrims heard that so great a prince was ill, they were struck with deep grief and mourning and frequently came to visit him. [Col. 0578D] Among them the duke and bishop of Venice, together with their leading men, were admitted to greet, see, and speak with the duke himself. Being admitted, they offered and gave the duke remarkable and unusual gifts in gold and silver vessels, purple cloth, and costly garments, because of the love and longing they had always felt to see him.

Duke Godfrey received what they offered with the greatest charity. Addressing them kindly, he sent them back to their naval lodging, declaring that he was held by some illness; but that on the next day, if it should be somewhat lighter for him, he would present himself before all those who wished to see and know him, and would then gladly enjoy their shared conversation.

But that same night, as the pain and bodily weakness increased [Col. 0579A], he ordered his attendants to carry him to Jerusalem because of the excessive disturbance of the naval host. Therefore at that time he was unable to share the promised fellowship with the Venetian pilgrims.

## Chapter XX.—By the duke’s counsel, a siege of the castle of Caiphas is prepared

When they learned of the duke’s severe illness, the duke and leaders of the Venetians approached Werner of Greis and Tancred, asking them to speak with the duke about what they should do: whether they should first besiege and reduce some city on the seacoast before going down to Jerusalem, or wait until, by God’s gift, the duke recovered his health.

Tancred had meanwhile hastened from Tiberias to Japhet [Joppa], having learned of the duke’s severe [Col. 0579B] illness. Then both leaders consulted the duke about what they had heard from the Venetians. Counsel having been taken with him, though he was ill, and with the other leading men, it was decreed that the Venetian pilgrims should surround the castle called Caiphas with a naval siege, while Tancred, in the duke’s place, together with Werner, should establish the siege on land, so that the city might be besieged and crushed from both sides, sea and land.

When the engines by which Caiphas was to be overcome on land and sea had been prepared, mournful news was brought to Joppa that Duke Godfrey, the supreme prince, had already died. Therefore all, Venetians as well as Franks, were troubled; abandoning the entire apparatus of the siege, they came in haste to Jerusalem. They found the duke so overcome and burdened [Col. 0579C] by illness that he could scarcely utter a word. Yet, consoling the leading men as best he could, he declared that he was recovering from this illness.

At this reassurance from the duke, after the Venetians had worshipped at the Lord’s tomb and visited the holy places, Tancred and Werner returned with Patriarch Dagobert to Joppa and, without delay, renewed their preparations to the last detail. After fifteen days they set out with every kind of engine and crossbow, and arrived at Caiphas by sea and land. But Werner remained at Japhet [Joppa], because he was suddenly seized by illness, and from there was carried to Jerusalem on a litter.

## Chapter XXI.—The death of the glorious duke and of the knight Werner

[Col. 0579D] Four days after Werner had been brought to Jerusalem, the duke began to suffer more severely from his illness. Having confessed his sins with true compunction of heart and tears, and having received communion of the Lord’s body and blood, thus armed and protected with a spiritual shield, he was taken from this light.

At the death of so distinguished a duke and noblest athlete of Christ, there was great lamentation and excessive weeping among all the Christians there—Franks, Italians, Syrians, Armenians, Greeks—and among very many Gentiles, Arabs, Saracens, and Turks, for five days.

Then Werner, the duke’s kinsman and an illustrious knight, likewise died. He was honourably and according to Catholic rite buried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, in the portico of the basilica of Saint Mary the Virgin and mother of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0580A], on the eighth day after the death of the most noble duke and prince of the holy city of Jerusalem.

## Chapter XXII.—The siege of the castle of Caiphas

While the most glorious duke lay ill at Jerusalem for a period of five weeks, the patriarch, Tancred, and the whole Venetian force, with their duke and bishop, set out from Joppa by sea and land for the city called Caiphas, as had been decreed before the duke’s death. They besieged it from sea and land with a marvelous and very tall engine, and with seven stone-throwing machines called *mangenas*, in order to overcome the city’s defenders and inhabitants.

When the engines, together with the great machine, had been brought against the wall, and the men of Gaul were attacking it from every side with a fierce assault [Col. 0580B], the citizens—who were inhabitants of Jewish descent, living by the grant and permission of the king of Babylon in return for tribute—rose upon the city walls and strongly resisted its defence. The Christians, suffering various injuries, lost all hope after fifteen days and completely withheld their hands from every attack.

Nor is this surprising. For Tancred, unlike his custom, did not courageously bring faithful aid with his men, because envy gnawed at his heart: Duke Godfrey, while still living and lying sick in bed, had granted the city as a benefice to Geldemar, surnamed Carpenel, a distinguished and noble knight, should it be captured.

## Chapter XXIII.—At Tancred’s urging, the slackened siege is somewhat renewed

[Col. 0580C] The patriarch, recognizing Tancred’s envy and bitterness of spirit, employed every incitement and persuasion in his power to approach him. He began to soothe Tancred and calm his anger, so that the city, strongly defended by the Jews, might not remain so steadfast in its position to the disgrace of the Christians, of whom no small part had been worn down.

The patriarch also inserted this condition: if, with God’s consent, the city were captured, it should, by counsel of the faithful, be handed over to him who had laboured more in its destruction. For he said:

> “You see, dearest brother Tancred, how the Venetian duke, defeated and exhausted by war with all his force, has departed and applies no further strength. His own men too, terrified, have now withdrawn their fleet far from the city, as far as the middle [Col. 0580D] of the sea.”

Hearing the patriarch’s words and his good exhortation in Christ’s name, Tancred put aside all bitterness and replied: “He would no longer, on any pretext, refrain from assaulting and attacking the city, although another had received the grant of that city when it had not yet been besieged or captured, and although the strength and force of Geldemar Carpenel could not be compared with his own.”

Having said this, he quickly sounded the horns and, by this signal, instructed the knights to renew the interrupted assault around the city and overcome the strength of the Jews who were stoutly defending it.

## Chapter XXIV.—What the bravest knights endured there

Upon hearing Tancred’s signal, the entire body [Col. 0581A] of knights present, both those of the duke and those of Tancred, hastened to arms. Armed, they rushed together and mounted the engine without delay. Winric, the duke’s cup-bearer, an outstanding knight; Wicker the German, praiseworthy in the sword-stroke and in the Turkish tongue [or “Turkish learning,” *lectione* uncertain]; and Milo of Clermont, knights of the duke, went up.

But among all the Venetian knights they found no one on the engine except one man, whom no danger of death could frighten from its defence. When this Venetian young warrior saw them rushing to his aid, he breathed again from his imminent distress in great joy, bursting out with these words:

> “All the men of our people have withdrawn from me, and I alone of all have remained. But henceforth, God permitting, I shall not part from you until I learn the outcome of our assault and undertaking, whether in the city’s ruin or our own [Col. 0581B]. Therefore let us now stand together in the Lord’s name. Although we are few, God’s power is great for all things, and for his grace we are ready to press on and endure dangers.”

Without delay, after these four had joined and united in Christ’s name, at the Venetian’s exhortation, twenty knights of Tancred were immediately added to them, all united in purpose: they would either penetrate the constructed tower of the city from this engine, or perish before that very tower in the same place.

Suddenly seizing double axes, axes, and iron mattocks, they vigorously broke through the opposing tower, having undermined it. The Jewish citizens, joined by bands of Saracens, immediately and stoutly resisted them; from the tower they cast down oil, boiling pitch, fire, and tow—namely, a great [Col. 0581C] conflagration—so that the Christian knights might be consumed by smoke and heat upon the engine, while the city and its tower remained unconquered with their inhabitants.

At last the Christian knights, not despairing of dying for Christ, stood fearless, enduring every hardship by day and night, until their shields, burned by flames, shattered by slings, and pierced by iron spikes, could be seen to have suffered grievous damage.

## Chapter XXV.—The town of Caiphas is stormed

Then, when the following day dawned and the Lord Jesus had mercy upon his own, the Jews and Saracens saw that the Christians were unconquerable and could not be kept back from the tower and its assault by flames or weapons. They promptly abandoned the tower, no longer able to hold it [Col. 0581D], and fled; after them the whole city likewise turned to flight.

The Christian knights pursued the hostile citizens through the middle of the city and cruelly killed them. Victorious, they opened the city gates and admitted the entire Christian army. There they plundered all they found: innumerable riches in gold and silver, clothing, horses and mules, barley, oil, and wheat.

The Venetians, still remaining at sea with anchors cast, now learned of the Franks’ victory and the capture of the city. Quickly raising their anchors, they arrived and killed some of the Gentiles; but they found no money there.

## Chapter XXVI.—Geldemar is expelled, and Tancred takes possession of the castle of Caiphas

[Col. 0582A]
