After the city of Caiphas had been captured, Geldemar Carpenel, because he had received it as the duke’s grant if it were captured—and did not yet know that the duke had died—called together his knights and foot soldiers to retain and fortify the city. But Tancred’s forces, more numerous and stronger, took possession of the city walls and towers and expelled Carpenel and his people from the city.

Carpenel considered that at this moment he could do nothing better than leave the city with all his men and withdraw to the very strong and wealthy castle called Saint Abraham, toward the mountainous country and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. The duke had subdued this castle after a short assault, having driven out the Gentiles [Col. 0582B]. It is six miles distant from Jerusalem, and is said to have been built and inhabited by Abraham, the first patriarch, who was also said to have been buried there.

The Turks and other Gentiles and Jews honoured and venerated this stronghold with great devotion; it is likewise observed and revered with no less solemnity by Catholic worshippers.

## Chapter XXVII.—By counsel of the leading men, Bohemond is summoned to rule in Jerusalem, but is captured on the journey

When Patriarch Dagobert and Tancred there learned of the duke’s death, they conspired together that they would give Geldemar Carpenel nothing from the city of Caiphas, but would deal with it as they pleased; and that thereafter they would similarly deliberate and dispose freely in every respect [Col. 0582C], as they wished, concerning Jerusalem, the kingdom of Duke Godfrey.

They therefore took counsel in the city of Caiphas to send an embassy to Tancred’s uncle Bohemond at Antioch, asking him to come to the land of Jerusalem with all his equipment and take possession of the kingdom before any heir of Duke Godfrey should occupy his throne.

This embassy of the patriarch and Tancred was sent at once. But its bearer, a man named Morellus, secretary of the patriarch, because he had been sent deceitfully and contrary to the oath which the patriarch himself had made with Tancred to the duke—that, if he should die, they would surrender the kingdom of Jerusalem to none but his brothers or someone of his blood—fell, through the opposition of God’s wrath, into the hands of Count Raymond at Laodicea [Col. 0582D]. Thus the entire embassy and its letters came to nothing, and the treachery was everywhere exposed.

At that time Bohemond, by divine judgement, had assembled three hundred horsemen in the month of August and set out toward the city of Malatya. He had been summoned to help the Christians by letters and an embassy from Gaveras, duke, prince, and lord of Armenia and of that city, because Donimanus, prince of the Turks, had besieged the city, which was grievously hard-pressed in his hand.

When Donimanus heard of Bohemond’s arrival with his forces and that he was not far from the city’s siege, he took five hundred knights from his army and met him on the plain of that region. He joined battle with him amid an unbearable hail of arrows, until Bohemond’s strength was worn down and his whole company [Col. 0583A] was overcome—slain, or made fugitives and scattered. Some were immediately cut to pieces; others were captured alive and held, together with their prince Bohemond. They were carried away into exile to Nixandria, a city of that same Turk, and bound in iron chains.

## Chapter XXVIII.—Donimanus, prince of the Turks, is defied by the besieged Christians of Malatya

After Bohemond, his kinsman Richard, and the other leading men of his household had been captured, Donimanus returned in great triumph to the city of Malatya with their spoils and the heads of those who had been beheaded. He sent an embassy in advance to Gaveras, demanding that he surrender the city into his hand, since he held Bohemond captive and had crushed all his cavalry [Col. 0583B], on whom rested all the Christians’ hope and chief confidence; otherwise, he said, Gaveras could not live before the Turks.

But Gaveras, understanding Donimanus’s boasting, declared that he would not at all open the city to him under these threats, nor obey any of his commands, while he still knew that Baldwin, prince of Edessa or Rohas, was alive and unharmed and had heard no report of any misfortune to him.

Hearing this, Donimanus, the magnificent prince of the Turks, spoke with great arrogance and gave this answer to the man:

> “Do not now place excessive hope or confidence in him. For I hope that before long I shall have Baldwin himself, as I have Bohemond.”

## Chapter XXIX.—Baldwin wishes to free Bohemond, but accomplishes nothing

[Col. 0583C]

Meanwhile Bohemond, despairing of his life and safety, secretly sent Baldwin, through a certain Syrian and without the Turks’ knowledge, a small lock of hair from his head as a sign of his captivity and grief, asking him to come to his aid without delay and rescue him from the Turks’ hands before he should reach their unknown and barbarous peoples.

On the third day after Bohemond’s capture, Baldwin took one hundred and forty armoured horsemen and descended into the plains of the city of Malatya to rescue Bohemond, his brother in Christ, if, with God’s favour, he could join battle with the Turks by some effort in a suitable place.

But Donimanus, frightened by the bold arrival of Baldwin and by the great martial strength [Col. 0583D] of his knights, immediately struck camp and fled with all his cavalry, turning toward the Sea of Russia and his own land. He rejoiced that he had seized Bohemond, so renowned a prince and head of the Christians, but feared that he might lose him through the Christians’ strength or skill.

When Baldwin learned of his flight, he pursued him for three days. Yet, fearing to pursue farther because of the treachery of false Christians or enemy ambushes, and because he had not many knights, he returned to Malatya. Gaveras, prince of the city, received him kindly and delivered the city into Baldwin’s faith, hand, and protection. Presenting him with the entire treasury of the city, together with many costly garments [Col. 0584A], Gaveras begged that Baldwin accept them as his reward; but Baldwin retained nothing of all that had been offered him.

Recognizing Gaveras’s goodwill and constancy of faith, Baldwin stationed fifty knights with him in the city to guard and hold its walls; he himself returned to Rohas with the rest. Afterward Donimanus, having learned of the departure of so formidable a prince and knight, gathered his forces anew and again besieged the city of Malatya for many days. But the city was stoutly defended by the aforesaid fifty young warriors whom Baldwin had stationed there, and remained untouched and unconquered by the enemy, until at last Donimanus, exhausted by war and wearied by the long siege, and frightened by Christian aid, abandoned the city [Col. 0584B] and thereafter ceased to besiege it.

## Chapter XXX.—Baldwin is invited by envoys to receive the kingdom of Jerusalem in his brother’s place

Meanwhile, after Baldwin had returned to Rohas from Malatya, a cruel embassy came to him: his brother by the same mother, Godfrey, the magnificent prince, had died at Jerusalem, and the whole kingdom of that land, with the death of so devout a ruler, had now been left desolate among the Christian people.

When he heard this sorrowful embassy, Baldwin’s heart gave way to excessive tears and lamentations. Yet, as a man of remarkable self-control, he outwardly showed something far different at the death of his dearest brother than what was in his heart.

The messengers of this embassy were Robert, bishop of Rames or Rama; Robert the knight; and likewise Gunther. They had been sent by Geldemar Carpenel [Col. 0584C], Robert son of Gerard, Rudolph of Mozon, Josfrid the duke’s chamberlain, Winric the Fleming, his steward Matthew, Wicker the German, and Arnulf, prelate of the Temple of the Lord. They conveyed the message in this manner:

> “The knights and leaders of the kingdom of Jerusalem, who have hitherto served under the most Christian duke, greet you in the name of Jesus Christ, Son of the living God. By their decree and counsel we have been sent here, so that you may know that your brother Godfrey, duke and prince of Jerusalem, has been taken from this light. Therefore they unanimously invite you to come quickly, receive the kingdom in your brother’s place, and sit upon his throne. For they have bound themselves by agreement to receive no other than his brother or one of his blood, both because of his inestimable goodness and extreme generosity, and because of the oath by which they affirmed [Col. 0584D] that they would never allow a foreigner to reign or sit upon the throne of Jerusalem.”

Baldwin listened kindly to the embassy and their words, promising that, after no long time, once he had arranged his affairs, he would go down to Jerusalem and, God prospering him, receive and govern the kingdom by their counsel.

## Chapter XXXI.—Baldwin, about to set out for Jerusalem, places his namesake over the city of Rohas

Having warmly commended the envoys and sent them back toward Jerusalem, Baldwin, duke of the city of Rohas, soon summoned all his faithful men, asking each separately whether he wished to go to Jerusalem or remain [Col. 0585A] in the region of Rohas.

Likewise he sent letters to Baldwin of Bourcq, a nobleman of his kin, son of Count Hugh of the castle of Rorstet, requesting that he leave Antioch and the service for pay, come down to the land of Rohas, receive this city as a benefice, rule in Baldwin’s place, and fight its enemies. He fully explained to him the death of his brother Godfrey, that most famous prince; how the most powerful men of Jerusalem had invited him to possess the kingdom; and how he himself would go there afterward.

This same Baldwin [of Bourcq], having formerly set out from Jerusalem and Ascalon with the others to join Bohemond, had remained at Antioch down to that day in military service and paid employment. These arrangements having been made, and Baldwin of Bourcq having arrived from Antioch at the appointed time [Col. 0585B] and been placed upon the throne and in the authority of the city of Rohas, Baldwin, the first and magnificent brother of Duke Godfrey, gathered four hundred distinguished horsemen and a thousand foot soldiers and set out by the royal road first for Antioch.

All the knights and guards of the city came out to greet him and offered him the city if he wished to become its prince or lord. There he rested three days amid honour and rejoicing, courteously heard all the citizens and guards in every matter, answered them wisely, and greatly comforted them in their despair over Bohemond’s loss. Yet he wholly declined to take charge of the city in Bohemond’s place.

## Chapter XXXII.—Struck by a dreadful report of an imminent battle, Baldwin proceeds with few men to meet it

[Col. 0585C] On the fourth day, setting out from Antioch in great cheerfulness, he came peacefully with all his force to Laodicea. After enjoying rest there for two days, he waited for the arrival of the delayed people who were following him.

When all his forces had been gathered, a report reached his ears that a large host of Gentiles, both Turks and Saracens, had assembled from various places and lands to confront him face to face and had resolved to prevent him from proceeding further. From the city of Damascus alone, it was said, twenty thousand Turks had gathered there in arms; the number of the other Gentiles could not be determined because of their incalculable multitude.

Therefore part of Baldwin’s army, shaken by fear and despairing of life, fled in the silence of the night. Others, feigning illness, declared that they could by no means follow him farther. At dawn, Baldwin learned that his army had melted away. Deeply moved by grief, but not at all afraid, he exhorted all whom he found ready to fulfil their vow:

> “I see that, through fear of death and of this new report, our people have been diminished and dispersed. Yet I do not fear the nations assembled against us, nor do I hesitate to continue the journey I have begun. Therefore I exhort those who remain, in the faith of Christ, that, as they go with me to Jerusalem, they be frightened by no peril of death, but proceed with steadfast courage, placing with me all their hope in the Lord God. But those who doubt and are fearful, not moving a step from this place with me [Col. 0585D], may return wherever they think safe.”

Having said this and asked all concerning the road, he found that all who were present were unanimous and agreed upon the journey. Yet, when he went down to Gybel and spent the night there, of the four hundred horsemen and thousand foot soldiers scarcely one hundred and forty horsemen and five hundred foot soldiers remained with him [Col. 0586A]. All the rest had slipped away and scattered from him through anxiety at the reported coming of the Turks.

Baldwin, nevertheless without fear, proceeded peacefully from the plains and region of Gybel, because the citizens had received him honourably and gently, with an abundant supply of necessities.

## Chapter XXXIII.—Concerning the same

Then, passing the city of Tortosa, he came to Tripoli [Col. 0586B]. The prince of the city received him faithfully and gladly, providing all the food required by the army. There he learned that the king of Damascus and Geneadoil, prince of the Saracens from the extensive region which they call Camolla after its camels—over which Geneadoil ruled—and men from all the cities on the coast of the Palestinian sea, as well as from the mountains and various other places, had gathered to oppose him in the narrow passes and very rugged rocks near the city of Beirut, or Baurim.

Baldwin, undismayed by this cruel report, declared that in Christ’s name he would endure all things and would never delay his journey to Jerusalem because of so many thousands of nations gathered in one place, but would fight them to blood and death.

Having spoken thus [Col. 0586C], he travelled by day; when night approached, he halted to lodge at the foot of the difficult mountains. There he was told that all the enemies had without doubt gathered there to prevent the passage, and that battle would be joined on the following day. Therefore his heart was somewhat shaken and his strength failed, because few men remained with him.

Nevertheless, when the next day dawned, Duke Baldwin, strengthened in the Lord Jesus, continued his journey until he reached the place where the multitude of his enemies stood, all their forces prepared to meet him, as he had heard. Discovering as he proceeded that they were not far away, at the burning heat of midday his men put on arms, mail coats, and helmets. With lances [Col. 0586D] couched and banners raised, they hurried through the narrow passes to meet the Gentile bands, fighting with them for a long time in the most constricted places.

At last, as the unbearable force of the Turks and Saracens prevailed, they drove the Christians and their prince Baldwin from the pass with bows and javelins. After this prolonged struggle, because night was falling, both sides held their hands from battle.

That same night Baldwin moved a little distance from the foot of the mountain, pitched a few tents, and spent the night there, eating sparingly. There he counselled his men that none of them should separate from him in any way until the entire force of the following pilgrims had gathered, so that on the next day, by careful foresight, they might enter every danger more safely and, receiving martyrdom [Col. 0587A] for Jesus’ name, not hesitate to endure any adversity.

## Chapter XXXIV.—Feigning flight, he returned and won a glorious victory

After these measures had been decreed and the Christian people had consented to Baldwin’s word, the Turks and Saracens lit a thousand fires among the mountains that very night—far more, that is, than their army needed—in order to frighten the Christian people.

Geneadoil, prince of Camolla, after the fires had been lit and having learned from informants how small Baldwin’s forces were, approached the duke of Damascus and proposed that they attack the Christians in their camp while they were weary and asleep. But the other leaders opposed this advice, saying:

> “It is not [Col. 0587B] a useful or safe plan for us Turks to engage in battle under the shadow of night, lest we be suddenly surrounded and killed by the Saracens, who have always hated us, and lest both the spoils of the Franks and our own be taken away. Rather, if it pleases you, let us wait until the dawn of day, when we can provide for ourselves in every respect.”

Thus Geneadoil’s counsel was defeated.

On the next day, Baldwin, watchful and ever alert, understanding that the Turks were already close at dawn, led the entire army of the faithful back into a plain behind them, as though he had begun to flee. When all the Gentiles saw this and thought that he was fleeing in fear, they pursued hard on horseback, sending forward five hundred horsemen and fifteen thousand [Col. 0587C] foot soldiers.

But Baldwin, ever an undaunted knight, seeing that the enemies were closely pursuing him and that a great part of their army had now come down across the whole plain, immediately wheeled his horses back with all the Catholic knights and charged the Turks swiftly. A fierce battle was joined, and about four hundred Turks were killed there by sword, lance, and arrow.

The rest of the multitude, still following in the pass, could not aid their own men because of the narrowness of the paths. Now despairing of life, they turned to flight. Thus Baldwin, by God’s grace, gained victory and captured forty-eight of the leading Turks in that battle. He gathered no plunder except excellent horses, because all the herds [Col. 0587D], together with the Gentiles’ spoils and tents, remained on the other side of the narrow pass.

When that severe battle ended at the ninth hour, Baldwin remained in the aforesaid plain and pitched tents, since there was a spring of sweet water there and sweet-tasting reeds, by which they were refreshed. No more than two knights, Walter Tauns and Baldwin Tauns, were found to have fallen there; only a few were wounded. The prisoners were likewise placed in tents and committed to custody.

When evening came, Baldwin, refreshed with his men, sat among the prisoners to inquire what were their origin and parentage. Among them was found the prince and tetrarch of Damascus, who was said to have offered a very great treasure as the ransom for his life.

## Chapter XXXV.—How shrewdly Baldwin forestalled Tancred’s deception

[Col. 0588A]

When the king of Damascus, Geneadoil, and all the Gentile leaders heard of their men’s defeat, the capture of many, and Baldwin’s triumph, they fled throughout the night. They feared that, at dawn, they might be found on the other side of the mountain and attacked by a bold Christian charge, punished by a capital sentence, or, if overcome by the Saracens of the region, counted as nothing and beheaded.

For it is the custom of the Saracen people to fear and obey any new victors, but to despise and persecute the defeated.

Baldwin, learning of the flight of all of them, broke camp at sunrise with the booty of horses, Turkish prisoners, and spoils, and went to the cities of Sidon and Gibeloth [Col. 0588B]. Passing through there without hindrance or danger, he turned aside to Sur, that is, Tyre, where he and his men were conveniently refreshed with lodging and provisions.

After this, passing Ptolemais, which is Acre or Accaron, he suffered no opposition or hostility from it or from those cities because of the victory and reputation they had heard concerning him. Thus he arrived peacefully at Caiphas and remained there for several days.

## Chapter XXXVI.—Tancred, frightened by Baldwin’s arrival alone, and Baldwin’s entry into the holy city

Unaware of the whole deception, Baldwin eagerly desired to find Tancred there and speak with him, and to conduct all his affairs [Col. 0588C] everywhere by Tancred’s counsel. But Tancred, knowing nothing of Baldwin’s arrival, had gone to Jerusalem to corrupt the leaders and guards of the Tower of David, so that either his uncle Bohemond or he himself might obtain the kingdom. He did all this at the instigation, with the help, and by the consent of the patriarch.

Therefore, at Caiphas, when he learned of Tancred’s deceit and cunning, carried out with the consent of Patriarch Dagobert, Baldwin, an illustrious and prudent man, summoned Hugh of Falkenberg and Robert, bishop of the city of Rames or Rama, concerning these matters. By counsel of his own men he immediately sent them to Jerusalem, so that they might forestall the entire plot; for he feared that through some treachery or promise of money he might lose the Tower of David and the kingdom of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0588D] When these matters had been completed, certain worthy knights of Duke Godfrey’s household—Rudolf, Geldemar, Wicker the German, and Rudolf of Montpizon—were on the road toward the city of Caesarea, pursuing the Saracens. Entirely unaware of Baldwin’s arrival, they first learned the matter from the aforesaid brethren: namely, that Baldwin had come to take possession of Jerusalem in his brother’s place and was still staying as a guest at Caiphas. Without delay, rejoicing at the arrival of so eminent a prince and worthy heir of Jerusalem, they gathered their companions and arms and hurried to Japhet, that is, Joppa. There they found Tancred, who had returned angrily from Jerusalem because he had been unable to enter the city, laying siege to it; and they informed him that Baldwin was present and intended to take possession of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0589A] When Tancred heard of Baldwin’s very near arrival, he immediately raised the siege of Joppa. He returned to Caiphas by another road, unwilling to meet Baldwin, who was returning from Caiphas, upon the direct route. Baldwin, however, setting out from Caiphas, met the aforesaid knights of Duke Godfrey’s household, who reported everything concerning Tancred to him. Then, hastening with him to Joppa, they stayed there for two consecutive days. Thereafter, having arranged affairs at Joppa, he went down to Jerusalem with all his following and with the booty which he had carried off from Baruth, that is, Baurim, including forty-five captive Turkish soldiers. He ordered that these be placed in the custody of the Tower of David and carefully guarded.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—After inquiry into the property of his deceased brother, he is urged by valiant men to undertake valiant deeds.

[Col. 0589B]

Finally, on the fourth day after he had entered Jerusalem, Baldwin assembled everyone, great and small, from the entire body of Christians, and inquired concerning the household goods of his brother Godfrey, his arms, his money, and the fiefs of each knight and powerful man. They testified that they possessed none of his brother’s goods, but that these had been dispersed in alms for the poor and in payment of debts. They produced the fiefs, however, according to what had been assigned to each from the revenues of the cities.

He patiently received all their answers. After discussing certain goods and arms, though accepting their explanations, he remained silent, restoring to each man his respective fief. Therefore, confirmed by the oath of all, he sat gloriously enthroned, exalted in power in the throne of Jerusalem. It was about the feast of St Martin, bishop of Tours, in the month of November,

[Col. 0589C] when Baldwin came to Jerusalem and was established by all, great and small alike, as king and lord.

Thus Baldwin having been gloriously placed upon the throne of Jerusalem, all the princes and knights of Duke Godfrey’s household came into his presence and spoke to him thus:

“You are the brother of Duke Godfrey, a most glorious and renowned prince. Therefore all the nations of the heathen round about, having heard of you, have been terrified at your arrival, because they know you to be great and most famous in war. Accordingly, it befits you to perform some notable deed, so that the lands of the heathen may stand astonished and never cease to marvel. Thus the name of your brother, prince of Jerusalem, shall live again in you

[Col. 0589D] and be magnified.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Besieging the city of Ascalon, after several days he raises the siege without accomplishing his purpose.

Having heard the counsel of his men, Baldwin secured the land of Jerusalem and the surrounding cities with faithful guards. Taking one hundred and fifty knights and five hundred foot-soldiers, he left the city of Jerusalem at the ninth hour of the day; and when evening came, he lodged beside a spring of fresh water, where the highlands end. Then, on the fifth day from there, rising up, he descended with all the strength of his men upon the city of Ascalon. In that city a thousand Arab horsemen sent from Babylon were stationed to defend its walls, lest the power of the new prince should suddenly burst upon it unawares.

There Baldwin’s knights, having pitched tents before the city walls, remained for two days without assault.

[Col. 0590A] But on the third day the Arab soldiers, making a sortie with the citizens, fought frequent engagements with them, until at length both sides suffered no slight losses among their own men. After another two days, and a very great slaughter of Saracens together with severe wounding of the Franks, King Baldwin prudently called his men back from the siege of the city, saying:

“These enemies of ours, trusting in the protection of their walls and in their great multitude of citizens, can easily prevail, should fortune oppose us, through the constant reinforcement of their own forces; while our men may perish heedlessly beneath arrows. Therefore it is expedient to move our camp away from this city.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—How ingeniously he conquered the people called Azopart, who lay hidden underground.

While these counsels were being discussed, Baldwin learned

[Col. 0590B] that in the wilderness between Ascalon and Babylon the Azopart, a most foul people, lay hidden in underground caves, waiting to harass and kill pilgrims wishing to journey to Jerusalem. As soon as he learned of the wickedness of this people, he moved his camp from Ascalon and besieged the caves with his army. He caused fire to be thrown into them, wishing to discover whether, because of the extreme confinement caused by smoke and heat, they would emerge from the grim and unheard-of caverns.

Yet none came out from all of them except two, who stood before him in the hope that they might find mercy and life. Baldwin, observing these dreadful and filthy men, addressed them in friendly fashion concerning all that he had heard about them; and, clothing them in costly garments, he asked about their people and kinship. Revealing everything to him as they were questioned, and judging him to be merciful toward them, they earnestly begged that one of them might remain with Baldwin while the other returned to the caves and familiar places, so that he might lead forth before the prince’s presence his companions enclosed in their intricate dwelling, remarkable stronghold, and inaccessible pit, in the hope that they too might find favour in his sight.

[Col. 0590C] Entering the pit, displaying the king’s clothes and gifts and speaking of his kindly reception, he immediately brought ten of his companions into the presence of the king and his nobles. Meanwhile, while the other man had gone back into the pit, he who had remained with Baldwin was beheaded by the king’s attendants. Likewise, the companion who, by vain hope and the promise of fine clothing, had led ten men out from the caves was secretly removed

[Col. 0590D] and immediately beheaded with nine of them. A tenth man, to whom the entire slaughter of his fellows remained unknown, was spared alive.

Taking this man apart, clothing him in honourable and soft garments, and soothing him with his speech, Baldwin immediately enticed him to return to his underground companions and urge them to come out. He asserted that he would treat them kindly, honour them with splendid gifts, grant them all the places of the region as fiefs, and conduct all affairs according to their counsel. Deceived and enticed by these promises, the wretch returned to the caves in a costly garment. He told all his accomplices of the prince’s friendliness and generosity, making the report more lavish than he had heard it; for he believed that his companions who had been removed and beheaded were alive and had been sent to guard Baldwin’s own cities.

## CHAPTER XL.—On the same matter.

[Col. 0591A]

The Azopart, buried beneath the ground in an immeasurable and inaccessible network of excavations, heard their companion’s favourable report—first threats, then splendid promises—and about thirty came forth. Standing before the prince himself, they were graciously received from his lips; then immediately led away from his sight, as though to receive gifts, all underwent capital punishment, except one, who alone remained with Baldwin out of all the thirty.

Baldwin treated this man alone with remarkable honour, though he knew nothing of the slaughter of his accomplices. He sent him also back to the aforesaid caves, that he might report to the men underground the honours and gifts bestowed by Baldwin and urge them, won over by his own enticement, to leave their refuge. Thus, again and again deceived by vain hopes, two hundred and thirty came forth,

[Col. 0591B] all of whom were beheaded without delay by the prince’s command, because they had inflicted the gravest evils upon pilgrims passing toward Jerusalem: despoiling some and slaughtering others. This great crime had always remained unavenged, because no one had previously been able to drive them from that cavern by force or by any device.

When these two hundred and thirty had been beheaded, and their wickedness had been repaid upon their own heads through the ingenuity of the most Christian prince, in vengeance for the pilgrims, only their women and children remained in their caves, along with the spoils of very many people. Understanding the men’s death, since no one returned to them thereafter, they did not dare at all to emerge. Therefore Baldwin, greatly enraged against them, ordered wood, straw, and tow to be brought before the mouth of every cave

[Col. 0591C] and set alight, until the heat and smoke should compel them to come out. At last, overwhelmed alike by the excessive smoke and heat, the mothers with their children—deprived of the support of their men—came forth, though unwillingly, and were immediately handed over and divided among the soldiers as booty. Some of them, with their mothers, were redeemed for a price; others were beheaded together.

## CHAPTER XLI.—While he leads his troops through difficult places, many perish from cold.

After this Baldwin set out for the castle called St Abraham’s, and lodged beside the foul-smelling waters of Sodom and Gomorrah, suffering there a great lack of food and fodder for the horses. While they were exploring the mountains in search of

[Col. 0591D] necessities, certain inhabitants informed them that, if they proceeded a little farther to a place called the Palms, they would find abundant wealth and supplies of food, by which they and their horses might recover their strength.

Hearing this, some young men—about forty—secretly detached themselves from the army and ran ahead to collect money and booty. But they found nothing except provisions and plentiful game, with which they filled their bellies; nor did they drink any wine or other beverage, but only springs of sweet water. Refreshed there in the place of the Palms, they rose and reached the mountains of Arabia. Having crossed them, they lodged between two mountain peaks. There, during the night, they sufficiently refreshed themselves with the necessary food which they had brought in the baggage of mules, camels, and asses,

[Col. 0592A] finding absolutely nothing there except fresh water.

They crossed these mountains, their difficult crags, and narrow passes in five days, with severe and immeasurable toil. On the sixth day, after traversing the mountains, they encountered the greatest dangers upon their furthest summit: horrible hail, terrible ice, unprecedented rain and snow. When this violence and terror came upon them, about thirty foot-soldiers died from the cold.

## CHAPTER XLII.—The city of Susumus is destroyed by fire.

After the difficult and perilous passage through the mountains and crags, they descended into a valley. Riding all day, they crossed the plain; and in the evening they encamped in a certain very wealthy village, where they lodged with their prince Baldwin and were refreshed with necessities.

[Col. 0592B] There certain Saracen scouts came to seek the favour of so great and mighty a prince and to obtain their lives. They revealed to the prince a nearby city called Susumus, exceedingly rich in resources, and said that it could easily be occupied and taken by assault. Baldwin, having learned this, departed from the aforesaid village on the fifth day and descended upon the city of Susumus in the evening. Finding its houses and every part of the city empty, he rested there securely in lodgings. For at news of his approach all the heathen fled from this region and city, since the city was considered weak because it had no wall.

There, for eight days, they rested in security without hindrance or any enemy attack, pursuing the heathen in the surrounding country each day

[Col. 0592C] and killing many whom they found. At dawn on the ninth day, by Baldwin’s command the city of Susumus was demolished and burned. They plundered the city’s spoil—herds and other goods everywhere—and, turning through another region in the mountains, ravaged the known haunts of the Saracens, gathering booty from every place.

At last, after eight days, burdened by various hardships, difficult terrain, and sometimes hunger, they prepared to return to the aforesaid foul-smelling waters. Coming to the village of the Palms, they found no food except the fruit of date-palms, with which they revived bodies wearied by travel and fasting for want of food.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—At Bethlehem, on the Nativity of the Lord, Baldwin is anointed king.

[Col. 0592D] Thereupon, returning by way of the castle called St Abraham’s, they came back to Jerusalem by the route by which they had come, on the third day before the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. There, after taking counsel with the patriarch and all his nobles, he resolved to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord at Bethlehem. On that same holy and solemn day, consecrated and anointed king of Jerusalem, he was crowned amid great glory.

For he would not, and did not presume, to be exalted, adorned, and elevated as king with a diadem, gold, or precious gems in the city of Jerusalem, where the Lord Jesus, King of kings and Lord of lords, humbled and obedient unto death for the redemption of the world, had been crowned with dreadful and sharp thorns. On the following day, departing from Bethlehem, he returned to Jerusalem

[Col. 0593A] and held his court and council, with all his chief men, in the palace of King Solomon for the three days of that same festival, remaining honourably for fifteen days in the royal city. During those days the king sat in power upon his throne, in order to render judgment and justice among his fellow Christians, if any wrong had been inflicted upon anyone or any quarrel had arisen, desiring to deal with everything equitably and settle it in a peace that was not feigned.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—At the king’s first session, Tancred is accused, summoned, and refuses to appear.

Geldemar, seeing that the lord king had sat down to administer justice, stood before him and made grave complaint concerning the injuries that Tancred was inflicting upon him in regard to the city which he had received as a gift from the hand of Duke

[Col. 0593B] Godfrey, and had earned through military service if it should be taken; and which Tancred now, having heard of the duke’s death, was holding by force and unjustly.

When Geldemar’s complaint had been received, the king, on the counsel of his men, first sent an embassy to Tancred, requiring him to come up to Jerusalem and make answer concerning Geldemar’s complaints and the wrongs done to him. Tancred replied that he would make no answer on these matters before Baldwin, because he did not recognize him as king of the city and judge of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

The king, however, again taking counsel with his men, sent him an embassy a second and third time, asking him not to evade justice, lest anyone thereafter should accuse the king or assert that the king had acted otherwise than justly and patiently against a fellow Christian and one of the Christian princes.

At last Tancred, anxious about what he should do after the third admonition, took counsel with his followers how he might answer and speak with the king, if it pleased him, between Japhet and Assur, from the opposite bank of the river dividing those two cities; for he feared to come to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0593C] When the king understood Tancred’s answer and request, he assented to his wish on the counsel of his elders, and on the appointed day set out for the same river-place between Japhet and Assur for a conference. After various counsels had been exchanged there, they agreed to meet again at Caiphas after fifteen days, because they had been unable to settle anything at that time. Thus Tancred went to Caiphas with the patriarch, while the king returned to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XLV.—After making peace with the king, Tancred, chosen duke, departs for Antioch.

[Col. 0593D]

Meanwhile, after a short interval, an embassy was sent from Antioch to Tancred by Bohemond’s nobles, asking him to come down to them and possess the principality of Antioch in Bohemond’s place, since he was his heir. Tancred, after taking counsel on the matter, resolved to depart for Antioch. Nevertheless, he decided to await the appointed day on which he was to have a conference with the king at Caiphas, lest, if he departed before that day, it should be counted against him as the disgrace of flight.

Accordingly, on the appointed day the king and Tancred met there at Caiphas for a conference. They became reconciled and friends, all complaints being set aside. Tancred restored into the king’s hand not only the land and city of Caiphas, but also the fortress and

[Col. 0594A] tower of Tiberias, which he had obtained as a gift from Duke Godfrey, because they belonged to the kingdom of Jerusalem; and he disclosed to him the embassy from Antioch.

Yet Tancred firmly stipulated this condition in the whole agreement: if he returned from Antioch after one year and three months, he should hold the lands and cities as a fief; but if he did not return within the stated period, he would never again seek these lands and cities from the king. These terms having been mutually granted in great friendship, the king received the lands and cities on that condition. He entrusted Tiberias to Hugh of Falkenberg’s garrison for custody and as a fief, and restored Caiphas to Geldemar Carpenel—while preserving this pledge: that, if Tancred returned after the aforesaid term, everything should be restored into his hand by the king’s gift.

After these decrees and the conclusion of peace, the king withdrew to Jerusalem. Tancred, however, went down by land as far as Antioch with all his cavalry and a force of five hundred foot-soldiers, to take possession of it.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—The king appeals against the patriarch to the Apostolic See.

Not long thereafter, the king of Jerusalem challenged the patriarch before the whole Church concerning the treachery which he had practiced with Tancred against him: namely, that the worthy heir should not succeed Godfrey, but that Bohemond, of foreign blood, should possess the kingdom. The king charged him with this crime, of which he was strongly accused by his own nobles, alleging that the fraud itself had now been exposed in letters sent to Bohemond through Morel, the patriarch’s secretary, but seized on the road.

[Col. 0594C] This dispute and discord between king and patriarch began day by day to grow ever stronger, until at last King Baldwin, angered by the patriarch’s ferocity and obstinacy, appealed to Paschal, the Apostolic and Roman pontiff, for judgment and justice: for investigation of so wicked a betrayal, of incited murder, and of discord, which the patriarch, as the intercepted letters showed, was striving by every means to bring about among the leaders of the Christians and the new and still tender Church.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—The Apostolic Lord sends Cardinal Maurice to Jerusalem as investigator.

Paschal, shepherd of the Holy Roman Church and examiner of Christian faith and religion throughout the whole world,

[Col. 0594D] complying with Baldwin’s prayers and those of the Holy Church of Jerusalem, sent Brother Maurice, one of the twelve cardinals, as legate of the Holy Roman Church to Jerusalem, upon the counsel of the faithful. In the Apostolic Lord’s stead, he was to confirm the patriarch in the episcopal chair, if he were examined and cleared according to his merits and fault; or, if convicted and justly condemned by Apostolic sentence, to depose and punish him.

Accordingly, by command of the Apostolic Lord Brother Maurice journeyed to Jerusalem. He greeted King Baldwin and the whole Church in the word of the Apostolic Lord, gave his blessing, and declared that he would hear, in all justice and truth, the king and the children of Holy Church obedient to God, and that by Apostolic authority he wished to turn every evil into good.

[Col. 0595A] Baldwin and the entire Church of the faithful gave thanks to God for this and answered that they would obey Apostolic commands in all justice and truth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—The patriarch, charged by the king on many grave counts, is suspended from office.

Thereafter, without delay, on the appointed day and with a council of faithful bishops and abbots assembled, in the hearing of all present and in the presence of the legate of the Holy Roman Church, King Baldwin maintained under the testimony of the entire Holy Church of Jerusalem that the patriarch standing before them was guilty of perjury, of betraying the kingdom of Jerusalem, and of plotting murder—that Bohemond might kill Baldwin on the road by which he was coming up from Rohas to Jerusalem—as the intercepted letters showed. Therefore, he declared, the patriarch could not continue to exercise episcopal office unless he could clear himself of these charges.

[Col. 0595B] Unable to excuse himself at all from the accusations laid against him, and especially from the sacrilege concerning the wood of the Holy Cross, of which he had diminished and dispersed a portion, he was suspended from divine office. A period of respite was nevertheless granted him, in case he might find some defense.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—On the Lord’s Supper, grieving that he was deprived of his office on that day, the patriarch placates the king with promised gifts.

Meanwhile the month of March came in its proper order, the Lenten fast began to be observed, and the solemn day of Easter drew near, on which chrism and oil for the sick must be consecrated. When therefore the day arrived for commemorating and consecrating the oil and chrism, on which the Lord Jesus supped with his disciples, the cardinal ascended the Mount of Olives—where that sacrament of chrism and oil is customarily performed—wearing a white stole and garments suitable for so divine a work, and did not permit the patriarch to be present in any capacity.

[Col. 0595C] But Patriarch Dagobert, seeing himself deprived of his office, which on that day all patriarchs, his predecessors, had customarily exercised on the same Mount of Olives while consecrating chrism and oil, came humbly and suppliantly to the king with tears. He began to urge that on this day he should not be so lightly and shamefully expelled from his office and thereby become a subject of talk in the mouths of all pilgrims.

The king strongly resisted and objected to him many things which the patriarch had undertaken against him. Yet Dagobert, increasingly troubled, pressed him all the more with prayers, reminding him how he had anointed and consecrated him king. But since even so the king did not listen, he secretly offered him three hundred talents of bezants. Corrupted by this, the king thereafter acceded to every request of the patriarch. And the king rejoiced at the promise of so great a sum because he was greatly pressed by want and now needed it to reward the service of his soldiers. He immediately rose, went to Brother Maurice, and spoke to him in these words:

[Col. 0595D]

## CHAPTER L.—The king addresses the cardinal concerning the restoration of the patriarch.

“Brother Maurice, this Church of ours is still considered new and tender. Therefore we do not wish it, nor does it please our wiser men, nor do we find it advisable in our council, that Jerusalem should so suddenly be deprived of its justice and that the patriarch should be removed from his office on so celebrated a day. Otherwise discord might arise among us during the Paschal days, to the confusion of pilgrims and the glorying of the heathen.

“Therefore we earnestly ask you not to refuse to hear us—who have maintained this holy Church with our blood and fought for it unto death—and not to take too severely at this time the matter which we have made known to you concerning the patriarch, until we see whither his defense tends or what end it reaches. For the time will not pass without our returning sufficiently to the equity of judgment in all things. For this reason, and because it pleases all the faithful, we ask you to allow him at this time to exercise his episcopal office,

[Col. 0596A] to consecrate the chrism and oil himself, and to grant indulgence and reconciliation, according to the rite of the Holy Church of Jerusalem, to pilgrims who have journeyed here from distant lands.

“After the solemnity of Easter, which it is now necessary to celebrate in the highest charity and concord, we have resolved, with your counsel, to deal with him in such a way that either he shall remain in his office if cleared, or, if convicted, be deprived of episcopal dignity.”

## CHAPTER LI.—On the friendship between the cardinal and the patriarch, the king’s reconciliation, and the agreement of the heathen with the king.

Moved by these words and blandishments, the cardinal yielded in every respect to the will of the king and the nobles. Removing his official vestments, he allowed the patriarch to consecrate the oil and chrism and celebrate the solemn Easter with every divine office.

From that day the cardinal and patriarch were joined in the closest friendship, amassing for themselves heaps from the offerings of the faithful and enjoying, night and day in secluded places, abundance of food, wine, and drink—all this, however, without the king’s knowledge.

[Col. 0596C] Meanwhile, while this reconciliation between the king and the patriarch was taking place in the same month of March, and the earth and woods revived as winter departed, the days began to lengthen, and the serenity of the air grew brighter day by day, behold: envoys from all the cities of the heathen came to the king’s palace. Some came deceitfully, some sincerely; they greeted the king with gifts and tribute and sought to establish peace with him, so that they might travel safely through the land for their business without fear of danger, and cultivate their fields and vineyards without alarm.

The king, being a newcomer and in need of much treasure for paying his soldiers’ agreed wages,

[Col. 0596D] consented to receive all that was offered him by the heathen cities—Ascalon, Caesarea, Ptolemais, and Sur, that is, Tyre—but rejected Assur and its gifts. To the others he granted peace and security from himself and his men until after the term of holy Pentecost.

## CHAPTER LII.—On the mutual embassies of the heathen.

Scarcely had the term of this peace reached its middle when the aforesaid cities sent envoys to the king of Babylon, reporting that, unless he soon came to their aid and expelled the Franks from the kingdom of Jerusalem, necessity would compel them to surrender themselves into the hands of the Franks’ king, because they could no longer resist the Christians.

[Col. 0597A] The king of Babylon, understanding the extreme need of his cities, sent back this message and assurance to all their citizens and amirals: that, without any delay, he would gather armed forces and come to the aid of all the cities. All these reports and plans were unknown to King Baldwin and to all the faithful dwelling in the kingdom of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LIII.—On the ransom of the Turks.

Meanwhile, a frequent embassy of Turks came from Damascus to Jerusalem to the king concerning the ransom of their captives, whom he had overcome and captured in the very narrow passes of Baurim and had brought to Jerusalem, imprisoning them in the custody of the Tower of David. He took counsel with his nobles to receive payment for the captives, since in a foreign land, new and unfamiliar, he had great need of money for the agreed wages.

[Col. 0597B] Thus he spared all forty-five captives, whose necks he had resolved to cut off, and received the unheard-of sum of more than fifty thousand gold bezants. He released them all alive and unharmed from fetters and chains, sent them out from the Tower of David, and dispatched them peacefully into the land of Damascus.

## CHAPTER LIV.—How the city of Assur is subdued.

At the same time, in the month of March, fleets of Genoese and Pisans arrived by ship at Joppa and dropped anchor there. Waiting for the Lord’s Easter, they finally came to Jerusalem to celebrate that day of the Lord’s Resurrection. When they had celebrated it with every devotion, they approached the king and earnestly requested permission to occupy and take by assault whichever city of the heathen he wished.

[Col. 0597C] Understanding their desire, the king resolved to besiege Assur by sea and land. He himself, setting out from Jerusalem with all his force, encircled the city and its walls on the landward side; the Pisans and Genoese, aboard their ships on the shore, watched its seaward exit.

Before the third day of the siege was completed, the citizens of Assur sought to make peace with the king: they asked permission to leave the city with their lives and limbs unharmed, taking their property, and to surrender and abandon the city into the king’s hand. The king, on his men’s advice, spared the inhabitants, promising that they might depart peacefully with everything that they could carry upon their necks; and he granted them safe conduct as far as Ascalon, without fear of death.

He entered the city with the whole multitude of horse and foot, rested there for eight days,

[Col. 0597D] and took counsel with the lord patriarch and the nobles of his kingdom concerning the remaining cities.

## CHAPTER LV.—The city of Caesarea is besieged.

At last all agreed that an embassy of the king should be sent to the amiral and leading men of Caesarea, ordering them to surrender the city to the king; otherwise they should know for certain that he would besiege it, and that, if it were taken by force, everyone found within it must be put to the sword.

The amiral and all the inhabitants of the city replied in these words: “Far be it from us that we should surrender ourselves and our city into the hand of the king of the Christians, when we shall soon be delivered by the king of Babylon, and not long ago received his letters.”

When the king learned of their boast, he left Assur in great anger with the lord patriarch, leaving guards there, and marched upon Caesarea, stationing his forces around it on every side.

[Col. 0598A] There were around the walls orchards of extraordinary extent, like the densest forest, beyond measure in every beauty and abundance of fruit. The king ordered them to be cut down with axes, lest Saracen ambushes among the dense foliage, shooting arrows from concealment, should harm the army.

When these had been cleared, he maintained the siege around the walls for fifteen days, constructing a siege-engine by which he could take the city and terrify its citizens. When the engine had at last been completed in every detail and raised by the army above the walls, it was extended high into the air, and the bravest fighters were stationed upon it to attack the city’s walls and defenders.

Then, by the king’s order, all were commanded to assemble early in the morning before the patriarch and king, from every place and tent, to receive his exhortation and carry it out in assaulting the city.

[Col. 0598B] When morning came, behold, at the king’s command all Christian horsemen and foot-soldiers were present before the patriarch and king. Having confessed their sins, received absolution, and communicated in the Lord’s body, they vigorously attacked the city by sea and land with the Pisans and Genoese.

These men, having lain idle all winter at Laodicea, had come up to Jerusalem in March, as related above, to celebrate the sacred and solemn Easter. They had been deprived of their Pisan bishop, who had secretly withdrawn from them and gone down with Bohemond and Baldwin to Jerusalem after its capture, and had been established by Duke Godfrey in the patriarchal see.

## CHAPTER LVI.—At last the city of Caesarea is overcome.

On that day the lord patriarch carried the Lord’s Cross before him for the protection and defense of the Catholic people, clothed in a holy white stole as though in a breastplate. The whole force of combatants did not hesitate to follow him up to the walls.

[Col. 0598C] With a hard and heavy assault they drove the citizens, thrown into confusion, back from the walls; and thus, suddenly applying ladders to the wall, they forced their way into the middle of the city. Seeing the Franks spread throughout the city and unable to resist them, the Saracens fled together to another fortification of the city, where an extremely spacious and strong wall divided the city on the inner side toward the sea.

There they stood for a while in resistance upon the walls, attempting defense in vain, spending the day with arrows, firebrands, and slings. At last, when the ninth hour of the day came, the citizens, burdened by repeated and unceasing assaults, and exhausted and overcome by a hail of both mangonel shots and arrows, fled trembling through the streets and various parts of the city.

[Col. 0598D] The Franks pursued them and, climbing these walls likewise by ladders, made a great slaughter among them: killing some, taking others captive, and everywhere seizing very great spoils of gold, silver, and precious purple cloth. The city’s priest, an aged man, was captured there, and five hundred Azopart were beheaded, having been sent there by the king of Babylon for payment of wages.

The aforesaid priest, brought before the king, was bound by his command in shackles; his women also were captured and put in fetters, in order to recover the talent of countless silver which the priest had buried through fear of the Christians. Once the city had been crushed and captured, the king rested there, with an abundance of every necessity, from the days of Pentecost until the Nativity of St John the Baptist.

[Col. 0599A] During those days he released the aforesaid priest unharmed in limb, after he had been ransomed for a thousand bezants by the citizens of Ptolemais, that is, Acre.

## CHAPTER LVII.—How, having heard the report concerning the Babylonians, the king awaits their arrival.

After this the king withdrew to Joppa in great glory, leaving Arpin of Bodvordis, a magnificent prince, in the city to guard its walls and gates. While the king was staying at Joppa, an embassy and report from Meravis in Babylon made known

[Col. 0599B] that all the Babylonians had gathered under arms and had resolved to give battle with him after eight days.

Hearing this, the king summoned all his followers together. By their counsel he departed from Joppa and, after three weeks had elapsed, encamped upon a very broad plain between Ascalon and Rames, together with the patriarch, all his equipment, and the entire household of his brother Duke Godfrey.

But while they waited long in that place for the enemies’ coming, and none of them had yet descended in fulfillment of his boast, the king dismissed each of his men to his own place. He himself peacefully inspected the nearby cities—Caiphas, Assur, and the others.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—How the king approached the patriarch, that either he himself should provide soldiers, or should give the king some money with which to procure them.

[Col. 0599C]

Not long after this, the king was pressed by his soldiers in the city of Joppa for the money which he owed them under the agreed payment in solidi. They had rendered much service also to his brother Godfrey, prince of Jerusalem, and were now serving no less zealously for his cause and honour. Accordingly, he went to Jerusalem and addressed the patriarch, asking him to grant him some money from the offerings of the faithful; by distributing it among the soldiers, he would make them willing to remain with him. Otherwise, they declared that they did not wish to remain within the bounds of Jerusalem and defend the Holy of Holies. Having heard the king’s request, the patriarch took a night’s delay and, returning on the following day, declared that he possessed two hundred marks of silver, for the needs of the brethren serving God there, and no more; he graciously permitted these same funds to be distributed at the king’s direction. The king believed the patriarch’s statement and accepted the silver offered. But Arnulf, chancellor of the Holy Sepulchre, and several others, to whom the whole sum and the offering of the Lord’s Sepulchre were known, maintained that the patriarch was by no means telling the truth, but had secretly stored away an immeasurable quantity of money in his own coffers. At Arnulf’s assertion and the people’s suspicion concerning the hidden treasure, the king became exceedingly angry and began to press the patriarch strongly to furnish and retain soldiers, paid in solidi from the offerings of the faithful, so that they might resist the power of the pagans and protect and defend the pilgrims and the whole Church from their plots and attacks.

## CHAPTER LIX.—How a dispute arose between the king and the patriarch

The patriarch, bound by the tie of private friendship to Brother Maurice, legate of the Holy Roman Church, so that together they feasted lavishly on the goods of the land and divided the offering of the Holy Sepulchre at will in his chamber, utterly disregarded listening to King Baldwin. He placed his hope and confidence in the promises of the apostolic cardinal, who had been bribed, and in the belief that by a small entreaty and a gift of gold he could corrupt and placate the king.

Although the king repeatedly urged the patriarch to provide forty soldiers and, by granting them money, make them willing for the work of war, the patriarch would not listen to him in any respect on these matters. One day it happened that this same patriarch, reclining in his house with Brother Maurice as usual, was feasting splendidly on varied foods, drinking no small quantity of wine, and passing the day securely in revelry. At last it was reported to King Baldwin that, while feasting daily in such luxury, they were consuming without measure or number the vows of the faithful; and that the king could ascertain this not only by report, but readily by sight.

## CHAPTER LX.—The dispute between the king and the patriarch in the presence of Cardinal Maurice

Without delay, while they were reclining at table in the same pursuit of feasting, the king appeared, having entered after the door was knocked upon, with certain of his leading men. Rebuking these fathers harshly, he burst out in these severe words:

“You spend yourselves in feasting; we, day and night, endure tribulations for the safety and perils of our brethren. You gratuitously devote the vows of the faithful to your pleasures; you know nothing of our distress and want. As the Lord lives, henceforth you shall receive nothing from any offering of the faithful, nor shall you any longer fill your bellies so delicately from it, unless you undertake to provide soldiers paid in solidi. For whence comes your right to take so freely and so powerfully the offerings and gifts of the faithful from the Lord’s Sepulchre, convert them into luxurious foods, and give no help whatever to the needs of the faithful? We redeemed Jerusalem—the holy city and the place of the longed-for Sepulchre—with our blood, and continually bear the burdens of toil and warfare for the defence of the holy places; and will you deprive us of the offerings of the faithful? Far be it from me to permit such a deed, or that your hands should hereafter be filled from these things. Certainly, either you shall drink with us the cup which we are about to drink, and are drinking in this time of distress, or take care that you receive nothing further from the Church’s possessions.”

At this, the patriarch burst out no less angrily, saying:

“You have acted without right counsel in rebuking us so rashly and forbidding us the Church’s goods, since it belongs to justice that those who serve the altar should live from the altar. Do you presume to make the holy Church tributary and servile—the Church which the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, made free from slavery by his blood, and committed and left to her guardianship? Take care that you presume no further to speak or act in these matters, which do not belong to you at all, lest by such bold attempts you incur, by judgment, the curses of the apostolic lord.”

Brother Maurice merely listened while they contended with one another, but urged them toward peace and concord.

## CHAPTER LXI.—The patriarch, overcome by argument, promised to provide soldiers, but scorned to fulfil his promise

But the king, no longer enduring the patriarch’s answer and harshness, is said also to have spoken sternly and impatiently:

“Take care that you do not readily raise against me again and again this argument—that those who serve the altar should live from the altar—when extreme necessity demands rather that Christian soldiers be fed from the altar than that the Saracens should violently carry off and divide the gifts of the faithful from the Sepulchre, while neither our soldier nor our priest receives anything. As the Lord lives, I shall not only consume the offerings of the faithful and distribute them to our soldiers; I shall also tear gold from the Lord’s Sepulchre and altar, so that the soldiers and defenders of the Christian people and the kingdom of Jerusalem may be supported. Afterwards, when it pleases the Lord God, and the pride or threats from the kingdom of Babylon have ceased and the land is quiet, we shall restore everything. Nor shall we be reluctant to enrich the church of that Sepulchre as is fitting, and to adorn it with richer gold, gems, or workmanship.”

After these words, the patriarch, overcome by the king—a man learned in letters—promised, on Brother Maurice’s advice, to provide thirty soldiers paid in solidi. Yet before long, weary of them, he took away a talent of incalculable money and left the soldiers unfunded and without pay. As the king perceived his hypocrisy day by day, he pressed him more forcefully and urged him concerning his military obligation. The patriarch, on the contrary, made deaf ears to everything; so obstinate was he in spirit.

## CHAPTER LXII.—The patriarch is deprived of authority over, and of the offerings of, the Lord’s Sepulchre. The patriarch’s money is disclosed to the king

The patriarch, sorrowful and sad, accordingly withdrew to Joppa. There, with the king’s consent, because he held priestly rank, he passed the time of autumn and winter in peace. Then, at the beginning of March, in the first year of Baldwin’s reign, he sailed to Tancred at Antioch.

His chamberlains, however, were seized and detained. Compelled by threats and fear of beatings, they declared that the patriarch had buried twenty thousand Byzantine gold pieces; and they reported that he possessed so much silver that its weight and number still remained unknown to everyone. Brother Maurice, however, because he was legate of the Roman pontiff, the king retained with himself in every honour he could show; he provided carefully for him and treated him graciously in all things.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—The king distributes money to his soldiers; a cruel embassy arrives from Babylon

Meanwhile, while the king was occupied with these and other various matters, distributing the revealed money among his excellent soldiers and rewarding each according to his service, a cruel message came down from Babylon: namely, that Meravis, who was second in the kingdom, was hastening with the entire force and equipment of the king of Babylon and would soon make war upon him.

When King Baldwin received these grim reports, he did not admit them carelessly or readily to his ears. But, departing from Jerusalem in September, on the solemn Nativity of Mary, mother and virgin, in the first year of his reign, he entered the city of Joppa with all his infantry and cavalry. Having garrisoned its walls with many of his own men, he hurried to meet the enemy with only three hundred horsemen and a thousand foot soldiers, in order to learn whether the report of war that had reached him was true.

When morning came, standing on the plain of Ramla, he saw the intolerable forces, numbers, and arms of the Babylonians advancing through the lands and districts of Ascalon—about two hundred thousand, both horsemen and foot soldiers. The king and all who were with him were not merely astonished, but shaken with terror.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—Three divisions of the king’s army are crushed and fail before the Babylonians

Nevertheless, perceiving that he could not avoid the danger or escape the enemies who stood not far away, the king arranged five divisions, composed of cavalry and infantry alike.

In the first division was Belvold, a most noble knight. When battle was first joined, he was killed with all his men by the pagans, except for one soldier who, having had a hand cut off there, scarcely escaped the danger of death.

Then Geldemar Carpenel, a most valiant knight commanding the second division, attempted to break through the midst of the enemy and aid his comrades in peril. He fell beneath the irresistible hand of the enemy with all his followers and helpers. Only William and Erkenbold escaped alive.

Hugh of Tiberias, a warlike young man stationed in the third division, rode swiftly through the midst of the enemy and fought them severely for a long time. At the end of the engagement, exhausted and overcome by the weight of battle, he scarcely escaped from the middle of the storm, all those of his company having been killed and crushed there.

Seeing so grievous a destruction of his men, the king was violently shaken with fear, along with the two divisions that remained with him. Nor was this surprising: they expected to undergo the same sentence of death at any moment.

## CHAPTER LXV.—Admonished by bishops, the king prostrates himself before the Lord’s Cross

Then two catholic bishops, Gerard and Baldwin—of whom Gerard bore before him the Lord’s Cross for the confusion and blinding of the Saracens and the deliverance of Christians—addressed the king gently and by way of correction:

“We fear, lord king, that because of the discord which has arisen between you and the lord patriarch, victory may today be hindered for our men. We therefore urge you to be reconciled with him and so make satisfaction to the Lord God of peace, that we may be delivered from the present danger.”

The king replied, “You have advised rightly.” Saying this, he dismounted from his horse, fell to the ground before the Lord’s Cross, and worshipped the Lord of heaven. He then gave this answer to the bishops:

“Most beloved fathers and brothers in Christ, most learned shepherds and teachers, the judgment of death is at hand for us. Countless enemies stand against us with bows, spears, and flashing swords. I would not today set myself against men whom the Roman Empire, the kingdom of France, and England could not penetrate and conquer by force, unless, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord God should deliver me from their hands in such a way that I shall not make peace with him until he has first been canonically cleared, before the apostolic see and the whole Church, of the treachery which he committed.”

## CHAPTER LXVI.—After confessing his sins, the king breaks through the enemy’s midst, while Bishop Gerard bears the Lord’s Cross before him

Having said this with an oath, he confessed his sins before the same bishops. Then, having received communion of the Lord’s body and blood, he left ten armoured knights with Bishop Gerard, who bore before them the wood of the Holy Cross.

The king himself mounted a horse called *gazela* in the Saracenic language, because it is swifter in course than other horses. He sent forward the fourth division which he had formed from the knights of Jerusalem, men most experienced and vigorous in war, so that they might strike and fight the enemy in the onset.

This fourth division, charging boldly at the king’s command, engaged the adversaries; but, unable to bear the burden of battle because of their multitude, it began to give way in flight. Yet when the king learned of its flight and rout, it was greatly relieved. For at once he arrived with his fifth division, fought a fierce battle with the enemy, and, renewing the attack, inflicted no small slaughter and carnage.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—The wondrous victory of the Lord Jesus and of his Holy Cross

While the king thus broke through the enemy’s ranks and covered the fields with the bodies of the slain, a most renowned emir rushed with violent fury against the bishop bearing the Cross, intending swiftly to cut off his head. But, forestalled by divine vengeance and a blow from God, he was choked by sudden death and expired.

Then another emir suddenly attacked the Christian king himself. Immediately the king’s spear pierced his horse through the neck; and with the same blow and thrust it manfully pierced the emir himself through breast and liver. Thus both horse and rider were killed by the Christian king.

When the two emirs, great commanders of the Babylonian army, had died—the first by divine vengeance, the other transfixed by the king’s spear—the king and all his men recovered strength. In the power of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Cross, they charged through the densely massed divisions of the Saracens and inflicted unprecedented slaughter upon them until evening, when, exhausted on both sides, each side withdrew from battle. But the king and the remnant of the faithful, holding the open plain, spent the night in the enemy’s camp. The despairing Saracens remained that night on the summit of a mountain.

Here indeed it is evident how the power of the Holy Cross prevails not only against the missiles of invisible enemies, but also against the weapons of visible ones. For in the first, second, third, and fourth divisions the pride and strength of the pagans prevailed in victory; but in the fifth division, in which the wood of the holy and venerable Cross was borne before the king and his companions, the entire power of the unbelievers began to weaken, be humbled, and be trampled down. Their fiercest leaders too, giving glory neither to God nor to the Holy Cross, but rushing boldly and foolishly against it as it stood opposed to them, were overtaken by sudden death and perished.

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—When battle was renewed, the Catholic king exhorts his men

After this Christian victory, which was won in September, on the very evening of the Nativity of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, at sunrise on the following day some Frenchmen still alive and unharmed hastened to arm again with their king, suspecting that battle still threatened from the pagans. But none were found or seen anywhere on the plain of the region.

As the king returned with only forty knights and two hundred foot soldiers, who had scarcely escaped, twenty thousand Saracens unexpectedly appeared in the open plain. They had besieged Joppa and had not taken part in yesterday evening’s battle, but had fiercely assaulted the city at Meravis’s command. Since there was no place by which the king could turn aside from them, he resolved to resist and encouraged them all in a great and bold voice:

“Behold, our enemies come to meet us in full armour. We, however, exhausted by battle, escaped only late yesterday from the hands of our adversaries, God alone protecting us, after overcoming the enemy. All our nobles and knights except ourselves have fallen. What then shall we few men do against so many thousands, still untouched by battle? We are few and weary from yesterday’s battle; there is neither place nor possibility of turning aside from them. Therefore I know not what counsel to give, except that in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the power of the Holy Cross, we all stand and fight against the unbelievers. For God is able to deliver us from their hands as well, just as yesterday he delivered us from the hand of enemies more numerous and stronger. But if we are destined for death and destruction, let us have confidence and hope that, if in this present world we allow our bodies to be slain for the name of Jesus and for the holy places of Jerusalem, in the world to come we may preserve our souls for eternal life together with our brethren who were slaughtered and crushed for Christ in yesterday’s battle.”

## CHAPTER LXIX.—The king’s glorious victory and return to Jerusalem

Strengthened by the king’s exhortation in the hope of eternal life, all the knights and foot soldiers, seeing the enemy’s troops advancing from afar, quickly put on their arms. Keeping the Lord’s wood always before their faces, they joined fierce battle with the enemy.

The Saracens, blinded and weakened, fear being instilled in them by the presence of so venerable a wood, did not persist long in battle. When they saw the Christians’ boldness and the overwhelming ruin of their own men, some fled toward Ascalon and others toward the mountains of Jerusalem; defeated and scattered, they sought refuge, while the king pursued them mercilessly in grievous slaughter.

Returning from the enemy’s slaughter, the king gathered together his very few companions and turned aside to Joppa with fresh spoils—gold and silver, horses and mules, and abundant wealth. There he took off his iron mail and purple garment; they were visibly, truly, and beyond doubt wholly soaked with the gore and blood of enemies. The king spent that night there in joy, merriment, and an abundance of food.

The citizens, however, rose up and hastened into the plains of Ascalon. By the transport of asses and camels they brought into the city of Joppa the tents, gold, silver, and many precious spoils of the slain pagans which the king and his very few companions had been unable to carry away. Then, when the light of the following day shone forth, the king ascended to Jerusalem in great glory. From all the enemy’s spoils and plunder, he bestowed tithes upon the hospital and Christ’s poor.

## CHAPTER LXX.—The death of Wicker, an outstanding German knight

Wicker the German, however, was seized by severe fevers in the same year, a little before this battle, and died in August; he was buried in the city of Joppa. With his sword—the sword with which he cut a Turk in two through armour and clothing in the middle of the bridge at Antioch—he would have brought the king no small aid here, had death not intervened to end his life.

One day in the district of Joppa, this magnificent knight, protected by his shield, attacked a great and terrible lion which often devoured men and herds near the mountains and was attempting to attack a grazing horse. The lion came toward him face to face with swift foot and leap; Wicker struck it with a blow of that same most sharp sword, forcefully splitting its brain into pieces, and left the cruel and fearless beast dead upon the plain.

# BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER I.—How, in the first year of King Baldwin, an innumerable multitude of Lombards set out through Bulgaria for Jerusalem

At the same time when this battle was fought in September and King Baldwin gained his bloody victory, in the first year of his reign, an innumerable people of Lombards from the kingdom of Italy, having heard of the notable Christian victory after the capture of Antioch and Jerusalem, gathered from various regions of Italy. They travelled prosperously through the kingdom of Hungary as far as the kingdom of the Bulgars, wishing to increase and aid their fellow-Christian brethren.

Among the same undertaking and company were men of the highest rank: the bishop of Milan; Albert, illustrious count of Blandratz; his brother Guy, an outstanding knight; Hugh of Montbeel; Otto, son of the sister of the aforesaid Albert, surnamed Altaspata; Wigbert, count of the city of Parma; and the other leading men of Italy, men of remarkable nobility and commanders of the army. Gathered to about thirty thousand, they entered, as stated above, the land and kingdom of the Bulgars with a strong hand.

## CHAPTER II.—The emperor of Constantinople permits these Lombards to buy and sell in the Bulgarian towns, and forbids them plunder

Having entered, they sent messengers to the emperor of Constantinople, requesting that, by his grace and grant, they might purchase for a price the necessities of life in the land of the Bulgars, which belonged to his kingdom and authority, and thus pass peaceably through his territory.

Having received the embassy and petition of so distinguished and Catholic an army, the king of the Greeks graciously granted all that they requested, subject to this condition: that so great a gathering should not ravage any places belonging to his jurisdiction by violence, nor disturb them through a rashly raised sedition. On this condition he granted them permission to buy and sell in the towns of that Bulgarian kingdom, abounding in bread, wine, meat, and every rich provision: namely, the towns of Panidos, Rossa, Rosto, Dedamis, the town called Natura, Sasalabria, Adrianople, and Philippopolis; lodged by these places, they were to sustain their lives peaceably and abundantly from the goods of the land.

## CHAPTER III.—The Lombards disregard the emperor’s edict and attack Greeks and Bulgars; but, soon summoned by the emperor, they proceed to Constantinople

When they came into this land, they transgressed the king’s command, nor did the commanders and leaders of the army heed it. Instead, they plundered everything without measure or reason, taking their property from the Bulgars and Greeks without any purchase, seizing their livestock and poultry, and—what is shameful to say of a Catholic people—devouring these things during the season and fast of Lent.
