Moreover, in the aforesaid places and cities, through greed for the objects stored within them, they broke open the chapels of the pious emperor himself, in the face of so great a multitude.

Likewise, in a deed dreadful to hear, one of their parasites impiously cut off the breasts of a woman defending herself. When the emperor heard this cruel disgrace and intolerable devastation inflicted upon the kingdom of the Bulgars by these men, together with the complaints of his people, he sent messengers to the chief men and commanders of the host, ordering them not to remain any longer in these regions, towns, and cities, but to hasten to him by the royal road at Constantinople, the city which is the head of all Greece.

They accordingly came to Constantinople and, by the king’s order and decree, pitched their tents on this side of the shore of the sea called the Arm of St George, along the bank of its channel for a distance of three miles. They remained there for two months in the springtime before any company from the kingdom of France or Germany joined them; there too, by many injuries as was their custom, they provoked the emperor himself to anger and hatred.

## CHAPTER IV.—The emperor, injured by the Lombards, forbids buying and selling there; they unanimously besiege his palace

The emperor, repeatedly provoked by many injuries, feared that the force of diverse nations would be enlarged by such great and numerous troops; then, made more daring, they might rise against the city of Constantinople in rebellion through greed or some pretext. He warned them not to remain longer in those places or on the shore, but to depart from there as quickly as possible and lodge within the borders of Cappadocia and Romania, near the ports of Civitot and Rufinel, until the legions and forces that were to arrive should assemble with them.

But they unanimously replied that they would by no means cross the arm of the sea until they had obtained more substantial forces of both Franks and Germans. Hearing this obstinate answer of the Lombards—that they would not remove themselves from the occupied seashore before the arrival of their expected companions—the emperor forbade them the right to buy and sell. At once a lack of the necessities of life arose among the people for three days.

Seeing the king’s anger, the prohibition of life’s necessities, and thus the pressure of famine among the people, all the Lombards, horsemen and foot soldiers alike, suddenly put on their arms. With mattocks, iron hooks, and hammers, they gathered at the gate and walls of the principal palace of the city, at the place called St Argenius. Breaking in and entering at two places, they first killed a young man of the emperor’s own blood, then killed a tame lion which was greatly beloved in the emperor’s palace.

## CHAPTER V.—When the emperor is finally reconciled through the bishop of Milan, the Lombards leave Constantinople and arrive at Nicomedia

The bishop of Milan, Count Albert of Blandratz, Hugh of Montbeel, and the other wiser and leading men of the army, recognizing that this most evil sedition would harm themselves and their men more than it could benefit them, rose up among the people and forbade the evil to continue. At last, now by threats and now by persuasion, they restrained the people and sent each man back to his own place.

When this most serious conflict had been calmed, the bishop and the count came by ship to the emperor himself across the same arm of the sea, since they were quartered more than a mile from the city and royal palace. Entering confidently before him, they tried to soften his mind and recall him from angry indignation, affirming under oath that they were innocent of this deed and that these evils had been stirred up and caused by senseless and incorrigible men.

The emperor, in turn, laid before them the offence of earlier injuries, then the outrages which they had recently committed in his presence: the destruction of his palace, the killing of his kinsman, and the slaughter of his lion. But the aforesaid leaders, shrewd, restrained, and eloquent in their replies, attempted by every means to soothe the emperor’s anger, first excusing themselves upon oath that these evils had been done in no way by their will or consent.

At last the emperor, appeased by their humble defence, through the intercession of such great leaders graciously forgave the pilgrims all that had been inflicted upon him. Nevertheless, as he had determined on the advice of his men, he again urged them to cross the arm of the sea. So anxious was he about the invasion and disturbance of his kingdom that, by great gifts of gold, silver, and purple cloth, and by still greater promises, he attempted to induce these men to make this multitude willing to cross the arm of the sea.

Corrupted by the emperor’s great gifts and promises, Albert of Blandratz, trusting him excessively, accepted ten horses together with other precious things. But the bishop, with prudent foresight, rejected all these things offered to him, fearing that, if the army crossed, it would be harassed by the Greeks and handed over to be killed by Turkish arms.

When the emperor saw the bishop’s steadfastness, he sought reconciliation with him by every means. Yielding to his request, he again granted the pilgrims permission to buy and sell, and on both sides a treaty for maintaining peace was confirmed. At the same time Count Raymond came down from Laodicea to Constantinople. He was of great assistance to the pilgrims in reconciling the emperor, becoming his foremost and closest associate in every counsel and decree above all those who went up to Jerusalem. At last, after the Lord’s Easter had been celebrated, the Lombards crossed the arm of the sea after several days and reached the city of Nicomedia.

## CHAPTER VI.—Conrad, master of the stables of Emperor Henry, joins the Lombards at Nicomedia with certain princes of western France

Likewise Conrad, master of the stables of Henry III, emperor of the Romans, arrived at Constantinople with two thousand Germans. Once made known to Emperor Alexius, he found favour in his eyes, being loved above all others and honoured with magnificent gifts. He too crossed the arm of the sea and joined the Lombard leaders.

Thereafter Count Stephen of Blois, moved by penitence, prepared to return to Jerusalem; likewise Stephen, duke of Burgundy; Milo of Bray; Guy Redhead; Hugh and Bardolf of Breis; Engelrad, bishop of Laon; the Viscount of Firmament; Reynold, bishop of Soissons; Baldwin of Grandpré, a most handsome knight; Dudo of Clermont; and Walbert, castellan of Laon. All these, from the kingdom of western France, joined the Lombards with all their forces there in the city and region of Nicomedia; they are reported to have come together in that same city from various lands and regions and to have remained within its territory.

## CHAPTER VII.—How, at Pentecost, an innumerable Christian army left Nicomedia and directed its march toward the region of Paphlagonia

Then, as the holy day of Pentecost approached, about two hundred and sixty thousand people, gathered into one body from different parts of the world—with the sons and wives of many, with clerics and monks, and with a great multitude of idle common people—requested a guide from the emperor of Constantinople. Granting their request, he appointed for them Count Saint-Gilles, who was his intimate associate, together with five hundred Turcopole horsemen, so that under his guidance and direction they might continue their journey and prudently manage all things.

These arrangements having been made, and Count Raymond made counsellor and leader of the army, Stephen of Blois resolved to travel by the route through the land of Nicomedia and Romania which Duke Godfrey, Bohemond, and the first army had taken, because it seemed to him and many of the company to be safe and favourable. But the Lombards, confident in their numbers, stubbornly maintained that they would go through the mountains and the region of Paphlagonia. They said that they would even enter the kingdom of Khorasan by force and either wrest Bohemond from Turkish captivity and free him, or, relying on their own strength, besiege and destroy the city of Baghdad, capital of the kingdom of Khorasan, and thus powerfully rescue their fellow-brother from his chains.

Stephen of Blois, Raymond, and the other leading men, understanding the Lombards’ extremely fierce obstinacy and excessive boasting about Bohemond’s deliverance, and unable to turn them from their error, set out by the route that they sought, with Count Raymond himself leading, accompanied by the Turcopoles and the emperor’s great equipment.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The people indulge unlawfully in lust on their march, utterly destroy the fortress of Ankara, and cut down the Turks’ neighbouring crops and grain

After three weeks had passed, while the pilgrims were still travelling prosperously and feasting abundantly, and while many among the people were indulging unlawfully in lust and engaging greatly in incestuous intercourse, on the very vigil of St John the Baptist, the Forerunner of the Lord, they came to mountains difficult to climb and very deep valleys, and then to the fortress called Ankara.

There they attacked the Turks whom they found. Continuing the assault until mid-morning, they utterly destroyed the fortification, cutting down two hundred Turks there. Yet six of their leaders, hiding themselves, escaped the danger of death in the silence of night.

They restored this fortress to the emperor’s soldiers, because it had belonged to his kingdom and had been lost through the Turks’ unjust invasion. They then proceeded to the stronghold of Gargara, ravaging the crops and all the sown fields of the region, because they could not damage the stronghold owing to its fortification, rendered strong and impregnable by its situation and the nature of the terrain. They left this stronghold unharmed and unconquered by the entire host. The Turks rejoiced greatly, since their fortress—vainly besieged by the Christian bands—now remained unharmed and undefeated.

From that day onward, they pursued the army; unable to follow as closely because of fatigue, they made attacks and killed men with frequent showers of arrows.

## CHAPTER IX.—Count Raymond, corrupted by Turkish gifts, leads the army along a desert route; Christians perform guard-duty in relays throughout the army

The Christian people then reached many cities and fortresses whose names are unknown. From these, the Turks sent gifts and abundant provisions, thereby turning aside the leading Count Raymond and the emperor’s soldiers. Thus bribed, they led the whole army through deserts, trackless places, wildernesses, and arid ground. There Turkish ambushes continually encountered them and slaughtered all those in the army delayed by carelessness or exhaustion.

Having recognized the ambushes, the very severe pursuit, and the destruction of the people, the leaders of the army decreed that guards from their people should be placed before and behind. About seven hundred Frankish knights were always to go ahead at the front and keep watch; likewise about seven hundred Lombards were to protect and await at the rear their weary and following brethren.

But when the Turks learned that the Lombards were guarding the rear of the army, more than five hundred of them, massed together with bows and horses, suddenly raised a loud cry and attacked them from behind, harassing and wounding them swiftly with a hail of arrows. At last, terrified by the prospect of death, the Lombards fled at the speed of their horses, abandoning the wretched foot soldiers exhausted by the journey. The Turks killed about a thousand of these in a grievous slaughter during this first guard-duty.

At dawn the next day, when the cruel news of the destroyed people had been carried to the camp, all the leading men of the army were troubled. They reproached the Lombards severely because the army had been crushed and diminished through their softness and sloth. Therefore they resolved to appoint other guards for the weary people following at a distance; but no one offered himself for guard-duty except the duke of Burgundy. With five hundred armoured horsemen, he guarded the army so effectively that not a single person of the people perished during his day’s watch.

## CHAPTER X.—The Turks fight a battle with Raymond, and the Christian companies, massed together because of the enemy, march in confusion through the wilderness
The following day, after Stephen’s watch [Col. 0610D], Count Raymond kept watch for his day. Seven hundred Turks, gathered together, attacked him vigorously at the ninth hour of the day in very narrow places, and engaged him in a severe battle of arrows. But the count resisted manfully and lost no more than three of his men, apart from some who were there wounded by grievous arrow-wounds. Therefore Count Raymond, seeing that a difficult battle pressed upon himself and his men, and that the increasing Turkish forces were bringing violence against him, sent back seven knights at full speed to the army, which had already advanced a distance of seven miles, so that some force might be sent to help him and his men, who were being excessively and long distressed by the enemy’s attack. When this message of the count was heard [Col. 0611A], ten thousand horsemen were immediately separated out; clothed in mail, covered with helmets, and with shields laid over their breasts, they retraced their route that same day to bring help to the count, supposing that all the Turkish forces had assembled. But the seven hundred Turks, seeing the count’s steadfastness and the bold relief-force returning, swiftly took flight and hid themselves in the mountains. From that day, their forces having been joined, Raymond and all the leaders and captains of the ten thousand, with the entire body of horsemen and the company of weary foot-soldiers, came together again on their return to the mass of the army. Thereafter they did not presume, with any confidence, to divide themselves or to range about separately anywhere, because of the continual assaults and the excessive numbers of the Turks.

## CHAPTER XI.—How the army, wandering in the wilderness for fifteen days, endured the most grievous miseries of thirst and hunger.

[Col. 0611B]

Thereafter, continuing their journey for fifteen uninterrupted days, they advanced ever farther into wildernesses and places uninhabitable and dreadful, across most rugged mountains. Finding nothing there—neither man nor beast—they began to be constrained by severe hunger; for neither gold nor silver could help anyone, because no kind of food could be found which might be bought for a price. If any Provençals went ahead—five hundred, or two hundred, or three hundred—to seek provisions, they were surrounded by the Turks and immediately killed; the following army is said to have found them daily mutilated. For this [Col. 0611C] Provençal people desired plunder and robbery more than all the rest, and for that reason were exposed to greater peril than the others through a heavier disaster. Only the rich and distinguished men, who had brought flour, bread, dried meat, or bacon in carts from the port of Civitot and from the city of Nicomedia, had sustenance for life. Severe want compelled the rest to gnaw leaves, the bark of trees, and the roots of plants, and thus to fill their bellies.

## CHAPTER XII.—Concerning a thousand Christian foot-soldiers who, while gathering barley in a valley, were surrounded and burned by Turkish fire.

Pressed by this want, a thousand foot-soldiers from the army, on the border of a city named Constamnes, discovered new barley, though not yet ripe. Nevertheless, laden with this grain, they descended into a certain valley and kindled a fire from shrubs and tamarisks [Col. 0611D], intending to shake the grains of unripe barley, scorched and roasted by flames, from the stalks in order to fill their bellies. Likewise, they learned to cook in order to mitigate their hunger certain little fruits of a strange and unheard-of kind—the bitter fruit of some bushes—found and gathered there in the desert. But, detected by the cruel Turks, they were crowned with martyrdom. For, since because of the difficulty of the terrain, valleys, and mountains no access to them lay open to any enemy, and there was no possibility or artifice for harming them with arrows, the Turks kindled an abundant fire from branches of shrubs and dry grassy material and filled the valley all around with it; as a result, a thousand men were burned. When the dreadful report of the burning and destruction of this Catholic legion [Col. 0612A] was spread through the camp, all the Christian princes were terrified. Therefore, from that day onward, for six continuous days, always gathered into one body, they arranged their march so that the foot-soldiers might appear among the horsemen, ready alike for every danger and for defence.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The Turks, twenty thousand strong, fighting the Christians with their leaders Doniman and Solyman, lost seven hundred men.

Thus six days were completed, and behold: the Turks Doniman, Solyman, Carageth, Brodoan of Aleppo, men from the mountains of Phlagonia, and men from the whole kingdom of Antioch, twenty thousand archers armed with horn and bone bows, confronted the Christian companies. Having observed all their circumstances and hardships, they resolved to attack them in battle on Friday. On that day the army of Christ’s faithful overcame the narrow and laborious passes of Phlagonia [Col. 0612B], and, coming out upon an open plain, pitched camp at the ninth hour of that same day, Friday, in order to rest. And behold, the Turks approached and, shouting loudly according to their custom, surrounded the whole army and began a severe battle on both sides. At times the Turks rushed upon the camp in sudden assault, harassed the Christian knights, and transfixed them with arrows. At times the Franks and Lombards, although weary and burdened by the journey, rose up, indignant at so many repeated assaults, and frequently drove them back, until seven hundred Turks fell. Of the Christians none were struck down; for that day the Turks could not break into or scatter those gathered into one body [Col. 0612C]. But the Turks, seeing that on this day they achieved nothing by slaughtering Christians, while very many of their own had fallen, returned sad and grieving to their camp as evening covered the earth. Likewise the Christian army, having stationed watches and guards around the camp, rested that night, all storm of war having ceased.

## CHAPTER XIV.—Where the Christians destroyed a Turkish stronghold, but, caught in an ambush, lost about seven hundred men.

The following Saturday, three thousand men of the Christian army and their leaders, Conrad and Bruno, his sister’s son, with other very brave men, left the camp and plain. Reaching the district of the city of Marecsh, after completing two miles of their journey, they attacked a Turkish stronghold [Col. 0612D]. The Turks defended it in vain; without delay the Christians destroyed it, plundered all the necessities of life found there, and put the Turks whom they found within to the sword. Rejoicing in this successful outcome, and carrying great and abundant Turkish spoils with them to their tents, the Christians descended through certain exceedingly rugged and rocky mountain passes. There they were surrounded by Turkish ambushes, harassed and transfixed with arrows. Being little able to resist because of weariness, the burden of their booty, and the narrowness of the terrain, about seven hundred perished, leaving all the spoils and plunder of the Turks there, though unwillingly. Those who escaped their hands came back singly and scattered, like men defeated and crushed, to the camp at evening, sad [Col. 0613A] and grieving. For the remainder of that day the army mourned for the loss of its men and rested in its tents, without any assault. Likewise, on Sunday both Turks and Christians ceased from every attack and storm of war.

## CHAPTER XV.—The Bishop of Milan exhorts the whole army to confess its sins, and the entire multitude is arranged in five battle-lines with its leaders to fight the enemies.

On Monday, when the first sunlight was already shining, the Bishop of Milan rose in the midst of the army. Moved by the divine Spirit, he foretold that battle would come that day; and, addressing the people of the living God, he exhorted all to come to confession of their sins. In the name of Jesus, by apostolic authority, he absolved them from the bonds of sin; after granting indulgence to all, he sanctified and blessed them with the arm of St Ambrose, Bishop of Milan [Col. 0613B]. Moreover, the Lord’s Lance, which Raymond had brought with him, was raised to sanctify and bless the people. After this blessing and confession of their purification, Stephen, Duke of Burgundy, a most renowned knight, formed a battle-line from his own people. Raymond retained the Turcopoles and Provençals in his own line. Conrad, constable of Emperor Henry III, summoned to his line the Alemanni, Saxons, Bavarians, Lotharingians, and all the Germans. The Bishop of Laon, Engelrad, Milo, Wido, Hugh, Bardolf of Breis, and Walbert of the city of Laon formed a line from the Frankish contingent. The Bishop of Milan, Albert of Blandraz, Wido his brother, Otto of Altaspata, Hugh [Col. 0613C] of Montbeel, Wigbert of Parma, and all the Lombard horsemen and foot-soldiers formed for themselves a very dense battle-line. When the lines had thus been arranged, the Lombards were stationed in the front, because their forces were considered irresistible, so that they might attack the Turkish lines nearest to them, standing firm and impenetrable face to face against them. Then the individual Christian battle-lines, stationed everywhere to right and left, confronted the individual lines of the heathen, often driving them into flight and often renewing battle against them. But the Turks, cunning and skilled in warfare, after retreating a little way suddenly checked their reins and, striking back with a hail of arrows, killed men and horses with grievous wounds.

## CHAPTER XVI.—The Lombards, fighting in the front line, give way; after them the remaining lines flee and scatter with their leaders.

[Col. 0613D]

The Lombards, therefore, who had been stationed in the front line, fought severely and long against the Turks. But their leader Albert, unable after excessive and prolonged resistance to bear the weight of battle, especially because of the failure of the horses, which had been weakened by hunger and could do nothing, took flight with the battle-standard which he carried in his right hand. Thus the whole Lombard host, with its leaders and princes, was driven in flight as far as the tents. Conrad, however, an undaunted knight, seeing the battle grow more severe and the Lombards fail and take flight, suddenly rushed forward with his own line and attacked and scattered the Turks from the first hour of the day until after noon [Col. 0614A]. At last, overcome by the excessive and continual shower of missiles, he took flight with a force long worn down by hunger and exhausted in strength, and himself returned to the tents. Stephen likewise, wishing with the Burgundians to aid his crushed and fleeing brethren, charged with his line and attacked the enemies vigorously. But at length, after a long struggle, he turned his back with all his men, countless numbers of his people having been killed there and destroyed by Turkish weapons; and he fled back to the tents in the same manner. Stephen of Blois, seeing all things turn to disaster for both Lombards and Franks, rushed forward with all the Franks in his line to aid his brethren and restrain the Turks, and did not cease fighting until evening [Col. 0614B]. At last the Count of Blois, overcome and crushed by the unbearable Turkish force, powerful in arrows and bone bow, was brought back to the camp in the same flight as his companions, many noble men of his household having been defeated and slain. There fell in his line the most illustrious men: Baldwin of Grantpreit, Dudo of Clermont, Wigbert of Mont-Laon, guardian and defender of that city, a friend of God, a most fierce knight, tall of body, and many powerful men and leading members of the army, whose names we cannot all know or discover. Count Raymond, meanwhile, hastening with the imperial Turcopoles and his Provençal squadrons to relieve his companions in the same battle, suddenly struck down many Turks. But thereafter, fortune proving too adverse, many of his own being struck down and diminished by arrows [Col. 0614C], the Turkish battle became overwhelmingly strong, until the whole troop of Turcopoles, terrified and scattered in flight, turned aside to the place of the tents, abandoning the count amid the dangers; almost all his Provençal knights were cut to pieces.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Count Raymond, defeated in battle, flees toward the mountains with ten knights and occupies a very high rock; rescued from it by his companions, he takes flight with all his men at midnight.

Seeing, therefore, the flight of the Turcopoles and the irretrievable ruin of his own men, the count did not remain longer in the danger of death threatening him. Barely escaping from the weapons, he turned toward the mountains and through narrow places, and stood upon the summit of a certain very high rock, difficult of ascent [Col. 0614D], with only ten companions. From there he and his men attempted, so far as they could, to resist the Turks pursuing and besieging him. When all who had escaped Turkish weapons had returned to the tents, Stephen, Count of Blois, inquired of all the principal men who had returned from battle or fallen under arms. He was immediately informed that Raymond had taken refuge upon the summit of the rock, and that unless help were brought to him, he could never escape the hands of the Turks. At this, Count Stephen, gathering again two hundred companions in mail and helmets, hastened to free Raymond from Turkish attack. Having put to flight the Turks who were pursuing him and suddenly cut down about thirty men, he took the count safely down from the rock and brought him unharmed [Col. 0615A] back to the tents. The strongest Christian battle-lines had been defeated and crushed and driven by the cruel battle as far as the tents; the victorious Turks returned with the spoils of Franks and Lombards alike to their own camp, scarcely two miles from the Christian station, yet winning on that day a very sorrowful and bloody victory. For three thousand fighting men of their company fell in the same battle in which Christian knights, burdened by the weight of their sins, were by divine judgment delivered to unbelieving and impious men for punishment. That same night, when Count Raymond had been freed from the summit of the rock and the Turkish siege through the assistance of Stephen of Blois and Conrad the constable, and brought back to his brethren in camp, all who had fled from slaughter and battle to the tents began to prepare fires and necessary provisions; they also gathered wood and brushwood for cooking food, by which they might restore their bodies, weary and fasting [Col. 0615B]. And behold, when the first silence of night had fallen, the same Count Raymond, seized by some fear—I know not what—and despairing of life, equipped the horses of all his men and all the imperial Turcopoles with bridles and saddles, and took flight. Fleeing throughout that night and hastening along a route through mountains and trackless places, he is said to have reached a castle of the emperor named Pulveral.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—After Raymond’s flight, all the leaders of the army, with the remaining multitude, abandon their tents and wives on the road and take swift flight.

[Col. 0615C]

When this flight of his became known and was spread among the people, such fear seized everyone that not one of the princes remained. All, great and small, noble and ignoble, despairing of life, hastened to flee as far as Synoplum, the emperor’s stronghold, unaware that the hearts of the Turks too were no less troubled by fear of flight. The Christians left behind their tents and all their equipment, with all their carts, their tender and dearly loved wives, and all the household goods required by so many nobles and so great an army. Without delay, through scouts, the report of so sudden a flight reached the ears of the Turks. Not long after crushing the Christians and gaining victory, they too had returned to their own camp, so that on that night they might refresh with food and sleep their limbs, wearied and burdened by the slaughter of Catholic knights [Col. 0615D].

## CHAPTER XIX.—How the Turks plundered the tents of the fugitives and slaughtered some of their wives, while taking others captive.

Hearing this, the Turks immediately rose, roused and summoned all their men with trumpets and horns, and—as men ever wakeful for the slaughter of enemies—were present at the Christians’ tents at first light. There they cruelly attacked the most noble women and distinguished matrons, both Frankish and Lombard; impiously seizing and binding them, they sent more than a thousand away among barbarous peoples and into an unknown language, as though they had plundered dumb cattle, and placed them in perpetual exile in the land of Corrozan [Col. 0616A], as in a prison and locked chamber. They killed the others, who were somewhat advanced in age, by the sword. The land and kingdom of Corrozan is so enclosed by mountains and marshy waters that any captives who enter it once can no more leave it than cattle can leave a pen, unless by the Turks’ licence and permission. Ah, what great grief! What miseries might be seen there, when such tender and most noble matrons were carried off as booty and led away by impious and horrible men—men whose heads are shaved before and behind, on right and left, in the manner of a neck; whose scanty hair, hanging down from these four necks, bristles in uncut locks; who also have uncut and long beards; and who are said in their appearance to resemble only foul and unclean spirits. Truly there was no small grief there; no slight fear seized the delicate matrons; no faint wailing of women was heard in the camp, where their beloved husbands—some killed, others fleeing under the pressure of utmost necessity—left them miserable and desolate in the hands of their assailants [Col. 0616B]. Some were in turn abused by unlawful and foul intercourse, and, after very great torment, were beheaded; others, pleasing to their eyes by cheerful countenance and beautiful appearance, were sent, as we have said, among barbarous peoples.

## CHAPTER XX.—How, after plundering the women, the Turks pursued the fleeing Christians, cutting them down in various slaughter and collecting their abundant spoils left along the road.

Having found and captured so many honourable women in the tents of the fleeing Christians [Col. 0616C], the Turks pursued at speed both horsemen and foot-soldiers, clerics and monks, and the whole female sex who had escaped from the camp in flight. They mowed them down with the sword no differently than a reaper is accustomed to mow ripe grain with his sickle. They spared neither age nor rank; only beardless youths, men suited for military service, did they take captive, intending also to carry them away in exile with the distinguished matrons to Corrozan. They seized an unheard-of quantity of money, left in the middle of the road by the fugitives, exhausted with weariness; besides this, soft garments, various furs, grey squirrel, ermine, marten, innumerable gold-woven stuffs of wonderful beauty, workmanship, and colour, as well as horses and mules [Col. 0616D], more than any number or writing could record. At last it wearied them to carry all these things away.

## CHAPTER XXI.—How one hundred and sixty thousand of the Christian army were killed by thirst and hunger, flight and Turkish bloodshed in battle.

The land and mountains, as those who saw these things with their eyes and scarcely escaped the judgment of death attest as true, were so covered, in the destruction and flight of so great an army, with Byzantine coins, uncoined gold, inestimable silver, and scattered denarii, that for more than three miles fugitives and pursuers seemed to walk upon gold, jewels, silver and golden vessels, marvellous and precious stuffs, and fine silk garments. The whole road flowed with the blood of the slain. Nor is this surprising, since more than one hundred [Col. 0617A] and sixty thousand fell there beneath the sword and arrow of the savage Turks. They were easily overcome and cut down by the enemy because of the long hunger by which they had been exceedingly afflicted and exhausted of strength, so that they could offer no resistance. Such hunger lay upon them in the deserts of Phlagonia that an ox-hide was bought for twenty solidi; a little loaf which could be enclosed in the palm of the hand was sold for three solidi in the money of Lucca; and the carcass of a horse, mule, or ass was valued at six marks. In this most savage flight, two worthy knights from the company of Stephen of Blois, while hastening along the road away from the pursuing Turks, encountered a certain stag coming from the mountains in the opposite direction, startled by the shouting and tumult of Turks and Christians; it became an obstruction in their path. Both fell over it by chance and were immediately beheaded by the enemies [Col. 0617B].

## CHAPTER XXII.—How the surviving Christian people, wandering and fugitive with their leaders, returned to Constantinople.

Thus the army, so crushed and fugitive, hastening to escape upon horse or mule, arrived scattered in flight at the city of Synoplum, which the emperor’s soldiers defended; and, continuing always to flee, part of it returned as far as the imperial city of Constantinople. Stephen, Duke of Burgundy; Stephen of Blois; Conrad, constable of the Roman emperor; the Bishop of Milan; the Bishop of Laon; the Bishop of Soissons; Wido Rufus; Hugh; Bardolf; the other chief men; and all who could escape the most grievous Turkish weapons returned to Constantinople [Col. 0617C], fleeing by mountains and trackless routes. Count Raymond, however, entering Synoplum by steep mountain paths and the depths of valleys with the Turcopoles of the Greek emperor, having left behind all his companions and leaders, spent the night there; on the following day he embarked upon a ship and was conveyed by sea to Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Concerning four hundred Christians who escaped the pursuing Turks, and another thousand soldiers who, when the Turks turned back, fell with their throats cut by Turkish swords.

Meanwhile, the small remnant of the army—the scattered remains of the Christians—followed the tracks of Count Raymond and the others by the same road; about four hundred, coming together out of their separate flight [Col. 0617D], were pursued from Tuesday to Wednesday by Solyman, Doniman, and Balas of Sororgia, still unsated with slaughter. Following the same route by which they were heading after the fugitive leaders toward Synoplum, they pursued them in order to cut them down and capture them. But they did not dare to follow them farther, because they had gone too far on account of the emperor’s forces and city, and so they turned back. On their return, they slew scatteredly that same day a thousand of the dispersed and delayed persons who came in their way, cutting off their necks. There the nobleman Eraldus, native of the city of Cadelim, met the impious tyrants and fell beneath their arrow. Engelrad, likewise from the same country, Dudo, an outstanding knight, Arnold, son of the bailiff, Walter of Castelens, and very many most powerful knights [Col. 0618A], whom the speed of their horses could not help, encountered the same executioners and were killed by arrows.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How the emperor kindly received at Constantinople the dispersed leaders and counts of the army as they fled to him; how he was hostile to Raymond but afterwards became his friend; and how the Bishop of Milan died there.

Count of St-Gilles and the other chief men, on entering Constantinople, were kindly received by the lord emperor. But he began to be somewhat angry with Raymond because, in fleeing, he had withdrawn and separated himself from his other companions, Stephen and Conrad. Taking this occasion, Raymond replied that he had acted thus because he feared that they would rise against him [Col. 0618B], since he had first begun flight from the camp with the Turcopoles, and because they might suppose that he had fled treacherously and by the emperor’s counsel. Soon afterwards the emperor’s anger ceased. He had pity upon them all, and relieved all who had been stripped of possessions and left empty-handed with magnificent gifts of gold, silver, arms, horses, mules, and clothing. Throughout all the autumn and winter he allowed them all to remain with him and recover strength amid every abundance and generosity of necessities. While they stayed there, the Bishop of Milan departed this life; the bishops and all the faithful gave him Catholic funeral rites.

## CHAPTER XXV.—How at the same time the most noble Prince William, departing from the kingdom of western France with fifteen thousand foot-soldiers added to his force, came down through arid Bulgaria.

[Col. 0618C]

At the same time, and in the first year of the reign of King Baldwin, the count and most powerful prince of the city of Ninive, commonly called Navers, named William, left the land and kingdom of western France. Making his journey through Italy, he crossed the deep sea by ship to the port called Brandiz, with fifteen thousand fighting men, horsemen and foot-soldiers, apart from an innumerable number of women, and withdrew to a city named Vallona. Having landed there, he came down to the city of Salonica, situated in the region of Macedonia and the land of the Bulgarians. There he was peacefully received in lodging by the inhabitants with every justice and kindness; theft, robbery [Col. 0618D], plunder, and unjust contention were forbidden under penalty of death, lest the army cause any injury in the emperor of Constantinople’s land, as the Lombards had done shortly before.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—How the same count, arriving at Constantinople with all his equipment, was received by the emperor and honoured with many gifts.

Thereafter, after a long journey and various lodgings, this distinguished count proceeded with all his forces and equipment to Constantinople. Kindly and honourably received by the emperor, he was ordered to pitch his tents for lodging on the shore of the Sea of St George outside the walls of the city. Three days later, by the emperor’s command, the count and the entire army crossed the arm of the sea [Col. 0619A], and, pitching their tents at a marble column which bears a gilded ram on its summit, not far from the arm of the sea, they remained there for fourteen days, around the feast of the Nativity of St John the Baptist. Each day the count was brought by ship into the emperor’s presence, and returned honoured and commended by him with no few gifts. The emperor also frequently sent to pilgrims and the humble people a kind of coin called a *Tartaron*, for the support of life.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—How the count and his army, leaving Constantinople, reached Stancona, a city of the Turks.

Finally, after the Nativity of St John, they departed from Civitot. Not staying there long, they left the route which the earlier army of Duke Godfrey and Bohemond had taken. Passing through very dense forests over a journey of two days, they reached Ancras—the very place which Count Raymond and the Lombard force had recently captured, beheading the Turks found in it—wishing to join in arms and forces the Lombard army which had gone on shortly before. But after remaining one day at the site of the aforesaid city and being unable at all to catch up with the Lombards, who continued their journey through Phlagonia, they left them to their left and took the road on the right leading to the city of Stancona, intending to remain there for some time and hear something of the Lombards’ fate [Col. 0619B].

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—Where the Turks encountered and harassed them in battle, killing a Lombard count with an arrow.

[Col. 0619C]

Before they had yet approached the city, Solyman and Doniman returned with Turkish forces and arms, scarcely eight days after the recent slaughter of the Lombards. Learning that the Count of Navers was following, they hastened by familiar paths through hills and valleys and encountered him there. Cruelly attacking with arrows, they harassed the army for three days by most severe warfare and bitter wounds, setting ambushes before and behind. Yet they had not as yet gained victory in those places, although many bands of pilgrims, unwisely following slowly because of weariness, fell under repeated assault [Col. 0619D]; and one Henry, a Lombard by birth, a distinguished count in his own land, died among his companions, transfixed by an arrow.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—The Christians resisted the Turks; after attacking Stancona in vain, they reached the city of Reclei, where about three hundred perished, parched by thirst.

For the Christian knights, still resisting the Turks manfully, killed very many and frequently drove others into flight; and they could readily drive them back, so long as they suffered no shortage of water and the strength of their horses had not failed. Thus the Christian knights, defended on the march from the repeated attacks of the Turks, reached Stancona. Finding there a Turkish guard and forces in the stronghold, they vigorously assaulted the walls; while the enemy within resisted them desperately [Col. 0620A], many were killed on both sides. Accomplishing nothing in this assault upon the stronghold, they moved their camp away and came to the city of Reclei. There the army languished under thirst so intolerable for three days that more than three hundred perished there by a most grievous death; the rest, still alive, were exhausted in strength and weakened by lack of necessities, and could offer little resistance. Tormented by this unbearable thirst, some of their companions climbed to the summit of a lofty rock and stood there, in hopes that they might spy water somewhere. But they saw only a city, empty of inhabitants and ruined, and supposed that water was in it; yet none was found, for its cisterns and wells had recently been demolished and filled in by the Turks.

## CHAPTER XXX.—The Turks, fighting the Christians, pursued the defeated and fleeing William; and concerning the flight of Robert and another William.

[Col. 0620B]

Shortly afterward the Turks learned that the army had already been weakened by the grievous suffering of thirst and could offer little resistance. They immediately pursued and attacked it with arrows, waging a severe battle on both sides throughout an entire day. Falling on both sides beneath sword, bow, and lance, they filled the whole very broad valley with their blood; and the ground of that region was covered with the thickly packed bodies of slain men and women. At last, as this most savage battle pressed on, the Christians’ strength was weakened by thirst and could therefore offer less resistance; Turkish fierceness began to gain strength and force the defeated Christians [Col. 0620C] cruelly into flight. They pursued the count, already defeated and fleeing from battle, as far as the city of Germanicoplam. Robert, brother of this count, and William of the city of Nonanta, the army’s standard-bearer, who was the first to turn his back, escaped Turkish arms with all the horsemen and fled to the aforesaid city of Germanicoplam, leaving the wretched foot-soldiers in the hands of the fierce enemies.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—How, after the duke’s flight, the Turks killed the remaining Christians and took their wives captive.

Seeing the flight of the Christian people and their leaders, the Turks raged in cruel slaughter among the people [Col. 0620D] and throughout the whole Christian company. Only seven hundred, fleeing through precipitous mountains and dense forests, were spared their lives. After this Turkish victory and the mournful slaughter of Christians, about a thousand wives of Christ’s soldiers were taken captive and led away by the horrible enemies into an unknown and foreign land. Horses and mules, silver and gold, and most precious clothing of every kind were plundered and carried off, enriching and filling the land and kingdom of Corrozan with excessive wealth and spoils. These most cruel wars and most savage massacres of Christians took place in the month of August, when summer is accustomed to be made more severe by the heat of the sun and the intolerability of thirst.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—How Count William, deceived by Turcopoles, reached Antioch at great risk.

[Col. 0621A]

The Count of Navers, who had scarcely escaped danger of death, had still retained, in fleeing from Turkish hands, something of his possessions and resources, and had barely made his way to the city of Germanicoplam. There he secured as guides, by much entreaty and payment of a large reward, twelve Turcopole soldiers of the Greek emperor, stationed there to defend the walls, for the road leading to the castle of St Andrew on this side of the city of Antioch. His purpose was to pass through Antioch in this way and continue his journey to Jerusalem. But the Turcopoles, faithless men, did not keep faith with him. Blinded by greed, they despoiled the count and his companions of their goods [Col. 0621B], leaving them naked and on foot in a desert and trackless place, and returned to Germanicoplam by familiar paths with the plunder. The count, sad and grieving, and especially distressed by the destruction of the Christian army, nevertheless completed, as he had vowed, the route under poor and mean covering, patiently accepting every adversity; at last, amid various hardships, he reached Antioch.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Tancred, the new prince of Antioch, assists the fugitive William.

Tancred, having become Prince of Antioch after Bohemond’s captivity, grieved for this same most noble count, so crushed by impious Turks and stripped of possessions. He furnished him with excellent and honourable new clothing and enriched him with magnificent gifts of horses and mules [Col. 0621C]. He kept him with himself for several days, until he had abundantly restored with the good things of the land—wine, oil, and the sweetness of meat—his limbs, made wretched and exhausted by thirst, fasting, wakefulness, and the fatigue of travel. Then, after the affliction and bitterness of soul and body had been relieved, William might undertake the road to Jerusalem, as he had vowed, in the spring season, after waiting there for and gathering together some of his scattered companions who had been left behind.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—How William, prince of Poitou, Welf, Duke of Bavaria, and Countess Ida entered Bulgaria with an armed host.

After a short interval, namely eight days after this recent slaughter, Count William, prince of the Poitevins, of the blood of Henry III, Emperor of the Romans, having peacefully crossed the kingdom of Hungary, entered the land of the Bulgarians with Welf, duke of Bavaria, and the noble countess Ida of the march of Austria, in a vast host of horsemen, foot-soldiers, and women, numbering more than one hundred and sixty thousand, and with abundant equipment. There, as easily happens among an unruly and incorrigible people, discord arose; and, after the Bulgarian duke named Guzh had been vexed by various injuries, William descended upon the city of Adrianople, unconquered in the strength of his followers. But the bridge leading into the city had been occupied and closed by the duke.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—How Rudolf died in the battle at the bridge, and how the duke of the Bulgarians surrendered.

Accordingly, while the Pechenegs and the other Cuman soldiers of the emperor’s realm fiercely prevented passage over the bridge with bows and arrows [Col. 0622A], and the Christians no less vigorously strove to cross it, so cruel a battle was fought on both sides that Rudolf, a man of very great nobility, born of Scegonges and kinsman of Prince William himself, was struck by an arrow and died there; Hartwig of Saint-Médard was taken prisoner; and so were very many others, whom it would take too long to recount individually.

Indeed, in that same battle, while the outcome shifted on both sides amid varied and immense destruction, it happened that the duke of the Bulgarians himself fell into the hands of William and his men and was held captive. At length, after counsels had been held on both sides that very day, all returned to concord; the captives were restored, and the Pechenegs and Cumans were pacified.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—With the Bulgarian duke appeased, William returns to Constantinople and is honored with gifts by the emperor.

[Col. 0622B]

Thereafter the agreement, the duke and his followers having been appeased, advanced so far that the duke not only granted the Christian pilgrims peaceful passage over the bridge and did not deny them permission to buy necessities, but also assigned an escort to all as far as Constantinople, without deceit or hindrance. In that city Prince William, Duke Welf, and Countess Ida remained for five weeks. They made known to Lord Emperor Alexius the whole vow which they had made concerning Jerusalem; and therefore, having bound themselves to him by an oath of fidelity, they deserved to receive many gifts of necessary provisions and permission to purchase necessities.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—When William’s army reaches the city of Stancona, the Turks block the springs and cisterns.

[Col. 0622C]

After this, as the time of harvest approached, they crossed by ship the arm of the sea of Saint George at the emperor’s command and persuasion, landed in the territory of the city of Nicomedia, and, continuing their journey through the pleasant places with which that region abounds, pitched their tents and stayed there for two days. Departing thence, they withdrew to Stancona. There, their provisions for life having been consumed by the long journey, both men and beasts were weakened by severe hunger and then by intolerable thirst.

Nor was this surprising. The Turks, having preceded them along the route, had burned all the crops before the face of this multitude; they had blocked wells, cisterns, and springs, so that, reduced by the utmost necessity of hunger and thirst [Col. 0622D], they might easily be overcome in battle.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—William and Welf fight the Turkish leaders before the city of Reclei, and the Christians take flight.

Therefore William, Welf, and their companions, seeing these wickednesses and stratagems of the Turks, attacked the cities under Turkish control—namely Phiniminum and Salamia—and destroyed them with great slaughter; nor did they spare from devastation any places round about subject to them. From there they descended to the city of Reclei, where a rushing river, long and eagerly desired, was sufficient for all.

But Selymanus, Donimanus, Carati, and Agunich, Turkish princes, suddenly confronted these unwary pilgrims on the opposite bank [Col. 0623A], with innumerable troops and weapons, preventing men, horses, and all beasts from watering amid a hail of arrows, until the Christians, worn out from afar and thus exhausted, could endure no more.

Accordingly, after a very great, long, and most savage contest, conducted from either of the marshy and deep banks, all the Christians took to flight and were crushed in unheard-of slaughter by their impious pursuers. Some, thinking to escape so cruel a martyrdom, separated from the multitude and went into a certain meadow, seeking to lie hidden in the hay; but they were not spared their lives: about three hundred there perished, transfixed by arrows.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the flight of the bishop of Auvergne and Duke Welf, and the death of Countess Ida.

[Col. 0623B]

The bishop of Auvergne and all his following, seeing Christ’s army thus scattered in flight and crushed by impious executioners, themselves fled to the foot of the mountain where the river Reclei rises, leaving horses and everything behind; and yet few escaped. Likewise Duke Welf, stripped of his mail-shirt and all else, fleeing through the mountains, was scarcely rescued from the enemy’s hand.

Many thousands of Germans, Franks, and Gascons, who were far from the mountains, are reported to have been killed there. Whether Countess Ida was captured and carried away, or torn limb from limb beneath the hooves of so many thousands of horses, remains unknown to this day; except that they say she was transported, among so many thousands of noblewomen, to the land of Corrozan for perpetual exile.

### CHAPTER XL.—How Tancred, prince of Antioch, received William as he fled through the mountains.

The count, with only one attendant-at-arms, fleeing through mountains and unknown roads from the weapons of his enemies, at last reached a city called Longinach, near Tursolt, governed by Bernard surnamed the Foreigner. Bernard kindly received him and supplied him with all necessities of life.

A few days later Tancred, prince of Antioch, heard that so eminent a prince was living there in poverty, stripped of his possessions and all things and greatly humbled. He took pity on his fellow-Christian brother and prince; and therefore, after taking counsel, he sent soldiers from Antioch to meet him, received him honorably, and, while he remained with him for several days [Col. 0623D] and feasted on the good things of the land, renewed him with precious garments.

### CHAPTER XLI.—How the princes scattered by war assembled at Antioch after gathering an army.

After the destruction of the Lombards and of William, prince of Navers, and likewise of William, count of Poitou, and Welf, duke of Bavaria, all those who had been scattered or had wintered at Constantinople or elsewhere came separately from every place to Antioch at the beginning of March, leaving behind their remnants: namely Albert of Blandraz, Conrad the constable, Stephen of Blois; likewise Stephen, duke of Burgundy; Count Raymond; William, count of Poitou; Welf, duke of Bavaria; the bishops Engelrad of Laon [Col. 0624A], Manasses of Barcelona, and other bishops of Italy. Having come together by ship at the port of Simeon the Hermit, they remained at Antioch for some time.

### CHAPTER XLII.—At the prayers of the princes Raymond is released from bonds by Tancred and is placed over the captured city of Tortosa.

Bernard the Foreigner, however, at that time held Count Raymond captive at that same port, because he was charged with having betrayed to death the Lombards and others who had been on the same expedition. Tancred, having received him into his custody at Antioch, kept him imprisoned.

The Christian princes who had assembled there, after a few days remembering their fellow-brother and Christian prince, and seeing him thus held in bonds by Tancred without examination [Col. 0624B], earnestly prayed Tancred, in Christ’s name, to release so great a prince and restore him to his own. Tancred, yielding to the prayers of his pilgrim brethren, restored him after bringing him out of prison, on this condition: that he should seize no land on this side of the city of Acre and should be bound by oath to observe this.

After receiving back Prince Raymond, they all saluted Tancred and returned from Antioch as far as the city of Tortosa. They besieged and captured it, and brought it under their authority. Raymond himself remained there by common counsel to guard its walls, since he seemed a prudent and skilled man in resisting enemies. The others resolved to continue their journey to Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—After worshipping at the Lord’s tomb in Jerusalem, Duke Welf returns to Cyprus and dies.

Duke Welf, avoiding this siege, went down to Jerusalem to worship, together with Reynold, duke of Burgundy, brother of Stephen and governing Burgundy in his stead. Reynold, who had set out for Jerusalem before the Lombard expedition and had wintered at Antioch until then, was seized by sickness and died and was buried on the road.

Welf therefore reached Jerusalem and, having worshipped the Lord Jesus and his tomb, returned by ship after a few days to the island of Cyprus. There he too was seized by illness, died, and was buried.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—How, after conquering Tortosa, the princes celebrated Palm Sunday at Joppa with King Baldwin.

[Col. 0624D]

The other aforementioned princes, after the capture of Tortosa, set out directly with ten thousand men as far as the city of Baurim. There they found King Baldwin, forewarned by an embassy, coming to meet them with a great force; for they feared to pass through the regions and cities of the gentiles without the escort of so renowned and powerful a new king.

Then, after resting with him during the night, they set out the next day with their forces united. Arriving at Joppa fifteen days before holy Easter, they remained there for eight days, including the solemn day of Palms itself. Thereafter, leaving Joppa on Palm Sunday, they went up to Jerusalem. They remained there seven days [Col. 0625A] and, awaiting the fire from heaven on Holy Saturday of Easter, visited the holy city with prayers and almsgiving.

Conrad the constable and Engelrad, bishop of Laon, being somewhat delayed, followed their brethren as far as Japhet; there they too joined the others at the Lord’s Easter.

### CHAPTER XLV.—After celebrating Easter at Jerusalem, the princes make peace between the emperor and the king.

Therefore, having assembled in Jerusalem from every place during this second week after Easter, and having splendidly and joyfully celebrated the holy festival with the king, they recalled the evils and dangers suffered by the pilgrims. They advised King Baldwin to urge the emperor of Constantinople, with the greatest humility in his power [Col. 0625B] and gentle entreaties, concerning the miseries of Christians: namely, that he should cease from the destruction and betrayal of Christians, aid the Church of Jerusalem, not heed Turks and Saracens, and not refuse fully and faithfully to provide every necessary supply from the garrisons and places of his realm as far as Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—A report spreads among the people that the Lombards were killed by the emperor’s design.

For a report circulated among the Catholic people that, by the emperor’s secret and treacherous counsels, the army of the Lombards had been led by Count Raymond and Turkish cavalrymen through the deserts, trackless places, and wildernesses of Flagania, so that it might there be easily overcome and killed by the Turks when exhausted by hunger and thirst [Col. 0625C].

But, as was reported by truthful and noble men, he was by no means to be blamed for this wicked crime. For he had repeatedly warned and instructed the army concerning the wildernesses, lack of provisions [Col. 0626A], and Turkish ambushes in the trackless country of Flagania, and therefore that they could not travel safely and securely by that route.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—Baldwin sends gifts to the emperor, who clears himself of treachery.

King Baldwin graciously accepted the counsel of all and sent to the emperor, as a gift, two tame lions which were especially dear to him, by Archbishop Gerhard and the bishop of Barcelona, in order to confirm their alliance and friendship. The emperor received favorably the king’s whole petition together with the gifts presented to him; and, taking an oath in God’s name concerning every suspicion of the slaughter of the Lombards which Christians entertained against him, he cleared himself. He promised henceforth to show mercy to all [Col. 0626B], and declared that he wished to honor and love King Baldwin.

During the same embassy, the emperor decreed that the bishop of Barcelona should clear him before Paschal, the Roman pontiff, of the betrayal laid to his charge.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—The emperor sends gifts to King Baldwin, but at Rome he is accused before the pope of his treachery.

A certain knight Engelrad, returning to Jerusalem, honored by the emperor with great gifts, brought good news: that the emperor wished to keep friendship and faith with King Baldwin and would no longer harm pilgrims. But the bishop resisted the emperor somewhat, because of his faithlessness toward the Franks, which he had wrung from him.

Accordingly, in bitterness of spirit he went to Rome and accused the emperor himself in the church at Benevento [Col. 0626C]. Therefore, after letters from that apostolic lord had been obtained, a grave complaint against the emperor was made among all the princes of Gaul.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0625]

### CHAPTER I.—How some Christian princes returned home, while others remained with the king at Jerusalem.

[Col. 0625C]

Afterward, as the gathering of Christians diminished day by day, some returning by ship and others scattering through different regions on their return journey [Col. 0625D], Conrad, constable of the emperor of the Romans; Albert of Blandraz; Stephen of Blois; Stephen, prince of Burgundy; Otto surnamed Altaspata; Arpinus of Buduordis; Hugh of Falckenberg; Hugh of Lezenais; Baldwin of Hestrut; Gutman of Brussels; Rudolf of the castle of Alos in Flanders; Hugh of Botuns; Gerbodo of the castle of Wintine; Rotger of Roscit; and very many other noble and distinguished men, who had then assembled from every place to celebrate holy Easter and had happily observed that holy time in all devotion and fullness of charity, remained with the king in the city of Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER II.—On the burning of the church of Saint George by the Babylonians, and the flight of Robert, bishop of the city of Ramla.

[Col. 0626C]

As the feast of holy Pentecost then approached and the body of Christians had been greatly reduced, some having returned by ship and others by land, an innumerable army of the king of Babylonia, larger than ever before, descended from Ascalon—some by ship, others over dry land on horseback and with abundant military equipment. They burned the church of Saint George, a mile from the city of Ramla, together with all whom they found in it fleeing before them with cattle and flocks. Moreover, they devastated the crops of the region—the pilgrims’ new labor and the hope of the entire year.

Robert, bishop of that city, a most Christian man, seeing so great an army suddenly fall upon the country with flames and plunder, and intending, after capturing Ramla, to descend upon the city of Jerusalem in order to assault its walls and besiege the king with the Christian people, immediately mounted his horse [Col. 0627A]. Escaping the enemy attack, he rode ahead to Jerusalem in order to inform the king how great an army had descended from Babylonia and how all the crops and neighboring places of the city of Ramla had already been consumed by flame and plunder.

### CHAPTER III.—King Baldwin gathers an army against the Babylonians.

Therefore the king, the entire household of Duke Godfrey, his brother, and the other nobles who still remained with him, hearing that so many thousands of adversaries had come to destroy the Catholic peoples, hurried to arms without delay. Already assembled and armored to the number of seven hundred, they advanced with the king against the enemy assaults, on the royal road, with trumpets, horns, and purple standards.

Scarcely had the king and his men emerged from the mountains of Jerusalem when, behold, in the valley and the broad plain of Ramla, hostile formations of Saracens, Arabs, and Azoparts approached with countless thousands of horsemen and foot-soldiers, intending by this force to recover Jerusalem and to overthrow the king and Christ’s faithful.

### CHAPTER IV.—King Baldwin engages the Babylonians; some of his leading men perish in the battle.

The king and all his following, seeing the enemy battle-lines stationed so near, laid aside every fear of death and took no thought for sparing their lives. Fiercely and in one accord they rushed through the midst of their enemies toward the thousands of them, penetrating the ranks by military strength and multiplying great slaughter with their weapons.

But while these seven hundred men—a small force indeed, yet outstanding and very brave knights—sought thus to penetrate by killing and breaking the enemy’s barriers, the intolerable people called Azoparts, placed among the midst of the thousands of gentiles, met the king and his men with clubs fashioned like hammers from iron and lead. Striking not only the knights but even their horses violently upon the head and other limbs, they drove them from the battle by heavy blows. Others, surrounding the distinguished men with arrows and slings, afflicted them without cease, like unending hail falling from heaven, until the king and all his men, unable to endure the force any longer, turned to flight.

Rudolf of Alos, Gerbodo of Wintino, Gerhard of Avennis, Godfrey the Short in stature, Stabulo, chamberlain of Duke Godfrey [Col. 0627D], Count Host of the castle of Rura, Hugh of Hamach of the land of Poitou, Hugh Botuns, Gerhard Barson, and all the rest perished among the enemy. Fifty of them fled toward Ramla and were admitted through the city gates. Lithard of Cambrai, Rotger of Roseit, Philip of Boulogne, Baldwin of Hestrut, Walter of Berga, Hugh of Burg, and Addo of Keresi fled toward Japhet, where ten thousand men met them, hastening to aid the king. But when they heard from these men of the king’s misfortune and of their own destruction, they returned in flight to the same city.

### CHAPTER V.—On the siege of Ramla and the flight or deliverance of King Baldwin.

Those men having been admitted into the city with the fugitive knights [Col. 0628A] and the gates shut, the Saracens pursuing them returned to their company and besieged the city of Ramla, pitching their camps on every side.

The king, despairing of life because of the city’s weakness, escaped through a breach in the wall with only Hugh of Brulis, who was staying at Gezela, and his attendant-at-arms, and fled toward the mountains of Jerusalem. Wandering all day and night, he traveled in vain, until the greater part of the Saracens met him as he wandered and made for Jerusalem. Flight through the mountains having been barred to him by them, he was grievously pressed by their pursuit and did not know where to begin wandering.

Understanding that he could not escape through the mountains, when the next morning had already dawned and he had recognized the road somewhat, the king withdrew toward the Christian city of Assur, though he was slightly wounded through his mail-shirt by the arrows of his pursuers [Col. 0628B]. He labored greatly day and night in mountains and trackless places until at last, standing in the open plain without rest, food, or fodder for his horse, he began to recall the region and its roads.

When morning came, he entered Assur. There Rorgius, who had received and held the city of Caiphas as a benefice, welcomed him with great joy, for he had thought that Baldwin had fallen with the others. Thus the king, having escaped the siege of Ramla and the hand of the Saracens, came to Assur. The others—Conrad, Arpinus, Stephen of Blois, Stephen of Burgundy, and other distinguished knights—entered a certain tower of the same city for protection.

### CHAPTER VI.—The Saracens storm the tower of Ramla, kill some Christian princes, and take Constable Conrad captive.

[Col. 0628C]

On the next day the Saracens, together with the Azoparts, having broken through the city walls with great force, began vigorously to batter and storm the tower itself with iron hooks and mattocks. At length, when the tower had been hollowed out, they kindled fire and smoke within it, so that the knights, pressed and suffocated by heat and smoke, might either perish or come forth.

But the outstanding knights chose rather to be consumed in honorable defense than to be suffocated and destroyed by a miserable death. On the third day, calling upon the name of Jesus and trusting in his grace, they came out and fought the Saracens fiercely face to face. With much bloodshed and slaughter among them, they avenged their own lives.

Conrad, incomparable in courage and strength, made great slaughter of the Saracens with his sword, until all who were present, astonished and terrified, stood far off from him and withheld their hands. They begged him to cease his dreadful killing and accept their right hands as a pledge that he might live, and so surrender to the king of Babylonia, until, when the king’s wrath was appeased, so famous and remarkable a knight might find favor in his eyes and, after imprisonment, receive rewards. And this was done.

Arpinus likewise was captured and spared, because truthful witnesses there made known that he had been a knight of the Greek emperor. All the others, together with Stephen and the other Stephen, the highest princes, were beheaded there.

### CHAPTER VII.—How the citizens of Jerusalem, terrified by King Baldwin’s flight, received consolation.

[Col. 0629A]

Meanwhile King Baldwin remained at Assur for these three days in order to learn the outcome of events. But this cruel report flew to Jerusalem, greatly terrifying all its inhabitants, and the whole city was turned to mourning and weeping. Indeed, the hearts of all were so dissolved by fear that they were preparing to leave the city by night and in darkness, unless a certain Gutman, born at Brussels, who had barely escaped, had brought them much consolation and repeatedly warned them not to leave the city hastily until they learned whether King Baldwin still survived.

At length, after a little while, news was brought that the king was still safe [Col. 0629B]. Hearing this, all rejoiced and took courage. Therefore, from then on, spreading themselves daily along the walls, they defended the city against Saracen attacks. The Saracens, in the pride of their victory, repeatedly assembled here in troops to provoke the Christian citizens.

### CHAPTER VIII.—With Constable Conrad imprisoned, the Babylonians terrorize the city of Japhet and King Baldwin’s wife with siege.

The others having been beheaded, while Conrad and Arpinus were received into the Saracens’ hands and sent as prisoners to the city of Ascalon, Meravis and all the powerful men of Babylonia advanced with great force and a strong hand toward the city of Japhet. With repeated assaults, engines, stone-throwing devices, military equipment [Col. 0629C], and attack, they harassed the men found in it.

Having cut off Gerbodo’s head and his legs, clad and shod in costly purple, they displayed them to the defenders of the city, asserting that they were those of King Baldwin because he resembled him. They urgently pressed the defenders to leave the city and come into the power of the king of Babylonia with sound limbs and life unharmed.

The Christians, believing it true and seeing the king’s head and legs displayed from afar, were seized with utter despair. They consulted together about departing with all their possessions and escaping by ship. During these days the queen, Baldwin’s wife, was in the city of Japhet itself; overwhelmed likewise by terror and grief at the death of her most beloved king, she too was considering flight with the others.

### CHAPTER IX.—King Baldwin arrives by ship at Japhet and is received joyfully by the citizens.

[Col. 0629D]

But after seven days had passed, the king left Assur, boarded a ship called a *buza*, and sailed with a few men to Japhet together with Goderic, a pirate from the kingdom of England. He raised and displayed in the air, toward the rays of the sun, a banner fixed upon a spear, so that the Christian citizens, recognizing this sign, might have confidence that their king lived and, not easily frightened by enemy threats, might not shamefully flee or be compelled to surrender the city. For he knew that they despaired greatly of his life and safety.

When the Saracens saw and recognized his signal, that division which was blockading the city by sea came against him with twenty galleys and thirteen vessels [Col. 0630A] commonly called *Cazh*, intending to surround the king’s *buza*. But, with God’s aid, as the sea’s waves swelled and resisted them from the opposite direction, while the king’s *buza* glided and flew easily and swiftly through the storms, it suddenly arrived in the harbor of Joppa, deceiving the enemies, after six Saracens had been struck and wounded with arrows from the ship.

When he entered the city and stood safe before the eyes of all, the spirit of all who had been grieving and mourning his death until then revived, because the head and king of the Christians and prince of Jerusalem had been received still alive and unharmed.

### CHAPTER X.—The Saracens briefly withdraw on learning that King Baldwin has returned, then renew the siege of Japhet.

[Col. 0630B]

The midday heat was already burning, and the king immediately mounted his horse and went out through the city gates with only six most distinguished knights, in order to provoke the surrounding Saracens and make it visible to all that he was still alive and safe.

When they learned that the king was alive and well, the whole multitude of gentiles removed their tents from Joppa and withdrew to the plains of Ascalon. They remained there for three weeks, until they learned whether any force was being increased for King Baldwin’s assistance. For the king had sent embassies throughout the castles, cities, and regions to all his brethren seeking aid.

But because Tancred, Raymond, and Baldwin of Bourg were too far away, they could not bring help at that time. The Saracens then came from Ascalon and renewed the siege around Japhet, until fifteen days had passed [Col. 0630C].

### CHAPTER XI.—On the Christian fleet.

Meanwhile, while this siege was under way, two hundred Christian ships arrived at Joppa in order to worship at Jerusalem. Bernard Witrazh of the land of Galicia, Hardin of England, Otto of Roges, and Hadewerck, one of the most powerful Westphalians, are reported to have been their leaders and commanders.

The Saracens who were blockading the city by sea on its upper side, seeing so many Christian battle-lines present, resolved to fight them in a naval assault. But the Christian ships, prevailing by sails and oars and by a more favorable wind through God’s mercy, strongly repelled the gentiles’ forces and came to rest on land. Joined by the citizens and the king himself as helpers, they entered the city; but the greater part remained encamped with tents pitched opposite in the open plain.

It was Tuesday in the month of July when these Christian forces, by God’s protection, came by sea to aid those distressed and besieged. But the Saracen troops, seeing that the Christian force boldly joined them face to face in a nearby camp, removed their tents in the middle of the night and settled more than a mile away, until at daybreak they might decide whether to return to Ascalon or harass the citizens of Japhet with repeated assaults.

### CHAPTER XII.—How King Baldwin, fighting the Saracens, overthrew three thousand of them.

[Col. 0631A]

From that Tuesday, while the Saracens remained unmoved in the pride and arrogance of their multitude and harassed the Christian people with many terrors of arms, when Friday approached King Baldwin left Japhet with trumpets and horns. With a strong force of horsemen and foot-soldiers, amid loud cries thundering on both sides, he attacked their strength in cruel battle.

The Christians who had arrived by ship likewise joined King Baldwin with dreadful shouts and loud clamor and fiercely attacked the Babylonians, afflicting them with most savage and deadly blows. Worn out by battle and unable to endure the force any longer, the Babylonians fled toward Ascalon [Col. 0631B]. Others, believing that they could escape their pursuers by entrusting themselves to the sea, were swallowed up by the intolerable heaving of the waves.

Thus the city of Joppa was freed with its inhabitants. Three thousand Saracens fell that day, while few Christians were found to have perished.

### CHAPTER XIII.—How Baldwin returned triumphantly to Jerusalem and, after the first slaughter of his men, obtained aid from Christian princes through envoys.

King Baldwin, therefore, having gloriously won triumph over his enemies, spent that night in Joppa with great joy, together with all the pilgrims who had assembled and possessed much spoil. When the next day dawned [Col. 0631C], he went to Jerusalem with all the pilgrims, ordering all things peacefully and powerfully and commanding that the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre at Jerusalem be opened to pilgrims so that they might worship Christ and fulfill their vows.

Before all this, when the aid of the new pilgrim army had not yet arrived, King Baldwin, anxious and greatly despairing because of the death of his men, sent an embassy to Tancred at Antioch and to Baldwin of Bourg in the city of Edessa. He asked them to hasten to his aid, declaring that otherwise he would soon lose the entire region of Syria and the kingdom at Jerusalem. He reported the Saracens’ audacity and stubborn victory, and how great a disaster his distinguished knights had recently suffered at the enemy’s hands.

They immediately gathered an army: Tancred in the territory around Antioch [Col. 0631D], and Baldwin at Edessa, with seven hundred horsemen and a thousand foot-soldiers. On the appointed day they met together at Antioch, taking with them Prince William of Poitou, who had recently, after the Lord’s Easter, returned to Tancred from Jerusalem after worshipping at the Lord’s tomb. They now descended through the valley of Damascus and Camolla, passed by Tiberias, and reached Caesarea of Cornelius, where they pitched their tents and spent the night.

In the morning they encamped by the river Assur, intending to lodge only one mile from Japhet. They had come down in the autumn season, in the month of September, when the abundance of every crop is usually overflowing.

### CHAPTER XIV.—How King Baldwin, supplying necessities to the arriving princes, consented to their intercession for Patriarch Dagobert.

[Col. 0632A]

King Baldwin, then staying in the city of Japhet and learning of the arrival of such brave men, appointed distinguished messengers to meet them and provide all necessities of life—bread, meat, wine, oil, and barley—to refresh the knights and their horses, weary from the long journey.

Dagobert, rejected by the same king, was in the company of these distinguished men. Believing that he would recover the patriarchal dignity, he intended to descend to Japhet with Tancred. Therefore Tancred, Baldwin of Bourg, Count William of Poitou, and William the Carpenter [Col. 0632B], having taken counsel about restoring the patriarch, sent an embassy to the king. They demanded that he restore the patriarch to his seat, declaring otherwise that they could not possibly go down to Ascalon to avenge their men.

Having heard this embassy, the king reluctantly consented to their entreaties, though he was greatly angered with the patriarch because money had been concealed.
