Nevertheless, overcome by the counsel of his men, he yielded to these mighty intercessors, on the condition that they should first descend upon Ascalon against the arms and soldiers of the king of Babylonia; afterward, he would deal with every matter concerning the patriarch by equitable judgment and with their counsel.

He also decreed that all these matters should be done under the examination of Robert, a Parisian cardinal, bishop, and legate. After the death of Maurice some time before, Robert had been sent by Paschal, Roman pontiff [Col. 0632C], to investigate and correct unlawful matters of the holy Eastern Church in these eastern lands.

### CHAPTER XV.—How King Baldwin, with the princes whom he had received, besieged Ascalon and killed the Babylonian emir in battle.

Tancred, Baldwin of Bourg, William, and the other William, having heard the king’s promise, advanced with him against Ascalon, under pledge of faith and in the strength of their arms and followers. For eight days they besieged its walls, devastated vineyards, crops, and all hope of that year, and repeatedly assaulted the walls.

At last, while they were raging there in repeated assaults and attacking the towers and walls, a most noble emir of the king of Babylonia, named Merdepas, who had remained to defend the citizens, suddenly burst out from the city with great force. With the sword and a hail of arrows, he attacked the Christian men among his followers. But by God’s grace and power he was swiftly killed and crushed by the Christians.

When Merdepas, the most renowned emir of the king of Babylonia, had thus been slain, all the gentile citizens of Ascalon were subdued and despaired of resisting further; they shut the gates in the Christians’ faces. Seeing that his men’s assaults and labors were in vain, the king withdrew, at the counsel of his leading men, from the city which seemed impregnable by human strength. He turned aside to Joppa with Tancred, Baldwin of Bourg, William, and the other William [Col. 0633A], where they feasted together in all glory and joy.

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the investiture of Patriarch Dagobert and the council held concerning him at Jerusalem.

Thereupon, after consultation had been held there with the bishops, abbots, and all the ordained clergy, and by the judgment of all the Fathers present, he was reinvested with every honor and dignity of which the king had deprived the patriarch, brought back to Jerusalem, and honorably restored to the episcopal chair. Thus, when Patriarch Dagobert had been brought back to Jerusalem and restored to the seat of his majesty, a council was appointed for the following day in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre. There suitable witnesses and accusers assembled in the presence and hearing of the lord cardinal and of the whole Church: Baldwin, bishop of the city of Caesarea; the bishop of Bethlehem; [Col. 0633B] Robert, bishop of Ramla; Arnulf, chancellor and archdeacon of the Lord’s Sepulchre; and many clerics.

There some accused him persistently and emphatically of simony; others of the murder of Greek Christians on the island of Cephalonia, committed by the Genoese at his instigation; others of betraying King Baldwin; and still others of concealing offerings and money given by the faithful. Present likewise at that council were Engilhard, bishop of Laon; similarly the bishop of Piacenza, the bishop of Tarsus, and the bishop of Mamistra; and other bishops and archbishops, reckoned at eighteen. The abbot of Saint Mary Latin, the abbot of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and the abbot of Mount Tabor were also present; and about six others from the land of France are reported to have sat there. [Col. 0633C]

## CHAPTER XVII.—On the deposition of the aforesaid patriarch and the appointment of Evermar in his place.

There, amid so great an assembly of distinguished men, while the aforesaid cardinal presided and examined the matter with impartial judgment, the patriarch, overcome and confounded by suitable witnesses concerning treachery and the other charges, fell silent. Since he proved rebellious and disobedient in making satisfaction to God and to the cardinal, and persisted obstinately in his perverse defence, he was deposed by the judgment of all the faithful and struck with anathema.

But Tancred and the other princes, seeing that the matter had reached its conclusion by the unalloyed judgment of truth, resisted no longer. Having taken leave of the king, they returned with him to the lands of Antioch and Edessa, taking with them the deposed patriarch, who, as they say, had been absolved at the entreaties [Col. 0633D] of so many magnates. The king himself remained at Jerusalem in great joy and glory. Without delay, by the counsel of the same Cardinal Robert and by election of the clergy and all the people, a certain Evermar, a man and cleric of good repute, renowned and cheerful in distributing alms, succeeded as patriarch in Dagobert’s office and place. With every zeal for religion and upright conduct, in brotherly love and charity, he served God there in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and was a faithful helper to King Baldwin against the Saracens and unbelievers.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—How, when the princes sailed home from Jerusalem with one hundred and forty thousand Christians, three hundred of their ships perished, partly through enemies and partly through the waves.

[Col. 0634A]

Accordingly, Tancred returned with the other princes, and more than one hundred and forty thousand pilgrim men who had assembled to worship at Jerusalem that year. Wearied by their long delay, they prepared ships with sails and oars; having taken leave of the king, they put out upon the high sea to return to the land of their birth, when the waters were calm and free from every violence and storm of winds.

But after they had scarcely sailed two days in calm weather, around the winter equinox the fair weather began to break up. Terrible winds arose; the ships were everywhere tossed by a violent tempest, hurled about and shattered by savage storms. At last the sailors and pilgrim men, exhausted and overwhelmed by swelling waves, were carried into the deep, some with their sails and oars destroyed; others, scattered by violent blasts of wind, were cast over an unknown sea and made wanderers, and reached Accaron. Others came to Sagitta, others to Ascalon—cities held by the gentiles—and were either captured, slaughtered, or drowned in the waters. [Col. 0634B]

There were three hundred ships of Christians that perished, and scarcely a tenth part of these is said to have been saved. When news of the disaster to so great a multitude was heard in Jerusalem, the king and all the men and women of the city gave themselves over to excessive mourning and lamentation, because so many thousands of their fellow brethren had been destroyed by so bitter a death, not only by the waves but also by the arms of the gentiles.

## CHAPTER XIX.—How, in the third year of his reign, King Baldwin besieged the city of Accaron, but by no means conquered it.

[Col. 0634C]

After this, in the third year of his reign, King Baldwin was greatly angered against the city of Accaron, because ambushes and attacks upon pilgrims had often issued from it. When winter’s severe cold had now passed away and the mildness of spring was breathing forth, after the octave of Easter of the preceding year—in which he had fought battles on the plains of Ramla and, after all his men had been shattered, had scarcely escaped the Saracens’ strength with a few remaining knights—he gathered an army of five thousand men and came to the walls of the aforesaid city.

Having laid siege to it on every side, he attacked it for five weeks with the discharge of mangonels and the height of siege engines, [Col. 0634D] so that the citizens, unable any longer to endure the force and the very frequent, grievous blows of soldiers and stones, were compelled to surrender the city into the king’s hand, having obtained their lives. For three Saracens had already gone out from the city—entirely unnoticed by the rest—to placate the king and obtain mercy for their lives. They reported to him every disaster and the loss of brave men and citizens, and that all within were so shaken by fear that, if he attacked the city strongly just once more, it would without doubt be delivered into the king’s hand with its gates opened.

The three had scarcely finished their speech and counsel with the king when, behold, at evening twelve galleys came down from Sur, that is Tyre, and from Tripla, that is Tripoli, cities of the kingdom of Babylon, carrying many armed knights and [Col. 0635A] one huge ship containing five hundred fighting men. All that night they entered the city and spread themselves through its walls and streets. Without delay, not waiting for daylight, they kindled a rapid fire with sulphur, oil, pitch, and tow and hurled it upon the king’s siege engines, so as to drive off from the city the men who were continually shooting arrows down from above and vigorously attacking it.

## CHAPTER XX.—How, when Reynold, the king’s archer, perished in the battle, the king himself withdrew from the siege of Accaron.

But when their arrival was known and fire was already repeatedly falling around the siege engine, a certain knight of the king, Reynold, highly skilled in archery and master of the archers, urged his companions to defend it. He himself took up a Balearic bow and struck down more than one hundred and [Col. 0635B] fifty Saracens with mortal wounds.

When morning came, the battle began to rage and grow fiercer on both sides. Saracen soldiers repeatedly burst forth from the gates and struck some of Christ’s pilgrims with lances, grievously wounding some and extinguishing others in sudden death. That same day, while Reynold carried on much fighting and slaughter against the enemy from the siege engine, standing too heedlessly and fearlessly in the open, a stone shot from a mangonel suddenly struck him upon the head. He died; by the king’s command his body was carried away and buried on Mount Tabor by religious monks.

The king, however, saw that the strength of the Saracens prevailed because of the intolerable multitude that had newly flocked by sea from the aforesaid [Col. 0635C] cities to assist this city, and because the force of his own men, burdened not only by battle but also by the long siege, was failing in its ability to resist. By the counsel of his magnates he ordered fire to be set to the siege engine, and, deeply troubled and grieving, withdrew, since he had been unable to achieve a favorable result at that time.

## CHAPTER XXI.—While King Baldwin devoted himself somewhat to hunting, he attacks sixty Saracens with ten companions.

In the same year in which the king left Acre unconquered and went up from Joppa to Jerusalem to rest there somewhat after suspending warfare, one day about the month of July he went hunting with only ten knights. As he entered the wooded highlands adjoining the city of Caesarea and occupied himself with this recreation, about sixty Saracens came down from Ascalon and Acre to lie in ambush for Christians, so that they might cut down and plunder those whom they caught either on the plain or in the highlands.

Then certain men of the Christian faith happened to meet them. Relying upon excessive boldness, the aforesaid gentiles resolved to pursue, kill, and despoil them, so that they might return to their cities in glory and victory with the spoils of the faithful. As the Saracens, with this cruel intention, followed the tracks of the Christians, and the entire region was stirred and terrified by reports of them, because their strength was thought greater than it was, King Baldwin—ignorant of all this and intent only on hunting—was informed that the Saracens had entered the region to ambush and slaughter the people of the living God, and that he ought therefore to come quickly to their aid in this emergency. [Col. 0636A]

On hearing this, he nobly urged the ten companions who were with him to pursue the enemy without delay and never permit them to leave the region unpunished, but to fight them bravely and recover the booty and plunder of their fellow brethren. Immediately forgetting the art of hunting, Otho Altaspata, Albert of Blandraz, and the others who had been hunting with the king—though unarmed with hauberk, shield, and lance, yet girded only with swords and carrying quivers, with all fear of death cast far away—spurred their horses and, following the Saracens’ track directly, chanced upon them already in view. Drawing arrows and swords, [Col. 0636B] they suddenly charged and fiercely joined battle on both sides.

## CHAPTER XXII.—King Baldwin is secretly wounded by a certain Saracen among the thickets, and, carried back to Jerusalem, is treated.

But King Baldwin, charging more fiercely than all the rest through the midst of the enemy and multiplying slaughter with his sword, unexpectedly came to a halt beside thickets in a low wood while his horse sped at full gallop. There a Saracen soldier, who had hidden among branches and shadowy leaves, pierced him with a concealed lance through thigh and loins.

Without delay, streams of blood poured heavily from the cruel wound of so mighty a king. His face began to grow pale, his spirit and strength to fail, and his hands to cease their sword-strokes, until at last he fell from his horse to the ground and was believed to have breathed his last, as though dead and slain. When his fellow knights saw this, they were immediately moved by immeasurable grief and began more fiercely and vigorously to kill and pursue the enemy, until some were killed and others scattered, turned to flight, and escaped through mountains and trackless places.

Thereafter they surrounded the king, weeping greatly, placed him upon a litter, and carried him to Jerusalem amid the extreme lamentation of men and women. They procured for him highly skilled physicians, by whose art and skill the king and mighty champion might recover from this mortal wound. [Col. 0636C]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—How the city of Joppa was besieged by the Babylonians, and how Christians arriving by ship fought against the Saracens.

[Col. 0636D]

When this wounding and grave illness of King Baldwin became known, the king of Babylon and Meravis gathered an army from all his realm and came down upon Joppa in a naval expedition. They anchored off the seaward side and besieged it. Meanwhile the men of Ascalon, coming by land at the king’s command to give assistance, joined in battle on both sides, from within and from without, and sought to conquer it by various assaults.

While this siege was underway and the citizens of Joppa and their Ascalonite enemies contended against one another in prolonged battles, two ships unexpectedly arrived with a company of Christians bound to worship in Jerusalem. One was the smaller vessel called a galley; the other, the larger one, was called a dromon. The larger ship, which contained more than five hundred men besides women, [Col. 0637A] approached secretly in the dark of night by sudden rowing, unnoticed by the army of the gentiles and having deceived the guards of the night watches; it came to rest in the harbor and on the shore of the city of Joppa.

But battered by the exceedingly violent and swift course and by the burden of goods and people, it split and gaped open and became embedded in the sand. When the Saracens saw it damaged by its difficult course and overly hasty flight, stuck in the mud of the sandy shore, they quickly came by ship to strike the shipwrecked people, plunder their goods and all necessities of life, and divide them among themselves.

But the Christians who were standing upon the very shore of Joppa, having gathered to see what would happen and to help the shipwrecked, saw their fellow Christians in danger. Resisting with vigorous attack, [Col. 0637B] they drove away the troublesome multitude, until, with God’s help and the gentiles repulsed, they prevailed in rescuing their brethren.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—On the other Christian ship, which suffered shipwreck and was wholly destroyed by the enemy.

The other, smaller ship did not cut the water under a true helm; rather, driven astray by an ignorant master, it rushed in blind night by sudden and easy course upon the enemy ships. When this was perceived, the ship’s master secretly escaped in a small boat with seven companions, leaving the ship abandoned among the enemy.

There were one hundred and fifty men on that ship, besides women; seven knights with their horses; and a great quantity of arms. When the gentiles perceived [Col. 0637C] that this Christian vessel had blundered into their midst, they encircled it on every side and throughout the night harassed its occupants with savage attack. The Christians, in turn, resisted bravely, until dawn. Then, unable to endure any longer the missiles and force of so many thousands, and ceasing to defend themselves, all were captured and beheaded with the seven knights and all the women, except only one squire, who by rash daring barely escaped by swimming amid the surging storms.

The enemy plundered all the spoils of those killed or drowned, divided them among themselves, and rejoiced and exulted that this fortunate chance of victory had so unexpectedly fallen into their hands.

## CHAPTER XXV.—How, upon Baldwin’s arrival, the Saracens abandoned the siege of Joppa, and both sides cultivated their fields.

[Col. 0637D]

But King Baldwin, learning of the long siege around Joppa and the destruction of his fellow brethren, had now recovered his health to some extent. He resolved to go down to Joppa, so that, once news of his arrival had been heard, the Saracens might be less able to frighten the Christian citizens and remain in the city’s siege.

The Saracens, however, hearing of the arrival and sound health of so mighty a king and believing that forces would be available to him, dared not remain there any longer. Taking advantage of the month of October and the winter season, when the storms of the sea rise more fiercely, they prepared their return without delay.

The king and the Christians of Joppa resolved to pursue them with swift boats and oars, if perhaps any sailing safely and slowly might be captured. [Col. 0638A] But at that time neither an opportunity nor any vengeance for the blood of their Christian brethren was granted. The king himself and all Christ’s faithful dwelling at Joppa rejoiced over all that had gloriously befallen them; encouraged, they slept securely and thereafter cultivated their fields and vineyards.

As the king recovered, the men of Ascalon dared less to harass the men of Joppa by war. They too enjoyed peace; and because the king’s force was free from war, they likewise rested, working diligently and unstintingly that year in crops and vineyards.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—How the city of Gibelet, conquered by the Pisans, was subjected to Count Raymond.

In the following year, as the season of March approached—namely, the fourth year of Baldwin’s reign—the Pisans and Genoese who had assembled at Jerusalem for worship again set out from Laodicea, where they had wintered, and arrived at Gibelet with a naval force. There Count Raymond met them from the city of Tortosa, seeking their assistance and strength to conquer Gibelet itself, so that, after the Saracen citizens had been driven out, the city might belong to Christians.

Readily yielding to his entreaties, they besieged the city with a great multitude of ships and attacked it vigorously. The count besieged it by land and battered it with repeated assaults and siege engines until it was taken and conquered, with its citizens, and delivered into Count Raymond’s hand and subjected to him. [Col. 0638B]

## CHAPTER XXVII.—The Pisans, summoned by the king’s entreaties, join him in harassing the city of Accaron by siege.

[Col. 0638C]

Not long after the capture of that city, an embassy of King Baldwin came to the Genoese and Pisans, conveying his abundant greetings. Then the king made a very earnest request of all of them: for the cause of God and the saints of Jerusalem, they should attack Ptolemais, now called Acre, by laying naval siege to it at sea; he himself, with God’s help and the forces of Christ’s faithful, would establish the siege on land.

Having heard the king’s request and exhortation, they all rejoiced and immediately came by ship and in strong force to Acre, or Accaron. The king encamped by land around the circuit of the walls. There, after making stone-throwers and siege engines for some days, they then attacked the city and its citizens everywhere, bravely and relentlessly, until the strength and hands of the Saracens were exhausted for resistance and they dared attempt nothing further. [Col. 0638D]

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—The amir of Accaron, counselling his citizens, resolves to deliver the city to King Baldwin; the king and patriarch deliberate concerning the besieged, who seek assurances.

When the amir of the city saw that his people had failed in their defence and, having no hope of help, no longer dared stand against the king’s power, he requested that peace and a suspension of war be granted, so that he might deliberate on how the city could be delivered into the king’s power while its citizens were saved.

At last, at the amir’s request, peace was established with pledges exchanged on both sides, [Col. 0639A] and the people ceased from every attack. Then the amir called together the whole assembly of Saracens and held an anxious consultation. Before all, he spoke in this manner:

> “For a long time we have defended this city even to the shedding of blood. But now we expect no help from our king of Babylon or from his cities, as was formerly customary, because of the harassment of the naval blockade. Therefore, if it were now agreeable to all our people, in this final extremity the city ought to be surrendered and opened to King Baldwin before we perish by his arms and, perishing, finally retain neither life nor city.
>
> “Accordingly, if my counsel appears useful and no sounder course can now be found, before the city is opened to him, let a treaty be established between us [Col. 0639B] and him, so that we may depart unharmed with our wives, children, and all our possessions, having everywhere a peaceful road without impediment or ambush from his men.”

All accepted this counsel of the amir, and it was immediately made known to the king: namely, that, with assurances pledged in good faith, peaceful departure should be given to the citizens, and that they would thereafter open the city gates and cease resisting the king. King Baldwin and Patriarch Evermar therefore consulted their men concerning this: if they opposed the citizens’ petition and denied them faith and covenant, and if the citizens feared to leave the city except in safety, the city could not be conquered without Christian death and danger.

They accordingly granted the petition on these terms: once the city was surrendered and opened, its people might depart peacefully with all their possessions and fear no danger. [Col. 0639C] But the Pisans and Genoese, inflamed by greed for the gentiles’ property, replied that this must not be done, so that the city’s riches and its incalculable treasures might be carried off peacefully.

At last, corrected and appeased by the king and the lord patriarch, they gave assent in all matters to what seemed more important for the Christians’ safety. Thus peace was promised and confirmed to the Saracens by the king’s oath, and the city and its gates were opened on that holy and celebrated day of the Lord’s Ascension.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—How the Pisans unjustly killed the Saracens as they left the city.

The king and his army entered the city. The leaders of the city and the other inhabitants departed peacefully [Col. 0639D] with their wives, children, livestock, and all their property. But the Pisans and Genoese, seeing them depart with all their household goods and their unheard-of wealth being carried away, were violently blinded by greed. Forgetting the faith and compact they had made with the king, they suddenly rushed through the middle of the city, killed the citizens, and seized gold, silver, purple cloths of various kinds, and many precious objects.

The people of Galilee, who had entered the city from the landward side with the king, saw the Pisans running through the city, killing citizens, and plundering unheard-of treasures. They too burned with the flames of greed and forgot their oath; they put about four thousand citizens to the sword, plundering their treasure, clothing, livestock, and all their countless riches.

When this unjust riot had finally been quieted, [Col. 0640A] the king was greatly angered at the injury done to him by the Pisans and Genoese, because of the oath. Therefore, lest it be believed that the pledged faith and covenant had been violated through his deceit and consent, he summoned his companions and household men and intended to punish this crime severely. But the lord patriarch intervened, repeatedly throwing himself at the king’s feet, and by prudent counsel made the king peaceful; he restored peace and concord on both sides.

## CHAPTER XXX.—On five hundred Arabs who attacked Joppa in battle and slew Otho.

In the same year after the capture of Ptolemais, also called Accaron and commonly Acre, when September was already half past, on the very day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, about five hundred Arab horsemen, armed and rising from Ascalon, came down upon Joppa. When the sun blazed at the middle of the sky, they stood before the city gate and attempted to challenge the Catholic knights to battle.

And behold, Otho Altaspata, nephew of Albert of Blandraz and a fearless young knight, with only the twenty men present to guard the city, put on helmet and took lance and met the five hundred horsemen. Challenging them in much mounted combat and rashly attacking their forces, they were at last mingled in the middle of the immense enemy host and could neither be drawn out nor return, until Otho, with five brethren, is said to have been killed there by the enemies’ weapons.

Immediately the Saracens and Arabs dismounted, cut off the heads of the slain, and carried them with them [Col. 0640C] to Ascalon as a token of victory, so that the sight might encourage the citizens to venture upon something further.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—On sixty Arabs plundering the city of Caesarea, whom King Baldwin defeated.

Scarcely seven days had passed after this when sixty Arab fighting men, desiring by some notable deed to win for themselves a name alike for glory and victory, set out for the city of Caesarea on the feast-day of the apostle and evangelist Matthew, in the hope that they might encounter some unwary Christians.

But no one met them. They therefore drove off cattle and sheep belonging to Christians, found grazing before the city walls, in order that Christians might leave the city and pursue them and thus be punished by hostile stratagem. As they carried away this booty, the Christian citizens of Caesarea, stirred by anger, went out from the city—nearly two hundred, with only one mounted knight. He had long been weakened by fever, had only slightly regained his health, and they pursued the Arab soldiers with bow, arrow, and lance in order to recover and bring back the plunder. [Col. 0640D]

The Arabs, resisting bravely and carrying off the booty, repeatedly drove the Christian foot-soldiers into flight. Indeed, they killed the still-ailing knight, who pressed them in close pursuit; they cut off his head and carried it away in the bags of their squires, in which they were accustomed to carry fodder for their horses.

Without delay, it was reported to King Baldwin, staying at Japhet or Joppa, that sixty Ascalonite soldiers had gone aside to plunder Caesarea. Having only forty knights with him, he sent thirty of them through the highlands, so that they might get ahead of every path by which he expected the enemy to return. He himself took ten men and set out by the direct route from Joppa to Caesarea, in case the aforesaid sixty soldiers should meet him, so that they might receive fitting recompense for the harm they had done Caesarea.

After the king and his men had travelled some distance, Arab squires and servants, sent ahead with the booty and the Christian knight’s head, met them, neither knowing the king nor being known by him. The sixty armed and mailed soldiers followed farther behind on the same road. The king and his men seized the squires and questioned them about the direction in which they were travelling; opening their packs, [Col. 0641B] they found in one man’s sack the head of a Christian knight.

When it was seen and recognized, the cruelty of the men of Ascalon was revealed. The king immediately compelled the captured squires, by threats and terror of punishments, to disclose the entire occurrence, threatening that, if they would not, he would punish them all there with a capital sentence. They at once declared that their masters were following them by the same road by which they themselves had come, and had intended to return through the highlands to Japhet.

On hearing this, the king immediately covered his breast with his shield, took up his lance, and with ten companions hastened along the road toward the enemy, fearing that some report might cause them to leave that route. Not far beyond, the sixty Arabs approached and carelessly charged upon the king and his men, suspecting neither the king nor any ambush there on the road. [Col. 0641C]

As they had so carelessly fallen into the king’s hands, the king struck his horse’s flanks hard and his men did no less. With a sudden shout and charge they attacked, burst through their midst, pierced some with lances, unhorsed others, and raged mercilessly in slaughtering them with the sword. At last, as the king’s strength prevailed and he penetrated and scattered the Arabs like straw, the enemies, unable to bear the weight of the combat any longer, turned their backs. Ten of them were captured and held, besides those who perished by arms. No fewer than forty of their horses were also taken, together with their arms and spoils, with which the king returned to Joppa in great glory and in vengeance for his beheaded knight.

From that day Japhet and all cities of the faithful that heard this rejoiced and were strengthened. Thus the king’s name was exalted throughout all the territories of the men of Ascalon and of all the gentiles, who greatly feared and marveled that the king, with ten companions, had in so successful an encounter crushed some of sixty Arabs and led others away captive. [Col. 0641D]

## CHAPTER XXXII.—How Raymond built a new fortress against Tripoli, in which he died and was buried.

At the same time and in the same year, Count Raymond gathered a force of Christian people from various places and realms and besieged the city of Tripoli, commonly called Tripla, for many days and years, seeking to conquer it by engines and arms. But while he laboured in vain for a long [Col. 0642A] time against it and its walls, he could not compel its surrender by the pressure of famine, because aid frequently came to it from Babylon, Ascalon, Sagitta, and Sur, while an abundance of supplies was available by sea.

Count Raymond therefore, after consultation with his men, decided to construct a new stronghold from which the city might always be assailed and to which his men might constantly return for protection from hostile attack. This stronghold was called the Mount of the Pilgrims, because there pilgrims and Christian knights would always have a defence against the strength of the gentiles.

But after two years had passed since the capture of Ptolemais and the building of this new stronghold called the Mount of the Pilgrims, the count died in February, after the Purification of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and was buried with Catholic rites in the same new fortress which he had built. [Col. 0642B]

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Where Emperor Alexius promised a large sum of money for Bohemond’s ransom.

Meanwhile, while the aforesaid prolonged business was being conducted concerning Acre, also called Ptolemais, over the redemption of its citizens and the surrender of the city, Emperor Alexius of Constantinople—who had always regarded Bohemond with suspicion, lest he expel him from the empire—repeatedly offered by embassies and letters a sum of two hundred and sixty thousand Byzantine coins to Donimanus, the mighty prince of the Turks. He sought to have Bohemond, prince of Sicily, whom Donimanus still held in chains, placed under his authority, wishing him to perish either in perpetual exile or everlasting condemnation, so that he might no longer harm the emperor’s realm [Col. 0642C] by any scheme.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—How Solyman, because of the money promised by the emperor, harassed Donimanus with war.

Solyman, formerly prince of the city of Nicaea, learned that the emperor was promising this immense sum of money for Bohemond’s ransom. By a cautious and private embassy of letters, he urged his fellow ruler Donimanus to make him a participant in so much money, because they had always been friends and companions in wars and in many plunderings. But Donimanus, coveting the whole weight of this treasure and wishing to keep it undivided, took up a crafty pretext and altogether refused to let this be done.

Solyman took this grievously. Breaking the friendship and alliance [Col. 0642D] that he had made with Donimanus, he began to oppose him with continual attacks and to lay waste what belonged to him. Indeed, having brought forces against him in battle for the third time and harassed him with many ambushes, he defeated him and put him to flight.

Thus Donimanus, assailed and humiliated by Solyman’s contrivance, began amid much lamentation and frequent sighs to recount this misfortune of his in the hearing of all his friends, in order that by their assistance he might obtain some revenge for the injuries done him.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Where Bohemond gave counsel concerning all these matters.

While Bohemond, still held in chains, gradually listened with a shrewd ear to these complaints of Donimanus, prince of the city of Nixandria, he began secretly to ask the guards and attendants what it was that made Donimanus, so great a prince, grieve, and why his entire household was now more troubled than usual.

At last, one day, when Donimanus learned that Bohemond had asked about his injuries and wrongs and had sighed deeply over them, he went down to the place of imprisonment where Bohemond was kept bound in iron chains. He recounted to him the ambushes and adversities that Solyman had inflicted upon him over the money offered to him by the emperor for Bohemond’s ransom, because he had refused Solyman a share of it. He knew Bohemond to be a shrewd man and an inventor of great counsels, so that, on hearing this, he might perhaps learn how to repay Solyman fittingly for his injuries.

Bohemond responded to him with the wisest counsel he could give concerning all that he had learned from him: [Col. 0643B]

> “From all these things that oppose you, you can take counsel sound enough to repay Solyman easily upon his own head for everything he has done to you and yours—if only you had not so rashly made an agreement with Emperor Alexius concerning this immense sum of money and my sale.”

Thereupon Donimanus, burning with intense concern for avenging his injury, more urgently begged Bohemond to teach him what counsel he judged sounder. Bohemond immediately replied:

> “If you are willing to refuse the emperor’s money, accept from me half of so great a sum, restore me to my former liberty, and free me wholly from these manacles on whatever terms may please you, I swear by my God that I shall bind myself to you with an inseparable bond of love and fidelity—and indeed all the Christian princes shall do likewise.
>
> “My friends and kinsmen, both those in Antioch and those in Rohas, and those dwelling in Jerusalem and in every place, shall join themselves to you under the same bond of faith, always taking counsel and acting for your honor and safety. [Col. 0643C]
>
> “But if you give more attention to the money offered you for my destruction than to the faith, friendship, and service of myself and my brethren, be certain that the money will diminish and be divided from day to day; and know that, so long as even one lives and prevails in these regions, the hatred, enmities, and harmful designs of my kinsmen and brethren can never be wanting against you and your land.
>
> “But if you give heed to me, to the service of my men, and to friendship; if you refuse the emperor’s money and receive from me what I have pledged, though it be a smaller sum, be certain of the friendship of all my brethren. Believe without doubt that their military service will always stand ready for you in all your affairs, in all faith and subjection. For, made allies and friends on both sides under oath, we shall easily conquer, by your strength and ours, not only Solyman himself, who thus lifts himself up and swells with pride against you and plans to injure you; we shall also subdue the land he holds once he is conquered and expelled. And we shall moreover bring the emperor’s realm and lands under our rule as soon as you determine.” [Col. 0643D]

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—Donimanus, having taken the counsel of his friends, restores Bohemund to liberty upon payment of the former ransom.

Donimanus, having heard and accepted these words and promises of Bohemund, [Col. 0644A] began, no little tossed in mind by conflicting considerations, to be troubled over what he ought first to choose and what to reject. He therefore gave him this reply:

“All that I have heard from your mouth is highly pleasing, if you fulfil what has been said by deeds of unbroken faith. But it is not fitting that I should give you my hand without the counsel of my own men. Therefore, after shortly taking counsel with them and laying before them your purpose and proposal, I shall either quickly do what you urge, or acquiesce in the counsels of my people—without, however, abandoning what is more advantageous.”

Then, after some days, counsel having been taken, all that Donimanus had heard from Bohemund and reported to his men was approved. Therefore they thought that his request and proposal ought no longer to be rejected, but that it should be carried out as beneficial and useful to all—on this fixed and firm condition, however: that each party, observing its own law [Col. 0644B] and profession, should preserve the friendship and treaty unimpaired.

This was accordingly done. Half the money which the emperor had promised was remitted to Bohemund, and permission was given for only one hundred thousand bezants to be paid and received. Once this had been settled and granted, Donimanus sent an embassy to the emperor declining the talent of gold which he had offered.

Bohemund, therefore, exceedingly rejoicing because, after enduring chains and imprisonment for two years, he had now, by God’s mercy, found favour in Donimanus’s eyes and very great leniency concerning his ransom, sent to all his kinsmen and friends, both to Antioch, to Rohas, and to Sicily, to collect money and bring it, once collected, on the appointed day to the territory of the city of Malatina, [Col. 0644C] where he was to be brought back and restored, and where peace and a treaty with Donimanus were also to be confirmed.

Immediately, all who heard of his ransom were filled with joy and exultation. Eagerly carrying out his command, they gathered and assembled, bringing to the aforesaid place on the appointed day money raised and made up from every quarter. There they found Donimanus and Bohemund, as had been decreed; they paid over the money itself, by number and weight, to Donimanus and his men; and, a treaty of friendship having been struck on both sides, they were reconciled to one another and made friends.

When this money had been received and stored by Donimanus’s private attendants and chamberlains, Bohemund, hands having been pledged and commended in a bond of highest affection, was sent back free from every obligation, with his men, to Antioch. There he was received, honoured, and brought in with no small rejoicing by all the fellow-Christian citizens.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—Solyman, because of Bohemund’s ransom, sends hostile letters to Donimanus.

When Solyman learned this, he took it very ill because he had been unable to share in the money. Speaking therefore against Donimanus, he stirred up the Soldan, king of Corrozan and Baldach—which is a city and the capital of the Turkish kingdom—with all the princes of the gentiles, to oppose him and deprive him thereafter of the king’s aid and favour. For, without the king’s knowledge, he had released Bohemund: a warlike man, so astute in every matter of war, and one who always plotted evil and snares against the Turks and the kingdom [Col. 0645A] of the Turks and Greeks.

Not long after these malicious embassies, prompted by Solyman’s accusation, had been sent to the king of the Turks, the king’s anger and the indignation of all the Turkish magnates reached Donimanus’s ears. They terrified him and his men with various threats and greatly troubled them. One day Solyman wrote a letter in these terms:

“Donimanus, brother and son of the Turkish people: until now you have been a distinguished man, acceptable to the king and to the whole kingdom of the Turks because of the wars and victories which you have achieved. But behold, your name has been greatly diminished; and now you have become utterly despised before the king of Corrozan and your whole nation, hated by all, because you allowed Bohemund to be ransomed [Col. 0645B] so cheaply and considered our counsel in this agreement and ransom as worthless and of no account.

“But if you wish to amend that disgrace and appease the king’s wrath and that of the great men of Corrozan, summon that same Bohemund—whom we regard as more dangerous than all other Christians—to the place which I shall designate, as though for assistance; and then, when our ambush has been laid, he shall suddenly be surrounded and seized. Otherwise, know that you will never recover the king’s favour, nor escape the hands and wrath of the Turks.”

Donimanus by no means consented, lest his own good faith and that of all Turks should appear cheap in the eyes of Christians and the other gentiles.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—After Bohemund’s return to Antioch, the Turks attempt to besiege the city of Rohas.

After this, in the same year in which Ptolemais, or Acre, was captured, [Col. 0645C] in the month of May, Bohemund returned to Antioch from exile and chains. Geigremich, a great prince of the Turks, kinsman of Corbahan and brother of Sochoman—who, after unjustly invading the kingdom of Jerusalem, had now lost it through the power of the king of Babylon, and at the first arrival of the Christian army had fled to Damascus to be protected there by the Turks—was one of the most powerful men of the kingdom of Corrozan. Having assembled an army of sixty thousand Turks, he advanced in great pride and strength to besiege the walls and fortifications of the city of Rohas, which is also called Edessa.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—Count Baldwin, Bohemund, and Tancred, confessing their sins, assemble an army and draw up battle lines against the Turks.

Baldwin of Burg, the prince of that city, appointed by King Baldwin, was alarmed by the arrival and sudden report [Col. 0645D] of this immeasurable multitude. He summoned and disposed for the defence of the walls all who were with him in the gathering of paid troops. Moreover, leaving the city, he sent an embassy inviting Bohemund and Tancred to bring aid and increase his strength, begging and entreating them in the Lord’s name not to permit Turkish pride to prevail over their Christian brethren.

When this embassy had been received, a force was immediately collected from all the places and castles of Antioch: about three thousand cavalry and seven thousand infantry came to the appointed place, namely the plains of the city of Aran or Caran, where Baldwin awaited their arrival with all the people whom he had assembled. There an Arab informed Count Baldwin, Bohemund, and Tancred that that Turkish host was hastening to approach and besiege the walls and storm the defences of the city of Rohas. On hearing this news of so many enemies coming upon them, they moved their camp and all their equipment to the river Cobar, which flows in its channel from the regions of the kingdom of Babylon as far as these parts. There, after pitching their tents, they are said to have spent the night upon the riverbank.

Then, at first dawn, they broke camp and took their stand upon the plain of the city of Racha. There they confessed before the patriarch of Antioch and Benedict, bishop of the city of Rohas, all their sins and offences; they restored every discord to charity; and, forming twenty battle lines, they deployed on the right [Col. 0646B] and left to resist the enemy, aid their Christian companions, and thus more lightly bear the burden of war.

The battle lines had scarcely been drawn up when, behold, Sochoman, on the right wing with thirty thousand brave fighting men and archers, approached to give battle with bold onset and the dreadful din of trumpets. Bohemund, Tancred, and all the knighthood of Antioch no less promptly hurried to meet him face to face, armed with cuirass and helmet and a shield-wall, shouting stoutly amid trumpets and horns.

On the left Baldwin of Burg and Gozelin of Cortona—who held Turbaysel as a benefice granted by Baldwin himself—met them in armour, with lances, swords, and swiftest horses. From both sides they loudly sounded trumpets and horns and joined battle. Bohemund and Tancred, fighting the enemy on the right wing, by God’s mercy began to prevail, attack, and lay low the enemy, until their strength failed and they took to flight. Five hundred Turkish soldiers fell in the battle conducted by Bohemund on the right; nearly two hundred Christians were slain.

Baldwin of Burg, Gozelin of Cortona, and the other distinguished knights, stationed with their battle line more than a mile from Bohemund, heard that Bohemund and Tancred had already engaged and were prevailing. Eager to join and mingle with the line of Bohemund and Tancred in support, they attempted at full speed to break through and crush the dense, opposing ranks of the enemy. But suddenly ten thousand Turks rose from ambush [Col. 0646D] and fiercely confronted them with bow and arrows, attacking them heavily and piercing them with arrows until the whole force was turned to flight. Some were captured and killed, while many others were carried away into everlasting exile.

### CHAPTER XL.—On the beheading of eighteen clerics and the capture of Count Baldwin, prince of Rohas.

In this most cruel rout, eighteen clerics and three monks, who had assembled to strengthen Christ’s soldiers with spiritual weapons, were beheaded. Bishop Benedict was captured and carried off. Indeed Baldwin himself, prince of Rohas, excessively eager for slaughter and advancing rashly, without opportunely awaiting Bohemund’s victorious standards, was defeated, [Col. 0647A] captured, and carried away.

Tancred, descending gloriously from the immediate Turkish slaughter but dismayed by the disastrous news, flew at once with his men to pursue the Turks, now victorious through the slaughter of Baldwin and his followers, in order to rescue the captives. But they escaped by their hasty flight. Only the bishop, with merely three knights, was freed and brought back.

At last, as night drew on and day was already departing, Bohemund and Tancred returned to their camp with all their company, to restore limbs exhausted that day by the immense burden of war.

### CHAPTER XLI.—Bohemund and Tancred flee after Baldwin’s capture, and Tancred is appointed in Baldwin’s place.

Then, at the first cockcrow, when Baldwin’s absence was discovered, they were seized by sudden fear and all hurried in swift flight to the city of Rohas, so that they might arrive beforehand to defend the walls and fortifications, lest the city be surrendered to the Turks, advancing in the wake of their victory.

But the citizens of Rohas, themselves Christians, hearing of the misfortune and destruction of their men and of the carrying away of so great a prince, were turned to lamentation and mourning; yet they were greatly comforted in their protection of all the Christian soldiers. For that day was the most celebrated Sunday festival for the Christian people.

When the following day dawned, the Armenian citizens of that city, after taking counsel with all who had assembled to lament so illustrious a prince, installed Tancred in Baldwin’s place, until such time as they might see whether Baldwin could be ransomed or freed. Bohemund then returned with his men to Antioch, Tancred having thus been established in Baldwin’s place to hold the city and its principality. [Col. 0647C]

### CHAPTER XLII.—The Turks surround the city of Rohas with a siege, and Tancred resists them as best he can.

After this, eight days having passed, while Tancred maintained the garrison of Rohas and its walls by vigilant guard, Geigremich and his men, exulting in the success of their victory and Baldwin’s capture and hoping to attempt still greater things, became exceedingly enraged against Tancred. They believed that they could now easily drive Tancred and his lordship from the city of Rohas and exterminate all the power of the Franks. Therefore, from every place and throughout the kingdom of the Turks, they assembled forces far greater than before. With these, in a strong hand, they descended into the plain of Rohas [Col. 0647D] to besiege its gates and walls, pitching their tents over a wide area.

When he saw so many thousands, so many tents, and so many varied armaments of the enemy, Tancred began to be deeply troubled, because he had only a small force of Frankish soldiers with which to meet and resist the united and countless Turkish legions. Taking counsel, therefore, he secured the city with a faithful guard; and, encouraging the citizens, he promised without long delay to engage these hostile bands and act bravely.

Understanding his comforting words and perceiving him to be a man of great confidence and boldness, all the citizens and soldiers of the city spread out over the walls and fortifications, met and repelled the enemy from afar, and did not delay to secure the bars and gates with every possible care.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—Tancred sends letters to Bohemund for the rescue of Rohas; Bohemund hastens to him with three hundred men.

[Col. 0648A]

But while battles were long joined on both sides, Tancred, a man shrewd in every military undertaking, secretly sent an embassy to Antioch in these terms:

“To his lord and uncle Bohemund, the magnificent prince of Antioch appointed by God: Tancred wishes prosperity and life.

“Since you departed from us and set me as guardian and defender of the city of Rohas in the place of our faithful brother Baldwin, Geigremich and Sochoman, having reassembled their strength and forces, have occupied the city of Rohas and its walls in a sudden siege. Their purpose is to storm the towers and fortifications, slaughter the citizens and plunder the city, and to take me captive, as they did Baldwin, [Col. 0648B] and carry me away among barbarous nations.

“Therefore, mindful of the charity which you have always shown toward Christ’s faithful, we have resolved to make known to you our tribulations and dangers, so that, understanding our evils and distress, you may swiftly summon companions and friends from Antioch and the other places and hasten along the way to relieve us, besieged and oppressed; diminish the Turks’ threats and boasting; and, in Christ’s name, drive them from the present siege.

“For you ought to consider that we are few in this land of pilgrimage. Thus there is no reason why, from any weariness of labours or wars, we should easily fail against enemies who watch with every care and diligence to conquer and destroy us. Rather, bearing one another’s burdens always, in season and out of season, let us endure as one and advance as one, patiently bearing adversity [Col. 0648C] and prosperity alike. But if sloth should seize us, or if some resentment delay us or make us negligent in aiding our brethren, I see nothing more advantageous than that we should leave the land and yield to enemies who rise up against us without ceasing. For it is evident that, being few, if we are divided, overcome by weariness, and fail, we cannot live and stand against the strength of our enemies.”

Hearing this, Bohemund hastily gathered three hundred horsemen and five hundred foot soldiers and set out to liberate his nephew and the Catholic inhabitants of the city of Rohas. Yet, because of the difficulty of the terrain and mountains, or the seven days’ journey, he seemed to delay greatly for those suffering daily assaults and attacks from the Turks.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—Before Bohemund arrived, Tancred at sunrise puts the Turkish camp and all its forces to flight.

Accordingly, while Tancred, the brethren, and the citizens waited for him day after day with many sighs, but Bohemund did not come at the hoped-for time and they utterly despaired, they unanimously vowed that they would rather die than be carried into exile in Corrozan and cruelly tortured by the impious with diverse punishments.

And behold: the citizens and soldiers assembled together and resolved upon battle. At the first dawn they would march out from the city in arms and companies, hasten silently to the camp, and, when close, loudly sound trumpets and horns; then they would suddenly attack the enemy, still weighed down by sleep and [Col. 0649A] sleeping securely and unsuspectingly. Thus, unable to rush to arms, the enemy would be cut down in the swiftest slaughter.

Carrying out what had been resolved, they marched from the city as soon as first light rose, equipped with every armour and strength at their command. With sudden crashing noise and a mighty shout they attacked the enemy camp, striking with the sword’s edge men still overcome by the previous day’s wine and wholly off their guard, until the plain before them was flooded with corpses and streams of blood.

As more of the day passed, Tancred’s force and power began increasingly to prevail, and a more terrible fear seized the enemy. Terrified by the excessive slaughter, they were driven into flight as far as the tents of the army commanders. At length Geigremich and Sochoman, seeing [Col. 0649B] all their camp crushed and turned to flight, scarcely mounted their horses with all those who had camped beside them, abandoned all their tents along with their other possessions, spoils, and pay, and hastened in flight, Tancred continually pursuing them by many routes.

### CHAPTER XLV.—When Bohemund encountered the fleeing Turks, a most noble lady was captured by Tancred’s companions.

The enemy having thus been scattered and made fugitives, and Tancred constantly cutting them down from behind, Bohemund, by God’s will and mercy, encountered the fugitives that same day with all his company. He knew that they had strongly occupied the plain during the night, but he was wholly ignorant that Tancred had fought them in so early a battle.

Now, however, like a prudent man skilled in warfare, when he understood that Turkish pride and strength had ebbed away and that they contemplated nothing but flight, he greatly rejoiced to see the victorious standards of the Christians pursuing them with loud cries. Joining his own strength and forces with theirs, he too pursued the fugitives and is said to have laboured without respite throughout the whole day in killing and capturing them.

In this rout and grievous crushing of the Turks, Geigremich and Sochoman barely escaped with a few men. But a most noble lady of the kingdom of Corrozan, who had furnished no small equipment, aid, and strength, was captured and held there by Tancred and his companions. Then, after this victory had thus been won through the mercy of God and the Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0649D] Bohemund, Tancred, and all the Christian soldiers peacefully took abundant Turkish spoils, with which they entered the city of Rohas in great joy and glory.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—How the Turkish princes and King Baldwin interceded with Bohemund and Tancred for the lady, and what they replied.

After several days had passed, an embassy from Geigremich and the powerful men of the kingdom of Corrozan approached Bohemund and Tancred in the city of Rohas concerning the lady’s ransom. They requested that Baldwin of Burg, whom they held in prison, be released in exchange for her restoration, or that fifteen thousand bezants should be sent by them for her return.

When Geigremich’s embassy and the capture of so noble a lady had been reported as far as Jerusalem, King Baldwin sent a humble embassy with many prayers, asking Bohemund and Tancred to restore Baldwin, their brother and prince of Rohas, by restoring the captured lady, and declaring that no money ought to be considered good or desired before this.

They graciously answered the king’s request in these terms:

“To their lord Baldwin, most Christian king of Jerusalem: Bohemund and Tancred offer unceasing service. We have resolved gladly to obey all your commands concerning the ransom of Baldwin, our friend and companion; this has always been and remains our concern. But at present it is necessary to conceal and suppress this matter in silence, if perhaps we may extort some money, to be delivered with Brother Baldwin himself in exchange for this lady; for we are in very pressing need of it [Col. 0650B] to reward the soldiers who labour unceasingly with us.”

Their reply was thus smooth and fair enough; but it contained neither good faith nor truth, nor any desire to ransom the man, because of their ambition for the city and its revenues. These, through its various business transactions and exchanges conducted solely within its walls, were reckoned at forty thousand bezants annually, apart from the revenues furnished by the many castles and districts belonging to the same city.

Thus satisfying the king with a friendly reply and promise, Bohemund returned to Antioch, while Tancred remained to guard and fortify the city of Rohas.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—How, after Bohemund departed for Italy against the Greek emperor, Tancred defeated the Turks in battle.

In the following year after the capture of Baldwin of Burg, and in the fifth year of King Baldwin, Bohemund departed not only for Italy but also for Gaul, seeking forces and stirring up princes against Alexius, king of the Greeks. Tancred was left at Antioch in his uncle’s place to guard the city, while Tancred’s authority was established at Rohas.

Brodoan, the magnificent prince of the city of Aleppo and brother of the Turks, seized this opportunity. Treacherously withdrawing from Tancred’s friendship and treaty, he heavily plundered the places and cities dependent upon Antioch. Moreover, after driving out the bishop of the city of Albariæ [Col. 0650D] and destroying many churches of God, he could not be satisfied even with this plunder and slaughter. At last, bringing forth from his land ten thousand cavalry and twenty thousand infantry, he advanced in great pride and boasting to attack the city of Antioch and overcome Tancred.

When Tancred learned that Brodoan’s intolerable and numerous strength and army had grown, he and his men were greatly frightened. Nevertheless, without delay he sent messengers to Turbaysel, Rohas, and Maresch, summoning to assistance all the Catholic men in the surrounding region and appointing their assembly at Antioch.

When they had gathered to the number of one thousand cavalry and nine thousand infantry, the bishop addressed them all, exhorting them not to doubt because of the multitude of their enemies, but confidently to resist in God’s name and strength, certain of victory with God’s help. After a three-day fast had been proclaimed and completed at the pontiff’s exhortation, Tancred descended with ten thousand cavalry and infantry as far as the bridge of Farfar, where they stayed overnight.

At dawn on the following day, Tancred and his men, having formed their battle lines and raised their standards, advanced toward Artesia in cuirasses, with shields and lances. There Brodoan, with countless cavalry and equipment, had occupied the entire country. On learning of the Christians’ arrival and that of their prince Tancred, he ordered battle lines and wedges to be formed; and at the third hour of the day battle was joined on both sides.

As the battle continued, with excessive sword-slaughter until the ninth hour, by the help of the Lord Jesus the Christian battle lines stood unconquered; the gentiles’ lines, however, were shattered, scattered, and alike turned to flight. Tancred and his men pursued them, killing some and taking others captive and bound, together with the spoils of their arms and horses. On the following day, after taking and distributing the spoils and arms of the enemy, Tancred returned to Antioch in great glory and joy of victory. All Christ’s faithful and the citizens of Antioch rejoiced greatly together with their lord patriarch and the bishop of that city, giving thanks to God and the Lord Jesus Christ, by whose mercy and protection so Catholic a prince, saved from the enemy multitude, triumphed.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the preparation for war between King Baldwin and the admiral of the Babylonians.

[Col. 0651C]

In the second year after the capture of the city of Acre, a great force and armament of the king of Babylon advanced by sea and land in the month of August, in order to besiege the city of Japhet, or Joppa, and storm it from the naval force. On the plains near the city of Ascalon they encamped, intending to invade the region suddenly from land and sea on both sides and thus more easily overcome King Baldwin and his men unexpectedly.

King Baldwin was then staying at Japhet. As soon as he saw the naval army, he understood the Babylonians’ stratagems and devices: they had occupied the city from the seaward side so that, while the king and his men were struggling and occupied in defending it against them from the water, the remaining gentile forces might rush in from the plains of Ascalon and suddenly storm Japhet.

But the king, recognizing their fraud and learning that their force had lain in the plains of Ascalon for three weeks, did not fail to keep their approach and intended attack upon Japhet secret and undisclosed, nor did he cease to summon allies and collect arms, so that throughout that whole interval he might remain prepared and fortified and, on whatever day they descended, be able to run to meet them with his own forces.

Hugh of Tiberias, Rorgius of Caiphas, Gunfrid of the Tower of David, Hugh of Saint Abraham, Eustace Granarius, Gutman of Brussels, a castle of Brabant, Lithard of the city of Cambrai in Gaul, Pisellus of Tournai, and Baldwin of Hastrut, castles of Flanders—[Col. 0652A] all these, summoned by the king to provide aid, gathered with forces of Christian cavalry and infantry collected from every side.

There was also in the king’s company a valiant young Turk named Mahumet, armed and attended by one hundred Turkish archers. Through the avarice and contrivance of his stepfather, he had been driven from his paternal seat and from the land of Damascus; he had now entered into a treaty with the king, that he might be faithful and ready to him in every military assistance.

When the Saracen legions saw that their frauds and ambushes had become known to the king, and that he had foreseen them and gathered the Christian force from every quarter for aid, they moved camp from the plains of Ascalon and advanced, in the pride of their multitude, as far as the place called Abilin.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—After summoning the patriarch of Jerusalem, King Baldwin, strengthened in the Lord, triumphs over the Babylonians.

When the king perceived their arrival and knew beyond doubt that they had already drawn near, he sent an embassy to the lord patriarch in Jerusalem, asking him without delay to summon a body of the faithful and hasten to increase his strength and provide aid against the enemy.

On hearing the king’s message, the patriarch gathered one hundred and fifty infantrymen, equipped them with arms, and set out toward Rames, as had been arranged for him by the king’s command. After this the king and all the faithful gathered for the business of war, fortified by communion in the Lord’s body and blood, marched out from the city of Japhet on Friday, six thousand strong. Lithard of Cambrai, because he was prudent and faithful, was left in the city with three hundred men against the naval force.

The king descended with all his company and standards to Rames, where he stayed on Saturday awaiting Lord Evermerus, patriarch, with all the force of Jerusalem. When the patriarch and the other faithful from Jerusalem had already arrived, at the dawn of Sunday the king arranged five [battle divisions; the source is defective] from the cavalry and infantry to engage the enemy. The king himself remained undaunted in the rearmost line among the horsemen, to strengthen and exhort his men. Only a small number of horsemen, namely one hundred and sixty, stood about him—nor is it surprising that they were few, because horses continually failed in this land.

When the king had made these arrangements, and all Christians had been blessed with the sign of the Holy Cross by the lord patriarch, standards and banners were raised, trumpets and horns sounded without cease, and the king and his men prepared to advance against the enemy camp, so that by anticipating battle they might no longer allow the troops of the unbelievers to advance with impunity.

The gentiles likewise, learning that the king was now so near with his forces, marched from their camp armed, with standards and horses and an intolerable shrieking of trumpets. They came to meet them in a great multitude of forty thousand, no less eager themselves to join battle. Thus, when the two armies appeared upon the plain, trumpets sounded mightily on both sides, [Col. 0653A] and the hosts of Christians and unbelievers fought fiercely from the first morning of Sunday—the last day of August—until the ninth hour. Then, weakened by God’s grace and mercy, the Saracens took flight from the Christians who were cutting them down and pursuing them, and hastened to retreat into Ascalon.

### CHAPTER L.—On the slaughter of seven thousand gentiles and on Count William.

In that battle seven thousand gentiles fell, and the admiral of Ascalon also fell. The admiral of Acre and the admiral of Assur, who had obtained their lives from the king and surrendered their cities, then fled to Ascalon before that year; they were captured with all their possessions.

King Baldwin, having received this victory through the help of God and the Lord Jesus Christ, entered Joppa in great glory with all the spoils of his enemies. Of his own company only one hundred perished, including the distinguished knight Reinard of Verdun, whom the king and the whole Church mourned with great lamentation, rendering him Catholic funeral rites.

The naval force was stationed beside the city. Expecting their own side’s victory and the rout and destruction of the pilgrims, they had vowed to burst suddenly into the city. But when they saw the severed head of the admiral and chief man of Ascalon, and learned of the flight and slaughter of the men of Ascalon and Babylon, they departed sorrowful and despairing from their station off the city of Japhet, rowing swiftly away. They sailed to Tripla in hope of refuge and spent the night there; at dawn they sailed back to Ascalon and Babylon. [Col. 0653C]

Count William of Sartengis, after the death of Count Raymond, his uncle, had succeeded by hereditary right to the land and cities of Camolla. After his uncle’s death, he was then vigorously attacking the same city of Tripla, or Tripoli, from the new fortress called the Mount of the Pilgrims, which Raymond himself had strongly fortified. Yet he could neither oppose nor hinder this naval force, sheltered at Tripla, because of its confidence in the water and the unbearable multitude of the city’s people, who always streamed to their aid on the shore. Nevertheless, with persistent effort and attack, the count tried to impede their return, at one time by artillerymen, at another by archers; but, trusting in the abundant waters, they reached Ascalon safely and powerfully, without opposition or harm.

### CHAPTER LI.—How King Baldwin, having defeated the Babylonians, burned the crops of Ascalon, while the army was alarmed by the cries of wild beasts of the forests.

After the battle and victory which the king won at Abilin, between Ascalon and Rames, the king’s land was quiet, and great fear shook the hearts of the men of Ascalon and Babylon. For they had so often been defeated, fallen, and fled before the king’s small force that they no longer had any hope of resisting or surviving before him.

While they sat in this grief and despair, however, and rested for the course of eight months, cultivated their vineyards, rejoiced that the king sometimes ceased from arms, and eagerly sought to placate him with mutual peace and gifts—all attempting this in vain unless they surrendered the city of Ascalon into his hands—the spring months passed, when crops, fruits, vineyards, and every hope of the year put forth flower and fruit and promise the coming harvest near at hand.

When all these things appeared in abundance and fullness, and all the fields of Ascalon were now hastening toward harvest, the king gathered plentiful soldiers and arms from Jerusalem and every place giving him assistance. During Rogationtide, when in those regions all crops quickly ripen for harvest, he occupied the land of the men of Ascalon, cutting down vineyards, fig trees, and trees of every kind with a strong hand. Indeed, he burned with fire the crops which did not suffice as fodder for horses, camels, [Col. 0654B] and the other herds, so that even by this irreversible loss a hard and unconquerable people might at least be softened to bow their necks.

Thus, after the whole region had been devastated not only by plundering hands but also by fire, the king prepared to return to Jerusalem with part of his army. All who were in his company proceeded by the mountain route, sounding with an immense blare of trumpets and horns and shaking every mountain and valley through which they were to pass in their strength with no small terror.

At this incalculable noise of so great an army, many wild beasts, startled and frightened from their dens and mountain wildernesses, wandered here and there in unfamiliar deviation from their paths. Nor was this surprising: even birds in flight could not endure the uproar of the shouting crowd, but, stunned by the loud cries, fell from the air into the midst of the multitude, failing in flight.

Thus, while diverse frightened beasts wandered from their dens and marvelled at this unheard-of clamour, it happened by unhappy chance that a timid little doe came down from the mountains and, in blind bewilderment, hastened in flight among the people. As soon as the foremost of the army saw her, they pressed hard upon her from every side with the speed of their horses—some seeking to seize her first, others to share in the hunt. [Col. 0654C]

### CHAPTER LII.—On Arnolf, a most noble youth slain in the mountains, whose head the men of Ascalon sent back with letters to King Baldwin.

While, among these men, the squire of the most noble young man Arnulf, a worthy knight and lord of the castle of Aldenardis, [Col. 0654D] pressed hard upon this beast as it hastened toward the mountains and eagerly strove to overtake it, the girths of his horse broke amid the same exertion of the chase; and thus, falling from the horse, he was thrown to the ground and ceased from the pursuit. But the horse, startled by the noise of the shouting crowd about it, rushed at an uncontrolled pace toward the mountains, allowing no one to approach or seize it, until, escaping through the mountain passes, it was seen no more.

Several men then hastened to seek the runaway horse, and Arnulf hastened also. But after they had sought it long and not found it, wearied by the difficulties of the mountains, they all turned back. Arnulf alone, troubled by concern for the horse, and unable to do without the service and attendance of his squire, [Col. 0655A] went farther in search of the horse, in the hope that he might perhaps find and bring it back. Yet, through grievous adverse fortune, the horse indeed was found, but the glorious young man never returned to his companions.

For Arab ambushes were lying hidden there. They had come down from Ascalon to the secluded mountain heights to observe and learn of the burning and ravaging of the country, and to take vengeance, upon any men from the army who might carelessly encounter them, for the plunder and flames which they had suffered. Seeing the most noble young man wandering alone and unarmed along mountain ridges and slopes, they attacked him with sudden cries and weapons. Though for a long time he vainly tried, with drawn sword, to resist and defend himself, at last, worn down and exhausted by a prolonged and relentless assault, [Col. 0655B] pierced through the body and vitals by lances and arrows, and falling from his horse amid much blood, he was killed; and they carried his head to Ascalon as a token of victory.

His horse, finally, running through the passes and precipices of the mountains, could not be caught by the heathen; until, having left the mountains, it returned to the king’s army, stained with the blood of its lord and rider and furnishing all with plain evidence of his death. For when the king and the whole body of Christians saw it dripping with blood, they concluded beyond doubt that Arnulf had fallen unsuspectingly by Ascalonite arms. Without delay, spreading through the mountains to pursue and seek out the enemy, they found only [Col. 0656A] Arnulf lying dead and headless; the Arabs they could not discover at all.

They took up his lifeless body and brought it to Jerusalem, where they rendered him Catholic funeral rites in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, at the Latin church of Saint Mary, mother of the Lord Jesus; and there he was honourably buried. The king mourned over him with great weeping on the day of the funeral; all the princes of the army wept as well; and the noble wife of Count Baldwin of the Hamaeans (*Hamaicorum*) wept over him with most bitter tears, because he had come as companion and fellow-traveller from the distant land of France to worship at Jerusalem. Nor should it seem strange that this young man deserved the weeping and lamentation of so many great men: he was gracious and well known to all, and he had never withdrawn from any military action under a dishonourable reputation.

On the third day thereafter, [Col. 0656B] after so illustrious a knight had been committed to burial, the Ascalonites sent his head, which had been requested by envoys, back to Jerusalem, with a letter hanging from one of his hairs and containing words to this effect:

> The Ascalonites send to King Baldwin the head of the slain knight and most noble man for no cause of affection other than that his grief, and that of those who look upon it, may be renewed and increased; and that they may recognize how the loss of so great a man can in no way be compared with or assessed against all their own losses and burnings, and that, upon the beheading of so great a knight, the Ascalonites should no longer wish to remember or grieve over their losses.

# BOOK TEN

## CHAPTER I.—How, in the seventh year of the reign of King Baldwin, a great people sailing to Jerusalem sought the escort of that king.

At the same time, in the seventh year of the reign of Baldwin, Catholic king of Jerusalem, a very great naval force of the Catholic English people—about seven thousand men in ships which they call *buzas*—together with another force brought from the kingdoms of Denmark, Flanders, and Antwerp, cast anchor in the harbour of the city of Joppa. They resolved to remain there until, having received the king’s permission and escort, they might safely be allowed to worship in Jerusalem.

The more distinguished and eloquent among them approached the king and spoke as follows:

> May the king live in Christ, and may his kingdom prosper day by day. Men and knights [Col. 0655D] professing Christianity have sailed here, by God’s assistance, from the distant lands of the kingdoms of England, Flanders, and Denmark, across the vast waters of the boundless sea, in order to worship at Jerusalem and see the Lord’s tomb. We have therefore come to entreat your clemency in this matter: that, by your favour and under your escort, we may peacefully go up to Jerusalem, worship, and return.

## CHAPTER II.—The king receives the pilgrims with great joy and consults his men as to how he may use their aid against the Saracens.

The king graciously heard their whole petition [Col. 0656C] and granted them an escort of valiant armed men, who led them safely by known paths, free from every attack and ambush of the heathen, as far as Jerusalem and all the holy places. When the pilgrims and Christ’s new arrivals had been brought there, they fulfilled their vows to the Lord in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and returned joyfully to Joppa without any hindrance.

Finding the king there, they pledged themselves to assist him in all things toward whatever undertaking his mind might turn. Receiving the men kindly and ordering that they be lodged, he declared that he could not give an answer to so sudden a proposal until he had summoned his leading men and taken counsel from the lord patriarch as to what course they might most usefully and suitably pursue, and so not waste such a willing army to no purpose. Accordingly, [Col. 0656D] after a few days he summoned the lord patriarch, Hugh of Tiberias, Gunfrid, keeper and provost of the Tower of David, and the other chief men of his military force, and arranged to hold an assembly in the city of Ramla, that he might consult them as to what he ought most usefully to do.

## CHAPTER III.—The king, following the counsel of his men, orders the English to wait at Joppa for the siege of Sidon.

When they had met on the appointed day and offered various reports and opinions, it finally seemed to all that the sounder counsel was that the city of Sagitta—that is, [Col. 0657A] Sidon—should be besieged, in the hope that, with God’s help and the strength of the new army by land and sea, it might be overcome. Then all present who urged its siege, because it was one of those heathen cities constantly in rebellion, were instructed and warned by the king that each should return home and provide himself with the necessities and arms for this expedition.

Each withdrew to his own place, and Hugh of Tiberias withdrew as well, a foremost warrior against hostile attacks, who could not be wearied by wars and ambushes, by day or night, in the land of the heathen, so long as his life remained unharmed.
