The king’s embassy then immediately ordered the whole English multitude not to move their tents or fleet from the city of Joppa, but to await the king’s command there without impatience. [Col. 0657B] The embassy further explained to all that the king and all his chief men had resolved to besiege and take the city of Sagitta by land and sea, and that their help and strength would be needed there; and that for this reason the king and patriarch were going down to the city of Acre to construct engines and mangonels for battering the walls and their inhabitants, while they were meanwhile to remain at Joppa until the king’s order became known.

All agreed to do so in accordance with the king’s command; they undertook to await his embassy in the harbour of Joppa and answered that they would obey in all things, even unto blood.

## CHAPTER IV.—While the king was preparing engines, the Sidonians promised him a large sum of money if they were not besieged.

[Col. 0657C] The king went down to Acre with the patriarch and all his household. For forty days he made and assembled engines and many kinds of siege-machines, arranging with the utmost care for everything that seemed best suited to assaulting the city. When this zeal and purpose of the king came to the ears of the inhabitants of Sagitta, and they heard that the overwhelming forces of armed men had gathered at Joppa to aid the king, they were greatly terrified. They feared that they would be consumed and subjugated beneath the king’s sword, just as the other cities—Caesarea, Arsuf, Acre, Haifa, and Tiberias—had been crushed and subjugated.

Having taken counsel, they promised the king, through secret intermediaries, a very great sum in Byzantine coins, and also a great talent [Col. 0657D] each year, if only he would spare their lives by not besieging and assaulting their city. These negotiations were therefore conducted day after day between the king and the citizens; they pressed the king concerning the ransom of their city and their safety, offering ever greater gifts. The king, anxious and concerned over the payment in solidi which he owed his soldiers, devoted himself wholly to money. Nevertheless, because he feared that Christ’s faithful might reproach him, he did not yet dare to accept it.

## CHAPTER V.—While Count Hugh was plundering the district of Suet, the Saracens took the booty from his companions; how Hugh, struck by an arrow in that slaughter, gave up his spirit; and of his brother’s death.

Meanwhile Hugh of Tiberias, having summoned a force of two hundred [Col. 0658A] horsemen and four hundred foot soldiers, withdrew into the land of the Grossus Rusticus, called Suet, very rich in gold and silver, abundant in herds, and bordering the territory of Damascus. There he seized enormous wealth and herds, sufficient for the siege of Sagitta, and from which he would also distribute generous shares to the king and his companions.

When this booty had been gathered from every direction and carried as far as the city of Belinas, called Caesarea Philippi, the Turks living at Damascus and the Saracens, inhabitants of the region, learned of it. Gathering everywhere in troops, they pursued Hugh’s company to recover the booty and advanced as far as the mountains through which Hugh’s infantry were leading it. There a fierce struggle arose on both sides: Hugh’s men [Col. 0658B] resisted in order to retain the booty, while the others strove with all their strength to recover it. At last the Turks and Saracens prevailed, and the booty was taken back.

When Hugh and his knights, who were on the mountainside, suddenly learned this, they immediately wheeled back on loose rein through the narrow and rocky passes, fought fiercely with the enemy, and came to the aid of their infantry. But through unhappy chance the battle went badly. For Hugh, unarmoured in a hauberk, was at once carried into the midst of danger; and while attacking and striking down the heathen in his accustomed manner, he was struck by an arrow from behind, which passed through his breast and liver, and expired in the hands of his men.

After the heathen troops had returned with the recovered booty and dispersed by dark and difficult paths over the rugged hills, Hugh’s knights placed his dead body upon a bier [Col. 0658C] and brought it to Nazareth, which lies near Tabor. There, amid much weeping and lamentation, this distinguished prince and mighty champion was honourably buried according to Catholic rite. His brother, named Gerhard, was then suffering from a severe illness. When he heard of his brother’s death, his bodily affliction was intensified by grief, and after eight days he too died and was laid, according to the custom of the faithful, beside his brother’s tomb.

## CHAPTER VI.—How the king received money from the Sidonians and sent the English army home.

After the tearful funerals of these celebrated princes, the king, taking advantage of the death of these men, foremost in his army, [Col. 0658D] agreed secretly, without anyone’s knowledge, to accept the money offered for postponing the siege of the city of Sagitta. Yet he pretended that he was not making peace with the Saracens, but still wished to complete the work he had begun.

He therefore sent an embassy to Joppa, instructing the English knights to sail down to Acre and deliberate with him about the siege and assault of the city of Sagitta. Rising at the king’s command, they immediately came, spreading on the tall masts of their *buzas* purple sails marked in varied colours and raising their purple-and-silk banners. Casting anchor off the shore of the city, they lodged there.

On the following day the king summoned his secretaries and companions and explained to the chief English and Danes his grief over Hugh’s death [Col. 0659A] and the death of his brother, and how much confidence he had placed in them in military affairs. Therefore, now that they were lacking and dead, he must necessarily postpone the siege of Sagitta and dismiss for the present the army which had been assembled. When the king’s decision had spread among the people, the army dispersed; and the English, Danes, and Flemings sailed away again with sails and oars, took leave of the king, and returned to the land of their birth.

## CHAPTER VII.—The king, strengthened by the Sidonians’ money, returned to Tiberias and appointed Gervase in Hugh’s place.

The king, having received from Sagitta fifteen thousand Byzantine coins for the safety of the city, went with all the cavalry of his household to Tiberias. There he arranged [Col. 0659B] a guard of valiant men who might defend with equal courage the land which Hugh had held by the king’s gift and had acquired and subdued through great and continual battles; who might keep enemies at a distance and in no way allow them to cross the mountains.

Accordingly, he appointed in Hugh’s place Gervase, an illustrious and most noble man, born in the kingdom of western France, skilled and experienced in war. He set him over Tiberias and the whole region, knowing him to be loyal and exceedingly fierce in war against every incursion of heathens, Saracens, Turks, and Damascenes.

## CHAPTER VIII.—While the king remained at Tiberias, the Ascalonites killed five hundred Christians near the river of Ramla.

Meanwhile, while the king lingered there over these affairs, [Col. 0659C] the men of Ascalon learned of his absence, the departure of the new army, and the deaths of Hugh and his brother. They hastily sent embassies to Sur, that is Tyre; Sagitta, that is Sidon; and Beirut, that is Baurim, instructing them to assemble armed forces on an appointed day. Thus, falling upon Ramla, that is Rama, and Joppa, they would attack the unsuspecting Christians, killing some and carrying others away captive.

In accordance with the Ascalonites’ summons, men gathered from every direction, numbering as many as seven thousand horsemen. With great force they burst into the plain of the fields of Arsuf and Ramla with sudden cries. There, in October, on Wednesday, the very feast-day of the blessed martyr Dionysius, they found unsuspecting pilgrims, unaware of so great a multitude, near the river [Col. 0659D] flowing between Arsuf and Ramla. They charged fiercely with lances and arrows, and no fewer than five hundred were cut down and beheaded.

## CHAPTER IX.—When the Ascalonites attacked Ramla, Rotger met them in battle with his knights.

Exulting excessively in the power and strength of their arms after the destruction of so many pilgrims, the Ascalonites and the other heathens of the king of Babylon immediately came onto the plain near Ramla to assault the city and challenge its inhabitants to battle, should any come out—as their boldness had always been accustomed to resist. On that day the Christian citizens and knights were unprepared and undefended; moreover, no more than eight [Col. 0660A] mounted knights were found for the city’s defence and protection.

Terrified, these men and a certain defender of theirs named Baldwin, believing that all the forces and equipment of the king of Babylon were present, immediately left the city on eight very swift horses. Entering Joppa, they reported to Rotger of the castle of Resset, who commanded the city of Joppa, and to the other fellow Christians, that the Ascalonites and the entire power of Babylon had occupied the plains of Ramla and would beyond doubt hasten without delay to the walls of Joppa.

On hearing this, every knight and foot soldier in Joppa, suddenly alerted by Rotger, armed themselves at the city gate and marched out to meet the enemy, drawing near so that by every kind and strength of arms they might prevent the enemy from reaching the walls and entrance [Col. 0660B] of the city.

## CHAPTER X.—Of the Ascalonites’ ambush, and the valour of Rotger and his knights in battle.

But the Ascalonites and Arabs deliberately concealed their forces in the hiding places of the mountains opposite. They sent forward men mounted on horseback and highly skilled with lance and bow, so that, riding at utmost speed to the city gate, they might draw the city’s men farther out until, falling into the ambush, they would be surrounded on every side; then, bursting from their concealment, the enemy might kill some of the unwary men and take others captive.

Rotger and his fellow soldiers, armed and ready, went out to meet them and did not refrain from fighting the Arabs. Spending a great part of the day in mounted struggle and manoeuvring, they were distressed by severe wounds [Col. 0660C] and exhausted by great labour. At last, as the Christians pursued farther because of their favourable success, while the Arabs deliberately gave way from time to time, the enemy forces began to emerge from the mountains and to appear and approach everywhere in excessive and innumerable numbers.

But although the Christians believed this war had been sent from Babylon, they were not shaken by fear. They resisted bravely and placed their hope of life in the Lord Jesus, for whose name and love they had left behind every kindred of flesh and blood.

## CHAPTER XI.—Of the knight Gerhard, at whose urging the Christian army fled to the city of Joppa.

[Col. 0660D] At this point a knight named Gerhard, of King Baldwin’s household, who held a share of the revenues of the city of Joppa in return for military service, came at full speed on horseback into the midst of the Christian ranks. He declared that the enemy’s strength and numbers were innumerable and so overwhelming that the present Christian force could never withstand them; it would therefore be more prudent for knights and foot soldiers to return to the city’s defences and protect the walls.

Some men were greatly angered by these words of discouragement, rebuked those made fearful by Gerhard’s words, urging them to stand and fight. Others, however, shaken by excessive fear, cried out that Gerhard’s counsel should be followed now that the king was absent. In a moment, through this division, the Christian host was so thrown into disorder and scattered that it undertook a general [Col. 0661A] flight toward Joppa, as bees are wont to fly and scatter before a whirlwind.

## CHAPTER XII.—The Saracens pursued the fleeing Rotger and killed forty Christians before the city.

Seeing that the men had failed through fear and taken flight, the Saracens and Arabs vigorously urged on their horses and pursued the fugitives without mercy. They cruelly struck them with lances and arrows, except those who escaped through the city gate. Rotger, Gerhard, and the other Christian knights escaped through the speed of their horses; but in the rush of flight they trampled down the slow and miserable foot soldiers, and no one was permitted or able to rein in before those pursuing and chasing them. The sole hope of life for those striving was the city gate—to enter it.

At length, as the one party pressed them with fierce pursuit and the other struggled in a great crush for possession of the gate, [Col. 0661B] certain slower Christians were shut out. Before the gateway and city walls they fell beneath the weapons of the impious heathen, and about forty were beheaded there.

## CHAPTER XIII.—How the Saracens destroyed Arnulf’s castle in a siege, taking captive the governor of that fortress.

[Col. 0661B] Having gained this victory, the Ascalonites at once attempted to force the city walls. But taking away the heads of the beheaded men, they rejoiced in the favourable outcome of the battle and returned to the territory of Ramla amid trumpets and horns. In great pride they besieged Arnulf’s castle, which stood toward Jerusalem in the mountains, [Col. 0661C] built with walls and ramparts by command of the Catholic king for protection of the country.

After besieging it for two days, they so terrified its inhabitants by the threat of mangonels and engines that Gunfrid, keeper and provost of the fortress and Tower of Jerusalem, who now also commanded this garrison of Arnulf’s, scarcely obtaining his life, sought the pledged right hand of the Saracens, surrendered himself, and opened the garrison gate to the enemy. Entering, they at once destroyed the fortress walls, struck down those whom they found by the sword, and reserved only Gunfrid, whom they carried captive to Ascalon.

## CHAPTER XIV.—After winning their victory, the Saracens attacked a Christian dromon in the harbour of Joppa with eight galley ships.

[Col. 0661D] Then, beginning on Friday after that Wednesday which followed the feast of Saint Dionysius the martyr, the Ascalonites, joyful and exalted in their triumph, fitted out eight galleys and placed in them archers and very powerful men. They resolved to put in at Joppa, thinking that they might encounter the Christians’ forces or ships and overcome them by capture or sinking.

And behold: arriving at Joppa early in the morning with great force and the sound of trumpets, they observed from afar in the harbour of the city an enormous ship, called a *dromon*, laden with various goods and necessities of life. Attacking it on every side, they stripped it in a fierce assault and pierced with arrows the only two men left to guard it.

But the Christian citizens of Joppa, seeing that the Saracens [Col. 0662A] prevailed, had killed the guards of the *dromon*, and stripped it of its goods, hastened to its aid with lances, bows, and slings, until that very great ship was recovered and retained. The small boat which was always attached to the *dromon* to lighten it, however, the Saracens violently tore away; and they carried it off, laden also with much wealth.

## CHAPTER XV.—The king, roused by news of these evils, set out from Tiberias against the Ascalonites with six thousand men.

Thus, after the Christian brethren and their cities had twice and thrice been struck by so great a disaster and misfortune, the report flew everywhere and came grievously to the ears of King Baldwin in the district and city of Tiberias. [Col. 0662B] It greatly moved him because, having dismissed his allies and forces, he had spared the cities and places of the Saracens, and because they had dared thus to deceive him by means of the money mentioned above.

He therefore returned to Joppa without delay. Having assembled five hundred horsemen in hauberks and helmets and as many as six thousand foot soldiers, he wished to march upon Ascalon in vengeance for his men. He advanced as far as the Place of Palms, at the boundary of the castle of Beroart, two miles distant from the city of Ascalon.

## CHAPTER XVI.—The king, at his men’s counsel, returned to Jerusalem without battle; and Rorgius of Haifa died.

There, after taking counsel with his men, he considered that at this time no assault on Ascalon [Col. 0662C] would profit him, whether in the grainfields, vineyards, or destruction of trees: the region had repeatedly been so thoroughly ravaged by fire and plunder in the preceding days that nothing outside the city had been left untouched. Moreover, the citizens and Arab soldiers did not allow any of their men to come out from the city walls.

The king thereby tempered the anger in his heart which he had conceived in vengeance for his men. He therefore returned to Jerusalem with the lord patriarch, postponing vengeance for them. In the same year Rorgius, who governed Haifa by the king’s gift, was seized by severe illness and languished for a long time, until at last his bodily affliction increased and ended his life. He was honourably buried according to Catholic rite beneath the eaves of the portico of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Of a ruler of the city of Femia, slain by his associate Bother, whom his citizens pursued.

[Col. 0662D]

At the same time of year when King Baldwin postponed the siege of Sagitta and dismissed the English knights, and Hugh of Tiberias was killed by the bow and arrow of a Turk, a certain ruler of the city called Femia, who exercised immense power far and wide over the surrounding land, was regarded as generous and favourably disposed toward Christian and pilgrim retainers. A Saracen named Bother, who remained with him under a military engagement and agreement for payment in solidi, bore great envy and resentment against him. At last, one day, when opportunity served his malice, Bother invited him treacherously to dine; he was ensnared by deceit and ambushes concealed in the house, and slain by Bother’s accomplices. [Col. 0663A]

When he had thus been treacherously killed, the citizens of the city, ignorant of this cruel deed, blazed with intense anger against Bother, repeatedly gathering courage to avenge their ruler and destroy those who had dared to lay hands upon him.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—When Bother sought Brodoan’s help, Tancred was invited by the citizens but was not admitted.

Bother, therefore, lodging in one of the city’s strongest towers and distrusting the citizens, especially because they were Christians, [Col. 0663B] secretly sent messengers to Brodoan, ruler of the city of Aleppo. He asked him to come down suddenly with assembled forces, seize and take the city of Femia, and, after they had pledged one another their right hands, possess the city and its territory together.

When the Christian and Armenian citizens learned this, they were greatly terrified, fearing that they would again [Col. 0663A] be subject to the rule of the heathen tyrant Brodoan. Placed under the hand of the traitor Bother, they sent messengers to Tancred, because he was a Christian man and a foremost warrior, asking him to take forces and companions, come to them, seize the lordship of the city and country, and hold it thereafter.

He immediately gathered seven hundred horsemen and a thousand foot soldiers and set out for the city, but was not admitted. For Bother, the wicked traitor, had corrupted all the citizens and chief men of the city with flattering promises and great gifts, and had broken the spirits and hearts of all through threats and terrors.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Tancred withdrew for a time and, after Easter, enclosed the city of Femia in siege.

Tancred, seeing the citizens hostile to him, [Col. 0663C] pitched his tents before the city walls. After he had spent three weeks there, he could make no progress in any of his assaults. The traitor had alienated everyone. The Lenten fast had already passed its middle. Therefore, seeing that he could achieve nothing at that time, Tancred broke camp and returned to Laodicea and Antioch.

Not long before, he had besieged Laodicea and, after overcoming and subduing it, had taken it from the hand of the Greek king and his garrison into his own power. After celebrating the eight days of holy Easter with Christian rite and honour, Tancred reassembled his companions and forces and went down to Femia. He brought up engines and mangonels on every side, hoping that the conquered city might be delivered into his hand, rather than [Col. 0663D] into Brodoan’s, and that the citizens might be punished along with the traitor.

## CHAPTER XX.—How, while Tancred attacked Femia, the two sons of the murdered ruler aided him against Bother.

Meanwhile, while he laboured fruitlessly with assaults and machines around the city and could not terrify the citizens, and many days had already passed, the two sons of the treacherously murdered ruler—who, when they heard of their father’s death, had barely escaped Bother’s hand under cover of night and fled to Damascus, where they had stayed with their kinsmen for fear of Brodoan and Bother—now heard that Tancred had again besieged Femia and that Brodoan could do nothing against him. They sent messengers to Tancred, asking whether it seemed useful and acceptable to him and his men that they should come to aid him and avenge their father’s blood. [Col. 0664A]

Tancred heard their messengers and sent them back graciously. He gladly assented to their coming to aid him and made an agreement with them concerning all that he intended to do around the city and against the citizens and Bother. In accordance with their pledge, they took one hundred Arab and Turkish soldiers and came to Femia, to Tancred’s camp. They spoke to him thus:

> This land and city were the seat of our father and forefathers; but through Bother’s envy and greed we have been driven from them and made exiles. Therefore we now seek refuge and aid with you; we seek and enter into pledged faith. If we take these walls, we do not begrudge them to you; we seek no hope of recovering them. Rather, we grant them to you willingly. [Col. 0664B] Thereafter, you shall do and render to us, in return for military service, whatever seems fitting to you.

Thus, after right hands had been pledged, they found Tancred favourably disposed and prepared to fulfil all these terms toward them.

## CHAPTER XXI.—When the Christians had enclosed the city, Bother and his citizens surrendered themselves into Tancred’s hands.

Without delay, continual assaults and the throwing of stones were made from outside; but everything appeared to be done in vain until at length the whole city was enclosed by a ditch and rampart, so that no one could leave from within through any open exit. Thus the citizens, pressed by hunger, and the traitor who lived in it were surrendered into Tancred’s power and custody. And so it was done.

For the citizens and that same traitor, crushed by intolerable hunger [Col. 0664C] and unable any longer to withstand Tancred’s force, begged that they might be spared and promised that, if right hands were pledged to them, they would open the city gates. Tancred then took counsel with his men, who were wearied by the tedium of the long siege and had now sat there until the month of August. He agreed to Bother’s and the citizens’ request: namely, that he would pledge his right hand to Bother, spare the citizens, enter the city peacefully, and possess it once it had been surrendered. Thus it was done, and the city was handed over.

## CHAPTER XXII.—The sons of the murdered ruler ask Tancred to have Bother killed.

Indignant at this, the sons of the murdered ruler urgently approached Tancred with their petition, saying:

> Such an evil man and such a wicked traitor [Col. 0664D] ought not to be received or kept alive, but utterly erased from the land.

Tancred answered them with complete gentleness:

> It is not Christian practice to violate the faith which we have pledged to this man, though I know him well to be perverse and perjured. Rather, it is ours to keep faith and truth with every people. Therefore we grant him his life and safety of limb. But his accomplices, to whom we have granted no pardon, shall be in your hands, whether for death or life, in vengeance for your father’s blood, as soon as we first depart from this siege and our army has prepared its return home. And in all matters advantageous to you, my hand shall not fail you.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—How, after the victorious Tancred returned to Antioch, the sons of the murdered ruler pursued Bother’s friends.

[Col. 0665A]

After these words, Tancred, the city having been surrendered to him and a guard of his own men established in it, returned to Antioch with Bother and the other hostages, under the faith given and received. He placed the sons of the treacherously murdered ruler in charge of many places in the territory of the city.

After Tancred’s departure, these sons remained in that district and killed Bother’s accomplices, guilty of their father’s death. Others aware of and guilty in that same murder, whom they caught in repeated ambushes, they either maimed in their limbs or strangled by hanging.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How King Baldwin reconnoitred, with fifteen armed men, the Turkish army advancing against him.

[Col. 0665B]

Then, after Hugh’s death, King Baldwin returned that same year from Tiberias and the land of Suet to Ptolemais, having celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there, in the eighth year of his reign, in order to rest from the labour of travel. There he immediately heard that the ruler and king of the city of Damascus, of Turkish stock, had assembled arms and equipment, had resolved to besiege Tiberias and take Gervase—appointed in Hugh’s place—and no longer feared the king’s strength.

Hearing this, the king immediately hastened to resist the Turks with a small force, about forty knights. Leaving the coast, he advanced boldly into the mountains with fifteen young companions skilled in arms and horsemanship, together with other [Col. 0665C] chosen men, to reconnoitre the entire Turkish army and its forces. The Turkish force amounted to about three thousand fighting men. Having now reconnoitred all their forces and seen their tents, he cautiously returned by byways and known paths to his companions.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Of the five Turks honoured by King Baldwin, at whose prompting three thousand Turks were put to flight.

[Col. 0665C] Scarcely had the arms been laid down, scarcely had the horses been stripped of bridles and saddles, when, at evening, five Turks came into the king’s camp. They were envoys of the others; after discussing and negotiating at length concerning various matters and the making of peace, they were received kindly. Laden with gifts of costly clothing, silver vessels, and [Col. 0665D] Byzantine coins, and commended by the king with friendly words, they returned to their camp after much conversation.

Honoured by the king with this favour and distinction, these five thereafter began to favour his cause greatly. They magnified sevenfold the strength and equipment which they had seen, and extolled it among the Turkish assembly, wishing to repay him worthily for all the benefits and gifts which the king had bestowed upon them. When the Turks and their leaders heard these things from their own men and believed much of what they reported, they were seized by great fear and began to flee in every direction, while night covered heaven and earth.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—The king, after the Turks had scattered in flight, summons his army, proceeds to Jerusalem, and performs the Ash Wednesday rite of ashes.

[Col. 0666A]

Having learned this from informers, the king pursued them at the first dawn of day, until, fleeing through the countryside, they escaped behind the walls of Damascus. When they had escaped into their defences and shut themselves in, the king decided to make his return; and after some days he came to Bethlehem, where on the feast of the Epiphany he was solemnly crowned. Staying there for eight days over various military affairs, he proceeded first to Jaffa, then to Nablus, which they call Samaria, and which this same King Baldwin had subdued without military display, in order to arrange the affairs of these cities, lest any trickery or deceit could work against them. Then, after nine days, having summoned allies from all the surrounding places, he returned to Jerusalem in February, where, at the beginning of the fast, on Mount Sion, his head having been sprinkled with ashes in the Christian manner by the hand of Baldwin, bishop of Caesarea Cornelia, he performed the Lenten rite.

### CHAPTER XXVII.—How the king, hastening against three thousand Turks, employed the guidance of a priest of the Syrian Christians.

Thus, when the season of Lent had begun, on the following day, having taken five hundred knights, he set out, on the advice of a certain Syrian named Theodore. This man had learned that three thousand Turks had come down from Damascus into the ancient valley of Moses, to fortify a certain stronghold, so that no member of the king’s people might have a route there for purposes of trade. The king therefore set out to destroy the stronghold [Col. 0666C], which the Turks, at the request and with the consent of the Arabs, had established there in order to bar passage to all Christians.

Then, for eight days, making his way through the foul-smelling waters of Sodom and Gomorrah, through desert places and the difficulties of the mountains, he arrived, with all his companions worn down by severe exhaustion, at the dwelling-place of certain Syrian Christians. There he stayed as a guest and was sufficiently refreshed, both he himself and all his followers. Learning, therefore, that they were Christians, he summoned their priest, intending to inquire of him about the new stronghold and the intentions of the Turks, and sought his advice about everything. Rising at dawn with the king, the priest travelled faithfully and truly for three days, serving as his guide through the road and country, until at last, under his guidance, the king rested in lodging at a safe place [Col. 0666D], not far from the stronghold and the Turks.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—How the Syrian priest, coming into the camp of the Turks, compelled them all to flee by his persuasion.

At dawn on the following day, that same priest and guide rose and entered the Turks’ camp. Reporting everything otherwise than it was, he spoke in this fashion:

“King Baldwin, coming down from Jerusalem with a huge force, has devastated the little settlement which was ours. We have been scattered; I alone of them have reached you, and scarcely escaped, to warn you not to wait for his arms and forces. For his escort and military array are no more than one mile away from you.”

When this report had been heard, such fear, by God’s will, seized the hearts of all [Col. 0667A] that, leaving their tents behind at once, they hastened into general flight. Hardly had the darkness lifted, hardly had morning dawned, when behold, King Baldwin descended into the valley amid the sound of trumpets and the clash of arms. But he found no Turk, killed no one, and captured no one; for throughout that night they had taken flight at no slow pace.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—Concerning the Arabs hidden in mountain caves, whom the king compelled to come out with fire and smoke.

The Arabs, by whose counsel the Turks had gathered there from Damascus, despairing of their lives, suddenly hid themselves from the king’s presence in mountain caves and dark hiding-places like mice. They vanished with the herds and household goods which they had brought there to help build the stronghold. The king, however, descending into the valley with his army [Col. 0667B], searched the excavations throughout the region and, having pitched tents, besieged the mouths of the caves.

But since even so he could not compel the men to come out, at last he kindled fire and smoke before the cave mouths and forced them all to emerge. Some of them were immediately slain by arms, others captured and carried away—to the number of sixty—while all their spoils were taken from the cave, together with many asses, cattle, sheep, and goats.

### CHAPTER XXX.—The king, having gained victory, returns to Jerusalem laden with booty, and comforts the places of his kingdom by visiting them.

After these successes, the king returned with all his force and with the booty he had taken as far as the Jordan River, gathering Syrian brethren and fellow Christians from all parts of the region and taking about sixty with him because of fear of the Arabs. There the booty was divided between the king and the knights. Then, after two days had passed, the king went up to Jerusalem with his share of the booty, which had fallen to him as one third of the division. All Christian pilgrims and citizens came out to meet him with delight and joy.

After four days had elapsed, he went down from Jerusalem to Jaffa and stayed there for some time. He also came to Acre, where he dealt extensively with the affairs of his kingdom; and, as Easter approached, he returned to Jerusalem on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper. There, at this holy solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, he was gloriously and canonically crowned. Eight days later he again set out, going down through the castles and cities to Ptolemais; he also proceeded to Tiberias [Col. 0667D], in order to strengthen his people by military support against Turkish ambushes and threats.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—How, when the people of Ascalon besieged Jaffa, the citizens, encouraged by the king, went out through the gates against them and prevailed.

Behold, the people of Ascalon, rejoicing in his absence, came out three thousand strong onto the level fields of the city of Ramla. Accomplishing nothing there, they came in great anger and besieged Jaffa. When this cruel report reached the king, who had by then returned from Tiberias to Ptolemais, he sent sixty men valiant in arms and war by ship to Jaffa, to assist the citizens and to tell them that the king would follow them without delay with an assembled force.

When the citizens heard that the king’s aid had preceded them [Col. 0668A] and that the king himself would shortly follow, they opened the gates and went out to resist their enemies. The two sides joined battle: eighteen Saracens fell, while thirteen Christians were killed. The remaining Saracens, thinking that the king was present and that this was why the citizens now resisted more boldly, took flight, the Lord Jesus prospering His own. The Christians pursued them vigorously and struck only sixty of their horses with arrow and lance; nevertheless, they seized none of them. Without delay the king, as he had promised, came to Jaffa in a great display of arms; but since his own citizens had already won the victory with God’s aid, he enjoyed the desired rest there with his men.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—Where the king compelled the people of Ascalon, who wished to build a stronghold against the Christians, to flee.

[Col. 0668B]

Four days later the king returned to Jerusalem to arrange the kingdom’s affairs and enjoy some rest. Suddenly word reached him that the people of Ascalon, having summoned Turks from Damascus under an agreement for payment, had resolved to fortify a stronghold in order to capture the castle called Saint Abraham’s and destroy the one then held by a certain Walter, surnamed Mahomet, who had received it by the king’s grant after the death of Rorgius.

When the king learned these alarming reports, he selected and took seventy worthy knights, hurried there, and rested for the night in lodging at Saint Abraham’s. At the dawn of a Friday, with the horses loosened and their reins released, he fell upon the camp of the Ascalonites in a great charge, amid the blare of horns and the tumult of shouting [Col. 0668C]. Unaware and stunned by so sudden a storm, they were immediately forced into flight.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—While the Christians were intent upon booty and were almost overwhelmed by the enemy, the king came to their assistance, after the enemy had been greatly despoiled.

But his Christians, blinded by greed for enemy possessions and too busily occupied in gathering and carrying off spoil from their enemies’ tents, forgot warfare and arms. The people of Ascalon and the Turks, observing that they were more intent on booty than on pursuing their fleeing enemies, regrouped everywhere and joined battle with them. They killed five of the king’s distinguished knights, among them Hugh of Cassel and Albert, surnamed Apostolius, who were slain by arms [Col. 0668D].

Yet the king, with God’s help, scarcely having recovered his men’s strength, gained the advantage and finally won the victory. Thirty of the enemy fell by his sword, sixty were carried away captive, and others escaped by flight. The king and his men brought to Jerusalem thirty-three camels, sixty-eight horses, much booty, and many tents, rejoicing and exulting over this victory.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—The people of Ascalon, making attacks before Jerusalem, lost five men.

Meanwhile the people of Ascalon, by no means forgetting their quarrel, assembled at Jerusalem with arms and forces, skirmishing there all day in horsemen’s charges with the youths. But five of them, after much fighting [Col. 0669A], are reported to have been captured there with their horses and spoils. Seven Christian infantrymen who had gone out to resist are said to have been beheaded. Thus the terrors and threats of the pagans were greatly checked.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—How King Baldwin attacked and despoiled Babylonian merchants near the Jordan.

After some days had passed, word was brought to the king that Babylonian merchants would be beyond the Jordan River under cover of the darkness and silence of night, and would descend to Tyre, Beirut, and Sidon to send merchandise to Damascus. He was told that he could seize much booty from them and relieve the poverty of his people. Having heard everything in order, he took sixty knights [Col. 0669B], rose in the night, and went down to the riverbank.

But seeing that the merchants’ forces were too numerous, he deferred fighting them face to face. Instead, secretly turning aside from them, he soon shouted against and attacked the rearmost men with vigour. He struck down eleven with the sword and took forty prisoners. They brought to Jerusalem eleven camels carrying *zucra* [sugar], four laden with other spices and precious goods, and seventeen carrying oil and honey. By their abundance the entire region of pilgrims was relieved and strengthened.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—Where, after Count Baldwin was redeemed from captivity by Gozelin, Tancred became his enemy.

After this, in the eighth year of King Baldwin’s reign [Col. 0669C], Gozelin of Turbessel, a most faithful knight, redeemed Baldwin of Bourg from the hand of Geigremich, a very powerful Turk, by giving one hundred thousand byzants. Baldwin had granted him land and territory in return for military service. Gozelin had gathered this sum, obtained through urgent entreaty from all Christian princes and men, great and small, and from all the places and cities of the faithful.

Thus Baldwin was redeemed and brought back with every honour to the city of Edessa. Tancred, however, left that city, which he had received to hold in custody. From then on hostility and envy grew so greatly between the two princes that, having assembled forces, neither ceased from harming and opposing the other by plunder and ambush.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—Baldwin, defeated by Tancred, is besieged, but is freed by Gozelin’s skill and the intervention of Geigremich, prince of the Turks.

[Col. 0669D]

At last, on a certain day, one setting out from Antioch and the other from Edessa, they marched forth in arms and military array with their forces, and fiercely joined battle. Very many of Baldwin’s party were slain and overcome, and many more captured. Baldwin himself scarcely escaped from the field and was besieged in the city of Tuluppa by Tancred and his men.

Gozelin, who had barely escaped from the field and the enemy, knowing that Baldwin was besieged by Tancred, went to Geigremich. He urgently pressed and begged him to aid his ally in their reciprocal compact and free from Tancred’s siege so famous a man and kinsman of the king of Jerusalem. Geigremich immediately, without summoning any Turks, ordered it to be made known throughout the whole region that he would come to Tuluppa with forty [men; the source is grammatically uncertain] on an appointed day [Col. 0670A] for Baldwin’s release, so that his forces might assemble there to him from every side.

Tancred, learning of the Turk’s resolve to liberate Baldwin, withdrew his camp from the siege. Baldwin entered the city of Edessa in joy and exultation, forgetful of past injuries.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—How Henry, emperor of the Romans, recovered his constable Conrad through the king of the Greeks.

At the same time Conrad, constable of Henry III, emperor of the Romans, a man distinguished in every military undertaking, was brought out of prison and chains through an embassy and petition made by the emperor himself to the king of the Greeks, and by that king to the king of Babylon. On account of affection and reciprocal obligation, he was restored to Alexius, the great king of the Greeks [Col. 0670B].

King Alexius rejoiced greatly when Conrad was received alive and unharmed. Having honoured him with magnificent gifts, he sent him back to Henry, emperor of the Romans, more welcome than all gold and silver, purple cloth, and precious stones. For he judged that nothing sweeter or more precious among gold and silver, purple and precious stones could suffice for him.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—How Bohemond, returning from Italy with an army, besieged Dyrrhachium, a Greek city.

After this, in the second year following Conrad’s restoration, Bohemond came by ship to Valona with an army of Christians gathered from various kingdoms of Gaul and Italy [Col. 0670C]. He suddenly seized it and subdued all the surrounding places belonging to the Greek kingdom. Having subdued them, he turned against Dyrrhachium, a great city very powerful in resources and in the entire strength of its citizens and soldiers. Pitching tents around its walls, he besieged it with a vast multitude. For he had twelve thousand fighting horsemen and sixty thousand infantry soldiers.

### CHAPTER XL.—How, while Conrad remained in Italy, Bohemond attacked the walls of Dyrrhachium.

Conrad, having been sent back by the Greek emperor [Col. 0670D], then remained in Italy because of serious discord which had arisen, through envy and the counsel of wicked men, between the lord emperor Henry and his son Henry V, king; he did so lest, exerting himself in favour of either one, he should grievously offend the other.

Accordingly, when the siege had been established on every side in springtime, Bohemond ordered engines and stone-throwing machines to be made for attacking the city. For many days he battered the walls and towers with repeated blows of stones, and harassed the citizens and all inhabitants with vehement assault. The citizens, on the other hand, hurled from their engines fire-pots filled with fuel that water could not extinguish; throwing various kinds of fire upon all the work of his engines, they resisted with arrows and slings with all their strength, for the matter was one of life and death to them.

### CHAPTER XLI.—How Bohemond met the king of the Greeks in battle when he came, while continuing his attack upon Dyrrhachium.

[Col. 0671A]

At last, while he harassed the city and its citizens with repeated assault and military skill and had already spent the whole summer season in warfare, the king of the Greeks assembled an innumerable army and came down into the plains of the city of Bothilia to assist Dyrrhachium and drive Bohemond and all his company from the siege.

When the emperor’s tents had been pitched in the aforesaid places and plains, one day’s journey from the territory of Dyrrhachium, the emperor’s soldiers—both the foreign Franks who served the emperor for agreed payment, and the Turcopoles, Cumans, and Pechenegs—formed a body of ten thousand, armed and armoured with lance and bow [Col. 0671B], and resolved to attack Bohemond and his men in their camp.

But Bohemond, learning the matter from informers, met them as they approached on the open plain. Engaging in battle with a charge, he killed a thousand by sword, lance, and arrow, and sent the rest in flight as far as the emperor’s tents. Afterwards Bohemond renewed his assault more fiercely for the destruction of Dyrrhachium, bringing up engines and stone-throwing machines in the hope that the guards, terrified by his new victory, would open the gates to him. But the defenders of the city could not yet be softened or intimidated by these threats and attacks; instead, with every effort and military art, they resisted those bringing force against them.

### CHAPTER XLII.—Concerning three hundred of Bohemond’s knights killed by the Turcopoles.

[Col. 0671C]

Later, on a certain day, when provisions and fodder for the horses had failed Bohemond’s forces, three hundred knights and seven hundred infantrymen were sent to gather plunder in Greek territory. An innumerable multitude of Turcopoles, Cumans, and Pechenegs—the emperor’s soldiers—came against them. In the fierce battle that followed, as many as three hundred of Bohemond’s knights were killed there, and many more were carried away captive.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—Where Italian princes, corrupted by Greek gifts, turned Bohemond away from the siege.

While these conflicts, ambushes, daily raids, and most grievous slaughters continued on both sides for almost a year [Col. 0671D], Bohemond’s army was burdened by the weariness of the prolonged siege. Many withdrew, and the naval contingent, reduced by lack of bread and other necessities, sailed to Italy. Meanwhile the emperor’s naval strength was brought in with an abundance of all food and weapons.

Wido, Bohemond’s sister’s son, William Claret, and the other leading men of the army, corrupted by the emperor’s money and blandishments, pressed various grave arguments upon Bohemond. Now they cited the shortage of food, now the dispersal of the people and naval army, now the resources sent into the city by the emperor; and they attempted to turn him away from the siege and bind him to the emperor in friendship.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—Concerning Bohemond’s reconciliation with the king of the Greeks, who granted permission to those travelling to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0672A]

At last Bohemond saw that his followers had melted away, that many had gone over to the emperor’s assistance, and that they worked less and less in assaulting the city. He accepted his men’s counsel and was reconciled to the emperor for an immense weight and quantity of unspeakable gold, silver, and precious purple cloth.

Having been reconciled and received infinite gifts and treasures, he embarked and returned to Apulia, deceiving and in no way rewarding all who had endured with him long labours and the burdens of war around Dyrrhachium. Recognizing Bohemond’s fraud and departure, these men begged the emperor’s clemency that he might peacefully allow them to continue their road through his kingdom to Jerusalem [Col. 0672B].

After this peace had been arranged, the emperor returned to Constantinople and granted all of them a route through his kingdom without any hindrance, just as he had promised and affirmed under oath when he entered into alliance with Bohemond and all the leading men of Gaul and Italy then present.

### CHAPTER XLV.—King Baldwin, having assembled forces, besieges Sidon.

In the same year, as autumn approached, King Baldwin assembled forces from every quarter, by sea and land, from the various peoples of the Italian realm: namely, Pisans, Genoese, Venetians, Amalfitans, and all those who are accustomed in the manner of pirates to attack [Col. 0672C] and despoil seafarers. In August he besieged the city of Sidon by sea and land, setting mangonels and engines against the wall all around on the landward side. With the masts of ships raised as towers and prepared for battle, he attacked it from the water with a strong force for many days, repeatedly assaulting it stoutly with great strength of his men.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—Concerning the most noble lady of the pagans, whom King Baldwin captured through his soldiers with four thousand camels.

When this siege had been made and arranged, after some days the king learned from informers that a certain noble and exceedingly wealthy lady from the kingdom of Arabia had camped beyond the Jordan, beside the hills, because of the rich pastures, with an innumerable herd of camels, cattle, sheep, and goats [Col. 0672D]. About five hundred men, rich in herds and livestock, were settled there with her and all her household in safety.

The king immediately sent secretly to Jerusalem for William, son of Robert, prince of the Normans, ordering him to take the soldiers whom he had left to guard the city, together with infantrymen, hasten beyond the Jordan, attack the unsuspecting Arab Saracens while they grazed their herds in security, and take captive the men and women with all their herds.

William hastened from Jerusalem in accordance with the king’s command. He took two hundred horsemen and five hundred infantrymen, and, crossing the Jordan’s fords, suddenly fell with all his force upon the camel-guards. But he found the Saracens resisting fiercely and defending themselves and their herd with bow and arrow [Col. 0673A]. At last William and his men prevailed. Only two of their own distinguished men were killed; they slew many pagans and captured many others, together with young girls and boys and the aforesaid most noble lady. They brought to Jerusalem about four thousand camels with the remaining herds—an incalculable booty. From their sale much gold was received and, at the king’s command, divided among the soldiers.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—Concerning two towers of Sidon, one of which was overthrown by divine providence.

Meanwhile, when the king was attempting to break into a certain tower of the city of Sidon by a greater assault and repeated blows of stones and had almost pierced it, the king’s purpose was restrained by the advice of Arnulf, clerk and chancellor. He said that so excellent a structure could not be rebuilt for less than two thousand byzants, and that after a few days it could be preserved for the king’s possession without destruction or the throwing of stones, once it had been handed over.

There was another tower in which apostates and betrayers of the faith from Provence, of Count Raymond’s following, had been placed for defence. They mocked and derided the Lord’s wood—the cross—which the king had brought from Jerusalem to protect God’s people. Making a cross contrary to themselves and fastening it to the top of that tower, those foolish and malicious men presumed to dishonour it with spittle and urine.

The pious king and all the people mourned this, and called upon the God of heaven with tearful voice, asking that He might open the fountain of His mercy and show the apostate men and foolish Saracens that they had not acted rightly in presuming to inflict blasphemy upon the divine majesty [Col. 0673C]. Soon their prayers were answered: without human labour, that tower was so shaken and destroyed, as evening was approaching, that not one stone remained upon another, and the unbelieving men were buried and suffocated beneath its collapse.

Seeing this power of God, the king and his men planned to enter the city through that tower. But because night was coming on, after taking counsel together in the evening, they deferred the attempt until daylight.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—How the Christians entered a naval battle against Babylonians sent to aid the people of Sidon.

[Col. 0673D]

But that same night men and abundant arms came from the kingdom of Babylon to the citizens of Sidon: fifty ships and eight triremes, which they call *Catti*, arriving at Ptolemais amid trumpets and horns. During the day their journey had been somewhat delayed by a contrary windstorm. When the governor of the city of Acre learned of this, he sent an urgent embassy by night to notify the king, so that hostile forces might not do harm without preparation.

At dawn, moreover, a multitude of ships from the city of Tripoli joined them with strong force and irresistible armour, adding strength to the Babylonians so that, having seized the harbour by force, they might remove the station of the faithful ships and the king’s blockade. Seeing from afar the peoples approaching in strong and irresistible force, the Christians went out from the harbour to resist them [Col. 0674A]. They fought with them in a fierce naval engagement and remained long in alternating attacks.

But unable to withstand the force of so many, the Christians scarcely escaped to land, not to the harbour. Three of their ships were overcome and captured, and all found in them were slain and beheaded. The Saracens seized the harbour in strong force.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—The king, fighting the Babylonians, won a victory, though many of his companions were killed.

On the following day Saracen soldiers, armoured and armed, came out from the city gates with their forces and drew up in their strength as far as the king’s tents, believing that they would defeat and drive him away. But the king, forewarned of the people rushing upon him, met them with only five hundred horsemen and four thousand infantrymen [Col. 0674B]. Joining a fierce battle, he killed about fifteen hundred of them by the edge of the sword and pursued the remaining multitude—namely forty thousand men—as they fled to the city’s defences.

Five hundred of the king’s army are said to have fallen that day. Giselbert of the castle called Cuiun, a distinguished man and very skilled in warfare, also fell after much exertion in that day’s struggle. The king and his men mourned him greatly and buried him according to the custom of the faithful.

When evening had come, the Saracens had fled into the stronghold, and the king, still unharmed, held the field in victory, a reliable message informed him that he must by no means wait for the light of the next day, because of the Turks whom the Sidonians had summoned from Damascus for a payment of thirty thousand byzants. Their number was about fifteen thousand [Col. 0674C].

### CHAPTER L.—Because of the Turks, the king burns his tents and withdraws from the siege, briefly giving himself to hunting.

The king, therefore, trusting the reliable message, yielded to prudent counsel. He sent all those seriously wounded ahead to Ptolemais and set fire to his own ships, all the engines, and the tents. As evening approached, while these were reduced to ashes and embers, he waited in the field for daylight itself.

When daylight appeared, the king moved his camp away from the siege and headed for Acre. He remained that day in the hills and refreshed himself by hunting, pursuing boars in the customary manner and course of hounds. He caught about five, meanwhile putting out of mind the anxieties and loss of his men.

### CHAPTER LI.—The Christian people are filled with joy at the king’s return.

[Col. 0674D]

Meanwhile there was grievous mourning and desolation among the men and women in the city of Acre, because they still knew nothing of the king’s life and safety. They had heard that many of their own had fallen and that all the array of ships and camp had been consumed in flames. After some delay, the king came out from the hunt and hills and entered Ptolemais. The entire Christian people received him as though restored from the dead with shouts of exultation; weeping for excessive joy, they repeatedly kissed his head and hands.

### CHAPTER LII.—The Turks’ demand of the people of Sidon for the promised sum of money.

Behold, after the king had withdrawn from the siege and been received at Acre with glory and joy [Col. 0675A], the Turks from Damascus came in a vast array of horsemen before the gates and walls of Sidon. But, since the gates were shut, they were not admitted. Then a certain Dochinus, governor of Damascus and commander of the Turkish army, demanded thirty thousand byzants from the leading men and inhabitants of the city, because they had been summoned to aid them and, on hearing of their arrival, King Baldwin had deferred the siege.

But the citizens and leading men of the city declared that they could in no way raise so great a sum; they entirely denied any such agreement, saying that, from fear for their lives, they had promised the Turks so many thousands of byzants merely to make them more eager to come to their aid, since so large a payment was being offered. Hearing this, the Turks and their leaders burned with violent anger [Col. 0675B]. For ten days they did not cease attacking the city, now employing force, now threats, declaring that they would call King Baldwin back for the Sidonians’ utter destruction.

At last the Sidonians, burdened by Turkish assaults and despairing because of their threats, offered nine thousand byzants. Though the Turks repeatedly refused these, in the end overcome by weariness and fearing the king’s strength and attack, they accepted this small amount and returned to Damascus.

### CHAPTER LIII.—Concerning four thousand Turks whom Gervase, lord of Tiberias, pursued with eighty armoured men.

Before this siege of Sidon, as Rogationtide approached—that is, before Pentecost—the same Turks left Damascus with four thousand armoured horsemen [Col. 0675C] and entered the region of Tiberias. Having set ambushes on either side, they sent ahead three hundred men on very swift horses, who by their usual charge and assault were to draw the men out from the fortification until they reached the place of ambush.

Gervase, a most renowned and noble man from the kingdom of France, who at that time by the king’s grant governed the city and fortress of Tiberias, learned that the Turks had rushed in. Without delay, he called about eighty fellow knights, mounted and equipped with weapons and armour, and two hundred infantrymen exceedingly bold in battle. He pursued the Turks sent ahead at a swifter pace than usual, without waiting, on anyone’s advice, for the following infantry.

### CHAPTER LIV.—Gervase, his men having been killed in battle, is captured alive; King Baldwin mourns greatly.

[Col. 0675D]

The Turks, retreating in pretended flight toward the place of ambush, led Gervase into the midst of the enemy through rocky and trackless mountain places, while his horsemen and infantry were greatly exhausted by their immoderate pace. Then the Turks burst forth from ambush, surrounded Gervase and his men on every side, and overwhelmed them in a fierce charge, ceaselessly shooting bow and arrow against them. They did not allow those vainly sent into flight to return to the mountains.

Terrified by such a multitude, Gervase took flight with a small band across a certain level stretch of marshy ground. But, weary and out of breath from the long pursuit and the softness of the watery soil, they failed in their running. As the Turks enclosed the men on every side, they prevailed greatly against them with arrows and swords [Col. 0676A].

Despairing of flight and life, and seeing the Turks already rushing around their flanks, Gervase and his men forcefully turned their horses’ reins against the enemy. Though very few, they nevertheless avenged themselves with much blood by their right hands, striking down many Turks and there falling among the fierce enemy in an honourable death. None of all these escaped except two squires, who reported the event at Tiberias; the rest were either killed or captured.

Gervase too was captured and carried to Damascus, bound in chains and committed to careful custody. All who heard this cruel report concerning so distinguished a knight and the destruction of his men mourned for many days with vehement grief, weeping and great lamentation. Even King Baldwin—though always hardened against every adversity with the ferocity of lion and boar—was now shattered in spirit, though he wholly concealed his sorrow beneath a cheerful expression [Col. 0676B].

### CHAPTER LV.—An embassy of the Turks to King Baldwin concerning Gervase and the cities of Haifa and Ptolemais.

Some days later Turkish messengers spoke to King Baldwin at Acre in this manner:

“We hold Gervase captive and still alive. If you wish to receive him sound and unharmed, restore to our power the three cities of Ptolemais, Haifa, and Tiberias. Otherwise, know that he can in no way escape the danger of death.”

Having heard this, the king took counsel with his men and replied in these words:

“If you sought gold, silver, or any precious thing for Gervase’s safety and ransom, you could undoubtedly obtain from us more than one hundred thousand byzants [Col. 0676C]. But as for the cities you demand: even if you held my full brother, all my kindred, and all the leading men of the Christian people in your chains, we would never surrender these cities for their lives—much less for one man alone. If you kill him, our strength will not therefore be diminished; rather, with God and our Lord, it is not impossible that someday we shall repay you for his death.”

### CHAPTER LVI.—The Damascenes, failing to obtain the cities from the king, mockingly kill Gervase in the middle of the city.

When the king had thus answered and the Turks no longer had hope concerning the aforesaid cities, Gervase was brought forth into the middle of Damascus. After much mockery, he was pierced by Turkish arrows and breathed out the spirit of life. When this distinguished knight Gervase was dead, Soboas, one of the most powerful Turks, ordered his head cut off. He ordered the skin of the head, with its white and luxuriant hair, left uncut for a long time, to be stripped off and dried because it was of remarkable beauty, so that it might always be raised on a high spear as a sign and memorial of victory, to stir up grief among Christians [Col. 0676D].

### CHAPTER LVII.—How Evermerus brought to King Baldwin letters from the Roman synod and the apostolic lord concerning his restoration.

In the same year in which King Baldwin withdrew from the siege of Sidon, Lord Evermerus, patriarch of Jerusalem, returned from the Roman synod, which he had attended in order to clear himself of every complaint and accusation brought against him by the king and Chancellor Arnulf. In the midst of the Roman Church and in the hearing of the apostolic lord, he made the man who spoke unjustly against him fall silent, his mouth stopped. By the judgement of the Holy Roman Church, he was sent back to the king with letters and the seal of that apostolic lord, Paschal, directing that he should henceforth retain the patriarchal see honourably and without offence [Col. 0677A].

But the king would not listen to the embassy or to the letters bearing the Roman pontiff’s seal concerning his restoration. The patriarch therefore remained in the city of Acre, to see whether the king’s disposition toward him might still, with God’s help, be softened.

### Chapter LVIII.—The King Confirms His Decision: Evermerus Is Deposed, and Gobelin Obtains His See

[Col. 0677B]

At last, since the king, further incited by Arnulf, continued to oppose the patriarch and would not permit him to return to the patriarchal see, it was resolved, on the counsel of many, that Evermerus should voluntarily relinquish the dignity of his patriarchate without councils or judgment and without any hope of recovering it, lest the holy and still newly established Church of Jerusalem be deprived for so many days of a pastor’s watchful care amid this hatred and contention. Thus, after Evermerus had voluntarily and without any hope surrendered the honor of the patriarchate, a certain cleric named Gobelin was substituted for him, by the election of the king, Arnulf the chancellor, and the whole Church; and all acclaimed that Evermerus should become archbishop of Caesarea of Cornelius, which had recently been left without a pastor. [Col. 0678A] Although it was unjust that this dispute should be settled in this way, unless one of them had been condemned by a decree and judgment of the canons, nevertheless, because the Church of Jerusalem was still inexperienced and tender, the Apostolic See allowed it to be done. And so, by the king’s grant and the assent of all the faithful, each was elevated to an office of honor.

### Chapter LIX.—On the Patriarch’s Embezzlement

While these matters were being conducted between the king and the patriarch—the latter denying that he possessed money, while the former demanded money or soldiers—a certain Christian, envoy of Roger, brother of Bohemond, arrived from Apulia and stood before the king. In the hearing of the whole Church, he testified that a few days earlier he had brought to the patriarch one talent of gold, namely a thousand Byzantine coins, so that the patriarch might divide it in just and faithful portions for the envoy’s sins and for the repose of his own soul and those of his family: one portion, that is, for an offering at the Lord’s Sepulchre, for the use of the brethren serving God there; another for the maintenance of the hospital for the sick and other infirm persons; and a third for the king, to strengthen and reward soldiers lacking possessions and arms. [Col. 0678B] But the patriarch, blinded by avarice, kept everything for himself and distributed nothing from the talent either to these persons or to those, as had been enjoined and arranged with him. Convicted before the king of this enormous fraud and breach of trust by suitable witnesses, and no longer able to defend himself, he fell silent. Therefore he was immediately, without delay, deprived of authority over, and the offerings of, the Lord’s Sepulchre; while his chamberlains, dependents, and counsellors were seized and sent into custody.

# Book Eleven

[Col. 0677]

### Chapter I.—William, Count of Sartangis, Having Defeated the King of Damascus, Besieges the Fortress of Arqa

[Col. 0677C]

At the same time when King Baldwin returned from the siege of Sidon, William, Count of Sartangis, fought a battle with the king of Damascus, named Hertoldinus. Having crushed him and his forces in the plain of the castle of Mount Peregrinus, William returned in victory and glory with a thousand mailed horsemen and much plunder. He then besieged with great force the fortress of Arqa, which Duke Godfrey, during the first expedition, had been unable to overcome by many engines or by force. This he did after having inflicted widespread devastation of crops and produce throughout the region every year, acting on the advice of a certain Saracen, because the inhabitants of the place suffered an extreme scarcity of provisions. [Col. 0677D]

### Chapter II.—William Obtains the Same Fortress, Overcome by Hunger

For three weeks he inflicted heavy attacks upon the defenders of the fortress with engines and crossbows, allowing no one either entrance or exit, until the fortress—naturally fortified and unconquerable by human strength—was pressed by famine and surrendered to him. And so it happened. For after three weeks had passed, all the inhabitants were so oppressed by hunger that, on the mountain side where a siege could not be maintained, they pierced the walls and abandoned the fortress, empty of cattle, full of weapons, but with its money and every precious thing already carried away. [Col. 0678C]

When one of William’s army perceived that no defence was being made from the fortress walls, he secretly climbed over the barbicans and walls to investigate; he saw and detected no one, and immediately reported this to his lord and prince William and to all his companions. They at once entered after breaking the bolts and gates, took possession of and fortified the towers and walls, and, retaining the fortress thereafter, invaded and continually ravaged the entire region as far as Damascus.

### Chapter III.—How Bertrand, with the Pisans, Occupied Amiroth, a City of the Greeks

[Col. 0678D]

In the same year, during Lent, at the beginning of March, Bertrand, son of Count Raymond, assembled from every quarter in his own land forces of fighting men and mailed horsemen. With forty galleys carrying four thousand men—one hundred fighting men placed in each galley, apart from the sailors—he sailed from the place and city of Saint-Gilles and arrived at Pisa, a city of Italy. There he took aboard Genoese who had joined in the same vow to go to Jerusalem; after mutual pledges had been confirmed, eighty of their galleys were added to his force. He sailed to Amiroth, a city of the Greek emperor, where they forcibly gathered food and necessities of life from every direction. [Col. 0679A]

### Chapter IV.—How Bertrand, Summoned by the King of the Greeks, Became His Man and Was Rewarded by Him

The emperor soon learned that Bertrand, son of Count Raymond, had occupied Greek territory with a great force and had not hesitated to lay it grievously waste. He immediately sent envoys to him, inviting him to come to him under the protection of his leading men; they were to confer concerning peace, and Bertrand was to receive from the emperor’s gift whatever sum of money he wished. He was also to be restored in the emperor’s friendship and fealty in his father’s place, and then to pass through the emperor’s land with his men. [Col. 0679B]

Bertrand immediately obeyed the king’s command. Leaving the sea by the Arm of Saint George, he went with some selected members of his company to speak with the emperor in his palace; he bound himself to him by oath and became his subject. Then, having received many gifts of gold, silver, and purple cloth from the emperor, he resumed his voyage and set sail as far as the port of Saint Symeon, which Tancred then held under his authority.

### Chapter V.—Tancred, Invited by Bertrand, Hastens to Meet Him

[Col. 0679C]

Bertrand at once, on the counsel of his men, sent messengers to Tancred, ordering them to greet the man and to announce his own arrival and the equipment of his companions, earnestly requesting that Tancred would not refuse to confer with him. Understanding that Bertrand had arrived in great force, Tancred summoned his men from every quarter and came from the city of Antioch to meet him at that same port. They exchanged kisses and spent that night together in great rejoicing. When morning came, Tancred asked why he had arrived.

### Chapter VI.—Bertrand’s Request for Restoration of His Share of Antioch, and Tancred’s Answer

After many courteous words had passed between them, Bertrand asked Tancred, with every expression of humility, not to refuse to restore to him that part of Antioch which his father had first seized on entering the city. [Col. 0679D] Tancred did not reject his request, but imposed this condition: Bertrand must provide him aid and strength in besieging and recovering the city of Mamistra, which Tancred had recently lost after it had been delivered to the emperor through Armenian treachery; otherwise he would give no answer concerning these matters.

Bertrand, however, would not agree to Tancred’s request for the siege of this city, because of the fealty which he did not deny that he had promised to the emperor. Yet, if Tancred were willing, he promised to besiege and take Gibel, because it was a city of Saracens. Tancred again reminded him of Mamistra, but said nothing whatever about Gibel. [Col. 0680A] Bertrand replied that, because of the oath he had made, he would undertake nothing against the emperor or his city.

### Chapter VII.—Tancred, Angered with Bertrand, Warns Him to Leave Antioch as Quickly as Possible

At this Tancred, deeply angered, rejected him and warned him quickly to pass through the land under Tancred’s authority with his company, lest Tancred bring great harm upon him and his men with an assembled force. Immediately an order was issued throughout the whole region that no one should presume to sell necessities of life to Bertrand or his men, if he valued the safety of his limbs.

Hearing this, Bertrand and his men resumed their voyage from the port and came as far as the city of Tortosa, which Count Raymond had newly conquered and taken, and which William of Sartangis then held as his own. [Col. 0680B] It was opened to them without opposition; Bertrand and his men lodged there and feasted on the produce of the land.

### Chapter VIII.—How Bertrand Challenged William Concerning His Father’s Land, and How Tancred Assisted William

When day came, Bertrand sent envoys to his kinsman William, asking him not to deny him the land of Camolla, which his father had seized at the beginning of this expedition, if he wished to retain Bertrand’s service and friendship. William replied that he could not easily comply with this request, since, upon Raymond’s death, the land had fallen to him as an inheritance, and he had defended it from enemies for many days through great dangers and labours.

At length William, troubled by this embassy, took counsel with his men and sent messengers to Tancred, asking him to assist against his kinsman Bertrand; Tancred was to receive Bertrand’s forces and land from his hand, and William would thereafter be his man and knight. [Col. 0680C] Hearing this, Tancred promised Count William every assistance and appointed a day on which he would meet him at Tortosa; then, with their arms and forces joined, they would drive Bertrand and his gathered company from the land and city.

### Chapter IX.—Bertrand’s Embassy to King Baldwin against the Aforesaid Princes, and His Siege of Tripoli

When Bertrand learned of this plan and alliance, he departed from Tortosa and, hastening by sea, on the third day besieged the city of Tripoli with great force by land and sea. [Col. 0680D] Having laid the siege, he sent envoys to Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, to report that he had besieged Tripoli; that William of Sartangis and Tancred, having denied him his father’s cities, had formed an alliance and were preparing to use force against him; and that he therefore greatly needed the king’s aid against these injuries, declaring that he wished to remain in the king’s service.

### Chapter X.—King Baldwin Orders William and Tancred to Meet Him at Tripoli

The king graciously heard his envoys and promised aid. He immediately summoned Pagan of Caiphas and Eustace, surnamed Granarius, and sent them as envoys to Tancred and William with these words:

“Know that Bertrand, your fellow-brother and fellow-Christian, son of Count Raymond, has sought our aid concerning the wrongs which you now inflict upon him regarding the land and cities of his father; this must not be done. [Col. 0681A] For it pleases the whole Church of Jerusalem that you come down to us at Tripoli and restore the cities unjustly taken, both to Bertrand and to Baldwin of Le Bourg and Joscelin of Turbessel; and that, after counsel and an assembly have been held together, we return to concord. Otherwise we shall not be able to retain the land into which we have lately entered against the surrounding enemies, Turks and Saracens.”

### Chapter XI.—The King Arrives at Tripoli and Receives Bertrand as His Man

Meanwhile the king went down to Tripoli with five hundred horsemen and as many foot soldiers, passing peacefully through Tyre, Sidon, and Baurim, because after the siege of Sidon they had obtained from the king, for much gold, a firm and inviolable peace in order to cultivate their crops and vineyards. [Col. 0681B]

Bertrand rejoiced when he saw the king and his force, and there became the king’s man by oath. Three weeks of this siege and assault had already passed before the king’s arrival; neither engines nor the blows and terrors of any mangonels had been able so to shake or overcome the city that its gates were opened to Bertrand, unless the king’s presence had intervened.

### Chapter XII.—How the King Reconciled Four Princes at Tripoli

Having heard the king’s will and message, Tancred restrained William from anger and every assault until they could speak face to face with the king and proceed to him at Tripoli. They immediately gathered seventy men, distinguished horsemen, and went to Tripoli. Shortly afterwards Baldwin of Edessa and Joscelin of Turbessel followed them with a great cavalry force, as the king had commanded. [Col. 0681C]

When all had assembled there and all injuries on both sides had been recounted before the king and his faithful men, Baldwin of Le Bourg and Tancred were reconciled, Tancred graciously forgiving Baldwin for what Baldwin had unjustly held. Bertrand and William also made peace, on the condition that William should retain Arqa and the other places he had acquired, while no one should hinder Bertrand from holding what his father had acquired. The king restored to Tancred the city of Caiphas, the Temple of the Lord, Tiberias, and Nazareth together with all their revenues, having received Tancred’s fealty, so that henceforward he might remain steadfast in the king’s service and affection. [Col. 0681D]

### Chapter XIII.—After the Reconciliation of the Princes, the People of Tripoli Surrender Themselves to the King

When they learned of the concord of such great princes, the Saracens, no longer able to endure the force brought against them and seeking peace, agreed to surrender the city to no one except the king. Having obtained preservation of life and limb, they especially trusted in his faith, lest the Pisans and Genoese, in violation of treaty, should attack them with arms, as they had the people of Ptolemais, and lest they should not be allowed to leave the city peacefully.

The king, having received the city, gave them his hand that they might depart safely, carrying away no more than they could bear on their shoulders. And behold, the city and its gates were opened; the Pisans, Genoese, and the whole army entered, spread everywhere, and fortified the walls and towers. [Col. 0682A]

### Chapter XIV.—On Five Hundred Men of Babylon Hidden in an Underground Cave and Discovered by a Woman

Five hundred mailed and armed soldiers, sent by the king of Babylon to defend the city with its inhabitants, heard that an agreement had been made to hand over the city into Christian hands. They concealed themselves from those entering and searching the city in an underground dwelling, remarkably constructed in masonry. They had vowed and conspired that, in the silence of the first night, they would yield to no sleep until they emerged from their subterranean hiding place and, rushing unexpectedly upon all who were sleeping and resting securely, cut them down with arms amid an outcry.

But a certain woman, captured by Christians in the first taking of the city and severely tortured for money, was at last greatly distressed and near death. [Col. 0682B] She spoke thus to her tormentors:
