“If you were willing to spare my life, restrain your hands from the punishments by which you afflict me, and allow me to leave my chains free, I would undoubtedly provide for your safety and that of your fellow-brethren; and I would disclose to you something by which your lives might remain unharmed, though shortly you will be destroyed, trusting in security, by treachery and remarkable craft. But if I deceive you in any of this, inflict upon me the harsher torments you have devised, and do not allow my life to remain upon the earth for one further hour.”

The soldiers, marvelling at the woman’s words and steadfastness, held secret counsel among themselves and promised her, on their faith, that they would spare her if they found that the truth of these matters agreed with her words. [Col. 0682C] The woman then disclosed the affair and every plot to all of them exactly as it stood, saying:

“Before the capture of this city and the agreement for their safety, the citizens had determined by crafty and secret counsel that five hundred mailed soldiers, excluded from the Christians’ treaty, should enter a certain underground dwelling and conceal themselves there with weapons beneath the buildings of this city. When darkness had fallen and you were sleeping in security, they were all to emerge with a rush and tumult and kill you, unsuspecting and ignorant of this plan, with their weapons.”

When this device for the destruction of Christians had been revealed by the woman to certain Catholic soldiers, and by the soldiers to King Baldwin and the other leading men, [Col. 0682D] the king and all the men, gathered together in arms, immediately rushed upon them and besieged the place from every side. Finally, after the men within had made little resistance, they were overcome by force and heavy assault, bound and brought out, and struck with the sword’s edge; none of them was spared. The woman, however, in accordance with the pledge given her by the faithful, was thereafter free from prison and chains; and all her possessions, both buildings and other property, were restored to her without opposition.

### Chapter XV.—Count William Is Killed by His Squire, and King Baldwin Besieges Baurim

Shortly afterwards William of Sartangis, because of a trivial injury and quarrel in which he had mistreated his squire, was struck through the heart by an arrow in a secret attack made by that man and died. Thus Bertrand alone acquired and subjected the fortress of Arqa and everything under William’s authority. [Col. 0683A]

After the city of Tripoli had been taken and subdued, King Baldwin, on the counsel of Bertrand, son of Count Raymond, whom he had appointed over that city, summoned all men of the Christian name in the following year. In December, amid the cold of winter, he besieged the city of Baurim, called Beirut. It is situated in a narrow and scarcely passable mountain defile, offering a route from the highlands down beside the shore of the deep sea. Bertrand’s ships and those of the Pisans arrived from Tripoli by sea for the city’s siege; while on the plain of the fields the tents of the king and his men were pitched with a great force of Franks, mounted and on foot, ready for every assault. [Col. 0683B]

For many days he besieged it. Daily, and without restraint, he battered and struck the towers and walls with stone-throwing engines, allowing neither citizens nor defenders any respite; moreover, by cutting down and laying waste vineyards and crops, he terrified the city greatly.

### Chapter XVI.—An Embassy from Count Baldwin to King Baldwin: Edessa Was Besieged through Tancred’s Counsel

After some days of the siege had passed and springtime was already approaching, envoys of Baldwin of Le Bourg came from the city of Edessa. They informed the king that, through Tancred’s prompting and suggestion, Turkish princes—namely Arangaldus, Armigazi, and Samarga from the kingdom of Khorasan—had besieged Edessa with a great multitude. [Col. 0683C] They had grievously devastated the country in every direction, harassed Baldwin with continual attacks, and pressed the city with numerous assaults.

The envoys further declared that Baldwin and all the citizens were compelled by the utmost necessity of hunger and defence; therefore, before long, they would need the king’s help against so many thousands of Turks, lest the city, together with its possessions and inhabitants, be taken and subjugated, and lest Baldwin and his men be subjected to a capital sentence. When the king heard this, he ordered the envoys, under penalty of death, to keep this ungrateful report silent. He himself concealed it in remarkable silence, lest, upon hearing of the Turks’ pride and audacity, men’s hearts should be frightened and they should work less vigorously toward the city’s destruction. [Col. 0683D] Thus the king was silent, and the envoys were silent. He pursued no other aim than that engines, showers of stones, and assaults should be brought against the city walls until the inner strength of the Saracens had been subdued, the surrendered city had been opened, and the citizens were either punished by the sword or captured as conquered men.

### Chapter XVII.—While King Baldwin Vigorously Assaults Baurim, the Citizens Voluntarily Surrender

At last, after the gates with their bolts and the walls had been severely battered, the amir of the city fled by ship at night with many desperate men to the island called Cyprus, which belonged to the Greek realm. They had no confidence that they could survive or remain in defence of the city, because no aid came from the king of Babylon as the days passed.

The citizens, seeing [Col. 0684A] that the amir and all the commanders had fled, that the city could not be held against the Christian king, and that an intolerable war had for so long threatened from every side by land and sea, could endure no longer. They asked that hands be given to them and their lives spared, so that, once the gates were opened, they might leave the city safely. This was done. Hands were given; the citizens departed in peace; and the city was taken and opened on Friday, the day before the Saturday of holy Pentecost.

But of those who were still found in the city—who, foolishly remaining behind, had not departed under the treaty—about twenty-one thousand were killed by Bertrand and the Pisans. They found little in the way of precious clothing or any adornment. For the despairing inhabitants had gathered what was more valuable in the middle of the city and melted it by fire; gold, silver, and precious vessels had been secretly and gradually carried by hidden routes at night to the island of Cyprus. [Col. 0684B]

### Chapter XVIII.—After Taking Baurim, the King Proceeds to Jerusalem and Exhorts the Princes to Liberate Edessa

After the city was taken, the king appointed guards in it and returned to Jerusalem. There, after celebrating the feast of Pentecost, he for the first time disclosed to Bertrand and to all his own household and that of Jerusalem the siege of Edessa, or Rohas, and the wrongs suffered by Baldwin of Le Bourg, as he had learned them from the envoys. He exhorted them all in these words:

“By the grace of God and the will of our Lord Jesus Christ, our purpose and victory concerning Beirut have been accomplished, although we fought to take it for a long time. [Col. 0684C] But now I seek the goodwill of you all, that we may aid the city of Edessa and Baldwin, who is besieged there. Let no one turn away, since they are brethren, ready to assist us in every need. For charity requires us inviolably to give aid and not hesitate to lay down our lives for brethren and friends.”

### Chapter XIX.—At the King’s Exhortation, Bertrand and the Others Set Out for Edessa

At these words of the king, all who were present from the kingdom of Jerusalem willingly undertook the expedition to Edessa, to bring aid to their besieged fellow-Christians, to make war upon the Turks, and to give their lives for their brethren. They renewed their preparations; forgetting the labours still fresh from Beirut, they set out on the road to Edessa at the beginning of June, in helmets and mail, in companies of seven hundred chosen horsemen, and with a force of three hundred foot soldiers highly skilled with bow and lance. [Col. 0684D]

Thus the king departed, and Bertrand departed with his forces, from the city of Jerusalem, which had been secured by the vigilant and careful foresight of soldiers; the other cities under their authority had also been fortified. They went down into the plains and region of Armenia and arrived at the city of Edessa after a journey of one month. On hearing of the king’s arrival, many Frankish and Armenian Christians came to join them in aid from various places and fortresses, by hundreds, sixties, and fifties. They had scarcely reached the River Euphrates when his army had increased to fifteen thousand fighting men.

### Chapter XX.—On the King’s Arrival, the Turks Leave Edessa; and Count Baldwin Accuses Tancred

[Col. 0685A]

When he entered the territory and borders of the city with this strong force, amid the splendour of banners and helmets glittering in the brilliant rays of the summer sun, with the great sound of trumpets and the tumultuous arrival of the people, the Turks learned through their scouts that he was approaching. They tore down their tents and withdrew from the siege, moving their camp into the territory of the city of Harran, six miles from Edessa, where they remained until they could learn and determine whether they could meet and resist the king’s forces and troops.

After they had been absent from the besieging position at Edessa for one day, Baldwin of Le Bourg rejoiced at the report of the king’s arrival. Hastening from the city to meet him with four hundred warlike horsemen and ten thousand Armenians, [Col. 0685B] he informed him that the Turks had turned toward Harran, but were still waiting in camp and listening for news of the king’s intention, being excessively confident in four hundred thousand horsemen. He reported that these men had assembled for the siege of Edessa through Tancred’s counsel and prompting, and that Tancred was in every respect hostile and opposed to him.

### Chapter XXI.—King Baldwin’s Embassy to Tancred and Their Conference

Having heard Baldwin’s complaint concerning Tancred’s injuries, the king, on the counsel of his men, sent an embassy to Tancred at Antioch, summoning him to come down to the king and the principal men of the Christian army. If Baldwin had wronged Tancred in any respect, the king declared that he wished to settle everything either by equitable judgment or by the harmonious counsel of the leading men in the presence of the Christians. [Col. 0685C]

Tancred strongly resisted coming. At last, on the counsel of his men, he came down with fifteen hundred mailed soldiers to hear and answer all the accusations made against him by Baldwin of Le Bourg, and to set out before all men whatever accusations he had against Baldwin. On arriving, he greeted the king and was graciously received by him.

Then the king, in the presence of the assembly of the faithful, asked him why he had led Turks against brethren and fellow-Christians when he ought rather to have aided the Christians. Tancred did not attempt to excuse himself; he replied that he had not aided them for this reason: Baldwin, governor of the city of Edessa, had shown him no regard, although in former days Edessa itself and many other cities of that kingdom had belonged to Antioch and had paid annual revenues to the ruler of Antioch. [Col. 0685D]

### Chapter XXII.—The King Addresses Tancred Concerning Reconciliation with the Princes

King Baldwin gently restrained Tancred in this complaint, saying:

“My brother Tancred, you demand an unjust thing; nor should you speak of any tribute as a just grievance against Baldwin, although the cities have hitherto paid it to Antioch. For in all that God shall subject to our rule, we are to have nothing to do with the law of the Gentiles. You know, and it is known to all Christians, how, when we left our land and kindred, seeking exile for the name of Jesus and abandoning our inheritances, we resolved that whatever any one of us should seize in this land of our pilgrimage from the kingdoms and lands of the Gentiles which he had conquered, he should hold peacefully and freely. No one was to raise a hand against him in injury, but rather each was to give assistance and lay down his life for his brethren. [Col. 0686A]

“Therefore know that you have no just complaint against Baldwin, since the ordinances of the Gentiles do not agree with ours. By firm counsel we have agreed upon this: if the affairs of Christians should prosper so greatly that we establish a king, we should follow him as our head, ruler, and defender, subject to him for preserving and extending what is ours. Therefore, from fear of God and by the just judgment of all Christians now present, you must return to concord and turn your mind away from every grievance you hold against Baldwin. [Col. 0686B] Otherwise, if you wish to ally yourself with Gentiles and plot against our people, you cannot remain a brother of Christians. We too are ready, according to our decree, to be helpers and defenders in all things for our Christian fellow-brother.”

Tancred understood that the king had rebuked him justly in the judgment of all, and that he had no just defence against these words. He returned to concord and friendship; moved by penitence because he had plotted anything with Gentiles against his fellow-brother, he promised henceforth to remain an unfailing, pure, and faithful helper of his brethren, as he had vowed at the beginning of the expedition.

### Chapter XXIII.—After Reconciling the Princes, the King Drives off the Turks and Reconciles All Christians in the Region

[Col. 0686C]

After this peace had been arranged, their forces and arms having been joined, the king and Tancred pursued the Turks toward Harran in order to fight them. But when the Turks learned of their reconciliation, they fled, dispersing through byways and mountains. Many from their company were nevertheless destroyed; livestock and a considerable quantity of provisions were seized and carried off.

King Baldwin returned from the pursuit and destruction of the enemy and stayed for a few days in the land of Edessa, repairing and settling everywhere the hatreds and disputes he found among Christians.

### Chapter XXIV.—The King and Tancred Cross the Euphrates; Five Thousand Christians on the Other Side Are Killed by the Enemy

[Col. 0686D]

The king and Tancred had scarcely reached the River Euphrates in haste, travelling continuously by day and night, when the Turks, gathering forces and troops from every direction, swiftly pursued them in order to strike them from behind and attack them with arrows, charging and shouting as was their custom.

But the king, learning of their approach and audacity, hastened to cross the river with his entire force in only two boats. Yet by unhappy chance, after the king and Tancred had crossed with a large part of their army, both boats, too heavily laden with arms and soldiers, began to founder and sink amid the waves. Thus the rest of the force, about five thousand men remaining on the other side of the water, could no longer be conveyed across either by oars or by any aid. [Col. 0687A]

Without delay, the Turks arrived in great numbers in the heat of midday. Charging fiercely upon the wretched multitude, which could not escape the river crossing, they cruelly killed them with bows and arrows, while the king, Tancred, and all those stationed on this side of the river looked on. The king became deeply sorrowful and grieved because the boats had perished and he had been unable to aid his men as they fell before his eyes.

### Chapter XXV.—The King Brings Count Baldwin, Fleeing from Battle, Back Safe to Edessa

After this bloody slaughter the Turks returned into the land of Edessa. Baldwin of Le Bourg, who was following the king with three hundred horsemen, met them. Unable to turn aside, he dared to engage them in battle. But the Turks, prevailing through the strength of their numbers, pierced them all with arrows. Baldwin alone fled toward the mountains and scarcely escaped their hands.

On the following day the cruel report of this grave disaster reached the ears of the king and Tancred. [Col. 0687B] They immediately prepared boats and crossed the river with their men, intending to exact a fitting penalty if they found the Turks anywhere. But, finding and seeing none of them, they found Baldwin of Le Bourg desolate, sorrowful, and weeping over the slaughter of his men; with a strong Frankish force they brought him alive and unharmed to Edessa.

### Chapter XXVI.—On Magnus, King of Norway, Who Came to Venerate Jerusalem

Meanwhile Magnus, brother of the king of Norway, came in great array, heavily armed and with a strong force: forty ships and ten thousand fighting men. Having sailed for two years around the broad sea from his own kingdom, he cast anchor at the port of the city of Ascalon for the whole duration of a day and night, to see whether any men from the city would come out to meet him by land or sea, with whom he might enter into some encounter, whether by design or chance. [Col. 0687C] But the Ascalonites remained silent and did not dare to come out; on the following day he arrived at Jaffa, desiring to venerate Jerusalem.

### Chapter XXVII.—On the Men of Babylon Sailing against Baurim, and on Christian Ships Fighting Them

A few days later, an incomparable naval force came from the kingdom of Babylon to the city of Beirut, or Baurim, to recover the city if an opportunity should be given. It consisted of galleys and of biremes and triremes, commonly called *catti*, equipped with towers and fitted out for war. After remaining there for a day and provoking the Christian guards, they were unable to injure or overcome them by any device.

They gained no advantage by force or skill; instead, while besieging the city in a wide circuit, they observed from the masthead ships in the distance. Three had come from Flanders and Antwerp, commanded by William, Starcolphus, and Bernard, sailing to venerate Jerusalem. A fourth, from the Greek kingdom, carried various merchandise and provisions and had likewise set out by sea for trade. [Col. 0688A]

When they saw these ships and recognized the sign of Christianity, the enemy strove from every side with oars, buzes, and galleys to surround and capture them. Hastening toward them with great exertion of rowing, they forced them into flight by a heavy pursuit. But, with God’s grace assisting, they hastened their course with swifter sails and oars. One escaped to the city of Caiphas, whose Christian inhabitants gave it aid from land with bows and arrows. Two others, shaken by the weight of their great hulls, escaped between Caiphas and Acre after the water became too shallow, Christians likewise hurrying to aid them. The fourth, from the Greek kingdom, being delayed too greatly, was captured and retained, and stripped of all its goods.

### Chapter XXVIII.—How the Ascalonites, Warring against Jerusalem, Were Defeated by the Christians
[Col. 0688B] At the same time, in the same month of August when these events were taking place, the people of Ascalon, rejoicing at the absence and prolonged expedition of King Baldwin, and judging that only slight forces of soldiers remained in Jerusalem, gathered five hundred horsemen and resolved to besiege and capture the city and to challenge in battle the men who were in the citadel of the Tower of David. But Christ’s faithful, having learned of their plan and approach, sent throughout Ramla, Assur, Joppa, Caiphas, and Caesarea to all who obeyed King Baldwin, urging them without delay to hasten to Jerusalem by day and night and defend the city and its citadel from the enemy assault.

They immediately hurried from every side, entered the city in the silence of night, and strengthened the gates with watchful guards, both clergy [Col. 0688C] and women, and the towers with the loyal diligence of soldiers. The remaining three hundred soldiers, massed with weapons and arrows, descended on horseback and on foot through the hills to the place where the road of the Ascalonites was expected to pass. And behold, the Ascalonites arrived in a great body of cavalry and with full equipment, meeting the Christians in the open field. When battle had long been joined with weapons and arrows, at last the Ascalonites turned their backs. The Christians pursued them, killed two hundred, and brought horses and much spoil, together with many captives, to Jerusalem in joy and unexpected victory.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—How the naval force of the Babylonians attacked Ptolemais, and the king came to the aid of its citizens.

The naval force which had sailed out from Babylonia and was preparing ambushes for the Christians at sea turned from Baurim toward Ptolemais. Rising in great strength from the height of their ships’ masts, they so oppressed and harassed the defenders of the city in war that, invading with a multitude and strength of ships, they held almost the entire harbor for about eight days. Meanwhile, while great devastation was occurring in the city of Ptolemais, and scarcely did the harbor-chain resist the enemy so that they might not seize the city, King Baldwin, Bertram of Antioch, and Rohas, with their entire force still undivided, prepared to return. On hearing of the Babylonian gathering and attack against Accaron, they hastened by the quickest route, so that they might assist their own men and free them from hostile attack.

### CHAPTER XXX.—How King Baldwin gloriously conducted King Magnus to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0689A]

But the king, having left part of his army to assist the Christian citizens of Ptolemais, first turned, on the advice of prudent men, to Joppa, to the king of Norway, so that, hearing from his own lips, he might know what action was first required and could be undertaken. Soon, after the two had been bound together by every bond of affection, the king named Magnus earnestly begged King Baldwin to proceed with him on the road to worship in Jerusalem, by the authority of the Lord Jesus, who commands His faithful first to seek the kingdom of God, and afterward to find all things useful to those who seek; then to undertake whatever he might choose, or to besiege a city with his naval army.

King Baldwin most willingly complied with the desires of King Magnus and his leading men [Col. 0689B]; and he did not refuse to go with them to Jerusalem, as he had vowed. Accordingly, when both kings ascended into the holy city, all the clergy in white garments and in every adornment of divine worship came forth in hymns and songs with all the citizens and people, and conducted the kings with all their retinues as far as the Lord’s Sepulchre with cries of exultation. King Baldwin indeed led King Magnus by the hand, honorably and with familiar affection, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, which urges us to “outdo one another in showing honor” (Rom. 12:10). He led him and showed him all the holy places and those matters known to himself, and for several days provided for him with abundant service and royal display. Then, that they might be strengthened more and more in affection and faith, [Col. 0689C] he went down with him in a strong force to the River Jordan. There, after the Catholic rite had been performed in the name of the Lord Jesus, he brought King Magnus back to Jerusalem safe, in glory and rejoicing, and secure from every danger.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—How these two kings besieged Sidon after the Babylonians had returned home.

After returning to Jerusalem, they convened the church and, by common counsel, resolved to besiege by land and sea Sagitta, or Sidon, which had often resisted the king and inflicted many injuries and grievances upon pilgrims; and never to withdraw until the captured city had been delivered into Christian hands. Without much delay, King Baldwin and Bertram, having gathered forces, encamped with abundant equipment for the siege of the city of Sagitta [Col. 0689D], setting up engines and stone-throwing devices with which the city might be attacked daily.

King Magnus moved his naval forces from Joppa and put in at the city of Sagitta, so that by besieging and attacking it from the sea he would allow neither entrance nor exit on that side. The Babylonian naval force, understanding that the equipment and forces of these most powerful men and great kings were present by land and sea, withdrew from the harbor of Ptolemais and its attack to the harbor of Sur, that is, Tyre. There it delayed, lest King Magnus should disturb it in naval battle while it was found at the siege of Ptolemais. Yet some of the Babylonians, relying on very swift *buzæ*, ranged to and fro over the open waters with great effort, if perhaps by some chance they might overcome and carry off Catholic men. [Col. 0690A] But the Babylonians succeeded not at all; therefore, fearing the boldness and skill of King Baldwin, they returned to Babylonia by sea.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—King Baldwin and his men, surrounding the Sidonians, brought up several engines.

King Baldwin and Bertram, having summoned their forces, established the siege from land; the king of Norway, casting anchor with all his host, secured his position on the seaward side around the city. With the siege thus placed, they pressed the walls and towers of the city with every effort, by assaults and frequent breaches; while the citizens, on the other hand, stoutly resisted from within with weapons and stone-throwing engines. They brought up an engine that had been constructed over many days and placed in it men with Balearic bows, who, elevated by the height of the engine’s platforms, looked down over the walls [Col. 0690B] into the city, the towers, and its defenses; and thus, striking through lanes and streets, they afflicted the inhabitants with intolerable blows.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—The Sidonians attempt to burn the king’s engine by a hidden excavation, but are cleverly forestalled by him.

But the citizens, seeing that the engine rose above the city and harmed its inhabitants, made, in the darkness of night, an excavation beneath the foundations of the walls, with great effort and remarkable skill. Their purpose was that, after the excavation had been made through the walls as far as the station of the engine, they might carry dry wood and fuel for fire into it; and when these had suddenly been reduced to ashes, the engine might collapse with the earth and instantly suffocate the men placed in it. But the king, forewarned of this wicked device by the report of certain persons, [Col. 0690C] moved the engine away from the place of excavation; and thus the Sidonians’ labor was spent in vain.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—After a long siege, the Sidonians surrender to King Baldwin, and about five thousand leave the city.

At last, after the course of six weeks, the Sidonians, seeing that they could accomplish nothing against the engine, that the city and its gates were continually shaken by stone-throwers, and that they were no less hard pressed by the naval assault, while the Babylonian naval force was absent, asked that terms be granted them and that the city, with its towers and keys, be surrendered into the king’s hands, on this condition: that the *amiraldus*, the governor of the city, and those of his party might depart peacefully with their possessions, carrying as much as they could bear upon neck and shoulders.

The king, wearied by the long siege and assault, after taking counsel [Col. 0690D] with the king of Norway, Count Bertram, and the other sensible men, yielded to the Sidonians’ request. Thus, after the city had been surrendered and opened to his power, about five thousand Sidonians departed peacefully with their *amiraldus* and their possessions, making for Ascalon; those who remained were brought beneath the king’s yoke and into his servitude.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—How the *amiraldus* of Ascalon secretly came to Jerusalem and surrendered Ascalon.

After this, the city having been placed in the hands and keeping of his men, King Baldwin went up to Jerusalem in glory and victory on the feast-day of Saint Thomas the Apostle. There, after the Nativity of the Lord had been gloriously and according to Catholic rite celebrated, his name was exalted in victory throughout all the cities of the pagans [Col. 0691A]; and fear seized all who heard that everything had prospered for him, and for many days they ceased from every attack and assault.

Thereafter, when Easter of the Lord had been solemnly celebrated by King Baldwin and by the whole Church, the *amiraldus*, that is, prince of Ascalon—whether touched, I know not, by a spirit of fear or of divine love—began through intermediaries to address the lord king and to negotiate with him concerning the surrender of the city. At length the same *amiraldus*, after giving and receiving a pledge of faith, entered Jerusalem to the king and disclosed everything to him, as he had determined in heart and mind concerning the surrender of the city, the admission of the king himself and his men, and the devotion of fidelity to be shown toward the king and his followers.

Finally, when the purity of his devotion and purpose of mind had been recognized and established, and mutual pledges of faith had been exchanged, it was decreed [Col. 0691B], first by the counsel of the king and his princes, that the king should remain in Jerusalem, but that three hundred of his military and fighting men should go down with the *amiraldus* to Ascalon, enter the city, take possession of its towers, and subject all the citizens to the king. Going down accordingly, as had been decreed, they entered the gates with the assistance and consent of the *amiraldus*, seized the walls, and brought the citizens under the king’s authority.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—The embassy of Count Baldwin to King Baldwin concerning the coming of the Turks, and the report that the son of the Babylonian king was descending upon Ascalon.

Without delay, when the aforesaid soldiers had taken possession of the city and, from the hand of the *amiraldus*, had transferred everything to the king’s power, while the king sat in Jerusalem in great might and glory, envoys of Baldwin of Burg entered before the king and spoke as follows:

“The Turks [Col. 0691C] from the kingdom of Khorasan, having marched out in great strength with two hundred thousand stout horsemen, have besieged the fortress of Turbaysel, laying waste the land with plunder and every devastation against the Christians. He [Baldwin of Burg], having gathered forces of horse and foot, descended as far as the place called Solome. There, while he delayed for several days because of the Turkish forces that had assembled from Damascus to oppose him, a grievous report became known: the son of the king of Babylonia had descended upon Ascalon, in order to attack the Christian soldiers found there and restore the city to his own authority.”

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—When King Baldwin descended upon Ascalon, the son of the Babylonian king, admitted by the citizens, killed the Christians found there.

[Col. 0691D] On hearing this, the king postponed his journey and returned to Ascalon, if perhaps he might assist his men. But the citizens who inhabited the city, seeing the force of Babylonia present and the absence of King Baldwin, assembled one day, struck the *amiraldus* down at sword’s edge, and, opening the gates, admitted the son of the king of Babylonia into the city. Once admitted, before King Baldwin could reach the territory of Ascalon, he killed at sword’s edge all the Catholic soldiers who were dispersed along the walls, terrified and suddenly overcome. He then strengthened the city with bolts and every Saracen guard.

King Baldwin therefore hastened onward; but when he learned of the destruction of his men, the loss of the city through the citizens’ treachery, and the killing of the *amiraldus* by fraud, he returned to Jerusalem, since at that time [Col. 0692A] there was no opportunity to assault the city and avenge his beheaded men.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—How Count Joscelin pursued two hundred thousand Turks besieging Turbaysel and marching toward Antioch.

Meanwhile Malducus, Arongaldus, Armigazi, and Samarga, who had gathered an army of two hundred thousand horsemen and besieged Turbaysel, spent two months digging beneath the mountains of that fortress with immense effort, so that the wells and cisterns might run dry and they might capture Joscelin, defender of the place, together with those dwelling with him. But after excessive labor, seeing that they made no progress in demolishing and digging through the mountains, they proceeded from there toward Antioch with one hundred thousand men. The other hundred thousand, because of the excessive and protracted delay, during which the necessities of life were diminishing, resolved to return to the land of Khorasan.

Joscelin, learning of their return and division, pursued those returning with one hundred and fifty horsemen and one hundred infantrymen. Falling upon those who followed behind and had been delayed, encumbered with wagons of provisions, he cut down a thousand and carried off to the fortress great booty with spoils. [Col. 0692B]

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—Concerning the hundred thousand Turks who wickedly beheaded the hostage-son of Brodoan, prince of Aleppo.

The remaining multitude of one hundred thousand Turks reached Aleppo and begged Brodoan, prince of the city, to receive their wives, young sons, and daughters for protection until they should see the outcome of their victory. But he refused them, because peace existed between him and Tancred. He promised them only that he would give aid to neither side, either one or the other; and for this reason he gave his son to them as a hostage.

The Turks held his son; after a little while, violating their pledged faith, they firmly declared that they would behead him unless he aided them and sheltered their sons and daughters, together with their wives and baggage, within the walls because of the uncertain outcome of war. When he refused because of the treaty he had made with Tancred, they did not shrink from putting his son to death by capital sentence before the eyes of his father and the sight of all his people. Having thus so wickedly and treacherously beheaded Brodoan’s son, they went to Caesarea Philippi, situated near the mountains of Gibel, one day’s journey from Antioch [Col. 0692D]; there they pitched their tents above the River Farfar and encamped.

### CHAPTER XL.—The gathering at Antioch of King Baldwin and the Christian princes against the Turks.

Joscelin, hearing that the Turks had turned from Turbaysel, which is Bersabee, toward Antioch, hastened without any delay to Antioch to aid Tancred, with one hundred horsemen and fifty infantrymen. Baldwin of Burg also hastened with two hundred horsemen and one hundred infantrymen; Pagan of Sororgia likewise with fifty horsemen and thirty infantrymen. In addition, Hugh of Cantalar, namely of the estate of Hunnine, joined the aid with his companions.

Richard, governor of the city of Maresch, also came [Col. 0693A] with sixty horsemen and one hundred infantrymen; likewise Guy of Gresalt, William of Albin, Guy surnamed Capreolus, ruler of the cities of Tarsus and Mamistra. The bishop of Tarsus came, and also the bishop of Albaria. William, son of the count of the Normans, who held lordship over the city of Tortosa, which Tancred had taken from Bertram, joined with his followers. Engelger, governor of the city of Femia, came with two hundred horsemen. Bonaplius came, holding the city of Sarmit; Guy surnamed Fraxinus came, holding the city of Harich; Robert of Sidon, Rotger of Montmarin, holding the fortress of Hap; Piractus, holding Talaminiam. Pancras and Corrovasilius of the city of Crasson came; likewise Ursinus from the mountains of Antioch [Col. 0693B], and also Antevellus and his brother Leo.

Martin, count of Laodicea, came; Tancred had made that city subject to his own right after driving out and defeating the soldiers of the Greek emperor. Robert of the Old Bridge also came, an outstanding and tireless knight who had often plundered the lands of the pagans by military force. All these were Tancred’s soldiers; men from the entire principality of Antioch assembled in the royal city. King Baldwin had likewise hurried there from Jerusalem after the destruction of his men in the city of Ascalon; with him were Bertram, Eustace Granarius, Walter of Saint Abraham, the lord patriarch Ghibelin, and the remaining multitude of the faithful. About four thousand gathered in that same place in a strong force and passed the night until morning. At dawn [Col. 0693C] they proceeded as far as the castle of Giril.

### CHAPTER XLI.—How sixteen thousand Christians drew up their battle-lines against the Turks and were endangered by severe famine.

On the third day after they had assembled in one body from all places and fortresses, they arranged their battle-lines and set out on the road toward Caesarea, where the Turkish forces had gathered like the sand upon the seashore. The Christian army amounted to about twenty-six thousand horsemen and infantrymen, fighting men. Seeing that the Christian force had approached, the Turks crossed to the other bank of the River Farfar and pitched their tents there in a broad place.

[Col. 0693D] They remained in that place on both sides for sixteen days. But the Christians could not engage the Turks in a set battle because of the latter’s extraordinary raiding and circling over the fields in every direction, which they contrived against the Christians by the speed of their horses. These Turks also compelled all the surrounding towns and fortified places, by great threats and terrors, not to bring anything for sale to the Christians. Therefore, for six days they were so pressed by want of bread, and especially of fodder for horses, that more than a thousand seemed likely to perish through famine and pestilence.

### CHAPTER XLII.—How, though battle-lines were repeatedly drawn up on both sides, the Turks took flight.

On the fifteenth day the Christians again arranged their ranks; the Turks arranged theirs as well. Thus, when three battle-lines had been drawn up on both sides, the Christians, exceedingly eager for the slaughter of the enemy, advanced with excessive haste against the hostile formations. But having moved too far away from their companions, and being harassed by an unrestrained hail of arrows, they returned in flight to the army, with many wounded and with very many men, together with horses, mules, and all their spoils, taken captive.

[Col. 0694A] Seeing their men exhausted in battle and driven back in flight as far as the army, Baldwin and Tancred raised the sign of the Holy Cross and, with loose reins, charged against the Turks in hope of salvation and victory. But the Turks, in their customary manner, fled by hundreds and hundreds, by thousands and thousands, never allowing battle to be joined with them. Then, when a certain day had dawned, the Turks took counsel and returned to the land of Khorasan, because they had been unable to harm Antioch, and because the Christian force had confronted them and could not be frightened away either by battle or arrows. These events occurred at the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, in autumn, when all crops are usually reaped and gathered.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—How, after the departure of the Turks, Tancred besieged the fortress of Gerez for many days.

[Col. 0694B]

In that same year, after the departure of the king and the other great men who had come together to aid him, Tancred retained his forces and, in October, strongly besieged the fortress of Gerez, called Sarepta of the Sidonians because it had once been subject to the king of Sidon. But he found it fortified with Turkish weapons and guards; it was also found to be exceedingly strong on every side by the construction of its towers and walls [Col. 0694C]. This almost impregnable fortress lay six miles from the city of Aleppo, which Brodoan defended by his arms.

Tancred, seeing the fortress extremely strong and very securely defended by the Turks, ordered engines and stone-throwers to be made over many days. Disposing his men around the fortress on every side, in twelve divisions, he attacked it day and night, battering down its towers and walls. Tancred also surrounded his own men with a most secure rampart and strengthened it with vigilant guards, lest the enemy suddenly and cunningly break in upon him or his men, divided among the siege positions, engage them in battle, and thus easily defeat them.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—How Tancred at last overcame the city of Gerez by many devices and obtained its entire territory.

[Col. 0694D]

Thus Tancred, having brought his engines against the wall and towers and stationed his men under the protection of the rampart, inflicted destruction on the fortress for many days. Then, on a Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord, the principal castle, shaken by repeated blows of stones, collapsed. Falling from on high, it crushed by its fall and unbearable weight the two towers adjoining it, and thus opened a way for Tancred and his followers.

Tancred now pressed the enemy in the fortress more closely and vigorously than before, striving to come face to face with them within under a roof of shields. But he still could not confidently enter because of the mass of stones blocking the approaches [Col. 0695A], and because hostile missiles hurled by the Turks opposed him. The Turkish defenders of the fortress, seeing the ruin of their towers and that Tancred had besieged them for a long time and had resolved to continue until the fortress was taken, asked that terms be granted. Having taken from them purple cloth and other valuables in gold and silver, he allowed them to leave the fortress, and they surrendered themselves to his power. Thus Tancred became possessor and lord of this fortress and of the entire region.

### CHAPTER XLV.—How Tancred besieged another fortress, named Vetule, with a certain *amiraldus* allied to him.

In the same year, during Lent, after Sarepta had been captured, its walls and towers rebuilt, and guards stationed there, Tancred gathered forces and besieged for three months the castle called Vetule, situated in the mountains [Col. 0695B] in the region of Gibel. But he left one side unbesieged because of the difficult terrain and the forces of the Saracens, who were more abundantly stationed on that side. The siege having been laid, they collected plunder everywhere, captured pagans, and inflicted much damage.

At length a certain *amiraldus*, seeing that the regions were being grievously ravaged by Tancred’s army, made a treaty with him that Tancred should not enter his territory for plunder. In return, he would besiege the unbesieged side of the fortress, because he knew paths which no skill of the Franks could discover, being untraceable. This was done. For after making this treaty with him, Tancred assigned him ten horsemen and one hundred infantrymen as assistance, so that under his guidance and with his local knowledge [Col. 0695C] he might occupy the unbesieged position beforehand, allowing no exit or entrance there.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—While this *amiraldus* and Tancred were surrounding Vetule in siege, he barely escaped by flight when the citizens burst out from the city.

The *amiraldus*, taking Tancred’s soldiers with him and gathering five hundred of his own men, besieged the difficult positions. There they built lodgings and encampments, intending to maintain the siege there for some days, and were heavily burdened by labor and exertion. Wearied and exhausted by the difficult route and work, and sunk in heavy sleep, they were unexpectedly attacked in their camp at the first watch of the night by Turks and Saracens with many thousands. At the same time all the defenders burst from the fortress; when the signal and shouting were heard, they fought until morning and cut down one hundred infantrymen.

The *amiraldus*, grievously wounded, barely escaped with ten knights; but the five hundred soldiers, entering the fortress with the Saracens in false faith, were separated from their leader and *amiraldus*. [Col. 0696A]

### CHAPTER XLVII.—How Tancred, after a long siege, obtained the city of Vetule and all its region.

[Col. 0696B] Tancred, always undaunted, strengthened the siege still more and brought twelve mangonels against the city walls, until within one month he had battered through the barbicans and towers into the interior of the fortress. But when the defenders saw that they could in no way endure the stone-projectiles, in the silence of one night they set fire to certain wooden buildings and escaped by flight. Tancred, seeing at evening that the fortress was burning and learning that the men had fled, boldly entered with his companions, fortified the towers with his own garrison, and began to conquer and subdue the region.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—On the death of Duke Bohemond.

[Col. 0696C] In this year Bohemond, Tancred’s uncle, was seized by illness and died at the city of Bari; he was buried according to Catholic rite in the church of Saint Nicholas. This was at the time when Henry V, king and fourth emperor, cruelly overcame at sword’s edge in Rome many enemies resisting him with hostile force, and powerfully and gloriously retained the kingdom and empire by the hereditary right of his forebears.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0695]

### CHAPTER I.—How King Baldwin took counsel concerning the siege of Tyre.

[Col. 0695D]

In the second year after Sidon had been captured and Tancred had attacked and taken Sarepta, King Baldwin, having summoned the whole Church of Jerusalem from all the places under his authority, took counsel about besieging Sur, which still rebelled and inflicted injuries upon fellow Christian brethren by land and sea, and had withdrawn from all tribute and agreement which it had falsely promised to the king. When all had been admonished and volunteers for this siege had been found, a day was appointed on which they should assemble and, according to the king’s decree, pitch tents, surround the walls with a rampart, and hem them in.

### CHAPTER II.—How the Tyrians made and concluded an alliance with the prince of Damascus against the king.

[Col. 0696D]

When such news sounded in the ears of the Tyrians, they were greatly alarmed and made an alliance with a certain Dochinus, prince of Damascus, so that they might obtain protection and assistance from him and, with his consent and permission, convey the treasures of the city and their more precious possessions for safekeeping into a treasury and storeroom at Damascus. They also asked him to send archers and defenders of the city to assist them for stipulated payment, promising to give him and his men twenty thousand Byzantine solidi.

### CHAPTER III.—Concerning Reinfrid, a Christian knight, through whose guidance the nobles of Tyre were put in chains by the king.

[Col. 0697A]

This agreement, therefore, having been mutually made, confirmed, and established by exchanged pledges of faith, the citizens of Tyre approached a certain Reinfrid by name, a Christian man and distinguished knight of the king. They promised and gave him a reward of one thousand Byzantine coins, so that under his guidance they might peacefully transport the loads of their treasures to Damascus and return unhindered with camels and wagons.

But Reinfrid, a fickle man who did not greatly care if he violated faith toward pagans and unbelievers, reported everything to the king and disclosed the day on which they would travel to Damascus with all their forces and precious goods, asserting that the king could capture and retain all these things without opposition. On hearing this, the king [Col. 0697B] immediately summoned infantry and two hundred knights and ordered them to block and carefully watch the roads by which the men would set out for Damascus with their loads.

And behold, in the silence of night, when all things are usually at rest, the Tyrians came onto the Damascus road with their camels, innumerable gold, silver, purple cloth, and every kind of precious ornament, led by the aforesaid Reinfrid. Suddenly the king’s ambush fell upon them: some were killed, others seized; and they carried off limitless treasures, precious purple, and silk of diverse colors and workmanship, together with Reinfrid himself, in the wagons of camels and mules.

### CHAPTER IV.—How the prince of Damascus assisted the Tyrians, and how the king besieged them.

Marvellous and unheard-of treasures were captured there, and the king generously bestowed them with liberal hand upon soldiers long oppressed by want. After these men had been captured, some killed, and a few escaped, Dochinus, in whom they had hoped for refuge, was deeply troubled. Without delay he sent to the city of Tyre five hundred soldiers skilled with arrow and bow, so that they might forestall the king’s siege, resist the king and his men from the city, and assist the citizens for stipulated payment.

King Baldwin therefore, descending from Jerusalem in strength and with an equipment of ten thousand men, occupied the city walls on land, having pitched camp on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle. On the seaward side, however, at the city’s flank and harbor, the naval blockade was not of great strength or armament. For the king of the Greeks had promised that forces would be present there by water [Col. 0697D]; but, as winter came on, they were not assembled.

### CHAPTER V.—How, while the king was enclosing the city, the Tyrians came out through the gates but were soon wonderfully repelled by the king, and killed some who entered with them.

After the king had secured the siege and surrounded himself and his army with the protection of a ditch and rampart, lest an attack by opponents should burst upon them unexpectedly, he assaulted the city by force and attacked its towers and walls with every kind of war-engine, repeating fierce assaults day after day. But the Turks, who confound and resist with a hail of arrows, were spread out along the walls and towers opposite; without restraint they multiplied Christian casualties and grievous wounds, and smothered the crowd rushing toward the gates and iron bars by incessant casts of stones and by pouring out sulphur and boiling pitch.

At length, one day after many assaults and protracted labors, while the army outside rested a little and held its hand from the work of war, and while within the Tyrians and their Turkish soldiers kept silence—though they had nevertheless resolved suddenly to rush from the gates against the king’s camp—in a moment they resumed their arms, donned hauberks and helmets, and, opening certain gates, dared to rush in a great multitude into the open flatness of the fields, where the king and army now dwelt forgetful of war, as far as the places of the tents. They pierced many with arrows and, with great and dreadful shouting, threw the whole army into commotion.

[Col. 0698B] And behold, without delay all the astonished Christian soldiers flew at them from every camp, armed with weapons, lances, and hauberks, striving with great strength on both sides. At last, however, the Christians prevailed and forced the fleeing Tyrians back into the gate. Thus, as both parties became intermingled—the one in swift flight, the other in rapid pursuit—they powerfully entered the city. The Turks and Tyrians, seeing that the Franks had already entered the city with them, turned against those pressing them from behind. Resisting stoutly and mounting the walls, they repelled with every sort of missile the army still striving to enter, until they prevailed by their strength, shut the gates, and held about two hundred men within the walls.

There the glorious and noble knight William of Wanges, and likewise William, of remarkable boldness and military renown, were captured with their distinguished companions, knights and infantrymen, and perished by capital sentence [Col. 0698C]; many others were bound in chains.

### CHAPTER VI.—How the Tyrians remarkably burned two Christian engines with pitch and sulphur.

Then, after some days, seeing that neither assault nor stone-throwing engines caused any harm at all to the citizens or the walls, the king ordered two engines to be made, rising to great height above the walls and constructed with two storeys. One of these was completely built and erected at the expense and through the labor of Eustace Granarius, an illustrious knight and foremost member of the king’s household and council. Eustace himself, with chosen young soldiers, remained in it; morning, noon, and evening, they killed some Tyrians and wounded others with every kind of missile as they moved through the city, observing the towers, walls, and all parts of the city.

The soldiers of the king posted in the other engine attacked Turks and Tyrians no less vigorously, and, striking down with Balearic bows those who advanced from the gate, killed them. The Tyrians, in turn, prepared stones to batter the engines and those dwelling in them. But the engines, clothed in hides of bulls, camels, and horses, and in wicker screens, withstood without injury or movement the impact of stones, iron stakes, and flaming missiles. Seeing that they could not harm the engines in this way, the Tyrians attempted to destroy them by another device. They raised a tree of great height with ropes and fashioned from a large timber a broad and spacious ring, in the manner of a crown; they fastened it with iron chains to the top of the tree. [Col. 0699A] Around this wooden circle they spread pitch, sulphur, wax, fat, and mingled tow, and set it alight with a fire unquenchable by water. They drew it by ropes as far as that part of the walls where Eustace’s engine stood.

Suddenly, belching excessive flame, it was released from the tree onto the engine. Intolerable flames surrounded it on every side and consumed it in a great, irresistible conflagration, along with a large number of the men who tried to shake off and extinguish the fire but could not escape. By the same method and contrivance, the king’s engine too was burned and reduced to nothing. Thus, although both engines were burned, the king remained undaunted in the siege, wishing still to subdue the city either by famine or by some device.

### CHAPTER VII.—The Tyrians’ embassy to the prince of Damascus, and the king’s return to Jerusalem after their arrival.

[Col. 0699B]

At last, recognizing the king’s steadfastness and unshaken resolve, the Tyrians secretly sent an embassy to Damascus, asking the great prince Dochinus to aid them. They promised him a large sum of money and swore that they would always remain in his aid and service. He immediately assembled twenty thousand horsemen and descended through the mountains to the borders of Tyre, intending on the following day to attack the king and his men in their camp, and thus free the city from the king’s hand and siege.

On the very day when this Dochinus, or Duodechinus, entered the borders of Tyre through the mountains, seven hundred men-at-arms with sixty worthy knights from the king’s army went out to seek fodder for the horses [Col. 0699C]. By chance and unknowingly they fell upon the arms and forces of the Turks. All of them were slain and cut down by their enemies with arrow and sword, except for a few who scarcely escaped and reported what had happened. When the king learned that so many thousands had assembled nearby and had killed his men-at-arms and soldiers, he took counsel with his leading men, who had been worn down by the long siege and exhausted of both resources and provisions. He struck camp; and on the Sunday before Palm Sunday, passing through Ptolemais and the other cities, he entered Jerusalem on the holy and celebrated day of Palm Sunday through the gate facing the Mount of Olives—the gate through which the Lord Jesus also entered, riding upon an ass. He entered with his followers and with certain distinguished envoys of the Greeks who had come to him [Col. 0699D] while he was still engaged in the siege.

He spent that holy week visiting the holy places, in prayer, the distribution of alms, and confession of sins. On the holy day of Easter, crowned at the command of the lord patriarch, he celebrated solemnly and royally, with every honour and glory, on account of the envoys of the Greek emperor.

## CHAPTER VIII.—How King Baldwin plundered Idumaean merchants, and how Tancred, prince of Antioch, died.

Having there celebrated the Easter solemnities for eight days, he set out with two hundred knights and one hundred foot-soldiers for the Valley of Moses, in the regions of Arabia, in order to gather some booty there [Col. 0700A], by which he might enrich impoverished soldiers, stripped of their goods, and encourage those who were dispirited. The envoys of the Greek emperor, honourably commended and enriched with magnificent gifts, were sent back to Constantinople.

Hardly had he entered the regions of Arabia when, behold, Idumaeans—whom modern people call Bidumi—merchant men, with immense quantities of diverse merchandise on mules and camels, came into the hands of the king and his men. Being altogether unable to escape, they were stripped of all their wealth: gold and silver, precious gems, purple cloth of various sorts and workmanship, and likewise spices. Many were taken captive and brought to Jerusalem, where they were committed to custody; their booty and spoils were divided among the soldiers.

In the same year Tancred, who ruled Antioch, was seized by a severe illness and died during the Advent of the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0700B]. He was buried according to Catholic rite in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, and left behind great mourning among almost all who were nearby when they heard of his death.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the arrival of the Turks against Jerusalem, and how the king in response assembled an army.

After the death of so famous and warlike a man, and of a most formidable vanquisher of the Turks on every side, when March came and the new spring began to breathe, the aforesaid Malducus—himself one of the most powerful men of the kingdom of Corrozan—assembled about thirty thousand of the strongest Turkish troops. He planned to proceed as far as Damascus, take with him Dochinus, likewise a Turk and the unjust prince of the Damascenes, attack the cities held by the king, and then, if events succeeded according to his desire, advance upon Jerusalem to subdue and destroy the Christians [Col. 0700C].

When news of this famous prince’s muster was spread through the region of the city of Edessa, Armenian messengers were sent to King Baldwin to report his entire undertaking and preparations, so that, forewarned and having summoned his own forces, he might meet the enemy more safely and easily in resistance. Having heard the messengers’ words, the king immediately sent an embassy to Antioch, to Rotgerus, a most distinguished young man and knight, son of Tancred’s sister, who had been installed in Tancred’s place and held the principality of Antioch. He asked him to make every effort to come without delay to his aid, with arms prepared and forces assembled, as it had been decreed from the beginning that Christians should assist their Christian brethren [Col. 0700D].

Rotgerus, without delay upon receiving the king’s embassy, resolved to come to the king with seven hundred knights and five hundred foot-soldiers; but he was somewhat delayed in gathering arms. The Turks, hastening along the road to Damascus, encamped at the Sea of Galilee. They besieged the garrison of Tiberias and spent much time on this side of the Jordan, occupying Mount Tabor and striving to destroy Christian settlements everywhere. For three months they had powerfully continued their outrages, raids, and oppression of the Christians, laying everything waste, sparing no one, keeping watch for ambushes night and day, and harassing the soldiers of Tiberias with frequent assaults and warfare.

## CHAPTER X.—Concerning fifteen hundred Christian pilgrims, for whose sake the king crushed two hundred Turks in battle.

[Col. 0701A]

In these days fifteen hundred pilgrims, who had remained in Jerusalem for the Easter solemnity, prepared to return. But fearing to pass through the region of Tyre, they approached the king with humble prayer, asking that they might deserve to have his escort through Tyre, lest they be attacked by the inhabitants of the city, since, exhausted and weighed down by great poverty, they could offer little resistance. Seeing their determination to return, the king assembled three hundred soldiers and kept the road with them as far as the mountains of Tyre.

But he lingered for a little while in a mountain hiding-place and sent the pilgrims ahead, in order to discover whether any force of the citizens of Tyre would appear to pursue the Christian pilgrims [Col. 0701B]. After they had been sent ahead, about five hundred soldiers of the city of Tyre sallied forth. They pursued the pilgrims, who were passing at some distance from the city, intending to kill and capture them; with loud shouting and the blare of trumpets, they thundered forth to terrify them.

But the king, hearing this outcry, swiftly rose from his hiding-place and ambush and came upon the soldiers from behind. He inflicted a great slaughter, until the Saracens, defeated and crushed, took flight and retraced the road to Tyre. They did not enter its gates before two hundred of them had been captured and killed. The pilgrims continued their journey on that day alone; but on the following day, hearing that the Turks were present with so many thousands, they took counsel and returned to Ptolemais, remaining there with the king.

## CHAPTER XI.—The king engages the Turks, is scattered in flight, and some of his men fall in battle.

[Col. 0701C]

The king, therefore, understanding that the Turks’ audacity had grown excessively burdensome, that they had collected plunder far and wide, and had rarely rested from assault, was deeply angered. He summoned all those who were around Jerusalem and in all the cities which he possessed; gathering about seven hundred knights and four thousand foot-soldiers, he swore and declared before the pilgrim army that he would no longer wait for Rotgerus and the more distant Christian princes, nor endure any longer the arrogance and outrages of the Turks.

Immediately, gathering both the new pilgrims and the others at Ptolemais, he resolved to pitch camp beyond the Jordan, on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0701D], precisely in the place where the Turks’ tents had hitherto stood amid pleasant and delightful meadows. The crafty Turks, learning this through informants, struck their tents and withdrew to Mount Tabor, as though they feared the king and were hastening to flee, not daring to engage him in battle.

But scarcely had the tents been pitched when Malducus and Dodechinus, with the whole company of their followers, burst out from the mountains of Tabor. Like the sand of the sea, they fiercely rushed with bow and arrow upon the camp of the king and his men, fighting with severe battle and cruel wounds and attacking the Christian battle-lines. At length the king and all his force, unable to withstand the might of so many thousands, took flight. About fifteen hundred were killed, besides the knights, thirty of whom were slain [Col. 0702A]. There fell Reinerus of Brus, an undaunted knight; Hugh, a noble young man and distinguished knight; and others whose deeds and wars are most worthy of praise and remembrance.

## CHAPTER XII.—The king, having assembled sixteen thousand men, powerfully drove the Turks from the Jordan in a second encounter.

Scarcely had the king escaped, while the Turks held the open country in victory, when on the following day Rotgerus, successor and heir of Antioch, son of Tancred’s sister, arrived with four hundred knights and six hundred foot-soldiers. He was greatly distressed at the king’s misfortune and the fall of his men, because his delay on the journey had prevented him from being able to assist in the previous day’s battle. The prince of the city of Tripoli also came, no less dismayed that the king’s camp had been so cut down by the Turks [Col. 0702B].

Shortly afterward very many Christian battle-lines arrived by ship as far as Ptolemais. From all directions, by sea and land, those who came together amounted to sixteen thousand. When so many thousands had quickly assembled, the king, with the counsel of all present, resolved to attack the Turks, who still persisted beyond the Jordan in their fierceness, so that, with God’s aid, he might repay upon their heads the evil which they had tried to inflict upon himself, his followers, and the whole region.

But when the Turks heard of the king’s coming and intention, they withdrew from the district of the Jordan and entered Romania, besieging and taking many fortresses and cities of the Greek emperor.

## CHAPTER XIII.—How the wife of the duke of Sicily hastened to King Baldwin’s marriage-bed with a great retinue.

[Col. 0702C]

Afterward, when the king and all his force had returned to Ptolemais from pursuing the enemy, at the beginning of August word reached the king that the most noble wife of Roger, duke of Sicily, brother of the magnificent prince Bohemond, was hastening with great eagerness to the king’s marriage-bed after the death and funeral rites of her aforesaid husband. She came with an abundant display of great wealth and a very large escort of soldiers.

She had two triremes, each carrying five hundred men highly trained in war, together with seven ships laden with gold, silver, purple cloth, and a multitude of precious gems and garments; besides weapons, coats of mail, swords, helmets, and shields shining brightly with gold, and every other equipment which the most powerful men customarily provide for the defence of ships [Col. 0702D]. Indeed, on the ship in which the aforesaid lady intended to reside, a mast covered with the purest gold cast its rays afar in the brightness of the sun; and both ships, their projecting beaks adorned with gold and silver in workmanship, were a marvellous sight to all who beheld them.

In one of the seven ships were Saracen men and archers, very brave men, resplendent in the brilliance of precious garments. They were brought as a gift for the king, and were regarded as inferior to none in the region of Jerusalem in the art of archery. When the arrival and splendour of this lady became known, the king sent three ships, called *galeidae*, filled with distinguished men highly skilled in naval combat, to meet her. But because the sea swelled in a storm of winds, they could neither meet nor join her [Col. 0703A]. For the force of the winds drove the ships far away, until at last, about the ninth hour in the evening, they were received into the harbour and inlet of Ascalon. The sailors could not, despite futile efforts, maintain their course over the waters because the wind opposed them too violently.

## CHAPTER XIV.—With what glory the king joined that lady to himself, after her soldiers had been liberally rewarded by her.

The Ascalonites, always hostile to Christian men, immediately recognized the Christian banners and hastened forth in iron-clad *galeidae* and with weapons to meet and fight them. But after a lengthy struggle and repeated attacks from both sides, one Ascalonite *galeida*, carrying fifty soldiers, was crushed and sunk [Col. 0703B]; the rest were overcome and driven back.

Without delay, the Christians prevailed in victory on every side. Gathered into one body, with God’s favour, when a calm breeze had returned and all the fury of the sea was stilled, they left the harbour and anchorage of Ascalon in great strength. Thus Ptolemais was reached in peaceful sailing.

As soon as the king learned of the arrival of this most glorious lady, he came to meet her as she disembarked, accompanied by all the leading men of his kingdom and all the servants of his household, in garments of varied kind and beauty, in royal dress, with horses and mules gleaming with purple and silver, with trumpets and every sweetness of musicians. The streets were spread with wonderful and varied carpets, and the lanes shone with purple hangings in honour of this most noble lady, most renowned for her treasures [Col. 0703C], as kings ought to be exalted in every glory and pomp.

She was led in with this joy and praise and joined to the king in a permanent marriage. A great preparation and adornment for the wedding was made in the royal palace of the city for several days. Very many treasures were transferred by her into the king’s treasury; through these the king and all those who had lost arms in the Turkish wars were now relieved and enriched beyond estimation.

When the wedding was over and the king of Jerusalem intended to go up with his bride, Rotgerus, honourably commended by the king, prepared to set out for Antioch. The new queen gave him one thousand marks of silver, precious purple cloth, five hundred bezants, and excellent mules and horses; besides this, ordinary soldiers who had come from afar to assist the king received no small rewards of gold and silver [Col. 0703D].

## CHAPTER XV.—How, after the Christians’ departure, the Turks devastated Greek territory and destroyed the city of Stamiria.

Thus, while certain men were eager to return to their own lands, some travelled overland through Romania and reached the city of Stamiria. There they were kindly received in lodging by the Greeks, Christian men, with every necessary provision. Without delay, the Turks—who had been driven by the king out of Galilee and had taken and crushed the cities and towns of the Greek emperor, reducing them to nothing through plunder and spoils—attacked the walls of this city and set a siege around it, inflicting great force, threats, and terror upon its citizens.

Not many days afterward [Col. 0704A], after terrible assaults, they attacked the principal gate of the city with overwhelming force. The Greek soldiers, effeminate men, offered little resistance. With axe and hatchet they smashed the gate; when the defenders were at last exhausted, they rushed in together. Attacking all alike, citizens and pilgrims, with arrow and bow, they committed no small slaughter, carried off many persons, and removed all the money and valuables found there.

In the same city, some forty men from the Christian army who were staying for the sake of hospitality were captured and beheaded. Yet this was not without abundant vengeance in their own blood: for with incalculable courage and fighting, repulsing and killing many Turks at the gate which they had been stationed to defend, they held out unconquered until their adversaries were admitted through the gate defended by the Greeks [Col. 0704B].

## CHAPTER XVI.—Concerning seven thousand Christians who crossed the sea and all perished by shipwreck.

About seven thousand persons continued their return by sea. Sailing with favourable sails and without storm, on the feast of St Martin they reached the harbour and anchorage of the island of Cyprus. They cast their anchors into the deep and hastened to go ashore from their ships. Without delay, a strong and violent wind, such as sailors had not heard for many years, descended upon the sea. It caused an intolerable movement and raging; it shook the ships, broke their ropes with its force, tore the anchors from the deep, and raised storms against the vessels so greatly that ship dashed against ship without helmsman, suffering mutual destruction [Col. 0704C]. Thus that whole gathering of Christians, with all its equipment, was swallowed in a miserable drowning.

None escaped except two *buzas*, out of a total of thirteen ships. On the following day, when the sea’s fury had subsided, so many thousands of bodies, noble and ignoble, were cast ashore by its repeated flood that they could scarcely be buried by the faithful over the plain of the fields during the course of three weeks.

## CHAPTER XVII.—How King Baldwin’s soldiers fought gloriously in a naval battle against the Babylonians.

In the second year after King Baldwin’s marriage, a large army of the king of Babylon arrived by sea as far as Tyre on the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary [Col. 0704D]. There, some plotting ambushes against the Christians and others conducting trade in goods, they remained until after the third day following the Nativity of that Virgin, and then prepared to return.

As they approached Ptolemais, they formed naval battle-lines, fortified with every kind of equipment against Christian forces. Two ships of greater strength and number guarded the rear; yet, heavily burdened with goods and people, they followed at a distance of more than a mile. The citizens and the king’s soldiers at Ptolemais, who according to custom were spread daily over the walls, saw the sails and masts of the Babylonian pagans rowing away. At once they donned coats of mail and helmets; about four hundred men embarked in three *galeidae* and put out upon the waves, in order to seize the following ships after harassing them by some naval stratagem [Col. 0705A].

One of the two ships, heavily laden with arms and people, was wholly unable to escape. It began to resist with great defensive use of arms from the ninth hour until evening. But at last, after heavy slaughter inflicted on both sides, it began to fail in strength. It was captured and brought to the harbour of the city of Caiphas. At Caiphas certain captured and wounded Saracens were left committed to custody; the uninjured were sent on to Ptolemais in their captured ship, together with certain wounded Christians.

After the wounded Christians had been put ashore from the three *galeidae*, the remaining uninjured Christians, taking additional companions with them in two *galeidae*, pursued the ship which, more heavily loaded and impeded with goods, soldiers, and arms, was travelling more slowly [Col. 0705B]. They now vigorously assailed and encircled it with five *galeidae*. The enemy defended themselves no less vigorously and fought manfully for their lives with every kind of weapon and volleys of arrows. At last, after excessive martial labour from morning until midday, with both sides worn down, the ship of the pagans, called a *cattus*, almost escaped, defended and freed from their hands.

The men and soldiers of Ptolemais watched this from the walls and saw that the Christian *galeidae* had become exhausted. Taking counsel, they decided to send two hundred men to aid them. Thus the ship, continually harassed and overcome from every side by frequent attack from those vessels, was forcibly brought to Ptolemais in the evening. Two *galeidae* came out from Sur, which is called Tyre, to assist them; but seeing the steadfastness of the Franks and the failure of their own side, they fled back to their own city [Col. 0705C].

There were one thousand very strong fighting men on this ship. At the king’s command, the citizens surrounded them throughout the night with many watches and armed guards. Their innumerable goods were divided among the soldiers. Of the Saracens, some were beheaded; others were ransomed and released for an immeasurable price.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—How the prince of Damascus deceitfully killed another Turkish prince.

After these events, in the following year, the aforesaid Malducus, one of the most powerful Turks, returned to Damascus from the regions of Romania after a great slaughter and killing of Christians. He was exalted in name and fame among the Turks and all the pagans because, more than all others, he had exercised a wider tyranny over Christ’s faithful [Col. 0705D].

Therefore Dochinus, prince of the Damascenes, stirred by grievous envy and indignation, devised Malducus’s death by every stratagem he knew. Yet he did so secretly, lest he incur the hatred of his own people, by whom Malducus was greatly loved because of his lavish generosity and military valour. Accordingly, although he often laboured by deceitful contrivance to bring about his death, and among his many devices found no opportunity to kill him, he finally found this means for his treachery, by which he might kill the man and erase his name.

He approached four soldiers of the Azopart race with gifts and magnificent promises, asking that they secretly stab him with concealed weapons on a festival day, in the privacy of his oratory, while he was occupied with the ceremonies of the pagan rite [Col. 0706A]; thus they would deserve to receive gifts from him. Secretly admitted into the oratory, they attacked Malducus as he entered and confidently performed the ceremonies. Piercing him together through the breast with sharp iron, they killed him while he knew nothing at all of it, and escaped in flight.

Dochinus, who was privy to this treachery and murder, at first concealed the fact. But when he heard from his own men that the deed had been done, he began, with feigned tears and great lamentation but no feeling in his heart, to complain of the death of so magnificent a prince. He ordered the authors of his death to be pursued and sought everywhere. But after a short time his fraud began to become known among the Turks; from that day he fell into their hatred and enmity, suffering many plots because of his altogether inexcusable treachery [Col. 0706B].

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the great pagan expedition against Antioch, which King Baldwin destroyed through his army.

In the second year after Malducus’s murder, Burgoldus came forth from the kingdom of Corrozan; Brodoan, king of Aleppo; and Cocosander of the city of Lagabria. With forty thousand Turks, a great expedition, and intolerable armament, they advanced into the territory of Antioch. They pitched their tents in the plains of the cities of Rossa, Royda, and Femie. Breaking down and capturing the suburbs of these towns with stone-throwing engines, though unable in any way to harm Femie itself, they devastated the whole district with plunder and fire.

They took the cities of Tommosa, Turgulant, and Montfargia with overwhelming force and a strong hand [Col. 0706C]. They captured and carried away in chains William, the Christian prince of Perce and commander of those garrisons. Of the others found in them, they killed some by capital sentence and held others captive. They are said to have remained in these regions for eleven weeks.

At that time King Baldwin was staying at Jerusalem. Invited to aid Christ’s soldiers, he hastened toward Antioch with five hundred knights and one thousand foot-soldiers. With him went Dochinus, prince of Damascus, now bound in loyalty to the king, with a very large body of cavalry. Punctus, son of Bertrannus of Tripla—that is, Tripoli—was present in the same company with two hundred knights and two thousand foot-soldiers [Col. 0706D], travelling by the royal road as far as the city of Taramria.

There Rotgerus of Antioch and Baldwin of Rohas met them with ten thousand horsemen and foot-soldiers; they encamped and remained in that land for eight days. Hearing of the king’s presence and the size of his forces, the Turks resolved to flee toward the city of Malatina in the mountains, because they despaired of engaging him.
