When the king learned of the Turks’ withdrawal, he prepared to return with his men. He took with him Tancred’s wife, daughter of the king of France; by the king’s counsel she was joined in marriage to that same Punctus, and the wedding was celebrated gloriously at Tripla, in every abundance and richness. Tripla had been left to him by his parents in hereditary right.

## CHAPTER XX.—How, after King Baldwin returned to Jerusalem, the Turks, having reassembled their forces, were routed.

[Col. 0707A]

After the king’s return, the Turks immediately returned in force to Gastum, Harech, and Synar, cities of the Franks. They invaded the land and mercilessly devastated everything found there. Hearing this, Rotgerus and Baldwin were greatly distressed at the king’s departure, because he had already gone far away and could not be recalled. Therefore, after taking counsel and deciding not to send messengers to him in vain, they assembled fifteen thousand of their own men of every kind, both Franks and Armenians.

The Turks had divided into three companies upon the River Farfar, which runs between the two cities Caesarea Stratonis and Femie. At first light, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, Rotgerus and Baldwin formed battle-lines and attacked the Turks [Col. 0707B]. When battle had been joined, fifteen thousand Turks fell; few Christians are reported to have died. When the first army had thus been crushed, Rotgerus advanced with a great shout against the second. All the enemies, stunned by fear, fled toward the fords of the aforesaid river, where they were engulfed and suffocated by the waters.

The third army, astonished by this victory of the Catholics, sought refuge in confusion through error of the roads and happened to reach the district of Camolla, in a valley near the fortress of Malbech. There Dochinus met them with eight thousand men and fought fiercely against them, killing three thousand and carrying off one thousand captives [Col. 0707C]. Among these fleeing Turks were many of Malducus’s lineage and blood, who had often been bitterly hostile to Dochinus because of his treachery and wicked murder of Malducus. As their kinsmen, they brought complaint of their relative’s death before great and small alike in the land of Corrozan and sought to exact vengeance for his killing.

For this reason Dochinus was always anxious and suspicious; he now adhered more faithfully to King Baldwin and the Christian faithful, with whom he was allied, and did not cease in any way to injure the Turks.

## CHAPTER XXI.—How King Baldwin set out with a small force for Mount Sinai.

In the third year after King Baldwin had celebrated the above-mentioned marriage royally, in autumn he set out with two hundred knights and four hundred foot-soldiers for Mount Oreb, commonly called Orel [Col. 0707D]. There, in the course of eighteen days, he strengthened a new fortress, so that he might more powerfully attack the land of the Arabs; merchants might thereafter be allowed passage in either direction only by the king’s grace and permission; and no enemy ambush or force might suddenly arise without being exposed to the king’s faithful men stationed in the fortress. Thus the royal fortress would be an obstacle to the enemy.

When the fortification of this stronghold had been secured on every side against enemies, the king—always eager for new enterprises—secretly summoned sixty distinguished knights and set out toward the kingdom of Babylon, in the hope that he might accomplish something notable by capturing Saracens and Idumaeans or attacking cities. Passing through the desolate places of the vast wilderness, with an abundance of food carried on the backs of mules, he is said to have reached the Red Sea [Col. 0708A]. There he and his followers refreshed themselves by bathing from the severe heat of that land and were nourished with fish from that sea.

Hearing that monks serving God lived there on Mount Sinai, he resolved to hasten down the slopes of the mountain to them for prayer and conversation. But at the request of messengers sent to him by the monks, he did not ascend, lest the monks, rendered suspect because of the Catholic king, be driven by the pagans from their mountain dwelling. It was reported that the city of Babylon could be reached from there within four days.

## CHAPTER XXII.—King Baldwin prudently returns from Mount Sinai to Jerusalem at his followers’ warning.

But because his force was small, with which he had descended silently through the places of the wilderness [Col. 0708B], and because his arrival was now beginning to become fully known owing to certain delays, his friends advised him not to proceed farther, but to return as quickly as possible and safely to Jerusalem in secrecy. For if either the king’s entrance or departure became known, more than a hundred thousand pagans of every kind would have converged in arms to meet him and occupied all the roads on every side.

Accordingly, yielding to his followers’ counsel and leaving that country by the precautions he knew, he resolved to return through the valley of Hebron and the fortress of St Abraham. Staying there overnight with his men, he abundantly refreshed their tired bodies with the provisions of that land. Then, taking the road which leads to Ascalon, he gathered all the spoil wandering over the plains of Ascalon: two hundred camels, very many herds of cattle, and flocks of sheep and goats [Col. 0708C]. With these he returned powerfully and without pursuit to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—How King Baldwin, stricken at Ptolemais, was relieved of illness through many alms.

A few days later, having gone down to Ptolemais, he began to fall seriously ill at the beginning of March, and day by day the affliction of his body became worse. Therefore, uncertain of his life, he ordered that part of his treasures—gold and silver vessels and many thousands of bezants—be distributed to the poor for his sins and the salvation of his soul. He likewise ordered without delay that the wine, grain, oil, and barley which he had at Jerusalem and in many other places be distributed to the poor [Col. 0708D], orphans, and widows.

He assigned a portion indeed to his household; and to his household soldiers and newcomers, and to all who had served him in military aid under agreements for pay in solidi, he gave bezants, gold, silver, and abundant purple cloth. He ordered all his debts to be paid and firmly instructed that they should not be an impediment to his soul.

But by God’s will, who gives life to all who repent and defers death, health was restored to him who already had no hope of living, through the prayers and tears of orphans and widows. His bodily weakness was relieved, and Christ’s athlete wholly recovered. For news of his very severe illness had already spread, and Babylonian naval forces had come to Tyre to attack the cities of the Christians upon the king’s death. But when they heard of his health and restored soundness, they immediately retraced their sea-route to their own region and departed without any opposition [Col. 0709A].

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How the patriarch rebuked the same king, and how he repudiated that unlawful marriage.

After the king had recovered from his illness, Arnulf, chancellor of the Lord’s Sepulchre, was elected and appointed patriarch, after the death of Bishop Ghibelin. He then went to Rome, was kindly received by Paschal, bishop of Rome, and returned. Having cleared himself of all accusations, he began, by the admonition and command of the same apostolic bishop, to rebuke and admonish the lord king [Col. 0709B], that he should remove from his marriage-bed the aforesaid lady whom he had taken as wife, because of the adultery which he had committed with his first wife, descended from Armenian princes, in that he had defiled lawful marriage by adulterous unions with her.

He also declared him barred on the ground of consanguinity with that same lady, who was descended from Frankish blood. Following this admonition, a council was convened in the city of Ptolemais, in the church of the Holy Cross. The king was separated from his wife, Arnulf the patriarch taking action and the whole clergy, together with the king himself, judging the matter. She, sad and grieving, released from this marital bond by synodal law, returned by ship to Sicily. From that day onward the king persisted in observing the imposed penance; touched and admonished by God, he subdued his body with remarkable abstinence and chastity from all unlawful acts [Col. 0709C].

## CHAPTER XXV.—How the city of Pharamia was captured.

After some time, when the complaint was heard concerning all the hardships inflicted by the people of Ascalon upon pilgrims coming to or returning from Jerusalem, King Baldwin, having taken counsel with his men, resolved to attack the king of Babylon himself; so that, if perhaps his land, kingdom, and riches were devastated, Ascalon would be less able to behave proudly and rebelliously, since it was accustomed often to be sustained and exalted by the wealth of that kingdom and its stores of arms. And now, as spring was beginning to breathe, he set out with two hundred and sixteen knights and four hundred foot-soldiers trained and experienced in warfare, [Col. 0709D] proceeding by way of arid and solitary places with wagons of provisions. From all the regions of Arabia through which they passed, whether bound to him by allied friendship or showing him any regard, they took neither booty nor anything else. At last, after eleven days of uninterrupted travel with the whole force mentioned above, the Nile, which flows through the land of Egypt, opened before him; descending into it, they washed away their sweat. Moving camp thence, on a Thursday before mid-Lent, in the month of March, they arrived at the territory of a certain city called Pharamia, exceedingly well fortified with walls, gates, and ramparts. This was a most beautiful city of the kingdom of Babylon, no more than three days’ journey from Babylon. On the following day, Friday, having arranged the battle-lines [Col. 0710A] and standards of their very small army, clad in mail and helmets, they attacked that city, empty of defenders, and entered its open gates with force, assault, and a great shout. There they found an unheard-of abundance of necessities: wine, wheat, oil, barley, meat, fish, and everything that can be eaten. A great quantity of gold, silver, and every kind of precious ornament was found there. For all the inhabitants of the city, suddenly hearing the report of the king’s approach so near at hand, had forgotten every thought of defense and of their possessions, intent only upon flight; they had withdrawn far from the city, caring only for life and safety. The king and his men, refreshing bodies wearied and burdened by nine days’ travel and by the incalculable heat of that torrid region, found food and drink in abundance; and they rested on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, doing everything as they pleased.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—King Baldwin, after taking Pharamia, fell ill unto death.

But on Sunday, the day which divides the fast, prudent men concerned for their safety came together before the king and spoke as follows: “We are few; and now our strength has become known to the city and kingdom of Babylon. Babylon, moreover, is said to be no more than three days’ journey from here. Therefore let us take counsel together, that, leaving this city, we may continue the route to which we have pledged ourselves and make no delay here.”

Accordingly the king, complying with the counsel of his men, at first light warned his companions, demolished the city walls, [Col. 0710C] and set fire to all the buildings, towers, and houses. More than anyone else he devoted all his strength to that devastation, lest it should thereafter furnish the Babylonians with strength and aid. Yet while, as has been said, the king labored more vigorously and attentively than all others in demolishing the walls and burning the buildings, his limbs were excessively afflicted by heat and exertion; he was seized by a violent illness, and the suffering of his body began to increase more and more. When darkness had fallen and the sun had wholly set, despairing of life, he summoned the leading men of his army, revealed the weakness of his body, and declared that he could not now escape death.

On hearing of the king’s despair and desolation, all, from least to greatest, began to groan; excessive weeping [Col. 0710D] and tears burst forth from their eyes, and great desolation came upon everyone. For none had any hope or confidence of ever returning to Jerusalem; rather, they thought that in this exile they were doomed to perish under a sentence of death.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—The king’s consolation and command to his soldiers concerning his death and burial.

To strengthen them, though he was grievously afflicted, the king said: “Why, most valiant men, so often proved in dangers, are your spirits disturbed at the decline of myself alone, and why are weeping, desolation, and grief multiplied? No, my most beloved brothers and sweetest fellow-soldiers: do not let the death of myself alone so soften and fail your hearts, and weaken you also in a foreign land and among enemies. Remember, in God’s name, that my [Col. 0711A] strength is that of one man, and that there are still among you very many whose strength and counsel differ little or not at all from mine. Therefore be most valiant men, and do not begin to become effeminate in sorrow over my death; rather, you ought to be concerned how you may cautiously return by the strength of your arms and retain the kingdom of Jerusalem, as you pledged yourselves to God from the beginning.”

Having said this, he earnestly entreated and admonished all who were present, in faith and obedience, that if he died they should never bury his lifeless body in this land of the Saracens, lest it be made an object of mockery and derision among the nations; but that, by every skill and effort within their power, they should carry his corpse back to the land of Jerusalem and bury him beside his brother Godfrey. Hearing this, and scarcely restraining themselves from weeping, [Col. 0711B] they replied that he imposed upon them a heavy and unbearable burden, since in the days of extreme summer heat it was impossible to preserve, touch, and carry any corpse. The king pressed them further and urged all not to refuse this labor for the sake of conveying him home.

After these words he prayed as follows: “As soon as I am dead, I beg you to open my abdomen with an iron blade and remove my entrails; but preserve my body with salt and spices, wrap it in leather or cloths, and carry it back to Jerusalem for Catholic funeral rites and burial beside my brother’s tomb.” Without delay he summoned Addo, a cook of his household, and bound him by oath to cut open his abdomen and remove his entrails. To him he said: “Know that I shall shortly die; and therefore, as you love me—or as you loved me while living [Col. 0711C] and well, remain faithful to me now that I am dead. Disembowel me with the blade; rub me thoroughly, inside and out, with salt; do not spare to fill my eyes, nostrils, ears, and mouth. Do not cease to carry me back with the others. Know that by doing this you fulfill my desire and keep faith with me.”

Having made these arrangements, on Tuesday he began to be tortured more violently by his illness, unto death, before the eyes of his leaders and faithful men.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—The soldiers’ inquiry as to who should hold the crown after him; and the conveyance of his body to Jerusalem.

Seeing his life failing, they asked him—because he was a man of great wisdom, while he was still alive and well—whom he wished to be appointed or crowned heir [Col. 0711D] of the kingdom of Jerusalem after his death, so that, by his counsel and decree, a king might be established more certainly and without dispute. He designated the kingdom for his brother Eustace, should he come; but if he were unable because of age, then Baldwin of Bourg should be chosen, or such a man as would govern the Christian people, defend the churches, remain steadfast in faith, fear no power of adversaries, and be not easily corrupted by payment.

Having said this, the man most noble in the land of his birth, Lorraine, of most noble blood; the king most glorious and victorious in the kingdom of Jerusalem; the most valiant athlete of God—breathed out the spirit of life, steadfast in the faith of Christ and purified in confession of the Lord, fortified by reception of the Lord’s body and blood. When this most renowned prince had thus died in a barbarous land, the distinguished [Col. 0712A] princes and fellow-soldiers, knights and foot-soldiers, dissolved in excessive tears with great wailing and lamentation because of grief. They would have renewed their weeping still more had they not been seized, upon the loss of so great a prince, by fear in a land hostile on every side.

Therefore, concealing his death and all grief, as he had earnestly requested, they cut open his abdomen; his entrails were taken out and buried, while his body was salted inside and out, and his eyes, mouth, nostrils, and ears were treated with spices and balsam. Sewn into leather and wrapped in cloths, it was placed upon horses and securely fastened, so that no stratagem of the heathen might detect that he had died and thereby embolden them, swarming from all sides, to pursue the bereft army. Once the lifeless body had been thus prepared, it was cautiously carried in this conveyance through the foreign land, through deserted and pathless places. By way of the district of the valley of Hebron, where the fortress and burial-place of the holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are honored by the faithful even to the present day, [Col. 0712B] they returned, having continually, day after day, guards of armed knights and foot-soldiers to right and left.

Then, arriving with the king’s dead body upon the plains of Ascalon, they raised their standards, formed their columns, and, trusting solely in military strength, are said to have passed without hindrance or attack by their adversaries, until on that same holy and celebrated day of Palm Sunday they entered the highlands of Jerusalem together with the royal corpse.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—How they laid the king in a royal tomb, and how the lord patriarch immediately fell ill and died.

[Col. 0712C]

On that same day the lord Patriarch had descended from the Mount of Olives with his clergy after the blessing of palms. Brothers from the Temple of the Lord and from all the churches came to meet him, assembling for the feast in hymns and praises, in celebration of that holy day on which the Lord Jesus, seated upon an ass, deigned to enter the holy city Jerusalem. Thus, while all Christian gatherings were assembled for that solemnity in praises of God, behold, the dead king was borne into the midst of those singing psalms. At the sight of him voices were hushed and praises subdued; abundant weeping, both of clergy and people, was heard.

Nevertheless, when the Office of Palms had been completed, and all had entered through the gate called the Golden Gate, through which the Lord Jesus, coming to his Passion, entered, together with the dead king, [Col. 0712D] it was resolved by common counsel that the lifeless body should immediately be committed to burial. For all considered it burdensome and unfitting that a body long kept, and already foul-smelling, should be preserved longer. Without delay, when the Catholic funeral rites had been performed and the body had been commended to the earth by the lord patriarch, he was placed beside the tomb of his full brother Godfrey, at the place of Calvary, in the vestibule of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, in a mausoleum such as befits kings. There, in memory and honor of his name, he was set above the other buried persons, in a great and magnificent work of polished white marble; just as his brother Godfrey had been exalted with the same honor of a mausoleum.

When this most renowned prince of Jerusalem had been buried, the venerable Patriarch Arnulf, through grief at the death of so great a king and athlete of Christ, was seized with a violent illness. After being ill for three weeks, he ended his life and was laid beside the burial-place of the patriarchs.

## CHAPTER XXX.—How, after the burial of King Baldwin, his nephew Baldwin of Bourg was elected and anointed king by all, after the consecration of the new patriarch Gormond.

On the same day on which King Baldwin was buried and Patriarch Arnulf began to fall ill, the clergy and people of the nascent Church, bereft of so great a king and defender, began to consider restoring the kingship. They said that it was not a useful policy for the place and people to remain long without a king and the consolation of a defender, lest the place and land, defended by no one, should perish. Although different persons [Col. 0713B] said different things, at last all approved that Baldwin of Bourg should be placed upon the throne of the kingdom of Jerusalem, because he was an undaunted knight, had often endured many dangers in strongholds for the safety of Christians, and had resolutely retained the land of Rohas, defended from every hostile assault.

It was immediately acclaimed that he should rightfully receive the crown of the kingdom and that the lord patriarch should create and elevate him as king. For that same Baldwin had come to Jerusalem to worship on the feast day, unaware of all that had happened. The patriarch, still alive though ill, saw the people’s devotion and steadfastness toward Baldwin. Although Baldwin resisted somewhat, declaring that the wealth of Rohas was sufficient for him, the patriarch graciously gave his assent and [Col. 0713C] anointed and consecrated him king and lord of Jerusalem.

Baldwin, anointed and consecrated king, was splendidly honored on the day of the holy Resurrection; he was exalted with dignity amid rejoicing, gladdened during those holy days, and most devoutly performed the justice of God in all things. On the appointed day, as is just and as the laws teach, he summoned all the leading men of the kingdom to the palace of King Solomon, conferred benefices on each, received from them faith and oath, and honorably sent each man back to his own affairs. He subjected to his authority the cities of Naples, Samaria, Joppa, Caiphas, the castle of Saint Abraham, Ptolemais, Sagitta, Tiberias, and the other cities and places belonging to the kingdom of Jerusalem. He assigned some of their revenues to his leading men, [Col. 0713D] and attached others to his own table.

After the death of King Baldwin and Patriarch Arnulf, and after Baldwin too had been anointed king, Gormond, a man of good conduct, was elected patriarch by all the clergy and people. Consecrated by the holy bishops, he received the episcopal throne of Jerusalem, to govern the people of the living God and strengthen the new and holy Church of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Concerning four thousand Idumaean herdsmen, by whom Christian soldiers, while pursuing them on the holy day of Easter, were slain in various places.

In the second year of the reign of Baldwin of Bourg, the new king of Jerusalem and lord of the city of Rohas, certain Saracens of the kingdom of Arabia, and others of the Idumaean people, whom modern men call Bidumos, drove from their land and region herds [Col. 0714A] of more than thirty thousand camels, one hundred thousand cattle, and countless thousands of sheep and goats. They led them to pasture in the territory of the kingdom of Damascus, following there an abundance of grass, with the permission and consent of the lord of the land of Damascus, under an agreement concerning the *byzantii* which that lord was to receive from them.

More than four thousand horsemen and foot-soldiers went out of Egypt and Arabia with these many thousands, armed with lance and sword and abundantly supplied with all necessary provisions, to guard the flocks. While they peacefully and attentively kept watch over their herds in the territory of the kingdom of Damascus, fearing nothing because of their confidence in Dochin, prince of Damascus—by whose favor and permission they were spread over the pastures with their wives and children, as is the custom of the heathen—the report of so many herdsmen who had come there from a distant land reached the ears of Joscelin of Courtenay. By the gift of King Baldwin, brother of Godfrey, he held in fief the land and revenues of Tiberias, since, being of high birth, he was the son of the aunt of Baldwin of Bourg, now made king of Jerusalem.

Therefore, when Joscelin learned of this innumerable multitude of herds in a remote and solitary place, he did not delay to inform Godfrey of Bures, a distinguished man and most famous knight in every work of war, from the territory of the city of Paris, and his brother William; and he urged both brothers to attack the booty. They accepted his exhortation and, after warning and assembling one hundred and sixty horsemen—men most daring in war and most eager for plunder—and sixty foot-soldiers most fierce [Col. 0714C] with bow, lance, and sword, set out for the same region where the herdsmen and guards of the herds, mighty Arab, Egyptian, and Idumaean soldiers, were encamped, while the cattle, sheep, and goats wandered widely in length and breadth.

When they reached the place, Joscelin, with fifty knights in one line, was posted on the right to give aid. William, with an equal number of knights arranged in his column and clad in helmet and mail, remained posted at a distance on the left, to furnish support to his companions engaging in battle. Godfrey of Bures retained sixty knights in his line and, stationed in the center with all his company of sturdy foot-soldiers, boldly attacked the herdsmen and the leaders of the herdsmen, attempting to carry off the booty. Pressing the plunder with all his strength, he advanced too far into the hands of the defenders of the flock.

Four thousand men, hearing the horns and signals, came up in an instant to recover their herds. Surrounding Godfrey and his men, they fought fiercely with them, until Godfrey and his very few men, unable to endure the force of so many, fell—about forty men armed with bow, lance, and sword; men most valiant and, until that day, undefeated in every battle. Each was enriched with revenues of lands and possessions of places, and in military service each had knights under him: one twenty, another ten, another five, or at least two. Only eight were carried off captive; the rest perished by the enemies’ weapons. [Col. 0715A]

When William heard the shouting of men fiercely fighting one another, he mounted his horse with his men and wished to aid those in distress; but he was delayed by error of route among thickets and arid places, and thus could not come to the assistance of his companions in their great danger. Joscelin, understanding the overthrow and destruction of his valiant men, himself boldly rushed into the hands of the cruel enemy; but, since his companions had already been killed and crushed, he could be of no assistance. More than two hundred Saracens are reported to have been slain in the same battle. Of the sixty Christian foot-soldiers scarcely ten escaped through byways and shady places.

These most grievous losses of distinguished knights occurred on the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection, when all Catholic men customarily rest from labor and every conflict [Col. 0715B] and devote themselves to almsgiving and prayer. I think, therefore, that for this reason they were delivered into the hands of their enemies: because on so holy a day they were eager for plunder, and consequently were deprived of the aid of their men, who wandered astray through impassable places.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—King Baldwin II assembled an army to take vengeance on his enemies; the Idumaeans placate him with money.

After the most valiant men had been slain in this lamentable massacre, a cruel report concerning the death and misfortune of the named leaders swiftly reached King Baldwin, who had departed from Jerusalem and was staying at Ptolemais. By their aid and counsel the Church of Jerusalem had been strengthened and was greatly advancing day by day. On hearing this, and learning of the death [Col. 0715C] of his beloved knight Godfrey, his heart was shaken by violent grief and his countenance lost all cheerfulness. The hearts of all who had been overflowing with joy during those Easter festivities were changed into mourning and groaning throughout all the streets and squares of Ptolemais.

Without delay, summoning all the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem to avenge their slain brethren, and gathering an army from every place inhabited by Christians, the king came with six thousand men as far as Bethan and ordered his tents to be pitched across the plain. That same night the army of Jerusalem and the others who had assembled began to grow weary of this expedition and vengeance, because the city of Damascus was very near and fortified by Turkish arms. Meanwhile, as they hesitated thus, the Idumaeans, terrified by the report [Col. 0716A] of the new king’s approach and distrustful of Turkish aid and of the Turks’ fickle loyalty, decided to give the king four thousand *byzantii* for the killing of their men, so that henceforth, by his favor and consent, they might safely and peacefully guard their herd and no violence be inflicted upon them. The king, seeing the steadfast unwillingness of his people to march on, permitted this to be done by the counsel of his men. Having received this sum of gold, the king returned to Ptolemais, ordering alms to be given and many Masses celebrated for the soul of Godfrey and the souls of the other slain men.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Concerning seven hundred Christian pilgrims who, after visiting the Lord’s Sepulchre, were killed by most wicked Saracens on their return.

Likewise, in that same second year of King Baldwin II, on the Holy Saturday of that Resurrection on whose following day Godfrey and the aforementioned knights were slaughtered by the Idumaeans—when the continuous grace of God from heaven, to strengthen faith in the Lord’s Resurrection, causes a flame suddenly to arise in the lamp of oil placed in the Lord’s Sepulchre, to kindle the Paschal candle on that night—about seven hundred pilgrims, having worshipped the Lord Jesus before his venerable tomb and seen the miracle of the divinely kindled fire, descended from Jerusalem with joyful and cheerful hearts in order to visit the waters of the Jordan according to the rite of the faithful. When they had proceeded from the hill country as far as the castle of Cuschet and Burgewins, in a desert place, behold, Saracens from Tyre and Ascalon [Col. 0716C] appeared, fiercely attacking the pilgrims with arms and joining battle with them. The pilgrims, being unarmed, worn down by many days on the road, and weakened by lack of food for the name of Jesus, were quickly overcome and turned to flight. The impious executioners pursued them, killed three hundred by the sword, and took sixty captives.

When these miseries and killings were heard of in Jerusalem and its environs, the king and Lord Patriarch Gormond, with all men, were afflicted by great grief. Therefore they immediately sent knights to avenge the slaughtered faithful. But these hastened to arms and took the road in vain; for after this massacre the Saracens had fled and entered within the walls of Tyre and Ascalon with their Christian captives and Christian spoils.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1125: FRANCO, ABBOT OF AFFLIGEM

[Col. 0715]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 199)

Franco, second abbot of Affligem in Brabant from 1109 to 1130, while still a monk wrote for his predecessor Fulgentius, abbot of Affligem, twelve books *On the Grace, or Beneficence, of God*. They were published at Antwerp in 1565 and at Freiburg in 1620. Prefaced by Fulgentius’s letter requesting the work from him, they are printed in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume XII, and the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume XXI, pp. 293–327. At the end of Book XII, p. 326, there is an elegiac poem, noted by Henry of Ghent, ch. 39, and by Trithemius, ch. 367 and II, 104 of the *Illustrious Benedictines*. They report that Franco wrote *On the State of Future Glory* in verse; Cave wrongly thought it had been lost. Leyser incorrectly distinguishes from that work the verses appended to the books *On the Grace of God*.

There are also two letters of this Franco in volume XXI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 327: “That a monk who has cast off the habit cannot be saved”; and, p. 328, a consolatory letter to nuns and sisters at Bigard near the forest. The treatise *On the Course of the Spiritual Life*, arranged in twelve distinctions or books, which Oudin mentions in volume II, p. 959, I do not think differs from the twelve books *On Grace*. Yet Oudin also cites two manuscript works of Franco: one *On the Fast of the Four Seasons*, and the other *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*.

[To which writer of this name the book *On the Institution of the Eucharist* ought principally to be assigned, I do not know. Father Martene found it in the monastery of the Canons Regular of St Augustine, of the Agony of Christ, near the city of Tongeren, with this title: “Franco, humble monk, *On the Institution of the Eucharist*.” See *Literary Journey*, vol. II, p. 198. Mansi.]

[Col. 0717]

# THE TWELVE BOOKS OF FRANCO, ABBOT OF AFFLIGEM, ON THE GRACE OF GOD.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons, twelfth century, part II, p. 293.)

## LETTER OF ABBOT FULGENTIUS TO THE MONK FRANCO.

[Col. 0717]

[Col. 0717A] FULGENTIUS, humble servant and called abbot of the Church of Affligem, to his dearest brother and son FRANCO: with greeting and paternal affection, may you possess forever the joys of the holy and second Resurrection.

I had asked you, most loving brother and son, and you had promised, as is your custom, that you would obey: namely, that you should write some small treatise on the Grace of God, beneficial to my blindness and to others like me, who are accustomed to stammer about the grace of God, since we quite fail to know what the grace of God is. Therefore I ask you again, and command you under obedience, that, spreading the sails of your understanding to the breath of the Holy Spirit, you begin to write in the Lord’s name, knowing without doubt that holy love and obedience, which are never without reward, will supply the powers which inexperience denies you. Begin from the beginning of God’s creation and continue to the last day, when “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” and God “shall be all in all”; and continue to that time when he will say to his elect: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.” May the Lord Jesus, who called us into his grace and glory, deign to make us sharers in that kingdom.

But when you come to the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, where he says, “Take and eat. This is my body,” I beg you to linger there, commending more attentively his wondrous love toward us and that ineffable privilege and grace of love: that he deigned to refresh us with his most holy body and blood, though John the Baptist, of exceptional holiness, confessed himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his shoe. May the Holy Spirit, therefore, who, when the days of Pentecost were completed, filled the hearts of Christ’s disciples, fill [Col. 0718B] your soul and heart with like power and sweetness of ardor, so that you may pour forth a good word acceptable to God and worthy of heavenly reward, pleasing to the brothers and to all the children of holy mother Church. Farewell in Christ.

## FRANCO THE MONK’S PREFACE TO ABBOT FULGENTIUS.

[Col. 0717]

[Col. 0717B] To Lord FULGENTIUS, venerable Father, rightly to be honored by the name and office of the highest Father, FRANCO, his son unworthy of so great a father: filial affection with due obedience.

Beloved Father, since, in your praiseworthy desire, you wish not to be found ungrateful to the Grace of God—to whom every creature rightly gives thanks, each in its own voice, as to its Creator—and since, like an eager merchant, you search with holy eagerness to find that most precious pearl, the treasure of the riches of God’s grace, you lay an unbearable burden upon our weak neck, a burden in no way proportioned on an equal scale to our powers—if I may say so without offense to your prudence. For you ask, indeed, by that modest and humble authority of yours command, that I compose some small treatise on the Grace of God, beneficial to infants still drawing the milk-flowing breasts of holy mother Church: those who still, as you say, stammer about God’s grace; who do not yet speak of grace itself with a full voice; who, because of the immaturity of their understanding, do not yet fully recognize either the benefit of grace or the very Author of grace.

It is a holy work, a truly divine work, a work full of every usefulness, a work to be pursued with every praise; a truly supercelestial gift, beyond the telling of all tongues of human poverty—indeed, beyond even angelic eloquence. For what else shall I call the grace of God but God himself? For if the power of God, the wisdom of God, his beauty and his glory are believed to be nothing other than God himself, then likewise the grace of God is believed—if rightly believed—to be God himself. And who is sufficient to speak worthily of God?

Consider then, I beseech you, my Father, how weighty is the burden of your command; and place beneath it the shoulder of your holy intercession to lighten it. Supported, therefore, by the patronage of your prayers, I shall undertake what you command, considering that God, the most gracious distributor of his gifts, so honors the rich with higher gifts that he does not at all cast aside the poor. He who commands the rich to offer him gold, silver, precious stones, and other things which the hands of the wealthy can more easily obtain, gladly receives from the poorer even offered goats’ hair; and he preferred the two mites of the Gospel widow to all the gifts of the proud synagogue.

And lest anyone perhaps attribute this little work—whatever it may prove to be—of poor ability to presumption and confidence in my own learning, I set at its very threshold the title of obedience, placing your letter before detractors as a kind of imperial edict, so that they may regard me as excused because I obey commands. May that ever-watchful guardian preserve you in safety; and may that grace which you love advance you unto old age and the fullness of Abraham’s days.

# THE TWELVE BOOKS OF FRANCO, ABBOT OF AFFLIGEM, ON THE GRACE OF GOD. BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0719]

[Col. 0719C] As I am about to write on the Grace of God, I invoke the very Author of grace, that, with his aid, I may worthily bring to its proper end and with Catholic understanding the task I have undertaken at his command—for “he who hears you,” he says, “hears me”—so that, just as grace shines forth at once in the title at the beginning of the work, so also at its end thanksgiving may resound for the work brought to completion. Gathering, therefore, all things as it were into the bosom of my heart, and considering each one more carefully—whatever things we know or believe to have been created (we know visible things; we believe invisible things)—I find nothing among them all that does not rightly render thanks to its Creator. For it was created by his wisdom when it did not exist, and it has from him the power to remain in the dignity of its received creation.

For even those highest things among God’s creatures, the blessed ranks of blessed spirits, distinguished for the ministry of their Creator in an order wonderful and ineffable to us, likewise—indeed, much more—fall down before their Creator, ascribing wholly to his grace what they are, what they know, and what they can do. And, as sacred Scripture testifies, they unceasingly render thanks to him with their voices, both for the excellence of their creation and [Col. 0720C] for the continuance of their blessedness. Hence the prophet Isaiah, raised by the prophetic Spirit, testifies that he saw the Invisible One seated upon a lofty throne, and heard two seraphim—the ranks nearest to the divine majesty, burning more intensely, according to their name, from the flame of his love—crying out to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts.”

But that supreme power and incomparable might, Creator of all things and Governor of all, containing all things and needing none, alone grants all things freely to everyone in such a way that it receives no recompense from anyone. For in the same prophet, when he rejects the victims of Jewish superstition, saying, “What use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?”, he plainly indicates that he needs nothing, adding: “I am full.” Whatever is full needs nothing in respect of that in which it is full. From this fullness John also, greatest among those born of women, had drawn, when he said: “From his fullness we have all received grace for grace.”

Since, therefore, the divine essence is full in itself and filled from nowhere else, it follows that it created all things which it created, not from any need of itself, but solely through the grace of its goodness. Rightly, then, every creature and every order, angelic as well as human, serves it; and whatever dignity, usefulness, honor, and glory shines throughout the whole creation is rightly ascribed wholly to the Creator’s grace. And this is the true blessedness of all things that have been made: that they refer all things to the praise of him from whom they have even their very being.

Because the apostate angel, puffed up by the greatness of his own splendor, refused to do this, and wished to ascend above the height of the clouds—that is, to transcend by proud presumption the very glory of angelic dignity—and to become like that divine majesty inaccessible to every creature, he was crushed by the undertaking of such impiety and, [Col. 0721B] cast out from the midst of the fiery stones, was thrown down, by the just sentence of the righteous Judge, into the baseness of earthly dust. Nor would that proud spirit, inventor of pride, have been content with this goal—namely, attaining the likeness of the Most High—unless this goal had been boundless.

Over his unhappy fall, under the figure of the prince of Tyre, the prophet Ezekiel is commanded to take up a prophetic lament and, lamenting, to say:

“You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty;  
you were in the delights of God’s paradise.  
Every precious stone was your covering:  
sardius, topaz, and jasper;  
chrysolite, onyx, and beryl;  
sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald;  
gold was the workmanship of your adornment,  
and your openings were prepared on the day when you were created.  
You were the outspread and protecting Cherub, and I placed you  
upon the holy mountain of God, in the midst [Col. 0721C] of fiery stones.  
You walked perfect in your ways from the day of your creation,  
until iniquity was found in you.”

O how wonderful is the power of the Creator in the prince of Tyre! O how lavish is the outpouring into his creature of the Giver of all good things! He created this prince from nothing, endowed him with the fullness of wisdom, adorned him with perfect beauty, and covered him with every precious stone—that is, with the manifold glory of virtues.

This is that Lucifer who rose in the morning, who, because of the excessive splendor of his brightness, turned the faces of those who looked upon him toward himself. The true Sun, God, illuminator of all stars, alone surpassed him by the greatness of his incomparable splendor. O Lucifer, Lucifer, how brightly you would have shone, had you been willing to recognize your illuminator; [Col. 0721D] had you referred back to him the brightness bestowed upon you by him!

Alas, how destructive you are, pride—even to the heavenly powers themselves—enemy of all good things, worm and moth of all beauty and integrity! Gather together, kings of the earth, and be astonished; all peoples, attend and marvel; and you, earth and ashes, be frightened by this example. Beware, O human being, of the touch of pride. Behold: that morning star, ascending brilliant and radiant from its rising, is suddenly darkened by the cloud of pride rising from his own heart’s corruption; and he who boastfully declared that he would rise above the stars of God is suddenly turned—alas!—into a sulphurous torch and, driven by the whirlwind of majesty, plunged into the darkness of the abyss.

Where now is that empty swelling, that wretched prince? Is this how one ascends above the height of the clouds? Is this how one mounts the throne which you boasted you would raise above the stars of God? Is this to be like the Most High? Do you not know, wretch, that humility reigns even in the heights? But your pride cannot perceive either what humility is or where it reigns. Hear, therefore, O earth; hear and tremble: for even the firmament has been weakened, and heaven, torn apart, has lost so many thousands of angels. This is the cause of the grief and prophetic lament which, instructed by the prophetic Spirit, he raises over the prince of Tyre.

“Gold,” he says, “was the workmanship of your adornment, and your openings were prepared on the day when you were created.” Trembling and afraid, I put my finger into these invisible openings; yet, guided by divine grace, I grope as one attempting to explore dark things with a trembling hand. A seal or pearl is pierced not from within, but from without. Therefore the openings of this seal were prepared on the day of its creation not by itself, but by the hand of its Creator, through which wisdom divinely infused might teach the prince of Tyre that his shining in God’s likeness had been bestowed upon him by divine grace.

Since we understand gold as meaning understanding, gold was the workmanship of this prince’s adornment when, illumined by the light of wisdom, he discerned the difference between Creator and creature; when he preserved equality with those who shared his nature; when, as a creature, he rendered obedience to the Creator. Made an outspread Cherub by this abundance of knowledge and greatness of gifts, and protecting those beneath him by the eminence of his dignity, he was placed among the fiery stones, upon the mountain [Col. 0722C] of God: that is, among the elect spirits burning with the fire of divine love, raised by grace and not by merit to the highest summit of divine contemplation.

We have heard from where and to what height grace raised the prince of Tyre; let us now hear to what depth ungrateful pride cast him down. “You walked,” he says, “perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you.” “In you,” he says, “was it found”: it was not breathed in from elsewhere, nor persuaded by another.

“In the multitude of your trading your inward parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned; and I cast you out from the mountain of God, and destroyed you, O protecting Cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up in your beauty; you destroyed your wisdom in your beauty. I cast you upon the earth; I gave you before the face of kings, that [Col. 0722D] they might see you.”

The Lord gave the prince cast down and rejected before the face of kings when, as the disciples returned from preaching and took a certain human pride in the expulsion of demons and the performance of signs, he said: “I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning.”

“In the multitude of your iniquities and in the iniquity of your trading, you defiled your sanctification.” It was wholly wicked and unjust trading: that a creature raised from nothing by the gift of its Creator to such glory should seize for itself, by tyrannical usurpation, the likeness of its Creator. But because he wished to seize it by robbery and violate the divine holiness, he defiled even that angelic sanctification which he possessed by nature.

“I will therefore,” he says, “bring forth fire from your midst which shall devour you.” And rightly so: from where such impiety had proceeded, thence also should come forth the avenging flame to punish it. “And I will make you ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you”—not because a spirit is dissolved into ashes, but because, stripped of angelic glory, he was reduced as it were to the baseness of ashes. “All who see you among the nations shall be astonished at you; you have become nothing, and you shall not be for ever”: not because he ceased to exist substantially, but because, by apostatizing from God, he lost blessed existence.

Nor have I set forth in sequence, though somewhat at length, the wretched fall of this apostate and the prophet’s lament over him without purpose, but in order to show more clearly, by contrast, how greatly the blessed spirits are debtors to the grace of God, [Col. 0724A] by whose gift, while others fell from so lofty a summit of dignity through the impulse of pride, they themselves remained steadfast in the eternal stability of their blessedness. But if this is so of spirit, what of flesh? If of an angel, what of a human being? If of heaven, what of earth? Therefore he too is cast down to earth and set before those born of earth as an example, so that they may be terrified by the fall of so great a prince and, not ungrateful for received grace, may likewise enjoy their blessedness eternally with the blessed spirits.

Having considered these matters concerning that more excellent creature, according to the slenderness of our understanding, let us pause a little for breath, so that, our strength restored and the Holy Spirit going before us, we may complete the journey we have begun concerning the Grace of God.

## Preface to the Second Book

[Col. 0723]

[Col. 0723B] As I am about to sail, at your command, venerable Father, upon this great and wide sea, I confess that I entrust the little boat of my poor intellect to uncertain waves not without fear: lest perhaps, with the helmsman’s eye led astray by some sinister star, I strike upon the Syrtes, or be swallowed in the whirlpool of Charybdis, or fall among the dogs of Scylla to be devoured. And I fear that, while rashly seeking the pearl hidden in the deep, I may myself perish in the depths, suffocated by Egyptian waters and deprived of life-giving breath.

Raise therefore, I beg you, your untiring hands to heaven with Moses, and pray for favorable winds for the sailor, so that the pearl which you seek, divinely revealed to me through your prayers, may enable me, with ship and cargo safe, joyfully to reach the harbor of salvation. With sails therefore spread at your command, I shall be borne out upon the deep by him who breathes from the south; and wherever the impulse of the Holy Spirit drives me, I shall follow gladly and with thanksgiving.

## Second Book

[Col. 0723]

[Col. 0723C] The Wisdom of God, reaching from end to end, filling all things and embracing all things, from whom nothing can be hidden and nothing can perish, had brought that numerous multitude of angels to the fullness of integrity which was pleasing in his sight. Yet, although this multitude was protected against the fall of those who became proud, its full number in God could not itself suffer loss. Therefore, lest any loss should seem to have occurred in his creation, he formed within himself a wonderful plan of restoration: that he might transform a certain lower material, by the art of his wisdom, into the same glory.

Before I speak of this material’s creation and dignity, I shall permit the eyes of my heart to range a little through the breadth of the elements of the world, so that, having surveyed this great house and examined more carefully the beauty and ornament of its wonderful structure and its varied furnishings, I may estimate from the great glory of the house how great is the glory of the lord of the house. Both glories—the glory of house and of lord—proclaim the craftsmanship and commend the grace of their Creator.

Therefore the Wisdom of God, intending to make, for the restoration of the heavenly ruin, a human being—an earthly angel, so to speak—first created for him a house in which he might dwell. He set its foundations in the solidity of the earth; he extended its length from east to west; he spread its breadth from south to north; he raised its height to heaven, which he placed over the whole structure like a vault, protecting it as a kind of roof. And so that sufficient light might be present for this great house, he fixed in heaven the sun, [Col. 0724C] moon, and stars, great and splendid lights, so that from above they might shine upon the whole house and render their lord unfailing service in grateful succession.

The field is clothed with flowers; the trees are clothed with leaves and made fruitful with fruits, so that they may offer new fruits to the new lord when he comes forth from the secret counsel of God’s wisdom into public view, and may provide him a pleasing spectacle through the variety of their beauty. All the elements present themselves festively: heaven gladdens all things with the cheerfulness of its countenance; the air dances with the melody of birds; earth, about to receive its lord, adorns itself with splendid cultivation and many colors; sea and rivers likewise rejoice in their rippling waters and fish, which meet one another in swimming, as is the way of those who rejoice, and applaud in their own fashion.

Nor have I mentioned these things as mere entertainments, to delight the ears of my hearers or stir up applause for myself, but so that from consideration of them the human being may understand how greatly indebted he is to God, who created him solely through the grace of his goodness for this glory; who ordered elements so splendid for his service, assigned to his use whatever swims in the waters, walks upon the earth, flies in the air, and gleams in heaven. But woe to the human being who, on the last day, is found ungrateful for so great a grace, whether by living badly or by ascribing to his own merits the fact that he lived well—if indeed it can rightly be called living well.

The necessary resources for human use having therefore been prepared, he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” O condescension! O grace! Who can think of it worthily? Who can express it in words? Who can love it as it deserves? He does not say, “Let us make man in the image of an angel, in the image of an archangel, in the likeness of cherubim or seraphim.” But what does he say? “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” What is man but mud? For man was made from clay. And what else is it to say, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” than, “Let us fashion mud and make a god”? “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High,” says Scripture, which, as Truth testifies, cannot be annulled. Divinity shines in mud as an image in a mirror, and mud has been made firm into God.

O mud, how base and abject you were! Behold how firm, how pleasing, how glorious you have become, after you were taken into the hands of the heavenly potter. Recall, therefore, what you were; consider what you are. Recall the baseness of your material; consider the dignity of the one who formed you. And, thus firmly established, always stand with steady foot, lest you ever slip from the hand of your potter.

The vessel of election commended this potter’s art and the power of his art when, with apostolic authority reproving vessels ungrateful to their potter, he said: “Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” The prophet Jeremiah, known to God before he was formed and sanctified before he was born, is commanded to go up in prophetic understanding into this potter’s house; and, in the figure of the potter into whose house he was commanded to descend, to admire this potter’s art, work, and power, and, by the example of the broken and remade vessel, to console a grieving people with a joyful promise.

But because that potter, remaking what was broken, served that particular time, let us return to our own potter. At the beginning of time he was not remaking what had been broken, but forming what did not exist; when from his clay he formed not one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, but one vessel alone, in perfect beauty, for honor and glory. To this glory of creation, this special gift of God’s image, and this heavenly privilege, free choice was also bestowed upon the human being by the Creator’s gift, so that one who could distinguish good and evil by reason and understanding might also have the power to choose what he wished. Thus, to the greater praise of the giver and glory of the one who uses it rightly, he might flee evil and seek good not from the necessity of a divine command, but from the inclination of his own choice.

For that which is done from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness is not truly called good. “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts fear out.” Therefore that which is not grounded in the root of love is falsely called good. And how great a grace is this! For what master says to his servant, “Do what you wish, servant, if you wish”? What master sets his servant free, so that he need not serve if he does not wish to? What potter forms clay and does not form it for his own use? Yet our potter, bestowing all things upon his work and needing it for absolutely nothing, leaves the created human being free in his own choice and grants him the option of choosing whatever he wishes.

What is more fitting to God’s image than to recoil from the foul and embrace the honorable? What better accords with reason than to choose virtues and detest vices? Both, namely good and evil, are set before him: the use of the one is urged; the other is forbidden. The reward and end of each are proclaimed: eternal life for the one, death—likewise eternal—for the other. Thus, clothed with every beauty and protected on every side, he introduces the human being into the paradise of delight which he had planted from the beginning. He grants him the use of every tree in paradise, but forbids one. For how would a servant know that he had a lord unless he received a command? “From every tree of paradise,” he says, “eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.”

Alas! From that invisible enemy, that inventor of all malice and deceit, who accomplishes more through tricks than through strength, the human being could not be safe even in paradise, because he proved ungrateful for so great a grace. Blown upon by the spirit of pride and overthrown by the deception of the ancient serpent, while he wished to be like the Creator, he could not remain what he had been created. For while he sought, through tyrannical power, to rule himself—which belongs to God alone—unbridled in pride, he cast off with rebellious neck the obedience due to the most gentle Ruler, under whose governance he had been safe. And while he sought the false divinity which the devil had promised, enslaved by sin he lost the true divinity and the immortality of body and soul which grace had bestowed.

Then that most health-giving tree, created by God and planted in paradise, which had been for the obedient a tree [Col. 0726C] of the knowledge of good, became for the disobedient a tree of the knowledge also of evil. For, stripped of the glory of immortality and ashamed at the disgrace of his nakedness, he learned how great an evil it is for a human being to resist God, for a creature not to obey the Creator.

O cruel pride, mother of cruelty! O envy, cruel daughter of a most evil mother! Have you become more blessed because this man has become wretched with you? Do not rejoice; do not exalt yourself, for the lost man has not perished utterly, nor has he been utterly destroyed by the point of your malice. Now you shall see the power of our potter; now you shall marvel—or rather, grieve—at the skill of his art: for he who, in the old man, had formed dust moistened with heavenly dew into angelic glory will, in the new man, raise that same form by the wonderful and wondrous wisdom of his art above every virtue, principality, and power, to the right hand of God the Father.

Therefore he gathers up the fragments of the broken vessel. “Adam, where are you?” he says, so that his seeking of the lost may be a sign of love and a means of consolation. The transgressor is accused of his transgression; penance is imposed upon the guilty; sweat of the brow and scarcity of food are inflicted; the exile from paradise is thrust into this valley of tears; his bloodied conscience is pricked by thorns and thistles. But lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow and utterly crushed by despair, the work of human redemption is immediately enacted in mystery in the very first offspring of the human race.

For righteous Abel, first in the type of the supreme priest, performing the office of priesthood, commends to God through the innocence of his life the sacrifice offered from the firstborn and chosen sheep. When Cain, his brother, devoid of fraternal love, saw that Abel’s offering was accepted, he envied it; and, goaded by envy, himself first pierced by the point of his own malice, killed the innocent man. Abel had no crime other than that he was innocent. Behold: already in mystery, the blood of the true Abel cries out to God the Father for the sin of paternal disobedience, [Col. 0728A] asks pardon for the transgressor, excuses guilt through innocence, and sets the sin of the world at the price of its own blood. But concerning the benefit of this blood and the worth of its price, since we still walk in the darkness of the shadow of things to come and have not yet proceeded in speech to the rising of the true Sun, let us defer the matter until the fullness of time and the coming of Truth.

## Short Preface to the Third Book

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727A] The Word of God is like spices: the more it is ground, the more it gives off fragrance; and the more finely it is sifted through the spiritual sieve, the sweeter is the taste found in it. In this little work, through the favor of the very grace of which I speak, I experience this to some extent in myself: the more vigorously I grind it with the pestle of my tongue, the more I taste its sweetness [Col. 0728A] and the more I love it. Having therefore tasted beforehand how sweet is the fruit of labor, I shall gladly persevere in the work I have begun, invoking that anointing from heaven which, by anointing them, refreshes the weary limbs of laborers and will supply the strength necessary for those at work.

## Third Book

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727B] In the preceding part of this work, I lamented with the prophet the fall from heaven of Lucifer, who, plunged into the darkness of the abyss, is known to have been sought by no mercy of God, nor ever to be sought. Then, in the creation of man, I marvelled at the greatness of the Creator’s grace: that he created the lowliness of clay in his own image and likeness. When man had been ensnared by the serpent’s craft and cast out of Paradise, God in his devised goodness had compassion on him; and he who allowed an angel of such great brightness to perish was tenderly concerned for the restoration of his clay. Recognize, therefore, O man, how much you owe to the most kindly Lord, who neither allows one who is perishing to perish, nor is turned aside by an adversary, but pursues the fugitive with fatherly love, calls him back, speaks gently to him, and, when he has returned, not only forgives his crime but also promises him a kingdom.

[Col. 0727C] O lavish goodness, O ineffable kindness, O grace to be pursued with every act of thanksgiving: you withdraw yourself from no one; you are not overcome by the enormity of anyone’s crime; you are everywhere at hand, nourish all things, strengthen all things, protect all things, preserve all things. O stubborn servant, O ungrateful one, why do you not love the Lord, whom you experience everywhere as so merciful and so kind? What is this hardness of your heart, which cannot be melted by so great a fire of love? But let us return to the delightfulness of grace and rejoice in contemplating it.

This grace did not fail the righteous Noah in the time of tribulation, when it washed, as by a baptismal flood, the whole earth infected by the filth of sinners—for all flesh had corrupted its way. It showed him the timber by which he might be saved and might save others; it instructed him beforehand to fit out the ark for his own salvation and that of his household:

[Col. 0727D] how he was to construct it, how to join it together, and with what to coat it. And lest it should be idle at any time, in the mystery of the resurrection it preserved the human race—or rather, the seed of the human race—in eight souls. From those few grains sprang that most fertile

[Col. 0728B] harvest of Abraham’s race.

This grace led the righteous Lot out from the burning of Sodom, when it protected him beneath the shadow of its hand amid the burning wicked; as from the flame of lust, so also from the flame of sulphur. Further, after Abraham had been brought out from Ur of the Chaldeans and led by the grace of the one calling him into the land of promise, the darkness of ignorance gradually faded away and the light of faith poured itself into a blind world. When the covenant had been established with Abraham, God, the most kindly comforter of mourning Zion, promises the very author of grace and mediator of the covenant: “In your seed,” he says, “all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed.”

Whence comes this joyful promise? Whence this new blessing? By what merit of yours, O man? It had been said to you—and this indeed you had deserved—“Cursed is the earth in your work.”

[Col. 0728C] Does the flower of blessing rise from the root of cursing: that truly blessed seed, that truly holy shoot, which sanctifies the whole mass, corrupted by the leaven of sin, through the sprinkling of its blood? What, then, is this seed? “He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though of many,” says the Apostle, “but as of one: ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ.” Behold Abraham’s seed; behold him concerning whom the promise was made to Abraham; behold the expectation of the nations, the blessing of the nations. This is that true seed, that Gospel grain, which, cast into the furrows of faith, bears a most abundant fruit.

Already it sends its root on high; already it fastens its root in Abraham’s very faith—a root that can never be dried out by any heat, nor at all torn up by any heretical hand. Already in the faith of the one Abraham that holy root grows together, which later will spread in a multitude of branches throughout the whole

[Col. 0728D] breadth of the world and, at the time of harvest, will be multiplied by the faith of the nations as by the abundance of fruits.

Behold, you who love grace, you who inquire into the greatness of grace: lift up the eyes of your mind and look upon the author of grace. Consider that grace works even in the very

[Col. 0729A] shadow of things to come; and that without grace the salvation of humankind is not even foreshadowed. Abraham was old and had taken a barren wife, now also an aged woman. Even if she had not been barren, because she had already passed the time of bearing children—for she was ninety years old—she could not give birth. Age, barrenness, and the capacity for childbearing excused their ordinary office, so that, when the law of nature had ceased, faith might have merit.

Scripture records that God led Abraham outside and, having shown him the brightness and multitude of the stars, said: “Consider the stars; if you can, count them. Your seed shall be made equal to them”—the seed which, from one son of promise, as though from a grain of blessing, will spread to east and west, north and south. Abraham is rightly led outside to receive the promise, because faith is not enclosed

[Col. 0729B] within the narrow bounds of human impossibility. “Abraham believed the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Abraham did not distrust or doubt; he considered neither his own old age nor that of his wife. He looked to the Almighty who promised and most certainly believed that he who had deigned to promise was also able to perform.

Thus from the father’s faith is born the son of promise: the joy of both parents and the hope of multiplying the seed. He receives his name from joy, because he shares the joy of his birth with the whole household; indeed, he is called Isaac as a type of him at whose birth a heavenly messenger announces joy not to one household but to the whole world. His rejoicing mother nurses the little heir; the trembling old woman diligently performs the office of a nurse. His aged father exults,

[Col. 0729C] prepares a feast, celebrates a festival—not so much because he himself has received a son, as because, in the son of promise, the salvation of the whole world and the redemption of humankind are promised, as the prophet understands.

In the mystery of that redemption, tested and commanded to sacrifice his beloved son Isaac—so that the flame of fatherly love might blaze more fiercely through so many names of affection—he obeys gladly. He girds on the sword, takes up his son, prepares the wood; nor does he then waver concerning the promise when he draws the sword against his son’s throat. His devotion to God overcomes paternal affection; and because he acknowledges God as Father, he does not know himself to be a father. Thus he stands with arm outstretched, a faithful servant ready to obey; he stands above his victim, a devoted priest,

[Col. 0729D] most certainly trusting that his offering would be the more acceptable to God the sweeter the affection he bore for his only son.

O blessed Abraham, with what praises shall I extol you? With what proclamation shall I magnify you? Rightly were you established as father of many nations, for upon your faith is founded the multitude of believers. What of innocent Isaac? What of the victim acceptable to God? He does not resist, kick back, contradict, or murmur. He rejoices that he has been chosen as a victim for God; he delights that his father’s obedience has been proved in him. But because the immortal one could not die, and Isaac, the only son of his father, bore the figure of the only-begotten Son of God, an angel cries out from heaven to the faithful servant not to stretch out his hand against the boy.

But the prophet, with prophetic eyes turned back behind him toward generations yet to come, sees and understands a ram caught by its horns among brambles;

[Col. 0730A] and, because without the shedding of blood there is no remission, he offers it in place of his son.

I have briefly touched upon the faith of our father Abraham, the promise of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the blessing of the nations in Christ. In these grace especially shines forth, and it is grace that I have undertaken to commend; in these human wisdom claims nothing for itself, nor does human effort. For this reason also, I think, the holy patriarchs received barren wives by God’s hidden counsel—Abraham, Sarah; Isaac, Rebekah; Jacob, Rachel—in whose actions, marriage, and offspring the sacrament of Christ and the Church was foreshadowed: so that, when nature’s assistance fails, humanity may understand itself to be saved by grace alone and not by merit.

Now, for the son of promise, to propagate

[Col. 0730B] the promised offspring, a worthy wife is sought. From the house of the wise man a wise servant is chosen, mature in years and judgment. With his hand placed beneath his master’s thigh, he swears by the God of heaven, and prophetically signifies the mystery that the Lord of heaven would be born from Abraham’s thigh. Thus the servant is sent to his master’s land and kindred. He employs prudent counsel: he takes his place beside the fountain of water, so that in the clear waters of wisdom he may behold the beauty of form of the wife to be betrothed. And because he perhaps himself understands the sacrament of this betrothal, he pours out prayer, asks assistance from heaven, casts a lot, and entrusts the choice to God.

By “lot,” however, I mean the sign which he himself set before himself and counted as a lot: that the maiden who came out to draw water, and was so diligent in drawing it

[Col. 0730C] as to suffice both for him and for watering the camels, would be worthy to enter into marriage with the patriarch. Behold: in this mystery too grace was present. It itself filled the servant with the spirit of counsel; it itself established the kind of lot; it itself chose the wife. Yet Rebekah, called by lot to the fortune of the bridal chamber, remains barren and does not fulfill a wife’s office, so that the patriarch might understand grace to be necessary even in the promise and obtain fruitfulness for his wife through prayers.

Nor was grace absent in the struggle of the little ones in the womb. Not yet born, they foreshadow the contest of two peoples and contend for precedence; and it belongs to grace that one overcomes the other, though neither had done anything good or evil. He who is born later is preferred to the earlier one. One of them lives at home and is protected under the roof of protecting grace;

[Col. 0730D] the other wanders outside, while he boasts proudly within himself, like that Gospel Pharisee, about Abraham’s seed, the observance of the received law, the diverse ritual of ceremonies, and sacrificial victims. Concerning the election of one and the rejection of the other, the Apostle treats at greater length, overflowing with the stream of apostolic eloquence. Whoever desires to know his judgment on these matters should turn his gaze toward that apostolic heaven which declares the glory of God and hear him thunder forth his own words.

Isaac loves Esau with fatherly affection, as he hunts outside and, as it were, toils for his own righteousness. But Rebekah cherishes Jacob within with motherly tenderness, since he presumes nothing from himself. Isaac intends, as a type of the Jewish people, to bless the firstborn; but grace, the mother, places beneath the blessing right hand the people of the nations. She herself counsels the stratagem by which the blessing is to be taken; she herself teaches the art of feigning; and, when her son trembles, she herself performs the cook’s office.

[Col. 0731A] Truly a loving mother, who does not refuse a maidservant’s work in order to obtain the blessing for her son. Truly a wise woman, who knows how to cook and season kids in such a way that they equal—or even surpass—the savour of goats and deer.

For the Good Shepherd, having set forth the parable of the hundredth sheep and the tenth drachma, each lost and found, says: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing repentance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance.” Rebekah knows, as one instructed by her husband and as a wife attentive to her husband, what food pleases Isaac more, what kind

[Col. 0731B] of seasoning tastes sweeter and is more savoury. Among women there is no other like Rebekah: so wise, so energetic, so devoted, so diligent. By the craft of her wisdom she strips the kid’s skin in such a way that she does not leave it naked; she sheds its blood in such a way that she does not take away its life.

Thus the old man, delighted by the savour of Rebekah’s seasoning and made happier by a draught of wine, asks for a kiss as he is about to bless his son; he gives a kiss, because there is no blessing without the kiss of love. In blessing him, therefore, he invokes upon his son abundance from the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth: that, sprinkled from above with the dew of wisdom, he may

[Col. 0732A] spiritually discern spiritual things and from the fatness of the earth produce the fruits of mercy.

Thus, thus does grace the mother always labour for the son whom she loves; thus she advances the gentle, thus the humble. Thus she never ceases to present the sons of adoption to God the Father, as though to one whose sight is dimmed and who does not impute the sins of former ignorance, that they may be blessed daily.

Something similar happens in us. The one born first within us is red and bloody, wholly hairy with the roughness of vices; he pursues carnal things, values spiritual things at nothing, loves a dish of lentils more than his birthright, and sells the dignity of the firstborn for the cheapness of lentils—a thing so great for so paltry a price. But the one born later is simple and gentle, pursuing spiritual things and valuing carnal things at nothing. Like a wheel, he scarcely clings to the earth for a moment,

[Col. 0732B] but strives with his whole effort to raise himself to heavenly things. In order to inherit the paternal blessing, he purchases his brother’s birthright with a dish of lentils—a thing so great for so paltry a price. But that the younger should overcome the elder and the later supplant the earlier is not a matter of merit but of grace, since the former is first by the order of birth and first obtained the kingdom of sin in our body. From that kingdom the grace of God has delivered us and transferred us into the kingdom of his Son. Since in that kingdom eternal rest from all our labours is promised to us, let us now rest, wearied from this work.

## Preface to the Fourth Book

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731B] Just as colour then shines more brightly and appears more beautiful when applied by the painter’s hand to the underlying panel, and one colour is distinguished from another by the pleasing variety introduced by the painter, so any writing is usually more pleasing to readers when divided into books or volumes and interwoven, as it were, with a manifold variety of colours through fittingly introduced examples, figures, and testimonies.

Accordingly, as I pass through the most delightful paradise of the ancient Fathers, I pluck certain flowers from it and bring them into this present little work, so that from the brightness and beauty of

[Col. 0732C] heavenly flowers my rustic discourse may find whatever small measure of favour among its hearers. For this reason I introduce the examples of the holy Fathers and their wondrous deeds, impossible to human weakness: that divine grace may be more clearly apparent in their deeds, precisely insofar as human strength is seen to have failed in them and human counsel to have proved inadequate. Let this volume, then, take its beginning from Jacob’s departure into a foreign land, in whose election and blessing the preceding narrative set its conclusion.

## Fourth Book

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731D] Jacob, therefore, fearing his raging brother, who threatened him with death on account of the blessing taken from him, is persuaded by his mother and, already instructed in that Gospel saying, “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another,” and that apostolic saying, “Give place to wrath,” sets out into exile, accompanied by his father’s blessing. Deprived of his parents’ comfort, he is received into the bosom of God’s compassion to be cherished.
