By divine compassion’s own ordering his journey is directed; by its own advance a nightly lodging is provided for the traveller.

When, therefore, he had come to a certain place, he lay down to sleep after sunset, placing a stone beneath his head. His body slept in purity, but his spirit kept watch with God; and, like the bride in the words, “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch,” he sang, as it were, as one loving the bridegroom in spirit, as

[Col. 0732D] it were. Thus, for the blessed exile so blessedly asleep, the heavens are opened, God’s secrets are disclosed, and the mysteries of peace to be restored through love as mediator between the heights and the depths, between God and humankind, are shown.

For, raising his eyes, he flies above earthly things and penetrates heavenly ones. He sees the ladder of love resting on two commandments as on two sides, and holding the Law and the Prophets together in those two by an indissoluble bond, stretched from earth all the way to heaven; and he sees the angels of God ascending and descending by it. He sees also the Lord above, resting upon the ladder as the principle of love, and saying to him: “I am the Lord God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you sleep I shall give to you

[Col. 0733A] and to your seed; and your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth. You shall spread abroad to west and east, north and south; and in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. I shall be your guardian wherever you go, and I shall bring you back to this land; nor shall I leave you until I have fulfilled all that I have said.”

Established in his parents’ house, enclosed by their protection, and soothed by the service of servants, he hears nothing divine and sees nothing divine. But as an exile and fugitive, deprived of every human help, he finds God as guardian and protector and receives, by God’s promise, the promise that in his seed the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.

But Jacob, understanding the mystery of the vision and already beholding the time of grace with spiritual eyes, raises up as a pillar the stone upon which he had rested the head of faith, as upon the author of grace. Pouring oil over it, as though bringing down the Spirit from heaven, he prophetically signifies by the stone anointed by his hand that Christ is to be placed in the foundation of the Church. “For no one,” says the Apostle, “can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

[Col. 0733B] Marveling at the greatness of such grace, he says: “Truly the Lord is in this place.” But what is great or wonderful about the Lord being in that place? In what place is the Lord not? Indeed, he is the place of all places, the time of all times: from him all things arise, within him all things run their course, and to him all things return. Yet Christ, the stone conceived of the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin, and anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions,

[Col. 0733C] is the place in which the Lord truly is. “And I did not know it,” he says. Something similar—indeed, the very same thing—is said by another prophet, and more than a prophet, who, seeing the Holy Spirit descend from heaven upon the Lord and remain, says: “And I did not know him.”

And Jacob, in fear, says: “How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.” Truly the stone raised as a pillar and imbued with heavenly anointing is the house of God, because in it “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” It is also the gate of heaven, because through the key of faith in him heavenly things are opened, and through him, the Mediator, we enter to God the Father.

Now let us proceed in the order of the narrative to Joseph and set him before our face as a transparent mirror of grace. Sold as a slave through the envy of malicious

[Col. 0733D] brothers, he did not lose the liberty of his noble mind, being preserved by divine grace. As a type of Christ, tempted by the hand of an unchaste mistress, like an adulterous Synagogue, he left his cloak—as though his body were handed over into the hands of the wicked—and victoriously gained the palm of chastity.

Withdrawn from his father’s presence through his brothers’ malice and taken from the land of his birth into a foreign land, he possessed the grace of divine providence everywhere present. It did not fail him either when he was disgraced by the charge of adultery or when he was shut in prison. For innocence is safe even in prison and free even in chains. Thus Joseph, enclosed within the confines of prison, walks with God in the courtyard of his heart, speaks with God, philosophizes with God. Though he sees no human beings,

[Col. 0734A] he understands the mysteries of dreams, and in the restoration of the cupbearer and the condemnation of the baker prophetically foretells the calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews.

Both men, namely the cupbearer and the baker, know beforehand, from Joseph’s prophecy, what is to come upon them after the mystery of three days, because at one and the same time, by one and the same sacrament, the two peoples receive different wages according to their merits. For when, through faith in the Holy Trinity, the people of the nations is taken up to the service of the eternal King, so as to press wine from the vine which says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman,” and by its most sweet taste make glad the heart of the God who feasts with them, then the faithlessness of the Jews—which fails in the Trinity because it does not receive the Son—is punished in its head; so that those who had been the head among the holy Fathers

[Col. 0734B] may become the tail in an adulterous and degenerate generation.

But because the grace of divine mercy is most present precisely when hope of human consolation has already entirely vanished, that exile and unknown man, bought as a slave for a slight price, who as one guilty of a crime—and so great a crime—against his master had been shut in prison for punishment, is suddenly, by divine appointment, raised from the wrong of imprisonment to the rulership of all Egypt. He is set over the administration of so great a kingdom; and he who perhaps had suffered hunger in prison, forewarned by the spirit of counsel, delivers not Egypt alone but the whole world from famine.

But Joseph, gentle and a most steadfast guardian of his humility even in his glory, already taught in spirit by that precept of the Law, though it had not yet been published—“You shall not remember the injury of your fellow citizens”—recognizes his brothers while remaining unrecognized,

[Col. 0734C] because those who had lost brotherly feeling deservedly did not recognize their brother’s face. Yet because rotten wounds require iron and cautery, he rages against the guilty with a dove-like severity; he strikes the offenders with the two wings of love; and, having instructed them by salutary discipline, he reminds them of the violation of love.

“Rightly,” they say, “do we suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother when we saw the anguish of his soul as he pleaded with us, and we did not listen. Therefore this tribulation has come upon us.” Yet even in raging he does not rage; rather, in raging he loves more and gives better counsel, so that by the cleansing medicine, the bitterness of envy being boiled away, they too may put on the bowels of mercy and, sprinkled with the honey of brotherly sweetness, may also recognize brotherly faces in the mirror of love.

Behold, careful observer of grace: fix your eyes upon this transparent

[Col. 0734D] mirror, and, if you can, contemplate its greatness of brightness with eyes undazzled. What grace was this, what kind and how great, which in sudden transformation raised one sold, enslaved, poor, exiled, condemned, and shut in prison to be ruler of a mighty kingdom?

The same grace saved little Moses from Egyptian waters—from heretical waters—lest he be drowned. It adopted him as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; indeed, through the son it adopted the mother as its daughter. And it cried to him with the prophetic voice: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty.” This grace brought little Moses, whom his mother the Synagogue could not raise to perfect manhood,

[Col. 0735A] to mature strength—so much so that he pierced with the sword an Egyptian disputing with a Hebrew and, as it were, striking him with the fist of perverse doctrine; then he hid him in the sand and covered what was earthly with earthly dust.

For this, he was betrayed by the very man whom, as a righteous man in mercy, he had reproved because of the injury inflicted on his brother. Sought by Pharaoh for death, he escapes by flight from the hand of those seeking his life, having as guide on the way and protector of salvation the one whom, immediately after his birth, when abandoned by his earthly father and exposed by his mother, he had had as his protector. O compassion, O mercy, O grace: when a father abandons, you do not forsake; when a mother exposes, you gather up; and when parental love dries up, you abound all the more.

“Can a woman forget

[Col. 0735B] her infant?” asks Isaiah—or rather, through Isaiah the Lord says to Zion: “that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Even if she should forget, yet I shall not forget you.” For although divine consolation never fails its faithful ones, nevertheless it is more abundantly present and protects more abundantly when the rage of persecutors rages more violently and burns more fiercely.

Hence Moses in the wilderness marvels that the bush burns and is not consumed, because it is overshadowed by the cloud of God’s mercy standing in the midst of the bush. For when the Lord stands in the midst of the Church, whatever fire of persecution may inflame it, it is not burned; rather, purified like gold in the furnace of tribulation, it is made purer than gold.

But Moses, who as a human being had fled from Pharaoh’s presence in human fear, strengthened by the grace of the divine address,

[Col. 0735C] returns more steadfastly. With the ten plagues of the rod of the Law he instructs the Egyptians, oppressors of God’s people; but, since they are not corrected, he overwhelms them for punishment in the waves of the sea, through which he conveys the children of promise by a new way to the land of promise.

What in these things, and in all these things, do you claim for yourself, human weakness? Why do you, empty dust, vaunt yourself over empty things? For the fiery overshadowing of the bush, the division of the sea, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the passage of the children of Israel are the work of God’s grace, not of your merit.

Moreover, when by these and other deeds and signs, of which I pass over many in the interest of brevity, the splendour of grace shone upon the blind, the trumpet of the Law also sounded for the deaf: so that the human being, to be restored by divine compassion to the ancient state of the first creation,

[Col. 0735D] might first learn by many teachings that he could find the way of recovery by no wisdom of his own, no power of his own, and no merits of his own, but by the grace of his Creator alone.

“Listen, Israel,” says the lawgiver, sounding the trumpet of the Law: “Today you shall cross the Jordan

[Col. 0736A] to possess nations greater and stronger than you, great cities fortified up to heaven, a great and exalted people, the sons of Anak, whom you yourself have seen and heard of, against whom no one can stand. Know, therefore, today that the Lord your God himself will go before you as a devouring and consuming fire, to crush, destroy, and scatter them before your face. Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed them before you: ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this land,’ when these nations have been destroyed because of their impieties. For you shall not enter to possess their land because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart; but because they acted wickedly, they were destroyed as you entered, and so that the Lord might fulfill his word,

[Col. 0736B] which he swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Know, therefore, that the Lord your God has not given you this excellent land as a possession because of your righteousness, for you are a stiff-necked people.”

What could be clearer or more manifest? Behold: neither by your sword nor by your bow, O human being, did you overcome the fiercest nations, trained in war from ancient times, against whom no one can stand; nor did you possess a land abounding in every good thing. And lest perhaps you should say, “If I did not obtain victory by my own strength, I nevertheless deserved it by my righteousness,” hear that you are a most stiff-necked people, and that you entered the land flowing with streams of milk and honey not so much for your own sake as for the righteousness of the fathers, because of God’s sworn promise.

Do not, therefore, be ungrateful for such great benefits. Prefer nothing to his love, who freely bestowed all these things on you. His love is sweeter than every sweetness, more sweet than every honeyed delight; compared with it, the sweetness of temporal things is found more bitter than gall.

[Col. 0736C] O at what cost to our inward sweetness do we injure ourselves when, with adulterous eyes after the likeness of transgressing Adam, we desire outward things; when, in contempt of the Creator, we love the creature more than the Creator; when, for certain trifles unworthy even of Christian eyes to behold, we offend the minds of our brethren and dissolve with contentious temper the brotherly love which is the bond of perfection. For to Christian eyes nothing except Christ ought to appear beautiful, and to the Christian heart nothing except

[Col. 0736D] Christ ought to taste sweet. May he himself, in order to season the affections of our souls with the savour of divine sweetness, boil away with the fire of his love the harmful humours of carnal affections—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Short Preface to the Fifth Book

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735D] “Deep calls to deep at the sound of God’s waterfalls.” Therefore, in order that the Gospel deep may become clear to us, let us first look through its waterfalls into the

[Col. 0736D] prophetic deep, and, with attentive ear, listen to what prophecy, when invoked by the Gospel, answers.

## Fifth Book

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737A] Therefore let the prophet David first sound for us the prophetic trumpet, and declare what from ancient times he learned from his fathers concerning the grace of God. “For thou, O Lord,” he says, “didst destroy the nations by thy hand and plant them; thou didst afflict peoples and cast them out. For they did not possess the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them; but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou wast pleased with them.” For in saving us it is not our merits but his own goodness that pleases God; nor is he won over so much by our service as appeased by his inborn goodness. By his right hand he protects us, by his arm he defends us, and by the illumination of his countenance—that is, by the spirit of counsel—he instructs us. But, as he speaks of the past, so he speaks also of the future: “My King and my God, command salvations for Jacob. Through thee we shall scatter our enemies; in thy name we shall trample down our adversaries. For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me.”

[Col. 0737B] Behold: with the same meaning, because with the same Spirit, lawgiver and prophet, like two cherubim with faces intent upon the mercy-seat, sing in harmony; and they attribute possession of the promised inheritance not to their own toil, skill, strength, military courage, or finally to their arms or merits, but to the grace of God, of which it is truly a gift.

But as Scripture records concerning that mighty man of whom this strong man, strong in hand, bore the type: “Jesus began both to do and to teach.” The grace which he proclaims in David’s words he also commends by deeds. For though he was humble and insignificant in his own eyes, he was found great in the eyes of the Lord,

[Col. 0737C] chosen for kingship by divine judgment, and anointed by the prophetic hand for the establishment of his kingdom—not with a lentil, but with a horn of oil. Having therefore undertaken care of the people and administration of the kingdom, when the foreign enemies attacked and peace was disturbed, he voluntarily exposed himself to danger; and, as a good king, he took thought more for the common good than for his own safety. Armed with the shield of faith, he alone at that time did not fear that monstrous Goliath—better called a monster than a man—huge in body, savage in spirit, accustomed to war, and puffed up by victories. For who would not fear so dreadful a monster? What warrior would not hide himself from his face?

But our David, the least indeed in bodily stature among his brothers, yet greatest in faith, most beautiful in appearance, and suffused with rosy redness in the mystery of Christ’s blood,

[Col. 0737D] did not know how to fear the enemy of God’s people and blasphemer of the holy Name. Fearless, and not terrified by the monstrous size either of body or weapons, he prepares to avenge both the injury to his people and the blasphemy against the name of the living God. Saul persuades him, therefore, to put on Saul’s own breastplate; he is covered with a helmet and girded with a sword. But burdened rather than equipped by all these things, hindered rather than protected, lest he seem to have placed hope of victory in the king’s weapons rather than in God, he again takes off the royal breastplate, removes the helmet, and unbuckles the sword.

What else does this deed seem to you to signify by the defender of God’s people, if not to sing by his actions: “For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword shall not save me”?

[Col. 0738A] He therefore betakes himself to familiar and invincible defenses, armed with apostolic armor: the breastplate of faith, the helmet of hope, and the sword of God’s word, knowing that the enemy of God cannot be overcome except through God’s word. He seeks no weapons of war. As a shepherd he takes the shepherd’s staff; he gathers from the brook five most clear stones, as though smoothed by the hand of God and inscribed by the finger of God; he hides them in a shepherd’s pouch; he meets the proud enemy face to face and drives one into his shameless forehead. With a single blow he crushes that enormous beast which challenged men one by one to single combat, and, victorious, cuts off the blaspheming head with its own sword.

Behold how David, though untrained for war, proclaims both by deed and by word that one must place confidence in God’s grace rather than in one’s own strength

[Col. 0738B] or weapons; how he strips himself of the royal breastplate so that grace may clothe him better; and how he seeks no weapons other than shepherd’s staff and stone to crush the most monstrous enemy—by which, as the prophet understands, the prince of the opposing power was to be slain by Christ.

Having thus slain, by God’s power rather than his own, the enemy of God’s people, and having gloriously triumphed over adversaries on behalf of all, he was thereafter established in the kingdom after his enemies had been subdued. He prepares, at royal expense and with royal generosity, to build a house for the Lord; he resolves to make a dwelling worthy of God. And because the wise man governs all things by counsel, he shares his counsel with the prophet, asking the Lord’s will concerning the devotion of his own will.

[Col. 0738C] But because human poverty is insufficient to build a house worthy of God, God commends his devotion indeed, but does not approve the work by divine judgment. Instead, he declares that one shall come forth from David’s womb and shall reign upon his throne with everlasting dominion, one so beloved and so uniquely chosen from among the sons of men that God shall be a Father to him, and he, with equal honor, shall be a Son to God.

“He,” he says, “when your days have been fulfilled, when the legal ceremonies have now been completed, and you sleep with your fathers, shall lay the foundations of the ecclesial house in the faith of the Gospel. He shall build its lofty walls upon columns of hope; and lest they be dissolved by any force of winds or rains, he shall coat them within and without with spiritual bitumen, as he once did that ark in the flood. He himself, finally, to bring to fitting completion the beauty of so great a house, shall set upon it the summit of charity, on which all the precepts of the Law and the Prophets depend.”

[Col. 0738D] But the Son promised to David—indeed, in David to the whole world—is alone found worthy among the sons of men: so wise, so rich, and abounding in such fullness of every good that he may build a house worthy of God. For he alone, taught from ancient times and from eternity, knows from what stones the house of God must be built; by what rule each stone must be squared; which must be laid in the foundation; which must be raised into columns; by what quality one is to be joined to another; by what variety of colors the house is to be adorned;

[Col. 0739A] and finally, by what celebration of praises and sweetness of melodies it is to be dedicated. His coming to build the Lord’s house is awaited; his wisdom, fitting for so great a work, is proclaimed. In this promise David glories more than in his royal throne.

In this promise is an admirable dispensation of God’s word: when he was about to promise such great things to a man—however great and holy, still a man—things exceeding human merit, things unattainable even by the excellence of angelic dignity itself, he first calls him back to himself and reminds him from where he was taken, by what means, to what place, and through whom he was brought. He recalls the lowliness of the pastoral office and the height of imperial authority: from the one he was raised by grace, to the other brought by power. He says that he himself was companion on the journey and protector in dangers;

[Col. 0739B] that he exalted David’s name through kingdom, riches, wars, and victories, and made it equal to the names of the mighty of the earth. Thus, first fortifying the fragility of the human mind by the remembrance of humility, against the poison of pride as by a kind of spiritual antidote, and then enumerating the blessings he had bestowed as testimony to great grace, he promises, as the crowning fullness of benefits, to establish forever also the throne of David’s promised son.

“King David entered,” Scripture says, “and sat before the Lord and said: ‘Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that thou hast brought me thus far? And this also seemed too little in thy sight, O Lord God, unless thou shouldst speak also concerning the house of thy servant into the distance.’” And a little later: “Because of thy word, and according to thy heart,

[Col. 0739C] thou hast done all these great things, so as to make them known to thy servant.”

“He entered,” it says. And where did he enter? Clearly, admonished through the prophet’s mouth by the Lord’s words concerning such numerous and great benefits, and moreover by promises far greater still, he enters the innermost chamber of his own heart. He sets himself before himself; on one side he weighs his own merits, on the other the divine benefits. And because his merits are far unequal to the benefits, he sits before the Lord, humbles himself before the Lord, and ascribes all things to the grace of him from whom he remembers that all had been freely bestowed upon him. “Because of thy word,” he says, “not because of my merit; according to thy heart,” not according to any plan devised by man.

Behold how a powerful king, a wise king—and therefore truly powerful because

[Col. 0739D] wise—commends grace by deeds, proclaims grace by word, and teaches that there is no protection safer for a human being than the help of God’s grace.

Isaiah, however, understands divine grace to be necessary for human frailty in every respect, and asserts that, when grace is removed, he does not hesitate to compare all human righteousness to the filthiest cloth of a menstruating woman. “We have all become as an unclean thing,” he says; “all our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth.” But David, groaning that he is guilty, humbly confessing his guilt, and skilfully composing a most devout prayer—very useful for all guilty persons in supplication—now presuming upon the goodness of the most forgiving Lord with hope of pardon, says: “Thou shalt sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” What,

[Col. 0740A] then, is more unclean than a menstruous cloth, or what is cleaner than snow? Who can reach this abyss of the riches of God’s grace, unsearchable by all human curiosity and impenetrable to all philosophical acuteness? By the slight sprinkling of the lowly herb hyssop, it so swiftly and powerfully washes perfectly away menstrual filth—indeed, our iniquities, fouler than menstrual filth itself—that its abundance of whiteness surpasses even the whiteness of snow.

Yet I do not call the sprinkling of the lowly hyssop slight in such a way as to have it understood as powerless; rather, it is slight, subtle, divine, and so powerful that without its sprinkling there is no cleansing at all from the menstruous stain, no sanctification of the holy tabernacle, of the book itself, of the people, or of anything whatever.

[Col. 0740B] What and how great is this grace, O sons of grace? From where, I ask, did it begin? Where does it end? Indeed, it neither began nor ends, but flows eternally from the eternal fountain; and in due season it enters the hearts of the elect as a fourfold river, richly watering, with timely and late rain, the bridegroom’s bed of spices so that it may produce the shoots of virtues.

This is that grace—this, I say, is the grace—which can cause the Ethiopian, who according to Jeremiah cannot change his skin, to cast off his native blackness more quickly than speech; which, by a mere nod, changes the leopard mottled with the diversity of heretical doctrine into the most pleasing whiteness of one faith.

I delight still to fix my eyes in admiration upon so great a grace, and from God’s own words to gather the most ardent zeal and most kindly affection of the most merciful Creator toward the human soul.

[Col. 0740C] In Jeremiah the Lord rebukes Jerusalem for committing fornication with idols, and in Jerusalem he rebukes the human soul for committing fornication with vices. Like a most merciful husband jealous for an adulterous wife, soothing her while she trembles under consciousness of her offense, and calling her back to the lawful bed after granting pardon for her incest, he is jealous, he soothes, he calls back; and, contrary to the custom of men, he declares that he will do this: that his incestuous, prostituted, adulterous wife need only return, and he will restore both the companionship of the marriage-bed and the dignity of her name, together with the undiminished love of former affection.

“It is commonly said,” he says, “If a man dismiss his wife, and she depart from him and take another husband, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But thou hast committed fornication with many lovers; yet return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive thee.

[Col. 0740D] Lift up thine eyes straight before thee, and see where thou hast not prostituted thyself. Thou didst sit in the ways, waiting for them, like a robber in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land by thy fornications and thy wickedness. Therefore the showers of rain have been withheld, and there has been no latter rain. Thou hast acquired the brow of a harlot; thou wouldst not blush. Therefore at least from this time call upon me: ‘My Father, thou art the guide of my virginity.’”

O mercy, O kindness, O marvelous, O wondrous charity! What was ever more merciful? What ever sweeter? We wretches, we whitewashed tombs, who outwardly make a show of holiness by the name of singularity and the garb of humility,

[Col. 0741A] while inwardly we breathe forth the rot and stench of dead men’s corpses—if we see a sinner, one like ourselves, we disdain and despise him. For we have cast our own sins behind our backs and fix our eyes on another’s speck, neglecting our own beam. If we see one fallen, if we see one wounded by robbers, we neither pity nor sympathize; we do not bind the wounds, nor raise the prostrate person with a comforting hand. Because we have no bowels of mercy, wretched men pass by the wretched.

We do not deem such a person worthy of a kiss or even of speech. The very bread we share with mice and throw from the table to dogs, we shudder, with Pharisaic arrogance, to share—as though it were sacrilege—with one who shares our nature and the name Christian. We do not remember

[Col. 0741B] the command which we have received, frequently heard, and frequently read: “Thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian, because thou wast a stranger in his land.” There is none of us who has not been exiled in Egypt, who has not served Pharaoh, who has not gathered straw for him as fuel, who has not groaned bent beneath his burden. And if we have been led out from the house of bondage and the furnace of iron with Christ as our guide, let us not abhor the Egyptian, in whose land we were strangers.

If we hear a Hebrew longing for the promised land but still groaning beneath the Egyptian burden, crying out, let us pity him and run to him. And so that we may fulfill Christ’s law, let us set the shoulder of brotherly charity beneath our brother’s burden. But—what I cannot say without grief—we have forgotten the fear of the Lord and pass by his commands with a deaf ear, and our brother’s need with dry bowels.

[Col. 0741C] But, to return to what preceded: he who alone is uniquely clean, alone clean among the sons of men, into whom nothing defiled enters, beside whose purity even angelic purity itself fails to escape being filth—he does not disdain us, reject us, or shrink from us in that foulest and most loathsome brothel of the heart.

Alas for grief! Alas for shame! What is horrible even to say: prostituted to the devil, the corrupter of souls, and—to speak foul things foully—defiled in our whole activity from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, that is, from the least thought to the completed deed: such people, so filthy, so worthless, so cast down, the most humble and merciful Lord does not abhor, despise, or reject. He takes such persons to himself in marriage; he gently entreats those conscious of so great a crime and terrified by their conscience to return to him.

He sends envoys skilled in reconciliation; he does not charge them with faithlessness or reproach them with adultery;

[Col. 0742A] and himself ordering the message of the embassy, he says: “Speak to her heart”—that is, soothe her and call her—“because her wickedness is completed, her iniquity is forgiven.” He recalls the fidelity of the first betrothal, the greatness of the dowry, the union of two in one spirit, the adornment and beauty of their shared bedchamber, the delight of the kiss, and the sweetness of the embrace. By these and such things he softens her when she trembles, restores confidence to her distrust, and finally, when she returns, sends out to meet her neither servants nor friends: he himself first meets her, first rushes to embrace her, first to kiss her. And when the feast of such great joy has been celebrated with fitting exultation, he brings his beloved into the chamber of spices.

Delighted beyond measure—indeed beyond every human measure—by his sweet presence, embrace, and kisses, she is now powerless through the excessive heat of her love. She scarcely sustains herself—indeed, she does not sustain herself—but, languidly falling back upon her beloved’s neck, she testifies to the greatness of love by the greatness of her voice and jubilation.

[Col. 0742B] “Daughters of Jerusalem,” she cries, “daughters of Jerusalem, strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.”

I judge this languor sweeter than every state of health; I do not doubt it stronger than death itself; I consider it preferable to kingdoms and thrones, and in comparison with it I value gold and mud alike. Yet though I love it in my heart as a tiny spark of small love, and proclaim it with my mouth, I confess that I do not yet know what is the bride’s languor from love of the bridegroom.

Therefore, whoever you are, avid for the food of grace and insatiable in your desire for inward sweetness, break into this chamber of spices, I say, whether with Gospel importunity or by secretly entering in stealthy silence. Having seized the private moment of bridegroom and bride, seek there, learn there, what is the greatness of grace—not from me, a most poor man who is himself ignorant of these things.

[Col. 0742C] Yet meanwhile, if you wish, feed upon these dishes of our poverty; and nourish yourself with the sweet kernel of Gospel wheat, somehow shaken out through the sieve of obedience and sprinkled with the oil of charity. But if anyone loves straw more, let him gather it for himself throughout Egypt wherever he will, and if he wishes, build a city for Pharaoh. As for me, I neither offer charity, a thing of such value, for sale in exchange for worthless straw, nor do I buy it myself.

May the Ancient of Days bless your holy head, venerable Father—in whom all things are mature and none grows old; for what is becoming old and aged is near destruction—and may he swiftly crush beneath your feet the common adversary of us all. Amen.

## Preface to the Sixth Book: On the Grace of the New Testament

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741D] Mariners skilled in navigation are accustomed, according to the character of the winds, to stretch or draw in the fold of the sail, to set it obliquely or directly; and the more swiftly they hasten to cross over, the more freely they loosen the sail to the wind, so that the laden ship may complete its course all the more quickly as the force of the wind pressing from behind [Col. 0742D] more greatly assists its motion.

Therefore, as my keel of obedience ploughs the sea of so great a mystery, I see that the sail of my poor intellect must not be drawn in, but, with the fold of pious desire expanded, must be spread wholly before the Holy Spirit. With all my inmost being I must cry out with the prophet: “Come, O Spirit, from the four winds.” For if the prophet is commanded to invoke the Spirit’s power in order to give life to dry bones, then a type of one people, how much more does necessity lie upon me—of most slender spirit, writing concerning the life of all nations in Christ—to invoke and earnestly entreat the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, that, taught by him, I may be able, within the capacity of human narrowness, to speak of the greatness of life-giving grace and the manner of its giving life?

[Col. 0743A] Therefore I invoke him with voice, heart, prayers, and desires, that, as beneath his shadow that glorious womb of the glorious Virgin swelled, and as, led by him from the Father’s bosom through the bridal chamber of that same womb, the heavenly bridegroom came forth to us, so from his [Col. 0744A] visitation I may conceive the catholic understanding of the incarnation of God’s Word and, in language suited to the utterance of stammering infancy, bring forth into the world that Word which was in the beginning.

And I earnestly pray that the most gracious Comforter may not so abhor the filth of an unclean hut that, offended, he passes by his little servant and leaves his poor man unconsoled in this sweat of his brow. But just as I divided the completed part of this work concerning the sacrament of the Old Testament according to the number five, so I have judged it fitting to mark the remaining part, in honor of the sevenfold Spirit, with the number seven.

## Sixth Book

[Col. 0743]

[Col. 0743B] Though innumerable counsels of God’s wisdom were available by which he could abolish the handwriting of sin that stood against us, he chose especially that means through which redeemed man might learn his Redeemer’s wondrous love toward him and receive from God’s own virtue an example of virtue to be imitated.

For I do not think that God’s omnipotence should be confined to that cause as though by necessity, nor that humanity was assumed by God and into God because man could not otherwise be redeemed. I confess that man could not be redeemed otherwise, because the Redeemer willed no other way. The cause, therefore, was the will of his goodness, not some necessity of impossibility; it drew in the almighty hand so far that, if he did not become man, he could not redeem man.

[Col. 0743C] But wondrous, ineffable, and incomprehensible to every understanding was this condescension: that God should become man, fullness should empty itself, bread should hunger, strength should grow weary, life should die. But why was this? That the man assumed by God might become God; that he who emptied himself might fill the emptied; that, hungering, he might feed those who fast; that, wearied, he might strengthen the exhausted; that, dead, he might give life to the dead.

Perfectly great grace; wondrous condescension; so great an emptying of so great a majesty. How emptied, do you suppose, was he who is immeasurable, enclosed in the very small and most pure womb of one little virgin? How emptied was the Almighty in the tender years and limbs of infancy, powerless even over himself? How emptied was he who alone is singularly rich and sufficient unto himself: he who clothed the heavens with light, wrapped in swaddling-clothes?

[Col. 0743D] How emptied was that ineffable joy of angels when he wailed in a cradle and wept for the cause of the first parent’s misery? How finally was that majesty, to be adored by virtues and dreaded by powers, emptied when mocked by sinners and smeared on the face with spittle?

Yet lest anyone suppose that the power of divine majesty was so emptied in the assumed humanity that God’s omnipotence failed in our weakness or was diminished in any part of itself, let such a person distinguish, in the same person, the property of each nature, understanding that the weak things are to be attributed to the man and the divine things to God. Therefore the emptying of the Son of God must be believed to be nothing other than the dispensatory concealment of divine majesty in the Son of Man.

[Col. 0744B] Since, therefore, the good shepherd had chosen this particular way, as we have said, for seeking the lost sheep, he employed a new mode of creation in creating the new man. And it was fitting that he who came to heal the mass corrupted in Adam should be born not from the seed of corruption but from the power of the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, the most beautiful bride among the daughters of men was sought, from whose womb, like a bridegroom from his chamber, he might come forth to us, beautiful beyond the sons of men. A seal worthy of God’s wisdom was sought, beneath which he might seal the mystery hidden from the ages. Glass, most pure and most solid, was sought, through which the sun of righteousness might send fiery rays to put the darkness of the nations to flight, and from which the purity of the glass might receive an increase of brightness without suffering any loss of integrity.

[Col. 0744C] Who was this bride, so elegant and fair? Where on earth was she so beautiful that she might draw the Son of God from the Father’s bosom and, by the pious violence of the bonds of charity, draw him captive into her embrace? Long sought and awaited by the prayers of many saints, she was at last found: that exceptional and especially worthy, uniquely beautiful Virgin Mary.

But by whom was she found? By a human being? By any prince of the heavenly host? Rather, by the Creator himself of angels and men; by the Wisdom of God itself, which proceeds eternally from the mouth of the Most High, which is sharper than every two-edged sword, which reaches even to the division of soul and spirit, joints and marrow, and which alone is sufficient to search out the thoughts and affections of each person, indeed the very origins of thoughts and affections.

[Col. 0744D] Wisdom itself ordained Mary for itself as bride from eternity; in the fullness of time Wisdom itself sanctified Mary’s most chaste womb as its tabernacle; Wisdom itself adorned its temple in Mary with all glory and beauty beyond the loveliness of all visible and invisible creatures—as much as it willed, and as befitted the one to be born from her.

“For Wisdom,” says the Wise Man, “has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven columns.” Wisdom itself, plainly without a man’s assistance,

[Col. 0745A] built itself a house in Mary; Wisdom itself hewed out lofty columns for its house, supported by which the most chaste womb of the most sacred Virgin remains unshaken in the everlasting stability of its modesty.

Having found a virgin chaste and holy—indeed so chaste and holy as to be espoused to the Son of God—the workshop of the Holy Spirit, by the skill of the supreme Craftsman, prepares the ornaments for so great a virgin and for the future mother of so great an offspring. With what zeal, what diligence, what eager devotion, what adornment, my poverty cannot express; but they were such as befitted the mother of Christ, the shelter of the Holy Spirit, the queen of heaven, the empress of queens.

One messenger is chosen from many thousands: worthy of so great a king, fitted for so great a mystery, most expert in such a friendly embassy, gentle and mild in rendering reverence to virginal modesty. He is called Gabriel, because he is the messenger of God’s strength.

[Col. 0745B] He is sent, therefore, to go quickly, because the fullness of time had now arrived; to bring fitting betrothal gifts to the beloved bride, to offer adornments no less glorious to the glorious Virgin, and then, after presenting the gifts, to deliver in due order a new greeting, unheard of by the world: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women.”

O how full of grace was she whom even angelic dignity itself greeted so devoutly and dutifully! “Hail,” he says, “full of grace, to be filled with the Holy Spirit and to fill, through the fullness of thy womb, the emptiness of the whole world!” O what grace, what blessing of Mary, through which Eve’s curse was healed!

“The Lord is with thee.” In a wondrous and astonishing manner, the same one is bridegroom with the bride and son from the mother: bridegroom with the bride, in creating a new man; son from the mother, in making himself a new man.

[Col. 0745C] “The Lord is with thee,” not merely by the general grace of blessing by which he is with the other saints and thus also with thee, but by the singular prerogative of grace: as a son is with his mother, so the Lord is with thee. The Lord is with thee to sanctify thy womb; the Lord is with thee to join human nature to himself in thy flesh; the Lord is with thee to water the garden-bed of thy womb with a new blessing; the Lord is with thee to bring forth from the paradise of thy womb the fruit of the divine shoot, which alone among all the fruits of the sons of men knows not the worm of corruption.

“Blessed art thou among women.”

[Col. 0745D] Blessed among women, blessed above all women, the glory of women, the blessing of men and women. Rightly, I say, blessed among women, since with the hand of reconciliation she has wiped from all women the reproach of the ancient deception. For what if guilt is through Eve and righteousness through Mary; if guilt’s punishment is through Eve and forgiveness of guilt through Mary; if the ancient curse is through Eve and the new blessing through Mary? Finally, if death is through Eve, life likewise is through Mary.

Rightly, therefore, every condition, every age, every rank honors Mary with the angelic greeting; rightly every voice, every tongue, and every conscience proclaims with the angel concerning Mary: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women.”

[Col. 0746A] Alarmed by this unfamiliar form of greeting, that noble young virgin, her face cast down, is silently agitated, silently reflects within herself, and before rendering to the one who greets her the courtesy of a reply, prudently weighs in the balance of her heart the nature and manner of the greeting.

Mary, most faithful guardian of her modesty, was like the solitary turtledove, withdrawing and fleeing, remaining alone with herself in the solitude of her heart, sitting in the little nest of chastity, and feeding the young of holy meditation with the fruits of contemplation until they grew into the strength of perfected virtue. Mary, a friend of seclusion and devoted to quiet, was constantly in her chamber and very rarely in public. She hated commotion and fled encounters, lest, through being frequently seen, she contract—even if not a stain upon conscience or reputation—that which one rarely escapes who voluntarily plunges oneself into crowds of people.

Let virgins hear; let those who profess the discipline of the cenobitic arena hear:

[Col. 0746B] those who, forgetful of their profession and impatient of quiet, run about through provinces, fortresses, and towns, and under the pretense of service to their Church—but in truth with the salvation of their own soul betrayed—shamelessly plunge themselves, contrary to the reverence due their habit, into the tumults of people and the mud of worldly affairs.

But what have Christ’s servants to do with the world’s mud? What have citizens of heaven to do with the inhabitants of this age? What has a pearl to do with a dung-heap? What has a solitary person to do among a crowd?

I say this not to disparage Christ’s ministers and the ministers of Christ’s servants—may such impiety be far from the mind of Christ’s poor man. Far be it from me to blame those whom God praises, condemn those whom God commends, or reproach those whom I judge rather worthy of praise and honor, to whom I myself gladly offer reverence.

[Col. 0746C] For Christ’s ministers imitate their Lord, who came forth from the Father’s bosom into this valley of tears and, in the sweat of his brow, provided rest for us. Those, therefore, are his imitators who labor outwardly with the Apostle amid toil and misery, so that they may provide inward rest for their brothers. Thus, that in God’s tabernacle the fine linen and hyacinth, purple and scarlet—which cannot bear the injury of rains—may remain untouched, they themselves bear the assaults of storms. They are anxious and troubled about many things with Martha; and, so that their brothers may have leisure and taste how sweet the Lord is, they themselves taste from the cup mixed with gall how bitter the world is.

Thus, having said these things, as it were incidentally, by way of admonition to myself and to those like me, let us turn our eyes to Mary, the most pure mirror of virginity [Col. 0746D], and see how she received the angel who greeted her. She is astonished at the novelty of the greeting; having been greeted, meanwhile she keeps silence, lest by responding she should seem too forward—a thing unbecoming to a virgin. But the prudent envoy, respecting virginal modesty and soothing her alarm, says: “Do not fear, Mary; do not fear. You have found favour with the Lord; do not fear. You have found favour with God; therefore I called you full of grace. You have found favour with God, and therefore have deserved to bear the Son of God. For behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son—not merely any son, but a great one; not the son of an earthly father, but the Son of the Most High. Do not wonder; do not disbelieve my words, since you see that the barriers of virginal modesty remain secure. Your womb shall be filled, but the seal [Col. 0747A] of the womb shall not be broken. You shall bear a son, yet he shall not diminish the honour of his mother. You are a virgin; you shall be a mother—blessed because a virgin, more blessed because a mother; yet you alone shall possess this privilege for ever. For as in childbirth you have had, and shall have, no equal, so in the privilege of this endowment you shall have no other comparable to you. Nor should you despair of becoming a mother because you know neither your own husband nor his father. For he who chose you in time to be his mother has already possessed a Father from eternity. He has a Father, but does not yet have a mother; and therefore I have been sent to you, to betroth you to him by faith. Therefore give faith and receive the offspring; and you shall be a blessed mother, because you shall bear God and man.

“Wonderful are the things I say—wonderful and unheard-of—but they are not impossible to the Almighty. Your womb is an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain; but it is well enclosed and firmly sealed precisely because it is open to God alone. Do not fear for your chastity, my lady, dove without gall: you are the mother and bride of my Lord, because your barriers are not to be opened, either in conception or in childbirth. The sun enters and leaves through glass without breaking the glass: shall the creator of the sun be unable to preserve his mother undefiled? But if you ask the cause of my coming and the benefit of your childbirth, hear the name of your son and understand the fruit of your womb. He shall be called Jesus; he shall be a saviour, and he comes to save. Rejoice therefore, my lady; rejoice that you have been chosen by so great a grace to be the mother who bears the Saviour of the whole world.”

To these and other such words—indeed, to far other words, although not spoken by the angel, yet inspired by the Holy Spirit who was to come upon her into Mary’s most pure heart—she gives credence; she hesitates at nothing, doubts nothing [Col. 0747C], but faithfully believes that the Almighty will fulfil what he promises shall come to pass. She compares, I suppose, the angel’s words with the prophet’s words, what she hears with what she had read; and she believes what she hears all the more readily because the angel does not disagree with the prophet. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” says the prophet, “and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.” Isaiah foretells: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Gabriel echoes: “Behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son.” Isaiah prophesies, “His name shall be called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us”; Gabriel announces to Mary, “He shall be called the Son of the Most High.” She weighs, compares, and examines both, I suppose; and she gives the more abundant faith to the new words inasmuch as they accord more harmoniously with the old.

She therefore now believes without hesitation that she will conceive and that she will give birth [Col. 0747D], but she asks how this is to happen, because she had read this neither in the prophet nor heard it from the angel. “How,” she says, “shall this be, since I do not know a man?” How shall this be? No man has been known by me: whence shall I have a son? I am a virgin: how shall I be a mother? How shall this be? This is not the law of Adam’s children: that a woman should conceive without a man, or a child be born without a father. By this law, in this order, all the ages from the beginning until our own have run their course: a woman is made pregnant by a man, and a child is begotten by a father. Who has seen or heard the things you affirm? They are unaccustomed in experience, unknown to sight, unverified by hearing. How then shall this be?

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Divine are the things I announce; mighty works [Col. 0748A] of the Almighty are those I proclaim. Thus the Almighty willed; thus the Almighty ordained—he who made all things in heaven and on earth that he willed. God’s will is not governed by the order of nature; rather, the order of nature is directed according to God’s free will. Nor should one say that what the Lord of nature has decreed shall be so occurs outside nature’s course. The Holy Spirit shall come upon you. By the power of the Holy Spirit he shall be created in your womb, who, as two natures meet in one person, shall be held equal to the Holy Spirit. And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Do not fear, mirror of chastity, the heat of lust: you shall be shaded by the power of the Most High. As shade removes heat and provides refreshment, so the intervening power of the Most High shall exclude the heat of sin and pour divine dew into the hidden places of your womb. [Col. 0748B] Therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God. Rightly shall that be born holy which is conceived from the Holy Spirit; justly shall he be called the Son of God who is created by the power of the Most High. This is the order; this is the manner of virginal conception and childbirth: the will and omnipotence of God.”

Thus fittingly instructed and sufficiently taught, Mary says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word. I am the Lord’s handmaid; I am his handmaid, and he may use me as he pleases. I consider my condition; I acknowledge myself a handmaid; I offer to my Lord the will of devoted service. With ready devotion I carry out the obedience required of me. It is much to me—very much—that I deserve to be called a handmaid. My littleness does not attain to that most excellent title, that I should be called the mother of the Lord. [Col. 0748C] Let it be done to me according to your word: let him who was the Word in the beginning be made flesh in me. Let it be done to me, that I may be found worthy, through whom the world may find the grace of reconciliation. Let it be done to me, that on earth I may provide the hospitality of my body for him who thereafter may receive me in heaven into the fellowship of his kingdom.”

I thought these matters concerning the fullness of grace which flowed divinely into the womb of the glorious Virgin, and from there streamed forth into the whole world, should be treated at greater length, in order to show the greatness of God’s grace, bestowed upon humanity through Mary with no preceding merits. Whatever Mary possesses by her special prerogative, the grace of God bestowed it; divine compassion provided it for the salvation of the whole world. Mary’s good is the common good [Col. 0748D] of all, and from Mary’s fullness the desolation of the nations has been filled. Whoever thirsts with eager throat for the sweetness of grace, approach with due reverence the fullness of Mary’s womb. So great a richness of compassion flows from it, so great a sweetness of compassion, that neither does its abundance know deficiency nor its sweetness satiety. Drink, then, drink from this fountain of compassion. Drink, that it may fill your eager throat; but do not suppose that by drinking you extinguish your thirst. Love of eternal things has this characteristic: it always inflames the desire of those who love, and never produces in lovers any weariness of itself.

No mind can estimate, no tongue suffice to recount, how great a grace God bestowed upon humanity through Mary, the glory of virgins: Mary, star of the sea, light of the wandering, hope of the despairing, consolation of the sorrowful [Col. 0749A], common joy of all Christ’s faithful. We have not yet satisfied our desire in her praise, nor do we believe that it can ever be satisfied amid the failing condition of this corruptible life. Yet once the sweetness of her praise has been tasted, our desire is kindled more and more; but by daily remembrance of her and frequent repetition of her most sweet name, the heat of devout longing is cooled as though by a certain divine dew. For after the singular name of her beloved Son, which is above every name, heaven and earth name no other name from which devout minds may conceive so much grace, hope, sweetness, and consolation. For as often as those who love her hear that most sweet name, Mary, so often from the devout hearing and sweetness of the name heard [Col. 0749B] they draw within themselves some indescribable delight.

For the name of Mary contains in itself something wonderfully sweet and divine, so that when it sounds it breathes the fragrance of beloved sweetness into friendly [Col. 0750A] hearts. And this concerning the name Mary is wonderful—indeed very wonderful—that, though heard a thousand times, it is always heard as though new. Mary, holy virgin, mother worthy of God, most gracious comforter, most loving reconciler, most powerful advocate of her own. I may seem to anyone excessive in praise of Mary—our Mary, I say, our Mary—but only to one who is both ungrateful to the mother and impious toward the Son. It still pleases me, and will please me for ever, to linger over the praises of the glorious Lady, the glorious Virgin, and the most glorious Mother; but since we have drawn out the discourse at length, let us end this discourse concerning Mary in praise of Mary, giving thanks for all the benefits bestowed upon us through the devout Mother, to her most loving and only Son, who with [Col. 0750B] God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Preface to Book Seven

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749B] It is the custom of Holy Scripture to support itself mutually by its testimonies, as though by certain columns, and to establish matters difficult and incredible to human distrust by the example of another matter equally difficult. For divine speech accommodates itself to its hearers and meanwhile nourishes with the tenderness of milk those whom it does not yet see fit for solid food. Thus, when in Ezekiel the Lord promises that the captivity of the Jewish people shall be released, and they, measuring God’s power by their own weakness, believe this impossible even for God because of the magnitude of their calamity, he sets forth a likeness and persuades the unbelieving by comparison with something more difficult and more unfamiliar to belief. He sets before [Col. 0750B] the prophet exceedingly many bones, stripped of flesh, with their sinews loosened, and so dry that even the prophet’s faith doubts whether they can be restored to life. At the Lord’s command, as the prophet prophesies, more swiftly than speech they are clothed with flesh and joined together by sinews; and when the Spirit blows from [Col. 0750C] the four winds, they are given life and restored to their former state of life upon their feet. As these things were set before the house of Israel as a portent, so the barren old woman Elizabeth was set before the glorious and perpetual Virgin Mary as an example, that in Elizabeth as in herself she might learn the omnipotence of God, by which, whenever and however he wills, he reverses nature’s course.

## Book Seven

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749C] “And behold,” says Gabriel, “Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age, because no word shall be impossible with God.” If you consider the order of nature, you find nothing of this in Elizabeth. Nature does not demand childbirth from an old and barren woman; and even if she were not barren, old age would owe nature nothing of the kind. But if she is both old and barren, by what law of nature did she conceive? Yet when nature failed, grace prevailed, because no word is impossible with God.

But because obedience is the cause and grace the subject-matter of this little work of mine, it would be absurd to pass over in silence the herald of grace. For the herald of grace is conceived by grace, born through grace, filled while still in his mother’s womb with his mother’s grace, and receives from grace the name John, that is, “the grace of God.” It pleases me, therefore, to look back to what preceded and set these things out somewhat more fully in their order.

The eternal Judge, about to enter the court of the world, did not wish to come suddenly and unexpectedly upon the accused; rather, he took care to send a worthy herald before his face [Col. 0750C], who might declare repentance to the accused and prepare a path of mercy for the coming Judge. For it belongs to a kindly judge that, as he appears strict and terrible to the obstinate, so he appears merciful and gentle to the penitent. And it was surely fitting that the herald of so great a Judge should himself be commended by great proclamations, so that from the herald’s dignity the world might learn how great was the Judge’s excellence.

Accordingly, a messenger is sent from heaven—not just any messenger, but Gabriel the archangel—to Zechariah, priest of the Lord, at the time of sacrifice. Thus, while he directs from the altar of his heart to heaven the incense of prayer, he may be gladdened by a heavenly messenger concerning the granting of his petition. And the time suits the mystery, and the mystery suits the time: while the priest within offers God the people’s vows with the fragrance of incense and the people themselves outside implore God for their salvation, then the priest within, in the secrecy of his heart, may learn from the angel the hidden counsels of God concerning the birth of the Lord’s forerunner and the people’s salvation.

But Gabriel the archangel, most skilled in such an embassy [Col. 0751A], stands at the right of the altar of incense, as though proclaiming by his position that the things he announces are matters of the right hand. He is beautifully placed at the right of the altar of incense because he announces that the people’s prayer, offered through the priest, has been heard. Beautifully, I say, at the right of the altar of incense, because he announces the strength of God’s right hand. At this vision the devout priest, wholly intent on divine things—and all the more so because terrified by the angel—burns with silent thought within himself, wondering who he is, whence he is present, and what he wants of him. He does not believe him to be a human being, since at that time and in that sacred place—namely, at the hour of incense and within the enclosure of the veil—he had suddenly presented himself among holy things. He marvels the more, trembles the more; believing the visitor to be something divine and rendering reverence to divine things, he waits reverently until he who had come reveals the cause of his coming [Col. 0751B].

“Do not fear,” says that gracious consoler of the trembling; “do not fear, because those who offer to God the sacrifice of praise as a fragrant offering of sweetness ought not to fear at our entrance. Do not fear, because what I announce is not sorrowful: it is welcome, joyful, and full of gladness. Your prayer has been heard, offered gratefully to God as though for the salvation of the people and for the redemption of the whole world. Your prayer has been heard, now accepted through the merit of him who shall be priest and victim. Your prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth your wife shall bear you a son—not merely a son of flesh, but also of promise; not of nature, but of grace. For now that the womb of bleary-eyed Leah has been exhausted by the birth of six sons, the time is at hand when Rachel, more beloved and made fruitful by grace, will begin to bear sons of the right hand. And to teach you everything, he shall be called John [Col. 0751C], because he shall be accounted of great grace and great merit before God. For he shall be great before the Lord, already chosen for a great work and later to be taken up by the Lord for a great work. He shall be great because he shall be the herald of him whose greatness has no end. He shall be great because he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb. He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, he whose power shall create him in that womb. For when the office of begetting in the father and of giving birth in the mother has already died, whose gift is this but that of the Holy Spirit? He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit, nourished by the sweetness of the Holy Spirit; and therefore he shall eat nothing unclean, nor drink wine or *sikera* [strong drink]. For one who tastes with the palate of the heart how sweet the Lord is pays little attention to outward flavours; but one who fasts from inward sweetness longs for the husks of swine. And many shall rejoice at his birth, because he shall announce their joy to the world. Many shall rejoice at his birth; but after him shall come one at whose birth both heavenly and earthly things shall exult.”

For these oracles of the angelic assurance, the unbelieving priest—and, with its priest, that faithless people—is punished with silence, until it inscribes the name John upon the tablet of faith; and until, at the end of the world, the veil of unbelief is taken from its heart, it understands from the Holy Scriptures that the time of grace has almost passed and the day of judgment is at hand, and through confession of the true faith may merit, along with the office of speech, also the gift of prophecy. Meanwhile, Zechariah having been punished with the just penalty of his unbelief, the divine promise does not delay. Elizabeth conceives [Col. 0752A], marvels and is amazed that she has conceived, not yet understanding what novelty or miracle is taking place within her. The bashful old woman hides herself; she strives to conceal God’s mighty works, unaware how renowned throughout the world he was to be who would be born.

The eager and devout Virgin is present: Mary is present, having been told by the angel of Elizabeth’s conception. Perhaps turning over in her mind the saying of the Wise Man, “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things,” she hastens to visit her kinswoman; the Mother of the Lord herself, with dutiful devotion, greets first the mother of the servant, always bearing the palm, both of virginity and of humility. Come now: without dispelling the thick cloud, fix your gaze, if you can, on grace’s most pure splendour itself; and, borrowing the eagle’s keen sight, examine it carefully as an attentive observer. But perhaps you will say: “What are these things to me? What has righteousness to do with the unrighteous [Col. 0752B], the merits of saints with a sinner, the humility of a servant with the insignia of the Lord, finally, a human being with the mighty works of God?” Very much indeed. For in order to clothe his servant with his glory, the Lord put on the form of a servant; and what God accomplished in the assumed human being, he bestowed upon humanity. Take comfort therefore, O human being, take comfort; presume that this grace also is yours through your Lord’s kindness, and believe without doubt that even the last member is to be glorified with its head.

When the Mother of the Lord’s greeting was heard, the handmaid of the Lord was filled with the Spirit of the Lord; and because she recognized through the Spirit a great grace, she cried out with a loud voice because she had great faith: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. Blessed are you among women [Col. 0752C], who alone, before all women, have deserved the privilege of this blessing. Blessed is the fruit of your womb, from whom the bread of heaven is made. Blessed is the fruit of your womb, by whose sweetness the most bitter hunger of the world is driven away. Blessed is the fruit of your womb, without whom even the angels do not live in heaven. And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Whence to an unworthy little handmaid is it granted that I should be thought worthy of a visitation by so great a lady? Whence to the wife of a soldier, that she should be visited by the mother of the emperor? For behold, when the voice of your greeting sounded in my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy.”

O grace, O miracles! The empress visits the handmaid; the emperor gladdens the soldier. The lady honours her servant with the service of a greeting; the lord endows his servant with a prophetic spirit. The mother of the Judge humbles herself by serving the handmaid; the Judge sends his herald before his face, having given him his commission [Col. 0752D]. But the handmaid receives her lady with due reverence and loves her more, the more gracious she finds her. She is not proud, is not puffed up like Hagar, nor does she lift up her neck; rather, giving thanks for the service, she declares herself unworthy of her lady’s arrival. And because she humbly prostrates herself before the mother of her Lord, she receives from the Son, as a gift for the honour paid to the mother, the spirit of prophecy. Nor does the little one in the womb cease from his office; he too, perceiving that his Lord is present, dances with joy. He does not yet recognize his mother’s face, yet, enclosed in a virginal womb, recognizes his Lord. The servant recognizes the Lord, the soldier the king, the herald the judge; and because he sees that the Judge is now beginning to enter, he proclaims to the world, so far as he is able, with the exultation [Col. 0753A] of joy, the coming of his Judge.

O novelty! O miracle! O spectacle most beautiful and unknown to the theatre of the world! Our little ones in the womb play with one another in their play, but not as Ishmael mocked Isaac, one mocking the other. The most gracious Lord plays with his devoted servant by pouring grace into him; the humble little servant plays with his loving Lord by rendering such thanks as he can meanwhile offer. The Lord plays with the servant by revealing his coming; the servant plays with the Lord by prophesying his coming through the movement of his body. Behold, our little ones strive as those in Rebecca’s womb did; but not that one may supplant the other, but that each may commend the other to the world. Christ commends John as a most faithful servant; John commends Christ [Col. 0753B] to the world as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. Christ commends John, saying: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen”; John commends Christ, saying: “He who comes after me has been made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie.”

These friendly offices of mutual commendation are anticipated in the joys of the little ones in the womb, while the Lord of the servant rejoices together in his holiness, and the servant exults that he has been found worthy to be called the servant of the Holy One of saints. This is that wondrous grace, unheard of in all ages, which I can neither conceive in thought nor utter with my tongue. Wonderful grace: those who do not yet freely enjoy the life of the world nevertheless together bring about the freedom and life of the world—one by prophesying in gesture, the other by giving life through grace. Wonderful grace, I say [Col. 0753C], because those who cannot yet benefit themselves already provide for the world.

Having thus considered the exultation of the little ones, and having above spoken briefly of how greatly Elizabeth exulted and how she blessed the glorious Mother and the fruit of her womb, let us now consider the joy, praise, and song of the Mother of the Lord, as her Son may deign to reveal them. Various songs are found in the Holy Scriptures, differing from one another according to the greatness of events or the weightiness of mysteries; and it belongs neither to my littleness to understand nor to expound the reason for them all.

For in Exodus there is a song sung to God by the children of Israel for Pharaoh’s overthrow, with Mary leading in song with a timbrel; and this, I think, is found to be the first of all songs [Col. 0753D]. For the first victory over Pharaoh is granted to us when God fights for us: when in baptism, of which that sea was a figure, the entire kingdom of sin is destroyed with its king, the devil, so that not even one Egyptian remains who pursued God’s people from behind. And lovers of grace should note this in Pharaoh’s drowning: God’s people neither meet nor engage in battle with that most monstrous beast, invincible to every human power; rather, by grace alone that strong armed one, who until then possessed all his goods in peace, is drowned while the people merely watch.

There is also another song in the Book of Judges, Deborah’s song for Sisera’s death; by him we understand some opposing power [Col. 0754A], which likewise oppresses and persecutes God’s people and, after they have been delivered from Pharaoh’s power by God’s right hand, again and again tries to impose the tribute of sin. There is also another song in the Book of Kings, that of our Hannah—that is, of grace—who poured forth prayer to God, not for the death of her enemies but for the fruit of her womb; being heard, she offered God a sacrifice of praise and uttered a song of exultation. Boasting, she sang that by the dignity of one son the grace of God had made her greater than the numerous offspring of her rival.

But since it is not my purpose now to review all the songs of ancient history, I shall come to Solomon’s most celebrated one among the songs, called, because of a certain—indeed great—excellence of its own, not merely a song but the Song of Songs. There is no fear of an enemy there, no pain from a closed womb; there, with none remaining barren, all come up from the washing with twin offspring; there the daughters of Jerusalem sing in sweet melodies that contemplative nuptial song of bridegroom and bride. I judge that the one special song of Mary, which she offered to the Lord from the first fruits of her womb, who had given the blessing, is to be preferred to all these and other divine and mystical songs. Nor am I mistaken in this judgment; for as the fruit of Mary’s womb holds primacy among all fruits, so Mary’s song rightly holds the first place among all songs. For those songs were figures and served the truth which speaks in the Gospel: “I am the truth.” And our bride, embracing [Col. 0754C] and kissing her Beloved, and singing in the ears of friends those words of love which escape human understanding and feeling, enjoys a far greater joy than Solomon’s bride, burning with longing and impatient of delay, who cries out in the impatience of love: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Having offered these preliminary remarks in commendation of the glorious Virgin’s song, let us stop up the ear of the heart like an asp against the clamour of the world, and listen more attentively to how our timbrel-player resounds from on high. Therefore, after such great joy had been celebrated at the arrival of the Mother of the Lord—as great as those who were worthy to be present knew—the blessed Mother, wholly filled with the presence of her Son’s divinity, seeing great things and feeling great things, sings with great joy of heart: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Great, wondrous, divine things are being done [Col. 0754D], and in the valley of tears the joys of angels are celebrated. He who contains heaven lies hidden in the narrowness of one womb, and he who sustains all things by his will is borne by the womb of one maiden. What tongue of flesh could suffice to praise worthily such great gifts and boundless benefits? What understanding could comprehend them? The weakness of flesh does not bear the weight of such majesty; understanding fails, the tongue is insufficient. Let my soul, then, magnify the Lord—not because it itself is sufficient, but that, as more worthy than flesh by its condition, it may find some worthier thanksgiving in an ecstasy beyond itself.

Deceitful lips and a deceitful heart act deceitfully when the tongue sounds one thing while the heart desires another. But whoever, in praise of God or concerning God’s praise, seeks anything other than God [Col. 0755A], that person’s soul does not magnify the Lord; rather, it magnifies what it esteems great in its heart, what it loves more than God. But because the blessed Mother could prefer no created thing to the love of her beloved Son, for that incomparable gift uniquely bestowed upon her she magnifies the Lord, as she had learned from the law, with all her heart, with all her soul, and with all her mind.

“And my spirit has exulted in God my Saviour.” Her spirit rightly exults confidently in God, whose soul magnifies the Lord. One exults in honours, another in riches, another in children; this person in one way, that person in another. Mary’s spirit exults in God alone. Rightly she magnifies thus, rightly she exults thus, she who declares with humble confession that her humility was regarded by God and that she was raised from a handmaid into the glory of maternal dignity [Col. 0755B]. “He has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid; from this time all generations shall call me blessed.” Because he saw me humble, he made me glorious; because I was humble in my own eyes, I pleased his eyes. For humility is the beauty of the soul, the elegance of its form, the adornment of a virgin, the guardian of modesty. Humility adorns the face, commends the life, enlightens the understanding, preserves one’s actions. The Lord regarded it in Mary, approved it, loved it, and rewarded it in Mary with so great a recompense that no generation passes without blessing Mary. One generation passes and another comes; Mary’s praise never fails in any generation. Mary’s praise is an unfailing fountain: the farther it extends, the more abundantly it is filled; and the more abundantly it is filled [Col. 0755C], the more widely it spreads.

Therefore every generation rightly blesses Mary, through whom every generation obtained blessing. For she is blessed not only with the general blessedness shared with the other elect, but also with a special gift above all mortals. Every generation rightly blesses Mary, I say, because he who is able to do whatever he wills has done great—indeed very great—things with her. “He who is mighty has done great things for me,” she says, “and holy is his name.” See how the mother of grace attributes the entire work of grace to grace. She does not say: “He has done great things for me because I am a virgin, because I am holy, because I am worthy”; but because he is mighty, holy, and merciful. Because he is mighty, he powerfully accomplishes great things; because he is holy, he loves holiness and restores holiness [Col. 0755D]; because he is merciful, he mercifully forgives.

Because he is mighty, he can grant to a virgin both the honour of motherhood and preservation of virginal modesty. Because he is mighty and holy, he can change the Ethiopian’s skin and, having wiped away native blackness with his almighty hand, make it whiter than snow. Because he is mighty, he will bind the strong man; because he is holy, he will sanctify the defiled; because he is merciful, he will open even to the thief the gate of paradise. For his power shall not be weakened by my weakness, his holiness shall not be defiled by the likeness of sin, nor shall he, in dispensing mercy, forget the judgment of justice.
