“But his mercy is unto generations and generations for those who fear him”—not for those who despair, scorn, mock, heap sin upon sin [Col. 0756A], and from day to day kindle for themselves ever more fiercely the flame of Gehenna. Therefore, in order to offer mercy, the Lord urges sinners toward repentance; and those whom he cannot draw with gentleness he strikes with terrors, so that those whom love of the promised kingdom does not soften may at least be broken by the hammer of fear at the dread of Gehenna. Thus the Mother of mercy, beneficially providing for the sick world, after pouring the gentleness of oil into its wounds to soothe pain, also mingles the sharpness of wine to consume corruption, tempering the sweetness of mercy with the bitterness of fear, so that fear may not crush into despair nor mercy raise people up into freedom to sin. “His mercy,” she says, “is unto generations and generations for those who fear him.”

But the daughter of David, taught by her father to sing mercy and judgment to the Lord, having sung the Lord’s mercy for the consolation of the humble, also mentions judgment in order to terrify the proud: “He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.” This is that exalted arm in which God the Father always fights, in which he always triumphs gloriously. This is that outstretched hand which is read of in the prophets, which is now held over little children as a rod of threat, and which, at the end of the world, Isaiah testifies shall be laid upon Assyria—that is, the devil and his followers—never to be raised by any hand, any pity, or any aid. Alas, with how heavy, alas, with how immovable a mass it shall then be laid upon the ungodly—this hand which, because it is now felt light through mercy’s mitigation, is easily despised [Col. 0756C]. Then pride, which now strikes heaven with its head, shall be hurled from the seat of its height into the depths of hell; then that humility pleasing to God, which now creeps on the ground as though weak, shall be exalted to a seat at God’s right hand. “For he has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble.”

Although these words may generally be interpreted of all the proud, they may also be understood of the Jews, proud of their observance of the law and glorying in the nobility of Abraham’s race. Since they seek to establish their own righteousness, which is from the law, they refuse to submit to God’s righteousness, which is in Christ Jesus. For Carmel has been counted as a forest, and the forest as Carmel: the unbelief of the Jews has been rejected and the faith of the nations chosen; and, with the wilderness of the Synagogue transformed into fruitfulness, the strangers of the Church eat [there] [Col. 0756D]. Therefore the hungry people of the nations is filled with good things, and the people of the Jews, once rich, is sent away empty.

“For he has received Israel his servant,” and that most broad bosom of God’s mercy has gathered in the multitude of the nations. For he is truly Israel who beholds God with the eyes of faith, who does not limp in faith, who walks behind the Lord with firm step and on a straight path. For *Israel* is interpreted not only “a man seeing God,” but more correctly also “upright of God.” But that Israel according to the flesh is not gathered by the breadth of God’s bosom: it sold the dignity of its birthright for a paltry lentil, and, following the killing letter, does not seek the life-giving spirit. Yet as that Israel according to the flesh was justly expelled at justice’s command because of its unbelief [Col. 0757A], so our Israel has been introduced into its place solely by the hand of God’s grace.

“For he has remembered his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever.” God spoke to Abraham that he would receive Israel his servant when he foretold that Abraham’s seed would be made equal to the stars of heaven. He spoke the same thing to Abraham when he promised that all nations would be blessed in his seed. He spoke likewise to David when he foretold that one from the fruit of his womb would sit upon his throne, whom at the chosen time he would adopt as his Son in a special manner, though before all times he had begotten him as equal to himself. Likewise he spoke to our other fathers [Col. 0758A], when in the offering of Isaac, the sale of Joseph, and innumerable other such figures, he prefigured the mysteries of his incarnation and of human redemption.

Let what has been said about that noble song of the glorious Virgin suffice—not according to the dignity of the song, but according to the slenderness of my understanding. Holy Mother Church has tasted this song, so sweet, so pleasant, and so full of every spiritual delight, and has instituted so celebrated a use of it that no day throughout this age now passes on which she does not sing it in evening praise, for the praise of the glorious Mother and of her most glorious Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Preface to Book Eight

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757B] At your command, venerable Father, as I set down in my blunt style the great and magnificent gifts of God’s grace, I return in almost every word to that same grace, praying that in its accustomed goodness it may deign, through an unlearned tongue, to reveal itself to its lovers. Yet I do not know how I may commend it more lovingly than by recalling those wondrous proclamations of Christ’s charity which, in assuming humanity for humanity’s redemption, he either powerfully performed as God or graciously endured as man. Whoever desires to know their whole multitude [Col. 0758B] and completeness should turn over the volumes of the holy Gospels and the apostolic library. Our purpose is to pluck a few flowers from many for the adornment of our little garland. These few things which I insert I distinguish not with the variety fitting to them, but with such as I know; and I humbly entreat the reader to pardon my toil, since, while I myself stammer, I am compelled to teach others how to speak of God’s grace. But let us continue what we have begun.

## Book Eight

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757C] Now, as the fullness of time drew near, and that night approached which illumines all days from the beginning, the bridegroom of the Church—promised by the ceremonies of the Law and by the oracles of the prophets—comes forth from his bridal chamber: Christ is born from Mary. Upon the way, the Way is born; the beauty of souls is wrapped in swaddling-clothes; no place is found for the Saviour in the inn of the synagogue; the food of life is laid in the manger of the present Church, so that, because he had multiplied his mercy, he might nourish human beings and beasts unto life. The place was indeed fitting to the mystery: for he who was the living bread was laid in a manger. Wearied animals return to their accustomed mangers and seek the wages due to their labour, so that, refreshed by their master’s abundance, they may again devote themselves, in dutiful turn, to the service of their keeper. Behold, our little one, who is to refresh the weary, [Col. 0757D] is placed in the midst of his manger; and because the teacher had come from heaven, he sets up a chair for himself in the manger. Though, as a little child, he cannot yet speak with his voice, he already cries out as it were in his wailing: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

But lest even the time of infancy should pass without the activity of grace, the author of grace, in accordance with the prophetic oracle and the foreshadowing of his name, though still seemingly powerless over himself, declares war upon the prince of this world. Having led men, by the more radiant star, to recognition of the true light, he swiftly strips the spoils [Col. 0758C] from that strong man who had hitherto possessed his court in peace. For this is that distinguished warrior whom Isaiah foretold would be born of the prophetess—that is, of Mary, ever inviolate and ever virgin. To him the prophet gives, as a presage of the future, the name: “Hasten to take spoil; make haste to plunder.” For this warrior hastens greatly and moves with great speed: while crying in the cradle, he seizes the weapons of the strong—indeed, the strongest weapons of the strong. He declares war, not upon any ordinary soldier, but upon the very prince of spiritual wickedness; and, after the leaders of his army have been frightened merely by the announcement of his coming light, he commands the Magi to serve in his camp and strips the tyrant of his chosen weapons.

Great, and incomparably great, is this grace freely bestowed upon lost humanity, which deserved nothing but punishment: that heaven should serve the wailing little child in a star; [Col. 0758D] that angels should sing praises; and that the most venomous head, which had pierced the heel of the first human being with its viper’s tooth, should be crushed by a foot still weak in itself. Great indeed, and worthy to be pursued with laudatory proclamation, would that grace have been had he remained in the form of God, crushed the serpent’s head with the foot of his majesty, and freed the human being bound in its coils. But who can worthily wonder at that grace—at that grace, I say—that immeasurable goodness deigned not only to have such merciful compassion upon our misery, but, having assumed our humanity, to suffer even [Col. 0759A] our misery itself? Who can worthily marvel at so glorious a victory, in which our king triumphs so gloriously over that ancient prince, grown old in evil days, not in his own majesty but in our weakness, so that while still wrapped in swaddling-clothes he carries captive across, not merely the outermost, but the foremost commanders of his enemy’s army?

This most illustrious victory of our king—his enemy’s confusion—is our glory. For lest that proud one should insult his Creator over humanity’s fall, he grieves that in the very one whom he had conquered he himself has been conquered. Having thus freely sampled these firstfruits of grace in the Magi, the firstfruits of the nations, let us turn the course of our discourse back to the cradle of our king and see how the good shepherd also drenched the Jewish fleece with the dew of his grace.

While shepherds watched over their flock with pastoral care, [Col. 0759B] an angel, radiant with angelic brilliance, stood before them and announced that the Saviour of the world had been born. He made known that, since the sorrow of the ancient sentence had been abolished for all the people, he would become the author of eternal joy: “I announce to you,” he says, “great joy, which shall be for all the people: for there is born to you today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.” Truly this was a proclamation worthy of the birth of so great a king: that to a mourning people, worn down beneath the yoke of Babylonian and Roman servitude, peace and joy should be proclaimed at once at their king’s birth.

Such are the fruits of grace; such shoots spring from that divine root. Grace arises for us from God the Father in Christ, and with it abundance of peace. For when the prince of peace is born, the wall of enmities is dissolved; the author of dissension is dragged away in chains; and captivity, [Col. 0759C] released into obedience to its king, having received power, treads with a now free foot upon the haughty neck of that proud one who raised himself above the heights of the clouds, and joyfully sings to its redeemer: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.”

Wonderful also is this grace of the Lord Jesus Christ: he judged that the new joys of his birth should first be announced, not to Herod or to the chief priests, but to shepherds—rustic men, yet simple and righteous. For as he chose to be born among the poor, so he judged it fitting that the joys of his birth should first become known to the poor. Moreover, we have learned on Luke’s testimony that Jesus “began to do and to teach.” Therefore, he who came first to do and then to teach, first displayed in himself [Col. 0759D] the pattern of humility and poverty which he was to teach. Thus he chose to be born among the poor; he foresaw a stranger’s lodging for his birth; and because amid the unbelief of the Jews he found nowhere to lay his head, he crossed over to the wilderness of the nations, alien from the Law and covenant, from the knowledge and worship of God.

These works, then, of such divine mercy are not, O human being, distinctions earned by your merit, but marks of God’s grace. They are to be embraced by you so much the more dearly and always venerated more devoutly, because he bestowed all things freely and demands no repayment. For even the service which he seems strictly to demand of you as necessary is itself an act of inexpressible grace. What could you contribute to that supreme blessedness, which admits no increase and knows no diminution, if you offered service [Col. 0760A] and honour? Or what could you take away if you did not offer them? Thus, in commanding you to serve, he benefits you, so that by the merit of your devotion that immeasurable mercy may, as though justly bound, faithfully reward you for your obedience with an eternal reward.

It is fitting also that I should not pass over in silence the most glorious athletes, contemporaries of their king, who contend in an unheard-of manner of fighting and triumph through an extraordinary mode of victory. In them, though their age could neither know the zeal for warfare nor have desired the prize of victory, grace alone conquers the enemy, and innocence alone merits the palm. I mean those blessed and truly innocent ones who, through Christ’s grace, obtained the glory of martyrdom before they could know the cause of martyrdom. Happy little ones, who deserved to confess Christ’s name by their blood [Col. 0760B] before their tongue. Happy little ones, who deserved to enter victoriously from the arena of the world into the kingdom before they knew how to engage an enemy. Blessed martyrs, white with the snow-white robe of innocence and blooming with rosy blood, who deserve to follow wherever he goes, the Lamb of God. For he himself was the cause of their punishment, and he is also the crown of their glory.

When bloody Herod, the executioner, hears that Christ has been born, and hears that he is to be king of the Jews, he is disturbed and driven by the furies of his impious mind: he trembles, turns pale, is shaken with fear, and loses his composure. He dreads the name of king because he does not understand the manner of this kingship. For he had obtained the kingdom of the Jews neither by noble birth nor by merit, but had invaded by tyranny—and retained by cruelty—that noble kingdom due, by the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, to the royal tribe of Judah. [Col. 0760C] Therefore, when the king of righteousness is born, injustice trembles; when piety is about to reign, cruelty rages.

But why do you rage impiously? Why are you tortured by envy? Why do you fear the Saviour’s coming? Why do you tremble at the name of the gentlest and humblest king? He has not come to take away temporal things, he who grants eternal recompense to his soldiers. He does not need an earthly kingdom, he who presides over heaven. Lay aside, then, your empty fear; compose your agitated mind; and, in order to reign more happily under him, faithfully do what you pretend to do—adoring your king, whether you wish it or not, with your neck bowed in submission.

But the deceitful fox hides for a time within the dark recesses of his faithless mind, feigns joy in his face, devises treachery in his heart, and, while promising to go and worship him, prepares to kill him when found. [Col. 0760D] Yet the malice of the human mind attempts in vain to mock the wisdom of God, just as a slippery serpent tries in vain to set its tracks by a soft movement upon the hardness of rock. For the Lord, who had appointed one time suitable for his birth and another for his passion, each suited to its mystery, does not disdain to be carried into Egypt by foreign hands—he who endured having his own hands fastened to the cross—not so much fleeing Herod as fulfilling a mystery. For he already signified that his name was to flee Judaea before the chief priests and the madness of the clamouring people, instigated by their king, the devil, and was to be carried by the apostolic mouth into the lands of the nations.

But the bloody beast, thirsty for blood with burning jaws, thinks itself deceived while it is deceived; because it could not, as it desired, attack the throat of the newborn king, [Col. 0761A] it poured out its rage upon the innocent army of little children, so that, by strangling the little children of the same age as its king and prostrating the entire army, the one whom it alone and especially sought might not escape the bite of the raging beast. Thus the bodies of little children are struck down by the swords of executioners, but are borne to the heavens by angels’ hands. The most savage executioner rages on earth, but the most serene judge crowns in heaven. Truly happy, truly blessed, are those who deserved eternal life before they were able to enjoy this present life, for whom entry into this life was passage into eternal life.

In the great glory of these holy little children, I delight to contemplate the greatness of the giver of grace. Although their weak and immature age could neither fear the punishment of death nor know how to hope for the reward of faith, he nevertheless does not allow [Col. 0761B] the glory of their martyrdom or the fullness of their reward to be diminished because they suffered for him. For, as blessed Jerome testifies, even in mature age it is the cause, not the punishment, that makes the martyr.

In the same way, the devil, who ruled in Herod, persecutes Christ born in us, in the hope that he may deceitfully kill him while he is still little within us and keep us captive under the ancient yoke of his dominion. For when Christ is born in us and brought to manly strength, all the Egyptian idols in the temple of our heart fall, and the kingdom of sin, together with all the works of confusion in which the devil reigns, perishes. Knowing and anticipating this, he rages and roars and prowls like a roaring lion; and, so as to trip up the unwary, he transforms himself into an angel of light, pretends that he will worship the newborn king, smears the rim of the cup with honey, [Col. 0761C] and conceals poison in its depths.

For while we rest and enter the Lord’s way with a confident step, the cunning plotter insinuates himself on the right as an angel of light and suggests one contrivance of his deception after another: that we gain nothing in our present place, and that from the things we seek to acquire we incur much loss through the company and negligence of those with whom we live. He accuses superiors of being unmerciful, proud, irreligious, worldly: of zealously pursuing their own concerns, neglecting those of others, not extending a hand to the fallen, and offering the sick neither compassionate feeling nor the help of consolation. Among the brethren he marks one for pride, another for envy; he accuses this man of talkativeness and that man of vanity; finally, he insists that scarcely anyone can be found to whom one may safely entrust oneself.

Therefore one ought to withdraw to this or that place—or, since one will nowhere find people like oneself, of such good zeal and pious desire, to migrate into remoter regions and solitude. There, no obstacle will be met in the pious desire arising from the importunity of evil people; there will be quiet, silence, assiduous prayer, frequent fasting; there, holy conduct and an angelic life; there, tears and sighs; in short, everything will succeed according to one’s wish. [Col. 0761D] By hissing these and other such things into our heart, the ancient serpent tries to lead away every unwary and simple person from the Lord’s flock, so that, once a transgressor of the holy profession has no one to sustain him, it may easily cast him down, entangled in its coils; and, once he finds no one to raise him up, it may freely suffocate him when cast down.

Thus, thus the inventor of all fraud, while advising things seemingly holy and useful, pretends to worship Christ in order to kill him once found; and once he is killed, it may thereafter possess more freely the kingdom of sin which it had held within us until then. But although it kills in the flesh Christ’s little ones—of whom he himself says, “Allow the little children to come to me”—it does not capture the citadel of faith. And although, having received power, it sifts the elect, it is itself deceived: sending the purest fine flour to the table of the heavenly king, it retains for itself the unclean bran of its own deceit.

We read something similar about impious Pharaoh: he ordered the little Hebrew boys to be slaughtered, while the females, who weaken the strength of warriors, were to be preserved. For he says to his people: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel is numerous and stronger than we are. [Col. 0762B] Come, let us deal wisely with it, lest perhaps it multiply. And if war should arise against us, it may join our enemies, overcome us, and depart from the land.” Therefore he commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill the males but preserve the females.

The ancient enemy who raged in Pharaoh already knew at that time that war was threatening him; he knew it and feared it. Therefore, in order to stir up the Egyptians against God’s people, he prophesied from his own domestic mouth that war would be brought upon them by that very people. But he prefigured the time of Christ’s grace and the victory of the Christian people, when the one who speaks in the Gospel, “I came not to bring peace but a sword,” raises war against him throughout the world; and he is daily overcome, as though unarmed and weak, under Christ’s leadership even by the little ones whom Pharaoh judged should be drowned in the river.

The people of the Hebrews is added to the enemies of the Egyptians when the Jew joins the people of the nations in unity of faith, and both peoples, with equal courage, wage common war against their common enemy. When Christ grants victory, each people comes up victorious from the Red Sea and joyfully sings: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured; horse and rider he has cast into the sea.” [Col. 0762C] But where God’s people are granted free passage to the land of promise, destruction is prepared for pursuing adversaries; and the wave that makes a way for the humble overturns the wheels of hostile chariots so that it may also engulf the proud rider.

Now divine mercy is accustomed to grant the aid of its protection more especially when every help of human power and resource has failed, so that where human weakness falls beneath the sickle of tribulation, it may know that its escape is due neither to its own strength nor to its merit, but to God’s grace. For in this the most gracious physician of souls especially provides for human salvation: at times he leaves a person to himself and withdraws the hand by which he sustained him in weakness, so that, when left to himself, the person falls and learns from that fall that he cannot stand without God. Thus he may cling more firmly to his protector and refer all things to the praise of him whose gifts they all are. [Col. 0762D] For a person is plainly impious toward God if he attributes to his own merits what belongs to the grace of God.

In all these matters consider, O human being, how great thanks you owe to your liberator. While you stand and look on, he defeats your enemies by an insensible element against insensible beings; and, once your enemy has been cast down by his right hand, he proclaims you victor, praises you as victor, and grants a crown to your head—the sign and reward of victory. And, so that you may marvel at and love still more the kindness and power of your protector, attend to the savagery and pride of your enemy.

Who would not be terrified even at the mere hearing of this most savage being, who boasts in the swelling arrogance of his proud heart that he has found the strength of nations as though it were a nest and gathered the whole earth as though it were abandoned eggs? For he says: “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood; I have removed the boundaries of peoples, plundered their princes, and like a powerful man have brought down those seated on high. My hand has found [Col. 0763B] the strength of peoples as a nest; and as abandoned eggs are gathered, so I have gathered the whole earth. There was none to move a wing, open its mouth, or chirp.”

Who hears of so great a strength in his enemy without his ears ringing? Who sees others falling from on high and does not himself, placed below, tremble? Yet what is more exalted than Peter’s throne, or stronger than Stephen’s rank? And nevertheless, Judas seated upon the apostolic throne he drags down with the hook of avarice; Nicholas, standing in Stephen’s rank, he overthrows, enticed by the allurements of lust.

And who would not marvel at the terror of this most cruel one, who boasts that, after gathering the whole earth, he found no one to move a wing, open his mouth, or chirp? Nor is this surprising. Whoever pursues earthly things is earth-born and has the wings of the soul bound by the birdlime of desire. When gathered by the devil into the number of the lost, he cannot move a wing or fly away; and, possessed by a demon, like that mute man in the Gospel, [Col. 0764A] he can neither open his mouth nor freely contradict in speech the one who holds him captive. But whoever is heavenly and, having taken up the wings of a dove, strives toward heavenly things, freely flies out of the devil’s snares and, with open mouth and free voice, taunts the ancient deceiver. “In vain is the net cast before the eyes of those with wings.”

What, then, is more wonderful than this conflict, and what more glorious than this victory? For when frail humanity, weakened by the defect of its corruption, encounters the devil, what else can I say than that a little worm enters combat with an angel? Most beautiful indeed—most beautiful—is this spectacle of so unequal a duel, for angels and human beings alike. The ancient enemy stands gnashing and raging, casting forth foam from his rabid mouth and vomiting threats; and, because in Christ’s presence he possesses no strength, he attempts either to ensnare the unwary by fraud [Col. 0764B] or drive away the fearful by terror. Thus he coils himself in a thousand folds, whirls about like a mill in a thousand deceptions, and with such subtlety and speed slips from one deceit into another that, as his swiftness often deceives the eyes, a person does not know where the twisting serpent begins or where it ends.

But the little worm of Christ, safe beneath the shadow of his wings, sees and laughs at its enemy tearing itself with its rabid mouth. In silent speech and with a devout heart, crying to the Lord with Moses, it overcomes the adversary by prayer. Christ is present as spectator of the contest and protector of his soldier. Since he grants victory from heaven, the apostate angel is cast down by one act of pride into hell, while the little worm, borne upward by Christ’s grace, climbs to heaven to be crowned. This victory is yours, O Christ, eternal conqueror; [Col. 0764C] to you belong thanksgiving, praise, and glory, who live and reign for endless ages. Amen.

## Preface to Book Nine

[Col. 0763]

[Col. 0763C] It ought not to trouble the reader if I briefly answer on my own behalf those who perhaps think I deserve reproach because, having begun to write about God’s grace, I have wandered with unrestrained course across the breadth of the Old and New Testaments. For, as I hastily cross the very broad field of both Testaments, I touch upon a few examples of divine mercy which offer themselves to one in haste, [Col. 0763D] so that from these the reader may understand what he ought to think concerning God’s grace in other cases also.

Let the person who judges this blameworthy weigh one thing from another and estimate invisible things from visible: for a colour bound to a cloth does not obtain the same favour through the mouth of one praising it as it does when, applied with becoming variety to panels laid beneath it, it displays its own brightness to beholders’ eyes. So too the grace [Col. 0764C] of which we speak—ineffable in speech and incomprehensible in thought—pleases readers more greatly in proportion as it shines more clearly from the continuous text of Holy Scripture, with examples applied as though by a painter’s hand.

I could indeed state briefly, and as it were confine excellent colour to cheap cloth, that whatever dignity and grace stand out in all created things proceed from that fount of supreme goodness. But the honey of heavenly grace does not offer so sweet a taste of itself to the palate of our heart unless, through the works of its mercy themselves, it drips from the bride’s lips as though through the openings of its honeycomb. Therefore let us carry out what we have begun and, with our loins girded, complete by grace’s guidance what remains of the journey we have undertaken.

## Book Nine

[Col. 0763]

[Col. 0763D] In the preceding discussion, when we treated Pharaoh’s cruelty, we also recalled the crossing of the children of Israel, when the liquid element, to defend God’s people, rose up on the right and left into the stable support of walls, while nature was astonished but the Lord of nature gave the command. Let us now see how our leader, girded [Col. 0765A] with strength, enters the waters of the Jordan to complete the mystery of that Red Sea; and how he who at the beginning separated waters from waters by the firmament set between them now likewise separates the waters of the Jordan from one another through a spiritual judgment interposed, just as Joshua once did. He sets the upper waters in the solidity of a wall, but allows the lower waters, flowing away from him, to pass by just judgment into the Sea of the Wilderness and the Dead Sea, utterly alien from life, until they wholly fail away.

But let us first see why he wished to approach the waters of baptism: was it because of a need in himself, or because of grace toward us? Filth is washed by water, and what is defiled is cleansed by water. Why, then, did he wish to be washed with water, he who had no filth? What then shall we say? Did he approach a bath uselessly, in which there was nothing defiled to be cleansed by the bath? He therefore wished to be baptized for us, and, for our sanctification, sanctified the waters by the immersion of his most holy body. For all human nature had been infected and defiled in Adam by the poison of the serpent’s persuasion; nor was there any washing by which it could be cleansed except the sacrament of Christ’s baptism. And that which was dead through sin could not be given life except through life-giving water.

For the first thing to breathe and live came forth from the waters, as Sacred Scripture testifies; and what water brought forth alive was the first to deserve God’s blessing. Moses, the writer of sacred history, when describing the creation of heaven and earth and carefully setting out separately the works of each of the six days, says concerning the first day, [Col. 0765C] the third, and the fourth: “And God saw that it was good,” yet he mentions no sacrament of blessing conferred. Concerning the second day, however—the day that divides the waters—the divine word does not report that God pronounced it good, perhaps itself indicating by silence that divine judgment does not approve whatever divides unity. But concerning the fifth day it speaks thus: “God also said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living soul, and birds above the earth, beneath the firmament of heaven.” And a little later: “And God saw that it was good; and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth.”

See how life is born from waters for a world that was dead; and after it has been made alive, the sanctification of God’s blessing is bestowed, and thereafter grace for increase [Col. 0765D] and multiplication is added. For the blessing of God’s right hand cannot be idle; rather, from the grace of God’s blessing, an abundance of every good always overflows.

Likewise, before the coming and baptism of the Saviour, death had occupied the whole breadth of the world, and a deadly sleep had overwhelmed all Adam’s children, so much so that one lying dead could not be awakened either by the lawgiver crying aloud or by the prophetic trumpet sounding. But when our Elisha saw that the child lying down did not rise either through the servant sent beforehand or through the staff laid upon him, he had compassion upon the grieving mother. He deigned to approach the lying child, contracted himself to the measure of the little one, and, placing mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, and hands to hands, [Col. 0766A] he warmed him with divine heat and raised up the one who could not be raised by any assistance of human weakness.

See how greatly the true Elisha, our Lord Jesus Christ, contracts himself: he assumes even the form of sin, seeks the baptism of sinners among sinners, and, by touching the waters himself, washes us. But amid these matters it is worth asking why almighty God, intending to forgive the sins of the world, judged this visible element should be taken up into the work of invisible grace as though for some supplementary purpose. Who, even if unbelieving, could believe that the Almighty cannot forgive our sins without it? And who, even if mad, would dare to say either that something is commanded by God uselessly or that something which does not cooperate with salvation itself is employed in the ministry of our salvation?

Therefore this visible element, I think, was taken up into the sacrament of our redemption as necessary. By “necessary,” however, I mean necessary not to omnipotence itself but to our slowness. For if, misled by the error of our unbelief, we scarcely believe what we see with our eyes and touch with our hands, how could the dimness of our sight fix its gaze, with the sharpness of faith unharmed by the rays of the invisible sun, unless the heavenly physician anointed the eyes of our heart to behold invisible things with the salve, as it were, of visible things? Hence, when sending his disciples to preach, he said: “Go, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”

For the teacher sent to preach is entrusted with the care of healing the sicknesses of souls. But [Col. 0766C] a physician applies treatment in vain if the sick person despairs of recovery. Therefore, so that the sinner may flee to the remedies of repentance with undoubting faith, let him learn from the visible healing of another’s body what he ought to hope from the almighty physician concerning the invisible sickness of the soul. Likewise, let the one who has fallen asleep into death through the deadly sleep of sin learn, through this visible raising of bodies at the invocation of Christ’s name, also to believe in the invisible resurrection of the soul through faith in Christ. And let the person who grieves that he has been stained with the unclean colour of heretical doctrine, different from his own worship the Lord with bent knee, and from the cleansing of bodies not despair of recovering the purity of faith. But the person possessed by a demon and violently driven headlong through crimes [Col. 0766D] and disgraceful acts, if he turns to the Lord with his whole heart and full faith, should not doubt that the malignant spirit—however hostile, however violent—will be driven from the inner chamber of his heart by the Lord’s command.

Therefore, just as signs and wonders are performed visibly so that things which cannot be seen may be believed, so also the visible element itself has been taken up into the work of heavenly grace to strengthen believers’ faith. And the element accords very fittingly with the mystery: as this washes bodily filth, so the other, by forgiving sins, washes the filth of souls. Therefore, as we have said, the Saviour enters the streams of the Jordan to sanctify them for our sake, so that, once the channels of sin have been dried up, he may halt our downward course and, as we persevere in the sweetness of grace received, no violence of temptations may again roll us unwillingly into the Dead Sea—that is, into the deep and most bitter abyss of vices.

For whoever, after liberty has been restored to him by Christ, willingly enslaves himself again to the ancient service of unclean spirits is rolled into the Sea of the Wilderness, entirely deserted by the grace of heavenly visitation, and into the Dead Sea—for “the soul that sins, it shall die”—not so much driven by his enemy’s violence as enticed by the allurements of his own desire.

Thus, when the Lord was baptized, heaven was opened, the Holy Spirit came in the form of a dove, and the Father sounded from heaven in a voice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” This is the grace, power, and sanctification of Christ’s baptism: through it, baptized persons receive forgiveness of all sins through faith in the Holy Trinity. O how glorious a council in the presence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit! [Col. 0767B] O how joyful a spectacle even for the heavenly powers! Blessed the Baptist who deserved to see these things; blessed the one who deserved to hear them; blessed also the one who faithfully believes what he hears; but happier still is the one who, after being washed once by Christ’s baptism, keeps his conscience henceforth clean from defilements.

“Opened,” says blessed Luke, “opened was heaven.” And when had heaven been closed to him? When had it been closed to him without whom it could not even exist? How could the firmament open itself to him without whose governance it would waver in weakness? Rather, it was opened for us by the key of Christ’s baptism, for us to whom it had previously been shut by the bar of original sin. Heaven was suitably opened then so that humanity might learn what key had opened the heavenly places to it.

“And the Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove and remained upon him.” The dove is ever the Spirit’s familiar bird: the simple bird for the simple one; free from the bitterness of gall for sweetness itself; bearer of the olive branch; friend and messenger of peace. O how delightful a dwelling in the most pure breast of the lover of purity! O the Lord’s condescension and grace! O the servant’s honour and glory! [Col. 0767C] Would that this most gentle bird might find rest in our breast: it circles in most gentle flight, seeking a humble and quiet place in which to rest. Blessed is the soul that provides lodging for Christ when he is a stranger. Blessed is the conscience that offers refreshment, under the shadow of pious desire, to the Spirit circling and burning with ardour.

But these are the things of saints. In our breast, may he at least find rest for a moment—he who could at some time find a stable and eternal dwelling only in that most pure and most loving little breast of our Lord Jesus Christ. For this is he—this one man, unique and alone—long awaited, greatly desired, whom those seven prophetic women, sick with love, cry out to in the near-impatience of excessive love, saying to their beloved: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called over us: take away our reproach.”

“Take away our reproach!” Alas! The one made in the image of his maker, created for the honour and glory of his creator, is called not the image and mirror of his maker but, by a perverse name, the reproach of his giver of life. Alas! Who will give [Col. 0768A] water to my head and fountains of tears to my eyes, that I may weep not for those slain of one people but for the reproach of the whole human race? In all humanity none is found whose name may worthily be called over these women, who may be honour and glory to these women, who may take away—or rather, who may not increase—the stain of disgrace.

Therefore these seven women, namely the seven spiritual graces, complain in a mournful voice, saying: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be called over us: take away our reproach. From the beginning we have surveyed the human race; we have examined patriarchs, righteous persons, and prophets. ‘All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one.’ Therefore we rest in you. Let your name, then, be called [Col. 0768B] over us: take away our reproach. You are he whom we have always desired; you of whom we sang in our instruments: ‘A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.’ We cherished the root; we brought forth the shoot; we overshadowed the woman in labour; we produced the flower. We therefore rest in him by right.”

These seven women are the sevenfold Spirit, who, distributing diverse gifts to each person according to his will, remains always the same and undivided in himself. No believer doubts that he needs nothing. He asks only that the invocation of Christ’s name remove its reproach from their midst, so that the vessels of the eternal tabernacle, cleansed by the sprinkling of his blood, may be worthy to receive the outpouring of the blessing of his graces.

Accordingly, when the Lord descended into the Jordan, the Spirit too descended from heaven; and He rests upon His breast with all the greater confidence because He finds in Him nothing to disturb His repose. But what does it mean that He is now seen to have descended upon Him from whom He is believed never to have departed from the very hour of His conception? Does He now for the first time visit His temple, which He had consecrated in the virginal womb? Therefore, the Holy Spirit’s appearing in bodily form above the Lord when baptized teaches our faith that, for those baptized in Christ, heaven is opened and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit received, they are adopted as children of God. For through the Spirit [Col. 0768D] forgiveness of sins is given; through the Spirit comes the adoption of children, as the Apostle testifies to the Romans: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father. For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.”

When, therefore, the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon the Lord, lest the sacrament of our faith remain incomplete, the testimony of the heard voice also declared the presence of the Father. For the paternal voice was heard—and truly a paternal voice: a gracious voice, a herald of loving-kindness, which condemned the old sentence and introduced new grace: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” O new and unheard-of testimony of God the Father concerning a man! [Col. 0769A] Once, when human wickedness had multiplied, when all flesh had corrupted its way and every thought of the heart was at all times bent upon evil, the Lord said, inwardly touched with grief of heart: “I will destroy man, whom I created, from the face of the earth; for I repent that I made them.” The sentence of the just Judge against the guilty was indeed deserved and just; yet pitiable for wretched man was the repentance of so merciful a Creator concerning His own creation.

But now, in the channel of the Jordan, beholding that Man concerning whom divine providence never repents, He speaks over Him with a gentle voice and commends Him alike by the privilege of love and holiness and by the privilege of dignity. He commends Him as the Son to be adored by reason of His dignity, to be venerated by reason of the singular privilege of His love, and to be imitated by reason of that special holiness in which He has always pleased God the Father. “This,” He says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Behold what dignity, grace, and benefit the sacrament of baptism has bestowed on us: dignity, that God the Father should adopt us as His children; grace, that He should cherish and sanctify those adopted with paternal love; benefit, that He should so advance the sanctified from virtue to virtue that He Himself may always be well pleased in us.

Let us therefore remember what we were and behold what we are; from these we shall readily gather what we have obtained through the grace of God. Yet would that we might either be permitted not to know, or might have no desire to repeat, what we were; and that we might defend by the worthiness of our conduct the dignity of adoption as children of God which we glory in having attained. We were rebels against God; we became transgressors of His command; and, by the sentence of our condemnation, were made exiles from paradise and a sport to the ancient enemy. [Col. 0769C] And truly, what greater mockery for the ancient enemy, and disgrace to our race, could there have been than that he should pluck down our strength with his proud hand as though it were a nest, as we mentioned above, while there was none among us even to move a wing or yelp with open mouth?

Human weakness, once its foot was set in motion with a wavering step, could not stand upon that slippery ground of sin; but as the devil daily drove it toward worse things, it fell so low that the fool said in his heart, “There is no God,” and man, blinded by the darkness of his ignorance, bent his knees to wood and stone. Shame! That rational man should bow his neck to senseless [Col. 0769D] wood, and worship a stone that does not know that it is worshipped! Shame! To seek help from one who did not know how to help himself, and to consult concerning one’s own condition one who could not stand unless fixed with nails! Where then, O man, was the dignity of your creation? Where was the splendor of the divine image impressed upon you by God’s hand? How did you become forgetful of your own power? How did you choose to be subjected in so degraded a slavery to irrational things, over which you ought to have ruled by both the nobility of your nature and the governance of reason? How was it that you, who had been made in the image of God, worshipped the image of a dog and a serpent?

Such were the shoots we put forth from that rotten root of paternal corruption; such milk we sucked from the breast of our mother, Gentile religion; thus were we taught by the devil our father. But when we heard the true Father crying aloud: [Col. 0770A] “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty,” when we acknowledged God as Father, we were adopted as children of God. The most gracious Father does not reproach those who return with the filthiness of idols or the husks of swine; but moved by paternal love, He rushes into their embrace and offers the kiss of peace as a sign of reconciliation. The services of servants are assigned to us as to children; everything is presented for our adornment—the robe, the ring, the shoes, the insignia of paternal nobility. The place of former dignity is restored, and a festive banquet is prepared for our exaltation, with rejoicing friends.

Who would not be astonished at the depths of such mercy? What hardness of the human heart, set aflame by this fire, would not melt? [Col. 0770B] For what rich and mighty man would deign to adopt as his son a servant base by birth and infamous in life? And what great thing would it be if a human being adopted a human being, a mortal a mortal, a corruptible being a corruptible being, as a son? But when God adopts man as a son—the Almighty one who is weak, the Eternal one who is temporal, so base and so unworthy—who can sufficiently marvel, who can worthily proclaim it, who can render to Him who adopts a return of due service, not to say of love, proportionate to it?

For I, to speak what I feel, pursuing this grace with breathless course along its tracks, cannot grasp it; and the nearer and nearer I come, the more clearly I see that it is incomprehensible. Yet this too ought to be considered in these names of compassion: that He who is supremely good and supremely [Col. 0770C] merciful preferred to invite the willing by tenderness rather than compel the unwilling by threats and terrors, calling Himself father, nurse, mother, and hen, while from affectionate mercy He calls us sons, little children, and chicks.

In one place the Lord speaks to Jerusalem as though the most gracious father were tenderly speaking to a little child: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion upon the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you.” Even if, He says, it were possible for a woman, trampling the law of nature and neglecting affection, not to be moved toward her own offspring nor to pity the son of her womb, nevertheless it can by no means happen that I, who am the Creator of nature, should forget those whom I created. You will find many other passages like these in [Col. 0770D] Holy Scripture, from which you may learn the wonderful affection of the most merciful Creator toward His creature.

Therefore, O man, warned by so many and such great benefits and by the very name of mercy, strive to adorn with your conduct the dignity bestowed upon you, lest, if it is empty and idle in you, it also be fruitless. Consider carefully how much labor people expend, with what zeal, and finally at the peril not merely of life itself but even of the soul, in order to acquire temporal things and gather up perishable possessions—where neither the possessions nor their possessor can remain long. Let it then shame the child of the kingdom to be found less zealous in preserving the glory of his adoption than the child of perdition in heaping up perishable things and accumulating for himself punishments that will last forever. Let it shame him to sadden, even slightly, that most serene [Col. 0771A] countenance of his Father, who deigned to adopt him into such glory. Let it shame him, I say, to forsake the incomparable delights of his Father’s table and defile with the unclean husks of swine the mouth sanctified by his Father’s kiss.

Let him always consider the greatness of paternal love; and let him also dread, should he be found ungrateful, the intolerable severity of paternal indignation. Let him set before his eyes the immeasurable reward of slight labor, and, conversely, the inescapable punishment of momentary pleasure. Let him fear the coming examination of the dreadful judgment, in which, when the gifts of mercy bestowed upon us have been recalled, the debt of fitting service will be exacted from us with strict scrutiny. Before the tribunal of the Judge there will be recalled the dignity of our creation, [Col. 0771B] the glory of the divine likeness, the love of redemption, the shedding of precious blood, adoption as children, and the promised blessedness of the kingdom of heaven. There will also be recalled the aids granted for fulfilling the commandments, the weakness of the enemy, and our own negligence.

O how great then will be the confusion of the trembling conscience! Alas, how bitter! Alas, how late! Alas, how fruitless then will repentance for past sloth be! O if only it were now permitted to behold that countenance of our confusion; O if only it were now possible to soften that strict judgment by a reformed life. Then, when conscience accuses, there will be no defender; now, when life is corrected, there will then be found no accuser.

You therefore, chosen race, holy offspring, royal stock, live worthily of God, worthily of so great a Father, as children of God and most beloved children, so that you may then receive Him joyfully as Father, whom you now serve with filial affection. It is not for children, when their father comes, to tremble or seek hiding places, but with exultant spirit to rush eagerly to meet him, each striving to be first to approach, to embrace him eagerly, kiss him most affectionately, and attest their boundless joy at the arrival of their most sweet father by their meeting, gestures, applause, kisses, and embrace. Such children—so devoted, so pious, so diligent—the most gracious and serene Father receives with paternal gladness, gathers countless children into one embrace with arms spread wide, presses His sweet children to His most sacred breast, and soothes them with gentle hand and gentle speech.

“Now, my children, [Col. 0772B] now my most beloved ones, now you blessed of my Father, enjoy with me the glory of my kingdom. Now recognize how great is the dignity of your adoption, and reap with joy what you sowed in tears. The times of your labor and sorrow have now passed more swiftly than a runner; but the times of your refreshment and joy, while I remain, cannot pass away. Therefore, because you gladly fulfilled what I commanded, freely receive what I promised.”

On that day, illumined by the splendor of the divine countenance, man will be able to recognize what grace of God, and how great, was shown toward him. And because he will find nothing in himself worthy of such bounty, he will render eternal thanks to the Giver, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Preface to the Tenth Book

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771C] The path of virtues is steep and laborious, and is not easily climbed by any human being unless the grace of which we speak directs the ascending person’s steps. Therefore I too, lame in almost both feet, commanded to climb this loftiest—not merely mountain, but mountain of mountains—am greatly afraid at the difficulty of the matter. For although it is glorious to strive toward the heights, it is sufficiently shameful to tumble downward with an ineffective step. It is not difficult for anyone to walk over level ground, where the walker neither pants anxiously nor fears utter ruin if he slips.

But since, as the injunction of obedience hanging at the threshold of this little book contains, I am commanded to discuss the sacraments of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, I am compelled to ascend the very summit of our faith—an ascent than which I have experienced nothing more laborious, nor anything more dangerous in a fall. And though I wait, at the foot of the mountain, for the descent and touch of the merciful physician with the leper, I am compelled suddenly to climb the heights with John and James and, while the scales of my blindness have not yet been removed, to contemplate the glory of the transfigured Lord.

Yet I have this one consolation amid the difficulty of this work: I did not rush into it by any rash presumption, but was compelled by the force of obedience to attempt it, if perhaps I might be able, with uninjured foot, to follow the tracks of grace going before faith. For I judged it better to proceed little by little, however weak my step, than to be found disobedient by failing even to attempt what was commanded. Let us therefore undertake what remains, with the help of Him who commanded it.

## Tenth Book

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771D] Our Lord Jesus Christ, knowing that the root of pride cannot be torn out from the human race except by the hand of the heavenly husbandman, pursues it everywhere with the hoe of His word, lest, if it is not dug up, every fruit be corrupted by the poison of its root and what might have been healthful with a sound root become deadly when that root is corrupt. Knowing, then, that the human mind is eager for glory and seeks things higher than itself to such an extent that it sometimes wishes to ascribe even the gifts of God’s grace to itself, He applies the plaster of humility to that harmful swelling, teaching that whoever exalts himself must be humbled, and conversely, whoever humbles himself must be exalted.

Indeed, He judges that divine benefits ought so entirely to be referred to the praise of God that He declares His teaching not to be His own and humbly affirms that He can do nothing of Himself. If the power of God and wisdom of God assigns to God the Father the glory of His teaching and work, how much more should human weakness do so? If the vine attributes the richness of its root to God who waters it, how much more should the branches? For what could a branch possess unless, so to speak, it conceived the bud in the embrace of the root, in some hidden womb of nature, and brought forth the grape? “I am,” He says, “the vine; you are the branches. As the branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.”

For this purpose the heavenly husbandman grafts the branch, raises it up, digs around it, and cultivates it: that it may cleave to the root and become one with the root; that it may live from the root, bear fruit from the root, and bear fruit that remains, while knowing that the glory of all the fruit belongs to the vine. For then it truly lives, when it humbly recognizes from whom it lives. Therefore, in order that the merciful cultivator may root out that most evil root of pride from the field of our heart, He says, “My teaching is not mine,” and, “I can do nothing of myself.”

And when He had reproached the cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—in which He had frequently taught and performed many mighty works—for the hardness of their obstinate minds and the faithlessness of their unbelief, declaring that Tyre and Sidon and the land of the Sodomites would fare more leniently on the day of judgment, He thus glorifies the Father concerning the faith of the apostles and believers: “I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it was well pleasing before you.”

And see how everywhere He commends grace, everywhere proclaims the Father’s glory. “I give thanks,” He says, “to you, Father, Lord [Col. 0773C] of heaven and earth.” He attributes nothing to Himself from the faith of believers, claims nothing for Himself from the instruction of disciples—He who had chosen, called, instructed, and justified them. He Himself distinguishes vessels of wrath from vessels of mercy; He Himself assigns different persons to this or that work of His ministry; He chooses twelve by special grace, instructing them more familiarly in private; outside, He proposes parables to the crowds, while at home He explains to His disciples what He has set forth. Yet attributing none of these things to Himself, but referring all things to the Father’s glory, He gives thanks for the rejection of the proud and the election of the humble, saying: “I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

Diligent reader, [Col. 0773D] attend carefully to how the Only-Begotten of God, coeternal with the eternal Father—sharing with Him one substance, the same glory, one and the same counsel, and an undivided work—refers all that is His to the glory of the Father alone, in order to teach you, a mere human being, weak and powerless, to whom you ought to refer all that is yours, if indeed it is worthy of God. For He does not say, “We have hidden these things and revealed them,” but, “You have hidden and revealed them.” It is as if He said: “I called; you inspired. I held the book; you opened it. I set forth the law; you expounded it. I sounded in their ears; you sounded in their hearts.”

O grace, O mercy, O wisdom! Thus, yes thus, the merciful physician provides for His sick person; in this way He digests with a healing purgative the harmful humors spread throughout the limbs, striving both to dry up the very spring from which poisons flow and, as far as lies in Him, to remove the causes [Col. 0774A] and origins of the disease, lest, if the spring begins once more to bubble up with its old poisons, He lose both the labor of His skill and its expenditure.

From this confession of our Lord, therefore, let the lover of grace learn how and to whom he ought to give thanks, and let him know that, however much good he finds in each individual thing, so much grace of God is present in each. For no one, however sharp his intelligence, will ever be able to discover how great grace is in itself—unless perhaps he has measured how great the immeasurable is.

Again, when He was about to feed five thousand with five loaves and four thousand with seven, He took the loaves in His hands, gave thanks, blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to distribute to the crowds. About to perform a miracle, He first gives thanks for the power bestowed upon Him, and only then uses the power received in the performance of the miracle. Such abundance of blessing followed the thanksgiving that, though so many thousands were fed from few loaves, the remaining fragments overflowed into twelve and seven baskets. And the dispensation of grace in this feeding of the crowd is wonderful: how some are fed with barley loaves, others with wheat loaves.

But still more wonderful is the division of graces in the feeding of the word, of which those loaves were a type: how the same word, according to the palate and taste of those who eat, tastes like barley to some and wheat to others. Barley is coarser in husk and harsher in taste, the food of servants and fodder of beasts; wheat, however, is softer to the touch and sweeter in taste, and is brought to the tables of masters. Those, therefore, who still serve the Lord in a spirit of slavery and servile fear [Col. 0774C] find the taste of barley in God’s word. But those who serve the Lord in the spirit of love and love God with the chaste fear which remains for ever and ever draw from God’s word a wholly different taste, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

Thus, refreshed by the wondrous and ineffable sweetness of the word, they reject with a nauseated stomach the hardness of barley and the food of servants, as free people, as children, as those delicately nourished; and chewing again with insatiable throat the sweetness once tasted, and joyfully uttering from the heart the good word, they sing with gladness: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” There is something else concerning the word of God that I wonder at still more: the same word sometimes produces in one reading or chanting it almost no taste of its own savor, while at other times it surpasses, when tasted, all the sweetness of honey.

For it often overflows with such abundance of honeyed sweetness that it enters the thirsty soul, parched by the heat of its longing, like a torrent, and draws the whole person after it with a certain holy violence. Often, suspended with all his mind toward heaven and carried by the word of God into forgetfulness of himself, a person thinks of nothing besides Him on whose love he feeds. Then, having cast off the cloak of earthly care, he is borne upward in a fiery chariot with Elijah; and in him is truly fulfilled what is written of Enoch: “And he was not found, because God translated him.” For one who is at other times raised by the free flight of holy desire toward heaven is not found in the earthly dregs, having been translated by God; and the more he becomes accustomed to the purest [Col. 0775A] ether, the more he recoils from earth’s muddy and stinking marshes.

But when, by the necessity of the flesh, he is compelled like an eagle to descend to earthly things, then he truly laments that he is a stranger; then groans break forth, then sighs strike his breast, then showers of tears flow, and, distressed by the defect of his corruption, he does not so much sing as howl mournfully: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been greatly a stranger.” Yet the reason a person does not enjoy this sweetness whenever he wishes, and does not always find it in the word of God, is often the defect of his inward palate and the punishment of previous sluggishness; but sometimes it comes through the dispensation of God’s grace, which wonderfully orders all things. For if it were always present at will, a person would not seek it with such desire; or perhaps, what is more ruinous, deceived by a familiar presumption, he would believe it the fruit of his own labor and not the gift of God.

But the Lord knows how to dispense His gifts, what to give to whom and when; and so He distributes the talent of the word among His servants according to the ability of each, wishing no one to be without profit. Having spoken of these mystical loaves according to the place and measure of our little ability, let us pass to the true bread that descended from heaven, earnestly beseeching Him with all the affection of our heart that, in His accustomed goodness, He may deign to be present to one writing of Him, so that by His inspiration I may write things worthy of Him and profitable to readers.

Therefore, at the banquet of the most holy supper, when He had brought to an end the typical Passover celebrated with the legal ceremonies, He substituted the true and eternal Passover by the offering of the true Lamb. In His immolation, Love itself and the grace of which we speak offered itself, as it were visibly, for our eyes to behold. “No one has greater love than that one should lay down his life for his friends.” But if laying down one’s life for friends is such great love that no greater could exist, what manner of love, what greatness of love, is it to lay down one’s life for enemies? For when a life is laid down for friends, friendship is returned in kind; but when a life is laid down for enemies, it is rightly called love, rightly called grace. “But God commends his love toward us,” says the Apostle, “because, while we were still sinners and enemies, Christ died for us.” This is the commendation of that immense love [Col. 0775D] worthy of God. This is the manifestation of unsearchable grace: Christ dies for sinners out of gratuitous goodness; the Son of God is made a spectacle, and God is exposed to human insults.

Therefore, when the flesh of the typical lamb had been consumed and the legal ceremonies, as I have said, completed, the true Lamb Himself, who takes away the sin of the world, took bread in His hands and, blessing and breaking it, gave it to His disciples in these words: “Take and eat; this is my body.” The good Shepherd, about to lay down His life for His sheep and, having completed the course of His dispensation and fulfilled the mystery of our redemption, about to return to the Father, was bound to His flock by an indissoluble bond of love and could not long be absent from it in bodily presence.

He, therefore, who took maternal flesh into [Col. 0776A] His hands and turned the flesh He had assumed into the work of our redemption, likewise takes bread into His hands and, by the power of the divine blessing and of the Word—which He Himself is—changes it into His body, the sacrament of our salvation. He breaks the bread as one having power to lay down His life and to take it up again. Though the persecutor seizes, binds, strikes, mocks, spits upon, and crucifies Him, it is He who breaks the bread; it is He who performs the mystery of the Passion. For unless He Himself broke the bread, unless He permitted Judas the power to betray Him and the Jews the power to crucify Him, the former would spread his snares in vain and the latter stretch out their hands in vain.

Indeed, when Pilate said, “Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to crucify you?” He showed that this power was granted, not inherent: “You would have no power over me,” He said, “unless it had been given you from above.” He demonstrates the same thing by deeds to the servants who had come to seize Him, when with one gentle word, saying, “Whom do you seek?” He casts them raging to the ground. Thus the Gospel grain is ground by the hands of the Jews, baked in the fire of the Passion, and, made the living bread by the Word of life, becomes life-giving nourishment for the faithful.

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to the disciples, saying: “Drink of this, all of you. This is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” Taking the cup, he gave thanks. Everywhere he gives thanks; everywhere he instructs us to give thanks to God—yet especially at the point of his passion, when, the more the flesh falters and trembles from its weakness, [Col. 0776C] the more it needs the hand of divine consolation to support it as it wavers. “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” says the Creator and knower of flesh and spirit.

Since, therefore, he who made us knows our weakness, and knows that we, frail and unarmed, cannot resist one strong and armed unless a stronger protector defends us against the implacable hatred of the ancient enemy, he has granted us the unconquerable protection of daily bread. The Lord knows that our adversary, infected from ancient times with the gall of envy, rages against us with tireless malice; nor can any treaty arise between parties at war without injury to our salvation. The merciful examiner of hearts knows also that the path of our corruption is dark and slippery, [Col. 0776D] and that no human being can pass through it unharmed. Since, therefore, we are daily endangered, daily fall, daily grow sick, he has deigned to show us daily his presence in the mystery of his body and blood, that by it we may be freed, raised up, and restored to strength.

And because bread strengthens the human heart and wine also gladdens it, he rightly instituted that the mystery of his passion should be celebrated under the appearances of bread and wine. For he is the true bread, who strengthens the hearts of the faithful lest they fail in this vast wilderness; who banishes the hunger that leads to death; who satisfies our desire with good things—not with the punitive satiety that torments and produces disgust, but with a satiety that always renews strength and never creates disgust. For this food, of which he says, “My flesh is truly food,” is truly wonderful; [Col. 0777A] and the eating of this food is insatiable: the more it is taken, the more it is hungered for; and the more it satisfies the eater, the more it stirs the hungry person to eat further.

Nor is any cup like the Lord’s cup, which so gladdens its drinker with divine and inexpressible delight that it swallows up every remembrance of former sorrow. And not only this: it so intoxicates the drinker with its innate sweetness that it sends him into ecstasy of mind, so that he says to father and mother, “I do not know you”; that he denies himself to himself and, in a manner, does not know himself; so that he no longer sees the way of the world which he has so often entered, nor is any longer able—or indeed willing—to plant steps reeling from drunkenness in the slippery love of the unclean world. Thus, thus—indeed far otherwise, for ineffably—the bread of Christ, which is truly his flesh, [Col. 0777B] strengthens the hearts of the faithful; thus the cup of the Lord, which is truly his blood, gladdens the hearts of those who drink.

And fittingly the mystery of our redemption is recalled in those forms in which one thing is made from many. For bread is made from many grains, and wine is pressed from many berries. The crushed, moistened, and compacted grains come together in such great unity, and all become so completely one, that you cannot distinguish one grain from another; nor can sight, touch, or taste discover what belonged to which. Having been separated by the sieve’s judgment from the roughness of the chaff, all pass into one appearance, one flavor, and one smoothness, so that nothing unlike appears in their form, nothing tastes contrary to itself, and nothing feels different from itself in touch.

[Col. 0777C] If, then, things that grow from the earth are thus united and made indivisible, how much more those which are born from the evangelical grain and the seed of divine blessing. For that evangelical grain fell into the earth so that, having died, it might send down roots and spread throughout the whole breadth of the world, and that which had fallen alone might rise multiplied by the faith of the nations. This grain, therefore, ground in the mill of the passion and moistened, as it were, with the water of the peoples’ faith, has been united to us by such an indissoluble bond of love that from many grains one bread might be made, and from individual members cleaving to their head by the same bond of love, one body.

For this reason, as Scripture says, a man left father and mother and clung to his wife, so that the two might be one flesh: bridegroom and bride, [Col. 0777D] Christ and the Church. He left the Father when, made a little lower than the angels, he emptied himself; when, though handed over, he did not go out [to resist]; though suffering, he did not threaten; when he kept himself within the confines of our weakness without laying aside the power of paternal strength. He also left his mother—the synagogue, his mother according to the flesh, not according to the spirit. For flesh is the mother of flesh; faith is the mother of the Word. Since she did not recognize him whom she bore and did not believe him whom she had foretold, she lost both the affection and the name of motherhood.

But he clung to his wife, the Church gathered from the nations; because she offered her inviting bridegroom the dowry of faith, she deserved fellowship with him in one spirit and one flesh. The communion of unity should likewise be considered in wine, which flows together from many [Col. 0778A] berries into one liquid under the pressure of the winepress. And beautifully the memorial of the Lord’s passion is enacted in these things, both of which in some manner suffer: they are ground and pressed. For just as grains are crushed so that bread may be made, so grapes are trodden so that wine may flow.

“For all who wish to live in Christ Jesus,” says the Apostle, “suffer persecution.” And, as blessed Peter testifies, Christ suffered for this purpose: that he might leave before us the footprints of his passion, so that by following them and suffering with the sufferer, we might reach, by the rough path of passion, the joy of resurrection. Therefore, let whoever is delighted by the sweet taste of this wine not refuse the pressure of the winepress. For this reason water is mixed with wine in our mystery, and thus an acceptable sacrifice is offered to God: because then we offer to God the pleasing victim of Christ’s passion, [Col. 0778B] when we ourselves share in his sufferings by suffering with him.

For when our Lord delivered his body and blood to his disciples to be received in the mystery of bread and wine, he gave the command that they should do this more frequently in remembrance of him. For then we offer worthily, then we receive worthily, when in offering and receiving we recall the abundance and greatness of his love, and do not evade suffering like things through the gift of him for whose sake we suffer.

As a type of this wine which drips from the winepress of the cross, two scouts carry on a pole a cluster from the land of promise, in whose marvelous size and wondrous sweetness the people might taste beforehand the most abundant and sweetest fruits of their promised inheritance. For two men carry the cluster on a pole because two—if I may use another comparison—[Col. 0778C] walls come together in one cornerstone; and from each people, namely Jews and Gentiles, chosen scouts and preachers carry about the mystery of the cross and the power of him who hangs upon the cross.

In its infinite greatness—for “the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no number to his greatness”—and in its inexpressible sweetness, we taste beforehand the sweetness of future blessedness, insofar as the bitterness of our corruption permits. In its honey-sweet affection, so to speak—for whatever I may say is far too little—in that honey-sweet affection we taste our promised land, truly flowing with streams of milk and honey, and all the fruits of our land forever tasting the same sweetness. Therefore the Prophet, who had tasted these things, [Col. 0778D] comforting himself, sings joyfully: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

And by a sufficiently elegant comparison both mysteries, of the stone and of the cluster, correspond to one another. For just as the cornerstone holds together in the middle both walls approaching from opposite directions, so the cluster hanging in the middle joins both bearers, the one going before and the one following.

But there are some who, while they look too closely at the visible appearance of this most holy mystery, become dim-sighted in faith regarding the reality itself. They hesitate over how, while the former taste and appearance of bread and wine remain, the substance of bread and wine can pass into another substance, that of Christ’s flesh and blood. But reflection upon God’s omnipotence can easily heal this weakness of faith: nothing difficult for his creatures is impossible [Col. 0779A] to the Almighty, who was able to create all things from nothing by a word and to transform one thing into another according to his will.

To speak of something from our own experience, not of God’s power—for to God all things are equally possible—it is easier to transform what exists into whatever form he wills than to form from nothing what does not exist. “Has the Lord’s hand been shortened, that it cannot save?” Can he who created heaven and earth by a word for humanity’s service not turn the smallest portion of bread and wine into his true body for humanity’s salvation?

Therefore let the faith of the Christian heart not waver concerning the truth of Christ’s body, lest one bear the name of Christian profession in vain and celebrate the sacraments of divine religion in vain. For without faith [Col. 0779B] it is impossible to please God. Though someone enters the Church, participates in the Church’s sacraments, and answers “Amen” to the solemn prayer, he does these things idly—indeed, perniciously—if he does not possess faith in what is being done.

It is near to folly to wish to examine all the sacraments of our faith and the works of divine power by the feeble reasonings of human wisdom, and to confine God’s omnipotence within the narrow limits of our impossibility. For what else can I call the attempt to comprehend every work of divine power by human understanding than to make God conform to man, so that he cannot do what man does not understand? And whence would faith have such merit if it had proof in every detail through ordinary human experience? But Christian sobriety prefers devoutly to believe what it has heard [Col. 0779C] rather than, by not believing God’s words, to become impious toward God.
