Its reward for faith is God himself, in whom it has believed. Great, therefore, is the merit of Christian faith, to which so great a reward is given in return.

Having considered these matters concerning the sacrament of our salvation, not according to its majesty but according to our weakness, let us recall briefly, as he himself grants, how we ought to do this in remembrance of Christ. One who approaches faithfully and receives devoutly ought to bring back from the belly of memory the food of life, like a clean animal chewing the cud upward, and to chew over by the throat of devout reflection the work of piety.

Let Christ’s devout guest, who sits down at that great table, remember by what bonds of love the Son of God was brought from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the Virgin; [Col. 0779D] with what zeal for our salvation the impassible and eternal God was moved, who, having become man, became passible and mortal for us. Let him remember [Col. 0780A] how the innocent one was given over to our punishments; with how many reproaches, injuries, and penalties he was afflicted. Let him remember that face into which angels desire to look, smeared with spittle, struck with blows, the shame of the cross, the bitterness of gall, and death more bitter than gall.

Let him also recall, with a devout feeling of compassion, the most bitter stretching of all the members of the innocent Lamb upon the gallows, and that most bitter piercing with nails. Above all these things, let him marvel at the voluntary passion and the unchanging gentleness of the sufferer. Nor let him pass over that most health-giving wound from which flowed the medicine for our wounds. For when the side of the Lord, already dead, was opened by the soldier’s lance, blood and water came out: blood of redemption, water of baptism.

[Col. 0780B] Thus from the side of the dead one life came forth, because our Adam fell asleep upon the bed of the cross so that he might bring forth from his side that Eve—the Church—who is truly the mother of all the living. Recalling all these things with the most devout affection of heart possible, and worshipping with the whole contrition of his spirit, let him return to himself; and, tasting at that great table such sweet dishes of love, let him consider within himself what he shall render to the Lord for them: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?”

Exhorting himself to similar things, and urging himself on with the devout spurs of love, let him offer to God the cup of his vows and, relying with unhesitating hope upon God’s help, say: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” For then a person celebrates the mystery of Christ’s passion healthfully in remembrance [Col. 0780C] of him, when, by Christ’s aid, that person prepares himself for like things: when, having been made to drink the most bitter gall of false brethren, he endures; when afflicted with injuries, he does not grieve; mocked, he laughs; worn down by punishments, he rejoices; and he supplies in his own body what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings.

Such a one truly eats life from the Lord’s table; such a one truly drinks life from the Lord’s cup; and according to Christ’s promise, he too lives in Christ, and Christ lives in him. It is not for our smallness to comprehend the breadth of this love and the height of this grace; nevertheless, it is devout for us always to stretch toward it. Let us therefore strive unceasingly to give thanks to him who turned his body into our food and his blood into our drink: Jesus Christ our Lord, who [Col. 0780D] lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## PREFACE TO THE ELEVENTH BOOK

[Col. 0779]

[Col. 0779D] Now that, with the grace of God directing our course, the little ship of faith, as we believe, has escaped safely from rocky places into safer waters, we make toward what lies farther on with easier sailing; nevertheless we keep our eyes fixed upon the same grace which we have followed before. For the one who stands at the prow to guard against dangers, if, as the sea smiles upon him, he turns his eyes backward in greater confidence of a safe return, neglecting what lies ahead, often brings his ship and all its cargo—[Col. 0780D] which he had preserved among the rocks by more careful navigation—to ruin on the open sea.

And often a ship tied up by its rope in harbor through carelessness is dashed about by the violence of winds, and through the negligence of the one who tied it suffers in port what it also suffers from the force of a storm amid the waves. Navigation upon the sea of this world is never safe; for even if at times the gentleness of the winds makes the breeze calmer, the fierce pirate [Col. 0781A] devil, ever greedy for our destruction, is never milder at any time.

But when our king stands at the prow, the cruel tyrant, fearing the presence of his majesty, is afraid to approach more closely; fleeing timidly in various directions, he does not dare attack those sailing, unless perhaps, when our faith sleeps, Christ has fallen asleep, and through our negligence the nail of faith has been lost, a contrary wind drives the tossing little ship [Col. 0782A] into the impious and bloodstained hands of the cruel pirate.

Therefore, strengthened by the protection of our king, let us raise the mast of the cross, spread open the sail of our heart to the Holy Spirit, and, with Christ as helmsman, direct the course of the work we have undertaken toward the desired shore.

## ELEVENTH BOOK

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781A] Throughout the whole course of this work, we have especially sought to commend the grace of God, [Col. 0781B] a matter which we have treated from the beginning both with arguments and with examples, but most clearly in the preceding section, where, arriving in the order of our narrative at the most holy mysteries, we discussed the unity of Christ and the Church, head and members, under the example of grains and berries.

For we said that, just as many grains compacted into one make one loaf, and many berries flow together into one liquid, so many members, joined to their head by an indissoluble bond, make one body. Christ is the head of this body, and his Church is its members. This saving exchange of the two natures, namely divine and human, was begun in the most sacred womb of the glorious Virgin, but was confirmed in the tribunal of the cross, by the intervening death of Christ’s blood, in the New Testament. [Col. 0781C] A blessed exchange, in which we exchanged weakness for power, misery for blessedness, mortality for immortality, humanity for God.

Among all who exchange, he is the most generous: he received what was worthless and returned what was precious; he assumed what was human and bestowed what was divine; he clothed himself in man and clothed man with God; he who was without sin underwent the penalty of sin and freed us at once from sin and from sin’s penalty. Therefore the exchange which the Son of God entered into with us he confirmed by the covenant of his blood.

For humanity could not have been joined to God unless the wall which stood between God and humanity, dividing them, had been removed from the midst. Nor could the hard, long-standing wall of sin be demolished by human hand or skill, because all human offspring, by natural descent, were liable to sin; and among human beings no one could be found who might make satisfaction for human sin. Therefore a man was necessary who was immune from sin, who, while innocently paying sin’s penalty, might take upon himself the cause of all sinners, and, sin being destroyed by a punishment not owed, might join creature to Creator, humanity to God, in himself—the mediator of God and human beings.

[Col. 0781D] Therefore, sin of the whole world having been appraised, and the foundation of transgression undermined by the price of Christ’s blood, the wall of enmity fell; and humanity, freed from sin, became one with God through intervening grace. For the perseverance of this holy union, the head prays to the Father for the members, Christ for the apostles, saying: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be [Col. 0782A] one as we also are.” And a little later: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through [Col. 0782B] their word: that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you; so may they also be one in us, that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.”

Listen, human being; listen to the voice of your God. Listen, member; listen and recognize the affection of your head. As man he asks for humanity, but as God he grants what he asks. “That they may be one,” he says, “as we are one. I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one.” The Only-Begotten is in the adopted son; the Father is in the Only-Begotten; and thus, through the Only-Begotten, the Father is in the adopted son. This is the fruit of the Only-Begotten’s prayer: the perfection of the adopted one.

There is no other form of perfection than the restoration of the whole universe into unity, when all things gather themselves into him from whom they subsist as created things. Thus, though the operation of individual members is diverse, the unity of the body remains whole in the bond of love. This unity truly embraces all things by the power of the Creator; it enters each thing in a different manner, yet, while filling all things, it does not divide itself, and while distributing itself to individuals, it does not diminish its own fullness.

[Col. 0782C] So too from this unity all things spread forth like members from a head; and each performs its own function in such a way that, even amid the diversity of its administration, it never springs away from the unity of the head. Rather, member clings to member, and all things become so completely one that all suffer in one, and all are glorified in the glory of one.

In this supreme unity, creator and giver of life to all, which contains all things and fills all things, the Holy Trinity subsists; in this unity the Son of God united himself to the son of man in the same person. The supremely good one preferred this good of unity not only to all earthly things but even to the duty of piety itself—not merely when performed for any saint, but even when performed for the Holy of Holies—when he said: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her.”

For Martha had received the Lord as a religious woman, a devoted disciple, and a kind hostess; therefore she was occupied with the matters of religion, devotion, and hospitality. Mistress and servant alike, she ordered, hurried, prepared, and served. But because there were many things which the hospitality due to so gracious a lord and so beloved a teacher [Col. 0783A] required, she burned with activity, ran about, and labored for breath; and because she could not attend to every individual thing, weighed down by anxiety, she was troubled and disturbed.

Thus the servant interrupts her lord, the disciple her teacher, and asks him whom she had received as a guest to judge against her sister. “Lord,” she says, “do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her, then, to help me.” But Mary sat at the Lord’s feet, devoutly hungry for the nourishment of the Word, driving away all transient and superfluous cares, like troublesome flies before her eyes, with the hand of discernment; from the very fountain of unity she drew that one thing which was necessary.

The prudent little bee hovered about Christ’s mouth and sucked the dripping honeycomb from his lips—whose breath was sweeter than honey; and whatever she could seize by the diligent service of listening, [Col. 0783B] she carried into the hive of her heart. Therefore, exceedingly delighted by the sweetness of the Word and fattened by the richness of true grain, she either did not hear or ignored her murmuring sister, deeming it no small loss of inward sweetness to lend even a moment’s ear to her complaining sister.

Thus, disregarding the complaint of her sister, who was appealing the Lord against her, because with blessed Job she had chosen hanging upon the mouth of Christ, she was flooded with the delights of the mind flowing from his lips, despising the murmuring of the belly. But the Lord, whom one sister had invoked as judge against the other, tempered his judgment toward both parties: he preferred the desire of one without condemning the labor of the other.

For the Lord knows that although the fruit is sweeter than the root, the fruit draws its sweetness from the root. Thus, although contemplation surpasses action, devout action greatly assists contemplation. For anyone who desires to ascend to the summit of contemplation must first exercise himself in the pursuit of holy action.

“Martha, Martha,” he says, “you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary.” You are anxious, troubled, stretched out in many directions; the things you strive to grasp are fleeting. You pour yourself out through the cracks of cares, and complain that you are exhausted. Like a torrent watering fields, do you draw up mud and grieve because you are troubled? You water the field of your heart by works of piety; in watering it you make it fruitful, but you cloud your eye with the dust of anxiety.

[Col. 0783C] Yet one thing is necessary. The one is not divided, not disturbed, not drawn off in different directions; it remains always the same and is never stained by another’s dust. While humanity stood with unmoving foot in this one, it neither suffered the injury of circumcision nor required the grace of baptism. But when those most evil shoots sprang up from the poison of sin, Peter’s knife was applied to cut away what was harmful; and after dust stirred up by the devil’s whirlwind from worldly cares had defiled our faces, bright with the image of God, the saving water flowed from Christ’s side to wash us.

Therefore one thing is necessary. This is the better part; Mary chose it, and it shall not be taken from her. Upon the stable and immovable firmness of this unity rest the foundations of Christian profession: faith, namely, and baptism, and the Church itself, the spiritual mother of spiritual children.

[Col. 0784A] For because God is one and the Lord is one, the confession of the true faith must likewise be one in every people and nation. And because the adoption of God’s children in Christ through the Holy Spirit is one, the regeneration of all into that same adoption must likewise be uniform. The same Spirit brings about this unity among diverse peoples, diverse ages, and also diverse professions of Christian religion, so that, just as many members different in form and function make one body through the same Spirit, so diverse peoples, ages, and professions may come together through the same Spirit of adoption into the unity of Christ’s body.

Therefore water is mixed with wine in the sacrament of Christ’s blood, because in the sacrament we are joined to Christ, so that [Col. 0784B] the one who receives faithfully also becomes one with him. He himself testifies to this when he declares concerning his flesh: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Thus we suffer with the sufferer, die with the one who dies, rise with the one who rises, and are glorified together with the glorified one.

Therefore, let dust, taken up by divine mercy into this participation in glory, recognize from the very glory of its assumption how great is the grace of the one who assumed it. For from no other consideration, I think, does the splendor and greatness of grace shine forth so clearly as from the comparison of human merit and divine benefit.

When, therefore, we celebrate the mysteries of Christ’s passion and our redemption, let us not only recall devoutly the sequence of events, but also crucify ourselves with our vices [Col. 0784C] and desires, so that, when the old person has been buried, we may rise with Christ into the new person. For “Christ, rising from the dead,” says the Apostle, “dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.”

And as though people were asking why he had said this, he continues: “So you also, reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but living to God in Christ Jesus.” Reckon yourselves dead to sin, for Christ died to sin once—that is, for the destruction of sin, not his own, which he did not have, but that of the whole world, which he took away by dying. For death is the punishment owed to sin. Therefore, when the innocent one paid the debt of sin’s penalty—he who owed nothing to sin—he delivered those who were liable both to sin and to sin’s punishment.

[Col. 0784D] So great was the price of the one death of Christ that it equaled—indeed outweighed—the debt of the whole world. Therefore it is no longer necessary for him to die a second time: by dying once, he erased, through the bond written in his blood, the record not only of preceding sins but also of future ones. He says, then: “So you also, reckon yourselves dead indeed to sin but living to God in Christ Jesus.” Just as Christ died once for the destruction of sin, so you too die once to sin, so that it may no longer live in you or hold dominion over you as it has until now.

For sin does not live when it finds no consent in us, when we do not yield to its persuasion, when we freely resist it as it seeks to break in. [Col. 0785A] Therefore the lover of Christ, the imitator of Christ’s passion, ought to die once to sin and once to the world, so that, sin having died, the life of God—the eternal life—may succeed in us. This is to live to God: to live eternally, to devote oneself to virtues, not to look back, to stretch oneself toward the things ahead, and never to cease from the pursuit until, attaining one’s desire, one deserves to lay hold upon the beloved of one’s soul.

This, therefore, is to die with Christ: to die once to sin. And this is to rise with Christ: to live to God, as we have said. This glory of the first resurrection, and this blessed life still in a corruptible body, is a gift of grace and a foretaste of that eternal and unfading glory. For it is impossible for anyone to rise in the future body unto glory who has refused in the present life to awaken in soul from the sleep of sin to life.

But in every spiritual discipline beginnings are laborious and endings joyful, because “weeping will remain at evening, and joy in the morning.” At the evening, indeed, of our mortality, when we sow the seeds of good works, we weep over the misery of our exile and the lengthening shadows of ignorance. But when the morning of our hope dawns and the sun of righteousness shines, after we have reaped abundant fruits of grace from slight labor, we shall exult with inexpressible joy.

Therefore our Lord, who at the ninth hour, as the day declined toward evening, brought grief to the world by giving up his spirit, postponed the joy of his resurrection until morning, so that by the morning joy he might console—indeed abolish—the evening weeping. For this purpose he took our weeping upon himself on the evening of his passion, that on the morning of his resurrection, dispersing the cloud of our sorrow, he might pour upon us the joy of his glorification.

[Col. 0785C] For the kind teacher, seeing the minds of his disciples troubled by the bitterness of his passion and grieving over the removal from them of so loving an instructor, comforted them with the comparison of a woman in labor: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come. But when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish for joy that a human being has been born into the world.” And, explaining what is the sorrow of the pregnant woman and what the joy over the child born, he adds: “Therefore you too now indeed shall have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

When the Lord was delivered to death and drank the cup of our bitter transgression, this holy woman—the holy Church, bound to her bridegroom by the inseparable love of the same Spirit—drew into herself through the mouth of her beloved the taste of bitterness. Suffering with the sufferer and dying with the one who dies, she is pierced by the nails of sorrow and suffers in the bitterness of grief what he suffers in passion. For it cannot happen in any way that she should remain unaffected by the pain of him with whom she is one flesh and the same spirit: “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church,” says the Apostle; and, “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

[Col. 0786A] Therefore this holy woman, conceiving from the spirit of sorrow, has grief; and like a solitary turtledove, deprived of the comfort of her mate, she fills the inner chamber of her heart and the secret place of their common bridal chamber with lamentations. For bearing deep beneath her breast the wound of love, she feeds as one grieving upon tears and the bread of sorrow. She searches all things, looks about at everything; and as her soul melts with the fire of longing, she is meanwhile nourished by the very longing with which she is afflicted.

She tempers the heat of desire with tears; and because she sees the face of her beloved, for her sake, smeared with spittle, watering that face abundantly with tears, she now offers to her beloved a sacrifice of thanksgiving. But when the Lord rises and is glorified in the robe of immortality, she gives birth from the conception of sorrow to the spirit of exultation. She tears her sackcloth of mourning, clothes herself with the mantle of joy, and, because of the joy of glorification, no longer remembers the anguish of the passion.

She exults at the splendor of the risen one, [Col. 0786B] dances for joy at the glory of the triumphant one, and no longer grieves—indeed, rejoices—that she lost for a time him whom she deserved to receive back so glorious and adorned with so many spoils. She rejoices that the prince of death has been triumphed over in her flesh; she rejoices that in the Lord the first portion of her body ascends in triumphant procession to God the Father, confidently hoping with unshaken hope that she is to be raised up in all her members to that place where she rejoices that she has already been exalted in her head.

She rejoices that in the head has now been accomplished what she hopes will someday be accomplished in the members. “Death has been swallowed up in victory”; and, triumphing over the one who had conquered her, she repeats in exultation: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” Where now is that sting of sin by which you pricked and wounded [Col. 0786C] my children, bound under the yoke of your slavery because of the debt of the first transgression? Where now is that insolent boasting of yours? “I gathered the whole earth, and there was none to move a wing, or open its mouth, or chirp.”

Behold, that earth, watered by the blood of its Lord, now bears fruits of righteousness for its cultivator—the earth which, when you were its cultivator, bore thorns of idolatry. Look now whether you can find among human beings one who, from fear of you, dares move a wing. Look now—if indeed, overwhelmed by shame, you are able to raise your brazen face—who is this man who flies so freely from the lower regions and penetrates heaven with such power.

This is he who is free among the dead. Having broken your nets with the foot of innocence, he not only escaped free, but, while you look on and gnash your teeth, drew out his faithful ones, whom the snares of your malice had entangled, without your being able to resist. [Col. 0786D] Behold, he moves a wing; behold, he beats his wings; weighed down by no burden of corruption, with the free rowing of his wings he cuts through the air, and, to the astonishment of the heavenly powers themselves at the new and unheard-of miracle, the man joins himself to the right hand of God the Father.

Behold, he opens the mouths of infants and nursing children and perfects praise in their mouth; and from their mouths he does not so much chirp as prattle, declaring that your deceit has been mocked and your power crushed. Where, therefore, O hostile death, is your victory? Where is your boasting? It has been shut out, ground down, reduced to nothing.

Therefore the holy woman, a mother by grace, who gives birth in pain, gives birth to joy—not joy which gladdens for an hour and passes away, but joy which occupies every affection of the soul and remains forever.

It now pleases us to contemplate, and also to admire, the work of grace, and, at the final touch of the work, to proclaim the skill of its maker. For the final touch of a work shows how great is the artist’s mastery. Look now, O children of grace, and turn your eyes to the Author of grace; recognize from what condition he assumed human nature, and to what height he advanced it. For this is that nature which was indeed well created by God the artificer, and, from the softness of clay, made firm unto eternity by the fire of divine inspiration. Had it not rested the foot of pride upon what was forbidden by presumptuous daring, it would not have been shaken from the stability of its eternity by the hand of the sinner. But when it turned from the warmth of divine love to the cold and shadow of the serpent’s persuasion, deprived of divine fire, it was contracted by the frost of sin [Col. 0787B], and at last, by the decree of divine judgment, was dissolved into the lowliness of dust as death crushed it.

Thus wretched man, made unstable dust, began to be swept away by the whirlwind of the diabolic tempest, and violently driven and dashed upon the precipices of vices and errors, so that of that earthen vessel and jar of the heavenly potter not even a potsherd remained fit, according to the prophetic utterance, for carrying a coal from the fire or drawing water from a pit. Is this, wretched and pitiable man, that blessedness promised to you by the deceiver? Is this that glory of your divinity? Vain was the serpent’s hiss to which you foolishly lent your ear; and therefore, miserably deceived in grasping at vanities, you neither obtained what you hoped for nor were able to retain what you possessed [Col. 0787C]. For you did not deserve to be God, which you sought by robbery; nor were you able to remain what you were—namely, immortal.

I do not say this in order that I, myself wretched, may insult our misery, but that I may indicate the greatness of our misery: so that, having more carefully inspected the deformity of the material, we may all the more admire the power of the grace that reforms us. It is no great skill to hammer a precious vessel out of selected gold metal; but to fashion a beautiful vessel out of any base and contemptible material—this is the mark of outstanding art, this of exceptional praise.

Therefore the kindly potter was pleased to moisten once more, with the rain of heavenly grace, his vessel shattered by a mighty breaking and dissolved into ashes; to compact it into a mass; and from the fragments of the old vessel to restore a new vessel [Col. 0787D], more precious than the former. But lest it should again be dissolved by the flood of a turbid torrent and the inundation of sin, he applied the furnace of the cross; and, with the exceedingly powerful fire of suffering kindled, he placed within it the unfired vessel. Since it had been compacted and formed by the work of the Holy Spirit, it did not crack in the fire.

But why do I say that it did not crack? For it not only preserved in the fire the strength divinely bestowed upon it, but also emerged from the fire purer; because he who, at the Father’s command, endured the reproach of the cross, received by the Father’s gift authority over heaven and earth. For, glorified by the glory of the Resurrection, and indicating to his disciples, who were to be witnesses, the manner of that same glorification, he said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” “Has been given to me,” he says; and see how he ascribes to grace the authority [Col. 0788A] which he declares was given to him. Although he possesses all things in the Father and bestows all things with the Father, he mentions nothing of the power of his divinity, but refers the grace of received authority to the glory of the Giver.

Therefore, O lover and seeker of grace, stretch out now the bosom of your narrow heart—stretch it out more widely—and gather from this immense expanse whatever you can; for no bosom of human narrowness can wholly contain so vast a gift of grace. “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” he says. Who would ever have believed that this could come from dust? For human nature, which by the force of divine judgment is dissolved by death into dust, is rightly called dust even before it comes to be what it will be. Who then would ever have believed of dust that it would receive authority over heaven and earth?

How great, do you suppose, is this artificer—how great—who so compacts, so strengthens, so exalts dry and unstable dust, that he sets it over not only earthly things but heavenly things as well? What do you suppose this artificer would make from choice material, who makes things so great and such things from what is base and almost nothing? Yet our artificer needs neither base nor precious material: his own merciful will is material sufficient for all things. How much, then, does man owe to God, by whose gift he presides in his Head even over heaven? This is the greatness of God’s grace, truly beyond estimation, truly incomprehensible, through which human nature has been exalted above every principality and power of angelic rank.

This miracle, unheard of on earth, was unfamiliar in heaven: that a human being should ascend powerfully to heavenly things, not in a fiery chariot nor with angelic assistance [Col. 0788C], but by his own power; and, while thrones and dominions stood amazed, should join himself to the right hand of God the Father, there to reign with equal right for ever. At this miracle, so great and so unfamiliar, angelic dignity was astonished. While some went before and cried aloud, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be raised up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter,” others asked: “Who is this King of glory? Who is he? Whence is he? We know God as the King of glory; this one whom we see is a man. Whence then is this novelty? Whence comes equality of kingdom and glory to man with God? Is this perhaps also a work of omnipotent grace? Has grace itself, which created us for this glory, also glorified man into God?”

This is that grace—this, indeed, is that grace—which was hidden from the ages in the secret counsel of the wisdom of our God [Col. 0788D]. This is what lay hidden from eternity and appeared at the fitting time; it shows how great its mercy and how great its power are, when it exalts man into God. This is truly “the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

O how mercifully changed, O how happily transformed, was that sorrowful sentence upon man: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go”—for he who was assumed into God passed over to God, and God and man sat down at the Father’s right hand. Although each nature remains unconfused in its own property, yet both natures remain undivided from one another in the same person. This, therefore, is the change of the right hand of the Most High.

Behold, the man for whom his own earth, by the sentence of righteousness, produced thorns and thistles, is now worshipped in supplication by heaven [Col. 0789A] and earth. Behold, that nature, once dark and contemptible because sinful, now shines above all things and is venerable to all because it justifies all. Therefore we too rightly honour it, rightly worship it, because to it, thus assumed and thus glorified, we ourselves owe whatever we are.

We must therefore rejoice with it as servants, as neighbours, as friends: servants by condition, neighbours by contemplation, friends by devotion. We must rejoice with it and congratulate the merciful shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep; who drew the hundredth sheep, half alive, from the lion’s mouth in order to restore the sum of our wholeness; who in one work supplied us with cause for a threefold joy. For the first and chief joy arising for us is over the victory of our King; the second, over the redemption of our companion; the third, over the restoration of our wholeness [Col. 0789B].

This triumph of our King is the more glorious because it is the more unusual. For though in battle strength is always contested on both sides, in the opposite manner our King’s victory is achieved through weakness. He did not deem it worthy to contend against a feeble enemy by the strength of his majesty; rather, he set before the cruel tyrant a human being who had once been his captive, and through the captive overcame the captor. Thus, in the glorification of our Redeemer and of ourselves in him, the excellence of divine grace stands pre-eminent—grace which could in no way be greater, unless perhaps, far be it, something greater than God could be found.

Let us therefore admire in the one and same Lord Jesus Christ both the glory of what was assumed [Col. 0789C] and the grace of him who assumed it; and let us know that through grace offered to us we must attain the glory promised to us. A reward is set before labour: immeasurable for what is slight, eternal for what is momentary; adoption together with the Only-Begotten; everlasting possession of the kingdom together with the Father. Only let us heed the Apostle exhorting us, and by no means receive the grace of God in vain.

For we receive the grace of God in vain when, not cooperating with God’s grace, we do not render thanks worthy of God. We receive the grace of God in vain when we pass through the acceptable time and the day of salvation without any benefit to our salvation. But woe to the person who receives God’s grace in vain; who reduces to nothing in himself the work of God’s mercy; who dissipates the counsel of his salvation; who, by living ruinously, nullifies the bond-document of human redemption. For to the children of perdition the work of redemption shall be as though it had not been; indeed—and this is graver still—the fire of Gehenna and damnation shall be an added burden to them [Col. 0790A]. For it would have been better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

But the feet of the saints, Ezekiel testifies, are straight feet, firm steps; and, brought out by angelic visitation from doomed Sodom and instructed by the example of Lot’s wife, they neither turn the mind back toward burning Sodom nor turn back the step of good work toward the slippery pleasures of the flesh. For she, because she looked back with feminine curiosity, hardened into a pillar of salt. Although through the penalty of transgression she acquired for herself the hardness of stone, she nevertheless imparts to those who taste it the seasoning of the wisdom of salt [Col. 0790B]. “When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser.” This too is a gift of grace: that the fool may serve the wise, and the punishment of the reprobate may instruct the elect unto life.

Therefore the saints, weary of the habitation of Sodom and its sulphurous stench, hasten toward the mountains and stretch themselves daily forward in progress, until by breathless running they occupy the very summit of the mountains and have as their rewarder the one whom they had as helper in their course.

But since the grace of which we speak is a special gift of the Holy Spirit, and since from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation we have arrived, by the footsteps of this grace itself, at the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension, it remains that we should also speak of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit himself, insofar as he shall deign to inspire us [Col. 0790C]. But the discourse must now be closed; nor should the fullness of that grace be poured into a vessel already full. Reserved for its own beginning, it must be set down in the seventh volume.

The number is also especially fitting to the mystery: because the Spirit is sevenfold in his gifts, let a sacred number sing his praises. For although the following volume is the twelfth in the total number of the whole work, yet, in the division by which we assigned five volumes to the sacrament of the Old Testament and seven to the New Testament, it is found to be the seventh, in honour of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, to whom, with God the Father and his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, be honour and glory through the infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## PREFACE TO THE TWELFTH BOOK

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789D] With the yearly expectation of the coming of the Holy Spirit now approaching, and being about to set the final hand to the present little work, I implore in most humble prayers the grace of that supreme artificer and teacher of angels and human beings: that he may direct my trembling hand according to the rule of his wisdom, and may worthily complete, by himself, the work devoted to his name.

For he pours upon Aaron’s beard the ointment which descends from the head, and does not leave even the hem of his garment exempt from the abundance of his outpouring. Therefore, since we see the beard of our Aaron dripping with the dew of ointment, we, the slender fringes of his garment, await a drop of the poured-out liquid. Now, as a man’s beard is an indication of manly strength, so the fringes hanging from the garment are an ornament and beauty to the fullness of the entire garment [Col. 0790D].

The breadth of this mystery ought neither to be enclosed within the narrowness of a little preface, nor should the brevity of a little preface be extended to the breadth of allegory. Let us therefore reserve the breadth of the mystery for its own field; and, our weary limbs having been anointed with an infusion of healing oil, our sinews and bones restored by divine anointing to their former strength, let us traverse the little that remains of our journey begun, with the grace we proclaim itself as our guide.

## TWELFTH BOOK

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791A] As I enter upon the final part of this work, that prophetic testimony concerning Aaron’s beard immediately presented itself at the very threshold of the little preface; I postponed its fuller exposition for the breadth of the present volume.

That Aaron, then, the first priest under the Law, serving by legal ceremonies as a type of what was to come, bears the type of our Redeemer, to whom God the Father swore—and does not repent of his oath—“You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.” For he has no need daily to enter, in another’s blood, into the copies of the true Holy of Holies: having obtained eternal redemption, he entered once for all into the holy places, made both priest and victim; he alone, found innocent among humankind, became in his own person a victim fit and sufficient to exhaust the sins of others [Col. 0791B].

Nor does our high priest need to shed another’s blood for the ignorance of his people, since he values the sins of the whole world at the price of his own blood, a price that far surpasses and outweighs them. Therefore, once the victim of redemption had been consummated upon the altar of the cross, he entered the very Holy of Holies and stood before the face of God the Father as propitiator for us, expiating the ancient contumacy of the servant by the voluntary obedience of the Son.

For what was there that the most merciful Father would not forgive, when he saw his only-begotten Son, after the offering of his suffering had gone before, pleading for the guilty? For what sin would he not grant pardon to the Son who pleaded, since he possesses with him from eternity the same will and the same substance? How could he fail freely to restore to his Only-Begotten his inheritance, unjustly seized but justly redeemed [Col. 0791C], when he granted him also a seat at his right hand?

Therefore, when our Head had been glorified and anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, the beard of our Aaron, which had long since flowered when watered with the dew of the Word, was to be soaked with drops of healing oil. Thus the beard, surrounding the mouth like the household of the descending Word, might first receive the grace of the flowing oil; and then at last that healing liquid might diffuse itself over the garment beneath. Nor could the sacred hem of the garment remain exempt from this flood of oil, although it was the extremity and support of the fullness of the whole garment.

By the beard of our high priest we understand the apostles; by the garment, the remaining believers; by the outermost hem of the garment, would that we might truly understand our own humility [Col. 0791D]. By the softness and richness of the oil we understand the grace of the Holy Spirit, which flowed down from the Head upon the beard when our Lord Jesus Christ sent him from the Father to the disciples, as he had promised.

Thus St Luke, the writer of the Acts of the Apostles, records concerning him:

> “When the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them [Col. 0792A], and the Holy Spirit sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

“Suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” because the Holy Spirit, when he comes, teaches heavenly things. This is that mighty spirit in which the Lord shatters the ships of Tarshish; no force resists his omnipotence. When he shakes the hearts of the fleshly-minded, he overthrows from its foundation the tower of pride and every structure of sin.

The fire of divine inspiration was necessary to melt the coldness of human unbelief, so that apostolic hearts, numb with the frost of human fear, might receive the flame of divine love, and thus at last burn up with fiery tongues the straw of another’s error. Therefore, since these things were to be accomplished by the coming and grace of the Holy Spirit, the Invisible One appeared in fiery tongues, so that by visible things it might be shown what the invisible Spirit, who had come, was doing within.

The nature of fire burns, kindles, and illumines. But the love of God, who is a consuming fire, burns away harmful things, kindles cold things, and illumines dark things [Col. 0792B]. It burns away the old man with his defilements; it kindles the numbness of human weakness; it illumines the blind and leads the erring back onto the way of truth.

Therefore, when this saving fire entered the hearts of the disciples, it kindled them with the torches of love to bear witness to Christ; and lest the barbarian world of the nations should remain deprived of the proclamation of Christ, the heralds of faith, having received the Spirit, spoke in the tongues of all peoples. O wondrous power of the Holy Spirit in teaching! Within scarcely the space of one complete hour [Col. 0792C], he both teaches the disciples all truth and grants them strength of faith and steadfastness of spirit for testimony. O gift beyond estimation, O incomparable grace!

The apostolic band, which had fled from before the face of the raging people, terrified by the Lord’s Passion, and had hidden in an upper room for fear of the Jews, suddenly shines forth, clothed with power from on high; and, taking up the prophetic wedge in testimony, it proclaims in free confession that he who had died is the Author of life.

See, to add also Solomon’s saying: the little hare, a weak people, which before had trembled fearfully at the sound of those entering, once it placed its lair in the strength of the rock, rises like a lion from its lair to the prey in the onset of the Spirit, driven by the hunger of holy desire [Col. 0792D]. It now fears no encounter; indeed, it boldly rushes to meet Christ’s enemies, crying and roaring, trampling down and crushing, and felling so many thousands of the beasts of the forest by the terror of its roar alone.

How great, do you suppose, was the roar of Peter, prince of the apostles—how great, how terrible—when, after delivering a discourse on the outpouring of the Holy Spirit to the gathered and astonished crowds, he struck down three thousand unbelievers by his word and united them to the number of the faithful by their confession of Christ’s name? And how great was that roar when, after the soles and ankles of one lame man were made firm at the invocation of Christ’s name, the foundations and feet of five thousand were made firm and planted in the faith of Christ [Col. 0793A]?

By whose gift? By whose aid? By what power or wisdom, finally, were all these things accomplished? Was it human power? No: they were accomplished by the power of the grace of the preacher himself, of the Judge presiding within, and of him who brandishes from the apostolic mouth a two-edged sword. For the Lord says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father.”

Yet who would have believed this of Peter: that he whom a lowly servant-girl had struck down with the dart of her tongue would, by his word, lay so many thousands low before Christ? Who would have believed that the pillar, knocked by the battering ram of fear into the pit of denial, would be restored to its former state of strength? But, raised by a threefold confession after it had been cast down by a threefold denial, it stood more firmly; and in its own fall it learned how to help those who fall [Col. 0793B]. In this, so to speak, momentary fall of his, the merciful shepherd mercifully provides for his flock: that human presumption may tremble in the falling of Peter, and fallen weakness may not despair in Peter’s rising.

But, to return to my beginning and look again to the grace of which we speak: from that time the horn of saving oil flowed more abundantly into all the members of Christ’s body, and the grace of the Holy Spirit was spread more widely through the whole breadth of the world. For, when the children of the kingdom had degenerated and been cast into outer darkness, the poor and weak were to be gathered from the four quarters of heaven to the wedding feast of the heavenly King, to fill the place of Jewish unbelief and receive among the twelve tribes the inheritance of the blessing once promised [Col. 0793C].

“In your seed,” God says to Abraham, “all nations shall be blessed.” Therefore, when this blessing was poured out by God the Father in Christ Jesus through the Holy Spirit upon all nations, the Gentile world, hearing the voice of the Lord who called it, began to give thanks for its invitation; to wash away the filth of idolatry in the font of baptism; and to cover the shame of its ancient nakedness with the new robe of innocence and the wedding garment of love.

And when the trumpet of the Gospel sounded, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” and that of the Apostle, “The form of this world is passing away,” it began to despise what was passing as though already past, and to love what was flourishing no more than what was dry. For, with the foot of faith planted upon the stability of the unshaken Rock, and with the eye of the heart fixed in an unblinking gaze upon the eyes of its Beloved [Col. 0793D], it could no longer know what was passing away or love what was failing.

For how could it perceive the torrent of the passing age when it was fixed upon eternity? How could it love anything foul when it was betrothed to the heavenly King, whose beauty of countenance eclipses the brightness of the sun? How could it even bring its lips, sanctified by the kiss of the heavenly Bridegroom, toward the taste of the love of this world, more bitter than gall, when at the table of the heart it ate divine honey presented by its Beloved?

Thus it began, desiring eternal things, to despise temporal things; and, from this stormy tempest, daily to sigh anxiously toward the harbour of eternal rest. Wearied by its pilgrimage, it began to utter with lamenting groan that apostolic cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall free me [Col. 0794A] from this body of death?” And, languidly reclining its head upon its Beloved’s breast and cooling the heat of its desire in the shadow of future consolation: “The grace of God,” it says, “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Not merit, not works of the Law, but grace alone. Through whom? Not through a human being, not through a lawgiver, nor finally through the Law itself, but through Jesus Christ, who made both the Law and man.

From this it comes that the steadfastness of the devout, kindled by the desire for eternal things, laughs at tyrants’ threats, rejects promised riches and dignities, gladly endures the tortures of executioners that open to it an entrance into the kingdom, and voluntarily mounts the gleaming instruments of iron, seeking for itself eternal refreshment.

Whence comes this human strength? Whence this steadfastness of spirit? Whence this human constancy, that one who lately feared the leaves of words stirred by tyrannical fury now does not dread chains and beatings, prisons and crosses, frying-pans and burning plates, while the flame of the Holy Spirit burns within [Col. 0794B]? Your grace, O Christ—your grace, I say—works all these things. It is given freely to all in such a way that it is never preceded by anyone’s merit or desire; rather, it itself precedes all, helps all, and grants to all that they may arrive.

The words of the Lord himself bear witness to this, when, rewarding faithful servants with a worthy recompense, he honours them with the grace and title of friends: “I shall no longer call you servants,” he says, “because the servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father.”

It belongs to a friend diligently to observe the mind of his friend. Hence “friend” (*amicus*) is said, as it were, to be the guardian of the mind (*animi custos*). Rightly, therefore, he honours his faithful ministers with the proclamation of his friendship, since he had entrusted to them the secrets he had heard from the Father. But lest a weak mind should ascribe to itself what belonged to God, and believe that it had attained this glory of God’s friendship by its own merit, he warns them to turn back the eyes of their minds to the beginning of the way and consider carefully through whose showing they found the way, and under whose leadership they arrived so far [Col. 0794C].

“It was not you,” he says, “who chose me; but I chose you and appointed you, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain.” Therefore the privilege of friendship is the gift of the one who chooses, not the merit of the chosen. The fruit of the grafted twig is likewise the gift of the husbandman who grafted it. It is grace that chose; grace that appointed; grace that bestowed fruit; grace that brought it through to maturity. Whatever excellence or spiritual zeal shines forth in a human being flows from this fountain of mercy.

Although there are almost as many witnesses to this fact as there are professors of the faith, it is nevertheless pleasing to bring forward two from among many, in whom subsequent grace shines more clearly because no merits of theirs preceded it [Col. 0794D].

Let the apostle Paul enter first: once an assailant of the Christian faith, now its most valiant defender and the most faithful champion of God’s grace. If you examine his works, you find that he deserved wrath rather than grace. Led by the thread of the killing letter, he attempted to extinguish the life-giving Spirit. He knew that the Law had been given by God through Moses, but did not yet rightly understand that it was veiled in figures and ceremonies. Nor did he perceive how absurd it was to believe that the sins of the people were cleansed by the blood of an animal, unless the price of that blood came to their aid which believing peoples daily drink in faith.

Thus darkened by the shadow of the Law, he began to persecute the children of light and declared the witnesses of truth to be defenders of falsehood, and therefore rightly to be slain as enemies of the Law and truth. He began, therefore, to rage like a ravening wolf among Christ’s sheep: to strangle those present, rage against those absent, and seek letters from the chief priests for Damascus [Col. 0795A]. Nor could the insatiable beast satisfy the frenzy of its madness by those it had devoured, so long as it knew even one remained whom it could strangle.

But after, in its swollen spirit breathing threats and slaughter, the madness of the rulers had breathed upon it through the letters entrusted to it, it exults, hurries, and, taking companions of the same zeal, hastens the journey, lest it suffer any loss to its fury by going too slowly. But where are you rushing, savage beast? Against whom are you raging, bloody animal? Do you not know that the faster you run, the sooner you fall into the snare? Or are you unaware—to address you meanwhile in your own words—that God’s patience leads you to repentance? He thunders from heaven, while you wage war from earth against him. You abuse the patience of mercy; it is necessary that you experience the severity of justice. That Nazarene, that crucified one, whom you insult as though dead, will pierce your neck, raised against him, with the dart of light.

It happened, then, that as he approached Damascus [Col. 0795C], while Christ’s little flock called for help from heaven, heavenly light surrounded the adversary of light. It first exacted from the persecutor the penalty of blindness and afterward, when the darkness of his former ignorance had been driven away, restored the wanderer to the way. Nor did he deserve to hear the voice of divine correction until the foot of pride had been tripped and he fell face downward to the earth.

For he heard a voice terribly rebuking him from above, asking why he so cruelly persecuted below the innocent and the suppliant: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? What have I done? What have I deserved? When did I harm you? When did I grieve you? Was it for this that I suffered for you, that I should endure these things from you? Was it for this that I gave my hands to be pierced with nails for you, that you should pierce my inward parts with the sword? Why do you persecute me? Long ago my indignation would have boiled up against you, had not great mercy preserved you until now.”

Wholesomely admonished and restored to himself by this voice crying from heaven, he began, stunned, to wonder within himself what the voice he had heard might be, whose it was, and whence it came; as though saying: “What miracle is this? What do I hear? A voice which sounded from heaven accuses me of persecution. Who is it that accuses me? I persecute the disciples of that Nazarene, and this with zeal for God’s Law—and am rebuked from heaven? What has the Crucified to do with heaven? What has a transgressor of God’s Law to do with God? Yet I will ask who it is that rebukes me, because the terror of the voice I heard and the punishment of blindness inflicted show that he who speaks is terrible.”

“Who are you, Lord?” The brilliance of the emitted light shows that you are Lord [Col. 0796A], and the punishment of my correction, so sudden, proclaims your power. “Who are you, Lord? I know no Lord in heaven save one; and to him I supposed that I was rendering service by this zeal and effort of mine. Who are you, Lord? Deign to reveal yourself—who you are—so that I too may know the manner of my service.”

“I am Jesus the Nazarene,” he says, “whom you persecute. I am that Jesus, that Nazarene, despised by you, mocked by you, crucified by your forefathers. But it is hard for you to kick against the goad; for the more you kick against the goad, the more you wound your heel upon it. Therefore cease—at last, cease—and set a limit to your fury, lest, if you pass beyond the boundary of my patience, you deserve no longer correction but destruction [Col. 0796B].

“For the blindness which has been cast upon your eyes from the cloud of your unbelieving heart is the penalty and punishment of your former ignorance: so that you, who in the faith of the whole Trinity were darkened, having impiously cut me off from unity with the Father by the sword of your unbelief, may pay for the darkness of your impious heart by three days’ blindness of the eyes. But I grant pardon to your ignorance, and illumine the darkness of your unbelief with rays of truth, so that, the veil removed and your face unveiled, you may see and recognize him whom you formerly read in the Law and did not know.”

But Saul, trembling and astonished—astonished, indeed, at the profound blindness of his ignorance, and trembling at the dreadful majesty of the one speaking—both renders reverence to God and promises obedience to the Lord. As a suppliant servant, he asks what the kindly Lord wishes and commands: “Lord, what do you wish me to do [Col. 0796C]? What do you wish, Lord, that I should do, so that I, who incurred wrath by persecution, may find grace by obedience? Do not look to my merits, which are liable to condemnation, but to the remedies of your mercy, which are always near to salvation. Foolishly deceived, because I had been instructed carnally in the Law, I had placed the sum of salvation in the justifications of the Law; and therefore I had laid hands upon you yourself, the Lawgiver and, as I now truly understand, the Author of grace. I now understand, though late, that the discipline of the Law was the pedagogue of Christian freedom, and that once human infancy had advanced to perfection under you as teacher, the instruction of the Law was no longer necessary. What then do you wish, Lord, that I should do? I am ready myself to suffer what I inflicted on your servants; I am ready to die for you, whom I mocked as dead.”

“Rise,” says the Lord, “rise and enter the city. There you will find a sheep; hear her as your teacher.” The wolf is sent to the sheep, that he may learn gentleness; that together they may approach the fountain flowing from the right side, and, when the wolf has been submerged, the sheep may emerge [Col. 0796D]. Behold the delightful spectacle of our grace: a sheep leads the wolf captive. She licks the shaggy creature, arranges the bristling one, gives milk to him who previously drank the blood of the devout. The sheep delights in his touch; the wolf, forgetting his ferocity,

> Casting off his savage countenance, he grows gentle into a lamb.  
> Nor does she grieve that her charge yields to sickness;  
> she removes the scales from his eyes and restores his sight.  
> Then she applies the washing made sacred by the name of baptism.

Where Saul perishes, Paul comes forth from the deep. [Col. 0797A] Thus Grace, his mother, raises her neophyte to be an Apostle, and from the furnace of testing brings forth the most pure vessel of election, so that he may offer the drink of faith to Jews and Gentiles—a faith which he had formerly persecuted in believers. But the cup of the word which he had received he first offers to his unbelieving mother; yet she, drunk upon the cup of gall which she had also offered to her Lord upon the cross, rejects the saving draught, ungrateful alike to him who sends and to him who offers it.

Therefore he turns to the widely scattered Gentiles and begins to gather from among them the wandering sheep, so that, when sheep from both folds had been collected into one, there might be one fold and one shepherd, and he who had redeemed them might himself feed them. But, lest his service prove unequal to the affront, he runs forth from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, spreading the name of Christ through villages, castles, towns, and provinces [Col. 0797B], and maintaining by arguments from the Law and the Gospel that the sum of human salvation consists in the worship of the Christian religion. By word he teaches; by example he persuades; and with a wondrous and unheard-of affection of charity he wishes himself accursed for his brothers, desiring that all men should be as he himself is. Some he begets for Christ; others, miscarried from the faith, he bears again in travail; and, lest anything of their fatherly nobility degenerate in his children, he labours with a mother’s solicitude. He gives milk to little ones in Christ; he strengthens adults in faith with solid food. Among the former he judges himself to know nothing except Christ, and him crucified; among the latter he disputes concerning heavenly secrets and mysteries hidden from the ages.

Meanwhile—or rather, because of—these pursuits of piety, he is bound in chains, beaten with rods, overwhelmed with stones, and shut in prison. [Col. 0797C] Yet because the word of God can neither be bound nor shut up, he flies everywhere in letters, forms the conduct of life, supports the weary with the outstretched hand of consolation, and promises eternal rewards in exchange for momentary tribulation and happy perseverance. With the weak he is weak; for those who are scandalized he burns; and, to sum up all briefly, that he may gain all, he becomes all things to all.

But we have by no means placed the vessel of God’s grace upon the table of our little work in order to recount anew the whole course of his apostolic calling, labour, and suffering; rather, in his election and the summit of apostolic dignity, we may behold the greatness of that grace of which we speak. He himself marvels at its greatness in himself, and with humble confession declares himself unworthy of the apostolic dignity. [Col. 0797D] For when he was speaking of the Lord’s resurrection and was adducing as witnesses of it those to whom the Lord appeared, he said: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” But lest he should seem ungrateful for God’s grace, he remembers the benefit bestowed upon him and attributes all that he is, not to his own merits or labours, but to the giver of every good: “By the grace of God,” he says, “I am what I am; and his grace in me was not empty.”

And if anyone wishes to run through the text of his Epistles, he will find that in almost every letter Paul is concerned to rebuke those who claim God’s grace for themselves from legal ceremonies or from their own works, and to subject them to God’s grace, to which all things are rightly subject. But since this discourse hastens to its end, and these Epistles are readily available to their readers, I refrain from inserting them here, sparing the reader’s weariness.

There are also very many—indeed innumerable—others in the catalogue of saints, in whom almost every trace of virtue had been effaced; yet, when grace reformed and restored them, they suddenly shone in Christ’s Church like bright lights. For nothing is impossible to omnipotent grace, which often recalls to life those who are despaired of precisely in order to grant hope of revival to others equally despaired of. I promised, however, to produce two witnesses—two from many thousands—in whom God’s grace shines more especially; and when I have presented one of them, let the other now present herself.

[Col. 0798B] Let that woman therefore come forward—once notorious in a celebrated city; notorious, I say, not for good repute but for infamy; the disgrace of honour, the shipwreck of modesty. Since it is established what she was before she washed, wiped, and anointed the Lord’s feet, let us see what she returned from the banquet of mercy to be. For, having heard that salvation reclined in the house of Simon the leper, and that the oil of grace had flowed even to cleanse lepers, she recoiled inwardly from the horror of her most foul leprosy; and, seeing herself the more clearly, she blushed the more deeply. Amid the diners she presented herself, guilty but devout; and, though her tongue was silent, her tears disclosed what she sought, what she asked, and what she needed.

For she knew to whom she had come, before whom she had fallen, whom she was imploring, and that [Col. 0798C] before God the sorrow of the heart accomplishes more than the cry of the voice, and that before so merciful a judge prayers of tears obtain more swiftly than those of the tongue. Therefore, by bathing the Lord’s feet with tears, she cleansed her conscience of its stains; and, by repeatedly pressing kisses upon them, she reconciled the ancient enmity through the service of diligent devotion. And because not even that which was insensible had remained untouched by the slavery of sin, she humbly offered that very thing also in satisfaction for sin: she wiped with her hair the feet which she bathed in tears—the hair with which she had formerly often drawn behind her, as with chains, captive bands of young men.

She also applies to the holy feet ointment of genuine nard, commending in the genuine nard the integrity of faith. Thus, thus the sinful woman clinging to the Lord’s feet—sinful, I say, but penitent; weeping and piercing herself through with the sword of grief—offered herself to God as a sacrificial victim for her sin. For she knew, on the prophet’s testimony, that God cannot despise the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart. [Col. 0798D] Thus she performs in herself the office of a priest; and, first shedding the blood of sin, from which the righteous man longs to be delivered, she cuts her own victim into pieces, while she examines her former life in the balance of her heart, dividing it, as it were, limb by limb according to its individual acts.

Carefully considering every act and finding nearly all of them unclean, she releases the entire fountain of compunction into tears, so that the torrent of tears may carry away everything filthy which, from her former way of life, had settled at the bottom of her conscience. Therefore she spares herself no sorrow and restrains no weeping, in order that the wave of tears, serving in place of baptism, may wash the defiled victim; and, having washed it with tears, she commends it with kisses so that it may become acceptable. She also applies, to banish the most foul stench, the sweetest fragrance of ointment: she who had spread a foul stench from the cavern of lust through the hearts of the devil’s attendants now spreads, through the mouths of Christ’s diners, the fragrance of sweetness from the alabaster of penitence.

It delights one to behold the sumptuous banquet of our King and to distinguish the various dishes set before him by their flavours. Simon, who had invited him, had presented his dishes to the Lord as to a righteous man, with doubtful faith. The Evangelist says nothing of their seasoning, because they were not seasoned with evangelical mustard. For Simon saw the mustard seed as tiny in the man, [Col. 0799A] [Col. 0799B] and therefore, blinded by Pharisaic self-conceit, did not understand the force of the mustard hidden in the divinity, which seasons souls with faith. Thus, by his prejudgment, he oppresses the wretched woman and judges mercy—judging who and what the woman was, while reproaching him as though he did not know who and what she was. “If this man,” he says, “were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner.”

But enough of Simon’s dishes: because they are unseasoned. Our hunger more eagerly seeks Maria’s seasoning. Maria, I suppose, as one nurtured in the Law, knew that Isaac gladly ate the kids cooked and seasoned by Rebecca’s art, and that the cooking of the kids signifies the conversion of sinners. Perhaps she had also heard the Lord, speaking in parables concerning the remedy of repentance, say that there is joy in heaven over the conversion of one penitent sinner rather than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no remedy of repentance. [Col. 0799C] Therefore, assuming the confidence of hope, she hastens to the remedies of divine mercy, seasoning the dead corpse of her soul with the mixture of compunction and repentance, lest unseasoned corruption produce decay and decay exhale a stench.

Crushing her whole self in the mortar of her heart with the pestle of humility, and reducing herself, like spices, as it were to the finest powder, she sets before the Lord’s feast the most pleasing banquet, adding to each dish the most delightful seasoning of true love. Thus, as Maria brought forward these sweet and pleasant dishes one after another, the Lord’s hunger was satisfied. He had indeed come invited to the Pharisee’s house and had reclined at table; but because he abhorred Jewish superstitions, he remained spiritually fasting even in the midst of the meal. [Col. 0799D] He rejoices, therefore, in the dishes for which he had come; he delights greatly in these exquisitely prepared dishes of repentance; and because the heat of love had blazed in Maria’s heart, our Joseph is intoxicated at noon with the wine of compunction and repentance.

A wondrous and unheard-of sight! While the miserable woman weeps, Mercy smiles; for unless the miserable woman were present, Mercy would, as it were, be idle. Pharisaic but false righteousness assails the guilty woman; but as she trembles, clemency interposes itself as her shield. Setting forth the parable of the two debtors, justice absolves the one who owed more, because she also loved more. “Do you see this woman?” he says. “Though you did not pour water upon my feet, she has watered them with tears. [Col. 0800A] Since she entered, she has not ceased to kiss my feet, whereas you did not even give a kiss to your guest, as is the custom of those who invite. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she has anointed my feet with ointment so precious and so abundantly that the whole house has been filled with its fragrance.”

These are signs of great devotion; these are unquestionable testimonies of true love. She loves greatly, she loves deeply, who serves piety with such diligent devotion. Because, therefore, she loved much, she merited much and obtained forgiveness for many offences. O loving-kindness, O mercy, O grace! Who has heard such things? Who has seen their like? A sinful woman entered, clothed in the rags of sins; she suddenly departs holy, in the shining robe of holiness. No long course of years or days intervenes; chaste fasts do not wear away the drunken excess of sensuality; deep sighs do not batter the breast, the fortress of sin. Rather, grace alone intervening, the captive of sin becomes free, and one so guilty is granted the prerogative of so great a gift.

[Col. 0800B] Let the world hear; let the people gather; let them behold, wonder, and inhale: the whole house has been filled with the fragrance of ointment. Let no sinner, by reason of the enormity of any sin, despair of pardon. Maria stands as witness to what kind of thing grace is, how merciful and how powerful—the grace that heals. Whatever the wound may be, however deep or putrid, it is not incurable for our physician, provided only that it receives the applied plaster of repentance. See how many wounds, how deep and how putrid, were suddenly healed in Maria by that grace of the Redeemer which we proclaim. See: she stands healed; see how, with great thanksgiving, she magnifies the greatness of the grace by which [Col. 0800C] she was healed. See: standing on the shore, she calls to the harbour of repentance those who have suffered shipwreck in sensuality and helps those who rise up by extending the hand of her merciful intercession. For this holy sinner became the most faithful reconciler of sinners and the most kindly comforter of the wretched, because, having experienced in herself the bitterness of sufferings, she knows best how much mercy those who suffer need.

But why do we linger longer over the benefits bestowed on Maria, when every day we marvel at the gifts of the same grace in those who are saved throughout the world? Did the fragrance breathed from Maria’s ointment vanish idly into the air? Whence does so great a multitude of penitents daily flow into the house of the Church, in which our Redeemer reclined in our humility, [Col. 0800D] unless the fragrance of the ointment draws them? Drawn by this fragrance, persons of every rank, age, and sex race eagerly to the house of salvation, seeking the touch of the Saviour because they are wounded by sin.

What force other than repentance, accompanied by its army of sins, assaults heaven? Desiring to invade a right not its own and to gain by force the inheritance of the saints, a share not due to it, it sends beforehand to the grace that bears the keys of heaven its household servants, who know its secrets best—tears and sighs—so that, after payment in the accepted coin of proved currency, namely pure confession and thereafter holy conduct, repentance itself may open the gate of the kingdom that guilt had closed against it. For to whom was the gate of the kingdom ever opened except by grace? Who among the heavenly tribes ever obtained the allotted cord of inheritance unless grace assigned the lot? [Col. 0801A] Who came to the throne of the eternal King to be crowned, whom grace did not bring? Who there merited a victor’s crown, unless grace placed it upon him? For she herself opens; she herself leads onward; she herself pleads the cause of suppliants; she herself gives each person rewards according to merits.

Therefore repentance, wishing by holy violence to batter the barriers of heaven, hires the army of grace at the wage I have mentioned, trusting that every way will be open if it deserves her aid. With grace thus aiding sinners, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. This is the grace which holds from eternity the primacy in creating, giving life, and sustaining life; she possesses in herself the power of protecting, advancing, and bringing persons to the measure of the full age of Christ.

[Col. 0801B] She is the one who in the mother’s womb compacts the clay of our formation; she distinguishes each limb in its proper place; she gives life by solidifying what was fluid; and she nourishes by breath and food, as she knows how, the little child enclosed in the prison of the womb, while the mother is inactive and not yet capable of providing this nourishment. Then she brings forth the little human being, still unaware that he is human, from the darkness of the womb into this visible light, so that, cast into this valley of tears, he may weep for the exile to which his condemnation has sentenced him, and may seek by weeping, groaning, and such supplication as he can meanwhile make another womb from which he may be reborn more blessedly.

But gracious Mother Grace, taking pity on her little child’s tearful groaning and on the original sin of innocent age, returns one unhappily born to the womb of Mother Church, that he may be born again more happily, by the wondrous and ineffable power of divine creation. [Col. 0801C] In one and the same act she puts the sinner to death and gives life to the human being, so that one born for death may be reborn for life; one born for exile, for a homeland; one born for the world, more happily for God. Thus she receives him, born and brought forth far more blessedly than at his first birth, rejoicingly in her lap; she gives milk, cherishes, and nourishes him; and when grown, she hands him over to spiritual teachers to be instructed in heavenly disciplines—yet she herself does not abandon him.

For she teaches the teachers what they ought to teach: how they should train her novice to crush beneath the foot of reason the flower of youth that smiles upon the world, and to restrain with the bridle of the fear of the Lord youthful spirits—ardent, unbridled, and rushing by the force of the flesh into the pit of sensuality. She teaches further that the flesh, as an intimate of vices, must not be weakened by indulgence; nor must the fire of youth be inflamed by the heat of sensuality. [Col. 0801D] Rather, both must be tempered with such moderation that the flesh, serving the spirit as a maidservant, neither collapses beneath its burden from excessive affliction nor, becoming too wanton, rejects with a rebellious neck the spirit’s rule.

She also warns her neophyte to guard most carefully against that most evil worm, pride; and, lest a perverse root find in him any fuel, always to remember that he is earth and ashes. She warns him diligently to watch the most wicked head of that serpent, than which none is more wicked, so that, once its venomous head has been crushed, no fear may remain concerning the rest of its body.

Having instructed the soldier in these and similar disciplines, Christ’s grace, our armour, clothes him in apostolic armour. [Col. 0802A] She fortifies his breast with a breastplate, his head with a helmet, and hangs the shield from his neck by a light strap, so that it can easily be moved wherever care for protecting the body requires. And because “the sword of the mighty is always upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night,” she girds his loins with the sword of the word, so that he may restrain the overflow of sensuality with the girdle of chastity and repel the assaults of lust with the sword of the Spirit.

Nor does the sword of Christ’s soldier hang idly from his thigh, but serves as a sign to beholders that no one except a man girded with chastity can drive back attacking evil spirits. Thus, armed on every side with spiritual weapons, Mother Grace also fills her adopted son with the spirit of counsel, since splendid arms themselves often burden a combatant more than they help him where counsel does not direct the battle. “It is necessary,” she says, [Col. 0802B] “my son, that you know what enemy you are about to encounter: whether he is visible or invisible, whether he relies on strength or on deceits, so that, recognizing the nature both of the battle and of the enemy, you may more easily guard against each.

“Your enemy is that ancient and utterly evil one, blackened from the beginning by the corruption of envy. He begrudges you the glory of your adoption—a glory which, had he remained humble, would have been both yours and his—which he was stripped of when his own pride despoiled him so completely that he does not even grieve that he is naked. He begrudges you this glory, yours and formerly his; he is distressed that you aspire to it; he lies in wait upon the road by which you will ascend; he meets you armed as you climb, in order to bar you from the way of the kingdom to which he himself does not aspire.

“But do not be terrified by his armour or fear his darts, which faith in Christ has so blunted that they can have no effect in causing harm if they find a breast fortified by the shield of faith. [Col. 0802C] Therefore do not tremble when he threatens harsh things, since he is powerless; nor listen when he promises pleasant things, since he is deceitful. Pass by with a deaf ear both his empty threats and his vain promises.
