If he hurls missiles against your face, receive the coming blows with your shield; and, lest he inflict a side wound, do not neglect to protect your flank also by drawing up the shield.

“Pierced by the nails of Christ’s cross and deprived of strength, he has turned to deceit; and when he accomplishes nothing in open battle, he transforms himself into an angel of light, falsely claiming to be a minister of salvation and deceiving the unwary beneath an appearance of virtue. For he assumes a thousand forms of deceit and, whirled about by the force of his malice like a millstone, prowls roaring around Christ’s sheepfold, that by whatever means—whether through manifest vices or hidden ones veiled under an appearance of good—he may devour those drawn away from Christ’s flock. [Col. 0802D]

“Therefore, my son, guard your heart with every vigilance, and never open the gates of your heart to the most cunning tempter. For by no means can he break the seal of Christ’s cross unless perhaps—may it never be!—softened by the blandishments of his deceit, you freely choose to admit the most savage enemy within your walls. Excluded in this manner, he turns to other devices of fraud, attempting to climb the fortress of your heart by the ladder of vainglory. He declares that you are holy, pleasing to God, and his conqueror; while deceitfully pretending himself weak, powerless, overthrown by your prudence, and cast down by your virtue. He tells you falsely that nothing further need be feared by you who have crushed beneath your foot an enemy so fierce as though he were a powerless worm.

[Col. 0803A] “But the most wicked plotter makes no mention of the power of God or Christ’s grace. He praises your strength and magnifies your victory, magnificently indeed but deceitfully, by secret suggestion, so that if you lend your ear to his flattery and attribute Christ’s victory to your own powers or merits, then, abandoning the foundation of humility, you may fall from the height of exaltation into the depth of destruction. But if he finds your mind founded upon deep humility and cannot overthrow it with this battering-ram of pride, he brings up another engine: a nocturnal revelation. He stands beside you in sleep, radiant, predicting many future events and sometimes interweaving true things, so that, having been relaxed by sleep and divinely endowed with the spirit of prophecy, you may believe yourself equal to the apostles. But do not believe the liar, who is the father of falsehood, for the testimony of falsehood is utterly unworthy of truth; and, while he is believed to speak truth, he strives more grievously to overthrow.”

Grace thus forewarns and fortifies her novice, then leads him out to the arena of conflict, imploring aid from heaven for him as he engages. [Col. 0803B] As heavenly clemency protects her soldier and Christ’s power has won so distinguished a victory over the most savage enemy, the loving mother rejoices, exults, and dances; she presents her victor to the eternal King to be crowned, approves the lawful contest of her soldier, and asks for rewards worthy of the victor’s labour. What and how great are the rewards received by the discharged soldier of Christ, no earthly person can sufficiently describe.

Therefore all that we are, all that we live, our birth into the world, our rebirth in Christ, our becoming superior through the Redeemer’s gift to the ancient enemy to whom we are naturally inferior, our becoming stronger through the power of the Holy Spirit despite the weakness of the flesh, our struggle under the unequal lot of nature, and our receiving the palm of victory while Christ triumphs in us—all this belongs to the grace of God. [Col. 0803C]

But the rewards of the saints, which are still hidden from us in the present and reserved for future knowledge, are, just as they are unknown to sight and untested in experience, also beyond expression in speech. Yet lest they should not be loved if wholly unknown, divine serenity has placed between our darkness and its brightness a certain mirror, through which, by directing the gaze of faith as best we can, we may behold the joys of eternal brightness laid up for us and be inflamed with all the ardour of our minds to merit them.

Concerning this contemplation of ours through the mirror of faith, the vessel of election discoursed elegantly, employing an apt comparison from human age. For when he commended charity to the Corinthians and had spoken with apostolic eloquence at length concerning its praise, he said at last: “Charity never fails; prophecy shall be made void; tongues shall cease; knowledge shall be destroyed; but charity never fails.” And, as though introducing the reason why such great gifts of the Holy Spirit are made void and destroyed, he says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.” Prophecy is made void and knowledge is destroyed because they are partial; because what they accomplish is imperfect; because what they know is immature. “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, [Col. 0804A] thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.” Thus, when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial shall be made void.

When the sun shines bright, the stars that were formerly clear are hidden—not because they lose their brightness, but because, overwhelmed by the splendour of so great a radiance, they do not appear. So too, in eternal brightness prophecy shall be made void, but in order to be fulfilled; knowledge shall be destroyed, but in order to be perfected. When they have been fulfilled and perfected, this temporal emptying, compared with eternal fullness, will be as though it had not been. Thus prophecy now speaks as a child, and knowledge understands as a child, because now we see through a mirror and in an enigma; but when we attain to the perfect man, then we shall see face to face.

[Col. 0804B] Let us now, if you please, weigh in the balance of judgment that part by which the saints now know and prophesy. Since no estimation of ours can equal even that part, we shall see that the whole and perfect reality is beyond comprehension by sense, beyond expression by speech, and beyond valuation by any comparison whatsoever. Let us see what portion fell to the blessed Apostle himself who speaks these things; none can show it more faithfully than he who received it. “I know a man,” he says, “in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—such a one caught up even to the third heaven.”

What is this, blessed Apostle, that you say? What depths do you, true vessel of election, sound? You know in part, and yet you search out the secrets of the third heaven? If you received the whole, where would you penetrate? If, bound by a body which corrupts and weighs down the soul, [Col. 0804C] you penetrate so far, where will you fly when released? As holy Thomas said, “Lord, we do not know where you are going,” so I too say, Apostle: we do not know where you fly.

O most excellent portion, O portion truly apostolic! “And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.” It is a great portion of humanity for a human being to hear what it is not permitted a human being to speak. You see, then, that the complete, whole, perfect reality is ineffable, since even the small portion of that whole is ineffable.

Who, therefore, being sane, would demand impossibilities from me, most poor and truly speechless in the face of these mysteries? Who would demand [Col. 0804D] that I describe what are those joys of eternal blessedness and blessed eternity, where God will be all in all, when I cannot describe how great are those gifts of the saints, where God is still all things in each individual?

For in this present time of imperfection God is all things in each individual, when he distributes to each as he wills: to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances; to one firmness of faith, to another certainty of hope, to another the foundation of humility, to another the surpassing excellence of charity. These things to some, other things to others: though those final gifts of salvation without which no one is saved are found in all who are saved, they are present in one to a lesser degree, [Col. 0805A] in another more abundantly.

“To each,” as the Apostle says, “is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness,” for the completion of imperfection, so that he who is now all things in each individual may one day be God all in all. Therefore, when in that eternal blessedness of the saints one person receives what is now divided among individuals, how great, think you, will that reward be, and what joy?

Human narrowness cannot comprehend the joys of that eternal brightness, where nothing will intervene to cause sorrow and nothing will be lacking to bring delight:

> No mourning resounds there, for there is no pain there;
>
> Nothing there causes regret, weariness, or shame;
>
> There is no sin there, which holds dominion here.
>
> That region knows nothing of what serves vice.

[Col. 0805B]

> Death, hated by all, is not even seen there,
>
> Nor is it to be feared by you; there is everlasting life.
>
> There is no need there for ploughs or dark rains
>
> To nourish dry seeds lest they perish.
>
> For all there is one bread, a marvellous gift,
>
> Which you always eat, yet do not diminish by eating.
>
> Wonderful, yet true: there the appearance of things is new;
>
> God, who truly is food, is there the bread.
>
> Anxiety, pestilence, sickness, and weakness, be far away:
>
> You oppress earth-dwellers; you flee heaven-dwellers.
>
> Sacred Scripture stands witness to what kind of garment is there:
>
> Whoever is washed in the laver is clothed with Christ.
>
> If you keep this garment, you will not be found naked:
>
> Now bright in one robe alone; then in both robes.

[Col. 0805C]

> From eternity the city stands upon that heavenly mountain:
>
> Who can tell how bright are the walls it bears?
>
> It is enclosed by a four-sided wall that will never fall;
>
> It stands supported by faith, and by no other stone.
>
> It is strong with towers, accessible through twelve gates;
>
> It shines with perpetual light and has no night.
>
> Peace is tranquil there; no fear of an enemy is there;
>
> The holy multitude rejoices in everlasting gladness.
>
> Nations flock together; no one forbids their entrance,
>
> And there they enjoy the lot promised to them.
>
> All hasten with swift and very easy step;
>
> A throng of elders is borne along, mingled with a choir of young people.
>
> Rich Grace summons the citizens hence to their rewards,
>
> So that all who come may receive what is due to them.
>
> She bestows gifts on them; a crown is given to each.
>
> There shines the bright, blood-purple company.

[Col. 0805D]

> The more harshly one has been afflicted, the more splendidly is one clothed,
>
> Shining in the snowy throng in a rose-coloured robe.
>
> Then there are also sufficiently glorious rewards for virginity:
>
> Free from the enticements of the flesh, it becomes renowned.
>
> For great merit, a snow-white companion follows the Lamb,
>
> Removes the mirror, and fixes its gaze upon him.
>
> This sight so fills the hungry mind,
>
> That nothing remains which it can grieve to lack.
>
> All are blessed who enjoy so abundant a gift,
>
> That they receive so much that they desire nothing more.
>
> With such gifts is every faithful person endowed in heaven,
>
> Who is devoted with a loving heart to Christ’s service.
>
> Gracious Grace freely bestows so great things upon her children;
>
> We believe every good thing to be her gift.

[Col. 0806A]

> But you ask: if it is freely given, what do you merit?
>
> Know that your very willing is itself hers.

Having set out these matters concerning the joys of eternal blessedness—not according to their worth, but according to our small capacity—I shall turn back my dry little stream to its source, offering a gift of poor talent to the pious memory of him at whose command I undertook this work. I undertook it at the command of our venerable father Fulgentius, first abbot of the abbey of Affligem, then flourishing in Christ’s religion. Living, he impressed upon our hearts living traces of Christian poverty, monastic humility, and fatherly charity; and, passing to the joys of paradise, he left them for us to imitate.

As founder of the said monastery and its first instructor in monastic observance, he established in that barbarous wilderness of the nations—not, I say, by confession of faith, but by the practical display of it—a lodging place for Christ, who was a stranger and often passed through there. [Col. 0806B] Since many people of diverse rank, profession, and age flocked there from different regions and sought Christ in his guest-house, he devoted many to Christ’s service; so that during the time of his residence he deserved to be father, in various places, to more than two hundred and thirty monks, nuns, and brothers living under the rule of obedience.

While, in the manner of a faithful servant, he distributed the measure of wheat to them and was no less concerned for temporal assistance, no one but he who bore it can know what heats of distress and what agonies of heart that holy soul endured. Yet, though often scorched in the furnace of poverty and refined by much fire of tribulations, he did not crack; rather, the more harshly he burned, the purer he emerged. Therefore our Fulgentius now shines, as we hope and trust, in that eternal brightness, where we beg him to intercede for our disobedience, whom here we had as teacher of obedience.

[Col. 0806C] To him, therefore, I offer the fruit of my obedience, that he may correct what he judges needs correction—what, illuminated by the light of truth, he surely knows better than I—and may offer the corrected work to the Author of Grace as, would that it might be, an acceptable gift. For I find in myself nothing, absolutely nothing, which I dare offer to the judgment of that strict Judge for examination, unless perhaps, through the intervention of the grace which I preach, I may deserve to be purified by that cleansing coal which one of the seraphim took from the altar with tongs and rendered the lips of the prophet Isaiah clean.

Nor do I need cleansing only of the lips, but also of the heart and of the whole body; and because, in my own judgment, all that belongs to me is defiled, all awaits the coal of divine purification. Therefore I flee to the omnipotence of him for cleansing, whose praises of mercy I have extolled in this small work, not with worthy praises but according to my powers, that he may strip me, his unworthy herald, of Ethiopian skin and inborn blackness and place me within that most broad bosom of grace, which embraces alike heavenly and earthly things and yet suffers no narrowing of its breadth.

[Col. 0806D] For although both priest and Levite pass by me in misery, wounded and half-dead, I nevertheless hope, O most merciful Samaritan, that you will not pass by your creature until you bind up the wounds, temper the biting wine with gentle oil, moderate severity deserved by negligence with mercy necessary for one dying, and heal the sick person whom you have received into the hands of any of your servants—yet at your own expense.

In return for this praise of grace, I ask you, O Lord Jesus Christ, Author of Grace, to join me to the company of those who praise you, rejoice in you, and give you thanks, so that, with the sight of grace made clear by the eye-salve of grace, I may contemplate your face—O sweetest, O most lovingly beloved, and sweeter than every sweetness—and so that, when the cloudiness of the mirror has been removed, I may see in you yourself what, and of what kind, and how great is that grace of yours which saves all things.

This is the grace that shines in angels, assigns thrones to apostles, triumphs in martyrs, distributes palms to [Col. 0808A] virgins, rejoices with all the righteous, and celebrates with you, O holy Trinity, in eternal praises with thanksgiving worthy of all. Now at the end of the work, let praise and thanksgiving be given to him who is beginning and end: from him all things receive their beginning, and by his grace each is also brought, in its order, to the end of completion.

If any reader finds upon this table of poor talent anything which he judges useful even for the nourishment of little ones, let him know that it belongs to God’s grace. Whatever he finds unseasoned and tasteless, let him know that it belongs to my inexperience and grant pardon. For no branch can do anything without the vine, nor can we without the Author of Grace, who lives and reigns through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0807]

## LETTER OF THE MONK FRANCO: THAT A MONK WHO HAS CAST OFF HIS HABIT CANNOT BE SAVED

[Col. 0807B] To Lantbert, called by God’s grace to adoption as a son of God, Brother Franco—a monk in habit, would that he were one in deed—wishes that you may savour not the things of fleshly prudence, which is hostile to God, but the things that are of God.

Having read, my brother, the letter—whether yours or that of the man who, though he had been a monk, has now become a fugitive—and recalling the question you put to me concerning apostasy through abandonment of the sacred habit, I remembered that verse: “To excuse excuses in sins.” I remembered also that ancient and disobedient Adam, who even now, in the sons of disobedience, when they presumptuously desire and attempt forbidden things, ashamed of himself, flees from the most serene light of God’s countenance to the hiding places of his dark heart; and, in order to excuse sins—or rather, to heap sin upon sin—as though to cover his shame, sews together fig leaves.

Among their company is that man of yours, I know not by what name he ought to be called, since he is now neither cleric nor monk: for he has cast aside the habit of the one and unlawfully usurped that of the other. As he learned from his father, he now sews together fig leaves to cover his nakedness, setting before us country people a question as light as leaves, empty of every weight and solidity of truth. He maintains that whatever he pleases is permitted to him: yesterday a monk, today a cleric, tomorrow or the day after a soldier—if only he did not fear for his skin. O order without order! O falling away, not advancement! O how much better, how much more salutary, if he would uncover his wounds to that most merciful and almighty physician, and seek from him, by weeping, groaning, and sighing day and night over his festering wounds, the plaster made from the precious blood of the undefiled Lamb! [Col. 0807D]

He ought to have remembered that Gospel prodigal and, guided by his example, at last nauseated by the husks of swine, to have longed for the delights of his father’s table; so that, displaying his sin rather than concealing it, and humbly confessing rather than defending it, he might receive, by the pardon of the most merciful Father, both the first robe and the ring, the badge of paternal nobility. Having thus said these few things beforehand for the admonition and consolation of our fugitive, I shall turn to the objections and, with the Holy Spirit breathing upon them, dissolve the spiders’ threads that obscure the light of truth for weak understandings.

You ask me what I think of the judgment of the most blessed man Benedict: whether I should absolve one whom he condemns, and what I should say about one whom he calls a mocker of God. Far be it from me—far, I say, utterly far from me—to clothe my thoughts in such impiety that I should ever proclaim things contrary to that saint, concerning whom Gregory, the holy bishop of the holy apostolic see, testifies in the second book of the *Dialogues*, written on the life of this blessed man, that he possessed the Spirit of God and was endowed with prophetic grace; whose holy teaching is commended by a holy life and confirmed by signs and miracles worthy of all admiration.

For what else did he teach than what he learned from him whose Spirit he had? “No one,” says the Lord, “who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Therefore the monk who renounces parents, possessions, pleasures, and finally—what is both highest and ultimate—his own will; who humbly bends his neck beneath Christ’s yoke of obedience, puts his hand to the plough. If, at the devil’s prompting, he should at any time cast off his habit and take it back again, he undoubtedly looks back.

I do not sufficiently understand why you introduced that chapter of the Apostle: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked,” unless perhaps it was to weaken the judgment justly pronounced by the blessed man against a deserter from the holy and highest profession—as though he had wrongly called the apostate monk a mocker of God, who, according to the Apostle, cannot be mocked. But plainly one kind of mockery, as the Apostle says, does not fall upon God; another is that which our lawgiver asserts is inflicted upon God by a monk. [Col. 0809A]

And what you add—that the sacred habit consecrated by solemn blessing confers no benefit of salvation—how can anyone hear this patiently? Who can bear it with composure? Is the holy ordinance of holy Church to be considered frivolous? Is the blessing solemnly performed according to ecclesiastical custom upon the vestments and implements of ecclesiastical ministry empty? Is the invocation over such things of the holy and undivided Trinity to be considered ineffectual? Is the sacrament of chrism and oil to be judged superfluous, as containing and conferring nothing of salvation? And is sacred baptism as well? These things are impious—plainly impious—and alien to the mind of all Catholics.

For vestments consecrated by the invocation of Christ’s name for ministry and for the use of God’s ministers—Christ, in whom are sanctified all things in heaven and on earth—bestow salvation and increase holiness, provided that the life and conduct of those who use them are worthy, so that the invocation of the holy Name may bestow an increase of holiness upon them. Yet upon those who live wickedly and unworthily in a holy habit, that habit, I do not deny, confers no salvation; rather, it is for them a testimony and an accumulation of condemnation.

Therefore, as you claim, a monk cannot cast aside the habit of his profession without harm to his salvation and assume the habit of a cleric; for every habit has now become unlawful for him except that in which he made profession.

Now let us examine the very examples by which you vainly strive to prove what ought not to be proved—examples supplied by that teacher of yours in a new profession, who teaches a monk, in perverse order, to profess himself a cleric, and which have been adapted to strengthen falsehood. They attack this pestilential teaching rather than defend it; they weaken it rather than strengthen it.

“Abraham,” you say, “the hermit, took on military dress and sought out and recovered his niece Mary, who had been deceived by a false monk.” Very well: Abraham temporarily assumed military dress in order to seek his niece. Did he therefore cast off the monastic habit forever? Abraham put on an alien habit for a certain moment of time, so to speak; he did not cast off his own. He was moved by zeal for his niece, not hatred or weariness of the monastic profession.

The work of piety excuses Abraham’s momentary change of dress; and that the pious old man’s loving concern for his niece was pleasing to God is testified by that niece’s praiseworthy conversion. Yet even during that very interval he performed the work of a monk, not of a soldier; and, when the work of piety had been completed, he returned rejoicing with his spoil to the hermitage. He removed the garment which he had put on to conceal himself and, as he had done until that day, so also thereafter, served Christ commendably in both the habit and practice of the monastic profession.

But you relate that the blessed John the Evangelist pursued the fugitive young man, not with apostolic gait but riding swiftly on a horse. What does that prove? Did he lose his apostolic rank because he rode a horse? I am astonished—and justly—that you have presumed to compare the work of our Redeemer and the mystery of our redemption with a detestable deed. For who of sound mind equates good with evil? Who compares virtue with vice? Who, possessing a healthy mind, compares God with man in a work so utterly unlike? [Col. 0810B]

Alas! That supreme Lord of virtues, whose greatness has no end and whose wisdom no number, did not disdain to appear like us in the form of our humility, poor and weak. But this man of yours disdains the habit of monastic humility, conformed to the Lord’s cross; moreover, he boasts that he has cast it off, philosophizes elegantly that he acted rightly, and, having strengthened his proposition with suitable testimonies, draws the following conclusion: “The transgression of one’s profession does no harm.”

But if the profession of a monk is holy—which he himself does not dare deny—and if transgression against holiness does not escape the liability of guilt, then transgression of profession is harmful to the transgressor.

I have at hand, my dearest friend, very many testimonies from both Testaments to choke this new kind of monster. I also have many and innumerable examples of holy Fathers who served in this holy profession. If I wished to gather their dense forest together, I should extend the brevity of a letter into the breadth of a book. But run through in memory, if you please, all who have professed this holy calling; and if from among all the chosen you can bring forward even one who abandoned his habit and ended his life with a praiseworthy end, I yield.

Let us now, at the end of the work, fall before him who is beginning and end, that, as the loving Shepherd, he may seek the wandering sheep with his customary tenderness; having found it, place it upon his merciful shoulders; and, amid the rejoicing of his friends and exultation of the angels, restore it to the remaining flock, its number made whole in perfection. May he who keeps Israel keep you safe and free from every stain of the unclean world, dearest brother.

[Col. 0809]

## Consolatory Letter of the Same Author to the Nuns and Sisters at Bigard near Forest

[Col. 0809D] To his beloved sisters, called by Christ in Christ’s love into the paradise of Bigard, and, as we hope, to be led by Christ himself, their guide, from Bigard into the paradise of heavenly delights: their own F., brother by sacrament, servant by office.

Grace to you and an abundance of consolation from that unfailing fountain of sweetness, our Lord Jesus Christ. Though he waters the whole surface of the earth—that is, our souls—with evangelical rains and the dew of the Holy Spirit, and makes it fruitful by watering it, he nonetheless overflows full within himself and remains forever full.

Dearest daughters, true sisters, born into sisterly affection toward me from the virginal womb of holy mother Church, without any desire of foul flesh, the Holy Spirit overshadowing: he himself is my witness, who alone presides within as witness and judge of conscience, with what loving and sincere affection I love you; how I long for you all in the inward parts of Jesus Christ; and how I desire and pray that, on the day of the Lord, you may all be found worthy of your calling, profession, and espousal.

For you are that glorious bride, that renowned bride, betrothed by his own blood to the Son of the Most High King, as a testimony of his exceeding love. For you, daughters—for you—those evangelical wedding festivities have been prepared with royal magnificence. For you the oxen have been slaughtered; for you the fattened fowls have been killed; for you that fatted calf, richer than every rich sacrifice, has been offered. And, for the worthy and most solemn celebration of the joy of your wedding, symphony, chorus, and every kind of music have been supplied by angelic ministry.

Therefore, since you have been betrothed with such love, endowed with such a dowry, chosen with such condescension, and advanced to so great a height of glory, keep watch with every vigilance, my sisters, lest that unavoidable eye find in you anything unworthy of a queen and the bride of so great a king; lest he find in your hearts any adulterous affection, he who counts every unlawful desire of the heart as adultery.

That pure and simple eye cannot look upon anything defiled, nor does he wish to possess the bed of our heart jointly with an adulterer. For the bed is narrow, as the prophet says: it cannot hold both; and the short cloak cannot cover both. “For what agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” None at all. O how far apart are this bridegroom and the adulterer, and how unlike are the affections toward them! For the love of the former is sweeter than every sweetness; but that unclean love of the latter is fouler than every foulness and more bitter than every bitterness.

Therefore, with every effort and every safeguard, my daughters most dear to me, let us guard the entrances of our senses, lest while we sleep that ancient enemy, the slippery serpent—more cunning than all beasts of the earth—creep in craftily, winding invisibly and gliding almost imperceptibly.

Indeed, that common adversary of all good things, though he loves no one and hates all, especially abhors and persecutes the holy name and holy way of life of monks and nuns, because they have renounced that most wicked head a second time and issued him a second bill of divorce: first in holy baptism, and secondly in the holy profession of a holy way of life.

Nor ought our care to be less, or our attention more relaxed, because we have departed from the world in body—though would that we had departed in heart—and because, enclosed by walls, we have been separated from common human society. Paradise was much stronger and much safer than our walls; yet because Adam did not guard sufficiently against the snares of this slippery enemy, he was not safe even in paradise. Therefore no place is found safe for a human being against an untiring and ever-watchful enemy wherever that person himself grows dull and falls asleep from guarding himself.

For the battle we wage is domestic: the enemy with whom we fight is within. He is not shut out by walls but is swiftly driven back by the divinely kindled arrows of faith. Yet he is not utterly extinguished; defeated and crushed beneath the Lord’s foot, he again attacks with shameless brow and again joins battle.

Therefore let us not believe that our own strength suffices, or our own skill prevails, to guard against and overcome so hostile an enemy. Rather, pouring out our hearts to God in devout tears and urgent prayer, let us implore his aid, that he who knows all things and can do all things may uncover the enemy’s snares and swiftly crush all his strength beneath our feet.

If, when that bloodthirsty beast has been weakened by God’s power, some respite should at times smile upon us, let us not attribute it to our own strength or our own merits, as though we had conquered by our own power or obtained victory from God by our merits. The humble Lord does not wish his servants to swell with pride over his gifts; he does not wish them, through benefits bestowed on them, to seize tyranny against him, claiming that what belongs to divine grace is their own power.

“For what have you,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” And the prophet: “Does the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or does the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?”

Therefore, that we may preserve what has been divinely bestowed upon us and deserve what is yet to be bestowed, let us cultivate humility before all else. Humility raises from earth to heaven, whereas pride hurls from heaven into the depths of hell.

Let my daughters be kind and humble toward one another; let them be prompt in obedience and devoted in service. Let them be hands to the weak, eyes to the blind, staffs to the infirm, that they may become more pleasing to their Bridegroom and Lord in proportion as they are more ardent, for his name’s sake, in rendering service to their sisters. Yet, while doing these things, let them seek no present reward for their labor, so that they may find a more abundant fruit in the future. “For whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap.”

Whatever gain you acquire, entrust to Christ for safekeeping; whatever labor you expend, send it beforehand before your face into the kingdom of heaven, where whatever has been laid up is neither destroyed by moth nor lost through theft. May he deign to bring us to the blessed eternity and eternal blessedness of that kingdom—he who deigned to adopt us as sons—through his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with him and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

But I beg you, pray for my lords and brothers who are with me, to whom, by the obligation of obedience, I render service as a servant, that they may suffer loss in nothing, but that almighty God, from the abundance of his mercy, may supply whatever they lack through the office of my service. [Col. 0813A]

Pray also for me, a sinner, dearest daughters, that the loving Lord may deign now to call back his outcast; that, stripped of these filthy garments and restored also with the ring as a sign of reconciliation, he may clothe me with the first robe and the shoes of immortality, and, now long disgusted with the husks of swine, bring me into the house of the eternal banquet amid the rejoicing of angels. Farewell, most beloved sisters; and, when you have read our letter, intercede also for our sins.

I also beg you to send this little exhortation of charity to the sisters at Forest, who are most dear to me in Christ, so that, because I have great confidence in them, they may together with you pray to the common Lord for me, a sinner: that the merciful Judge may deign both to absolve his guilty servant, who has lain prostrate at his feet for so many years to seek pardon, from the bonds of sins, and to lead him forth from the tent of this body, and offer to the angelic spirits the festal joy over the lost sheep found again.

Since I love them in the same spirit and affection as I love you, I write them the same things as I write you, changing only the name; may their holy prayers obtain that I may rejoice with them in the kingdom of God. Amen.

## Appendix to Franco

[Col. 0813]

# Chronicle of Affligem

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IX, p. 407.)

## Notice

A certain monk, whose name is unknown, wrote after 1122 the origins and history through the immediately following years of the monastery of Affligem, situated near Asse and Aalst. For this purpose he used the accounts of brethren who had been present at the events from the beginning, as well as charters preserved in the abbey archive. Yet he did not carry the history down to his own times, but stopped at the beginning of the twelfth century, adding only one notice concerning the vision of Abbot Fulgentius in the year 1109.

In the same century another monk of Affligem, who added a continuation to Sigebert, excerpted the expanded little book. In the seventeenth century Simon Guillermot, subprior of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut, copied it from an old codex; his transcript was used by:

1. D’Achery, who inserted the work under the title *Historia Affligemensis* in the *Spicilegium*, vol. X, pp. 585 ff., and by De la Barre, vol. II, pp. 769 ff., of the other edition. We have reprinted their text after collating it with

2. the Affligem Continuation in our edition of the *Scriptores*, vol. VI (*Patrologia*, vol. CLX). We have restored several usages of the twelfth century in the spellings *caritas*, *domnus*, *elemosina*, *inicere*, *subicere*, and in writing the names *Heinricus*, *Rodulfus*, and *Odulfus*. The continuation printed in D’Achery, being composed in the middle of the seventeenth century by Odo Cambier, had to be omitted.

# Chronicle of Affligem

[Col. 0813B] ## Preface

Because the course of slipping time removes from younger generations the memory of the past, it seemed very useful to me to commit to writing, for the knowledge of posterity, how, at what time, and by what founders the monastery of Affligem was begun, according to what we received from those who were present at its events and survived from that time down to our own.

### 1.

At the time when a dispute arose between Pope Gregory—who was also called Hildebrand—and Emperor Henry IV of that name [Note: [Col. 0813] “henr.” in the first edition, consistently.], it happened that holy Church was oppressed and harassed by diverse necessities and adversities. For since the head itself, composed of kingship and priesthood, had been made sick by the disease of discord, the remaining body could not remain sound and free from illness.

Then indeed simony, the sole survivor of ancient heresies, and the irreverence of married priests had become so prevalent throughout the world that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were already for sale among secular rulers, and there was almost no distinction between the lives of laypeople and clerics. Moreover, the followers of the emperor, excommunicated by the apostolic see, punished with plundering, tortures, and even death those whom they saw unwilling to communicate with them.

But the merciful Lord, having compassion on the misery of his own, raised up many religious persons inflamed by his Spirit, that they might set up a hedge and stand in battle for the house of Israel. One of these was Wederic [Note: [Col. 0815] “wethericus” in the second edition.], priest and monk of the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent, a man highly distinguished by secular nobility and, what is greater, by divine religious devotion. Strengthened by permission of apostolic authority, he travelled through the provinces of Flanders and Brabant, sowing the word of God and turning the people of God from their sins by his preaching.

By his exhortation six knights were moved to compunction: Gerard surnamed the Black, then most famous in those provinces for prowess in arms; Cinelin and Harger; also Vulbodo, Geldulf, and Tibald. Leaving behind everything they had acquired unjustly, they followed the poor master of the poor as poor men and remained with him for about three months. Then, burning with desire for a stricter life, they asked this same father and teacher what they ought henceforth to do, and how they might receive from the Lord the forgiveness of sins that he had already promised them.

### 2.

At the same time Lord Anno, bishop of the church of Cologne—[Note: [Col. 0815] namely, “was.”]—was held to be conspicuous before God and men in deed and name, endowed with zeal for all religion. [Note: [Col. 0815] Thus the first edition; “the aforesaid” in the second edition.] To him the aforesaid Wederic sent his sons, now eager for their own salvation, earnestly exhorting them to direct the course of their actions according to Anno’s command and counsel.

Accordingly, as they had been instructed, they hastened without delay to Cologne and came to the bishop. In humble confession they disclosed the detestable condition of their former life, and then sought from him a remedy of penance according to his judgment. Being a man of the highest prudence, he persuaded them to return to the place where they had committed their crimes, declaring that it was expedient for them to devote to divine service by voluntary affliction the place which they had formerly polluted by plundering innocent persons.

There, in short, they should reconcile themselves to divine mercy through good works, where they had provoked it to anger through unlawful pursuits; there they should renounce the devil and his deeds, where they had voluntarily been companions in his destructive service. Encouraged by these most salutary answers of the blessed man, they swiftly returned to their native soil. On the vigil of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, 28 June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083, they assembled at a deserted place called Affligem [Note: [Col. 0815D] Cf. the charter of Count Henry of Brabant, 1086, where it is called *Hafflingem*.], in order, according to the command of the man of God, to devote themselves there to the labor of penance where they had earlier committed deeds requiring penance.

This place was then suited only to gatherings and conspiracies of robbers, both because it was deserted and because it lay beside a public road by which merchants and pilgrims came from all directions. Robbers stationed in this nearby place of ambush carried off booty from them. When they assembled, the men brought with them only three loaves of bread, received as alms, one cheese, and a few tools; and they began to cultivate that deserted land. First, according to the measure of their strength, they resolved to build a very small oratory; then a house for the poor, another house for arriving guests, and for themselves also a hut in which to live.

### 3.

Now there was a knight named Gerard, called the White, most notorious in this province for cruelty and strength. Among other evidences of his ferocity, with the Lord permitting it, he one day voluntarily incurred the guilt of homicide. When, after committing the crime, he was returning home, the enemy of humankind appeared to him on the road and, terrifying him with a dreadful vision after his customary manner, left him almost lifeless.

But he, fearing God’s judgment upon him and believing himself already enslaved to the one whom he had served for a long time, nevertheless considered whether he might somehow escape that one’s right over him. He hurried to the aforesaid brothers, laid aside there all the fury of his savagery, and by God’s grace at once appeared changed from a wolf into a lamb. His conversion was such a wonder to all that, because of the great novelty, one person told another that this man, so cruel and so savage, had been converted; and, because of his sudden transformation, the whole province gave thanks to the supreme God.

In the same year, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, 8 September, there came to them a knight named Henrard. From repentance for homicide, the whole world had likewise become worthless to him. He began to examine the site of the place and the manner of life of its inhabitants; and when the austerity of their life and labor, and the unity of those laboring, pleased him, he returned home, renounced all that was his, and came on the approaching feast of Saint Remigius, 1 October, resolved henceforth to remain with them.

Thus, as it is written, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1), they lived together in great sweetness and peace, directing their attention to nothing except what would advance the salvation of souls; their bodies they sustained either by labor of their hands or by alms of the faithful.

### 4.

Lest any ecclesiastical person or secular power should oppose their undertaking, they sought and obtained the consent of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, and also of the cleric Herbert, who, living in England, held the altar of Asse, upon land in whose parish these brothers had settled. Countess Adela of Leuven, likewise consulted on the matter, graciously consented with her two sons Henry [Note: [Col. 0817] “henrico” in the first edition, consistently.] and Godfrey, to whom the freehold belonged. Nor content with these, they approached Emperor Henry; and on the day on which he was first crowned, 31 March 1084, they sought and received his consent and that of the count palatine, to whom part of the freehold pertained.

But while they pursued the matter more than was necessary, wishing through excessive and simple-minded inquisitiveness to secure themselves on every side, they hindered themselves. For they had heard that a monk of Lobbes had once lived there; so they came to Lobbes to the abbot and asked his permission. Although he had no certain claim to the place, whether in writing or by anyone’s testimony, nevertheless, led by their very petition into hope of acquiring it, he opposed them entirely unless they subjected both themselves and the place to his lordship and obedience.

When the brothers refused this, they went to Henry, bishop of Liège, explained the whole matter carefully, and begged him to reconcile the abbot to their request. The bishop summoned the abbot; and when he gained nothing with him, some elders of the church of Lobbes were summoned, and the bishop began to discuss the affair with them. Although they too resisted strongly, they could not establish by any argument that they had any right in the place. Therefore, to secure peace between the two parties and remove from posterity an occasion for controversy, the bishop promised that he would give the church of Lobbes an exchange for that estate. Thus the abbot and monks consented and renounced their claim. The brothers then returned to their own place and pressed on with the work they had begun.

### 5.

After this they began to desire the monastic life and habit, judging that nothing remained through which they could become nearer to God. They went to Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, disclosed their desire, and asked him to provide certain men who might instruct them in the order they desired. The bishop, being a pious man and rejoicing in their devotion, ordered them to say from what monastery they wished to take teachers.

Aquicinctum [Note: [Col. 0817D] Anchin.], recently founded, was then held in high repute because [Note: [Col. 0817] “qui” in the edition.] it was more famous than other monasteries both for brotherly charity and for the strictness of holy religious observance. They therefore asked that brethren from this monastery be lent to them for a time. The bishop sent them to Aquicinctum with his commands and letters, beseeching the abbot and convent to grant without hesitation what God’s poor requested for his honor.

Alard, the first abbot of that place, then presided over the Lord’s flock. Obeying both episcopal authority and brotherly charity, and hoping also through this occasion to subject the place being built to himself, he sent with them his prior, Titubald by name, and another brother called Rodulf. [Note: “Sent” supplied by D’Achery.] When they arrived, they were greatly pleased by the situation and attractiveness of the place. Not long afterward they instructed their abbot to come and inspect it.

The abbot, announcing a definite day for his arrival, ordered them to meet him at Tournai with horses and lead him from there as far as Affligem. Thus, when he had been brought as he had arranged and arrived on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, both the undertaking already begun and the site pleased him.

### 6.

It happened that on that same day Lord Fulgentius arrived, who was afterward, by God’s ordering, made abbot. A native of Brabant and a monk of the monastery of Saint Agericus at Verdun, he had served irreproachably in the Lord’s camp for almost twelve years.

When Theoderic, bishop of that city, was excommunicated because of the emperor, and the abbot of the monastery and the other brothers abstained from communion with him and would not submit to the obedience of an excommunicated man, a great dispersion of the brethren took place, so that the monastery, then most renowned, was almost reduced to nothing.

Then this man of whom we speak departed and returned to his homeland, taking with him a companion named Herimann. Having heard the report of this new foundation, he often came there. Seeing voluntary poverty of spirit and bodily humiliation in labors displayed in various ways, he marvelled; marvelling, he delighted in it, so much so that he determined to establish his stability there forever.

Thus, as stated above, he came on the very day when the abbot of Aquicinctum arrived, as though he were henceforth already to remain with them. On the following day, celebrated for the glorious Ascension of the Lord, the abbot blessed the monastic garments and gave them to two of the men, namely Henrard and Gerard. [Note: Supplied by D’Achery.] After remaining there no more than two or three days, he departed. But when, after nearly half a year, he recalled his own monks, Lord Fulgentius, having taken his companion Herimann, remained with those brothers and instructed them in what was fitting for monastic order and the salvation of souls.

### 7.

In the fourth year from the beginning of the foundation, 1087, they summoned Lord Bishop Gerard. On his arrival, he dedicated the place in the presence of Lord Count Henry, who both granted it liberty and increased its endowment by twenty *mansi* of land.

The devil, enemy of every good thing, envying these happy undertakings, attempted to hinder them; for he foresaw that, if the affair should come to completion, many would be taken away from him and joined to the Lord’s camp. He therefore corrupted one of the first founders named above, namely Vulbodo, and, having tripped him up by his suggestions, compelled him to depart, as he had removed Judas from the company of the apostles and Nicholas from the fellowship of the deacons.

After leaving and, like a dog returning to its vomit, plunging himself again into the world, he came not long afterward to the monastery, demanding that a sixth part of everything that had been produced at the place should be given to him. Since he was one of the original six, he maintained that a sixth share of the goods belonged to him.

On Lord Fulgentius’s advice, the brothers replied that, so long as he had remained with them, he had held all things in common with them; but because he had departed of his own accord, he could thereafter have no share in what was held in common. When he obtained nothing, wishing to avenge his rebuff, he went to Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, accusing two monks of having fled from that bishop’s jurisdiction. He said that, having come into Brabant, they were spreading many shameful reports both about the bishop himself and about the emperor; therefore, he claimed, it was expedient that they be driven away, lest the imperial majesty and the bishop’s authority be brought into contempt through their accusations.

The bishop, excessively credulous of these lying charges, wrote to Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, directing him to expel those monks from the place and not permit them to remain anywhere within the bounds of his diocese. Although Bishop Gerard greatly favored the brothers and the place which he himself had already dedicated, nevertheless, because of fear of the emperor, through whose gift he had received the bishopric, and also because of the bishop of Verdun, whom he knew could both benefit and harm him with the emperor, he commanded the brothers to leave and not remain any longer in his diocese.

The brothers bore this command most bitterly. Since they could find help nowhere else, they fled to Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and carefully explained to him who they were, where they had settled, and what they had suffered from the bishop of Cambrai because of the false accusation of a perverse man.

When the archbishop heard their case, he had compassion upon their unjust affliction and sent orders to Bishop Gerard, commanding by virtue of obedience that he cease from harassing Christ’s poor and not presume to trouble them any further. Thus the brothers obtained their desired security and thereafter suffered no further molestation from the bishop.

Thus the Lord, helper and protector of his own in all things, is present with mercy especially in tribulations. His providence does not fail in the ordering of his own affairs: he crushes to nothing the snares of hostile adversaries rising up against them, and with mighty hand restrains and calms the unjust oppressions of his own.

8. In that same year (1087), namely the fourth from the beginning of the building work, a cleric of distinguished character, a young man named Arnulf, drawn by divine prompting [Col. 0819D], arrived on the feast of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary and joined the little flock. Having lived irreproachably in the holy profession for many years, he was afterwards recognized as having benefited that same church greatly by his diligence and intelligence, counsel and assistance. From his youth until the day of his death, for about sixty-four years, he laboured not sluggishly in the Lord’s vineyard; inflamed by the ardour of his holy purpose, he bravely bore the burden and heat of the day, and left us an example of his patience—or rather, perseverance—well worthy of imitation.

[Col. 0820A] From the fourth year until the sixth, that is, for two years, living together in the greatest tranquillity and peace, and already tasting in some measure how sweet the Lord is, they vied in zeal for their holy purpose. Although the number of brethren did not increase greatly during these two years, they grew ever more in virtues; like the merchant in the Gospel, having sold all things, they eagerly sought with their whole intention to buy the precious pearl. For who could adequately recount how great was the harmony of charity that united them, when each strove to advance his neighbour, as himself, to ever higher and better pursuits of virtue? I do not think it necessary to relate their patience in labours and hardships, in such great rigor [virtute; perhaps vitae, “of life,” or victualium, “of provisions.” Dachery.—“I would prefer to read vitae.” Note: [Col. 0819] 9] and austerity and poverty of clothing [Col. 0820B] and poverty, while demolishing and building; for I know that this is most familiar to all sound-minded persons. Some indeed who did not possess the Spirit of God were driven into flight by the excessiveness of the labours; but those whom true love of God had kindled, when they saw the fall of the wicked, were, as is read in Job (41:16), terrified and purified.

But in the sixth year (1089), the fragrance of so great a religious life, being unable any longer to remain hidden, burst forth. The scent of such great virtues spread abroad in every direction through provinces, cities, villages, and castles, so that it summoned even strangers and persons remote from their homes, drawn to admiration and reverence for the servants of God.

Accordingly, very many, both clerics and laymen, began to flock to [Col. 0820C] them: some from a desire for conversion, others in order devoutly to commend themselves to the patronage of God’s servants. Indeed, in that year, with God’s favour, their number increased so greatly that their community attained the perfect number of twelve, counting clerics and laymen together.

9. But because they had no help of a spiritual father under whom they might bear the standards of holy warfare, and whom they might obey in all things as standing in Christ’s place, they began to be exceedingly troubled about this matter and diligently to discuss among themselves the election of an abbot. The two monks mentioned above, namely lord Fulgentius and his companion Herimannus, intended in this business to rely upon the counsel and help of their own abbot, lord Rodulfus [Col. 0820D], both because he surpassed almost all the abbots of that age in prudence and religious devotion, and because they had first received the habit of their holy purpose under him.

Having therefore taken counsel, they kept lord Fulgentius at home with the brethren, and sent Gerard the Black, together with the aforesaid Herimannus, to Liège at the feast of Saint Lambert, to meet the abbot. The abbot suggested to them that they choose for themselves a certain monk of his, named Laurence, a native of that province, who had formerly held the office of prior in his monastery. The aforesaid brethren, arriving at Liège, found the abbot as they had hoped. They approached him, explained the reasons for their [Col. 0821A] journey, sought his counsel and help, and asked that the aforementioned monk be given them as abbot, if this did not displease his wisdom.

When he had heard this, the abbot, being a prudent and provident man, by God’s prompting proposed to them a sounder and more useful counsel. He firmly urged that they should instead choose the man whom heavenly providence had appointed for them, namely lord Fulgentius. And lest he, being a meek and humble man, should persist in declining this burden, the abbot sent through the same brethren letters bearing his authority as testimony, commanding and ordering him to put away every excuse and to assent without delay to the will of God and to the brethren’s election. As for the monk whom they requested, he declared that he could by no means summon him, because, after the aforesaid dispersal of the brethren of that monastery [Col. 0821B], he had gone with others into a foreign and remote province.

Cheered greatly by these answers and counsels, and strengthened by the authority of the letters, the aforesaid brethren bade him farewell and hurried home. Concealing and hiding the whole affair as though nothing had been done, they kept silence for several days. For they said that, if the course of events became known through any hint of report, he would prefer to evade such an office rather than undertake it, and would secretly take flight.

10. Now about the feast of All Saints a cry again arose among the brethren. The devout flock complained that it could do nothing without a shepherd; and at last, with the consent of all, the day of election was fixed for the feast of Saint Martin [Col. 0821C]. Preparing for this day by prayers and almsgiving, fasts and vigils, harsh disciplines of scourging, and daily tears, they implored the grace of the Holy Spirit that, through the envy of the ancient enemy, it might not suffer so great a harmony among the brethren to be dissolved or disturbed in any way.

But the merciful Lord, who is always near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. 144:18), moved by such great prayers, granted the will of those who fear him and, as follows in the same Psalm (ibid., 20), carefully guarded them from every stealthy intrusion of discord. What more need be said? The appointed day arrived on which that humble community had determined to elect a shepherd for itself. After prayer had first been offered, they came, as was customary, into chapter, and began to discuss matters appropriate to the occasion and time. [Col. 0821D] In a marvellous way all voices and wills agreed upon one judgment: “We judge lord Fulgentius, divinely appointed, most worthy of this honour and office. With one voice we all choose him as our shepherd and father.”

But he, as a man of remarkable humility, on the contrary advanced various and diverse excuses, declaring with tears that he was unworthy of pastoral office; finally, with many protestations, he affirmed that he would accept that burden for no reason whatsoever. While he pleaded thus with tears, the aforesaid brother Herimannus immediately rose, brought forth into the midst the letters of his abbot which had hitherto been concealed, openly declared the command of [Col. 0822A] obedience and the peril of disobedience, and urged him to grant assent to the brethren’s request in obedience to his abbot. [Note: [Col. 0821] 10 “Obedience” appears to have dropped out.]

But, as simple persons are sometimes stubborn in the purpose of their minds, he would not alter his decision in any way, believing that by weeping, crying out, and lamenting he could resist their request. Yet they remained, with remarkable constancy, steadfast in the same resolve; and at last, moved inwardly by zeal for God, they burst out with these words:

“The Lord who, by provident dispensation, has appointed you for us his servants, though unworthy; who has made the wills of us all agree through the counsel and command of your abbot—he has undoubtedly also ordained that you should benefit us. But why say more? If you resist further, you will suffer compulsion. Henceforth, whether you will or no, [Col. 0822B] you shall become our father.”

At these words, rising and beginning the appropriate psalmody [Note: [Col. 0821] 11 “that is, psalmody.”], they rushed upon him unanimously, laid hands on him, and with pious violence dragged him—carrying rather than leading him—to the altar. Completing the remaining customary rites upon him by force and according to rule, they placed him in the abbot’s seat. But when he perceived that the humble persistence of his excuse and resistance had been frustrated in hope and effect, fearing that he himself might become for them the first cause of disturbance, he at last yielded, overcome by their importunity, and accepted the burden imposed upon him, unwilling though he was, with fear and reverence.

11. Meanwhile it happened, by God’s will, that a cleric native to Flanders, a man distinguished in appearance, learning, birth [Col. 0822C], and every virtue, named Hugh, heard of the renown for virtues possessed by this monastery. Having heard, he was eager to see; having seen, he desired to share in all its vows. Coming therefore, as has been said, he found almost greater things than fame had proclaimed. Testifying that all he had heard was true, he immediately began to discuss making his stability with them secure.

The brethren, giving countless thanks to the supreme Shepherd for the arrival of so venerable a man, rejoiced greatly in the Lord, and frequently urged him speedily to fulfil in act the pious desire he had conceived in his mind. He received their salutary admonitions as good ground receives seed; having established his stability among them as they advised, he afterwards brought forth from himself very abundant fruit.

[Col. 0822D] Since the abbot had not yet been confirmed, according to ecclesiastical custom, by episcopal blessing, he was compelled by the brethren to set out with his companions for Cambrai. This Hugh, of whom we are speaking, still clothed in clerical dress, was his travelling companion. Arriving at Cambrai (1088), the abbot, on the feast of Saint Gregory [Note: [Col. 0821] 12 “George,” witness 2.], in the seventh year, was confirmed by episcopal blessing and authority; while the aforesaid cleric was raised to the ministry of the diaconate. Having completed the business of his office, they returned prosperously. Learning that an ordination was to take place at Tournai on the second Saturday, they sent the often-mentioned cleric there in haste [Col. 0823A] to be ordained priest.

Having received the honour of the priesthood, he swiftly returned to the place chosen for him. There, laying aside the display of secular dress and taking up the garment he had long desired, he escaped naked from the shipwreck of this world by a happy course. Thus he began to be first in zeal for all religious observance and virtue, though he had been last in the order of conversion. When the brethren saw the shoots of such great virtues growing in him, by common counsel and consent they entrusted to him the office of prior on the fifteenth day after his conversion. Thus indeed, as it is written, “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14): after setting aside the pride of this world and descending, in human estimation, to the humble conversion of poor monks, within the span of one month he rose step by step to the summit of deaconship, priesthood, and the priorate.

Raised to this honour, he strove in all things to submit himself to the abbot and to obey his commands in everything. Conversely, the abbot did not set himself before him as lord or master, but, wisely considering their shared humanity and human frailty, showed himself by the humility of service to be a servant and minister not only to him but also to all others. How great was the charity and harmony then uniting those subject to them, when peace and love born of such true humility united even their prelates! Or what scandal of discord could ever secretly steal in among subjects, where those set over them contended even for the lower place? Thus, each most devoutly bearing the other’s burdens, they exercised, with charity [Col. 0823C] and concern for the flock entrusted to them, its care for nearly thirty-five years, until the death of lord Fulgentius [Note: [Col. 0823D] (3) In 1120 according to the Affligem Supplement; nevertheless, Rodulfus of Saint-Trond visited him alive in 1121, and his successor Franco appears in a charter of 1123.]. Throughout the entire period in which they both remained alive and well, they continually exhorted one another, by words and examples alike, to persevere in regular discipline.

12. (1091.) Meanwhile, through the grace of God, who truly prefers the conversion of sinners to their death, it happened that a certain lord of a neighbouring castle, a man named Heribrand, illustrious in birth according to the splendour of this world, exceedingly rich in estates and possessions, and endowed with every secular dignity, grew weary of transient and perishable things and resolved with all eagerness to seek true riches that do not diminish. Troubled and terrified by a nocturnal vision, he longed that the desire of his conversion might be fulfilled as quickly as possible.

The order of the vision, as it is reported, was as follows. Sleeping with his wife Adela, a most devout and honourable woman, he saw himself suddenly brought before the dreadful judgment of God, heard, condemned, and violently dragged by impious torturers to places of punishment. Terrified by so sorrowful a sentence, in the overwhelming anguish of his spirit he began to reflect with bodily grief upon the perpetual misery of the place appointed for him. Since no aid, no hope remained to him, but [Col. 0824A] in despair he believed that he was now to be plunged into the dreadful abyss of that hell, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, immediately appeared to him. Gently comforting him as he trembled, he checked his fear with these words: “Do not fear, Heribrand; do not fear, but know without hesitation that by my intercession and aid you shall be redeemed from these torments.”

At this sight he awoke, and turning to his wife, declared, still panting, that he had been terrified by a grave dream. She replied: “I do not know what or what kind of dream it was, but a plain sign of great fear and sorrow still remains upon you.” He recounted the vision to her in order and added at the end: “Certainly it is fitting that worthy thanks be rendered to most blessed Peter, who faithfully stood by me, unworthy though I was, in so great a need; that devout service be repaid for his countless benefits [Col. 0824B]; and that henceforth we live in such a way as to escape so terrible a sentence. And, that I may openly reveal my intention to you, from this point, if you consent, I shall leave the world and faithfully serve the supreme King and his glorious apostle.”

She replied: “Far be it from me to resist so pious a resolve in any way, or to be opposed to your salvation—indeed, to my own. Rather, whatever good you resolve to do, I shall gladly assent, becoming your fellow-worker according to my means.”

When he learned of his wife’s ready consent, he was greatly rejoiced and fixed a definite day for carrying out his purpose. On that day, intending to bid final farewell to the whole company of his household, he gathered them together. Therefore, girded with the last belt of his knighthood and raising his own banner [Col. 0824C]—that is, armed against spiritual wickedness—he hastened to Affligem, followed by friends and kinsmen, as though going to war. Entering the church of Saint Peter, no longer with his wife but with his sister, he laid aside the garb of warfare and made himself for ever the servant of almighty God and his chosen apostle. Thus both exchanged the freedom of the world for God’s service by a blessed offering.

On that day, before witnesses, he gave to the same church a certain portion of his patrimony in Flanders. Because of the inconvenience and remoteness of the places, this was sold there; with the same silver he bought for himself another piece of land in the neighbourhood here. But since their children had not yet grown up and still needed their parents’ counsel and assistance, the mother, in view of their weakness, with the abbot’s permission sometimes went down to advise them. The father, however, remained steadfast in God’s service as long as he lived. Therefore, that it might become known to all with how great a mercy and kindness of God he had been summoned—or rather, drawn—to this holy purpose, before the thirtieth day after his conversion he was seized by fever and, in true confession, closed the last day of this life. The aforesaid wife, seeing that her husband’s marvellous conversion was followed so swiftly by its reward, blessed the merciful Lord with all cheerfulness and devotion, he who wonderfully drew those whom he had foreordained to [Col. 0825A] life; and she spent the remainder of her life in his holy service under the habit of holy religion.

13. We have briefly touched upon these matters concerning lord Heribrand and his noble wife, as our present purpose required. Now let us extend the account by relating how their sons followed in their father’s footsteps.

Of his five sons, although at different times and ages, all came to us. Each separately brought together for us different portions of his patrimony; all of them together left God himself, who had given these things, as their heir in their own stead. One, though married, despised fleshly pleasures and allurements and, leaving [Col. 0825B] the world with wife and children, increased the Lord’s flock by a larger number and enriched it with a more ample possession of estates. Another, after his wife’s death, undertook divine warfare with his sons and daughters. Another, free from the bond of marriage, devoted himself to divine service all the more devoutly because he was more free.

The first two of these, not by birth but by conversion, namely Ingelbert [Note: [Col. 0825] 13 “Iggelbertus,” witness 2.] and Siger, flourishing in the first bloom of youth, when the world was already smiling upon and flattering them, regarded its enticements as nothing. They despised the bond of marriage as an obstacle to their desire; delighting in the Lord rather than in the world, they became monks and sought eternal rather than transient things. They also resolved to confer their entire possessions upon the monastery.

But who can alter the decree of divine providence? Those very men who then violently seized things that were not their own afterwards restored not only what they had unjustly taken, but also everything due by right to their own possession—indeed, they restored even themselves to the same church to which they had caused injury.

After the passage of a few years, their brother lord Folcard, who was first by birth, was struck by illness and prompted by the example of his younger brothers to follow in their footsteps. Recovering from that illness, he afterwards lived in holy observance all the more devoutly because he had remained longer in the world. He gave the church eight oxgangs of his patrimony, leaving all the rest, though unwillingly, to his daughter. His conversion was opposed by his brother lord Onulf, who greatly resisted [Col. 0825D] our cause and benefit. Among other words of opposition and arrogance, he affirmed on oath that he would never become a monk, even if he knew that he was to be led alive down to Tartarus.

Not long afterward, Onulf himself was seized by a most serious illness. He was troubled by fear of death and disturbed by an accusing conscience. Because he had utterly lost all hope of bodily recovery, he anxiously sought whatever remedy there might be for his soul. What more need be said? Having laid aside every fear and repenting of his rash oath, he asked with all humility and modesty for the habit [Col. 0826A] of holy religion which he had formerly detested. Brought to the often-mentioned church, he most devoutly commended himself, his wife Gertrude, their two sons Godfrey and Walter, and one daughter, with all their possessions and substance, to the living and true God. Shortly thereafter, in the same devotion of penitence, he ended his life.

His sons, being committed to letters, and followed by divine grace, attained the rank of priesthood. Finally lord Arnulf, himself beneficially wounded by the dart of divine fear, came with two sons and as many daughters, and further enlarged the possessions which had been allotted to him by his brothers.

14. Having described their conversion, let us for the sake of necessity employ for a little while a reversed order, and return to speak of lord Ingelbert of Calfstert, brother of lord Heribrand [Col. 0826B]. This Ingelbert, while striving bravely with his retainers to defend a certain castle of his own right that enemies had unjustly invaded—he being a valiant man in arms—was severely wounded by a lance-thrust and became lame.

Thus, long and greatly wearied by the violent pressure of wars, he at last wisely returned inwardly to himself. Since he found no peace outwardly, he resolved to establish inward peace with himself by the covenant of a devout way of life. Having sought salutary counsel, he reflected with himself upon his conversion; and, for his own edification, he frequently visited the brethren of the aforesaid monastery and spoke with them. Hearing from them what was more salutary, he eagerly strove to fulfil it in deeds to the best of his ability. Yet he bore with distress the intolerable loss of his goods. For he wished to confer all that he possessed upon the church in which he had vowed to serve God; but, because he could in no way rescue these things from the assaults and attacks of enemies, he was wholly uncertain what would be more useful for him to choose.

At length, considering that it would be more useful and salutary for him to confer upon the brethren at least some benefit from these possessions than to leave the whole to be plundered by enemies, he approached Count Henry, who at that time held the highest position in those territories. He delivered into the count’s hands all that belonged to him by right. In return, the count gave him [Col. 0826D], for the use of the brethren, four of his knights living near the boundaries of the aforesaid church, together with all their possessions: namely Siger and his brother Herminiannus [Note: [Col. 0825D] (4) “Herimannus?”] of Ecclegem, Titubald of Thidalmont, and Renizo surnamed Ridderman, that is, his huntsman. After receiving permission from him, Ingelbert returned to Affligem, immediately changed his secular habit, and, now victorious over every enemy, secured for himself the charter of perpetual peace.

15. Under what humility and gentleness he carried out his holy purpose seems worth briefly relating for our edification. A man of such nobility and renown drove asses bearing the brethren’s grain to the mill. Like the lowest servants, he carried his own bread in his bosom; at the hour of the meal, he sat upon his sack, as upon a seat spread with carpets, and with thanksgiving ate the food brought to him. He kindly shared it with all, even with the servants whom he found there and who seemed almost unworthy to serve him, treating them as brethren.

But these are small matters. He himself washed the brethren’s shoes, he himself anointed them with his noble hands, and he himself very often washed the feet of his servants as well. Yet even this is too little. I shall relate one further incident, which seems to me to surpass every measure of humility. One day [Col. 0827B], without anyone’s knowledge or command, he began to clean the latrine below from the stench of filth. Then one of the brethren, seeing this by chance, came to the abbot and reported that lord Ingelbert was standing there and doing this work.

Alarmed, the abbot hurried outside and found the venerable man engaged in the aforesaid task. Overwhelmed with astonishment, he cried out: “What are you doing, brother? What are you doing?” But Ingelbert, lowering his face to the ground, replied: “I am engaged, venerable Father, in a work that is very necessary.” The abbot, marvelling at such humility, compelled him to leave immediately and forbade him under threat to continue this task any longer. Then Ingelbert said: “Gladly, beloved Father, I would finish the work I have begun, did I not fear to transgress the command of your holiness [Col. 0827C]; nevertheless, I shall do as you order.”

16. His nobility and dignity were indeed great according to worldly standards. But in order to gain true dignity, he somehow forgot what he had been and, by humility, made himself lower and more contemptible than all. No one ever saw him angry; no murmur ever sounded from his mouth; he never allowed himself to be honoured more than another.

One day, returning from a journey, he had almost failed from bodily weakness, thirst, and hunger. A brother who met him asked whether he had eaten; he answered that he had not. The brother said to him, “Then I shall go and prepare a meal for you.” He replied, as if in jest: “Go, go, and prepare us a good refreshment.” But on the following day he reproached himself for this word, and groaned deeply that even so slight an expression of his own will and desire had crept in upon him.

Endowed with such and so great virtues, and desiring daily to enlarge the possessions of the church, he again approached the aforesaid Count Henry and suggested that what he had formerly given should be increased [Note: [Col. 0827] 14 “and that,” editions.]. The pious count graciously assented to his prayers, as was fitting, and granted him in perpetuity for the use of the church those possessions which we now hold at Wawere [Col. 0827D].

17. (1096.) Meanwhile it happened that the two sons of Lady Ida, countess of Boulogne—Duke Godfrey [Col. 0828A] and his brother Baldwin, each of whom afterwards, one after the other, obtained the sceptre of the kingdom—resolved to set out for Jerusalem, in order that, with God’s help and by a mighty hand, they might restore to the Christian religion the holy places then held under siege by unbelievers and impious men.

Gathering an army of the faithful from far and wide, they came into the territories of this province also, where they bestowed generous benefactions from their own patrimonies upon many poor monasteries. When this became known, brother Godfrey surnamed the Black, because he had known the aforesaid Duke Godfrey before his conversion, hastened to meet him at Ghent, where he had by chance then arrived. With many prayers he begged him, on his return journey, to turn aside to Affligem for hospitality.

The devout and pious duke did not wish to make light of such earnest prayers.
