Therefore, after he had dispersed almost all his army in various directions lest the brethren be burdened too much by them, he turned aside to the monastery mentioned above with his brother Count Baldwin, with Count Godfrey—who later valiantly bore the ducal banner—and with the others whom he retained with him [Col. 0828B]. Received by the brethren with due honour and reverence and shown every kindness, he wished to repay the brethren’s benefits. Accordingly, he went with his nobles to the altar of Saint Peter, and there, with the consent of his brother Baldwin, legally offered to the same church, in accordance with the statutes of princes, five manses of his patrimony in the place called Huglintrau.

But because their brother Count Eustace was not present at this donation, all the brethren felt no small fear that after their departure they might suffer some harmful adversity from him. Therefore, after consultation, some of the brethren hurried to Boulogne and requested that this benefaction of his brothers be confirmed by his authority. He not only did not oppose his brothers’ gift, but added whatever belonged to his own right and, with his mother’s assent—or rather at her urging—established it as valid and unshaken in perpetuity.

Thereafter the mother of these noble sons, herself equally generous and noble, while travelling later in these regions, chose lodging at the same monastery. Among other benefactions of her liberality, she most devoutly gave the brethren the altar of Genappe, which belonged to her by right, freely and discharged from every [Col. 0828D] exaction.

18. (1099.) After this, a noblewoman named Eremberga gave us Frasne [Note: [Col. 0827] 15 “the cell of Fraxinium,” witness 2.] with her sons, for the souls of herself and her parents. Anseele was built at his own expense before his conversion by Adin, the biological brother of lord Abbot Fulgentius. He bought with his own money the surrounding land which we still possess; and when he had completed everything there, as though for his own use, he followed his brother’s footsteps and received under him the habit of holy religion.

Hillinus of Baltersem, with a certain son of his named Gislebert, our monk, gave us two parts of the allod at Vertejic [Col. 0829A], of which we are heirs; a noblewoman of Leuven named Geva freely made up the third part. At Eversberghe, we also bought another allod from Arnulf of Stenherhe [Note: [Col. 0829] 16 “Stenherke?”] for twenty-two marks. In exchange for it, we obtained from Franco, castellan of Brussels, three parts of another allod, which we now enjoy at Esschen; this allod was worth so much more because we bought its fourth part from Godeson of Wesenbecca for twenty-three and a half marks.

A certain citizen of Leuven named Helricus, who became a monk with us, gave us one manse of land at Levedale. Rembald of Dofle also received in this place the habit of holy religion and brought us the allod on which is situated a certain manor called Berchem. A knight of Ascha named Gislebert Clinhleunt likewise came to conversion with his wife and gave us also the whole fief which he held from Duke Godfrey, whose man he was. The same duke granted all these things to our liberty; in its possession we established the manor of Colried.

The sons of Onulf of Meltburch, namely Walter and Emelinus, their maternal uncle Wiscolo of Putige, and his sons, sold the allod which they held jointly, on which we established the manor called Upper Jeten. Moreover, Rodulf of Gunchelberga, leaving behind the things of the world and burning with desire for a holier life, became a monk with us and granted us a part of his allod at Zellehe [Col. 0829C]. We bought the other part, which had fallen by inheritance to his daughter and her husband, from both for a price; on possession of this allod we built two manors there.

19. It should be known that almost all the lands which we hold on this side of Ascha were bought piecemeal from the dependants of Duke Godfrey, dwelling there either by benefice or hereditary right. From that same pious duke we obtained freedom for all of them. Further, we bought from Arnulf of Vilvorde the allod at Cobbeghem, in wood and open land, at a very high price—namely one hundred and forty marks—and, with Duke Godfrey’s cooperation, confirmed it for ever to our church by a stable agreement [Col. 0829D].

Moreover, Lady Remundis of Aalst and her two sons Baldwin and Ivamus granted us sites for two mills at Erenbodeghem and offered to our church the altar of the same village, which belonged to them by their own right. But we feared to receive God’s gift from lay persons; therefore we diligently insisted that we should receive this donation instead from the bishop. They consequently gave the same altar to the bishop of Cambrai, according to our request [Col. 0830A], and we canonically received it from the bishop, the gift being valid and confirmed under his authority.

The same two brothers also gave us land lying before our gate, extending in length for the space of two manses. Afterwards the elder of them, namely Baldwin, was seized by severe illness. Before his death he became a monk and, at his own wish and request, was brought all the way to us. Then, with his brother’s consent, he gave us in Flanders, at Testreet, a certain allod of pastureland, whose revenue amounts each year to ten pounds of silver.

20. At Oosterzele, Arnulf of Wintica gave us three manses of his allod, expecting in return an eternal rather than a temporal benefit. Afterwards, having been gravely wounded in warfare, he left the world and became a monk with us; his wife too lies buried with us. William of Volsar, a nobleman, inflamed by the same desire, received with us the habit of holy observance and gave us a third part of his allod at Sconart [Col. 0830B]; we bought the other two parts for a price. Siger of Erenbodeghem, also a convert, added one manse there.

The young Count Robert gave us the place of Saint Andrew [Note: [Col. 0829] 17 “the cell of St Andrew situated near Bruges,” witness 2.] as an alms-gift (1100). Although the altar of the same place belonged to him by right, because it is a spiritual gift he caused it to be given to us with secure permanence by the bishop of Noyon, in whose diocese that place is situated [Col. 0830C].

His son, the illustrious Count Baldwin, wishing to confer upon us a benefit of his generosity, considered what he might best give that would be more useful and nearer to our needs. Learning that a certain allod near us was held by the brethren of Saint-Bertin, he made an agreement with them, gave them a full equivalent in exchange within his own territory, and gave us, in remembrance of himself, the aforesaid allod of six manses in extent.

Two full brothers, free in status, lived together undivided near the castle of Rodenburch in Flanders, both still remaining free from the companionship of marriage. Inflamed by one desire, they diligently discussed between themselves the salvation of their souls. They set before one another how small and contemptible all earthly things are in comparison with eternal ones; at last they resolved unanimously to renounce the world and worldly occupations.

Therefore, leaving their native soil with all that they had, they became exiles seeking their true homeland. Having passed by several wealthier and nearer monasteries, they preferred to join the fellowship of our poverty. They gave their house, which they had inhabited together, with all its equipment, with herds [Col. 0831A] and flocks, fields and possessions, where we possess a manor to this day, subsequently enlarged by additional estates.

Accordingly, from Count Theodoric and Countess Clementia we also bought, for a large price, two estates which, in the usage of their language, they call *pecorias* (“cattle-estates”). We received from both parties the deed of donation, secured by the count’s seal and confirmed in perpetual validity, in the presence of the chief men and barons of the land [Col. 0832A]. In addition, Flanders provided us with many revenues in estates and silver. We sold a good many of the estates there because of the distance and inconvenience of the locations, but usefully spent the proceeds on purchasing other properties nearer to us.

## Vision of Lord Fulgentius, First Abbot of This Place

[Col. 0831]

[Col. 0831B] Fulgentius, first abbot of Affligem, saw two biers being borne to heaven. One, it was said, belonged to the Archbishop of Canterbury, the other to the Abbot of Cluny. One ascended on the Wednesday of one week; the other likewise on the same weekday of the following week. Within a few days the event proved the truth of the vision. For Lord Anselm the archbishop departed at daybreak on Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper (21 April 1109); while the holy elder, Abbot Hugh, as was said above, after the celebration of the Resurrection, was released from the flesh on the Sunday of that same week, namely on the eighth day, at evening (28 April).

## In the Year of the Lord 1125: Hugh of Ribemont

[Col. 0831]

## Notice

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, XI, 113)

Hugh of Ribemont is known to us only through an excellent letter addressed to G. of Angers, who had put to him certain questions concerning the nature and origin of the soul. Since Hugh designated the person to whom he wrote only by the first letter of his name, we can offer only conjectures on the matter. It nevertheless seems highly probable that the letter G. means Graphion of Angers, who taught at Reims during the episcopate of Rainaud de Martigné, archbishop of that city. This appears from an act of that prelate dated 1127 (*Martène, Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 368), where one finds the subscription of Graphion the teacher: “The mark of Master Graphion of Angers,” etc.

But whatever may be the identity of the person to whom Hugh addressed this letter, it is a very important document and does credit to its author. In it he answers several very subtle and difficult questions in a manner showing him to have been a skilled philosopher and a very enlightened theologian. It contains, in summary, the various systems concerning the origin and nature of the soul, and clearly establishes the Church’s teaching concerning original sin. He shows that the soul is not a part of the Godhead, as some have falsely maintained, since it is subject to change and sin; that it is erroneous to say it is corporeal, since it is spirit; and that it is another error to believe that souls are joined to bodies in order to expiate faults committed in another life, since, according to the Apostle, Jacob and Esau had done neither good nor evil before their birth.

Graphion had asked him whence the soul of each individual comes. He answers that opinions are divided, but that Scripture does not expressly teach us whether the souls of Adam’s descendants derive their origin from that which God created in the first man, or whether He creates new ones for each human being. In relation to original sin, he then asks: if souls do not derive their origin from Adam’s, and if they are without sin when they are united to bodies, how do they contract original sin? For how could this sin be imputed to the flesh alone, which comes from Adam and, being without reason, cannot be capable of sin? How can one who has not sinned be punished for another’s sin?

But, says our author, we know that after Adam sinned, his body experienced the movements of concupiscence and acquired an inclination toward sin. Therefore, when the soul is united to flesh inclined toward sin, it does not indeed find the flesh guilty of sin, but disposed to commit it. By uniting itself to the flesh, the soul itself consents to it: it gives it life, loves it, abandons reason, and at once gives itself wholly to the senses. Thus, in yielding to that inclination that leads toward sin, it consents to it; and by consenting, contracts it. It sins, therefore, by its will and not by necessity; and because it sins, it deserves to suffer the penalty due to sin. It is therefore justly damned unless the Church assists it by purifying it through the baptism necessary to it, as faith teaches us. He then cites the authority of Saint Augustine to prove that sin does not come from God and that man does not commit it by necessity, but by his will.

[Col. 0833] Hugh answers several other questions on the same subject of the soul’s origin, which had been proposed to him by Graphion or which he proposed to himself. He again cites Saint Augustine, in whose writings this single letter sufficiently shows that he was very well versed. Dom Martenne published it in his *Treasure of Anecdotes*. It is regrettable that a writer with so much talent for writing, insight, and precision either left us no other productions of his pen, or that they have not come down to us.

[Col. 0833]

## Letter of Hugh of Ribemont to G. of Angers

He answers the question proposed: whether the soul of the first man was made from nothing, and how sin is contracted.

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 481, from the manuscript of Clairmarais.)

[Col. 0833A] HUGH of Ribemont to G. of Angers.

Love commands me to answer your question; incapacity refuses. Affection bids me; negligence forbids. Goodwill urges me; difficulty denies. But one who truly loves gives his whole self, with all his affection, wholly to the one whom he loves; for a friend he despises difficulty, casts away negligence, and does not plead incapacity. Therefore I answer you who inquire—not as I ought, but according to my ability.

You ask me whether the soul given to the first man was made from nothing, or from pre-existing matter. If we say, from matter: was it corporeal or incorporeal? If it is said to have been made from corporeal matter, then a body may indeed seem capable of being made from a body, but not a spirit from a body. For how can the intellectual life of a rational essence be made from corporeal matter [Col. 0833B]?

But if you say, from incorporeal matter, what is that matter? If that matter was rational, what use of reason did it have? If it was without sin, it seems not to have been formed into a soul, but deformed, since the soul so often incurs sin. But if it was irrational, how can what is irrational be the matter of a rational soul? If, moreover, it lived, was it blessed or miserable? If blessed, it was surely better there, for here it incurs many troubles through the soul. But if miserable, what evil merits had preceded?

Those are mistaken who believe the soul to be a part of the divine substance, since the soul is mutable, incurs sin, and pays penalties to the Lord for sins. Those too are mistaken who call the soul a body, since it is spirit—not Creator, but created. Those likewise are mistaken [Col. 0833C] who say that souls are poured into bodies as a punishment for the evil desert of a previous life, since the Apostle says that Jacob and Esau, not yet born, had done neither good nor evil.

You also ask: from where are the individual souls of individual persons made? We answer: different persons hold different opinions. But we do not read that Holy Scripture has manifestly determined whether the remaining souls are propagated from the first soul given to the first man; whether new ones are created for individuals; or whether, already existing from the beginning, they either are sent by the Lord or descend into bodies by their own spontaneous will [Col. 0834A].

If, therefore, souls do not come by propagation, and are without sin when they enter bodies, whence do they incur original sin? For who will impute sin to the flesh alone that comes from Adam, since it lacks reason? And how does one who has not committed sin incur the penalty rightly due for another’s sin?

But we know that after Adam sinned, his body contracted the movement of concupiscence and the tinder of sin. Therefore, when the soul is united with flesh possessing the tinder of sin, it finds that flesh not sinful, but capable of sinning. United to it, the soul consents to it, gives it life, and loves it. Hence it sometimes sets reason aside and first devotes itself wholly to bodily senses [Col. 0834B]. But while it consents to the tinder of sin, it contracts sin by consenting. It therefore sins voluntarily, not by necessity; but that which sins justly bears sin’s penalty. It is consequently justly damned unless help is brought to it through the Church.

But we say: if it sins voluntarily, it can refrain from sin; it can be without sin. Therefore it does not sin necessarily; therefore the sacrifice of our redemption is not necessary. But what is the point of these things? For the faith of the Church testifies that Christ is necessary; that baptismal grace is necessary; that our redemption is necessary. Why, then, is guilt necessary? But if it is necessary, how is it voluntary? Yet every sin is from the will.

For Augustine says: “I am certain that the soul has fallen into guilt through no fault of God, through no necessity of God or of itself, but by its own will” [Col. 0834C].

What then? Attend more carefully to what we have already set forth. Every soul, invisibly bound to flesh possessing the tinder of sin, does indeed consent to the flesh as it contracts the movement of concupiscence. Therefore every soul sins. If every soul sins, guilt is necessary in respect of the act; consequently our redemption is also necessary. Thus we say that repentance is necessary for all believers living in this life: necessary, indeed, not because those restored to goodness by grace can, with grace helping them, be without sin, but because the tinder of sin and the law in the members are always left for combat in this life [Col. 0835A]. Hence we always fall, and always ask the Lord to forgive what is owing from us. Therefore, as long as we live, we necessarily ask forgiveness, because, with respect to the act, we necessarily sin.

You also ask: if new souls are daily made from nothing, how is it true what is written: “He who lives for ever created all things together”? We answer that all things were indeed made together. For at that time individual things were made either in their own actuality or in matter. Therefore souls that are now, as some hold, newly made from nothing were also made there by likeness. For the first soul was made in the image and likeness [Col. 0835B] of God, and this same nature exists in every individual soul.

You further ask: if the soul is not propagated by descent, when is it infused into the body—when semen is emitted; after emission, when conception occurs; or after conception, when the embryo is formed? We read, indeed, in Moses: “If someone strikes a pregnant woman and she miscarries: if it has been formed, let him render life for life; if it has not been formed, let him be fined money” (Exodus 21). From this we wish to understand that a soul is never infused before the body has first been formed, because it is fitting first to prepare the house and then for its inhabitant to enter. In Adam, indeed, the body was first formed, and afterward the spirit was breathed in.

But perhaps, by a spontaneous movement, once the body has already been formed [Col. 0835C], the soul begins to exercise its power—though it may have been present there before, quiet and without movement. For how could it have grown together, coagulated, and advanced as far as form, if it had first been inanimate?

Those, however, who assert that a soul is infused from the parent along with the semen of the flesh—if they derive soul from soul through bodily semen, what do they prove except that the soul is a body? But if they derive an incorporeal soul from an incorporeal source, what do they mean? Is a part infused from the soul, so that it may grow together into a soul which is to be formed? Yet extension, growth together, and division into parts belong not even to the soul but to the body. And if the father’s soul transfers its whole self into the son, so as to make a soul in the son without loss to itself, what else is this than to say that there are not many souls, but one soul of all?

Augustine says [Col. 0836A]: “It is astonishing if any human understanding comprehends how, just as one lamp is lit from another and another flame comes into being without loss to the first, so a soul is made from the parent’s soul in offspring, or propagated in offspring: whether the incorporeal seed of the soul flows by some hidden and invisible path separately from father to mother when conception occurs in the woman; or, what is still more incredible, lies concealed in the woman’s body. But when seed flows out fruitlessly and no conception occurs, does the seed of the soul not go out at the same time? Or does it return, with the utmost swiftness and in an instant of time, to the place from which it went out? Or does it perish? And if it perishes, how is the soul itself immortal when its seed is mortal? Or does it receive immortality when it is formed, so that it may live?”

Likewise: “If the origin of the soul is hidden, provided its redemption is clear, there is no danger. We do not believe in Christ in order to be born, but in order to be reborn, however we may have been born.”

Likewise: “Although I do not know how it can be explained whether the soul descends by propagation or not, I nevertheless believe that the most clear authority of divine utterances would exist on this matter also, if man could not be ignorant of it without loss to promised salvation” [Col. 0836B].

Likewise: “It is not permissible to doubt that no one drew the Mediator’s soul from Adam. For if no soul is propagated from another, when all are held bound by propagated flesh of sin, how much less should it be believed that Christ’s soul could have come from the propagation of sin—he whose flesh came from a Virgin, conceived not through lust but through faith? But if the remaining souls are held liable through the sin of the first sinful soul because they are propagated from it, then surely the soul which the Only-Begotten joined to himself either did not draw sin from that source or was not drawn from it at all. For he who loosed our sins was not unable to draw for himself a soul without sin; and he who created a new soul for that flesh which he made from earth without a parent was not unable to create a new soul for the flesh which he took from a woman without a man” [Col. 0836C].

I wished to write these things to your affection, since I could refuse you nothing whatsoever. If, therefore, you begin to doubt on the basis of these matters, seek from the wise those things which wise men have doubted. But if, God willing, you are able to find anything better on these questions, do not be reluctant, in repayment of love’s debt, to write back to me also. Farewell, dearest friend.

## In the Year of the Lord 1125: Pontius, Abbot of Cluny

[Col. 0835]

## Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, IV, 1134)

[Col. 0835C] Pontius of Mergueil, son of Peter, Count of Mergueil, formerly prior of Saint Martial—or, as others hold [Col. 0836C], a monk of Saint Pontius, according to the Library of Cluny, col. 1310—or a monk of another church than Cluny [Col. 0837A], according to the *Chronicle of Saint-Bertin*, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, col. 605 (accounts which are not mutually inconsistent), was at last elected successor of Blessed Hugh in 1109. On the seventh day before the Ides of May [9 May] he received blessing from Guy, Archbishop of Vienne.

Indeed, in that very year, which is elsewhere said to have been the first of Pontius’s ordination, Hugh of Lusignan, his cousin, showed himself generous to him in connection with a certain church; and Pope Paschal II confirmed his privileges in the tenth year of his pontificate, indiction II.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] (1) See *Bibliotheca Sebus.*, pp. 440 and 443.]

In the following year Peter, Bishop of Saintes, confirmed to Pontius the abbey of Saint Stephen, which his predecessor Ranulf had granted to Saint Hugh. Likewise, Amelius, Bishop of Toulouse; Bernard Ato, viscount of Béziers; Peter Raymond, brother of the said bishop; and Adela, wife of Peter Raymond and sister of Pontius, Abbot of Cluny, restored to him in the same year the church of Saint Columba with its dependencies and appurtenances, according to the cartulary of Moissac [Col. 0837B].

[Note: [Col. 0837D] (2) Ibid., p. 441.]

With Amelius consenting, together with Raymond the provost and the canons of Saint Stephen, Pontius, Abbot of Cluny, and Ansquitinus of Moissac received as a gift the church of Saint Mary of La Dalbade from Gerald, steward of the hospice of Saint Mary the Golden, according to the charters of Blessed Mary the Golden.

In 1116 Emperor Henry sent envoys to Paschal II, of whom Pontius was the first; he was said to be the pope’s kinsman. He carried out this embassy excellently and prudently, as also many other undertakings for securing peace in the Church. One of these embassies in particular is expressly described in a charter of Guy, Bishop of Geneva, who in 1119 granted to “Pontius, abbot, our friend,” the church of Condominium with all its appurtenances, for his own soul and those of his predecessors, etc.: “William, Bishop of Châlons, also being present, who was setting out with the aforesaid abbot to Lord Emperor Henry on behalf of peace between kingdom and priesthood,” etc. [Col. 0837C].

Orderic Vitalis calls this Pontius, in Book XII of his *History*, “the son of the Count of Mergueil, closely related by blood to kings and emperors, godson of Pope Paschal II, at whose command he was educated among the Cluniacs; teachable from childhood, agreeable, steadfast in virtues; he was of middle stature and fair complexion.”

John of Ypres agrees in the *Chronicle of Saint-Bertin*, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, col. 605: “A certain young man, Pontius, noble by birth [Col. 0837D] and a monk of another church, had been elected to a bishopric; but, when men of higher counsel objected, the pope appointed another bishop and earnestly commended this Pontius to the venerable Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.”

Moreover, his character, religious devotion, and knowledge of letters matched his other endowments. Equipped with these advantages, he defended the privileges of his monastery modestly but vigorously at the celebrated Synod of Reims in October 1119; Orderic, in the cited book, records the speech he delivered before the council on this matter.

His religious devotion and noble birth are also clearly proved by the following incident [Col. 0838A]. Observing that the wine offered at Cluny during the sacred solemnities of Mass was ordinary wine, he admonished his aunt, Lady Judith, Countess of Auvergne. She gave one hundred gold pieces to purchase a vineyard; and for this alms the venerable Abbot Lord Pontius promised the countess that at Cluny an anniversary observance would be performed in perpetuity for her son William, Count of Auvergne, for his wife, for the count’s sons Robert and William, and for his daughter Judith.

There survives Letter XXXII of Paschal II to Pontius, concerning the prohibition of giving Communion by intinction. It directs that the Eucharist be received so that the Body and Blood are received separately, except by the sick and infants. This proves that communion under both kinds was then in use and continued even for infants [Col. 0838B]. There is also another letter, XLVII, of the same supreme pontiff, granting pontifical ornaments to Abbot Pontius.

His successor, Pope Gelasius II, fleeing Italy, was most generously given thirty horses by Abbot Pontius; in return Gelasius gave the monastery of Cluny a distinguished privilege. He died piously in that monastery and was buried there. Calixtus II was then acclaimed pope there in his place. He granted Pontius and his successors as abbots authority to exercise everywhere the office of a Roman cardinal; allowed Pontius to admit into his monastery monks of every kind except the excommunicated; and further confirmed the monastery’s churches and all its possessions. The bull was issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February], indiction XIII, in the second year of his pontificate [Col. 0838C], 1120. Another bull of the same pope addressed to the same abbot and dated 1122 may be found in the *Bullarium Cluniacense*.

Nor should it be omitted that Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, dedicated to Pontius the *Life of Saint Hugh*, his predecessor; and that William, Bishop of Périgueux, granted him the church of Saint Theodore of Rocaboucort in 1121.

[Note: [Col. 0838D] (3) Vol. II of the new *Gallia Christiana*, col. 486, documents.]

Furthermore, Peter the Venerable narrates his deeds at greater length in Book II of the *Miracles*, chapters 12 and 13. From him Spondanus transcribes the following in his *Annals*: After Hugh’s death, Pontius was elected by the Cluniacs to his seat. For several years he lived quite modestly with his religious brethren. Subsequently, however, he began to undermine the monastery and gradually alienate the brothers’ minds from himself by various disturbances. Therefore, after discord had continued for about ten years, Pontius went to Rome to Calixtus. There he resigned the abbatial office—though the pope refused his resignation—about April 1122 [Col. 0838D], after he had held office for thirteen years, and immediately withdrew to Jerusalem with the intention of staying there.

[Note: [Col. 0838D] (4) See the Chronicle of Alberic under the year 1122.]

Later, however, changing his mind, he returned to Gaul and invaded Cluny by force of arms. He cruelly harassed and expelled the monks; like a barbarian, he plundered the abbey’s gold and silver vessels, villages, and lordships; and with fire, sword, plunder, and slaughter he raged with impunity in a religious place. Hearing of this scandal, Pope Honorius sent Cardinal Peter [Col. 0839A], who, together with Humbert, Archbishop of Lyons, struck Pontius and his adherents with anathema.

Pontius was then summoned to Rome to undergo judgment in the dispute and clear himself; but sentence was pronounced, and he was deposed from every ecclesiastical dignity as an invader and sacrilegious man. Several letters of Pope Honorius on the matter survive, addressed to Abbot Peter and to the monks of Cluny. In one of them he speaks thus:

> “Pontius, indeed, enemy of the ordinances of Blessed Benedict and hammer of the monastic order, had renounced the abbey of Cluny into the hand of our predecessor Pope Calixtus, of blessed memory, without hope of recovering it, and had bound himself by vow to live in Jerusalem forever. Yet, contrary to the will of God and to ours, in proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption he occupied the monastery of Cluny” [Col. 0839B].

Hence another letter, written to the monks of Cluny themselves, forbids them to return to Pontius, formerly abbot, without permission from Peter, then abbot. The acts of the deposition and excommunication of this Pontius are preserved in the codex of Celles-sur-Belle, from which our Dom Claude Estiennot extracted them and inserted them in vol. IV of his *Historical Fragments*, fol. 31.

Finally, scarcely a month after this misfortune, he died at Rome in 1125, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], according to notes to the Library of Cluny, the calendar of Saint Leonard of Bellême, and the necrology of the abbey of Saint Giles preserved in the library of the Dominican Friars at Chambéry—not on the fourth day before the Ides, as is read in the Cluniac Chronicle of Francis de Rivo. Elsewhere, however [Col. 0839C], the day of his death is recorded as 28 December and the year as 1126; this is more consistent, for the *Bullarium Cluniacense* contains a letter of Pope Honorius to Abbot Peter, dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October], indiction III, 1126, in the second year of his pontificate [Col. 0840A], from which it is clear that Pontius was still alive.

I conclude Pontius’s history with the words of the *Chronicle of Vezelay*:

[Note: [Col. 0839C] (5) Labbé’s Library, vol. II, p. 301.]

> “By command of the apostolic see, the brother of the Count of Melgueil was arrested without a hearing, and kept in custody in the tower called ‘the Seven Halls’ until his death, namely the fifth day before the Kalends of January [28 December]. He was buried like a poor man—indeed, like a captive—beside Saint Andrew, who had formerly governed the monastery of Cluny excellently for fourteen years.”

These words, however, may suitably be interpreted from other sources as follows: he was not heard because he had refused absolution from excommunication, maintaining that he could be excommunicated by no one—a response judged insane [Col. 0840B]. “He was kept in custody”: so too John of Ypres, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, col. 660. “Like a poor man”: Pope Honorius II, writing to Peter, Abbot of Cluny, in Letter 1, says of Pontius:

> “Although he had often been warned concerning the evils inflicted upon Cluny and had refused to do penance, nevertheless, out of reverence for this monastery, of which he had been a monk, we caused him to be honourably buried.”

He was in fact first buried near Saint Andrew, but was later translated to Cluny, where his tomb may be seen in the greater church near the chapel of Saint Martin. It portrays the man with his feet bound, because he died excommunicated, and with hand and foot cut off. His *Life* is extant in the Library of Cluny, p. 551. See also Hugh Menard’s observations on the Benedictine Martyrology under 29 December, p. 429 [Col. 0840C].

[Col. 0839]

## Statutes of Abbot Pontius

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., II, 183.)

[Col. 0839C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let all the brothers and sons of the holy monastery of Cluny, present and future, know that I, Brother Pontius, a sinner and unworthily called abbot, considering how Blessed Odilo, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, established a general commemoration of all the faithful departed [Col. 0839D], and how our pious predecessor Lord Abbot Hugh celebrated for several years an anniversary observance for brothers who had died in his time, in the first year of our ordination, by common counsel, decreed and confirmed before all in the chapter of Cluny by this present charter that henceforth a universal memorial of all brothers and sisters of our congregation who have died from the foundation of the place itself should be solemnly observed on the vigil of All Saints.

We established it especially on the vigil of All Saints because the general commemoration of all the faithful departed is to follow immediately. It seems right to us that first a special remembrance of our own should be devoutly observed among us, and that afterward a universal intercession should follow both for our own departed and for all the faithful departed [Col. 0840C]. It was also established so that all those saints and elect of God, whose feast is anticipated and honoured, may deign through this office of fraternal devotion to commend the souls of these same brothers to the divine majesty by their holy intercession.

We therefore command that this commemoration be observed under the following terms: not only at Cluny, but also in all our abbeys, priories, and cells, now and for as long as the monastery of Cluny remains in holy religious observance, a solemn office with Mass shall annually be devoutly celebrated on that same day, according to what is suitable for the places and their brothers. All the brothers, according to their order and according to the grace God has given to each one, shall gladly perform Masses and psalms for their departed brothers [Col. 0841A], so that whatever has not been rendered during the year to brethren who have died through ignorance or negligence may be made good entirely to the praise of God.

That they may strive to fulfill this more devoutly, we have joined to this work of mercy the deceased parents and relatives of all our brothers, praying that Almighty God may make them participants in these and the other good works of our congregation. The first prayer for the brothers shall be said: “God, giver of pardon”; the second for the sisters: “We beseech thee, O Lord”; the third for parents: “Incline, O Lord.”

When the vigil falls on a Sunday, this observance for the departed brothers shall take place on the preceding Saturday or Friday [Col. 0841B]. We also judged it fitting that, just as a pious intercession is offered to the divine majesty for the repose of the departed, so fraternal mercy should likewise be bestowed upon the living, for health both of body and soul.

We therefore decree that I myself, during my life, and our successors throughout the ages, shall provide from our own resources a general meal for the community of Cluny on that day, namely the vigil of All Saints; and that on the following day, the feast of All Saints, we shall feed three poor persons with bread and meat for every brother then present at Cluny [Col. 0841C]. If the feast falls on a Friday, this feeding of the poor with bread and meat shall occur on the following Saturday or Sunday.

We command that the same feeding of the poor be carried out in all our places, so that abbots, priors, or deans shall diligently arrange for three poor persons to be fed, in accordance with the circumstances of time and place, for every brother whom they have with them in their respective places [Col. 0842A]. Let this ordinance of mercy not appear burdensome to them, for Christ Jesus, who gave himself for our salvation, demands this from us as though it were his own: if we wish to have him favourable to us, we must feed him in the poor and needy.

Moreover, our place has always, through God’s mercy, grown toward better things through the salutary institutions of the holy Fathers. The brothers themselves will finally be readier and more devout both for spiritual and temporal duty when they reflect that so great a work of mercy must be rendered to them every year, as though by obligation [Col. 0842B]. It will therefore be a great act of charity if abbots, priors, and deans, under this general commemoration, provide their brothers some special meal on that day, so that all things may work together for good to those who love God.

Therefore let this day’s commemoration be observed, as we have said, in psalms, Masses, prayers, and almsgiving, so that, God granting and all the saints interceding, the living may deserve to attain a blessed end and the departed to enjoy eternal joys; so that strength and grace may be given to me, a sinner, in this obedience laid upon me; and so that mercy may be granted to us all on the day of the great judgment among the holy departed [Col. 0842C]. Amen.

[Col. 0841]

## Pious Ordinances of Abbot Pontius

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, III, 63.)

[Col. 0841C] Grant made by Pontius, Abbot of Cluny [Col. 0841D], to Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo.

Let the entire congregation of this venerable monastery, both present and future, know that Lord Pontius, the reverend abbot of this monastery, ordered concerning Lord Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, that after his death a thirty-day course of Masses be diligently performed for him by the brothers, with ringing bells, full office, and a general Mass. The meal which the dean of Galliniac provided on the vigil of Saint Matthew after Bernard’s death shall be provided on the day of his anniversary.

II.

[Col. 0842D]

Another grant made to Eskil, Archbishop of Lund.

Let all know that the entire community of this Church granted to the distinguished Lord Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, which is the metropolitan see of all Denmark, after his death every benefit in all respects equal to that performed for one of the brothers of Cluny, both at Cluny and in all its dependent places. For he was a great lover of this place.

[Col. 0843]

## Letter of Hugh, Monk of Cluny, to Lord Pontius, Abbot of Cluny

In which are discussed certain matters concerning Saint Hugh and Abbot Pontius himself: how he was made cardinal, and how devoutly he revered the ashes of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, brought to Cluny in the time of Saint Majolus, Abbot of Cluny.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 557.)

[Col. 0843A] To the most serene father, Pontius, Abbot of Cluny, his lord: Hugh, servant.

When I consider your excellence, Father, I do not dare to speak before you unbidden. But since I see that certain matters worthy of remembrance concerning the great holy Hugh, your predecessor, have been passed over in silence, if your graciousness bids me speak, I shall set forth briefly a few things out of many, small matters out of the greatest. I marvel indeed that those prolix writers, who composed such large volumes about him, omitted these things. What I relate is very well known to those now living, but, as you command, has been committed to the memory of posterity.

Blessed Hugh had once set out to visit the Frenchmen. On reaching the district of Beauvais, he entered Gournay upon the river Aronde. There the illustrious man Albert received him honorably. The man’s wife, named Ermengard, also reverently came to meet so great a guest. When the saint saw her, inspired by a prophetic spirit he said: “Lady, you are pregnant; you shall bear a son who, as it shall please God, will become a monk.” Hearing what she had not previously known about herself, the woman wondered. Those present, marking the oracle they had heard, rejoiced. Afterwards, in accordance with the word of the servant of God, the pregnant woman bore a son. The boy grew up and, assigned to the profession of arms, entered military service; and, as men of that kind are unhappily wont to do, he became ruinous.

Meanwhile the saint, full alike of days and virtues, ended his final day in the Lord. At that time Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, the glory of bishops, eminent in learning and conspicuous in holiness, was in Italy at Pavia. While blessed Hugh was departing from this present life [Col. 0843C] and being granted eternal life, the bishop saw distinguished companies being prepared to go forth with lights and with the other things customarily displayed solemnly in a procession. When the bishop asked who it was for whom so glorious a triumph was awaiting, the answer was given that this festive devotion of the saints was proceeding to escort Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny. The bishop wondered and disclosed this to his companions; and, when he had returned to Gaul and noted the time at which he had seen it, he found that the saint had departed at Cluny at the very time shown to him at Pavia.

After the saint’s death, you were happily elected and worthily appointed to the office of so great a Father. Led by the Lord, you went down into the aforesaid regions of France [Col. 0844A]. There, according to your noble custom of preaching good things to all, you found the young man of whom the saint had prophesied; having found him, you summoned him; having summoned him, you brought him out. We saw him at Cluny as a monk named Landric, for many years endowed with excellent morals. Thus, most gracious Father, thus your most holy predecessor Abbot Hugh, whom you loved greatly—indeed, whom you love—proved to have shone also in prophecy among his other virtues. Thus, at the dissolution of his body, revealed to a bishop, he is recognized as a fellow-citizen of the heavenly beings. But let my insignificance now be silent; let your charity rather consider how lofty these things are. For I, so very lowly, ought to have feared to speak of this height.

Finally, in the year 1118 from the Word born of the Virgin, Pope Paschal having died—he had governed the summit of the Roman see for eighteen years and more—Gelasius was chosen by a Catholic election and consecrated pope, a man highly learned, generous in almsgiving, and prudent in counsel. When Henry IV, emperor of the Romans, was raging against the Church, Gelasius withdrew to the sea, sailed for Gaul, and first sent a messenger from Pisa to announce his coming to you. For the Roman pontiff has you, namely the abbot of Cluny, as his own and special son in the regions of Gaul. You met him at Saint-Gilles and most elegantly supplied him and his large retinue with mounts and all other things in abundance.

When he had been made ill by the hardship of the sea, you most dutifully cared for the pope on the soil of your birth—the land which your father Peter, the powerful and noble count of Mergueil, had contested against the right of the apostles Peter and Paul and had thereby acquired [Col. 0844C]. When he had recovered and wished again to reach his Cluny, he passed through Lyons in Gaul and descended to Mâcon. There, worn down by a very severe illness, he most urgently commanded that he be carried to Cluny. Brought there and received with the highest reverence, after completing one year and four days of his episcopate, surrounded in his own house by bishops and cardinals amid the brethren, the shepherd himself rested in peace at his own Cluny.

After him the venerable Guy, archbishop of Vienne, was elected at Cluny by the Catholic Church and was thus ordained Pope Calixtus. He surpasses others in the height of earthly nobility, but shines more beautifully through the splendor of heavenly charisms. He returned to Cluny a second time, and there devoutly celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision and Epiphany. While he frequently spoke, among other matters, about the life and miracles of blessed Hugh, he did not attend to whatever prolix little documents had been written about these matters, but gladly accepted authoritative persons brought before the chapter of Cluny, who testified more convincingly concerning what they had seen and heard about the saint. With bishops and cardinals alike concurring, the pope decreed, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, that the feast-day of so great a confessor, approved by so many and such great virtues, should be celebrated.

On the day of the Lord’s Epiphany the pope went forth solemnly crowned, surrounded by an abundant choir of bishops and cardinals. The Roman military force then present attended him according to its custom [Col. 0845B]. How many nobles of Burgundy followed him! The sacred convent of Cluniac brethren came to meet him with most splendid ceremony: a community exalted by humility, enlarged by charity, instructed by discipline, and fortified by discernment.

On that same day, with the common assent of those of his household who sat around him, the fortunate Pope Calixtus granted to the Church of Cluny, his special and own church, that the abbot of Cluny should always and everywhere exercise the office of Roman cardinal. With his own hand the pope invested you with a ring, so that it might be manifest to all that Cluny, together with you and what is yours, is properly considered the peculiar possession of the Roman pope alone; and, by the Lord’s providence, it neither has ever been nor shall in the future be under the jurisdiction of another bishop or of any other power.

As the pope was about to depart on the following day, he entered the chapter of Cluny [Col. 0845C], commendably commended himself in his humility to the prayers of the brethren, strengthened them with blessings, and departed after recalling the memory of the aforesaid confessor. Let it suffice that I have said these things, and let your favor grant me pardon. But I beg that your fatherhood not be offended when my unworthiness presumes to ask you something.

You know, Father, that Pope Cornelius, glorious martyr, carefully placed the bones of Peter and Paul, removed from the Catacombs: those of Paul on the Ostian Way, and those of Peter in the Vatican. Their ashes, however, he reverently deposited in a fitting vessel in the monastery of Saint Paul. In subsequent years this monastery was entrusted to Saint Odo, your predecessor, and through him the vigor of the Cluniac order shone there for some time. At length, when the city was disturbed by seditious tumults, which that city most often suffers by unhappy custom, and evils pressed hard, the departing monks carried with them that vessel of apostolic ashes, these sacred pledges, and quickly reached Cluny.

In the days of Saint Majolus, the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Bourges, dedicated the monastery of Cluny and worthily deposited the aforesaid vessel of apostolic ashes in a column beneath the principal altar [Col. 0846B]. But when, Father, in your days, after the monastery had been built anew in a remarkable work, you ordered the old one demolished and the cloisters enlarged, you prudently preserved that aforesaid altar unmoved, and in its place, by divine counsel, caused the head of the old monastery to remain. For there, as those who have experienced it firmly believe, the grace of prayer and abundance of tears are fittingly found. There, through pious correction, the burden of sins is laid down. There the apostolic ashes—an inestimable treasure, Father—are visited with frequent reverence.

Because you often seek them in prayer, I beg you, though trembling, yet strengthened by your mercy, that before those most sacred apostolic ashes you may sometime deign to remember me, you who do not cease to show mercy to your own. And while you often commemorate in supplicatory prayer the holy confessor, blessed Hugh [Col. 0846C], I beg you to obtain that he may deign to assist also that mother whom you brought with you from France together with her three sons, and whom you piously received as a mother at Marcigny, her sons at Cluny. And because I have spoken much, I beg your pardon.

[Col. 0845]

# PIOUS DONATIONS MADE TO THE CLUNIACS UNDER THE GOVERNMENT OF ABBOT PONTIUS

## I. Peter, bishop of Bourges, grants and confirms to Cluny the church of Carandigna.

[Col. 0845C–D]  
(MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, I, 246, from the Cluniac cartulary of Colbert.)

To the most reverend community of the holy Church of Cluny: P[eter], by God’s grace bishop of the Church of Bourges, greeting and sincere love in Christ.

We do not believe that your prudence is unaware how pious, just, and consonant with Christian faith it is to honor, assist, and love religious men; and how evil, wicked, and contrary to the salvation of souls it is to attack and trouble them and to take away their rights. Moved, therefore, by this consideration, I have resolved to honor, assist, and love your church, whose order’s good reputation has spread far and wide [Col. 0846C]. Accordingly, I give, grant, and confirm to you and to your Church of Cluny [Col. 0846D] the church of Carandigna with all its appurtenances, which Alfonso, emperor of blessed memory, formerly bestowed upon you and your church for the remedy of his own soul and of the souls of his parents.

## II. Letter of Baldwin, count of Flanders, to Pontius, abbot of Cluny—confirming to him the abbey of Saint-Bertin.

(MARTÈNE, ibid., p. 334.)

To Lord P[ontius], reverend abbot of the holy Church of Cluny: BALDWIN, count of Flanders, and CLEMENTIA, countess, eternal happiness in Christ.

[Col. 0847A] Desiring that matters pertaining to religion should remain firm, lest the crafty enemy be able to overthrow what has been well begun, we make known to your serenity that we now willingly grant anew to you and your successors, for the remedy of our souls, and declare fully ratified, all pretext set aside, that concession concerning the church of Saint-Bertin which my lord Count Robert, while still living, with my own consent, granted and confirmed in writing to your predecessor, Lord Abbot Hugh of pious memory.

Moreover, that this our concession may remain firm in the sight of princes, we have confirmed it with their assent and caused it to be subscribed with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lambert, abbot. Sign of Walter, treasurer. Sign of Rainier [Col. 0847B], notary. Sign of Bernard, chaplain. Sign of Alard. Sign of Rotger, castellan of the island. Sign of Walter, castellan of Courtrai. Sign of Raiger, steward. Sign of William, steward. Sign of Ulric, cupbearer. Sign of Guy.

Done in the year of the Lord 1112, in the town of Ypres, on the day before the Ides of April.

## III. Charter of William, archbishop of Besançon, concerning Haute-Pierre.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 577.)

WILLIAM, by God’s grace archbishop of the holy Church of Besançon, to the venerable Father Lord PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors lawfully appointed in perpetuity.

It belongs to the pastoral office to uproot and destroy, to lay waste and scatter, to build and plant. Therefore, since almighty God has placed us over his people for this purpose: that we may cultivate the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts through regular discipline, strive to uproot vices, destroy superfluities, and implant the seedlings of virtues; and since we cannot accomplish this by our own strength without fellow-workers, we must enlist from every place experienced cultivators, men of virtue, who, laboring manfully until evening, may take refuge at the breasts of our consolation beneath the shelter of divine protection, and, eating the fruit of their hands’ labors with us, may gain for themselves and for us the denarius of eternal blessedness.

Because the Church of Cluny is known to have, above other churches of Gaul, very skilled cultivators of this sort of spiritual husbandry, and many more of them [Col. 0847D], assenting to the petitions of our venerable brother Walcher, prior of Gigig… [lacuna], we have given and granted the church of Haute-Pierre, formerly deprived of monastic religious life, to you, O abbot of Cluny beloved by God, and to the most holy community of that place, to inhabit and, with God as author, to form more watchfully in the religion of the monastic order.

Done at Besançon in the church of Saint John, with the approval of Pontius, prior of Haute-Pierre; Lord Stephen, canon of the same church and cantor of Besançon; Lord Mainerius, dean; Lord Bernard, master; Lord Manasses, archdeacon; Stephen, treasurer; Burchard and Hugh, archdeacons; and many others. Afterwards, at Cluny, on the third day before the Ides of August, I myself was present in your chapter [Col. 0848A], and, together with those who were with me, approved and confirmed the same, saving our rights and due customs. Now likewise, by the page of the present privilege, we approve, grant, and confirm to you and your successors the aforesaid church of Haute-Pierre with all its appurtenances, saving, as stated above, our rights and due customs.

Indeed, if any person, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, let that person be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord until making due satisfaction and amending the offense; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. For those who preserve these provisions, peace and tranquility. Amen.

## IV. Charter of Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, concerning the church of Saint Columba.

[Col. 0848B]  
(Ibid.)

I, AMELIUS, by God’s grace bishop of Toulouse.

Recognizing that the church of Saint Columba, situated in the territory of Toulouse in the district of Cher, beside the river Hers, belongs by right to Saint Peter of the monastery of Cluny, I restored to Cluny, into the hand of Lord Abbot PONTIUS, that church of Saint Columba together with the churches belonging to it, saving the right of the Church of Toulouse. I did this because of the great and very dear affection preserved from ancient times until now between our predecessors and the Fathers of Cluny, and because of the sincere and truly brotherly friendship which I have especially with the aforesaid abbot and shall always endeavor to maintain; and so that I may deserve to share in the Cluniac fraternity in all their good works. I wish and pray that all my lawful successors who approve this act and charter may share in that good.

Our canons of the see of Toulouse, Arnald William the archpriest and the others, approved this act. Viscount Bernard Aton also restored that church with its appurtenances and made a new donation of it to Cluny, into our hand and that of the aforesaid abbot, insofar as it could belong to him; granting that, with his consent, any of his vassals holding anything from the goods of the aforesaid church of Saint Columba should restore it. Moreover, my brother Peter Raymond [Col. 0848D] and his wife Adila, who was the sister of the aforesaid abbot, freely restored whatever they possessed from the goods of the church; and together they gave their son, a boy named William, to become a monk at Cluny.

Sign of Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, who redonated and approved the church of Saint Columba with its appurtenances to Cluny and confirmed this charter concerning it.

Sign of Raymond, archbishop of Auch, who was present at both donations, namely those of the bishop and the viscount.

Sign of Arnard Raymond, provost. Sign of Arnald William, archpriest. Sign of Isarn, prior of Frigdel. [Col. 0849A] Sign of William, chaplain. Sign of Bernard Aton, viscount. Sign of Bernard of Villamod.

Moreover, very many other monks, clerics, and knights were witnesses.

Done at Saint Eulalia near Carcassonne, in the hand of Lord Pontius, abbot of Cluny, in the year 1110 from the Incarnation of the Lord, under Lord Paschal II, with Louis reigning as king of the Franks.

Albert the German wrote it when requested.

## V. Charter of Riquin, administrator of Toul, concerning the cell of Frondon.

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Father [Col. 0849B], Son, and Holy Spirit: RIQUIN, by God’s grace administrator of Toul, to PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, and his successors lawfully advanced in perpetuity.

The height of apostolic dignity must be honored unceasingly by all the faithful with ever more earnest devotion, because it is manifest that, through their merits and teaching, the holy Church shines like the sun and moon; founded upon the rock, it rejects the incitements of heretical depravity and does not accept its allurements. Therefore, although devoted service ought to be offered to all whom the King of heaven has made sharers in his kingdom and glory, yet it is fitting more urgently and vigilantly to devote the service of heartfelt desire to him whom God has specially established as ruler of the Church redeemed by his blood: who, after God, is guardian of the flock and shepherd of the sheep, keeper of heaven’s gate, and prince of the apostles.

Accordingly, the holy Church of Cluny, triumphantly marked by the name and title of blessed Peter, shines incomparably under the prerogative of religion. With the bodily eyes closed and cast down, it teaches us, in spiritual fervor, eagerly to contemplate heavenly things. It is, if I may truly say so, the universal household and court of the supreme Householder, in which sacred proclamations of praise ring out to God. From this blessed company and unconquerable army, the heavenly Jerusalem takes to itself purple-clad ranks, who sit upon thrones of judging orders and wear flourishing garlands. Most happy and blessed is the devotion which faithfully serves the offices and worship of so celebrated [Col. 0849D] a congregation and church.

Although unworthy, desiring to be an executor and participant in its benefactions and prayers, I have resolved, according to my means, to enlarge it with necessary resources and to establish canonically what it possessed in our diocese. Therefore, for the perpetual peace of your monastery, Pontius, most beloved son in Christ, we make known to posterity the settlement of the case of the cell of Frondon, decided in our time.

Bertricus by name, abbot of Moyen-Moutier, appearing before our tribunal in the general synod, brought a complaint against Wicard, prior of the cell of Frondon. He asserted that Odoin, an illustrious man, had made a gift and investiture of that cell to Saint Peter of Moyen-Moutier in the presence of free witnesses; but that, having later revoked the gift, the Church of Cluny had invaded it irrationally and even presumptuously. The aforesaid Odoin, then present there, denied this entirely; he offered to swear, producing free witnesses, that he had never made any donation of it to the Church of Moyen-Moutier.

The prior, however, using wiser counsel, asked for a delay until the next synod, in order to consult his abbot on the matter, as the case required. Because of the length of the journey and the remoteness of the abbot, and as the difficulty of the matter pressed, he extended this delay to the third synod. At length, before the whole synodal assembly, he produced a charter bearing the seal of our fortunate predecessor of pious memory, Pibo. It contained that Lord Odoin, through the hand of the aforesaid bishop, had freely made a donation of the cell of Frondon, together with all its appurtenances, to Saint Peter of Cluny; and that the abbot of Cluny had already peacefully possessed it under his administration for nearly thirty years [Col. 0850B].

Finally Odoin himself came forward decisively and proved by oath, employing six free witnesses, that these matters stood thus. Overcome by so evident a reason and so convincing an inquiry, the abbot of Moyen-Moutier departed disappointed in his vain hope. The prior of Cluny then requested that what belonged to our office be done concerning the matter.

Therefore, by the ban of God and our own, and also by pontifical authority, we decree and forbid that anyone henceforth bring a claim against the Church of Cluny concerning the cell of Frondon; otherwise, let that person find upon his soul the curse of most severe judgment and have no part in the lot of God’s elect, unless, making worthy satisfaction, he repents. But may divine mercy grant to you and all yours perseverance in your saving purpose in his holy service; and may the Lord make your face like adamant and flint, so that with great freedom you may rebuke the rebellious house.

Therefore, in order to exclude every future controversy, we have decreed that this page of record be made; confirming it lawfully with our seal, we have delivered it to be strengthened by the signs and testimony of our faithful men.

Sign of Riquin, bishop. Sign of Theomar, abbot of Saint Mansuetus. Sign of Vindric, abbot of Saint Aper [Col. 0850D]. Sign of Stephen, primicerius. Sign of Berengar, dean. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Gotbert, archdeacon and cantor. Sign of Odoin. Sign of Theodoric of Saint-Hilaire. Sign of Theodoric of Calmont. Sign of Equin of Barbanville. Sign of Gerard of Blanteries. Sign of Adelin of Girancourt. Sign of Walter of Calmont. Sign of Walter and Theodoric, his brother, of Vinricourt.

These things were done at Toul, in the general synod, in the greater church of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, in the year 1111 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fourth indiction of our ordination, epact 9, concurrent 6, Henry IV being emperor, and our Lord Jesus Christ happily reigning. Amen.

## VI. William, bishop of Périgueux, gives to Cluny and Abbot Pontius the church of Saint Theodore of Rocaboucort.

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, 486.)

William, by God’s grace bishop of Périgueux, to the venerable Lord PONTIUS, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors lawfully appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of the wise has provided that the deeds of their times be perpetuated through the service of writing, lest they be able to be obliterated from the memory of posterity by the passage of future time. Therefore I wish it to be made known by the letters of this present document to those present and absent alike that I, bound by the necessity of my office to care for all churches of our diocese and desiring the rights of religion to be observed in them, give and grant to be held forever, to God and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and to Lord Pontius, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and his successors, the church [Col. 0852A] of Saint Theodore of Rocaboucort.

This is done with the counsel of the clerics of the see of Périgueux—namely William of Nanclart, Arnald, William, Iterius of Sauzet, and many others who were present with us—and with the concurrent gift and grant of the canons of the same church, namely Iterius, Gardra, Helias of Sauzet, Peter Iterius, Gerald Ferron, Peter Hugh, and many others. It is further approved and confirmed by Lord Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman Church, in the presence of the clerics of the Church of Angoulême, Richard and his brother William, nephews of that same legate, together with Eudrard the chaplain and Theaum, his notary.

That this gift may be held securely without another’s claim and may remain ratified, I authenticate this charter with the protection of our seal and invest the aforesaid abbot of Cluny, under the testimony of the same our clerics; and of the monks: Pontius, prior of Berbezil; Gerald Robert, prior of Mont-Berulph; and Arnald, prior of Rocenac [Col. 0852B]. This gift was made in the year 1121 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Calixtus presided in the apostolic see and King Louis reigned in France, with the Lord Jesus Christ reigning everywhere. Amen.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1125: PETER LEONIS AND GREGORY, LEGATES OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0851]

# LETTERS OF PETER LEONIS AND GREGORY

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 687 and 697, from the manuscript of Saint-Vaast.)

## I. Letter of Peter Leonis, priest, and Gregory, deacon of Saint Angelus, cardinals, to Angelrannus, bishop of Amiens—ordering him to ensure the restoration to Saint-Vaast of Arras of the altar of Campanioles.

(Year 1125.)

P. Leonis, priest, and G., deacon of Saint Angelus, cardinals and legates of the apostolic see, to their venerable brother A., bishop of Amiens: greeting.

Our most beloved brother, the abbot of Saint-Vaast, has complained to us very greatly that Guy, a knight, transferred a certain altar of Campanioles from the right of Saint-Vaast into the control of the monastery of Montreuil. This is wholly contrary to reason and the authority of the saints. Therefore we command and order your brotherhood to have that altar restored to the right and authority of the aforesaid monastery of Saint-Vaast.

> **Note [Col. 0851] (1).** Peter Leonis later became the antipope Anacletus, who contended with Innocent II for the papacy.

## II. Letter of Peter Leonis, priest, and Gregory, deacon of Saint Angelus, cardinals, to A., abbot of Anchin—concerning the dependents granted by Baldwin’s widow to the church of Blessed Mary.

(About 1130.)

P. Leonis, priest, and G., deacon of Saint Angelus, cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See, to their venerable brother A., abbot of Anchin: greeting and affection.

We have read the account of the case between the canons of Blessed Mary and the abbot of Saint-Vaast, which your brotherhood communicated to us; and, according to the tenor of the document which you sent us, this is our judgment. If the abbot of Saint-Vaast can prove that, before Baldwin’s widow granted those dependents to the church [Col. 0853A] of Blessed Mary, the said dependents had been adjudged by judgment of the city’s scabini to that woman and her children, and had been adjudged to Saint-Vaast to be possessed peaceably, her donation will have no force. Likewise, if he can show that the earlier donation to the monastery of Saint-Vaast was made not conditionally but absolutely, the second will have no validity. Likewise, if the landed estate on which the dependents reside belongs to Saint-Vaast, those dependents cannot be transferred to another church without the abbot’s assent.

> **Note [Col. 0853] (2).** That is, the cathedral church dedicated to Blessed Mary.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1128: JOHN MICHAELENSIS

[Col. 0853]

# NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, XI, 67.)

All that is known about John Michaelensis is that he attended, in January 1128, a council held at Troyes, where he performed the functions of secretary. Indeed, he himself seems to suggest this in the prologue to the Rule of the Templars attributed to him. Aubert Le Mire, who first made this Rule public in his *Chronicle of the Order of Cîteaux*, from a manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, claims that Saint Bernard was its author. In this he has been followed by all those who have subsequently had occasion to speak of the Knights Templar and their Rule.

Haeften (*Disquisitiones Monasticae*, tract IX, disq. IX, p. 86), after Stellartius, observes that this Rule was given to them by Saint Bernard, but in a style very different from that of the holy doctor; and that one might say he wished to adapt himself to the capacity of these good knights, if his discourse addressed to the same knights were not as eloquent as the other works of the holy abbot. Manrique, under the year 1128, cites two texts to prove that the Rule in question is Saint Bernard’s work. But Dom Mabillon shows, in the warning which he placed at the head of one of the saint’s writings (*Opera S. Bernardi*, I, p. 571), *On the Praise of the New Knighthood, Addressed to the Knights of the Temple*, that the two texts offer nothing favorable to this view but, on the contrary, entirely overthrow it.

> **Note [Col. 0853A] (1).** “Certainly, although the authority of our composition is commended by the very great number of religious Fathers who assembled in that council through divine admonition, nevertheless we ought not pass over in silence those in whose presence, and while they expressed the true judgments, I, John Michaelensis, by the grace of God deserved to be the humble scribe of this present document, by command of the council and of the venerable abbot of Clairvaux, to whom this task had been entrusted and was due.”

It appears from the first passage that, when the Council of Troyes charged Saint Bernard with composing a Rule for the Knights Templar, the saint transferred the task to John Michaelensis. Dom Mabillon explains it thus, and that is indeed its true meaning. If one wishes, one may dispute the term *scriba* (“scribe”), maintaining that John Michaelensis was only a copyist or secretary; but at least it is certain that the text does not mention Saint Bernard as having composed any Rule for the Templars.

As for those who might claim that John Michaelensis gives himself only the title of secretary and not author, we ask them whether the function which the Council of Troyes had assigned to Saint Bernard was merely that of scribe or secretary. John Michaelensis states that he performed the task which they had wished to assign to that holy abbot, and which belonged to him: *cui creditum ac debitum hoc erat*, “to whom this had been entrusted and was due.” He therefore composed the Rule himself and was not a mere copyist. One must nevertheless admit that there is a certain obscurity in the first text, which may have given Le Mire, Manrique, and others occasion to err; but a little attention would have prevented this mistake.

As for the second passage, it does indeed say that the Council of Troyes ordered that a Rule be drawn up for the Templars, but the author of the Rule is not named in it either directly or indirectly. Monsieur de Villefore, in his *Life of Saint Bernard* (Book II, pp. 124–125), says that the plan of giving a Rule to these knights seemed vast and remarkable to all the assembled prelates; and that, in honor of the letters of Pope Honorius and the patriarch of Jerusalem, they invited Bernard to compose the Rule requested by the knights. But Saint Bernard did not judge it fitting, adds Villefore, to take this care upon himself, and the Rule was made by someone else.

William of Tyre (Book XII, ch. 7) and James of Vitry (Book I, ch. 65) mention the Rule given to the Knights Templar at the Council of Troyes. Had Saint Bernard been its author, would these two historians have failed to say so? Yet they observe a profound silence concerning the author. A manuscript in the Cottonian Library states that this Rule was drawn up and written by John Michaelensis, by order of the council and of Saint Bernard. Moreover Alberic, a monk of Cîteaux, says that these knights were given the Rule of Saint Augustine; and the *Monasticon Anglicanum* likewise places them under the Order of Saint Augustine. It would be rather surprising if a Cistercian monk such as Alberic, living in the abbey of Trois-Fontaines, not far from Clairvaux, had been unaware that Saint Bernard composed this Rule, if he had actually been its author.

But what proves beyond reply that the Rule of the Templars cannot be Saint Bernard’s work is the difference between the style of the Rule and that of the holy abbot of Clairvaux. The Rule is [Col. 0855] filled with barbarous terms and Latin of the lowest quality. It displays none of that elevation of mind, nobility of style, taste for piety, or unction which reign in all Saint Bernard’s writings and characterize his genuine works. We shall not dwell further on refuting an opinion which destroys itself; it is sufficient to cast one’s eyes upon the work in question to become convinced that it is not by Saint Bernard.

It is certainly true that the Council of Troyes, wishing to carry out the intentions of Pope Honorius II and the patriarch of Jerusalem by drawing up a Rule for the Templars, selected Saint Bernard as more capable than anyone else of doing it well. But the holy abbot transferred the task to John Michaelensis, who composed it during the council itself, since it was read and approved there, as the author attests. There have, however, been several subsequent additions. It consists of seventy-two chapters, the same number as the Rule of Saint Benedict, from which its author borrowed several matters.

The purpose of this Rule is to combine monastic life with the profession of arms. It forbids the reception of children, lest they later repent of their commitments. In the year 1128 the Knights Templar numbered only nine; six of them appeared at the Council of Troyes, with Hugh of Payns, their first Grand Master, at their head. It may be presumed that they carried with them to Palestine, where they returned in the following year, the Rule which had been drawn up for them.

It has been published in various collections. André Favin included it in his *Théâtre d’honneur et de chevalerie* (Book IV, p. 16; 4, 1659), printed at Paris by Robert Foüet in 1620, quarto. The editor attributes it to Saint Bernard, although, by his own admission, it is not found among Bernard’s works. It was printed in the *Necrology of the Order of Cîteaux*, together with a letter of Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, in which that prince asks Saint Bernard to give a Rule to the Knights Templar; in Chrysostom Henriquez’s *Fasciculus sanctorum ordinis Cisterciensis*; in the tenth volume of the councils edited by Fathers Labbe and Cossart; and elsewhere.

M. Le Bœuf (Dissertations on the History of Paris, vol. II, p. 119), speaking of composers of ecclesiastical chant in the twelfth century, cites a certain Michalus, highly praised by Doctor Alain, as having corrected errors committed in this art:

> Music rejoices in Doctor Michalus,  
> And corrects its errors under such a master’s direction.

Would it be rash to conjecture that this Michalus might be the same person as our John Michaelensis? In any event, this musician is wholly unknown to us.

# RULE OF JOHN MICHAELENSIS FOR THE TEMPLARS

(LABBE, *Councils*, X, 923.) COUNCIL OF TROYES. [Note: [Col. 0855A] (2) Tyre, recounting the acts, time, and place of the council, writes as follows in book XII, chapter 7: “A council having been held in France at Troyes, attended by the lord archbishops of Reims and Sens with their suffragans, also by the bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See, and by the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux with many others, a rule was established for them and a white habit assigned, by command of Pope Honorius and Stephen, patriarch of Jerusalem. Although they had already been engaged in this undertaking for nine years, they were only nine in number; from that time their number began to increase and their possessions to multiply. Later, in the time of Pope Eugenius, it is said that they began to sew crosses of red cloth upon their mantles, in order to be more conspicuous among others—both the knights and [Col. 0856A] their lower-ranking brethren, called sergeants. Their estate grew so vastly that today they have, more or less, three hundred knights in their convent, clad in white cloaks, apart from the other brethren, whose number is almost countless. They are said to possess such extensive holdings both beyond and on this side of the sea that there is now no province in the Christian world which has not bestowed a portion of its goods upon the aforesaid brethren; and they are said today to possess resources equal to royal wealth. Since, as we have said, they have their dwelling beside the Temple of the Lord in the royal palace, they are called the brethren of the knighthood of the Temple. Although for a long time they maintained themselves in an honourable purpose, prudently fulfilling their profession, they neglected humility—the guardian, as is recognized, of all virtues, which, voluntarily seated low, has no place from which to suffer a fall—and withdrew themselves from the lord patriarch of Jerusalem, from whom they had received both the institution of their order and their first benefits, refusing him the obedience which their predecessors had rendered him. [Col. 0858] They also became very troublesome to the churches of God, withholding tithes and first-fruits from them [Col. 0858A] and wrongfully disturbing their possessions.”] In this council the Templar knights, in the ninth year of their institution, were assigned, together with their Rule, the white habit, in the year of the Lord 1128, during the pontificate of Pope Honorius II.

[Col. 0855]

# NOTICE

(MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, book LXXV, no. 28.)

Matthew, formerly prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, was made cardinal and bishop of Albano by Honorius. Sent into Gaul with legatine authority toward the end of the preceding year, he held a council at Troyes at the beginning of this year, [Col. 0857] attended by Rainaud of Reims and Henry of Sens with their suffragans, and many abbots, foremost among them Stephen of Cîteaux and Bernard of Clairvaux. We learn the time at which the council was held from the prologue of the Rule of the Knights of the Temple, which was approved at that council: namely, on the feast of Saint Hilary, in the year 1128 from the incarnation of the Son of God, in the ninth year from the beginning of the aforesaid knighthood, which took its origin from Master Hugh of Payns.

This prologue was written, and the judgments of the Fathers recorded, by John Michaelensis at the command of the council and of the venerable abbot of Clairvaux, to whom this task had been entrusted and was due—namely, that he should be the council’s secretary. The same author recalls each of the bishops and abbots present at the council. These abbots were: the abbot of Vézelay, namely Rainaud, who not long afterward became archbishop of Lyons and legate of the holy Roman Church; the abbot of Cîteaux, namely Stephen; Hugh, abbot of Pontigny; Roger, abbot of Trois-Fontaines, whom Guy succeeded in the following year; the abbot of Saint-Denis of Reims; the abbot of Saint-Stephen of Dijon; and Guy, abbot of Molesme. Nor was the aforementioned Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux absent, and those named above freely praised his judgment aloud.

Matthew had repeatedly invited him to the council by letter.
