Bernard excused himself on the ground that, scorched by the burning heat of a raging acute fever and exhausted by sweats, weak flesh could not suffice for a willing spirit (BERNARD, letter XXI); but at last he had to obey the legate’s command. Besides the bishops and abbots, Alberic of Reims and Master Fulgery were also present at the council; and among the laity, Count Theobald, the count of Nevers, and Andrew of Baudement. Finally, Hugh, master of the knighthood, came with several of his disciples, who set before the Fathers the manner and observance of their institution. It therefore pleased the council that their Rule, examined and approved by the Fathers, should be committed to writing. This was done by John Michaelensis, secretary of the council.

This Rule is woven almost wholly from the words of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and consists of the same number of chapters, namely seventy-two. Its author is believed by many to have been Saint Bernard; yet it is enough to attribute to him the book *In Praise of the New Knighthood*, addressed to the Knights Templar and dedicated to Master Hugh.

[Col. 0857]

# RULE OF THE POOR FELLOW-SOLDIERS OF CHRIST AND OF THE TEMPLE OF SOLOMON

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0857A] Our address is directed first of all to all who despise following their own wills and desire, with purity of mind, to serve as soldiers of the highest and true King: let them choose, with the most earnest care, to take up the splendid armour of obedience, to fulfil it, and to fulfil it perseveringly. Therefore we exhort you who until now [Col. 0857B] have embraced secular knighthood, in which Christ was not the motive but only human favour, to hasten to join forever the fellowship of those whom the Lord has chosen from the mass of perdition and, by gratuitous mercy, has formed for the defence of the holy Church.

But above all, whoever you are, O soldier of Christ, in choosing so holy a way of life, you must bring pure diligence and steadfast perseverance to your profession. This way of life is known to be so worthy, holy, and exalted before God that, if it is observed purely and perseveringly, you will deserve to obtain a share among those soldiers who gave up their souls for Christ. For in it the military order has now blossomed and shone anew—a military order which, having despised zeal for justice, strove not to defend the poor or churches, as was its duty, but to seize, plunder, and kill.

It is therefore well with us that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ has continuously sent his friends from the holy city into France and Burgundy, who do not cease to offer their souls as a sacrifice pleasing to God for our salvation and for the propagation of the true faith. Therefore, with all rejoicing and brotherly [Col. 0858B] affection, and at the request of Master Hugh, in whom the aforesaid knighthood had its beginning, we gathered together, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, from various dwelling-places of the province beyond the mountains, at Troyes, God leading us, on the feast of Saint Hilary in the year 1128 from the incarnation of the Son of God, the ninth year from the beginning of the aforesaid knighthood.

We deserved to hear, chapter by chapter, from the mouth of Master Hugh himself, the manner and observance of the order of knighthood. Whatever, according to the limited measure of our understanding, seemed absurd to us, and everything which at the present council could not be reported and reckoned up in a memorable manner, we have not lightly but deliberately and unanimously entrusted to the providence and discernment of our venerable Father Honorius and of the illustrious Stephen, patriarch of Jerusalem—who were not ignorant of the fruitfulness and necessity of religion in the East [perhaps *regionis*, “region”]—and likewise to the counsel of the common chapter of the poor fellow-soldiers of Christ.

Indeed, although the authority of our formulation is greatly commended by the very large number of religious Fathers who assembled at that council under divine prompting, we ought not to pass over in silence those in whose presence, and while they uttered their true judgments, I, John Michaelensis, by command of the council and of the venerable abbot of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 0859D] (3) Understand Saint Bernard.], to whom this task had been entrusted and was due, deserved by divine grace to be the humble secretary of the present document.

## Names of the Fathers Sitting in the Council of Troyes

First sat Matthew, bishop of Albano, by God’s grace legate of the holy Roman Church; then Rainaud, archbishop of Reims; third, [Col. 0859B] Henry, archbishop of Sens; then their fellow bishops: Rancidus, bishop of Chartres; Goffelinus, bishop of Soissons; the bishop of Paris; the bishop of Troyes; the prelate of Orléans; the bishop of Auxerre; the bishop of Meaux; the bishop of Châlons; the bishop of Laon; the bishop of Beauvais; the abbot of Vézelay, who not long afterward became archbishop of Lyons and legate of the holy Roman Church; the abbot of Cîteaux; the abbot of Pontigny; the abbot of Trois-Fontaines; the abbot of Saint-Denis of Reims; the abbot of Saint-Stephen of Dijon; the abbot of Moles . . . . [of Molesme].

The aforementioned Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux was not absent, and those named above freely praised his judgment aloud. There were also Master Alberic [Col. 0860A] of Reims and Master Fulgery, and many others whom it would take too long to enumerate. Moreover, concerning the unlearned, it seems fitting to bring forward as witnesses lovers of truth: Count Theobald, the count of Nevers, and Andrew of Bandinento [Baudement], who, with the most earnest care, examined what was best and moderated what seemed absurd to them, were present at the council.

Master Hugh himself, master of the knighthood, was indeed not absent; and he brought with him some of his brethren: Brother Godfrey, Brother Rorallus, Brother Geoffrey Bisol, Brother Pagan of Montdidier, and Archembaud of Saint-Amand. This Master Hugh, with his disciples, made known to the aforesaid Fathers, according to the compass of his memory, the manner and observance of the small beginning of his military order, which took its beginning from him who says, “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

It therefore pleased the council that the counsel there carefully examined by the file and consideration of the divine Scriptures, yet with the providence of the pope of Rome and the patriarch of Jerusalem, and likewise with the consent of the chapter of the poor fellow-soldiers of the Temple which is in Jerusalem, should be committed to writing, lest it be consigned to oblivion. It was to be observed inviolably, so that they might worthily deserve to arrive, by a straight course, at their Creator—whose sweetness surpasses honey so greatly that, in comparison with it, the bitterest wormwood is as nothing—through the aid of him whom they serve and may serve through endless ages of ages. Amen.

# HERE BEGINS THE RULE OF THE POOR FELLOW-SOLDIERS OF THE HOLY CITY

[Col. 0859]

## I. How They Are to Hear the Divine Office

[Col. 0859C]

You who have renounced your own wills, and others who serve as soldiers with you until a fixed term, with horses and arms, for the salvation of souls and for the highest King, should diligently strive universally to hear Matins and the whole complete service, according to canonical institution and the custom of the regular teachers of the holy city, with devout and pure affection.

This is especially owed by you, venerable brothers, because, despising the light of this present life and the suffering of your own bodies, you have promised forever, for the love of God, to hold the raging world as worthless. Refreshed and satisfied with divine food, and instructed and strengthened by the Lord’s commands, after the completion of the divine mystery let none fear [Col. 0859D] battle, but let him be ready for the crown.

## II. How Many Lord’s Prayers They Are to Say if They Cannot Hear the Divine Service

If any brother is perhaps absent on business of Eastern [Col. 0860C] Christendom—which we do not doubt has happened often—and for such absence does not hear the divine service, we commend and unanimously affirm aloud that he should say thirteen Lord’s Prayers for Matins, seven for each of the Hours, and nine for Vespers. For those engaged in this saving labour cannot come at the fitting hour to the divine office. But, if possible, the appointed Hours should not pass before the prescribed duty has been performed.

## III. What Is to Be Done for Deceased Brothers

When any remaining brother pays to death, which spares no one, that which cannot be taken away, we command that the chaplains and clerics who, together with you until the fixed term, serve the highest priest in charity, offer solemnly to Christ, with purity of heart, the appointed office and Mass for his soul. The brothers present, remaining overnight in prayers for the salvation of the deceased brother, shall pay one hundred Lord’s Prayers [Col. 0861A] for the deceased brother until the seventh day. From the day on which the brother’s death has been announced to them until the aforesaid day, let the number one hundred, the completeness of perfection, be observed with brotherly observance.

Further, by divine and merciful charity we beseech, and by pastoral authority command, that every day, just as it was given and is due to a brother in turn, what is necessary for the sustenance of this life—in food and drink only—be supplied to some poor person until the fortieth day. We altogether forbid all other offerings which the voluntary poverty of the poor fellow-soldiers of Christ had customarily rendered indiscriminately to the Lord at the deaths of brethren, at the Paschal solemnity, and on other solemnities.

## IV. Chaplains Shall Have Only Food and Clothing

[Col. 0861B]

We command, with vigilant care, that other offerings and every kind of alms, however made, be rendered to the unity of the common chapter, whether to chaplains or to others residing temporarily. Therefore the servants of the church shall have food and clothing only according to authorization, and shall not presume to possess anything more, unless the master voluntarily gives it to them in charity.

## V. Concerning Knights Who Remain for a Fixed Term and Die

There are knights dwelling mercifully with us for a fixed term in the house of God and of the Temple of Solomon. Therefore, with ineffable compassion, we ask, beseech, and finally earnestly command you that, if meanwhile dreadful power brings any one [Col. 0861C] to his last day, some poor person shall have, for his soul’s sake, seven days’ sustenance out of divine love and brotherly devotion.

## VI. No Remaining Brother Shall Make an Offering

We have decreed, as was said above, that no remaining brother shall presume to make another offering; but day and night, with a pure heart, let him remain in his profession, so that he may be able in this to make himself equal to the wisest of the prophets:

> “I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115),

and, in my death, I will imitate the death of the Lord. For as Christ laid down his soul for me, so I too am ready to lay down my soul for my brothers. Behold a fitting offering; behold a living sacrifice pleasing to God.

## VII. Concerning Excessive Standing

[Col. 0861D]

Since a most truthful witness has declared to our ears that you hear the divine office by standing excessively and without measure, we do not command this to be done; indeed, we censure it. Rather, when the psalm “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord” has ended, with the invitatory and hymn, we command all—strong and weak alike—to sit, in order to avoid scandal.

While you are sitting, at the end of each psalm, when the *Glory be to the Father* is recited, we direct you to rise from your seats and pray toward the altars, out of reverence for the Holy Trinity there named; the weak are to bow. Likewise, at the recitation of the Gospel, at “We praise thee, O God,” and throughout Lauds until the conclusion of “Let us bless the Lord,” we prescribe standing; and we command that the same [Col. 0862A] rule be kept at the Matins of Saint Mary.

## VIII. Concerning the Refection of the Community

We believe that you take food together in one hall—better called a refectory. There, when something necessary is required, because of ignorance of the signs it should be requested gently and privately. At table, always request whatever is necessary for you with all humility and submissive reverence, as the Apostle says: “Eat your bread in silence” (2 Thessalonians 3). And the Psalmist should encourage you in saying: “I set a guard upon my mouth,” that is, “I resolved within myself that I should not offend with my tongue” (Psalm 38), that is, “I guarded my mouth lest I speak evil.”

## IX. Concerning Reading

[Col. 0862B]

At dinner and supper let holy reading always be recited. If we love the Lord, we should desire with most attentive ear his saving words and commands. The reader of the readings shall indicate silence to you.

## X. Concerning the Eating of Meat

During the week, unless the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, the feast of Saint Mary, or All Saints should occur, three meals of meat are sufficient for you; for habitual eating of flesh is understood to be an honourable [perhaps *onerosa*, “burdensome”] corruption of bodies. But if such a fast falls on Tuesday that the eating of meat is withheld, let it be supplied to you abundantly on the following day.

On Sunday, to all remaining knights and likewise to chaplains, two dishes seem undoubtedly good and fitting in honour of the holy Resurrection. Let the others, namely squires and servants, remain content with one dish, with thanksgiving.

## XI. How Knights Ought to Eat

It is generally necessary that they eat two by two, so that one may diligently look after the other, lest harshness of life or secret abstinence be introduced into every meal. We judge it just, moreover, that each knight or brother should have for himself alone an equal and equivalent measure of wine.

## XII. That on Other Days Two or Three Dishes of Vegetables Shall Suffice

On other days—namely Monday, Wednesday, [Col. 0862D] and Saturday—we believe that two or three dishes of vegetables or other foods, or, so to speak, cooked pottages, suffice for all; and we command that this be observed, so that anyone unable to eat from one may be refreshed from another.

## XIII. What Food Is to Be Taken on Friday

On Friday, in reverence for the Passion, we commend that Lenten food be sufficient once for the whole community, excluding the weakness of the sick, from the feast of All Saints until Easter, unless the Nativity of the Lord or the feast of Saint Mary or of the Apostles occurs. At another time, unless a general fast occurs, let them eat twice.

## XIV. After Meals They Shall Always Give Thanks

After dinner and supper we command without exception that, in the church, [Col. 0863A] if it is nearby, or otherwise in the same place, thanks be rendered, as is fitting, with a humbled heart to our highest provider, who is Christ. By brotherly charity they ought, and are commanded, to distribute scraps to servants or poor persons, while reserving whole loaves.

## XV. That the Tenth Loaf Shall Always Be Given to the Almoner

Although the reward of poverty, which is the kingdom of heaven, is undoubtedly due to the poor, nevertheless we command you—whom the Christian faith undoubtedly recognizes as belonging to their number—to give daily the tenth of all bread to your almoner.

## XVI. That the Collation Shall Be at the Master’s Discretion

When the sun leaves the eastern region and descends toward Iberia [perhaps *Ibernam*; likely “Iberia”], after the signal has been heard, as is the custom of that region, you must all proceed to Compline; and we desire that you first take the general collation. We place this collation at the master’s direction and discretion: when he wishes, it may be taken with water, and when he mercifully commands, suitably with diluted wine. But this must not be done to excessive fullness or luxuriance, but sparingly, for we see even wise persons become apostates.

## XVII. That Silence Shall Be Kept after Compline

After Compline has ended, you must go to bed. When the brothers leave Compline, they shall no longer have permission to speak in public unless necessity compels; but let each speak gently to his squire whatever he has to say. Perhaps, as you leave [Col. 0863C] Compline, some great necessity may compel you to speak with the master himself, or with the person to whom authority over the house is due after the master, concerning military business or the state of our house, because the day is not thought sufficient for this.

We command this to be done thus because it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10); and elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18). In that conversation we altogether forbid buffoonery, idle words, and words provoking laughter. As you go to bed, if anyone has spoken anything foolish, we command him to say the Lord’s Prayer with humility and a devotion to purity.

## XVIII. That the Weary Need Not Rise for Matins

[Col. 0863D] We do not commend that weary knights rise for Matins, as is evident to you. Rather, with the consent of the master, or of the person entrusted by the master, let them rest and say the prescribed thirteen prayers in such a way that their minds agree with their voices, according to the Prophet’s saying: “Sing wisely to the Lord” (Psalm 48); and: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to thee” (Psalm 137). We commend this unanimously to you. But this must always remain at the master’s discretion.

## XIX. That Common Provision Shall Be Maintained among the Brothers

The divine page reads: “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 2). Therefore we do not say that there should be favouritism, but that regard must be had for infirmities. Let the one who has less need give thanks to God and not be grieved; while the one in need should humble himself because of his infirmity, not exalt himself because of the mercy shown him; thus all members will be at peace. We forbid anyone to adopt excessive abstinence; rather, let them earnestly maintain the common life.

## XX. Concerning the Quality and Manner of Clothing

We command that clothing always be of one colour, for example white, black, or, as it is called, coarse brown (*burella*). To all professed knights we grant white garments in winter and summer, if possible, so that those who have put aside the dark life may recognize that through brightness and whiteness they are reconciled to their Creator. What is whiteness but complete chastity? Chastity [Col. 0864B] is security of mind and health of body. Unless every knight perseveres in chastity, he cannot come to eternal rest and see God, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “Pursue peace with all, and chastity, without which no one shall see the Lord” (Hebrews 12).

But because such clothing must be free from the appearance of arrogance and excess, we command that all have such garments as enable each man by himself, without difficulty, to dress and undress, and to put on and take off his shoes. The official responsible for this service shall diligently ensure that he does not give garments too long or too short, but distributes them according to the measure of each wearer’s size. Those receiving new garments shall always return their old ones [Col. 0864C] immediately, to be stored in the wardrobe or wherever the brother responsible for this service shall decide, for the use of squires and servants, and sometimes of the poor.

## XXI. That Servants Shall Not Have White Garments, That Is, White Mantles

We emphatically oppose this practice, which existed in the house of God and of the soldiers of his Temple without discernment and without the counsel of the common chapter; and we command that it be cut off utterly as a particular vice. For formerly servants and squires possessed white garments, from which intolerable harms arose. In the regions beyond the mountains certain false brethren arose—married men and others—saying that they belonged to the Temple although they belonged to the world. They brought so many affronts and harms upon the military order; and the resident servants, through pride, caused many scandals to arise from this.

Therefore let them always have black; but if such cannot be found, let them have whatever can be found in the province where they live, or what may be purchased most cheaply in one colour, namely coarse brown (*burella*).

## XXII. That Only Remaining Knights Shall Have White

No one, therefore, is permitted to wear white cloaks or possess white mantles except the knights of Christ named above.

## XXIII. That They Shall Use Lambskins

By common counsel we have decreed that no remaining brother shall ever possess skins, a fur garment, or anything of the sort belonging to bodily use, including [Col. 0865A] a covering, except lambskins or ram-skins.

## XXIV. That Old Garments Shall Be Distributed to Squires

The official or distributor of clothing shall faithfully and equally strive, with every care, always to distribute old garments to squires and servants, and sometimes to the poor.

## XXV. Whoever Desires the Best Shall Have Inferior Things

If any remaining brother, as his due or from an impulse of pride, wishes to have fine or superior things, he will undoubtedly deserve the meanest things because of such presumption.

## XXVI. That the Quantity and Quality of Garments Shall Be Observed

It is necessary to observe the quantity according to the size of bodies and the amplitude of garments. Let the distributor of clothing be attentive in this.

## XXVII. That the Distributor of Clothing Shall Above All Preserve Equality

As was said above, let the official consider their length by equal measure, with brotherly regard, lest anything attract the eyes of whisperers or accusers [perhaps *eriminatorum*]; and in all the matters stated above, let him humbly consider God’s recompense.

## XXVIII. Concerning Excessive Hair

All brothers, especially resident brothers, ought to have their hair cut so that it may be seen to be orderly and according to rule both before and behind. The same rule shall be observed without deviation with respect to the beard and moustaches (*grenniones*), lest excess or the vice of affectation be displayed.

## XXIX. Concerning Beaks and Knots

Beaked shoes and knots are plainly heathenish. Since this is acknowledged to be abominable by all, we forbid and prohibit anyone to possess them; indeed, he must be entirely without them. We do not permit, but altogether prohibit, others who serve temporarily from having beaked shoes, knots, excessive hair, or immoderately long garments. For those who serve the highest Creator need cleanliness, inwardly and outwardly, as he himself attests when he says: “Be clean, because I am clean.”

## XXX. Concerning the Number of Horses and Squires

[Col. 0865D] Each of you knights may have three horses, because the exceptional poverty of the house of God and the Temple of Solomon does not at present permit an increase beyond this, except with the master’s permission.

## XXXI. No One Shall Strike a Squire Serving without Pay

For the same reason we allow only one squire to each knight. But if that squire serves any knight freely and charitably, the knight may not beat him or punish him for any fault whatsoever.

## XXXII. How Those Who Remain for a Fixed Term Shall Be Received

We faithfully command all knights who desire with purity of heart to serve Jesus Christ in the same house for a fixed term [Col. 0866A] to purchase horses suitable for this daily service, arms, and whatever is necessary for them. Then we judge that the horses should be appraised fairly and advantageously, with equality preserved on both sides. Let the price be recorded in writing, lest it be forgotten. Whatever is necessary for the knight, his horses, or his squire, including horseshoes and their iron fittings, shall be supplied from the same house in brotherly charity, according to the house’s resources.

If meanwhile the knight loses his horses through any event in this service, the master shall provide others, as the house’s means require. When the time comes for returning home, the knight shall give half the price out of divine love; and, if he wishes, receive the other half from the common funds of the brethren.

## XXXIII. That No One Shall Act According to His Own Will

[Col. 0866B]

It is fitting that those knights who regard nothing dearer to themselves than Christ should, for the service they have professed, and for the glory of highest blessedness or fear of hell, maintain unceasing obedience to the master. It must be maintained so that, as soon as anything is commanded by the master or by the person to whom the master has given authority, they know no delay in performing it, as though it were commanded by God. Of such persons Truth itself says: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Psalm 17).

## XXXIV. Whether It Is Permitted to Go through the Town without the Master’s Command

Therefore we beseech and firmly command the knights dwelling in the house who have abandoned their own will, [Col. 0866C] and others serving for a fixed term, that they shall not presume to go into the town without the master’s permission, or that of the person entrusted with this duty, except at night to the Sepulchre and to the stations contained within the walls of the holy city.

## XXXV. Whether It Is Permitted for Him to Walk Alone

Those walking in this manner shall not dare to begin a journey, by day or night, without a guard—that is, a knight or resident brother. In the army, after they have been lodged, no knight, squire, or other person shall go through the quarters of other knights in order to see or speak with someone, without permission, as was said above.

Thus we affirm by counsel that, in such a house ordered by God, no one is to serve as a soldier or rest according to private ownership; rather, everyone shall devote himself wholly according to the master’s command, so that he may imitate the saying of the Lord: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5).

## XXXVI. That No One Shall Ask Specifically for What He Needs

We command that this particular custom be included among the others and kept with every consideration because of the vice of asking. Therefore no resident brother should specifically and by name ask for a horse, a mount, or arms. How then? If his infirmity, the weakness of his horses, or the weight of his arms is known to be such [Col. 0867A] that proceeding thus causes common harm, let him come to the master, or to the person whose duty it is after the master, and show him the reason in true faith and purity. Thereafter the matter shall lie at the discretion of the master, or after him of the procurator.

## XXXVII. Concerning Bridles and Spurs

We do not wish gold or silver, which are private riches, ever to appear on bridles, breast-straps, spurs, or stirrups; nor may any resident brother buy such things. But if old equipment of this kind is given charitably, let the gold or silver be coloured so that its shining colour or adornment may not seem an occasion of arrogance to others. If new things are given, let the master do with them whatever he wishes.

## XXXVIII. No Covering Shall Be Had on Lances and Shields

No covering shall be had on shields and lances, nor pennons on lances, because this is understood to be not beneficial but harmful to us.

## XXXIX. Concerning the Master’s Permission

The master may give horses, arms, or any other thing to anyone.

## XL. Concerning the Trunk and Bag

A bag and trunk with a lock are not permitted; we set this forth so that no one may possess them without permission of the master or of the person entrusted with the affairs of the house after him. This present chapter does not apply to procurators and those living in different provinces, nor is the master himself included.

## XLI. Concerning the Sending of Letters

No brother may in any way receive or send, whether from his relatives, from any other persons, or between brethren, without the command of the master or procurator. Once a brother has permission, the letters may, if the master wishes, be read in the master’s presence. If anything is sent to him even by his relatives, he shall not presume to receive it until it has first been reported to the master. But this chapter does not include the master or the procurators of the house.

## XLII. Concerning the Recounting of One’s Own Faults

Since every idle word is known to generate sin, what will those who boast of their own faults say before the strict Judge? The prophet certainly shows that if one must sometimes refrain even from good speech because of silence, how much more must one abstain from evil speech because of the punishment of sin. Therefore we forbid and strongly prohibit any resident brother from daring to recall to his brother, to anyone else, or concerning anyone else, the follies which, to speak more plainly, he committed so outrageously in the world in military affairs, or the pleasures of the flesh with most wretched women. If he happens to hear someone recounting such things, he shall make him be silent; or, as quickly as he can, he shall depart from there with the swift foot of obedience and not offer the ear of his heart to the seller of oil.

## XLIII. Concerning Gain and Acceptance

But if anything is given freely to any [Col. 0868A] brother without gain, let him bring it to the master or steward. If, however, his friend or relative is unwilling to give it except for his own use, he shall by no means receive it until he has permission from his master. Let the person to whom a thing has been given not be vexed if it is given to another; rather, let him know certainly that, if he is angered by this, he acts against God. The officials to whom this ministry concerning trunk and bag is specially owed and granted are not included in this aforesaid rule.

## XLIV. Concerning Horse Feed
This is a useful provision for all; we have established this precept so that henceforth it may be observed without deviation. No brother, however, may presume to make a linen or woollen eating-cloth specially for that purpose, nor may he possess any, except a small tablecloth.

### XLV.—That no one dare exchange or request anything

[Col. 0868B]

One further matter remains: no brother may presume to exchange his own possessions with another brother without the master’s permission, nor to ask for anything, except from brother to brother, and then only if the thing is small and cheap, not substantial.

### XLVI.—That no one catch a bird with a bird, nor travel with one who does so

We unanimously judge that henceforth no one may dare catch a bird by means of a bird. For it does not become religious persons to cling thus to worldly amusements, but rather willingly to hear the Lord’s commands, to devote themselves frequently to prayers, and daily in prayer to confess their sins to God with tears or groaning. No brother may presume, for this principal reason, to go in the company of a man engaged in such pursuits with a hawk or another bird.

### XLVII.—That no one strike a wild beast with bow or crossbow

It is fitting to conduct oneself with every religious observance, simply and without laughter, humbly, speaking not many words but reasonable ones, and not loudly. We specially enjoin and command every professed brother not to dare go in the wood with bow, crossbow, or javelin; nor may he accompany anyone doing this, except in order to protect him from a treacherous pagan. Nor may he dare shout or chatter with a dog, or spur his horse through desire to take a wild beast.

### XLVIII.—That a lion always be struck

For it is certain that this has been especially entrusted and assigned to you: to lay down your lives for your brothers and to remove from the earth the unbelievers, who continually threaten the Son of the Virgin. For of the lion we read that he himself goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5); and that his hand is against everyone and everyone’s hand against him (Gen. 16).

### XLIX.—Hear judgment in every matter brought against you

We know indeed that the persecutors of holy Church are innumerable and hasten incessantly, and ever more cruelly, to harass those who do not love contention. Therefore let the judgment of the council be weighed with calm consideration in this matter: if anyone in the regions of the East, or anywhere else, brings any claim against you, we command you to hear judgment through judges who are faithful and true lovers of you [Col. 0869A]; and we command you without deviation to do what shall be just.

### L.—That this rule be observed in all matters

We command that this same rule be permanently observed in all things wrongfully taken from you.

### LI.—That all professed soldiers may possess land and men

By divine providence, as we believe, this new kind of religious life took its beginning from you in the holy places: namely, that you should join military service to religion, and that religion, armed through military service, should proceed to strike the enemy without guilt. We therefore judge it right that, since you are called soldiers of the Temple, you yourselves, on account of distinguished merit and special worth, may have a house, land, and men [Col. 0869B], possess cultivators, govern them justly, and receive the due service specially owed to your institution.

### LII.—That unfailing care be taken of the sick

Above all, unfailing care must be given to sick brothers, so that they may be served as though Christ himself: thus that Gospel saying, “I was sick, and you visited me,” may be kept in memory. They are indeed to be borne carefully and patiently, because through such persons heavenly recompense is undoubtedly gained.

### LIII.—That necessities always be given to the sick

We command the officers responsible for the sick, with every observance and vigilant care, faithfully and diligently to provide, according to the resources of the house, whatever is necessary for the maintenance of their various illnesses [Col. 0869C]—for example meat, fowl, and other things—until they are restored to health.

### LIV.—That one not provoke another to anger

No small precaution must be taken that no one presume to stir another to anger, because the highest mercy has bound poor and powerful alike in the kinship and divine brotherhood.

### LV.—How married brothers are to be received

We permit you to receive married brothers in this manner: if they seek the benefit and participation of your brotherhood, each is to grant to the unity of the common chapter, after death, his share of property and whatever more they acquire; meanwhile they are to lead an honorable life and strive to do good to the brothers, but they may not wear a white garment and white mantle [Col. 0869D]. If the husband dies first, he is to leave his part to the brothers, and his wife is to have from the other part the means of living. For we consider it unjust that brothers of this kind should remain in one and the same house with brothers who have promised chastity to God.

### LVI.—That sisters no longer be admitted

It is dangerous henceforth to gather sisters together, since the ancient enemy has driven many from the straight path of paradise through female companionship. Therefore, dearest brothers, so that the flower of integrity may always appear among you, it is no longer lawful to follow this custom.

### LVII.—That brothers of the Temple not associate with excommunicated persons

[Col. 0870A]

Brothers, this must be greatly avoided and feared: no soldier of Christ may presume in any way to join himself to a person publicly and specifically excommunicated, or receive his goods, lest he likewise become *anathema maranatha* (“accursed at the Lord’s coming”). But if he has merely been interdicted, it will not improperly be lawful to associate with him and charitably receive his goods.

### LVIII.—How secular soldiers are to be received

If a soldier from the mass of perdition, or another layman, wishing to renounce the world, desires to choose your communion and way of life, do not assent to him immediately; rather, according to Paul’s saying, “test the spirits whether they are from God,” and so let entry be granted him. Let the Rule therefore be read in his presence [Col. 0870B]; and if he carefully obeys the precepts of the Rule set forth, then, if master and brothers wish to receive him, let the brothers be summoned and let him disclose to all, with complete sincerity, his desire and petition. Thereafter the period of probation is to depend wholly upon the master’s consideration and prudence, in accordance with the respectability of the applicant’s life.

### LIX.—That not all brothers be summoned to secret counsel

We do not command that all brothers always be called to counsel, but those whom the master recognizes as suitable and prudent in counsel. When, however, he wishes to deliberate about greater matters, such as giving common land [Col. 0870C], debating the Order itself, or receiving a brother, then it is fitting, if the master wishes, to summon the whole congregation; and, having heard the counsel of the common chapter, let that be done which the master judges better and more useful.

### LX.—That they ought to pray silently

We command by common counsel that brothers pray, as the disposition of mind and body requires, standing or sitting, yet with the greatest reverence, simply and without shouting, so that one may not disturb another.

### LXI.—That they receive the pledge of serving-men

We have learned that many from different provinces, both retainers and squires, fervently desiring the salvation of their souls, wish to bind themselves for a term in [Col. 0870D] our house. It is useful that you receive their pledge, lest perhaps the ancient enemy secretly or improperly suggest something to them in God’s service, or suddenly drive them from their good purpose.

### LXII.—That boys, while they are young, not be received among the brothers of the Temple

Although the rule of the holy Fathers permits boys to be kept in a congregation, we by no means approve your burdening yourselves with such persons. But anyone wishing to give his son or kinsman permanently to the military religious life should support him until the age at which he can manfully, with armed hand, remove Christ’s enemies from the Holy Land; then, according to the Rule, let the father or parents place him among the brothers and make their petition known to all. For it is better not to vow in childhood than, after he has become a man, to draw back disgracefully.

### LXIII.—That the aged always be honored

The aged must be supported with compassionate consideration according to the weakness of their strength and diligently honored; nor are they in any way to be held strictly to matters necessary for the body, while the authority of the Rule is preserved.

### LXIV.—Concerning brothers who travel through different provinces

Brothers sent through different provinces should endeavor, as their means permit, to observe the Rule in food, drink, and other matters, and live irreproachably, that they may have a good testimony from outsiders. Let them not defile the profession of religion by word or deed [Col. 0871B], but above all offer to all with whom they associate an example and seasoning of wisdom and good works.

Let the man with whom they resolve to lodge be adorned with the best reputation; and, if possible, the host’s house on that night should not lack a light, lest the dark enemy bring about slaughter—God forbid. Where they hear that soldiers who are not excommunicated have assembled, we say they should go there, considering not so much temporal advantage as the eternal salvation of those souls.

We approve that those brothers sent thus to overseas regions in hope of conveyance receive persons wishing permanently to join the military Order, on this agreement: that both meet in the presence of the bishop of that province [Col. 0871C], and that the prelate hear the applicant’s wish. When he has heard the petition, let the brother send him to the master and brothers in the Temple at Jerusalem; and if his life is honorable and worthy of such fellowship, let him be received mercifully, if it seems good to master and brothers.

But if he dies meanwhile, let the whole benefit and brotherhood of Christ’s poor and fellow-soldiers be bestowed upon him as upon one of the brothers, in return for his labor and hardship.

### LXV.—That food be distributed equally to all

We also judge that this ought fittingly and reasonably to be maintained: food is to be allotted equally, according to the resources of the place, to all brothers remaining there. For regard to persons is not useful; consideration of infirmities is necessary.

### LXVI.—That the soldiers of the Temple possess tithes

[Col. 0871D]

We believe that, having left abundant riches, you have subjected yourselves to voluntary poverty; hence we have shown that you who live the common life may justly possess tithes in this manner. If the bishop of the church to whom the tithe is rightfully due wishes charitably to give it to you, he ought, with the assent of the common chapter, to grant you those tithes which the church then appears to possess.

But if any layman still wrongfully holds it from his patrimony, and, strongly reproving himself for this, leaves the same to you, this may be done at the will of the superior alone, without the chapter’s consent.

### LXVII.—Concerning light and grave faults

If a brother, in speech, military service, or otherwise [Col. 0872A], commits any slight offence, he is voluntarily to reveal his offence to the master in making satisfaction. For slight offences, if they are not habitual, he is to undergo a light penance. But if, while he is silent, the fault becomes known through someone else, he is to be subject to a greater and more manifest discipline and correction.

If the offence is grave, he is to be removed from familiarity with the brothers and not eat with them at the same table, but take his meal alone. The whole matter is to rest upon the master’s dispensation and judgment, so that he may remain safe on the day of judgment.

### LXVIII.—For what fault a brother is no longer to be received

Above all it must be provided that no brother, powerful or powerless, strong or weak, seeking self-exaltation and gradually growing proud, remain undisciplined by defending his fault. If he refuses amendment, let stricter correction be applied to him [Col. 0872B]. If, after pious admonitions and prayers poured out for him, he refuses amendment and raises himself more and more in pride, then, according to the Apostle, let him be rooted out from the pious flock: “Remove the evil one from among you” (1 Cor. 5).

A diseased sheep must be removed from the society of faithful brothers. Yet the master, who ought to hold staff and rod in his hand—the staff, indeed, by which he supports the weakness of others’ strength, and the rod by which he strikes the vices of offenders with zeal for rectitude—should strive to act by counsel of the patriarch and spiritual consideration, lest, as blessed Maximus says, either lax gentleness fail to restrain the sinner, or immoderate severity fail to recall the offender from his fall.

### LXIX.—That from the Paschal solemnity until the feast of All Saints each may receive only one linen shirt

[Col. 0872C]

Meanwhile, on account of the excessive heat of the eastern region, we compassionately provide that from the Paschal feast until the solemnity of All Saints each person be given only one linen shirt—not as a due, but solely as a favor—for one who wishes to use it; at other times, however, all are generally to have woollen shirts.

### LXX.—How many and what kinds of bedding are necessary

We approve by common counsel that those sleeping separately, one in each bed, should sleep no otherwise unless a very great reason or necessity occurs. Each is to have bedding or bedclothes by the measured provision of the master [Col. 0872D]. We believe that a sack, mattress, and coverlet are sufficient for each.

Whoever lacks one of these is to have a rug, and may properly use a linen covering, that is, a *velus*, at all times; they are to sleep clothed in shirts and always sleep in drawers. While the brothers sleep, a lamp must never be lacking continually until morning.

### LXXI.—Concerning avoidance of murmuring

By divine admonition we command you to avoid and flee as a kind of plague rivalry, envy, spite, murmuring, whispering, and detraction. Let each therefore take care with watchful mind not to blame or rebuke his brother, but diligently heed within himself the Apostle’s saying: “Do not be an accuser or a whisperer among the people” (Lev. 19) [Col. 0873A].

When he clearly knows that a brother has committed some fault, let him peacefully and with brotherly kindness correct him alone, according to the Lord’s command; if he does not hear him, let him bring in another brother; but if he despises both, let him be publicly rebuked before all in the assembly.

For those who speak ill of others are greatly blind, and those who do not guard themselves from spite are exceedingly unfortunate; hence they are plunged into the ancient malice of the crafty enemy.

### LXXII.—That the kisses of all women be avoided

[Col. 0874A]

We believe it dangerous for every religious person to gaze too intently on women’s faces; therefore no brother may presume to kiss widow, virgin, mother, sister, aunt, or any other woman. Let Christ’s soldiery therefore flee women’s kisses, by which people are often endangered, so that with pure conscience and secure life it may dwell forever in the sight of the Lord.

# In the Year of the Lord 1127: Walter, Canon of the Church of Thérouanne, and Galbert of Bruges, on the Life and Martyrdom of Blessed Charles the Good, Count of Flanders

*(Bollandists, Acta Sanctorum, March, vol. I, 2 March, p. 152)*

[Col. 0873]

## Preliminary Commentary

### § I. The Life of Blessed Charles written by contemporary and other authors. His name entered in martyrologies. His bones elevated.

[Col. 0873B]

1. At Bruges, the most celebrated city of the Flemings, on 2 March 1127, Blessed Charles the Good, margrave or count of that most noble province, died as a martyr, murdered by several seditious men in the church of St Donatian. Divine mercy soon showed his virtue more eminently to the world through miracles wrought at his body; hence most of the princes of Flanders hastened there as quickly as possible to avenge the most wicked murder.

At that time the ecclesiastical government of the territory of Flanders was chiefly subject to the bishops of Tournai and Thérouanne. The former, who was at the same time bishop of Noyon, was called Simon, son of Hugh the Great, brother of Philip I, king of the Franks; Simon was cousin of Louis VI, called the Fat, who then ruled the Franks, both being descended from King Henry I as grandfather.

In Galbert’s *Life of Blessed Charles* below, no. 38 [Col. 0874B], Bishop Simon is called brother—namely, half-brother on the mother’s side—of Charles the Good’s wife. For his mother Adelaide, or Aleidis, after the death at Tarsus in Cilicia on 18 October 1102 of her first husband Hugh the Great, married again Count Rainald of Clermont and bore him Margaret, afterwards taken as wife by Charles the Good. The royal family of Charles the Good is explained below in the Acts.

2. The other bishop presiding over the church of Thérouanne was Blessed John, a man illustrious for holiness and learning, who laid aside this mortal flesh on 27 January 1130. We published his distinguished Acts, written by a contemporary author, under that day.

At this blessed bishop’s command Walter, canon of the same church of Thérouanne, and, as ancient codices state after the Acts themselves, archdeacon by rank and formerly intimate with Blessed Charles himself, wrote with great judgment [Col. 0874C] the lineage, life, death, and avenging of Count Charles.

In the manuscript *Universal Chronicle* of Theodoric Paul of Gorinchem, Walter is called a priest of Bruges. He himself states below in the *Life*, no. 29, that Charles summoned him to Ypres by command and that he was present with him on the third day before the Kalends of March, that is, three days before the murder; and in no. 40 he recounts what, speaking with the count that same day, he had learned from him concerning his inclination and desire for martyrdom.

Since he was not at Bruges when the holy count was killed, in no. 45 he testifies before God that what he reported of Charles’s death and miracles he knew by the testimony of the religious men Lord Elias, dean of Bruges, Fromold, provost of Furnes, and other clergy and laity who declared they had seen these things.

In no. 56 he says that he learned it from the report of a cleric summoned by Provost Bertulf when Walter was departing for Ypres. And in no. 70 he says that very many truthful and religious men who had been present testified to him when he inquired, one of whom, Absalom, abbot of St Amand, he judged worthy to name on account of his holiness [Col. 0875B].

He pursued the events which, as he writes at the end before the epilogue, “were completed within almost two months after the count’s death.” Walter evidently published this *Life*, composed by himself, in the months immediately after the death.

He frequently mentions William of Ypres, descended through his father Count Philip from Robert the Frisian; in no. 73 he records only that, after being made count of Flanders by King Louis of France and William the Norman, he “was entrusted to the castellan of Lille for safekeeping,” which occurred on 27 April. But he is silent that the same William was led captive to Bruges about 9 September, as Galbert writes in the other *Life*, no. 131.

We give this *Life* from very ancient manuscript codices of the cathedral church of St Donatian at Bruges, of Dunes Abbey, and another manuscript of our own; and collated it with the version published at Paris in 1615 from the library of St Mary of Igny, without naming its source, by Jacques Sirmond. Yet Philip Alegambe in the *Bibliotheca Societatis Jesu*, Valerius Andreas in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, Aubert Miraeus in the *Fasti Belgici*, Antonius Sanderus in *De sanctis Flandriae*, and others attribute that edition to him.

The same *Life* occurs in a manuscript hagiology of the library of the regular canons of Rouge-Cloître near Brussels and in a manuscript codex at the monastery of St Martin of Tournai.

[Col. 0875D]

3. Galbert of Bruges, public notary of his city and in most matters an eyewitness, wrote another *Life of Blessed Charles*. We infer that he observed everything before him with the greatest care from what he writes in no. 59:

> “Amid so many dangers of nights and contests of days, when I, Galbert, had no place for writing, I noted the sum of events on tablets until, having awaited some peace of night or day, I might arrange this present account according to the course of events; and, as you see and read, being hard pressed, I transcribed it for the faithful. Nor did I note what each individual did, because of the confusion and endlessness; but with attentive mind I recorded only what, in the siege, was brought together by common edict and deed for battle and its cause; and I compelled myself, as though unwilling, to commit this to writing.”

That notaries of this kind then held great authority with counts is clear from what is narrated in this *Life*, no. 31 and following, concerning the notary Fromald. A charter published by Miraeus in *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgii*, c. 139, indicates that in 1130 he subscribed among the more distinguished men to Theodoric of Alsace’s donation to the monastery of Cercamp.

We give this *Life* from a very ancient manuscript codex, which we hold to have been written in Galbert’s own time or not long after, and have collated it with two Bruges manuscripts. André Duchesne had another manuscript codex, from which he cites much in his *Histoire généalogique des familles de Guînes, d’Ardres, de Gand et de Coucy*, published by him in 1631 [Col. 0876B].

Olivier Vredius subsequently had the same codex and used it often in the *Genealogia comitum Flandriae*; it is now kept at Ypres by his son-in-law Jean-Baptiste Bonart, syndic of that city, from which I had certain passages collated.

The same *Life* was formerly translated into French; Petrus Scriverius testifies in *Principes Hollandiae aeri incisi et commentariis antiquorum auctorum illustrati* that he had its manuscript codex in his library, and transcribes some passages on p. 42:

> “From the trustworthy account,” he says, “of Galbert of Bruges, an eyewitness, who recounts the Life of Charles the Good and these same things in a separate booklet.”

But we do not accept his opinion that Galbert wrote in French, since the elegance of language shining in the passage transcribed from him does not appear to have belonged to that age, especially among foreign Flemings. Moreover, the most ancient and very many codices are in Latin, the language in which we have no doubt he wrote, just as public acts were then customarily drawn up by notaries.

This history is carried on, as no. 25 says, “through distinctions of days and of deeds done on those days, to the vengeance recorded at the end of the little work.” From these words it might appear that the author later added the narrative of the Flemings’ defection from William the Norman, count, the election of Theodoric of Alsace, and the various wars waged by each side up to William’s death.

Since these do not pertain closely enough to Blessed Charles, we would prefer to omit them if they existed printed elsewhere. But because extracts from them are cited by André Duchesne and Olivier Vredius [Col. 0876D], and because we too cite some below so that correct knowledge of the family of the van Straten may be had, we give the work entire, so that the reader may acquire full knowledge of the events.

4. Suger, created abbot of St Denis near Paris in 1123 and dead in 1152, flourished in the same age as Count Charles. From his pen we have the *Acts of Louis the Fat*, king of the Franks, into which he inserts a compendium of the events surrounding the death of Blessed Charles and its avenging, published in almost the same words in the continuation of Aimoin, book V, c. 51; we place it below before the other, already mentioned, longer Acts.

We also have an ancient rhythmic poem containing a lament over Count Charles’s death and its avenging [Col. 0877A], found in a very ancient codex by the aforementioned Jacques Sirmond, copied by him, and sent from Paris to Antwerp in 1634. There are also several epitaphs formerly composed for Blessed Charles and printed by Jacobus Meyer in book IV of the *Annals of Flanders*.

5. Aelnoth, a monk of Canterbury, wrote the *Life and Martyrdom of St Canute*, king of Denmark, a few years after his death. Johannes Meursius published it at Copenhagen in 1631, having accurately corrected the edition printed at Copenhagen at the beginning of this century and illustrated it with his notes.

Appended in a manuscript codex to this *Life of St Canute* was the *Passion of St Charles*, count of Flanders, called Canute’s son; it too was printed twice with it. Its author is anonymous and perhaps Danish, but certainly not sufficiently acquainted with French, Flemish, and even English families [Col. 0877B]. Meursius, a man more learned in Greek antiquity than in the histories of these regions, did not notice that writer’s errors, as we have elsewhere observed concerning Danish matters. We omit those Acts, lest the bulk increase, since a curious reader may read them in print.

6. Three hundred years ago lived John Iperius, abbot of St Bertin in the city of Saint-Omer, who, delighted by historical study, wrote a *Chronicle of his monastery*, which we possess in manuscript. In part 2, chapter 41, he deals with the life and death of Blessed Charles and adds certain benefits bestowed on his monastery which are not reported by others. Omitting the rest, we annotate these on the former *Life*, as also matters narrated differently in the manuscript *Chronicle* of the monastery of St Andrew at Bruges.

Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite of Ghent, reckoned among learned Belgians two hundred years ago, calls Charles in book 7 of *De patronatu beatissimae Dei Genitricis semperque virginis Mariae de Monte Carmeli*:

> “the martyr Charles, son of Canute, martyred king of the Danes; shield of the just, sword of the wicked, who consecrated to Jesus Christ the first fruits of his military service in Jerusalem, mother of the New and Old Testament and workshop of our salvation, to be defended.”

7. The author of the manuscript *Florarium sanctorum* commemorates Count Charles among the other saints with this encomium:

> “In Flanders, at the town of Bruges, the deposition of Blessed Charles, martyr, count of the Flemings, son of Blessed Canute the martyr, illustrious king of Denmark, father of the poor and most devoted protector of churches. About the year of salvation 1127, in the eighth year of his rule, in the church of St Donatian, before the altar of St Mary, while reciting Psalm 50, after the first three penitential psalms had been said, and distributing alms to the poor, he was killed for righteousness’ sake by the hands of his servants; Christ immediately making known by many signs that he was acceptable to him.”

Hermann Greven and John Molanus celebrate him likewise in their additions to Usuard. Galesinius has this in his Roman Martyrology:

> “At Bruges (rather, Bruges), St Charles, martyr. He, son of Canute, martyred king, received the crown of martyrdom with no less glory.”

Petrus Canisius inscribed the following words in his *Martyrology* published in German:

> “Likewise, the blessed memory of the holy martyr Charles, count of Flanders, who rests at Bruges in the cathedral church of St Donatian” [Col. 0878A].

Saussay, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, records him among the other saints of this region in these words:

> “At Bruges in Flanders, then under the metropolitan see of Reims, St Charles, surnamed the Good, count and martyr of this province, son likewise of St Canute, glorious martyred king of Denmark.”

A compendium of his life and death is then attached; the basilica is called that of St Domitian, whereas it is that of St Donatian, bishop of Reims. Other matters, which we shall reject below, are added from the cited Meyer and Molanus in the *Index of the Saints of Belgium* and their *Nativities*. Miraeus in the *Fasti Belgici*, Baldwin Willotius in the *Hagiologium Belgicum*, Antonius de Balinghem in the *Fasti Mariani*, and others likewise celebrate him.

8. “His sacred bones,” says Miraeus, “were raised from the tomb and are reverently preserved in the sacristy of the canons of the cathedral church of St Donatian. He was a man of very tall stature, namely nine feet tall; and the limbs and bones, which are still seen there with great admiration, corresponded to that bodily length.”

Molanus adds:

> “On the same day a sermon on his merits is delivered in the sacristy and the relics displayed to the people. Those suffering from fever often drink from his wounded skull. At the place where he fell, above the high altar, the elders erected a cross with four nails in his memory, as crosses are customarily erected everywhere on roads in memory of those slain” [Col. 0878C].

Molanus continues:

> “Charles Philip de Rodoan, fourth bishop of Bruges, through zeal of devotion and pious affection which he had for the bones of the once most illustrious Count Charles the Good, cruelly murdered before the altar of the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the ambulatory above the choir, where a certain chaplaincy of the Most Holy Trinity is founded, resolved, with the consent of the lords of the chapter, to have the casket containing the said bones honorably adorned with red velvet, the said chapel enclosed and adorned at his own expense, and the casket transferred and placed above the altar of that chapel.
>
> “Having deliberated on the matter, the lords of the chapter agreed to the said adornment of the casket, the enclosure of the chapel, and the translation of the said casket, after the chapel had first been enclosed, on 23 February 1516. But afterwards, at the proposal and urgent request of the same most reverend bishop, for various alleged reasons moving their minds, the said lords of the chapter decreed on 1 March 1590 that tomorrow and thereafter a solemn Mass of the Most Holy Trinity should be celebrated in memory of Charles the Good, once count of Flanders, unjustly slain, as it had been celebrated.” [Col. 0878D]

These words are entered in the cited register of capitular acts of the same church of Bruges; an extract, subscribed also by Mr Matino, secretary, was procured for us by Arnoldus Crabcels, archdeacon of Bruges, licentiate in both laws and sacred theology.

So that no knowledge of deeds done or written might be lacking to us, we ourselves went to Bruges and inspected each thing in person [Col. 0879A], and venerated the sacred bones of Blessed Charles in the sacristy of the canons of the cathedral church of St Donatian.

### § II. A little tale of Charles’s death found in the Flemings’ vernacular Annals and inserted into the histories of later writers

9. What we have hitherto considered concerning the authors who described the life and death of Blessed Charles and the vengeance taken upon the criminal murderers is such that scarcely sounder evidence regarding any saint could be hoped for. For they mostly committed to writing matters at which they themselves were present and which they saw done, or at least related what they had received from those who had witnessed these things with their own eyes.

Various authors then independently composed their respective Acts in far-separated places, unaware of one another’s writings: Walter the archdeacon at Thérouanne, [Col. 0879B] Galbert the notary at Bruges, and Suger, abbot of St Denis, at Paris. With them agree the authors of the ancient rhythmic poem and epitaphs, the chronicler of the monastery of St Andrew, Abbot Iperius of St Bertin, and the anonymous Dane concerning Blessed Charles’s death.

John Brando the Fleming may be added, of the Cistercian Order and doctor of sacred theology, who died at Bruges in the refuge of Dunes in 1428 and agrees completely in the manuscript *Chronodromus*. This work exists in three volumes, very neatly written on parchment, at Louvain in the College of Arras.

There is another manuscript *Chronicle* at the Jesuit college in Louvain concerning the counts of Flanders down to Louis of Male, or the year 1381, which agrees. I omit Robert Gaguin, Nicolas Gilles, and other earlier writers of French affairs who agree in this controversy [Col. 0879C].

Furthermore, in our annotations we have compared the actions of particular persons with most contemporary historians, who left to posterity in writing events then done in the Low Countries, France, Germany, Denmark, England, Italy, and far-off Palestine. Ancient charters of kings, princes, bishops, and especially of the counts of Flanders—the forebears of Blessed Charles and his later successors—were of the greatest assistance in establishing the truth from every side.

10. Meanwhile, with all these matters disregarded, a monster was compounded from contrary, diverse, and mutually conflicting notions. It was accepted by very many, even by men not without learning, [Col. 0879D] almost as a divine oracle, and inserted into the Chronicles of Flanders. There exists a similar chronicle in the common Flemish vernacular, printed at Antwerp in 1531. We found its earlier part, carried down to the year 1488, written by hand at Bruges in a manuscript whose last leaves are mutilated. What is related in these chronicles concerning the murder of Blessed Charles is circulated separately; and even now it is “read annually at Bruges before the doors of the church, after six horns have first been sounded by the lords of as many estates or feudal holdings subject to this proclamation,” as these matters are reported in Jan Lernout’s Commentary on the Nature and Worship of Count Charles, and likewise on his Murder and the Revenge Soon Taken upon His Assassins.

Lernout was counted among men devoted to humane letters. Valerius Andreas, in his *Bibliotheca Belgica*, following others, reports that “he was Justus [Col. 0880A] Lipsius’s inseparable companion in surveying the academies and antiquities of France, Italy, and Germany.” But Andreas is mistaken in saying that the little work on the Life of Charles the Good, composed by him, was published at Paris. His son Jacobus Lernutius had it enlarged by himself and printed at Bruges in 1621 after his father’s death. In his preface he states that, “having examined my father’s paper furniture,” he found it “written very incorrectly and hastily; and therefore I applied the file, interpolated it, and added certain things which I judged appropriate to the subject.”

On account of these words, we judge that the elder Lernout composed those things in his youth, when he had not read even one of the authors cited above, none of whom he mentions anywhere; and that afterwards, having become acquainted with them, he cast aside that commentary [Col. 0880B] as misshapen, unpolished by the final application of the file, indeed unworthy of having his name attached to such tales by a learned man. In the margins appear Terence, Sallust, Cicero, Apuleius, and Cujas, cited for uncertain words and turns of phrase, though not without the mark of a youthful mind.

11. Blessed Charles had scarcely assumed the helm of Flemish government when Clementia, mother of the deceased Count Baldwin and then married to the duke of Louvain, attempted, with several princes joined to her, to depose him from power. “Hence,” says Lernout, “there arose a savage war . . . When Oudenaarde resisted the woman and refused to acknowledge the authority of the ruler, she violently attacked the ancient town of the Nervii and gave it over to the soldiers for plunder, the citizens being put to the sword [Col. 0880C] to a man, from bald man, as the saying goes, to bald man, and the houses wholly consumed by fire. Yet some writers of our history relate that the city and citizens were treated more mildly, and maintain that only the leading rebels were punished, while the city remained unharmed and the inhabitants’ property safe. Whatever the truth may be, let the authors bear responsibility for it. I have followed the vernacular annals which I saw, and I offer no judgment in a disputed matter.”

Thus Lernout, who proceeds from the same vernacular annals as follows: “The instigators and helpers of so cruel a deed were the Count of Monts and the Count of the Shrine of St Paul, together with the Count of Hesdin . . . who, besides the destruction of Oudenaarde, brought many evils upon Flanders.” So he writes; but, offering no judgment of his own, he leaves credit [Col. 0880D] to the authors—namely, to that vernacular chronicle of Flemish affairs and to the several writers whom he said related a milder treatment of the city and citizens. He seems to mean Mejer and Marchantius, whom he cites later and of whom we shall speak more fully below. Marchantius is silent on these matters.

Mejer’s words are these: “Clementia attacked and burned Oudenaarde, and is said there to have inflicted the final punishment upon certain citizens.” Thus Mejer gives a milder version of the chronicle, in which it is merely written that “citizens were killed.” Lernout added “to a man, from bald man to bald man,” so that he could employ the phrase as a proverb. But we judge that nothing at all was then done against Oudenaarde, and that events occurring after the murder of Blessed Charles have been wrongly transferred to this occasion.

Walter the archdeacon, who was alive then, [Col. 0881A] carefully describes below, in chapter 3 of the Life of Blessed Charles, the military disturbances stirred up by the said Clementia, without any mention of this destruction of Oudenaarde. But after the murder of Blessed Charles, “at Oudenaarde the Count of Monts had fortified himself and his followers, in order to invade the county of Flanders, which he claimed belonged to him more rightfully by kinship.” Soon, about 17 April, “Baldwin of Aalst and Razo, with a very great army of Ghent, besieged the castle of Oudenaarde. Then the Count of Monts, with the burghers of the same place, charged the men of Ghent with a military assault; he put them to flight, killed some, wounded others, and took many captive. Indeed, the greater part of the fugitives were drowned in its waters, having been conveyed by ship to arrange the siege beforehand. Then, at the beginning of May, [Col. 0881B] King Louis went toward Oudenaarde, where the Count of Monts had ravaged our land, travelling through Ghent. But our count, William the Norman, had gone ahead of the king and by violent force burned the suburb as far as the stone tower; and so more than three hundred persons, who had taken refuge in the church of that place, were burned, they say. On the fourth day before the Nones of May, Thursday about noon, the count returned.”

So writes Galbert, who was then living at Bruges, below in the *Life*, nos. 108, 114, and 122. Thus the suburb itself had remained untouched and intact until that time; it was then burned not by the Count of Monts but by William the Norman, who had been made count of Flanders. Nevertheless Mejer dared to write: “The Count of Monts, returning as an enemy against the Flemings, burned Oudenaarde in anger, where very many persons are said to have been consumed in the chief church.” [Col. 0881C] But those burned were in the church of the suburb. Let these remarks be made on the occasion of Lernout, who adheres to the vernacular annals.

12. Olivier Vredius of Bruges, a vigorous investigator of Belgian antiquities, especially Flemish ones, strove to discover and establish their history and truth from the charters of princes and contemporary writers. He was preparing for the press a commentary *On the First Counts of Flanders down to Charles the Dane, with the Forestier Tale Rejected*, as this title is given in Valerius Andreas’s *Bibliotheca Belgica*. But death forestalled him, and he did not publish—or perhaps did not complete—that treatise [Col. 0881D]. In any case, he rightly intended the Forestier tale to be rejected, though the vernacular annals, together with Mejer and Marchantius, propose it as the beginning of all historical truth.

Whether Vredius intended to conclude that commentary with the Acts of Blessed Charles, or rather to exclude them, has not yet been possible to discover. Certainly, had he read more carefully what those annals insert concerning Blessed Charles and compared it with contemporary writers, he would have rejected it too as a most foolish tale—especially those matters concerning the murder of the holy count, its occasion, and the revenge taken upon the parricides, as they are narrated both in those annals and in the annual public proclamation customarily made at Bruges.

We judge that the origin of this embellished fiction is plainly to be traced [Col. 0882A] to vernacular plays, commonly called the *romanciae* of the rhetoricians, which used to be performed publicly amid the gatherings of cities, with a prize offered. We assign this drama to the fifteenth century of Christ, when Bruges was regarded as the most celebrated market among the cities of the Low Countries and counted seventeen tribes of kingdoms and nations, which were accustomed to maintain their houses and colleges there.

In this comedy the Hanseatics had their own scene. Lernout calls them the profit-seeking nation of the Oosterlingen. Although they only began to assemble more than a hundred years after the murder of Blessed Charles, they are introduced as if, having brought a great quantity of grain by ship from the north, they had Bertulf the provost and his brother Lambert as purchasers. These Hanseatic associations or commonwealths were subject to four most famous cities: Lübeck, Cologne, Brunswick, and Danzig. Under Lübeck were counted Hamburg, Rostock, Wismar, Stralsund, Lüneburg, Stettin, and other neighboring cities. Among these the first commercial alliance began in the twelfth century, especially about the year of Christ 1260 or 1270; and thereafter some corporate body of cities confederated with one another was established about the year 1322—unless that date should rather be called the first member of a complete body. To it, about the year 1364, [Col. 0882B] John Isaac Pontanus asserts in book VIII of the *Danish History*, p. 494, that the metropolitan city of Cologne was added as a second member.

These are approximately the times [Col. 0882C] when Bruges gradually grew into the commercial mart of Flanders, when it entered into what they call a mercantile league and made agreements with the several nations. Sanderus, book I, chapter 2 of the *History of Bruges*, relates that this was done with the Hanseatic cities in 1392. At that time 255 years had elapsed since the murder of Blessed Charles; and throughout nearly the following fifteenth century this abundance of merchandise continued at Bruges. We assigned the supposed comedy to this period above. Yet in that century I find no historian who borrowed even a single falsehood from this tale.

13. Paulus Aemilius, a native of Verona, lived in the sixteenth century and died a canon of St Mary’s at Paris in 1529. In his widely praised Commentary on the deeds of the Franks, book V, under Louis VI, called the Fat, he included the unspeakable murder of Blessed Charles [Col. 0882D] and reduced into a compendium the aforementioned fiction, excerpted from the vernacular annals of the Flemings. He may be excused by the reader on this account: he had not seen Walter the archdeacon and Galbert the notary, the principal writers of the Life of Blessed Charles, and believed the Flemish annals should be followed in preference to Suger and the continuator of Aimoin.

Somewhat younger than Paulus Aemilius was Jacobus Mejer, a Fleming from the district of Bailleul, who died in 1552 and was buried at Bruges, at St Donatian’s. In book IV of his *Annals of Flanders* he maintains that “a certain Walter, a monk, wrote concerning the life and death of this Charles to John, bishop of [Col. 0883A] Thérouanne, but Galbert of Bruges wrote much better and more fully.” Yet he is mistaken in making Walter a monk; others identify him as archdeacon of the church of Thérouanne, and we have said that this Life was written by him with great discernment.

Moreover, we cannot sufficiently marvel that Mejer, while so often neglecting these authors, adhered to his own vernacular annals. The censure which he himself passed at the end of the year 1473 in book XVII upon Robert Gaguin seems applicable to him: namely, that “those commentaries which he followed, written in the provincial language, are wholly foolish and false in many places.” Perhaps these vernacular Flemish annals deserve a sharper censure in this history of Blessed Charles, since the fiction plainly continues. Yet Mejer is followed by Petrus Oudegerstius, in the *Annals of Flanders* published in French by the Plantin press in 1571; Jacobus Marchantius, in the four books of *Commentaries Describing Flanders*, published by the same press in 1596; John George, canon of Bruges, in his Flemish Life of Blessed Charles; Antonius Sanderus, in the recently issued sumptuous volumes of *Flanders Illustrated*; [Col. 0883B] and others of the same sort, who mingle all kinds of fables without any examination of the facts. We shall present a few of them.

### § III. Further Examination of the Same Tale concerning the Murder of Blessed Charles

[Col. 0883C] 14. Walter and Galbert describe the famine and want which afflicted Flanders during the two years before the murder of Blessed Charles, and commend the count’s exceptional generosity toward the poor. From this public famine the fictional comedy, or form of proclamation, begins. First, a certain almoner of the count is established, named Tammardus, and said to have been killed with the count on the same day. Thus he would be Themardus, castellan of Brugburg, whose death, together with that of his two sons Walter and Gillebert, Walter describes in no. 42 and Galbert in no. 26 and following.

But what is immediately added makes clear that this Themardus, castellan of Brugburg, and Thancmarus of Straten—of whose family we shall speak below—were fused into one and the same man in the said form of proclamation and in the vernacular annals of the Flemings. Paulus Aemilius, Oudegerstius, and Lernout follow them. Mejer, however, correctly distinguishes from Themardus of Brugburg another Tagmarus, though he also makes him the count’s almoner. The ancient writers refrain from that title. The occasion seems to have been given by Walter, when in no. 25 he reports that Charles “had great zeal in dispensing alms to the poor, and especially to monks.”

Once this scene is played, Bertulf the provost and his brother Lambert are brought onto the stage. They are surnamed Stratii—a name which, as we shall show below, is wrongly attributed to them—and they purchase from the Hanseatic or Oosterling merchants already mentioned grain conveyed by ship from the north. They likewise buy all the tithes belonging to neighboring monasteries, carry them to their storehouses, and fill the granaries with heaps of grain. [Col. 0884A] Then the count, moved by the tears of the needy, decrees that Tammardus should sell a great quantity of grain found in their granaries partly at a fair price, partly—if the recipients were needy—give it out freely by measure, leaving them a sufficient portion for their own livelihood. When they indignantly refused to receive the money collected from the grain sold, he ordered it distributed to the poor.

This is a thoroughly plausible scene, presented by all the recent writers, including Mejer, Marchantius, and Sanderus; yet no ancient writer mentions it. Walter reports that, because of the previously noted scarcity, Count Charles reduced the price of bread and prohibited drinking-parties. Galbert even praises the prohibition of brewing beer, the price imposed on wine, and the order to sow legumes. But neither charges Bertulf the provost or his family with the disgrace of hoarding grain [Col. 0884B], although both authors otherwise carefully investigate the causes of hatred and expose every crime both of Provost Bertulf and of his father Erembald—as will become clearer than daylight below.

15. With Bertulf and his brother Lambert inflamed by anger and hatred, Lambert’s son Burchard, or Borsiardus, intending to avenge an injury on his uncle’s advice, occupies part of the estate of his adversary Tammardus. The boundaries, formerly properly laid down to divide the fields, are fraudulently moved to positions convenient and advantageous to him. Lest the scene appear too meagre to the spectators, peasants are introduced, trying by Burchard’s orders to steal away all the ripe cherries gathered from Tammardus’s orchard.
