Tammardus’s servants appear, resist boldly, attack with their fists, and are driven back. The cherries are forcibly seized and carried to Bertulf; applause is given for the victory. A complaint brought by Tammardus to the prince results in Lambert, together with Burchard his son, being summoned to the tribunal. But they defy the summons and do not appear. They order their followers to break down Tammardus’s doors, shake fruit from the trees, and carry it off as stolen property. Yet while Burchard’s servants gather another’s fruit, Tammardus’s retainers attack them and grievously wound them; they are carried home in a cart.

Then their masters, intending to avenge this defeat, hurry to Tammardus’s country estate and order the trees cut down from the root and the manor wholly destroyed. Having perpetrated this deed, they kill Tammardus’s uncle by the sword and the latter’s pregnant daughter. The accusation is brought before the prince, an inquiry is held, and Burchard is declared guilty [Col. 0884D] and required to make good the entire damage.

I omit the rest of this scene, which may be read in the cited form of proclamation, in the vernacular annals, and in Lernout. It is enough to observe that none of this is reported by the ancient writers of the Life; indeed, in the records of the monastery of St Andrew, which we shall cite below, Tangmarus is said to have flourished with descendants even in the time of Robert of Jerusalem, and therefore to have wished to convey his possessions for the construction of that monastery.

16. John Iperius, to demonstrate Blessed Charles’s piety toward ecclesiastics and religious men, narrates that the abbot of St Bertin approached the count on the feast of Epiphany and complained of oppression inflicted by a certain knight. [Col. 0885A] This subject was thought suitable for embellishing the comedy. Accordingly Count Charles, as Flemish custom represents him on the celebration of that day, is created king in play and, giving himself over to every delight and festivity, distributes offices and magistracies jokingly among various guests amid banqueting and drinking. The complaint made by the abbot is brought forward; Lambert, with his son Burchard, is invented as the oppressor.

Provost Bertulf is summoned and comes gladly, expecting to take a splendid part in the banquet. But after the abbot’s complaint is repeated, he is sharply rebuked and threatened with a heavy penalty together with his brother unless he promptly satisfies the abbot and his monastery. Paulus Aemilius recounts all this, along with the other matters already cited, at greater length.

17. After these events, a conspiracy to kill the count is said to have been made at Ypres. Besides the kinsmen, eight canons of Ypres are fictitiously drawn into it. Friday is appointed as the suitable day for carrying out the murder, because every week on that recurring day the count was accustomed to check hunger only by drinking beer and eating bread; clothed and dressed in haircloth, barefoot, wearing a long garment with a purse hanging at his side, he would go to church and remain there until all sacred rites had been performed and he was called at the hour of dinner.

[Col. 0885B] The count is said to have returned to Bruges on Tuesday, the final day of the Bacchanalia, which that year closed February; and then, on the following Friday, 3 March, to have been killed by Burchard while praying in the church without any company. As skilfully and ingeniously devised as these things appear, [Col. 0885C] so foreign are they to the truth. The count summoned his barons to Ypres for the third day before the Kalends of March, which then fell on the first Sunday of Lent. On the next day, at their counsel, he ordered Burchard’s fortification demolished. Returning to Bruges, on the Kalends of March he answered the provost’s arrogant embassy and pressed for restitution. The assassins conspired to kill him on the following night; and on the morning of 2 March, Wednesday after the first Sunday of Lent, he was slaughtered in the church.

Thus writes Walter the archdeacon, who had been summoned to Ypres by the count and could know what had been done; and Galbert the notary, who saw all things at Bruges with his own eyes, gives a fuller account. Paulus Aemilius writes that he was killed on Ash Wednesday itself. [Col. 0885D] Mejer, in assigning the day, followed Galbert the notary. But in making Robert and Lambert, Bertulf’s brothers, who had already died, guilty of the conspiracy, he errs greatly, as shall be shown below.

The same Mejer reports that “three days after the murder the count’s body was honorably buried in the church of St Christopher near the market.” But on that day, 4 March, “the noble body was conveyed to the upper chamber of the church of St Donatian and enclosed in a tomb constructed as the necessity of that time required.” So Galbert writes, no. 41. On 14 April, after the upper chamber had been occupied, “the body of Blessed Charles was found there; at its head stood a burning candle, which those traitors had placed in honor of their lord.” So again Galbert, no. 105. Yet in no. 149 he states that, “on the tenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0886A] of May, Friday, after seven weeks of his first burial had passed, the count’s tomb in the upper chamber was demolished and his body reverently taken up from it . . . and, with the king accompanying, was carried by the bishop and three abbots to the church of St Christopher.” Mejer preferred to follow recent little tales rather than Galbert of Bruges, an eyewitness whom he had nevertheless declared to have written “much better and more fully.”

18. The comedy hitherto presented was transformed into a mournful tragedy, and vengeance began to be taken upon the assassins. Everything in the form of proclamation, the *Annals of Flanders*, and the commentaries of Paulus Aemilius and Lernout is filled with mistakes and errors, various ones of which Mejer and others have copied. We do not wish to dwell upon them, lest we weary the reader [Col. 0886B]. Let those unwilling to rest content with the truth presented by Walter, Galbert, and the others compare for themselves what is set forth concerning each individual. We shall touch upon some matters in the notes; here we observe only a few.

To Lambert, brother of the provost and father of Burchard, who had already died, are attributed many actions actually performed by his brother Desiderius Hachet, then castellan of Bruges, of whom most writers are silent. Lambert is said to have escaped by night from the tower of St Donatian; but, discovered and captured, he was placed on a butcher’s block, his hands and legs cut off, red-hot irons thrust into the stumps, and then he was hanged on a gallows, to become food for birds. Mejer likewise reports this from the Flemish annals.

Galbert, no. 80, deals with a certain Lambert Archei, who is said likewise to have escaped in flight, been captured, and held in custody. [Col. 0886C] Perhaps these details were attributed to that Lambert, together with the punishment inflicted upon “the knight George, chief among the traitors, who with Borsiardus, Lambert’s son, had killed the count; after both his hands were cut off, he was struck with a sword, cast through the feet into the sewer, and drowned,” as Galbert writes in no. 51. But whatever gave rise to the error, no ancient writer mentions any Lambert Nappin then surviving.

[Col. 0886D] 19. A similar fabrication is adopted in recounting vengeance taken upon the guilty and criminal murderers. In the vernacular *Annals of Flanders*, the Form of Proclamation, Lernout’s Commentary, and other works, all the actions performed in this vengeance are splendidly attributed to William of Ypres or Loo, son of Count Philip, brother of Robert of Jerusalem. Before Blessed Charles, he had a right of succession to the county of Flanders, unless he had been born of an illegitimate union, as will be clearly established below.

Thus he is imagined, as soon as he heard of Blessed Charles’s murder, to have hastened at once to Bruges and to have returned there repeatedly; to have investigated the deed’s circumstances and causes; summoned soldiers; ordered the castle or borough besieged; created a new magistracy; prescribed punishments for the captured Lambert and the other accused; and finally, after administering Flemish affairs for nine weeks as the true successor, to have come to Bruges for the fourth time and reported to King Louis how many accomplices in Charles’s murder he had punished and by what methods. These and other fictions may be read in the said vernacular annals [Col. 0887A] and Lernout’s commentaries.

On the contrary, when, on 16 March, two weeks after the murder of Blessed Charles, a report was spread among the leaders of the siege that “William of Ypres had been granted the county by the king, they took it indignantly. Therefore they joined in oath and pledged faith to one another that they would never serve as soldiers under him while he remained count of Flanders. For he was suspected by all and marked as implicated in the betrayal of Lord Count Charles.” So Galbert, no. 57.

For on 6 March they knew that “Godescalcus Thaihals had come from Ypres to Bruges as a messenger to the provost and the other accomplices in treason, and had openly conveyed greetings and friendship from William of Ypres, his intimate friend, together with the readiest assistance in every matter so far as lay in his power. As for the rest—which it is shameful to relate publicly—having been brought [Col. 0887B] into the chamber, he stripped himself naked. Hence the whole household put confidence in William, calling him and treating him as count. In this the wise observed William’s awareness of the treason: he had thus greeted the traitors at the height of their crime and had offered them, with all his power, the most ready aid by pledge, writing, and assurance.” Galbert gives this account in no. 44.

Walter adds in no. 64 that “William, as soon as he heard of the count’s death, claimed the county for himself that same day, occupied the strongly fortified town of Aire, and brought under his control St Venant, Cassel, Bailleul, Ypres, and also the territories of Bergues and Veurne.” Yet, seeing that the traitors were closely besieged by other Flemish nobles, William himself feigned that he was their enemy. When Isaac, the provost’s nephew through [Col. 0887C] his sister, had been captured and was being taken from Thérouanne to Aire, “he looked for William himself, believing that through him he could escape, because he had been privy to the treason. But after that count arrived, dissembling his guilty awareness, he ordered Isaac hanged.” This occurred on 23 March, as Galbert himself states in nos. 80 and 127.

Indeed, the provost himself, who had arranged “for the writs and accounts of the revenues to be kept” for William, was about to suffer the ultimate punishment. When William asked him who “were still secretly harmful and guilty in the death of Count Charles,” he replied before all that William knew them as well as he himself did. Then, seized by fury, that William ordered him killed. These details are found in Galbert, no. 93.

[Col. 0887D] 20. Meanwhile William the Norman, both offered by the king and chosen by the nobles, had become count of Flanders. But because William of Ypres held him in contempt, “the king bore with difficulty the arrogance and disdain of the adulterine Count of Ypres,” as Galbert relates in no. 90. Therefore Ypres was besieged and captured by the king, the rest of Flanders subdued, and William was taken from Ypres to Lille. There, from 26 April until about 9 September, he was held captive. Then he was taken to Bruges and “shut up in the uppermost chamber, with sentries and guards set over him to watch him most carefully.” Again, on 8 October, “he was taken from Bruges to Lille and entrusted to the castellan of that place.” So Galbert, nos. 121, [Col. 0888A] 131, and 135. These were the first occasions on which he entered Bruges after the murder of Blessed Charles.

Mejer writes these things about William under the same year, 1127: “William of Ypres, having sworn allegiance to the Norman and laid aside the title of ruler, is released from custody. But, contrary to the faith pledged to the Norman, he defects to Stephen, king of the English; immediately returning by sea with a great English force, he advances upon Sluys and ravages the surrounding fields—an enemy to the Norman more dangerous than one of uncertain allegiance to his country.” We do not discover from where Mejer drew these dreams.

[Col. 0888B] The vernacular annals state that, after Ypres was taken, this William was held captive at Saint-Omer but released through the entreaties of the nobles. He then went to England and complained to the king about the injury done him; the king granted him the county of Kent, where he lived for about twenty-four years. That William was in England and fought for King Stephen about 1140 is established from the Norman and Huntingdon chronicles and from a gift made to the monastery of St Bertin, printed by Vredius in his *Genealogy of the Counts*, p. 147. But we are here dealing with 1127, when, as we have said, he was held in custody at Bruges and especially at Lille.

21. Indeed, in the following year, 1128, when a great part of Flanders had defected to Thierry of Alsace, “William of Ypres”—as was learned at Bruges on 27 March—“was brought out of captivity and came to Kortrijk in order to aid William the Norman with his own counsel and forces and those of his followers.” So Galbert, no. 152. But when Count William died from his wound on 27 July, [Col. 0888C] Thierry of Alsace took peaceful possession of all Flanders, leaving William of Ypres as former lord of Loo.

On 22 August of that same year, in Thierry’s letters confirming the customs of Saint-Omer, William de Loo subscribed before Iwan of Ghent and Daniel of Dendermonde, by whose chief efforts Thierry had been summoned and had accepted the county. Du Chesne published those letters in book IV of the *Proofs of the House of Ghent*, p. 208. Miraeus likewise, in chapter 141 of the *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgii*, produces letters of the same Count Thierry, by which in 1130 he confirmed estates granted to the monastery of Loo, before witnesses including William, son of Count Philip, and others.

[Col. 0888D] This is William of Ypres or Loo, of whom Mejer states that he “died in the monastery of Loo on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, 1172; and that in his own time his tomb was opened, and his feet and legs still lay intact, much larger than those of any person then living.” So he writes. Robert, William’s son of Loo, is mentioned in a charter of Philip of Alsace, published from the archive of Furnes Abbey by the cited Vredius, p. 148.

From this it is also clear that Paulus Aemilius, Mejer, and others are greatly mistaken when they report that possessions were permanently taken away from all who had conspired in any way in the murder of Blessed Charles. In what follows this will be refuted as a wholly empty invention. On William of Ypres’s actions in England and his earldom of Kent, the chronicles of Normandy and England may be consulted.

### § IV. The Murder of Blessed Charles, Committed by the Erembalds, Wrongly Attributed to the Straten Family

[Col. 0889A] 22. While we are preparing for the press this whole sequence of various writers on the life and murder of Blessed Charles the Good, and elucidating each item by its appropriate notes, we stood struck with great amazement that certain more recent writers of Flemish history, who imply that they have themselves read these materials, should proclaim the men of Straten or the Stratiani guilty of the unspeakable murder of so great a prince, and should say that this most powerful Straten family then flourished at Bruges—although no ancient writer, if their records are read carefully, has provided the slightest occasion for writing this.

There was near Bruges an illustrious Straten lineage, favored by Count Charles. [Col. 0889B] It derived its name from the nearby lordship of Straten, adjoining the city and near the abbey of St Andrew, which was carved out of that lordship. Another and exceedingly powerful family, which we shall presently call the Erembald family from its progenitor, was hostile and inimical to it with inveterate hatred. Their disputes grew into a kind of civil war. The house of Straten was attacked and ravaged by the Erembalds, and the count’s authority was violated. When the nobles of Flanders had been summoned to render judgment, the Straten family was declared innocent, the Erembalds guilty, and certain houses belonging to the latter were demolished. Enraged and maddened by this, the Erembalds cruelly slaughtered Blessed Charles as protector of the Straten family. Having established this, we shall proceed to distinguish the two families through a continuous comparison of events.

[Col. 0889C] 23. Abbot Suger writes below, no. 39, that these murderers, whom we call Erembalds, were “low-born and drawn from the dregs of servile condition.” Galbert, no. 12, relates that they “were of servile condition according to the lines of their kindred, and therefore strained in every way to remove themselves from the servitude of the count, who claimed them for his own service.” Walter adds in no. 24 that “this seemed to be the first occasion of the murder; from it they began to exercise the most grievous hatreds against the count.”

Therefore Erembald, from whom the rest descended, came from these dregs of servile condition. Galbert, no. 113, asserts that “Erembald was born at Veurne,” came to Bruges, and became “the man and knight of Boldrannus, castellan at Bruges. He repeatedly [Col. 0889D] committed adultery with his lord’s wife, and she, adulterous herself, promised the viscountcy to her adulterer if her husband should soon die. Accordingly, the adulterer continually plotted his lord’s death and, during an expedition commanded by the count, in the silence of night threw him into the depths of the Scheldt. Having returned, he married his adulteress and purchased the viscountcy with his lord’s wealth.” Thus Galbert. The viscountcy means the office itself of castellan.

But the indicated expedition was that of Baldwin the Pious, or Baldwin of Lille, great-grandfather of Blessed Charles the Good. [Col. 0890A] Drawn into a military alliance by Godfrey the Great, duke of Mosellan Lorraine, he took arms against Emperor Henry III; on the imperial bank of the Scheldt he destroyed the fortress of Ename, seized the castle of Ghent after a long siege, and, after making peace with Emperor Henry, restored the cities of Cambrai and Antwerp, which he had occupied. These matters are found in Jacobus Mejer, book III of the *Annals of Flanders*, under the years 1046 and 1050.

But Sigebert begins that war in 1047 and says it was ended by Pope Victor in 1057. He writes that Baldwin invaded the county of Hainaut, burned the town of Huy, and besieged Antwerp; but that Emperor Henry, while Baldwin fled, crossed the Scheldt and captured many leading Flemings besieged within the city of Tournai. From these accounts the time when Baldrannus, castellan of Bruges, was thrown into the Scheldt and Erembald substituted in his place is more than sufficiently shown. [Col. 0890B] The office of castellan then remained with Erembald and his descendants for eighty years.

24. Miraeus, *Donations of Belgium*, book II, chapter 25, and *Survey of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 98, published a grant made in 1067, indiction V, by the same Count Baldwin of Lille to the monks of Saint-Winoc at Bergues. After Count Baldwin, his wife Adela, and their sons Baldwin and Robert, its subscribers included Erembald, castellan of Bruges, Erkenbert the provost, and many others whose names Miraeus omitted. But Sanderus, in *Flanders Illustrated* and in his treatment of the district of Franconatus, p. 292, asserts that in those times “the family of the de Straten was powerful and wealthy, and is mentioned in the charters of Baldwin of Lille” for the year 1067, of which we have spoken: Athelard de Stratis [de Straten; Col. 0890C] appears with Abbo de Rodanburch.

In the same *Survey*, chapter 112, Miraeus produces another charter of Robert of Jerusalem, by which, in 1089, he makes Rainer, provost of the church of Saint Donatian, perpetual chancellor of Flanders. After Provost Rainer and several canons and others, the subscribers include Erembald, castellan of Bruges, and his son Rodbert; likewise Athelard de Stratis. At the beginning of book IV, Mejerus lists the chief nobles flourishing in these times, among whom are found Erembold, castellan of Bruges; Albo, who is the Abbo of Rodenburg mentioned above; and Adelard of Straten. Thus the Erembald family was plainly distinct from the Straten family, though both flourished in great esteem among the Flemings.

[Col. 0890D]

25. Erembald had five sons: the previously mentioned Rodbert or Robert, castellan of Bruges after his father’s death; Lambert Nappin—these two are considered the eldest, and to have died before the murder of Blessed Charles; Bertulph, provost of Saint Donatian; Desiderius Haket, likewise, as will be shown below, castellan of Bruges; and Welfric, or Wlfric, or Guelric, surnamed Cnop. Here are various anciently attested surnames—Haket, Nappin, Cnop—but nowhere is *de Straten*, or anything similar, suggested. That surname remained with the descendants of Athelard de Straten. Among them were Thagmar, or Thancmar, who had no children, and then Berenvold, or at least other unnamed persons, from whom were descended the grandsons of Tagmar, to be discussed below.

When Robert of Jerusalem was campaigning in the Holy Land, he made a vow and ordered his wife to build the abbey of Saint Andrew on the estate of Betferkerca. Tagmar de Straten had earlier urged him toward that distinguished undertaking, since he too gave very many possessions to the same monks and was regarded as a secondary founder, as we ourselves have transcribed from the ancient records of this monastery. In Miraeus’s *Survey*, chapter 125, there is a charter of Baldric, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, by which, “in the year 1105, indiction VIII, he granted to the altar of Betferkerca the right of freedom, on condition that monks should be established there.” Among the subscribers were Bertulph the provost, Robert the castellan, and Lambert Nappin, three brothers born to their father Erembald; likewise the aforementioned Tagmar de Stratis.

By what contrivance Bertulph became provost, Galbert explains in no. 92 in these words: “Bertulph could remember how he had been violently intruded and placed over the living provost Ledbert, an honourable man who endured everything for God’s sake, and had unjustly and against God usurped pre-eminence in the temple of God,” etc.

But Robert, castellan of Bruges, according to Sanderus, *Affairs of Bruges*, book I, chapter 7, “signs the charter of Baldwin—or rather Baldric—bishop of Noyon and Tournai, by which, in the year 1096, the altar of Oostburch, together with the chapel dependent upon it, situated in Isendica, is given to the monks of Saint Peter at Ghent.” But since Baldric was made bishop after Radbod’s death in 1098, the assigned year is erroneous.

Again, according to Sanderus: “Another—or rather the same—Robert, castellan of Bruges, in [Col. 0891C] 1109 signs the charter of Robert of Jerusalem concerning a gift made to the monastery of Formeselle. The same man in 1101 confirms the privileges of the church of Saint Donatian.” Is this correct? For Mejerus, under that year, asserts that the privileges granted to that church by Count Robert were subscribed by Erembald, castellan of Bruges, with his son Robert; Athelard of Straten; and others.

Galbert, no. 113, places Robert, also castellan after Erembald, second among Erembald’s sons; and after Robert himself declares that his son Walter succeeded as hereditary castellan, third in the succession of the viscounty. In book II of the *Proofs* appended to the *Genealogical History of the Families of Ghent and Guînes*, p. 67, André du Chesne published part of a charter of Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, confirming in 1113 an exchange made by the church of Saint-Bertin of the village of Oosterseele for other property. Among the subscribers to this grant was Walter, castellan of Bruges.

26. But when this Walter died at a very young age, he was succeeded by his uncle Desiderius Haket, son of Erembald and brother of Provost Bertulph. In a charter of the same Baldwin for the church of Formeselle, cited by du Chesne, p. 188, Haket signs in 1115 as castellan of Bruges; likewise, in another charter for the benefit of the same church of Formeselle, in du Chesne, p. 68, in 1117, indiction X, he signs as Hachet, castellan of Bruges.

The same du Chesne, in book II of the *Proofs* for the *Genealogical History of the Bethune Family*, p. 19 [Col. 0892A], published a charter of Count Charles by which, in 1122, he confirmed “the privileges granted by his predecessors to Wulveric, abbot of the church of Saint Bavo at Ghent”; among the witnesses is Haket, castellan of Bruges. These are acts of Haket alone.

The same Count Charles the Good, and his butler or cup-bearer Walter with his brother Cono, endowed the abbey of Aldenburg. The charter concerning this matter, signed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August in 1119, indiction XII, was subscribed by Bertulph, provost of Bruges; Desiderius Haket, castellan; and Lambert Nappin—three brothers and sons of Erembald; likewise Thancmar de Straten and Berenvold de Straten. See Miraeus’s *Survey*, chapter 168.

Walter de Straten and his two brothers appear to have been sons of the said Berenvold. They are frequently called Tagmar’s grandsons [Col. 0892B], because, after their father’s death, they lived with him on his lordship of Straten, as will be clear from what follows. After Lambert Nappin’s death, there survived his sons Burchard, or Borziard—also called by the Anonymous Dane Fromold, surnamed Borchard—and Robert, called by the same Anonymous author Lambinus Morunnater. Robert, later castellan, had sons Walter, whom we have said was castellan in his youth, Albert, and then, by a second wife, Robert, commonly called “the boy.”

Their lordship was at Ravenscot in the territory of Bruges, “very strongly fortified for defence,” as Galbert testifies in no. 47. But Borziard had a house which he fortified not far from Straten, or perhaps on the lordship of the lords de Straten. Hence began hatreds, disputes, and armed incursions between the two families. As Galbert says in no. 15: “The count supported the just cause of Thancmar de Straten; but Bertulph the provost summoned all the knights, by payment, influence, and entreaty, to aid his nephews against Thangmar, and indeed brought in five hundred armed knights and countless foot-soldiers, and ordered iron tools and axes to be brought,” etc.

In this attack upon Thangmar’s dwelling, Robert, brother of Borziard, fell, Galbert testifying in no. 26. They suspected that he had been killed by Henry of Locris, a knight fighting for the lords de Straten. What happened to Albert, whom Galbert in no. 11 calls Bertulph’s third nephew, is nowhere stated; thus he too seems to have perished when, “with a large and powerful force assembled” (in Walter’s words, no. 28), “they raid nearly the whole region, break into houses, plunder all movable goods, strip the poor, hang some, and slaughter most with the sword.” This occurred while Count Charles was absent in France. On his return to Ypres, Charles, by decision of the nobles of Flanders, arranged that Borziard’s stronghold should be overthrown, burned, and utterly destroyed.

When he returned to Bruges, Charles admitted mediators for Borziard and assigned him a new house, but elsewhere, far from the Straten estate. For, as Blessed Charles says in Galbert, no. 16, “because, dwelling beside Thancmar until then, he had never engaged in anything but disputes and seditions, with plunder and killing.” From this one may infer the great power of each family.

27. After these events, six leaders of the faction conspired to kill Count Charles; Bertulph the provost directed them by his counsel. They were Guelric or Wlfric, brother of the provost; the latter’s two nephews, Burchard or Buziard, son of Lambert Nappin, and Robert the boy, son of Robert the castellan, though he had been drawn in by the others quite unwillingly; then Isaac, a kinsman of the provost, William of Viroviacum, and Ingrasnus of Esnes. So Walter relates with Galbert, no. 34.

Mejerus adds as three leaders of the faction Robert and Lambert Nappin, brothers of Bertulph, though they had already died, and William, Lambert’s son. But because ancient writers are profoundly silent about him, we judge that this William never existed in reality, and was produced solely in the fabulous Flemish-language annals.

After Blessed Count Charles had been murdered on 2 March by the hand of the utterly impious Borziard, “on that same day,” says Galbert, no. 35, “those traitors made an expedition against their enemies, namely against Thangmar and his men at Straten, and found their settlements deserted and their courts empty. For, having heard of the crime committed in the count’s death, they feared for themselves, especially because they had lost their defender [lacuna]. Then those traitors, attacking both Thangmar’s settlement and his court, plundered all the weapons and household goods within, together with a great booty of the cattle and clothing of the peasants of that village; and so, after plundering throughout the entire day, they returned in the evening.”

These events, Galbert—an eyewitness—states took place at Straten, not, as Mejerus says, at Orscampo or Oostkamp, far from there near the new canal of Ghent.

## § V. The Affairs of the Erembald and Straten Families after the Murder of Blessed Charles

[Col. 0893C]

28. Desiderius Haket, castellan of Bruges, then came to the defence of the Erembalds, his brothers and nephews. Under his leadership, Galbert says in no. 46, the suburbs were fortified by the citizens. Against them “Gervasius, chamberlain of Saint Charles, took up arms and on 7 March besieged the settlement of Ravenschot, very strongly fortified for the defence of the traitors. On 8 March, when Robert the boy, whose settlement it was, made an unsuccessful sortie against the besiegers, Ravenschot was destroyed by fire and arms; and near Bruges the house of Wlfric Cnop, brother of the provost, who had sworn the death of the count, was burned.” So Galbert, nos. 47 and 48.

He then records that “on 9 March Gervasius, received within the suburb, besieged the traitors within the castle” [Col. 0893D]. The people of Bruges captured it on 19 March, and afterward, as will be related below, the church of Saint Donatian. Then, according to Galbert, no. 74, “the grandsons of Thancmar de Straten set up their banners in the provost’s house proudly, gloriously, and powerfully, and treated as their own whatever they found inside. They sent out the grain and wine which they had brought in from their countryside at Straten. But the citizens broke the wine-vessels and shut the gates of the suburb so that no one might escape, crying that Thancmar and his grandsons ought justly to be hanged, since on their account the count had been killed, the provost and his nephews besieged, and several members of their family slain and condemned to a most shameful death.

“And the besieged men, the castellan Haket and Robert the boy and others, from the higher tower, were beckoning with arms and hands, imploring them to destroy those enemies through whose fault so grave a crime had been committed—men who had so arrogantly climbed into the provost’s house and affixed their victorious banners, while, at the time when the castle was captured, they themselves slept at home and in their own countryside,” namely at Straten, where they had been taken under the protection of the princes.

On 23 March Isaac, the provost’s kinsman, was captured and hanged. On 30 March William the Norman was declared count of Flanders; in place of Desiderius Haket—who escaped from the tower on 1 April and hid at Lissewege with his son-in-law—Gervasius was made castellan of Bruges on 2 April. Then on 11 April Provost Bertulph was hanged at Ypres; on the 14th of that month the upper chamber of the church of Saint Donatian was occupied, and its tower surrendered on the 19th. Punishment was inflicted on 5 May, when Wlfric, the provost’s brother, and twenty-seven other accomplices were thrown from the tower and perished. Bursiard was afterward hanged, and Robert the boy beheaded at Cassel.

29. In the following year, 1128, after Thierry of Alsace had been raised to the countship, the Flemings gradually deserted William the Norman. The men of Straten adhered to William, even against the people of Bruges, who on 26 March, after receiving Thierry, “made an expedition before Thancmar’s house. But the next day, very early in the morning, Thancmar and his grandsons burned their own house and dwellings at Straten, because, if they had not done so, Daniel and Juan with their Thierry would have done so,” as Galbert testifies in no. 151 and the following section.

But “on 11 April [Col. 0894C] Thancmar’s grandsons attacked the Bruges men at Harenas, summoning the citizens to undertake military service; on 23 April Thancmar’s grandsons burned the house of Fromold the Younger at Berenhen; and on 12 June they burned a house near the castle of Bruges. But Gervasius, castellan of Bruges, coming against them, captured Walter, Thancmar’s grandson, through whom the occasion and cause of the entire sedition and conflict arose between Borsiard, betrayer of Count Charles, and Thancmar.

“But the citizens of Bruges clapped their hands for joy because Walter had been captured: he had been the head and beginning of every evil in our land, and through his intrigues Count Charles had been betrayed—not because he himself had betrayed him, but because he had compelled his enemies Borsiard and his companions to betray him.”

So Galbert, no. 174, adding that he says this “according to popular opinion and the fury of those who then wished to hang the aforesaid captive Walter, or to destroy him by a new and unheard-of manner of death, had the count permitted it.” Then, on 11 July, Walter was released from captivity in order to recover from his wound, after two brothers had been provided as hostages. On the twenty-fifth day of the same July, Walter, having been brought back into captivity, released them, as Galbert narrates more fully.

From these words, whereby, “according to popular opinion and fury,” Walter de Straten was proclaimed “the head and beginning of every evil,” he seems wrongly to have been numbered among the leaders of the Erembald faction and to have supplied the occasion for calling them Straten men or Stratenians.

30. After William the Norman died of his wound later in the same month of July [Col. 0895A], Thierry of Alsace received peaceful possession of Flanders, approved also by the kings of France and England. In the second year of his countship, 1129, he confirmed donations made to the monastery of Aldenburg, subscribed, along with others, by Thancmar de Straten. Thancmar likewise subscribed the charters of donation made by the same Count Thierry for the abbey of Quercetanum in 1130. See Miraeus, *Survey of the Churches of Belgium*, chapters 139 and 168.

“Thancmar, or Tachmar, was a man distinguished by power and wealth. Having no succession of children, he made Christ heir of his possessions and bestowed them on the monastery of Saint Andrew. His devotion grew so much that he professed the monastic life there, lived commendably, and died a holy death.” So Sanderus writes in the cited *Flanders Illustrated*, p. 292, from the account of Henry Zypaeus, abbot of the said monastery of Saint Andrew.

From this it is clear that we rightly distinguish this Thangmar from Themard, castellan of Brugburg, who was killed with Blessed Charles. In Sanderus, Richard vander Straten later subscribed charters of the said Thierry of Alsace; he was perhaps another of the brothers of Walter vander Straten discussed above. Another Richard, lord vander Straten, is also said to have lived in 1230. Sanderus adds that the lordship of Straten afterward belonged to the Coster, Dudezele, Halmaal, and Gistel families. But at Bruges we learned that it now belongs to the prince of Chimay and count of Middelburg.

[Col. 0895C]

31. These remarks about the Straten family are sufficient. Only a few things remain to be said about the Erembald family, or the family of traitors. Paulus Aemilius states that “no restraint was exercised toward any of the conspirators: not only was atonement for the slain count demanded by the death of the guilty, but all who were connected with them by any relationship, and indeed those even somewhat known to them, were either struck down by the sword or, through fear, chose voluntary and long exile for themselves, their neighbours detesting and cursing them.”

Mejerus adds that “among some it has been handed down that part of these parricides, exiles from their country, came to Ireland and, with the permission of the king of England, cultivated there an island named Gerina; there they increased into so great a people that they at one time dared to rebel against the king himself. In Flanders their buildings were razed to the ground, and the power to restore them was removed forever. All their fields and possessions were condemned to the heaviest taxes; their posterity was cursed and condemned for eternity.”

So Mejerus and those who followed him write. But this seems wholly unacceptable to us, as is clear from what has been said above about William of Ypres, son of Count Philip. The matter will become especially clear in the case of Desiderius Haket, castellan of Bruges, brother of Provost Bertulph and uncle of Burchard or Bursiard.

As soon as Blessed Charles had been murdered, he “went up with his men into the count’s house to take possession of it,” and undertook the protection and guardianship of his brothers, nephews, and the other conspirators. Then “he violently extorted all Blessed Charles’s keys—the keys of the house, the chests, and the coffers in the house—and brought them under his own control.” Galbert narrates this as having happened on the first day, nos. 26 and 36.

Later, while he was enclosed and besieged with the others inside the burgh, he was so hated by others that “a certain Robert of his household, his runner and servant, was intercepted in the middle of the market, killed, and dragged into the marshes.” Indeed, William the Norman could not be accepted by the people of Aldenburg as the new count unless he and the king promised “that Haket the castellan and the other traitors should never thereafter be heirs in the county of Flanders.” These statements occur in Galbert, nos. 51 and 89.

Meanwhile the besieged obtained permission for a conference, at which Haket pleaded for the release of all, demanding perpetual exile for the accused, but full and secure freedom for himself, Provost Bertulph, and Robert the boy, whom he wished to treat as innocent with himself. Walter the knight replied for the besieging multitude and pronounced all guilty without exception: “Therefore henceforth,” he added, “we renounce, condemn, and cast away the faith and homage which we have hitherto kept toward you.” When the answer was finished, all took up straws and renounced their service, homage, faith, and security toward them. So Galbert, nos. 64 and 65.

But “on the first of April,” as he says in no. 86, “on Friday, the day of the Preparation, Castellan Haket escaped alone from the tower, went to Lissewege, and hid there with his daughter, whom a knight of high rank and great wealth had formerly married there. For the fugitive was waiting to see what he should do next.” The next day, “on Holy Saturday of Easter,” Gervasius was “made castellan in the castle of Bruges” [Col. 0896C] in Haket’s place.

32. The knight mentioned was named Walter Crommelin, or Clomliin. According to Galbert, no. 149, he was among the first to bring assistance to the citizens of Bruges against William the Norman. Both he, Haket’s son-in-law, and Haket’s son Robert survived into the time of Thierry of Alsace and retained peaceful possession of their property.

André du Chesne presents two striking testimonies of this in the *Proofs* for book II of the *Genealogical History of the Families of Ghent and Guînes*. Having on p. 70 produced a charter of Thierry of Alsace confirming the possessions of the abbey of Saint Peter at Ghent, he adds the following on p. 71:

“Another charter of Thierry, count of Flanders, by which, in the presence of his principal barons, he causes to be settled and wholly decided a dispute between the abbot of Saint Peter and Haket, formerly castellan of Bruges, concerning the fact that, within the bounds of the parish called Liflinga, the aforesaid church has from ancient times possessed Bercaenas on the seacoast, to which certain new land has been joined and formed by accretion from the sea. These things were done under the seal and sign of the aforesaid Count Thierry. Witnesses: Juan of Aalst, Daniel of Dendermonde, Gerard of Oudenaarde, Wenemar, castellan of Ghent, Baldwin of Belle, Everard of Ghent, Christian of Gistel. Done at Bruges in the year of the Incarnate Word 1133.”

So he writes there. Of the named barons, Juan of Aalst, Daniel of Dendermonde, and the castellan of Ghent had each, with his own knight, besieged the burgh of Bruges from 10 and 11 March [Col. 0897A], and with others “renounced the service, homage, faith, and security of Castellan Haket and the others.” Yet now these same barons, with their Count Thierry, settle and decide a dispute concerning a definite possession of Haket.

The same page 71 adds the following concerning Haket’s son and son-in-law:

“A charter of the same Thierry, count of Flanders, by which he settles the dispute between Giselbert, abbot of Saint Peter at Ghent, and Robert, son of Haket, formerly castellan of Bruges, and Walter Crommelin, his son-in-law, concerning land at Testrep and the tithe of Groede. The sign of Count Thierry, and the sign of Iwan of Aalst, Daniel of Dendermonde, Gerard of Oudenaarde, Raso the butler, Thierry the chamberlain, Michael the constable, Wenemar castellan of Ghent, Ghislebert castellan of Bergues, Baldwin castellan of Lens, Walter of Nivelles, Baldwin of Belle, Gervasius of Ythelhem, Everard of Ghent, Walter Crommelin. Done at Bruges in the year of the Incarnate Word 1133, indiction XI, while King Louis reigned in France and Thierry ruled in Flanders, in the sixth year of his rule.”

In the aforementioned grant made by the same Count Thierry in 1130 to the abbey of Quercetanum, Walter Clomliin, the same son-in-law of Haket, subscribed.

33. We omit accumulating further evidence, since from these points it may sufficiently be inferred that, under Count Thierry, an *amnēstia*—that is, an oblivion of injuries and of the past unto perpetual forgetfulness—was effected. That lineage did not remain cursed and condemned for eternity, as Mejerus, Marchantius, and Lernutius tried to prove from the fabulous formula of a proclamation said to be read before the church doors. Lernutius, indeed, because the count was purportedly killed on a Friday, reports that the curse was customarily pronounced “on the first and second Friday of the month of March.”

But because it was certainly established from Walter, Galbert, and other ancient writers that Blessed Charles was killed on 2 March, a Wednesday, the condemnation began to be proclaimed on the sixth day before the Nones of March [2 March]. And, if Mejerus is to be believed, it was done to the sound of a trumpet; yet Marchantius wrote that the lineage was cursed by a horn-blower. All these things, upon seeing this account, ought better to be omitted, since God, the first Truth, is not honoured by so dense a mass of falsehoods.

## § VI. A Correctly Ordered Series of the Castellans of Bruges and the Provosts of Saint Donatian Relevant to This History

[Col. 0897D]

34. Since later writers had almost no knowledge of the castellans and provosts of Bruges, of whom we have already spoken, I repeat their catalogue. The castellans were Boldrannus under Baldwin of Lille, about the year 1050; Erembald for more than forty years; his son Robert; then Walter, born to that Robert; Desiderius Hakettus, also a son of Erembald; after his removal, Gervasius, chamberlain of Blessed Charles; and after Gervasius’s death, Radulf, also called Gervasius de Praet. These last subscribed, in 1143, a charter of Count Thierry for the church of Saint Mary of Tronchiennes [Col. 0898A].

Whether this second Gervasius was the son of the former, or whether he rather provided later writers with an occasion for error in calling the earlier man de Praet, we leave for others to investigate. Gervasius of Ythelhem, already mentioned, was alive at the same time.

Sanderus calls Castellan Gervasius “of Bruges,” which we likewise do not accept. For in book I, chapter 7 of *Affairs of Bruges*, when presenting the ancient castellans of Bruges, Sanderus displays great ignorance of the succession: he ignored Boldrannus; placed Robert before Erembald and then again added him as though he were another person; indeed, he does not state that Robert was Erembald’s son. Nor does he make Walter, Erembald’s grandson, Robert’s son—though he correctly places Haket after Walter, he says nothing of who Haket was.

Worst of all, under the note for 1120, Arnulf de Nielles is placed either as castellan of Bruges or as a relative of the castellans of Bruges, having been mentioned in charters of Manasses, count of Guînes, and his wife Emma. Du Chesne published those charters in the previously cited *Proofs*, p. 39, but omitted Arnulf and the other witnesses. Yet immediately on pp. 40 and 41 Arnulf, or Ernulf, de Nieles appears among the witnesses for 1120 and 1128, with absolutely no addition either of the dignity of castellan or of kinship with castellans. But, excluding Arnulf, it is entirely certain from the evidence stated above that Desiderius Hakettus was castellan of Bruges from 1115 to 1127. When he was removed, Gervasius succeeded him; after Gervasius’s death, Radulf succeeded.

35. We have also identified the provosts of the church of Saint Donatian: Erkenbert, Rainer, Ledbert, and Bertulph [Col. 0898C]. In Bertulph’s place, as Galbert relates below in no. 120, Roger was appointed; he died in 1157, as we ourselves read on a sepulchral stone in the choir of Saint Donatian.

Meanwhile Sanderus, *Affairs of Bruges*, book II, chapter 1, and, following him, the authors of volume II of *Gallia Christiana* in their treatment of the bishops of Bruges, offer an absurd succession, though it is called “accurately compiled.” Omitting Ledbert, they nevertheless enumerate eight men: Erkenbert, Rainarius, Bertulfus, Chancellor Guido, Bertulphus, Rodgerus, Arnulphus Stratensis, and Rogerius.

Of these, Bertulfus, Bertulphus, and Arnulphus Stratensis—named as distinct persons despite intervening names, with Bertulphus differing by only one letter—are one and the same person, “when Charles the Good was murdered.” Likewise Rodgerus and Rogerius, wrongly distinguished, are a single person. The death of the last should not have been assigned to 1147, since his sepulchral inscription indicates that he died ten years later.

Guido the chancellor is inserted because he “subscribed the foundation of the abbey of Saint Andrew made by Robert of Jerusalem in 1105.” But they do not seem to have read the charter of foundation, which, as stated above, was subscribed by Provost Bertulph with his two brothers. Hugh, chancellor of Roeselare, subscribed in 1130 a donation made to the monastery of Aldenburg, but should not on that account be numbered among the provosts of Bruges, even though no provost is found to have subscribed that donation, which may be seen in Miraeus’s *Survey of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 139.

## § VIII. The Murder of Blessed Charles, from the *Deeds of Louis the Fat, King of France*, by Abbot Suger

[Col. 0899A]

36. “We have resolved briefly to recount, avoiding tediousness, a most excellent deed—the noblest that he accomplished from his youth to the end of his life—not how it was done, but what he did, though it demands a fuller narration. The renowned and most powerful Count Charles, son of the king of the Danes through the aunt of Lord King Louis, had succeeded by the strongest right of kinship Count Baldwin, son of Robert of Jerusalem. He governed the very populous land of Flanders as energetically as he did diligently: an illustrious defender of God’s Church, conspicuous for generosity in almsgiving, and an eminent guardian of justice.

Because he was bound by the honour he had received, he fittingly pressed certain powerful men—low in birth but exalted by wealth, who were proudly striving to exclude his line of kinship from lordship—before the judgment of the court. For they were the dregs of servile condition. They, namely the provost of the church of Bruges and his men, men most proud and notorious traitors, most cruelly plotted against him.

When, therefore, on a certain day Charles had come to Bruges, he was present at the church of God very early in the morning. Prostrate upon the pavement and holding a prayer-book in his hand, he prayed. Suddenly a certain Buchard, nephew of the aforesaid provost, a savage attendant, with others of the same utterly wicked stock and other accomplices in the foulest treachery, approaches from behind the man praying—indeed silently speaking with God. Carefully drawing his sword, he gently touches the count’s neck, prostrate upon the ground, so that it should rise a little and unexpectedly present itself to the striker’s sword; then, bringing the blade down upon him, the impious man with one blow most wickedly beheads the pious man, the servant his lord.

Those standing by, accomplices in the impious murder, drank his blood and, like dogs raging over abandoned corpses, delighted in tearing the innocent man to pieces. They gloried exceedingly that they had been able to accomplish the wicked purpose they had conceived and the iniquity they had brought forth. Adding iniquity to iniquity, blinded as they were by their wickedness, they slaughtered, by a most unhappy kind of miserable death, without preparation and without confession, whatever castellans and whatever barons of the nobler count they could encounter, whether in that church or outside in the castle. Yet we consider it greatly beneficial to them that they were found praying in church and thus slain for loyalty to their lord, since it is written: ‘Where I find you, there I shall judge you’ (Ezekiel 24:14).”

“The fierce men then buried the count in that very church, lest he should be mourned and buried honourably outside, and lest a devout people, stirred by his glorious life and still more glorious death, should rise to avenge him. Turning the church itself into a den of thieves, they fortified both it and the count’s house adjoining the church. Having prepared every provision of food, they resolved in the height of their pride both to protect themselves from there and to bring the land under their control.

Therefore, astounded by the horror of so great and wicked a deed, the barons of Flanders who had not consented to it performed tearful funeral rites and avoided the taint of treason by reporting this to their lord King Louis—not to him alone, but, as the report flew, throughout the whole world. Moved both by love of justice and affection for his kinsman, the king was roused to avenge so great a treachery. Neither the war of the king of England nor that of Count Theobald detained him. He entered Flanders boldly, burning with all the force of mind and action to destroy the utterly wicked men with the utmost severity.

He appointed as count of Flanders William the Norman, son of Robert of Jerusalem, count of Normandy—for by right of kinship it belonged to him. When Louis came down to Bruges, fearing neither the barbarism of the land nor the foul kinship-line of the traitors, he besieged and constrained the traitors shut up in the church and tower. He forbade supplies other than their own; by God’s providence, even these were ill-suited to their needs. When he had worn them down for some time by hunger, pestilence, and the sword, they left the church and retained only the tower, so that the tower might retain them.”

37. “Now, therefore, when they despaired of life, when their lyre had already been turned to mourning and their organ into the voice of those who weep, the most wicked Buchard, with the agreement of his companions, escaped by flight. Seeking to leave the country but unable to do so—his own iniquity alone preventing him—he returned to the stronghold of a certain friend and intimate. Seized at the king’s command, he was subjected to a carefully devised miserable death: bound atop a high wheel, exposed to the rapacity of ravens and birds, his eyes gouged out from above and his entire face torn apart, pierced a thousand times from below with arrows, lances, and javelins; then, most wretchedly killed, he was thrown into a sewer.

But Bertold, the head of iniquity, having likewise resolved to flee and having wandered about rather freely here and there, returned through pride alone—for he said, ‘Who am I, or what am I?’ He too was captured and, exposed to the king’s judgment, was condemned to the deserved and most miserable death. Hanged on a gallows with a dog, whenever the dog was struck, it turned its rage upon him and devoured his whole face by biting. Sometimes also—horrible to tell—it defecated; and thus, more miserable than the most miserable, he ended his wretched life with everlasting death.

Those whom he had shut in the tower he compelled by many hardships to surrender; one by one, he threw them down before him with their necks broken. One of them also, named Isaac, who out of fear of death had been tonsured in a certain monastery, he stripped of monastic status and fastened to a gallows.

Having thus gained the victory at Bruges, the king with his men hastened to Ypres, a most excellent fortress, against William the Bastard, supporter of the treason, in order to take vengeance on him as well. By messengers sent to them, he won over the men of Bruges by threats as much as by promises. While William confronted him with three hundred knights, one part of the royal army rushed upon him, while another boldly occupied the castle from a side gate. Once it had been secured, the king expelled William, disinherited, from all Flanders. And because he had aspired by treason to possess Flanders, he deservedly possessed nothing in all Flanders.

Thus Flanders, washed and as it were rebaptized by these and various modes of vengeance and by the shedding of much blood, had William the Norman appointed as count; and the king, with God’s aid, returned victoriously to France.”

38. Adela, the aunt of King Louis and mother of Blessed Charles, is said to have been the uterine sister of Bertha, daughter of Florentius, first count of Holland. Bertha, married to Philip I, king of the Franks, bore him the said Louis. But Gertrude, Bertha’s mother, after the death of her first husband Count Florentius, married Robert the Frisian as her second husband; by her he begot Robert the Younger of Jerusalem, [Col. 0902A] Adela, the mother of Blessed Charles, and Gertrude, mother of Thierry of Alsace, later count of Flanders. Moreover, Galbert thus relates at no. 94 what is reported concerning a dog used in Bertulf’s punishment: “The enraged crowd of Ypres twisted a dog’s entrails around the provost’s neck, and set the dog’s mouth against his mouth as he breathed out his life, thereby equating him and his deeds with the dog.”

[Col. 0901]

# THE EARLIER LIFE, BY WALTER, ARCHDEACON OF THE CHURCH OF THE MORINI

(From three manuscript codices and the edition of Jacques Sirmond.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0901B] To his lord and father, deservedly to be cultivated with every reverence of devotion for his holiness, JOHN, bishop of the holy Church of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0901C] We stated above, §1, that Blessed John died on 27 January 1130, not yet three years after the murder of St Charles.], Brother WALTER, the unprofitable servant of his condescension: the due service of complete submission.

1. The venerable authority of your fatherhood has commanded my humility that, because in these our times crimes most dreadful, committed by wicked men in these regions, have been perpetrated—crimes abominable to the whole world—and because, in vengeance for them, the greatly terrifying judgments of divine justice have been displayed, weighed in the most equitable balance of recompense according to their enormity; and because all these things, as unheard-of to past generations as they are marvellous to the present, I should set forth in writing as they occurred and transmit them in writing to the knowledge of [Col. 0901C] posterity.

Your providence has decreed that all these things should be written and preserved in writing to be made known to future times, so that, when they are read or heard, good people, considering so great an equity of the heavenly Judge, may grow more ardently in love of him; and evil people, recognizing so terrible a judgment of divine vengeance, may through fear of him restrain themselves from their perversity. To your command has also been added the friendly request of Lord Goscelin the dean and of our brethren, a request which I must always receive with every honour; and I desire with fervent longing to obey them in all things pleasing to God.

Therefore, constrained by the authority of your holiness and fraternal charity, I shall undertake what you enjoin—helped by him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent [Col. 0902B] and who waters, and by watering makes fruitful, the dryness of my tongue with the dew of his grace. I rely more upon the power of obedience than upon that literary learning which I have not yet attained to such a degree that I should dare this work.

2. Since this too pleases you, I shall endeavour, avoiding every blemish of falsehood and the uncertainty of common report, nevertheless to recount in a simple narrative, as far as I can, the things that were done. Thus, being less intent upon the superfluous trappings of words and elaborate rhetorical ornaments, I may avoid wearisome prolixity, yet not be found, through striving after excessive brevity, to conceal from the reader’s knowledge the truth necessary concerning those events which I either saw myself or learned beyond doubt from the testimony of truthful men. [Note: [Col. 0901C] This period was omitted without warrant in Surianus’s fourth edition [Col. 0902C]. We indicate the chapter titles appended to this preface, and afterwards divide the text in our customary manner, while retaining the author’s own chapter divisions written in the margin.]

[Col. 0902C] And, so that everything said may emerge more clearly, I have arranged to mark out the entire sequence of the following little work, summarized under concise headings and with the numbers of the several pages prefixed. Thus the page may not, as it were, remain blind and cause the reader weariness, and a more ready approach may lie open to finding what is sought. If I do not treat each matter in its natural order, I beg the reader not to be troubled by it. When later events introduce themselves, I may sometimes fittingly set them forth beforehand by anticipation; and I may sometimes add earlier matters by recapitulating them in an artificial order—provided always that, where reason requires it, it is sufficiently clear what happened at what time.

## PART I. The deeds of Blessed Charles in youth under the counts of Flanders, Robert the Frisian and Robert the Younger: the journey to Jerusalem

[Col. 0903B]

[Col. 0903C] 3. (**CHAP. I.**) Therefore, in the year 1127 of the incarnate Word, in the fifth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, peace having been removed from our land, tranquillity disturbed, honour destroyed, and nearly all human happiness extinguished, there began a detestable origin of wars, hardships, shameful deeds, and every kind of misery. For on that same day of that year, in the life of one man the lives of many were endangered; and from the wrongful death of one man, the deserved deaths of many were propagated in a terrible sequence, by the just judgment of God.

Then, indeed, according to the prophet, “the iniquity of our fathers returned into remembrance before the Lord” (Ps. 108:14), and our ancient sins began to be struck with fresh vengeance. Thus, when he in whose hand, after God, the safety of the people had hitherto rested was removed from their midst, it might be manifestly understood that the sentence of divine judgment, formerly hidden in the secrecy of God’s foreknowledge, had now come publicly forth. For on that very day Charles, count of Flanders, was killed at Bruges in the church of St Donatian by the abominable crime of certain men, to the ruin of [Col. 0903D] very many. He was the son of Canute the martyr [Note: [Col. 0903D] St Canute, king and martyr of Denmark, is honoured on 10 July, the day on which he was killed; on that day we shall give various accounts of his deeds. From this St Canute’s brother Eric the Good, likewise king of Denmark, was born St Canute Lavard, king of the Obotrites and duke of Schleswig; he was killed on 7 January, on which day we have illustrated his deeds.], [Col. 0904C] formerly king of Denmark [Note: [Col. 0903D] All writers of that time commonly wrote “Dacia” for Denmark. Peter, abbot of Celle, book VIII, letter 19, addressed to the archbishop of Lund: “Your Denmark is remote from our France”; and shortly afterward: “Its appearance is one and the same in Denmark and in France.”], and of Queen Adela, whom Roger, duke of Apulia, afterwards took as his wife. But, that we may more clearly show both the occasion of his killing and the punishment of heavenly vengeance terribly visited upon those responsible for his death, it is pleasing to resume the beginning of our little narrative somewhat further back.

4. (**CHAP. II.**) His father, the aforesaid king, after he had been killed through the treachery of his own men in the church to which he had fled in fear of death [Note: [Col. 0903D] In the year of Christ 1086, in the city of Odense, or Othensia, in the church of St Alban, the British martyr, whose feast is 22 June.], was counted among the martyrs by the Danes, because the Lord worked signs and wonders through him; from that time to the present he has been held in great veneration. But the queen, with her little son, returned to Flanders, to her father Robert [Note: [Col. 0904D] Robert seized the county in 1072. Galbert sets forth much concerning his genealogy and the county violently wrested away by him, nos. 109 ff.], [Col. 0904D] the most valiant margrave [Note: [Col. 0904D] The counts of Flanders were formerly called margraves because they guarded the border of the western kingdom of France.], grandson, through his daughter Adela [Note: [Col. 0904D] Adela married Baldwin the Pious, or of Lille, in 1027; after his death she became a nun and lived in the monastery of Messines near Ypres, which she herself had founded, dying there in 1079. Charles’s mother was called Adela after this grandmother.], of Robert [Note: [Col. 0904D] This is Robert, son of Hugh Capet, who succeeded him when he died in 997 and lived until 1031.], formerly king of the Franks, surnamed the Frisian, and to her most noble mother Gertrude [Col. 0905A], descended from an illustrious Saxon stock [Note: [Col. 0905C] He married Gertrude, widow of Florentius I, count of Holland, in 1063, and, becoming guardian of his stepson Thierry, ruled Holland and Frisia; for this reason also he may seem to have acquired the surname “the Frisian.” Gertrude is called the daughter of Herman, or Heyman, duke of the Saxons, whom Giles of Liège, monk of Aurea Vallis, calls Bernard. Gertrude died in 1113 and was buried at Veurne.]. After she had remained there for some time, her parents gave her in marriage to the aforesaid Duke Roger [Note: [Col. 0905C] Roger, son of the Norman Robert Guiscard, is well known for his successful expedition against the Saracens. Baronius places Robert’s [Col. 0905D] death in 1085; others place it earlier, and Parisius later. Yet that Roger was in authority in October 1085 is indicated by an offering made to the church of St Sophia at Salerno, reported by Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VII, under Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno. Baronius, from Peter the Deacon, relates that Roger died in 1111.].

She bore Roger a son named William [Note: [Col. 0905D] William was made duke of Apulia and Calabria by Paschal II and Gelasius II. See Baronius for the years 1114 and 1118.], who, upon his father’s death, succeeded to the duchy and greatly ennobled the honour he had received by nobility of character and vigour. But when he heard of the death of his only brother, he was at first inconsolable in grief, and then himself began to decline mortally. When he knew that he was in danger, he summoned the archbishop of Salerno [Note: [Col. 0905D] This was Romuald, ordained in September 1121 and dead on 21 January 1136; Ughelli provides further information.] and the bishop of Troia. Desiring to have confirmed by their testimony what he had already done while sound in health, he assigned, for perpetual possession, whatever movable or immovable property he appeared to own in the land to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0905B] and to his most holy vicar Pope Honorius [Note: [Col. 0905D] Honorius II was consecrated on 21 December 1124 and died on 16 February 1130. From this the reader may learn why the pope initially denied Roger, count of Sicily, the title duke of Apulia.], from whose sacred mouth I frequently heard this very thing. Thereafter he departed this light in confession of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0905D] On 26 July of the same year, 1127, in which St Charles was killed. See Falco of Benevento in [Col. 0906C] his *Chronicle*.].

5. This Charles of ours, having passed through the years of childhood and reached adulthood, after receiving the belt of knighthood, devoutly went to holy Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0906C] After it had been captured in 1099; hence Galbert, no. 9, relates that the kingdom of Jerusalem was offered to him when he later became count.] to visit the Lord’s sepulchre. There, bearing arms against the pagans, enemies of our faith, he served Christ the Lord vigorously for some time; and he dedicated to him, whom he prudently recognized as the one whom above all others he must serve, the first fruits of his labours and deeds. Soon afterwards, through divine ordering, he returned to Flanders to his uncle Robert the Younger, the margrave [Note: [Col. 0906C] Called “the Younger” because he ruled Flanders with his father for about seventeen years, but after his father died in 1094 he ruled alone.], and was received by him with the honour fitting for such a young man.

[Col. 0906A] 6. (**CHAP. III.**) Since we have now incidentally made mention of this glorious prince, it seems worthwhile to recall briefly some outstanding marks of his virtues. This is that renowned Count Robert, son of Robert the Frisian, who, when he heard the decree of that Council of Clermont, holy and to be remembered with the memory of all saints [Note: [Col. 0906C] That council was held in November 1095, at the instigation of Blessed Peter the Hermit.], concerning the rescue of the venerable place of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection from pagan hands and its recovery for the Christian faith, immediately judged, according to evangelical teaching, that wife and children, and finally everything he possessed in the world, must be placed after the service of Christ the Lord. Bearing the emblem of Christ’s cross upon his shoulders and following, as far as he could, Christ’s bodily footsteps, he hastened eagerly with others inspired by the same grace to fulfil with the entire constancy of faith [Col. 0906B] the command of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0906C] William of Tyre, book I, chapter 17, lists first “Hugh the Great, brother of Philip king of France; second, Robert count of the Flemings; . . . eighth, Godfrey duke of Bouillon.” Robert’s journey is described in book II, chapter 16 and following, as also in Tudebodus and other writers on this expedition.].

In that expedition, and in the capture of the cities of that land, especially Antioch [Note: [Col. 0906D] Antioch was taken on 3 June 1098. Tyre, book I, chapter 21, writes that among the first to climb its walls were “the lord count of Flanders and Lord Tancred, by whose guidance the others were directed.”] and holy Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0906D] Jerusalem was stormed on Friday, 15 July 1099, at the ninth hour. Tyre, book VIII, chapter 18: “Immediately after Duke Godfrey entered the count of Flanders and the duke of the Normans.” Hence Robert was surnamed “of Jerusalem.”], he gave innumerable splendid proofs of his courage and excellence. The history written about the deeds of the Franks who captured Jerusalem for Christ contains some of these. For his praise it is enough here to recall only this: because of the invincible steadfastness of his spirit, he is recorded as having been called “the son of George” even by the Arabs and Turks [Note: [Col. 0906D] Tudebodus, book IV, recounts the battle joined with the Turks under the leadership of Duke Godfrey, Robert count of Flanders, and Hugh the Great, when “St George, Theodore, and Demetrius were their leaders from heaven”; terrified, the Turks fled. Thus he could have been called by them the son of St George; this is also noted in a manuscript chronicle of the monastery of St Andrew which he himself founded.].

7. (**CHAP. IV.**) Therefore, after the unbelieving nations had been defeated by the mighty hand of the Lord, and Arnulf had been raised to the dignity of patriarch in the holy city, and Duke Godfrey to the royal diadem, [Col. 0906C] he returned prosperously to his own land, [Note: [Col. 0906D] Tyre, book IX, chapter 13: “These things having thus been accomplished, the princes beloved of God and devoted to God, the lords count of the Normans [Col. 0907C] and of the Flemings, having happily completed the journey of pilgrimage undertaken by them, prepare to return to their own lands.”] and for the remainder of his life governed his land happily with great and distinguished moderation.

## PART II. Flanders is offered to Blessed Charles by Count Baldwin, and he accepts it

8. (**CHAP. V.**) A short time after the aforesaid reception of our Charles, Robert died in France, near the city of Meaux, after being ill for a few days. [Note: [Col. 0907C] The author prudently passes over the occasion of so great a man’s death: namely, that, fighting against the English in the Norman war to be mentioned shortly, he fell from his horse near Meaux on the river Marne, was crushed, and died on the third day thereafter. Meyer places his death in 1111; but a charter signed by him in the following year, 1112, produced by Oliverius Uredius in *On the Seals of the Counts of Flanders*, p. 9, shows that he died in that year. In that same year Baldwin [Col. 0907D] his son still signed a charter for the monastery of Alciacus in Artois, in Miraeus, *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgii*, ch. 128.] He was buried in the monastery of St Vaast, in the city of Arras, amid the great grief of all; and he left as heir his son Baldwin, a young man, whom he had received from his most noble wife Clementia [Note: [Col. 0907D] Clementia was the daughter of William and sister of Stephen, princes of Burgundy; she was also sister of Guy, archbishop of Vienne, who became Roman pontiff in 1119 under the name Calixtus II.].

Not long afterwards, having received from King Louis [Note: [Col. 0907D] This is Louis VI, called the Fat, Baldwin’s cousin, born of Bertha, uterine sister of the aforementioned Robert of Jerusalem and of the mother of Count Charles; king of France from 1108 to 1137.] both the gift of knighthood and his paternal inheritance, [Col. 0907B] he made especial use of Lord Charles’s counsel and was formed by his instruction. In a short time he grew to such an eminence of courage and martial vigour that all who observed his worth found him remarkable, and he became wholly formidable not only to neighbouring counts and dukes but even to kings themselves. Yet as his strength shone beyond the measure of his age through sudden advances, so it could not endure long, because God’s hidden providence opposed his undertakings.

For at that time he had taken under the protection of his patronage and supplied with military arms the dispossessed young William [Note: [Col. 0907D] This is William the Norman, who became count of Flanders after the murder of St Charles.], son of Count Robert [Note: [Col. 0907D] Robert, the second son of William the Conqueror, king of England, who died on 6 September 1087, received Normandy from him and, together with the count of Flanders and others, captured Antioch and Jerusalem. Meanwhile, when his elder brother William Rufus, king of England, died childless on 2 August 1100, their youngest brother Henry I seized the English kingdom and was crowned on the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. Robert returned to Normandy in that same year, vainly claimed the kingdom of England as due to him as elder brother, and in 1106 was defeated and captured in battle; the following year he was deprived of his eyes, and he died miserably in 1134. These matters are found in Matthew Paris and others.], son of William, king of the English, surnamed Pileatus (“the Clad”), that is, the Robert who had begotten him from Queen Matilda, sister of the aforesaid Robert the Frisian, as also his brothers William and Henry, and whom his own brother Henry, king of the English, held captive. [Col. 0907C]

Baldwin had resolved, with all his strength, to restore to William his inheritance of Normandy, which William’s uncle had acquired after the capture of his father. [Col. 0908A] He therefore harassed it with heavy and repeated incursions. He had already subjected a great part of it to himself, with its towns and fortresses; and he compelled nearly all the rest to tremble exceedingly at fear of his sword, since King Henry himself was unable to defend it either by strength of arms or abundance of wealth. But truly, as the Prophet says, “There is no strength, no counsel against God” (Prov. 21:30). Truly, he alone is mighty who, whenever and however he wills, is able to reduce the power of all to nothing.

9. (**CHAP. VI.**) While Baldwin was doing such things and planning much greater ones, the shield of a certain hostile knight, as they say, struck and crushed his forehead. From the collision there arose a small swelling in the place where the saving sign of the cross was customarily impressed upon him; [Col. 0908B] and all the summit of that great power, which had risen so quickly as though into a great mountain, still more swiftly subsided and, appearing for a little while like smoke, vanished. For, despite the care of physicians, his illness daily worsened. At last, in the town of Roeselare [Note: [Col. 0908C] A quite pleasant town in Flanders, in the territory of Ypres toward Bruges, called by some Rollarium and by Charles the Bald Rossat, in the land of the Menapii; in Flemish, Rousselare; in French, Roullers.], he received the monastic habit with the utmost devotion and humble supplication. Worn out by the sickness for about ten months, he died on 17 June in the year of the Lord 1119. His body was conveyed to the monastery of St Bertin [Note: [Col. 0908D] Situated in the town of Saint-Omer.], where, amid the immeasurable weeping of all the nobles of the land and sorrowful lamentation, he was buried before the altar of the Holy Cross on 19 June of the same month.

10. (**CHAP. VII.**) Nevertheless, although his mother, with certain others concurring, strongly opposed this on account of her affection for William [Note: [Col. 0908D] In the other *Life* he is called William of Ypres; and in charters Uredius prints in the *Flemish Genealogy*, p. 147, he calls himself “William of Ypres” and “William, son of Count Philip.” Sugerius and others call him a bastard, spurious, and illegitimate. Galbert, no. 77, says that his low-born mother never ceased, while alive, to card wool. Had Marchantius read this, he would not have asserted with so much effort that William was born of lawful marriage.] son of Count Philip [Note: [Col. 0908D] He is commonly called Count Philip of Ypres or of Lo; he himself calls Lo the village of his possession, in Uredius’s evidences for the *Flemish Genealogy*, p. 146. Lo is in the district of Veurne, where there is a distinguished abbey. His charter in Miraeus, *Notitia Ecclesiarum Belgii*, ch. 114, indicates various gifts made by him to it.], son of the aforesaid Robert the Frisian. Philip had married the countess’s niece [Note: [Col. 0908D] We have discussed above Robert of Lo, born from that marriage.], and she was most eager that she should succeed her son.

Before Baldwin departed this life, however, he himself appointed this glorious man Charles, of whom we have undertaken to speak—having often proved his excellence and ability in many matters—and entrusted to him the whole charge of governing and arranging all affairs. [Col. 0909A] Earlier he had also joined Charles in marriage to the noble maiden Margaret [Note: [Col. 0909C] Rainald was born to the count of Clermont and Margaret, who had six sisters. Of these, Felicia married the holy king of Aragon; Adelaide was mother of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, assistant to St Norbert in founding the church and monastery of Prémontré. Andrew du Chesne discusses this lineage from a manuscript history of the restoration of the church of Laon, *Genealogia Castellionensis*, book II, chapter 6, p. 18 of the evidences; there Charles is called that distinguished count of the Flemings.], daughter of Count Rainald of Clermont, and had granted him the county of Amiens [Note: [Col. 0909D] Formerly the counts of Amiens had been Ingelram and his son Thomas, called counts of Coucy. But because Thomas had been deposed by King Louis on account of his wicked life, he was embittered by hatred and was always hostile to Blessed Charles, as is said below.] together with the castle of Incre [Note: [Col. 0909D] We read in an addition to our manuscript *Chronicle of Sigebert of Gembloux*, continued to 1164, that Count Baldwin granted the castle of Encres to Charles, his cousin, in 1115. Incra, or Encra, is in Picardy, in the same region as Amiens toward Artois, on the river of the same name, which joins the Somme near Corbie. The name Albert was lately imposed upon it in hatred of the Italian Concini, who had held from it the title of marquis.].

I would judge that all these things were done not so much by the young man’s own will as by the ordinance of the heavenly Judge, who by his hidden inspiration bent as he willed the mind and will of one too youthful and less fitted for mature counsels.
