For it is written: “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord, and he turns it wherever he wills” (Prov. 21:1). [Col. 0909B] Had the decree of divine will not ordained that this should happen, the love of one man would never have outweighed in Baldwin’s mind the love of three persons—his mother, his male cousin, and his female cousin. The signs of subsequent events made this most plainly evident. For who, I ask, cast down with such speed the enormous billows of martial storms raised so violently against him, unless it was he who wished, through the ministry of this man, for a time to provide tranquillity for those whom he had made? Hence the Psalmist: “He made its storm into a breeze, and its waves were stilled” (Ps. 106:29).

## PART III. Blessed Charles’s noble spirit: stern toward the wicked, benevolent toward the good and the wretched, especially in the time of famine

11. (**CHAP. VIII.**) For after he had assumed the helm of governing this land in the manner already set forth, Countess Clementia, pricked by blind envy for the reason stated above, immediately united herself in marriage with the duke of Louvain [Note: [Col. 0909D] This was Godfrey the Bearded, or the Younger, count of Louvain. Emperor Henry IV, after Henry of Limburg had been captured and deprived of office for rebellion, had granted him in 1116 the duchy of Brabant and Lower Lotharingia, together with the margraviate of Antwerp. [Col. 0910C] He died in 1140 and was buried at Affligem, leaving five children by his first wife Ida.], aided by the treachery of certain nobles of the land. [Col. 0910A] She broke the agreement of peace which her son, Margrave Baldwin, had made while near death between Charles and herself; and, with her husband’s consent, that of the count of Mons [Note: [Col. 0910C] The count of Mons, or Hainaut, was then Baldwin III, son of Baldwin of Jerusalem and Ida. Flanders was due to him as grandson of Baldwin VI, count of Flanders.], and that of King Louis of France, who, as many thought, secretly favoured their undertaking, she prepared to expel Charles from the borders of Flanders, of which she then held about twelve towns.

Count Hugh [Note: [Col. 0910C] “Hugh of Candavene,” says the aforementioned manuscript addition to Sigebert, “was expelled from the castle of Encres in 1115,” which, as we said, had been granted to Count Charles; “when in 1117 he was laying Flanders waste by plunder and fire, Count Baldwin besieged the castle of St Paul, but was reconciled with him through the mediation of Count Eustace of Boulogne.” After Blessed Charles’s death Hugh subscribed the charter by which William the Norman, received at Saint-Omer on 17 April, as Galbert relates at no. 107, confirmed the customs of the city; it is printed in du Chesne, *Genealogy of the Béthune Family*, book II of the evidences, p. 21. In Galbert, no. 154, he adheres to Thierry against the Norman on 30 March 1128. Yet Anselm of Gembloux testifies in his *Chronicle* that in 1131 “he burned the town and church of St Riquier in the district of Ponthieu.” Meanwhile, because he is called “of Campo Avenae” or “Candavene,” Janus Lernutius writes in the *Life of Blessed Charles* that “a report reached him from Hainaut that very many brigands had established a base in the fortress of Avesnes under Count Hugh, heir of the fortress, which fortress they commonly called St Paul,” etc. Avesnes is a town of Hainaut on the borders of Picardy. But what had this to do with Blessed Charles, since he held no lordship in Hainaut? The subject here is the town of St Paul, then subject to Artois, eight miles from Arras and six from Saint-Omer.] of St Paul, surnamed Campus Avenae (“Field of Oats”), seeing this opportunity to practise his malice, likewise began to renew his ancient and long-established hatred against Charles, to raid the parts of the land adjoining his own, and, according to his custom, more fiercely than usual to devastate everything by fire and plunder.

12. (**CHAP. IX.**) Therefore, while all these men unanimously conspired for Charles’s destruction and stirred up on every side savage tumults of war to the ruin of our people, he who by the hidden judgment of his power “scatters the counsels of nations,” reproves “the thoughts of the mighty,” and rejects “the counsels of princes,” looked down from his holy height: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon earth, to hear the groaning of those in chains and to release the children of the slain” (Ps. 72:10). To his faithful servant Charles he graciously granted both undaunted confidence to wage war against them and unconquerable power to defeat them all.

For all that din of wars roaring around him was checked as swiftly by victory as it had been raised by the ferocity of pride. “Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high” [Col. 0910C] (Ps. 92:6). I do not think it so remarkable that he quickly restrained the movements of so many princes and their most stubborn rising, as that, with almost no shedding of blood, [Col. 0911A] he inspired all of them with the utmost terror of himself. Thus, once they had obtained from him whatever terms of peace, none dared ever again to renew the reins of rebellion, or to give even the slightest occasion for such a suspicion of himself.

13. Therefore the countess—now, more unhappily, a duchess—overborne by her husband’s unexpected successes, sought peace from Charles and was compelled to surrender to him four of her towns: Diksmuide [Note: [Col. 0911C] Dichesmuda, Dicasmuda, and Dicimuda, now commonly Diksmuide, between Ypres and Nieuwpoort.], Bergues [Note: [Col. 0911C] Called Bargium or Bragium by others; commonly Bergues-Saint-Winoc, a well-known town near Dunkirk.], Aire [Note: [Col. 0911C] Aire, a very strongly fortified town of Artois, not far from the river Lys, beside which, in neighbouring Flanders, lies the church of St Vaast.], and Saint-Venant [Note: [Col. 0911C] *Guerpire*, or *werpire*, derives from the Germanic word *werpen*, “to cast” or “throw,” because a right and lordship were transferred and renounced by the throwing of a straw. Thus in the *Miracles of Blessed Bertilia*, published by us in the Addenda to 3 January, one reads “feudal land lawfully sold and surrendered (*guerpita*).” See further Vossius, *On Faults of Speech*, book II, chapter 23.]. She who had formerly planned to obtain what was another’s unjustly through war, having lost much of what was her own, learned to be content with the remainder and to rejoice in peace. Yet Charles kept his faith fully with her, as with everyone, and thereafter treated her with every honour and humanity.

[Col. 0911B] 14. But Hugh persisted in his insolence. Charles subsequently destroyed the castle of St Paul after it had been surrendered to him, leveled all its fortifications, and compelled Hugh, against his will, to live more peaceably in the future and to devote himself to agriculture, which he had previously prevented by raging destructively throughout the surrounding country. But afterwards, as they say, necessity changed into willingness: Hugh seemed gladly to embrace this way of life, and, as long as that same prince lived, judged it more advantageous to rejoice in the security of peace than to disturb others and be disturbed through the losses caused by plundering and fires.

15. Count Walter of Hesdin also, caught making ready a rebellion and conspiring with Hugh through his habitual folly and perversity, he expelled him not only from his castle but from the country as well, and appointed another as his successor.

> **Note:** Hesdin, or Hesdinium, an ancient town of present-day Artois, once had its own counts. Among them, in 1065 Count Walter (perhaps this man’s grandfather) subscribed to a charter of the Count of Guînes; see Chesneau on this family [Col. 0911D]. Then Ingelram or Ingelramnus, Count of Hesdin, restored in 1072 the church of the monastery of Auchy, which had been destroyed by barbarians, and in 1079 confirmed donations made to that monastery. Baldwin, Count of Flanders, declares him to have been Walter’s uncle in a charter signed in 1112, “and restores to him his land”; thus Walter seems to have rebelled repeatedly.

But in the final year of his life, taking pity on him, he granted him certain adequate revenues for the necessary maintenance of life. He also so thoroughly subdued the Count of Montaigu and Thomas, Count of Coucy, who habitually disturbed our side to the utmost of their power, that they not only refrained from inflicting injuries upon others, but also, whether willing or unwilling, endured in peace those unexpectedly inflicted upon themselves. Thus, when every disturbance of war had been calmed by God’s aid, the land was silent before him.

> **Note:** Anselm, Count of Hesdin, subscribed in 1127 to the previously mentioned charter of William the Norman on behalf of the people of Saint-Omer; perhaps he was appointed in place of the expelled Walter.

> **Note:** Coucy, or Cociacum—commonly Coucy—in the district of Laon, formerly belonged to the archbishops of Rheims, having been given by King Clovis to St Remigius. There Thomas, besieged by Louis the Fat, “was wounded to death; brought before the king and conveyed to Laon, he breathed out his most foul spirit, deprived of the divine Eucharist—a most abandoned man, hostile to God and men alike, who spared neither clergy through fear of ecclesiastical punishment nor people through any human feeling, slaughtering everything and laying everything waste.” Suger and Abbot Guibert of Nogent describe these and other crimes of his in the treatise *On the Murder of Galdric, Bishop of Laon*.

16. (CHAPTER X.) Having obtained this tranquillity of peace, I am wholly unable to explain in words what a man he showed himself to be, and how great. Devoted to God, he humbled himself with every humility before all His servants—that is, the prelates of churches and persons of every religious order—and, reverently obedient to their commands, patiently and humbly endured the reproofs with which they judged that he should be corrected according to time and circumstance. With complete gentleness he promised amendment and greater caution for the future.

> **Note:** Iperius, part II, chapter 41, relates the following, which belongs here: “Toward God and ecclesiastical and religious men he was so humble and devout that he often asked them to rebuke him at an appropriate time and place for his shortcomings, and to pray God for him. In his court he always caused the affairs of religious persons and churches to be dispatched first, saying that those who attend to God’s service ought not to be detained in the courts of princes. Thus it once happened that this Abbot John entered the count’s court on the day of Epiphany [Col. 0912D], and the count said to him: ‘Lord Abbot, who is singing the high Mass for you today, on this holy festival, in your church?’ The abbot said: ‘Lord, there are a hundred monks in the monastery, so some worthy man can celebrate it.’ And the count said: ‘On so great a feast you ought to be in your community, singing with those who sing psalms, feasting with those who dine, and refreshing your monks who have laboured in God’s service. For our forefathers assigned you revenues for this purpose.’  
> ‘Lord,’ said the abbot, ‘necessity compels me, for a certain knight oppresses us.’ The count replied: ‘It would have been enough for this to be conveyed to me by letter or messenger; for it is my office to defend you, and yours to pray God for me.’ Calling the knight, he said: ‘By the faith which I owe to Baldwin, my predecessor, I declare: if I hear any more of this, I shall have you boiled, as he did a knight who was plundering a widow.’ Thus the knight desisted, and the abbot returned comforted.”

This appears the more praiseworthy in his character because it is rarely and with difficulty found in others who hold not merely worldly but even ecclesiastical eminence. For most men, once they have attained the summit of even a modest power and begun to receive honour from their subjects, immediately forget their natural condition and their own frailty; raised up, as it were, upon some pinnacle of vanity, they despise others, whom they refuse to recognize as their equals by the order of nature. They believe themselves wiser and more worthy than all those whom they surpass through the lot of rank.

While they devote themselves to the pleasures of the world, become defiled with the filth of vices, and are vainly exalted by the swellings of pride, they utterly disdain to be corrected by anyone’s rebukes; indeed, they are often made more hostile rather than improved by them. Thus, fearing neither God nor men, like unbridled horses they rush headlong into vices. And so that, according to Scripture, those who are filthy may become still more filthy (Rev. 22:11), it is brought about by the dreadful judgment of the Almighty that not only is reproof absent to restrain them, but flattery is commonly present to nourish their vices. Their subjects, that is, not only fail to rebuke what their rulers do wrongly, but also—so that “the sinner may be praised in the desires of his soul”—often praise, from a desire to please, what they ought to censure from zeal for righteousness. Hence Ezekiel was told: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute and not like a man who rebukes, because you are a rebellious house” (Ezek. 3:26). And through the prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you” (Isa. 3:11).

17. (CHAPTER XI.) But our venerable margrave Charles showed himself gentle and humble toward those who corrected him, and often even gave thanks. By devout entreaty he asked them to obtain for him by their prayers divine assistance, so that he might do what they said. For he judged that in this he was obeying and yielding not so much to men as to God, whose embassy they discharge. He knew and wisely observed that Truth Himself said in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me; and he who receives you receives me” (Luke 11:16).

Nor did he burden churches or the people under his authority with any exactions, as is the corrupt custom of other princes. Rather, by diligently providing for the public welfare of all, he relieved them in many ways; and, in the manner of a loving father, carefully provided for everyone in common.

18. This may indeed be proved by the fact that, when in the two years before his death sterility of the land and scarcity of crops had brought about a great shortage of provisions, he mercifully remitted to his peasants a large portion of the rents from which he himself had to live and maintain his household. He also completely prohibited for a time not only superfluous but often necessary brewing and drinking, and imposed moderation upon the immoderate; thereby, with fatherly care, he wisely secured for all the sustenance necessary for life.

> **Note:** Anselm of Gembloux, under the year 1125: “A most severe winter, continuous for six weeks and very harmful. A severe famine everywhere, with many persons of both sexes perishing.”

He also decreed that anyone selling bread should sell not one loaf, as was customary, but two loaves, however small, for each penny, so that every poor person who perhaps did not have a penny might have the means of purchasing with a halfpenny.

19. What, I ask, would he do in great matters, who so carefully provided in the least? At a time when he saw that there were many needy people, he assigned one hundred of them to each of his estates—for he had many—and commanded that they receive from his own resources a daily allowance. Moreover, in whatever city, town, or village he might be, countless persons flocked to him every day. He distributed food, money, and clothing among them, especially with his own hands. Thus the memory of those present records that at Ypres on one day he gave away seven thousand eight hundred loaves.

For he allowed no one to leave him empty-handed; he frequently stripped off and gave away even the very costly garments which he wore. For he had heard that evangelical saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 25:40); and this: “What you have done to one of my least ones, you have done to me” (Matt. 5:7). He was so affected by their miseries that, when he saw them troubled or afflicted in any way, he grieved for them with all his heart, himself fulfilling, according to his measure, what the Apostle says of himself: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 2:29).

And lest in all this he should be regarded as conspicuous for an exceptional and singular degree of generosity, he repeatedly invited others also to this work of mercy, not merely by example but by exhortation. For he said that so great an opportunity for acquiring the kingdom of God must by no means be neglected by the devout minds of believers; rather, they must sow in blessing in the present, so that in the future they might reap eternal life from blessing.

## PART IV. The occasion of the hatred stirred up against Blessed Charles

20. (CHAPTER XII.) But, in order that, according to the same Apostle, he might become all things to all men (1 Cor. 9:12), as he was gentle toward the humble, so he appeared severe to the proud: soothing the former with lamb-like mildness and deterring the latter with lion-like severity. He also restrained with such strict severity those unjust oppressions by which they were accustomed to crush the poor, that he both delivered the needy from the hand of sinners, according to the Prophet (Ps. 81:4), and curbed the malice of the wicked lest it rage beyond measure. Thus those whom love of justice did not moderate might at least be restrained by fear of punishment.

He also checked with extraordinary severity the formerly untamed ferocity of the barbarians inhabiting the maritime regions of Flanders, who, having set aside the fear of God, were accustomed cruelly to shed human blood. He absolutely forbade the erection of the signals which they used to raise aloft in order to summon their confederates to battle, and which, in the madness of their furious lust for war, they called in their language *bacchae*.

> **Note:** Even now in the Belgian language *bake* is called a lookout, beacon, signal, or coastal marker, for the nighttime approach of ships.

He was either loved or feared by all to such a degree that among that great multitude of a savage people scarcely anyone could be found who thought it safe to oppose in even the slightest matter his ordinances promulgated for the public benefit.

21. The extent to which he was a champion of truth and justice may be inferred from this: he diligently showed himself steadfast in fulfilling promises and wholly discerning in investigating the merits of cases. Nor did God’s grace fail him in this; instructed by it, he examined all matters requiring consideration with a marvellous keenness of subtle judgment. Detecting and reproving injustice, exalting and defending equity, he upheld justice in all things to the best of his power.

In all these matters he frequently observed this order: whenever clerics or religious monks, compelled by some necessity, had cases to plead in his court, he heard their complaints before all others and decided their causes; only then did he turn to other business. For he judged it utterly unworthy and inappropriate that those who ought to devote themselves to reading or prayer should linger in court or in the conduct of such affairs, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4).

22. (CHAPTER XIII.) Since, then, this illustrious man excelled in these and many other virtues, which all that we can say is insufficient either to enumerate or explain, the more good men delighted in his virtuous efforts, the more the wicked were tormented. For they saw, and grieved, that by his uprightness the lives of those whom they envied were safeguarded and their own efforts were thwarted. Since their wickedness, restrained by the chains of fear of him, was not permitted to rage as it wished to the destruction of others, they considered their own safety endangered by his survival; and whatever they saw added to others, they thought subtracted from their own advantage.

Spurred by these incentives of greed and goads of rapacity, they first began to envy him, then to nurse secret hatred against him, and finally, loosening their tongues in detraction, to tear the life of the just man with canine teeth. In this they rightly followed in the footsteps of their Jewish forefathers, who are shown to have persecuted the Lord and Saviour with the same malice that the Prophet had long before described in their person: “Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is useless to us and opposed to our deeds” (Wis. 2:12).

23. (CHAPTER XIV.) At that time there was a certain provost of Bruges, named Bertulf, archchaplain and chancellor of the Flemish court. Since the world smiled upon him, he had amassed immense riches; for he possessed very extensive estates both through paternal inheritance and through the liberality of princes, namely Charles and his predecessors. So that no temporal prosperity might seem lacking to him, he attained the height of the greatest power, with a great crowd of kinsmen, friends, and dependants—whom he had beyond number—obeying him.

Miserably satiated with all these things, he was raised up into pride. This, indeed, as I confidently judge, would never have happened to him under God’s protecting grace, had he wished to use humbly, as provisions for the journey through this valley of tears, God’s good creation granted us for that purpose, rather than perversely to enjoy and delight in it.

Root out, good husbandman, the thorns from the soil of my heart, so that in it the seed of your word may bring forth fruit, if not a hundredfold or sixtyfold, then at least thirtyfold. Hear me as that wise man petitions you: “Give me only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. 30:8); and, as the patriarch Jacob desires, “bread to eat and clothing to cover me” (Gen. 28:20).

But, to return to my subject: while this son of the world flourished in all the goods of this world, abundance of riches produced power for him, and power in turn begot and brought forth pride. Lifted up by it, he despised others; swollen with excessive arrogance, he could no longer contain himself. And because such as is the master of the household, such are his servants, his nephews and dependants—whom the unhappy man nourished and loved too carnally, to their own ruin—began to suffer from the same plague as he did, while their wickedness issued forth as though from fatness.

24. (CHAPTER XV.) It happened that a certain noble knight brought an action against another nobleman in the count’s court concerning the violation of a truce. The latter, when the stigma of servile status had been cast against him because he had married a kinswoman of that provost, who was said to be the count’s bondwoman, answered by repudiating the charge as a free man [the Latin is corrupt or uncertain]. Therefore the entire kindred of the provost flamed with an intolerable anger against Count Charles and that knight; for the slander seemed to extend to them all.

> **Note:** A truce, an armistice, or temporary pledge of faith given to an enemy: called by later Greeks τρέβα and τρεύα; in German, *treuwe*, “faith.”

> **Note:** *Placitare*: that is, to dispute, litigate, or submit a matter to judgment. Thus Vossius, book IV of *On Faults of Speech*, chapter 16, where he cites this passage.

The case was therefore long debated, but it was finally resolved in this way: the woman whose status had been challenged was personally to establish her freedom, with the consent of the count, by the hand of twelve nobles; while the count’s claim against the rest of that family was to remain intact.

> **Note:** The controversy concerning the status of the two families is discussed in §§4 and 5.

This postponement of that accusation was thus thought to have been the first occasion for the murder of Lord Charles. From it they began to entertain the bitterest hatred against him.

25. (CHAPTER XVI.) Therefore that ancient serpent, the enemy of the human race, perceiving this opportunity to exercise his malice, immediately thrust himself into the midst of the malicious and proud. Having placed the throne of his kingdom in the minds of those over all the children of pride he glories to reign, he craftily prepared another snare by which they might more frequently be entangled and cast down.

For a certain Burchard, nephew of that provost—namely, son of Lambert, the provost’s brother—a man exceedingly proud and great in his own eyes, bore grave enmities, though arising from the slightest causes, against his neighbour Thancmar, who was said to show great zeal in spending alms upon the poor, especially monks, and against Walter, Thancmar’s nephew. On both sides there were no small killings of men. But Charles, God’s servant, frequently exacted from them the terms of truce by the authority entrusted to him by the Lord, and repeatedly compelled them, though unwilling, to make peace. He sought to be counted among those to whom Truth Himself promises: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

> **Note:** From this has been taken the occasion for inventing that Burchard was Blessed Charles’s almoner, as was said above.

26. (CHAPTER XVII.) But the provost and his people, who thought themselves stronger and prouder, suspected that Charles was directing his efforts to protect the other party. Since, conscious of their own wrongdoing, they were inwardly tortured by envy, they complained that what he strove to do for the common good was being done to their own detriment.

Thus, prompted by goading envy, enraged by raging anger, and puffed up by pride, they suddenly attacked Thancmar, who was unsuspecting and feared no evil because of the truce. Breaking the covenant of peace, they burst into the lower court and compelled him, in great distress, to flee to the upper fortification. They cut down the brushwood and scattered, demolished, and ruined everything found below. When Thancmar had suffered this injury, he brought a just complaint before the count, declaring both the damage inflicted upon him not without contempt for the count and the grave danger in which he had stood.

Summoned to answer the charge on a day and at a place appointed by the count, they chose to add contempt to contempt rather than excuse their absence even through a representative.

27. (CHAPTER XVIII.) The prudent man patiently overlooked this injury, deciding meanwhile to wait for them and still gently invite them to correct so grave an offence. Later, when he had spoken privately with the provost at Bruges about all these matters and rebuked him with sufficient moderation, as was his custom, the provost promised that on the following day he and his people would make full amends. Nevertheless he disregarded this promise: neither did he come himself nor bring them to make satisfaction.

But the count, repeatedly provoked, though he did not doubt that all this was done in contempt of him, bore it with equanimity. Even then he delayed to exact just punishment from the obstinate, and once more waited with forbearance for amendment.

## PART V. Public robberies suppressed by Blessed Charles on the counsel of the barons

28. (CHAPTER XIX.) But all this was in vain. Abusing his patience and promising themselves impunity thereafter on that account, they fell into worse courses under the impulse of pride. Whereas they ought to have corrected their earlier errors through repentance and, even late, appeased the just wrath of their lord by making satisfaction for their faults, they resolved rather boldly to heap fault upon fault and aggravate excess with excess.

For, taking advantage of the count’s absence when he had perhaps gone to France—for his presence was always burdensome to all workers of iniquity, like an intolerable prison—they gathered a large and powerful force of knights. Raiding almost the whole surrounding region, breaking into houses and carrying off every movable thing, they despoiled the poor; they hanged some and slaughtered most by the sword. Since this had never formerly been customary, it seemed exceedingly intolerable and cruel to everyone. For from ancient times it had been established by the counts of our land, and had until then been observed almost as law, that however great a war might arise among any persons, no one in Flanders should presume to plunder anything or seize or despoil anyone.

29. (CHAPTER XX.) When the revered guardian of his country returned and learned the atrocity of such great crimes, he was deeply grieved. Since these deeds had been committed during the holy peace, that is, within Septuagesima, he resolved, as was fitting, to avenge not so much his own injury as God’s.

But, desiring to determine how it ought to be punished, he summoned his barons to assemble at Ypres on the third day before the Kalends of March. I too was present there by his command, though for another matter. He set before their ears every event in the order in which it had occurred, and, lest he seem to avenge himself alone, requested their counsel about everything. Nor were there lacking persons who lamented that they had been unjustly robbed by the men of Bruges and subjected to blows and insults, and who implored justice for their disgrace with tearful complaints.

When different persons had expressed different opinions, all finally agreed that the count himself should personally visit those districts, investigate more certainly by sight and hearing what had been done, and then proportion the measure of punishment to the measure of guilt. Although he was not wholly unaware of their wicked schemes against him—especially as the aforesaid Burchard had long before been accused of saying, “If someone killed the count, who would avenge him?”—he nevertheless determined to go, and ordered a considerable number of knights to accompany him.

30. (CHAPTER XXI.) Setting out with them on the next day, he saw houses ruined and all possessions plundered and scattered, and learned that not even the smallest means of subsistence had been left to the poor. Moved on the one hand by the tears of the wretched and on the other by his innate compassion, he groaned deeply; drawing long sighs from the depths of his heart and shedding tears, he grieved marvellously.

First, he burned, overthrew, and utterly destroyed Burchard’s nearby stronghold, as the seedbed and root of so great an evil. Then, intending to deal more carefully with these and other matters, he went that same day to Bruges—alas, never to return. On the following day, namely the Kalends of March, while he remained there and examined the cases of individuals with his customary equity, the day declined toward evening. The sun, showing that the warped minds of wicked men were deprived of the light of truth, left those regions of the world which it customarily illumined with its rays; it withdrew spiritual light from them and bodily light from these, and brought the desired opportunity for the children of darkness to do works of darkness. For “he who does evil hates the light.”

31. (CHAPTER XXII.) Then, it is said, the provost summoned to himself Guy of Steenvoorde and a few others who appeared to be familiar with the count. Imposing his embassy upon them, he sent them to the count’s court as though they were about to ask pardon for his nephews. Carrying out what they had been ordered, they immediately approached the count and laid before him, as they say, not so much a peace proposal as a complaint:

> “Let the punishment and disgrace of Burchard be enough, lord, to have satisfied your anger thus far; let it be enough that you have burned his dwelling-place to the injury of himself and all his family. Now restrain the impulses of your wrath, vainly aroused against him; spare the afflicted young man, forgive at last one assailed by excessive insults. Let him now, if it please you, find a place for mercy with you, he whom undeserved punishment has more than sufficiently saddened and tormented. Restrain also the force of your hatred and anger against his family, and appease by a belated satisfaction those whom you have grievously offended.”

> **Note:** Steenvoorde, in ancient sources *Stenasforda* and *Stenafvordt*, is a celebrated town in the territory of Cassel. Its lord, Wido or Guy, subscribed the letters of Blessed Charles, Count, for the monastery of Lo in 1123, in Miraeus’s *Notitia*, chapter 134. Guy’s wife is called below, no. 49, the sister of Isaac, kinsman of Provost Bertulf; but in Galbert, no. 94, she is called Bertulf’s niece. Isaac and this wife of Guy therefore seem to have been born of a mother who was the provost’s sister.

32. The hero gave them this very brief reply:

> “Why do you so insist that I have given way to my passions and undeservedly inflicted shameful injuries upon your Burchard? What requital worthy of Burchard’s great offences has been made if one little house of his is burned while he himself remains unpunished? Did not justice rather demand that he restore in full what he took from the poor and undergo in his own body the penalties for such great crimes? Let him therefore restore justly what he has unjustly seized, acknowledge the condition of his family, and so find the mercy he seeks. For by what reasoning can he obtain pardon while retaining the plunder of the poor?”

33. (CHAPTER XXIII.) When this was reported to the provost, although nothing could have been said more justly than the count’s argument, since it accorded with the commands both of the Law and of the Gospel, he nevertheless ought to have yielded to truth and reason. Instead, his mind blinded, he began to rage more wildly; excessively inflamed by his passions and kindled by a diabolical spirit, muttering dreadful things and breathing grave threats, he supplied spurs to his followers as they rushed on and weapons to them in their fury. Those whom he ought to have restrained, he incited still more with the goads of his anger.

The madness of the demented and the frenzy of the furious were further increased because the aforesaid envoys had not acted sincerely. Distorting the count’s words and inflaming the proud minds of the young men still more severely, they said that they would never obtain mercy from the count unless they all declared themselves to be his slaves.

## PART VI. Blessed Charles’s final pious acts; the murder committed

34. (CHAPTER XXIV.) Thus those who had moved from folly into madness immediately formed a deadly plan, the provost together with those envoys being physically absent—as one who did everything while seeming to do nothing—and began to discuss the detestable crime of killing their lord. The devil forestalled their counsels by inspiring them, furthered them by cooperating, and carried them forward by inciting them. At last six leaders of their faction came to this decision of iniquity: Guelric, the provost’s brother; the aforesaid Burchard; Robert, son of Robert, another brother of the provost; William of Wervik; Ingrasnus of Esen; and Isaac, kinsman of the provost. They conspired to kill the count as soon as possible, binding themselves by a compact of faith—or rather, faithlessness—to accomplish the deed and conceal it until it was accomplished.

> **Note:** Wervik, on the Leie or Lys river, is a town between Menin and Kortrijk. The above-mentioned Guy of Steenvoorde and William of Wervik subscribed the letters of Blessed Charles, Count, for the Abbey of Marchiennes, issued in 1125, indiction III, concurrent 3; see Chesneau, *On the Family of Béthune*, book II of the *Proofs*, p. 20.

> **Note:** Esen is a manor near Diksmuide, described by Sanderus in *Flandria Illustrata*, p. 316; its lord is called by Iperius Ingrasnus, or Ingesramus of Esen. Below, no. 75, his paternal uncle is called Theodoric of Diksmuide, a powerful man. Theodoric of Esen subscribed a donation to the Abbey of St Andrew in 1105; perhaps he was this man’s father.

> **Note:** In the vernacular Chronicle of Flanders, in the form of a proclamation and in Lernutius, this conspiracy is invented as having been made at Ypres on the feast of St Vincent, 22 January; the chief of the conspiracy is made Lambert, brother of Provost Bertulf, though he had already died. The preceding discussion addresses this and other related points.

35. These things were done at night: deeds of darkness, though night belongs to the absence of light. Although all was carried on in secret, it could not remain hidden. Rumours brought reports of it, and he himself was informed that plans concerning his danger were being made. Yet he could not be persuaded to believe this. His conscience did not merely fail to accuse him of having done anything wrong in this affair; it truly justified him for a work of righteousness.

I readily believe that this came about by the just and hidden judgment of God: so that, as his merits, our sins, and their abominable crimes demanded, the palm might be hastened for him, sorrow for us, and just punishment for those traitors. For thus, as we may piously believe, it was fitting that he should be granted the desired rest; that we should be deprived of a defender and protector of whom we were unworthy; and that those wicked men should be visited with a punishment commensurate with their crime. O marvellous providence of almighty God in all things!

36. (CHAPTER XXV.) When that night had passed, the glorious prince, having lain groaning in his bed somewhat longer than usual, rose, washed his hands, and then, devoutly as was his custom, hastened to perform a work of mercy. For he had so ordered his life that on every day he dedicated the beginning of his actions to the Lord: before proceeding to church, he distributed alms to the poor with his own hands.

Because of his immense devotion to Christ, he was accustomed to do this barefoot. He allowed no one to assist him in this office of piety; carrying each dish to each person, he kissed the hands of every individual with the greatest reverence. He had recently added to this religious observance that every day he would clothe five poor persons in new garments and shoes.

Having humbly offered this sacrifice of almsgiving upon the altar of holy faith, he at once went to church, about to offer himself besides as a victim of propitiation. He was accompanied by no knights, for they were dispersed everywhere among lodgings and chapels. Before the altar of St Mary, Mother of God, situated in the upper part of the church of St Donatian, he prostrated himself in prayer. There, after praying for some time, repeatedly bending his knees and commending himself more intently to the Lord, he finally cast himself face-down upon the pavement. Placing his little book before him, he began in supplication to chant the seven penitential psalms for the cleansing of his sins.

37. Meanwhile, while the clergy—that is, his chaplains—were chanting, according to ecclesiastical custom, the first and third hours of the day together with the Lord’s Prayer, and were already reciting the prayers of the third hour, he was reciting the fiftieth psalm, itself the fourth of the penitential psalms, after the three already mentioned. For he was accustomed to pray in such a manner that those standing around could hear him.

Then Burchard, master of treachery and leader of the crime, with six sword-bearers drawn from the retinue of the provost and his own, unexpectedly stood behind him at his side. With naked sword he first touched him lightly, so that he might extend his head to be struck. When Charles raised his head and turned his face toward him, Burchard, raging, struck that most venerable forehead—the overthrower of the proud and raiser-up of the humble—with a mighty blow, and dashed his brain upon the pavement.

His accomplices then rushed in to commit the same deed and all struck him together, though in vain, since the first blow had sufficed for his death. They cut down his head with many wounds and almost severed his right arm together with the hand which, that very hour, had extended a coin—or rather coins—to a poor woman asking alms and held others to distribute to further petitioners.

38. (CHAPTER XXVI.) But now I wish to turn my pen briefly aside from the sequence of the narrative and consider, however inadequately, the enormity of so great a crime and the most cruel savagery of those criminals.

O most wicked Burchard, what have you done? O most mad Bertulf, to what have you consented? O all accomplices and agents of this most criminal deed, what did you devise, what did you do, what did you accomplish? Whom did you kill, why, when, where, and how? Certainly your lord; certainly because of his justice; certainly in Lent; certainly in a church; and certainly without any reverence.

Let your crime, if you please, be compared with that of your detestable Jewish forefathers. They killed their Lord, not so much with their hands as with their tongues, outside the gate of the city; yet they did not at all recognize Him as their Lord. “For if,” as the Apostle says, “they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). But you did not shrink from killing with both tongue and hands, in a holy place and at a holy time, Him whom you undoubtedly knew to be your lord.

Therefore you have not merely equalled the crime of your forefathers by your own crime, but, if it may be said, surpassed it. You must therefore fear—and fear exceedingly—lest those whom you seem to have surpassed in guilt should also surpass you in the severity of your punishment. Following their example, you have fittingly lost both place and nation; and, lest you should lose them, you did not fear to commit so great an abomination. These, indeed, are only the beginnings of sorrows, unless you repent worthily.

39. (CHAP. XXVII.) But now let us turn away from these sorrows and consider the joyful, and every way gladly commemorated, circumstances of our Charles’s blessed end. For if we examine it with diligent discernment, we may reasonably perceive [Col. 0922C] that he had something in common with the martyrs—speaking, of course, without prejudice to their reverence. For, as it is written, “It is not the punishment so much as the cause that makes martyrs.” [Note: Augustine, on Psalm 34.] But what, I ask, was the cause of this, so to speak, martyrdom, except justice? For he was killed because he would not turn aside from the straight path of equity; he was therefore killed for the testimony of truth.

40. And so that you may know that he had not wholly failed to realize that the danger of death had long before been plotted against him by those most criminal men, and yet had not retreated because he trusted in the justice of his cause: at the assembly of magnates gathered at Ypres on the third day before the Kalends of March, as stated above, when mention was made of Burchard’s most wicked design, hear what pearl he brought forth from the treasure of a good conscience—for “the righteous is as confident as a lion” [Col. 0922D]:

> “I shall go,” he said, “and, under God’s protection, I shall go in safety. And even if it should perhaps happen that I am killed there, to die for justice will certainly be not so much dangerous as glorious. As for vengeance, God will provide.”

Moreover, so that you may infer that he said this not casually or lightly, but thoughtfully, hear what I myself learned from him. For when, on the evening of that same day, the provost of the regular clerics dwelling in that place told me that certain laymen, driven by their arrogance, had made threats against him, and asked my advice as to what he ought to do, we jointly brought the matter before Charles, as the defender of the humble. We received from his mouth—or rather, as later became evident, through his mouth from his heart—this reply [Col. 0923A]:

> “Whatever threats they make against you, I am certain that, so long as I live, they will dare to harm you in no respect. But even if it should happen that you are killed for truth, what death, I ask, could be more glorious than this? For what surpasses martyrdom in glory?”

Surely, in my judgment, he would not have said this unless he burned with the love of martyrdom.

41. You have therefore seen what was the cause of his death; now see, if you please, what his work was. Certainly, he had long before confessed his sins and was then doing penance for them. At that same hour, as has been said, he was devoted to prayer, which he also rendered more acceptable to the Lord by almsgiving. And if any stains from earthly contaminations still adhered to him [Col. 0923B], it is credible that they could be wiped away by the shedding of blood and the bitterness of death. Thus his murderers dug for themselves the pit of death, but introduced him through the gate of death to the entrance of life; they stripped him of the garment of mortality and clothed themselves in their own shame as with a double cloak.

## PART VII. B. The supporters of Charles slain. The body borne upon a bier. Miracles, veneration, burial.

42. (CHAP. XXVIII.) Having committed this murder, while still thirsting for blood, they attacked Themard, castellan of Brokburg, who happened to be nearby, after the others had fled, and pierced him with many wounds. [Note: Brokburg, or Burburg, is a town in western Flanders near Gravelines. The family of this castellan is discussed at length in the manuscript History of Guînes, from which much has been printed by du Chesne, book IV of the *Proofs*. Themard—elsewhere Thevard—castellan of Brokburg, subscribed charters of Blessed Charles dated 1119, 1121, and 1125. His sons Walter and Gilbert, likewise killed with him, and Henry, who survived and succeeded his father as castellan of Brokburg, are mentioned by Galbert, no. 150. We have above corrected the identification of this man with Tengmar. The Paris edition printed “Thangmar of Bruges.”]

When this was done, the conspirators previously mentioned, each with his retainers, arrived [Col. 0923C]. Searching without resistance throughout the whole town, populous and extensive like a city, they zealously pursued everywhere those whom they had long before marked out for death. Two of these men—the sons of the aforementioned castellan—were cruelly killed: Walter, still remaining in his lodging and, alas, resisting bravely but in vain; and Gilbert, attempting to escape outside the town in altered dress with the castellan of Courtrai. [Note: Courtrai, or Curtrai, is a distinguished city of Flanders on the River Lys. Its castellan Walter subscribed a charter of Count Baldwin in 1115; Rodeger subscribed letters of Thierry in 1145.]

They then returned to seek Walter the steward, whom they feared had escaped by flight. [Note: Galbert calls him Walter of Lokeren. He subscribed a donation made to the church of Saint Nicholas at Veurne in 1120 and to the monastery of Saint Winoc in 1121. There are two places called Lokeren: one in Waasland on the River Durme, another in the territory of Ypres toward Bailleul. Since the latter is nearer Veurne and Bergues-Saint-Winoc and lies in Flanders proper, it is meant here.]

But when they learned that the castellan had made confession to a priest, received the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, and had not yet died [Col. 0923D], they again rushed upon him in the church. Seizing him by the feet and dragging him violently over the rough unevenness of the steps [Col. 0924A], they dashed and shattered his head against each step. Then, dragging him before the doors of that same church, while he still struggled in his last moments, they expelled his spirit by a renewed slaughter.

When they had long searched for Walter and could not find him, and had already despaired of discovering him, a certain boy is said to have betrayed him and pointed out to his pursuers the hiding-place that had quite opportunely concealed him in so great an emergency. When Walter realized that he had been betrayed, he immediately fled at full speed and anxiously ran as far as the altar of Saint Donatian. With the veil hung before the altar, he covered himself as best he could. The ministers of the devil pursued him there, seized him, and, arrogantly denying him the opportunity to make confession—the only thing he asked—dragged him out of the church and killed him [Col. 0924B].

43. (CHAP. XXIX.) Thus the body of Lord Charles, while his servants lay hidden here and there and, through fear of death, dared appear nowhere, lay for some time in the place where he had been murdered, since there was no one to bury him. At length it was borne down by the ministry of the clerics and placed in the middle of the choir, where it was attended by the mournful rites of those grieving. Yet few openly lamented him, or dared show any sign of grief or sorrow at his death. So great was the fear of the traitors, who had even decreed that he should by no means be buried there, lest his tomb appear as a reproach to them for posterity.

When Arnulf, abbot of the monastery of Blandinium, heard this, he came swiftly on the following day and wished to carry him away to be buried in his own monastery. [Note: Arnulf—called Arnold by some—was abbot from 1117 to 1132. Together with the castellan of Ghent, he had been sent to Aachen; at the feast of Epiphany in this year, 1127, he was with Emperor Lothair and reported to him that Blessed Count Charles stood ready to render every submission. Thus Anselm of Gembloux.] [Col. 0924C]

The provost and his men willingly consented; and when the abbot had prepared a bier, clerics and laypeople alike, stirred at once by the Spirit of God, took courage to resist. They vehemently objected, and even began violently to confront and reproach them face to face with weapons:

> “If you took our lord from us so that he might not live, must you also take him from us when dead? You who caused us not to have him alive, allow us at least to have him dead. For we trust that him whom we had as patron and protector while living, now that he has been slain as a martyr, we shall have much more as a faithful intercessor before God.” [Col. 0924D]

What more need be said? At last they prevailed over the provost’s party and the abbot [Col. 0925A], and brought back their lord’s body to be buried in the upper part of the church. At that hour, while the people’s faith burned and—as it is fitting truly to believe—the merit of venerable Charles demanded it, I shall not pass over the miracle worked by divine mercy.

44. (CHAP. XXX.) There was a boy whose sinews had been contracted from the cradle, so that he was not only unable to walk but could not raise himself from the ground in any way. He was small in stature, yet very widely known because of his affliction. For he had lived for about eight years on the alms of the monks of Saint Andrew at Bruges and had been supported by their benefactions. [Note: The manuscript chronicle of the monastery of Saint Andrew, chapter 5, relates it thus: “In the nineteenth year after the foundation of our monastery, in the time of the venerable Father Alard, our second prior, a boy came to the gate of our monastery seeking alms. From the cradle his sinews had been so contracted that he could not merely fail to walk, but could not even raise himself from the ground. Moved by compassion for his misery and poverty, our prior Alard, most merciful toward the poor, brought him into the monastery and provided him abundantly with food and clothing for eight years.”]

The prior there made him some device by which he could manage, with assistance, not so much to walk as to crawl. He gradually began to move himself in whatever fashion he could; eventually he came as far as Bruges [Col. 0925B] and stayed for some time in the house of Reinger the toll-collector. [Note: Lernutius, drawing on his fabulous *Annals*, calls the cripple “Rogekinus, the toll-collector.” Meyer says that “a young man named Roger was carried away by Renger the toll-collector.”]

[Note: The same manuscript chronicle adds: “Meanwhile he received frequent alms from the aforesaid Count Charles. But when the news of his most unjust death spread everywhere, this cripple shed the bitterest tears over the loss and unjust death of so merciful a patron. Urged by emotion, he went to the church of Blessed Donatian, in which that most wicked crime had been committed. In the manner he was able, he climbed the steps and found the body of the blessed count and martyr lying there abandoned and stained with its own blood. Drawing long and deep sighs from the bottom of his heart for a very long time, he did not cease to fill heaven with groans over so great a crime. At last, because of love for the dead man, he anointed all his limbs, deadened by weakness, with Charles’s blood—not because he had any hope of recovering health, as he later confessed, but solely from the devout affection of love that he had borne toward one who had done him such great kindnesses. But almighty God, wishing to show how great was the merit of the man whose death was being mourned, suddenly restored to perfect health one who could not even have suspected that this might happen to him. Leaving his devices there, he sprang down the steps upon his own feet like a roe deer and ran through the whole city, where his singular misery had made him very well known, showing everyone that he had been restored to complete health.”] [Col. 0926C–D]

This man, then, being present at that hour beside the venerable body, fell down in supplication beneath its bier and devoutly begged for the longed-for gift of health. Suddenly those sinews, long contracted, began to be loosened by wholly divine power; his weak limbs began to rise and were strengthened and made firm for walking. Thus, by God’s grace and the merit of the holy man, he was completely restored to full health, so that no trace of his former disability remained in him. Therefore, he who had come weak and sorrowful departed healthy, rejoicing, and giving thanks to God. And because this took place before a crowd, it could certainly not remain hidden.

45. (CHAP. XXXI.) Those who were present and recognized the martyr’s glory through so manifest a miracle gave immeasurable praises, with rejoicing, to the Lord who bestowed such grace [Col. 0925C]. At once one could see countless men and women of both sexes and of different ages eagerly hurrying from every quarter: reverently wiping up his blood with linen cloths; scraping it even from the pavement with iron instruments; gathering with veneration hairs of his head or beard, torn off by the swords of raging men; and storing all these things away with every diligence and devotion, to be preserved thereafter for their protection [Col. 0926A].

Nor was this without effect. For a cap of his, preserved by someone, is said through God’s grace, faith going before, to have conferred many benefits of healing upon sufferers from fevers. And lest anyone, in unbelief, should accuse me of inventing all these things and speaking from myself, I call God to witness that I learned through the testimony of the religious Lord Elias, dean of Bruges, Frumold, provost of Veurne, and other clerics and laypeople who affirmed that they had seen them, the things that I have related concerning his death and miracles. [Note: Fromold, provost of Veurne, subscribed a donation to the abbey of Formeselles near Ypres in 1117 and to the church of Saint Nicholas at Veurne in 1120.]

But when the faithful, rejoicing, marveled at the first miracle accomplished, and, marveling, rejoiced, and the bells were rung in praise of God, Bertulf is said to have asked what the commotion meant. When the matter had been explained as it occurred, he not only refused to believe or repent [Col. 0926B], but turned to mockery and derision and ordered even the doors of the church to be barred, lest the devout people should gather there.

46. (CHAP. XXXII.) These events took place on Thursday, as stated above, after Charles had been killed on Wednesday, the sixth day before the Nones of March. Thus, through fear of the provost, the gathering of clergy and people was restrained, and the burial of Lord Charles was delayed until Friday. On that day a few of his men and dependants came together and buried him in the place where he had been killed, in a sarcophagus made of stones and mortar upon the pavement. But since reason and ecclesiastical authority did not permit the priests and clerics to perform this in a place of homicide polluted by human blood, they commended him to the Lord in another church through solemn celebrations of masses [Col. 0926C] and prayers. [Note: Galbert writes that it was the church of Saint Peter outside the walls, no. 42.]

## PART VIII. Vengeance upon the wicked evildoers; three of them slain.

47. While the provost and his followers rejoiced as though their adversary had been overthrown, and planned and considered how to acquire the principality for themselves, as though there were no one to oppose them, they did not know what vengeance was being prepared for them by the terrible judgment of divine severity. While they rejoiced over the blood and the plunder of Charles’s treasures [Col. 0927A], which they had seized, the just Judge and most equitable Requiter secretly disposed their punishment.

O ineffable goodness and justice of God! He waited for his impious Jewish persecutors until the forty-second year after his Passion, mercifully granting them that interval for repentance. [Note: These years are reckoned from the consulship of the two Gemini down to the second year of Vespasian, as many were accustomed to reckon.] But because they neglected to repent, failing to recognize that God’s patience invited them to repentance and storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, they perished in horrible punishments in that same year. Yet for these persecutors of a just man He justly shortened the time and scarcely postponed vengeance until the eighth day. For the former, because the Church was still in its infancy among them, were, I believe, to be tolerated mercifully for longer; but these, because the Church was now mature in them and was scandalized by them, were more swiftly and justly to be judged [Col. 0927B].

48. (CHAP. XXXIII.) For behold: on the eighth day, as though Lord Charles were in some sense rising again to avenge himself, Gervase, their neighbor, an honorable and upright man, gathered about thirty of his own knights and attacked the castle of Bruges. [Note: Gervase the chamberlain subscribed, in 1123, letters of Blessed Charles for the monastery of Saint Peter at Ghent.] Since they did not dare resist him, because the fear of God had fallen upon them, he entered and forced them to take refuge in the inner fortification. I should not doubt that this was accomplished by divine power, since they were far superior in number, strength, and fortification. But the hand of the Lord strengthened the few faithful and made weak the strength and courage of the many unbelieving.

Moreover, heavenly grace so changed the hearts of the citizens of Bruges that they not only refused to favor the unjust party of their lords, or to offer help to those who favored it, but utterly abhorred their association. Joining Gervase, they immediately besieged them in the fortress to which they had fled [Col. 0927C]. [Note: That is, Burchard, the knight George, and the servant Fromald, as Galbert states, no. 51. Robert, messenger of the castellan Haket, is also reported slain there on the same day, 9 March.]

Two of those who had cooperated in the murder of Lord Charles were intercepted and seized in the sight of the others, so as to punish and shame them. They were tortured, as was fitting, with various shameful punishments, then finally killed, and thrown partly into the sewers, where their lords looking down from the walls could see them.

49. (CHAP. XXXIV.) Isaac, one of the conspirators, a powerful and wealthy man, lived some distance away in a strongly fortified place. At that time he had entered the church of Blessed Mary unjustly and irreverently [Col. 0927D]—for one who had not feared proudly to violate a church ought humbly to have avoided entering a church. By this circumstance he happened to be cut off from the siege; making no provision whatever for his house, since he desired to preserve his life [Col. 0928A], he immediately escaped by flight.

His brother Desiderius, who had joined Gervase against his own kin to avenge the blood of the just man, at once broke into Isaac’s house and with his own hands consigned all its fortifications to the flames. Had he found Isaac himself there, there is no doubt that he would have killed him in vengeance for so great a crime. See how deeply the hatred of wickedness had been inspired in them: it even overcame the natural affection of kinship. For in one who had made himself an accomplice in such monstrous wickedness, Gervase had no regard for blood relationship, nor Desiderius for fraternal ties.

Isaac, however, hiding in the daytime where he dared and wandering by night wherever he could, came to the house of his sister, whom the aforementioned Guy of Stenford had as his wife. Under her guidance he fled as far as the monastery of Saint John of Thérouanne, built upon a hill overlooking our city [Col. 0928B]. [Note: The monastery of Saint John is believed to have been founded by King Theuderic of France in expiation for the murder of Saint Leodegar. When the city was destroyed, the monks migrated to Bailleul and later to Ypres, where the monastery is still called Saint John’s.]

For, compelled by divine or human fear, he wished to become a monk. He had intended to wait there for a monk of Ename to give him the habit, but he could not remain concealed. [Note: Ename is a monastery on the River Scheldt near Oudenaarde; its abbot Gislebert subscribed a charter of Blessed Charles in 1122.]

50. (CHAP. XXXV.) Rumor spread the report, and it was immediately made known throughout the whole city, that the men who had killed Charles, father of their country, lay concealed in the monastery of Saint John. Arnulf, therefore, son of Eustace the advocate, desiring also to avenge the count’s blood—whose vengeance, he now heard, the whole world itself was conspiring to effect—sent his officers there at nightfall to guard the abbey on every side throughout the night [Col. 0928C], lest those hiding in the darkness should be able to escape anywhere. [Note: Lernutius, with his *Annals* and a formulary of proclamation, substitutes for Arnulf the knight Herman of Heest. Arnulf’s father Eustace subscribed letters of Blessed Charles at Aire in 1125.]

When Isaac learned that snares had been prepared for him, trembling, he fled to Lord Folquin, the abbot. By humble and very persistent entreaty, he at last obtained from him the monastic habit he desired. [Note: Ingebert, abbot of Saint John, subscribed a charter of Blessed John, bishop of Thérouanne, in 1122; Folquin succeeded him.]

Nevertheless, on the following day Arnulf came with his men to the monastery. He ordered Isaac, brought out and discovered through his own confession, immediately to be stripped of his monk’s clothing and dragged tumultuously, naked and barefoot, with his hands tied behind his back, to the city. There, to ensure that no trace of monastic profession remained upon him, all the hair of his head was completely shaved off. Citizens of both sexes and every age stood round on all sides [Col. 0928D], crying, “Let the traitor and betrayer be hanged at once, or burned alive!” Arnulf himself also strove with all his strength to carry this out. At last his father and mother intervened and, against their son’s will, obtained that Isaac should be kept alive for a while [Col. 0929A].

It is credible that this also happened by divine action, so that the transgressor might be tormented longer both by the suffering of present punishment and by fear of impending death, and might meanwhile be afflicted, if unrepentant, by eternal torments, or, if repentant, by purgatorial ones.

51. After several days had passed, Lord William, son of Count Philip, whom we have mentioned above and who had already occupied a large part of this land after the count’s death, came to Thérouanne. From the wife of the advocate—for he and his son were then absent—he obtained the surrender of Isaac. He had a rope tied round Isaac’s neck, led him with him to Aire, and, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, had him hanged in the hearing of all the people, as Isaac confessed his crimes and declared himself deserving of every punishment. [Note: Lernutius says that “Isaac, compelled by tortures, freely confessed after being released from punishment that on the day the count was killed he had slaughtered with his own hand more than twenty-five senators and officers of the prince”; he then lists the “naval men, authors of the conspiracy.” These statements are drawn from the formulary of proclamation and fabulous *Annals*.]

[Note: The same Lernutius, with his sources, asserts that Isaac was “tied naked to the tail of a wild horse; whipped at the end of every street; had hands and feet cut off in the marketplace; was then carried to the gallows; and, after his head had been cut off, was fastened to the gibbet, bound by a strap beneath the armpits.” Meyer did not dare repeat this fabrication, saying only that he was “put to death on the gallows after various tortures.”]

## PART IX. Punishment inflicted upon Bertulf the provost and Guy of Stenford.

[Col. 0929B]

52. (CHAP. XXXVI.) When the aforesaid siege had been begun at Bruges by Gervase and Desiderius, as stated, Baldwin of Ghent [Note: This most ancient Ghent family is fully illustrated by du Chesne, who in book IV discusses this Baldwin’s great-grandfather Rudolph, his grandfather, and his father, also named Baldwin and surnamed the One-Eyed and the Bearded. All were counts of Alost. Galbert, nos. 53–54, states that this Baldwin’s brother Juvan came with the castellan of Ghent on 10 March, and that the next day the four others mentioned here came. In no. 136 he says that Baldwin died on 24 October of this year. Meyer states that “Baldwin of Ghent died in 1125 and was succeeded by his brother Juvan.” Yet among those who “came to Bruges to besiege the parricides,” he includes Baldwin of Ghent, and later, at the end of 1127, adds: “In the same year Baldwin of Ghent, by far the most illustrious of the Flemish nobles, renounced all worldly concerns, wholly devoted himself to religion, and later died in the abbey of Affligem.” But Galbert says that he “received the monastic habit when he breathed his last.”] and Daniel of Dendermonde [Note: Dendermonde is a city at the confluence of the Dender and Scheldt, between Ghent and Antwerp. Daniel, its lord, descended from the said Ghent family; his great-grandfather Reingot of Ghent was brother of Rudolph, whom we have also called the great-grandfather of Baldwin and Juvan.] came from the east; Walter of Lillers [Note: Lillers is a town in Artois not far from Aire. Galbert calls its lord Count Butelgir—that is, steward or cupbearer. Together with the already named Baldwin, Juvan, and Daniel, he subscribed letters of William the Norman for the men of Saint-Omer, cited above.]; Richard of Wulveringem [Note: Galbert calls him Richard of Woldman; a nephew of Thangmar of Straten married his daughter.]; and Thierry of Dixmude [Note: Thierry was uncle of Ingrannus, who had conspired in the murder.] came from the west. Having gathered an army, they joined the same siege and confirmed by oath that they would not depart until they had captured and punished those murderers.

After a few days had passed and several assaults had been made, on one day they climbed the wall on the southern side and boldly threw themselves inside. They violently attacked those traitors [Col. 0929C] and compelled them all to flee into the church of Saint Donatian, which they had previously polluted with a foul murder. This was indeed fittingly deserved. For it was especially appropriate that, in that place which they had not feared cruelly to disgrace in contempt of God and his saints, they should be forced against their will to endure the hardships of a long siege [Col. 0930A], of vigils, hunger, and thirst, and the continual terrors of an impending death.

53. (CHAP. XXXVII.) But on the day before this happened, while they were shut in within and others besieged them from without, it is uncertain whether through the negligence or the contrivance of the besiegers—for some say, and more certainly, that several had been bribed with money [Note: Galbert, no. 70, says that 400 marks were given to the aforesaid Walter Butelgir, or Walter of Lillers; in no. 136 he reports money given to others.]—the provost was given an opportunity to escape. Lowered from the top of the wall to the ground by a rope and secretly led out from the siege with the help of certain men [Note: Galbert, no. 76, says that “a shrewd knight, brother of Fulk, canon of Bruges, was given him as guide.”], he traveled at night and lay hidden by day, fleeing in wretchedness, and as one worthy of pity, to the house of Alard of Warneton [Note: Warneton, or Wastena, lies on the River Leie between Comines and Armentières. Galbert agrees, no. 76, and calls it Warneton; the vernacular *Annals* have Watene, and Lernutius Watenum. But that place lies between Cassel and Saint-Omer.], whose wife was Agantrude, the provost’s niece and former castellan of the castle called Saint-Omer [Col. 0930B].

When he had remained hidden there for nearly three weeks, uncertain rumors and the conjectures of the common people began to spread word of his presence. No longer daring to keep him there, they transferred him each night to different places, in order somehow to conceal his flight, whose discovery they greatly feared.

54. After the Easter days had passed, on the eighth day after the Lord’s Resurrection—that is, the Sunday octave—the report of this concealment came to the aforementioned Lord William, who happened then to be at Ypres. On hearing it, he immediately sprang up, mounted his horse, and set about searching for the provost with great noise and haste. They searched Alard’s house and all his hiding-places, as well as the house of his daughter, where that wretched man was said to have rested on the preceding night [Col. 0930C]. When they did not find the man they sought, they became violently angry. First they burned both houses, as though polluted by the presence of a pestilential man and therefore requiring purification by fire. Then they seized Alard’s aforesaid daughter, threatening to maim her limbs on the following day unless the provost were surrendered [Col. 0931A].

Lord William also renounced Alard’s homage, and, having declared him his enemy, seized his entire fief. [Note: *Diffiduciare* means to establish enmity or hostility. Ivo of Chartres, Matthew Paris, and Thomas Walsingham, cited by Vossius, *On the Faults of Language*, p. 679, use the word.] [Note: In Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum Angliae*, book I: “The king seized the bishopric,” that is, invaded it or laid hands upon it; the usage is common elsewhere.] He gave security by faith and oath concerning the dishonoring of Alard’s daughter, on the condition stated above, and so departed.

55. (CHAP. XXXVIII.) With matters thus brought to a crisis, Alard and his people began to deliberate on what had to be done. Since on the one hand they saw that no indulgence could be granted to his daughter and, on the other, that no advantage toward their safety could come from the provost’s own destruction, they finally resolved to surrender the provost, thereby gaining safety at least for Alard’s daughter. So that he might justly be compelled to suffer what he was accused of having done, they had him brought out of the house in which they had concealed him, through the agency of a certain woman, and handed over to those who had been prepared to seize him [Col. 0931B].

That same night he was brought to the castle of Warneton and kept there until dawn. There he asked that a priest be summoned to him. Doing penance for his sins, he made confession to God and to the priest in the sight of all; prostrate upon the ground and striking his breast with his fists, he humbly prayed that the Lord might grant him forgiveness.

56. At daybreak, when those who had taken him urged him to proceed on horseback to Ypres, he refused altogether to ride, preferring to go on foot, barefoot though there was frost. When he had set out, he summoned to himself one of the clerics from whose account we learned these very details, and began to sing the Ambrosian hymn, *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—antiphonally with him [Col. 0931C]. When this was finished, he completed the Hours of Blessed Mary, singing with the same devoutness of supplication. Then he turned to psalmody and strove silently and attentively to chant psalms to himself.

When the men of Ypres came to meet him and led him into Ypres, striking him everywhere upon the head with fists, rods, stones, and the large sea-fish caught in those regions, and subjecting him to every kind of insult, he persisted always in patience—or rather, some might say, in hardness and silence—and almost until his very death he unceasingly meditated upon the psalms.

Then, suspended on the gallows by neck and arms and battered by many blows from those striking him, he was at last put to death in this manner. [Note: Drawing from the vernacular *Annals* and the formulary of proclamation, Lernutius wrote and believed the following: “By night he was carried from Ypres to a forest a mile from the city, sewn into the hide of a disemboweled ox, and hung alive from an accursed tree in the wilderness; on the fourth day he was found dead.” Meyer preferred to follow Walter, who, he says, had written from the testimony of the cleric present when Bertulf requested this.]

I do not think the following should be passed over concerning him: while he was prosperous [Col. 0931D–0932A], he especially abhorred insults and mockery of this kind. For from the reports of certain members of his household I learned with certainty that, whenever conversation among his servants happened to turn to the saving Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ and others praised Christ’s patience, he was accustomed to say:

> “I wonder why the Lord was willing to endure such things. Certainly, if such boys (*garciones*) insulted me in this manner, I would vigorously avenge my wrongs, especially if necessary; and I would at least throw spittle in the face of anyone mocking me.”

[Note: The French word *garçon* means “young man”; hence we have often rendered *garciones* in that sense.]

See how those things which he was accustomed to judge most unbearable, he was himself compelled to endure, to the increase of his misery.

57. (CHAP. XXXIX.) At that same hour Lord William of Ypres went forth and proceeded to investigate the case of Guy of Stenford, who had lately been accused of the same crime—namely, of having offered counsel and assent to the count’s death. This Guy had entered into single combat on that account against his accuser Herman, surnamed the Iron [Man]. In the first encounter and in the second he had been superior in the fight; and, though he himself was armed with an equally heavy hauberk and helmet, he had thrown the same Herman, burdened by the excessive weight of his armour, to the ground and crushed him beneath the fall of his own body and so great a load. Yet Herman, strengthened by courage, rose as if he felt no weight at all, and, reversing their positions, began to press him who, as has been said, had been superior in the second encounter, to confess the crime committed. Why say more? At length he was defeated by divine judgment, convicted of the crime of which he was accused, and finally condemned to the punishment of death. When this had taken place at Reningas [Reninga in the district of Ypres, commonly Reningels; we discussed it on 2 February in connection with the Life of St Adalbold, duke, §3. Lambert of Rinenghelles, with Anselm and his brother Baldwin, subscribed Count Theoderic’s charter for the monastery of Lo. in 1130. Miraeus, ch. 130. Our manuscript here has “Rinningas.”], they immediately seized him, dragged him to Ypres, and hanged him, now himself most wretched, beside that miserable provost on the same gallows, on the same day, the third before the Ides of April [11 April].

[Note: Lernutius, drawing upon the stories mentioned, says: “Guy and ten canons of St Martin’s, because they had taken part in the counsels, were deservedly punished by William of Lo: Guy was condemned to death and ordered to be killed; the canons were shut up in prison and prolonged their lives on bread and water in the shame and sorrow of a black cavern, without any hope of seeing daylight. Of these, five were detained in the episcopal quarries, at Tournai, and an equal number at Teerenburg.” This is sheer invention.]

58. After they had hung there for some time and begun to pollute the air with their stench, the burgesses again took counsel and decreed that they should be cast out beyond the town [thus Berthulf was not, from the beginning, hanged outside the city, as the tale indicates] and there set up more carefully. For they could not refrain from torturing and mocking even the dead, since they lamented that by these men’s treachery they had been bereaved of such a father and lord. Accordingly, they erected a tall tree and placed upon it a cartwheel; then, sewn into ox-hides so that they might last longer, they set them upon it, joined together face to face and bound as though in a mutual embrace. But after a few days had passed, their corpses were secretly removed from there and buried.

[Note: “In the monastery of Formeselles,” says Iperius; but Lernutius says, “in the church of St Martin.”]

O truly dreadful judgments of divine severity! For who would ever have suspected, to say nothing of Guy, that the provost of Bruges—indeed, the most splendid son of this age, abounding in all the riches of this world, and, after the count alone, almost the most powerful man in the whole land—would descend to such misery that he was permitted neither to live dishonourably nor even to end this life honourably? But He who casts down the mighty from their seat, who knows the lofty from afar, and who by the most discriminating judgment of His justice renders to each according to his deeds, was uniquely powerful to cast down their height and reduce their power to nothing, whenever and however He willed.

## PART X. The punishment inflicted on Burchard, killer of Blessed Charles

59. (CHAP. XL.) Now that Burchard whom we have recalled as the first to strike the head of the venerable count Charles, after enduring many hardships while besieged, escaped for a short time by human aid; but, since divine counsel opposed his undertakings, he was entirely unable to escape. For, as later became clear from his confession, after leaving that tower he first hid for some time.

[Note: Lernutius, from vernacular annals and the text of a proclamation: “Burchard fled from Bruges to the monastery of Quercetum with several servants.
