There they hid for four days in the cell of a regular canon, covered by a white garment; they took care to have themselves marked with a large tonsure, as though they were monks, living according to the prescribed rule, and in such a guise hoped to reach Brabant and escape the pursuing Nemesis.” Mejerus copied this account, but omitted the companions. Let credibility rest with them.]

Then, at night, taking with him certain companions for the journey, whose fidelity he did not doubt, he began his flight, judging it wiser to seek distant regions, so that, unknown among strangers, he might hide himself more safely and thus, by prolonging a needy and miserable life, somehow extend it. When he came to a certain water [Iperius calls it the Lys, but Mejerus the Scheldt; Lernutius places it near Antwerp] which he had to cross by boat, he found a little vessel ready on the bank and at once boarded it. When he tried to push it away from land in order to direct it to the opposite bank, it remained motionless, weighed down by the hidden force of divine power, and could not be moved from its place. When he perceived this, he began to exert all his strength and to strain with every effort he could make to draw it away from the bank. After struggling long and accomplishing nothing at all, he called his companions and invited them to assist him. They immediately ran up in astonishment and devoted all the strength they possessed to moving that one small boat; nevertheless it remained motionless like a wall, since divine power made it wholly immovable.

O detestable madness of Burchard! Burchard makes light of and disregards the enormity of his own crime, while he curses and recoils from an insensible piece of wood. A small boat resists the powerful thrusts of strong men, though it is ordinarily moved and turned about with ease by the hand of a single boy. Yet these are Your works, Christ: You turn those who wander to the way of truth and bend the proud toward the grace of humility; lest You condemn them eternally, You often punish them in time. For now, through the immovability of the boat, You warned this wicked man to recognize his own wickedness and dread Your justice—You who once rebuked the folly of the prophet Balaam through the speech of an ass.

60. Thus at last that wretched man, pierced by this miracle and finally returning to himself, abandoned the boat, cast himself upon the ground, struck his guilty breast with his fist, and, shedding abundant tears, began with much groaning to undergo repentance for his guilt. For he had never previously repented of this sin. When, after his lament, he again tried to move the boat and saw it immovable as before, now more certainly understanding the will of God, he began to despair of his temporal safety and immediately, sad and grieving, returned to his customary hiding places.

61. (CHAP. XLI.) After he had already lain hidden in various places for many days, he happened, near Lille [Insula is understood to mean the chief city of Gallic Flanders], to turn aside, under the guidance of one of his servants, into a certain hut. He sent that servant, the guide of his journey, to the house of his uncle Bernard to ask for bread with which he might restore his famished soul—for he was hungry. The servant, wishing to carry out what he had been commanded, willingly obeyed his order; arriving at the house, he asked, for his master’s use, as though for a man accustomed to luxuries, for fine bread. But by the wondrous judgment of the Almighty, he who sought his master’s safety found death; and, desiring to provide the hungry man with the food he needed, he prepared for the guilty man the torments he had deserved. For on this occasion he disclosed his master, simply, though through other persons, to the aforesaid Bernard; he thought that he ought by no means to conceal his nephew from one who was, as it were, his uncle. But by the just judgment of God it came about that he who had not feared to kill his lord was himself betrayed to death by his own servant.

[Note: Lernutius embellishes the matter from his customary tales as follows: “In the city of Lille he had three uncles: Hugh, lord of Alwenii; Bernard, lord of Roubaix; and Oliver, powerful lord of Baudevennii. When he came to them, they had assembled to dine together. To offer some respectable pretext for his arrival, he said that he was contemplating Cyprus, in order to establish a home and residence for himself on that island. Before departing for such remote shores, he said, he had come to bid farewell to his relatives, and he asked for a definite sum of money with which, once paid, he could complete that long journey.” So it is reported there.]

Bernard at once informed his brother Hugh of the same matter. Hugh therefore, after consulting with his brothers, although he would rather have saved his nephew than betrayed him, if he had dared, nevertheless announced to the castellan of Lille [this was Roger, who in the following month, as castellan of Lille, together with his son Robert, subscribed the above-mentioned letters of William the Norman for the people of Saint-Omer] and the burgesses that he had found Burchard, and ordered them to come quickly and punish, with such vengeance as they judged worthy, the man guilty of so great a crime. Had he wished to spare him, there is no doubt that he himself would have run a grave danger to his own safety.

62. (CHAP. XLII.) When the people of Lille heard Hugh’s command, they immediately went forth with great uproar, seized Burchard, led him to Lille, and prepared a gallows for him in the marketplace. But, awakened by fear of eternal damnation so as to be afraid, and encouraged by contemplation of heavenly mercy so as to hope, he began sternly to accuse himself and publicly to declare that he deserved every punishment. Finally, he demanded that his right hand, which had rendered its bloodstained service in shedding righteous blood, be cut off as a penalty to wash away so great a crime and gain pardon. When no one could be found to do this, he asked at least that he be granted the means to cut it off himself. But consenting to be denied both requests, he returned again to accusation of himself and invocation of heavenly mercy.

Thus, openly confessing and bewailing his guilt, imploring the regard of divine mercy, and, to encourage more confident hope in that mercy, recalling mercies shown to sinners of old, he moved all the bystanders’ hearts to compassion and pity; by his mournful lamentation he brought almost everyone to shed tears, and he strove by every means he could, through temporary pains of the flesh, to escape eternal punishments. He therefore voluntarily offered his limbs to torture; fastened in the spokes of a wheel [Note: Lernutius presents the familiar tales thus: “Inserted among the spokes of a wheel, with his whole body smeared with honey and honeycombs, he sat upon a lofty post, unable to move his limbs. Above him were placed dense lattices from a grove to keep off ravens and other carnivorous birds, lest he be torn apart by their beaks; instead he was exposed to the stings and bites of flies, bees, and hornets, which consumed the skin and flesh of the living man, tearing him little by little to the deepest bones. The torture lasted six days and more.” Mejerus preferred, rejecting these tales, to recount Gualter.], and raised upon a high stake, he persevered in the same devotion, confession, and supplication from the ninth hour of the day until twilight on the following day, and died.

[Note: Lernutius adds: “One of his household servants, Everard, hearing that his master was now being carried off to punishment, escaped by flight into the Ardennes forest; there he fell into a well, not by accidental mischance, and was drowned.” This he gives from vernacular annals, whereas Mejerus tells it differently: “But his servant Everard, having received at Cassel money from men acting in his master’s name, fled into the Ardennes, where he was thrown from his horse into a certain river and perished.” Earlier writers are silent.]

## PART XI. Various contests concerning the successor of Blessed Charles in the county of Flanders; William the Norman is installed

63. (CHAP. XLIII.) But it is now fitting to turn the narrative back to earlier events and relate things which happened before but have hitherto been omitted by us. For not everything that occurred at the same time could also be told at the same time. Therefore, after the margrave had been killed at Bruges, as has been said, news of so great an evil immediately spread everywhere and on that very day extended nearly thirty leagues. Everywhere there was mourning; everywhere groaning and great grief among clergy, monks, peasants, the poor—finally, among all who wished to live in peace and tranquillity and to maintain, and be protected by, justice. But every robber and wicked man, as though released when the bonds by which they had been held were broken—for, as then became plainly evident, they had been restrained more by fear of Charles than of God—began to throw everything into disorder, despoil merchants and travellers of their goods, and often bind and imprison them. So great was the frenzy and wickedness of depraved men that not even reverence for the holy season—for it was Lent—could restrain them.

64. Yet, through the merciful aid of almighty God, their madness was quickly checked. For the prelate William, kinsman of Lord Charles, as soon as he learned from a messenger of the count’s death, claimed the county for himself that same day, though in vain. He seized the strongly fortified town of Aire and compelled all its inhabitants to swear fidelity to him. After he had likewise subdued Saint-Venant, Cassel, Belle, Ypres, and also the districts of Bergues and Furnes, he swiftly repressed the movements of robbers within those territories and ordered peace to be maintained. The other barons of the land also, conferring with one another and inspired by God, agreed to peace, and each endeavoured to defend his own district.

65. (CHAP. XLIV.) But the magnificent king of the French, Louis, on hearing that his kinsman Charles had died and that William had seized, especially without the king’s assent, an honour not due to him, was greatly angered. Desiring both to deprive William of the dignity he had usurped and to avenge the death of his friend, he came to the city of Arras about the middle of Lent. He ordered to come there also the young William, called count of Normandy, who, as we recalled at the beginning of this little work, had been wickedly disinherited by his uncle Henry, king of the English, and who had recently married the queen’s sister [this was Joan, sister of Adelaide, wife of King Louis; Orderic Vitalis discusses her in book XII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, fol. 884].

While they remained in that city for nearly fifteen days, several parties repeatedly came before the king seeking the county of our land and asserting that it belonged to them: namely Arnulf [Galbert calls him Arnolaus. He was born in Denmark from the sister of Blessed Charles, whether she was Ingerta or Cecilia; Pontanus discusses their marriages in book V of *Danish Affairs*, fol. 198 ff.], nephew of Lord Charles; Baldwin of Mons; and envoys of the aforesaid William, who had already violently occupied the previously mentioned part of our land. At last the queen, by God’s hidden but, I think, just dispensation, prevailed; after skilfully inclining the minds of certain magnates to agree with her, she secured the lordship of the county for her brother-in-law, the count of Normandy, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March].

66. (CHAP. XLV.) His uncle [Henry I, king of England, who, as stated above, held William’s father captive], fearing that William’s power might increase to his own detriment, strove with all his heart and every art he could employ to diminish it. He therefore sent his nephew Stephen of Blois [Stephen, later king of England, was born of Adela, sister of King Henry, and Stephen, count of Blois], count of Boulogne [Boulogne, or Bononia, a city of Belgic Gaul on the British Sea; Stephen had acquired its county through marriage to Matilda, only daughter and heir of Eustace, count of Boulogne] and Mortain [“Mortain, an impregnable fortress on the boundary of Brittany and Neustria.” Thus Rigord in the *Deeds of Philip Augustus*. Stephen had received its county as a gift of King Henry after the count of that place had been captured, as Orderic testifies, book II, fol. 811. Here Neustria denotes that part of it which is Normandy]. Through him and other envoys of his party, distributing many gifts and promising more, Henry stirred the minds of many powerful men. He declared that Flanders was his inheritance and belonged to him by right through his uncle Robert of Cassel; by these means he won them to his support and allied to himself the duke of Louvain, his father-in-law [Godfrey the Bearded, whose daughter Adelaide King Henry had married], the count of Mons, Thomas of Coucy, and the oft-mentioned William. He urged and incited all these and their supporters to oppose the king’s will and settlement and to hinder in every way the advance of the new count—not so much in order that he himself might obtain Flanders, which perhaps he had already despaired of doing, as to weaken and destroy the count’s forces, which he suspected would be dangerous to himself.

67. After some time the king, together with the count, left the city of Arras. He first recovered Lille, then Ghent and Bruges, though with difficulty at that time, since supporters of the English party created many obstacles almost everywhere; and he strengthened the siege by his presence. Thereafter, after Easter, the count returned by way of Lille and Béthune as far as our city of Thérouanne, where he was received with great joy by clergy and people and remained two days. Then, after obtaining the castle called Saint-Omer, whose castellan and burgesses welcomed him willingly, though on certain promised conditions [Chesnaeus, in the proofs to book II of the *Genealogical Family of Béthune*, p. 20, cites part of letters in which Count William says: “Not wishing to oppose the petition of the burgesses of Saint-Omer—especially because they received my claim to the consulship of Flanders with willing hearts, and because they have always behaved toward me more honourably and faithfully than the other Flemings—I grant them in perpetual right the laws or customs written below and order them to remain ratified . . . Done in the year 1127, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April], Thursday, the feast day of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian.” Osto, castellan of that city, and his son William subscribed, as did Stephen, count of Boulogne, and very many others cited by us above], and remaining there a few days, he again passed through Thérouanne and returned to Lille.

## PART XII. The church of Bruges is reconciled; the body of Blessed Charles is reburied; miracles; Flanders is pacified

68. (CHAP. XLVI.) Meanwhile the king had compelled Robert and the other Bruges murderers to leave the tower into which they had fled, surrender themselves, and submit to imprisonment and chains. From their account the miracle I shall relate became known. From the time they were besieged and confined in that tower of the church, they took no pleasure in the taste of any food which they had carried there in no small quantity, any more than if they had been eating earth. But after they came out and surrendered, they immediately recovered the taste they had lost for so long. When Robert was thirsty and was offered wine of the very kind which he had customarily drunk while confined there, he praised its excellent taste and swore that he had not drunk good wine from the beginning of the siege. He did not know that he had drunk from the same wine he had formerly used to drink. When this was pointed out to him, he recognized God’s work in the chastisement of His sinners and, together with the others, praised the divine goodness.

69. The king ordered that the church of St Donatian, polluted in many ways not only by the shedding of blood but also by their abominable and filthy habitation, should be cleansed after all its defilements had been removed. He further ordered that the venerable body, which had been buried there more negligently than was fitting, be carried to another church [Galbert writes: the church of St Christopher in the marketplace, no. 119], so that its funeral might there be attended to more carefully and that it might afterwards again be buried in the church with the honour appropriate to it. This was done.

70. (CHAP. XLVII.) But the miracle which divine condescension showed there ought not, it seems, to be passed over in silence. For many truthful and religious men who had been present testified to me when I inquired; among them it is fitting to name here, because of the merit of his holiness, Lord Absalon [Absalon, abbot of St Amand, subscribed the letters of Count Theoderic by which, in 1135, he confirmed the possessions of the monastery of Marchiennes. We treated St Amand and this abbey at length on 6 February, his feast day]. When they had opened the tomb in which the venerable body had been laid fifty-three days earlier [“Seven weeks had now passed,” says Galbert—namely 22 April. We have noted above the error of Lernutius and Mejerus, with their vernacular annals and text of a proclamation], they found it so free from corruption, for the glory of God and the manifestation of the holy martyr, that not even the faintest vapour of slight decay rose from it to offend in the least the noses of those standing about, or of those handling and caring for the body. Yet although it had already lain in the tomb for the period we have stated, it remained susceptible to handling, with wounds raw and entirely fresh, as though he had been killed on that very day. Moreover, so great a fragrance of sweetest perfume divinely spread and filled the whole place that no one could doubt that God had wished to glorify His faithful servant. “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes.” This is judged all the more marvellous because we regard scarcely anything among human corpses as more foul-smelling.

71. Therefore the church was reconciled according to ecclesiastical custom through the ministry of Lord Simon, bishop of Tournai [concerning Bishop Simon, uterine brother of the wife of Blessed Charles, see above, §1], whom the king of France had summoned for that very purpose. The aforesaid body was also brought back with the greatest devotion and reverence of clergy and people, and on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April] was buried in the middle of the church, to rise in glory at the last judgment.

72. (CHAP. XLVIII.) When all these things had been solemnly accomplished with the honour they deserved [In the vernacular annals of Flanders, the following matters concerning Ypres are suppressed, as is William’s capture, because all the actions hitherto splendidly performed are attributed to him; see above, §3], the king marched to Ypres with such an army as he could assemble. The next day, the sixth before the Kalends of May [26 April], the count, as agreed, energetically advanced with an army from the other side to meet him, and the king arrived there about the sixth hour. The oft-mentioned William, son of Philip, showing less reverence than he ought for the majesty of royal dignity, boldly met him outside the town, relying on the arms and courage of many strong men whom he had allied with himself, and began to fight most fiercely against the whole army. Yet while he thought that he was acting bravely—while he resisted his enemies with utmost stubbornness and directed and renewed his battle-line against them—the wretched man did not know what pit of temporal misfortune and adversity was being prepared for him.

For some burgesses, who had sworn fidelity to him not merely once but often, had conspired with certain other men to betray him. They sent envoys to the king and swore that they would open the gates to him and hand William over. Woe to the world because of offences! Or rather, woe to Flanders because of betrayals! It is astonishing, and no less lamentable, that an unhappy land which had happened to lose its lord through treachery could obtain another only through treachery. A few of the men of Ypres had arranged this betrayal. They had judged it more advantageous to obey the king’s will than William’s commands and to submit to a power they suspected. This, they say, was not because they blamed his person in any respect, but because they feared that the rule of certain of his relatives would prove too unrestrained.

73. (CHAP. XLIX.) Accordingly, after fighting on both sides in various charges from the sixth hour until the ninth, on the northern and eastern sides, by means of a banner deliberately placed on the topmost summit of the church of St Peter as the signal for the impending betrayal, they summoned the divisions of the opposing party. They opened the southern gate and admitted them into the town. These men at once ran through the whole town, devastating everything by plunder and fire. William then at last perceived that he had been abandoned and took flight, which was all that he saw remained to him; but his flight was too late. Daniel of Dendermonde pursued, seized him as he fled, stripped him of his arms, and delivered him as a captive to Count William. Thus Ypres, plundered and burned that same day from the northern gate to the southern gate and taken by an innumerable multitude of soldiers, saw the king and count go to the monastery of Messines, bringing captive William with them. On the following day, after entrusting him to the castellan of Lille to be guarded, they proceeded to Aire; receiving it in surrender, they very easily subdued Cassel and the rest of that inland Flanders. Then at last they returned again to Bruges to avenge the death of the honoured Charles.

## PART XIII. The remaining accomplices in the killing of St Charles punished; two escape by flight

75. (CHAP. L.) They also caused Guelric, brother of the provost, whom we have mentioned above as having conspired in Charles’s death, together with nearly twenty-eight other prisoners brought from prison [this took place on 5 May and is described at length by the eyewitness Galbert, no. 123], to be thrown down from the high tower. Thus those murderers perished by torments proportionate to so great a wickedness. Although not all had sinned equally in counsel or deed, nevertheless, by consenting to wickedness and helping wicked men, they had all bound themselves, as it were, by equal bonds of iniquity. Therefore, since they had not shrunk from being joined in their fellowship, they were not undeservedly punished by the same penalty.

But Robert, whom we have also shown above to have been among the conspirators, was thought incapable of being safely punished there, because he was greatly loved by the people and seemed in certain respects more excusable than the others. They therefore resolved to take him away with them. When they had brought him as far as Cassel, and he showed much repentance for his guilt, they had him executed outside the town by beheading.

75. (CHAP. LI.) While these things were taking place, Ingelram of Esen, one of the aforesaid conspirators, had hitherto excused his sins by relying on the protection of his uncle Theoderic of Diksmuide. Blinded by the darkness of his treachery, he had not been ashamed brazenly to present himself before the king and count; and if anyone dared accuse him of this crime, he had boasted that he would defend himself manfully. But he began to lose confidence. At first he hid for some time among his own people; then, finding an opportunity, he put everything aside and, eager to secure his own safety, fled his homeland. Up to the present time—that is, while I write this—he has never appeared again anywhere in our land.

[Note: Concerning him Lernutius, from the Annals of Flanders: “Ingelram of Esen subsequently went to Germany and lived at Mainz on the Rhine. In that town a quarrel arose between him and a certain citizen; during their dispute he inflicted a mortal wound upon him, and death followed. For the crime he was brought before the magistrate, shut in a sack, thrown into the river, and died by a fate deserved by his crimes.” This is reported there; Mejerus believed and copied it. Let credibility rest with them.]

76. (CHAP. LII.) But William of Viroviacum, likewise one of the conspirators, as became clear from the confessions of others—I had left him almost untouched, being intent upon the others and awaiting the issue in his case—could not conceal his wickedness for long. What he had done in secret was immediately revealed by evident proofs. For directly after the count’s murder and the plundering of his treasure, he returned to Viroviacum and carried off with him no small share of it. Yet he was not allowed long to rejoice in the fruit of his wickedness. While he exulted over his enemy’s fall and insolently rejoiced at another’s losses, sudden fear seized him and drove him, terrified, from the borders of Flanders.

For he heard that his brother Lambert [perhaps Lambert of Reddenburch, concerning whom similar things are reported; his son Walter is numbered by Galbert, no. 70, among the leaders of those besieged in the tower of St Donatian], who was innocent, as had become clear from the outcome of the judicial combat he had entered in the court of the oft-mentioned William, was being accused in connection with the count’s death. He also learned that that same William, to whom he had already rendered homage by deceit, had formally renounced him. He began to be afraid. At first he prepared to defend himself; but on the following day, so violently did the goads of a guilty conscience drive him, though no one had yet pursued him, that he committed himself to flight. Taking with him his wife, a few of his men, and such possessions as he could carry away, he fled on the sixth day after the count’s death. “For, as Scripture says, ‘the wicked flee when no one pursues’” (Prov. 28).

77. The castellan of Kortrijk, who had formerly been his enemy, as soon as he heard of his flight, advanced upon Viroviacum with an armed force of many knights. Having plundered all his movable property, he destroyed the entire fortification and, meeting no resistance, burned it so completely that not even a stump remained in the place. William himself had reached a certain village near Tournai; pursued by the people of Tournai, who attempted to seize and punish him, he lost his wife, the greater part of his men, and almost all his possessions. Barely obtaining a horse, he escaped and withdrew into the region of the Nervii [these Nervii must, as is done here, be distinguished from the people of Tournai and placed in Hainaut, as we have elsewhere shown], content with only two companions.

There he entered a certain monastery of monks and, moved more by human than divine fear, as later became clear, presumptuously took the tonsure and habit of monastic life. Yet a few days later, on the pretext of his wife—whose consent, he claimed, he had not obtained before doing this—he abandoned monastic life and immediately returned to the secular world and to the arms he had left behind, without any retraction. In this deed he made sufficiently plain how feignedly he had adopted that religious purpose. For if the bond of his wife compelled the bond of religion to be dissolved, why did he not abstain from arms, by which he had so long wronged those around him? Did the law of marriage compel that too? By no means. For if he truly repented of his crimes, then, after laying aside arms, he ought, even if his wife insisted so strongly upon the marital debt, to have remained with her, eaten his bread in the sweat of his face, and worn himself out in strict fasting.

But now, as we have learned from many reports, he takes no care to appease God’s wrath even by repentance. Rather, with hardened heart, he “makes excuses for sins,” and, provoking God rather than appeasing Him, he does not fear to increase sins by sins. He should therefore fear—and we also for him—that, because he delays turning to the Lord, the wrath of God may come suddenly and destroy him in the time of vengeance. Perhaps he is also kept there so long despite others’ wishes in order that, if he does not repent during the time granted him and proudly abuses God’s gift of mercy, he may at the end be struck more severely by God’s just judgment.

[Note: Mejerus and Marchantius report that “William of Viroviacum, driven from Viroviacum by the prefect of Kortrijk, was eventually captured in Germany and worn down by prolonged tortures at Strasbourg; his wife was buried alive at Tournai.” Let credibility rest with the authors.]

The same may not unreasonably be thought concerning the aforesaid Ingelram. All these things were completed within about two months after the count’s death.

## EPILOGUE
78. Behold, most reverend Father, I have obeyed your will—indeed, your command—and the devout request of my brethren, as far as I was able. Venturing to touch upon a subject so greatly surpassing both the measure of my talent and my powers of expression, as the work itself shows, I have exposed myself alike to the reproach and ridicule of many. [Col. 0942C] For a fool, while he remains silent, is often believed to be wise. His silence is thought to proceed not so much from poverty of understanding as from the safeguard of humility. Thus I too, had I kept altogether silent, might indeed have been considered wise; but I would not thereby have been any wiser. Now, however, because I have disclosed my ignorance by writing, the learned men into whose hands this work may perhaps come will be offended with me: some will disparage me as foolish; others will mock me as presumptuous; others will judge me an ignorant man; and some will rightly cry out that I am a fool. What, then, holy Father, can excuse one whom such clear evidence convicts? I might indeed plead, as a suitable excuse, the obedience imposed upon me by your authority; but I judge it better [Col. 0942D] to endure such censures [Note: [Col. 0942D] The word “to endure,” or something similar, seems to be missing.], even if I could somehow escape them, than, by stubbornly excusing my ignorance, to add deceit to so great a heap of my sins, deprive myself of the fruit of humility, [Col. 0943A] and vainly exalt myself into the arrogance of vanity. For it is more profitable for me to be known as foolish—which I am—than to be thought wise—which I am not. The former can produce a humble and not unfruitful fear; the latter, however, may produce, God forbid, a ruinous swelling of pride. May He graciously deign to turn this away from me together with all other filth of vices—He who condemned every kind of pride by His own humility. Amen.

[Col. 0943]

# SECOND LIFE, BY GALBERT THE NOTARY

(From several manuscripts.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0943B]

1. Among the princes of kingdoms whom we have known in our own region, there had flourished an utmost zeal to win glory and praise through deeds of warfare; and an equal desire for good government was present in them. Yet the Emperor of the Romans, Henry [Note: [Col. 0943D] Henry V is meant, who died at Utrecht in 1125 and had formerly been excommunicated by Pope Callistus II.], ruled with less power and fame. After reigning many years, he died without an heir. Likewise, the king of England [Note: [Col. 0943D] Henry I, king of England, discussed above in chapter 2.] lived in his kingdom without children, with less fame and strength than Count Charles, margrave of Flanders, our natural lord and prince. Charles, distinguished in warfare and noble by royal blood, ruled the county from his seventh year as father and advocate of the churches of God; he was generous toward the poor, gracious and honourable among his nobles, cruel and cautious against [Col. 0943C] enemies. Though without an heir, he was betrayed and slain by his own—indeed, by his most wicked—servants, and died for justice.

In undertaking to describe the death of so great a prince, I have not laboured after elegance of expression or sought to distinguish varied rhetorical colours, but have pursued only the truth of events. Although in a dry style, I have committed to the memory of the faithful, by writing, the extraordinary manner of his death. Nor, when I applied my mind to this work, did I possess either an appropriate place or opportunity of time; for our place was at that same time distressed by fear and trouble, so that, without exception, clergy and people alike were equally endangered by the destruction both of their possessions and of their lives. Therefore, amid so many adversities and within the most confined limits of place, [Col. 0943D] I began to restrain a mind tossed to and fro, as though in the Euripus, and to confine it within the manner of writing. In this exertion of my mind, one tiny spark of charity, nourished and exercised by its own fire, kindled utterly all the spiritual virtues of my heart; and thereafter granted freedom to write to my outward man, whom fear had possessed.

2. Concerning this effort of mind, which, placed in such straits, I have commended for the common hearing of you [Note: [Col. 0944D] He seems to be addressing the citizens of Bruges.] and of all the faithful: if anyone strives to bark or carp at it, [Col. 0944B] I care little. For I am made secure by the fact that I speak a truth open to all who were struck with the same danger together with me, and commit it to be remembered by our descendants. Therefore I ask and exhort that, if the dryness of this style and the small handful of this little work should come into anyone’s hands, he should not mock or despise it. Rather, let him marvel, as a new wonder belonging solely to our time, at what has been written and brought together by God’s ordering; and let him learn not to despise or hand over to death earthly authorities, whom we must believe have been set over us by God’s ordinance. Hence the Apostle: “Let every soul be subject to every authority, whether to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by God” (1 Pet. 2:13). “As” (*tamquam*) is not comparative [Col. 0944C] here, but confirmatory: in Holy Scripture *tamquam* is used for what truly is; as in “as a bridegroom,” that is, truly a bridegroom.

Certainly the murderers, drunkards, fornicators, and slaves of every vice in our land did not deserve to have set over them a good prince—religious and devout, catholic, after God the supporter of the poor, advocate of the churches of God, defender of his country—and one in whom the remaining power of earthly rule might receive a model for governing well and material for serving God. Seeing, therefore, the advancement of the Church and of the Christian faith, as you will hear below, the devil shook the stability of the earth—that is, of God’s Church—and troubled it by deceits, betrayals, and the shedding of innocent blood.

# CHAPTER I. The illustrious deeds of Blessed Charles in the county. The Roman Empire and the kingdom of Jerusalem offered to him.

[Col. 0944D]

3. Charles, then, son of Cnut, king of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0944D] Cnut, Cnuto, or Canute are names applied indiscriminately to kings of Denmark; the father of Blessed Charles was Saint Canute IV of that name.], and born of a mother descended from the blood of the counts of Flanders, was reared from childhood in our country by that kinship of affinity, until he attained mature strength of body and mind. Once he had been armed with the honours of knighthood, he undertook noble deeds against enemies; [Col. 0945A] he attained an excellent reputation and the glory of a name almost equal to that of great and powerful men. Our nobles had for many years earnestly wished for him as their prince, if this might somehow come about. Thus Count Baldwin, a most valiant young man, at his death entrusted both his realm and his princes to his nephew Charles, and commended them under the protection of faith.

4. With the prudence of greater counsel, the pious count began to make arrangements for restoring peace and recalling the laws and rights of the realm. Little by little, peace was gathered and established from every side; and in the fourth year of his countship, through him all things flourished, all things smiled, all things enjoyed the security of justice and peace and abundant gladness. At length, seeing that the grace of peace was pleasing to all, he proclaimed throughout the bounds of the realm that all who dwelt and conducted their affairs either in the market-place or within fortified places should live together in tranquillity [Col. 0945B] and security, without the use of arms; otherwise they would be punished with the very arms they carried. Under this regulation bows and arrows, and afterwards every kind of weapon, were laid aside in market places as in peaceful places.

By the favour of this peace, people governed themselves by laws and justice, applying every resource of intellect and study to legal pleadings: so that each might defend himself, when accused, by the strength and eloquence of rhetoric; or, when attacking an adversary, might deceive him by an oratorically embellished variety of figures. Then rhetoric possessed its exercises both through cultivation and by nature; for many unlettered persons had been granted by nature herself modes of eloquence and rational paths of conjecture and argument such that those trained and learned in rhetorical art could by no means withstand or turn them aside. But because these men again, by their deceits, came together in the courts against the less cautious faithful and sheep of Christ, God, who surveys all things from on high, did not disdain to chastise His deceivers: so that He might show by punishments to those to whom He had granted the good of eloquence for salvation that they had used that good for their own destruction.

5. Therefore the Lord sent scourges of famine, and afterwards of pestilence, upon all who lived in our realm; but first He deigned to call them back to repentance by the terror of signs, since He foresaw them inclined to evil. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1124, [Col. 0945D] in the month of August, an eclipse and an unnatural failure of light appeared to all inhabitants of the earth in the body of the sun, about the ninth hour of the day [Note: [Col. 0945D] Among other astronomers, Sethus Calvisius recorded this eclipse as having been observed by English writers to have occurred on 17 August, and describes it accurately.]. The eastern disk of the sun was darkened and gradually cast strange clouds over the remaining parts; yet they did not darken the entire sun at once, but only part of it. Nevertheless, the same cloud traversed the whole circumference of the sun, passing from east to west only within the circle of the solar substance. Therefore those who noted the condition of peace and the wrongs committed in legal proceedings foretold to [Col. 0946A] all the peril of a coming famine and death.

And when men, both lords and servants, were not corrected even in this way, the want of a sudden famine came, and thereafter the scourges of pestilence descended [Note: [Col. 0946D] In 1125, two years before the death of Blessed Charles, as Walter indicates.]. Hence in the Psalm: “He called for famine upon the land, and broke every staff of bread” (Ps. 104:16). During this calamity, no one could sustain himself with food and drink in the customary fashion. Instead, contrary to custom, a feaster consumed at one meal only as much bread as he had formerly been accustomed to consume over several days before this time of famine. Thus, through excess, he became glutted; and all the natural passages of the receptacles, stretched by an excessive filling of food and drink, were weakened in their natural function. Men wasted away through crudity and indigestion, yet still suffered hunger until they breathed their last. [Col. 0946B] Many also became swollen and nauseated by food and drink, though these things were indeed abundant for them.

During this time of famine, in the middle of Lent, even the people of our land dwelling near Ghent, the rivers Leie [Note: [Col. 0946D] The Legio—elsewhere Legia or Lisa—flows into the Scheldt at Ghent.] and Scheldt ate meat, because bread had wholly failed them. Some, while travelling to towns and fortified places where they might obtain bread, perished of hunger before completing even half their journey. Around the villages and estates of the rich, and around castles or strongholds, the poor, having dragged themselves with miserable steps in search of alms, died begging. Wonderful to say: no one in our land retained a natural complexion; rather, a pallor akin and proper to death was upon all. Healthy and sick alike languished, because one who had been sound in bodily constitution became sick on seeing the misery of one dying. [Col. 0946C]

6. Not even thus were the wicked corrected—those who, at that same time, as is said, had conspired against the life of the most pious Count Charles. But the noble count laboured in every way to support the poor, distributing alms in his castles and places, both personally and through his officers. During that calamity he supported one hundred poor persons at Bruges every day, giving each of them one very large loaf, from before the aforesaid Lent until the new harvest of that year. He had made the same provision in his other fortified places.

In the same year the lord count decreed that whoever sowed two measures [Col. 0946D] of land at sowing-time should sow one further measure with beans and peas, because this kind of pulse bore fruit more quickly and earlier, and thus the poor might sooner be supported if the misery and deprivation of famine should not cease during the year. He issued the same command throughout his entire county, thereby providing as far as he could for the poor in the future. He also sternly rebuked those of Ghent who had allowed poor people to die of hunger before the doors of their houses when they could have fed them.

He likewise forbade the brewing of beer, so that the poor might have a more plentiful and better supply [Col. 0947A] if citizens and inhabitants of the land ceased brewing during the famine. For he ordered bread to be made from oats, so that the poor might at least prolong life by bread and water. He ordered a quarter of wine to be sold for six pennies and no more dearly, so that merchants might cease from their abundance and purchase of wine and exchange their wares, in the necessity of famine, for other provisions by which they might have a more ready supply and support the poor more easily.

From his own table he daily withheld food sufficient to support one hundred and thirteen poor persons. Moreover, from the beginning of that Lent and of his devout fast—in which he was soon betrayed and fell asleep in the Lord—he gave each day to one poor person new clothing: namely a shirt (*camisia*) [Note: [Col. 0947D] *Camisia*, used for an undergarment, occurs in the old Salic Law, title 6, and in Fortunatus, Book I of the Life of Saint Radegund. From it later arose the word *chemise* in the modern French language, which did not yet exist in those times. Perhaps *cama*, as is now the case among the Spaniards, was once used among the Goths and ancient Germans for “bed,” so that *camisia* was called the garment in which one sleeps.], tunic, furs, cloak, breeches, stockings, and shoes (*subtulares*) [Note: [Col. 0947D] In ancient codices one finds *subtulares*; perhaps *subtalares* should be substituted, so that they are shoes, as it were “under the ankles.” In the Life of Saint Gudila, 8 January, no. 8, *subtalares* is read, where Garneveltius thinks *subtulares* should be restored; but with only a vowel changed, these words can readily be confused.]. He continued this until the day on which he died in Christ. Having carried out this distribution and merciful bestowal upon the poor, he would go to church, where, prostrate in prayer, he sang psalms to God; and there, after hearing the sacred office according to custom, he distributed money to the poor while lying thus prostrate before the Lord. [Col. 0947B]

7. While Charles, margrave of Flanders, lived in his county adorned with peace and glory [Note: [Col. 0947D] “Henry V lost life together with his kingdom at Utrecht in 1125, on Thursday in Pentecost.” Anselm of Gembloux, *Chronicle*. Some maintain that he died two days later.], the Roman Emperor Henry died, and the kingdom of his empire was left desolate and disinherited without an heir. Therefore the wiser men among the clergy and people of the Roman and German kingdom laboured by every means to provide themselves with a man noble both in birth and character for the imperial rule. Having examined the princes of lands and kingdoms, they deliberately formed a plan that the wiser and more powerful men in the realm should solemnly send suitable envoys—namely, the chancellor of the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0947D] The archbishop of Cologne was Frederick, from about 1100 or somewhat earlier until 1131; on 23 September of this year, 1125, he crowned Lothair of Saxony emperor at Aachen. A contemporary anonymous writer in his Life relates that Saint Norbert was ordained to holy orders by him.] of the city of Cologne, together with Count Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0948D] Count Godfrey seems to have been the count of Namur, brother of Saint Albert, bishop of Liège. When the said Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, had established Albert against the intruder Alexander, Count Godfrey defended him by arms.]—to the pious Count Charles of Flanders. In the name of all the clergy and all the people of the German kingdom and empire, they were to entreat and beseech his power and piety to assume, solely out of charity, the honours of the empire and royal dignities together with their resources. For all the best men, both clergy and people, awaited with the most just desire his election, that, by God’s gift, he might deign to come among them; that they might unanimously exalt him by coronation and the elevation of the Empire; [Col. 0948A] and establish him as their king under the law of the Catholic emperors, his predecessors.

8. When Count Charles heard the embassy and petition, he took counsel with the nobles and peers of his land about what he should do. But those who loved him with a just love and the power of affection, and venerated him as a father, began to grieve, to lament his departure, and to fear that their country would suffer grievous ruin if he should leave it. At last those most wicked traitors, enemies of his life, advised him to seize the kingdom and its honours among the Germans, persuading him how great a glory and fame it would be for him to be king of the Romans. Those wretches laboured by what cunning and what deceits they might be rid of him—the man whom, later, when they could not remove him, they betrayed while he was alive and striving against them for the law of God and men.

Therefore Count Charles remained in his county at the request of those who loved him, committing and establishing peace and the welfare of his country, so far as lay in him, for all: catholic, good, devout, a worshipper of God and a prudent ruler of men. When he intended to undertake deeds of secular warfare, he had no enemies around his land, whether in the marches or within his borders and boundaries; for they feared him, or, joined to him by a covenant of peace and friendship, they instead exchanged gifts and presents with one another. Yet, for the honour of his land and the exercise of his soldiers, he sometimes undertook the contests of secular warfare against some [Col. 0948C] count or prince of Normandy or France, and sometimes beyond the kingdom of France. There he practised tournaments with two hundred knights; in this he heightened his own fame and the power and glory of his county. Whatever fault he committed through this frivolity, he made amends for before God by the manifold redemption of almsgiving.

9. During his lifetime it also happened [Note: [Col. 0948D] Baldwin, son of the count of Retesta, became king of Jerusalem after the death in 1118 of Baldwin, brother of Godfrey of Bouillon; then he was captured in 1123, but was freed not long afterwards. The writers of the Holy Land expedition praise him highly enough that it seems some matters carried out far from Flanders are here reported from public rumour.] that the king of Jerusalem fell into Saracen captivity, and the city of Jerusalem sat desolate without its king. As we learned, the knights of the Christian name who had devoted themselves there to Christian warfare hated him, because that captive king had been miserly and parsimonious and had not governed the people of God well. They therefore took counsel and, by common consent, [Col. 0949A] sent letters to Count Charles, asking him to go up to Jerusalem, assume the kingdom of Judaea, and possess in that place and holy city the crown of the Catholic empire and royal dignity.

But after taking the counsel of his faithful men, he refused to abandon the land of Flanders, which, had life remained with him, he would have governed well and much better than he had governed it thus far—if those most wicked traitors, full of the devil, had not killed their lord and father, full of the spirit of piety, counsel, and strength. Alas for the sorrow: that they should remove so great a man from God’s Church, one whom the Church, the people of the eastern empire, and the holy city of Jerusalem together with the Christian people had desired, resolved, and jointly petitioned to establish as king.

# CHAPTER II. The cause of the hatred stirred up against Saint Charles

[Col. 0949B]

10. The powers of my soul fail me, and together with his memory the greater power within the soul—namely, reason—for praising the good Count Charles. In merits you, princes of the lands, are all inferior to him: less powerful, unskilled, undiscerning, and disordered in character. For in the end of his life Count Charles was, among the religious children of the Church, such a man as his merits placed him above rulers and many philosophers of the Christian faith. And although he may once have been a sinner and criminal, at the end of a good life all things worked together for his good and the everlasting salvation of his soul through the fruit of repentance. Hence also he says:

> No one ought to be called blessed  
> before death and his final funeral rites.
>
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.136

[Col. 0949C] And the Apostle: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to His purpose” (Rom. 8:28). Therefore in a holy place, in holy prayers, in holy devotion of heart, in the holy season of the Forty Days, in the holy distribution of alms [Note: [Col. 0949D] The relics of these saints are still preserved at Bruges in the highest veneration, enclosed in silver tombs or reliquary heads; we ourselves saw them there with no little admiration at their outstanding splendour. Saint Donatian is patron of the city and of the whole diocese, and the cathedral church is dedicated to him. His feast is also observed by the people on 7 October, when we shall treat of the translation of his body.], before the holy altar, and among the holy relics of Saint Donatian, archbishop of Rheims, [Col. 0949D] Blessed Basil the Great, and Saint Maximus, raiser of three dead men [Note: [Col. 0949D] As we were told, a large portion of Saint Basil’s spine is preserved. Of Saint Maximus there are two ribs, a leg, two bones of the arm, and five finger-bones. Thus Sanderus, Book II of *Bruges*. Saint Maximus is commemorated on 27 November, Saint Basil on 14 June.], unclean dogs, filled with the devil, cut the throat of their lord.

For no one is so irrational, dull, or stupid as not to judge those traitors worthy of the lowest and unheard-of punishments—those servants who, by an unheard-of betrayal, destroyed their own lord, whom they ought to have guarded. It was therefore a marvel, and especially worthy of remembrance, that although we have seen many emperors, kings, dukes, and men of consular rank, we have neither seen nor heard of any man whom it so well became to be lord and father, advocate of the churches [Col. 0950A] of God, as it became him. For he knew how to be a lord, father, advocate, merciful, gentle, ready to grant requests, fitted for the honour of God and the adornment of the Church. This is surely sufficiently credible, because after the death of so great a man all bore witness concerning his merits—friends and enemies, strangers and neighbours, noble and ignoble, and inhabitants of whatever land had heard even his outstanding reputation—how great his merit must be believed to have been before God and men, since, in executing God’s justice and for the salvation of those whom he governed, he died in the manner of a Christian ruler. Those who were men of his peace, magnifying their treacheries against him, betrayed him, as in the Psalm: “For the man of my peace, who ate my bread, magnified treacheries against me” (Ps. 40:10).

[Col. 0950B] 11. After God’s mercy had withdrawn the scourges and wholly removed the adversity of the season, He began to bestow the abundance of His favour upon the lands. He commanded granaries to be filled by the fruitfulness of crops, the world to overflow with wine and other provisions, and, by a certain pleasantness of the seasons, the whole land blossomed anew at the divine command.

The pious count, wishing therefore again to restore the good order of the realm, inquired who among his dependants were unfree, who were servants, and who were free in the kingdom. While court business was being conducted, the count was often present, hearing the dispute concerning secular freedom and the condition of servants: namely, that in great matters and general cases free men did not deign to make answers to servants. He laboured to trace those who belonged to his dependency and to claim them [Col. 0950C] for himself.

One provost, Bertulf of Bruges, and his brother the castellan of Bruges, with their nephews Borsiard, [Note: [Col. 0950D] Robert, Borsiard’s brother, is said below, no. 26, to have been killed in a skirmish.] Robert, [Note: [Col. 0950D] Albert is called in the Life by the anonymous Dane the son of Robert the Castellan, and therefore the cousin of Borsiard and of the said Robert. He is mentioned no further.] Albert, and the other leading members of that kindred, strained every device and resource to escape and evade the servitude and dependency of the count; for they too belonged to the count’s dependency and were of servile condition.

12. Having at length taken counsel, that provost gave his marriageable nieces, whom he had brought up in his house, in marriage to free knights, so that, as it were by the occasion of these marriages, he and his own people might somehow gain access to secular freedom. But it happened that a knight who had married the provost’s niece challenged another knight to single combat in the count’s presence; the challenged man was free by the descent of his kindred. In a contemptuous answer, the challenged knight indignantly declared that he was not of servile condition, but descended through the lines of his race from free rank, and for that reason would not enter single combat as the equal of the challenger. [Col. 0951A] For whoever, though free, had married a bondwoman according to the count’s law, after possessing her for a year was no longer free, but became of the same condition as his wife.

The knight therefore grieved because he had lost his freedom through the wife by whom, when he married her, he had expected to become freer. The provost and his people also grieved; and for this reason they strove by every means to withdraw themselves from the count’s servitude. Therefore, when the count learned from proof of the truth and the report of the elders of the realm that they unquestionably belonged to him, he attempted to claim them for his servitude. Yet because the provost and his kinsmen had not, from the time of the count’s predecessors until then, been challenged or called to account concerning their servile status, the matter was consigned to general oblivion, as though it had been dormant and neglected through many ages, unless it had been recalled to the truth of memory in the aforesaid challenge to combat. [Col. 0951B]

13. Moreover, the provost, together with the entire succession of his nephews, was more powerful in the realm after the count, and more distinguished in reputation and religious standing; he maintained that he himself was free, as were both the ancestors and descendants of his kindred, and with a kind of superstition and arrogance he pressed this claim. He laboured by counsel and power to withdraw himself and his people from the count’s possession and dependency; and he often reproached the count in these terms:

> “This Charles from Denmark would never have ascended to the county had I wished otherwise. Now, then, since he has become count through me, he does not remember that I have done him good; indeed, he is striving utterly to reduce me and my whole kindred to servitude, asking the elders whether we are his servants. But let him inquire as much as he wishes: we always shall be and are free, and there is no man on earth who can make us servants.”

Yet he spoke boastfully in vain. For the wary count had understood the provost’s disparagement and that of his men, and had also heard of their fraud and betrayal. Since the provost and his men could not secure the success of their defence without losing the freedom they had usurped, he preferred to perish with the whole succession of his nephews rather than be made the count’s bondsman. At last, by the deceit of a perverse and wicked design, they began privately to deliberate upon murdering the most pious count, and eventually to seek a place and opportunity to kill him. [Col. 0951D]

14. The provost was thus glad that the quarrels and disturbances which had arisen between his nephews and Thancmar—whose just cause the count favoured—gave him occasions for betraying the count. For by money, influence, and entreaty he had summoned all the knights of our province to assist his nephews against Thancmar. He besieged Thancmar on every side in the place where he had entrenched himself, and at last, having assembled a force, attacked the besieged men with great violence. Breaking down the barriers of the gates, he cut down the orchards and hedges of his enemies. Yet he acted in absence, as though he had done nothing; all things he did by counsel and deceit, while outwardly pretending every goodwill. He told his enemies that he grieved because his nephews committed so many quarrels and homicides—though he had urged them to every wickedness. [Col. 0952A]

In the aforesaid encounter, very many wounded and dead fell on both sides that day. When the provost learned that the engagement had begun, he himself went down to the carpenters working in the brothers’ cloister and ordered their iron tools—that is, their axes—to be carried there, so that with them they might cut down the tower, orchards, and houses of his enemies. He sent throughout every house in the suburb to collect axes, which were carried there with the greatest speed. When his nephews returned at night with five hundred armed knights and countless foot-soldiers, he brought them into the cloister and the brothers’ refectory, where he refreshed them all with a varied provision of food and drink; and over this he was joyful and triumphant.

As he continually afflicted his enemies in this way [Col. 0952B] and incurred the greatest expenditure upon those assisting his nephews, first the armed retainers and afterwards the knights began to plunder the peasants, so that they seized and consumed the cattle and herds of the villagers. Whatever the peasants possessed for their own use, the provost’s nephews violently seized and assigned to the maintenance of themselves and their followers. But from the beginning of the realm no count had permitted robbery to be committed in the kingdom, because great death and conflict resulted from it.

15. The peasants therefore heard that the count had come to Ypres. By night and secretly, as many as two hundred went to him; falling at his feet, they begged for his fatherly and customary aid—that he should order their goods restored: their livestock and herds, clothing and silver, and every other furnishing [Col. 0952C] of their houses, all of which the provost’s nephews and those who had fought with them by night and day in that siege expedition had plundered.

The count, deeply troubled by the grievances of those complainants, summoned his counsellors and also many members of the provost’s kindred, asking them by what punishment and strictness of justice this crime should be judged. They advised him to destroy Borsiard’s house by fire without delay, because he had committed robbery upon the count’s peasants. They especially advised that the aforesaid house be destroyed because, as long as it stood, Borsiard would continue to perpetrate quarrels, robberies, and homicides, and would wholly lay waste that neighbourhood. Having taken counsel on this matter, [Col. 0952D] the prudent count went down and burned the house, utterly destroying his dwelling.

Then Borsiard, the provost, and their accomplices grieved beyond measure: both because the count seemed in this action to have given consent and assistance to their enemies, and because the count daily challenged them concerning their servile status and laboured by every means to make them his bondsmen.

16. And so, after the house had been burned, the count went up to Bruges. Having been granted a house and seated there, those close to him came and warned him, saying that the provost’s nephews intended to betray him, since they now had a suitable occasion in the burning of the aforesaid house. Yet even if he had not done this, the count would no less have been betrayed by them. After the count had eaten supper, mediators came before him on behalf of the provost and his nephew, asking the count to turn away his indignation from them and receive them mercifully into his friendship. But the count answered that he would deal with them in all justice and also mercifully, if from then on they were willing to put aside quarrels and robberies; moreover, he promised that he ought to restore to Borsiard an even better house. Nevertheless, on the site where the house had been burned, he swore that, while he held the county, Borsiard would henceforth hold no possession, because, dwelling beside Thancmar until then, he had never committed anything but quarrels and disturbances against enemies and citizens, along with robbery and slaughter. [Col. 0953A]

The mediators, however, were partly aware of the betrayal and did not trouble the count much about reconciliation. When the servants went to pour drink, they asked the count to order better wine brought. After drinking it, as drinkers are accustomed to do, they asked to be served once more, and still more abundantly, so that, after obtaining a final and later permission from the count, they might go away as though to sleep. At the count’s command, drink was served abundantly to all present, until they had received final leave and departed. [Col. 0953B]

# CHAPTER III. The nocturnal conspiracy to murder Saint Charles. The enormity of this crime weighed.

17. [Note: [Col. 0953D] Just as the narrative of the preceding chapter and of this one agrees plainly with what we reported as described by Walter, indeed also by Suger, so it differs utterly from what has been assembled in the vernacular Annals of Flanders, the Form of the Bruges Proclamation, and Lernutius’s Commentary. We touched on some points in the preceding Commentary.]

Accordingly Isaac, Borsiard, William of Wervik, Ingrannus, and their accomplices, having obtained the provost’s consent, hastened to do what, even by the free exercise of their will, they would not have done under the necessity of divine ordinance. For immediately those who were mediators and intercessors between the count and the provost’s nephews went to the provost’s house and announced the count’s reply: namely, that they could obtain no favor either for the nephews or for their aforesaid supporters; he would deal with them only as the strictness of justice and the censure established by the leading men of the land should determine.

Then the provost and his nephews went into a chamber. Having summoned whomsoever they wished, and with the provost himself guarding the chamber door, they gave their right hands to one another, pledging themselves to betray the count. For this crime they summoned Robert the Younger, inviting him to give his right hand and to do with them the same thing which they themselves were undertaking, for which they had pledged their right hands to one another.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Robert the Younger, son of Robert the Castellan, brother of Bertulf the Provost. The byname “the Younger,” or in Flemish Kindt, was given both to him and to his father; by this surname various families are called. Neither is mentioned in the said Annals and other tales. On the contrary, Meyer mentions not only the son but also the father Robert, though he had died twelve or more years previously, as is clear from what was said above. [Col. 0954D]]

But the youth, prudent through the strength of a noble spirit, perceived that the matter for which they pressed him would be grave. He resisted, unwilling ignorantly to submit himself to their compact unless he first knew what deed they had resolved to undertake. [Col. 0954A] When they still compelled him, he withdrew and hastened to leave by the door. But Isaac, William, and the others cried out to the provost, who was then doorkeeper, not to permit Robert to go out until, compelled by his command, he had done what they demanded of him.

At once the youth, ensnared by the provost’s blandishments and threats, returned and gave his right hand under their terms. Though ignorant what he was to do with them, once he had immediately been bound with the traitors, he asked what he had done. They replied: “This Count Charles is striving by every means for our destruction, and hastens to reduce us to his slaves. We have now conspired for his betrayal, and henceforth you must carry out that same betrayal with us, both in counsel and in deed.”

18. Then the terrified youth, wholly dissolved in tears, [Col. 0954B] said: “Far be it from us to betray our lord and the count of our country. Indeed, if you do not desist, I shall go and openly reveal your betrayal to the count and to all men; and, God willing, I shall never render counsel or aid in this undertaking.”

As he fled from them, they forcibly held him back, saying: “Listen, friend: as though we were seriously intending to carry out the aforesaid betrayal, we have now disclosed it, in order to test by this whether you would remain with us in any grave enterprise. There is indeed something else which we have still concealed from you, for the sake of which you are bound to us by faith and compact; that we shall tell you later.” Then, as though turning the affair into a jest, they disguised the betrayal.

Each of them went down to his own place, leaving the chamber.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] Lernutius says that this conspiracy was made at Ypres on the feast of St Vincent, 22 January; this comes from the fabulous Annals.]

When Isaac at last reached home, he pretended to be going to sleep—for he was waiting for the silence of the night. Soon mounting a horse, he returned to the castle, went down to Borsiard’s lodging, summoned him and such others as he wished, and they withdrew separately to another lodging, namely that of the knight Walter. When they had entered, they completely extinguished the fire in the house, lest the lit fire reveal to persons awakened in the house who they were and what business, contrary to custom, they were conducting at that hour of night.

Secure in the darkness, they took counsel that the betrayal should be carried out at once in the morning. They chose from Borsiard’s household the bolder and more daring men for this crime and promised them great riches. To knights who should kill the count they offered four marks, and to serving-men who should do the same, two marks; and [Col. 0954D] they bound themselves by a most wicked compact.

[Note: [Col. 0954D] It cannot easily be determined how a mark ought to be valued. Matthew Paris, in his History under the year 1235, maintains that each mark was reckoned at 13 shillings and 4 sterlings. But the valuation seems to have varied among different peoples.]

Isaac therefore returned to his house about dusk, after he had encouraged the others by his counsel and arranged them, willing and ready, for so great a crime.

19. When the day came, exceedingly dark and [Col. 0955A] foggy, so that no one could distinguish anything from another at the length of a spear, Borsiard secretly sent several servants into the count’s court to watch for his departure to the church. The count had indeed risen very early, distributed alms to the poor in his own house, as was his custom, and then went to church.

But, as his chaplains related, when he had composed himself in bed to sleep during the night, he was troubled by a certain anxious wakefulness. His mind was confused and disturbed; harassed by manifold thoughts, he now lay on one side, now sat up in bed, and appeared altogether wearied within himself. When he had proceeded on the way toward the church of St Donatian, the servants who were watching for his departure ran back and announced to the traitors that the count had gone up into the upper chamber of the church [Col. 0955B] with a few companions.

Then that frenzied Borsiard, with his knights and servants, all taking naked swords beneath their cloaks, pursued the count into that same upper chamber. They divided into two parties, so that by neither passage of the chamber might any of those whom they intended to betray escape. And behold, they saw the count lying prostrate, as was his custom, beside the altar on a low stool, where he was devoutly chanting psalms and prayers to God, while also distributing coins to the poor.

20. It must be known what noble and eminent man, what outstanding count, these most impious and inhuman servants betrayed. His ancestors had been the better and more powerful persons who had flourished from the beginning of holy Church, whether in France, Flanders, Denmark, or finally under the Roman Empire. From their stock the pious count had sprung in our own time; reared from childhood into perfect manhood, he never departed from his fathers’ and royal forebears’ noble customs and native virtues of life.

Having performed many distinguished and excellent deeds before becoming count, he took the road of holy pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Crossing the depths of the sea, he finally ascended to Jerusalem after many dangers and wounds often endured for Christ’s love, with the most desired and joyful fulfillment of his vow. There also he fought stoutly against the enemies of the Christian faith; and thus, after reverently worshipping at the Lord’s tomb, he returned to his homeland.

In the hardship and distress of that pilgrimage, this pious servant of the Lord learned—as he often related while governing the county—how great was the want suffered by the poor, with what pride the rich were puffed up, and by how much misery the whole world was shaken. Therefore he was accustomed to stoop to aid the needy, to be strong amid adversity, and not to be exalted in prosperity; and, as the Psalmist teaches, “The ruler’s honor loves judgment” (Ps. 98 [Vulgate 98; English Ps. 99]). He governed the county by the judgment of princes and prudent men.

21. When the life of so glorious a prince had received martyrdom, all the inhabitants of the lands, struck by the infamy of his betrayal, grieved exceedingly. And, marvelous to relate, when the count was killed in the Bruges castle in the morning of one day—namely Wednesday—the report of his impious death struck the citizens of London, in England, [Col. 0956A] on the following day about the first hour; and about evening on that same second day it disturbed the people of Laon, [Col. 0956D] who are far distant from us in France.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Laon is in upper Picardy, on the borders of Champagne; it is also called Lugdunum Clavatum, commonly Laon. Far from it, at the confluence of the Saône and Rhône, is the very famous trading city of Lyons.]

We learned this through our scholars, who were studying at Laon at that time, and likewise through our merchants, who were occupied in trade in London that same day. No one could have traversed the stated intervals, whether of time or place, so swiftly either by horse or by ship.

22. For carrying out this crime of betrayal, it was also ordained by God that the audacious and presumptuous descendants of the predecessors of Provost Bertulf should survive, while the others had been forestalled by death. While they lived, these men had been powerful persons in their country, weighty in influence and abounding in wealth; but the aforesaid provost lived in the clergy with most severe harshness and was not a little proud.

For it was his custom, when someone very well known to him came into his presence, to pretend through the pride of his heart not to recognize him, and indignantly to ask those sitting near him who the man was. Only then, if it pleased him, would he greet the person summoned. When he had sold someone a small canonical prebend, he gave him investiture without any canonical election—indeed, by force. No one among his canons dared either silently to rebuke him or openly to do so.

In the aforesaid community of brothers at the church of St Donatian there had formerly been canons very devout and perfectly learned—namely, at the beginning of the provostship of this most arrogant prelate. Repressing his pride, they kept him constrained by orthodox counsel and teaching, lest he presume to do anything dishonorable in the Church. But after they fell asleep in the Lord, the provost, left to himself, was borne wherever his own inclination and the impulse of arrogance drove him.

Since he was the head of his family, he strove to prefer his nephews—exceedingly nurtured by him and finally girded with knighthood—to all others in the land, and he labored to make their fame known everywhere. Thus he armed his kinsmen for disputes and seditions and set enemies against them for them to attack, so that the report might fly throughout all places of how great were the power and strength of himself and his nephews, whom no one in the kingdom could resist or overcome.

At length, when he was accused before the count of servile condition, and when the count exerted himself to prove that he and his entire succession had been slaves, he was humiliated, as has been said. He then strove by what escape and what cunning he might oppose his servitude, and by what strength preserve his usurped freedom. When he could not otherwise persist in obstinacy, he brought to a criminal conclusion, through himself and his followers, the betrayal which he had long avoided, both among his own people and among the peers of the realm.

23. But the most merciful God deigned again to call his own back by the terror of signs. Near our region, bloody waters appeared in ditches as a sign of the coming slaughter. By this they might have been recalled from their crime, had they not, in the hardened zeal of their hearts, conspired [Col. 0957A] to betray the count.

Moreover, they often discussed who would avenge the count if they killed him; though they did not know what they were saying, they marked out “Who?” as an innumerable name: countless persons not capable of being entered under a fixed number. For the king of France with a great army, together with the princes of our land and an innumerable multitude, assembled to avenge the death of the most pious count. Nor has the misery of this fate yet run to its end: rather, from day to day they have not ceased to avenge the aforesaid death of the count upon all who are suspected or guilty, wherever fugitives and exiles may be found.

24. Therefore we inhabitants of the land of Flanders, who lament the death of the count and great prince, mindful of his life, entreat, exhort, and beseech that, having heard the true and certain account of both his life and death, whoever hear it may ask for his soul the glory of eternal life and everlasting blessedness with the saints.

In the following arrangement of this Passion, the reader will find distinctions of the days and of the events done on those days, down to the vengeance recorded at the end of this little work: vengeance which God alone carried out upon the princes of the land, whom he removed from this world by the severity of death, and by whose counsel and aid the betrayal was begun and brought through to its conclusion.

## CHAPTER IV. The killing of St Charles and of four others. The flight or captivity of certain persons.

25. In the year 1127, [Col. 0957C] on the sixth day before the Nones of March—that is, on the second day of that month—after two days of the second week of Lent had passed, when Wednesday next dawned, with the fifth concurrent, the sixth epact, about morning:

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Disregarding this exact calculation, the vernacular Annals, the Form of Proclamation, and Lernutius’s work say that he was killed on 3 March, the sixth weekday after Ash Wednesday. Paulus Aemilius and others say on Ash Wednesday itself; but they need no refutation.]

[Note: [Col. 0957D] In place of the seven concurrents, the seven letters of the alphabet—F, E, D, C, B, A, G—were adopted. Therefore, with the fifth concurrent, the dominical letter was B. [Col. 0958D] See Petavius, *De doctrina temporum*, book 6, chapter 28.]

While the pious count lay in prayer at Bruges in the church of St Donatian, formerly archbishop of Rheims, in order to hear the morning Mass, he was, out of the pious custom of his almsgiving, distributing gifts to the poor. His eyes were fixed upon the reading of the psalms and his right hand was extended for the giving of alms. For his chaplain, who performed this office, had placed many coins before the count, which he distributed to the poor in the course of prayer.

The service of the first hour had also ended, and the responsory of the third hour had ended, when the *Pater noster* was prayed. As the count, according to his custom, prayed attentively and aloud while reading, then at last—after all their counsels, oaths, and mutual assurances—the murderers and most wicked traitors left the count, devoutly praying and giving alms, prostrate in humble supplication before the divine majesty, pierced by swords, repeatedly transfixed, and dead. Thus, washed from sins by streams of his own blood [Col. 0958A] and having completed life’s course in good works, God granted the count the palm of martyrs.

At the final moment of life and death, amid all the blows and sword-strokes, he turned as best he could his face and his royal hands toward heaven. Thus he surrendered his spirit to the Lord of all and offered himself to God as a morning sacrifice.
