The bloodied body of so great a man and prince lay alone, without the veneration of his followers or the due reverence of his servants. Therefore all who heard the outcome of his death followed that mournful funeral with tears and, lamenting, commended to God so great a prince who had met his end in martyrdom.

26. They also killed the castellan of Bruges, first wounding him to death, then dragging him shamefully by the feet from the upper chamber [Col. 0958B] to which both he and the count had gone up, and dismembering him with swords outside at the doors of the church. Yet this castellan had confessed his sins to the priests of that church and had received the body and blood of Christ according to Christian custom.

For immediately after the count had been killed, those swordsmen, leaving the count’s body and bringing this castellan back to death in the upper chamber, rushed out against those enemies from the count’s court who were present, in order to kill them as they wandered in the castle, as they pleased. They pursued into the count’s house a certain knight Henry, whom Borsiard suspected in the matter of the death of his brother Robert. Henry fell at the feet of the castellan Haket, who had himself gone up with his men into that same house to hold it. Haket received Henry and, together with him, Walter of Lokeren’s brother, and preserved them from their assailants.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] There is no mention of Haket in the said Annals and other accounts; Lambert, Borsiard’s father—already dead—is substituted in his place.]

27. At that same moment, the two sons of the castellan of Bruges were betrayed to the same swordsmen, while they were confessing their sins to priests in the upper chamber of the church. The knighthood of these sons and their conduct alike were well commended by all. They were called Walter and Giselbert: brothers by birth, equals in knighthood, worthy in the nobility of their handsome appearance to be loved by all who knew them.

When they heard at once of the slaughter of the count and their father, they tried to flee. But, at the Sands, at the exit from the suburb, the most wicked traitors rode out after them in pursuit.

[Note: [Col. 0958D] The place called the Sands is now commonly called the Friday Market.]

One brother, named Eric, was thrown from the horse on which he was fleeing by a wicked knight, one of those who had betrayed the count; once thrown down, he was killed together with the pursuers. The other brother, springing from the doorway of his lodging to escape, was likewise met and pierced through with swords. One of our citizens, Lambert Berakin by name, cut him down as he fell with his axe, as though he were a piece of wood [Col. 0959A]. Thus they sent those slain brothers to the holy blessedness which is in the supercelestial life.

28. Moreover, they pursued for one league the fleeing Riquard of Woldman, a powerful man of that town, [Note: [Col. 0959D] Woldman, or Woman, a village near Diksmuide.] whose daughter a nephew of Thancmar had married, against whom the provost and his nephews had until then carried on disputes and seditions. He had gone up with his knights to the count’s court, as had many princes who that day were preparing to go to court.

Frustrated in this pursuit, the traitors returned as far as the castle, into which the clergy and people of our place had flocked and wandered about, stunned by the turn of events. Those who had formerly stood in the count’s friendship while he lived feared without doubt and for the time being hid themselves, withdrawing from the sight of those traitors. Those who depended upon the count’s friendship from his court quickly turned to flight and escaped while the people were in tumult.

Gervasius, the count’s chamberlain, whom the right hand of God armed first to avenge the death of his lord, fled on horseback toward his Flemish kinsmen. A certain John, a servant of the count who was accustomed to guard his chamber and whom the count had loved above his servants, fled from morning on horseback by back ways until noon. At noon he reached Ypres and published there the death of the count and his men.

At that time merchants from all the kingdoms around Flanders had gathered at Ypres for the feast of the Chair of St Peter, when the universal market and fair were held. They conducted business in security under the peace and protection of the most pious count. At the same time merchants had come down from the kingdom of the Lombards to that same fair. From them the count had bought a silver *kanna* for twenty-one marks, wonderfully wrought, which deceived those viewing it concerning the drink it contained.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] *Kanna*, a word very familiar to Flemings and Germans, is the same as the Latin and Greek *cantharus*, a drinking-cup; below, no. 100, it is called a silver wine-vessel.]

When the report struck all those gathered for the fair from their various places, they packed their belongings and fled by day and night, carrying with them the disgrace of our land and spreading it everywhere.

29. Therefore every man who had heard even the report of him mourned that count of peace and all honor. But in our castle, where our lord and most pious father Charles lay slain, no one dared openly mourn the outcome of his death. Looking upon their own lord as though he were unknown, seeing their own father as though he were a stranger, they restrained their grief and sighs without tears. Yet they bore those griefs all the more heavily within because they did not dare to seek relief in tears and wailing.

For the provost’s nephews and that most criminal of men, Borsiard, with his accomplices, had returned to the castle immediately after their enemies’ flight and sought Walter of Lokeren, whom both he and his soldiers hated most fiercely. For Walter had been of the count’s counsel and had injured them in every way, having urged the count to reduce to slavery the entire kindred of the provost.

Walter himself, distressed by fear, had hidden in the organ loft—that is, in a certain dwelling for the church’s organs—in the same upper chamber in which the count lay slain. He had remained there from the time when the count was being killed until those wicked men returned to the castle about noon after putting their enemies to flight.

They burst through the doors into the church and, running about with naked swords still bloody, with great shouting and clatter of arms, searched around the chests and stalls of the brothers of the church, crying Walter’s name aloud. They found the castellan of Bruges, whom they had wounded to death in the upper chamber, still breathing. Dragging him by the feet, they finally killed him at the church doors.

While he was still breathing in the upper chamber, an abbess of Auriniacum had received his ring from him so that she might bring it to his wife as a sign of his death and as a token of all that he had instructed the abbess to convey to his wife and children. He himself did not know of their death until after his own.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] The monastery of Auriniacum in western Flanders is mentioned again at no. 66.]

30. Meanwhile Walter of Lokeren was sought both within and outside the church. One of the church guards had hidden him, and Walter had left his cloak with him. But from the place where he lay hidden, when he heard the clamor of arms and heard himself called by name, confused by the terror of death and thinking he might be more safely preserved in the church, he ran out. Leaping down from the high vault [Col. 0960C] of the schoolrooms, he fled through the midst of his enemies as far as beneath the choir of the church, crying loudly and piteously to God and the saints.

That wretched Borsiard and Isaac pursued him with their own hands—Isaac, at once servant, chamberlain, and man of Count Charles—raging in the holy place with swords drawn and horribly bloodied. They were indeed exceedingly furious and fierce of face, large in stature, grim, and such that no one could look upon them without terror.

Borsiard seized Walter by the hair of his head and, raising his sword, stretched himself out to strike him. He wished to delay this not for an instant, because he held in his hands the enemy for whom he had so desired. Yet, through the intervention of the clergy, he postponed Walter’s death until he could lead him outside the church as he had seized him.

The captive, certain of death, went crying, “Have mercy upon me, O God.” They replied, “We must repay you with such mercy as you have deserved from us.” After thrusting him away from themselves and leading him out into the castle court, they cast him to their servants to be killed. The servants put him to death as swiftly as possible, burying him beneath swords, clubs, nails, and stones.

[Note: [Col. 0960D] This is the foundation for the fabrication of others that he had killed twenty-five senators or ministers of the prince with his own hand; we have given Lernutius’s words above.]

31. Meanwhile, returning to the sanctuary around the altar, they searched whether anyone was hiding there whom they had adjudged to be killed [Col. 0961A], and they sent servants in to search it.

In the first sanctuary, Baldwin the chaplain and priest, and Godebert, the count’s clerk, were hiding beside the altar. Distressed by fear alone, they remained there, relying upon the altar. In the second sanctuary, Odger the clerk and the younger Fromold, notary and a member of Count Charles’s court more intimate with him than the rest—and therefore more suspected by the provost and his nephews—had taken refuge; Arnold, the count’s chamberlain, hid with them.

Odger and Arnold had covered themselves under a single carpet, while Fromold made himself a hiding-place beneath bundles of palm branches. Thus they waited for death. The servants who had been sent in searched and turned over every curtain, cloak, book, carpet, and the palms [Col. 0961B] which the brothers yearly carried on Palm Sunday. They first found Odger and Arnold. They had earlier found Eustace the clerk, Walter of Lokeren’s brother, sitting with Baldwin and Godebert, without knowing who he was. Those who were found promised the servants searching them that they would later give them money if they concealed them.

32. When the servants had at last returned to the choir to Borsiard, Isaac, and the others, those who had been sent in adjured them to report whether they had found anyone. Once the disclosure was made, Isaac was seized by sudden and violent rage against the younger Fromold, so that he swore by God and the saints that Fromold’s life could not be redeemed by an amount of gold as great as the church itself.

He turned the rage of all against Fromold, crying that no one had more maliciously spoken against the provost and his nephews to the count. Isaac immediately burst through the doors, seized Fromold at close quarters, and prepared to lead him away.

When Fromold saw him, he did not believe that Isaac had come to seize him but that he would redeem him from death. He said: “My friend Isaac, I beseech you by the friendship that has existed between us until now: preserve my life, and consider my children—your nephews—whose welfare I have preserved through the count, lest, if I am killed, they become without a protector.”

Isaac replied: “You shall receive the pardon which you have earned by maligning us before the count.”

Meanwhile a certain priest came apart to Fromold, advising him to confess his sins to God and to him. After he had done so, despairing of life, Fromold drew a gold ring from his finger and sent it through the priest to his daughter. Meanwhile Isaac consulted with Borsiard about what he should do: whether to kill him there, or spare his life for the time being until they had extorted from him the whole treasury of the count, together with that from Arnold the chamberlain, whom they held captive before them.

33. Meanwhile the canons of that place ran to the uncle of the younger Fromold, urging him to approach the provost for his nephew’s life. They had seen him placed in the very act of death, and Isaac had sworn to kill him. The old man hastened up with the brothers of the church to the provost in his house, fell at his feet, and begged and implored [Col. 0962A] him to protect his nephew’s life.

At last the provost sent a messenger to forbid his nephews from harming the younger Fromold. But when they heard the messenger, they sent word back that this could not be done, even if he himself were present. When he heard the report, the old man fell again at the provost’s knees, demanding that he himself go down to save Fromold.

The provost went, indeed, not with a quick pace but with an exceedingly slow one, as a man who cared little for someone he regarded as highly suspect. At length he reached the sanctuary, in which nothing holy but everything perverse was being done. At the request of the clergy, he took under his protection all those held captive there, but on this condition: that when Isaac and his nephews demanded the persons entrusted to him, the provost would return those captives.

34. [Col. 0962B] The provost therefore returned and brought those entrusted to his protection into the chamber of his house, keeping them under most careful guard. He said to Fromold, whom he had taken away captive: “Know, Fromold, that at the coming Easter you will not possess my provostship, as you hoped. Nor had I deserved this from you, that you should speak against me in this manner.” Fromold swore that he had acted innocently.

Nevertheless, no one in the count’s court had been so intimate with him while he lived, nor so dear to him, as the aforesaid Fromold. For after its burning, Fromold had rebuilt from the ground up the house with royal construction, in a better and more fitting design than it had ever possessed before. In comparison with it, no house in the world was reckoned better or more useful.

Thus, while they were held imprisoned, shut inside and locked up, they at least had place and time to mourn the pious count: not their lord, but their father; in familiar intercourse their equal; merciful, humble, gentle, beneficial to rich and poor in the realm alike. Those captives could not speak to one another for grief, except in sighs and sobs drawn from the deep sadness of their minds.

Miserable was the crime in which servants were not permitted to die with their lord and father, but had to endure the greater misery of living after him. With him they would have passed more nobly from this world, in an excellent and most honorable death before God and men, than they could live in grief at their lord’s death and behold traitors flourish under another count’s rule—God forbid.

While they were overwhelmed in this faintness of spirit, no friend dared even secretly approach them to offer words of comfort. Indeed, if anyone did approach, he was deprived of life.

## CHAPTER V. The burial of Blessed Charles and others. The miracle of a lame man healed. The plundering of goods.

35. Meanwhile, the bodies of those killed—namely the castellan and Walter of Lokeren—were carried from the castle. The castellan and his beloved sons were placed together on ships and conveyed to their own homes and castles.

The provost walked about in his house with his canons, excusing himself as far as he could in words, saying that he had known nothing beforehand of this betrayal. That same day the traitors made an expedition against their enemies, namely Thancmar and his followers at Straten, [Col. 0963A] and found their settlements empty and their courts deserted.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Straten and its lineage were discussed above, §4.]

For when they heard of the crime committed in the count’s death, they feared greatly for themselves because they had lost their defender. If they should perhaps be shut in and pressed by siege from the traitors, they thought, no helper would remain for them, since they had finally learned that all the peers of the realm had consented to the betrayal. They believed that much graver dangers threatened in the future both themselves and the whole kingdom. Caring nothing for their possessions, but considering only whether they might preserve their lives, they fled to safer places.

Then the traitors invaded both Thancmar’s settlement and his court, plundering all arms and household goods within, together with a great booty of livestock and clothing belonging to the peasants of that village. Having thus plundered throughout the whole day, they returned in the evening.

Nor did these men alone carry out plundering in our vicinity. Many others who had known beforehand of the betrayal hurried at once to the routes of the merchants going to the fair held at Ypres and robbed them together with their goods. When he heard of the murderous betrayal, William of Ypres believed that he would henceforth obtain the county. He compelled all merchants, from whatever place they came, whom he could seize at the fair to swear security and fealty to him and his men. Otherwise he did not permit them to leave him, but held them captive until they had performed all things and given him their guarantees. He did all this by the counsel of the provost and the latter’s traitorous nephews.

36. [Col. 0963C] Already, as that same day declined toward evening, by the common counsel of the provost, his nephews, and their accomplices, they demanded from the younger Fromold, whom they held captive, the keys to the count’s treasury. Likewise, they forcibly extorted all the keys of the house and of the chests and coffers in it. Borsiard, Castellan Haket, and Walter, son of Lambert of Reddenburch, took these into their power.

37. Nothing meanwhile was done concerning the body of the count—though the priests had secretly made the commendation of his soul at the time when they also gave Christ’s communion to his castellan—because the body still lay bloody and alone in the very position in which he had been killed.

The brothers of the church therefore carefully considered what they should do with it and what rites they should prepare for him, since no one dared, even secretly, to perform the divine office in the same church in which so great a slaughter and crime was known to have taken place. At last, having received permission from the provost and with the brethren’s consent, the elder Fromold wrapped the noble body in linen, placed it on a bier in the middle [Col. 0964A] of the choir with due veneration, set four candles beside it according to our custom, and afterward attended carefully to all else.

Women alone sat around that funeral, keeping watch with pious lamentation throughout that day and the following night. Meanwhile the traitors took counsel with the provost and their castellan by what stratagem the count’s body might be removed, lest a body buried in their presence should bring them everlasting reproach. Having craftily devised their plan, they sent to Ghent for the abbot, that he might take the count’s body away from our place and bury it after its removal to Ghent.

Thus that day, full of grief and miseries, came to its close: the day on which the source of all the evil and disturbance that had arisen, and would arise in greatest measure, among the kingdoms around us had emerged.

[Col. 0964B] 38. On the following night the provost ordered the church to be secured on every side with arms and watches—the upper chamber and the tower of the church—so that, should an attack by the townspeople occur, he and his men might take refuge in those places. That night, at the provost’s command, armed soldiers entered the upper chamber of the church, guarding the tower and its exits with continual watches, fearing an assault and attack by the citizens against them on the following day and thereafter. On the Sunday after the count’s death, the provost sent greetings to our bishop Simon of the see of Noyon.

The bearer of the letter was Ralph, a monk of St. Trudo, in which letter he begged the bishop to reconcile to God the church in which the count, betrayed without his knowledge, lay.

> [Note: [Col. 0963D] The monastery of St. Trudo was formerly in the village of Oedeghem, where religious women now reside; from there it was transferred to the city, to a place called Quercetum, where an abbey of regular canons still stands. In book 1, chapter 51, of his *Belgian Donations*, Miraeus publishes a letter of donation made to this monastery in 1130 by Count Theodoric. St. Trudo, patron of this place [Col. 0964D], is commemorated on 23 November.]

He also offered grounds for his defense, by which he might canonically prove his innocence before all clergy and people. Thus that messenger was captured and thrown from his mount, and did not reach the bishop. Hearing this, the provost was greatly afraid for himself.

On Wednesday and Thursday, the provost sent through a certain youth to Walter of Frorerdest, adjuring him by the faith which he had pledged to the provost and his nephews to hurry to his aid with all his strength; and he sent him four hundred marks of silver. But Walter, having received the money, pretended that he would come, and never came, except to harm him and his nephews.

> [Note: [Col. 0964D] Bruges manuscript: *Forerdeslo*. It appears to be Ulaerslo, near Diksmuide.]

But Bishop Simon, who was the uterine brother of the wife of Count Charles, placed the church of Bruges castle under interdict and struck those sacrilegious traitors with the sword of anathema. He altogether forbade any of the faithful to join their conspiracy or assist them; and, if anyone did so, he condemned under anathema all their helpers in the aforesaid evil.

> [Note: [Col. 0964D] A brother by the same mother, as explained above.]

39. On Thursday, the fifth day before the Nones of March, the abbot for whom they had sent to Ghent arrived at dawn in the castle, having ridden all night, and demanded from the provost and his nephews the count’s body, as they had promised him.

> [Note: [Col. 0964D] Lernutius, on the authority of his own reports, asserts that the abbot of St. Peter’s, or Blandinium, together with other nobles, transferred the body to the market-place, to the church of St. Christopher, and buried it; then besieged the traitors.]

The provost had gone out and, having summoned the castellan and his nephews who had betrayed the count, was taking counsel with them as to how the abbot might remove the body without disturbance. At once the poor, who were awaiting alms to be distributed by the provost for the count’s soul—having understood the plan sooner, since apart from the poor no citizens wished to go with them or associate with them any longer—began to spread abroad that the abbot had come by trickery and in concert with the traitors in order to carry away the funeral bier.

He had caused a bier to be prepared, upon which the body was to be placed and transported by horses. Meanwhile the poor followed the provost wherever he went, crying: “Lord, may it never happen that the earthly remains of our father and so glorious a martyr are removed from our place [Col. 0965B]. For if this happens, this place and its building will henceforth be destroyed without mercy. Yet the enemies and persecutors who will come upon this castle will have some pity and compassion, so as not utterly to destroy the church in which the body of the blessed count has been reverently buried.”

A great rumor about removal of the body spread among the citizens. The provost and that abbot hurried, before the report was stirred up in the city, and he had the new and freshly made bier brought as far as the door of the church, for the removal of the corpse. Soldiers had entered to lift the bier standing in the middle of the choir, together with the count, and transfer it to the other bier standing at the door.

[Col. 0965C] 40. Then the canons of that church rushed up and forcibly set back the bier in the choir, saying that they first wished to hear from the provost why he had ordered this. They went out into the castle, where the provost and his nephews stood; and with them was a very great crowd of citizens who had heard the report that the body was to be taken away. One of the elders spoke before all the people:

“Lord Provost, if you wished to act justly, you would not, without the consent and counsel of the brethren, have given away so precious a martyr, so great a ruler of the realm, so great a treasure of our church—him whom divine mercy and dispensation granted to us as a martyr. There is therefore no reason why he should be taken from us, among whom he was chiefly raised and lived, and among whom, by God’s ordinance, he was betrayed for righteousness’ sake. Indeed, if he is removed, we fear the destruction [Col. 0965D] both of this place and of the church. Through his intercession God will spare us and have mercy upon us; lest perhaps, if he is taken from us, God avenge without any mercy the betrayal committed among us.”

But the provost and the traitors, turned to anger, ordered the body to be taken up. With a great cry, therefore, the brethren of the church rushed to the doors of the church, shouting that, so long as they lived, they would not permit the body of the most pious Count Charles and martyr to be taken away; rather, they would die there than allow its removal. Then indeed one might have seen clerics armed with boards, benches, candlesticks, and every implement of the church with which they could resist. Instead of a trumpet they rang the bells, and thus summoned all the citizens of the place. When these understood what was happening, they rushed up armed, with swords drawn, and surrounded the count’s bier [Col. 0966A], ready to resist if anyone attempted to remove it.

41. While turmoil arose both inside and outside the church, divine mercy chose to calm its children from madness and the tumult of arms. For weak and lame persons lay beneath the bier; and amid the very tumult a lame man whose foot was joined to his buttock began to cry out and bless God, who, for the merits of the pious count, had restored to him in the sight of all present the natural power of walking. The report of this miracle therefore calmed everyone.

But the provost, castellan, and those traitors had gone up into the count’s house, fearing the disturbance; and they sent word to the citizens that they should do nothing concerning removal of the body against their will. That abbot therefore returned, glad to have escaped. The provost [Col. 0966B], however, went back and forth, consulting with the traitors and arranging what they should do according to the outcome of events.

Immediately the brethren of the church sought craftsmen and workmen who knew, in the urgency and necessity of the moment, how to construct a burial vault for the count in the place where he had received the palm of martyrdom. They hastened to do this by every means devised for the purpose, lest through some trick the body, still unburied and therefore all the easier to remove, should be stolen from them. Thus that day, full of disturbance and deceit concerning the removal of the sorrowful corpse, came to an end.

42. On Friday, the fourth day before the Nones of the same month, the canons and the provost gathered in the church of St. Peter outside the walls to perform the customary funeral rites; and, the tomb now prepared, the Mass of the faithful departed for the soul of the pious count was celebrated there. Very few besides the canons made offerings; for no one from the household offered except Baldwin the chaplain, Odger the Younger, and Godebert, clerics of the count.

Afterward the provost and the brethren returned to the church of Blessed Donatian, where the corpse lay. When the poor had been admitted into the church, the elder Fromold distributed coins, though through the hands of the provost, to all needy persons who wished to receive them, for the salvation of the soul of Charles, the pious count. The elder Fromold did this not without tears; indeed, he expended more tears of compassion than coins. For there was a very great gathering of poor persons who received alms.

When the distribution of alms was completed, [Col. 0966D] the noble body was carried into the upper chamber. The provost, standing nearby beside the tomb, at last wept for the count, whom the guidance of reason made him recognize as father of the whole region of Flanders. He mourned him as the man whom, with an obstinate mind, he had disdained to recognize. The count was enclosed in a tomb constructed for the necessity of that time; and, though not as befitted him, nevertheless, as subsequent work and craftsmanship allowed, he was laid beneath and enclosed.

Surely his soul, purified by the sufferings of martyrdom, possesses the rewards of his merits with Him who ordained for him in this manner to die to the world and to live in the heavenly county with God Himself and the Lord—to whom belong dominion, praise, honor, and glory through ages without end. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI. The growing insolence of the traitors begins to be checked by Gervase, the count’s chamberlain.

[Col. 0967A]

43. On Saturday, the third day before the Nones of March, Fromold the Younger was released from captivity about the evening of that day. This was accomplished only through the very great efforts of his intercessors with the provost and his nephews. At last they released him on this condition: within the next eight days after his departure from imprisonment, he must either be reconciled to the villains into whose hands he had fallen, or else renounce his country and thereafter live in exile.

He went down to his house with his friends and household, who had been worn beyond words by grief and fear of death, both for him and for themselves. Before he was captured, his servants had not dared go anywhere, without believing that they would immediately be pursued because they belonged to his household. He therefore feasted with his friends and household, being certain that he would renounce his country rather than return to the captivity of the traitors who had betrayed their lord, who loved them above others and whom he himself almost loved more than himself. Before ever making peace with them, he would choose perpetual exile. For it is exceedingly hard, and contrary to nature, for a man to be at peace with his enemy, since every creature, if it can, flees from what is hostile to it.

After he had supped, he made arrangements for his household and possessions; and, having taken leave of each person, he distributed grain, cheeses, and meat to his servants for their sustenance for a time. He hoped that, by God’s ordering, he would yet joyfully and securely possess all the things which [Col. 0967C] he was now leaving from necessity and out of love for the most pious count. He departed with his father-in-law beyond the castle and the suburb in which he had hitherto lived. His friends followed him as far as they were permitted, commending him to God with lamentation and tears.

At the same time, the aforesaid traitors—most obstinate in every wickedness—made a raid against Thancmar and his men, their enemies. There they suffered a most disgraceful repulse and returned to the castle in fear and shame.

44. On the Sunday immediately before the Nones of the first month, Godescale Thaihals came from Ypres as messenger to the provost at Bruges, with these words: “My lord and your intimate friend, William of Ypres, sends you greetings and friendship, and openly promises you and yours the readiest assistance in all things, insofar as lies in his power.”

> [Note: [Col. 0967D] In the vernacular annals and in the proclamation formula, he alone, or almost alone, acted by his own authority against the traitors; how rightly he did so is clear from this passage and what follows.]

But the rest, which it was shameful to report publicly, after all had applauded him, he revealed to the provost, William of Wervik, Borsiard, and the few others whom they had admitted with them into the chamber. From then on the whole household placed confidence in William with joy, to such an extent that they called and accepted him as count.

In the secrecy of this message, the wise and those who drew inferences marked William with the stigma of treachery: he had greeted the traitors of our place when their crime was fully ripe, and had offered them, by pledge, writing, and assurance, the promptest aid of all his power. When the messenger returned, the merchants of Flanders, from whatever place they had assembled at the market in Ypres, were seized and compelled to give William faith, security, and homage, and thus accept him as their count. This was done by the counsel of the provost and his party, hoping that they had therefore betrayed the pious Count Charles with impunity.

> [Note: [Col. 0967D] That is, with impunity.]

Indeed, William would have been raised to the countship at that time if he had immediately come down to Bruges to avenge his lord and kinsman, the betrayed count. But because matters had not thus been ordained by the Lord, both the other princes and the people of the land had to follow the divine ordering and become united in avenging the death of the most pious count.

Moreover, inhabitants of the suburb of our place openly entered the counsels of those lords—the provost, that is, the castellan, and his wicked nephews—and investigated the secrets of their plans, so that, by cleverly discovering their deceits and schemes, they might thereafter be more cautious. At that time the provost and his associates did not cease to solicit and entrap everyone, so that they might favor them, by giving and promising many things. For he told William that he would give him the county; and therefore he urged him to receive homage and assurances from all the Flemings whom he could compel by force or price [Col. 0968C]. The provost sent word to the men of Furnes who had remained in his friendship that they should make themselves secure men and vassals of William.

45. He also sent letters to the bishop of Noyon, offering his defense that he had been privy to nothing in counsel or deed concerning the betrayal of the count. He further declared that, with the utmost affection, he would give counsel and aid to the children of the church—that is, to himself and his canons—by reconciling the churches and by coming swiftly in person, with the authority of his episcopal office, for the celebration of the divine services. He sent letters in the same terms to John, bishop of Thérouanne.

He ordered Robert of Kerseca, who had married the provost’s niece, to fortify his house and lands as strongly as possible [Col. 0968D], until he had established William of Ypres as count.

> [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Kerseka* is also read as *Kaseka*. What if it is Kemseca in the territory of Waas? Hugh of Kemseca, lord of this place, is mentioned in a letter of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders, dated 1166, in Sanderus’s work on Waas. Someone has suggested that perhaps *Kacskercka*, or *Kacsikinskercka*, should be read: the name of a settlement near Diksmuide, whose natural situation was suited to every kind of fortification.]

This Robert had been a free knight before marrying the provost’s niece; but after he had held her for a year, he belonged to the count in servile condition according to the law of the counts of Flanders. Hence there had arisen a most destructive conflict between the pious Count Charles and the provost and his adherents concerning servitude and freedom.

The provost also sent for those Flemings who lived near the sea and were his neighbors [Col. 0969A], ordering them to come with their forces to aid him and his nephews, should anyone in the realm and county rise up to take vengeance.

46. He sternly commanded our citizens to enclose the places of the suburb with ditches and fences, so that they might defend themselves against anyone whatsoever. At the same time, the citizens did enclose the suburb, but with a purpose wholly different from that advised and commanded to them, as afterward became apparent. Thus, under the leadership of the castellan, the citizens plundered outside the suburb the fences and timber of the murdered count and of Fromold the Younger, who, deprived of his property, was awaiting exile; they also took everything else that appeared useful for making a fence. They built towers, battlements, and exits [Col. 0969B] for the common defense against enemies.

All, clergy as well as people, hastened to complete this work. There was consequently no rest: they kept watch at night and worked by day, until the enclosure of the suburb was completed and guards were appointed at every gate, tower, and battlement, so that no one might go out unless known, and no one be admitted unless a citizen.

47. On Monday, the Nones of March, God drew the swords of divine vengeance against the enemies of His church, and moved the heart of a certain knight, Gervase, to carry out vengeance more fiercely and swiftly than had then been expected. Thus, gathering his wrath, that knight raged against those criminals with all the might of his forces. With a fierce infantry host, a circle of knights, and a dense array of weapons, he surrounded himself against the enemies of God. Rushing forward, he besieged a stronghold named Ravenschot, which had been very strongly fortified in defense of the traitors.

> [Note: [Col. 0969D] This is Ravenscot in the district of Bruges, or Franconate, near the river Lieve, opposite Eeklo. Yet this place appears to have been nearer to Bruges and to have ceased to exist after being destroyed by fire and arms.]

The place was invincible and inaccessible both because of the difficulty of its situation and because of its fortifications. Gervase took great spoil in livestock from that castle and its neighbors. For at that time all who belonged to those criminals lived in security, believing that no one in the whole world either wished or could rise against their lords, because those wretches had committed so audacious a crime against their lord the count. God had blinded them, so that they possessed neither reason nor counsel; but, cast headlong into every evil, drunken with wrath and madness, they wandered in fear and terror—both those who had betrayed the count and all who remained in their aid.

Since they believed themselves secure and regarded everyone in the realm either as beneath them or as their friend [Col. 0970A], they had not guarded against an attack upon themselves. Therefore, when Gervase made his attack at Ravenschot, he took enormous plunder. But those who were besieged, caught by the unexpected attack, were deeply astonished, especially because they were so few to defend themselves against so many thousands. Despairing of their lives, they immediately surrendered to Gervase on condition that they might depart with their lives and limbs safe.

Once they had been expelled, the horsemen and foot soldiers who had besieged the stronghold rushed in and laid waste everything they found inside. Those who had surrendered during the siege—that is, the men of the traitors—fled by night as far as our place, reporting the event to the provost and his men. From then on they were continually afraid [Col. 0970B], their frame of mind changing from the pride and arrogance with which, until that time, they had been fierce, excessive, and without humility.

Robert the Younger, whose stronghold was soon to be destroyed by fire and sword, tried with a few men to make a sortie against the besiegers; but when he learned of so great a multitude, he abandoned the attack. It would take too long to relate the fear and grief suffered by those traitors and, conversely, the joy in which all the rest apart from them exulted, because with one and the same understanding they perceived that God Himself had begun vengeance on every side.

48. On Tuesday, the eighth day before the Ides of March, the stronghold of Ravenschot was burned and destroyed by fire and arms; and near Bruges the house of Wulfric Cnop, brother of the provost, who had sworn to the count’s death, was burned.

> [Note: [Col. 0970D] No mention of this Wulfric Cnop occurs either in the cited Annals or in the proclamation formula.]

Gervase therefore advanced with his forces toward the castle in which the traitors had fortified themselves. He made circuits and raids, forestalling their routes around the suburb of the castle. When our burgesses heard that God had begun vengeance so swiftly, they rejoiced in conscience alone; they never dared openly to congratulate the avengers, because the traitors still confidently and powerfully came and went among them. Privately, however, they gave thanks to God, who in the place of horror and confusion deigned to look again with eyes of mercy upon His faithful people, and who was hastening to destroy those most wicked murderers who had hitherto scourged the people of the Lord by plunder, fires, wounds, and every kind of disturbance.

They sent secret messengers to Gervase and his men, making an agreement of mutual faith, friendship, and most faithful security. Moreover, they swore to avenge their count, and to admit Gervase’s army among them inside the suburb on the following day, receiving them as brothers within their fortifications. When Gervase and his men heard the embassy, I cannot express with what greater joy and more righteous spirit they received the messengers’ words, knowing that whatever they did in vengeance had been ordered by God. Gervase and his men swore with the messengers of our citizens [Col. 0971A] and entered into the same oaths of faith and security, for the avenging of their lord and the most just count of our land. All this was hidden from those traitors and from most of our citizens, except a few wiser people of the place, who privately and by night formed this counsel, salutary for all.

## CHAPTER VII. The siege of Bruges castle begins. Military forces join. Punishment inflicted upon certain captured traitors.

49. On Wednesday, the seventh day before the Ides of March, when the eighth day of that blessed count had dawned—he who had passed from earthly things to the true octave—Gervase, by agreement with our citizens, was received inside the suburb [Col. 0971B], at the Sands, west of the castle. This was to be the greatest ruin for those traitors.

But before this, on that same day, he had terrified Borsiard, Robert the Younger, and their accomplices by the burning of houses. Seeing houses aflame in every direction, they had gone out from the castle to observe those who were setting the fires, in case they might perhaps attack them. On the eastern side of the castle, three taller houses were burning, their flames driven by gusting winds. Citizens, together with Borsiard and his soldiers, who did not know of the agreement made between the burgesses and Gervase, made sorties to watch; and the greater part of them, armed, went out with those villains. Isaac too, who while the pious Count Charles lived had been chamberlain and a member of the count’s counsel and household, and who was the head of the betrayal [Col. 0971C], rode out with his soldiers.

At last, when knights on both sides had drawn close to one another, the traitors, seeing that they could not withstand so large an army because they were very few, turned to flight. Their pursuers followed at full speed and drove them as fugitives back into the castle. When they had at last reached the suburb, Borsiard and his men paused for a little before the house of Desiderius, Isaac’s brother, seeking counsel as to what they should now do. Meanwhile Gervase, pursuing them violently, came to the gates of the suburb on its western side. There, having given and received assurances from the citizens, he burst in with a very strong force. The citizens still remained quietly in their houses, as was customary. It was toward evening [Col. 0971D], and many citizens had sat down to their meal, unaware of this action.

50. While those traitors were thus taking counsel and stood bewildered concerning their flight, they scarcely noticed their pursuers bursting through the streets, attacking them with spears and lances, arrows, and every weapon. Great tumult, the crash of arms, and the thunder of cries disturbed all the citizens, who rushed to arms and made ready. Some, wholly ignorant of the pact [Col. 0972A], prepared to defend the town and suburb against Gervase. Others, who knew what had happened, rushed with all their strength alongside Gervase and drove the fleeing traitors into the castle.

When the agreement, pledge, and oath between Gervase and the citizens had become known among the citizens, they then together rushed across the bridge of the castle against those who, on the side of the criminals, were resisting from the castle in battle. At another bridge, leading toward the provost’s house, there was a great conflict of fighting, in which men fought hand to hand with lances and swords. At a third bridge, on the eastern side of the castle and extending to the castle gates, a most violent engagement took place. Those inside, unable to endure the fierceness of battle, broke the bridge and shut the gates above themselves.

Wherever the citizens gained access to the men of the castle [Col. 0972B], the fighting was most fierce, until the latter could endure no longer. Since they had been intercepted and betrayed by the citizens, whether willing or unwilling, those wretches were driven back inside the castle; a great part of them were wounded, overwhelmed by fear and grief, and exhausted by the fatigue of battle.

51. Meanwhile, at the beginning of Gervase’s incursion into the suburb, Isaac fled from the place where they had been taking counsel and took refuge in his own rather strong house. Having crossed the bridge which led from the suburb to his house, he dismantled and broke it, lest anyone pursue him in flight.

At that time George, a knight and one of the foremost traitors, who had himself killed the count together with Borsiard, was captured. Desiderius the knight, brother of Isaac the traitor, threw him from his horse and cut off both his hands.

> [Note: [Col. 0971D] Desiderius is also praised by Walter; nevertheless, some stigma is laid upon him below, no. 73, in the words of Robert the Younger. At no. 137 he is said to have died on 17 December and to have been privy to the conspiracy.]

Although Desiderius was the brother of a traitor, he had not been privy to the betrayal. That most wretched George, his hands cut off, fled to a place where he hoped to hide; but he was immediately accused to a certain Walter, a knight of Gervase, and brought out. Sitting on horseback, that knight ordered a very fierce young swordsman to kill him. The man rushed upon George, struck him with his sword, and threw him to the ground; then, after casting him by the feet into a sewer, the swordsman forced him to drown as a deserved punishment for his evil.

A certain Robert, called Haket, a runner and servant of the castellan’s household, was also captured and killed in the middle of the market-place; he was dragged into the marshes [Col. 0972D]. Another utterly wicked servant of Borsiard, named Fromald, was likewise captured. He had fled and hidden between two mattresses, clothed in a woman’s surplice in order to disguise himself. Drawn out from there, he was led into the middle of the market-place. Before all onlookers he was hanged, transfixed with a pole through the hams and legs, his head hanging downward, so that his private parts faced toward the castle, to the disgrace and shame of those traitors, who stood besieged at the count’s gallery and battlements and watched this done for their own reproach.

> [Note: [Col. 0972D] A *lobium* is a projecting part of a building beyond a wall or partition, beneath the roof.]

Meanwhile they did not cease shooting arrows at one another, hurling stones, and casting missiles from the walls.

> [Note: [Col. 0973D] That is, to shoot, after the French expression *tirer*. So also in chapter 8, no. 61.]

52. At last, when day had ended, fear and watchfulness prevailed on both sides during the night; they laid snares for one another, in case anyone should steal away from the besieged to escape, or anyone should secretly slip over the walls to assist the besieged. Throughout the whole siege, therefore, both sides maintained watches and ambushes.

The besieged very often made assaults upon the besiegers on individual nights with most violent fighting, and the struggle was fiercer by night than by day. By day the besieged did not dare show themselves because of their shameful crime; they hoped somehow to remain concealed and escape, so that, if they did escape, no one might suspect them of the crime of betrayal. Therefore they fought the more fiercely at night, because they believed that, through the leaders of the siege who had assented to them, they might perhaps later emerge and easily clear themselves of the charge.

But the leaders cared nothing for what they promised the besieged or how many oaths they swore, provided only that they might extort from them the pious count’s money and treasure. They were right to take from the besieged the count’s treasure and many additional gifts, since no pledges and no oaths were to be observed toward men who, as most wicked servants, had betrayed their lawful and natural lord. And indeed, from their enemies they sought the saving observance of pledges and oaths that were owed them not at all—men who had brought death upon their lord and the father of the entire county.

More justly, therefore, those who had loved the count even in death, who had assembled for vengeance and there endured fear, watches, wounds, assaults, and all the adversities customarily suffered in a siege, should have obtained the castle, treasure, and comital possessions after their lord’s death than those most wicked traitors, who had destroyed both—the place and its wealth. The besiegers and besieged frequently discussed matters with one another in such terms. But in their replies the besieged offered only the excuse of the betrayal.

53. On Thursday, the sixth day before the Ides of March, the castellan of Ghent came with his forces to the siege, as did Iwan, brother of Baldwin of Aalst.

> [Note: [Col. 0973D] Siger, castellan of Ghent, subscribed the charters of donation of Blessed Charles.]

During the preceding night of that Thursday, Isaac—knowing and condemning himself as privy to the crime, for fear of death pressed upon him—fled with his sole squire. His wife, servants, maidservants, and entire household fled also; and wherever they could remain in so constricted a flight by night, they hid. They left their house, court, larger furnishings, and all other property which they had hitherto possessed freely and powerfully, abandoned and without protection, as plunder for their enemies [Col. 0974A].

On hearing this, early in the morning the castellan of Ghent and Iwan rushed in with a multitude from the siege, plundering everything they found useful to carry away. At last they put burning torches beneath the roofs and set fire to the houses, courts, and everything found there that could be consumed by fire.

> [Note: [Col. 0973D] Walter, no. 49, relates that Isaac’s house was burned by his own brother Desiderius, evidently aided by the knights summoned to protect it.]

All these things were destroyed with the greatest speed by the conflagration, the wind’s fanning, and the violence of the weather; and everyone bore witness in astonishment that no building and timber-work of such scale had suffered annihilation so swiftly.

54. On Friday, the fifth day before the Ides of March, Daniel, one of the peers of the realm, who before the betrayal of the count had been closely allied with the provost and his nephews, hastened to the siege. With him came Richard of Woldman, Theodoric, castellan of the town of Diksmuide, and Walter Butelgir, the count’s butler.

> [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Butelgir*: in Flemish *butelier*, in French *boutilier*, a word derived from *buto* or *button*. In Anastasius the Librarian: “Pope Leo III made a silver *button* with its basket.” Hence *butica* and *buticula*, as also *butellarius* and *buticularius*, terms used by Hincmar and others, signifying a steward, pantry-master, or cupbearer, as will shortly become clear.]

Each of these princes came with all his forces to avenge the death of the count and his lord. After all had assembled with our citizens, and after all the leaders in the siege had also been summoned, before they were permitted to enter the suburb they swore that they would inviolably preserve its places and possessions for the safety and benefit of our citizens. Then, with one mind and assault, they swore to attack, overcome, and, God willing, defeat the adversaries and most impious murderers; to spare none of the accused their lives; not to lead out or save the accused by any stratagem of their own; but to destroy them and proceed by the common judgment of the nobles, for the honor of the realm and the safety of its inhabitants [Col. 0974C]. This was confirmed, while preserving the property of the citizens, their own property, and the property of all who labored in the siege to avenge the count’s death.

55. On the fourth day before the Ides of March, Saturday, an order went forth from the princes that all who had taken their places in the siege should attack the castle on every side where they had access. About midday the knights armed themselves together with the citizens and went round, attacking the castle gates with fire. In this assault they burned the postern beside the provost’s house. But while they attacked the larger gates of the castle, having drawn up a dry heap of hay and straw and summoned a soldier to set the straw alight, those attacking were overwhelmed from inside the castle with stones, stakes, lances, and arrows. Thus countless men, struck down from the battlements as though by millstones, were wounded and crushed; scarcely escaping with their lives from beneath the vaulted gatehouse, where they had sheltered in order to tend the fires, they fled, leaving helmets and shields behind. Whoever was pursued by a stone cast down from above, however great his courage and strength, suffered a most grievous fall, so that he fell utterly prostrated and broken, dying and lifeless. In this attack one man-at-arms outside the walls, pierced through the heart by an arrow, died. There was great shouting and uproar on both sides, a most severe engagement; the clangour of weapons and crash of blows resounded in the higher hollow of the air. At length the battle continued into evening; and since those outside had gained nothing but death and injury, they withdrew from the walls and battlements of the castle. Gathering part of their multitude, they became anxious about the danger of the coming night. The besieged, however, were thereby increasingly encouraged, because they saw their assailants, afflicted by so many falls and wounds, driven back from the walls.

## Chapter VIII. The forces of the besiegers increased. The arrival of the Countess of Holland. Relics removed from the church. The castle fortified by the besieged.

[Col. 0975B]

56. On the third day before the Ides of March, Sunday, peace was outwardly observed on both sides. On the preceding day before the Ides of March, Monday, and on the following Tuesday, the burghers from Ghent assembled for the siege, together with a most eager crowd of plunderers from the neighbouring villages. For their castellan had commanded them to gather their strength and community, arm themselves, and make an attack upon the castle separately and on their own account, as men glorious in battle and skilled in fighting and overcoming the besieged.

When they heard that they were to make a separate assault in the siege, they gathered to themselves all archers, ingenious craftsmen, bold robbers, murderers, thieves, and every sort of man presumptuous enough for every crime of war. They loaded thirty wagons with weapons; men came running on foot and horseback, hoping that they would acquire vast wealth if perhaps the besieged surrendered to them. Their army was indeed powerful and innumerable. When they approached the gates of the suburb, they dared to enter violently; but the whole multitude of the siege force which met them inside opposed them face to face. Fighting would almost have broken out on every side, had not the wiser men restrained themselves in each line.

For, giving and receiving right hands, they bound themselves by faith and the oath of an oath, that they would join the siege with the same purpose, the same arms, and the same counsel, while preserving the place and possessions of our citizens; and that they would retain with themselves only those native men who were shrewd in battle, sending the others back behind them. Thus those men of Ghent entered with a very great multitude and filled the ground around the castle. Then their workmen and craftsmen prepared ladders by which they might scale the walls. At the same time Razo Butelgir returned from Saint-Gilles and came, most justly grieving over the death of his lord the count, with his force to the siege.

> [Note: Col. 0975D] This is Razo of Gavere, who subscribed to many charters of Blessed Charles and of the succeeding counts, sometimes also as Razo the *butellarius* (“cup-bearer” or “butler”) and Razo the *pincerna* (“cup-bearer”). Gavere lies in the district of Aalst.

57. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, Wednesday, at *cum sanctificatus* [the Mass incipit; reading uncertain], on the night of Saint Gertrude, the Countess of Holland arrived at the siege with her son and a great multitude accompanying her. She hoped that all the princes of the siege would choose her son as count, because our citizens and many of the princes had urged this upon her. The countess enjoyed great favour with them, and laboured to turn the minds of all the nobles toward friendship with herself by giving and promising many things.

> [Note: Col. 0975D] This is the beginning of the Mass on Wednesday after the fourth Sunday of Lent, which Wednesday fell that year in the night, as is said here, or on the vigil of Saint Gertrude, that is, 16 March.

On that day Froolsus and Baldwin of Somerenghem pretended that they had come from William of Ypres. They announced to the princes of the siege that the king of France had granted the county to William of Ypres, and by this made anxious all those who had promised to choose the son of the aforesaid countess. Thus those pretended knights cunningly proclaimed such a falsehood as truth, in order by that stratagem to delay the assent of the princes of the siege to receive the son of the aforesaid countess as count. Hearing this, the princes were indignant at the possibility that it might be true: that William of Ypres had been endowed with the county by the king. They therefore swore together and bound themselves by faith that, while he remained count of Flanders, they would never serve in arms under him; for he was suspected by all and marked as implicated in the betrayal of the lord count.

> [Note: Col. 0976D] This is Petronilla, daughter of the duke of Saxony, married to Floris II, Count of Holland, surnamed “the Fat.” When he died in the flower of his age in 1122, she, as widow, vigorously administered—beyond what was expected of her sex—the government of the county entrusted to her, as guardian for her son Dirk VI. After her death she was honourably buried in 1144 in the monastery of Rijnsburg which she had built. Meyer says nothing of this countess’s arrival, for which error he is reproved by Scriverius.

58. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, Thursday, the canons of Saint Donatian climbed the walls on ladders on the southern side of the castle. From that side they sent out their chests and reliquaries of saints and relics, with the permission and consent of the princes, and transferred to the church of Blessed Christopher, situated in the middle of the marketplace, the curtains, hangings, tapestries, mantled and silk copes, sacred vestments, heaps of books, church utensils, and all else belonging to the church.

The provost allowed, through the intervention of the elder Fromold, the removal of the written accounts and registers of the count’s revenues, which he had kept for himself and his William of Ypres, because he saw that his fortune had wholly changed; just as, though unwillingly, he permitted all the chests of saints and the furnishings of the church to be carried away. Thus the church of Saint Donatian was at last left alone and deserted to the traitors, who made of it their brothel, latrines, kitchens, and ovens, and who, being unclean, did all unclean things.

The most pious Count Charles, servant of God, still lay alone in the place where he had received martyrdom, left to his traitors. Therefore, after everything permitted to be removed had been carried out, the canons, weeping and without the customary reverence, bore the relics of the saints amid grief, sighs, and lamentation. No one besides the clergy and a few persons carrying the sacred things was allowed near the walls of the church. Armed men stood on both sides, guarding themselves; yet amid so many weapons they venerated the saints, offering peace and safe passage to those bearing them.

This was a strange and very unusual procession. Algerus, the provost’s chamberlain, dressed in a clerical cope according to clerical custom, carried the cross. Since he despaired of his life, he escaped by this disguise. All good men, and all the citizens, grieved at this turn of events. Yet they rejoiced that they had secured the relics of the saints, which would have been left in the church as prey to the enemies and plunderers of the place had they remained there, as later became evident after the castle’s capture and the invasion of the church.

[Col. 0977B]

59. It should be noted that amid so great a tumult of events and so many burnings of houses—houses into whose suburban roofs they had shot burning arrows from within at night, while thieves outside also sought to steal something for themselves—and amid so many dangers of nights and contests of days, I, Galbert, had no place for writing. Therefore I noted the substance of events on tablets, until, waiting for some peace by night or day, I might arrange this present account according to the course of events. Thus, constrained as I was, I faithfully copied it down for you according to what you see and read. Because of the confusion and infinity of events, I did not record what each individual did; rather, with attentive mind I recorded only what, in the siege, was brought together by common decree and action for the battle and its cause. I was compelled, almost against my will, to commit this to writing.

60. The construction of the ladders was as follows. First a broad ladder, with its rungs, was made according to the height of the castle walls. On its right and left were woven very tough rods in the manner of a wall. At the front of the ladder likewise stood a joined wall. Upon this ladder, laid lengthwise, was placed another ladder, narrower and longer, constructed in the same manner; so that after the larger ladder had been raised, the smaller ladder might slide down within the wall, while the walls woven at the right, left, and front would stand as protection for those climbing on every side.

[Col. 0977D]

61. This must not be passed over: many had been enclosed within the castle who were not guilty of the count’s death either by deed or consent, but had been shut in together with the guilty on the day when they were first enclosed within the walls. Likewise, many had voluntarily entered with the criminals; although they had not been present at the actual, material killing, they nevertheless assented to the guilty. Still others had entered during the first and subsequent days of the siege for the sake of reward and gain.

Among them was one monstrous young archer, skilful and swift in shooting, named Benkin. He went about the walls fighting, now running here, now there; at times he alone seemed to be several men, since he inflicted so many wounds from inside and never ceased. Whenever he aimed at the besiegers, his shots were recognized by everyone: either he struck unarmed men with a grave wound, or with a discharged arrow he pursued armed men and, though they were not wounded, stunned them into flight.

> [Note: Col. 0977D] Below, in nos. 117 and 119, he is called Coterellus, where his flight and punishment are discussed.

Also present among those guilty men was the knight Weriot, who had remained a thief and robber from his youth. He caused great slaughter among those attacking outside the walls by hurling down and casting stones, using only his left hand. Moreover, an innumerable number of guilty persons and helpers were within the walls, labouring day and night in watches, fighting, attacks, and varied toil. They had filled up the castle gates from bottom to top on the inside by bringing earth, stones, and dung, lest, after the gates had been burned and fired, the attackers should perhaps enter from outside. Indeed, after fires were applied on the eastern side, the great gates had almost been burned through, and a very large opening would have stood exposed had they not blocked it with the aforesaid mass of materials.

Finally, when they had blocked the inner exits of the gates with stones and heaps of earth, both the besieged and the besiegers destroyed from outside the bridges on either side which had formerly led to the castle. Thus no entrance remained for enemies, nor exit for the besieged.

62. Having thus secured themselves at their exits, the besieged laboured to block the southern doors of the church, the doors of the count’s house leading into the castle, and the doors extending from the cloister into the castle; so that, if by some misfortune they lost the count’s court, they might withdraw into the count’s house and the provost’s house, as well as into the brothers’ refectory and cloister and into the church.

The church of Blessed Donatian stood built round and high, roofed with tilework and crowned with pots and bricks. For formerly the church roof had been supported by a construction of timbers, and the same basilica had borne an elaborate bell-tower structure raised to a height. Thus it surpassed others by the splendour of its dignity, like a royal seat, dispensing safety and peace in the midst of the country, and justice and law to the fathers of the land on every side.

> [Note: Col. 0978D] That is, while the rear part of the church had not yet been added.

Since all the timberwork had formerly been consumed by the ravages of fire, they had therefore devised, against the danger of fire, a stone structure made of pots and bricks which the element of fire could not burn. On the western side of the same church, a very strong tower rose from the fabric of the church to a greater height, dividing at its summit into two sharper towers. A wall enclosed the provost’s house, the brothers’ dormitory, the cloister, and indeed the whole castle; and this wall, which they had at last presumed to secure for themselves, stood higher and stronger, with battlements and a wall-walk for fighting outward. Although the wall itself was strong and the means of ascent secure, they laboured night and day to make themselves safer within, for they now understood that they would have to fight against the whole world.

## Chapter IX. Fruitless negotiations between the parties concerning an agreement. The castle taken. Flight of the besieged into the church.

63. At last they could remember their proverb: “If we kill Charles, who will come to avenge him?” And indeed they were innumerable; and, apart from God, the number of those coming to avenge him was uncertain. Therefore the interrogative and indefinite force of *quis* (“who”) in their proverb received its true and full meaning.

It should be known that those vigorous knights were inside with the guilty men, and were always more ready in spirit to go out or to fall and slip down outside from the wall, if they had found an opportunity; for all who were besieged with the guilty were generally enrolled under the stigma of traitors. When the princes of the siege learned this, they gathered counsellors and men of greater wisdom, approached the walls, and held a parley with all who were besieged inside.

They ordered that those among the besieged who were not guilty be summoned to the walls for public view, and offered them permission and power, if they wished, to depart from the besieged with their lives and limbs safe, provided that their innocence was manifest. Furthermore, apart from the guilty, if any wished to depart and prove their innocence according to the judgment of the princes, they could leave under the same liberty. But no indulgence would be granted to the guilty, who had committed a crime so monstrous and hitherto unheard of; rather, they would suffer an unheard-of destruction and a hitherto unheard-of bitterness of death.

Accordingly, under this edict and agreement, very many came out, because their innocence was manifest or because those who were less believed were ready to prove it.

64. At length the provost, with a sadder countenance and having laid aside the sternness and pride of his majesty, came in a shattered state of mind to the parley; and his brother, the castellan Haket, addressed the besieging party humbly in these words. The castellan Haket was spokesman for the provost and all the besieged, speaking alone for them all. He replied to the princes:

> “Lords and our friends, who have pity on us: if anything else had happened to us, you ought, by some trace of our former affection, to extend toward us such offices of mercy as you can, without injury to your own honour and resources. We therefore ask and beseech you, princes of this land, and remember how many benefits of affection you have received from us. Have pity on us, who together with you lament and mourn the death of the lord count, condemn the guilty, and would entirely expel them from among us, were we not unwillingly preserving in them the kinship of our own blood.
>
> “Nevertheless, we beseech your power: hear us concerning our nephews, whom you call guilty. Let them obtain through you liberty now to depart from the castle; then, after a penalty has been imposed upon them for so monstrous a crime by the bishop and magistrates, let them go into perpetual exile, that in this way they may somehow deserve to be reconciled to God in sackcloth and penitence—the God whom they have gravely offended.
>
> “But we—I, the provost, and Robert the Boy—together with our men, are ready to satisfy everyone, according to the judgment of every rank, that we are innocent of the deed and consent of the betrayal. We are wholly prepared to prove our innocence in this matter, if any man under heaven deigns to receive the proofs of our defence. My lord the provost offers, before the whole clergy, to undertake however severe a proof of his innocence, since he testifies that his conscience is clean.
>
> “Again we ask you to permit our nephews, who are guilty and marked in the betrayal, with their lives and limbs safe, to have liberty to go into exile; and permit us to be cleared by a true judgment of proof—knights to be examined according to secular law, clerics according to the divine writings. But if you abhor to do this, we prefer to live thus besieged together with the guilty rather than come out to you and die shamefully.”

65. When the castellan Haket had finished his speech, a knight of the siege, named Walter, began to reply:

> “We ought henceforth neither to remember any benefit from you nor rightly to observe any trace of former affection. You violently shut away the lord count, who ought to have been buried and mourned by us as was fitting; you participated with the guilty in the treasure of the realm and unjustly possess his royal court. You are the most impious traitors to your lord, and from now on nothing belonging to the kingdom and county pertains to you.
>
> “For you unjustly possess everything, both your own lives and external property, since you have made yourselves men without faith and without law. You have therefore armed against yourselves all who profess the Christian name, because you betrayed the ruler of this land, for the justice of God and men, during the holy season of Lent, in a holy place, while he lay prostrate in holy prayers before God. Therefore we renounce, condemn, and cast away the faith and homage which we have hitherto observed toward you.”

> [Note: Col. 0979D] *Exfestucare*: to renounce a right, possession, or lordship by taking up a rod or straw and handing it over or throwing it away; as was said on 6 February in the *Acts of Blessed Hildegund*, p. 920.

The whole multitude of the siege was present at this parley. Immediately when this reply ended, they took up straws and renounced the homage, faith, and security of those besieged men. They separated from one another with anger and fixed determination: those outside to storm the place, those inside to resist.

66. On that same day we heard from the retainers of the abbess of the monastery of Aire the fate of Isaac. On the same night in which he had fled, when he believed that he had reached Ghent, he arrived near Ypres. From there he fled as far as Steenvoorde, a village of Guy, his brother-in-law. There, after taking counsel, he went down by night to Thérouanne and secretly assumed a monk’s habit.

> [Note: Col. 0980D] Rather, he was Isaac’s brother-in-law, since, as is said below in no. 94: “Guy had married Isaac’s sister, the provost’s niece.” Walter agrees in no. 49.

But rumour and the universal search pursued the fugitive, so that he could in no way remain hidden and the truth was immediately discovered. The son of the advocate of Thérouanne, when he learned of Isaac, burst into the brothers’ cloister and found him hiding in the church in a cowl, as though meditating upon psalms.

> [Note: Col. 0981D] Arnulf, son of Eustace; so Walter, no. 50.

When he had brought Isaac out under arrest, he bound and beat him with rods and fetters, and thus extorted from him the disclosure of the guilty persons in the count’s betrayal. Isaac confessed concerning himself and named other guilty men, adding that there were many who had known of the crime and had assisted the guilty men who actually delivered the count, namely by the material sword. He also spoke of his conspiracy of treachery with Bosiard and William of Wervik, Ingrannus of Esna, Robert the Boy, Wlfric the provost’s brother, and a few other most wicked murderers included with them.

Some reported that Isaac said that, when one oak tree was undermined in the orchard adjoining his house, he had hidden money deep among its roots. The knights of our place searched for it, digging everywhere down into the bowels of the earth, but in vain.

67. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, Friday, ladders were brought against the walls, and the two sides attacked one another with arrows and stones. Those who brought the ladders advanced protected by shields and clothed in mail. Many followed to watch how the ladders would be raised to the walls, because they were heavy from greenness and moisture and of great weight: they were about sixty men’s feet in height; the lower ladder was twelve feet broad, while the upper was much narrower but somewhat longer.

As the ladders were dragged, the hands, voices, and cries of those dragging them assisted, and their shouts resounded in the upper air. Then the men of Ghent, armed, protected with shields those pulling the ladders. Hearing and seeing the hauling, the besieged mounted the walls and went out upon the battlements, raining down innumerable casts of stones and a thick shower of arrows against those handling the ladders.

But spirited and daring young men, setting up small ladders which ten men normally carried, wished to anticipate the assault of the larger ladders and climbed the wall one after another. Yet whenever anyone attempted to reach the top and get over the wall, those hiding inside and lying in wait for the climbers struck the man clinging to the ladder down with spears, poles, and missiles. Thus no one remained so daring or swift as to dare enter among the besieged by the smaller ladders.

Meanwhile others tried to pierce the wall with masons’ hammers and every kind of iron implement, but after tearing away a large part of the wall they withdrew frustrated. When the crowd pulling the ladders had climbed near the walls and fighting became fiercer on both sides, as stones were hurled down from within, the darkness of deep night prevented both parties from fighting. Having suffered many injuries, the men of Ghent waited for the following day, when the whole siege force together with them would set up the larger ladders by force and enter among the besieged.

68. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, Saturday, at dawn the besieged, harassed in different parts of the castle, had given their limbs rest after their daily battles. They felt somewhat safer because on the preceding day they had fought nobly against the men of Ghent from outside. In that confidence, when day had been announced, the wall-watchers went inside the count’s house to warm themselves by the fire because of the harsh cold and winds, leaving the court of the castle empty.

Our citizens climbed in on the southern side, where the saints’ relics had been removed, by slender, portable ladders which one man could carry. Once inside, they silently and without shouting assembled themselves in great battle formations, fortified for combat. At once they arranged for the lesser men among them to go to the great gates, remove the heap of earth and stones from the gates, and make an entrance for all those standing outside, who still did not know of this action.

They had also found one castle gate on the western side firmly closed with nails and an iron bar, but not blocked by any mound of earth and stones. The traitors had kept this gate unobstructed in order to admit and dismiss through it whomever they wished. At their first approach our burghers immediately opened it with swords and axes; and amid a stirred-up clamour and clash of arms they threw into panic and tumult the army around the castle.

Thus a very powerful force of the siege rushed within the castle: some to fight, others to plunder whatever they found within, and others to enter the church, seize the body of Blessed Count Charles, and carry it to Ghent.

69. Then those traitors, lying in the count’s house in deep sleep, were awakened by terror and unending shouting. Ignorant of the course of events, they ran about to see what caused the cries. When they understood that danger threatened them, they leapt to arms and held their position before the doors, awaiting battle.

Some of them were intercepted at one of the gates as our citizens entered the castle: several knights who had been assigned to guard the eastern gates. Encountering the tumult with the citizens who had entered, and unable to do more, they surrendered themselves to the mercy and compassion of their captors. Others, despairing of their lives if captured by the citizens, slipped down from the walls. One of them, the knight Giselbert, fell headlong while climbing down and died.
