When some women had dragged him into a house and were preparing his funeral, the castellan Theodoric and his men, having learned that he was dead, tied him to a horse’s tail, dragged him through every street of the suburb, and finally threw him down into a cesspit in the middle of the marketplace.

> [Note: Col. 0982D] Above, in no. 54, he is called the castellan of Diksmuide.

When the citizens understood that the traitors meant to resist before the doors in the count’s house, they climbed the stairs leading to those doors, chopped the doors to pieces with axes and swords, entered among the besieged, and drove them through the middle of that house as far as the passage through which the count had customarily gone from his house to the church of Saint Donatian.

In this passage, which was vaulted and constructed of stone, there was a great battle. There the citizens fought hand-to-hand with swords alone, because the besieged refused to flee any farther. Testing their strength and courage to the full, both sides stood motionless like the wall itself, until the citizens, gathering their force, did not fight but rushed upon the besieged and put them to flight.

Among these was Borsiard, monstrous and wrathful, fierce and undaunted, stronger in bodily power; he continually stood facing the citizens, wounding and striking down many, and with the hammer-like blow of his sword knocking down very many men stunned by it. They also drove Robert the Boy into flight. No one wished to lay a hand upon him because they had heard that he was said to be innocent of the betrayal; indeed, all the more because he had remained beloved by everyone in the realm both before and after the betrayal. That noble man had neglected to flee, but followed the fugitives at the request of his friends. Had it not been for his sake, they would then and there have captured Borsiard and his knights, together with all the persons guilty of the betrayal.

When the traitors withdrew into the church, the citizens pursued them no farther. Instead they returned to plunder, running through the count’s house, the provost’s house, the brothers’ dormitory, and the cloister. All who were present in the siege did likewise, hoping perhaps to obtain the count’s treasure and the household goods of the houses within the walls.

In the count’s house they plundered many mattresses, tapestries, linen, cups, cauldrons, chains, iron bolts, shackles, fetters, leg-irons, cords, iron collars, handcuffs, every iron implement of imprisonment, the iron doors of the count’s treasury, and the lead water-pipes which had conducted rainwater from the roofs. They believed that they could take these things without blame. In the provost’s house they also seized beds, chests, seats, garments, vessels, and all his household goods. How limitless was the quantity of grain, meat, wine, and beer which they seized in the cellars of the count, the provost, and the brothers, I leave untold. In the brothers’ dormitory, which was furnished with precious and costly clothes, they exercised such great plunder that from the time of their entrance into the castle until nightfall they did not cease going back and forth carrying things away.

## Chapter X. The flight of the provost. Dissensions among the besiegers. The lower church taken. The tower, with the upper story of the church, held by the besieged.

70. Thus nothing was left to the besieged except the church alone, together with the provisions they had carried into it: namely wine, meat, flour, cheeses, legumes, and other necessities of life. It must here be stated who were the leaders among the besieged: the castellan Haket, Borsiard, Robert the Boy, Walter son of Lambert of Reddenburg, and Wilfric Cnop.

The provost Bertulf, on the third night—that is, Thursday night before the capture of the castle—gave as much as four hundred marks to Walter Butelgir and escaped alone, suspended by ropes from beneath his gallery. He trusted that Walter more than any man on earth. Yet Walter brought him over to a desolate place, namely the Moor, and left him there alone, exposed to his enemies and abandoned to flight, although in that place unknown to him he did not know where to flee or whom to avoid.

> [Note: Col. 0983D–0984D] *Mor*, or rather *Moer*, is in Flemish a marshy, boggy place. Below, in no. 89, a similar place is noted as being in the territory of Aardenburg, to which the provost was perhaps taken.

The besieged, having climbed the tower of the church, cast millstones down upon those wandering in the castle and brought a grievous fall upon those carrying off the plunder of all the household goods; many were crushed and perished fatally. The victors of the castle immediately directed arrows against the windows of the tower, so that no one in the tower could put his head out through the windows without receiving a thousand arrows and a thousand sling-stones. The whole tower stood bristling with arrows stuck in it.

Since neither side achieved anything in this way, the besieged set fire to the roof of the schools adjoining the church, wishing thereby to burn the provost’s house, to which that roof was adjacent. But frustrated in this action, they ran about below on the church floor, in the choir, and in the inner sanctuary, armed and watchful, lest anyone dare enter among them through the windows or violently burst in through the church doors.

71. Very early in the morning, a young man from the crowd of Ghent climbed a ladder to the great window of the church sanctuary. Breaking with sword and pole through the glass and ironwork, he boldly slipped inside and opened a chest in the sanctuary to search for plunder. Bending down, he began to turn things over and move his hand here and there, when the heavy chest lid fell suddenly upon that thief and robber, struck him, and hurled him back dead.

The same dead man lay there covered by a heap of feathers for a long time, for a very great heap of feathers lay in the sanctuary. Meanwhile, when the men of Ghent had waited long for that young man and he did not return, they wished to climb forcibly through the window. They had sent that youth ahead as the boldest man, through whom they might test entry into the church; and thus they believed that they could obtain the count’s body.

Against them our citizens met with arms, and never allowed the men of Ghent even to speak in their presence about removing the count’s body. Our citizens were exceedingly indignant—more than anyone would believe me—that any men should attempt to remove the body from our place. As the parties contended, they drew swords against one another, and a general tumult and rush to battle arose.

The besieged meanwhile assailed the victors as much as they could. But the wiser men, hearing the uproar and learning of the victory and dispute—namely, that the men of Ghent claimed that they ought by right to take the count’s body with them to Ghent because they had frightened the besieged by their ladder-machines and forced them to flee from the castle, while our citizens asserted in response that the Ghent men’s machines had accomplished nothing and had done nothing in the siege but steal and impose heavy expense upon our place—calmed the tumult by ending the dispute, saying:

> “Do not contend; instead, let us wait together until God gives us and the realm a good and lawful count. By the counsel of that count, the princes of the realm, our bishop, and the whole clergy, provision may then be made concerning the body.”

72. Having thus made peace in this fashion, the assailants of the church appointed [Col. 0985B] armed and bold men for the attack. Their forces having been gathered, they entered violently and rushed toward the church-door facing the cloister; they drove the besieged from the lower pavement up to the upper chamber, in which they had wickedly and treacherously delivered up the most worthy count in the land. The servants too were shut in with their lord, although they had been enclosed with their lord the count against their own will.

Then at last the men of Ghent entered the sanctuary and sought the young man whom they had sent in that morning through the principal window of the sanctuary. They found him crushed among feathers and dead—though some falsely claimed that Borsiard had killed him when he carelessly made his way down into the church. For it is not possible to describe how great a shower of stones had been cast from the upper chamber upon the victors on the pavements of the church [Col. 0985C], nor how many were buried, crushed, or wounded by darts and arrows. The whole choir of the church lay covered by a heap of stones, and nowhere could the pavement be seen. The walls, glass windows round about, statues, and likewise the brethren’s seats and stalls were thrown down; and everything was so confused and ruined that no holy and intact appearance remained in the church. Rather, disfigured by a shameful and shapeless ugliness, it stood more dreadful than any prison.

For the besieged in the upper chamber had prepared defenses for themselves from chests, altar-boards, forms, benches, and the rest of the church furnishings, binding them together with bell-ropes. They also broke up the bells and the lead with which the church had formerly been roofed, burying some beneath it [Col. 0985D]. Below, indeed, in the church—that is, in the choir—the fighting was extremely fierce; but such slaughter was inflicted from the tower and its doors that I cannot adequately describe it or recount the multitude of those struck and wounded.

73. Accordingly, Gervasius, knight, chamberlain, and counsellor of the counts of the realm, seized the upper house of the count with great courage and ordered his standards fastened upon the summit of the fortress of the house. This was done in resentment against the besieged, who, on the very first day of the siege—even on the day when impious servants had delivered up their lord—had borne standards against their enemies. Thus that William of Ypres bore standards, as though he were lord and count of the land, against certain persons who had refused to pay him the count’s revenues, because they had sharply rejected him as count [Col. 0986A].

Those traitors, indeed, acting with no humility on the first day of the siege—because they believed that the princes of the realm were accomplices in their crime and secure with them in the same loyalty and friendship—had arrogantly set up their standards on the highest tower of the count’s chamber, on the summit of the church tower, on the three lesser towers, on the gallery of the provost, and likewise at the gateway exits. By this it might appear that they were the masters, awaiting the great men of the realm, their friends and accomplices, by whose power they would destroy the siege and leave unavenged their betrayal of the count.

Desiderius, Isaac’s brother, took possession of the lower house of the count with our citizens, and had fixed his standard upon the larger gallery of the count. When Robert the Boy saw him passing from the tower in the castle, he reproached him as follows [Col. 0986B]:

> “O Desiderius, do you not remember that until now you advised us to betray our lord the count? You gave assurance and security concerning this; and now, seeing our misfortune, you rejoice and persecute us. Would that I were permitted to come out! I would challenge you to single combat. I call God to witness that you are a greater traitor than we, since formerly you betrayed our lord and now betray us!”

He endured this reproach, not without the notice of all.

74. In the house of the provost too, the nephews of Thancmar—on whose account, as they say, the betrayal was partly committed—had proudly, gloriously, and forcefully set up their standards. All took this very ill, and our citizens were especially distressed, because before the time of the betrayal the provost and his household had been religious men, behaving amicably toward them and treating with honor all who lived in our town and in the realm [Col. 0986C].

After these men had seized the houses and affixed their standards, they possessed as their own whatever they found within. The hearts of our citizens therefore swelled against Thancmar’s nephews, and they sought an occasion to fight and kill them. Thus, toward evening on that Saturday, when Thancmar’s nephews were sending out to their country estate the grain and wine that they had seized in the provost’s house, our citizens met them in the cloister. Drawing their swords, they cut open the wine-vessels; an immense tumult arose, and the citizens shut the gates of the suburb so that none of those nephews might escape.

But the besieged had summoned citizens who had formerly been their friends [Col. 0986D], imploring them to destroy those enemies, through whose agency they had committed the most grievous crime. Since Thancmar’s nephews could not resist the citizens in that same house of the provost, they sought to escape secretly. Thancmar himself, fleeing, reached the exit of one gate; and, because it was closed, when asked what had caused so great a tumult, he lied that fighting was occurring between the besieged and the besiegers. At last he hid in a little house, until he could see what would happen to his nephews.

As the citizens crossed in arms by the bridge of St Peter and by the castle bridge, Walter the butler and the other leaders of the siege met them, vigorously restraining the tumult. So many men stood in the marketplace with lances that one might have thought the surface of the lances a very dense forest [Col. 0987A]. Nor was this surprising, since on that same day people from throughout the whole realm had poured into the suburb: some for plunder, some for vengeance, and especially to carry away the count’s corpse, while others came to witness all that was happening there.

All cried that Thancmar and his nephews ought rightly to be hanged, because through their fault the count had been killed; the provost and his nephews had been besieged; and many members of their household had been slain and condemned to a most shameful death. Therefore, they said, they could not endure that the men be spared, but should condemn them to a death more shameful and cruel: for by fraud, sedition, and a corrupt bargain, they had betrayed to the count their lords—the provost and his brothers, together with his nephews, who were the more powerful and noble men of the county.

The leaders could scarcely restrain the enraged citizens, because the castellan Haket and Robert the Boy, standing in the higher tower with the friends and kinsmen of those citizens, beckoned with arms and hands for an attack upon Thancmar’s nephews [Col. 0987B]. These men had so arrogantly gone up into the provost’s house and set up victorious standards, as if they had captured the castle by their own strength—although, when the citizens violently entered the castle, Thancmar’s nephews had been sleeping at home and on their country estate.

At length the tumult was calmed on this condition: that they should leave the house at once, shamefacedly remove the standards they had set up, and depart. Under the hazardous escort of the leaders, they then withdrew. They so distrusted the citizens that each nephew of Thancmar departed on horseback, with his own escort riding beside him [Col. 0987C]. Thus the house was left under the protection of the knights and citizens of our town; and the grain and wine were divided among the leaders of the siege and the citizens, through whose strength the victory had been achieved that day.

75. At last, as that day closed, it made men exceedingly anxious about keeping watch during the following night—in the castle court and the brethren’s cloister, as well as in the provost’s house, refectory, and the brethren’s dormitory. For the besieged had adopted the plan of burning the roofs of the cloister and houses around the church, so that the besiegers might have no access to them by any route. Astounded by this, the night-watchers remained sleepless in vigilant anxiety and fear. Often the besieged went out secretly during the night and struck fear into the guards [Col. 0987D].

Moreover, in the confined space of the church tower, the traitors ordered their watchmen throughout every night of the siege to sound trumpets and bugles and blow the horn, still hoping to escape because the princes of the realm, by letters shot into the tower on an arrow, offered them friendship and aid.

76. The provost, having as guide the brother of Fulk, a canon of Bruges—a treacherous knight—rode on the Thursday night already mentioned, by Walter the butler’s command, to Kaihem, a village belonging to Walter and Borsiard.

> [Note: [Col. 0987D] Caihem, or Kejem, below Diksmuide, not far from the Ypres river.]

After hiding there briefly [Col. 0988A], and having been denounced, he fled by night with one companion to Furnes, to his wife. From there again, because he could not remain hidden on the holy night of Good Friday, he passed through Warnestum, as we heard that same night; he persisted in his flight, going barefoot and voluntarily enduring punishment for his sins, that God might pardon so great a sinner for his offense against the pious count.

This is quite credible, since when he was captured shortly afterward, the soles of his feet appeared flayed: on his night journey he had struck his feet against stones so often that blood flowed from them. And truly this man suffered most grievously: he who had formerly lorded it over all, who flourished in the riches and honor of this world, and who, amid luxury, feared the sting of a flea as though it were a spear—behold, alone and an exile within his own territory, he wandered alone [Col. 0988B].

Let us return from this digression to the watches of the aforesaid night. As besiegers and besieged mutually inflicted nocturnal terrors upon one another, both sides, exhausted and wearied, had exchanged day for night in order to sleep.

## Chapter XI. William the Norman, successor to Blessed Charles in the county of Flanders; other claimants. Plots arranged to carry his body to Ghent.

77. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, Sunday, on the feast of Abbot Benedict, Louis, king of France, sent from Arras to the leaders and barons of the aforesaid siege greetings, assurance, aid [Col. 0988C], and in addition every favor in avenging his nephew Charles, the most just count of Flanders—one more worthy, he said, to have been king than the count of most wicked traitors:

> “At present I have no opportunity to come over to you, since I came down here more hastily with few men, having heard and learned the outcome of the affair and the siege. It did not seem prudent to me to fall into the hands of the traitors of the land. For, as we have learned, there are still many who grieve for the besieged, defend their crimes, and labor in every way for their escape.
>
> “Therefore, since the land is disturbed and conspiracies have already been formed against William, who seeks to seize the realm by force; and nearly all the towns have sworn against him that they will by no means receive that William as count, because he is illegitimate—

> [Note: [Col. 0987D] Abbot Suger above calls him a *bastardus*, ‘bastard.’ [Col. 0988D] Marchantius should be corrected, since he wishes to clear him of this stain.]

> —born, that is, of a noble father and a low-born mother, who, while she lived, never ceased carding wool—I desire and command you to assemble before me without delay and, by common counsel, elect a useful count, one whom you agree shall rule over you as your equal, and over the land and its inhabitants. For the land cannot long remain without a count except at greater danger than that now threatening it.”

78. When the letters had been read before all, and before they had yet answered the king’s letters whether they would go or not, another messenger arrived from the count Charles’s nephew [Col. 0989A], conveying greetings to the leaders of the siege and an expression of his natural affection toward all inhabitants of the land:

> [Note: [Col. 0989D] This is Thierry of Alsace, cousin of Blessed Charles; both were descended from two sisters, daughters of Robert the Frisian.]

> “It is certain to all of you that, after the death of my lord the count, the realm of Flanders belongs by right of kinship to my lot and authority. Therefore I wish you to consider and act cautiously regarding the election of my person, and I ask you, having been forewarned, not to make me an outsider to the realm. For by right and by the claim of kinship, if you send for me, I shall come as count—just, peaceful, approachable, and a careful provider for the common advantage and welfare.”

Then the leaders, together with all who had heard the letters sent by the count’s nephew from Alsace, declared them fictitious and gave no attention to making an answer [Col. 0989B], because the commonwealth was in distress; the king was hastening a meeting nearby; and they foresaw that they could not deliberate about electing that nephew without lengthy proceedings.

79. Anticipating the most useful course, in obedience to the king’s command they prepared to leave on Monday and Tuesday. Yet afterwards, by deliberate and particular counsel, the leaders summoned the citizens, rushed to arms on that same Sunday, and attacked the besieged in the tower. This was done in order to more completely break the spirit of the terrified besieged and make them fearful, so that when the leaders suddenly departed to the king, they would not dare leave the tower or flee.

A severe conflict indeed took place on both sides [Col. 0989C]; and the besieged still did not know why they were attacked on Sunday, when all the other Sundays in the preceding time had been observed in peace. The leaders accordingly left on Monday and Tuesday to speak with the king at Arras, having arranged for men to guard the tower cautiously and faithfully, armed day and night, so that none of the besieged might slip away.

80. On the tenth day before the Kalends of April, Wednesday, Isaac, my liberator, was captured and hanged. Three weeks after the count’s murder, before the Annunciation of St Mary and before Palm Sunday, Lambert Archei escaped from the tower, fleeing by boat to the village of Michem.

> [Note: [Col. 0989D] Did the tale arise from this of Lambert Nappin, Borsiard’s father, who is counted among the accomplices in the vernacular annals, by Meyer and others? Formula of proclamation.]

He had shared Borsiard’s counsel and had always acted wickedly, advising, acting, and inciting his lords to every crime [Col. 0989D]. Therefore he was hated by all who had heard of his deceptions during the siege. From the beginning of the siege, when he was confined within the castle, until the time when he escaped, he was active in everything undertaken inside: exceptionally skilled with the bow and especially powerful in hurling spears and every sort of missile. He had inflicted deadly slaughter upon the enemy.

When he fled, the citizens searched for him at dawn and throughout the entire day on which he escaped. For, as he stole away from the tower, Borsiard cried out to those besieging the tower when and to what place his counsellor and intimate associate had fled [Col. 0990A]. At last the citizens surrounded the village in which the fugitive had hidden; they dragged him from his hiding-place and brought him back captive. They would have put him to death by hanging in our marketplace, had the leading men of the siege been present at that time; they had gone to Arras to deliberate concerning the realm.

Finally, he was entrusted, under pledge of safe conduct, to a certain Gerbert, one of our citizens and his kinsman. Gerbert held him bound in chains under vigilant guard until he should be brought before the chief men of the county, so that it might be determined by their judgment what they decreed should be done with him.

81. On the ninth day before the Kalends of April, Thursday, Woltra Cruval reported to our people that the king of England had concluded an agreement with William of Ypres, supplying him with limitless money and three hundred soldiers to assist him in obtaining the county of Flanders [Col. 0990B]. Although this was false, he spread it abroad by simulated deceit as though it were credible.

For it was certainly established that William of Ypres had received five hundred pounds of English coin from Count Charles’s treasury through the hands of the nephews of Provost Bertolph. These most impious traitors had tried to set that same William above themselves and the realm. He had obtained money, counsel, and help from them; and in letters sent and returned daily they discussed their mutual intentions and the secrets of their consciences.

Thus the aforementioned knight falsely claimed that William had received monetary gifts from the king of England [Col. 0990C], wishing to conceal William’s treacherous complicity. William had in truth accepted money secretly sent by the traitors, with which he might purchase paid soldiers (*solidarii*), so that once he had obtained the county by force, the traitors might then accomplish their wishes through him.

> [Note: [Col. 0990D] Soldiers were called *solidarii*, either because they received a *solidus* as pay, or because they were maintained by wages. See Vossius.]

No one seeking high office in the realm wished openly to accept any counsel or embassy from the traitors, because he would immediately be branded as a traitor. Therefore William concealed his involvement and falsely stated that the money had been sent him by the king, as if he had nothing in common or secret with the traitors. Yet before the siege he had openly sent the provost and his people greetings and aid in sealed letters [Col. 0990D].

At that time Giselbert, nephew of the traitors and castellan of Bergues, who was under the accusation of treason, had escaped to the castellan of Saint-Omer, offering to prove his excuse and innocence before the king and the fathers of the realm.

> [Note: [Col. 0990D] Frolulph, castellan of Bergues, subscribed the letters of Blessed Charles in 1121. He was succeeded by Giselbert, nephew of the traitors.]

82. On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, Friday—the Annunciation of the Lord, on which day the Lord also suffered—celebrated in the Saturday before Palm Sunday, a scheme and deception of the men of Ghent was devised [Col. 0991A]. With the guidance of the chief herald, the knight Ansbold, certain of our citizens who consented, and likewise the agreement of the traitors, it was arranged that they should enter the castle on the night following that Saturday. By the hands of the traitors, the brethren of the Ghent monastery were to receive the body of the most pious count through the windows of the upper chamber, gather it in bags and sacks, and carry it away.

Two monks had indeed waited throughout all that time for an opportunity to steal the body. While those who had guided the monks walked armed around the tower, the frightened watchmen sounded horns all around; and the summoned citizens and tower-guards rushed against the chief herald [Col. 0991B], the knight Ansbold, and their accomplices, putting them to flight and wounding some who were overwhelmed by fear of death.

The monks had promised their helpers a hundred marks of silver if, by their means, they obtained the count’s body. When it became known that the monks wished to take away the count’s body secretly, by payment, or by any other means, the wary citizens devoted themselves, with an anxious and watchful crowd, to still stricter surveillance.

83. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April, Palm Sunday, our people of Bruges assembled in the field adjoining the suburb, within the town enclosure. Having summoned Flemings from every direction around us, they jointly swore upon holy relics as follows:

> “I, Folpert the judge, swear that I shall elect such a count for this land [Col. 0991C] as will profitably govern the realm of his predecessor counts and be able powerfully to maintain its rights against the enemies of the country; who will be affectionate and merciful toward the poor, devoted to God, walking the path of uprightness, and such a man as both wishes and is able to promote the common good of the country.”

Thereupon all the leading citizens swore likewise: Alard the alderman of Isendica, with those subject to his authority; Hajolum of Oostburg, with the leaders of that place; Hugh Berlensis of Reddenburg, with the stronger men of that locality; and from Lapscheure, Oostkerke, Uitkerke, Lissewege, Slype, Gistel, Oudenburg, Lichtervelde, and Jabbeke, all the stronger and better men took the same oath.

> [Note: [Col. 0991D] Reddenburg, called Rodenburg by others, now Aardenburg, is a town of Flanders toward Zeeland, where Isendica and Oostburg are situated. The remaining places lie all about in the territory of Bruges, or the Franconate.]

There was a very great multitude united in this oath.

[Col. 0991D]

84. On the third day before the Kalends of April, Wednesday, at the ringing of the bells, our leaders returned from Arras. They had gone to the king to deliberate about the realm and elect a count in accordance with the counsel of Louis, emperor of France, the counsel of all his barons, and the choice of our land; and, after prudent examination of what seemed advantageous for the country, they returned joyfully with this report, proclaiming greetings and assurance on behalf of the king and barons [Col. 0992A] to us, to all the inhabitants of the land, and especially to those who had labored through the continual siege to exact vengeance for the death of Lord Count Charles:

> “Louis, king of France, sends greetings and favor to all good sons of the realm; and, with royal power in the strength of God and the force of arms, the unconquerable assistance of his presence. Foreseeing with grief the grave ruin of the country together with the betrayal of the count, we have assembled to exact vengeance with the severity of rigor and a punishment unheard of before this time. And in order that henceforth the land may be reconciled and restored under its count, newly elected by us, obey and carry out whatever you hear in the following text of this letter.”

Accordingly Walter the butler produced the king’s sealed letters before all our citizens [Col. 0992B], who had gathered in the aforesaid field to hear the king’s command. Confirming the testimony of the letters orally, he said:

> “Hear, our citizens, what counsel and business have been undertaken before the king and his barons and examined by prudent judgment. The princes of France and the foremost men of Flanders, by royal command and counsel, have elected for you and this land as count William the Boy, born in Normandy: noble in lineage, indeed, and reared among you from infancy into boyhood and then into a vigorous youth. It is clear that he has been accustomed to every good custom; and you will be able suitably to shape him, as you wish, into a man gentle and teachable in every good character.
>
> “I, Robert of Béthune, have elected him, together with Baldwin of Aalst and his brother Iwan, castellan of Lille; and the other barons have raised him to the county [Col. 0992C]. We have given him loyalty, security, and homage according to every custom of his predecessor counts of Flanders. He has also rewarded our labor by granting us the lands and estates of the traitors, who by the judgment of all the leaders have been condemned to outlawry. It is established that nothing remains to them, either in property or mercy, except a death still most grievous and unimaginable.

> [Note: [Col. 0992D] This is Robert IV, surnamed the Fat, whose distinguished deeds are related by du Chesne, book II of *The Family of Béthune*, chapter 4, and in the *Proofs*, pp. 13–23.]

> “Therefore I command, wish, and sincerely advise you inhabitants of the suburb, all of you present, to receive as your lord and count the newly elected William, to whom the county has been granted by the king. Moreover, whatever may lawfully be granted by his authority—such as tolls and land-rents—he will willingly remit to you the toll, if you desire it jointly, and the rent of your dwellings within the suburb. I announce this myself on behalf of the king and the new count: he will remit these without deceit or malicious contrivance.”

Having heard the letters and the voice of their bearer, the citizens deferred their answer concerning the acceptance or election of the new count. They wished first to summon the Flemings with whom they had established oaths concerning the election, so that together they might either grant acceptance or reject the letters of the royal embassy. Since they had prolonged the day with lengthy deliberations, the citizens withdrew from the place of assembly, sending messages throughout that night to the Flemings, that they might approve or reject the election made in the person of the new count [Col. 0993A].

## Chapter XII. The arrival in Flanders and at Bruges of Count William with the king. Oaths made on both sides.

85. On the day before the Kalends of April, Thursday, after the citizens had met with the Flemings, they agreed by common counsel that on Holy Saturday twenty knights and twelve of the oldest and wisest citizens should go out to meet the king’s envoys for a conference at the town of Ravenschot; and that the men of Ghent should wait there for our people’s arrival [Col. 0993B]. For the people of Bruges, from the towns and castles of Flanders, stood in such mutual security and friendship that they would neither approve nor oppose anything concerning the election unless jointly.

In this matter our citizens of Bruges did nothing without the counsel of the men of Ghent, who were seated nearer them at their side. They went therefore as previously arranged on that same Holy Saturday. The king too, as he had arranged at Arras, came down with the newly elected count to Lille, where homage was rendered to the count, as at Arras. From there he came down to the town named Dinsa, upon the road by which he intended to go to Ghent.

> [Note: [Col. 0993D] Dinsa, or Densa, is called a castle and town in the letters of Count Thierry under the year 1152. It lies on the river Lys between Ghent and Courtrai; the title of marquisate is now attached to it.]

In that town the king awaited the men of Ghent, who were to receive the new count according to his command and the election of the foremost men of the land [Col. 0993C]. Thus it was agreed harmoniously between our people and the men of Ghent concerning the reception of the newly elected man, that they should receive him as count and advocate of the whole land.

86. On the Kalends of April, Friday, Good Friday, the castellan Haket escaped alone from the tower and passed through Lissewege, where he hid with his daughter. A knight, of great lineage and full of wealth, had formerly married her there.

> [Note: [Col. 0993D] Robert Crommelin, as was stated above from Count Thierry’s letters.]

That fugitive was awaiting what he should do next. On the fourth day before the Nones of April, Holy Saturday of Easter, certain of our citizens and men of Ghent who had returned from the conference elected William as count for themselves and their country, rendering homage, loyalty, and security to the count according to the custom of his predecessor counts.

On the same day Gervasius [Col. 0993D] was made castellan of our castle at Bruges by the king and the new count. Yet this office did not fully recompense his merit, though he had done so many and such great things in the siege, which I earnestly commend to the memory of readers. For at the very moment when Count Charles was being betrayed, he ran about the castle weeping, tearing his hair and clothes, clapping his hands, and crying:

> “Alas, that I alone cannot avenge my lord, the most just prince of our land [Col. 0994A], whom no man dares defend or avenge!”

There he, Gervasius alone, began the vengeance, and later, with God Himself fighting alongside him, happily brought it to completion.

87. On the third day before the Nones of April, holy Easter Sunday, on the feast of the virgin Theodosia, with dominical letter B:

> [Note: [Col. 0993D] Theodosia, a Tyrian virgin, suffered at Caesarea [Col. 0994D] in Palestine. Very many place her feast on this third day of April; others place it on the preceding day.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0994D] In another of our copies, the fifth: the letter, apparently V, indicating the title “Virgin,” was taken for a numeral.]

the clergy and people waited in suspense for the arrival of the king and count among us. On that day those most wicked traitors communicated in the body and blood of Christ. Yet it is unknown through what priest this was done. On the same day the besieged and most wicked traitors harassed with arrows those passing through the castle, prolonging their lives—with no limit of faith or reverence—while awaiting the most shameful death that was to come upon them [Col. 0994B].

88. On the Nones of April, Tuesday, “Water of wisdom”:

> [Note: [Col. 0994D] These words begin the Introit of the Mass on this day; this mode of expression is frequently noted.]

at nightfall, the king, together with William, the newly elected count and marquis of Flanders, came to Bruges, to our suburb. The canons of St Donatian went out to meet him, bringing the relics of the saints and receiving the king and new count joyfully in solemn procession according to royal custom.

On the eighth day before the Ides of April, Wednesday, the king and count assembled with their men, our knights and citizens, and many Flemings, in the customary field. Chests and relics of the saints were brought together there. Silence having been ordered, the charter of the church’s liberty and the privileges of St Donatian were read before all [Col. 0994C], in the presence of king and count: so that neither the king in his own person nor the count might rashly oppose what was written in the pages of the privileges, ratified by Catholic Roman pontiffs and never violated by any Catholic kings or counts; but that, rather, he might revere these enactments by the prerogative of royal dignity and strengthen them by the command of his authority.

The brethren of that church declared that, by the pope’s grant, they possessed the liberty to elect a provost canonically and without simony, as the wording of their privilege contained. They further declared that if the king were present, he would raise the canonically and non-simoniacally elected provost to the ministry of his office and the dignity of prelacy, and install him in the office of prelacy [Col. 0994D]:

> “But if the king were absent, the count, exercising the office of the same power, should make the confirmation of the canonically elected provost and install him in office, both in his own person and on behalf of his men, according to the custom of his Catholic princely predecessors.”

The small charter of the agreement made between the counts and our citizens concerning remission of toll and the rent of their dwellings was also read. In return for electing and receiving the person of the new count [Col. 0995A], they were to receive from the count this liberty: henceforth neither they nor their successors in our town should pay toll or rent to the count or his successor. Rather, endowed with this perpetual freedom as written in the charter of agreement, they demanded an oath from the king and count together to confirm that liberty—namely, that neither king nor count, either personally or through officials, would trouble our citizens or their successors in our town regarding payment of toll and rent; but would preserve inviolate, in good faith, without malicious contrivance and without reservation, both the canons’ privileges and the remission of tolls and rent.

Under this compact, therefore, the king and count swore upon the saints’ relics in the hearing of clergy and people [Col. 0995B]. Afterwards the citizens likewise swore fidelity to the count, as was customary, and rendered him homage and assurances, as they had formerly done to his predecessors, the natural princes and lords of the land. To make our citizens well disposed toward him, the count further granted them authority and permission to amend and improve their customary laws from day to day according to the circumstances of time and place.

89. Finally, after all things had been confirmed by the oath of those swearing, the king and count returned to their lodging. There, in the hearing of all, letters of this kind were delivered by the leading men who had carried out the siege at Reddenburg [Col. 0995C]:

> “We too, the executors of this siege, shall elect the newly elected count of Flanders on our part, upon this condition: that you condemn and abolish, removing henceforth from us and the inhabitants of our district, the customary military expeditions, moreover the unjust exactions of princes, and the new tolls which have recently and contrary to the customary law of the land been established at Reddenburg by Lambert’s deceitful counsel. Our peasants must have freedom to go out and pasture their livestock on the land called Mor, without the unjust compulsory purchase instituted by Lambert.
>
> “Furthermore, concerning the very burdensome compulsory redemption of dwellings at Erdenburg, we wish to establish a middle course through king and count: namely, that each of those payments which the sons, after their fathers’ death, have hitherto redeemed for sixteen pence according to the assessment of the dwellings, should be redeemed for only twelve pence [Col. 0995D].
>
> “We establish this rule for ourselves: if an expedition is proclaimed on behalf of our count, a man who has no lawful excuse shall pay the count twenty shillings as amends. On all these matters we demand your assent, lord king, and the grant and confirmation of the new count, so that he may confirm by oath everything we have set down in this charter and that is established as publicly proclaimed in the hearing of all.
>
> “We admonish and beseech both the person and all-powerful authority of the king and of the count, that they may never permit Provost Bertolph [Col. 0996A], his brothers Ulfric Cnop, the castellan Haket, Robert the Boy, Lambert of Reddenburg with his sons, Borsiard, and the remaining traitors ever afterward to become heirs in the county of Flanders.”

When such a charter had been read in the sight of all, the new count swore that he would confirm and grant in good faith, without malicious contrivance and without reservation, everything they had demanded of him. Thereafter, throughout the rest of the day, those who had previously been enfeoffed by the most pious Count Charles rendered homage to that count, receiving anew in like manner their fiefs, offices, and everything they had previously held by right and law.

90. On the seventh day before the Ides of April, Thursday, homage was again done to the count, and in this manner the terms of fealty and security were completed. First they performed homage thus: the count asked whether he wished to become his man wholly; and he replied, “I do.” Then, with joined hands enclosed by the count’s hands, they were bound by a kiss. Secondly, he who had done homage gave faith to the count’s spokesman in these words: “Upon my faith I promise that henceforth I shall be faithful to Count William, and shall fully observe homage to him against all men, in good faith and without deceit.” Thirdly, he swore the same upon the relics of the saints. Then, by the rod which the count held in his hand, he granted investitures to all who had made security and homage, together with the oath, upon this compact.

On the same day Eustace of Steenvoorde, first killed by the citizens at Saint-Omer, and afterwards thrown into the conflagration of the house to which he had fled, was burned to ashes. Under the charge of treason he had deserved to suffer such a death. On the same day at Bruges the count gave Baldwin of Aalst four hundred pounds less twenty, because after the king he had been especially influential in the county through his strength and counsel.

On the sixth day before the Ides of April, Friday, homage was likewise done to the count. On the fifth day before the Ides of April, Saturday, the king went to Wijnendale [Note: [Col. 0995D] Wijnendale near Torhout.] to confer with that William of Ypres, the usurping count, concerning the making of peace between him and the true and new count. But to that usurping count it seemed utterly beneath him to enter into agreement with the true count of Flanders, or to make any settlement of peace, because he held him in contempt. “The king, therefore, taking grievously the arrogance and scorn of the usurping count of Ypres, and disdaining him, returned to us.”

On the fourth day before the Ides of April, Sunday, our count was to have gone to Saint-Omer by counsel of the king and princes; but because he had few men with him on the road in whom he could trust, he returned to us by night.

## CHAPTER XIII. Punishment inflicted upon Provost Bertulf and Guy of Steenvoorde. The tumult of the citizens of Bruges pacified.

91. On the third day before the Ides of April, Monday, Provost Bertulf [Col. 0997A] was delivered into the hands of that usurping count. The latter had therefore sought him with particular zeal and persistent effort, searching out the place where he lay hidden, so that, having captured him and made public that he had taken the provost of Bruges, he might chiefly restore the reputation of his power by inflicting a severe vengeance upon him. For, as we have written above, at the height of the treason he had sent to the same provost and his followers an open greeting from Ypres; thereby he had rendered his own reputation most shameful and treacherous throughout all the borders of the kingdoms.

Thus, when he had captured him as a fugitive and exile in his own country and among his relatives, he nevertheless could not sufficiently devise by what punishment of death he should destroy one said to be privy to the treason. And although that usurper seemed by such arguments of cunning and craft to prove [Col. 0997B] his own innocence, nevertheless God, whom nothing withstands, by whose authority it was said, “Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed” (Matthew 10:26), made known this inhuman shame and the traitors of so great a prince to His faithful, condemned them, proscribed them, and cast them down.

So great was the tumult, shouting, and concourse of the people of Ypres and of the whole surrounding district around that one captive man that we cannot adequately describe it. As they say, dancing, leading choruses, and offering diverse applause, they went before and followed the provost, dragging him with long ropes on his right and left, so that the line of those dragging him extended far in length and spread broadly apart from one another. Thus that man, formerly worthy and most powerful, was publicly mocked shamefully and disgracefully by all. Entirely naked except for his breeches, [Col. 0997C] covered with mud and stones, he was dragged along. Except for the clergy and a few who had formerly known the religious man, no one pitied him.

92. Worn down by so many injuries, wounded by so many insults and blows, he awaited from afar the punishment of his death. Before the eyes of his mind all that he had done might deservedly have been recalled to memory, if the crowd rushing upon his death had granted him any time to live. He might indeed, if he ought, have remembered how, violently intruded and unjustly set over the living Provost Ledbert—a worthy man who endured all things for God—he had usurped preeminence in the temple of God against God; how he had bartered little prebends by the Simoniac heresy; [Col. 0997D] how he had armed his nephews from the revenues of the Church for every crime; and how at last, by his consent or counsel, he had delivered to death the Catholic and most noble prince Charles, born of royal stock. As he confessed amid the anguish of his punishment, he could have defended him against treason, had he wished.

Before the eyes of his mind he might have set how much favour among the clergy, how much honour, reputation, wealth, influence, and reverence God had freely bestowed upon him—yet, while he possessed that grace of God, of which he was the steward, as though it were his own and natural, he had utterly failed to remember it. For thirty-six years he had been entangled in all the virtues and vices aforesaid in such a way that he seemed incapable of being disentangled. If anyone wishes to hear the complexity [Col. 0998A] of his lineage and the magnitude of his deeds, it is plain that he must believe rather in the wondrous combat of God and the hand which He exercised for their destruction. And although I may seem here to have an opportunity to describe his genealogy, yet I judge that I have sufficiently laboured for the work undertaken and shall refrain from such descriptions; for I have proposed to narrate the outcome of the siege, not the illegitimate origin of the provost and his kin.

93. Therefore the man went on—once glorious, now dishonoured; once venerable, now vile—with unmoved countenance and eyes fixed upon heaven. Unless I am mistaken, he invoked without vocal sound God, merciful toward the human condition, in which He Himself, clothed in it, rules human beings in the kingdom of the world; but in the secret of his mind he invoked Him as his ever-present helper. [Col. 0998B] Then one of his persecutors struck his head with a club and said: “Most arrogant of men, why do you disdain to look upon and speak with the princes and with us, who have power to destroy you?”

But he took no care to look at them. He was hanged in the middle of the marketplace of Ypres, beside the punishments of thieves and robbers, upon a gallows. They pulled off his breeches so that the more shameful parts of his body might be exposed. There was no shameful or disgraceful thing which they did not inflict as part of his punishment. Upon that gallows his arms were stretched out in the form of a cross and his hands inserted; his head was thrust through a hole in the same gallows, so that the rest of the man’s body, hanging from those limbs as though strangled by alien nooses, might die. When he was first hanged, and upon that instrument [Col. 0998C] of the gallows the man still supported his body somewhat upon the joints of his feet, so as at least thus to prolong the span of his wretched life, that usurping Count William came to him amid the many thousands who were stoning and pelting him. He ordered silence and said:

“Tell me then, O provost, I entreat you by the salvation of your soul: tell me, I beg, who, besides you and Isaac, and besides the openly declared traitors, are still secretly guilty and criminal in the death of my lord Count Charles?”

Before all he replied: “You know as well as I.”

Then William, seized by rage, ordered stones and mud to be thrown at that provost and that he be killed. And behold, those who had assembled in the market to buy fish [Col. 0998D] tore the man’s body apart with iron hooks, clubs, and stakes. Nor did they allow him long to remain supported by that aid of the instrument upon which he braced himself with the joints of his feet; rather, forcing him away from that support, they inflicted hanging and the loss of life amid the darkness of a most bitter death.

As he died, he made complaint concerning the treason by which Walter, a knight of Sarran and his own man, had betrayed him to that same death in which he was now dying; Walter, who ought to have given him guidance, had deceived him. The raging mob of Ypres then twisted a dog’s entrails around the provost’s neck and placed the dog’s mouth against his own as he was already expiring his vital breath, equating him and his deeds with a dog.

94. At the same time Guy, a renowned and strong knight, [Col. 0999A] who had been foremost in the counsel of the counts of Flanders, had conspired in the same treason because he had married the provost’s niece, namely Isaac’s sister. Therefore a certain Herman the Iron, a strong knight, immediately after Count Charles’s murder, and in the presence of that usurping count of Ypres, challenged Guy to single combat for having wickedly betrayed his lord. Guy declared that he was always ready to defend himself against the charge of treason brought against him. A day was appointed for them: the same day on which the aforesaid provost also endured the torments of his death.

Immediately after the provost’s death, all who were present returned to the court where the combat had been proclaimed between Herman the Iron and Guy, and both sides fought fiercely. Guy threw his opponent [Col. 0999B] from his horse and, as often as he wished, struck down with his lance the man attempting to rise. Then the opponent, running nearer, pierced Guy’s horse with his sword and disembowelled it. Guy finally fell from it and, drawing his sword, attacked his adversary.

Their encounter was unbroken and exceedingly fierce, with alternate sword-strokes, until, wearied by the weight and burden of their armour, both cast away their shields and, with the strength of wrestlers, hastened the victory of the contest. Herman the Iron fell prostrate to the ground, and Guy lay upon him, striking the knight’s mouth and eyes with iron gauntlets. But Herman, lying prone, as is read of Antaeus, gradually recovered strength from the coolness of the earth (Aeneid I, §14), and cunningly, while he rested, made Guy secure in his expectation of victory. Meanwhile, gently withdrawing his hand down to the lower edges of the hauberk, [Col. 0999C] where Guy had not been protected, he seized him by the testicles and, gathering all his strength for a single moment, thrust him away from himself. In that wrenching blow the whole lower nature of his body was ruptured; Guy fell so utterly that he cried out that he was defeated and dead.

Then the count, wishing in every respect to preserve his own reputation in this combat, ordered Guy, already dead, to be hanged beside the provost upon the same gallows, so that, as they had been equals in betrayal, so they might be equals in death by torture.

95. Afterwards the bodies of both men were placed upon cart-wheels, fixed upon a very high gibbet, and displayed for all passers-by to see. Their arms, bent toward one another’s necks as though in mutual embraces, marked out an image of their betrayal and counsel concerning the death of their lord, the glorious and most pious Count Charles, though they had now been dead for three days. Then one of the king’s squires came to us, [Col. 0999D] reporting in the king’s presence the outcome of the two men; he had been there that day and had seen both the provost and Guy hanging at Ypres.

It was immediately proclaimed to those besieged in the tower that their lord the provost had been captured and was dead, and that nothing remained to them except to surrender themselves to the king, to be treated according to the wickedness of their deeds. Thus pain and anxiety, mourning and sighing afflicted those miserable men, stripped of every hope of life: fear and despair besieged them more strongly than the leaders of the siege.

96. On the same day Gervase ordered the carpenters to dismantle the wooden tower [Col. 1000A] which had been erected earlier to attack the walls and now stood useless. He commanded its strongest beam, specially separated from the others, to be prepared and made into a battering ram with which the wall of the church might be breached. But while the archers of the besieged were trying to shoot arrows at the workmen from the summit of the tower in which they lived, the bow, with an arrow set upon it, fell from the archer’s hands at the very moment when, with the bow bent by the tension of its string, he hurried to draw it.

The knights who saw this, who had been promptly present and stationed over all the work of the craftsmen, protecting those working skillfully upon siege-engines—such as battering rams, sheds, throwing-machines, ladders, and similar devices by which they are accustomed to destroy walls and structures of stone—prophesied an evil outcome from the fall of the besieged men’s bow and arrow.

97. That same day toward evening, a serious tumult arose between Gervase and his men, and our citizens. For by command of the king and order of those leaders of the siege who were endeavouring swiftly to hasten the destruction of the besieged, and who throughout the whole period of the siege had spent great sums and laboured continually in watches and assaults, a general decree had been confirmed by their common counsel and royal edict: no one among the entire besieging multitude was to dare approach the tower and speak with the besieged, lest perhaps it be disclosed to them by what device they might be captured. A law was also established for transgressors: if anyone acted against this decree, he was to be cast into captivity [Col. 1000C] and punished by the common judgment of the princes.

Accordingly, one of the citizens, who had married the sister of a besieged knight, secretly approached the tower and asked his brother-in-law for vessels and clothes which he had lent him; and the knight returned the vessels he possessed. As that citizen passed through the marketplace on his return, one of Gervase’s knights, who had received the king’s, the princes’, and his lord’s command, together with authority to arrest transgressors of the decree, pursued him and forcibly brought him as a captive to the count’s house.

Immediately an immeasurable tumult arose among the citizens. Rushing to arms, they attacked the count’s house and Gervase’s household, who defended themselves stoutly from within. For the citizens cried that they would never endure anyone’s lordship; indeed, it lay within their own power to correct this wrongdoing. After they had continued the disturbance for some time, Gervase spoke these words in their midst:

“You know, O citizens and my friends, that at your request both the king and the count have now appointed me viscount of our place. In accordance with the decree of the king and princes, my knight has now arrested a citizen and neighbour of yours as a transgressor of the decree. By this deed you have personally slighted my dignity; you have attacked the count’s house and my household within it; and at last, without cause, you have rushed forth under arms in the king’s presence. Therefore, if you wish, I relinquish the viscountcy because of the injury inflicted upon me; I dissolve the faith and security established between us, [Col. 1001A] so that it may be clear to all of you that I do not seek lordship over you. If it pleases you, then, let us meet before the king with arms laid aside, so that judgment may be given between our people and yours.”

When he had finished his speech, they went up together before the king and were again reconciled to one another in faith and friendship as before.

## CHAPTER XIV. The siege advanced. The upper storey of the church occupied. Veneration of the tomb of Blessed Count Charles.

98. On the second day before the Ides of April, Tuesday, the king went up into the brothers’ dormitory with his wiser men and counsellors, carefully to determine at what point they might skillfully make an assault upon the church. The dormitory building was joined to the church, so that siege-engines might be prepared there [Col. 1001B] to breach the church wall and enter against the besieged. For when those miserable men could not hold the lower parts of the church, they had blocked with wood and stones the stairs leading up to the upper storey, so that no one could ascend and they themselves could not descend; they were trying only to defend themselves from the upper storey and the church towers.

Between the columns of the upper storey they had set up lookouts and fighting-positions from piles of chests and heaps of benches, from which they might cast stones, lead, and heavy objects upon those attacking the church. Likewise, before the openings of the tower windows they had hung tapestries and mattresses, so that they might perhaps not be struck from within by slings and crossbows [Note: [Col. 1001D] *Arbalistis*, as though *arcubalistis*; hence the French word *arbalète*, a bow furnished with a stock or crossbow.] when the tower was attacked from without. At the very summit of the towers stood the stronger youths among the besieged, [Col. 1001C] who cast millstones upon those moving about in the castle court.

Thus, having arranged their affairs in disorder within God’s church, they awaited the end of their death. They paid no reverence or honour to the blessed corpse which lay buried among them in the upper storey, except only this: scarcely recognizing their lord whom they had betrayed, they set a wax candle at his head, which burned continually in honour of the good count from the first day of the siege until the day on which entry was forcibly made against them. They had also placed flour and legumes around the count’s tomb, taking them daily for their own use and thereby sustaining life.

99. While the king and his men were diligently examining and marking out the point for breaching the church, Robert the Boy, [Col. 1001D] putting his head out through one of the church windows, spoke to the king’s knights and begged them to act as his messengers to the king. He humbly declared that he wished to submit himself to every judgment of the princes and barons of the land, his lord the king, so that by their law he might deserve either to live through the merit of his defence, or, if he could not clear himself, to be destroyed by a sentence of punishment.

No man dared bring the words of the messenger into the king’s presence, so gravely was the king angered even to see those traitors. Yet our citizens, the king’s knights, and all who heard how humbly the young man had pleaded with the lord king, were moved to tears and pitied him, praying for the Lord’s mercy on his behalf.

100. [Col. 1002A] On the Ides of April, Wednesday, the besieged invented a false report concerning the death of Borsiard: namely, that when a quarrel had arisen between Robert the Boy and Borsiard, he had fallen pierced by a sword. They believed that by this the minds of the princes might be softened from severity, so that they would not henceforth attack with such fury as before; and from the tower they announced Borsiard’s death, falsely spreading the report. Others asserted that he had escaped.

When he heard this, the king understood that those besieged men were now losing confidence, failing through fear and anxiety. With steadfast resolve he ordered his knights to arm themselves and attack the church. This was done so that, weakened and wearied in that encounter, the besieged might thereafter be unable to endure so many repeated assaults and attacks, but might rather yield and give the place of victory to the Catholic King Louis and his knights. [Col. 1002B] From midday until evening the attack was fierce on both sides, in hurling stones and shooting missiles.

101. On that day the king received from Dean Elias the keys of the sanctuary of the Church of Saint Christopher, because he had been informed that Count Charles’s treasure had been deposited in that sanctuary. When the king entered, he found nothing except saints’ relics. The truth was that the provost, as though a gift in the division of the plunder, had received from his nephews a gold cup with its cover and a *canna*, that is, a silver wine-vessel, from the robbery of the count. He had offered these same vessels to God for the work of the church, for the salvation of his soul.

When the siege was taking place and the brothers removed the relics and saints’ shrines from the castle, they secretly placed those two vessels in a certain chest, under the pretence that they were holy relics, and carried them out together with the other relics of the saints. The aforesaid dean entrusted that chest for safekeeping to a simple priest, Eggard, in the Church of the Lord Saviour, sealed under the veneration due to the most worthy relics. [Col. 1002C] How devoutly that simple priest received the chest, placed it in the sanctuary, poured out prayers, and sought the salvation of his soul, was evident from the testimony of his fellow priests in that church. Throughout the night he set before it lighted candles, tapers, lamps, and lanterns, believing that he could not sufficiently venerate those relics.

Indeed, that priest had sufficiently deserved that, when those vessels were restored to the new count, he should drink good wine once or more often from the same vessels. The king, therefore, searching everywhere for this treasure, had sent investigators and spies to collect Count Charles’s treasure secretly, but achieved nothing in this matter. The king even compelled Robert the Boy, on the second day before his departure for France, to be beaten with whips, so that, if he remembered anything concerning the treasure or knew who possessed any part of it, he might inform the king. By his accusation, on the same day the new count and the king obtained the aforesaid vessels, as we shall say below. Other besieged men proclaimed that Borsiard had fled, so that they might be attacked less fiercely under that falsehood.

102. [Col. 1003A] On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, Thursday, the battering ram—the engine made for breaching the church wall—was brought into the brothers’ dormitory, within the same enclosure outside which, on the inner side, the body of the good count lay committed in burial to his God. At once the builders of the ram raised ascending stages high in the air; and, after removing the wooden wall of the dormitory which stood nearest the church, they brought the top of the stages up to that point, so that any armed men who dared might advance by steps as far as the wall of the church.

For in the first construction of the church building, according to the arrangement of the old work, there was a window at that point toward which the builders had now directed the stages. But they held the approach of the engines somewhat lower, arranging the blows of the ram beneath the window, so that after breaching the stone wall they might freely occupy that same window as a doorway. The steps were very broad, and ten knights at once could stand abreast at their front to fight.

After these things had been arranged, they suspended the largest beam by ropes over those steps on that side for piercing the church. They attached loops to it, and placed armed men by the loops, who would pull the ram backward from the church, lift it high, and then, withdrawn by strength and force, strike it skillfully and methodically against the church wall. [Col. 1003C] Over the heads of those ascending, coverings of interwoven branches were fitted into and fastened to beams, so that, even if the roof of the dormitory were somehow broken by the besieged, the men driving the ram might work safely beneath the woven branches. They also set wooden walls before themselves for protection, so that they might not be wounded from within by missiles and arrows.

Accordingly, after the ram had been drawn back from the church wall by ropes as far as the men holding it with outstretched arms could do so, in one charge and one shout they hurled the ram’s exceedingly weighty rush and fall upon the church with all the strength and utmost effort of their bodies. At every blow a great mass of stones fell to the ground, until the whole masonry and wall at the point struck was pierced through. The ram’s head was reinforced with very solid iron fittings, so that it could suffer no injury by any device other than what it inflicted upon itself through the force of its own weight and strength. Thus the long labour of battering, [Col. 1003D] begun at midday, ended after evening.

103. Meanwhile, the besieged, sensing the weakness of the wall and that the breach would soon be made, uncertain and irresolute as to what they should do, finally prepared burning coals within, smeared with pitch, wax, and butter, and threw them onto the roof of the dormitory. Immediately the coals clung to the tiles and, as the wind blew, sent up flames, so that great raging flames seized the roof on every side. From the upper tower they threw millstones upon the dormitory roof at the point where the ram was breaching the church, seeking both to protect the fire set upon the roof so that no one might extinguish it, and to protect themselves from the danger of entry by crushing with stones, cast from above, those who were breaking through the church.

The overwhelming mass and magnitude of the stones did not impede the men working the ram. When the knights saw flames darting above their heads, one of them climbed onto the roof and, amid so many showers of stones and missiles, scarcely extinguished the fire. Then, after so many blows of the ram, a very large opening appeared in the church wall. It had been breached more quickly than was expected because, since the time of the church’s ancient burning, rain and inundating showers had left the whole church building as though rotten: it had remained bare without a wooden roof until then.

Then an immeasurable shout rose outside; and all who had attacked the besieged at the doors, in the lower choir, through the windows, and in every place where they had been able to gain access, learning that the church had been breached, fought with fiercer spirit and most eager boldness for victory. They had attacked steadily on both sides from midday until evening, almost failing from the labour of battle and the heaviness of their armour.

104. But when they understood that the ram had made a breach, refreshed and strengthened in spirit, they began—as though they had only then first rushed to arms—to harass the besieged and pursue them without restraint. The wretched besieged, though few in number, were still fewer in combat, since they did not have the advantage of fighting together in one place. They had to resist separately at every approach: at the doors, windows, choir, and especially at the place which the ram had now occupied. Having already suffered the miseries of life, they now expected loss and destruction at the hands of their enemies.

Those within the church who had hurled stones, arrows, spears, stakes, and missiles of every kind against the men operating the ram were the more fearful because they were few, because their accomplices were fighting separately and nearly failing from long exertion against so great an army, and, moreover, because they lacked weapons with which to protect themselves. Yet they resisted as far as they dared.

But the men operating the ram, the other knights of the king, and the armed, bold, and battle-eager young men of our city, when they beheld the besieged opposite them, regained their courage. They held before the eyes of their hearts how honourably it would be to die for father and country, [Col. 1004D] how glorious a victory lay before the conquerors, how wicked and criminal were those traitors who had made Christ’s church into a den for themselves, and—what seemed more evident—how eagerly and greedily they themselves rushed upon the besieged because of the plunder of their lord count’s treasure and money, and hurried for that cause alone.

Whatever their spirit may have been, without order, without battle, and without any regard for weapons, they hurled themselves in one rush through the middle of the opening, so that by rushing in together they deprived the besieged of place and time to fight or kill anyone. They did not cease from falling in until, without interruption, they had made themselves, as it were, a bridge. By the wondrous dispensation of God’s grace, they entered without mortal danger to their lives: some falling, some stumbling, some driven in by force, some struggling to rise after a fall and falling down, others—as commonly happens in such a tumult—rushing in disorder. With voices and shouts, the noise of running and falling, and the clangour and crashing of arms, they filled not only the church but the whole castle and its neighbourhood inwardly; while outside they praised and blessed God for the victory by which He had honoured His conquerors, exalted the king and his men, glorified above all things the name of His majesty, cleansed His Church in part from its defilers, and granted that His glorious martyr and leader of the good should then at last be mourned, surrounded by the devout veneration and prayers of His faithful.

105. Therefore, what had not previously been permitted was at last permitted to the younger Fromold: out of long desire and ardent spirit, to offer vows to God for the salvation of his lord the count; to make a sacrifice of tears and contrition of heart; and to rejoice with joy at seeing the place where his lord lay buried. Then for the first time he prepared funeral rites for his lord, whom he had been unable to see for all those days after he was buried—that is, forty-four days. For he had seen not the body but only the tomb from outside. He desired and prayed in word and heart that God, on the day of the common resurrection, might grant him at last to see his lord Charles the prince exalted with double glory among the faithful rulers and supreme princes of His present Church, to remain with him, and to be blessed with him forever in the glory of contemplating the Holy Trinity.

He considered it a great gift that he was permitted to mourn death beside his lord’s tomb, lament the fall of the whole country, and render with highest love the last offices to him whom he had loved while living and who had now been betrayed by his servants. He did this not without tears.

“O God, how many vows of Your faithful did You deign to receive on that day! And whatever worship of God had been interrupted in that church was indeed compensated at that hour by the greatness and multitude of the righteous prayers.”

A burning candle stood at the count’s head, placed there by those traitors in honour and veneration of their lord. After the attackers had rushed into the church against the besieged and a clamour had arisen as the latter fled, those most wicked men withdrew from the breach, the doors, and their defensive positions. Having climbed the tower, they resisted their pursuers upon the stairs in order to defend themselves.

The most Christian victorious knights of the king of France therefore hastened to block and close the stairs with stones, wood, chests, beams, and other materials, so that none of the besieged might descend into the upper storey in which the count lay. The king ascended into the church, mourned the death of his nephew Charles, and set a guard to watch the tower more carefully. Thus the king’s knights watched the tower and those besieged within it in alternating guards.

Whatever was found in that upper storey that could be plundered became everyone’s spoil. At last the canons of the same church ascended by ladders from the choir to the upper storey and appointed some of the brothers to keep vigils around the count’s tomb each night. Though the church’s furnishings had been broken, so that nothing remained in its former condition, they found, God guarding them, the altars and altar-tables unmoved. Rejoicing with joy, the brothers regarded whatever they later obtained as received not by right or merit, but solely by God’s gift.

Thus God brought that day to a conclusion—“to the conclusion” [*in conclusionem*, as printed]—of His enemies and to the victory of the faithful, exalting the name of His dominion unto all the ends of the earth. Yet those besieged did not cease to establish watches for themselves in the tower, blow horns, and act imperiously in so confined a condition, as though they still possessed some homage, not recognizing themselves to have become most miserable. For they had been given over to a reprobate mind. Whatever they did thereafter was pleasing neither to God nor to men, but rejected and hateful.

106. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, Friday, the people of Bruges assembled before the king, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and did reverence to his dignity, begging that, in consideration of their prayers and services, he grant Robert the Boy freedom to leave the besieged and receive the lawful clearing of his innocence. The king assented that he would grant their requests, saving the honour and favour of his own person together with that of the princes of the land, without whose counsel he had determined to do nothing in the matter.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, Saturday, the castellan of Ghent came in advance with Arnold of Geraardsbergen [Note: [Col. 1005D] *Grandberga* and *Grandmontium* are contracted forms for *Gerardiberga* and *Gerardimontium*, a town within the territory of Aalst. In the Chronicle of Saint Bavo it is called the land of Aalst and Geraardsbergen. Thus Johannes van Waesbergh of Geraardsbergen described it in a separate book.], and with the leading men of his district gathered together, earnestly petitioning the king in every way for the liberation of Robert the Boy. The king told him that he could grant them nothing consistent with his honour without the common counsel of the princes; otherwise he would act against his faith and oath.

## CHAPTER XV. The new count received at Saint-Omer. The right of rival claimants. The descendants of Count Baldwin of Lille indicated. The household of Provost Bertulf notorious for adultery and homicide.

107. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, on the Sunday “The Good Shepherd has risen,” word was brought to the king that the new count of Flanders had been joyfully received with honour at Saint-Omer, according to the custom observed for the predecessors of the counts of that land. For boys carrying bows and arrows had gone out to meet him: nimble and swift in their encounter with the count, advancing in bands, pretending as though to resist him in battle, girded and prepared, with their bows bent and strings drawn, so that, if need arose, they might attack the count and his men with arrows. Seeing the boys’ approach, the count and his men asked through an intermediary what they wanted. They cried out to the count that it was their right to obtain from him the fief which their boys had always held from his predecessors: namely, freely to roam in the woodland clearings on saints’ feast-days and in summertime, catch little birds, shoot squirrels and foxes, and devote themselves in recreation to such boyish pursuits.

> “We have therefore hitherto done these things freely, and we wish henceforth, by your permission, to renew the customs of our games.”

Accordingly the citizens, armed, next came out to meet him, awaiting the return of their boys and the arrival of the new count. Count William, who was just reaching youthful maturity and had scarcely passed beyond boyhood, good-naturedly and indulgently granted the boys their games; and, amid applause and encouragement with the boys, he seized their banner and standard and took delight in it. They began to sing his praises and to raise the sounds of dancing, when the citizens, watching from afar, saw the count solemnly received by the boys and coming down to them surrounded by applause and reverence for peace.
