Thus, after count and people had assembled together, the clergy of that place came in procession to meet him with incense and candles, in exaltation of his honour and glory, as is customary at the reception of those newly obtaining counties. Resounding with shouts of joy and harmonies of song, and with all the citizens applauding, they received him and solemnly brought him into the church amid the same sweetness of melody. There the canonically elected man devoutly rendered to God the duty of prayer; and people and clergy likewise prayed for him, that, while he administered the county, God might so govern and protect him that thereafter they might render what was due to both the count and God in peace and security. After the reception, they performed homage and gave assurances. He had come down to Saint-Omer from the city of Thérouanne.

108. At that same time Hugh of Campagne-lez-Hesdin and Walter of Forerdeflo, with their men, made an assault upon the castle of Aire, where that adulterine Count William of Ypres had shut himself and his followers in and strongly fortified the place and castle. For he had seized the county and had violently occupied many of the castles and strongholds of Flanders: the castle of Ypres, the town of Formeselles, the castle of Cassel, the fortress of Veurne, the castle of Aire, and the entire district surrounding the aforesaid castles, as well as the castle of Bergues and others. [Col. 1007D] For he was illegitimate in the line of the counts, and believed that he had acquired the county through that kinship by marriage. They threw down two knights of the aforesaid prince and gained five horses.

At the same time Baldwin of Aalst and Razo, with a very large army of Ghent, besieged the castle of Oudenaarde, in which the count of Mons had established and fortified himself and his followers, in order to seize the realm of Flanders, which more justly belonged to him by right of kinship.

109. For, to trace somewhat more deeply the origin of the earlier counts, Baldwin the Bearded was the founder of the lineage of the succeeding counts.

[Note: [Col. 1007D] This surname “the Bearded” is generally assigned by others to the father of this Baldwin, Baldwin IV, son of Arnulf the Younger. Thus the signature added to a charter of King Robert of France in the year 1034 reads, “the signature of Baldwin, count of Flanders, of the worthy beard”; he died in that same year and was succeeded by his son Baldwin V, surnamed the Pious and the Islander, who died in 1067.]

When he died, he was buried at Lille. He left two sons as heirs of the land of Flanders, Baldwin and Robert. While still living, their father ordered both to take wives. He caused Baldwin—

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Baldwin VI, called “of Mons” because he acquired Hainaut through his wife; he died in 1070 and was buried in the monastery of Hasnon, as was his wife Richildis, who died in 1086.]

—to marry Richildis, countess of Mons, in Hainaut. By her, her husband begot two sons: one was called Baldwin [Col. 1008B], the other Arnulf. Robert, then, took as wife Gertrude, countess of Holland. After the settlement had been concluded, he begot by her the abbess of Messines, and Gertrude—

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Gertrude, married to Duke Theoderic of Upper, or Mosellan, Lorraine, son of Gerard of Alsace, bore Simon, Theoderic, Gerard, and Henry. Of these Simon succeeded his father in Lorraine when the latter died in 1115, and himself died in 1129. Theoderic governed Alsace and afterwards Flanders. *The Origins of Alsace and Lorraine*, published by Hieronymus Vignier, pp. 112 ff. Henry was bishop of Toul.]

—the mother of Simon and Gerard; she became duchess in Alsace, for Duke Theoderic had married her. He also begot Adela, the mother of Count Charles, who, separated from her first husband, married the duke of Salerno. Her first husband also, King Cnut of Denmark, having been betrayed by his own men and slain in church, possesses the lot of the saints, having died a martyr for justice.

While that first father, Baldwin, lived, he spread out his sons, one on his left and one on his right, like two wings with which he might fly throughout all his lands. He himself alone ruled the middle region, namely Flanders.

110. [Col. 1008C] When, full of good days, he had died, his elder son Baldwin, count of Mons, obtained the county of Flanders with his wife Richildis. Fearing therefore that some disturbance or betrayal might be committed against himself and his sons by his brother Robert, he required his brother to render homage and give assurances to himself and his sons. Since, after taking counsel with the magnates, he knew this to be advantageous both to the country and to himself, he summoned his brother Robert, count of the Waters—

[Note: [Col. 1008D] Robert the Frisian is called “of the Waters” because he held the islands of Zeeland together with the neighbouring part of modern Flanders, called the Land of the Four Ambachten, places lying everywhere amid waters.]

—and convened his court at Bruges, together with the peers and barons of his entire county. In the presence of them all he declared these words:

> “I, Baldwin, count of Flanders, wishing henceforth to provide against the possibility that my sons and the inhabitants of my land may suffer any injury or disinheritance through the wiles and betrayals of my brother, entreat and command my brother Robert, count of the Waters, to swear faith and assurance to my sons after my death: [Col. 1009A] that after my death he shall inflict neither force nor deceit upon my sons by fraud or stealth; but, so long as he lives, he shall swear and maintain faith, in his own person and that of his men, toward my sons—that is, his nephews—as fully as can be known. And I shall give him many gifts and presents upon this condition.”

Accordingly, in the church of Saint Donatian at Bruges, an oath was made upon countless relics of saints, which Count Baldwin had ordered brought forward, in the presence of all who at that time were peers and princes in the land. Having received the gifts, the count returned.

111. When Baldwin, Richildis’s husband, died at Bruges, his son Arnulf, to whom the country belonged, returned with his mother toward Mons and the neighbourhood of the sea, and lived about Cassel, Saint-Omer, and those districts. [Col. 1009B] For that young man had not yet received arms, but had embraced the valour of knighthood.

Robert, count of Holland, heard that the country had been left to his nephews, who were still small in age, and that the boys’ mother had withdrawn herself with them from the frontier district near Bruges. This gave him both occasion and opportunity for betrayal. Secretly and treacherously he sent to the princes and leading men of the coastal district—at IJzendijke, Oostburg, Reddenburg, and Bruges—and to the maritime Flemings; by payment and promises he bound them to himself, so that through them he might obtain the county of the land and drive out his nephews, who were little children and incapable.

He had a cleric in his household who was a faithful messenger of this betrayal. When this man came so often to Bruges and the borders of Flanders, a rumour began to spread that the cleric was the messenger of treachery. Then, seeking to evade suspicion, on another occasion, while again carrying his lord’s orders to the princes, he pretended to be blind. Preceded by his guide, he followed with hands raised and feeling his way with a staff; and thus, blind in heart and eyes, he carried out the betrayal that brought death and blindness.

When the count of Holland had won the goodwill, pledged faith, and assurances of all the princes of the country, he embarked on ships and came secretly into Flanders with an armed force only. Having secretly summoned all the traitors, on a certain night they gave their accomplices a signal to set fire to a house at a place called Clipello, and to gather there at the signal of the flame. When all had assembled at that signal, their band was numerous and strong. They then openly went in pursuit of the boy Arnulf, who at that time was staying unsuspectingly at Cassel with a few men. Even those aware of the betrayal urged their boy-lord to make war against his traitorous uncle, promising that because he was resisting justly God would grant him victory.

Thus the boy Arnulf, encouraged for battle, met them with very few knights. In the tumult of battle, his own servants, who had armed him and knew the fittings of his armour, cast down their boy-lord as though they were strangers rather than servants [Col. 1010A], and cut his throat with swords.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] In the year 1072.]

After their lord had been betrayed, all who had fought on the boy’s side were put to flight. Some were killed and expired on the spot; others, mortally wounded, endured death after a few breaths of life. Many indeed were dead, many wounded, and many captured.

As Count Robert, secure from the enemy, ranged through his army, a certain Wulfric Kabel, who had remained faithful to the boy and did not know that he had been killed, attacked the traitorous Count Robert vigorously and with his own force, and took him captive. When the tumult of that day had subsided, all the peers of the country assembled, besieged that castellan Wulfric on every side at Saint-Omer, and compelled him to surrender Count Robert. When he had surrendered him, they established Robert as count of the country.

The brother of the betrayed boy Arnulf, who survived, was named Baldwin.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] Baldwin, called “of Jerusalem,” by Ida, daughter of Emperor Henry IV, left Baldwin III, [Col. 1010D] who by Yolanda, daughter of Gerard of Wassenberg, begot Baldwin IV, called “the Child.”]

He left heirs after him, from whose line comes this boy count of Mons, a valiant knight who is to obtain Flanders by right. Now, having heard of the betrayal of Count Charles, he claims his country and inheritance, the whole of Flanders, by hereditary right. He therefore does what he can; yet little of what belongs to him is done for our new count. In this ancient betrayal one should note the prophetic saying: “For God is accustomed to correct the iniquities of the fathers by the severity of vengeance unto the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 5:9).

112. That Robert who first betrayed his nephew is to be counted first. His son Robert, who lies at Arras, was second both in succession and in the county. After him his son, Count Baldwin, who lies at Saint-Omer, was third. After him came the fourth count, the best count of all counts, a star and foremost light of earthly rank; in his betrayal and martyrdom God brought to an end the corrective vengeance for the ancient betrayal, and conveyed to the rest of the saints him who was slain for the justice of his country, in the very place where the oath had formerly been sworn.

In the second betrayal God accomplished both things: he exercised vengeance for the old betrayal and immediately received among the holy martyrs the man dying for justice. Therefore, after that Count Robert who had betrayed his nephew had occupied the county, he always regarded with suspicion the traitors of Flanders who had handed over the county to him, and never allowed them to approach his counsel. Seeing themselves scorned and despised by their count, they separately formed a plan to kill the count by treachery and to raise Baldwin, brother of the betrayed boy Arnulf, to the county—as was just, since he was the more rightful heir of Flanders. Again, as formerly, they met in a deserted place to deliberate on bringing death upon their lord.

When they returned after obtaining an opportunity for betrayal, one of the knights involved in the plot threw himself at the count’s feet and accused the other accomplices in that wicked [Col. 1011A] treachery, who had sworn the count’s death. The accused men were summoned by the count to battle, convicted: some were beheaded, others condemned to exile, and many outlawed. Finally—if it were fitting to hear it, which indeed it is not, though it should be written for astonishment alone—in the fourth or third generation of the line, God in turn avenged the ancient betrayal upon the stock of the traitors by new perils and a new kind of casting down.

113. It is fitting now to recall somewhat more fully the origin of the provost’s family and his nephews. Boldran was castellan at Bruges, and his wife was named Dedda or Duva. A knight, Erembald of Veurne by birth, was Boldran’s man.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] This family was discussed above, §3.]

An expedition was ordered for the Flemings—

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Under Baldwin the Pious, or the Islander, as has been demonstrated in the same place.]

—and they proceeded by horses and ships for the defence of their country, as far as the place of danger and assault upon the land. [Col. 1011B] While they were sailing their ships down the river Scheldt, Boldran the castellan, his knight Erembald, in whom he trusted above the others, and many others besides, all clad in mail and ready for battle, were overtaken by night. They cast anchor in midstream to await daylight.

But this Erembald frequently committed adultery with the wife of his lord the castellan. The adulterous woman too, it is said, had promised her adulterer the viscounty, should her husband die soon. Therefore the adulterer was always plotting his lord’s death. In the silence of the night, as the castellan stood at the side of the ship to urinate, Erembald ran up behind him and hurled his lord far from the ship into the depths of the rushing water. This happened while the others slept; no one but that adulterer knew where the childless castellan had gone, drowned as he was.

Erembald then returned, married his adulteress, and bought the viscounty with the resources and wealth of his lord. By this wife he begot Provost Bertulf, Haket, Wulfric Cnop, Lambert Nappin, father of Borsiard, and Robert also, who became castellan after him in the second place. After Robert, his son Walter succeeded as heir in the third rank of the viscounty; after him Haket was castellan, in whose time Count Charles was betrayed.

Thus in this fourth degree the ancient casting-down of Boldran was punished in his descendants by this new casting-down [Col. 1011D], which occurred from the battlements of the count’s chamber at Bruges. Perhaps, by God’s dispensation, the sin of the parents was punished in them, as is read in Exodus, where the Lord says to Moses in chapter 33 of the same Exodus, when God gave laws concerning all things:

> “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me.”

114. Let us return to describe the event at Oudenaarde. The count of Mons, with the burghers of that place [Col. 1012A] and a charge of knights, fell upon the men of Ghent. Having put them to flight, he killed some, wounded others, and captured many. Indeed, the greater part of the fugitives were drowned in the very waters by which they had been transported in ships to arrange the siege. The count and his men prevailed in those parts. He had also taken the castle of Ninove—

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Ninove, called by others Nienhove, a town on the river Dender in the territory of Aalst.]

—and had placed in it his keenest and strongest followers.

On the same day at Bruges, an esquire escaped from the tower by rope. He was immediately captured, dragged to prison, and shut in there to await, though unwillingly, the day of his destruction.

## Chapter XVI. Surrender of those besieged in the tower. Reconciliation of the church of Saint Donatian. Funeral rites of Blessed Charles. Ypres taken.

115. [Col. 1012B] On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, Monday, our citizens again fell at the king’s knees, begging for Robert’s release. But the king, angered by those who troubled him so often, despised them. In wrath he ordered his servants to go quickly and cut down the tower with iron tools. They immediately began to demolish the tower below with those tools.

As they cut it down, mortal terror seized the besieged, so that they suffered immeasurable panic. Food and drink disgusted them; all their senses were dulled and languished. Wasted by hunger and thirst, although they had enough with which to sustain life, they called out to those whom they saw wandering outside in the castle court, awaiting already in part the fall and ruin of the tower being cut down. They said that they were drying up from the violent aridity of thirst and languishing from hunger and famine. By a wondrous dispensation of God, their own wine, already drawn and drunk, became sour and stinking and tasteless to those traitors; their grain and bread tasted rotten, and insipid water was of no benefit to them. Disgusted by the rotten taste and smell, they almost failed from hunger and thirst.

Compelled by this want, they sought permission to leave the tower and go to whatever other place the princes should decide they were to go. The cutters of the tower had already removed its steps, and only a little remained, which, once cut down shortly, would bring a most grievous fall and collapse.

116. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, Tuesday, when they understood that the greater parts of the tower had been cut through and that the danger of collapse was imminent [Col. 1012D]—for at every stroke of the hammers they felt reverberations and shaking at the tower’s summit, and, in infinite fear, perceived the tower as if already trembling and quaking—they took counsel to surrender themselves to the king’s power before they should be crushed and suffocated in the tower’s collapse and fall.

The boy Robert called for himself and his accomplices to surrender to the king, on the condition, however, that Robert himself should be held without imprisonment, although the others were to be thrust into prison. After the princes had deliberated, the king granted the besieged liberty to leave in accordance with their request [Col. 1013A], since it was highly advantageous that they should surrender willingly and without danger of death to the besiegers and those cutting down the tower.

They went out one by one, twenty-seven in all, toward the provost’s house, through a window slanting toward the tower stairs. Those who were more corpulent descended by ropes from the larger window of the same tower. The boy Robert was entrusted to the king’s knights to be guarded in the upper chamber of the count’s house; all the others were thrown into prison. Finally, as though doing a great thing for our citizens, the king entrusted Robert to their custody in fetters and chains, on condition that they should later surrender him to king and count to be dealt with by judgment of the princes. The citizens received the still adolescent young man into custody as a great gift upon the stated condition.

117. Here it should be noted how God reduced those traitors to a small remnant, both in lineage and in place. Before this crime, certain stronger and better predecessors of the same blood had died, whom it would take long to enumerate by name. At last these worst men were left, through whom God’s dispensation was completed: the betrayal accomplished, the country laid waste, plunder practised, and the hand of all armed against all.

When they believed that they had committed with impunity all the things they had treacherously done, and that no human being dared inflict vengeance, vengeance was left to God alone. He immediately confined and frightened them, so that they did not dare go outside the district of our town. Instead, they took counsel to fence and dig round our town and suburb, as we mentioned above. On the eighth day after the count’s death they were shut up in the castle through siege; then, after our men had taken the castle, they were driven into the tower and more closely confined; then they were thrown into prison, so cramped that they could not all sit together unless at least three or four stood.

Darkness, heat, stench, and sweat infected them, together with the horror of a desperate life and the disgrace of an uncertain future death. It would indeed have been granted them as a great gift of mercy had they been permitted to die as thieves or robbers perish by hanging. While they were preparing to leave the tower, one of the young men, having thrown down his sword, dared leap from a higher window of the tower and swiftly summon courage for flight. Though condemned by awareness of his guilt, he was prepared to enact in his body the liberty of his courageous spirit. Yet in the very attempt others held him back, and he endured going to prison with them.

Many of our citizens, seeing the young man’s danger and the captives’ misery, wept, because they could not without tears see their lords taken captive to prison. At last those pale wretches came out, bearing on their faces the marks of betrayal, hideously marked by livid discoloration and starvation. Then, as they emerged, an innumerable crowd rushed into the tower [Col. 1014A] and carried away as plunder everything found there.

While our people were rioting and running about in the tower, Benkin the coterel escaped by a rope let down from the tower to the ground, and hid as best he could until, during the night, he fled to the island in the sea called Wulpen.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] At the extremity of Flanders opposite Zeeland, separated from Cadzand only by the interposition of a very narrow stream.]

All, unanimously searching for him, believed that he had hidden even in drains and filthy places. Almost everyone then present at the siege struggled to climb the tower in hope of profit and of obtaining the count’s treasure. Then Gervase the castellan put armed knights inside, who thereafter prevented the disorderly people and those wishing to climb up. He secured the traitors’ best wine, including the count’s cooked wine, bacon—

[Note: [Col. 1013D] *Bacones*: lard or pork; French and English *bacon*; Flemish *baecke-speck*.]

—twenty-two *pisae* of cheese—

[Note: [Col. 1014D] A *pisa* of cheese is a fixed quantity of cheese. Thus Count Theoderic, among other donations made in 1130 to the monastery of Ter Doest at Bruges, grants four *pisae* of cheese from the alms of his table.]

—legumes, wheat flour, excellent baking implements, and all the best household furniture and vessels which they used. Yet none of the count’s treasure was found there.

118. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, Wednesday, the king went to Reddenburg to inspect the site and see how Lambert, accused and branded with the crime of treachery, had fortified himself there under siege. On that day, through the brightness of the sun and the mildness of the air, God renewed the world about us, because he had expelled from the sacred place the traitors and defilers of the temple and shut them in prison.

Rejoicing in these gifts of God’s grace, the brethren of the church, by every sort of washing, cleansed the floors, walls, and altars of the church, leaving nothing unwashed. They rebuilt the steps that had been cut away and, as though the church had been renewed, adorned their place with new furnishings and rebuilding.

119. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Thursday, a deer-hide covering was sewn in which the count’s body might be placed, and a shrine was also made in which they might lay and enclose it.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Friday, seven weeks having now passed since his first burial, the count’s grave in the upper chamber was opened, and his body was reverently removed from it with incense, frankincense, and spices. The brethren of that church had believed that the count’s body would by then stink and that no mortal could endure the stench, because it had remained buried in the upper chamber for seven weeks from the first Friday, the day of burial, until the Friday that followed, the tenth day before the Kalends of May. They therefore arranged that, as the body was raised from the tomb, incense and frankincense should be put beside the count’s resting place and burned in a fire, so that if any stench breathed forth from the tomb it might be suppressed by the power of the wholesome fragrance.

When the stone was lifted and they perceived no stench, they wrapped the body in deer-hide and placed it on a bier in the middle of the choir. The king awaited in the church, with a gathered multitude of citizens and all others [Col. 1015A], until the bishop and three abbots with him came in procession from the church of Saint Christopher with all the clergy and with the shrines of Saints Donatian, Basil, and Maximus, to meet the funeral procession and the king at the bridge of the castle, and to carry the blessed body back with tears and sighs to the same church of Saint Christopher.

There the bishop, with the whole choir of priests, celebrated the commendation and the Mass of All the Faithful Departed for the salvation of the good count’s soul. On that same day Benkin the coterel was captured.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] *Coterelli* are called people of lower rank because they live in huts and cottages; hence the word *cota* or *cotta*. Rigord, *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus*: “The count of Poitou had sent a multitude of coterels to Ralph’s castle as relief.”]

Bound to the upright beam of a wheel, he suffered the destruction of his life and became a spectacle for all. He had deserved to die miserably by that torture at Haren.

120. On the ninth day before the Kalends of May, Saturday, an edict went forth [Col. 1015B] from the king and princes that the citizens should make ready and prepare at Ypres and Staden—

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Staden, called Stathan by others, three hours’ journey from Ypres toward Bruges; Sanderus depicts its town hall in an engraving in *Castellania Iprensis*, p. 398.]

—for a siege. On the eighth day before the Kalends of May, Sunday, the church of Saint Saviour at Bruges was consecrated. That church had been burned by a conflagration, and its altars broken. On the seventh day before the Kalends of May, Monday, because the altars of the church of Blessed Donatian had not been broken, the bishop celebrated the church’s reconciliation early in the morning.

Then king and people, preceded by the bishop, abbots, and all the clergy of that place, went in procession to the church of Saint Christopher. Bringing the body of the blessed count, our lord and father Charles, back to the church of Blessed Donatian, they solemnly commended the body to God in the middle of the choir and suitably enclosed it in a tomb. When the funeral rites had been solemnly completed, the king and bishop installed Roger—

[Note: [Col. 1016D] Roger, or Rogerius, provost of Bruges, subscribed to the charters of Theoderic of Alsace in 1130 and 1136. We have demonstrated above that he died in 1157.]

—in the office of provost among the brethren of that church.

On the same day the king and our castellan Gervase, with a great army and together with our citizens, set out toward Staden and Ypres. It was also the feast of Mark the Evangelist. It should be noted that on that day God bestowed three great gifts upon the church of Saint Donatian: he deigned to reconcile that church to himself; he granted that the body of the good count should be kept in it; and he provided Roger to that same church as provost.

121. On the sixth day before the Kalends of May, Tuesday, the king and count besieged Ypres with a large army. A tourney took place, and the knights on both sides engaged fiercely, when that adulterine Count William fought with three hundred knights against the new count at one of the gates. Then those utterly wicked men of Ypres, as they had separately agreed with the king, admitted the king and his immense army by another part of the town. Rushing in, they suddenly raised cries and set houses on fire. They also practised plunder, while that adulterine Count William of Ypres came out to meet the raiders, unaware that both the castle and he himself with his followers had been betrayed.

The king and count captured him and carried him prisoner to Lille for safekeeping. Many had gone over to him after the death of Count Charles—chaplains and officials, men in pay and servants from the count’s daily household—because that adulterine count of Ypres was descended from the line of the counts. The men of Veurne also served with him, intending that, if he should establish himself in the county, they might destroy their enemies by his strength and power. But because God strikes the minds of the wicked, the contrary befell them. When their enemies heard that William of Ypres had been captured, they attacked the hostile possessions, houses, and households, and destroyed by fire and sword all the substance of those whom they hated. Thus it was not enough for those wretches that they were captured; they also suffered the loss of their goods at home.

So God pursued those traitors, who had conspired with their count of Ypres in the death of the lord and protector of the land, both in warfare and at home. Our count therefore took possession of everything which William of Ypres had held; he also captured his knights and drove many from the land. Thus our side acted victoriously that day, and returned with applause and very great plunder.

## Chapter XVII. Punishment inflicted on many guilty persons. The vessels of Blessed Charles restored. A new inquiry into the accomplices.

122. [Col. 1016C] On the Kalends of May, Sunday, news was brought to us at Lille that Borsiard had been captured, bound to the upright beam of a wheel, lived through that day and the following night, and then perished in the ruin of his shameful death. He deserved to die without end, if he could have died so many times, since because of his crime so many after him were punished, outlawed, hurled down, hanged, and beheaded. At his destruction all the faithful gave thanks to God, who had deigned to expel so great a murderer from his church.

It was fittingly ordained amid the past troubles of the times that, with the pleasantness of the month of May, God should restore the grace of peace and the stability of our land, Borsiard having been suspended and his accomplices captured. The king then turned and went toward Oudenaarde, where the count of Mons had attacked our land, passing through Ghent. Our count had preceded the king and, by violent action, had burned the suburb as far as the stone tower.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] How ineptly these matters are reported by Meyer—or rather transferred by him, and by the vernacular annals and others, to the beginning of Blessed Charles’s county—has been discussed at length above, §3.]

Moreover, many who had taken refuge in the church of that place were burned together, as many as three hundred, it is said.

123. On the fourth day before the Nones of May, Wednesday, the king returned to Bruges without the count. On the third day before the Nones of May, Thursday, later, about midday, the count returned to us. The brethren of the church of St Donatian first received him in procession; after prayer and an offering had been made to God at the altar according to the custom of his predecessors, the count himself returned to Count Charles’s house, entered it in state, and dined there. There was a very great commotion and crowd around and within the castle, waiting to see what would be done with Robert and the prisoners.

The king therefore left his lodging and came to the count. But since the house was full of people, attendants, and soldiers, the count went down into the square and courtyard of the castle. All who had been standing in the hall followed him. When they saw the house empty, as he had arranged beforehand, he had the doors of his house barred; then, taking only the leading men with him, he went up again. They then decided from which side of the tower-chamber those traitors should be cast down.

When this had been arranged, the king and count sent guards to the prison, who were cunningly to summon out first Wulfric Cnop, brother of Provost Bertulf. Those sent lied to the prisoners under a pretence of concealment, saying that the king intended to deal mercifully with them. Under this hope of mercy, they came out of prison without delay. Yet they were not permitted to leave all together. First they led out Wulfric, conducted him through the inner parts of the house to the battlements of the highest tower, bound his hands behind his back, and, as he looked down upon the beginning of his death, the guards threw him down.

The wretch, clothed in nothing but a shirt and breeches, fell to the ground with his whole body shattered and crushed, retaining little life; he immediately breathed his last in death. Thus made a spectacle and an everlasting disgrace to his family—indeed, to the whole land of Flanders—he perished unmourned by anyone.

Second, they brought out Walter, a knight, son of Lambert of Reddenburg, to the precipice. His hands were bound in front, not behind, and they were about to cast him down at once. But he begged the king’s soldiers standing nearby, for God’s sake, to grant him time to pray to God; moved by pity, they allowed him to pray. When he had finished praying, this young man of notably handsome appearance was hurled down. Falling to the ground, he underwent the danger of death and immediately expired.

A knight named Eric was also led away and similarly cast down. He fell upon a wooden ladder and tore out a rung which had been fastened with five nails. It was remarkable that, though thrown from such a height, he still sat upon the ground and signed himself with the sign of the holy Cross. When women wished to touch him, one of the soldiers threw a great stone among them from the count’s house and thus prevented their approach. Certainly he could not long survive inwardly intact; for even that which he lived after the fall was not life but the misery of dying.

To omit the order of enumeration, all the rest likewise were thrown down: twenty-eight in all. Some of them hoped to escape because they had been innocent of the betrayal. But because fate drew them on—or rather divine vengeance compelled them—they were thrown down together with those guilty of betrayal.

124. On the day before the Nones of May, Friday, on the feast of St John, when he was put into the vat, the king, beginning his journey home, departed from Bruges and took with him the boy Robert as a prisoner. As the young man departed, our citizens of Bruges followed him with tears and heavy lamentation, because they had loved him greatly. Yet, because of the disgrace attaching to the man of our town, they did not dare follow him further.

Looking back upon the weeping and pity of the citizens, he said: “Behold, my friends, since you cannot save my life, at least pray to God that He may deign to have mercy on my soul.”

He had not gone far from the castle when the king ordered the feet of that young man to be fastened beneath the belly of the horse upon which the prisoner rode. After the count had provided the king with an escort, he returned to us in the castle.

125. On the Nones of May, Saturday. Afterwards Dean Elias returned to the new count the silver drinking-cup and the golden cup of Count Charles, with its golden cover, which Provost Bertulf had entrusted to the dean when he took flight. The boy Robert had revealed this treasure to the count before leaving Bruges because, as they say, the king had extorted from him by scourging the information whether he knew of anything from the count’s treasure that had been stored away.

Many were astonished at the simplicity of Dean Elias. Although he had hitherto lived with the severity of a kind of sanctity, by receiving this plunder he had gravely departed from the tenor of sanctity and simplicity which he had professed—for it is forbidden by divine authority: “Do not touch what is unclean …” He returned that treasure to the count unwillingly, sufficiently showing by this how much he had loved the plunder.

He also said that Provost Bertulf had bestowed those vessels upon the church of St Donatian for the salvation of his soul, believing that thereby he could excuse his own innocence. In this too we all plainly learned that the provost had received the count’s vessels for his own use in the division of the treasure; and, unable to take them with him when fleeing, he left this most wretched plunder with his dean.

126. It will subsequently be possible to speak of the penitence of Borsiard and of those who, with him, had betrayed the count—Isaac and others. They assert that Borsiard acknowledged his sin, grieved and repented of it, and begged all the spectators of his gallows to cut off the hands with which he had killed his lord Charles. He begged all, at least, to pray and entreat God for the salvation of his soul, since he had deserved no salvation in this life; and, insofar as he knew and could, he called upon almighty God to be merciful to him.

Moreover, when those who were thrown down looked downward from the battlements, they signed themselves with the sign of the holy Cross and, invoking the name of Christ Jesus, cried aloud even while falling. But because those traitors were excommunicated immediately after the deed had been committed, they were not absolved by the bishop either before or after their destruction, owing to the strictness of justice; and therefore they lie buried outside the cemetery, at crossroads and in open fields.

[Note: Lernutius, drawing on his Annals, asserts: “By the king’s command they were carried outside the city into the fields, adjoining the boundaries of St Bavo and St Andrew, and hung there for a long time as a foul spectacle to travellers.”]

127. Isaac, then, while hiding among monks in a monastic habit, foresaw the crowd rushing upon him and said to the abbot: “My lord, if I had the will to fight, I would not allow myself to be taken without the slaughter of many. But because I acknowledge myself guilty of betrayal, I embrace every evil and temporal death itself, so that in this present life there may be punished in me the grave sin which I committed against my lord.”

The son of the advocate of Thérouanne then came forward, seized Isaac, and threw him into chains until that illegitimate count of Ypres should arrive and judge him.

[Note: These matters should be referred to no. 80, where his punishment, inflicted on 23 March, is briefly discussed.]

Isaac too awaited that same William, believing that he could escape through him because William had been privy to the betrayal. But after that count had come, concealing his own guilty knowledge, he ordered Isaac to be hanged because he had betrayed Count Charles.

On the road by which he was being dragged to be hanged at the castle of Aire, Isaac openly declared that he had betrayed his lord. He begged the tumultuous crowd to overwhelm him with mud, stones, and clubs, believing that no punishment in this life could be sufficient for one who had committed so great a crime. Thus he welcomed the blows, strokes, stones, and all his punishers, and gave them thanks because they deigned to destroy so grievous a sinner.

At last, when he reached the place of hanging, he greeted the trunk of the tree, kissed the ropes and the tree together, fastened the noose around his own neck, and said: “In the name of the Lord, I embrace the punishment of my death, and I beg you all to pray to God with me, that whatever I, miserable man, have sinned against my lord may be punished in me by this bitterness of death.” Thus, lifted by the noose, he deserved to die shamefully.

[Note: These matters also pertain to chapter 13, where the punishment of the provost was discussed.]

128. Provost Bertulf had received many signs from God of his death. For when the keeper of the church at Bruges was ill in his chamber, the provost entered to visit him; immediately the beams supporting the roof over his head broke, so that he scarcely believed that he had escaped from the chamber.

At another time, a great beam in his house at Bruges fell—not driven by a man or by wind—directly upon the chair and seats beside it, where the provost customarily sat with power and imperiousness. He himself was at Furnes at the time, and everything caught in that collapse was utterly shattered.

At another time, when the provost was passing through Ypres beside the gallows set up in the marketplace, on which he was later hanged, he said to his knights: “Almighty God, what was it that I dreamed last night? In a dream I saw myself standing fixed upon this very gallows.” He mocked such a vision and regarded it as nothing.

But we heard something of his punishment, and nothing of repentance. The boy Robert was taken as far as Cassel and, by the king’s command, beheaded; but, having confessed his sins, he forgave his executioner for delivering him to death.

## Chapter XVIII. Investigation into the accomplices and helpers of the traitors, and the plunderers of Blessed Charles’s money. Various persons privy to the betrayal die.

129. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, Saturday, the vigil of Pentecost, Eustace, newly appointed castellan of Furnes by the new count of Flanders, brought Oldger, formerly chamberlain of Provost Bertulf, as a prisoner with him to Bruges before all the members of the count’s court. The prisoner was to inform the count which canons or laymen had obtained from Provost Bertulf, or from the provost’s nephews, the treasure and spoils of Count Charles.

He accused Dean Elias of having three hundred marks; Canon Littera, two hundred marks; Robert, keeper of the church, mattresses, cloaks, and silver; Master Ralph, six silver cups; and Robert, son of Lidgardis, one hundred marks of silver. Oldger had fabricated such lies in order thereby to earn the favour of escape.

Yet this seemed likely to many, because Dean Elias had already, upon the accusation of the boy Robert, returned to the count a silver drinking-cup weighing twenty-one marks and a golden cup with its golden cover, weighing seven marks of gold. It appeared that both that dean and some of his canons still retained much silver, as later became clear.

For Robert, keeper of the church, freely entering and leaving among those traitors throughout the siege, had received from them a very large sum of money on condition that, if the traitors escaped, he—the priest and keeper—would return what he had received for safekeeping. After those wretches had been condemned, that keeper wished craftily to conceal the money. He therefore pretended that he was going to Jerusalem, loaded three and a half strong palfreys, and left our castle early in the morning. In this way he carried off Count Charles’s plunder to offer it to Christ in Jerusalem.

[Note: We have indicated, in the Life of Charles, Abbot of Villers, 29 January, no. 16, that *palefredi* or *palfredi* means horses. Vossius and others discuss the origin of the word.]

Because of this deed, everyone’s suspicion turned upon those canons. On the same day Littera returned to the count three marks of silver which he had retained from the provost’s silver.

130. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, holy Pentecost Sunday, the count, Castellan Gervase, Walter of Frorerdeslo, and the Flemish knights who were present swore that they would preserve the peace throughout the whole land of Flanders to the best of their power.

131. After the feast of the Nativity of St Mary, which falls on the sixth day before the Ides of September, namely Saturday, our count had William of Ypres—whom he had captured during the assault upon Ypres—brought to Bruges. He shut him in the uppermost chamber of Bruges castle with his brother Thiebald Sorel.

[Note: Thiebald is mentioned nowhere else; perhaps he was only a half-brother. The name was rather common at that time. For Tietbald of Vitry and Tretbald of Vermelles signed Count Thierry’s charter for the monastery of Marchiennes in 1135, in Chesnaeus, book II of the *Proofs concerning the Béthune Family*, p. 24.]

After they had remained imprisoned together for six days, Thiebald was entrusted for safekeeping to a knight named Everard of Ghent. William of Ypres was immediately forbidden to look out through the windows, but was allowed only to walk about inside the house. Guards and watchmen were also placed with him, who watched him with the utmost care.

132. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, Friday, on the night of St Lambert, the count commanded the best and most faithful persons from every neighbourhood around us and from the citizens of Bruges, together with Castellan Gervase, to swear for the honour of the land that they would truthfully declare: who killed Count Charles, or who killed those slain with that aforesaid count; who plundered the count’s goods and those of the persons killed with him, or the goods of the count’s men and household; who joined himself in support of the traitors after the death of the lord of the whole country; who had remained with those most wicked men before or after the siege; who, without the leave of the princes who were besieging the castle and those within it, had led out the traitors and their accomplices and for that reason secretly received money and the treasure of Count Charles from them; and who had afterwards detained and aided those whom the king and count, by the common counsel of the barons of the land, had condemned as guilty and decreed should be outlawed.

After the oath they sat together in the count’s house and accused before us one hundred and twenty-five persons. At Reddenburg they accused thirty-seven with Lambert, whom they had marked as guilty of betrayal.

133. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, Saturday, the feast of St Lambert, the count, intending to go toward Ypres, demanded a toll from our citizens of Bruges. But the count was unwelcome to them because his knights had been enfeoffed with the revenues of that toll from the time of all his predecessors as counts. His knights harassed the count because he had remitted the toll to the citizens of Bruges, from which they had hitherto held their fiefs. They maintained that the count could not lawfully remit it without the consent of his knights, nor could the citizens lawfully have asked the count to remit it to them. Thus hostility was stirred up between the citizens and the count with his knights.

According to the law of the siege established by the princes, the count and his men then sought to proceed against those accused. The statute and decree were as follows: whoever led any of the besieged out against the will of the leaders of the siege should be condemned to the same penalty which the person led out would have suffered.

Now many of the besieged had secretly been led out for payment. The relatives of those who had been killed while besieging the traitors therefore fell at the count’s knees, begging him to hand over to them for killing or punishment those who had secretly, furtively, and treacherously led the besieged away, or to expel such seducers from the land. Compelled by this consideration, the count ordered the accused to stand before him, intending to deal with them according to the law of the siege.

But they replied that they had not been lawfully accused, but out of envy and hatred, not for the sake of truth. Nevertheless, they earnestly begged the count to deal with them according to the judgment of the scabini of the land, both concerning the charge of betrayal and concerning every ground of suspicion.

Several of the accused were reconciled with the count, though the nephews, sons, and kinsmen of those slain in the siege still pursued them, either because they had spirited away traitors who had betrayed Charles, lord of the land, together with the fathers of these accusers. Such were the sons of the castellan of Bruges, who even in the new count’s presence hurried to accuse Everard of Ghent, because for money he had led out those besieged men who had killed their father and brothers together with the count of their country.

When this was heard, the greater part of the accused withdrew, their own conscience gnawing at them. The count therefore took counsel and, having summoned his barons, decreed that he should outlaw those accused men who had done homage to Count Charles and had also aided the traitors while besieged with them; that he should admit others to make satisfaction; and that he should mercifully receive others into his favour without judgment.

134. It happened, by the stern and terrible judgment of God, that Walter of Frorerdeslo, one of the peers of the land, while on a military expedition, was thrown from his horse by the force of his own riding, was completely shattered and lay ill, and shortly afterwards died.

It was indeed true that he had been privy to the betrayal of his lord and father of the entire land of Flanders. To ensure that he might stand in the most certain security with the traitors, he united in marriage to the niece of Provost Bertulf an adopted son of a shoemaker, whom his wife had falsely claimed to be his son. For Walter had believed the boy truly to be his own son, whom the mother had long deceitfully pretended to have borne as the wife of Walter aforesaid. But the infant whom she had borne had died immediately in childbirth.

She therefore substituted the shoemaker’s son, who had been born at about the same time; and she secretly gave her own dead child to the shoemaker’s wife, paying her to confess that she had borne that dead child and to conceal from her husband what had been done. When that stolen and adopted son had grown up, and everyone believed him truly to be Walter’s son, the provost came and gave his niece—the daughter of his brother—to that stolen son as wife, so that through that marriage they might stand together firmly through every fortune and become bolder, stronger, and more powerful.

After Walter’s death, however, his wife publicly declared that the boy was not her true son but an adopted one, whom Walter himself had pledged to a certain man of Bruges for three hundred pounds. Thus the contrivance of the provost was deceived by God’s contrivance: wishing proudly and gloriously to exalt his own family through that marriage, he joined it, deceived by God’s artifice, to the son of a shoemaker.

No one dared lay hands upon Walter, although he had been privy to the betrayal. For he was the peer of that land, second only to the count. But God, to whom vengeance was left, removed him from the sight of the faithful by a lingering death.

135. On the eighth day before the Ides of October, Saturday before the feast of St Richarius, William of Ypres was taken by the count’s order to the Islands and entrusted to the castellan of that fortress.

[Note: Meyer wrote that by this time William had fled to England and, with the king’s forces, captured Sluys. We have said that this fabrication is most effectively refuted by the present passage when compared with no. 152, where he is said to have been brought out of prison on 27 March of the following year.]

The count feared our citizens, and also those outlawed from the land, lest by some trick they free William from imprisonment at Bruges and violently attack the castle.

It should be noted that, after Count Charles was killed, Borsiard and his accomplices in that crime, in the manner of pagans and sorcerers, on the night when Count Charles was first buried, took a cup full of beer and bread. Sitting around the tomb, they placed the drink and bread upon the table of the sepulchre, eating and drinking over the body of the blessed count in the belief that no one would by any means avenge him.

136. On the ninth day before the Kalends of November, Monday, before the feast of St Amand, Baldwin of Aalst died. He too, one of the peers among the peers of Flanders, had been marked by the evil of complicity in the betrayal of his lord Charles, and not long afterwards breathed his last, having left this life.

The occasion of his death was slight. While he was blowing a horn, and the passage within was already swollen with wind, and all the strength of his head laboured to blow, the marrow of his brain was suddenly shaken from its natural place and burst out through an old wound in his forehead. When the swelling of the wind and of his own breath had burst it open, the brain matter which had lain in his skull boiled forth, blocking the passages of the nostrils, eyes, and throat; and so, dying, he endured the deadly blows of God’s sword.

At last, as he breathed his final breath, he received the monastic habit and so departed from the world in the manner of a Christian knight.

These two aforesaid leaders of the land died near one another, though separated by an interval; and all inhabitants of the land spoke and remembered them, discussing their sudden deaths. After the death of Lord Charles, God had deprived them of life by so swift a judgment and arranged for them an occasion and manner of dying from so slight a cause.

They had indeed acted contrary to Christian custom during the siege with the provost and others whom they had led out of captivity. Having received money from the provost and his men, after leading them away by byways contrary to the decrees of the king and princes, they left them naked and alone in open places, until those men, wandering and travelling through fields and villages, were captured and destroyed by the extermination of a most wretched death.

137. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, Saturday, after the third week of the Lord’s Advent had ended, in the same year, on the Ember Days: Desiderius, brother of Isaac, that aforementioned traitor, died. Being privy to the betrayal, he did not deserve to enjoy longer the happiness of life.

From the time of the siege he had not dared to appear openly at the count’s court, except secretly. For many in our county would have challenged him to judicial combat and convicted him of betrayal if he had gone openly to court. Moreover, the new count forbade Desiderius, even if he happened to come to court, to serve him drink; for Desiderius had been one of the cupbearers at court.

## Chapter XIX. The occasion of the Flemings’ defection from Count William the Norman.

138. On the Ides of August past—thus, on the feast of St Peter in August—after the fair had been held in the Islands, the count wished to arrest one of his servants there in the marketplace and ordered him seized. The citizens of the Islands rushed to arms, drove the count and his men out of the suburb, beat some members of his court, threw Normans into the marshes, and injured many others in various ways.

The count immediately besieged every quarter of the Islands and compelled the citizens to pay him fourteen hundred marks of silver, if only in that way they might be reconciled. Consequently the greatest hostility arose between those citizens and the count, so that thereafter they stood mutually suspicious of one another.

139. On the third day before the Nones of February, Friday after the feast of the Purification of the Lord’s Mother, the citizens of Saint-Omer rose against the count because he unjustly wished to impose upon them the castellan of that place, who had violently plundered the goods and property of those citizens and still strove to plunder them. The count also besieged Saint-Omer with a heavy army.

But the citizens secretly introduced Arnold, nephew of Count Charles, did homage to him, and gave securities that, should the new count persist in the unjust siege, they would turn to Arnold. At the same time snow, ice, cold, and an east wind fell fiercely upon the face of the earth. They therefore feared the count’s attack and paid six hundred marks of silver to secure reconciliation. From this arose the greatest hostility between those citizens and the count, and thereafter they became suspicious of one another.

140. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, Thursday before Septuagesima, the citizens of Ghent rose against their castellan because he had always acted unjustly and perversely against them. He went to the count, who brought him and the citizens together in order to reconcile them.

[Note: Extracts from what follows to the end were published by Chesnaeus in the *Proofs concerning the Family of Ghent*, beginning at p. 205.]

The count, wishing to oppress the citizens and violently impose the aforesaid castellan upon them, waited there for some days. Then the citizens, as they had agreed with Prince Daniel and Iwan, brother of Baldwin, called the count to account. All having assembled at Ghent, Iwan was appointed spokesman of the citizens and began as follows:

“Lord Count, if you had wished to treat our citizens and your citizens of Bruges, and us their friends, according to law, you ought not to have inflicted upon us wrongful exactions and oppressions. Rather, you ought to have defended us from enemies and treated us honourably.

“But now, contrary to the law and to the oaths which we swore for you concerning the remitted toll, the confirmation of peace, and the other rights which the men of this land had obtained from the good counts, your predecessors, especially in the time of Lord Charles, and from yourselves: you have in your own person broken those things, violated both your own pledged faith and ours, we who swore the same oath together with you.

“It is clear how much violence and plunder you committed in the Islands, and how unjustly and perversely you persecuted the citizens of Saint-Omer. Now you will likewise, if you can, treat the citizens of Ghent badly. But since you are our lord and lord of the whole land of Flanders, it is fitting that you deal with us reasonably, not violently, not perversely.

“Let your court, if you please, be held at Ypres, a place in the middle of your land. Let the leaders from both sides, our peers, and all the wisest men among clergy and people meet in peace and without arms, with calm minds and after careful consideration, without deceit or malicious contrivance; and let them render judgment.

“If you can henceforth retain the county while preserving the honour of the land, I wish you to retain it. But if you are such a man as one without law, without faith, deceitful, and perjured, depart from the county and leave it to us to entrust to some suitable and lawful man. For we are mediators between the king of France and you, so that you should do nothing of consequence in the county without the honour of the land and our counsel. Behold: you have perversely treated, contrary to faith and oath, both us, your sureties before that king, and the citizens of almost the whole of Flanders—contrary to the oath of the king himself and ours, and thereafter of all our leaders in the land.”

141. The count then sprang up and would have performed the formal renunciation of homage against Iwan, had he dared because of the uproar of those citizens. He said: “I therefore wish, rejecting the homage which you rendered me, to make myself your equal and without delay to prove by war against you that I have hitherto acted well and reasonably in every respect in the county.”

But Iwan refused and fixed a day: Thursday at the beginning of the fast, the eighth day before the Ides of March, when they should meet peacefully at Ypres.

The count therefore went down to Bruges and, summoning the knights of that neighbourhood, commanded them to hasten with him to the appointed day, armed and ready for him. Having summoned the citizens at Bruges, he complained to them how dishonourably Iwan and his men, if they could, were expelling him from the land, and begged them to stand faithfully with him. They agreed.

Accordingly, on the appointed day the count came up with an armed force and filled Ypres with knights and *coterelli*—men of lower rank—prepared and equipped for battle.

[Note: *Coterelli*, that is, persons of lower status, as stated in chapter 16.]

Iwan and Daniel also came up near Ypres, namely at Roeselare, and sent messengers ahead to the count saying: “Lord Count, because the day was fixed in the sacred season of fasting, you ought to have come peacefully and without deceit and arms, proceeding reasonably; but you have not done so. Rather, you stand ready to fight against our people. Iwan, Daniel, and the citizens of Ghent command you: because you have come to kill them treacherously, they do not delay, through us, to renounce the homage which they have hitherto kept inviolate toward you.”

Those messengers formally renounced homage on behalf of their lords and departed.

142. Before this time Iwan and Daniel had sent through the towns of Flanders this message of greeting: “Let us mutually give hostages and sureties, if you wish to live honourably in the land, so that, should the count seek to fall violently upon you or us, we may everywhere run together to our mutual defence.”

The towns most willingly agreed to do this, provided that, with the honour of the land and their own honour preserved, they could be rid of this utterly perverse count, who attended to nothing except how he might persecute his citizens by cunning. They added:

“Behold how the merchants and all the traders of the land of Flanders are besieged because of this count, whom you substituted in the county for the most worthy father Charles. During this year we have consumed our resources; moreover, whatever we gained in another time, either this count has taken away or we have consumed while shut up and besieged within this land by his enemies. Consider, therefore, by what means we may be rid of this robber and persecutor of ours, while preserving the honour of the land and yours.”

Meanwhile the count at Ypres was laying snares for Daniel and Iwan, gathering to himself all the knights of the land.

143. On the fifth day before the Ides of March, the first Sunday of Lent, a true report struck us: the young Thierry, nephew of Count Charles, had come from Alsace to Ghent and was waiting there until this count and his Normans should be expelled, so that he himself might be received as count.

It is very remarkable that Flanders should receive so many lords and at the same time be prepared to receive the boy from Mons, Arnold, whom they had secretly introduced at Saint-Omer, this man who now waited at Ghent, and our own pretended count. The castellan Thierry and his kinsmen and friends hastened to receive this Norman as our count; those at Saint-Omer, Arnold; those at Arras and in the borderlands, the count of Mons; and Iwan, Daniel, and the citizens of Ghent, this Thierry as count.

144. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, Friday, the citizens of Bruges rushed into the castle, seeking to discover whether the younger Fromold had filled the count’s house with grain, wine, and other provisions to be kept for the use of Count William. On the same day, hearing that the count was coming into the suburb of Bruges, they closed the gates against him should he arrive, no longer wishing to regard him as count.

145. On Ember Saturday, after the full first week of the fast had passed, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, the feast of the virgin Gertrude, Castellan Gervase ordered all inhabitants of his viscounty to prepare themselves, so that they might assemble at Torhout, equipped for war, on the Wednesday after the aforesaid Saturday, waiting there until our Count William should lead them to fight against Daniel and Iwan.

146. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the feast of Abbot Benedict, our castellan Gervase returned from Torhout to Bruges with his men. He reported that Arnold, nephew of Count Charles, had for a second time been secretly introduced into Saint-Omer by certain citizens.

When he learned this, William, count of Flanders, hastened from Ypres with a strong force to Saint-Omer, drove Arnold, while under siege, into the church of St Bertin, and wished to burn the church. He compelled Arnold, and those besieged with him, to renounce Flanders altogether.

147. On that same day the count returned to Ypres, preparing to attack Iwan and Daniel on the following day with the force summoned at Torhout. On the same day, namely Wednesday, our citizens and our maritime Flemings swore an association, that from then on they would stand together to defend the honour of their town and country.

148. On the tenth day before the Kalends of April, Friday, letters having been sent, the men of Ghent, together with Iwan and Daniel, told our citizens of Bruges that until the following Monday they should decide whether they intended wholly to remain with the citizens of Ghent and wholly to renounce the count’s homage, or wholly to persist with Count William and oppose the citizens of Ghent and their lords and friends. After the appointed day, they were unwilling to remain in uncertainty with the people of Bruges.

149. On the ninth day before the Kalends of April, Saturday: “Rebecca said” [Note: that is, the Saturday before the Third Sunday in Lent, when, in the Mass, part of chapter XVII of Genesis is read in place of the Epistle.]. The people of Bruges had heard that the count was hastening down from Alstra [Note: Alstra, commonly Alteren, in the district of Ghent, near the right bank of the new canal by which one travels to Bruges.] to Bruges; they denied him access to their town and castle. Through the castellan Gervase they sent word to the count that he should turn elsewhere until he had expelled his enemies from Flanders, and only then would they restore to him the town and castle at Bruges. They also required of the same castellan Gervase that he declare to them whether he had resolved either wholly to remain with them in the same allegiance and security, or wholly to withdraw from them together with his count.

That same day, about evening, they saw the count passing by us toward Maldegem; our citizens immediately sprang to arms and would have stood against the count at the city gates, if he had come down to Bruges; and they shut the gates against him on every side. That same day Cono, brother of the dead Walter of Frorerdeslo, came over to our citizens and, in the middle of the marketplace before everyone, swore that henceforth he would faithfully stand with the citizens, with all his power. The knights Walter [Note: Walter Crommelin, son-in-law of Hacket the castellan.] of Lissewege and his men, and Hugh Snaggaerd of Oostkerke and his brothers, were allies of our citizens.

## Chapter XX. The Election of Thierry of Alsace as Count of Flanders. The Death of Lambert of Reddenburg.

150. On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, Sunday, the Annunciation of St Mary, the Gospel was read: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.” The countess of Holland [Note: Petronilla, mother of Thierry VI, discussed in chapter 8.] and her foster-brother Count Thierry [Note: Since, together with his sister, he was for a time acting on behalf of her son.] sent to our burghers—both clergy and people of our neighbourhood—the greetings of the citizens of Ghent and of themselves:

> “Whatever you lawfully possess through our predecessor-counts, you shall possess more securely through me, if indeed you install me in the county. I shall grant peace and free passage for trade to your merchants and to those of all Flanders; and my sister the countess will grant the same, provided, however, that we give one another hostages for my reception by you and for the granting of free trade to you.”

Immediately the castellan Gervase went to the count at Maldegem, advising him to go up toward Ypres, because at Maldegem he would be held almost as under siege if the men of Ghent perhaps made an attack upon him. The men of Bruges immediately sent for Daniel, asking him to come down to them at Bruges with his force.

Meanwhile Arnold, whom they had formerly received as count at Saint-Omer, was striving, with the aid and counsel of the king of England, to obtain the county of Flanders, together with Henry, castellan of Broekburg [Note: Henry, son of Themard, who was killed with Blessed Charles; as constable and castellan of Broekburg he subscribed Count Thierry’s charter of 1151, in the Proofs to the History of the House of Ghent, p. 203.]. Thus the land of Flanders was divided: some, still preserving allegiance and homage to Count William, served with him; others desired Thierry, as Daniel, Iwan, the men of Ghent, and the men of Bruges did; others Arnold, as did those at Saint-Omer and that region; while others believed that the count from Mons ought to be preferred. Thus, amid so great a division, the land was laid waste.

151. On the seventh day before the Kalends of April, Monday, the castellan Gervase refused henceforth to remain with our people of Bruges, because they had denied Count William access to their town and castle, had closed the gates against him, and had chosen Thierry as their count in addition. Therefore, outside the castle of Bruges, Gervase summoned the leading citizens and addressed them as follows:

> “Because I still keep faith with my sole lord, Count William, from whom, under the law of the world, I cannot separate without loss of honour, I cannot have leave to remain with you who have shown such contempt for the count. But because I love you, I shall go to the count and plead for you, so that he may grant you a delay until next Sunday and inflict no injury on you. Thus, if I can reconcile you with the count, I shall do so; but if not, I shall warn you of every injury which the count will inflict upon you, insofar as I can know it beforehand. I ask that you honourably safeguard my wife, sons, daughters, and possessions, which still remain inside the castle, until the appointed day.”

All our citizens granted him this, faithfully promising to observe it. That same day Stephen of Boulaere [Note: Boulaere, near Geraardsbergen, at this time a barony comprising twelve villages. Stephen of Boulaere had accompanied Count Robert to the Holy Land. William of Boulaer subscribed Iwan of Ghent’s charter of 1139 for the monastery of Tronchiennes, in Miraeus, *Codex Donationum*, ch. 94.] entered among us with about forty knights. Our knights made a raid before Thancmar’s house. That same day Iwan [Note: Iwan married Lauretta, daughter of Thierry, in 1140.] and Daniel brought Thierry of Alsace to Bruges in order that he might be received as count. Our citizens met him, acclaiming him.

152. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April, Tuesday, in the morning, Thancmar and his nephews burned their own house and dwellings at Straten, because, if they had not done so, Daniel and Iwan, with their Thierry, would have burned them. We learned indeed that Iwan and Daniel had not yet made homage and an oath of security to that Thierry, but were leading him through the castles of Flanders in order to move the people and knights to elect him count. For Iwan and Daniel could not conduct the election without the permission and assent of the duke of Louvain. They had, indeed, both given their word to the duke that they would not elect that Thierry count without the duke’s consent.

That same day we heard that William of Ypres, released from captivity, had come to Courtrai, perhaps to aid Count William, expelled from Bruges and Ghent, with his counsel and the strength of his followers. Since Iwan and Daniel, two of the peers and leading men of Flanders, had received very many gifts from the king of England and were to receive more for expelling his nephew—namely our Count William—they had resolved to do nothing without the counsel of the king of England or of the duke of Louvain. The king of England and that duke were to give the duke’s daughter to Arnold, nephew of the most pious Count Charles, whom at the same time the men of Veurne and the castellan of Broekburg had received as count, through the counsel and assistance of the king of England.

At last our citizens asked Iwan and Daniel: “Why, then, have you brought this Thierry all the way to us, if you are not first, and we second, to make him allegiance, security, and homage?” They answered: “Because when he came to Bruges, he came with us, and we with him, so that he might see the situation of the place and test in what spirit the men of Bruges, and those joined to them in friendship and security, would receive him.”

On the fourth day before the Kalends of April, Thursday, the knights of Oostkerke, whose names were entered on a parchment, sent themselves and many others to Count William at Ypres and renounced the allegiance and homage which they had formerly made to that count.

153. On the third day before the Kalends of April, Friday, the men of Bruges awaited the return of Daniel and Iwan, who had earlier secretly left the suburb with their knights. They had appointed this day to our citizens, on which the men of Ghent, Bruges, and those allied with them were to make homage and oaths of security to Thierry of Alsace. Before this Friday, in the leap year, the corresponding day in the previous year had been the Wednesday immediately before Easter.

That same day in the evening Iwan, Daniel, and Hugh Campo Avenae (“Oatfield”) returned to us at Bruges. It was reported that William of Ypres, who had been captured, had been set free by Count William of the Normans. Immediately after they had dined, both leaders and people assembled at the exit of the castle, at the Sands; there they elected Thierry of Alsace count of all Flanders. Iwan and Daniel made homage to him in the presence of all. A law was granted allowing all who were held outlawed for the betrayal of Count Charles to return to the court of this new count and, if they dared, to clear themselves: if a man was a knight and belonged to the count’s court, according to the judgments of the peers and vassals of the land; otherwise, according to the judgments of the land’s aldermen, each person so accused was to purge himself.

The count, his leading men, and the people of the land further granted liberty, for the condition of the commonwealth and the honour of the land, to improve all the laws, judgments, practices, and customs of those inhabiting the land. It should be noted that, on this same weekday in the preceding year, the leaders of the siege returned from Arras. Having left us to elect a count for the land according to the counsel and command of King Louis—Iwan and his brother Baldwin of Aalst, Walter of Frorerdeslo, and the other peers of the land—they returned to us in high spirits and announced that they had freely and lawfully elected William, the boy from Normandy, as count and lord of our whole land, together with the king of France.

And while Count William was sitting with his barons in a certain upper chamber at Ypres, taking counsel about what he ought to do against Thierry, newly elected as count only by the men of Ghent, Bruges, and their accomplices, the chamber itself fell to the ground, and those trusting in it fell with it, so that one of them almost died, suffocated by the fall.

154. On the day before the Kalends of April, Saturday, meanwhile clergy and people returned to the Sands. Upon the bier of St Donatian the count swore, as we have said before; and hostages, Iwan and Daniel, were given between the count and the clergy and people, to guarantee that the count would fulfil all that he had sworn and would not knowingly deceive them. Then the men of Ghent swore allegiance; thereafter the men of Bruges made allegiance and homage to the count.

That same day Lambert of Reddenburg came to Bruges to clear himself of the charge of betrayal. On the Kalends of April, Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*, in the middle of Lent, Thierry was received as count and entered St Donatian’s church at Bruges in procession. According to the custom of his predecessor-counts, he took his seat; he dined in the hall and house of the counts. Throughout the day our men of Bruges worked to bring in the castellan Gervase, whom they had faithfully loved. Yet some men of Bruges, retainers of that same Gervase, acted wickedly against him, having separately formed a plan with a certain Walter, son-in-law of Hacket the castellan, whom they were trying to put over Gervase.

155. On the fourth day before the Nones of April—Saturday in the previous year, the holy Saturday of Easter, but now Monday—the castellan Gervase entered the castle of Bruges to Count Thierry, amid a multitude of his knights and burghers who had faithfully loved him. Standing before everyone, he said:

> “Lord Count Thierry, if God had granted us and our country this favour—that we had had you present immediately after the death of our lord and your nephew Charles—we would have received no one but you into the county. Therefore I make known to all that I have wholly departed from Count William; I have renounced the homage, allegiance, and security which I have hitherto maintained toward him, because the peers of the land and the whole people have condemned him, as one wandering still in the land without law, without faith, and without the justice of God and men. They have received you, the natural heir and just lord of the land, with honour and love. Therefore I wish to make homage and allegiance to you as the natural lord of the land, of whose condition we are; and I wish to receive from you the office and fiefs which I have hitherto held from your predecessors. If anyone, on Hacket’s behalf—who was castellan immediately before me—claims the viscounty against me, I shall be ready to answer before you and the peers of the land.”

When his speech was ended, he became the man of Count Thierry. Then, throughout the rest of the day, and for several days afterward, all those who ought to be enfeoffed in the county made homage to the count. The count immediately hastened to establish peace throughout his county between those who had hitherto carried on mutual quarrels, disputes, and serious fighting.

156. On the eighth day before the Ides of April, Friday, Lambert of Reddenburg cleared himself by the ordeal of hot iron, in Count Thierry’s presence, of the betrayal and death of Lord Count Charles. Daniel and Iwan were not present.

157. On the fifth day before the Ides of April, Monday, certain men of Ypres came before Count Thierry in the loggia of his house at Bruges, declaring that the count would come to aid the citizens of Ypres on the condition that, if the citizens expelled Count William from Ypres, Count Thierry would enter among them on the following day to assist them.

158. On the fourth day before the Ides of April, Tuesday, Count Thierry, with his vassals and the burghers of Bruges, made an expedition against his enemies, who were stationed at Oudenburg and Gistel. Since they were strongly fortified on every side for resistance, the count and the citizens returned halfway along the road.

That same day the king of France sent our citizens the following letter:

> “I wish you to send me eight prudent men from among yourselves at Arras on Palm Sunday. I shall summon an equal number of the wiser men from each castle of Flanders. Before them and all my barons, I wish reasonably to examine what is the matter of dispute and conflict between you and your Count William, and I shall immediately work to establish peace between you and him. If any citizen does not dare to come to me, I shall provide safe-conduct for his journey there and back.”
