The citizens immediately deliberated how to answer the letter, saying: “Before William was received as count, the king swore that he neither wished nor ought to receive any purchase-price or payment for the election of that count; yet afterwards he openly received a thousand marks as a price and payment, and is perjured. Likewise, whatever he remitted to the citizens in tolls, and whatever he swore together with the king that he would preserve inviolate, he violently broke. Though the count had given hostages to confirm all that he had remitted and granted to the citizens, he deceived those hostages.

“Finally, when at Ypres he appointed a day for us and the peers of the land, to settle with us, as all the inhabitants of the land know, he pre-emptively occupied that castle with armed force in order to act violently against us and compel us to whatever he pleased. Thus, contrary to reason and to the law of God and men, he shut us in this land, so that we could not trade; indeed, we have consumed, without profit, trade, or acquisition of goods, whatever we had formerly possessed. Therefore we have a just cause for expelling him from the land.

“Now we have elected as our count the more just heir of the land, the son of the sister [Note: Inno, the aunt. They were cousins, sons of two sisters.] of Count Charles: a faithful and prudent man, raised up according to the custom of the land, established by our allegiance and homage, worthily imitating the nature, customs, and deeds of his predecessors. We therefore make known to all—to the king and his princes, alike to our contemporaries and successors—that nothing belongs to the king of France concerning the election or installation of the count of Flanders … [Note: Something seems to be missing, such as “if it happens that he dies,” or similar words.] whether he dies without an heir or with an heir: the peers of the land and the citizens have power to elect the nearest heir to the county, and possess the liberty to raise him up in that county. By the law governing the lands which the count held as a fief from the king, when the count dies, his successor shall give the king only armour for that fief. The count of the land of Flanders owes the king of France nothing further; nor has the king any claim by which he may, by authority, purchase, or payment, impose a count upon us or prefer anyone.

“But because the king and the counts of Flanders had hitherto stood connected by kinship, for that reason the knights, nobles, and citizens of Flanders gave the king their assent to elect and install that William as their count. Yet what is owed by kinship is wholly one thing; what is established for the examination of justice by the ancient tradition of the predecessor-counts of Flanders is another.”

159. On the third day before the Ides of April, Wednesday, the feast of Pope Leo, Thancmar’s nephews attacked the men of Bruges at the Sands, summoning and enticing the citizens, who had not yet eaten, and Count Thierry with his knights, to engage in fighting. The bell-ringers of the churches and the knights sounding trumpets drove them far from Bruges. Subsequently the better-equipped among our knights and citizens again advanced against their enemies at Gistel and compelled some of them to be glad if perhaps they might be permitted to make homage to our Count Thierry and give hostages upon this condition: that they would never deceive him.

160. On the ninth day before the Kalends of May, Monday after Easter Sunday, our Count Thierry rode to Lille and secured those neighbouring districts. Meanwhile Lambert of Wingene, with a few knights, made an expedition against Bruges; together with Thancmar’s nephews, he burned the house of Fromold, the younger notary of the count, a defensible house at Beernem.

At the same time Count William had gone up to the king of France at Compiègne, a place in France, to receive counsel and assistance from the king as to how he might retain Flanders. He freely restored to our bishop Simon of the see of Noyon twelve altars which he had held as fiefs, in order that the bishop might act as advocate and defender of the churches of God in Flanders, on the condition that the bishop should condemn by ban and the sentence of excommunication all citizens of the Flemish land who had received Count Thierry and advanced the power of his county, and who had imposed him upon Count William by force and without judgment. On this agreement the bishop sent letters to Ghent and suspended the churches there from divine office.

161. On the day before the Kalends of May, Monday, Lambert of Reddenburg, who had lain under the charge of betrayal until he satisfied Count Thierry through the ordeal of hot iron, was besieging his enemies at Oostburg with a very strong force. He had gathered to himself from the surrounding sea islands almost three thousand men, friends, and kinsmen. Against him, the men of Reddenburg assembled a strong force of infantry and cavalry.

When the one party came to besiege and the other to free the besieged, a messenger of Count Thierry intervened—namely the castellan Gervase—wishing to postpone the battle until they could make peace in the count’s presence. But Lambert and his men were stubbornly intent on killing the besieged; they would not delay at all from striking them. Thus, while so many thousands launched their assault and the besieged defended themselves bravely, suddenly the knights of Reddenburg, who had awaited the issue of the battle in another house as assistance to the besieged, sprang forth armed, some mounted and some on foot, though few in comparison with the besiegers.

Those who sprang out immediately raised an immense noise and shouting into the air, so terrifying and utterly confounding the besiegers that they took flight, cast away shields and weapons, and stripped themselves for running in their flight. Then those previously besieged came out in force of arms, while the men of Reddenburg pursued from behind those who had fled and cut down the leaders and captains of all those enemies. Of the infantry they killed whom they wished. The number of wounded was countless, and the number of free men slain was—

162. In this battle it should be noted that Lambert, who recently had cleared himself by hot iron of having betrayed Count Charles, was now killed. For as long as he acted humbly toward God, God pardoned him what he had done in his lord’s death. But after his release from the ordeal of hot iron, Lambert and his men, without any regard for mercy, proudly besieged a few men with three thousand; and, obstinate to the utmost of their ability, they would spare them neither for God’s sake nor for the sake of the oath they had made to Count Thierry, that they would stir no sedition in their own persons or those of their followers. They would not postpone the battle and slaughter of the besieged. He deserved, therefore, to be killed: forgetful of God’s mercy and of the dispensation by which God had preserved him alive, he seemed deserving of death with all his followers, unless indeed he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, as he had promised God and the Church.

For when a servant humbly acts with the Lord concerning his guilt, the Lord pardons the servant who acts according to the law of repentance. But when a man acting justly is perversely treated by another man, and God is called in as judge between the two, God aids the fidelity of the just party, casts down the unjust man from his cause, and confounds him in his obstinacy. Hence it happens that in war one wicked man is overthrown, while in the judgment of water or iron a wicked but repentant man does not fail.

It should further be noted that those killed at Oostburg had originally, by their counsel and schemes, set Count Thierry up at Ghent and Bruges and violently imposed him upon Count William of Normandy. And although Thierry was Flanders’ natural heir, a just and pious count, while Count William of Flanders was dishonourable and a persecutor of the citizens of the land, nevertheless those who now lie miserably slain did not give counsel justly. Nor can they be called innocent of betrayal of their lord, since through their counsel and violent schemes Count William still remained in his land of Flanders.

## Chapter XXI. Battles and Military Incursions between William the Norman and Thierry of Alsace.

163. On the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the night of Wednesday, those who were still held under siege by the citizens of Ghent in the count’s house, because they persisted in supporting Count William, came out and burned many houses in the streets. While the citizens laboured to put out the fire, they cut down with axes the projectile engines—namely mangonels [Note: Beka, *On the Bishops of Utrecht*, under John II: “Applying mangonels to batter the towers.” He also frequently writes *manganae*, as below in no. 181 *magnella* is used.]—by which they were bringing down the stone house and tower in which the besieged were living.

That same day, Wednesday, Gervase, castellan of Bruges, with knights wished to besiege those at Wingene who supported Count William. But those valiant knights met Gervase, wounded him, captured two of his squires, and gained horses and palfreys.

164. Thus, on the third day before the Nones of May, as the year turned, the anniversary day was approaching of all those cast down from the tower for the death of Count Charles. It should be noted that in this same week Lambert son of Ledewif and several others were killed at Oostburg; by their counsel and betrayal Thierry was violently imposed upon William the Norman in Flanders.

In the same week the king of France was endeavouring, on the day before the Nones of May, the Sunday *Misericordia Domini*, to summon archbishops, bishops, all synodal persons among the clergy, abbots, and the most discerning men among clergy and laity, counts, barons, and the other princes, to assemble before him at Arras. He intended to hold counsel concerning these two counts: which of them he should expel by royal power, or which he should establish. At that time Thierry was at Lille and William was moving about at Ypres.

The whole land was afflicted with dangers—robberies, burnings, betrayals, and plots—so that no prudent person lived securely. Both sides therefore awaited the counsel or judgment that would be delivered in the court and assembly of so many prudent and discerning men, and feared what dangers might come; for they feared that every danger would befall them.

It should be noted that almost all to whom the Flemish land had been forbidden for the betrayal of Count Charles, under the judgments of the leading men and barons of the land, returned at this time by this pretence and deceit: if anyone dared call them to account for the betrayal, those challenged would answer either in the count’s court, if he was a knight, or before the aldermen and judges of the land, if of lower condition. Yet no one had as yet been challenged or answered.

165. It should also be remembered that, when Count Thierry had first gone up to Lille, a certain enchantress met him as she descended into the water which the count was about to cross by a bridge near the enchantress. She sprinkled the count with water. Thereupon, so they say, Count Thierry became sick in heart and bowels, so that he loathed food and drink. When his knights grieved over him, they seized the enchantress, bound her hands and feet, laid her upon burning straw and stubble, and burned her.

From that time until the seventh day before the Ides of May, Cono of Frorerdeslo at Wijnendale, and those who at Wingene bore arms with Lambert against Count Thierry and his followers, did not cease to plunder nearby villages and peasants and violently carry off their goods. The men of Bruges, however, surrounded themselves with new ditches and defended themselves by watches and ambushes of their own and of their knights. At that time the village of Oescamp was completely plundered by the knights of Count William.

166. On the day before the Ides of May, Monday, the men of Bruges attacked those at Wingene. Many on both sides were wounded and some killed. Yet the fortified place of those besieged was not destroyed.

167. On the Ides of May, Tuesday, Count William, having gathered his knights, attacked a crier at Oescamp, drove him into the church of that village, and besieged him shut inside. Setting fires against the doors of the church, he burned the doors themselves. Meanwhile our burghers met him armed at Oescamp; when they saw the count, his knights, and the flames in the church, they fled in terror, and many were captured that day.

While the count was riding out in pursuit and chasing our citizens, the crier of Oescamp sprang from the church with a few others, escaped the danger of the fire, and one of the knights who had left the church in that escape was captured. But our burghers fled in frightened terror, also because they were conscious that they had unjustly expelled and betrayed that same Count William; some hid in field ovens, from which they were pulled out and carried away captive.

168. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, Monday, report came from Lens that the king of France had fled from Lille, where he had besieged our Count Thierry for four days. At the same time the men of Ghent disembowelled a certain enchantress and carried her stomach around their town.

169. On the fourth day before the Kalends of June, Tuesday, Count William, having assembled a very great force of knights and foot-soldiers, attacked Bruges. With energetic and spirited assault, he pressed as far as our gates, ramparts, and inside our ditches. On both sides some were killed and very many wounded. At last, in the evening, he returned to Jabbeke [Note: Jabbeke is one hour’s journey from Oudenburg, according to Straten.].

170. On the third day before the Kalends of June, Wednesday, Count William again seized peasants, knights, and armed men at Oescamp and carried them off violently to Wijnendale and Oudenburg.

171. On the day before the Kalends of June, the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, Count William sent from Oudenburg a monk named Basil, directing his notary Basil to hurry to him because the shepherds and keepers of his estates and revenues had come into his presence to render an account of their debts. That monk was detained at Bruges by Iwan, the castellan Gervase, and Arnold, nephew of Count Charles, who had come to Bruges from Broekburg on the preceding day.

At the same time Count William ordered Oudenburg to be enclosed and strengthened with ditches, where he had arranged to receive himself and his followers. No countryman around us was safe: with all his household goods, he either fled and hid in the woods, or came into Bruges, scarcely secure there either in life or possessions.

172. On the fourth day before the Ides of June, holy Pentecost Sunday, Count Thierry came to Bruges, having secured the surrounding villages around Ghent; he was received by our people with the greatest joy.

173. On the third day before the Ides of June, Monday, certain knights and brigands who supported Count William came out from Jabbeke. Pretending to bear peace, they exchanged conversation and greetings with a knight who was on our side. This knight’s house was a defensible and very strong one; all who lived around it, and many citizens of Bruges, had brought their possessions there to preserve them more safely.

They caught that knight while he was moving securely in his courtyard, killed him by inflicting wounds, and, after driving out the knight, violently took possession of the house. Count Thierry immediately flew there joyfully with an innumerable multitude, besieged them, and compelled the besieged to surrender. Yet he allowed them to depart with their limbs unharmed; and on Tuesday, the day before the Ides of June, he duly restored the knight and lord of that house to his own house.

174. On that same day before the Ides of June, the knights of Count William, who had been stationed at Oudenburg, Jabbeke, and Straten in order to lay snares for our Count Thierry and our people, heard that Thierry had made a siege with all his force in remote villages outside Bruges. About sixty raiders rushed up and burned a house near the castle of Bruges, wishing to draw out our citizens, whom they might perhaps capture in that way. They attacked us chiefly in order to recall Count Thierry from the siege by the smoke and flames of the fire.

The castellan Gervase, meeting the attack of the ambushers with his knights, captured two valiant knights: Walter, nephew of Thancmar, through whom the occasion and cause of the whole sedition and conflict had originally arisen between Borsiard, that betrayer of Count Charles, and Thancmar; and another knight with Walter. Walter himself, however, was mortally wounded in that capture. The citizens of Bruges clapped their hands together for joy, unable sufficiently to show one another their delight at so favourable an outcome. For at last, after so many evils, so many plunderings and burnings of houses, and so many murders committed among us, that Walter was captured by our men—the man who was the head and beginning of every evil in our land, through whose plots Count Charles was betrayed; not because he himself had betrayed him, but because he had compelled his enemies Borsiard and his followers to commit the betrayal. [Note: Hence arose the occasion for writing that Blessed Charles was killed by the men of Straten, as stated above.]

I say this, however, according to popular opinion and according to the fury of those who would then have hanged the aforesaid captive Walter, or destroyed him by some new and unheard-of manner of death, if the count had allowed it. For, seeing the fire near Bruges, Count Thierry was already returning from the siege with all his multitude; but before he arrived, those two were captured and the other ambushers driven back in flight.

175. That same day Walter of Somergem [Note: Somergem, in the district of Ghent, three miles from the city. Sanderus, book IV of *Rerum Gandavensium*, p. 177, discusses the antiquity of this family and states that Bernard and Walter of Somergem lived under Philip of Alsace.] and the knights and foot-soldiers with him, who were fighting on our side, were captured at Haltra. That same day Daniel and Iwan captured fifty knights at Rupelmonde against the duke of Louvain. That same day the men of Ypres secretly sent letters to the men of Bruges, asking that some of the wiser men from each side meet privately in a safe place and deliberate usefully concerning the honour of the county.

176. On the fourteenth and thirteenth days before the Kalends of July, Count Thierry had gone up to Ghent with Count Frederick [Note: [Col. 1038D] Frederick is named as Thierry’s brother by the Vignerus cited above, *Origins of Alsace*, p. 115.] and assembled an innumerable army from Axel, Bouchaute, Waas, and those neighbouring regions. He also brought engines for hurling missiles, [Col. 1038C] by which he might overthrow the fortified houses and strongholds of his enemies. He arrived with a formidable army at Tielt [Note: [Col. 1038D] Tielt, a town in the district of Kortrijk, endowed with the rights and privileges of the citizens of Harelbeke by William the Norman, as Sanderus reports from Gramaye in *Flandria Illustrata*, p. 427.], and besieged the house of the knight Folket.

Accordingly, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, Wednesday, the men of Bruges met the count with their castellan Gervase and an innumerable multitude of Flemings who had conspired with them. They encamped outside on the following night around the aforesaid house. Count William therefore surveyed the army nearby, to see how large was the crowd and force besieging his knight. Nor was he little distressed by that injury and by the advancing arrogance of the besiegers. For Count William had chosen to die first rather than endure so great a disgrace to himself.

Accordingly, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, Thursday, the fourth day before the feast of St John the Baptist, early in the morning at Oudenburg he devoutly received penance for his sins from the abbot of that place, a religious and prudent man. He vowed to God that henceforth he would be the protector of the poor and of the churches of God. Likewise all his valiant knights made vows; having cut their hair and discarded their ordinary clothing, they put on shirts and mail-coats together with their other arms. With humble vows before God and with most resolute zeal, [Col. 1039A] they advanced to battle and came to the summits of a hill overlooking the army of Count Thierry; there they prepared themselves for battle.

177. Count William accordingly formed three squadrons of cavalry and himself commanded the first line of his men, intending as its leader to deliver the first assault. Opposite him Count Thierry likewise drew up his lines. In one of these Thierry himself and the castellan Gervase were leaders; Count Frederick was in another. With shortened lances, they gradually engaged each other on both sides with the strength of lance and sword, and countless men fell. They fought hand to hand, as though offering themselves to death; they rushed amid the very weapons of their enemies. Indeed, they had previously resolved that they would die in battle rather than be expelled from the county.

For in the first attack Daniel, who commanded Count Thierry’s soldiery, wished to throw himself upon Count William’s wedges of troops. There Count Frederick was unhorsed, and opposite him Riquart of Woldman, already bound in a prior binding, was taken captive; for many, indeed innumerable, reciprocal bindings took place. At last they fought with swords.

178. But the division and wedge in which Count William was fighting began to fail and turned backward in flight; Daniel pursued it with his men. While both sides laboured—the one in fleeing, the other in pursuit—the second division of Count William’s wedges, which lay concealed for an ambush, sprang forth against the faces of Daniel and his men. Since they had been encouraged and equipped for battle with fresh strength [Col. 1039C] and a united purpose, hesitating in nothing, they shattered those pursuers with lances and swords.

Then Count William, swiftly rebounding from flight, recovered himself with his men; in a single charge, with manly spirit and bodily strength, he pressed upon the violence of arms and the dispersal of his enemies. Therefore all who had foreseen the perils of battle threatening them alongside Count Thierry scattered in different directions, throwing away their weapons and fleeing utterly naked, so that none remained with their count except ten knights. Count William and his men, casting off their mail-coats and mounting their horses more lightly equipped, at last reaped the fruit of their victory: they killed some enemies and captured others.

179. About midnight Count Thierry returned to Bruges; but where Count William went, we have not heard. Then the wives of our district mourned their lost husbands, sons their fathers, and male and female servants their masters. Seeking news of the disaster and misfortune of the battle, they languished through the whole night and thereafter in weeping and sighing. At earliest dawn, when our people went out for their dead, they were again captured by William’s soldiers. So grievous a persecution and so manifold a captivity of our people had never been heard of in our parts before this deed of war. An immense sum of money was paid to Count William and his men to ransom our captives; and so, in a manner, our land was plundered anew.

At last, hearing that Count William before entering battle had humbly subjected himself to God, undertaken the remedy of penance, and cut off his hair and superfluous garments, he and all his men, after their military misfortunes, our citizens together with their Count Thierry cut their hair and garments. Our priests too, following the example of their enemies, at last preached penance. After so many injuries, plunderings, and captivities inflicted upon our people, they proclaimed a universal fast, carried crosses and shrines of saints to the church of Blessed Mary at Bruges, and there all the Bruges clergy excommunicated by name Count William the Norman: Dean Thancrannus, and the priests Eggard, Sigebodo, Heribert, the elder Fromold, and Thierry. They also caused Count Thierry to vow before all that, if [Col. 1040B] any of the men of Ypres should turn to him, he would receive them mercifully; and likewise he would not disinherit any persons from the whole county who turned to him.

180. On the eighth day before the Kalends of July, Sunday, the feast of St John the Baptist, in the church of Blessed Mary, a crucifix which stood on the pavement for the faithful to adore was itself, by God’s power, lifted upward from the place where it had stood firmly fixed; it would have fallen to the pavement unless one of the church custodians had caught it in his hands before its fall. This custodian again fixed the crucifix in its accustomed place; but after he had gone away, the same crucifix was again lifted from its fastening, as before, and began to fall. Then all who stood there in adoration ran up and fastened it again, supposing that [Col. 1040C] the fall had occurred through negligence in fixing it. But after examining all around, they established that no negligence had caused this.

181. On the fourth day before the Nones of July, Wednesday, at the translation of Martin, bishop of the Church of Tours, Count William the Norman besieged with a formidable army the house of the chief reeve in the village of Orscamp. He brought engines for hurling missiles, a mangonel and a *pyrrira* [uncertain engine-name], to overthrow the aforesaid house. But Count Thierry, with the citizens of Bruges and Flemings from around Bruges, positioned themselves around the ditches and hedges of the same house, together with Arnold Wineth. A river divided the two armies, fortifying the aforesaid house on its eastern side.

[Col. 1040D] Yet on the side from which William launched his attack, that house was secure with hedges and ditches. Thus many on both sides were killed or wounded in the onset of battle and mutual fighting, but the house, its ditches, and its hedges stood firm. At length they raised a tower on one side and an opposing tower on the other; having climbed them, they fought more fiercely. Then William’s army, because a west wind blew hard upon the opposing wedge of enemies, ordered hay, grass, house-roofs, brushwood, and every material that could serve to fill the ditches to be brought from all directions, so that they might thus enter upon the enemies opposite them.

But those inside threw fire, more readily burning with pitch, old grease, and wax, upon the machine; and everything that had been thrown in was consumed by fire. [Col. 1041A] The smoke from that burning contrivance, driven by the shrieking wind, rushed into the eyes of those who had kindled the fire from within; many were struck down, overwhelmed by lances, missiles, and arrows. William remained in that siege for six days; during those days, the soldiers of both armies practised so many feats of arms and so many skirmishes. For, since the river was deep between the two enemies, throughout the siege William’s soldiers sought fords and crossings of the river by which they might cross without delay, eager for fighting and war, being stronger in arms and more numerous in men.

Therefore, on the sixth day, the seventh day before the Ides of July, Monday, about evening, seeing that he was making no progress in the siege of that house, William ordered four hundred soldiers to cross by the fords of the river. [Col. 1041B] They burned the house of the knight Ansbold and the houses of his brother and sisters. Then his army withdrew; but our people fled to Bruges, and neighbouring people dwelling around us, fleeing with all their household goods and livestock, entered with us into Bruges, stupefied with trembling and fear, and passed that night without sleep. On the same day the monks of St Trudo and their cell situated near Orscamp were utterly plundered, so that not even books or a chalice for sacrifice remained there.

182. It should be noted that none of the wiser men among our Bruges people dared to speak the truth about our disaster, misfortune, and flight. For whoever professed any truth was branded as a traitor to our district [Col. 1041C] and a supporter of Count William, and was immediately threatened with death. Nor is this surprising, for God hardened their hearts so that they would not hear the whole truth.

Yet the crosses and processions carried through the churches by the clergy provoked God more to anger than to appeasement, because in obstinacy of mind, evils, pride, and resistance to the authority placed over them by God, they had risen up. Every soul ought to be subject to higher authority, as the Apostle says (Romans 13:1). Therefore, if misfortunes befell that place from which the worst betrayals had arisen—wars, seditions, murders, and the everlasting disgrace of all Flanders—was not that same place justly due for every evil? And if the church of the brethren at Bruges suffered, was it not deservedly so, because the provost of that church had brought in the cause of evils?

And although no one dared announce the ban and anathema of our archbishop, bishop, and his other suffragan bishops, we truly heard and knew that we had deservedly been placed under ban and forbidden the divine office, because we had set one count over another and through this had brought countless deaths upon all. Our priests and the clergy of our district prepared themselves to fight with the people and mob, ill mindful that they ought to stand as a wall for the house of Israel.

[Col. 1042A] 183. On the fourth day before the Ides of July, Wednesday, at the translation of Benedict the abbot, Christian of Gistel and the brothers of Walter Pennatus Mendacium came to Bruges under Daniel’s safe-conduct. Christian gave his son as a hostage, and the two aforesaid brothers remained as hostages for their brother Walter, who was fettered in the count’s house at Bruges. Christian and his knights therefore took Walter with them, until they should see whether he recovered or died, since he lay near death from his wound.

## Chapter XXII. The Death of William the Norman. Thierry’s Peaceful Government

184. On the fourth day before the Ides of July, Thursday, the Duke of Louvain besieged Aalst [Note: [Col. 1041] Aalst, a principal city of Imperial Flanders, situated between Ghent and Brussels, with an important territory; formerly reckoned as part of Brabant.] with a formidable army. Count William of Flanders came to his aid [Col. 1042B] with four hundred knights. Meanwhile many false reports about the aforesaid siege circulated among the people of Bruges.

185. Meanwhile it happened at Bruges that a water-mill, submerged by the waters and collapsing on every side, was destroyed; and the water which had fortified the castle and suburb of Bruges on the south flowed away almost entirely at the place where the mill had dammed it. The citizens, alarmed by this, ran together and blocked the escaping water with dung, wood, and earth. They therefore attributed the undermining of the mill to a secret act by their enemies, because after the waters had drained away their castle and suburb lay open to the enemy’s entrance.

[Col. 1042C] Many soothsayers, both laymen and priests, were present, flattering our citizens by predicting to them whatever they knew the citizens wished to hear. But if any wise person spoke truthfully concerning the siege, or the dangers threatening the place and its citizens, he was assailed by them with the most contemptible rebuff and fell silent. Meanwhile our citizens still laboured to extort money from one another, which they might send to Count Thierry for the campaign of the aforesaid siege. The people of Ghent laboured likewise. Iwan and Daniel, together with Count Thierry and a strong knight, sufficiently tested in war, were besieged in Aalst.

186. On the eighth day before the Kalends of August, Wednesday, the feast of St Christopher, Walter Pennatus Mendacium was brought back into captivity at Bruges; and the hostages who had been given and held for him until that time were restored.

187. On the sixth day before the Kalends of August, Friday, after the Transfiguration of the Lord on Mount Tabor, the Lord deigned in some measure to set an end in this sedition to his foreknowledge and at the same time to our persecution. For Count William the Norman, when he had exposed himself before the enemy in the assault on the aforesaid siege near the castle of Aalst, was thrown from his horse. As he regained his feet and lowered his right hand toward the edges of his armour, one of the enemy infantrymen sprang forward and, piercing that right hand of the count [Col. 1043A] in the palm with a lance, drove it through the middle of the arm that was joined to the hand, inflicting a mortal wound.

His knights gathered him up, their lord dying by a pitiful fall. Concealing his death from the enemy throughout that entire day, they suppressed voices and cries of sorrow, afflicted with all the more acute anguish of mind and confusion. The Duke of Louvain then eagerly sought to make peace for himself and his men with our Count Thierry, and entrusted the causes of all their mutual discord to the judgment of Iwan, Daniel, and the king of England. When the settlement was commended and agreed by both sides, the duke asked our Count Thierry to grant Count William safe conduct to return peacefully with his men from the siege. When Count Thierry had given the duke his full assent in this matter, the duke said: “Behold, William the count, whom your valour pursues as so great an enemy, has died from a mortal wound.”

Then each person sprang forth: some on either side to mourn the fall of so great and eminent a knight; others to urge their enemies to exult; others to announce it to those who had remained at home, so that they might conduct their affairs cautiously, only watchfully and with foresight. For everywhere there flew the rumour and report of that prince’s death, and those who had fought in the count’s faith and security withdrew to safer places. Then, with unending lamentation and loud trumpet-blasts, they carried the body of the valiant knight, placed upon a bier, to Saint-Omer for burial.

[Col. 1043C] 188. Count Thierry, however, pursued his enemies everywhere, devastating them by fire, capturing and destroying them, except those who had obtained his favour before the burning, whether by money or otherwise. Thus Count Thierry came up to Ypres on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, Sunday, with innumerable knightly assistance and took Ypres. But the citizens, knights, and hired soldiers of Bruges went out, plundered the village of Ridevorda, and burned houses.

Lambert of Ridevorda, Lambert of Winchina, some men of Folket and Tielt [Note: [Col. 1043D] Folket’s house at Tielt is established above, no. 176.], and many others from our borders who had fought in Count William’s aid withdrew into the fortified place of Wynendale. Those citizens of Ypres [Col. 1043D] who had stood on William’s side also fortified themselves at Formesela against Count Thierry, together with Isaac [Note: [Col. 1044D] Isaac of Formesele subscribed to the frequently cited letters of Blessed Charles in 1121.]; there most intense fighting was carried on.

It should be noted that, since the Bruges district was in such great danger that the citizens believed they could find a remedy for themselves only from God alone, and therefore sought to appease God with the sacrifice of their hearts, God aided them according to his usual dispensation. For he slew Count William by the sword of his judgment, but in such a way that he died not in his own cause but in the cause of another’s battle—namely, that duke in whose assistance he was fighting. Therefore we people of Bruges were regarded as innocent of his death, [Col. 1044A] since none of our people had caused his death; indeed, at the very time when he departed this life, we feared beyond doubt that he would come to besiege us.

The knights from Oostkerke too, who had depended upon the counsel of Count Thierry and ours, reproached us on the very day on which Count William died, saying that we had been traitors, and withdrew from us. Meanwhile a messenger came to Bruges to announce Count William’s death. On hearing it, the citizens and all our people gave thanks to God for so great a deliverance of themselves and their possessions.

189. Thus God’s wondrous dispensation ordained that this prince should die in this manner: that he should perish while assisting the aforesaid duke besieging Aalst, outside our county. And although he fought in part against our count and our people, that battle and siege were in fact undertaken for no one’s cause other than the duke’s. Although Count William gladly attacked our people on any occasion and had therefore especially joined the duke’s aid, his battle and the death allotted to him there by God were imputed only to the duke. For in this he had been the duke’s soldier; he died there not primarily for the county, but for the duke’s safety and honour, like any other hired soldier.

Some maintain that, after expelling Count William, our people set Count Thierry over him and supported Thierry with silver, counsel, and every resource, both advice and money; and that they placed him in camps and in every place where they could forestall William, to oppose and resist him. [Col. 1044C] In that way, they could not be proved innocent of William’s death. Others say that the duke attacked Thierry because he foresaw that, if Thierry should perhaps rule and remain in the Flemish county, he might inflict many evils upon him in the future, perhaps expel him from the duchy, or at least violently take away that dower for which Count Thierry was striving to summon the duke before the emperor.

For a like reason Count William fought Count Thierry in the duke’s aforementioned siege: he knew that Thierry was being weakened, by which stratagem he might be able to expel him from the county. Yet he knew that Thierry had been set over him unjustly and treacherously. Thus Count William could reasonably have fallen there both for the duke’s cause and for his own injury; and Count Thierry could rightly have resisted the duke and Count William there, both for the dower demanded from the duke and because the county had been treacherously transferred.

190. Let it therefore be asked: since God wished by the death of one man to restore peace to the country, why did he rather ordain that Count William should die, who possessed the more just claim to govern the land? Why did Count Thierry, who seemed to have been imposed unjustly, not die sooner? Or by what justice did God grant the county to one who had violently seized the dignity?

[Col. 1045A] If, therefore, neither of them had received the county properly, it ought justly to have been taken from both. Yet because the county belonged to Count Thierry by hereditary right, he possesses it lawfully. And even if he appears to have seized it unjustly, nevertheless, long before the election of the William who died, he had requested from the leading men of Flanders by letters what belonged to him. Although he was not heard by them at that time either, he ought no less to seek and recover his inheritance, which had been unjustly taken from him and unjustly sold to another by the king of France.

Therefore, after so many disputes, we assign the more just cause to Count Thierry, who cannot be said to have been unjustly set over Count William. Rather, that dead count was most unjustly set over Thierry and made count by purchase through the king’s authority, by an act of power. Thus, by ancient justice, God preserved Thierry’s life and restored him to his inheritance, and removed by death from the county the man who, however powerfully he might have lived, would have devastated the whole land, stirred all its inhabitants to civil war, and confounded the laws of God and men. God, by strict law, judged him to enter the way of all flesh, not without his evil deserts.

For Count William will not confess that, after death, anything he possessed in life remains with him among the shades whom he sent ahead to places of punishment, except praise for his soldiery; for he was called good in warfare. Thus God corrected according to the rule of his strict judgment an injury which no human power either could or would correct. Therefore he brought upon the people of Flanders anger and the scourges [Col. 1046A] of his indignation, because it had been within everyone’s power beforehand to deliberate, foresee, examine, and investigate with utmost diligence; and to appease God with contrite heart and the sacrifice of a devout mind concerning whom they should set over themselves and their country as lord, and to love and honour the one elected.

Because they neglected this, they endured as a tyrant and devastator, exacting every kind of evil, the man whom they had heedlessly received as lord. After his election and reception into the county, the princes, bailiffs, [Note: [Col. 1045D] It should rather be read “bailiffs”; on the origin and meaning of this word, much may be found in Spelman’s *Glossary*.] or counsellors of the land taught him none of the honourable ways of the preceding counts; rather, they instructed him in plunder and in cunning, deceitful pretexts by which they might procure and at times violently extort infinite sums of money from the citizens and burgesses of the land.

[Col. 1046B] 191. Thus Thierry, margrave of Flanders, ruled from the time of William’s death. Having passed through the towns—Arras, Thérouanne, Saint-Omer, Lille, and Aire—where, according to the custom of his good predecessors, he was honourably received by clergy and people and confirmed by faith and homage, he finally went up to the kings of France and England to receive from them fiefs and royal gifts. Both monarchs—the king of France and the king of England—were pleased with our Count Thierry, and gladly granted him the investitures of the fiefs and benefices which the most holy and pious Count Charles had held from them.

[Col. 1045]

# ANCIENT RHYTHM

From a manuscript of Jacques Sirmond, Society of Jesus

## § I. Lament for the Death of Blessed Charles, Count of Flanders

[Col. 1045C]

Alas, grief! The duke of Flanders and defender of the Church,

The good guardian of his country and cultivator of justice,

The cunning of traitors, the wickedness of the impious,

Full of grievous envy, slew for justice’s sake.

O unhappy Flanders! O cruel, O impious land!

What madness seized you? What perverse wickedness?

That you should spurn your duke, seek his death,

Lay snares, and kill your protector?

Through him you had flourished and been clothed in splendour;

You had gained pre-eminence and excelled many in honour.

But because you have played the harlot, you have become a transgressor;

You have dared what ought not be dared, and are to be despised above all others.

O unhappy, wretched, cruel, pestilential land!

Why did you inflict wounds, shedding the entrails of your father?

[Col. 1045D]

Why did you perpetrate this crime, disturb the laws of peace,

Violate justice, and cut the throat of your father?

What did you lack, you impious sons of cruelty,

Conscious of so great a crime and ignorant of the fear of God?

Not gold, clothing, estates, nor the resources of horses:

Therefore, amid great abundance, you perpetrate wicked deeds.

O day full of sorrow, substance of our mourning!

[Col. 1046C]

By which our peace is ended through malignant offspring.

A day to be deprived of every light, darkened by a gloomy storm,

Because the country is deprived of its protection and government.

Mourn shamelessly, Flanders, worthy of grievous misery;

Punishments of death beyond searching await you.

Formerly you were pre-eminent; now you have become foolish.

Your guilt demanding it, reciprocal slaughter will be returned.

## § II. Another Lament

Charles, jewel of counts, illustrious duke, flower of knights,

We grieve that you, undeserving, suffered death.

Your prudent moderation and diligent vigilance

Carefully kept all things safe for your country.

The impious feared you; the sons of peace loved you;

To the good you were a place of refuge, to the wicked a punishment.

Sweet France mourns you; Burgundy groans for you,

Nearby Brittany too, and moreover our own country.

[Col. 1046D]

Overflowing in a river of tears without end,

It weeps, bereft of government and deprived of protection.

O what goodness of constancy, what steadfast patience!

He dies for justice, through whom the country stood firm.

While he was in church, intent on psalmody,

Praying to God with devout mind, an impious band emerged.

At once swords are drawn; sons cut down their father;

Four innocent companions are killed with him.

[Col. 1047A]

Joined in holy love, they are delivered to the outcome of death;

Their destruction becomes Flanders’ confusion.

Here the father is cut down with two sons by swords,

And, snatched away by the impious, they enjoy heaven’s joys.

Soon their kindred, sharing in their fate,

Mourn and groan with devout hearts, as their condition requires.

Let them now cease from mourning; let them endeavour to pour forth prayers.

It is fitting to seek aid for their souls through the gift of prayers.

Merciful clemency of God, transfer those slain for your grace

To the joys of heaven, that they may be with you in glory. Amen.

## § III. Vengeance for the Death of the Same Count

The count’s death, hateful to all peoples,

To be wept for with continual tears and unheard of in the ages, having been described,

The cruel punishments of the impious are described,

Which they endured in Flanders for their wickedness.

[Col. 1047B]

The just power of God, wishing such great crimes,

Liable to punishment, to be punished with justice,

Sends from the south a judge, a worker of justice,

And an avenger of wickedness, to repay the impious.

Thus the king of France comes, intending to provide for the country,

An enemy of wickedness and a friend of justice.

He enters into great counsel concerning how to punish

The impious band that created discord through murder.

He speaks with the princes and complains of their unspeakable deeds.

The counsel is considered; at last sound advice is offered:

They urge the royal mind to cross into Flanders

To punish the monstrous wickedness of the monstrous men.

The king, relying on this counsel, goes there with his company,

To deliver them to destruction for their evil deed.

Hearing this, the guilty sons of iniquity,

Fearing the force of sovereign power, seek a place of refuge.

They enter a most secure castle, most suitable for fighting,

With hearts entirely ready to defend their most wicked crime.

[Col. 1047C]

But Isaac escaped; he pretended to be a monk,

Covered with a sheep’s skin, though within he was a fierce wolf.

Captured, he confessed that he had sinned, committed so great a crime,

And plotted the count’s death when he ought to have honoured him.

He is convicted by his own mouth and led to torture;

Thus he is hanged high: he receives what he deserved.

The king therefore enters Flanders, seeking the impious band,

By God’s grace intending to execute justice upon them.

Royal power arrives; with engines it encircles the walls;

It attacks the buildings in which the impious people lie hidden.

[Col. 1048A]

Battle is fought on both sides; enemy attacks enemy;

One is cut down by a sword, another pierced by a javelin.

Charity gives strength to these men; weakness grows in those;

Equity gives these courage; iniquity takes courage from those,

Who, deprived of counsel, despair of aid

And fear that so great a punishment will be imposed for murder.

The head of this wickedness, worthy of no pardon,

Is let down from the battle through a window in the rampart.

Despairing of pardon under the compulsion of conscience,

The wretch flees by byways, fearing death’s destruction.

He moves here and there and struggles to flee death,

But he gains no benefit from concealment, he who is burdened by this crime.

It became known that the provost, thus secretly let down,

Had fled so as not to undergo the destruction merited by his deeds.

He is sought through the lands everywhere; at last found, he is captured,

Delivered to judgment, and suffers what he deserved.

[Col. 1048B]

The executioners seize him and put a noose around his neck;

He is dragged to the rack: such punishment befits the guilty man.

He is placed upon the rack and beaten with fists and clubs;

He suffers savage scourges and so dies in torment.

After he is dead, he is hanged upon the gallows;

He deserves such treatment, having been proved a traitor.

Let us return to the other sons of iniquity,

Accomplices in treason, most wicked above all others.

Hearing the report that their leader had been treated thus,

The wretches do not cease to lament within as they watch him being destroyed.

Burchard is soon exposed; fleeing, he wanders and is captured;

Captured, he is led to death and dies suspended from a wheel.

When the impious band hears that he too suffers punishment,

Despairing of pardon, it surrenders the walls of the castle.

The illustrious king enters the castle, and his army,

Anxious for the count, runs forward pouring out groans.

[Col. 1048C]

He causes the tomb to be uncovered; uttering a plaintive groan,

He weeps and laments the jewel of counts, who had governed the people well.

When these expressions of grief are ended and the traitors captured,

They are bound in fetters to be handed over to executioners.

Their punishment is discussed and their disgrace determined;

It pleases the royal will, which orders them to die by being thrown down.

They fall from the height of the fortress and are delivered to death:

They deserve this punishment, they whose delight is treason.

[Col. 1047]

# ANCIENT EPITAPHS

Published from manuscripts by Jacob Meyer.

## I

[Col. 1047C]

Here lies the father of orphans, helper of widows,

[Col. 1047D]

Saviour of his country, zealous guardian also of the churches,

Peace and life to his own people, terror and death to his enemies.

When peace had been established everywhere among his subjects,

Charles, count of the Flemings, offspring of Danish royalty,

Died here; innocent, he perished.

Prostrate in prayer, slain at the Lord’s altar,

He became for justice a sacrifice pleasing to God.

May he who flourished in life rest in peace when dead.

## II

[Col. 1048C]

Count Charles departed by the sword and treachery of his own men;

[Col. 1048D]

Vengeance followed: the death of the guilty was harsh and grievous.

## III. Found in a monastery on the Rhine, not far from Andernach

Through you while living, Charles, your Flanders shone

Glorious and blessed in renown, peace, and prosperity, mighty.

[Col. 1049A]

At your death peace perishes, renown lies fallen, each plunderer possesses goods,

And violence without law rages everywhere.

You did not nullify the soldier’s office by that of judge:

You were both soldier and judge, strong and just.

In restoring churches, worshipping God, and feeding widows,

You were Martha, Mary, and the Good Samaritan.

By arms, law, and threats you subdued your enemies and your own people.

[Col. 1050A]

Punishing deeds already done, and future ones by fear,

You generously and gently gave gifts to the good, pardon to the wretched, punishment to criminals, and laws to be maintained.

Because you conducted the affairs of arms and peace bravely and wisely,

You were greater than Caesar.

A servant, justice, a church, and Caesar, second only to Mars—cause, place, and light—were yours in death.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1130: BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF DOL

[Col. 1049]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana Vetus*, vol. II, p. 566)

[Col. 1049B] Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil in Anjou, a writer celebrated in his age, was elected to the see of Dol and consecrated on the very day of the Nativity in 1114. Orderic Vitalis, an Englishman, writes the following about him in Book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*:

> “I resolved reverently to honor the aforesaid elder, whom I knew well. He was a citizen of Orléans, monk and abbot of Bourgueil, trained in liberal studies and venerable for the merits of his religious life. From there, on account of his piety and wisdom, he was raised by ecclesiastical election to the rank of the archbishopric of Dol. In his episcopate he retained the monastic life and, as circumstances allowed, generally lived with monks. For he ruled over untamed Bretons, whose perversity he could not endure; therefore he frequently left these insolent and lawless people and fled into Normandy, where the Church of Dol had, from the time of St Samson, while Hildebert was king of the Franks, estates upon the river Risle, which it possessed quietly and peacefully. There, by his writings and teachings, [Col. 1049C] he stirred his hearers to the worship of God; and he visited the neighboring monasteries, namely Fécamp, Fontenelle, Jumièges, and many others, strengthening them in the fear of God by sacred sermons. At last he died in a good old age, and was buried at Préaux in the basilica of St Peter the Apostle, before the crucifix.”

He had received the pallium from Pope Paschal II at the Council of Reims, which he attended. He is also called archbishop in the record of an investiture of a certain church performed by Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and apostolic legate, and likewise in several charters from the archives of Bourgueil and Fontevrault.

He left various literary monuments. Orderic, in the cited ninth book, especially mentions his *History of Jerusalem* in four books, published in the volume on the eastern expeditions undertaken by the Franks, in the collection of Jacques Bongars, the learned French author. In the preface to that work Baldric himself says that he began it when nearly sixty years old. It begins with the year 1095, in which this memorable [Col. 1049D] pilgrimage to the East began, and ends with the capture of the city of Jerusalem. The same work also shows that he himself attended the Council of Clermont. But hear Orderic’s words:

> “Baldric, archbishop of Dol, [Col. 1050B] composed four books with distinction, in which he truthfully and eloquently described the entire narrative from the beginning of the pilgrimage to the first battle after the capture of Jerusalem.”

He also elaborated a Life of the blessed Samson, bishop, as well as the deeds of the bishops of Dol; likewise, a manuscript Life of St Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, survives in certain libraries. In addition, at the command of Petronilla, the first abbess, he wrote the Life of Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Order of Fontevrault. In its prologue he speaks thus:

> “Lady Petronilla, you have imposed a great and heavy burden upon our weakness, since I am disturbed by many a storm of this shifting world, and especially of Lesser Brittany, in which I dwell among scorpions and am surrounded by a twofold, bestial ferocity.”

Michael Cosnier, parish priest of Poitiers, first brought this work to light and edited it with notes.

He also delighted in poetry and composed several historical poems, in which he identifies himself as Baldric of Anjou [*Andegavensis*], [Col. 1050C] and abbot of Bourgueil. Moreover, Cosnier observed in his *Analecta*, from one of Baldric’s own poems, that he was not native to Orléans, as Orderic is cited as saying, but was born at Meung-sur-Loire. Baldric’s poems were first edited and published from an old manuscript at Poitiers by François Duchesne, royal historiographer, son of the most learned André, in volume IV of the *Writers of the History of France*.

He completed the course of mortality on 7 January 1131, and this epitaph is found in the church of St Samson above the Risle:

> Let it be known to those present and future that Baldric, of good memory, archbishop of the Church of Dol, dedicated this church in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of St Samson, most blessed confessor, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1129. In the same year he dedicated the church of St Lawrence of Marisco, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, both of which belong by right to the holy Church of Dol. This Baldric governed the Church of Dol for twenty-two years and forty-four [Col. 1050D] days; and on the thirtieth day after the consecration of this present church he died in the confession of Christ and sleeps at Préaux. May his soul possess eternal rest.

[Col. 1051]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XI, p. 103.)

[Col. 1051A] 1. Baudri produced a great number of works, both in verse and prose. In his youth he had a taste for poetry, which he continued to cultivate not only after renouncing the world, but even while he was abbot of Bourgueil. He does not, however, seem to have excelled in it except in relation to his age, in which he acquired a reputation. “He was a poet by no means undistinguished in his own time,” says Father Mabillon of him [Note: [Col. 1051D] *Annales*, book LXV, no. 68.]. Mabillon further admits that there is little useful matter in the poems that remain to us, except insofar as they make known the great men of his time, in whose honor he made verses, whether during their lives or after their deaths. M. Duchesne printed part of them in the fourth volume of the *Historians of France*, from p. 232 to p. 278.

Dom Mabillon, in the supplement to his *Diplomatics* [Note: [Col. 1051D] Mabillon, ch. 11, no. 8, p. 51.], says that he saw in an old manuscript, now belonging to the Ottobonian Library, [Col. 1051B] poems by Baudri, some of which have not yet been printed. Among those not yet published is one in which Baudri expresses his sorrow that the stylus which he had used for ten years to write upon his tablets had broken. Dom Mabillon did not consider this piece—in which the author describes the use of the stylus—serious enough for his purpose to publish it. But he reports several verses from another poem in which Baudri describes his tablets. They were not, according to ordinary usage, of black wax but of green wax, apparently because that color fatigues the eyes less. He jokes about the stylus which a certain Lambert of Angers had made for him to write on those tablets, and praises the abbot of Sées, who had given him a bag in which to put them.

Among M. Duchesne’s manuscripts, now preserved in the King’s Library, there are, in the nineteenth volume, p. 537, [Col. 1051C] verses of Baudri that are merely an extract from a more substantial poem which he had made on William’s conquest of England and addressed to Countess Adela, daughter of that conqueror [Note: [Col. 1051D] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 747.]. This fragment bears the following title: *Verses of Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, on the conquest of England by William, duke of the Normans, taken from the larger poem dedicated to Countess Adela.*

We shall not pause here to identify the various epitaphs by our author that have been separately published in different writers, such as that on Bérenger, printed by Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 1051D] Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, ch. IV, p. 102.], etc. “Baudri,” says M. Le Bœuf [Note: [Col. 1051D] *Dissertation sur l’Histoire de Paris*, vol. II, p. 61.], “is better known for the abundance than for the delicacy of his poetry. It was he who set the fashion for the style of panegyrics, which was very easy to compose if one was content to say in verse that a given person was a second Cicero, another Virgil, an Aristotle; that he surpassed Homer; that Nestor, Ulysses, Croesus, and Quintilian were united in a certain person; that another was the Plato and Socrates [Col. 1051D] of his age.” This is not praise of Baudri’s [Col. 1052A] poetry; nor do we believe it deserves such praise. As for his prose, he succeeded somewhat better, though not sufficiently to deserve to be called an admirable Cicero—a title given him by one of his friends in a letter of which we shall have occasion to speak.

2. The most substantial work we possess by Baudri is his *History of the Crusade*, which occupies third place in Bongars’s collection. The author was about sixty when he composed it, as he says in his preface, and his sight had been weakened by age—*seniles oculos*, “aged eyes.” Thus he did not write, or at least did not complete, this work until after he had been placed in the see of Dol. Indeed, generally speaking, all the works we possess from him, except some of his poems, are productions of his old age, which did not prevent him from writing or from undertaking long journeys.

To return to his *History of the Crusade*: it is divided into four [Col. 1052B] books, containing the principal events of this celebrated expedition from the Council of Clermont, where it was proclaimed, to the victory which the crusaders won over the infidels shortly after taking Jerusalem—that is, on the twelfth day of the following August. The author makes a considerable chronological error by placing the capture of that city in 1098; for all historians unanimously agree that it was taken by the crusaders on 15 July 1099.

Baudri had not been a witness of the events related in his history, since he had not accompanied the crusaders on their expedition, although he had attended the Council of Clermont. His work [Note: [Col. 1052D] *Histoire littéraire*, vol. I.] was composed from that of an anonymous writer which had fallen into his hands. Since no one valued the anonymous writing because its style was very bad, Baudri—who otherwise believed it accurate—undertook to revise it, to make it tolerable to read [Note: [Col. 1052D] *Gesta Dei per Francos*, p. 80 ff.]. But he did not confine himself [Col. 1052C] to correcting its style: he inserted what he had learned elsewhere about this famous crusade.

Wishing to assure himself still further of the truth of the facts, he sent his work to Peter, abbot of Maillezais, his intimate friend, who had travelled to the Holy Land, and asked him to give it its final polish. The letter he wrote to him on this subject, and the reply of that abbot, immediately precede Baldric’s prologue to his history [Note: [Col. 1052D] *Ibid.*], which forms part of Bongars’s collection. Such precautions as Baldric took to perfect his history should give us a favorable opinion of it. Father Mabillon [Note: [Col. 1052D] *Annales*, book LXXV, no. 95.] regarded it as his principal work, and it is indeed the work which does the author most honor.

It begins, like that of the anonymous writer, with the Council of Clermont and ends, as we have already said, with the great victory which the crusaders won on 12 August 1099 over the Sultan of Babylon. Thus its text, which through a [Col. 1052D] manifest error gives 1098, must be corrected. Orderic Vitalis [Col. 1053A] [Note: [Col. 1053D] Orderic, book IX, p. 776.] held it in such high esteem that he drew from it everything he reports concerning the crusade. Le Baud [Note: [Col. 1053D] Le Baud, ch. XXIV, p. 170.], following his example, drew from it the greater part of what he says about the taking of Jerusalem in his *History of Brittany*.

As for the history used by Baldric, which is the first in Bongars’s collection, everyone now knows that it is the work of Theudbode, a native of Poitou, which was corrupted by an anonymous writer who suppressed the author’s name. This led M. Duchesne to restore it in his collection of the *Historians of France* [Note: [Col. 1053D] Vol. IV, p. 777.]. It is preceded there by a learned preface by M. Besly, the distinguished magistrate of Poitou, to whom we owe this discovery and who communicated it to M. Duchesne. Thus, in order to judge Baldric’s work soundly, one may compare his history with the two editions, the more exact of which is in the collection of the historians of France. For the anonymous writer took [Col. 1053B] liberties that marred Theudbode’s work; and since Baldric had no other text before his eyes, he himself might be corrected from that edition.

3. This is the place to speak of a writing which M. Mesnard [Note: [Col. 1053D] Mesnard, manuscript *History*, p. 219.], in his manuscript history of Anjou, and Father Le Long [Note: [Col. 1053D] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 203.] attribute to Baudri: namely, glosses on the Pentateuch. “He wrote unpublished little glosses on the Pentateuch,” says M. Mesnard: *Scripsit glossulas super Pentateuchum nondum editas.*

What doubtless gave occasion for attributing glosses on the Pentateuch to him is what he says in his letter to the abbot of Maillezais. There he asks the abbot to send him glosses on the Pentateuch of Moses which the abbot had shown him during his visit, and of which he had read a portion to him without naming their author. They had greatly pleased Baudri, who expressed a desire to have them complete and asked his friend to have them copied in a script and with forms that would not tire his age-weakened sight: *tali compactum charactere talibusque figuris quae seniles oculos non offendant*—“written in such a script and with such letter-forms as do not offend aged eyes” [Note: [Col. 1053D] *Gesta Dei per Francos*, p. 82.].

Baudri adds that, if his friend grants what he asks, it will be seed from which he will gather an abundant harvest, because he himself will place observations between the lines and extract the hidden senses [Note: [Col. 1053D] “For I think indeed that, once you have agreed to this for me, you will bring forth a student in me and receive a manifold harvest from the seed that has been sown. I shall indeed add interlinear interpretations and, wherever they lie hidden, draw out the inner kernels,” etc.]. If the abbot of Maillezais satisfied the bishop of Dol in this matter—as is probable, and as he gave him reason to hope in his reply [Note: [Col. 1053D] “The little glosses on the Pentateuch, which their restless seeker seeks by knocking, we shall send, copied out, to that venerable fatherhood as quickly as we can” [Col. 1054D]]—it is likely that the prelate in turn kept his word by adding his observations to the writing he requested. This no doubt gave occasion to attribute glosses on the Pentateuch to him, although it is clear that they were not his. They may have been the work of the abbot of Maillezais himself, who, in reading part of them aloud, perhaps did not wish through modesty to disclose himself as their author.

4. *Deeds of the Bishops of Dol.* This history of the archbishops of Dol is probably not different from Baldric’s chronicles, which Le Baud [Note: [Col. 1054D] Le Baud, pp. 70, 74, 112, 115, 118, 119, 120, 150, etc.] frequently cites in his *History of Brittany*, and of which [Col. 1053D] Symphorien Guyon [Note: [Col. 1054D] Guyon, eleventh century, p. 337.] says in his history of Orléans: “Baudri wrote the annals of his church from St Samson down to his own time.”

The extracts found in Le Baud indicate that Baldric’s particular aim was to establish, at least by possession, his alleged metropolitan right over Brittany, which he traces back to St Samson. Father Le Long [Note: [Col. 1054D] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 203.] assumes that the acts of the archbishops of Dol were printed in Cosnier’s notes on the Life of Robert of Arbrissel, published at La Flèche in quarto in 1641. Yet they are not found in that edition.

5. The same motive that led Baldric to give the acts of the archbishops of Dol led him to write the Life of St Samson. This is very different from the Life published by Du Bosc, or Du Bois, in his *Library of Fleury*, as well as from that found in the first century of Benedictine saints, among their acts published by Dom Mabillon [Note: [Col. 1054D] Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, p. 166.]. In the Life of St Samson found in the Library of Fleury, he has only the title of bishop. St Dubricius laid hands upon him about the year 501, says Adrien Baillet [Note: [Col. 1054D] Baillet, 28 July], and made him a regional bishop—that is, an apostolic missionary—without assigning him any particular see [Col. 1054B]. This overturns Baldric’s system, which makes him archbishop of Dol, where certainly there was no bishop until long after Samson’s death. Baronius [Note: [Col. 1054D] Baronius, year 559, no. 33.] assigns no see at all to this holy prelate. Bollandus was content to insert in his collection the Life of St Samson published by Father Mabillon.

6. After the death of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, which occurred in 1117, Petronilla, first abbess of Fontevrault, wrote to Baldric to urge him to compose the Life of this holy founder, whom he had known particularly well [Note: [Col. 1054D] Cosnier, notes on Baldric, p. 125; Bollandus, dedicatory epistle; Cosnier’s epistle in Bollandus, *ibid.*]. At first the prelate wished to excuse himself, on the ground that, being of decrepit age, exposed to the stormy waves of the world, and obliged to live among an undisciplined people, he would be overwhelmed by the weight of such an undertaking. Nevertheless, he yielded and soon satisfied the pious abbess by writing the Life of Blessed Robert [Note: [Col. 1054D] Bollandus, 25 February, p. 603; Baillet; Cosnier]. It may be regarded as a precious monument of twelfth-century monastic history.

What is especially noticeable is a striking character of truthfulness. Baldric applies himself solely to giving a complete idea of the apostolic missionary’s penitential life, of the discipline he established at Fontevrault, and of the poverty of his first disciples. He enters little into the detail of his actions and so neglected dates that he did not even determine the year of the monastery’s foundation. Thus it is less a life than a funeral eulogy of Blessed Robert. Baldric lacked documentary materials; he even complains of this in his dedicatory epistle to Petronilla.

We possess, under the name of Andrew, Robert’s confessor and companion in his journeys, a very detailed account of Robert’s final illness and death, of which Andrew had been a witness. These two works have always been joined together in every edition published to this day. Bollandus inserted the two writings in his collection [Note: [Col. 1054D] p. 603.], under 25 February, with notes sent to him from Fontevrault. An edition appeared at La Flèche in 1641 with this title:

> *The Beginning of Fontevrault; or, the little work of Baldric, bishop of Dol, concerning Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, and Brother Andrew’s supplement to the history of the Life of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel; edited and prepared by Michael Cosnier, priest of Poitiers, parish priest in the same place.*

[Col. 1055A] This edition contains notes by the editor and questions concerning the authority of the abbess.

We find a translation of the Life of Robert printed in Paris in 1585, and in Angers the following year, under the title: *Chronicle of Fontevrault, containing the Life of Robert of Arbrissel, by Baldric of Dol and Andrew, monk of Fontevrault, translated into French by Yves Magistri, or Yves Michel, of the Order of Friars Minor* [Note: [Col. 1055D] Langlet, *Méthode historique*, vol. III, p. 146.]. The same Life was translated from Latin by Jean Chevalier, Jesuit, in octavo, at La Flèche in 1647, by Griveau [Note: [Col. 1055D] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 280.]. The next year, in the same town and by the same printer, the Life of Blessed Robert appeared again through the care of Sébastien Ganot, religious of Fontevrault, with a dedicatory epistle to the queen regent [Note: [Col. 1055D] *Bibliothèque de Fontevrault*.]. In that edition the Latin and French stand in two columns.

7. The Life of St Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, [Col. 1055B] closely followed that of Blessed Robert, unless it preceded it [Note: [Col. 1055D] Possevino, vol. I; *Neustria pia*, p. 282; Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. III, p. 498; Pomeraye, *History of the Archbishops of Rouen*, p. 189.]. It is at least certain that it appeared before 1120, since Baldric dedicated it to Ursion, abbot of Jumièges, who died about that year. Indeed, he undertook it only at the request of that abbot and his monks.

St Hugh had been monk and abbot of Jumièges before being placed in the see of Rouen. After his death, in 730, he was buried in the church of that abbey, which he had richly endowed during his life. This may be seen in the Chronicle of Fontenelle, written in the time of Louis the Pious. Ursion and his monks wished to renew the memory of this great man, which had seemed buried in oblivion since the incursions of the Normans who devastated the country around the middle of the ninth century. They asked Baldric to write his Life.

But what success could be expected? All the ancient records had been dispersed by the barbarians. There existed only a badly composed Life of the saint, written about the middle of the tenth century [Note: [Col. 1055D] Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. III, p. 499.]—that is, [Col. 1055C] two hundred years after St Hugh’s death—by a religious who, lacking the necessary records, could only collect popular traditions, ordinarily liable to countless gross errors and anachronisms. Baldric worked from such a Life and composed his Life of St Hugh.

Had he possessed critical judgment, he could have observed its gross errors by comparing it with the Chronicle of Fontenelle [Note: [Col. 1055D] Chronicle of Fontenelle, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 495.], which reports nothing but accurate matter concerning the holy archbishop of Rouen. But far from entertaining any suspicion about the false and invented facts with which this Life is full, he regarded them as true and considered the author accurate in his simplicity: “I do not deny that those writings are simple, but nevertheless I know them to be true” (*Scripta illa non diffiteor simplicia, sed tamen scio veracia*).

Thus, in revising the Life of St Hugh, he corrected nothing in it and adopted all the false facts scattered through it. This caused great confusion in the history of the archbishops of [Col. 1055D] Rouen. Instead of the true St Hugh, archbishop of Rouen—son of Drogo, duke of Champagne, and Adaltrude or Anstrude, daughter of Waratto, mayor of the palace—Baldric gave us, on the basis of accounts full of false, invented, and now universally rejected claims, another alleged St Hugh, son of Charlemagne, who was never archbishop of Rouen. It is true that Charlemagne had a natural son named Hugh; but the testimony [Col. 1056A] of the best historians establishes that this Hugh was only priest and abbot, not bishop, and that he perished in 844 in a battle fought between the troops of Pepin, son of Pepin, king of Aquitaine, and those of Charles the Bald.

We shall not pause here to expose the falsehood of the accounts reported by the anonymous writer and adopted by Baldric. The authors who have discussed them before us have anticipated us; moreover, it has already been done in discussing the Chronicle of Fontenelle and the anonymous writer, two manuscripts of whose work are preserved in the library of Jumièges.

The continuators of Bollandus did not believe that the Life of St Hugh written by the anonymous author, or Baldric’s Life, deserved a place in their collection. Like Dom Mabillon, they confined themselves to pointing out their gross errors and making an extract from the Chronicle of Fontenelle, which contains the summary of the life of this holy archbishop of Rouen. Arthur du Moutier published in his *Neustria pia* [Col. 1056B] the Life written by the anonymous author of Jumièges and revised by Baldric.

8. Around the year 1120 Baldric composed the history of the translation from Rome to Jumièges of the head of St Valentine, priest and martyr at Terni in Umbria [Note: [Col. 1055D] Bollandus, 14 February, p. 758; Du Cange, new ed., under *Colonia*, vol. II, 14 February, p. 758.]. At the beginning of his work he declares that the simple and candid account which the monks of Jumièges gave him of what they knew bore such a mark of truth that it served him in place of authentic documents, and that the miracles related after his narrative rested likewise upon their testimony [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Accepting the monks of Jumièges’ unimpeachable sincerity, ancient simplicity, and pure account as a substitute for authority, and their testimony as authority for the miracles.”].

Bollandus, who published this account, observes that St Valentine was bishop of Terni, not a simple priest as Baldric believed; and that Valentine the priest and martyr was not the one of Terni but the one honored at Rome. M. Baillet [Note: [Col. 1056D] Baillet, 14 February.] states that the history of the translation of St Valentine’s head from Rome to Jumièges was written by Baldric in 1020. This is an error of the author, or rather [Col. 1056C] of the printer: 1120 must be read.

9. M. Duchesne [Note: [Col. 1056D] Duchesne, *Series of Authors*, p. 152.] attributes to Baldric three writings on the celebrated abbey of Fécamp, entitled as follows: first, *Names and deeds of the abbots who governed the monastery of Fécamp*; second, *On the revelation of the monastery of Fécamp*; third, *Description of the monastery of Fécamp, by Baldric, archbishop of Dol.*

The second of these three writings, printed in the *Neustria pia* [Note: [Col. 1056D] *Neustria pia*, p. 193.], is dedicated to William of Ros, third abbot of Fécamp, who died in 1107. This date, without mentioning the difference between the style of that writing and that of Baldric’s other works, seems sufficient to prove that he was not its author.

As for the first and third, they are merely one work furnished with two different titles. Besides these two, it has still others: *Account of the monastery of Fécamp*; *Baldric’s letter to the monks of Fécamp*; *Itinerary*. One is [Col. 1056D] surprised at so many titles being given to one and the same writing [Note: [Col. 1056D] Du Cange, new ed., vol. IV, p. 491.]. Yet not one is unsuitable. In the work in question, a letter to the monks of Fécamp, Baldric recounts his travels, and so it may be called an *Itinerary*. He speaks of several abbots who governed the abbey of Fécamp and describes that house in considerable detail; thus the letter could bear the various titles just reported: *Description of the monastery of Fécamp*, etc.; *Account of the monastery*, etc.

Thus the three writings on the abbey of Fécamp attributed to Baldric are reduced to one alone. It is a glorious monument for that celebrated monastery. The author observes, regarding the generosity with which hospitality was exercised at Fécamp, that it was an established custom there to give presents to guests when they departed. There was already an organ in the church at that time—then no common thing—and Baldric highly applauds the practice. He writes at length about William of Ros and reports that he was still mourned, although several years had already elapsed. He gives a fine eulogy of Roger, William’s successor. Orderic Vitalis says of this in his history [Note: [Col. 1057B] Orderic, book XII, year 1118.]: “Baldric, bishop of Dol, vividly sketched his distinctive virtues.”
