Dom Mabillon, in his *Annals* [Note: [Col. 1057C] *Annales*, book LXXI, no. 33.], reports the praises Baldric gives Abbots William and Roger in his letter [Col. 1057B] to the monks of Fécamp. Father Arthur du Moutier inserted this letter in its entirety in his *Neustria pia* [Note: [Col. 1057C] p. 227.].

10. Baldric is held to be the author of a History of St Valerian, who suffered martyrdom under the Emperor Commodus at the castle of Trenorque, or Tournus, between Chalon and Mâcon. Garnier and Falcon, monks of the abbey of Tournus—now a collegiate church of secular canons—wrote the acts of St Valerian about the beginning of the twelfth century. We possess Garnier’s acts and others without an author’s name; but these seem to be the same, apart from a few altered expressions.

M. du Bosquet, bishop first of Lodève and then of Montpellier, printed the latter in his *Gallican History* [Col. 1058A] [Note: [Col. 1057C] Book V, pp. 102–205.]; and Father Chifflet printed them in the *History of Tournus* [Note: [Col. 1058B] Vol. II, p. 33.]. They are also found in the two histories of Chalon known as the *Illustrious Orbandale*, with this difference: in one they have a preface and conclusion, which are absent from the other. Messrs Baillet and de Tillemont make little of these acts [Note: [Col. 1058C] Baillet, 4 September; Tillemont, vol. III, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 602.].

“It is believed,” says M. Baillet, “that the latter acts, published by M. du Bosquet, have as their author Baldric, bishop of Dol, who lived at the end of the eleventh century.” Father Chifflet maintains this, but offers no proof. Abbé Juenin considers them earlier and attempts to prove that they were written, at latest, at the beginning of the ninth century [Note: [Col. 1058C] Juenin, Part I, p. 11.]: first, because they say nothing of the translation of St Valerian, which took place in 980; second, because Ado seems to have seen them and drawn from them what he says of St Valerian in his Martyrology. We leave the reader to judge whether these reasons are decisive.

But whether the acts of St [Col. 1058B] Valerian published by M. du Bosquet are Baldric’s work or that of a writer older than he, they have neither more nor less authority. Even if we possessed the history by the bishop of Dol, which appears to be different, it would add no authority to them; therefore it is easy to console oneself that it has not reached us.

11. In the Library of Lambeth [Note: [Col. 1058C] Cave, p. 568.] there is preserved a manuscript containing a treatise *On Visiting the Sick*, attributed to Baldric. The same treatise, without an author’s name, is also found in a manuscript in the Library of Vienna, Austria. From what we have reported, the reader is able to judge Baldric’s person and writings.

[Col. 1057]

## FOUR BOOKS OF BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF DOL, ON THE HISTORY OF JERUSALEM

(Bongars, *Gesta Dei per Francos*, I, p. 81.)

## BALDRIC’S DEDICATORY LETTER TO PETER, ABBOT OF MAILLEZAIS
[Col. 1057D] Love forbids me silence and leads me into prolixity; love takes away leisure and draws me into business; love forbids me to be silent and compels me to speak and write. All this is the work of a love not new, but long-standing and continuous, though in some manner renewed. I had a particular and unique friend, who had made me wholly his own and took pleasure in himself only through me—I mean Lord Geoffrey, a venerable man, by parentage of Évreux, abbot of Maillezais, a man worthy to be remembered and described, had not the burden of pressing circumstances produced an obstacle for me. I truly returned his affection, insofar as I could, because in loving him I wished in no way to be his inferior. At last he rested in a praiseworthy end; yet he had first voluntarily laid aside the abbacy, so that he might devote himself more freely to contemplation and serve God Himself with fewer distractions.

Peter, his kinsman, afterwards a suitable shepherd, a man sufficiently energetic and well fitted for so great a charge, succeeded him in that same office, with Geoffrey’s own consent. For the monks of Maillezais elected him and chose him for themselves; and by placing over themselves as abbot the man whom they chose for love of his uncle, they showed in him the very affection they had borne my lord Geoffrey—although many merits also proclaimed him worthy of the abbacy. As he entered successively upon his uncle’s honour, so he remained his heir in the most becoming generosity of character. Thus, thanks be to God, we have this Peter surviving the good Geoffrey, very much in harmony with our own age and manners.

Therefore I, Baldric, by the grace of God archbishop of Dol, now write to him; and with all my heart I greet my Peter—mine, I say, and yours. I greet you, my Peter, as ruler of Maillezais; I greet you as my dearest brother; I greet you as a pilgrim and traveller to Jerusalem. I give thanks to my God, sweetest brother, who guided you forth and brought you back. I give thanks to my God who directed your foot aright; who orders all your affairs and has ordered them thus far. May He also, I pray, continue to order them, and may He, I implore, make His countenance bright upon you.

I also give you thanks, the tenor of which perhaps you have not yet heard, since you have not yet heard what I am about to command; and yet, in a certain manner, what I have resolved to enjoin upon you has already been done—as if you had already answered me: “Consider it said; consider it done.” I resolve to command you rather than request you, because I prefer to be imperious with one in whom I have confidence than to press, as an importunate and wearisome petitioner, upon one from whom I am compelled to despair. I thank you because you are such a one as I may trust, whom I may ask—or command.

Peter, my dear and reverend priest, graciously receive these expressions of my thanks in the love with which I speak them. Even if someone carps at them obliquely as premature, a person of sound judgment will judge them timely. For nothing can be untimely which is adorned by the kindness and title of distinguished affection. For the splendid and polished privilege of friendship produces delightful playfulness. Those who doubt one another are not truly friends; for friendly intimacy is blighted where either party’s confidence is begrudged.

But lest I be reproved as ungrateful to myself—for ingratitude is the stepmother of every good reputation—I give thanks to myself, because I have someone whom I may command. For I am not deprived of every consolation of friends when I may exercise authoritative command toward you. What I command is this: recently, in your chamber, you showed me some explanatory glosses on the Pentateuch of Moses; you yourself read them, but did not know how to name their author. They pleased me because they explained the sequence of the words and clarified whatever was obscure.

Therefore I command your fraternity, by commanding, to send me that little book, transcribed for my request: let it be written in such a hand and with such letter-forms as will not offend aged eyes, as will provide a path to the reader, so that the doubled lettering may not seem to split itself apart, and as will not blunt our understanding through ugliness. But if you can find elsewhere the remainder that is lacking, either indicate it to me, so that I may obtain the whole; or, generously enough, order it to be bought for me at your expense. For I think that, after you have complied with me in this, you will bring forth a diligent student in me, and from the seed cast down will receive a manifold harvest. I shall indeed add interlinear explanations and, wherever hidden, draw out the inner marrow. I shall add further whatever has been cut short; I shall correct whatever is superfluous. I shall dedicate the whole to your name and, as an unwearying investigator, commend it to future readers as something that will profit them, with your little book leading the way.

I do not doubt that you will solemnly perform what I have commanded. But there is another thing that I ask, desire, and in which I shall take great delight. Do not be barren toward me by failing to write back; visit me with such an embassy, and thus greet me—an exile and pilgrim in nearer Britain. I shall embrace it as another self; and you, always desire me as your neighbour, as another yourself.

I have sent you for correction the little book which I composed, in whatever fashion, *On the Journey to Jerusalem*. I wish you to restrain and polish it by regular critical judgment, and to send it back to me, together with this letter, not unrewarded. Meanwhile let us greet one another, that each may live and prosper, and that we may see one another again. Amen.

## PETER, ABBOT OF MAILLEZAIS, TO BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF DOL

[Col. 1059D] As your Holiness, experienced in such matters, has subtly and quite succinctly observed, that “love in no way loves silence,” we have long learned by experience, most reverend Father. For it banishes leisure and, by drawing the mind of the lover—who delights in the things belonging to love—toward what is love’s own, it kindles it indescribably.

But whence comes this to me: that a letter of my lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as its sound reached my ears, all that was within me exulted in my womb. Just as clouds of dark and gloomy air flee before the onset of the North Wind, so, at the sight of it, the phantoms of every thought and the weight of every biting care were expelled. No place remained for any sadness when the matter of such great and desirable joy had arrived.

Let others read and sweat over the immense volumes of philosophers; for me, the writings of my admirable Cicero suffice, and by their inexplicable sweetness refresh the soul of the reader. Let my most loving friend then believe whatever the ancient poets sang: only let him visit me in prose or verse, and, when I am weighed down by the fatigues and occupations of various affairs, revive me again and again through the frequent and sweet consolation of his letters.

If I undertook to describe his most gracious goodness of character and his most illustrious deeds, I should stand dumb before the magnitude of so great a subject and fear that, not by explaining them but rather by the inadequacy of my ignorance, I might obscure them by diminishing them. It is therefore sufficient—and wiser—to contemplate with admiration the many and great qualities of the pious Father, and, embracing and loving him with the arms of one’s whole mind, to delight in love.

Yet to whom shall I ascribe this indissoluble affection, for which I return thanks? To my own worthiness, or to his charity, which incorporates whomever it chooses into itself? It must altogether be assigned to him; it must all be imputed to him, who has joined an ant to himself and bound it fast with the glue of everlasting brotherhood. Therefore let him unhesitatingly command whatever pleases him, whatever comes into his heart, of his purchased servant; and, considering not the fulfilment of his command but the devotion of the one who fulfils it, let him assess it accordingly.

I am, I confess, I am his purchased servant. But whose servant? Surely of him whom, from his earliest years, the worthy proclamations of a praiseworthy life commend; who, ascending from virtue to virtue, deserved to be raised to the summit of the priesthood; and who, both by the ploughshare of holy preaching and by the example of good works—rebuking and exhorting—raises the people subject to him to lofty things upon the wings of virtues.

Truly blessed and beloved of God is the land of Brittany, illuminated by the flashes of so great a star. The East exults, adorned by the teaching of the apostolic Fathers and by its most glorious palm; let the West likewise rejoice, distinguished by the titles of so great a primate. Let that fierce people lay aside, in some measure, its inborn ferocity as it hastens to the honeyed eloquence of its watchman. Let no natural foolishness be imputed to it any longer, now that it is instructed by the teachings of so wise a bishop.

O admirable and praiseworthy mercy of the heavenly dispensation! In order to have mercy upon the fierce and to exclude foolishness, it sent to tame their bestial stiff-neckedness a most gentle patron, seasoned with the salt of incomprehensible wisdom. By visiting them, he enriched them; but he deprived us of the most welcome sight of him. By visiting, I say, a barbarous people long buried beneath the darkness of ignorance, he enriched them with an incomparable treasure, and withdrew from us a shepherd shining among our countrymen like Lucifer, the morning star.

My longer discourse would have turned toward him, had not the stormy tempest of so pressing a persecution, thundering against us, intervened. For the present, then, let his kindness kindly receive this very little offering; let him see it and not disdain to read it, looking not at the surface of its literary style but at the affection of its sender, who lays himself, heart and body, beneath the traces of his feet.

And because, with the divine page as witness, “a hidden treasure and concealed wisdom are worthless,” we shall send to his venerable fatherhood as soon as we can the glosses on the Pentateuch which the unwearied investigator seeks by knocking. For we do not doubt that, from this very small handful, we shall gather again a hundredfold fruit of multiplied harvest, profitable to succeeding posterity. Above all, however, we earnestly request that, as he promised in every detail, he correct them: scraping away every superfluity and carefully inserting whatever is lacking.

We also return the Jerusalem book, sent to me, a Jerusalem pilgrim, with the letter placed at its head and filled with wonderful sweetness. Yet I wonder, not a little and with astonishment, with what mind he sent the aforesaid little book to one ignorant and watered with scarcely a drop of learning, to be restrained and polished—especially since no poet would dare presume such a thing. For where the chaining together of many thoughts harmonizes, where the joining of parts proceeds with regular judgment and free movement, and where a careful reader finds nothing discordant, what remains to be corrected? But now, with humble greeting, we bring our speech to an end and earnestly pray that we may deserve to see the Father whom we long for.

# THE HISTORY OF JERUSALEM OF BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP  
## THE PROLOGUE OF LORD BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP, TO THE HISTORY OF JERUSALEM BEGINS

[Col. 1061D] BALDRIC, abbot of the brothers of Bourgueil, and afterwards, by the mercy of God, though unworthy, archbishop of the people of Dol, [wishes] all Christians to love peace and truth.

[Col. 1062D] Blessed be our Lord Jesus Christ, author of the Christian name and most invincible ruler, and most wise extender of Christendom. Dearest brothers, it is fitting that you bless Him and praise Him in all His works, and never forget His unfailing mercy toward us. He changes kings and times; He corrects the pious in order to advance them; He punishes the impious in order to correct them—for in Him there is nothing unmerciful.

In our times He stirred up almost all Christendom, wherever it was upon earth; and, so that Christian soldiery might assemble to rescue Jerusalem, in which He suffered, from the hands of the filthy Turks who ruled it as a captive woman, He unanimously incited His faithful people. For it must not be believed that, without divine inspiration, men abounding in every possession would be willing to go on campaign from the western region to the eastern, abandoning estates and homes, sons and wives, and to set out joyfully amid innumerable calamities in order to fight against barbarous nations with His strength.

For who has ever heard of so many princes, so many dukes, so many knights, so many foot-soldiers fighting without a king, without an emperor? Indeed, in this army neither did one man command another nor did another rule another; no one determined what seemed his own private concern, except what the common counsel of the wise decreed, except what the decision of the people approved. It is certain, therefore, that the Holy Spirit, who blows where He wills, both encouraged them to undertake such great labours and inspired among them an unbroken concord.

I have endeavoured to commend the course of this History to posterity in my own style, though it is not sufficiently polished, although the weakness of my small talent could not adequately expound so great a burden. Yet although in our days there was a great abundance of Sallusts and Ciceros, there was a barren lack of anyone willing to devote himself to this not ignoble task. Indignant, as it were, with our elders, who were sleeping and idle, I undertook this work; and, lest a history worthy of narration should yield to envious oblivion, I set my hand to writing when nearly sixty years old.

Certainly, if more eloquent persons undertake this same work more successfully, I do not in any way prejudge their eloquence if they correct me. I ask only that they not disparage my labour through envy or the fault of arrogance. Yet I did not deserve to take part in this blessed army, nor have I narrated things seen by myself. Rather, some compiler, suppressing his name, had issued a very rustic little book concerning this matter; nevertheless, he had woven together the truth. But owing to the uncouthness of the manuscript, noble material had become cheapened, and its unpolished and unadorned reading at once repelled even simpler readers.

Therefore I approached this study not from desire for empty glory or swollen pride, but, anxious that it might please succeeding Christendom, I committed it to little sheets of parchment. And although I am a Christian, descended from Christian forefathers, so that I now possess the sanctuary of God, as it were, by inheritance and have asserted an hereditary title to the Christian possession; and although I have abhorred paganism with all my strength as excluded from the law of God—yet, in setting forth the truth of history, neither love nor hatred nor the other vices shall knowingly precipitate me toward either side. Thus I shall not, by disparaging pagans, rashly favour Christians as a liar and falsifier; nor, if the gentiles performed anything bravely and boldly, shall I, begrudging their courage and boldness, take anything away from them.

I shall apply myself with moderation to setting forth the truth, and I shall restrain by the judgment of truth the partiality of my mind—which, nevertheless, I owe above all to Christians. For if I diminished the strength of the gentiles more than was just, I should detract from the courage and labours of Christians, while proclaiming with reckless exaggeration that our people fought against an unwarlike nation. Therefore I shall briefly recapitulate what I observed in the aforesaid book; relying on the reports of participants who were present there, I shall insert what I have heard, and thus, with God’s help, complete the work I have undertaken. Let us now apply our pen, waiting for the undertaking already mentioned. May God, the rewarder of all good things, repay for good to me the benefit of this presumed little work. Amen.

The prologue ends.

# THE HISTORY OF JERUSALEM BEGINS  
## How Christians from remote parts of the world, with the greatest labour, sought it out, conquered it, and held it. BOOK I

[Col. 1063D] Those who have read even lightly the books of historians, or who have eagerly lent their ears to the accounts of chronologers, know Jerusalem, the metropolis of all Judaea: a city neither undistinguished nor unknown, many times adorned beyond measure with royal honours, many times besieged by tyrannical enemies and razed to the ground, bereft of her own children when they were led away captive, and subjected to the various tumults of time before the coming of the Saviour.

Moreover, no one is ignorant—unless perhaps someone rashly and shamelessly tramples underfoot the page of the Gospel—that Christ, preaching over it, wept and foretold its destruction. How this happened will readily become clear to anyone reading the deeds of Titus and Vespasian, which the most eloquent Josephus consecrated in celebrated prose. The buildings themselves still testify that it was rebuilt and marked by Christian distinctions, and honoured with most fitting church buildings; and the lofty walls with which the entire city is surrounded bear witness to it.

Yet because, in the time of its own Christianity, that city obeyed its Christ less than it ought, it was again subjected to an earthly ruler and served him, because it gradually disdained to serve the heavenly emperor. Thus it became tributary for a long time to the Babylonian admiral, having strayed from its Christ in proud stiff-neckedness. Hence those colonists of the city who escaped death or captivity served profane masters, while gentile newcomers ruled over its native children.

The holy temple of God was indeed polluted; the court of God became, irreverently, a gathering-place for foreign gentiles. The house of prayer became a den of robbers, and Mother Church was changed into a stepmother for her own children. It is true that they allowed the church of the Holy Sepulchre to be preserved with somewhat greater honour—not because they cared greatly for the Christian religion, but because in this way they served their own interests and greed. Christians came from remote parts of the world for prayer and honoured that sanctuary with lavish offerings. But the gentiles afflicted the Christians who gathered there with every kind of forced service, and thoroughly stripped the pilgrims of the rich resources they had brought: they compelled them unwillingly on the road to hire transport, prevented them from entering the long-desired and long-sought city until they had paid the price of admission, and thus impoverished them through various exactions. Finally, they often tore souls from their injured bodies, worn out by tortures.

The barbarous people had also turned other churches to private uses: either stabling their beasts in them or, what is more shameful, doing whatever else was disgraceful there. Thus they provoked God against themselves, having abominably dishonoured God and defiled holy places by unlawful and foul acts. Therefore the divine counsel resolved to punish them and decided, through those over whom they had ruled, to drive them from the places consecrated to God.

For the gentiles had already extended their dominion as far as Antioch, and had likewise defiled the glorious places of that holy city. Thus they had provoked against themselves the wrath of the Almighty, because they had sent the stench of their deeds up to heaven. We sometimes saw among ourselves beggars and exiles who were citizens of Jerusalem; we saw natives of Antioch lamenting the downfall of the holy places and, reduced to poverty, humbly imploring public alms for themselves. Some of us pitied the needy, for we heard the same things from our pilgrims whenever they returned.

For the purpose of public preaching, Urban, bishop of Rome, came into Gaul; and, as he was an eloquent sower of words, he scattered the word of God everywhere. After a general council had been held at Piacenza, the aforesaid pope shortly afterward came to Clermont. There, with many bishops and abbots of Gaul, he again held a general synod. After first dealing with matters pertaining to the faith, he added the following address concerning the grievous misfortunes of the Christians of Jerusalem and Antioch.

Countless powerful and honoured men had also flocked to the council from many regions, although proud in the belt of lay knighthood. Seated therefore in the pulpit, he spoke as follows:

> “We have heard, most beloved brothers—and you have heard—that, without profound sighing, we cannot recount the great calamities, inconveniences, and dreadful sufferings with which our Christian brothers, members of Christ, are scourged, oppressed, and wronged in Jerusalem, Antioch, and the other cities of the eastern regions. They are your brothers, kin from the same womb; for you are children of the same Christ and of the same Church. In their own inherited homes, they are enslaved to hereditary or foreign masters, or driven from them; they beg among us, or, what is more grievous, they wander in exile, are sold, and are beaten in their own patrimonies.
>
> “Christian blood, redeemed by Christ’s blood, is shed; and Christian flesh, related to Christ’s flesh, is subjected to unspeakable outrages and wicked servitudes. In those cities there is mourning everywhere, misery everywhere, groaning everywhere. I speak in sorrow: in churches where divine sacrifices were once celebrated, alas, behold, stables are prepared for their animals. Wicked people have occupied the holy cities; the Turks, filthy and unclean, rule over our brothers.
>
> “At Antioch blessed Peter first sat as bishop. Behold, in that very church the gentiles have established their superstitions and shamefully expelled from the house dedicated to God the Christian religion which they ought especially to have observed. Estates of saints assigned for stipends, and the patrimonies of nobles entrusted for the maintenance of the poor, are subjected to pagan tyranny; after converting them to their own uses, cruel masters abuse them. God’s priesthood is trampled to the ground; God’s sanctuary—horrible sacrilege!—is profaned everywhere. If Christians still hide there, they are sought out for unheard-of tortures.
>
> “Brothers, we have until now almost refrained from speaking of holy Jerusalem, because we greatly fear and blush to speak of it. For that city in which, as you all know, Christ Himself suffered for us, has, because our sins require it, been brought under the filth of pagans and withdrawn from the service of God—to our shame, I say. For this is an accumulation of reproach for us Christians who deserved it, a great disgrace. Whom does the church of Blessed Mary now serve—the church in which she herself was buried bodily in the valley of Jehoshaphat?
>
> “And why have we passed over the temple of Solomon—or rather, of the Lord—in which barbarian peoples now place and worship their images against all right and justice? We refrain from recalling the Lord’s Sepulchre because some among you have seen with your own eyes to what great abomination it has been surrendered. There the Turks violently seize the offerings which you have often brought there as alms; there they heap innumerable mockeries upon our religion.
>
> “Yet in that place—and I do not speak of unknown things—God rested, there He died for us, and there He was buried. How precious and desirable is the place of the Lord’s burial, a place beyond comparison! Nor has God even there ceased to perform His annual miracle: on the days of His Passion, when every light in the sepulchre and in the surrounding church has been extinguished, the lamps, extinguished, are relit by divine radiance. Brothers, whose breast is of such flint that so great a miracle does not soften it? Believe me: a man is brutish and dull-witted whose heart is not struck into faith by so present a display of divine power.
>
> “Yet gentiles see these things together with Christians and are not corrected. They are indeed frightened, but are not converted to the faith; nor is this surprising, since blindness of mind rules them. You who are present, you who have returned, know better yourselves with how many afflictions they have wronged you—you who there sacrificed your possessions and your blood to God. We have said these things, dearest brothers, so that we may have you yourselves as witnesses to our speech.
>
> “There remain many more miseries of our brothers and devastations of the churches of God, which we could recount one by one; but tears and groans press upon us, sighs and sobs press upon us. Let us weep, brothers—come, let us weep—and, weeping from the depths with the Psalmist, let us groan:
>
> > ‘O God, the nations have come into thy inheritance;  
> > they have defiled the temple of thy holiness;  
> > they have made Jerusalem a watch-house for fruit.  
> > They have given the corpses of thy servants  
> > as food to the birds of heaven,  
> > the flesh of thy saints to the beasts of the earth.  
> > They have poured out their blood like water  
> > around Jerusalem,  
> > and there was none to bury them.’  
> > (Psalm 78)
>
> “Woe to us, brothers! We, who have now become a reproach to our neighbours, an object of derision and mockery to those around us, let us grieve and suffer with our brothers, if only in tears. We, made the refuse of the people and worse than all others, should lament the most savage devastation of the most holy land.
>
> “We may rightly call that land holy, for there is not even a footstep in it which was not illumined and sanctified by the body or shadow of the Saviour; by the glorious presence of the holy Mother of God; by the beloved passage of the apostles; or by the blood of martyrs, poured out and to be drunk in. How blessed, O Stephen the protomartyr, were the stones that crowned you! How fortunate, O John the Baptist, were the waters of the Jordan that served you in baptizing the Saviour!
>
> “The children of Israel, led out from the Egyptians, who prefigured you when they crossed the Red Sea, claimed that land for themselves by their arms, with Jesus as their leader. They expelled the Jebusites and the other intruders, and inhabited the earthly Jerusalem as an image of the heavenly Jerusalem.
>
> “What are we saying, brothers? Hear and understand. You who are girded with the belt of knighthood pride yourselves with great arrogance; you tear your brothers to pieces and are divided among yourselves. This is not Christ’s knighthood, which tears apart the Redeemer’s flock. Holy Church reserved knighthood for the aid of her own people, but you have wickedly perverted it into wickedness.
>
> “To speak the truth, whose heralds we ought to be: you do not truly keep the path by which you go to salvation and life—you who oppress orphans, plunder widows, commit murder and sacrilege, and despoil what belongs to another. You expect the wages of robbery for shedding Christian blood; and, as vultures scent corpses, so you seek and pursue wars in distant regions. Certainly this way is most evil, because it is altogether remote from God.
>
> “But if you wish to provide for your souls, either lay aside as quickly as possible the belt of such knighthood, or go forth boldly as soldiers of Christ and hasten to defend the Eastern Church. For from her have flowed the joys of all your salvation; she distilled into your mouths the words of divine milk; she offered you the most holy teachings of the Gospels.
>
> “Brothers, we say these things so that you may both restrain murderous hands from fratricidal slaughter and set yourselves against foreign nations on behalf of those who belong to the household of the faith. Under Jesus Christ our leader, may you, the Christian battle-line, the most unconquered battle-line, contend for your Jerusalem better than those ancient sons of Jacob themselves, and attack and conquer the Turks who are in it, more wicked than the Jebusites. Let it be beautiful for you to die for Christ in that city in which Christ died for you. But if it happens that you die before reaching it, count that as dying on the road, provided Christ finds you in His own service. God gives the same reward of the denarius to the first hour and to the eleventh” (Matthew 20).
>
> “It is dreadful, brothers, dreadful, for you to stretch out a rapacious hand against Christians; it is a lesser evil to brandish the sword against Saracens—indeed, it is a singular good, because it is charity to lay down one’s lives for one’s brothers. Do not, however, be anxious about provisions for tomorrow’s journey; know that those who fear God lack nothing, nor do those who love Him in truth. Even the wealth of your enemies will be yours: for you will despoil their treasures, and either return victorious to your own lands or, made purple by your blood, attain an everlasting prize.
>
> “You ought to serve such a commander, whose power lacks nothing and whose rewards lack no pay to render. The road is short, the labour very moderate, and it will repay you with so unfading a crown. Therefore let us now speak with prophetic authority: ‘Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty one’ (Psalm 44:4). Gird yourselves, I say, and be mighty sons, because it is better for you to die in war than to see evils befall your people and the holy things. Let not the enticing blandishments of women and of your possessions soften you so that you do not go; nor let the labours to be endured frighten you into remaining.”
>
> Turning to the bishops, he said: “You, brothers and fellow bishops, fellow priests and fellow heirs of Christ, proclaim this same message throughout the churches committed to you, and preach with all your voice and courage the road to Jerusalem. After confessing ignorance of their sins, bargain securely with Christ for heavenly pardon. And you who are going will have us as intercessors for you; may we have you as fighters for the people of God. It is ours to pray; let it be yours to fight against the Amalekites. We shall extend tireless hands toward heaven in prayer with Moses; you, fearless warriors, draw and brandish the sword against Amalek.”

When the apostolic lord had clearly made known these and similar things to those present, some wetted their faces with tears, others trembled, and others debated the matter. But among all those at the same council, as we saw, the bishop of Le Puy, a man of great name and highest nobility, named Naimarus, approached the lord pope with a joyful countenance. Bending his knee, he sought and obtained leave and blessing to go. Moreover, he received a command from the apostolic lord that all should obey him, and that he himself should, by virtue of his office, protect and assist the army in all things, since everyone knew him to be a bishop of great courage and singular ability.

Thus, when a worthy chief had been found for God’s army, a great multitude of nobles gave their assent, and immediately all sewed the banner of the holy cross upon their outer garments. For the pope had commanded this and had been pleased that those departing should make this sign. The supreme pontiff had indeed preached that the Lord had said to His followers: “If anyone does not carry his cross and come after me, he cannot be my disciple.” “Therefore,” he said, “you ought to fasten the cross upon your garments, so that by this you may travel more safely and furnish an example and encouragement to those who see you.”

While these things were taking place, behold, envoys of the count of Toulouse, namely Raymond of Saint-Gilles, suddenly arrived. They reported and testified before the council that he himself was going and had already fastened the cross upon himself. “Countless knights also,” they said, “have joined him, and he will lead with him a very great number of people from his own lordship.” They added:

> “Whoever belongs to God, let him join him, for he will share his wealth with the needy and will deny to none of the travellers his help and counsel. Behold, thanks be to God, two voluntary leaders have already come forward for the Christians who are to go: behold, priesthood and kingship; clerical and lay order agree in leading the army of God. The bishop and the count represent Moses and Aaron anew for us.”

On hearing this, any who had been faint-hearted yesterday took courage today, and everywhere clothed themselves with the holy cross. The council was dissolved, and each of us hastened back to his own home. The bishops preached, and now the laity too cried out the same message with freer voice. The word of God was sown, and the number of those bound for Jerusalem increased daily. Those who remained were ashamed, while those who intended to go on pilgrimage now openly gloried. People encouraged one another, and individually discussed these matters in corners and at crossroads. Indeed, they say that certain signs happened divinely for the accomplishment of these things—signs whose truth we do not at all fail to recognize.

(AD 1095.) [Col. 1070A] In the year of the Incarnation 1095, on the day before the Nones of April, Wednesday, the twenty-fifth day of the moon, an immense falling movement of stars was seen by countless observers in Gaul, so dense that, had they not shone, they might have been thought hail. Some even supposed that they had fallen; yet we do not rashly presume to affirm anything concerning their setting. We know, however, Truth itself bearing witness, that at some time the stars will fall from heaven (Matthew 24:29). As for their motion or flashing, if anyone doubts it, let him either believe us or at least accept our annals, in which he will find it recorded. What this convergence especially portended we do not at all determine, particularly since it has not yet been granted us to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but through parables and certain correspondences they compared the movement of the stars to the movement of Christendom. [Col. 1070B] For in the following year (1096) the synod was held at Auvergne, and the expedition was begun. Besides all this, a certain inward desire was inspired among Christians, so that nearly all would have undertaken the journey had they possessed the means for its expenses. Fathers rejoiced as their sons departed; wives rejoiced as their most beloved husbands went away, yet grieved the more because they themselves remained behind. Nevertheless, more departed than husbands who were scarcely, if at all, likely to return hastened away from their wives. And, in a strange manner, the emotion of joy drew tears from both alike, as usually happens at the deaths of loved ones.

Yet “the remedy exceeded its measure,” because in some persons the desire to go crept beyond what was proper. Many hermits, recluses, and monks, not wisely enough abandoning their dwellings, went on the expedition. Some indeed set out for the sake of prayer, having received permission from their abbots; but more slipped away in flight. [Col. 1070C] Many also among the common people displayed crosses which they boasted had been divinely born upon their bodies; and certain little women presumed the same. But this was found altogether false. Many, moreover, applied hot iron to themselves in the form of a cross, either from the contagion of boasting or in display of their good intention. But enough of these matters. By such reports the concourse of those departing increased so greatly that their number became numberless. We have inserted these things lest we seem either to have passed anything over or to be reproached for having indulged our countrymen in their vanities.

[Col. 1070D] Nor did that report stir only common people and those living on this side of the mountains; it also summoned palatine counts and royal princes: namely Hugh the Great, brother of the King of the Franks; Robert, count of Normandy, son of William, king of the English; and another Robert, count of Flanders. In the regions of Germany Duke Godfrey received this message, together with his brothers Baldwin and Eustace; likewise another Baldwin, count of Mount. Beyond the mountains too—that is, in Apulia—this message became widespread, and called Bohemond, a man of great ability, son of Robert Guiscard and brother of Duke Roger; it joined to him his nephew Tancred and Richard of the Principate. Moreover, if I ventured to speak of men of consular rank, I should neither pass Ralph of Baugency over in silence, nor omit Ebrard of Puiset, nor conceal anything concerning Centorius of Bieria or William Amanei, nor should my pen disdain many others, who nevertheless made themselves illustrious by their distinguished deeds and conducted themselves praiseworthily in God’s army. Yet envious oblivion shall not pass over these or others when a suitable occasion presents itself.

[Col. 1071A] The aforesaid men, having undertaken God’s expedition, approached Constantinople, city of the imperial majesty, with innumerable peoples. Nor could this thunderclap be hidden from England or the other sea-girt islands, though separated from our world by the abyss of the roaring sea. Indeed, rapidly spreading report encouraged and armed the Britons, the Gascons, and the farthest Gallic peoples. [Col. 1071B] The Venetians also, Pisans, Genoese, and those who inhabited the shores either of Ocean or of the Mediterranean Sea, covering the sea with ships laden with arms and men, engines and provisions, ploughed the waters; and those who went by land covered the whole face of the earth like locusts.

The aforesaid Germans had to pass through Hungary, and they passed through it. A certain Peter, the great Hermit, had preceded the following host with many Germans and very many Franks and had arrived at the imperial city. Yet he found there many Lombards, Longobards, and again Germans who had gone before him; and, in accordance with the emperor’s reply, they were awaiting the coming army. Meanwhile the emperor had ordered a market to be supplied to them in the city, as was right. He had also commanded them not to cross a certain arm of the sea, called the Arm of Saint George, until the great army which followed should arrive. “For,” he said, “if you act otherwise, savage pagans will rush upon you and destroy this unwarlike legion”—as indeed later happened.

[Col. 1071C] For that people, without king or leader, gathered indiscriminately from various places and living without discipline, greedily fell upon the property of others. They stripped and sold the lead with which churches had been roofed; they also demolished palaces and behaved wickedly in every respect. When the emperor learned this, he was greatly angered, since he saw that they were already ungrateful for his benefits. He therefore compelled them, expelled from the city, to cross the strait. Having crossed, they again committed many unlawful acts against Christians: devastating the countryside like enemies, they burned both houses and churches. At last they came to Nicomedia.

[Col. 1071D] There they separated the Lombards, Longobards, and Germans from the Franks; for the Franks were fiercer and more unmanageable, and therefore more inclined to every evil. The other peoples, after removing the Franks, appointed a certain Rainald over themselves; and under his command they entered Romania. Advancing beyond the city of Nicaea for four days’ journey, they found a certain fortress called Exerogorga, empty of all inhabitants, whether through fear or design is uncertain. Entering it to lodge there, they remained there, since they found it full to overflowing with every kind of provisions. When the Turks learned this through their scouts, they hastened without delay to surround the fortress.

[Col. 1072A] Rainald had gone out from the fortress with his men to lay an ambush for the approaching Turks. But the Turks prevailed and struck many of them down with the sword. Those who could fled and were received into the fortress; when it was surrounded on every side, the Turks immediately cut off their water. For the spring and well that supplied the fortress were outside it, and the Turkish army, strongly enclosing them on both sides, watched them without ceasing. Nothing is harsher for those in distress than lack of water; nothing more swiftly captures secure places than the suffering of unbearable thirst. The Christians were therefore compelled to draw and drink the blood of their pack-animals. Others dipped cloths in muddy cisterns and, if they found any moisture, were not ashamed to squeeze it into their mouths. [Col. 1072B] It is said—though it is very shameful—that some urinated into their hands and drank it. Others, if they happened to find damp or cool ground, dug it up; and either lay naked upon it, face upward, or placed it on their breasts, that they might at least in some fashion be cooled. Who could have lived amid such pressing anguish? Yet, though dying, they endured this great hardship for eight days, while the priests present spoke to them as follows:

> “[Col. 1072C] Endure, brothers, for God is present in order to test you. Therefore do not despair even in these great tribulations; rather, act courageously, so that you who have provoked His wrath may now, placed in extremity, beat upon His abundant mercy for yourselves. Placed in such distress, you will be able to deserve His aid if with your whole heart you flee to His help. Long ago in the desert of Sinai He commanded the rock to be struck, and waters flowed out, and our fathers drank their fill. He is still of the same power; He is still of the same mercy. If He does not now hear you, it is our fault; if He does not now regard you, it is our negligence. Remember that we have grievously offended and angered Him, we who have grown enormously wealthy through the plundering of our brethren’s property and through the destruction of churches beyond all telling.”

[Col. 1072D] The priests repeated these things to them daily; but they could not be made to drink the wine of contrition. They rotted like beasts in their own filth; hardened in heart like Pharaoh, they could in no way make satisfaction to God for their sins, and therefore they perished. They stopped their ears, deafer than asps against the voice of those who charm wisely, and therefore truly acted foolishly. Indeed their leader Rainald took counsel with the Turks and agreed, if he could, to betray his brothers to them. He went out with many men, pretending to proceed to battle, and as a deserter fled to the Turks.

Those who remained were compelled to make a dishonourable surrender; and—O wretched deed!—turned to despair, they committed an abominable apostasy against the Lord. But those who bore witness to their faith either underwent the sentence of death, were set up as targets and shot with arrows, were torn apart from one another, sold for a paltry price, or carried into captivity—some to Antioch, some to Khorasan, some to Aleppo, or wherever it more pleased their captors, triumphant and leading captives captive, to take them. [Col. 1073A] Yet, through the unshaken constancy of Christian faith, they came to rest in a glorious end.

The Christians suffered this first persecution on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September]. When the Turks again heard that Peter the Hermit and Walter, surnamed “Without Possessions,” were in another town called Civitot near Nicaea, they set out to pursue them. Emboldened by their second success, and like raging wolves or a savage tiger, they bent more eagerly upon shedding blood. Already confident of victory, they came running and encountered Walter, whom they slaughtered together with many who were with him. Peter the Hermit had already returned to Constantinople because the contentious people would not consent to obey him. Since the Turks found them unprepared, they overcame them more easily.

[Col. 1073B] They also beheaded a certain priest of the Lord while he was devoutly celebrating the solemnities of the Mass. Those who could escape alive fled, hiding among reeds, woods, or mountainous places. Others held the fortress of Civitot in order to defend themselves; the Turks immediately besieged it, brought very much timber from every direction, and prepared to set both fortress and men on fire. [Col. 1073C] But the Christians, now placed in the uttermost despair, became more courageous—for “despair sometimes makes men bolder”—and boldly cast fire upon the timber. Thus they escaped the fire, but did not wholly escape the imminent danger of death. For the Turks seized the entire fortification of the castle, and the Christians whom they captured they killed, enslaved, or mocked with every sort of insult.

This second suffering befell them in October. Behold: within a short interval of time and a small space of land, Christendom was twice crushed, twice punished, twice chastised. We do not doubt that this happened to them for the expiation of their crimes, to restrain the folly of the less cautious, and for the necessary discipline of the army that followed. [Col. 1073D] For those still encamped on this side of Constantinople, upon hearing this—many fugitives had returned, and the emperor had bought all their weapons so that, being unarmed, they might do less harm to his own people—waited for one another, so that, after sharing counsel, trusting in their leaders’ aid and supported by military forces, they might enter the enemy’s land, having first made the Deity favourable to them by the pure confession of prayers.

While these things were taking place, Duke Godfrey, Baldwin and Eustace his brothers, and Baldwin of Mount were travelling through Hungary with their companies and drawing near to Constantinople. The bishop of Le Puy and Count Raymond were making their way through Slavonia. Hugh the Great, the count of Flanders, and Robert duke of the Normans, passing Rome with their fellow-soldiers, arrived in Apulia. [Col. 1074A] Bohemond, hearing that such great multitudes of Franks were approaching—for a man of such importance could not remain ignorant of so widely proclaimed a report—investigated the merits and insignia of each. He ordered an excellent cloak to be brought, cut it into small pieces, distributed a cross to each of his men, and kept one for himself. So great a concourse of soldiers suddenly gathered to him that Count Roger, while under siege—for each of them was engaged in a certain siege—was left almost alone. Grieving that he had lost his people, he returned to Sicily with a few men.

[Col. 1074B] Bohemond, being a man in every respect most moderate, made modest preparation for his route and transport. With his nobles and abundant forces of armed men, he crossed the sea and at last, with a calm oar, landed in the regions of Bulgaria. The names of those who adhered to him on this expedition and had been joined to him in other wars are these: Tancred, son of the Marquess; Richard of the Principate; his brother Ranulf; Robert of Anxa; Ermannus of Canni; Robert of Surda Valle; Robert son of Turstan; Humphrey son of Ralph; Richard son of Count Ranulf; the count of Rusinolo with his brothers; Boellus of Chartres; Alberedus of Cagnano; and Gunfredus of Monte Scabioso. All these united unanimously with Bohemond and swore that they would obey him with the utmost devotion, inseparably, on the way of God.

Hugh the Great and William, son of the Marquess, hastily entered the sea at the port of Bari and, sailing, arrived at Dyrrachium. [Col. 1074C] But the duke of that city, one of the emperor’s princes, judging them—as indeed they were—to be great and capable men, ordered them seized, since they were not yet sufficiently protected by military squadrons and auxiliary bodies of infantry. He therefore had them diligently escorted under watchful guard to Constantinople, so that the emperor might determine concerning them as he pleased and might thus require homage and fealty from them. That duke appears chiefly to have acted thus in order that the matter itself might demonstrate, by such proofs, the devotion he bore to his emperor, and might bind the emperor to himself more closely.

[Col. 1074D] Duke Godfrey, first of all the dukes, arrived at Constantinople two days before the Nativity of the Lord and pitched camp near it. Bohemond, waiting for his followers who were striving to catch up with him, advanced slowly and thus, by proceeding little by little, prudently waited for them day after day. Soon afterward the emperor assigned the duke lodging in a suburb of the city. The men-at-arms of the ducal army, without any caution, ran outside the city to bring in straw and other necessities. For they as yet suspected nothing hostile from the emperor, who had voluntarily offered them lodgings.

But the emperor had secretly ordered his Turcopoles and Pechenegs to attack and kill those who went out day after day, keeping the closest watch for this purpose. The losses of his men were reported to the duke, and the unexpected ambushes of the Turcopoles became evident to him. [Col. 1075A] Baldwin therefore went out to protect his men and, if possible, to destroy the ambushers. Finding them pursuing his own troops, he unexpectedly attacked the unwary enemy and defeated them. He killed some and, fearless, presented sixty others alive and captured to his brother the duke. When Emperor Alexius—for Alexius was his name—heard this, he was very angry and continually devised evil in his heart against Christ’s army.

The duke, informed of the emperor’s furious agitation and taking precautions for the future, left the city and set up his camp where he had first pitched his tents. When night came, by the emperor’s command the duke’s camp was attacked and his army subjected to many injuries. But the duke, being exceedingly shrewd in such matters and a most valiant fighter, had wisely stationed guards to keep watch around the tents and commanded each man to remain alert, for he was not ignorant of the emperor’s tricks. [Col. 1075B] The attackers were swiftly repulsed; seven of them were killed, and the duke boldly drove the fugitives in flight as far as the city gate. Returning to his tents, he remained there nearly five days. Meanwhile the emperor was devising evil against him, while the duke was more anxiously taking counsel for himself and his men; the emperor forbade him passage through the imperial city, while the duke awaited the arrival of the nobles who followed.

At last, leaving nothing untried—for he was a perceptive and resourceful man—the emperor made an agreement with the duke under the pretext of peace: if he crossed the Arm [of Saint George], the emperor would always send him an abundant market and provide all who lacked necessities with the requisite assistance, provided only that he might be secure concerning the duke’s oath. [Col. 1075C] The emperor did this in order to remove the duke and his forces from that region, lest he be able to use the counsels and assistance of the princes who were arriving. The duke accordingly crossed over, after mutual pledges had repeatedly been made and received with the emperor concerning the promises.

Meanwhile Bohemond came into the valley of Adrianople and addressed his followers there in the following public speech:

> “Nobles and fellow-soldiers, henceforth we must all proceed cautiously. Caution is very necessary for us, especially since we are journeying from our homeland for God. We are pilgrims for God; we are soldiers of Christ. Let us restrain greedy hands from plundering the homes of Christians. [Col. 1075D] The time will come when we shall enter hostile land, when we shall be enriched and rejoice from their abundant spoils. Whatever Christians provide us with a market, let them come safely and return safely. The land in which we are is Christian land; therefore you may not plunder it. Let us take food there only as a blessing, and let us not strip our brothers’ goods beyond what the need of life requires. But you, our chiefs and companions, who are more mobile, take more vigilant care of the infantry; advance early enough while waiting for them, so that they do not fail on the way, and pitch your tents in good time. And because, thanks be to God, you are more wealthy, pour out your goods as alms to the poor. Keep the Lord ever present before your eyes.”

Having spoken thus, the most prudent hero fell silent and ordered the camp moved from the valley. [Col. 1076A] At last they came to Castoria, where they solemnly observed the Nativity of the Lord. After remaining there for some days, they could not obtain the market they sought. For the inhabitants of that city alleged that they were not pilgrims at all but warriors and tyrants. Driven by hunger, they were therefore compelled to seize oxen, horses, asses, and whatever else suitable for eating could be found. Leaving Castoria, they next encamped in Pelagonia.

There was there a very strongly fortified castle of heretics, richly supplied with every good thing. Attacking it on every side, they utterly destroyed it, burning its inhabitants with it, being enemies of heretics. For all these travellers equally hated Jews, heretics, and Saracens, all of whom they called enemies of God. [Col. 1076B] After the castle had thus been razed to its foundations and all its inhabitants exterminated, they struck their tents and came to the river Vardar. Bohemond crossed it with part of his army; another part, namely the count of Rosinolo with his brothers, remained behind.

The emperor’s men, who were ranging about as scouts while watching the roads, saw that the army was divided. Charging the count and his men, they hoped easily to overcome them, since the army had been separated from them. When Tancred learned this, whether by a messenger or through the uproar—for they were not yet far from the others—he urged his swift horse with the spurs and flew to them like lightning. Having crossed, or rather swum, the intervening river, he promptly brought aid to the count. [Col. 1076C] Two thousand knights followed Tancred; having likewise crossed the river, they gave assistance. Immediately, contrary to the Turcopoles’ expectation, they prevailed over them, put them to flight in battle, and gloriously triumphed over the fugitives.

[Col. 1076D] Having killed some and captured many more, they brought them bound before Bohemond. He questioned them why they so cruelly opposed his expedition, especially since he was not hostile to their emperor. They answered: “Posted on the emperor’s pay, we can do nothing other than what he commands.” Bohemond was angered at the emperor, but restrained himself. He dismissed them unpunished, but warned them with threats to prevent them from harming his people thereafter. Yet he is said to have told his companions:

> “Since we must pass through the emperor’s territory, let us restrain the swelling of our spirit and, so far as we can, avoid provoking him unjustly. It is the height of folly for a man to pour out all his spirit where an aroused mind will produce no result. Rather, it is the mark of prudence for a man subject to another’s power to conceal himself when he cannot satisfy his own power. It is prudent to defer until the proper time what one cannot accomplish immediately. Conversely, he deserves rebuke for sloth and cowardice who, when unable to do more, thunders with threats, but when able, forgets the wrong that has been done. If we can, let us overcome the emperor by benefits; if not, let us bear with equanimity and conceal the injuries inflicted upon us.”

[Col. 1077A] So he spoke and silently contained the anger of his heart. This battle occurred on Wednesday at the beginning of the fast. There is no doubt that the pilgrims fought unwillingly that day, except insofar as the necessity of self-defence pressed upon them.

Meanwhile the emperor’s envoys met Bohemond—for Bohemond had already sent his men to him—to conduct him safely through that land and provide them a market everywhere. For this purpose the emperor sent one of his *corpalatii*, a man very close to him and exceedingly capable. This man always went ahead and, speaking with the local officials on the emperor’s behalf, continually prepared a market of saleable goods for them. They came to a certain castle which, because it abounded in grain, cheese, wine, and oil, they were eager to attack. [Col. 1077B] The inhabitants neither prepared a market for them nor admitted any of them, so greatly did they fear them. But Bohemond vigorously forbade the attack, lest perhaps the emperor find some fault in it, although Tancred and others strongly opposed him to his face. Nevertheless, the judgment of the man forbidding it prevailed.

When morning came, the inhabitants went out to meet him, carrying crosses before them, begging pardon, and offering him whatever pleased him. He willingly granted them pardon and passed on. He came to the city called Serra, where they had a sufficient market. Bohemond then acted wisely: he came to an agreement without any bitterness with two *corpalatii*, and that day they became the closest of friends. [Col. 1077C] On account of their friendship, he ordered all animals seized by his men, wherever found, to be restored. The *corpalatii* restored all things to the persons to whom they belonged; consequently, the mourning of those who wept was turned into joy.

Then, as time required, they encamped from place to place and came as far as the city of Rusa. There, after sufficiently procuring all necessities—for the Greek people eagerly desired to see Bohemond—they pitched their tents on Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper. Leaving his people there, Bohemond went with a few men to the emperor and said to his men: “Conduct yourselves moderately. I shall go ahead of you to prepare your passage; but approach the city with restraint, and do everything wisely.”

[Col. 1077D] Tancred, the head and leader of Bohemond’s force, saw that the Christians on expedition were impoverished and destitute, and felt immeasurable compassion for them. He therefore resolved to lead them by another road where they might find provisions. They entered a valley rejoicing in fertile soil and full of bodily nourishment, where they celebrated the Lord’s Passover. When the emperor heard that Bohemond had arrived—whom he greatly feared, since he had often heard of his prudence and courage, and had himself fought and prevailed against him, once and again, along with his father Guiscard—he received him honourably and supplied him abundantly outside the city, as befitted them both.

[Col. 1078A] While the emperor had ordered a conference with Bohemond, Duke Godfrey had returned to Constantinople, leaving his own men beyond the Arm, because the emperor was sending him no market, contrary to his agreement. The bishop of Le Puy and the count of Saint-Gilles were also present, having again left their multitude behind them. Having taken counsel with his men—for the Greek people are very skilful in counsel—the emperor addressed each leader through envoys, requiring all of them to render him both homage and fealty, and then to cross over in safety. The nobles of the imperial city, taking precautions lest the Franks, assembled together, rise against them and deprive them of their goods, had advised the emperor thus, so that they might at least live securely from the Franks. For the Franks altogether avoid perjury.

[Col. 1078B] The emperor sought this cleverly; the Franks stoutly refused. The Franks maintained that they owed an oath to none but God, whose soldiers they were on the expedition. To this the emperor responded by refusing passage, while promising henceforth both market and escort, affirming that he himself would go after them and bring them assistance with all his forces. The Franks were distressed: they refused to swear an oath, especially because the Greeks would otherwise permit them no passage. What were they to do? They did not wish to fight Christians; they could not obtain peaceful passage; and they abhorred returning home with the purpose for which they had gone left incomplete.

[Col. 1078C] At length, many, compelled by necessity and somewhat induced by the emperor’s promises, adopted this resolution: they would satisfy the emperor on this condition, that he should command an oath to be sworn to them regarding whatever he promised them. And this was entirely done. They therefore swore to Emperor Alexius concerning his life and honour, that they would take neither from him so long as he faithfully maintained what he swore. But the count of Saint-Gilles resisted more than the others; indeed, he restlessly considered how he might avenge his men upon the emperor. Nevertheless, the common judgment of the leaders prevailed, and they recalled the spirited count from this intention. He swore, therefore, but was not brought to render homage, for he declared that he would rather die than render homage to the emperor. The Greeks say that the count’s oath was sufficient, since they could not extort what they demanded beyond it. Immediate orders were therefore given concerning embarkation.

[Col. 1078D] Meanwhile Tancred arrived with the army entrusted to him. Hearing that the emperor had required an oath from the elders, he hid among the common people with Richard of the Principate and, hastening to the ships, crossed over quickly. Bohemond, however, briefly said to his men who were about to cross:

> “Hasten your march and do nothing rashly. I shall remain awhile longer to speak about the market, lest we appear to have acted without deliberation. Walk prudently, neither too slowly nor making war foolishly. It often happens that the folly of some hinders the causes of the wise. See, therefore, how cautiously every one of you walks, and let each warn the other more carefully.”

[Col. 1079A] Having said this, he urgently ordered the crossing. Behold, the envoys of the bishop of Le Puy and likewise of the count of Toulouse were present again. The count therefore remained with his people until satisfaction had been given to him and to Bohemond concerning the market.

Godfrey, with the others, came to Nicomedia and remained there with Tancred for three days. When it was learned that no road lay open by which so many and such great hosts could proceed, the duke sent three thousand men to level the steep places of the rocks and mountains. Taking axes, adzes, mattocks, and various other iron tools, they cleared thickets and brushwood and made level the precipitous parts of the mountains, preparing a road for the army. They also set up lofty markers which those following could recognize, lest they lose their way. They arrived at Nicaea on the day before the Nones of May, that is, 6 May.

Now Nicaea is the capital of all Romania. When the camp had been laid out and the tents pitched, Nicaea was besieged—a city [Col. 1079B] most strongly fortified, seeming impregnable because of its walls rising toward heaven and the adjoining lake encircling one side of the city. There the Christians suffered a grievous shortage of bread, so that, whenever a single loaf could be found, it was bought for twenty or thirty denarii; for the emperor had not yet sent them a market. But God provided for His own: Bohemond soon arrived, bringing an abundant market by land and sea. Thus an unexpected and sudden plenty of provisions came upon the whole army of Christ.

On the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, they began to attack the city and to raise wooden engines against the height of the wall. For two days they fiercely assailed the city and attempted also to undermine the wall. The pagans within, on the contrary, pressed on stoutly, defended their walls and homes with great force, hurled stones and missiles, protected themselves with shields, and boldly opposed the oncoming storm of arrows. [Col. 1079C] On the other side, the Franks left nothing untried: sheltering beneath a roof of interlocked shields, they avoided the shower of missiles and repeatedly harassed the besieged, though often exhausted.

Meanwhile the citizens sent messengers and, since the city could not be watched on the side where the lake extended, summoned aid from their countrymen and neighbours, saying: “Hurry in through the southern gate without fear. For the southern gate is still free from every siege.” On that very day, namely the Saturday after the Ascension of the Lord, that gate was entrusted to the Count of Toulouse and the Bishop of Le Puy, [Col. 1079D] since both had arrived that day. As the Saracens came rushing up confidently, the count, armed unexpectedly, met them; his whole army stood splendidly under arms; and all, trusting in the sign of the holy Cross, manfully repelled the barbarian folly. That people, having lost no small number of their men, shamefully turned to flight and was easily overcome by the Franks. The count therefore entered his tents that day with a great trophy.

The besieged citizens again sent messengers to speak of aid and, by oath, to testify to their hope of battle and certainty of victory. Their allies came in crowds, rejoicing together, declaring that victory was in their hands, and already delighting in the prospect of plundering their enemies’ spoils. Each brought out his own ropes [Col. 1080A] with which to lead captive Christians, bound, to his home. For they trusted both in the great numbers of the assembled nations and in the strength of their own courage; they also despised the Christian people, as being worn down by the length of their journey, by hunger and thirst, and by many other hardships. Thus, gathered rashly from the mountain summits, they descended and strove to rush as far as the city.

The Franks met them again. For the Franks, neglecting nothing, guarded every road; they attacked them again, overcame them again, and put them again to flight. Having consigned many to destruction, they returned victorious. They also brought back many heads of the slain, which the slingers hurled [Col. 1080B] into the city, to the joy of the besiegers and the terror of the besieged.

Yet the pagans did not resist the Christians with less spirit: now they hurled missiles from the battlements and defended the walls; now they advanced and disturbed the very camp. Against them Count Raymond and the Bishop of Le Puy assigned men continually to undermine the tower which rose threateningly over their tents, and to persist, despite exhausted strength, in the task assigned to them. Attacking the city, they drove back the resisting inhabitants with crossbows, bows, and slings—for you would have thought the incoming missiles a hailstorm. They sent men prepared for battle as far as the walls and prudently protected them, lest the townsmen contrive any harm against them. They undermined the tower to its foundations; having inserted timbers and set fire [Col. 1080C] in the perforated wall, they returned unharmed to their own men.

The fire immediately took hold of the timber. When it had burned, the overhanging tower weakened; splitting open through its cracks, the whole structure collapsed in ruin. But because it was night, the Christians could not and would not fight against the city, intending to do so on the following morning. This delay greatly benefited the besieged and greatly harmed the Christians. For during the night the pagans tirelessly rebuilt the wall. They passed that night without sleep, slackening in nothing but mutually encouraging one another to defend their city.

At daybreak the Franks were greatly astonished at the unexpected rebuilding of the wall, praised their opponents’ untiring labour, yet grieved because they were compelled to remain there longer. [Col. 1080D] For the defenders had suddenly raised the masonry so high that the Christians could not harm them at all on that side. Thus the Christians’ labour was rendered useless: their undermining of the walls did them no good. Behold, Count Robert of Normandy had arrived.

All these besieged the city, pitching their tents nearby. On one side Bohemond and Tancred besieged it; beside them stood Duke Godfrey with his brother Baldwin and Eustace. Next came the Count of Flanders, a vigorous man and a most daring knight. Beside him were Count Robert the Norman, Stephen of Chartres, the Count of Saint-Pol, Conan son of Count Geoffrey, Ralph of Gaël, Roger of Barneville, [Col. 1081A] and very many others. At the southern gate the Count of Toulouse and the Bishop of Le Puy, as has been said, kept watch. Thus they enclosed it all around, so that no one could enter or leave except where the city was surrounded by the lake. For the inhabitants sailed securely across the lake in the Christians’ sight and brought in by ship what they needed.

Thus the army of Christ besieged the city. “O splendid camp! O majestic tents! Who has ever seen such tabernacles? Let that flattering tale of Troy cease; let those tents of the Pelasgians become worthless; let the deeds and names of those chiefs be henceforth obscured. There Ulysses exercised his cunning; Ajax displayed his boldness; Achilles showed his hardness. Here the Christians showed forth dove-like simplicity, and in arms practised a pure and glorious warfare. Pure in conduct, vigorous in body, courageous in heart, they fought; for they safeguarded their souls and renounced every unlawful desire and pleasure of the flesh. They shone in arms and were especially becomingly adorned in their morals.” [Col. 1081B]

I confess, and confess truly, that if Balaam (Num. 24:3) had been worthy to behold so fair a sight, he would have preferred these tents to the tents of Israel. For in the Christian camp he would have found neither a Midianite woman whom Phinehas ought to pierce with a dagger (Num. 25:6), nor a malignant serpent whom he should torment for its wickedness. In brief, that army resembled the beautiful Church; indeed, it possessed such beauty that we may not rashly say Solomon sang of another when he declared: “Behold, [Col. 1081C] you are beautiful, my beloved, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon” (Song of Songs 1:4).

In this expedition the commanders themselves fought and themselves kept watch, so that one could not tell how a commander differed from a soldier, or a soldier from a commander. Moreover, there was such common ownership of all things that scarcely anyone called anything his own; rather, as in the primitive Church, almost all things were held in common among them. They had utterly banished brothel and prostitution far from their camp and were especially concerned with moral uprightness. Women nevertheless lived there among the men, but either in marriage or in lawful service. If anyone was convicted of any indecency, he was rebuked and punished publicly, so that fear might be instilled in the rest, or severe vengeance was taken upon him. For daily the bishops preached [Col. 1081D] about continence and abhorred every prostitute and every abuse from the midst of the camp.

Those soldiers eagerly exposed themselves to their enemies’ swords for their brothers, and rejoiced wonderfully if they were thought worthy to die in avenging injuries done to their neighbours. “O Gaul, exalted above all lands! Behold how beautiful are your tents in Romania! Armed, you set out from western Europe and pitched your tents and the stakes of your pavilions in Asia. May God preserve and perpetuate this unanimity of your good will, so that you may proceed safely to the Jerusalem for which you long.”

Meanwhile the Turks laboured hard both to defend the city and to restore the walls, never resting from their reconstruction. Besieged on every side by land, they committed themselves safely to the lake in order to bring in provisions. [Col. 1082A] They went and returned before the Christians’ eyes, and however great the Frankish army might be, it could not harm them. But who escaped their vigilant ingenuity? The Franks, men most prudent in every respect, adopted a plan to take even the lake away from the townsmen. They therefore sent an embassy to Constantinople—formerly called Byzantium, from which we still call the coinage of that city Byzantine denarii—requesting that the emperor, by his sovereign command, send a plentiful fleet to Civitot, where there was a convenient harbour, and that, since delay harmed those who were ready, he should allow no postponement in dispatching it.

“Moreover,” they said, “send us oxen and carts to carry rafts over the mountains [Col. 1082B] and woods as far as the lake. If you do this, you will certainly recover the city of Nicaea, which we besiege and which the Turks violently took from you; for they will have no escape if we cut them off from their shipping.”

At the emperor’s command, oxen were quickly brought, sailing vessels reached the harbour of Civitot, and the emperor’s Turcopoles were also present. Boats were placed upon carts and, with oxen serving this task, were hauled with great labour to the shore of the lake. On that day they did not launch them into the lake, judging it better to wait for night. They seem to have done this in order to approach the city unexpectedly by lake and seize the townsmen’s shipping before they knew it. When the sun had set and night lay upon the earth, [Col. 1082C] they launched the ships into the lake and entrusted them to the Turcopoles.

At dawn, as the day was whitening, the ships, furrowing the lake, advanced in order toward the city. When the citizens saw from afar the lake covered with ships, they marvelled and supposed perhaps that aid was coming to them. But once they had proof that those ships had been prepared against them, and that their own shipping, as it had been yesterday and the day before, no longer lay open to bring them provisions, they stiffened with fear and, drained of blood, despaired. For, disturbed by this sudden reverse, everything had happened contrary to their expectation. They could no longer resist in rebellion, with innumerable nations gathered against them. For a city besieged by land and lake, there was no hope of safety, no place of escape, except the disgrace of surrender, which attends all the defeated.

[Col. 1082D] Unfamiliar weapons terrified them, and the very gleam of the weapons unnerved the besieged. They knew the Franks to be a fierce and warlike people, unwilling to desist from an undertaking until everything fell out according to their wish. They knew them to be wholly merciless—slayers of their people, whom they themselves had provoked. Therefore, deliberating over the imminent danger, they sent to the emperor and offered terms for themselves under a law of surrender:

“Let your imperial faith, which must not be violated, make us secure concerning our families and our small possessions. Receive the surrendered city under the covenant of your protection; command that we depart unpunished, and we shall restore your city to you. Protect us from these executioners, who will yet grievously harass you, [Col. 1083A] and cause us to be brought into your presence. We shall obey your commands if you likewise respond to our wishes. Let it be permitted us to serve you; let it be permitted us, alive, to rise up and fight for your empire or your person. Do not charge it against us that, while we were able, we fought against you; for then we lived under the law of war. Grant us life and make us subject to you; from enemies make us your devoted servants. If—God forbid—you afterwards find us ungrateful to you, repay our ingratitude as it deserves, with our bodies punished and finally our heads cut off. For we shall be more faithful to you in proportion as your benefits make us more indebted to you. Let the emperor’s generous liberality spare the conquered and subdue the proud.”

When the emperor heard this, the event subsequently proved that, envying the Christians’ success, [Col. 1083B] he secretly granted the embassy’s request. He ordered his attendants to bring the men who surrendered themselves and their possessions safely to Constantinople, and carefully to arrange for the preservation of the city. In accordance with the emperor’s command, everything was done: the city was surrendered, and the pagan people were brought unharmed to the imperial city. As has been said, the emperor received them not merely with freedom from captivity but with the honour of liberty, and honoured them, once maintained with great generosity.
