He is said to have done this so as to attach the rescued men to himself, invite others to surrender, encourage them at a suitable time against the Christians, and, when opportunity offered, rebel through those persons against whom he secretly felt envy. Yet he bestowed many gifts upon the poor Christians [Col. 1083C] in order, by this hidden pretence, to conceal what he was hiding in his heart and reserve himself and his schemes for suitable future machinations.

After the city’s surrender, the Christian people withdrew from the siege. Many Christians died there: some from hunger, some by the sword, others by some other destruction. They regarded these as happily crowned with martyrdom, because they gave up their bodies out of compassion for their brethren. Among the pagans too, through the varied events of war and the disasters of the attacking forces, one might have seen many bodies slaughtered and found many unburied corpses scattered everywhere.

The Christians remained there for seven weeks and three days; when the city had been taken—or rather surrendered—they turned their steps elsewhere. The emperor had ordered that the possessions of that city should not be made public spoil. They would not have wished to spend so many days there either, since, after wasting their resources and many days, it seemed that they had sacrificed everything to the emperor: both the blood they had shed and the wealth they had brought, which they had diminished beyond measure. Nor did they rejoice in the rich spoils [Col. 1083D] acquired through deaths of many kinds. They therefore regretted the long siege, since they had not taken possession of the city in the manner of a conquered town; for if at least the enemies’ goods had been declared public booty, the poverty of the needy might have been alleviated and their exhausted expenses somewhat repaired.

They therefore did not bear Alexius’s command with equanimity, though they deferred the matter because they could then achieve nothing. Here the seedbed of hatreds first became visible; here the nourishment of enmities was discovered; here the incentives of discord began to sprout; here the semblances of rivalries seemed to grow. For because Alexius had not acted rightly toward them, they began to contemplate revenge against him. Let the first book therefore end here: after the first city had been overcome, though they had not obtained it as they wished, the Christian army prepared to go elsewhere to wage war. Meanwhile let the Christians proceed, while we apply ourselves to the work begun, with the light of dawn rising.

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

On the day when the siege was lifted, they came to a certain bridge, where the Christian army [Col. 1084B] pitched its tents. They stayed there two days; on the third day, before the morning star had whitened at dawn, they hastily set out. Because the night was dark, in uncertainty they took an uncertain road.

Divided from one another, they completed a journey of two days in two separate columns. In one column were Bohemond, Robert the Norman, Stephen Count of Blois, Tancred, the Count of Saint-Pol, Walter of Saint-Valery, his son Bernard, Gerard of Gournay, William son of Viscount Ranulf, William of Ferrières, Hervé son of Dodeman, Conan son of Count Geoffrey, Ralph of Gaël, his son Alan, Riold of Loheel, Alan, seneschal of the holy Church of the Archbishop of Dol, and many others. [Col. 1084C] In the other were the Count of Toulouse, the Bishop of Le Puy, Duke Godfrey, Baldwin, Hugh the Great, and the Count of Flanders, with abundant companies of travellers.

On the day after the second, Turks as innumerable as the sand of the sea gathered against Bohemond. Seeing the Christians and trusting in their great multitude, they attacked them boldly and in concert. Anger and fury encouraged them; they were also indignant that foreigners should lay waste their possessions, and they felt most bitterly that the Christians had dared to capture Nicaea. But Bohemond, seeing the countless multitude of enemies threatening and attacking his men with rapid speech and savage sword, stood undaunted and spoke with good judgment to his companions:

[Col. 1084D] “Most valiant soldiers of Christ, behold, the time for fighting has come. Cast away every fear which makes even men womanish, and manfully provide for your own defence. Tirelessly endure the blows of those attacking you; trusting in the aid of Jesus Christ, stretch forth your warlike hands and, while there is time, show the strength of your forefathers. I beg you, let not the glory of the Franks be dishonoured through our negligence, nor the holy name of Christians become cheap through our sloth. The situation is desperate; war confronts us; a numerous enemy is near. Yet nothing has befallen you beyond your expectation or desire: everything has happened according to your wish. For this you left your homeland; for this you came: you have always desired war. [Col. 1085A] Behold what you have long wished and prayed for; behold, they have surrounded us on every side. But, O unbroken race, O most unconquered people, do not be afraid, for God is truly with us. If anyone is fearful, let him summon a courageous spirit in this crisis—or at least hide his fear through shame. Now we need arms and courage; it is not a time for sloth or inexperience. Why delay with words? Let each now speak to himself.”

Then he ordered the tents to be swiftly made ready and commanded the companions who had moved farther away from him to come forward to aid them. “Unless you hasten,” he said, “the unavoidable danger of death presses upon us. The report of battle is not doubtful: we see it with our eyes and feel it in our wounded bodies. Come now, Christians, [Col. 1085B] run to us and defend both us and your commonwealth. The danger in which we stand is common; the peril in which we struggle is common.” Then he said: “You infantrymen, vigorously and wisely pitch the tents; you knights, advance with me to meet them and tirelessly bear the toil of battle. We have come as warriors for Christ; let us not fail in this battle of Christ. Let each man tell himself what he knows must be done in such an undertaking.”

Meanwhile the Turks arrived shouting and fiercely harassed the Christians with arrows, javelins, and close blows. No rest was granted to the weary; one could see every Christian body streaming with blood or sweat. The Franks, on the other hand, bore the weight of war without ceasing; they sometimes prudently delayed their charges against the enemy; at times resisted with swords; awaited the summoned allies; and wavered in nothing. [Col. 1085C] From the third hour of the day until the ninth the Christians endured this violence of battle.

That day women were especially necessary to the combatants: they quickly offered water to the thirsty and strengthened the fighters with encouragement. The field of Mars glowed, for both sides fought with all their strength. The Christians were distressed, since they were often attacked in their very camp. The other army disbelieved Bohemond’s envoys, doubting the certainty of the battle. For it could not imagine that any people would dare to seek battle against a tenth part of its army. But once this report spread throughout the whole army [Col. 1085D] and envoys were sent in addition to envoys, the duke, a most vigorous knight, Count Stephen, a prudent and moderate man, and Hugh the Great with their fellow soldiers flew to the aid; Baldwin and his brother Eustace likewise came undaunted with their comrades. The Bishop of Le Puy followed behind them, as did Raymond, Count of Toulouse.

The hearts of the already exhausted Christians marvelled where so great a people, so suddenly and beyond expectation, had emerged against them. For the enemy covered mountains and valleys; wherever there were plains, all were filled with dense formations of troops. They were Saracens, Agulans, and Persians, whose number they reckoned at three hundred and sixty thousand, apart from the Arabs, whose gathering [Col. 1086A] was uncounted.

Meanwhile the needed and expected assistance was desired. They said, “Would that it might come!” They spoke to one another: “Let us keep secret what we eagerly hope. With God’s help today we shall triumph over those now savagely attacking us; today we shall be enriched and rejoice in their wealth. Meanwhile let us be silent and endure.” Thus they encouraged one another, and the contest was carried on with swords drawn and brandished toward death. Unless God had then been present in the camp of His own people and prepared aid for the exhausted, that very day would have brought the whole expedition to an end.

The allies whom they had summoned arrived suddenly. The Bishop of Le Puy, with his great army, took the enemy in the rear; on another side the Count of Saint-Gilles, Baldwin, and Eustace rode swiftly; [Col. 1086B] from the right Duke Godfrey charged, together with Hugh the Great and Robert of Flanders, a knight most ready in every respect. Robert the Norman was already fighting with Stephen of Blois, Tancred, and Baldwin. The pagans, astonished that they were unexpectedly pressed by enemies both in front and behind, entrusted themselves to flight and turned their backs in retreat. The Christian sword cut them down to utter destruction, and many met death in diverse ways. Those who could hid in hiding places. Many thousands of barbarians were slain there, because the Christians fell heavily upon those who had pursued them mercilessly throughout the day.

William the marquis, Tancred’s brother, died that day, and Geoffrey of Mont Scabious—men highly martial, of good character, and distinguished. [Col. 1086C] Besides these, many Christian knights and infantrymen fell.

For we do not dare call the Turks unwarlike: they are exceedingly powerful in cunning, flourish in bold courage, and fight with an unturned sword. They also very frequently inflict death upon enemies from afar, because they use bows and rely on many instruments of war. Yet at that time they had greatly unlearned the practice of fighting, because they had enjoyed a long period of leisure. They nevertheless boast that they derive their genealogy from Frankish stock and that their forefathers departed from Christianity. They also say that none should naturally wage war except themselves and the Franks. If, however, they returned to Christianity, then they would rightly glory that they had sprung from Frankish lineage.

For the present, let this suffice: unquestionably they are men cunning, ingenious, and warlike; but, alas, alienated from God. [Col. 1086D] Therefore that nobility from which, as they say, they originally proceeded is darkened, because they have not been grafted into the true olive, which is Christ.

This battle occurred on the Kalends of July, 1 July. The Christians gave thanks to their Christ, who had rescued them from the hands of their enemies and filled them with His consolations. Therefore they celebrated that day as a feast and offered God worthy praise.

After the enemy had thus been crushed and fled far away, the Christians turned to plundering their tents, since they themselves, being in flight, could not remain there long. There was found there much gold and silver, [Col. 1087A] pack animals, mules and horses, oxen and camels, rams and asses; they found abundant household goods in their pavilions. Laden with varied riches, they returned to their own men in triumph and with inexpressible joy. Thus there was great rejoicing in the Christians’ tents; they celebrated that day, giving thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, the prosperer of their journey and life.

The victory was therefore solemnly observed: they had been delivered from every distress, not by their own hand but by divine power, and were filled with every abundance of good things. Nor was report content merely to rouse the neighbouring cities: it began to terrify distant and foreign nations and to carry the name of Christianity to the ears of remote peoples. The Christians’ illustrious deeds were proclaimed, and all alike feared the military force which was coming upon them.

Thus it happened that Suleiman, son of the elder Suleiman, fleeing from Nicaea, encountered ten thousand Arabs. When they learned that he was fleeing, they said to him: [Col. 1087B] “Madman and wretch, why are you fleeing?” Suleiman answered them: “Formerly I thought that I could overcome and conquer the people of the Franks, but the outcome has been reversed: we have been defeated, and therefore wander fugitively here and there. For we saw—or think we saw—their multitude so widely extended that no one could sufficiently reckon their array. You would have been able to marvel and be astonished, for they are more numerous than the stars of heaven. We, still trembling, scarcely escaped their legions. Shaken by this overwhelming terror, we can scarcely yet breathe for trembling. Therefore, if you believe us, flee before they catch you while you are hiding. For no little city will be able to resist, since they have succeeded in taking Nicaea, our metropolis.”

When they heard Suleiman, they attempted to flee. But when they came to the castles or cities in which Syrians lived—who themselves bore the name of Christianity—they deceitfully addressed them, saying: “We have conquered the Franks. They have so completely perished that we have utterly erased their memory from this land; if any have survived, they are hidden in tunnels.” Thus they spoke to the unsuspecting inhabitants and were received within the gates. Once inside, they plundered the towns, houses, and churches of those who knew nothing; [Col. 1087D] they carried off whatever was precious and desirable, including sons and daughters, and thus mocked them everywhere. For they forestalled the arrival of the Franks; before the latter came, the former had departed.

When the Christians heard these things, they pursued them and pressed on with their journey. They entered a waterless and uninhabitable land, where they perished from hunger and thirst even unto death. If they happened to find unripe crops, they plucked ears of grain, rubbed them, chewed them, and swallowed them. While many failed for lack of such scant provisions, others somehow survived. There their pack-horses and asses died; many glorious knights were compelled to go on foot; and those able to do so employed oxen in place of conveyances, either to carry themselves or their goods.

Not long afterwards they entered a most fertile land, full of provisions and every good thing, except that they could by no means replace their horses as mounts. [Col. 1088A] They came to Iconium. At the inhabitants’ persuasion, because that settlement suffered from a shortage of water, they filled their skins to refresh themselves. After completing a day’s journey, they came to a certain river, where they rested for two days and recovered.

Scouts, who always ran ahead of the army either to make provision for it or to seize fodder and other necessities, advanced to Heraclea. In that city was a large gathering of Turks, waiting to see whether they could harm the Christians. They had laid harmful ambushes, if they could, for the scouts. When the Franks found them, they boldly attacked and easily scattered them in flight. Thus the city of Heraclea, the Turks having been expelled, was immediately reduced to Christian rule; and they spent four days there.

There Tancred, a man indeed of singular bravery, and Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, a man in no way inferior to Tancred in worth, separated themselves from the others [Col. 1088B] and entered the valley of Betrentot with their forces. Tancred, again separated from Baldwin, came with his knights to Tarsus. The Turks came out of the city and met them prepared to resist. Tancred manfully struck down those who attacked him as enemies and drove them, fighting, in flight back into the city itself. Tancred, a man equally fearless in all things, made camp with loosened reins near the city walls.

Without delay Baldwin arrived, requesting that Tancred join him amicably in taking the city; Tancred wholly refused. When night followed, the Turks left the city and took flight. At the very beginning of night, the inhabitants of that city came out after the Turks and cried loudly: “Franks, conquerors and lords of the world, the Turks have departed; the city stands open—come! Run, most unconquered Franks, to receive the city; run, do not delay! Why do you linger?” The sentries of the camp heard them shouting, not quietly or in secret; but because it was night, [Col. 1088C] both counsel and action were postponed until daylight.

[Col. 1088D] At dawn the leading citizens came and surrendered themselves and their possessions to the Christians. Wanting to restrain the quarrels which they heard among the disputants, they replied not unwisely: “Illustrious lords, cease these disputes for the present. We desire and pray that you come peacefully; but otherwise let that Tancred rule us, who yesterday fought so gloriously against the Turks while we watched in admiration.”

Baldwin would not agree, but wished either to claim half the city for himself or at least to make all of it public spoil by plundering it together. Tancred said: “Far be it, Baldwin, that we should enrich ourselves with the plundered possessions of our brethren. They themselves ask for me; they themselves desire me; they entrust their lives to me—and shall I, like a ravening wolf, devour the prey entrusted to me? Far be that, I say, [Col. 1089A] from me.”

For the Syrians who inhabited those cities were Christians, although the Turks ruled over them. Baldwin would not yield to Tancred’s arguments. Longing to carry through his own judgment, he resolved to rush eagerly into making the city public spoil. His whole concern was either the plundering of the inhabitants’ homes or the attempt to claim half the city. Tancred neither wished nor could struggle longer against Baldwin’s opposition, because Baldwin’s army had the larger forces. Having given the signal to his men and with his trumpets sounding, he withdrew somewhat embittered. Yet, being moderate in his anger, he restrained himself and did not intend, even because of the injuries done to him, to disturb the journey toward Jerusalem. Thus Baldwin alone gained possession of all Tarsus.

Without delay, however, two excellent cities, Azera and Mamistra, [Col. 1089B] and very many castles were surrendered to Tancred.

Other nobles, with their forces, had entered the land of the Armenians. There they found a very strongly fortified town; but, because they did not wish to delay there longer, they passed it by without attacking it. They judged that it was not worth exhausting the whole army for a single castle. Not far away was a certain city, Alfia, which at once surrendered to the newcomers. A certain man of the military belt, Simeon by name, a native of that country, sought and received that city in order to defend the land; and he remained there with all whom he could. The larger army proceeded onward. They also came to Caesarea of Cappadocia, which had been destroyed down to the ground; yet its ruins, still standing in some fashion, bore witness to how great that Caesarea had been. Departing thence, they directed their march toward another beautiful city, rich in fertile soil, Plastentia, which the Turks had shortly before besieged for three weeks; but because it was impregnable, the Turks had been wholly unable to take it. It therefore immediately opened itself, not unwillingly, to the Christians. A certain Peter of Alfia readily obtained the city, which he had requested from the nobles, in order to guard and conquer the country in fidelity to the Holy Sepulchre and to Christianity. It was heard during that expedition that the Turks who had besieged the city were not far ahead of the army, intending, if possible, to harm them. But Bohemond, a diligent man in military affairs, summoned such soldiers of his own as he wished and carefully pursued them, [Col. 1089D] in case he might perhaps find and attack them somewhere. Yet he accomplished nothing, because he could not find them.

They next came to Coxon, a noble and populous city, which the inhabitants of that place gladly surrendered along with their Christian brethren. There the weary army rested for three days. It was reported to the Count of Toulouse that the Turks who had been guarding Antioch had departed in flight. Therefore, having taken counsel with his men, he selected persons to send ahead to investigate the matter carefully and to reconnoitre everything else diligently. For this purpose there were dispatched men of consular rank, not ignorant of military discipline: the Viscount of Castellon, William of Mont-Pèlerin, Peter of Roa, and Peter Raimund, with many soldiers. They came into the valley of Antioch and heard a different report there. They heard [Col. 1090A] that the Turks had abundantly prepared themselves to defend the city. But Peter of Roa, separating from the others, entered the valley of Rugia. Finding very many Turks, he struck them severely, overcame them, and put them to flight. Those Armenians, hearing of the Christians’ favorable successes and the pagans’ repeated misfortunes, surrendered to Peter the city of Rusa and certain castles.

Things thus went favorably for them, but not equally so for the larger army. Setting out on the march, they advanced by creeping over mountains exceedingly rough and rocky. Through these, neither their companies could proceed in file, as they had the day before and two days earlier, nor could even their pack animals creep onward; rather, men and beasts alike were grievously burdened. Nor, when they were confined in the narrow way, was there any outlet elsewhere. Thus those struggling and failing were crushed and battered [Col. 1090B] along the pathless road. In their extreme distress they groaned, clasping their hands tightly and gnashing their teeth. Horses slipped into immense precipices; and the very narrow track produced, by its gaping breaches, an obstacle for all. Many, having there lost either horses or pack animals together with the goods laid upon them, were impoverished. Some sold, for a trifling price, servants, mail-coats, or helmets; others threw them far from themselves, since there no one, not even an unarmed man, could remain unencumbered. Their one concern, and not without fear, was to bring away their own bodies. When they had barely escaped those disastrous straits, they turned aside to a certain city called Marafin. The inhabitants of that city brought them an abundant [Col. 1090C] market. Having stayed there for a while, until they might recover somewhat, they awaited Lord Bohemond, who, as has been said, had recently departed from them in pursuit of the Turks.

After this they entered that famous valley, broad and fertile, in which lies the royal and renowned city of Antioch, the metropolis and chief city of all Syria, where Peter, chief of the Apostles, adorned the episcopal chair. Now, by the hidden judgment of God, though not an unjust one, with many churches destroyed and some irreverently converted to secular uses, it was enslaved, alas, to Turkish abominations. The scouts, who customarily ran ahead of the following army, as they approached the Iron Bridge [Col. 1090D] found countless Turks hurrying to fortify Antioch. Therefore, making a sudden attack upon them—for the Christians always marched armed—they threw them into confusion in an abrupt encounter. Having killed many, they brought back to their own camp, which had been pitched on the riverbank, the mules which the Turks were leading to the city, loaded in many ways with provisions and various stores. Great joy therefore arose in the camp, both because of the victory and because of the excellent booty which the scouts had brought back. They did not cease to give thanks to God, lest they seem ungrateful to him by whose aid, they acknowledged, such happy successes had befallen them. They said: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Psalm 115). Thus daily and continually [Col. 1091A] they rendered praise to God, and with devout prayers and humble hearts implored him as protector in all that they had to do.

Bohemond, never yielding to idleness or sleepiness—for he was a restless man—came secretly with four thousand soldiers near the gate of Antioch, watching in case any persons might secretly enter or leave. At daybreak the army struck its tents where it had been, set out, and came to Antioch. On Wednesday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], it pitched its tents and vigorously besieged the city at three gates. The other side was not besieged at all, because it was confined by cliffs and mountains so extended and inaccessible that no place there could be adapted [Col. 1091B] for a siege. So great a fear seized the Antiochenes and all those stationed round about that none of their raiders dared await an encounter. Thus they were nearly silent for fifteen days.

The land adjoining Antioch, because the valley was fertile, was exceedingly productive: full of vineyards, pleasant with fruits and crops, wooded with trees, rich in gardens, and abundant in pasture. There were many Armenians and Syrians in the city. They were indeed Christians, but greatly subject to the Turks. Pretending flight, they boldly went out into the camp, begging and seeking public alms. Because their wives were within the city, they returned to their household homes; and, as malignant spies, they faithfully reported to the Turks whatever they heard in the camp. This, it is said, harmed the Christians not a little: “Nothing injures those at war more than learning the enemies’ secrets, and, against preparations already made, devising opposing preparations, and frustrating or forestalling the enemies’ plans.” When the counsels of the camp had been disclosed to the Antiochenes, they began gradually to come forth boldly and to hem in the pilgrims outside. [Col. 1091C] If they prevailed, they attacked and slaughtered the unwary; and, after committing their raids, they either returned to the city or withdrew unharmed to safer places. Thus they blocked all the roads around about, so that everything was closed against the Christians both from the sea and from the mountains. And so it happened that those outside were now more severely besieged than those hiding inside.

There was not far away a sufficiently fortified castle called Areth, where those who frequently attacked the Christians were dwelling. When the nobles learned this, they grieved greatly at the hostile incursions, because those wicked men had dared to draw their bloody swords against the holy people. For already many had perished through the plots of the natives. They therefore sent men to meet the Turks and lure them on as they themselves retreated. Bohemond, wholly devoted to warfare, lay hidden in ambush. The Christians, seeing the Turks pursuing them most fiercely, feigned flight as they had been instructed, immediately turned their backs, and knowingly veered toward the place where Bohemond was concealed. Yet in that encounter—or rather, that flight—two Christian soldiers were killed.

[Col. 1092A] Then Bohemond, a most valiant fighter, sprang quickly from the place where they had halted; attacking the Turks, he killed many and took some alive. He ordered these to be beheaded ceremonially before the city gate as a spectacle. He is said to have done this in order that those in the city might be terrified for their punished fellow-countrymen, and perhaps thereby be deterred from pursuing the Franks in such a manner. For often, when penalties are inflicted on some, others are intimidated. Yet those in the city, made more savage, often climbed the higher towers, shot at the Christians from the battlements, and by every means they could kept them at a distance from the city. Their arrows flew even before Bohemond’s tents; indeed, a woman struck by an arrow there died, because the Christians had established their camp near the city. Having again taken counsel, the men of the camp built a castle upon the summit of the mountain called Maregard, which overhung Bohemond’s tents, so that the camp might be protected from Turkish attacks. In the succeeding days, each of the leaders guarded it in turn according to his allotted watch.

Meanwhile provisions dwindled, because they dared neither make raids nor had a market. What they had found in the valley, having made no provision for the morrow, they had consumed lavishly. Little remained in their camp, and what did remain diminished through daily consumption. Food was therefore altogether exceedingly expensive. And the feast of the Nativity of the Lord was now approaching.

[Col. 1092C] Those leaders spoke among themselves, intending to take counsel on how the people might be fed. The greater men, with paternal concern, supported the lesser. Now famine was becoming dreadful, since all fodder and provisions failed from day to day. They said: “Let one part of us go far away to forage for grain and plunder; let another, reinforced division guard those who are plundering; let another remain in the camp; and let us leave nothing untried. Soldiers of Christ, let us never grow slack in idleness. Why do we delay? The Christian people are already, in great part, in danger.”

Then Bohemond spoke first: “If it seems sound to you, nobles and lords, the Count of Flanders and I will go out; and whatever God grants, you shall see. Meanwhile keep watch over the camp and do nothing negligently.” The counsel was approved, [Col. 1092D] and the assembly dissolved. Having carefully celebrated Christ’s Nativity, the Count of Flanders and Bohemond, armed, set out—not without the tears of those remaining—with more than twenty thousand soldiers and footmen. They quickly scattered through the settlements of the Saracens.

But Saracens, Arabs, and Turks had gathered from Jerusalem, Damascus, and many other towns of various regions: immense peoples, so that they might aid Antioch. Hearing that the Christians had dispersed throughout their territory, they rejoiced greatly, hoping certainly to overcome them, since they thought them few and foreign. In the dead of night, therefore, they arranged two battle-lines in ambush, one in front and the other behind, so that at daybreak, when they attacked them, [Col. 1093A] the Christians could escape neither way, but would be assailed from both sides.

But the Count of Flanders, a man mighty in arms, and Bohemond rushed upon them with one accord. Invoking the name of Jesus and raising the sign of the holy cross which they always bore before them, they fought most resolutely and severely afflicted their enemies. Many of them were killed; but the Christians were little enriched by their spoils, for they had no leisure either to pursue or despoil them. Meanwhile the Turks stationed to guard the city, hearing that Bohemond had departed, came out of the city more boldly and were already ranging through the camp itself. They reconnoitred to discover which tents were more weakly defended.

One day, therefore, they rushed together into the camp [Col. 1093B] and attacked the Christians closely and all at once. For they had not yet heard that their own men had been defeated. On that day many Christians were killed, because those Ishmaelites pressed fiercely upon the camp. That day the Bishop of Le Puy lost his standard-bearer, who carried his banner. Had not muddy rough ground separated the city from the camp, making passage either impossible or difficult, the Turks would repeatedly have ridden at full rein through the tents and raged against the Christian people, who had now grown somewhat weak.

Bohemond, returning from the Saracens’ country after the battle, had found little to plunder. He climbed other mountains in case he might find elsewhere something which, once plundered, would benefit either his companions [Col. 1093C] or those awaiting him. But the land had already been reduced to such desolation that many returned empty-handed. Thus they had labored in vain, except that they had won a notable triumph over the Turks. Yet no victory extinguishes hunger where everything fit to eat is lacking. Brief is the joy which the want of bread makes sorrowful. They returned to the camp, which dreadful famine was wounding.

The Armenians and Syrians, natives of that land and insatiably greedy for gain, seeing the Christians return empty-handed, ran to advantageous and more remote places. Buying up provisions wherever they found them, they carried them to the camp and sold at a high price what they had bought cheaply. Indeed, they sold one donkey-load for eight purple garments, which were valued at one hundred and twenty solidi [Col. 1093D] of denarii. Disease and pestilence therefore contaminated the camp, and everywhere those without means to buy died of disastrous hunger. Those who were wealthier nevertheless bestowed many gifts on the needy, who begged from door to door. Yet they could not sustain so many thousands for many days.

Some therefore thought of secretly deserting the camp. William Carpenter and Peter the Hermit took counsel to flee secretly; and they fled. Tancred found and seized them, reproached them shamefully, and compelled them to return to the army. He exacted from them an oath and pledge that they would return and make satisfaction to their brethren. William was brought to Bohemond’s tents. Bohemond restrained him with reproachful words and punished him with fitting [Col. 1094A] compulsory services. He said: “What have you dared to do, O disgrace and reproach of all France? Why did you wish to weaken the hearts of your fellow-brethren, so that, following your example, they might abandon the enemy of God and not return? Have you alone seized upon a safety born of fear, so that, leaving us behind, you might escape unharmed? Most wretched of all men, you ought to have remained in the camp of God and laid down your glorious life for your brethren. Now, therefore, for all the days of your life upon earth you shall be dishonored.”

Meanwhile Franks came to Bohemond and pleaded with him for William, whom he held; he promptly yielded to them. Yet, so that he should not depart again, William swore an oath with their approval. At this time the Christians’ horses had failed to such an extent that scarcely a thousand knights in that entire and great army still had mounts. Men and horses suffered alike; there was no hope of escape unless God showed favor to those who sighed and cried out to him. Their hearts and mouths fled to their Lord; and, because they despaired of earthly aid, they placed all their hope in God. “Thus God mercifully reproved them, that they might turn to him with their whole heart; and that, if any impenitence lay hidden in them, they might be purified, being refined by the fire of contrition and the misfortune of pressing necessity.” Famine increased daily, and all, terrified by fear, wasted away. To intensify their dread there was added rumor, a foreboding herald of evil and magnifier of reports, announcing that the Turks were about to arrive.

[Col. 1094C] A Greek from Constantinople, named Tagingus, had come from the emperor’s side. He commanded the attendants whom the emperor had sent to the army. His courage failed more than that of the others through fear of death; he came to the nobles and, concealing the immense fear he felt, began thus:

“I see, illustrious lords, that you are placed in utmost anxiety and surrounded by every hardship. All provisions have been consumed; the horses are dead; the camp is besieged. We who besiege are more severely besieged than those whom we besiege. They ride out, they make raids, they attack us fiercely; we are surrounded on every side, so that we dare not go out at all. We expect no helper. Every market is forbidden us. To endure these things long is nothing else [Col. 1094D] than to perish moment by moment. I pity your generosity, Conscript Fathers, you who have come from the uttermost regions of the earth to die among these foreign peoples, unless you either believe me or adopt a better plan. Whose breast of iron would not be moved by the destruction of so many Christians? Believe me, Conscript Fathers; I do not speak of unknown matters: I am not in a land unknown to me. I could sufficiently provide for myself if I intended to desert you. But may my soul be blotted from the book of the living if I ever withdraw myself from your holiness, unless I always share your necessities. Yet meanwhile my soul is weary of your miseries, and unless I can help you, I shall wholly die in bitterness. Therefore accept my counsel, when I have spoken it well. As stated before, I do not wish, while alive, to withdraw from the enemy unless I had devised some better benefit for our companions. I am a member of the emperor’s household, as you know; I am known to all the Greek people.

“A thought has therefore entered my heart which, although the thing I propose is burdensome and laborious to me, I disclose to you. I am ready to fly to the ports and to the emperor, and there to obtain an imperial decree, so that all may hasten to assemble to aid you; that they may bring in abundance flour and wine, meat and cheese; and that the emperor’s faithful subjects may generously supply you with whatever provisions they possess. I shall also endeavor, if life remains to me, to bring you a great many horses. And lest you mistrust me, I shall speak truthfully: whatever I freely offer, I shall faithfully perform. I leave my tents and my companions here, intending to return at once; and I swear upon these most holy things that I shall carry out all this in good faith.”

[Col. 1095B] Thus he swore and departed. The multitude believed him, and all the people earnestly implored him to hasten his return. But he went away, wickedly perjured, and never returned. By this pretext he provided for his miserable life. Meanwhile the impoverished people secretly departed, going where they thought they might live. No one dared go toward the sea, because roads and pathless places were guarded. Yet ships had put into harbor that could have helped them, if access to them had been open.

Then again a fresh rumor spread: countless Turks were coming, and imminent death was immediately threatening all. They were so numerous that a broad expanse stretching for many stadia in every direction would scarcely have contained them. Again there was a new fear; suddenly they were afraid as though they had never feared until then. Bereft of sense and bloodless, they grew pale, and many bowed their drooping heads. Yet the nobility called for deliberation concerning battle. All the nobles whom we have mentioned above assembled; all encouraged one another for battle, since among them none was lukewarm and none faint-hearted.

Bohemond, however, setting forth his counsel, added: [Col. 1095D] “I see, thanks be to God, that you are all of one mind and that no one in this matter differs from another. I therefore judge it superfluous to lead so many nobles, so many prudent men, through roundabout arguments, when I see that you are already united in the same purpose. You all yearn for battle; you all believe it will contribute to the common safety. I too approve this; I urgently demand it. For I beg that we do not die sluggishly or unwarriorlike, nor become a reproach and disgrace to all Christians. If it should happen that we die, let us at least die gloriously in battle. To die without glory is as though we were compared to senseless beasts, made like brute cattle.

“As for the people of God committed to us, we shall see many die. What distinguishes lord from servant, nobleman from commoner, rich from poor, knight from foot-soldier, unless the counsel of us who preside benefits them and our protection assists them? If the Turks rule over me unpunished, I no longer wish to live. You, lords of consular rank and illustrious men, light and flower of victorious [Col. 1096A] France, glory and model of warlike knighthood, fight for yourselves and lay down your lives for your brethren. Let us invoke the name of the Lord Jesus: either we shall rejoice in rich spoils, or we shall die a distinguished death. At least secure concerning our souls, we shall not die as cowards are accustomed to die.

“Finally, we are neither so many nor so strong that we can sustain two battles. But, O all you soldiers, let us leave the camp; for this seems to me fair and useful. Let us march out fearlessly to meet them. But all of you foot-soldiers remain in the camp: a fortification for the camp and an obstacle to those in the city. Keep watch all night without sleep; or relieve one another in watches. Support yourselves; each one of you fight for yourselves—indeed, let each defend the other. Above all, carefully guard the gates of the city that are before you, lest, if they are opened, the enemy may range freely among you. Henceforth, as the will in heaven shall be, so let it be.”

Having said this, they armed themselves and fortified themselves with holy communion, and went forth from the camp, not without grievous laments from both companies. Neither side trusted in itself: neither priest nor woman, neither common person nor soldier; neither those going out nor those remaining hoped ever again to enjoy one another’s sight. Both sides rushed into the embraces and kisses of their loved ones, and all were moved to tears. The soldiers lodged between the river—which in its ancient name was called Daphnes, and which flows past Antioch—and the lake; for they had heard that the Turks had assembled at Castle Areth beyond the Iron Bridge.

[Col. 1096C] The nobles assembled before dawn, for in such pressing danger they had been unable to sleep. At the first light of dawn they sent out knowledgeable scouts to report to them concerning the Turks. Without delay they saw them hurrying from the other bank of the river. They had formed two large battle-lines, and a very great force followed behind. The scouts swiftly returned, shouting: “What need is there of words? Look: there they are. Do not delay, for they are near.” The nobles discussed how to arrange the battle and entrusted the matter to Bohemond. “Come,” said Bohemond, “each of you summon your men; and, when the signal is given, let each of you fight with his own battle-line. Where there is need of lances and swords, carry out the task; and do not forget the deeds and blows of your fathers.”

Accordingly six battle-lines were arranged. Five of them advanced first, to bear the weight of battle and effectively drive back the hostile army by striking it. Bohemond, last with his own line, moved forward gradually, ready to provide for and assist all; and, if the Turks overcame the foremost lines, to receive the whole onset of the battle. Trumpets sounded, horns resounded, and the cry of both multitudes was heard. Shield struck shield, boss struck boss; when lances broke, swords were blunted, and both legions pressed forward hand to hand. Turkish reinforcements arrived and began fiercely to drive back the Christians. The Franks could not withstand so great an assault by so many proven contingents, but, wavering, [Col. 1097A] were compelled to yield. So great was the shouting, din, and rain of missiles that even the air itself was darkened.

Bohemond groaned, seeing them on every side as though he were all eyes, and said: “Christ, sustain thy Christians.” Then he added: “Robert”—for Robert, son of Gerard, bore his banner—“spur your swift horse hard; be an undaunted aid to the wavering Christians. Remember, I beg you, our ancestors, and do not in anything tarnish the shining renown of the Franks. Know that help from heaven will come to us immediately; but God wills that we, like strong athletes, should deserve and win the prize.”

Robert, fortified by the sign of the holy cross and surrounded by supporting companies, hurried to the scene and, a most daring knight, stood against the bloody Turks. He attacked those faithless men so fiercely that he made the streamers of Bohemond’s banner fly in the faces of the Turks, and somewhat terrified them with his loud cry. At the attack and shout of that standard-bearer, the Franks, recovering courage, rushed unanimously upon the Turks. With daggers brandished, they pressed more savagely upon those who pressed against them. The clash of arms was great, and sparks struck out from bronze helmets flashed like fire. Wounds met wounds, and the fields were purple with excessive blood. You might see entrails hanging out; you might see severed heads and mutilated bodies lying everywhere. The Turks were terrified by overwhelming fear, and suddenly, as their formations gave way, committed themselves to flight. The Christians pursued them beyond the Iron Bridge, striking down, trampling, and slaughtering them.

[Col. 1097C] Many Turkish soldiers were killed there, because that battle had no foot-soldiers. The Christians, having won a great trophy, returned to their own people, bringing many horses of which they had special need, and much spoil which their own hands had won in battle. Great joy therefore arose in the camp, and all gave God fitting thanks. But the Turks returned in great disgrace to their Castle Areth, with broken spirit and downcast faces. Having stripped it completely, they set it on fire and fled. Seeing this, the Armenians and Syrians occupied the narrow places and inflicted great damage upon the fleeing Turks: they killed many, brought back some alive, and restored the aforesaid castle, subdued to the Christians, [Col. 1097D] to them.

The Franks in the camp also brought one hundred heads of those killed, to console their own people and dishearten the besieged. They even presented them to the envoys of the Admiral of Babylon, who had at that time been sent to them from Babylon and were lodging in tents beside them. Those who had remained in the camp fought against the Antiochenes throughout the day, continually guarding three city gates to prevent them from breaking out.

This battle was fought on the Ides of February [13 February], Tuesday, which preceded the beginning of the Lenten fast. Those who had fortified the city, more fiercely inflamed to anger, attacked the Christians more ardently and did not cease at all from raiding them. Although hitherto they had always been defeated in battle—some killed, others wounded, others captured, and all the remainder put to flight and scattered—yet there was such a multitude in the city that they continually disturbed the camp, frequently sprang out, and still more frequently destroyed the Christians by deaths of every kind.

[Col. 1098A] Besides this, the Christians were afflicted by great hardships, because they dared neither abandon the siege nor march far from the camp. The surrounding regions had been reduced to such desolation that they supplied them with no provision of food. The Turks, indeed, knowing the advantageous places, both rode out to forage for grain and more attentively laid snares for the Christians. Whatever cities, castles, and towns there were, every man and every woman, all those near or far, were hostile to the Christians. Every place was blocked lest merchants should perhaps come to them. Thus they were in dreadful danger from lack of food.

The nobility, therefore, anxiously and compassionately sought to provide for the common people. They said: “You see that we make no progress. This city is impregnable. We cannot even surround it completely. Inside, it overflows with an abundance of food; outside, we are endangered by miserable famine. Those hiding within are nearly more numerous than we who are outside. Yet if they would speak of battle, we would gladly hear it. Look: the walls themselves defend them even if they sleep. Before our eyes, they range everywhere. What evil, finally, do they suffer? Rather, it is we who suffer, so grievously confined. Let us therefore do one thing, beneficial to us all and, as it seems, especially harmful to them. Do you see that mosque (Machomaria) built before the city gate? There is a bridge there, sufficiently useful for their supplies. Let us build a castle there; once it is fortified, we shall be able more easily to resist them and aid our people. For after our enemies lose both bridge and passage, we shall move about more freely and safely, and shall also pass the nights more securely in the camp.”

[Col. 1098C] This proposal seemed good to them. The Count of Toulouse said to them: “Let us build the castle as you say, and I shall guard it when fortified.” Bohemond also added: “If my counsel seems acceptable to you, Conscript Fathers, let us go to the port of Saint Symeon. I too will go with you, and will bring that force, however small, which awaits us there and which may faithfully aid us and effectively complete this appointed work. There are many ships there and many of our companions; but, though summoned, they do not dare approach because every place is full of the impious plunderer. Let us, however, continue our campaign, always prepared for battle, and let us be cautious and watchful for those whom we bring as reinforcements. Those who remain with the baggage must take diligent care to defend the camp and must labor tirelessly on the designated work. Nothing must be undertaken sluggishly; both this and that must be attempted vigorously.”

The Count of Saint-Gilles joined Bohemond, and they hurried to the port of Saint Symeon. Those who remained in the camp, girded with swords, prepared themselves unanimously to begin the castle. [Col. 1099A] The Turks, no less ready and not inferior either in number or in arms, boldly met the Franks. They attacked the Christians so fearlessly that they put them to flight and killed many. Great sorrow therefore arose in the camp; they mourned in their tents and were silent that day.

At last the Turks, having learned that the Count of Toulouse and Bohemond had gone off to the port, set suitable secret ambushes and devised how they might harm the Christians. Behold, the Christians were returning from the port, bringing with them a force neither sufficiently armed nor very warlike. The Saracens surrounded and hemmed them in from every side, attacked them fiercely, and strove to assail them with every onslaught of missiles. Thus they attacked them now with arrows, now with swords, now with lances, now with thrown weapons [Col. 1099B]. They cut them down without mercy, crying out against them and gnashing their teeth. The Christians, being few, could not long endure the cruelty of those raging against them; and, because they could not resist, they were compelled to save themselves by flight. Those who could either hide or escape survived; the rest, overtaken by their deadly lot—alas!—fell.

More than a thousand Christians were slain in that encounter; and behold, grief in the camp was doubled and increased: yesterday and today paganism had triumphed over Christendom. Behold, paganism, raised high in insolence and applauding, had today humiliated mournful Christendom. Yet such are the outcomes of wars; such are the changes of men and times [Col. 1099C]. No one has ever succeeded happily always; no one ever will rejoice, or has rejoiced, in uninterrupted prosperity. Therefore in prosperity adversity must be guarded against; and in adversity prosperity must be hoped and prayed for.

The report that the Christians had been defeated filled the ears of those who had remained behind, and so all the people lamented together. For they did not know whom to reckon alive and whom dead. Yet very many, crawling through the mountains, had escaped and returned as swiftly as possible to the tents. Bohemond, however, returning by a shorter route, arrived before the Count of Toulouse and gave a true report of the Christians’ disaster. The Christians, more stirred to anger than terrified, advanced unanimously against the Turks and attacked them bravely [Col. 1099D]. The Saracens on the opposite side stood firm, thinking that they could prevail, just as they had lately prevailed over the Count of Toulouse and Bohemond. They also believed that the Franks had been weakened by that very fear, while they themselves had grown stronger through their successful result.

Thus the battle was fought most fiercely on both sides. The Turks had crossed the bridge and boldly met the Christians. The Christians, like a wild beast provoked by the bites of dogs or wounded by the point of a hunting-spear, roused by the slaughter of their comrades and brethren, thirsted eagerly for Turkish blood and exerted themselves utterly to avenge their own. The pagans, terrified because what had occurred exceeded their expectation, immediately turned their backs to those striking them and tried to escape in flight. Once flight had begun, the whole legion shamefully lost its manliness.

[Col. 1100A] The fugitives were hindered both by the narrow bridge and by the swift, deep river; for they had to cross by one or the other, or by both. No one could wade through the river near the bridge, and scarcely anyone could swim across it. So great a multitude of horsemen mounted the bridge at once that one impeded another and many suffocated one another. They could have crossed more easily one by one than in a mass. Meanwhile the Christians pressed upon those who were giving way, by no means forgetful of the wrongs done to their brethren and themselves; most eager avengers of their own shed blood, desirous of victory, and intent upon subduing the city. Thus those insatiable slayers pressed hard upon them, using lances and swords against them at close quarters. Whomever they could, they either hurled into the river or pierced with deadly swords [Col. 1100B], so that the river itself seemed stained with blood and covered over with corpses. Indeed, if any tried to swim across or sought to crawl around the bridge, they were killed by those pressing upon them and overwhelmed by every kind of calamity.

That day dawned upon the pagans as a day of death, on which scarcely anyone could avoid dying. The Christians pressed upon the fugitives, pressed upon those trying to swim, and bore down upon those who had fallen. No one withheld his hand from blood; every Christian drenched his sword in the blood of the slain. From the spectacle of the walls and fortifications, the women looked upon the miseries of their people and envied the Franks’ ever-successive successes.

In that battle there died twelve leaders of the Turkish forces, whom they call *admirals*, distinguished and eminent nobles; and fifteen hundred soldiers, capable and very brave men, who had long watched diligently over the city’s defence [Col. 1100C]. Moreover, profound fear restrained the rest from thereafter shouting arrogantly against the Christians or rushing presumptuously upon them. Nightfall ended that battle. Those who could escape alive entered the city bloodless and exhausted, and thereafter could not recover their former strength. The Christians too returned triumphantly to their own people, bringing with them many horses and abundant spoils, which they needed greatly. They rejoiced in the Lord Jesus and, giving thanks, advanced day by day toward a better condition.

[Col. 1100D] On the following day, the Turks came out from the city at earliest dawn, gathered whatever corpses they could find, and buried them beyond the bridge at Machomaria, before the city gate. Very many, however, they left drowned in the river, of whom they could say: “He is covered by the river who has no urn.” Those whom they buried, they accompanied with treasures of cloaks and precious garments; and they added bows, quivers, and many bezants to the provision for the dead. When the Christians learned this, partly drawn by desire for the spoils and partly stirred to inflict grief on the Turks, they dug up the buried men and insulted the exhumed bodies with sufficient disgrace. Whatever desirable property was found with them they seized [Col. 1101A], and, gathering the bodies together, threw them contemptuously into one pit.

They sent four pack-mules laden with the heads of the slain to the port, so that the envoys from Babylon who happened to be there might see them and be struck dumb with grief. The citizens, seeing this, grieved beyond measure and were saddened even unto death. Thus they groaned, wailed, and lamented all that day, and daily wasted away.

On the third day they began to build the castle mentioned above; and they decided to fortify it with the very stones which they had taken from the graves of those they had disinterred. When it was sufficiently fortified, they confined their enemies more tightly and kept diligent watch lest they should venture outside. The Franks, now more secure, ranged through the mountains [Col. 1101B] and more freely occupied themselves with bringing in straw and whatever other provisions. On the other side of the river, where the Christians had not yet pitched their tents, the Turks could move about safely, since they feared no Christian there.

The Christians therefore took counsel together: “If,” they said, “some among us were to occupy and defend a castle built over there, we should be safer, and this city, more diligently besieged, would more easily waste away. Certainly every opportunity of bringing in supplies would be cut off from them, and all forage would be wholly denied them.”

All approved this plan; yet everyone, and especially each individual, feared crossing the river in order to take up residence. One man feared for himself, another likewise; and no one trusted himself to defend the castle [Col. 1101C]. One man, withdrawing himself, invited and urged another; yet no one sought that castle for himself. At last Tancred spoke and made an agreement with the chief Franks concerning the guarding of that castle. He therefore summoned his fellow soldiers and his companies and added to his association any others he could enlist; he took possession of the fortified castle and established how the besieged city should be vigorously opposed. His men watched roads and trackless places, and his confederates kept restless watch wherever they were stationed.

One day, as on the day before and the day before that, Syrians and Armenians were abundantly carrying into the city whatever was necessary. Tancred swiftly attacked them when he found them; taking all that they were transporting [Col. 1101D], he triumphantly rejoiced in the rich spoils and provisions. Thereafter such great fear seized the city that both the citizens and all who contemplated aiding the citizens were terrified. The city now lacked every supply and was in danger of great misery, having consumed nearly all that it possessed and being unable to have anything brought into it. For they were surrounded on every side, and above all the entire traffic of commerce was cut off from them.

Yet we do not set forth one by one all the calamities suffered either by the townspeople or by those dwelling in the camp, because we cannot do everything. Both sides suffered great misfortunes in turn; nevertheless, fortune more often smiled serenely on those in the camp while they fought. For the Franks were fiercer in disposition, braver by nature, and more experienced in war [Col. 1102A]; and for this purpose they had undertaken their journey to distant regions and foreign peoples. Endowed with endurance, they bore every hardship cheerfully. In their pressing necessities they called upon God as their helper, and frequently made devout satisfaction to him for their human transgressions.

There was in the besieged city a certain *admiral*, descended from Turkish stock, named Pirrus, who had entered into a pact of friendship with Bohemond through faithful messengers. Not, as I think, because he had ever seen Bohemond, but because flying report had brought him much good news of Bohemond and he had no doubt at all of his prudence. Thus they frequently conversed through trustworthy interpreters and known signals [Col. 1102B].

Bohemond sometimes urged him toward Christianity; sometimes he persuaded him to surrender the city by many promises. As a shrewd man, he left nothing unattempted. At one time he frightened him with the misfortunes threatening the city; at another he attracted him by the abundant rewards which God gloriously destines for Christendom. Thus Bohemond said:

“I wish, my dearest Pirrus, to persuade you to act in all things according to the custom of true friendship: that is, to bury within yourself the secrets that I entrust to you; to keep our mysteries, which are entrusted to you alone, and not betray them to anyone; and henceforth, let not friend distrust friend, intimate distrust intimate. Therefore act swiftly in all that has been discussed: think earnestly of surrendering the city to me, of acquiring freedom for yourself [Col. 1102C], and above all of accepting Christianity [Col. 1103A]. Nothing you wish shall be lacking to you, and we promise to grant you whatever you demand. Unless you do all these things—which are both useful and honourable—you will err exceedingly and will without doubt show that you were never our friend.”

Pirrus yielded to these or similar words; lending a ready ear to the messengers who questioned him, he finally broke out into these instructions. For God had now inspired him as to what he ought to do and had dropped into the ear of his heart how he should answer Bohemond according to his wish:

“I assent to your commands, my dearest friend. For I know you to be a moderate and honourable man. Moreover, I do not fail to understand how highly we ought to value the name and virtue of friendship, whose highest degree is to will the same thing and not to will the same thing. I do not wish you henceforth to hold before me whatever dangers threaten the city. We are not people to be frightened by your threats. The city, as you see, is impregnable. But I wish you to speak of your Christianity, for which I ardently long [Col. 1102D], which I see to be invincible, and whose glory I do not at all deny.

“In short, that I may speak more briefly and satisfy you, I place my soul in the hands of my intimate friend and place this city in the keeping of my friend. Three well-fortified towers are under my guard; I shall surrender them to your officers. And lest you distrust me in anything, I shall send you my son as a hostage, so that those whom you send may hasten with greater security. But lest I be accused of treachery, I attribute everything I plan to do wholly to your Christianity.

“Do not begin in such a way that, failing, you succumb with the undertaking unfinished. For then death would threaten me and mine, and henceforth no one would have any opportunity to surrender the city. Therefore do not delay or dissemble, for delay has harmed those who were prepared. But, once counsel has been received and action hastened, either abandon the matter altogether or bring the enterprise to completion.”

When Bohemond heard this, he rejoiced exceedingly. Yet for a time he restrained face and mouth, lest some inward movement of his spirit be detected through foolish joy. Then, speaking to the nobles, he finally opened his lips:

“You see, assembled fathers, that I cannot set forth without deep sighs the calamities with which we are afflicted and the hardships that strike this people. But why should I mention common men, when you, offspring of illustrious blood, grow pale from hunger, waste away from weariness, and languish under toil? A grievous plague has infected our camp, brought on by grievous need [Col. 1103B]. It has long been our lot to keep watch under the open sky and sleep beneath the clear air. Bitterly cold nights assail us. This entire land is hostile to us: its fields have been reduced to wilderness and are tilled with no plough, or only rarely. At the season when others gather their harvests, we reap no ears of grain, nor have we a market to furnish food to our people. The citizens, who know this region, cannot be prevented from going out and returning.

“It is disgraceful to leave this city unconquered; and oh, would that we might all die rather than depart without the city having been surrendered or destroyed [Col. 1103C]. Already secure concerning misfortunes, we do not know whether fortunate success will come to us. But how long shall we endure continual death here? This city, as you see, is impregnable. What use here would battering-rams, ballistae, or any engines for assaulting a city be? It remains, therefore, that we turn to experiments of counsel, since devices for engagements with whatever weapons do not help us.

“Let each of you, then, assembled fathers, attempt whether by money, friendship, threats, or any means he can gain this city for himself; and let us willingly grant it to whoever can accomplish this by whatever ingenuity. For why do we delay here for so long? What profit will there be in subduing the city if, before it is subdued [Col. 1103D], the whole Christian army is destroyed by deaths of every kind? Therefore, if you judge that my counsels ought to be accepted, deliberate openly; and let us grant—grant indeed—to the man who can subject this city to himself. And ask that each of us may carry this out effectively.”

At length the eloquent hero fell silent. The response of the assembled nobles was as follows. I think that, already understanding his speech by conjecture, they had anticipated it: they believed that Bohemond was speaking, as it were, for himself alone. Therefore they answered him somewhat indirectly:

“Far be it from us,” they said, “that one should be preferred above another, so that this city should be specially bestowed upon any one of us [Col. 1104A]. We are brothers and equals by fraternal right and equal lot. Once we have taken it, we shall divide it. It is fitting and just that, as we share the labour, so we should share the honour: let us capture it together and together receive our allotted portions of it.”

With these words the assembly dissolved. Bohemond kept silent, and meanwhile the matter, being delayed, came to no result. Thus the man of consummate prudence restrained himself, lest, if he had heard anything he did not wish, it should be detected by a change in his expression.

Not long afterwards, a rumour foretelling evil spread widely through the camp: Turks, Publicans, Agulans, Azimites, and many other pagan peoples were said to be approaching and to have declared war against the Christians. Soon trustworthy messengers arrived, attesting the certainty of the imminent danger [Col. 1104B].

The Christian leaders then spoke among themselves and of their own accord proposed to Bohemond: “You see the critical point to which our situation has come. If, therefore, by entreaty or price, even with our aid, you can obtain this city, we unanimously grant it to you—saving in all things the oath which, with your approval, we made to the emperor. If therefore the emperor comes to assist us and keeps the sworn agreements, we do not wish to live perjured; but, as has been said with your permission, we grant it to him. If not, it shall always be subject to your authority.”

At once Bohemond began again to press Pirrus with repeated messages and earnestly urged his friend not to weave delays. Pirrus, asking no questions, gave this prompt answer to one who was urgent in counsel; he also sent his son as a hostage [Col. 1104C], saying:

“Let your herald proclaim aloud in your camp that the Frankish people, prepared today, are tomorrow to enter Saracen territory in order to plunder it. Thus our purpose will be concealed from both ours and yours. Our people will rest less anxiously, supposing that the greater multitude of your nation has gone a long distance away. But after your tents have gone out, let them return by suitable routes in the silence of night. Meanwhile, you secretly bring a ladder to the wall, hurry, restrain all disturbance, and climb the wall swiftly and confidently, because I shall deliver up my towers, as I promised you. You must arrange what remains to be done and bring the outcome to pass by your swords. Do not neglect, as though sluggish, anything that must be done. I shall remain sleepless and watchful, awaiting your arrival.”

Bohemond assigned the duty of making proclamation to one of his servants, who was called, for some reason unknown to me, “Mala Corona” (“Evil Crown”). Going through the entire camp, he shouted loudly that the appointed time had been proclaimed by the nobles for going to plunder the land of their enemies [Col. 1104D].

Bohemond entrusted the secret of all his plans to Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, the Count of Saint-Gilles, the bishop of Le Puy, Robert the Norman, and certain other nobles. Tancred and his advisers had known the whole matter from the beginning. Stephen of Blois was absent; claiming to be detained by serious illness, he had departed to Alexandretta for recovery until he should regain his health.

Accordingly, the Christian army, ignorant of this matter, left the camp as evening fell; led through certain byways, it returned by short detours near the city before dawn had yet broken [Col. 1105A]. Meanwhile Bohemond instructed his close followers:

“Prudently place this ladder, which I have prepared, against that wall which you see. Act wisely and silently, and climb confidently. Pirrus, our friend, will make you safe and establish you as masters in his towers. I have his son with me as a hostage. But once you have mounted the towers, accomplish the remaining task with the sword. Let none fear; let no one be dismayed. The ladder is fixed to the wall and fastened from above to the battlements. Hasten, therefore, and climb without fear.”

[Col. 1105B] The first to climb was a Lombard named Paganus, though not altogether without fear. Nor is that surprising, since he feared betrayal, was crossing into unknown places, dreaded every possible outcome, and continually imagined the horror of death before him. Nevertheless about sixty men followed him. Pirrus gathered them with the greatest care and stationed them in his towers. When he saw that no larger number was following, he is said to have spoken in his mother tongue: “Michro Francos echome”—that is, “Alas, alas! We have few Franks.” For he feared that they were too few to defend, much less to fight, and that they might fall with him into the hands of the Turks.

Thus he directed his complaint against Bohemond as though he were unmanly and sluggish, taunting him with friendly reproaches. That Lombard descended in great haste by the ladder on which he had first climbed and said to Bohemond, waiting at a distance: “What are you doing? Are you asleep? Send quickly those whom you mean to send, for we have now taken three towers unharmed. Otherwise you have lost us, the city, and your friend, who has poured all his hope and soul into your bosom.”

Bohemond and those with him rejoiced; more quickly than the word, they hastened forward, seized the ascent, and, urging one another on, each now outstripped the other. Thus many had already climbed and many were still climbing when those in the towers and other fortifications of the walls raised loud cries [Col. 1105D]. They also occupied other towers and now ran about, shouting through the walls and streets. Whomever they could find, they slaughtered, sparing no one who came before them.

For the citizens had scarcely awakened and were still drowsy. Worn out by the hardships of the long siege, they lay helplessly exhausted. Unaware of what had happened, they came out of their houses unarmed; stunned by sleep and the sound of shouting, the cautious encountered the incautious, hoping that they were their own people. They called the Christians together as though they were their own; but wherever they met them, they fell like sheep and were cut down. Then, by chance, Pirrus’s brother by blood was also slain. Such are your events, blind and untimely night! Such are your tumults, dark hours!

[Col. 1106A] Meanwhile so great was the crush of men climbing the ladder that the ladder itself split apart and broke up. No person of sound mind can doubt that this brought both grief and great hindrance upon the Christians. The Frankish ranks were visible outside the walls, but they could offer no help to those fighting above and within. Thus no small sorrow arose there.

But not far from the ladder was a certain gate which the Christians, exploring on previous days, had seen. Feeling for it on their left side, they found it; breaking it open, they entered as quickly as possible. Then a greater din arose, and a fuller opportunity for battle came to the Christians; while the Turks, buried in sleep and wine, met a harsher extremity of slaughter. Those pagans, trying to flee the threatening danger, ran into the Christians; and while they strove, unknowingly, to avoid the attack, they fell into sudden peril of death.

Bohemond, since nothing can be done swiftly enough for a desiring mind, impatient of delay, ordered his banner to be carried into the city and placed opposite the citadel in the city, upon a higher hill [Col. 1106B]. For the Franks had entered the city in such force and prevailed so completely over that circumcised people that, after countless men had been killed, they drove whatever remained either into the castle overlooking the city or into any other places of refuge. That night no mercy was granted to age, sex, or any condition. The night was uncertain, and thus made no distinction of sex.

Day dawned. Those who remained in the camp, roused by the tumultuous people and the resounding trumpets [Col. 1106C], saw and recognized Bohemond’s banner and rejoiced at the city’s capture. They ran to the gates, entered, and struck down any Turks they found attempting to escape. That day saw a very great slaughter of pagans. That night and that morning brought deadly fortune upon the Antiochenes.

Some, indeed, escaped alive through the gates because they were unknown to the impetuous Franks. Cassianus, the Turkish lord, hid himself among the fugitives and somehow escaped alive, not into lesser misfortune but into misfortune deferred. He reached Tancred’s territory, trembling beyond belief. It is uncertain whether he departed wholly deprived of refuge or hurried about seeking help from his fellow-countrymen. This much is certain: if he had entered his castle [Col. 1106D], he would have provided more advantageously for himself and his people.

At last, his own horses and those of his companions exhausted, he was compelled to halt. He turned aside into a small hut and hid there, though not securely enough. When the inhabitants of that district—Syrians, that is, or Armenians—learned of this, they rushed upon him, seized him, cut off his head, and brought the severed head before Bohemond, so that they might thereby earn his favour and be granted and obtain the freedom they desired.

The end of Cassianus, a most distinguished man, was obscure and miserable. Such are your rewards, worldly prosperity! Such are your wages, false and deceptive Fortune! The pagans yield too much to fate and fortune [Col. 1107A]. Behold, unhappy Cassianus, Antiochene leader and *admiral*, today, overtaken by miserable chance and miserable disaster and mocked by hostile fates, is slain. Behold, a royal descendant, like someone born in dung, is shamefully punished with his body left unburied. His belt and scabbard were valued at sixty bezants; for those peoples take great pride in such ornaments and clasps.

The streets [Col. 1108A] and all the spaces between the buildings of the city were so densely occupied with corpses that no one had free passage: the crossroads and lanes were obstructed by the bodies of the slain. Thus overwhelming horror and stench assailed every traveller. Accordingly the city of Antioch, except for the citadel, was taken; and Cassianus, as has been said, was shamefully cut down on Wednesday, the third day before the Nones of June [3 June].

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1107]

[Col. 1107B] While Antioch was being besieged, many had flocked to its assistance and many were still flocking there. But when the city was taken, of those who had arrived some were killed, some were received into the citadel, and others sought safety for their lives in flight. Those who were still coming, hearing the report of the Antiochenes’ downfall, stopped and deliberated whether to depart far away or draw nearer.

Report urged them to depart, for it everywhere announced the Christians’ successful outcomes; and from their successes people anticipated still greater successes. Consequently the greatest fear entered every breast. Anger urged them to approach, because of the hostile slaughter of their fellow-countrymen; shame also urged them, because the audacity of the foreign invaders had not yet been checked. They likewise trusted in the vast multitude of nations gathered together [Col. 1107C] and in their own singular courage, as they boasted.

Moreover, they said that it would be disgraceful unless the many checked the folly of the few; unless natives drove intruders from their territories; unless they avenged the blood of their own people shed by enemies; unless they diligently protected their children, wives, household gods, and the remaining furnishings of their homes and hearths.

Their prince and commander was Curbarannus, a man most warlike, second to none in boldness, endowed with prudence, abundant in wealth, surrounded by military assistance, desirous of glory, swollen with boastful pride, a man of great renown, commander of the soldiery of the sultan of Persia. While Antioch was being besieged, Cassianus, the *admiral* of Antioch, had invited him by many embassies to hasten to liberate Antioch [Col. 1107D], promising that he would send him back honoured with much money.

Curbarannus, both to receive the promised payment and, especially, to extend his own renown, received permission from Caliphas, the apostolic leader of his people, to rage against the Christians. He gathered innumerable peoples—namely Turks, Saracens, Arabs, Publicans, Azimites, Kurds, Persians, Agulans, and countless others—and formed an immense army. Having assembled abundant forces from every side, which no one could number, and having further added to this company the *admiral* of Jerusalem and the king of Damascus, Curbarannus advanced toward Antioch.

In that expedition, as has been said, were about three thousand Agulans, all clad in iron armour; they feared neither arrows nor lances and bore no weapons into battle except swords. As these men approached Antioch [Col. 1108B], Sensadolus, Cassianus’s son, came to meet them, sorrowing over the captured city and wasting away over the death [of his father]. One might have seen tears streaming down his beardless youthful face, tears that would move even an adamant breast to pity and stir it to render assistance.

He then poured forth words of this kind into Curbarannus’s bosom:

“Most invincible prince, wounded by hostile fortune, I come before you as a suppliant and ask aid from your generous munificence. I pray that the mercy owed to the wretched may move you and that the human feeling of common flesh may compel you. Consider, I pray, the circumstances into which I have fallen; weigh the changes of human affliction. Fortune, which now looks upon me with a sidelong glance, formerly smiled on me; then I rejoiced in an excellent father and a renowned city.
