“You must fear the same misfortune for yourself [Col. 1108C]. In your favourable successes, you must reflect beforehand upon guarding against adversities. It belongs to a fortunate and generous man to regard others’ calamities as his own and to extend abundant mercy to another’s misery. Therefore help me with the disposition in which you would wish help to be given to yourself if fortune had touched you with my affliction.

“If you wish to triumph over the Christians, you can easily destroy them; you will acquire a great name for yourself and restore our people to freedom. But if you neglect to fight against them, what remains except that they should strive to bring your house and family to ruin? Unless this people is vigorously checked, it longs to advance to Chorasan; beyond all measure it attempts what exceeds its strength and makes mighty threats.

“Behold, they have gained Antioch, an impregnable city, by ingenious treachery [Col. 1108D]; and these rash people besiege the citadel which overlooks the city. Against our people, these worthless refuse bark with Coturnosian gaping [reading uncertain: *hiatuque Coturnoso*]. Hasten, therefore, and quickly come to my aid. You shall not depart unrewarded, nor shall I be ungrateful for your benefits. Moreover, I shall render you perpetual homage and shall hold in your allegiance the city which you restore to me.”

“No,” said Kerbogha, “I have decided not to act thus. But if you wish me to exert myself for you with all my strength, place the citadel in our hands, and I shall entrust it to my own retainers. Once I am secure concerning you, as I have said, I shall attack that rabble with every effort; otherwise I shall protect only my own territory.” Sensadolus, unworthy of assistance, yielded to Kerbogha’s demands and surrendered the stronghold [Col. 1109A] to the power of his protector.

On the third day after the city had been handed over to the Christians, Kerbogha also took possession of the stronghold; and the messengers of the aforesaid prince rode about near the city. The rest of the army followed behind, and they pitched camp at the Iron Bridge. They immediately stormed that fortification and killed everyone at once, except the lord of that castle, whom they bound with iron chains. When the battle of which we shall speak later was ended, he too was found alive and in chains.

The next day came, and Kerbogha pitched camp between the river and the lake; and there they spent two days. He entrusted the restored castle to one of his intimates and said:

“I know your loyalty, courage, and self-command; and therefore I shall entrust this city [Col. 1109B] to your vigilance. I knew, I say, that you would rejoice in our honour; and so I commit this very great honour to your fidelity. Guard it therefore prudently, and attend vigilantly to the duty imposed upon you. Many men, as you know, are devoted to me and would obey all our commands more swiftly than speech; but I weigh your loyalty above theirs, set your diligence before their diligence, and compare no one to your shrewdness.”

Astonished, the other replied: “If, saving your favour, I could avoid this decision of yours, I should wish you to transfer this present command to anyone else. But if, before you rebuke me for any disloyalty and I perceive your mind to be hostile toward me, I must receive this castle, then only on this condition: [Col. 1109C] that, if you are defeated in a hand-to-hand battle in the field, I shall, out of regard for my life, open the castle to the Franks.”

Kerbogha replied: “I have not found your prudence and integrity untested. Whatever happens, I grant this according to your stipulation.”

Once the castle had been entrusted and accepted, as has been said, Kerbogha, who had arrived with certain of his men, returned to the camp in the valley where his army had pitched its tents. Those Hagarenes had seized from some poor Christians certain utterly worthless weapons—namely, a rusty sword and a fairly useless little spear. They presented these to Kerbogha in mockery of the Franks, saying: “These are the weapons of war, these exceedingly precious arms, which those locusts brought from beggarly Gaul. With these [Col. 1109D] they threaten to conquer us; with these they struggle against us.”

Kerbogha smiled, took the weapons in his hands, and said mockingly:

“The Franks have not yet encountered any men. Are these the weapons in which they trust? Are these the semblances of arms by which they suppose they captured Antioch by deceiving it through treachery? Yet, vainly, they boast of this, since we have retained the stronghold which commands Antioch, fortified with ramparts and soldiers, and shall afflict those enclosed within with every injury. Let us therefore rouse ourselves, O nation of ours, always most unconquered; and let that wretched people discover in the first encounter whether we are beasts of burden or men. Let us drive the refuse of that people from our borders and, [Col. 1110A] O unbroken race, pursue them without ceasing even into their own lands. I consider it the greatest disgrace, my nobles, if we have defended ourselves and prevailed in our own land, unless, by rendering them like for like, it should be granted us to destroy them and all that belongs to them in their own land.

“Antioch, a royal and renowned city, is the capital of all Syria. They occupied it not by arms but by treachery; not by war but by their promises and flatteries. Let us therefore shake it free by fighting; and, once they have been expelled, let us attack their lands.”

He summoned his secretary and said: “Write letters to be read in Khorasan, containing this message:

“To our Pope, the Caliph, and to King Sulayman the Great: perpetual safety and boundless honour. Know [Col. 1110B] that those locusts, who possess no homeland of their own and are called Christians, have irreverently emerged from their hiding places and, as you have heard, have most insolently presumed to attack our land. But we, trusting in your goodwill and in our own arm, have set out to repress the folly of that people, and shall easily reduce them to servitude. Yet we judge this too little for us unless we also cover their borders with our bands and swallow up all their goods.

“Meanwhile, rejoice, all our friends, and beget sons, who, while we campaign in a distant region, may replace those whom we have brought with us and may possess our territories until we return. For our part, we have fortified the stronghold commanding the city of Antioch, which has been surrendered [Col. 1110C] to us, and are now deliberating how we may fight against them. So that you may see against whom we are to fight, we have sent you their glorious weapons, in which you will be able to observe how trifling are the bearers of such arms. And that you may rejoice still more fully, we now have enclosed those who took Antioch by their tricks, and we do not doubt their surrender. Therefore give yourselves abundantly to your desires and pleasures; farewell, all our friends and counsellors. May Sulayman, mighty and great king, especially prosper. For I swear that I shall in no way return until, after Syria and Romania have been restored to freedom, I have also subjected Apulia to my dominion.”

While these things were happening, the mother of the aforesaid Kerbogha, who was in the city of Aleppo, came to her aforesaid [Col. 1110D] son, lamenting over what she had heard concerning him. She was old and full of days, being a centenarian, and was prescient of things to come. This fortune-telling woman also drew many inferences from the constellations; she was not ignorant of divinatory arts, and was acquainted with many disciplines. Weeping, she said to her son:

“Why, dearest son, have you undertaken this business of war without consulting me? Did you suppose that, because I am decrepit, I had become foolish? Believe me: understanding still flourishes within my worn-out body; loose skin and the wrinkles of old age still shelter a lively mind. Indeed, you could reveal your counsel to no one more faithfully, no one who would love you more closely or advise you more judiciously. What can be compared with maternal affection? [Col. 1111A]

“Why then, man of leaden heart, have you presumed to leave your mother unconsulted and unbid farewell? O flinty breast and adamantine heart, which the memory of your mother did not soften, which reverence for an affectionate mother did not compel to conversation! For though the body has withered, understanding still lives and flourishes, unbroken. Finally, sweetest son, what a great and ineffectual undertaking you have embarked upon without me, at least to weigh the matter in the balance of counsel beforehand. You ought to have measured with what unconquerable people you were about to fight; you ought to have considered how unaccustomed to battle are the forces which you have gathered from every quarter.

“For, not concealing the truth in any respect: our people are golden; theirs is iron. Ours too is sufficiently spirited and, in action, no less effective; but it is inexperienced and much unpractised [Col. 1111B] in this kind of hardship, since the old age of this nation has flourished greatly in peace. Moreover, the God of the Franks is truly almighty; unless they gravely offend him, he always protects them as victors. In our regions, flesh of my flesh, your name has been spread widely enough; but your arm has not yet been sufficiently proved against Christians. Unless you cease from attacking them, one of two things will happen: either, triumphing over the Christians, you will be more glorious; or, defeated—may it not be so—you will stain the title of your valour.

“Further, if you yielded to your mother’s advice, you would recover from this rashness and withdraw yourself and your people, on some honourable pretext, from this presumptuous enterprise. But if not, it is certainly dangerous [Col. 1111C] for you to entrust yourself to doubtful fortune. For it is uncertain to which side Mars will smile; yet I fear for ours, because the ferocity of those executioners, their habitual practice of warfare, and their own cunning utterly dismay me. All these matters ought to have been considered with wiser caution. But since you have begun according to your own will and cannot be removed from these undertakings—for you are an obstinate man—lest I omit anything flattering: in this battle, if you engage, you will be defeated, and your army will be stripped of its rich treasures. Many will be killed; you will escape alive, but you will nevertheless die this year—alas for me!—by a sudden death.”

The aged woman, failing in tears, had ended her speech, when her son, boastfully, replied briefly:

“I wonder, my mother, with what face you have pronounced a victory for the Christians, when [Col. 1111D] they cannot be compared with our people either in numbers, arms, or courage. I alone have more powerful, warlike men devoted to me than they possess in their entire expedition. Yet what false interpreter announced these things to you? Nevertheless, I want you to be silent, lest perhaps you weaken the spirit of our army by your enervating talk. Return, therefore, sweetest mother, and await the outcome, wishing for better things. They are men, as we are; and we shall fight against unclean and uncircumcised men, not against God, nor will God fight against us. We are surrounded by an equal lot of mortality. Only those will die more swiftly whose hands prove slacker, whose spirits grow less bold in refusing to defend themselves. But you, mother, wholly worthy [Col. 1112A] of reverence, farewell; and do not yet believe that the time foretold by our lots and omens—namely, that the Christians will possess our land—has arrived.”

Having said this, the warrior hero fell silent. Having kissed her son, his mother, her cheeks drenched in tears, anxiously returned to her home; and she brought into Aleppo, that most strongly fortified city, the wealth which she could gather from every quarter, to be preserved.

On the third day after this, Kerbogha, armed, rode toward the town entrusted to him. The Christians, seeing the battle-lines advancing in order and drawing near to the city, went out to meet them; and, prepared for battle, believed that they could resist them. But the multitude and strength of those Ishmaelites were so great that the Franks were at once compelled to retreat into [Col. 1112B] the city, fearing to withstand the impetuous peoples. Because the narrowness of the gates could not grant them free entrance, many perished, suffocated by the rush itself.

The Turks attacked them fiercely; day was already failing, and no rest was given to the weary. Thus, when the day had been exhausted, welcome night cast its shadow over the land. Great despair therefore fell upon the Christians. Yet some consoled others and urged them toward battle on the following day. But certain men, more fearful than right and honour allowed and forgetful of affection for their brethren, planned flight by night; and, to the disgrace of all their kin and descendants, fled still more disgracefully.

They did not remember how shameful it was, after abandoning brothers and comrades-in-arms, without bidding friends farewell or consulting their leaders, to be lowered over the wall by ropes, to make manly strength shamefully effeminate, and to go mad before it was necessary. For those who formerly fled from battles after leaving their companions were called traitors to their comrades, and vengeance was often exacted upon their heads. I shall not fail to name certain of these men; I would name them all if I knew them all by name. We ought not spare the disgrace of men who, through excessive fear, did not spare their own reputation.

They were William of Grandmesnil, and his brother Alberic, Guy Trousseau, and Lambert the Poor. Terrified by fear of the previous day’s battle and anxious to flee the next day’s, they were lowered by ropes over the wall; and, to their perpetual disgrace, they were called stealthy rope-walkers [Col. 1112D]. Thus at the dead of that night they slipped away by ropes and reached the harbour of St Symeon on foot, with hands and feet torn raw. They walked all night through steep precipices; and, travelling with many companions toward the aforesaid harbour, they stopped in exhaustion and said to the sailors lingering in the port—for there were indeed many ships in the harbour:

“What are you doing here, wretched people? All the Christians whom you await have been beheaded and destroyed. No one but ourselves escaped alive, and you are still idly delaying. The Turks have besieged Antioch, which we had subdued—indeed, they have taken it. They have beheaded everyone else, and we have scarcely escaped their swords while making our way to you this night. Break your moorings, therefore—break them quickly, I say—and drive through the sea with your oars [Col. 1113A]; for if you delay, you will see what we say.”

Aroused by rumours of this kind, the sailors—some having cut their anchors loose—were already ploughing the sail-bearing sea and slanting their crackling sails into the winds. While this was occurring, behold, Turks suddenly flew in, scouting the shore; they slaughtered the unprepared and frightened sailors, ravaged and plundered the vessels lingering in the harbour after setting fire to them, and tore apart the idle men as they pleased.

Those who remained in the city endured throughout the day the weight of Turkish warfare. Already exhausted, they could no longer bear such great labours; so, adopting a sudden plan, they built a wall of unworked stones, without mortar, between the city and the stronghold, so that the Turks might not have free passage against them. That barrier afforded [Col. 1113B] the Christians timely help, but created a troublesome obstacle for the Turks. The townsmen ran as far as the wall, but were immediately driven back by the Franks, and so the assault of the pagans was frustrated. The Franks, with all diligence, stood armed at the wall; they gave themselves neither to sleep nor to the care of any other need.

Meanwhile famine gradually gained strength, and the Christians were compelled to devour horses, asses, and whatever else was unclean. Set amid great misery, many despaired; yet others sighed from the depths of their hearts to God. A prudent man never ceases to consider how he may escape necessity. Nor does anyone escape more easily than the man who makes the Lord his helper. Thus they called upon the Lord [Col. 1113C], and he heard them and sent them a certain priest, who spoke as follows:

“Brothers and my friends, hear the vision which I saw. Lest you suppose it a phantom or a delusion of dreams: if I lie, I want you to punish my presumption. Having resolved to spend the night in the church of the holy Mother of God, to intercede, I say, on our behalf, I do not know whether awake or half asleep—God knows—I saw our Lord Jesus Christ, though I did not recognize him. His most holy Mother was there also, and Peter, most holy prince of the apostles. I saw them all; yet, as I have said, like a man beside himself, I did not recognize my Lord and that holy company.

“The Lord said to me, ‘Do you recognize me?’

“I understood the voice of the questioner but had not yet recognized the person asking; and I replied, ‘Not at all, my Lord.’

“Then a splendid cross appeared shining above his head. Again he asked me the same question, and I replied, ‘If I understand rightly, my Lord, from the sign of the cross placed upon your head I perceive that you are the Crucified One and our Redeemer.’

“He said, ‘It is indeed as you say.’

“Then, my cheeks bathed in tears, I fell sobbing at his feet and added: ‘Lord, have mercy upon us. Lord, remember your people. Lord God, help us.’

“The Lord said to me: ‘Even until now I have helped you. For I allowed you to take Nicaea, protected you in many battles; under my leadership you conquered and prevailed at Antioch, and [Col. 1114A] during that siege I granted you many things as you wished. But, ungrateful for my benefits, you have become proud against me; your iniquity has come forth as from fatness. You, an injurious people, have provoked me like pagans by fornicating with women—whether foreigners or of your own profession, yet illicitly. This singular stench has reached heaven and turned my eyes away from you. Therefore I shall repay your ingratitude and shall not spare the prostituted and whoring multitude.’”

Then the Mother of Mercy and blessed Peter fell at the merciful feet of the Redeemer and softened the wrath of the one who threatened by these entreaties:

“Lord, for so many years a pagan people possessed this house, which was a house of prayer, and—shame!—defiled it with their impurities. And [Col. 1114B] behold, because the offences of a few demand it, are you angered so as to destroy all your Christendom, which delivered this house from them with its own blood? Spare, Lord, spare; spare your people, and do not give your inheritance to destruction, so that the nations may rule over them.”

The Holy of Holies yielded to the prayers of his suppliant Mother and Apostle, and, now with a more cheerful countenance, said to me:

“Go and tell my people: remove from among yourselves the brothel, prostitution, and every abuse; wash away your crimes with tears; return to me, and I shall return to you; and within five days I shall provide you with timely assistance. For I am God, who has nothing unmerciful in him. Meanwhile let them daily chant: ‘Our enemies have gathered together and glory in their strength. Break their might [Col. 1114C], Lord, and scatter them, that they may know that none fights for us but you, our God. Scatter them in your strength, and cast them down, O Lord, our protector.’ Let them continually sing these and other passages pleasing to the Godhead.”

The priest said these things and added:

“Brothers and my lords, do not disbelieve my lowliness, for I do not speak fabricated evasions, nor do I deceive you, deluded by fantastic imaginings. If you wish, I shall even make trial of this matter, lest, God forbid, you despise the Redeemer’s command which I have proclaimed to you. Throw me down from the summit of any tower, or cast me into fire; and when you see me unharmed, then at last believe. Otherwise, know that I have spoken inventions.”

[Col. 1114D] The Bishop of Le Puy ordered the Gospel and the cross to be brought before them. Upon these the priest, satisfying the people, swore that he had seen the vision in due order exactly as he had testified in that assembly. Immediately all the people turned to lamentation, and each urged the other to confess his guilt. You might have seen the faces of Christians bathed in tears; their heads covered in ashes, and barefoot, people of every age, with no person excepted, hastened everywhere through the churches to pray. They sought help and asked for counsel.

The Lord then inspired them with this counsel, which they accepted unanimously. One of them said:

“My lords, let us swear to one another that henceforth none of us shall withdraw from this holy company so long as he lives [Col. 1115A], until we have kissed the Sepulchre of the Lord our God, for whose sake we have undertaken this journey. Then, after taking leave also of the brethren, let those who wish return to their own homes.”

This speech pleased the whole assembly. Therefore all the leaders whose names you have found recorded above swore. Tancred too swore and added that, so long as he could keep sixty knights with him, he would in no way depart from the road to Jerusalem. Thus the whole congregation of Christians was heartened, strengthened, and exceedingly rejoiced by participating in such an oath.

There was also there a certain pilgrim named Peter. Before Antioch was occupied, Saint Andrew had appeared to him, questioned him, and said:

“What are you doing, good man?”

Peter replied: “Who are you, my lord?”

He said to him: “I am Andrew, apostle of Christ. I want you to know that, after you enter this city and go into the church of blessed Peter, you will find in that place”—and he indicated the place—“the lance which pierced the Saviour’s side upon the cross. For whatever touched that saving and most holy dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit upon the gibbet of the cross is sacred and especially to be embraced by all Christians.”

Having said this, the blessed apostle disappeared. On hearing this, the pilgrim kept silent; for he did not wish to reveal the apostle’s response to anyone, judging that he had seen this vision as one dreaming. Nevertheless, as the pilgrim later related, blessed Andrew led him all the way to the place [Col. 1115C] and showed him everything that had long lain hidden there.

After the city had been captured and, as has been said, Christendom severely crushed, blessed Andrew appeared to him again and said:

“Why, faint-hearted man, did you not take the lance?”

Peter replied: “Who, Lord, would believe what I heard?”

“Do not despair,” said the apostle, “do not despair. But know for certain that all that I told and showed you is true. Know that this revelation will greatly benefit the weary Christians, for through the lance saving confidence will flow forth to them. Within five days the Lord will visit them and powerfully rescue them from the hands of their persecutors.”

Peter disclosed to his companions this counsel divinely imparted to him. But the people did not believe and mocked the man who testified [Col. 1115D]. He persisted, affirming on oath that Saint Andrew had appeared to him twice and had announced such things to him, and had earnestly commanded him not to conceal any longer the secret entrusted to him. At last they believed his oath, and their spirits recovered their former strength, as though awakened from sleep. For now two heralds had appeared who agreed concerning their salvation and God’s favour. Now, therefore, more secure in God’s help, they rejoiced in the Lord as if they had already conquered.

Meanwhile, the Turks who were in the castle did not cease at all from harassing the Christians, but attacked the Franks with all diligence. One day, before the Franks’ eyes, they shut up three Christians [Col. 1116A] in a certain tower; nor did the Franks dare to bring aid to those enclosed. They had been worn down by many afflictions and still wasted away, receiving no consolation except hope.

Two of the three, badly wounded, came out of the tower. The third man alone defended himself bravely throughout the day against the Turks’ assault. He struck down two Turks without aid from anyone, and alone with his hand withstood the pursuing bands. We have said this so that we might not omit to relate how greatly the Christians had by then been terrified: they saw their brethren attacked, yet dared not, though standing there, to struggle for them.

That most valiant fighter was called Hugh Forsenatus, of the army of Godfrey of Mont-Scabieux, a man indeed great-souled and bold, and worthy of especial praise [Col. 1116B] among all warriors. Since the arms of his own men did not help him, let our page at least commend this glorious knight to succeeding generations. Alas, with how many and how great calamities had the spirits of the Franks withered! They saw one of their own fighting all day and did not help him; they heard him crying out and did not answer. Though they were called leaders, they did not come together; though trumpets sounded, they hid in their houses. Indeed, unarmed and spiritless, they detested the battle for which they had long prayed; now, as though lifeless, unwarlike, and without glory, they preferred death.

Bohemond and the leaders, seeing the army thus failing, so that the men neither wished to defend themselves nor could be led even as far as the wall which separated the city from the stronghold by however slight a division, ordered a great fire to be kindled and part of the city burned, so that in this way at least they might leave their houses and hiding places, in which at last, emasculated, they were skulking quite shamelessly [Col. 1116C]. The fire was lit in that part of the city where Cassian’s palace stood out. The leaders were troubled and grieved because, when called to battle, the men gave them none of their customary respect.

Without delay the fire gained force, because an old accumulation of timber furnished fuel to its crackling flames, while the burning wind supplied impetus and strength. Therefore all who had lodged in those houses, scarcely snatching up their possessions, were forced to flee to their leaders, each of whom had taken up a position at the city gates for watch duty. From the third hour of the day until midnight the fire did not cease, and about two thousand houses and churches were burned. The fire then died down, because all the violence of the winds had vanished.

The Turks of the stronghold had now prevailed over the Franks, who could scarcely protect themselves; almost nothing but weapons separated the two sides. The affair was now conducted by arm and hand alone, and they fought at close quarters on both sides; the battle was not interrupted even for a moment. The Turks, more numerous and strengthened by more abundant food, relieved one another in turns, left nothing unattempted, attacked the Franks boldly, thrust themselves voluntarily into engagements, and encouraged one another. The Franks, on the other hand, staggered under excessive distress and could take neither food nor sleep, since [Col. 1117A] no rest was allowed them. He who had bread was not permitted to eat it; nor could anyone refresh his parched mouth even with water saved for the purpose, since they had no leisure even to breathe.

Amid so great misery they began to raise another wall of flint and mortar, since the Turks had easily thrown down the one which they had erected without mortar. They also built a wooden engine, so that the Christians might defend themselves more securely. Nor did warfare cease meanwhile, because the indefatigable Turks laboured by every means to prevent the wall from being raised.

Dark night had concealed the colours of all things; and a fire was seen from heaven to threaten from the west and to rage as though falling among the Turkish camps. Their camp was not far from the city, for they had pitched their nearest tents in the valley. Although the fire did them no harm or injury, it nevertheless struck them with great fear and sadness, but brought comfort and joy to the Christians; for that sign from heaven shone upon both peoples. Some of the Turks immediately abandoned their camp in fear and lodged wherever they could, namely near Bohemond’s gate.

Those who remained in the stronghold fought throughout the day with the Christians and could not be torn away either by the Christians’ deaths or exhaustion. They pressed on with lances and missiles and matched wound with wound. The force remaining in the camp so encircled the city that no entrance or exit was open to anyone by day. At night someone could occasionally get out, but secretly and not without fear [Col. 1117C].

Thus famine increased day by day and afflicted the Christian army more grievously than can be believed or expressed. Many died of hunger. Those alive scarcely moved; their faces appeared pallid, hideously disfigured by emaciation, worn thin by prolonged fasting. In that calamity you saw no spendthrifts; indeed, you saw even the richer men needy, and all, formerly stout in flesh, made lean by starvation. A small and very poor loaf of bread, if it could be found at all, was bought for a Byzantine coin. It is better, I think, to be silent concerning wine than to speak of it, since scarcely any leader there even tasted wine. Horseflesh or ass-flesh was reckoned an imperial delicacy. A hen cost fifteen solidi; an egg, two solidi; a walnut was valued at one denarius [Col. 1117D]; every cheap article cost many staters. They eagerly plucked, boiled, and devoured leaves of fig trees, vines, thistles, and any other trees they found. They cooked dry hides of horses, asses, camels, and buffaloes and ate them. Besides this, they endured many other calamities and privations.

For hunger compelled them to chew greedily and swallow foods formerly rejected with disgust. Nothing was so foul or tasteless that hunger did not assign it flavour, or strip away the shame that might have prevented its being tasted. That wretched people endured this continual suffering for thirty-six days. Therefore let no one doubt that we have spoken truth, and let no one murmur. What food could have sustained [Col. 1118A] those who had harvested no crop, found no granaries, inhabited a city devastated by a long siege and finally burned, and received no market goods from the natives—no one can reasonably determine. One may indeed marvel, but cannot adequately decide whence they lived so long.

Nor ought this to be laid accusingly to God, for whose sake they endured such things: he chastens in order to correct, and with paternal affection scourges every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12:6). Even in those scourges he is merciful; and his hidden goodness does nothing perversely or without mercy, for the judgments of God are never unjust. But Christ so disposed matters concerning his Christians that, amid those afflictions, they might recover strength beyond the barbarians’ expectation; and, when their enemies thought them exhausted, might prevail. In their oppressions, which befell them in order that they might be tested to the uttermost, they chanted without ceasing:

“Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Psalm 113).

Thus, reproved by these things, they cried from the depths and were mercifully heard; and they were raised above their enemies.

Meanwhile Count Stephen of Chartres, whom the elders had chosen to preside over their counsels and public affairs, a man eloquent and of exceptional learning, had withdrawn to Alexandretta for recovery, being detained, as he said, by a slight illness. All awaited his return, since they had appointed him their leader and counsellor. They hoped also that, if he returned, his experience would be of great benefit to all [Col. 1118C]. He had fallen ill and departed before the city was taken, as has been said. But when he heard, through reports concerning this and other armies, that the Turks had surrounded the city—for Alexandretta is not far distant from Antioch—he secretly climbed the mountains overlooking the lower-lying city, so that he might learn fully the strength, deficiencies, and preparations of both armies. He saw the Turks’ innumerable tents, and themselves spread out like the sand of the sea over many stadia; he saw also the city surrounded, and recognized that a small band of Christians was shut within.

Believing therefore that his companions had either already all been destroyed, or were about to be destroyed at once—for what else could an inexperienced man suppose?—he was greatly terrified, and with those present began a hurried flight and departed secretly [Col. 1118D]. Yet he acted very imprudently, because he had spoken with no one from the Christian expedition. He ought first to have sent one of his own men secretly, neglecting nothing rashly; to ascertain truly what was being done within; and, if possible, to consult them carefully. He ought not to have taken wholly for himself the fear threatening all, nor to have fled disgracefully like any common man. For it would have been more glorious for him to die with his brethren than to survive as a fugitive and return to his homeland. Later, returning from his homeland to Jerusalem, he expiated this offense, touched by contrition of heart; and thus made satisfaction to all. But for the time being, unconsidered fear drove him into dishonorable flight. This was long held against him as a reproach [Col. 1119A], until he washed away his fault; and it greatly harmed those shut within as well.

For after he had returned, plundered his castle, and was hastening onward in his flight, he met the emperor at Philomelium. Calling him aside, he said: “You should know for certain that Antioch has been taken by the Christians; but the Turks have retained the citadel, which towers over and is most strongly fortified against the city. And behold, they surround and besiege the city, attacking it from the defenses of the citadel; or rather, as I suppose, they have already taken it and all the men have perished. Therefore take counsel for yourself and for the people you lead. I give this counsel: return as swiftly as possible, lest perhaps you fall into the hands of those pursuing us and all of you perish in the twinkling of an eye. But if you act otherwise, I tell you that shortly—though too late—you will repent of this rashness.”

[Col. 1119B] The emperor immediately summoned his council and the Franks, many of whom were with him; for on both sides, Gallic and Greek people were streaming in great numbers to aid the besieged. He laid out the matter in order before them and said: “The Franks to whose aid we were hastening now require assistance greater than our own, because they have either all already been swallowed up in death or carried away into captivity. They would therefore need either a helper able to restore them to life, or one strong enough to bring them back from the distant captivity into which they are said to have been taken. For this is the testimony of the count who is here; yet we can do neither. The time has forestalled the aid we were preparing for them. What more can we do? Since all have been destroyed, what profit could our assistance bring them [Col. 1119C]? To make a laborious and costly journey where one can achieve nothing is utter madness. Therefore it seems good to us to return quickly, lest we too be destroyed to no purpose. For behold, the Turks, more insolent than usual and more savage than tigers because of the blood they have shed, will easily prevail if they attack us, since our own men, hearing these reports, will immediately lose heart and falter. Let us return, therefore, and postpone our undertaking to a future time. A day will come, I say, when we shall set out to avenge the blood shed by the treacherous Turks. For the present, I would have our men die a sudden death; but let us return, that we may live, and let us preserve and restore them for wrath and vengeance. Meanwhile, by imperial edict we order this land behind us to be devastated [Col. 1119D], so that, if the Turks should ever come out against us, they may be compelled to withdraw because they find nothing here. Moreover, we command that the people inhabiting this region be transferred into Bulgaria, so that we may not be accused of having forgotten anything.”

Thus the Franks returned unwillingly and lamented most bitterly. Many poor pilgrims also died here and there, being long weakened by illness. Guy, Bohemond’s brother, was with the emperor while the rumor-bearing count spoke. Hearing this prophecy, he was greatly grieved and wept from the very marrow of his heart’s anguish. Wailing, he cried: “Alas, my brother and dearest lord Bohemond, what has happened? How have you fallen, hope of the people of God? Do we suppose that you deserved this [Col. 1120A]? Woe is me! Why did I not perish instead? O God, why have you judged thus? Why have you so abhorred your people? Why have we become a reproach among the nations? Who will grant me, sweetest brother Bohemond, that I may die for you? Let my soul die, O people of God, O leaders worthy of every title of praise, at your death.”

As he spoke thus, he tore his beardless cheeks with hooked nails and plucked out his fair hair; and he moved all his hearers to lamentation. Scarcely comforted, though his grief was not soothed, he was compelled to return with the emperor. An immeasurable sorrow also stole over the people of God. For bishops, abbots, and priests almost ceased for three days from prayers and praises of God, and sighed with deep groans. Guy too continually lamented on the journey [Col. 1120B], groaned, and poured forth many insults against the aforesaid count. Indeed, on that day the whole army was so stupefied that, terrified by mental shock, they nearly lost their senses; at last, however, they recovered themselves and more devoutly again sent forth to God plaintive cries, propitiatory prayers, and mournful complaints.

The emperor, too ready to believe the words of the man of Blois, returned to Constantinople to secure his own repose, having given no aid whatever to the besieged Christians in that singular necessity. Behold how greatly Stephen of Chartres harmed the army of God: while consulting for himself alone and abandoning his brethren and fellow-soldiers, he turned the emperor’s helping presence away from them and, an untruthful bearer of reports, disgorged rumors other than those proper for him to convey. Yet we do not doubt that this occurred by God’s dispensation [Col. 1120C], he who orders all things sweetly and does not permit even one sparrow to fall to the ground by chance. For if Emperor Alexius had arrived and overcome the Turks, the victory would have been attributed to his people rather than to the army of God, and credited to the multitude of Greeks rather than to Frankish valor.

But those who were in the city turned to God and placed their whole hope in things above, because they had been compelled to despair of human aid. Therefore they spoke among themselves about seeking the Lord’s lance; for they had great confidence in it, if it could be found, because the apostle Andrew had promised this from God. They went accordingly to the church of Blessed Peter and, after carefully marking the place, debated the matter there for a long time [Col. 1120D]. The opinion of the majority prevailed, and they entrusted that task to thirteen vigorous and industrious men, who were to dig there diligently. Thus they dug from morning until evening and finally, with that same Peter to whom it had been revealed present, found the lance. When it was lifted with fitting reverence, a public cry arose; a joyful rush was made toward it, as was due, and it was kissed with every devotion. You might have seen people moistened with tears, forced from them by joy; you might have perceived the joy brought forth by the discovery of so great a thing. Such gladness arose among them that, all listlessness removed, thereafter they remembered no sorrow. And from that time they dared to deliberate about war.

[Col. 1121A] They therefore resolved to send envoys to the Turkish leaders, who might report their replies to them through an interpreter. They sent two: Peter the Hermit and a certain Herluin, not unacquainted with the Turkish language. These two men, sufficiently knowledgeable and capable Christians, spoke thus to Kerbogha and his men:

“The leaders of the Christians and the entire Christian army send us to you, asking you henceforth to desist from attacking them and to cease persecuting Christians. For why have you pitched your tents against them and made ready your weapons, brandishing them for war? What harm do they do you? What concern is Antioch to you, for which you have assembled? If you wish to contend by right, is not this land, justice so directing, the Christians’ land? Did not blessed Peter designate it for Christianity through his preaching [Col. 1121B]? Did he not himself preside there as bishop? Yet you, relying upon proud tyranny, after killing our brethren, have bound it under your own dominion. Behold, again in rash daring you prepare to make war upon them. Does it seem just to you that, if they now desire to recover their own land and make no attempt whatever to take anything of yours from you, you should in turn rise with swords girded against innocent men?

“They command, therefore, that if you withdraw peacefully, they will allow you to carry away all that is yours; and, if you wished, they would freely give you something of their own. But if, which would be better, you longed for baptism, they would gladly grant you that sacrament; they would restore this land to your rule; and they would place themselves before your enemies on your behalf, like brothers born of the same womb [Col. 1121C]. But if you gird yourselves with the sword and dare to contemplate battle, he will fight more securely whom the justice of the very cause for which he fights protects. Yet we, in the will of God, shall gain God as our helper and have justice as our ally. If you have any reply, we shall hear it.”

Then Kerbogha is said to have replied with a grim countenance: “We judge very differently. Your Christianity, which is idolatry and abomination, we utterly reject and abhor. Will your Crucified One, whom you put forward—he who could not rescue himself from the reproach of the cross—rescue you from our hands? We wonder with what mouth you presume to call your own the land which we have possessed for so long, and which our forefathers possessed before that superstitious Peter of yours; but by his deceits he turned them away from worship of their Deity and seduced them, deceived into your most trifling sect [Col. 1121D]. Moreover, this land has been ours by right from ancient times, and our strength, once you are wiped out, will immediately restore it to us. If you would be willing to become Turks with us—which would be altogether necessary for preserving your lives—we would entrust to you this city and many other regions; we would raise all who are foot-soldiers to be horsemen; and we would fight for you everywhere. But if you reject even this, consider flight; for we shall provide for ourselves by subduing the land—or rather, it is already subdued.”

The envoys took the road back and returned in haste, making the Christian army more certain of the impending war. Meanwhile famine grew stronger [Col. 1122A], and fear of the Turks still somewhat unmanned the hearts of the trembling Christians. At length, by the priests’ order, after three days of fasting had been completed, processions with litanies held through the churches, and each Christian fortified with the most holy viaticum, they arranged the battle.

They established six divisions within the city. In the first division were Hugh the Great with the French and the Count of Flanders; in the second, Duke Godfrey with his warlike army; in the third, Robert, duke of the Normans; in the fourth, the bishop of Le Puy, carrying with him the lance which the Christians wished to be borne before them and regarded as a great safeguard and protection. Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles also remained behind, to watch lest the Turks descend from the citadel and rush freely on foot into the city [Col. 1122B]. Tancred, a distinguished prince and soldier, commanded the fifth division. Bohemond presided over the sixth, that he might provide for all and be wholly present in the needs of each. Bishops and priests preached and prayed; standing in elevated places, they marked all with the sign of the venerable cross.

They marched out in order through the gate before the Mosque. Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that, as they went out of the city, a little shower fell, like a dew-laden drop. It so gladdened horses and riders sprinkled as though by morning dew that the horses, as if exhilarated, began to neigh; the riders’ spirits were sweetened, and they became more vigorous and cheerful, all feeling themselves readier and more agile. Yet the rain was so fine and slight [Col. 1122C] that they could scarcely have called it rain; they felt certain dewy drops more than they saw them. This has been reported to us by many credible persons. Who could doubt that this was the bounty of a divine gift? Who could fail to recognize in the sprinkling of those drops the blessing of God visiting his own? Thus, strengthened by greater confidence, they advanced to battle.

Kerbogha is said to have remarked: “They are hastening more to flight than to battle.” Such was his boldness and folly that he thought no nation would dare to come against him. Yet when he saw that they did not turn aside fearfully either this way or that, but advanced at a measured pace, he was again not ashamed to say: “Will these contemptible little dogs perhaps dare to undertake battle?” He is also said to have been somewhat afraid [Col. 1122D], and to have grown pale with savage anger. For earlier, seeing the Christians come out, he had said to his men: “Let them come this far, so that we may swallow them more freely within our power. Let them come out; let them approach. For we shall at once surround them, prevail, and suffocate them.”

The Christians, however, proceeded step by step, and no one rushed ahead of another disorderly. Therefore Kerbogha, as has been said, froze with greater fear; his customary bodily strength failed, and his spirit grew cold. Secretly he ordered his steward, whom they call an admiral, who was in charge of his affairs, that if he saw a lit fire smoking at the head of his army, he should know that his men had been defeated; and that man was immediately to give the signal, gather all his own men, and withdraw, lest perhaps the people with him, or those in the tents, should all perish [Col. 1123A].

Kerbogha, observing the ordered divisions and seeing forces greater than he had heard of, began craftily to draw back little by little toward the mountains, so that the Franks, thinking that he fled, might pursue headlong and, being thereby thrown into disorder, could more easily be harmed. Then the Turks too, accomplishing nothing in this way, dispersed from one another. One part came from the sea; others stood in place, hoping that they could enclose the Christians. Conversely, the Franks, not ignorant of the enemy’s ambushes, took a portion from the division of Duke Godfrey and Robert the Norman, established it as a seventh division, and placed over it a certain Reynald. They immediately met the pagans coming from the sea. The Turks fought fiercely against them and struck many with arrows or inflicted upon them other cruel kinds of death [Col. 1123B]. The other Christian companies arranged themselves in a line extending from the sea to the mountains; the intervening distance is said to have been about two miles. From both the mountains and the sea the Turks pressed them shrewdly, surrounding and attacking the Christians on every side.

Behold, thanks be to God! From those same mountains an innumerable army was seen to emerge, mounted on white horses and carrying white banners in their hands. Many Christians—and, as they think, pagans also—saw this, and, wondering, hesitated over what it might be. At last both sides recognized that a sign had been given from heaven. For they recognized the leaders of that host advancing with their standards: Saint George, Saint Demetrius, and Saint Mercurius [Col. 1123C]. This vision struck great fear into the Saracens, but increased the Christians’ hope. It encouraged the latter and utterly disheartened the former. Many who were present testified that this occurred; yet not all could see it, but only those to whom the Lord wished to reveal his secret. To some he revealed it for confusion, to others as a manifestation of imminent victory. Let no one accuse us of falsehood, for we invent nothing from our own hearts; we testify what we have heard, and our testimony from the mouths of those who were present is true.

The pagans fighting on the sea-side, once unable to bear the weight of battle, set fire to the grass, as Kerbogha had foretold, so that those in the tents, seeing it [Col. 1123D], might flee and carry away whatever spoils they could. Once the signal mentioned above was recognized, they fled swiftly and restlessly; trembling, they seized their more precious possessions. But the Christians fighting opposite them now turned the battle toward their tents, where they knew that the greater part of the enemy’s strength had remained. The Turks still resisted with all the obstinacy they could muster: some fought, while others busied themselves plundering the tents.

Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and Hugh the Great rode by the river, where once more the greatest mass of combatants was assembled. Attacking them steadfastly, they drove them back in unison. Those pagans pressed obstinately, and the battle was fought relentlessly on both sides. Bronze helmets rang like struck anvils [Col. 1124A]; fire flashed in little sparks; swords were shattered; men, their brains dashed out, fell to the ground; hauberks were torn; entrails spilled out; exhausted horses sweated, and neither horses nor riders were granted any rest. The packed ranks were now scarcely separated from one another by the narrow interval of weapons; some drove against others at close range, and hands repelled hands, feet feet, bodies bodies. Yet fear, divinely sent upon the Turks, terrified them; the invincible steadfastness of the Franks made them marvel and stand aghast, and forced them into flight.

Thus the whole legion began to collapse, and neither trumpet, drum, clarion, nor herald could call them back. For it is impossible for so many peoples, once flight has begun, to return again and fight again [Col. 1124B]; the very onset and common terror dishearten them and hurl them onward in flight. The fleeing Turks turned toward the tents, where they thought many of their men, left there as reinforcements, remained; but while the others fought, these had fled after seeing the fire kindled, as has been said. The Franks, restraining their hands and eyes for a time from plundering the pavilions, pursued them diligently and without mercy, killing them, and drove them as far as the Iron Bridge; they pursued them still farther, slaughtering them everywhere, as far as Tancred’s castle.

At last, returning to their tents, they seized whatever was desirable and carried into the city treasures of every sort; countless horses and beasts of burden; wool-bearing sheep; abundant provisions; and everything necessary for those in need [Col. 1124C]. For the pagans have this custom: whenever they march against an enemy, whether to provide for their necessities or from vainglorious ostentation, they take abundant wealth with them; they make horses, asses, and camels carry burdens; they have sheep and cattle driven along for food; and they omit neither grain, flour, beans, oil, nor wine. When all these things had been brought abundantly into the city and the desired victory obtained, they blessed God with worthy praises, recognized him visibly as their protector and defender, and raised jubilant hymns to heaven.

The Syrians and Armenians inhabiting those regions, seeing that the Turks had been irretrievably defeated in battle [Col. 1124D], blocked the familiar mountain passes and occupied the narrow paths; drawing swords, they inflicted immense slaughter upon them. They massacred them like wandering sheep, since, through extreme terror, they had forgotten every means of defense. The admiral who had remained in the city’s citadel, to whom Kerbogha had entrusted that castle, saw his men disgracefully scattered far and wide. Before all the Franks had returned, terrified by fear, he asked for and received a Christian banner, which he placed in a higher position in the citadel. He is understood to have done this so that mercy might be shown both to his own men and himself, and so that there might be no doubt about surrendering the citadel. The banner was that of the Count of Saint-Gilles, since it was nearest at hand when requested [Col. 1125A].

When the Lombards saw this, they were vehemently indignant because Bohemond’s banner had not been raised, though their comrades had granted him the city under the earlier agreements. To settle the dispute peacefully, the admiral returned the count’s banner and raised Bohemond’s on the tower. Having requested a time for discussion, he spoke concerning peace and the safety of his fellow-soldiers. Bohemond and the admiral therefore agreed that those defenders of the castle who wished to become Christians should, secure in their lives, be treated with Christian generosity; but those who wished to retain their own law should be escorted unharmed to safe places, and should not there be deprived by deceitful demands of what they had brought with them. This agreement was confirmed by all, and the citadel was immediately surrendered to Bohemond. Not long afterward that admiral was baptized [Col. 1125B] and endowed with the generous munificence of the Franks. Later he used to say that he had adopted Christianity in a special way long before. Those who resisted the Christian faith returned under Bohemond’s escort to their own country.

This battle was fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul. After the pagans had thus been defeated, others driven far from the city, and the Christians, with Christ as their leader, won their glorious triumph and rendered worthy praises to God, the leaders of that illustrious Christian host came together. Having taken counsel, they sent Hugh the Great, a capable man, to Emperor Alexius at Constantinople, that he might hasten to receive the city which they had won for him through calamitous sufferings [Col. 1125C], and likewise preserve inviolate the sworn agreements made with them. For they themselves did not in any way wish to depart from their obligations. Let him therefore come, so that neither party might be defrauded of promises and duties.

“Let him come to us,” they said, “and, as he agreed with us, let him henceforth provide us with an unremovable companion on our journey to Jerusalem. We do not wish yet to seek any pretexts concerning the oath we made to him, though we certainly could; nor should he advance any excuse for not coming and keeping his own oath. For perjury consists in the thing itself, not merely in an appearance of perjury, unless, all deceit removed, you labor to observe your oath even beyond your strength.”

Hugh the Great went to discharge this embassy. But although he had performed many things bravely by hand and counsel in that expedition [Col. 1125D], he greatly failed in this respect: like a messenger of raven kind, he did not afterward return to his brethren as he had promised and ought to have done.

After the aforesaid Hugh had departed for the emperor, the Frankish leaders held a council and deliberated on conducting the people of God to Jerusalem. They said: “This people, which has suffered many calamities in order to merit the sight of the tomb of the Lord its God, now exhausted by many misfortunes openly complains of delaying the journey no longer; and we too, worn by great weariness, make the same complaint. Let us therefore determine what is most useful for them. We judge that no further delays should be introduced except those imposed by unavoidable necessity. But nevertheless, each matter must be weighed not impetuously but carefully and moderately [Col. 1126A]. The land through which we are to travel lacks water; summer is excessively hot; at present we could not endure the harshness of the climate. We have been exhausted in strength and resources by a long siege. Let us therefore pause and rest; let us restore our wounded and sick; and meanwhile have pity on our poor. Let us wait for the moist season after the solstice and avoid the harmful course of Cancer and Leo. At the Kalends of November the weather will grow cooler; then, gathered together, let us unanimously undertake the journey agreed upon. Otherwise we would afflict the whole people with untimely heat. Let this counsel be explained more fully to the crowds demanding it. We must avoid an unmanageable season, and we judge this most beneficial for all.”

This was announced throughout the entire army and was at last approved by all. The leaders and their households dispersed through neighboring regions to spend the summer; the needy followed them in order to live. For the leaders had said: “If anyone is poor but sound in body, let him join us, and we will support all, assigning each a wage. Let the sick be sustained by public alms until they recover.”

There was in the same army a certain knight of no little spirit, one of Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles’s household, named Raymond Pilet. He gathered to himself many men, knights and foot-soldiers. Having assembled as large an army as he could, he boldly entered the land of the Saracens. Passing beyond two cities, he came to a certain castle [Col. 1126C] called Thalamania. Since the inhabitants of that castle were Syrians, they surrendered themselves to him of their own accord. They rested in that place for about eight days.

They were then told that a well-filled Saracen castle lay not far away. Girding on military belts and shielding themselves with coverings of cloth, they attacked the castle on every side, pressed it hard, prevailed, plundered it, and utterly destroyed those settlers. Yet those who wished to convert to the Catholic faith they spared unharmed. They returned to their former castle, rejoicing in victory. On the third day they set out again and came to a city near them called Marram [Col. 1126D]. Many pagans from Aleppo and other neighboring cities had assembled there and came out against them for battle.

Thinking that they would fight, the Franks at once prepared themselves for battle in the customary manner of soldiers in camp; but the enemy’s empty hope deceived them. The Turks cautiously withdrew toward the city, neither fleeing nor fighting at close quarters; rather, by a certain stratagem they avoided battle and then attacked the Franks again with swift movement. They charged them, wheeled about with the easiest of turns, and their horses, swiftly brought round, readily wheeled again. The Franks sustained repeated assaults and could not safely avoid the attacks of those pressing upon them; for if they attempted to retreat, the pagans would press upon their rear as they withdrew—which indeed happened later. Thus they endured until evening both labor and the burning of thirst, for the heat was extreme. When they could no longer endure either the toil or the plague of thirst, since no water for refreshment could be found, they attempted and agreed to return gradually, in a compact body, to their castle [Col. 1127A].

But the feeble and undisciplined people—namely the foot-soldiers and Syrians—despising order and neglecting the soldiers’ command, began to flee in scattered groups, seized by excessive fear. The pagans pressed upon them tirelessly, pursued those who showed their backs, and struck them down; more savage than wolves, they spared no one. The prospect of victory and the opportunity of the moment supplied them with strength. Many of the common and faint-hearted people were killed; some died by the sword, others were suffocated by the distress of parched throats. Those who escaped alive returned with their Raymond to their castle and remained there several days. This slaughter occurred in the aforesaid month of July.

For success did not always attend the Christians. The Lord was correcting them for their arrogance, lest their minds perhaps become somewhat swollen with pride because of their frequent victories. But those who had remained in Antioch, their wishes fulfilled, enjoyed peace and joy—except that their leader and protector, the bishop of Le Puy, seized by a grave bodily affliction, began to fall ill; and, growing weaker, took to the bed of sickness. Addressing his sorrowful sons in fatherly speech and abundantly consoling them, he entered upon the way of all flesh and, as his illness worsened, departed in the Lord. Then immoderate mourning arose throughout Christ’s whole army [Col. 1127C], because he had been the counsel of nobles, the hope of orphans, and the support of the weak; a military man for soldiers, he instructed and trained clerics in a clerical manner; he shone with singular prudence, eloquent and gracious, all things to all men. Accordingly, they venerated him with their whole hearts as father and lord, because he inwardly gave each one affectionate protection.

The grieving army celebrated his funeral with episcopal honor. Having prepared his body with such spices as they could obtain, they accompanied it with imperial gifts; and the companies of orphans buried their departed father weepingly and solemnly in the church of Blessed Peter. The people could scarcely be torn from his tomb, tearing their hair and faces [Col. 1127D]. They offered long-lasting tears for the dead bishop; after wiping them away, they once more took counsel for themselves.

But the Count of Saint-Gilles, never yielding to idleness or sluggishness, but continually making war upon the pagans with zeal, entered the land of the Saracens and came to Albara, a city of no small distinction among them. His army stormed and took it by force; it reduced all the city’s inhabitants, of both sexes, to nothing by killing them, and subjected the conquered city to his dominion. They sent to Antioch, for consecration, an elected bishop there, a prudent and honorable man. Thus they appointed him bishop in that place, a worthy steward for the Christian people. When matters pertaining to religious worship had been arranged there, the month of November approached [Col. 1128A]. The agreed time for departure was now at hand, and all were concerned with completing the journey. All the chief men assembled at Antioch, where the greater part of the army had spent the summer. They found the people rejoicing and exulting, except that they had buried the bishop of Le Puy on the Kalends of August.

Once all had assembled, they began to discuss the pressing matter, lest they be further delayed from their journey. Meanwhile Bohemond openly complained concerning the city because he did not yet hold all of it under his authority. He spoke to them about the allied agreements which they had made with him when the city, not yet taken, was under siege. They had agreed to grant him dominion over the whole city until the matter should be referred back in its entirety to the emperor [Col. 1128B]. But the Count of Saint-Gilles could in no way be softened from continually speaking of the oath which he had made to the emperor, as Bohemond himself had approved:

“I do not wish,” he said, “to be charged with perjury anywhere, nor meanwhile will I allow you alone to rule this city. Let the city at least remain under common guardianship, and let us discuss the completion of our journey more freely. But if not, let our peers and equals decide what is just.”

This was the unappeasable dispute between Bohemond and the Count of Saint-Gilles. All the elders and those most distinguished by experience assembled in the church of Blessed Peter, to see whether so great a conflict might be calmed. The claims of both litigants were heard attentively, while they awaited the decisions of learned judges. They withdrew for private deliberation, and the knowledgeable men argued clearly and at length [Col. 1128C]. Judgment was postponed, lest discord increase. Therefore Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, Robert the Norman, and the other chief men said:

“Since at present we can give no judgment that will not displease one party, let us, insofar as we can, defer this matter under the pretext of peace; meanwhile something will occur.”

They answered those awaiting their decision: “At present we can give no judgment; but we wish and approve that, with this matter peacefully deferred, we hasten our journey. When it has been completed, either by judicial process or by the authority of our counsel, after we return with God’s favor—trust us in this—we shall reconcile you with one another.”

This was entirely accepted, and it was confirmed, with hands placed in the hands of the bishops, that they would proceed thus straightforwardly [Col. 1128D]. Bohemond therefore fortified the castle restored to him with provisions, men, arms, and guards. The count similarly fortified the palace of the admiral Cassianus, which he had occupied, and the tower above the bridge from the port of Saint Symeon. Their ambitions and hostilities were so great that neither trusted the other, each fearing that the other might seek the city for himself beneath a concealed ambition. Nor is this surprising, in view of the honor and advantage involved.

Antioch is indeed a most beautiful and strongly fortified city, exceedingly rich in abundant revenues. Within it are four fairly high mountains, on one of which—the highest, that is—stands a citadel towering above the entire city. Below, the city is properly built [Col. 1129A] and encircled by a double wall. The inner wall is broad, raised into the air, and constructed and joined together from great squared stones. In the structure of this wall are four hundred and fifty towers, adorned with very handsome battlements and protected by defenses; the outer wall is not of such great height, but is nevertheless of marvelous beauty. It contains three hundred and forty churches. By reason of its great primacy it has a patriarch, to whose patriarchate one hundred and fifty-three bishops are subject. On the east it is enclosed by four mountains; on the west, a river named Farfar flows past the city walls. Eighty-five kings raised, exalted, and ennobled it in founding it; the greatest and first among them was Antiochus, [Col. 1129B] from whose name Antioch seems to have received its designation.

And because it was of such authority and nobility, the Franks were unwilling rashly to abandon it after conquering it, since it had been the head of all Syria, had extended its primacy far and wide, and was to subject even distant regions to them. The Christians had besieged and taken it for eight months and one day. Again, once the city itself had been taken, the Gentiles held them besieged within it for three weeks. During that prolonged siege such a multitude of Gentiles gathered that no one recalls ever seeing or hearing of a more numerous concourse of peoples. Therefore they rested there for five months and nine days. With so many circumstances confronting them, they were unwilling to leave it carelessly, but entrusted it to faithful protection. [Col. 1129C] The count, however, and Bohemond each entertained private designs concerning it.

Accordingly, as has been said, they fortified the city; and in November, intending to set out elsewhere, after putting every matter in order, they departed from Antioch. Count Raymond left with his army and, having passed through two cities, Rugia and Albaria, arrived on the fifth day before the Kalends of December at Ma'arrat, a fortified and wealthy city filled with many nations of Hagarites. On the following day he began to assault the city; but, hindered by its walls and defenders, he achieved nothing then. Bohemond followed and arrived at the aforesaid city on Sunday. On the next day, namely Monday, they vigorously attacked the city. They set ladders against its wall and all day harassed the guardians [Col. 1129D] of the walls by various assaults, yet likewise did them little harm. For the ladders had been raised to the wall, but as the Turks shouted and fought against them, no one dared to climb. Those citizens also believed that they could resist these men just as they had thwarted Raymond Pilet; but in the end their presumptuous hope deceived them.

For Count Raymond had a wooden engine constructed, which, so that it might be more easily moved, he had placed upon four wheels. It was of such height that it looked down upon the summit of the walls and matched even the elevation of the towers. They therefore brought that structure up beside a certain tower. The battle-signals of horns and trumpets sounded [Col. 1130A]; armed companies surrounded the walls; crossbowmen and archers launched missiles; and those in the wooden tower hurled enormous stones upward. Priests and clerics humbly entreated God to defend His Christendom, granting them safety and victory. William of Mont-Pèlerin was in the engine, with many others. Since that structure rose higher than the walls, they injured the defenders more easily, for stones cast from above fell upon them. Struck upon their shields, helmets, or heads, they readily perished and utterly failed. They also had iron hooks with which they ceaselessly harassed one another.

Nevertheless, the Turks in the towers attacked the Christians with arrows and stones, [Col. 1130B] threw into the engine the fire called Greek fire, and allowed nothing to remain idle. The Christians in turn poured out oil, which especially extinguishes that fire; attempted the ascent and drew back their feet; and those who had mounted the walls were afraid, yet failed in nothing. Thus the battle was prolonged until evening. So tireless was the valor of the Hagarites that they boldly repelled the Christians’ stratagems.

Yet Gulferius de Turribus, a man of high birth and marvelous boldness, of Limousin lineage, was the first boldly to climb the ladder and set foot upon the wall. Some climbed after him, but not many, for the broken ladder split apart. Yet he defended the wall bravely and, having driven back the pagans, summoned his companions by gesture and voice. [Col. 1130C] Meanwhile another ladder was hastily set up, and many foot-soldiers and knights climbed it. At last so many ascended that they occupied a great part of the wall and drove back the citizens in battle. The pagans nevertheless rose up and attacked the Christians with all their strength. They assailed them several times with such force that some Franks, overcome by fear, let themselves down from the wall. Yet many remained upon it; they endured and repaid the frequent assaults until the Christians had undermined the wall and opened an entrance. When the Turks learned this, they were terrified even to despair and cast themselves into irrevocable flight.

Thus the wealthy city of Ma'arrat was taken at evening, on Saturday, the third day before the Ides of December. It seemed good [Col. 1130D] to the leading men of the city, in such misery of terror, to gather with their children, wives, and household goods in the palace above the gate, so that at least the suddenness of death might be postponed and they might gain a moment in which to live. For all who are about to die deem it the greatest gain if they can prolong life a little. The Christians entered the conquered city and greedily carried off whatever treasures they could find, whether in houses or in pits. They pursued the slaughter of the Saracens with such effort that they scarcely allowed anyone to live. Thus nowhere in the entire city—no street, corner, house, or any place—was free from corpses; the steps of passersby were grievously impeded [Col. 1131A] by the dead bodies piled together.

There was there none of the fear which the dead ordinarily produce in the living, because they had become accustomed everywhere to having the dead beside them as though they were alive. Only the stench troubled them; for to smell them, see them, or sleep among the dead without disgust had already become habitual. Of those gathered in the palace, some were killed; others, by Bohemond’s order, were led to Antioch either for servitude or for sale. All were thus scattered after their goods had been plundered; for those who gave out on the road were either crushed beneath stones or pierced with swords. Thus the unhappy citizens of Ma'arrat suffered the extermination described above. The Franks remained in that city for a full month and three days. The bishop of Orense fell sick there, departed [Col. 1131B] from those below, and flew upward to those above.

From this delay a severe famine befell the army, because horses and horsemen had consumed everything they had found in the city; nor, with the whole country devastated, could they find even the smallest thing outside the city, and they had no market. As a result, through this very prolongation, this famine exceeded the hunger they had endured at Antioch. They were therefore compelled to touch with unsated teeth every dishonorable, unfamiliar, harsh, and even unlawful thing. It was reported and established that many ate Turkish flesh—that is, human flesh—roasted on spits and baked over fires, biting it without shame. They would thus slip out secretly from the city, kindle fires at a distance, cook it, and, after consuming their abominable meals, return—as though they had done nothing of the kind—thus providing for their wretched [Col. 1131C] lives.

This report nevertheless became public in the army; but because hunger prevailed, punishment was deferred. The leading men, however, struck breast [Col. 1132A] and mouth, and remained silent in horror. Yet it was not imputed to them as a crime, because they cheerfully endured that famine for God’s sake and made war upon their enemies with enemies’ hands and teeth. They committed unlawful acts, indeed, but crushing necessity compelled the law to be violated. For camp-famine desires everything and rejects nothing. What do you not compel, cruel hunger? For it is an incurable plague, and when food is taken away hunger increases day by day. A human being can endure no affliction less easily than hunger; hence it has often happened that certain starving men, as though dreaming, attacked themselves with their own teeth. For nothing is more intolerable to a human being than hunger.

Others who truly wished to act more honorably cut open the bodies of the Turks, because they found bezants in their entrails; and the Christians took for themselves the gold which they had swallowed. The Christians suffered so great a pestilence of starvation at Ma'arrat; indeed, many perished from overpowering hunger. There again they spoke of reconciliation between Bohemond and Count Raymond; when this accomplished nothing, Bohemond at once departed angrily for Antioch, and the journey to Jerusalem was disrupted to the detriment of the peoples. For the private quarrels of princes ruin and afflict their subjects when one disagrees with another. While each seeks what is his own, he grows cold toward the common good; and peoples are abandoned to common destruction where their leaders do not take thought for one another. Thus the people journeying toward Jerusalem were greatly hindered by [Col. 1132C] the private grievances of their leaders. Let this third book therefore now end, and let us gird ourselves anew to begin the fourth.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1131]

[Col. 1131C] The true cause of the mutual hostility among the princes was Antioch. The occasions for their complaints were these: one publicly alleged before all that he had made an oath to the emperor, which he was wholly unwilling to violate; the other said that the city had been granted to him by all, and therefore wished to retain the gift made to him. Yet both claims were true; and although that was the situation, because they could not be reconciled, this was a great hindrance to the entire army.

After Bohemond had withdrawn to Antioch, Count Raymond sent his envoys to the princes who were at Antioch and addressed them, asking them to meet him at Rugia for a conference. The summoned princes came to Rugia—namely Duke Godfrey, Robert the Norman, and Robert of Flanders—and brought Bohemond with them. They spoke, as they had yesterday and the day before, about reconciling the great men. When again the affair produced no result, those princes returned sorrowfully to Antioch, because they had still achieved nothing toward hastening the march. Neither the count nor Bohemond wished to go, since they were still fiercely disputing over the city. Bohemond would not go unless the entire city were handed over to him; nor would the count go unless Bohemond accompanied them.

The count returned to Ma'arrat, where the Christian army was endangered by famine. [Col. 1132D] Stirred to compunction in heart, he generously mastered his own will and undertook to proceed toward Jerusalem in order to provide for God’s soldiers. He put the cause of God before either his own wish or advantage. It is indeed the highest virtue in princes if they rule themselves, provided they are not stubbornly obstinate; for excessive obstinacy in leaders endangers all their subjects. The count therefore commanded himself not to harm Christendom altogether. Accordingly, he arranged by orders that Cassianus’s palace should be carefully fortified.

Thus he left Ma'arrat on the Ides of January, barefoot, and voluntarily joined himself to the pilgrim people. For, humbled, the count displayed this sign of his undertaken pilgrimage. Great joy therefore arose among the people [Col. 1133A] of God. As they proceeded, the count of Normandy joined them at the city of Capharda, and there they rested three days.

The king of Caesarea then concluded an agreement of peace with the counts. For he had often sent his envoys before Ma'arrat and had stipulated this agreement: that he would remain peaceful toward the Christians and willingly furnish them many things, unless the untamed Frankish race were bent upon disinheriting him or devastating his kingdom. He further gave them assurance that, so long as his kingdom were spared, no obstacle whatever would be made for the Christians, and he would provide them with an abundant market. They received this pledge from the king of Caesarea and continued on their way with greater confidence.

Leaving Capharda, they encamped beside the river Pharfar [Col. 1133B] near Caesarea. But when the king saw that the Franks had lodged near his city, he was greatly displeased, being ashamed to have the camp of foreigners so near him.
