He said: “Unless at first light you remove your camp from the suburb of our city, you will violate the treaty made, and we shall forbid you the market promised to you and provide for ourselves.”

When morning came, he sent two of his men to show them how to cross the river and lead the army into fertile country. They entered a rich and prosperous valley, above which stood a castle; that castle immediately gave assurance of safety to the counts. They plundered there about five thousand animals. They also found much varied food there, and the entire army of Christ was refreshed by its freely available abundance. [Col. 1133C] The inhabitants of the castle also gave the army horses, purest gold, and much money; and they swore that henceforth they would in no way harm the pilgrims or subsequently deny them a market. They stayed there five days.

Then, departing thence, they arrived at a certain castle of Arabs. The lord of the castle immediately came out to speak with them and negotiate peace. Once peace acceptable to both sides had been made, they moved to another city, most beautiful in walls and rich in every good, situated in a valley and named Cephalia. The citizens of that city, terrified at the arrival of the Franks, left the city in fear; [Col. 1133D] frightened, they abandoned gardens full of vegetables and houses filled with food and wealth, and fled heedlessly. Having gladly taken possession of all these things, the Franks moved on the third day. They crossed in descent a high and immense mountain range and again came down into a fertile valley, where they rested twelve days.

Not far from the valley was a castle full of Saracens, which the Christians strove vigorously to take by assault; and indeed they would have conquered it had not the Gentiles driven out herds of animals, beasts of burden, and cattle. The Christians plundered these and thus rested that night away from the castle. They returned to their tents, leading with them the animals which the garrison had released. At dawn the Franks, having gathered their tents, returned to the same castle, [Col. 1134A] thinking to pitch their camp there. But the pagan people, exceedingly terrified, withdrew by night and left the castle empty of men. Entering hastily, the Christians found it, though deserted by people, nevertheless full of every consoling abundance: there was no lack of wheat, wine, flour, barley, or oil. If anyone remained needy there, the misfortune of poverty was produced for him by the misfortune of idleness.

There they devoutly celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary on the second day of February. Envoys of the king of the city of Camela came there to the counts. The king of that city sent the counts abundant gifts and made peace with them. He also said that he would never harm Christians, but rather would love and honor them, provided only that the Christian people rendered him like treatment.

The king of Tripoli sent his envoys quickly to the counts, bringing them ten horses, four mules, and an immense weight of gold. Having offered these, the envoys added: “The king of Tripoli sends these words: namely, that you may have peace and friendship with him, and love him in truth just as he loves you.” The counts neither made peace with him nor accepted the gifts; rather, they confidently replied: “We reject all these things from you, until you strive to become a Christian.”

Leaving that excellent valley, they came on the day before the Ides of February to a certain castle called Arqa, beside which they set their camp. That town was fortified by an innumerable multitude of pagans and throngs of Arabs and Publicans. [Col. 1134C] They defended themselves bravely.

Fourteen Christian knights went toward Tripoli, which was not far from the army. They found sixty Turks leading before them many people—Saracens, Turks, and Arabs, about fifteen hundred in all—and many animals. The Christians fiercely attacked them, killed six of them, took as many horses, put the others to flight, and carried off the animals. For the unconquerable fierceness of the Franks terrified all, both those nearby and those far off. God worked in them in such a way that even now fourteen overcame sixty and routed the remaining multitude, snatching the animals from their very jaws.

From the army of Count Saint-Gilles, Raymond Pilet and Viscount Raymond set out; and with not many knights they ranged before the city of Tortosa, where there was a considerable multitude of pagans. When it had become late, they withdrew secretly to a place and, having kindled fires in several suitable positions, spent the night there as though the whole army had arrived. When the sun had risen, the Franks assembled to attack the city; finding it empty, they occupied it, while the castle remained under siege. There was another city not far from this one, called Maraclea. The admiral who governed it made an agreement with the Christians and brought Frankish banners into it.

Meanwhile Duke Godfrey, the count of Flanders, and Bohemond came as far as the city of Lichia. [Col. 1135A] Bohemond again separated from them and returned to Antioch, which he greatly desired to be his own. The duke and the count besieged a city called Gibellum.

Count Raymond heard that the Gentiles were coming with great bodies of fighting men and were preparing an unequivocal battle against the Christians. He therefore sent to his companions besieging Gibellum, saying: “A certain battle threatens us, and troops of pagans are gathering against us. Therefore make peace with the city you are besieging; come more swiftly to protect your brothers. It is better for us to gather and fight than to be separated from one another and defeated. Battles take little time, but victory brings the greatest gain; sieges consume much time, and besieged towns are scarcely subdued. Wars will bring nations and kingdoms under our rule; enemies subdued by war will vanish like smoke; when battle is completed and the foe conquered, a vast dominion will lie open to us. It is therefore good that we join together, because if we can deserve to have God as leader and guide, we shall without doubt immediately triumph over our enemies. Hasten, I say, lest our adversaries find us unprepared when they arrive.”

The duke and count gladly heard the embassy, for they hungered eagerly for battle. They made peace with the admiral of Gibellum and, having received from him gifts—gold, mules, and other things agreeable under the agreement—they left the city and departed to aid their brethren; but they did not then find the Turks whom they expected. Thus, disappointed of the battle [Col. 1135C] they desired, their desire for fighting was disappointed that day. They lodged beyond the river and besieged that castle from that side.

Not long afterward certain Christians rode to Tripoli, seeking to do what harm they could to those Gentiles. They found those people drawn out beyond the city—the Arabs, the Tripolitans themselves, and the Turks—likewise awaiting the Christians’ raid and lurking as though in ambush. Then each side fiercely attacked the other. The Hagarites withstood their first assaults for a while and struggled for some time. At last, when struck, they turned their backs; and in that retreat they lost many of their own. Many of the more noble citizens also fell there.

Women, mothers, and virgins, watching from the battlements, called down evils upon the Christians, grieved and groaned for their own; and yet perhaps some of them in their hearts applauded the courage of the Franks. So great was the slaughter of pagans and the shedding of blood that day that the river washing the city seemed to have reddened; and the citizens’ cisterns, situated within the city, which that river supplied, were fouled with that blood. The greatest grief and mourning therefore descended upon the Tripolitans, both for their leading men who had been slaughtered and for their cisterns polluted by the vile inrush of blood. Stricken by two disasters in one day, they shed double tears: they were distressed that the Franks had unexpectedly gained the trophy of victory, and grieved at the bloody defilement of their cisterns, which [Col. 1136A] they valued highly. The Tripolitans were terrified to the point of collapse and, besieged thereafter without a siege, did not dare to leave the city gate. Their neighbors suffered the same misfortunes. Rejoicing in the victory they had won, the Franks returned to their own, singing hymns to God.

On the following day knights from the army rode beyond the valley of Desem to plunder the land. Finding oxen and asses, sheep and camels, numbering nearly three thousand, they returned joyfully to the camp laden with such great booty. They remained before that castle, because it was very difficult to take, for three months and one day. They also celebrated Easter there, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

The Christian ships of which we spoke at first had put into a fairly safe harbor [Col. 1136B] near the castle. They supplied that army with wheat and wine, cheese and oil, beans and bacon, and a market of every abundance. For this reason they had encamped there so long: shipping sustained them, and they often went out to plunder the rich country. They went out, I say, and because they were in no way disappointed of their purpose, they returned more joyfully and were strongly spurred to range out again.

Many Christians were also killed there, for Saracen swords were not always blunt; their soldiery was not always inactive, nor their hands powerless. They killed Anselm of Rabamont and William the Picard, men of high birth and skilled in warfare, whose illustrious deeds were plainly known in that army of Christ. Many others fell also, whose names may He preserve in the memorial of life; for we cannot recount everything about everyone.

The king of Tripoli frequently addressed the Christian leaders through envoys, testing their minds in every way, so that, after giving him gifts, they might make peace with him, abandon the castle, and accept the agreed payments. The Christians set before him the matter of Christianity and could not otherwise be turned from their purpose. That king resisted Christianity greatly, because he feared and reverenced the laws of his fathers and the customs of his ancestors.

As time advanced, the new crops had turned white, because that region is heated by greater warmth than lands on this side of the mountains; and therefore an earlier [Col. 1136D] summer ripens earlier harvests. In the middle of March fresh beans were gathered; on the Ides of April wheat was cut, and the autumn of the vintage returned.

The Norman duke, the count of Flanders, the count of Toulouse, and Tancred then spoke concerning the road to be completed, because the favorable season was already pressing on, indeed had almost passed. Therefore, abandoning the castle which they had long besieged, they came to Tripoli and made an agreement with the Tripolitans. The king gave them fifteen thousand bezants and fifteen horses of great value, and restored three hundred pilgrims whom he had long held captive. Finally, under the pretext of peace, he provided them with a market, by which all were refreshed; and he firmly pledged that, if they could at any time overcome the war which the admiral of Babylon was preparing against them, he himself would become a Christian and hold his land in their fealty.

They therefore departed from the city in the middle of May. They had to go on, and they traveled all day by a narrow, steep, and trackless road; in the evening they reached a castle called Bethoron. Then they approached a city situated on the seashore, called Zebaris. There, because of a shortage of water, they endured the severe distress of excessive thirst. Greatly weakened by it, they made their way to the river Braim; there both men and beasts of burden were refreshed with drink.

On the day of the Lord’s Ascension they had to proceed by a narrow road. There they feared an attack by the Gentiles throughout the day; yet, though fearful, [Col. 1137B] they did not cease advancing. Standard-bearers and armed knights went before and guarded the whole army against ambushers. Those responsible for baggage followed, and helpers of the pack-animal drivers. Behind, the military order hastened along, and all attended to the needs of all. Thus every day the baggage-carriers moved along in the middle, and the masses of unarmed people accompanied them. Trumpets sounded, and they proceeded by stages along the road so that the weaker might not fail. They kept watch by turns at night; and where greater fear threatened, there a more vigilant watch was prepared.

They allowed nothing to be done rashly or disorderly. The undisciplined were punished, the ignorant instructed, the rebellious rebuked, the incontinent reproved for their lack of self-restraint, and all alike were urged to almsgiving. All also cultivated moderation and chastity; and, so to speak, there was a kind of school of moral discipline in the camp. Such was the order and pattern of those journeying to Jerusalem. So long as they maintained this rigor of discipline and abounded in charitable affection, God was visibly present among them and fought His wars through them. We have said this in order that, by praising those men, we might rebuke the life and conduct of those undisciplined persons who later succeeded to this glorious expedition in arrogance. For among human beings nothing is more useful than discipline.

Having crossed those mountains, in which enemies were feared, without encountering an enemy, they came to a city beside the sea, [Col. 1137D] called Baruch; from there to another called Sagitta; then to another called Sur; from Sur to Acre; from Acre to the castle called Cayphas; and from there they came to lodge near Caesarea, where on the day of Pentecost, the fourth day before the Kalends of June, they rested. When that day had been solemnly completed according to Christian custom, they gathered their tents and, having again traversed the journey that lay before them, arrived at the city called Ramla. There they halted, weary from the road. The citizens of that city, respecting their arrival because they had not dared to fight the Christians in that district, left the city empty and escaped in flight.

Beside this small city was shown an honorable church in which the most precious body of the blessed martyr George had rested, because, having been held there by pagans, that blessed champion completed his blood-soaked course. In former times this place had had a bishop; but now, subjected to paganism and having lost the dignity of a pontiff, it was ingloriously placed beneath the proud domination of the Saracens. The Christians groaned, drawn solely by love for unconquered George. For they wished always to deserve him as companion and defender, since they had heard and seen him in the battle of Antioch as their leader and forerunner, fighting against the erring people; indeed, the Gentiles commonly say that he is always hostile to them. They saw the walls of the church adorned with buildings, yet deserted by people. They therefore restored its former dignity to the desolate city and placed over it an elected bishop. For they trusted in the Lord [Col. 1138B] that the region would be subjected to them, and therefore strove to restore the fullness of Christianity.

But because the restored bishop did not yet possess estates from which he could live—for all the lands of that church were producing briars—the Christians offered him tithes of their resources. With these generous contributions gathered, the aforesaid pontiff could live and restore the church. They also exhorted him to preserve the purity of faith and to summon the people to the Catholic faith. They urged him to endure calmly the desolation of that impoverished land, because He who long ago became poor in order to restore Christians, having nowhere to lay His head, when invoked would, as One who does not refuse prayer, work effectively with him [Col. 1138C]. For he should know that He had said to His fellow workers: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

After arranging these matters at Ramla, they decided at dawn that the journey to Jerusalem should be hastened. The signal having been given, they set out upon the road; and, as they had long desired, that day they reached the city itself. Jerusalem is not far from Ramla, but about twenty-four miles away. On the night before they came to Jerusalem, no night, I think, was more burdensome or tedious to them on the journey. It was a kind of aggravation of their long-established hunger. For when food is shown to a hungry man on the day before yesterday, yet not offered to him, with what desire, think you, is he stirred anew, as though by a fresh hunger? So those who had taken the road to Jerusalem and had endured so many unseasonable nights on its account—when they knew that they would be there on the next day—how great an impediment do you suppose that lingering night imposed upon them? Other nights had brought them cold, fear, or battles; this night, which was more grievous, inflamed desire by postponing it. They scarcely believed that the day would come, though they knew that it would come—the day that would satisfy their prayers and show them the city they desired.

That morning was awaited, and they knew it would soon dawn; but because it seemed to be delayed, their deferred longing increased. For to a desiring mind, nothing comes quickly enough. Day dawned, and the tireless people of God climbed the mountains lying before them. They went [Col. 1139A] joyfully, because that day was to bring an end to the labors of years. It was a desirable day, like the last day of a hired laborer. But when they reached the place from which they could behold Jerusalem itself, crowned with towers, who could worthily recount how many tears they shed? Who could fittingly express their feelings? Joy wrung sighs from them, and immeasurable gladness produced sobs. At the sight of Jerusalem all halted and worshiped; bending the knee, they kissed the holy ground. All would have walked barefoot, had fear of the enemy not commanded them to go armed. They went and wept; and those who had assembled to pray hastened first to fight, bearing arms.

They wept over that city over which Christ Himself had wept; [Col. 1139B] and, wonderfully, they besieged on Tuesday, the eighth day before the Ides of June, the city over which they wept. They besieged it, I say, not as stepsons besiege a stepmother, but as sons besiege a mother. They besieged it not with that siege of which the Lord had said: “Behold, days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you, and hem you in, and your children who are within you” (Luke 19). Now, on the contrary, friends surrounded it, and its children hemmed in the strangers and adulterous intruders. For behold, it had no children within it to rule in concern for it; rather, it endured alien and foreign masters, lawless and impure men, who tyrannized over it in captivity beneath an oppressive yoke. They therefore besieged it not in order to capture it while free, but to free it while captive.

Robert, duke of the Normans, besieged it from the north, beside the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, where he fell asleep in the Lord after being stoned by the Jews; next to him the count of Flanders pitched his tents. From the west Duke Godfrey and Tancred besieged it; from the south the count of Saint-Gilles besieged it—namely, on Mount Sion, near the church of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, where the Lord Jesus supped with his disciples. Thus Jerusalem, besieged by her own children, was shut in; within, however, she was profaned by the Muslim peoples.

On the third day some Christian knights went out from the camp—Raymond Pilet, Raymond of Taurina, and several others—either to survey the country or to plunder. They overcame and put to flight two hundred Arabs whom they encountered; [Col. 1139D] they killed many, and seized thirty horses there. Having done this, they returned cheerfully to their own side. On Monday they vigorously attacked the city and, as they believed, would indeed then have prevailed, had they prepared ladders in sufficient number. Yet they demolished the outer wall and brought one raised ladder against the inner wall. Christian knights ascended it in turns; they fought hand-to-hand upon the wall with the Saracens, striking them with swords and lances. In that engagement many from both peoples were killed, though more of the gentiles perished. When the trumpet sounded the recall, the Christians at last abandoned that assault and returned to camp.

Meanwhile the provisions they had brought with them failed; bread was no longer to be found for purchase [Col. 1140A], nor could they go out to gather grain. For that country is wholly without irrigation—indeed, scorching and exceedingly dry—and therefore ill suited to beasts of burden and animals, being poor in pasture; nor is the land wooded, and consequently it is less fruitful, except that it produces palm and olive; it also bears vines. The Jordan, they suppose, is separated from Jerusalem by nearly thirty stadia; it has lakes, but they are distant. The city has its own cisterns from which it is supplied. At the foot of Mount Sion is the spring of Siloam, but it could scarcely sustain a few people; nevertheless it helped, and a little water was purchased at great cost. They led their horses to drink, not without extreme fear, for six miles.

Meanwhile word was announced in camp that Christian cargo ships had arrived in the port of Jaffa, which we believe was called Joppa by its ancient name [Col. 1140B]; this greatly pleased everyone in the camp. The leaders considered how they might make safe the journey there and back for those carrying necessities from the ships, for Joppa or Jaffa is about eight miles from Ramla. The people of Ascalon, or native inhabitants, wandering in the mountains or in the cuttings and steep ravines, sometimes attacked and slaughtered travellers. This disturbance, or report, interrupted the passage of merchants’ supplies.

To carry this out, at first light Raymond Pilet, Acard of Montmerle, William of Sabra, certain knights, and some foot soldiers went out from the army of the count of Saint-Gilles and proceeded toward the sea. Trusting in their courage, they advanced in arms toward the port. [Col. 1140C] We do not know whether through strategy, through delay while lingering behind, or through ignorance of the road, they became divided from one another. Thirty knights, taking another route, were separated from the others. These thirty encountered one hundred Arabs, some Turks and Saracens from the army of the admiral, and boldly attacked them; battle was joined. But their opponents stubbornly resisted and, trusting in their numbers, the many surrounded the few; for this is the Saracens’ manner of fighting. They had now enclosed the Christians and, chattering confidently about their deaths, expected victory, when a messenger, shouting to Raymond Pilet, roused him thus:

> “Unless you fly with utmost speed to your fellow soldiers to bring them aid, you have certainly lost them all. They are already surrounded by enemies, though [Col. 1140D] they still defend themselves somehow.”

They gave their horses rein and drove the chargers with bronze spurs; swifter than speech, they all flew to them. With shields held before their breasts, they drove back the throngs with spears, scattered those who opposed them, and each man struck down his adversary to the ground. They fell suddenly upon foes unaware of them and committed the entire matter to the sword. Thus they gained the advantage. The enemy twice re-formed their ranks and thought they could resist, but accomplished nothing. The Franks again fell upon them fiercely and thus freed their own men from that assault, except that they lost Acard of Montmerle, a most daring knight, and several foot soldiers. The Turks therefore turned their backs and hastened into flight; but many were pierced by the pursuing spears. [Col. 1141A] The Christians pursued them for nearly four miles. They also captured one hundred and three horses and one man alive, who, under compulsion, set out in order everything that was being prepared against the Christians.

Meanwhile, during the siege of Jerusalem, a violent thirst raged and pressed hard upon the Christian camp. They used to sew together fresh hides of oxen, buffaloes, and horses; made into sewn skins, these carried water for six miles. They led their horses there to water them, but the gentiles lay in ambush for them and grievously harassed them from the narrowness of the terrain. Yet the water which they conveyed as though rescued from disaster was so foul-smelling that even the horses rejected it: when they smelled it, they wrinkled and contracted their nostrils and sneezed from the nausea of disgust. This suffering was exhausting, [Col. 1141B] for people can endure hunger longer than thirst. If any signs of springs were found, either the gentiles had blocked them and diverted their flow elsewhere, or lurking bandits waiting to do harm guarded them. The Kidron and other streams had dried up in the burning heat. Barley bread in camp was costly. The natives, hiding in caves and caverns, had removed all provisions. Thus the Christian army was endangered day after day by such great distress.

The appointed leaders assembled for counsel and discussed what must be done amid such calamities. They said:

> “Distress is on every side: bread has failed; water is lacking. We ourselves are grievously besieged while we think that we are besieging this city. We scarcely dare leave the camp, [Col. 1141C] and then return empty-handed. By our long delay we have incurred this scarcity, and unless we take precautions we shall incur a worse one. By arms and bodily strength, without engines, we cannot storm this city. The walls stand in our way, the ramparts stand in our way, the towers stand in our way; the hostile defenders within, who abound, stand in our way. What then, conscript fathers, do you advise? Let us have pity on this people and at last undertake something beneficial to us all, harmful to the citizens shut within, and freeing us from these labours.
>
> “Yet the gravest difficulty is that such undertakings require materials. This land is not wooded; if we could find trees anywhere, we would certainly strive to make engines capable of overlooking these walls [Col. 1141D] and equalling the height of the loftier towers. Let us therefore seek beams from houses, or carry off timbers from churches, or construct compact engines from any other material, and attack this city with all our strength; otherwise we waste our time in vain.”

At last they found timber, though at a great distance from the place, and brought it with great labour. Carpenters were summoned from the whole army, by whose skill the engines might be constructed. They now applied themselves urgently to the task: some dressed the rough surface of the timber, others hewed it, others bored it, others joined timber to timber; and in a short time they raised the engines. Duke Godfrey was constructing one at his own expense, and the count of Toulouse had likewise ordered another to be erected at his expense. [Col. 1142A] The craftsmen worked diligently at these tasks.

No less tirelessly, the Hagarenes concerned themselves with fortifying the city; by night they laboured to raise the towers higher and busied themselves without rest in defending the city. Meanwhile, the more discerning men explored which part of the city was less strongly defended. On a certain Saturday, in the depth of night, they moved Duke Godfrey’s engine there; at sunrise they raised it on the eastern side. On the first, second, and third weekdays thereafter they prepared and fitted it together with all diligence. The count of Saint-Gilles raised his engine on the southern side. Because of their great protection, these engines may be called wooden fortresses.

The count moved his fortress close to the wall, but between the wall and the fortress there lay a deep [Col. 1142B] precipice, wholly impassable for the approaching tower. Such engines cannot be led down into sloping ground or directed against mountainous places; to be moved, they always require level ground. Therefore heralds proclaimed through the army that “whoever throws three stones into that ditch shall receive one denarius for the stones thrown.” Everyone to whom these delays had become tiresome—for one could scarcely find a little water to refresh the tongue for a denarius—either gladly laboured to carry stones or eagerly desired to assault the city.

Before attacking the city, bishops and priests clothed in priestly vestments addressed the people. One, standing in an elevated place, began as follows:

> “Hear, [Col. 1142C] brothers and lords. Although you yourselves know everything we are about to say to you now—for you have heard these things many times already—yet it is most beautiful, sweet, and delightful always to speak concerning the Lord our God; and you must continually hear and understand effectively.
>
> “In this city before you Christ redeemed you; here God established Christianity; from here the sacrament of Christianity flowed even to us. We have come from our own lands in order to pray here and kiss the tomb of our God. This city which you see is the entire cause of our labour. Yet this Jerusalem is an image of the heavenly Jerusalem. It is the form of that city for which we long.
>
> “Do you see with what obstinacy [Col. 1142D] men who are base, foolish, and so utterly foreign dispute it with us? Do you see with what stupidity those who have no right to it contend that what ought to be ours belongs to them? Finally, you know with what rashness they pollute God’s sanctuary and to what countless abominations they have subjected the holy city.
>
> “Certainly, if you will consider rightly and carefully, this Jerusalem which you see, to which you have come, in which you are present, both prefigures and points toward that heavenly city. Behold, visible enemies dispute this one with us; but invisible enemies besiege the paths leading to the other, against whom spiritual conflict must be waged. It is harder for us to struggle against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places than against the flesh and blood that we see. Those who snarl in that little city are the shadow [Col. 1143A] of those others and are inferior and weaker than their masters. If these men, who are almost nothing, can conquer and take from us the city we see, what, think you, will their lords do—‘when servants dare such things’? Certainly we should fear that the heavenly city may be shut against us and taken away from us, if, through our sloth, our house is abandoned to malignant guests.
>
> “We shall be wholly unwarlike and ineffective in spiritual combat if we do not rise against foolish dogs that cannot bark strongly, effeminate and unarmed men, fearful of every death. Wake up, therefore, household of Christ; wake up, ready-equipped knights and foot soldiers. Steadfastly seize this city, truly our commonwealth; and attend to Christ, who even today is outlawed and crucified in this city. [Col. 1143B] With Joseph, take him down from the cross for yourselves; place that incomparable treasure, that desirable treasure, in the tomb of your hearts; and manfully wrest him from these impious crucifiers.
>
> “For as often as these evil judges, accomplices of Herod and Pilate, mock or force your brothers into service, so often they crucify Christ; as often as they torture and kill them, so often they thrust Longinus’ lance into Christ’s side. They indeed do all these things; and what is worse, they scoff at and reproach Christ himself and our law, and provoke us with reckless speech. What then are you doing? Is it right for you to hear these things, to see them, and not groan? I speak to fathers, sons, brothers, and grandsons: if an outsider struck one of you, would you not [Col. 1143C] avenge your blood? How much more ought you to avenge your God, your Father, your brother, whom you see reproached, outlawed, crucified; whom you hear crying, desolate, and asking for help: ‘I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the nations there was no man with me’ (Isa. 63:3).
>
> “Act, therefore, and confidently fit your weapons to yourselves. Steadfastly attack this city as God’s fellow-workers, and let it be beautiful for you to die for Christ in this land, for those for whom Christ died in this city. You begin the war; he, your leader, will furnish the resources of battle and the reward of good will and glorious action.”

The heroic speaker had ended, and all, now girded with arms, attacked the city unanimously. Each now spoke to himself; each was his own priest and bishop. Thus on Wednesday and Thursday they pressed the city by night and by day. Having first undertaken prayers and fasts, sighs and almsgiving, and fortified themselves by communion in the sacred viaticum, they attacked the city at first light on Friday, but could not prevail. Those on the towers or walls helped one another and continually hurled fire and stones. The count of Toulouse, after filling the ditch—for only after three days and nights had he scarcely completed it—brought his tower to the wall and was angered at the delay suffered by his men.

But at the hour when the Lord suffered according to the will of the Jews, the Christians, mindful of that passion, as though their strength had been newly renewed [Col. 1144A] and a new boldness had come upon them, fought bravely with all their might—Duke Godfrey and his brother Eustace leading, and the others following those leaders. Then a knight named Letaldus climbed the wall and, fighting steadfastly, cried out. Others immediately followed him. Those who had defended the walls until then fled in all directions and no longer concerned themselves with protecting the city. The multitude of Christians, entering the city, pursued the fugitives and spared no one.

The admiral, who commanded the Tower of David, terrified, surrendered himself to the count and immediately opened for him the gate at which pilgrims had been violently squeezed for their money in order to enter; there they customarily paid tolls, [Col. 1144B] otherwise they were mercilessly restrained at the gate. Citizens fleeing to Solomon’s Temple gathered there and still dared to defend themselves within it. They launched fierce attacks upon the Christians there, but when they saw that they were accomplishing nothing, they threw down their swords and submitted their necks to death. No one knows the number of those killed; but their blood, flowing through the Temple, reached to the calves of those walking there, and there were great heaps of corpses throughout the city. For the Christians spared neither age nor sex nor rank nor any condition, pursuing them with such hatred because they had appropriated for unlawful uses and disgracefully defiled the Temple of the Lord, the church of the Holy Sepulchre, Solomon’s Temple, and other churches. [Col. 1144C]

Some had fled onto Solomon’s Temple. Having asked for and received Tancred’s banner, that they might at least thus be saved, they waited for whatever fate came; yet they gained little or nothing, for the Christians did not spare even them. Except that they kept alive for a time certain persons to carry out the dead, and afterward either sold them or removed them from the light above. Tancred was nevertheless greatly saddened by this; yet he did not rage against the Christians on that account. He therefore remained silent and wholly restrained himself from that disturbance. The count of Toulouse ordered the admiral, who had entrusted himself to him and surrendered the citadel of David, and the others with him, to be conducted unharmed as far as Ascalon. He had made such an agreement with them and wished to preserve his compact inviolate. [Col. 1144D]

They did not plunder or burn that city in the manner of a subjugated city; rather, finding its houses filled with every good, they reserved them as property for their own households, and many generously shared what they had found with the poorer people. Now rejoicing in the long-desired triumph, their hands washed from slaughter, many barefoot, joyful and weeping for joy, hurried in bands to kiss the Sepulchre of the Saviour; there they offered joyful gifts and peace-offerings. Who could now adequately explain that joy? Let each person rather reflect within himself and consider how great it must have been, than accuse me, a barren and word-poor interpreter. I therefore leave each one to himself, so that no one may rise against me even on this account. For the joy was immense, when all had attained what they had long awaited. There they saw the end of their labour; and now, more secure, from present things they imagined that rewards of future goods would come to them.

They arranged for the removal of the corpses, because horror and an utterly monstrous stench were growing strong. They assigned this work to living gentiles; and, because these were insufficient, they again entrusted the same task to poor Christians for payment. Later they piled the bodies upon pyres and burned them, thus cleansing the city of its filth. They remained in the city, giving worthy thanks to God, the prosperer of their journey and labour and the mighty victor over the faithless gentiles. [Col. 1145B] They ascribed this victory not to their own strength, but attributed the whole to God, who had worked in them both the willing and the ability. They also restored the churches to their dignities and fitted each for the work of prayer. In each they poured out tears and fulfilled their vows all day with the incense of contrition. They observed those days as solemn ones and, as it were, kept sabbath, celebrating the feast-days of a certain Jubilee. They established as a festival the day on which they recovered the city: the fifteenth day of July, Friday. All who rejoice and applaud at the liberation of that city and the victory of the Christian people rightly love that triumphal day.

They also deliberated concerning the establishment of a king there, and the leading men spoke among themselves as follows:

> “We give thanks to our Lord, illustrious nobles, who has given glory to his name and granted victory to us his servants. You see, our magnates, to what harbour of rest God has brought the public cause of our journey; you see in what condition he has placed the summit of our common desire. Why should we recapitulate each thing that he has done through us, or we through him? Behold, the time approaches when some of us, our long-desired purpose now fulfilled, will think of returning home. But before this holy assembly is dissolved, we must provide to whom the government of this city is to be entrusted: to whom the people who [Col. 1145D] remain here may look, and who, as a wise guardian, may devote care to their protection. What profit is it that we have obtained this city at the cost of a thousand deaths, if—God forbid!—we should happen not to preserve it? Why did we come here from the ends of the earth? Why did we endure so many and such great labours, hastening toward another quarter of the sun, if at last we return while the city is left without counsel? Let us first take counsel for the city, so that afterward those who are to return may more freely take counsel for themselves.
>
> “This city from ancient times possessed royal dignity and at the same time held patriarchal eminence. For, passing over Melchizedek, Abraham’s contemporary, if we come to more recent times and trace the genealogy and line of kings from David to Josiah and from the Babylonian deportation, we shall seem to have woven a sufficiently long tale; yet we shall have proved that this city had kings. Moreover, we do not doubt that James, the brother of the Lord, presided here as bishop. Therefore we judge it worthy of apostolic dignity; modern Christianity has applied its title of dignity to a patriarch. [Col. 1146A]
>
> “Let us therefore consider a man who suitably excels in royal virtue: who presents himself as God’s servant with respect to God, and knows himself to be king with respect to men; who loves God’s worship, cherishes the people, and commands the army. For this monarchy, adjacent to the Saracens, cannot be defended without soldiers. We say the same concerning a patriarch, since these two necessities must be provided for. The kingdom needs the priesthood; the priesthood must be sustained and protected by the kingdom.
>
> “Since you know that each of these matters is most necessary, and other business remains for us to consider, let us omit words and come to action. Let us choose Duke Godfrey and appoint him over this city. Many qualities meet in him which belong to royal dignity. As we all know, he is a man of royal blood, descended from forefathers professing Christianity, skilled in warfare according to Frankish custom, and most effective in military affairs in heart and arm. Therefore, in every respect he has been singularly approved in this expedition. Serenity especially shines in him; clemency flourishes in him—twin sisters especially becoming to rulers. He uniquely loves generosity, because he has lavishly expended his whole patrimony and everything he possessed upon this army, [Col. 1146C] or rather has wisely invested it in God’s service. He will be an enemy to the gentiles and a brave protector to Christians. Finally, to use another’s words and briefly contain the fullness of a fitting ruler: he is one who knows ‘to spare the subjected and to subdue the proud.’
>
> “Let us therefore now address him with the divine oracle and command him with authoritative injunction: ‘Hear, O son, and see, and forget thy people and thy father’s house; and come into the land which I shall show thee, and I will make thee into a great nation’ (Ps. 44:12). He has brothers; he has kinsmen, acquaintances, and relatives; he has beneath him many knights, all of whom will freely remain with him and wage God’s wars with him.
>
> “But you, most excellent prince, whom God has today chosen as king, be a soldier of God and fight the battles of the Lord: we lay this charge upon you from God.”

And laying hands upon him they took hold of him, saying:

> “Behold, after God we appoint you king. May the Lord be with you, direct your actions, increase for good the pre-eminence of your character, and afflict his enemies in your hands.”

They said the same concerning the patriarch, for he would be most necessary both to God’s people and to the king. “At present no better person occurs to us for election than Lord Arnulf, a man very highly educated in the liberal arts. Let us approach him and appoint him deputy over this charge, until by deliberative counsel we decree that either he or another is to be enthroned. For we know [Col. 1147A] that he excels in the strictness of justice and is powerful in eloquence; moreover, very many qualities suitable to a bishop concur in him. But because we cannot establish this decision at present—for we hasten to other matters—we judge that the matter of whoever is to be enthroned should be deferred. Except that we name Lord Arnulf to fulfill the bishop’s duties and meanwhile answer with a shepherd’s voice. He himself may be enthroned the day after tomorrow, if perhaps he consents to those who ask him; or however the matter ought to turn out, it shall be deliberated. For behold, swearing and lamenting, he resists most firmly lest he himself become pontiff; yet at least he will assist by giving counsel. For the present let the episcopacy be exercised by counsel, until he whom God provides as suitable may exercise it by office.”

On the eighth day after the city had been captured, the duke was elected king.

Meanwhile messengers came to Tancred and Count Eustace, telling them to proceed quickly to receive the city of Neapolis; for the inhabitants of that city wished to surrender themselves into their hands. Taking attendants and many retainers, they came to the city, which immediately made peace with and surrendered to them. They remained there and rested joyfully until the duke—indeed, the king—sent swift messengers to them, saying:

> “We have heard, and it is certain, that the Babylonian admiral is at Ascalon and is preparing a great war there against us. Hasten, therefore, and come, so that we may boldly meet them before they can [Col. 1147C] shut us up in the city. Once enclosed, we could not fight them on equal terms. For those shut in have difficult exit and entry, and unsuitable fear often troubles them. But if we meet on an open field, with God as guide, the outcome will be freer and easier for us. We are indeed readier than they in arms and strength. We wish to meet them where they still expect nothing to fear.”

Leaving the city, they immediately ranged through the mountains, seeking whether they might perhaps find Saracens anywhere whom they could harm in any manner. They came near the sea to the city of Ramla and found many Arabs going in advance of the admiral’s army. Attacking them with all confidence of spirit, without delay they scattered them; after killing some, [Col. 1147D] they kept others alive so that they might report news to them, inform them concerning the admiral and his army, and enable them, once they had heard, to take more careful precautions. They examined every detail exactly: who they were, how countless a people they were, what they were preparing, and in what place they meant to gain the advantage. The captives explained these things in full, having bargained for their lives.

Tancred spoke thus by messengers to the king and leaders:

> “Know beyond doubt that war is prepared against us at Ascalon, and that almost the whole world has assembled and conspired, believing that they will violently crush and subjugate us. Come, therefore, and, gathering all your strength, ‘let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us’ [Col. 1148A] (Ps. 2:3). If, as you have ordered, we meet them fearlessly, we shall for that very reason prevail over them much more easily. They assemble to besiege us and bring their engines to storm the city; let us rise against them unexpectedly. For once they see events proceeding beyond their expectation, they will be astounded and wither away; then they will flee wherever they can. But we shall drive our swords hilt-deep into their vitals and triumph victoriously over them.”

The king proclaimed through a herald that all should prepare themselves for the war of which they had been warned and should eagerly follow the king’s banner.

> “For our enemies,” he said, “are all gathering at Ascalon to come into battle against us. Therefore all go forth to meet them, and let no one remain behind except the infirm.”

Thus on Tuesday the king, the appointed patriarch, the count of Flanders, and the bishop of Martirano left the city. The count of Saint-Gilles and Robert, duke of the Normans, refused to depart until they should be more certain of the admiral’s attack. “Why,” they said, “should we tire ourselves in vain? Let us first ascertain the matter; then we shall go out with greater confidence.” Yet they sent scouts from among their own men, knights who would report certain news, so that they too might believe the report without hesitation. Having seen all that was being prepared, these returned at a rapid gallop and faithfully testified to what they had seen.

The king also, not fully trusting their message, sent the bishop of Martirano to Jerusalem to testify before the leaders concerning all that was being prepared. [Col. 1148C] He would hasten the matter more effectively, having seen these things with his own eyes and having left the king’s side that same day. The bishop of Martirano, as he was carrying the counts’ stated words to the patriarch and king—for he had already spoken with the count of Toulouse and the Norman—fell into the hands of pagans. It is uncertain whether he was carried away or killed, but afterward he did not appear. The count of Toulouse and the Norman, with many others, went out to war and left Jerusalem on Wednesday.

The clergy, the small number of weak people who remained in the city, Peter the Hermit, and the unwarlike multitude of women conducted processions from church to church, intent upon prayer and fasting, that God might show favour to his people, utterly overthrow their enemies before them with a strong hand, [Col. 1148D] and bring them back defended from their enemies with the joy of safety and triumph. The clergy, as has been said, devoted themselves to masses and other prayers.

The leaders then assembled with their armies at the river opposite Ascalon. There, finding abundant herds, they were enriched by rich booty, and all who were in need were refreshed. Three hundred Arabs came pursuing the Franks. The Christians rushed against them and, capturing two of them, drove the rest in flight as far as their army. No longer was the report of battle uncertain: what doubtful rumour ordinarily conveys ambiguously to the ears, the certain reality itself showed to the eyes of all, [Col. 1149A] once they had seen one another beyond doubt. After that attack the Christians returned to camp and rested that night—unless rather all devoted themselves to watches and prayers.

In the evening the patriarch caused the following proclamation and prohibition to be made: that no Christian going out to battle on the following day should occupy himself with plundering spoils, lest he be less ready for battle and the very burdens of the spoils make victory harder for him; after the battle, once the enemy had been conquered, they should rejoice in rich spoil and burdens, and devote themselves to despoiling the defeated enemy.

The sun had risen over the earth, and the people of God were considering the coming battle. They entered a valley beside the seashore, lovely in its beautiful plain; there each arranged and drew up his forces in separate bodies. [Col. 1149B] The king carefully deployed his division; Robert, count of the Normans, his; the count of Toulouse, his; the count of Flanders and Gaston, theirs; Count Eustace, his; Tancred, his. Each of these arranged his archers and infantry; and, with these sent forward, they advanced slowly.

They were instructed how they should shout their battle-cries, how they should stand firm, how, by striking, they should pierce enemies deemed impenetrable; and how they should frequently look back to their standards, fearing nothing, and harden themselves to endure hostile blows—although they had learned all these things in other battles successfully fought.

No less, on the opposite side, the pagans massed in wedges, more numerous than the stars; and their countless legions stretched from side to side in battle-lines. They sent forward a certain people whom they called Ethiopians [Col. 1149C] and stationed them in one place, commanding them to remain immovable. With their knees fixed upon the ground, but with the right knee set back, protecting their upper bodies with small shields, they used arrows and swords. They had been ordered neither to retreat even for a moment nor to go beyond the place they occupied by so much as a step. Moreover, the military companies, arrayed as they had been, held their assigned positions.

Because they feared the excessive effects of thirst, owing to the heat, the dusty haze, the exertion, and the long duration of the fighting, they had hung little vessels full of water from their necks, so that, refreshed by them, they might either resist more steadily or pursue fugitives more tirelessly. Of their own flight, indeed, there had been no mention, since they already believed themselves victorious. For they trusted in their innumerable multitudes [Col. 1149D], in the spirited courage of their peoples, and in imperial commands that they should never flee. For it had been decreed: “Let those who flee be punished without fail by execution.”

When battle had been prepared on both sides, and they came to the place from which the Franks could now see the pagans somewhat more closely, we are told that the Christians paused briefly; raising their eyes to heaven and fixing their knees upon the ground, they prayed, for they hoped for help from heaven. When they had prayed briefly and the sign of the life-giving cross had reverently been applied to their foreheads, they rode forward with greater confidence. The pagans had now halted and waited motionless.

On the right wing by the sea rode the count of Toulouse. On the [Col. 1150A] left the king hastened with his contingents. In the middle, meanwhile, fought the Norman, the count of Flanders, Tancred, and others. But what is one against a hundred? What are ten against a thousand? Yet truly He who once caused this to be sung in the choir, “Saul struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand” (1 Kings 18:7), worked no differently on that day among the Christians.

The Christians, crying out in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, attacked them courageously. Robert, count of the Normans—behold, a man often to be named by his own name for this noble deed—saw from afar the standard-bearer of the emir, who had a golden apple at the top of his spear; the spear itself shone fittingly white, being covered with silver. Recognizing him, he charged boldly through the midst of the ranks against him and wounded him grievously [Col. 1150B] unto death. This struck no small fear into the pagans. The count of Flanders likewise attacked them fiercely. Tancred, undaunted, assailed them through the middle of their tents. The pagan soldiers immediately took to flight. The Ethiopians stood dumbfounded.

But the king and certain Franks turned against the Ethiopians and, lingering there for some time, cut them down with swords crosswise like grain in a field; severing their bodies, they hewed them in halves. The fields were sprinkled—rather, flooded—with blood, and everywhere were strewn the corpses of the pagans. The Christians pursued them as they fled, for the pagans, trembling through God’s power, had no opportunity to catch their breath and did not catch it in any manner.

For, if the pagans are to be believed, they themselves often reported afterwards that they were so stunned that, though their eyes were open, they could scarcely see the Christians, yet could do them no harm at all. They did not dare rise up against the Christians or, though many, bark back against the few. They fled, therefore: some climbed trees or rocks, wishing to escape death; others entered the hiding-places of caves for the same reason. The Christians pressed hard against them, forcing some over precipices, piercing others with daggers, cutting the throats of others; in general, they spared no one.

Thus a deadly day had fallen upon the pagans, a day on which not even one was granted an opportunity of escape—except those who could somehow get away. The count of Saint-Gilles, fighting by the sea, killed innumerable men and drove the fugitives toward [Col. 1150D] the city. But because the city was some distance away from them, those left behind exhausted either immediately fell when struck or threw themselves into the sea, and thus, headlong, rushed from death into death. To those whom the Franks could overtake in their running, no respite was granted.

The emir’s fleet covered the whole sea, and that people awaited the outcome of the battle. But, seeing that a fortune other than that which they had hoped for threatened their own side, they boarded their boats, set their sails obliquely to the wind, and so sailed back to their homeland. That day, therefore, was exceedingly adverse to those Babylonians. It was a day of tribulation and dispersal, a day of death and confusion. Yet those who could do so fled into the city.

They say that the emir, scarcely still breathing, groaned deeply and thus [Col. 1151A] lamented:

> “Creator of all things, what is this? What has happened? What hostile fate has harmed us? Alas for me! What unspeakable disgrace! What enduring reproach has befallen our people! A beggarly people, a small people, has prevailed against our people! Whence comes this? Having made an agreement, I brought here two hundred thousand soldiers, and foot-soldiers without number, whom I believed would prevail over the whole world. Yet now, lest I lie, they have been so disgracefully defeated by fewer than a thousand cavalry and thirty thousand infantry.
>
> “Either their God is almighty and fights for them, or ours is angry with us and rebukes and chastises us with excessively severe fury. Whatever the case may be, one thing shall follow: I shall not rise against them again, but rather shall return to my own land, dishonoured for as long as I live.”

Having said this, he lamented tearfully and mourned from the depths of his heart.

> “I swear,” he said, “by Mohammed and by all the divine powers of the gods, that hereafter I shall not retain soldiers under any agreement, [Col. 1151B] since I have been driven out by an alien and foreign people. I brought every kind of weapon and engine of war in order to besiege them in Jerusalem, and they forestalled me in battle two days’ journey away. Alas for me! What more can I say? I shall always be dishonoured in the land of Babylon.”

When the slaughter was finished, the Christians returned to plunder the tents of the Ishmaelites. There they found [Col. 1152A], to state it briefly, whatever valuable household goods can be imagined: silver, gold, provisions, flour, and oil; herds of countless animals; every display of ornaments; heaps of weapons; and whatever else could be better. Having plundered all these things, they returned joyfully to the holy city of Jerusalem and rendered worthy thanks to God in each of the churches.

Robert, count of the Normans, bought the emir’s standard from those who had retained it after the emir was wounded, for twenty marks of silver, and placed it in the Lord’s Sepulchre as a memorial of the memorable triumph. Another bought the same emir’s sword for sixty bezants. Thus indescribable joy arose throughout all Christendom.

Thus the Christians liberated Jerusalem from the hands of the impious Turks in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098 [Note: [Col. 1151B] Read: 1099.], and, with Christ as their leader, triumphed over them many times. This great battle occurred on the day before the Ides of August; and Christendom throughout the world was exalted, thanks be to God.

[Col. 1152B] We now close the fourth book of this history with the battle, marvelously won by God’s assistance a few days after the capture of the city; and, our promise thus fulfilled, we rest.

Here ends the History of Jerusalem, composed by Baldric, archbishop of Dol.

[Col. 1151]

# THE ACCOUNT OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE HEAD OF ST VALENTINE THE MARTYR TO JUMIÈGES IN GAUL, BY BALDRIC, BISHOP OF DOL

(Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, February, vol. II, p. 758.)

## NOTICE

1. Jumièges, an ancient Benedictine monastery, lies on a peninsula of the River Seine, about five leagues from Rouen, in whose diocese it is situated. In the church of this monastery is preserved the head of St Valentine the martyr, brought there from Rome. Distinguished by many miracles and set forth for public veneration, it is honoured by an annual feast. Baldric, bishop of the city of Dol in Armorican Brittany—or, as he himself writes, metropolitan pontiff—who flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century, wrote the history of this translation and its miracles. From his pen we have a History of Jerusalem, divided into four books and published among the *Deeds of God through the Franks*. He begins it with the year 1095, from which that military expedition in the East takes its beginning, and ends with the capture of Jerusalem, which occurred five years later.

Orderic Vitalis describes him in his *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, where, near the end, he relates the following concerning the author:

> “He was a citizen of Orléans, a monk and abbot of Bourgueil, educated in the liberal studies and venerable for the merits of his religious life. Thereafter, because of his religion and wisdom, he was advanced by ecclesiastical election to the rank of archbishop of Dol. In his episcopate he retained the monastic life and, as opportunity allowed, commonly lived with monks. For he presided over the untamed Bretons, whose perversity he could not endure. Therefore he frequently left those insolent and lawless men and fled to Normandy, where the Church of Dol, on the River Risle, had estates from the time of St Samson, while Hildebert was king of the Franks, and possessed them quietly and peacefully.
>
> “There, by his writings and teachings, he stirred his hearers to the worship of God; he visited the neighbouring monasteries—Fécamp, Fontenelle, Jumièges, and many others—and strengthened them by sacred sermons in the fear of God. At length he died in a good old age and was buried at Préaux, in the basilica of St Peter the Apostle, before the Crucifix.”

These are the words of Orderic, who completed his history in the year of Christ 1041. At another time we shall discuss other Acts of saints written by the same Baldric.

2. Frederick Flovet, one of our associates, communicated to us this history of the translation of St Valentine’s head and of the miracles from a manuscript of the church of St Ouen. Bishop Baldric cites, for the authority of this writing, at no. 1, “the trustworthy sincerity, ancient simplicity, pure report, and testimony concerning miracles of the monks of Jumièges.” And at no. 17, after recounting the miracle by which health was restored to Brother Hugh, the precentor, he adds: “We drew this from his own mouth, while other brethren who had witnessed it with him were listening.”

3. It is not equally clear to which St Valentine this sacred head should be considered to belong. At no. 2 he is called “a priest of Terni.” Yet the saint of Terni was a bishop; and St Valentine the Roman is said to have been a priest, and his head is said to be preserved among the Romans in the church of St Sebastian. In the year 1605, however, the body of Valentine the bishop was found at Terni in a leaden coffin. The Spaniards likewise believed that it was preserved in the monastery of St Benedict of Bages, at Rubricata near Barcelona, and that his head, conveyed to the city of Toro in the diocese of Zamora, was kept in a silver casket. These reports seem to be understood of another saint of the same name, Valentine.

# THE HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION BEGINS

[Col. 1153]

## CHAPTER ONE. The head of St Valentine is brought from Rome to Jumièges. Veneration follows the liberation of the fields from an invasion of animals.

[Col. 1153A]

1. How the head of the most blessed Valentine was brought at length to Jumièges, our style, though very unpolished, does not shrink from writing, as the trustworthy sincerity of the brethren related it to us and as the ancient and admirable simplicity of the Fathers themselves had handed it down. I therefore, Baldric by name, priest—though unworthy—of the holy Church of Dol and metropolitan bishop by rank, judging the pure report of the monks of Jumièges sufficient authority, have taken care to set down in writing what I heard concerning the translation of the head, and likewise a few things which, among the many miracles the Lord deigned to work through him, I learned from their testimony and believed.

2. A certain man who exercised the priesthood, hastening to the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer, went to Rome and, God prospering him, completed the journey he had undertaken. Yet he had arranged certain ascents in his heart: if he could by any means find relics of saints, he would carefully bring them back and carefully preserve them. The priest, lodging in a certain man’s house, disclosed to someone his desire, in case he might perhaps find some consolation for it.

While they were speaking of these matters, someone appeared who mentioned Valentine, priest of Terni: “My dear friend, I could give you his head, not because I am enticed by a desire for profit, but because I am very concerned that the province beyond the mountains may rejoice and be made illustrious by it. And if you distrust what I say, I wish you at least to believe me when I swear, for I declare that what I say is indeed true.” Thereupon he willingly swore this to the priest, uncovered after the oath the head of Valentine, which he knew to be hidden, and, in handing it over to the priest, fulfilled his promise. The priest in turn, adjured to treat the head honourably, gave his pledge; and so they took leave of one another. The priest understood, therefore, that the Lord had made his journey prosperous, since He had made him attain the object of his vow.

[Col. 1154A]

3. The priest returned bearing the long-desired treasure and placed all his hope in Valentine’s prayers. Unharmed, he crossed the harsh and pathless mountains and cliffs and finally arrived in Neustria. The priest entrusted the protection of that most holy head where he chose; and, some time afterwards, it was brought to the monastery of Jumièges and given to the members of that church, where he himself became a monk.

For the time being they placed it behind the altar of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, because they did not yet dare to proclaim it publicly. Much time passed, and an antiquity now growing old had nearly effaced these reports. Yet among those brethren there was frequent talk and continual conversation concerning Valentine. Some of them knew the place in which [Col. 1154B] the head was hidden, but they did not wish to reveal it to any outsider. They deferred the matter until the Governor of times should grant them a fitting time. They feared that what had been kept hidden might be demanded of them.

They had now placed that noble relic in an ivory casket and set it among other old chests. Some indeed doubted whether they perhaps possessed another head in place of Valentine’s head. They had heard only of the oath, but were exceedingly afraid in their hearts of perjury. Nor had blessed Valentine yet made himself clearly known to them by any manifest signs.

4. It happened at one time that the gracious God visited the farmers of Jumièges and gently chastised them; He no longer wished His servant, whom He had decreed should benefit Neustria, to remain hidden. Therefore the King of kings, the wondrous Craftsman, sent an army of His vengeance, destined to harm the people of Jumièges greatly and, unless they cried to Him quickly, to destroy all their crops. He sent, I say, little animals to attack and overcome humankind, resembling mice and called *mulotes*; they devastated all cultivation and, in a wondrous fashion, hostile squadrons cruelly assailed human beings: they cut down the sown crops, consumed the grain, and reduced cultivated land to wasteland.

Thus, indeed, the most serene One sometimes prepares evil visitations against us, that we may be corrected, may cry out, and may not lose heart, in order that we may be heard. The people of Jumièges cried out to the Lord—to whom they ought indeed to have cried—because scarcely anything remained from those animals. For neither by day nor by night did they cease consuming the crops; but that hostile swarm, with hostile tooth, cut down every height of the harvest. You might have seen those wild legions roaming through the fields, and there was no one able to resist divine vengeance. Therefore they cried to the Lord from the depths of their hearts. At length He heard them and thus delivered the afflicted, for they were compelled to confess that this suffering and scourge had proceeded from no other source than God’s vengeance.

[Col. 1155B]

5. In the church of Jumièges there was among the religious brethren a certain religious man, to whom St Valentine appeared once in church and then again. He was of venerable appearance, clothed in a white mantle and adorned with priestly vesture. In an authoritative voice he said to him:

> “Go and tell the brethren to carry through the fields and this district our head, concerning which some are uncertain—for I am Valentine—and to go around the crossroads and streets. God will truly be merciful to them if from now on they remember us more promptly on this account.”

The man disregarded this, thinking it a dream. On the following day Valentine appeared again and repeated the same words. Nor did the monk then comply, but remained silent and waited.

On the following night, while the brethren were nearly finishing the prayers of Matins, Valentine appeared reprovingly and rebuked the negligent monk in a voice which many could hear:

> “How long will you pretend not to know? How long will you be idle? Do you not see what great disasters threaten this land? Go, speak; delay no longer. But if . . .”

Some men heard him speaking and heard the sound, yet did not understand the words. The man to whom the command had been given was summoned; terribly stirred by Valentine’s threats, he recounted the first and second vision and reproached himself for his negligence.

6. After he had spoken of the third conversation, they believed him because they had heard the reproving voice. Immediately all hastened without delay, adorned [Col. 1155D] the casket of blessed Valentine for carrying, and placed it upon a litter, reverently bending their necks beneath it, because they had such confidence in the Lord. The inhabitants flocked together in crowds, poured out prayers and tears, and, chastened to some degree, held a procession. Through the intercession of blessed Valentine, they sought and expected deliverance in his compassion. They performed litanies and led Christian dances in procession around the place.

That most holy bier contained the noble propitiatory object which was carried, and in it, after God, they placed singular trust. A marvelous thing! Those *mulotes*, an army hostile—indeed very hostile—to men, as though they had perceived Valentine’s rebuke, from that time gathered together unharmed and hastened toward the River Seine, whether of their own accord or compelled by Valentine’s command. They entered the inescapable channel of the river [Col. 1156A], were submerged, and, caught in its vast whirlpools, were drowned. For the Almighty, in order to show the power of His beloved servant, exterminated that destroying host and thereby spread abroad the name of His Valentine.

7. The fishermen, catching this unprecedented providence in their nets, wondered and were astonished. Thus, within a few days, those *mulotes* were swallowed in deep gulfs, and all the inhabitants rejoiced at their disappearance. For that evil army had not yet completely threshed everything into destruction, since Valentine’s prayer had forestalled the plague. They therefore harvested what they found remaining, rejoicing more over so immediate a miracle than they were almost distressed by the preceding loss; for they had with them a faithful patron, a ready hearer, an effective helper, their lord Valentine, to whom they had commended themselves.

They also trusted that through blessed Valentine the Lord would deliver them from every other distress, because they promised that thereafter they would honour him more worthily. This miracle was spread abroad throughout the surrounding region, and it became common on every tongue that the most blessed Valentine was ready to hear. They therefore promptly prepared a more beautiful receptacle in which he might rest or be carried about, and adorned the casket with silver through their generous gifts.

## CHAPTER II. Fires extinguished through the help of St Valentine; pestilence and drought removed.

[Col. 1156C]

8. The power of this martyr, so often to be named, was often proved in quenching destructive fires. The large and extended workshops of the servants stood adjacent and contiguous to the monks’ workshops, so that scarcely a narrow space separated the two. Fire, carelessly banked under ashes, kindled and immediately seized the whole house of those buildings. The blazing fire raged with crackling flames and gravely threatened the monks’ dwellings, indeed threatening damage to the church itself. The wind blew toward the monks’ roofs, and leaping sparks and flames were carried into the buildings of God’s servants.

The monks were chanting Matins; but necessity compelled them to interrupt the chanting because they feared the danger that threatened. They had now lost every hope [Col. 1156D] of escape, when some of them brought forward Valentine’s bier and almost thrust it into the flames, setting it against the raging fire. They left that casket among the nearest houses and withdrew, because they could not endure the force and heat of the kindled fire. At that same moment the wind ceased, and a wind contrary to it began to blow; thus the fire, turned back upon itself, dwindled and died out.

You might see a beam of a house burned on one side, while the other side remained unharmed. All rejoiced to furnish testimony to so immediate a miracle—for who would not have rejoiced?—praising God and blessed Valentine aloud. For the more abundant that martyr was in miracles, the more glorious he was to them and to the neighbouring peoples.

[Col. 1157A]

9. Again it happened that, in the night-time, a stealthy fire found fuel prepared for itself in a house and seized it; no longer hidden, it leapt beyond the roof of the house and, with black vapours, attacked and consumed everything wooden. The force of the smoking conflagration reflected itself upon the stars, and a mass of dense embers threatened danger to the church itself; for the opposing wind drove sparks back upon the church.

The relics of St Valentine were brought, and at once the wind seemed as though ashamed, the fire departed from its rage, and all its most violent heat immediately fell silent.

10. We have also experienced the power of holy martyr Valentine in other miracles. He often moderated an excessive mortality among human beings and revealed by manifest signs how great was his merit with God. To recall a few instances among many, I shall add something further, so that God may be glorified in these things also and blessed Valentine magnified.

In recent times a horrible mortality fell upon the inhabitants of a certain village, apparently called Durclerus. The grievous plague entered so deeply among those mortals that every day either ten corpses, or at least seven or six, were carried out, scarcely to be buried by the survivors. Those who had seemed well only recently, afflicted by swift disease, sought and followed those whom they had carried out for burial yesterday or the day before. In that disaster, whoever felt even a little pain expected nothing but untimely death.

They had to some extent ceased performing the customary funeral rites, because all alike—or each person individually—feared for himself. The tears that survivors are accustomed to offer for the buried, which affection for their loved ones draws forth through human sympathy, they shed, in an order reversed, for themselves while still alive; for, now secure concerning the dead and as though their lamentations for them had dried up, whenever one of their own was struck by illness, they wept only for the person soon to die.

That trembling and anxious people turned their grief and lamentations toward the Lord and begged that blessed Valentine be brought to them, for that place both was and is a possession of the brethren of Jumièges. Why delay longer? That propitiatory object was brought there to be embraced, and they felt the help of the saint of God. Those who were ill, thanks be to God, immediately recovered strength; and afterwards none died except by natural death and after a more prolonged sickness. That people rejoiced and exulted because the evil pestilence had fled; they gave thanks to God and commended themselves from their hearts to the most blessed Valentine.

[Col. 1157D]

11. Since we have once mentioned escape from mortality through holy Valentine, and since we were present at this event, let us recount another consolation bestowed upon people through Valentine. In the place called Blinguitutum, mortality began to rage and to ravage that district. A message was sent to Jumièges. The people and the leading men of that settlement begged that most holy Valentine be brought there, since the village lay very near to it.

Valentine was sent there and immediately showed how much he prevailed with God. The plague was calmed and subsided; holy Valentine returned to his own place [Col. 1158A] with great rejoicing and a great procession, which we too deserved to attend. Since Valentine is found ineffective in nothing, on the third day the inhabitants of that land followed him, giving thanks and announcing that the plague had ceased. They further added: “Those who lay in their beds and had, as it were, wasted away in a trance while you were with us—behold, through our holy Valentine they have recovered.”

12. Though many things remain, I judge that one further matter should be added in writing, a thing which can in no way be reckoned anything but a miracle. The grass had withered and the crops had turned pale, because unseasonable drought had dried out the earth. Every field, dusty, threatened barrenness, and every God-fearing person lamented.

The people of Jumièges proclaimed a procession, at which one might have seen the devotion of the people. Nor could Valentine remain unmoved, as the necessary and fitting companion of the procession; through him, indeed, everyone had hope in the Lord. There is a church in honour of St Philibert, separated from Jumièges by some distance but well suited for prayer. They set out for it on foot and reached the oratory.

The sun shone in excessive heat, and the sky showed no cloud; rather, it was clear. Meanwhile the monks went with their colleague, blessed Valentine, to lay their complaint before God and obtain rain; nor did they doubt concerning this. For who would doubt when he appointed Valentine as an intercessor on his behalf?

They entered the church and hastened to celebrate sacrifice. While I write or reread this, I am so shaken with joy that I can scarcely express what I feel. The sky began of itself to darken slightly with little clouds; then it thundered a little, and then again a little; immediately abundant rain began to fall. When Mass had been celebrated, that choir of monks sat down, waiting in case the rain might cease; for they could not return to the monastery, disturbed by the excessive downpour.

Then the bare sky brightened a little, the density of the clouds held back its waters, and the weather permitted those brethren an opportunity to return. They returned and watched the impending rains with reverence; yet they were not distressed by escape from the rain. Indeed—and this is the more astonishing—the rain fell, as they saw, on their right and left [Col. 1158D], but did not strike the procession. They returned to the monastery, gladdened by the rain for which they had prayed and in no way harmed by that rain.

## CHAPTER III. Various sick persons, having invoked the patronage of St Valentine, are healed.

13. It is impious to be silent about Valentine; it is pious, when one has been compelled, to speak about Valentine.
