Those guilty of impious silence and ingratitude must be reproved, especially those who see these and other things yet are silent, who conceal the glory of Valentine when it ought to be enlarged, who obscure him when he ought to be publicly commended. Let them therefore correct their fault and speak; let them add writings to writings, because the supreme Creator [Col. 1159A] does not cease to add miracles to miracles.

The brethren had now gone out again with their Valentine to request rain and were returning. The abbot’s groom—whom we understand to be the master of the horses—had long lost the use of sight and had fallen into despair on that account. His relatives saw Valentine’s casket present and ran to bring the groaning man; holding him by the hands, they sounded some noble thing in his ears and set him before Valentine as he approached.

The procession halted briefly because they pitied their servant. The attendants put a wooden collar around his neck, to hold a candle, and attached it to the saint’s tomb. He touched the casket, kissed it most tenderly, and prayed with sobs concerning his infirmity. Those present—there were many [Col. 1159B] present—added their prayers to his and did not cease from supplication. Ranulf—for that was his name—made a vow and an offering for himself, groaning for his own sake. Within a few days, after he had fulfilled his obligation to Valentine concerning himself, he recovered both senses completely, because he had chosen Valentine for himself.

14. These things are indeed few, since more and greater things remain. The nephew of the same groom, a young man, soon afterwards was seized by a severe sickness, lay in bed, and became gravely ill. He became ill, I say, for he lost both sight and hearing and, besides this, fell into a fit of madness. The young man’s relatives grieved and invoked Valentine in heart and voice for one who was unconscious. Through his relatives’ invocation his sight was restored to him, while his hearing remained somewhat benumbed. His madness too had subsided a little, but he was still utterly ill.

He was led by the hand to Valentine, and people groaned in prayer for him. They placed him beneath the saint’s bier; what he was to do was indicated to him more by sign than by word, for his ears were stopped shut. He slept briefly and immediately rose completely well.

15. A certain woman went out at midday to inspect her crops, but she saw something—I do not know what—and fell into madness. Her own people restrained her unwillingly and bound her in chains, since she could not otherwise be kept under control. She was brought bound to Jumièges, where they well knew that Valentine, their lord, lived eternally with God. She was brought, I say, wounded by a mad spirit, and that unclean woman was led into the church.

Because of her uncleanness, however, they sent her out of the monastery and placed her outside in the courtyard. That dwelling of the saint was washed, and they gave the washing-water to the madwoman to drink. She drank it and immediately recovered; and after giving thanks, she returned unharmed to her own home.

[Col. 1159D]

16. Since a brief mention has been made of persons turned to madness and healed through that blessed saint, another matter, not unlike it, occurs to mind; nor do we dare pass it over or conceal it, lest perhaps we be deprived of the patronage of that same protector.

A certain old woman, younger than the woman mentioned above, became mad through an accident and grew excessively savage. Whether because she lacked friends, had suffered a very grievous injury, or was neglected by her neighbours, she wandered everywhere and was restrained by no one. Her frenzy consequently grew continually worse, because she roamed as a vagrant through crossroads and fields. Some followed her in mockery and often laughed at her madness.

Such is worldly ignorance and childish frivolity: people very often laugh where they ought to grieve. She had become an object of horror and fear to all who feared that the singular enemy of humankind might devise some evil against them through her. It was night for them by night and day, because sleep is renounced by persons made senseless in this manner.

The feast-day of blessed Valentine arrived, and a considerable crowd gathered. While Masses were being celebrated, they brought her before the saint; and, while they were still being celebrated, that madwoman recovered [Col. 1160B] her former reason. They gave thanks to God and willingly offered praises to blessed Valentine.

17. Let us also offer praises to Valentinus, who is ever at hand as a ready hearer for all Christians, and especially for the monks of Jumièges. Let no one complain that we set new miracles before old ones, miracle beside miracle, since they are not unknown. We anticipate times by times, since we ourselves are anticipated by those who recount them, though with modest insistence.

A certain precentor in the church of Jumièges, named Hugh, was laid low by a severe bodily illness in the infirmary. The feast of Valentinus was at hand, and the brethren spoke to Hugh concerning the evening office: “You will not be able,” they said, “to go to church; therefore you must celebrate Vespers here separately. We shall remain here with you and, as far as we can, keep the feast. For since the day before yesterday you have been troubled by many painful sufferings.” “Far be it from me,” he said, “that I should hear it here; rather, I will force myself to go there, where is the head of my lord Valentinus!”

He went in order to hear the office; he went to kiss the shrine; he went to pray and return. He did not reach the monastery itself, for health met him on the way because of his devotion. Thus he obtained that, once the praises had been completed, he should return healed and take food while hungry; for in the preceding days he had lost his appetite for eating, which, once cured, he recovered. He was also present at Matins with the choir of brethren; and, as though he had suffered nothing throughout the night, on the following day he performed the office of precentor. We drew this account from his own mouth, while other brethren who heard him and attested it with him were present. [Col. 1160C–D]

18. Another brother, named Turald, somewhat advanced in age and himself invested with priestly rank, suffered severely in his left breast and had long been afflicted for many days. He could scarcely stand and could scarcely breathe, since both his body and his bed seemed to be turning in his illness. The time came when the feast of Valentinus had to be celebrated. Turald, no longer master of himself because illness held sway over him, resolved to hurry to the church; but he could not do so by himself until, after summoning the infirmarian, he leaned upon him, and thus hastened to church with trembling step. For he placed his hope in St. Valentinus and did not wish to be deprived of his feast.

He lay beneath the bier; and after the completion of seven psalms and the conclusion of the litanies, he rose to kiss the shrine. But because he was short in stature, he could not kiss it at all. Yet the shrine made an exceedingly great noise, so that the attendant, who had gone some little distance away, heard the ringing sound. The monk was alarmed, fearing that some misfortune had happened to the shrine; but after carefully examining everything and realizing that the matter was otherwise, he became reassured, came to himself, and was made well. For Valentinus had sported with him by making a sound as a sign of rejoicing, not by speaking. [Col. 1161A]

19. Time would fail me—or I would fail time—if I presumed to recount individually all that the Lord has chosen to accomplish through Blessed Valentinus. Yet, omitting many things, let us at least confine ourselves to a few.

A certain brother, Ursio, a man of great repute, was prior of the church of Jumièges; he shone abundantly both through integrity of life and through learning. But just as empire does not protect an emperor, kingship a king, or principality a prince from death, so honor and letters protect no one from illness. We may, indeed, defer it and derive some benefit meanwhile, but in the end we cannot wholly escape. Thus the prior suffered, though neither learning nor honor had sufficiently fortified him.

For nearly twelve days he lay without food, because his appetite had departed from him. Weak in every limb, he wasted away and failed from moment to moment. Then the merciful remembrance of Valentinus came into his mind, since even for one without appetite the patronage of so great a protector was not to be neglected. He asked an attendant to support him by leading or carrying him to the shrine of the blessed man, since his feet could not carry him there by themselves. He was barefoot, without his monkish stockings, for the illness had gained a powerful hold over him. Supported over his whole body, he was brought there and entered beneath the elevated shrine. He prayed, made a vow, and wept; and, healed, he returned without support wherever he wished. For Valentinus refuses an answer to no one who touches him with the ointment of piety: he is present for the desolate, present for the afflicted, present for all who are miserable. [Col. 1161B–C]

20. Harmful humors sometimes dominate human beings, and through their excess they suffer burning vapors. This affliction arises from a disordered defect of phlegm or blood, though it often comes through the hidden judgment of God. Its nature is such that this fiery heat can scarcely be quenched except by death, or, more often, through the mercy of God when invoked. This suffering illness deprives its victims of sleep, for they are continually gnashing their teeth and merely howling. This disease resembles madness, because the decaying flesh stinks, smokes, and wastes away.

Two people suffering thus, one a man and the other a woman, stood before Blessed Valentinus, crying out horribly and yet urgently begging his aid. Out of their poverty one offered a wax foot, the other a hand, because those were the limbs in which they were helped. Both were healed, and each returned sound and unharmed to his or her own home. For Valentinus is powerless in nothing, unless someone proves ungrateful and unworthy toward him. [Col. 1161D–1162A]

21. Truly God is wonderful in his saints, he who alone performs great wonders; and in him Valentinus lives, himself a worker through him and not idle. For no one known to cleave to God can be idle.

Behold, again through Blessed Valentinus—or rather, Valentinus through God—help was given to a poor woman whom the Lord God had previously struck with blindness. The holy visitations of almighty God are many, and his healings are innumerable. Yet in both there is grace of God so manifold as to be beyond speech. He strikes in order to heal; he heals in order to save; he saves in order to crown and glorify. He deprived the aforesaid woman of sight, to whom through the Lord he had decreed to give aid through Valentinus. And I believe that she had sinned; but the hidden judgment of God foresaw that this would be for his praise and for the memorial of his faithful servant. For it is written: “Neither this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God might be made manifest in him” (John 9:3). In her case it was thus:

“The wife of a certain servant of Jumièges—that is, the servant who was the almoner-monk—fell into a most grievous sickness, so that, with almost every limb disabled, she lay weak upon her bed for a long time; or rather, she suffered there. For the illness was extremely severe, so that scarcely a breath remained in her. While this affliction continued, she was deprived of the sight of her eyes and hopelessly consigned to great misery. Time passed upon time, and the woman lamented helplessly. In dreams she scarcely attained any sleep at all; or rather, half-dead, she languished deprived of light. Whatever health she possessed was wretched, for she existed wholly in lamentation. A long time thus passed, and she almost despaired of her eyes.

“Yet her husband spoke to his wife and gently consoled the mourning woman. By now the pupils of her eyes had begun to discharge, so that recovery was considered still more hopeless. ‘If, my wife,’ he said, ‘you made a vow to Blessed Valentinus, whose feast-day this is, professing yourself the saint’s handmaid, and if you rendered him your annual capitation, I believe you would recover, because he is a most effective helper with the Almighty.’

“The sorrowful woman, whose heart in particular was gnawed by inward afflictions, willingly agreed. Following her forerunner with quickened step, she ran to church on the feast-day. She made her vow, prayed, slept, and—to the astonishment and applause of the people—returned to her home enlightened, without a guide. Thereafter she rendered each year to Blessed Valentinus the promised capitation; and not without reason, since she had found in Valentinus a powerful refuge for herself. Her long mourning was turned into enduring joy, because, once darkness had been driven away, she thereafter possessed the aid of sight. The brethren, weeping for joy, rang the bells in praise of God and sang a jubilant song, judging it sacrilegious to remain silent concerning such mighty works.” [Col. 1162A–D]

22. Another brother fell ill and almost failed entirely; he was earnestly loved by the other brethren because he was adorned by good conduct. The season of Lent arrived, yet he had to be sustained with meat. At last they feared for the brother’s death and, according to Christian custom, he was anointed with the oil of the sick. Nevertheless, returning somewhat to himself, he urged the attendants more by a sign than by speech to place him before Blessed Valentinus, in case he might perhaps be helped by the saint’s prayer. This was done, and immediately he was cured of that illness and went away well. [Col. 1163A; 1164A]

[Col. 1163]

# LIFE OF ST. HUGH, BISHOP OF ROUEN

> **[Note: [Col. 1163] See the literary notice on Baldric above, col. 1055, no. 7.]**

BY BALDRIC, ARCHBISHOP OF DOL.

(Edited by the Rev. Father Arthur du Monstier, *Neustria pia*, p. 282, from a manuscript codex of St. Vedast at Arras.)

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 1163B]

I. BALDRIC, by the grace of God archbishop of the Bretons, to URSIO, venerable abbot of the monks of Jumièges, and to the reverend congregation of that same place: obedience and blessing.

Any material not enhanced by the craftsmanship of a polisher is of less value to those who behold it. Gold and silver, ivory and wood, marble and every kind of stone, when adorned by no carving or polish, are merely what they appear to be; but if the hand of a polisher is applied to them, they immediately become more precious from being precious. In much the same way, any noble history is cheapened unless it is elegantly narrated; unless an eloquent style gives it color, it loses its nobility. Likewise, unless melody commends songs, unless sonority and graceful articulation beautify reading, their very lack of harmony disfigures it, and a tiresome cheapness steals over it. It is clear, therefore, that added euphony is as valuable in each thing as negligence or incompetence is harmful in all things.

But you, brethren of Jumièges—gem of the monastery, praiseworthy gem—by command and entreaty have enjoined upon our humility that I should write something concerning the conversion and manner of life of Lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, a man almost supremely holy from his mother’s womb, and should cast the censor’s correcting eye upon the little book written on this subject long ago. I refrain, however, from either praising or disparaging that book; nor do I presume to correct it, since I am by no means adequate to this task and burden.

For Blessed Hugh sprang forth from royal stock, and so great a subject ought to be undertaken with royal polish and a palatine pen. For who am I to write it? Who, I say, am I, whom no Ciceronian eloquence accompanies, that I should be adequate to this? Yet who am I, that I should not obey your lord abbot and you, our brethren and lords—or rather, charity itself? Therefore, wholly yours, I have complied with you; and I shall set forth briefly, as I can, the deeds of my lord Hugh. Perhaps the Holy Spirit also has arranged that I, archbishop of the Bretons, should proclaim the archbishop of the Northmen, a monk a monk; that, preserving truth, I should extol him and draw forth a little from noble material. May that most blessed Hugh himself, and your prayers, dearest brethren, implore for me the Paraclete Spirit as co-worker and helper. Amen. [Col. 1163B–1164C]

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1163]

[Col. 1163D]

II. I wish those who read what we have briefly arranged concerning Blessed Hugh to be persuaded and entreated not to rise too violently against us or assail our simplicity, because, as though presumptuous, I have drawn new things from old and have, as it were, cried out over their writings. I do not deny that those writings are simple, but I know that they are true. Charity and obedience compelled me to apply my hand to them.

Nor shall I linger over writing the miracles which God performed through Lord Hugh, though they are many; rather, as far as I can, I shall explain his holiness and manner of life. In touching upon miracles, I shall almost pass over those things which may be common to faithful and unbelieving persons; as it is written that the Lord will say to those who boast of miracles, “I do not know you.” Indeed, Hugh so sanctified his infancy, adolescence, and all the remainder of his life that, so long as he lived, he endured a long martyrdom. Like a beautiful rose, he flowered among thorns; bedewed with almsgiving, fasting, and his tears, he reddened as though crimsoned with his own blood, and neglected nothing that befitted religious devotion. For, according to the command of his Jesus, he bore his cross until, crucified, he passed to the crucified Jesus. [Col. 1164D–1165B]

III. It is very difficult for those who have taken care to read the successive genealogy of the kings of the Franks—as it is written—not to know from what parents Hugh’s line proceeded. For among the most noble reckoning of those kings there emerged one supremely noble among nobles: Charlemagne, emperor of Gaul and Italy, son of the patrician Pippin, invincible in war and yet incessantly warlike.

The army of this Charlemagne defeated and captured in a certain conflict a duke of Bavaria named Tassilo; having at last triumphed over him, not without loss and heavy labor, it presented the captive to the emperor in Francia. The king condemned him to exile but, granting him his life, permitted him to become a monk in the monastery of Jumièges—a place which then, and long afterward, flourished in great abundance of resources and rigor of observance.

The emperor took Anstrudis, Tassilo’s daughter, into his marriage-bed, and begot from her a son whom he wished to be called Hugh. Anstrudis loved this child of hers very tenderly and nursed him at her breast, until, when he was already in his fourth year, she entrusted him to King Charles to be brought up at court and to be greeted and honored there as the emperor’s son. The lord emperor, rejoicing with paternal spirit over him, exulted greatly and committed the infant to faithful guardianship. The boy advanced in age and grew greatly in favor with the courtiers. [Col. 1165B–D]

IV. The time came when the boy of royal stock had to be sent to receive instruction in letters. An order concerning him was given to a master who was to devote care to this matter. Thus Hugh was joined to a company of boys of the same age, so that he might apply himself more readily to school. As is the custom in the teaching of letters, he first saw the elementary characters presented to him on a little parchment sheet. He was not yet five years old, and already labored earnestly in this apprenticeship.

He seemed, however, to absorb that exercise beyond his companions; and whatever was impressed upon him was shaped in his little breast as in soft wax. For his mind possessed remarkable capacity, lively retention, and a sagacious diligence beyond childhood; not without the admiration of his master, who was already compelled to foresee something great in Hugh. The Holy Spirit too was already prefiguring in the child something that would one day benefit all the people of Gaul. He surpassed the measure of childhood and anticipated the curiosity of his attentive master. Nor was he praiseworthy only in grasping letters; he was already somewhat eloquent in conversation. At times he won over his master with promises and exhortations, that he might apply himself still more diligently to Hugh’s school studies. For he appeared already to be living through his seventh year, yet pursued an apprenticeship beyond that of a seven-year-old. [Col. 1165D–1166A]

V. The king heard such reports of his son—for a father’s heart could not long be distant from his firstborn—and, when Hugh had been brought to him, embraced and kissed him. He marveled at the keen answers of so tender a child and at the greatness hidden in the little breast of his son. Beyond his reception of learning, moreover, a certain uprightness of life adorned him. He did not devote himself to childish games, nor did he hunger for royal spectacles; rather, step by step he ripened toward more advanced things.

Delighted by his son’s disposition, the emperor sent him to the church of the most blessed Dionysius, that he might be reared and taught there among the servants of God. For the king judged it beneficial for his son to be nourished where no device of evil might defile him. He was received into the school, and the king’s son was carefully brought up. His intelligence seemed all the more capacious because his blood was more exalted. Yet he did not disdain discipline on account of royal eminence: devoted to school, he was subject even to the rod. Indeed, he loved the rod, so that he might attain discipline more readily. For his mind was not inflated with any pride because he was born from royal stock.

You might have supposed him one of the humbler pupils among his fellow students, because he was not in the least exalted by the high rank of either side of his family. He often preceded his masters and fellow pupils in rising for Matins, so that it was plainly evident that, in so diligent a pupil, there was an unusual novelty of discipleship. For whatever he heard, with a thirsting heart he seized for himself beyond ordinary human capacity; and from a few things he inferred many. He blushed deeply if he was ever found idle. His masters marveled, and all marveled, since they could not but wonder what so great and such an abyss of learning portended.

He himself won his masters by prayers, hired them at whatever price, or even compelled them to persist in their lessons and somehow satisfy his hunger. Thus he was the subject of much and very frequent conversation. Meanwhile Hugh was approaching his fifteenth year and maturing; and, having ranged through the books of Cicero and Varro, another thought was already active in his breast: the love of God, which he had long conceived, and from then [with *tunc* added in f.] the birth-pangs of that conception pressed upon him. He no longer wished to be occupied with the sophistries of chatter, but resolved henceforth to devote himself to divine concerns. [Col. 1166B–D]

VI. A thought of this kind entered his mind: that he should hasten to the thresholds of the apostles, to be supported by their patronage. He thought it fitting first to reveal his desire to such great teachers, whom he knew to be the princes of all the apostles. He also resolved to enroll for himself as master the special vicar of Peter—or rather, of God. For he judged that his vow would receive whatever increase through those senators who held the primacy of the whole apostolate.

Having obtained from his master permission to return to the palace—for he always wished to remain subject to his masters—he came to his father in order to confess his intention. He was received with a cheerful countenance and spent some time with the palace clergy. One day, while the clergy were awaiting the emperor at Mass, they held, as often happens, an uncertain discussion about certain divine matters. Each said what he thought, but no one reached the core of the issue. Hugh listened silently to each person’s opinion and did not refute this man or that. He avoided pride by remaining silent before he was asked.

At last the discussion came to him, and an answer was requested from him. They hung upon the speaker’s lips and marveled at the wisdom of his exposition. For he did not seem to speak with a human mouth, but spoke as one filled with the Spirit of God. Thus he pleased them all; and there was no lack of someone to report to his father the prudence of the son, at which the father rejoiced exceedingly. From that time Charlemagne began to hold him dearer and decreed that greater honor should be shown him by his attendants. From that time he called him more familiarly; and if any important matter arose, he listened to him more attentively.

The emperor then gave him all his royal rights in two abbeys: namely, the place of Rebais and the Cross of St. Ouen, together with very beautiful estates suitable for his income. He learned also that Hugh intended to journey to Rome, and immediately granted him permission; he lavishly prepared the mounts appropriate to a king’s son. He also wrote to the venerable Pope Leo, that he should receive Hugh as befitted the emperor’s son. For Hugh was most dear to him and worthy of every welcome. Whatever Hugh might ask of the pope, the king commanded that he should grant him without difficulty; that he should love him with a father’s affection and strengthen him in every good thing through the affection of charity. [Col. 1167A–C]

VII. Now, what a companion he showed himself to his fellow travelers; how pleasant, generous, kind, and magnificent toward all who were in need; how sober at meals, how sparing toward himself; how affable, how restrained in speech, how diligent in prayer and vigil—this is not for us to declare, since none of us can do everything. And when Rome was reached, what sobbing tears he offered, with what sorrow he afflicted himself in the hearing of God and Blessed Peter, he knows better to whom this young man of good disposition wholly vowed himself. You might have thought him already dead to the flesh, so earnestly did he kiss the ground. He humbly commended himself to the patronage of all the saints in whose dwelling places he moved about.

At last Hugh was solemnly received by the lord pope and honored in all things as a king’s son. They addressed one another with spiritual joy and shared themselves mutually in reciprocal intercourse. In the course of their other conversations of piety, Hugh opened to the lord pope the desire hidden in his heart and chose to enter the clerical state. The pope heard the young man’s wish and hesitated whether he should favor his requests. He feared the emperor on either account: he feared to shave the son without consulting the king, and likewise feared to offend the royal will of the son.

At last it came into the apostolic’s heart that it was better to comply with the young man where God would be served than to neglect so great a matter where God would be offended. He expected that he could be reconciled with the king after his displeasure, provided only that he might merit God’s favor. And he added: “The king, in his letters, commanded us to satisfy his son’s will in all things. He did not expressly mention the tonsure; but he who says ‘in all things’ excepts nothing. Therefore let us do that whereby we may gain God. Let us lay the foundation; God will give the increase.”

And immediately, when scissors had been brought, Hugh himself promptly cut off the locks he had seized and, sobbing, offered them to the Lord God. You might have seen those standing by weeping with him in pious compunction and foreseeing greater things concerning Hugh. Thus Hugh became the adopted son of the lord pope, to whose commands the good young man had wholly devoted himself.

Having been made a cleric, the most humble Hugh prostrated himself at the feet of Lord Leo, that thereafter, wherever he might be, he might be specially supported by his prayers. He offered the curls of his hair to Blessed Peter, that by this sign he might be wholly dedicated to the clerical state. He also said: “In the course of time, God cooperating, I profess that I shall become a monk in our homeland, in a certain household of God—namely, in the monastery of Jumièges.” At the fitting time, having remained with him for a long while, he was ordained deacon by the hand of the supreme pontiff. At last, honored with many relics of saints, which he had eagerly requested one by one, he returned to Francia with a prosperous [perhaps “swift”] step. [Col. 1167D–1168C]

VIII. Nor should it be passed over in silence that, as he departed from Rome, the Lord God deigned to work through him. For he no longer wished his soldier to remain hidden, now that he proclaimed his God through the clerical status publicly assumed.

A certain demoniac, cautiously bound—for he was tormented by the excessive frenzy of a demon—was brought before the most holy Hugh, accompanied by many of his own people, who urgently begged for him. Meanwhile the wretched man tore himself to pieces and cried out horribly; whatever he touched he violently rent apart, for his madness was immense. Most holy Hugh halted, moved by the prompting of the Holy Spirit. He could not lack the prerogative of mercy, in whom the abundance of the Holy Spirit dwelt.

When the demoniac saw him, he immediately seemed stunned and swiftly fell to the ground. For already the evil spirit was devising what the Holy Spirit was beginning. Blessed Hugh asked the bishops who were present and accompanying him to give their blessing, since they too ought to indicate it beforehand. He himself, fearless, approached the madman and placed upon him the wood of the holy cross. Rebuking the evil spirit in the name of the Lord, he commanded it to depart without doing harm and not presume to torment the man again. He also gave him holy water to drink, signed him with his own hand, and expelled the disturber of God’s servant from a place not its own.

All marveled, and after this Hugh’s holiness could no longer be kept silent. Moreover, in confirmation of the miracle, that frenzied man, restored to himself, well and joyful, traveled on with that holy company and, safe and sound, rejoiced with the others in praises of God. [Col. 1168D–1169A]

IX. On his return, that holy man was never idle. His prayer was continual, his fasting continual, his practice of psalmody continual; his almsgiving abundant, his contemplation frequent. Although Hugh had been accustomed to each and all of these things before his apprenticeship in the clerical state, yet, once his head had been shorn and he had received the order, he was as though transformed, since from that time his spirit was diligently made contrite in every good work.

At that time Charles resided at Trier in his palace. Someone came and announced to the king the arrival of his son, commanding Hugh to hasten to him as quickly as possible. For the king was possessed by a great desire to see him. He also sent a large part of his household to meet him; many others joined them, marveling at his transformation. Some grieved and wept; others, whose minds were sounder, rejoiced.

At the king’s court was Hugh’s full brother, named Drogo, himself adorned by praiseworthy conduct. He hastened to meet his brother; kissing him and embracing him in fraternal arms, he wept most abundantly. He wept, I say, as though he already saw dead the man whom he saw made a cleric—not because he disparaged the clerical state, since he himself aspired to the same calling, but because brotherly affection wrung tears from him and had found excessive sobs. Thus he wept and wasted away in weeping.

Hugh said to them, and especially to his brother: “You, brother, and you all ought to rejoice over me, for such is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” The father rose to meet his arriving son; after kissing him, he made him sit beside himself. The king’s eyes grew moist for his son, as though restored to life and returned, and he remained long in an embracing kiss. The emperor delighted in both his sons, but especially in Hugh. [Col. 1169B–D]

X. While they sat beside their father at table, letters were brought: one concerning the misfortune of the church of Rouen, another concerning that of the church of Metz, each reporting that the shepherd of its people had died. The clergy and people of each church also said: “O king, with united supplication we pray that we may be granted your two sons as our bishops—for Drogo, of whom we have just spoken, was also very learned. We have canonically elected them; only let not the assent of the great Caesar be lacking to us.”

When the letters had been read, Augustus was silent for the moment, until he had summoned many of his bishops and nobles to consult concerning the matter. For this reason Charles held a special council at Aachen, seeking counsel concerning the churches left desolate. In those days illustrious kings did not act rashly or precipitately in such a matter, but conferred deliberately and at length with bishops and religious men, always preferring God’s will to human intrusions. The letters were again read, and the envoys spoke wisely and distinctly.

The holy synod recognized that the Holy Spirit had been the leader and initiator of this matter; for human judgment could not have made an election so fitting and harmonious. The two brothers, two olive trees, two great luminaries, were brought into the midst; and concerning them, what the Holy Spirit had dictated was established. The king confirmed by his authority the election that had been made and the agreement of the bishops. He commanded Hugh to be sent to the people of Rouen and Drogo to those of Metz.

He also placed under Hugh, who was the elder, the abbeys and all royal possessions which the king held by hereditary right in that diocese, to serve during his lifetime for his son’s expenses and for the uses of Christ’s poor. In the same manner he assigned Drogo the province of Metz with its royal rights. This synod was held at Aachen on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October [19 September], in the year 702 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while the great King Charles reigned.

The aforesaid brothers, to whom this had happened beyond their expectation and desire, were astonished and uncertain what they chiefly ought to do: comply or resist. To resist, they regarded as disobedience; to comply, they regarded as a kind of human ambition. They would nevertheless have ventured to resist, had they not been compelled under adjuration by God. Nor could anyone deny that a matter proceeding so favorably had issued from divine providence.

Since the following day dawned as Saturday and was the autumn fast, the holy synod ordained them priests; and on the next day, namely Sunday, consecrated them bishops. They knew, indeed, that delay in such a matter was harmful. The august emperor sent them forth to the sees divinely appointed for them, assigning suitable envoys to each and abundant necessary resources from the royal treasury. [Col. 1169D–1170C]

XI. Rouen received Hugh with great rejoicing, and all came out to meet him with exultation and joy. Thus that same venerable man Hugh succeeded to the see of the church of Rouen as the twenty-third after Mallonus, the first bishop of that city; in governing the monastery of Fontenelle he was seventh after St. Wandregiselus, and in governing the monastery of Jumièges he was seventh after Blessed Philibert and sixth after Lord Aichard.

On that day his table, worthy of so great joy, first refreshed the little poor, and afterward fed the grown ones. Neither on that day nor on others was reading absent from his table, lest chatter creep into the meal. Then he began to devote himself to rebuilding the churches of God. He decreed that a church in honor of the apostle James, ruined from its foundations, should be rebuilt. He commanded that the brothels, houses of prostitution, prostitutes’ quarters, and every public abuse in the city should be destroyed, so that purity and chastity might be cultivated more freely.

He also summoned to himself from throughout his diocese servants of God—clerics and monks, nuns and widows—so that he might learn individually of their holy manner of life and relieve their poverty if anything should perhaps be lacking. He also commended himself to the acquaintance and prayers of each one. At fixed times holy and eloquent Hugh called together his people and, discoursing on the delightfulness of the Scriptures, often taught them and kindled them toward heavenly desire. He held councils among his bishops, in which he argued richly and abundantly concerning moral holiness. For he did not wish any time to pass in which he might be idle from divine works.

Nor do I suppose that anyone departed from an assembly of the councils until he had received his abundant greeting and blessing for the use of travel. Indeed, he desired nothing as his own, but made all his possessions common, above all for the benefit of the poor. Nor should it be left unsaid that abundant banquets were prepared daily in Hugh’s court because both the dignity of the church of Rouen and the eminence of royal blood demanded it. He shared these banquets with the poor and with visitors; he himself, however, always rose from the abundant table either fasting or hungry. The seasoning of reading was never lacking from his table, because his inner person especially delighted and lived by it.

It happened, therefore, that one day the reader gave this opening at the beginning of the reading: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation; for it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdoms of heaven.” And he immediately added: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of God.” And again: “Blessed are you who now hunger, for you shall be filled.”

This reading struck fear into the man of God, so that he understood himself to be especially rebuked. From Septuagesima until Palm Sunday, he therefore lived with the brethren of Jumièges, keeping silence and watching in fasting and prayer. Still clothed as a cleric, he was already living as a monk. [Col. 1170D–1171C]

XII. Then, after a few days had passed, when his father had died and the people of various regions had been summoned, judging himself unworthy, out of humility, to be bishop and declaring this openly, after governing the church of Rouen for twenty-six years, he obtained leave from his people and moved to Jumièges. There he became a monk and laid aside the dignity of archbishop. For nearly ten years he lived there in this mortification of the flesh, and the royal shoot had cast himself down into the dung-heap of universal usefulness.

One day, when the solemnity of Matins had been completed, that blessed man, remaining in church to perform his customary private prayers, watered the pavement with tears and assailed heaven with supplications. Barefoot, he disregarded the cold of marble and winter. Wholly in heaven, he cared nothing for earthly discomfort. Then fevers attacked Hugh, announcing to him that death was near. He was shaken by the fevers; yet, because he was still held back a little from the path of the fathers, he was distressed. For with the Apostle he desired “to depart and be with Christ.” Nevertheless, he ordered the abbot and the brethren of Jumièges to be summoned to him; he also called his successor, the archbishop of Rouen. To them he foretold the dissolution of his body and commended himself to their prayers.

[Col. 1172B] Strengthened by reception of the Lord’s body and blood, but first anointed with the liquid of holy oil and the other signs of Christian religion, he rendered up his spirit to God. The pale company of monks embalmed with spices his little body, worn out by holy works. The ever-to-be-named Hugh departed on the day before the Ides of April, in confession of the true faith and in the consummation of true religion.

The whole course of blessed Hugh’s manner of life and struggle was a kind of military service acceptable to God, which began at once to shine in his very childhood. He was abundant in almsgiving; discerning and subtle in preaching; a lover of poverty; a constant observer of fasting; a foster-child and honourable vessel of sobriety; and a despiser of all carnality. He chose and made peculiarly his own obedience and humility, those two outstanding sisters, closely joined to him; and among the monks of Jumièges he lived and slept as the gentlest of monks.

[Col. 1172C] He shone as the worker of many miracles, though he always wished them to remain hidden. We have left those deeds to be arranged by a more celebrated pen; seeking rest for our hand, we have withdrawn it from so great a harvest. This blessed man lived seventy-four years, always serving under arms, solely that he might deserve the robe. He flew away to the place appointed for him by God, an old man and full of days. For venerable old age is not long duration nor something reckoned by the number of years, but that which pleases God and is well ordered.

The sorrowing and orphaned flock of Rouen and Jumièges, whom he had reared with paternal affection, performed for him solemn and mournful obsequies. Yet they knew reasonably that they should rejoice more concerning him whom the God of gods had called to heaven, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1173]

## BALDRIC’S ITINERARY, OR LETTER TO THE PEOPLE OF FÉCAMP

(*Neustria pia*, p. 227.)

[Col. 1173A] **BALDRIC, archbishop of Dol, to the people of Fécamp.**

### 1.

Caught up to the summit of the mind, I wished to revisit the colonies through which I had once passed as a guest; and I began to delight and walk through each of them. “I went down into the garden of fruit trees, to see the pomegranates” (Song of Songs VI). I saw the lofty cedar of Lebanon, Cluny, and smiled upon it; I beheld the fragrant cypress, Marmoutier, and rejoiced exceedingly. I admired the rich paradise—Bourgueil—which had long nourished me among its pomegranates, and I took delight in it; especially because I had been its keeper and gardener for almost six lustres.

Then, taking an occasion not dishonourable, of my own accord I crossed over to Lesser Brittany, chiefly because in our rose-garden there were springing up, as commonly happens, bastard shrubs. Since, on rooting them out, I either ignored them or could not remove them, I fled; for I preferred to migrate rather than persist in stripping out brambles. I feared indeed that I should fail beneath the laborious burden; and already the restless Poitevin storm had begun wickedly to blow.

[Col. 1173B] Therefore, raised higher and placed in the episcopal chair, I, William, formerly abbot of Bourgueil and adorned in the see of Dol with the archiepiscopal pallium, began to travel through the territories of the Bretons on this side [of the sea]. Yet in those plains I could by no means find roses like those of Bourgueil. Either they had somewhat withered, or they had utterly dried up, or, uprooted entirely, they showed no evidence even that they had once existed; rather, that wilderness displayed desert, uncultivated ground, and grim salt-marshes.

Like Achsah, daughter of Caleb, sitting upon an ass, I began to sigh (Josh. XV)—not because I repented of our migration or wished to return to former treasures, but because I desired to see a more abundant richness of flowers than I saw. For a little while I persisted in clearing the fields of stones and planting olives; but, overcome by the barbarous exhalation of the maritime land, I stopped, and, because I had laboured in vain, I blushed deeply.

### II.

Confounded by shame, I sailed back to England, in the hope that there I might find something which, my works having been left behind, could at least refresh me with an image not unlike the things I had lost. O how much gold and silver I found there! How great an abundance of rich food! How much joy and exultation! How lavish the brethren, how eloquent, how pleasant, how admirable! I rejoiced and, in comparison with England, judged the Brittany in which I had begun to dwell to be exile.

[Col. 1174A] I rejoiced, I say, because I was gladdened by the fragrance of religion with which almost that whole region was aflame. Good God! What fragrant roses, what gleaming lilies I perceived there! What scent of rich spices I breathed in! How I was clasped in friendly embraces; how I was urged, with no feigned importunities, to remain with each of them! Yet, as I suppose, they did not esteem me anything great, apart from being a pilgrim; rather, compelled by the charity overflowing in them, they compelled me.

For they sang that Paschal responsory: “Remain with us, for evening is drawing on, and your day, already declining, is turning toward its setting. It is therefore fitting that henceforth you should rest in this household of God.” Perhaps I offered excuses and little excuses to a few of them, and, not without common tears, hastened my return.

### III.

Normandy is a province adjoining and contiguous with the land of the Bretons, separated from and bounded by it only by a small river called the Couesnon. I resolved to enter and explore it, and I entered. There truly I found paradisal dwellings; there I saw the inhabitants of the clouds, the choirs of cenobites; there I was received by those servants of God with immense joy and compelled to rest.

I examined the habits of each man: whether perhaps, by contrivance, they had made themselves cheerful for the hour to a passing visitor; whether they were affable to us out of reverence for our person; whether they honoured guests purely for God’s sake; whether this was merely for appearance or a proof of charity.

[Col. 1174C] What shall I say? On the first day of our arrival they were good; but on the following day they had become so much better that, had I not recognized the faces I had seen yesterday, I should have thought them not the same men but others. I gave thanks; and because God had reserved for himself seven thousand who had not bent the knee before Baal (III Kings XIX), I recognized this without doubt. In thanksgiving and exultation of mind I travelled through Normandy, and I had to come to the most welcome community of Bec. There I truly found the full assistance of all religious life; for there could in no way be detected either pretence, flattery, or changeability, but a certain sincere moderation of natural uprightness. Of that place it could surely be said: “Nothing in excess.”

After I had spent the night there, I asked the venerable abbot for permission to depart, but did not receive it. For that instrument of the Holy Spirit and charity immediately replied: “Father, we too have read, have not consigned it to forgetfulness, and indeed have taken it as an example: ‘And they compelled him: Remain with us’ (Luke XXIV). Certainly, saving your reverence, those words were words of faint-heartedness, not of the expansiveness of charity. You must therefore be compelled, and we compel you.”

[Col. 1175A] I accepted that playful speech as a divine response and yielded. I recognized that God dwelt among human beings and spoke in them, and I reproved my own faint-heartedness.

### V.

At last, finally torn away from afar, I saw Fécamp—of which I had heard much from pilgrims—like the rising of dawn. At the very entrance of that most limpid dwelling, I confess, I was astonished. For, amid the most seemly arrangement of splendid buildings and between walls of stone, brethren, devoted to monastic frugality and worthy of royal pomp, came out to meet us. Greeting my lowliness and, as it were, dancing with the foot of charity, they revered me not as an unknown man but as one familiar and of their household from their very cradles.

[Col. 1175B] In a wonderful manner every one embraced and congratulated me, though until that time they had neither seen nor heard of me. Old men hurried with younger men, and each blushed to arrive last. Whoever came later excused himself for his lateness, and all together applauded me. The venerable abbot had flown to us first, since he had first heard of our arrival. He spoke on behalf of all; yet every one spoke for him and for himself. Each anticipated the other in expressing the same affection of kindness.

The sweetness of the people and fullness of charity disposed matters thus. But our iron people would abhor such a thing, being deprived of the honeycomb that drips with true charity. Blessed simplicity does not know suspicion; but suspicious perversity does not know simplicity. Yet the judgment of charity is better than the ordering of human tradition.

I was received into the cloister and invited into the furnace of souls—the purgatorial chapter. They hung upon the mouth of my discourse; some were moved to tears, not because my speech had any flavour, but because charity hopes all things, believes all things, and neglects no one.

[Col. 1175D] Some spoke with us privately and, sighing, complained about their souls. In all of them I found the Holy Spirit dwelling; and they were, God knows, found without fault. For one is not faulty who is now the reprover of whatever fault there may have been.

### V.

A certain person named Adelelm, exceptionally learned in liberal letters, was assigned to me as guide, guardian, and attendant. So long as I was there, he remained familiarly at my side. I questioned him privately about the domestic concerns of the monastery, and he answered each matter eloquently.

Concerning the surviving abbot, as one newly elevated, he conveyed many good things and promised greater ones. At length, with sobs, he turned his speech to the one who had recently died:

[Col. 1176A] “My lord, this church has had rulers worthy of remembrance; but the lord Abbot William, of good memory, who lately died, shone out above his predecessors and fellow provincials as the glittering sun rises above the other lights. Endowed with great learning, first archdeacon of Bayeux, then monk of Caen, and finally abbot of Fécamp, a reverend and white-haired man, once the majesty of religious life, he exalted this house by the discipline of his character, enlarged it in its buildings, and—what was especially outstanding in him—enriched it with a community of brethren.

“Many noble laymen and clerics, stirred by the fragrance of his religious life, put off [the old life] for conversion and voluntarily put on the monk’s habit, being formed by his holy institutions. I myself, who speak with you, was far away when I heard the good reputation of our lord William. Attracted by it, and with the permission of our abbot—for I had, and still have, another abbot—I came to Fécamp in order to attach myself to him. I was received gratefully, although I was a manikin of no importance.

[Col. 1176B] “He himself gathered together all of us whom you see; but we were more numerous than we now are, for almost a hundred of us followed our leader after his departure. Lord Father, infer and consider what manner and greatness of table it was, whose such remnants you still behold. The vigour of the Order has endured. He instructed us by words and examples and bound us all to himself in his paternal affection.

“For, not to conceal the truth, for God’s sake he was everything to everyone. Therefore our tears follow him; therefore our sighs accompany him. Who can remember him with dry eyes? We offer ourselves to you, reverend Father, because, as we believe, we have sent you beforehand—not lost you—as our patron to the court of our God. While you were ours, who was more abundant in tears? On your bed, sighing, you contended with yourself; in the crowd you were peaceful with us. In a corner of the church or in the solitude of your pallet, you were wholly troubled. You pleaded with yourself over our offences; and, O sweetest father, you mercilessly crucified yourself for the brethren’s sins, should any have occurred.

[Col. 1176C] “Whose offence did you not make your own through compassion? As many times as any man—or I, wretch that I am—sinned, so many times did you sacrifice yourself. You often spent the night in prayer, and, groaning, disturbed the God of perfect rest. Without offence you argued with him; and by friendly argument, like another Solomon, you made him peaceful toward yourself and toward us. You redeemed us with alms, because you faithfully distributed what was entrusted to you.

“What poor person’s need ever found your hand barren? What church did not receive your generosity? You went about the corners and crossroads even of lepers, to speak familiarly with them, often even to kiss their elephantine hands. You entered their little huts, that you might assist all in their needs and that the distress of every miserable person might know you. Who can unfold the breadth of your heart, dear Father? I shall therefore do better, from this point onward, to refrain from speaking of you. The holiness of your good manner of life cannot be fully expressed in words.

[Col. 1177A] “Yet, thanks be to God, we have one of your own, heir to your worth: our abbot, formerly familiar to you, the lord Roger—a man sufficiently capable, a minister, we hope, suitable, and a master who will benefit us. But circumstances themselves have changed, rulers have changed, and manners have changed. It is human to lament what we have lost, because we utterly despair of improvement.”

Having said this, the distinguished man fell silent, but did not at once cease his lamentations. My own eyes too grew wet, for I sympathized with his narration. We interrupted our conversation and hastened to attend to other matters.

### VI.

I viewed the extent of the church, the beautiful spaciousness of God’s house, and the abundant splendour of its ornaments; he also described the extent of its estates, and I marvelled at each thing.

[Col. 1177B] I then gave thanks, because the faithful had bestowed upon God—whose all things were—so many and such great gifts, useful for the needs of the poor. And, not to pass over the community of brethren in silence, I saw in that house many men of one habit, one mind, and one identity, so that there might rightly be read there: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

If you asked of anyone, “Who is that man?” he praised him so highly that you would scarcely believe anyone else could be compared with him. This was not because he lied, for in each was something on account of which he might deservedly be extolled. Yet each preferred the other to himself; and this all proceeded from mutual love and from the discipline of the monastic Rule.

Their knowledge of letters so abounded that many had fully attained the wealth of Holy Scripture and committed it to memory. Yet they did not for that reason listen less eagerly to others speaking, nor did they despise the rest as less learned; rather, for humility’s sake, they embraced all who came.

[Col. 1177C] Seeing them frequently devoted to prayer, often watered with tears, suitably attentive to frugality, speaking words of edification in silence, attending monastic assemblies, and neglecting nothing of their office, I saw soldiers of God fighting against the ancient serpent. Therefore they were always under arms; they awaited the robe, and for that reason fought without weariness. Such a legion, such an army, such a fellowship had feared lord Abbot William as lord, heard him as master, and loved him as father; and all still sighed for him.

### VII.

There was one thing in that church which pleased me not moderately, something which David included in his songs for the praise and stirring of God: “Praise the Lord,” he says, “with strings and organ” (Ps. CL). There I saw a musical instrument constructed of bronze pipes, which, roused by crafted bellows, produced a sweet melody. Through a continuous octave and the resonance of harmony it united low, middle, and high voices, so that it might seem a choir of harmonizing clerics, in which boys, old men, and young men met and were gathered, rejoicing. They called it an organ, and set it in motion at fixed times.

[Col. 1178A] Yet I do not fail to know that there are many who, having no such thing in their churches, run down by murmuring those who do have it—men whom we dare to call slanderers and detractors—because they do not know how to explain what organs signify to us. These men have forgotten that lyric poets composed verses for the psaltery. Perhaps they have not read that most holy David soothed Saul’s frenzy when he was possessed, by the modulation of strings (I Kings XVI). They have certainly learned that Elisha, in order to calm himself after the king of Israel had grievously angered him, commanded his attendants: “Bring me a psalmist.” And while the psalmist played, the hand of the Lord came upon him, making him gentle (IV Kings III)—that is, the Holy Spirit came. For the spirit of wisdom could not enter an angry and ill-disposed soul. It entered, then, one made cheerful through the ministry of the psaltery.

Therefore we do not err if, so far as we can, we imitate the footsteps of such great fathers. Yet we do not doubt that the Lord delights in these things; rather, many ecclesiastical furnishings of this kind are made, like golden, silver, or silken ornaments, for God’s praise and to stir the dullness of the human body.

[Col. 1178B] I myself do not take great pleasure in organ music; but through it I am stirred to understanding: namely, that just as many pipes of varying weight and differing size, moved by one wind, unite in a single song, so human beings ought, inspired by the Holy Spirit, to unite in one judgment and come together in the same will.

Moreover, if by carving we make rough timber serviceable, and by polishing we compel unworked stones into a useful work, what do you judge ought to be done with rational human beings? That they may be joined together, they must be shaped; that they may agree, they must be cemented with the glue of charity, lest they fall apart. All this the organs placed in church teach me. Are not we also organs of the Holy Spirit?

Finally, let anyone who removes these things from the church remove from it every vocal sound as well, and, with Moses, pray with unmoving lips; let him wait until the Lord says to him: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV). But if we do not reject jubilation or harmonious vocal sound, let the envious speak, let the critics speak, let those who disagree with themselves say what is to be done.

[Col. 1178D] We state plainly that organs are good, if we understand their mysteries and draw from them spiritual harmony. For the ruler of all things indicated this harmony to us when he joined together elements greatly discordant in themselves and bound them with harmonious rhythm. This is what organs, drums, and cymbals provide for me; this is what the psaltery and the voices of those who rejoice provide—except when we pronounce the Scriptures syllable by syllable and distinctly.

If, therefore, we have organs, we promise to use them according to ecclesiastical custom; but if we do not, we may do without them without sacrilege. Hearing the organs, let us be joined in inward harmony and cemented by a twofold love.

### VIII.

Moreover, in the same church I saw a wheel which, by some artifice I know not, descended and ascended, continually turning. At first I thought it a vanity, until reason drew me away from that understanding. At last, through these signs of the fathers of old, I understood

[Col. 1179A] that Fortune’s wheel, adversary of every age, often throws us down to the depths; then again, a flattering deceiver, it promises to raise us to the summit of height. Yet it turns in a circle, so that we may beware the unstable dizziness of fortune and not trust the rolling of a wheel which smiles and flatters falsely.

Those wise teachers of old did nothing without deliberation. In making such things, they invited us to understanding. Thus Moses indicated this when he spoke through enigmas and gave testimony concerning animals that chew the cud and do not chew the cud, those to be eaten and those not to be eaten; he signified the same concerning fat, the same concerning kidneys, when he wrote (Lev. XI; Deut. XIV). Whatever things of this kind they did—and we do—can be a reading for us, if anyone is capable of reason. We are urged in every particular to take precautions against dangers.

[Col. 1179B] Those brethren often see these things, wonder at them, and are taught in this way why they were made. But for us, who have now become foolish, these things have become worthless, and thus we disparage them because we lack the intellectual eye. It is not difficult for anyone to say, “This is black,” if he does not know how to distinguish that this is white. Yet I attribute this more to present foolishness than I impute it to ignorance of inventions. Shall I cast away a chasuble if I do not know what a chasuble is? Whatever remains of the institutions of the fathers for our investigation, let us not immediately despise; but, as it is written (Lev. XIX), let us burn it with fire.

### IX.

The abbot of Fécamp frequently prolonged conversation with us amid those delays. In that discussion I discovered sufficiently that he was simply a servant of God, for he often wished to discuss the salvation of souls. He poured his complaints into our bosom, lamenting and groaning over many things. He confessed that the abbacy was a heavy and great burden and that, if he could do so without blame and without disgrace, he would gladly leave it. He hated every vice with perfect hatred, yet he was not jealous. So far as I could ascertain, he was generous, not prodigal, and sober even at feasts.

[Col. 1179D] I asked permission to depart and scarcely obtained it, because he earnestly begged me to rest with him for many more days. Yet overcome by our insistence and importunity, he finally consented. Meanwhile, privately summoning our chamberlain, he filled our travelling bag with his generosity and, without my knowledge, told our servant:

“These things are few for the present; but if God grants life, we shall make amends.”

Our servant, having taken the money, came to speak with us secretly and revealed the abbot’s pious theft of gold for us. I was surprised, but not offended; rather, I began to inquire why he had done this.

“It is the custom of this monastery,” he said, “and it has descended to us from our predecessors, that no person whatever should leave us without a gift, unless he has felt the charity of this church. You would have felt it more generously, reverend Father; but I am hindered by the fact that I am still new in this rank and, compared with our father lord Abbot William, ignorant and unlearned.

[Col. 1180A] “Yet you shall not leave fasting, because it is winter and it is written: ‘If I send them away fasting to their own homes, they will fail on the way’ (Mark VIII).”

After the meal I departed and happened, on the road, upon a two-wheeled wagon laden with the abbot’s provisions, making its way to the place where I was to lodge. At his word, I say, the abbot had already arranged that very lodging, had joined to our party his nephew and his own attendants to serve us, and had not omitted to give me certain garments as well. We were served carefully; at first light, scarcely able to tear ourselves away from one another, we returned to our Brittany.

### X.

After two years had passed, I returned to Fécamp and was received with no less joy than before. Then, as I was departing, the abbot gave me a Mauzerian cup, which I received with complete eagerness—as he was indeed sure that I would—because it displayed a most elegant turning, form, and material, and a precious stone, namely chalcedony, adorned the top of its cover. He added several other things as well.

So that he should not send me away empty-handed when I was going to Rome, in that same year he sent me golden consolation, thereby showing that he still remembered me. I have said these things in order to praise the generosity of the church of Fécamp and the liberality of its abbot, and to show myself not unmindful of the benefit received.

[Col. 1180C] I returned a third time and, as it seemed to me, was met with greater joy than ever before. Although the proverb commonly says, “Fish and guests stink after three days,” I was received more carefully on my third visit and was provided for with more attentive care. The men of Fécamp did not tire of showing themselves more cheerful and more pleasant in countenance. They protested and swore that, so far as concerned them, the proverb—which I had said to them in jest—was false, because they had never grown weary of me and indeed begged for my more frequent return.

They begged, therefore, that I should return for the dedication of the church, which they were to celebrate annually and festively and which was near at hand, and that I should in no way fear becoming a burden.

“For,” they said, “we are more saddened by our departure than by our arrival. We speak simply, because we blush to speak with one heart while holding another in the heart. It is not ours to speak anything feigned, for the community of Fécamp knows purity. Our possessions, thanks be to God, have been enlarged; the resources of the sanctuary committed to us are abundant. Why should we murmur against hospitality? Does not God love a cheerful giver (II Cor. IX)? And are we not commanded to be hospitable to one another without murmuring (I Pet. IV)?

[Col. 1180D] “It is a great danger if we grow lukewarm in the good of hospitality, because God abundantly provides for our church that by which our hospitality is sustained. Our house has hitherto known no creditor; it knows how to give, but does not know how to lend at interest.”

I yielded to the petitioners’ requests and pledged myself to return. The abbot, however, was absent, since unavoidable necessity detained him. Yet I found as many abbots as almost as many brethren—not because they behaved without order, but because individually and collectively they all devoted themselves to serving us. There was one Robert, one of the priors, still beardless yet old beyond his years, grey in mind, with abundant hair; he was the abbot’s chaplain and a man of admirable chastity. He ministered with such care and made preparation with such diligence for the early celebration of Mass that he almost compelled me to celebrate daily and obliged me to carry out ecclesiastical services.

### XI.

But, that I may not pass over the site of Fécamp, I shall briefly conclude concerning the place of Fécamp. That place, like a garden of paradise, lies in a lovely valley between two hills, enclosed on one side by cultivation and on the other by a most pleasant wood.

[Col. 1181B] The wood seems of such uniformity that it might be thought to have sprung up on one and the same day, or to have been cut down from its height to an equal level. The tops of its boughs, foliage, and small branches are so dense that, by their shade and greenness, they delight the ground and the eye, repel the burning heat of the sun, and withstand the onset of rain. The trees rise a little from their trunks, though they are not very tall, and make for pleasant walking.

The Ocean Sea lies close to Fécamp, for it is not even a mile distant from the place. It abounds in fish, produces daily ebb and flow, and has a tranquil harbour. A valley is watered by clear fresh water. It has springs, is suitable for gardens, and nourishes fruit-bearing trees. The stream that flows past the castle has pleasing and useful courses. The very noble castle is encircled by strongly fortified walls.

[Col. 1182A] The natural river Seine is about fifteen miles from Fécamp; fishing is abundant, and that catch supports Fécamp. The monastery is built high with very handsome walls and is in large part covered with lead. That hall is called the Gate of Heaven and the Palace of God himself, and is likened to the heavenly Jerusalem. It gleams with gold and silver, is adorned with fitting silk hangings and relics of saints, and especially glories in the invocation of the Holy Trinity and in the custody of the blood of the Lord Jesus, gathered from his limbs when he was buried by Nicodemus, as blessed John testifies (John XIX). Pilgrims flock to it solemnly and in companies, especially because the place is dedicated in honour of the most high God.

I embrace, love, extol, and venerate that place with my whole effort. Our brethren, fellow-soldiers, abbot, and monks: greetings from us; and count me, I ask, among your friends and faithful ones. I do not love you merely because you are generous to me, but because, as I believe, you possess true religion and endeavour to assist everyone for Christ’s sake.

[Col. 1182B] I love you for your community; I commend myself to you because of my need. May God increase my desire to satisfy you; may he make your kindness serene toward loving me; and may he help and stir both us and you to serve him. Amen.

[Col. 1181]

## LIFE OF BLESSED ROBERT OF ARBRISSEL, BY BALDRIC

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXII, under Robert of Arbrissel.)

[Col. 1181]

## HISTORICAL POEMS OF BALDRIC, BISHOP OF DOL

(Edited by Duchesne, *Scriptores historiae Francorum*, IV, p. 151, from an old manuscript codex in the library of the distinguished Alexandre Petau, senator of Paris.)

### On the mortuary roll of Abbot Natalis

[Col. 1181C]

On the roll, many anxiously reap  
A certain sequence of discourse, always beginning from Adam.  
But while they lament the sin of the first-created man,  
They often labour in vain to append many things.  
But now we must speak of Abbot Natalis;  
Therefore what may profit has been added in writing.  
May Natalis, cultivator of monastic religion,  
Be joined, through Christ’s mercy, to the citizens of heaven.

[Col. 1182C] Nicholas, by your prayers and merits protect him,  
Who, while living, chose to have you as his patron.  
We should make, breathless, a poem for Natalis,  
If much poetry could benefit the faithful.  
But since the babblings of odes are of no benefit,  
Let us, I pray, put aside the trivialities of odes.  
Intent upon prayers, briefly inscribe the places,  
Lest an over-active pen bring waste to the page.  
While he lived, he was a firm pillar of the Church;  
Therefore may his soul, foster-child of Jerusalem, live there.

[Note: [Col. 1181C] Alternatively: “may a heavenly foster-child be his.”]

### On Abbot Natalis

[Col. 1183A]

Abbot Natalis had enlarged these buildings,  
And Pope Urban had consecrated what was newly made,  
When God, Nicholas, summoned his foster-child,  
To whom he gave eternal sleep in a solemn burial.

Here Natalis now lies, reduced to ashes in the flesh;  
May no guilt harm him because of the flesh’s defilement.

### Another on the same subject

Abbot Natalis, the special flower of abbots,  
Shows what man is: earth made beneath the earth.  
A white-haired man, a holy man of abundant merit,  
While living he benefited this Church far and wide.  
But dead, he adorns it with his sacred bones,  
Which this stone cherishes like a nurse.

Here, Nicholas, your devoted servant clung to you;  
[Col. 1183B] therefore now remember your servant.  
Commend to Christ him whom Christ has taken from the world,  
And protect him by the right of your patronage.

### On the roll of Rainald of Reims

If my Muse could in any way help the dead,  
I ought truly to have continued my Muse.  
But two things rather must be done for the dead,  
Which use and law mark out for us to do.  
For law and compassion weep for the dead,  
And the neighbour prays for souls to be saved.  
Therefore let us set down a brief Muse as a memorial,  
And let what is useless to instruction be far from our work.

Let us weep in sympathy for Rainald of Reims,  
But let us pray in aid of the patriarch.  
For you, best Father, our faces are wet with tears.  
[Col. 1183C] We pray for you; pray, we beseech you, for us.

The letter of the roll gathers beyond propriety many matters,  
Which, sparing frivolities as it were, we pass over unpunished.  
And it was fitting to spare the scanty sheet.

### On the roll from Le Mans

The page of the roll brings forth double sobs:  
First it wept for Johel, and finally for Hoel.  
One was an abbot; the other a bishop by order;  
These men had been, as it were, the sun of Le Mans.  
God touched both alike with one swift death,  
That they might be transferred to the great stars of heaven.

The examples of both alike shine upon us;  
May they both now illumine our darkness.  
But if any fault bestowed stains upon them,  
[Col. 1183D] may the Almighty grant them pardon for that fault.

Meanwhile, city desolated by such great patrons,  
Pour forth prayers for yourself, and remember yourself.  
Choose whom you wish; yet choose those who will benefit you,  
Whose rule may profit those subject to them;  
Whose teaching may offer you the two Testaments,  
And whose celibate life may fit them for the citizens of heaven.

The men of Bourgueil send you these written verses,  
Which it was fitting to send with prayers offered beforehand for you.  
May also the bowels of fraternal compassion compel you  
To commend our people—and us—to God in prayer.

### Epitaph for Hoel of Le Mans

Hoel died by an untimely event,  
The sun of the people of Le Mans and glory of bishops.  
Sweet in speech, second to none in piety,  
[Col. 1184A] he was for all an example of religious life.

His own people and neighbouring regions mourn him,  
Whom they rightly venerated as father of his country.  
Therefore they visit him, laid here according to solemn custom,  
And make vows before his holy tomb.

### Another epitaph
Faces grow wet, hearts groan, and bodies wither,  
when the inscription carved upon this tomb is read.

This inscription declares that Hoel, weighed down by death,  
made peoples orphaned by his death.

The city of Le Mans especially wept for him,  
the bishop whom the Lord had given them.

The holy bishop rests bodily in this tomb;  
may the bishop’s spirit attain the stars of heaven.

### Epitaph of Simon of Agen

[Col. 1184B] Simon, the aged man, bishop of Agen,  
was a Cicero in legal causes, a Cato in character.

Returning to his native soil, among the people of Bourges,  
he died and was buried in his own earth.

Holy Mary of Dol now shelters the bishop’s bones;  
the land of Dol had also sheltered him as a boy.

### In the roll for the Archbishop of Bourges

When, like a swarm, rolls have come to us,  
every roll announces death to me, not life.

Thus it is a cruel messenger, forever announcing that  
which ever assails us with tears and grief.

The roll reported the death of Rainald of Reims.  
Indeed, we saw the pallid limbs of Durand,  
when Pope Urban summoned us to Clermont.

[Col. 1184C] The roll of Hoel of Le Mans moved us.  
There remains now the document concerning John of Orléans.

Yet, if we wish to count abbots among these,  
the page of the roll laments many abbots.

Poitiers laments Gerald, and Le Mans Hoel;  
Angers, moreover, laments Natalis as dead.

I pass over many—some whom negligence removes,  
others whom forgetfulness takes away while I attend to other matters.

At last a roll came concerning a great bishop,  
whom a matter of singular affection commended to me.

He shone, as he deserved, with a double honour—  
if we call a double burden a double honour.

He was himself abbot at Dol and likewise bishop of Bourges,  
and presided over both sees without ambition:

[Col. 1184D] compelled rather by the advantage of both houses,  
and constrained by the holy direction of the lord pope.

Savage death carried off this vigorous Audebert in his youthful years,  
death which knows how to spare no one.

See: the letter of the roll gives me living tears.  
My inquiry will always make these tears return.

Audebert, do not depart from my heart;  
nor, if our prayers have any power, be rejected.

Therefore, brethren, provide for him by setting one of yourselves in his place—  
city of Bourges and flock of Dol—

and offer prayers for our dead;  
touch your common Father with a common petition,

that he may grant your shepherd a seat above the heavens.

### Invective against the roll-bearer

I beg that the courier may now spare us his so frequent coming;  
[Col. 1185A] through excessive use we dread his words too much.

May the prelates live, for whose death there wander  
the ravenous vulture, the black raven, and the flying courier,  
and likewise the owl, singing a dire omen to mortals.

They signify deaths and foretell corpses.  
Thus the roll always brings news of someone’s death.

Therefore let him be wholly banished from our gatherings—  
he who always announces death, who announces distress.

For if he comes often, he will lack the payment of a coin.

See, he has lately told me that Audebert has died  
and that the sun of the world has hidden beneath a cloud.

What will you do, Bourges, with so great a shepherd slain?  
What will you do, flock of Dol, now that your abbot is dead?

Take up lamentation, your face bathed in tears:  
both of you have lost an incomparable patron.

[Col. 1185B] And desire that I too, his colleague, remain in grief,  
whose vehement complaint will know no end.

Let him share in tears who shared in love.  
Companion while he lived, may I be companion while he dies.

### Epitaph

For the merit of his life, Audebert, a holy man,  
was granted a double honour: bishop and abbot.

Bourges had him as bishop, Dol as abbot.  
In word and deed he was sufficient for both.

His body is enclosed in a small holy tomb;  
now adorned with a double gift, a double honour.

Farewell, Audebert: may peace and everlasting light be yours.

### On the same man

That happy day shone with a fortunate sun,  
when Dol and Bourges were joined.

[Col. 1185C] These twin sees, at last under one shepherd,  
were made one after grievous disputes.

The city of Bourges scarcely snatched Audebert mutually into the episcopate,  
and then Dol as abbot.

Made bishop through the disputes of friendly contention,  
his own flock, wherever it was, retained him.

This Audebert, having discharged his double honour,  
succumbed to death while burdened with this charge.

Here rests the most holy dust of a holy patron.  
Father, often look upon your people from above.

### On the same man

Father Audebert, most holy father and bishop,  
see: Dol grieves for you; the city of Bourges grieves for you.

You ruled these places named above as father to these, bishop to those,  
[Col. 1185D] so that neither was devoid of your love.

See, you lie here—if the body is ashes and bones are body—  
may the spirit find rest in the Lord.

The learned bishop, whose body rests in this earth,  
was enriched by abundant learning.

He was abbot at Dol and priest at Bourges alike;  
one man benefited and presided over each place.

Though still in youthful years, unexpected death removed  
the common charge from this Audebert.

This monument shelters the body laid here;
