may the Almighty shelter the bishop’s soul.

### On the same man

Bourges languishes at your funeral, Audebert;  
how vehemently love awakens for you, and grief restrains it.

Yet Dol is not assailed with lesser lamentation,  
[Col. 1186A] whose flock burned with excessive love for you.

You were a dear abbot to these, an archbishop to those,  
for you could nourish both at full breasts.

You go to Christ, calling you by fitting signs,  
and as though preparing worthy rewards for your merit.

At every moment, patron, remember us,  
and help the flock redeemed by life-giving death.

### The same, on the same man

Hearer of poets, and himself the guide of poets,  
bishop at Bourges, but at Dol both bishop and abbot;

though by his conduct surpassing the years proper to youth,  
he vowed himself, while young, to the religion of monks.

This Audebert, buried in solemn fashion,  
sleeps, he who consecrated his life with a fitting end.

May he now also often look upon us from on high with Christ.

### On Rainald the clerk

[Col. 1186B] Rainald by name, whom this tomb shelters,  
was an outstanding clerk who knew how to flatter no one.

No one was ever more faithful among friends,  
and let this inscription now be his proof of faithfulness.

At Angers, leaving tears behind at his death,  
he slept in Christ; may Christ be with him.

### On the same man

Our age rejoiced in a restored Cato  
until it deserved to have Rainald for itself.

For he was keen in speech and keen in righteous deeds,  
an example of sobriety to all.

Abundant learning enriched him to the honour of his character;  
a torrent-like abundance of intellect raised him up.

See, Rainald, you lie as ashes. If any stain of sin clung to you,  
[Col. 1186C] may the highest grace of God cleanse it away.

### On the same man

The writings of the ancient Catos usually exalt their admirable morals  
for our own times and theirs.

But your great faithfulness, Rainald, a hundred times surpassed  
Cato’s, together with his constancy in justice.

Energetic in deeds, ready and keen in speech,  
you were an ornament of the clergy, an ornament of the people.

See, Rainald, you lie dissolved in a small tomb;  
may the Almighty grant you the forgiveness you need.

### On Guy

Guy, soon to depart for Jerusalem,  
bearing in his mind the duties of holy knighthood,

a man full of resources, you fell, anticipated by a good death;  
[Col. 1186D] here you are restored to the bosom of your native soil.

That day which preceded the sixth day of the sixth month  
alarmed the people of Angers by your death.

Now, therefore, Guy, may Christ, the heavenly guide, establish you  
in the peace of that Jerusalem. Amen.

### On Ralph

A very wealthy man, yet not a slave to wealth,  
generous to the poor, compassionate toward the wretched,

Ralph lies here, made dust from a rich man;  
once he was Angers’ abundance of counsel.

At your death, Ralph, grief takes possession of your city,  
and it humbly prays that you may live to God.

### On Ralph

Man, soon to become earth, why do you vainly pride yourself?  
This Ralph, laid here, teaches you what you are.

[Col. 1187A] The equal of the foremost citizens of Angers  
in eloquence, intellect, and abundant provision,

because he generously distributed his possessions among many needy people—  
then a man, now he becomes earth. Have mercy on him, O God.

### Again, on the same man

The people of Angers, shaken by bitter misfortune,  
have here laid down their great fellow citizen in tears.

Here, therefore, Ralph, you lie—once very wealthy,  
no small part of the people of Angers.

Yet you expended your own possessions freely in Christ;  
may God now repay you still more generously.

The morning sun and the twelfth day of May—  
alas, you hastened too much—brought your funeral.

### On the inscription of a house

You who praise Roman palaces, intent on their constructions,  
[Col. 1187B] praise instead this great work of John.

Here sculpture is fitting; the arrangement of stones harmonizes.  
Poitiers is praised for this work

as much as Rome is praised for its marble columns.  
Indeed, abundance of resources produced this work.

### On the same house

Whoever considers this building can know  
how prudent and how wealthy that John was.

By directing the masons and pouring out expenditures,  
he erected this structure equal to royal buildings.

### On Rainald the abbot

Philosophy rested in her beloved  
Rainald, whom she had made her vessel.

Here he flourished as abbot of Saint Cyprian,  
[Col. 1187C] enriching the church in discipline, possessions, and lands.

Almost every possession which the place had formerly,  
the father’s care made twofold.

At last the readier part of Rainald went to the stars;  
the part that was earth became earth.

### On Benedicta the recluse

Benedicta, a recluse, lay hidden here for many years,  
long rejoicing in contemplative repose.

Bride of God, clinging to the embraces of her bridegroom,  
she rested joyfully in peace amid those embraces.

This small prison was a pleasant home for her;  
now her dust lies here, while her spirit holds the stars.

### On Clarembald

Prudent in legal affairs, a sturdy knight in arms,  
born of free blood and full of wealth:

[Col. 1187D] now, Clarembald, you rest here partly as ashes,  
a cause of grief and lamentation to the citizens of Angers.

May your spirit dwell among the stars while earth covers earth;  
may you, now new earth, finally possess the heavens.

### On Pope Urban

Pope Urban, whom France called Odo,  
whom the land had brought forth as a tender boy,

was abandoned by the vital airs when dying,  
he in whom the world’s eloquent tongue thus fell.

So that the surviving world might lack a teacher like him,  
weeping Rome here laid her own to rest.

### On the King of the English

He who, with heaven indicating and a comet foretelling,  
subdued the English by innumerable massacres;

who was duke over the Normans and Caesar over the English;  
[Col. 1188A] who poured out wealth as from a flowing spring:

William, powerful in sovereignty, wife, and children,  
died and at once left all these things behind.

### On the son of the aforesaid man

Nobility, kingship, prudence, abundance of goods  
could not keep William from dying.

His father conquered Normans and English by war;  
the son held both peacefully.

Alas, harsh fortune! While he pursued stags,  
an arrow shot at wild beasts struck him down.

### On the same man

He who was great among kings and admirable to the world,  
who by his worth was both king and count:

a count over the Normans and king over the English, whose father  
[Col. 1188B] subdued the English by Norman soldiery—

while he hunted stags, William fell by the whistling arrow of a companion.  
He was king; behold, he is ashes.

### Again, on the same man

You who read this inscription, recognize that buried beneath  
is the king of the English, now a little dust.

Here you lie, William, son of William,  
who, fierce in fierce warfare, subdued the English by the sword.

While you pursued stags, another also aimed his blow;  
you yourself suffered a death intended for a stag.

### Again, on the same man

At his command Norman and Englishman trembled;  
with a wealthy hand he often showered riches.

Not differing from his father William in deed or name,  
[Col. 1188C] he had been a distinguished count and king.

In a strange death, intent upon stags, he endured a bow;  
thus too this great man is buried beneath this earth.

### On Ramnulf

Great father Ramnulf, venerable old priest,  
chamber of virtues, rich dwelling of God:

after conquering the Evil One with every virtue,  
you promptly depart, freed from flesh, to those above.

Here, great old man, your bones rest solemnly,  
and this tomb has been given to your bones.

Behold, your rejoicing spirit abides above the eternal stars;  
father, often look upon your people from above.

### On the same man

Ramnulf was another Tobit in a distant age:  
having lost his eyes, he worshipped God in spirit.

[Col. 1188D] Satisfaction for the poor, rest for the weary, a path for the fallen,  
he was a priest, a sacrifice pleasing to God.

A pleasing fragrance of incense, burned like incense,  
giving his soul to heaven, he returned his bones to the ground.

Here, Ramnulf, you lie buried in solemn fashion,  
but you live in a more solemn citadel of heaven.

Death brought perpetual lamentation upon the people of Angers  
when it took the young Martel away from those above.

The good prince had restored golden ages to the world,  
making the times peaceful after wars were stilled.

While he laboured to heal peace once more after it had been harmed,  
a cruel arrow struck him while intent upon peace.

Here, Martel, you lie, noble heir of Martel,  
whose deeds worthy of Mars gave you your title.

[Col. 1189A] You were a lover of peace, and so a lover of peace  
that nevertheless you were warlike Hector himself.

You would have reformed the age and the people in the toga;  
had you lived, you would now have been Octavian.

Sparing subjects and curbing proud necks,  
you had attained the height of an excellent prince.

A cruel arrow forestalled your successes,  
secretly aimed by a traitorous archer.

A martial cause made you be called Martel,  
but Geoffrey was the name bestowed upon you.

Here rests a virgin who, unmarried,  
married Christ: God’s bride, knowing no marriage.

Constant in heart, Constance shone in name,  
of the illustrious lineage of noble fathers.

[Col. 1189B] Abundant learning enriched her mind,  
so that she might be thought a divine Sibyl.

See, beneath this tomb the dead virgin turns to ashes;  
may her spirit, flying away, dwell on high among the stars.

Hugh, first bishop of Die and afterwards bishop of Lyon,  
a great son of the Roman Church,

whom the Roman pope requested as his legate—  
coming to a synod, alas, he died.

A chamber of virtues, a hall of divine nectar,  
the man of Susa buried in this earth.

Justus rejoiced, a good host in so great a guest,  
whom God had sent him as an exceptional companion.

Lyon, mourn: your solemn councils  
fell with the death of the Father.

## Inscriptions suitable for the deceased named below

### On John, Archbishop of Dol

[Col. 1189C] Splendid from his forefathers, himself the glory of his forefathers,  
a Breton by nation, this man is buried in this tomb.

Leaving behind arms, homeland, children, and mother,  
a duke now becomes at once a monk from being a duke.

Because he lived honourably, he was chosen bishop  
of the metropolitan see named Dol,

so that he who had been their count might, as bishop, provide counsel—  
and might provide better counsel as bishop than as count.

He came to the pope and asked to be consecrated by him;  
while this was delayed, he died in the Lord.

[Col. 1189D] Here is laid a worshipper and lover of religion,  
whom the Bretons mourn and holy Wisdom shelters.

If you ask his name, know that his name was John;  
and, if the day of his death: give the tenth of the tenth [10 October].

### On William of Montsoreau

The inextricable hour gathers without delay  
servants with nobles and boys with old men.

If nobility could prolong lives,  
a man of ennobling house would not die.

Alas, William, you had nobility enough;  
yet you are nobly taken away to those above.

Within a small grave are bones of great lineage;  
this grave holds your noble limbs.

If you injured anyone, if you deserved anything ill,  
yet may Christ be present; may you enjoy peace. Amen.

### On Lord Berengar

[Col. 1190A] All Latin eloquence languished but flourished  
while it was vigorous at Tours in master Berengar.

But Latin eloquence, once flourishing, now languishes,  
since envious fate removed so great a light from Tours.

The door of life was closed to you in January, doctor—  
or rather, in January the door of life was opened to you.

See, great old man, your dust lies beneath this vault,  
yearning for the return of its proper condition.

And though the hope of your merits promises you forgiveness,  
let the reader hasten it by making a devout vow.

### On Frodo of Angers

Whatever a Latin scholar knew of the quadrivium and trivium,  
you, Frodo, had heard all of it fully.

A diligent scholar, you almost surpassed the Latins;  
[Col. 1190B] when a brief hour struck you with grievous death.

Carried away from Angers and buried in English tombs,  
you gladden the English with Angevin dust.

Englishmen, reverently keep Frodo’s ashes,  
and make his soul glad with your prayers.

### Again, on the same man

Frodo, what profit was it to know the depths of books,  
with your Aristotle worn out night and day?

What did Ovid’s poetry, to which you clung for so many years, profit you?  
What are Cicero, Statius, and Virgil to you now?

All these together promised you a golden age, Frodo;  
yet black day took all these things away together.

The accursed hunger for gold led you into English kingdoms;  
much learning and much hope of gain were yours.

Weeping Angers commands the English to need your body;  
[Col. 1190C] let learned readers command the heavenly dwellers to receive your soul.

### Again, on the same man

Frodo, labour had made you the equal of great poets;  
now death has made you the equal of the shadow that flees.

An exile from Angers, you had tirelessly travelled the world,  
seizing little learning and devoting yourself to studies.

At last golden hope invited you to the English;  
there unexpected death carried you and your hope.

Let all who devote themselves to studies lament you, Frodo,  
for when you died, a great part of them fell.

See, dead, you lie: dust made from dust.  
I pray that God may be gracious to you, Frodo.

### On Peter, Prior of Dol

Peter, adorned with the honour of the priorate of Dol,  
prudent in deeds and himself the rigor of the order:

[Col. 1190D] after you overcame the bishop of Bourges,  
as he strove to tear apart this place,

with peace restored and the brethren’s resources multiplied,  
at last, oppressed by too-hasty death, you died.

Your death has brought us tears that must endure;  
but special love asks for diligent prayers.

This stone shelters Peter—alas, alas—now ashes;  
Christ, living stone, may you shelter his soul.

### Again, on the same man

The community of Dol rightly made you prior, Peter,  
for your virtue had preferred you to itself.

Richard, bishop of Bourges, ravaging the aforesaid flock,  
succumbed, overcome by your worth.

You improved your subjects in discipline and resources,  
[Col. 1191A] powerful in counsel and endowed with eloquence.

See, this stone shelters our Peter in bodily form;  
but you, Almighty One, shelter his soul.

### Again, on the same man

Peter, you were dean, and rightly dean, Peter,  
for, as you ought, you were all things to all.

The brethren of Dol grievously mourn your death,  
whose affairs you had strengthened by excessive effort.

You so opposed Richard of Bourges  
that the bishop himself yielded to your speech.

See, Peter, as one buried, you inhabit a decaying tomb.  
May your spirit, seeking the heights, inhabit the stars.

### On the canon without private property

Rainald, the flourishing rose of the clergy of Poitiers,  
eloquent, truthful, and a lover of religion,

[Col. 1191B] was the first to establish for you, land of Poitiers,  
a canonry possessing no private property.

Having completed the course of a life so well ordered,  
at last lifeless he is placed beneath this tomb.

O highest priest, be a dwelling for his spirit;  
and Christ, remember your priest.

### On Godfrey of Reims

A joyful treasure of great philosophy  
and a great Muse perish when Godfrey dies.

This ornament of the clergy, another sun fit for the world—  
had he himself lived long, he would have sufficed for the world.

But unrestrained death put its bridle heavily upon him  
and, envious, carried away a great radiance from the world.

Reims has his body; may heaven be the soul’s dwelling.  
Rich urn, farewell to rich bones.

### Again, on the same man

[Col. 1191C] To be mourned by the world, but especially by the city  
called Reims, here, Godfrey, you lie.

Especially attended by the rich tears of the clergy,  
you have at last been returned to your mother’s bosom.

Lamp of the people of Reims and of the Latin clergy,  
you wring tears from all by dying.

Gaul embraced you with such great love  
that it grieves not to have lain down with you at the same time.

Now, insofar as mourning Gaul can walk upon her feet,  
she still accompanies you with laments and prayers.

### Again, on the same man

The man whom this stone covers would not have been equalled by Tully,  
if both had belonged to the same age.

[Col. 1191D] For such wisdom had filled this poet  
that you would think him to have surpassed the Romans.

Finally, he was as great as flying fame, published through the world,  
has made whatever men it pleases great.

The devouring envy of death—alas!—took him from the world.  
Alas, Godfrey, you now lie in a small grave.

His mother, Reims, receive his divine ashes;  
and you too, Christ, be the dwelling of his soul.

### Again, on the same man

What powerful nature scarcely bestowed all together upon anyone,  
it had bestowed all upon you, Godfrey:

beauty, riches, character, memorials of descendants,  
a discerning heart, abundant intelligence;

a countenance equal to your intellect, love of flourishing study—  
yet all these things could not keep you from dying.

[Col. 1192A] See, a small urn contains your distinguished limbs;  
Reims gave you birth, and Reims also possesses you.

Happy city, revere your own, made happy by his dust;  
may heavenly citizens shelter their fellow citizen.

### Again, on the same man

Until antiquity itself blots out these letters,  
or a hostile hand is banished from celebrated honour,

that Godfrey, whom the bright Muse produced second only  
to Ovid, whom abundant learning filled—

see: eternal fame still endures for Godfrey,  
and will endure while fame can fly.

Reims gave him birth, and Reims buried him:  
earth honours earth, but his spirit dwells among the stars.

### On Alexander of Tours

When death has inflicted countless tears upon the world,  
[Col. 1192B] it now inflicts greater tears.

For Alexander, the particular ornament of young men,  
died, oppressed by untimely death.

Still an adolescent, he had not lived twice ten years  
when the beautiful rose withered from what it had been.

He was a canon of Tours, a boy of lofty talent—  
once a rosy flower, now muddy ash.

And if beauty and age drew stains upon him,  
yet forgive him, O King, giver of both.

### On the same man

Although my care has given inscriptions to many tombs,  
it has given none more mournful than this inscription.

For Alexander lies here: grief to the world at large,  
and especially to his own people, the flower of youth.

His beauty surpassed the beauty of young men  
[Col. 1192C] more than saliunca surpasses the rose, or the violet the broom-flower.

At last you would see the dead man’s limp neck  
like lilies cut off from their stalks.

The clergy of Tours weep for him, and so does everyone  
who feels compassion for tender age.

### Again, on the same man

Whatever greater beauty nature could possess,  
it had bestowed equally upon Alexander.

Though it had bestowed whatever things are thought beautiful,  
yet he is dead: see, he lies here as ash.

He scarcely reached four years beyond fifteen  
when death took all things from him together.

See, the glory of beautiful flesh stinks, though worthless;  
but, God, forgive what he deserved ill.

### Again, on the same man

[Col. 1192D] You who hasten hastily to the doors of the present church,  
stop, if you wish to know whom this stone covers.

Here rests the dust of one Alexander,  
whom unique beauty had set before the world.

Here among young men, like the most conspicuous star,  
he was pleasing to clergy and pleasing to people.

Here, when he was about twice ten years old,  
the tender flower, touched by grievous sun, fell.

You who read these lines, if you pity the one turned to ashes,  
say in prayer: “God, spare the tender boy.”

### On William, Bishop of Angoulême

Noble exemplar of noble men, William, and their glory—  
alas! here you rest, turned to ashes by swift death.

You were bishop by order, count by the blood of your forefathers,  
[Col. 1193A] prudent in deeds, second to none in speech.

Angoulême, grieve, bereft of so great a patron;  
see, you languish, deprived of the guidance of your bishop.

Fear destruction: deprived of guidance, you languish,  
for you know none comparable to him.

Yet, unhappy city, revere your father’s limbs.  
Say also: “May William’s spirit pass beyond the stars.”

### On Eriland

Eriland, whom abundant learning raised as a great radiance for the world,  
you lie here, to be mourned by the world.

Great old man, equally charming in speech and conduct,  
you would have sufficed for the world had you lived long.

Neither death nor old age could have harmed anyone, if you  
had not known death or old age in such a way.

But because dying is common and life slips away,  
[Col. 1193B] let there be restraint in tears and room for prayers.

While your earth covers you, may your bones rest gently;  
and may peace with Christ be yours, Eriland.

### As above, on Peter the prior

Death, unrestrained, rages as though its reins were broken.  
For it takes young men, and it takes old men too.

But whatever it has taken, whatever wicked deed it has done,  
in striking Peter it has dared a greater crime.

This Peter was a monk of Dol  
and dean of that same house.

Acting prudently, he governed that house so  
that, alive, he now causes living tears by his death.

Now, Peter, you lie here—if Peter is bones and ash;  
may God’s spacious house be a dwelling for your spirit.

### On Gerald of Orléans

[Col. 1193C] Gerald, outstanding teacher and great sophist,  
strength of the Church and pillar of clergy and people,

hope of orphans, generous supporter of widows,  
light and particular ornament of Orléans;

a man grey-haired, strong in the governance of character,  
from whose understanding enfeebled old age took nothing:

at last, touched by the common image of death,  
he put off what he was; his portion of earth is given here.

His living spirit slips away into the thin airs;  
yet, if anything from muddy affairs clung to it,

may Christ’s merciful compassion wholly expiate it.  
Reader, assist these prayers by adding “Amen.”

### On Odo, Abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély

You who hurry past the memorials of this tomb,  
[Col. 1193D] pause your step, I ask, to read its inscription.

Here lies the glory and particular ornament of abbots,  
abundance for the poor, Odo himself needy.

A lover of piety, exemplar of monks, he fittingly  
benefited the church of Angély.

At last, lulled to rest by a peaceful death, he rested:  
Odo, strength of the church and vigour of the order.

You who read this, do these two things for Odo: make devout prayers,  
and make yourself anxious about the fear of death.

### On Ralph, Archdeacon of Poitiers

Having fittingly discharged the honour of the archdeaconry,  
counsel of the people, light of the clergy of Poitiers,

Ralph, whom the height of excellent wisdom had richly endowed,  
lies here, dust made from dust.

City of Poitiers, mourn, bereft of so great a minister.

[Col. 1194A] In grief strike your breast; tear your hair in disarray,  
since you lack a person equal to him.

Yet never restrain your petitions amid tears,  
that Ralph’s spirit may obtain forgiveness.

Let boy and old man, and the reader too, ask this same thing.

### On Bishop Durand

Here lies the venerable bishop Durand by name,  
whose gracious life commended him to God.

The highest grace of God granted him  
a splendid funeral, whose form was a triumph.

Pope Urban, having summoned a general synod,  
called twice a hundred Fathers to attendance.

On the third day before the tenth day of December  
the light of his present life was taken from him.

Clermont, reverently keep these holy ashes,  
[Col. 1194B] and be more secure under his patronage.

### On the same Durand

In muddy times, a man of great energy,  
Durand restored golden ages.

As bishop he made Clermont most worthy of a bishop;  
as a religious man he made it worthy of God.

You would say that his funeral resembled a triumph  
and showed the marks of God who ordered it.

Urban was present, surrounded by a hundred bishops;  
the number of abbots was greater still.

When the mournful third day before the tenth of December came,  
the day of return is now a feast-day of mourning.

### On the Count of Poitiers

If worldly glory produced monuments faithful to their subject,  
none would produce one more fittingly than you, duke.

[Col. 1194C] You were a high-born man, an ornament to the world, duke of Aquitaine,  
terrible to the enemy, father of your country.

But, William, let your inscription—and your work—be known:  
the work of this Church in which you are buried.

### On a young knight

Godfrey, second to none in spirit or beauty,  
rests, lulled by untimely death.

Stronger in spirit than his tender limbs could be,  
before the age of knighthood he took up a knight’s arms.

The boy of high nobility slept in Christ.  
He was not fifteen years old, but would have been fifteen  
if he had been permitted to live fifteen days more.

In flowering May, this rose withered as a rose;  
the fifth day before the end closed both his day and his years.

[Col. 1194D] This monument holds him entrusted to it,  
and Godfrey becomes a monument of tears to his own people.

### On Elpe, Countess

Beauty, age, and royal great-grandfathers did not remove  
the bounds of death from you, whom such fates had placed,

Elpe, so that neither would have disgraced you as queen.

### On Burchard, the good knight

If I set a hundred tongues in motion for you, Burchard,  
I could not match your praises.

For no one’s virtue will be comparable to yours,  
however many men poetry may magnify.

You alone so subdued the men of Turin  
that they believed you to be a thousand men.

Guardian of the widow Agnes and tamer of criminals,  
you fall as avenger of a wife’s adultery.

[Col. 1195A] The noble body born at Tours rests here;  
may the spirit have a home in the Lord.

### Again, on the same man

If anyone recounts Achilles’ deeds in admiration,  
let him recall Burchard’s deeds as greater.

Second to none in the valour of body or mind,  
had he lived long, he would have been another Julius.

[lacuna]

### Again, on the same man

Whatever powerful nature distributed among many virtues  
in making men good,

that, Burchard, bountifully generous, it had wholly given you,  
reproducing in you all the heroes at once.

Whatever others have received in parts,  
[Col. 1195B] you alone attained completely and in full.

Prudent in speech, robust and keen in arms,  
you were Cicero as advocate, Hector as warrior.

But while, for a small lordship of the duke at Tours,  
you hasten thunderously against the Lombards,

and subject that people to yourself by words and arms,  
you fall by the treachery of the people and of your wife.

See, nothing of you remains but dust and bones.  
Peace be with you: wars indeed were the cause of your death.

### On Raherius, the most daring man

The deeds of heroes used to be inscribed upon tombs  
so that posterity might read how great they had been.

But your deeds, Raherius, ought especially  
to be inscribed by the pen, for you were exceptional.

[Col. 1195C] For nature had made no one your equal,  
so that you alone surpassed all leaders.

A treacherous spear pierced both your sides  
while you wished to be a protector to your soldiers.

Happy urn, shelter him who terrified the vast world;  
may there be no terror for his body or his soul.

### On the same man

Trusting in his winged horse, he rushed like lightning upon the enemy,  
offering himself as an assisting shield to his own men.

Raherius fell—none was more daring—  
his two sides pierced by an enemy weapon.

He breathed out his spirit, suddenly mixed with blood,  
made a grievous example to soldiers.

He grievously paid the cruel wages of warfare,  
for which he gave both body and soul;

[Col. 1195D] and if God’s bride dares approach her bridegroom for such a man,  
let her herself pray to God for Raherius.

### As above

Raherius, a strong knight like another Achilles,  
unequalled in any respect by Hector’s praises,

whom mighty nature had adorned throughout the world  
with the titles and virtue of knighthood:

alas, he died by the blow of one soldier,  
having bought so harsh a reward of warfare.

Lamentation remains to soldiers for so great a knight.  
O that tears may benefit his soul!

His magnanimous body is entrusted to a small urn;  
may his spirit find the better lot it deserved.

### Again, on the same man

A strong breast, blond hair about the face,  
[Col. 1196A] a beard beginning to grow, and still few years:

these were slight grounds, Raherius, for living,  
yet they had offered you hope of a long life.

Nature had bestowed a bold heart  
and a strong hand on no one more than upon you.

The blow of a single soldier took all these things away at once;  
indeed, it compelled you to die by sudden death.

At last you are now enclosed as dust in a small tomb;  
but the place of your soul is now known to God.

And if bold faith offers prayers for such men,  
let gracious faith offer prayers for you also.

### To his shield

Shield, now bereft of your master, rest—  
no master equal to Raherius will there be.

Live, destined to behold feast-days for a long age;  
[Col. 1196B] for no spear is now to be feared by you.

For if Raherius lived, or anyone his equal,  
such great leisure would not be owed to you.

His death makes rest for you; his life would make labour.  
But that labour would be worthy of honour for you.

Never second, always first, you would go against the enemy;  
you would neither know anxious retreat nor flee.

Let those who see you weep for so great a knight,  
and may you long endure, placed upon his monument.

### On the man to whom it happened

You who read the laments above your buried men,  
you who are accustomed to mourn five lesser men crushed by misfortune,  
pour out your tears for me, now ruined.

I was a great count, father of my country, enemy to enemies,  
William by name, all things to all men in every station of life.

[Col. 1196C] But now, having obtained the final lot, as each one does,  
I have died not by my own law but by the law of Him who commands,

whose law changes all things into another being.

Alas for me! Reader, nothing more remains of the count  
than that your prayers may improve what I have done.

Read this, now enclosed and buried beneath this vault:  
where man is buried by the common law, I shall rise again.

### On Osanna

Reader, if perhaps you ask what I was and what I am:  
I was born a girl; now I have become ashes.

I entered marriage solely from love of offspring;  
I died while giving birth to my tenth child.

Nor was the child born by the ancient manner of birth:  
after his mother had been cut open, the son was extracted.

[Col. 1196D] The cause of my marriage became the cause of my death.  
I was a count’s wife; Osanna was my name.

But what do rank, riches, and abundance of children profit?  
Christ, help me; be my dwelling.

### On Guy

Exiled from my city, while I pursued books  
as though they were fleeing from me, and devoted myself to studies,

alas, a lamentable hour fell upon me;  
for unexpected death came upon me.

See, my body turned to ashes rests beneath this tomb.  
May my spirit obtain the better lot it has deserved.

Yet constancy of faith and confession of sin  
at some time make me secure of forgiveness.

What I await, however, may the multitude of readers  
[Col. 1197A] and their company of votaries together hasten for me.

I was a citizen of Tours, Guy by name,  
of patrician stock; now Reims possesses me.

### On John

When John dies by untimely death,  
he is released from death’s cruel dominion.

For he rather lives who seems thus to have died.  
No artifice of pleasure clung to him.

His age had scarcely completed half a year;  
the day of baptism itself was also the day of death.

Therefore Christ’s grace alone benefited him,  
though it justly precedes those without merit.

Thus there is abundant cause for rejoicing at John’s death,  
since in dying he needed no prayers.

### On the boy Odo
[Col. 1197B] A small urn and a modest stone placed over the urn  
indicate that they contain but a little substance.

What this stone weighs upon are the bones of a tender boy—  
if, indeed, a single day sufficed to harden his bones.

This boy was almost born and reborn at the same time;  
he could scarcely live, and soon deserved to die.

Yet the name imposed by hastening death  
is made clear by these signs: the boy Otto lies here.

**On Burchard, again.**

Although Tours may have surpassed Roman achievements  
by the distinctions of its soldiery and by its worth,

yet you, Burchard, surpassed the men of Tours  
by the distinctions of your soldiery and by your worth.

But when at last you confronted Lombard treachery  
as avenger and pursued the guilty,

[Col. 1197C] Your adulterous wife betrayed you to enemies and culprits;  
thus, a great man, you fell from a slight wound.

This tomb now covers your high-minded body;  
but spare your spirit, gracious God.

**On Troilus.**

No age is exempt from the wound of death:  
here I lie, Troilus, a lifeless young man.

**On Rainald, Archbishop of Rheims.**

Christ’s grace had bestowed upon the people of Rheims  
Rainald, a light and steadfast pillar.

Taken also from the church of blessed Martin,  
he greatly benefited the church of Rheims.

Death struck him while he flourished in so great a pontificate,  
and likewise left the see vacant.

[Col. 1197D] His orphaned citizens, weeping for so great a bishop,  
placed here the body of their pontiff.

Let this people render fitting honours of earth to his clay;  
may the Almighty grant pardon to his soul.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January],  
he left the world and entered heaven.

**In the mortuary roll for William, abbot.**

Since William hastened to true being,  
although he first seemed to have gone to non-being,

yet, if in his haste he hastened by the straight path,  
all the friends of the Church judge that they should rejoice.

But if any error harmed him as he hastened,  
let the pious concern of the brethren ask forgiveness for him—  
a concern that, devoted, suppliant, and diligent, knocks upon God.

[Col. 1198A] Therefore we have said to Him: “Spare William, Redeemer,”  
that He may likewise grant pardon to us; say this for us,  
so that mutual prayer may unite us though far apart.

**In the mortuary roll for Adam, abbot.**

This is consolation for the desolate Burgulians:  
from Adam comes what your Adam has endured.

But grief over death is, as it were, made nothing,  
especially since Christ’s death is our remedy.

The physician will not be lacking unless there is no one for him to heal.  
O happy illness, whose cure is Christ’s death.

You too mourned because you were bereft of a good father.  
Surely you grieved more for your father than for yourselves.

Nor is it strange: the love of the heart drew forth tears.  
But let this pain fall away. God is the medicine of pain.

Provide for the Father by making pious vows for the Father,  
[Col. 1198B] and also for yourselves, by now supplying yourselves with a Father.

**Lament for his master.**

Mirror of teachers, beloved teacher,  
worthy to be matched with the titles of the great,  
O Hubert, man revered for your virtues,  
I offer unceasing tears at your funeral rites.

Your death is cruel to me.

When you have been taken from me, what joys remain to me?  
The capacity for rejoicing has failed.  
There is granted, alas, a most abundant store of mourning  
and perpetual complaint.

Woe to my life!

Hubert, paternal guardian of his country,  
a bright lamp, has fallen at Meung.  
Since then the light of this day has been sad for me;  
[Col. 1198C] I scarcely know what I am doing when I act.

Your death is cruel to me.

Grief burns our hearts to the marrow;  
a rare breath scarcely restores our inward parts.  
Hubert’s death becomes the cause of groaning;  
hence comes frequent panting.

Woe to my life!

Where have you gone, my other self—rather, my very self?  
Love long ago joined us in this bond,  
nor does death now subject us merely to the same lot.  
For me, to have died and to enjoy you would have been glory.

Your death is cruel to me.

Since then I mourn more with tears,  
and for that very reason I rejoice more—an unfamiliar thing.  
[Col. 1198D] The more the matter of tears displeased me,  
the more their sad weight pleases me.  
That both displeases and pleases: each is pleasing.

Woe to my life!

Sobs have produced halting verses.  
No poetic barriers keep elegies away from you, teacher;  
our complaint repeatedly says:  
“No remedy,” it says, “can alleviate this illness.”

Death, which will join me to you and you to me, pleases me.  
Death, I pray, come late.

**On Gerard, carried off at Laon.**

While Gerard increased praises by his praises,  
Angers possesses what is worthy of great praise:

as greatly as Cicero and Virgil in Latin learning,  
so brightly did another Aristotle shine among us.

[Col. 1199A] Light and glory of the clergy, a sun sufficient for the world,  
he brought forth for the world both quadrivium and trivium.

Yet fortunate was the Burgulian abbot,  
who claims Gerard as his own.

He died at Laon, but he lives among the Burgulians;  
and now they ransom his long life with prayers.

Therefore let whoever is rich in a deceased body  
commit him to the earth with special honour.

**Again, on the same man.**

Manegald, nourished abundantly at your breasts,  
later in time, almost earlier in learning,

Gerard was drawn from your bosom and came to the Andegavians,  
bringing both difficult and plain sayings.

By his own praise he multiplied the praises of Laon,  
expounding the arts with easy grace.

[Col. 1199B] Laon too envied Burgueil its possession of him,  
and Burgueil, smooth-tongued, snatched away the one whom Laon envied.

Now let Gerard rest with the Burgulian  
until one or the other is committed to the tomb.

O that neither death nor mischance may separate them  
until the white swan first turns black;

and until the black raven flies with white wings,  
until the returning Loire flows toward Laon;

and until the shrill cicadas fall silent and are strong,  
and old age or pain harms neither.

**To the same man, that he become a monk.**

[lacuna]

I myself know a place that, flourishing, gives birth to leisure—  
books, writing-tablets, and everything suited to students.

It is the place Burgueil, and a river called the Change  
[Col. 1199C] waters its gardens with an unceasing, crystal stream.

And in this place is a site almost removed from crowds,  
which protects the brothers from worldly anxiety  
and nourishes in its bosom the enduring children of peace.

Nearby the meadows are green, and the forest borders them.  
Let whoever strives to be upright purchase this place; let him redeem it.

**On the abbot of La Sauve-Majeure.**

Since the faithful customarily pray for the dead  
and perpetuate tears for those dear to them,

there is no need for either in the case of Father Gerald,  
who lived on earth as a citizen and inhabitant of heaven.

He dedicated La Sauve-Majeure to monks and to the Lord,  
voluntarily exiled from his native land.

[Col. 1199D] His native France became worthless to him, and he left it,  
coming to the woodland tracts of Bordeaux.

Behold, the woodland land now sends forth settlers for heaven,  
which flourished through Gerald, its cultivator.

Behold, the happy soul rejoices in the hall of heaven;  
may his body, laid here, bring joy to peoples.

**Again, on the same man.**

Here lies the most holy abbot of La Sauve-Majeure,  
the splendour of abbots and glory of monks.

He cultivated forests and made fallow fields for Christ,  
so that spikenard might produce roses and the willow apples.

This place, formerly woodland and savage ground,  
by his example is now the gate of heaven.

A man grey-headed, a man of perfect integrity,  
a citizen of heaven, has fallen asleep in the Lord.

[Col. 1200A] People of Aquitaine, embrace the body of so great a Father,  
whose fragrance of religious life still lives for you.

Gaul, rejoice with Gerald, whom you bore;  
and here venerate his holy ashes.

**Again, on the same man.**

Dove-like in mind, severe in the ardour of zeal,  
sweet in speech, outstanding in character;

generous to the poor, sparing toward himself, serene of countenance,  
compassionate toward all, with a heart that poured forth liberally.

Abbot Gerald lies here, buried in respect of the flesh;  
for his liberated spirit has taken possession of heaven.

The Gallic people, his mother, gave him to the Aquitanian people,  
and he cultivated the ancient forests of Bordeaux.

He benefited that land and that people so greatly  
that now both people and land bear fruit through him.

[Col. 1200B] This place, richly adorned, is wealthy in his precious bones;  
may the honour shown to his bones benefit the peoples.

**On the same abbot.**

A white dove of God, far removed from stains and wrinkles,  
whom no blackness of sin harmed;

like a soldier discharged from service and carried off to the king’s rewards,  
the abbot’s spirit claims the stars for itself.

But the ash that is joined with him from the earth  
rests in this soil, rightly called man.

His native land, France, which had been sweet to him,  
he freely abandoned, following in Abraham’s footsteps.

The worthy guest and first inhabitant of La Sauve-Majeure,  
he occupied these woodland tracts and cultivated them for God.

Gerald by name, a vigorous man, thirsted for things on high;  
here his body rests, his spirit possesses the heights.

**On the same abbot.**

[Col. 1200C]

Wise as a serpent, simple as a dove, Gerald,  
angelic in appearance, a pleasing swan in old age;

a lion in zeal, a suppliant lamb in suffering,  
gentle, mild, upright in religious life.

When with the divine plough you had subdued this land  
and gathered countless brothers to yourself,

at last touched by the common likeness of death,  
you gave your soul to heaven and your limbs to the bosom of the earth.

Pray for us, Gerald, venerable Father.  
There is no need for us to ask anything else for you.

**To Audebert, archdeacon of Le Mans.**

I judge you worthy to be matched with renowned poets,  
although you outshine those poets in achievement and fame;  
nor do you differ from Virgil in elegance.

[Col. 1200D] Having spoken briefly of Berengar of Tours,  
you seemed to us, unless I am mistaken, a great Homer.

**To the brother of Count Stephen.**

Farewell, Philip, mouthpiece of the lamp, boy of lofty promise;  
hail, destined one day to become a bright light of the clergy.

Though rank and more advanced age place me before you,  
love alone compels me to write to you.

I write what may benefit a growing boy  
and what befits both our age and our rank.

Receive as from a friend what love has fashioned, what I offer in friendship;  
keep it as a friend, and read it when alone.

For I do not wish my words to wander at the crossroads:  
no one except the unhappy has been free from envy.

Just as the line of lofty blood ennobles you,  
[Col. 1201A] so may the line of character likewise ennoble you.

Willingly submit to the rod and hands of your teacher;  
while there is time, learn diligently and turn over books.

The time will suddenly come when your age advances you,  
when nobility calls you away from study.

For if then, when asked, you do not know how to reply,  
even should you become a bishop, you will be a mute little ass.

Take care not to be too harsh toward fellow pupils;  
rather, remember that you are to be a pupil.

Do not reproach anyone with what he has done with you,  
nor with what a friend has told you in private.

If you are angry, nevertheless charge no one with a fault;  
for perhaps another time you will be at peace.

Nobility, a rash tongue, and insolent manners  
neither agree with one another nor fit together well.

[Col. 1201B] Born from noble forefathers named Odo,  
you were born that you might renew the Odos of old—

who lived in such a way that one was Julius in arms,  
Augustus in peace, Solomon in riches.

Indeed, one of them added Octodurum to his dominions  
and acquired Augusta under his own rights.

And he begot Theobald, foster-child of peace,  
from whom you, Philip, descend as the offspring of a prince.

Therefore, you whom so many leaders among your ancestors  
and counts among your forefathers adorn with ancient nobility,

give signs worthy of your nobility;  
by your own character outshine your ancestors.

Whether, Philip, I have spoken with kindly love,  
you yourself can discern from the sequence of thought.

If my words sound like uncouth rusticity,  
[Col. 1201C] believe me: I could not speak better.

It is the defect of one who does not know, not the fault of one unwilling:  
though I have not spoken well, I have said what I wished to say.

Finally, regard what you feel and what our will desires  
as though our poems themselves had uttered it.

May your diligence adapt the words to my wishes  
and value the force of my wishes more than the words.

Value the letter because a friend sent the letter;  
love what bears before it the name of friendship.

Now remember me; I too shall remember one who remembers,  
and may not even death divide us from ourselves.

**To Countess Adela.**

You go, my little letter, to see unfamiliar courts,  
to see the marriage chambers of kings and counts.

You go to win me the favour of an outstanding countess,  
[Col. 1201D] provided that you first win her own favour.

Win her favour by saying: “Hail, Countess;  
hail, rather, you worthy of the title Queen.”

She is, if you do not know, the daughter of that king  
who subdued the untamed English by the sword;

who struck with fierce steel the Northmen, resisting their father’s laws,  
and placed them beneath the yoke.

He led storm-tossed depths along the shore  
and, as it were, joined shores to shores.

Although he exceeded imperial expenditure,  
he possessed such abundance of resources

that scarcely could anyone reckon his treasures—  
lavish toward soldiers and lavish toward the Church.

Finally, he was so great that by himself he made the world  
[Col. 1202A] tremble at the name of his empire.

Yet it is uncertain which lineage of her two parents  
was the more equal and the more illustrious.

Her father, born of fathers and grandfathers, a count,  
had exalted his forefathers by his own worth.

He had added as much honour to his present fortunes  
as their fortunes had once added to his ancestors.

Nor was his wife inferior to so great a husband,  
whom royal nobility elevated.

She, powerful by descent from powerful nobility,  
was a noble shoot of the land of Flanders.

Thus fate had made these two equals, as it were twins,  
that they might be a special model of marriage.

The queen adorned the king; the king adorned the queen;  
each was an ornament, and the other’s ornament.

[Col. 1202B] The daughter succeeded her father, no less in worth,  
except that she does not bear the arms of a soldier.

Yet she would bear arms, were not the custom to forbid such work;  
nor is it fitting for tender limbs to be burdened with iron.

There is, however, one thing in which the daughter surpasses her father:  
she applauds verses and knows how to devote herself to books.

She also knows that rewards for poets are her concern:  
no one leaves her generosity empty-handed.

Moreover, she possesses an overflowing power of composition  
and knows how to prefer poems to poems.

Therefore do not be afraid: she is exceedingly gracious;  
she herself will grant time, and she herself will grant a place.

And, as I think, the countess will not send you away empty,  
though you are unpolished; she will act according to her custom.

Nor will she give you the little that you have deserved;  
[Col. 1202C] she will give what is her own praise and glory.

Her generosity is now almost known throughout the world;  
her gifts now summon men from the ends of the earth.

She is known to me, though I am not known to her;  
rustic simplicity concealed me from her notice.

Nor would I now dare to send a poem to her,  
but she ordered that she wished to have my poem.

Recently she heard something of our poetry  
and, applauding, indicated that I should add more.

I add it not because it can be equal to her worth,  
but that it may gain strength from her worth.

A great subject has ennobled my poems;  
my poems do not ennoble the subject.

Integrity of character and a chaste heart honour her;  
[Col. 1202D] noble offspring and love for her husband adorn her.

There are, nevertheless, many men whom distinction, integrity,  
and their own beauty can commend to women.

Who would attempt this woman? But what good would attempting do?  
She keeps the inviolable pledges of her marriage-bed.

Unusual distinction and incomparable beauty commend her,  
together with the charm of her conversation.

But who could soften so hard a flint?  
They look upon her to no effect, yet it delights them to look.

They deem the rewards great while feeding on empty hope,  
and by longing for her they provoke their own eyes.

Nor is it surprising, since her beauty shines so greatly,  
that she ought to surpass all maidens.

I would have seen her, had I not blushed as a rustic;  
indeed, while speaking to her, I blushed to look upon her.

[Col. 1203A] Then, unless my wandering eyes had turned aside,  
she would at once have drained every word from me.

At the sight of the Gorgon, very many are thus  
immediately deprived of their proper functions.

And before Circe many have likewise grown rigid,  
for they could not bear the goddess’s gaze.

Thus I scarcely saw her, yet I remember having seen her  
as I remember dreams that I have seen.

So I often recall that I have seen the new moon—  
or when I scarcely see, or think that I see myself.

I scarcely saw her; but, as I myself remember,  
her beauty is to be preferred to Diana’s.

**To the same woman, for the cloak she had promised him.**

The cloak which I ask, which I have asked—if you give it, Adela—  
should befit the giver and at the same time befit the recipient.

[Col. 1203B] No woman is greater to me; no woman is better to me:  
from a countess you will become a queen to me.

Our poems also will make you greater;  
by our poem you will be spread throughout the wide world,

so that Cyprus and farthest Thule may know you—  
Ethiopians, Indians, the Gaetulian, and every island.

I indeed speak great things, but I know how to speak great things  
since I have taken a countess as my subject.

You yourself supply me with poem and pen;  
you yourself will give breath and fill my open mouth.

You pay earned rewards to poets;  
you compel silent bards to become eloquent.

Therefore, Countess, revisit your poet as he speaks,  
and return, O lady, to the writer the cloak as his reward—

[Col. 1203C] a cloak gleaming with Phrygian gold,  
a cloak whose gem-studded circumference adorns the breast;

so that, when this cloak clothes my limbs from above, it may bear you upon its breast—  
a cloak that displays a price worthy of a countess,

which I may rightly call the countess’s cloak.

As you surpass queens and countesses,  
so may this work surpass the cloaks of queens and countesses—  
a work that makes you enduring beyond the stars.

I ask for great things, if you did not know how to repay still greater things.  
You yourself disdain the faint-hearted who ask for little.

I do not ask for things too lofty, nor do I aim at things too lofty:  
by whatever ornament, you ought to adorn your servants  
and at the same time enrich the treasuries of churches.

To have asked this is mine; let it be yours to grant it.  
Answer me so as to favour the right of each of us,

[Col. 1203D] and take care that the cloak lacks not even its own fringe.

**To Cecilia, daughter of the king of the English.**

Royal maiden, hail—hail, I say, royal maiden;  
a maiden then to be preferred to Roman girls,  
a maiden now to be preferred to maidens of her own age,

whom her august father made equal to the kings of the English;  
whom beauty of form together with love of virginity  
and excellence of character adorn with great praise;

whom her own zeal for reading splendidly adorns;  
whom a husband nobler than her father has graciously won.

Therefore, maiden, strive to please your husband.  
For you have not married just any bridegroom from the common herd,

but one more outstanding, whose beauty may make you endure.  
What the abundant language of books will say to you—

behold, maiden, whatever I may be able to do,  
[Col. 1204A] I offer myself according to my ability, or further if you wish.

I heard that you had kept a certain sister,  
whose fame once struck my ears;  
her name has escaped me, though I remember having seen her.

She was from Bayeux, but was then Angevin.  
If it please you, greet her on my behalf,  
and write back to me her name and your own.

**On Duke Roger.**

You whose father’s worth won you a duchy by warfare,  
whom peace and your father’s abundant worth make equal to him:

hail, Roger, illustrious duke, hail for long;  
make a special Burgulian greeting to yourself.

Yet your deeds outstrip our fellow countrymen,  
for your name is proclaimed throughout the whole world—

whether because you lavish rich rewards upon soldiery,  
[Col. 1204B] or because, a prudent man, you manage public affairs,  
which stand firm and are not to be shaken in your days;

or because you enrich churches with boundless gifts,  
or because at this time you invite the Muses  
by your generosity, so that Apollo cannot be silent.

**To the bishop of Ostia.**

Odes which, I wish, will please him to whom they are sent—  
I, a little man, direct them to great Odo.

Odo, glory of bishops and singular ornament,  
the pope’s counsellor, rule of justice,

strength of the Church, an unshakable pillar:  
Burgueil sends a greeting that he may welcome.

Burgueil sends greeting to the great patriarch,  
that Odo may secure for me acquaintance with the bishop.

Guido has celebrated you in my hearing;  
[Col. 1204C] by many indications he has made you known to me.

Guido carried your name into our world,  
and that man was to me the herald of so great a man.

Your bearing among nobles, which does not exceed the proper measure,  
made you known to me.

Guido said that you possess cheerful manners  
and speech fitting to those manners.

And, as he told me, rich literature enriches you,  
and you delight in the Muses of poets.

If you wish to sing, you sing with sweet melody;  
besides this, your face and expression are cheerful.

Sweet in address, open and wholly available to all,  
you cheer the sad and restrain the foolish.

Now alive, you are another Cicero, mouth of orators;  
[Col. 1204D] alive, you are Aristotle, skilful in words.

These present times, which are like a ship without a helmsman,  
have wished you to become their governor.

Those who made you Odo, as Rome made Odo bishop of Ostia,  
will soon make you lord of Rome.

Here provident fates have already begun to spin;  
here we discern them and now favour them.

Made heir to Odo in the pontificate,  
you will soon be appointed to the papacy.

This place, this name, and this abundance of speech signify it;  
the integrity of your lofty mind foretells it.

The garb of tunic-clad religion indicates it;  
the same Cluny produced you both.

It nurtured you both; Ostia raised you both:  
one was pope, and the other will be no less so.

[Col. 1205A] O that I may then flourish in surviving life,  
that then I may sing of you with all my voice!

Then Orpheus shall not be able to surpass our Muse,  
if our trumpet sounds with full breath.

For now my little boat is carried under stolen sails,  
since every kind of pirate makes a din.

They tear an innocent man with the teeth of detraction,  
and envy cries that I am deserving of death.

They object that I touch writing-tablets after the proper time,  
that I do not walk with lowered eyebrow.

Yet I whisper, and I also ponder psalms with myself;  
I look about with sidelong glances.

Since envy, like a thief, is a cruel stepmother to worth,  
for that reason I am often chilled in my studies.

But if your protection were willing to defend me,  
[Col. 1205B] if only you would love my poems,

the creeping ivies would soon spread more luxuriantly,  
whenever I should be supported by a bold sword.

Whenever I touch the lyre in bold performance,  
whenever I strike the Muses with a full plectrum;

whenever, fearless, I dare to be called a poet,  
whenever I hold the reeds with an untrembling hand.

If by word or by any signs you mock my poems,  
Odo, I do not fear thunderbolts—

thunderbolts which one defended by great Rome should fear?  
What should he fear whom your hand, O Odo, protects?

Deign to keep me under your favour, greatest Shepherd,  
so that, safer, I may see Rome if need be;

so that, safer with you as guide, I may behold Roman palaces,  
which my rusticity, without a guide, would fear.

[Col. 1205C] Now, secure as though of your affection,  
I commend to you what I desire utterly.

Do not make me, who presume upon you, ashamed.  
I ask what is due; give it to me, for you can.

If the asp blocks its ears in every possible way  
so as not to admit our prayers;

if you deny what is asked and can restore what was denied;  
if your heart is closed to my prayers;

if you are unwilling, without loss, to give what you can give,  
you are not he whom I hope for, whom I myself sing as yours.

O how I should hope, though I live far off and far away,  
that—may God avert it—you would do this to me!

Odo is my only son—indeed, my fellow abbot—  
for whom, devotedly, I stand at your feet.

[Col. 1205D] For the man of Rheims, who has wholly deserved the pope’s wrath,  
weighs his hand too heavily upon him.

For he placed the diadem upon King Philip  
and now in this matter also disregards the pope’s authority.

Therefore, Odo, I pour out my very heart  
that you may accomplish this easy matter for me.

Support his claim to the abbacy in proper order,  
so that that son of mine may be restored.

May what Roman authority confirmed in him  
remain unshaken and valid.

You can and ought, unless you despise me, Odo,  
to restore him as abbot to Saint-Remi.

I shall not be ungrateful: in gratitude I shall add  
gifts to poems, poems to gifts.

[Col. 1206A] Behold, exhausted, he has been unable to return;  
but if you command him to come, he will come.

He will now be secure if you write that he may return;  
we shall know that he is to be restored.

If you wish to send what you judge useful to us,  
know that Guido is in my place.

Guido lives for me: great, good, and faithful,  
of great weight and no small name.

Honour him now as you honour us,  
for he flourishes in the gracious simplicity of his character.

Many occasions extend this ode into prayer;  
but now, with brief conclusion, remember me, Odo.

**Again, on the same man.**

Without end I most earnestly wish my Odo well:  
my Odo, hail; hail, future pope.

[Col. 1206B] That I call you mine, presumption compels me to say—  
so very small a monk calling so great a bishop his own.

You whom I have never seen, whom I have absorbed only through my ears,  
I am compelled by excessive love to call mine.

I have admitted you wholly into my heart,  
for I have learned that you love poems.

You praise poets and offer rewards to poets,  
cheerful, wise, a dove free from gall;

compassionate toward the wretched, helper of strangers,  
more than all others free from harshness of character.

A greatest orator, a singular lover of poets,  
you invite my reeds to study.

I desire you such; I long for you such—  
as you are, and as I deserve you to be.

I ask you to owe me what friend owes friend,  
[Col. 1206C] friends whom unquestioned love has bound together.

Between such persons there is never a divided will:  
they think, live, and die as one.

Behold, if you deem me worthy, I pledge myself such a friend to you.  
O that you may favour my wishes, Odo!

If you give yourself to me, if you deign to be ours,  
among singers I shall be another Orpheus.

Now, too confident in your affection,  
I dare to make entreaty for my dear ones.

I commend my Burchard, whom I love greatly,  
to your protection and your counsel.

Guido’s household is burned by great poverty;  
Odo, rain down dew-bearing riches upon it.

**To Lady Emma.**

[Col. 1206D] Emma, glory and ornament of monastic sisters,  
receive the greeting sent by Burgueil.

Burgueil sends you greeting and offers this prayer:  
may it join you to me and keep you joined to me.

For philosophy has nurtured you with her own honey  
so that milk now flows from your breasts.

This was recently evident to me when I read your poems,  
which you had sweetened with unbought nectar.

Swarms of women pupils run to you  
that the bees may be refreshed by the honey of their mother bee.

If your order admitted male pupils,  
I myself would wish to be your pupil.

**To Amatus, archbishop.**

It is a bishop’s law to grant pardon to one who asks;  
he who forbids pardon dissolves the law.

[Col. 1207A] Best of bishops, thus favour me as I ask,  
so that your deeds may prove you a bishop to me.

Therefore graciously open ears long assailed,  
and let me, as a suppliant, find the pardon that I request.

With clouds removed, look upon me with a serene brow;  
I shall amend whatever is required, if I deserve pardon.

But if not, surely our complaint will touch their equals,  
so that bishops may correct such things.

**Verses of Odo to the abbot.**

This greeting your Odo sends you, Baldric,  
which he desires you to write back to him.

Recently, friend, I possessed and read your little book;  
I could scarcely believe it a work of this age.

So great was its weight of words, so great its eloquence,  
that Virgil might be believed to have composed it.

Hoping that my name was written among your friends,  
I turned over your book three and four times.

[Col. 1208A] Yet there was not even a slight mention of me there;  
this matter disturbed my mind greatly.

Surely, eloquent man, you judged me unworthy  
of being made perpetual in a poem of yours.

Yet the urn, the hare, the raven, the crab, and little asses—  
you yourself being witness—shine as stars in heaven.

And after so many illustrious names of great men,  
worthless little beasts possess the heavenly realms.

After the illustrious names of many great men,  
make your heavenly page receive me too.

I ask that one distich may cling to the margin of your book,  
by which your Odo may be read as inscribed.

If you deny what I seek by my merits and prayers,  
I shall nevertheless wrest it from you by my importunity.

I shall often send you these commonplace poems of mine,  
and so extract by persistence what I request, though you resent it.

[Col. 1207]

## BALDRIC’S POEM ON HIS WRITING-TABLETS: A FRAGMENT

(Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Supplement, p. 51, no. 11, “On the instruments which ancient notaries and copyists used for writing.”)

As regards the stylus, the ancients used it especially for writing on waxed tablets. We read in an old codex, now in the Ottobonian Library, poems of Baldric, abbot of Burgueil, partly published and partly not made public. Among them is one poem, mournful—indeed festive—on a broken stylus, which Baldric had used for writing on waxed tablets for ten years. Had the matter not been too slight for our purpose, I would reproduce the entire poem, in which the author describes the whole craft and use of the stylus.

This brings to mind Leo Allatius, who, having lost the pen which he had used exclusively for writing Greek for forty years, grieved so deeply that he could scarcely restrain his tears. In another poem Baldric plays upon his writing-tablets, which were coated not, as usual, with black wax but with green wax, doubtless to refresh the eyes. He also plays upon the stylus suited to them, which a certain Lambert of Anjou had made; and he praises the abbot of Sées, from whose gift he had received the pouch in which those tablets, scarcely half a foot in length, were enclosed. He especially commends their small size and form in these verses:

Your page measures scarcely eight verses in width;  
in length, however, it scarcely holds a hexameter.

Yet in you are likewise eight tablets,  
which make fourteen little pages.

For the outer ones lack wax on one side;  
thus eight make fourteen.

Thus they hold twice six, and they hold a hundred poems;  
the multiple little pages do this as well.

In his verses he also celebrates Gerard and Hugh, his notaries or scribes, who transferred his poems from waxed tablets onto parchment.

## ACTS OF SAINT VALERIAN, MARTYR, BY BALDRIC, AS IT SEEMS

(Chifflet, *History of the Abbey of Tournus*, proofs, p. 33, from the manuscripts of Acey, Chalon, and several others.)

[Col. 1209A] The glorious contests of the most blessed martyrs, undertaken for the honour of Christ our Lord and God, are celebrated with continual observances and an annual solemnity, so that, when the devout people come to know the faith of the martyrs, they may rejoice that these men have triumphed and may trust that they themselves will be protected by their patronage.

For it is well known that Eusebius, the historian of holy memory, bishop of the city of Caesarea, a most blessed priest of outstanding life, most learned also in ecclesiastical instruction and worthy of reverence throughout the world for his exceptional diligence, set forth—as far as, with the help of the divine Spirit, he was able to discover it by tracing the truth of what occurred—the cities, places, and towns of the several provinces that deserved to be adorned by the heavenly triumphs of martyrs, and during whose reigns, by an organized enforcement
[Col. 1209B] of official duties, innumerable persecutions were conducted. Though he did not expound the complete passions of each individual martyr, he nevertheless truthfully indicated to devout and faithful Christians the grounds on which they ought to be written or celebrated.

Thus this faithful worshipper cultivated the grace of God diffused throughout the whole world. Just as abundant harvests arise from the fertility of a field from a small seed of wheat and increase in multiplied plenty, so, through the account of the aforesaid man, the passions of martyrs, flowing out from the source of one book and disseminated in the writings of the faithful, have watered the whole world and are to be celebrated. We, however, following the order of events, have taken care to write the passion of Saint Valerian the martyr with that devotion which, Christ triumphing, we have learned was accomplished with most certain truth.

[Col. 1209C] Therefore, in the times of Emperor Antoninus, a most severe outbreak of persecution arose, to such a degree that it was publicly proclaimed throughout all the provinces of his empire by general authority and established by imperial decrees that wherever a person of the Christian religion should be found, without distinction of rank, sex, or condition, that person, after being afflicted by diverse tortures, should be punished by beheading.

At that time, in the city of Lyons, the greatest and chief city of Gaul, Pothinus, bishop of holy memory—whose consummation in martyrdom revealed the merits of his life—was regarded as a most learned instructor of Christians. As the aforesaid historian relates, he was seized by the persecutors along with forty-eight other martyrs and consigned to prison darkness; and fifty souls confessing Christ’s glory were thrust together into one prison. Of these, Saint Marcellus and Saint Valerian, summoned at night by an announcing angel, were released together. One of them made for the country of the Sequani, the other for that of the Aedui, with the Arar between them, by the prompting of divine providence: so that, through their instruction, the hearts of the pagans might attain to the grace of heavenly religion and the named provinces might always be fortified by the particular patronage of martyrs.

[Col. 1210A] At that time, after the glorious contest of Saint Marcellus’s martyrdom, accomplished under the examination of the governor Priscus, and after no long interval, the governor himself hastened from the city of Lyons to Tournus. He travelled at the herald’s proclamation, by public road in mule-drawn vehicles, and by the river Saône in ships, with his company divided; for Tournus, then called a military granary because soldiers’ grain-rations were distributed there, he reached when the day was already declining into evening.

There, when he learned through the report of mad pagans of the passion of Saint Marcellus, which had taken place in the city of Chalon, he discovered, by pagan accusation, that Saint Valerian had there a most secluded cell for prayer and had already made many people Christians.

[Col. 1210B] Then the utterly wicked governor spent that same night turning over cruel thoughts. When daylight came, as the cruelty of his mind demanded, he ordered his officers to seek out Saint Valerian and bring him before his eyes.

When the soldiers dispatched to his hut arrived, he, supposing them to be Christians in the charity of grace, invited them in the manner of hospitality. They first observed him, saw that he had the sign of the cross both inside his cell and marked upon his own face, and immediately seized him. In the zeal of their searching inquiry, they asked what that sign was which they had found inside his hut, or which he seemed to have marked upon his face when they came to him.

Then Saint Valerian answered: “This is the sign of salvation, in which the Lord of heaven and earth, Jesus Christ—reigning before the ages with the Father and the Holy Spirit and enduring for eternity—redeemed us by his Passion and, by dying, broke the bonds of death and bestowed upon us the rewards of eternal life.”

Then they said: “Therefore do you, companion of Marcellus, declare that you are a Christian?”

Saint Valerian answered: “I freely profess, in a voice that shall remain to the end, both that I am the companion of Saint Marcellus and that I am a Christian.”

Accordingly, when chains had been put upon him and his hands bound behind his back [Col. 1210D], as though he were guilty of a criminal offense, he was presented by the officials to the governor Priscus. When Priscus saw him, inflamed by the harshness of a beastly heart, he said: “Are you Valerian, who preaches Christ’s name and will perish through a superfluous error [Col. 1211A]? Or have the things done to your companion Marcellus, deceived by a similar error, perhaps not come to your notice? Take counsel for yourself by venerating the divinities of the immortal gods. Acknowledge those whom the authority of the most sacred emperor decrees are to be worshipped: whom our fathers too beheld, whose most holy images we worship, and whose offspring most manifestly rule the heavens. Worship therefore almighty Jupiter, and Juno, his wife and sister; likewise Venus, the daughter of so great a god; Vulcan and Mars, at once her brothers and husbands. If you do not do so, you will be punished with torments far more severe than those inflicted on your colleague Marcellus.”

Saint Valerian replied: “That you are governor and judge of the provinces is declared by the staff surrounding you [Col. 1211B]; but the error of the Gentiles shows you ignorant of all knowledge. How is it that, by your emperor’s wicked religion, you overthrow the decrees of emperors? What are these divinities of which you speak? The statutes of the laws command incest to be punished; yet with sacrilegious speech you profess as almighty god one whom you have not denied to have been the husband of his own sister, and you judge that I ought to worship his daughter Venus, the wife of his brother. Do you declare crimes venerable in divinities and condemnable in human beings? You confound yourself fully and abundantly by your own error. And you threaten that you will inflict upon me the torments of my most blessed brother Marcellus—torments overcome in a glorious contest? Would that you recognized yourself as defeated both by his courage and by your own pronouncement, and worshipped, with sound judgment, God, the Lord of heaven and earth, ruler and maker of all things [Col. 1211C]; who suffered without guilt, that by his death he might free us from the eternal guilt of death, and by his resurrection show us the assurance of everlasting salvation—whose kingdom is found to have neither end nor beginning. He is the true God, who is found not [Col. 1212A] in metals or stones, but in the temple of faith and in the grace of eternal blessedness.”

Governor Priscus said: “Do you not fear the torments that surround your punishment? And, as though you were going to justify [variant: judge] the judge, do you utter certain empty ravings? Now, as you fail under tortures, you will prove more plainly either the power of my divinities or the vain power of your God.” Saint Valerian replied: “Those tortures which you name have already been overcome by my fellow soldiers who went before me.” Then the most savage governor ordered the holy martyr of God, suspended from a post, to be torn with iron claws. And since, aided by Christ, he was not wearied by any torments but persisted in praise of the Lord, and since the wicked governor feared that through his perseverance many would come to the true religion [Col. 1212B] of the Christian faith, he ordered him to be released and then killed by the stroke of the sword in the place where we now venerate the relics of his body.

Then Saint Valerian, remembering the grace and glory of Saint Stephen, the first martyr and deacon, looked toward heaven and saw him offering a crown to his eyes—to him who did not fear, in dying, to grant martyrdom its victory. Thus the holy martyr consecrated that place with his body, while his spirit ascended to the kingdoms of heaven. As we celebrate his annual feast, let us pray for his patronage with devout minds: that he may increase the faith of the people, protect his own province, and preserve by his merciful intercession all the people attached to his worship; and that the devoted and faithful writer who has celebrated his triumph [Col. 1212C] may be defended by his patronage with eternal grace in this present age and in the age to come, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong dominion and power with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1211]
