## BALDRIC OF DOL’S CHARTER, CONFIRMING ALL THE GOODS OF THE MONASTERY OF ST FLORENTIUS  
*(Year 1109)*

[*Spicilegium*, ed. de la Barre, vol. III, p. 459.]

[Col. 1211D] Since things well done by the ancients are very often corrupted by modern people, and since the persistent greed of those ignorant of rights often disturbs not only secular but ecclesiastical rights [Col. 1212D], I judge it not unfitting, in view of the exigency of affairs and the condition of the times, to support the institutions of predecessors by the agreement of successors as though with certain props [Col. 1213A], and to fortify them with certain safeguards, so that one eager for another’s property may find nothing upon which to lay hands. With this consideration in mind, a certain matter was thus conducted by the monks of Saint Florentius.

When Lord Baldric, archbishop of Dol, was returning from Rome in the second year of his ordination, bringing with him the pallium—that is, the completion of his rank—he lodged at Saint Florentius in Saumur on the day before the Nones of March. On the following day, which then fell on a Sunday, he entered the chapter-house; and after he had spoken with the brethren, they asked him to grant them most firmly all the things which they possessed within his bishopric and which depended upon the consent of his authority, and to protect them by his authority. He promised that he would do this. [Col. 1213B]

Accordingly, three days later, on the day on which he was to depart, he caused the board to be struck very early in the morning; and, when the brethren had assembled [Col. 1214A], he entered the chapter-house and granted them everything as they had requested—while preserving, however, the claims of the canons of Saint Samson and of the church of Saint Mary situated in the castle of Dol. Witnesses of this grant are John, bishop of Saint-Brieuc, who had come with him and was present; Lord Abbot William of the same monastery; Orgerius, the prior; and all the other brethren then present in the community of Saint Florentius, whom it would be tedious to enumerate. The same Bishop John also granted us whatever we possessed in his bishopric and whatever we might acquire therefrom.

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1109, in the second Roman indiction, lunar cycle VIII, Paschal term XIV, on the Kalends of May, the day of Easter itself, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, the twenty-first day of the moon.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1130: HONORIUS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1213]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils* XXI, 319)

[Col. 1213C] Honorius, formerly called Lambert, was born at Bologna and was bishop of Ostia. At the assembly of princes at Worms, when Emperor Henry was freely relinquishing the investiture of bishops, he absolved him from the bond of anathema by the authority of the Apostolic See, whose legation he was exercising. He was elected pope on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January in the year of Christ 1124, in the time of Henry V, king of Germany, and Henry IV as emperor. Against him, in a schism, there was created the pseudo-pope Theobald, cardinal of Saint Anastasia, distinguished by the name Celestine II. But because the stronger party was with Honorius, says the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Theobald’s supporters, seeing the course of events, went over to Honorius.

The abbot of Ursberg says nearly the same thing in almost the same words, adding that Lambert had been very long approved in the Roman [Col. 1213D] Church and was known on both sides in the legation in which he had formerly labored vigorously in the German regions for the reconciliation of kingdom and priesthood; that he was consecrated with the unanimous favor of the clergy both far away and nearby; and that, according to the custom of that see, he was called Honorius, truly worthy of so great an honor.

William of Tyre alone, in book XIII of the *History of the Holy War*, chapter 15, says of this pontiff’s election: “In that same year, 1124, Pope Calixtus II, of happy memory, departed this life. A certain Lambert, a native of Bologna and bishop of Ostia, was appointed in his place; he was called Honorius. He was elected amid a dispute with a certain Theobald, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. Because Honorius’s election had proceeded less canonically, after twelve days he freely rejected and laid aside the mitre and mantle in the presence of the brethren. But the brethren—bishops, cardinal-priests, and cardinal-deacons alike—seeing his humility and providing against introducing some novelty into the Roman Church in the future, corrected what had been wrongly done and improved it. Authorizing the same Honorius anew [Col. 1214D], they fell at his feet and rendered him their accustomed obedience as their shepherd and universal pope.”

This is William of Tyre’s account of Honorius’s election. Pandulph, quoted by Baronius, says nearly the same thing in nearly the same words: “He bestowed the pallium upon William, archbishop of Tyre, the first of the Latins to have been consecrated by Garmond, patriarch of Jerusalem; [Col. 1215A] and in letters addressed to the bishops and clergy of Tyre, and also to the aforesaid Garmond, patriarch of Jerusalem, he ordered them graciously to receive and religiously obey as their archbishop the man to whom he had granted the pallium by right.”

“Moreover,” says William of Tyre, “he sent with him Lord Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, legate of the Apostolic See, an eloquent and very learned man. Through him he wrote a letter to Bernard, patriarch of Antioch, warning him, under penalty of suspension, to restore to the lord of Tyre the suffragans whom he was keeping from him. At the beginning of his pontificate he excommunicated and deposed Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, for repeatedly showing contempt toward the Apostolic See.”

Peter the Deacon says: “He held in extraordinary honor Saint Bernard, marvelous in that age and like a certain star fallen upon the earth; Hildebert, archbishop of Tours; Norbert, apostle of many nations; Hugh of Saint Victor, theologian of Paris; [Col. 1215B] and other men outstanding in talent, learning, religious devotion, and piety. He confirmed by a rescript as sacredly and lawfully established the decrees of the synod of Nantes, by which two rights were taken away from Conan, count of Brittany, with his assent. And he wholly abolished, to the great benefit of all Brittany, that evil abuse—rather than custom—by which, upon the death of a husband or wife, all the deceased’s movable goods and everything recovered from shipwreck passed not to the children or lawful heirs but to the treasury.”

Papirius Massonus says: “He deposed Otto, bishop of Halberstadt, who had been accused and convicted by his canons of receiving thirty solidi for consecrating a certain church, and substituted Rudolph for him.” The *Chronicle of Hirsau* says: “After Duke William of Apulia and Calabria died without children, he compelled Roger, count of Sicily, who had seized his territory, by force and arms to swear the customary oath of fidelity to the Roman Church. Ill-informed, he absolved Louis the Fat, king of France, an usurper of ecclesiastical goods and rights, whom Stephen, bishop of Paris, had bound with just censures; for this reason Saint Bernard rebuked him severely enough in two letters. [Col. 1216A] In his time, a certain Tanchelm, founder of the heresy of the Adamites, deceived many at Antwerp by his eloquence and diligence. For he denied that reception of Christ’s body and blood aided salvation; he set priests and bishops at naught; and he ordered those who did not assent to his heresies to be killed through his followers—for he had about three thousand soldiers who followed him everywhere. Norbert of the Premonstratensian Order was appointed bishop of that place to eradicate this heresy from human minds. He made such progress through his sermons that nearly all were converted to the Catholic faith, bringing into the church the Lord’s body [the Eucharist], which they had kept shut up in chests and holes for ten years.”

Robert, continuator of Sigebert, says: “In his time nearly the whole nation of the Pomeranians, subdued by Boleslaus, duke of the Poles, and the great king of the Goths, having embraced the Christian faith through the preaching of Otto, bishop of Bamberg, passed into Christ’s camp.” Helmold, chapter 41. Olaus, book II, *On the Northern Peoples*, chapter 7: “And when at last Pope Honorius, after the death of Henry V, who had died without an heir, had freed Lothair, duke of Saxony, designated by the common consent of the nobles in the year of the Lord 1125 as successor to the kingdom and empire, from civil war against Henry’s rebellious nephews through his sister—namely Conrad and Frederick, dukes of Swabia—by pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against them, as Freising attests, he died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year 1130. He had held the pontificate for five years, one month, and seventeen days.”

“And he made,” says Pandulph in Baronius, “many ordinations in the City,” etc. When ill, he had himself carried from the Lateran palace to the monastery of Saint Andrew, and there died in peace; he was buried in the basilica of the Savior.

[Col. 1215]

## [LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES]

[Col. 1217]

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF HONORIUS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

## I. He takes the canons of the Church of Saint Vincent at Bergamo under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Year 1125, 19 February)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, IV, 450.]

[Col. 1217A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALBERT, archpriest, and the brethren living canonically in the mother church of Saint Vincent at Bergamo, and to their successors remaining in the same religious observance, forever.

The care of the universal Church, etc. Therefore [Col. 1218A], with merciful kindness we assent to your petitions, beloved sons in the Lord, and receive the church of Saint Vincent, together with the community of your congregation and everything pertaining to it, under the protection of the Apostolic See. By the authority of this present privilege, we decree that whatever goods or possessions have been bestowed upon your church by Catholic bishops or religious kings, whatever it rightfully possesses at present, and whatever it may in the future justly and canonically acquire through the Lord’s generosity—in churches, towns, villages, tithes, market tolls, or other things—shall be preserved always firm and entire for you and for your successors living according to the rule [Col. 1219A].

We therefore decree that, so long as you remain in observance of canonical discipline, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, all shall be preserved for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. We further forbid that either the bishop or any person may divert the goods of your community to private uses, grant them to others as benefices, or alienate them by other means from the brothers’ prebends or from the common good. Leases, exchanges, and investitures of estates shall be conducted by the common counsel of the brethren [Col. 1219B], and neither the bishop nor any persons whatever may usurp this right, while preserving nevertheless the canonical reverence due to the Catholic bishop of Bergamo. But if anyone in the future, etc. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, indiction III, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

## II. He confirms the goods and privileges of the monastery of Rheinau.  
*(Year 1125, 24 February)*

[Zapf, *Anecdota Monumenta historiae Germaniae illustrantia*, vol. I, p. 471, Augsburg, 1785, quarto.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ DIETMAR, abbot of the monastery of Rheinau [Col. 1219C], and to his successors to be regularly appointed forever.

> **Note [Col. 1219D]:** A double concluding formula occurs in papal rescripts: namely, “forever” and “greeting and the apostolic blessing.” The former is used in bulls of greater importance and intended to endure for a long time; the latter in other, shorter rescripts which are to be carried out at once. Thus Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI.

Just as no effect ought to be granted to those who request unjust things, so the petition of those desiring lawful things ought not to be delayed. Therefore, dearest son Dietmar, assenting to your requests, we confirm by this present page of privilege to your venerable monastery of Rheinau whatever is known to belong to that monastery through the lawful donations of the faithful; and also whatever it may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful. May these things remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree, under threat of divine judgment [Col. 1219D], that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, harass it with reckless vexations, or grant them as a benefice. Instead, all things shall be preserved whole and entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. No advocate shall be appointed, nor may anyone by any device intrude or interfere [Col. 1220A], except one whom the abbot has chosen. If he opposes the abbot in any matter, he shall lose the authority granted to him, and the abbot shall choose another by apostolic authority.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of the same place, or of any successor of yours, no one may be installed there by any trickery or force, except one whom the brethren choose by common consent, or whom the sounder part of their counsel elects. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly, attempts to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends, let him lose the dignity of his honor and power; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment; let him be cut off from the most holy body of the Lord; and let him be anathema, to be burned in fire on the last day of the Lord. Amen.

[Col. 1220B] I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hands of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Frederick, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the year 1126 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction III.

> **Note [Cols. 1219D, 1220D]:** Substitute the fourth indiction. On this point Mabillon, in the cited book II, chapter 25, no. 9, writes: “Certain bulls are found whose reckoning anticipates our more recent one,” where he gives examples from these very years. Ailmericus, or Emericus, is often found subscribing bulls as cardinal, but never with the title of librarian, otherwise customary, as occurs in the present bull.

In the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

## III. Confirmation concerning the abbey and election of the abbot at Saalfeld, according to the foundation of Hanno of Cologne and Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz; and incorporation of the parishes of Neuhofen and Crölup; and that no one may establish or consecrate a church within the lord abbot’s territory or jurisdiction, nor may dogs be maintained or payments be made to hunters.  
*(Year 1125, 24 February)*

[*Thuringia sacra*, p. 698.]

[Col. 1220C]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ WALTHER, abbot of Saalfeld, and to all who are to succeed him, forever.

Since the dignity and authority of the Apostolic See, over which by the Lord’s dispensation we preside, has this highest purpose: that provision may be made through it for the whole Church throughout the world and that all congregations and holy places may be ordered, established, and defended by it, we make known to all our sons—that is, to all Christ’s faithful—and we will, for the remedy of our soul and for the interest of the holy apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1220D], that their place and abbey called Saalfeld shall remain and be confirmed according to the foundation of the venerable Hanno, archbishop of Cologne, its founder, and of his collaborator Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz, in whose diocese it is situated on the river called the Saale.

We therefore will, establish, and command under threat of perpetual anathema that this place remain [Col. 1221A] stable and undisturbed in perpetual peace, safe and fortified against every violation and disturbance and under favor. The monks who live there according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the custom of the monastery of Siegburg, and who have free election concerning their abbot, shall choose from among themselves one worthy to be abbot, if there is such a man; otherwise they shall receive as abbot one from the monastery of Siegburg, from which they derive their customs. No one may compel an abbot once installed to any courtly service.

We confirm by the sanction of our authority the goods and possessions of this place which the venerable Hanno, other bishops, and the faithful have granted there or will grant to me. The place shall hold firmly under its own right the parish called Neuhofen, the parish called Crölup, and all other parishes and churches in that land [Col. 1221B], as the venerable Hanno ordained; and no one may construct or consecrate a church in that province without the abbot’s consent.

And because the people of that land, before the venerable Archbishop Hanno undertook the work through that monastery and the other churches which he founded, were pagan and still appear half-pagan, we grant and give authority, as the same Bishop Hanno and Archbishop Sigefrid ordained by testament, that the abbot of that place and the monks whom he has assigned for this purpose shall have power there to preach God’s word, baptize, bury, visit the sick, and receive confessions, so that the spark of Christianity still alive there through them may by no means be extinguished but may be kindled ever more [Col. 1221C] to the honor of the holy, supreme, undivided Trinity.

Let the monks of Saalfeld possess the mountain called Coburg, with all estates belonging to it; the village called Sevrinveldin and another called Sidemaresdorff; the market at Moderin; and the estates of a certain Reginald, which amount there to nearly twelve *mansi*; and elsewhere the village called Ilmina, with its mill and all its appurtenances; also the grove and forest which once belonged to the chamber. As Archbishop Hanno granted these, so may they possess them with all villages and newly cultivated lands established there.

> **Note [Col. 1221D]:** Moderin is called Medera, not far from Wiesenfeld in Franconia.

And if anyone, from the time of Archbishop Hanno to the present, has usurped any newly cultivated land there without the abbot’s permission, or wishes henceforth to usurp one [Col. 1221D], unless he repents and acknowledges the rights of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and their monks, let him be anathema forever. Likewise we decree concerning those who wish either to remove from or withhold from those monks the tithe paid throughout the land from each *mansus*, consisting only of two modii, because it is especially the endowment of the monastery and the daily provision prepared for those who serve the Lord. Therefore no bishop, no bishop’s reeve, and no knight may henceforth interfere in that tithe if he wishes to be cherished in the bosom of Mother Church.

We also forbid, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that on the monastery’s property, according to the custom of that province [Col. 1222A], dogs be maintained or payments made to hunters; nor may the place be burdened or oppressed by the violence of bishops, advocates, or any other persons whatsoever. For it is the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, fortified and enclosed inwardly and outwardly by us and our successors: there Martha may serve; there Mary may be granted peace and behold how sweet the Lord is; there “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” is often heard and sung beforehand, together with prayers for all the Lord’s people and for us.

To these customs we add this also, and make it known by the sanction of our authority to all the faithful: a certain free man named Adelbert of Conize and his wife Christina, for the remedy of their souls and of those [Col. 1222B] of their parents and relatives, have granted to the Lord and his apostles Peter and Paul at Saalfeld all the estates which they possessed in the land called Orla: namely, at Coniza, Buchio, Brisinnice, Quezin, and wherever else they lie, with all their appurtenances—ways and non-ways, revenues and returns, fields and woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, mills, meadows, pastures, and dependents.

They granted all these under the condition that whoever is abbot of Saalfeld shall have under his authority the advocate of those goods, and shall entrust that office, without benefice and without succession by any heir, to whomever he wishes. No one shall have a benefice from those goods, except the persons exempted with their benefices when this conveyance was made. Those transferred from the household are to be called servants: those from the abbey of Saint Michael at Siegburg and from the abbey of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne. Those transferred so that they remain as they formerly were may enjoy only this status arising from such household membership: whoever among them is declared culpable in court shall make amends with only thirty denarii, and shall pay half of those denarii—that is, fifteen.

The aforesaid knight Adelbert and his wife Christina shall hold the advocacy of those estates and the estates themselves with every benefit for as long as they live, unless they freely choose to relinquish them. After both their deaths, however, the abbot and his brethren shall freely and fully possess them as alms for the benefit of the monastery, the poor, and Christ’s hospice. If anyone [Col. 1222D] wishes to violate this or inflict any violence upon these decrees, let him know that, by the authority of Christ’s apostles Peter and Paul and by the sanction of our power, he is to be condemned with all the wicked, robbers, and invaders to anathema and everlasting fire—unless, promptly moved by worthy repentance, he takes care to amend his ways.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, through the hand of Dilmaric, chancellor and librarian of the Holy Roman Church; in the year 1125 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction III, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

> **Note [Col. 1222D]:** The chronological indications are corrupt. Jaffé.

## IV. Privilege for the Camaldolese Congregation.  
*(Year 1125, 7 March)*

[Mittarelli, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. III, p. 306, from an ancient manuscript of Saint Michael’s, Pisa.]

[Col. 1223A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, prior of Camaldoli, and his brethren, both present and future, forever.

By the providence of God, the dispenser of all good things, the care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us, so that we may cherish religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore all lovers of the Christian faith ought [Col. 1223B] to love religion and diligently foster venerable places together with the persons themselves dedicated to divine service.

Accordingly, dearest sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive your place, with all that pertains to it, into the protection of blessed Peter and our own protection, and fortify it by the patronage of the Apostolic See. Therefore, by the present charter of privilege, we ordain that the condition of the Hermitage of Camaldoli shall always remain in the strength of its religious life; that the order of monastic observance established throughout your whole congregation shall not be altered through anyone’s arrogance; and we forbid any brother of your congregation, after having made monastic profession, to depart without the permission of the prior and a reasonable permission of the brethren. [Col. 1223C] Should he presume to depart and, after a second or third warning, scorn to return, he shall be subject to a sentence of excommunication until he has made fitting satisfaction.

Moreover, no bishop shall, without canonical examination, prohibit the divine office in churches governed by brothers of that congregation. The monks of your churches may also, when a city or parish is under a general interdict, celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors and with diocesan clergy excluded. Further, those who travel on account of service to the servants of God dwelling in the Hermitage of Camaldoli shall be molested by no one in going, returning, or staying.

Whatever you now justly and lawfully possess, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors remaining in that [Col. 1223D] religious life. We have judged that the following should be expressly named:

the church of Saint Donatus, called Fonsbonus, with its hospice and all its goods; the monastery of Saint Mary at Poplena; the monastery of Saint Saviour near the city of Florence; the monastery of Mount Muri; the monastery of Saint Peter at Cerreto; the monastery of Saint Mary at Policiano; the monastery of Saint Peter at Fontiniano; the monastery of Saint Justus at Volterra; the monastery of Saint Mary at Morrona; the monastery of Saint Frigidian and the monastery of Saint Michael within the city of Pisa; the monastery of Saint Sabinus in the territory of that city; the monastery of Saint Stephen at Cintoria; [Col. 1224A] the monastery of Saint Saviour at Cantignano; the monastery of Saint Peter at Puteoli; the monastery of Saint Saviour at Salvamunda; the monastery of Saint Mary at Agnano; the monastery of Saint Peter at Rota; the monastery of Saint Saviour of the Berardingi; the monastery of Saint Vigilius in the borough of Siena; the monastery of Saint Peter in vivo Montiis Armiati [reading uncertain]; the monastery of Saint Quiricus at Rosa; the monastery of Saint Sabinus at Clio; the hermitage of Fleri, with its monastery; the monastery of Saint Virianus; the monastery of Saint Bartholomew at Anglari; the monastery of Saint Mary at Trivio; the hermitage of Saint Peter at Fajolo; the monastery of Saint Mary on the Island; the monastery of Saint Mary at the Lake; the monastery of Saint Angel near the castle of Bristi; and the small monastery of Saint Christina in the same estate.

In the March of Camerino: the monastery of Saint George; the monastery of Saint Martin at Accole, with the church called the Hermit. On the island of Sardinia: the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Zaccari; the church of Saint Eugenia at Samanar; the church of Saint Michael and Saint Lawrence at Vanari; the church of Saint Mary and Saint John at Altazar; the church of Saint Mary at Contra; the church of Saint John and Saint Simeon at Salverano; the church of Saint Nicholas at Trulla; the church of Saint Peter at Scano; and the church of Saint Paul at Cotroniano.

Furthermore, we decree that whatever you may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire, by the Lord’s gift, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1224C] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid hermitage and your congregation, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, to be of benefit in every way to the religious brethren and the poor.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in the future to violate rashly this charter of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not make amendment by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and [Col. 1224D] blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But to all who preserve what is just for the aforesaid hermitage or congregation, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the severe Judge, find the reward of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

+ **THE EYES OF THE LORD ARE UPON THE RIGHTEOUS.** I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church. + I, Guido, bishop of Arezzo, subscribe. + I, Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, subscribe. + I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli, subscribe. + I, Vitalis, bishop of Albano, subscribe. [Col. 1225A] + I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, subscribe. + I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, subscribe. + I, Desiderius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, subscribe. + I, Sigizo, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sixtus, subscribe. + I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore, subscribe. + I, John, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, subscribe. + I, Rodulf, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, subscribe.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of March, in the third indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Honorius [Col. 1225B] II, pope.

### V. To Henry, bishop of Verdun.—That he restore, or cause to be restored, what was taken from Abbot Lawrence of Saint Viton. He adds that he is aggrieved because, when summoned, Henry scorned to come to Rome. (1125, March 11.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 257.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Verdun: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our son Lawrence, abbot of Saint Viton, came to us and complained that the market of Mount Saint Viton, the toll together with a measure of wheat, jurisdiction and correction of measures, and the tithes on wine sold outside the city, [Col. 1225C] which he lost during the conflict, had been taken from him by your predecessor. We therefore command your fraternity to restore to him what was taken.

**Note:** [Col. 1225D] The conflict over investitures, waged at Verdun in the time of Bishop Richard, was made the subject of a lengthy history by Lawrence of Liège in his *History of the Bishops of Verdun*, vol. II of the folio *Spicilegium*, p. 247 ff. [Col. 1226D] See the supplicatory tract of Abbot Lawrence addressed to Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, in Martène, vol. I, *Anecdota*, col. 374.

Concerning Richer of Bu, who invaded his freehold in the estate of Baron and inflicted various other injuries upon him, administer due justice. If you neglect to restore the rights of his monastery, which were confirmed by our predecessors, do not doubt that we shall regard this as a grave matter. We are, moreover, greatly aggrieved that, when summoned by our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory and by us, you scorned to come to us and to the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### VI. To Peter, abbot of Cluny.—Privilege for Cluny. (1125, April 2.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 323.]

[Col. 1225D]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of the venerable monastery of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

The incomprehensible and ineffable mercy of divine power has established us, by this ordering of providence, in the administration of the Apostolic See, so that we may strive to exercise paternal concern for all [Col. 1226A] Churches. For the holy Roman Church, which retains the primacy over all Churches granted to it by God, ought, like a loving mother, to provide for each Church with unremitting vigilance. To her, indeed, all must have recourse as to their head and mother, that they may be nourished from her breasts, defended by her authority, and relieved from their oppressions.

It is fitting, therefore, that churches and venerable places—especially those belonging to the special right and peculiar possession of the holy Roman Church, which, by God’s will, we serve—should receive the honour of a more special prerogative and be strengthened by the protection of apostolic authority. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Peter, abbot, graciously yielding to your just requests, we also confirm by the present decree, with the Lord as author, whatever liberty, protection, and authority our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Roman Church—especially Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal II, popes of apostolic memory—conferred upon your monastery and the places belonging to it, by prudent judgment. Among these the following were thought fit to be noted by their proper names: the abbey of Saint Giles, etc.

In all priories and cells now subject to your government without their own abbot, no one shall presume at any future time to appoint an abbot. You or your brethren may elect priests for the churches, provided that they receive the care [Col. 1226C] of souls from bishops or the bishops’ vicars without payment. If, which God forbid, those persons refuse from perversity to confer it, the priests shall obtain by the benevolence of the Apostolic See permission to celebrate the offices.

The brethren of your places shall receive the consecrations of churches or altars from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated, if those bishops are willing to provide them freely and without improper dealing. Otherwise, they shall receive the sacraments of those consecrations from whatever Catholic bishop they prefer. Nor may anyone disturb the brethren of your cloister or of your places on account of alms properly given for the salvation of the living or the dead; rather, they may receive, for the use of God’s servants and the poor, the offerings of both men and women brought to them.

We also ordain that brethren of your cells, wherever situated, shall not suffer suspension of the divine offices because of any interdict or excommunication. Instead, both the monks themselves and their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to monastic profession, shall celebrate the offices of divine service and perform the rites due to burial behind closed church doors, with diocesan clergy excluded. We also grant you permission to receive into conversion, at your places, secular clerics or laymen, except those excommunicated for specified crimes. [Col. 1227A] We confirm by the present charter of our decree the boundaries of immunity of your place established by our aforesaid predecessor Pope Urban: namely, that no person of whatever status or power may presume to make an incursion, seizure, or robbery, or commit homicide within those boundaries.

Furthermore, we decree that no one at all may rashly disturb your venerable monastery and its dependent places; rather, their possessions and other goods, already given for the salvation of souls or hereafter, through God’s mercy, to be given, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in the future rashly to violate this charter of our constitution, [Col. 1227B] etc. … saving in all things the right of the Roman Church and the reverence due to the Apostolic See. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Unalis, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, have assented and subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of the Apostles, have subscribed. [Col. 1227C] I, Rossemagnus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Gregory, have subscribed. I, Cosmas of Saint Mary in [lacuna], have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angel, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the third indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of our pontificate.

### VII. He informs the monks of Cluny that he has graciously received Abbot Peter. He commands that they not go to Pontius, former abbot, against Peter’s will. (1125, April 2.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 140.]

[Col. 1227D] HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We render praise and thanksgiving to divine mercy because, under its protecting power, we have learned that your steadfastness remains in the unity of concord and that the observance of religion shines among you. We ask that, firmly persisting in the good beginning which you have made, you labour with unwearying zeal effectively to perform what is pleasing to God.

We received our most beloved son Peter, abbot, who came to us, with paternal kindness out of regard for you and affection for him; and we diligently granted both his requests and yours. We restored to him and to the monastery of Cluny, saving the right of the holy Roman Church, the abbeys of Saint Giles, Saint-Bertin, and Saint Benedict on the Po, in order that religion might be reformed and preserved in them. [Col. 1228A] Sending him back to you with the execution of our letters, we ask your charity to love him with special affection and, as a father and the guardian of your souls appointed by God, unanimously honour him by obedience and humble submission. We also beseech you in the Lord to assist us by your prayers.

We command that no monk professed at Cluny shall presume to go to Pontius, formerly abbot, without the consent of our aforesaid son Peter, abbot. If anyone does, attempts, or presumes to attempt this, we shall hold valid the sentence which the aforesaid abbot pronounces against him.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of April.

### VIII. He commands Peter, abbot of Saint Giles, to return to obedience to the Cluniacs. (1125.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, instruments, 190.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Saint Giles, and to the monks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the providence of God, the dispenser of all good things, the care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us, so that we may cherish religious persons and strive by every means to preserve religion pleasing to God. [Col. 1228C] For no service is ever rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion.

It was indeed in this concern for charity that our predecessors, Roman pontiffs of apostolic memory, formerly entrusted the monastery of Saint Giles to the abbey of Cluny for the establishment and preservation of religious excellence. But in recent times, after the death of your abbot Hugh, when your place, oppressed by the incursions of wars and afflicted by many persecutions, could not remain without a pastor’s comfort, our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory appointed you, beloved son Peter, as abbot. From the letters which he sent to the abbot of Cluny, we understand that he did this, as is evident from the tenor of his intention, with the right and reverence of [Col. 1228D] the monastery of Cluny preserved.

We therefore command and direct all of you to return without objection to the submission and obedience of our most beloved son, the abbot of Cluny. And you, Abbot Peter, within forty days after receiving these letters, shall go in suppliant devotion to the monastery of Cluny, promise obedience to its abbot, and make profession to that monastery, all pretext set aside—while preserving in all things the right of the Roman Church, the abbot’s blessing, and the reverence of the holy Apostolic See. If you prove contumacious, you shall incur the indignation of blessed Peter and of us.

Given at the Lateran.

### IX. To the abbot and monks of Saint-Bertin.—He commands them to return to submission and obedience to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny. (1125.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 41.]

[Col. 1229A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Bertin, and to the monks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The peace of the Church, concord among brethren, and unity of religion are accustomed to join things below to things above, and earthly things to heavenly. Therefore we rejoice, as a debt of paternal charity, that you, unanimously devoted to divine service, are pleasing to God and men through religious devotion. You should ascribe this not to merits or to your own prudence, [Col. 1229B] but to God and to the care of the Church of Cluny, to which our predecessors entrusted the duty of establishing and preserving religion in your monastery; and this, with divine clemency’s favour, has also brought great increase in temporal and spiritual matters.

We therefore command and direct you humbly to return without objection to the submission and obedience of our most beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny. And you, son abbot, within forty days after receiving these letters, shall go in suppliant devotion to the monastery of Cluny, promise obedience to its abbot, and make profession to that monastery, all pretext set aside. If you prove contumacious, you shall incur the indignation of blessed Peter and of us.

[Col. 1229C] Given at the Lateran, etc.

### X. To the monks of Saint Benedict on the Po.—He commands them to show obedience and reverence to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, and to receive the abbot whom he gives them with the counsel of the chapter of Cluny. (1125.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 41.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks of Saint Benedict on the Po: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The peace of the Church, concord among brethren, and unity of religion are accustomed to join things below to things above, and earthly things to heavenly. [Col. 1229D] Therefore we rejoice, as a debt of paternal charity, that you, unanimously devoted to divine service, are pleasing to God and men through religious devotion. You should ascribe this not to merits or to your own prudence, but to God and to the care of the Church of Cluny, to which our predecessors entrusted the duty of establishing and preserving religion in your monastery; and this, with divine clemency’s favour, has also brought great increase in temporal and spiritual matters.

We therefore command and direct you to render obedience and reverence, without any opposition, to our most beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny; to receive reverently the abbot whom he shall appoint with the counsel of the chapter of Cluny; and to take care humbly to obey him as the shepherd of your [Col. 1230A] souls, while preserving in all things the right and reverence of the Roman Church. If you have presumed to appoint an abbot by yourselves, we shall judge your act void and exact full justice from you. Therefore by these letters we warn and command you, within forty days after their receipt, to go to the monastery of Cluny and obey without resistance the abbot whom the abbot and brethren of Cluny shall give you.

### XI. To Thurstan, archbishop of York. (1125, April 5.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 143.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THURSTAN, archbishop of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to divine clemency because we are safe and well in the City, in the tranquillity of peace. Since we love your person, we wish that controversy concerning primacy between the Churches of York and Canterbury should be decided only in our presence.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of April.

### XII. He commends John, legate of the Apostolic See, to archbishops, bishops, etc. (1125, April 12.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 327.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1230C] brothers and sons—archbishops, bishops, abbots, nobles, and all other clerics and laymen established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although you dwell at the ends of the earth, the universality of the Christian faith nevertheless brings you under the pastoral care of the apostle Peter. For when it was said to Peter, “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John 21), certainly no sheep or lamb belonging to Christ’s fellowship was excepted from that special pastoral charge entrusted to Peter.

Moreover, the authority of our most holy father Pope Gregory and the preaching of blessed Augustine make manifest that, by allotment, the kingdom of England belongs to blessed Peter and the Roman Church. By this duty of our office, therefore, we are moved to provide for you, who are far away, with more attentive care. Accordingly, we have committed our authority in your regions to our Christian son John, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, vigilant in sharing our solicitude. [Col. 1230D] He will deal, with the assistance of your love and through the cooperating patronage of the holy apostles, with the correction and stability of the Churches, the increase of religion, and all other matters that appear to require approval or disapproval.

We therefore ask, admonish, and command you to receive him reverently as the vicar of Saint Peter, hear him humbly, and, at his summons, solemnly hold synodal assemblies with him, so that by his diligence and yours those things in your kingdom needing correction may be corrected, and those needing strengthening may be strengthened through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

### XIII. To the canons of Tours.—He confirms the sentence of excommunication against Fulk, count of Anjou. (1123, April 12.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 322.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clerics of the mother church of Saint Maurice at Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1231B] Just as good and humble sons should be more closely bound by the bonds of paternal affection, so the ungrateful and disobedient ought to be restrained by the rigour of justice. We have learned that Fulk, count of Anjou, scorned to observe the judgment, concerning the divorce of the unlawful marriage of his daughter and William, son of Count Robert, rendered by our beloved son J., cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, together with our other brother bishops and wise men, after suitable witnesses had given evidence. Moreover, what is more serious, we have learned that, in insult to blessed Peter and the holy and Apostolic Roman Church, he seized the messengers sent to him by the aforesaid legate, held them in strict custody for two weeks, presumed to burn their beards and hair with flames, and publicly burn the letters [Col. 1231C] in the open air.

The same legate therefore proclaimed a sentence of interdict over the count’s own land and of excommunication upon his person. Having taken counsel with our brethren, we confirm that sentence until fitting satisfaction is made, and command that the interdict be observed.

Given at the Lateran, on the day before the Ides of April.

### XIV. To John, legate of the Apostolic See.—He commands him diligently to carry out in England the legation received from Calixtus II. (1125, April 3.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 327.]

[Col. 1231D] HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as it is the duty of good sons to obey their fathers with the humble devotion of submission, so it is incumbent on fathers to provide for their sons with kindly affection of charity. We therefore entrust to your prudent care and solicitude the charge over the kingdom of England committed to you by our predecessor Pope Calixtus II of blessed memory. We beseech you in the Lord, as a wise and discerning son of the Roman Church, to labour zealously and honourably in those matters which pertain to the honour of God and the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April.

### XV. He commends John, cardinal and his legate, to David, king of the Scots. (1125, April 13.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 329.]

[Col. 1232A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DAVID, illustrious king of the Scots: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Devout and humble disciples of blessed Peter ought diligently to carry out whatever they know concerns the honour of the Holy Roman Church. Therefore we request and command your nobility to receive reverently our beloved son John, cardinal, to whom we have entrusted our authority in those regions, and to honour him. You shall also cause the bishops of your land, when summoned by him, to assemble at his council. We entrust to this our legate for careful investigation and examination the controversy long disputed between Thurstan, archbishop of York, and the bishops of your land. We reserve the final judgment to the decision of the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April.

### XVI. At Bishop Peter’s request, he receives the Church of Montefeltro under protection. (1124, April 21.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, II, 844.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, bishop of Montefeltro, and to his successors to be canonically promoted for ever.

[Col. 1232C] The authority of our office exhorts us to labour for the condition of the Churches and, with God’s saving help, to provide for their peace and welfare. Accordingly, dearest brother in the Lord, Peter, we receive the holy Church of Montefeltro, over which you preside by God’s will, into the protection of blessed Peter and our own protection. By the authority of this privilege, we decree that whatever possessions and goods your Church of Montefeltro now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to it.

We have judged that the following should be expressly named: the chapel of Saint Pancras; Saint Martin’s on the Mount; the chapel of Saint Sophia; the chapel [Col. 1232D] of Saint Mary in Plebe with its estate; the parish church of Saint Lawrence at Folia with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Michael with its estate; the monastery of Saint Mary at Scriptino with all its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint John at Carpineo with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Marinus and the estate at Carpineo; the parish church of Saint Cassian at Pisino with all its appurtenances and its entire estate; the chapel of Saint Theodore with its appurtenances, and the land in the valley of Cava and at Molledano; the parish church of Saint Theonistus in the place called Corma with all its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Marinus with its castle and all its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Agatha with all its appurtenances, and the estate called Farnito in the place [Col. 1233A] called Ovilione; the parish church of Saint Martin at Murisiano with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Hilary with its appurtenances; the parish churches of Saint Mary in Vico with their appurtenances; the parish churches of Saint Stephen at Murlo with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Martin in the wood with its appurtenances; the parish churches of Saint Peter in Cultu with their appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Peter ad Missam with its appurtenances; the whole estate of Herman; the whole estate of Adinus; the monastery of Saint Saviour on the estate; the whole cell of Faustus with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin at Vivedo with all its appurtenances, together with the castle called Casale d’Ilice; the parish church of Saint Cassian in the field of Juvenicus with all its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Mary in Romania with all its appurtenances; [Col. 1233B] the parish church of Saint Mustiola with its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Severinus with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Proculus with its appurtenances; and one-third of the estate of Atilianus; one-third of the estate of Bacunianus; one-third of the estate of Stabulum; one-third of the estate of Justi; together with the whole field called Martii; three small parcels of land from the estate of Atilianus, called Plegae; the whole estate of Plegnus; the estate of Alfidiarum, called the Flat Field; the whole estate of Frigi; the whole estate of Antimaria; the whole estate of Columnella; the estate beyond Collina; the whole chapel of Saint Archangel; the estate of the valley of Donatulus; the whole Licinian holding; the whole estate of Ausi; the cell of Faustus; the greater and lesser Scannullae in their entirety; the chapel [Col. 1233C] of Saint Agatha with the castle called Petra Anellaria; the whole chapel of Saint George; the whole estate of Cervianus; the estate of Capicianus; the estate called Grilena with all its appurtenances in the Castle of Felicity; the chapel of Saint Martin at Castagnolo; the chapel of Saint Sophia at Aquatario; the whole chapel of Saint Mary at Methavistis; the church of Flora at Scapinio; the estate of Sititianus; the estate of Campo Piano with all its appurtenances; and the new castle called Petrella—while preserving in all things the right and reverence of the Roman Church.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may, etc. If anyone, etc.; but to all, etc. Amen.

[Col. 1233D] I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Honorius II, pope.

### XVII. To Didacus, archbishop of Compostela. (1125, May 1.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 430.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to DIDACUS, archbishop of the Church of Compostela: apostolic greeting and blessing.

Your presence, brother [Note: [Col. 1233D] I would read “brother.”], should doubtless make known to you that this priest, named Bernard, has come to us from your regions and has reported very many good things to us about you; and that in our presence he complained of the knights of Salamanca—indeed, enemies of God—who most inhumanely invaded a certain church which he governed as best he could and stripped him of all his goods. Therefore we lay upon you a command of obedience and earnestly ask you, as our son, not to refuse to admonish by apostolic authority the bishop of Salamanca, who is your suffragan, that he cause the goods of the aforesaid church to be restored to this cleric and that he by no means omit to impose upon those robbers what is canonically due. If he scorns to do so, let him be struck by canonical justice. [Col. 1234B] We also ask you to deign, for God’s mercy, to assist somewhat this man reduced to such poverty.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May.

### XVIII. Privilege for the canonical community of Porto. (1125, May 4.)

[Fantuzzi, *Monumenta Ravennatia*, vol. VI, p. 41.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ JOHN, provost, and his brethren professing the canonical life in the church of Saint Mary at Porto, and to their successors remaining in the same religious life for ever.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by the Lord, the disposer of all good things, so that we may love religious persons [Col. 1234C] and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God; for no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless it proceeds from the root of charity and is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore all lovers of the Christian faith ought to cherish religion and to foster with greater care venerable places together with the persons devoted to divine service therein, so that they may be troubled by no vexations of wicked men or wearied by oppressive and burdensome exactions.

Accordingly, assenting to your petitions in the Lord, dearest sons, we receive both you and your church, with all that belongs to it, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own safeguard. We decree that whatever you now lawfully possess, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Moreover, by the authority of this present privilege we decree that the aforesaid church shall be exempt from every extraordinary levy: namely, if at any time the archbishop of Ravenna, [Col. 1234D] or, upon his departure, clerics or laymen of that church, should happen to travel to the Roman pontiff on any business or to the emperor, no exaction in silver, horses, or anything of this kind may be made from them out of that church; nor may any burden ever be imposed there by lodging. Furthermore, when war threatens and the citizens of Ravenna raise a contribution either for soldiers or for fortifying the city, we likewise decree that the oft-mentioned church shall be exempt from every levy, while in all things the rights of the Church of Ravenna established by the enactments of the holy Fathers are preserved.

If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that church may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. [Col. 1235C] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, Boniface, cardinal-priest, have subscribed. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon, have subscribed. I, Gerard, of Saints Aquila and Prisca, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, the cardinal-priest of St. Balbina, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Nones of May [4 May], in the third indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Honorius II.

## XIX. The privileges of Paschal II and Calixtus II for the abbey of St. Walburga are renewed and enlarged. (1125, 11 July.)

[Wurtwein, *Nova subsidia diplomatica*, vol. VII, p. 56.]

[Col. 1235D] HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ BERTHOLF, abbot of the monastery built in honour of the holy apostles Philip and James and of St. Walburga the virgin, in the diocese of Strasbourg, namely in the place called Sacred Wood (*Sacra Silva*), and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Since without the cultivation of true religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor service acceptable to God be rendered, it belongs to apostolic authority to love religious persons and to protect religious places—especially those which belong to blessed Peter and pertain in a special manner to the Roman Church—by the safeguard of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Bertholf, graciously receiving your just petitions, we strengthen under the patronage of blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church the monastery of Sacred Wood, over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. It has been offered to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church under an annual payment of one gold coin, and dedicated in honour of almighty God, the holy apostles Philip and James, and St. Walburga the virgin, following the example of my predecessors Paschal and Calixtus II, Roman pontiffs.

We decree that all things bestowed upon that monastery by the religious princes Duke Frederick and Peter, founders of that place, or by other faithful persons from their own right, and whatever may hereafter, by God’s bounty, be given, offered, or acquired by other lawful means, shall remain peaceful and inviolate to you and your successors. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb that place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

When the abbot of that place, or any of his successors, dies, no one may be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, elect according to the love of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Moreover, in accordance with the decree of our predecessor Pope Calixtus, you shall possess without any opposition from the brethren of Salsen or from any other persons the tithes of livestock and produce [Col. 1236C] which you gather throughout the whole land of Sacred Wood by your own labour or expense. Your peasants, however, shall pay their tithes to the priests of their respective parishes. We also confirm to the brethren serving God there the use of the same forest—for building and heating according to their lawful need, for obtaining water and providing for their own convenience, and pasture for their animals throughout the whole forest—as it was granted by the liberality of our aforesaid sons Emperor Henry and his nephew Duke Frederick, as well as Count Peter.

If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the oft-mentioned monastery may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the reward of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon of the Holy [Col. 1237A] Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of July [11 July], in the third indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

## XX. To Henry, bishop of Verdun.—He commands him to come before him at the next feast of the Epiphany to answer concerning the ordination of Conrad, bishop of Toul, and the complaints of the abbot of St. Vitonus; meanwhile he is to refrain from episcopal office. (1125, 3 October.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 258.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Verdun: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessor, Pope Calixtus of pious memory, summoned you by his letters to come to him during the past Lent, in order that you might give a reasonable answer concerning the ordination of that intruder Conrad of Toul.

> [Note: [Col. 1237D] Conrad had been elected bishop of Toul in 1107 by certain canons, while Riquin of Commercy was elected by others; Riquin soon secured for himself the votes of both parties. Conrad, however, remained unconsecrated until the time of Calixtus II, as we learn from this letter.]

After his death, we too set you a date to come before us concerning the same matter; but you, puffed up by the swelling of pride, utterly refused to come. Moreover, we commanded you to restore to the abbot of St. Vitonus what was rightfully his monastery’s and to return what had been taken. Afterwards you presumed to take from him those very things and certain others besides. Therefore, because of such grave offences, we command and order you by these present letters to come before us at the next feast of the Epiphany to answer; meanwhile, you are to abstain entirely from episcopal office.

[Col. 1237C] Given at Benevento, on the fifth Nones of October [3 October].

## XXI. He receives the monastery of St. Paul of Argon under protection and confirms its possessions. (1125, 21 November.)

[See Lupi, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis*, II, p. 923.]

## XXII. He confirms the original foundation of the monastery of St. Martin of Ahusen. (1125, 27 November.)

[Petri, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 190.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the monks of the monastery of St. Martin of Ahusen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as assent ought to be denied to unreasonable petitioners, so we ought to meet the requests of those who seek what is just with kindly assent. Accordingly, we have considered the devotion of the noblemen Count Palatine Adelbert and his brothers Udalric and Walter deserving of approval. In the diocese of Augsburg, in the district of Alba, they offered, together with their father Count Palatine Manegold of distinguished memory, for the salvation of his soul, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as their own freehold, with everything belonging to the same place, an estate of their own right called Ahusen, where a church, the house of blessed Martin, has been built . . . They request that this offering be confirmed by our authority.

We therefore decree by the authority of this present enactment that both the aforesaid place and all things belonging to it shall always remain whole and inviolate under the protection of the Apostolic See. No person whatsoever may disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support they were granted.

Upon the death of the abbot of that place, no one may be set over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall regularly determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God. In the election of your advocate (*advocatus*), [Col. 1238B] the abbot shall have free authority, with the counsel of his brethren, to choose a person whom he recognizes to be good and useful for defending the liberty of the monastery.

We also decree that the burial ground of that monastery shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Likewise, we confirm the exchange (*concambium*) which is known to have been made, with the consent of both parties and the acquiescence of the founders, concerning the place on which your monastery is situated, with the church of St. Peter at Tetingen, to whose parish it belonged. You shall receive ordinations of monks and consecrations of altars or churches from the bishop in whose diocese [Col. 1238C] you are, provided that he possesses the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to grant what is requested without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive those sacraments from him, if he grants them under the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold coin annually to the Lateran palace.

If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person violates this page of our constitution, or knowingly attempts rashly to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1239A] on the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of the most holy Pope Honorius II.

## XXIII. Confirmation of the foundation of the cell of St. Mary at Breisach. (1125, 27 November.)

[Petri, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 232.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Abbot OTTO and his brethren professing the canonical rule in the church of St. Mary, situated in the county of Breisach, in the place called the Black Forest, and to their successors who, by the grace of almighty God, shall remain in the same religious life in perpetuity.

[Col. 1239B] We perceive, by God’s ordering, that we have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See so that we may lend our ear to just petitions and ought, insofar as the Lord grants, to spread religion. Since therefore you, dearest sons in Christ, inspired by divine grace, have proposed to establish your conduct under the discipline of regular life and to serve almighty God in common according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, we rejoice in your vows with paternal affection. Accordingly, we grant your petition our fullest and devoted assent, and receive both you and your place under the protection of the Apostolic See.

You have resolved to make it tributary to the Roman Church on the counsel and at the instigation of Bruno, provost of Strasbourg, a man of outstanding energy, who [Col. 1239C] built your church at his own expense upon his own freehold and endowed it by grants of his goods and possessions. We also confirm by the authority of this privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed, and forbid anyone, after making profession, to possess anything as his own or to depart from the cloister without leave of the abbot or community.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one may be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or force except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, shall regularly determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God. No one may interfere in that election except those whom your religious community shall summon. In the election of your advocate (*advocatus*), [Col. 1239D] the abbot shall have free authority, with the counsel of his brethren, to choose one whom he knows to be good and useful for defending the monastery’s liberty. If he proves to be a usurper rather than an advocate and seizes the monastery’s goods instead of defending them, the abbot shall have authority, with the brethren’s counsel, to appoint another advocate more useful to himself.

You shall receive ordinations of clerics and consecrations of altars or churches from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he has the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to grant them to you without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive those sacraments from him, if, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants them.

[Col. 1240A] We strictly forbid an assault, under any pretext, upon the precinct of your monastery. If, however—which God forbid—it happens that violence is inflicted in your court by the shedding of blood, the raising of blows, or anything of this sort, your church is not to be prohibited from divine offices on that account, unless a general interdict has been imposed. Furthermore, we decree that the tithes of your labour and livestock, which are cultivated at that place itself through your expense and labour, shall remain peaceful and inviolate to you; nor do we permit you to be disturbed on this matter either by the bishop of that diocese or by anyone else.

By apostolic authority we command that the exchange made between your church and St. Gall shall remain inviolate for all future time. We also decree that the burial ground [Col. 1240B] of that monastery shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who desire to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Moreover, we decree that whatever goods shall hereafter be justly and canonically acquired through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors, so long as the observance of the canonical order flourishes there by the Lord’s favour. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

As a token of this favour received from the Roman Church, you shall pay the Roman pontiff a priestly stole every two years. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person violates this page of our constitution, or knowingly attempts rashly to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here and hereafter they may receive the fruit of blessed [Col. 1240D] recompense and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. The episcopal right being reserved. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

## XXIV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of St. Ulrich at Neresheim. (1125, 27 November.)

[See *Wirtembergisches Urkundenbuch*, Stuttgart, 1849, I, p. 367.]

## XXV. To Geoffrey, abbot of Savigny.—He confirms the goods granted to the monastery of Savigny. (1125, 9 December.)

[Martène, *Thesaurus*, I, p. 361, from a Savigny manuscript.]

[Col. 1241A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GEOFFREY, abbot of Holy Trinity at Savigny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The pastoral care has been entrusted to us by God so that we may strive both to establish religion pleasing to God and, once established, preserve it with diligent care. Accordingly, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Geoffrey, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Thurstan, archbishop of York, we have considered your reasonable requests deserving of assent.

For we decree that the monastery of the Blessed Trinity at Savigny, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, shall retain secure and inviolate for you and your successors whatever it now justly and lawfully possesses; and whatever you may hereafter acquire, by God’s bounty, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, or the gifts of princes, shall be preserved secure and whole to you, with due reservation of the right and reverence owed to the diocesan bishop.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If anyone knowingly attempts, by rash presumption, to act contrary to this our constitution, let him know that he will incur the sentence of anathema.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of December [9 December].

## XXVI. To S., king of Norway.—That he restore Bishop Ralph of Orkney to his former position. (1125, 9 December.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, p. 144.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ S., illustrious king of Norway: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1241D] It has been reported to us that our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of York, consecrated Ralph himself for Orkney. Afterwards, however, as we have learned, another person was intruded there. Yet either one person shall hold the episcopal see, or none shall. Therefore by these present letters we command your nobility to restore to the aforesaid Ralph the episcopal see—namely, Orkney—with its parish and other appurtenances, as the rightful bishop and pastor of that place. And let your care for the future guard against incurring God’s wrath on this account.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of December [9 December].

## XXVII. To the bishop of Whithorn.—That he go to Thomas [read: Thurstan], archbishop of York, from whom he is to receive consecration. (1125, 9 December.)

[Ibid., p. 145.]

[Col. 1242A]
