HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son, bishop-elect of Whithorn (*Candida Casa*): greeting and apostolic blessing.

No pride in being subject to one’s worthy prelates befits one to whom it is granted by the Lord to preside over others. Therefore by these present letters we command you to go, for consecration, to our dearest brother Thomas, archbishop of York, as to your own metropolitan; and from his hand, in the presence of the grace of the Holy Spirit, receive consecration with humble devotion.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of December [9 December].

## XXVIII. To G., archbishop of Canterbury, etc., and to the king of the English. (1125, 9 December.)

[Ibid., p. 147.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers G., archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, and all bishops established throughout the kingdom of England, and to his dearest son in Christ H., illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as our . . . so you ought to preserve their dignity inviolate for your brethren; [Col. 1242C] therefore we command you to permit, without any opposition, our dearest brother Thomas [read: Thurstan], archbishop of York, in accordance with ancient custom and the prerogative of the Church of York, to have the cross carried before him and to crown the king in the customary manner.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth Ides of December [9 December].

## XXIX. Privilege for the Church of York. (1125.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, p. 335.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THURSTAN, archbishop of York, and to his successors to be canonically promoted in perpetuity.

[Col. 1242D] Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound by the apostolic office entrusted to us to love our brother bishops with intimate charity, preserve for the churches committed to them by God their due rights, strive for their well-being, and, with the Lord’s help, provide beneficially for their peace and advantage.

Therefore, dearest brother Archbishop Thurstan, we confirm in perpetuity to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of York over which, by God’s appointment, you preside, the metropolitan suffragans of the Church of York and whatever parishes are known to belong to that church by episcopal or metropolitan right.

Desiring, with God’s help, that the ancient dignity of the Church of York be kept whole, we forbid by apostolic authority that henceforth either the archbishop of Canterbury demand any profession from the archbishop of York or the archbishop of York make one to Canterbury; nor may York in any way be subject to Canterbury’s jurisdiction, as has been wholly forbidden by blessed Gregory. Rather, in accordance with the ordinance of that same father, this distinction of honour shall be preserved between them forever: he who was ordained first shall be considered first.

Moreover, if the archbishop of Canterbury is unwilling freely, and without exacting submission, to consecrate the archbishop-elect of York, the archbishop-elect of York shall freely be consecrated by his own suffragans or by the Roman pontiff. We confirm by the authority of this present privilege for the Church of York the ancient customs of its liberty and the possessions which you now [Col. 1243B] lawfully hold or may hereafter, by God’s bounty, justly acquire. We decree that no one may take them away, diminish them, or dare to harass them with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

We further add to this present chapter that the churches of St. Andrew of Hexham, St. John of Beverley, St. Wilfrid of Ripon, St. Mary of Southwell, and St. Oswald of Gloucester shall always remain whole and undisturbed, in all possessions, liberties, and customs, to you and your successors and likewise to the Church of York.

If therefore any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

## XXX. He confirms the rights of the Church of Ravenna. (1125.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, II, p. 365.]

[Col. 1243D]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUALTER, archbishop of Ravenna, and to his successors to be canonically promoted.

The most holy Roman Apostolic Church was established by our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, as head and hinge of all things. It is therefore not fitting for the members to depart from the head, but rather to obey the exalted reason and heavenly providence of the head. The governing discernment of the head, moreover, considering the dutiful acts of individual members, distinctly preserves each one’s right, rank, and divinely established nature; and, with social charity free of envy, preserves for all noble churches the dignity of their antiquity.

Moved by this consideration, we desire to preserve without any diminution the honour of the renowned Church of Ravenna, the special daughter of the Apostolic See itself. Therefore, venerable brother Gualter, whom we love in full charity in Christ for your Church’s vigour, learning, religion, and uprightness of character, we assent with paternal affection to your reasonable petitions.

By this page of the present privilege we confirm the bishoprics of the province of Emilia, namely Parma, Piacenza, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, Ferrara, Adria, Comacchio, Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Bobbio, Cesena, and Ficocle. Furthermore, we confirm to you the exarchate of Ravenna, which belongs to the Roman Church, and the monasteries of St. Albert and St. Hilary, together with the other monasteries and possessions belonging to your church, which have been bestowed by authentic privileges from our predecessors and Catholic kings.

[Col. 1244B] We also entrust the care of the monastery of Pomposa to your religious person, while preserving the right of our Church, so that by your diligence it may be reformed in regular discipline. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb our Church of Ravenna, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit both of your uses and those of the clergy and poor.

If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Boniface, cardinal of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal of the Holy Apostles, have subscribed. I, Benedict, cardinal of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed. [Col. 1244D] I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Clement, have subscribed. I, Conrad, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd, have subscribed. I, Desiderius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. I, Peter of Pisa, cardinal-priest of St. Susanna the martyr, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal of the title of St. Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Vitalis, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Guilidinus, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, the count, deacon of St. Mary in Agro, have subscribed. I, G., cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Portico, have subscribed. [Col. 1245A] I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, G., cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed; and many others.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

## XXXI. To the bishops of Provence.—On behalf of the monastery of Lérins: that they restore what has been taken and cause others to restore it. (1125.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, p. 265.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers AUGERIUS, bishop of Riez; BERENGARIUS, bishop of Fréjus; PETER, bishop of Nice; and MANFRED, bishop of Antibes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1245B] Our sons, the abbot Gorinus and the monks of Lérins, set before the jaws of the Saracens and fearing captivity, chains, and the dangers of death, complain to us tearfully concerning you: that you presume forcibly to take away certain churches from them. Though they expected necessary protection from you, with the proper order reversed they experience unbearable loss.

We therefore command your brotherhoods to restore the aforesaid churches promptly and in full to the monastery of Lérins. They also complain most pitifully concerning your parishioners: namely Peter of Alanson, the wife of William Anger, and the knights of Montbrison, who, after plundering their estate, ravaged and laid it waste by fire; and concerning the same wife of William, who utterly reduced another estate, together with its monastery, to desolation. Therefore we command you to compel them to make satisfaction to the monastery of Lérins and its brethren.

But you, bishop of Antibes, are to warn your parishioner Fulk—

> [Note: [Col. 1245D] Fulk of Grasse, brother of William.]

—that he must come to a peaceful agreement with the brethren of that place concerning the money which our predecessor Pope Paschal of blessed memory directed should be given to the monastery of Lérins from the funds prepared for the journey to Jerusalem which Fulk had vowed to undertake; that he must restore the money which the brethren gave from the monastery treasury to ransom him from the Saracens, and which he swore to repay; restore the estate belonging by right to the monastery which he took from it; and make satisfaction to the abbot and monks for the castle of Aureiluc [Arluc], which he presumed to devastate. [Col. 1245D] Otherwise, we shall be unable to refrain from the sentence of our office.

Given at the Lateran.

## XXXII. To Gerard, bishop of Chieti. (1125–1126.)

[Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, II, II, p. 1007.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of Chieti: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our son Giso, abbot of the monastery of St. Clement of Pescara, came before us and complained in our presence against your parishioner Rainald of [Col. 1246A] Tocco that he was forcibly taking from him the church of St. Mary at Pesile. We therefore command your brotherhood to admonish the same Rainald to restore the church to the aforesaid abbot. Otherwise, if he proves contumacious, do not delay in exercising full justice against him. For we shall, by God’s authority, ratify whatever you canonically do in this matter.

### XXXIII. To Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela. (A.D. 1126, Jan. 10.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 442.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1246B] We have received, with the charity which was due, the envoys with letters sent to us by your brotherhood. But since many affairs pressed upon us, and because of our recent accession, we have not at present been able to respond to your requests. Let, however, the discerning prudence of your brotherhood take care that you strive to use, and not misuse, the dignity of the pallium, which the clemency of your holy mother, the Roman Church, has granted you as a sign of humility.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.

### XXXIV. To the Same. (A.D. 1126, Jan. 10.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1246C] HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although certain sinister and superstitious reports concerning your person have reached our ears, nevertheless, since you profess yourself a most devoted son of the Roman Church, we desire to love you with true charity and do not wish lightly to give a hearing to any informer concerning you. But conduct yourself with such humility and devotion that you may be able fully to retain the favor of blessed Peter and of ourselves.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of January.

### XXXV. To Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln—Confirmation of the Privileges of the Church of Lincoln. (A.D. 1126, Jan. 30.)

[WILKINS, *Concilia M. Britann.*, vol. I, p. 406.]

[Col. 1246D]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALEXANDER, bishop of Lincoln, and to his successors lawfully to be installed, in perpetuity.

The pious and diligent concern of a mother’s solicitude is accustomed sweetly to rear tender children and wisely to provide adults with the means by which they may be supported. Correspondingly, the holy Roman Church, founded upon Peter’s faith, holds primacy among all Churches: she nourishes the little and weak with the milk of her wisdom; but supplies the mature and devout with the food of deeper knowledge [Col. 1247A] and, so that they may be freer to devote themselves to divine service, defends them from the assaults of enemies by the protection of the Apostolic See.

Moved therefore by this consideration, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the Church of Lincoln, over which, beloved brother Alexander, bishop in the Lord, you preside by God’s appointment; and, by its authority, we strengthen it with defense and privilege against the molestation of wicked men. Therefore may the goods and possessions which it justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter be able canonically to acquire through the Lord’s bounty, remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of Lincoln.

Among these we have thought fit to record by their own names: namely, in the city of Lincoln, the borough called Willingtorp; Hundegata; the church of All Saints; [Col. 1247B] Netella, Luda, Stou, Noritona, Newerca, Staford, Lidentona, Spaldewic, Buchendara; the manor situated near the city of Leicester; Chilesbei, Eroposeia, Banebiria, Tama, Nundentona, Dorchecestria, Woburna; the abbey of Egenesham, with all appurtenances of all the aforesaid; the episcopal parish of Lindsey; Northamptonshire, Leicestershire, Hampshire, Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Huntingdonshire, and part of Herefordshire.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever, cleric or layman, may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit of ecclesiastical uses. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page [Col. 1247C] of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, the third day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1247D] 1126, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XXXVI. Privilege Confirming the Possessions and Goods of the Monastery of St. Theoderic at Reims. (A.D. 1126, Feb. 10.)

[VARIN, *Archiv. admin. de Reims*, vol. I, p. 279.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Saint [Col. 1248A] Theoderic, situated in the territory of Reims, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

A desire shown to pertain to the religious vocation and the salvation of souls must, by God’s authority, be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, beloved son in Christ William, abbot, assenting to your reasonable requests, we receive into the protection of blessed Peter and our own protection the monastery of Saint Theoderic, over which you are known to preside by the Lord’s appointment. By this present decree we confirm to you and to your successors, advanced there in the fear of God, all possessions and all goods which that place now lawfully possesses.

Among these, the following seemed fit to be stated by their own names: namely, [Col. 1248B] the whole village of Saint Theoderic itself, free and unmolested, and exempt from advocacy, county jurisdiction, viscounty jurisdiction, and every secular exaction, according to the charters of Kings Lothair, Charles, and Henry; together with the adjacent hamlet called Villare-sub-Silva; likewise, the demesne holding in the village of Pouillon; the demesne holding in the village of Tilly, with its dependent lands; and in all these, jurisdictional authority, justice, and an oven, with the entire tithe; the village of Francs with the entire tithe. Since all these are contained under one parish, it is free on the ground that it does not pay those annual provisions at the synod; and the priests whom the abbot appoints there need not attend the assemblies of deans called the Kalends unless they wish to do so voluntarily, though otherwise they shall render canonical obedience to them. [Col. 1248C]

The demesne holding in the village of Trigny or Mazelles; justice, jurisdictional authority, and the ban-oven throughout the whole village, with the entire tithe and certain lands lying in the village of Cavaillon and belonging to Trigny itself; the tithe of the village of Châlons, which belongs to the parish of Trigny itself; the tithe of the village of Chanat, which belongs to the parish of Saint Theoderic, as does the village of Francs. Three mills at Vidula, with all the water and fishing rights of that river, from the division of the river above the mill of Maschot as far as the mill of Macele, together with a fourth part of that mill and the marsh adjoining that water, for the grass-right of which the peasants of Châlons render corvée service to Saint Theoderic at Trigny. The village of Nocturniacum, with jurisdictional authority and justice; [Col. 1248D] the demesne holding in the court of Brimercy; rent-paying lands in the village of Mairy and likewise at Gaugia.

In the diocese of Reims, these altars: Trigny; Herimundivilla; Summopi; Spoia; Seilisas; Ida; Thelina.

> [Note: Col. 1247D. A privilege of Eugenius, issued in 1148 and found in the Cartulary of Saint-Thierry, fol. 391, adds here: “de Puteolis.” See the notice of this same privilege in Morlot, no. 358.]

> [Note: Col. 1247D. The privilege of 1148 adds: “… with the chapel [Col. 1248D] of Vosiers, with two parts of the tithe and three mills.”]

In the bishopric of Laon, these altars: Wreivilla; Hupenci Court; Berturi Court; Agubi Court; Condet; Domnamaria; Ansoldi Court; Saint Theodulf, which is called Guast.

> [Note: Col. 1248D. The privilege of 1148 adds: “… with a demesne holding and three parts of all the land adjoining that village.”]

In the bishopric [Col. 1249A] of Noyon, two altars and churches, and the full tithes of Atheiis and Emina, and seven holdings of land in the village of Atheiis itself. In the bishopric of Tournai, these altars: Guartengen; Kercova, with the chapel of Guarnereia.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. The bull of 1148 adds: “… Dotheniis with the chapel of Coengio; the church of Petengio.”]

In the bishopric of Cambrai, these altars: Bernis, with the chapel of Quadromonte; Elefella.

> [Note: Col. 1250D. The bull of 1148 adds: Scalnasia.]

Whatever else the same monastery may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire shall remain secure and unimpaired to it; and the aforesaid altars shall be free and without incumbents. Saving in all matters the rights and reverence due to the archbishop of Reims and the other bishops, and canonical customs.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1249B] or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for every useful purpose of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1249C] and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Haimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XXXVII. Confirmation of the Discipline and Possessions of the Brethren of St. Mary of Prémontré. (A.D. 1126, Feb. 16.)

[HUGO, *Annales sacri ord. Praemonstrat.*, vol. I, preliminary matter, p. 9.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1249D] sons, NORBERT, brother in Christ, and the canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Prémontré, and to their successors professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Those who follow the footsteps of apostolic discipline renounce worldly pomp and possessions and serve the Lord with all their strength. If these, then, bring to completion the good which they have begun, at the Judge’s final examination they will obtain the robe of immortality and everlasting glory. Since, therefore, inspired by divine grace, you have resolved to live religiously and lead there the canonical life according to the institution of blessed Augustine, we confirm your purpose by the authority of the Apostolic See and exhort you to persevere steadfastly in it for the remission of your sins.

We therefore ordain that in your churches, in which brethren professing the canonical life dwell, no person whatsoever may alter the order established there according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Nor may any bishop in future dare to expel from your churches brethren of this religious order; nor may any person professing the canonical life dare to depart from those churches or cloisters without the common permission of the community. No bishop, abbot, monk, or any person whatsoever may receive one who has departed without the security of letters from the community. We also confirm by this page [Col. 1250B] of our present writing the goods and possessions which you justly and lawfully possess.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names: namely, the Church of Saint Martin of Laon in the diocese of Laon; the Church of Saint Mary of Viviers in the diocese of Soissons; the Church of Saint Mary of Floreffe in the diocese of Liège; the Church of Saint Mary and of the blessed Peter and Paul at Cappenberg in the diocese of Münster; the Church of Saint Mary at Wollar in the same diocese; the Church of Saint Mary at Clostat [Elcostad] in the diocese of Mainz; the Church of Saint Annalis in the diocese of Metz; the Church of Saint Michael at Antwerp in the diocese of Cambrai; the circuit of the same valley, from the place called Halierpré to the valley of Rochard, with the three adjacent valleys, and from the stream toward Vois, as the valleys extend.

The two parts of the tithe which you hold in the village of Crespi through the bishop of Laon, and the other things which you possess in that village by the grant of our beloved son Louis, king of France. The freehold of Clairfont; the freehold of Romengeis with a mill; three holdings at Bolmont; one holding at Anisy with a mill; one holding at Fraisne; one holding at Versigny; three and a half holdings at Souppy; the whole freehold called Bonnuel. One house at Soissons with vineyards and lands; vineyards in the district of Laon, in the villages called Broiencourt, Ursignicourt, and Montarcume.

Whatever else you may in future be able canonically to acquire by grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors who persevere in the purpose of holy religion. [Col. 1250D] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb those churches, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit of regular brethren and the poor, saving the canonical jurisdiction of diocesan bishops.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all preserving the rights of those churches may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Haimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Honorius II, [Col. 1251B] pope.

### XXXVIII. Confirmation of the Foundation of the Church of Cappenberg. (A.D. 1126, Feb. 27.)

[HUGO, ibid., preliminary matter, p. 369.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ NORBERT and his brethren, professing the regular life in the Church of Saint Mary at Cappenberg, and to their successors in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive in every way to spread religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever acceptably rendered to God unless it proceeds from the root of charity and is preserved by the purity of religion. Thus, out of this concern for charity, we have reasonably judged that your requests should be granted.

We therefore decree and, by apostolic authority, establish that no person whatsoever may alter the order established according to the Rule of blessed Augustine in the Church of Cappenberg, for the construction of which Count Godfrey, his brothers, and Otto, their co-heir, offered the site to God, Saint Mary, and the holy apostles; or at Varlas and Hofstadt, where brethren professing the canonical life dwell. No bishop in future may dare to expel brethren of this religious order from those churches; nor may any person professing the canonical life [Col. 1251D] dare to depart from those churches or cloisters without the common permission of the community. No bishop, abbot, monk, or any person whatsoever may receive one who departs without the security of letters from the community.

We therefore prohibit and altogether forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to enter, occupy, or fortify as a castle Cappenberg and its precinct by force or fraud. We also confirm by this page of our writing the goods and possessions which the aforesaid three persons, and the freeholds which other faithful persons have lawfully bestowed upon those churches from just alms for the use of the canons.

Among these we have thought fit to record by their own names: namely, Werne, Nette, Alsteden, Heile, Cappenberg, [Col. 1252A] Mangethe, Curete, Sorbeke, Wifecle, Wisheim, Spelchorp, Hasela, Lancklar, with all their appurtenances: namely, meadows and pastures, roads and trackless places, streams and watercourses, mills, woods, and fields. Whatever else you may in future be able canonically to acquire through the grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors persevering in the purpose of holy religion.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb those churches, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit of regular brethren and the poor, saving the canonical jurisdiction [Col. 1252B] of diocesan bishops. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of those churches may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1252C] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XXXIX. Privilege for the Monastery of St. John the Evangelist at Kaltenborn. (A.D. 1126, Feb. 27.)

[*Thuringia sacra*, p. 304.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, GODESCALC, provost, and his brethren in the Church of Saint John the Evangelist at Coldenbrunna, professing the canonical life, both present [Col. 1252D] and future, in perpetuity.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious persons and to defend their places by the protection of apostolic guardianship. Our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Calixtus, as we learn from his writing, fortified with the protection of apostolic guardianship your Church of Saint John, which the nobleman Wimannus established from his own estates for the regular life in the diocese of Halberstadt. Accordingly, favorably assenting to your requests and following in the footsteps of that lord, we establish by apostolic authority the order of canonical life which you have professed, and strengthen your church by this page of the present writing.

For we decree that all possessions and goods justly bestowed upon that place from their own right, whether by the aforesaid Wigmann or by any faithful persons, or which it may hereafter happen to receive justly and canonically through God’s bounty, shall remain forever secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved entire for every useful purpose of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the provost of that place, no one may be placed over it through any artifice or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, elect according to God. If anyone, having learned the tenor [Col. 1253B] of this decree, should rashly attempt—God forbid—to act against it, let him incur the loss of his honor and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XL. Privilege for the Church of St. Mary at Piacenza. (A.D. 1126, Mar. 9.)

[CAMPI, *Dell’ Historia di Piacenza*, vol. I, proofs, p. 528.]

[Col. 1253C]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the mother church of Saint Mary and Saint Justina at Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may give diligent thought to the condition of the Churches and, with the vigilant concern of paternal affection, provide for their welfare; so that through the assiduity of our labor they may increase in spiritual and temporal goods, and we may thereby receive our due reward from God. Therefore, most dear sons in Christ, favorably yielding to your petitions made through our venerable brother [Col. 1253D] Arduin, bishop of the city of Piacenza, we have resolved to strengthen by the aid of apostolic defense the Church of Piacenza of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, and of the holy martyr Justina, in which you serve the Lord.

We confirm by this page of our present writing to you and your successors the possessions and goods which you justly and lawfully possess: those granted to you by the religious bishops of Piacenza who have departed this world, or by that same brother of ours, the bishop who at present presides over your Church; those offered from their own right by faithful men; and those acquired by other means—while certainly preserving the jurisdiction and due reverence of your bishops.

In like manner, we confirm the chapel of Gosolongo [Col. 1254A] and the parish church of Verdeto, with their appurtenances, which the aforesaid brother Arduin, bishop, has generously granted for your use with paternal kindness. Whatever else you may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through God’s bounty shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for every useful purpose of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1254B] But upon all who preserve the rights of that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1254C] on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XLI. He Receives the Monastery of St. Blaise into Apostolic Protection and Confirms Its Free Advocacy. (A.D. 1126, Mar. 28.)

[GERBERT, *Hist. Nigrae Silvae*, vol. III, p. 59.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTOLD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise, situated in the diocese of Constance, namely in the place called the Black Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by the Lord, provider [Col. 1254D] of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and spread in every way the religion pleasing to the Lord. For no service is ever acceptably rendered to the Lord unless it proceeds from the root of charity and is preserved by the purity of religion. Therefore we graciously assent to your petition and strengthen the monastery of Saint Blaise, over which you preside by God’s appointment, with the protection of the Apostolic See, together with all things belonging to it.

We decree that whatever the same monastery today justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved entire for every useful purpose of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

You shall receive the consecration of altars or churches, the ordination of monks, chrism, holy oil, and the other things belonging to episcopal office, from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide them freely and without wrongful exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what you have requested. [Col. 1255B]

We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Moreover, no opposition by any bishop or provost may prevent you from receiving laymen or clerics living in the secular state for conversion. Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it by any fraudulent artifice or force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Furthermore, saving the reverence due to the bishop of Constance, we confirm to your monastery the cell in the forest of Schwarzwald, built by Saint Reginbert, [Col. 1255C] together with all possessions, estates, and lands belonging to it.

> [Note: Col. 1255. Here is the repeated confirmation to the monastery of St. Blaise of the cell of St. Reginbert.]

We also confirm that arrangement concerning the liberty and advocacy of your monastery which Henry IV, emperor of blessed memory, established; which our predecessor Pope Calixtus of happy memory strengthened by the privilege of his authority; which our beloved son Lothair, king, fortified by the firmness of his decree; and which we have ratified by the common deliberation of our brother bishops and cardinals. Namely, in electing an advocate, the abbot shall have free authority, with the counsel of his brethren, to choose such a person as he knows to be good and useful for defending the monastery’s liberty, one who desires to hold and administer that advocacy well, not for earthly gain but for the love of God, the remission of his sins, and the reward of eternal blessing.

But if, being a vexatious claimant rather than an advocate, he seizes the monastery’s goods instead of defending them, and, having been warned once, twice, or three times, in no way makes amends, the abbot shall have authority, with the counsel of the brethren, to appoint there another, more useful advocate. Thus, as was determined by judicial decision of the aforesaid Emperor Henry and our aforesaid son King Lothair, the liberty of your monastery shall in every respect be exempt from the jurisdiction of the Church of Basel. As a sign of our protection and of the liberty granted [Col. 1256A] to your monastery, you shall pay one gold coin annually to the Lateran Palace.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal [Col. 1256B] peace. Amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

### XLII. He Confirms the Monastery of Wiblingen and Its Goods, and Receives It into Apostolic Protection. (A.D. 1126, Mar. 28.)

[As above, p. 55.]

[Col. 1257B] HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WARNER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin called Wiblingen, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

Desire which is shown to pertain to the purpose of religion and to the salvation of souls must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore we, beloved son in Christ, having been moved by your petitions presented through our venerable brother Udalric, bishop of Constance, strengthen by the privilege of apostolic authority the monastery of St Martin, over which, by God’s ordering, you are known to preside. It was received by our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Urban, into the special right and protection of the Apostolic See. We decree that whatever estates and whatever goods the aforesaid church now possesses, whether by the gift of its founders, Count Hartmann and his brother Otto, or by the just offering of other faithful persons, and whatever it may hereafter be able lawfully and canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1257C]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, to serve the uses of those for whose support they were granted, saving nevertheless the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Constance. He may, however, in no way impose any exaction or custom harmful to the peace of those living under the rule. [Col. 1257D]

After the religious Count Hartmann, the advocacy of that monastery shall be administered by his heir whom the abbot and brethren have chosen. If he should afterwards prove useless to the monastery, they shall remove him and appoint another. We decree that burial in the same place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wishes of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Furthermore, by a decree to remain in force forever, we establish that no living person may claim in your monastery any condition of proprietary right, hereditary right, investiture, or any authority whatsoever that may harm the brethren’s liberty and peace. [Col. 1258A]

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks to be promoted to sacred orders, from the bishop in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he possesses the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to furnish these freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what is requested.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one may be placed over it by any craft of insinuation or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of St Benedict. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually one gold bezant to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen. [Col. 1258B–C]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hiemeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1125. [Note: [Col. 1257] The year 1126 must be placed here, when the fourth indiction and the second year of the pontificate of Honorius II—elected 21 December 1124—were running.] In the fourth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XLIII. * He receives the monastery of St Lambert into protection and confirms its possessions and rights, imposing upon the monks an annual rent of one bezant. (Year 1026, 29 March.)

[“In the Imperial archive at Vienna, from Pertz’s papers.” JAFFÉ, *Regesta Rom. pont.*, p. 553. Opening words: “Because without spring.”]

XLIV. Brief to all bishops and magnates of Gaul, that they restrain Pons, formerly abbot of Cluny. (Year 1126, 24 April.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 336.]

[Col. 1258D]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable fathers, archbishops, bishops, barons, and other faithful persons established throughout France, Aquitaine, and Burgundy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The devil, enemy of all goodness, sought to sift the religious life of the brethren of Cluny like wheat. For he drew Pons, swollen with a spirit of arrogance, from regions beyond the sea by the hook of ambition, in order to disturb brethren devoted to divine service; and he brought it about that the monastery of Cluny was occupied by him. Therefore, sending to you from the bosom of the holy Roman Church our beloved son Peter, cardinal-deacon, we command your charity that, following his counsel, you take the utmost care to expel the invader Pons from the monastery of Cluny, its dependent houses, and all its appurtenances. For this same son of ours, Peter, in our stead, will confirm the sentence of anathema against Pons and all his supporters. Take care also to uphold and honor our beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

XLV. To the monks of Cluny.—That they reject Abbot Pons. (Year 1126, 24 April.)

[MANSI, ibid., p. 337.]

[Col. 1259B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all monks and lay brothers belonging to the monastery of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly grieved because, as we have learned, Pons, driven by a diabolical spirit, has seemed by reckless daring to disturb the unity of the sacred community and the state of religious life. Although woe is to that man through whom scandal comes, scandals must nevertheless arise for the testing and purification of the good. [Col. 1259C] For the strength and courage of a soldier are known in war, and the steadfastness of religious faith is proved in adversity.

Therefore, sending to you from the bosom of the holy Roman Church our beloved son Peter, cardinal-deacon, we command that, remaining firmly in the unity of charity, you give no counsel or assistance whatsoever to that Pons; rather, abstain from him in every way as from a schismatic and an invader. For this same son of ours, Peter, in our stead, will confirm the sentence of anathema against Pons and all his supporters. We command, moreover, that you humbly show obedience and reverence to our beloved son, the abbot of Cluny, as to your shepherd and the ruler of your souls.

[Col. 1259D]

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

XLVI. To Humbert, archbishop of Lyons.—On the same matter. (Year 1126, 24 April.)

[MANSI, ibid.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable HU . . . ., archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are grieved because, as we have learned, Pons has rashly disturbed the religious life of Cluny. We therefore give thanks to your brotherhood because, as a lover of religion, you resisted him manfully. With urgent vigilance, strive by every means, both through ministers of the Church and through secular powers, to drag him from the monastery and put him in prison. We immediately send from our side a legate, who will give you counsel and assistance in accomplishing this.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Formula of excommunication against Pons and the Ponziani.

This is the excommunication pronounced by Cardinal Peter, legate of the holy Roman Church, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the authority of Lord Pope Honorius, whose office he exercises, against Pons the invader and schismatic, against the burgesses of Cluny, and against all their supporters, at the synod of Lyons, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the presence of consenting bishops, abbots, many priests, and clerics.

[Col. 1260B]

Because Pons, contrary to the will of God, of Lord Pope Honorius, and of the whole Roman Church, has seized the monastery of Cluny by the irrational violence of laymen, we, following the mercy of the Roman Church more than the severity of justice, summoned him to us three times, by letters as well as messengers, so that he might hear from our mouth the will of Lord Pope Honorius on this matter and obey him in all things as the universal Father of the whole world. But because he refused to obey Lord Pope Honorius, in whose stead we act, and refused to repent of the crime of invading the Church which he had committed, we will no longer suffer this injury done to God and the Apostolic See to remain unavenged.

By the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of Lord Pope Honorius, who has entrusted to us full power to act in his stead in this matter, we confirm in the present synod the sentence of excommunication justly pronounced anew against the same Pons and all his supporters by Lord Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, legate of the holy Roman Church and of Lord Pope Honorius, and by his suffragans. Renewing it again, we bind the aforesaid Pons, the monks adhering to him, and likewise the burgesses of Cluny with the bond of anathema, until they come to their senses and return to fitting satisfaction. [Col. 1260C]

We also command under anathema that no one presume to ring bells, celebrate divine offices, or hold chapter in the churches or workshops within the circuit of the wall of Cluny, or outside it within the enclosures or dependency of the whole borough, until Pons departs from there and ceases this assault. Moreover, we bind by the same bond of anathema those who have received, or shall hereafter receive or give, anything from the treasury of the church of Cluny by way of donation, sale, or pledge.

Furthermore, we place under interdict the dependent houses in which Pons has intruded his own priors—namely, Souvigny, together with Prior Eustorgius and his supporters; Marseille with its prior; Laizi; and its prior; Paray with its prior—so that divine offices may not be celebrated there. Finally, we interdict every office of Christianity in the places mentioned above, except baptism for children and penance for the dying who wish to turn from this wickedness, after security has been given into the hands of Lefald Vincent and of others who maintain obedience to the Roman Church and fidelity to Abbot Peter. [Col. 1260D–1261A]

We bind with the same bond those who carry provisions or arms, for price or gift, to the burgesses of Cluny in defense of this crime.

XLVII. He restores to Roger, archbishop of Pisa, the right of consecrating the bishops of Corsica and grants him the pallium. (Year 1126, 21 July.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 343.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROGER, archbishop of Pisa, and his successors canonically appointed forever.

For this purpose we know that we have been established, by God the author of all good things, in the holy mother Catholic and universal Roman Church, which is the seat of justice: that we may preserve its rightful due to all churches and, if we learn that anything has been wrongly done, bring it back to the path of rectitude by the counsel of reason, so that matters needing correction may be corrected by judicial order and things rightly established may remain in the strength of their vigor. [Col. 1261B]

Our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban, out of regard for justice and charity, with the counsel of bishops and cardinals and the assent of other faithful persons, entrusted and subjected to the Church of Pisa and to Daibert, who then presided over it, and to his canonically succeeding successors, the government and ordering of the bishoprics of the island of Corsica. He also promoted Daibert himself as archbishop of the island of Corsica and commanded the Corsican bishops, under obedience, to obey him as their metropolitan.

For, during the great and long tempest of schismatics which the Roman Church was then suffering, he had made the city of Pisa liable to many labors. Corsica, moreover, had cooled in its subjection and obedience to the Roman Church, both through the length of distances and through the negligence of its pastors, the insolence of its lords, and the lack of legates of the Apostolic See. Given over to dissolution and dispersal, it had almost abandoned the discipline of ecclesiastical order. [Col. 1261C]

Accordingly, that same predecessor of ours fittingly responded to the merits of so many benefits conferred by the Pisans, and in due charity provided for the Corsican Church, which is nearer to the Pisans. Afterwards his successor Pope Gelasius, from the same regard of charity, confirmed by the authority of his privilege the same right and dignity which Pope Urban had bestowed upon the Church of Pisa. When he had been taken from this light, our predecessor Pope Calixtus, for the same reason, strengthened with the protection of his privilege what had been granted and confirmed to the Church of Pisa by his predecessors Urban and Gelasius.

But the Genoese, envying the honor of the Pisan people and unable to endure their advancement with equanimity, seized this matter as an occasion and made war against the Pisans. Hence, through the exaction of sins, there occurred slaughter, fires, and many captivities of Christians, while the Saracens’ boldness in raging against Christians greatly increased. Furthermore, the Genoese, coming to the City, diligently endeavored to stir up the Roman clergy and people, persuading them that it would be a great loss to the Roman Church unless the dignity granted to the Church of Pisa were taken away. [Col. 1261D–1262A]

They asserted that the Roman Church was the cause and support of this war, and that, if the consecration of the Corsican bishops were recalled to the Roman Church’s own jurisdiction, peace and concord would undoubtedly arise between themselves and the Pisans. Moved by these reasons, Lord Pope Calixtus, a lover of peace, revoked, for the sake of peace, that grant to the Church of Pisa made by his predecessors and confirmed by himself, and annulled it by the text of his document. Yet neither in his time nor in ours has concord between the Pisans and Genoese been achieved.

After the government of the Roman Church had been entrusted to us by God, you, brother Roger, archbishop of Pisa, and the consuls came to us and humbly asked us to render justice concerning the consecration of the Corsican bishops. This had been granted to the Church of Pisa by our predecessors Urban, Gelasius, and others, and had been removed without prior fault on the part of the Pisans and without judgment. The Pisans likewise being present, the Genoese subsequently came before us and nonetheless asked that we confirm the removal effected for them by Pope Calixtus. [Col. 1262B]

We carefully urged both parties to make peace, but could obtain peace from them neither by entreaties nor admonitions. For the Genoese who had come to us declared that they had not been sent by their people for this purpose and could not go beyond their instructions. Therefore, after taking counsel with our brethren the bishops and cardinals, we agreed that reason required both peoples to be compelled to peace. We accordingly sent our legate, a count then cardinal-deacon, with our letters to Genoa and Pisa, ordering them to confirm by oath in his hand that they would obey our commands concerning the consecration of Corsica and the war until the approaching feast of St Michael.

When that term had passed, both parties came before us. We labored diligently to establish peace between them, although without success. Finally, when we asked them to confirm by oath that they would obey our commands, the Genoese said that they could not do so because the term of their consulate had expired. Then, by the common deliberation of the Pisan council, we received their oath concerning this matter; and, lest the Genoese allege against us any reasonable excuse, we granted them a second and a third term by our messengers and letters. [Col. 1262C–D]

They neither came nor sent a canonical excuse for themselves. Since, therefore, the dispute remained between the Roman and Pisan Churches and the Pisans did not cease seeking the right of their Church, we summoned our brethren the archbishops, bishops, and abbots who fully knew the case and the manner of the act done by our predecessor Calixtus. When they had gathered in the sacred Lateran palace in the Lord’s name, we handed them the registers of our predecessors Urban, Gelasius, and Calixtus. We carefully showed what had been done by us since we assumed the burden of the Apostolic See and how greatly we had labored to arrange peace between the parties, asking them, in the charity with which they had come, to advise us according to what the grace of the Holy Spirit revealed to them. [Col. 1263A]

Afterwards, adjured by the faith which they owed to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, they replied that they were constrained by no cause other than divine charity to give the counsel which they gave; this counsel they issued in writing, ratified by their own hands. The words of that document are these:

“By the prompting grace of the Holy Spirit, Lord Honorius, bishop of the most sacred and Apostolic See, asked the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of various provinces for counsel as to what ought justly and canonically to be done in the matter of the Church of Pisa. It seemed reasonable to them that the privileges and decrees of Urban, Gelasius, and Calixtus of blessed memory should remain unshaken, and that the Church of Pisa, despoiled of the Corsican bishoprics without a judicial procedure proper to the case, ought to be restored to them.” [Col. 1263B]

The archbishops Walter of Ravenna, Romuald of Salerno, Otto of Capua, and Roffred of Benevento subscribed to this document; likewise the bishops William of Orvieto, Guido of Arezzo, Gregory of Terracina, Pandulf of Teano, Clarissimus of Assisi, Robert of Aversa, Richard of Gaeta, Transmund of Segni, John of Cales, Gualfred of Siena, Geoffrey of Sessa, Ranulf of Caserta, James of Faenza, Otto of Sutri, Peter of Civita Castellana, Benedict of Nepi, Ildito of Soana, Gerard of Amelia, Benno of Cesena, and Peter of Tuscania; and the abbots Matthew of St Lawrence of Aversa and John of St Sophia, together with John, prior of Camaldoli. Also present were the other bishops Benedict of Lucania, Andrew of Luni, Illandus of Massa, Peter of Chiusi, and Otto of Todi. The absent Oldegarius, archbishop of Tarragona, and the bishops Walter of Maguelonne and Gottfried of Florence gave their assent and counsel in letters of their own. [Col. 1263C]

Moreover, our fellow brethren, the bishops and cardinals, assembling together in the Lord, began to deliberate among themselves; and all but one deacon judged that Pope Urban had lawfully been entitled, by the authority of the Roman Church, even against the will of the bishops of that island, to establish the bishop of Pisa as guardian and metropolitan of the Corsican Church. They further judged that his successors, Lord Gelasius and Lord Calixtus, were likewise entitled to confirm the same arrangement by their privileges. And because the dignity granted and confirmed to the Church of Pisa by so many Roman pontiffs ought not to have been taken away without manifest fault and judgment, they again judged that the same dignity ought to be restored to it and that the privileges issued by those Roman pontiffs concerning that grant should be preserved unshaken. This was also approved by the honored men Peter, prefect, the consuls, and the other wise and noble men of the Roman city. [Col. 1263D]

Therefore, recognizing as just before all men what had been commended by the archbishops and abbots, judged by the cardinals, and approved by the barons, we invested you, dearest brother Roger, archbishop of Pisa, with the pastoral staff for the consecration of the bishops of the island of Corsica. Now, therefore, according to the judgment of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, the counsel and approval of the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and the assent of the Roman nobility, we decree that the privileges issued to the Church of Pisa by our predecessors Urban, Gelasius, and Calixtus shall remain in force and unimpaired. By the text of the present privilege we restore to you, and through you to the Church of Pisa, the consecration of the bishops of Corsica, so that, according to the tenor of the privileges already mentioned, you may have authority as the proper metropolitan of that island to govern, ordain, and consecrate its bishoprics and bishops, and to summon them to synod both in the metropolitan Church of Pisa and on the island itself, for the honor of God and of that Church of Pisa. [Col. 1264A–B]

We also confirm to you and your successors the use of the pallium, granted by our predecessors to your predecessors for precedence over that island, on the days specified above: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Hypapante, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the three feasts of blessed Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, the nativities of St John the Baptist and of the holy Apostles, the Commemoration of All Saints, the consecration of churches, the consecration of suffragan bishops and clerics, the annual anniversary of your own consecration, the feast of St Sixtus, the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the anniversary of the dedication of the Church of Pisa, the feasts of the holy martyrs Stephen, Lawrence, and Ephysius—whose body rests in that church—and the solemnity of blessed Agatha, virgin and martyr. We also grant that, throughout the Pisan diocese and the island of Corsica, a cross may be carried before you and your successors. [Col. 1264C]

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 1264D]

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have signed. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed. I, Boniface, cardinal-priest of the title of St Mark, have signed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Apostles, have signed. I, Benedict, cardinal-priest of the title of Eudoxia, have signed. [Col. 1265A] I, Conrad, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd, was present and have signed. I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of the title of Damasus, have signed. I, Sasso, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen, have signed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Susanna, martyr, have signed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus, have signed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Callixtus, have signed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus, have signed. I, Sigito, cardinal-priest of the title of SS Marcellinus and Peter, have signed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St Sabina, have signed. I, Gerard, cardinal-priest of the title of SS Aquila and Prisca, have signed. I, Ubert, cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement, have signed.

[Col. 1265B] I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, have signed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico, have signed. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore, have signed. I, Stephen, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, have signed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas, have signed. I, Angelus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Domnica, have signed. I, Hyacinth, prior-subdeacon of the sacred basilica, have signed. I, Hermann, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, have signed. I, Nicholas, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, have signed. I, Silvius, prior of the subdeacons of the Cross, have signed. I, Peter, subdeacon, have subscribed. I, Caleph, subdeacon, have subscribed. [Col. 1265C] I, Matthew, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, have signed. I, John, however unworthy a subdeacon, have signed. I, Bobus, subdeacon of the sacred palace, have signed. I, Gerard, subdeacon, have signed. I, Stephen, subdeacon of the sacred palace, have signed. I, Boniface, clerk, have signed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XLVIII. He confirms Peter, abbot, in the abbey of Cluny, and condemns Pons as “excommunicated, invader, plunderer, sacrilegious person, and schismatic.” (Year 1126, 20 October.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 338.]

[Col. 1265D]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The care of the universal Church entrusted to us by God, dispenser of all good things, does not cease constantly to urge our mind to preserve unshaken the state of religious life and to safeguard due liberty for religious places. Yet holy mother Church, which for a time is partly a pilgrim on earth, is purified by the storm of many oppressions and tested in the furnace of severe persecution; gazing toward heaven, she sighs in grief until she is united there in presence with the one who, rewarded with the prize of the unfading crown, rejoices in the contemplation of her Creator. [Col. 1266A]

But the ship of blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of heaven, over which Christ presides as helmsman, though struck by many storms and tossed by terrible blasts of wind, will nevertheless never suffer the loss of shipwreck; rather, it will safely reach the harbor of tranquility with those who cleave to it.

Pons, indeed, enemy of blessed Benedict and hammer against the precepts and monastic order, had renounced the abbey of Cluny into the hands of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Calixtus, without hope of recovery, and had bound himself by vow to live permanently at Jerusalem. Yet, against God’s will and ours, he occupied the monastery of Cluny in proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption. Disturbing the splendor of the religious life of the brethren of Cluny, which had shone throughout all Gaul, he infected the hearts of the simple with the poison of his wickedness. [Col. 1266B]

Furthermore, adding sacrilege and the disgrace of rapacity to his former sins, he plundered the sacred vessels and the monastery’s treasury, which had been set aside from the offerings of the faithful for the use of the poor when need should arise; and he squandered the greater part of it to retain soldiers, archers, and crossbowmen. Because, hardened in such obstinacy, he would in no way come to his senses, our venerable brother Humbert, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication.

After we had learned by trustworthy report that such danger and such devastation of religious life threatened the monastery of Cluny, we judged it proper to send into those regions our beloved son Peter, cardinal-deacon, from the bosom of the holy Roman Church. By our command and authority he bound Pons the invader and his supporters with the bond of anathema. [Col. 1266C]

After this, you, beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, and the same Pons agreed to come before us on the octave of St Michael next following and to obey the judgment of ourselves and the Roman Church concerning the aforesaid controversy and transgression. To ensure that neither party should deceive the other concerning this, you both furnished hostages in the presence of the aforesaid beloved son Peter, cardinal-deacon. When the appointed term arrived, you presented yourself before us. Pons, however, came to the City with monks and burgesses, but was not yet absolved, together with his followers, from the bond of excommunication. [Col. 1266D]

In accordance with ecclesiastical usage, he was repeatedly required by our brethren to make satisfaction for the transgression for which he had been excommunicated and afterwards, in the proper order of reason, to be permitted to plead his case. Yet, swollen with a spirit of pride and, in his accustomed manner, extending his tongue into denials and entanglements of words, he scorned to make satisfaction to us and to the Roman Church. We did, indeed, receive some monks who had come with him after receiving their satisfaction and admitted them to plead their case.

Then, through our most dear son Matthew, prior of St Martin of the Fields, whom you had appointed advocate and defender of your cause, you humbly alleged that you had been canonically elected abbot of Cluny according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, confirmed by our predecessor of happy memory Pope Calixtus and by ourselves, but had now been expelled by Pons the invader and his unfaithful accomplices, the burgesses; and that the monastery’s goods and treasury had been dispersed. You asked that restitution be made to you for what had been taken and justice done for the injury inflicted. [Col. 1267A]

The monks who had come with Pons, on the other hand, cried out that Pons, their shepherd, had been fraudulently taken from them and had never relinquished the governance of the monastery of Cluny. They were immediately refuted when the volumes of the registers of Pope Calixtus, a man of apostolic character, were produced, together with the testimony of witnesses who had been present at the time. To set down his words addressed to Pons, they are these:

“We command you to desist from such frivolity and not dare in any way to trouble the abbey of Cluny which you renounced into our hands without hope of recovery. But if you become a transgressor of our command, you will lose the favor of blessed Peter and ours; and if at any time you appeal to us, you will not be heard.”

Likewise, among other things, he wrote to the community of Cluny:

“We have learned from many reports that jealousies and contentions are being stirred among you, and we are greatly distressed. For Pons, who formerly presided over your monastery, does not cease to divide your concordant unity and trouble the simplicity of your minds. Therefore we command your entire community that, if you desire to save your souls through obedience to blessed Peter, you shall at once cast away every schism and unanimously and devoutly render humble submission and obedience to our dearest son Peter, abbot of Cluny. You shall place no further hope in that Pons, who in our hands utterly renounced the abbey of Cluny without hope of recovery; for what we have decided concerning him in this matter we shall change on no ground whatever. But if any of you should violate this command of ours, if he is distinguished by the title of an abbacy or any prelation, or holds advancement in an order, he shall suffer loss of his dignity and rank and be subject to the sentence of anathema.” [Col. 1267B–C]

He wrote likewise concerning him to you, dearest son Peter:

“As for what we have determined concerning that Pons, who formerly presided over the abbey of Cluny and who entirely renounced it into our hands without hope of recovery, we do not wish to change it for any reason.”

Therefore, as the office of judge required, after a more diligent investigation of the matter, and with the counsel and common assent of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, with Peter, prefect of the City, other Roman nobles, and jurists approving, we invested you in full, by abundant justice, with the abbey of Cluny, with the obedience of its monks, and with all things belonging to that abbey both externally and internally. Releasing the hostages you had given for the execution of justice, we bound those whom Pons and the burgesses had pledged on their side. [Col. 1267D]

We also condemned the burgesses, with the legal penalty applied, to restore to the monastery the treasury of Cluny and repair the other damage, into your hand, since we know that the responsibility belongs to you; the remission of that penalty, however, is entrusted to your discretion. Furthermore, condemning Pons as excommunicated, invader, plunderer, sacrilegious person, and schismatic, we confirmed by apostolic authority the sentence issued against Pons by our predecessor of blessed memory, Lord Pope Calixtus: namely, that he should at no time recover the abbey of Cluny. If anyone hereafter attempts to violate this judgment of our determination, let a layman be struck with the sword of anathema, and let a cleric be punished by deprivation of honor and office. [Col. 1268A]

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1268B] I, bishop of Porto, was present.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XLIX. Privilege for the nunnery of Fontevraud. (Year 1126, 1 November.)

[PAVILLON, *Life of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel*, documentary proofs, p. 625.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ P., abbess of the monastery of St Mary of Fontevraud, and to the daughters succeeding her and regularly appointed forever.

[Col. 1268C] The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by the Lord, the ruler of all, so that we may strive by every means to promote religious persons and forms of religious life pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless it proceeds from the motive of charity. Therefore, beloved daughter in the Lord, Abbess P., mercifully inclined by your reasonable petitions, we grant our assent.

Accordingly, we have judged that the monastery of St Mary of Fontevraud, whose governance we hope has been entrusted to you by the Lord, ought to be fortified by the protection and defence of the Apostolic See, lest it be burdened by any compulsory services or harassed by the vexations of wicked persons, and so that, with a pure heart and in purity, you may perform God’s service more freely.
