Whatever else, moreover, you may in future be able justly and lawfully to acquire, by the Lord’s gift, through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall be preserved firm and entire to you and your successors.

Furthermore, as the same founders declared and as their charter contains, we decree under the protection of the Apostolic See and Roman liberty that the same monastery shall always remain free and exempt from every condition of other persons: that is, no person of whatever dignity or order shall be interposed between the Roman pontiff and you and your successors, nor shall the abbot of Vendôme be compelled in any way to attend a council at which the pope is not personally present.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors, with every dignity belonging to it, the church of Blessed Prisca situated on the Aventine Hill, with all its appurtenances, just as your predecessors are known to have held it in the time of our predecessors. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit, we decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person shall henceforth presume by any cunning or pretext to take from you or your successors the aforesaid church of Blessed Prisca or the dignity of that church.

Should it happen that a legate of the Roman Church visits the aforesaid monastery of Vendôme, let him be received there charitably, and let the necessities of the body be diligently supplied to him according to the means of the place. Yet that legate shall not dare personally to dispose or correct anything in that place, nor presume under the pretext of his legation to trouble the superior of the place or the brethren; but if he learns that anything requires correction, he may report it to the pope. If anyone wishes to bring a case against that place concerning any matters, neither the abbot nor the brethren shall answer him at all before consulting the Roman pontiff, because whatever is disposed of or determined without our judgment or that of our successors shall be void.

As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay twelve solidi of your currency annually to the Lateran palace. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by fitting satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to stern vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, [Col. 1296B] amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, G[?], cardinal of the title of the Holy Apostles, have subscribed.

I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Calixtus, have subscribed.

I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed.

I, Girard, priest-cardinal of the title of Fasciola, have subscribed.

I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of St Balbina, have subscribed.

I, Rusticus, priest-cardinal of St Cyriacus, have subscribed.

I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Giles, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed.

I, John, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.

I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

[Col. 1296C]

I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of St Angelo, have subscribed.

I, Saro, priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen, have subscribed.

I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Equitius, have subscribed.

I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Anastasia, have subscribed.

I, Goselin, priest-cardinal of the title of St Cecilia, have subscribed.

I, Sigizo, priest-cardinal of the title of St Sixtus, have subscribed.

I, Eibert, priest-cardinal of the title of St Clement, have subscribed.

I, Deusdedit, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed.

I, Jonathan, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, [Col. 1296D] deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1129 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XCI. Commands Suger, abbot of St Denis, to provide for the discipline of the nunnery at Argenteuil, restored to the monastery of St Denis by Stephen, bishop of Paris. (Year 1129, April 23.)

[Gallia Christiana, VII, documents, 52.]

HONORIUS, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ SUGER, abbot of St Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1297A] The love of religious life and the unity of charity will then be maintained in the perfection of their state, if what is restored by the members of the Church through a reasonable arrangement is strengthened by its head. Therefore, though unworthy, having been placed by the Lord in the See of Blessed Peter the Apostle, to which Christ granted primacy over all Churches, we wish to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and we confirm with more earnest care by apostolic authority what has been established by our brethren.

For our venerable brother Stephen, bishop of Paris, as we have learned by inspection of his letters, granted to you, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Suger, and to the monastery of St Denis, for the sake of religious observance and without prejudice to the rights of the Church of Paris, the monastery of Argenteuil. Certain women of bad life were said to be living there; and he had also learned from ancient royal charters that the monastery belonged by right to the monastery of St Denis. This he did in the presence of our venerable brethren Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See; Renaud, archbishop of Reims; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; and Goselin, bishop of Soissons; and at the urging of our dearest son Louis, the illustrious and glorious king of the Franks. The grant was made on the condition that you provide for the women in religious places where they can save their souls.

> [Note: [Col. 1297] He ratified this restoration in 1129, in the seventh indiction, at Reims, during the solemn anointing of Lord Philip, the glorious king, son of Louis.]

We therefore confirm by our authority what the aforesaid Stephen, bishop of Paris, has decreed concerning the aforesaid monastery for the restoration of religious observance, and we will that it remain firm in future times. We command your belovedness, therefore, to strive with diligent vigilance to establish religious and monastic observance in the aforesaid place; and, lest any one of the aforesaid women perish through your fault, to provide for them with careful concern in religious places.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

XCII. For the monastery of St Martin of Nevers. (Year 1129, April 27.)

[Gallia Christiana, XII, documents, 338.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, prior of the church of St Martin situated in the suburb of Nevers, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life there: greeting in the Lord.

It befits the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious men and to defend their places by the protection of fatherly kindness. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Prior Stephen, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Martin at Nevers, over which, by God’s ordinance, you are known to preside, and we strengthen it by this page of our present writing.

Let the possessions and goods which that church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may in future acquire, by the Lord’s gift, through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors, without prejudice to the rights and due reverence of the bishop of Nevers. We have thought fit to specify by their proper names: [Col. 1298A] the two churches of Luciniac with their appurtenances; the chapel of Bafias; the church of Buciac; the church of Moresca; the church of Coloncello; the church of Bazolis; the church of Spiriac; the church of Mont Rumilion; and the church of St Ouen.

We also confirm to you the grant of grain offered at the dedications of churches, which Fromund, bishop of Nevers, bestowed upon your church. Let the canonical order established there be inviolably preserved forever in future times. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or wear it down with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, for the benefit both of yourselves [Col. 1298B] and of the poor. If anyone, therefore, in future, etc.

I, Honorius, bishop of the catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1129 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XCIII. Takes under protection the monastery of St Mary of Curatio, and grants to those who visit the monastery on certain days “one hundred and fifty years’ remission of imposed penances.” (Year 1129, September 13.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, IX, 274.]

[Col. 1298C]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all and each of Christ’s faithful: greeting and apostolic blessing in perpetuity.

The desire which you set forth out of [love?] of religion and show to concern the salvation of souls ought always, with God as its author, to be fulfilled with some measure of favour. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, … of the monastery situated in the place called Curatio, dedicated in honour of the Virgin, which a certain son of ours, Roger of Marturano, constructed and offered to the holy Roman Church: following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Alexander II, Gregory VII, Urban II, Paschal II, and Calixtus II, we protect it by the authority of the holy Apostolic See and strengthen it by the privilege of indulgence.

Therefore, desiring that it be enriched with indulgences and spiritual graces and frequented in honour of the Virgin, we mercifully remit in the Lord, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and the authority of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, one hundred and fifty years of the penances imposed upon all and each truly penitent and confessed person who reverently visits that place on the feasts of the same glorious Virgin—namely her Nativity, Purification, Annunciation, and Assumption—and on the feast of the Holy Innocents, and who gives alms and lends assisting hands for the repair of that church; this remission extends also throughout the octaves [Col. 1299A] of the aforesaid feasts.

Given at St Mary of Curatio through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of September, in the third indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

> [Note: [Col. 1299] The chronological indications are corrupt, and the authenticity of the bull is not established. Jaffé.]

XCIV. Privilege for the monastery of St Mary of Amelungsborn. (Year 1129, December 5.)

[Leukfeld, *Antiquitates Michaelsteinenses et Amelunxbornenses*, Wolfenbüttel, 1710, quarto, p. 21.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son … abbot of the monastery of St Mary at Amelungsborn, [Col. 1299B] in the diocese of Hildesheim, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A pious desire which is shown to concern the purpose of extending religious observance ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot, granting fair and favourable assent to your just and reasonable petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own the monastery over which, by God’s ordinance, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that the monastic order established there according to the Rule of St Benedict and the Cistercian reform shall be inviolably observed in perpetuity. We further establish that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and reasonably possesses, or may in future acquire by the Lord’s favour through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of other faithful persons, or other just means, shall remain firm, peaceful, and entire to you and your successors, always without prejudice to the canonical rights and due reverence of the diocesan bishop.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful device or violence, save one whom the brethren by common consent—or at least the sounder part of the brethren—shall, according to the fear of God and the strictness of your order, provide to be elected, whether from their own community or, if necessity requires, from another. And as we specially grant to your person the right to wear the mitre, dalmatic, sandals, and ring, so, by the same apostolic authority, we permit and confirm forever to all your regularly elected successors the use of these things at all solemnities of the saints, festive processions, and synods.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever, whether of small or great esteem or authority, may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with other reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, firm, and undisturbed, wholly useful for the support and governance [Col. 1300A] of those for whose use they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that guilty person makes fitting amends by adequate satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to stern vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that holy place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, [Col. 1300B] amen.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1129 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius III.

XCV. Privilege for the church of St Martin of Tours. (Year 1129, December 19.)

[*Défense de l’église de Saint-Martin de Tours*, supporting documents, p. 14.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in Christ, the canons of the church of Blessed Martin of Tours, present and future, to be established in perpetuity.

Placed by the Lord in the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought, by the office imposed upon us, to love and honour all God’s churches, but especially those which belong particularly to the right and possession of the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your reasonable petitions, we strengthen by the protection of the Apostolic See and confirm by the page of our writing the church of Blessed Martin of Tours, which belongs by proper right to Blessed Peter and adheres more particularly to the Holy Roman Church.

We establish that whatever goods and possessions that Church now justly and lawfully possesses shall remain firm and unimpaired to you. We have thought fit to record by their proper names: the borough of St Peter Puellar, with its appurtenances, granted to you by our beloved son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks; [Col. 1300D] the church of St Paul of Cormery; the church of St Mary of Bellomont; the church of St Cosmas with their dependencies; and also the liberty and immunity, honours and benefices conferred upon your church of Blessed Martin through the writings of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Adeodatus, Leo, Adrian, Sergius, Gregory, Paschal, and Calixtus; through those of the archbishops of Tours Crotbert, Ibo, and Airard; or through royal charters. Whatever else you may in future acquire, by God’s gift, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall be preserved whole and inviolate to you.

Let your cloister remain free and peaceful as far as the projections of the walls, as it is known to have remained until now. Let the priests dwelling within the precinct of the Church—in their cells, in your oratories, in the church of St Venant, and in the church of St Peter called *de Cardoneto*—continue in the liberty in which they are known to have remained in former times. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Blessed Martin, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact, wholly useful for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, and the ordinations of canons who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the archbishop of Tours, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the same sacraments. Moreover, if one of your canons is also a canon of the archbishop’s churches, and has renounced his benefice, the archbishop shall have no power to excommunicate him.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes fitting amends by adequate satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to stern vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

THE EYES OF THE LORD ARE UPON THE RIGHTEOUS.

I, Honorius, bishop of the catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh indiction, in the year [Col. 1301D] 1129 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Honorius II.

XCVI. To P[elagius], archbishop of Braga.—Commands him to appear before him on the coming Sunday on which is read: “I am the good shepherd.” (Year 1129.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 492.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother P., archbishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It pleased the Roman pontiff to honour the Church of Compostela and to grant suffragans of the metropolitan see of Mérida to our venerable brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela. But after the death of G., bishop of Coimbra, a suffragan of the aforesaid metropolitan see, your brotherhood, as we have learned, presumed to consecrate a bishop in that Church, disregarding the reverence due to the Apostolic See. Since we cannot pass over without examination the injury thereby inflicted upon our venerable brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela, and the contempt shown to the Holy Roman Church, we command and enjoin upon your brotherhood that, on the coming Sunday on which is read “I am the good shepherd,” you come before us prepared to answer for such grave excesses.

XCVII. To Didacus, archbishop of Compostela.—Gives thanks because he visited him and the Holy Roman Church, etc. (Year 1129.)

[Flórez, *ibid.*, p. 491.]

[Col. 1302B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to your brotherhood because you visited us and your holy mother, the Roman Church. We have graciously received the messengers sent to us by you and have carefully considered what was contained in your letters. But we have sent our beloved son Hu. [Humbert or Hubert], priest-cardinal, from our side to the regions of Spain, and have entrusted him with our authority. Therefore let your brotherhood receive him graciously, treat him honourably, and diligently assist him in ecclesiastical affairs for the honour of God and Blessed Peter.

Moreover, when, by the Lord’s favour, he returns to us, we shall take counsel concerning those matters which our beloved son King A. and your messengers requested on your behalf. We have also directed in writing that the archbishop of Braga, because of the presumption he committed in consecrating the bishop of Coimbra, should come before us on the coming Sunday on which is read, “I am the good shepherd,” to answer for it.

XCVIII. Recommends to A[defonso], king of the Spains, his legate Hubert, priest-cardinal. (Year 1129.)

[Flórez, *ibid.*, p. 491.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ A., the illustrious king of the Spains, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Ask your elders with what affection and how great a devotion your grandfather, King A. of illustrious memory, loved Blessed Peter and the Holy Roman Church, and they will tell you that for this reason victory was granted to him by the heavenly power, and that by often fighting he defeated the Saracens, enemies of the Christian name. We rejoice that, following in his footsteps, you reverence and love churches and ecclesiastical persons; and we pray the divine clemency that you may attain advancement from good to better. We have dispatched Hubert, cardinal-priest, from our side into the regions of Spain, and have entrusted our authority to him. Therefore, out of reverence for St. Peter and ourselves, let your nobility receive him kindly, so that, supported by the assistance of royal power, he may, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, correct the disorders of your realm and confirm what has been well established. But when, by grace granted, he has returned to us, we shall be able to deliberate more freely concerning what you have requested on behalf of our brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela. Out of regard for your affection, moreover, we command our aforesaid legate to render justice to M., archdeacon of Ourense, for whom you have petitioned.

XCIX. To Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg.—He confirms the replacement by Premonstratensians of clerics living insufficiently religious lives. (1129.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred Order of Prémontré*, vol. II, ch. 109.]

[Col. 1303B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother NORBERT, Archbishop of Magdeburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

What we recognize to have been justly and reasonably established by our brethren, we willingly confirm by apostolic authority. As we have learned from examination of the writings which your brotherhood has sent us, and from the report of your messengers, you have placed elsewhere, providing for their needs as a pious father, the clerics who had been living insufficiently religious lives in the church of St. Mary at Magdeburg, and because of this had diminished the goods of that church; and in that same church of Blessed Mary you have established religious men professing the canonical life. Since this is recognized as having been justly done by your prudence through zeal for God and with a view to religion, we decree it ratified.

Given at the Lateran, in the year 1129.

C. To Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg. (1129.)

[MEICHELBECK, *History of Freising*, vol. I, part I, p. 309.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother CONRAD, Archbishop of Salzburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Church of Freising and Bishop Henry have complained before us, through their letters and messengers, grievously against you: namely, that you endeavor to invalidate the arrangements which he made after obtaining the favour of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of happy memory and of the Roman Church; that you also overturn altars consecrated by him; and that you judge and dispose concerning his parish, not as metropolitan, but as though you were its own bishop. We, however, neither desire nor ought in any way to defend his sins or those of any other person. Yet if you desire, in accordance with what you see fit to do through zeal for justice, to free the Church of Freising from the aforesaid person, it is reasonable that you proceed canonically in this case. For we are ready both to hear it and, God granting, to determine it. In the meantime, refrain from every harassment both of his person and of his parish.

CI. He receives under protection the monastery of St. Peter in the Black Forest and confirms its privileges. (Between 1125 and 1130.)

[SCHANNAT, *Vindications of Documents*, I, I, 162.]

[Col. 1304A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ EPPON, abbot of the monastery situated in the Black Forest, in the place called the cell of St. Peter, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

The incomprehensible and ineffable divine mercy has placed us, by this ordering of providence, in the administration of the apostolic see, so that we may endeavour to exercise paternal concern for all churches. For this Roman Church, which by the Lord’s grant holds the primacy of all churches, ought, like a diligent mother, to provide for each church with vigilant care; for all must have recourse to it as to their head and mother, so that they may be nourished at its breasts and relieved from oppressions. It is therefore fitting that churches and other venerable places, especially those belonging to the special right and singular ownership of the Holy Roman Church, which we serve by God’s authorship, should receive the honour of a more particular prerogative and be strengthened by the protection of apostolic authority.

Accordingly, since Duke Berchtold, a man of eminent nobility, built a monastery in the county of Breisgau, in the diocese of Constance, in the forest called the Black Forest, in honour of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and subjected that estate to the right of the Roman Church, we, confirming his devotion by apostolic authority and assenting to your reasonable requests, beloved son Eppo, abbot, following the example of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Urban II, receive that place to be specially cherished under the protection of the apostolic see. By the present page of privilege, moreover, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever lands or possessions the aforesaid Duke Berchtold, together with his wife Agnes and his sons, has conveyed, and whatever other men have offered to our monastery from their own right, as well as whatever you may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you.

We decree, therefore, that no person may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away or diminish the possessions subject to it, or harass them by any rash vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and shall in every respect benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Furthermore:

[lacuna]

… are cultivated or maintained at your own expense and labour, we decree shall remain quiet and unimpaired for you; nor do we permit you to be disturbed in this matter by the bishop of the same diocese or by his officials. We establish that the burial-place of that monastery shall be altogether free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. You shall receive the ordinations of monks and the consecration of altars or churches from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to confer what is requested without impropriety; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive the sacraments from him, supported by the authority of the apostolic see.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God, regularly provide to be elected. The advocate whom you shall appoint for your rights shall have no power to dispose of anything in your monastery.

[lacuna]

CII. He confirms the possessions of the Church of Hadmersleben. (Between 1124 and 1130.)

[LEUCKFELD, *Antiquities of Katelenburg*, Leipzig and Wolfenbüttel, 1713, quarto, p. 83.]

[Col. 1305B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ THIETMAR, provost of the Church of Hamersleben, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

Those dwelling in the house of the Lord, united in sincerity of love, preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; for, through pure prayers continually poured forth, they incline the most merciful Creator with a pure mind, so that earthly things may be joined to heavenly things and may together be associated with those above. For just as the inward spirit governs and gives life to the structure of the human body, so the flourishing of a religious mind exists and the beneficent divine inspiration is the saving guide.

[Note: [Col. 1305D] Something is missing.]

Therefore, because we have learned that you, beloved son in the Lord Thietmar, provost, live religiously, devoted to divine service, we have judged that your reasonable requests should be granted. Accordingly, we strengthen by the protection and guardianship of the apostolic see your places—namely, the cloister of Hamersleben, the cloister of St. John the Baptist at Halberstadt, the cloister of St. Lawrence at Schöningen, the cloister of Kaldenburnen, the cloister of Reichenberg, the cloister of St. George at Berk, the cloister of Becigheroth, and the cloister of Ammensleve—as well as the persons of the brethren serving God there, together with the goods and possessions which you presently possess justly and lawfully, or may in future, by the Lord’s grant, be able to acquire by just means.

We establish that the religious order instituted in those cloisters according to God, the holy apostles, and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and established by you in the observance of religion through sacred institution, shall be inviolably observed for all future time: namely, that every brother, whether canonically set over others or regularly subject, shall live religiously in the aforesaid places; and that no bishop or other ecclesiastical or secular person shall presume to violate your persons or cloisters by exaction, violence, or disturbance. Rather, so that you may be able more freely and without all molestation to devote yourselves to divine service, you and your goods, received under the protection of the apostolic see, shall remain in due liberty.

Moreover, you may receive into your congregation secular clerics coming from anywhere, provided they are not excommunicated and, having sought permission from their own prelates, have resolved to serve God with you. If anyone should rashly presume to oppose this our confirmation, unless he makes worthy satisfaction, let him, as a despiser of an apostolic command, be deprived of the dignity of rank and office.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

CIII. To the Archbishops of Bourges, Tours, Bordeaux, Auch, and Dol. (Between 1124 and 1130.)

[MARTENE, *Anecdota*, III, 885.]

[Col. 1306B]

By divine ordering, although unworthy, we have been placed in the watchtower of our fathers the apostles Peter and Paul; we are therefore bound to apply ourselves to the children of the Church with the zeal of paternal affection. For this reason, as far as we can, we exercise pious care before God for all; and those to whom, whether because of the excessive distance of lands or sea, or because of the diverse pressing affairs of the Roman Church, we cannot offer our presence, we visit through legates of the apostolic see whom we send.

Therefore, concerning our beloved brother G. [Gerard], bishop of Angoulême, whom both our predecessors, the pontiffs Paschal and Calixtus of holy memory, and we ourselves have deemed worthy of veneration as a prudent and wise man of God, we ask, exhort, and command your whole body to receive him reverently; and you shall take care humbly to obey him as our legate and vicar of the apostolic see, etc.

CIV. Privilege for the Church of Meaux. (Between 1124 and 1130.)

[DU PLESSIS, *History of the Church of Meaux*, vol. III, p. 24, from the cartulary of the Church of Meaux.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BURCHARD, bishop of Meaux, and to his successors to be canonically promoted for ever, etc.

[Col. 1306D] … We establish that all clerics and laypeople dwelling in the villages of Resbac and Jotré shall be subject to the Church of Meaux by parochial right, and that everything belonging to parochial right from them shall be preserved free and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also decree that the abbot of Resbac and the abbess of Jotré shall render canonical obedience to you and your successors. Their blessing likewise, just as it is known to have been administered hitherto through your predecessors, shall henceforth be conferred through you and your successors. The promotion of monks to ecclesiastical orders shall also be administered by the bishop of Meaux, provided that he is willing to confer them freely and without impropriety, etc. …

CV. Privilege for the monastery of St. George of Prüfening. (Between 1125 and 1130, 21 January.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. XIII, p. 146.]

[Col. 1307A]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HERB., abbot of the monastery of St. George of Prüfening, situated between Regensburg and the Danube, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting to the mercy of apostolic governance to love religious persons and to defend their places by the protection of apostolic guardianship. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Herb., abbot of the monastery of St. George of Prüfening, assenting to your reasonable requests through the intervention of our venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, we receive under the guardianship of Blessed Peter and our protection the same monastery of St. George over which, by God’s authorship, you preside, and we strengthen it by the page of this our writing.

Accordingly, the goods and possessions which the aforesaid monastery of St. George presently possesses justly and lawfully, or may in future, by the Lord’s grant, acquire through the liberality of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors regularly appointed. Furthermore, we confirm for you the tithe granted by our aforesaid brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, which he is known to have obtained from Arthuic, bishop of Regensburg, through an agreeable exchange.

[Note: [Col. 1307] See Laurent Hochwart, in the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Regensburg*, book II, chapter 22, in Oefele, *Writers on Bavarian Affairs*, vol. I, p. 186, no. 6.]

We also establish that the religious order instituted in your monastery according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed for all future time. Upon your death, now abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, but only one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict provide to be elected.

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your own labour cultivated at your own expense, or from your gardens and orchards. And lest anyone, on the pretext of advocacy, should attempt to impose exactions upon your monastery, alienate, sell, or grant your goods as benefices, we prohibit this in every way.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact, to benefit in every respect the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted, without prejudice to the due reverence owed to the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt rashly to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

+ I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

CVI. Privilege for the Church of St. Margaret of Baumburg. (Between 1125 and 1130, 27 January.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. II, p. 180.]

[Col. 1308B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GODISCALC, provost of the Church of St. Margaret of Baumburg, and to his successors to be canonically appointed for ever.

Whenever something is requested from us that is recognized as consistent with reason, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and provide suitable support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Godiscalc, provost, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and the apostolic see, and strengthen by the page of our writing, the Church of Blessed Margaret of Baumburg, over which, by God’s authorship, you are known to preside.

We establish that what Count Berengar has bestowed upon your aforesaid church out of devotion, and whatever possessions and goods it presently holds justly and lawfully, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have directed that the following be stated by their proper names: Megilingen with its appurtenances; Perhenmos; Handburt with a mill and one estate; Hoffstet with one estate. Whatever further things you may in future be able to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall be preserved quiet and entire for you and your successors, without prejudice to the right and due reverence of the diocesan bishop.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that church, take away or retain its possessions when taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and shall in every respect benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. As a sign of this protection received from the apostolic see, you shall pay one gold piece annually to the Lateran palace.

Upon the death of you, now provost of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall canonically provide to be elected in the fear of God. Certainly, after making profession, none of you may possess private property or leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or congregation. We grant to you and your successors the tithes of your newly cleared lands, with all objection by episcopal officials removed, so that by God’s grant you may remain for ever in peace in the vocation you have undertaken.

If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt rashly to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

CVII. Confirmation of the foundation of the Church of Denkendorf. (Between 1125 and 1130, 27 January.)

[*Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 260.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONRAD, provost, and his brethren in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Denkendorf, professing the canonical life, both present and future, for ever.

[Col. 1309C]

The authority of the office entrusted to us exhorts us to concern ourselves for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s saving help, to provide for their peace and benefit. For it is recognized as worthy, honourable, and fitting that we who have been assumed to the governance of churches should protect them from the malice of wicked persons and fortify them by the patronage of Blessed Peter and the apostolic see.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Conrad, provost, assenting to your reasonable requests, we receive under the guardianship of Blessed Peter and our protection, and strengthen by the page of our writing, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Denkendorf, with its goods, offered by the most illustrious Count Berthold upon the glorious Jerusalemite Sepulchre of the Lord for the remedy of his soul, and over which, by God’s authorship, you are known to preside. We establish that whatever possessions and goods that church presently possesses justly and lawfully, or may in future be able to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, the benefactions of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors, without prejudice to the right and due reverence of the diocesan bishop.

Upon your death, now provost of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common assent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine provide to be elected. You shall receive chrism, oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordination of clerics from the bishop of Constance, provided he enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to confer these freely upon you and without impropriety; otherwise, you shall receive the same sacraments from whichever bishop you prefer who is supported by the authority of the Roman Church.

Furthermore, in electing an advocate the provost shall have free power, with the counsel of his brethren, to choose such a person as he recognizes to be good and useful for defending the liberty of the monastery, one who desires to hold and administer the advocacy well, not for earthly advantage but for the love of God, the forgiveness of sins, and the reward of eternal blessedness.

Adding these provisions, we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact, to benefit in every respect the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt rashly to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Honorius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February [26 January].

CVIII. To the canons of the Church of St. Fridianus at Lucca. (Between 1125 and 1130, 29 January.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucchese edition, IV, 588.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the canons of the Church of St. Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our most distinguished son A., your prior, appearing before us, laboured with many efforts and great urgency of prayers that we might release him and his brethren from their obligation to the Lateran Church. But moved by the grave necessity of that church, we were unwilling not only to release them from this burden, but even compelled the prior himself, unwilling and reluctant, to remain with us for a while, so that through his industry we might provide for that church.

We therefore command and direct you to persevere, as you have begun, in the service of God. If the aforesaid prior summons any one of you to this end, that he may be placed over the Lateran canonry, let none of you resist. Rather, whoever is charged with this by him, whether from among those who are with you or from others who dwell in your obediences, shall, with every contradiction removed, accept this obedience for the honour of God and the benefit of the aforesaid church.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January].

CIX. To the same persons. (Between 1125 and 1130, 5 February.)

[Ibid.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., prior of St. Fridianus, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know that it is pleasing to us that the purity of your good intentions and the strength of your religious life do not cease to shine forth acceptably before God and human beings. For we desire that the love of your brotherly charity may advance from strength to strength, so that you may be able to receive a reward from the fruit of good works and, by the example of a good life, make others also imitators of your footsteps. We entreat you in the Lord Jesus Christ to assist by your prayers us who labour under the care and solicitude of the whole Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of February [5 February], etc.

CX. He confirms the law of Henry, sometime emperor, concerning the non-administration of an oath by clerics, issued at Rimini on the third day of April. (Between 1125 and 1130.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 362.]

Following the footsteps of our predecessors, who declared that graver questions ought to be settled by the supreme pontiff, and having carefully investigated the counsel of our brethren, we have, with God’s help, decided this issue conclusively. We find, accordingly, that the laws provide that no cleric may presume to swear an oath; but elsewhere it is written that all principal persons, at the outset of a lawsuit, shall take an oath against calumny. Some jurists and other wise persons have doubted whether a cleric ought to take the oath or may delegate this duty to another person.

For since that edict of the constitution prohibiting clerics from swearing had been promulgated by Marcus [corrected reading: Marcian] Augustus, addressed to Constantine, prefect of the praetorium, concerning the clerics of Constantinople, it was believed not to apply to others. [Variant opening: *cum* (“since”) for *quia* (“because”).] Therefore, in order that this doubt may be entirely removed from all persons, we confirm the interpretation of our son H., formerly emperor [alternative reading, syntactically uncertain: *ab omnibus decisionem quondam clerici filii nostri H. imp.*—“by all, the decision of our son H., formerly a cleric, emperor”], made, as we have received it, in the third year of his reign; and we decree that the constitution of Emperor Marcus [corrected reading: Marcian] ought to be interpreted so that it is judged to apply generally to the clerics of all churches.

For since Emperor Justinian decreed that the canons of the Fathers ought to have the force of laws, and since in certain canons it is found that clerics must by no means dare to swear, it is fitting that the whole clerical order be considered, beyond doubt, exempt from taking an oath. Moreover, the text of the principal enactment [variant: *principis*, “of the prince”] is known to be in our possession as follows:

> “We therefore, preserving the intention of each law, divine and human, decree and, by imperial authority, establish beyond challenge [variant: irrevocably], that no bishop, priest, cleric of any order, abbot, monk, or nun shall be compelled on any ground to take an oath in any cause or controversy, whether criminal or civil. Rather, they may, if they know it expedient for their church, delegate such a duty to other suitable defenders; yet with this qualification: no bishop shall dare to swear without consulting the Roman pontiff, nor any cleric without consulting his own prelate.”

We command all bishops, all priests generally, and the entire clergy to observe this provision in such a manner that whoever acts against this constitution shall know that pardon will thereafter be denied him. We do not take as an example or precedent our own recent action otherwise in the case of our brethren and fellow bishops of the Churches of Areana [as printed] and Sens, because we assented to their will and petition.

CXI. Confirmation of the foundation of the canonry of Beuron; likewise, grant of abbatial blessing and investiture with the pastoral staff. (1124, 10 October.)

[*Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 213.]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, professors of the canonical life in the church called Buron, consecrated in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, between two mountains on the bank of the River Danube in the territory of Constance, and to their successors canonically living for ever.

[Col. 1312C]

Just as assent ought to be denied to those requesting unreasonable things, so we ought to meet you, who request just things, with kindly assent. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the special fostering protection of the apostolic see, as a proper possession, and defend by the authority of this privilege against the malice of all wicked persons, the Church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin. Peregrinus, illustrious and noble, of pious memory, built it on his own land and offered it as his own free estate to Blessed Peter the apostle and his holy Roman Church; and in it you, dearest sons, serve God under the discipline of the regular life.

Accordingly, by the present decree we establish that whatever your church justly possesses today, or may in future justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors under the protection of the apostolic see. Since we have learned from the report of your messengers that your church presently remains vacant, we decree that no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom your convent by common consent, or the sounder part of your convent, shall, in the fear of God, provide to be elected either from your congregation or from another of the same profession. This shall henceforth be observed in your church.

Your elected prelate shall be invested with pastoral care by the bishop of Constance, provided that he is Catholic and stands in the favour of the apostolic see. If it pleases your brotherhood, moreover, your prelate shall, by our authority, be adorned by your bishop with abbatial ordination and the bearing of the pastoral staff. From him also you shall receive chrism, sacred orders, and the dedications of churches, provided, as stated, that he is Catholic; otherwise, you shall receive these from any other bishop, while in all respects preserving the canonical right and due reverence of your Catholic bishop.

By our authority we free your brotherhood from subjection to every other person whatsoever. We also grant your church free burial: that is, no one shall oppose the devotion and final request of those who have decided to be buried there. Furthermore, we establish that none among you, after making profession, may possess private property or be free to leave your cloister without the permission of your prelate and the entire congregation. If anyone leaves and, after warning, refuses to return, your provost shall have authority to bar such transgressors everywhere from their offices and from communion; and no bishop, abbot, or provost shall receive one so barred.

Upon the death of any advocate either of your monastery or of any of your estates, no one shall presume to claim the advocacy as though by hereditary right, except one whom your prelate, judging him useful and suitable with the counsel of the brethren, chooses for this purpose and commits the advocacy to him. If the advocate so chosen is negligent and useless in your affairs, administers the office entrusted to him badly, and after warning does not amend, he must cease from the office imposed upon him at the request of your prelate; and another, who zealously carries it out for the love of God and for the redemption of his own soul, shall be substituted for him.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that church, take away or retain its possessions when taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire for the uses of you and your successors, and shall in every respect benefit the alms given to the poor and the reception of pilgrims. As a sign of this benefaction received from the Roman see, you shall pay annually to the Lateran palace one gold bezant, or silver of the same value.

And so that this authority of our protection may remain firm and unshaken for ever, we have caused this document to be drawn up and marked with the impression of our seal. If, therefore, hereafter any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, duke, prince, count, viscount, judge, advocate, or person of any rank whatsoever violates the page of our decree or knowingly attempts rashly to act against it, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve that place's rights may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome by the hand of Hymmericus, acting vice-chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the fourth indiction, on the second lunar day.

## CXII. He confirms the liberty of the monastery of Altaich (the Upper).

(22 March 1126.)

[Monumenta Boica, XII, 98.]

[Col. 1314B]

HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful: apostolic blessing and greeting.

We confirm by our authority, as it is written, the privilege of liberty of the monastery of Altaich, and bind it under the ban of Saint Peter and our own, so that no one may unjustly inflict any violence upon that place or its possessions, or do it any harm; and if anyone transgresses this, let him know that he is condemned by eternal anathema.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in order to approve and declare the diligence of good men, we make known and commit to the memory of posterity, so that [Col. 1314C] all sons of the Church, present and future, may know and acknowledge in what manner the place called Upper Altaich was established for the service of almighty God and committed to Roman liberty. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1125, in the eighth indiction, on the third day before the Ides of December, indeed in the first year of Lothair, king of the Saxons, by God’s permission and through the strenuous efforts of Lindeger, abbot of the same place, Frederick, advocate of the Church of Regensburg, with the consent of his wife, and Count Albert of Windeberch, with his wife and very young children—under whose hereditary jurisdiction that place belonged—came together at the same place with many friends, noble men, and their distinguished followers.

Therefore, admonished and moved to contrition by the Holy Spirit, they entirely alienated from their own use and power that same place with all its appurtenances—[Col. 1314D] fields, vineyards, woods, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands—which they themselves or their parents had given, or which belonged to that place by some right of grant arising from their kinship and close relationship, or which had been bestowed upon it by their knights, any of their predecessors, or any persons whatsoever. Without recourse or opposition by any person, they gave, transferred, and bestowed it upon God and Saint Peter, and decreed that it should be free forever, plainly for the salvation and absolution of their own souls and those of their parents.

Therefore, lest this transfer and confirmation should ever be broken or annulled by any person, whether by themselves or their descendants and heirs, [Col. 1315A] by common counsel they decreed to entrust the same place jointly into the hands of the aforesaid Count Albert: namely, so that he, going to Rome, should confirm and establish this entrusting upon the altar of Saint Peter in the presence of the bishop of the apostolic see and the princes of the Romans. This was on the condition that each year a gold coin should be paid from it as testimony, and that the place should thereafter be subject to no service owed to any person—king, prince, or bishop.

Moreover, this transfer was made on these terms: that the monks serving God there should have the authority to elect as abbot, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, whomever they wish, whether from among themselves or from elsewhere, provided that the man elected receives the staff from the altar.

This further condition concerning the advocacy was agreed between them: that Frederick, who at that time was advocate, if he should father a son, should himself and his descendants always retain the rights of advocacy; but if he should die without children, the rights of advocate should pass to Count Albert and his descendants, and whichever among them was the elder by birth should be advocate. Yet this advocate shall retain there no right or power other than that which is set down below. Once a year he must hold a judicial session with the household, and he may exercise it nowhere but in that same place. If, however, the usefulness of the place requires that he come there, the following shall be supplied to him for his service: six urns of wine and one of mead; twenty urns of beer; four measures of grain and the same number of pigs; and twelve measures of oats. Yet if he holds court there, [Col. 1316A] all these things shall be given to him there; they shall not be carried elsewhere, nor shall he have power to give or grant them to anyone as a benefice. If, however, that advocate proves burdensome to the brethren and useless to the monastery, he shall be removed and another substituted.

The witnesses to all these matters were pulled by the ear: Frederick the advocate; the two sons of Count Albert, Perchtold and Albert; Dietrich of Ponchusen; Dietmar and his brother Ekkeric of Silichigin; Dietmar of Weniggesdorf; Marchwart of Elbermundesdorf; Werigant of Wolfoha; Ratpot of Slipphingen; Eberhart of Rota; Willehalm of Geppenheim; Werinheri of Holzen; another Werinheri and Gotfchalch of Heninchouen; Altman of Welichinberch; Swiker of Perindorf; Ovdalrich of Ahahovsen; [Col. 1316B] Liupolt of Uhesigen; and Gozpolt of Routenbach. All these noble men and their knights: Adelhart of Hiuttae; Gotpolt of Rovberdof; Goswin of Hagabach; Engilschalch of Landoldesdorf; Landold of Landoldesberch; Wolchmar of Mennaha; Gozpreth of Harda; Gumpolt of Herimutesdorf; Eppo of Drahfala; Rovdolf of Fremichesberch; Adelbrecht of Houedorf; Megingoz and his brother Hiltibolt; Marchuuart and Werinheri of Nuzbach; Perinhart of Gebinchoven; Marchwart of Niuenchirichen; Sigibot of Chounenzhella; Pabo of Geswenta; Hagano of Gezhusen; and very many others.

Given in the Lateran palace, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the third indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, Otto being chancellor of the holy Roman see.

[Col. 1315]

# APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF POPE HONORIUS II

(MANSI, Councils, XXI, 325.)

## I. Pope Honorius says to the Lord Archbishop of Salzburg, who, through his legate, consults the apostolic see concerning certain matters already settled:

[Col. 1315C]

Writings concerning these cases were issued long ago and are in the possession of the lord archbishop himself. He has no need to inquire about them or to await some new writing from us. Let him use the ancient writings; for, since he holds the seat of God, he will have our assistance in whatever matters the ancient traditions of the Fathers support for him.

[Note: [Col. 1315] Concerning the matter at issue, see the following determination.]

## II. The same Gerhoh recounts this definition of faith, delivered by the same Honorius.

The blessed-memory Pope Honorius first stood by me when Master Luitinfus, among the masters of France, was at his court. While this man was attempting to establish that Christ, insofar as he is man, is indeed the natural son of a human being, but the adoptive Son of God the Father, [Col. 1315D] and while I, on the contrary, maintained that adoption did not belong to the assumed man in respect of his being the Son of God, the aforesaid Pope Honorius supported me. He had been stirred to this by a small book presented to him by a certain Lateran canon, a man powerfully learned in letters, and read through by me. In it there was carefully investigated the difference between desired sons, who are also admittedly called proper and natural sons, and adopted sons, who are by no means equal to natural sons.

Then, therefore, when the designation “adoption” had been refuted in Christ, the proper and natural Son of God and man, I, exalted upon the rock and strengthened in the faith of Peter, returned from the city with joy, holding it certain that what Peter said concerning the Son of Man to erring men [Col. 1316C–D] was true, and that he himself did not err when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

## III. Decree of Honorius.

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Saint Thomas of Canterbury has it in Letter 97, p. 118.]

[Col. 1317A]

It should be the concern of all bishops to make the names of excommunicated persons known both to neighboring bishops and to their own parishioners alike, and, once posted in a public place before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who come, so that, by this twofold diligence, ecclesiastical entry may certainly be denied to excommunicated persons and every pretext of excuse removed from all.

[Col. 1317]

# LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO HONORIUS

## I. Letter of Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the apostolic see, to Honorius.

—He replies to Honorius’s sixty-fifth letter and reports what was done at the Council of Reims. (1127.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 266.]

[Col. 1317B]

To the most reverend Father and Lord HONORIUS, by the disposing mercy of God supreme and universal pontiff of the holy Roman Church, MATTHEW, servant, though unworthy, of the Church of Albano: with the earnestness of faithful prayers for your welfare.

Concerning the case of the men of Luxeuil, whom your fatherhood had commanded us, in accordance with the tenor of the letters of Pope Paschal of blessed memory, to invest, [Col. 1317C] we nevertheless carefully investigated their case. Reserving any right which the men of Dijon may possess, we summoned both parties to Reims on the Kalends of August. [Note: At this Council of Reims was issued the decree of Matthew, bishop of Albano, which Marlot recounts, vol. II, p. 301.] There, when very many bishops and abbots of that land had gathered for the business [Note: [Col. 1317D] Especially because of the deadly conflict which had hitherto existed [Col. 1318D] between Count William of Flanders and his rival Thierry of Alsace.] that had arisen there, we began carefully to investigate this matter in the common hearing of the brethren, according to the tenor of your letters.

We examined more closely the letters [Note: We do not possess these letters of Paschal II.] in which the aforesaid Pope Paschal had, as they claimed, commanded that they be invested; but nothing concerning this investiture was expressly contained in them. On the other hand, the men of Dijon produced in the assembly the privileges of our lords, namely of the same Pope Paschal and of Pope Calixtus of good memory, [Note: [Col. 1318D] For Calixtus’s letters, issued in 1124, see Perard, p. 216, or *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII.] in which these possessions were confirmed separately. By other writings and arguments they maintained that the men of Luxeuil had never been invested with the possessions they demanded.

Having heard this, we directed our brethren—the archbishops of Reims (Rainald) and Sens (Henry), and the bishops of Chartres (Geoffrey), Paris (Stephen), Beauvais (Peter), Soissons (Joslen), Laon (Bartholomew), Noyon (Simon), Châlons (Elbert), Troyes (Atto), and Meaux (Burchard)—to withdraw for consultation. After taking counsel together, on the basis of the reasons we have set forth and many others, they adjudged the investiture to the men of Luxeuil, provided, however, that the men of Luxeuil should remain in the condition in which they were [Col. 1318B] when they received the letters of Your Holiness. And so that this case may, by God’s grace, be concluded in your presence by the deadline set by you, we remit them to you.

We do not wish the prudence of your fatherhood to be unaware that almost all the people of that land, except the men of Luxeuil, testify that the men of Dijon possess the right; and, dearest Father, we earnestly ask you to uphold it.

## II. Of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see.

—He replies to Honorius’s fifty-fourth letter. (1127.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 350.]

H. to the most holy and universal pope; A., by the grace of God [Col. 1318C] humble servant of the holy Church of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see: the obedience due to so great an apostolic authority, and reverence most devoted to so great a Father.

Having received Your Holiness’s letters concerning the case of that brother—if indeed he ought to be called a brother—who usurps the bishopric of the holy Church of Würzburg, we learned that the whole course of the case had been reported to your supreme apostolic authority very differently from what it was, since many things are wont to be accomplished by surreptitious means. For he lodged complaints against us with Your Holiness, saying that he suffered injury from us and was oppressed contrary to justice.

But in this case, God and our conscience bearing witness, we have done nothing that can conflict with canonical rules; nothing for which we should be suspect to Your Holiness; nothing which anyone who has examined the case more fully could reproach. Whatever we have done in this case, we have done not from zeal of bitterness but from zeal for justice; not moved by any hatred but from regard for our office; not against the canons of the holy Fathers but according to the canons.

We know indeed, according to the divinely inspired rules of the holy Fathers, that a bishop ought not to be deprived of his bishopric before the outcome of his case is known. But Your Most Holy Apostolic Authority knows well that this judgment of the holy Fathers must be understood of doubtful episcopal cases, not manifest ones. The utterly shameless case and [Col. 1319A] certain crime of the man in question admit no appearance of lawful defense or just excuse. It is therefore clearer than daylight to all that he attained to the rank of so great a priesthood neither by any privilege of merits nor by any preceding election; but, by tyrannical violence, he was thrust into the Lord’s sheepfold. He entered not through the door but broke in by another way, through ambition and the Simoniacal heresy, most shamelessly as a thief and robber. What we cannot say without great sorrow and compunction of heart is that he has usurped for himself the place of the lawful shepherd, whom the holy Church of Würzburg, from among her own sons, had elected by the common vote and consent of clergy and people, with our approval and consent, to be canonically enthroned: a man noble in birth and character, most thoroughly trained in ecclesiastical discipline, [Col. 1319B] Catholic in faith, prudent by nature, chaste, sober, humble, affable, learned, instructed in God’s law, discerning in the meanings of Scripture, and in every respect most worthy of the priestly name and honor.

## III. Of the clergy of Rouen.

—Concerning the election of Hugh as Archbishop of Rouen. (1130.)

[*Spicilegium*, ed. de Labarre, III, 484.]

To the lord and universal pope HONORIUS, the Church of Rouen: all obedience and subjection in Christ.

By a common election we have chosen your son Hugh, abbot of Reading, as our bishop. On this matter we sought and obtained the assent of our lord Henry, king of the English. We asked that he be released and made free for us by the bishop of Salisbury, under whose authority he performed the office of abbot, and we received him in freedom. But because, upon his own disclosure, we learned that we could not have him without the assent of your authority—especially since we read that this was written in your letters sent to the aforesaid king of the English: “We retain him under our own right and lordship as a special cleric of Blessed Peter and of the Holy Roman Church”—we ask that he be granted to us by Your Sublimity. We shall hold him all the dearer insofar as we rejoice that he has been bestowed upon us from the seat of your exalted authority. With humble supplication, dearest Father and Lord, we ask that he be granted to us by your grace in such a manner that we may rejoice that he remains forever under no right or power except your sole gracious protection.

[Note: [Col. 1319] See the letter of Henry I, king of the English, to Pope Innocent II, under Innocent II, at the year 1143.]

# LETTERS OF HILDEBERT OF LE MANS TO HONORIUS

(See under Hildebert below.)

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1130: VIVIANUS OF PRÉMONTRÉ

[Col. 1319]

# HARMONY, OR TREATISE ON FREE CHOICE AND GRACE

(MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, IX, 1073, from the manuscript codex of the royal college of Navarre.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

Vivianus of Prémontré comes to light here for the first time, hitherto unknown, together with his *Harmony*, or *Treatise on Free Choice*—unknown, I say, because neither the Premonstratensian library of John Pagi mentions him, nor Casimir Oudin, himself once a member of Prémontré, who carefully investigated and accurately listed the authors of his order in the supplement to Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, nor finally do any other compilers of libraries mention him.

Vivianus was, as may be inferred, one of the first disciples of Saint Norbert, and he wrote not long after the foundations of his order had been laid. At least these words of his seem plainly to indicate it: “Vivianus, the least of the poor Church of Prémontré”; for they entirely bear the character of a newly founded religious community. Saint Norbert’s first monastery was founded in a deserted place in the diocese of Laon, divinely indicated beforehand, in the year of Christ 1120. We therefore judge that Vivianus wrote his *Harmony* about the year 1130, shortly after Saint Bernard had composed a treatise on the same subject, which Vivianus mentions; according to Mabillon’s testimony, this happened before 1128.

In this treatise Vivianus followed the teaching of the abbot of Clairvaux, which he also declares to have been “the chair of teaching of certain others.” Moreover, we owe this little work to the kindness of the most distinguished Lord Davole, librarian of the royal college of Navarre, who shared with us a codex written almost in the author’s own age.

## PROLOGUE TO GERARD, DEAN OF SAINT-QUENTIN

[Col. 1321]

[Col. 1321A] To GERARD, dean and master of the church of Saint-Quentin, VIVIANUS, the least of the poor Church of Prémontré: may you happily await the gift of future liberty.

You know, and we know, of the controversy between two persons concerning freedom of choice; perhaps you remember, and we remember, that you gave assent to one of their positions. Afterwards, we had in our hands a certain book which Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, composed on free choice and grace. In it we found the aforesaid position, which we had also previously heard debated by others. We therefore send it to you in this treatise, set forth according to the words of the aforementioned wise man and of certain others designated as occupying the chair of teaching, so that you may examine and consider it—not because, being wise, you may thereby become wiser; for in matters of this kind you are sufficiently wise of yourself—but because we think that the view which pleased your judgment when heard in passing and only once will please you when examined more attentively and repeated ten times.

# HARMONY

[Col. 1321]

[Col. 1321B]

### 1.

Every good thing, as Scripture teaches, shines forth more beautifully when brought into common view. Hence our Creator, who outwardly needed no aid of administration—indeed, who is the highest good, supreme blessedness, and wholly sufficient to himself, and was so, since his power, wisdom, and goodness can neither increase nor diminish—this Lord, I say, so powerfully wise and so wisely good, created the rational creature, namely angel and human being, and infused into them the light of reason and understanding.

For he willed that the creature, illuminated by these eyes, should behold its Creator; should know him when beheld; should love him when known; and should imitate him whom it loves, as far as it can. He did not will this in order that he himself might shine forth more beautifully [Col. 1321C]—for that is impossible with respect to himself—nor did he do it because he could thereby become richer, he to whom nothing could be lacking. Rather, he did so in order to make the created thing beautiful, rich, and blessed, displaying himself to it as most beautiful and showing it the riches and blessedness of his divinity.

In this aforesaid creature, and in the fabric of the world likewise, prepared so that the whole might serve humanity, the power of so great an artificer is perceived and known through their magnitude, his wisdom through their beauty, and his goodness through their usefulness. Although all these agree universally in this, namely that a good creature was made by the good God, according as God saw all that he had made and, behold, they were very good, nevertheless it is not ours to teach or say how greatly the rational creature differs from the irrational or insensible creature; for everyone who uses the endowment of reason, if willing to attend, discerns this.

For this creature, created in the image of its Creator according to freedom of choice, on which all merit depends, alone can become miserable [Col. 1322B] or blessed: miserable, by sinning and being alienated from its God; blessed, by being restored to its source through repentance, confession, and satisfaction. According to what I have said, the definition of free choice seems applicable to it, as some define it thus: “Free choice is voluntary and free consent”; or thus: “Free choice is the capacity of the rational will by which good is chosen, grace cooperating, and evil is chosen when grace deserts it.” Thus *free* is referred to the will, and *choice* (*arbitrium*) to reason.

For it consists in these two, namely will and reason. It belongs to reason to see what ought or ought not to be chosen; it belongs to will to desire. Therefore reason, like an attendant, points out the way, advising that which it sees should be done and dissuading from its opposite. Will, like a mistress, draws reason along with itself wherever it inclines. For will is not drawn by reason; reason merely shows what it ought to desire. Rather, reason is drawn by will and led into things contrary to reason itself. And although it naturally belongs to reason to oppose the will in evil—that is, to judge that it ought not to be done—it may nevertheless be overcome and consent.
