Reason was given to will to instruct it, not to destroy it; it would destroy it if it imposed upon it any necessity preventing it from freely turning itself, according to its choice, either toward good or toward its opposite. If, against the resistance of reason, either of these occurred—namely, if the will could not turn itself wherever it wished—the will itself would no longer be will. For where there is necessity, there is no longer will, nor freedom, and therefore no merit. Will alone, which is always free and can never be compelled, is judged before God and merits either blessedness or misery. The senses and appetites do not make one blessed or miserable; otherwise brute animals would share in blessedness or misery. Nor do intelligence, memory, or other such things make one just or unjust; thus, even if they have slowness or instability, these are not imputable.

### 2.

And in order to show more fittingly what we intend, we think it necessary to go back a little further. Among corporeal things, life is not the same as sensation, sensation is not the same as appetite, nor is appetite the same as consent. In every body, life is an inward and natural motion, active only within; sensation is a vital motion in the body, alert also toward what is outside; appetite is the natural force bestowed upon an animate being for eagerly moving the senses. Consent, however, is a spontaneous nod of the will, or also the mind’s free disposition of itself.

Will is a rational motion presiding over sensation and appetite, having reason always as its companion wherever it turns, and in a manner, as we have said, as its attendant—not because it always moves from reason, but because it never moves without reason. Thus it does many things through reason against reason itself: that is, through reason’s quasi-ministry, against its counsel or judgment. Hence the saying: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” [Col. 1323B] (Luke 16:8); and again: “They are wise in order to do evil” (ibid.). For prudence or wisdom cannot be present in a creature, even in evil, except through reason.

Thus, although we have life together with trees, sensation and appetite—indeed, a comparable life—with birds, what is called will distinguishes us from both. The consent of this will, certainly voluntary and not necessary, while it makes persons either just or unjust, also by merit makes them blessed or miserable. Such consent, therefore, is not inappropriately called free choice because of the inalienable freedom of will and the unchanging judgment of reason which it always and everywhere carries with it. It is free of itself by reason of will; it is its own judge by reason of reason. And therefore, because it is compelled by no force and no necessity, it is rightly, as we have said, judged before God and merits good or evil.

But how can good or evil be imputed to that which is acknowledged not to be free of itself? Necessity excuses both; where necessity exists, there is no freedom, and hence no merit, and therefore no judgment. [Col. 1323D] Yet in such cases original sin must always be excepted, since it is known to have a different rationale.

### 3. Liberty is threefold. Liberty from necessity.

After setting down certain matters that needed to be prefaced, let us consider something concerning the threefold liberty. We shall then set forth the opinions of certain persons, differing somewhat from one another. They say different things, yet seem to produce a kind of harmony. For harmony is called the concord of diverse sounds brought into one; and those who, although they think or express different things, are nevertheless found not to depart in any way from the path of truth, seem to produce such harmony.

Therefore one liberty is from necessity, another from sin, another from misery. Liberty from necessity belongs equally and without distinction to God and to every rational creature, good as well as evil. It is neither lost nor diminished by sin or misery; it is no greater in a just person than in a sinner, nor in an angel than in a human being. Thus the consent of the human will, turned toward good through grace, makes a person freely good and free in good insofar as the person becomes willing and is not dragged unwillingly. Likewise, when it descends voluntarily into evil, it is no less free than spontaneous in evil, being led by its own will and not compelled from elsewhere to be evil.

And just as the heavenly angel, or God himself, remains freely good and through no external necessity, so likewise the devil freely falls into evil and persists in it by his own voluntary motion, not by another’s impulse. It must indeed be understood that free [Col. 1324B] choice is not so called because it ranges or operates with equal power or facility between good and evil. It could fall by itself, and can still do so; but it cannot rise again except through the Spirit of the Lord. Otherwise neither the holy angels, who are so good that they cannot be evil, nor the transgressing angels, who are so evil that they cannot become good, would be said to possess free choice. We too shall lose this [supposed equal capacity] after the resurrection, when some of us shall be inseparably joined to goods and others to evils.

Yet neither God lacks free choice nor does the devil, because the fact that God cannot be evil is not caused by a weak necessity but by a will steadfast in good and voluntary steadfastness; and the fact that the devil cannot recover toward good is not caused by some alien violent oppression but by his own obstinate will in evil and voluntary obstinacy. Free choice is therefore called free rather because it makes the will equally free whether in good or evil, since no one can be called or be either good or evil except willingly.

For the same reason, free choice is not inappropriately said to be equally disposed toward good and evil: namely, because what is equal in each case is not ease in choosing, but freedom in willing. By this prerogative of divine dignity the Creator uniquely marked the rational creature: as he himself was under his own authority and was good by his own will, not by necessity, so too the creature might in some measure be under its own authority, so that it could become evil only through its own will and be justly condemned; or remain good and be saved by merit. This does not mean that its will could suffice for salvation, but that it could by no means attain salvation without its own will.

For no one will be saved unwillingly. Nor do the words read in the Gospel, “Compel them to come in” (Luke 14:23), or elsewhere, “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44), present any obstacle. For the gracious Father, who wills all to be saved, though he may seem to compel and draw as many as he does toward salvation, approves no one as worthy of salvation whom he has not first approved as willing. His purpose, when he terrifies and strikes, is to make them willing, not to save them unwillingly, so that, when he changes an evil will into a good one, he transfers freedom rather than removes it. For will, [Col. 1325A] whose inseparable companion is always freedom, cannot be changed except into another will. Free choice follows will everywhere in such a way that, unless will itself wholly ceases to exist, it does not lack free choice.

But will endures equally in evil as in good; consequently, free choice remains whole equally in evil as in good. And just as will, even when placed in misery, does not cease to be will but is called and is a miserable will, just as it is a blessed will, so no adversity or necessity can destroy free choice, or even in any degree diminish it in itself. Therefore freedom of will remains even where there is captivity of mind, fully as much in evil persons as in good, though more ordered in the good; likewise whole, according to its mode, in the creature as in its Creator, though more powerful in the Creator.

Ambrose shows that God possesses free choice by writing thus to Gratian: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). The Apostle also says that one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). “As he wills,” he says—that is, according to the choice of free will, not in obedience to necessity. There is no other free choice in God than the divine will, which does all things not by necessity but by goodness alone; for goodness is his nature.

Against what we have said, that angels cannot sin, some commonly object what Jerome says: “God alone is one into whom sin cannot fall; all other beings, since they possess free choice, can bend their will in either direction.” But how this should be understood may be inferred from the words of Isidore: “Angels are mutable by nature, immutable by grace.” Hence it must be granted that good angels can sin by their nature—that is, their nature does not oppose this; nevertheless it must not be granted simply that good angels can sin. Rather, they cannot sin—that is, the grace by which they have been confirmed opposes this.

### 4. Liberty from sin.

There follows liberty from sin. There is a liberty from sin, of which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17). And elsewhere: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God” [Col. 1325D] (Romans 6:18), and so forth.

This is what Augustine means: “A human being, using free choice badly, destroyed himself and it.” The liberty from necessity was not lost, but liberty from sin was lost. “For whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). This liberty from sin belongs only to those reformed by the gift of grace, not because they are entirely without sin, but because sin does not rule in them; and this is properly called liberty.

In doing evil, as some hold, free choice is not properly said to be free, since reason there disagrees with will. For will desires what reason opposes. Here it must not be omitted that before sin nothing hindered the will toward good and nothing restrained it toward its opposite; without the obstacle of difficulty, will desired the good. But after sin, [Col. 1326A] before free choice is restored, it can be pressed down by concupiscence and overcome. After restoration, before the confirmation that will occur in the future, it can be pressed down but not overcome. After confirmation, it can neither be overcome nor pressed down.

There are those who say that no one in this world can claim liberty from sin for himself; but this is true if slight or venial sins are not excepted. For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). But one who asserts that such liberty can be claimed means liberty from grave sins.

### 5. Freedom from misery

There follows the question of freedom from misery, concerning which the Apostle says: “The creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21). Concerning this, as some assert [Col. 1326B], no one shall be liberated; rather, they say, the punishment of sin always accompanies us in this life.

But there are those who say that holy persons who have already received the firstfruits of the Spirit, and who, with Mary, have chosen the better part, are sometimes, in an excess of contemplation, caught up in the Spirit and taste, however slightly, the sweetness of heavenly blessedness—although rarely and fleetingly—and that then they are free from misery. For those who already hold the part that shall not be taken away undoubtedly experience what is to come. But what is to come is blessedness. Blessedness and misery, moreover, cannot coexist at the same time. Therefore, whenever they share in the former through the Spirit, they neither feel nor taste the latter. Yet, as it seems to me, only those who have experienced this ought to be believed concerning it.

But whatever may be the case with others, the Son—who [Col. 1326C] came to set free free choice, not from necessity, but from sin and the punishment of sin, concerning whom it was said to the Jews, “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free” (John 7:36)—possessed both freedoms: namely, freedom from sin and freedom from misery. The former he possessed in power and in act, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53); the latter not in act but in power, because no one took his life from him, but he himself laid it down. Finally, as the prophet testifies: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7). Thus, having been born of a woman and made under the law—that is, under the law of misery—in order to redeem those who were under that same law, he alone, free among the miserable and sinful, might shake both yokes from the necks of his brethren.

He himself possessed freedom from necessity [Col. 1326D] even by virtue of his human nature; he possessed the remaining freedoms by divine power. The first freedom he bestowed upon us in the creation of nature; by grace we are restored in the second; the last is reserved for us in our homeland. Let the first, therefore, be called the freedom of nature; the second, the freedom of grace; the third, the freedom of life or glory.

For first, we were created as a noble creature with free willing and voluntary freedom. Second, we are re-formed in innocence as a new creature in Christ. Third, we are raised in perfect glory as a creature in the Spirit. The first freedom, therefore, has much honor; the second, very great strength as well; the last, the fullness of delight. By the first we excel the other living creatures; by the second we subject the flesh; by the third, death. Or rather: just as in the first he subjected beneath our feet sheep, [Col. 1327A] oxen, and the cattle of the field, so also through the second he casts down, levels, and crushes beneath our feet the spiritual beasts of this air, concerning whom it is said: “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. 73:19).

Finally, in the last freedom he will submit us more fully to ourselves through victory over corruption and death, when, namely, “the last enemy, death,” shall be destroyed, and we shall pass, as was said, into “the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” It is by this freedom that Christ will set us free when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father (Gal. 5:1).

### 6. The saints after death are free from sin and misery. In this world man is not free from sin and misery

It must also be known without doubt that perfect freedom from sin and misery belongs to perfected souls released from the flesh, together with God and Christ [Col. 1327B] and the angels above the heavens. For holy souls, although they have not yet received their bodies, lack something of glory, but have absolutely nothing of misery.

Yet free choice is by no means named from this freedom—whether freedom from sin or that called freedom from misery—but solely from that freedom which is called freedom from necessity, because “voluntary” appears, conversely, to be contrary to “necessary.” For from the freedom called freedom from sin it might perhaps more suitably be called free counsel; and, likewise, from the freedom called freedom from misery it might rather be called free delight than free choice. For choice is judgment. As it belongs to judgment to discern what is permitted, so it surely belongs to counsel to determine what is expedient or inexpedient; and to delight to experience what pleases [Col. 1327C] or does not please.

In this life, the freedom of choice alone remains full and intact in human beings, both after sin and before sin. Freedom of counsel, however, exists only in part and in a few spiritual persons who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, so that sin no longer reigns in their mortal body. Freedom of counsel prevents sin from reigning; but the fact that sin nevertheless does not wholly disappear is the captivity of free choice.

But when that which is perfect comes, then that which is partial shall be abolished. That is, when freedom of counsel is full, there will no longer be any captivity of choice. This is what we daily ask in prayer when we say: “May your kingdom come.” This kingdom has not yet come wholly into us; nevertheless, each day it gradually comes, and little by little extends its boundaries more and more, in those at least whose inward person is renewed day by day through God’s help. Only contemplatives, however, as has already been said, when they are lifted up in an ecstasy of mind on the wing of contemplation, enjoy in some measure the freedom of delight, and even this only to a very small degree and on the rarest occasions.

### 7. The first human possessed every freedom in Paradise, but in an inferior degree

Next it must be considered how, or to what extent, the first human being in Paradise possessed all three freedoms of which we have spoken: freedom of choice, counsel, and delight; or, in other names, freedom from necessity, sin, and misery.

He always retained the freedom of choice unshaken, both after sin and before sin [Col. 1328A]. But if he had possessed the other two fully, he would never have been exiled from Paradise. Each of them has two degrees, a higher and a lower. The higher freedom of counsel is the inability to sin; the lower is the ability not to sin. Likewise, the higher power of delight is the inability to be troubled; the lower is the ability not to be troubled.

Thus, in his creation, the human being received the lower degree of each freedom, together with full freedom of choice, and fell away from both when he sinned. He fell from being able not to sin into being unable not to sin, having wholly lost freedom of counsel. Likewise, he fell from being able not to be troubled into being unable not to be troubled, having wholly lost freedom of delight. Only freedom of choice remained, as a punishment—the very freedom through which he lost the others. [Col. 1328B] He could not lose that alone.

For, having become a slave of sin through his own will, he deservedly lost freedom of counsel. And, having become through sin a debtor to death, how could he thereafter retain freedom of delight? Therefore, from the three freedoms he received, by abusing that which is called freedom of choice, he deprived himself of the others. He abused it in that, having received it for glory, he turned it to dishonor, according to the testimony of Scripture saying: “Man, when he was in honor” (Ps. 48:13), and so forth.

Among living creatures, the power to sin was given to the human being alone, by the prerogative of free choice. It was given, however, not so that he should thereby sin, but so that he might appear more glorious if he did not sin while being able to sin. For what could have been more glorious for him than for it to be said of him what Scripture attests, saying [Col. 1328C]: “Who is this man? We will praise him” (Ecclus. 31:9). Why is he so praiseworthy? “For he has done wonders in his life” (ibid.). What wonders? “Because he could transgress, and did not transgress; do evil, and did not do it” (ibid.).

As long as he remained without sin, therefore, he preserved this honor; when he sinned, he lost it. He sinned because it was free for him to do so; and surely it was free to him from no other source than freedom of choice, through which he had the possibility of sinning. Yet the fault was not the giver’s, but the abuser’s: he turned to the practice of sin the very capacity that he had received for the glory of not sinning.

For although he sinned from the ability he had received, he sinned not because he could, but because he willed. For when the devil and his angels transgressed [Col. 1328D], the others did not transgress—not because they could not, but because they would not. The fall of the sinner, therefore, must be ascribed not to the gift of power, but to the fault of the will.

Yet, although the fall comes from the will, the fallen person no longer has it freely within his power to rise again by will; for even before the fall he could not advance to something better by any effort of his own without superadded grace. The will was indeed given the ability to stand so as not to fall, but not the ability to rise again if it fell. No one can climb out of a pit as easily as he can slip into it.

The human being fell by will alone into the pit of sin; but it is not enough that he should will, nor is it in his power, to rise again, since now, even if he wills, he cannot avoid sinning. What then? Has free choice perished because he cannot avoid sinning? By no means. Rather, he has lost free counsel [Col. 1329A], through which he formerly possessed the inability to sin. And because he is indeed unable not to be troubled, it follows that the miserable person has also lost freedom of delight, through which he had formerly possessed the ability not to be troubled.

Thus free choice remains even after sin; and although miserable, it remains intact. The fact that a human being is not sufficient by himself to shake off sin or misery does not signify the destruction of free choice, but the deprivation of the other two freedoms. For it does not belong to free choice, so far as it is concerned, nor has it ever belonged to it, to be able or to be wise, but only to will. It does not make the creature powerful or wise, but only willing.

Hence the Apostle says: “So that you do not do whatever things you wish” (Col. 3:22). Willing, as I have said, belongs to us from free choice—not, I say, willing good or willing evil, but simply willing. For to will good is progress; to will evil is decline; but willing simply is that very thing which either advances or declines. So that it might exist, creating grace made it; so that it might advance, saving grace makes it; so that it might decline, it casts itself down.

Free choice itself makes us willing; grace makes us well-disposed. From the former comes our willing; from the latter, our willing good. Simple affections belong to us as if from ourselves, such as willing and fearing; their additions come from grace, such as willing good, fearing God, and loving God. This is simply that grace orders the dispositions which creation has given, so that virtues are nothing other than ordered affections.

One affection is ordered, another disordered. Disordered is the will; hence it was said: “You do not know what you ask” (Mark 11:33). He taught ordered will who said: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). He said this then in words, but afterwards also by example, saying to the Father: “Not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26:89).

Likewise, fear was disordered when “there they trembled where there was no fear.” He taught ordered fear who said: “Fear him who can cast soul and body into Gehenna” (Matt. 5:29). Love was disordered; hence it was said: “People loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19). It is ordered when the Bride asks in the Song of Songs: “Set love in order within me” (Song 2:4).

Where something similar is found, let something similar be said. We received these affections, both those just mentioned and others, in the condition of nature, so that we might be some kind of creature. [Col. 1329D] But we received their ordering in the visitation of grace, so that we might be God’s creature. Hence free will makes us our own; evil makes us the devil’s; good makes us God’s.

Therefore, recognizing what came from nature and what he expected from grace, the Apostle said: “Willing lies near at hand to me, but I do not find the accomplishing” (Rom. 7:18). He knew certainly that willing belonged to him from free choice; but that grace was necessary to him in order that his willing itself might be perfect.

For this we need a double gift of grace: true wisdom, which is the turning of the will toward good; and full power, which is the confirmation of that same will in good. Perfect conversion toward good is such that nothing pleases except what is fitting or permitted. Perfect confirmation in good is such that nothing that pleases is lacking. Then at last the will will be perfect, when it is wholly good and abundantly fulfilled in goodness [Col. 1330A]. This we await in the future life, where there will be true wisdom with respect to righteousness, and true power with respect to glory.

“True” and “full” have been added: the former to distinguish it from the wisdom of the flesh, which is death, and likewise from the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God; the latter to distinguish it from those of whom it is said: “The powerful shall be powerfully punished” (Wis. 6:6).

And because, as was said, the human being cannot possess true wisdom or full power through freedom of choice, he therefore has need of Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God. As wisdom, Christ infuses true wisdom into him through the restoration of free counsel; as power, he restores full power [Col. 1330B] through the repair of free delight. Thus by the one he may be perfectly good and know sin no more; by the other, fully blessed and feel no adversity. But we await this in the future, when both freedoms now lost shall be fully restored to free choice—not as they have been granted to any righteous person in this world, however perfect, nor as they were granted even to the first human beings in Paradise, but as the angels now possess them in heaven.

### 8. The image and likeness of the Creator are contained in the three freedoms

I think that in these three freedoms—choice, counsel, and delight—is contained the very image and likeness of the Creator in whose image we were made. The image, indeed, is in freedom of choice; but in the other two freedoms a certain twofold likeness is marked [Col. 1330C].

Perhaps this is why free choice alone suffers no diminution or defect whatsoever: in it, above all, a certain substantial image of the eternal and immutable divinity seems to be impressed. For even though it had a beginning, it knows no end; it receives no increase from righteousness or grace, and no loss from sin or misery. What is more like eternity?

In the other two freedoms, however, because they may not only be diminished in part but wholly lost, there is recognized a more accidental likeness, laid over the image, of divine wisdom and power. For we lost them through fault and recover them through grace; and every day some advance more and some less in them, or fall away from them. They may even be lost in such a way that they can no longer be recovered. They may also be possessed in such a way that they can in no manner be lost or diminished.

The human being was created in Paradise in a degree of this twofold likeness of the wisdom and power of God—not the highest degree, indeed, but one nearest to it. For what is nearer to inability to sin or be troubled, in which holy angels undoubtedly already stand and God always exists, than ability both not to sin and not to be troubled, in which the human being was certainly created?

Having fallen from that degree through sin—or rather, we having fallen in him and with him—we received through grace, not that same degree again, but a lower degree in its place. For here we cannot be altogether without sin [Col. 1331A] or misery; nevertheless, with grace helping us, we can be overcome neither by sin nor by misery.

The highest angels possess the highest degree of divine likeness; we possess the lowest; Adam possessed the middle; demons possess none. The spirits above were given to endure without sin and misery; Adam, to exist without them, but not also to remain so; we, not even to exist without them, but only not to yield to them. But the devil and his members, just as they never will resist sin, so they can never avoid the punishment of sin.

Therefore, when these two freedoms—counsel and delight, through which true wisdom and power are ministered to the rational creature—are varied by God’s dispensation, according to his will and for different causes, places, and times, so that they are possessed in small measure on earth, fully in heaven, moderately in Paradise, and not at all in hell; while freedom of choice is not changed even somewhat from the condition in which it was created, but is always possessed in some manner, so far as it is concerned, by heaven, earth, and hell: rightly the former two are assigned to likeness and the latter to image.

And indeed, the authority of Scripture testifies that in hell both freedoms have perished—that is, those said to belong to likeness. For that true wisdom exists there not at all—which is understood to come from freedom of counsel—is made manifest by the place where it is written: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it; for there is neither work nor reasoning nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten” (Eccles. 9:10). And elsewhere: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” [Col. 1331C] (Wis. 1:4).

Concerning power, moreover, which is given through freedom of delight, the Gospel speaks thus: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 25:30). For what is the binding of hands and feet except the complete removal of power?

Nor could likeness even have been found in this world; the image would still have lain here ugly and disfigured, had not that woman of the Gospel lit a lamp—that is, had the wisdom of God not appeared in the flesh—swept the house, namely the house of vices, and sought her drachma which she had lost (Luke 15:8), that is, her image. Stripped of its native beauty and foul beneath the skin of sin, it lay hidden as though in dust. Having found it, she wiped it clean, lifted it from the region of unlikeness [Col. 1331D], renewed it in its former beauty, and made it like the glory of the saints—or rather, would at length render it wholly conformed to herself—when that saying of Scripture is fulfilled: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

And truly, to whom did this work more fittingly belong than to the Son of God? Since he is the brightness and express image of the Father’s substance, bearing all things by his word, he appeared equipped from both sources: with the means to reform what was deformed and to strengthen what was weak. By the brightness of his image, banishing the darkness of sins, he made it wise; and by the power of the Word, he made it strong against the tyranny of demons.

Therefore the Form itself came, by which free choice was to be re-formed, because it had to be re-formed from that from which it had been formed, if it was to receive its former form. Form, however, is wisdom; conformity accomplishes in the image within the body what form accomplishes in the universe.

Now Wisdom “reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). It reaches from end to end: that is, from the greatest angel to the smallest worm, from the greatest creature to the least, or from the highest heaven to the lowest regions of earth. It reaches mightily, not by movement or local diffusion, but by a certain substantial and everywhere-present power, by which it most powerfully moves, orders, and governs all things. And it does this sweetly: that is, with no difficulty but by peaceful will.

Or it reaches from end to end—that is, from the origin of the creature to the end appointed by the Creator, whether the end toward which nature presses it, cause hastens it, or grace grants it. Thus free choice should endeavor to rule its body as wisdom rules the universe; and it should do this mightily, by resisting vices, and sweetly, by resting in conscience: that is, not from sadness or necessity, which is the beginning rather than the fullness of wisdom, but with ready and cheerful will, which makes the sacrifice acceptable, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

### 9.

It must also be known that between the divine Spirit and the desire of the flesh there holds a certain middle place that which in the human being is called free choice—that is, the human will. It hangs, as it were, between the two upon the precipitous slope of a very steep mountain. It is so weakened in its desire through the flesh that, unless the Spirit diligently helps [Col. 1332C] its weakness through grace, it is not only unable, by ascending from strength to strength, to attain the summit of righteousness—which, according to the Prophet, is like the mountains of God (Ps. 35:7)—but also, rolling downward through its own weight from vice into vice, always plunges headlong. This is owing not only to the law of sin implanted in the members from the beginning, but also to dispositions imbedded by the habitual practice of earthly dwelling.

At this point one may object from the Apostle’s words: “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). These words may seem to compel the will and rob it of freedom. But however greatly a person may be pressed by inward or outward temptations, the will will always remain free with respect to choice, since it will nonetheless judge by its own consent.

With respect to counsel or delight, however, while the desire of the flesh and the misery of life resist it, the will feels itself less free, but not at all evil, provided that it does not consent. Similar is the complaint commonly made by some: “I want to have a good will, but I cannot.” But this in no way prejudices freedom of choice, as though the will suffered force or necessity in this respect; rather, it plainly testifies that it lacks the freedom called freedom from sin.

For one who wills to have a good will proves that he has a will. He cannot will to have a good will except through will. And if he has will and [Col. 1333A] freedom, but freedom not from sin but from necessity, then in not being able to have a good will when he wills it, he indeed feels that freedom is lacking to him—but surely freedom from sin. He grieves that his will is oppressed, not destroyed, by that from which he is oppressed; and without doubt he has a good will in some manner, in that he wills to have one.

For what he wills is good, and he could not will a good thing except with a good will, just as he could not will an evil thing except with an evil will. When we will good, the will is good; when we will evil, the will is evil. In both cases there is will; in both cases there is freedom. Necessity yields to will.

But when we cannot accomplish what we will, we indeed perceive that freedom from sin is in some sense captive or miserable, yet not lost. If an objection is made from Peter’s sin—that he seemed to have lost free choice when he denied out of fear—then he was undoubtedly already such when he heard from him from whom nothing could be hidden: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:75).

That weakness of will, revealed through the fear that came upon him, was not produced but made known; it made known how he loved himself and how he loved Christ—not to Christ, but to Peter. For Christ knew beforehand what was in the human being. Peter sinned not by hating or despising Christ, but by loving himself.

A will cannot be compelled except by itself; nor, as was said long ago, can it be changed into another will. It compelled itself. If it compelled itself, then as both compelled and compelling, it seemed to lose freedom there and also to recover it. For it suffered from itself the force which it inflicted upon itself. But what the will suffered from itself was from will; what was from will was no longer from necessity but voluntary; and if voluntary, free.

The person whom his own will compelled to deny was compelled because he willed; indeed, he was not compelled, but consented—not to another’s power, but to his own will, namely that by which he desired by every means to escape death. He denied while grieving, but not except while willing. Of those in whom the will was sound it is written: “They may be killed, but they cannot be bent.”

### 10. What free choice does in the human being

We have said that free choice is deprived of its freedom by no necessity or adversity. Yet, although it remains thus stable, it must be known that it itself accomplishes only the human being’s salvation—or rather, God’s grace accomplishes salvation in it or through it.

Perhaps someone will ask here: What does free choice do in the human being? We answer briefly: it is saved. Remove free choice, and there will be nothing to save; remove grace, and there will be no means by which it may be saved. The work cannot be accomplished without these two: one by whom it is done, the other to whom—or in whom—it is done.

God is the author of salvation; free choice is merely capable of receiving it. God alone can give salvation, and free choice alone can receive it. Therefore what is given by God alone and to free choice alone cannot exist without the consent of the recipient any more than without the grace of the giver. Thus free choice is said to cooperate with grace that works salvation [Col. 1334A] when it consents—that is, when it is saved. For to consent is to be saved.

### 11. What grace is. God works salvation through creatures in three ways

It should be considered that grace awakens free choice when it sows a thought; heals it when it changes its affection; strengthens it when it leads it to action; and preserves it lest it experience failure. It works in this way with free choice, yet it precedes it in the first instance and accompanies it in the others. It precedes so that free choice may thereafter cooperate with it; yet what is begun by grace alone is completed jointly by both, so that they work together, not separately; at the same time, not in turns, throughout each advance; not partly grace and partly free choice, but each accomplishes the whole work undividedly.

This one accomplishes the whole, and that one accomplishes the whole; but as the whole is in free choice, so the whole is from grace. It must therefore be confessed that salvation belongs not to free choice but to the Lord.

Nevertheless, to establish our merits, he deigns to employ the ministries of creatures—not because he needs them, but through them or from them he brings about their advancement. Therefore he works the salvation of those whose names are written in the book of life: sometimes through a creature without the creature itself; sometimes through a creature against the creature itself; sometimes through a creature with the creature itself.

Many things beneficial to human beings are done through insensible creation, and likewise through irrational creation. They are said to be done without the creature itself because, lacking understanding, it cannot be conscious of them. God also does many things useful for salvation through evil human beings or angels; but because they are unwilling, he does them against them. For, while wishing to harm, they help: as much as the useful action benefits others, so much does their perverse intention harm them.

But those through whom and with whom God works are good angels or human beings, who both do and will what God wills. For those who consent in will to the good which they accomplish in deed share in the work that God performs through them. What can the creature through which something is done, but without which it is done, deserve? What can the creature through which and against which it is done deserve except wrath? What can the creature through which and with which it is done deserve except grace?

Therefore no merits are gained in the first case, evil merits in the second, and good merits in the last. But it must be confessed that these things occur in those whom grace has preceded. For God works these three things in us: to think good, to will, and to accomplish. The first he does without us; the second with us; the third through us.

We must take care, when we perceive these things being done within us or with us, that we attribute them not to ourselves but to God’s grace alone. What else do our words express than what the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16)? He does not say this, of course, as though anyone could will or run in vain; but so that the one who wills or runs may glory not in himself, but in him from whom he received both willing and running: “For, O human being, what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

You are created, healed, saved. What of these is from yourself, O human being? What of these was not impossible to free choice? You could neither create yourself when you did not exist, nor justify yourself when a sinner, nor raise yourself when dead [Col. 1335A].

Therefore, if you are wise in the right way, you will confess a threefold operation—not of free choice, but of divine grace, in it or concerning it. The first is creation; the second, reformation; the third, consummation. First, we are created in Christ into freedom of will. Second, through Christ we are re-formed into the Spirit of freedom. Thereafter, with Christ, we are to be confirmed in the state of eternity.

For what did not exist had to be created in him who existed; what was deformed had to be re-formed through the Form; and the members could not be perfected except with the Head. This will be completed when “we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ,” when Christ, our life, appears, and we too shall appear with him in glory.

But since consummation is to take place concerning us and in us, not from us; and creation takes place even without us; reformation alone, which in some manner takes place with us through voluntary consent, is reckoned to us as merit. It consists in our fasts, vigils, continence, works of mercy, and the other exercises of virtues, through which our inward person is clearly renewed day by day.

For this inward renewal consists in three things: uprightness of intention, purity of affection, and remembrance of good action, through which memory, conscious of itself in a good way, shines brightly. Since it is certain that these are done in us by the divine Spirit, they are God’s gifts. But because they occur with the consent of our will, they are our merits; yet both the will and the merit are from God.

For there is no doubt that both willing and accomplishing, for the good will, are from God. Otherwise, if what we call our merits are rightly so called, they are certain seedbeds of hope, incentives to charity, signs of hidden predestination, omens of future blessedness, and the way to the kingdom—not the cause of reigning. Nor do we need a long discussion of this matter, since human consummation ought rather to be called a beginning, and Paul says: “If by works, then it is no longer by grace” [Col. 1336B] (Rom. 11:6).

*Here ends the treatise on free choice and grace, which, if it please, may henceforth be called HARMONY, because in it a concord brought into unity from diverse sounds is gathered together. Amen.*

[IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1130: ABBOT GAUSSELMUS.]

[Col. 1335]

## LETTER OF ABBOT G. TO A., PRIOR OF SAINT VICTOR OF MARSEILLES

He reproves the brothers of Marseilles because they disinterred a dead man, and complains that they do not render him the reverence due to him.

(From the archives of Saint Victor, extracted by Dom Furnerius; edited by Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 691.)

[Col. 1335C] To A., his deeply cherished friend, prior of Marseilles, and to the entire holy community: G., a sinner, [Note: [Col. 1335D] This is undoubtedly Abbot Gauselm, who is said in the brief Marseilles chronicle in Labbe to have presided for only a single year, and who immediately withdrew to Sainte-Baume out of zeal for perfection, intending to devote himself to the exercises of contemplation—a fact that surprises me has hitherto been passed over by writers.], wishes right understanding, discernment, and fulfillment in deed.

Scripsit mihi tua dulcis fraternitas se sincero mentis affectu parvitatis meae dilectioni quondam inhaesisse, quodque verum esse fateor, multimodas pietati tuae gratias refero, adjiciens me tibi ejusdem charitatis spontaneam reddidisse vicissitudinem, quod reali argumento facile probari potest, quod nunquam voluntati tuae contrarius esse volui; imo forsitan contra quorumdam persuasiones te semper ad meliora informare atque provehere studui. Quod vero scripsisti me te et alios charissimos fratres nostros quasi despectissimos servos dimisisse, salva pace tua dico quod hoc modestius dici posset, quoniam [Col. 1336C] nullatenus vos deserens contempsi, imo semper corde et animo vobiscum sum. Verum cogente necessitatis articulo, corpore tantum non longe secessi a vobis, et negotio vobis noto locum praebere volens, quod corpore praesens facere nequirem. Conquesta est tua dilectio quod non transmisi tibi speciales litteras: quod non fuit, charissime frater, charitatis oblivio, sed rei familiaris assidua occupatio, et praecipue quod laboriosum est mihi scribere, cum visus oculorum meorum aliquantulum ex aegritudine capitis obtenebretur. Propterea quod querimoniae tuae, charissime frater, rationabiliter respondere curavi, nec, si placet, verbis meis tuae benignitatis aures accommodare non renuas, sed sicut pro te et pro aliis conquestus es, ita pro te et pro aliis, [Col. 1337A] ut universaliter respondeas, justa ratio poposcit. Quaero igitur a te, charissime frater, quo peccato merui contra sanctorum decreta pontificum, et contra omnem ecclesiasticam institutionem, tam coeli a vestra paternitate feriri sententia, ut ad omnipotentis Dei contemptum et beatae Virginis Mariae, deinde ad nostrum dedecus, corpus cujusdam miseri paralytici defuncti in coemeterio hujus speluncae a vobis sepeliri prohibetur, et post sepulturam multo sudore fabricatam? Quis vestrum, si alicui injuriae hic imputari posset, infra capitulum vestrum vel extra me appellavit? vel cujus audientiam vel judicium, sive et regularem correctionem subterfugere tentavi? Quis vestrum potest me notare, ut postquam ad hanc veni speluncam, cupiditatis vitio [Col. 1337B] vinctus aliquid exigerem vel acciperem a defunctis? quo igitur commisso tanta multari merui contumelia, ut sepultura vacua hiatu suo ridiculum transeuntibus praebeat? Certe, charissime frater, aut vos quorum praecepto, ut sanctissimus frater noster dominus Guido testatur, neminem vestrum excipiens, hoc factum est manifeste . . . . . mihi canonicam auctoritatem, cujus fulti praesidio haec fieri praecepistis, aut ego, antequam sopiatur tam contumeliosa injuria, eoram metropolitano circumstantibus suffraganeis episcopis, sanctorum auctoritate canonum probabo vos ordinis vestri incurrisse periculum adjiciendo tunc . . . . supersedeo. Praeterea dic mihi, charissime frater, quis vestrum postquam in hac spelunca pauperrime inclusus sum, excepto W. Biterrensi, [Col. 1337C] proprio compellente negotio, spontaneae visitationis gratia . . . sive laetificare sua praesentia voluit? Nescis tu, charissime frater, quod nuper nulla ratione, nullis precibus potui a vestra paternitate impetrare ut transmitteretur mihi Berengarius sacrista citissime reversurus? Breve colloquium valde necessarium fuerat. Et ne . . . . . . . a vestra beatitudine mihi charitatis janua clauderetur, scit vestra sanctitas quod nullo modo a vobis peccatis meis exigentibus impetrare merui, ut in tam sancto B. Joannis festo mitteretur mihi aliquis ex fratribus ad concelebrandum tantae solemnitatis officium: sed vix transmissa est mihi cappa curta, vetus et disrupta, sub maxima comminatione ut in crastinum solemnitatis reportaretur, et quod aliquantula, falsa tamen [Col. 1337D] reverentia obstante, per vos ipsos me adhuc ex toto dehonestare erubescitis. Elegistis ex vobis qui mihi frequentes inferendo contumelias, desiderio vestro satisfaciat, domnum videlicet Guidonem, virum illustrissimum, huncque virtutum flore decoratum, cujus vita gloriosa et admirabilis religio non solum nos peccatores circumstantes, verum etiam omne Massiliense monasterium illustrat. Ipsi a vestra laudabili prudentia, ut proprio perhibet ore, injunctum est, ut irritando me ad iram saltem defunctorum [Col. 1338A] corpora . . . . . . tumulari prohibeat, quia, ut vir clarissimus ac verae obedientiae amator, quod vere praeceptum est, nullatenus facere negligit, sed ad obedientiae cumulum adjicit plurima derisoria ac contumeliosa verba. Quid enim, charissime frater, ista mihi innuunt, nisi ut dicam cum propheta: Filios enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me? Et alibi: Isti labiis me honorant, cor autem eorum longe est a me. Et in Evangelio: Ecce quomodo amabant eum. Sed haec ad praesens omittenda censeo, quod ad reseranda cordis mei arcana tempus meum nondum advenit, tempus autem vestrum ad me floccipendendum, ad me vituperandum, semper est paratum. Verumtamen, nisi vestra sanctitas circa me caute egerit, ego sanctitatis vestrae servus, qui [Col. 1338B] hactenus contemptus tacui, laesus silui, quandoque sicut parturiens loquar, proindeque fraternitatis tuae laudabilis dulcedo in proximo B. Victoris festo jubet me venire ad se; non recuso venire, si quis honeste me deducere voluerit, paratus ex toto corde puraque mentis devotione ad honorem Dei et B. Virginis Mariae et praefati gloriosi martyris, necnon et sanctae matris nostrae Massiliensis utilitatem, remoto omnino totius amaritudinis zelo, corroborare et confirmare quod melior pars, praeeunte Spiritus sancti gratia, elegerit, secundum B. Patris nostri Benedicti praeceptum et animarum nostrarum desiderabilem salutem. Si vero, quod absit! aliqui sinistrae partis contra B. Benedicti normam, sive contra consilium domnorum et fratrum nostrorum Dominum timentium, [Col. 1338C] pravitates suas fovere cupientes aliquid religioni adversum agere voluerint, scito quod ego qualiscunque peccator monachus quondam a vobis catholice electus, et adhuc a nemine depositus, nulli tradam pastoralis officii virgam, imo fortissimus praeliator ascendam ex adverso, opponens me murum pro domo Israel, et stabo in praelio in die Domini, clamans cum Legislatore: Si quis Domini est, jungatur mihi. Postremo quod laudabilis amicitia tua, sicut quondam fidelis mihi fuit et jucunda, et humiliter obediens, ita in eodem se semper perseveraturam asserit, debitas tibi grates persolvo, et si in aliquo tibi necessarius fuero, necessitudini tuae ultroneum me offero. Denique reddens vicem tuae dilectioni, licet tibi specialiter scripserim litteras, [Col. 1338D] tamen si in conspectu omnium fratrum eas legere volueritis, satis mihi placet, hoc tantummodo tuae discretioni committens, ut simpliciter intelligas et intelligendo prudenter discernas quorum respectu superius scripta querimonia a me sit promulgata, et sicut in prima fronte epistolae ita et in fine omnes domnos nostros et charissimos fratres per te iterum salvari optamus. Vale, valeant et ipsi, et ut pro me servo tuo omnipotentem Dominum exorare dignentur, flexis genibus humiliter imploro.

Your sweet brotherhood has written to me that it once adhered, with sincere affection of mind, to love for my lowliness. Since I acknowledge this to be true, I return manifold thanks to your piety, adding that I have freely rendered you the same return of charity. This may readily be proved by actual evidence: I have never wished to oppose your will; indeed, perhaps against the persuasions of certain persons, I have always endeavoured to train and advance you toward better things.

But as for your writing that I abandoned you and our other dearest brethren as though you were utterly contemptible servants, I say—saving your peace—that this might have been said more moderately. For, in no way abandoning you, have I despised you; rather, [Col. 1336C] I am always with you in heart and mind. Yet, compelled by a pressing necessity, I withdrew from you only in body, and not far away, wishing to make room for a matter known to you, which I could not accomplish while physically present.

Your affection complained that I had not sent you a personal letter. This, dearest brother, was not forgetfulness of charity, but continual occupation with household affairs; and especially because writing is burdensome to me, since the sight of my eyes is somewhat clouded by an illness of the head. Therefore, since I have taken care reasonably to answer your complaint, dearest brother, do not, if you please, refuse to lend the ears of your kindness to my words. And just as you have complained on behalf of yourself and others, so just reason has required that you answer generally on behalf of yourself and others. [Col. 1337A]

I ask you, therefore, dearest brother: by what sin have I deserved, contrary to the decrees of the holy pontiffs and to every ecclesiastical ordinance, to be struck by so severe a sentence from your fatherhood, that—to the contempt of almighty God and of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and then to our disgrace—the body of a certain poor dead paralytic is forbidden by you to be buried in the cemetery of this cave, even after a grave has been made with much labour?

Which of you, if any injury could here be charged against someone, summoned me either within your chapter or outside it? Whose hearing, judgment, or regular correction have I sought to evade? Which of you can accuse me that, since I came to this cave, bound by the vice of avarice, [Col. 1337B] I have demanded or received anything from the dead? What offence, then, have I committed such that I deserved to be punished with so great an outrage, so that the empty grave, with its open mouth, offers passers-by a spectacle for ridicule? Surely, dearest brother, either you—by whose command, as our most holy brother Lord Guy testifies, with none of you excepted, this was openly done—[lacuna] shall show me the canonical authority on whose protection you relied in ordering this to be done; or I, before so insulting an injury is hushed up, shall prove before the metropolitan, surrounded by the suffragan bishops, on the authority of the holy canons, that you have incurred peril to your order—adding then [lacuna]. I refrain.

Moreover, tell me, dearest brother: since I have been enclosed in utmost poverty in this cave, which of you, except W. of Béziers, [Col. 1337C] compelled by some personal business, has wished of his own accord to visit me [lacuna] or to gladden me by his presence? Do you not know, dearest brother, that recently I could obtain from your fatherhood by no argument and no prayers that the sacristan Berengar should be sent to me, though he would return very quickly? A brief conversation was exceedingly necessary.

And lest [lacuna] the door of charity should be shut against me by your blessedness, your holiness knows that, because my sins demanded it, I could in no way obtain from you that on the most holy feast of St John one of the brethren might be sent to me to celebrate together the office of so great a solemnity. Rather, scarcely was a short, old, torn cope sent to me, under the gravest threat that it should be returned on the day after the feast; and, notwithstanding some slight yet false reverence, [Col. 1337D] you are still ashamed to dishonour me completely in person.

You have chosen from among yourselves one who, by inflicting frequent insults upon me, may satisfy your desire: namely Lord Guy, a most distinguished man, adorned with the flower of virtues, whose glorious life and admirable religious observance illumine not only us sinners around him, but also the whole monastery of Marseille. By your praiseworthy prudence, as he himself declares, he has been ordered, by provoking me to anger, at least to forbid the bodies of the dead [Col. 1338A] to be [lacuna] buried. For, as a most illustrious man and lover of true obedience, he by no means neglects what has truly been commanded; but, to crown his obedience, he adds many mocking and insulting words.

For what do these things suggest to me, dearest brother, except that I should say with the prophet: “I have nourished and brought up children, but they have despised me”? And elsewhere: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” And in the Gospel: “See how he loved him.” But I judge that these matters ought for the present to be omitted, because my time for unlocking the secrets of my heart has not yet come; whereas your time for making little of me and reproaching me is always ready.

Nevertheless, unless your holiness acts cautiously toward me, I, the servant of your holiness, who [Col. 1338B] have hitherto been silent when despised and silent when injured, shall one day speak like a woman in labour. Accordingly, the praiseworthy sweetness of your brotherhood commands me to come to it for the approaching feast of St Victor. I do not refuse to come, if someone is willing honourably to conduct me there. I am prepared, with my whole heart and with pure devotion of mind, for the honour of God, of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of the aforesaid glorious martyr, and also for the welfare of our holy mother of Marseille, wholly laying aside every zeal of bitterness, to strengthen and confirm what the better part, led by the grace of the Holy Spirit, shall choose, according to the precept of our blessed father Benedict and the desirable salvation of our souls.

But if—God forbid—some of the sinister party, wishing to foster their perversities, should undertake anything contrary to religion, against the rule of St Benedict or against the counsel of our lords and brethren who fear the Lord, [Col. 1338C] know that I, however unworthy a sinner and monk, once canonically elected by you and not yet deposed by anyone, shall hand the staff of the pastoral office over to no one. Rather, I shall rise up as a most resolute combatant against them, setting myself as a wall for the house of Israel; and I shall stand in battle on the day of the Lord, crying with the Lawgiver: “Whoever is for the Lord, let him join me.”

Finally, because your praiseworthy friendship declares that, as it was once faithful, pleasant, and humbly obedient to me, so it will always persevere in the same way, I render you the thanks due to you; and if I may be needed by you in anything, I freely offer myself to your need. In return for your affection, although I have written this letter to you especially, [Col. 1338D] nevertheless, if you wish to read it before all the brethren, it is quite agreeable to me. I entrust only this to your discernment: that you understand simply, and, by understanding, prudently distinguish on whose account the complaint written above has been issued by me. And, as at the beginning of this letter, so also at its end, through you I again wish salvation to all our lords and dearest brethren. Farewell; may they also fare well. On bended knees I humbly beg that they may deign to entreat almighty God for me, their servant.

## In the Year of the Lord 1130: Domnizo, Priest and Monk of Canossa

[Col. 1339]

## Historical Notice

*(FABRICIUS, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis, II, 55.)*

Domnizo—otherwise Donizo or Donnizo—a priest and monk of Canossa of the Order of St Benedict, wrote in two books, in hexameter verse and for the greater part leonine verse, the *Life of Countess Matilda*, the most celebrated ruler of Italy, who died in the year of Christ 1115. It was first published by Sebastian Tegnagel in his collection of ancient monuments, Ingolstadt, 1612, quarto; then, more correctly from a Roman manuscript, in vol. I of G. G. Leibniz’s *Brunswick Writers*, p. 629; and finally, more carefully corrected from the Padolirone and Reggio manuscripts and enriched with many verses, with the notes of the aforesaid Leibniz and of the most distinguished Muratori, in vol. V of the *Thesaurus of Milanese Writers on Italy*, p. 335.

Vossius, p. 773, has already observed that Domnizo was himself present at most of the events which he records, and that he favoured the papal party zealously against Emperor Henry IV. No one, however, has yet produced the prose work of Domnizo mentioned by Sandius, in which he treats of the chastity and other virtues of Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, as well as certain of the same matters found in the metrical *Life of Matilda*.

[Leibniz first published Domnizo’s history written in prose from the Lucca manuscript of Francesco Maria Fiorentini; Muratori subsequently published it from that source in *Rerum Italicarum*, vol. V, p. 389. There occur there all those matters concerning the virtues and chastity of Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, which Sandius here noted in Fabricius. This, therefore, is the history written in prose, not by Domnizo himself but by some other author. Thus Fabricius has no reason to say that no one mentions that prose work of Domnizo: it has not been mentioned as composed by Domnizo, but, as drawn from Domnizo, it is very well known. —MANSI.]

[Col. 1339]

## Domnizo’s *Life of Countess Matilda*

*(See Patrology, vol. CXLVIII, in the appendix to Gregory VII.)*

## In the Year of the Lord 1130: Abbaud, Abbot

[Col. 1339]

## Notice

*(FABRICIUS, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis, I, 1.)*

Around the year 1130 Abbaud, an abbot otherwise unknown, published a brief treatise *On the Breaking of Christ’s Body* against Peter Abelard.

[Col. 1341]

# Treatise of Lord Abbaud, Abbot, on the Breaking of Christ’s Body

*(MABILLON, New Edition of the Analects, p. 52.)*

## Prefatory Notice

After Berengar’s heresy had been condemned, questions and controversies concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist arose, even among Catholics, from the formula of confession proposed to him by the Church at the Roman council, concerning the sense of the words in which that formula was framed. One question concerned the breaking of Christ’s body. Some maintained that this breaking took place only in the sign or symbol, not in Christ’s body itself; others, by contrast, contended that it occurred in the body itself, on account of the words of Berengar’s first confession, which anathematized as heresy the claim that Christ’s body could not sensibly be handled by priests’ hands, broken, or ground by the teeth of the faithful, except in the sacrament alone.

The authors of the first opinion asserted that after the conversion of the substance, the appearances or accidents of bread—wherein the breaking occurred—remained in the Eucharist. Others denied this, judging, as Abbaud says here, that whiteness or roundness cannot be separated from the body itself, which is white or round.

Among the former, Peter Abelard was not the least. Walter, abbot of St Victor’s at Paris, attacked him under this description as a heretic. Four books by that author survive in a Victorine manuscript against the four “labyrinths” of France—as he himself calls them—namely Abelard, Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert of Poitiers. Thus, in book III, chapter 11, speaking against Abelard:

> At last he comes to Berengar. For this heretic maintained that everything occurred in figure and sacrament, and nothing in reality. But afterwards, convicted before Pope Nicholas and many bishops, he confessed and even swore that bread and wine after consecration are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of Christ; and that they are sensibly handled by priests’ hands, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful, not only in the sacrament but also in reality. Behold the Catholic faith. But this schoolman explains it thus: “It is indeed truly so,” he says, “but only in the sacrament” [that is, the breaking, below]. Again he says: “That breaking and division may certainly be said to occur, not in the substance of the body, but in the sacramental form of bread itself, so that the breaking and division is truly such for it, since it occurs not in the substance but in the sacrament, that is, in the appearance.” Again: “There is there a true division [breaking?] and partition which occurs in the bread, that is, in the form of bread.” Again: “The breaking and those parts which are seen to occur there occur in the sacrament, that is, in the visible appearance. Therefore Berengar’s words must be distinguished thus: Christ’s body is said to be sensibly handled by priests’ hands, and also broken and ground by teeth, not merely in the sacrament but in reality. It is indeed truly so, but only in the sacrament. Therefore there is there a true grinding and division.” Behold: while he distinguishes by his customary argumentations the Catholic faith, which requires no distinction whatever, he proves himself another Berengar. For just as the latter asserted, “Everything occurs, but only in the sacrament,” so does this man. Berengar, however, when corrected, added to the sacrament and the breaking, and also to the grinding by teeth, the reality which he denied; this man, on the contrary, removes reality from all these things when he asserts that everything takes place not in the substance but in the visible appearance, the form of bread, and the sacrament alone.

Walter’s accusation against Abelard is not, however, fair at this point. Abelard admitted the true body of Christ in the Eucharist, but maintained that the breaking and grinding occurred not in the body itself but in the appearance of bread.

Abbaud the abbot agrees with Walter’s opinion concerning the real breaking of Christ’s body in this treatise, which we have excerpted from a manuscript containing the sermons of Abbot Christian. Christian seems to me to have been abbot of the monastery of St Peter at Chartres; but of what place Abbaud was abbot has not yet become known to me, although he lived in the same century as Abelard, namely the eleventh.

[Col. 1341A] The Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was handed over, took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat. This is my body, which shall be delivered up for you.” I therefore believe that the bread which he took he made his body by blessing it. Accordingly, he broke his body; and concerning that same body of his, now blessed and broken, he said to his disciples: “This is my body.” Nor do I believe less firmly that he broke it than that he blessed it, gave it to his disciples, or finally said, “This is my body.”

But perhaps someone says that the Lord’s body could then truly be broken because it was still mortal; [Col. 1342A] now it cannot be broken because it is already immortal. What then is the meaning of the Apostle Paul’s saying: “The bread which we break, is it not a sharing in the body of the Lord?” Perhaps someone is troubled because he did not say, “The body which we break,” but “the bread which we break.” Consider what he says elsewhere: “Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup”; yet no Christian doubts that he there speaks of the body and blood of Christ. For Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were persevering in the teaching of the apostles and in the communion of the breaking of bread.” [Col. 1343A]

Pay attention, I beg you. Certainly the same bread is blessed, received, and distributed. Yet the Apostle preferred to say, “The bread which we break,” rather than “the bread which we bless,” receive, or distribute. Moreover, since the same bread is daily offered to God for the salvation of the whole world, why did he not at least say “the bread which we offer,” rather than “the bread which we break,” when he could certainly have said this most appropriately? And why likewise did the Evangelist not use “bread of blessing,” “bread of communion,” “bread of distribution,” or at least “bread of offering,” rather than “bread of breaking”? Surely apostolic and evangelical speech, by its authority, strengthened precisely that point concerning which it was apparent that doubt could arise more readily; perhaps, indeed, because this expression also more fittingly accorded with the mystery.

[Col. 1343B] For the very Wisdom of God, which assumed to itself in unity of person the animate body of which we speak, although it remains wholly unimpaired in itself, is nevertheless broken for us when it is expounded; and we, by sharing spiritually in it, truly live to God. Conversely, Jeremiah laments the failure of teachers: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

But it is one thing when the truth of an event is investigated according to the literal character of the deed; another when the mystical rationale of the same event is examined allegorically. For example, we read in the Gospel that after the resurrection the Lord entered to his disciples while the doors were shut. First, according to the literal character of the event, one asks how that was a true body which entered to the disciples through closed doors. Then follows the mystical rationale of the same event: namely, unless the garden has been enclosed, the bride vainly entreats the bridegroom, “Let my beloved come into his garden.” Or, to speak more plainly and briefly: unless the doors of your heart have been shut against the desires of the world, spiritual grace cannot enlighten you. [Col. 1343C]

But here, where we are treating the literal character, we have interwoven the spiritual rationale, because we understand that the Wisdom of God, which orders all things sweetly, fittingly disposes bodily events according to the pattern of spiritual things. The Psalmist also testifies: “You have made all things in wisdom.” Therefore, supported by the spiritual rationale and according to the faith of the Gospel, which says, “He blessed and broke,” and also of the Apostle, who says, “The bread which we break,” and of Luke the Evangelist, who says, “Bread of breaking,” [Col. 1343D] I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth unto salvation that the body of Christ is truly broken by the priest’s hands.

Perhaps I am here mocked by those who know that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, not half or maimed, but wholly intact. As though the Apostle, when he said, “The bread which we break is a sharing in the body of the Lord,” had forgotten him of whom he so often reminded us that he sits at the right hand of the Father; or had forgotten him of whom he declared with such constancy that, having risen from the dead, he dies no more and death no longer has dominion over him. How then is it asked of one and the same body that it remains whole in heaven and is broken on earth? [Col. 1344A]

Here especially appears what I said above: the Apostle and the Evangelist particularly employed the word “breaking” so that by their authority that point might be established concerning which the human heart would more easily doubt. For the assertion seems very contrary to itself when it is proclaimed concerning one and the same body that it remains whole and is broken. But human insufficiency does not suffer these straits; human weakness cannot set limits to divine power, even if rashness attempts it. For what is impossible with human beings is possible with God.

Otherwise, is this alone asserted concerning Christ’s body that is contrary to human reason and impossible according to the law of human bodies? Is it not also asserted concerning that same body that, through the mystery of his birth, it came forth to human sight from the Virgin’s closed womb, and that, through the resurrection, it entered to his disciples through closed doors; and that he showed himself both tangible and yet incorruptible? Here are three things, so that this may not now be the sole but the fourth of things which reason does not comprehend, though faith grants them to divine power. [Col. 1344B]

Let each of the others, indeed, see what he thinks. But for myself, I consider it pious and good to believe that that body, which the great and utterly incomprehensible sublimity of the Deity willed to be its own, surpasses by a certain ineffable, singular, and divine power not merely mortal but even immortal and heavenly bodies by an immense distance. Besides, to wish to reason about that body according to the law governing other [Col. 1344C] bodies is to seek the living among the dead. Let the human being, then, who is not able to investigate and enumerate the weaknesses of his own body, cease to think lofty thoughts about God’s body; let him learn to agree with the humble. Let him remember that a certain wise man, speaking of God, said: “Do not be curious about too many of his works.”

Yet let us suppose someone grants that Christ’s body is not truly broken, and let us see what fruit follows from this. Tell me, I beg you: how can I know that the Evangelist speaks truly when he says, “This is my body,” if he deceived us when he said, “He broke”? Likewise, if the Apostle lies when he says, “The bread which we break,” how shall I believe that he speaks truth when he continues, “is a sharing in the body of Christ”? [Col. 1344D] Thus, whoever does not grant that Christ’s body is truly broken has, so far as lies in him, broken the whole faith of so great a sacrament. But far be it that the Evangelist and the Apostle should be thought false; far be it that every word should be thought impossible with God!

Someone may say that not everything is to be ascribed to divine power; many matters must be investigated with the sharpness of reason. I, with the Apostle, now know in part, awaiting the time when I come into Galilee and there see him face to face. Yet, if anyone does not disdain the humble counsel of a little man, let him in no way investigate this mystery of the divine body by reason, but believe the evangelical authority without doubt. The Lord “has hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.” “Turn your eyes away from me,” he says; “they have made me flee away.” [Col. 1345A]

I too once thought, when I was little, that no understanding could ever attain, even in however small a degree, how earthly bread could be changed into Christ’s body. I had resolved that it must only be believed most firmly on divine authority and not investigated at all. But afterwards my God enlightened my darkness, so that I saw—although through a mirror and in an enigma—that which, before seeing it, I had believed most firmly. For the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” So also concerning the matter now in our hands, I do not see how one and the same body can both be broken and remain whole; nevertheless, I believe it with absolute certainty. For God is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, so that what I do not see and yet believe, I may one day see and rejoice in. For blessed are those who have not seen and have believed. [Col. 1345B]

Yet, lest the troublesome and violent discord of these apparent contradictions, when one and the same body is affirmed both to be broken and to remain whole, lead anyone into unbelief, and lest he suppose that nothing of the kind can be found in Scripture, let him consider what is written in Luke’s Gospel. Jesus says: “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” And immediately the Evangelist says: “They laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.” See what a contradiction this is. For if, according to Jesus, she was not dead, how did they know that she was dead? If they thought her dead when she was not, surely to think is one thing and to know another. But if they held it certain that she who lived was dead, this was error, not knowledge. Thus either she was dead, and Truth spoke contrary to truth when it said, “She is not dead”; or Truth spoke truly and the Evangelist falsely when he said, “knowing that she was dead.” But neither conclusion is admissible. [Col. 1345C]

Certainly, there is a greater contradiction in someone’s being both dead and not dead than in something’s being broken and remaining whole. For it is much easier to restore what has been broken than to raise the dead. The former is sometimes done by a human being; the latter is always the work of God alone.

We must therefore have recourse to another passage of the Gospel, where the Lord, speaking of the dead, says: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living; for all live to him.” Observe that he did not say simply “they live,” but “they live to him”: that is, he does not deny that they are dead to human beings, but denies it to God. For eternity—to which things future are things already done, and to which the consummation of all things is already known—when it wills, speaks of things not according to that instability which they now suffer by their natural mutability, but according to the state which they shall eternally receive from the immutability of their Creator. Therefore it is rightly said of the dead—if indeed they are to live eternally with God after the resurrection—“All live to him,” because that state of immortality awaits them immutably, whereas death, which now holds them temporarily, will one day cease to be. [Col. 1345D]

And he rightly denies that the girl is dead, since he intended not to abandon her to death but restore her to life—he who made all things at once, though the nature of time does not permit them to occur all at once. [Col. 1346A] Consider, therefore, whether in the same way it may be said that what is broken for us remains whole for God. He who spoke concerning the bodies of his servants, saying, “All the hairs of your head are numbered,” and “not a hair of your head shall perish,” although according to us nearly all hairs have perished—would it be surprising if, with him, any particle, however tiny, of his own body could perish, even though the same body is divided into many parts by being broken and is eaten by many?

Therefore his body is always whole to him whose providence permits no particle of it to perish. With us, local division is proof of breaking, because we consider a limb broken when we see it severed from itself and divided in place. But with God, just as it is truly said, “With respect to time, a thousand years are as one day, and one day as a thousand years,” so it may equally truly be said, with respect to place: a thousand places, however many places one wishes, or indeed all places, are with God as one place. For to him who is always wholly present everywhere, local absence cannot make anything absent; local distance cannot make anything distant; local division cannot divide anything. [Col. 1346B]

Therefore, what is broken with us because it is locally divided remains whole with God, to whom all places are one place. Since this can be said even of other corporeal things, how much more of that body which is personally united to that substance which is always wholly present everywhere? For that reason alone, it may not altogether implausibly be maintained that it remains whole even when broken, because in a wonderful and [Col. 1346C] ineffable manner it has become one with that substance and remains one with it even at the very time of its breaking; that substance receives no breaking in any way and always remains wholly unimpaired—namely, the Deity itself, ever unbroken and undivided.

This can be maintained for another reason also. Among us, a limb which is broken and divided from its body is certainly dead. But every particle of that body, even when broken, is not merely alive but is life itself, if anyone receives it faithfully. Therefore, what retains the power—and more than the power—of something whole even when it is broken may rightly be called whole. [Col. 1346D] Yet I do not say these things as though so great a mystery had been revealed through me or so great a question solved.
