I have done only this: that the assertion of both breaking and wholeness may not be judged wholly absurd. Let better persons speak better on this point, and more learned persons more learnedly. Would that I might hear from someone the most certain explanation of so great a mystery!

Above, indeed, we defended the breaking of the Lord’s body on evangelical and apostolic authority; meanwhile we omitted the testimony of our eyes. For truly the truth of the Gospel is a more certain testimony than the sight of our eyes. We more readily grant that our eyes may deceive us than that the Gospel may lie. Yet our Lord Jesus Christ himself, when blessed Thomas doubted his resurrection, satisfied him not so much by prophetic testimonies as by the evidence of his own eyes. Therefore, the testimony of our eyes does not seem to me wholly to be despised. [Col. 1347A]

The man who denies that the Lord’s body is broken must therefore be pressed to say whether he believes that what we consecrate and break on the altar is Christ’s body. If he grants it, he does not deny the breaking of Christ’s body. If he denies it, let every faithful person judge whether he ought to be judged faithful; let that man himself see whom he wishes to believe, since he believes neither evangelical authority nor his own eyes. But let us, with the disciples, recognize the Lord in the breaking of bread.

I had considered answering also those who say that the body itself is not broken, but that something is done in its whiteness and roundness. But, reflecting that it is foolish to dispute about whiteness and roundness in Christ’s Gospel, I have put away ears that love such things and left such matters to dialecticians—or [Col. 1348A] indeed to children—especially since anyone can easily see that whiteness or roundness cannot be separated from the body itself, which is white or round, so that these things cannot separately and individually be broken unless that body itself is broken. And truly, what need has any faithful person, in this matter of faith, for such circumlocution of words? Let each person simply and plainly profess whether he believes that Christ’s body is truly broken by priests’ hands or not.

I ask, indeed, that no one judge me presumptuous because I, a very small man, have presumed to write about so great a matter. Since I have been thought not to believe rightly, I could not fail to defend my faith in whatever small discourse I could compose.

## In the Year of the Lord 1130: Bruno, Bishop of Strasbourg

[Col. 1347]

## Notice

*(Gallia Christiana, new edition, V, 797.)*

[Col. 1347B] Bruno, formerly provost of Honau, in which office he established the sale of wine in 1104, was afterwards elected bishop of Strasbourg in 1123, having previously been a canon of the Church of Bamberg, in place of the deposed Cuno, according to the archive of the canons of Honau. In 1125 he subscribed a charter of Emperor Henry V, perhaps for Lure, for B., bishop of Strasbourg, is recorded as subscriber to the same emperor’s charter for Lure, dated 5 Kalends of July, year 1123, indiction XIII; where 1125, indiction III, should be read.

Certainly, in that year, on the fifth or sixth day before the Kalends of January, he subscribed at Strasbourg to the privilege which Emperor Henry granted to the monastery of St Blasien. In the following year, 1126, Bruno and Eberhard, who succeeded Bruno, contended for the bishopric of Strasbourg, according to the charter concerning the foundation and dedication of the monastery of St John near Tabernas in the diocese of Strasbourg. Bruno, for an uncertain reason, was deposed, and Eberhard was put in his place by Emperor Lothair.

[Col. 1347]

# Letter of Bruno to Gerhoh, Provost

*(R. P. Bernard PEZ, New Treasury of Anecdotes, vol. I, part II, p. 221.)*

[Col. 1347C] To Lord G., provost, a religious and learned man: B., a sinner, may you eat of the hidden manna.

Amid the heavy pressures and various tumults of a world collapsing and rolling its lovers along with itself, I have examined your writings as far as I could. I have observed your zeal, your studies, [Col. 1348C] your struggle, and your learning; and I have judged that what the queen of the South said concerning King Solomon ought truly and confidently to be declared concerning you: namely, that the report which speaks of your praises is less than the treasure of wisdom which reveals itself to one who approaches more closely and digs more deeply. [Col. 1349A]

John the Baptist knew and pointed out the Lamb of God in one respect, and in another respect did not know what he was to recognize through the dove descending and remaining upon him. Certainly something of this kind has happened to me concerning you: I knew you, but neither as such a man nor in your entirety. Therefore, having tasted your writings, though hurriedly and only on the surface, I earnestly and with ardent desire long that the favour of your writings and likewise your most sweet presence may be granted to me, so that matters which are closed or seem to present a question may be opened, as it were with certain keys, through mutual conference and friendly conversation. May almighty God, mindful of us, preserve for a long age your safety and that of all who dwell with you in Christ.

## In the Year of the Lord 1131: Frederick of Cologne

[Col. 1349]

# Letters and Diplomas of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne

*(D. MARTENE, Amplissima Collectio, I, 661, 674, 681.)*

I. Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the clergy of Liège.—He rebukes them because, in a hasty election, even admitting excommunicated persons to their assembly, they cast their votes for Alexander; he summons them before his tribunal at the monastery of Inda. (Year 1121.)

[From the manuscript of St Lawrence at Liège.]

[Col. 1349B]

F., by the grace of God humble minister of the holy Church of Cologne, to the entire clergy at Liège: search the testimonies of the Lord, that with their whole heart they may seek him.

We received your letter, sent to us through Brother Nicholas, with paternal affection. In it you appear both to desire our presence and, like sons of obedience, to offer yourselves to be corrected by our counsel if in any matter you have exceeded the bounds of your own judgment. We wish you to know one thing: we would have been ready to come down to you and to provide for you with due fatherly care, had we not perceived your offences to be so manifest, so contrary to the decrees of the holy canons, to our authority, and to your own salvation.

For, when your bishop Lord Frederick, of blessed memory, died, we sent you letters of consolation, lamenting your desolation with paternal tears and earnestly exhorting you to fix your hope upon the Lord’s consolation. But because at that time we were occupied with weighty affairs of Church and Empire, we admonished you by our proper authority to postpone your election until you could have our counsel and until our return; for we wished to make provision for your weakness, for temporal peace, and nevertheless for a canonical election.

But meanwhile, refusing to comply with divine ordinance and with our admonition, you admitted into your assembly a multitude of those who, at your request, were held excommunicated by the lord pope, by us, and even by your own bishop. There, prejudicing our authority, taking counsel with excommunicated persons, and rebuilding what you had destroyed, you made yourselves—what we cannot say without deep grief—transgressors, defiled by fellowship with the excommunicated.

We have indeed clear proof of this wretched fault: your letters sent both to the Church of Cologne and to your venerable son Andrew.

> [Note: Andrew, the provost major, later became bishop of Maastricht.]

In these letters you stated, quite rashly, that you had received Alexander as your lord and bishop; and, to crown your inexcusable conduct, you added in a conspiratorial compact that you neither wished nor were able to accept any counsel against him.

> [Note: This Alexander, as we have seen above, had wished, after Otbert’s death, to obtain the bishopric by money. After St Frederick had been killed by poison, he sought it again; but God, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, raised not the ambitious Alexander but the humble Albero, primicerius of Metz and brother of Duke Godfrey of Louvain, to the see of Liège.]

But if you have conspired in this matter, why is our coming down to you, or the presence of our counsel, requested? Why is obedience to us so frequently and insistently promised by your mouths and writings, when it is destroyed by the insolence of this conspiracy, fixed in your hearts, as you assert?

We marvel—and not a little—at your calling yourselves in writing the whole Church of Liège. For, to say nothing of the archbishop’s dignity by which we ought to be a more eminent member of the Church of Liège, the charity of our brotherhood, which until now has shared and been companion to your tribulations, appears contemptuously repudiated. And if it is again the Church, why do you exclude her whom alone we recognize and confess to be the Church of Liège: Provost Andrew; the archdeacons Henry and Steppo; Master Stephen; and the religious abbots Ralph of St Trond and Heribrand of St Lawrence at Liège; and others who, although separated by differences of place, are nevertheless your brethren in unity of spirit?

> [Note: Brusthem must here be corrected: he numbers Archdeacon Henry and Reppo, or Steppo, among Alexander’s faithless supporters. Perhaps Emmo should be read in place of Henry; Emmo is there placed among Frederick’s adherents.]

> [Note: Ralph of St Trond and Heribrand of St Lawrence at Liège.]

These are beyond doubt testified to be the Church of Liège by the obedience of good simplicity, and by the persecution which they have suffered and daily suffer for righteousness’ sake.

Nor can we pass over this: contrary to the statutes of the holy canons, with the chrism and oil of the present year neglected—indeed despised—and with old oil kept back for many years, anointings are still being performed in certain of your archdeaconries by priests, contrary to the canons and to our authority; for through disobedience they presume to celebrate divine offices with excommunicated persons.

It would take long to enumerate how many and how great offences have provoked the Lord’s forbearance, and how presumptuously you have acted against our authority. For you have not only estranged yourselves from the Church of God, but have also drawn into partnership in your transgression those who had until now remained sincerely with us. Therefore, since fatherly visitation of consolation is not owed for offences so manifest and hateful to God, but rather the rebuke of fitting severity must be applied, we summon you to the see of Cologne, against which you have inflicted so grave a prejudice. If, as you have written, you wish to correct your offences by our counsel, then, following the example of the evangelical Father, we shall gladly receive the offspring that had perished, under the witness of both Churches, namely the Church of Cologne and the Church of Liège which is with us.

Nevertheless, out of abundant consideration, if this humility of yours requires it, we shall meet you at St Cornelius at Inde on the fourth day before the Nones of September [2 September], together with the sons of the aforesaid Churches, prepared mercifully to receive those who have been corrected in a spirit of gentleness and to instruct them.

> [Note: A monastery of the Order of St Benedict, two hours from Aachen, founded by Benedict of Aniane, confessor of Emperor Louis the Pious; the head of Pope St Cornelius is believed to be kept there.]

And since Alexander, through Godescalc, a cleric of Maastricht, in the presence of the Church professed obedience and submission to us, and through the same man informed us that he wished to submit to our counsel concerning all his offences, we sent him word that we would remain in the aforesaid monastery on the third day before the Nones of September [3 September], so that, should he perhaps wish reasonably to submit anything, he might be heard by the ears of the Church.

But if any among you has zeal for the Lord, let him not fail to admonish, rebuke, reprove, entreat, and pray for him, that he may mercifully spare himself and the Church of Christ, lest he begin to be held infamous—he who has so often been expelled from the thresholds of holy Mother Church by the apostolic lord, by us, and by his own bishop. For repeated rejections make his person infamous and thus notorious to the Church, so that he not only fails to attain what he wickedly seeks, but also incurs danger to his rank and order—things which the gentleness of the Church still tolerates him to retain out of the affection of maternal mercy.

We write these things to you, dearest brethren, in a spirit of charity, not in order to shame you, but, as we stated in our earlier letters, in order to bring you—who need consolation in both spiritual and temporal peace—back to the bosom of the Church’s unity.

## II. Diploma of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, for New Corvey

He confirms for it the tithes from demesne holdings in his episcopate, granted long ago in a solemn council in the time of Emperor Arnulf. (A.D. 1120.)

[From a manuscript of New Corvey.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be known to the faithful of both the present and future age that the venerable Erckenbert, abbot of Corvey, because of a recently arisen harassment by certain persons directed against himself and his monastery, sought our protection. He asked that we grant him a privilege confirming the tithes which, from ancient times, are paid to his monastery from demesne holdings in our bishopric, according to the consent and subscription of Willibert, Archbishop of Cologne, and of the nineteen bishops who had assembled in a synod in the time of Emperor Arnulf, and according to the concession of all his successors.

> [Note: At the national synod of Mainz in 888 it was decreed that churches established in antiquity were not to be deprived of tithes or other possessions and that these were not to be assigned to new oratories. At that synod the privileges of Corvey and Herford were confirmed by a solemn decree, subscribed by nineteen bishops together with Willibert of Cologne. Since their names have not been found either by Labbe and Cossart in the General Councils, or by Sirmond, Serrarius, and others, we produce them here from the decree published in the *Annals of Paderborn*: Fulco of Reims; Willibert of Cologne; Thiadmar of Salzburg; Redbodo of Trier; John, Archbishop of Rouen; Hildegrim, Bishop of Halberstadt; Adalcar, Archbishop of Hamburg; Arn[?], of Würzburg; Liaward of Vercelli; Rodbert of Metz; Adalhelm of Worms; Godethaneus of Speyer; Wicbert of Hildesheim; Deth[?] of Verdun; Dodilo of Cambrai; Honoratus of Beauvais; Herdilo of Noyon; Balthramnus of Strasbourg; Waldo of Freising; and Thiadulphus, Bishop of Chur.]

To his reasonable petition I, Frederick, by God’s grace Archbishop of Cologne, gave my consent, as pious as it was just; and I ordered this charter of our authority to be made for him, both to renew and to strengthen the enactments of earlier authorities. In it I decreed valid not only the subscription of the aforesaid archbishop and of the other archbishops assembled in the aforementioned synod, but also the concession of all my predecessors. I acknowledge and permit to that Church the tithes which it possessed in the bishopric of Cologne before our time—especially those which it is known to have held from its demesne at Lachem, whether on the Rhine or in other demesne holdings—concerning which it complained that an unjust and unprecedented objection had been raised against it.

That greater faith and reverence may be shown to this decree of our authority, and that it may more effectively support the defence of those to whom it is entrusted, we have added inviolable force both by the impression of our seal and by the terrible sanction of our ban. We further establish and decree, by the power and in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that this present testament shall remain unchangeable and inviolate throughout all ages: striking its violators, unless they repent, with the severity of anathema and eternal curse, while promising its guardians and defenders the sure hope of everlasting reward.

Done and confirmed in the famous court and assembly of Goslar, in the year of the singular Nativity 1120, in the seventh indiction, during the reign of Henry V, August Emperor of the Romans; in the pontificate of Lord Calixtus; in the nineteenth year of our episcopate; and while the most reverend Abbot Erckenbert happily guided the chariot of the Church of Corvey.

## III. Diploma of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, for the Monastery of Grafschaft

(From the autograph.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. FREDERICK, by the favouring mercy of God Archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne.

We are admonished by the authority of the Holy Scriptures and instructed by the examples of our predecessors, the archbishops of this holy see of Cologne, to visit with the hand of charity the places of saints and monasteries of brethren, so that, building something upon the pious foundation of our predecessors, we may be found sharers in their reward with the supreme Shepherd.

With this purpose, visiting the monastery of Grafschaft, founded by Lord Anno, archbishop of blessed memory, we have bestowed certain of our possessions for the use of the brethren of the aforesaid church, hoping to obtain with him, the founder of that place, a portion in the land of the living.

Accordingly, when a certain man named Jalen, within the bounds of our court at Badelich, had sold his allod to Abbot Wichbert of the aforesaid monastery, we confirmed that same allod to St Alexander—that is, to the monastery of Grafschaft, founded in honour of St Alexander—adding to the church whatever the aforesaid Jelen had held by our right in common enjoyment with all those dwelling under our jurisdiction.

Furthermore, since the aforesaid church possessed three and a half pounds from the tithe of Soest by the gift of our venerable predecessor Lord Anno, and the unjust violence of estate-stewards had usurped the lease of that same tithe, we restored the lease to it and confirmed by our proper authority that it should not thereafter be deprived of it.

We likewise restored to that church the tithe of the vineyard of Thielbach, which our predecessor Lord Sigewin had bestowed upon the church of Grafschaft as part of its endowment on the day of its consecration, but which had been alienated from the church by the stewards of Bacharach. We established by like authority that the vineyard or its tithe should be preserved for the brethren in perpetual freedom.

And so that the aforesaid church of Grafschaft may possess without any disturbance these things written above, and also those things which the ever-memorable generosity of Lord Anno bestowed upon it, we have confirmed them by the power granted to Blessed Peter and by the authority of our ban. To their guardians we promise joys which eye has not seen nor ear heard; but we threaten unjust claimants and invaders with the punishments of Gehenna, where their worm does not die and their fire is not extinguished.

And so that this confirmation of our grant may pass down to posterity unshaken in remembrance, we strengthen it by the attestation of this privilege and the impression of our seal. We also set down the rights and possessions which Lord Anno of pious memory bestowed upon the same church, and these likewise we confirm by the authority already stated.

This confirmation was made at Cologne, in the presence and with the assent of many faithful servants of Blessed Peter and honourable persons, whose names we have judged worthy to be recorded as testimony to this confirmation:

Provosts: Henry of the House of St Peter—that is, the cathedral church dedicated to St Peter, still called in French *le Dôme*—Ekkebert, dean of the same place; Godfrey of St Severin; Henry of the Holy Apostles; and Theoderic of St Mary in the Steps.

Abbots: Gerard of St Pantaleon; Alban of St Martin; Rupert of Deutz; and Cuno of Siegburg.

> [Note: From this you may correct Bucelinus in *Germania Sacra*, who assigns the beginning of Gerard’s administration as abbot of St Pantaleon to 1138. Since Archbishop Frederick, author of this diploma, died in 1131, the beginning of Gerard’s abbatial dignity must necessarily be placed earlier.]

Free men: Hermann, advocate of the same church, and his son Gerard; Thietmar; Gerard, Count of Jülich; and Engelbert of Kent.

Ministerials of St Peter: Hermann, advocate of St Peter; Almar; Henry of Aldentorph; and many others.

These, moreover, are the possessions conferred upon the monastery of Grafschaft by its generous founder, Lord Anno: the church of Worumbach, etc.

## IV. Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the Milanese

He exhorts them to resist the enemies of the Church.

(From a manuscript of St-Germain-des-Prés.)

To the consuls, captains, all the militia, and the whole people of Milan: FREDERICK, by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Cologne, [wishes you] to act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.

Great and exceedingly praiseworthy is the Lord in this City of God, which is adorned with glorious liberty and therefore founded in the exultation of the whole earth, while it disdains to be cast down by any unjust powers. Therefore, since glorious things of you are spoken throughout the whole world, illustrious City of God, preserve your liberty, so that you may likewise retain the dignity of this name. For as long as you strive to resist powers hostile to the Church, you shall enjoy true liberty, Christ the Lord, its author, helping you.

Let, therefore, the praiseworthy justice and the dignity of your name handed down from your fathers to us strengthen your constancy, beloved friends, together with the unanimous applause of us all and of all honourable men. For all of us who are princes of Lotharingia, Saxony, Thuringia—indeed, of all Gaul—are united in affection toward you. Just as we are joined in one body of the realm, so we shall always be found ready to live with you in the same justice and the same liberty of laws.

Moreover, should you require our help or counsel, let the prudence of your judgment determine how you wish it to be done; our diligence will be found most ready to carry it out. Therefore, whatever pleases you collectively, we desire to be informed of in writing—not because we distrust you, but because we wish to rejoice in your replies, so that what cannot be done by bodily presence at this time may at least be afforded us through the service of your letter, whose office it is to make absent persons, as it were, present and to unite among friends conversations both sweet and confidential. Farewell. Strengthen in the Lord the other cities which are with you.

## V. Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the Church of Liège

He directs that they are not to receive, in the see of Liège, a man intruded through simony by royal nomination.

(From a manuscript of St Trond.)

F., by God’s grace humble minister of the holy Church of Cologne, to the archdeacons, provosts, deans, scholastics, cantors, and all Catholics of the Church of Liège: never to turn aside from the holy purpose on account of any necessity.

By evangelical authority, scandals must come, so that, when the son of perdition is revealed, all who have been predestined to the lot of heavenly recompense may be made manifest and proved. Therefore, forewarning your brotherhood, we admonish, entreat, and command you, under the obligation of holy obedience, that you do not receive `[lacuna]`, who comes to you under the title of bishop-designate by the violence of royal intrusion. For by his rash invasion he deprived our see, so far as lay in him, of its archiepiscopal honour; and he despised you, upon whom he wished to be imposed without canonical election. Nor did he fear, through simoniacal ambition, to forestall the truce of your election fixed for the named day, which both your Church had requested and the authority of our see had granted.

Accordingly, being ready to punish every disobedience, we have prepared against him and against all his followers, or those communicating with him, a sentence of anathema, from which we desire the obedience of your brotherhood to be delivered.

## VI. Form Letters of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne

(*Spicilegium*, III, 474.)

To the most reverend BRUNO, most sincere in the worship and life-giving devotion of religion, Archbishop of the holy Church of Trier: FREDERICK, humble servant in CHRIST of the venerable Church of Cologne and of its people, [wishes him] abiding glory with the joy of prosperity and everlastingness in Christ, Prince of shepherds.

> [Note: “Most reverend.” In this letter the numerical signs customarily appended at the end are not found, doubtless through the ignorance of the copyist. For there is a twofold order of numerals in ancient formulae of letters of this kind, as appears from examples reported by Sirmond in vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*. The first expresses the letters of the Greek-written word ΑΜΗΝ, “Amen.” The second order gives the sum of the numerical values, both common and proper, of each form letter. Both orders appear corrupted in Frederick’s letter, as do also the five Greek characters appended in final order in the copy, which we cannot reproduce here owing to the lack of suitable type. They were, first, a double mark—the one called by the ancients *ennacos*, indicating the number nine hundred—then the letters T, Π, and Σ, or C, for thus it was anciently written. Yet, according to the rules for form letters, the following letters ought to have been subscribed: Φ, Ρ, Λ, Ο; namely Φ for the first letter of the writer Frederick, Ρ for the second letter of Bruno to whom the letter is written, Λ for the third letter of Baldwin the recipient, and Ο for the fourth letter of Cologne, from which it is written. If a fifth were to be used, it should have been Ε, for the fifth letter of Trier, to which it is written. To all these the indiction should have been added.]

Keeping the most salutary decrees of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, we canonically address your God-worthy and pious fatherhood, and reverently approach your holiness under the designation of a form letter. We inform you that we have given these letters dimissory to a certain present deacon of ours named BALDWIN, who, having been canonically brought up in your diocese, we have promoted from the order of clerics to the rank of deacon. Fortified by these canonical credentials and with our permission, he may dwell in your parish under the protection and governance of your dear charity. If uprightness of character and worthiness of learning are found in him, we faithfully consent that you promote him to the order of priesthood; and we commend him to you to be canonically cherished and guided in the bosom of holy Mother Church.

We have therefore determined to secure this letter on either side with Greek letters and judged that it should be sealed with the ring of our Church. May Christ, Prince of shepherds, deign long to preserve your brotherhood unharmed for the keeping of his flock. I XL VIII I. [DCCC DCCC, CCC].

# A.D. 1117. Richard, Abbot of Préaux

## Historical Notice concerning Richard

(Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXX, no. 11.)

Geoffrey, or Gaufredus, the fourth abbot, administered the monastery of Préaux for seven years. He caused the church of that place to be dedicated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [17 October], on which day the dedication of the church of St Peter of Préaux is noted in the old calendar. In the same calendar Gaufredus is said to have died on the third day before the Kalends of September [30 August], not of December as in *Neustria Pia*.

> [Note: Page 509.]

His successor Richard, a man of outstanding piety and learning by no means slight for his age, was called “of Furnells.” He had first been trained in monastic discipline and letters at the monastery of St Vigor in Bayeux, under Robert of Tombelaine, the last abbot of that place. When Odo, the bishop and founder of the monastery of St Vigor, was held in chains, Robert returned to Mont-Saint-Michel, of whose monastery he was a monk.

> [Note: Orderic, book II, p. 709.]

After Robert’s departure, that new community of monks, deprived of a ruler, was quickly scattered. Among them Richard, being eager to learn, sought learned and religious men in other monasteries: Anselm of Bec, Gerbert of Fontenelle, and Gontard of Jumièges, in whose company he lived for some time.

Finally, after the death of Gaufredus, abbot of Préaux, he was chosen to govern that abbey. He did not discontinue the study of sacred letters, as his various unprinted moral commentaries upon many books of Holy Scripture testify. He composed them amid the burdensome occupations of his office, and throughout them he repeatedly says that he finds relief in these studies. He had already spent twenty-eight years in those sacred studies when he dedicated his *Commentaries on Genesis* to Anselm, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, styling himself repeatedly “a servant of the Lord’s Cross.” Yet Orderic says that these commentaries—or perhaps a part of them—had been inscribed to Maurice, abbot of St Launomarus at Blois.

In that letter to Anselm he explains the aim of his studies in these words:

> “Moreover, the Lord knows the poverty of my knowledge. The witness of my conscience—or rather of my intention—speaks to him without pretence: I do not presume upon my own powers, nor do I expend labour to explain the intricate mysteries of the Mosaic law for the applause of mortals or the profit of passing reward. For in the beloved fellowship and companionable love of that law almost twenty-eight years have now passed, during which I have shut myself wholly within it. While I toil in pursuing its commandments, I find great rest; and whenever the prevailing importunity of worldly affairs frequently tears me away from its embraces, I undergo no small labour.”

He explains the same disposition of mind more fully in the prologue to his commentary on the Book of Numbers, published after his exposition of Deuteronomy. This prologue is addressed to Adelelm, a most learned priest, as Orderic testifies, and a monk of Flavigny, who, serving reverently with the monks of Holy Trinity at Fécamp, grew old among them.

> [Note: Ibid.]

Let readers permit us to reproduce here the beginning of that prologue, in order to illustrate the pious author whose works, in my opinion, will never come to light:

> “After the solicitude of pastoral care, after the noisy administration of public affairs, after the most troublesome altercation of a rustic multitude almost devoid of reason, I can scarcely revisit the inner chamber of my mind and weigh the loss of my life; nor do I find any escape anywhere. I complain and grieve deeply, son Adelelm, because where formerly I was accustomed to behold tranquillity of mind and the brightness of continual reading, there I am now compelled, without doubt, to endure in the depths of my heart a tumultuous crowd of thoughts and the dust of worldly dwelling. For he who searches the reins and hearts of all knows that I would rather bear the austerity of a subject than the staff of pastoral government,” etc.

As for Richard’s other commentaries, he dedicated the Proverbs of Solomon to Pontius, Abbot of Cluny, and his exposition of the Song of Songs to his son Maurice. In these and his other commentaries, moreover, he testifies that he suffered from censorious critics.

## Prologue of Richard on Leviticus, addressed to Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury

(About A.D. 1100.)

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 575, from a manuscript of St Vaast at Arras.)

Here begins the prologue to the Book of Leviticus, produced by a certain servant of the Lord’s Cross.

One of the inhabitants of the house of the children of Israel, to ANSELM, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury: [wishes him] to offer to the supreme priest a living, holy, rational sacrifice.

Since I do not doubt, most beloved and greatly venerable among the members of Christ, that diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit are active in you: first, because, placed amid the cares of ecclesiastical affairs, you devote yourself vigilantly to the search for wisdom not only in the daily hours but even in stolen hours of the night; and secondly, because you are able to set forth in eloquent speech, with eloquence at hand, what you understand in the law of the Lord. Likewise, because you wonderfully restrain the throng of the ignorant and unruly by the wall of your patience and remain unmoved under their importunate assaults.

Therefore, seeing such a prerogative of virtues implanted in you, I have decided to entrust to your judgment my exposition of the Book of Leviticus. Nor do I wish anyone to suppose that, in proclaiming your praises, I have indulged in rhetorical display and anointed your head with the oil of a sinner, so that I might gain you as protector and defender of my trifles more readily than some other advantage, as certain people think. If they do not believe my words, let them at least believe my deeds.

For if you are a true lover of divine wisdom, you will not know how to spare anyone whom you discover to be its destroyer. This thing becomes so much more hateful to me as I delight more fully to experience wisdom’s delightful embraces. Moreover, deeply dreading the mouths of those who speak wickedly—men who each compete rather to embrace the wasting of life in sleep than to endeavour to pursue the gain of most welcome labour in expounding the mysteries of the sacred Scriptures—I ask you, my lord, to read through this work with a wakeful mind; and whatever offends sound understanding, cut it away with the blade of catholic faith. And where anything is less than it ought to be, I ask again that you supply it as seems good to you. Thus may the hissing of certain persons afterward be restrained, their poisonous and gnawing tooth blunted, and this book, commended by your authority and by careful examination, be circulated more safely to the ears of many.

But if anyone should judge me presumptuous and undertaking a work beyond the strength of my intellect, I entirely deny the one charge but confess the other to be in me. Yet, because very many maintain that I have fallen into the fault of presumption by undertaking to explain the text of Leviticus and to produce with an abundant pen a lengthy work, let the venomous tongue at last grow weary, and rather turn back the weapons forged upon the anvil of envy against an archbishop and a multitude of religious persons whom the gift of divine grace has willed to set over the children of the heavenly Jerusalem. For I obeyed their commands.

With a running, commentarial pen I completed the entire work in seventeen books. The testimonies of Scripture with which I had often sought to surround the things I wrote at dictation, I endeavoured, according to my custom and as the simple multitude of believers demanded, to expound as though they were the words of the book. Thus, committing my right hand to the right hand of the Most High—who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap—I humbly undertook the whole long labour that he himself supplied to me and willingly offered it to those who requested it.

Let assessors of others’ works know that the Lord is accustomed sometimes to minister many good things to his children through weak vessels, especially when some poor lover of wisdom bends diligently over its flowers and, with a groaning breast, frequent sighs, and at times a little stream of tears following, knocks upon wisdom’s ears. What mortal, I ask, could endure for two or three years the importunity of any needy person continually seeking nourishment at his door with repeated cries, without sending out at least crumbs falling from his table?

I confess that for twenty-five years I lay day and night before the gate of supreme wisdom, imploring with all the desires I could that she would bring me, thirsty as I was, into the wine-cellar and relieve my poverty with the wine of incomparable joy. And because, as Truth declares when it says, “Knock, and it shall be opened unto you,” divine mercy likewise opened its door to me when I knocked and gave me abundantly, according to my desire, those things which I sought to give to others. Everyone who lacks wisdom should ask God, and it shall be given to him.

Certainly, I have sometimes seen one poor man rather more importunate than the rest in requesting the alms necessary for his body, and therefore very often obtaining by the force of continual crying what he desired, and distributing what he had thus extracted to his sluggish companions. By imitating this practice, I am said to be importunate toward my Lord Jesus Christ; and if he does not give to me because I am his friend, nevertheless because of my importunity he will rise and give me as many loaves as I need.

## Epitaph of Richard

(*Neustria Pia*, 510.)

Light, flower, vessel of his country, of monks, and of philosophy—  
Abbot Richard, the whole house, lies here.

Whatever the Law had woven, his tongue unwove;  
and whatever any man had entangled in the ancients, he explained.

May the God of life grant perpetual life  
to him whose death assigns the third Kalends of February [30 January].

# A.D. 1133. St Stephen, Third Abbot of Cîteaux

## Historical Notice

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, April, vol. II, p. 496.)

### Chapter One.—Birth; monastic life; pilgrimage. Entry into Molesme and Cîteaux; his priorate.

1. The principal founders of the Cistercian Order were St Robert, Blessed Alberic, and the St Stephen already mentioned, whom the tables of the Roman Martyrology propose for commemoration on this day. We gave the life of St Robert, Abbot of Molesme and regarded as founder of the Cistercian Order, on 29 April of this month.

> [Note: See *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII.]

There we examine more fully the beginnings of the whole Order and cite various matters concerning St Stephen, which are touched upon here only in passing; to these we refer the kindly reader, lest the bulk of the work grow too large. We gave the life of Blessed Alberic on 26 January, from the *Fasciculus of Saints of the Cistercian Order* compiled by Chrysostom Henriquez. He had included it in book I, distinction 2, and had appended in distinction 3 the Life of St Stephen, which the curious reader will find there. From various sources, and especially from both books of the *Exordium of Cîteaux*, we select the principal matters.

2. On the origin of St Stephen, Angelus Manrique, in his introduction to the *Cistercian Annals*, chapter 2, no. 4, writes as follows:

> “Stephen, surnamed Harding, was noble by birth, English by nation, and a monk by profession; he had adopted this manner of life from adolescence, receiving the habit at the monastery of Sherborne. For the sake of study he had first crossed from England to Scotland, and then to France, to Paris. There, after sampling secular letters, he drank deeply of sacred learning; diligent in labour, profound in intellect, outstanding in meditation; and one in whom—as I use the words of William of Malmesbury, book IV, *On the Kings of the English*—‘knowledge of letters accorded with religion: gracious in speech, cheerful in countenance, always joyful in spirit in the Lord.’ Having laid these firmer foundations, after some years he set out for Rome to visit and venerate the holy thresholds, taking with him as his companion in study a cleric. Remarkable in so young a man, though religious: no occupations or distractions, no business, could prevent him from devoutly chanting the entire Psalter every day. Even amid the discomforts of travel, the demands of nature, and works toward one’s neighbour required by both tables of charity, there was time and place for chanting the Psalter, while the same cleric responded alternately—a faithful companion and ready for every good work.”

Thus the *Greater Cistercian Exordium*, book I, chapter 27, written in the twelfth century by a monk of Clairvaux; and Manrique asserts, for the year 1106, chapter 1, no. 5, that “the history of St Stephen is most fully illuminated” by it. But in no. 5, chapter 2, of the *Introduction*, he adds the following.

3. “After visiting the holy places at Rome, I believe that Stephen Harding conceived a vow of an even more perfect life; both happily returned to Gaul, when, as they passed through the territory of Langres, Molesme within it—recently made famous—gave them an occasion to turn aside to the monks. Stephen perceived that he was due to a new foundation, a new monastery, or rather, to a future order; and Robert and Alberic lacked a third person for the weaving of that threefold cord which would never be broken and would bind so many men with heavenly bonds. Yet a sharp temptation did not fail to confront his fervent spirit, under the stronger appearance of piety: the old companionship had to be dissolved and severed, the cleric now for the first time dissenting from him and refusing to remain at Molesme. Parents and brothers once left behind, wealth abandoned, worldly glory despised, pleasures and delights overcome, caused the man of God less trouble than the impending loss of one good and proven friend, though it might be compensated by the fellowship of so many saints. But at last a hidden power overcame his wavering mind, a power preparing Stephen for Cîteaux. The new guest increased the community of Molesme, to the joy of the angels and the wasting-away of demons; Robert and Alberic, abbot and prior, and all their other brethren rejoiced equally.”

4. Molesme later became corrupted through abundance and proved incapable of correction. St Robert abandoned it, leaving its care to Blessed Alberic; but Alberic, after suffering beatings and imprisonment, withdrew with St Stephen into the wilderness called Unicus. Yet all were recalled to Molesme and reformed many things. Since they could not reform everything, they planned to build a new monastery; having obtained authority for this from the apostolic legate, they chose Cîteaux, chiefly through the action of St Stephen. Of him the *Exordium* cited above, book I, chapter 10, says:

> “When the movement for renewing religious life had arisen, Stephen himself, first among the foremost, laboured with most ardent zeal and pressed in every way for the establishment of the place and order of Cîteaux; of which he was afterwards, by God’s ordinance, to be appointed pastor and teacher.”

Perhaps he was also sent to Duke Odo of Burgundy to seek assistance. We have set out all these matters in the Life of St Robert.

5. The monastery therefore began to be inhabited on 21 March 1098, under St Robert as its first abbot. But when, by papal command, Robert returned to Molesme in the following year, Blessed Alberic was advanced to the abbacy, and St Stephen was appointed prior by him. Together with Alberic, Stephen increased the rigour of discipline, promoted confirmation of the monastery by Paschal, and especially assisted in framing the first statutes of Cîteaux. Thus the beginning of the Cistercian reform was established and the white habit adopted. There is some tradition that St Stephen delivered a sermon at the death of Blessed Alberic, who was taken from this life in 1109; it is found, together with the remaining Acts of Alberic, under 26 January.

## CHAPTER II.—He is made abbot: his first statutes. The poverty of the house divinely relieved. His attentiveness in prayer. Humility.

6. The author of the *Greater Cistercian Exordium*, book I, chapter 27, cited by Manrique for the year 1109, chapter 2, writes:

> “After the death of their second shepherd, the Church of Cîteaux, still poor and small, met to deliberate on the election of an abbot without respect of persons. Through the grace of the Holy Spirit acting among them, they chose a good man, Stephen by name, English by nation, who had left Molesme with them: a man of conspicuous holiness, adorned by the grace of every virtue, a lover of the wilderness and a most fervent imitator of holy poverty. When this had been done, by the Lord’s gift, as we have said, he immediately began, as a faithful and prudent steward, to consider with the most devout attention of mind how he might advance and raise up his newly founded order—still unstable in many respects, since it had not yet been fully developed and bore the marks of sheer poverty—and strengthen it by such moderation that it might bear much fruit for the Lord Jesus.
>
> “Having therefore summoned his brethren and taken counsel with them, both he and his brethren forbade the duke of that land, or any other prince, ever to hold his court in that church, as they had formerly been accustomed to do on feast days. Then, lest anything should remain in God’s house, where they desired to serve God day and night, that savoured of pride or superfluity, or that might at any time corrupt poverty, the guardian of virtues, which they had voluntarily chosen for God’s sake, they further decreed that they should keep no crosses of gold or silver, but only wooden ones painted with colours; no candlesticks except one of iron; no censers except of copper or iron; no chasubles except of fustian, linen, or cloth, and without gold or silver; nor albs or amices except of linen, likewise without gold or silver. They entirely gave up all cloaks, copes, dalmatics, and tunics. They wished their chalices to be not gold but silver, and, if possible, gilded; the communion tube to be silver and, if possible, gilded; and stoles and maniples to be of cloth only, without gold and silver. They also decreed that altar cloths should be of linen, plain and without pictures; and that cruets for the service of the altar should be without gold or silver.”

7. Thus far from the cited *Exordium*. The indicated dukes of that land were the dukes of Burgundy, descended from Robert, king of France. Of these, Odo I, great-grandson of King Robert and founder of this monastery, had died in 1102. At that time his son Hugh was living; Hugh died in 1142 and was succeeded by Odo II, Hugh’s son, who survived until 1152. The epitaph of these three is preserved at Cîteaux in the chapel on the right side of the church.

Manrique investigates several matters concerning the sacred vestments especially rejected and henceforth not admitted. The term *pallia* (“cloaks”) seems to be taken in a general sense, with copes—namely choir copes or pluvials—for priests, dalmatics for deacons and subdeacons, and tunics for the thurifer and acolytes carrying candles, treated as species under it. The *fistula*, or communion tube, was used by those who received Christ’s blood besides the celebrant. We have seen this rite still observed among the Cluniacs in solemn Masses. Cajetan, part I, question 80, article 12, question 3, notes that “in some places in the Cistercian Order communion is administered under both kinds.” We have also seen that this applied to nuns of the same order, on 13 April, in the Life of the Venerable Ida of Louvain, book III, no. 10.

8. On the poverty of the order under St Stephen, extending even to begging, the said author of the *Exordium*, book I, chapter 23, gives the following account; it is repeated from him by Helinand, monk of Cîteaux—who flourished about 1212 at Froidmont—in Vincent of Beauvais, book XXVI of the *Historical Mirror*, chapter 2:

> “I remember hearing Master Peter the Chanter of Paris, a most upright and learned man, relate concerning this Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, that when one day his cellarer informed him that there was nothing in the monastery with which even for one day the needs of the brethren could be supported, he replied: ‘Saddle two donkeys for us.’ When they were saddled, he made one lay brother mount with him, and ordered him to beg bread door to door in one village, while he himself did the same in another; and, having done this, they were to meet at a place he had designated.
>
> “As they were returning to the appointed place, they met one another. The abbot saw that the lay brother’s sack was much fuller than his own, and said with a smile: ‘Where did you beg? As I see, you gathered in a richer street than I did.’
>
> “The lay brother replied: ‘That priest whom you know very well filled my sack.’
>
> “Hearing this, the abbot groaned and said: ‘Woe to you! Why did you accept anything there? Did you not know that that priest was ordained simoniacally, and that what he received is leprosy and plunder? As the Lord lives, we shall taste nothing at all of everything he gave. Far be it from us to eat his sin and have it incorporated into us.’
>
> “Having summoned the shepherds of sheep, who were not far away, he emptied the entire sack of the lay brother into their laps.”

The same author of the *Exordium* tells several similar stories; and in book I, chapter 31, he says:

9. “The holy feast of Pentecost was at hand, and on that most sacred day scarcely enough loaves could be found in that house to suffice for the brethren. Then the brethren, greatly rejoicing, as though they were being fattened on the very poverty that they endured for God’s sake, began to sing the Mass of so great a solemnity with the utmost devotion and joy of heart. And behold, before Mass was finished, they received with much thanksgiving an abundant blessing sent to them unexpectedly, from the storehouses of God’s grace. In these and similar events, the man of God, perceiving how truly Scripture says, ‘Nothing is lacking to those who fear him,’ admired the Lord’s generosity and mercy toward himself and his brethren; he advanced more and more in holy religious life and gloried in the narrowness of blessed poverty as in every kind of wealth.”

The same author of the *Exordium*, in chapter 34, then relates the following, which should be joined to this.

10. “At one time, when the house of Cîteaux was constrained by great poverty, the venerable Abbot Stephen called one of his brethren and, speaking to him in the Spirit of God, said: ‘You see, dearest brother, that we are severely pressed by want, and that our brethren are near to perishing through hunger, cold, and other hardships. Therefore go to the fair at Vercelliacum [possibly Vercey], which is close at hand; and purchase there three wagons, with three strong draught-horses for each, which we greatly need for carrying our burdens. When you have loaded those wagons with cloth, provisions, and other necessary things, bring them back with you, returning to us in joy and prosperity.’

> “The brother replied: ‘I am ready, lord Father, to obey your commands, if you give me money with which to purchase those supplies.’

> “The venerable abbot answered, in his poverty placing magnificent confidence in the mercy of God: ‘Truly, brother, know that when I anxiously and carefully sought how to relieve the necessities of our brethren, only these three denarii were found in this house. Take them, if you wish; and for everything else that is lacking, the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ will provide for you. Go therefore in confidence, for the Lord will send his angel with you and make your journey prosperous.’

The brother accordingly departed for Vercelliacum and was received as a guest by a certain faithful and God-fearing man. When that man learned the reason for his journey and the brethren’s need, he immediately went to a very wealthy neighbour of his, who was desperately ill and almost dying, and was distributing his possessions among the poor. Having told this sick man of the want of the Cistercian monks, whose holiness was already renowned in that region, he summoned the aforementioned brother to his house and, while dying, gave him so great a sum of money that he could sufficiently purchase everything the abbot had enjoined upon him.

11. “Having therefore obtained the three wagons with their nine draught-horses, he equipped and loaded them with everything that he knew to be useful for the brethren’s needs. Thus he who had come empty-handed returned to his brethren full and joyful, in accordance with the abbot’s prophecy. As he approached Cîteaux, he sent a messenger to inform his abbot both of his arrival and of the outcome.

> “On hearing this, the venerable father rejoiced greatly in the Lord, and summoning all the brethren together said: ‘The God of mercies, the Lord, the God of mercies, has acted freely and generously. Truly nobly, truly splendidly have you acted, our Steward and Shepherd, opening your hand and filling our poverty with your blessing.’

Then they formed a procession and went out to meet the arriving brother as far as the gate. The abbot himself went forth vested in sacred garments and carrying his pastoral staff, while ministers preceded him with cross and holy water. Thus they solemnly received the alms with much thanksgiving, not as bestowed by a human being, but as mercy sent down from heaven by the Lord, God their saviour.

This prudent and spiritual man, as may be understood, wished by this solemn reception of the gift to admonish his sons, both those then present and their descendants, to preserve the grace of this miracle in continual remembrance, and to learn from it, in all their necessities, to place devout confidence in God’s mercy. For he never abandons those who hope in him, but is always the most merciful comforter of his poor and a helper in times of tribulation.”

Thus far the author of the *Exordium*, in Manrique under the year 1110. To this we add what happened to Stephen when he was ill after being bled, as reported in book II of the *Exordium*, chapter 30:

12. “Once the poor Abbot Stephen had been bled, and because the house was poor the cellarer—upon whom, by the command of the Rule, the care of the poor and sick rests—had nothing at hand from which to prepare some more nourishing food for his poor and sick abbot. Loving his abbot with sincere charity, he ran about, in case he might perhaps find something somewhere through which he could show outwardly the charity that burned within him. And behold, a large bird flew up carrying in its claws a fish of no small size; immediately it dropped the fish before the eyes of those who marvelled and departed, leaving the cellarer an abundant prey sufficient to provide for his abbot’s bloodletting.”

But from book I of the same *Exordium* must be added what is narrated in chapter 32.

13. “Moreover, how far Stephen was from being deaf to the author of the holy Rule, who commands that we should stand for psalmody in such a way that our minds agree with our voices, will be clear from what we now relate. It was his custom, when the reading at collation had been completed and he entered the church, to grasp the church door with his hand and press his fingers firmly, as if making a sign; just as people are accustomed to make a sign or measure, so that, reminded by it, they may impress more deeply upon memory what they do not wish to forget.

> “Since he did this often, one day a brother, encouraged by familiarity, asked why he did it. The holy Father replied: ‘I tell all my thoughts, which I am compelled to admit during the day because of the duty laid upon me of administering the house, to remain outside and not dare enter at all, but to wait until tomorrow, so that I may find them here first thing.’”

Thus far that source. Similar things are related of St Bernard, who may have learned this from St Stephen, his abbot. Then chapter 33 adds:

> “How great his humility was, and how much he hated every display of pride, is sufficiently shown by his pastoral staff, with which he used to proceed in festal processions. Preserved to this day in the treasury at Cîteaux out of reverence for so great a Father and held in great veneration, it seems not very different from the ordinary walking-sticks upon which old and infirm people commonly lean.”

## CHAPTER III.—Comfort amid the despondency caused by the failing prospect of successors, from the appearance of a deceased monk and from a dying man’s vision. The arrival of St Bernard and others.

14. William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, book I of the Life of St Bernard, chapter 3, writes:

> “At that time the new and little flock of Cîteaux, under Stephen, a venerable man and abbot, was becoming deeply weary because of its small number, and every hope of successors into whom the inheritance of that holy poverty might pass was failing. All men venerated in them the holiness of their life, but recoiled from its austerity. Suddenly, by a divine visitation so joyful and so unexpected, it was made glad, so that on that day that house seemed to have received from the Holy Spirit this answer: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who did not bear; break forth in cries, you who did not travail; for the children of the desolate are more numerous than of her who has a husband’ [Isaiah 54:1], ‘of whom afterwards you shall see children’s children for many generations.’”

But how, in that desolation, St Stephen addressed a dying monk is narrated thus in the *Greater Exordium*, book III, chapter 28:

> “You see, dearest one, how great is the weariness and failure of spirit in which we are placed, because we have in some measure entered the narrow and constricted way which our most blessed Father Benedict set before us in the Rule. But whether this manner of life of ours pleases God is not sufficiently clear to us, especially since all the neighbouring monks judge us as inventors of novelties and promoters of scandal and schism.
>
> “Above all, the dart of most bitter sorrow pierces my heart: our small number. One by one, death intervening, we are daily taken from our midst; and, as I greatly fear, this newly begun religious life will end together with us. For the Lord has not yet deigned to associate with us capable persons suited to the humility of holy poverty, through whom we may hand down to posterity the pattern of this institution of ours.
>
> “Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love we have entered the narrow and constricted way which he sets before his followers in the Gospel [Matthew 7:13], and by virtue of obedience I command you that, after your death—at the time and in the manner decreed by the grace of that same Lord—you return to us and make us certain concerning our condition, insofar as his mercy shall will.”

The sick man replied: “I will gladly do, lord Father, what you command, provided that, aided by your prayers, I may be permitted to fulfil your command.”

15. “A few days had passed after his death. The venerable abbot, with the community of brethren engaged in work, had given the signal for rest, as was customary. He too, having withdrawn a little from the others, was intent upon prayer, sitting with his head covered by his hood. And behold, that deceased brother, suffused with great splendour of brightness, stood before him; yet he appeared rather to be suspended in the air than standing upon the earth.

> “When asked how he was and what his condition was, he replied: ‘Well, most well, Father; I am well. May it be well with you also, because through your teaching and care I have been made a participant in that endless joy, that incomprehensible peace of God which surpasses all understanding. To attain it, I patiently and humbly endured the hard labours of our new order.
>
> “‘And now, in accordance with your command, I have returned, announcing to you, Father, and to your brethren the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since you commanded rightly that you should be made certain concerning your state, hold firmly, with every scruple of doubt removed, that your life and way of life are holy and pleasing to God. Moreover, the sorrow that devours your heart so greatly because you are leaving no successors will very soon be driven from you and turned into rejoicing and exultation. For the children of your barrenness shall yet say in your hearing: “The place is too narrow for us; make room, that we may dwell” [Isaiah 49:20].
>
> “‘For behold, from this very time the Lord has begun to do great things with you, sending you many persons. Among them will be very many noble and learned men, who will fill this house so that, flying out from it like swarming and overflowing colonies of bees, they will penetrate many regions of the world; and from the seed of the Lord that has taken root in this place, they will bring into the heavenly granaries many sheaves of holy souls, gathered from all parts of the world.’”

Having heard this, the holy abbot, filled with joy and exultation, gave thanks from the inmost depths of his heart to divine mercy, proving by happy experience how truly Scripture testifies: “For the Lord does not abandon those who hope in him” [Psalm 33:23].

16. “Meanwhile the heavenly messenger prepared to depart; but, wonderful to say, he did not presume to do so without the blessing of his spiritual Father. He therefore said to the abbot: ‘It is time, lord Father, for me to return to him who sent me; and therefore I ask that you dismiss me strengthened by your blessing.’

> “The astonished and frightened abbot replied: ‘What, I ask, is this that you say? You have passed from corruption to incorruption, from vanity to truth, from darkness to light, from death to life; and you ask a blessing from me, who still mourn miserably under all these things? This seems contrary to every integrity of law and reason. Rather, I ought to be blessed by you; and therefore I beg you to bless me.’

> “He answered: ‘It is not fitting thus, Father. For the power of blessing has been granted you by the Lord, since you are placed at the summit of dignity and spiritual teaching. But for me, your disciple, who through your saving instruction escaped the defilements of this world, it is desirable to receive a blessing. I shall by no means depart from here unless I have merited your blessing.’

The abbot, filled with astonishment and wonder and not daring to resist further with obstinacy, raised his hand and blessed him. Thus that holy soul disappeared, restoring the visible form it had assumed to the secret realm of invisible things.

17. “On another occasion, to one of the brethren who was about to enter upon the way of all flesh, there appeared in a vision an innumerable multitude of people washing their garments near the oratory of that church, beside a most bright fountain. In that vision it was said to him that this fountain was called Ennon [Aenon]. When he reported this to the abbot, the great man immediately understood that a divine consolation was signified by it.”

Thus far the author of the *Exordium*. The final words are read in the cited Life of St Bernard, chapter 3, where there is added:

> “The abbot then gave abundant thanks to God through Jesus Christ, much rejoicing in the promise, but still more afterward in its fulfilment.”

St Jerome, in *Hebrew Places*, says: “Ennon, where John baptized, as is written in the Gospel [John 3], is a place still shown even now, eight miles from Scythopolis, between Salim and the Jordan.”

18. The aforesaid William opens chapter 4 of the Life of St Bernard thus:

> “In the year 1113 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the fifteenth from the establishment of the house of Cîteaux, Bernard, servant of God, about twenty-three years old, entered Cîteaux with more than thirty companions and, under Abbot Stephen, bowed his neck beneath Christ’s sweet yoke. From that day the Lord gave blessing, and that vineyard of the Lord of hosts yielded its fruit, stretching its branches unto the sea and its shoots beyond the sea.”

These words agree with what is set out in the *Lesser Exordium*—said to have been composed in 1120 by the first Cistercian Fathers—chapter 18:

> “Therefore in those times the Lord visited that place. For by God’s grace he brought at one time to that church so many learned clerics and noble laymen—men powerful and equally noble even in the world—that thirty entered the novices’ cell together with joy. There they successfully completed their course, bravely struggling against their own vices and the incitements of evil spirits.
>
> “Encouraged by their example, old and young, and persons of different ages in different parts of the world—seeing, that is, in these men that what they had previously feared impossible was possible—began to gather there, submit their proud necks to Christ’s sweet yoke, ardently love the hard and harsh commands of the Rule, and make that church wonderfully joyful and unfailingly strong.”

## CHAPTER IV.—Various monasteries built under him. New statutes. The document called the Charter of Charity.

19. The manner in which the Cistercian Order began to spread beyond its first dwelling is related by Manrique in words drawn from the cartulary of La Ferté:

> “So great was the number of brethren at Cîteaux that neither their resources sufficed for them nor the place in which they lived could suitably contain them. The brethren therefore resolved to seek another place, where some of them, separated from the others in body but not in soul, might serve God devoutly and according to the Rule.
>
> “While Abbot Stephen carefully and diligently sought such a place, this discussion came to the knowledge of Lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, and the canons of that city, and also to the ears of two counts, namely Gaudelric and William, and of other distinguished men. They rejoiced greatly, surveyed their land in every direction, and at last, by God’s will, found a place suitable for the aforementioned monks, where they might serve God and live according to the Rule.
>
> “The two aforementioned counts gladly granted them a portion of the woodland called by the inhabitants of that region Bragne. Let it therefore be recorded for pious posterity that on 18 May in the year of the Lord 1113, the monastery of La Ferté, situated above the Grosne—the first daughter of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Chalon—was founded by the most illustrious counts Ganderic and William. Its church of the most blessed Virgin Mary was consecrated by the most reverend Walter, bishop of Chalon, in the presence of Joscelin, bishop of Langres, the aforesaid most venerable counts, and many other men distinguished for piety.
>
> “On 16 May, the vigil of that dedication, the venerable Father Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux, went there and brought with him Brother Bertrand and twelve other religious, for the propagation of religious life.”

Thus the cartulary of La Ferté. Similar material occurs in the *Greater Exordium*, book I, chapter 33, which adds:

> “Nor do we doubt that Stephen had first acquired the place itself with its buildings for them by paternal care—not, I say, by payment, but by the fragrance of virtues—and had also supplied from the patrimony of Cîteaux relics, chalices, ornaments, vestments, books necessary for the divine office, for table use, and for reading in the cloister, together with all else required for the observance of religious life, according to the custom instituted by him in his order.”

This monastery lies about ten Roman miles from Chalon.

20. In the following year, 1114, another monastery was added, called Pontigny, four leagues from the city of Auxerre, in whose diocese it was founded. It was the second daughter of Cîteaux; about one hundred monasteries are said to have been subject to it, as thirty were to La Ferté. The third daughter was Clairvaux, in the diocese of Langres, five leagues from that city; it is said to preside, or at least formerly to have presided, over about eight hundred monasteries.

On its origin William, book I of the Life of St Bernard, chapter 5, says:

> “When it pleased him who had separated Bernard from the world and called him, through a more abundant grace to reveal his glory in him and to gather through him into one the many children of God who were scattered abroad, he put into the heart of Abbot Stephen the purpose of sending his brethren to build the house of Clairvaux. When they departed, he appointed the same Lord Bernard their abbot; they indeed marvelled, since they were men mature and vigorous both in religion and in worldly affairs, and feared for him, both because of his youthful age and because of bodily weakness and his lesser experience of external administration.”

In 1661 we spent several days at Cîteaux and reverently visited the oratory in which St Bernard, with the other novices, was said to have undertaken his pious exercises. We then also visited the monasteries of La Ferté and Pontigny, being everywhere received with kindly charity and assisted in gathering the Lives of the Saints.

In an ancient chronology of monasteries are read these words:

> “In the year 1115 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [25 June], the abbey of Clairvaux was founded; on the same year and the same day, the abbey of Morimond.”

This appears to refer to the monks sent by Stephen from Cîteaux to the said monasteries. Morimond was the fourth daughter of Cîteaux, also situated in the diocese of Langres, on the borders of Lorraine and the County of Burgundy.

There followed the construction of very many monasteries. From a most ancient chronology, Carolus de Visch lists in the *Library of Cistercian Writers* more than ninety erected in Stephen’s time, not only throughout all the provinces of Gaul, but also in Italy and Spain, England, Germany, and Sweden. Thus, as was said above, “the Order stretched its branches unto the sea and its shoots beyond the sea.” Yet below only twenty are indicated as having been founded.

21. Among these was the distinguished monastery of Bonnevaux, founded by Guy, archbishop of Vienne, later supreme pontiff under the name Callistus II, as the Chronicle of Bonnevaux relates in these words:

> “In the year 1117 from the Incarnation of the Lord, when Lord Guy, legate of the holy Roman Church and archbishop of the Church of Vienne, but now Catholic pope, was returning from the council which he had held at the castle of Dijon with an assembly of many bishops, abbots, and other religious persons, he came to the new monastery commonly called Cîteaux. He asked Lord Stephen, abbot of that place, to build a monastery in his archbishopric of Vienne, where monks living under a Rule and an abbot might devoutly implore God’s mercy for himself, for all the clergy, and for the people entrusted to him.
>
> “The same abbot, having consulted the monks committed to his care, assented to his request and came to Vienne. By the counsel and assistance of the aforementioned Lord Pope Callistus, he began to build a monastery in a certain valley, which the same pope ordered to be called Bonnevaux, ‘Good Valley.’ It should be known that all the expenses necessary for this work were supplied by the provision or administration of that same pope.”

Thus far.

22. As monasteries thus began to be founded and the Cistercian Order to expand, Stephen, after a chapter had been held at Cîteaux [Col. 1372B], prescribed for his brethren notable laws or statutes (they call them the *Charter of Charity*). “But considering,” as is read in both *Exordia*, “that these statutes could not be firmly established without the considered authority of the Apostolic See, and imitating the example of his predecessor, he sent them to Rome with the agreement of his abbots and brethren. He humbly requested of Lord Calixtus II, then pontiff of the Apostolic See, that he should decree that those measures which Stephen had established with his fellow abbots and brethren for strengthening the discipline of the monastic order should remain ratified and unshaken by apostolic authority. The Supreme Pontiff graciously assented to his petition and promulgated a decree confirming the order, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1109 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1372C], in the first year of his pontificate.” So it says there.

This *Charter of Charity* contains thirty chapters, which may be read in Manrique under the said year, chapter 4. There, from a manuscript of Clairvaux, chapter 5 adds the following: “The venerable Father Stephen, ever watchful in prudence and wonderfully provident, established outstanding laws in order to cut off the shoots of schisms, which, if they grew up, might stifle the fruit of mutual peace before it could arise. He wished that document fittingly to be called the *Charter of Charity*, because its entire sequence breathes only those things which belong to charity; so that it appears almost everywhere to pursue nothing other than this: ‘Owe no one anything, except to love one another.’ This Charter, drawn up by that Father, confirmed by the aforesaid abbots, was also fortified by the authority of the apostolic seal [Col. 1372D].” So it says there.

The pope’s diploma itself is found in chapter 7. But the regulations subsequently established by St Stephen were collected together after his death; Manrique published them, divided into eighty-seven chapters, under the year 1134, chapter 6. All of these may be seen in his work.

## CHAPTER V.—The laying down of the abbatial burden: illness, death, and veneration

23. “When blessed Father Stephen, as is read in the *Greater Exordium*, book I, chapter 37, had vigorously administered the office entrusted to him according to the true rule of humility of our Lord Jesus Christ, he was worn out by advanced old age, so that his eyes grew dim and he could not see, and he laid aside pastoral care. There succeeded him [Col. 1373A] a certain unworthy man named Wido, who, though endowed to no small degree with outward gifts, like a whitewashed tomb, was inwardly foul with the rottenness of vices. When, at the very beginning of his promotion, he was receiving the profession of the brethren according to custom, the same servant of God Stephen saw in the spirit an unclean spirit coming to him and entering his mouth. Scarcely one month had passed, and behold: by the Lord’s revelation his impurity was laid bare, and the spurious plant which the heavenly Father had not planted was immediately uprooted from paradise”; and the most holy man Raynard was substituted for him.

24. “When the time was at hand for the old man, whose labours had earned their reward, to be introduced into the joy of his Lord, and to lie down in order to ascend from the last place of poverty, which he had chosen in this world according to the counsel of the Saviour [Col. 1373B], to the banquet of the supreme householder, certain brethren assembled, including abbots of his order—for their number is said by that time to have grown to twenty—that they might attend with most devout services and prayers their faithful friend and most humble Father as he returned to his homeland. When he was already in agony and near to death, the brethren began to speak among themselves, declaring a man of such merit blessed and saying that he could go securely to God, since in his own time he had produced such fruit in the Church of God. On hearing this, and gathering his spirit as well as he could, he said in a voice as if reproving them: ‘What are you saying? Truly I tell you that I go to God so trembling and anxious, as though I had never done anything [Col. 1373C] good. For if there was any good in me, or if through my littleness any fruit could arise by the cooperation of God’s grace, I fear and tremble greatly lest I may perhaps have retained grace within myself less worthily or less humbly than I should.’

“Thus armed with the shield of perfect humility, which sounded from his lips and flourished in his heart, he put off the human being. Powerfully repelling all the most wicked darts of the adversary, whether fiery or sulphurous [Col. 1374A], he passed safely through the sharpest storms and ascended crowned to the gates of paradise. The sacred remains of his body were reverently buried beside the relics of his predecessor, so that those who had been one spirit and one faith in this life might not have unequal glory in eternal blessedness.” Thus far the said *Exordium*.

25. The ancient tables of Cîteaux report that he died in the year 1134, on 28 March. Henriquez and Bucelinus place him on that day in their martyrologies, as does Saussay in the *Gallican Martyrology*, whose encomium is as follows:

“Likewise, on this day, the deposition of St Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux, a man of conspicuous holiness and adorned with the grace of every virtue. A most ardent emulator of holy poverty and most eager lover of the wilderness, having happily completed the warfare of religious profession, after he had enlisted many recruits into Christ’s camp, among them St Bernard, leader of others, he was joyfully summoned to the prize of heavenly glory. His blessed memory, inscribed in the Church’s sacred records, shines illustriously among the nativities of the saints, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

For the present day, 17 April, the following is read in the Roman Martyrology: “At Cîteaux in France, St Stephen, abbot, who first inhabited the wilderness of Cîteaux and joyfully received St Bernard when he came to him with his companions.” He is widely celebrated on the same day in monastic martyrologies. His sarcophagus may still be seen at the entrance to the church of Cîteaux, toward the chapter-house cloister [Col. 1374C], with this inscription:

“Here are buried together the holy and venerable Fathers, abbots, founders, and enlargers of the monastery and Order of Cîteaux: Lord Alberic, Lord Stephen, Lord Raynard, Lord Gozovinus, Lord Fastradus, etc. May their blessed souls, living unto almighty God, always be mindful of us.”

[Col. 1373]

# THE CENSURE OF ST STEPHEN, THIRD ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX, CONCERNING CERTAIN PASSAGES OF THE BIBLE

(Mabillon, *Works of St Bernard*, III, XI.)

[Col. 1373D] Brother STEPHEN, abbot of the New Monastery, to the present and future servants of God, greeting.

As we resolved to write this history, among the many books which we had gathered from different churches, in order that we might follow the more truthful one, we encountered one which differed greatly from nearly all the others. Because we found it fuller than the rest, we gave it credence and wrote this history according to what we found in that book [Col. 1374D]. But when it had been set in order, we were greatly disturbed by the disagreement among the histories; for sound reason plainly teaches that what has been translated from the one fountain of Hebrew truth by one translator—namely, blessed Jerome—whom our people had now adopted to the exclusion of other translators, ought to have one and the same sense.

There are, however, certain books of the Old Testament which our translator translated not from Hebrew but from the Chaldaean [Aramaic] language, because he found them thus among the Jews, as he himself writes in the prologue to Daniel; and we have received these, like the other books, according to his translation.
