Therefore, greatly wondering at the disagreement among our books, which we had received from a single translator, we approached certain Jews skilled in their Scriptures and questioned them with the utmost care, in the Roman language, concerning all those places of Scripture in which were found those portions and verses which occurred in our aforesaid exemplar and which we had already inserted into this our work, but which we did not find in many other Latin histories. As they turned over many of their books before us and explained to us in Roman words the Hebrew or Chaldaean writing at the places about which we questioned them, they found none at all of the portions or verses [Col. 1375B; Col. 1376A] that troubled us.

Accordingly, trusting the Hebrew and Chaldaean truth, and the many Latin books which did not contain these passages but agreed throughout with those two languages, we entirely erased all those superfluities, as is apparent in many places in this book, and especially in the books of Kings, where the greater part of the error was found. We now ask all who are to read this volume that they by no means add hereafter to this work the aforesaid superfluous portions or verses. It is sufficiently plain in what places they stood, because the erasure of the parchment does not conceal the same places.

We also forbid, by the authority of God and of our congregation, that anyone presume dishonourably to handle this book, prepared with great labour, or to make any mark with his nail through its writing or in its margin [Col. 1376B].

> **Note:** [Col. 1375B] Below is read: “From the acts of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order, year 1196. At the petition of the late archbishop of Lyons, who requests that the Gospel reading concerning the Lord’s Passion, read according to Matthew on Palm Sunday, be corrected, the abbot of La Ferté is instructed diligently to inquire what is thought on the matter in the churches of Cluny and Lyons, and to endeavour to report it at the following Chapter.
>
> “Year 1200. Let the words ‘They divided my garments among themselves’ be written in the text of the blessed evangelist Matthew wherever they are lacking.”
>
> This censure is found in a codex of the Bible at the monastery of Cîteaux. Stephen, its second abbot, caused the said codex to be written, as this concluding notice testifies: “In the year 1109 from the Incarnation of the Lord, this book came to the end of its writing, while Stephen II governed the monastery of Cîteaux as abbot.”

[Col. 1375]

# SERMON OF THE MOST BLESSED STEPHEN AT THE DEATH OF HIS PREDECESSOR

(MANRIQUE, *Cistercian Annals*, under the year 1109, chapter 1, no. 19.)

[Col. 1375C] If sorrow has made us equals in the loss of so great a good, a weak comforter will be one who himself needs consolation. You have lost your venerable Father and the director of your souls; I have lost not only a Father and director, but a companion and fellow-soldier, and an outstanding athlete in the wars of God. The venerable Father Robert, from the infancy of religious life, had nurtured him in a single house by singular teaching and equal piety.

He is absent from us, but not from God; and, if not from God, neither will he be absent from us. For this is particular and proper to the saints: when they depart from life, they leave their body to their friends and carry their friends in their mind. We possess the little body and singular pledge of our most beloved Father, and he himself has carried all of us in his mind with pious affection. And if, brought to God, he is united with him in inseparable love, he has similarly united us who are in him. What more is there to mourn?

A happy lot; happier still is he to whom this has happened [Col. 1376C]; most happy are we, raised to such a presence. For nothing more joyful can befall Christ’s athletes than, laying aside the garment of flesh, to fly to him for whose love they have endured so many labours. The fighter has received the prize; the runner has seized the reward; the victor has attained the crown; the possessor asks the palm for us.

Why then do we grieve? Why do we mourn one who rejoices? Why are we sorrowful over one who exults? Why, with mournful voices, do we cast ourselves down in complaint before the Lord, if he, raised to the stars, grieves at this—if the blessed can grieve—he who with constant desire asks for us an end like his own? Let us not grieve over a soldier who is safe; let us grieve over ourselves, stationed in battle. Let us turn sad and mournful voices into prayers, beseeching our triumphant Father not to permit the roaring lion and cruel adversary to triumph over us.

[Col. 1375]

(It appears among the letters of St Bernard as no. 45. See the *Works of St Bernard*, below.)

II. [Col. 1377] Letter of Abbot Stephen, Hugh of Pontigny, and Bernard of Clairvaux to Pope Honorius.

(It is St Bernard’s forty-ninth letter.)

# [THE CHARTER OF CHARITY]

[Col. 1377]

# PREFACE TO THE CHARTER OF CHARITY

All its manuscripts, and subsequently several Roman pontiffs, testify first of all that this first constitution of the Cistercian Order received from its authors the name *Charter of Charity*. Above all, Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Adrian IV, Alexander III, and Clement IV consistently affirmed this name when each confirmed it.

Nor are reasons lacking for so honourable a title. Besides the fact that Clement IV says that it was thus designated from the *charity* breathed forth in every direction by its decrees, Calixtus II—who first consecrated it by a special diploma—declares that it was sanctioned by the consent, common deliberation, and mutual charity both of all the abbots and monks of the same order and of the bishops in whose dioceses their first monasteries had been established. Its authors were so far from attempting to impose upon their brethren through it any exaction of earthly advantage or temporal goods, as they themselves put it, that they rather willed assistance to be provided by the others with the greatest charity whenever any of them should fall into need or ruin.

Add that, as their successors judged in the prologue of this same constitution, foreseeing by this constitution the shipwreck of mutual peace, they determined by what compact and in what manner—indeed, by what CHARITY—their monks, separated bodily among abbeys established in different parts of the world, should be joined indissolubly in spirit. So much concerning the name of this constitution.

As for the decrees contained in it, all are chiefly reducible to two heads: the formation of conduct and the governance or administration of the Order. Its first head prescribes the Rule of St Benedict for the formation of morals, and that Rule alone, as sufficient if it is observed accurately and literally. The remaining heads serve the governance of persons and administration of monasteries, most wisely regulating monastic visitations, the election of abbots, the authority of father-abbots, the holding of the General Chapter, and other matters of that kind. By these, to mention this incidentally, they seem to intend to refer all jurisdiction, superiority, and authority in this Order to the proper abbots, the father-abbots, and the General Chapter.

Concerning the author of this constitution, the following seems more probable: St Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux, was indeed its principal author, though not its only one. For, as we have mentioned above, the same constitution was sanctioned by the common consent and deliberation of all the abbots and monks, as Calixtus II, Eugenius III, and Clement IV expressly declare.

Moreover, although it is not known in what precise year it was written, it is entirely certain that it was confirmed in 1119 by the same Supreme Pontiff Calixtus II.

[Col. 1377]

# CHARTER OF CHARITY

(*Cistercian Nomasticon*, Paris, 1664, folio.)

Before the Cistercian abbeys began to flourish, Lord Abbot Stephen and his brethren ordained that abbeys should in no way be founded in the diocese of any bishop before that bishop had accepted as valid the decree drawn up and confirmed between the monastery of Cîteaux and the other houses born from it, in order to avoid scandal between bishop and monks. In this decree, therefore, the aforesaid brethren, foreseeing the future shipwreck of mutual peace, made clear, established, and bequeathed to their successors the compact and manner, the charity, by which their monks, separated in body among abbeys established in different parts of the world, should be bound together indissolubly in spirit. They also judged that this decree should be called the *Charter of Charity*, because its statute repels every burden of exaction and pursues only charity and the benefit of souls in divine and human matters.

# THE CHARTER OF CHARITY BEGINS

[Col. 1377]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the singular agreement among persons of this Order regarding the interpretation and practice of the Rule of St Benedict and the other usages and ceremonies

[Col. 1377A]

Because we recognize that we are all, though unprofitable servants, servants of one true King, Lord, and Master, we impose upon our abbots and fellow-brethren, monks whom God’s mercy has through us most wretched men established under regular discipline in various places [Col. 1378A], no exaction of earthly advantage or temporal goods. Desiring to benefit them and all the children of holy Church, we resolve to do nothing toward them that may burden them or diminish their resources, lest, while we desire to abound through their poverty [Col. 1379A], we be unable to avoid the evil of avarice, which according to the Apostle is proved to be the service of idols. Yet, out of charity, we wish to retain care for their souls.

> **Note:** [Col. 1379D] This is the first reason why they gave this constitution the name *Charter of Charity*.

Thus, should they ever attempt, God forbid, to depart from their holy purpose and the observance of the holy Rule, they may through our solicitude return to uprightness of life.

### I. The Rule is to be observed without a novel interpretation

We now will and command them to observe in every respect the Rule of blessed Benedict as it is observed at the New Monastery. They are not to introduce another interpretation in the reading of the holy Rule; rather, as our predecessors, the holy Fathers—that is, the monks of the New Monastery—

> **Note:** [Col. 1379D] Here arises the second reason why this statute may be called the *Charter of Charity*.

—understood and observed it, and as we today [Col. 1379B] understand and observe it, so they too are to understand and observe it.

### II. The customs are to be the same in all monasteries

Because we receive into our cloister all their monks who come to us, and they likewise receive ours into their cloisters, it therefore seems fitting to us, and we also will, that they possess customs, chant, and all books necessary for the daytime and nighttime offices and for Masses, according to the form of the customs and books of the New Monastery, so that there may be no discord in our practices, but that we may live by one charity, one Rule, and like customs.

### III. Privileges contrary to the statutes of the Order are forbidden

No church or person of our Order shall dare to seek from anyone a privilege against the common institutions of the Order, or to retain one obtained in any manner whatsoever [Col. 1379C].

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the visitations of the father-abbots and their mutual observance of honour toward one another

### IV. The abbot of Cîteaux is to be received as abbot of the mother of the Order

When the abbot of the New Monastery comes to any of these monasteries for visitation, the abbot of that place, recognizing that the church of the New Monastery is the mother of his own church, shall yield to him in every place of the monastery. The visiting abbot shall occupy the place of that abbot for as long as he remains there, except that he shall eat not in the guest-house but with the brethren in the refectory, for the preservation of discipline [Col. 1379D], unless the abbot of that place is absent.

> **Note:** [Col. 1380D] The third reason why this constitution is called the *Charter of Charity*: namely, the mutual display of honour and reverence which it commands.

### V. How visiting abbots are to be received

All visiting abbots of our Order shall act similarly. If several arrive and the local abbot is absent, the first among them shall eat in the guest-house. The following is excepted: the abbot of that place, even in the presence of a higher abbot, shall bless his novices after their regular probation.

### VI. What the abbot of Cîteaux must avoid in daughter-houses

The abbot of the New Monastery shall also take care not to presume to deal with, arrange, or interfere [Col. 1380A] in anything belonging to the house he has visited contrary to the will of its abbot or brethren.

### VII. What he may do in the same houses

But if he perceives that the precepts of the Rule or of our Order are being violated in that place, he shall endeavour, with the advice of the abbot present, charitably to correct the brethren. If the abbot of the place is absent, he shall nevertheless correct whatever disorder he finds.

### VIII. The father-abbot is to visit the daughter-house

Once every year the abbot of the mother church, either personally or through one of his fellow abbots, shall visit all monasteries which he himself has founded. If he visits the brethren more often, they should rejoice the more on that account.

### IX. The first four abbots are to visit Cîteaux

The first four abbots—of La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond—shall themselves visit the house of Cîteaux together [Col. 1380B], on a day fixed among themselves, apart from the annual Chapter, unless perhaps serious illness prevents one of them.

### X. Reverence is to be shown to abbots when they come to Cîteaux

When an abbot of our Order comes to the New Monastery, fitting reverence shall be shown to him by its abbot. He shall occupy that abbot’s stall and eat in the guest-house if the abbot is then absent. But if he is present, the visitor shall do none of these things, but shall eat in the refectory. The prior of the place shall arrange the business of the monastery.

This shall be the rule between those abbeys which have not begotten one another: every abbot, in every place of his monastery, shall yield to a visiting fellow abbot, that the saying may be fulfilled: “Outdo one another in showing honour” (Romans [Col. 1380C] 12).

### XI. When many abbots assemble, who is first

If two or more assemble, the first among the arrivals shall hold the higher place. All, however, apart from the abbot of the house present, shall eat in the refectory, as we have said above. Elsewhere, wherever they meet, they shall hold their rank according to the age of their abbeys, so that he whose church is older shall be first. Wherever they sit together, they shall humble themselves mutually.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the establishment, authority, and form of the General Chapter

### XII–XIII. An abbey that founds another has a right in it. Abbots are to come to the General Chapter

When, by God’s grace, one of our churches has so grown that it can build another monastery, it too shall observe among itself and its brethren the arrangement which we maintain among our brethren, except that they shall not hold an annual chapter among themselves. Rather, every year all abbots of our Order shall come to the General Chapter at Cîteaux, setting every excuse aside, except those prevented by bodily infirmity. They must nevertheless send a suitable messenger through whom the necessity causing their delay [Col. 1381A] may be communicated to the Chapter. Those also are excepted who live in more distant regions and arrive at the time appointed for them in the Chapter. If anyone should presume to be absent from our General Chapter for any other reason, he shall seek pardon for his fault at the Chapter of the following year and shall not escape without serious correction.

### XIV. Matters to be dealt with in the General Chapter

At this Chapter they shall deliberate concerning the salvation of their souls; they shall establish whatever needs correction or addition in the observance of the holy Rule or the Order; and they shall restore among themselves the good of peace and charity.

### XV. The failings of abbots are to be corrected in the same Chapter

If any abbot is found insufficiently diligent in the Rule, excessively occupied with secular matters, or blameworthy in any respect [Col. 1381B], he shall there be charitably denounced.

> **Note:** [Col. 1381D] *Clametur* here means the same as “let him be accused” or “let him be reported.”

Having been denounced, he shall ask pardon and fulfil the penance imposed upon him for his fault. This denunciation may be made only by abbots.

### XVI. If there is disagreement over correcting someone, whose judgment must be followed

If any controversy should arise among any of the abbots, or if such grave fault should be brought to light concerning one of them that he deserves suspension or even deposition, whatever is decided on the matter by the Chapter shall be observed without reconsideration. But if the affair should come into discord through diversity of opinions, the decision shall be held inviolably which the abbot of Cîteaux and those who appear to possess sounder judgment and greater fitness shall make. This shall be observed: none of those to whom the case particularly pertains [Col. 1381C] may take part in the decision.

### XVII. Monasteries suffering want are to be helped by others

If any church should fall into intolerable poverty for any reason, the abbot of that monastery shall endeavour to make the matter known before the whole Chapter.

> **Note:** [Col. 1381D] Here is yet another and new reason for the name *Charter of Charity*, namely, the aid granted to a monastery suffering poverty [Col. 1382D].

Then each abbot, kindled with the greatest fire of charity, shall hasten to support the want of that church from the resources bestowed on him by God, according to what he has.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the election of abbots

### XVIII. On the death of an abbot, how the election of a successor is to be made

If any house of our Order is deprived of its own abbot, the senior abbot, from whose house that house sprang, shall have all care for its administration until another abbot is elected there. On the appointed day for the election, abbots also, if any were produced by that house, shall be summoned; and with the counsel and will of the father-abbot, the abbots and monks of that house shall elect an abbot [Col. 1381D].

### XIX. On the death of the abbot of Cîteaux, who must be present at the election of his successor

Because the house of Cîteaux is the mother of us all, while it lacks its own abbot, the first four abbots—namely, those of La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond—shall provide for it and have care of that house [Col. 1382A] until an abbot has been elected and established there. On a fixed and named day for the election of the abbot of Cîteaux, abbots whose houses sprang from Cîteaux shall be summoned at least fifteen days beforehand; and also others whom the aforesaid abbots and brethren of Cîteaux know to be suitable. The abbots and monks of Cîteaux, gathered in the name of the Lord, shall elect an abbot.

### XX–XXI. Who may be elected abbot of a mother church. No one of another Order is to be elected abbot

> **Note:** [Col. 1382D] By “abbot of the mother church” understand the father-abbot, or the abbot of the house which has begotten another.

Every mother church of our Order may freely take for itself, if necessary, an abbot not only from the monks of its daughter churches but also from their abbots. No church of ours shall elect for itself [Col. 1382B] as abbot a person from another Order; nor may any of our houses be given to monasteries outside our Order.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the resignation and deposition of abbots

### XXII. How an abbot wishing to resign is to be admitted

If any abbot, because of his own unfitness or faint-heartedness, asks his father, the abbot of the house from which his own house sprang, to be released from the burden of his abbacy, that father-abbot shall take care not lightly to assent without a reasonable and very necessary cause. Even if the necessity is great, he shall do nothing in the matter by himself; rather, after summoning some other abbots of our Order, he shall act according to what they jointly know ought to be done.

### XXIII. How an abbot is to be deposed, if his faults require it

If any abbot becomes known as a despiser of the holy Rule, a transgressor of the Order, or as consenting to the vices of the brethren entrusted to him, the abbot of the mother church, personally or through his prior, or in whatever way he can most suitably do so, shall admonish him concerning amendment up to four times [Col. 1382C]. If he is not corrected even thus and is unwilling voluntarily to resign, a considerable number of abbots of our congregation having been assembled, they shall remove the transgressor of the holy Rule from his office. Thereafter another worthy man shall be elected, with the counsel and consent of the senior abbot, by the monks of that church together with such abbots as belong to it, as has been stated above.

### XXIV. How a deposed abbot is to be punished if he resists

If the person who is deposed, or his monks, God avert it, should choose to be obstinate and rebellious and refuse altogether to submit to the decisions, they shall be subjected to excommunication by the abbot of the mother church and by his other fellow abbots [Col. 1382D]. Thereafter he shall restrain them as he can and knows to be expedient.

### XXV. Where those who repent may go

If any of them thereafter comes to himself, desires to rise from the death of his soul, and to return to his mother, he shall be received as a penitent son.

### XXVI. No one may transfer elsewhere without his abbot’s consent

Apart from this cause, which must always be avoided with the greatest care, no abbot shall retain without the consent of the other abbot a monk belonging to any other abbot of our Order. No one shall introduce his own monks to live in the house of another without that person’s consent [Col. 1383A].

### XXVII. How the abbot of Cîteaux is to be corrected

Likewise, if, God forbid, the abbots of our Order should discover that our mother, the Church of Cîteaux, is growing lax in its holy purpose and departing from the observance of the Rule or of our Order, they shall admonish the abbot of that place through the first four abbots—namely, La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond—acting in the name of the other abbots, up to four times, that he may correct himself and take care to correct the others [Col. 1383B]. All else said concerning other abbots shall be diligently carried out in his case if he appears incorrigible, except that, if he does not voluntarily resign, they may neither depose him nor pronounce anathema upon him while contumacious. They must wait until the General Chapter, or, if it should then appear impossible to await it, until another assembly has been called. The abbots whose houses sprang from Cîteaux, together with certain others [Col. 1384A], shall be summoned, and they shall depose the unfit man from his office; then they and the monks of Cîteaux shall endeavour to elect a suitable abbot.

### XXVIII. What if he and his monks do not submit?

If that abbot and the monks of Cîteaux should choose obstinately to resist, they shall not hesitate to strike them with the sword of excommunication.

### XXIX. Where those who repent may take refuge

If afterward any of these transgressors at last comes to himself and, desiring to save his soul, flees to any one of our four churches—La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, or Morimond—he shall be received, with regular satisfaction [Col. 1384B], as a member of the household and co-heir of the church, until he is at some time restored, as shall be just, to his own reconciled church.

### XXX. Where the General Chapter is then to be held

Meanwhile, the annual chapter of the abbots shall be held not at Cîteaux but wherever the four abbots named above have determined.

[Col. 1383]

# THE OLDER USAGES OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER

(*Cistercian Nomasticon, or the Older Customs of the Cistercian Order*, Paris, 1664.)

# PREFACE

[Col. 1383] Since, as we saw above, the authors of the first constitution of the Cistercian Order, or *Charter of Charity*, prescribed the same manner of living and acting for all monasteries and persons of the Order, they directed that this little book, compiled from the usages and ceremonies hitherto observed, should be given to each monastery in order to bind them together by the same customs and rites. The whole Order subsequently embraced the guidance of this book so fully that from that time it scarcely thought of acquiring another.

Therefore, although this book has already appeared in print once and twice, we again allow it to go forth publicly in this new edition and enlargement, collating several of its manuscripts and restoring it to the form in which it first existed. It is furnished, however, not bare as hitherto, but with notes and observations; it is divided, for greater clarity, into five parts according to the diversity of subjects which it treats; and there have been added and marked those matters which were from time to time appended to it for the institution of the celebration of certain feasts, without any alteration whatever of titles or chapters.

And, so that at the very threshold we may set before the reader a rough outline of it:

The first part sets forth the arrangement of the Cistercian Breviary and Missal, according to the Rule of St Benedict.

The second, beginning with chapter 52 and continuing to chapter 70, treats, according to the older usage of the Church, of the ceremonies to be observed both in the canonical hours and in the celebration of Masses.

The third, extending from chapter 70 to chapter 89, sets forth the manner of acting and the rites to be maintained in the other regular exercises.

The fourth, extending from that same chapter 89 to chapter 102, treats of the care of the sick and the suffrages for the dead.

Finally, the fifth, extending from that same chapter 102 to the end of the book, describes fully and wisely the duties of the weekly officers or ministers who succeed one another each week in ecclesiastical and regular services, and likewise the offices of superiors and of every kind of official.

Having thus given some preliminary account, however imperfect, of the purpose and arrangement of this little book, if anyone should inquire into its date and age, we would assign to it antiquity rather than any definite year. Yet it is more probable that it was compiled either together with the *Charter of Charity* or immediately afterwards. This is evident, among other things, from the fact that it is listed among the books that must necessarily be possessed at the first foundation of every monastery, in chapter twelve of the *Institutes* of the same Order, issued in the year 1134 by Saint Raynard, fourth abbot of Cîteaux, approximately fifteen years after the confirmation of the *Charter of Charity*. Of its author or compiler, however, nothing is certain.

## PART ONE. Arrangement of the Cistercian Breviary and Missal according to the Rule of Saint Benedict

[Col. 1385]

### CHAPTER I. On the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 1385A]

In the Advent of the Lord, Isaiah shall be begun at Vigils on the first Sunday, and thereafter shall be read throughout Advent, not only at Vigils but also in the refectory, as time permits. On the same days, when after Vespers and Lauds, and at Mass, a commemoration of Advent itself and of some saint must be made, the commemoration of Advent shall be made first, and that of the saint afterwards.

In the third week of the same Advent, the Ember fasts shall be observed every year; and the homilies on the Gospels belonging to the three days of those fasts shall be read at Vigils. Their first lessons are to be pronounced by such deacons as the cantor chooses. On the Thursday of that week, the sermons of Saint Augustine on the Incarnation of the Lord—namely, “We read that holy Moses” (*Legimus sanctum Moysen*) and “You, I say, I address, O Jews” (*Vos, inquam, convenio, o Judaei*)—are to be recited at Vigils. [Col. 1385B]

But if the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle should fall on that same Thursday, the aforesaid sermons shall be read on the Tuesday of that week. It must nevertheless be understood that the antiphon assigned, as the Antiphonary indicates, to the fifth day before Christmas at the *Benedictus*—that is, “Do not be afraid” (*Nolite timere*)—is not omitted even if that fifth day falls on a Sunday, but is said at the *Benedictus*. The Sunday antiphon, namely “Hail, Mary” (*Ave Maria*), shall be left aside.

### CHAPTER II. How the Responsories at Vigils Are Divided on Ferial Days in Winter

[Col. 1385C]

All Responsories sung on Sundays from the Kalends of November until Easter, and the Responsories of the Epiphany, namely “Today in the Jordan” (*Hodie in Jordane*), shall be divided into sets of three for each ferial day through Friday. On Friday they shall be repeated from the beginning, except on those days which have their own proper Responsories: namely, before and after Christmas, before Easter, and while the Responsories “Lord, not in your anger” (*Domine, ne in ira*) are sung.

Further, whenever “Beholding” (*Aspiciens*), which is sung on Sunday with three verses, is repeated on ferial days, it shall be sung with the last verse only. If a feast of twelve lessons intervenes, the three Responsories which ought to have been said on the day occupied by the feast shall be said on the first day following the feast which is free. [Col. 1385D]

### CHAPTER III. On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, after the Nocturns, the Vigil for the Dead shall be celebrated in the customary manner; and everything else shall be performed as on other ferial days, with genuflection, until the Vespers of Christmas. The exception is that the Mass of that day, after Prime, shall be celebrated without genuflection and with the reverence with which it is sung on Sundays. [Col. 1386A] At it only one collect shall be said, unless there should happen to be a deceased person present. The prophecy of Isaiah before the Epistle shall be read by whichever brother the cantor calls upon.

In chapter, after the first verse of the first lesson, which begins, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judaea” (*Jesus Christus Filius Dei in Bethlehem Judae nascitur*), the whole community, prostrate in reverence for the holy Nativity, shall make a short prayer. When the abbot rises—or the prior, if the abbot is absent—the others too shall rise and sit down; and the reader shall then continue the rest of the lesson.

But if the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on a Sunday, it shall be celebrated as follows. Invitatory: “Lift up your heads” (*Levate capita vestra*). In the first nocturn: antiphon, “O Lord, in your strength” (*Domine, in virtute*); psalms, “O Lord, in your strength” (*Domine, in virtute*) and “My God, my God, look upon me” (*Deus Deus meus, respice*), with the rest as in the Breviaries. Verse: “Today you shall know that the Lord is coming” (*Hodie scietis quia veniet Dominus*). The lessons, however, shall be those written in the Lectionary for the Fourth Sunday in Advent itself: “Hear me, you who pursue what is just” (*Audite me, qui sequimini quod justum est*). In that first nocturn the Responsories shall be read: “Sound the trumpet” (*Canite tuba*); “It shall not be taken away” (*Non auferetur*); “I must decrease” (*Me oportet minui*); “Behold, he now comes” (*Ecce jam venit*). [Col. 1386B]

In the second nocturn: antiphon, “The Lord is defender” (*Dominus defensor*); psalms, “The Lord is my light” (*Dominus illuminatio*) and “To you I cry” (*Ad te clamabo*), etc. Verse: “On the morrow the iniquity of the earth shall be blotted out” (*Crastina die delebitur iniquitas terrae*). Responsories: “Virgin Israel” (*Virgo Israel*); “I have sworn, says the Lord” (*Juravi, dicit Dominus*); “We do not depart from you” (*Non discedimus a te*); “Consider how great he is” (*Intuemini quantus sit*).

At the Canticles: antiphon, *Alleluia*; canticle, “Lord, have mercy on us” (*Domine, miserere nostri*). Verse: “A shoot shall come forth” (*Egredietur virga*). Gospel: “When she had been betrothed” (*Cum esset desponsata*). Homily of Origen, [Col. 1386C] from which four lessons shall be read, as they are marked in the book. The first of them shall be read, on Sunday, by the weekly deacon; on ferial days, by whomever the cantor chooses. Responsories: “Sanctify yourselves” (*Sanctificamini*); “Be steadfast” (*Constantes estote*); “Sanctify yourselves, children of Israel” (*Sanctificamini, filii Israel*); “There shall be born for you” (*Nascetur vobis*). Gospel after *Te Deum laudamus*: “When the mother of Jesus had been betrothed” (*Cum esset desponsata mater Jesu*). Collect: “O God, who [by the Redemption]…” (*Deus qui nos Redemptionis*).

At Lauds: *Alleluia*; psalms, “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*) and “Give thanks to the Lord” (*Confitemini Domino*), etc. Chapter: “Behold, I come quickly” (*Ecce venio cito*). Responsory: “Today you shall know” (*Hodie scietis*). Hymn: “Splendour of the Father’s glory” (*Splendor paternae gloriae*). Verse: “Be steadfast” (*Constantes estote*). At the Gospel Canticle: antiphon, “He shall rise like the sun” (*Orietur sicut sol*). Collect: “O God, who [by the Redemption]…” (*Deus qui nos redemptionis*). For the commemoration [Col. 1386D] of Sunday: antiphon, “Hail, Mary” (*Ave Maria*); verse, “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord” (*Emitte agnum, Domine*); collect, “Stir up, O Lord, your power” (*Excita, Domine, potentiam*).

The morning Mass of Sunday, namely “Remember us, O Lord” (*Memento nostri, Domine*), shall be said with its collect, unless a deceased person be present. But the principal Mass shall be that of the Vigil, namely “Today you shall know” (*Hodie scietis*). *Alleluia* and “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum Deum*) shall be said. The prophecy of Isaiah before the Epistle shall not be omitted.

[Col. 1387A]

At the daytime Hours, *Alleluia*. The verses of the Vigil shall be as follows: at Terce, “Today you shall know” (*Hodie scietis*); at Sext, “On the morrow the iniquity of the earth shall be blotted out” (*Crastina die delebitur iniquitas terrae*); at None, “Be steadfast” (*Constantes estote*). At Terce, however, the chapter and collect are those of the Vigil. At Sext and None, they are as on the three preceding Sundays.

At Vespers only the first antiphon over the Psalms shall be said, namely “Before they came together” (*Antequam convenirent*), with the psalms “The Lord said” (*Dixit Dominus*), “I will give thanks” (*Confitebor*), “Blessed is the man” (*Beatus vir*), and “Praise, O servants” (*Laudate, pueri*): that is, four psalms under one antiphon. Chapter: “Paul, servant of Christ Jesus” (*Paulus servus Christi Jesu*). Responsory: “O Judah and Jerusalem” (*O Juda et Jerusalem*). Hymn: “Give heed, you who govern” (*Intende, qui regis*). Verse: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (*Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini*). At the *Magnificat*, antiphon: “When she had been betrothed” (*Cum esset desponsata*). Collect: “O God, who [by the Redemption]…” (*Deus qui nos redemptionis*). After these Vespers, no commemoration [Col. 1387B] of Sunday is made.

### CHAPTER IV. On the Nativity of the Lord

On the night of the Nativity of the Lord, the cellarer shall arrange for two lay brothers to prepare a fire in the warming-room, so that the monks may warm themselves at intervals, if the cold requires it. When the collect after the Gospel has ended, the community shall leave the church. Lamps having been lit in the cloister and lavatory by that brother who customarily carries a light at intervals after the Nocturns in chapter, the brothers shall sit in the cloister, and whoever wishes may warm himself.

Then, when the time requires it, the sacristan shall ring the bell gently, and the altar ministers shall prepare themselves for the Mass “The Lord said to me” (*Dominus dixit ad me*). At this Mass they shall be helped in vesting and unvesting by the two brothers who will do the same again later at the morning Mass, namely after Lauds. When the ministers have prepared themselves, the bell shall again be rung for the brothers to assemble in choir; the aforesaid Mass shall be celebrated as on the feast of one apostle. When Mass has been completed, after an interval, while the brothers sit in the cloister, the sacristan shall ring the bell in the order already prescribed, and the Lauds of Matins shall begin. [Col. 1387C]

After the Lauds of Matins, the brothers shall sit in the cloister according to the rule set out above. The *secretarius* [Note: [Col. 1387D] *Secretarius*, that is, the sacristan.] shall summon the altar ministers by the customary signal to prepare themselves, regulating this interval after the Lauds of Matins so that, as dawn begins, the Mass “Light shall shine” (*Lux fulgebit*) may begin. At this Mass no private Masses shall be sung until the Offertory is completed, except Masses for lay brothers who are to communicate. This morning Mass shall be celebrated as on Sundays, and the sick brothers and those assigned to various duties shall go to Communion.

As soon as the brothers leave choir after this Mass has been celebrated, the sacristan shall ring the bell. As on feast days the interval is customarily kept between the Lauds of Matins and Prime, so the same shall be observed between this Mass, “Light shall shine,” and Prime. When the bell has again been rung, the brothers shall come into choir for Prime and make the customary [Col. 1388A] prayer. After Prime they shall enter chapter.

### CHAPTER V. On the Octaves of the Lord

On the following three days, the morning Mass shall be “A child is born to us” (*Puer natus est nobis*).

On the first of these three days, namely Saint Stephen’s Day, the first collect at this Mass shall be “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God” (*Concede, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus*); the second, “Give us, we beseech you” (*Da nobis, quaesumus*). Then the Epistle: “The grace of God has appeared” (*Apparuit gratia Dei*); Gospel: “A decree went out” (*Exiit edictum*).

On the second day, namely that of Saint John the Evangelist, the first collect shall be “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”; the second, “Your Church” (*Ecclesiam tuam*); the third, “Give us, we beseech you.” Then [Col. 1388B] the Epistle: “Kindness has appeared” (*Apparuit benignitas*); Gospel: “The shepherds were speaking” (*Pastores loquebantur*).

On the day of the Holy Innocents, the first collect shall be “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God”; the second, “O God, whose [day this is]” (*Deus, cujus hodierna die*); then, “Give us, we beseech you”; in the fourth place, “Your Church.” Epistle: “Grace has appeared” (*Apparuit gratia*); Gospel: “A decree went out” (*Exiit edictum*).

It should nevertheless be noted that if Saint Stephen’s Day falls on Sunday, or if a deceased person is present at the morning Mass on Saint John’s Day, the Epistle “Grace has appeared” and the Gospel “A decree went out” shall be said. On the day of the Innocents, however, the Epistle shall be “Kindness has appeared” and the Gospel “The shepherds were speaking.” Likewise, if [Col. 1388C] Saint John’s Day falls on Sunday, or if a deceased person is present on the day of the Innocents, the Epistle shall be “Kindness has appeared,” and the Gospel, “The shepherds [were speaking].”

On that day, at Vespers, the first commemoration shall be of Saint Thomas; [Note: [Col. 1387D] The commemoration and feast of Saint Thomas of Canterbury were not in the earliest Usages, but were added here in the year [Col. 1388D] 1191, in which year his feast was received and prescribed by the general chapter.] then of the Nativity, and of the octaves of the saints. Everything else concerning Saint Thomas shall be done as noted in the books. His feast shall be celebrated in full, both by night and by day. The arrangement assigned for the preceding three feasts shall be observed: namely, concerning the commemorations to be made, the arrangement of the morning Mass when Sunday occurs, and a deceased person if one is present.

At the Introit of the principal Mass: “The righteous man shall rejoice” (*Laetabitur justus*). Collect: “Be present, O Lord” (*Adesto, Domine*), etc., as on the feast [Col. 1388D] of Saint Vincent. If it is Sunday, after Lauds a commemoration of Sunday shall first be made, namely “While deep silence” (*Dum medium silentium*); then of the Nativity; then of the octaves of the saints in order. The morning Mass shall be “While deep silence.” First collect: “Almighty everlasting God, direct [our acts]” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, dirige*). Second: “Be present, O Lord.” Third: “Grant.” Afterwards, [the commemorations] of the octaves of the saints. At Vespers one antiphon over the Psalms shall be said: “This holy man for the law” (*Iste sanctus pro lege*).

On the day after Saint Thomas’s feast, unless it is Sunday, the brothers, when Nocturns are completed, shall immediately go, as usual, to read by the lamp; and after Lauds, without an interval, [Col. 1389A] Prime shall follow. When it has been said, Mass shall be celebrated as on Sundays: namely, “A child is born to us.” Collects: “Grant, we beseech”; “Give us, we beseech”; “Your Church”; “O God, whose day this is.” Epistle: “Grace has appeared.” Gospel: “A decree went out.”

After Mass the brothers shall devote themselves to reading until the second hour. Then, after Terce has been said, they shall go to chapter, and afterwards to manual labour. It should also be noted that at the Vigils of this day the exposition of the Gospel, namely “A decree went out,” is to be read and pronounced by a deacon, as at twelve lessons. If this day is Sunday, let it be done as the books prescribe.

### CHAPTER VI. How the Offices of Masses on Sundays from the Nativity of the Lord until Septuagesima Are to Be Arranged Each Year

[Col. 1389B]

The first Sunday which falls after the Nativity of the Lord shall always have, at the morning Mass, the office “While deep silence” (*Dum medium silentium*). Likewise, the first Sunday which falls after the Epiphany shall always have, at the morning Mass, the office “On the lofty throne” (*In excelso throno*), except that if, because Septuagesima is imminent, the office “All the earth” (*Omnis terra*) must be sung together with the history “Lord, not in your anger” (*Domine ne in ira*), then “On the lofty throne” shall be said on the day after Epiphany.

It should be noted that when Sunday falls on the third day after Epiphany, and thereafter until the Octave of Epiphany, the collect “We beseech you, O Lord, [grant our vows]” (*Vota, quaesumus, Domine*) shall be continued every [Col. 1389C] day after the Octave of Epiphany, at Lauds and Vespers, until the following Sunday, on which “All the earth” is to be sung. The same Mass, namely “On the lofty throne,” shall be said on the same days—that is, after the Octave of Epiphany—as directed in the chapter [Note: [Col. 1389D] “In the chapter,” that is, in the chapter on Masses.] on Masses to be said on ferial days, provided that the office “All the earth” has not been said during the Octave of Epiphany or before it.

When, however, five weeks occur between the week in which “On the lofty throne” is sung and Septuagesima, then “All the earth” shall be sung in the first two weeks and “Worship God” (*Adorate Deum*) in the last three. Each of the weeks [Col. 1389D] in which “All the earth” is sung shall have its own proper collect, with the Epistles and Gospels belonging to it; and likewise the final three weeks in which “Worship” is sung, as follows.

In the first week the office “All the earth” is said. Collect: “Almighty everlasting God, who [order heavenly things together]” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui coelestia simul*). Epistle: “Having gifts” (*Habentes donationes*). Gospel: “A wedding took place” (*Nuptiae factae sunt*).

In the second week likewise the office “All the earth.” Collect: “Almighty everlasting God, [look upon] weakness” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, infirmitatem*). Epistle: “Do not be wise in your own eyes” (*Nolite esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos*). Gospel: “When Jesus came down” (*Cum descendisset Jesus*).

In the third week the office “Worship God.” Collect: “O God, who [in so many trials]” (*Deus qui nos in tantis*). Epistle: “Owe nothing to anyone” (*Nemini quidquam debeatis*). [Col. 1390A] Gospel: “As Jesus was going up” (*Ascendente Jesu*).

In the fourth week likewise the office “Worship God.” Collect: “Your household” (*Familiam [tuam]*). Epistle: “Clothe yourselves” (*Induite vos*). Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed” (*Simile est regnum coelorum homini qui seminavit*).

In the fifth week likewise the office “Worship” shall be said with the aforesaid collect, Epistle, and Gospel.

But when four weeks occur within the aforesaid interval, “All the earth” shall be sung in the first two, and “Worship God” in the last two. When only three weeks occur within the aforesaid interval, “All the earth” shall be said in the first of those three weeks with the first two collects, namely “Almighty everlasting God, who [order heavenly things together]” and “Almighty everlasting God, [look upon] weakness,” and with the Epistles and Gospels belonging to them. Thus, on [Col. 1390B] Thursday, “Almighty everlasting God, [look upon] weakness” shall be begun at Lauds. On that same day the Mass “All the earth” shall be sung with the Epistle and Gospel belonging to it, and shall be retained at both Vespers and Lauds through Saturday. The final two weeks, however, shall be conducted as described above for four weeks.

And when, within the often-mentioned interval from “On the lofty throne” to Septuagesima, only two weeks occur, the first shall be arranged as described for three weeks. In the second, in which “Worship God” is sung, the two collects, namely “O God, who [in so many trials]” and “Your household,” with their respective Epistles and Gospels, shall be treated in the same manner.

But when only one week occurs between that of “On the lofty throne” [Col. 1390C] and Septuagesima, then the cantor shall take care, as best he can, to complete both these offices with the above-mentioned collects and with the Epistles and Gospels belonging to them during the two weeks: namely, the first, in which “On the lofty throne” is sung, and the second, before Septuagesima—provided that they could not be completed in that second week before Septuagesima owing to a solemnity of twelve lessons or the commemoration of some saint who has a proper office [Note: [Col. 1390D] *Proprietatem*: that is, a proper office.] in the Gradual.

What we have said must be observed concerning the brevity of time, the saying of two collects in one week with their Epistles and Gospels, and the beginning of the second collect on Thursday. If this has been prevented by a deceased person present, a solemnity of twelve lessons, or the commemoration, on Thursday, of some saint who has a proper office in the Gradual, the cantor shall complete the whole on the first day which he finds free from such impediments after that Thursday and before Sunday. [Col. 1390D] If Friday also is occupied by any of these, then the Sunday Mass shall be sung on Saturday. Therefore, whether on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, wherever the cantor first finds a place free from a saint’s proper office, the Sunday office shall be completed; nor shall it be postponed because of a deceased person present, but both Masses shall be said. The same [Col. 1391A] shall likewise be observed whenever any Sunday Mass has not been said in the community.

### CHAPTER VII. On Saint Sylvester

The feast of Saint Sylvester shall be celebrated in full, both at night and by day, and the commemoration of the Nativity of the Lord shall be retained. Mass shall be arranged as follows. At the Introit: “Your priests, O Lord” (*Sacerdotes tui, Domine*). Collects: “Grant, we beseech, almighty God, that [we may follow blessed Sylvester]” (*Da, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus ut beati Silvestri*); “Grant, we beseech, almighty God”; “Give us, we beseech, O Lord”; “Your Church”; “O God, whose day this is.”

If it is Sunday, after the morning Lauds there shall first be a commemoration of Sunday, namely “While deep silence,” and then of the Nativity; afterwards, of the octaves of the saints in order. The morning Mass [Col. 1391B] shall be “While deep silence.” Collect: I. “Almighty everlasting God, direct our acts.” II. “Grant, we beseech, almighty God, that [we may follow blessed Sylvester].” III. “Grant, we beseech, almighty God”; afterwards, those of the octave of the saints.

At Vespers one antiphon of a confessor shall be said over the Psalms, namely “The Lord knew him” (*Cognovit eum Dominus*). But the chapter and everything thereafter to the end shall be of the octave of the Lord’s Nativity. The first commemoration shall be of Saint Sylvester, then of Sunday, and thereafter of the octaves of the saints.

### CHAPTER VIII. What Is to Be Read at Vigils after the Circumcision of the Lord until Septuagesima

[Col. 1391C]

After the Circumcision of the Lord, the Epistles of Paul shall be read at Vigils on ferial days until Septuagesima. This does not apply, however, on Sundays: rather, sermons of the authoritative Fathers on the Nativity, Circumcision, or Epiphany of the Lord shall be read until the Responsories “Lord, not in your anger” are sung. But if the time from the Circumcision until Septuagesima is short, the Epistles of Paul shall be read not only in church but also in the refectory, in accordance with the cantor’s direction.

### CHAPTER IX. On the Vigil of Epiphany

On the Vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord, the Mass shall be “A child is born” (*Puer natus*); collect, “Our hearts” (*Corda nostra*); then “O God, who [are the author of eternal salvation]” (*Deus qui salutis*), and the other customary collects. It should be understood that the collect “Grant us, your servants” (*Concede [Col. 1391D] nos famulos*) is not counted among the customary collects; it too shall be omitted from the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord until the day after Epiphany. Epistle: “Kindness has appeared.” Gospel: “After Herod’s death” (*Defuncto Herode*).

If the Vigil of Epiphany falls on Sunday, this Mass set out above, with its collect, Epistle, and Gospel, shall be sung after Terce. The morning Mass, however, shall be “A child is born,” with the collect “O God, [author] of salvation,” the Epistle “Kindness has appeared,” and the Gospel “The shepherds were speaking.” It should be noted that when this [Col. 1392A] Vigil falls on Sunday, the collect “O God of eternal salvation” (*Deus qui salutis aeternae*) is said at night after the Gospel, at Lauds, and at Terce; but the collect “Our hearts” is said only at the principal Mass.

### CHAPTER X. On “Lord, Not in Your Anger” and “I Will Bless the Lord”

From the Octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, the Responsories “Lord, not in your anger” (*Domine, ne in ira tua*) shall be said at Vigils on Sundays, and “I will bless the Lord” (*Benedicam Dominum*), etc., on ferial days, as they are found in the Antiphonary. The Sunday antiphons at Nocturns, and the ferial antiphons at the first nocturn, shall be said until Easter; at Vespers over the Psalms, until the Lord’s Supper; and from the Octave of Pentecost [Col. 1392B] until the Nativity of the Lord. The antiphons assigned to the second nocturn on ferial days shall be said only in Lent.

*Alleluia* shall be said from the Octave of Pentecost until Lent. [Note: [Col. 1391D] “Alleluia, etc., until Lent.” This is according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 15.] The Invitatories assigned for ferial days shall be used until the Passion of the Lord, and from the Kalends of November until Advent. The short Responsories at Nocturns shall be used from the Octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of November. The short Responsories at Lauds and Vespers shall be used until Septuagesima, and from the Octave of Pentecost until Advent of the Lord. The antiphons at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*, and all the short verses, shall be used until Lent, and from the Octave of Pentecost until Advent. The antiphons over the Psalms at Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None shall be used until [Col. 1392C] Palm Sunday, and from the Octave of Pentecost until Advent.

If a feast of twelve lessons intervenes, these items shall nonetheless be said on the days to which they are assigned after the feast. The same shall be done after the Octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary. It should be noted that when “Lord, not in your anger” is sung five times, the final lessons and final antiphons are repeated if necessary; and when it is sung four times, the final antiphon is repeated.

### CHAPTER XI. On Septuagesima

The Responsories “In the beginning” (*In principio*) shall be said in Septuagesima and Sexagesima, both on Sundays and on ferial days during this period. From Septuagesima until the Sunday on which books are distributed [Note: [Col. 1391D] “Until the Sunday on which,” etc.: that is, until the [Col. 1392D] first Sunday of Lent, on which books are distributed to the monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, as will be said below.], such portion of Genesis shall be read at Vigils as may suitably suffice, at the cantor’s discretion, for the Vigil lessons throughout this period. Whatever remains after the Vigil readings, together with the subsequent books as far as the Books of Kings, shall be read in the refectory. Careful provision shall be made that these are finished before the Sunday on which the office “Judge me, O God” (*Judica me, Deus*) is sung.

Nevertheless, on Sundays the homilies on the Sunday Gospels shall first [Col. 1393A] be read in the refectory, or whatever else must be read on any day because of some feast. Therefore, on the first Sunday of Septuagesima, after the homily—or something else concerning a feast, if there is one—has been read in the refectory as stated, the reading of Genesis, or of the other books, shall begin at the point at which the cantor foresees that the Vigil lesson should end by Lent.

From the first Sunday of Lent, on which we distribute books, at Vigils in church on ferial days we use Saint Augustine’s treatises on the Psalms until the Sunday on which Jeremiah is begun. But if the Purification of Saint Mary falls on Septuagesima Sunday, the history shall be begun at Vigils on Monday: namely, the Book of Genesis, with its preface and the Responsories “In the beginning God [created]” (*In principio Deus*); and on the following Sunday the Vigil lessons shall be said: “Therefore the Lord God took the man” (*Tulit ergo Dominus hominem*). [Col. 1393B]

### CHAPTER XII. On the Tracts

In Septuagesima and thereafter, on all Sundays and feasts of twelve lessons, at the principal Masses until Easter, all Tracts shall be sung antiphonally by the two choirs. The same shall be done on Good Friday with the Tract “Deliver me” (*Eripe me*). At the Vigils of Easter and Pentecost, “Praise the Lord, all nations” (*Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes*), and on Ember Saturdays likewise the Tract “Blessed are you” (*Benedictus es*), shall be sung antiphonally by the two choirs.

This Tract is begun by the choir of the Invitatory; [Col. 1393C] the other choir shall continue, “And praiseworthy [are you]” (*Et laudabilis*), etc.; and so it shall be done with each verse. At the end, the first verse shall be repeated by the one who began it, and sung through jointly by both choirs. At the end of the aforesaid Tracts too, both choirs shall sing together. All other Tracts shall be sung together by the whole choir and community.

It is not customary for a Tract to be said on ferial days outside Lent, except on Ember Saturdays, the Vigils of Pentecost, and principal and private Masses for the dead. Nor is one said at morning Masses on Sunday, either within Lent or outside it, unless the morning Mass is of Sunday because the Mass of the feast, after Terce, is not to be repeated. For on ferial days in Lent [Col. 1393D] “Lord, not according to [our sins]” (*Domine, non secundum*), the Tract “From my necessities” (*De necessitatibus meis*), and “Lord, hear my prayer” (*Domine, exaudi orationem*) are not omitted on Wednesday before Easter for any solemnity. Tracts sung antiphonally shall be begun in the choir in which the Invitatory is located. The cantor, or the person performing his office at Mass, shall begin the other Tracts in whichever choir he is.

### CHAPTER XIII. On the Beginning of the Fast

On Wednesday at the beginning of the fast [Note: [Col. 1393D] “Beginning of the Fast” is understood as Ash Wednesday.], after Prime has been said, the brothers shall go out into the cloister, and the altar ministers shall prepare themselves to celebrate Mass, as on other [Col. 1394A] days. Then, when the priest is vested in alb and maniple and the bell has been rung, the brothers in the cloister shall remove their shoes; leaving them in that place, they shall enter the church and stand in their order with their faces turned toward the altar. The weekly altar ministers, having removed their shoes in the vestry, shall come into choir.

After this the cantor shall begin the antiphon “Arise” (*Exsurge*); as he begins it, they shall turn to face one another. Then follows the verse “O God, our ears have heard” (*Deus auribus nostris*) and the *Glory be to the Father*. Next, the weekly minister of the Mass shall say the verse, “Show us, O Lord” (*Ostende nobis, Domine*); and, with the brothers prostrate on the stalls [Note: [Col. 1393D] “On the stalls,” namely, on the upper part of the lower choir.], there shall follow, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), the *Our Father*, “and lead us not [into temptation],” and the whole Psalm “May God have mercy [on us]” (*Deus misereatur*) with the *Glory be to the Father*. Verse: “And let [the brightness of the Lord] come upon us” (*Et veniat super nos*). “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*). “Let us pray” (*Oremus*): “Grant us, O Lord, protections” (*Concede nobis, Domine, praesidia*). Afterwards they shall rise and stand with their faces toward the altar until the Introit of Mass. [Col. 1394B]

Then, after the abbot has received the stole and pastoral staff from the sacristan and has blessed the ashes, previously placed by the sacristan in the sanctuary, facing north in the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 1394D] *Presbyterium* here denotes that part which extends from the first step of the choir to the altar itself.], and sprinkled them with holy water, the antiphon “Hear us, O Lord” (*Exaudi nos, Domine*) shall be sung, and the others as found in the books. When “Hear us, O Lord” has been begun, the abbot, having laid aside his stole, shall come before the step and, kneeling beneath it, first receive the sacred ashes from the weekly minister of the Mass. Having received them, he shall rise, resume the stole, stand upon the step, and, facing the choir, cast the blessed ashes upon the head of each person, beginning with the altar ministers, while all kneel upon the ground. While the ashes are imposed, whoever wishes may sit. If the community is large, the ashes shall be distributed in different places according to the abbot’s direction. When all have been admonished through the imposition of ashes to remember their own corruption, the abbot, having laid aside his stole, shall come into choir. [Col. 1394C]

If the abbot is the weekly minister of the Mass, the cantor shall assign the Mass to another. In the abbot’s absence, the weekly minister of the Mass shall bless the ashes. Once they have been blessed, he shall first receive them, together with his minister, from one of the priests vested in a stole, whom the cantor has notified beforehand. The weekly minister himself shall impose ashes on the person from whom he received them, and then return to his place. The person who gave him ashes shall also give them to all the others who approach in the order of their conversion [i.e. monastic profession]. It should be understood that while this office of ashes is performed, the person whom the cantor appoints must hold them before the abbot.

When the antiphon “Let us change our garments” (*Immutemur habitu*) has begun, the priest and minister shall put on their shoes and, when the bell has been rung, approach to celebrate Mass. All the others shall remain barefoot until Mass is completed, and shall then put on their shoes again in the cloister. Further, outside the choir, the prior, assisted by some brother, shall impose these ashes upon members of the household and guests, if present. [Col. 1394D]

It should be understood that the Tract “Lord, not according to [our sins]” (*Domine, non secundum*) [Col. 1395A] is said both on this day and on the other three days of each week during Lent—namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—until Wednesday before Easter. The sole exception is the Wednesday after the first Sunday of Lent, on which Wednesday the Tract “From my necessities” (*De necessitatibus*) is sung. The canonical preface, namely “Who by bodily fasting” (*Qui corporali jejunio*), shall be said both on this day and on every other day of Lent at the Mass of the fast, until the Lord’s Supper.

### CHAPTER XIV. On the Feasts of Saints Which Fall from the Beginning of the Fast until Palm Sunday

If, on ferial days between the beginning of the fast and Palm Sunday, a feast of twelve lessons on which we work occurs, first the Mass of the fast shall be said, omitting the customary collects. It shall be sung by the weekly minister of the preceding week, and the community shall hear it throughout. Once it is completed and the community has put its shoes on again, if it is Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, the Mass of the feast shall follow, sung by the weekly minister of the present week. After the Offertory, private Masses shall be celebrated. The ministers shall be assisted in vesting and unvesting for this Mass by those who did the same at the preceding Mass. Lay brothers shall not attend this Mass. The same shall be observed for the feast of Saint Maurice when it falls during the Ember fasts in September. [Col. 1395B]

At the *Te igitur* of the first Mass in Lent, the community shall prostrate itself upon the stalls; the Hours of the whole day, however, shall be performed without genuflection and shall be of the feast. But if it is a feast on which we do not work, [Col. 1395C] the first Mass shall be that of the fast, though not solemnly; and the brothers shall prostrate themselves at the *Te igitur*. This shall not be done at the solemn Mass after Terce. It is certainly to be remembered that genuflection at the *Te igitur* does not take place on a day of twelve lessons except in Lent.

### CHAPTER XV. On the First Sunday of Lent and the Observance of That Season

On the first Sunday of Lent, after Prime, while the morning Mass is being sung, the cantor, assisted by such brothers as the prior may assign him at his request if he needs them, shall bring the books which are to be given out in chapter and arrange them properly before the abbot’s seat, with something spread beneath them. On that day in chapter the reading from the Rule concerning the observance of Lent—namely, “Although at every season” (*Licet omni tempore*) [Note: [Col. 1395D] From chapters 49 and 48 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]—and the final portion of the preceding chapter, namely, “But in the days of Lent” (*In Quadragesimae vero diebus*), shall be read. [Col. 1395D]

When this has been read and expounded, the cantor, by the abbot’s command and with his assistants or others if necessary, shall distribute the books. Receiving them with both hands in joy at the divine Scriptures, the monks shall each bow deeply and gladly. It should be understood that sick monks shall attend this chapter, in order to receive books with the others.

Afterwards the abbot shall appoint brothers who, according to the Rule, shall go about the monastery throughout the year during the hours when the brothers are free for reading, insofar as they perceive it necessary. They shall look after the workshops, cloister, oratory, chapter-house, dormitory, warming-room, refectory, kitchen, and parlours, lest anyone be found conducting himself improperly. For this purpose they may enter the aforesaid places, except the parlours. [Col. 1396A] [Note: [Col. 1395D] By “parlours” understand the place adjoining the regular cloister, to which, according to chapter 72 of this book, the monks were accustomed to withdraw in order to speak with the prior concerning matters necessary to them. [Col. 1396D]]

On this day, after Compline, let the crosses be veiled and a curtain be stretched before the presbytery. [Note: [Col. 1396D] Curtain: that is, the veil which is hung between the choir and the presbytery during this season of Lent alone.] It shall remain thus on all non-festal days throughout Lent, until after Compline on the Wednesday before Easter. But on Saturdays and on the vigils of saints’ feasts of twelve lessons, before Vespers the curtain is to be drawn back from before the presbytery; and on the following day, after Compline, it is to be let down again. Likewise, it is to be drawn back for a Mass for a deceased person presently laid out, and for the exequies, at the words *Enter not into judgment*, until the seven Psalms are ended after the burial; and for the blessing of a novice. At Mass on non-festal days, so that the priest may freely ask the abbot, if he is present, for the blessing before reading the Gospel, the subdeacon shall draw back slightly the corner of the curtain on the abbot’s side, and, once the blessing has been given, shall let it fall again as before. The deacon, however, shall approach the curtain where it has been raised, asking for the blessing.

During these holy days of Lent, according to the instructions of our blessed father Benedict, we ought to devote ourselves particularly to prayer. Therefore, each brother, according to an established custom, shall every day offer private prayer to the Lord in the church during reading-time, unless a deceased person presently laid out prevents this. If during these days of Lent the cross behind the altar is taken down for any deceased person, or for communicating or anointing a sick person, it shall be uncovered until restored to its proper place, namely above the altar.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Two Weeks before Easter

On the two Sundays before Easter, *Glory be to the Father* is not said at *Asperges me*; rather, after the verse, the chant is repeated from the beginning. At other times, after the *Glory*, the repetition is made at *Lavabis me*. During these fourteen days, in which *Glory be to the Father* is not said at the Introit of Mass, except at Masses of solemnities and on non-festal Masses not belonging to Lent, the altar ministers, who, while that Introit is sung, stand at the entrance to the choir awaiting the time to enter, shall immediately enter and proceed to the altar when they hear the verse of the psalm begun after the Introit has been sung once through.

During these days the cantor shall divide the book of the prophet Jeremiah, to be read both in church and in the refectory, into two parts. One part shall be read in church on non-festal days at Vigils, until the Thursday before Easter. This part shall begin near the beginning of the book itself, a little before the point where the eighth Lesson ended at Vigils on Sunday night, namely: “See the word of the Lord. Have I become a wilderness?” From that point the cantor shall appoint from this prophecy, according to the greater or lesser length of the nights in each year, as much as he judges sufficient for the purpose stated. But when he judges that the portion to be read only in church should end, he shall have it begun in the refectory on the Sunday on which this prophecy was begun at Vigils—provided, however, that the homily of blessed Pope Gregory on the Gospel, “Which of you convicts me of sin?”, has first been read—and it shall be continued to the end of the book, taking care above all that the entire book be read within these days.

## CHAPTER XVII. Order on Palm Branches

[Col. 1397B]

On Palm Sunday the abbot shall perform the exorcism of the water; then he himself shall begin Terce. When it is ended, taking the pastoral staff, he shall bless, upon the step of the presbytery, the branches of trees placed there by the sacristan before Terce, and afterwards sprinkle them with holy water. When this has been done, the cantor, after offering a branch to the abbot, shall begin the antiphon *The Hebrew Children*; and immediately the sacristan, with his assistants and with those whom the prior has directed, shall distribute the blessed branches to the monks and novices, and shall give the remainder to the lay brothers, household, and guests, if present. Meanwhile, when the aforesaid antiphon is finished, another antiphon, *The Hebrew Children*, shall be sung.

[Col. 1397C] When these matters have thus been arranged, as the cantor begins the antiphon *The Crowds Go Forth to Meet*, the subdeacon shall go out carrying holy water, followed by the deacon with the unveiled cross. The community shall follow him in the order in which it stands in choir, with the monks preceding the lay brothers, so that the abbot—or, if the abbot is absent, the priest of the week—shall go last; after him the novices, and after the novices the lay brothers. The procession shall take place only through the cloister. The prior shall take care that nothing unsuitable be found in the cloister while this procession, or the other procession at the Purification or Ascension, is performed.

When the antiphon *The Crowds Go Forth to Meet* is finished, the antiphon *They Gathered Together* is begun; and while it is sung, the first station shall be made in the part adjacent to the dormitory. When it is finished and the verse *But One* immediately follows, the brothers shall move from that place, and the second station shall be held beside the refectory. At the repetition of this antiphon, namely *What Shall We Do, Since This Man*, they shall proceed to the final station near the church. At every station the deacon and subdeacon shall have their faces and the cross turned toward the community; both while walking and while standing, the subdeacon shall be before the deacon.

At the final station, when the cantor begins *Hail, Our King, Son of David*, the community shall bow to the cross, with knees and hands placed upon the ground. Then all shall rise and thereafter remain standing, facing the cross, until *Glory and Praise* is begun.

Meanwhile, while this antiphon *Hail, Our King* is sung, [Col. 1398A] the sacristan shall carry the lectern—which before Terce he placed in the chapter house—together with the text of the Gospels and the stole, to the place where the deacon is to read the Gospel: that is, before the church door. Near the end of the aforesaid antiphon *Hail, Our King*, the deacon shall hand the holy cross to the subdeacon; and the subdeacon meanwhile shall, as directed, set down the holy water. [Note: [Col. 1397D] “He shall set down,” or *jussum ponat*, means the same as “he shall place it on the ground.”] When the deacon has put on the stole, he shall move a little away from the lectern and ask the abbot for a blessing. Then, turned towards the east, he shall read the Gospel, with the subdeacon standing before him holding the cross and facing the community. When it has been read, he shall put off the stole and receive the cross; and the subdeacon shall take up the holy water again. The community also shall then stand with faces turned toward one another.

Two brothers, who should already have been instructed by the cantor, shall enter the church near the end of the Gospel; and, with the door closed, standing with faces turned toward the procession, [Col. 1398B] they shall sing the verses *Glory and Praise*, as arranged in the book. When they have finished, and the same brothers have repeated the opening of the same verses, *Glory and Praise*, they shall return to the procession and stand in their own order. When these things have been done, the abbot shall begin the responsory *As the Lord Entered*, and all shall enter the church singing it. On entering the choir, they shall lay the branches they carry in their hands upon the step of the presbytery; the sacristan shall immediately remove them. Where the deacon has set down the cross, it shall remain there unveiled until after Compline.

[Col. 1398C] Afterwards Mass shall be celebrated as on the feast of one apostle. It should be known that guests may not take part in the processions through the cloister, nor enter the chapter house for the addresses, unless there is some person of such distinction that this ought to be allowed. During this week no deacon shall receive the Gospel according to the regular rotation, nor shall any priest receive the week for Mass; rather, the cantor, with the abbot’s advice, shall assign these offices on the table. Nevertheless, the deacon may be changed on Saturday if necessary.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the Passions Are to Be Begun

For the Passion at this Mass, both *The Lord be with you* and *Glory to you, O Lord* are said. At the Passions on Tuesday and Wednesday, *The Lord be with you* is said, but *Glory to you, O Lord* is not said. On Friday, neither *The Lord be with you* nor *Glory to you, O Lord* is said. Whenever *Glory to you, O Lord* is not said before the Passion, the brothers do not sign themselves with the sign of the cross.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Wednesday before Easter

On the Wednesday before Easter, after regular Vespers, the office for the dead shall be said with its antiphons and collects, as on other days. The curtain [Note: [Col. 1398D] That is, the veil which had hung stretched before the high altar during Lent.] shall be removed after Compline.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Lord’s Supper, Parasceve, and the Vigil of Easter

From the Thursday before Easter until the Monday after the Octave of Easter, nothing shall be done for the dead, except the daily Mass. This, however, is omitted on Parasceve, on the following Saturday, and on Easter Day; on that day, nevertheless, the priest of the week singing the daily Mass of the Resurrection shall say the collect *Incline, O Lord*, and, if it is a trental, shall add *O God, whose property it is*.

On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday before Easter, after the nocturnal praise has been completed, when the brothers are seated in the cloister at the lights, and the sacristan sees that the time has arrived at which, according to the Rule, Lauds are to be sung near daybreak [Note: [Col. 1399D] “According to the Rule”: that is, according to the Rule of St Benedict.], he shall light one candle and place it on a candlestick on the first step of the presbytery. Thus, on Thursday the bell is rung; but on Friday and Saturday the brothers are summoned to the Hour by the board. Meanwhile, while the hymn of that Hour is sung, all the lights of the church, except the aforesaid candle, shall be extinguished by the sacristan. When the cantor begins the antiphon at the *Benedictus*, the same sacristan shall extinguish that candle also. When the abbot begins the *Our Father*, he shall carry into the choir for the saying of the collect the lighted candle which, before the one at the *Benedictus* is extinguished, must be hidden in a concealed place.

## CHAPTER XXI. Again, on the Lord’s Supper

On the Thursday before Easter, Mass shall be celebrated solemnly after Prime, as on the feast of one apostle and without genuflection; and all, both lay brothers and others, shall communicate at the high altar, unless the size of the crowd requires otherwise. The deacon shall place as many hosts to be consecrated [Col. 1399C] as are sufficient to provide Holy Communion for all the brothers on that day and to permit a portion of the sacrament to be reserved both for the office of the following day and for the sick.

After the peace, the body of the Lord shall be taken from the vessel upon the altar and placed upon the paten, to be consumed at that hour. The cloth also shall immediately be removed from that vessel, and another, presented by the sacristan at that hour, shall be placed in it. When this substitution has been made by the sacristan, the abbot, or whoever sings the Mass, shall immediately reverently place in the previously mentioned vessel the portion of Holy Communion to be reserved for the next day. Then the old cloth, carefully shaken out over the paten, shall be burned over the sacrarium, and its ashes thrown into it. It should be known that on this day [Col. 1399D] no one is to sing a private Mass, except for communicating lay brothers when the number requires it; and that Mass itself shall be of the day. But the Mass of Saint Mary, at which no one is to communicate on this day, and the daily Mass for the dead, shall be sung.

After Sext, the porter, unless the abbot has directed someone else, shall select as many poor persons as there are monks in the monastery. They are not all to be received for prayer, but shall remain in one place until they are led to the Mandatum. Meanwhile, while None is sung, the lay brother who is assistant to the monk responsible for the guesthouse, together with the other lay brothers summoned by the cellarer, shall lead the poor into the cloister and make them sit and remove their shoes, beginning from the church door by which the monks ordinarily leave the church and enter the cloister. [Col. 1400A] They shall bring there the vessels, cloths or towels needed for the Mandatum, and hot water, and shall arrange all things in proper order; the cellarer shall provide these vessels and other necessities.

When None has been said, the brothers shall leave the church, beginning with the seniors, in the same order as on non-festal days and at Christmas—namely, one after another—they go into chapter. The abbot shall pass all the poor persons as far as the last, and they shall perform the Mandatum for the poor in the cloister. The lay brothers, as fellow-workers in that holy Mandatum, shall carefully and adequately provide water and towels to the monks performing it. The cellarer, who hands the money for the poor to the monks, shall indicate to the monks at the end of the order that they are to complete the office of the Mandatum for the sick and absent monks, and for the porter, in the persons of the poor placed at the end of the line. Those sick persons from the infirmary who are able to be present may sit there.

After they have washed, dried, and kissed the feet of the poor, the monks shall wash their own hands. When this has been done, each brother shall give one coin to each poor person. The coins are to be given with bent knees, and the hands of the poor are to be kissed.
