Then the brothers shall rise together and, again asking forgiveness before the poor [Note: [Col. 1400D] “Asking forgiveness”: that is, kneeling with hands placed upon the ground.], shall say: “We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple.” Afterwards they shall go to manual work, if time permits. Then [Col. 1400C] the poor shall be led to the guesthouse, where the abbot with his assistants shall pour water over their hands, and afterwards they shall be refreshed. It should be known that all persons arriving on this day are, out of reverence for the Lord’s Mandatum, to be charitably refreshed at a suitable hour with bread and broth.

When the Mandatum of the poor is completed, the sacristan shall immediately summon as many brothers as he requires and uncover the altars; he shall properly arrange and put away the coverings removed from them. At Vespers the wooden board shall be struck, and that Hour shall be sung aloud as on other days. From this point no bell shall be rung in the church until the Mass on the Vigil of Easter, nor in the refectory or on the clock. It should also be known that from this point the verses in the refectory before and after food, and *Benedicite* with the blessing of the drink before the collation, and likewise the verses in chapter, shall be said more softly and in a low voice until after Vespers on the Vigil of Easter.

After the community has risen from the table, the brothers appointed by the table in chapter on that day for the Mandatum shall carry into the cloister the hot water which they themselves must previously have heated. If the abbot sees that help from the lay brothers is required in drawing, heating, and carrying the water into the cloister, the cellarer shall supply it adequately through the lay brothers. After a short interval, [Col. 1401A] the brothers shall go in the customary way to the refectory for *Libere*. Then the sacristan shall strike the board for the Mandatum. The community of monks shall sit in the cloister, as on Saturdays for the Mandatum, with the prior taking the abbot’s place; the cantor shall begin the antiphon *The Lord Jesus*, with sick persons who can be present in attendance, and with lay brothers seated on either side—namely, after the last monks and after the last novices.

Then the abbot and his assistants, girded with towels, shall wash, dry, and kiss everyone’s feet; the abbot, however, shall wash only twelve feet, namely those of four monks, four novices, and four lay brothers. If the number of novices is insufficient, the number shall be made up from the lay brothers. Assistants shall be assigned to the washers in this manner: two to the abbot, and one to each of the others, to provide them sufficiently with water and towels. Whenever they pass before the prior, both the abbot and the others shall bow. When the service has been completed, the abbot shall wash the feet of his two assistants, and the others shall wash one another’s feet. Finally, one of those assigned to him—the prior, namely—shall wash the abbot’s feet in the same place, while the other dries and kisses them. Afterwards both the abbot and the others shall pour water over one another’s hands.

Then, clothed in their cowls, they shall come to the place where the kitchen weekly servers customarily bow on Saturdays after the Mandatum, and there they shall bow. Then, when the prior rises and yields place to the abbot, all shall rise together; and when he is seated, all shall sit. At collation, the Gospel reading, namely *Before the Feast of the Passover*, shall be read, as on other days, by the deacon whom the cantor has directed, sitting down. [Col. 1401C] The end of this reading lies within the abbot’s discretion. Thereafter Compline shall be said more quietly in a moderate voice, though the sound of the psalmody must ring out clearly and distinctly. From this point the same shall be done at all Hours in psalmody and chant, except at Vigils and Lauds, until Vespers of Easter.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Parasceve

On Parasceve, after a short interval following Lauds, the brothers shall remove their shoes in the dormitory, and the sick in the infirmary, unless they are too seriously ill. Then the board shall be struck, and the community shall come into choir; a short prayer [Col. 1401D] shall be made at the stalls. [Note: [Col. 1401] A short prayer means the *Our Father* and *Hail Mary*. A solemn prayer means the *Our Father*, *Hail Mary*, and Creed.] The solemn prayer shall be completed in the customary manner before Terce. When Prime has been said, all shall follow the abbot, in the order in which they stand in choir, and enter chapter. The abbot shall sit on the right with his choir, and the prior on the left with his own choir, at the entrance of the chapter house; after them all shall sit in the order in which they processed, and shall recite the entire Psalter. When the Psalter is finished, the brothers shall devote the whole day to reading. After None, the abbot and ministers shall vest for the office.

Meanwhile the sacristan shall cover the surface of the altar with clean coverings, and one of the ministers shall light two lamps about the altar, as is customary on festal days. [Col. 1402A] Then, after the board has been struck, the community shall come into choir, and the reading *In Their Affliction* shall be read without a title by a brother previously instructed by the cantor. When he begins it, the abbot and ministers shall enter at the altar barefoot, omitting the customary prayer before the altar. When the reading is ended, the tract *Lord, I Have Heard* shall be said, then the collect *O God, from Whom Even Judas*—but *Let us bend the knee* is not said.

Then the reading *The Lord Said to Moses and Aaron* shall be read by the subdeacon, likewise without a title and wearing the maniple. He shall read it plainly as another Lesson, not as an Epistle. When it has been said, the tract *Deliver Me, O Lord* shall be sung; then the Passion and the solemn prayers shall follow, namely, *Let Us Pray, Beloved*.

Near the end of these prayers, [Col. 1402B] the sacristan shall spread some coarse linen before the altar in the presbytery, where the cross is to be adored. Two priests or deacons, forewarned by the cantor, shall put on albs for the office of the cross. Before the words *Through our Lord* at the end of the last collect are finished, they shall come behind the altar and, when the prayer has ended, take up the veiled cross which the sacristan had placed there before None; they shall carry it to the step of the altar, as the abbot and ministers depart from the altar. Then, supporting the cross by some suitable object, one holding it on the right and the other on the left, they shall sing, with bent knees, *My People*.

Two brothers before the step of the presbytery shall say three times *Agios*—“Holy”—bending the knee once at the first, after *O Theos*—“O God”—has ended, and rising to continue the rest. The choir shall repeat *Sanctus*—“Holy”—three times, likewise bending the knee at the first, after *Sanctus Deus*—“Holy God”—has been said. This shall be done in the same way a third time, both by the choir and by the brothers. While the final *Holy God* is begun, those holding the cross shall adore it briefly. When the chant is ended, uncovering it, they shall begin the antiphon *Behold the Wood of the Cross*; immediately all shall ask forgiveness opposite it. The other crosses shall be uncovered by the sacristans.

The abbot alone, then after him the deacon and subdeacon together, in albs without maniples, and thereafter monks and novices two by two, and all the lay brothers, shall adore and kiss the cross in the presbytery, prostrate with their whole body, but only briefly. While the adoration is performed, they shall stand with faces turned toward the altar; one may sit, however, if desired. The porter shall come at that hour, adore, and depart; he shall immediately return [Col. 1402D] to the gate. It should be known that, in adoring and kissing the cross, they are to observe the order which they follow in approaching for the peace and Communion. Meanwhile the chants belonging to this office shall be completed. It should also be known that, as the abbot directs, several crosses may be offered for adoration at other altars both to monks and lay brothers. While this is being done, the prior, attended reverently by the sacristan or another brother whom he has summoned by signal, shall present another cross for adoration outside the choir to guests, if present, and to the household. When all have adored, those holding the cross shall raise it and begin the antiphon *Above All Things*; immediately [Col. 1403A] the community shall ask forgiveness opposite it. The monks shall restore the cross to its place above its altar.

Then the abbot and deacon, having resumed with the subdeacon the things which they had laid aside at the altar, shall approach barefoot as before and shall make the prayer and say the confession. When this is done, the deacon shall place on the altar the corporal, previously laid by the sacristan upon the credence. The abbot, carrying the Lord’s body together with the vessel containing it, shall set it beside the corporal. When the deacon has arranged on the altar, as is customary for Mass, the chalice containing wine mixed with water and offered to the abbot, the abbot, having first used incense, shall open the vessel, wash his fingers, and take the Holy Communion from the vessel and place it on the corporal.

Then, without elevating either the Lord’s body or the chalice, [Col. 1403B] he shall say in a moderate voice: *Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts*, and *Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord*. At the words *Through the same our Lord*, etc., he shall divide the Lord’s body into three parts. Afterwards he shall say *For ever and ever* in a low voice; and when all answer *Amen*, he shall put one part into the chalice, saying nothing. The deacon, having made the censing and washed his hands, shall stand with the subdeacon where he customarily stands for the collects, until he ought to approach the altar to communicate.

Neither *The peace of the Lord* shall be said nor peace given; no forgiveness shall be requested from the community; nor shall *Lamb of God* be sung. Then the abbot and ministers shall communicate. Meanwhile the brothers shall keep their faces turned towards the altar. When the ministers have communicated, [Col. 1403C] the community shall leave and put shoes upon their feet. The cellarer shall ensure that warm water is available in the cloister, so that anyone wishing to wash his feet may do so.

Before Vespers the sacristan shall remove the coverings from the altar. Then, when the board has been struck, Vespers shall be celebrated. At mealtime the lay brothers shall clean the church. The monks in the refectory shall give thanks in the manner of servers; and the aforesaid lay brothers shall clean the cloister and chapter house after Compline.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Vigil of Easter

On the Saturday of the Easter Vigil, the concurrentes, epacts, and indictions for the year of the Lord shall be written on a slip prepared by the cantor and attached on that day to the candle to be blessed. After Sext [Col. 1403D] the sacristan shall adorn all the altars. After None, when he has struck the board gently, the abbot and ministers shall vest in sacred garments. The sacristan shall carry the lectern [Note: [Col. 1403D] Lectern: that is, the pulpit from which the Gospel is read.] on which the Gospel is read, with the book of the Gospels laid upon it, to the step of the presbytery where the abbot customarily performs the blessings. He shall carry the candle to be blessed upon its candlestick, its weight likewise not exceeding three pounds of regular bread, and place it at the right side of the lectern.

When these things are ready, the board shall be struck again for the brothers to assemble in choir. Then fire brought in a dish with live coals shall be blessed, and the abbot, standing upon the step of the presbytery, shall sprinkle it with holy water. [Col. 1404A] Meanwhile all lights in the church shall be extinguished and afterwards lit from the blessed fire. When a candle has been lit from it, the Paschal candle shall be blessed by the deacon, clothed in a stole and facing the altar, while the subdeacon stands at his right holding the candle in his hand. When, in reading, the deacon comes to the words, “Receive, holy Father, the evening sacrifice of this incense,” the cantor shall take care to press five grains of incense into it in the form of a cross. When the same deacon pronounces the words “A glowing fire kindles,” he shall take the light from the subdeacon’s hand and make the candle blaze. Then the subdeacon, having extinguished his candle, shall go to his place. The Paschal candle shall burn until after Compline on the following day; it shall remain in the place where it was blessed until the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

When the blessing has been completed, the reading *In the Beginning God Created Heaven and Earth* and the others shall follow, without titles. The deacon shall put off the stole and return to his place wearing the maniple. It should be known that the dish with the aforesaid coals is not to be taken out of the presbytery until the Paschal candle is lit, so that if the lighted candle should happen to go out, it may be relit from the same coals. The abbot, wearing the chasuble, shall come alone to the altar once the reading *In the Beginning God Created Heaven and Earth* has been begun, but shall by no means make the customary prayer before it. The choirs shall then face one another and shall duly complete the remaining readings, with their collects and tracts, [Col. 1404C] as they stand in the books.

It should be known that the order of brothers reading these lessons begins with the seniors; but on the Saturdays of the Ember Days, with the juniors. The cantor must nevertheless take care that those who read may, according to the Rule, [Note: [Col. 1404D] See the Rule of St Benedict, chapter 48.] edify the hearers. When the readings, chant, and collects have been celebrated, the abbot shall return to the vestry, leave his chasuble there, and thus go to his place. As he departs from the altar, the Litany shall be said by two brothers before the step of the presbytery, with both choirs responding together. When they arrive at the words *We sinners beseech you: hear us*, the abbot and ministers shall enter the vestry and prepare themselves for Mass.

Then, after the Litany, the cantor—or the succentor, if the Invitatory belongs to his choir—shall solemnly begin *Kyrie eleison*. Three lamps and two candles around the altar shall be lit from the blessed fire, and the abbot shall approach the altar with the full ministry, make the customary prayer, and then say the confession. While he pronounces the hymn *Glory to God in the Highest*, and the cantor continues *Peace to humankind*, the bell shall be rung until the words *Lord God, heavenly King* are said. No private Mass may be said by anyone on this day. At this Mass *The peace of the Lord* shall be said, but not *Lamb of God*. After *The peace of the Lord*, everyone shall immediately turn in his place to face the altar until the abbot says *Let us pray* after *The Lord be with you*. If the cantor judges that the daylight will not suffice for all to be completed in daylight, [Col. 1405A] he shall see to it that the vespertinal Lauds are sung somewhat less slowly than on other days. After the meal, they shall perform the Mandatum in the customary manner.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Saints’ Feasts Falling after the Saturday before Palm Sunday until the Octave of Easter

If the feast of our blessed father Benedict, or another feast of twelve lessons on which no work is done, falls after the Saturday preceding Palm Sunday until Thursday of Easter week, it shall be observed on that Thursday. If there are two such feasts, the first shall be observed on Thursday, the next on Saturday.

[Col. 1405B] But if, from the Saturday preceding Palm Sunday until the Lord’s Supper, and from Thursday of Easter until after the Octave, a feast of twelve lessons on which work is done occurs, commemoration of the feast of twelve lessons shall be made at Vespers on the vigil, at Lauds, at Mass, and at Vespers of that day. The feast of which a commemoration is customarily made shall conclude with the usual commemoration. But if, from the Lord’s Supper until Thursday of Easter, a feast of twelve lessons on which work is done occurs, or one of which we make a commemoration, no mention of it shall be made.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Easter Week

For the three days following Easter Day, [Col. 1405C] the brothers shall devote themselves to reading and shall not work, because we keep those three days solemn in veneration of the holy Resurrection, as the feast of an apostle. Invitatories, however, are never sung except at twelve lessons, by two brothers. On the other three following days we work, but nevertheless celebrate the daily Mass solemnly. At this Mass there shall also be two ministers, namely a deacon and subdeacon; two lighted candles beside the altar; and incense after the Offertory. It should also be known that on Easter Day and the three following days, *Glory to God in the Highest*, the Preface *Truly it is worthy, O Lord, at all times*, and *Communicantes* and *Hanc igitur oblationem* are repeated at both Masses.

On the remaining following days [Col. 1405D] when we work, one daily Mass shall be celebrated after Terce; at it *Glory to God in the Highest*, the aforesaid Preface, *Communicantes*, and *Hanc igitur oblationem* shall be said every day. *I believe in one God* is sung only on Easter Day.

This should be remembered: on Easter Monday, at the morning Mass, the collect of the day is not said as on the other following days, because the collect on Easter Day and that on Monday have one secret prayer and the same post-Communion. On the other days, namely Tuesday and Wednesday, at morning Mass the first collect shall be of the Resurrection and the second of that day. Only one Mass shall be celebrated on the three following days. During these three days, after the first collect of the weekday, [Col. 1406A] shall be said the collect of the Resurrection: *O God, who on this day through your Only-begotten Son*.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Eighth Day of Easter

On the Sunday within the Octave of Easter, the first Mass shall be *He Is Risen*, and the second *As Newborn Infants*; and the Preface *Truly it is worthy, O Lord, at all times*, *Communicantes*, and *Hanc igitur oblationem* shall be said at both Masses. The second Mass of this day shall be celebrated with the reverence used for the feast of one apostle. It should be known that the Gospel read at the greater Mass on this day, namely *When It Was Evening on That Day*, after it has been read in full on Sunday, is customarily divided into two parts on the remaining non-festal days of that week. The first part begins at the beginning and extends to *Thomas, One of the Twelve*; [Col. 1406B] the second begins from that point and continues to the end.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Season of the Resurrection

From the Octave of Easter until the Rogation Days, the Alleluias said at the greater Mass on Sunday shall be repeated alternately on non-festal days. The same applies throughout the Octave of the Lord’s Ascension. It should be known that from Easter until the Ascension of the Lord, on every Sunday the morning Mass should be of the Lord’s Resurrection, namely *He Is Risen*, unless a saint’s feast prevents it. At that Mass, however, neither the Preface *Truly it is worthy, O Lord, at all times*, nor *Communicantes*, nor *Hanc igitur oblationem* shall be said. If, as stated, the morning Mass is of a saint, then the collect of the Lord’s Resurrection, namely *O God, who through your Only-begotten Son*, shall be said after the collect of the saint, that is, before the Sunday collect.

If a feast of twelve lessons falls on that Sunday, the Mass shall be that of Sunday, and the collect of the Resurrection shall be said after that of the feast. Yet if the dedication of a church or the Finding of the Holy Cross falls on a Sunday during this season, the Sunday Mass shall be transferred. On the Sunday before the Ascension of the Lord, however, it is not to be transferred under any circumstances.

Moreover, in the week after Easter Week, the Acts of the Apostles are read in the refectory. While [Col. 1406D] the responsory *You Are Worthy, O Lord* is sung in church, the book of Revelation is begun. When the responsory *If I Forget You* is begun, the Catholic Epistles are read.

From the Saturday of the first week of Easter until the Octave of Pentecost, no responsory is said at Mass, except for the dead. Nevertheless, on non-festal days and at morning Masses, one *Alleluia* shall be said, except on the Saturday within the Octave of Easter when a twelve-lesson feast on which no work is done falls on it. At greater Masses, however, two *Alleluias* shall be said.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Rogation Days

After Terce on the Rogation Days, once the bell has been rung as it is customarily rung for Mass, [Col. 1407A] two brothers standing before the step of the presbytery shall sing the Litany. The brothers in both choirs shall respond together, standing with faces turned towards one another as they customarily do at Mass. At *We sinners beseech you: hear us*, the ministers shall leave and prepare for Mass: the deacon, if present, taking the stole, and the priest the chasuble.

If a feast of twelve lessons on which no work is done falls on one of the three Rogation Days, that feast shall be observed in full on the same day. If the feast of Saint Peter of Tarentaise falls on these days, two Masses shall be sung after Terce. After Prime, however, there shall be the Litany and then the Mass of the fast, with commemoration of the feast then occurring; after Terce, another Mass of the solemnity. [Note: [Col. 1407] What is noted here concerning St Peter of Tarentaise was added to the ancient usages by the general chapter in the year of the Lord 1197.] On these three days no mixed wine is taken.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Lord’s Ascension

At Vespers on the Ascension of the Lord, the lighted Paschal candle shall not be extinguished until after Compline on the following day. It shall then be removed from the church. Commemorations of saints which may fall on that day are to be omitted, unless a commemoration of some saint follows on the next day; for then a commemoration shall be made at Vespers on Ascension Day. The same shall be done on the Wednesday within the Octaves of Easter and Pentecost.

At the procession held in the cloister, at the first station let the responsory *Men of Galilee* be sung with its verse. At the second, the responsory *Father, while I was*. At the third, the verse *Holy Father*, with repetition; and, where necessary, let *Glory be to the Father* be sung with repetition. At the entrance to the church, the antiphon *O King of glory*. On the two following days after the octave, “on this day” is not said in the Collect.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Vigil of Pentecost

On the Vigil of Pentecost let the brethren be free for reading from Terce until Sext, and let those who wish sing Masses—but not the Mass of the Vigil. Before None the office is celebrated, and the remaining matters are performed as on the Vigil of Easter, except that neither fire nor candle is blessed; that the bell for the *Kyrie eleison* of the Mass is not rung; and that the *Agnus Dei* is sung.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Its Octave

It should be known that after the day of Pentecost the antiphon *Daughters of Jerusalem*, and the other chants proper to the Resurrection, are omitted; nor is *Alleluia* placed at the end of any chant except where it is found written in the books. Concerning feasts of saints occurring in this week, the order established for feasts in Easter week is to be observed.

On Wednesday within the octave, the morning Mass is of the fast; the principal Mass is of the feast, namely *The Spirit of the Lord hath filled*, which is solemnly celebrated after Terce. On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday of the same week, no more than one Mass is celebrated in convent after Terce. On the three fasting days we do not say *Glory to God in the highest*, except on Wednesday at the principal Mass after Terce; nevertheless, the Preface *Who, ascending above all the heavens*, and *Communicantes* and *Hanc igitur oblationem* are retained on every day of that week. Throughout Pentecost week Mass is solemnly celebrated as in Easter week.

On the three days following Sunday, only two Collects are said at the morning Mass: one, *O God, who on this day*, and the other of the present day. On Thursday one Collect is said, namely *O God, who on this day*. On Friday two: the first of the day, the second *O God, who on this day*; this latter is omitted on Saturday. On that Saturday nothing concerning the feast of Pentecost is sung at Vespers, but rather concerning the Holy Trinity. The history *God of all* is to begin on the second Sunday after Pentecost, or on another Sunday if that one is not free.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Sunday Offices from the Octave of Pentecost until Advent

From the octave of Pentecost until the first Sunday of the Advent of the Lord there are twenty-eight weeks when the period is longer, but twenty-three when it is shorter. There are twenty-four Sunday offices. Accordingly, in the longer period the last four offices are each said for two weeks: that is, *All that thou hast done*, with its Collect, Epistle, and Gospel, is said for two weeks; *In thy will*, for two; *If thou shouldst mark iniquities*, for two; *The Lord saith, I think*, for two. If three weeks exceed the number of offices, the same is done with the last three offices; if two, with the last two; if one, *The Lord saith* is said twice. But when the number of weeks is less than the number of offices, *In thy will* and *If thou shouldst mark iniquities* are said in one week. *The Lord saith* is said twice in the final week, provided that on Sunday the Collect is *O God, our refuge and strength*; the Epistle, *Be ye imitators of me*; and the Gospel, *The Pharisees went away*. During the week the Collect is *Stir up, O Lord*; the Epistle, *Behold, the days are coming*; and the Gospel, *When he had lifted up*.

This is to be observed: all Sunday Collects which are said two at a time are so arranged during the week that the one said on Sunday is repeated at Lauds and Vespers on the following weekdays until the other begins. Once the other has begun, it is said at Lauds and Vespers until the following Sunday. It is to begin, if possible, on Thursday.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Solemnities on Which We Do Not Work and Which Do Not Fall on Sunday

On all solemnities on which we do not work and which do not fall on Sunday, even if there is a commemoration of some saint, both Masses are nevertheless of the solemnity, except on the feast of blessed Bernard [Note: [Col. 1409D] The name and commemoration of St Bernard were not in the ancient customs; they were added by the General Chapter in A.D. 1165, after his canonization, which occurred in the preceding year, as is evident from the bull of Alexander III, Roman pontiff, who enrolled this holy father in the catalogue of saints.], and on the Beheading of St John the Baptist; and excepting feasts occurring from the beginning of Lent until after the octave of Easter, the Ember fasts and Rogation days, and those occurring in the week of the Nativity of the Lord or of Pentecost. But at the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross, since the Vigils are partly of saints and partly of the Holy Cross, the morning Mass is of the saints—even should the feast fall on Sunday—and the principal Mass is of the Cross. If the Finding of the Holy Cross falls on the Sunday before Ascension, the morning Mass is of Sunday and the principal Mass of the Cross.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Solemnities on Which We Do Not Work and Which Fall on Sunday

Again, on solemnities on which we do not work and which fall on Sunday, unless they are those feasts at which a sermon is delivered in chapter, the morning Mass is of Sunday—unless it must be deferred because of a proper office of some saint or because of a recently deceased person—and the principal Mass is of the solemnity. Yet if the Purification of blessed Mary falls in Septuagesima, Sexagesima, or Quinquagesima, the morning Mass is of Sunday and the principal Mass of the solemnity. Before Advent, however, when a single Sunday office must occupy two weeks, that office is not repeated on the second Sunday at morning Mass if a twelve-lesson solemnity is celebrated on it, but both Masses are of the feast. The same is done before Septuagesima. [Note: [Col. 1410D] “The same is done,” etc. These final words were added to the ancient Customs, since they are not found in all the older manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Solemnities on Which We Work and Which Fall on Sunday

On solemnities on which we work and which fall on Sunday, likewise the morning Mass is of Sunday—unless deferred because of a recently deceased person—and the principal Mass is of the solemnity, except within the octave of the Manifestation of the Lord, when approaching Septuagesima requires that *O Lord, rebuke me not in thy anger* be sung therein; and except in Advent, Septuagesima, Quinquagesima, and Lent. Yet if the feast of St Ambrose falls on Palm Sunday or on the octave day of Easter, at the morning Mass the Collect of St Ambrose is said.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Sundays on Which a Twelve-Lesson Solemnity Is Not Celebrated

On Sundays on which a twelve-lesson solemnity is not celebrated, both Masses are of Sunday, unless perhaps there is a commemoration of a saint whose office is designated in the Gradual, or the Vigil of some saint prevents it, or a recently deceased person has intervened. Yet on Palm Sunday, even if there is a commemoration of a saint, the morning Mass is of Sunday; and on the octave day of Easter it is of the Resurrection. On the one day following the feast of St Thomas the Martyr [Note: [Col. 1410D] What is prescribed here concerning blessed Thomas the Martyr was added to the ancient Customs in A.D. 1191 by order of the General Chapter, as we have already noted above.], if it falls on Sunday, the first Mass is of Sunday and the second of the octave of the Lord, namely *A child is born unto us*.

On the three days following the Circumcision of the Lord, if a Sunday occurs, the first Mass is of the octaves of the saints; the second, of the octave of the Lord, namely *A child is born unto us*. But if, during the octave of St John the Baptist or of the Apostles Peter and Paul, a Sunday falls on one of the four days assigned to the Masses of those saints, the morning Mass is of the octave and the principal Mass of Sunday. On Sunday within the octave of the Manifestation, the morning Mass is of Sunday and the principal Mass of the octave, unless *All the earth* is to be sung on that Sunday. When that happens, the morning Mass is of the octave and the principal Mass of Sunday.

Likewise, on Sunday within the octave of the Ascension of the Lord or of the Assumption of blessed Mary, if no twelve-lesson solemnity occurs, the morning Mass is of Sunday and the principal Mass of the octave. But if on other days within these octaves a twelve-lesson solemnity on which we do not work occurs, unless perhaps a sermon ought to be delivered in chapter at that solemnity, the morning Mass is of the octave and the principal Mass of the feast.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. In What Order Masses Are to Be Said on Ordinary Days

From the octave of Theophany until the beginning of Lent, and from the octave of Pentecost until Advent, every Monday a Mass for the Dead is said in convent. Tuesday and Thursday are of Sunday; Wednesday, for the familiars; Friday, of the Holy Cross; Saturday, of blessed Mary.

From the octave of Easter until the Sunday before Ascension, and in Advent until the Nativity of the Lord, the same order is observed, except that from the octave of Easter until the aforesaid Sunday, every Wednesday, the Mass for the familiars being omitted, the Mass *He is risen* is said. In Advent on Friday, because the Mass of the Holy Cross is not said, the Sunday Mass is repeated—unless a twelve-lesson solemnity occupies one of these days, or such a commemoration of a saint as has a Mass assigned in the Gradual, or the Vigil of some solemnity, or an Ember Day or Rogation day, or a recently deceased person, or such commemorations of the dead as we observe solemnly; and except on days assigned to those Sunday offices which, after the day of Epiphany or after *In thy will* or *The Lord saith*, sometimes remain to be discharged on ordinary days because Septuagesima or Advent is imminent; and when a Sunday Mass cannot be said on its proper Sunday because of the necessity of some solemnity or of a recently deceased person.

When it happens that some Mass cannot be said on its proper Sunday, it is sung on the first day after that Sunday which the cantor finds free from the aforesaid occurrences. Within the octaves of the Lord and of saints, let what is written in the ruling concerning their octaves be observed. On the Friday after the octave of the Ascension, the Mass of the Holy Cross is sung, unless an occasion arises for that Mass to be omitted, as it ordinarily is at other times. It should be noted that, if the Mass for the Dead cannot be said in convent on Monday because of any of the above-mentioned occurrences, it is said on the first day of the same week free from them.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Number of Collects at Mass

On ordinary days no more than four Collects are said at Mass in convent, except in the octaves of the Lord, and in commemorations and octaves of saints, and on the four days following the day of the Circumcision, and on the Friday after the octave of the Ascension; or if the abbot has added only one Collect to be said, or if there is a recently deceased person. Also excepted is the thirty-day observance held after the general chapter of abbots, whose Collect, namely *God, the giver of pardon*, is continued throughout all thirty days—except on twelve-lesson solemnities—at Vespers, Lauds, and Masses alike.

Even if several Masses are celebrated on one day, it is said at only one of them. It should be noted that we never say at Mass a Collect of Sunday, or of the Holy Cross—that is, *O God, who [of] thy only-begotten Son*—unless Mass of these is celebrated in convent on that day. In Advent, however, the Sunday Collect is said daily at Mass, except at Masses for the Dead, Ember fasts, and the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

When, however, Sunday commemorations have been sung at morning Lauds on the day after a solemnity which fell on Sunday, although the Sunday Mass perhaps must be deferred, the Collect is nevertheless said at the morning Mass. It should also be noted that at every morning Mass, if it is not the same as the principal Mass or not of the same saint, the Collect of the principal Mass is said first after the Collect of the morning Mass—except when the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord or of the Manifestation, or the Vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary, falls on Sunday. But the Collect *O God, who through thy Only-begotten Son* is to be said as ordered in its proper ruling. [Note: [Col. 1411] “In its proper ruling,” that is, in chapter 27 of this book.]

In some manuscripts there is added: “And the Collect of the Holy Spirit is not to be said in the Mass of the Trinity.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Four Histories Sung from the Kalends of August until Advent

If the Kalends fall on Sunday, the history begins that day. But if the Kalends fall on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, the history is taken up on the Sunday preceding those Kalends. If the Kalends occur on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the history is introduced on the following Sunday. Therefore, if the feast of All Saints falls on Thursday or Friday, the books of Maccabees are to be read and sung at Vigils until the following Sunday, on which the prophet Ezekiel is to begin to be read and sung.

But if the feast of All Saints falls on Sunday, it is celebrated that day; and on the following night, namely Monday, the prophet Ezekiel and the responsory *I saw the Lord* begin. On the following Sunday, however, the lessons belonging to the beginning of that book are not read because of the preface, since it is not customary for them to be read twice; rather, other lessons are read, those entitled in the lectionary for the second Sunday. This prophet is to be read for three weeks, on ordinary days and Sundays alike. What remains to be read from it at Vigils, after its reading there has ceased, is read in the refectory. When Daniel is finished, the twelve prophets are read in the refectory.

## CHAPTER XL. In Which Week the Ember Fasts of September Are to Be Observed

If the first day of the Kalends of September falls on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, the days of fasting are to be observed in the week of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. But if the Kalends of September fall on Thursday, Friday, Saturday, or Sunday, they are to be observed in the week in which the feast of St Matthew the Apostle occurs.

## CHAPTER XLI. How Books Are to Be Read in the Refectory from Pentecost until the Kalends of November

During the time when *God, hearer of all* is sung, until the Kalends of August, the four books of Kings are read, and afterwards the two books of Paralipomenon. From the Kalends of August until the Kalends of September, while *In the beginning God* is sung, we read the Proverbs of Solomon, then Ecclesiastes, then the Song of Songs, the Book of Wisdom, *Love righteousness*, and afterwards the book of Jesus son of Sirach, namely *All wisdom*.

At the Kalends of September, when *If we have received good things* is sung, Job is read. In the same month another history is substituted, namely *I beseech thee, O Lord*; then first the book of Tobit is read, then Judith, afterwards Esther, and finally Ezra. This history, namely *I beseech thee, O Lord*, is begun neither before the day before the Ides of September nor after the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, but on whichever Sunday occurs within those seven days—except that when the solemnity of the Holy Cross falls on Sunday, *I beseech thee, O Lord* is said on the Sunday preceding the feast. At the Kalends of October the two books of Maccabees are read while *May the Lord open* is sung. When they have been read through, we read the four books of the Gospels in the refectory only, up to the Passion narratives; omitting the Passion narratives, what remains is read. The other books to be read at other times have been arranged above in various chapters.

It should be noted that when a history is renewed, the book then begun with the responsories is begun in church with its preface; but it is read in the refectory from the point where the eighth lesson ended. In the first book of Maccabees, however, the reader begins in the refectory where the fourth lesson ended. This need not be observed for the other books to be read in the refectory at the same time after the first has been read through, as it is observed for the first book which we begin first in church.

But if the history is deferred because of an intervening feast, the book is nevertheless read at table with its preface, to be begun again in church when the history is sung.

It should be known that the responsory from the history entitled for Vespers, even if it is postponed once or twice because of an intervening feast, is said at the first free Saturday; unless, indeed, that history has already been sung on Sunday or during the week.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Antiphons to Be Said on Saturdays

The antiphons from the Old Books and the Epistles of Paul which are said at the *Magnificat*—namely *Speak, Lord*, *They all knew*, *But these things were written*, *Brethren, be strengthened*, and similar ones—are said on the Saturdays to which they are assigned, either at the *Magnificat* or in the commemoration. Any remaining are omitted that year. If any are lacking, the final ones are repeated. Whenever a Sunday Mass which cannot be said on its Sunday is discharged on an ordinary day, the antiphons assigned to the *Magnificat* and *Benedictus* from the same office are said that day, provided that they cannot be said on their Sunday. This sometimes happens before Advent and Septuagesima because of the brevity of the season.

It should be noted, however, that when, because of shortness of time, the antiphon *Lord, was not the good seed* is said at the *Benedictus* on the Saturday before Septuagesima, the antiphon *Gather first the tares* is omitted at Vespers of the same day. The same is done with the antiphons *A marriage was made* and *When the wine failed*, when Septuagesima falls on the tenth day before the Kalends of February. All other Sunday antiphons assigned to the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*, with their Collects, when a twelve-lesson solemnity is celebrated on their Sunday, are said after *Let us bless the Lord* at Lauds and Vespers in commemoration of Sunday. Yet on that Saturday they are not said when nothing of Sunday will be observed on the next day. This occurs before Advent, when one Sunday office occupies two weeks; for then the antiphons of that office are not repeated on the second Sunday if a twelve-lesson solemnity is celebrated on it.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Feasts of Saints Falling on Sundays or on the Ascension of the Lord

Feasts of saints on which we do not work, if they fall on the octave day of Easter, the day of the Ascension, Septuagesima, or a Sunday on which a history must begin and which has no following Sunday, are celebrated on the next day. The Purification of blessed Mary, however, is never deferred. If that history has two or more Sundays and those Sundays perhaps have principal feasts, the history is said on the feast which appears of lesser authority, and the feast is said on the following day.

But lesser feasts on which we have twelve lessons and work are omitted in such a circumstance; a commemoration is made at Vespers and Lauds, and the morning Mass is of the saints, followed by another commemoration at Vespers of that day. Yet the morning Mass is not of St Ambrose if his feast falls on Palm Sunday or on the octave day of Easter; rather, his Collect is said. Where the aforementioned necessity does not intervene, lesser feasts are neither omitted nor deferred, but celebrated on their own day, even if some history must begin which has another Sunday on which it can be sung—except if a feast of this sort falls on the Sunday of Septuagesima.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Feasts of Saints Falling on Saturdays

On Saturdays of Advent, Septuagesima, Quinquagesima, and Lent, if there is a feast, Vespers of Sunday are said and a commemoration of the saint is made. The feasts of the Purification and Annunciation of blessed Mary, St Benedict, and the Dedication of the Church, and any feast on which we do not work that falls on Saturday within the octave of Easter, are excepted from this rule: these feasts have their Vespers in full, and a commemoration of Sunday is made. On all other Saturdays all feasts have their Vespers in full, unless other solemnities occur which must take precedence over them. It should be noted that the feast of St Matthias—which must always be kept on the second day of the bissextile period—if it falls on any Saturday other than the Saturday preceding Sexagesima in a leap year, is celebrated on that Saturday, that is, on the first day of the bissextile period.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Vigils of Saints

When the Vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary falls on Sunday, the morning Mass is of Sunday and the principal Mass of the Vigil. But on the Vigil of St John the Baptist, of the Apostles Peter and Paul, of other apostles, of St Lawrence, or of All Saints, if it is Sunday, the morning Mass is of the Vigil and the principal Mass of Sunday. On the Vigil of All Saints, the first Collect is of the Vigil itself, namely *O Lord our God, multiply*. The second is of Sunday, if it is Sunday; the third, of St Quintinus. If it is not Sunday, the second is of St Quintinus; the third, *Almighty everlasting God, who [art] the God of the living*.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Octaves of the Lord and of Saints

Throughout the octaves of the Manifestation, the Ascension of the Lord, and the Assumption of blessed Mary, the Mass of the octave is celebrated daily, unless there intervenes a feast of some saint having an office assigned in the Gradual; or a Sunday Mass which could not be said on its Sunday becomes due; or a twelve-lesson solemnity which ought to prevent it occurs; or there is a recently deceased person; or the customary Mass for the Dead is due to be said in convent; or such a commemoration of the dead as we observe solemnly intervenes.

It should be noted that if the Finding of the Holy Cross falls on Sunday within the octave of the Ascension, after *Let us bless the Lord* at Lauds, commemoration is first made of the martyrs, then of Sunday, and then of the Ascension of the Lord. The morning Mass is of the martyrs: after their Collect, the Collect of the Holy Cross is said; then of Sunday; then of the Ascension. But that Sunday Mass, namely *Hear, O Lord, the voice*, is deferred. On Sunday within the octaves of the Assumption and Nativity of blessed Mary and of the Ascension of the Lord, everything appointed in the books is said of the octaves, both by day and by night.

Nevertheless, if the feast of blessed Bernard occurs on this Sunday [Note: [Col. 1415] The Mass to be said on the feast of St Bernard was composed by the supreme pontiff Innocent III and prescribed for the whole Order by the General Chapter of A.D. 1202.], everything is of the feast except the morning Mass, which is of the octave. The Sunday Mass is deferred to be said during the week. On Saturday at Vespers, however, and on Sunday at Lauds and Vespers, after the commemoration of the octave, a commemoration of Sunday is made. But when this same Sunday falls within the octave of St Lawrence, everything is said of Sunday; and at Lauds commemoration is made first of the octave, then of St Lawrence, and afterwards of St Mammes. The morning Mass is of Sunday: after its Collect the Collect of the octave is said, then of St Lawrence, and afterwards of St Mammes. The principal Mass is of the octave.

Within the octave of the Nativity of St John the Baptist, on the first day after the solemnity, a Mass of the Nativity itself is sung in convent unless a recently deceased person prevents it, or unless a Sunday Mass which could not be said on its Sunday is then to be discharged. If any of these prevents the Mass of St John from being sung that day, the Mass of St John is sung on the fourth day from the Nativity, unless one of the aforementioned causes likewise prevents it. But if the Mass of the Nativity itself has been said in convent on the first day after the solemnity, on the fourth day from that Nativity the Mass for the Dead is said in convent, unless it was said in the same week before that Nativity, or unless that fourth day is Sunday. If it was said in the same week before that Nativity, the Mass of St John is again said on that fourth day—unless it falls on Monday. If it is Monday, the Mass for the Dead is said. Yet it is not sung unless the Mass of the octave has first been sung once.

Within the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the same is observed on the fifth or seventh day from their solemnity: the Mass of those apostles is sung unless some aforementioned cause prevents it. On the remaining days, from the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist until the octave day of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Masses of the saints written in the Calendar are sung. It should certainly be noted in these octaves that, in the commemoration of St Paul, after *Let us bless the Lord* at Lauds, commemoration is first made of St John the Baptist, then of St Peter; the same commemoration is made at Mass on the same day. Likewise, commemoration of St Stephen, blessed John the Evangelist, the Holy Innocents, and St Andrew the Apostle is made daily at Lauds, Vespers, and Mass during their octaves; and Mass is celebrated for them on the octave day. Of the octaves of St Agnes the Virgin and St Lawrence the Martyr, nothing else is done except a commemoration at Vespers and Lauds on the octave day; and the Mass proper to that day is discharged for them.

Commemorations of the saints John and Paul, Pope Leo, and the other saints which commonly occur during the octave of St John the Baptist, the Apostles Peter and Paul, or the Apostle Andrew, must always be announced first after regular Vespers; then follow the other commemorations belonging to the aforesaid octaves of saints. The commemoration of Saints Caesarius and Benignus is made not at Vespers or Lauds, but only at the morning Mass.

When only three antiphons are used over the psalms at Vigils, and psalms occur which are divided at the fourth place, such as *Do not be emulous* and *Give ear, O my people*, the third psalm and the whole fourth are said beneath the second antiphon. The fifth alone, namely *O Lord, do not*, and likewise *The nations have come*, are said beneath the third antiphon.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Purification of Holy Mary

At the Purification of Holy Mary, after Terce the abbot blesses the candles previously brought by the sacristan, and afterwards sprinkles them with holy water. When the cantor has presented a lighted candle to the abbot, he begins the antiphon *A light for revelation*, adding also the verse *Now lettest thou depart*, as is found in the books. Meanwhile the sacristan, aided by his assistant and by those ordered by the prior, distributes the remaining candles to the monks, novices, lay brothers, household, and guests, if present.

Then a procession is made through the cloister. At it the deacon carries the cross and the subdeacon the holy water; and they conduct themselves in going and standing as we have prescribed for the Palm procession. At the departure of the procession, the cantor begins the antiphon *Hail, full of grace*. When it is finished, the other antiphon follows, *Adorn thy bridal chamber*; after it the antiphon *Simeon received an answer* is inserted. Three stations are made, one station for each antiphon. At the entrance of the church the abbot begins the antiphon *Today the blessed Virgin*. When all have entered and the aforesaid antiphon is finished, Mass is solemnly celebrated.

After the deacon has read the Gospel and has presented to the abbot the offering to be consecrated to God, and the deacon himself has arranged that offering upon the altar in the customary manner, the abbot returns his candle to the sacristan; the deacon offers his candle to the abbot, and afterwards the subdeacon. Then the abbot comes to the step of the presbytery, and the others, beginning with the priors, offer their candles, kissing the hand of the abbot or, if the abbot is absent, of the priest. The sacristan and his assistant receive the candles from the abbot’s hand and extinguish them. Then the abbot returns to the altar, censes it, and washes his hands. But if the feast of the Purification of Holy Mary falls on Sunday, the abbot performs the exorcism of the water in the customary manner before Terce, and the procession takes place after Terce.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Canticles

The canticles of the Nativity of the Lord—namely *The people that walked in darkness*—are said on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, of the Circumcision, of Theophany, and on the octave day of Theophany; likewise on every Sunday within those days, unless a twelve-lesson feast of some saint is celebrated on that Sunday; and on the Purification of Holy Mary. The Easter canticles, namely *Who is this that cometh from Edom?*, are said on every Sunday from Easter until Pentecost, unless another feast is celebrated; and on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, its octave day, and the day of Pentecost.

At the Dedication of the church let the canticles *I was glad*, *Unless the Lord*, and *Praise Jerusalem* be said. At the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross: *O Lord, I have heard*, *Glory be to the Father*; *For iniquity*, *Glory be to the Father*; *Thou hast gone forth for salvation*. At the Annunciation, Assumption, and Nativity of blessed Mary; on Sunday within the octave of her Assumption; on her octave day; and on the feast of one Virgin: *Hear me, ye that bring forth divine fruit*. At the feast of St Michael the Archangel: *O Lord, have mercy upon us*; and on all Sundays except those mentioned above. At the Nativity and Beheading of St John the Baptist, and on the feast of one martyr and one confessor: *Blessed is the man who is found in wisdom*. On the feasts of apostles, evangelists, and many martyrs: *Ye saints of the Lord*.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Feasts on Which We Work

The feast days with twelve lessons on which we work are these: the feast of St Sylvester; the octave of Epiphany; the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian; Agnes, virgin and martyr; the feast of St Agatha, martyr; the Chair of St Peter; Thomas the Confessor; the octave of the Ascension; John and Paul; the Commemoration of St Paul; the octaves of St John the Baptist and of the Apostles Peter and Paul; the Finding of St Stephen; Dominic the Confessor; the octave of St Mary; Maurice and his companions; Remigius, bishop; Cecilia, virgin; Pope Clement; Lucy, virgin. [Note: [Col. 1417D] Besides these days, the ancient Customs numbered those of St Gregory the Pope, St Ambrose the bishop, St Peter the bishop, St Augustine the bishop, St Jerome the priest, and St Catherine, virgin and martyr. They were removed from this chapter when two conventual Masses began to be celebrated on those days; and they were removed because, according to these Customs, on feasts with two Masses the monks were free for reading and prayer, but not for manual work. [Col. 1418D]]

## CHAPTER L. At What Times and in What Order the Office of the Dead Is to Be Celebrated

The Office of the Dead is performed daily, except on twelve-lesson days, on one day within the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, on the three days before Easter, and throughout Easter week and Pentecost week. Therefore, from the Kalends of November until the first Sunday of Lent, during the interval following Vigils, the Office for the Dead is performed on ordinary days.

[Col. 1418D] In this office, when the weekly brother begins the Antiphon while standing opposite the other choir, the brothers shall sit in their seats; and the weekly brother himself, having begun the Antiphon, shall sit down after bowing toward the altar. The other Antiphons, however, shall be begun by the brothers in alternation, as at the regular Vespers, standing and bowing as the weekly brother has done. The weekly brother who is to say the verse after the Psalms shall rise and, standing opposite the altar, say the verse. When it has been said, he shall bow and sit again while the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”) is said. [Col. 1419A] Afterwards, rising and lifting his seat, and bowing to the altar, he shall begin the Lesson. When it is finished, he shall bow again. Likewise, he shall bow at the end of each Lesson and of each verse. And, when the verse of the third Responsory has been said, he shall sit down. When *Laudate Dominum de caelis* (“Praise the Lord from the heavens”) has ended, the brothers shall rise while they say *Requiem aeternam* (“Eternal rest”). They shall do likewise at Vespers after *Confitebor* (“I shall confess”), saying *Requiem aeternam*. This verse, namely *Requiem aeternam*, shall always be said by the choir to which it properly belongs alone. When the Antiphon after *Laudate Dominum de caelis* has been said, the weekly brother shall begin *Ego sum resurrectio et vita* (“I am the resurrection and the life”); and *Benedictus* (“Blessed”) shall be sung somewhat more slowly, and likewise the *Magnificat* (“My soul magnifies”) at Vespers for the dead.

Therefore, once the Antiphon after *Benedictus* has been sung, [Col. 1419B] the brothers shall prostrate themselves over the stalls, if it is the time for prostration; otherwise, they shall lean upon the *misericordiae* [Note: [Col. 1419] They shall lean upon the misericordiae, that is, while sitting in their seats, with the sleeves of their cowls crossed over their knees.], and say the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”) silently. Then the weekly priest shall begin the Psalm *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”), which shall always be said at Lauds for the dead, both in summer and winter, and which each choir shall recite in alternation. When it is completed, and *Requiem aeternam* (“Eternal rest”) has been said as after the other first Psalms, the priest shall say *A porta inferi* (“From the gate of hell”), and *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), and afterwards the Collects in the customary order. When these are completed, and *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and *Requiescant in pace* (“May they rest in peace”) have been said, all shall answer, “Amen,” before rising; then, rising and bowing to the altar, they shall depart. After the Vespers of the day, however, Vespers for the dead shall be said [Col. 1419C], together with the Psalm *Lauda, anima mea, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, my soul”), before the Collects begun by the weekly priest.

From the first Sunday of Lent until the feast of All Saints, the office for the dead shall be celebrated after the Vespers of the day; namely, Vespers shall first be said for the dead themselves, and then the Vigil shall follow. When the third Responsory has been said, the weekly brother, facing the other choir, shall say, *Audivi vocem de caelo dicentem* (“I heard a voice from heaven saying”), and shall not bow either before or after it. When the community has responded, *Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur* (“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord”), they shall prostrate themselves or sit, as stated above. Near the end of the Vigil, namely after the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”), the Psalm *Lauda, anima mea, Dominum* (“Praise the Lord, my soul”) shall be said, begun by the weekly priest. The Lauds for the dead themselves shall be performed [Col. 1419D] on the following day, between Matins, Lauds, and Prime.

The whole office for the dead shall be said in summer in the order which we have established for winter. This office is celebrated in the week in such an order that on Monday three Psalms are said, namely *Verba mea* (“Give ear to my words”) and the others, unless they were said on the preceding Sunday; and the first three Lessons, namely *Parce mihi, Domine* (“Spare me, Lord”) and the others. On Tuesday, the three middle Psalms, namely *Dominus regit me* (“The Lord rules me”) and the others, with the Lessons, namely *Responde mihi* (“Answer me”) and the others. On Wednesday, the last three Psalms, namely *Exspectans exspectavi* (“Waiting, I waited”) and the others, with the Lessons, namely *Spiritus meus attenuabitur* (“My spirit shall be weakened”), [Col. 1420A] and the others; and thus they shall be repeated on individual days if necessary.

But if a feast of twelve Lessons falls on Monday, then on the Monday which follows the feast and is free, the same first Psalms shall be said. If, however, after those first Psalms have been said, another feast of twelve Lessons intervenes, the order shall not be changed; rather, on the next free weekday the three middle Psalms shall be said, and on another day the last three; on the following day they shall be repeated from the beginning.

## CHAPTER LI. In what order the Collects for the dead are to be said

*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus cui numquam* (“Almighty everlasting God, to whom never”), for the brothers of the congregation and likewise for our fathers, mothers, sisters, and dependants, shall be said first [Col. 1420B]; then *Fidelium Deus omnium* (“God of all the faithful”). These two shall be said continually, both at Vespers and Lauds, or at the Vigil joined to Vespers. In the Thirty-Day observance held after the general chapter, *Deus veniae largitor* (“God, giver of pardon”) shall take precedence, both in the office and at the conventual Mass for the dead, unless a deceased person is present. If at another time we hold another Thirty-Day observance, *Deus cui proprium* (“God, to whom it properly belongs”) shall be said; if a deceased person is present, *Inclina* (“Incline”) shall always be said singly in the first place, except in the principal offices for the dead, in which this alone must follow the first Collect.

At Mass, however, there are only two Collects: namely, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus cui numquam sine spe* (“Almighty everlasting God, to whom never without hope”), and *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus qui vivorum* (“Almighty everlasting God, who … of the living …”). If a deceased person is present [Col. 1420C] and Mass is said for him, the Collect *Inclina, Domine* (“Incline, Lord”) and *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus qui vivorum* (“Almighty everlasting God, who … of the living …”) shall be said, unless it is the solemn Thirty-Day observance, in which *Deus veniae largitor* (“God, giver of pardon”) is inserted. If Mass cannot be celebrated for him, that Collect shall nevertheless be said. But if the deceased person present is a bishop, *Deus qui inter apostolicos* (“God, who among the apostolic …”) shall be said only on the day of his burial.

At the daily Mass for all deceased brothers and dependants of our order, the Collect *Inclina, Domine* (“Incline, Lord”) shall be said. If a deceased person is present, the second Collect, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus cui numquam* (“Almighty everlasting God, to whom never”), shall be said for him singly. Then, if we are holding a Thirty-Day observance, *Deus cui proprium est* (“God, to whom it properly belongs”) shall be said, or *Deus veniae largitor* (“God, giver of pardon”) if it is the solemn Thirty-Day observance. For [Col. 1420D] at Mass in the community we hold no Thirty-Day observance except that solemn one held after the general chapter. It should be known that in the three Masses which we owe for each deceased person, the Collect *Inclina, Domine* (“Incline, Lord”) is said singly, unless it is ordered to be said in the plural in Chapter.

## CHAPTER LII. On the principal offices for the dead

On the commemoration of all the faithful departed; on the commemoration of our parents, brothers, sisters, and all our kinsfolk and benefactors; on the day on which, after the annual chapter, we solemnly commemorate [Col. 1421A] all monks, novices, lay brothers, and dependants of our order who died in the preceding year; and on the anniversary of all deceased bishops and abbots of our order, which is held on the fourth Ides of January: we perform a solemn office with Vespers, Vigils, and Lauds. The Psalms are sung standing, and somewhat more slowly, at Vespers, Vigils, and Lauds alike.

When the weekly brother has said the verse before the Lessons, they shall sit upon the *misericordiae*, silently saying the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”); then, when the Lesson has been begun, they shall sit in their seats until the third repetition of *Libera me, Domine, de morte* (“Deliver me, Lord, from death”). The cantor must begin this Responsory while standing. As soon as he has begun it, he shall bow, and sing the succeeding verses, bowing only after the last verse [Col. 1421B]. All monks who belong to the community must attend these offices and Masses, unless a serious cause prevents them.

At the office of all the dead and at the Mass [Col. 1422A], *Fidelium Deus* (“God of the faithful”) alone is said, unless a deceased person is present. At the commemoration of our parents, *Deus cui proprium* (“God, to whom it properly belongs”) alone; and on the anniversary of bishops and abbots, *Praesta, Domine, quaesumus* (“Grant, Lord, we ask”) alone. In the solemn Thirty-Day observance held after the general chapter, the first is *Deus veniae largitor* (“God, giver of pardon”); the second, *Praesta, Domine, quaesumus* (“Grant, Lord, we ask”), for the king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1421D] That is, King Philip Augustus of the Franks, whose commemoration was added here to the ancient Usages by order of the general chapter in the year 1223.]; these alone shall be said at the offices and at Mass, unless a deceased person is present. On the anniversary of bishops and abbots, whoever does not wish to sing privately for them shall say the Collect.

At these Masses the Responsory *Si ambulem* (“If I walk”) and the Responsory *Absolve* (“Absolve”) are sung jointly by both choirs in the community. But whoever sings privately shall say the Responsory *Requiem aeternam* (“Eternal rest”) and the Tract [Col. 1422B] *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”). If any of these days occurs on Monday, or on the day after a feast of twelve Lessons, Vespers for the dead shall be held after the regular Vespers.

## PART TWO. [Col. 1421] On the ceremonies to be observed both in the canonical Hours and in the celebration of Masses

## CHAPTER LIII. How the Priest and Ministers are to conduct themselves at festal Masses

[Col. 1421C]

On days of twelve Lessons, the priest shall vest for celebrating Mass with a deacon and subdeacon; the weekly brothers of the preceding week shall assist them in vesting. Once they are vested, the deacon and subdeacon, wearing maniples, shall go to prepare the altar: asking pardon at the altar-step, placing the Text [Note: [Col. 1422D] By “Text” understand the Book of the Gospels.] upon the lectern, and the Missal upon the altar at the right-hand corner. At the left-hand side they shall place the wiping-cloth under the pall, if a blessed object is placed upon it. Four palls, without a towel, must be placed upon the altar. Afterwards they shall prepare the service-table beside the altar, upon which the ministrations are made, placing upon it the chalice with corporal [Col. 1421D] and offertory-cloth, the seats in which the priest and ministers sit, and the piscina. At Terce both shall remain in the presbytery with the priest, where they may also sit during the Psalms. When Terce has ended, they shall go out. One of the ministers who assisted them in vesting shall ring the bell, light the two candles customarily burning on either side of the altar, and, if necessary, prepare the concealed lamp, lighted, upon the altar. The other shall assist the priest in putting on the chasuble. Afterwards he shall pour water over his hands. The deacon shall take the stole and wash his hands with water given him by the minister; likewise the subdeacon. The priest and deacon shall dry their hands with the cloth assigned to them; the subdeacon, with the other cloth.

When the minister has rung the bell, they shall leave the vestry and arrange themselves before the altar which is at the first station, facing the entrance to the choir: the subdeacon first, the deacon after him, and the priest last. They shall remain thus until *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”). When they move from there, they shall bow before that altar. Then, on entering, they shall bow again at the step of the presbytery; and, ascending, the deacon shall turn to the right and the subdeacon to the left. The priest shall pass between them to the altar, and as he passes they shall bow to him. Then the priest, bent before the middle of the altar, shall make his prayer; likewise the deacon behind him, and the subdeacon behind the deacon. When it is completed, they shall straighten themselves. Then the priest, having kissed the altar, shall sign himself. The deacon, signing himself, shall bow and go to kiss the left-hand corner of the altar. Having kissed it, he shall bow [Col. 1422D] and go to the right side, standing beneath the altar-step a little away from the wall; the subdeacon behind him.

The priest, descending beneath the altar-step, shall bow near the middle of the altar in order to make the confession, with the deacon at the right and the subdeacon at the left; and they shall make confession to one another, the priest beginning. The ministers shall call the priest “father,” and the priest shall call them “brothers,” even if he is their junior in rank; this is not to be done otherwise. When this has been said, they shall straighten themselves, and the priest shall approach the book at the right-hand corner of the altar. If they cannot complete this confession at that hour, they shall say it later when they are free. If the deacon has time before the priest says *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), he shall place the corporal upon the altar and [Col. 1423A], rinsing the chalice inside with water, place the bread upon the paten and wine in the chalice, with the subdeacon assisting him.

It should be noted that, whether it is the deacon or the subdeacon who serves, he shall pour in the wine first, and then hand the water-cruet to the priest when he sees that he is more at leisure; the priest shall pour the water into the chalice. Then, placing the paten upon the chalice, he shall cover it with the offertory-cloth, and afterwards go down beneath the altar-step on the right side. If, while the deacon is serving, the priest says *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”) or *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), the deacon shall interrupt the service and go behind the priest. If *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is said, he shall bow briefly after it has been said and return to serving. After *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), he shall reverently draw down [Col. 1423B] the middle of the chasuble [Note: [Col. 1423D] “The middle of the chasuble,” namely its front portion.]; then, turning to his place, he shall bow, with the subdeacon after him. If other Collects remain, they shall return to perform what remains of the service. When it is completed, they shall return to where they stood before, but without bowing, except at the first Collect. If no Collect remains, the subdeacon shall descend to read the Epistle before the step of the presbytery, opposite the middle of the altar and facing it, bowing before he begins to read and after he has read. If he should make an error in the Epistle itself, once it has been read he shall make satisfaction there: first placing the book upon the stall and placing his hands on the ground beneath the step, over his alb, without bending the knees, on festal and private days alike. Meanwhile, until the Gospel, the priest may sit and read in the Missal [Col. 1423C], and the deacon may sit at his direction and read in the Text, if he wishes. When the Epistle has been read, the subdeacon shall sit beside the deacon, or, if necessary, go into the choir to sing with the others. If the priest sits and the deacon wishes to look ahead at the Gospel, he shall do so at the lectern.

When the time comes to read the Gospel, they shall rise. The priest shall return to the right-hand corner of the altar, placing the Missal upon it. The deacon, placing the Text upon the lectern, shall turn to the abbot and humbly ask a blessing, silently saying, *Domne, iube benedicere* (“Master, please give a blessing”); or to the priest if the abbot is absent. Turning toward him, the priest shall say this blessing: “May the Lord be in your heart and in your mouth, that you may worthily proclaim the Gospel of Christ.” When it has been given, he shall turn his face back toward the altar as it was before, remaining thus until after *Gloria tibi, Domine* (“Glory to you, Lord”). While this is said, he shall sign himself and turn his face toward the Gospel, standing in trembling. The deacon, having received the blessing, shall turn to the book. When he has said, *Sequentia sancti Evangelii* (“The continuation of the holy Gospel”), he shall sign himself as the others sign themselves when *Gloria tibi, Domine* (“Glory to you, Lord”) is said. Once the Gospel has been read, if he has made an error in it, he shall turn eastward and make satisfaction in the manner of the subdeacon. Then he shall bow toward the east. Afterwards he shall bring the open book to the priest to be kissed, showing him with his finger the beginning of the Gospel which he read. He himself shall also kiss it [Col. 1424A] after the priest, and return it closed, beneath the pall, upon the lectern. After the end of the Gospel, the priest, turning his face toward the altar, shall begin there *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), or *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”). Meanwhile, while *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) is sung by the community, he shall stand in the same place until, when it has been sung, he says *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) and *Oremus* (“Let us pray”). Then, taking the book, he shall place it at the left-hand corner. After the Gospel, the deacon shall unfold the corporal, which has three folds in its width and four in its length, placing the middle of its width in the middle of the altar. Immediately after *Oremus* (“Let us pray”), with his hands covered by the offertory-cloth, holding the foot of the chalice with his left hand and the paten with his right, he shall offer both together to the priest, kissing his hand once. The priest, receiving both together, shall put them down [Col. 1424B] beside the corporal on the right side, leaving them for the deacon to prepare; then he shall move to the left-hand corner of the altar and remain there until he receives the censer to incense the chalice. The deacon, having placed the offertory-cloth upon the altar, shall put the chalice upon the corporal at the second fold of the front, right, and left portions, and the bread before the chalice, turning the corporal back over it. If there are several hosts, he shall place one separately and the others together; then he shall carry the paten and offertory-cloth back to the service-table. Meanwhile, as these things are being done by priest and deacon, the minister whose office it is shall hold the censer before the abbot, or before the priest if the abbot is absent, while the subdeacon holds the incense. When the incense has been put in the censer, he who holds the censer shall offer it to the priest, kissing his hand. The priest, receiving it, shall incense the chalice in this manner: he shall swing it once around the chalice; incense the right side of the altar above once, the left once, and likewise the front once. As he does this, the deacon shall put his hand beneath the priest’s arm, holding his chasuble so that he may act more freely. When this is done, he shall give the censer back to the deacon. Then, having washed his fingers with water poured from the cruet by the subdeacon and received in the basin prepared for this purpose, and dried them with the linen assigned for this purpose, he shall pray, bent before the altar. The deacon shall first incense the right side of the altar twice from outside; then, raising his hand, incense the cross twice, and passing behind the altar to the left [Col. 1424D] side, incense it and likewise the cross. He shall then give the censer to the subdeacon, who shall put it where it is customarily placed. The deacon himself shall return behind the altar-step on the right, so that, when the priest turns to the choir saying, “Pray, brothers, for me,” he may draw down the middle of his chasuble. Then, bowing low, he shall withdraw to his place, where he shall stand until the priest says *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”). The priest, having said *Orate, fratres* (“Pray, brothers”) moderately, so that he may be heard, shall turn his face back to the altar by the same side by which he turned toward the choir. Afterwards he shall move to the book at the left-hand corner, silently saying *Oremus* (“Let us pray”), for the first Secret and for the second if one or more follow. [Col. 1425A] Meanwhile the minister who offered the censer to the priest shall bring water to the deacon and subdeacon for washing their hands. The priest shall take care not to separate those fingers with which he must handle the Body of the Lord after washing them with water, except when he makes crosses over the host and chalice or signs himself.

When he has finished the Secrets, he shall return to face the middle of the altar, saying *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”), but without raising his hands until *Sursum corda* (“Lift up your hearts”). On hearing *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”), the deacon shall come behind the priest, bowing low to the altar, and stand facing the priest until the *Pater noster* (“Our Father”). At the same time the subdeacon shall take the paten covered with the offertory-cloth and come behind the deacon, bowing low [Col. 1425B] around the altar. [Note: [Col. 1425D] “Bowing low,” that is, inclining.] Then, straightening himself, he shall put his left hand beneath his right arm, in order to carry the paten more lightly. The subdeacon shall sign himself with the paten at *Sanctus* (“Holy”). The deacon shall likewise sign himself, remaining bent while he says *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus* (“Holy, holy, holy”), briefly and silently. When the Preface has ended, the priest shall bow before the altar, saying *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus* (“Holy, holy, holy”) briefly; and, signing himself, shall immediately begin *Te igitur clementissime Pater* (“Therefore, most merciful Father”), until he says *Uti accepta habeas* (“That you may graciously accept”); then he shall straighten himself, proceeding through the Canon as it stands in the book. When he comes to *Qui pridie quam pateretur* (“Who, on the day before he suffered”), he shall take the host and, raising it somewhat above the chalice, bless it between the other fingers which he has kept for this purpose. If there are several, without putting down the one he holds, he shall bless them all together; and again he shall hold it with both hands until he says, *Hoc est enim corpus meum* (“For this is my body”), and then return it to its place. When he says *Simili modo postquam coenatum est* (“In like manner, after supper had been eaten”), he shall take the chalice, grasping the corporal and chalice between both hands, and raise it a little until the point of making the sign [Note: [Col. 1425D] At the general chapters of 1210 and 1232, priests were ordered [Col. 1426D] to elevate the host after the consecration, and all who were present to ask pardon or bend the knee.]; then he shall put it down, making the sign of the cross above it. Having done this, he shall raise it as above until he says, *In mei memoriam facietis* (“You shall do this in remembrance of me”), and then let it go. When beginning *Supplices te rogamus, omnipotens Deus* (“We humbly beseech you, almighty God”), he shall bow before the altar until he says, *Ex hac altaris participatione* (“From this participation in the altar”); then he shall straighten himself, kiss the edge of the altar before the chalice, and sign himself after he has signed the Body and Blood, namely when he says [Col. 1425D], *Omni benedictione* (“With every blessing”). When he says *Nobis quoque peccatoribus* (“And to us sinners also”), he shall strike his breast lightly once.
