When the deacon sees him make the second sign of the chalice after the bow, namely when he says, *Sanctificas* (“You sanctify”), he shall come to the priest’s right. Having first kissed the altar, he shall suitably prepare to uncover the chalice on the right side with his right hand, while the priest begins on the left side with his left hand. The deacon, placing his left hand beneath his arm to hold in his alb-sleeve lest it touch the corporal, shall put the fingers of his right hand beneath those of the priest in holding the chalice, while the priest makes three crosses over the uncovered chalice [Col. 1426A], saying, *Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso* (“Through him, and with him, and in him”), and a fourth before the rim of the chalice while saying, *Est tibi Deo* (“To you, God”). When he says *Omnis honor et gloria* (“All honor and glory”), he shall hold the Body of the Lord over the chalice with both hands. When the priest begins, so that all hear, *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”), he and the deacon shall raise the chalice a little until after *Oremus* (“Let us pray”) has been said; then it shall be put down and covered again by both, each from his own side. Then the deacon, bowing before the altar, shall withdraw to where he stood. When the priest says *Panem nostrum quotidianum* (“Our daily bread”), the subdeacon shall approach the deacon and offer him the uncovered paten, kissing his hand. Afterwards he shall withdraw a little toward the wall on the right. The deacon, receiving the paten, shall offer it to the priest after *Sed libera nos a malo* (“But deliver us from evil”), kissing his hand. [Col. 1426B] Having offered it, he shall come to the place where he stood before the Preface, handing the offertory-cloth to the subdeacon. The subdeacon shall put it away folded; having put it away, he shall return behind the deacon. The priest, receiving the paten, shall place it under the corporal. If it is a Mass at which the community goes to receive the peace, he shall place it upon the corporal. Having said *Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine* (“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord”), before saying *per eundem Dominum nostrum* (“through the same Lord our”), he shall place the Body of the Lord upon the paten, moving the paten slightly to the right of the chalice; and, saying *Per eundem Dominum nostrum* (“Through the same Lord our”), he shall break the Body of the Lord over the chalice into three parts. Having said *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”), he shall make one cross in the chalice at *Pax Domini* (“The peace of the Lord”), another at *Sit semper* (“May it always be”), and a third at *Vobiscum* (“With you”). After he has said *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”) three times [Col. 1426C], and placed in the chalice the part of the Lord’s Body which he holds in his right hand, saying the entire prayer *Haec sacrosancta commistio* (“May this holy mingling”), silently, he shall turn his mouth toward the deacon and kiss him; the deacon shall kiss the subdeacon, with each bowing to the other; and the subdeacon likewise another, if he seeks the peace by going to the step. Having given the peace to the deacon, the priest shall place upon the paten that part of the host from which the ministers are to communicate. Having placed it there, he shall say the prayer *Domine Jesu Christe* (“Lord Jesus Christ”); when it has been said, he shall immediately take the Body of the Lord together with the chalice in both hands, draw it to himself, and receive the Body of the Lord over the chalice, then the Blood. Then, placing the uncovered chalice upon the corporal, he shall turn [Col. 1426D] to the right-hand corner of the altar. Having put the paten there with the hosts, he shall take from the vessel prepared by the deacon a host, which he shall put on the paten; and one or more, when necessary, of those that are there he shall put back in that vessel. This shall be done only on Sundays and on Maundy Thursday. That vessel shall remain upon the altar until after Mass. When this has been done, the priest shall communicate the deacon and subdeacon from the third part, and then communicate from the other hosts all the others who are to receive. As far as he can, he shall take care that no part of the Lord’s Body remains.

When the deacon approaches for communion, [Col. 1427A] without kissing the priest’s hand, he shall raise the front of his alb, bend his knees beside the altar, and, with his head thrown back and his mouth fittingly open beneath the priest’s hand, receive the Body of the Lord. Having received it, he shall rise and bow low. The subdeacon shall do likewise; after doing this, taking the tube [Note: [Col. 1427D] By “tube” understand the instrument prepared in the form of a tube for receiving the Blood of Christ. Communion under both kinds was subsequently abolished for ministers of the altar and laity alike, both by councils of the Church, as will be noted below at chapter 58 of this book, and by the general chapters of the order, as appears from the following definition of the general chapter of 1261: “Since grave dangers have already arisen, and graver ones may arise in the future, from receiving the Blood of the Lord which members of the order customarily receive from the chalice after Holy Communion, the general chapter ordains [Col. 1428D] that lay brothers and nuns of the order, except ministers of the altar, shall not approach the chalice in the customary manner.”], if it is then needed, he shall go leftward behind the altar. If it is not then needed, he shall follow the deacon. The deacon, coming before the chalice, shall bow and receive it at the priest’s direction, and take the Blood from the same side of the chalice as the priest; he shall not touch that side with his hand until it has been rinsed with wine. If only one or two are to communicate after him, he shall administer the Blood to them from the same side of the chalice from which he received it, holding the chalice in his right hand and placing his left under [Col. 1427B] their chins. Those who are to receive, whether deacons or subdeacons, holding the foot of the chalice with their left hand, shall fit it to their mouths as seems expedient to them. But if there are more, after receiving the Blood, the deacon shall place the chalice there upon the left-hand corner of the altar, holding it, while the subdeacon stands by and assists in this fashion: he shall hold his right hand outstretched beside the outer rim of the chalice and hold its foot with his left hand. The deacon shall hold with both hands in the chalice the tube which the subdeacon has previously prepared. Before placing himself to hold the chalice in the manner stated, the subdeacon shall first receive the Blood with the tube. While the brothers receive the Blood, wine shall be poured into the chalice by the deacon as required, from the cruet which the subdeacon previously prepared beside the altar. If anything of the Blood remains, he shall drink it with the chalice after returning the tube to the subdeacon. Before returning the tube, as far as possible, he shall empty it of the Lord’s Blood by drawing upon it from both ends; and he shall return the chalice to the priest without kissing his hand. The subdeacon, holding the tube crosswise before his face, shall go behind the altar to the priest to serve him wine in the chalice. Before the priest receives the chalice, if any whole hosts remain after the communicants, he shall put them back in the vessel. Having received the chalice, he shall rinse his fingers in it; then, placing it upon the altar, he shall go to the piscina and wash his fingers in water. Having dried them with the middle of the linen [Col. 1427D] prepared for him for this purpose, he shall return to the altar to drink the wine which he left in the chalice. Having drunk it, he shall rinse the chalice again with wine. Having consumed this, he shall place it upright upon the altar beside the paten. Likewise, it shall not be laid on its side even at private Masses. Thereafter the subdeacon, holding the tube, shall stand at the altar [Col. 1428A], facing the paten until the end of the Collect. Meanwhile the deacon shall fold the corporal upon the altar, and, turning to the Postcommunion, carry the Missal back to the right-hand corner of the altar.

When the priest begins the Collect after *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), the deacon, drawing down his chasuble, shall bow until *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“For ever and ever”). Then, straightening himself, and after *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”) or *Ite, missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”) has been said, he shall bow. Then, going to the altar, he shall transfer from it the chalice and paten to the service-table, consuming there with his tongue any portion of the Lord’s Body remaining upon the paten. Afterwards, taking the tube, he shall rinse it with wine, then the paten; after drinking this, he shall pour in more wine, rinsing the inside of the chalice, and consume it again. A third time he shall pour in wine, rinsing it in the same manner, and the subdeacon shall consume it [Col. 1428B]. If necessary, he shall pour in wine yet another time. When these have been washed and dried with the linen with which the priest shortly before dried his fingers, he shall put them away, together with the corporals and chalices. When Mass has ended, the priest shall bow before the middle of the altar, praying alone without the deacon. Having done so, he shall straighten himself and, kissing the altar, sign himself.

If it is Sunday, he shall give the blessing for the reader at table which is contained in the book [Note: [Col. 1428D] See the Rule of St Benedict, chapter 38.]. Then, bowing, he shall withdraw with his chasuble let down, which before Mass he had borne raised over his arms to the altar. If the deacon and subdeacon have already completed what they had to complete, they shall precede him in the order in which they came to the altar at the entrance of Mass. The priest, having removed [Col. 1428C] his sacerdotal vestments, shall come to the step [Note: [Col. 1428D] That is, the step of the presbytery.] where the Epistle is read and ask pardon as on festal days. On private days, however, he shall bend the knee immediately upon withdrawing. [Note: [Col. 1428D] Moreover, note that almost all these ceremonies fell into disuse, and that the rites of the Roman Church were substituted in their place by the general chapters of the order—namely by the general chapters of the years 1618 and 1628, and those which followed.]

## CHAPTER LIV. On Masses at which there is only one minister

If there is only one minister at Mass, the priest, vested in stole and maniple, shall go with the minister to prepare the altar. If the minister is a deacon, he shall perform the altar-service insofar as pertains to himself and the subdeacon. When the Epistle has been read, however, he shall not leave the choir; rather, he himself shall pour water from the cruet into the basin and dry himself with the towel with which the priest dries himself before the Secrets. Before he, having received the Blood from the chalice, withdraws to the left-hand corner [Col. 1428D], the one who assisted the priest in vesting shall approach with the tube prepared beforehand, assisting him in every respect as the subdeacon customarily does. But if the minister is a subdeacon, when he goes to the altar before the priest, he shall turn rightward [Col. 1429A], bowing low to the priest. At the confession he shall stand at the right. He shall place the Missal at the right-hand corner of the altar and the Text at the left, removing the latter after the Gospel. After the Epistle he shall wash his hands where the deacon also does. He shall serve the bread and wine and offer the paten and chalice. He shall draw down the chasuble, and always receive the peace and communion, except at a Mass for the dead, at which he may neither receive the peace nor communicate. When he is to read the Epistle, he shall bring the Epistolary into the church before vesting, and carry it back from there after Mass. The priest, in order to read the Gospel, shall ask the abbot for a blessing, but shall not descend from the altar-step. When the Gospel has been read, he shall say *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) there, if it is to be said. Then he shall immediately withdraw to the right-hand corner of the altar, where he shall say *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”). [Col. 1429B] When *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) is not said, he shall say *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”) where he read the Gospel.

It should be known that on all days when the community communicates, several hosts may, when necessary, be consecrated at the morning Mass and distributed upon the paten to communicants. In that case, if possible, the minister shall be a deacon—namely, the one assigned to the Gospel in the preceding week. But on all other private and festal days only one host shall be consecrated at every Mass; the priest, holding its third part over the chalice, shall distribute it to communicants, and then the Blood, in the manner above stated for the deacon, unless a deacon is present. It should also be known that no one ever kisses the abbot’s or priest’s hand except at Mass, and then only in the places defined above; and when the pastoral staff is given to the abbot in the community; and at the Purification of Blessed Mary, at the offering of candles.

## CHAPTER LV. In what order water is to be blessed.

On Sunday, when the signal for Terce has been rung, the church servant, having prepared a small stand upon the step of the presbytery, shall place salt and water upon it, together with the sprinkler; and, when the ministers and priest have vested and the altar has been prepared as stated above, the signal shall again be rung to summon the community. Those arriving shall arrange themselves as for Mass. This they shall always do at Terce when Mass is to follow immediately. When the ringing has ceased at the prior’s signal, the prayer shall be said. When it is complete, the priest, carrying the collectary, shall come before the step of the presbytery. Having arrived there, he shall bow to the altar. Then he shall bless the salt and water in the same manner as is set forth in the collectary, holding his hand over them while he recites the exorcism. When he has cast the salt into the water in the form of a cross and completed the exorcism, he shall hand the book to the subdeacon, who shall remove the salt-cellar and set it apart upon the step of the presbytery.

When the cantor has begun the antiphon, the priest shall take the sprinkler, dip it in the water, and go up to the altar, bowing at the altar-step. Then he shall sprinkle water before the altar and, beginning on the right side, go round it while sprinkling, until he reaches the front; there, bowing, he shall sprinkle the presbytery on both sides. Meanwhile the minister shall take water from the ewer containing the blessed water into any vessel, and, carrying another sprinkler, shall sprinkle the cloister and the workrooms: namely, the chapter-house, parlour, dormitory and the necessary rooms of the dormitory, warming-house, refectory, kitchen, and cellar.

> [Note: Col. 1429.] Observe the antiquity of the use of blessed water, not only upon persons but also in all the places of monasteries.

On returning from the workrooms, if any of this water remains, he shall pour it into the receptacle appointed for this purpose at the entrance to the church. He shall put the vessel he carries and the sprinkler away in the vestry. The priest, standing on the step of the presbytery, shall sprinkle first the abbot, then himself, then the ministers and the others approaching from the upper end of the choir, between the forms and the seats, as they stand in choir at that hour. Returning downward through the middle of the choir, each shall go up to his own place; and the novices who stand before the forms, having been sprinkled with water, shall return there. Those outside the choir or behind the choir, both monks and novices, shall come by the upper entrance of the choir and return through its middle. With respect to lay brothers (*conversi*), each church shall act according to the arrangement of its own oratory.

When the antiphon is finished, the priest, interrupting the sprinkling, shall turn toward the altar and say the collect *Exaudi nos* (“Hear us”) where he stands. When Terce has begun, after the *Gloria Patri*, he shall resume the sprinkling already begun. If it has not perhaps been completed by the *Gloria* of the first psalm, the priest shall stand in the same place and suspend the sprinkling until after the *Gloria Patri*; when it is complete, he shall return to his place and sit with the ministers. Then the sacristan shall bring water to the guests and household, put some into the vessel from which they ordinarily take water, and then into the vessel of the lay brothers.

When Terce has been said, on Sundays, on solemnities when no work is done at any season, and on feasts on which work is done in summer, the cantor shall immediately begin the Introit, even though the board is then being struck for a dead person. He shall do likewise on private days in summer, unless the Mass is such that it ought to be interrupted for a person recently deceased.

## CHAPTER LVI. How the community is to conduct itself at Masses

[Col. 1430D]

On all days on which two Masses are to be celebrated, at the second Mass the *Kyrie eleison* shall begin in the choir where the Invitatory is; at the first Mass it shall begin in the other choir. At the Mass of the night on the Nativity of the Lord, it shall begin in the choir of the Invitatory. When it is finished, they shall turn toward the altar. If the priest says *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, when the cantor begins, *Et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis* (“And on earth peace to people of good will”), they shall restore their faces as they were. When they say *Adoramus te* (“We adore you”), they shall bow, rising at *Glorificamus te* (“We glorify you”); and they shall similarly bow at *Suscipe deprecationem nostram* (“Receive our supplication”). At *Cum sancto Spiritu* (“With the Holy Spirit”), however, they shall sign themselves and turn toward the altar. When, after *Dominus vobiscum* (“The Lord be with you”), they have responded *Et cum spiritu tuo* (“And with your spirit”), they shall lean upon the misericords until the Epistle begins. Then, rising, they shall stand until the Gospel, as they stood while singing the Introit. At the greater Mass, however, they may sit together meanwhile if they wish. At the morning Mass, after the first *Dominus vobiscum* until the Gospel, anyone who wishes may sit; and after the *Sanctus* until the end of Mass, except during the *Agnus Dei*.

At all principal feasts, as also on other days, the Responsories and Alleluias are sung jointly by both choirs. At the end of Responsories and verses, at every Mass, the entire neume shall be sung, in order to avoid discordances. It should also be known that whenever only one Alleluia is said at Mass, whether a Responsory is said or not, the first neume of the Alleluia is omitted; but after the verse, in the repetition, the same Alleluia is sung with its complete neume. But when two or more Alleluias are said at one Mass, they shall be sung complete with their neumes, without repetition, except the one immediately before the Gospel, which is repeated. It should be noted that at the Vigil of Easter and of Pentecost only one Alleluia is said, but it is not repeated.

At the end of the chant before the Gospel, the brothers shall turn their faces toward the altar and sign themselves when they say, *Gloria tibi, Domine* (“Glory to you, Lord”). If *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) is to be said, when the cantor continues *Patrem omnipotentem* (“the Father almighty”), the choir shall turn to face the opposite choir. When they come to *Homo factus est* (“He was made man”), they shall ask pardon as on feast days. When they say *Adoratur* (“He is adored”), they shall bow, rising at *Et conglorificatur* (“And is glorified with [the Father and the Son]”). When they say *Et vitam futuri saeculi* (“And the life of the world to come”), they shall turn their faces toward the altar.

When the cantor begins the Offertory, they shall turn and stand as before. When it has been sung, they shall turn again toward the altar until the priest says *Orate, fratres* (“Pray, brethren”); then they shall return to the misericords until *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (“Through all ages of ages”). Then they shall rise and, with their faces turned toward the altar, stand thus until the *Sanctus*. Afterwards the choirs shall turn to face one another and bow while saying, *Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus* (“Holy, holy, holy”); when they begin *Pleni sunt caeli* (“Heaven [and earth] are full”), they shall rise, and sign themselves when they say *in nomine Domini* (“in the name of the Lord”). Having said the final *Hosanna in excelsis* (“Hosanna in the highest”), they shall turn their faces toward the altar and stand thus until *Per omnia saecula saeculorum*.

> [Note: Col. 1431D.] “They shall stand thus,” because at that time neither the host nor the chalice was elevated after the consecration.

Then they shall lean upon the misericords until they respond, *Et cum spiritu tuo*, after *Pax Domini sit semper* (“May the peace of the Lord be always [with you]”). Immediately rising, they shall stand face to face until after the first *Agnus Dei*. Then each shall ask pardon in his own place, bending the knee, except the ministers of the altar; and, after a pause long enough for one *Pater noster* to be said, the cantor shall begin the second *Agnus Dei*.

> [Note: Col. 1431D.] “They shall ask pardon, bending the knee.” This is the perpetual practice of the Cistercian Order: at the remembrance and mention of sins, the monks prostrate themselves as a sign of penitence and in hope of pardon.

If it is a day for prostration, after the *Sanctus* has been said they shall lean upon the forms until they respond, *Et cum spiritu tuo*, after *Pax Domini*. Then they shall do as has just been stated.

## CHAPTER LVII. Concerning the Peace

> [Note: Cols. 1431D–1432D.] The Peace—whether conveyed by an instrument or by an embrace—is nevertheless always given by a kiss to those who are to communicate, as is clear from the rubrics of the Missal and from these chapters.

No one shall receive the Peace unless he is about to communicate, except perhaps the prior, when it is necessary for him to give it to guests; or the subprior in the prior’s absence; or, if both are absent, whoever is then the senior of all those in choir. On Sundays and feasts when the brothers customarily go to Communion, the prior of those wishing to communicate shall come to the step and receive the Peace from the subdeacon. When he has returned to the altar, those who are to communicate shall approach the prior in their order, so that the prior remains at the step where he received the Peace until the first person after him has received the Peace from him. When he has given it, he shall withdraw to the right-hand choir of the novices, leaving at the step the person to whom he gave it. That person too, after giving the Peace to the next, and leaving there likewise the person to whom he gave it, shall move behind the prior.

While these make confession to one another, the rest shall follow in order, in the way described for the first persons, receiving the Peace from one another and arranging themselves in order behind the prior, two by two, confessing to each other. After confession they shall turn their faces toward the altar, and shall not return to their stalls until after receiving Communion. The last monk shall give the Peace to the novice who meets him in the middle of the choir, and who shall carry it to the lay brother when he appears at the choir-door. Then, arranging himself last with the next-to-last, he shall make confession.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning Communion

Meanwhile those who are first shall approach Communion in their order. On coming to the step nearest the altar, they shall lean upon the joints of their hands; then, having gone up the step, bent the knee beside the corner of the altar, and received the Eucharist, when they have risen they shall bow. Thus they shall pass behind the priest to the chalice.

> [Note: Col. 1432D.] “To the chalice.” This practice of receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist under both kinds has been abolished by the Church, as we have already said; see the Council of Constance, session 13; the Council of Basel, session 30; and the Council of Trent, session 5, under Pius IV, canon 1.

There, bowing again, they shall drink, and bow once more. As they return from the altar, the sacristan, standing at the head of the left choir of novices, shall offer wine to each, bowing; and each in turn shall bow to him before and after receiving it. This must be done not only here but everywhere, whenever they give or receive anything. When these things have been done, they shall bow toward the altar and go up to their stalls. This order concerning the Peace and Communion shall be observed at both Masses.

If anyone should at any time wish to communicate alone, having received the Peace from the minister, he shall confess either to the abbot, if he is present, or to the first person whom he finds standing in the right-hand choir. When Communion has been said, if the community communicates, those who wish may sit meanwhile until *Dominus vobiscum*. Those who remain standing shall turn their faces toward the altar until the priest says *Dominus vobiscum*; then they shall sit upon the misericords until the final *Dominus vobiscum*. Then they shall rise facing the altar, and, when *Deo gratias* (“Thanks be to God”) has been answered, they shall bow and depart. If it is Sunday, however, they shall neither bow nor depart until after the reader’s blessing.

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning private Masses

Throughout the year the brothers may sing private Masses during the time of reading; and after the Offertory of the community Mass, even in Lent, except on the Wednesday at the beginning of the fast. But on Lenten feasts upon which work is done, and on the feast of Saint Maurice when a fast-day falls, the rule set out in Chapter Fourteen shall be maintained.

> [Note: Col. 1433D.] “Are sung,” namely, in the community.

On days, however, when two Masses are sung, immediately after the first the priests may sing privately wherever the abbot considers suitable, except for fast-day Masses. In Lent, if a feast on which no work is done falls during the week, they shall not sing except after the Offertory. But if they have time to sing before the greater Mass, they shall not be permitted to omit that Mass.

On every day on which they fast and do not work, anyone who wishes and is free may sing Mass until None; in Lent, until Vespers. Whenever anyone doubts whether, by singing, he will be forestalled by the hour, he shall ask the sacristan by a sign: if the sacristan assents, he shall sing; if he refuses, he shall refrain. Whoever wishes to sing shall have two witnesses—that is, two assistants—one of whom must be a cleric capable of ministering to him.

> [Note: Col. 1433D.] “Two witnesses,” that is, two assistants.

If he is only an acolyte, he shall not presume to carry the chalice to the altar, to minister the bread and wine, or to offer them to the priest; but he may perform the other duties. If he is a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, he may minister the bread and wine in the chalice and offer them to the priest; nevertheless, only the priest who sings shall mix in the water. If the other brother is a layman, he must presume to do none of these things, except bring water and pour it for the priest before the priest is vested in sacerdotal garments, or light a candle or lamp. Both he and the other laymen may go up into the presbytery, not only for Mass but whenever necessary; nevertheless, they shall not go up upon the altar-step unless they are commanded to do so for some necessity, or when they communicate.

> [Note: Col. 1433D.] “The altar-step, however,” etc.: namely, because of reverence for the most holy sacrament.

Masses for the dead are not customarily sung on Sundays and solemnities on which a sermon is usually given in chapter, unless someone has recently died. The daily Mass customarily said for our deceased brothers is to be omitted only on Good Friday and the following Saturday, and on Easter Day, Pentecost, and Christmas Day. Yet on the days of Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas the weekly celebrant of that daily Mass shall sing the Mass of the feast at the altar where that Mass is customarily sung, and shall say the collect *Inclina* (“Incline”) in second place; if it is a trental, he shall add *Deus cui proprium* (“God, whose property it is”).

If, on one of those three days, a person recently deceased should arrive, the said weekly celebrant shall omit the Mass of the feast and say Mass for him. He shall say the first collect for him, namely *Inclina*; the second, *Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, cui numquam* (“Almighty everlasting God, to whom never …”), for those for whom *Inclina* was said; and, if it is a trental, the third, *Deus cui proprium*. At both community Masses, so long as the body is present, a collect shall be said for him. Those who sing privately shall say only a collect for him, both before burial and afterward; nevertheless, anyone who wishes may sing for him.

Those who sing private Masses, both they and their assistants, shall moderate their voices so that others suffer no hindrance. If anyone sees an altar-cloth laid upon the altar, he shall not presume to sing upon it without the direction of the person who placed that cloth there. Nor shall he make preparations around the altar at which he is to sing after the general—that is, community—Mass has begun, until the Offertory has been sung, except at the morning Mass, when priests may sing after Prime.

> [Note: Col. 1434D.] “General,” that is, community.

The priest, having vested and sprinkled his fingers with water, shall say the confession before the altar-step, standing in the middle between his assistants, so that the cleric is on his right and the layman on his left. One who has sung for the dead may insert other collects for any necessity, provided that he does not exceed the number of three collects, unless by the abbot’s command he adds a fourth. Collects of the Holy Trinity, of the Holy Spirit, or of the Saints shall not be said. At other Masses too, except on days on which it is not permitted to sing for the dead, collects for the dead may be inserted. He shall not give the Peace unless guests attending that Mass, or a brother intending to communicate, are present. Otherwise he shall conduct himself as the priest does in the community.

At every Mass the priest shall kiss the altar only three times, and his chasuble shall be drawn for him as often. It should be noted that abbots, monks, and lay brothers, when they hear Mass in churches not of our Order, receive the Peace like others if it is offered to them.

## CHAPTER LX. On which days two Masses are sung

> [Note: Cols. 1434D–1436D.] In ancient manuscripts, among these feast days are not listed the days of Saints Robert, Bernard, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Catherine, or the Crown of Thorns; indeed, neither are Saints Eligius, Edmund, and Malachy. The reason is that such saints’ feasts had not yet been instituted, or at least had not yet been received by the Order, when these Usages came to light.
>
> Moreover, if anyone wishes to know in what years and by which general chapters most of these saints’ feasts were eventually received and prescribed for the Order: the feasts of Saint Malachy, bishop, and Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, were received and prescribed by the General Chapter in 1191; the feast of Saint Julian of Le Mans, by the General Chapter in 1193; the feast of Saint Peter of Tarentaise, archbishop, by the General Chapter in 1197; the feast of Saint John before the Latin Gate, by the General Chapter in 1222; the feast of our holy father Robert of Molesme, founder of the Cistercian Order, by the General Chapters of 1222 and 1259; the feast of Saint Eligius, by the General Chapter of 1230; that of Saint Dionysius, by the General Chapter of 1232; the feast of the reception of the Lord’s Crown, by the General Chapter in 1240; the feast of Saint Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury, by the General Chapter in 1247; the feast of Saint John Chrysostom, granted to the Bernardine college where the principal part of his head is kept, by the General Chapter in 1251; the feast of Blessed Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers, by the General Chapter in 1255; the feast of Saint Peter Martyr of the same Order, by the General Chapter in 1256; and the feast of Saint Francis, founder of the Order of Friars Minor, is recorded as received only by the General Chapter in 1259. His commemoration, however, had long before been prescribed, namely by the General Chapter in 1228.
>
> The feast of Saint Ursula and her companions was granted to the scholars of the College of Saint Bernard in Paris in 1258, and soon afterwards permitted to the whole Order by the General Chapter in 1262. The feast of our holy father Bernard was placed among the feasts on which, according to the usage of the Order, a sermon must be delivered in chapter—that is, among the principal feasts of the Order—by the General Chapter in 1260. It had begun to be celebrated much earlier, as noted above, but with less solemnity.
>
> In the text of this chapter, where “thousand virgins” is read, perhaps “virgin martyrs” would be better read. For the Roman Church celebrates this feast under the name of Saint Ursula and her companions, not under the name of the Eleven Thousand Virgins.

On the Nativity of the Lord; on the Circumcision and Epiphany of the Lord; on Easter Day and the three following days; on the Ascension of the Lord; on Pentecost and the three following days; on the feasts of Saint Stephen, Saint John, the Holy Innocents, Saint Thomas the Martyr, and Saint William, bishop; on all solemnities of Blessed Mary; on the feast of Saint Vincent, at whose Vespers the twelfth Responsory, namely *Gloria et honore* (“With glory and honour”), shall be said; on the Conversion of Saint Paul; on the feast of Saint Matthias the Apostle; on the solemnity of Saint Benedict; on the feasts of Saint Mark the Evangelist, Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, Abbot Robert, and Philip and James; on the Invention and Exaltation of the Holy Cross; on the Nativity and Decollation of Saint John the Baptist; on the feasts of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Mary Magdalene, James the Apostle, Saint Peter in Chains, Saint Lawrence, Abbot Saint Bernard, Bartholomew the Apostle, Matthew the Apostle, Michael the Archangel, the Lord’s Crown, Dionysius and his companions, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Luke the Evangelist, Simon and Jude, All Saints, Saint Malachy the Bishop, Martin the Bishop, Saint Edmund, Andrew the Apostle, Saint Catherine the Virgin, Eligius the Bishop, Nicholas the Bishop, Thomas the Apostle, and the Dedication of the church; on diocesan feasts; and on every Sunday, two Masses are sung, and the brothers are free for reading. But garments are neither beaten out nor spread in the sun.

## CHAPTER LXI. When the priest and ministers ought to go up to the altar

At Mass for the dead, and at the morning Mass when two Masses are to be sung, the priest and ministers shall go to the altar at the beginning of the Introit. At the other Masses they shall wait until the *Gloria*.

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning *Kyrie eleison*

At Mass, *Kyrie eleison* is always begun in the choir where the Invitatory is, except at the morning Mass when two Masses are sung. It is said nine times alternately: the choir in which it begins says *Kyrie eleison* four times, with *Christe eleison* inserted once; while the other says *Kyrie eleison* twice, with *Christe eleison* inserted twice. Both choirs together shall finish the final *Kyrie eleison*. At the regular hours, however, and everywhere else, the whole community shall say *Kyrie eleison* once and pause, *Christe eleison* once and pause, and again *Kyrie eleison* once.

## CHAPTER LXIII. When “Gloria in excelsis Deo” and “Ite missa est” are sung

At the Vigils of Easter and Pentecost; on every Sunday; on feasts of twelve Lessons outside Advent and Septuagesima; and throughout the octave weeks of Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost, at every Mass *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and *Ite missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”) are said, except at fast-day Masses, which do not fall on Sunday.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On which days the customary collects are to be omitted

From the Vigil of Christmas until the Circumcision; from the Lord’s Supper until the octave of Easter; from the Vigil of Pentecost until the Octaves; on Sundays and on all feasts of twelve Lessons, even if two Masses are celebrated in the community, the customary collects are to be omitted at both Masses. Likewise, on the Saturday of the Ember Days and at all principal offices for the dead, these same collects shall be omitted.

## CHAPTER LXV. On which days “Credo in unum Deum” is said

On the Nativity, Circumcision, and Epiphany of the Lord; on Easter, the Ascension, and Pentecost; and on every Sunday, at every Mass, unless it is for the dead, *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) shall be said. Further, on the Invention and Exaltation of the Holy Cross and on the solemnity of the Lord’s holy Crown; on all solemnities of Holy Mary; on all solemnities of apostles and evangelists; on the feast of All Saints; and on the Dedication of the church, it shall be said only at the Mass proper to that solemnity.

> [Note: Col. 1436D.] “The Lord’s Crown,” that is, the reception of the Lord’s Crown: a feast instituted by the General Chapter in 1240 at the request of Saint Louis the King.

## CHAPTER LXVI. When the brothers ought to go to the Peace and Communion

On the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost, the brothers must receive the Peace and communicate, every excuse being set aside, unless perhaps the abbot has prohibited someone. On every Sunday, whoever can shall communicate. Priests, however, who sing during the week, if they do not sing on Sunday, may communicate or not at their own discretion. On the other days, anyone who perhaps did not communicate on Sunday may communicate if he wishes.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On which days three lamps are to burn, and on which days sermons are held in chapter

No more than five lamps shall be kept in the oratories. Of these, one shall be placed at the step of the presbytery, another in the middle of the choir, and a third behind the choir. These three must be lit at Vigils, at Mass, and at Vespers on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, Palm Sunday, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, Trinity, all solemnities of Holy Mary, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the solemnity of Saint Benedict, All Saints, Saint Bernard, and the Dedication of the church. At the commemoration of all the faithful departed, they are lit only at Vigils and Mass. On these days also—except transferred feasts and except the commemoration of the dead—sermons are held in chapter. They are also held on the First Sunday of Advent and Palm Sunday. Whoever wishes may keep the remaining two lamps for lay brothers and guests, and light them whenever he wishes. Where necessary, however, it is permitted to have more lamps for private Masses.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. How the brothers are to conduct themselves on Sundays and feast days

When they hear the signal for Vigils, the brothers shall rise and, prepared, enter the church, bowing to the first altar. They shall always do this whenever they pass before any altar. Then, bowing again to the high altar, they shall enter the choir from the upper end. For they do not ordinarily enter or leave from the lower end when the seniors stand in the lower choir, except the abbot, the prior, and the others who stand nearest the abbot or prior on either side.

Whether the abbot is present or absent, as many may enter or leave from the lower as from the upper end, and may go or return between the abbot’s and prior’s stall both to read their assigned Lessons and to receive blessings, as each abbot judges expedient according to the arrangement of his own oratory. It should be noted that, when the abbot enters the choir, only two bow to him, whether they are abbots or monks: one in his own choir, and the other nearest him in the opposite choir. Likewise, in the choir of novices, one bows on each side. Nor shall anyone arriving bow to the abbot standing in his stall, except those four. This must nevertheless be observed: if, before those who customarily stand nearest the abbot have entered, others enter, and no one yet stands between them and the abbot, as many of these as enter from either choir shall bow to him.

When they reach their places, they shall stand with faces turned toward the altar until the signal stops. Likewise, they shall stand before every hour of the day and before Masses. When the signal has ceased, they shall say the customary prayer upon the misericords: that is, *Pater noster* (“Our Father”) and *Credo in Deum* (“I believe in God”). At the sound, all shall rise, turn toward the altar, sign themselves, and, bowing again, stand there. When the priest slowly and drawn out says *Deus in adiutorium meum intende* (“O God, come to my assistance”), they shall bow deeply, with hands joined, until *Domine, ad adiuvandum me festina* (“O Lord, make haste to help me”) has been completed with the same slowness and gravity. They shall do likewise wherever they bow. At all times when the community is in church, at every hour, the priest shall reverently and slowly say *Deus in adiutorium meum intende*, and the community shall respond *Domine, ad adiuvandum me festina*, etc. There shall be a pause before *Gloria Patri* and before *Sicut erat*, even if what follows is to be said more quickly. Then the work of God shall be celebrated.

*Venite, exsultemus Domino* (“Come, let us rejoice in the Lord”), with the Invitatory, shall be said before the step of the presbytery by two brothers: namely, he who is serving the present week for the Invitatory and he who served the preceding week. On coming to the step they shall bow; after beginning the Invitatory they shall bow again; and thereafter they shall bow only at the end of each verse. After the repetition of the Invitatory they shall bow once more and return to their rank. On private days, however, the person singing the Invitatory shall not bow before beginning it. From the beginning of the Invitatory until *Gloria Patri* is said, the brothers shall keep their faces toward the altar; then the choirs shall bow toward one another until *Sicut erat in principio* (“As it was in the beginning”). In the same way they shall bow whenever *Gloria Patri* is said in the community, except at the blessing of water, at a novice’s blessing, at the Purification of Saint Mary while the candles are distributed, at the beginning of the fast while ashes are given, and at *Gloria et honor Deo* (“Glory and honour to God”) while the cross is adored on Good Friday.

If the abbot happens not to be present at the *Gloria* after *Venite*, he shall make satisfaction before the presbytery, as he customarily does at other hours when he is absent for the *Gloria* of the first psalm, and then come to his stall. After the hymn has begun, no one shall leave the choir until it is finished, except for an unavoidable reason; nor shall anyone leave during the other hymns, except *Jam lucis orto sidere* (“Now that the light of day has risen”), when Prime is sung immediately after Matins without an interval. Nor shall the priest who is to sing Matins for the sick leave before the hymn has begun.

No one shall sit from the beginning of *Deus in adiutorium* until after the hymn. Then, with hands folded upon their knees, they shall sit together during the first psalm and stand during the second; thus they shall proceed through the remaining psalms, and likewise in the second Nocturn. The abbot is not obliged to observe this rule. If anyone leaves and is not to return to that office, he shall bow before leaving. If the abbot leaves, one of the converted monks shall follow him with a light into the hidden places.

The abbot shall begin the first antiphon, or the Alleluia, in the first Nocturn. If he is absent, it shall be begun by the senior member in the choir where the Invitatory is. The weekly officer shall begin the remaining Alleluias. Whoever begins an antiphon or Alleluia shall stand reverently and a little away from the footboard until the metrum, and shall not bow until the first verse is completed.

> [Note: Col. 1439D.] *A podio*: that is, away from the board upon which the feet of those chanting the psalms rest.

The person immediately below him shall begin and intone the psalm, by day and by night, likewise standing a little away from the footboard until the metrum. But when the last of the clerics begins his own antiphon, only then shall the person above him begin the psalm. The same is to be observed at all offices for the dead, except that the person beginning the psalm does not rise while the others are seated. The person beginning the antiphon, without waiting for the end of the verse, shall bow and sit down. At the principal offices for the dead, however, he shall wait for the end of the verse and then bow.

It should be noted that whenever the last person in the choir has begun his antiphon, the next-to-last and the others senior to him, in reverse order, shall begin whatever antiphons remain to be said in the same choir, even if one of them has already begun another antiphon at that office. This may occur at offices for the dead, or perhaps sometimes at the regular Vigils because of the small number of monks. If an antiphon has been assigned to the abbot and he is absent, if the Invitatory is in the right choir, the monk standing beside him shall begin it and then his own; if it is in the left choir, he shall act similarly. In the same way, each person shall begin the antiphon of the person standing above him if he is absent. No one arriving late, except the abbot who begins the first antiphon, shall begin an antiphon assigned in chapter to another person; it shall be begun by the person to whom it was assigned.

At the end of the final antiphon of the first, second, and third Nocturn, on feast days as well as private days, the brothers shall turn toward the altar, and the versicle shall be said by the weekly officer, who alone bows after the versicle. The same shall be done at every versicle said at the other hours. If the reader must say the versicle, calling another person to say it, while the next-to-last verse of the sixth psalm before the *Gloria Patri* is being said, he shall bow toward the middle of the altar and proceed solemnly through the middle of the choir, bowing before the abbot. If another abbot is seated in the prior’s place, he shall bow once between them. On coming to the book, with body bowed toward the abbot, not carrying a lantern and with hands folded, he shall ask the blessing in the same voice in which he is to read, both there and elsewhere. Having received it, he shall not read until the commotion of those sitting down has ceased.

On returning from the reading, he shall bow between the abbot’s and prior’s stall, turning his head briefly toward the abbot. If there are two abbots, he shall bow once between them toward the altar; then, coming before the step, he shall bow. On feast days he shall prostrate himself upon the joints of his hands; on private days, upon his knees, placing his cowl beneath his hands. Then, bowing, he shall return to his seat. In the same way all shall make satisfaction, upon the joints of their hands, in the place where they are, whenever they incur a fault in the oratory, without turning right or left. We do not customarily make satisfaction merely for a mistake in chant notation.

Thus shall he conduct himself who is to read the first, fifth, and ninth Lesson. Those who read the other Lessons shall go to read while the Responsory is being sung before the verse. All readers shall see to it that the burning candle may suffice for the next reader. Those who sing the Responsories shall rise at such a time that they can lift the seat before beginning the Responsory. Having begun it, they shall bow, and likewise after the verse; but if the *Gloria* is to be said, they shall bow not after the verse but after the *Gloria*.

When the responsory *Aspiciens* is sung [Col. 1440B] with three verses, the singer bows only after the third verse. No one is to read two Lessons, or sing two responsories, or both a Lesson and a responsory within one nocturn, unless necessity compels it; likewise, no one of higher rank is to precede one of lower rank, except in the Gospel. When the reader begins, the brothers are to turn toward him and stand thus until he says, “And the rest.” He who has read the twelfth Lesson, once he has read what concludes in the Lectionary, is to say, “But thou, O Lord,” unless the cantor has directed him to read something suitable for the day, or something else. For the sacristan, when he sees that he has risen earlier than he ought, customarily warns the cantor by a sign to have the twelfth Lesson prolonged. Then he who reads it is not to finish it [Col. 1440C] until the sacristan signals or the clock sounds. When it has been read, he is neither to extinguish the candle nor close the book, if the Gospel is to be read from it.

Moreover, while the brothers sing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”), they are to bow at *Sanctus, sanctus* (“Holy, holy”), rising at *Pleni sunt* (“Full are”); and, when they finish the canticle, they are to turn toward the altar. When they have said, “Glory to thee, O Lord,” making the sign of the cross, they are to turn toward the reader of the Gospel, which must be read at the lectern from which the Lessons at Nocturns are also read. After *Te decet laus* (“Praise is due to thee”) has been said, turning toward one another, they are to bow until after *Cum sancto Spiritu* (“With the Holy Spirit”); then they are to sit on the misericords until after the end of the Collect. If he who reads the Gospel commits a fault, he is to make satisfaction between the abbot’s and the prior’s seats.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On Lauds

At Lauds, after *Deus misereatur nostri* (“May God have mercy on us”) has ended, and at Vigils after the hymn has ended, no one is to sit in choir until the first verse of the following psalm has ended [Note: [Col. 1440D] “Until the first verse,” etc. This should be noted, because many either do not know it or neglect it.], nor is anyone to leave. But whoever leaves is, upon returning, to remain standing for two verses before sitting. Likewise, at Vigils and at Prime, anyone who has left choir is to remain standing for two verses. At Prime at every season, except on Sunday, all are permitted to sit in the same order as at Vigils. At Prime on Sundays [Col. 1441A], and at Vespers at every season, we stand during the first and third psalms and sit during the rest. Those who leave choir must take care not to remain outside for more than two psalms, and that no more than two standing beside one another leave together.

He who sings the responsory is to bow before beginning it, and bow again after the verse. At its repetition, the choir is to turn toward one another. If the Invitatory is in the right choir, the cantor is to begin the hymns on all feast days, both at Vigils and at the other Hours, except Sext and None; these are to be begun by the one accustomed to begin them on ordinary days. If the cantor is absent, they are to be begun by the one appointed to intone the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*. If the precentor is in the left choir [Col. 1441B], he is to begin; if he is absent, the one appointed to begin the aforementioned canticles is to do so. On ordinary days, both at Vigils and at the other Hours of the day, the hymns should be begun by the one who begins the psalm, when the weekly officiant begins the antiphon. At every season, whoever begins the hymns is to stand apart from the step. At *Kyrie eleison* they are to sit on the misericords, as at the other Hours. When the weekly officiant begins *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”), all are to rise [Col. 1442A]; when it has been said, they are to bow. At the other Hours they do not rise until after *Deo gratias* (“Thanks be to God”), except at Vespers.

If it is Sunday, they are to stand facing the altar until the blessings [Note: [Col. 1441D] “Blessings.” On these blessings see chapter 35 of the Rule of St Benedict and chapter 108 of this book.] over the cooks are completed. If a commemoration is made, they are to stand thus until *Oremus* (“Let us pray”), and then sit on the misericords, not rising until after *Deo gratias*.

In winter, if a day of labour and fasting coincide, Prime is to follow immediately after the response “Amen”; otherwise, after *Deo gratias* they are to bow and leave. Then, if it is daylight, the sacristan is to ring the signal gently; if daylight has not yet appeared, it is not to be rung. In the meantime the brothers are to sit in the cloister by a light kindled by the church servant, but are not to read. When daylight has come, the signal is to be rung gently and an interval allowed, so that those who wish [Col. 1442B] may put on their shoes, go to the necessary place, change dressings for ailments, or wash their hands; anyone who wishes may sit in the cloister. On returning for Prime, except on Sunday, they are to sprinkle themselves with holy water and stand in their stalls until the signal ceases. Then they are to make the same prayer that they made at Vigils; and, Prime having been sung in the same manner, Mass is to follow.

## PART THREE. On the observances to be kept in regular exercises

[Col. 1441]

## CHAPTER LXX. On chapter and confession

After morning Mass, the sacristan is to ring the signal to summon the brothers to chapter [Note: [Col. 1441D] “To chapter”: this chapter is meant in the sense of chapter 46 of St Benedict’s Rule, where he orders one who has offended in any matter to come before the community [Col. 1442D] and there publicly disclose his offence and undergo the penance imposed upon him.]; nor is he to stop it until the blessing has been given. On hearing the signal, the brothers are to assemble in chapter, bowing before their seats. When they have sat down, they are to bow to one another. When the abbot, or any other person who is to preside over chapter, enters, all are to rise for him, bowing only to the abbot as he passes; when he has sat down, they too are to sit. But the man who is to sit beside the abbot is to make a deep bow toward the abbot from his place, though not upon knees or elbows, and then sit. The same is to be done in every place by anyone who is to sit beside him, except in church. For in church the brothers neither make such reverence to one another [Col. 1441D] nor do so at table, nor during the night.

When the reader comes before the lectern, he is to open the book and bow for the blessing. After the first reading, he is not to say, “But thou, O Lord”; but after he has read through “And of many other saints,” the brothers are to rise and turn eastward, saying the verse found in the collectary, namely [Col. 1442C], “Precious in the sight of the Lord,” the weekly priest beginning it. When he has said, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son,” they are to prostrate themselves over the upper seats, or bow upon their knees according to the season, all saying together, “Lord, have mercy.” Those sitting near the entrance of the chapter-house, on either side, are to prostrate themselves upon the ground facing east; those who bow are to do as those seated in the abbot’s seat; all the others are to bow facing them. When the priest says, “And lead us not into temptation,” they are to rise, remaining upright until the priest says, “Direct and sanctify”; then they are to bow. This bow is to be made alike at every season. The reader too is to bow or prostrate himself before the lectern as those near the chapter-house entrance do. When “Who made heaven and earth” has been said, they are to sit [Col. 1442D], provided that he who presides over chapter sits first. After sitting, they are not to bow to one another as before.

When all have sat down, the reader is to begin the reading from the Rule. When it is finished, he is to say, “But thou, O Lord”; and, taking the tablet, he is to read the brief [Note: [Col. 1442D] “Read the brief”: that is, the schedule containing the names of the officials for the following week.], if it is to be read that day. If the subprior presides over chapter and the reader is his prior, then, if he announces him, he is to name him “brother”; and in the same way he is to name himself. While the brief is read, anyone who hears his own name is to bow. If a weekly duty has been assigned to anyone who knows that, owing to some difficulty, he cannot perform it, he may ask for mercy concerning it in the present chapter; he may not do so outside it. If this happens through grave necessity, he is to ask pardon in the following chapter and state the necessity.

After the tablet has been read, the commemoration of the brothers is to be announced thus: “Commemoration of all deceased brothers and familiars of our Order.” Then he who presides over chapter is to say, “May they rest in peace”; and, when “Amen” has been said, the reader is to bow and offer the book to the abbot. The abbot is either to receive and expound it, or indicate that it should be carried to another. The reader is to show that person [Col. 1443B] the passage which he is to expound, and then go to his place. On reaching it, he is not to bow before his seat; but after he has sat down, he is to bow as the others did when they first sat. If he is crossing from the left side to the right, or from the right to the left, he is, on arriving before the lectern, to bow eastward and then cross to his place.

After “Bless, ye” has been said by him who presides over chapter, the passage is to be expounded, even on Good Friday. If anyone arrives before “Bless, ye” is said, he is to bow before his seat. When he has sat down, he is to bow as he would if he were present at the first confession. But if he comes afterward, while the seated community is bowing, he is to say “Bless, ye” in a low voice, so that those sitting around him may answer, “The Lord.”

[Col. 1443C] Once the passage has been expounded, no one is to presume to speak or ask pardon until he who presides over chapter says, “Let us speak of our order.” Then, if a deceased person is to be absolved, he is to be absolved at the cantor’s prompting. Afterward, if the last day of the thirty-day commemoration is to be remembered, the cantor is to commemorate him. Then, if a brief [Note: [Col. 1443D] Here *breve* means a schedule containing the name of someone recently deceased.] for a deceased person is to be read, it is to be read by the cantor, but only at the command of him who presides over chapter. When it has been announced, the abbot is to say, “May he rest in peace.” After all have said “Amen,” he is to appoint whatever seems fitting for that person’s soul.

Afterward, anyone who knows himself guilty in some matter is to ask pardon. Then accusations [Note: [Col. 1443D] “Accusations,” that is, charges or denunciations; see chapter 46 of the Rule of St Benedict.] are to be made, if any are to be made. He who brings an accusation is not to use circumlocutions in it [Col. 1443D], but is to say plainly: “That man did this.” But he who is accused, as soon as he hears his name, is, without answering, to ask pardon at his seat [Note: [Col. 1444D] “Ask pardon”: that is, prostrate himself upon the ground.]. When questioned by him who presides over chapter, “What do you say?”, he is to answer while prostrate, “My fault.” At that man’s command he is to rise; if he is guilty, he is humbly to confess his fault and promise amendment henceforward. But if he does not regard himself as guilty, the person who accused him is not to repeat the accusation unless questioned; another person, however, if he knows that the accused is guilty, may state it.

It should be understood that the accused is not to make an accusation on that same day against the man who accused him. When someone rises for judgment after being accused by another, he is to make satisfaction as many times as he is accused in that proceeding. While he lies upon the ground, no one is to speak. But after he has risen, whatever is to be said about him in that proceeding is to be said, lest he be compelled to rise after he has sat down, unless some reasonable cause against him should arise later in chapter. If someone comes voluntarily for judgment, he is to confess under one request for pardon all the negligences that he intends to confess. But if another compels him to rise by making an accusation, then, after that accusation has been dealt with, should he wish to say something concerning himself, he is to ask pardon again.

If several are before judgment together, the first is to stand in the middle and speak first. When he has spoken [Col. 1444B], he is to be judged at once and dismissed from judgment, unless the abbot makes him, or any one of them, remain there after the others have been dismissed, to undergo a graver judgment if his fault is greater than theirs. The others are likewise to be judged one by one and dismissed one by one, unless all have the same cause, so that they may be dismissed together.

Those dismissed from judgment are to return to their seats by passing behind those standing. No one is to be accused by more than three persons, except by him who presides over chapter, and except if he later commits some fault in the chapter itself. Nor is anyone, on account of one accuser, to ask pardon more than once, even if that person speaks of several faults concerning him, unless, as excepted above, he commits another offence in that same chapter. No one is to presume to speak in chapter [Col. 1444C] unless accusing another, being accused by another, or when someone has lost something—apart from the abbot and prior, and certain seniors to whom the abbot has given consent—unless commanded or questioned by the abbot, or himself intending to ask something concerning the order.

If, by chance, someone at the abbot’s command presents to chapter the greeting of the lord pope, the community is to rise and make a deep bow. At the greeting of a king, bishop, abbot, or any other similar person, they are to make a deep bow while seated. Likewise, they are to bow when the abbot orders them to make some common prayer; likewise for those whom he wishes to promote or demote, restore to their rank, bind by penance [Col. 1444D], or absolve [Note: [Col. 1444D] See chapter 2 of the Rule of St Benedict.]; and likewise all to whom he orders something to be done.

No one is to accuse another on suspicion alone, except concerning what he has heard, seen, or heard reported. When an accusation has been made against someone who is to be beaten in that proceeding, he who presides over chapter must take care that he is not beaten by the person who accused him [Note: [Col. 1444D] Ibid., and chapter 28.]. Once the abbot has ordered the person to be beaten to remove his clothing, he is immediately to sit in the place where he is standing; taking off his cowl, he is to place it before himself on his knees. Through the neck-opening of his tunic [Col. 1445A], he is to draw out his arms and the whole upper body as far as the belt; and, standing with bowed head, he is to say nothing except, “My fault; I will amend myself,” which he is to repeat frequently. Meanwhile, no one else is to speak, unless perhaps one of the priors humbly intercedes for him. He who beats him is not to cease beating until the abbot commands; when he has stopped, he is to help that brother dress. Once dressed and standing, the brother is not to move until the abbot says, “Go, sit down”; then, bowing, he is to go to his place.

It should also be known that one of lower rank ought not to beat a superior—for example, a deacon a priest—but an equal may beat an equal, or a superior an inferior. Care must also be taken that no one outside chapter speaks to anyone, or makes signs, concerning [Col. 1445B] the faults or secrets dealt with in chapter.

If a bishop, an abbot of monks or regular clerics, or even a king enters chapter, all are to rise and bow to him as he passes before them. If he asks for affiliation, it is to be granted to him, all standing, by the book [Note: [Col. 1445D] “By the book”: that is, by the Rule of St Benedict, with almost the same ceremony as is described in the ancient book of customs, distinction 15, final chapter.]; and after “Amen” has been answered, the abbot likewise is to request from him a share in his good works. After he has remained as long as seems proper to him who presides over chapter, the prior, or one whom the abbot commands, is to lead him to the guesthouse before the community leaves, unless the abbot wishes to retain him until the end of chapter. If he is a monk, cleric, or layman, affiliation having been granted while seated, he is to be escorted by any brother.

[Col. 1445C] If anyone, after the brothers have entered chapter, leaves it without being commanded, except because blood is flowing from his nostrils, because he is vomiting, or to bring a tablet to be read, he must make satisfaction. No one is to ask permission to leave except a cook or one charged with an obedience, someone compelled by natural necessity, someone to whom the abbot has previously given instruction, or someone who is to be sent on a journey. When they need it, these customarily ask by a sign for permission to leave in order to perform their office.

When the matters to be dealt with have been dealt with, all are to rise, turn eastward, and he who presides over chapter is to say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” After all answer, “Who made heaven and earth,” they are to bow eastward and all leave, unless someone remains [Col. 1445D] for confession or illness. Yet while anyone is confessing, no one is to remain there unless occupied with a like task. For during all times of reading—though only before the midday meal, and also in the interval before Prime—they may make confession there.

After they have therefore sat down, the prior is to say, “Bless, ye”; and when “The Lord” has been answered, the prior is to continue, “God be with us”; and when “Amen” has been answered, he is briefly to confess [Col. 1446A] the faults for which he asked pardon. Having said these, he is immediately to add: “For these and all my other sins, I confess myself guilty and beseech pardon.” Then the prior, having pronounced absolution over him, is to impose penance. Next, if he wishes, he may briefly strengthen, admonish, or rebuke him as seems expedient. If anyone, for confession, detains someone who hears confessions after the signal for Mass, or calls him away from Mass into chapter, he is, with both standing, to make his confession briefly.

## CHAPTER LXXI. How the brothers are to conduct themselves during reading

[Note: [Col. 1445D] In accordance with this chapter, our monks were permitted to devote all the time remaining to them from the Divine Office and manual work to either reading or prayer, and this in accordance with chapters 48 and 53 of the Rule of St Benedict.]

The brothers who leave chapter are to sit for reading, except those whose responsibility for offices leaves them no time to read. When they have completed these duties, however, they are to return [Col. 1446B] to reading. They may go into church for prayer not only then but at every time of reading and during every interval when they are not sitting; they are neither to keep their hoods on their heads, nor read, nor hold a book. Likewise, when the work of God is celebrated in church, they are neither to keep their hoods upon their heads nor read, except those who do not know the Psalter and those who have need to look ahead, read, or sing something for the service then at hand.

Those who sit in the cloister are to conduct themselves devoutly, each reading his own book, except those who sing from Antiphonaries, Hymnaries, or Graduals, and those who look ahead at their Lessons, which the cantor, or any brother qualified for this task whom he has appointed, is to hear. Nor are they [Col. 1446C] to disturb one another by asking questions, except about long and short vowel accents, a word which they do not know how to read, or the beginnings of readings at table, at collation, and, when necessary, at Vigils; such questions are to be exceedingly brief. If anyone keeps his hood upon his head while reading, he is to wear it in such a manner that it can be perceived whether he is asleep or not.

If anyone needs to go elsewhere, he is to put his book back in the book-cupboard [Note: [Col. 1446D] The *armarium* was a cell or place between the church and the chapter-house prepared for preserving books.]; or, if he wishes to leave it at his seat, he is to signal to the brother sitting next to him that he should guard it. This sign may also be made after Vespers. If anyone wishes to take from another a book from which the latter is reading or singing because he needs to consult it, he is to hand him another book, and the one to whom he hands it is to let him have it peacefully. If he does not wish to lend it [Col. 1446D], the requester is to bear this peaceably until he makes a complaint concerning it in chapter. They are to conduct themselves thus while sitting.

While walking, they are to proceed humbly and, with heads uncovered, make reverence to one another when they meet [Note: [Col. 1446D] “Making reverence.” This reverence is identical with the blessing of which St Benedict speaks in chapter 63 of his Rule. Both are made by uncovering the head and inclining the body. By this Peter the Venerable established the thirteenth distinction between Cistercians and Cluniacs.]. If they meet the abbot, they are to step aside and make reverence to him. Such reverence is to be made everywhere outside the dormitory whenever they meet the abbot or one another. [Col. 1447A] At work, however, when they meet one another, they neither make mutual reverence nor say “Bless, ye.” It should be noted that no visiting abbot is bowed to in the cloister otherwise than as to a monk, except the one occupying the abbot’s seat and their own abbot. No one is to make a sign by means of his hood, nor call anyone from afar by voice or sound. It should be noted that at all times of reading the brothers may wear their night-clothes [Note: [Col. 1447D] “In night-clothes”: that is, the footwear and garments which they use at night.]. If anyone in any way scandalizes a brother with whom he does not usually speak, he is to tell the prior; then, if the prior commands, after calling that brother, he is to lie prostrate at his feet [Note: [Col. 1447D] “Lie prostrate,” according to chapter 91 of the Rule of St Benedict.] until the offended brother, appeased, raises him.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Which workshops the brothers should enter, and when

[Col. 1447B]

### § I. On the kitchen

No one is to enter the kitchen, except the cantor and scribes to smooth a tablet; to melt ink [Note: [Col. 1447D] *Incaustum*: that is, ink.]; to dry parchment; and the sacristan or another person to light the church lamp, put coals in the thurible or small pan, or bless salt. Yet even these are not to enter if they find a sufficient fire in the warming-room. The abbot’s cooks and the infirmarian are also excepted for the duties of their office, as is anyone called by the cook to put a cauldron on the fire or take it off.

### § II. On the refectory

Likewise, no one is to enter the refectory except the infirmarian and the cooks of both kitchens—the abbot’s, namely, and the brothers’—for the duty of their service; those summoned from the refectory to help them [Col. 1447C]; all others who need to drink; and the church servant, for the salt-cellar.

### § III. On the warming-room

They may enter the warming-room both for the purposes stated above and to grease their undershoes, bleed themselves, or warm themselves. This must be done decently and not barefoot in another’s presence. It should nevertheless be noted that those brothers who, according to the Rule [Note: [Col. 1447D] Chapter 48.], make the annual circuit of the monastery cloisters may enter these three aforementioned workrooms.

### § IV. On the parlours

They are never to enter the parlours. If they have some business there, they are to ask at the door by a sign or sound; and then, if permission is granted, enter. During reading-time, no more than [Col. 1447D] two are to speak together there with the prior, unless the prior judges that necessity requires him to summon more. When they have completed the business for which they entered, they are to leave quickly unless detained.

### § V. On the dormitory

They are to enter the dormitory whenever they need to; on entering it, they are to put their hoods upon their heads. When entering the necessary house [Col. 1448A], they are, as far as possible, to hide their faces in their hoods, and sit with their sleeves folded before them and their cowl hanging down to their feet. If they sit in scapulars, they are nonetheless, as far as possible, to cover themselves in front. They are not to sit in the dormitory except when putting on or taking off their shoes, or when changing tunics if they choose to do this sitting; and then they are to sit on their own beds or footstools.

When leaving and dressing, they are to do so decently and carefully, lest they appear naked. They customarily do this not outside the dormitory but beside their own bed; and those who sleep outside are likewise to do so beside their own beds. The abbot may grant scribes, cellarers, infirmarians, and the cooks of both kitchens permission to lay aside cowls and scapulars, to whichever of them and wherever he sees fit [Col. 1448B]. They must nevertheless ensure that they are without cowl or scapular as little as possible. No one may even gird himself without one of these two garments. No one is to climb straight into bed, but from the side-board [Note: [Col. 1447D] *Sponda*: that is, the footstool mentioned above; or, if one prefers, the front side of the bed upon which they sat and from which the monks then drew their feet up into bed.], turn his feet into the bed. They are not to lie upon blankets, except young monks and infirm persons who are outside choir; all of these, if they wish, may place them on poles in summer. No one is to shake garments there or make signs, except perhaps with the abbot or prior, or when someone calls another on behalf of the abbot or prior.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the *mistum*

If it is a dinner-day, the signal for the *mistum* [Note: [Col. 1448D] What the *mistum*, mentioned here and in chapter 38 of the Rule of St Benedict, is, is described below: it consists of a quarter of a pound of bread and a third of a hemina of wine, and nothing else. For St Benedict permits nothing else with this *mistum* or breakfast except drink and bread, as is clear from chapter 35 of the Rule.] is to be struck three times in church before Sext. If it is a fast-day, it is to be struck the same number of times after Sext. On hearing it [Col. 1448C], the refectory reader and cook are to come to the refectory. If either is absent, the one present is not to wait for him. If both are present, the lower-ranking man is to say, “Bless, ye”; the higher-ranking man, giving the blessing, is to say, “May the Giver of all good things bless the food and drink of his servants.” After the *mistum*, he is to say silently: “Deign, O Lord, to repay with eternal life all who do us good for thy name’s sake.” The youths who take the *mistum* before Terce are to do likewise.

The measure of the *mistum* is a quarter of a pound of bread and a third of a hemina of wine. After the *mistum* has been taken, if anything remains, they are to return the bread to the chest and the wine to the vessel. It should be understood that from the beginning of Lent until Easter—except Sundays—the *mistum* is not taken, nor on the three Rogation days, the four Ember days, or the vigils [Col. 1448D] of the Lord and saints.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. How the brothers are to conduct themselves in winter on ordinary days from Vigils until Terce

From the Kalends of November until Easter, except from Christmas until the Octave of Epiphany, on ordinary days [Col. 1449A] the brothers are to prostrate themselves at Vigils [Note: [Col. 1449D] “Prostrate themselves”: namely, over the choir benches. “For prayer”: that is, for the *Pater noster* and the *Credo in Deum*.] for the prayer and for “O God, make haste to help me,” over the benches; and at *Kyrie eleison* they are to sit on the misericords, as at the other Hours. The remaining matters are to be completed according to the Rule [Note: [Col. 1449D] “According to the Rule”: that is, according to chapters 8 and 9 of the Rule of St Benedict.], as we have stated above.

After Vigils, or after the Office of the Dead if it is to be said, a light having been kindled by the church servant before the book-cupboard and in the chapter-house, the brothers are to sit in the chapter-house itself, and those who wish are to read. They are not to sit in corners unless reading. They are to wear their hoods in such a way that it can be recognized whether they are asleep or not. On hearing the clock, those who need it are to go to the necessary place, so that, when the signal is rung, all may be ready to enter choir. The church servant must ensure that the light burns before the book-cupboard during all that interval. If the abbot wishes a light to burn in the cloister while the brothers perform the work of God in church at night, he may do so. The sacristan is not to stop the signal until the abbot makes the sound for prayer [Note: [Col. 1449D] “For prayer”: that is, for saying the *Pater* and *Ave*.]. This is not done at the other Hours, except at Vigils and Prime at every season, and at Terce from the Ides of September until Easter, when we labour and fast.

Anyone absent from the prayers that are made before the regular Hours is to ask pardon in chapter, except the prior or another who has charge of the community; the cellarers and the guest-house monk; the cantor during reading-time; and those hearing Mass. Nevertheless, all must attend the prayers at which the *Pater noster* and *Credo in Deum* are said. Yet none of these is exempt from the prayers [Col. 1449C] made at both Vespers on feast-days. If, after Matins, daylight has not yet appeared, the sacristan is to kindle a light and an interval is to be made; the brothers may sit in the cloister if they wish, but are not to read.
