When daylight appears [Note: [Col. 1449D] “When daylight appears,” so that, in accordance with chapter 8 of the Rule, Matins or Lauds might be performed at the beginning of daylight. Thus Lauds was followed by Prime, Prime by Mass, and Mass by Terce, after which they entered chapter. This was from the Kalends of November until Easter, on ordinary and feast days on which they devoted themselves to labour or manual work.], the signal is to be rung. After the prayer has been made, they are to make the sign of the cross and bow over the benches or misericords, if the season requires it; they are to do likewise at all Hours after the prayer has been made. When the priest has finished “O God, come to my assistance,” at “Glory be to the Father” they are to lean over the benches or bow, as the season directs; and they are to do likewise at every Hour of the day. Prime having been said, Mass is to be sung. After Mass, the signal for Terce having been rung, the brothers entering church are to sprinkle themselves with holy water; when the signal stops, prayer is to be made as at Vigils. Terce having been sung, they are to go to chapter as stated above; and the same is to be done on feast-days on which we work [Col. 1450A]. A monk may carry a scapular with one or more tunics, beneath one or two cowls, when necessary.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On labour

When chapter has ended [Note: [Col. 1449D] “When chapter has ended”: that is, at approximately the sixth hour, according to chapter 48 of the Rule of St Benedict.] and the brothers are ready for labour [Note: [Col. 1450D] “For labour.” This is the eighth distinction between our monks and Cluniacs: our monks, but not theirs, devoted themselves to manual work according to the Rule of St Benedict. See Peter of Cluny, Letter 47, Book IV of the *Letters*.], the tablet is to be sounded by the prior or subprior, or by another if the prior orders it, should they perhaps be occupied with something of greater usefulness. At its sound all are to assemble [Note: [Col. 1450D] “All are to assemble,” etc. See the aforesaid chapter of the Rule.], except the infirm and those assigned to various offices. Yet the servant of the infirm, unless he is detained by the care of the sick, the cantor, sacristan, guest-master, and master of novices are to assemble like the others, unless the abbot has excused any of them from this in chapter because of some more important occupation [Col. 1450B].

If the prior is at home, he is always to sound the tablet [Note: [Col. 1450D] “Tablet”: that is, a wooden instrument intended to summon the brothers.] and arrange the work in the parlour. But if he is outside choir, the subprior or the person appointed is to sound the tablet; nevertheless, sitting in the parlour, the prior is to arrange the work. If anyone wishes to remain behind for any necessity, he is to state his reason to the prior and do what seems right to him. If the prior permits him to remain, he himself, prompted by that brother, is to provide what he is to do after he has completed the task for which he remained behind.

If some grave necessity prevents the prior from sounding the tablet and arranging the work as stated, the subprior or the person appointed is to do the same, arranging everything by signs if possible [Note: [Col. 1450D] “By signs,” etc. St Benedict gave occasion for the signs which R. P. Julian Varnier transcribed at length in his Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict, both by imposing perpetual silence upon his monks and perhaps by allowing necessities to be requested by sign rather than voice at meals (chapter 38).]. If it cannot be done by signs [Col. 1450C], he is to speak, but with the utmost brevity and only concerning the work. If the abbot or prior wishes to keep anyone back, the person detained is to signal to him who strikes the tablet; if he cannot do so before labour, he is to indicate it afterward. The prior is to distribute the tools and other implements necessary for labour as he sees fit.

Those going out shall follow the prior, or whomever the prior has appointed; likewise after work. The departure for work, the beginning and end of the rest-period, and the return from work are to be indicated by the sound of some object rather than by voice. The abbot shall appoint a mature brother to follow the community when it goes to work or returns from it. When they have reached the work, they shall not multiply signs among themselves, nor presume to speak—except perhaps briefly, necessarily, and quietly with the prior, apart from the brethren, concerning the work itself. [Col. 1450D–1451A] The prior also shall speak rarely when the abbot is absent, and, when he is present, most rarely, out of reverence for him.

It should nevertheless be noted that, in the abbot’s absence, the prior may hear confession there if necessary. But the subprior, even when both abbot and prior are absent, may not hear confession there, except concerning some matter such as a delusion in a dream, or when someone has committed an offence there; and even this is to be done briefly, standing. For when they are present, he is in no way to intervene.

They shall neither rest nor go elsewhere for any necessity without permission. But if it happens that they go away, once the necessity has been met they shall return to work promptly. If the reader, cook, or refectory-servant is there, on hearing the signal for the *mixtum* [the light meal], or before the signal is struck, according as they are working farther from or nearer to the monastery, they shall ask the prior’s permission to leave, and also what they ought to do after the *mixtum*. When they rest, insofar as the condition of the weather and the situation of the place permit, they shall rest near the prior. During their rest they shall not make signs to one another.

It should be known that during work no one may read, nor even carry a book to the work. No one, moreover, without cowl or scapular, whether there or elsewhere, may speak or make signs. On hearing the signal for the Hour—

> [Note: Col. 1451D. “For the Hour,” namely both Sext and None.]

—they shall stop work, even if they are to sing the Hour there. Those who are in church shall sing promptly, yet preserving a measured gravity. The same is to be done when the community is working in the cloister or within the boundaries. If the prior has not heard the signal, whoever hears it, whether at hay-cutting time or otherwise, shall signal him. The one in charge of the work, even if he is not a priest, shall always himself conclude the prayers before the Hours. He shall himself say the versicles and responsories, or assign them to another. If he is a priest, then, in the absence of the weekly officiant, he shall also begin the Hours and either himself supply, or assign to another, the Little Chapters, the *Our Father*, and the Collects. Yet the prior and subprior, if they are deacons, shall reserve the *Our Father* for themselves; if they are below that rank, the one who sings the Hour shall complete everything.

When the community is working within the boundaries and perhaps carrying wood or something similar that can be left without damage, when they hear the signal struck before the Hour, they shall leave there what they are carrying and hasten to the Hour. If they are within the auditorium or cloister when they hear the aforesaid signal, they shall carry their burdens to the designated place and then hasten to prepare themselves for the Hour. If they are carrying something that cannot safely be left carelessly, such as bread, wine, provisions, or similar things, they shall seek a suitable place and leave it there. If they are working beyond the boundaries and are not required to come to the monastery for the Hour, they shall say the Hour there and afterwards take up their burdens again. [Col. 1451D–1452A]

On returning from the work, they shall put the implements they brought where implements for work are customarily prepared, or return them to the prior. The exceptions are shears, hoes, forks, rakes, and sickles, which throughout the season of pruning, hoeing, hay-cutting, or harvest each person customarily keeps by his bed.

If at that time the Hour of the Work of God is being celebrated in the oratory, all shall hasten to arrive before the Work of God begins. But if the *Gloria* of the first psalm has been said, unless the *Kyrie eleison* has already begun, they shall, if possible, gather together and, with the prior leading, come to the step—

> [Note: Col. 1451D–1452D. “To the step,” namely of the presbytery. Our fathers ordered those who arrived late for the Work of God to stand there, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 43, which requires such negligent persons to stand in the last place or separately from the others, as punishment for their negligence. Thus our Cistercians assigned the step of the presbytery for this penance or satisfaction, as a place especially suitable for it: there they would stand apart from the others, last of all, and could easily be seen by everyone—both of which Saint Benedict requires.]

—with the priors arranged in the middle; and, in the absence of abbot and prior, the overseer of the work shall stand in the middle. Then they shall ask pardon before the step, either kneeling on the ground or, according to the season, merely lowering their hands upon their cowl to the ground. At the *Kyrie eleison* they shall prostrate themselves on their knees or bow, according to the season, until the end of the Hour.

If they have received permission to go into the stalls, they shall first bow to the one granting permission, then toward the altar; thus they shall proceed into the stalls, making satisfaction there upon the knuckles of their hands. This is always the manner in which they must make satisfaction among the stalls, except for one making satisfaction for a graver fault. It should be noted that the person granting permission shall not bow toward the altar before making the sign of permission; rather, with his right hand extended and turned upward, he shall move it from his left side across his breast to the right. Then they shall bow to one another, and afterwards toward the altar. [Col. 1452B–C]

Those who remain in the cloister after the community has gone out to work shall not make signs among themselves for as long as the community is outside. Cooks, however, those who prepare the refectory, and those who correct books may make signs to one another concerning their necessities. Likewise, those to whom permission to make signs has been given on account of some office assigned to them may make signs where, and with whom, this is prescribed for them.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the meal

After the Hour—

> [Note: Col. 1452D. “After the Hour.” Note that our brethren customarily went immediately after the Hour of the divine office to table, so that they might pass to bodily refreshment only through prayer and after spiritual food.]

—the prior, or one appointed by him, shall strike the signal. But if through negligence the food is not yet prepared, he shall not strike until it is ready; nor shall the brethren wash their hands, but meanwhile shall sit reading until the signal is struck. The same rule is to be observed at all meals.

When their hands have been washed and dried, they shall enter the refectory; and, coming before their seats, they shall bow toward the principal table. Then they shall rise and remain standing until the prior comes. If the prior is long delayed—which the prior ought altogether to avoid—anyone who wishes may sit meanwhile. When the prior comes, they shall rise for him. The prior shall bow before his seat before striking the bell; and the bell shall be rung at each meal long enough for the entire psalm *Miserere mei, Deus* (“Have mercy upon me, O God”) to be said. While it is being rung, whoever is in his place shall not go elsewhere until the verse is finished.

When it has been ended, the community shall say *Benedicite* (“Bless [us]”), and, when the verse and the *Gloria Patri* have been said, choir shall bow toward choir, saying: “Glory be to the Father; *Kyrie eleison*; and silently, *Our Father*.” When the priest has said, “And lead us not,” he shall rise and, standing toward the principal table, say: “Let us pray. Bless, O Lord, thy gifts,” etc., making one sign of the cross; and so he shall complete the entire blessing. When it is completed, the brethren shall rise and go to the tables. [Col. 1452D–1453B]

The cellarer and cooks shall see that both dishes are placed upon the tables before the bell is rung, if the abbot judges this expedient.

> [Note: Col. 1453C. “Both dishes.” In this consisted the fifth distinction established between our brethren and the Cluniacs: our brethren, unlike theirs, were content with the two regular dishes prescribed by chapter 39 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.]

Once the bell is rung, if any dishes still have to be brought, they shall not be brought until the reader begins to read. But if, when the reader begins, one entire dish still remains to be served at table, it shall be brought in order: first two bowls, one for the prior or abbot if he is present, and after “For the departed,” three—

> [Note: Col. 1453D. “After ‘For the departed,’ three.” Behold the piety of our brethren toward the dead. These portions of their dishes were given to the poor.]

—then two on the right side and two on the left, and so two on this side and two on that, until the last. Once the common food has been served, if the cellarer wishes to add something—

> [Note: Col. 1453D. “Add something.” Understand this of the special portions which, out of piety and mercy, were permitted for the weakened and infirm beyond the regular dishes; they will be mentioned often below.]

—for mercy’s sake to those whom the abbot has specified to him, he himself shall bring it to them and distribute it as he wishes; he shall do the same for the weakened brethren.

Once the reading has begun, the brethren shall uncover their bread, the prior doing so first. From then on, no one shall leave the refectory, nor shall anyone walk about while eating. No one shall wash his cup there with his hand; whoever wishes may wipe it. No one shall wipe his hands or knife on the napkin unless he has first wiped it with bread. Whoever wishes to take salt shall take it with his knife. Whoever drinks shall hold the cup with both hands. If anyone sees that another lacks something which he ought to have, he shall request it from the cook or cellarer. The person who sets something before another and the person before whom it is set shall bow to one another. The person to whom the prior sends something shall first bow to the bearer, then rise and bow humbly toward the prior.

> [Note: Col. 1453D–1454D. “Of the common food,” that is, of the regular dishes. To touch briefly here on the daily diet of our ancient monks:
>
> 1. It is clear, as appears from several chapters of this book, especially chapters 76, 84, and 90, that they had for their daily food a pound of ordinary bread and a hemina of wine, in accordance with chapters 39 and 40 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.
>
> 2. It is clear that, whether they took two meals or only one, they had each day two cooked dishes, which, according to Stephen, bishop of Tournai, in his letter to Robert of Pontigny, were supplied to them by field crops of legumes or garden vegetables.
>
> 3. It is clear that they sometimes allowed special portions to the weakened, feeble, and infirm out of piety and mercy; according to James, cardinal of Vitry, in chapter 14 of his *History of the West*, these were customarily prepared from fish, eggs, milk, and cheese.
>
> 4. It is clear that in summer, at harvest time, on days when they worked, they had one dish at dinner and another at supper, and that the latter was cooked, as appears from chapter 84 of this book. Consequently, on other days, if they supped at all, they took only fruits, vegetables, or the new growth of legumes, and these raw.
>
> From these matters alone it is evident that these poor of Christ not only obtained their food by the labour of their own hands, in rustic fashion, but also imitated the fare of the poor. More importantly, as the same Cardinal of Vitry testifies, feeding on straw like oxen from the Lord’s herd, they reserved the grain for those who came to them; for they served white bread to guests and kept coarse bread and second-grade bread for themselves. If this seems too harsh to anyone, let him learn from our holy father Bernard that exercise gives things flavours which idleness removes. For, as he says in his letter to Nepos, vegetables, beans, gruel, and coarse bread with water are repugnant to one at rest, but to one who labours they seem great delicacies.]

No one shall share the common food with anyone. But if something has been added for someone, unless it was given him by the cellarer because of bloodletting or illness, he may give only to the person sitting beside him on his right and to the person on his left; these persons, however, may give it to no one. If he gives it to only one person, that person may give it to the one beside him, but it shall proceed no further. The prior, like the others, shall strictly observe this rule concerning special portions. Guests, however, shall not give their general drink to another, nor may another receive it.

If anyone eating or serving commits an offence in any way, he shall ask pardon before the step. When the prior makes a sound with the knife, he shall rise, bow, and return to his place. When the bowls have been removed, the cook shall collect the spoons first from the right side, beginning with the prior; then from the left, beginning with the one next to the prior. [Col. 1454A–B]

When the prior wishes the reading to end, he shall say to the reader, “But thou”; and, after the response “Thanks be to God,” they shall cover what remains of the bread. When the reader has bowed, the prior shall strike the bell. They shall immediately rise and stand before the tables in the same order in which they stood before the meal, saying the verse begun by the cantor after the bell has ceased. When it has been said, they shall bow and go out chanting *Miserere mei, Deus*, begun by the cantor and sung with him by those standing in the right choir in church; the second verse shall be sung by the left choir. Thus they shall sing the remaining verses alternately, proceeding two by two, with the younger brethren leading. Yet the prior, or whoever is presiding over the community, shall follow them alone, between the two choirs. If an abbot is present, the prior shall go with a companion, while the abbot goes alone; if two abbots are present, they shall go together.

As the brethren enter the church, the first of the clerics to enter the choir shall strike the signal, if he can suitably do so. Entering the choir, they shall arrange themselves as for Mass, their faces turned toward the altar, until the *Gloria Patri*; then they shall prostrate themselves upon the forms, or, if the season requires it, bow, and afterwards sit upon the misericords. When the thanksgiving is finished, they shall rise, bow, and depart reverently. [Col. 1454C–1455A]

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the servers

Then the bell shall be rung to summon the servers. When gathered, they shall say the verse in a moderate voice. In the absence of abbot and prior, the one first in order of conversion, unless someone of higher rank is present, shall always bless the food. The table-reader shall ask a blessing from one of higher or equal rank and, before the meal, shall say the reading: “God is love; and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.” Afterwards he shall say: “May the God of peace and love always remain with us all.”

If the reader himself is of higher rank, one of the clerics shall ask his blessing and say both readings. But if no cleric is present, a lay brother shall ask the blessing, and the reader himself shall say the reading. The rule concerning special portions shall be observed as set out above. If, however, no one besides him is in that part of the refectory, he may cross to the other part and give to whomever he wishes.

After the meal, when the reading has been said, they shall there say the verse in a moderate voice, adding *Miserere mei, Deus*, with faces turned toward one another, never prostrating themselves there at any season. When the thanksgiving has thus ended, the table-reader shall always ring the little bell after the servers’ meal, except when in summer the brethren sleep after dinner, long enough for one *Our Father* to be said. Once this is finished, Vespers shall not be rung until they can go to their necessities and, if time permits, review the readings. [Col. 1455A–C]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On Vespers

At Vespers the weekly officiant begins the first antiphon; the second is begun by the one standing before all others in the other choir, abbots excepted; the third by the one standing after the weekly officiant; and the fourth by the second in the other choir. In the absence of the weekly officiant, whoever begins the first antiphon, whether superior or inferior to the weekly officiant, if someone inferior to him arrives beside him, shall name him to begin the third antiphon.

> [Note: Col. 1455D. “Shall name [the antiphon] to be imposed”: namely, for a guest-brother or newcomer, in order to avoid confusion in the divine office.]

If no inferior is present and someone superior comes beside him after the first antiphon, he shall name him to begin the third antiphon. The one beginning the second antiphon in the other choir shall act similarly. Whoever sings the responsory shall bow before beginning it, and bow again after the verse. When a responsory from a history is sung, once it has begun both the one who begins and the others shall turn their faces toward one another. The hymn shall be begun in the manner described above for Lauds. If a blessing is to be given to one returned from a journey, it shall be given before the commemorations, if these occur; and the brethren shall stand facing the altar until the blessing is completed. The same shall be done at all the Hours, whether for those setting out or returning, except at Compline when we lie prostrate upon the forms. [Col. 1455D–1456A]

## CHAPTER LXXIX. How the brethren are to conduct themselves after Vespers at all times

After Vespers, while seated in the cloister, they shall not read or sing loudly, nor make signs, except by command concerning guests, or to request permission to drink; or when someone, on behalf of the abbot or prior, calls another; or when someone signals the person sitting beside him to keep his book. They shall not sit together, nor shake out garments with a rod, except during hay-cutting and harvest, when they do not have reading-time before Sext. [Col. 1456A–B]

## CHAPTER LXXX. On drinking after Vespers

> [Note: Col. 1455D. “On drinking,” that is, on the beverage.]

When the sacristan strikes the signal in church, they shall gather in the refectory to drink—

> [Note: Col. 1455D. Properly “to drink,” because they took nothing but drink.]

—and, bowing before their seats, shall sit down, the prior sitting first. After he has rung the bell, and after the cantor has first said *Benedicite*, the weekly officiant shall say the blessing. Whoever arrives later shall, coming before the step, ask permission to drink; once he has received it, he shall bow there and go to his seat without bowing again. He shall not join those sitting in the higher seats, but shall sit on the seats before the tables and drink there, unless perhaps he ought to sit at the head of a table.

Then the prior shall strike the bell once—

> [Note: Col. 1455D–1456D. “Strike.” Namely, so that, once permission to drink had been given by this signal, they would begin to drink only together and after their superior.]

—after which no one shall enter the refectory. After an interval, three further strokes shall follow; at these they shall rise and bow before the tables or at the heads of the tables, and depart. Whoever is absent from this drinking shall make satisfaction in chapter, except the cellarers, infirmary officials, hospitaller, porter, those occupied in receiving guests, and those whom the abbot judges should be excused for definite reasons. Yet all who can suitably be present ought not to be absent. At these drinkings, as at those held in summer after None, if anyone commits a fault before the stroke of the little bell, he shall make satisfaction there; if afterwards, he shall ask pardon in the chapter on the following day. [Col. 1456B–D]

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the conference-reading

> [Note: Col. 1456D. “At the conference-reading,” that is, at the reading of the *Conferences* of John Cassian, according to chapter 42 of Saint Benedict’s Rule. Saint Benedict wished these Conferences or the Lives of the Holy Fathers to be read at this very hour, that is, before Compline, in the presence of the whole community, rather than other books of sacred Scripture, because they are easier to understand.]

Those coming to the conference-reading shall bow, and then sit down, even if the signal has not yet been rung. Once the brother who is to read has arrived, he shall sit at the lectern; having opened the codex, he may read there silently until the abbot arrives. On Saturdays, while feet are being washed, although he sits in that seat meanwhile, he does not customarily read there.

When the abbot arrives, all shall rise; and those before whom he passes shall bow to him. They shall rise only for the prior, or for whoever presides over the community, and, once he has sat, they shall sit. Then the reader, having received the blessing, shall read. All shall attend this blessing except the prior, or another presiding over the community; the cellarers; the refectory-servant and his assistants; the grange-master; the hospitaller; the master of novices; the abbot’s servants; and those who ring the signal for the conference-reading.

Meanwhile, anyone absent from the drinking may drink alone in the refectory without permission, even in a scapular. If the abbot judges it expedient, he shall appoint a mature brother to sit continuously near the refectory door during the reading after dinner, so that, should anyone wish to drink, he may signal him and that brother may go with him for his assistance. If he is absent—which he ought nevertheless to avoid—the person in need may go to drink without making any sign. In abbeys where such a brother has not been appointed, he shall ask permission by a sign from one of the more mature brethren, and so enter and drink.

The abbot shall not ask permission to drink or to undergo bloodletting; nor shall the prior, except from the abbot; nor the subprior, except from the abbot or prior. When the reading is finished, all shall rise; and, standing facing east, the abbot shall say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord,” and the community shall respond, “Who made heaven and earth.” Then all shall bow and enter the church.

If anyone does not come to the conference-reading early enough to be seated before “But thou” is said, when the hymn of Compline begins he shall go before the step of the presbytery and remain there facing the altar, conducting himself thereafter like those in choir until the end of the prayer after Compline. If a blessing is given to someone returned from a journey, the person making such satisfaction shall move aside near the step, and, when the blessing has been given, make the customary prayer there. [Col. 1456D–1457C]

## CHAPTER LXXXII. How the brethren are to conduct themselves after Compline

When Compline has been said, after the priest says, “The blessing of Almighty God,” the brethren shall sign themselves; and, after “Amen” has been said, they shall say the prayers *Our Father* and *I believe in God*. If a blessing is to be given to one returned from a journey, and the community is prostrate upon the forms, it shall by no means rise, nor shall the priest who gives the blessing. But if they are seated on the misericords, they shall rise and stand facing the altar while the blessing is said; once it has been said, they shall sit again on the misericords and make the customary prayer. The brother himself shall make the prayer in the place where he received the blessing, provided that he was with the others in choir for Compline.

When the prayer is complete, the abbot, going out, shall sprinkle each brother with holy water as they go out after him in order. They shall immediately put their hoods on their heads and, going nowhere else except the sacristan, those who sleep outside the dormitory, and those remaining for the vigils of a deceased person present there, all shall enter the dormitory. No one shall leave it except the sacristan, cellarer, hospitaller, keeper of the infirm, and one going to perform the *mandatum* [the ceremonial washing of feet]. They must not lie down without cowl, tunic, and stockings—

> [Note: Col. 1457D. “Without cowl, tunic,” etc.: namely, so that, in accordance with chapter 22 of the Rule, they should sleep clothed.]

—[Col. 1457C–1458A]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. How the brethren are to conduct themselves in summer, concerning vigils and until after Vespers

From Easter until the Octave of Pentecost, on ordinary days, *Venite exsultemus Domino* (“Come, let us rejoice in the Lord”) is sung by one brother with the invitatory; from the Octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of November, it is sung alternately by the two choirs, like *Domine, quid multiplicati sunt* (“O Lord, how many are they multiplied”). During this period—that is, from the Octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of November—the brethren shall prostrate themselves upon the forms for prayer, except during the Octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary. The rest shall be completed, as stated above, according to the Rule.

During the interval after Nocturns, those who wish may sit in the cloister, with a light kindled by the church-server if necessary. After Matins they shall say Lauds for the departed. When these have been said, and after an interval as on feast days, they shall put on their day-shoes and take their knives; and they shall do this whenever they customarily put on their day-shoes. Then, having been sprinkled with holy water and having made the prayer according to the season, they shall say Prime. Then they shall go to chapter; afterwards, to work until the first signal for Terce. On hearing it, those who are to sing Mass shall prepare themselves. Meanwhile they may go to confession in chapter; they may also pray and read—

> [Note: Col. 1458D. “They may pray and read,” because both were freely permitted to them during these intervals.]

—When the ministers have put on their vestments, Terce shall be sung. If one of the ministers is the weekly officiant of the *Iuvitatorium* [perhaps *Invitatorium*; materially uncertain], the one who ought to replace him in his absence shall fulfil that office. After Terce, Mass shall be sung; after Mass, they shall sit in the cloister.

If it is a fast day, after all has been celebrated in the order stated, they shall enter the dormitory after Sext, lay brothers leading, and rest in their beds until the eighth hour. Then the sacristan, awakened by the sound of the clock, shall ring the bell as is customarily done on other days. At this signal the brethren, having risen and put on scapulars, shall wash their hands if they wish; then, when the board has been struck, they shall work until the first signal of None. If it is a day on which the weekly officiants ought to take the *mixtum*, the sacristan shall ring for the *mixtum* during that interval for as long as he judges appropriate. Once the meal has been taken, they shall arrange the rest of the day as on ordinary winter days.

On the vigil of Pentecost, the sacristan must regulate the period of sleep after Sext so that the following interval may suffice for the office to be celebrated before None. When the brethren have been awakened by the customary signal, the altar ministers shall immediately prepare for the office; meanwhile the community shall devote itself to reading, and, once the ministers are vested, the signal shall be struck.

But if it is not a fast day, after Terce, when it is time to receive the *mixtum*, the sacristan shall strike the signal in the manner described. After Sext they shall go to the refectory. When they are proceeding after the meal to prayer, no one shall meet them; nor when they go out after the verse, nor when they go to the refectory after None, nor when they go to the dormitory after Compline, nor when they enter chapter. [Col. 1458B–1459A]

When all leave the church and follow the prior in the order in which they stand in choir, no one shall separate himself from the community until they enter the dormitory, except the sacristan and those who sleep outside the dormitory. No one shall leave the dormitory without permission, except the sacristan, cellarer, hospitaller, assistant—

> [Note: Col. 1459D. “Assistant.” By “assistant” understand one who, in accordance with Saint Benedict’s Rule, must be given to each official to help him, when necessary, in matters belonging to his office.]

—the abbot’s cooks, keeper of the infirm, subporter, or porter, if a matter of his office arises at that time.

After the meal, the servers, chanting *Miserere mei, Deus*, shall complete the verse there, never prostrating themselves at any season. Then they shall enter the dormitory. The cellarer shall carry the servers’ bowls back to the kitchen so that the brethren do not find them in the refectory after None. As soon as he is free, he shall take his place in the dormitory like the others. When the signal to rise is given, the cooks shall hasten to prepare water in the lavatory for washing and in the refectory for drinking. The rest, having prepared themselves and washed their hands, shall either enter choir or sit in the cloister until the signal is struck. [Col. 1459A–B]

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On drinking after None

After None has been said, they shall go to the refectory, the younger brethren leading, in the order in which they stand in choir, proceeding two by two. The prior shall follow alone, or the subprior if the prior is absent. Arriving before their seats, they shall bow, then enter the tables and remain standing until the prior sits. The cooks of the preceding week, as soon as they have entered, shall wipe the cups around and fill them inside with water; then they shall stand facing the principal table until the prior rings the bell. When he rings it, they shall come to the step. After the bell has ceased and *Benedicite* has been said, the weekly officiant shall give the blessing; and, after the response “Amen,” the one first at the prior’s right shall offer him the cup. The one on the left shall offer a cup to the person on the same side next to the prior.

Those who wish shall drink from their allotted measure of drink—

> [Note: Col. 1459D–1460D. “Those who wish shall drink,” etc. Thus at this hour they generally took nothing but pure water. If anyone wanted to drink something else, he took that much away from his customary drink allowance. The “measure” mentioned here means the regulated quantity of drink granted to each under the Rule, namely the *hemina* of which Saint Benedict speaks in chapter 40 of the Rule. It acquired the name *justitia* (“just measure”) from the fair moderation by which the same saint so regulated his monks’ drink that they did not drink wine to satiety, but more sparingly.]

Where it is necessary that the cooks of the present week also serve with them, the senior men arranged in the middle shall bring cups to those we have mentioned. The younger shall begin with the younger brethren placed last. Meanwhile, while the brethren drink, they shall keep their faces turned a little away from those drinking. Once the brethren have drunk, any server who wishes to drink shall set before himself the cup from which he served the others. Then, coming to the step, they shall bow before the prior. When he strikes the bell once, they shall withdraw without bowing before their seats and drink, if they wish, at the heads of the tables or before the tables. Once they have drunk, the prior shall strike the bell again with three consecutive strokes. Then they shall rise and bow again before departing. The servers shall put away the cups from which they offered water, where they are to be stored. [Col. 1459B–1460A]

As soon as they come to the dormitory, if they need to go to the necessities, they shall do so before taking off their cowls. The same is to be observed after work: they are not to go to the necessities before putting on their cowls. This order shall always be observed both before and after work. Those who return after Compline by command concerning guests may, however, go to the necessities before resuming their cowls. When they have prepared themselves for work, the board shall be struck.

After Vespers, once the office for the departed has been completed and the signal struck as stated above, they shall come to supper. If apples, raw vegetables, or some other such thing are to be distributed generally to the brethren, the cellarer may bring them around the tables before the verse, when he is free. If he distributes them after the verse, they shall be brought by the cooks or those assisting them. Then, collecting the bowls again, they shall put them upon the serving-table. [Col. 1460A–B]

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On the time of hay-cutting and harvest

During hay-cutting and harvest, the priest and ministers shall prepare themselves immediately after chapter to sing Mass. During hay-cutting, the community may attend this Mass and sing private Masses while it is being sung, if the abbot or prior judges it appropriate. On vigils and feasts of twelve lessons, those who are to sing privately shall not begin until after the offertory. When Mass has been sung in community, they shall immediately go out to work.

At harvest time, for this Mass, when the community is not present, the weakened and infirm brethren outside choir and from the infirmary shall assist in all things according to their ranks as necessary. Once it has been sung, the ministers themselves, gathered together, shall follow the others to work. The prior shall arrange how they are to know where to follow the community and who will lead them there.

In either season, if it rains after Mass has been sung in the morning, the monks may be at reading after Terce and may celebrate private Masses, if the abbot or prior judges this suitable. It should be known that at all solemnities of twelve lessons on which they work, and on vigils of saints, the community must hear Mass. At these times the community customarily works until Sext. Before Prime, if it is necessary to go out, dine outside the monastery, and sleep if need be, the cook and reader may take the *mixtum*. Those who remain in the abbey and eat in the refectory shall always give thanks in church, except the servers. [Col. 1460B–D]

Each person may be given a pound and a half of ordinary bread daily wherever needed, and it may be distributed to individuals according as time and place require. During this period, except on days when the brethren devote themselves to reading, they shall have one dish at dinner and another at supper, if possible. If the community has milk, whether cooked or raw, it shall count as one of the general dishes. Honey, however, shall never and nowhere be made into a general dish unless this seems good to the abbot because of a shortage of dishes and an abundance of honey.

It should be noted that during this period, when one dish is given at supper by command of the abbot, the weekly kitchen-officiant may assist the cellarer and take his meal with the servers. Where there are four weekly kitchen-officiants, two shall serve for a whole day; where there are two, one shall likewise serve. If they are far from the oratory, they may, if necessary, work after the signal for Vespers or any Hour has been struck; this must never be done at another time. Once Vespers has been sung there, they shall go to the monastery. If necessary, the prior may leave some behind there; yet they must not be absent from the servers’ supper. Even then this should occur rarely, and at another time never. [Col. 1461A–B]

When a monk sends his men to the granges, he must by every means ensure that, while going there or returning thence, and especially while staying there, they observe silence. He must also see that houses are prepared where they may eat together decently and in good order, and likewise sleep together, each in a separate bed according to the Rule. A lamp is to burn where they sleep. They must beware of making signs either with the lay brothers or with the household servants. Nor are they among themselves to make signs at unsuitable hours or places. No one is to cross the appointed boundaries without permission, nor proceed by wandering about and seeking byways [Col. 1461C]. At their table, the person whom the prior directs is to read. On Sundays and feast days they are to devote themselves to reading. No abbot is to send any community of monks to a grange except for gathering crops. These matters and other things suitable to this season cannot everywhere be observed equally; therefore each abbey shall act according to the situation of its locality and the judgment of its abbot or prior. Yet when the community is present in the abbey, if they must hasten to work in the morning, it is permissible to sing more quickly at the abbot’s discretion.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On shavings

[Note: At the request of our most reverend father, Lord John, priest-cardinal of St Lawrence in Lucina, who at the command of the lord pope asked the General Chapter that, out of reverence for the sacrament of the altar to be received, the number of shavings in the Order should be increased, the following arrangement was approved: there are to be twelve shavings, namely, at the Nativity of the Lord; at the Purification of Blessed Mary; on the first Sunday of March; at Easter; at the Ascension; on the Vigil of St John the Baptist; on the Vigil of St Mary Magdalene; on the Vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary; on the Vigil of her Nativity; on the Vigil of St Dionysius; on the Vigil of All Saints; and on the first Sunday of Advent. The shaving of lay brothers remains in its former condition. From the General Chapter of the year 1257. Cols. 1461D, 1462D.]

At the Nativity of the Lord; on Quinquagesima Sunday; at Easter; at Pentecost; on the feast of St Mary Magdalene [Col. 1461D]; at the Nativity of St Mary; and on the feast of All Saints, the brethren are to be clipped and shaved. The cooks are to heat and bring water into the cloister. The keeper of the combs, shears, razors, and whetstones is to sharpen and prepare them. The brethren whom the abbot commands are to clip the others. Those who have been clipped are to shave one another, and this in the cloister [Col. 1462A], except for the sick who are in the infirmary. The crown is to be shaved, not merely clipped a little above the ears. No one, unless invited, is to presume to shave another or make a sign that he wishes to do so; nor may anyone who has been invited dare refuse. One is not to give another the sign for shaving until after the table-bell has rung.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On the procession for bishops

For receiving a bishop, the brethren are to be summoned into choir by the bell.

[Note: Observe that St Peter Mauricius, Abbot of Cluny, held this to be the tenth distinction between our Order and the Cluniacs: our brethren, unlike theirs, acknowledged their own bishop (Letter 17, Book V). Col. 1462D.]

Then, at the cantor’s signal, someone is to take holy water; with it going before, the abbot is to follow, then the community and the novices, two by two, with the priests preceding in the order in which they stand in choir. When all have gone out and are standing in order before the monastery gate, the porter, or some other suitable person commanded by the abbot for this purpose, is meanwhile to go out and bring the bishop to meet them [Col. 1462B]. As he approaches, all are to kneel before him. When they rise, the abbot is to offer the sprinkler to the bishop, kissing his hand. And when the cantor begins the responsory *Hear, O Israel*, if there is one bishop, or *Let your loins be girded*, if there are several bishops, the novices are to enter first, then the rest, with the lay monks preceding, so that the abbot goes last, holding the bishop by the hand.

When they come into choir and the bishop applies himself to prayer, the abbot is to take his own place, with the others arranged after him as for Mass. When the responsory has been sung through, the abbot, raising the bishop, is to lead him to chapter, where all are seated in order. Having received the bishop’s blessing, the person to whom the cantor gives the sign is to read the lesson [Col. 1462C].

[Note: “Read the lesson,” namely from Holy Scripture, in accordance with chapter 53 of the Rule of St Benedict, which directs that the divine law be read in the presence of guests, so that they may be edified. Col. 1462D.]

When it is finished and *Benedicite* has been said, the abbot is to kiss the bishop and his companions, unless the bishop first wishes to say something for edification. Then all rise and bow for the bishop’s blessing, which the abbot must request unless the bishop has already given it in the oratory. When “Amen” has been answered, they are to depart, and the bishop is to be conducted to the guest-house.

It should be known that the community goes out to receive no one except its own bishop and archbishop, legates of the Apostolic See, the king, the lord pope, and its own abbot. This procession is not to be made more than once for any of them, except the lord pope.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On receiving guests

Guests are to be announced to the abbot of the place, or to the prior if the abbot is absent. If a guest is to be announced while they are seated for collation, he is to be announced to whomever is conducting the collation; and, at that person’s signal, the porter is to signal one of the brethren appointed to this task by the abbot of the monastery. For every abbot ought in his own monastery to appoint for his porter certain men whom he judges suitable for this duty [Col. 1463A].

If a guest arrives while Compline is being sung, the porter, taking a book and a light kept concealed, is, if necessary, to be present near the end of Compline at the abbot’s stall and announce the guest to him. At the abbot’s signal, he is to signal one of the persons appointed by him; that person, taking the porter with him, is to receive the guest. At other hours, the person signalled to receive the guest is to take a book and bring another brother with him.

Those who meet guests are to remove their hoods from their heads, if they are then worn, and thus, prostrate upon their knees, lead them to prayer.

[Note: “Prostrate upon their knees.” This was the ninth distinction between our Order and the Cluniacs: our brethren, unlike theirs, prostrated themselves in greeting guests, according to chapter 64 of the Rule of St Benedict. Col. 1463D.]

When they have entered the church, the person charged with that office is to sprinkle them with holy water. Afterwards they are to pray, bowed or prostrate, as the season requires [Col. 1463B]. But if the receiver is a bishop or an abbot, he is to offer the sprinkler, kissing the guest’s hand; and, having conducted him to the place where he should pray, he is to withdraw a little with his companion behind the praying guest and pray as stated above. When the prayer is complete, they are to sign themselves and go out.

The person who must read the sentence is to say *Benedicite*. Then they are to kneel once before them all; rising, they are to kiss them, and afterwards sit down. When the sentence has been read, if the guest needs an explanation, it is to be explained to him. Then he is to be taken to the guest-house or presented to the hospitaller; the brethren, however, are to return to the cloister. It should be known that those sent to receive guests, if they cannot return in time, are to lose neither the versicle nor the collation. Nor do those lose them who administer Communion or anoint the sick, or hear their confessions when they are at the point of death [Col. 1463C].

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On sending brethren on a journey

No one is to be sent on a journey except for the monastery’s benefit. A person to be sent away may receive a blessing at Lauds—unless Prime immediately follows—and at the other hours, except Compline; on ferial days he may also receive it at Nocturns. When he is to receive it, he is to rise and go to the step, and, turning himself according to the season, either bow or prostrate himself. On returning, however, he is not to turn himself, but is always to prostrate himself.

If he is with the abbot, whether going out or returning [Col. 1463D], he is always to place himself after the abbot for the blessing or prayer after Compline, or for satisfaction after the *Gloria* of the first psalm. If he cannot wait for the principal Mass, he may communicate at the morning Mass. If, inside the monastery gate, he is overtaken by the first signal of a canonical hour, or of chapter or collation, he is to return.

[Note: “He is to return,” so that, indeed, nothing may be preferred to the Work of God, according to chapter 43 of the Rule. Col. 1463D.]

A person leaving the monastery is not to eat before the monastery gate, nor anywhere within half a league [Col. 1464A] of the monastery; but this is permitted to one travelling through and not returning the same day. When leaving or returning, he is not to speak to anyone within the monastery without permission.

If he is to say the Hours by day and it is a day for prostration, he is to apply himself to prayer on the ground while saying *Glory be to the Father*; then he is to kneel again, maintaining silence until he comes to the place where he continues the Hour already begun.

[Note: “He is to kneel.” This too was the eleventh distinction between our brethren and the Cluniacs: our brethren, unlike theirs, as Peter of Cluny himself testifies, knelt at the canonical Hours while on a journey, according to chapter 50 of the Rule of St Benedict. Cols. 1463D, 1464D.]

Both by day and by night, while he is not riding, he is to say the Hours standing, unless he is seriously burdened. But one who goes to granges or cellarages, or to any dwelling belonging to the house from which he departs, is not to receive a blessing unless he expects to spend the night away. The same applies to one returning from there, unless he has spent the night away or eaten in a town.

Blessings given to those travelling or returning are to be spoken in the same tone in which the collect of the canonical Hour was said, except at Lauds and Vespers [Col. 1464B]. It should be known that only guests who have received a blessing may celebrate Mass before the Gospel of the community Mass. An abbot leaving on a journey before Terce in summer, or returning after Terce until None in winter, may celebrate or hear Mass on fast days and on feasts of twelve lessons, during Easter and Pentecost week, at the Nativity of the Lord, and at the principal offices for the dead.

They are to keep the customary fasts, both in summer and winter, according to custom, unless some abbot has made the traveller dine with him, and this only in the monasteries of that abbot; or unless a bishop, archbishop, or legate of the Apostolic See does so. But the principal fasts—on which it is customary in our Order to eat only Lenten foods—he is to observe according to custom. He is not to speak at table; he is not to eat fat; nor is he to lie on feathers, unless perhaps he cannot obtain straw or something similar on which to lie without great labour or expense. It should be known that both abbots and monks may carry with them a cloak, commonly called a bed-covering, and a pillow.

[Note: “May carry.” This was permitted them so that, in accordance with the Rule, even while travelling they might sleep upon a mat and a cloak. See chapter 55 of the same Rule. Col. 1464D.]

Anyone who wishes to use a cloak as bedding may do so, provided only that these things are not costly or ornate. On returning home, unless he returns on the very day on which he departed, he is immediately to go to prayer. Before entering the oratory, he is to sprinkle himself with holy water [Col. 1464D]. He is to pray in choir—if he does not find the community there—bowed or prostrate according to the season. If he finds them there, but not saying a canonical Hour, he is to pray outside the choir. For he must enter the regular Hour as soon as he arrives: he is to join those chanting if he arrives before the *Gloria*; but if afterwards, he is to make satisfaction at the step, unless he finds the *Kyrie eleison* already being said. If he finds the oratory door locked, he is to pray there.

If he is within the monastery precinct when the signal is sounded in church for the meal [Col. 1465A], he loses the versicle if he does not hasten there. If he finds the refectory bell being rung, he is to turn aside to the refectory in order to begin the versicle with the others. If he finds it already begun, he is to go and pray. After prayer, he is to signal the cook or cellarer whether he should enter; if the latter assents, he is to enter and say the versicle silently, standing and bowing as is customary in the community, and say the blessing, but he is not to make the sign of the cross. He is always to observe this equally at both dinners and both suppers, except that he is not to signal for admission to the servants’ meal.

If he arrives late for the servants’ meal, they are not to wait for him; nor, when they leave, is he himself to move. Likewise, if he arrives for the drinks because of the community, or because the signal for collation has rung [Col. 1465B], he is not to move—provided, however, that he arrives for collation before its end. If he comes at the signal for collation, or at the collation itself, he is immediately to join the community, finish with them [Col. 1466A], and eat after Compline. If he comes at Compline, he is to do likewise; if after Compline, he is likewise to eat and then complete Compline there in chapter. What we have said about the meal is also to be observed by those who return on the same day on which they went out; they must nevertheless take care to arrive always for the first meal.

It should be known that whenever a monk or lay brother of our Order arrives at any abbey of our Order, he is in every respect to observe the order of his own monastery. In church, however, he is not to intone a psalm or antiphon, say a lesson or responsory, or perform anything belonging to the office of the priest-weekly server, the inviter, or the weekly server, until the abbot commands. If he holds a priorship or another obedience [Col. 1466B], he is to do nothing by virtue of that obedience. A prior, however, takes the first place after the prior of that place.

## PART FOUR. On the care of the sick and the suffrages for the dead

[Col. 1465]

## CHAPTER XC. On those vomiting or bleeding, and their attendants

[Cols. 1465B–C]

If a priest’s blood flows from his nostrils during Mass, water is to be brought to him in the sanctuary by the attendants, for receiving the blood and washing himself. If this happens to ministers, they are likewise to be attended outside choir. But whenever this or vomiting occurs to anyone else, the brother charged with this duty is to follow him as he goes into the cloister; and if it is night, he is to stand beside him with a light and attend him, until he has washed himself and returns to choir. If at that time *Come, let us rejoice* or the first psalm of another Hour is being sung in church, he is to return to choir at the *Gloria*. Once it has been said, he is to return quickly to the sick man.

But if the afflicted man is not present at the *Gloria*, and this happens to him in the community, he is to go to his stall without making satisfaction. If it happens to him outside the community [Col. 1465D], he is not to make satisfaction at the step; instead, coming through the middle of choir before the abbot and making a sign of his necessity, he is to return to his stall. If it happens in the refectory, his attendant is not to return from there, but is to signal the cook or cellarer to help him. If the afflicted man returns to table before the community leaves, he is to eat what he was going to eat. The community is not to wait for him, nor is he, if he rises, to stop eating for this reason. If he returns after the community has left, he is not to wait for the attendants, but is to eat immediately and, after silently saying the versicle, depart. If it happens that an attendant does not see someone vomiting or bleeding, whoever sees it is to tell him.

## CHAPTER XCI. On bloodletting

[Note: *Minutio* is so called either from diminishing blood or from diminishing strength. Col. 1465.]

[Cols. 1466B–C]

The brethren are not to be bled during harvest-time, in Advent, in Lent, during the first three days of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, or when a principal fast falls on the second or third day. Nor may one be bled who is outside choir because of illness, until he has re-entered choir. The weekly servers of Mass, the kitchen, or the refectory reading are likewise not to be bled, unless, because of grave necessity, permission is granted to those asking mercy in chapter. A person returning from a journey is not to be bled on the same day, except by counsel of the abbot.

It should be noted that they may be bled four times a year, and, if it can suitably be done, they are to be bled in these months: February, April, and September. The fourth bloodletting is to take place about the feast of St John the Baptist. When part of the community is to be bled [Col. 1466D], the prior is to say in chapter: “Those who sit at this or that table are to be bled.” Care must be taken that the day not fall on the second, third, or fourth day of a feast of twelve lessons. Yet it remains at the abbot’s discretion not to forgo bloodletting for those whom he judges should be bled. He must nevertheless ensure that those are bled without whom the vigils can suitably be celebrated.

If the dinner hour falls between Terce and Sext, that is, after the Gospel, or before it if necessary; or, if it is a fast day, between Sext and None; and, at either time, after None if necessity requires: after a fire has been kindled in the warming-house by the person whom the prior directs, they are to prepare themselves for bloodletting. Meanwhile the bloodletter is to come by order of the prior. Those who have been bled may go to take a light meal [Col. 1467A] in the refectory, if they wish and have time.

Thereafter, during every period of reading or labour, a person who has been bled may either lie in his bed or sit in chapter and in the cloister until he enters choir. Likewise, while outside choir, he is neither to read nor sing. It should be noted that those who have been bled, and the sick who are outside choir, do not ask private pardons in church until they have re-entered choir, except at the Lenten prayer. In summer, when the community fasts, those who have been bled are to eat after the Gospel. Likewise, in winter, on feasts when the community devotes itself to reading, a person who has been bled is not to leave the cloister or perform any duty of his obedience, except the prior, sacristan, cellarer, or master of novices. But if he is a cook, he is to notify the kitchen prior; if he holds an obedience [Col. 1467B], his assistant is to fulfil his function. If he must sing, read in church or outside church, perform the washing of the poor, or do anything else, he is to notify someone about it, and that person is to do it for as long as he remains outside choir.

The weekly inviter, however, need make no sign concerning his office, nor the weekly server of Mass concerning his, except only concerning Mass. For the rest, a person who has been bled, as long as he remains outside choir—and, on the third day when the community is occupied with reading, during work-time—is not to make a sign except concerning confession, hearing Mass, or drinking. At the Hours he is to enter church, sitting down immediately upon arrival at his first entrance; after prayer he is to sign himself while seated. Then he is neither to prostrate himself nor bow at the *Gloria*, nor stand except at the *Magnificat*, the *Te Deum laudamus* [Col. 1467C], the Gospel, and the *Benedictus*. At private Masses, if necessary, he may assist when asked, and for this purpose cross to another part by the front of choir. He may also assist at common Masses when the community is absent. But after the Hour he is to depart before the others.

On the first and second days, in the absence of the community, he may, if necessary, enter choir and sit only for the psalms. In other respects he is to conduct himself there as a healthy man. The sick man from the infirmary, and one who is outside choir during haymaking and harvest, are to do likewise, except that he is not to begin an antiphon, intone a psalm, or perform the office of weekly server of Mass or inviter, if another is present who can and ought to do this. In the refectory, however, a person who has been bled is to behave like the others [Col. 1467D] and distribute nothing from his food.

[Note: “From his food,” that is, from the *pitancia* granted to him in addition to the regular pottages. Col. 1467D.]

For in winter, on the first day, he is to be given half a pound of white bread in addition to the common bread, with one *pitancia*. If it is Sunday, he is to receive the same as in summer. On the second and third days, he is to be given, at the mixed meal after Terce, one *pitancia* [Note: *Pitancia*, from *pietas*, is a dish better than the regular pottage. Col. 1467D] with a whole pound of white bread and common bread. On the fourth day, both in winter and summer, he is to receive a *pitancia* with the pottages. In summer, for three days he is to be given for dinner the common pottages and a pound of white bread, in addition to common bread, with one *pitancia* [Col. 1468A]. At supper, for three days, he is to be given a *pitancia* of whatever kind.

His attendant, or the person sitting beside him, may, if necessary, cut his bread and serve him other things, but only on the first day.

[Note: “To cut his bread,” etc., because at that time they were bled almost to the point of fainting. Hence the many indulgences granted them in this chapter. Col. 1468D.]

After the meal he is to go with the others to church; turning aside, as we have said, he is to stand in the first section until the community enters choir, and then, sitting down, complete what remains of the thanksgiving. But if the church has only one altar, both then and at the daytime Hours he is to withdraw to chapter. If it is summer, after None he is to precede the brethren going to the refectory for drinks, and, when the prior enters, stand until he sits down.

After collation, when the brethren enter choir, he is at once to turn aside and sit in the customary place, and, signing himself after prayer, go out if he wishes [Col. 1468B] to sing Compline in chapter. When it has been sung and prayer finished, he is to sign himself, sprinkle himself with holy water, and return to bed or, if he wishes, to the oratory; yet he is to enter the dormitory before the others. When the signal for vigils is rung, he is to enter church and sit down; after the prayer, signing himself, he is to go to the infirmary or chapter to sing vigils. At these vigils shorter readings than those in the community may be given; and under one blessing three readings, if only three are to be said, or four readings on feasts of twelve lessons, may be read.

The priest who is first there according to the order of conversion is to perform the entire office, if he can complete it, except those parts belonging to the ministry of the abbot or prior, if either is present; but he is to assign the readings to others, if someone is present who can read. If he cannot complete the entire office, the person whom he indicates is to complete it [Col. 1468C]. In the absence of priests, clerics of the other grades are to observe the same rule among themselves.

It should be known that the Office of the Dead, or anything else, is not permitted to be sung here, except the principal Offices of the Dead and that for a person who has died that day, on days when the community celebrates it. If he is alone, either in chapter or in the infirmary, an assistant who can help him complete the office is, if possible, to be provided; when it is completed, he is to go to sleep. For he must not sing the other Hours of the day outside, but hear them wholly within. At Prime, those who have been bled are to return to church. On feast days, while the signal for chapter is rung, they are to enter chapter like the others [Col. 1468D]; but on other days they are to enter behind choir, between the seats of the abbot and prior, arranging themselves in their order, where they are not to ask pardon unless someone is called out. If it is a fast day, on the second and third days they are to receive the mixed meal in the refectory after Terce.

On the third day, they enter choir at Prime on every day, both summer and winter. On that day they may sit in choir for two psalms, namely the first and second, at all the daytime Hours; at Vespers and Prime, however, they are not to sit except as the community does. During work-time, they are neither to sing nor read in the cloister [Col. 1469A], nor are they to go into the oratory for prayer. During work-time and reading-time, they may rest in bed shod and upon their blankets; and they may always do this, except when the community is sleeping in the dormitory. On the third night they are to remain away from vigils, unless it is a principal feast, namely one on which a sermon is given in chapter. On the fourth day they are to prepare for work like the others; yet the prior ought, because of their bloodletting, to assign them lighter work or remit work altogether.

## CHAPTER XCII. On the sick outside choir

Whenever anyone leaves choir because of illness, in the following chapter he is to ask pardon for it, even if he was ordered to remain out, and state the reason for his departure [Col. 1469B]. If he is the weekly kitchen servant, he is to receive the blessing for departure with his companion on Sunday; at the daytime Hours on ferial days he is to prostrate himself like the others. He may return to choir at any Hour of night or day, if he wishes, and also at Mass. In every other respect, while he remains outside choir, he is to behave like one who has been bled, except that he is not to take the mixed meal and is voluntarily to ask pardon in chapter.

But if anyone has an illness so definite and manifest that it can evidently be seen or understood that he is unable either to keep the community observance or to benefit in the infirmary, his illness is to be declared in chapter; and thereafter, in church, he is to sing, read, and work where and in whatever manner the abbot provides, insofar as his illness permits and the abbot appoints. But anyone whose illness is not definite, if he has not recovered after one or two days [Col. 1469C], is to enter the infirmary at the abbot’s discretion.

It should be known that one who has returned from a journey, if he is publicly put out, need not ask pardon for it in chapter. Those who come from a journey are not bound to receive a blessing for this, but they are to ask pardon.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the sick in the infirmary

Those in the infirmary may speak with the infirmarian, but only in a specified place appointed for this purpose, silently and only about necessities. Anyone wishing to enter it is to ask and receive permission from the infirmarian by a sign before entering. As long as any one person is with the infirmarian [Col. 1469D], another has no permission to enter.

But a person so sick that he lies continuously, or compelled to lie in bed by a sudden severe illness—such as fevers or another grave condition—may meanwhile speak with the infirmarian, and the infirmarian with him, if necessary; and this also quietly. But when he has recovered sufficiently to walk about here and there, he is to observe the usual silence, unless the abbot judges it expedient that someone still detained by grave illness be spoken to further at his bedside.

They are not to speak at table, nor after the signal of a canonical Hour has been given [Col. 1470A] until the service itself is completed, except those unable to rise from bed on their own. They are to sing vigils in the infirmary, as stated above, when they begin in church; and only the principal Offices of the Dead are to be said there. Gathered together, they are to sing the daytime Hours. Afterwards, anyone wishing may go to church for the Hours, and to Mass daily unless seriously burdened.

It should be noted, however, that those burdened by illness are not to kneel either in church or in the infirmary, at the Hours or at Mass, except at the *Agnus Dei*. At the blessing, novices are to be in choir in their proper order, and those who wish may sit. Anyone who wishes to communicate outside choir is to receive the peace from someone of the community who is going to communicate. If the person who must give peace to guests happens to be absent [Col. 1470B], he is first to bring it to the sick, and then they are to approach Communion in their proper order; and this only at the morning Mass.

They are not to assist or serve at Masses except during harvest-time. They may not enter church except when the Work of God is being celebrated there, nor remain in the cloister; nor may they make signs to monks observing the community rule. Rather, as far as they can, they are to keep from being seen by them or by other people. Yet if anyone has an illness that neither greatly weakens him nor disturbs his appetite for eating, such as swelling, an incision of the limbs, or something similar, such a person is not to lie on a mattress, relax the customary fasts, or change the foods of the refectory.

A person with a non-manifest illness is neither to read [Note: That is, in the refectory or church; he could read privately. Col. 1469.] [Col. 1470C] nor work. But one whose illness is evident is to read and work, not according to his own judgment, but at the hours appointed for him.

If anyone is such as to presume to disturb the others, murmur against this institution for the sick, or transgress in any respect, he is to be corrected. If, though corrected often, he does not amend, then, if the abbot thinks fit, his perversity is to be declared in chapter, where, being summoned, he is to be reproved before all. If he still does not correct himself, then, if his illness permits, he is also to be subjected to regular discipline.

They are not to return to the community until they have first informed the abbot; having received his permission, they may enter choir at whatever Hour they wish, but fasting, unless they are to be sent on a journey. If an abbot who is a guest of our Order is in the infirmary [Col. 1470D], he may speak either with two persons only or with individuals, except the attendants assigned to him. Any abbot in the infirmary, once he has recovered enough that he no longer lies bedridden but goes out and comes in, must observe the monastic rule of silence from the *Gloria* of the first regular psalm of Compline. But if he is afflicted by severe illness, he may act according to his need, preserving in all things propriety and gravity. If a bishop of our Order is in the infirmary, one may speak with him after Compline.

## CHAPTER XCIV. In what order the sick are anointed

[Col. 1471A]

For anointing a sick person, the signal is to be rung for as long as it takes to say one *Our Father*. After a short interval, the signal is to be rung again for the same length of time. Then the abbot is to put on alb, stole, and maniple, taking the pastoral staff. If he is absent, the cantor is to do this, or the person whom the cantor directs. Once he is vested and the signal has rung once, the community is to come into choir. Beginning the psalm *Blessed is he that understandeth*, then *Judge me, O God*, and after that *With my voice*, they are to proceed, adding the *Glory be to the Father* to each psalm, in the order in which they stand in choir. The priests are to follow the abbot, after the cross, with a light kept concealed and holy water. If necessary, the last psalm is to be repeated [Col. 1471B].

The sacristan, proceeding in his order, is to carry the oil and cotton or a cloth for wiping away the anointing. Whenever the words “By this holy anointing” are spoken, the cotton or cloth is to be used, and afterwards he is to burn it in the piscina appointed for this purpose. When they reach the sick person, after the psalms are finished, the minister of anointing is to say, “Peace to this house,” and the community is to answer, “Amen.” Immediately the priest is to continue, “The Lord be with you,” and say this prayer: “Almighty everlasting God, who through blessed James …”

When this is finished and “Amen” answered, the sick person is to say his *Confiteor*. If he does not know it or cannot say it, striking his breast he is to say: “Through my fault: for all my sins, I beg you, pray for me.” Then the entire community is to say to him: “May he have mercy upon you,” etc. Afterwards, if the abbot is present, he is to say this absolution: “The Lord Jesus Christ,” etc. If the abbot is absent, the person who anoints is to say: “Pardon and remission …” When this has been said, the anointer is to offer him the cross to kiss. When this has been done and the cross restored, he is to say, “By this holy anointing,” etc., and thus perform the rite of anointing.

When the sick person has been anointed, the community is to say the first psalm *Bless the Lord*; then the *Our Father* and the prayers written in the Collectary are to be said, followed by the prayers: first, “Let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, brethren”; second, “May the Lord be propitious”; third, “Grant pardon, Lord, to your servant”; fourth, “May God the holy Father bless you”; fifth, “May the God of heaven bless you”; sixth, “May God the Father who in the beginning … bless you,” etc. [Cols. 1471C–D].

When these things are completed, all are to leave. If he must immediately receive Communion, the person who anointed him, or another in his place if necessary, is to go with the ministers to church. Having washed his hands in the piscina, he is to bring Holy Communion with the chalice covered by the offertory veil, preceded by the cross, a light, and holy water. Another person, between the light and water, is to carry a wine-flask for sprinkling the fingers into the chalice. When they come to the sick man, the person carrying the water is to sprinkle him. The priest is then to say to him: “Behold, brother, the body of our Lord Jesus Christ which we bring to you. Do you believe that this is that in which are our salvation, life, and resurrection?” When he answers, “I believe,” the priest is to instruct him to say the *Confiteor*, if he is a monk. When this has been said, the priest, together with those present [Col. 1472A], is to say, “May Almighty God have mercy upon you”; afterwards he alone is to add, “Indulgence …” Then he is to communicate him, saying: “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life.”

If he is a lay brother, or a monk who does not understand letters, the priest is to explain the same to him in the vernacular (*Romane*); and the lay brother is to confess in the vernacular that he has sinned in thought, word, and deed. Likewise, a monk is to confess in the vernacular if he does not know his own *Confiteor*. The same is to be done whenever anyone is afflicted by grave necessity. For the direction that the sick person be questioned concerning his faith is understood not of all sick persons, but only of those who have been anointed and those who seem to be at the point of death. Likewise, on other occasions when sick monks or lay brothers communicate, the priest is to permit no negligence to occur [Col. 1472B], but speak of the matters necessary for this purpose. When he has communicated, they are to depart.

## CHAPTER XCV. How matters are to be conducted concerning a dying person

When anyone has drawn very near to death, he is to be placed on the ground upon a cloak, with ashes first laid in the form of a cross beneath him, and a mat or some straw. Then the board is to be struck repeatedly in the cloister, and, wherever the community is, the signal in church is to be rung four times, in the manner determined above for anointing a sick person, when it is rung twice. If the community is within the cloister, all are to run quickly to the dying person, saying the *Creed* two or three times, loudly enough to be heard. If it is outside, it is to come as quickly as possible, yet with gravity—except perhaps only in haymaking or harvest-time [Col. 1472C]. In some grave necessity, the Collectary is to be brought to the abbot, and the sacristan is to bring the stole and staff, taking with him someone to carry the cross, a light, a thurible, and blessed water.

If they sit down for the collation, upon hearing the board struck the reader shall say, “But thou, O Lord,” and the abbot, “Our help.” Whoever is not then present shall not make satisfaction at the step, but on the following day shall ask pardon in chapter. If they are in the oratory for Masses or the canonical hours, or on Saturday for the Mandatum, the abbot or prior and those whom the abbot directs shall go. But if the cantor sees that, by hastening, the others can suitably come to the deceased, they shall complete the work begun more quickly than usual [Col. 1472D] and follow the others. If, however, it is a principal solemnity, Vespers or Nocturns shall not for this reason be said more quickly. This is to be observed especially on the principal solemnities.

And it should be known that on Sundays and feast days Lauds or Matins, which according to the Rule ought to follow Nocturns immediately, shall not be interrupted even if the board is struck at that hour; likewise neither shall Prime on ordinary days after Lauds in winter. Nor shall the Office of the Dead, wherever it ought to follow, be interrupted because the board is struck. Therefore, when the Litany has been said, if he still lives, the seven penitential Psalms shall be said; but if he has not yet died, they shall depart, leaving the cross and holy water there.

When the soul has departed, the cantor shall begin, “Come to his aid,” the others following the same chant [Col. 1473A], and then: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.” Then: “Let us pray. To thee, O Lord, we commend.” After that Collect the dead man shall be carried away to be washed. The prior shall arrange by whom and in what manner he is to be washed and wrapped.
