Meanwhile, with the brethren arranged separately from the deceased around the abbot as in choir, insofar as the place permits and as each abbot has prescribed in his own monastery, and with the lay brothers separately present, the abbot shall continue with the remaining Collects: namely, “God of compassion,” and “of the dreadful wound,” “thy way,” “Almighty and everlasting God, who [of human …],” “Receive, O Lord, the soul of thy servant”; adding to it, “The portion of the blessed resurrection.” After this, when the community has answered “Amen,” the Psalter shall immediately be begun with “Blessed is the man” [*Beatus vir*].

After the washing of the body, when it has been brought back, the abbot, sprinkling it with holy water and censing it, shall say aloud for all to hear the Lord’s Prayer. When the abbot has said, “And lead us not,” and the others have answered, “But deliver us from evil,” the abbot shall say, “From the gate of hell”; then, “Let not the enemy prevail against him”; and after “The Lord be with you,” “Let us pray. O God, to whom alone belongs …” When he has begun this, the ministers shall proceed to the head of the procession with the cross, covered lantern, thurible, and holy water.

When the Collect has been said and the community has answered “Amen,” the cantor shall intone the Responsory, “Deliver me, O Lord, from death”; and thus they shall carry the body into the church, following the cross in the order in which they stand in choir: the lay monks preceding the clerics, after whom [Col. 1473C] the abbot shall walk with stole and staff, or whoever has performed the office; then the novices; then the deceased, borne by four or more whom the prior has appointed, followed also by the lay brothers.

While the deceased is being carried into the church, if a canonical hour is being sung, the cantor shall observe what is being sung. If the Gospel, or “Thee, God, we praise” [*Te Deum laudamus*], or any Responsory is being said, they shall wait a little in the cloister until it is finished, and then enter singing. But if the choir is singing anything else, they shall not delay entering; and the choir, interrupting what it was singing, shall sing with them until, after the Collect, it resumes what had been interrupted.

Upon arriving at the church, they shall place the body in the choir, unless it is so foul-smelling that it cannot be placed in the church. The abbot [Col. 1473D] shall determine where the body is to be placed. When the chant is finished and the brethren are arranged at the deceased’s head with cross, thurible, and holy water, in the order in which they came to church, and with a light set upon a candlestick at the deceased’s head, the abbot, standing behind them, shall make the commendation. Meanwhile the brethren shall face one another. When the commendation has been made, they shall leave the holy water and cross there.

When this has been done, those who had left during the Hour shall go to chapter, begin the Hour again, and complete it. They shall not begin Vigils, Lauds, and Vespers again from the beginning, but from where they left off. Having supplied what was omitted up to that which is being sung in choir, they shall return to the community, without making satisfaction, whenever they had gone out.

Moreover, if the board is struck while the Office [Col. 1474A] for the Dead is being said, leaving a few in choir as the cantor directs, the community shall go out to the deceased—unless it is a principal office, which may not be interrupted; in which case they shall do as was said concerning the canonical hours. If they had interrupted chapter, they shall return there and complete what remained, and the deceased who is present shall be absolved there. But if the abbot is absent at that time, he shall absolve him in the first Chapter at which he is present.

If they had interrupted the refectory, they shall return to the meal, even in Lent; but neither a signal shall be rung in church nor a bell in the refectory, nor shall the verse be repeated, nor shall the reader ask a blessing; rather, he shall begin where he ended. Those who had not yet begun to eat, remaining with the body, shall eat afterward. In every way the abbot shall provide that the body is never left alone.

Immediately after the commendation is completed, sitting in choir in the order in which they entered and in which they ought to be evenly placed at all intervals, they shall begin the Psalter where they left it in the infirmary, if it was begun. If it was not begun, they shall always begin from the beginning, saying the entire verse “Eternal rest,” while the signal is rung for the Hour. If they finish the Psalter before the body is buried, they shall say the complete Office of the Dead from the hour of the meal until night: *Placebo* (“I shall please”) and *Verba* (“Words”); after the second Psalter, *Placebo* (“I shall please”) and “The Lord shepherds”; after the third, *Placebo* (“I shall please”) and *Exspectans* (“Waiting”).

From nightfall until after Sext of the following day: *Verba mea* (“My words”) and *Exsultabunt* (“They shall rejoice”); “The Lord shepherds me” and *Exsultabunt*; *Exspectans* and *Exsultabunt* [Col. 1474C]. The weekly priest shall read the lessons; if it is day, the one whom the cantor appoints shall read them. When this has been sung through, they shall begin the Psalter again. If they finish it too, they shall perform the second office in the same way, that is, “The Lord shepherds me.” If the deceased is still above ground, they shall again begin the Psalter; when it is finished, they shall complete the third office in the same way.

All these offices shall be said in chant, in a moderate voice. The Responsory “Deliver me, O Lord” shall not be said except in the third office; and it shall be said with only the first verse and a single Collect, namely “Incline, O Lord.” The Psalters shall end with “Eternal rest” said in the singular. Whatever is said for him while he remains unburied shall be said in the singular.

[Col. 1474D] When the deceased is present in church, if the community celebrates the Office of the Dead after Lauds and Vespers, those in the infirmary shall celebrate it likewise. Those who have said Vigils in chapter shall say the Office of the Dead as it is to be said in choir. Those keeping watch around the deceased, unless they have already said the Office of the Dead after the Psalter is finished, shall not omit that office after the regular Vigils and Lauds which they have said there.

In the customary office performed after Vespers or Nocturns, the first Collect shall be said for him, and then the customary Collects—unless it is the solemn Office of the Dead. In that solemn office, after the first Collect only this shall follow, at Vespers, Lauds, and Mass alike. If Mass is said for him [Col. 1475A], his Collect shall be said first in the community: namely, “Incline [thy ear],” and “Almighty and everlasting God, who [art God] of the living”; but if it is a solemn thirty-day observance, “God of pardon” shall be inserted.

## Chapter XCVI. Likewise concerning the dead after they are in church

On every day on which we fast, both summer and winter, if anyone dies from the beginning of None until the beginning of Lauds, he shall be buried after Mass has been said following Prime. If he dies from the beginning of Lauds to the end of Prime, he shall be buried after Terce. If he dies from then until Terce, he shall be buried after Sext. If he dies from the beginning of Terce until Sext, so that Mass can be had before Sext, he shall be buried before None. If Mass cannot be had before Sext, it shall be had after Sext [Col. 1475B], and he shall be buried between None and Vespers. If he dies between Sext and None, Mass shall be said before None; None, if necessary, shall be deferred; and he shall be buried after the second meal. In Lent Mass for the deceased may be said after None, and he shall be buried after the first meal.

At times when we do not fast, if he dies from the meal until Lauds of the following day, he shall be committed to burial after Mass has been said following Prime. If from Lauds until the end of Prime, he shall be buried after Mass has been said following Terce. If from then until Terce, he shall be buried before Sext. If from Terce until Sext, he shall be buried after Mass has been said following None. But if from the signal for Sext until the meal, the Hour and Mass shall be said more quickly, and after Mass the brethren shall take their meal; [Col. 1475C] the deceased shall then be buried after None.

If two deceased persons, to be buried at different hours, should occur, and Mass can be had for them together, they shall be buried together at the hour when the second is to be buried, if this can suitably be done.

## Chapter XCVII. Concerning watches around the deceased

When watches are to be kept around the deceased, if there is time, the cantor shall designate on the board those who are to keep watch. Dividing them into two groups, the first group shall keep watch during half the interval from Compline until Nocturns, while the others sleep meanwhile; and according as he sees fit, it shall say Matins for itself. Near the end of the first interval, the one charged by the prior [Col. 1475D] shall go; having checked the time on the clock according to the sacristan’s indication, if it is time, he shall go to the beds of each who ought to keep watch and wake them. When they have entered choir, the first group shall withdraw; and the latter shall say Matins for themselves and thus keep watch until Nocturns. When the community comes, having indicated to the cantor the Psalm where they left off, they shall return to their beds to sleep.

But if the cantor has not time to write down those who are to keep watch, he shall designate by hand in choir those who ought to keep the first watch. He shall write down the second group and show those written down to one of the first group, who shall wake them; and both groups shall proceed as has been said. If the community rises for the deceased near the time of Vigils, it shall keep watch until Vigils.

At the hour of the meal, those who remained with the body [Col. 1476A], when the community comes in for grace, shall tell those entering the Psalm where they left off; and, going out by the rear of the choir, they shall go to the refectory to eat with the servers. If in summer a watch must be kept after the meal, those who kept watch before None shall sleep after None. No one shall be sent on a journey from the time a brother has died until the body is laid away, unless grave necessity compels; and even this shall not be done without the abbot’s permission. Those assigned to offices shall attend the deceased as reason directs. In the community, if possible, Mass for him shall be said solemnly with the Responsory “Though I walk” and the Tract “Absolve, O Lord.”

## Chapter XCVIII. In what order Masses or Collects are to be said for a deceased person who is present

[Col. 1476B]

On all days on which two Masses are sung in the community, if a deceased person is present, the first shall be said solemnly for him with two Collects, namely “Incline, O Lord,” and “Almighty and everlasting God, who [art God] of the living.” The second shall be said with the Collects which ought to have been said at the first Mass.

Nevertheless, in Lent and the fasts of the Ember Days; on Sundays on which a Mass of some vigil is to be said in the morning; on Sundays; from Septuagesima until Easter; on the octave-day of Easter; in the Advent of the Lord when a solemnity of twelve lessons, on which we are accustomed to work, falls on a Sunday; when the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on Sunday; on the Sunday when “While all things were in quiet silence” [*Dum medium silentium*] is said; [Col. 1476C] on the three Sundays before Lent; on the Sunday before Ascension when an observance of rest from work occurs; on a Sunday when some history is begun; on the sixth day after the Nativity of the Lord; on the three days on which we work in the weeks of Easter and Pentecost; at Sunday offices which cannot be deferred; also at principal fasts and principal Offices of the Dead; on octaves of saints and their proper offices, whose office is marked in the Gradual, except for Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus when they occur on the Sunday before Ascension; and on the octave of Saint Lawrence when a Sunday falls within it: on all these days, I say, the Mass of the day and the proper Collect for the deceased who is present shall be said, and nevertheless [Col. 1476D] Mass for the deceased who is present shall be said in the community.

Yet on the three days before Easter, neither privately nor in the community shall Mass for a deceased person who is present be celebrated. On the Lord’s Supper and on Saturday, however, if a deceased person is present, the Collect for him shall be said at Mass. On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, all Masses in the community shall be of the feast, and the Collect shall be said for the deceased person who is present; privately, however, anyone who wishes to sing for him out of devotion may do so. Those who sing of the feast shall say the Collect for the deceased, both after burial and before it.

Since it must in every way be avoided that any brother be committed to burial without his own Mass, if it can suitably be done, the deceased person who is present [Col. 1477A] shall have Mass in the community, even if one or two Masses have been sung or are to be sung on the same day. But if necessity of time or a principal solemnity does not permit it, at least a private Mass shall be said for him, if the hour does not prevent it; and he shall be buried according to the divisions of hours which we have set forth.

It should be known that, on account of this necessity, Mass for the deceased may be said on all fast-days outside Lent until None, in Lent until Vespers, and in periods when we do not fast until the meal.

If no one is present in the community who can sing this in the customary manner, a brother returning from a journey, if there is one, shall perform it. If he is absent, someone from the infirmary shall do so. If he too is not there, a brother who has suffered an illusion [Note: [Col. 1477D] “An illusion”: therefore, except in a necessity of this sort, those who had suffered an illusion were not accustomed to celebrate Mass.] shall do it [Col. 1477B]. But if he too is absent, the abbot or one of the priest-brothers of the monastery may sing a second Mass.

Nevertheless, whether the deceased is present, before burial, or after it, on that same day no one shall presume to sing Mass except for him, apart from the aforementioned three days—unless, by the abbot’s disposition, the brethren ought to communicate, or officials ought suitably to hear Mass on some principal feast.

## Chapter XCIX. In what order he is to be carried to the grave

When he is to be carried to the grave, the abbot shall be clothed in alb, stole, and maniple, with staff. When the signal has been rung as for Mass, those who sing the Psalms, after the Psalm is ended [Col. 1477C], shall turn toward the altar. The abbot, and those carrying the cross, light, incense with the thurible, and holy water, shall arrange themselves at the deceased’s head in this manner: first the water, then the light, then the cross, and last the abbot. The thurifer shall stand beside the abbot, so that whenever the abbot censes the body at the end of each Collect, he may hand him the ready thurible. The cantor, or one whom he appoints, shall hold the Collectary for him. Meanwhile the brethren shall turn toward one another.

When the office is completed, the thurifer shall take his place in his order, namely between the light and the water. Then, when the cantor has intoned the antiphon, they shall go out singing the Psalms: “When Israel came out” [*In exitu Israel*]; “Give thanks,” 4 [*Confitemini* 4]; “As”; “Remember, O Lord, David”; “Lord, thou hast proved”; “Lord, I cried”; “With my voice,” 2. After the Psalms shall be said the verse “Eternal rest,” and the antiphon “The choir of angels” [*Chorus angelorum*], and immediately “Most merciful Lord” [*Clementissime Domine*], in chant; and while “Lord, have mercy on the sinner” is said, all shall ask pardon.

They shall proceed in the order in which they stand in choir, with the priests going before, so that the abbot goes first, that is, after the cross, while the novices go after the monks. Four brethren, or more, appointed by the prior, clothed in scapulars beneath their cowls, shall lift the body. Someone, however, shall remain to guard both the church and the cloister.

When they arrive at the grave, the abbot and ministers shall arrange themselves at the head of the pit. Those bearing the body, placing it on the south side [Col. 1478A], shall take off their cowls and be ready to bury the body. When it is buried, having put their cowls back on, they shall return to choir in their order. The brethren, with their faces turned toward one another and standing apart from the abbot, singing after them, shall arrange themselves so that the seniors are on the side of the deceased.

Meanwhile the abbot, performing the office with only the ministers answering him, if the grave is not yet ready when he reaches “Of rashness indeed” [*Temeritatis quidem*], shall say the following Collects, reserving that one. When it has been prepared, before he begins that Collect, he shall sprinkle the body and then the grave. Then, having censed the body, he shall hand the thurible to the one who is in the grave, so that he may cense it. The body shall immediately be lowered, and shall again be sprinkled by the abbot and censed by the one in the grave. When it has been covered, the abbot shall throw earth upon it once. When this has been done, he shall withdraw opposite the grave, beginning “Of rashness indeed,” with the cross, light, thurible, and holy water arranged before him; and thus he shall complete what remains.

When these things have been completed, beginning the seven penitential Psalms, they shall return to church in reversed order, that is, with the lay monks going before; and, if there are novices, they shall go first. Having entered the middle of the choir, they shall stand in the order in which they came, until the priests prostrate themselves at the upper end. Meanwhile the abbot, having removed his priestly vestments, shall prostrate himself in the presbytery before the altar, and the seniors after him. If another has performed the service, having removed his priestly vestments, he shall prostrate himself in the first rank among the seniors. After the Psalms, “Eternal rest” and what is contained in the Collectary having been said [Col. 1478C], they shall depart.

Brethren who are outside choir because of illness, and those who have been bled, shall, if able, stand in their order for the dying man’s departure, for the burial, and for the seven Psalms after burial. Otherwise, they shall make their inability known to the abbot; but they shall be permitted to be absent from those things done for him in church. Those in the infirmary, if able, shall likewise go out to the grave in their order. On returning to the church, they shall prostrate themselves outside choir, as novices do. The lay brothers, however, shall be in their own choir or in the rear choir.

Then several briefs shall be made [Note: [Col. 1478D] “Briefs,” that is, slips requesting from other monasteries prayers and suffrages for the deceased.], to be given to the porter for distribution to travellers. Whatever is done for him before he is committed to the earth shall be beyond the obligation due to him. This obligation [Col. 1478D] is that the Collect for him shall be said in the community at the Office of the Dead, at Vespers and Lauds, until the thirtieth day: namely, “O God, whose special property it is”; and this same Collect shall be repeated in the daily Mass for the same number of days.

When these are completed, on the thirtieth day he shall be absolved in chapter when the cantor makes commemoration, and then he shall be joined to the Collect, namely “Almighty and everlasting God, to whom never …” Each priest shall say three private Masses, and each cleric a Psalter; those who do not know it shall say “Have mercy upon me, O God” [*Miserere mei, Deus*] one hundred and fifty times. Those who do not know that either shall say the Lord’s Prayer the same number of times.

If anyone of our Order should arrive and die there [Col. 1479A], as much shall be done for him as if he had professed in that house; nonetheless, the same shall be done for him in his own house.

At the time of the Cistercian chapter, on the day following the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, after the sermon delivered in chapter, while all stand devoutly, our deceased shall be absolved by him who presides over the chapter, saying: “May the souls of our brethren and familiars who have died this year rest in peace.” All answering, “Amen,” shall say *De profundis* (“Out of the depths”); then, bending the knee even on Sundays, they shall say the Lord’s Prayer. The presider shall say: “And lead us not into temptation”; “From the gate of hell”; “The Lord be with you”; “Let us pray. O God, giver of pardon,” etc.; and at the end, after “The Lord be with you,” “May they rest in peace.” “Amen.”

In the same manner absolution shall be made on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September] in every abbey of our Order, when the cantor makes commemoration; and on the same day at Vespers the solemn thirty-day observance shall begin, unless perhaps the following day is a principal fast-day or a Sunday. When this occurs, the absolution shall indeed not be deferred; but on the day of Saint Maurice—unless that too is followed by a Sunday—the solemn thirty-day observance shall begin at Vespers, and the following day, then the first of the thirty-day observance, shall be performed solemnly.

After the absolution of the dead, he who presides over the chapter shall continue and say what further is to be done for them, and this is the obligation: three portions of food every day in every abbey of our Order; from every priest, twenty Masses within the year; from the rest [Col. 1479C], ten Psalters; from those who do not know the Psalter, “Have mercy upon me, O God” one thousand five hundred times, or the Lord’s Prayer as often.

In all these matters, if before they have been discharged someone among our parents or familiars, or even among the brethren of our Order, dies, he may be included, unless perhaps someone has not yet discharged them through his own negligence. Yet if anyone, although he is still bound by the obligation of the chapter, or at other times while he owes some Mass for the dead, wishes out of devotion to sing from the present solemnity, it shall not be reckoned to him as negligence. From the time this absolution has been made, each person shall strive devoutly to discharge what he owes to his brethren, as the Lord has given to each, without waiting [Col. 1479D] for the abbots’ return from chapter.

When the abbots return from the Cistercian chapter, on the first day on which each is in his own chapter, at the cantor’s prompting they shall again be absolved with bending of the knee, even on Sundays and feast days. On every day of the thirty-day observance, the Collect of the thirty-day observance shall be said for them in the community—except on days of twelve lessons—both at Masses and at Offices. Beyond all this, one Mass daily, except on Christmas Day, Good Friday, Easter Saturday, Easter Day itself, and Pentecost, shall be said both for them and for all others of our Order who have departed from this world or depart from it daily.

### Form of briefs to be written for a deceased person

[Col. 1480A] On the first of August, in the monastery of N., Dom N. of N., priest and sacristan of the same monastery, died; for whose soul we request your prayers in charity, and we shall pray for yours. And similarly in comparable cases, changing what must be changed: namely, the day, place, name, rank, and office, as the case requires.

## Chapter C. Concerning our relatives

The deceased fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and blood-relatives of the brethren of our Order ought to be absolved by name in the Cistercian chapter, in the assembly of abbots, on the final day. The same shall be done in all abbeys of our Order on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, after the solemn absolution of our brethren, and on the first day when each abbot, returning from Cîteaux, enters his own [Col. 1480B] chapter. In these absolutions, however, only “May they rest in peace” shall be said. They shall also share in all those things which the general chapter decrees to be done for the brethren.

For them, too, once a year, in common, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November], a principal office shall be solemnly performed throughout all our abbeys. But when a monk asks mercy for his father, mother, brother, or sister—for it is not permitted to ask it for other relatives—the deceased shall be absolved, and each priest shall say the Collect for him in a private Mass; the remaining brethren shall say the seven penitential Psalms, or “Have mercy upon me, O God” an equal number of times, or the Lord’s Prayer as often.

## Chapter CI. How sick guests are to receive communion

[Col. 1480C] When the hospitaller sees that a guest ought to receive communion, he shall tell the prior, who shall arrange which priest is to do this and who is to go with him. The priest, having washed his hands and clothed himself in alb, stole, and maniple, shall take from the vessel in which it is reserved a portion of the Lord’s Body. Holding it above the chalice with both hands, covered with the offertory veil, he shall go to the sick man, the brethren preceding him in this order: first, one with holy water and fire in a covered lantern; second, one with wine in a cruet; third, one with an uncovered cross. Those before whom they pass shall prostrate themselves on their knees; when they return, however, they shall merely bow.

When they have come to the sick man, the priest, inquiring into his faith, shall communicate him. Then he shall moisten his fingers with wine in the chalice, which he shall administer to him [Col. 1480D], holding his left hand beneath the man’s chin; and, moistening the chalice again with wine, he shall give it to him. He may speak of what is necessary for him for this rite. But if they see that he is not yet approaching death, leaving the cross and holy water there, they shall return in the order in which they came.

## Chapter CII. How a guest is to be buried

When a guest has been reported dead, the prior shall arrange how the soul is to be commended, and the hospitaller how the body is suitably to be prepared. When the prior sees that the time is fitting, he shall send a priest with Collectary and stole, and two brethren with cross, holy water, a light in a covered lantern, and thurible, and whatever he wishes for carrying him to church, chanting in a moderate voice. The prior shall ensure that the body is not left alone or without a light.

If meanwhile the Office for the Dead or Mass is being sung, the Collect for him shall be said second. At another Mass it shall be said in the place where Collects for the dead are customarily said. At whatever hour the grave is ready, he may be buried, even after the meal. Then, the signal having been rung, the brethren shall arrange themselves around the deceased. When, however, the community is at work, it is not bound to come for the burial of the dead man; the smaller bell alone shall be rung twice.

The priest appointed by the cantor, wearing a stole over his cowl, and the others whom he has selected, with cross, holy water, fire in a covered lantern, and thurible, arranged in the usual way, shall perform the office plainly [Col. 1481B], that is, without singing, unless perhaps the abbot considers that it ought to be sung out of reverence for the person. When it is completed, he shall be carried to the grave as is customary. When he has been buried, if the cantor sees fit, he shall interrupt the psalmody and say “Eternal rest,” then “The choir of angels,” afterward “Most merciful [Lord].” When this is finished, the priest, having completed the Collect which he says, shall say aloud the Lord’s Prayer; then, “And lead us not”; “Eternal rest”; “From the gate of hell”; “Do not hand over, O Lord, the souls to beasts”; “O Lord, hear [my] prayer”; “The Lord be with you”; the Collect, “Absolve, O Lord,” and after it, “O God, by whose mercy.” When it has been said, they shall depart.

The sick and those who have been bled, and those assigned to different offices, may be absent from this service when necessary [Col. 1481C]. It should be known that all priests and all religious persons who die in the guest-house are carried into choir, and no others unless the abbot sees fit; and their exequies are sung. Yet pardon is not asked at “Most merciful [Lord],” nor are the seven Psalms said after burial, because these things are to be done only for a monk, lay brother, or novice of our Order.

Fugitives, both monks and lay brothers, lying in the infirmary for the poor, shall be given the habit when they appear to be at the point of death, and shall be carried to the monks’ infirmary if they are monks, or to the lay brothers’ infirmary if they are lay brothers [Note: [Col. 1481D] Note that at that time fugitives were customarily received only in the infirmary for the poor, unless they had returned to the monastery before their illness. Perhaps, however, this may be understood of fugitives who had fled from the monastery more than three times, to whom our people, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 29, denied return unless they were at the point of death. This is, according to Peter the Venerable, the sixth difference between our observances and those of the Cluniacs (*Epistle* 17, book IV of his *Letters*).].

## Chapter CIII. Concerning novices

A man wishing to become a monk, having made his request, shall not be brought into chapter until after four days. When he has been brought in, he shall prostrate himself before the lectern [Note: [Col. 1482D] See chapter 58 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]. Asked by the abbot what he seeks, he shall answer, “The mercy of God and yours.” When, at the abbot’s command, he has risen, the abbot shall explain the severity of the Order and inquire into his will. If he answers that he wishes to observe all things, the abbot shall say, after the rest: “May God himself, who has begun [Col. 1482A] in thee, bring it to completion.” When the community has answered “Amen,” he shall bow and withdraw to the guest-house. He shall act in the same manner each time he comes into chapter after the Rule has been read. On the third day, however, he shall be brought to the novices’ cell. From then, the year of probation shall begin.

In church, at work, and at collation, he shall attend the community in his order as the monks do. After the Hour he shall leave choir before the monks; after Compline he shall make his prayer outside choir. At the same hours as the monks he shall work, rest, read, and sleep. He shall eat the same food and wear the same garments, except for the monastic habit, in place of which he shall have a cape and mantle, or furs. He shall not make signs with the monks, nor receive the tonsure or orders.

If it happens that someone bound by a marriage tie is received, unknown to the monks to be so bound, he shall be expelled when it becomes known [Col. 1482B]. But if afterward he produces the seal of his bishop, or a reliable witness, that his wife, having vowed chastity, has released him, he may be received, to undergo anew an entire year of probation. If he has already received the monastic habit, he shall likewise depart. If he dies in the cell, the same shall be done for him as for a monk. If a lay novice, not daring to take the monastic habit, asks to become a lay brother, he may be received.

When one who wishes to become a monk has completed the year of probation [Note: [Col. 1482D] “When the year has been completed,” etc. This, according to Peter the Venerable in his *Epistle* 17, book IV of the same *Letters*, is the first distinction between our observance and that of the Cluniacs: they admitted their novices to profession before the probationary year was completed.], summoned in chapter before all, he shall dispose of what is to be done with his possessions, if he has any. Afterward, if he is a layman, his tonsure shall be blessed by the abbot in church, with the cantor and sacristan attending him; and the abbot shall complete the blessing as it is contained in the Collectary [Col. 1482C]. The sacristan shall burn the hair in the piscina assigned for this purpose. Then he shall be tonsured as a monk.

If Mass is to be celebrated later that day, immediately after the Gospel he shall come to the step of the presbytery and read his profession, if he can read [Note: [Col. 1482D] “If he can read.” Therefore, illiterate persons were sometimes received even among us at that time, and this in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict (ibid.).]; otherwise his master shall read it for him. When it has been read, the novice himself shall make the sign of the cross upon it, and then, bowing, he shall come to the altar, asking pardon at its step. Then, rising, he shall place the profession on the right horn of the altar, kissing it; and bowing again, he shall return to the step.

Meanwhile the abbot, standing at the right horn of the altar, shall take up the paper. Meanwhile the novice shall say three times the complete verse, “Receive me, O Lord,” asking pardon [Col. 1482D], with hands and knees placed upon the ground, on feast days as well as other days, whenever he has finished it. The community shall answer the same verse three times, adding “Glory be to the Father,” “Lord, have mercy,” and the Lord’s Prayer.

The abbot shall say, “And lead us not”; and when the brethren answer, “But deliver us from evil,” the cantor shall begin the Psalm “Have mercy upon me, O God,” to be sung alternately by each choir [Col. 1483A] with the *Gloria*, at which no bow is to be made, just as none is made at the *Gloria* said after “Receive me, O Lord.” The novice, having asked pardon three times after “Receive me, O Lord,” shall immediately humble himself at the feet of the abbot [Note: [Col. 1483D] “He shall humble himself at the feet”: that is, by this ceremony he was, according to the Rule, joined to the community.] and of the abbots, if there are more than one, and of the ministers. Then he shall humble himself before the prior and go through his choir, humbling himself at the feet of each individual. Returning again through the middle of the choir, he shall proceed through the right side as he did through the left.

If the prior is absent, unless the abbot is in the left choir, he shall go through the right choir before the left. Then, going out into the rear choir, he shall prostrate himself at the feet of the sick, if they are present. Having done this, returning through the middle of the choir, he shall prostrate himself below the step.

[Col. 1484A] Near the end of the Psalm, the abbot, coming with staff to the step, shall say, “Save thy servant,” etc., and four Collects shall follow. When these are completed, the novice shall rise. Then, after the cowl has been blessed and sprinkled with holy water, the abbot, stripping the novice of his own garments, shall say, “May the Lord strip thee,” etc.; and the brethren answering “Amen,” shall clothe him in the cowl, saying, “May the Lord clothe thee,” etc., the brethren answering “Amen.” Thus he shall be placed in choir.

After this, the abbot, returning to the altar, shall say “I believe in one God,” or “The Lord be with you.” But if he is not to be blessed at Mass, he shall be blessed immediately after Sext. It should be known that every abbot, even in the presence of a senior abbot, shall bless his own novice [Note: [Col. 1484D] See the *Charter of Charity*, chapter 2.].

## Part Five. Concerning the offices of weekly officers, superiors, and officials

## Chapter CIV. Concerning the weekly priest and his ministers

[Col. 1483B]

The weekly priest begins the Hours and all the chapter-readings; at Lauds and Vespers he says “The Lord be with you,” “Let us pray,” and the Collects; and at commemorations, the verses, “Let us pray,” and the Collects. But at the Collect of no commemoration does he say “The Lord be with you,” nor “Through Christ our Lord,” except after the last, when nothing follows. When Prime or *Exsultabunt* follows, however, he says daily “Through the Lord,” but not “The Lord be with you,” nor “Let us bless the Lord.” He gives blessings to the cooks and to those setting out on a journey and returning, as they are contained in the book. He says all these standing, and does not bow except after the chapter-readings. At the other Hours, prostrate or seated upon the [Col. 1483C] misericords, he says “The Lord be with you,” “Let us pray,” and “Let us bless the Lord”; and at the Office of the Dead he begins the Psalms, namely *Out of the depths* and *Bless the Lord, O my soul*, and says, “From the gate of hell,” etc. In Chapter and in the refectory he says the verse and blessings. In the absence also of the abbot, prior, and subprior, he performs in every respect the subprior’s office in church, except that he neither rouses the brothers nor moves from his place. If he is absent, the priest who stands above him in choir performs all these things for him; if no one stands above him, the one who stands below beside him does so. If there is no priest in that choir, the first in the other choir performs the same things. This order is not to be observed if he has been sent on a journey or is in the infirmary.

[Col. 1483D] At work, if he is present, he begins the Hours. He blesses the candle on the Purification of Saint Mary; ashes at the beginning of the fast; branches on Palm Sunday; and fire on Holy Saturday, and sings the solemn Masses. In his own week he sings the general Masses; and in the following week, when there are two Masses, he sings the morning Mass; and at the general Masses he assists in vesting and unvesting and in the other things needed there. In the third week, when there are two Masses, he does likewise at the morning Mass. When the deacon alone distributes the Blood to the brothers, as we said much above, he assists him in the subdeacon’s place. The minister, if he is a subdeacon, reads the Epistle; if a deacon, the Epistle and Gospel, in his week at the general Mass, and in the following week at the morning Mass. In the second and third weeks he assists at Masses, as we said concerning the priest.

### CHAPTER CV. On the weekly officer of the Invitatory

At the time when the Invitatory is sung on ordinary days, the weekly officer must, every day of his week, sing alone on ordinary days, “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord”; and, both in that week and the following one, at the Twelve Lessons with a companion. In the following week, if he is outside choir, he entrusts his office to another. He sings the verses at all the Hours and the Responsories at Lauds and Vespers in church. At the second Nocturn he intones *Alleluia*; at the canticles and the daytime Hours, the Antiphons and *Alleluia*; at Vespers he must intone the first Antiphon; at Lauds and Vespers say “Let us bless the Lord”; and read in Chapter. At the Office of the Dead he begins the first Antiphon; says the verses, lessons, and verses of the Responsories; and intones the Antiphons at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*.

If he is absent, the one who stands next to him above him performs all these things for him, unless he has been sent on a journey [Col. 1484D] or is in the infirmary; if he has no superior, the inferior does it. If the one superior to the weekly officer happens himself to be the weekly Mass officer, or ought to sing the Hours for another, he signals to someone to perform the Responsories and verses in the weekly officer’s place. Likewise, the one below him does so if he is the weekly [Col. 1485A] Mass officer and, by some occurrence, the office of the Invitatory has fallen to him.

The one who is below the weekly officer of the Invitatory always intones the Psalms and canticles, while the weekly officer begins the Antiphon. In summer, at Nocturns on ordinary days, after the lesson he sings the Responsory, “O Lord, [open] my lips”; “May God have mercy upon us”; “Whoever wishes”; “When I called”; and all hymns on ordinary days; and on feasts he begins at Sext and None. It should nevertheless be noted that, when the last of the clerics is weekly officer of the Invitatory, the one immediately above him must perform all these things.

### CHAPTER CVI. On the church servant

The church servant at Nocturns must light candles for the lessons and Responsories, [Col. 1485B] and at Lauds for “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), unless it is broad daylight, and for the Collect. Likewise, at the intervals in the cloister and in Chapter, and when necessary he must light the lamp for Compline. It also belongs to him to replenish the lamps in church whenever necessary; to provide light if it is lacking; coals in the brazier; water for washing hands before Masses; salt and water for blessing on Sunday before Terce; and live coals in the censer before the Gospel—or afterwards, if *Credo in unum Deum* is said—to carry into church. He must also return to the refectory after Mass the salt-cellar from which he took it. For all these things, if he cannot find them within the cloister, he may go outside.

### CHAPTER CVII. On the weekly reader

[Col. 1485C]

On Sunday, after the principal Mass, the table-reader, prostrating himself before the step of the presbytery and beginning on the right side, shall say three times the entire verse, “O Lord, [open] my lips,” and, having received the blessing, bow. He shall indicate to the cantor what and where he ought to read. At the signal, he shall take the *mistum*, as we said above; before the prior enters the refectory, placing the book on the lectern and having chosen an appropriate beginning, he shall have it open when the prior arrives. While the verse is said, he shall sit there; when it is finished, he shall rise and, turning toward the prior, humbly request a blessing from the same place. Having received it, if he is to read a homily, he shall begin, “At that time”; and after “and the rest” has been omitted, shall continue, “a homily [Col. 1485D] on the same reading.” While he reads, he must give ear to the prior, so that he may understand if the prior corrects him. If he understands what is corrected, he shall say it humbly; if he does not understand, he shall begin the verse again. He shall do this as often as he knows that the prior has grunted for this reason. When the reading is finished, carrying the book unfastened, he shall descend without delay; having set down the book, he shall bow; then, taking it up again, he shall depart to a place where he cannot be seen by the community. When the Bible is read in the refectory, the number of the chapters shall be stated by him. When the thanksgiving in church is ended, he shall ring the small bell, unless some abbot, or the prior of that place, or the subprior in the prior’s absence, is to eat with the servants. In the following week he shall read at [Col. 1486A] the conference. But if he is outside choir, in the infirmary, or sent on a journey, so that he cannot read at table, the cantor shall assign another, who shall read and take the *mistum* as long as he is absent.

### CHAPTER CVIII. On the weekly officers for the washing of guests’ feet

When the board is struck for the washing of feet after Compline, the brothers appointed for this on Sunday in Chapter shall put on their scapulars and follow the guest-master in their order. Coming to the guests, they shall remove their hoods. The senior shall wash feet on the first day [Note: [Col. 1485D] In this office of humility and charity, Peter the Venerable of Cluny testifies that there was a ninth difference [Col. 1486D] between our people and the Cluniacs: ours, but not theirs, washed guests’ feet.]; the junior shall dry them, but they shall not kiss them. On the second day the reverse shall be done, and so they shall proceed through the remaining days alternately. This done, they shall wash and dry their hands. Then, arranged so that [Col. 1486B] the seniors are in the middle, with knees bent and hands lowered to the ground before the guests, they shall say, “We have received mercy, O God”; then, rising, they shall bow and depart, drawing their hoods back over their heads.

### CHAPTER CIX. On the weekly kitchen officers

On Sunday, after Matins, those leaving the kitchen shall prostrate themselves before the step of the presbytery, beginning on the right side; then, bent over, they shall say, “Blessed art thou, O Lord.” Having received the blessing, they shall rise, bow again, and return thus to choir. Those entering shall follow, prostrating themselves in the same manner and saying their verse bent over. Having received the blessing, they shall bow and depart as the former did, [Col. 1486C] unless a commemoration is to be said. Wherever the abbot decides, during that interval, clothed in their day-clothes and scapulars, if they have time, they shall draw water for washing hands wherever needed; and, entering the kitchen, shall do whatever then needs doing. When two Masses are to be sung, if both are clerics or both laymen, the one who is to serve that day shall hear the first, the other the second, and communicate if he wishes. If one is a cleric and the other a layman, the layman hears the first, the cleric the second. If either is to say the Mass, Gospel, or Epistle, he hears the one to which his office pertains, and the other hears the other. On principal fasts both hear Mass.

[Col. 1486D] If, on principal fasts, a festival day should occur, the one serving that day shall go to the kitchen at the principal Mass. On their first day the senior, taking the *mistum*, shall serve; on the second, the junior; and so on the remaining days they shall serve in turn. During reading-time both shall work together in the kitchen, unless the one whose day it is—that is, the one who is to serve first—signals the other to read. In Lent they do not go to the kitchen before Terce, except on Sunday. It belongs to them to prepare water in the refectory for drinking, at both meals and for both drinks, and in the washing-place for washing hands. When sharp frost threatens, they shall provide hot water with [Col. 1487A] bowls in the cloister, near the washing-place, wherever necessary; and prepare water for shaving the brothers.

He who serves the novices at their meal, before carrying dishes to the monks, shall summon them by sound; shall prepare necessities for the brothers who, because of negligence, eat outside the refectory; and, after they have eaten, shall gather up again what remains. If he lacks anything, he shall request it from the cellarer by a sign. The other, after the meal, putting on his scapular and coming into the kitchen, shall clean and keep the novices’ bowls, if he finds them in the cloister with their remnants, together with the servants’ bowls. In summer, however, he shall not do this until after None.

[Col. 1487B] Where there are four weekly kitchen officers, two shall serve one day and two the next, in alternation. On the day when they do not work in the kitchen, they shall go with the community to work where the abbot decides. On Saturday they shall wash the towels for hands and feet, first in hot water and afterwards in cold. They must also wash the washing-place and the water-receptacle in the kitchen, sweep what is necessary, and put there what is needed. They shall sweep the kitchen and carry the rubbish to the designated place. When necessary, they shall heat water for the washing of feet. They shall prepare cut firewood for lighting the fire on the next day. Immediately after Vespers, if it is a fast-day; after the servants’ meal, if it is Lent; or after their supper, if it is a dinner-day, they shall return to the cellarer the vessels and other things which they received in the kitchen, [Col. 1487C] and the cellarer shall hand them to the one entering. If any of the things to be returned are missing, they shall make satisfaction in Chapter and report what is lacking.

When these have been returned, they shall prepare the things necessary for the washing of feet. As soon as the signal has rung, clad in scapulars, they shall put off their cowls in Chapter and come thus into the cloister. When, therefore, the abbot begins the Antiphon—namely *Postquam*—or, in the abbot’s absence, the cantor, the senior of those entering the kitchen shall wash the abbot’s feet and the junior shall dry them, proceeding in this way through the others on the left side. The junior of those leaving shall wash feet and the senior dry them, proceeding likewise through the others on the right side. To prevent this order being disturbed, if there are two abbots, the lesser abbot shall sit on the right side [Col. 1487D]. Those who finish more quickly shall cross to the other side and assist the others. Whenever they pass before the one presiding over the conference, they shall bow reverently. The one who washes feet and the one whose feet are washed shall bow to one another after the washing; likewise the one who dries and the one whose feet are dried. No one shall take off his shoes until the abbot has taken off his. When they are unshod, they shall take care as far as possible that their bare feet do not appear, but remain hidden beneath the cowl. Sleeves must not hang down while they sit, but they shall arrange them suitably before themselves. Before the reading, all shall have put their shoes back on.

When the washing of feet has been completed and the hands and vessels washed, they shall put back the vessels and towels where they are customarily put. Then, [Col. 1488A] taking up their cowls in Chapter and laying their scapulars in the cloister upon the seats, they shall come before the abbot in such order that the one who will sit last beyond the abbot is first in going; and the rest shall follow in the order in which they will sit. Thus the one who will sit last on the side from which they came shall proceed, and then all together, bowing before the abbot, shall go to their seats without bowing; but, after sitting down, they shall lower their heads. If one of them, compelled by some necessity, cannot complete his office, another shall serve in his place and take the *mistum* as long as the need lasts. Nevertheless, even if he is outside choir, he shall receive the Sunday blessing; but if he enters the infirmary, the one who completed the office for him shall receive it.

### CHAPTER CX. On the abbot’s cooks

[Col. 1488B]

The abbot’s cooks shall take turns doing the kitchen by weeks. If at any time one cannot accomplish it alone, he may call his companion for assistance; but both shall not serve at the meal, and they shall maintain silence according to the usual custom. They shall admit no one into the kitchen, the key of which they shall keep. The lay brother of the guesthouse shall also have the other key; he must assist them in all things and keep the utensils of that kitchen, as the monks do. They may enter the monks’ kitchen and refectory for the sake of their office. They shall hear Masses as we have directed above concerning the cooks. He whose week it is shall, [Col. 1488C] in the morning after Prime, clothed in scapular and day-clothes, receive only as much pulse [Note: [Col. 1487D] “Only as much pulse,” because evidently abbots used the same dishes as the monks.] as can suffice for the abbot and arrivals.

Before the hour of the meal he shall prepare the abbot’s table. If there are no guests, he shall summon by a sign two monks whom the abbot wishes to eat with him, and carry their cups and portions. If it happens that they return for some reason, they shall not be charged with having missed the verse. As soon as these monks have completed the verse after the meal, they shall bow and depart without waiting for permission, unless the abbot keeps them. If the abbot’s meal is prolonged beyond the brothers’ meal, when they know that the community has gone to church, they shall return to the cloister with the abbot’s permission [Col. 1488D].

Moreover, as soon as his companion can duly leave the community, he shall come to the refectory door and present himself to his companion; at his signal he shall remain to serve the abbot, if necessary. When he departs after finishing, he shall collect the napkins and vessels, carry the cups and portions of the monks, if present, into the refectory, and perform all the other things his companion would do. Before the conference or meal the weekly officer shall prepare drink for the abbot in the refectory, or, if the abbot orders it, in the guest-house. On Saturday, at the same hour as the general cooks, he shall hand over the key and kitchen utensils to the incoming companion. It should be known that for the table-reading they are to be entered in writing both when the abbot is absent and when he is present [Col. 1489A].

### CHAPTER CXI. On the abbot

The abbot must have the first and proper place in the right choir; conclude the prayers; intone the first Antiphon at Nocturns; give blessings to the readers; sing the twelfth Responsory; begin *Te Deum laudamus*; read the Gospel; throughout the whole week of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, and at the Twelve Lessons, intone the Antiphon at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*; begin, at the processions on the Purification of Saint Mary, *Hodie beata Virgo*; on Palm Sunday, *Ingrediente Domino*; and at [Col. 1489B] the Ascension of the Lord, *O Rex gloriae*. He must say the *Pater noster* aloud for all to hear at Matins and Vespers; take the weekly Mass duty like the others, and also sing solemn Masses on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord and on the day itself; at Epiphany; on Palm Sunday; on the three days before Easter and on Easter itself; at the Ascension; on the vigil of Pentecost and on the day itself; on all solemnities of Saint Mary and on the Vigil of her Assumption; on Saint Benedict’s day; on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; of the Apostles Peter and Paul; of Blessed Bernard; at the Dedication of the church; on the feast of All Saints; at all principal Offices of the Dead; and for a present deceased person—even if he has been defiled by a nocturnal emission.

[Col. 1489C] On the Purification of Saint Mary, he blesses candles; at the beginning of the fast, ashes; on Palm Sunday, branches; on Holy Saturday, fire; and he blesses the novices’ crowns and the novices themselves. He presides over Chapter and the Conference. In Chapter he must impose upon and absolve the brothers from the duties of the prior, subprior, and cantor, and the penances of lighter and graver fault; likewise, he may promote or degrade whomever he wishes. He may impose and absolve the rest within and without; hear confessions; give holy water after Compline to those leaving church; sleep in the dormitory; and eat in the guest-house [Note: [Col. 1489D] “Eat in the guest-house”: this was the twelfth difference between Cistercians and Cluniacs: abbots of the Cistercian Order ate with guests [Col. 1490D] in accordance with chapter 56 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, whereas Cluniac abbots did not.]. If he breaks a fast because of a guest, he shall nevertheless eat at the usual hour, namely after None. When guests are absent, he must have at least two monks at table; he shall keep silence at table insofar as he reasonably can. When he comes in from outside after Compline, he shall eat in the refectory unless guests are present. Likewise, after Terce when he has been bled; there also he may drink whenever he wishes.

It should be known that, when the abbot has denied something to anyone, he must not presume to ask or receive it from another. If anyone asks the cellarer for something that he refuses to give him, and afterwards asks the prior for the same thing, he must take care not to conceal from him that the cellarer denied it to him. Likewise, anyone who approaches the abbot about something [Col. 1490A] which the prior refused to give him must by no means fail to tell the abbot, in that very request, that the prior denied it to him. Whoever presumes otherwise should know himself guilty of deceit.

It should be noted that when monks kiss the abbot, they shall bend the knee before him and, after the kiss, bow deeply. We do not offer such a kiss of peace within the abbeys of our Order to one arriving from a journey unless he has first prayed. When the abbot is in the infirmary, he shall not sing Masses either privately or in community, unless perhaps, out of devotion, when there is a present deceased person; and this applies to one who can and wishes. But one who is continually in the infirmary may, by a Cistercian chapter, sing both privately and in community. It should be known that an abbot under a lighter fault [Col. 1490B] may perform his whole office, provided only that his satisfaction is not impeded.

### CHAPTER CXII. On the prior

The prior must stand in church in the first place of the left choir; in Chapter and at the conference sit beside the abbot on the right side; perform the week of the Invitatory, yet not read in Chapter; read the twelfth lesson; strike the board for work and lead the brothers there if the abbot does not go; and, when he does not go, entrust this only to the subprior, if the subprior goes to work. When necessity requires, he shall strike the board to summon the brothers to Chapter and ring the signal for washing; he shall ring the refectory bell [Col. 1490C] in the community and for the servants when present. If, upon arriving from outside, he finds the bell being rung or the verse being said, he shall enter, while the subprior, after ringing the bell sufficiently, returns to his place. If the subprior has already sat down, he shall enter as the other monks do; and the subprior, withdrawing a little, shall sit at the bell, and thereafter perform his office. He shall do the same at Chapter and at the conference. He shall perform the kitchen week, unless a greater advantage prevents it, and serve on his day. If he lies in the infirmary, he shall conduct himself more strictly and shall not speak simultaneously with more than two persons, and that in a designated place, unless perhaps, in the abbot’s absence, it is at times necessary to speak with more people for some counsel [Col. 1490D] or to hold Chapter for the sick. Indeed, if great necessity arises and the abbot is absent, the community may go to hold the common Chapter. If it seems good to the abbot, he shall also hear confessions in Chapter.

For the rest, whether the abbot is present or absent, he shall act within and without concerning all things and in all matters according to the abbot’s will, except that he shall not occupy the abbot’s place in church; sing solemn Masses in his place; bless candles, ashes, branches, fire, a crown, or a novice; give the blessing for the Gospel; anoint a sick person; bury a dead person; [Col. 1491A] promote or degrade anyone, or have anyone ordained; send anyone under a grave fault or absolve anyone therefrom; expel a monk from the monastery; receive a novice unless the abbot orders it; or hear confession of criminal matters, except from one at the point of death. The care of works, flocks, or granges shall not be entrusted to him, for his own office is sufficient. If he is not a priest but only a deacon, he may give the blessing to the reader in Chapter, in the refectory, and at the Conference, though he must not do so in church. He may also say the *Pater noster* in church, begin *Te Deum laudamus*, and read the Gospel lesson.

### CHAPTER CXIII. On the subprior

[Col. 1491B]

It belongs to the subprior to rouse the brothers in choir, even when the prior is present, and, when necessary, to correct the other matters belonging to the cantor and sacristan. At reading-time in the cloister and at intervals in Chapter, he shall take careful care that the brothers conduct themselves in an orderly fashion. If commanded, he shall hear confessions during reading-time: those of monks in Chapter, but those of novices, lay brothers, and infirmary patients where he is assigned. When the prior serves at the meal, he shall sit at the bell; go alone last to the thanksgiving; stand as superior in choir; and, in the abbot’s absence, sit also at the washing of feet. But after the washing of feet, when the prior bows before him with his companions, he shall give way a little.

[Col. 1491C] When the prior leaves the monastery, the subprior shall neither speak nor do anything belonging to the prior’s office, except by the prior’s command, until something occurs that specifically belongs to the prior’s office—for example, presiding over Chapter if the abbot is absent; striking the board for work; ringing the signal for the meal, or the bell for drinks. In his absence he shall give or arrange nothing except where the prior cannot suitably be awaited, or where something happens which must not and cannot be deferred. If the prior happens to be in the infirmary, the subprior shall act within and without at the abbot’s discretion—or, if the abbot is absent, by the prior’s counsel.

It does not belong to his office to change his place in church or read the twelfth lesson. Likewise, [Col. 1491D] he shall not change his place in Chapter or at the Conference if the abbot is present. If the prior, returning from a journey, eats with the servants, he may meanwhile speak within and without. If he is in the infirmary, he shall presume nothing more than the others. If the prior is outside the monastery or in the infirmary, the subprior shall act in the prior’s place at Vigils and in Chapter; and, eating with the servants, or taking the *mistum* with those who have been bled in winter, he shall sit at the bell.

### CHAPTER CXIV. On the master of novices

The master of novices must teach his novices their rule; rouse them in church; and, wherever they conduct themselves negligently, correct them by word or sign as far as he can [Col. 1492A]. At work, however, unless he is then the prior of the community, he shall not speak with them without first receiving permission, nor sing or read in their cell. He must provide for their needs as far as possible. He shall bring them into Chapter to hear the sermons. For manifest negligences, when they ask pardon before him, he shall impose penance. He shall keep written in the cell the first day of their entry; and announce to the abbot when the Rule is to be read to them. Whoever reads it shall read separately from the others during reading-time and work-time. When it has been read, he shall report this to the abbot in Chapter and summon them at his command. When the year is complete, he shall bring them for blessing, even on the very day on which each entered, provided that he heard the Rule before Chapter. If he cannot complete hearing the Rule before [Col. 1492B] Chapter, he shall be blessed on the next day, or thereafter, from the time he has heard the Rule. For novices who cannot read, he shall read their professions in church; have ink ready for affixing them to the cross, as also for visiting monks; lead and bring him back to the monks’ feet, if necessary; prepare holy water and a cowl; and assist him there in taking off and putting on [his garments]. Afterwards he shall carry his cup and portion into the refectory, show him the bed which the prior has directed, and on that same day indicate to him there the necessary matters. Then, for two months, he shall speak with him in the auditorium beside Chapter, as also with visiting monks.

### CHAPTER CXV. On the sacristan and his assistant

[Col. 1492C]

The sacristan must regulate the clock and have it sound daily before Vigils to rouse him; and in winter before Lauds on ordinary days, unless it is daylight. After rising, he shall have the dormitory and church lit, and place a light in the cloister if necessary. He shall unlock the church doors; for it belongs to him to secure, close, and open all the doors of that church whenever necessary. He shall sound for Chapter, the *mistum*, drinks, the Conference, and all the Hours, and shall not stop except at the prior’s signal—apart from the *mistum* and drinks, and except at Vigils and Prime at all times, and at Terce in winter when fasting and working. Yet he shall not fail to sound for Chapter and the Conference [Col. 1492D] until the blessing has been given. If he sounds them earlier or later than they should be, or if there is light at the Conference, he shall make satisfaction in the following Chapter. If, at a Vigil of Twelve Lessons, he delays so much that it is necessary to sing more quickly and abbreviate the lessons, he shall make satisfaction before the step of the presbytery, standing bent over from “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) until after “Thanks be to God” (*Deo gratias*). He must also end the twelfth lesson by signal or clock if it is prolonged beyond the point at which it ends in the breviary.

When Vigils or Hours are to be sung earlier, he shall inform the cantor; make candles and tapers and place sufficient numbers in various parts of the church. He shall carry them to the tables and to the conference when a negligence occurs; distribute them to the cellarer, infirmarian, and those who need them [Col. 1493A], and keep and distribute tallow candles. He shall prepare the stole and staff for the abbot whenever necessary. He shall suitably arrange candles, ashes, branches, and fire upon the step of the presbytery for blessing. After the blessing, with his assistant and those ordered to help, he shall distribute candles and branches to all. He shall remove branches after the procession and receive the candles from the abbot’s hand after the offertory.

For anointing a sick person he shall carry consecrated oil and tow or a linen cloth for wiping, and after wiping burn it in the piscina. He shall attend the abbot at the blessing of the crown and burn the hair in a secret place of the church. He shall keep, prepare, and whenever suitable change the Gospel-book, Missal, vessels, vestments, linens, and other furnishings necessary in church [Col. 1493B] and at the altar. Washing separately in a vessel set apart for that purpose the corporals, offertory-cloths, towels with which the priest’s fingers are dried after Communion, and the altar-cloth upon which the corporal is spread, he shall throw each washing into the piscina. He shall give the altar-cloth, together with the other linens, to the cellarer to be washed; but he himself shall wash the rest in a pot set apart for this purpose, with heated lye-water. When they have been washed and carefully dried, clothed in an alb with a stone, commonly called a *lisca*, he shall polish the corporals. Folding them, he shall divide the width into three parts, draw the left part over the middle, lay the right upon it, and store away the rest folded.

[Col. 1493C] Likewise, clothed in an alb, he shall make hosts in a place covered with clean linens, even outside the precincts if necessary, but in silence. Two brothers, clothed in scapulars, shall assist him in such a way that he need handle with his hands nothing but the hosts themselves. One of them shall tend the fire carefully; the other shall hold the iron instrument for baking the hosts. While they make them, they shall not speak. When this is finished, the sacristan shall carefully separate suitable from unsuitable ones and preserve them in the cleanest repository. If they should at any time become damp, they shall be suitably dried in the cloister.

Once a week, if he is a priest or deacon, he shall take care to wash the chalices decently inside and out with his own fingers, together with his assistant, after first washing his hands, [Col. 1493D] and throw the washings into the piscina. Afterwards, washing his fingers over the piscina, he shall dry both them and the chalices on the towel hanging above between two linens, and shall do this at reading-time. If he is neither priest nor deacon, he shall warn the prior to order another to do these things. Likewise, once a week he must wash the cruets and portions of his ministry. He shall sweep the presbytery pavement whenever necessary and extinguish the church’s negligences.

### CHAPTER CXVI. On the cantor and his assistant

The cantor must stand in the right choir and the subcantor in the left. Each shall rouse the brothers of his own choir for Vigils and singing. Each shall correct, in his own choir and in the other if the other has not corrected them, negligences concerning the intoning of [Col. 1494A] Antiphons, Psalms, short Responsories, hymns, and verses; and shall see to it that the brothers stand or sit in proper order. At Masses he shall begin “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) and, on feast-days, begin [the chants], except at Sext and None. Moreover, the cantor may cross into the other choir for any negligence, and the subcantor for an intolerable one; and each may correct negligences from his own choir in the other, if necessary. The subcantor shall not presume, while the cantor is present and unoccupied, to perform the other duties belonging to the cantor. If the cantor is absent or occupied, he shall perform everything for him.

It belongs to the cantor to bring books into church and carry them back; prepare them for the sick and those who need them; [Col. 1494B] provide before all others for the Work of God in the oratory; at the sacristan’s signal sing more quickly and abbreviate lessons. When opportune, however, he may do either without the sacristan’s signal. He shall begin the *Alleluia* and Antiphons after Psalms; those for commemorations and repetitions of the Invitatory and Responsories; the Responsories for the dead and their repetitions; and Antiphons after Psalms. He shall distribute books in church as required; prepare for the reader of the twelfth lesson what should be said for reading; intone the Antiphon at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat*, announce in singing to the abbot the one he is about to begin, and now begin the canticle. At Masses he shall begin the Introit, Responsories, *Alleluia*, Tract, Offertory, *Sanctus*, [Col. 1494C] the *Agnus Dei* three times, and Communion. At *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and *Credo in unum Deum*, after the priest, he shall add “And on earth peace to men” and “the Father almighty.” He shall correct in every respect all who make mistakes in church, except those reading the lesson from the lectern at Nocturns. Outside church he shall presume nowhere to do so, unless ordered, except when the moon and brief are announced in Chapter. He shall write on the board those who are to say the readings at Masses on fast-days; “Glory, praise, and honour” (*Gloria, laus et honor*), “My people” (*Popule meus*), and “Holy” (*Agios*); and, when they sing two by two, the litanies. When only one lesson is to be read at Mass, he shall give prior notice by signal.

To the remaining duties—namely, the Mass of Saint Mary; the Mass for the dead; Mass in the community [Col. 1494D]; the Gospel; the Epistle; the Invitatory; service in church; reading at table; cooking; and performing the washing of guests’ feet—the cantor shall designate brothers on the board. Those who perform their duties for more than four days shall be counted as having served a week; if for fewer, they shall serve the week again. Likewise, at the Lord’s Supper, he must enter on the board those assigned to the washing of the monks’ feet; to readings to be read in church and responsories to be sung; to Masses on the Nativity of the Lord, on the Vigil of Easter and Pentecost; and to those things said at those Masses. If any of these assignments needs to be changed after the brief list has been read in chapter, he must notify both the person whose name he removes and the person whose name he enters. He must remedy their omissions (except those concerning the kitchen), either himself or through another. [Note: [Col. 1495D] “To remedy their omissions.” Some here understand “omissions” to mean candles, allegedly so called because they signal the hour of the Divine Office. But anyone who reads attentively the opening words of this chapter, where the cantor is charged with correcting omissions concerning the Psalms, Antiphons, short Responsories, hymns, and versicles to be set down [Col. 1496D], will judge that by these “omissions” nothing other than defects occurring in such matters is meant.] He must make full provision, except for the kitchen, for the duties of those who are sent on a journey or are in the infirmary. Before they are sent on a journey or enter the infirmary, if they hold any duty, they must inform the prior, and the prior in turn the cantor.

He shall determine the readings in the cloister; show them to the readers, and listen himself or through another. He shall receive professions from the abbot’s hand and keep them. The abbot shall provide for the making and safeguarding of documents and books, assigning this responsibility to whomever he chooses. To give out and receive books, the cantor may go as far as the scribes’ doors, but may not enter. Likewise, with respect to the common books—namely Antiphonaries, Hymnaries, Graduals, the Lectionary, Collectary, Calendar, and the books read in the refectory and at Collation—he may go as far as the doors of the novices [Col. 1495B], the infirm, and the scribes, and ask there by signal, but may go no farther unless commanded by the abbot. After Collation he must secure the book-cupboard, keeping it locked during work, sleep, meals, and while Vespers are sung. At holy water; at the washing of feet; on Ash Wednesday; at all processions: he shall begin all versicles and Antiphons, except when the abbot is present. After the abbot rises, the abbot himself shall begin; likewise he shall begin “Today the Blessed Virgin,” the Responsory “As He Entered,” and the Antiphon “O King of Glory,” which three the cantor shall recite or prompt to him.

On the first Sunday of Lent, while the morning Mass is sung, he shall place the books in chapter and afterwards, at the abbot’s direction, distribute them to the brothers together with their assigned portion [solatium; Col. 1495C]. On the Vigil of Easter he shall attach to the Paschal candle a written slip containing the years of the Lord, the epacts, concurrents, and indictions, together with five grains of incense. He shall determine who is to carry water, fire, and the cross when an infirm person is to receive communion or anointing. If the abbot is absent, he shall anoint the sick person and bury the dead, or assign another to do so. At the Office for the Dead, whenever *Kyrie eleison* is said, he shall begin it. When the abbot has served the week of Masses, he shall say the versicle and blessings for him in the refectory. For blessings and the anointing of the sick he shall prepare the Collectary for him and hold it open before him. Whenever *Kyrie eleison* is said there, he shall begin it. He shall count the thirtieth day for the dead from the day following their burial; announce it in chapter [Col. 1495D]; write the briefs to be sent out for them; and also read the briefs in chapter. It should be known that if a deceased person dies before the end of Compline, the current day is to be designated in the briefs sent out for him. But if he dies after the end of Compline, the following day shall be designated in the briefs. Whenever the abbot is absent from the monastery at the death of a monk or lay brother, he shall be reminded, at the first chapter he attends, to absolve the deceased.

## CHAPTER CXVII. On the Infirmarian

[Col. 1496A]

The servant of the sick is accustomed to hear morning Mass and communicate at it. When a sick person goes to the infirmary, he must bring there a cup, a *justitia* [“allowance-vessel”], [Note: [Col. 1496D] *Justitiam*: that is, a vessel into which the regulated drink is poured.] and the bedding of his bed. Thereafter, he may speak with him concerning his necessities in the appointed place, as stated above. At Matins he shall light a candle, carry the books necessary for this purpose, and return them to the church. On Sundays, after Terce has been said in the infirmary, he shall bring holy water there. He must arrange for someone able to sing the Hours and read the lessons there more fluently, and assign this task to him. Before Compline he shall return to the book-cupboard the books that have been in the infirmary.

[Col. 1496B] The prayers generally enjoined in chapter for all the living and dead; any matter established or altered in common; or any public reproof directed against them—after the first Hour at which they gather following the chapter has been sung through, he shall recite these to them, while they maintain silence. But everything else said or done there he shall entirely keep silent about. He must not read or work there, unless he is occupied with their equipment or detained by their serious illness. He shall request necessities from the cellarer by signal, or also by word, wherever and for as long as the abbot sees fit.

If several persons are eating and, with everything ready before them, can serve one another, he shall go to the Hour or to the meal. But if there is only one, he shall remain with him if the sick person wishes [Col. 1496C], not only while he takes nourishment but also for Collation and Compline, if these are completed near nightfall; and for Vigils, unless the prior, with his consent, sends another. After the *Gloria* of the first psalm at the Hours, he shall keep silence, except in the case of those utterly infirm. He may enter the kitchen and refectory to serve them. On Saturday he shall wash the feet of those who wish it and shake out their clothes. When they return to choir, he shall restore to the refectory and dormitory the things he had carried away.

When anyone has come very near to death, he shall lay him on the ground upon a sackcloth, and immediately strike the board repeatedly before the cloister door. He shall heat water for washing the body, prepare the bier, bring it back from the grave [Col. 1496D], and keep it. Unless this has been assigned to another, it also belongs to him to preserve the blood of those who have been bled; to clean vessels stained with that blood; and in winter, after Vigils or after Matins or Prime, to make a fire in the warming-house. It should be known that once the infirmarian has begun to go to the meal, he shall not return, even if he cannot arrive before the versicle; rather, he shall miss the versicle, unless perhaps he is compelled to return because guests have arrived. Those who serve abbots or bishops of our order may, after Compline has been sung in the community, drink water outside the community in the refectory or before the refectory.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. On the Cellarer and His Assistant

The cellarer may speak with everyone except monks and novices of our order.
