It also belongs to him to prepare dishes for the cooks of both kitchens, to put salt into the common dishes, and to divide these among bowls, unless the abbot at some time judges this impossible. He must not alter the common food or drink for anyone except those who have been bled, nor add anything for anyone, unless by the prior’s command. Yet the prior himself must act in this matter, as in all matters, according to the abbot’s will, as stated above. Guests of our order are also excepted, [Note: [Col. 1497D] “Of our order”: because at that time it was not permitted to admit others, especially laypeople, into our refectories. In the course of time, however, this is recorded as having been granted to monks of certain monasteries of the Black Order and to Carthusians, in the book *Antiquar[um] Institutionum* and in the booklet of *Definitions*.] for whom the cellarer may provide an extra portion (*pitantia*) on the first day only. When he does so, he must carry it himself.

He shall prepare bread and wine or *sicera* [a fermented drink] in the refectory at the appropriate hour for distribution. For those who eat up to a third of a loaf at dinner, he shall add coarser bread at supper where it is available. He shall inspect the brothers who are eating at least once, both at dinner and supper. He may leave the dormitory whenever he wishes; and, when eating with the servants, may leave the refectory. If needed, he may take from the leftovers of food; the rest he shall leave to the porter. When the brothers sleep after Sext, he shall remove the servants’ bowls from the refectory [Col. 1497C]. On Saturday he shall receive by count from those leaving the kitchen the vessels and utensils of the kitchen, and return them to those entering. He shall not remove any of these things from the kitchen without the cooks’ direction.

If any person who has completed the kitchen duty is absent from the blessing after Matins, he shall receive the blessing on his behalf. On days when the brothers devote themselves to reading, he shall send two lay brothers to the kitchen to help them, both in washing bowls and in the other necessary tasks; and likewise, on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, two to the warming-house to make a fire. On Good Friday, after Vespers, he shall have lay brothers clean the church; and after Compline, the cloister and chapter-house [Col. 1497D]. He shall bring lay novices into chapter for their petition, and after a year for the making of profession; and shall first notify the person presiding over chapter of this. He shall communicate at morning Mass. At the Lord’s Supper he shall arrange for lay brothers to heat water, prepare the vessels and linens needed for the washing of poor persons’ feet, and lead lay brothers into the cloister for the washing of the monks’ feet. On Good Friday after the Office he shall place hot water in the cloister.

All these things shall be done by the one who regularly serves at the first meal. For when the cellarer is occupied with more important affairs [Col. 1498A], the subcellarer may serve, even in the cellarer’s presence, to the extent the abbot judges useful; and then may speak with lay brothers and household servants. He shall not speak to the cellarer himself except in the hearing-room beside the kitchen, or to guests in the cellar, if the cellarer is in the monastery. Only the one who serves the infirmarian may speak to him, wherever and for as long as the abbot sees fit. If the cellarer is absent, he shall carry out that office in every respect. But he must take every care not to do anything against the cellarer’s will; rather, he shall consult him in every matter and distribute everything according to his counsel. It should be noted that no more than two lay brothers together may speak within the abbey with the cellarer or his assistant, unless they have been called by him because of some pressing necessity [Col. 1498B].

## CHAPTER CXIX. On the Refectory Officer

The refectory officer may communicate at morning Mass. When the brothers eat twice before Sext, or eat once before None or before Vespers, it belongs to his duty to prepare bread and wine or *sicera* for the novices in the designated place. In the refectory he shall distribute napkins, spoons, bread, and wine or *sicera* among the tables. For this he may summon the cook. He shall save the novices’ leftover bread and drink when he finds it in the cloister. When the brothers eat once, he shall collect the napkins before the drink, and the drink afterwards. If it is supper-time, he shall do these things after the servants’ supper [Col. 1498C]. He shall not leave the cloister unless the cellarer is present.

## CHAPTER CXX. On the Guest-Monk

The guest-monk may speak with the guest lay brother, with all guests, and with those who eat or sleep in the guest-house; but outside the gate he shall speak neither with the guest lay brother nor with guests. It belongs to him to provide what and when guests are to eat, and how and where they are to sleep, and to serve them at meals; but while the community is eating, he may not do so unless ordered. He must prepare the washing of feet, himself or through another. When it is prepared, he shall strike the board three times slowly in the cloister [Col. 1498D], go before the monks, or the abbot as well, both on the way there and back, and, if it is night, assist as necessary with a light in performing the washing of feet. He must care for sick guests, both poor persons and others. If the washing of feet must be performed after the monks have gone to rest, he shall do it with the cellarer as best he can. At the Lord’s Supper he shall see that the poor prepare themselves properly in the cloister for the washing of feet.

## CHAPTER CXXI. On the Porter and His Assistant

After Lauds the porter shall go to the gate. If Prime happens through negligence to be said before daylight has become bright [Col. 1499A], he shall go after Prime. When a guest knocks, he shall open the door with the response, “Thanks be to God.” After the guest has said, “Bless [me/us],” [Note: [Col. 1499D] This blessing and salutation constituted the twelfth distinction between our order and the Cluniacs, as Peter of Cluny attests, *Epistle* 17, book IV.] he shall humbly ask who he is and what he wants. When he understands that the guest is to be received, he shall receive him kneeling within the gate. Then, having seated him beside the porter’s cell, he shall say: “Wait here a little while, until I notify the abbot concerning you; then I shall return to you.” Going to the abbot, if he does not find him, he may look for him in all the monastery’s workshops, except that he shall not enter the infirmary but inquire at its door by sound or signal. Having announced the guest to both the abbot and the person who is to receive him, he shall return quickly to the guest and instruct him how to conduct himself when the brothers come to meet him [Col. 1499B]. Thereafter he shall not speak to him, except when he is leaving.

When the departing guest wishes to go out through the gate, the porter shall bow to him in the same way as was stated for his entrance. If someone from the neighborhood or an acquaintance comes to the gate, once he has learned what he wants, he shall make him wait outside the gate until he learns from the abbot what is to be done with him. But if he is such a person as ought neither to be announced nor to remain there, he shall allow him to enter and go wherever he wishes. After recognizing monks and lay brothers of our order, he shall not speak with them. If a guest knocks at the gate while an Hour is being celebrated in church, he shall say, as usual, “Thanks be to God” and “Bless [me/us]” [Col. 1499C]; and after receiving him, shall, if necessary, say that it is not their custom to speak while the Hour is celebrated, asking him to wait until he answers him after the Hour. Guests may be announced until the second signal.

Small children are not ordinarily brought to prayer. Nor are those who come with women received within the cloister; food is instead given them outside with the women. Neighboring women, however, are given nothing there, except in time of famine if the abbot orders it. The porter shall keep loaves in his cell for distribution to passers-by. He shall work at the gate wearing a scapular; and as soon as he hears the signal for an Hour, he shall put on his cowl, remaining there reverently while the Hour is celebrated and conducting himself, as he can, like the brothers in church [Col. 1499D]. On a day when two Masses are celebrated, the subporter shall go to the gate before Prime, and the porter shall hear the first Mass and communicate, if he wishes and if it is an appropriate day, and shall then be in chapter. Meanwhile the subporter shall be at the gate; on days when a sermon is given in chapter, however, they shall go to the sermons in turn. On Good Friday the porter shall adore the cross in church with the others.

He is accustomed to eat with the servants, while his assistant keeps the gate and gives alms to passers-by. The assistant also customarily carries his vessels to the kitchen to collect food leftovers, receiving in them the dishes for the dead and whatever else the cellarer gives [Col. 1500A]. After rising from the meal, he shall distribute these things to the poor at the gate. He must not omit that distribution on account of the Divine Office that follows, but, using few and measured words, shall promptly complete what he has begun; and after completing it, shall perform, as best he can, the Divine Office he delayed. In summer, after Prime or None, he may sleep in the dormitory if he wishes, while his assistant guards the gate. He shall remain at the gate until after Compline; then, coming into the cloister, if he finds the church door locked, he shall say outside the prayer which the brothers say in choir after Compline; then, sprinkling himself with holy water, he shall enter the dormitory. If he is at any time being bled, sick, assigned to kitchen duty, or occupied by any other business [Col. 1500B], his assistant shall perform for him all the things stated above. When the subporter has heard Mass or eaten in the refectory, the prior shall likewise arrange for someone to guard the gate for him. The subporter shall not speak with a guest when the porter is present.

## CHAPTER CXXI. On the Meal Versicle

When the brothers eat twice, at dinner after “Bless [us]” the entire verse “The eyes of all” is said: “Glory be to the Father,” *Kyrie eleison*, and the Lord’s Prayer. Then, after the priest has said, “And lead us not,” and all have responded, “But deliver us from evil,” there follows, without “The Lord be with you,” “Let us pray: Bless, O Lord, these gifts of yours which from your bounty we are about to receive: Through the Lord,” etc. Afterwards the prior shall give the reader the blessing: “May the King of eternal glory make us participants in the heavenly table.” After dinner the entire verse “Let them confess” is said, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son”; and then the priest says: “We give you thanks, almighty God, for all your benefits, who live,” etc. Then, after Psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” has been sung, “Glory,” *Kyrie eleison*, and the Lord’s Prayer are said. After the priest has said, “And lead us not into temptation,” and the response, “But deliver us from evil,” the following five versicles follow, the priest saying the first part and the community responding with the last: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor”; “I will bless the Lord”; “In the Lord”; “Magnify”; “Blessed be the name of the Lord.” Then, without “The Lord be with you” [Col. 1500D] or “Let us pray,” the priest says: “Deign, O Lord, to repay with eternal life all who do us good for your name’s sake”; and “Let us bless the Lord,” to which the community responds, “Amen,” and “Thanks be to God.”

Before supper, however, the whole verse “The poor shall eat” is said, and the blessing over the reader: “May the King of eternal glory bring us to the everlasting supper.” After supper the entire verse “He has made a memorial” is said, followed by: “Blessed be God in his gifts, and holy in all his works, who lives,” etc., as stated above. When we eat once only, “The poor shall eat” is said before the meal and “He has made a memorial” afterwards. The rest is as stated for dinner.

[Col. 1501A] This blessing is given to the reader in chapter: “May divine help always remain with us.” This is given at Collation: “May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us a quiet night” [Col. 1502A]. This is given at the drink: “May the Giver of all good things bless the drink of his servants. Amen.”

# [HISTORY OF THE BEGINNING OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BEGINNING OF THE CISTERCIAN MONASTERY AND ORDER

(*Nomasticon Cisterciense*)

This history of the nascent Cistercian order is brief indeed, but certain and ancient, being contemporary with the order itself and written at the same time by those who founded the order. Therefore, gladly consider it here—long ago transmitted by Aubertus Miraeus in his *Chronicle* and elucidated by us in certain places—and, as you read, attend not only to this order’s original simplicity and humility, but also to the zeal and devotion of its first founders toward the sincere and literal practice and observance of the Rule of our most holy Father Benedict.

# FIRST HISTORY OF THE NASCENT CISTERCIAN MONASTERY AND ORDER, COMMONLY ENTITLED *THE BEGINNING OF THE CISTERCIAN MONASTERY AND ORDER*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1501B]

We, the first founders of this church of Cîteaux, make known to our successors by the present writing how canonically, by what authority, by what persons, and at what times the monastery and the pattern of life of these men took their beginning. Thus, when the sincere truth of this matter has been made public, they may love more steadfastly both this place and the observance of the holy Rule, begun here by us in whatever measure through God’s grace; may pray for us, who have borne without ceasing the burden and heat of the day; may labor in the strait and narrow way shown by the Rule until their last breath; and so, laying aside the burden of the flesh, may happily rest in everlasting repose.

## CHAPTER I. At What Time Saint Robert, Abbot of Molesme, First Laid the Foundations of the Cistercian Monastery and Order

[Col. 1501C]

In the year 1098 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Robert of blessed memory, first abbot of the Church of Molesme, [Note: [Col. 1501C] Molesme is a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the duchy of Burgundy and the diocese of Langres, founded by Saint Robert.] founded in the diocese of Langres, and certain brothers of the same monastery came to the venerable Hugh, then legate of the Apostolic See and archbishop of the Church of Lyons. They promised to order their life according to the custody of the holy Rule of Father Benedict. In order to carry this out more freely, they earnestly requested that he extend to them the support of his assistance and apostolic authority. The legate gladly favoring their desire, laid the foundation of their beginning by the following letter [Col. 1502B].

## CHAPTER II. Letter of the Legate Hugh to Robert, Abbot of Molesme

“Hugh, [Note: [Col. 1501C] This Hugh, formerly bishop of Die and legate of Gregory VII in Gaul, became archbishop of Lyons in the year of the Lord 1080 under that same pope; and, again serving as legate in those regions under Urban II, granted these letters to Saint Robert and his brothers, authorizing them to found the new Cistercian monastery.] archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, to Robert, abbot of Molesme, and the brothers with him who desire to serve God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

“Let it be known to all who rejoice in the advancement of holy mother Church that you and certain of your sons, brothers of the monastery of Molesme, stood before us at Lyons and declared that you wished henceforth to adhere more strictly and perfectly to the Rule of most blessed Benedict, which until now you had kept lukewarmly and negligently in that monastery [Col. 1502C]. First, in the sight of God and of us, you established that you wished to imitate that Rule itself, the institutions of monks, and upright practices fitting to religious life. Since it is evident that this cannot be fulfilled in the aforesaid place for many obstructing reasons, we, providing for the welfare of both parties—that is, those departing from it and those remaining there—judged it beneficial for you to withdraw to another place which divine generosity might designate for you, and there to serve the Lord more wholesomely and peaceably.

“Therefore, while you were present—namely Robert the abbot and the brothers Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Letald, and Peter—and all whom you may decide, according to rule and by common counsel, to associate with yourselves [Col. 1503A], we both advised you then to observe this holy purpose, command you to persevere in it, and confirm it forever by apostolic authority through the impression of our seal.

“But I confirm before God and his saints that I shall preserve in your hand the same profession and stability which I made in your presence in the monastery of Molesme, in this place called the New Monastery [Note: [Col. 1503D] “New Monastery,” that is, Cîteaux.] under obedience to you and your successors, to be regularly appointed in your place.”

## CHAPTER III. The Departure of the Cistercian Monks from Molesme and Their Arrival at Cîteaux

After this, strengthened by such great authority, the aforesaid abbot and his companions [Col. 1503B] returned to Molesme. From that religious company of brothers they selected companions who shared their vow regarding the Rule, so that, between those who had spoken with the legate at Lyons and those summoned from the monastery, there were twenty-one monks. Accompanied by such a company, they eagerly made their way to the wilderness called Cîteaux. This place lay in the diocese of Chalon and, because at that time it was dark with thick forest and thorn-bushes, was inaccessible to people and inhabited only by wild beasts. When the men of God arrived there, they realized that the place was the more suitable for the religious life which they had now conceived in heart and for which they had come thither, precisely insofar as it was more despised and inaccessible to worldly people. Having cut down and cleared away the dense forest and thorn-bushes [Col. 1503C], they began to build a monastery there, with the will of the bishop of Chalon and the consent of the man to whom the place belonged.

For while these men were still at Molesme, often inspired among themselves by God’s grace, they spoke, complained, and grieved over violations of the Rule of the blessed Father Benedict. They saw that they and the other monks had promised by solemn profession to keep this Rule, yet had by no means observed it. Therefore, as we have said, they came to this solitude by the authority of the legate of the Apostolic See, so that they might fulfill their profession through observance of the holy Rule. Then Lord Odo, [Note: [Col. 1503D] This Odo, four years later, having planned and prepared an expedition to Asia and being on the point of leading his army across, says Paradinus, was cut off by an untimely death and buried at Cîteaux; there also his second-born son Henry became a monk.] duke of Burgundy, pleased by their holy fervor and requested by letters of the aforementioned legate of the holy Roman Church, completed entirely from his own resources the wooden monastery they had begun [Col. 1503D], provided for them there abundantly in all necessities for a long time, and richly supported them with lands and livestock.

## CHAPTER IV. How That Place Rose to the Status of an Abbey

At the same time, the abbot who had arrived received from the bishop of that diocese the pastoral staff with care of the monks, by order of the aforementioned legate. He caused the brothers who had come with him regularly to establish stability in the same place [Col. 1504A]; and thus that church rose, by canonical and apostolic authority, to the rank of an abbey.

## CHAPTER V. How the Monks of Molesme Troubled the Pope’s Ears for the Return of Abbot Robert

Not much time having elapsed, the monks of Molesme, at the wish of Lord Geoffrey their abbot, who had succeeded Robert, approached Pope Urban at Rome and began to ask that the aforementioned Robert be restored to his former place. Moved by their importunity, the pope directed his legate, the venerable Hugh, that, if possible, the same abbot should return and that the monks who loved the wilderness should remain in peace.

## CHAPTER VI. Letter of the Lord Pope Concerning the Return of Abbot Robert

[Col. 1504B]

“Urban, [Note: [Col. 1504D] This is Urban II, chosen from the Cluniac order in the year of the Lord 1088.] bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother and fellow bishop Hugh, vicar of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We have received in council the great outcry of the brothers of Molesme, urgently demanding the return of their abbot. For they said that religious life in their place had been overthrown and that, because of that abbot’s absence, they were held in hatred by princes and all their other neighbors. At length, compelled by our brothers, we command your charity by these present writings, signifying that it is agreeable to us that, if possible, that abbot be brought back from the wilderness to his monastery. If you cannot accomplish this [Col. 1504C], let it be your concern both that those who love the wilderness may rest undisturbed and that those in the monastery may devote themselves to regular discipline.”

After these apostolic letters had been read, the legate summoned trustworthy and religious men and determined concerning the present matter what is written below.

## CHAPTER VII. Decree of the Legate Concerning the Entire Affair of the Monks of Molesme and Cîteaux

“Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyons, to his dearest brother Robert, bishop of Langres: greeting. What we have determined concerning the affair of the Church of Molesme at the conference recently held near the port of Ansilla,” etc. See under Hugh of Lyons, *Patrologia*, vol. CLVII, col. 524.

[Col. 1504D] The abbot approved and did all these things, absolving the Cistercians from the obedience which they had promised him in that place or at Molesme. Lord Walter, bishop of Chalon, released the abbot from the care of that church. Thus he returned, together with certain monks who did not love the wilderness. By this arrangement and apostolic dispensation, therefore, the two abbeys remained in complete peace and liberty. Returning, the abbot carried with him to his bishop the following letter as a shield of defense.

## CHAPTER VIII. Commendation of Abbot Robert

[Col. 1505A]

“To my most beloved brother and fellow bishop Robert, bishop of Langres: Walter, servant of the Church of Chalon, greeting.

“Let it be known to you that Brother Robert, to whom we had entrusted the abbey situated in our diocese, called the New Monastery, has been absolved by us, according to the decision of Lord Archbishop Hugh, from the profession which he made to the Church of Chalon and from the obedience which he promised us. He himself has absolved and set free from the obedience they had promised him those monks who decided to remain in the aforesaid New Monastery. Therefore do not hesitate henceforth to receive and honorably treat him. Farewell.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the Election of Alberic, First Abbot of the Church of Cîteaux

[Col. 1505B]

Thus bereft of its shepherd, the Church of Cîteaux assembled and, by a regular election, promoted as its abbot a brother named Alberic, [Note: [Col. 1505D] Although Alberic is here called the first abbot of Cîteaux, he must nevertheless be called only the second, at least if Saint Robert is reckoned as the first abbot of that place—as the context of the chapter itself makes clear. Alberic was elected in the year of the Lord 1099, so that Saint Robert presided over Cîteaux only for a year and three or four months.] a learned man, sufficiently skilled in divine and human learning, a lover of the Rule and of the brothers. He had long held the office of prior in both the Church at Molesme and this one, and had labored vigorously and long to bring about their migration from Molesme to that place; because of this affair he had endured many reproaches, imprisonment, and beatings.

## CHAPTER X. On the Roman Privilege

[Col. 1505C]

Having undertaken the pastoral care, though strongly unwilling, the aforesaid Alberic began, as a man of remarkable prudence, to consider what storms of tribulation might someday shake and harass the house entrusted to him. Foreseeing the future, he sent two monks, John and Ilbod, to Rome with the brothers’ counsel, asking Pope Paschal through them that his church might remain peaceable and safe beneath the wings of apostolic protection, forever free from the pressure of all ecclesiastical and secular persons. The aforesaid brothers, supported by sealed letters of Archbishop Hugh, John and Benedict, cardinals of the Roman Church, and Walter, bishop of Chalon [Col. 1505D], went to Rome successfully and returned before Pope Paschal himself, [Note: [Col. 1505D] Pope Paschal II, chosen from the Cluniac order as supreme pontiff in the year of the Lord 1099, is said to have erred regarding the investitures of benefices, which he granted back and forth to Emperor Henry IV—or Henry V, according to others.] while held captive by the emperor, fell into error. They brought back that pope’s privilege, drawn up in every respect according to the abbot’s and his companions’ wishes. We have considered it fitting to preserve these letters, together with the Roman privilege, in this little work, so that our descendants may understand with how great counsel and authority their church was founded.

## CHAPTER XI. Letter of Cardinals John and Benedict

[Note: [Col. 1506D] These two cardinals were then active in Gaul, having been sent there by Paschal II to reconcile Queen Bertha with Philip I, king of the Franks.]

[Col. 1506A]

“To Lord Father Paschal, worthy everywhere to be proclaimed with exceptional praise: John and Benedict, wholly at your service.

“Since it belongs to our office to provide for all churches and to extend a hand to the just requests of petitioners, and since Christian religion, supported by the aid of your justice, ought to increase, we earnestly entreat your holiness to incline the ears of your mercy toward the bearers of this letter, whom certain religious brothers have sent to your fatherhood at our counsel. They request that the command concerning the peace and stability of their religious life which they received from your predecessor, our lord Pope Urban of blessed memory, and which, in accordance with the tenor of that command, the archbishop of Lyons, then legate, and other fellow bishops and abbots determined between them and the abbey of Molesme, from which they departed for the sake of religious life, may remain forever unshaken by a privilege of your authority. For we ourselves have seen them and bear witness to their genuine religious life [Col. 1506B].”

## CHAPTER XII. Letter of Hugh of Lyons

“To the most reverend Father and his lord, Pope Paschal: Hugh, servant of the Church of Lyons, wholly at your service. These brothers, bearers of the present letters,” etc. See above, col. 525.

## CHAPTER XIII. Letter of the Bishop of Chalon
[Col. 1506C] “To the venerable Father Pope Paschal, Walter, bishop of Chalon, greeting and due submission. As Your Holiness ardently desires that the faithful may advance in true religion, so it is fitting that they should not lack the shelter of your protection and the comfort of your consolation. We therefore humbly request that you may deign to approve what was done concerning those brethren who, through a desire for a stricter life, withdrew from the Church of Molesme on the counsel of holy men, and whom divine mercy has placed in our bishopric. The bearers of this letter, sent by them, stand before you in person. According to the decree of your predecessor, and the decision and written instrument of the archbishop of Lyons, then legate of the Apostolic See, and of the fellow bishops and abbots—a matter in which we were present and, with others, were its authors—may you deign to confirm by the privilege of your authority that that place shall remain for ever a free abbey, while preserving the canonical reverence due to our person and to our successors. Moreover, the abbot whom we ordained in that same place and the other brethren earnestly implore this confirmation from your mercy, as a safeguard for their peace.”

## CHAPTER XIV. A Roman Privilege

[Col. 1507A]

“Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable Alberic, abbot of the New Monastery, situated in the diocese of Chalon, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever. The desire which is shown to concern a religious purpose and the salvation of souls,” etc. See under Paschal, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII.

## CHAPTER XV. The Ordinances of the Cistercian Monks Who Came from Molesme

Thereafter that abbot and his brethren, mindful of their pledge, arranged to establish and unanimously resolved to observe in that place the Rule of blessed Benedict. They rejected from themselves whatever conflicted with the Rule: namely, frocks and pelisses, woollen garments and hoods, straw bedding, and various dishes in the refectory; likewise fat, and all other things opposed to the purity of the Rule. Thus, making the rectitude of the Rule the standard of their entire manner of life, in ecclesiastical observances as well as in all the rest, they were made equal or conformed to the footsteps of the Rule. Having put off the old man, therefore, they rejoiced to have put on the new.

And because neither in the Rule nor in the Life of Saint Benedict did they read that this same teacher possessed churches or altars, offerings, burials, or tithes belonging to other people; or ovens, mills, estates, or peasants; nor that women entered his monastery, nor that the dead were buried there, except for his sister, [Col. 1507C] they renounced all these things, saying that where Saint Father Benedict teaches that a monk should make himself a stranger to secular pursuits—

> [Note: [Col. 1507D] Saint Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 4, “On the Instruments of Good Works.”]

—there he plainly testifies that such things ought not to occupy the actions or hearts of monks, who ought, by fleeing them, to pursue the etymological meaning of their own name.

They also said that the holy Fathers, who were instruments of the Holy Spirit, and whose ordinances it is sacrilege to transgress, distributed tithes into four parts: one, namely, to the bishop; another to the priest; a third to guests coming to that church, or to widows and orphans, or to poor persons who had no livelihood from elsewhere; and the fourth, finally, to the repair of the church. Since in this allocation they did not find a place for the monk who possessed his own lands from which he might live by working himself and through his livestock, [Col. 1507D] they refused to appropriate these things to themselves as though they were another’s right.

Behold: having despised the riches of this world, these new soldiers of Christ, poor with the poor Christ, began among themselves to consider by what contrivance, craft, or occupation they might support themselves in this life, together with guests and rich and poor persons who came to them, whom the Rule commands them to receive as Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 1507D] These *conversi*, or lay brethren, are discussed more fully in their *Usages*.]

They then determined, with the permission of their bishop, to receive bearded lay converts, and to treat them in life and death, excepting monastic profession, as themselves; and also hired labourers. For without their assistance they did not understand how they could fully observe the precepts of the Rule by day and by night. They also resolved to receive lands remote from human habitation, vineyards, meadows, forests, and waters, for making mills solely for their own use and for fishing; as well as horses and various livestock useful for human need. And when they had established agricultural granges anywhere, they decreed that the aforesaid lay brethren, not monks, should administer those houses, because the dwelling-place of monks, according to the Rule—

> [Note: [Col. 1507D] Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 66.]

—ought to be within their cloister.

Because those holy men knew also that blessed Benedict had built monasteries not in cities, castles, or villages, but in places removed from the throng of people, they promised to imitate him in the same respect. And as he organized the monasteries he had founded in groups of twelve monks, with a father abbot added, so they affirmed that they would act.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Their Sadness

The aforesaid man of God, namely the abbot and his community, was somewhat saddened because in those days scarcely anyone came there to imitate them. For the holy men were eager to entrust to successors, for the salvation of many, the treasure of virtues discovered through heaven’s gift.

> [Note: [Col. 1507D] See William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, in Book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, ch. 8, [Col. 1508D].]

But almost all who saw and heard of the unaccustomed and almost unheard-of severity of their life hastened to withdraw from them farther in heart and body rather than to draw near, and did not cease to doubt their perseverance. But the mercy of God, who inspired this spiritual warfare in them, did not cease magnificently to enlarge and bring it to perfection for the advancement of many, as what follows will show.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Death of the First Abbot and the Appointment of the Second, and on Their Ordinances

> [Note: [Col. 1508D] Observe again here that Saint Robert is not numbered among the abbots of Cîteaux.]

Alberic, the man of the Lord, having been happily trained in regular discipline for nine and a half years in the school of Christ, passed to the Lord, glorious in faith and virtues, and therefore deserved to be blessed by God in eternal life. He was succeeded by a certain brother named Stephen—

> [Note: [Col. 1508D] He was called Stephen Harding; he succeeded Saint Alberic about A.D. 1109, when he was absent, says William of Malmesbury.]

—an Englishman by birth, who had himself come there with others from Molesme and was a lover of the Rule and of the place. During his time, the brethren together with that abbot forbade the duke of that land or any other prince ever to hold his court in that church, as they had formerly been accustomed to do [Col. 1509A] on feast days.

Further, lest anything should remain in the house of God, where they desired devoutly to serve God day and night, that savoured of pride or superfluity or might at any time corrupt the poverty which they had freely chosen as the guardian of virtues, they confirmed that they would retain neither gold nor silver crosses, but only wooden ones painted with colours; no candlesticks except one of iron; no censers except of copper or iron; no chasubles except of fustian or linen, without silk, gold, or silver; no albs or amices except of linen, likewise without silk, gold, or silver. They entirely gave up silk cloaks, dalmatics, copes, and tunics. They retained silver, not gold, chalices, though gilded if possible; a silver tube, likewise gilded if possible; and stoles and maniples of silk only, without gold or silver. They expressly commanded that altar-cloths be made of linen and entirely without decoration, and that wine cruets be made without gold or silver.

In those days the same church grew in lands, vineyards, meadows, and granges, and did not decline in religious devotion. Therefore in these times the Lord visited that place, pouring out the bowels of his mercy upon those who prayed to him, cried to him, wept before him, drew long and deep sighs day and night, [Col. 1510A] and had almost approached the door of despair because they were nearly without successors. For by God’s grace he sent at one time to that church so many learned and noble clerics—men powerful and noble in the world—that thirty entered the novices’ cell together with eagerness, and, fighting bravely and well against their own vices and the promptings of evil spirits, completed their course.

Encouraged by their example, old and young people and persons of various ages in different parts of the world, seeing that what they had previously feared to be impossible in observing the Rule was possible in these men, began to flock there, to bend their proud necks beneath Christ’s sweet yoke, to love ardently the hard and harsh precepts of the Rule, and wonderfully to gladden and strengthen that church.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Abbeys Which They Built

From then on they established abbeys in different dioceses. These grew daily by so abundant and mighty a blessing of the Lord that within eight years twelve monasteries were found to have been founded among those who had specially gone forth from the Cistercian monastery and others who had sprung from them.

> [Note: [Col. 1509B] These twelve monasteries born from Cîteaux are named as follows: La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, Morimond, Preuilly, Trois-Fontaines, La Cour-Dieu, Bonnevaux, Le Bon-Rayon, Cadouin, Fontenay, and Le Mansiade or Mansus Adae.]

[ABOUT THE YEAR 1132: JOHN THE MONK.]

[Col. 1509]

# JOHN THE MONK’S LETTER TO ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, ON THE THREE MASSES TO BE CELEBRATED AT THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, AND ON THE FEASTS COMMEMORATED WITHIN ITS OCTAVE

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 712, from the Echternach manuscript)

[Col. 1509C] To ADALBERO, archbishop of Trier and legate of the Apostolic See—

> [Note: [Col. 1509C] There were two archbishops of Trier named Adalbero: one, who seized the see of Trier in 1005; the other, elevated in 1132 from the office of primicerius of Metz, a pious man and founder of the monastery of Himmerod. We judge this letter to have been written to the latter rather than to the former.]

—JOHN, eternal salvation and glory.

Because some years ago I published for certain friends a little book on the Mass office of the Lord’s Advent, I do not wish to repeat what I have said. Rather, I shall explain what follows from that point and what I have not yet treated, first, namely, the Mass office of the Sunday of the Nativity. Here the question first arises why on that day itself three Mass offices are celebrated: one Mass at cockcrow, another at earliest dawn, and a third in full daylight. For why is done then what is done nowhere else throughout the whole year: namely, that the Church generally solemnizes two Masses in a single night, something she is not accustomed to do on any other night?

There are those who explain it thus: these three Masses signify three periods—one before the Law and grace, and therefore wholly in darkness; a second under the Law, which was obscure through enigmas and finally ended in the light of grace, whence it begins in darkness, though darkness now declining, but ends with the light already dawning; and a third in the fullness of day, which is the present age of resplendent grace. Yet for this same reason and in this same order, three Masses ought likewise especially to have been celebrated at Easter, the feast of feasts, or on every feast of the Lord, or even every day. Others say other things, and each abounds in his own sense.

But we, preserving the view of all others, say that the entire office of the three Masses concerns the Nativity of the Lord itself. The fact that two Masses are performed at night signifies the two births of Jesus Christ: one eternal, from the Father; the other temporal, from the Mother. Both are incomprehensible to us, and lie hidden, as it were, beneath certain darkness from the eyes of our weakness. For if we look to his divine generation from the Father, who could fully grasp or express what it is for the Son of Man to be begotten by God the Father, as the prophet says: “Who shall declare his generation?”—so that you understand: no one.

For blessed Ambrose says that this birth exceeds the knowledge of angels and archangels, principalities and dominions, all heavenly powers, and those who dwell in houses of clay and have an earthly foundation. Rightly, therefore, the first Mass, indicating this full birth of Christ, is entirely performed in darkness, because, although it is incomprehensible even to the heavenly spirits who know all things, it is almost wholly concealed from us, enveloped in earthly darkness, except insofar as the lights of the Scriptures, shining in our midst, disclose it to our eyes. These lights, proceeding from the entire office of this Mass, shine into our hearts, so that, just as the eternal birth of the Word of God is indicated by the time of night itself, as we have said, so too it may be declared by the official testimonies of the Mass itself.

For, to examine each point briefly: the Introit, “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” does it not more clearly than light itself proclaim the manner of so great a generation from the mouth of the Son himself, born from the Father? What else does “The Lord said to me” mean except: “God the Father uttered me, the good Word, from his heart”? And what else does “You are my Son” mean but: “In the beginning was the Word”: God the Son, with God the Father, begotten from the Father himself? What does “Today I have begotten you” mean except that that ineffable generation has neither beginning nor end and is always most perfect? For “today,” which belongs to present time, declares that in that supreme generation there is nothing past or future, since all that belongs to it is always present. And “I have begotten,” which is in the perfect tense, indicates that it is always completely itself, a generation to whose utterly intact perfection nothing greater or lesser can ever accrue, remaining for ever the same.

The Gradual, “With you is the beginning on the day of your power,” etc., is the voice of the Father testifying to that same Son concerning his own generation, [Col. 1512A] that the Son is always coeternal with the Father in equal power of divinity, and has proceeded unto the perfection of eternal blessedness for all the saints, begotten from the substance of the Father before every creation of angels or the world. The Alleluia, “The Lord said,” is the one of which we spoke in the Introit. Although the Gospel recounts the generation of the Word made human, it nevertheless includes especially the divine generation in one word when it says of the blessed Virgin: “And she brought forth her firstborn Son.” Appropriately, “firstborn,” so that the discerning reader may understand that he whom the Virgin bore was already the Firstborn from the Father.

The Offertory and its verse proclaim that all must rejoice and sing because the Lord has come into the world: he is the day to be proclaimed from day to day, that is, the Son from the Father, and the salvation of God the Father. The Communion is “In splendours,” but this was explained above. Thus this Mass announces Christ’s first birth both by its very time and by all the parts of its office. Seek the second Mass and the Mass of the day in Amalarius.

Let us now turn aside to the question of the Mass office of the three following days. For there too is a question requiring explanation: why the feasts of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, then of Saint John the Evangelist, and finally of the Holy Innocents, are on their respective days placed before the Nativity of Christ the Saviour, when during the four days following the Lord’s Nativity no feasts of servants, of whatever rank, ought to take precedence over the Lord’s Nativity. For example, if within the first four days of Easter or Pentecost the feast of any saint, of whatever merit, occurs, it is omitted [Col. 1512C] or transferred to another day, and the Lord’s celebration is preferred in every respect. By the same rule, the feasts of these saints ought not to have been set before but beneath the Lord’s Nativity, unless a definite reason of mystery lay in them.

Moreover, the Assumption of Saint John at Ephesus, where he lies, is celebrated and said to have taken place on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

> [Note: [Col. 1511D] In the very ancient Echternach Calendar, written a thousand years ago, “The Reception of Saint John the Apostle at Ephesus” is entered on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. Likewise, in the ancient Martyrology of Saint Jerome, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July: “At Ephesus, Saint John, apostle and evangelist.” And in the ancient Gellone Martyrology: “The feast of the dormition of Saint John the Apostle.”]

Stephen too is the protomartyr, and there is no historical certainty that the Holy Innocents suffered on those very days. But, to resolve the proposed question, we say that a mystery lies in this ordering of the feasts. This mystery is that at Christ’s Nativity it was granted to us that Christ and the Church, reborn in Christ, should be one body and one spirit, and that the two should be one flesh. The Church, therefore, was reborn and incorporated with Christ made flesh; she celebrates together Christ’s Nativity, made for her sake, and her own Nativity in Christ—that is, the Nativity of her head and of her members.

On the first day is celebrated the Nativity of Christ, who is the Church’s head. The Church has three orders: one of martyrs, another of teachers, and a third of all faithful persons and subject peoples. But lest an undiscriminating confusion arise from the innumerable multitude, all the innumerable martyrs are honoured under the celebrated name of the one protomartyr Stephen, who first returned to the Saviour himself the cup of suffering [Col. 1513A] which Christ the Saviour had tasted for all, and whose example all the others follow. Likewise, the innumerable order of all teachers is glorified under the name of John, beloved by Christ, who, as apostle and evangelist, is the first and chief teacher of the Churches. The innumerable multitude of all subject faithful persons is likewise commemorated under the name of infants and sucklings, who by their innocence already prefigured the simple faith of the righteous.

Therefore, since the holy Church of God, as she had already borne in Adam the image of the earthly man, now also bears in Christ the image of the heavenly; and since she who in the first Adam, who was earthly and from the earth, was stained with earthly things, has now become heavenly in the second Adam, who came heavenly from heaven, she rightly celebrates at the Nativity of her head the blessed heavenly birthdays of all her members, so that the birth of the entire ecclesiastical body into eternal life may be solemnized together.

For the divine Law of Moses itself also indicates figuratively this birth of the entire ecclesiastical body. Containing all the sacraments of the Church, when it had set forth separately the rites and ceremonies of the three feasts chiefly celebrated in the year—Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—it finally delivered the observance of the Feast of Tabernacles and said among other things: “On the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm branches, boughs of trees with thick foliage, and willows from the stream; and you shall rejoice before [Col. 1513C] the Lord.”

It is clearer than light that Passover and Pentecost in the Law already foreshadowed figuratively our Passover and Pentecost in the grace of the Gospel. The Feast of Tabernacles likewise prefigured the Nativity of Christ, when he placed his tabernacle in the sun, appearing visibly to the world beneath the covering of flesh. Under the very tents of the Incarnation—that is, through faith—he introduced all of us who believe in him, and has always protected and still protects us from the snares of spiritual wickedness. Hence the Law itself warns us, saying: “Let your descendants learn that the children of Israel lived in tabernacles,” so that all believers may hold for certain that under faith in the incarnate Word, to whom we are incorporated through rebirth by water, we are protected from the face of the malignant enemy, [Col. 1514A] who goes about seeking someone to devour.

For the construction of these tabernacles, then, on the first day is taken the fruit of the most beautiful tree: that is, on the first day the Incarnation of Christ is celebrated, Christ who feeds us with his flesh and blood, which are the fruits of our life. For he is the tree of our salvation, described in the first Psalm and in the Apocalypse as planted beside streams of water. After taking the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm branches are taken for constructing the tabernacles: that is, after the celebration of the Saviour’s birth, the crowns of victorious martyrs are celebrated for the completion of the Church’s orders; this is indicated in the commemoration of their protomartyr. Then are taken the branches of trees with thick foliage: that is, the teachers who proceed from Christ himself, the tree [Col. 1514B] of life, with the manifold teaching of truth, like branches with dense leaves; this is represented in the feast of blessed John, the supreme teacher. The willows from the stream follow. Though fruitless, they nevertheless put forth leaves and are green; they are the common little people, who, although placed in the world and scarcely bearing any fruit of righteousness, nevertheless live and are saved by faith. They are signified in the celebration of the Innocents, who had not yet learned either to speak or to cooperate.

With these matters completed, let us briefly touch at the end of this writing upon the rationale of the Sunday falling within the days of the Lord’s Nativity, lest we omit anything concerning the Mass office of this feast. This Mass occurs and is celebrated on an uncertain day, and signifies the faith of the Synagogue, which at the end—though it is uncertain when—will believe in Christ. Thus the future receiving of the Synagogue, together with the rest of the body of the Church, is already celebrated at Christ’s Nativity.

The Introit, “While all things were in quiet silence,” is the voice of the Synagogue itself, testifying that it was blinded by unbelief when Christ was born. The Gradual, “Fairer in beauty,” and “My heart has overflowed,” are the voice of the Father, as though testifying to the Jews themselves that Christ is God and his Son, which they do not now believe. The Gospel and the Communion, taken from the Gospel, while they recount that the child Jesus was brought back from Egypt, indicate that the faith of Christ will at the end of the world return from the Gentiles to the Jews, when their unbelief has been extinguished.

# IN THE YEARS OF THE LORD 1137 AND 1134: DROGO, CARDINAL AND BISHOP OF OSTIA

[Col. 1513]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, II, 65)

Drogo, formerly a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Saint-Nicaise near Rheims, prior and abbot of Laon, bishop of Ostia and cardinal from 1130 to 1138, wrote a book, or sermon, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion*, found in both editions of the *Orthodoxographi* and in the *Libraries of the Fathers*; in the latest Lyons edition, however, it appears in volume XXI [Col. 1515]. Attached to it, on p. 341, is the book *On the Creation and Redemption of the First Man*, first published in 1622 from a manuscript codex of the library of Elne; also, on p. 344, *On the Sevenfold Grace of the Holy Spirit and the Beatitudes*, and on p. 345, *On the Divine Offices, or Canonical Hours*.

[Col. 1515]

# SERMON OF CARDINAL DROGO ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE LORD’S PASSION

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, XXI, 329.)

[Col. 1515A] “Do not fear, daughter Zion; behold, your king comes to you, gentle, and sitting upon a colt, the offspring of a yoked beast” (Matt. 21; Zech. 9). Come, Lord Jesus, come, desire of all nations, for my soul has grown drowsy from weariness at your delay, and my eyes have languished for want of your light. Rise, beloved sun, so that man may go forth to his work and to his labour until evening, and may work not for food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternity. Do not fear, daughter Zion. Fear belongs to the small; therefore you are still a daughter, because you fear. You are not yet Jerusalem, but daughter Zion—that is, “watchtower.” Learn, then, to keep watch; do not fear, because fear disturbs the eye. A cheerful pupil looks out clearly. Faith is the pupil of your eye. Just as the pupil of the eye is exceedingly delicate, and, unless it is diligently and carefully protected by the eyelids, is impaired by the touch of the slightest and finest dust, so the sharp sight of faith, unless it always keeps [Col. 1515B] watchful guard, is disturbed by nothing more quickly.

But do not fear, daughter Zion; behold, your king comes to you. The sun rises for you, to guard, enlighten, and lead you where there is no dust. He comes to you gentle: as he himself is, so he wishes you to be; become gentle in bearing his yoke. Let him sit upon you, his she-ass, and upon the colt, offspring of the yoked beast. And what is this she-ass? It is that which is called flesh and woman, and *virago*, “woman from man,” because she was taken from man. And who is her colt? The male, man. And how is he her colt? “For that which is spiritual is not first, but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15). The gentle king sits first upon the she-ass, afterward upon the colt: first the flesh is tamed [Col. 1515C] so that it may be fit for the yoke; then the colt is born, nourished, and strengthened, so that it may be able to bear its rider. And why is he the offspring of a yoked beast? Because woman is subject to man, and man is the head of woman (1 Cor. 11); yet he is the offspring of a yoked beast because man is through woman, while she herself shall bear in pain. Let the gentle king sit upon both, making peace, so that they may not oppose one another.

He comes to you gentle, and do you not go to him? “Go out from” the land (Gen. 12) of your flesh, and from the kindred of your mother, and from the house (ibid.), that is, the memory of your father. Your father is an Amorite, and your mother a Canaanite (Ezek. 16). Forget this father, and then the king will desire your beauty. Great is beauty [Col. 1516A] if you hear and see and incline your ear. You hear by obedience; you see by understanding; you incline your ear by humility. This is beauty; this is the whole glory which is within, in golden fringes (Ps. 44). The gentle king desires this beauty of yours.

Go out, therefore, from the city, because “he saw,” he says, “iniquity and contradiction in the city” (Ps. 54). Go out with the Hebrew children, who simply pass forth to meet the Lord. Spread olive branches in the way (Matt. 21), and offer works of mercy for his feet. Take palm branches, that you may triumph over the princes of darkness. Let nothing remain in you which does not come forth to meet Jesus, for not even a hoof was to be left in Egypt to Pharaoh. Let hands and heart, and tongues, sing together: “Hosanna in the highest.”

“You have indeed seen, Lord God, the affliction of your people who are in Egypt,” and you inclined your heavens and came down to free us. Lord, a little rest has been granted me from the most harsh works of darkness, by which the importunate taskmaster [Col. 1516B] Pharaoh sorely afflicted my mind; and the preparation of your Sabbath has now gladdened my soul. Yet I have not reached the cave, where I may more fully discern the pustules and moles which stain my face and are greatly displeasing in your eyes. For though I wash myself with nitre and multiply for myself the herb *borith* (Jer. 2), I am stained by my iniquity.

And now, Lord, the days of your Passion ought to press upon us more strongly than Pharaoh’s overseers; for in your works are righteousness and peace and joy in the [Col. 1516C] Holy Spirit. But we sleep while you, Lord, pray for us, because our eyes “were heavy at that time” (Matt. 26). Awaken us, that we may watch and pray, lest we fall into temptation, for tribulation is near us. How quickly the eye closes lest it see you; our foot slips into this great and spacious sea, with ships, where are creeping things without number. They mock the attentive soul by the phantasms of its dreams and draw it into the heart of the sea, whence return to the heights is not easy unless you send forth your hand from on high and deliver us from many waters. Awaken us, Lord, that we may watch and pray with you even one hour.

[Col. 1517A] But who is there that watches with you for one hour? For you have been withdrawn from us as far as a stone’s throw, and you agonize at length, so that a drop of your blood runs down to the earth (Luke 22). You are far withdrawn from us, because the stone was cut from the mountain without hands, and the stone was cast and struck Goliath upon the forehead and the statue upon its feet. This is your casting far from us, because as our forerunner you entered for us even into the inner places behind the veil, where you always intercede with the Father. But would that the drop of blood which sweats from your agony might run down even to the earth; that the earth might open its mouth, drink it, and cry to you—and with you to the Father—better than Abel’s blood! (Gen. 4).

But who, Lord, watches with you one hour? Even in heaven there was silence only for about [Col. 1517B] half an hour (Rev. 8); how much less shall we watch with you for one hour on earth? (Matt. 26). How often you return to us and find us sleeping (ibid.), and yet kindly awaken us; and again you go away a second and a third time, saying the same words? (ibid.). But as soon as you depart, sleep takes us again, and we cannot watch except while you are with us and awaken us. You come in the second and third watch (Luke 12), but blessed is that servant whom you then find watching (ibid.). No mention is now made of the first and fourth watches, because neither earliest age receives the faculty of watchfulness, nor latest age the hope of long sleep.

And what is this, Lord, that on returning the third time you grant abundance of sleep? “Sleep now,” you say, “and rest” (Matt. 26). Do you grant one sleep in which there is rest, [Col. 1517C] and forbid another in which the eyes are heavy? So it is. For one who watches in you sleeps sweetly, is still, and rests in his sleep; but one who sleeps away from you, like a drunkard by night (Jer. 23), is grievously tossed about without knowing why.

“My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26), you say. The soul is sorrowful when it awaits the tribulation of death; for who knows whether it goes to the left or to the right? Who knows how to answer one who rebukes him, when the Judge speaks like a woman in labour? (Isa. 42). Therefore let the sorrowful soul become like the pelican of the wilderness: let it hate the city and their assemblies of blood; let it grow pale in the leanness of solitude; and, like the night-raven among the ruins of Scripture, let it seek its food through the whole night, and fly forth as a sparrow over the [Col. 1517D] roof, watching and wary of when the thief may come.

Or do you not see Judas, how he does not sleep? How wakeful are the eyes of avarice! How it ranges over the whole world! His hand does not cease, his foot does not cease, and he heaps up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. Yet Simon sleeps, James sleeps, and John. Why? Because they do not consider what is soon to happen; the magnitude of danger drives away sleep. Did Peter sleep in the courtyard? Did those sleep who fled after leaving him? Did the young man sleep when they seized him and he, casting off the linen cloth, fled naked? (Mark 14). Yet it was cold, because Peter stood and warmed himself (John 18): the magnitude of danger makes one forget both cold and hunger.

Awake at last, awake, wretched [Col. 1518A] soul—if not through love, at least through fear. Consider at least the torment which you are soon to suffer in death. Surely no cross is harsher than death. Death itself, I say, is the harshest cross prepared for you, toward which you hurry daily without heed. See how death crucifies you: the body stiffens, the legs stretch out, the hands and arms fall, the breast gasps, the neck fails, the lips foam, the eyes grow fixed, the face sweats, the countenance becomes dreadful, and grows pale like a potsherd. This cross awaits you. I do not know whether death is sweeter on a soft bed or upon a hard cross, except that the cross cuts short pain more quickly. What we see and feel is light compared with what the soul already tastes within. For sensation quickly departs from the body, but death always accompanies the soul that is its own.

“When the living creatures moved, the wheels beside them moved likewise” (Ezek. 1). If our life advanced, the whole of Holy Scripture would walk with us; but because, walking on foot through marshes and rocks, we stumble, [Col. 1518B] the wheels scarcely follow us. The Passion of the Lord is celebrated, and we devote ourselves to pleasure! From the cross he cries to us: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is a sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1); and there is no one to hear, no one to console, no one to answer.

“I thirst,” he says (John 19). Lord, for what do you thirst? Is thirst, then, a greater torment than the cross? You are silent about the cross and cry out about thirst? “I thirst”—for what? For your faith, your salvation, your joy; the suffering of your souls concerns me more than the torments of my body. “O all you who pass by the way, attend [Col. 1518C] and see whether there is a sorrow like my sorrow.” Attend to my sorrow, so that in my sorrow you may see your own sorrow; my sorrow is the image of your sorrow. What you observe in my body, observe also whether a like sorrow is not in your heart. Pass from yourselves to me; pass from me into yourselves; and see whether there is in you sorrow like my sorrow. “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves, daughters of Jerusalem” (Luke 23). For that sorrow which you pass by and do not heed is more to be wept for than my sorrow; for I was struck because of your crime.

These things, gracious Jesus, you cry to us from your cross; and, if not by words, nevertheless by the deed itself. What shall I answer you? What shall I say, or what shall I repay? Thus you have made your body a mirror of my soul. I did not know [Col. 1518D] the insults and terrors, and Satan striking me unceasingly with blows, unless I saw the art of your healing, curing like by like, and weighed in the balance (Job 6) on this side your calamity and on that my iniquity. You gave your body to those who struck you, and your cheeks to those who plucked them; you did not turn away your face from those spitting upon you (Isa. 50), so that your blows might remove my blows, your scourges expiate my scourges, and the reproaches of those who reproached you might remove from me everlasting reproach. These are the spotless wrappings of your flesh, with which you bound my wounds, merciful Samaritan, that you might set me upon your beast and lead me to the inn; for truly you bore our infirmities [Col. 1519A] and carried our sorrows, and by whose stripe we have been healed (Isa. 53).

Thus Christ is struck with blows, his face veiled, in the house of the high priest, because the Christian is struck with blows in the house of conscience, when his mind is blinded. What Christ suffered publicly, I suffer secretly; what he suffered outside at the hands of Caiaphas’s servants, I suffer within through Satan’s dealings. For “sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128): they have veiled my face, fixed my face upon the ground, made my back their anvil, and sinners have built upon my back. But I am still contained within the house where the girl dies and is raised; for there too Peter denied, saying, “O man, I am not” (Matt. 9). I regard man, not God; I fear man, not God, whose truth I deny.

Does Peter not seem to you [Col. 1519B] to have had his face veiled in these words? Hence he was struck with blows a third time, because he denied a third time. And Paul asked the Lord three times to remove from him the angel of Satan who struck him with blows (2 Cor. 12). Therefore both apostles were struck with blows; both suffered shipwreck—Peter within, Paul without. Satan would indeed, if he had been permitted, have sifted Peter by striking him with blows as wheat (Luke 22), until he had shaken out from him every particle of faith. “But I,” he says, “Peter, have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Matt. 26); therefore Christ looked upon him, and he went out and wept bitterly. Peter had his face veiled until Christ looked upon him. But did he not look upon him even earlier? He did; but Peter did not look back at Christ who looked upon him, because he had his face veiled. Hence another Evangelist rightly says, “And Peter remembered” (ibid.); Christ’s looking upon Peter was Peter’s remembrance. Therefore, when you remember your sins with weeping, you are seen by Christ; indeed, when the veil has been removed, you see Christ.

“And he went out” (ibid.). He denied because he did not wish to remain within; yet when he denied, he went out. Out from where? From Christ’s house, from the house of the faithful. But when he went outside the house of Caiaphas, he was brought into Christ’s house. How many today say, “We are of Christ’s house, we are of the house of the Church,” and yet belong to the house of Caiaphas—that is, hypocrisy? What Peter did by denying, these do by affirming; but unless, through confession, they go out [Col. 1519D] and weep bitterly, they do not enter Christ’s Church. The bitterness of tears washes the veil from the eyes.

Christ, then, was struck with blows in Caiaphas’s house because Peter was struck with blows in Caiaphas’s house; and what Peter suffered from Satan within, Christ endured outwardly from Satan’s servants. “Attend and see whether there is a sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1). Consider which suffered the heavier reproaches: Christ outwardly in his body, or Peter inwardly in his heart?

But now let us go to Pilate. “When morning came” (Matt. 27), he is brought bound to Pilate. So long as guilt lies hidden, it is night; but when it begins to become known, morning comes. Then he is bound by the chief priests and delivered to Pilate—that is, to the prince of darkness—as the Apostle commands such a person to be delivered to Satan for the destruction [Col. 1520A] of the flesh (1 Cor. 5). The young man is carried from the house to the gate of the city (Luke 7), where Pilate sits upon the tribunal; for judgment was customarily held at the city gate.

Pilate, having seized him, scourged him. Often, while guilt is uncovered, it becomes unrestrained through the sinner’s shamelessness; the scourges increase, the wounds multiply, for “many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. 31). With these scourges the Pharaoh of this world struck the children of Israel (Exod. 5). After this he is handed over to soldiers to be mocked (Matt. 20): this is spiritual wickedness. See the order of misery: from the chief priests he is delivered to the prince of darkness; the latter, having enslaved him by his scourges, exposed him to his soldiers for more profound mockery, and then finally for crucifixion. For after the cross no punishment remains, because sin is ended by death; [Col. 1520B] but when death has now been avoided, the sinner is tormented by a greater mockery of demons.

For, stripping him of the garment of all Christian beauty, they place around him, as though in royal splendour, a scarlet cloak—that is, a garment mixed with blood—when, because of cruel bloodshed, he is both honoured and surrounded by many. Hence, “plaiting a crown of thorns” (Matt. 27), they put it upon his head: while heaping upon him thorny riches from plundering the poor, they raise his head to the kingdom of pride. For money claims for itself what Wisdom was accustomed to say: “By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just” (Prov. 8). Where money is, there is the king, there is a multitude of dependants. Hence they put a reed in his right hand [Col. 1520C] (Matt. 27). For the power and kingdom of the wicked is a reed shaken by the wind; Christ’s kingdom, however, is an iron rod. And fittingly the reed is placed in his right hand, because “their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. 43).

What follows is clearer than light: bending the knee, such persons mock him rather than serve him. “Hail, King of the Jews,” and “spitting upon him” (Mark 15), they praise him with superfluous praises—“for the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” (Ps. 10). “They took the reed and struck his head with it” (Mark 15). From such rulers their soldiers receive the power to harm and devour the poor; yet all of this will return upon the head of him by whose authority they defend themselves. This is the third death, when one sits stinking in the chair of pestilence (Ps. 1). By these deaths the unhappy soul is afflicted before the final death of the cross; and, what is more wretched, it delights in such reproaches as though they were great honours, and is daily led thus to the cross, itself bearing the punishment of its condemnation.

But what is meant by this: after the mockery, the cloak is removed and he is clothed again in his own garments? It is that often proud Adam, when through the pain of the flesh he enters the borders of death, lays aside his pride and returns to consideration of his own decay. There he either finds, by divine mercy, the fruit of repentance, or after the dreadful judgment is broken down by a twofold crushing. Thus Herod, resplendent in royal apparel, when the people acclaimed him more than was fitting, was immediately struck by an angel; stripped of the cloak, he put on his own garment and, consumed by worms, [Col. 1521A] expired. Was he not rightly mocked? “Hail, King of the Jews” (Mark 15). Why are you proud, earth and ashes? (Ecclus. 10). Why do you glory in shining clothing? “The moth shall be spread beneath you, and the worm is your covering” (1 Macc. 9). This is your garment; those who wrapped you in a scarlet cloak mocked you.

Thus Antiochus and Herod, enemy of the Lord’s birth, after laying aside borrowed garments, expired amid their own worms. Return at last, sometime, to your heart; return, old Adam. See where and how the new Adam sought and found you. I shall show you in his body the disgraces of your soul. Was it not enough that, through blows and novel kinds of mockery, he ran after you as you fled, crying out and pitying you, and that he followed, found, and seized you even as you were breathing out your soul at the final punishment of the cross? For who was that thief but Adam? From the time when he first committed the murder of his own self in paradise, he remained guilty before Christ and hid himself, until, finally consumed and seized at the point of the cross, he could flee and hide no longer.

[Col. 1521B] There at last, when seized, he turned to you, good Jesus; he confessed his guilt; he willingly embraced punishment. For you warned him not to shrink from suffering what he saw you also suffering with him. Thus he alone, the one man out of the whole world, clung to you; and therefore he alone out of the whole world entered paradise with you, where he was established so firmly, no longer as a guardian of paradise but as a citizen and member of God’s household, that he can no longer fall from it. O most blessed thief—indeed, no thief, but martyr and confessor! [Col. 1521C] For he turned necessity into willingness, changed punishment into glory, and the cross into triumph. In you, most blessed confessor and martyr, Christ gathers up the remnant of faith from the barrenness of the whole world. While the disciples fled and Peter denied, you rejoiced to become his companion and fellow-sufferer in the Passion. You were Peter upon the cross; and Peter in Caiaphas’s house was the thief. Peter was this thief so long as, hiding within, he denied Christ without; and thus you preceded Peter into paradise, because he who embraced you upon the cross, your leader and guide, introduced you with himself as his faithful and glorious soldier on the very day on which he himself entered.

“I am needy and poor” (Ps. 69), Lord, and lame from my mother’s womb (Acts 14); and behold, I sit [Col. 1521D] at the gate of your temple called Beautiful (Acts 3), neither able nor willing to enter. Rather, begging outside in need of your good things for the sustenance of my flesh, I seek the airy and false images of men, in which I may heap up for myself the talent of iniquity, burdensome bundles. And behold, it is the ninth hour of prayer (ibid.); Peter and John, your apostles, go up to your holy temple to pray (ibid.), while I cling to earth and mud, thinking earthly and vain thoughts. As others enter, I remain outside, not seeking with them the things that are your Father’s, but those of my first father, which daily put me outside and which have wickedly desired me.

Behold, it is now the ninth hour of prayer; the day has declined, night is near. When I rise early in the morning, I shall find nothing in my hands of those things for which I now beg. It is, I say, the ninth hour of prayer. At this hour you prayed while hanging on the cross; you prayed, bowing your head, crying with a loud voice (John 19), and expired. You prayed, bowing your head in the spirit of humility and crying with a loud voice—with the highest and most secret affection of fatherly love and love for us. In that powerful cry, Lord, you expired; and you still retain with you the same disposition of compassion which you then had for us, because your love does not know how to grow cold.

It was the ninth hour of prayer. And why was the ninth hour an hour of prayer? Because about the ninth hour darkness came—[darkness came until the ninth hour]. The horror of darkness which covered the whole earth had to be driven away; the darkness of the peoples had to be repelled, a darkness which had begun to abound from the time when you began to walk in the breeze after noon, from the time when you did not cease crying, “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. 3), following at the back of one fleeing and hiding himself, so far as was possible for him who was expelled from the paradise of delight and came even to the punishment deserved by his iniquity.

[Col. 1522B] “We receive the due reward of our deeds; but what has this man done?” (Luke 23). O Adam, how late you burst forth into these words! Only now have I found you. “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (ibid.). Therefore it is the ninth hour of prayer. At the ninth hour he prayed; at the tenth he entered paradise. Therefore the lame man did not enter the temple, because he had not yet reached the tenth generation; but Peter said to him: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts [Col. 1522C] 3).

Truly you are the mountains to which I lifted up my eyes, from whom help shall come to me; but “my help is from the Lord” (Ps. 120), because you said, “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” At Christ’s word you let down the net, and at Christ’s word you raise the lame man. At Christ’s word his feet and soles are made firm. What are his feet? Faith and fear. And what his soles? Hope and love. Therefore Peter and John appropriately ascended together, one bearing the emblem of faith, the other that of love. They ascended to your temple, Lord, to pray together with you, so that they too might enter together with you into the paradise of your sanctuary. For at your death the veil which was over Moses’ face was torn (Exod. 4). But they would not enter alone, because neither did you, Lord, enter paradise alone. You bring in the thief; they bring in the lame man. Yet the thief is no longer in paradise a thief, nor the lame man in the temple lame: for how is he lame who stands and walks, leaps, and praises the Lord? Or how is he a thief if he is with Christ in paradise? “For evil shall not dwell beside you” (Ps. 5).

The thief had been a thief when he hid before confession; but after prayer he was righteous. For what did he pray? “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23). O great faith, O great love! He prays for future things, not present ones; he does not wish to be taken down from the cross, but to be placed in Christ’s kingdom. For what else does he say but, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1)? I do not know what Paul desired more than this thief did. “Remember me!” O contrite and humbled heart! What less or more humble request could he have made than that Christ should remember him? “Remember me”—me, I say, so unworthy, so sinful. I know my iniquity, and my sin is before me; I am ashamed to raise my eyes to you. Against you alone have I sinned; you alone can cleanse me from my sin. I did evil against you when I wished to hide myself from you. I am a thief of my own soul; indeed, I committed murder. I wished to conceal it, but I did evil before you. Remember me; have mercy on me. I have deservedly come into this misery, since I deserted your blessedness. I was rich, and behold how poor I have become! I could eat and delight in every tree of paradise, and behold, I am tormented and die on this tree. Remember me: I had forgotten you, but when you are angry, you will remember mercy.

“Have mercy on me according to [Col. 1523B] your great mercy” (Ps. 50). I see in you mercy both great and your own—that is, mercy fitting for you, which caused you to descend to misery like mine for my sake. “We receive the due reward of our deeds” (Luke 23); but what have you done? I see you like me in punishment, whom I see so unlike me in deed! You could not follow me farther. Whence did you come? You came forth from the highest heaven (Ps. 18) and from the Virgin’s womb, beautiful in form; and you hang with me upon the tree! Who brought you here? Mercy alone. According to this great mercy of yours, have mercy on me, God. You are God, not merely man; you are God, and I am man—your creature, whom you made in your image and likeness. God, have mercy upon your image.

But in what shall I recognize that you have mercy? In this: I see in you an image like my own, suffering the same misery with me. What remains, then, but that I should hope in so great mercy? Who, I say, could despair? Therefore, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” You go to your kingdom; you have completed your business. You came for this purpose, that you might lead me back with you. I desire to go with you, and I neither tremble at nor am ashamed of suffering this most bitter death.
