For how could I tremble where I saw you with me? “Even though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for you are with me.” Or how could I be ashamed of what I saw you, Lord of heaven, bearing? “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him I shall be ashamed when I come in [Col. 1523D] my majesty, and that of my Father and the holy angels.” “Whoever does not carry his cross” (Luke 14) “and follow me is not my disciple.” This is your saying: whoever is ashamed of this saying, him you will be ashamed of. For whoever is ashamed of your cross is ashamed of your glory. But as for me, may it be far from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The cross is your glory; the cross is your dominion. Behold, your dominion is upon your shoulder: you bear those who bear you. Whoever bears your cross bears your glory; whoever bears your glory bears you; but those bearing you, you bear upon your shoulder, because “your dominion is upon your shoulder” (Isa. 9). Therefore those who bear you are your dominion—for you reign in them. O greatest emperor, I know how—or whither—you bear your dominion upon [Col. 1524A] your shoulder. Your shoulder is high; your shoulder is strong; your shoulder reaches to the Father’s seat, above every principality and power and virtue. There you carry the hundredth sheep; there you lead Joseph’s sheep (Ps. 79). Joseph’s sheep is led to the Father’s right hand. Now Joseph’s sheep is exceedingly secure: Christ bears you upon his shoulder. His shoulder is strong; do not fear. It is high; do not look to the depths, because “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

“A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their return into the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). So long as I am a son of the old Adam, I bear a heavy yoke. If I were a son of the new Adam, I would bear a light yoke. What is the heavy yoke? A talent of lead. And what is the light burden? Christ’s cross. The former, as it is written, is drowned in mighty waters (Exod. 15); the latter swims upon the waters. A wondrous thing! Nothing is more frightening to man than to suffer the cross. But why do people fear the cross? Because they are thieves. If they were not thieves, they would not fear the cross; therefore whoever fears is a thief.

“How,” you ask, “is he a thief?” Hear Christ: “But you,” he says, “have made it”—that is, my house—“a den of thieves” (Matt. 21). “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are.” Thus people make themselves a den of thieves: they murder people and drag them into their den. What murder is greater than a man’s killing himself? Or what murder is graver: to kill the body [Col. 1524C] or the spirit? O how often a man kills his own spirit! How many murders does he commit within himself! Whenever he voluntarily and deliberately commits sin, what does he do but cut his own throat? “For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). The sword of the soul is sin; the death of the soul is sin. Whoever takes this sword in the hand of his own deliberation—that is, finds it acceptable and pleasing—first lays hands upon himself, first kills himself. “Let their sword enter into their own hearts” (Ps. 36).

Nor is it enough to kill once and rest; a thousand times and a thousand times they cruelly turn their hands against themselves. “Their feet are swift to shed their own blood,” men of blood and deceit. How deceitful? Because they heap the corpses of the dead [Col. 1524D] into their den and cover them with a mound of earth, lest either they themselves see them or others see them. They do not wish to see them, lest the stench of the corpse bring horror or shame upon their faces; they do not wish to be seen, lest, perhaps detected as thieving murderers, they be dragged away to dreadful punishments.

But in all punishments what is as dreadful as the cross? Therefore thieves fear the cross, because the cross is the avenger of crimes, the punishment of the wicked; with an even balance the cross judges and repays—on one side the guilty, on the other the innocent. Therefore the cross is terrifying to the wicked, but to the devout it is more gracious than all the trees of paradise. Did Christ fear the cross? Did Peter? Did Andrew? Indeed, he desired it: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 8). “With desire,” he says, “I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22).

[Col. 1525A] He ate the Passover with the disciples, and he ate the Passover when he suffered, when he passed from this world to the Father. “I have food to eat which you do not know; my food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4), and the Father’s will is that I drink the cup. Therefore upon the cross he ate and drank, became drunk, and slept. Cursed Ham laughed at his shame; and the sons, turning their backs, covered with a cloak the mystery of that deepest sleep. “For the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam; and he took one of his ribs, built it into a woman, and brought her to Adam” (Gen. 2). It is evident that Christ slept and was put to sleep; from his side the Church is daily built, fed, [Col. 1525B] nourished, and brought from the ends of the earth, that the Queen may stand at the right hand in golden apparel, surrounded by variety.

Therefore he ate the Passover upon the cross, because he ascended the palm tree and gathered its fruits. “When I am lifted up,” he says, “I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). What are “all things”? Heaven, earth, and hell. He drew the Father to himself, because his cry entered into the Father’s presence, into his ears; and the earth shook, the rocks were split, and the tombs opened because they heard the voice of the Son of God. Thus the Mediator of God and men, placed between heaven and earth, ate the Passover and gathered the fruits of the tree from every direction, drawing them into his body; for all things flowed to the tree of life, which was in the midst of paradise, because the sword which had barred the way was quenched.

[Col. 1525C] Who, then, should fear the cross any longer? For upon the cross hangs every fruit of life, because it is itself the tree of life in the midst of paradise. It is height, breadth, loftiness, and depth. It gathers and rewards the good; it destroys and condemns the evil. It is consolation for the sorrowful, refreshment for the hungry, glorying for the perfect. I may travel through heaven, earth, sea, and dry land, Lord, and nowhere shall I find you except upon the cross alone. There you sleep; there you feed; there you lie at noon (Song 2).

For your cross is faith, whose breadth is love, length long-suffering, height hope, and depth fear. Whoever finds you finds you upon this cross. Upon this cross the soul is suspended from the earth and plucks sweet fruits from the tree of life. Upon this cross, cleaving to its Lord, it sweetly sings: “You are my protector, my glory, and the lifter up of my head” (Ps. 3).

No one, therefore, seeks you, no one finds you, unless he is crucified. O glorious cross, take root in me, that I may ascend into you! But where did they crucify him? (John XIX.) At the place of Calvary. Blessed indeed is the place where the cross is fixed. Good is the baldness that is clothed with such foliage. To this baldness Elisha was ascending: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II). See whether our Elisha too is not bald: “The Son of Man,” he says, “has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke IX). See how bald he is who has nowhere to lay his head! He is bald because his kingdom is not of this world; our Elisha is bald because, when he was abandoned, all his disciples fled [Col. 1526A] (Matthew XXVI). For what are the disciples but the hairs of the head, all of which are numbered? (Matthew X.) Therefore, at the place of Calvary the standard of the cross is raised. “Because the daughters of Zion walked with outstretched neck and with beckoning eyes, the Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion” (Isaiah III). “May the Lord make bald the crown, the hair, of those who go about in their offences” (Psalm LXVII). He will make bald, he says, the crown of the daughters of Zion, and will make there a place of Calvary, so that the glorious cross of Christ may be fixed there where pride had made its seat for itself. “Enlarge your baldness like an eagle” (Micah I). The eagle, made bald, enjoys the clear sun; so the more the baldness of the soul is enlarged, the more purely the true light pours itself into it. But those who nourish their hair acquire for themselves condemnation of blindness and heaviness.

For this reason [Col. 1526B] Absalom lost the blessed vision of this light: his long hair weighed him down; it was cut only once a year, and he weighed his hair at two hundred shekels by the public weight (II Kings XIV). Thus, suspended by that very hair from a tree, he perished. Absalom, “the father’s peace,” is himself Judas, and everyone who, while at peace, is bitter bitterness to Christ (Isaiah XXXVIII). “Hail, Rabbi” (Matthew XXVI): by voice and kiss he brought peace to the Father; “with their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed” (Psalm LXI). “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm XL). He is one, and they are many. Behold Absalom; behold Judas; behold the body of Satan. But how did he nourish his hair? “He was a thief, and had the money-box” (John XII). This long hair weighed him down, and he was shorn once [Col. 1526C] in the year, when once he brought back the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the temple. He weighed them at two hundred shekels—the number of the unclean—and this by the public weight, not by the weight of the sanctuary; for, being led to repentance, he weighed his sin very heavily. “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matthew XXVII). Every word is full of weights, but by the public weight, not the sanctuary weight: because he was more ashamed of disgrace than of conscience, and weighed his own wickedness more heavily than God’s mercy.

Hear the sanctuary weight: “I have sinned; I have done evil before you; blot out my iniquity” (Psalm L). On the one hand, “I acknowledge my iniquity” (ibid.); on the other, I consider your great mercy: “Have mercy on me, O God” (ibid.). Hear also the public weight: “My iniquity,” Cain says, “is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Genesis IV). Therefore he brought back the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the temple (Matthew XXVII). See how greatly he valued them: he did not throw them onto a dung-heap, but into the temple. Surely he had always devoted his temple to such gods: “For covetousness is the service of idols” (Galatians V), and covetousness blinds the eyes of the wise (Deuteronomy I). See how the wretch was blinded! He preferred to destroy himself rather than let the coins perish. He consigned the coins to the temple and himself to the noose; he loved his heirs, who would gather those same coins from there, and who even now keep them in their Corban. He threw them into the temple, and, departing, hanged himself. Indeed, he had long since withdrawn from Christ and hanged himself in the noose of avarice; but what [Col. 1527A] he had done in secret became publicly known to everyone (Matthew X).

The character of the outward punishment disclosed the measure of the torment; for by the things through which a man has sinned, by these he shall be punished (Wisdom XI). “Hanging, he burst open in the middle” (Acts I): his belly was full, and it burst. The vessel burst in the middle, where Satan had his seat; thus the vessel of dishonour burst, because it was not among the potter’s vessels that are tested in the furnace (Ecclesiasticus XXVII). For this reason, he had no share in the potter’s field, in the burial-place of strangers (Matthew XXVII); rather, like a potsherd cracking over emptiness, he is broken apart, and all his entrails were spilled out (Acts I). Money is the entrails of the avaricious; these are scattered and lost, but men of mercy are gathered together. Judas and Absalom still hang by the hair of their heads, and the mule on which he sat passed on (II Kings XVIII). Do not [Col. 1527B] become like horse and mule, because the world passes away, and its desire. The hair of Absalom, by which he hangs, is avarice, “the root of all evils” (I Timothy VI); wherever this has taken root, an abundance of every evil’s hair will grow.

The mule, however, mixed from horse and ass, is the double-minded person who displays outwardly what he does not keep within. Such was Judas, such Absalom: outward piety, inward malice; double iniquity. The horse openly swells with pride; the ass walks simply; the mule is wicked and deceitful, and throws down the unwary.

Open to us, Lord, open to us the door of your side which is in your ark, that you may bring us in with the clean animals, seven and seven. You are the true Noah, whom God your Father alone found righteous [Col. 1527C] before himself (Genesis VI). “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew IV). You know your sheep, and they know you, because they are clean animals, seven and seven, who by sevenfold grace and works of light, having now attained Sabbath from Sabbath, are worthy to be inscribed among the eighth; and this number alone was saved in the ark.

Bring us also to yourself through the door of your side, which is the faith of the Church, and shut the door from outside (Genesis VII), until iniquity passes away. And when the flood has ceased, open the door again to us—not now the door of faith, but of hope—the door opposite the door shown to the prophet Ezekiel in the building of the mountain (Ezekiel XL). Yet in the meantime you have also a window in the ark, through which the Beloved puts forth his hand (Song V) and arouses his dove: [Col. 1527D] “Arise,” he says, “my friend, my fair one, and come” (ibid.). And when she flies out after you to seize you, you escape and ascend above the cherubim, and fly upon the wings of the winds (Psalm XVII), so that the foot of your dove finds nothing firm in you on which to rest, unless she returns again to your ark, and you, taking her in your hand, place her again in her little dwelling (Genesis VIII).

For it is safer meanwhile to wait and rest in the harbour of faith than, in pursuing you too far and fruitlessly, to fall into and drown in the impassable waters of the flood. For the waters flowing from the right side of the temple (Ezekiel XLVII), measured for a thousand paces, come up to the ankles; after another thousand paces, to the knees; again after another thousand, they rise to the loins; but after another thousand paces [Col. 1528A] the river grows and swells so greatly that it cannot be crossed (ibid.). One must instead return to the firm ground of the bank; therefore the holy living creatures went and returned (Ezekiel I). Likewise the dove, when she found nowhere for her foot to rest, returned to the ark (Genesis VIII). But the raven, once sent out, does not know how to return (ibid.), because, pursuing with no single eye, it is caught in the flood of vanity—and deservedly. For what has the dove to do with the raven? What has white to do with black? What has Judas to do with John? What has Christ to do with Belial? (II Corinthians VI.) Yet Christ sits in the middle between Judas and John; in the middle between the chosen and rejected thief; and Noah between raven and dove. But the raven, once sent out, did not return, because Judas, going out, was drowned in the air.

But why, O Lord, does [Col. 1528B] one of the soldiers open your side with a spear? (John XIX.) Who is that one soldier, unless perhaps he is the one who received your seamless garment by lot? It is indeed the unity of the faithful, which serves under you alone; its spear of preaching opened your side to all believers. For “the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Hebrews IV). This is that spear which the prophet Habakkuk calls a flashing lance (Habakkuk III). David took this spear, together with the water-jar, from the head of his sleeping enemy Saul (I Kings XXVI), because from the proud, envious, and negligent the word of wisdom together with grace is withdrawn. But Abishai, son of Zeruiah, wished to pierce the sleeping man once, so that there might be no need a second time, unless this David had graciously restrained him. For unless the merciful and long-suffering patience of God sustained the lazy and contemptuous sinner, Satan’s sword—that is, his own iniquity—would slay him eternally. For wicked Satan desires that one who sleeps should not add anything by which he may rise again (Psalm XLIX).

But merciful David repeatedly cries from the distant hilltop: “Will you not answer, Abner?” (I Kings VI [an apparent citation error for I Kings XXVI].) For you repay the sinner evil for good, most gentle David, and you admonish and wait longer for him to answer you one thing for a thousand. Yet to them your voice seems hostile because you disturb their restless sleep. “Who are you,” he says, “who cries out and disturbs the king?” (I Kings XXVI.) “At your rebuke, O Lord, those who mounted horses have slumbered” (Psalm LXXV), and their charioteer [Col. 1528D] does not wish them to awaken until he casts them into the deep. For the king of the wicked is pride: “he sleeps in the shade, in the secret place of the reed, in moist places, and the shadows protect his shadow” (Job XL). He is Abner, who protects Saul. “Why,” he says, “do you disturb the king?” Yet even the proud heart is sometimes pierced at David’s voice, though not unto correction. Proud Saul is bent by David’s most humble words, when David says: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and one flea, like a partridge in the mountains” (I Kings XXIV).

Not without reason does David compare himself either to a dead dog or to a flea: “a living dog is better than a dead lion” (Ecclesiasticus IX). Better is a dog alive to God and dead to the world than a proud and reprobate lion, dead to God and alive to the age. A flea is small [Col. 1529A] and both bites and leaps; so the humble righteous person confidently bites the vices of the carnal and leaps upon the mountains, where he has the safest refuge, so that he need not fear the adulterous partridge that pursued Elijah (III Kings XIX) and killed John the Baptist (Matthew XIV).

Give me, Lord, a portion in the land of the living, in the burial-place of strangers in the field of Aceldama (Matthew XXVII), which was bought at the great price of your blood. For there all our fathers were buried, who were strangers and pilgrims upon this earth; there Abraham buried his most beautiful wife Sarah in the double cave (Genesis XXIII). But why was it that he would neither receive the field itself freely, nor bury his dead in their chosen tombs? Because he did not believe that he could be saved freely, through himself, without the price of Christ’s blood; nor did he judge it good for himself to dwell in the foul-smelling tombs of the world. “Bury your dead,” they say, “in our chosen tombs” (ibid.). The world has chosen tombs: namely, those whom the summit of pride or the laboriousness of superstition makes conspicuous. All Egypt is full of tombs; for there was no house in which a dead person did not lie (Exodus XII). The children of Israel desired those tombs in the desert: “Were there no tombs for us in Egypt” (Exodus XIV), that our corpses should lie naked and unburied in the wilderness? The most holy patriarch would not bury his dead in such tombs. But where? In the double cave, where hope of good works and contemplative love rest; for Leah also lies buried there. Therefore Sarah and Leah were hidden together in the double cave [Col. 1529C].

The former, first barren and later already old, bore only one son of joy; the latter ceased bearing after six sons, except that at last she bore a daughter—the disgrace of the sacred lineage. A remarkable thing! This woman who had six sons is said to have ceased bearing (Genesis XXIX); the other, who had only one, is not recorded as having ceased bearing. But the active life has an end; the contemplative always bears fruit. The one gives birth in pain, the other in joy; yet both are buried in the same field. For Rachel was placed near Bethlehem beneath the stone of the cross laid over her (Genesis XXXV): plainly, she sits at Jesus’ feet, that from the house of bread she may always give birth fruitfully. Therefore Sarah and Rachel will never cease bearing. Leah, however, after six sons either ceases bearing altogether [Col. 1529D] or bears a daughter. She is carnal pleasure, which sometimes creeps in under the appearance of discernment into the active life; yet if she is truly a widow, she shall be saved—not through the begetting of a daughter, but through the bearing of sons (I Timothy II).

Thus the noble patriarchs were buried in the double cave together with their wives. For they dwelt in tents as strangers and pilgrims upon the earth; therefore both they and all their descendants possess, by inheritance, the burial-place of strangers. But why was Jacob, when old, buried there by his son Joseph with a greater splendour, sweetness, and glory than the rest? (Genesis L.) Perfect charity is represented by aged Jacob. In it the Father is buried with the Son—or rather, together with the Son—as he himself says: if [Col. 1530A] anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (John XIV). This is that glorious and sweet burial of the Father, the Ancient of Days, who buries in himself those who love him and hides them in the hiding-place of his face from the contradiction of men.

And the bones of Joseph—namely, the memorial of our Saviour—are daily carried out of Egypt by the children of Israel (Exodus XIII). For God did not leave Joseph’s bones in Egypt, he who detests foul-smelling and whitewashed tombs (Matthew XXIII). And God buried Moses; but his tomb has not been found by man to this present day (Deuteronomy XXXIV). Finally, who can ascend there where he ascended through the midst of the cloud to the highest mountain, and was there forty days and forty [Col. 1530B] nights, and saw and examined the pattern of the wondrous tabernacle which God had set up and not man? Therefore, to this day, when Moses is read (II Corinthians III), he has a veiled face, because his tomb is not found by mortal man.

In the same field of blood, the glorious line of kings also received its lot, those who were buried in the tomb of their fathers in Jerusalem. There likewise the vision of the prophets and the martial strength of the Maccabees were gloriously adorned. Let that once glorious tower of Babel, renowned among kingdoms and illustrious in pride, the tower of the Chaldeans, now be compared, if you please, to this burial-place of strangers (Isaiah XIII). What can be found like this our burial-place? There, language is divided into many tongues; here, five cities of Egypt no longer speak the Egyptian or Canaanite tongue [Col. 1530C], but one is called the city of the sun.

From that tower of Babel Jezebel was cast down: the mother of fortifications, worshipper of idols, artificer of avarice (IV Kings IX). When they wished to bury her, because she was a king’s daughter, they found only the skull, the extremities of the hands, and a wall sprinkled with blood. This indeed is the burial of the wicked; this is their worthy recompense: that nothing remains of them but the extremities of the hands, that is, scarcely the last traces of their deeds, and the skull—once the seat of pride—stripped of the glory of hair, because “I saw the wicked exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm XXXVI). This is Jezebel’s baldness, she who was clothed in meretricious adornment [Col. 1530D] and had painted her eyes with stibium, or antimony (IV Kings IX). The crown of pride has been made bald; no one now deigns to look upon it except one who wishes to abhor her wickedness, so that he may wash his hands in the sinner’s blood and, like a strong and swift horse, pierce, trample, and pass over the cast-down harlot with his hoof.

Here too a blood-stained wall was left behind, to terrify men of blood and deceit, who because of their avarice stone humble Naboth. But the utterly shameless dogs, lovers of corpses, incorporate adulterous flesh into themselves; hence they consequently lap its blood also, because they shall share alike in lust and in vengeance. There are, however, other dogs, made from enemies of the abyss, who suffer hunger for righteousness, who go about the city—not that of Babylon but of the Church—and [Col. 1531A] whatever they find there dead to vices, they consume and bury with themselves. But those whom the birds—that is, demons flying through emptiness—consume when dead outside the city: what sort were they? Such were Ahithophel, Absalom, Jezebel, and Judas, who, having received their soul in vain, also breathed it out in vain.

But let us return to the field of Aceldama, that we may admire and rather emulate the glory of the dwellings of the blessed. For “the memory of the wicked is with a noise,” but the memory of the righteous shall live for ever and ever. Such were Joseph, who was “a councillor, a good and righteous man” (Luke XXIII), and Nicodemus, once a servant of night but now of day, who, to anoint the Lord’s body, brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds (John XIX). Jesus loved such servants of his burial [Col. 1531B], who boldly wrest his body from the power of darkness and claim it as their own, so that each may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour (I Thessalonians IV), binding it with the laws of chastity and the linen cloths of discipline, and preserving it from the decay of worms by the mixture of myrrh and aloes. For these spices are bitter indeed, but they ward off corruption. The chastening of the flesh is laborious indeed, but otherwise neither mind nor flesh itself is kept incorrupt.

“About a hundred pounds.” O good and heaped measure! One must surely weigh between body and soul with most subtle discernment, so that each may rejoice to have its full measure, and there may be peace and equality between flesh and spirit, in order that due measure may be maintained and perfection not abandoned [Col. 1531C]. These are like the hundred pounds that keep the body of Jesus whole and sweet in the tomb of the faithful.

Behold, Solomon’s bed is surrounded by sixty strong men, all holding the sword and very skilled in war (Song III). Your bed, Jesus Christ, is greater than Solomon’s: it is your burial, in which on the Sabbath you rested from every work that you had accomplished. Your tomb is new and in a garden (John XIX), and cut out in rock, because your beloved, the faithful soul, is a garden enclosed; it is renewed daily in the knowledge of you and made firm upon the rock of your love, burying itself with you in the inner person, in the secret place of your tabernacle. There sixty strong men from among the strongest of Israel surround you, in whom are the works of the six days, good works and very perfect, so that in the six and the ten [Col. 1531D] of the law they may preserve your image and likeness.

These guard you better than the deceitful guard of the wicked: they are most skilled in war, able to drive away not only the enticements of the flesh but also the powers of the air and the terrors of night. But those who besiege the tomb by night like drunken men, “trembled with fear where there is no fear,” because the power of darkness cannot endure light; at the announcement of life they became as dead men (Matthew XXVIII; the printed citation reads “Malach. XXVIII”). Therefore the children of night do not guard you, but the children of day. Your brightness inspires them with terror, so that they flee from you; but to these it gives joy, that they may approach you. “While we were sleeping,” they say, “his disciples came and stole him away” (Matthew XXVIII). O liars! You spoke truth, but [Col. 1532A] “iniquity lied to itself” (Psalm XXVI). For those who are asleep cannot guard Christ; but “those who watch for me in the morning shall find me” (Proverbs VIII).

For while you sleep, what can appear to you but dreams? Behold, you have abundant money in your hands; guard it, if you can, lest thieves dig it out or steal it. For Christ’s disciples will diligently guard their own treasure: each person strives to preserve what he loves. Certainly Michal loved David more than her father Saul, and therefore let him down through the window and saved him (1 Sam. 19).

What is this? Michal, Saul’s daughter, the daughter once of pride: after she had married the beautiful David, she begins to hate her father. To her it is said in the psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your father’s house, and [Col. 1532B] the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44 [45]). Hence she lets David down through the window. Understand that window to be the one through which the Beloved puts forth his hand (1 Sam. 10 [probably Cant. 5:4]); through this window he is let down by his beloved to his beloved—that is, to himself—and is hidden in the inner person, where he may both live securely and remain concealed from the wicked.

For he hid himself and went out from the temple of faithlessness; because while he played the harp before Saul, in order to make the evil spirit of the Lord depart from him, that impious man attempted to pin him to the wall with a spear. But when David turns aside (1 Sam. 16), what does it mean that the spear is fixed in the wall, except that, when Christ’s grace has withdrawn, the hardened mind is pierced by the weapon of its own malice? And what does Saul, the king of darkness, hold more hateful even today than David, his son-in-law? Therefore, while David was absent, he took his daughter and gave her to another husband, obscure indeed, but strong of hand (1 Sam. 5 [probably 1 Sam. 25]); yet when David returns and receives the kingdom, he again claims her for himself, because he had betrothed her to himself with two hundred foreskins, from which he had cut away not only impurities of the flesh but also of the mind.

Woe to you sinners, O Lord, who besiege your tomb. For you truly turn aside from them, and they do not find you in your sweet and flowery bed; rather, they encounter the image of their own heart, wrapped in darkness, having at its head a goatskin (1 Sam. 19), the foul-smelling memory of their sins. Blessed, however, is the one who watches at your tomb, guards you, and wrestles at dawn with the angel of resurrection, not letting him go until he hears something of his wonderful name: so that Jacob’s name [Col. 1532D] may be changed into Israel (Gen. 35), and, after the river of sorrow has been crossed, the sun of righteousness may immediately rise for him.

“Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” (Matt. 27 [probably Mark 16:3]). The door of my mind is closed, Lord, and the stone of mortality, weighed down by the burden of my iniquity, presses upon my understanding. Human strength is altogether unable to remove it, unless your almighty Word comes from the royal seats—the Angel of Counsel—to tear down the wall of hostilities and open our understanding so that we may understand the Scriptures, and see the linen cloths set before us, the truest witnesses of your humility and resurrection. Whoever, with your help, can search you out in them will taste beforehand something of the glory of the resurrection which you have prepared [Col. 1533A] for those who love you, whose first-fruits you have already gathered into your bosom, offering them always before the face of your Father, roasted by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

And that angel, the herald of so great a joy, who rolled away the stone and terrified impious minds but gently soothed devout ones, forbidding them to fear—that angel, I say, bore witness to the blessed resurrection not only by word, but also by countenance, apparel, and touch. For he rolled away the stone and sat upon it (Matt. 28): the stone, I say, which is even now rolled upon us and presses down our face. This undoubtedly takes place in the first resurrection, that of the soul: the spirit in turn subjects beneath itself the burden of corruption that presses upon it, and, like judge and lord, assumes governance of that which is beneath it.

And what is signified by the whiteness of snow [Col. 1533B] and the appearance of the garments, except the chaste, cold, and spotless purity of our body? It is like the angelic brightness presiding within it, and supplies both testimony and obedience. But his inward aspect, where “the light of your countenance” is stamped, O Lord, is terrible and bright like lightning: terrible, that it may cleave apart and terrify the enemies of the soul; bright, that it may always appear, with righteousness, before you who are the true Light.

Such was the face of Moses (Exod. 3 [probably Exod. 34]) through fellowship with your Word: luminous and terrible, because it was horned to scatter the enemies, and veiled because of the radiance which fleshly eyes could not bear. And now, Lord, we know and rejoice that you have truly risen from the dead and are still far removed from us mortals, because you have ascended [Col. 1533C] upon your fiery horses (Hab. 3) and fiery chariot, which is manifold by ten thousands (Ps. 67 [68]). Nevertheless, your cloak has fallen to us from you and remains with us to this day: that is, the linen cloths of your body, through which we may experience the help of your power at the fitting time, so that your spirit may become double within us, and we may love in you both God and our neighbor.

The pains of death have surrounded us, and the tribulations of hell have troubled us. They have surrounded us—our garment of mortality, swarming with worms, which continually eat me and do not sleep. These are pains, forerunners of that greatest pain which comes upon us like an armed man and strives to overwhelm us unawares. And who is so provident [Col. 1533D] that he can endure its terror? Yet, whether we will or not, it must certainly be endured; it must certainly be passed through. But do not forget Elijah’s cloak, otherwise the torrent will not be divided for you without it.

There are also other torrents of iniquity—the sea of my sins—which trouble me; and would that they troubled me in such a way that I cried out in grief: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver!” (2 Kgs. 2). For the torrents of iniquity trouble me, taking away the light of my eyes, so that I cannot see most gracious Elijah when he is taken from me. For if I saw him, surely his spirit would become double in me and I would cry: “My father, my father!” The Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4). The double spirit cries doubly: [Col. 1534A] “My father, my father”: my father, creator; my father, restorer.

“My father, my father!” O affectionate cry! “The chariot of Israel and its driver” (2 Kgs. 13): you carry and rule, uphold and govern. Whom? Israel, believing in you, hoping in you, sighing toward you. Behold, you have been taken up: your Elisha will see you no longer. Yet your cloak remains with him in memory of you, so that the presence of your absence may continually both soothe his sorrow by increasing it and increase it by soothing it.

“Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22): this is the sacrament of your body, which we receive in remembrance of your body until you come. Your cloak is your flesh, with which clothed you came forth to us. You were indeed hidden from the faithless, but you showed yourself to your faithful ones, as you do even [Col. 1534B] today. Beneath this cloak your greatest strength is hidden (Hab. 3), O mighty Samson; and at last you did not conceal it even from the beloved woman who did not love you, in order to turn an enemy into a friend.

You loved the woman so greatly—not loving you, but persecuting you—that because of love for her your wisdom became foolishness and your strength weakness. But “the foolishness of God became wiser than men, and the weakness of God stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1), because, voluntarily sacrificing yourself to the Father and dying by your own power, you shattered the princes of darkness and crushed their kingdom. Your cross became, indeed, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles; but to those who believe, the power of God and the wisdom of God.

As long as we are in this body, we are away from you, [Col. 1534C] Lord. You do indeed walk with those who love you and who speak and grieve concerning you; yet your face is that of a stranger, and though you recognize them, you are not recognized by them. Truly you are that Joseph (Gen. 42) who spoke more harshly to his brothers as though they were strangers—not from indignation, but from compassion—while you both grieved over and rebuked those two walking on the road: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe!” (Luke 24).

Your brothers therefore come to you as strangers, but you graciously draw near to them. They come to you with the asses of their foolishness and slowness, and with sacks empty through poverty; but you fill them not only with grain, because you also return the money tied in the mouth of the sack. “When one sack was opened,” it says, “to give fodder to the beast, he found the money in the mouth of the sack. ‘My money has been returned to me,’ he said; ‘behold, it is in the sack. What is this that God has done to us?’” (Gen. 42). They come to you empty and foolish, but you send them back laden and abounding with the grain of your wisdom; moreover, you return the money of eloquence, bound by the authority of Scripture. For you make the tongues of infants eloquent, that they may give fodder to beasts that do not yet understand you, and a measure of wheat in its season.

Walk now with us, Lord, lest we be desolate and sorrowful on this road on which we travel; for you yourself once went before the children of Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night (Exod. 13), and at your command they struck their tents and raised them again. What is the cloud which goes before the true Israelites, [Col. 1535A] except your most true and most holy body, which we receive at the altar? In it the height of God and the immensity of your majesty are veiled from us; mortal weakness could not endure either its heat or its brightness unless the mediating cloud intervened, tempering the burning from above and marking out beneath a safe way to you.

Your whole army follows this cloud, Lord God of hosts. Whoever does not follow it is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes. For from it shines forth the path leading to life: the path of humility and patience, the path of gentleness and mercy, and everything which you have deigned to reveal to humankind through the mystery of your Incarnation. From this light the glory of Law and Prophecy shines upon us, because Moses and Elijah [Col. 1535B] appeared with you on the mountain, but a bright cloud overshadowed them (Matt. 17). For neither could they, any more than we, have been saved without your protection. Yet for them, as friends and members of your household—or rather, as the chief among your household members and friends—the cloud of your sacrament was transparent; whereas for us, lying cast down from the sight of your eyes, it is very dim.

But your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book, because beneath your cloud you nourish, perfect, and lead Joseph like a sheep. This is the pillar of cloud which went before the children of Israel by day; the pillar of fire by night is the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the apostles in fiery tongues, who illumines and lifts up the gloom of our blindness, so that we may relish the things above, [Col. 1535C] not the things upon earth. Thus the cloud is by day and the pillar of fire by night, because your flesh tempers the heat of divinity and the light of the Holy Spirit illuminates the darkness of our mind.

Therefore, while you spoke on the road with the two disciples who were traveling with you, and the cloud of a stranger covered your face, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scripture to us?” (Luke 24). The pillar of fire undoubtedly burned within, because the pillar of cloud spoke to them without. But when at last did they recognize you? “In the breaking of bread” (ibid.). And truly, Lord, you are not recognized except in the breaking of bread. The bread is your flesh. You broke your body with your own hands, because you had power to lay down [Col. 1535D] your life and to take it up again. You broke the body that appeared outwardly and showed the marrow that lay hidden within; for unless you suffer, you are not recognized: “There his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3).

And what is your strength, except gentleness, humility, wisdom, and obedience? These strongest and sweetest virtues you showed us in the breaking of bread—that is, in your Passion. By these virtues your flesh, which we are, is gradually nourished, brings to perfection, and is brought to perfection. First, indeed, between the two millstones of hope and fear, it is ground like grain, so that it may become new dough. Then, when it has passed into the form of bread, it is baked in the oven of sufferings. Afterwards, when you have blessed it with every spiritual blessing and said, “It is finished” (John [Col. 1536A] 19), you break even our body, which is in your hands and which we commit into your hands. There you are recognized, not in the appearance of a stranger, but in your own countenance: so that no longer may a spear open your side for us, but we may touch and see with a finger that you are, Lord, our God, father of orphans and judge of widows.

Do you not see this poor widow—my desolate soul—which has no one, neither brothers nor friends nor neighbors, from whom I may borrow empty vessels, not a few, which my sons may bring to me, and into which I may pour from the little oil that remains to me from you, so that you may display to all the fullness of your blessing? For I understand, Lord, that the empty vessels are certain literal and historical senses of your Scripture, [Col. 1536B] and they are not few, so that the whole world could not contain them.

The Babylonian king—that is, the ruler of pride—takes captive these vessels of your most holy temple and compels them to serve at his banquets, not to his glory but to his disgrace (2 Kgs. 2 [probably 2 Kgs. 24–25 / Dan. 5]). He arrogates to himself the knowledge of your law, drinks the wine of his prostitution in the vessels of the sanctuary, and defiles your gifts with the ointments of a harlot. Therefore, opposite the wall, a harsh but just sentence is written against them (Dan. 5): because every kingdom divided against itself shall be desolated and handed over to the Medes and Persians, who do not seek silver nor desire gold, but with poisoned and fiery arrows kill their little ones—that is, their foolish notions.

But you, Lord, will have mercy on the poor and desolate widow, lest that most wicked [Col. 1536C] and importunate creditor, who has lent me many talents of his iniquity at interest for my destruction, take away my two sons—the faculties of my inner soul—to serve him. It is good and salutary for me to ask to borrow vessels not a few, and by the blessing of superabundant oil to redeem my sins, and thereafter to live with my sons.

But because I have neither neighbors nor children from whom to borrow the exercise of my mind, as soon as I relax my hands that wicked creditor attacks me and compels my two sons—that is, understanding and affection—to serve sloth and his vain illusions. Therefore you, merciful defender of widows, since you are exceedingly rich and give abundantly to all: you, I say, [Col. 1536D] yourself lend to me both the vessels which you know to be useful for this purpose and the oil, so that all things may be yours and all may serve you. For I do not wish to carry your oil into Egypt, lest I sin against you, but only that I may not eat the bread of idleness; rather, that I may exercise myself all day in your righteous ordinances and live.

And behold, what the son of my memory has presented to me: as soon as it falls into my hands, I shall seize it. Elijah stood on the summit of the mountain, and the first captain of fifty was sent to him and was consumed by fire; the second likewise; but the third was preserved by the merit of humility and devotion (2 Kgs. 1). Behold, a vessel—but empty, because when taken in this way it rather echoes cruelty. Let it be filled with oil, and its harsh sound will cease.

For who is Elijah standing on the summit of the mountain except you, [Col. 1537A] Lord Jesus, who stand above with the Father? The first captain of fifty comes to you, sent by the world dry from excessive drought, and cries to you: “Man of God, come down from the mountain” (ibid.). For the world knows that it cannot be saved without you. Man of God and God-man: let the human being whom you seek move you to condescend to humanity. Come down from the mountain: no one can approach you unless you approach him; no one can ascend to you unless you descend to him. “Man of God, come down from the mountain.” You are the mountain raised above the tops of the mountains: come down and have compassion on us in the valley of tears.

“If I am a man of God,” he says, “let fire come down from heaven” (ibid.), and so forth. “For I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12), which I desire may be kindled and devour you and your fifty. I beseech you, [Col. 1537B] Lord, let that fire descend also upon me and devour in me the old person with his deeds. This is the first fifty which your fire devours, so as to make it rest from every servile work. The second fifty, however, is the active life itself, which likewise has an end, Sabbath after Sabbath. Your fire consumes this too as a burnt offering. In the first fifty, indeed, the goat is burned; in the second, the ram is consumed by fire. But the third, which is that of resurrection or contemplation, has no end, but lives always with Elijah.

Therefore it was well read in the Gospel concerning the one hundred and fifty-three great fish, all of which were reduced into one fish, placed upon the coals, which the seven disciples saw and with which they ate breakfast together with Jesus, who was the eighth (John 21). This very number, namely one hundred and fifty—the three fifties and the seven disciples—sounds forth rest in harmony. And as the individual fifties tend toward unity, so the seven tend toward the eighth, that is, toward Christ; and all agree in one.

But as Christ and all the elect are one body, one bread, one man, or one fish, so the devil with all the reprobate is one body and one enemy. “There is a great eagle, with great wings,” and so forth (Ezek. 17). An eagle, on account of the excessive keenness of spiritual nature; great, on account of the height of pride; the great wings adhering to and exalting him are the powers of evil spirits; the long extent of limbs, [Col. 1537D] wicked human beings, whose service he employs in waging war against the good. And rightly “long,” because they still come daily and endure until the end of the age, following the leadership of pride; full of feathers, of the deceits of fraud and of avarice, because he transforms the same arts in various ways in order to deceive.

He came to Lebanon, a soul once made white through the merit of faith and life. He took the marrow of the cedar: the incorruptible cedar is the height of hope, whose marrow is charity, which the devil especially strives to assault. He plucked away the topmost part of its branches and uproots from love of God the word of wisdom which is most excellent. And he carried it into the land of Shinar: that is, “of their stench,” which signifies vain glory.

“On that day the Lord will whistle for the fly which is at the end of the rivers of the land of Egypt, and for the bee which is in [Col. 1538A] the land of Assyria” (Isa. 7). Whistle, Lord, also for this unclean fly, my sinful soul, so that your good Spirit may lead me in the right way, that I may go to the lofty and mountainous land of promise, which is watered from your heights and awaits rain from heaven—not like the land of Egypt, which a river bubbling up from the earth wholly covers.

For there is no opposing mountain; there is no obstacle to Egypt’s desires. Rather, as they bubble up from the earthly mind over the exposed surface of the soul, they run down without delay. For the Egyptian river has seven mouths, deriving from one head, that is, pride. The last of these is understood as carnal lust, from which flies—ever lovers of impurity—are born. Nor does the abundance of grace despise even this fly; rather, [Col. 1538B] it whistles and calls her forth from the end of the rivers and joins her to the bee that was in the land of Assyria: “And they shall come and rest together in the torrents of the valleys, and in the caverns of rocks, and in all thickets, and in every hollow” (ibid.).

The bee is a virgin; but as long as she is in the land of Assyria—that is, of self-exaltation—she cannot make honey. For only the land of promise flows with milk and honey. Therefore, when grace whistles, the fly and the bee meet and rest together in the torrents of the valleys. In those torrents the bee is cleansed from the filth of pride, and the fly from that of lust. The torrents of the valleys are the disciplines of humility. Why torrents? Because any sorrow or difficulty involved in correcting vices soon passes away. Hence a woman has sorrow when she gives birth; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers [Col. 1538C] the distress (John 16). For labor is turned into love, weariness into longing, and bitterness into sweetness. Thus from the torrents of the valleys they advance to the caverns of the rocks.

The rocks are the fathers, most steadfast and strong in faith. In their sufferings, as in their own models, the fly and bee rest, nesting like doves. From there their hand does not cease, nor their foot; but constantly exercised in every thicket of good works, they finally come to the openings of contemplation. These are your works, Lord Jesus, because they are very good.

Thus you whistled for Mary Magdalene, from whom you cast out not one but seven Egyptian rivers. See how she rested in the torrents of the valleys. She entered among those reclining at table [Col. 1538D] and ran to Jesus’ feet; she poured torrents of tears over them. To wash her Lord’s feet she brought no waters but those of her own eyes, using her hair instead of linen cloths. Then, when her feeling grew more ardent and abundant, the coal, sprinkled with the rain of tears, blazed more fiercely (Matt. 26; Luke 7). You could see her fixing upon the sacred footprints kisses most frequent and insatiable; you could see the whole house filled with the sweetness of the ointment she poured out.

What then was she doing but resting in the torrents of the valleys, she from whom so many and such great torrents of grace were flowing? Hence, when her many sins had been forgiven her because she had loved much, she now, like a dove washed with milk, sat at Jesus’ feet beside the fullest streams, [Col. 1539A] while her sister Martha busied herself with much serving. What need is there to mention the office of burial which she anticipated: rising from the feet to anoint the head, while that foul tomb of avarice growled against her, unable to bear the fragrance of devotion? Such love could not die even when Christ was dying: while the men—that is, the apostles—fled and hid themselves, the undaunted woman stood weeping at the tomb (John 20). She had no wine, and burned wholly over the dead man. The body had been taken away, and she could not leave the tomb; the more it was removed from her hands and eyes, the more ardently her soul pursued it. Had it been possible, she would have filled the tomb with tears to ransom the body. “She stood,” it says, “weeping”: this alone remained to her from you. The body had been taken away, [Col. 1539B] but who could take away her weeping?

Yield, lady, yield full rein; and run forth, pouring yourself into untiring tears, until you attain your Lord who has been taken away—indeed, who has risen. Again and again bend down; look yet more often upon the empty place where he had been laid. The place itself provokes you more and more to weep, while it presents to you the absence of him whom you seek. “She saw,” it says, “two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid. They say to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?’” (ibid.). Surely, most gracious angels, you knew well what she was weeping for and whom she sought; why, by mentioning it again, did you stir her afresh to tears? But the joy of unexpected consolation was near; therefore let the whole force of sorrow and weeping run its course.

[Col. 1539C] “Turning around, she saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus” (ibid.). O tender, O delightful spectacle of devotion! He whom she seeks and desires both hides himself and reveals himself: he hides himself so that he may be sought more ardently; when sought, that he may be found with joy; when found, that he may be held with anxious care; and when held, that he may not be let go until he is introduced to make his dwelling in the chamber of his love. By this art Wisdom plays in the world, and her delights are to be with the children of men. “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” (ibid.). Do you possess him whom you seek and not know it? Do you possess true and eternal joy, and weep? Do you possess within the one whom you seek without? Truly you stand outside the tomb weeping (ibid.): your mind is my tomb; there I rest, not dead, [Col. 1539D] but living for ever. Your mind is my garden. You rightly supposed that I am the gardener: I am the second Adam; I work and guard my paradise. Your tears, your devotion, your longing, are my work. You have me within yourself and do not know it; therefore you seek without, and behold, I shall appear without, so that I may lead you back within and you may find within the one whom you seek without.

“Mary”: I know you by name; learn to know me by faith. “Rabboni”—that is, “Teacher”: this is to say, “Teach me to seek you; teach me to touch and anoint you.” “Do not touch me,” he says, as a man, nor as you previously touched and anointed one who was mortal: “I have not yet ascended to my Father.” You have not yet believed me equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. Believe this, then, and you have touched me. You see a man; [Col. 1540A] therefore you do not believe: for what is seen is not believed. You do not see God: believe, and you will see; by believing you will touch me, as that woman touched the fringe of my garment and was immediately healed (Matt. 9). Why? Because she touched me by her faith. Touch me with this hand; seek me with these eyes; hasten running to me with these feet. I am not far from you, for I am a God who draws near; I am the word in your mouth and in your heart. What is nearer to a human being than his own heart? There I am found within by all who find me; for the things seen without are indeed my works, but they are transient and perishable. I, however, their maker, dwell in the most hidden and purest hearts.

All power in heaven and on earth has been given to you, Lord Jesus (Ps. 8), great king, king of powers, [Col. 1540B] because you became obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross. Behold, your majesty has been raised above the heavens (2 Sam. 2), and all things have been subjected under your feet. David first reigned in Hebron seven years over Judah; afterward he was anointed over all Israel, and reigned in Israel thirty-three years. But when you, most mighty David, were anointed in Hebron only over Judah, Saul, the king of pride, had already died among them; otherwise, while he lived and sin ruled them, they would not say to you, “We are your bone and your flesh.” For who can be a member of Christ and at the same time a member of a prostitute? Or what agreement has Christ with Belial? “Behold,” they say, “we are your bone and your flesh” (2 Cor. 6); “and yesterday and the day before, when Saul was king over us, you [Col. 1540C] were leading Israel out and bringing it back” [cf. 2 Sam. 5].

And truly it is so: while the prince of darkness still reigns over us, you endure with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction; you go out before us, calling us to battle against vices; you free us and lead us, though unworthy, out of the hand of sins. Therefore Judah first—that is, confession—anoints you king over itself in Hebron. For once Saul is dead, it remembers your benefits and, confessing its error, makes a passage from sins to you, King of righteousness. But you reign over Judah seven years in Hebron because you render to them sevenfold into their bosom; and, having expiated them sevenfold from the vices over which proud Saul ruled, you restore them by your sevenfold power.

Afterward your kingdom passes into Jerusalem [Col. 1540D] over all Israel, because by the work of confession, once the senses have been enlightened, one comes to the vision of peace. There a place was made, and it is the mountain which you appointed for your disciples, that they should go into Galilee, see you there, and worship you after your resurrection; for now God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. The superabundance of grace despises this, but [the hisses of the kings of the earth; the reading is uncertain].

Moreover, you reign in Jerusalem thirty-three years. Thirty-three contains three tens: in the law, which consists of ten commandments, a threefold progress of the soul is understood—by living, meditating upon, or loving the law of God. Of the first it is said: “I will praise God in my life” (Ps. 145); of the second: “Your law is my meditation” (Ps. 118); of the third: [Col. 1541A] “How I have loved your law, O Lord” (ibid.). The three above thirty signify certain most excellent contemplatives who, through purity of conscience, fullness of wisdom, and perfection of charity, draw near to the supreme Trinity.

This is also the number of the mightiest men, who are most powerful in your army; yet even the most eminent among them do not attain to your wisdom and strength, for “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or be like the Lord among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). You are like the tenderest worm of wood (2 Sam. 23): born of a virgin, by your humility and charity you pierce every hardness; indeed, by the force of your Spirit you kill eight hundred princes of wickedness. Who is as strong as you? Who is as merciful, you who wept over Jerusalem [Col. 1541B] and made lamentation over the destruction of your enemies? And now, Lord, you grieve over Saul and Jonathan his son, who fall daily upon the mountains of Gilboa. For unless you grieved, you would not cry from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9).

For whom does Saul signify but proud prelates in your Church, who seem to themselves to stand head and shoulders above all the people? And what does Jonathan signify but young men teachable and of refined intellect, who, corrupted by the habits and conversation of their elders, cannot cultivate friendship with David except secretly, as though guarding against the snares of those who disparage and mock them? Rightly, therefore, kind David, you weep over Jonathan his son; for they would not be worthy of weeping if they had fallen well. But upon [Col. 1541C] the mountains of Gilboa, which run down into the deep, neither the dew of grace nor the rain of teaching shall come any more, because there the shield of the mighty was cast away (2 Sam. 1): Saul’s shield.

The shield of the mighty is hope in divine protection, by which the fiery darts of the devil are repelled. Saul was grievously wounded by archers, so much so that in despair he killed himself. Saul’s shield, however, is confidence in one’s own strength, which cannot resist the arrows of the uncircumcised. “Woe to those who have lost endurance!”—that is, the shield of the mighty. And, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man”: this is Saul’s shield. “For he shall be like a tamarisk in the wilderness,” because neither dew nor rain comes upon you, mountains of Gilboa. “How have the mighty fallen!” [Col. 1541D] For if they were mighty, how did they fall? And if they fell, how were they mighty? But: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength” (Jer. 9; 1 Cor. 1); rather, “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10), and “let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10).

For even if they are swifter than eagles, so that by quickness of intellect they soar above contemplatives; even if they are stronger than lions, so that by strength in action they surpass true preachers—yet if, presuming upon themselves, they cast away the shield of salvation, they will fall before their enemies. But whoever trusts in the Lord, like Mount Zion, shall not be moved for ever. Saul preferred to lean upon his own spear rather than lean upon the Lord; therefore the reed-staff of Egypt pierced his hand. His own spear and his own charioteer, who drove the chariot of his insolence, [Col. 1542A] killed him. “I knew,” he says, “that he could not live” (2 Sam. 1). The obstinacy of the arrogant does not know how to humble itself so that it may live.

Command, most righteous King David, command your servant—that is, the spirit of pure discernment—to kill in me this Amalekite, Saul’s armour-bearer, who even now daily dares to put his hand against the Lord’s Christ. Do not rain upon us quails, Lord: the desires of our flesh, which rise only two cubits from the ground because they do not attain the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Do not rain upon us flesh like dust, for flesh is dust and leads into dust. “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine” (Matt. 15): such is the end of all carnal pleasures. And, like the sand of the sea, winged birds (Ps. 73): [Col. 1542B] gluttony rejoices and flutters its little wings, but soon turns into the sand of the sea; luxury rejoices and flies briefly, but soon passes into the sand of the sea. Every sweetness of the flesh ends in bitterness; it briefly lifts the unhappy soul but soon weighs it down into the sand.

But you, Lord, are surely manna like coriander seed (Exod. 16), which, when crushed in the mill, yields whiteness and sweetness like cakes made with oil. This is the bread of angels which man ate. Unbelievers still say, “Manhu—what is this?” (ibid.), because they see your word as minute, humble, and seemingly contemptible. Therefore they return and desire the great meats of Egypt, because they do not know or taste the hidden inward flavor of manna, possessing every delight of sweetness (Wis. 16). They return to [Col. 1542C] flesh and dry it in the sun around the camp. A wondrous thing: under one and the same sun, flesh is hardened and manna melts (Exod. 16)! Flesh is dried so that it may last longer; the wicked are hardened so that they may more long satisfy their pleasures. But your manna melted when the sun grew hot, because “my soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5).

Shine warmly upon us, noonday sun, so that the manna may melt and its spices flow like a torrent in the south (Ps. 125). Gather, children of Israel, gather manna and grind it in the mill, and our soul shall be filled as with fatness and richness. The labor is troublesome, but fruitful: “You shall eat the labors of your hands, and already you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127) in the future. [Col. 1542D] Grind, I say, body and soul in the mill, and you shall find the body rich in marrow through fasts, labors, and vigils; the soul, through study of the divine law. Let not the law fall from the mouth of your heart; turn it over, turn it again, revolve and return it, and then you shall understand what savor manna has.

Thus did he who said: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118). Be a virginal bee; gather from the little flowers of manna. You have a garden of delight full of roses and lilies, painted in wonderful variety; whatever you find there is sweet and fragrant. Store it abundantly in your hive. And what more shall I say? One and the same food is honey to the bee, a spring of water to the deer, and bread that strengthens the human heart. This is bread made with oil: it heals the sick, strengthens the healed, gladdens the countenance, and possesses every delight and every flavor of sweetness.

[Col. 1543A] Where are the quails? Where are the dried meats? Surely they have rotted in the teeth of those eating them. If they rotted in the teeth, how much more in the stomachs? Indeed, even the beasts rotted in their own dung. But the bread of angels which man ate does not know decay; it does not go into the latrine, but tends upward. It leads humanity back to the place from which it drew its image. You are rich, Lord, and your granary does not fail. Feed your poor man today from the crumbs that fall from the table of your children. Your needy one cries at your doors because today he has nothing to eat. Lord, I am so weak that I cannot open my mouth. O how healthy was he who said, “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit!” (ibid.). Therefore, Lord, open my lips [Col. 1543B] and feed me with your praise: that is true food. Your entire city Jerusalem lives on no other food, because you satisfy it with the fat of wheat and make it drunk with the torrent of your delight.

Woe to those who fast from your praise: indeed, they sit upon their dung so as to drink the urine of their sins; that is, they gape after temporal things in order to satisfy the enticements of the flesh. To such you give a bronze earth and an iron heaven, so that no rain falls upon them for three years and six months, because they bear neither the fruit of faith nor that of good works. Let them have a bronze earth, because their lips ring like a cymbal; and an iron heaven, because they carry a hard and inflexible heart. Of such persons the Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God said, ‘Why do you recount my statutes and take my covenant into your mouth?’” (Ps. 69). These do not live by your praise, Lord, but die of hunger—not hunger for bread and water, but for your word.

[Col. 1543C] Yet you will not kill the soul of the righteous by hunger, because in the time of drought you commanded the raven and the widow of Zarephath to feed your servant Elijah (1 Kings 17). For you, Lord, feed those who feed you; hence the widow’s jar of flour and flask of oil do not fail as she feeds you. The raven feeds you, and the widow feeds you; but the widow with bread baked under ashes, the raven with evening meat. The sinner is a raven: Zacchaeus the tax collector was a raven; hence he flew up into a sycamore tree. “Today,” he says, “I must stay with you” (Luke 19): today the raven will feed Elijah. How did he feed him? “Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor” (ibid.); therefore he fed Christ, and the poor with Christ—[Col. 1543D] indeed, Christ in the poor. From what? From meats: that is, from temporal things. For to leave temporal and carnal things for Christ is to feed Christ with meat.

And this occurs in the evening, on the border of darkness and light, so that one may advance and it may be said, “Evening and morning were one day” (Gen. 1). First the raven feeds, then the widow; for the raven becomes a widow. The raven is changed into a dove and utters groans. Why? Because she is a widow; because the Bridegroom has died; because he washed her from her sins—that is, from the raven’s blackness. Her Bridegroom has died; therefore, in memory of him, she gathers two sticks so as to make for herself and her son—that is, the spirit—a little provision for the journey, and to die with her Bridegroom. But Elijah must first be fed, and from the very little flour of new kneading a small loaf baked under ashes must be made.

[Col. 1544A] Christ requires the firstfruits of our works, and requires us not to think lofty thoughts but to associate with the lowly, guarding against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (Matt. 16). This simple and humble understanding is the small loaf baked under ashes which Christ requires of us. A good woman ought not to be without flour or a little oil, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9). But whoever has a little flour or oil recognizes it in himself because he hungers and thirsts for righteousness. “I have,” she says, “only as much flour in the jar as a handful can hold, and a little oil in the flask” (1 Kings 17). The handful is a small capacity; the flour is the clean and subtle whiteness of faith; the jar is the watchful safeguard of humility, lest the wind of pride reduce so great a glory to dust and scatter it.

[Col. 1544B] Whoever has little within himself understands with what arms he ought to guard it, lest he lose even that. Therefore, Lord, the raven and the widow feed you in Zarephath of the Sidonians, while the cursed fig tree withered in the land of the Jews. Tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners go before the Pharisees into the kingdom of heaven. In the house of the Pharisee you recline outside; in the house of the sinful woman you feast within. Feed, Lord, the young of ravens (Ps. 146), the son of sinners crying to you, because “my father and my mother have forsaken me” (Ps. 26), but you do not forsake the one who hopes in you.

You have hardened our heart, Lord; you have hardened our heart so that we did not fear you; you have set a cloud so that prayer might not pass through. Take from us, Lord, as you have promised, the heart of stone (Ezek. 36), and give us a heart of flesh, so that you may place your Spirit [Col. 1544C] in our midst. When your Spirit comes, it lays down fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom, as a base and foundation. The fear of the Lord makes the heart stable, so that the house built upon sevenfold grace may remain unmoved. You know, Lord, how restless my heart is, and how unstable, like dust and like the sand of the sea, so that whatever I attempt to build upon it, I seem rather to pile up a ruin upon my head. How aptly it was said: “Jerusalem sinned a sin; therefore she became unstable” (Lam. 1). She sinned a sin, heaped up wickedness; therefore she became unstable—now outside, now inside, now chattering and wandering in the corners of streets, unable to endure rest or to stand in her house upon her own feet.

[Col. 1544D] Behold how well the harlot-like madness of my soul has been portrayed. And what shall I do? Return to your former husband, and do not spread your feet for every passerby. Therefore you have become unstable and vile, repeating your ways too often: Jerusalem sinned a sin; she repeated her ways excessively. Return, then, to your former husband and say to him: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). And he will say to you: “Keep your tongue from evil” (Ps. 33); restrain gluttony, slaughter lust, cut off every unlawful movement of your body. “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. 5). This is not enough: philosophers have done this; seekers of empty glory have done it; hypocrites do it. They have crucified their flesh, but have not received reward from Christ. Why? Because they did not have the fear of the Lord.

[Col. 1545A] “Pierce my flesh with your fear.” Many have pierced the flesh, not with your fear but with the swelling of vanity. This is not enough: pierce with your fear not only the lust of the flesh but also the lust of the soul. The lust of the soul is empty glory: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72). What difference is there between perishing by bodily impurity and by the soul’s lust? Therefore not only the cross of the flesh but also the cross of the soul must be taken up. Mortification of the members is the cross of the flesh; the cross of the soul is fear of the Lord. The fear of God pierces the soul so that it does not look to right or left.

There is also a third cross, that of the Spirit, which is charity. “I have been crucified with Christ,” says the Apostle (Gal. 2); “who shall separate me from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8). That cross—that is, charity—makes my heart fleshly, soft, and tender. Thus by the very tender calf [Col. 1545B] we understand Christ, crucified through excessive charity. Whoever reaches that cross passes through the thick cloud and pours out prayer in the sight of God. Thus too the cloud covered Moses on Mount Sinai for six days, but on the seventh day the Lord called him from the midst of the darkness. “The appearance of the glory of the Lord,” it says, “was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain, in the sight of the children of Israel. And Moses entered into the midst of the cloud and ascended the mountain” (Exod. 24).

For what is meant by the six days during which Moses is covered by the cloud, except those six virtues by which one ascends to wisdom? But on the summit of wisdom alone the burning fire of most ardent charity displays the likeness of divine glory. Whatever lies below the seventh degree of wisdom is counted darkness and cloud. [Col. 1545C] Therefore the first cross, through fear, devotion, and knowledge, crucifies the flesh. The second cross possesses the soul’s strength, counsel, and understanding: by strength it terrifies the devil; by counsel it directs the neighbor; by understanding it guards itself. But the third cross surpasses all these; and charity, gathered into unity, sleeping and resting in peace as one, rests.

“In the beginning, Lord, you created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), that is, angelic and human nature. But after this brief mention of angels, your discourse turns to humankind alone: “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (ibid.). We see, Lord, and it lies before our senses, this great and wondrous fabric of the world, which by its beauty and magnitude does not cease to proclaim immeasurable, incomprehensible, and eternal wisdom, [Col. 1545D] power, and goodness. Yet although these things surpass the understanding and eloquence of all mortals, I would rather direct the gaze of the mind toward the new heaven and new earth which you declare that you are now creating. For you say in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). What is this but a new heaven and a new earth? For from deeps you form earth, and from earth heavens. The sinner is a deep; but when you make light shine from darkness, so that they cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light (Rom. 13), you are known to have created a new earth and a new heaven.

Behold, Lord, I perceive that the earth of my mind is still empty and void, and darkness is upon the face of the deep. [Col. 1546A] It is empty because it wavers in miserable restlessness amid the empty trifles and phantasms of its own making, void of the fruits of good works. Or, as another translation has it, “invisible and unformed.” For it is like a kind of chaos, most hideous and entangled in its confusion, knowing neither its own end nor its beginning, nor the measure of its nature—except that it believes itself to have been wonderfully made from nothing by the supreme Creator, and after this life to be conveyed either to hell according to its merits or to heaven through the mercy of its maker. It is indeed unformed because it does not preserve the beauty of the virtues and the likeness of the divine image to which it was made similar. Therefore it is driven back into the abyss of its blindness, and its face is darkened by the shadows of its illusions.

[Col. 1546B] Such is my soul, my God; such is my soul: it is earth empty and void, invisible and unformed, and darkness is upon the face of the deep. Yet it says: “The deep gave forth its voice” (Hab. 3), and “the lower and dark deep calls upon the higher deep” (Ps. 41)—upon you, who surpass every understanding. The deep of my mind calls upon you, Lord, that even from me you may create a new earth and a new heaven. David called for this, and with David we call: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50). He already knew that something had been made of him, but he asked that he might be made a new creature, a new heaven and earth.

[Col. 1546C] “We have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us, the work which you performed in their days” (Ps. 43). This is the work done “in their days,” of which he says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). For you formed their hearts one by one, creating light in them and dividing light from darkness, calling the light day and the darkness night. This is the work you performed in their days and in the days of old. Of these days Abraham the elder, and many others, are remembered to have been full, just as were those to whom the Apostle said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). O best Creator, if you still perform this work which you performed in ancient days, why do you not perform this work also in my soul? For my soul is empty and void, and darkness is upon the face of the deep. Say, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1), and it will be! You have already created it so that it is something; [Col. 1546D] create it so that it may be light. Say, “Let there be light,” and there will be light.

You performed this work both in Lazarus and in Paul. The former’s face was bound with a cloth, because darkness was upon the face of the deep. From the latter’s eyes, when he was baptized, something like scales fell (Acts 9), so that with unveiled face he might behold the glory of the Lord. The things which continually make my heart sleep before you likewise made the apostles sleep in your agony: “their eyes,” it says, “were weighed down” (Mark 14). But now, Lord, it is time to rise from sleep (Rom. 23 [an erroneous citation]), as your trumpet sounds more frequently: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light” (Eph. 5). Illuminate my darkness, O Christ; say to my soul, “Let there be light,” and there shall be light.

[Col. 1547]

# The Book of Cardinal Drogo on the Creation and Redemption of the First Human Being

*(Bibliotheca Patrum, ibid., p. 341.)*

[Col. 1547A] That blessed and everlasting Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God, namely supreme power, supreme wisdom, supreme goodness, created a certain trinity in its own image and likeness: namely, the rational soul. In this soul there is set forth a certain trace of that supreme Trinity, consisting of memory, reason, and will. It was created in such a way that, remaining in God, it would be blessed through participation in him; but turned away from him, wherever it might betake itself, it would remain wretched. Yet this trinity chose rather to fall by the movement of its own will than to stand by the Creator’s grace through free choice.
