Thus through suggestion, delight, and consent it fell from that highest and beautiful Trinity—power, wisdom, purity—into a contrary and foul trinity: weakness, blindness, and impurity. For memory became powerless; reason, weak, imprudent, and dark; will, impure.

Moreover, memory, which while it stood contemplated the power of the simple Godhead, fell from it and, as though falling upon rocks, burst apart and shattered into three parts: affective, burdensome, and idle thoughts. I call “affective” those by which it is emotionally occupied—for example, concerns about necessary matters, eating, drinking, and countless other things; “burdensome” thoughts are those involved in external administrations; “idle” thoughts are those by which it is neither emotionally engaged nor burdened, yet is distracted through them from contemplation of eternal things—for example, if I think of a horse running or a bird flying.

Reason likewise has a threefold fall. Its function is to examine good and evil, true and false, advantageous and disadvantageous. In discerning these it is so blinded by darkness that judgment is often led to the opposite conclusion, taking evil for good, falsehood for truth, and what is harmful for what is advantageous, and conversely. It would never be deceived in these matters if it were never deprived of the light in which it was created. But because it fell from that light, without doubt it found nothing but the darkness of its own blindness. Hence it came about that it lost even the instrument by which it managed these things: namely, that threefold way of wisdom—ethics, logic, and physics—which we may call by other names, moral, speculative, and natural knowledge. For through ethics the good—that is, virtues—is chosen, and evil—that is, vices—is rejected. Through logic truth and falsehood are known. Through physics, the advantageous and disadvantageous are known: that is, what ought to be taken up for use and what rejected.

Will follows, and its ruin is likewise threefold. It ought to have clung to and loved the supreme goodness and purity alone; but by its own iniquity, falling from the heights into these low things, it loved the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition. What fall could be judged more unhappy than this, in which, as memory, reason, and will perish, the whole substance of the soul likewise perishes? Yet that blessed Trinity, mindful of its mercy and unmindful of our guilt, repaired this exceedingly grievous, foul, and dark fall of our nature.

Therefore the Son of God was sent by the Father and gave faith. After the Son, the Holy Spirit was sent; he taught and gave charity. Thus through these two—faith and charity—there arose hope of returning to the homeland. This is the trinity—faith, hope, charity—through which that immutable and blessed Trinity, as by a trident, led back from the mire of the deep to lost blessedness the mutable, fallen, and miserable trinity. Faith illuminated reason; hope raised memory; charity purified will.

Therefore, when, as has been said, the Son of God came as man, though he was God, like a good physician he gave precepts. By observing them, lost health would be restored. To establish faith in the precepts, he displayed signs; to persuade people of the usefulness of those same precepts, he promised blessedness. Faith is of one kind in relation to precepts, another in relation to signs, and another in relation to promises: namely, that by which we believe *in* God, that by which we believe God, and that by which we believe *God* [i.e. trust God]. Through faith in the precepts we believe in God. To believe in God is to hope in him and love him. Through faith in signs we believe God, who can do such things and can do all things. Through faith in promises we believe that he truly fulfills whatever he promises.

Likewise hope is threefold and proceeds from the aforesaid threefold faith. From faith in the precepts arises hope of pardon; from faith in signs, hope of grace; from faith in promises, hope of glory. Charity too is comprised under a threefold number: from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. We owe purity to our neighbor, conscience to ourselves, and faith to God. Purity means that whatever is done should be done either for the neighbor’s benefit or for God’s honor. Yet it must especially be shown toward one’s neighbor, because we are entirely manifest to God, whereas we cannot be manifest to our neighbor except insofar as we open our heart to that neighbor.

Two things create a good conscience in us: penitence and self-restraint. Through penitence we punish sins already committed, and through self-restraint we do not commit sins that would thereafter need punishing. This we owe to ourselves. After these follows unfeigned faith, which must be offered watchfully to God: lest either, on account of the neighbor to whom we devote ourselves, we offend God; or, on account of the conscience which we wish to keep in humility through penitence and self-restraint, we perform the obedience due to God’s commandments less fully. This is unfeigned faith.

It is called “unfeigned” in distinction from dead and feigned faith. Dead faith is that which is without works. Feigned faith is that which believes for a time and falls away in time of temptation. Hence feigned faith is called fragile.

[Col. 1549B] There is moreover another manner of rising again, comprised under the same number, set in correspondence with the fall of the first man. For Adam, placed in paradise, first lost attentiveness to God. Blessed Augustine testifies that the tempter would never have cast man out of paradise unless some pride had first gone before in the human soul, since it is most truly written: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16). Second, he lost justice, because he obeyed his wife’s voice more than the divine voice. For justice is the virtue that renders to each his due. Third, he lost judgment when, reproved after his sin, he indirectly shifted his own guilt onto the Creator through the woman, saying: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

Therefore, by the same steps of virtues through which man, placed in exile, deserved to be deprived and expelled from paradise, he must return. Judgment must accordingly be exercised first; then justice; finally, attentiveness must be applied. Judgment, indeed, is owed to ourselves, so that we judge and accuse ourselves; justice to our neighbour; and attentiveness to God. The prophet Micah shows us this way of return, saying: “I shall show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: namely, to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitously with your God” (Mic. 6). The Apostle testifies that Christ taught this way of salvation, saying: “The grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this world” (Tit. 2): soberly, that is, with respect to ourselves; justly toward our neighbour; piously toward God.

[Col. 1549D] He also more plainly introduced attentiveness to God, adding: “Awaiting the coming of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (ibid.). In many other passages of Holy Scripture this order and rule of life may be found, if diligently sought—for example: “Blessed is the man who remains in wisdom, who meditates in his justice, and considers in understanding the attentiveness due to God” (Ecclus. 14). For he remains in wisdom, and is wise, who here always judges himself, so as to escape God’s eternal judgment. “For,” says the Apostle, “if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged; but when we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, lest we be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11). He is wise, not according to the wisdom of this world, but according to that wisdom drawn from hidden things, through which, by God’s wonderful work, all the elect, worn down here by blows and pressures, may afterwards be built into the edifice of the true Solomon without the sound of a hammer.

“You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). In place of the paradise that we lost, Christ the Saviour has been restored to us. Therefore, just as four rivers are led forth from the one fountain of paradise to water paradise, so from the hidden recess of his breast proceed four fountains, from which arise four kinds of waters whereby the Church is watered throughout the whole world. The four fountains are truth, wisdom, power, and charity.

[Col. 1550B] From these fountains waters are drawn, a distinct kind from each: from the fountain of truth, waters of judgments; from the fountain of wisdom, waters of counsels; from the fountain of power, waters of aids; from the fountain of charity, waters of desires. In the waters of judgments we know what is lawful or unlawful; in counsels we discern what is expedient or inexpedient. But because temptations are not lacking to elect persons who rightly advance through these things—for they are tempted in two ways, either shaken by terrors or seduced by blandishments—they must be armed against terrors with the aids of divine power, and against blandishments with desires for supreme charity. For, as a certain holy man says, desires for better things overcome desires for worse things.

Or we may proceed thus: what profit is it to know what is lawful and expedient—which judgments and counsels certainly teach—if one cannot accomplish it?

[Col. 1550C] Therefore, after the waters of judgments and counsels, the waters of aids must be sought. Again, what avail knowledge and ability if charity is not the end of all these things? Rightly, then, after judgments, counsels, and aids, desires are drawn from the fountain of charity, so that whatever we know and say, whatever we do or suffer, may be brought to its completion by the end of eternal life.

But so that what has been said about the fountains and waters may shine forth more clearly, I think it should be demonstrated by examples from Scripture, and that the images of gold which we have put forward should be inlaid with silver. First, I think no one doubts that those four fountains flow from the breast of Jesus. But how the aforesaid waters are drawn from these same fountains must be worked out. Let David come, then, and declare why judgments proceed from the fountain of truth. He certainly seems to have understood this when he said: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance” (Ps. 16). For the holy man would not have called his judgment that which did not proceed from God’s countenance—that is, from truth.

[Col. 1550D] For he knew that the elect are ruled by the judgments of truth as with an iron rod; and because he felt himself to be under their rule, he sang exultantly: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18). And lest perhaps through carelessness they should stray from them, let them hear the Father’s voice, threatening through the same Prophet: “If they do not walk in my judgments and do not keep my commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with stripes” (Ps. 88).

The key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom disclosed these mysteries of divine judgment when he said: “It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God; but if first with us, what shall be the end of those who do not believe God’s Gospel?” (1 Pet. 4). This too was spoken concerning the elect. But there is another judgment concerning the reprobate, which likewise proceeds from truth itself. Thus it is said through Paul: “We know that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things” (Rom. 2). Truth itself embraces both judgments, saying: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

[Col. 1551B] It distinguishes the two when it likewise says: “These shall go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life” (Matt. 25).

If we have seen how judgments are drawn from the fountain of truth, let us see how counsels are poured forth from the fountain of wisdom. Who can doubt that the Apostle Paul is wise, when Peter, his fellow apostle, affirms that wisdom was given to him (2 Pet. 3), and the whole sequence of that apostle’s words breathes nothing but wisdom? Let him, then, offer counsels, and through them teach us what is expedient for those who are pilgrims and hasten toward the heavenly homeland. “Concerning virgins,” he says, “I have no commandment of the Lord; but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful. I judge, therefore, that this is good because of the present necessity: for it is good for a man to remain thus” (1 Cor. 7).

[Col. 1551C] If he had had a command concerning virgins, he would have done nothing other than what was commanded. But now, when both are lawful—to marry or not to marry—what could be said more concisely than that it is good for a man to remain thus, that is, to remain in virginity? Especially since the pressure of necessity commonly bears heavily, life’s very brevity urges us swiftly toward death, and the form of this entire world passes away. Likewise, when speaking of a widow, he says: “She will be happier if she remains thus,” that is, unmarried, “according to my counsel” (1 Cor. 7). And lest this counsel appear to have been drawn from his own heart rather than from the fountain of wisdom, he added: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid.).

But why do I linger over a few examples, when every sex, every age, every condition can find counsel for salvation in his words, if it seeks diligently? If anyone wishes to examine more closely whether it is true that counsels flow from wisdom, let him read the books entitled *Wisdom*, where the entire course of the discourse seems to breathe counsels. But if he studies to draw life from it more prudently and profitably, let him hear Wisdom herself healthfully inviting him: “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19). Do you ask whose commandments? “Fear God,” she says, “and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12).

[Col. 1551D] Let him hear, I say, that same Wisdom calling out with a mother’s affection: “Give me, my son, your heart” (Prov. 23). Oh, how I too would wish to suspend my heart upon her word, from whose wondrous mouth I hear such sweet counsels of life resounding! Oh, that I might dip the pen of my tongue in her fountain, so that I might be fit to set down profitably what remains concerning the two fountains, namely power and charity.

And because these four fountains so pour their savour into one another that whoever drinks from one is invited by a certain ineffable sweetness of love to another, I am pleased now to pass from Wisdom to Power, and, as far as Power itself aids me, to show how the waters of aids are drawn from it. As I said above, judgments of truth are twofold, since they determine what is lawful or unlawful; and likewise counsels of wisdom teach two things, namely what is expedient or inexpedient. So here too we recognize that double waters of aids are to be drawn from the fountain of power: waters that either wash the elect from faults or refresh them in torments.

[Col. 1552B] Let us take an example of both. The evangelist Luke relates that a certain woman who suffered from an issue of blood, having spent all her substance on physicians and yet being unable to be cured, came up behind and touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment; and immediately the flow of blood stopped. Jesus said, “Who touched me?” And when the disciples replied, “The crowds press and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” he answered again: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8). Behold what waters of aid that woman drew from the fountain of the Saviour’s power, by which she was washed from the flow of blood that no medical skill could heal.

But if anyone objects that the testimony cited has no relevance to the present work, because that woman seems to have been washed not from sins but only from bodily illness, let him know that it is the custom of divine power to heal the heart before the body. Thus elsewhere, when a paralytic was brought to him for healing, as a good and merciful physician, wishing first to heal what was more important, the mind rather than the flesh, he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9).

[Col. 1552D] And so, once the conscience has been healed, the body is consequently healed also, when it is said: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (ibid.). Thus the gift of faith first washed that woman’s heart inwardly, through which she deserved outwardly to obtain health of body. The Lord himself indicates this when he says: “Daughter, your faith has made you whole; go in peace” (Luke 8).

That waters of aid in torments are also drawn from this same fountain of power is shown by the three youths placed in the blazing furnace, for whom the flame itself grew cool (Dan. 3); and especially by that illustrious martyr Vincent, who, when he was grievously tortured, is said not only to have endured but even steadfastly to have challenged his torturer in these words: “Rise up,” he said, “and rage with the whole spirit of your malice. You shall see that through God’s power I am stronger while being tortured than you are who torture me.” Much more might be said abundantly about this fountain of power, but I pass over it briefly, because I long more eagerly to drink than to write from the fountain of Charity.

[Col. 1553A] We are invited to this fountain by the voice of our Redeemer, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink; and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). The evangelist then explained to what drink he invited us, saying: “This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (ibid.). What Spirit, if not the Spirit of charity, whom the world cannot receive, but whom only those who truly believe in him receive?

Let us therefore draw from this fountain waters of desires, and divide them into twin streams, so that, just as there are two commandments of one and the same charity, there may likewise be twin desires by which those commandments are fulfilled. For one desire is that by which God is loved for his own sake; another is that by which one’s neighbour is loved in God or for God’s sake. In the former there is no limit: God is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. But in the latter a certain measure is prescribed when it is said: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 19).

[Col. 1553B] The Prophet burned with the first when he said: “As the deer longs for fountains of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41); and likewise: “My soul desires and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83). Paul showed the second toward the Romans, to whom he wrote: “For I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace” (Rom. 1). And the Lord said to his disciples in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22).

[Col. 1554A] It should be noted that the human mind is spiritually stirred and advanced toward the former by three affections. Therefore it is commanded to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. The first affection is sweet, the second prudent, the third strong. Peter possessed the first when he dissuaded the Lord from dying: for he loved sweetly from the heart him whose Passion he feared. But when he heard, “Get behind me, Satan; you do not savour the things of God but those of this world” (Mark 8), rebuked by these words and understanding what good Christ’s death contained, he began prudently to love with his whole soul him whom he had previously loved only sweetly with his whole heart. Yet he did not then love with his whole strength; for had he done so, he would not have denied him because of the danger of death.

But after the Resurrection and Ascension, when the Spirit was given from above, he at last loved with his whole strength; for Christ’s sake he afterwards did not fear to undergo the dreadful punishment of the cross.

[Col. 1554B] We also exercise charity toward our neighbour in three ways: either so that charity itself may be built up where it is absent; or increased where it is present; or, at least, so that we may beware lest it perish or diminish where it is present. Whoever works this toward his neighbour with a pure affection will without doubt obtain more abundantly that charity which is directed toward God.

[Col. 1553]

## A Short Work of Cardinal Drogo on the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, or On the Sevenfold Grace of the Holy Spirit and the Beatitudes

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, ibid., p. 344.)

[Col. 1553C] The first grace is the fear of the Lord. Whoever has it hates every iniquity, according to that saying of the Psalmist: “I have hated and abhorred iniquity; I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. 118). For it is written: “The fear of the Lord hates evil” (Prov. 8); and again: “Fear God, and depart from evil” (Prov. 3). And of Job it is said: “A man fearing God and departing from evil” (Job 1).

Without this grace—the first of graces, which is the beginning of all religion—no good can spring up or endure. For just as security or negligence is the cause and mother of all sins, so the fear of the Lord is the root and guardian of all good things. Hence it is written: “If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house shall quickly be overthrown” (Ecclus. 27). For the structure of all virtues immediately inclines toward ruin if it loses the protection of this grace. Therefore Solomon says: “Be in the fear of the Lord all day, because you shall have hope in the end, and your expectation shall not be taken away” (Prov. 13).

[Col. 1553D] Hence the Apostle also says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2). And what more? Fear and religion are bound together; neither can remain without the other. Thus Simeon was called “a just and God-fearing man” (Luke 2). Thus too it is written in the Law: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him alone; to him you shall cling” (Deut. 6). Therefore Solomon says: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12).

We ought to possess this fear as most blessed Job declares that he possessed it: “I always feared the Lord as swelling waves over me” (Job 31). Through this fear of God we abandon all things, renounce the world, and deny ourselves, as the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 4 [cf. Matt. 16]). This divine fear, then, which subjects the person it wholly fills to poverty and separates him from evil, is first in the order of graces just as poverty is first in the series of beatitudes.

[Col. 1555A] Concerning it the Lord, placing it as the foundation of the other virtues, says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

The second gift is the spirit of piety, resembling the second beatitude set forth in the Gospel, of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). Of such people the Lord says in Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to announce [good news] to the meek” (Isa. 61). Moses also “was the meekest of all men dwelling on the earth” (Num. 12). Of such people Job says: “The Lord sets the humble on high and raises those who mourn to safety” (Job 5). Hence Solomon says: “Humility shall go before glory, and glory shall receive the humble spirit” (Prov. 15). Therefore it is said of the Lord: “He shall save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33); conversely it is said of the proud: “God resists the proud” (Jas. 4).

[Col. 1555B] “Before ruin the spirit shall be exalted; humility follows the proud” (Prov. 11 [citation printed as 2]). Pride casts down from the heights to the depths; humility raises from the depths to the heights. For the angel, becoming proud in heaven, fell into Tartarus; man, humbling himself on earth, ascends to heaven. The more exalted a person is, the humbler he ought to be. Therefore it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3). Thus the Lord himself says: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 20). Again: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke 17). Again he says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11 [citation printed as 15]).

Without the virtue of humility the other virtues cannot profit. Hence blessed Gregory says: “He who gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust in the wind.” For just as dust is scattered by the blast of a strong wind, so every good is swept away by the wind of vain glory. It is even far better to be a humble sinner than an arrogant righteous person, as the Lord clearly shows where he adduces the Publican and the Pharisee as an example (Luke 18). For, as a certain wise man says: “Humble confession amid evil deeds is better than proud boasting amid good deeds.”

[Col. 1555C] The third gift is the spirit of knowledge, of which we read in Solomon: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1). For true knowledge is to know that we are mortal, perishable, and frail, and that in this exile, this prison-house, this pilgrimage, this valley of tears, this place of miseries, we ought to grieve and mourn. Hence it is said in the third beatitude, corresponding to this third gift: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). Again: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6). Thus Solomon says: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14). “I judged laughter to be an error, and said to joy: ‘Why are you vainly deceived?’” (Eccl. 2 [citation printed as 22]). “The heart of the wise is where sadness is, and the heart of fools where mirth is” (Eccl. 7).

[Col. 1555D] True knowledge, therefore, is to know that all worldly things are perishable, momentary, and uncertain, according to what is read in Solomon: “All things are subject to vanity; they were made from earth and shall alike return to earth” (Eccl. 3). Again: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccl. 1).

The fourth grace is the spirit of fortitude, resembling the fourth Gospel beatitude, of which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5). For one who hungers and thirsts for justice is made invincible against every adversity and remains unafraid. Therefore Solomon says: “The righteous man shall be confident as a lion, without terror” (Prov. 28). Again: “Whatever happens to him shall not make the righteous man sad” (Prov. 12).

[Col. 1556A] All those mentioned by the Apostle were filled with this spirit of fortitude, of whom he speaks thus: “The saints endured mockeries and stripes, moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the slaughter of the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted; the world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 11). Endowed with this Spirit, the Apostle confidently said: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8), and so forth.

This Spirit sustains and governs the whole Church, and equips and fortifies it against hostile snares. Hence the bridegroom says in praise of the bride: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order” (Song 6).

[Col. 1556C] The fifth gift is the spirit of counsel, which causes a person to sympathize with and have mercy upon others; it corresponds to the fifth beatitude, of which it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). Thus Solomon says: “He who is inclined to mercy shall be blessed” (Prov. 11 [citation printed as 2]). We principally exercise this in three ways: when we fulfill the six works recorded in the Gospel; when we strive to correct sinners and bring them back to goodness; or when we most readily pardon injuries inflicted upon us.

This second manner of mercy, or spirit of counsel, caused God to empty himself and take the form of a servant (Phil. 2), so that he might correct the straying sheep and bring it back to its own fold. Thus the Apostle says: “He gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present wicked age” (Gal. 1). We ought to devote ourselves to this manner of giving counsel as the Apostle directs when he admonishes: “Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, entreat” (1 Tim. 4 [cf. 2 Tim. 4]).

[Col. 1556D] There is another manner of counsel, namely the virtue of discernment, through which we distinguish true virtues from virtues that are disguised or feigned; through which we cautiously recognize Satan himself, the author of hypocrisy. For, as the Apostle says, “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11); and, according to the saying of blessed Cyprian, “He enlists his ministers as though they were ministers of justice, asserting night to be day and destruction to be salvation.”

This virtue, the teacher and mistress of the other virtues, accordingly moderates and governs all the others from above, preserving them imperially and discerningly so that they do not stray freely either below or beyond the proper measure. Hence Boethius says: “Virtues hold the mean; if anything is done either below or beyond what is fitting, one departs from virtue.”

[Col. 1557A] The sixth grace is the spirit of understanding. It corresponds to the sixth beatitude, of which the Gospel says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Unless the mind’s vision has been diligently purified, it cannot clearly understand mystical and divine things. For as it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1). Hence Solomon says: “Evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 15). Elsewhere it is said: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1). Therefore whoever wishes to have sincere and lucid understanding should strive to escape the phantasms and clouds of depraved thoughts and to guard his heart with all diligence and caution. Hence Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4).

The seventh gift is the spirit of wisdom, namely a certain inward savour and most sweet taste.

[Col. 1558A] Hence the Church sings: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; be still and see; come to him and be enlightened” (Pss. 33, 45). By this inward taste of divine wisdom we taste beforehand the things above, contemplating how delightful and pleasant it is to be among the citizens of heaven, where nothing able to displease can be present and nothing pleasing can be absent.

This seventh grace corresponds to the seventh beatitude, of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5). For those who have a peaceful and serene mind savour heavenly things more sweetly and see them more subtly. For the more powerful a person is, the wiser he is shown to be. Hence Solomon says: “A man’s instruction is known through patience” (Prov. 19). Of such persons it is said elsewhere: “Great peace is for those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 1558B] These seven graces are the seven women taking hold of one man; the seven spirits resting upon the flower; the seven lamps shining in the lampstand; the seven eyes in the stone; and the seven spirits before the throne of God.

[Col. 1557]

## Cardinal Drogo’s Book on the Divine Offices, or Canonical Hours

(*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, ibid., p. 345.)

### Why Morning Praises Are Celebrated by the Faithful

[Col. 1557C] When the Lord was about to lead the children of Israel out from the harsh slavery of Egypt and from under Pharaoh’s hand, after many miracles by which he could not soften Pharaoh’s hardened heart, he powerfully performed one final miracle: by an angel striking them down, he killed the firstborn of the Egyptians. By this he greatly terrified Pharaoh and his people, and wonderfully liberated his own people.

For through Moses he commanded the people of Israel that all, each according to their families and households, should take an unblemished lamb; and, after eating its flesh according to what had been commanded them, should put its blood upon the doorposts of their houses, so that, seeing this sign, the striking angel might pass over unharmed those who belonged to them. But at midnight the destroying angel came.

[Col. 1557D] Wherever he saw the marks of blood upon the doorposts, he passed by; entering the houses of the Egyptians, he killed the firstborn in each of them, while preserving all the firstborn sons of Israel. Compelled by the power of this miracle, the king of Egypt dismissed the Lord’s people (Exod. 12–13).

In this event was figured our deliverance, which the Lord daily works spiritually in us, and by which we are made men, sons of Israel. For *Israel* is interpreted “one seeing God.” We are sons begotten in faith by the holy Fathers who saw the Lord, and by all others to whom God is seen. Since that miracle was performed in the middle of the night, we too ought to rise for nocturnal vigils with the Prophet, who says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Ps. 118), so that, by the cooperation of divine grace, we may be delivered from the invisible Pharaoh—that is, the devil—and from the slavery of Egypt, namely from the works of darkness.

[Col. 1558C] Therefore during nocturnal vigils the Lord must be prayed to, that by the sword of his word, invisibly piercing, he may strike down and annihilate in us the works of our former dark life, which we know are signified by the firstborn of the Egyptians. In these works we too served as captives of Pharaoh, that is, the king of darkness. “For whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8). While we obeyed our own pleasures, as the Apostle says, “You were once darkness” (Eph. 5), and, blinded, we obeyed malignant spirits.

But now, converted and made light in the Lord, as we keep vigil through the night before him with watchful gaze, let us also ask that he preserve inviolate in us, by the blood of the true Lamb, that faith by which we behold him and which was signified by the firstborn of Israel. For faith is the first and foundation of all virtues.

[Col. 1559A] Let that destroying angel, who “goes about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5), neither wound faith in us through the error of a perverse opinion nor kill it by making it sluggish through negligence in good works. “For faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). We shall be safe from him if, applying diligence and walking in the footsteps of the Lord’s humility, patience, and meekness, we maintain everywhere in life and conduct an imitation of the Passion signified by the blood of the lamb. If the devil truly perceives these signs in us, he will flee in terror, having no power able to prevail against us.

### On the Same Subject

As we are about to celebrate morning praises, established to be celebrated at the dawn of day in honour and reverence of the Lord’s Resurrection, which occurred very early in the morning, let us recall also the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea. This signifies our first resurrection, given to us in baptism, when the Lord delivered them from Egyptian slavery and from Pharaoh’s hand, so that, passing thence through the wilderness, they might at length enter the land of promise.

[Col. 1559B] That passage is reported to have taken place in the morning watch, whose final part is the dawn of day. Since all these things happened to them figuratively, they foreshadowed the truth that was to come to us. For because our baptism, consecrated by Christ’s blood, is understood through the Red Sea, our cleansing in baptism is fittingly figured by the passage of God’s people. There, putting off the dark contagions of our former error, freed from the malignant invader, and immersed with the Lord, we die; and, brought forth from the first death, we ourselves rise again into life, so that we may share in his Resurrection, which occurred very early in the morning.

[Col. 1559C] No one, however, can rise to glory in the second resurrection unless he has possessed the first in this life. As the first death is to be defiled by vices and entangled in one’s own desires, while the second is to lie subject to everlasting pains, so the first resurrection is to rise from vices in this life, while the second is to pass from corruption to incorruption, from exile to homeland, from darkness to light, and from punishments to rest. It is clear, therefore, that as the second death inevitably follows the first, so the second resurrection likewise accompanies the first mercy.

Let us therefore meditate in the Lord with David at morning, and anticipate him at daybreak, meditating upon his words, so that by his mercy he may grant us to rise from the first death, and, when he comes a second time, make us, conformed to himself, participants in his Resurrection. Thus may we pass through the wilderness of this life on an unblemished path, so that, under his guidance, we may be able to arrive at the land of true promise, the heavenly Jerusalem.

### On the Hour of Prime

[Col. 1560A]

The praise of the First Hour, as the hymn itself attests, in which we say, “Now that the star of daylight has risen,” was appointed by the holy Fathers to be celebrated at sunrise. If it is ever celebrated later or earlier, as circumstances require, provided that we render the office due to the Hour at a suitable time, let the fixed time of this and of the other Hours likewise be left to Him to whom all things are present. Therefore, when we assemble to celebrate this Hour, let us bless our Creator and give thanks to Him, who provides and cares even for our outward necessities, so much so that, besides the many other benefits of His goodness, He has deigned to furnish us with this visible sun—a creature so splendid in its beauty and so necessary in many ways for the service of our bodies and the illumination of our senses. [Col. 1560B]

For this bodily sun—to pass over the many other things which divine providence accomplishes through it—cleanses the world of darkness; by its approach it makes the region of heaven which we inhabit milder, driving away the cold; and, fertilizing the earth, causes the trees to bear fruit. Although these things deserve admiration, neither its usefulness should detain those who use it, nor its beauty those who behold it. We ought not to remain among these bodily things, which profit only for a little while, however numerous they may be in their own kind; but, as it is written: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1). Through the creature, which invites us to its Creator, let us seek in faith and love the Sun of Justice, namely the Lord Christ; [Col. 1560C] and we shall be able daily to find Him knocking at the door of our mind.

For through the bodily benefits bestowed upon us—which are subject to change and pass away—He admonishes us to seek the supreme Good, which He Himself is, unchangeable and ever abiding; and He truthfully promises that He will be found by those who seek faithfully and knock in love. For it is written: “Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7). Therefore, that He may be found by us, let us seek with a sincere heart and knock in love, beseeching His most merciful compassion, that He who is the true Sun of Justice, driving away the darkness of blindness and ignorance, may deign to rise and dwell in our minds. And because He has deigned to become our mediator and advocate, let Him approach the Father and make Him more merciful and propitious toward us, driving away the cold of vices; and let Him cause our earth—that is, our very hearts—to put forth shoots from the roots of holy thoughts, and outwardly to bear fruit without weariness through works sweetly fragrant to God. [Col. 1560D] Thus, thirsting in all things for true justice, may He Himself lead us unfailingly to Himself through Himself and draw us to that blessed and complete satisfaction; for He promises His faithful ones, saying: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5).

## On the Third Hour

Christ, the innocent Lamb, deigned at the third hour of the day to stand for judgment before Pilate, a most contemptible slave, on behalf of us sinners, [Col. 1561A] lest, when our sins accuse us amid the terror of the last judgment, we should be condemned as guilty. For He endured the cruel sentence of the Jews, who, for that reason, are said by the Evangelists to have crucified Him at that very hour, crying, “Crucify, crucify Him” (John 19), lest that final and most dreadful sentence should fall upon us, in which the rejected are told: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

He most patiently bore blows, spittle, scourges, the crown of thorns, and mockeries, that by His example He might invite us to patience, so that, tested in this life, we might through patience possess hope of eternal life. It is also shown to belong to the mystery of this Hour that the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven at the third hour to enlighten the Church, was poured into the hearts of the disciples. Let us therefore at this Hour, giving thanks, worship our Savior, who was willing to prepare for us benefits so necessary and so wondrous. [Col. 1561B] Let us also entreat that same free goodness, through which He willed this, that as the same Spirit gives us inward life, He who is the head of His own people may make us outwardly His members through good works; and thus may grant us, according to our measure, to become His imitators and to share in what He suffered. Delivered from an evil report—where it is promised that the just person shall not fear—we may deserve to hear the good and sweet utterance: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you by my Father” (Matt. 25).

## On the Sixth Hour

[Col. 1561C] The history of evangelical truth testifies that Christ, our salvation, ascended the cross at the sixth hour and allowed His innocent hands and feet to be pierced by a most savage executioner, so that by His wounds He might heal our wounds and by the gibbet of the cross remove from us eternal punishments. It is therefore fitting and salutary for us also, at the hour when the Son of God submitted those members which His supreme divinity had assumed for us to the pains of His Passion and the disgrace of the cross, to give thanks to so great a Majesty, the restorer of our nature.

And because, as He Himself declares, we can do nothing without Him, while attending His praises at the hour of His holy crucifixion, let us earnestly beg that He deny the aid of His mercy to no one. For there are two kinds of crucifixion: either the flesh is crucified with its vices [Col. 1561D] and desires, or the mind and will are, by divine help, restrained from vain and unlawful thoughts. May He make us persons crucified in body and soul, so that we may be fastened by His fear, lest the cunning tempter overcome us by the violence of vices; but, kindled with the fire of His love in noonday fervor, may we be formed and perfected for good works according to obedience to His commands. Thus, having fallen away from life through the forbidden tree, we may be able to return through the tree of obedience.

## On the Ninth Hour

Not without tears and sobs, if our frailty were sufficient, ought we always to assemble to celebrate the mysteries of the ninth hour. For this is that Hour in which Christ, the life of the living, in whom whatever was made was life, hanging on the cross for us, after all that had been foretold concerning Him up to the hour of His death had been fulfilled, bowed His head and, commending His spirit into the hands of the Father, gave up the spirit. [Col. 1562A]

Therefore, each day at this Hour let us call before the eyes of our mind that saving and venerable spectacle of the cross and of the Crucified One; and, worshipping with bowed minds and thanksgiving His soul as it leaves the body, let us beseech His merciful and unfailing compassion. By that love through which He willed to die for our sins and rise again for our justification, may He make us in this life die to sin and live to justice. And in our supreme necessity, when the soul leaves the body, may He assist us and, by the interposition of His unique death, protect us from the death of the soul and at last restore us to that blessed life which, speaking of His sheep, He promises: “And I give them eternal life” (John 10). [Col. 1562B]

## On the Evening Hymns

After the mysteries of the ninth hour have been performed, now more confident in the hope of divine mercy, we come with more cheerful hearts to celebrate the evening hymns more festively. For we believe and confess that the propitiation of the whole dispensation which the Lord Jesus fulfilled for us in the body, “unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2), ascended into the presence of the Father at that very Hour on the day on which He suffered; through it peace with Him was restored universally to the human race.

For all are saved with respect to the abundant mercy of our Savior, and no one is excluded from so great a benefit unless he prefers of his own will to perish. At that same Hour, on the day before He suffered, He prepared for us two benefits, by no means to be passed over and very necessary, and left them to be imitated in the very act. One was when He rose from supper and washed the disciples’ feet. In this He foreshadowed our earthly manner of life, denoted by the name of feet, which must necessarily be washed and cleansed daily by Him from the dust of offences which we continually incur, if we are to have a share with Him. [Col. 1562C]

The other was when He gave us the sacrament of His body and blood, which He left for us to perform at that Hour of consecration in remembrance of Himself, so that His Church, in the pilgrimage of this world, might not fail, but, having this life-giving provision for the journey, might meanwhile be nourished and strengthened by it, until we all meet Him in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4): that is, when the body of Christ will be made complete, all its members adhering to the head, and God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

Therefore, since the evening Hour is adorned with mysteries so great and so universal, let us attend it with more ready and expanded affections; and, rendering to the propitiator of all the thanks due from mouth and heart, let us persist in prayer, that whatever earthly dross we contract while living here He may wash away in the fountain of His mercy. Completing His goodness in us, may He so feed and sustain us in this life with the provision of His most holy body that, when we depart hence, we may deserve to be enrolled among those for whose reconciliation with God the Father [Col. 1563A] He offered so great a sacrificial offering of propitiation, and whose names are inscribed in the book of life before the ages.

## On Compline

Compline, the Hour which brings the departing day to its end, is celebrated by holy Church in honor of the Lord’s burial. At that time Joseph and Nicodemus—who had first come to Him by night—faithfully took Him down from the cross, prepared His body with spices, wrapped it in linen cloths, while the holy women watched attentively from afar where He was laid; and they performed these offices with the utmost devotion.

For that devotion of the women must not be passed over. Because they had loved Him fervently while He was alive and had seen Him die on the cross not without exceeding grief and tears, they carefully marked the place where He was buried, in order to return to seek Him again when they had prepared the ointments with which to anoint Him. [Col. 1563B] As we call their devotions and services to mind, who would not ardently desire with them to have stood by reverently and ministered with utmost care? Yet, since what can no longer happen may be supplied by spiritual things in place of bodily ones, it does no harm that we could not have been bodily present at that burial of the Lord’s body. Rather, venerating in faith what was done there, and buried with Him in love as regards the things of the world, let us strive to prepare in the secret place of our breast a resting-place for Him, in which He may not lie dead, but in which He, now living for ever, may delight as our life and rest in our conduct. [Col. 1564A]

Giving thanks, therefore, for these benefits, let us pray that He who searches hearts and reins may cleanse our inner house from the filth of vices, so that it may please Him to enter and dwell there. But lest we seem to have applied no diligence, before we fall asleep let us wash away with tears and repentance whatever we recognize that we have sinned during the day; let us meditate on the things of God; and by holy meditation prepare a place for Him within us, saying with David: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord” (Ps. 131).

If, therefore, while we sleep so great a guest inhabits the inmost chamber of the heart, then when we wake again and seek Him at the night watches, He will not be far away. The faithful soul will find Him ready in the bedchamber of its breast, where, in falling asleep, it had placed Him. [Col. 1564B]

## In the Year of the Lord 1118: Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble

[Col. 1563]

## Notice concerning Saint Hugh

(Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, April, vol. I, p. 36)

Among the illustrious men who flourished in the eleventh and twelfth centuries of Christ with an exceptional splendor of holiness may be counted Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble in Upper Dauphiné, a friend of Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusian Order, and of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Saint Hugh was born in the year of Christ 1053 and was ordained bishop in 1080, when he was about twenty-seven years old, as is read in the *Life*, no. 5. He departed to the Lord in the eightieth year of his age, the thirty-second of his episcopal consecration, in the year of Christ 1132, on the Kalends of April [1 April], the sixth weekday before Palm Sunday. That year was a leap year; in it, with the lunar cycle at 12, the solar cycle at 21, and the dominical letters C B, Easter was celebrated on 10 April. So much concerning his age.

The name of Saint Hugh occurs in various sacred calendars, both handwritten and printed. Among these are Grevenus and Molanus in the supplement to Usuard; Maurolycus, Galesinius, and Canisius; and, among monastic writers, Wion, Menard, and Dorganius. Bucelin composed a lengthy encomium upon him; Constantinus Ghinius entered him in the calendar of canons; and Saussaius praises him highly in the Gallican Martyrology. With all these he is thus commemorated in the Roman Martyrology: “At Grenoble, Saint Hugh, bishop, who spent many years of his life in solitude and, renowned for the glory of miracles, departed to the Lord.”

[Col. 1563]

## Second Notice

(Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 188)

Hugh was the son of Odo, a nobleman of Valentinois, a man very devout while still in military dress. In very advanced age he embraced the Carthusian institute; after spending about eighteen years in it, almost a centenarian, he surrendered his soul to God in the hands of his son Hugh, who had administered to him the anointing and the holy viaticum. Hugh’s mother was no less devout. After her husband’s death, wishing likewise to leave the world, she followed her son’s counsel, because women’s religious monasteries were then rare, and spent the remainder of her life in a private house in works of piety.

Hugh was born of these parents at a place in the district of Valentinois called Château, situated near the Isère. He attended school at Valence; when his studies were completed, wishing to keep himself free from every defilement, he was received into the household of Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, and was employed as his assistant in uprooting the shoots of simony and other vices of that age among clergy and laity alike.

Meanwhile, it happened that the same legate held a council at Avignon. The canons of Grenoble, who were without a bishop, came together there to request a shepherd. When Hugh was offered to them by the legate, he left nothing untried to avoid this dignity. But at last he was compelled to assume it. Since he refused to be consecrated by Guarmund, archbishop of Vienne, who was accused of simony, he went with the legate to Rome to be ordained by Pope Gregory. There, relieved by the counsels of the pontiff from the severe temptation by which he was afflicted, and honored by the goodwill of Countess Matilda, who gave him a pastoral staff and certain sacred books, he came to his church. There he found clergy and people in great disorder: incontinent and simoniacal priests; laymen devoted to usury and invaders of churches; and all this through the negligence of his predecessor bishops, who had consumed the resources of the episcopal household.

It is not easy to say how much labor and concern Hugh expended in correcting these corruptions. But when perhaps he observed that the results did not answer his desires, he withdrew, through a desire for a quieter life, to La Chaise-Dieu, not yet two years after his consecration. There he became a monk; fired by the examples of the holy men who were numerous there, and in turn inflaming them, he showed himself worthy alike of universal imitation and veneration. Yet after the space of one year, by order of Pope Gregory he was compelled to return to his church, bringing with him a rich increase of virtue and zeal. Thereafter he ordered his life so as to retain a monk’s life in the episcopate, joining religious men to his household. Among them was the venerable William, then prior of Saint-Laurent and later abbot of Saint-Theofred.

In the episcopate he displayed such modesty and such restraint of his senses, especially of his eyes, that he never fixed his eyes upon women; and such devotion that, when he heard confessions, he moved penitents to contrition by abundant tears.

To clarify the subsequent events, it is useful here to investigate in what precise year Hugh became and was consecrated bishop. The solution of this question depends on two points: namely, the year of the Council of Avignon, in which he was elected to the episcopate; and the year when the Grande Chartreuse was founded, which occurred about the sixth year of his episcopate. With regard to the first, the Council of Avignon was held after Pope Gregory had written to the people of Arles, [Note: [Col. 1565] Gregory, *Register*, book VI, epistle 21.] exhorting them to elect a bishop for themselves, who was elected in the aforesaid council, as was Hugh, as is evident from the Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny. But this letter was written “on the Kalends of March, in the second indiction,” and therefore in the year 1079. Thus neither election took place before that year or the following one.

Two arguments persuade me that it happened rather in 1079. One is that I hold it certain that the foundation of the Charterhouse, which took place about the sixth year of Hugh’s episcopate, must be placed in 1084. The other is that Hugh died, according to Guigo, in 1133, on the Kalends of April, “in at least the eightieth year of his age—for he was about twenty-seven years old when elected—and at least the fifty-second of his consecration.” If you compare these calculations, you must admit that his election took place in 1079 and his consecration at the beginning of the following year.

[Col. 1565]

## Extracts from the Cartulary of the Church of Grenoble

(Mabillon, *Opera posthuma*, vol. III, p. 358)

### I. On the Injuries Inflicted by Guy, Archbishop of Vienne, upon the Church of Grenoble and upon Hugh, Bishop of That Church, Concerning the District of Salmorieu

[Col. 1565A]

I, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, transmit to the knowledge of posterity how Guy, archbishop of Vienne, raised a claim concerning the district of Salmorieu, asserting that the Church of Grenoble unjustly possessed the aforesaid district because it belonged by right to the Church of Vienne. To settle this complaint, we came to Vienne; but since the case was then not heard, we appointed another day for a hearing. On that day they met again with him at Romans: Gontard, bishop of Valence, and Guy, bishop of Geneva; and with us, Pontius, bishop of Belley, and Landric, bishop of Mâcon. [Col. 1566A] There, by writings and other testimonies, we demonstrated that the Church of Grenoble had possessed that district for one hundred years and more. We stated that we were entirely ignorant when it had first possessed it.

In reply, the people of Vienne objected that, at the time when the Church of Grenoble had been laid waste by pagans, the district had been granted temporarily to the bishop of that city by the archbishop of Vienne. When the aforesaid bishops asked them whether they possessed any documentary records supporting this answer, they replied that they had no writing concerning it, but that common report alone sufficed. But the canons of Grenoble requested the bishops present to judge whether the bare and unsupported words of the people of Vienne should exclude the Church of Grenoble [Col. 1567B] from so ancient a possession.

The archbishop of Vienne, however, refused to hear judgment, because at that time he held in his hand the knights of that land, bound to make peace; and, taking the opportunity, he violently seized what he could not obtain by judgment. Concerning this invasion we made complaint to Pope Urban II. He therefore sent letters to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, who was then legate of the Roman Church.

Accordingly, relying on apostolic authority, the archbishop of Lyons caused each of us, by command of the lord pope, to come before him at Bâgé to settle so great a matter. Having heard the case on both sides, he judged that the Church of Grenoble should have full investiture of that which, as we have said, had been violently taken from it; and he promised to determine the claim at the first council to be held in Gaul. The archbishop of Vienne, however, contemptuous of the judgment of the apostolic legate, refused to restore the investiture to us. For at that time he had sent his legate with letters to Pope Urban at Rome, requesting him to confirm by privilege what belonged by right to the Church of Vienne. In obtaining this privilege, as he himself later confessed to us, he expended five hundred solidi in the Roman curia. [Col. 1567C]

In it he fraudulently and by deception caused the district of Salmorieu, which he had recently seized, to be included in writing, while the lord pope was wholly unaware of the complaint concerning that district. When we learned of this fraudulent privilege, [Col. 1567D] we sent to the lord pope with the greatest haste, complaining both of the contempt shown for the judgment of his legate concerning our investiture and of the fraudulent obtaining of the privilege. Pope Urban therefore sent letters to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and his legate, a copy of which is written below:

> “Urban … to his beloved brother and bishop Hugh of Lyons, etc.
>
> “Of our solicitude,” etc. See under Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLI.

Through the same legate he sent us letters in this form:

[Col. 1568A]

> “Urban … to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, etc.
>
> “Concerning your affair,” etc. See above, under no. 117.

Meanwhile Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, arranged to hold a council at Autun, and ordered us to attend, prepared to submit the complaint to the judgment of the whole council. At last our case came before the council. There, after many words, in order to prove that our case was unjust, the archbishop of Vienne produced with ostentation a writing, apparently worn away by great age. It stated that Baruinus, archbishop of Vienne, had granted to Isarnus, bishop of Grenoble, the church of Saint-Donatus and the district of Salmorieu until peace should be restored to the Church of Grenoble from the persecution of pagans by which it was then ravaged.

When it had been read, we recovered our breath from the fear they had instilled in us, asking the apostolic legate to keep that charter himself, since it undoubtedly bore false witness. For Baruinus, archbishop of Vienne, and Isarnus, bishop of Grenoble, were not contemporaries, as we had established from the catalogue of Lyons and from many other writings. Moreover, we invalidated and annulled that charter because Alcherius, bishop of Grenoble and predecessor of Bishop Isarnus, is known from many documentary testimonies to have possessed the aforesaid district of Salmorieu. And the Church of Grenoble had obtained the church of Saint-Donatus not through Baruinus, but through the grant of kings, namely Boso and his son Louis, as their royal decrees made clear. [Col. 1568B–C]

When the falsehood of that document had become known to us and it had thus been invalidated, the archbishop of Vienne began to evade the judgment which he had at first demanded with a certain importunity. The charter was suddenly removed from the sight of the council and of the legate himself; disregarding the judgment, he appealed to the authority of the aforementioned privilege. But it could offer him no support, since the lord pope had by his letters declared that this privilege had been extorted from him by deception, and had entrusted our case to his legate to be determined by canonical judgment. Thus the archbishop of Vienne, who had sought to defend his injustice by this escape, was left without it. [Col. 1568D]

The archbishops and bishops present, at the request of the apostolic legate, who feared disruption of the council, attempted to restore peace and concord between us. But because he refused to restore in full what he had seized from us, we judged it better to accept a synodal judgment than a useless concord. [Note: [Col. 1567D] So in our copy.] Fearing this greatly, and desiring, as it were, to escape the impending sentence of judgment, he promised to restore to us, by the counsel of his canons at Vienne, the right of the Church entrusted to us, as he had possessed it more advantageously than our predecessors. Accordingly, on the appointed day I came to Vienne; but he did not at all fulfill what he had promised.

Meanwhile Pope Urban arranged to celebrate a council at Piacenza, ordering the Gallican bishops to attend. As I was proceeding there to make complaint concerning so great an injury, I found the archbishop of Vienne in Italy at Saint Ambrose. In order to turn me back from my intended journey, during the week in which the pope had arranged to celebrate the Council of Piacenza, he pledged, on the advice of the archbishop of Lyons, that he would obey concerning our case. Trusting this, I returned home from the journey. But when I was preparing to come to Lyons on the appointed day, the archbishop of Vienne renounced the hearing. Thus shamefully deceived by him, and recognizing his deceits, I immediately resumed the journey I had interrupted; and, with the greatest haste, I arrived at Piacenza on the final day of the council. [Col. 1569A]

There, before the pope and the whole council, I set forth the violence which the archbishop of Vienne had inflicted upon us, his deceits, his contempt for the Apostolic See, and his refusal to obey the judgment of the apostolic legate concerning our investiture. When this had been heard, the pope, by judgment of the whole council, restored to us full investiture of the district of Salmorieu, annulled the privilege which, as stated above, the archbishop of Vienne had extorted by deception, and sent him letters concerning this, a copy of which is written below:

> “Urban, bishop … to Guy, archbishop of Vienne, etc.
>
> “For necessity and utility,” etc. See above, under no. 134.

The archbishop of Vienne refused to obey these letters; indeed, he dishonored their bearer with threats and insults. Accordingly, coming shortly afterward to the pope at Milan, I exposed the presumption and contumacy of the archbishop of Vienne against the Apostolic See. The pope therefore withdrew me from his jurisdiction and, by letters which we have taken care to append here, forbade clergy and laity dwelling in the district of Salmorieu to obey the archbishop of Vienne. [Col. 1569B–C]

> “Urban, etc., to his beloved sons, both clergy and laity dwelling in the district of Salmorieu, etc.
>
> “Because our brother of Vienne,” etc. See under Urban.

In the meantime it happened that the lord pope visited the Gallican Church. Coming to Valence to dedicate the greater church, and there addressing the archbishop of Vienne, he ordered both of us to appear before him at Romans on an appointed day to settle the dispute between us. In obedience to his command, I arrived there laden with ancient documentary testimony and sufficiently fortified by the counsel of bishops, clergy, and laity. But the archbishop of Vienne, puffed up with a spirit of pride, occupied the castle and defenses of the place with armed knights, so that if the pope should say anything contrary to his will, he might remain there in his own power. Therefore the pope, himself despoiled in this manner of his own right—namely, the abbey of Romans—could not determine our case. [Col. 1569D–1570A]

But I, mindful of the wrong done to me, took care at the Council of Clermont, which the pope held in the same year, to lay before the pope and the whole assembly our complaint, long pursued against the archbishop. The pope, sympathizing with our injury and labor, restored the district of Salmorieu in full to the Church of Grenoble, and withdrew me and the Church of Grenoble from the archbishop’s obedience for as long as he should contemptuously refuse to obey the apostolic command concerning this restoration. He then issued letters to the count and our parishioners as follows:

> “Urban, bishop … to Count Guigo, the clergy, and the people of Grenoble, etc.
>
> “The complaint of the venerable,” etc. See above.

[Col. 1570B] Count Guigo, stirred by the apostolic letters, approached the archbishop and obtained from him by threats and entreaties that he should restore the district of Salmorieu to us and to the Church of Grenoble, in accordance with the apostolic command. Present at this restoration, at the Chapel of the Granaries, were Gualterius, bishop of Albano, and Leodegarius, bishop of Viviers; the canons of the Churches of Vienne and Grenoble; the aforesaid Count Guigo; and also the leading men of that land.

Because bodily weakness kept me in Apulia for almost two years, the archbishop again presumed to seize that investiture. When this was reported to the pope through our legate, he warned by his letters his legate, the archbishop of Lyons, that by apostolic authority he should entirely restrain the archbishop of Vienne from injuring the Church of Grenoble and ourselves. I have placed a copy of those letters below:

> “Urban, bishop … to Hugh, vicar of the Apostolic See, etc.
>
> “How arrogantly,” etc. See above, under no. 223.

[Col. 1570C] At the same time, by divine mercy favoring us, it became known through more certain indications that the charter which the archbishop of Vienne had produced against us at the Council of Autun concerning the district of Salmorieu was false. The man to whom the writer of that charter, being held by illness, had confessed revealed this to us. The writer, named Sigibod, a monk of Saint-Ragnabert, was summoned through our friends, monks of the same monastery, to the monastery called Granier; there, before the altar of Blessed Mary, I adjured him under invocation of the divine presence, threatening excommunication.

At length the controversy was ended. By the common consent of the parties, the district of Salmorieu was divided into two equal parts, one of which went to the archbishop of Vienne and the other to the bishop of Grenoble. This was done at Lyons on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January] in the year 1107, in the presence of many bishops; and shortly afterward it was confirmed by Paschal II, whose bull on this matter was published from the cartulary of Grenoble after Theodore’s *Penitential*, vol. II, p. 536 (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII). [Col. 1570D]

[Col. 1571]

## Letters and Diplomas of Saint Hugh

### I. To the Archbishop and Canons of the Church of Tours: The Letter of the Crusaders concerning Affairs in the East

[Col. 1571A]

(This letter of Saint Hugh is found at the end of the letter of the leaders of the Crusaders, which is the fourth among the letters of King Godfrey. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLV.)

### I. Charter of Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, Forbidding Women to Approach the Charterhouse

(Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 646, from the archive of the Grande Chartreuse.)

Hugh, called bishop of the Church of Grenoble, to the priests and laity dwelling in the diocese of Grenoble: eternal greeting in the Lord.

[Col. 1571B] How greatly our brethren, the monks of Chartreuse, desire to please God is sufficiently shown by the world which they flee and by the harshness and solitude of the place in which they dwell. Since peace and quiet are most necessary to their desire, we have determined and commanded that a house be built beyond the bridge which is the boundary of their possession, in order to remove those things which are contrary to their purpose.

We therefore ask your charity and enjoin you by divine authority that women shall in no way pass through their land, nor men bearing arms. Moreover, within the bounds of their possession we forbid fishing, hunting, bird-catching, the pasturing and passage of sheep, goats, and all domestic animals. [Col. 1571C] May divine mercy multiply in its grace those who obey our admonitions, and grant them the same share which the monks themselves desire to have in all the good things which the servants of God perform there or will perform until the end of the age. But we leave the disobedient liable to divine judgment and shall have them punished by secular power.

Given in the month of July, in the year 1084.

### III. Charter of Leotard, Son of William, concerning the Fief of the Episcopal Cellar (*cellaria*)

(As above, from the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

I, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, make known to all that Humbert Pilosi, Dodo of Grenoble, Guigo of Lac, and Rostagnus were [Col. 1571D] with me at the court which William Leotard first held with me. He therefore surrendered one *mansus* [holding], which, as was proved there by witnesses, he had falsely claimed to hold as a fief of the episcopal cellarership; and because he had surrendered the holding and said that he possessed nothing else as a fief of the cellarership, with the aforesaid men approving, I granted him [Col. 1572A] also, each year, as a fief of the cellarership, ten solidi, and maintenance for himself alone in my household as long as I should remain there; and I gave him, or made any agreement with him, nothing else whatsoever. Afterwards Guigo Gerald brought an action against him concerning the *cabanaria* which he possessed at Miserey; and, in the plea which he held with Guigo Gerald before me, he confessed that this *cabanaria* was an ancient fief of the cellarership, which he had concealed at the first plea, when he surrendered the holding and falsely stated that he possessed nothing as a fief of the cellarership. And since he had unjustly and by fraud extorted from us ten solidi every year, after the death of that William his sons Beto, Leotard, and their other brothers held a plea before me. I gave them the ancient and true fief—namely, the *cabanaria* of Miserey, which their father had concealed and which, under the testimony of worthy men, he had confessed to be an ancient and true fief of the episcopal cellarership.

[Col. 1572B] I gave it to them as a fief of the cellarership, together with the houses and courtyards which they possess at Grenoble, and one oven which is beside their Calomentum, or beside the house of Stephen Coaiz; and, in my household, maintenance for one person alone as long as I should remain there. But I retained for myself the ten solidi which their father had extorted, and I gave them absolutely nothing else. It was established by this plea and agreement that Leotard should have no one else whatsoever in the office of cellarer, either independently or subordinate to himself; but if Leotard should not wish personally to hold the keys, or if he should hold them and alienate the episcopal goods in fief, I—and likewise each of my successors—shall entrust them to whomever I choose. He himself, however, shall retain the fief, while others serve the benefit of our household.

[Col. 1572C] The witnesses to this charter are Rostagnus, Guigo of Lanz, Odolric, Gualdinus, Fulco, canons of the Church of Grenoble, Guigo the convert, and many others. Afterwards I restored to them in fief the ten solidi which I had retained.

### IV. Charter of renunciation made by Leodegarius of Clariaco and others to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, concerning the whole land of Fabriis

(*Mémoires pour l'histoire du Dauphiné*, vol. I, p. 134.)

In the name of the Father, etc.

I, Leodebarius of Clariaco, and Peter Mallenus, Jarento Rufius, his mother and wife, Largerius the priest, his brother, and Silvius of Clavaissone, [Col. 1572D] all of us, in good faith and without deceit, have renounced and given the whole land of Fabriciis to God, to Blessed Mary, to Saint Vincent, to Saint Donatus, and to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble—to whom it had been adjudged by right of episcopacy at Rotmanis—and to all his successors, to be held and possessed by them in perpetuity.

[Col. 1573A] And we have sworn that neither we nor anyone by our counsel or consent will ever molest the bishops of Grenoble concerning the aforesaid land or the goods proceeding from that land. Witnesses of this renunciation are Hugh himself, bishop of Grenoble, into whose hand it was made; William of Clariaco; Obrias, dean of the Church of Grenoble; Guigo, prior of Saint Donatus; William, monk of Saint Gotfred; Peter Stephen, canon of the Church of Maguelonne, who wrote this charter; Oldric, the bishop’s steward; Adhemar Cabiscolus of Saint Donatus; Atenulphus Guaniola; Bortellus the episcopal officer and his two sons Hugh and Peter; William Bruno; Peter of Saint Andrew, the bishop’s marshal; and Rodulf of Alavard, nephew of the aforesaid dean.

[Col. 1573B] This charter was made in the month of May, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1128, on Thursday, the twenty-first day of the moon.

### V. Renunciation of a tithe made by Peter Gorga to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble

(Ibid., p. 135, from the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

[Col. 1574A]

Let it be known to the present and future sons of the Church of Grenoble that Peter Gorga, his wife, and his wife’s sister restored and renounced to God, Blessed Mary, Saint Vincent, Bishop Hugh, and his successors the tithe which they held in the *cabanaria* that they hold from Aimon the elder, according as Hugh himself should best determine for his own benefit and that of his successors. This renunciation was made into his own hand, in the presence of Peter of Vizille, Gerald of Savoy, Guigo the convert, and Mallenus, [Col. 1574B] cellarer of the count.

**LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS.** 1349

I.—Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the clergy of Liège. He rebukes them because, in a hasty election, having even admitted excommunicated persons to their assembly, they cast their votes for Alexander; and he summons them before his tribunal at the monastery of Inda. 1349

II.—Diploma of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, for New Corvey. He confirms to it the tithes from demesne holdings in his diocese, formerly granted in a solemn council in the time of Emperor Arnulf. 1352

III.—Diploma of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, for the monastery of Grafschaft. 1353

IV.—Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the people of Milan. He urges them to resist the enemies of the Church. 1354

V.—Letter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, to the Church of Liège. He orders them not to receive in the see of Liège one intruded by simony through royal nomination. 1355

VI.—Formal letters of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne. 1356
